steps: In a large bowl, combine 2 cups of Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee. Gradually add 1 cup of water, kneading until a soft, smooth dough is formed. Cover the dough with a damp cloth and let it rest for at least 20 minutes.
Boil 4 medium potatoes until they are fork-tender. Peel and mash them thoroughly in a mixing bowl, ensuring there are no lumps for a smooth filling.

To the mashed potatoes, add 1/2 finely chopped onion, 2 finely chopped green chilies, 1 inch grated ginger, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp garam masala, 1/2 tsp amchur powder, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder, and salt to taste. Mix in 3 tbsp finely chopped fresh coriander leaves. Combine all ingredients thoroughly to create a well-seasoned potato mixture.

Divide the rested dough into 8 equal portions. Take one portion, flatten it into a small disc, and place approximately 2-3 tablespoons of the potato filling in the center. Carefully gather the edges of the dough to enclose the filling, pinching to seal securely, and form a neat ball.

Lightly dust your rolling surface and the dough ball with Anveshan Khapli Atta. Gently roll out each stuffed ball into a round paratha, about 7-8 inches in diameter, ensuring the filling is evenly distributed and the paratha doesn't tear.
Heat a tawa (griddle) over medium-high heat. Place a rolled paratha onto the hot tawa. Cook for about 1 minute until you see small bubbles forming on the surface.

Flip the paratha. Brush 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee generously over the top side. Cook for another minute, then flip again and brush 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee on the other side. Continue cooking, pressing gently with a spatula, until both sides are golden brown and crispy, about 2-3 minutes per side.
Transfer the hot paratha to a plate. Immediately spread 1 tbsp of white butter over the top, allowing it to melt into the hot paratha. Repeat the process for the remaining dough and filling.
tips: For the best texture, ensure the potato filling is not watery. If it seems too moist, cook it lightly in a pan for a few minutes to dry it out.
Don't overstuff the parathas, as this can make them difficult to roll without tearing. Start with a moderate amount and adjust as you get comfortable.
Using a heavy-bottomed tawa helps in even cooking and prevents the parathas from burning.
Serving immediately with a generous dollop of white butter is crucial for the authentic Punjabi experience.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve Punjabi Masala Aloo Paratha piping hot with a generous dollop of white butter, a side of tangy yogurt, and a spicy Punjabi pickle for a truly authentic meal.

steps: In a large bowl, combine 2 cups of Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil. Gradually add 1 cup of water, kneading until a soft, pliable dough forms. Cover and let it rest for 20 minutes.
Boil 3 medium potatoes until tender. Peel and mash them thoroughly, ensuring a smooth consistency.

In a dry pan, lightly roast 3 Guntur red chilies, 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 tsp coriander seeds, 1/2 tsp urad dal, and 1/2 tsp chana dal until fragrant, about 2-3 minutes. Allow to cool, then grind into a fine powder.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan over medium heat. Add 2 minced garlic cloves and 10 curry leaves, sautéing until fragrant, about 1 minute. Add the mashed potatoes, the freshly ground spice powder, 1 tsp tamarind pulp, and salt to taste. Mix well and cook for 3-4 minutes, stirring continuously, until the moisture evaporates. Stir in 2 tbsp finely chopped fresh coriander leaves. Let the filling cool completely.

Divide the rested dough into 8 equal portions. Take one portion, flatten it slightly, and place about 2 tablespoons of the cooled potato filling in the center. Carefully bring the edges of the dough together to seal the filling, forming a smooth ball.

Lightly dust your work surface and the stuffed dough ball with Anveshan Khapli Atta. Gently roll out each ball into a round paratha, about 6-7 inches in diameter, applying even pressure to prevent tearing.
Heat a tawa (griddle) over medium-high heat. Place a rolled paratha on the hot tawa. Cook for about 1 minute until small bubbles appear on the surface.

Flip the paratha. Brush 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil generously over the top side. Cook for another minute, then flip again and brush 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on the other side. Continue cooking, pressing gently with a spatula, until both sides are golden brown and cooked through, about 2-3 minutes per side.
Repeat the process for the remaining dough and filling. Serve hot.
tips: Guntur red chilies are known for their intense heat. Adjust the quantity according to your spice preference.
Roasting the whole spices before grinding is essential for developing their full flavor and aroma.
Ensure the potato filling is completely dry before stuffing to prevent the parathas from becoming soggy.
Anveshan Groundnut Oil is a great choice for its high smoke point and neutral flavor, allowing the spices to shine.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve Andhra Masala Aloo Paratha hot with a cooling yogurt raita or a simple dal, to balance the fiery notes of the Guntur chilies.

variations.name: Classic Cheesy Aloo Paratha
variations.description: A modern cafe favourite that hides molten mozzarella and sharp cheddar inside a lightly spiced potato mash, wrapped in wholesome khapli-atta dough. Cut it open hot and the cheese pulls into long strings while the ghee-roasted crust stays shatteringly crisp.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Swapping maida for khapli atta makes this indulgent cheese paratha genuinely wholegrain

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee browns the crust evenly so the cheese inside melts before the outside scorches

steps: Boil 3 medium potatoes for about 15 minutes until utterly soft, then peel and mash them completely smooth and let the mash cool to room temperature so it will not melt the cheese prematurely.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and around 3/4 cup water for a full 8 minutes into a soft, elastic dough; rest it for 15 minutes under a damp cloth.
Mix the cooled mash with 2 minced green chillies, 1 tsp red chilli flakes, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1/2 tsp black pepper powder, 1/4 tsp salt and 3 tbsp chopped coriander until evenly seasoned.
Fold 3/4 cup grated mozzarella and 1/4 cup grated cheddar into the seasoned potato just before assembling, keeping the cheese in distinct shreds rather than mashing it in.
Stuff each of 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp of the cheese-potato mix, pinch shut carefully, and roll gently to 6-inch rounds; keep them slightly thick so the cheese cannot break through.
Cook on a medium tava for about 2 minutes per side, glossing each side with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee, until the crust is golden and you can feel the centre turn soft and molten when pressed lightly.
tips: Cool both mash and tava-fresh parathas briefly; cutting immediately lets all the molten cheese run out onto the plate.
Use low-moisture mozzarella; fresh varieties leak whey and burst the seams mid-roll.
Underfill rather than overfill on your first attempt, as cheese expands dramatically once it melts.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve quartered with a smoky tomato-chilli chutney or ketchup for the kids, and add a crunchy kachumber salad to offset the richness.

variations.name: Punjabi Cheesy Aloo Paratha
variations.description: Punjab's dairy pride turned up to eleven: grated paneer joins the cheese and potato, ajwain perfumes the dough, and each paratha is crowned with hand-churned white butter as it comes off the tava. This is the heaviest, richest paratha in the family and unapologetically so.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: A robust wholegrain shell to carry Punjab's triple-dairy filling of cheese, paneer and butter

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Only a lavish bilona-ghee roast does justice to a Punjabi cheese paratha

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp ajwain seeds worked directly into the flour, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 3/4 cup water; after 8 minutes of kneading the ajwain-scented dough should be soft and stretchy, so rest it for 15 minutes.
Boil 3 medium potatoes until a knife slips through easily, roughly 15 minutes, then peel, mash and cool completely.

Combine the cool mash with 1/2 cup crumbled paneer, 3 minced green chillies, 1 tsp anardana powder, 1/2 tsp garam masala, 1/2 tsp salt and 3 tbsp chopped coriander, working it into a cohesive, tangy-spiced base.
Gently toss in 3/4 cup grated mozzarella at the very end so the shreds stay whole and give a proper cheese pull later.
Stuff 8 dough balls generously with about 2.5 tbsp filling each, seal and roll into thick 6-inch rounds; the Punjabi style is stout, not paper-thin.
Shallow-fry on a medium tava with a full 2 tsp Anveshan Ghee per paratha, flipping twice and pressing the edges, until both sides are burnished deep gold, close to 2.5 minutes per side.
Slide onto plates and immediately drop 1 tbsp white butter on each hot paratha so it melts into the crust before serving.
tips: Kneading ajwain into the dough rather than the filling perfumes every layer and aids digestion of all that dairy.
Crumble the paneer finely; large chunks create air pockets where the melting cheese bursts through.
These are best eaten straight off the tava; the paneer firms up as it cools and the pull disappears.
variations.servingSuggestion: Nothing suits this better than a tall patiala glass of sweet lassi and a sharp onion-chilli sirka salad to cut through the dairy richness.

variations.name: Tamil Cheesy Aloo Paratha
variations.description: A darshini-meets-cafe creation where the cheese-potato filling gets a proper Tamil tadka of curry leaves, crushed pepper and hing in gingelly oil. The pepper's sharp heat slices cleanly through the melted cheese, so each bite finishes bright instead of heavy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The mild sweetness of emmer wheat lets the curry leaf and pepper tadka shine through

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil gives the cheesy crust a toasty South Indian accent

steps: Boil 3 medium potatoes for around 15 minutes until fully soft, then peel, mash smooth and spread on a plate to cool quickly.
Work 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and nearly 3/4 cup water into a soft dough, kneading for 8 minutes; cover and rest 15 minutes.
Crush 1 tsp black peppercorns coarsely in a mortar so some pieces stay cracked rather than powdered, which gives pops of heat in the finished filling.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil on medium, sizzle 15 curry leaves, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 inch minced ginger and 1/4 tsp asafoetida for 40 seconds until the leaves crisp, then stir in 1/4 tsp turmeric powder and pour it all over the cooled mash.
Season the mash with the crushed pepper and 1/4 tsp salt, mix well, and only then fold through 1 cup grated mozzarella in loose shreds.

Fill 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp each, seal, roll to gentle 6-inch rounds and toast on a medium tava with 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil per side until crisp and freckled brown, about 2 minutes per side, listening for the faint sizzle of melting cheese.
tips: Let the tadka cool for a minute before it meets the cheese-bound mash, or the mozzarella will clump into one lump.
Cracked pepper beats pepper powder here; powder makes the whole filling uniformly hot instead of giving bright bursts.
Fresh curry leaves crisped in oil are essential; dried leaves turn papery and flavourless inside the moist filling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Slice into wedges and serve with tomato thokku or a fiery red chilli chutney; a filter coffee chaser is entirely appropriate.

variations.name: Assamese Cheesy Aloo Paratha
variations.description: Assam's legendary bhut jolokia lends a slow-building, fruity inferno to this cheese-laden filling, tamed by cooling mustard-oil-kissed potato and a shower of coriander. The cheese is not just indulgence here; its fat is the only thing standing between you and the ghost pepper.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: A hearty wholegrain wrap that stands up to Assam's fiercest chilli

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Pungent wood-pressed mustard oil is the authentic Assamese counterpoint to bhut jolokia's fruity fire

steps: Boil 3 medium potatoes until completely tender, about 15 minutes, then peel, mash and spread the mash out to cool fully before it meets the cheese.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and roughly 3/4 cup water for 8 minutes into a smooth, supple dough; rest for 15 minutes.
Wearing gloves, deseed and mince 1/2 a bhut jolokia chilli very finely; even this small amount will season all 8 parathas emphatically.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it shimmers and loses its raw edge, about 1 minute on medium-high, then soften 1 finely chopped small onion and 1 inch grated ginger for 2 minutes and stir in the minced bhut jolokia and 1/4 tsp turmeric powder for a final 30 seconds.
Blend this tempering into the cooled mash with 1/4 tsp salt, 2 tsp lemon juice and 4 tbsp chopped coriander, then lightly fold in 1 cup grated mozzarella.

Stuff 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp of the fiery cheese filling, roll into careful 6-inch rounds, and cook on a medium tava with 1 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil per side until deep golden and molten-centred, about 2 minutes each side.
tips: Handle bhut jolokia with gloves and wash the knife and board immediately; its oils linger on surfaces for hours.
For a beginner-friendly version, swap the ghost pepper for 2 regular green chillies and keep everything else identical.
The mustard oil must be heated past its raw pungency first, or it will fight the chilli instead of framing it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a soothing bowl of plain curd and sliced cucumber, the traditional Assamese cooling agents against ghost-pepper heat.

variations.name: Goan Cheesy Aloo Paratha
variations.description: Goa's kokum meets melting cheese in this coastal riff, its sharp fruity tang doing what vinegar does in a Goan rechado, cutting straight through the richness. A little crushed black pepper and garlic sautéed in coconut oil complete the sunshine-flavoured picture.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The wholegrain base grounds this playful coastal combination of kokum and cheese

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil brings the Konkan coast to the tava, browning the crust with a tropical scent

steps: Soak 5 kokum petals in 3 tbsp warm water for 20 minutes, then chop the softened petals fine and reserve 1 tbsp of the deep pink soaking liquid.
Boil 3 medium potatoes until yielding to a knife tip, about 15 minutes, then peel, mash smooth and let the mash cool completely.
Prepare the dough from 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp melted Anveshan Coconut Oil and around 3/4 cup water, kneading for 8 minutes to a soft, even ball; rest for 15 minutes.

Warm 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil over medium heat and fry 6 sliced garlic cloves and 2 chopped green chillies until the garlic edges turn gold, about 90 seconds, then stir in 1/4 tsp turmeric powder and switch off.

Mix the tempering, chopped kokum, the 1 tbsp reserved kokum water, 1/2 tsp coarsely crushed black peppercorns, 1/4 tsp salt and 3 tbsp coriander into the mash, then fold in 1 cup grated mozzarella last.

Fill 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp of filling apiece, seal well since the kokum makes it slightly moist, roll to 6-inch rounds and toast on a medium tava with 1 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil per side until crisp and sun-gold, about 2 minutes per side.
tips: Chop the kokum very fine; whole petals create sour pockets instead of an even tang through the filling.
Add only the measured tablespoon of soaking liquid or the filling turns too wet to seal cleanly.
Dried kokum varies in intensity, so start with 4 petals if yours smell especially sharp and fruity.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a simple tomato salad dressed in coconut vinegar, or alongside sol kadhi for a full Konkan-style pairing.

variations.name: Classic Gobi Paratha
variations.description: Winter's favourite stuffed flatbread, packed with finely grated cauliflower that is salted, squeezed and spiced so the filling stays fluffy instead of watery. Roasted in bilona ghee, the khapli crust turns crisp while the gobi inside stays sweet and just-tender.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli's soft gluten forgives the tricky rolling that a moist gobi filling demands

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Grassy A2 ghee accentuates cauliflower's natural winter sweetness on the tava

steps: Grate 1 medium cauliflower on the fine side of a box grater to get about 3 cups, toss with 1 tsp salt and rest for 15 minutes, then squeeze the gratings hard in a muslin cloth until no more liquid drips out.

While the gobi drains, knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and close to 3/4 cup water for 8 minutes into a soft, pliable dough and rest it covered for 15 minutes.

Season the squeezed cauliflower with 2 minced green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 3/4 tsp red chilli powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric powder, 1/2 tsp garam masala and 3 tbsp chopped coriander, tossing lightly so the shreds stay airy.
Divide the dough into 8 balls; flatten one into a 4-inch cup, pack in 2 tbsp of the gobi mixture, pressing it down lightly, then gather and pinch the edges shut over the top.
Dust each stuffed ball with dry Anveshan Khapli Atta and roll softly into a 7-inch round, using patting motions with the pin rather than hard strokes so the shreds do not poke through.
Roast on a medium tava for about 2 minutes per side, brushing each side with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee, until golden-brown spots bloom and the cauliflower smells sweetly toasted.
tips: Salting and squeezing the gobi is the make-or-break step; skip it and the filling steams the dough into a soggy mess.
Season the cauliflower only at assembly time; salt keeps drawing out water even after squeezing.
The squeezed gobi liquid is flavourful, so use it instead of plain water when kneading your next batch of dough.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best with a slab of white butter melting on top, plus sweet dahi and gajar-gobhi pickle for a proper winter breakfast spread.

variations.name: Punjabi Gobi Paratha
variations.description: The Ludhiana-winter original: ajwain and anardana lift the grated gobi, the parathas are rolled thick, and each one leaves the tava under a slick of ghee and a knob of white butter. Hearty, tangy and built to fuel a cold December morning in the fields.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: A sturdy emmer dough that rolls thick, the way Punjab likes its winter parathas

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Punjab measures paratha quality in ghee; bilona ghee makes each layer flaky and fragrant

steps: Finely grate 1 medium cauliflower, mix with 1 tsp salt, rest 15 minutes and wring it out in a cloth until the shreds feel almost dry to the touch.
Knead a dough from 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 3/4 cup water, working it 8 minutes until springy; rest under a damp cloth for 20 minutes.
Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan over medium heat and crackle 1/2 tsp ajwain seeds for 20 seconds until their thyme-like scent rises, then pour the seeds and ghee over the squeezed gobi.

Add 2 tsp anardana powder, 3 minced green chillies, 1.5 inch grated ginger, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 4 tbsp chopped coriander to the cauliflower and toss until the sour-spicy seasoning coats every shred.
Shape 8 dough balls and pack each with a generous 2.5 tbsp of filling; seal firmly and roll into thick 6-inch rounds, patting the edges with your palm to keep them plump.
Roast each paratha on a medium tava with a liberal 2 tsp Anveshan Ghee, flipping twice and pressing with a spatula, until both faces are richly browned and flaky, close to 2.5 minutes per side.
Crown every hot paratha with 1 tbsp white butter the instant it leaves the pan so it melts into the ridges.
tips: Anardana's fruity sourness is Punjab's answer to the gobi's sweetness; amchur works in a pinch but halve the quantity.
Thick rolling is deliberate; a thin gobi paratha dries out before the filling heats through.
Serve within minutes of cooking; a Punjabi gobi paratha waits for no one, and neither should the butter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Bring out sweet lassi in a steel tumbler, sliced mooli with chaat masala, and mango pickle; that is the complete sarson-season table.

variations.name: Bengali Gobi Paratha
variations.description: Modelled on phulkopir dalna flavours, the grated cauliflower here is briefly sautéed in pungent mustard oil with kalonji, green chilli and a whisper of sugar, Bengal's signature balancing touch. The filling goes in cooked, so it tastes like the beloved winter curry folded inside bread.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Wholegrain khapli replaces the usual maida porota shell with something far more nourishing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Kacha ghani mustard oil gives the sauteed phulkopi filling its unmistakable Bengali bite

steps: Grate 1 medium cauliflower coarsely to yield about 3 cups; no salting needed here because this filling will be cooked dry in the pan.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and roughly 3/4 cup water for 8 minutes to a soft, even dough; rest it for 15 minutes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai until it shimmers and mellows, about 1 minute on medium-high, then crackle 1/2 tsp kalonji and 3 slit green chillies for 30 seconds.

Add the grated cauliflower with 1 inch grated ginger, 1/2 tsp turmeric powder and 1/2 tsp salt, and saute on medium heat, stirring often, until the shreds soften and every trace of moisture cooks off, 6 to 7 minutes.
Finish the filling with 1/2 tsp sugar, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder and 3 tbsp chopped coriander, then spread it on a plate to cool completely before stuffing.

Stuff 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp of the sauteed phulkopi each, roll gently to 7-inch rounds, and fry on a medium tava with about 1 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil per side until crisp and amber-spotted, around 2 minutes per side.
tips: Cooking the filling first is the Bengali way; it concentrates the cauliflower's sweetness and guarantees a dry, easy-to-roll stuffing.
The half teaspoon of sugar is not for sweetness but for balance; Bengali cooking uses it the way others use salt.
If the sauteed gobi still looks moist, spread it thin on a plate for 10 minutes; trapped steam is the enemy of a crisp porota.
variations.servingSuggestion: Eat the Kolkata way with begun bhaja and a smear of kasundi, or simply with thick misti doi on the side for contrast.

variations.name: Rajasthani Gobi Paratha
variations.description: Rajasthan's dry-heat pantry defines this one: whole dried red chillies are pounded with coriander seeds into a rough kutti masala that coats the grated gobi, and amchur stands in for fresh souring agents scarce in the desert. Roasted in ghee, it eats bold, rustic and warming.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Hardy emmer wheat matches the robust, sun-dried flavours of the Marwari kitchen

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: In Rajasthan ghee is both cooking fat and seasoning; bilona ghee delivers on both counts

steps: Grate 1 medium cauliflower finely, salt it with 1 tsp salt, rest 15 minutes and squeeze it bone-dry in a muslin cloth.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and nearly 3/4 cup water into a firm-soft dough over 8 minutes and set it aside, covered, for 15 minutes.

Dry-roast 4 dried red chillies, 2 tsp coriander seeds and 1 tsp fennel seeds in a hot pan for about 2 minutes until the chillies deepen in colour and the seeds smell toasty, then pound them into a coarse, flaky kutti masala.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium, add the pounded masala and 1 inch grated ginger for 20 seconds, then tip in the squeezed gobi and toss off the heat so the spices cling to every shred.
Mix in 1.5 tsp amchur powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric powder and 2 tbsp chopped coriander, tasting to confirm the filling is boldly sour-hot before you stuff.

Fill 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp of masala gobi each, roll into 6- to 7-inch rounds with light pats, and roast on a medium tava with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee per side until crusty and deeply freckled, about 2 minutes per side.
tips: Pound the roasted spices coarse, not fine; the uneven flakes are the signature of a hand-ground Rajasthani masala.
Fennel is the quiet hero here, cooling the chilli heat; do not skip it even if it seems unusual with gobi.
These parathas keep well for a day trip; the dry filling and ghee roast were designed for desert journeys.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with garlic chutney, a katori of plain dahi and green chilli pickle; add hot jaggery tea to complete the desert-winter mood.

variations.name: Kerala Gobi Paratha
variations.description: A thoran-inspired filling of grated cauliflower steam-tossed with fresh coconut, curry leaves and green chilli in cold-pressed coconut oil. The coconut keeps the gobi juicy and sweet, and the finished paratha carries the gentle, tropical aroma of a Kerala lunch pot.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Soft khapli dough wraps the delicate thoran-style filling without overpowering it

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil is the heart of a thoran and scents this paratha through and through

steps: Grate 1 medium cauliflower coarsely; this filling is pan-cooked so it needs no salting or squeezing beforehand.
Knead a soft dough from 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp melted Anveshan Coconut Oil and about 3/4 cup water, working it for 8 minutes; rest for 15 minutes under a damp cloth.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil on medium, fry 4 sliced shallots until their rims brown, about 2 minutes, then add 12 curry leaves, 3 chopped green chillies and 1 inch minced ginger and sizzle for 30 seconds.

Add the grated cauliflower, 1/2 tsp turmeric powder and 1/2 tsp salt, and cook covered on low for 4 minutes, then uncovered on medium for another 3 minutes, stirring, until the shreds are tender and dry.
Fold in 1/2 cup fresh grated coconut and 1/2 tsp roasted cumin powder, toss for 1 minute so the coconut warms through, and cool the thoran filling completely on a plate.

Stuff 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp of the coconut-gobi mixture, roll them gently into 7-inch rounds, and toast on a medium tava with 1 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil brushed per side until golden-freckled and aromatic, about 2 minutes per side.
tips: Cover-cook the cauliflower first so it steams tender, then dry it uncovered; the two-stage method keeps the thoran texture authentic.
Add the coconut at the end and only warm it; long cooking turns fresh coconut oily and dull.
A pinch of crushed pepper in the finishing toss deepens the flavour if your chillies are mild.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a sharp lime pickle and a cup of chukku kaapi or sweet chaya; for lunch, moru curry alongside is wonderful.

variations.name: Classic Garlic Aloo Paratha
variations.description: A garlic lover's spin on the beloved stuffed paratha, where golden-fried garlic is worked into the potato mash and a garlic-infused ghee gets brushed over the finished crust. The double layer of garlic, mellow inside and toasty on top, makes this the most aromatic paratha on the breakfast table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Ancient emmer wheat rolls thin without springing back, ideal for a generously stuffed garlic paratha

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Slow-churned bilona ghee carries the fried garlic aroma into every layer of the crust

steps: Boil 4 medium potatoes on high heat for about 15 minutes until a skewer passes cleanly through the centre, then peel and mash them smooth while still hot.
Combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, add roughly 3/4 cup water in stages and knead for 8 minutes into a soft, pliant dough; rest it covered for 15 minutes.

Melt 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan over low-medium heat and fry 8 minced garlic cloves slowly until they turn an even biscuit gold, about 2 minutes, taking care they do not brown further and turn bitter.

Scrape the garlic and its ghee into the mash, then add 2 minced green chillies, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi, 1/2 tsp salt and 3 tbsp chopped coriander, mixing until fragrant and uniform.
Shape 8 dough balls, tuck about 2 tbsp of garlicky filling into each, seal well and roll into 7-inch rounds with light, even strokes, dusting sparingly with dry atta.

Roast on a medium-hot tava for around 2 minutes per side, brushing each side with a little of the remaining Anveshan Ghee mixed with the last 2 grated raw garlic cloves, until crisp bronze patches appear and the garlic on the surface toasts fragrant.
tips: Fry the garlic on gentle heat and pull it at pale gold; it keeps cooking in the residual ghee and darkens one more shade off the flame.
Grating the raw garlic for the finishing ghee, rather than mincing, helps it toast evenly on the hot crust without burnt bits.
The filling freezes well for 2 weeks in portions; thaw fully before stuffing so the dough does not turn soggy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Cut into quarters and serve with plain whisked curd and lime pickle; a mint-coriander chutney doubles the fresh-versus-toasty garlic contrast.

variations.name: Punjabi Garlic Aloo Paratha
variations.description: Modelled on the hefty parathas of Amritsar's galis, this version loads the garlic-potato filling with anardana and ajwain-scented ghee, then finishes each hot paratha with a melting spoonful of white butter. The pomegranate-seed sourness against sweet fried garlic is what sets the Amritsari filling apart.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli's hearty wholegrain bite suits the robust Amritsari-style stuffing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Generous bilona ghee on the tava is non-negotiable for the shallow-fried Amritsari crust

steps: Pressure-cook 4 medium potatoes for 3 whistles, peel them warm and mash coarsely; Amritsari fillings keep a rustic, uneven texture rather than a smooth paste.

Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 3/4 cup water for 8 minutes until soft and stretchy, then rest the dough for 20 minutes so it rolls thick yet tender.
Warm 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium heat, crackle 1/2 tsp ajwain seeds for 20 seconds until sharply fragrant, then fry 8 roughly chopped garlic cloves until golden at the edges, about 90 seconds.

Empty the pan over the mash and season with 2 tsp anardana powder, 3 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1/2 tsp garam masala, 1/2 tsp salt and 3 tbsp coriander, kneading the spices through with your knuckles.
Make 8 dough balls and stuff each with a hearty 2.5 tbsp of filling; because the filling is generous, roll slowly to a thick 6-inch round, flipping the disc once midway to keep it even.
Shallow-fry on a medium tava with about 2 tsp Anveshan Ghee per paratha, pressing the edges until both sides are crisp, deeply browned and slightly flaky, about 2.5 minutes per side.
Top each hot paratha with 1 tbsp white butter just before it leaves the kitchen so it melts into the crags of the crust.
tips: Anardana clumps in the packet; rub it between your palms as you sprinkle so the sourness distributes evenly through the mash.
Roll these thicker than usual parathas; the Amritsari style is closer to a stuffed bread than a flatbread and needs the extra body.
No white butter on hand? Whip chilled cream for a minute and drain; the fresh unsalted result is exactly what dhabas use.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Amritsar way: with a tall glass of sweet lassi, sliced onions and a fiery green chilli pickle on a steel thali.

variations.name: Tamil Garlic Aloo Paratha
variations.description: Here the filling channels a Tamil poriyal: mustard-free but rich with curry leaves, crushed pepper-garlic paste and urad dal fried crisp in gingelly oil. The urad dal nubs add a surprise crunch inside the soft potato, a texture trick straight from the Kongunadu kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The wheat's natural sweetness balances the sharp pepper-garlic paste in this Tamil-style filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Nallennai, wood-pressed gingelly oil, is the classic Tamil frying medium and turns the crust deeply aromatic

steps: Boil 4 medium potatoes for 15 minutes until tender throughout, peel and mash them lightly, leaving the texture a little coarse the way a poriyal base would be.

Prepare the dough by kneading 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and close to 3/4 cup water for 8 minutes to a smooth, elastic ball; rest for 15 minutes under a damp cloth.
Pound 10 garlic cloves and 1 tsp black peppercorns into a coarse, sticky paste using a mortar and pestle; the uneven crush releases more aroma than a smooth blend.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil over medium flame, fry 1 tbsp urad dal until it turns the colour of cashew, about 90 seconds, then add 2 torn dried red chillies, 15 curry leaves and 1/4 tsp asafoetida and sizzle for 20 seconds.
Lower the heat, add the pepper-garlic paste and fry for a full minute until its raw smell disappears, then fold the entire tempering into the mash with 1/2 tsp turmeric powder and 1/2 tsp salt.

Stuff 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp filling each, roll into 7-inch discs, and toast on a medium tava with 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil per side until golden-brown and crisp at the edges, about 2 minutes a side.
tips: Fry the urad dal patiently to a cashew colour; underdone dal stays chalky inside the filling instead of crunchy.
The pepper-garlic paste must be fried until the garlic loses its raw sharpness, or the filling will taste harsh rather than warm.
These parathas stay crisp longer than ghee-roasted ones, making them excellent lunchbox candidates.
variations.servingSuggestion: Accompany with coconut thogayal or a simple tomato-onion chutney, and finish the meal with a tumbler of spiced buttermilk (neer mor).

variations.name: Rajasthani Garlic Aloo Paratha
variations.description: A tribute to lahsun ki chutney from Jodhpur, where whole dried Mathania-style red chillies are soaked, ground with garlic and cooked down before meeting the potato. The filling is brick-red, smoky and assertive, built for the desert habit of bold flavours that need no accompaniment.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Sturdy khapli dough stands up to the moist chilli-garlic chutney filling without tearing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Desert kitchens finish everything in ghee; here it rounds off the sharp chilli-garlic edge

steps: Soak 6 dried red chillies in hot water for 20 minutes until leathery-soft, then grind them with 12 garlic cloves and 1 tsp coriander seeds into a thick, coarse red paste, adding no more than 1 tbsp of the soaking water.
Meanwhile boil 4 medium potatoes for about 15 minutes until soft, peel and crumble them roughly into a wide bowl.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and around 3/4 cup water into a firm yet pliable dough, working it a good 8 minutes; rest 15 minutes.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium and fry the chilli-garlic paste, stirring constantly, until the ghee separates at the edges and the raw garlic smell turns sweetly pungent, about 4 minutes.
Mix this cooked chutney into the potatoes along with 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp amchur powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric powder and 1/2 tsp salt until the mash turns an even terracotta red.

Fill 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp of the red filling each, roll gently into 6- to 7-inch rounds, and roast on a medium tava with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee per side until crusty and darkly freckled, roughly 2 minutes per side.
tips: Cooking the chilli-garlic paste until the ghee separates is the critical step; an undercooked paste makes the filling taste raw and wet.
Deseed half the chillies before soaking if you want Jodhpur colour without the full Jodhpur burn.
The cooked chutney alone keeps a week refrigerated, so make double and spread it inside plain rotis too.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of thick, lightly salted dahi and slivered onions; in true Marwari spirit it also pairs superbly with hot masala chai at 5 pm.

variations.name: Odia Garlic Aloo Paratha
variations.description: Odisha's beloved panch phoron, the five-spice mix of mustard, cumin, fennel, kalonji and fenugreek, is bloomed in pungent mustard oil and folded through a garlicky mash, echoing the flavours of aloo bharta eaten with pakhala. Fennel's sweetness threads through every bite, softening the garlic's punch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Wholegrain khapli echoes the rustic, unpolished character of Odia home cooking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil is the backbone of an Odia bharta and gives this filling its rustic pungency

steps: Boil 4 medium potatoes until completely tender, around 15 minutes at a rolling boil, then peel and mash them fine while hot, bharta-style.
Knead the dough from 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and about 3/4 cup water; give it 8 minutes of steady kneading until smooth, then rest for 15 minutes.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pan until it shimmers and mellows, about 1 minute on medium-high, then drop in 1 tsp panch phoron and let the five seeds crackle and pop for 30 seconds.
Add 8 sliced garlic cloves, 1 finely chopped small onion and 3 chopped green chillies to the tempering and fry until the onion turns translucent and the garlic golden, about 3 minutes on medium.
Combine the tempering with the mash, 1/2 tsp turmeric powder, 1/2 tsp salt and 3 tbsp chopped coriander, working it together until the filling is streaked yellow and flecked with whole spices.

Stuff and seal 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp of filling each, roll to 7-inch rounds, and cook on a medium tava with 1 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil brushed per side until blistered nut-brown, about 2 minutes each side.
tips: Panch phoron must go into properly hot oil so the fenugreek toasts instantly; in lukewarm oil it stays raw and bitter.
Mash the potatoes finer than you would for a North Indian paratha; the Odia bharta texture should be almost creamy.
A day-old filling actually tastes better here as the fennel and kalonji perfume deepens overnight.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with tomato khajuri khatta, Odisha's sweet-sour date and tomato chutney, or simply with thick curd and a roasted green chilli.

variations.name: Classic Garlic Gobi Paratha
variations.description: Golden ghee-fried garlic is tossed through squeezed cauliflower shreds so every bite of this paratha carries a sweet, toasty garlic backbone. A final brush of garlic-infused ghee on the hot crust doubles the aroma without doubling the effort.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat's mild sweetness lets the double garlic layer take centre stage

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Garlic fried gently in bilona ghee turns candy-sweet instead of acrid

steps: Finely grate 1 medium cauliflower, toss with 1 tsp salt, rest for 15 minutes and squeeze the shreds in a muslin cloth until they stop dripping.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 3/4 cup water for 8 minutes to a soft, stretchy dough; cover and rest for 15 minutes.
Fry 8 minced garlic cloves in 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over low-medium heat until uniformly biscuit-gold, about 2 minutes, watching closely in the final 30 seconds when they colour fastest.

Pour the garlic and its ghee over the squeezed gobi, then season with 2 minced green chillies, 3/4 tsp red chilli powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi and 3 tbsp chopped coriander, tossing until fragrant.
Stuff 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp of garlicky gobi each, pinch the seams shut and roll into 7-inch rounds with soft pats of the pin.

Cook on a medium tava for about 2 minutes per side, brushing each side with the remaining Anveshan Ghee into which you have grated the last 2 raw garlic cloves, until the crust is crisp, golden and headily aromatic.
tips: Pull the frying garlic at pale gold, not brown; carryover heat in the ghee finishes the job off the flame.
Kasuri methi and garlic are natural allies; crush the leaves finely so they distribute rather than clump.
If prepping ahead, keep the fried garlic and the gobi separate and combine at assembly so the crunch survives.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain dahi whipped with black salt and a fresh tomato-onion kachumber; the acidity resets the palate between garlicky bites.

variations.name: Punjabi Garlic Gobi Paratha
variations.description: A dhaba-thick paratha where garlic meets anardana and ajwain in the gobi stuffing, rolled stout and shallow-fried in ghee until the crust flakes. The finishing knob of white butter melting over the top is not garnish in Punjab; it is policy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: A wholegrain upgrade to the dhaba classic that still rolls thick and soft

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The generous tava ghee that gives Punjabi parathas their flaky, burnished armour

steps: Grate 1 medium cauliflower finely, salt it with 1 tsp salt for 15 minutes and wring the shreds bone-dry in a cloth.
Knead a soft dough from 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and roughly 3/4 cup water, working it for 8 minutes; let it relax for 20 minutes.
Warm 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat, pop 1/2 tsp ajwain seeds for 20 seconds, then fry 10 roughly chopped garlic cloves until their edges catch gold, about 90 seconds.

Empty the sizzling pan over the gobi and season with 1.5 tsp anardana powder, 3 minced green chillies, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 4 tbsp chopped coriander, mixing until the sourness and garlic spread evenly.
Shape 8 dough balls, load each with a hefty 2.5 tbsp of filling, seal and roll into thick 6-inch rounds, patting the rim round with your palms.

Shallow-fry on a medium tava with 2 tsp Anveshan Ghee per paratha, pressing and flipping twice, until both faces are flaky and richly browned, about 2.5 minutes per side, then top each with 1 tbsp white butter straight away.
tips: Chop the garlic rough rather than mincing it; the bigger pieces stay sweet and chewy inside the thick paratha.
Anardana against garlic is the flavour heart of this recipe; taste the filling and add another half teaspoon if it reads flat.
Roll thick without fear; a proper dhaba paratha is nearly half a centimetre before it hits the tava.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside a tall sweet lassi, sliced radish with black salt and a strong pickle; eat with hands, no cutlery allowed.

variations.name: Bengali Garlic Gobi Paratha
variations.description: Garlic sliced thin and fried in smoking mustard oil with kalonji infuses this phulkopi filling with the fierce, warming flavours of a Bengali winter bhaji. A hint of sugar rounds the pungency, keeping the filling true to Kolkata's balancing instincts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Nutty emmer flour stands in beautifully for the usual refined porota base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Garlic fried in pungent kacha ghani mustard oil is a cornerstone Bengali flavour

steps: Coarsely grate 1 medium cauliflower; the shreds go straight to the pan, so there is no need to salt or squeeze them.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and close to 3/4 cup water into a soft dough over 8 minutes, then rest it for 15 minutes.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it shimmers and its sharpness mellows, about 1 minute on medium-high, then crackle 1/2 tsp kalonji for 20 seconds and fry 10 thinly sliced garlic cloves until golden at the rims, about 90 seconds.
Add the gobi, 3 slit green chillies, 1/2 tsp turmeric powder and 1/2 tsp salt, and saute on medium for 6 to 7 minutes, stirring, until the cauliflower is tender and every drop of moisture is gone.
Finish with 1/2 tsp sugar, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder and 3 tbsp chopped coriander, then spread the bhaji on a plate to cool completely before stuffing.

Stuff 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp each of the garlicky phulkopi, roll gently into 7-inch rounds and fry on a medium tava with about 1 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil per side until amber-blistered, around 2 minutes per side.
tips: Sliced garlic behaves differently from minced in mustard oil; slices toast to sweet chips while mince burns, so slice thin and even.
Do not shortcut the oil-heating step; raw mustard oil tastes harsh, while properly warmed oil tastes warmly pungent.
The pinch of sugar is a Bengali signature that heightens the garlic; it should never be detectable as sweetness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with kasundi for dipping and a wedge of gondhoraj or regular lime; hot cha in a clay bhar completes the picture.

variations.name: Karnataka Garlic Gobi Paratha
variations.description: Tamarind and garlic pull this filling toward the flavours of a Mysore-style gojju, with chana dal and curry leaves fried crisp in groundnut oil for texture. Tangy, gently sweet and deeply savoury, it is the most balanced member of the garlic gobi family.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Old-world emmer wheat matches Karnataka's affection for hardy heritage grains

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil crisps the tempering and toasts the crust the darshini way

steps: Grate 1 medium cauliflower coarsely into roughly 3 cups of shreds and keep aside, unsalted, for pan-cooking.
Prepare the dough with 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and about 3/4 cup water, kneading 8 minutes until smooth and supple; rest 15 minutes.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium and fry 1 tbsp chana dal until it turns deep gold, about 90 seconds, then add 2 torn dried red chillies, 12 curry leaves and 8 sliced garlic cloves and fry until the garlic browns lightly, another 90 seconds.
Tip in the gobi with 1/2 tsp turmeric powder and 1/2 tsp salt and saute for 6 minutes until tender and dry, stirring so nothing catches on the pan floor.
Stir in 2 tsp tamarind paste and 1 tsp jaggery powder, cook 1 minute more so the tang and sweetness glaze the shreds, and cool the gojju-style filling completely.

Fill 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp apiece, seal and roll to 7-inch rounds, then toast on a medium tava with 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil per side until crisp and handsomely spotted, about 2 minutes per side.
tips: Tamarind and jaggery must both be present; one without the other tips the filling out of the classic gojju balance.
Fry the chana dal fully golden before the garlic enters, since the garlic finishes faster and both must land crisp together.
This tangy filling pairs unusually well with a soft-boiled egg mashed on the side for a Bengaluru PG-room dinner.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and a small tumbler of sweet curd; on weekends, add a strong Mysore filter coffee to finish.

variations.name: Malwa Garlic Gobi Paratha
variations.description: Indore's love of crunch shows up as coarsely crushed roasted peanuts tossed with garlicky sauteed gobi, seasoned with fennel and lime in the jeeravan spirit. The nut-and-garlic pairing gives this paratha a street-side chaat energy no other regional take has.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The hearty emmer base keeps up with Malwa's peanut-heavy appetite

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Peanut filling cooked in wood-pressed groundnut oil makes the nutty theme sing twice

steps: Grate 1 medium cauliflower coarsely and pound 1/2 cup roasted peanuts into a chunky rubble, leaving several halves whole for crunch.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and near 3/4 cup water for 8 minutes into a soft, elastic dough; rest under a damp cloth for 15 minutes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium flame and fry 8 minced garlic cloves with 3 chopped green chillies until the garlic is golden and nutty-smelling, about 90 seconds.
Add the gobi with 1/2 tsp turmeric powder and 1/2 tsp salt and saute for 6 minutes until soft and dry, stirring often so the garlic at the bottom does not darken further.
Off the heat, fold in the crushed peanuts, 1/2 tsp fennel seed powder, 1 tbsp lime juice and 4 tbsp chopped coriander, then cool the filling completely on a wide plate.

Stuff 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp of the crunchy filling each, roll carefully into 7-inch rounds so the peanut pieces stay inside, and roast on a medium tava with 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil per side until golden and crisp, about 2 minutes per side.
tips: Crush the peanuts by hand in a mortar rather than a mixer; machine grinding releases oil and turns them pasty.
Lime juice goes in only after the pan leaves the heat, keeping its brightness intact against the rich nuts and garlic.
Sprinkle a pinch of jeeravan or chaat masala into the filling if you want the full Indore street-corner effect.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve Indore-style with spiced curd sprinkled with sev, a wedge of lime and cutting chai; leftover filling is excellent on buttered toast.

variations.name: Classic Masala Gobi Paratha
variations.description: A spice-forward gobi paratha where the grated cauliflower is coated in a full masala wardrobe of coriander, garam masala, cumin and kasuri methi before being sealed into khapli dough. Each ghee-roasted bite delivers layered warmth rather than plain heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The wheat's gentle nuttiness lets a complex masala blend stay in focus

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Blooming the ground masalas in bilona ghee unlocks their full aroma before they meet the gobi

steps: Grate 1 medium cauliflower finely, toss the shreds with 1 tsp salt and let them weep for 15 minutes, then twist them dry in a muslin cloth with real force.
Meanwhile knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 3/4 cup water for 8 minutes to a soft, elastic dough; rest it covered for 15 minutes.

Melt 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over low heat and bloom 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1/2 tsp turmeric powder for just 20 seconds until the kitchen fills with their scent.
Pour the bloomed masala over the squeezed gobi, add 1 inch grated ginger, 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi and 3 tbsp chopped coriander, and mix until every shred wears an even rust-orange coat.
Portion the dough into 8 balls, stuff each with 2 tbsp of the masala gobi, seal the pleats firmly and roll into 7-inch rounds using soft, patting strokes.
Cook on a medium tava, giving each side about 2 minutes and a brush of 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee, until crisp golden-brown patches appear and the spices smell toasted, not raw.
tips: Twenty seconds is all ground spices need in hot ghee; a moment longer and the coriander powder turns acrid.
Crush kasuri methi between your palms as you add it to wake up its aroma.
If your garam masala is older than six months, add an extra half teaspoon; ground spices fade fast.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling cucumber raita and lemon pickle; the mild raita gives the layered masala room to shine.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Masala Gobi Paratha
variations.description: Goda masala, with its stone flower, coconut and sesame undertones, gives this gobi filling the smoky-sweet depth of a Puneri bhaji. A crunch of toasted sesame and a groundnut-oil roast keep it firmly rooted in the Deccan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer's rustic crumb suits the earthy goda masala like a Puneri bhakri would

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is Maharashtra's daily fat and deepens the goda masala's roasted sweetness

steps: Grate 1 medium cauliflower coarsely to get around 3 cups of shreds; this filling gets cooked, so skip the salting stage.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and roughly 3/4 cup water into a supple dough over 8 minutes and rest it for 15 minutes.
Toast 1 tbsp white sesame seeds dry on low heat until they hop and turn ivory-gold, about 2 minutes, and set them aside.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium, crackle 8 torn curry leaves and 2 chopped green chillies for 30 seconds, then add the gobi, 1/2 tsp turmeric powder and 1/2 tsp salt and saute for 6 minutes until tender and dry.

Off the heat, stir in 2.5 tsp goda masala, 1 tsp jaggery powder, the toasted sesame and 3 tbsp chopped coriander; the filling should smell smoky-sweet and look dusky brown, so cool it fully before stuffing.

Stuff 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp of the goda-spiced gobi apiece, roll to 7-inch rounds without pressing hard, and roast on a medium tava with 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil per side until crisp mahogany spots develop, about 2 minutes per side.
tips: Goda masala goes in off the heat; direct frying scorches its coconut content and turns the filling bitter.
The teaspoon of jaggery mirrors the sweet edge Maharashtrian bhajis carry; do not omit it.
Leftover filling makes an excellent sandwich layer with a smear of green chutney next morning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a spoon of shengdana chutney (dry peanut-garlic chutney) and plain curd; a slice of raw onion completes the Puneri thali feel.

variations.name: Awadhi Masala Gobi Paratha
variations.description: Lucknow's refinement shows in this pale, fragrant filling: gobi cooked gently in ghee with white-spice warmth from fennel, cardamom and white pepper, then perfumed with a few drops of kewra water. It is a paratha that whispers its masala rather than shouting it.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: A tender emmer shell befitting the delicacy of Awadhi dastarkhwan breads

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Awadhi cooking is ghee-first; bilona ghee provides the rich, rounded base the kewra floats upon

steps: Grate 1 medium cauliflower finely and keep it unsalted; the moisture will be driven off in the pan the Awadhi way, by slow sauteing.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and close to 3/4 cup water for 8 minutes until silk-soft, then rest the dough for 15 minutes.
Chop 8 cashews fine and toast them in 1/2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over low heat until pale gold, about 90 seconds, then lift them out and reserve.

In the same pan, warm 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium-low, sweat 1 inch grated ginger and 2 minced green chillies for 1 minute, then add the gobi with 1/2 tsp salt and cook gently, stirring, for 7 minutes until soft, dry and barely coloured.

Take the pan off the heat and season with 1 tsp fennel seed powder, 1/4 tsp green cardamom powder, 1/2 tsp white pepper powder, the toasted cashews, 2 tbsp coriander and exactly 1/2 tsp kewra water, folding gently; cool completely.

Fill 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp each of the perfumed gobi, roll into 7-inch rounds with a feather-light hand, and roast on a medium-low tava with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee per side until evenly pale gold rather than dark, about 2.5 minutes per side.
tips: Kewra water is potent; measure the half teaspoon rather than pouring from the bottle, or the filling smells of perfume instead of food.
Keep the tava a notch lower than usual; the pale Awadhi crust should be blond-gold, never charred.
White pepper, not black, keeps both the colour and the gentility of the filling intact.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a saffron-laced raita or a light burhani, and cut into neat quarters as you would for a Lucknow dastarkhwan.

variations.name: Andhra Masala Gobi Paratha
variations.description: The masala here is a Guntur-style kaaram: dried red chillies pounded with garlic, cumin and curry leaves into a fierce red rubble that clings to every cauliflower shred. Sesame oil on the tava and a tamarind backbone make it taste unmistakably of coastal Andhra.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli's mellow sweetness gives the Guntur kaaram a fair fight

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil carries chilli heat the way Andhra kitchens intend

steps: Grate 1 medium cauliflower coarsely; the filling is stir-fried, so the shreds go in raw and unsalted.
Make the dough with 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and about 3/4 cup water, kneading a full 8 minutes; rest 15 minutes under cover.
Dry-roast 4 Guntur dried red chillies and 1 tsp cumin seeds on low heat until the chillies crisp and darken slightly, about 2 minutes, then pound them with 6 garlic cloves into a coarse red kaaram.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil on medium, crisp 12 curry leaves for 20 seconds, then add the gobi with 1/2 tsp turmeric powder and 1/2 tsp salt and stir-fry for 6 minutes until tender and completely dry.
Work in the pounded kaaram and 1.5 tsp tamarind paste, fry 1 more minute so the paste coats and darkens, then fold in 2 tbsp coriander and cool the brick-red filling fully.

Stuff 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp of kaaram gobi each, roll out to 7-inch rounds patiently, and roast on a medium tava with 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil per side until fiercely blistered, about 2 minutes per side.
tips: Pounding beats grinding for kaaram; a mixer turns the chillies pasty while the mortar keeps them flaky and potent.
Balance check: the tamarind should register right after the heat; add another half teaspoon if you cannot taste it.
Serve younger eaters first from a batch made with 2 chillies, then pound extra kaaram into the remaining filling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Offer with a bowl of chilled curd whisked thin, gongura pickle for the brave, and raw onion wedges as the traditional coolant.

variations.name: Odia Masala Gobi Paratha
variations.description: Panch phoron crackled in mustard oil is the flavour spine of this filling, its fennel and fenugreek weaving through soft-cooked cauliflower exactly as in an Odia phulakobi tarkari. A late hit of grated ginger and green chilli keeps the masala fresh rather than heavy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: An unfussy wholegrain wrapper true to Odisha's grain-first food culture

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil plus panch phoron equals the definitive Odia tarkari base

steps: Coarsely grate 1 medium cauliflower for about 3 cups of shreds and keep them ready by the stove, unsalted.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and around 3/4 cup water for 8 minutes into a soft, springy dough; rest for 15 minutes.

Bring 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to a light shimmer over medium-high heat so its raw bite mellows, about 1 minute, then crackle 1 tsp panch phoron until the mustard seeds within pop, roughly 30 seconds.
Add 1 finely chopped small onion and fry to translucence, about 2 minutes, then tip in the gobi with 1/2 tsp turmeric powder and 1/2 tsp salt and saute for 6 minutes until soft and dry.
Finish off the heat with 1.5 inch grated ginger, 3 minced green chillies, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder and 3 tbsp chopped coriander, then spread the tarkari filling to cool before stuffing.
Fill 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp apiece, seal, roll into 7-inch rounds and toast on a medium tava, brushing 1 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil per side, until nut-brown blisters form, about 2 minutes per side.
tips: Panch phoron needs genuinely hot oil so all five seeds bloom together; test with a single mustard seed first.
Adding the ginger and chilli after cooking preserves their brightness against the deep, toasty five-spice base.
This filling doubles as a side dish; make extra and eat it with dal-rice tomorrow, as an Odia household would.
variations.servingSuggestion: Wonderful with tomato khatta and a spoon of dahi; on hot days, serve alongside a bowl of chilled pakhala water for authenticity.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Aloo Paratha
variations.description: The dhaba-style breakfast staple of North India, stuffed with a fiery mash of potatoes, green chillies and crushed black pepper. Slow-ground khapli atta gives the crust a nutty sweetness that balances the double hit of fresh and dried heat, while a final brush of bilona ghee turns the surface blistered and crisp.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Stone-ground emmer wheat keeps the paratha soft for hours, so leftovers stay pliable in a tiffin

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A2 bilona ghee has a high smoke point, so the crust blisters golden without burning on the tava

steps: Boil 4 medium potatoes in well-salted water over high heat until a knife slides through with no resistance, about 15 minutes; drain, peel while warm and mash until completely smooth so no lumps tear the dough later.

Make the dough by rubbing 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, then adding 3/4 cup water a little at a time; knead for 8 minutes until soft, stretchy and no longer sticky, cover and rest for 15 minutes.

Mix the warm mash with 3 finely chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric powder, 1/2 tsp freshly crushed black peppercorns, 1/2 tsp salt and 3 tbsp chopped coriander until evenly speckled.

Divide the dough into 8 equal balls and the filling into 8 portions of about 2 tbsp each; flatten a ball into a 4-inch disc, cup it in your palm, place one portion of filling in the centre and pinch the edges together to seal completely.

Dust the stuffed ball with dry Anveshan Khapli Atta and roll it out gently and evenly into a 7-inch round, rotating a quarter turn after every few strokes so the filling spreads without bursting through.

Cook on a medium-hot tava for about 90 seconds until small bubbles rise, flip, spread 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee over the surface, flip again and press the edges with a spatula until both sides carry deep golden-brown spots, about 2 minutes per side.
Repeat with the remaining balls, stacking finished parathas in a cloth-lined box so steam keeps them supple until serving.
tips: Mash the potatoes while they are still warm; a cold mash turns gluey and forms lumps that puncture the paratha when rolling.
If a paratha tears while rolling, dab the tear with dry atta rather than water, which would glue it to the rolling pin.
The filling can be made up to a day ahead and refrigerated, but bring it back to room temperature or it will make the dough sweat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of chilled boondi raita and a wedge of spicy mango pickle; a glass of salted lassi rounds it into a full Punjabi-style breakfast.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Spicy Aloo Paratha
variations.description: Pune households flavour their potato stuffing with goda masala, the region's coconut-and-stone-flower spice blend that tastes smoky-sweet rather than sharply hot. Toasted sesame seeds add crunch and the parathas are pan-roasted in wood-pressed groundnut oil for an earthy, nutty finish typical of the Deccan kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat's low gluten makes it forgiving to roll around the chunky goda masala filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil mirrors the traditional Maharashtrian frying medium and deepens the goda masala's roasted notes

steps: Pressure-cook 4 medium potatoes for 3 whistles on medium heat, cool, peel and crumble them coarsely with your fingers rather than mashing, which keeps the filling pleasantly textured.

Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and roughly 3/4 cup water into a supple, non-sticky dough; work it for about 7 minutes, then rest under a damp cloth for 15 minutes.

Toast 1 tbsp white sesame seeds in a dry pan on low heat until they pop and smell nutty, about 2 minutes, then heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in the same pan and crackle 8 torn curry leaves and 2 chopped green chillies for 30 seconds.

Tip the tempering and sesame over the crumbled potatoes, add 2 tsp goda masala, 1/2 tsp turmeric powder, 1/2 tsp salt, 2 tsp lemon juice and 2 tbsp chopped coriander, and fold everything together until the mash turns an even dusky brown.
Shape 8 dough balls, stuff each with about 2 tbsp of the goda masala potato mixture, seal the pleats firmly and roll into 6- to 7-inch rounds using light, outward strokes.
Roast each paratha on a medium tava, brushing both sides with the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil, until the surface shows crisp mahogany patches, roughly 2 minutes per side.
tips: Goda masala scorches quickly, so it goes into the filling off the heat instead of being fried in the tempering.
If you cannot find goda masala, kala masala works, but do not substitute garam masala; the dish loses its signature sweet-smoky character.
Crumbled rather than mashed potato is authentic here; it also releases less moisture, so the parathas crisp better.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a dollop of homemade curd whisked with a pinch of salt and a side of Maharashtrian thecha for those who want an extra chilli kick.

variations.name: Bengali Spicy Aloo Paratha
variations.description: In Kolkata homes the potato stuffing is perfumed with pungent kacha mustard oil and crackled kalonji, the same pairing that defines aloo posto and jhaal dishes. The raw bite of mustard oil mellows on the hot tava into a warm, sinus-clearing sharpness that no other fat can imitate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The wholegrain sweetness of khapli tempers the sharp mustard-oil filling beautifully

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Cold wood-pressed mustard oil keeps its signature pungency, the soul of this Bengali stuffing

steps: Boil 4 medium potatoes until fork-tender, about 15 minutes on high heat, then peel and mash them fine while hot; a Bengali filling should be silky, not chunky.

Work 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil together, then knead in about 3/4 cup water for 8 minutes until the dough is soft and springs back slowly when pressed; rest it for 15 minutes.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a small pan until it just begins to smoke and its raw smell fades, about 1 minute, then lower the heat and crackle 1/2 tsp kalonji with 4 slit green chillies for 30 seconds until fragrant.

Pour this sizzling tempering over the mash, add 1 inch grated ginger, 1/2 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1/2 tsp salt and 3 tbsp chopped coriander, and beat with a fork until the filling turns pale gold and aromatic.
Portion the dough into 8 balls, enclose 2 tbsp of filling in each, pinch shut and roll out to 7-inch rounds with gentle pressure so the soft mash does not squeeze out at the seams.

Fry each paratha on a medium-high tava with about 1 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil per side, pressing with a spatula until the crust develops deep amber blisters, roughly 2 minutes per side, and serve straight off the pan.
tips: Always let mustard oil reach its light smoking point before tempering; skipping this leaves an acrid raw edge in the filling.
Kalonji burns fast, so add it only after the pan comes off high heat and count to thirty before pouring the tempering out.
Bengali households eat these with sugar-sprinkled tomato chutney; keep the filling extra spicy so the sweet side dish has something to fight.
variations.servingSuggestion: Offer with tangy tomato-khejur chutney and a few slices of raw onion rubbed with salt; a hot cup of milky cha makes it a proper Kolkata jolkhabar.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Aloo Paratha
variations.description: This take borrows the fearless heat of Guntur, folding coarse Guntur red chilli flakes, garlic and curry leaves into the potato mash the way an Andhra karam podi is built. Sesame oil in the pan adds the deep toasted aroma of a Rayalaseema kitchen and carries the chilli heat evenly through every bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli's gentle sweetness is the perfect foil for the aggressive Guntur chilli heat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil is the traditional Andhra roasting fat and gives the crust a podi-like toasted depth

steps: Cook 4 medium potatoes in boiling water for about 15 minutes until completely soft, then peel and mash them while steaming hot so the spices to come can bloom into the starch.

Bring 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta together with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and close to 3/4 cup water; knead vigorously for 8 minutes to a smooth, elastic dough and let it relax for 15 minutes under cover.
Dry-roast 4 Guntur dried red chillies on low heat until they darken a shade and turn brittle, about 2 minutes, cool them and crush into coarse flakes with a mortar and pestle.

Warm 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pan over medium heat, sizzle 6 sliced garlic cloves until light gold, about 1 minute, then add 12 curry leaves and let them turn glassy and crisp before switching off.

Fold the garlic tempering, crushed Guntur chilli flakes, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp tamarind paste, 1/2 tsp salt and 2 tbsp coriander into the mash until it glows brick-red throughout.

Stuff 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp filling apiece, roll each to a 7-inch disc with a light hand, and roast on a medium tava with 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil per side until fiercely blistered and crisp, about 2 minutes per side.
tips: Roast the Guntur chillies in a ventilated kitchen; their fumes are potent, which is exactly why the flavour is worth it.
The teaspoon of tamarind paste is not optional; Andhra heat always rides on a sour undertone that keeps the palate refreshed.
Scale down to 2 chillies for a family-friendly version without losing the garlic-curry leaf character.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Andhra way with a katori of chilled curd rice on the side, or with peanut chutney and a raw mango sliver to cut the heat.

variations.name: Kerala Spicy Aloo Paratha
variations.description: Inspired by the masala inside a Malabar erissery-spiced dosa roll, this version folds fresh grated coconut, black pepper and green chillies into the potato filling. Cooking in cold-pressed coconut oil scents the whole paratha with the unmistakable aroma of a Kerala tharavad kitchen at breakfast time.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The soft wholegrain crumb of khapli mimics the tenderness of a Malabar paratha without any maida

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil perfumes the crust with true Malabar aroma as it toasts

steps: Simmer 4 medium potatoes in salted boiling water for 15 minutes until soft to the core, then drain thoroughly, peel and mash them roughly, leaving a few small nubs for texture.
Knead a dough from 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp melted Anveshan Coconut Oil and about 3/4 cup water, working it for 8 minutes until velvety; cover and set aside for 15 minutes.

Crush 1 tsp black peppercorns coarsely, then heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil over medium flame and fry 4 sliced shallots until their edges brown, about 2 minutes, adding 10 curry leaves, 3 chopped green chillies and 1 inch julienned ginger for the last 30 seconds.

Stir 1/2 cup fresh grated coconut and 1/2 tsp turmeric powder into the pan and toast gently for 2 minutes until the coconut smells nutty but stays white, then mix this into the mash with the crushed pepper and 1/2 tsp salt.
Divide the dough into 8 portions, hide 2 tbsp of the coconut-potato masala inside each, seal the seams and roll out to 6- or 7-inch rounds on a lightly floured board.
Toast each paratha on a medium tava, drizzling 1 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil around the edges, until both faces are freckled deep gold and the coconut aroma rises, about 2 minutes per side.
tips: Toast the coconut only until aromatic; letting it brown makes the filling dry and takes the dish toward a chutney flavour instead.
Frozen grated coconut works if thawed and squeezed, but fresh coconut gives the filling its characteristic juicy sweetness.
Crushed pepper added off the heat stays bright and floral; frying it too long turns the whole filling bitter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best with a small bowl of coconut chutney spiked with roasted chana dal, or alongside sweet milky chaya poured from a height, Malabar tea-shop style.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Gobi Paratha
variations.description: A heat-lover's gobi paratha with a triple chilli charge: fresh green chillies, red chilli powder and cracked black pepper folded through squeezed cauliflower shreds. The bilona-ghee roast tempers the burn just enough to keep you reaching for the next wedge.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli's sweetness is the built-in fire extinguisher for this triple-chilli filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rich A2 ghee coats the palate and rounds off the sharp chilli edges

steps: Grate 1 medium cauliflower on the fine holes, mix the shreds with 1 tsp salt, wait 15 minutes, then wring them in a muslin cloth until they feel dry and fluffy.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and roughly 3/4 cup water for 8 minutes into a smooth, yielding dough; rest it for 15 minutes.
Crush 3/4 tsp black peppercorns coarsely and mince 4 green chillies fine; combining cracked and fresh heat gives the filling both immediate and lingering spice.

Toss the squeezed gobi with the pepper, chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder and 3 tbsp chopped coriander until vividly flecked throughout.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, pack 2 tbsp of the fiery filling into each, seal the tops and roll into 7-inch rounds with soft, patting strokes to keep the shreds inside.
Roast on a medium tava, about 2 minutes per side with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee brushed on each face, until crisp bronze spots appear and the chillies smell bright and toasty.
tips: Deseed half the green chillies to keep the flavour but lower the flame for mixed company.
A squeeze of lime over the hot paratha lifts all three chilli layers noticeably.
The filling holds overnight refrigerated, but stuff and roll only just before cooking so the heat stays fresh, not flat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Balance the burn with a big bowl of sweet boondi raita and a chilled glass of chaas; pickle is optional, courage is not.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Gobi Paratha
variations.description: Guntur chillies, the pride of Andhra's spice markets, are dry-roasted and pounded with garlic to lacquer the cauliflower in a rust-red coat. Fried curry leaves and a gingelly-oil crust give it the aroma of a Vijayawada mess hall at lunchtime.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: A calm wholegrain canvas for the loudest chilli in India

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil's toasted depth is the traditional partner to Guntur chilli heat

steps: Coarsely grate 1 medium cauliflower and set aside; it will be cooked dry in the kadai, so no salting is required.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and about 3/4 cup water into a supple dough over 8 minutes, then rest it, covered, for 15 minutes.

Toast 5 Guntur dried red chillies and 1 tsp coriander seeds in a dry pan on low until the chillies turn glossy and brittle, about 2 minutes, then pound them with 8 garlic cloves into a coarse, angry-red masala.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil over medium flame, crisp 15 curry leaves for 20 seconds, then add the gobi with 1/2 tsp turmeric powder and 1/2 tsp salt and stir-fry for 6 minutes until tender and moisture-free.
Add the pounded chilli-garlic masala and 1 tsp tamarind paste and fry for 90 seconds more so the garlic cooks through, then fold in 2 tbsp coriander and cool the filling completely.

Stuff 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp each of the Guntur gobi, roll gently to 7-inch rounds, and toast on a medium tava with 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil per side until deeply blistered and crisp, around 2 minutes per side.
tips: Open a window when dry-roasting Guntur chillies; the airborne heat is part of the authentic experience but hard on the eyes.
The garlic must lose its rawness in the pan or it will dominate the chilli; ninety seconds of frying is the sweet spot.
Refrigerated, the pounded chilli-garlic masala keeps a week and doubles as an instant podi with hot rice and ghee.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Andhra way with curd rice on standby, a wedge of lime, and thin slices of raw onion to douse the after-burn.

variations.name: Assamese Spicy Gobi Paratha
variations.description: A cautious quarter of bhut jolokia, the world-famous ghost pepper of Assam, is all this filling needs to hum with fruity, floral fire. Mustard oil and a shower of fresh coriander frame the heat the way an Assamese aloo pitika would.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Wholegrain emmer keeps this ghost-pepper special grounded and gut-friendly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Sharp kacha ghani mustard oil is Assam's chosen frame for bhut jolokia's floral heat

steps: Grate 1 medium cauliflower coarsely and keep it beside the stove; the moisture will cook off in the pan.
Knead the dough from 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and close to 3/4 cup water, giving it 8 solid minutes, and rest it for 15 minutes under a damp cloth.
With gloves on, mince 1/4 of a bhut jolokia as finely as you can; blot the board with paper afterwards and wash your hands twice.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to a shimmer over medium-high so its pungency softens, about 1 minute, then fry 1 chopped small onion and 1 inch grated ginger until pale gold, 2 to 3 minutes.

Add the gobi, minced bhut jolokia, 1/2 tsp turmeric powder and 1/2 tsp salt and stir-fry over medium heat for 6 minutes until the shreds are dry and tender, then finish off the heat with 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 4 tbsp coriander; cool fully.

Fill 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp of the smoky-hot gobi, roll into 7-inch rounds, and cook on a medium tava with 1 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil per side until handsome brown blisters cover both faces, about 2 minutes per side.
