ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The coarse emmer grind mimics the chakki atta used in Punjabi village kitchens

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Generous ghee-basting is what gives a true Punjabi paratha its shattering, crisp edges

steps: Chop 250 g washed spinach very finely with 1 inch ginger, sprinkle with 0.5 tsp of the salt and set aside 10 minutes, then squeeze out every drop of released water.

Toss the squeezed spinach through 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta along with 1 tsp anardana powder, 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi, 0.5 tsp garam masala, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt.

Work in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then knead with about 0.5 cup water, added gradually, into a soft dough; the spinach keeps releasing moisture, so stop as soon as it comes together. Rest for 15 minutes under a damp cloth.
Pinch off 8 balls, flatten each, dab with a few drops of ghee, fold into a square and roll out to a 6-inch square paratha for the classic layered dhaba look.
Cook on a hot tava over medium-high heat for 60 to 90 seconds per side, then spoon 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee around each side and fry, pressing with a spatula, until deep golden and blistered.
Top each hot paratha with a small pat of the 2 tbsp white butter just before it goes to the table so it melts into the layers.
tips: Salting and squeezing the chopped spinach first prevents the dough from going slack halfway through rolling.
No anardana on hand? Use 0.5 tsp amchur for the same tang, though anardana gives the truer Punjabi flavour.
Roll the folded square gently at the corners; pressing hard squashes out the ghee layers that make it flaky.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a tall glass of salted lassi and a spoon of gajar-shalgam pickle; in Punjab this paratha often stands in for both bread and sabzi.

variations.name: Bengali Palak Paratha
variations.description: Bengal treats spinach as palong shaak, and this porota carries that identity: the dough is bound and shallow-fried in pungent mustard oil, with kalonji crackling through every layer. The mustard sharpness against the sweet greens is unmistakably Kolkata. Slightly flaky, slightly chewy, it needs nothing more than a smear of kasundi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its gentle nuttiness stands up to mustard oil better than refined flour ever could

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed kachi ghani oil delivers the sinus-tingling pungency Bengali porotas are known for

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a small pan until it just smokes, switch off, and let it cool for 2 minutes to mellow its raw edge.
Blanch 200 g spinach for 90 seconds, refresh in cold water, squeeze hard and blend with 2 green chillies and 1 tsp ginger paste to a thick paste of about 3/4 cup.
Mix 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp kalonji, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp sugar and 1 tsp salt, then rub in the cooled smoked mustard oil until the flour feels like damp sand.
Knead in the spinach paste plus up to 0.25 cup water to form a smooth, medium-soft dough; rest it covered for 20 minutes so the kalonji perfumes the dough.
Divide into 8 balls, roll each into a thin 6-inch disc, brush lightly with mustard oil, pleat like a fan, coil into a spiral and roll again to build flaky layers.
Shallow-fry each porota on a medium tava with 1 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil per piece, about 2 minutes per side, until crisp, deep golden and puffed at the layers.
tips: Always smoke and cool mustard oil before kneading; skipping this leaves an aggressive raw bitterness in the dough.
The pinch of sugar is a Bengali signature that balances the mustard heat, so do not leave it out.
Scrunch each cooked porota gently between your palms while hot to separate the flaky layers.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with kasundi mustard, sliced cucumber and a simple aloor dom; a hot cup of sweet cha alongside completes the Kolkata breakfast picture.

variations.name: Kerala Palak Paratha
variations.description: A Malabar-inspired take where fresh grated coconut and curry leaves are kneaded into the spinach dough, and the layers are laminated with virgin coconut oil instead of ghee. The result is a softly flaky paratha with a tropical sweetness and crackle of black pepper. It tastes like the tea-shop porottas of the coast, gone green.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: A wholegrain answer to the maida used in tea-shop porottas, with far better flavour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil laminates the layers and scents the whole paratha like the Malabar coast

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan over medium heat, add 4 sliced shallots, 12 torn curry leaves and 1 chopped green chilli, and fry for 2 minutes until the shallots turn light gold.
Add 200 g chopped spinach and 0.5 cup grated coconut to the pan and cook for 3 to 4 minutes until the spinach wilts and the mixture is completely dry; cool it fully.
Blend the cooled mixture to a coarse paste, then knead it into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, 1 tsp crushed black pepper and up to 0.25 cup water until you have a soft, stretchy dough.
Rest the dough for 20 minutes, then divide into 8 balls and roll each as thin as you can, about 8 inches wide, brushing the surface with a little coconut oil.
Pleat each thin sheet into a ribbon, coil it into a snail shape, rest 5 minutes, and roll gently back into a 6-inch round to keep the layers intact.
Cook on a medium tava for about 2 minutes per side, drizzling 1 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil around each paratha, until golden with flaky, slightly crisped edges.
tips: Cooking the spinach-coconut mixture until bone dry is critical; any moisture will glue the laminated layers together.
Use fresh coconut, not desiccated; the natural oil in fresh gratings keeps the crumb tender.
Clap each cooked paratha lightly between both hands, tea-shop style, to fluff the layers apart before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coconut-milk vegetable stew or a fried-egg roast; a few banana slices on the plate is a very Kerala touch.

variations.name: Kumaoni Palak Paratha
variations.description: From the Uttarakhand hills, where cooks temper greens with jakhya, a wild mountain seed that crackles like tiny popcorn in hot ghee. That smoky tempering is folded through the spinach dough along with warming ginger and hill chillies. It is a rustic, cold-weather paratha with a texture and aroma no plains version can copy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Close cousin to the hardy hill wheats ground at Kumaoni gharats (watermills)

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Jakhya must crackle in properly hot ghee to release its wild, nutty smokiness

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai until it shimmers, add 1 tsp jakhya seeds and 2 broken dried red chillies, and let them crackle and pop for about 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 250 g roughly chopped spinach and 1 inch grated ginger to the tempering and stir-fry over high heat for 3 minutes until the leaves wilt and all moisture evaporates.
Stir in 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, cook for 1 more minute, then spread the mixture on a plate to cool completely.
Knead the cooled spinach tempering into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with up to 0.33 cup water, working it for 5 minutes into a firm yet pliable dough; rest 15 minutes.
Shape into 8 balls and roll each into a slightly thick 5-inch round; hill parathas are kept small and sturdy rather than paper thin.
Roast on a medium-hot tava for 90 seconds per side, then smear 0.5 tsp Anveshan Ghee on each side and cook until both faces carry deep brown, smoky spots.
tips: Do not walk away while jakhya crackles; it burns within seconds and turns bitter once it darkens.
If jakhya is unavailable, cumin seeds bloomed the same way work, though the paratha loses its distinct hill character.
These sturdier parathas travel well; wrap in foil for a trek-day lunch and they stay good for hours.
variations.servingSuggestion: Eat the pahadi way with bhang ki chutney or plain curd sprinkled with roasted cumin, and hot rhododendron or lemon tea on the side.

variations.name: Classic Dhaba-style Bhindi
variations.description: The bhindi masala of highway dhabas: okra seared until blistered, then folded through a rustic onion-tomato masala that clings to every piece. A final flourish of crushed kasuri methi and garam masala gives it that unmistakable smoky-tandoor aroma without a tandoor.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil takes the high heat needed to blister okra without any slime, adding a nutty dhaba-style depth

steps: Wash 500 g okra, then pat every piece completely dry with a kitchen towel; trim the crowns and cut into 1-inch pieces. Dry okra is the single biggest defence against slime.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a wide kadhai on medium-high and sear the okra undisturbed for 6-7 minutes, tossing only twice, until the edges blister and turn light brown. Lift the okra out onto a plate.
Add the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil to the same kadhai, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add 2 finely sliced onions and fry on medium heat for 6-7 minutes until deep golden.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute until the raw smell disappears, then add 2 finely chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder.
Cook the masala on medium heat for 4-5 minutes, mashing with the back of the ladle, until the tomatoes break down and oil beads appear at the edges.
Return the seared okra with 1 tsp salt, toss gently to coat, and cook uncovered on medium heat for 5-6 minutes so the okra stays firm and the masala turns jammy, not wet.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi between your palms over the pan, sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala, toss once and rest off the heat for 2 minutes before garnishing with 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Never cover the pan once the okra goes in; trapped steam is what makes bhindi gooey.
If the okra still feels sticky mid-cook, stir in 1 tsp of lemon juice; the acid cuts the mucilage instantly.
Sear the okra a few hours ahead and refrigerate; folding it into hot masala just before dinner keeps it perfectly crisp.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve straight from the kadhai with hot tandoori roti, a wedge of raw onion and a glass of salted chaas, dhaba style.

variations.name: Punjabi Dhaba-style Bhindi
variations.description: The Grand Trunk Road version, where the okra masala gets a lavish finish of white butter and a sharp lift of amchur. Extra onions cooked to a sweet melt make the base richer and darker than the everyday sabzi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee gives the okra the caramel-nutty richness that Punjabi dhabas get from their bhattis

steps: Rinse and thoroughly towel-dry 500 g okra, then slice into thick 1.5-inch batons so they hold their bite under the rich masala.
Melt 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai over medium-high heat and fry the okra for 7-8 minutes until it loses its raw green look and picks up brown patches; set it aside on a plate.

Add the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, splutter 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 30 seconds, then tip in 3 sliced onions and 2 slit green chillies; fry on medium for 9-10 minutes until the onions are a deep caramel brown.

Mix in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and sauté for 1 minute, then add 2 chopped tomatoes, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder and bhuno for 5 minutes until the ghee separates around the masala.
Fold the fried okra back in with 1 tsp salt and cook uncovered on medium-low for 6-7 minutes, tossing every couple of minutes, until each piece is glossily coated.
Sprinkle 1 tsp amchur and 0.5 tsp garam masala, toss for a final minute, then take the pan off the heat and crown the sabzi with 2 tbsp white butter so it melts into the hot okra.
tips: Caramelising the onions properly is non-negotiable here; rushing them leaves the masala pale and sweet-less.
Swap amchur with 2 tsp lemon juice added off the heat if you want a fresher, sharper tang.
Leftovers make a brilliant stuffing for grilled bhindi-cheese toast the next morning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with hot butter-brushed lachha paratha, a bowl of dahi sprinkled with roasted cumin, and sliced onions soaked in vinegar.

variations.name: Bengali Dhaba-style Bhindi
variations.description: A pungent, minimalist take built on raw-smelling mustard oil and crackled kalonji, with a mustard-seed paste that clings to the dherosh like a sharp golden glaze. No onion-heavy masala here; the heat comes from slit green chillies and the finish is a whisper of sweetness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed kachi ghani mustard oil delivers the nose-tingling pungency that defines Bengali dherosh bhaja

steps: Soak 2 tbsp yellow mustard seeds in 3 tbsp warm water for 15 minutes, then grind with 2 green chillies and 0.25 tsp salt into a smooth, sharp paste.
Wash 500 g okra, dry each pod fully, trim the tops and keep the pods whole with just a shallow slit down one side so the paste can seep in.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai until it just begins to smoke, about 2 minutes on high, then lower the heat so its raw pungency mellows without burning.
Crackle 0.5 tsp kalonji for 20 seconds, add the whole okra with 0.5 tsp turmeric and fry on medium heat for 8-9 minutes until the pods blister and brighten.
Whisk the mustard paste into 0.5 cup water, pour it over the okra with 0.75 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp sugar, and simmer uncovered on low for 5-6 minutes until the sauce thickens to a coating glaze.
Lay 2 slit green chillies on top, cook 1 more minute until their aroma lifts, then scatter 1 tbsp coriander and serve while the mustard bite is still lively.
tips: Never boil the mustard paste hard or it turns bitter; keep the simmer lazy and low.
Add a strained 0.5 tsp of the mustard soaking water to the paste while grinding for extra sharpness without bitterness.
For a shorshe-posto twist, replace half the mustard seeds with soaked poppy seeds for a creamier, gentler sauce.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over steaming gobindobhog rice with a slice of gondhoraj lime and crisp fried papad on the side.

variations.name: Kerala Dhaba-style Bhindi
variations.description: Vendakka mezhukkupuratti energy: okra stir-fried in coconut oil with shallots, curry leaves and cracked black pepper, then tossed with fresh grated coconut. It is glossy, gently spiced and full of toasty coconut sweetness rather than tomato tang.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed coconut oil perfumes the okra the way a Kerala cheena chatti would, without any refined-oil flatness

steps: Dry 500 g okra completely, then cut into thin 0.5-inch rounds; thin rounds crisp faster in coconut oil and shrug off stickiness.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a wide pan on medium, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds for about 30 seconds, then add 2 torn dried red chillies and 1 sprig of curry leaves until they crackle and glisten.
Add 10 sliced shallots and 4 chopped garlic cloves and sauté for 3-4 minutes until the shallots turn translucent with golden edges.
Tip in the okra rounds with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt and stir-fry on medium heat for 10-12 minutes, tossing every 2 minutes, until the rounds are browned and no longer stringy.
Sprinkle 1 tsp freshly crushed black pepper and 0.5 cup grated coconut and toss on low heat for 2-3 minutes so the coconut toasts lightly and coats the okra.
Finish with the second sprig of curry leaves and 0.25 tsp salt if needed, tossing once off the heat so the leaves stay fragrant and crisp.
tips: Use a wide, shallow pan; crowding okra rounds in a small kadhai steams them soggy.
Frozen grated coconut works if squeezed dry first, but toast it 1 minute longer.
For a richer temple-style version, add 1 tbsp of coconut slivers along with the shallots and let them brown.
variations.servingSuggestion: Spoon beside Kerala matta rice, a ladle of moru curry and a roasted pappadam for a proper naadan lunch line-up.

variations.name: Andhra Dhaba-style Bhindi
variations.description: Bendakaya vepudu with serious firepower: okra fried crisp, then tossed in a fiery Guntur chilli-garlic masala and brightened with a spoon of tamarind pulp. Roasted peanut crumble at the end gives every bite crunch against the heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil is the traditional Andhra frying medium; its deep nuttiness stands up to Guntur chilli heat

steps: Pat 500 g okra bone-dry and cut into 1-inch pieces; soak 1 tbsp tamarind in 2 tbsp hot water for 10 minutes and squeeze out a thick pulp.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a heavy kadhai on medium-high and fry the okra in two batches for 6-7 minutes per batch until crisp-edged and olive-brown; drain onto a plate.
Add the last 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds for 30 seconds, then brown 1 tbsp chana dal for about a minute until it smells biscuity.
Toss in 1 sprig curry leaves, 6 crushed garlic cloves and 1 large sliced onion and fry on medium for 5-6 minutes until the onion edges char lightly.
Lower the heat, stir in 1.5 tsp Guntur chilli powder and 0.5 tsp turmeric for just 20 seconds, then immediately add 1 tbsp tamarind pulp and 1 tsp salt so the chilli blooms without scorching.
Return the fried okra, toss on medium heat for 4-5 minutes until every piece wears the brick-red masala, then finish with 3 tbsp crushed roasted peanuts and the second sprig of curry leaves.
tips: Guntur chilli burns fast; always add the tamarind within seconds of the chilli powder hitting the oil.
Scale the chilli down to 1 tsp and add 0.5 tsp coriander powder if you want flavour-forward rather than fire-forward.
The peanut crumble goes in only at the end; cooked longer it loses its crunch and turns chewy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot steamed rice and a bowl of cooling curd on the side to tame the Guntur heat; a crisp appadam completes the plate.

variations.name: Classic Dry Capsicum
variations.description: A quick, no-gravy stir-fry where capsicum strips are seared over brisk heat with cumin, onion and a tangy hit of amchur. It stays deliberately dry and glossy, making it the ideal tiffin-box sabzi that never turns roti soggy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: Light wood-pressed sunflower oil lets the capsicum's own sweetness lead while giving a clean, non-greasy sear

steps: Deseed 4 medium capsicums and slice them into thin strips about 1 cm wide; slice 2 medium onions into similar strips so everything cooks at the same pace.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sunflower Oil in a wide kadhai on medium-high heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 30 seconds until they turn a shade darker and smell toasty.
Add the sliced onions and stir-fry on medium-high for 4 to 5 minutes until they soften and pick up light golden edges, then stir in 2 tsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 1 more minute.
Add the capsicum strips and toss on high heat for 2 minutes so they blister slightly at the edges instead of stewing in their juices.

Lower to medium, sprinkle 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and stir-fry uncovered for 6 to 7 minutes until the strips are tender-crisp and completely dry.
Dust 1 tsp amchur over the sabzi, toss for 30 seconds, then finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander leaves and switch off while the peppers still hold their bite.
tips: Cook uncovered throughout; covering traps steam and turns this from a dry stir-fry into a limp, watery sabzi.
A wide pan matters more than you think here, as crowded capsicum steams instead of searing.
Add amchur only at the end; cooking it long makes the tang bitter instead of bright.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pack it with soft chapatis and lemon pickle for the classic office tiffin, or spoon it over dal-chawal for a weeknight plate that needs no extra effort.

variations.name: Tamil Dry Capsicum
variations.description: Kudamilagai poriyal from Tamil homes, where diced capsicum is tempered with mustard, urad dal and curry leaves in gingelly oil, then dusted with sambar powder. A final shower of fresh coconut keeps it light, aromatic and unmistakably southern.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil is the traditional poriyal medium in Tamil Nadu, adding a deep toasted fragrance to the tempering

steps: Dice 4 medium capsicums into neat 1.5 cm pieces, discarding the seeds and white ribs, and keep 1/3 cup grated coconut ready for the finish.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadhai on medium heat, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds for about 30 seconds, then add 2 tsp urad dal and 1 tsp chana dal and fry until the dals turn biscuit-gold, about 1 minute.
Tear in 2 dried red chillies, add 15 curry leaves and 1/4 tsp hing, and let everything sputter for 15 seconds until the leaves crisp and shine.

Add the diced capsicum with 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, toss well, and cook uncovered on medium heat for 6 to 7 minutes, stirring every couple of minutes, until the pieces soften but stay squeaky-crisp at the centre.
Sprinkle 2 tsp sambar powder over the capsicum and stir-fry for 2 minutes so the spice coats each piece and loses its raw edge, adding 1 tbsp water only if the powder looks dusty.
Switch off the flame, fold in 1/3 cup grated coconut and toss for 30 seconds in the residual heat so the coconut warms through without browning.
tips: Fry the urad dal patiently to an even gold; underdone dal tastes raw while dark dal turns the whole poriyal bitter.
Any good homestyle sambar powder works, but one with fenugreek in it gives this poriyal its authentic backbone.
Add the coconut strictly off the heat so it stays white and juicy rather than dry and toasted.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as the dry accompaniment on a South Indian lunch plate beside sambar rice and rasam, or with curd rice and a fried appalam on hot days.

variations.name: Rajasthani Dry Capsicum
variations.description: Besan wali shimla mirch from Rajasthani kitchens, where capsicum strips are tumbled with roasted gram flour, whole dried red chillies and crushed fennel-coriander. Slow-roasted in ghee until the besan forms a savoury, nutty crust on every strip, it is a marwari lunch staple.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee roasts the besan coating to a rich, biscuity crust the way Rajasthani households traditionally make this sabzi

steps: Slice 4 medium capsicums into finger-thick strips. Coarsely crush 1.5 tsp fennel seeds and 2 tsp coriander seeds in a mortar so they stay gritty rather than powdery.

Dry-roast 1/2 cup besan in a heavy kadhai on low heat for 5 to 6 minutes, stirring constantly, until it darkens to a sandy gold and smells nutty; tip it out onto a plate immediately so it does not keep browning.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in the same kadhai on medium, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add 3 whole dried red chillies and 1/4 tsp hing and fry for 15 seconds until the chillies puff and deepen in colour.

Add the crushed fennel-coriander and immediately follow with the capsicum strips, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt. Stir-fry on medium heat for 6 to 7 minutes until the strips soften and their edges wrinkle.
Lower the flame, scatter the roasted besan evenly over the capsicum and toss gently for 4 to 5 minutes; the besan will absorb the ghee and juices and cling to the strips in a crumbly golden coating.
Sprinkle 1.5 tsp amchur, toss for a final minute until the coating smells toasty and tangy, and serve straight from the kadhai while the crust is still crisp.
tips: Roast the besan on low and keep it moving; even ten extra seconds can tip it from nutty to burnt.
If the besan clumps when added, drizzle 1 tsp more ghee around the edges of the pan instead of water, which would make it pasty.
This sabzi is best eaten fresh, as the besan crust softens on standing; re-crisp leftovers in a dry pan on low heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Marwari way with hot phulkas, a katori of dahi and a papad, or alongside dal-baati as the dry vegetable on the thali.

variations.name: Malwa Dry Capsicum
variations.description: From the Malwa plateau of Madhya Pradesh comes this rustic sookhi sabzi where capsicum is stir-fried with a coarse crush of roasted peanuts and sesame in groundnut oil. The peanut crumble toasts in the pan, giving every bite a sweet, earthy crunch with a green-chilli kick and a squeeze of lemon.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil doubles down on the roasted peanut crush, giving this Malwa sabzi a layered nuttiness

steps: Cut 4 medium capsicums into 2 cm chunks, finely chop 4 garlic cloves and 3 green chillies, and pulse 2/3 cup roasted peanuts into a coarse, pebbly crush.
Toast 1 tbsp sesame seeds in a dry kadhai on low heat for about 2 minutes, shaking the pan, until they turn pale gold and start to pop; tip them out and set aside.

In the same kadhai, heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add the chopped garlic and green chillies and fry for 1 minute until the garlic edges colour.

Add the capsicum chunks with 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and stir-fry uncovered on medium-high for 7 to 8 minutes until the chunks blister and soften but do not collapse.
Lower the heat, add the peanut crush and toasted sesame, and toss for 3 minutes; the crumble will toast against the hot pan and coat the capsicum in a golden, gravelly layer.
Switch off, squeeze the juice of 1/2 lemon over the sabzi, shower with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and give one final toss before serving.
tips: Keep the peanut crush coarse; a fine powder soaks up all the oil and turns the coating stodgy.
The lemon must go in off the heat, otherwise its brightness cooks away and leaves only sourness.
Swap half the capsicum with diced raw banana or potato for the heartier version Malwa farm kitchens make in winter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Eat it with hot bajra or wheat rotis smeared with a little ghee, and a raw onion wedge on the side for the true Malwa dhani experience.

variations.name: Odia Dry Capsicum
variations.description: An Odisha-style bhaja where capsicum and potato are shallow-fried in pungent mustard oil with the five-spice crackle of panch phoron. Garlic smashed into the tempering and a slow, patient fry give this dish its deeply savoury, home-kitchen character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Kachi ghani mustard oil is the soul of an Odia bhaja, its sharp aroma standing up to the earthy panch phoron

steps: Cut 3 medium capsicums into thick strips and 2 medium potatoes into thin half-moon slices; slice 1 onion and lightly smash 6 garlic cloves under the flat of a knife.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai on high heat until faint wisps of smoke appear, about 1 minute, then reduce to medium so the oil mellows.
Add 1.5 tsp panch phoron and 2 torn dried red chillies and let the five seeds crackle and pop for about 30 seconds, releasing their distinct fenugreek-fennel aroma.
Add the smashed garlic and sliced onion and fry on medium for 3 minutes until the garlic turns golden at the edges and smells sweet rather than sharp.

Slide in the potato slices with 1/2 tsp turmeric and half the salt, and fry uncovered on medium heat for 8 to 9 minutes, turning every few minutes, until the slices are three-quarters cooked with browned patches.

Add the capsicum strips, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining salt, and continue frying uncovered for 7 to 8 minutes until the capsicum wilts, the potato is fully tender and everything carries crisp, dark-gold edges.
tips: Slice the potatoes noticeably thinner than the capsicum so both reach doneness together in the open pan.
Fry patiently without a lid; bhaja means fried, and the crisp edges are the whole point of the dish.
The fenugreek seeds in panch phoron turn bitter if the tempering burns, so keep the flame at medium once they hit the oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside steamed rice and dalma for a proper Odia lunch, or with pakhala bhata and a roasted papad in the summer months.

variations.name: Classic Dry Lauki
variations.description: The everyday North Indian sookhi lauki: tender bottle gourd cubes clinging to a rustic onion-tomato masala, cooked without a drop of extra water so the gourd's own juices concentrate into flavour. It is light on the stomach yet deeply savoury, the kind of sabzi that disappears fastest from a weekday thali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed sunflower oil keeps this delicate gourd sabzi light and lets the cumin aroma stay clean

steps: Peel 600 g bottle gourd, halve it lengthwise, scoop out any mature seeds and cut it into 2 cm cubes. Finely chop 1 large onion and 2 medium tomatoes and keep everything within reach of the stove.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sunflower Oil in a heavy kadhai on medium heat until it shimmers, then add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them sizzle and darken a shade, about 30 seconds.
Add the chopped onion and saute on medium heat for 5-6 minutes until the edges turn golden brown, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute more until the raw smell disappears.

Tip in the chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt. Cook on medium for 4-5 minutes, mashing occasionally, until the masala turns glossy and oil beads appear at the edges.

Add the lauki cubes and toss for 2 minutes so every piece is coated in masala. Cover the kadhai, drop the heat to low and cook for 12-14 minutes, stirring twice, until the gourd is translucent and a knife slides through easily.
Uncover, raise the heat to medium-high and stir for 2 minutes to dry off any released moisture. Sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala and 2 tbsp chopped coriander leaves, toss once and switch off.
tips: Taste a raw sliver of lauki before cooking; if it is even slightly bitter, discard the whole gourd as bitterness intensifies on cooking.
Do not add water at any stage - lauki releases plenty of its own, and the covered low flame is enough to cook it through.
If the sabzi turns watery, finish it uncovered on high heat for 3-4 minutes instead of extending the covered time, which would turn the cubes mushy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with phulkas, a bowl of plain toor dal and a wedge of lime; a side of roasted papad adds the crunch this soft sabzi loves.

variations.name: Bengali Dry Lauki (Lau Bhaja Style)
variations.description: In Bengali homes lau is treated gently - no onion or garlic, just pungent mustard oil, crackling kalonji and slit green chillies, with a whisper of jaggery to round off the heat. The result is a pale golden, faintly sweet sabzi where the gourd itself is the star.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Kachi ghani pungency is the backbone of this niramish Bengali preparation - heat it till it smokes lightly to mellow the sharpness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A Bengali touch - a spoon of unrefined jaggery balances the mustard oil's bite without making the dish sweet

steps: Peel 600 g bottle gourd and cut it into thin batons about 4 cm long and 1 cm thick - Bengalis cut lau finer than the North Indian dice so it cooks quickly and stays silky.
Pour 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil into a kadhai and heat on medium-high until the surface ripples and a faint smoke rises, about 2 minutes; this step tames the raw pungency.
Lower the heat to medium, drop in 1 large bay leaf, 1 tsp kalonji and 3 slit green chillies, and let them crackle for 20-30 seconds until the kalonji smells nutty.
Stir in 2 tsp ginger paste and fry for 45 seconds, then add the lauki batons, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt and toss until every strip glistens yellow.
Cover and cook on low for 12-15 minutes, stirring gently every 4-5 minutes, until the batons turn translucent and tender but still hold their shape.
Uncover, sprinkle 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder over the lau and stir on medium heat for 2-3 minutes until any liquid evaporates and the pieces look glossy. Finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Never substitute the mustard oil here - it defines the dish; refined oil would leave it tasting flat and hospital-bland.
Keep the chillies slit but whole so they perfume the sabzi without making it fiery; diners can bite in if they want heat.
This tastes even better after resting 15 minutes off the heat, as the jaggery and mustard notes settle into the gourd.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with steamed rice and a simple masoor dal, Bengali-style; a spoon of this lau alongside crisp begun bhaja makes a quietly perfect vegetarian lunch.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Dry Lauki (Dudhi Bhaji)
variations.description: Dudhi chi bhaji from Maharashtra leans on goda masala - the state's smoky, stone-flower-scented blend - plus crushed roasted peanuts that soak up the gourd's juices. It is earthy, mildly sweet-spiced and completely different from the tomato-based northern version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil echoes the peanut garnish, doubling the nutty depth Maharashtrian bhajis are loved for

steps: Cut 600 g peeled bottle gourd into small 1.5 cm dice - smaller than usual, the Maharashtrian way, so the pieces cook fast and carry more masala per bite.
Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a kadhai over medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and wait until they pop vigorously, roughly 30 seconds.
Add 0.25 tsp asafoetida, 10 curry leaves and 2 chopped green chillies; they will splutter loudly, so stand back for the 15 seconds they need to crisp up.
Immediately add the diced dudhi with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, stir well, then cover and cook on low heat for 12 minutes, stirring once midway, until the dice are just tender.
Sprinkle 2 tsp goda masala over the gourd and fold it through gently; let it toast against the hot pan for 2 minutes so its smoky notes bloom without burning.

Stir in 3 tbsp roasted peanut powder and 2 tbsp grated dry coconut, cook uncovered for 2-3 minutes until the powder absorbs the pan juices and the bhaji looks dry and crumbly. Garnish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Goda masala scorches quickly - always add it after the vegetable is cooked, never into the initial tempering.
Grind the peanuts coarse, not to a paste; you want gritty pockets of nuttiness, not peanut butter coating the gourd.
No goda masala on hand? Use 1.5 tsp garam masala plus 0.5 tsp of the peanut powder toasted dark, though the flavour will be simpler.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft chapatis or jowar bhakri and a katori of varan-bhaat; a squeeze of lime just before eating brightens the goda masala beautifully.

variations.name: Kerala Dry Lauki Thoran
variations.description: A thoran treatment for bottle gourd: the cubes steam under a blanket of fresh coconut pounded with cumin, shallots and green chilli, all brought together in coconut oil with popping mustard and curry leaves. Every forkful tastes of the Malabar coast - clean, fragrant and barely spiced.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Unrefined coconut oil ties the tempering to the coconut crumble - the one fat a thoran cannot do without

steps: Dice 600 g peeled bottle gourd into small 1 cm cubes. In a mixer, pulse 0.5 cup grated fresh coconut with 2 green chillies, 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, 4 of the shallots and 0.25 tsp turmeric into a coarse, crumbly mixture - do not add water or grind it smooth.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a wide pan on medium; when a mustard seed dropped in dances, add the full 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them finish popping, about 30 seconds.
Add 2 dried red chillies torn in half, 12 curry leaves and the remaining 4 shallots, thinly sliced, and fry for 2 minutes until the shallots soften and turn light gold at the edges.
Add the lauki cubes and 1 tsp salt, toss for a minute, then cover and cook on low heat for 8-10 minutes until the cubes are just tender - they should still have a slight bite.
Scatter the coconut crumble over the gourd, fold it in gently, then cover again and steam on the lowest flame for 4-5 minutes so the coconut perfumes every cube without browning.
Open the lid, stir once and cook uncovered for 1-2 minutes only if there is visible moisture; the finished thoran should be fluffy and dry, never oily or wet.
tips: Fresh coconut is non-negotiable for texture; if using frozen, thaw it fully and squeeze out excess water before grinding.
Crush the coconut mixture coarse - a smooth paste turns the thoran heavy and pasty instead of light and fluffy.
A half teaspoon of coconut oil drizzled raw over the finished thoran, off the heat, is the classic Kerala finishing flourish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Spoon beside steamed Kerala matta rice with a ladle of moru curry or sambar; it also makes a lovely filling for leftover dosa the next morning.

variations.name: Rajasthani Dry Lauki with Ghee and Whole Red Chillies
variations.description: Desert kitchens cook lauki the assertive way: bloomed whole dried red chillies, fennel and asafoetida in ghee, with a final flourish of amchur for the tang that Rajasthani food gets without tomatoes. It is bold, tangy-hot and gloriously aromatic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan A2 Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee is the traditional Marwari cooking fat - its caramel notes stand up to the fierce chilli-fennel tempering

steps: Peel and cut 600 g bottle gourd into thick half-moons about 1.5 cm wide - the sturdier cut suits this masala-forward, onionless preparation.

Melt 2 tbsp Anveshan A2 Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat until fully liquid and fragrant, then crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1 tsp fennel seeds together for about 30 seconds until the fennel smells sweet.
Break 3 dried red chillies into halves, add them with 0.25 tsp asafoetida, and fry for 20 seconds until the chillies deepen to a brick red - do not let them blacken or they turn bitter.

Working quickly, add the lauki half-moons along with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, and toss for 2 minutes so the spices coat the gourd in the hot ghee.
Cover and cook on low for 14-16 minutes, stirring every 5 minutes; the gourd will sweat, soften and absorb the chilli-fennel masala until a spoon edge cuts through a piece with no resistance.
Turn the heat up for a final 2 minutes, dust 1 tsp amchur over the sabzi and toss until dry and tangy. Shower with 2 tbsp chopped coriander before serving.
tips: Fennel plus amchur is the signature Rajasthani pairing - do not skip either, as together they replace the sweetness and tang tomatoes would give.
Bloom the whole chillies just to brick-red; even 10 extra seconds turns them acrid and the whole sabzi tastes scorched.
For a richer dhaba-style touch, spoon an extra half teaspoon of warm ghee over the sabzi right before it goes to the table.
variations.servingSuggestion: This begs for hot bajra or wheat rotis smeared with ghee, a bowl of panchmel dal and a side of green chilli pickle - a proper Marwari thali corner.

variations.name: Classic Garlic Matar Paratha
variations.description: Sweet mashed peas meet a whole head's worth of golden-fried garlic in this deeply savoury stuffed flatbread. The garlic is browned slowly in ghee until mellow and toasty, so the filling tastes rich rather than sharp, and the khapli atta crust bakes up with crisp, buttery edges.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Stone-milled emmer flour gives the crust a wheaty depth that plain atta cannot match

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Garlic fried in slow-churned bilona ghee turns sweet and nutty instead of acrid

steps: Mix 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 3/4 tsp salt and 1 tbsp softened Anveshan Ghee, then knead in roughly 3/4 cup water until the dough is soft, smooth and leaves the bowl clean; rest it covered for 20 minutes.
Boil 1.5 cups green peas for 4 minutes until tender, drain fully in a colander and mash them coarsely while still warm.

Melt 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium-low heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add 12 finely chopped garlic cloves and fry slowly for 2 to 3 minutes until they turn an even light gold and smell toasty, not burnt.

Raise the heat to medium, add 2 minced green chillies, the mashed peas, 3/4 tsp red chilli powder, 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1/2 tsp garam masala and 3/4 tsp salt, and cook for 4 minutes until the filling is dry and clumps together. Stir in 3 tbsp chopped coriander and cool.
Shape the dough into 8 balls and divide the filling into 8 heaps of about 2 tbsp; flatten each ball into a cup, load the filling in, gather the edges to the top and pinch them closed.
Roll each stuffed ball into a 6-inch round on a lightly floured board, working from the centre outward so the garlic-pea layer spreads evenly to the edge.
Roast on a medium-hot tava for close to 2 minutes per side, brushing with the remaining Anveshan Ghee, until golden-brown freckles cover both faces and the kitchen smells of toasted garlic.
tips: Keep the flame low while frying the garlic; even ten extra seconds past golden turns it bitter and dominates the filling.
Squeeze the boiled peas in a clean cloth if they seem wet; a dry mash is the difference between an easy roll and a torn paratha.
Make a double batch of the filling and refrigerate half; it doubles as a terrific sandwich spread the next morning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best with a bowl of plain curd swirled with a pinch of black salt, sliced onions and a hot cup of adrak chai; leftover parathas roll beautifully around scrambled eggs.

variations.name: Tamil Garlic Matar Paratha
variations.description: Modelled on Tamil Nadu's poondu (garlic) preparations, this take fries the garlic in wood-pressed sesame oil with curry leaves and freshly crushed black pepper. The gingelly oil's toasty depth and the pepper's warmth give the pea filling a distinctly southern character, closer to a milagu poondu masala than a northern stuffing.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat rolls thin and crisp, ideal for soaking up fragrant gingelly oil

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed gingelly oil is the soul of Tamil tempering and deepens the garlic's flavour

steps: Work 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 3/4 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil together, adding about 3/4 cup water bit by bit, until you get a soft dough that dimples easily; rest it for 20 minutes under a damp cloth.
Simmer 1.5 cups green peas in salted water for 4 minutes until they yield to a spoon, drain them dry and mash roughly.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadhai on medium; splutter 1/2 tsp mustard seeds, brown 1 tsp urad dal for 40 seconds, then tear in 2 dried red chillies and 15 curry leaves and let them crackle for 20 seconds.

Add 12 sliced garlic cloves and fry for 2 minutes until pale gold, then tip in the mashed peas with 1.5 tsp crushed black pepper, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 3/4 tsp salt and cook for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring, until the mixture is dry, peppery and fragrant. Cool it fully.
Divide the dough into 8 balls and the filling into 8 portions of 2 tbsp; stuff, seal with a firm pleat-and-twist, and gently press each ball flat.

Roll into 6-inch rounds with easy strokes, dusting minimally, then cook on a medium-hot tava for about 2 minutes a side, drizzling the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil around the rim until both sides carry deep brown speckles.
Rest the parathas for 2 minutes under a cloth so the pepper aroma settles into the crumb before you serve them.
tips: Crush the peppercorns coarsely in a mortar just before cooking; pre-ground pepper loses the bright bite this filling depends on.
Let the urad dal turn properly golden in the oil, as its nutty crunch is a hallmark of Tamil-style seasoning.
If gingelly flavour feels strong to newcomers, cook with half sesame oil and finish with a light hand instead of the full drizzle.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and a small tumbler of sambar for dunking, or the Tamil traveller's way, with a spoon of curd rice and a piece of sun-dried vathal on the side.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Garlic Matar Paratha
variations.description: Goda masala, Maharashtra's smoky-sweet blend of dagad phool, coconut and sesame, transforms the garlic-pea filling into something earthy and faintly caramel-edged. A scatter of toasted sesame seeds pressed into the crust before roasting adds the region's signature crunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli's rustic sweetness sits naturally beside goda masala's warm coconut notes

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the workhorse fat of Maharashtrian home kitchens

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing smear of ghee rounds off the goda masala's smokiness

steps: Knead a soft dough from 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 3/4 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and around 3/4 cup water; it should feel like an earlobe when pressed. Rest for 20 minutes.
Boil 1.5 cups green peas for 4 minutes until soft, drain well and crush them into a coarse, dryish mash.
Toast 2 tbsp white sesame seeds in a dry pan over low heat for 2 minutes until they pop and smell nutty, then set them aside on a plate.

Warm 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in the same pan on medium, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then fry 10 crushed garlic cloves and 2 chopped green chillies for about 90 seconds until the garlic is blond and aromatic.

Stir in the crushed peas, 2 tsp goda masala, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 3/4 tsp salt, and cook for 4 minutes until the filling darkens slightly and holds together in a lump; fold in 3 tbsp chopped coriander and half the toasted sesame, then cool.
Portion the dough into 8 balls and the filling into 8 mounds of 2 tbsp; stuff and seal each ball, then dip one face into the reserved sesame seeds and press so they stick.
Roll each ball, sesame-side up, into a 6-inch round and roast on a medium-hot tava for about 2 minutes per side, brushing with the remaining 1/2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil until crisply spotted.
Slick each hot paratha with a little of the 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee just before serving so the spices bloom in its warmth.
tips: Goda masala scorches quickly because of its coconut content, so add it with the peas rather than into the hot oil alone.
No goda masala on hand? A stopgap of garam masala plus a pinch of toasted desiccated coconut and sesame gets you close.
Press the sesame layer on firmly before rolling; loose seeds jump off the tava and burn.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thecha, the fiery Maharashtrian green-chilli and garlic condiment, and a bowl of mattha, spiced thin buttermilk with coriander and ginger.

variations.name: Malwa Garlic Matar Paratha
variations.description: From the Malwa plateau of Madhya Pradesh comes this hearty rendition where coarsely crushed roasted peanuts join garlic in the pea filling. The peanuts lend a rich crunch and body reminiscent of the region's poha and sabudana khichdi toppings, making each bite nubbly, nutty and satisfying.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The hearty emmer crumb complements the peanut-studded filling of the Malwa plateau

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Cooking a peanut filling in wood-pressed groundnut oil doubles down on its toasty sweetness

steps: Prepare the dough by kneading 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 3/4 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and nearly 3/4 cup water for 5 minutes until supple; rest it, covered, while you cook the filling.
Pulse 1/2 cup roasted peanuts in a grinder to a coarse rubble; a few larger pieces are welcome, but stop well short of a powder.
Boil 1.5 cups green peas for 4 minutes until tender, drain completely and mash them with a fork, leaving a little texture.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium, sizzle 1 tsp cumin seeds for half a minute, then cook 10 minced garlic cloves and 3 chopped green chillies for 90 seconds until the rawness fades and the garlic turns straw-coloured.

Add the mashed peas, crushed peanuts, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 3/4 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp amchur and 3/4 tsp salt; stir-fry for 4 minutes until the filling is thick, dry and smells of toasted nuts. Spread on a plate to cool.
Divide the dough into 8 balls and the filling into 8 portions of about 2.5 tbsp, since the peanuts bulk it up; stuff each ball, twist the top shut and flatten lightly.

Roll out to 6-inch rounds, using gentle pressure so peanut bits do not pierce the dough, and roast on a medium-hot tava for roughly 2 minutes per side with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil until crusty and gold-flecked.
tips: Grind the peanuts coarse, not fine; a powder makes the filling pasty while a rubble keeps every bite crunchy.
The amchur is essential here as its tang cuts through the richness of the nuts, so do not skip it.
These freeze well: stack cooked parathas with parchment between them and re-crisp straight from the freezer on a hot tava for 90 seconds a side.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Malwa way with a bowl of sev-topped curd, a spoon of green coriander chutney and jaggery-sweetened lassi for a proper plateau breakfast.

variations.name: Goan Garlic Matar Paratha
variations.description: Goa's beloved kokum brings its wine-dark tang to a garlic-pea filling enriched with fresh grated coconut and cooked in cold-pressed coconut oil. The result is coastal and bright: sweet peas, sour kokum and toasty garlic in every mouthful, echoing the flavours of a Goan solkadhi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer's mild nuttiness lets the kokum's fruity sourness shine through the crust

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil ties the filling to Goa's coastline with its clean tropical aroma

steps: Soak 6 dried kokum petals in 3 tbsp warm water for 15 minutes until soft and deep pink, then chop them fine and reserve the crimson soaking liquor.
Meanwhile knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 3/4 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and about 3/4 cup water into a soft, elastic dough; rest it under a damp cloth for 20 minutes.
Cook 1.5 cups green peas in boiling water for 4 minutes until tender, drain thoroughly and mash them coarsely.

Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil over medium heat, pop 1/2 tsp mustard seeds, crackle 10 curry leaves, then fry 10 chopped garlic cloves and 3 slit green chillies for about 2 minutes until the garlic is golden at the edges.

Add the mashed peas, chopped kokum, 1 tbsp of the kokum liquor, 1/3 cup grated coconut, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 3/4 tsp salt; cook for 5 minutes, stirring often, until the mixture dries into a tangy, cohesive mass. Cool it completely.
Split the dough into 8 balls and the filling into 8 scoops of about 2 tbsp; enclose the filling inside each flattened ball, seal the seam with a pinch and rest for 5 minutes.

Roll each ball into a 6-inch round with a light hand and roast on a medium-hot tava for close to 2 minutes per side, brushing with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil until blistered bronze all over.
tips: Chop the softened kokum finely and distribute it well; a large piece in one bite is bracingly sour on its own.
Because coconut adds moisture, cook this filling a minute or two longer than usual until it truly stops steaming.
Swap kokum with 1 tsp tamarind pulp in a pinch, though you will trade kokum's floral, fruity sourness for a flatter tang.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a chilled glass of solkadhi and a simple salad of onion, cucumber and grated coconut dressed with lime, letting the coastal flavours carry the meal.

variations.name: Classic Garlic Methi Paratha
variations.description: Golden-fried garlic and fresh fenugreek are a made-for-each-other pairing: the garlic's sweetness rounds off methi's gentle bitterness in every layer of this khapli atta flatbread. A ghee tempering of cumin ties the two together for a paratha that perfumes the whole kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Long-fermenting emmer bran soaks up the garlic-ghee tempering and keeps the paratha aromatic even when cooled

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Garlic fried in slow-churned bilona ghee turns nutty-sweet rather than acrid

steps: Melt 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add 8 minced garlic cloves and fry 60 to 90 seconds, stirring, until the garlic is light gold and smells sweet rather than raw.
Tip 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta into a wide bowl, pour the warm garlic tempering over it and rub through with your fingertips until the flour is evenly speckled and faintly greasy.

Add 2 cups washed and firmly squeezed methi leaves, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, then knead with 3/4 cup water added in three additions for about 7 minutes to a soft, non-sticky dough; rest covered for 15 minutes.
Divide into 8 equal balls, flatten each in dry flour and roll to a 15 cm circle, rotating a quarter turn between strokes so it stays round and even.

Slide onto a tava heated on medium-high for 2 minutes; when bubbles rise after about a minute, flip, spread 0.5 tsp Anveshan Ghee, flip once more and press the surface until both sides carry golden-brown spots, around 2 minutes total.
Cook the remaining parathas the same way, wiping loose flour off the tava between each so the garlic flecks never scorch and turn bitter.
tips: Fry the garlic only to pale gold; a shade darker and its bitterness will fight the methi instead of flattering it.
For deeper flavour, rest the kneaded dough 30 minutes so the garlic oil migrates through the crumb.
A teaspoon of kasuri methi crushed into the dough intensifies the fenugreek aroma when fresh leaves are mild.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best with a bowl of plain dahi whisked with a pinch of black salt, or alongside a simple tomato-onion sabzi and lemon pickle for a complete weekday lunch.

variations.name: Tamil Garlic Methi Paratha
variations.description: A Tamil Nadu spin where garlic and vendhaya keerai meet a classic tempering of mustard seeds, urad dal and fistfuls of curry leaves in wood-pressed sesame oil. The result tastes like a cross between a paratha and a South Indian podi-smeared roti, toasty and deeply savoury.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat gives this South Indian style paratha a soft chew that plain wheat rotis rarely achieve

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Nallennai from a wood press is the backbone of Tamil tempering, adding its signature roasted fragrance to the crust

steps: Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a small kadai over medium heat, splutter 3/4 tsp mustard seeds for 30 seconds, then add 1 tsp urad dal and 2 torn dried red chillies and fry until the dal turns biscuit-brown, about 1 minute.

Add 8 crushed garlic cloves and 15 curry leaves to the same oil and fry another 60 seconds until the leaves crisp and the garlic edges colour; take the pan off the heat and let the tempering cool for 5 minutes.

Combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 2 cups squeezed chopped methi, 0.5 tsp crushed black pepper, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt in a bowl, pour in the cooled tempering and mix until every strand of methi is coated.
Knead with 3/4 cup water added gradually for 7 to 8 minutes into a supple dough that pulls cleanly off your palm, then rest it under a damp cloth for 15 minutes.

Roll 8 balls into 14 cm rounds and cook each on a medium-hot tava for about 90 seconds until the underside freckles, flip, smear 0.5 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, and roast the second side until crisp brown patches appear, roughly 2 minutes more.
Stack the parathas in a hot pack with a curry leaf or two between layers so the tempering aroma keeps building until serving.
tips: Cool the tempering before it meets the flour, or the hot oil will cook the atta into lumps.
Urad dal must be fully browned and crunchy; underdone dal stays chalky inside the paratha.
Swap half the water for thin buttermilk to get the faint tang of a Tamil kitchen's day-old dough.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut thogayal or a spoon of idli podi loosened with gingelly oil; a tumbler of sweet-salty neer mor alongside makes it a proper Tamil lunch.

variations.name: Bengali Garlic Methi Paratha
variations.description: Kolkata's porota-makers would approve of this one: garlic slow-fried in pungent kachi ghani mustard oil, folded with methi into flaky triangular layers. Kalonji seeds and a whisper of sugar give it the sweet-sharp balance Bengali breakfasts are loved for.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The tender emmer crumb flakes into layers beautifully when folded porota-style

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed shorshe tel gives the garlic a wasabi-like lift no refined oil can imitate

steps: Bring 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil just to smoking point in a small pan over medium-high heat, about 90 seconds, then lower the flame, add 8 thin-sliced garlic cloves and 1 tsp kalonji and fry gently for a minute until the garlic chips are blond and crisp.
Pour this fragrant oil with all its garlic and kalonji over 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta and rub it in; the flour should smell boldly of mustard and toasted garlic before any water goes in.

Fold in 2 cups washed, squeezed methi, 2 minced green chillies, 0.5 tsp sugar, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 3/4 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, then knead with 3/4 cup water for 7 minutes to a smooth, elastic dough and rest it 20 minutes under a damp cloth.
Roll each of 8 balls into a 12 cm disc, brush with a film of mustard oil, dust with dry flour, fold into quarters and re-roll into a 5 mm thick triangle to build the classic porota layers.

Roast on a medium tava 90 seconds a side until beige spots darken, then drizzle 0.5 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil around the edges and shallow-fry each face 45 seconds until the tips of the triangle turn crackly and deep gold.
Tap each porota sharply between your palms as it comes off the tava so the layers loosen and the steam escapes, keeping the crust crisp.
tips: Smoking the oil once and then cooling it is essential; unsmoked kachi ghani oil tastes raw inside dough.
Slice the garlic instead of mincing so it fries into little crisps you can taste in the finished layers.
These triangles freeze well half-cooked; finish them straight from the freezer on a hot tava for 2 minutes a side.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with cholar dal or begun bhaja and a smear of kasundi mustard; finish the meal with a small bowl of mishti doi for full Kolkata effect.

variations.name: Rajasthani Garlic Methi Paratha
variations.description: Modelled on the lehsun-heavy breads of rural Rajasthan, where dried methi and fiery Mathania-style red chillies survive the desert pantry. Roasted besan in the dough adds a sattu-like nuttiness, and the paratha is finished dhaba-style with a garlic-chilli ghee drizzle.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Hardy emmer wheat mirrors the rustic desert grains this recipe grew up on

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: In Rajasthan ghee is poured, not brushed; bilona ghee's caramel notes carry the garlic-chilli drizzle

steps: Soak 4 dried red chillies in 3 tbsp hot water for 10 minutes, then pound them with 10 garlic cloves and a pinch of the salt in a mortar into a coarse, brick-red lehsun-mirch paste.
Dry-roast 1/4 cup besan in a heavy pan over low heat for 3 to 4 minutes, stirring constantly, until it darkens a shade and smells nutty; cool it before it meets the dough.

Mix 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with the roasted besan, 1.5 cups squeezed fresh methi, 2 tbsp crushed kasuri methi, half of the garlic-chilli paste, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and the remaining salt, then rub in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee.
Knead with 3/4 cup water added bit by bit for 8 minutes until soft yet firm enough to hold a thick paratha, and rest it covered for 15 minutes.

Roll 8 balls into sturdy 13 cm rounds about 5 mm thick and roast each on a medium tava for 2 minutes a side, applying 0.5 tsp Anveshan Ghee per side, until the crust is deeply browned and crisp at the rim.
Warm the last 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with the reserved garlic-chilli paste for 60 seconds until it sizzles and smells roasted, and spoon this drizzle over the hot parathas just before serving.
tips: The double methi (fresh plus kasuri) is deliberate; kasuri brings the concentrated aroma desert cooks rely on in the dry months.
Keep the parathas thicker than usual; the besan makes thin ones brittle.
The garlic-chilli ghee also keeps for a week refrigerated and is superb over dal or khichdi.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a katori of dahi, a raw onion smashed open the highway-dhaba way, and lehsun ki chutney; it stands up well to gatte ki sabzi too.

variations.name: Kerala Garlic Methi Paratha
variations.description: A Malabar-inspired paratha where fresh grated coconut and garlic are sautéed in virgin coconut oil with shallots and curry leaves, then kneaded through the methi dough. It carries the gentle sweetness of a thoran in flatbread form, with a soft, almost parotta-like crumb.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer's soft stretch gets this whole-wheat bread surprisingly close to the tenderness of a Malabar parotta

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold wood-pressed coconut oil perfumes both the sauté and the tava, the twin signatures of a Kerala kitchen

steps: Warm 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadai over medium heat and sauté 4 sliced shallots, 8 minced garlic cloves, 2 minced green chillies and 12 curry leaves for 2 minutes until the shallots soften and turn translucent at the edges.

Add 1/2 cup grated coconut and 2 cups squeezed methi leaves to the pan with 0.5 tsp turmeric and a pinch of the salt, and stir-fry 3 minutes until the coconut smells toasty and the mixture is quite dry; cool completely, about 10 minutes.
Combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, the cooled coconut-methi sauté, 0.5 tsp crushed black pepper and the remaining salt in a bowl, mixing until the greens are dispersed through the flour.
Knead with 1/2 cup water added slowly, since the sauté already carries moisture, working the dough 7 minutes until soft and faintly springy; rest 15 minutes under a damp cloth.
Roll 8 balls into 14 cm rounds, handling gently because the coconut makes the dough short, and cook each on a medium tava for 90 seconds until pale spots appear, then flip.
Spread 0.5 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil on each side and roast, pressing lightly, until both faces are freckled golden brown, about 2 minutes more; the kitchen should smell like a Malabar tea shop.
tips: Cool the coconut sauté fully before kneading or the dough turns greasy and refuses to hold shape.
Frozen grated coconut works if thawed and squeezed; desiccated coconut does not, as it stays gritty.
These are best eaten fresh; the coconut crumb dries faster than plain parathas, so hold them wrapped in a cloth, not open.
variations.servingSuggestion: Wonderful with a fried-egg roast or vegetable stew, and startlingly good with a spoon of sweet mango pachadi; sulaimani tea on the side seals the Malabar mood.

variations.name: Classic Home-style Bhindi
variations.description: The weeknight bhindi ki sabzi every Indian kitchen leans on: dry-fried okra folded into a light onion-tomato base with everyday spices. It is quicker and gentler than the dhaba version, with each piece staying separate, tender and completely slime-free.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed sunflower oil keeps this everyday sabzi light while still carrying a clean, seed-sweet aroma refined oil never has

steps: Rinse 500 g okra ahead of time and let it air-dry fully on a towel, then trim and cut into 0.75-inch pieces with a dry knife.
Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Sunflower Oil in a wide pan over medium heat and fry the okra for 6-7 minutes, tossing occasionally, until the pieces look dry and lightly speckled; slide them onto a plate.
Pour the remaining 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Sunflower Oil into the pan, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then soften 1 large chopped onion for 4-5 minutes until pale gold.

Add 1 tsp ginger-garlic paste and stir for 45 seconds, then add 1 large chopped tomato, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder and cook 3-4 minutes until the tomato collapses.
Return the okra with 1 tsp salt and cook uncovered on medium-low for 6-7 minutes, folding gently every 2 minutes, until the pieces are fork-tender but still holding shape.
Dust 0.5 tsp amchur over the sabzi, give it one last toss and switch off; the tang wakes everything up right at the end.
tips: Wash okra hours before cooking, never minutes before; residual water is what creates slime.
A wide pan matters more than the flame here; okra piled two layers deep will steam instead of fry.
For tiffin boxes, skip the tomato and double the amchur; the drier version stays fresh till lunchtime.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best with soft phulkas, a katori of plain toor dal and a simple kachumber of cucumber and onion.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Home-style Bhindi
variations.description: Bhendichi bhaji the Deccan way: okra simmered with the warm, faintly sweet complexity of goda masala and thickened with roasted peanut powder. Fresh coconut on top makes it taste like a Pune home kitchen on a Tuesday.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Maharashtrian bhaji is traditionally made in groundnut oil; this wood-pressed one doubles down on the peanut notes already in the dish

steps: Dry 500 g okra thoroughly and cut into 1-inch pieces; keep 3 tbsp roasted peanut powder and 2 tbsp grated coconut measured and ready by the stove.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds for about 30 seconds, then add 1 pinch of hing and let it foam for 5 seconds.
Add 1 chopped onion and 2 chopped green chillies and sauté for 4 minutes until the onion softens and smells sweet, not browned.
Tip in the okra with 0.5 tsp turmeric and stir-fry on medium heat for 8-9 minutes, tossing every 2 minutes, until the pieces stop looking glossy and turn tender.
Sprinkle 2 tsp goda masala and 1 tsp salt, toss well and cook 2 minutes so the masala's cinnamon-sesame warmth coats the okra evenly.
Stir in 3 tbsp roasted peanut powder, cook 1 more minute until it binds the bhaji lightly, then finish off the heat with 2 tbsp grated coconut and 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Goda masala scorches quickly, so it always goes in after the okra is nearly done, never into hot bare oil.
No goda masala on hand? Grind 2 cloves, 1 inch cinnamon and 1 tsp sesame seeds with 0.5 tsp regular garam masala as a stopgap.
Add the peanut powder off a rolling flame; overheated peanut powder releases oil and turns the bhaji greasy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft jowar or bajra bhakri, a smear of thecha for the brave, and a bowl of mattha (spiced buttermilk).

variations.name: Gujarati Home-style Bhindi
variations.description: Bhinda nu shaak with the classic Gujarati sweet-sour balance: okra cooked gently with dhana-jeeru, then rounded off with jaggery and a squeeze of lemon. Toasted sesame seeds give the soft okra a delicate crunch and nutty finish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Gujarati shaak is built on groundnut oil; the wood-pressed version adds a roasted-peanut aroma that refined oil cannot

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A spoon of chemical-free jaggery powder gives the authentic gentle sweetness that balances the lemon in this shaak

steps: Towel-dry 500 g okra completely and cut into short 0.5-inch pieces, the small cut Gujarati kitchens prefer for quick, even cooking.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp ajwain for 30 seconds, then add 1 pinch of hing.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, stir for 30 seconds, then add the okra with 0.5 tsp turmeric and toss until every piece is coated in the fragrant oil.
Cook uncovered on medium-low for 10-12 minutes, stirring every 2-3 minutes, until the okra is soft, dry and no longer sticky when pressed with a spoon.
Season with 2 tsp dhana-jeeru, 1 tsp salt and 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook 2 minutes until the jaggery melts and lightly glazes the okra.
Finish with 1 tbsp sesame seeds toasted into the shaak for 1 minute, then switch off and brighten with 2 tsp lemon juice just before serving.
tips: The jaggery must go in only after the okra is fully tender; added early it makes the pods sweat and turn slippery.
Toast the sesame seeds separately in a dry pan if you want a more pronounced crunch on top.
This shaak reheats beautifully; splash 1 tsp water and warm it covered on low so the jaggery glaze loosens again.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve Gujarati-thali style with hot rotli, a bowl of kadhi, steamed rice and a spoon of chhundo on the side.

variations.name: Tamil Home-style Bhindi
variations.description: Vendakkai poriyal from a Chennai home kitchen: okra tempered with mustard, urad dal and plenty of curry leaves in gingelly oil, spiced with sambar powder and finished with fresh coconut. Dry, fragrant and made for mixing into hot rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Nallennai (gingelly oil) is the soul of a Tamil poriyal; this wood-pressed sesame oil brings that deep, toasty authenticity

steps: Wipe 500 g okra dry with a cloth, then slice into neat 0.5-inch rounds; small rounds are traditional for poriyal and cook through evenly.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in an iron kadai over medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds for 30 seconds, then brown 2 tsp urad dal for about a minute until golden and nutty.
Add 1 torn dried red chilli, 1 sprig of curry leaves and 8 sliced shallots and sauté for 3 minutes until the shallots soften and the leaves crisp.
Add the okra rounds with 0.25 tsp turmeric and stir-fry on medium heat for 9-10 minutes, tossing every 2 minutes, until the rounds brown at the edges and lose all stickiness.
Sprinkle 2 tsp sambar powder and 1 tsp salt and toss for 2 minutes so the spice toasts in the hot oil and clings to the okra.
Turn off the heat and fold in 3 tbsp grated coconut and the second sprig of curry leaves, letting the residual heat warm the coconut through.
tips: An iron kadai gives poriyal its signature toasted edge; stir a little more often since iron runs hot.
Homestyle trick for extra-crisp rounds: rest the cut okra under the fan for 20 minutes before frying.
Coconut goes in strictly off the flame; cooked coconut loses its fresh sweetness and turns chewy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as part of a Tamil meals plate alongside hot rice, vatha kuzhambu or rasam, and appalam.

variations.name: Kumaoni Home-style Bhindi
variations.description: A pahadi rendition tempered with jakhya, the wild Himalayan seed that crackles like tiny popcorn and tastes earthier than cumin. Cooked simply in pungent mustard oil with garlic and hill-style red chillies, it lets the okra and the jakhya do all the talking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Kumaoni kitchens cook almost everything in pungent mustard oil; this cold-pressed one smokes and mellows exactly like the hill-village original

steps: Dry 500 g okra completely on a towel, then slit each pod lengthwise into halves so the jakhya-scented oil can reach the seedy centre.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a heavy kadhai on high for about 2 minutes until it just smokes, then reduce to medium so the raw pungency softens.
Add 1 tsp jakhya seeds and let them crackle and pop for 20-30 seconds, then add 6 sliced garlic cloves and 3 whole dried red chillies and fry for 1 minute until the garlic edges turn golden.
Slide in the okra halves with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp coriander powder and toss until every piece glistens with the spiced oil.
Cook uncovered on medium-low for 12-14 minutes, turning gently every 3 minutes, until the okra is browned, soft inside and completely dry.
Season with 1 tsp salt in the final 2 minutes, then finish off the heat with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and 1 tsp lemon juice for a fresh mountain-air lift.
tips: Jakhya must go into properly hot oil or it stays hard and gritty; wait for a visible shimmer before adding.
No jakhya available? Cumin works, but toast it 10 seconds less as it burns faster than the hill seed.
Salt only at the end here; salting early draws moisture out of the slit pods and slows the browning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Eat pahadi style with thick mandua (finger millet) rotis, a bowl of bhatt ki churkani and a spoon of hill-garlic chutney.

variations.name: Classic Home-style Tori
variations.description: This is the everyday North Indian ridge gourd sabzi that cooks in its own juices until silky and spoon-tender. A simple cumin-onion-tomato base lets the gourd's delicate sweetness shine, while wood-pressed groundnut oil adds a gentle nutty depth. It is light on the stomach and comes together in one kadhai on a weeknight.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed from whole groundnuts, it keeps a mild nuttiness that flatters the gentle flavour of ridge gourd

steps: Lightly peel the ridges off 500 g ridge gourd, halve it lengthwise and cut into 1 cm half-moons; finely chop 1 large onion and 2 medium tomatoes and keep everything within reach.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium heat until it shimmers, then crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 30 seconds until they smell toasty.

Add the chopped onion and saute on medium heat for 5-6 minutes, stirring often, until the edges turn golden brown; stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 1 minute until the raw smell disappears.

Tip in the chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt; cook for 4-5 minutes, mashing occasionally, until the masala turns jammy and oil beads at the edges.
Fold in the ridge gourd, coat it well in the masala, then cover and cook on low heat for 10-12 minutes; the gourd will release its own water and turn translucent and tender.
Uncover, raise the heat to medium-high and cook for 2-3 minutes to evaporate excess liquid until the sabzi is moist but not watery, then finish with 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander.
tips: Do not add any water while cooking; ridge gourd releases plenty of moisture on its own and extra water makes the sabzi mushy.
Peel only the tough raised ridges and leave most of the green skin on for texture and colour.
If the sabzi turns watery, cook uncovered on high for a couple of minutes at the end instead of adding thickeners.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with phulkas and a bowl of plain dal, with a wedge of lime and sliced onions on the side for a classic everyday thali.

variations.name: Bengali Jhinge Tori with Posto
variations.description: In Bengali homes ridge gourd, called jhinge, is most loved when simmered with a creamy poppy seed paste and pungent mustard oil. Slit green chillies and nigella seeds give this version its unmistakable character, and a whisper of khandsari balances the mustard's bite. The result is a pale, delicate curry that tastes far richer than its short ingredient list suggests.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed kachi ghani mustard oil brings the sharp, peppery pungency that defines Bengali jhinge posto

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: A tiny pinch of unrefined khandsari rounds off the mustard oil's pungency the way Bengali cooks use a touch of sweetness

steps: Soak 3 tbsp poppy seeds in 4 tbsp warm water for 15 minutes, then grind with 1 slit green chilli into a smooth, thick white paste; a small mixer jar works best for this quantity.
Peel the ridges from 500 g ridge gourd and cut into 2 cm chunks, and dice 1 medium potato into 1 cm cubes so both vegetables cook through at the same pace.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai on medium-high until it just begins to smoke, then lower the heat and crackle 0.5 tsp nigella seeds for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add the potato cubes and fry on medium heat for 4 minutes until the edges look lightly golden, then add the ridge gourd, 0.5 tsp turmeric powder and 1 tsp salt and toss for 2 minutes.
Cover and cook on low heat for 8-10 minutes, stirring once midway, until the gourd releases its juices and the potato is fork-tender.
Stir in the poppy seed paste, 0.5 tsp Anveshan Khandsari and 2 slit green chillies, and simmer uncovered for 3-4 minutes until the paste coats the vegetables in a creamy, barely-wet gravy.
Sprinkle 2 tbsp grated coconut on top, switch off the heat and let the pan sit covered for 2 minutes so the flavours settle before serving.
tips: Always let mustard oil reach its smoking point once and then cool slightly; this mellows the raw sharpness without losing its character.
Grind the poppy seeds after soaking, not dry, or the paste stays gritty and the gravy will not turn creamy.
Keep the finished dish slightly moist; posto thickens as it cools and can turn pasty if you dry it out completely on the stove.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steaming hot plain rice and a wedge of gondhoraj or regular lime; Bengalis eat jhinge posto as the first, delicate course before dal and fish.

variations.name: Kerala Ridge Gourd Thoran
variations.description: A quick stir-fry from Kerala where diced ridge gourd is steamed open in the pan with a crumbly mixture of fresh coconut, shallots, garlic and green chilli. Cooked in wood-pressed coconut oil with a mustard seed and curry leaf tempering, it is dry, fragrant and ready in minutes. Every spoonful carries the sweet aroma of coconut against the mild gourd.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed from fresh coconuts, it doubles down on the thoran's coconut flavour instead of fighting it like a neutral oil would

steps: Dice 500 g ridge gourd into small 1 cm cubes after shaving off the tough ridges; small, even pieces are essential so the thoran cooks quickly and stays dry.

Coarsely crush 0.75 cup fresh grated coconut with 5 shallots, 3 garlic cloves, 2 green chillies, 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp turmeric powder using two or three short pulses in a mixer; keep it crumbly, not a paste.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a wide pan on medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds for about 30 seconds, then add 1 broken dried red chilli and 12 curry leaves and let them crisp for a few seconds.
