Add the diced ridge gourd and 1 tsp salt, toss to coat in the tempering, then cover and cook on low heat for 6-7 minutes until the cubes turn translucent, stirring once so nothing catches.
Scatter the crushed coconut mixture over the gourd, mix gently, cover again and steam on low for 4-5 minutes until the raw smell of shallot and garlic disappears.
Open the lid, stir-fry on medium heat for 2 minutes to drive off any pooled moisture so the thoran is moist but crumbly, then take it off the heat.
tips: Pulse the coconut mixture only briefly; a coarse crumble gives the classic thoran texture while a fine paste makes it heavy and wet.
Frozen grated coconut works if thawed fully, but fresh coconut gives noticeably more sweetness against the mild gourd.
If your gourd is very watery, salt the cubes lightly and rest them for 10 minutes, then squeeze gently before cooking.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside matta rice and a tangy pulissery or sambar for a proper Kerala lunch; it also folds beautifully into a wrap with leftover chapati.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Tori Bhaji with Goda Masala
variations.description: This homely Maharashtrian bhaji dresses ridge gourd in smoky-sweet goda masala, crushed roasted peanuts and a touch of jaggery, a combination found in kitchens across Pune and the Desh region. The peanuts thicken the juices into a nutty coating while the jaggery and chilli play off each other. It is rustic, deeply savoury and unlike any North Indian tori.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Maharashtra's everyday cooking fat; its roasted-peanut aroma echoes the crushed peanuts in this bhaji

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Chemical-free jaggery powder dissolves evenly into the bhaji, giving the gentle sweetness goda masala dishes are known for

steps: Trim the ridges off 500 g ridge gourd and cut it into thick 1.5 cm pieces; slice 1 medium onion thinly and coarsely crush 0.25 cup roasted peanuts in a mortar.
Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a kadhai over medium heat, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds until they finish crackling, then add 0.25 tsp asafoetida and stir for 5 seconds.
Slide in the sliced onion and fry for 4-5 minutes on medium heat until soft and just turning golden at the edges, which builds the sweet base the goda masala needs.
Add the ridge gourd along with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, toss well, then cover and cook on low for 8-10 minutes until the pieces are tender and glossy.
Sprinkle in 2 tsp goda masala, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and the crushed peanuts, and stir-fry uncovered on medium heat for 3-4 minutes so the juices thicken into a nutty coating.
Taste and adjust salt, then finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and rest the bhaji off the heat for 2 minutes before serving so the goda masala blooms.
tips: Add goda masala near the end of cooking; long frying dulls its delicate dagad phool and coconut notes.
Crush the peanuts coarsely rather than to a powder so you get little crunchy pockets in the soft bhaji.
No goda masala on hand? A half-and-half mix of garam masala and roasted coconut powder is the closest quick stand-in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with soft bhakri or chapati, a dollop of curd and a slice of raw onion; it also makes an excellent filling for a quick masala toast the next morning.

variations.name: Kumaoni Tori with Jakhya Tadka
variations.description: In the Kumaon hills of Uttarakhand, vegetables are stir-fried with jakhya, a tiny wild seed that crackles into a nutty, popping crunch no cumin can imitate. This tori keeps things spare, just garlic, dried red chillies, turmeric and pahadi patience, letting the mountain-style mustard oil tempering do the talking. It is the simplest recipe in this collection and arguably the most addictive.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Pahadi kitchens swear by pungent mustard oil for jakhya tempering; this wood-pressed one has the bite the dish needs

steps: Scrape the ridges off 500 g ridge gourd and slice it into thin 0.5 cm rounds; thin slices catch the jakhya tempering better than chunks and cook faster on a hill-style high flame.
Roughly smash 4 garlic cloves with the flat of a knife and slit 1 green chilli lengthwise so both release flavour quickly into the oil.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a heavy kadhai on medium-high until it just smokes, then reduce the heat and add 1 tsp jakhya seeds; they should crackle and pop like tiny fireworks within 15-20 seconds.
Immediately add 2 broken dried red chillies, the smashed garlic and slit green chilli, and fry for about 1 minute until the garlic turns pale gold and smells sweet.

Add the ridge gourd rounds, 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, toss well, and stir-fry uncovered on medium heat for 8-10 minutes, letting the slices sear lightly rather than steam.
When the gourd is tender with a few browned edges, squeeze over 2 tsp lemon juice, toss once and take the pan off the heat straight away.
tips: Do not substitute cumin for jakhya and cook it the same way; jakhya pops almost instantly, so have the next ingredients ready before it hits the oil.
Cooking uncovered is intentional here; covering makes the rounds watery while the pahadi style keeps them lightly seared and distinct.
Jakhya is sold online and in Uttarakhand stores as wild mustard or cleome seeds; buy a small pack, it stays fresh for months.
variations.servingSuggestion: Eat it the pahadi way with thick mandua (ragi) rotis or steamed rice and a bowl of bhatt ki churkani, with extra lemon on the side.

variations.name: Classic Masala Aloo Gobi
variations.description: The definitive North Indian home version: cubed potatoes and cauliflower florets braised in a slow-cooked onion-tomato masala until every edge is stained turmeric-gold. A final drizzle of bilona ghee rounds the spices into something deeply comforting rather than merely hot.

ingredients.name: Cauliflower
ingredients.note: about 500 g, cut into bite-sized florets

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed and nutty, it stands up to the long bhuno this masala needs

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the finishing drizzle that gives this sabzi its dhaba-worthy aroma

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Peel and cut 3 medium potatoes into 2 cm cubes and break 1 medium cauliflower into bite-sized florets; soak the florets in warm salted water for 10 minutes, then drain and pat completely dry.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a heavy kadai on medium heat until it shimmers, then crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 30 seconds until they turn a shade darker and smell toasty.
Add 2 finely chopped onions and saute on medium heat for 6-7 minutes until golden brown at the edges, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 1 minute until the raw smell disappears.

Add 2 chopped tomatoes along with 1/2 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt; cook for 4-5 minutes, mashing occasionally, until the masala thickens and oil beads at the edges.

Tip in the potato cubes, toss to coat in the masala, cover and cook on low heat for 8 minutes. Add the cauliflower florets, stir gently, cover again and cook for 10-12 minutes until a knife slides through both vegetables without resistance.

Uncover, raise the heat to medium-high for 2 minutes to evaporate any moisture, then sprinkle 1/2 tsp garam masala and drizzle 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the hot sabzi, tossing gently so every floret glistens.
Rest the sabzi covered off the heat for 2 minutes, then scatter 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander on top and give it one final gentle fold before serving.
tips: Pat the cauliflower bone-dry after soaking; wet florets steam instead of browning and the sabzi turns mushy.
If the masala starts catching before the vegetables soften, sprinkle 2 tbsp hot water down the sides rather than stirring vigorously, which breaks the florets.
Make the onion-tomato masala up to 2 days ahead and refrigerate; on a busy evening the dish comes together in 20 minutes.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile it beside hot phulkas with a wedge of lime and sliced onion, or tuck it into a toasted pav with green chutney for a quick lunch.

variations.name: Punjabi Masala Aloo Gobi
variations.description: The Amritsar-style take where the gobi is first pan-seared in ghee until blistered, then folded through a robust masala sharpened with amchur and perfumed with kasuri methi. It is richer and tangier than the everyday version, built for tearing into with butter-brushed rotis.

ingredients.name: Potatoes
ingredients.note: cut into thick wedges

ingredients.name: Cauliflower
ingredients.note: cut into large florets

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee replaces the usual dhaba butter and sears the gobi to a nutty blister

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: sliced thick

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: half julienned for garnish, half grated

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit lengthwise

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: roughly chopped

ingredients.name: Kasuri methi
ingredients.note: crushed between palms

steps: Melt 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide pan on medium-high heat and sear the cauliflower florets in a single layer for 5-6 minutes, turning once, until blistered brown in spots; lift them out and set aside.
In the same pan add the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add 2 thickly sliced onions and fry on medium heat for 7-8 minutes until deeply golden.

Stir in the grated ginger and 2 slit green chillies and cook for 1 minute, then add 2 chopped tomatoes with 1/2 tsp turmeric powder, 1.5 tsp Kashmiri red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt.
Bhuno the masala on medium heat for 5-6 minutes, pressing the tomatoes down with the back of the ladle, until it turns brick-red and the ghee separates at the sides.
Add the potato wedges, coat them well, splash in 1/4 cup hot water, cover and cook on low heat for 10 minutes until the potatoes are halfway tender.
Return the seared florets to the pan, fold gently, cover and cook on low heat for another 10 minutes until both vegetables are fork-tender but still holding their shape.
Sprinkle 1 tsp amchur and 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi over the sabzi, toss on high heat for 1 minute until dry and glossy, then finish with 3 tbsp fresh coriander and the reserved ginger juliennes.
tips: Searing the gobi separately before it meets the masala is the dhaba secret; skip it and you lose the smoky char that defines this version.
Crush kasuri methi only at the moment of adding; pre-crushed leaves lose the perfume within hours.
For a true truck-stop finish, spoon 1 extra tsp of warm Anveshan Ghee over each portion just before it reaches the table.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tandoori roti, a mound of lachha onions soaked in vinegar, and a tall glass of salted lassi to cool the tang.

variations.name: Bengali Masala Aloo Gobi
variations.description: Modelled on the winter phulkopir dalna of Kolkata kitchens, this no-onion, no-garlic take simmers gobi and aloo in a ginger-tomato gravy bloomed in pungent mustard oil. A whisper of jaggery balances the heat, and a spoon of ghee at the end is non-negotiable in any Bengali home.

ingredients.name: Potatoes
ingredients.note: quartered

ingredients.name: Cauliflower
ingredients.note: large florets, stem left long

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: kachi ghani pungency is the backbone of every Bengali dalna

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: pureed

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the traditional Bengali touch of sweetness, minus refined sugar

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the closing spoonful every dalna is judged by

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai on medium-high heat until it just begins to smoke, then lower the heat and wait 30 seconds so the raw pungency mellows.
Fry the cauliflower florets in the hot oil for 4-5 minutes until pale gold on the edges, lift them out, then fry the quartered potatoes for 4 minutes and set both aside.
In the remaining oil, temper 1 bay leaf and 1/2 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add 1 tbsp ginger paste and 3 slit green chillies and stir for 1 minute until fragrant.

Pour in the puree of 2 tomatoes with 1/2 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp cumin powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt; cook on medium heat for 5 minutes until the gravy darkens and oil floats on top.

Return the fried potatoes and cauliflower to the kadai with 3/4 cup hot water and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder; cover and simmer on low heat for 12-14 minutes until the vegetables are tender and the gravy clings thickly.
Switch off the heat, sprinkle 1/2 tsp garam masala and swirl in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee; keep covered for 3 minutes so the aromas settle before serving.
tips: Always let mustard oil reach its smoking point once and then cool slightly; skipping this leaves a raw bitterness through the dish.
Frying the florets before simmering keeps them intact in the gravy, so resist the shortcut of adding them raw.
This dalna tastes even better after an hour of resting; reheat gently with a splash of water rather than boiling it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle it over steaming gobindobhog rice with a slice of gondhoraj lime, or pair with soft luchis for a Sunday Bengali breakfast.

variations.name: Kerala Masala Aloo Gobi
variations.description: A Malabar-leaning stir-fry where the vegetables are tossed with crackled mustard seeds, curry leaves and hand-crushed shallots in virgin coconut oil, then blanketed in fresh grated coconut. Black pepper carries the heat, giving it a warmth entirely different from north Indian chilli-driven versions.

ingredients.name: Potatoes
ingredients.note: diced small

ingredients.name: Cauliflower
ingredients.note: small florets

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed aroma that makes this taste of a Kerala kitchen

ingredients.name: Shallots
ingredients.note: thinly sliced

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Black pepper
ingredients.note: coarsely crushed

steps: Warm 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a wide urali or kadai on medium heat, then pop 1 tsp mustard seeds for about 30 seconds until they finish sputtering.

Toss in 2 sprigs of curry leaves and let them crisp for 15 seconds, then add 10 sliced shallots, 3 slit green chillies and the chopped ginger; saute for 4-5 minutes until the shallots turn translucent and lightly pink at the edges.
Stir in 1/2 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, followed immediately by the diced potatoes; toss for 2 minutes so the spices coat every piece.
Sprinkle 3 tbsp water over the potatoes, cover and cook on low heat for 8 minutes, then add the small cauliflower florets, cover again and cook for another 10 minutes until both are just tender.
Uncover, raise the heat to medium and stir-fry for 3 minutes to drive off moisture, then add 1 tsp coarsely crushed black pepper and toss well so the heat blooms through the pan.
Fold in 1/2 cup grated fresh coconut, cook for 2 minutes just until the coconut warms and smells sweet, and take the pan off the heat while everything is still bright and loose.
tips: Add the coconut only at the very end; letting it fry too long turns it dry and takes away the fresh sweetness that defines the dish.
Frozen grated coconut works well here if thawed fully and squeezed of excess water first.
Crush the pepper coarsely with a mortar rather than using pre-ground powder; the uneven bits give little bursts of warmth.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with Kerala matta rice and a tangy pulissery, or roll it into a warm Malabar parotta with a squeeze of lime for a beach-shack lunch.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Masala Aloo Gobi
variations.description: A Pune-style sukhi bhaji where sweet-smoky goda masala, roasted dry coconut and sesame seeds do the work of a heavy gravy. It is darker, earthier and more aromatic than its northern cousin, meant to be scooped up with soft bhakri.

ingredients.name: Potatoes
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Cauliflower
ingredients.note: medium florets

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday fat of Maharashtrian kitchens, pressed the slow way

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Goda masala
ingredients.note: the signature Maharashtrian blend with stone flower and coconut

ingredients.name: Roasted dry coconut
ingredients.note: grated khobra, dry-roasted until tan

steps: Dry-roast 3 tbsp grated dry coconut and 1 tbsp white sesame seeds in a small pan on low heat for 3-4 minutes until tan and nutty, then tip onto a plate to cool.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds for 30 seconds, then add 1/4 tsp asafoetida and let it foam for a few seconds.
Add 1 finely chopped onion and saute for 5-6 minutes until soft and golden, then stir in 2 tsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute until aromatic.
Add 1/2 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp goda masala and 1 tsp salt, stir for 30 seconds, then immediately add the cubed potatoes and toss to coat before the spices scorch.

Cover and cook on low heat for 8 minutes, then add the cauliflower florets with a sprinkle of 2 tbsp water, cover again and cook for 10-12 minutes until both vegetables are tender but not falling apart.
Scatter the roasted coconut-sesame mixture over the bhaji, toss on medium heat for 2 minutes until every piece wears a nutty brown coat, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander.
tips: Goda masala burns quickly, so keep the flame low when it hits the pan and have the potatoes ready to follow within seconds.
If you cannot find goda masala, simmer 1 tsp garam masala with a pinch of grated jaggery and extra roasted coconut for a close stand-in.
Leftovers make an excellent stuffing for masala toast sandwiches the next morning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with jowar bhakri and a raw onion-koshimbir salad, or serve alongside varan-bhaat for a complete Maharashtrian thali.

variations.name: Classic Masala Aloo Matar
variations.description: The definitive North Indian curry of potatoes and green peas simmered in a well-fried onion-tomato masala. The potatoes soak up the spiced gravy while the peas keep their pop and sweetness, and a final flourish of garam masala ties it together. It is the dish most Indian homes reach for when the vegetable basket looks bare.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A sturdy wood-pressed oil that fries the onion-tomato masala to a deep colour without turning greasy

steps: Peel 3 medium potatoes and cut them into 2 cm cubes, finely chop 2 medium onions, and puree or finely chop 3 medium tomatoes; keep 1 cup green peas thawed and ready.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a heavy kadhai over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 30 seconds until aromatic.
Add the chopped onions and fry for 6-7 minutes on medium heat, stirring regularly, until they turn a deep golden brown; then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute more.

Pour in the tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1.25 tsp salt, and cook for 6-8 minutes until the masala thickens and oil separates at the sides.

Add the potato cubes and 1 cup green peas, coat them in the masala for 2 minutes, then pour in 1.5 cups hot water, cover and simmer on low for 12-14 minutes until a knife slides easily through a potato cube.
Lightly mash 3-4 potato pieces against the pan wall to thicken the gravy, sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala and 3 tbsp chopped coriander, and simmer uncovered for 2 minutes before switching off.
tips: Fry the onions patiently to a true golden brown; pale onions leave the gravy tasting flat and slightly raw.
Mashing a few cooked potato cubes into the gravy is the traditional way to get body without cream or cashews.
Fresh winter peas need 3-4 extra minutes of simmering compared to frozen ones, so taste one before finishing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle over steamed basmati rice or scoop up with hot phulkas; a side of boondi raita and roasted papad turns it into a complete lunch.

variations.name: Punjabi Makhani-style Aloo Matar
variations.description: Punjab takes aloo matar and makes it unapologetically rich: the masala is bhuno-ed in bilona ghee, mellowed with fresh cream and perfumed with kasuri methi. The gravy turns glossy and clings to every potato cube like a weekend treat. This is the version served at Amritsari homes when guests stay for dinner.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Slow-churned bilona ghee replaces the dhaba butter here, giving the makhani-style gravy its nutty, caramel richness

steps: Cube 3 medium potatoes into bite-size pieces, grate or finely chop 2 medium onions, and blend 4 medium tomatoes into a smooth puree for the silky gravy this version demands.
Melt 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds with 1 bay leaf for 30 seconds, then add the onions and fry for 7-8 minutes until they are a rich brown.
Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and saute for 1 minute, then pour in the tomato puree with 1.5 tsp Kashmiri red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1.25 tsp salt.
Bhuno the masala on medium heat for 8-10 minutes, stirring every couple of minutes, until it darkens, turns glossy and the ghee visibly pools around the edges.
Add the potatoes and 1 cup green peas with 1.5 cups hot water, cover and simmer on low for 12-14 minutes until the potatoes are completely tender and the gravy has thickened.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi between your palms into the pan, stir in 0.25 cup fresh cream and 0.75 tsp garam masala, and simmer gently for 2 minutes without boiling hard so the cream stays smooth.
Rest the curry covered off the heat for 5 minutes; the potatoes drink in the creamy gravy and the flavour deepens noticeably.
tips: Kashmiri chilli powder gives the trademark red colour with mild heat; using regular chilli powder at the same quantity will make it fiery.
Always crush kasuri methi between your palms just before adding to release its aroma fully.
For an even richer dhaba finish, top each serving with a small extra spoon of warm ghee instead of butter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best mopped up with butter naan or lachha paratha, alongside sliced onions soaked in vinegar and a tall glass of sweet lassi.

variations.name: Gujarati Sweet-Tangy Aloo Matar
variations.description: Gujarat balances every curry on the khatta-mitha axis of tang and sweetness, and this aloo matar is no exception. Jaggery melts into the tomato base while lemon sharpens it, and a hing-mustard tempering keeps it distinctly Gujarati. The gravy is lighter and brighter than its Punjabi cousin, made for scooping with soft rotli.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the default fat of Gujarati kitchens and lets the sweet-tangy masala stay light on the palate

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Unrefined jaggery powder gives the authentic Gujarati mithash that white sugar cannot match in depth

steps: Dice 3 medium potatoes into small 1.5 cm cubes so they cook quickly, finely chop 3 medium tomatoes, and slit 2 green chillies; notice there is no onion or garlic, in true Gujarati style.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium heat, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds fully, then add 0.25 tsp asafoetida, the slit green chillies and 1 tsp grated ginger for 30 seconds.
Add the chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp dhana-jeeru and 1.25 tsp salt, and cook for 5-6 minutes until the tomatoes collapse into a soft pulp.
Stir in the potato cubes and 1 cup green peas, add 1.75 cups hot water, cover and simmer on low heat for 12 minutes until the potatoes are soft enough to break with a spoon.
Dissolve 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder into the simmering gravy and cook uncovered for 3 minutes; the gravy should taste gently sweet behind the spice, not sugary.
Switch off the heat, squeeze in 1 tbsp lemon juice, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander so the khatta-mitha balance lands fresh and bright.
tips: Add the lemon juice only after the heat is off; boiling citrus turns the gravy bitter and dulls its brightness.
Taste after adding jaggery and adjust by the half-teaspoon; tomatoes vary in sourness and the balance is the whole point of this dish.
This version thickens as it sits, so loosen leftovers with a splash of hot water rather than cooking them again.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulka rotli, a katori of Gujarati kadhi and a spoon of chhundo on the side for the full thali experience.

variations.name: Kashmiri Saffron Aloo Matar
variations.description: Inspired by the yogurt-based, onionless gravies of the Kashmiri pandit kitchen, this aloo matar simmers in whisked curd scented with fennel, dry ginger and true saffron. The gravy is pale gold, aromatic and gently warming rather than hot. Saffron steeped in warm milk is swirled in at the end, turning a humble curry into something celebratory.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Kashmiri pandit cooking tempers spices in pure ghee; bilona ghee's clean flavour lets the saffron and fennel lead

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: Genuine Pampore saffron blooms into a honeyed aroma and golden hue that defines this gravy

steps: Soak 12 strands of Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside for 15 minutes; whisk 0.75 cup plain yogurt until completely smooth so it will not split in the pan.
Peel 3 medium potatoes and cut into thick wedges, then pat them dry; there is no onion, garlic or tomato in this gravy, so the potatoes must brown properly for flavour.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan on medium heat and fry the potato wedges for 6-7 minutes, turning occasionally, until golden on most sides; lift them out and keep aside.

In the same ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 3 cloves with 0.25 tsp asafoetida for 30 seconds, then lower the heat fully and stir in 2 tsp fennel powder, 1 tsp dry ginger powder and 1 tsp Kashmiri red chilli powder for just 15 seconds.
Take the pan off the heat, whisk in the yogurt in a steady stream, then return to low heat and stir constantly for 3-4 minutes until the gravy is smooth and gently bubbling.
Return the potatoes with 1 cup green peas, 1.25 tsp salt and 1.25 cups hot water; cover and simmer on low for 12-14 minutes until the potatoes are fully tender and the gravy coats a spoon.
Swirl in the saffron milk, simmer 2 minutes more until the gravy turns pale gold, and serve straight away while the aroma is at its peak.
tips: Whisk the yogurt smooth and add it off the heat, then stir continuously until it boils once; this is the only reliable way to keep it from curdling.
Fennel and dry ginger burn in seconds, so keep the flame at its lowest when they hit the ghee.
Crush the saffron strands lightly between your fingers before soaking to release far more colour and fragrance.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice as Kashmiris would, with a side of mooli chutney; avoid strong pickles that would bury the saffron's perfume.

variations.name: Andhra Guntur Aloo Matar
variations.description: This fiery take channels Andhra's kura tradition: potatoes and peas fried in wood-pressed sesame oil, loaded with Guntur chilli, garlic and curry leaves, then sharpened with a spoon of tamarind. The gravy is thick, brick-red and unapologetically hot. Every bite finishes with the toasty depth that only gingelly oil delivers.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil is the backbone of Andhra kura; its toasty depth stands up to Guntur chilli heat like no neutral oil

steps: Cut 3 medium potatoes into 2 cm cubes, slice 1 large onion, chop 2 medium tomatoes, and crush 6 garlic cloves roughly; soak a small lime-sized ball of tamarind if not using ready pulp.

Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil in a kadhai over medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then drop in 12 curry leaves and the crushed garlic and fry for 1 minute until the garlic edges brown.
Add the sliced onion and fry on medium-high for 5-6 minutes until deeply golden; Andhra gravies rely on well-browned onion for their body.
Stir in the tomatoes, 2 tsp Guntur red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric powder and 1.25 tsp salt, and cook for 5 minutes until the masala turns brick-red and pulls oil.
Add the potatoes and 1 cup green peas with 1.5 cups hot water, cover and simmer on low for 12-14 minutes until the potatoes are soft through.
Stir in 1 tbsp tamarind pulp and simmer uncovered on medium heat for 4-5 minutes until the gravy thickens enough to coat the vegetables thickly and the raw tang cooks off.
tips: Guntur chilli is seriously hot; halve the quantity on first attempt and build up rather than rescuing an over-spiced pot.
Frying garlic until its edges brown, not just translucent, is what gives Andhra gravies their signature aroma.
A pinch of jaggery is a traditional Andhra trick if the tamarind makes the gravy too sharp for your table.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot steamed rice, a spoon of extra sesame oil drizzled on top Andhra-style, and cooling curd on the side to temper the heat.

variations.name: Classic Masala Capsicum
variations.description: The homestyle shimla mirch ki sabzi found on North Indian dinner tables, where crisp-tender capsicum squares are folded through a slow-cooked onion-tomato masala. The peppers keep a slight bite while soaking up earthy coriander and cumin, and a nutty wood-pressed groundnut oil base gives the masala real depth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil has a gentle nuttiness that rounds out the sharp capsicum without overpowering it

steps: Deseed 4 medium green capsicums and cut them into 2 cm squares; finely chop 2 medium onions and 2 medium tomatoes and keep everything ready before you light the stove.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium heat and drop in 1 tsp cumin seeds. Let them sizzle and darken a shade, about 30 seconds, so their aroma blooms in the oil.

Add the chopped onions with a pinch of the salt and saute on medium heat for 6 to 7 minutes, stirring often, until they turn golden at the edges. Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute more until the raw smell disappears.

Tip in the chopped tomatoes along with 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and the remaining salt. Cook on medium for 5 to 6 minutes, mashing gently, until the masala thickens and oil beads appear at the sides.
Add the capsicum squares and toss to coat every piece in the masala. Cover and cook on low heat for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring twice, until the capsicum is tender but still holds a slight crunch.
Sprinkle 1/2 tsp garam masala and 3 tbsp chopped coriander leaves over the sabzi, toss once on high heat for 30 seconds so any moisture dries off, and take it off the flame.
tips: Cut all capsicum pieces the same 2 cm size so they cook evenly; smaller shreds turn mushy before the larger chunks soften.
If the masala sticks to the kadhai before the tomatoes break down, splash in 2 tbsp hot water and scrape the base rather than adding more oil.
The sabzi keeps well for 2 days refrigerated; reheat uncovered in a pan so the capsicum does not steam and lose its bite.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with phulkas and a bowl of plain curd, or roll it into a wrap with sliced onions and a squeeze of lime for a quick lunchbox meal.

variations.name: Bengali Masala Capsicum
variations.description: A charchari-style take from Bengali kitchens where capsicum and potato batons are cooked in pungent mustard oil with crackling kalonji and slit green chillies. A whisper of khandsari sugar at the end gives the dish that signature Bengali sweet-heat balance.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed kachi ghani mustard oil carries the sharp pungency that defines Bengali charchari; smoke it well before tempering

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: Unrefined khandsari sugar melts into the masala for the gentle sweetness Bengali vegetable dishes are known for

steps: Slice 3 medium capsicums into thick batons, cut 2 medium potatoes into similar finger-length batons, slice 1 onion thinly and slit 4 green chillies lengthwise.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai on high until it just begins to smoke, about 1 minute, then lower the flame; this mellows its raw pungency while keeping the flavour.

Scatter in 1 tsp kalonji and 2 of the slit green chillies and let them crackle for 20 seconds. Add the sliced onion and fry on medium for 3 to 4 minutes until translucent and lightly pink at the edges.
Add the potato batons with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1/2 tsp salt, and fry on medium heat for 7 to 8 minutes, tossing now and then, until the edges pick up golden spots.

Stir in the chopped tomato, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining salt, cook for 2 minutes, then add the capsicum batons and remaining green chillies. Cover and cook on low for 8 to 10 minutes until both vegetables are fork-tender.
Uncover, sprinkle 1 tsp Anveshan Khandsari over the sabzi and toss on medium-high heat for 2 minutes until any liquid evaporates and the batons glisten with the mustard oil coating.
tips: Smoking the mustard oil first is non-negotiable; skipping it leaves an acrid raw bite instead of the mellow pungency the dish needs.
Cut potato and capsicum to matching thickness so the potato finishes cooking just as the capsicum turns tender.
A final drizzle of 1/2 tsp raw mustard oil off the heat is a classic Bengali touch for extra aroma, if you enjoy its kick.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair it the Bengali way with steamed rice and a bowl of masoor dal, keeping a wedge of gondhoraj or regular lime on the side to brighten each bite.

variations.name: Kerala Masala Capsicum
variations.description: A thoran-inspired dry preparation where finely diced capsicum is steamed open-pan with a crushed coconut, shallot and curry leaf mixture. Cooked in aromatic wood-pressed coconut oil with a mustard-and-red-chilli tempering, it tastes unmistakably of a Kerala home kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed coconut oil perfumes the thoran with a fresh, sweet coconut aroma that refined oils simply cannot give

steps: Dice 4 medium capsicums into small 1 cm pieces. In a mixer, pulse 3/4 cup grated coconut with 4 shallots, 3 garlic cloves, 2 green chillies, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1/2 tsp black pepper powder just 3 or 4 times to a coarse, crumbly mix; do not grind it to a paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a wide kadhai on medium heat and pop 1 tsp mustard seeds, about 30 seconds, until the spluttering slows.
Add 2 torn dried red chillies, 15 curry leaves and the remaining 4 shallots, sliced, and fry for 2 minutes until the shallots soften and the curry leaves turn glossy and crisp.
Add the diced capsicum and 1 tsp salt, toss well, then cover and cook on low heat for 6 to 7 minutes, stirring once, until the pieces are just tender but still bright green.
Scatter the coarse coconut mixture over the capsicum, mix gently, cover again and steam on the lowest flame for 4 to 5 minutes so the coconut absorbs the pepper and turmeric and turns pale yellow.
Open the lid, raise the heat to medium and toss for 2 minutes until the mixture is dry and fluffy, with no moisture pooling at the base of the pan.
tips: Pulse the coconut mixture coarse and short; over-grinding releases oil and makes the thoran heavy instead of light and fluffy.
Frozen grated coconut works well if fresh is unavailable, but thaw it fully and squeeze out excess water before pulsing.
Leftovers make an excellent filling for dosa or can be tossed with cooked rice and a spoon of coconut oil for instant thoran rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside steamed Kerala matta rice with a ladle of sambar or moru curry, letting the peppery coconut crumble play against the tangy gravy.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Masala Capsicum
variations.description: Pune-style shimla mirchi bhaji perfumed with sweet-smoky goda masala and thickened with crushed roasted peanuts and sesame. Cooked in wood-pressed sesame oil, the peppers pick up a toasty, faintly caramel note that is unique to Maharashtrian home cooking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed sesame oil echoes the toasted sesame inside goda masala, tying the whole bhaji together

steps: Cut 4 medium capsicums into thin strips and finely chop 1 onion. Grind 1/2 cup roasted peanuts to a coarse powder and dry-toast 1 tbsp sesame seeds in a small pan on low heat for 2 minutes until they smell nutty and turn light gold.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadhai on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds for about 30 seconds, then add 1/4 tsp hing and let it foam for 5 seconds.
Add the chopped onion and saute on medium for 4 to 5 minutes until soft and lightly browned at the edges.
Add the capsicum strips with 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt. Toss, cover and cook on low heat for 7 to 8 minutes until the strips wilt but keep a gentle crunch.

Sprinkle in 2 tsp goda masala, the coarse peanut powder and the toasted sesame seeds, and toss on medium heat for 3 minutes; the peanuts will soak up the juices and cling to the peppers in a thick, crumbly coating.
Check the salt, finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and switch off once the bhaji looks dry and the goda masala smells warmly caramelised rather than raw.
tips: Goda masala scorches quickly, so always add it after the capsicum has softened, never into hot oil at the start.
If you cannot find goda masala, a mix of 1.5 tsp garam masala with 1/2 tsp of extra toasted sesame powder comes respectably close.
Keep the peanut powder coarse like breadcrumbs; a fine powder turns pasty and dulls the bhaji's texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft jowar or bajra bhakri and a spoonful of thecha for heat lovers, or tuck it into a chapati roll with a drizzle of curd.

variations.name: Kashmiri Masala Capsicum
variations.description: A gently spiced, curd-based preparation inspired by Kashmiri wazwan home cooking, where capsicum simmers in a fennel and dry-ginger scented yogurt masala. Saffron bloomed in warm ghee is swirled in at the end, staining the dish gold and lending a delicate floral finish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee gives the yogurt gravy its silky body and carries the saffron's aroma the way Kashmiri cooks intend

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: Genuine Kashmiri saffron strands bloomed in warm ghee turn the dish golden with a honeyed floral note no substitute can match

steps: Cut 4 medium capsicums into wide 3 cm diamond-shaped pieces. Whisk 1 cup thick curd until completely smooth and soak 12 strands of Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 1 tbsp of warm Anveshan Ghee, letting them steep while you cook.
Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan on medium, add 3 cracked cardamom pods, 3 cloves and 1/4 tsp hing, and let them sizzle for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the capsicum pieces and fry on medium heat for 5 to 6 minutes, tossing often, until the edges blister lightly and the pieces turn glossy.

Lower the flame fully, stir 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 2 tsp fennel powder, 1 tsp dry ginger powder and 1 tsp salt into 2 tbsp water to make a slurry, and pour it over the capsicum. Cook for 2 minutes so the spices lose their rawness without burning.

Keep the flame at its lowest and add the whisked curd one spoonful at a time, stirring constantly in one direction; after all of it is in, simmer uncovered for 6 to 7 minutes until the gravy thickens and coats the back of a spoon.
Swirl in the saffron-infused ghee with its strands, simmer for 1 final minute until the gravy blushes gold, and take the pan off the heat.
tips: Always add curd on the lowest flame while stirring continuously in one direction, or it will split into grainy curds.
Mixing the powdered spices into a water slurry before adding protects the delicate fennel and ginger from scorching in hot ghee.
This gravy thickens as it rests; loosen leftovers with a splash of warm water, never by boiling hard.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle over steamed basmati rice with a side of Kashmiri-style radish-walnut chutney, and let each diner catch a saffron strand or two on top.

variations.name: Masala Mooli Paratha
variations.description: A spice-forward upgrade of the winter staple: the squeezed radish filling is loaded with garam masala, coriander powder and a ghee-bloomed cumin tempering so every layer tastes seasoned, not just the centre. The masala is rubbed into the dough too, tinting the crust a warm ochre.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli's earthy flavour stands up to a heavy masala load where refined flour would taste flat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Blooming the whole spices in bilona ghee unlocks their oils and carries the masala through the filling

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp coriander powder and about 3/4 cup water into a soft ochre-tinted dough. Coat with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and rest 15 minutes.
Salt the 2 cups grated radish with 1/2 tsp salt for 10 minutes, then squeeze it in fistfuls until it stops dripping and feels fluffy-dry.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium-low and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 30 seconds until they darken and smell nutty, then pour the tempering over the squeezed radish.

Work in 1 tsp garam masala, the remaining 1 tsp coriander powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric, 3/4 tsp red chilli powder, 2 minced green chillies, the last 1/2 tsp salt and 3 tbsp coriander until the filling looks uniformly rust-coloured.
Portion the dough into 8 balls, stuff each with 2 tbsp of masala filling, seal the pleats on top and roll gently into 6-inch rounds, dusting as needed.
Roast on a medium-high tava about 1 minute per side dry, then with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee per paratha, flipping twice, until crisp golden-brown patches bloom and the spiced dough smells toasty.
tips: Seasoning the dough as well as the filling means even the sealed edges taste of masala rather than plain wheat.
Grind your garam masala fresh if you can; pre-ground masala older than three months goes dull and needs half a teaspoon extra.
If the filling tastes too sharp raw, remember the tava mellows radish considerably; do not over-salt to compensate.
variations.servingSuggestion: Cut into quarters and serve with boondi raita and a spoon of nimbu achar; the cool raita against the warm masala is the whole point.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Masala Mooli Paratha
variations.description: Goda masala, the sweet-smoky Maharashtrian blend with dagad phool and coconut, completely transforms the radish filling here, while toasted sesame seeds in the dough echo the state's love of til. It eats like a cross between a paratha and a thalipeeth, best with a dab of homemade curd.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer's rustic texture suits this thalipeeth-leaning paratha better than any polished flour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the everyday fat of Maharashtrian griddles and lets the goda masala shine

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing smear of ghee is the traditional Maharashtrian flourish over any masala bhakri or paratha

steps: Toast 1 tbsp sesame seeds on a dry tava over low heat for about 90 seconds until they pop and turn pale gold, then knead them into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt and about 3/4 cup water. Rest the dough 15 minutes.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium, add the 2 cups grated radish with 1 tsp salt and 1/4 tsp turmeric, and saute 5 to 6 minutes until dry and faintly golden.

Sprinkle in 2 tsp goda masala and 3 tbsp grated coconut and toast 1 more minute on low heat until the masala smells sweetly smoky, then mix in 2 minced green chillies and 3 tbsp coriander and cool completely.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, pack 2 tbsp of the goda-scented filling into each, seal firmly and roll out to 6-inch rounds using gentle strokes.
Cook each paratha on a medium tava with 1/2 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil per side, about 90 seconds a side, until sesame-flecked brown spots appear and the edges crisp.
Rub a thin film of Anveshan Ghee over each hot paratha the moment it comes off the tava so it soaks into the crust.
tips: Goda masala scorches quickly; always add it off direct high heat and never fry it longer than a minute.
If you cannot find goda masala, toast 1 tsp each of coriander and sesame with a pinch of cinnamon and clove as a stopgap, though the real blend is worth sourcing.
Cooked-filling parathas like this one freeze well; stack with parchment between and re-crisp on a dry tava straight from frozen.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a katori of thick dahi whisked with a pinch of salt, and a wedge of lime; a side of dry peanut-garlic thecha turns it into a full Puneri lunch.

variations.name: Odia Masala Mooli Paratha
variations.description: Odisha's five-spice panch phoron — fenugreek, nigella, cumin, fennel and mustard — is bloomed in mustard oil and folded through sauteed radish for a filling that tastes of the state's beloved mula bhaja. The paratha is griddled in mustard oil for a rustic, faintly bitter-sweet finish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Slow-milled khapli mimics the coarse whole wheat of traditional Odia kitchens

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Panch phoron only comes alive when sputtered in pungent kachi ghani mustard oil, the Odia way

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and roughly 3/4 cup water into a pliable dough; rest it 15 minutes under a damp cloth.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai until it shimmers and just smokes, lower the flame, and sputter 1.5 tsp panch phoron with 2 broken dried red chillies for about 30 seconds until the fenugreek darkens slightly.
Add the 2.5 cups grated radish, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt and cook on medium for 6 to 7 minutes, stirring, until the shreds wilt, dry out and pick up the five-spice perfume.
Mix in 2 minced green chillies, 1 tsp ginger and 2 tbsp coriander, then spread the filling out to cool fully for about 10 minutes before stuffing.
Shape 8 balls, load each with 2 tbsp of the panch-phoron radish, seal and roll to 6-inch rounds with a light hand so no fenugreek seed tears the dough.
Griddle each paratha on medium heat with 1/2 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil per side for 90 seconds a side, until reddish-brown blisters form and the crust smells nutty and sharp.
tips: Panch phoron must sizzle in hot oil before meeting the radish; raw fenugreek seeds anywhere in the filling would turn it bitter.
Keep the fenugreek fraction of homemade panch phoron slightly lower than the rest; it dominates if overdone.
A day-old batch of this filling tastes even better; refrigerate it overnight and stuff cold.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with dalma or simply a bowl of plain dahi and a roasted papad; a spoon of tomato khajuri chutney on the side plays beautifully against the five-spice.

variations.name: Andhra Masala Mooli Paratha
variations.description: Built around the searing fruitiness of Guntur red chillies, this take laces the radish with a coarse chilli-garlic-curry-leaf pounded masala inspired by Andhra karam podis. Griddled in groundnut oil, it is unapologetically hot, tangy with a touch of tamarind, and dangerously good with curd rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli's gentle sweetness is the perfect foil for the Guntur chilli heat packed into this filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Andhra kitchens fry their karam masalas in groundnut oil; wood-pressed keeps its deep roasted-peanut aroma

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and about 3/4 cup water into a soft, smooth dough; rest 15 minutes.

Dry-roast 4 Guntur chillies and 1 tsp cumin seeds on low heat for about 2 minutes until the chillies puff and deepen in colour, then pound them coarsely with 5 garlic cloves, 10 curry leaves and 1/2 tsp salt into a rough karam-style masala.
Salt the 2 cups grated radish with the remaining 1/2 tsp salt, rest 10 minutes and squeeze completely dry between your palms.
Massage the pounded chilli-garlic masala, 1 tsp tamarind paste and 1/4 tsp turmeric into the squeezed radish until every shred is stained brick-red.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, fill each with 2 tbsp of the fiery mixture, seal well and roll out to 6-inch rounds, keeping pressure off the centre.
Roast on a medium-high tava with 1/2 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil per side, about 1 minute a side over two flips, until crisp with dark toasted patches and the chilli aroma hits your nose.
tips: Deseed half the Guntur chillies if serving children; the flavour stays but the burn halves.
The pounded karam masala doubles as podi for idlis; make a double batch and store it dry for a week.
Tamarind tightens the filling; add it with the masala, never to the salted radish beforehand, or the shreds go soggy again.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Andhra way with a bowl of cold curd, a wedge of lime and a spoon of avakaya pickle; sweet lassi on the side is the smart insurance policy.

variations.name: Kumaoni Masala Mooli Paratha
variations.description: In the Kumaon hills radish is a winter staple, and its parathas are perfumed with jakhya — the wild mustard-like seed that crackles louder and toasts nuttier than cumin. Bhang jeera-style crushed coriander and a ghee roast give this mountain version its clean, herbal warmth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Heritage emmer echoes the old pahadi wheats still hand-milled in Kumaoni villages

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Pahadi households roast their winter parathas in homemade ghee; bilona ghee recreates that hill-kitchen flavour

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt and about 3/4 cup water into a soft dough, rub with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and rest 15 minutes under a plate.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium and crackle 1 tsp jakhya seeds for 20 to 30 seconds until they pop like tiny fireworks and smell nutty.
Add the 2.5 cups grated radish, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt and saute 6 minutes on medium heat until the shreds collapse and dry out completely.
Fold in 2 tsp crushed coriander seeds, 2 minced green chillies, 2 tsp grated ginger and 3 tbsp fresh coriander, then cool the filling fully on a plate for 10 minutes.
Shape 8 dough balls, stuff each with 2 tbsp of the jakhya-scented radish, seal the seams and roll gently into 6-inch rounds.
Roast on a medium tava, brushing each side with 1/2 tsp Anveshan Ghee, about 90 seconds per side, until freckled golden-brown and crisp at the rim.
tips: Jakhya must always be crackled in hot fat first; the seeds are unpleasantly gritty raw, and their magic is entirely in the pop.
If jakhya is unavailable, brown mustard seeds plus a pinch of cumin get you close, though the texture is softer.
Hill kitchens roll these small and slightly thick; two small parathas stay warmer on the plate than one large one.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bhang jeera chutney or plain radish-leaf saag and a glass of warm haldi doodh; in true pahadi style, eat them sitting in the sun.

variations.name: Classic Masala Palak Paratha
variations.description: A bolder cousin of the plain palak paratha, where the green dough is loaded with a full masala battery of garam masala, coriander, amchur and ginger. Every bite is spiced through rather than seasoned on top, so it needs no sabzi alongside. Ghee-roasting rounds the spices into a warm, toasty finish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat's naturally sweet crumb keeps the heavy masala from tasting harsh

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasting the spiced dough in bilona ghee blooms the garam masala as it cooks

steps: Blanch 200 g spinach in boiling water for 90 seconds, cool it in cold water, squeeze thoroughly and blend with 1 inch ginger and 1 green chilli into a thick puree of roughly 3/4 cup.
Whisk 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp garam masala, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp amchur, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt so the spices distribute evenly.
Add the spinach puree and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, and knead with up to 0.25 cup water into a soft, smooth dough that springs back slowly when pressed; rest 15 minutes covered.
Divide the dough into 8 balls and roll each into an even 6-inch round, dusting lightly with dry atta only when the disc starts to stick.
Cook each paratha on a medium-hot tava for about 1 minute until small bubbles rise, flip, cook 1 minute more, then brush both sides with the remaining Anveshan Ghee.
Press the edges with a folded cloth and roast a final 30 to 40 seconds per side until crisp brown patches form and the spices smell toasty.
tips: Mix the dry spices into the flour before adding the puree; adding them later leaves streaks of raw masala in the dough.
Add amchur last if adjusting spice levels; its tang sharpens noticeably as the paratha rests.
Leftover parathas crisp up beautifully next morning on a dry tava; skip the microwave, which turns them leathery.
variations.servingSuggestion: These are assertive enough to eat solo with plain curd and sliced onions, or roll one around a spoon of sweet mango chunda for a lunchbox wrap.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Masala Palak Paratha
variations.description: Goda masala, the smoky-sweet Maharashtrian blend with dagad phool and coconut, completely changes the personality of this paratha. Toasted white sesame kneaded into the dough adds crunch and nuttiness in every bite. It echoes the flavours of a Puneri kitchen more than any Punjabi dhaba.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli wheat is an heirloom Maharashtra staple, making it the natural flour for this regional take

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A ghee finish softens goda masala's smokiness into a rounded, sweet warmth

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A whisper of jaggery is the classic Maharashtrian counterpoint to goda masala's smoke

ingredients.name: Kokum-free tamarind is skipped; use lemon juice

steps: Toast 1.5 tbsp white sesame seeds on a dry tava over low heat for 2 to 3 minutes, stirring, until they turn pale gold and start to pop; set aside to cool.
Blanch 200 g spinach for 90 seconds, refresh in cold water, squeeze dry and blend with 1 green chilli into a thick puree of about 3/4 cup.
Combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 2 tsp goda masala, the toasted sesame, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt in a wide paraat.
Add the spinach puree, 1 tsp lemon juice and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then knead with up to 0.25 cup water into a soft dough; rest for 15 minutes under a damp cloth.
Divide into 8 balls and roll each to a 6-inch round; the sesame seeds will show as pale flecks through the deep green surface.
Roast on a medium tava for about 90 seconds per side, brushing each side with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Ghee, until golden spots form and the goda masala smells sweetly smoky.
tips: Every household's goda masala differs in strength; start with 2 tsp and add more to the next batch rather than overwhelming this one.
Toasted sesame can be doubled and pressed onto the rolled paratha surface for a decorative, crunchy crust.
The touch of jaggery is traditional, not optional; it bridges the bitter greens and the smoky masala.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with mattha (spiced thin buttermilk) and a dollop of metkut-spiked curd, the way a Puneri lunch plate would be laid out.

variations.name: Odia Masala Palak Paratha
variations.description: Odisha's beloved panch phoron - a five-seed blend of cumin, mustard, fennel, fenugreek and kalonji - is bloomed in mustard oil and worked through the spinach dough. The seeds pop against the soft crumb while the fennel leaves a cool, sweet aftertaste. It tastes of a Cuttack kitchen on a monsoon morning.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its rustic bite suits Odia home cooking, where breads are hearty rather than refined

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Panch phoron only comes alive when crackled in pungent kachi ghani mustard oil

steps: Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai until it just smokes, lower the heat, and crackle 1.5 tsp panch phoron with 1 broken dried red chilli for about 30 seconds until the mustard seeds pop.
Add 3 sliced garlic cloves, fry 30 seconds until golden, then tip in 250 g chopped spinach and cook over high heat for 3 to 4 minutes until wilted and dry.
Season the greens with 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, cook 1 minute more, and cool the mixture completely on a plate.
Knead the cooled tempered spinach into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, adding up to 0.33 cup water gradually, until you get a soft, supple dough; rest 15 minutes.
Divide into 8 portions and roll each into a 6-inch round, flouring lightly; whole seeds will stud the surface, which is exactly the look you want.
Cook on a medium-hot tava about 90 seconds per side, drizzling 1 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil around each paratha, until crisp-edged with deep golden blisters.
tips: Fenugreek seeds in panch phoron scorch first; pull the pan off the heat the moment they turn light brown.
Ready-mixed panch phoron varies; if yours is fenugreek-heavy, reduce to 1 tsp to avoid bitterness.
These parathas taste even better slightly cooled, when the fennel's sweetness comes forward.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside dalma or simply with a smashed-potato aloo bharta laced with raw mustard oil and green chilli, Odia-style.

variations.name: Andhra Masala Palak Paratha
variations.description: Fiery Guntur chillies, ground with garlic into a rustic paste, drive this Andhra rendition, mellowed only slightly by nutty wood-pressed groundnut oil. Curry leaves fried crisp are crumbled straight into the dough. It is the hottest paratha in this collection and proudly so.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The wheat's mild sweetness gives the Guntur heat something to land on

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the default fat of Andhra kitchens and tames the chilli burn with nuttiness

steps: Soak 4 Guntur dried red chillies in 3 tbsp hot water for 10 minutes, then grind them with 4 garlic cloves and a pinch of the salt into a coarse crimson paste.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a small pan over medium heat and fry 10 curry leaves for about 40 seconds until translucent and crisp; drain and crumble them.
Blanch 200 g spinach for 90 seconds, refresh, squeeze hard and blend into a thick puree; you need about 3/4 cup.

Combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with the chilli-garlic paste, crumbled curry leaves, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp coriander powder and the remaining salt, then knead with the spinach puree and up to 0.25 cup water into a soft dough. Rest 15 minutes.
Divide into 8 balls and roll each to a 6-inch round; the dough will be flecked deep green and red from the chilli paste.
Roast on a medium-hot tava for 1 minute per side, then spoon 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil around each paratha and fry until the surface blisters golden-brown, about 1 more minute.
tips: Deseed half the Guntur chillies for a family-friendly heat level without losing their fruity colour.
Grinding the chillies with garlic and salt, rather than using chilli powder, gives the authentic rustic karam texture.
Keep a bowl of cold curd on the table; it is the traditional Andhra remedy between fiery bites.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with sweetened thick curd or a coconut-based chutney; a strip of raw mango on the side plays beautifully against the heat.

variations.name: Malwa Masala Palak Paratha
variations.description: In the Malwa belt of Madhya Pradesh, crushed roasted peanuts go into flatbread doughs for body and crunch, and this paratha follows suit. Coarse peanut rubble, coriander and a hint of fennel turn the spinach dough almost cookie-nutty. It is substantial, warming fare built for Indore winters.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Malwa is old wheat country, and heirloom emmer honours that heritage

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee-roasting doubles down on the peanuts' toastiness for a rich Malwa-style crust

steps: Pulse 0.5 cup roasted peanuts in a mixer to a coarse rubble with some pieces the size of rice grains; do not grind to a paste or the dough turns oily.
Blanch 200 g spinach for 90 seconds, cool, squeeze firmly and blend with 1 inch ginger into a thick puree of about 3/4 cup.
Mix 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with the crushed peanuts, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp ground fennel, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt.
Knead in the spinach puree, 1 tsp lemon juice and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, adding up to 0.25 cup water, to form a soft dough; rest it for 15 minutes.
Divide into 8 balls and roll each gently to a 6-inch round; roll with light pressure so the peanut bits do not tear the surface.
Roast on a medium tava for about 90 seconds per side, brushing each side with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Ghee, until nutty-smelling and studded with golden-brown patches.
tips: Rub the roasted peanuts in a towel to remove skins before crushing; the skins turn bitter on the tava.
If rolling tears the dough around peanut bits, patch with a pinch of dough and keep going; rustic looks are authentic here.
A tablespoon of crushed peanuts pressed onto the top before roasting makes a lovely crunchy face.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a green-chilli-spiked curd raita and a piece of Malwa-style mango pickle; it also pairs surprisingly well with sweet milky chai.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Matar Paratha
variations.description: A winter-morning North Indian favourite where sweet green peas are mashed with green chillies, crushed pepper and ginger, then sealed inside a soft khapli atta shell. The filling is cooked dry in ghee so every bite is fluffy, flaky and sharply spiced rather than soggy. Slow-roasted on the tava, it develops crisp golden blisters while staying tender inside.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat's low gluten keeps the stuffed shell soft even after it cools in a tiffin

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee's nutty aroma blooms the cumin and crisps the crust without burning

steps: Knead the dough: combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 3/4 tsp salt and 1 tbsp melted Anveshan Ghee, then work in about 3/4 cup water a little at a time until you have a soft, smooth ball that springs back when pressed. Cover and rest for 20 minutes.
Boil 1.5 cups green peas in salted water for 4 minutes until just tender and bright green, drain them completely, then mash coarsely with a fork so some texture remains.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add the minced ginger and 3 chopped green chillies and fry until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add the mashed peas along with 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1/2 tsp crushed black pepper and 3/4 tsp salt; cook on medium heat, stirring, for 4 to 5 minutes until the mixture looks completely dry and pulls away from the pan. Stir in 3 tbsp chopped coriander and cool fully.

Divide the dough into 8 equal balls and the filling into 8 portions of about 2 tbsp each. Flatten a ball into a 3-inch cup, place one portion of filling in the centre, gather the edges over the top and pinch firmly to seal.
Dust the stuffed ball lightly with dry atta and roll gently with even pressure into a 6-inch round, rotating as you go so the filling stays centred and does not break through.

Roast each paratha on a hot tava over medium heat for about 2 minutes per side, brushing both sides with the remaining Anveshan Ghee, until deep golden-brown spots appear and the surface puffs in patches.
Press the edges gently with a spatula so they cook through, then transfer to a plate lined with a cloth and serve the parathas hot.
tips: Cook the pea filling until it is bone dry; any trapped moisture turns to steam on the tava and tears the paratha while rolling or roasting.
Chill the filling for 10 minutes before stuffing so it firms up and is far easier to seal inside the dough.
If a paratha tears while rolling, patch the spot with a small pinch of dry dough, dust with atta and continue rolling with lighter strokes.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of chilled curd whisked with roasted cumin powder, a wedge of lime and spicy mango pickle; a glass of masala chai completes the classic dhaba plate.

variations.name: Rajasthani Spicy Matar Paratha
variations.description: In the desert kitchens of Rajasthan, heat comes from sun-dried Mathania-style red chillies pounded with garlic rather than fresh green ones. The pea filling is laced with this smoky chilli-garlic paste, a whisper of hing and ghee-bloomed ajwain, giving a fiery, rustic paratha that pairs beautifully with cooling chaas.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli wheat handles the robust chilli-garlic filling without turning chewy on the hot tava

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rajasthani cooking is unapologetically ghee-forward; bilona ghee gives the authentic granular aroma

steps: Soak 5 dried red chillies in 1/4 cup hot water for 15 minutes until pliable, then pound or grind them with 8 garlic cloves and a splash of the soaking water into a coarse, brick-red paste.

Meanwhile knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 3/4 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and roughly 3/4 cup water into a soft, pliable dough; smear with a few drops of ghee and rest under a damp cloth for 20 minutes.
Simmer 1.5 cups green peas in boiling water for 4 minutes until tender, drain well and crush them coarsely so no whole peas remain to puncture the dough.

Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai over medium flame; sizzle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1/2 tsp ajwain for 30 seconds, add 1/4 tsp hing, then fry the chilli-garlic paste for 2 minutes until the raw garlic smell disappears and the ghee turns red.

Tip in the crushed peas with 2 tsp coriander powder, 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp amchur and 3/4 tsp salt; cook and stir for 4 minutes on medium heat until the filling is dry enough to hold its shape when pressed. Cool completely.
Portion the dough into 8 balls and the filling into 8 mounds of 2 tbsp each; cup each ball in your palm, tuck in the filling, twist the edges shut and flatten gently between your hands.
Roll each stuffed disc into a 6-inch round with light, outward strokes, dusting sparingly with dry atta, then roast on a medium-hot tava for around 2 minutes a side until crisp russet patches form.
Finish each paratha with a generous 1/2 tsp of the remaining Anveshan Ghee spooned over the hot surface so it soaks into the blisters before serving.
tips: Mathania or any sun-dried Kashmiri-style chilli gives colour with moderate heat; for a fiercer paratha keep the seeds, for milder discard them before soaking.
Fry the chilli-garlic paste until the ghee visibly separates and turns red, otherwise the filling tastes raw and sharp.
These parathas stay soft for hours, making them ideal travel food; wrap them in a clean muslin cloth while still warm.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a tall glass of salted chaas spiked with roasted jeera, a spoon of garlic chutney on the side and a few rings of raw onion sprinkled with lime.

variations.name: Bengali Spicy Matar Paratha
variations.description: Inspired by Kolkata's beloved koraishutir kochuri, this version cooks the spiced pea filling in pungent mustard oil with ginger, green chillies and a flutter of kalonji. The mustard oil is heated to its smoking point first, mellowing it into a deep, winey sharpness that defines Bengali winters.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: A wholesome khapli swap for the maida traditionally used in kochuri dough, with a nuttier bite

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed kachi ghani oil carries the nose-tingling pungency Bengali pea fillings depend on

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A final brush of ghee softens the mustard oil's edge and perfumes the crust

steps: Make the dough by rubbing 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 3/4 tsp salt, then adding about 3/4 cup water gradually; knead for 5 minutes to a supple, elastic ball and rest it, covered, for 20 minutes.
Blanch 1.5 cups green peas for 3 minutes in boiling water, drain, and blitz them with 4 green chillies and 1 tbsp ginger paste into a coarse, stiff paste without adding any water.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai until it just begins to smoke, about 2 minutes on high, then lower the flame and let it cool for 30 seconds so the raw pungency mellows.

Crackle 1/2 tsp kalonji in the oil for 20 seconds, add the pea paste with 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1/2 tsp sugar and 3/4 tsp salt, and stir-fry on medium for 5 to 6 minutes until the mixture forms a dry, rollable mass. Cool it fully.
Shape the dough into 8 balls, hollow each into a small katori, spoon in 2 tbsp of the pea filling, pleat the edges closed and rest the stuffed balls seam-side down for 5 minutes.
Roll each ball into a 6-inch disc using gentle strokes from the centre outward, flipping once midway so both faces stay smooth and the green filling shows faintly through the dough.
Cook on a medium-hot tava for roughly 2 minutes per side, drizzling the edges with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil, until crisp amber spots bloom across the surface.
Brush the finished parathas with 1 tbsp warm Anveshan Ghee and stack them under a cloth for 2 minutes so the crust softens slightly before serving.
tips: Always heat mustard oil to a light smoke and then cool it briefly; skipping this leaves an aggressive raw bite in the filling.
Grind the peas without water; a wet paste will leak through the dough and stick to the rolling pin.
The pinch of sugar is not for sweetness but to round out the peas, a signature of Bengali winter cooking.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Bengali way with a light aloor dom or simply a smear of kasundi mustard and thin cucumber slices, with sweet mishti doi to finish the meal.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Matar Paratha
variations.description: Andhra Pradesh brings its legendary Guntur chilli to the pea stuffing, tempered in wood-pressed groundnut oil with curry leaves and plenty of garlic. The filling is bold, garlicky and vividly red, mellowed just enough by the sweet peas so the heat builds sip by sip rather than scorching outright.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The sturdy emmer dough stands up to the oil-rich Guntur chilli filling without going limp

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the everyday fat of Andhra kitchens and lets the chilli flavour lead

steps: Bring the dough together with 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 3/4 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and close to 3/4 cup water; knead until soft and stretchy, then rest for 20 minutes under an inverted bowl.
Cook 1.5 cups green peas in boiling salted water for 4 minutes until they crush easily, drain thoroughly and mash them into a chunky mixture.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan on medium; pop 1/2 tsp mustard seeds, fry 1 tsp chana dal for 40 seconds until golden, then add 10 crushed garlic cloves and 12 curry leaves and fry for a minute until the garlic edges brown and the leaves crisp.

Lower the heat and stir in 2 tsp Guntur chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1/2 tsp turmeric for 20 seconds so the spices bloom in the oil without scorching, then add the mashed peas, 1 tsp tamarind pulp and 3/4 tsp salt.
Cook the filling for 4 to 5 minutes, mashing and turning, until it darkens to a deep red-green and no moisture pools at the bottom of the pan; spread it on a plate to cool.
Divide the dough into 8 pieces and the cooled filling into 8 balls of about 2 tbsp; stuff each dough round, seal the mouth tightly with a twist and flatten with your palm.

Roll into 6-inch rounds with light pressure, then roast on a medium-hot tava about 2 minutes per side, spooning the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil around the edges until both faces are freckled deep brown and crisp.
tips: Bloom the Guntur chilli powder off a low flame for only a few seconds; burnt chilli turns bitter and ruins the whole batch.
Frying a spoon of chana dal in the tempering adds the subtle crunch Andhra fillings are known for.
Tone the heat down by swapping half the Guntur powder for sweet paprika without losing the signature red colour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a katori of thick curd, a spoon of Andhra avakaya pickle and a slice of raw mango on the side; some sliced shallots dipped in salt make the perfect crunchy foil.

variations.name: Assamese Spicy Matar Paratha
variations.description: A daring take from the Northeast where a small measure of bhut jolokia, one of the world's hottest chillies, is tamed with ginger, fresh coriander and a squeeze of lime. Cooked in pungent mustard oil, the filling is bright, citrusy and fiercely aromatic, with the jolokia's fruity heat arriving as a slow, glowing finish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its gentle sweetness cushions the bhut jolokia's blaze better than refined flour would

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Assamese home cooking runs on sharp mustard oil; the wood-pressed version keeps its full aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Brushed on at the end, ghee carries the chilli's fruity notes and cools the palate

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 3/4 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and about 3/4 cup water into a smooth, springy dough; cover with a damp towel and set aside for 20 minutes.
Wearing gloves, deseed and mince half a bhut jolokia very finely; wash the knife and board immediately and do not touch your face while handling it.
Boil 1.5 cups green peas for 4 minutes until soft, drain them well and crush to a rough mash that still shows broken pea halves.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a wok until it shimmers and lightly smokes, about 90 seconds on high, then reduce the flame, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and fry the ginger juliennes for a minute until they curl and turn golden at the tips.

Add the minced jolokia and stir for just 15 seconds, then fold in the mashed peas, 1/4 cup spring onion greens and 3/4 tsp salt; cook on medium for 4 minutes until dry, switch off, and finish with 2 tsp lime juice and 1/4 cup chopped coriander. Cool completely.
Split the dough into 8 balls and the filling into 8 portions of 2 tbsp; encase each portion inside a flattened dough cup, pinch shut, and press flat between your palms.

Roll each one into a 6-inch circle, dusting lightly, and cook on a medium-hot tava for around 2 minutes per side, dabbing with the remaining 1/2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until crisp bronze patches appear.
Slick the hot parathas with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, rest them for a minute under a cloth, and serve while the crust still crackles.
tips: Half a deseeded bhut jolokia already delivers serious heat; first-timers should start with a quarter or substitute two regular green chillies.
Add the lime juice only after the pan is off the heat so its brightness survives and lifts the chilli's fruitiness.
Keep a bowl of sugar or a spoon of honey nearby when serving; water only spreads capsaicin burn while sweetness neutralises it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside a cooling Assamese-style mashed potato pitika with raw mustard oil and onions, plus a bowl of plain rice-washed curd to douse the jolokia's slow burn.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Methi Paratha
variations.description: The everyday North Indian methi paratha turned up a notch: fresh fenugreek leaves and green chillies are kneaded straight into khapli atta dough so every bite carries a pleasant bitterness and a slow chilli warmth. Roasting in bilona ghee gives the flatbread crisp, blistered edges and a soft, layered centre.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Stone-ground emmer wheat keeps this paratha soft for hours and adds a nutty depth that plain atta lacks

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee has a high smoke point, so the paratha crisps on the tava without any burnt aftertaste

steps: Wash 2 cups of chopped methi leaves in two changes of water, then squeeze them firmly between your palms and sprinkle over 1/4 tsp of the salt; rest 10 minutes and squeeze once more so the leaves release their bitter juice and will not make the dough sticky.

In a wide bowl combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with the squeezed methi, 3 minced green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp black pepper and the remaining salt, then rub in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until the flour looks like damp sand.

Add the 3/4 cup water a few tablespoons at a time, kneading for 6 to 8 minutes into a soft, pliable dough that springs back slowly when pressed and does not stick to your fingers; cover with a damp cloth and rest 15 minutes.
Divide the dough into 8 equal balls of roughly 60 g each, dust one ball with dry atta and roll it into a 15 cm round of even thickness, flouring lightly only when it starts to catch.

Heat a tava on medium-high for 2 minutes until a drop of water sizzles instantly, lay the paratha on it and cook 60 to 90 seconds until small bubbles rise and the underside shows pale brown freckles, then flip.

Spread 0.5 tsp Anveshan Ghee over the surface, flip again after a minute, ghee the second side and press the edges with a spatula until both faces are golden with deep brown spots, about 2 minutes more; repeat for all 8 parathas.
tips: Salting and squeezing the methi twice removes most of the harsh bitterness while keeping its aroma; skipping this makes the dough weep water as it rests.
If the dough turns sticky from the greens, knead in a tablespoon of dry khapli atta rather than extra water.
