Stack cooked parathas in a cloth-lined box so the steam keeps them supple for tiffin, up to 6 hours.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a bowl of thick salted curd, a wedge of lime and a spoon of mango pickle; on cold mornings pair it with masala chai sweetened with jaggery.

variations.name: Punjabi Spicy Methi Paratha
variations.description: A dhaba-style paratha from Punjab's wheat belt, where ajwain-scented dough meets a generous slather of white butter over the ghee-roasted crust. Crushed anardana adds a sour spark that plays against the fiery green chillies and the bitterness of winter methi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli's coarse bran gives the rustic, chewy bite Punjabi dhabas prize in their tandoori-style parathas

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasting in cultured bilona ghee recreates the smoky richness of a dhaba tava

steps: Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp ajwain in it for 30 seconds until it smells sharp and medicinal, then pour this tempering, ghee and all, over 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta in a paraat.

Rinse and squeeze 2 cups chopped methi dry, then add it to the flour along with 2 minced green chillies, 2 tsp anardana powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp salt, tossing everything until the greens are evenly flecked through.
Pour in 3/4 cup water in stages and knead vigorously for 8 minutes, slapping the dough against the bowl the dhaba way, until it feels supple like an earlobe; rest under a wet cloth for 20 minutes.

Pinch off 8 balls, roll each into a 12 cm disc, brush with a little of the ghee, fold into a half-moon and then a triangle, and roll again into a thick triangular paratha about 5 mm deep so it develops flaky layers.

Roast on a medium-hot tava for about 90 seconds per side until brown blisters form, then drizzle 0.5 tsp Anveshan Ghee around the edges and shallow-fry each side another minute, pressing with a cloth until the layers puff and crackle.
Slide onto a plate and immediately crown each hot paratha with 0.5 tbsp white butter so it melts into the crevices before serving.
tips: Crush the anardana coarsely just before using; pre-ground powder loses the fruity tang that defines this paratha.
The triangular double-fold traps ghee between layers, so do not skip it even when in a hurry.
Leftover parathas revive beautifully on a dry tava for 40 seconds a side; never microwave or they turn leathery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Do it the Amritsar way: serve with a tall glass of salted lassi, sliced onions sprinkled with chaat masala, and a ladle of homemade dahi on the side.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Spicy Methi Paratha
variations.description: Inspired by Maharashtra's thalipeeth tradition, this version folds warm, coconut-and-coriander scented goda masala, crushed roasted peanuts and toasted sesame into the methi dough. Wood-pressed groundnut oil on the tava gives it the toasty, nutty crust typical of Deccan griddle breads.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat's earthiness stands up to the strong goda masala better than refined flour ever could

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil doubles down on the peanut notes in the dough, a signature of Deccan griddle breads

steps: Toast 1 tbsp sesame seeds in a dry pan over low heat for 2 minutes, shaking constantly, until they turn pale gold and start to pop; tip them into a large mixing bowl to cool.

Add 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta to the bowl with 2 cups washed and squeezed methi leaves, 1/4 cup crushed roasted peanuts, 2 tsp goda masala, 2 minced green chillies, 3/4 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, then drizzle in 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and rub it through the flour.
Work in 3/4 cup water gradually and knead 7 minutes to a soft dough that holds a thumbprint without cracking; the peanuts should stay in visible coarse bits. Rest, covered, for 15 minutes.
Shape 8 balls and roll each between sheets of lightly oiled parchment into a 14 cm round about 4 mm thick, since the nutty dough is more delicate than plain atta dough.

Heat the tava on medium for 2 minutes, cook each paratha 90 seconds until the top surface dulls and bubbles appear, flip, then spoon 0.5 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil around the rim and roast until both sides carry deep golden patches, about 2 minutes more.
Press the edges gently with a folded cloth during the last 30 seconds so the thicker rim cooks through and turns crisp before you lift it off.
tips: Goda masala scorches quickly, so keep the tava at medium rather than high heat throughout.
If you cannot find goda masala, dry-roast 1 tsp coriander seeds, 2 cloves and 1 tbsp grated dry coconut, then grind; it is a close home approximation.
The dough keeps refrigerated for a day, but bring it back to room temperature before rolling or it will crack at the edges.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Kolhapur way with a dollop of thecha (green chilli-garlic crush), a katori of dahi and slivers of raw onion; it also pairs superbly with pithla.

variations.name: Bengali Spicy Methi Paratha
variations.description: West Bengal's love for pungent mustard oil transforms this paratha: the dough is kneaded with kalonji bloomed in smoking-hot shorshe tel, giving it the unmistakable sharp aroma of a Kolkata kitchen. A hint of sugar balances the methi's bitterness, a very Bengali touch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli's low gluten keeps this mustard-oil dough tender instead of tough, ideal for triangular Bengali porota

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Cold wood-pressed kachi ghani oil carries the nose-tingling pungency that defines Bengali griddle breads

steps: Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a small kadai over medium-high heat until it just begins to smoke and its raw pungency softens, about 90 seconds, then drop in 1 tsp kalonji and let it sputter for 20 seconds off the heat.

Pour the kalonji tempering over 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, add 2 cups squeezed chopped methi, 3 minced green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 0.5 tsp sugar, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 3/4 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, and toss until the oil darkens the flour evenly.
Knead with 3/4 cup water added gradually for about 7 minutes until you have a smooth, springy dough that leaves the bowl clean; cover and rest 15 minutes so the bran hydrates fully.

Divide into 8 portions, roll each into a 12 cm circle, brush lightly with mustard oil, fold in half and in half again, then roll the triangle out to a 5 mm thickness the way Bengali porotas are shaped.

Cook on a medium tava for 1 to 2 minutes per side until beige spots deepen to brown, then drizzle 0.5 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil around each side and fry 45 seconds more until the layers separate visibly and the edges crisp.
Rest the finished porotas upright against a bowl for a minute rather than stacking flat, so the crust stays crackly while the inside stays flaky.
tips: Always smoke the mustard oil once and cool it slightly; raw kachi ghani oil can taste unpleasantly acrid in dough.
The pinch of sugar is not for sweetness; it rounds off methi's bitterness the way Bengali cooks balance shukto.
For extra flake, chill the folded triangles 10 minutes before the final rolling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with alur dom or simply a smear of kasundi and cucumber slices; a cup of milky Darjeeling tea completes the Kolkata breakfast picture.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Methi Paratha
variations.description: Andhra's famous Guntur chillies set this paratha ablaze, mellowed by a garlicky sesame-oil tadka and crisp curry leaves crushed into the dough. It borrows the spirit of karam podi rotis served in Vijayawada homes, where every flatbread is expected to bite back.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The wholegrain sweetness of emmer tempers Guntur chilli heat so the paratha stays fiery yet moreish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil is the traditional Andhra roasting fat, lending a deep toasted aroma to the crust

steps: Make the tadka first: heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a small pan on medium, pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds for 30 seconds, then fry 6 minced garlic cloves and 12 curry leaves for about a minute until the garlic is pale gold and the leaves are translucent and crisp.

Scrape the entire tadka, oil included, into a bowl holding 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 2 cups washed and squeezed methi, 2 tsp Guntur chilli powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, crushing the fried curry leaves between your fingers as they go in.
Add 3/4 cup water little by little and knead for 7 to 8 minutes until the dough is soft and stretchy with a faint red hue throughout; cover with a damp cloth and rest 15 minutes.
Portion into 8 balls of about 60 g, dust with dry flour and roll each to a 15 cm round, keeping the pressure even so the fiery flecks do not tear the surface.

Roast on a tava preheated over medium-high for 2 minutes: cook the first side 60 to 90 seconds until bubbles swell, flip, spread 0.5 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, flip again and press until both faces show crisp mahogany spots, roughly 2 minutes.
Finish each paratha with a few drops more of the hot gingelly oil brushed over the top the moment it leaves the tava, so the chilli aroma blooms.
tips: Guntur chilli delivers slow, building heat; halve it to 1 tsp for children and add a squeeze of lime instead.
Frying the garlic only to pale gold matters, since darker garlic turns bitter next to methi.
These parathas taste even better an hour later once the chilli oil settles into the crumb, making them ideal for lunchboxes.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with cooling curd rice or a katori of thick perugu, plus a spoon of avakaya pickle for the brave; gongura chutney on the side is pure Andhra.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Mushroom
variations.description: The everyday North Indian mushroom masala that turns a humble fungus into a weeknight star — button mushrooms seared until browned, then tossed through a sharp onion-tomato masala punched up with green chillies and freshly crushed black pepper. The finish is dry-ish and glossy, the kind of sabzi that disappears before the rotis do.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed, so it stays nutty and stable at the high heat needed to sear mushrooms

steps: Wipe 500 g button mushrooms with a damp cloth instead of washing them, then quarter them; finely chop 2 medium onions and 3 medium tomatoes and slit 3 green chillies lengthwise.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sunflower Oil in a heavy kadhai on high heat, spread the quartered mushrooms in a single layer and sear undisturbed for 3-4 minutes until the edges turn golden brown, then lift them out and set aside.
In the same kadhai on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 30 seconds, add the chopped onions with a small pinch of salt and saute for 6-7 minutes until deep golden at the edges.

Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the slit green chillies and fry for 1 minute until the raw smell fades, then add the chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder.
Cook the masala on medium for 5-6 minutes, mashing occasionally, until it thickens and the oil separates at the sides of the pan.
Return the seared mushrooms along with 1 tsp salt, toss well, and cook uncovered on medium-high for 4-5 minutes so the moisture they release reduces into a thick masala that clings to each piece.
Crush 1 tsp black peppercorns coarsely, sprinkle over the mushrooms with 3 tbsp chopped coriander leaves, toss once and switch off while the mushrooms are still springy and juicy.
tips: Searing the mushrooms separately on high heat before they meet the masala keeps them meaty instead of rubbery and watery.
If the sabzi looks watery at the end, raise the heat and toss constantly for 2 minutes rather than covering the pan — trapped steam makes mushrooms limp.
Swap half the button mushrooms for oyster mushrooms for a meatier bite; sear them exactly the same way.
variations.servingSuggestion: Roll it into hot phulkas with sliced onions and a squeeze of lime for a quick kathi-style wrap, or serve beside dal-chawal on a weeknight thali.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Mushroom
variations.description: A fiery, garlic-forward vepudu from the Guntur belt, where the local sun-dried chillies do the talking. Mushrooms are stir-fried in gingelly oil with crushed garlic, curry leaves and a double hit of Guntur chilli — whole and powdered — for a dish that is brick-red, dry and unapologetically hot.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed gingelly oil, the traditional Andhra frying medium that deepens the chilli flavour

steps: Clean 500 g button mushrooms with a dry cloth and slice them thick; crush 8 garlic cloves roughly with the flat of a knife and slice 2 medium onions thin.

Warm 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a wide pan on medium-high, pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, then drop in 3 whole dried Guntur chillies torn in half and 2 sprigs of curry leaves — they should splutter and crisp within 20 seconds.
Add the crushed garlic and fry for about 1 minute until it smells toasty and turns pale gold, then tip in the sliced onions and saute for 5-6 minutes until they soften and brown at the edges.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 4-5 minutes on medium until they collapse into a jammy base.

Raise the heat, add the sliced mushrooms with 2 tsp Guntur red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, and stir-fry for 6-7 minutes until the liquid evaporates and the masala turns brick-red and dry.
Take the pan off the heat, shower over 2 tbsp chopped coriander leaves and rest the vepudu for 2 minutes so the chilli heat settles into the mushrooms.
tips: Tearing the dried Guntur chillies before tempering releases their seeds and gives the oil a deeper, smokier burn.
If Guntur chilli powder is too fierce for your table, cut it 50-50 with Kashmiri chilli powder to keep the colour but soften the heat.
This dish is meant to be dry — keep the flame high in the final stir-fry and never cover the pan.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot steamed rice, a spoon of Anveshan Ghee melted on top and a bowl of chilled curd on the side to tame the Guntur fire.

variations.name: Kerala Spicy Mushroom
variations.description: A Malabar-style pepper roast where mushrooms are slow-tossed with golden shallots, crunchy coconut slivers and crushed black pepper in virgin coconut oil. The heat here comes from pepper rather than chilli powder, giving a warm, aromatic burn with fennel sweetness underneath — toddy-shop food at its best.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed virgin oil whose aroma is the backbone of any Kerala roast

steps: Halve 500 g button mushrooms, peel and halve 12 shallots, julienne 1 inch of ginger, slice 5 garlic cloves and cut 0.25 cup of fresh coconut into thin slivers.
Coarsely pound 2 tsp black peppercorns with 0.5 tsp fennel seeds in a mortar — the mix should be gritty, not powdery, so it toasts rather than burns.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a cheena chatti or wok on medium, fry the coconut slivers for 2-3 minutes until they turn light brown and nutty, then push them to the side.
Add the shallots, ginger, garlic, 2 slit green chillies and 2 sprigs of curry leaves and saute for 5-6 minutes until the shallots are glossy and golden.
Tip in the halved mushrooms with 0.25 tsp turmeric powder and 1 tsp salt and toss on high heat for 5-6 minutes until their released water cooks off and the pieces start to brown.

Lower the heat, sprinkle the pounded pepper-fennel mix and 0.5 tsp garam masala over the mushrooms and roast, tossing every 30 seconds, for 3-4 minutes until every piece is coated in a dark, peppery crust.
Finish with the remaining sprig of curry leaves crisped in the hot pan for a few seconds before switching off.
tips: Pound the pepper just before cooking — pre-ground pepper loses the citrusy top notes that define this roast.
Shallots are worth the peeling effort here; regular onions turn the dish sweet and watery.
For toddy-shop authenticity, let the mushrooms sit in the hot pan for 2 minutes after switching off so a slight char develops at the bottom.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best with Kerala matta rice and moru curry, or tucked into a flaky Malabar parotta as a late-night snack.

variations.name: Bengali Spicy Mushroom
variations.description: A pungent, homestyle chorchori-inspired dish where mushrooms and cubed potato are cooked in raw-edged mustard oil with kalonji and a fresh mustard-seed paste. Slit green chillies bring the heat and a whisper of jaggery rounds off the sharpness, in true Bengali sweet-heat balance.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed kachi ghani whose sharp pungency is the soul of this Bengali preparation

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a spoon of unrefined sweetness that balances the bite of mustard, the Bengali way

steps: Soak 1.5 tbsp yellow mustard seeds in 3 tbsp warm water for 15 minutes, then grind with 1 green chilli and a pinch of salt into a smooth, sharp paste.
Quarter 500 g button mushrooms, dice 1 medium potato into 1 cm cubes, slice 1 onion and chop 1 tomato while the mustard soaks.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai on medium-high until it just begins to smoke, then lower the heat for 30 seconds so the raw pungency mellows without losing character.
Crackle 0.5 tsp kalonji in the oil, add the potato cubes and fry for 5-6 minutes on medium, stirring now and then, until they turn golden at the corners.
Add the sliced onion and cook for 3 minutes until translucent, then stir in the tomato, 0.5 tsp turmeric powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 2-3 minutes until soft.
Add the quartered mushrooms and the remaining 3 slit green chillies and cook uncovered on medium-high for 5 minutes, letting the mushroom liquor loosen the masala and then reduce.

Lower the flame, stir in the mustard paste and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder with a splash of water, and simmer gently for 3 minutes — do not boil hard or the mustard turns bitter — then scatter 2 tbsp coriander leaves and cover for 1 minute off the heat.
tips: Always soak mustard seeds before grinding; grinding them dry makes the paste bitter rather than sharp.
Letting the mustard oil reach its first wisp of smoke before cooking is non-negotiable for the authentic jhanj (pungency).
This tastes even better after resting 30 minutes, once the mustard settles into the potatoes and mushrooms.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steaming gobindobhog or basmati rice and a wedge of gondhoraj or regular lime — the citrus lifts the mustard beautifully.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Spicy Mushroom
variations.description: A rustic rassa-style dry mushroom preparation built on goda masala — Maharashtra's smoky, faintly sweet spice blend — with toasted dry coconut and sesame seeds ground into the masala. Cooked in wood-pressed groundnut oil, it has the deep, earthy character of village kitchens along the Deccan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed and full-bodied, the everyday cooking fat of Maharashtrian homes

steps: Dry-roast 3 tbsp grated dry coconut and 1 tsp white sesame seeds in a pan on low heat for 3-4 minutes until the coconut turns biscuit-brown, then grind coarsely with 6 garlic cloves and half of 1 chopped onion.
Thickly slice 500 g button mushrooms, chop the remaining 1.5 onions fine and chop 2 medium tomatoes.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium, splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, then fry the chopped onions for 6-7 minutes until they turn a deep golden brown.
Add the coconut-sesame-garlic paste and fry for 3-4 minutes, stirring constantly, until it darkens a shade and smells toasted.
Mix in the tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 4-5 minutes until the masala thickens and oil beads appear at the edges.
Fold in the sliced mushrooms with 2 tsp goda masala and cook uncovered on medium-high for 6-7 minutes, tossing often, until the mushrooms are tender and coated in a dark, clinging masala.
Sprinkle 3 tbsp chopped coriander leaves, toss once more and rest for 2 minutes before serving so the goda masala blooms fully.
tips: Goda masala burns quickly — always add it with the mushrooms, never into hot oil directly.
Roast the dry coconut low and slow; even slightly burnt coconut will turn the whole dish acrid.
No goda masala at hand? Use garam masala plus a pinch of stone flower (dagad phool) powder for a close approximation.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with soft jowar or bajra bhakri and a raw onion wedge, dhaba-on-the-Deccan style; leftover masala is superb stuffed into a vada pav.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Sattu Paratha
variations.description: The everyday fire-breather of Bihar's kitchens: a soft khapli atta shell hiding a crumbly roasted-gram filling punched up with green chillies, crushed black pepper and lemon. The filling stays slightly loose and nutty, so every bite spills warm, spiced sattu. Roasted in bilona ghee, the crust blisters and crisps while the inside stays moist.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Stone-ground emmer wheat keeps the shell soft and pliable, so the spicy filling never tears through

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Slow-roasted chana sattu has a deep toasty flavour that carries the green-chilli heat beautifully

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A2 bilona ghee crisps the crust and mellows the chilli burn with its caramel aroma

steps: Rub 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 1/2 tsp salt into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, then add about 3/4 cup water a little at a time and knead for 8 minutes to a soft, non-sticky dough. Cover with a damp cloth and rest for 20 minutes.

In a wide bowl, combine 1 cup Anveshan Sattu with the chopped onion, 3 minced green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 3/4 tsp crushed black pepper, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1/2 tsp salt, 3 tbsp coriander leaves and 1 tbsp lemon juice.

Sprinkle 2 to 3 tsp water and 1 tsp melted Anveshan Ghee over the sattu mixture and mix with your fingertips until it just clumps when pressed in a fist but still crumbles apart; it must not turn pasty.

Divide the rested dough into 8 equal balls. Flatten each into a small cup, place 2 tbsp of the sattu filling in the centre, gather the edges over the top, pinch to seal and rest the stuffed balls for 5 minutes.
Dust lightly with dry atta and roll each ball gently into a 6 to 7 inch round, applying even pressure so the filling does not burst through the edges.

Cook each paratha on a medium-hot tava for about 2 minutes per side until brown spots appear, then brush 1/2 tsp Anveshan Ghee on each side and press with a spatula until both faces are blistered, golden and lightly crisp, about 1 more minute per side.
tips: If the filling feels too dry and pours out while rolling, work in another teaspoon of water; if it turns sticky, rescue it with a spoonful of dry sattu.
The stuffed balls can be assembled up to 4 hours ahead and refrigerated under a damp cloth; roll and roast straight from the fridge.
Keep the tava at medium heat: too hot and the crust chars before the filling warms through, too low and the paratha turns leathery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with smoky baingan chokha, a wedge of lime and a tall glass of salted chaas to cool the pepper heat.

variations.name: Bihari Spicy Sattu Paratha
variations.description: The homeland version, eaten from Patna to Gaya, where the sattu filling is anointed with raw pungent mustard oil and a spoon of tangy mango pickle masala. Ajwain and kalonji are crackled in hot mustard oil before going in, giving the stuffing its unmistakable sharp, achari edge. It is rustic, fiery and intensely savoury.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli wheat mirrors the coarse desi atta used in Bihari homes and browns evenly on the tava

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Authentic Bihari flavour starts with properly roasted chana sattu that smells of the bhaad furnace

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed kachi ghani oil brings the nose-tingling pungency that defines this filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasting the paratha in bilona ghee balances the raw bite of the mustard oil inside

ingredients.name: Mango pickle masala, mashed from the jar

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt and roughly 3/4 cup water for 7 to 8 minutes until soft and springy but not sticky, then cover and set aside for 20 minutes.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a small pan until it just begins to smoke, switch off the heat, then drop in 1/2 tsp ajwain and 1/2 tsp kalonji and let them crackle for 20 seconds in the residual heat.

Pour this seed-infused oil over 1 cup Anveshan Sattu in a bowl, then add the onion, 4 minced garlic cloves, 2 green chillies, 1 tbsp mashed mango pickle masala, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 2 tbsp coriander; the mixture should hold together loosely when squeezed.
Shape the dough into 8 balls, press each into a bowl shape, spoon 2 tbsp of the achari sattu filling inside, twist the edges shut and flatten gently between your palms.
Roll each stuffed ball into a 6 inch disc with light, outward strokes, dusting with dry atta so the pungent filling stays sealed within.

Roast on a medium-hot tava for 2 minutes on the first side until speckled brown, flip, spread 1/2 tsp Anveshan Ghee over the surface and cook, pressing the edges, until both sides are deep golden and crisp, about 2 more minutes.
tips: Smoking the mustard oil before tempering removes its raw harshness while keeping the signature pungency intact.
Use the oily masala clinging to mango pickle pieces rather than the pieces themselves for an even distribution of tang.
These taste closest to a Bihari roadside dhaba when eaten within 10 minutes of leaving the tava, while the crust still crackles.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with chokha of roasted tomatoes and potatoes, a raw onion wedge and a final drizzle of mustard oil at the table, dhaba style.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Sattu Paratha
variations.description: A Deccan-style reinvention where the sattu filling meets fiery Guntur chilli powder, plenty of garlic and toasted sesame, echoing the flavours of Andhra podi. Roasting the paratha in nutty sesame oil gives the crust a deep, toasted aroma that stands up to the chilli. Expect slow-building, lingering heat rather than a sharp sting.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The sweet nuttiness of emmer wheat tempers the aggressive Guntur chilli heat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Roasted gram flour behaves like a podi base here, soaking up the garlic and chilli oils

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed gingelly oil is the classic Andhra roasting fat and doubles the toasty sesame notes

steps: Combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and about 3/4 cup water, kneading for 8 minutes until the dough is supple and bounces back slowly when pressed. Rest it, covered, for 20 minutes.
Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a small kadai over medium heat, add 6 minced garlic cloves and 10 shredded curry leaves, and fry for about 90 seconds until the garlic turns pale gold and fragrant.
Take the kadai off the heat and stir in 2 tsp Guntur red chilli powder for 10 seconds so it blooms in the warm oil without scorching, then scrape everything into a bowl with 1 cup Anveshan Sattu.

Add the chopped onion, 1 tbsp toasted sesame seeds, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 2 tbsp coriander to the sattu, then sprinkle 2 tsp water and mix until the filling clumps softly.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, stuff each with 2 tbsp of the garlicky chilli filling, seal the seams tightly and roll into 6 inch rounds with gentle, even strokes.

Roast each round on a medium tava, giving it 2 minutes per side, then drizzle 1/2 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil around the edges and cook another minute per side until the surface is crisp with deep brown patches.
tips: Blooming the Guntur chilli powder off the heat keeps its bright red colour and prevents an acrid burnt taste.
For genuine Andhra intensity use chilli powder made from whole Guntur sannam chillies rather than a generic blend; reduce to 1 tsp for a family-friendly version.
Leftover filling makes an excellent podi-style sprinkle over hot rice with a spoonful of ghee.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of chilled curd rice or thick perugu on the side; the cool dairy is the traditional Andhra counterweight to Guntur heat.

variations.name: Rajasthani Spicy Sattu Paratha
variations.description: A desert-kitchen take built for shelf life and bold flavour: no onion, no garlic, just crushed dried red chillies, hing and roasted coriander seeds folded into the sattu, in the manner of Marwari travel food. Amchur supplies the sour lift that fresh produce would in other regions. Generous ghee inside and out keeps every bite rich and crumbly.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Hardy khapli wheat rolls out thin without cracking, ideal for this dry desert-style filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Protein-dense sattu was the Marwari traveller's fuel; here it drinks up the chilli-hing ghee

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rajasthani cooking is unapologetically ghee-forward; bilona ghee perfumes both filling and crust

steps: Make the dough by working 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 1/2 tsp salt into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, then adding around 3/4 cup water gradually and kneading 8 minutes to a soft, smooth ball. Rest under a damp cloth for 20 minutes.

On a dry tava over low heat, roast 4 dried red chillies and 2 tsp coriander seeds for about 2 minutes, tossing constantly, until the chillies darken slightly and smell smoky; cool and crush coarsely in a mortar.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan on medium, crackle 1/2 tsp ajwain for 15 seconds, add 1/4 tsp hing, then immediately pour this tempering over 1 cup Anveshan Sattu in a mixing bowl.

Stir the crushed chilli-coriander mix, 1 tsp amchur, 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1/2 tsp salt and 2 tbsp coriander leaves into the sattu, sprinkling 3 to 4 tsp water until the filling presses together like damp sand.
Portion the dough into 8 balls, stuff each with 2 tbsp of the chilli-sattu filling, pinch firmly closed and roll out into 6 inch discs, flouring lightly as needed.

Cook on a medium-hot tava for around 2 minutes a side until dry brown spots form, then lavish 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee over each paratha and roast a further minute per side until flaky, crisp and deeply golden.
tips: Crush the roasted chillies coarsely, not to a powder; the little flakes give the classic Rajasthani bursts of heat.
Because the filling contains no onion, these parathas keep well for a full day at room temperature, making them ideal tiffin or travel food.
If you cannot handle whole-chilli heat, shake out the seeds before roasting; the smokiness stays, the fire softens.
variations.servingSuggestion: Present the Marwari way with lehsun ki chutney, a lump of churned white makkhan and sweet-sour ker sangri or plain dahi on the side.

variations.name: Assamese Spicy Sattu Paratha
variations.description: A Northeast-inspired scorcher that borrows Assam's legendary bhut jolokia, used in a cautious half-piece, with raw shallots, ginger and a squeeze of lemon in the sattu. Kneading and roasting in pungent mustard oil ties it to the Brahmaputra valley's everyday cooking. Fruity, floral chilli heat blooms a second or two after each bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The gentle sweetness of khapli wheat is a welcome buffer against the ghost chilli's intensity

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Earthy roasted gram cushions and carries the fruity bhut jolokia heat evenly through the filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Kachi ghani mustard oil is the backbone of Assamese kitchens, sharp and grassy

ingredients.name: Bhut jolokia chilli, deseeded and minced

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and close to 3/4 cup water for 8 minutes until soft, stretchy and non-sticky; rest covered for 20 minutes.

Wearing gloves, deseed and mince 1/2 a bhut jolokia very finely, then heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a small pan until it shimmers and fry the chilli with 4 sliced shallots for about 2 minutes until the shallots soften and turn translucent.

Tip the shallot-chilli mixture over 1 cup Anveshan Sattu and add 1 inch grated ginger, 1/2 tsp crushed black pepper, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1/2 tsp salt, 1.5 tbsp lemon juice and 3 tbsp coriander leaves.
Work 2 to 3 tsp water into the mixture with your fingers until it holds its shape when squeezed yet crumbles at a touch, tasting a pinch carefully to gauge the chilli level.
Divide the dough into 8 portions, cup each ball, fill with 2 tbsp of the fiery sattu mix, seal the top and roll into thin 6 to 7 inch rounds.

Roast on a medium tava for 2 minutes until the underside is freckled brown, flip, smear 1/2 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil on top and cook, flipping once more, until both sides are crisp and burnished, roughly 3 more minutes in total.
tips: Always wear gloves when handling bhut jolokia and never touch your face; wash the knife and board immediately with soapy water.
Start with a quarter chilli if you are new to ghost peppers; you can knead extra minced chilli into leftover filling later but you cannot take it out.
A teaspoon of sugar in the accompanying curd tames the burn better than water ever will.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside a cooling bowl of plain curd, sliced cucumber and a wedge of Assam lemon, letting each diner brace for the slow-blooming heat.

variations.name: Classic Stuffed Beetroot Paratha
variations.description: A jewel-toned North Indian breakfast paratha where sweet, earthy grated beetroot is sautéed with ginger and warm spices, then tucked inside a soft khapli wheat shell. The filling is cooked dry so the paratha rolls out clean without tearing, and slow-roasting in bilona ghee gives the crust a nutty, blistered finish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat's low gluten keeps this stuffed paratha soft for hours, so it never turns leathery in a tiffin

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee's high smoke point lets the beetroot sugars caramelise on the tava without burning

steps: Mix 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp of the salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then knead in about 1 cup water a little at a time until you have a soft, non-sticky dough. Cover and rest it for 15 minutes while you make the filling.
Peel and grate 2 medium beetroots on the fine side of the grater, then squeeze the shreds firmly in your fist over a bowl to press out as much juice as possible; a wet filling will tear the paratha.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium heat and let 1 tsp cumin seeds sizzle and crackle for about 30 seconds. Add the minced 1 inch ginger and 2 chopped green chillies and fry for 1 minute until fragrant.

Add the squeezed beetroot with 1 tsp coriander powder, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric and the remaining 1/2 tsp salt. Cook on medium heat for 5 to 6 minutes, stirring, until the mixture looks dry and glossy, then stir in 1/2 tsp amchur and 2 tbsp chopped coriander leaves and cool completely.
Divide the dough into 8 equal balls. Flatten one ball into a 3 inch cup, place 2 tbsp of the cooled beetroot filling in the centre, gather the edges over the top and pinch firmly to seal.
Dust the stuffed ball lightly with dry atta and roll it gently into a 6 inch round, using even pressure so the pink filling does not burst through the dough.

Roast each paratha on a hot tava on medium-high heat for about 2 minutes per side, brushing both sides with the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, until deep golden-brown spots appear and the surface puffs in patches. Repeat with all 8 parathas.
tips: Squeeze the grated beetroot twice, once before and once after salting, and save the crimson juice to knead into your next batch of dough for pink rotis.
Cool the filling fully before stuffing; warm filling releases steam and makes the dough soggy at the seams.
If a paratha tears while rolling, dab the tear with dry atta and roll only from the edges instead of the centre.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve two parathas per person with a bowl of thick salted curd, a wedge of lime and a sharp mango pickle; the cool curd plays beautifully against the sweet beetroot.

variations.name: Punjabi Stuffed Beetroot Paratha
variations.description: This is the dhaba treatment: a generously stuffed, sturdily rolled paratha spiked with ajwain and anardana, roasted until crisp and then crowned with a melting spoon of white butter. The filling gets pomegranate-seed tang and a coarse crush of coriander seeds for that unmistakable Punjab crunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Stone-ground khapli gives this dhaba-style paratha the rustic bite Punjabi tandoor breads are loved for

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasting in bilona ghee builds the shattering, layered crust that white butter then melts into

steps: Knead 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and roughly 1 cup water into a smooth, pliable dough that springs back slowly when pressed. Rest it under a damp cloth for 20 minutes.

Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan over medium heat, crackle 1/2 tsp ajwain and 1 tsp coarsely crushed coriander seeds for 30 seconds, then tip in 1 finely chopped small onion and fry for 3 minutes until light gold.

Add 2 medium beetroots, grated and squeezed dry, along with 3/4 tsp red chilli powder, 1/2 tsp garam masala and the remaining 1/2 tsp salt. Cook for 6 minutes on medium heat until the filling is dry enough to hold its shape when pressed, then mix in 1 tsp anardana powder and 3 tbsp chopped coriander and cool.

Shape the dough into 8 balls, press each into a wide cup and pack 2 heaped tbsp of filling inside. Pull the dough over the filling, twist off the excess at the top and flatten gently between your palms.
Roll each stuffed ball on a floured board into a thick 6 to 7 inch round; Punjabi parathas stay slightly thick so the crust can crisp while the middle steams.

Cook on a hot tava over medium-high heat, pressing the edges with a spatula, about 2.5 minutes per side with 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee shared between the parathas, until both faces are crisp and mottled deep brown.
Slide each hot paratha onto a plate and immediately top with 1/2 tbsp white butter per paratha so it melts into the crust before serving.
tips: Crush the coriander seeds coarsely on a chakla with a rolling pin rather than grinding them; the little shards are the signature dhaba crunch.
For an authentic sour edge, add an extra 1/2 tsp anardana instead of amchur, which keeps the filling dry.
Press the paratha edges firmly on the tava with a folded cloth so the thick rim cooks through and crisps.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a tall glass of salted lassi and sliced raw onion rings dipped in vinegar; in Punjab this paratha is breakfast, lunch and a challenge all at once.

variations.name: Bengali Stuffed Beetroot Paratha
variations.description: Bengal cooks its beloved winter beets in pungent mustard oil with kalonji and slit green chillies, and this paratha bottles that exact flavour. The raw bite of mustard oil mellows on the tava into a smoky sharpness that flatters the beet's sweetness far better than any neutral fat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli's gentle sweetness echoes the beet, so the mustard oil's pungency stays the star of this Bengali take

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed kachi ghani oil smoked to its haze point gives the filling its true Bengali nose-tingle

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A last brush of ghee on the roasted paratha rounds off the mustard oil's edge, the classic Bengali finish

steps: Make the dough by rubbing 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil into 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, then kneading in about 1 cup water until soft and springy. Rest, covered, for 15 minutes.
Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai on medium-high until it just begins to smoke and its raw smell fades, about 1 minute, then reduce the heat to medium.
Scatter in 1/2 tsp kalonji and 3 slit green chillies and let them pop for 20 seconds, then add 1 inch of grated ginger and stir for another 30 seconds until aromatic.

Add 2 medium grated and well-squeezed beetroots with 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1/2 tsp sugar and the remaining 1/2 tsp salt. Fry for 6 to 7 minutes until the beet darkens and turns dry, then finish with 1/2 tsp roasted cumin powder and cool the mixture fully.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, stuff each with 2 tbsp of the beet mixture, seal the mouth tightly and roll out to a 6 inch round with light, even strokes.

Roast each paratha on a medium-hot tava for about 2 minutes per side until freckled brown, then brush the hot surface of each with a little of the 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee just before taking it off the heat.
tips: Always let mustard oil smoke lightly and cool for a few seconds before adding spices, otherwise the filling tastes raw and bitter.
The 1/2 tsp sugar is not optional in a Bengali kitchen; it deepens the beet's colour and balances the mustard's heat.
Leftover filling makes an excellent beetroot bhorta the next day, mashed with a raw drizzle of the same mustard oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a smear of kasundi mustard and a simple aloo bhaja on the side, the way a Kolkata home would round off a Sunday jolkhabar.

variations.name: Kerala Stuffed Beetroot Paratha
variations.description: Inspired by the beetroot thoran of Kerala's lunch messes, this filling folds fresh grated coconut, curry leaves and crackled mustard seeds through the beets, all sautéed in cold-pressed coconut oil. The coconut keeps the stuffing loose and fragrant, so every bite tastes of a coastal kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The nutty emmer wheat wrapper stands in beautifully for a Malabar parotta without any maida

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil perfumes the thoran-style filling exactly like a Kerala tharavad kitchen

steps: Knead 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and close to 1 cup water into a supple dough, then let it relax under a damp cloth for 15 minutes.

Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a wide pan over medium heat and pop 1 tsp mustard seeds fully, about 40 seconds, before adding 12 curry leaves and letting them crisp for a few seconds.
Add 4 sliced shallots and 2 chopped green chillies and sauté for 2 minutes until the shallots soften and smell sweet.

Tip in 2 medium beetroots, grated and squeezed of their juice, with 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1/2 tsp black pepper powder and the remaining 1/2 tsp salt, and cook for 5 minutes until nearly dry. Fold in 1/2 cup fresh grated coconut, cook 2 more minutes until the mixture clumps softly, and cool completely.
Portion the dough into 8 balls and stuff each with 2 tbsp of the cooled coconut-beet filling, pinching the seam shut before dusting with atta.
Roll each ball gently to a 6 inch circle and roast on a medium-hot tava for around 2 minutes per side, drizzling the edges with a few drops of coconut oil, until golden patches bloom on both faces.
tips: Squeeze the coconut and beet mixture in your palm before stuffing; if liquid seeps out, return it to the pan for 2 more minutes.
Frozen grated coconut works, but thaw and dry-toast it for a minute so it does not water down the filling.
Tear, do not chop, the curry leaves into the filling for bursts of aroma in every bite.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a small bowl of moru curry or plain buttermilk spiked with ginger and curry leaves, keeping the whole plate light and coastal.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Stuffed Beetroot Paratha
variations.description: Goda masala, Maharashtra's smoky-sweet blend with dagad phool and coconut, turns the beet filling deep and complex, while crushed roasted peanuts add the crunch of a proper Deccan bhaji. Roasted in groundnut oil, this paratha tastes like a Puneri lunchbox at its best.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli is an old Deccan staple, so this wrapper is closer to the original Maharashtrian ghadichi poli than modern atta

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil doubles down on the peanut notes that anchor this goda masala filling

steps: Combine 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, then knead with roughly 1 cup water into a soft dough and rest it for 15 minutes under a plate.
Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai over medium heat, crackle 1/2 tsp mustard seeds for about 30 seconds, then add 1/4 tsp asafoetida and let it foam for 5 seconds.
Add 2 medium beetroots, grated and firmly squeezed, along with 1/4 tsp turmeric and the remaining 1/2 tsp salt, and sauté for 5 minutes until the shreds soften and dry out.

Stir in 1.5 tsp goda masala, 1 tsp crumbled jaggery and 1/4 cup coarsely crushed roasted peanuts, cook 2 more minutes until the masala smells toasty, then mix in 2 tbsp chopped coriander and cool the filling completely.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, cup each one open, pack in 2 tbsp of filling, seal the pleats at the top and flatten into a thick disc.
Roll every disc to about 6 inches and roast on a medium-hot tava for 2 minutes per side, pressing gently with a spatula, until both sides carry crisp brown freckles and the peanuts smell toasted.
tips: Goda masala scorches quickly, so always add it after the beetroot has softened, never into hot oil directly.
Pulse the peanuts to a coarse rubble, not a powder; whole halves tear the dough while powder disappears into the filling.
A pinch of extra jaggery rescues the filling if your goda masala batch runs bitter from dagad phool.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a spoon of shengdana chutney and fresh buttermilk seasoned with cumin, the classic Puneri thali companions.

variations.name: Classic Stuffed Carrot Paratha
variations.description: A winter-morning North Indian favourite where sweet red carrots are sautéed with ginger and cumin, then tucked inside a soft khapli wheat crust. The filling is cooked dry so the paratha rolls out without tearing, and each bite balances the carrot's natural sweetness with warm garam masala. Ghee-roasting gives it crisp, blistered spots and a rich aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat's low gluten keeps the stuffed crust tender, never chewy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee for the dough, the filling tadka and tava-roasting

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 3/4 cup water into a soft, pliable dough that springs back slowly when pressed. Cover and rest for 20 minutes so the emmer wheat hydrates fully.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 30 seconds until fragrant. Add 1 inch grated ginger and 2 finely chopped green chillies and stir for 30 seconds.

Add 2 cups grated carrot with 1/2 tsp salt and sauté on medium-high for 5 to 6 minutes until the moisture evaporates and the carrot looks dry and glossy. A wet filling will tear the paratha, so keep stirring until no steam rises.

Stir in 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder, 1/2 tsp garam masala and 1/2 tsp amchur, cook 1 minute more, then mix in 3 tbsp chopped coriander. Spread the filling on a plate and cool completely, about 10 minutes.
Divide the dough into 8 equal balls. Flatten each into a 3-inch cup, place 2 tbsp of carrot filling in the centre, gather the edges over the top, pinch to seal and press flat.

Dust with dry atta and roll each ball gently into a 6-inch round, keeping even pressure so the filling does not burst through. Cook on a hot tava on medium-high heat for about 1 minute per side until brown spots appear.

Brush both sides with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and roast, pressing gently with a spatula, another 30 to 40 seconds per side until the paratha puffs slightly and turns golden with crisp blisters.
tips: Squeeze the grated carrot in your palm before sautéing if it feels watery; drier filling means easier rolling and no leaks.
The filling can be made a day ahead and refrigerated; bring it to room temperature before stuffing so it does not stiffen the dough.
If a paratha tears while rolling, dab the spot with dry atta and roll from the edges inward rather than over the tear.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot off the tava with a bowl of thick curd whisked with a pinch of roasted cumin, and a wedge of lime pickle on the side.

variations.name: Punjabi Stuffed Carrot Paratha
variations.description: In Punjab's dhaba tradition, the carrot filling is bulked up with onion and kasuri methi, the dough carries a whisper of ajwain, and the finished paratha is crowned with a melting spoon of white butter. It is heartier and more robust than the classic, made for cold mornings with a tall glass of lassi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Stone-ground khapli gives the rustic, nutty crumb dhaba parathas are loved for

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Generous ghee-basting is non-negotiable for a true Punjabi paratha

steps: Rub 1/2 tsp ajwain seeds between your palms into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, add 1/2 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then knead with roughly 3/4 cup water to a soft dough. Rest it under a damp cloth for 20 minutes.
Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan over medium flame, add 1 finely chopped medium onion and fry 3 to 4 minutes until the edges turn light gold.

Tip in 1 inch grated ginger, 2 minced green chillies and 2 cups grated carrot with 1/2 tsp salt. Cook on medium-high, stirring often, for 6 minutes until the mixture is completely dry and smells sweet.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the pan, add 3/4 tsp red chilli powder and 3/4 tsp garam masala, toss for 1 minute, then cool the filling fully on a wide plate.
Shape the dough into 8 balls, cup each one and pack in 2 tbsp of the onion-carrot filling. Seal the pleats firmly, flatten, and roll into thick 6-inch rounds with light strokes.

Roast each paratha on a hot tava over medium-high heat, about 1 minute per side, then drizzle 1/2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee around the edges and fry 40 seconds per side, pressing with a cloth until deeply golden and crisp.
Stack the parathas and top each with 1 tsp white butter just before serving so it melts into the crust.
tips: Cook the onion until truly golden before adding carrot; raw-tasting onion turns the filling watery and sharp.
Roll these slightly thicker than a plain paratha; the chunky filling needs the extra wall to stay sealed.
Leftover parathas crisp up beautifully next morning on a dry tava, no extra fat needed.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a tall glass of sweet lassi and a sharp aam ka achaar; on weekends add a fried egg on top, dhaba style.

variations.name: Bengali Stuffed Carrot Paratha
variations.description: Bengal's love for pungent mustard oil and kalonji transforms this paratha entirely. The carrot filling is cooked in smoking-hot Anveshan Mustard Oil with nigella seeds and green chilli, giving it a sharp, nose-tingling edge that plays off the vegetable's sweetness. A light final smear of raw mustard oil is the unmistakable Bengali signature.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli's earthy flavour stands up to the assertive mustard oil

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed kachi ghani pungency is the soul of this Bengali take

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon in the dough keeps the crust supple against the sharp oil

steps: Make the dough by working 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 1/2 tsp salt into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, then adding about 3/4 cup water gradually. Knead 5 minutes to a smooth, soft ball and rest 15 minutes covered.
Heat 1 1/2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai until it just begins to smoke, about 1 minute on high, then lower the flame; this mellows its raw bite while keeping the aroma.
Crackle 3/4 tsp kalonji in the hot oil for 20 seconds, then add 3 slit green chillies and 1 inch julienned ginger and stir until the chillies blister lightly.
Add 2 cups grated carrot, 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1/2 tsp salt and 1/2 tsp sugar. Sauté on medium for 5 to 6 minutes until dry and faintly caramelised, fold in 2 tbsp coriander and cool completely.
Divide the dough into 8 portions, stuff each with 2 tbsp of the kalonji-carrot filling, seal the mouth tightly and roll out to 6-inch discs with gentle, even strokes.

Cook on a medium-hot tava about 1 minute per side, then brush with the remaining 1 1/2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and fry 30 to 40 seconds per side until golden freckles cover the surface and the edges crisp.
tips: Always let mustard oil reach its smoking point once before adding spices, or the filling will taste harshly raw.
A tiny pinch of sugar in the filling is very Bengali; it rounds out the mustard oil's pungency rather than sweetening the dish.
If serving guests unused to mustard oil, halve the final brushing and finish with ghee instead of oil on half the batch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a smashed-tomato kasundi chutney or plain aloo bhaja, and slit green chillies on the rim of the plate.

variations.name: Kerala Stuffed Carrot Paratha
variations.description: This coastal spin folds fresh grated coconut, curry leaves and cracked black pepper into the carrot filling, all sautéed in fragrant wood-pressed coconut oil. The result tastes like a thoran wrapped in bread, gently sweet, herbal and peppery. Shallots add a delicate allium note that onions cannot match.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Wholegrain emmer makes a softer wrap for the coconut-flecked filling than maida

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil perfumes both the thoran-style filling and the roast

steps: Combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, then knead in about 3/4 cup water until soft and elastic. Cover with a damp cloth and set aside for 20 minutes.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan on medium and pop 1/2 tsp mustard seeds, about 30 seconds, then add 2 sprigs of curry leaves and 6 sliced shallots. Fry until the shallots soften and turn translucent, about 2 minutes.
Add 2 chopped green chillies, 1 1/2 cups grated carrot, 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1/2 tsp salt. Sauté on medium heat for 4 to 5 minutes until the carrot loses its raw crunch and all moisture cooks off.
Fold in 1/2 cup fresh grated coconut and 3/4 tsp crushed black pepper and toast 2 minutes more, until the coconut smells nutty but stays white. Cool the mixture fully before stuffing.
Portion the dough into 8 balls, stuff each with 2 tbsp of the coconut-carrot mixture, pinch shut and roll softly into 6-inch rounds, patching any thin spots with a dusting of atta.

Roast on a medium-hot tava for about 1 minute per side, then drizzle the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and cook another 40 seconds per side until the surface turns golden with a light coconut sheen.
tips: Use only fresh or frozen grated coconut; desiccated coconut turns dry and gritty inside the paratha.
Crush the pepper coarsely just before cooking so its heat blooms without turning bitter.
Toast the coconut only until aromatic; browning it changes the flavour from sweet to roasted and overwhelms the carrot.
variations.servingSuggestion: Delicious with a small bowl of coconut-yogurt pachadi or a thin vegetable stew, and hot black kattan chai to finish.

variations.name: Kashmiri Stuffed Carrot Paratha
variations.description: A valley-inspired paratha that leans on Kashmir's pantry: saffron-infused dough, fennel and dry ginger in the filling, and mild Kashmiri chilli for colour without fire. Anveshan Saffron soaked in warm milk tints the crust pale gold and lends its honeyed aroma to every layer. It is the most delicate, festive member of this family.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The pale khapli crumb shows off the saffron's golden tint beautifully

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: GI-tagged Kashmiri threads bloomed in warm milk perfume the dough itself

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee-roasting echoes the richness of Kashmiri festive breads

steps: Soak 1/4 tsp Anveshan Saffron threads in 1/4 cup warm milk for 10 minutes until the milk turns deep amber.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, the saffron milk and about 1/2 cup water into a soft golden dough. Rest it, covered, for 20 minutes.
Melt 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium heat and sizzle 3/4 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add 2 cups grated carrot and 1/2 tsp salt and cook 5 to 6 minutes, stirring, until dry and sweet-smelling.

Season the carrot with 1 tsp fennel powder, 1/2 tsp dry ginger powder and 3/4 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, then stir in 2 tbsp raisins and cook 1 minute so they plump slightly. Cool completely on a plate.
Divide the saffron dough into 8 balls and stuff each with 2 tbsp of the fennel-carrot filling. Seal well and roll into 6-inch rounds, dusting sparingly so the golden colour stays visible.

Cook each paratha on a medium tava for about 1 minute per side, then brush with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and roast 40 seconds per side until pale gold with amber spots; avoid high heat, which dulls the saffron aroma.
tips: Crush the saffron threads lightly between your fingers before soaking to release maximum colour from fewer strands.
Fennel and dry ginger are the Kashmiri backbone; do not substitute garam masala or the character disappears.
Keep the tava at medium rather than high; gentle roasting preserves the saffron fragrance that fierce heat burns off.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sweetened thick curd or a cup of kahwa; for a festive plate, scatter slivered almonds over the buttered paratha.

variations.name: Classic Stuffed Gobi Paratha
variations.description: The definitive North Indian winter breakfast: a soft khapli wheat shell wrapped around a spiced, ginger-flecked cauliflower filling, roasted until blistered and golden. Squeezing the grated gobi dry is the old dhaba trick that keeps every paratha crisp outside and fluffy inside.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Stone-ground emmer wheat gives the shell a nutty sweetness and stays soft for hours in a tiffin

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee's high smoke point lets the paratha blister and crisp without burning

ingredients.name: Cauliflower, finely grated
ingredients.note: about 3 cups once grated

steps: Knead 3 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 1.25 cups water, adding the water gradually, into a soft, non-sticky dough. Knead 8 minutes until smooth and supple, then cover and rest 20 minutes.

Toss the 3 cups grated cauliflower with 0.5 tsp salt and set aside 10 minutes; then squeeze it firmly in fistfuls over the sink until no more water drips out. Dry gobi is what stops the parathas from tearing.

Mix the squeezed cauliflower with 1 inch grated ginger, 2 minced green chillies, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp amchur and 3 tbsp chopped coriander until evenly speckled with spice.

Divide the dough into 8 balls and the filling into 8 portions of about 3 tbsp each. Flatten a ball into a 4-inch cup, place one portion of filling in the centre, gather the edges over the top and pinch firmly to seal.
Dust with dry atta and roll each stuffed ball gently into a 7-inch round, using light, even strokes from the centre outward so the filling never breaks through.

Heat a tava on medium-high until a drop of water sizzles instantly. Cook each paratha 1 minute until bubbles appear, flip, spread 0.5 tsp Anveshan Ghee, flip again and press the edges with a spatula until both sides show deep golden-brown spots, about 3 minutes total.
Brush the finished parathas with another 0.5 tsp Anveshan Ghee each and stack them in a cloth-lined box so they stay soft and steamy until serving.
tips: Grate the cauliflower on the fine side of the grater; large shreds poke holes while rolling.
If the dough springs back while rolling, rest it 5 more minutes; relaxed gluten rolls thinner without tearing.
Filling can be made a day ahead, but salt it only just before stuffing or it will weep water.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot off the tava with a bowl of thick whisked curd, a wedge of lime pickle and sweet milky chai on the side.

variations.name: Punjabi Stuffed Gobi Paratha
variations.description: The dhaba original from the highways of Punjab, where ajwain and tangy anardana sharpen the gobi filling and the hot paratha is crowned with a melting pat of white butter. It is heartier, flakier and unapologetically rich compared with the everyday version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli wheat mirrors the coarse desi atta Punjabi dhabas grind fresh at the chakki

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A generous ghee-shallow-fry is what gives the true dhaba-style crackle on the crust

steps: Work 3 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee together, then pour in roughly 1.25 cups water in stages and knead 8 minutes to a pillowy, non-sticky dough. Rest it under a damp cloth for 20 minutes.

Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium heat and crackle 0.5 tsp ajwain for 20 seconds until fragrant. Add the finely chopped onion and grated cauliflower and stir-fry 4 to 5 minutes until the gobi loses its raw smell and turns dry.

Take the pan off the heat and stir in 1.5 tsp anardana powder, 0.75 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 2 minced green chillies and 0.5 tsp salt. Spread the filling on a plate and cool completely so it does not steam the dough.
Shape 8 dough balls, cup each one in your palm and pack in 3 tbsp of the cooled filling. Draw the dough up around it, twist off the excess at the top and flatten the pouch gently between your palms.
Roll each pouch on a floured board into a thick 7-inch disc; Punjabi parathas stay slightly thicker than usual so the crust turns flaky rather than crisp-thin.

Slap the paratha onto a hot tava over medium-high heat and cook about 90 seconds per side, spooning 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee around the edges on each flip, until both faces are patched with crusty brown and the surface puffs in spots.
Slide each paratha onto a plate and immediately top with 1 tbsp white butter so it melts into the crust before it reaches the table.
tips: Cooking the filling first drives off moisture, so you can roll these thicker and stuff them fuller than raw-filling versions.
No anardana? Crush 1 tsp amchur with a pinch of black salt for a similar sour hit.
Press the paratha edges down with a folded cloth while roasting; the rim is the last part to cook through.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a tall glass of salted lassi and a spoon of aam ka achaar; on winter mornings dhabas serve it alongside sarson da saag for a full Punjabi thali.

variations.name: Bengali Stuffed Gobi Paratha
variations.description: A Kolkata-style porota where the gobi filling is sautéed in pungent mustard oil with kalonji and green chilli, echoing the flavours of phulkopir dalna. The sharp, wasabi-like heat of the oil against sweet winter cauliflower is what makes this take unmistakably Bengali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The emmer wheat's faint sweetness balances the sharp mustard-oil filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed kachi ghani mustard oil keeps the nose-tingling pungency Bengali cooking is built on

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A final ghee brush is the classic Bengali finish on any porota

steps: Make the dough by rubbing 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil into 3 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, then kneading in about 1.25 cups water for 8 minutes until soft and elastic. Cover and let it relax for 20 minutes.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai on medium-high until it just begins to smoke and its raw sharpness mellows, about 1 minute, then lower the heat and crackle 0.5 tsp kalonji for 15 seconds.

Add 1 inch grated ginger, 3 minced green chillies and the grated cauliflower with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp sugar. Sauté 5 minutes on medium until the gobi is dry, faintly golden and smells nutty, then cool completely and fold in 2 tbsp coriander.
Portion the dough into 8 balls, hollow each into a cup and press 3 tbsp of the mustard-scented filling inside. Pinch the seams shut and rest the stuffed balls 5 minutes so the seal sets.
Roll every ball into a 7-inch round with gentle pressure, flouring lightly; if a little filling peeks through, patch it with a pinch of dry atta and keep rolling.
Roast on a medium-hot tava for about 90 seconds per side, drizzling 0.5 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil around each paratha as it cooks, until crisp bronze patches bloom across both faces.
Finish each porota with a thin swipe of Anveshan Ghee straight off the tava so the crust gleams and the aroma of ghee meets the mustard heat.
tips: Always let mustard oil reach its faint smoking point once before adding spices; skipping this leaves a raw bitter edge.
Bengali households add the pinch of sugar not for sweetness but to round out the mustard's bite - do not skip it.
These reheat beautifully on a dry tava; avoid the microwave, which turns the crust leathery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with begun bhaja (crisp fried aubergine slices) and a spoon of kasundi mustard relish for a true Kolkata breakfast plate.

variations.name: Kerala Stuffed Gobi Paratha
variations.description: A Malabar-inspired paratha where the cauliflower is folded through fresh grated coconut, curry leaves and cracked black pepper, then toasted in virgin coconut oil. It eats like a thoran wrapped in soft wheat, fragrant and gently sweet rather than fiery.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Soft khapli dough drinks up the coconut aroma without turning dense

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed virgin coconut oil toasts the crust with a sweet tropical fragrance no refined oil can match

steps: Combine 3 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt and 1 tbsp melted Anveshan Coconut Oil, then knead in around 1.25 cups water over 8 minutes to a soft, stretchy dough. Rest it, covered, for 20 minutes.
Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a wide pan over medium heat and pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, about 30 seconds, before adding 4 sliced shallots, 12 shredded curry leaves and 2 minced green chillies.

When the shallots turn translucent, about 2 minutes, tip in the grated cauliflower with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt and cook 4 minutes until dry. Off the heat, fold through 0.5 cup grated coconut and 1 tsp crushed black pepper, then cool fully.
Split the dough into 8 balls and load each with 3 tbsp of the coconut-gobi mixture, gathering the edges over the filling and pinching them into a tight topknot before flattening.
Roll each parcel into a 7-inch circle with a light hand, dusting with atta as needed; the coconut makes this filling forgiving, so roll it evenly thin.
Cook on a medium tava for roughly 2 minutes per side, spooning 0.5 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil over each flip, until the surface is freckled deep gold and smells of toasted coconut.
tips: Use only fresh or frozen grated coconut; desiccated coconut turns gritty inside the paratha.
Crush the pepper coarsely in a mortar - powdered pepper disappears, while cracked bits give bright pops of heat.
If the filling feels loose, squeeze it in your fist before stuffing; coconut binds better once compressed.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and a small bowl of Kerala-style moru curry (spiced buttermilk) for a complete southern breakfast.

variations.name: Rajasthani Stuffed Gobi Paratha
variations.description: A desert-style paratha with a rustic filling of gobi toasted with crushed dried red chillies, coriander seeds and a whisper of hing, roasted crisp in plenty of ghee. Rajasthan's dry-larder cooking shows in every bite: bold spice, no onion needed, and a crust sturdy enough for travel.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Hardy khapli wheat keeps these parathas soft even in Rajasthan's dry heat, tiffin-style

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rajasthani cooking measures hospitality in ghee - it crisps the crust and carries the chilli heat

steps: Bring together 3 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then knead with about 1.25 cups water for 8 minutes into a smooth, medium-soft dough. Cover with a damp cloth and rest 20 minutes.

Melt 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai over medium heat, add 0.25 tsp hing, then the 3 crushed dried red chillies, 2 tsp crushed coriander seeds and 1 tsp fennel seeds. Sizzle 30 seconds until the chillies darken a shade and smell smoky.

Add the grated cauliflower, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt and fry 5 minutes on medium, stirring often, until the gobi is completely dry and edged with gold. Stir in 1 tsp amchur and 2 tbsp coriander leaves, then cool the filling fully.
Divide the rested dough into 8 balls, press each into a cup and pack in 3 tbsp of the chilli-gobi filling. Seal the seams firmly and flatten each parcel between floured palms.
Roll out to slightly thick 6-to-7-inch rounds; Rajasthani parathas are kept a touch sturdier so they hold their crunch long after cooking.
Roast on a medium-hot tava about 2 minutes per side, spreading 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee generously on each face as you flip, until the crust turns a deep russet brown with crisp, ghee-fried edges.
tips: Crush the dried chillies by hand and discard most seeds if you want the smokiness without full desert-level heat.
These parathas keep well for a day trip; wrap in cloth, not foil, so the crust never sweats.
A pinch more fennel in the filling cools the chilli burn without dulling the flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Rajasthani way with lahsun ki chutney, a tumbler of chaas and raw onion rings sprinkled with salt and lime.

variations.name: Classic Stuffed Onion Paratha
variations.description: The North Indian breakfast workhorse: sharp raw onions salted, squeezed bone-dry and spiked with roasted cumin and amchur, then sealed inside soft khapli atta dough. Roasted in bilona ghee, the crust blisters golden while the onion inside turns sweet and jammy at the edges.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: stone-ground emmer wheat gives a naturally sweet, soft crumb that stays pliable for hours

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: 1 tbsp softens the dough, the rest roasts each paratha to a nutty, blistered crust

steps: Knead the dough: mix 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then work in about 3/4 cup water a little at a time. Knead for 8 minutes until the dough is soft, pliable and no longer sticks to your palm, then cover and rest for 15 minutes.

Finely chop 3 medium onions, toss them with the remaining 1/2 tsp salt and set aside for 10 minutes, then squeeze them hard between your palms to press out every drop of juice — the filling should look almost dry.

Season the squeezed onions with 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1/2 tsp amchur, 2 finely chopped green chillies, the grated 1-inch piece of ginger and 3 tbsp chopped coriander; mix until evenly coated.

Divide the rested dough into 8 equal balls. Flatten one ball into a 4-inch cup, place 2 tbsp of onion filling in the centre, gather the edges over the top and pinch firmly shut so no filling peeks out.
Dust the sealed ball with dry atta and roll it gently into a 6 to 7 inch round, easing off pressure near the edges so the onions do not tear through the dough.

Heat a tava on medium-high until a drop of water sizzles off instantly. Cook the paratha for about 1 minute until bubbles rise, flip, brush 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee on top, flip again and press lightly with a spatula until both sides show deep golden-brown spots, about 3 minutes per paratha.
Repeat with the remaining balls, brushing each side with Anveshan Ghee as it cooks, and stack the finished parathas loosely covered with a cloth so they stay soft and steamy.
tips: Squeeze the salted onions twice, five minutes apart — the second press removes the water that would otherwise leak and tear the paratha mid-rolling.
If the dough tears while rolling, dab the spot with dry atta and continue with feather-light strokes instead of re-balling, which toughens the crumb.
Roll and cook one paratha at a time; stuffed rounds left waiting more than 2-3 minutes start weeping onion juice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Slide each paratha straight from the tava onto the plate with a bowl of chilled dahi, a spoon of mango pickle and hot masala chai; a small pat of white butter melting into the top layer is the classic dhaba send-off.

variations.name: Bengali Stuffed Onion Paratha
variations.description: A Kolkata-style porota where the onions are softened in pungent mustard oil with crackling kalonji instead of going in raw. A whisper of khandsari sugar rounds out the mustard's bite — that sweet-sharp balance is the unmistakable Bengali signature.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: the emmer wheat's extensibility lets you roll the porota thin without the filling bursting

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed kachi ghani oil carries the sinus-tingling pungency this porota is built around

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined cane sugar that tempers the mustard heat the way Bengali kitchens intend

steps: Bring the dough together with 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and roughly 3/4 cup water; knead 7 to 8 minutes to a supple, smooth ball and rest it under a damp cloth for 15 minutes.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai on medium until it just reaches its smoking point, then lower the heat for 30 seconds — this mellows its raw edge without losing the aroma.
Crackle 1 tsp kalonji in the hot oil for 15 seconds, then add 3 sliced onions and saute for 5 to 6 minutes until they collapse and their edges turn light gold.

Stir in 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tsp Anveshan Khandsari, 3 chopped green chillies and the grated 1-inch knob of ginger; cook 1 more minute, fold in 2 tbsp coriander and spread the filling on a plate to cool completely.
Portion the dough into 8 balls, cup each one, spoon in 2 tbsp of the cooled onion filling, seal the pleats tightly and roll out into a 6-inch round with gentle, even strokes.

Roast each porota on a medium-hot tava, flipping every minute and drizzling the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil around the edges, until both faces are freckled deep brown and crisp, about 3 to 4 minutes each.
tips: Cooling the filling fully before stuffing is non-negotiable — warm onions steam the dough from inside and make it gummy.
If raw mustard pungency bothers anyone at the table, smoke the full 3 tbsp of oil once at the start and use it through the recipe.
A porota flipped often cooks flakier than one left to sit; keep it moving every 60 seconds.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with begun bhaja (crisp fried aubergine slices) and a smear of kasundi mustard, or simply a boiled egg mashed with green chilli and a drop of mustard oil for a proper Kolkata breakfast.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Stuffed Onion Paratha
variations.description: Built on goda masala — that smoky, faintly sweet Maharashtrian blend with dagad phool and roasted coconut — this version folds toasted sesame and dry coconut into the onion filling. Cooked in wood-pressed groundnut oil and finished with ghee, it eats like a stuffed cousin of kanda bhaji.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli's low gluten elasticity keeps the sesame-flecked crust tender, not chewy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed peanut oil is the everyday fat of Maharashtrian kitchens and deepens the nutty filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a final brush of bilona ghee glosses the goda masala's warm spice notes

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and about 3/4 cup water into a soft, springy dough; rest it covered for 15 minutes while you build the filling.

In a dry pan on low heat, toast 1 tbsp white sesame seeds and 2 tbsp grated dry coconut for 2 to 3 minutes, stirring constantly, until the coconut turns biscuit-gold and smells toasty; tip onto a plate.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in the same pan on medium, add 3 finely chopped onions and cook 5 minutes until soft and just starting to colour at the edges.

Add 2 tsp goda masala, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1/2 tsp salt to the onions, fry 1 minute until fragrant, then fold in the toasted sesame-coconut and 3 tbsp coriander; cool the filling fully.
Shape 8 dough balls, stuff each with 2 tbsp of the goda-scented filling, pinch the seams closed and roll into 6-inch rounds with light hands so the coconut flecks stay inside.

Cook each paratha on a medium tava with a drizzle of the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, about 90 seconds per side, until crisp and mottled brown; brush the hot stack with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee before serving.
tips: Goda masala scorches quickly — add it to the onions off the boil of the heat and never fry it longer than a minute.
Toast the sesame and kopra only until pale gold; dark toasting turns the filling bitter against the sweet spice blend.
Leftover filling makes an instant side: fold it into steamed rice with a spoon of ghee.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a katori of thecha (green chilli-garlic crush) on the side and a glass of chilled taak (spiced buttermilk) — the cooling salted buttermilk against the smoky goda masala is pure Pune comfort.

variations.name: Kerala Stuffed Onion Paratha
