variations.description: A thoran-inspired take where shallots stand in for big onions, sauteed in virgin coconut oil with mustard seeds, curry leaves and fresh grated coconut. Black pepper carries the heat, so the flavour is green, coastal and completely different from its northern cousins.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: ancient emmer wheat rolls thin enough to flake in layers, Malabar-parotta style

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed virgin oil that perfumes the shallot filling with fresh coconut sweetness

steps: Work 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and around 3/4 cup water into a soft, stretchy dough; knead 8 minutes, coat lightly with oil and rest 15 minutes.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadhai on medium; pop 1/2 tsp mustard seeds until they finish sputtering, then drop in the leaves from 2 sprigs of curry leaf and let them crisp for 10 seconds.
Add 15 thinly sliced shallots, 3 slit green chillies and the julienned 1-inch piece of ginger; saute 5 to 6 minutes until the shallots wilt sweet and translucent with golden tips.

Sprinkle in 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1/2 tsp salt and 1/2 tsp crushed black pepper, stir 30 seconds, then fold in 1/2 cup fresh grated coconut and cook 2 minutes more until the mixture is dry; cool completely.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, fill each with 2 tbsp of the coconut-shallot mixture, seal firmly and roll out to a 6-inch circle, dusting sparingly with dry atta.

Roast on a medium-hot tava for about 90 seconds a side, brushing with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, until the surface blisters into crisp golden patches and the kitchen smells of toasted coconut.
tips: Slice the shallots thin and even; thick pieces stay crunchy and puncture the dough when you roll.
Cook the coconut filling until it looks dry and fluffy — residual moisture from fresh coconut is the main cause of soggy centres.
Swap half the black pepper for crushed white pepper if serving kids; the aroma stays, the burn softens.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a small bowl of coconut chutney sharpened with a squeeze of lime, or alongside a fried egg basted in coconut oil for a Malabar tea-shop breakfast feel.

variations.name: Rajasthani Stuffed Onion Paratha
variations.description: Modelled on Jodhpur's pyaaz kachori, the filling is a robust fry-up of onions, crushed dried red chillies, fennel and roasted besan, all bloomed in generous ghee. The besan drinks up the onion juices, so every bite is dense, spicy and dry-crumbly in the true desert style.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: hardy emmer wheat mirrors the rustic grains Rajasthani households roll their rotis from

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: desert cooking runs on ghee — it blooms the whole spices and crisps the crust like a kachori shell

steps: Knead a firm-soft dough from 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 3/4 cup water; work it 8 minutes until smooth and rest under a plate for 15 minutes.

Melt 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium heat; bloom 1/8 tsp hing, 1/2 tsp ajwain, 1 tsp fennel seeds and 4 roughly crushed dried red chillies for 30 seconds until the fennel smells sweet and the chillies darken a shade.
Add 3 finely chopped onions and fry 6 to 7 minutes, stirring now and then, until they turn deep golden at the edges and lose their raw smell.

Sprinkle in 2 tbsp besan, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1/2 tsp salt; roast the mixture 2 to 3 minutes until the besan smells nutty and coats the onions like a crumble, then stir in 1 tsp amchur and cool the filling fully.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, stuff each with 2 tbsp of the kachori-style filling, pinch shut and roll gently to a 6-inch round — the besan-bound filling rolls out cleanly without tearing.
Roast each paratha on a medium tava, spooning the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over both sides, about 2 minutes a side, until crusty and freckled a rich reddish brown.
tips: Roast the besan patiently until nutty; underdone gram flour tastes raw and pasty against the sweet fennel.
Crush the dried chillies coarsely by hand for smoky flecks of heat rather than an even burn.
This filling keeps 2 days refrigerated, so make a double batch and roll fresh parathas each morning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Do it Jodhpur-style: serve with tangy tamatar ki launji or a spoon of garlic chutney, and finish the meal with a piece of jaggery to cool the palate.

variations.name: Classic Cheesy Matar Paratha
variations.description: A winter-morning favourite where sweet mashed green peas meet molten cheese inside a flaky khapli atta shell. The filling is tempered in ghee so the cumin blooms fully, and the cheese binds the peas so the paratha never bursts on the tava. Crisp outside, gooey inside — the definitive version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: stone-ground emmer wheat gives a naturally sweet, soft dough that rolls thin without tearing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee for the dough, the tempering and the final roast — its nutty aroma carries the whole paratha

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and about 0.75 cup water into a soft, pliable dough that springs back when pressed. Cover and rest for 15 minutes.
Boil 1.5 cups green peas in salted water for 4-5 minutes until they crush easily between your fingers, drain completely, and mash them coarsely so no whole peas remain to tear the dough.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium heat, splutter 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add grated 1 inch ginger and 2 minced green chillies and fry until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Tip in the mashed peas with 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt; cook for 3-4 minutes until the mixture looks dry and leaves the pan. Cool fully, then fold in 0.75 cup grated cheese and 3 tbsp chopped coriander.

Divide the dough into 8 balls. Flatten each into a 4-inch disc, place 2 tbsp of the pea-cheese filling in the centre, gather the edges to seal, and roll gently into a 6-7 inch paratha, dusting with atta as needed.

Roast each paratha on a hot tava on medium-high heat for about 90 seconds per side, brushing both sides with the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, until deep golden spots appear and the surface blisters.
tips: Cool the pea mixture completely before adding cheese, or it will melt prematurely and make the filling wet and impossible to seal.
If the filling feels loose, stir in 1 tsp of dry khapli atta — it absorbs moisture without dulling the flavour.
Stuffed, unrolled dough balls keep in the fridge for a day; bring to room temperature for 15 minutes before rolling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Cut into wedges so the cheese pull shows, and serve with a bowl of thick salted curd and a sharp mango pickle to cut the richness.

variations.name: Punjabi Cheesy Matar Paratha
variations.description: The dhaba treatment: a sturdier pea-and-cheese filling scented with ajwain and kasuri methi, roasted until crackly and then slathered with white butter while still hissing hot. Anardana powder adds the tangy backbone Punjabi stuffed parathas are famous for.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: the emmer wheat's high extensibility handles this generous dhaba-style stuffing without splitting

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasting in bilona ghee gives the crackly, layered crust a tandoor-like aroma

steps: Work 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 tsp ajwain, 0.5 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee together, then add roughly 0.75 cup water gradually and knead 8 minutes to a smooth, elastic dough. Rest it under a damp cloth for 20 minutes.
Pressure-steam or boil 1.5 cups peas until fully tender, about 5 minutes, then drain and crush them roughly with a potato masher — a little texture is welcome in the Punjabi style.

Sizzle 1 finely chopped small onion in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat until light brown at the edges, roughly 4 minutes, then stir in the crushed peas, 1 tsp anardana powder, 0.5 tsp garam masala, 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi and 0.5 tsp salt.
Dry the filling out over medium heat for 3 minutes until it holds together when pinched, cool it down, then mix in 0.75 cup grated cheese until evenly flecked through.
Shape 8 dough balls, cup each into a bowl, pack in 2 tbsp filling, pleat shut and roll out to a thick 6-inch round — dhaba parathas stay slightly fat so the crust chars while the middle steams.
Cook on a very hot tava, 2 minutes on the first side until brown blisters form, flip, drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee around the edges and press with a spatula until both faces are crisp and mottled.
Take each paratha off the heat and immediately crown it with 0.5 tbsp white butter so it melts into the crust before serving.
tips: Crush kasuri methi between your palms before adding — it releases far more aroma than whole leaves.
Pressing the paratha edges with a folded cloth while roasting forces the trapped steam out and crisps the rim.
No anardana? Use 0.5 tsp amchur, but add it off the heat so it stays bright and tangy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Do it the Amritsar way: pair with a tall glass of salted lassi and a spoon of sweet-and-sour lemon pickle on the side of the plate.

variations.name: Bengali Cheesy Matar Paratha
variations.description: Bengal's love of koraishutir kochuri inspires this take: a gingery pea filling perfumed with kalonji and green chilli, cooked and crisped in pungent mustard oil. The sharp oil against the mild cheese is a classic Bengali contrast of heat and cream.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: gives the kochuri-style shell a delicate, biscuity crumb instead of a chewy one

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed kachi ghani oil — its wasabi-like pungency is the signature of this Bengali version

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a final ghee gloss softens the mustard oil's bite the way Bengali kitchens do

steps: Rub 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and 0.5 tsp salt into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, then knead with about 0.75 cup water for 6-7 minutes into a supple dough. Rest, covered, for 15 minutes.
Blitz 1.5 cups boiled green peas with 3 green chillies to a coarse, grainy paste — Bengali fillings are smoother than north Indian ones, so avoid leaving whole peas.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just smokes and its raw sharpness mellows, lower the flame, and crackle 0.5 tsp kalonji seeds for 20 seconds.

Add 2 tsp ginger paste, fry for 45 seconds, then add the pea paste, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp sugar and 0.5 tsp salt; stir over medium heat for 4-5 minutes until the paste balls up around the spoon. Cool, then work in 0.75 cup grated cheese.
Portion the dough into 8 balls, stuff each with 2 tbsp of the green filling, seal firmly and roll into thin 7-inch rounds with light, even strokes so the filling spreads to the edge.
Fry each paratha on a medium-hot tava with 1 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil, about 90 seconds a side, until freckled deep brown, then finish with a thin smear of 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee across the hot stack.
tips: Always let mustard oil reach its smoking point once, then cool slightly — skipping this leaves an acrid raw edge.
The pinch of sugar is not optional in Bengali cooking; it rounds out the pea's sweetness against the pungent oil.
If the pea paste turns watery after blending, dry it 2 extra minutes in the kadai before adding cheese.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with alur dom on the side and a wedge of gondhoraj or regular lime — the citrus lifts the mustard oil beautifully.

variations.name: Kerala Cheesy Matar Paratha
variations.description: A Malabar-leaning version where the pea filling is folded with fresh grated coconut, curry leaves and crushed black pepper, all sizzled in cold-pressed coconut oil. The coconut keeps the filling juicy, and the cheese turns it into something like a molten thoran inside bread.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: kneaded soft and rested long, it flakes in layers the way a Malabar paratha should

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed from fresh coconuts — it perfumes the filling and crisps the crust with a tropical sweetness

steps: Make a soft dough from 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, 0.5 tsp salt and about 0.75 cup water; knead until silky, then rest 20 minutes under a damp towel.

Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan over medium heat and pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds until they finish sputtering, about 30 seconds, then fry 2 sprigs of curry leaves and 6 sliced shallots until the shallots turn translucent and lightly gold, 3 minutes.

Add 1.25 cups boiled, mashed peas, 0.5 cup fresh grated coconut, 1 tsp crushed black pepper, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt; toss on medium heat for 3 minutes until the coconut smells toasty and the mix is dry.
Spread the filling on a plate to cool for 10 minutes, then fold in 0.75 cup grated cheese so every spoonful has both coconut and cheese.
Divide the dough into 8 portions, stuff each with a generous 2 tbsp of filling, pinch closed and roll into 6-inch rounds, keeping the pressure light so the coconut does not poke through.
Toast on a medium-hot tava for about 2 minutes per side, brushing with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, until golden patches bloom and the edges crisp.
tips: Use fresh or thawed frozen coconut, never desiccated — dry coconut steals moisture from the filling and makes it crumbly.
Crush the pepper coarsely just before cooking; pre-ground pepper loses the floral heat this recipe leans on.
Leftover filling makes an excellent stuffing for grilled sandwiches the next morning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Plate with a small bowl of coconut chutney and sweet mango pickle, and serve alongside cardamom-spiced chaya for a proper Kerala tea-shop spread.

variations.name: Andhra Cheesy Matar Paratha
variations.description: Fiery and garlicky, this take grinds toasted Guntur red chillies with garlic into the pea filling, with sesame oil deepening the heat. The cheese plays the cooling role that curd usually does on an Andhra plate, taming the chilli just enough to keep you reaching for more.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: its gentle sweetness is the perfect counterweight to the Guntur chilli's aggressive heat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed gingelly oil, the traditional frying medium of Andhra kitchens, adds a deep nutty base note

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, 0.5 tsp salt and close to 0.75 cup water until smooth and stretchy, then let it relax for 15 minutes under cover.

Dry-toast 3 Guntur chillies and 1 tsp coriander seeds in a pan over low heat for 2 minutes until darkened a shade and smoky, then grind them with 6 garlic cloves and 0.5 tsp tamarind paste into a coarse red masala.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil on medium, crisp 1 sprig of curry leaves for 20 seconds, then fry the ground chilli-garlic masala for 90 seconds until the raw garlic smell disappears.

Stir in 1.5 cups boiled, mashed peas and 0.5 tsp salt and cook for 3-4 minutes until the filling turns brick-flecked and dry enough to pinch into a ball. Cool completely before folding in 0.75 cup grated cheese.
Shape 8 balls from the dough, load each with 2 tbsp of the spicy filling, seal the pleats and roll out to 6-inch discs on a lightly floured board.
Roast on a hot tava for around 90 seconds per side with 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil drizzled around each paratha, pressing gently until the surface is crisp with dark red-brown spots.
tips: Deseed one or two of the Guntur chillies if serving children — you keep the colour and aroma but drop the burn considerably.
Grinding the masala coarse, not to a paste, gives the filling the rustic kaaram texture Andhra cooks prize.
A quick 10-minute rest after roasting lets the cheese set slightly so the wedges cut clean.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with chilled sambaram (spiced buttermilk) and a spoon of gongura or lime pickle — the sourness is the classic Andhra counterpoint to chilli heat.

variations.name: Classic Paneer Paratha
variations.description: The definitive North Indian breakfast paratha: a soft khapli wheat shell wrapped around a crumbly, gently spiced paneer filling. Slow-roasting on the tava in bilona ghee gives it blistered golden spots and a nutty aroma that plain oil can never match.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Stone-ground emmer wheat kneads into a naturally soft dough that stays pliable even after cooling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A2 bilona ghee for the dough, the tava and the final brush — it is what makes the crust flake

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 1/2 tsp salt and about 3/4 cup water into a soft, non-sticky dough; knead for 5 minutes until smooth, cover and rest for 15 minutes.

Crumble 250 g paneer finely with your fingertips so no lumps remain, then mix in 1/2 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 finely chopped green chilli and 3 tbsp chopped coriander.

Divide the dough into 8 equal balls and the filling into 8 portions of about 2 tbsp each. Flatten a ball into a 4-inch cup, place one portion of filling in the centre, gather the edges over the top and pinch firmly to seal.
Dust the stuffed ball lightly with atta and roll gently into a 7-inch round, turning it a quarter after every couple of strokes so the paneer spreads evenly without tearing through.

Heat a tava on medium heat until a drop of water sizzles instantly. Cook the paratha for about 1 minute until small bubbles appear, flip, spread 1/2 tsp Anveshan Ghee, flip again and press the edges with a spatula until both sides show golden-brown spots, about 3 minutes total.
Repeat with the remaining balls, brushing each finished paratha with a little more Anveshan Ghee while still hot so the surface glistens and stays soft.
tips: Use fresh, moist paneer; if it feels dry, knead in 1 tbsp milk so the filling binds instead of spilling out while rolling.
Rest the rolled parathas no more than 5 minutes before cooking — the radish-free paneer filling is forgiving, but the khapli dough dries faster than maida dough.
Stack cooked parathas in a cloth-lined box; the trapped steam keeps them soft for up to 2 hours for tiffin.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a bowl of chilled salted curd, a wedge of lime pickle and sweet masala chai for a classic Delhi-style breakfast plate.

variations.name: Punjabi Paneer Paratha
variations.description: The dhaba original from Punjab's Grand Trunk Road: a thicker, generously stuffed paratha finished with a slick of white butter melting over the hot crust. Kasuri methi and ginger in the filling give it the unmistakable roadside-dhaba fragrance.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli wheat gives the sturdy yet tender base a thick dhaba-style paratha needs

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Punjabi parathas are shallow-roasted in ghee, not just brushed — be generous on the tava

steps: Make the dough first: work 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 1/2 tsp salt, then add roughly 3/4 cup water in stages, kneading 6 minutes to a supple, springy dough. Cover with a damp cloth for 20 minutes.

Grate 300 g paneer on the coarse side of a grater — grating, not crumbling, is the dhaba trick for an even filling. Season it with 1/2 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp anardana powder, 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi, 1 inch grated ginger and 2 minced green chillies.
Shape 8 dough balls and stuff each with a heaped 2 tbsp of the paneer masala, sealing the pleats at the top and flattening the ball between your palms before rolling.
Roll each ball into a slightly thick 6-inch round — Punjabi parathas stay chunky, so do not roll them paper thin or the filling will dry out on the tava.
Roast on a medium-hot tava with 1/2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee per paratha, pressing gently with a folded cloth and flipping twice until deep golden patches appear on both faces, about 4 minutes per paratha.
Slide each paratha onto a plate and immediately crown it with 1/2 tbsp white butter so it melts into the crust before serving.
tips: Anardana powder is the secret souring agent in Punjabi stuffings; if unavailable, use 1/2 tsp amchur but never lemon juice, which makes the filling watery.
Grated paneer packs tighter than crumbled, letting you overstuff dhaba-style without blowouts while rolling.
For an authentic finish, cook the last 30 seconds on a slightly higher flame so the ghee on the surface crisps into lacy brown edges.
variations.servingSuggestion: Plate with a tall glass of salted lassi, sliced onions sprinkled with chaat masala, and homestyle mango pickle — the complete Punjabi dhaba spread.

variations.name: Bengali Paneer Paratha
variations.description: A Kolkata-style take where pungent kachi ghani mustard oil does double duty — smoked into the filling and brushed on the tava. Nigella seeds and a whisper of sugar balance the sharp mustard heat, echoing the flavours of Bengali chhena dishes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The wholegrain nuttiness of khapli stands up beautifully to assertive mustard oil

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed kachi ghani oil — heat it to smoking once to mellow the raw pungency, the Bengali way

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A final ghee brush rounds off the mustard sharpness with sweetness

steps: Combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil, then knead with about 3/4 cup water for 5 minutes into a soft, elastic dough. Rest it under a damp cloth for 15 minutes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a small pan until it just begins to smoke, then take it off the heat, drop in 1 tsp nigella seeds and let them crackle for 20 seconds in the residual heat.

Crumble 250 g paneer into a bowl and pour the warm nigella-mustard oil over it. Add 1/2 tsp salt, 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1/2 tsp sugar, 2 minced green chillies and 2 tbsp coriander, mixing until the filling turns pale gold and fragrant.
Portion the dough into 8 balls, stuff each with 2 tbsp of the mustard-scented filling, seal the seams tightly and roll out to gentle 7-inch rounds on a floured board.
Cook each paratha on a medium tava, brushing both sides with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil, flipping until deep golden freckles form, roughly 3 minutes per paratha.
Finish the hot stack with a light brush of 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee so the pungent and sweet notes settle together before serving.
tips: Always smoke mustard oil once and cool it slightly before it touches the paneer — raw kachi ghani oil is too bitter for a filling.
The 1/2 tsp sugar is not optional in the Bengali palate; it lifts the mustard rather than sweetening the dish.
Leftover parathas revive perfectly on a dry tava; sprinkle a few drops of water and cover for 30 seconds to re-steam.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with begun bhaja (crisp fried aubergine slices) and a smear of kasundi mustard relish for a true Kolkata brunch.

variations.name: Kerala Paneer Paratha
variations.description: A Malabar-inspired paratha where fresh grated coconut, curry leaves and coconut oil transform the filling into something tropical and fragrant. The coconut keeps the paneer astonishingly moist, and each bite carries the toasty sweetness of the southern coast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat's mild sweetness mirrors the coconut instead of fighting it

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil perfumes both the tempering and the tava, Malabar style

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A small ghee finish deepens the toasted-coconut aroma on the hot crust

steps: Knead a soft dough from 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and about 3/4 cup water; work it for 5 minutes until it springs back when pressed, then rest 15 minutes covered.

Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadai over medium heat, splutter 1/2 tsp mustard seeds for 15 seconds, then add 12 curry leaves and 2 slit green chillies and fry until the leaves crisp and shine.

Add 1/2 cup grated coconut to the tempering and toast on low heat for 2 minutes until it smells nutty but stays white, then fold in 200 g crumbled paneer, 1/2 tsp salt and 1/2 tsp black pepper powder. Cook 1 minute and cool completely.

Divide the dough into 8 balls and the cooled coconut-paneer filling into 8 portions of about 2 tbsp. Stuff, seal the pleats and roll each ball into a 6-inch round with a light hand so the coconut does not pierce through.
Toast each paratha on a medium tava for about 3 minutes, flipping twice and brushing with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil until golden islands appear across both sides.
Brush the finished stack with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee while hot and let it rest 2 minutes under a cloth so the flavours knit together.
tips: Cool the coconut filling fully before stuffing — a warm filling steams the dough from inside and makes rolling impossible.
Frozen grated coconut works if thawed and squeezed dry; wet coconut will tear the paratha at the edges.
Crush 2 extra curry leaves into the dough itself for a fragrant green-flecked crust.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coconut-coriander chutney and sweet milky filter coffee, or alongside a thin vegetable stew for a Kerala tiffin experience.

variations.name: Rajasthani Paneer Paratha
variations.description: A desert-style paratha with fire and thrift in equal measure: crushed dried red chillies bloomed in ghee, plenty of ajwain in the dough, and a coarse, rustic filling. It is built to be robust — the kind of paratha that travels well wrapped in cloth, as Marwari lunches always did.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Hardy khapli wheat gives the firm, layered bite Rajasthani parathas are known for

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: In Rajasthan ghee is the flavour, not a garnish — it blooms the chillies and roasts the paratha

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp ajwain, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 3/4 cup water into a firm yet pliable dough; the ajwain goes into the dough itself, desert style. Rest 15 minutes.
Dry-roast 1 tbsp coriander seeds and 4 dried red chillies on a low flame for 2 minutes until brittle and aromatic, then pound them coarsely in a mortar — keep visible flakes, not powder.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan, tip in the pounded chilli-coriander mix and sizzle for 30 seconds so the spices bloom, then pour over 250 g crumbled paneer along with 1/2 tsp salt, 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp amchur. Mix well.
Divide dough into 8 balls, stuff each with a level 2 tbsp of the fiery filling, seal firmly and roll into thickish 6-inch rounds, dusting minimally with atta.
Roast on a medium tava with 1/2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee per paratha, pressing the surface with a spatula until deep russet spots develop on both sides, around 4 minutes each.
Rest the parathas 2 minutes before serving so the chilli-ghee aroma settles into the crumb rather than escaping as steam.
tips: Pounded roasted chillies give slow, rounded heat; chilli powder would make the filling harsh and one-dimensional, so take the extra 2 minutes.
These parathas keep for a full day at room temperature wrapped in muslin — ideal for travel tiffins.
If serving children, swap 2 of the dried chillies for 1 tsp sweet paprika to keep colour without the burn.
variations.servingSuggestion: Do as Marwari households do: serve with a katori of chaas spiked with roasted cumin, a spoon of garlic chutney, and raw onion rings.

variations.name: Classic Garlic Cabbage Paratha
variations.description: A North Indian breakfast staple where sweet shredded cabbage is sautéed with plenty of golden garlic, then tucked inside a soft khapli wheat dough. The filling is cooked dry so the paratha rolls out clean and crisps beautifully on the tava, with a nutty aroma from slow-browned garlic in ghee.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat gives this paratha a naturally sweet, nutty crumb that stays soft even after cooling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee browns the garlic without burning it and gives the crust its signature aroma

ingredients.name: Cabbage
ingredients.note: finely shredded

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: finely minced

ingredients.name: Green chilli
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Salt
ingredients.note: divided between dough and filling

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 1/2 tsp salt and about 3/4 cup water into a soft, non-sticky dough; knead for 5 minutes until smooth, cover and rest for 20 minutes.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium heat, splutter 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then sauté 8 minced garlic cloves and 2 chopped green chillies until the garlic turns pale golden, about 1 minute.

Add 3 cups finely shredded cabbage with 1/2 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1/2 tsp salt; sauté on medium-high heat for 5 to 6 minutes until the cabbage wilts and all moisture evaporates.
Take the filling off the heat, stir in 1/2 tsp amchur powder and 3 tbsp chopped coriander, and spread it on a plate to cool completely so it does not steam the dough.
Divide the dough into 8 equal balls, flatten each into a 3-inch cup, place 2 tbsp of cabbage filling in the centre, gather the edges over the top and pinch firmly to seal.
Dust each stuffed ball with dry atta and roll gently into a 6-inch round, applying even pressure from the centre outward so the filling does not tear through.

Roast each paratha on a hot tava over medium-high heat for about 2 minutes per side, brushing both sides with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, until deep golden-brown spots appear and the edges crisp.
tips: Squeeze the shredded cabbage with a pinch of salt for 10 minutes and wring it out before cooking if you want an extra-dry filling that never leaks while rolling.
Cook the garlic only to pale golden; it keeps browning in the residual heat and turns bitter if taken darker in the pan.
The cooked filling keeps refrigerated for 2 days, so you can make it ahead and roll fresh parathas in the morning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot off the tava with a bowl of thick curd, a wedge of lime and a spoon of garlic pickle; a glass of masala chaas turns it into a complete brunch.

variations.name: Punjabi Garlic Cabbage Paratha
variations.description: The dhaba-style version from Punjab, rolled thick, roasted on high heat and finished with a knob of white butter melting over the crust. The filling leans on ginger, garlic and garam masala, with kasuri methi rubbed in for that unmistakable roadside-tandoor flavour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The extra half cup makes a thicker, dhaba-style paratha that stands up to a heavy butter finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Generous ghee on the tava is what blisters the crust the Punjabi way

ingredients.name: Cabbage
ingredients.note: shredded

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: minced

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: grated

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Kasuri methi
ingredients.note: crushed between palms

ingredients.name: White butter
ingredients.note: for topping

steps: Bring 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta together with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and roughly 1 cup water; work it for 6 to 7 minutes into a supple dough, then cover with a damp cloth and set aside for 20 minutes.

Melt 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan over medium flame and fry 1 chopped onion for 3 minutes until translucent, then add 10 minced garlic cloves and 1 inch grated ginger and cook another minute until fragrant.
Tip in 3 cups shredded cabbage, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 3/4 tsp salt, and stir-fry on high heat for 6 minutes until the mixture looks dry and lightly caramelised at the edges.
Off the heat, crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the filling, sprinkle 1 tsp garam masala and 2 tbsp coriander, mix well and let it cool on a wide plate for 10 minutes.
Portion the dough into 8 balls, cup each one in your palm, pack in a generous 2.5 tbsp of filling, seal the pleats at the top and press flat.
Roll each ball into a thick 6-inch disc, keeping it noticeably thicker than a regular paratha so it stays fluffy inside.
Cook on a very hot tava for about 90 seconds per side with 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee brushed over both faces, pressing the edges with a spatula until they blister and char in spots.
Top each hot paratha with 1 tbsp white butter just before it leaves the pan so it melts into the crust.
tips: Press the paratha edges down with a folded cloth while roasting; the edges are the thickest part and need direct contact to cook through.
If you cannot find white butter, lightly whip chilled cream for 2 minutes and use the soft solids the way Punjabi homes do.
Caramelising the onion before the cabbage goes in adds the sweetness that balances the garam masala; do not rush that step.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a tall glass of sweet lassi and spicy mango pickle; for the full dhaba experience, add a katori of dahi whisked with a pinch of roasted cumin.

variations.name: Bengali Garlic Cabbage Paratha
variations.description: Inspired by bandhakopir torkari, the beloved Bengali cabbage stir-fry, this paratha carries the pungent kick of mustard oil, the sweetness of green peas and a whisper of sugar. Nigella seeds in the dough perk up every bite with their oniony crunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its wholemeal earthiness stands up to the sharpness of mustard oil in the filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed kachi ghani oil delivers the authentic nose-tingling jhaanj Bengali cabbage demands

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A final ghee brush mellows the mustard heat, the classic Bengali balance

ingredients.name: Cabbage
ingredients.note: shredded

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: sliced thin

ingredients.name: Nigella seeds
ingredients.note: kalonji, for the dough

ingredients.name: Green chilli
ingredients.note: slit

steps: Mix 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp nigella seeds, 1/2 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil, then knead in about 3/4 cup water for 5 minutes to a smooth, pliable dough; rest it covered for 20 minutes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai until it just begins to smoke, then lower the flame and let it cool for 30 seconds so the raw pungency softens.
Fry 8 sliced garlic cloves and 3 slit green chillies in the oil for 1 minute on medium heat until the garlic edges turn light brown and aromatic.

Add 3 cups shredded cabbage, 1/2 cup green peas, 1/2 tsp turmeric powder, 1/2 tsp salt and 1/2 tsp sugar; cook uncovered on medium heat for 7 to 8 minutes, stirring often, until the peas are tender and the pan looks dry.
Cool the filling fully, then lightly mash it so the peas break down and the mixture holds together when pressed.
Shape the dough into 8 balls, hollow each into a cup, spoon in 2 tbsp of the cabbage-pea filling, close the mouth tightly and roll into a 6-inch round on a floured board.
Roast on a medium-hot tava for 2 minutes on each side until brown freckles appear, then finish with a thin brush of 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee across the hot surface.
tips: Always let mustard oil reach its smoking point once and cool briefly before adding aromatics; skipping this leaves a raw, bitter edge in the filling.
Mash the peas coarsely rather than fine so you get sweet pops of texture inside the paratha.
Leftover filling doubles as a side dish; reheat it with a spoon of ghee and serve with plain rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tomato-khejur chutney and a few slices of cucumber; on a winter morning, a cup of milky cha alongside completes the Kolkata mood.

variations.name: Kerala Garlic Cabbage Paratha
variations.description: A thoran-inspired take where cabbage is tossed with fresh grated coconut, curry leaves and crackled mustard seeds before being folded into the dough. Cooking the paratha in coconut oil gives it a faintly sweet, tropical crust unlike any northern version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Stone-ground emmer keeps the paratha tender enough to fold around the coconut-flecked filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil doubles down on the thoran flavour and crisps the crust with a sweet aroma

ingredients.name: Cabbage
ingredients.note: finely shredded

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: crushed

ingredients.name: Green chilli
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Shallots
ingredients.note: sliced

steps: Work 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and about 3/4 cup water into a soft dough; knead 5 minutes until it springs back when pressed, then rest covered for 20 minutes.
Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan on medium heat and pop 1 tsp mustard seeds until they crackle, about 30 seconds, then toss in 2 sprigs of curry leaves and let them turn glossy.
Add 4 sliced shallots, 6 crushed garlic cloves and 3 chopped green chillies and sauté for 2 minutes until the shallots soften and smell sweet.
Stir in 3 cups shredded cabbage with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1/2 tsp salt; cook on medium flame for 5 minutes, tossing regularly, until the cabbage is just tender but still has bite.
Fold in 1/2 cup fresh grated coconut, cook 1 more minute, then spread the thoran-style filling out to cool completely before stuffing.
Divide the rested dough into 8 portions, stuff each with 2 tbsp of the coconut-cabbage mixture, seal the seams well and roll out gently to a 6-inch circle.
Cook each paratha on a medium-hot tava for about 2 minutes a side, drizzling the edges with the remaining coconut oil, until golden patches form and the coconut inside smells toasty.
tips: Use fresh or frozen grated coconut, not desiccated; dried coconut turns chewy inside the paratha.
Keep the cabbage slightly undercooked before adding coconut so it finishes cooking on the tava without turning mushy.
A few curry leaves crisped in coconut oil and crushed over the finished paratha intensify the aroma dramatically.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney or a quick tomato-onion salad, and pour strong South Indian filter coffee alongside for a proper Kerala breakfast spread.

variations.name: Andhra Garlic Cabbage Paratha
variations.description: A fiery rendition powered by Guntur red chillies, roasted chana dal powder and a hit of tamarind, echoing the flavours of Andhra vepudu. The dry chilli-garlic pounded together forms an intense masala paste that stains the filling a deep brick red.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The robust wheat flavour tames the Guntur chilli heat instead of disappearing behind it

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed peanut oil is the traditional Andhra frying medium and adds a nutty backbone to the masala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing swipe of ghee rounds off the chilli sting on the crust

ingredients.name: Cabbage
ingredients.note: shredded

ingredients.name: Roasted chana dal
ingredients.note: ground to a coarse powder

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and around 3/4 cup water for 5 minutes into a soft, elastic dough; rest under a damp cloth for 20 minutes.
Dry-roast 4 Guntur red chillies on a low flame for 2 minutes until deep and brittle, cool them, then pound with 10 garlic cloves and a pinch of salt into a coarse, brick-red paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium, crisp 1 sprig of curry leaves for 20 seconds, then fry the chilli-garlic paste for 2 minutes until the raw garlic smell disappears.
Add 3 cups shredded cabbage, 1 tsp coriander powder and 1/2 tsp salt; stir-fry on high heat for 5 to 6 minutes until dry, then mix in 1 tsp tamarind paste dissolved in a spoon of hot water.
Sprinkle 3 tbsp coarse roasted chana dal powder over the filling to absorb residual moisture, toss well and cool completely on a plate.
Split the dough into 8 balls, fill each with 2 tbsp of the fiery mixture, pinch the opening shut and roll into a 6-inch disc with light, even strokes.
Roast on a hot tava for roughly 2 minutes per side until crisp reddish-brown blisters form, then rub 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the hot parathas before stacking.
tips: Adjust heat by deseeding two of the four chillies; Guntur chillies bring genuine fire, not just colour.
The roasted chana dal powder is the secret to a bindable, non-leaky filling, so do not skip it.
Pounding the chilli-garlic in a mortar rather than a mixer keeps the paste coarse, which chars into flavourful flecks on the tava.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Andhra way with a dollop of chilled curd to douse the heat and a spoon of avakaya pickle for those who want even more; thin buttermilk with curry leaves is the ideal cooler.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Onion Paratha
variations.description: The everyday dhaba-style pyaaz paratha: a soft khapli wheat shell packed with sharp raw onions, green chillies and roasted cumin, toasted in ghee until blistered and crisp at the edges. The trick is squeezing the onions dry so the paratha rolls out without tearing. Each bite is sweet, pungent and gently smoky.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Stone-ground emmer wheat gives the dough extra stretch so the onion stuffing stays sealed

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee browns the crust evenly and carries the onion's sweetness without smoking

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 0.75 cup water into a soft, non-sticky dough; work it for 5 minutes until smooth, then cover and rest 15 minutes.

Finely chop 3 medium onions and 3 green chillies, toss with 0.75 tsp salt and set aside for 10 minutes; then squeeze the mixture firmly in your fist to press out all the released juice, which would otherwise tear the dough.
Mix the squeezed onions with 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp black pepper and 3 tbsp chopped coriander until every shred is coated in spice.
Divide the dough into 8 equal balls; flatten one into a 4-inch cup, place 2 tbsp of the onion filling in the centre, pleat the edges together, pinch to seal and dust with dry atta.
Roll each stuffed ball gently into a 6-inch round using light, even strokes from the centre outward so the filling does not burst through.

Heat a tava on medium-high flame; cook the paratha 1 minute until small bubbles appear, flip, spread 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee, flip again and press the edges with a spatula until both sides show deep golden-brown spots, about 3 minutes total.
Repeat with the remaining balls, stacking finished parathas in a cloth-lined box, and serve them hot while the crust is still crisp.
tips: Salting and squeezing the onions is non-negotiable; skip it and the parathas will leak and stick to the rolling pin.
Stuff and roll only just before cooking — a stuffed ball left sitting for 15 minutes turns soggy from onion moisture.
If a paratha tears while rolling, patch the spot with a small pinch of dry dough and dust generously with atta before continuing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve two per person with a bowl of thick salted curd, mango pickle and a few onion rings dipped in lemon juice for a proper highway-dhaba plate.

variations.name: Bengali Spicy Onion Paratha
variations.description: In Bengal the pyaaj porota gets its bite from pungent kasundi-style mustard flavours: onions are wilted in smoking-hot mustard oil with nigella seeds before stuffing. The mustard oil's sharp, wasabi-like heat mellows into a deep savoury note as the paratha toasts. It is a monsoon-evening favourite with a cup of milky cha.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli wheat's nutty flavour stands up to the assertive mustard oil in this Bengali take

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed kachi ghani oil delivers the authentic sinus-tingling jhaanj Bengalis prize

steps: Make the dough by rubbing 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, then kneading in roughly 0.75 cup water until soft and elastic; rest it under a damp cloth for 15 minutes.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai on high until it just begins to smoke and its raw sharpness fades, about 1 minute, then lower the flame to medium.

Crackle 1 tsp nigella seeds in the hot oil for 15 seconds, then add 3 finely sliced onions, 4 slit green chillies and 1 inch grated ginger; sauté 5 to 6 minutes until the onions turn soft and pale gold but not brown.

Stir in 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp sugar and 0.75 tsp salt, cook 1 more minute, then spread the filling on a plate and cool it completely before adding 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
Portion the dough into 8 balls, cup each into a small bowl shape, spoon in 2 tbsp of the cooled onion filling, gather the edges over the top and twist off the excess dough to seal.

Roll each parcel into a 6-inch disc with gentle pressure, then toast on a medium-hot tava for about 90 seconds per side, drizzling 0.5 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil around the edges, until both faces are freckled deep brown.
Rest the porotas 2 minutes under a cloth so the crust softens slightly in the Bengali style before serving.
tips: Always let mustard oil reach its smoking point once before adding spices, otherwise the filling tastes raw and bitter.
Cooling the sautéed filling fully is essential; warm filling steams the dough from inside and makes rolling impossible.
For an extra Bengali kick, smear a little kasundi mustard inside the dough cup before adding the onion filling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with aloo dum or simply a smear of kasundi and sliced cucumber, and finish the meal with hot lebu-cha (lemon tea) as they do in Kolkata's para stalls.

variations.name: Rajasthani Spicy Onion Paratha
variations.description: Rajasthan's desert kitchens toast whole dried Mathania-style red chillies and coriander seeds, pound them coarsely and fold them through the onion masala for a rustic, smoky burn. Besan is added to the filling to absorb moisture — an old marwari trick for travel-friendly parathas that stay crisp for hours.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The hardy emmer grain mirrors the coarse desert wheats traditionally used in Marwar

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rajasthani cooking is generous with ghee; bilona ghee gives the crust its khasta flakiness

steps: Combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 tsp salt, 0.5 tsp ajwain seeds and 1 tbsp melted Anveshan Ghee, then knead with about 0.75 cup water into a medium-soft dough; the ajwain will toast through fully during cooking. Rest 15 minutes.
Dry-roast 4 whole dried red chillies, 2 tsp coriander seeds and 1 tsp fennel seeds in a pan on low heat for 2 to 3 minutes until fragrant and brittle, then pound them coarsely in a mortar.
In the same pan, melt 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium heat and roast 3 tbsp besan for 3 minutes, stirring constantly, until it smells nutty and darkens a shade.

Toss 3 finely chopped onions with the pounded spices, roasted besan, 1 tsp amchur, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt; the besan will drink up the onion juices within 5 minutes, giving a crumbly, rollable filling.
Shape the dough into 8 balls, stuff each with 2 tbsp of the chilli-onion filling, seal by pleating, and roll into thick 5-inch rounds — Rajasthani parathas are kept smaller and sturdier.
Cook on a medium tava for about 2 minutes per side, spooning 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee over each face, pressing the edges until the surface is crisp, deeply spotted and khasta.
Crush each finished paratha lightly between your palms once, as done with khasta rotis, to open the flaky layers, then serve.
tips: Roast the besan patiently on low heat; under-roasted besan tastes raw and pasty inside the paratha.
Adjust the dried chilli count to your tolerance — 4 Mathania-style chillies give a warm glow, 6 give true Rajasthani fire.
These parathas keep crisp for 6 to 7 hours, making them ideal tiffin or travel food; wrap in paper, not foil, to preserve the crunch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the desert way with a wedge of raw onion, garlic-chilli chutney and a tall glass of chilled chaas seasoned with roasted cumin.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Onion Paratha
variations.description: An unapologetically fiery take built on Guntur red chillies, the pride of Andhra Pradesh. The onions are bound with a coarse podi-style paste of Guntur chilli, garlic and tamarind, so every layer carries tangy heat. Curry leaves crisped in hot oil finish the paratha with a southern perfume.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The wholegrain sweetness of khapli tames the Guntur chilli's aggressive heat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the traditional Andhra frying medium and deepens the podi flavour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A final gloss of bilona ghee rounds off the chilli burn on the finished paratha

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and around 0.75 cup water into a supple dough; cover and let it relax for 15 minutes while you build the podi paste.

Toast 5 Guntur dried red chillies in a dry pan on low flame for 2 minutes until they puff and darken slightly, then grind them with 6 garlic cloves, 1 tbsp tamarind pulp and 0.25 tsp salt into a coarse, brick-red paste.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium-high, crackle 12 curry leaves for 20 seconds until glassy, then add 3 finely chopped onions and sauté 4 minutes until just translucent.

Stir the Guntur paste, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt into the onions, fry 2 minutes until the raw garlic smell disappears, and cool the filling completely on a wide plate.
Divide the dough into 8 portions, stuff each ball with 2 tbsp of the cooled chilli-onion masala, seal the pleats firmly and roll out into 6-inch rounds on a dusted board.
Roast each paratha on a medium-hot tava, brushing with the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil, about 2 minutes per side until crisp, aromatic and mottled with dark blisters.
Slick each hot paratha with a little Anveshan Ghee the moment it comes off the tava so the fat melts into the spicy crust.
tips: Deseed two of the five Guntur chillies if you want the flavour without the full Andhra blaze.
Grind the podi paste coarse, not smooth — the little chilli flecks toasting against the tava are the signature of this paratha.
The tamarind keeps the filling moist, so roll these slightly thicker than usual to prevent tearing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Eat with a cooling bowl of thick curd rice or plain perugu and a spoon of avakaya pickle on the side — the classic Andhra fire-and-ice pairing.

variations.name: Kerala Spicy Onion Paratha
variations.description: Inspired by Malabar kitchens, this version folds fresh grated coconut and shallot-style small onions into the filling, tempered in coconut oil with mustard seeds and green chilli. The coconut turns lightly toasty as the paratha cooks, giving a sweet, nutty counterpoint to the pepper heat. It tastes like a thoran wrapped in flatbread.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Soft emmer dough laminates well, echoing the layers of a Malabar porotta

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil perfumes both the tempering and the tava, the Kerala way

steps: Work 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil together, then knead in about 0.75 cup water until you have a smooth, springy dough; rest it covered for 15 minutes.
Warm 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan on medium heat and pop 1 tsp mustard seeds fully, about 30 seconds, before adding 15 curry leaves and 3 chopped green chillies.
Add 2 chopped medium onions and 8 sliced shallots; sauté 5 minutes until soft and sweet, then fold in 0.75 cup grated coconut, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp black pepper and 0.75 tsp salt.
Toast the coconut mixture 3 more minutes, stirring, until it dries out and smells nutty like a thoran, then spread it on a plate to cool to room temperature.
Split the dough into 8 balls, hollow each into a cup, pack in 2 tbsp of the coconut-onion filling, crimp shut and flatten gently between your palms before rolling to 6 inches.
Cook on a medium tava for roughly 2 minutes a side, drizzling 0.5 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil around the rim of each paratha, until the crust turns golden with toasty brown coconut speckles.
Stack the parathas under a cloth for 3 minutes; the trapped steam softens them just enough to tear by hand like a porotta.
tips: Use fresh or frozen grated coconut, never desiccated — dried coconut turns gritty and steals moisture from the dough.
Cook the filling until visibly dry; coconut releases oil and water that will otherwise burst the seams while rolling.
Crushing the cooked paratha lightly between both palms fluffs the layers, the same move used on Malabar porottas.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a small bowl of coconut chutney or Kerala-style kadala curry and finish with sulaimani chai spiked with lime and mint.

variations.name: Classic Stuffed Mooli Paratha
variations.description: The winter breakfast staple of North Indian homes, where sharp white radish is tamed with salt, squeezed dry, and folded into a soft khapli atta shell. The filling stays juicy but never leaks, and the crust turns flaky and golden from a generous ghee roast. Peppery, warming, and best eaten straight off the tava.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat's low gluten keeps the paratha soft even after the juicy mooli filling goes in

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee's high smoke point gives the crust its blistered, nutty finish

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 0.75 cup water into a soft, non-sticky dough. Cover and rest for 20 minutes so the emmer wheat hydrates fully.

Grate 500 g mooli on the fine side of a grater, toss with 0.5 tsp salt and set aside for 15 minutes. Squeeze the radish hard in fistfuls until it releases nearly half a cup of juice and feels almost dry.

Mix the squeezed mooli with 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp grated ginger, 2 minced green chillies, 3 tbsp coriander, 0.5 tsp amchur and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt.
Divide the dough into 8 balls. Flatten each into a 4-inch cup, place 2 tbsp of filling in the centre, gather the edges over the top and pinch to seal completely.
Dust each stuffed ball lightly with flour and roll gently to a 7-inch round, easing the pin outward so the filling spreads without tearing through.

Heat a tava on medium-high until a drop of water sizzles instantly. Cook each paratha for about 1 minute until small bubbles rise, flip, spread 0.5 tsp Anveshan Ghee, and roast both sides, pressing the edges, until deep golden spots appear, 2 to 3 minutes total.
Stack the parathas in a cloth-lined box so they stay soft, brushing the top of each with a little more of the remaining Anveshan Ghee while still hot.
tips: Squeezing the salted radish dry is the make-or-break step; skip it and the paratha will tear while rolling.
Save the pressed mooli juice and knead it into your next batch of dough for extra flavour and zero waste.
If a paratha springs a leak on the tava, dab the spot with dry flour and press gently; it will seal as it roasts.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a bowl of thick homemade curd, a wedge of lime pickle, and sweet milky adrak chai on the side for the full Delhi-winter experience.

variations.name: Punjabi Stuffed Mooli Paratha
variations.description: The dhaba version from Punjab's wheat belt: a thicker, sturdier paratha with an ajwain-scented filling, roasted hard on the tava and crowned with a melting knob of white butter. It is rich, rustic food built for cold mornings and big appetites.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Stone-ground khapli gives the dense, wheaty bite Punjabi dhaba parathas are known for

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A heavy hand of A2 ghee on the tava is what makes the dhaba-style crackly crust

steps: Work 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee together, then add about 1 cup water bit by bit and knead 8 minutes to a smooth, pliable dough. Rest it under a damp cloth for 20 minutes.
Meanwhile grate 600 g mooli coarsely, salt it with 0.5 tsp salt, wait 15 minutes, then wring it out in a muslin cloth until no more liquid drips.
Warm 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp ajwain for 30 seconds until fragrant; pour this tempering over the squeezed radish so the raw seeds are properly bloomed.
Season the filling with 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp crushed pepper, 1 tsp anardana powder, 2 tsp ginger, 3 tbsp coriander and the last 0.5 tsp salt, mixing with your fingers.
Shape 8 dough balls, stuff each with a packed 2.5 tbsp of filling, seal the pleats firmly and roll to a slightly thick 6-inch round, keeping dhaba-style heft rather than rolling thin.

Roast on a medium-hot tava for 90 seconds a side, then slather each side with 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and press with a spatula until both faces are crisp and mottled dark gold, about 4 minutes per paratha.
Top every hot paratha with 0.5 tbsp white butter the moment it comes off the tava so it melts into the crust.
tips: Blooming the ajwain in hot ghee before it meets the filling stops any raw, bitter edge and doubles its aroma.
Anardana gives the true Punjabi sour note; if unavailable, use 1 tsp amchur but add it just before stuffing.
Press the paratha edges hard with the spatula while roasting; the rim is thickest and needs the extra contact heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Plate with a tall glass of salted lassi, sliced raw mooli from the leftover trimmings, and green chilli pickle, the way roadside dhabas on the Amritsar highway do.

variations.name: Bengali Stuffed Mooli Paratha
variations.description: A Kolkata-style take where the radish filling is cooked down in pungent mustard oil with kalonji and green chillies, echoing the flavours of mulo bhaja. The cooked filling is drier and more intense, and a final raw drizzle of mustard oil gives the paratha its unmistakable Bengali punch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli's nutty sweetness balances the sharp mustard oil in this Bengali-style filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed kachi ghani pungency is the soul of this paratha; refined oil cannot replace it

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Just a touch in the dough keeps the layers tender against the assertive filling

steps: Bring together 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and roughly 0.75 cup water; knead until supple, then rest 20 minutes under a damp cloth.
Grate 500 g mooli, mix with 0.25 tsp salt, rest 10 minutes and squeeze out every drop of juice you can manage.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai on medium-high until it just begins to smoke, then lower the heat and crackle 0.75 tsp kalonji with 3 slit green chillies for 20 seconds.

Add the squeezed radish, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp sugar; stir-fry on medium heat for 6 to 7 minutes until the mixture is dry, faintly caramelised and smells sweetly pungent. Cool fully, then fold in 2 tbsp coriander.
Portion the dough into 8 balls, cup each one, spoon in 2 tbsp of the cooled filling, pinch shut and roll out to a 7-inch disc with light, even strokes.
Cook on a medium-hot tava, brushing each side with about 0.5 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil, flipping twice until both faces carry crisp, bronze patches, around 3 minutes per paratha.
Finish the stack with a thin raw drizzle of the remaining Anveshan Mustard Oil for that sharp, sinus-clearing Bengali aroma.
tips: Letting the mustard oil reach its first wisp of smoke before tempering mellows its bitterness while keeping the pungency.
Cook the filling until genuinely dry; a wet mulo mixture will steam inside and make the paratha soggy.
The pinch of sugar is not for sweetness; it rounds off the radish's sulphurous edge, a standard Bengali trick.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with begun bhaja (crisp fried aubergine slices) and a smear of kasundi mustard relish for a proper Kolkata Sunday brunch.

variations.name: Kerala Stuffed Mooli Paratha
variations.description: A Malabar-inspired crossover where the mooli filling is toasted with fresh grated coconut, curry leaves and black pepper in coconut oil, like a thoran tucked inside a flatbread. The coconut soaks up the radish juices, so the filling is naturally fluffy and sweet-spicy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The wholegrain emmer base gives this coconut-laced filling a malty, earthy wrapper

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed coconut oil perfumes both the thoran-style filling and the tava roast

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and close to 0.75 cup water into a soft dough; rest it, covered, for 20 minutes.
Grate 450 g mooli, salt with 0.25 tsp salt, wait 10 minutes and squeeze firmly until the shreds feel dry to the touch.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan on medium; pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, then add 12 curry leaves, 2 chopped green chillies and 4 sliced shallots and saute for 2 minutes until the shallots turn translucent.

Tip in the radish, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt; toss on medium heat for 4 minutes, then stir through 0.75 cup grated coconut and 0.75 tsp crushed pepper and cook 2 more minutes until dry and fragrant. Cool completely.
Divide the dough into 8 balls and stuff each with 2 tbsp of the coconut-mooli thoran, sealing the mouth well before rolling to a 6.5-inch round.
Roast each paratha on a medium tava, wiping the surface with about 0.5 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil per side, until freckled golden brown and crisp at the edges, 3 minutes per paratha.
tips: Cool the coconut filling completely before stuffing; warm filling releases steam and blows open the seams while rolling.
Fresh coconut beats desiccated here, but if using desiccated, soak 0.5 cup of it in 2 tbsp warm water for 10 minutes first.
Fry a few extra curry leaves crisp in the leftover coconut oil and crumble them over the finished parathas.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a small bowl of coconut chutney and sweet milky filter coffee; for a fuller meal, add a ladle of Kerala-style moru curry (spiced buttermilk).

variations.name: Rajasthani Stuffed Mooli Paratha
variations.description: From the desert kitchens of Rajasthan comes a fiery, rustic paratha where the filling is charged with hand-crushed dried red chillies, coriander seeds and fennel, flavours borrowed from the state's famous besan and pyaaz kachoris. Roasted extra-crisp, it travels well and keeps for hours, true to marwari tradition.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Hardy emmer wheat mirrors the rustic, coarse-milled rotis of rural Rajasthan

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Desert cooking leans on ghee for moisture; here it crisps the crust and blooms the chilli masala

steps: Make a firm-soft dough from 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 0.75 cup water; knead well and rest 20 minutes.
On a dry tava over low heat, toast 4 dried red chillies, 1.5 tsp coriander seeds and 1 tsp fennel seeds for 2 to 3 minutes until they darken a shade and smell toasty, then crush coarsely in a mortar.
Grate 500 g mooli, salt with 0.25 tsp salt, rest 10 minutes and squeeze bone-dry between your palms.
Sizzle 0.25 tsp hing in 1 tsp hot Anveshan Ghee for 10 seconds, pour it over the radish, then work in the crushed spice mix, 0.75 tsp amchur, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp salt and 2 tbsp coriander.
Form 8 balls, load each with 2 tbsp filling, seal tight and roll into a 6-inch round a touch thicker than usual, desert-style.

Roast on a medium flame, giving each side a full 2 minutes before the first flip, then crisp both faces with 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee per paratha until the surface is deeply browned and crackly, about 4 minutes each.
tips: Toast-and-crush spices just before mixing; pre-ground powders lose the smoky depth this paratha depends on.
A slightly firmer dough and longer roast keep these parathas fresh for a day, which is why they were traditional travel food.
Control the heat by removing chilli seeds before crushing, or lean in and add a fifth chilli if your household likes it fierce.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Marwari way with lehsun ki chutney (fiery garlic chutney), a spoon of churned white makkhan, and chaas seasoned with roasted cumin.

variations.name: Classic Cheesy Dal Paratha
variations.description: A kid-approved upgrade of the humble dal paratha: spiced toor dal mixed with grated mozzarella that melts into gooey pockets inside a crisp khapli crust. The dal keeps it wholesome while the cheese pull keeps everyone at the table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Whole emmer sneaks fibre into a cheese-loaded favourite

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee browns the crust before the cheese inside can overheat and leak

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 0.75 cup water into a soft, smooth dough; cover and rest for 15 minutes.
Cook 0.75 cup thick toor dal in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat with 1 tsp roasted cumin powder and 0.25 tsp salt until completely dry, 4-5 minutes, then cool it to room temperature.
Combine the cooled dal with 0.75 cup grated mozzarella, 0.5 tsp chilli flakes, 0.5 tsp black pepper and 2 tbsp chopped coriander; the mixture should clump when squeezed.
Divide the dough into 8 balls; cup each ball, pack in 2 tbsp of the cheesy dal, pinch the opening firmly shut and rest the stuffed balls 5 minutes so the seal sets.
Roll each ball into a 6-inch round with soft, even pressure, stopping the moment you feel the cheese shift under the pin.

Roast on a medium-hot tava for about 1 minute per side until spotted brown, then crisp with the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, roughly 0.5 tsp per side, until the crust turns deep gold and the interior audibly sizzles.
tips: The dal must be bone-dry before mixing with cheese; any moisture makes the melted cheese steam and burst the seams.
Rest stuffed balls before rolling; a set seal is the single best defence against a cheese blowout on the tava.
Serve within 10 minutes of cooking; the molten cheese-pull window is short.
variations.servingSuggestion: Cut into wedges like a quesadilla and serve with spiced tomato ketchup for kids or green chutney whisked into curd for adults.

variations.name: Punjabi Cheesy Dal Paratha
variations.description: Amritsari indulgence at full volume: chana dal and shredded cheese laced with kasuri methi and garam masala, roasted thick and finished with a slick of white butter. It eats like a stuffed kulcha's rustic cousin.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: A sturdy heritage grain that carries a heavy dhaba-style filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Double-roasting in bilona ghee builds the crackly Amritsari crust

steps: Work up a soft dough from 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and roughly 0.75 cup water; rest it 20 minutes for easy stretching.
Fry 1 finely chopped onion and 2 minced green chillies in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium heat until golden at the edges, 3-4 minutes.
Add 0.75 cup thick cooked chana dal, 0.5 tsp garam masala and 0.25 tsp salt; coarsely mash and cook until the mixture is dry and crumbly, about 5 minutes, then cool it fully.
Rub 1 tbsp kasuri methi into the cooled dal, then toss through 0.75 cup grated processed cheese so the shreds stay distinct rather than pasting together.
Stuff 8 dough balls generously with the mixture, seal the pleats, and roll thick to 5-6 inches; a Punjabi paratha should feel substantial in the hand.

Roast on a medium tava 90 seconds per side, then crank the heat, spoon on the remaining 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and re-fry each side about 45 seconds until the crust blisters mahogany and crunches when tapped.
tips: Processed cheese holds its structure under dhaba-level heat better than mozzarella, which is why kulcha shops use it.
Onions must be fried until truly golden; half-cooked onion releases water into the cheese and softens the crust.
Assemble at most 30 minutes ahead; longer and the salt in the cheese weeps moisture into the dough.
variations.servingSuggestion: Crown with the 2 tbsp white butter at the table and serve with tamarind-onion chutney and a cold glass of sweet lassi.

variations.name: Andhra Cheesy Dal Paratha
variations.description: Guntur's famously fierce red chillies collide with cool, melty cheese in this Andhra-style paratha, mellowed by a toor dal base tempered in groundnut oil with curry leaves. Fiery, tangy and creamy in the same bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The mellow grain gives Guntur heat a soft landing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the everyday fat of Andhra kitchens

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and about 0.75 cup water into a soft dough; rest 15 minutes under a damp cloth.
Dry-roast 3 Guntur chillies on a low flame until glossy and brittle, about 90 seconds, then pound them coarsely with 6 garlic cloves into a rough, fiery paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium, crisp 10 curry leaves for 20 seconds, then fry the chilli-garlic pound for 1 minute until the raw garlic smell fades.
Add 0.75 cup thick cooked toor dal, 0.5 tsp tamarind paste and 0.25 tsp salt; mash and cook until dry, about 4 minutes, then cool completely before folding in 0.75 cup grated mozzarella.
Encase 2 tbsp of the mixture in each of 8 dough balls, seal well, and roll gently to 6-inch rounds without pressing hard over the centre.
Cook each paratha on a medium-hot tava about 1 minute per side until spotted, brushing the surfaces with the oil left in the tempering pan so no chilli flavour is wasted.
tips: Guntur chillies bring real heat; swap one of the three for Kashmiri chilli if you want colour with less burn.
Tamarind is the Andhra counterweight to both heat and cheese richness; do not omit it.
Pound the chilli-garlic coarse; a smooth paste disappears into the dal and loses its punchy flecks.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with chilled curd rice on the side, Andhra-style; the cool rice is the perfect firewall for the Guntur heat.

variations.name: Tamil Cheesy Dal Paratha
variations.description: A Chettinad-leaning mash-up where black pepper, fennel and curry leaves season the dal before cheese joins the party, all toasted in gingelly oil. The pepper's sharp heat cuts the cheese so nothing feels heavy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer's gentle sweetness plays against Chettinad pepper heat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil's toasty depth is non-negotiable in a Tamil tempering

steps: Mix 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, then knead in about 0.75 cup water until pliable; rest the dough 15 minutes.
Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil over medium heat, sizzle 0.5 tsp fennel seeds for 30 seconds until they smell sweet, then add 12 curry leaves and 4 chopped shallots.
Sauté the shallots until translucent and lightly browned, about 3 minutes, then grind in 1 tsp coarsely crushed black pepper and toast for 20 seconds.
Stir in 0.75 cup thick cooked moong dal and 0.25 tsp salt, mashing and drying the mixture over medium heat for 4 minutes; spread it out to cool fast, then fold in 0.75 cup grated mozzarella.
Fill 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp each of the peppery cheese-dal, twist the tops closed and roll softly into 6-inch discs.
Toast on a medium tava roughly 75 seconds per side, wiping the surface with the fragrant oil left from the tempering, until golden-freckled and puffed at the edges.
tips: Crush pepper fresh and coarse; its volatile heat is what keeps the cheese from tasting flat.
Shallots, not onions, give the authentic Tamil sweetness; if substituting onion, use only half a medium one.
Moong dal's light body lets the pepper and fennel lead; avoid swapping in heavier chana dal here.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a quick tomato thokku or podi mixed into gingelly oil; a filter coffee afterwards completes the Tamil café mood.

variations.name: Assamese Cheesy Dal Paratha
variations.description: A daring Northeast-inspired paratha that stings a masoor dal and cheese filling with a whisper of bhut jolokia, Assam's legendary ghost chilli, balanced by mustard oil and fresh coriander. Tiny amounts, huge character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The robust grain shell keeps the ghost-chilli filling honest

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Assam's kitchens run on pungent mustard oil; wood-pressed keeps it true

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A ghee finish cools the palate after each bhut jolokia flash

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt and around 0.75 cup water plus 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee into a soft dough; rest it for 15 minutes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, cool for 30 seconds off the flame, then return to medium heat and fry 5 minced garlic cloves until pale gold, about 90 seconds.
Add one quarter of a deseeded, finely minced bhut jolokia and stir for only 10-15 seconds; the fumes are potent, so keep your face back and the exhaust on.
Immediately add 0.75 cup thick cooked masoor dal and 0.25 tsp salt; mash and cook until dry, about 4 minutes, then cool fully and fold in 0.75 cup grated mozzarella with 3 tbsp chopped coriander.
Stuff and seal 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp filling each, then roll them out gently into 6-inch rounds on a lightly floured surface.

Roast each paratha on a medium tava about 1 minute per side until brown-spotted, then gloss with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee so the finish is rich and the heat stays smouldering, not scorching.
tips: Wear gloves or oil your fingers when mincing bhut jolokia, and never touch your eyes afterwards.
A quarter chilli for the whole batch is genuinely enough; taste the cooled dal before adding cheese and stop there.
No bhut jolokia? Use 2 fresh green bird's-eye chillies for a tamer but similar fruity heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve Assamese-style with a cooling side of plain curd and a wedge of lemon; a spoon of kaji nemu (Assam lime) pickle is the connoisseur's touch.

variations.name: Classic Cheesy Palak Paratha
variations.description: A kid-approved crowd-pleaser where sautéed spinach meets molten grated cheese inside a wholegrain khapli crust. The cheese binds the greens so the filling never spills, and every tear of the hot paratha pulls into gooey strands. It is the smartest way to sneak a full bunch of palak into a fussy eater's plate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Low-gluten emmer wheat rolls thin without springing back, ideal for a cheese-stuffed paratha

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee browns the crust to a biscuit crispness that contrasts the molten centre

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and about 0.75 cup water for 6-7 minutes into a soft, smooth dough; rest it covered for 15 minutes.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium flame, sizzle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, add 3 minced garlic cloves and fry until pale gold, about 1 minute.
Add 200 g finely chopped, squeezed-dry spinach with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.25 tsp salt; cook on medium-high for 4-5 minutes until the pan looks completely dry, then cool the mixture fully.
Mix the cooled spinach with 1 cup grated cheese, 0.5 tsp chilli flakes and 0.5 tsp crushed pepper — the mixture should clump together when pressed.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, cup each portion, pack in 2 tbsp of the cheesy spinach filling, seal the pleats tightly and roll gently into a 6-inch round.

Roast on a medium-hot tava for about 75 seconds per side, brushing with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, until golden spots form and the paratha puffs slightly; rest 1 minute so the cheese sets before cutting.
tips: Cool the spinach completely before adding cheese, or it melts prematurely and turns the filling watery.
Seal the dough pleats with a drop of water — melted cheese finds any weak spot and leaks onto the tava.
A minute of resting after roasting lets the molten cheese thicken so it stretches instead of gushing out.
variations.servingSuggestion: Cut into wedges like a quesadilla and serve with tomato ketchup for kids or green chutney spiked with mint for adults.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Cheesy Palak Paratha
variations.description: Goda masala — Maharashtra's sweet-smoky blend of dagad phool, coconut and sesame — turns this cheese paratha unmistakably Marathi. The spinach is sautéed with the masala and a scatter of roasted peanut powder before the cheese goes in, echoing thalipeeth flavours. It tastes like a Pune café mashup of tradition and indulgence.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli is an old Maharashtrian favourite — this emmer wheat is still farmed in the state's heritage belts

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Toop, as Marathi homes call it — bilona ghee blooms the goda masala's smoky spices

steps: Make a soft dough from 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and roughly 0.75 cup water; knead 7 minutes and rest 15 minutes under a damp cloth.
Melt 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium heat and fry 1 finely chopped small onion with 1 minced green chilli until soft and lightly browned, about 3 minutes.

Sprinkle in 1.5 tsp goda masala and stir for 30 seconds until the smoky aroma blooms, then add 200 g chopped, well-squeezed spinach with 0.25 tsp salt and dry it out over medium-high heat for 4 minutes.
Cool the mixture, then fold in 1 cup grated cheese and 2 tbsp roasted peanut powder until the filling holds together in a soft mass.
Shape 8 dough balls, stuff each with 2 tbsp of the goda-spiced filling, pinch shut and roll into 6-inch rounds; press 1 tsp sesame seeds, divided, onto the surface of the parathas as you roll.
