Roast sesame-side down first on a medium tava, about 80 seconds per side, gliding on the last 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until the crust turns crisp with dark golden patches.
tips: Goda masala scorches quickly — 30 seconds in ghee is enough; longer and it turns bitter.
Peanut powder is the moisture insurance here, absorbing any cheese whey so the paratha stays crisp.
If you cannot find goda masala, dry-roast 1 tsp sesame, 0.5 tsp coriander seeds and a pinch of grated dry coconut, then grind — a quick home approximation.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a Marathi-style thecha of pounded green chillies and garlic, plus a cooling bowl of mattha (spiced buttermilk).

variations.name: Gujarati Cheesy Palak Paratha
variations.description: Gujarat's love of sweet-savoury balance shows up here as a spoon of jaggery powder melted into the spinach before the cheese is added, alongside ginger and sesame. The result recalls the flavours of a methi thepla crossed with a cheese toastie — mildly sweet, gently spiced, deeply comforting. Rolled thin and roasted supple, it travels well in a tiffin too.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Thepla-soft and wholegrain — emmer wheat keeps this paratha pliable even at room temperature

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Gujarati farsan-makers prize good ghee; this bilona batch gives the crust its khasta finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Chemical-free jaggery powder melts evenly into the greens for that signature Gujarati sweet note

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp salt and around 0.75 cup water into a soft thepla-like dough; rest 15 minutes.
Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat and sizzle 1 tsp ginger paste with 1 tsp green chilli paste for 45 seconds until aromatic.

Add 200 g chopped, tightly squeezed spinach and 0.25 tsp salt, cooking on medium-high about 4 minutes until dry; in the final minute stir in 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder so it melts and glazes the greens.
Spread the mixture to cool, then combine with 1 cup grated cheese and 1 tbsp sesame seeds to form a cohesive, faintly sweet filling.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, enclose 2 tbsp filling in each, seal well and roll into thin 6.5-inch rounds — Gujarati flatbreads are rolled thinner than northern ones.
Cook on a medium tava roughly 70 seconds per side, brushing both faces with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, until soft with scattered golden-brown spots rather than a hard crust.
tips: Stir the jaggery in at the end of cooking the spinach; added early it can seize into hard bits instead of glazing.
Roll these thinner than usual — the sweet filling caramelises against a thin wall for the best flavour.
These stay soft for 6-8 hours, making them a great tiffin or travel paratha, just like thepla.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with chhundo (sweet mango pickle) and a cup of masala chai — the sweet-spice pairing Gujaratis grew up on.

variations.name: Tamil Cheesy Palak Paratha
variations.description: A Chennai-style twist that tempers the spinach with curry leaves, mustard seeds, urad dal and cracked pepper in gingelly oil before the cheese goes in. The urad dal adds tiny crunchy pockets, like a good poriyal, against the cheese's creaminess. Roasting in sesame oil gives the crust the toasty depth of a dosa griddle.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Wholegrain emmer takes on the gingelly-oil tempering like a parotta made honest

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil — nallennai — is the backbone fat of Tamil kitchens and this tempering

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A last-minute drizzle of bilona ghee, the way hotel-style Tamil parottas are finished

steps: Mix 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and 0.5 tsp salt, add about 0.75 cup water and knead into a soft, stretchy dough for 7 minutes; rest 20 minutes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil on medium, pop 0.75 tsp mustard seeds for 20 seconds, then fry 1 tsp urad dal until it turns biscuit gold, about 45 seconds.
Toss in 15 curry leaves — they will crackle sharply — followed by 200 g chopped, squeezed spinach with 0.25 tsp salt; cook 4-5 minutes on medium-high until fully dry.
Cool the tempered greens, then work in 1 cup grated cheese and 0.75 tsp crushed black pepper so the filling binds into soft clumps.
Portion the dough into 8 balls, hide 2 tbsp of filling in each, seal and roll out to 6-inch circles, keeping the pressure light over the centre.
Griddle on medium-high about 75 seconds per side until crisp-spotted, then finish each paratha with a few drops of the 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee while still on the tava.
tips: Fry the urad dal to a true golden brown before the leaves go in — underdone dal stays chalky inside the filling.
Crushed pepper beats chilli powder here; its sharp heat cuts the cheese's richness the Tamil way.
Slap the rolled paratha between your palms once before griddling to relax the dough for an even cook.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and a small tumbler of sweet-sour tomato rasam for dunking the crisp edges.

variations.name: Rajasthani Cheesy Palak Paratha
variations.description: Desert-style boldness meets gooey cheese: the spinach is cooked with crushed dried red chillies, garlic and ajwain, flavours borrowed from Rajasthan's lahsun chutney. Kasuri methi rubbed into the filling adds the smoky bitterness that balances the rich cheese. It is a fiery, garlicky paratha built for cold Aravalli mornings.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Hardy emmer wheat echoes the coarse desert attas Rajasthani rotis are famed for

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rajasthan cooks measure hospitality in ghee — this bilona jar earns its generous role here

steps: Rub 0.5 tsp ajwain and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, then knead with 0.5 tsp salt and close to 0.75 cup water for 7 minutes into a soft dough; rest 15 minutes covered.
Toast 3 dried red chillies in a dry pan on low for 1 minute until brittle, cool, and crush them coarsely with your fingers or a mortar.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium flame and fry 6 minced garlic cloves until golden at the edges, about 90 seconds, then add the crushed chillies and 1 tsp coriander powder for 20 seconds.
Add 200 g chopped, squeezed spinach and 0.25 tsp salt; dry the mixture out over medium-high heat for 4 minutes, then off the heat crumble in 1 tbsp kasuri methi and cool completely.
Blend the cooled greens with 1 cup grated cheese, divide the dough into 8 balls and stuff each with 2 tbsp filling, sealing the mouth firmly before rolling to a 6-inch disc.
Roast on a medium-hot tava around 85 seconds per side, lavishing on the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and pressing the edges until the crust is crisp and burnished.
tips: Crush the toasted chillies coarsely; flakes give bursts of heat while powder would just make the filling uniformly hot.
Rub kasuri methi between your palms as you add it to wake up its smoky aroma.
Scale the chillies down to 2 for kids — the garlic alone still carries plenty of Rajasthani character.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a spoon of fiery lahsun ki chutney on the side and a glass of chaas to douse the flames.

variations.name: Classic Cheesy Pyaaz Paratha
variations.description: A modern family favourite where sweet sautéed onions and molten mozzarella-cheddar pull apart in strings inside a nutty khapli wheat crust. Cooking the onions first concentrates their sweetness and keeps the cheese from turning the filling watery on the tava.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Wholegrain emmer balances the richness of the cheese so the paratha never feels heavy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasting in bilona ghee gives the crust a toasty aroma that boxed butter cannot match

steps: Knead 3 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 1.25 cups water for 8 minutes into a soft, silky dough; rest it covered for 20 minutes.

Melt 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat and sauté 3 finely chopped onions with 0.25 tsp salt for 6 to 7 minutes until they turn light golden and smell sweet, then cool completely on a plate.
Toss the cooled onions with 0.75 cup mozzarella, 0.5 cup cheddar, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp chilli flakes, 1 tsp oregano and 2 tbsp coriander until the cheese strands bind the mixture.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, flatten one into a 4-inch cup, pack in 2.5 tbsp of the cheesy filling, pull the edges together and pinch a tight seal at the top.
Roll each stuffed ball gently into a 6-inch round, slightly thicker than a plain paratha, so the melting cheese stays locked inside.

Cook on a medium tava for about 90 seconds until bubbles appear, flip, brush with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee, and repeat on the second side, pressing lightly, until both faces are golden-spotted and the paratha feels springy, about 4 minutes in all.
Rest each paratha 1 minute before cutting so the molten cheese thickens just enough to stretch instead of gushing out.
tips: Always cool the sautéed onions fully before mixing in cheese, or the cheese melts prematurely and turns the filling greasy.
Keep the tava at medium; high heat browns the crust before the cheese in the centre has melted.
Grate the cheese straight from the fridge — cold cheese is easier to portion and seals in neater pockets.
For kids' tiffins, make 12 smaller parathas from the same quantities and underfill slightly so they travel without leaking.
variations.servingSuggestion: Cut into wedges like a quesadilla and serve with tangy tomato-garlic chutney or ketchup on the side and a cold masala chaas to cut the richness.

variations.name: Punjabi Cheesy Pyaaz Paratha
variations.description: The dhaba blockbuster: a thick, hearty paratha loaded with onions, ajwain-scented dough and a mountain of melty cheese, finished the Amritsari way with a knob of white butter sliding off the top. Kasuri methi in the filling gives it that unmistakable Punjabi restaurant aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli's coarse grind gives these thick dhaba parathas their satisfying, hearty chew

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A generous ghee sear is non-negotiable for the crackly, layered Punjabi crust

steps: Rub 1 tsp ajwain and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee into 3 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, then knead with about 1.25 cups water for 8 minutes to a soft dough; rest 20 minutes so the ajwain perfumes it.
Chop 3 onions finely, sprinkle with 0.25 tsp salt, wait 10 minutes and squeeze them absolutely dry between your palms.

Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi between your fingers over the onions, then add 1 cup grated processed cheese, 2 minced green chillies, 0.5 tsp garam masala and 1 tsp red chilli powder and mix into a shaggy, sticky filling.

Shape 8 dough balls and roll two thin 5-inch discs per paratha; spread 2.5 tbsp filling on one disc leaving a half-inch border, cap with the second disc and press the edges firmly to seal — the double-disc method holds heavy cheese loads best.
Roll the sealed sandwich lightly to a 7-inch round, then roast on a medium-hot tava for about 2 minutes per side, lavishing each side with 1.5 tsp Anveshan Ghee until deeply browned and crisp.
Slide onto a plate, crown immediately with 1 tsp white butter per paratha and let it melt into the crust before serving.
tips: The double-disc sealing method is worth learning for any heavily loaded paratha; it never bursts on the tava.
Rub kasuri methi between hot palms before adding — the friction wakes up its aroma dramatically.
Processed cheese melts stringier than paneer; for a sharper bite swap half of it with grated aged cheddar.
variations.servingSuggestion: Do it dhaba-style: serve on a steel thali with dahi sprinkled with bhuna jeera, sirke wale pyaaz and a tall glass of sweet lassi.

variations.name: Tamil Cheesy Pyaaz Paratha
variations.description: A Chennai café-style mashup where the cheese-onion filling is laced with a curry leaf and pepper tadka made in wood-pressed sesame oil. The gingelly nuttiness, cracked pepper and crisp-fried curry leaves make it taste like milagu-jeera podi met a cheese toastie.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The emmer wheat's earthiness pairs naturally with nutty gingelly oil

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil is the soul of Tamil tadkas and crisps the crust beautifully

steps: Knead a supple dough from 3 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and roughly 1.25 cups water; work it 8 minutes and rest 20 minutes under a damp cloth.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadai on medium, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds for 30 seconds, then fry 15 curry leaves, 2 chopped green chillies and 1 tsp ginger until the leaves turn glassy and crisp.
Tip in 3 finely chopped onions with 0.25 tsp salt and sauté 6 minutes until golden at the edges; stir in 1.5 tsp crushed black pepper, cook 30 seconds more and cool the mixture completely.
Fold 1 cup grated mozzarella through the cooled pepper-onion tadka so every strand of cheese picks up flecks of curry leaf.
Stuff 8 dough balls with 2.5 tbsp filling each, seal the pleats, and roll into 6-inch rounds a touch thicker than usual to protect the melty centre.
Toast each paratha on a medium tava with 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil per side for about 2 minutes a side, until the crust turns deep gold with crisp lacy edges; rest 1 minute before cutting.
tips: Crush the pepper coarsely in a mortar rather than using powder — the sharp bursts of heat against the cheese define this recipe.
Fry the curry leaves until truly crisp; limp leaves turn chewy inside the melted cheese.
A teaspoon of idli podi mixed into the filling makes a wonderful, more pungent podi-cheese version.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and a small tumbler of filter coffee, or cut into strips and dunk into sambar like a cheeseful kothu snack.

variations.name: Andhra Cheesy Pyaaz Paratha
variations.description: Fierce Guntur chillies meet cooling molten cheese in this Andhra-style paratha, where the onions are cooked down with a garlicky red chilli paste before the cheese goes in. The contrast of sana-level heat and creamy cheese pull is what makes this version addictive.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The robust wholegrain crust carries serious Guntur heat without tasting thin

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the traditional Andhra frying medium and tames raw chilli harshness

steps: Soak 5 dried Guntur chillies in 0.25 cup hot water for 15 minutes, then grind them with 6 garlic cloves and 1 tsp coriander seeds into a coarse red paste.
Meanwhile knead 3 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and about 1.25 cups water for 8 minutes into a soft dough; rest it 20 minutes.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium, fry the chilli-garlic paste for 2 to 3 minutes until the oil separates and the raw garlic smell disappears, then add 3 chopped onions, 0.25 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp turmeric.
Sauté the onions 6 minutes until soft and stained brick-red, stir in 2 tbsp coriander leaves, then spread the masala on a plate and cool it fully before folding in 1 cup grated mozzarella.
Stuff 8 balls of dough with 2.5 tbsp of the fiery cheese filling each, pinch the seals shut and roll into thickish 6-inch rounds.
Roast on a medium tava with 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil per side, about 2 minutes each side, until the crust blisters mahogany-gold; rest a minute so the cheese sets to a slow, spicy pull.
tips: Frying the chilli-garlic paste until oil separates is the flavour make-or-break step; underfried paste tastes raw and acrid.
Scale heat by chilli count, not by skipping the paste — even 2 Guntur chillies keep the character while sparing your palate.
The cool creaminess of the cheese hides the heat at first bite; warn guests before their second paratha.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a katori of thick curd and a wedge of lime, plus sliced cucumbers to douse the Guntur fire between bites.

variations.name: Delhi-style Cheesy Pyaaz Paratha
variations.description: A tribute to Chandni Chowk's Paranthe Wali Gali, where parathas are shallow-crisped in ghee until shatteringly flaky. Here the onion-cheese filling is spiked with garam masala, anardana and chaat masala, so every bite has that sweet-sour street-corner punch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Rested khapli dough fries up extra flaky in the shallow ghee, old-Delhi style

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Paranthe Wali Gali fries only in desi ghee — bilona ghee recreates that aroma at home

steps: Make a soft, well-kneaded dough from 3 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 1.25 cups water; rest it a full 25 minutes, which helps it fry flaky rather than chewy.
Finely chop 3 onions, toss with 0.25 tsp salt, rest 10 minutes and squeeze out all their liquid into the sink.

Combine the onions with 0.5 cup crumbled paneer, 0.75 cup grated cheddar, 1 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp anardana powder, 1 tsp chaat masala, 2 minced green chillies and 3 tbsp coriander into a tangy, cohesive filling.
Portion the dough into 8 balls, stuff each with 2.5 tbsp filling, seal firmly and roll to 6-inch rounds of even thickness so they crisp uniformly.

Set a tava on medium heat with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee; lay a paratha in the shallow pool of ghee and fry 2 minutes per side, spooning hot ghee over the top and pressing the edges until both sides turn a crackly, deep gold.
Drain each fried paratha briefly on a rack, then finish with a light dusting of chaat masala while still glistening.
tips: Shallow-frying in a pool of ghee, not just brushing, is what separates a Gali-style parantha from a home one; drain on a rack to keep it crisp.
Anardana gives the authentic sweet-sour note; if unavailable, use 0.5 tsp amchur but the flavour will be flatter.
Crumbled paneer stretches the cheese and keeps the filling from oozing — a trick many Delhi vendors quietly use.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as they do in Chandni Chowk: with saunth ki meethi chutney, spicy aloo sabzi and a pyramid of sirka onions on a leaf plate.

variations.name: Classic Beetroot Paratha
variations.description: A ruby-pink stuffed flatbread where earthy-sweet grated beetroot is sautéed with cumin and chilli, then tucked into a soft khapli wheat dough. Cooking the filling first drives off the beet's moisture, so the paratha rolls out clean and crisps beautifully in ghee. The nutty depth of emmer wheat is a natural match for beetroot's sweetness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Stone-ground emmer wheat gives the dough a nutty flavour and keeps parathas soft for hours

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee for the dough, the filling tadka and roasting — it browns the crust without burning

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 3/4 cup water into a soft, non-sticky dough. Cover and rest 20 minutes so the emmer wheat hydrates fully.
Peel and grate 2 medium beetroots on the fine side of the grater, then squeeze them firmly in your fist over a bowl to press out excess juice.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium heat, splutter 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add grated ginger and 1 chopped green chilli and fry until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add the squeezed beetroot with 1/2 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder and 1/4 tsp turmeric. Sauté on medium heat for 6-7 minutes until the mixture looks dry and clumps together, then fold in 3 tbsp chopped coriander and cool completely.
Divide the dough into 8 balls. Flatten one ball into a 4-inch cup, place 2 tbsp of the cooled beetroot filling in the centre, pleat the edges shut and pinch off the excess dough.
Dust with atta and roll gently into a 6-7 inch round, rotating as you roll so the filling spreads evenly without tearing through.

Cook on a hot tava on medium-high heat for about 1 minute per side until brown spots appear, then brush both sides with the remaining Anveshan Ghee and roast 30 seconds more per side until crisp and blistered.
tips: Never skip squeezing the grated beetroot — the pressed-out juice makes the filling wet and tears the paratha; knead that pink juice into your next batch of dough instead.
Cool the filling fully before stuffing; warm filling steams the dough from inside and makes rolling impossible.
If a paratha tears while rolling, dab the spot with dry atta and roll only from the edges inward.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot off the tava with a bowl of thick chilled curd, a wedge of lime and mango pickle — the cool curd against the warm pink paratha is the whole point.

variations.name: Punjabi Beetroot Paratha
variations.description: The dhaba treatment: a generously stuffed beetroot paratha kneaded with ajwain, roasted till crackling on a hot tava and crowned with a melting spoon of white butter. Kasuri methi and amchur in the filling give it that unmistakable Punjabi tang. It is a breakfast built to fuel a full day in the fields.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli wheat mimics the coarse, flavourful desi atta Punjabi homes traditionally chakki-ground

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Punjabi parathas are roasted lavishly — bilona ghee gives the authentic khoya-like aroma

steps: Make the dough by rubbing 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 1/2 tsp ajwain seeds into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, then knead with about 3/4 cup water for 5 minutes until smooth and supple. Rest under a damp cloth for 20 minutes.
Grate 2 medium beetroots and 1 small onion, sprinkle with 1/2 tsp salt and set aside 10 minutes, then squeeze the mixture hard between your palms until no more liquid drips out.

Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium flame and toss in the squeezed beet-onion mixture. Cook 5-6 minutes, stirring, until it turns glossy and dry, then stir in 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi, 1 tsp amchur, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder and 3/4 tsp red chilli powder. Cool fully.
Portion the dough into 8 equal balls. Cup each ball, load it with a heaped 2 tbsp of filling, gather the edges over the top like a potli and press flat between your palms.
Roll each stuffed ball on a floured board into a thick 6-inch disc — Punjabi parathas stay slightly thick, so do not roll paper-thin.

Slap onto a hot tava on medium-high heat and cook 60-90 seconds per side until deep brown spots form, pressing the edges with a folded cloth so they cook through. Spoon Anveshan Ghee over both sides and roast until the surface crackles.
Top each hot paratha with 1 tbsp white butter just before it leaves the tava so it melts into the crust.
tips: Salting and resting the grated beet and onion draws the water out in one go — this dhaba trick keeps the thick filling from turning soggy.
Press the paratha edges firmly on the tava; the rim is the thickest part and stays raw if ignored.
For the true dhaba finish, cook the roasted paratha directly on the open flame for 5 seconds per side to blister it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a tall glass of salted lassi and a raw onion halved and smacked open with the palm — dhaba style — plus sweet mango chutney on the side.

variations.name: Bengali Beetroot Paratha
variations.description: Bengal loves beetroot in its winter torkaris, and this porota borrows that palette: pungent mustard oil, kalonji and slit green chillies against the beet's sweetness. The filling is cooked in smoking mustard oil for that sharp, nose-tingling jhaanj Bengalis prize. A final drizzle of raw mustard oil before serving is non-negotiable.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The emmer wheat's faint sweetness balances the pungent mustard oil in this porota

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed kachi ghani oil with real jhaanj — smoke it first to mellow the raw edge

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon in the dough keeps the porota layers tender against the assertive filling

steps: Combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then work in roughly 3/4 cup water and knead 5 minutes to a soft, pliable dough. Rest it, covered, for 20 minutes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai until it just begins to smoke, then lower the flame and let it cool for 20 seconds so the rawness burns off.
Scatter in 1 tsp kalonji and 2 slit green chillies; when the seeds crackle, add 1 tsp ginger paste and stir 30 seconds until aromatic.

Tip in 2 medium beetroots, grated and squeezed dry, with 1/2 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1/2 tsp sugar. Fry on medium for 6 minutes until the beet darkens and smells sweet-pungent, then spread on a plate to cool.
Shape the dough into 8 balls, stuff each with 2 tbsp of the mustard-scented filling, seal the pleats and flatten gently.
Roll into 6-inch rounds with light strokes, flouring as needed, and cook on a medium-hot tava about 1 minute per side until freckled brown.
Brush the porotas with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in the last 30 seconds on the tava so the raw pungency blooms on the hot crust.
tips: Always let mustard oil reach its smoking point once before cooking in it — skipping this leaves an acrid raw bite.
The pinch of sugar is not for sweetness; Bengali cooks use it to round out mustard oil's sharpness and deepen the beet's colour.
Leftover filling makes an excellent beetroot chokha the next morning with a squeeze of lime.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a simple aloo'r torkari or just thick tok doi (sour curd), plus an extra slit green chilli rubbed with salt on the rim of the plate.

variations.name: Kerala Beetroot Paratha
variations.description: Inspired by Kerala's beetroot thoran, this version folds fresh grated coconut, curry leaves and crushed black pepper into the beet filling, all tempered in coconut oil. The coconut keeps the stuffing moist and faintly sweet while pepper brings the heat, Malabar-style. The paratha is finished soft and pliable, closer to a Malabar-style flatbread than a crisp northern one.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: A wholegrain stand-in for the maida of Malabar parottas — all the softness, none of the refined flour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed from fresh coconuts, it carries the thoran aroma into both filling and crust

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and about 3/4 cup water until soft and stretchy, then rest 20 minutes under a damp towel.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadhai over medium heat and pop 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 4 sliced shallots, 1 chopped green chilli and the leaves of 1 curry sprig; fry 2 minutes until the shallots soften.
Add 2 grated and squeezed beetroots, 1/2 tsp salt and 1/4 tsp turmeric and cook 5 minutes on medium, stirring, until nearly dry.
Fold in 1/2 cup fresh grated coconut and 1 tsp coarsely crushed black pepper and cook 2 more minutes until the coconut smells toasty. Cool the thoran-style filling completely.
Divide the dough into 8 balls and stuff each with 2 tbsp of filling, pleating the dough closed and pressing out the air before flattening.
Roll softly into 6-inch rounds — the coconut makes this filling delicate, so use a light hand and patch any tears with dry flour.

Cook on a medium tava about 75 seconds per side, then glaze with the remaining Anveshan Coconut Oil and toss on a few torn curry leaves from the second sprig; roast 30 seconds until the leaves crisp against the bread.
tips: Crush the pepper coarsely in a mortar rather than using fine powder — the little bursts of heat are the Kerala signature here.
Frozen grated coconut works, but thaw and squeeze it first or the filling turns watery.
Keep the flame at medium; coconut in the filling scorches faster than a plain beet stuffing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and a glass of sambharam (spiced buttermilk with curry leaves and ginger) for a full Kerala breakfast plate.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Beetroot Paratha
variations.description: Goda masala — Maharashtra's smoky, coconut-and-stone-flower blend — transforms the beetroot filling into something dark, warm and faintly sweet. Roasted peanut powder adds body and a nutty crunch typical of Deccan cooking. Rolled thin and roasted in ghee, it tastes like a stuffed cousin of the beloved beetroot koshimbir.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat echoes the hearty jwari-bajri breads of the Deccan while staying easy to roll

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Goda masala blooms best in hot ghee, releasing its dagad phool smokiness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed peanut oil in the dough doubles down on the filling's roasted-peanut note

steps: Work 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and 1 tsp salt into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, add about 3/4 cup water and knead to a smooth, soft dough. Rest 20 minutes.
Set a kadhai on medium heat with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee; crackle 1/2 tsp mustard seeds, then add 1/8 tsp hing and 1 chopped green chilli and let them sizzle for 30 seconds.
Add 2 grated, well-squeezed beetroots with 1/2 tsp salt and cook 5 minutes until the shreds go limp and dry.
Sprinkle in 2 tsp goda masala and 3 tbsp roasted peanut powder, toss 2 minutes on low so the masala toasts without burning, then mix in 2 tbsp chopped coriander and cool.
Divide the dough into 8 portions, fill each flattened cup with 2 tbsp of the goda-spiced beet mixture and seal the pleats tight.
Roll into thin 7-inch rounds, dusting lightly, and roast on a hot tava about 1 minute per side until mottled brown.
Finish each paratha with a brushing of the remaining Anveshan Ghee and 20 more seconds on the tava so the goda masala aroma lifts off the crust.
tips: Goda masala burns quickly — always add it after the beetroot has cooked, never straight into hot ghee.
Peanut powder absorbs moisture, so if your filling still looks wet, an extra spoon of it will rescue the texture.
No goda masala on hand? Dry-roast 1 tsp coriander seeds, 2 cloves and 1 tbsp desiccated coconut and grind — it is close enough for one batch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Plate with a fresh beetroot-cucumber koshimbir, a dollop of homemade curd and lime pickle; a warm cup of masala taak completes the Maharashtrian thali feel.

variations.name: Classic Cabbage Paratha
variations.description: Finely shredded cabbage is salted, squeezed and folded straight into the spiced dough, so every paratha rolls out easily and cooks up with lacy, crisp edges. It is the simplest and most forgiving of all stuffed-style parathas — no sealing, no tearing, just honest everyday flavour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The emmer wheat's gentle gluten makes mixed-dough parathas roll thin without shredding the cabbage through

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Kneaded into the dough and used for roasting, it crisps the cabbage flecks at the surface into savoury lace

ingredients.name: Cabbage
ingredients.note: very finely shredded

ingredients.name: Water
ingredients.note: approximate; the salted cabbage releases its own moisture

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: grated

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Toss 2.5 cups finely shredded cabbage with 0.75 tsp salt in a bowl and set aside for 10 minutes; then squeeze the cabbage hard between your palms over the sink until no more liquid drips out.

In a wide paraat, combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, the squeezed cabbage, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, the grated ginger, 3 tbsp chopped coriander, 0.5 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee.

Rub the mixture between your fingers for a minute so the atta coats every cabbage shred, then add water a tablespoon at a time — usually about 0.5 cup — and knead 5-6 minutes into a soft, pliable dough. Rest it covered for 15 minutes.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, dust generously with dry atta and roll each into a 6-7 inch round; the cabbage flecks should show through the surface without breaking it.
Heat a tava on medium-high until water droplets dance on it, lay a paratha down and cook for about 1 minute until bubbles rise across the surface.

Flip, spread 0.5 tsp Anveshan Ghee over the cooked side, flip again after a minute and press gently around the edges until both sides are patched with golden brown and the cabbage edges smell toasty, roughly 3 minutes per paratha.
Cook the rest the same way, stacking them in a covered container lined with a kitchen towel so they stay supple.
tips: The squeeze is everything: skip it and the dough turns sticky halfway through rolling as the salt keeps pulling water out of the cabbage.
Save the squeezed cabbage juice for kneading if the dough feels dry — it carries flavour that plain water does not.
Roll and cook immediately once the dough is made; a mixed cabbage dough loosens if it sits for more than an hour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best with a bowl of plain curd whisked with a pinch of black salt and a fiery garlic chutney; add sliced radish and lemon wedges for crunch on the side.

variations.name: Punjabi Cabbage Paratha
variations.description: A robust, stuffed version in the Punjabi mould: the cabbage is sautéed with ajwain and anardana until sweet-tart, packed thickly into the dough, and the finished paratha is crowned with melting white butter. Hearty enough to anchor a whole winter meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: A sturdier khapli dough shoulders the generous dhaba-style stuffing without splitting on the tava

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Used with a heavy hand for roasting, the way Punjabi kitchens insist parathas be finished

ingredients.name: Cabbage
ingredients.note: shredded

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Anardana powder
ingredients.note: dried pomegranate seed powder for the classic Punjabi tang

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: minced

ingredients.name: White butter
ingredients.note: to top each paratha

steps: Knead 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 1 cup water for 8 minutes until smooth and springy; rest the dough under a damp cloth for 20 minutes.

Warm 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium heat, crackle 0.75 tsp ajwain for 20 seconds, then fry the chopped onion and minced green chillies until the onion turns translucent, about 3 minutes.
Add 3 cups shredded cabbage and 1 tsp salt and sauté on high heat, tossing constantly, for 5-6 minutes until the cabbage wilts, dries out and picks up light brown edges.
Stir in 1 tsp anardana powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp garam masala, cook 30 seconds more, then spread the filling on a plate and cool it fully before stuffing.
Shape the dough into 6 generous balls; flatten each into a cup, pack in about 3 tbsp of the cooled filling, pleat the edges closed and flatten gently between your palms.

Roll every stuffed ball into an 8-inch round with light strokes, then roast on a medium-hot tava, brushing each side with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and pressing the rim with a spatula until deeply golden and blistered, about 4 minutes per paratha.
Slide a spoonful of white butter onto each paratha straight off the tava so it melts into the crust as it reaches the table.
tips: Anardana is the make-or-break note here; if you cannot find it, stir in 1 tsp of dry mango powder off the heat instead.
Cook the cabbage until genuinely dry — Punjabi-style thick parathas trap any leftover steam and turn pasty inside.
These freeze well half-cooked: roast without ghee, cool, stack with parchment, and finish with ghee straight from the freezer.
variations.servingSuggestion: Plate with dahi sprinkled with roasted cumin, a wedge of raw onion and gajar-gobhi pickle; a glass of thick sweet lassi makes it a proper Punjabi thali.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Cabbage Paratha
variations.description: Inspired by kobichi bhaji, this version folds cabbage cooked with goda masala, peanuts and a whisper of jaggery into the paratha. Goda masala's toasty, faintly sweet complexity — coconut, sesame, stone flower — makes it taste unmistakably of a Pune home kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its rustic wheat flavour sits naturally alongside earthy goda masala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed peanut oil is the everyday fat of Maharashtrian bhaji and echoes the crushed peanuts in the filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The quiet sweet note every Maharashtrian bhaji carries against its spice

ingredients.name: Cabbage
ingredients.note: finely shredded

ingredients.name: Goda masala
ingredients.note: the signature Maharashtrian blend

ingredients.name: Roasted peanuts
ingredients.note: coarsely crushed

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Make the dough first: knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and about 0.75 cup water until soft and elastic, 6-7 minutes, then rest for 15 minutes under a bowl.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai over medium flame and pop 0.75 tsp mustard seeds fully — wait until the crackling stops, around 30 seconds — before adding the chopped green chillies.
Add 2.5 cups shredded cabbage with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt; sauté on medium-high for 5 minutes until wilted and dry with a few browned strands.

Lower the heat and season with 2 tsp goda masala, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 3 tbsp crushed roasted peanuts; stir for 1 minute so the jaggery melts into the spices, then cool the bhaji-style filling completely.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, cup each one, tuck in 2 tbsp of filling mixed with the chopped coriander, seal firmly and roll out to 6-7 inches, patching any thin spots with a pinch of dry flour.

Roast on a medium tava, drizzling the remaining groundnut oil around the edges, flipping every minute until both sides carry crisp mahogany spots, about 3-4 minutes each; the goda masala should smell warmly toasted, never burnt.
tips: Goda masala scorches faster than garam masala because of its coconut and sesame; always add it on low heat.
Crush the peanuts coarse, not to powder — the little nubs of crunch are half the pleasure of this filling.
If you make goda masala at home, add a pinch of dagad phool (stone flower); it is the note most shop blends miss.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Pune way with a katori of mattha (spiced thin buttermilk) and lime pickle, or alongside varan-bhaat for a fuller weekend lunch.

variations.name: Tamil Cabbage Paratha
variations.description: Borrowing from cabbage poriyal, this southern take tempers the filling with curry leaves, urad dal, mustard seeds and fresh coconut in sesame oil. The dal turns nutty and crisp inside the paratha, and the curry-leaf perfume announces itself the moment it hits the tava.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its soft gluten mimics the tenderness of parotta dough without any maida

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed nallennai is the traditional Tamil cooking fat and gives the tempering its deep aroma

ingredients.name: Cabbage
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Curry leaves
ingredients.note: torn

ingredients.name: Urad dal
ingredients.note: split, skinned

ingredients.name: Dried red chillies
ingredients.note: broken in half

steps: Knead a soft dough from 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and roughly 0.75 cup water; work it 7 minutes until it stops sticking to the bowl, then rest 15 minutes covered.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadhai on medium, splutter 0.75 tsp mustard seeds completely, then add 1 tbsp urad dal and the broken red chillies and fry until the dal turns biscuit-gold, about 1 minute.
Add 0.25 tsp asafoetida and the torn curry leaves — stand back, they will crackle — followed immediately by 2.5 cups chopped cabbage, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt.

Stir-fry on medium-high heat for 5-6 minutes until the cabbage is tender-crisp and dry, then fold in 0.5 cup grated coconut, cook 1 minute more and spread the poriyal-style filling out to cool completely.
Portion the dough into 8 balls, stuff each with 2 tbsp of cooled filling, seal the gathered edges with a twist and roll gently into 6-inch rounds on a floured board.

Roast each paratha on a medium-hot tava with a small drizzle of the remaining sesame oil, flipping every minute until both faces are freckled deep gold and the curry leaves inside smell toasty, about 3-4 minutes per paratha.
tips: Watch the urad dal like a hawk; it goes from golden to bitter in seconds and one burnt batch flavours the whole filling.
Tender-crisp is the target for the cabbage — Tamil poriyal never cooks it to mush, and that slight bite survives roasting beautifully.
A pinch of sugar in the filling is common in Kongunad homes and rounds out the asafoetida; add it with the coconut if you like.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and a small bowl of sambar for dipping, or roll it around a spoon of idli podi mixed with sesame oil for a lunchbox version.

variations.name: Bihari Cabbage Paratha
variations.description: A gutsy paratha in the spirit of Bihar's litti country: the cabbage is cooked in pungent mustard oil with garlic, green chilli and a spoon of roasted sattu that binds the filling and adds a smoky gram depth. Rustic, high-flavoured and built for cold mornings.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Wholegrain emmer stands up to the assertive mustard-sattu filling the way Bihari wheat doughs do

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Kachi ghani pungency is the backbone of Bihari cooking; smoke it briefly to mellow before tempering

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Roasted gram flour drinks up the cabbage's moisture and brings litti-style smokiness to the stuffing

ingredients.name: Cabbage
ingredients.note: shredded

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: roughly crushed

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil, rub to breadcrumb texture, then knead with about 0.75 cup water for 7 minutes to a soft dough; rest 15 minutes.
Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai until it just smokes, let it calm for 30 seconds off the flame, then return to medium heat and sizzle 0.5 tsp kalonji for 15 seconds.

Fry the crushed garlic and chopped green chillies for about 1 minute until the garlic edges brown, then add 2.5 cups shredded cabbage with 0.75 tsp salt and cook on high, tossing, for 5 minutes until collapsed and dry.

Sprinkle in 3 tbsp Anveshan Sattu, 1 tsp amchur and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and toast everything together for 2 minutes; the sattu should smell nutty and the mixture should hold together when pressed. Cool completely.
Divide the dough into 8 balls and the filling into 8 portions of 2 tbsp; stuff, seal the pleats firmly and roll each ball into a 6-7 inch disc with steady, gentle pressure.

Roast on a medium-hot tava, brushing sparingly with mustard oil, turning every minute until both sides are crisped and darkly freckled, about 4 minutes per paratha; the aroma should be sharp, toasty and faintly smoky.
tips: Sattu is your safety net: if the filling ever looks moist, another spoonful will dry it out without dulling the flavour.
Bihari food is unapologetically pungent, but you can roast these in ghee instead of mustard oil for a softer landing.
The same filling, moistened with a spoon of water and a squeeze of lime, doubles as an instant sattu-cabbage chokha side.
variations.servingSuggestion: Eat with baingan chokha or tomato chokha and a raw green chilli on the side, litti-style; a glass of salted sattu sharbat completes the Bihari spread.

variations.name: Classic Matar Paratha
variations.description: Sweet winter green peas, steamed and coarsely mashed with ginger, green chilli and roasted cumin, stuffed into soft emmer-wheat dough and griddled in ghee. The pea filling is cooked down until fluffy-dry so the paratha rolls thin without bursting. It is North India's favourite way to celebrate fresh matar season.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat's gentle sweetness mirrors the peas — the two grains-and-greens pairing tastes made for each other

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee for the tempering and the tava — its nutty depth is half the flavour of a matar paratha

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and about 0.75 cup water into a soft, pliable dough; work it 6-7 minutes, then rest covered for 15 minutes.
Steam or boil 2 cups green peas for 5-6 minutes until they crush easily between two fingers, drain thoroughly and mash coarsely — keep some texture, not a paste.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, add 0.25 tsp hing, then 1 inch grated ginger and 2 minced green chillies for 1 minute.

Add the mashed peas with 0.5 tsp salt, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp amchur; stir-fry on medium for 4-5 minutes until the mixture is dry enough to hold its shape when pressed. Cool completely.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, flatten each into a cup, fill with 2 tbsp of the pea mixture, seal the edges and roll softly into a 6-inch round, dusting with dry atta as needed.
Roast on a hot tava over medium-high heat about 1 minute per side, then apply the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee across the parathas and press until both faces carry deep golden-brown spots.
tips: Drain the boiled peas really well and dry-fry the mash — trapped steam is what makes matar parathas burst on the pin.
Amchur is the classic souring agent here; lemon juice makes the filling wet, so avoid swapping.
Fresh winter peas beat frozen for sweetness, but if using frozen, thaw and pat them dry first.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a dollop of homemade white butter and sweet-tangy tamarind-date chutney for dipping.

variations.name: Bengali Matar Paratha
variations.description: Modelled on Bengal's beloved koraishutir kochuri, this version perfumes the pea filling with ginger, green chilli and freshly ground roasted fennel, all sautéed in smoking-hot mustard oil. The fennel's sweet anise note against pungent mustard oil is the unmistakable Kolkata winter flavour. Rolled a touch thicker, it eats like a griddled cousin of the fried original.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: A wholegrain stand-in for the maida of kochuris — all the flavour, far better fibre

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Kachi ghani mustard oil, smoked and settled, gives the filling its authentic Bengali pungency

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing brush of bilona ghee — the gilded touch on every Kolkata breakfast bread

steps: Prepare the dough by rubbing 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and 0.5 tsp salt into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, adding about 0.75 cup water, and kneading 7 minutes until supple; rest 20 minutes.
Boil 2 cups green peas for 5 minutes until soft, drain fully and grind to a coarse, almost-smooth paste without adding any water.

Bring 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to its smoking point in a kadhai, switch off for 30 seconds to mellow it, then return to medium heat and sizzle 2 tsp ginger paste with 2 minced green chillies for 1 minute.

Add the pea paste, 0.5 tsp salt, 0.5 tsp sugar, 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder and 1 tsp roasted fennel powder; cook, stirring constantly, for 5-6 minutes until the mixture leaves the pan's sides and can be rolled into a ball. Cool fully.
Divide the dough into 8 portions, stuff each with 2 tbsp of the fennel-scented pea mash, seal carefully and roll into 5.5-inch rounds slightly thicker than usual so the soft filling stays cushioned.
Cook on a medium tava roughly 90 seconds per side until puffed in patches and freckled brown, then gloss each paratha with a share of the 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee.
tips: Grinding the peas smooth-ish, kochuri style, is what separates this from a North Indian matar paratha — do not leave it chunky.
Cook the paste until it genuinely leaves the pan; an underdone filling stays sticky and tears the dough.
Roasted fennel powder loses aroma fast, so grind it fresh from 1 tsp dry-roasted fennel seeds if you can.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Kolkata way with a light aloor dom (spiced baby potato curry) or simply with jaggery-sweetened tomato chutney.

variations.name: Punjabi Matar Paratha
variations.description: The Punjab rendition muscles up the filling with browned onions, crushed anardana and a proper garam masala, then roasts the paratha thick and crisp under spoonfuls of ghee. Pomegranate seed powder gives the peas a winey tang you find in Amritsari stuffed breads. Finished with white butter, it is unapologetic dhaba food.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: This heirloom wheat gives the thick Punjabi crust a satisfying, roti-like chew

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Dhaba parathas float in ghee — bilona quality means the indulgence actually nourishes

steps: Knead a soft dough from 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and roughly 0.75 cup water; give it a full 8 minutes of kneading and a 20-minute covered rest.
Boil 2 cups green peas until tender, about 6 minutes, drain well and crush coarsely with a masher.
Melt 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium-high and brown 1 finely chopped medium onion for 5-6 minutes until deeply golden — the browning is the Punjabi flavour base, so do not rush it.

Lower the heat, add 1 inch grated ginger and 2 chopped green chillies for 1 minute, then the crushed peas with 0.5 tsp salt, 0.75 tsp garam masala and 1 tsp anardana powder; fry 4 minutes until dry and fluffy, fold in 3 tbsp chopped coriander and cool.
Make 8 dough balls, pack each with a generous 2 tbsp of the onion-pea filling, pleat shut and roll to a 6-inch round about 0.5 cm thick.

Roast on a medium-hot tava 90 seconds per side, ladling on the remaining 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in stages and pressing with a spatula until the crust crackles and turns deep brown; crown each hot paratha with 0.5 tbsp white butter.
tips: Deep-browned onions and anardana are the two non-negotiables — skip either and it becomes a generic pea paratha.
Cool the filling before stuffing; warm filling steams the dough and makes rolling a sticky mess.
Press the paratha edges hard against the tava, as the rim is thickest and needs the most direct heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with dahi sprinkled with black salt, mango pickle, and if you are being properly Punjabi, a second paratha.

variations.name: Kumaoni Matar Paratha
variations.description: From the Uttarakhand hills, this paratha tempers its pea filling with jakhya — the wild mustard-like seed Kumaonis prefer over cumin — plus hill garlic and crushed coriander. Jakhya pops like tiny caviar in hot ghee, lending a crackly texture and a grassy, peppery aroma no plains spice can copy. Simple, honest mountain food.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Heritage emmer suits pahadi cooking, where old grains never went out of fashion

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Hill households treasure pure ghee from grass-fed cows — this bilona jar is the same tradition, bottled

steps: Bring together 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and about 0.75 cup water; knead 7 minutes into a soft mountain-roti dough and rest it for 15 minutes.
Boil 2 cups green peas for 5-6 minutes until they mash easily, drain completely and crush to a coarse rubble.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium-high and drop in 1 tsp jakhya seeds — let them pop and crackle for 20-25 seconds until the sputtering slows.

Add 4 minced garlic cloves and 2 chopped green chillies for 1 minute, then the crushed peas with 0.5 tsp salt, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp crushed coriander seeds; dry-fry 4-5 minutes until fluffy, fold in 2 tbsp coriander leaves and cool.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, stuff each with 2 tbsp of the jakhya-pea filling, seal the seams and roll to an even 6-inch circle.
Cook each paratha on a medium-hot tava about 80 seconds per side, brushing with the last 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, until crisp bronze patches bloom across the surface.
tips: Jakhya must audibly pop in the ghee before anything else goes in — that crackle is the whole point of the spice.
If jakhya is unavailable, brown mustard seeds are the nearest stand-in, though the flavour turns sharper.
Hill cooks crush coriander seeds on a stone rather than using powder; the coarse bits perfume every bite.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bhang ki chutney (hemp-seed chutney) or plain thick curd and a mug of hot pahadi buransh squash in winter.

variations.name: Awadhi Matar Paratha
variations.description: Lucknow's refined kitchens perfume the pea filling with kewra water, black cardamom and white pepper, keeping the heat gentle and the aroma regal. The peas are cooked in ghee to a silken mash, closer to a nimona than a rustic stuffing. A drop of kewra on the finished paratha announces the dish before it reaches the table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The soft, aristocratic crumb of emmer wheat suits Awadh's delicate, dum-cooked sensibility

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Awadhi cuisine is built on fragrant ghee — bilona-made, it carries the kewra and cardamom beautifully

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt, 2 tbsp milk and around 0.7 cup water into a soft, satiny dough; rest it 20 minutes for an extra-tender crumb.
Boil 2 cups green peas for 6 minutes until very soft, drain and grind to a fine, dry paste.

Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on low-medium heat, add the seeds of 1 black cardamom lightly crushed, and let them infuse for 30 seconds before adding 1 finely chopped small onion and 1 inch grated ginger; sweat gently for 4 minutes without browning.

Stir in the pea paste with 0.5 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp white pepper powder and cook on low for 5-6 minutes, stirring, until the mash turns glossy and holds together; off the heat sprinkle 0.5 tsp kewra water, mix and cool.
Shape 8 dough balls, enclose 2 tbsp of the perfumed pea mash in each, seal without trapping air and roll into delicate 6-inch rounds.

Roast on a medium tava about 75 seconds per side, painting on the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, until pale gold with light speckling — Awadhi breads are never hard-roasted; finish the stack with the last 0.5 tsp kewra water flicked over the top.
tips: Kewra is potent — measure with a teaspoon, never pour from the bottle, or the filling smells of soap.
Sweat the onions colourless; browning would coarsen the pale, courtly flavour this paratha is known for.
The spoonful of milk in the dough is an old Awadhi trick for a softer, richer crumb.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a light saffron-tinted raita and slivered pickled onions, as part of a Lucknawi-style breakfast spread.

variations.name: Classic Methi Paratha
variations.description: The everyday North Indian methi paratha, where fresh fenugreek leaves are kneaded straight into khapli wheat dough so every bite carries a gentle, pleasing bitterness. Slow-milled khapli atta keeps the layers soft for hours, and a final brush of bilona ghee gives the crust its signature nutty aroma. This is the version packed into countless Indian tiffins with a spoon of curd and pickle.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat absorbs the moisture of the methi leaves without turning the dough sticky

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: 1 tbsp goes into the dough for softness; the rest crisps the parathas on the tava

steps: Wash 2 cups chopped methi leaves in two changes of water, squeeze them firmly dry, then sprinkle a pinch of the salt over them and set aside for 5 minutes so they wilt slightly and lose excess moisture.

In a wide bowl combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, ½ tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, the grated ginger and minced green chillies, mixing the spices evenly through the flour.

Add the wilted methi, 2 tbsp curd and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then knead in about ½ cup water a little at a time until you have a soft, non-sticky dough; cover and rest it for 15 minutes so the bran hydrates fully.
Divide the dough into 8 equal balls, dust each with dry atta and roll into rounds about 6 inches across, keeping even pressure so the edges stay as thick as the centre.

Heat a tava on medium-high until a drop of water sizzles instantly, lay on a paratha and cook 1 minute until small bubbles rise, then flip, spread ½ tsp Anveshan Ghee over the surface and press the edges with a spatula until golden-brown spots appear, about 2 minutes per side.
Ghee the second side the same way, cook 1 more minute until both faces are blistered and crisp, and stack the finished parathas in a cloth-lined box so they stay soft.
tips: Always squeeze the washed methi leaves dry before kneading; trapped water will loosen the dough mid-way and force you to add extra flour, which toughens the paratha.
The curd tenderises khapli atta noticeably; if you skip it, add 1 extra tsp ghee to the dough to keep the parathas pliable.
The dough keeps refrigerated for a day, but bring it back to room temperature for 20 minutes before rolling or it will crack at the edges.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot off the tava with a bowl of salted lassi and a wedge of lime pickle, or roll one around scrambled eggs for a quick working-day breakfast.

variations.name: Bengali Methi Paratha
variations.description: In Bengali kitchens flatbreads meet the sharp pungency of shorshe tel, and this methi paratha is no exception. Cold-pressed mustard oil goes into the dough and onto the tava, while nigella seeds bloomed in the same oil add their oniony crackle. The result is a darker, more assertive paratha that stands up beautifully to aloo dum.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The wheat's natural sweetness balances the sharp mustard oil in this Bengali dough

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Smoke it lightly first to mellow its raw pungency, the classic Bengali trick

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a small pan on medium heat until it just begins to shimmer and its raw smell softens, about 90 seconds, then drop in 1 tsp kalonji seeds and let them crackle for 20 seconds before taking the pan off the heat.
Tip the chopped methi leaves into the warm oil and toss for 1 minute so they wilt and soak up the mustard-kalonji flavour; cool the mixture for 5 minutes.
In a large bowl mix 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, ½ tsp turmeric, ½ tsp sugar, the chopped green chillies and coriander, then fold in the cooled methi mixture with all its oil.
Knead in roughly ½ cup water, added in three or four splashes, until the dough is supple and springs back slowly when pressed; rest it covered for 15 minutes.
Shape 8 balls, roll each into a 6-inch disc on a floured surface, and cook on a medium-hot tava for about 2 minutes on the first side until pale spots form underneath.
Flip, drizzle ½ tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil around the edges, and press gently until deep golden patches develop on both faces, roughly 2 more minutes; finish all 8 the same way.
tips: Warming mustard oil until it shimmers before use removes its harsh bite while keeping the signature aroma; never skip this step for dough work.
Kalonji burns fast, so add it only after the pan is off direct high heat and keep the crackle to 20 seconds.
The little sugar in the dough is a Bengali balancing move against methi's bitterness, not a sweetener; do not increase it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with Bengali-style aloo dum or a runny egg curry, and keep sliced green chillies and a pinch of black salt on the side for true Kolkata street-stall character.

variations.name: Gujarati Methi Paratha
variations.description: Borrowing from the thepla tradition, this Gujarati take mellows methi's bitterness with jaggery and rounds it out with sesame and a spoon of besan. The dough is rolled thinner than a Punjabi paratha and cooked until flexible rather than crisp, which is exactly why theplas survive long train journeys. Sweet, spicy and faintly nutty all at once.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its low gluten lets these thepla-style rounds stay bendable even when cool

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Dissolves into the dough to tame the methi's edge the way Gujarati home cooks intend

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Used sparingly on the tava so the theplas stay supple, not fried-crisp

steps: Stir 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder into 3 tbsp sour curd and let it sit for 5 minutes until the jaggery dissolves completely into a caramel-tinted cream.

Combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 3 tbsp besan, 2 tsp sesame seeds, ½ tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp salt and 2 tsp ginger-chilli paste in a wide thali, rubbing everything together with your fingertips.

Add the chopped methi and the jaggery-curd mixture, knead briefly, then work in up to ¼ cup water only if needed to form a soft, smooth dough; the methi and curd release most of the moisture themselves. Rest for 15 minutes.
Pinch off 10 small balls and roll each very thin, about 7 inches wide, dusting lightly so the sesame seeds do not tear the surface.

Cook each round on a medium tava for about 45 seconds until the surface puffs in patches, flip, smear ¼ tsp Anveshan Ghee, and cook pressing lightly until soft brown freckles cover both sides, about 90 seconds total per side.
Stack the cooked theplas immediately in a covered container; the trapped steam keeps them flexible enough to fold into quarters without cracking.
tips: Add water very cautiously; curd plus wilting methi can turn this dough sloppy fast, and a stiff dough is impossible to roll thin.
These stay soft for 2 full days at room temperature, making them the ideal travel and tiffin flatbread.
If the rounds turn crisp instead of pliable, your tava was too hot; these want steady medium heat and quick handling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Gujarati way with chhundo (sweet mango pickle), a bowl of plain curd and masala chai; leftovers roll neatly around potato bhaji for lunchboxes.

variations.name: Kerala Methi Paratha
variations.description: A coastal reimagining where freshly grated coconut is kneaded into the methi dough and the parathas are toasted in cold-pressed coconut oil. Black pepper and curry-leaf-free restraint keep the focus on the sweet coconut against the bitter greens, a pairing straight out of Kerala's thoran logic. The crust picks up a faint toasted-coconut perfume that is unmistakable.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Sturdy enough to hold grated coconut in the dough without the rounds tearing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed, so the tava releases a true Malabar aroma as each paratha toasts

steps: Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadai over medium heat and soften the chopped shallots for 2 minutes until translucent, then add the methi leaves and toss for 1 minute until just wilted; cool completely.
Grind ¾ cup grated coconut briefly, three or four pulses only, so it turns fine but stays dry; over-grinding releases milk and wets the dough.
Mix 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with the ground coconut, 1 tsp salt, ¼ tsp turmeric, 1 tsp crushed black pepper and the minced green chillies, then add the cooled methi-shallot mixture.

Knead with about ½ cup warm water, adding it gradually, into a soft pliable dough; the coconut fat softens it further as you work, so stop as soon as it holds together cleanly. Rest 15 minutes under a damp cloth.
Roll 8 balls into 6-inch rounds with gentle strokes; if coconut shreds poke through, press them back in rather than adding more flour.

Toast each round on a medium-hot tava, 2 minutes on the first side, then flip and spoon ½ tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil around the rim, pressing until both faces show deep golden islands, about 2 more minutes.
tips: Only fresh or thawed-frozen coconut works here; desiccated coconut drinks up the dough's moisture and gives a dry, crumbly paratha.
Crush the pepper coarsely at home rather than using fine powder; the little bursts of heat are the point of this variation.
These are best eaten within a few hours, as fresh coconut shortens shelf life; refrigerate any extras and re-toast with a film of coconut oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside a mildly spiced coconut-milk vegetable stew or egg roast; a smear of sharp lime pickle cuts the richness perfectly.

variations.name: Rajasthani Methi Paratha
variations.description: Desert cooking taught Rajasthan to love dried methi and fierce red chillies, and this paratha honours both. Kasuri methi deepens the fresh leaves' flavour, ajwain aids digestion of the hearty wheat, and a coarse paste of soaked dried red chillies is worked right into the dough. Finished generously with ghee, it eats like a meal even with nothing but garlic chutney beside it.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its rustic, nutty grain matches Rajasthan's preference for robust country wheat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rajasthani parathas are unapologetically ghee-rich; it carries the chilli heat evenly

steps: Soak 4 dried red chillies in hot water for 15 minutes, then pound them with 4 garlic cloves and a pinch of salt into a coarse, brick-red paste using a mortar or small grinder.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp ajwain seeds for 30 seconds until fragrant, then pour this tempering over 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta in a paraat.

Crush 2 tbsp kasuri methi between your palms directly into the flour, add 2 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp salt, the chilli-garlic paste and the fresh methi leaves, and rub everything through until the flour looks speckled and evenly reddish.
Knead with about ½ cup water into a medium-soft dough that holds a thumbprint without sticking, then rest it 15 minutes under an inverted bowl.
Roll 8 balls into thick 5-inch rounds; Rajasthani parathas are rolled smaller and fatter than northern ones so they stay soft-centred.
Cook on a medium tava for 2 to 3 minutes per side, applying a full ½ tsp Anveshan Ghee to each face and pressing the edges until they blister into crisp, dark-gold patches.
tips: Layering fresh methi with kasuri methi gives a rounder, deeper fenugreek flavour than either alone; do not substitute one for both.
Pound the soaked chillies rather than blending with water; a wet paste dilutes the dough and mutes the chilli's punch.
If serving guests who fear heat, deseed two of the four chillies before soaking rather than reducing the count, which would flatten the colour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Do it the Marwari way: serve with lehsun ki chutney, a stack of onion rings sprinkled with salt, and a tall glass of chaas to douse the fire.

variations.name: Classic Mixed Veg Paratha
variations.description: The everyday North Indian stuffed flatbread that turns leftover vegetables into a hearty breakfast. A soft khapli wheat dough wraps a lightly spiced, ghee-sautéed filling of potato, carrot and peas, roasted until the surface blisters golden. Nutty emmer wheat and slow-churned bilona ghee give it a flavour plain atta parathas simply cannot match.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Long-fibre emmer wheat kneads into an extensible dough that rolls thin without tearing over the filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee both enriches the dough and crisps the surface into lacy brown spots on the tava

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and about 0.75 cups water into a soft, non-sticky dough. Knead for 5 minutes until smooth, cover and rest 20 minutes.
Boil 2 medium potatoes, 1 diced carrot and 0.5 cups peas in salted water for 10-12 minutes until a knife slides through easily, then drain thoroughly and mash while still warm.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds until fragrant. Add 1 inch grated ginger, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder, stir for 20 seconds, then fold in the mashed vegetables with 1 tsp salt.

Cook the filling for 3-4 minutes, stirring, until it looks dry and holds together when pressed. Mix in 3 tbsp chopped coriander and cool completely, then divide into 6 equal portions of about 3 tbsp each.

Divide the dough into 6 balls. Flatten each into a 4-inch cup, place one portion of filling in the centre, gather the edges over the top, pinch to seal and roll gently into a 7-inch round, dusting with dry atta as needed.

Roast each paratha on a hot tava over medium-high heat for about 1 minute per side until brown spots appear, then brush both sides with the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and press the edges with a spatula until crisp and golden, 1-2 minutes more.
tips: Drain the boiled vegetables well and cook the filling until dry; a wet filling will burst through the dough while rolling.
Cool the filling fully before stuffing, otherwise steam makes the dough sticky and hard to seal.
The stuffed balls can be shaped, layered with parchment and refrigerated up to a day ahead; roll and roast fresh.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot off the tava with a bowl of chilled homemade curd, a wedge of lime pickle and sliced onions sprinkled with chaat masala.

variations.name: Punjabi Mixed Veg Paratha
variations.description: The dhaba-style paratha of Punjab is thicker, more generously stuffed and unapologetically rich. The filling leans on potato and cauliflower punched up with amchur and crushed anardana, and each paratha is finished with a knob of white butter melting over the ghee-crisped crust. This is the paratha that built the reputation of Amritsar's breakfast lanes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Stone-ground khapli gives the sturdy yet tender crumb a thick dhaba paratha needs

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A generous ghee shallow-roast is what separates a Punjabi paratha from an ordinary roti

steps: Make the dough first: work 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 0.75 tsp salt, then add about 1 cup water gradually and knead 6 minutes to a supple, pillowy dough. Rest it under a damp cloth for 25 minutes.
Steam 3 medium potatoes and 1 cup small cauliflower florets for 12-15 minutes until completely tender, then mash coarsely and spread on a plate for 10 minutes so the moisture evaporates.
In a pan, heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium flame and soften 1 finely chopped onion with 2 minced green chillies for 3-4 minutes until light golden at the edges.

Tip in the mashed vegetables along with 1 tsp amchur, 1 tsp anardana powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt. Stir-fry 3 minutes until the mix is dry and tangy-smelling, then cool and portion into 6 balls of roughly 3 tbsp.

Pinch off 6 dough balls, roll each into a 5-inch disc, cup it in your palm, seat a filling ball inside, pleat the edges shut and roll out to a thick 7-inch paratha with even pressure so no vegetable peeks through.

Cook on a medium-hot tava for 90 seconds until the underside speckles brown, flip, spoon over 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, flip again and press the edges until both faces are deeply golden and crisp, about 4 minutes per paratha.
Slide each paratha onto a plate and crown immediately with 1 tbsp white butter so it melts into the crust before serving.
tips: Anardana powder is the dhaba secret; if unavailable, double the amchur but do not skip the sour note that balances the rich crust.
Steam rather than boil the cauliflower so the filling stays dry enough to roll thick parathas without leaks.
Rest the rolled parathas no more than 5 minutes before roasting or the filling's salt will draw out water.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair the traditional way with a tall glass of salted lassi, sweet mango pickle and extra white butter on the side for tearing and dipping.

variations.name: Bengali Mixed Veg Paratha
variations.description: Bengal cooks its vegetables in pungent mustard oil, and this paratha carries that unmistakable sharpness right into the stuffing. Potato, beans and cabbage are stir-fried with kalonji and green chilli in smoking-hot mustard oil, echoing the flavours of a classic torkari. The wasabi-like heat of cold-pressed mustard oil mellows on the tava into something deeply savoury.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The gentle sweetness of emmer wheat tempers the sharp mustard notes of this Bengali stuffing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed kachi ghani mustard oil must be heated to its smoking point to bloom its signature pungency

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A final ghee baste balances the mustard heat with a rounded, sweet finish

steps: Combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and 0.5 tsp salt, then knead in roughly 0.75 cups water for 5 minutes until soft and elastic. Cover and set aside for 20 minutes.
Boil 2 medium potatoes for 10 minutes until fork-tender and mash them. Finely shred 1 cup cabbage and chop 0.5 cups french beans into tiny pieces.
Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai until it just begins to smoke, lower the flame, and crackle 0.5 tsp kalonji with 3 slit green chillies for 30 seconds until aromatic.

Add the beans and cabbage with 1 inch grated ginger and stir-fry on high for 4-5 minutes until the cabbage wilts and picks up light brown edges. Fold in the mashed potato, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp sugar, cook 2 minutes more, then cool fully.
Shape the dough into 6 balls, hollow each into a small bowl, pack in about 3 tbsp of the mustard-scented filling, seal the pleats firmly and roll into 7-inch rounds with light, even strokes.

Roast on a medium-hot tava for about 2 minutes per side until blistered and brown, brushing each side with a little of the 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in the final minute so the crust turns glossy and crisp.
tips: Always heat mustard oil until it faintly smokes and then cool it slightly; skipping this leaves a raw, bitter edge.
Squeeze the shredded cabbage in your fist before frying to expel water and keep the filling roll-friendly.
The touch of sugar is authentically Bengali; it rounds out the mustard's pungency rather than sweetening the dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a spoonful of kasundi mustard relish and thick sweetened mishti doi on the side for a proper Kolkata-style contrast of sharp and sweet.

variations.name: Kerala Mixed Veg Paratha
variations.description: Inspired by the thoran technique of the Malabar coast, this paratha folds coconut-flecked, curry-leaf-scented vegetables into soft khapli dough. Carrot, beans and fresh grated coconut are tossed in cold-pressed coconut oil with mustard seeds bloomed until they pop. The result tastes like a Kerala sadya wrapped in warm flatbread.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli's nutty depth stands up beautifully to sweet coconut and fragrant curry leaves

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil perfumes the thoran-style filling exactly as a Kerala kitchen would

steps: Knead a soft dough from 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, 0.5 tsp salt and about 0.75 cups water, working it 5 minutes until it springs back when pressed. Rest, covered, for 20 minutes.
Finely dice 2 carrots and 0.75 cups beans into pieces no bigger than a pea so they cook through quickly and roll flat inside the paratha.

Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a wide pan over medium heat and pop 1 tsp mustard seeds for about 30 seconds, then toss in 12 curry leaves and 2 chopped green chillies and let them sizzle for 15 seconds.

Add the diced vegetables with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, sprinkle 2 tbsp water, cover and cook 5-6 minutes until just tender. Stir in 0.5 cups grated coconut and 0.5 tsp black pepper, fry uncovered 2 minutes until dry, and cool completely.
Divide dough into 6 portions, stuff each with about 3 tbsp of the coconut filling, pinch the seams closed and roll out gently into 7-inch rounds without pressing hard over the centre.
Cook each paratha on a medium-hot tava for around 2 minutes per side, dabbing lightly with the leftover coconut oil, until golden freckles cover both faces and the edges crisp.
tips: Fry the coconut only until dry, not browned, so the filling stays sweet and moist rather than toasty.
Fresh curry leaves are essential; dried ones lose the citrusy aroma that defines this paratha.
If the filling feels loose, mash a quarter of it against the pan; the crushed vegetables will bind the rest.
variations.servingSuggestion: Accompany with coconut chutney or a quick tomato-onion pachadi, and finish the meal with a small tumbler of spiced buttermilk (sambharam).

variations.name: Rajasthani Mixed Veg Paratha
variations.description: In water-scarce Rajasthan, parathas grew bold with dried spices instead of fresh produce, and this take honours that tradition. The filling of potato, peas and besan-toasted crumble is fired with crushed dried red chillies, coriander seeds and ajwain-scented dough. Roasted in ghee until deeply crisp, it carries the rustic punch of a Marwari kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Hardy khapli wheat mirrors the coarse desert grains traditionally milled for Marwari flatbreads

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rajasthani cooking prizes ghee as both cooking fat and flavour, crisping this paratha to a rich finish

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 0.5 tsp ajwain, 0.5 tsp salt and about 0.75 cups water into a smooth, medium-soft dough; rest it 20 minutes under a damp cloth.
Dry-roast 4 dried red chillies, 2 tsp coriander seeds and 1 tsp fennel seeds in a pan over low heat for 2-3 minutes until fragrant and brittle, then cool and pound to a coarse powder in a mortar.
Boil 3 potatoes and 0.5 cups peas for 10-12 minutes until soft, drain well and mash together while warm.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium flame, toast 3 tbsp besan for 2-3 minutes until nutty and sand-coloured, then add the mash, the pounded spice blend, 1 tsp amchur and 1 tsp salt. Cook 3 minutes until dry, then cool and divide into 6 portions.
