Stuff 6 dough balls with the spiced filling, seal the openings tightly and roll each into a 7-inch disc, keeping the pressure light at the centre so the crumbly filling stays put.

Roast on a medium tava about 2 minutes a side, then spoon 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over each paratha and press with a folded cloth until both sides crackle golden brown, roughly 2 minutes more per paratha.
tips: Toasting besan into the filling is the Marwari trick that absorbs moisture and adds a nutty savour.
Pound the roasted spices coarse, not fine; the little chilli flecks bursting on the tongue are the point.
These parathas keep well for travel; cool fully, wrap in cloth, and they stay tasty at room temperature for a day.
variations.servingSuggestion: Eat the desert way with garlicky lahsun ki chutney, a spoon of churned dahi and slivers of sun-cured ker sangri pickle if you can find it.

variations.name: Classic Dry Aloo Gobi
variations.description: The definitive sukhi aloo gobi: cauliflower florets and potato cubes cooked uncovered until their edges caramelise, coated in a clinging onion-tomato masala rather than swimming in gravy. Par-searing the vegetables separately in mustard oil keeps every floret intact and lightly charred.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil chars the gobi edges with a subtle pungency refined oil cannot give

steps: Cut 3 potatoes into 1-inch cubes and 1 medium cauliflower into bite-size florets; soak the florets in warm salted water for 10 minutes, then drain and pat completely dry.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a wide kadai on medium-high until it just shimmers, then sear the potatoes and florets in two batches for 4 to 5 minutes each until golden-edged but still firm; lift them out and set aside.
In the same kadai, add the remaining 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then sauté 2 finely chopped onions for 5 minutes until light brown.

Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until its raw smell fades, then add 2 chopped tomatoes, 0.75 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1.25 tsp salt; cook 4 to 5 minutes until the masala thickens and oil beads at the edges.

Return the seared vegetables to the kadai, toss to coat every piece, then cook uncovered on low for 10 to 12 minutes, turning gently every few minutes, until a knife slides through the potato and the masala clings dry to the florets.
Scatter 3 tbsp chopped coriander over the top, toss once more and switch off the heat.
tips: Cooking uncovered for the final stretch is what keeps this sabzi dry; a lid traps steam and collapses the florets.
Pat the soaked florets bone-dry before searing — wet gobi steams instead of browning and splatters the oil.
Choose waxy potatoes if you can; they hold their cube shape better than starchy ones in a dry stir.
Leftovers make a superb sandwich filling mashed lightly with a spoon of curd the next morning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulkas, a katori of boondi raita and lime pickle; it also packs beautifully into a lunchbox since there is no gravy to spill.

variations.name: Bengali Dry Aloo Gobi
variations.description: Modelled on the winter classic phulkopir dalna in its dry avatar, this version blooms panch phoron in pungent kachi ghani mustard oil and finishes with a whisper of Bengali garam masala and slit green chillies. A pinch of sugar at the end rounds the flavours the way every Kolkata kitchen does.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Kachi ghani pungency is the backbone of Bengali vegetable cookery; nothing else tastes right

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Replaces the customary pinch of white sugar with a warmer, mineral sweetness

steps: Cube 3 potatoes and break 1 cauliflower into medium florets; rub them with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt and let them sit for 10 minutes.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai on medium-high until it smokes faintly, then lower the heat and fry the turmeric-rubbed vegetables for 6 to 7 minutes until their surfaces blister pale gold; remove to a plate.
Add the last 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil, and when hot, tip in 1.5 tsp panch phoron; the fenugreek and nigella should crackle and darken within 30 seconds.
Stir in 1 tbsp grated ginger and 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp cumin powder and 0.75 tsp salt, and cook 4 minutes until the tomatoes slump into a jammy paste.
Return the fried aloo and gobi, add 3 slit green chillies and 3 tbsp water, and cook uncovered on low for 10 minutes, folding gently, until the vegetables are tender and the masala coats them dryly.
Sprinkle 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.5 tsp Bengali garam masala, toss for a final minute and rest the sabzi 5 minutes before serving so the flavours settle.
tips: Let the mustard oil reach its faint smoking point once before frying; this mellows the raw pungency the Bengali way.
Panch phoron burns fast — have the ginger and tomatoes chopped and ready beside the stove.
The jaggery is not for sweetness but for balance; do not exceed a teaspoon or the dish tips into dessert territory.
variations.servingSuggestion: Eat it Kolkata-style with steamed gobindobhog rice and a drizzle of raw mustard oil, or fold into a luchi for a Sunday brunch.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Dry Aloo Gobi
variations.description: A ghar-style Marathi bhaji where goda masala's smoky sweetness, roasted peanut crush and a final flourish of fresh coconut turn plain aloo gobi into something you would find in a Pune lunch dabba. Groundnut oil ties the peanut notes through the whole dish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the everyday Maharashtrian fat and amplifies the peanut garnish

steps: Prep 3 potatoes into small cubes and 1 cauliflower into florets, keeping both roughly the same size so they cook evenly.

Warm 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a heavy kadai on medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds for about 30 seconds, then add 8 curry leaves and 2 sliced onions and fry 5 minutes until the onions soften and pick up colour.
Add 1 chopped tomato, 0.75 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt and cook for 3 minutes until the tomato breaks down completely.
Slide in the potatoes and cauliflower, toss to coat in the masala, sprinkle 3 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 12 minutes, stirring twice, until a floret crushes easily against the pan wall.
Uncover, dust in 2 tsp goda masala and 3 tbsp crushed roasted peanuts, and stir-fry 3 to 4 minutes on medium so the moisture evaporates and each piece wears a dry, dark-spiced coat.
Finish off the heat with 3 tbsp fresh grated coconut folded through gently so it stays snowy against the brown masala.
tips: Add goda masala only near the end; prolonged frying turns its delicate dagad phool aroma bitter.
Crush the peanuts coarse, not to a powder — you want gravelly bites, not paste.
This bhaji is traditionally medium-spiced; bump the chilli powder to 1.5 tsp if you like Kolhapuri-level heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft chapatis or jowar bhakri, a wedge of lime and a spoonful of green chilli thecha for the brave.

variations.name: Tamil Dry Aloo Gobi
variations.description: A poriyal-style rendition from Tamil kitchens: the aloo and gobi are tossed with a mustard-urad dal tadka, plenty of curry leaves and a sprinkle of sambar powder, all in nutty gingelly oil. Fresh coconut folded in at the end keeps it light and temple-lunch fragrant.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil's toasty depth is the default cooking fat of Tamil poriyals

steps: Dice 3 potatoes into half-inch cubes and separate 1 cauliflower into small florets; steam or parboil both in salted water for 5 minutes until just fork-tender, then drain thoroughly.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a wide pan on medium, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds for 30 seconds, then add 2 tsp urad dal and 2 torn dried red chillies and fry until the dal turns biscuit-gold.
Throw in 15 curry leaves and 10 halved shallots and sauté 4 minutes until the shallots turn glossy and lightly caramelised at the cut faces.
Add the parboiled vegetables with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt, spreading them in one layer, and let them sit undisturbed 3 minutes to pick up golden crusts before the first stir.
Sprinkle 2 tsp sambar powder and stir-fry another 5 to 6 minutes on medium until the spice smells roasted and the vegetables look dry and speckled.
Kill the heat and fold in 4 tbsp fresh grated coconut so it warms through without toasting.
tips: Parboiling first keeps the poriyal quick and prevents the cauliflower from overbrowning before the potato cooks.
The urad dal must be fully golden before anything else goes in; pale dal stays chalky in the finished dish.
Any good homemade sambar powder works; if using store-bought, start with 1.5 tsp as they run saltier and hotter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside hot rice, a ladle of tomato rasam and appalam for a proper Tamil lunch spread, or tuck into a curd-rice bowl.

variations.name: Kashmiri Dry Aloo Gobi
variations.description: In the Kashmiri Pandit style, this aloo gobi skips onion and garlic entirely, leaning on fennel, dry ginger and a saffron-yoghurt glaze for its haunting aroma. The florets are ghee-fried until russet, then lacquered with saffron the way dum aloo gets its finish in the Valley.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Kashmiri Pandit cooking is built on ghee; bilona ghee gives the fried gobi its nutty russet crust

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: A few Pampore threads bloomed in warm water perfume and gild the entire dish

steps: Steep 0.25 tsp Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron threads in 2 tbsp warm water and set aside for at least 10 minutes until the water turns deep amber.
Cut 3 potatoes into thick wedges and 1 cauliflower into large florets; prick the potato wedges lightly with a fork so they drink in the spiced glaze later.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium and fry the potatoes and florets in batches for 6 to 8 minutes until russet-brown all over; drain on a plate.

In the ghee left behind, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 2 cloves for 30 seconds, then lower the flame fully and stir in 0.5 cup whisked curd one spoon at a time, stirring constantly so it never splits.
Season the curd base with 2 tsp fennel powder, 1 tsp dry ginger powder, 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt, then return the fried vegetables and toss to coat.

Pour in the saffron water, cover and cook on the lowest flame for 8 minutes, then uncover and reduce for 3 to 4 minutes, turning gently, until the glaze clings to every wedge and floret with a lacquered sheen.
tips: Whisk the curd smooth and add it off a rolling boil; high heat is the only reason curd splits in Kashmiri gravies.
Fennel and dry ginger are the flavour signature here — do not substitute garam masala or the dish loses its identity.
Crush the saffron threads between warm fingers before steeping to release double the colour and aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with steamed long-grain rice and a Kashmiri walnut chutney; a few extra saffron strands on top make it wazwan-worthy for guests.

variations.name: Classic Garlic Carrot Paratha
variations.description: A sunny breakfast paratha where sweet grated carrot is sautéed with plenty of garlic until the raw bite mellows into a savoury-sweet filling. The khapli atta shell turns crisp and blistered on the tava while the inside stays juicy, and the garlic perfumes every layer.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Stone-ground emmer wheat gives the dough a nutty flavour and keeps stuffed parathas soft for hours

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee is used three ways here: in the dough, for the garlic tadka, and to roast the parathas golden

ingredients.name: Carrot
ingredients.note: grated, from about 3 medium carrots

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: finely minced

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Green chilli
ingredients.note: finely chopped

steps: Knead the dough: combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then add about 0.75 cup water a little at a time and knead for 6-8 minutes until you have a soft, smooth, non-sticky dough. Cover and rest for 15 minutes.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle for 20 seconds, then add 8 minced garlic cloves and 1 chopped green chilli and sauté until the garlic smells toasty and turns pale gold, about 1 minute.

Add 2 cups grated carrot, 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.75 tsp salt; stir-fry on medium-high heat for 4-5 minutes until the carrot softens and all its moisture evaporates. Stir in 3 tbsp chopped coriander and cool the filling completely on a plate.

Divide the rested dough into 8 equal balls and the cooled filling into 8 portions of about 2 tbsp each. Flatten a ball into a 4-inch cup, place one portion of filling in the centre, gather the edges over it and pinch firmly to seal.
Dust the stuffed ball with dry atta and roll gently with light, even pressure into a 7-inch round, rotating a quarter turn between strokes so the filling stays centred and does not tear through.

Heat a tava on medium-high until a drop of water sizzles instantly. Cook the paratha for about 1 minute until small bubbles appear, flip, brush the top with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Ghee, flip again after 1 minute and press the edges with a spatula until both sides show deep golden-brown spots, about 3 minutes total.
Repeat with the remaining balls, stacking finished parathas in a cloth-lined box so they stay soft and warm until serving.
tips: Squeeze the grated carrot lightly before sautéing if it is very juicy; a wet filling is the main reason stuffed parathas tear while rolling.
Cool the filling fully before stuffing — warm filling steams inside the dough and makes the paratha soggy.
The dough can be kneaded up to 8 hours ahead and refrigerated; bring it back to room temperature for 20 minutes before rolling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve two parathas per person with a bowl of thick salted curd, a wedge of lime and some green chilli pickle; a tall glass of masala chaas turns it into a complete weekend brunch.

variations.name: Punjabi Garlic Carrot Paratha
variations.description: The dhaba treatment: a thicker, more generously stuffed paratha finished with a knob of white butter melting over the crisp top. Kasuri methi and ginger join the garlic in the filling, giving it the unmistakable punch of a Punjabi winter breakfast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The extra half cup makes sturdier dhaba-style dough that holds a heavy carrot stuffing without bursting

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Punjabi parathas are shallow-roasted lavishly; bilona ghee gives them their signature caramelised crust

ingredients.name: Carrot
ingredients.note: grated red Delhi carrots if in season

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: crushed to a coarse paste

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: grated

ingredients.name: Kasuri methi
ingredients.note: crushed between palms

ingredients.name: White butter
ingredients.note: for topping

steps: Make a firm-soft dough by mixing 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, working in about 1 cup water gradually; knead 8 minutes until the dough springs back when pressed, then rest it under a damp cloth for 20 minutes.

For the filling, warm 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan over medium flame, add the crushed garlic and grated ginger and fry until golden and fragrant, roughly 90 seconds, keeping the heat moderate so the garlic does not scorch.

Tip in 2.5 cups grated carrot with 1 tsp salt and cook on high heat for 5-6 minutes, tossing often, until the shreds look dry and slightly caramelised at the edges. Season with 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp garam masala and 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi, then spread on a thali to cool.

Portion the dough into 6 large balls for thick dhaba-style parathas and divide the filling into 6 mounds of about 3 tbsp each. Cup a dough ball in your palm, load in one mound, pleat the edges shut and rest the stuffed balls seam-side down for 5 minutes.
Roll each ball on a floured board into an 8-inch disc, using gentle outward strokes; if a shred of carrot pokes through, patch it with a pinch of dry atta rather than re-rolling.

Cook on a hot tava over medium heat: 1 minute on the first side, flip, spread 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee, flip again and press with a folded cloth so the paratha puffs in spots and turns crusty brown, about 4 minutes per paratha.
Top each hot paratha with a spoonful of white butter the moment it comes off the tava so it melts into the crust.
tips: Red winter carrots make the filling sweeter and more colourful; balance them with an extra pinch of chilli powder.
Press only the edges while roasting — pressing the centre pushes out steam and makes the paratha dense instead of flaky.
Leftover filling doubles as a quick sandwich stuffing or can be folded into scrambled eggs the next morning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Do it the Amritsar way: pair with sweet lassi in a steel tumbler, sliced onions sprinkled with chaat masala, and a spoonful of mango pickle on the side of the plate.

variations.name: Bengali Garlic Carrot Paratha
variations.description: Bengal's love of pungent mustard oil transforms this paratha: the carrot filling is cooked jhuri-bhaja style with nigella seeds and green chillies in smoking mustard oil. The result is sharper and more rustic than the ghee-roasted classic, with a distinct kick on the finish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat's slight sweetness balances the sharp mustard oil in this Bengali-style filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed kachi ghani oil must be heated till it just smokes to mellow its pungency before the tadka

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A final brush of ghee on the roasted paratha rounds off the mustard heat, Kolkata style

ingredients.name: Carrot
ingredients.note: grated

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: sliced thin

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit lengthwise then chopped

ingredients.name: Sugar
ingredients.note: the Bengali pinch that balances mustard's bite

steps: Work 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and roughly 0.75 cup water into a supple dough; knead until smooth, about 7 minutes, and set aside covered for 15 minutes.
Pour the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil into a kadhai and heat on high until it just begins to smoke, then lower the flame and wait 30 seconds — this step tames the raw pungency.
Scatter in 0.75 tsp kalonji, let it sizzle for 15 seconds, then add the sliced garlic and chopped green chillies and fry until the garlic edges turn light brown, about 1 minute.

Add the grated carrot, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp sugar and toss on medium-high heat for 5 minutes until dry, glossy and faintly caramelised. Cool the mixture completely before stuffing.
Shape the dough into 8 balls, stuff each with about 2 tbsp of the cooled carrot mixture, seal the pleats tightly and roll into 6-7 inch rounds with a light hand, dusting with atta as needed.
Roast each paratha on a medium-hot tava, drizzling a few drops of mustard oil around the edges; flip every minute until both faces carry crisp brown patches, about 3-4 minutes each.
Brush the finished parathas with a thin film of 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee divided among them while still hot, which softens the mustard sharpness beautifully.
tips: Never add kalonji to an unheated pan — it turns bitter; it should hit oil that is properly hot but no longer smoking.
If mustard oil tastes too assertive for your table, use it only in the filling and roast the parathas in ghee instead.
The filling keeps for two days refrigerated and also works stirred through hot rice as a quick carrot bhaja.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a Bengali-style tomato-khejur chutney or simply thick misti doi on the side; a few slices of cucumber with black salt complete the plate.

variations.name: Kerala Garlic Carrot Paratha
variations.description: A Malabar-inspired take where the carrot filling is enriched with fresh grated coconut, curry leaves and black pepper, cooked in coconut oil like a thoran. It is gently sweet, deeply aromatic, and tastes of a Kerala kitchen at breakfast time.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Long-fermenting khapli wheat rolls thin without springing back, ideal for soft Malabar-style parathas

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil carries the thoran-style tempering and scents the whole filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Added to the dough for pliability so the coconut filling stays the star

ingredients.name: Carrot
ingredients.note: grated

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: crushed

ingredients.name: Black pepper powder
ingredients.note: freshly cracked

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: finely chopped

steps: Bring together 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 0.75 cup water; knead for 7-8 minutes to a soft, elastic dough and rest it, covered, for 15 minutes.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadhai over medium heat, pop 0.75 tsp mustard seeds until they finish spluttering, then add the crushed garlic, chopped green chillies and curry leaves and fry for 45 seconds until the leaves crisp and the kitchen smells like a Kerala tempering.

Add 1.5 cups grated carrot with 0.75 tsp salt and stir-fry for 3 minutes on medium heat, then fold in 0.75 cup fresh grated coconut and 0.75 tsp cracked black pepper and cook 2 minutes more until dry. Spread the thoran-like filling out to cool fully.
Divide the dough into 8 balls; stuff each with 2 tbsp of the cooled coconut-carrot filling, gathering the edges into a tight topknot and pinching off any excess dough.
Roll each stuffed ball into a 6-7 inch round using soft strokes and a dusting of atta, keeping the pressure even so the coconut does not break the surface.

Cook on a medium-hot tava, spooning the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil around the parathas as they roast; flip every minute until golden freckles cover both sides, about 3-4 minutes per paratha.
tips: Use only fresh or thawed frozen coconut; desiccated coconut turns the filling dry and gritty inside the paratha.
Crack the pepper coarsely at home — its floral heat against the sweet carrot is the signature of this version.
If the filling releases moisture as it sits, drain it on a sieve for 5 minutes before stuffing rather than adding extra flour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a small bowl of coconut chutney or Kerala-style pineapple pachadi, and finish the meal south-style with a tumbler of hot filter coffee.

variations.name: Kashmiri Garlic Carrot Paratha
variations.description: An elegant valley-style paratha where saffron-infused milk is kneaded into the dough and the carrot filling is warmed with fennel and dry ginger — the twin souls of Kashmiri spicing. Mildly sweet, golden-hued and fragrant, it feels festive enough for a special breakfast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its warm, wheaty flavour lets the delicate saffron perfume shine through the dough

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Kashmiri breads are roasted rich; bilona ghee gives the flaky, festive finish this paratha needs

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: About 15 strands bloomed in warm milk tint the dough gold and perfume every bite

ingredients.name: Warm milk
ingredients.note: for blooming the saffron

ingredients.name: Carrot
ingredients.note: grated

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: minced fine

ingredients.name: Fennel powder (saunf)
ingredients.note: the defining Kashmiri spice

ingredients.name: Kashmiri red chilli powder
ingredients.note: colour and gentle warmth, not sharp heat

ingredients.name: Crushed walnuts
ingredients.note: a valley touch for crunch

steps: Soak 0.25 tsp Anveshan Saffron strands in 0.25 cup warm milk for 10 minutes until the milk turns deep amber, crushing the strands once with the back of a spoon to release colour.

Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, the saffron milk and about 0.5 cup water into a soft golden dough; work it 7 minutes until silky, then rest 15 minutes under a damp cloth.

Melt 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium heat, sauté 6 minced garlic cloves for 1 minute until pale gold, then add 2 cups grated carrot and 0.75 tsp salt and cook 4-5 minutes until the moisture is gone.
Season the filling off the heat with 1.5 tsp fennel powder, 0.75 tsp dry ginger powder, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 3 tbsp crushed walnuts; mix well and cool completely, about 15 minutes.
Divide dough and filling into 8 portions each; encase 2 tbsp of filling in every ball, sealing the seams with a firm pinch, and roll into 6-7 inch rounds with a floured pin.

Roast each paratha on a medium tava, brushing both faces with the remaining Anveshan Ghee, flipping every minute until they blister into golden-brown patches, about 3-4 minutes apiece; keep the heat moderate so the saffron dough does not scorch.
tips: Bloom saffron in warm, never boiling, milk — high heat kills its aroma and you lose the point of the recipe.
Fennel and dry ginger burn quickly, so they go in off the heat; this keeps their fragrance bright rather than bitter.
For a festive touch, roll a few extra crushed walnuts onto the surface of the rolled paratha and press once with the pin before roasting.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of plain kahwa-spiced tea or sheer chai and a dollop of fresh cream; a spoon of apple murabba on the side plays up the valley theme.

variations.name: Classic Garlic Dal Paratha
variations.description: A North Indian breakfast staple that turns leftover toor dal into a garlicky, golden-flaked flatbread. The filling is perfumed with slow-fried garlic and roasted cumin, and the khapli atta shell crisps beautifully in ghee while staying soft inside.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat's low gluten keeps the stuffed paratha tender, never chewy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee's nutty aroma blooms the garlic without burning it

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 0.75 cup water into a soft, non-sticky dough; cover and rest 15 minutes so it rolls without tearing.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle for 30 seconds, then add 8 minced garlic cloves and fry until pale gold and fragrant, about 2 minutes.

Stir in 1 cup thick cooked toor dal, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt; cook on medium, stirring, until the mixture leaves the sides of the pan and looks dry, 4-5 minutes. Cool fully, then mix in 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
Divide the dough into 8 balls; flatten one into a 3-inch cup, place 2 tbsp of the garlic-dal filling in the centre, pleat the edges shut and pinch off excess dough.
Dust with atta and roll gently into a 6-7 inch round, applying even pressure so the filling does not break through the surface.

Cook on a hot tava over medium-high heat for about 1 minute per side until brown spots appear, then brush both sides with the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee (about 0.5 tsp per paratha) and press the edges until crisp and golden.
tips: The filling must be completely dry and cool before stuffing; a warm or moist dal filling steams the dough and makes rolling impossible.
If a paratha tears while rolling, dab the spot with dry atta and roll from the edges inward rather than over the centre.
Both dough and filling can be made a day ahead and refrigerated; bring the dough to room temperature 20 minutes before rolling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot off the tava with a bowl of chilled boondi raita and a wedge of lime; a spoon of garlic pickle on the side doubles down on the theme.

variations.name: Bengali Garlic Dal Paratha
variations.description: Inspired by Bengal's love of shorshe, this version fries the garlic and filling in pungent mustard oil with nigella seeds and green chillies. The result is a sharper, more assertive paratha with the faint bitterness that Bengali kitchens prize.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Stone-ground emmer stands up to mustard oil's punch without turning dense

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed kachi ghani oil gives the authentic Bengali nose-tingling heat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A final ghee gloss softens the mustard's edge the Bengali way

steps: Make the dough by rubbing 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, then kneading in roughly 0.75 cup water until smooth and supple; rest it under a damp cloth for 15 minutes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just begins to smoke, then lower the flame and wait 30 seconds; this mellows the raw pungency while keeping its character.
Add 1 tsp nigella seeds and 2 slit green chillies to the oil, sizzle for 20 seconds, then fry 10 chopped garlic cloves until light golden, about 90 seconds on medium heat.
Add 1 cup thick cooked masoor dal, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt; stir-fry until the dal thickens into a scoopable, dry paste, 5-6 minutes, then cool completely.
Shape 8 dough balls, stuff each with 2 tbsp of the mustard-garlic dal, seal the pleats firmly and roll out to a 6-inch disc with light, even strokes.

Roast each paratha on a medium-hot tava for 60-90 seconds per side until blistered with deep brown spots, finishing with a thin smear of the remaining mustard oil, then glossing with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee divided across the batch.
tips: Always heat mustard oil to its smoking point once and then cool it slightly; skipping this leaves the paratha tasting raw and acrid.
Masoor dal cooks drier than toor, making it the safest choice for a filling that will not leak during rolling.
Chop rather than crush the garlic here; visible golden bits are part of the Bengali texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with begun bhaja (crisp fried aubergine slices) and a smear of kasundi mustard relish for a full Kolkata-style plate.

variations.name: Rajasthani Garlic Dal Paratha
variations.description: Borrowing from the fiery lehsun chutney of Rajasthan, this paratha packs stone-crushed dried red chillies and extra garlic into a rustic chana dal filling. It is bold, smoky and built for the desert habit of hearty one-flatbread meals.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its wholesome, nutty base tames the fierce chilli-garlic filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rajasthani parathas are unapologetically ghee-laden; bilona ghee earns it

steps: Combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 tsp ajwain, 0.5 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then knead with about 0.75 cup water into a firm-soft dough; rest 20 minutes under a plate.
Dry-roast 4 dried red chillies and 1 tsp coriander seeds on a low flame until brittle and aromatic, about 2 minutes, then pound or grind them to a coarse rubble.
Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium heat and fry 12 roughly crushed garlic cloves until golden at the edges, about 2 minutes, keeping the flame moderate so they do not bitter.

Tip in 1 cup thick cooked chana dal, the pounded chilli-coriander rubble and 0.5 tsp salt; mash and cook until the mixture is dry enough to hold a shape, 4-5 minutes, then brighten with 1 tsp lemon juice and cool.
Portion the dough into 8 balls, cup each one, load in 2 tbsp filling, gather the edges into a tight topknot and roll out to a thickish 6-inch round.
Cook on a medium-hot tava for about 90 seconds per side, then generously ladle on the remaining 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, pressing with a spatula until both faces are crisp, spotted and deeply golden.
tips: Chana dal must be pressure-cooked fully soft yet drained well; a watery dal will burst the paratha at the seams.
Grind the roasted chillies coarse, not fine; the little flecks give the true Rajasthani bite and look.
These keep well for travel; wrap in cloth while warm and they stay soft for 6-8 hours, a genuine desert-tiffin trick.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Rajasthani way with a katori of plain curd, raw onion rings and an extra spoon of lehsun ki chutney for the brave.

variations.name: Tamil Garlic Dal Paratha
variations.description: A Tamil-inflected take that folds curry leaves, black pepper and gingelly oil into a poriyal-style dal filling. The paratha picks up the deep, toasty fragrance of sesame oil, echoing the flavours of a Chettinad kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer's mild sweetness balances the pepper-heavy Tamil masala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil is the soul of Tamil tava cooking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A ghee finish rounds out the sesame oil, temple-prasadam style

steps: Work 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and 0.5 tsp salt into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, then knead with close to 0.75 cup water to a pliable dough; rest it, covered, for 15 minutes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pan on medium; pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds fully (listen for the crackle to slow, about 30 seconds) before adding 12 torn curry leaves.
Fry 8 sliced garlic cloves in the tempering until golden-edged, roughly 2 minutes, then grind in 1 tsp coarsely crushed black pepper and stir for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Fold in 1 cup thick cooked toor dal and 0.5 tsp salt, mashing and cooking on medium until the filling is dry, aromatic and holds together, 4-5 minutes; cool it completely on a plate.
Stuff 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp filling apiece, seal well and roll each into a 6-inch circle, flouring lightly whenever the pin starts to drag.
Griddle each paratha over medium heat for about a minute per side until freckled brown, then finish with a light brush of Anveshan Ghee, about 0.5 tsp per paratha, and serve hot.
tips: Crush the pepper coarsely just before cooking; pre-ground pepper loses the sharp Chettinad top note within hours.
Fry curry leaves until they turn glossy and translucent, not crisp-brown, so their oil perfumes the whole filling.
Any leftover filling makes an excellent side for curd rice the next day.
variations.servingSuggestion: Plate with coconut chutney and a small tumbler of sweet-sour pineapple rasam; the pepper in the paratha and the rasam mirror each other beautifully.

variations.name: Kerala Garlic Dal Paratha
variations.description: This coastal rendition works fresh grated coconut into the garlic-dal filling and cooks everything in virgin coconut oil, thoran-style. Sweet coconut, hot garlic and soft khapli layers make it taste like a Malabar breakfast in flatbread form.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its soft crumb mimics the tenderness of a Malabar parotta without maida

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil carries the thoran aroma into every layer

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and around 0.75 cup water into a smooth, elastic dough; rest for 15 minutes beneath a damp towel.
Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil over medium heat and sauté 8 sliced garlic cloves with 2 chopped green chillies and 10 curry leaves until the garlic turns pale gold, about 2 minutes.
Add 0.5 cup fresh grated coconut and toast, tossing constantly, until it dries out and smells sweetly nutty, 2-3 minutes on medium-low.
Mix in 1 cup thick cooked moong dal, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt; mash and cook until the filling is dry and mouldable, about 4 minutes, then spread on a plate to cool fast.
Fill 8 rested dough balls with 2 tbsp of the coconut-dal mixture each, pinch the seams closed and roll softly into 6-inch rounds without pressing the centre.
Cook on a medium tava, about 75 seconds per side, drizzling the last 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil around the edges until the surface blisters golden and the kitchen smells of toasted coconut.
tips: Use freshly grated or thawed frozen coconut, never desiccated; dried coconut turns gritty inside the paratha.
Moong dal keeps this filling light; if substituting toor, reduce the coconut to 0.33 cup or the filling will crumble.
Toast the coconut only until fragrant, not brown, to keep the filling sweet rather than bitter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a sharp Kerala-style tomato-shallot chammanthi or a fried egg on top for a hearty Malabar toddy-shop mood.

variations.name: Classic Garlic Paneer Paratha
variations.description: Golden garlic fried gently in bilona ghee perfumes both the paneer filling and the crust of this paratha. It is mellower than a chilli-forward paratha — the garlic turns sweet and nutty in the ghee, making this the version even garlic sceptics come back for.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Slow-milled emmer flour gives a tender crumb that lets the roasted garlic shine

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Garlic fried in bilona ghee turns sweet and golden instead of acrid — the heart of this recipe

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 0.75 cup water into a soft, springy dough. Cover with a damp cloth and rest for 15 minutes.

Mince 8 garlic cloves. Melt 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan over medium-low heat and fry the garlic slowly for 2 to 3 minutes, stirring, until it turns pale gold and smells sweet — stop before it browns.

Pour the garlic and its ghee over 250 g crumbled paneer, then mix in 2 minced green chillies, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp salt and 3 tbsp chopped coriander.
Split the dough into 6 balls and the filling into 6 portions of about 3 tbsp. Cup each ball, tuck in a portion of filling, gather and pinch the edges shut, then flatten lightly.
Roll each stuffed ball into a 7-inch round with light, even strokes, dusting with dry atta only when the dough begins to catch.
Cook on a medium-hot tava: 1 minute until bubbles form, flip, brush with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee, then roast each side about 2 minutes more until crisp golden-brown spots cover the surface.
tips: Golden garlic is sweet; brown garlic is bitter — pull the pan off the heat the moment the colour turns.
Save a spoonful of the garlic ghee to brush over the finished parathas for a double hit of aroma.
The filling freezes well for 2 weeks; thaw fully and pat dry before stuffing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best with plain thick curd whisked with a pinch of black salt, or alongside dal tadka for a comforting weeknight dinner.

variations.name: Punjabi Garlic Paneer Paratha
variations.description: This Amritsari-style rendition pairs raw-pounded garlic with grated paneer, kasuri methi and anardana, then finishes the hot paratha with a spoon of white butter that melts into the garlicky crust. It is bold, buttery and built for a heavy winter breakfast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Sturdy emmer dough holds the wet garlic-paneer filling without tearing on the tava

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Lavish basting in bilona ghee builds the crackly, layered crust Punjabi dhabas are famous for

steps: Bloom 0.5 tsp ajwain seeds in 1 tbsp hot Anveshan Ghee for 20 seconds, tip into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, and knead with about 0.75 cup water into a supple dough; rest 20 minutes.
Pound 10 garlic cloves with 2 green chillies in a mortar into a rough, juicy paste — the crush releases more punch than mincing with a knife.
Warm 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on low and fry the garlic-chilli paste for about 90 seconds until its raw sting softens but the aroma stays sharp.
Grate 300 g paneer and fold in the garlic paste, 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi, 1 tsp anardana powder, 0.5 tsp garam masala and 0.5 tsp salt, squeezing the mixture together so it binds.
Stuff 6 dough balls with heaped 3 tbsp portions, twist off the excess dough at the seal, and roll into thick 6-inch rounds — thickness keeps the garlicky centre moist.
Roast on a medium tava for about 90 seconds per side, drizzling 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee around the edges of each side and pressing with a spatula until crisp, deep-brown patches develop.
Top every paratha with 1 tsp white butter the moment it comes off the tava so it melts into the crust.
tips: Mortar-pounded garlic is non-negotiable here — a food processor chops instead of crushing and you lose half the aroma.
If the filling feels wet from the garlic juice, work in 1 tsp of dry atta before stuffing.
These reheat beautifully directly on a low flame for 20 seconds per side; skip the microwave, which turns the crust leathery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve dhaba-style with a tall glass of sweet lassi, sliced radish and a fiery red chilli pickle on a steel thali.

variations.name: Bengali Garlic Paneer Paratha
variations.description: Bengal marries garlic with its beloved kachi ghani mustard oil and a whisper of kalonji, giving this paratha a sharp, sinus-clearing character. The garlic is fried in the pungent oil until golden, so every bite carries that unmistakable Kolkata street-side aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The chewy emmer crumb mimics the satisfying bite of a Kolkata porota

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Garlic fried in wood-pressed mustard oil is a foundational Bengali flavour pairing

steps: Bring 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil just to smoking point, cool it for 2 minutes, then knead into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt and about 0.75 cup water; rest the soft dough 15 minutes.
Slice 9 garlic cloves into thin flakes rather than mincing them — the flakes fry into crisp golden chips that stay distinct in the filling.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil on medium until shimmering, crackle 0.5 tsp kalonji for 15 seconds, then fry the garlic flakes 2 minutes until light gold and toss in 3 chopped green chillies for a final 20 seconds.
Cool the tempering slightly and fold it, oil and all, into 250 g crumbled paneer with 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.25 tsp sugar, 0.5 tsp salt and 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
Stuff 6 dough balls with 3 tbsp of filling each, seal by pinching firmly, and roll into 7-inch rounds using a floured pin and minimal dusting.
Shallow-roast on a medium tava with 1 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil per side until crisped and freckled deep brown, roughly 2 minutes a side; the mustard-garlic aroma should be assertive.
tips: Garlic flakes overcook in seconds — lift the pan off the heat while they are still pale gold, as they keep darkening in the hot oil.
The tiny amount of sugar is the classic Bengali balancer for mustard oil's pungency; do not skip it.
For a street-style finish, crush one extra fried garlic flake over the paratha before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with aloo dum on the side and a smear of kasundi, the Bengali fermented mustard relish, for the full Kolkata experience.

variations.name: Tamil Garlic Paneer Paratha
variations.description: Inspired by poondu (garlic) dishes of Tamil Nadu, this version tempers whole smashed garlic with mustard seeds, urad dal and a storm of curry leaves in gingelly oil. The garlic goes in twice — fried for depth and raw-crushed for bite — over a pepper-warmed paneer base.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat toasts beautifully in gingelly oil, echoing the crust of a Madurai bun parotta

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil and garlic are inseparable in Tamil poondu cookery

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and around 0.75 cup water into a soft, elastic dough and rest it for 15 minutes.
Smash 7 garlic cloves under the flat of a knife; keep the remaining 3 aside to crush raw into the finished filling.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil on medium, pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, fry 1 tsp urad dal to a biscuit gold, then add the smashed garlic, 2 broken dried red chillies and 15 curry leaves and saute 2 minutes until the garlic edges brown.
Take the pan off the heat, stir in 0.25 tsp turmeric, cool 5 minutes, then combine with 250 g crumbled paneer, 0.75 tsp black pepper, the 3 reserved raw-crushed garlic cloves and 0.5 tsp salt.
Fill 6 dough balls with 3 tbsp each of the garlicky mixture, seal well, and roll gently into 7-inch discs, keeping the pressure even so the crisp bits do not pierce through.
Roast each paratha on a medium tava with 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil per side for about 2 minutes a side, until the crust is crisp, aromatic and stippled with brown.
tips: The double garlic treatment is the point: fried garlic gives sweetness, raw-crushed garlic gives bite — keep both.
Tear the curry leaves as they go into the oil; bruising releases far more of their citrusy oil.
A pinch of asafoetida in the tempering adds an authentic Tamil finishing note if you have it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tomato-onion chutney and a small bowl of curd rice; a strip of fried appalam alongside adds a pleasing crunch.

variations.name: Malwa Garlic Paneer Paratha
variations.description: From the Malwa plateau of Madhya Pradesh comes this hearty version where crushed roasted peanuts join the garlic-paneer filling, adding sweetness and crunch. Roasted in ghee with a coriander-fennel dusting, it tastes like a cross between a paratha and a Malwa-style stuffed baati.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The rustic emmer grain suits Malwa's wheat-centric farm cooking perfectly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Malwa cooks finish nearly every flatbread with a spoon of ghee; here it also fries the garlic

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A spoon of wood-pressed groundnut oil in the dough amplifies the peanut theme of the filling

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and roughly 0.75 cup water into a soft, non-sticky dough; rest it, covered, for 15 minutes.
Toast 1 tsp fennel seeds in a dry pan on low for 1 minute until fragrant, then pound them coarsely with 4 tbsp roasted peanuts into a gritty rubble — not a paste.

Melt 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium-low and fry 8 minced garlic cloves for 2 minutes until pale gold, then stir in 1 tsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder off the heat so the powders bloom without scorching.
Mix the garlic-spice ghee, the peanut-fennel crush, 2 tbsp chopped coriander and 0.5 tsp salt into 250 g crumbled paneer until it clumps loosely when squeezed.
Divide the dough into 6 balls and stuff each with 3 tbsp of the peanut-garlic filling, sealing the seams with a firm twist and pinch before rolling into 7-inch rounds.
Roast on a medium tava for about 2 minutes per side, brushing each side with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee, until the crust blisters golden-brown and the peanuts inside smell toasty.
tips: Coarse peanut rubble gives the signature Malwa crunch; over-grinding turns it into oily peanut butter that leaks.
This filling is fairly dry by design — sprinkle 1 tsp water over it if it refuses to hold together.
Fennel is the quiet star; toast it fresh rather than using pre-ground powder.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a bowl of Malwa-style spiced chhaas and green chilli pickle; on cold evenings serve alongside dal to mop up.

variations.name: Classic Masala Beetroot Paratha
variations.description: This is the beetroot paratha for spice lovers: the grated beet is cooked down with a full masala base of onion, ginger-garlic, garam masala and coriander powder before stuffing. The result is a deeply savoury, almost keema-like filling wrapped in nutty khapli wheat. Each bite delivers layered spice rather than plain beet sweetness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat's robust flavour stands up to the heavy masala without tasting bland

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee carries the garam masala through the filling and crisps the crust

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and roughly 3/4 cup water into a soft, pliable dough; rest it covered for 20 minutes.
Melt 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium heat and sizzle 1 tsp cumin seeds until they darken a shade, about 30 seconds.
Add 1 finely chopped onion and fry 4-5 minutes until golden at the edges, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until the raw smell fades.

Add 2 grated and firmly squeezed beetroots along with 1/2 tsp salt, 2 tsp coriander powder, 3/4 tsp red chilli powder and 1/4 tsp turmeric; cook 6 minutes, stirring, until the mixture is dry and glossy.
Turn off the heat, mix in 1 tsp garam masala and 3 tbsp chopped coriander, and spread the masala on a plate to cool completely.
Shape the dough into 8 balls, cup each one, pack in 2 tbsp of filling, pleat shut and flatten. Roll into 6-7 inch rounds with gentle, even strokes.
Roast on a hot tava on medium-high for about 1 minute per side until brown-spotted, then brush generously with the remaining Anveshan Ghee and cook 30 seconds more per side until crisp.
tips: Add garam masala only off the heat — cooking it further makes the filling bitter and dulls its aroma.
The filling should be dry enough to hold its shape when pressed into a ball; if not, cook it 2 more minutes before cooling.
Stuffed, unrolled dough balls keep in the fridge for a day — roll and roast fresh for a 10-minute breakfast.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with boondi raita and slivered onions soaked in lime juice; the cooling raita plays off the layered masala heat.

variations.name: Rajasthani Masala Beetroot Paratha
variations.description: Rajasthan's desert kitchen leans on dried whole red chillies, coriander seeds and hing rather than fresh produce, and this paratha follows suit. The beet filling is tempered with hand-pounded dried chilli and finished with a dusting of crushed fennel for a rustic marwari edge. Roasted till sturdy, it travels well — as any desert bread should.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Coarse wholegrain texture close to the chakki atta of marwari kitchens

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rajasthani cooking is unapologetically ghee-forward; bilona ghee keeps the paratha moist in dry heat

steps: Prepare a firm-soft dough from 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 3/4 cup water; knead 5 minutes and rest 20 minutes under a damp cloth.
Dry-roast 3 dried red chillies, 2 tsp coriander seeds and 1 tsp fennel seeds in a small pan on low heat for 2 minutes until fragrant, then pound coarsely in a mortar.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium, add 1/4 tsp hing and immediately follow with 2 grated, squeezed beetroots and 1/2 tsp salt.
Sauté the beet 6-7 minutes until dry, then stir in the pounded spice mixture, 1 tsp amchur and 1/4 tsp turmeric and toast 1 minute more before cooling completely.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, stuff each with 2 tbsp of the chilli-flecked filling, seal firmly and flatten between your palms.
Roll into slightly thick 6-inch discs and roast on a medium-hot tava about 90 seconds per side until deeply browned — Rajasthani parathas take a darker roast.
Slather both sides with the remaining Anveshan Ghee and press with a spatula for a final 30 seconds so the crust turns sturdy and crisp.
tips: Pounding the roasted spices coarsely, not grinding fine, gives the authentic khada masala bite of marwari food.
Amchur stands in for fresh souring agents scarce in the desert — do not swap it for lime juice, which wets the filling.
These parathas keep soft for a full day wrapped in cloth, making them ideal tiffin or travel food.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Rajasthani way with a katori of dahi, lehsun ki chutney and a piece of gud — the jaggery bite between spicy mouthfuls is the desert tradition.

variations.name: Tamil Masala Beetroot Paratha
variations.description: Beetroot poriyal meets flatbread: the masala here is a South Indian tempering of mustard seeds, urad dal, curry leaves and sambar powder cooked in sesame oil. The urad dal toasts to a nutty crunch inside the pink filling, a texture trick straight from a Tamil poriyal. Gingelly oil on the tava gives the crust its distinct Chettinad-style aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: A wholegrain wheat that rolls thin like a Tamil-style chapathi yet stays soft

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil — the default fat of the Tamil kitchen — perfumes both tempering and crust

steps: Mix 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, add about 3/4 cup water and knead into a smooth, soft dough. Rest 20 minutes.
Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadhai over medium heat; pop 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 2 tsp urad dal and 1 broken dried red chilli and fry until the dal turns golden, about 1 minute.
Drop in the leaves of 1 curry sprig, let them crackle 10 seconds, then add 2 grated and squeezed beetroots with 1/2 tsp salt and 1/4 tsp turmeric.
Cook 5-6 minutes until dry, sprinkle over 2 tsp sambar powder and 3 tbsp grated coconut, and toss another 2 minutes on low until aromatic. Cool the poriyal-style filling fully.
Portion the dough into 8 balls, fill each with 2 tbsp of the tempered beet mixture, seal and press flat.
Roll out to thin 7-inch rounds and cook on a hot tava about 1 minute per side until spotted deep brown.
Drizzle the remaining Anveshan Sesame Oil around the edges, scatter the second sprig of curry leaves onto the tava beside the bread and roast 30 seconds so their fried aroma clings to the crust.
tips: Fry the urad dal until properly golden — pale dal stays chalky inside the filling instead of crunchy.
Every sambar powder differs; taste the filling and adjust with a pinch of chilli powder before cooling.
A teaspoon of the filling folded into hot rice with ghee is the cook's treat while the parathas roast.
variations.servingSuggestion: Cut into wedges and serve with coconut chutney and a small tumbler of filter coffee, or alongside curd rice for a proper Tamil lunchbox pairing.

variations.name: Gujarati Masala Beetroot Paratha
variations.description: Gujarat's beloved sweet-spicy-tangy balance shapes this thepla-like paratha: jaggery melts into the beet masala while lime and green chilli push back. Sesame seeds in the dough toast against the tava the way they do on a good methi thepla. It is softer and thinner than northern parathas, made for stacking and travelling.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Rolls whisper-thin for thepla-style parathas without cracking at the edges

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Chemical-free jaggery dissolves evenly into the hot filling for Gujarat's signature sweet note

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed sing tel, the everyday oil of Gujarati homes, for tempering and roasting

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, 2 tsp sesame seeds, 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and about 3/4 cup water into a soft, rollable dough; rest 20 minutes.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium and fry 1 tbsp green chilli-ginger paste for 30 seconds until it stops spluttering.
Add 2 grated, well-squeezed beetroots with 1/2 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 2 tsp dhana-jeeru powder and cook 5-6 minutes until the shreds are dry and tender.
Stir in 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook 1 minute until it melts and coats the beet glossily, then finish with 2 tsp lime juice and 2 tbsp chopped coriander. Cool fully.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, stuff each with 2 tbsp of the sweet-spicy filling and seal the pleats without trapping air.
Roll thin, almost thepla-like, into 7-inch rounds and cook on a medium-hot tava for about 45-60 seconds per side until soft with light brown freckles.
Brush both sides with the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil and give each side a final 20-second press so the sesame in the dough toasts fragrant.
tips: The jaggery-lime pairing is the whole trick: always add lime off the heat so its brightness survives.
Roll these thinner than a normal stuffed paratha; the dry, jaggery-bound filling will not leak.
Stacked in foil, they stay soft for two days — the classic Gujarati travel-food quality.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with chhundo or kesar mango pickle and a bowl of plain dahi; for the full prava-bhojan experience, wrap a stack in cloth with fried green chillies tucked between layers.

variations.name: Odia Masala Beetroot Paratha
variations.description: Panch phoron — the five-seed blend of cumin, fennel, fenugreek, kalonji and mustard — is bloomed whole in hot oil and folded through the beet masala, giving every bite a different crackle. A hint of grated ginger and green chilli keeps it homely, the way Odia santula-style vegetables are spiced. Mustard oil on the tava finishes it with an eastern edge.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Hearty emmer wheat suits Odisha's rustic, lightly spiced flatbreads

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Kachi ghani pungency is essential for blooming panch phoron the Odia way

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A small measure in the dough tenderises the crumb against the sharp mustard notes

steps: Bring together 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then knead with about 3/4 cup water for 5 minutes into a soft dough and rest it 20 minutes.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai until it smokes lightly, cool 20 seconds off the flame, then return to medium heat and crackle 1.5 tsp panch phoron for 30 seconds until the fenugreek darkens slightly.
Add 1 inch grated ginger and 2 chopped green chillies, stir briefly, then tip in 2 grated and squeezed beetroots with 1/2 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1/2 tsp red chilli powder.
Cook 6-7 minutes on medium, stirring often, until the beet is dry and the five spices are evenly flecked through the pink mass; cool completely.
Shape 8 dough balls, load each with 2 tbsp of filling, gather the edges shut and flatten gently before rolling into 6-inch rounds.
Roast each paratha on a hot tava roughly 1 minute per side until brown blisters form across the surface.
Smear with the last 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and roast 20 seconds more per side so the crust picks up the oil's pungent finish.
tips: Watch the fenugreek seeds in the panch phoron — they turn bitter beyond light brown, so keep the blooming brief.
If mixing your own panch phoron, use equal parts of all five seeds but halve the fenugreek for a gentler blend.
The filling doubles as a side dish: pile any extra beside dal-rice as an instant beet bharta.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with dahi baigana (Odia yoghurt-brinjal raita) or simply thick curd whisked with a pinch of roasted cumin, plus a wedge of lime.

variations.name: Classic Masala Cabbage Paratha
variations.description: This is the cabbage paratha for spice lovers: the shredded cabbage is bhuno-ed with onion, ginger-garlic and a full masala battery of coriander, garam masala and chilli until it tastes like a dry sabzi. Stuffed and roasted in ghee, each bite is layered, warming and deeply seasoned.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The wholegrain wrapper has enough character to stand up to a heavily spiced filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bhuno-ing the masala in bilona ghee gives the filling its rounded, restaurant-style richness

ingredients.name: Cabbage
ingredients.note: finely shredded

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 0.75 cup water into a soft, smooth dough, working it a full 7 minutes; rest it covered while you cook the filling.

Melt 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat and fry the chopped onion for 3-4 minutes until golden at the edges, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook until the raw smell disappears, about 1 minute.

Add 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder with a splash of water and bhuno for 1 minute until the masala darkens and the ghee separates at the edges.

Tip in 2.5 cups shredded cabbage and 1 tsp salt, raise the heat and stir-fry for 5-6 minutes until the cabbage is dry and coated in masala; finish with 0.75 tsp garam masala and 3 tbsp chopped coriander, then cool completely.
Divide the dough into 8 balls; flatten each into a small bowl shape, load in 2 tbsp of filling, gather and pinch the edges shut, then flatten gently and dust with atta.

Roll each ball into a 6-7 inch round and roast on a medium-hot tava, brushing both sides with the remaining ghee, flipping every minute until deep golden spots form and the masala smells toasty, about 3-4 minutes per paratha.
tips: Bhuno the powdered spices with a splash of water so they cook through without burning — raw coriander powder tastes dusty in a filling.
Taste the cooled filling before stuffing; it should be slightly saltier than a sabzi since the plain dough will dilute it.
These reheat best on a dry tava rather than a microwave, which softens the crisp spots.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with boondi raita and a sharp onion-tomato kachumber; for a heavier meal, serve alongside dal makhani and let the paratha do the scooping.

variations.name: Gujarati Masala Cabbage Paratha
variations.description: Sweet, tangy and gently spiced in the Kathiyawadi thepla tradition: jaggery and lime balance the chilli, while sesame seeds toast on the surface as it roasts. The cabbage is kneaded right into the dough, making these thin, flexible and perfect for travel tiffins.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli's low-elasticity gluten rolls thepla-thin without springing back

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The everyday Gujarati fat, wood-pressed for a clean nutty finish that keeps theplas soft for days

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Dissolves into the dough for the sweet undertone every Kathiyawadi masala flatbread carries

ingredients.name: Cabbage
ingredients.note: very finely shredded, salted and squeezed

ingredients.name: Water
ingredients.note: approximate

steps: Salt 2 cups shredded cabbage with 0.5 tsp of the salt, rest 10 minutes, then squeeze out every drop of liquid you can; reserve the juice for kneading.

In a paraat, mix 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with the squeezed cabbage, 1 tbsp sesame seeds, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.75 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 0.75 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil.

Add 1 tbsp lime juice, the reserved cabbage juice and just enough water — around 0.5 cup total liquid — to knead a soft, slightly oily dough; work it 5 minutes, cover and rest only 10 minutes so the cabbage stays perky.
Pinch off 10 small balls and roll each very thin, about 7 inches across and barely 2 mm thick, dusting lightly with dry atta; thinness is what makes these flexible like thepla.

Cook on a medium tava: 40-50 seconds until the surface bubbles, flip, smear 0.5 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, flip again and press lightly until both sides show scattered brown freckles rather than large char spots, about 2 minutes each.
Stack the cooked parathas immediately in a covered dabba; the trapped steam keeps them pliable enough to roll without cracking even hours later.
tips: The jaggery is not optional here — without that sweet counterpoint the lime and chilli taste one-dimensional.
Rolled thin and cooked soft, these stay good for a day at room temperature, which is why they are Gujarat's favourite travel bread.
Swap a quarter cup of the atta for besan if you want a more pronounced Kathiyawadi flavour and extra binding.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve rolled with chhundo (sweet mango pickle) or alongside a bowl of kadhi; for the full highway-dhaba experience, add masala chai and a wedge of raw onion.

variations.name: Andhra Masala Cabbage Paratha
variations.description: Fiery and garlicky in true Guntur style: the cabbage is stir-fried with a coarse pounded paste of Guntur red chillies, garlic and cumin, so the heat blooms slowly and lingers. A squeeze of lime and fresh curry leaves keep the fire bright rather than heavy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its mellow sweetness is the perfect foil for the Guntur chilli blaze

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Andhra kitchens fry their karam pastes in gingelly oil; the wood-pressed version adds a deep roasted note

ingredients.name: Cabbage
ingredients.note: shredded

ingredients.name: Guntur dried red chillies
ingredients.note: soaked 10 minutes in hot water

ingredients.name: Cumin seeds
ingredients.note: pounded into the chilli paste

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and about 0.75 cup water for 7 minutes into a supple dough; rest covered for 15 minutes.
Drain the 4 soaked Guntur chillies and pound them with 8 garlic cloves and 1 tsp cumin seeds in a mortar into a coarse, rubbly karam paste — texture matters, so stop before it turns smooth.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadhai on medium, fry the karam paste for 2 minutes until the raw garlic smell fades and the oil stains brick-red, then throw in the curry leaves and let them crackle for 20 seconds.

Add 2.5 cups shredded cabbage, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt; stir-fry on high for 5-6 minutes until dry and flecked with red masala, then take it off the heat, mix in 1 tbsp lime juice and 2 tbsp coriander leaves and cool fully.
Shape 8 dough balls, stuff each with 2 tbsp of the cooled Guntur cabbage, seal the pleats with a firm twist and roll into 6-7 inch rounds without pressing hard over the filling.

Roast on a medium-hot tava with a thin drizzle of sesame oil per side, flipping every minute until crisp, deep-gold patches form, about 3-4 minutes each; the chilli aroma will sharpen as it toasts, so keep the exhaust on.
tips: Soaking the dried chillies before pounding gives heat without the acrid edge that dry-ground chilli can have in a filling.
Scale the Guntur chillies to your audience — even 2 makes a decidedly spicy paratha; the lime juice is what keeps the heat pleasant.
Leftover karam paste is gold: fry it in a spoon of sesame oil and toss with hot rice for instant kanda karam annam.
variations.servingSuggestion: Cool the fire with thick curd rice on the side or a glass of neer majjiga (thin spiced buttermilk); a spoon of avakaya pickle is for the truly brave.

variations.name: Odia Masala Cabbage Paratha
variations.description: Odisha's beloved panch phoron — cumin, mustard, fenugreek, fennel and kalonji — is bloomed whole in mustard oil and folded through the cabbage, giving the filling a five-spice crackle and gentle bitterness that is instantly recognisable from a bandha kobi tarkari. Understated, aromatic and quietly addictive.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: A rustic wholegrain shell suits Odia home cooking, which prizes simplicity over richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Panch phoron must bloom in pungent mustard oil to taste authentically Odia

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A final ghee brush after roasting, the way festive Odia parathas are finished

ingredients.name: Cabbage
ingredients.note: shredded

ingredients.name: Panch phoron
ingredients.note: the Odia five-spice whole seed mix

ingredients.name: Potato
ingredients.note: boiled and mashed, the classic tarkari partner

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit and chopped

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: julienned fine

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and about 0.75 cup water into a soft dough; work it until smooth, around 7 minutes, and rest for 15 minutes.

Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai until it shimmers and just smokes, ease the flame to medium and scatter in 1.5 tsp panch phoron; let the five seeds crackle and pop for 30 seconds until fragrant.

Add the julienned ginger and chopped green chillies for 30 seconds, then the shredded cabbage, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 0.75 tsp salt; cook on medium-high for 5 minutes, tossing, until wilted and dry.
Fold in the mashed boiled potato with the remaining 0.5 tsp salt and cook 2 minutes more, mashing lightly so the potato binds the cabbage into a stuffable tarkari; cool it completely on a plate.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, fill each with a generous 2 tbsp of the cooled mixture, seal well and roll out to 6-7 inches, flouring as needed to stop the seeds tearing through.

Roast on a medium tava, flipping every minute and drizzling drops of mustard oil at the edges, until both sides are blistered golden-brown, about 3-4 minutes per paratha; brush the hot parathas with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee divided among them.
tips: Panch phoron burns unevenly if the oil is too hot — the fenugreek should turn light brown, never black, or it will taste bitter.
The potato is the binder; without it the seed-flecked cabbage filling tends to spill when you roll.
This filling, loosened with a ladle of water and simmered, becomes a genuine bandha kobi tarkari for the next meal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with dahi baigana (Odia yoghurt-brinjal raita) or simply thick curd and tomato khatta; a piece of jaggery on the thali is a very Odia sweet full stop.

variations.name: Malwa Masala Cabbage Paratha
variations.description: From the wheat bowl of Madhya Pradesh comes a crunchy, warming version: roasted peanuts are pounded coarse and cooked into the cabbage with sesame, ajwain and a Malwa-style hit of coriander seed. The peanut crunch against the soft khapli crust makes this the most texturally interesting paratha of the family.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Malwa is wheat country; stone-ground emmer honours the region's roti-first table

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Doubles down on the peanut theme — the filling is cooked in the same nut it celebrates

ingredients.name: Cabbage
ingredients.note: shredded

ingredients.name: Roasted peanuts
ingredients.note: pounded coarse

ingredients.name: Coriander seeds
ingredients.note: crushed coarse

steps: Make a soft, rested dough from 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and roughly 0.75 cup water; knead 7 minutes and set aside under a damp cloth for 15 minutes.
Warm 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai over medium heat and crackle 0.5 tsp ajwain with 1.5 tsp coarsely crushed coriander seeds for 30 seconds until they smell citrusy and toasted.
Add 2.5 cups shredded cabbage with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt; stir-fry on medium-high for 5 minutes until the shreds soften and dry out completely.

Tip in 0.5 cup coarsely pounded roasted peanuts, 1 tbsp sesame seeds, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp amchur; toast together for 2 minutes so the sesame pops and the peanuts re-crisp, then stir in the coriander leaves and cool fully.
Portion the dough into 8 balls, stuff each with 2 tbsp of the peanut-cabbage mixture, pinch the seams closed and roll gently to 6-7 inches — the nut pieces will dimple the surface, which is fine.

Roast on a medium-hot tava with a little groundnut oil brushed on each side, flipping every minute until deeply golden and crisp, about 3-4 minutes per paratha; the peanuts inside should sound faintly crunchy when you tap the crust.
tips: Pound the peanuts, do not grind them — powder makes the filling pasty, while coarse rubble gives the signature crunch.
Sesame seeds jump out of the pan when they toast; keep a lid handy for the first 20 seconds.
Amchur added off high heat keeps its fruity tang; cooked too long it just tastes flat and sour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Do as Indore does: serve with sev-topped dahi, a spoon of spicy garlic chutney and cutting chai; leftover parathas crisped on the tava make an excellent base for poha-style toppings.

variations.name: Classic Masala Methi Paratha
variations.description: The dhaba-style upgrade of a plain methi paratha, where a full masala battery of garam masala, coriander powder and amchur is kneaded into the dough alongside the greens. Each round comes off the tava lacquered in bilona ghee, spice-flecked and aromatic enough to eat on its own. This is what North Indian highway kitchens serve when you ask for something with punch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Heirloom emmer wheat gives these spiced rounds a wholesome, slightly sweet backbone

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee blooms the garam masala on the hot tava, doubling its aroma

steps: Rinse and firmly squeeze 2 cups chopped methi leaves, then rub them with a small pinch of salt and let them sit for 5 minutes to draw out their bitterness and extra water.

In a paraat, whisk together 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp garam masala, 2 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp amchur, 1 tsp red chilli powder, ½ tsp turmeric, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder and 1 tsp salt until the flour is uniformly ochre.

Work in the squeezed methi, grated ginger and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then knead with about ¾ cup water, added in stages, into a soft dough that no longer sticks to the bowl; rest covered for 15 minutes.
Divide into 8 balls and roll each into a 6-inch round, re-dusting once mid-way so the spice-heavy dough does not grip the pin.

On a tava heated over medium-high flame, cook each round about 90 seconds until bubbles dot the surface, then flip and paint on ½ tsp Anveshan Ghee, pressing with a folded cloth until crisp bronze patches form.
Turn once more, ghee the second face, and cook a final minute until both sides crackle lightly when tapped; serve straight off the heat.
tips: Amchur is the quiet hero here; its tang keeps the heavy spicing from tasting flat, so do not omit it or swap in lemon juice, which weakens the dough.
Knead a minute longer than feels necessary; spices interfere with gluten, and the extra kneading restores softness.
Leftover parathas revive perfectly on a dry tava for 30 seconds a side; avoid the microwave, which turns the spiced crust leathery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best with a katori of dahi whisked with black salt and a raw onion salad; for a dhaba experience, add a slab of white butter melting on top.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Masala Methi Paratha
variations.description: Goda masala, Maharashtra's sweet-smoky signature blend of dagad phool, sesame and coconut, transforms this paratha into something closer to a methi thalipeeth. A spoon of jowar flour lends the characteristic rustic bite, and the rounds are toasted in ghee until the goda masala's caramel notes surface. Deeply savoury with a whisper of sweetness underneath.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Blended with jowar the thalipeeth way, it keeps the rounds tender where jowar alone would crack

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Toasting goda masala in slow-churned ghee coaxes out its coconut-sesame depth

steps: Melt 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan over low heat, stir in 2 tsp goda masala for 30 seconds until it smells of roasted coconut and sesame, then immediately scrape it into a mixing paraat to stop it scorching.
Add 1¾ cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, ¼ cup jowar flour, 1 tbsp sesame seeds, 1 tsp red chilli powder, ½ tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt to the paraat and rub the bloomed masala evenly through the flours.

Fold in 2 cups chopped methi and the finely chopped onion, then knead with about ½ cup water into a soft dough; the onion keeps releasing juice, so hold back the last splash of water until you are sure it is needed. Rest 15 minutes.
Shape 8 balls and roll them into 6-inch rounds between sheets of parchment if the jowar makes the edges ragged, patching any tears with a pinch of dough.

Cook each round on a medium tava for 2 minutes until the underside is freckled brown, then flip, spread ½ tsp Anveshan Ghee, and press until the goda masala scents the kitchen and both sides are richly bronzed, about 2 more minutes.
Rest the stack under a cloth for 5 minutes before serving; the brief steam softens the jowar and settles the spice.
tips: Goda masala is not garam masala; if you cannot find it, dry-roast 1 tsp sesame, 1 tbsp grated dry coconut and a pinch of cinnamon and grind them as a stopgap.
Chop the onion almost to a mince; larger pieces tear the rounds while rolling.
A skillet lid placed over the tava for the final 30 seconds gives these the soft-centred thalipeeth texture Maharashtrians prize.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of homemade dahi, spicy thecha on the side, and a drizzle of ghee on top the Puneri way; leftover rounds pair well with pithla.

variations.name: Andhra Masala Methi Paratha
variations.description: Guntur chillies, the pride of Andhra Pradesh, drive this fiery version where the masala leans on roasted chilli-garlic podi rather than northern garam masala. Groundnut oil, the region's everyday cooking fat, toasts the parathas to a deep crimson-flecked crust. It is unapologetically hot, with the methi's bitterness acting as the only brake.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its gentle sweetness is the necessary counterweight to Guntur chilli heat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is Andhra's default fat and stands up to high tava heat

steps: Dry-roast 5 Guntur chillies, 1 tbsp chana dal and 2 tsp coriander seeds in a kadai over low flame for 3 to 4 minutes, stirring constantly, until the dal turns golden and the chillies crisp without blackening; cool fully.
Grind the roasted mix with 6 garlic cloves and a pinch of salt into a coarse podi; it should look like rough red sand, not a smooth paste.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in the same kadai, crackle 10 curry leaves for 15 seconds, add the methi leaves and stir 1 minute until wilted, then mix in the podi and switch off; cool 5 minutes.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with ½ tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt, the methi-podi mixture and about ¾ cup water into a soft, faintly red dough; rest it 15 minutes under a damp cloth.
Roll 8 balls into 6-inch discs, flouring lightly; flecks of chilli and curry leaf should show through the surface.
