Toast each disc on a medium-high tava, about 2 minutes per side, brushing ½ tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on each face and pressing until the crust turns a deep russet with charred pinpoints.
tips: Roast the chillies on the lowest flame with constant stirring; one scorched Guntur chilli will make the entire podi acrid.
The chana dal in the podi is textural and also softens the heat; skipping it makes the paratha noticeably sharper.
For a milder table, serve with a bowl of cold curd rice on the side; it is the traditional Andhra antidote to chilli overload.
variations.servingSuggestion: Eat with a spoon of ghee-drenched kandi podi and plain curd, or alongside a simple tomato pappu, letting the paratha itself supply all the fire.

variations.name: Kumaoni Masala Methi Paratha
variations.description: From the Uttarakhand hills comes this quietly distinctive version tempered with jakhya, the wild mustard-like seed Kumaonis prefer over cumin for its superior crackle. The masala stays earthy and minimal, hill-style, with coriander, hill garlic and a touch of bhang jeera-like nuttiness from toasted sesame. Cooked in ghee, it tastes of woodsmoke kitchens and cold mountain mornings.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Close cousin to the hardy hill wheats traditionally ground in Kumaoni gharats

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Pahari kitchens finish almost every flatbread with ghee; here it also blooms the jakhya

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small iron pan over medium heat and add 1½ tsp jakhya seeds; they should pop and crackle noisily within 20 seconds, at which point add the 5 crushed garlic cloves and fry 30 seconds until golden.
Tip the methi leaves into the pan, toss for about 1 minute until they collapse and glisten, then remove from the heat and let the mixture cool for 5 minutes.
In a wide bowl, combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 2 tsp coriander powder, 1 tbsp coarsely ground toasted sesame, ½ tsp red chilli powder, ½ tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt.
Add the cooled jakhya-methi tempering and knead with roughly ¾ cup water into a supple dough that springs back slowly when pressed; rest it 15 minutes.
Roll 8 portions into 6-inch rounds, keeping them slightly thick in the middle the hill way so the centre steams soft while the edges crisp.
Cook on a medium tava for around 2 minutes each side, applying ½ tsp Anveshan Ghee per face, until the surface is mottled deep gold and the jakhya's toasty scent rises.
tips: Jakhya must always be crackled in hot fat first; raw seeds are bitter and gritty, and no amount of tava time fixes them.
If jakhya is unavailable, brown mustard seeds bloomed the same way come closest, though the crackle is softer.
The coarse sesame stands in for the hills' bhangjeera; grind it only roughly so it stays a texture, not a paste.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as they do in Almora, with bhaang ki chutney or plain radish-leaf saag and a tumbler of buttermilk; a spoon of hill honey on the last paratha is a local treat.

variations.name: Punjabi Masala Methi Paratha
variations.description: The maximalist Punjabi rendition: a robustly spiced methi dough shallow-crisped in ghee, then finished with a knob of white butter melting into the crust. Anardana adds the tang Punjabi parathas are known for, and the rounds are pressed hard on the tava for that shattering, layered exterior. This is Sunday-breakfast food, built to be eaten with both hands.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Stone-adjacent slow milling keeps the bran intact for a true Punjabi wholewheat crumb

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Punjabi parathas demand a generous hand; this ghee crisps without ever tasting greasy

steps: Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a ladle over the flame, crackle ½ tsp ajwain seeds in it for 20 seconds, and pour the sizzling tempering over 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta in a large paraat.
Add 1 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp anardana powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt to the flour and rub the ghee through until the mixture resembles damp sand.

Mix in the chopped methi, grated and squeezed onion and minced green chillies, then knead with about ½ cup water into a soft, elastic dough; punch it down twice during a 15-minute rest for extra pliability.
Divide into 8 balls, roll each to 5 inches, fold into a triangle with a smear of ghee between the folds, and roll again to a 7-inch triangle for flaky layers.

Slap each triangle onto a hot tava, cook 1 minute, flip and spread ½ tsp Anveshan Ghee, then press firmly all over with a spatula so the layers separate and crisp, about 2 minutes per side until deeply golden.
Crush each finished paratha lightly between your palms to open the flakes, crown with ½ tbsp white butter, and serve while the butter is still sliding.
tips: Squeeze the grated onion almost dry before it goes in; onion water is the top reason Punjabi paratha dough turns slack on the second rolling.
The triangle fold, not extra ghee, is what creates flake; keep the smear between layers thin.
Anardana gives a fruitier sourness than amchur here and toasts better against butter; find it at any Punjabi grocer.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Amritsari way with dahi sprinkled with roasted cumin, spicy mango pickle, and sweet milky chai; nothing else is needed or wanted.

variations.name: Classic Masala Mixed Veg Paratha
variations.description: A spice-forward cousin of the everyday veg paratha, where the filling is built on a proper masala base of browned onion, ginger-garlic and toasted ground spices. Garam masala and coriander powder folded through mashed vegetables give every bite a warm, layered heat. Khapli atta dough and a bilona ghee roast make it as wholesome as it is punchy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat's earthy flavour carries a heavy masala without turning bitter or dense

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The masala base is bhuno-ed in bilona ghee, which deepens every spice it touches

steps: Work 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and about 0.75 cups water into a soft, smooth dough over 5 minutes of kneading, then rest it covered for 20 minutes.
Boil 2 potatoes, 1 diced carrot and 0.5 cups peas for 10-12 minutes until completely tender; drain and mash them together while hot.
Melt 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then brown 1 finely chopped onion for 4-5 minutes until golden at the edges.

Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until the raw smell fades. Add 2 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp garam masala with a splash of water, and bhuno the masala 2 minutes until it glistens.
Fold the mashed vegetables and 1 tsp salt into the masala, cook 3-4 minutes until the mixture is dry enough to shape, then cool and divide into 6 portions of about 3 tbsp.

Stuff 6 dough balls with the masala filling, seal well and roll into 7-inch rounds. Roast each on a medium-hot tava for 2 minutes per side, finishing with a brush of the remaining 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until the crust is crisp and blotched deep gold.
tips: Bhuno the ground spices until ghee beads at the edges of the masala; underdone spices taste dusty inside a paratha.
Add garam masala at the end of the masala stage, not the start, so its aromatics survive the roasting.
Leftover filling doubles as a sandwich mash or can be rolled into cutlets the next day.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best with a katori of boondi raita and slivered green chillies in vinegar; a hot cup of masala chai on the side turns it into a full Sunday breakfast.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Masala Mixed Veg Paratha
variations.description: Goda masala, the smoky-sweet Maharashtrian blend scented with dagad phool and coconut, transforms this paratha's filling into something you would find in a Pune household. Potato, cabbage and peas are tossed with the dark masala, peanuts and a whisper of jaggery for the region's beloved sweet-savoury balance. Roasted in ghee, it is earthy, fragrant and quietly complex.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli wheat is a Maharashtrian heritage grain, making it the natural match for goda masala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee blooms goda masala's stone-flower smokiness the way refined oil never can

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A pinch of unrefined jaggery gives the filling the classic Maharashtrian sweet undertone

steps: Knead a pliable dough from 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and roughly 0.75 cups water; rest it 20 minutes while you cook the bhaji-style filling.
Boil 2 potatoes and 0.5 cups peas for 10 minutes until soft, then mash. Shred 1 cup cabbage as finely as you can.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium and pop 1 tsp mustard seeds, about 30 seconds. Add 2 chopped green chillies and the cabbage and fry 3-4 minutes until wilted and lightly caught at the edges.
Lower the flame and stir in 2 tsp goda masala with 0.5 tsp turmeric, letting the dark spices toast in the fat for 30 seconds until intensely aromatic.

Add the potato-pea mash, 3 tbsp roasted peanut powder, 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp salt; mash everything together over low heat for 3 minutes until dry, then cool and shape into 6 filling balls.

Stuff and seal 6 dough rounds, roll each to 7 inches and roast on a medium tava for about 2 minutes per side, gliding the last 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the surface until mahogany spots appear and the peanut aroma rises.
tips: Goda masala scorches quickly; always toast it on a low flame and for under a minute.
Peanut powder both thickens the filling and adds the crunch Maharashtrian bhajis are known for.
If you cannot find goda masala, kala masala works; garam masala does not — the stone-flower smokiness is the dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a dollop of thecha (green chilli-garlic crush) for heat lovers and a cooling glass of solkadhi or plain taak (spiced buttermilk).

variations.name: Andhra Masala Mixed Veg Paratha
variations.description: Guntur chillies, the pride of Andhra Pradesh, set this paratha's masala ablaze. The vegetable filling is fried in wood-pressed groundnut oil with curry leaves, crushed Guntur chilli and a sour edge of tamarind, in the style of a fiery vepudu. It delivers the clean, upfront heat Andhra kitchens are famous for, tempered by the sweet nuttiness of khapli wheat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The mild sweetness of khapli dough is the perfect foil for Guntur chilli fire

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the traditional frying medium of Andhra vepudu-style vegetables

steps: Bring together 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, 0.5 tsp salt and about 0.75 cups water, kneading 5 minutes to a soft dough. Rest 20 minutes under a damp cloth.
Dry-roast 4 Guntur chillies in a pan for 1-2 minutes until glossy and brittle, cool, and pound them coarsely with 5 garlic cloves into a rough, fiery paste.
Boil 2 potatoes, 1 diced carrot and 0.5 cups chopped beans for 10-12 minutes until tender; drain thoroughly and mash coarsely.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium-high, sizzle 10 curry leaves for 15 seconds, then fry the chilli-garlic pound for 1 minute until the raw garlic smell disappears.

Add the mashed vegetables, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tbsp tamarind pulp and 1 tsp salt. Stir-fry 4 minutes until the filling darkens slightly and dries out, then cool and portion into 6 balls.

Fill and seal 6 dough balls, roll to 7-inch rounds and roast each on a hot tava about 2 minutes per side, pressing the edges until crisp and deeply speckled; smear the last of the groundnut oil over the finished parathas.
tips: Guntur chillies bring heat and colour; deseed half of them if you want the flavour with slightly less blaze.
The tamarind should read as brightness, not sourness; start with less and adjust after tasting the filling.
Frying curry leaves until translucent-crisp before the paste goes in gives the filling its signature Andhra aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Do as Andhra homes do: serve with thick curd rice on the side or a spoon of avakaya mango pickle and ghee-fried papad.

variations.name: Odia Masala Mixed Veg Paratha
variations.description: Panch phoron — the five-seed blend of cumin, fennel, fenugreek, kalonji and mustard — defines Odia tempering, and here it is bloomed in mustard oil to spice a santula-style vegetable filling. Pumpkin and potato lend gentle sweetness against the bitter-aromatic seeds. It is a subtle, homely paratha that tastes of an Odisha kitchen at dusk.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Wholegrain khapli echoes the rustic, unpolished character of Odia home cooking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Panch phoron must crackle in pungent kachi ghani mustard oil to release its five-fold aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A restrained ghee finish, the way Odia festive breads are kissed with it at the end

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil, 0.5 tsp salt and about 0.75 cups water for 5 minutes into a soft, springy dough; rest 20 minutes.
Peel and dice 1 cup pumpkin and 2 potatoes into small cubes, and boil with 0.5 cups peas for 8-10 minutes until soft enough to mash. Drain very well, since pumpkin holds water.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai until it just smokes, cool it 30 seconds, then crackle 1.5 tsp panch phoron over medium heat for about 40 seconds until the fenugreek darkens a shade and the fennel smells sweet.

Add 1 inch grated ginger and 2 chopped green chillies, sizzle 30 seconds, then tip in the mashed vegetables with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt. Cook and mash for 4-5 minutes until the mixture is thick, dry and speckled with seeds; cool completely.
Divide the dough into 6 balls, tuck about 3 tbsp of filling into each, seal the pleats and roll softly into 7-inch discs, flouring lightly to prevent sticking.
Roast on a medium tava, about 2 minutes per side, until brown-spotted, then gloss each hot paratha with a little of the 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee just before it leaves the pan.
tips: Do not let the fenugreek in panch phoron go dark brown; a shade past golden is the line between aromatic and bitter.
Pumpkin brings the filling its Odia sweetness; squeeze the boiled cubes gently in a sieve if they seem watery.
This filling tastes even better rested; make it a few hours ahead so the five spices settle into the vegetables.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside dalma or a simple tomato khajuri chutney with dates, and end with a piece of chhena poda if you are feasting properly.

variations.name: Malwa Masala Mixed Veg Paratha
variations.description: From the Malwa plateau of Madhya Pradesh comes a paratha built around crunchy roasted peanuts, the region's staple crop. Coarsely crushed peanuts join potato and carrot in a cumin-coriander masala, giving the filling body, richness and pockets of crunch. Roasted in groundnut oil and finished with ghee, it doubles down on that toasty peanut character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Malwa's wheat-belt heritage meets its ancient emmer cousin in this hearty dough

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Cooking the peanut filling in wood-pressed groundnut oil layers nut flavour on nut flavour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The final ghee roast gives the peanut-studded crust its festive Malwi richness

steps: Knead the dough: 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and about 0.75 cups water, worked 5 minutes until supple. Cover and rest 20 minutes.
Pulse 0.5 cups roasted peanuts in a mortar or grinder until half is coarse crumble and half is powder; the two textures matter.
Boil 2 potatoes and 1 diced carrot for 10-12 minutes until soft, drain, and mash while warm.

Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan over medium heat, fry 2 chopped green chillies for 30 seconds, then add the mash with 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 2 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, cooking 3 minutes until dry.
Stir the crushed peanuts and 1 tbsp lemon juice through the filling, cook 1 minute more so the crumbs toast lightly, then cool and divide into 6 portions.

Stuff, seal and roll 6 parathas to 7 inches each. Roast on a medium-hot tava around 2 minutes per side, brushing with the remaining Anveshan Ghee until the crust is crisp and the peanuts inside smell toasted.
tips: Keep half the peanuts coarse; fully powdered nuts make the filling pasty and lose the signature crunch.
The lemon juice cuts the peanuts' richness — do not skip it or the paratha can feel heavy.
Roll these slightly thicker than usual; thin rolling shears the peanut pieces through the dough.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with green coriander-peanut chutney and a bowl of jeera-spiked chaas; in true Malwa spirit, a little kairi launji (raw mango relish) alongside is wonderful in summer.

variations.name: Classic Masala Paneer Paratha
variations.description: The dhaba-style breakfast staple of North India: a soft khapli wheat shell hiding a crumbly, masala-flecked paneer filling. Slow-roasting in bilona ghee gives the crust its signature blistered, golden crunch while the paneer inside stays creamy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat kneads into an extra-soft dough that stays pliable even after the paratha cools

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee has a high smoke point, so the paratha crisps without burning

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 0.75 cup water into a soft, non-sticky dough; it should spring back slowly when pressed. Cover and rest 15 minutes.

Crumble 250 g paneer finely with your fingertips so no lumps larger than a pea remain, then mix in 1 finely chopped small onion, 1 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp salt and 3 tbsp chopped coriander leaves.

Divide the dough into 6 equal balls and the filling into 6 portions of about 3 tbsp each. Flatten a ball into a 4-inch cup, place one portion of filling in the centre, gather the edges over the top and pinch firmly to seal.
Dust the stuffed ball with khapli atta and roll gently from the centre outwards into a 7-inch round, rotating a quarter turn after every few strokes so the filling spreads evenly without tearing.

Heat a tava on medium heat until a drop of water sizzles instantly. Cook the paratha 1 minute until small bubbles appear, flip, spread 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee over the surface, and cook pressing the edges with a spatula until golden-brown spots form, about 2 minutes per side.
Repeat with the remaining balls, wiping the tava with a dry cloth between parathas so loose flour does not scorch. Brush each finished paratha with a little more Anveshan Ghee while still hot.
tips: Press the crumbled paneer in a clean cloth for a minute before mixing; removing excess moisture stops the filling from tearing the dough while rolling.
If a paratha tears while rolling, dab the spot with dry atta and roll only over the intact areas — never re-ball a stuffed dough.
The filling can be made 8 hours ahead and refrigerated, but add the salt only just before stuffing or the onion will weep water.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve stacked in a cloth-lined basket with thick chilled curd, a wedge of lime pickle and sliced onions sprinkled with chaat masala.

variations.name: Punjabi Masala Paneer Paratha
variations.description: In Punjab the paneer paratha is an unapologetically rich affair: the filling gets punchy amchur and ajwain-scented dough, and the finished paratha is crowned with a melting pat of white butter. It is thicker, flakier and more indulgent than the everyday version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The nutty emmer wheat stands up to the robust Punjabi filling better than refined flour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Generous ghee-basting is what gives the Punjabi paratha its flaky, dhaba-style crust

steps: Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan on low heat and sizzle 0.5 tsp ajwain seeds for 30 seconds until fragrant, then pour this tempering into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta along with 0.5 tsp salt.
Knead the atta with roughly 0.75 cup water into a soft, supple dough that does not stick to your palm, then rub the surface with a few drops of ghee, cover and rest for 20 minutes.

Grate 300 g paneer on the large holes of a box grater and toss with 1 tsp amchur, 1 tsp anardana powder, 2 minced green chillies, 1 tsp grated ginger, 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi and 0.5 tsp salt until evenly speckled.

Shape the dough into 6 balls, cup each into a bowl shape and pack in a heaped 3 tbsp of the paneer mixture. Bring the edges together, twist off the excess dough at the top and flatten gently between your palms.
Roll each stuffed ball into a thick 6-inch round — Punjabi parathas are rolled deliberately thicker than usual so the filling stays juicy inside.

Roast on a medium-hot tava for about 90 seconds until the underside is freckled brown, flip, drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee around the edges and cook another 2 minutes, pressing so every part touches the hot iron and turns crisp.
Slide each hot paratha onto a plate and immediately top with 1 tsp white butter so it melts into the crust before serving.
tips: Grating rather than crumbling the paneer is the Punjabi trick — the fine shreds compact well and never burst through the dough.
Anardana powder gives a tang amchur cannot match; if using only amchur, increase it to 1.5 tsp.
Rest the rolled parathas no more than 5 minutes before roasting or the amchur will draw moisture and make the surface tacky.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a tall glass of salted lassi and a bowl of homemade white makhan; in true Amritsari style, add a side of spicy mango pickle.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Masala Paneer Paratha
variations.description: This take borrows the soul of Maharashtrian home cooking — smoky, sweet-spiced goda masala and a scatter of roasted peanut crush in the filling. The result is a darker, earthier paratha with a gentle warmth rather than sharp heat, finished in cold-pressed groundnut oil.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli's slight sweetness echoes the coconut-jaggery notes hidden in goda masala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the everyday fat of Maharashtrian kitchens and doubles the peanut aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A final ghee gloss softens the crust and rounds off the smoky goda masala

steps: Mix 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, then work in about 0.75 cup water to form a smooth, soft dough. Rest it covered for 15 minutes.
Dry-toast 1 tsp sesame seeds in a small pan on low heat until they pop and turn pale gold, about 1 minute, and tip them onto a plate to cool.
Coarsely crush 3 tbsp roasted peanuts in a mortar; you want gritty crumbs, not powder, so the filling keeps a crunch.

Crumble 250 g paneer and fold in 2 tsp goda masala, the toasted sesame, the peanut crush, 2 finely chopped green chillies, 2 tbsp chopped coriander and 0.5 tsp salt until the mixture smells warmly spiced.
Portion the dough into 6 balls, stuff each with about 3 tbsp of the filling, seal the seam by pinching and twisting, and roll into gentle 7-inch rounds on a floured board.
Cook on a medium tava, brushing each side with 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, until deep brown blisters appear, about 2 minutes per side; the goda masala should smell toasty, not scorched.
Brush the hot parathas with a thin film of Anveshan Ghee just before they leave the tava for a glossy, aromatic finish.
tips: Goda masala burns faster than garam masala because of its coconut content — keep the tava at medium, never high.
If you cannot find goda masala, kala masala works, but add an extra pinch of sesame to mimic the nutty depth.
A teaspoon of the peanut-sesame mix saved aside makes a lovely garnish over the accompanying curd.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a Maharashtrian-style thecha of pounded green chillies and garlic on the side, plus a katori of sweetened dahi to cool the palate.

variations.name: Bengali Masala Paneer Paratha
variations.description: Bengal swaps ghee-first cooking for the sharp, wasabi-like heat of pungent mustard oil, and the filling takes on kalonji and green chilli in place of heavy masalas. The pared-back spicing lets the paneer taste of itself, with the mustard oil delivering the signature bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Stone-ground emmer gives these parathas the rustic chew Bengalis prize in a triangular porota

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed kachi ghani mustard oil brings the nose-tingling pungency that defines this regional take

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a small pan on medium heat until it just begins to smoke, then switch off and let it cool for 2 minutes — this mellows its raw edge while keeping the aroma.
Pour the cooled oil over 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, rub it through, then knead with about 0.75 cup water into a soft dough. Rest under a damp cloth for 15 minutes.

Warm 1 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in the same pan, crackle 0.5 tsp kalonji seeds for 20 seconds, add 1 tsp grated ginger and 3 slit-and-chopped green chillies, and fry for 30 seconds until the ginger loses its rawness.

Take the pan off the heat and fold in 250 g crumbled paneer, 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.25 tsp sugar, 0.5 tsp salt and 2 tbsp chopped coriander; the residual warmth binds the filling lightly.
Divide the dough into 6 balls, stuff each with 3 tbsp of the cooled filling, seal well and roll into 7-inch rounds, flouring the pin rather than the paratha to keep the surface dry.
Fry each paratha on a medium tava with 1 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil per side until crisp, dappled and deep golden, about 2 minutes a side; the kitchen should fill with the sharp mustard perfume.
tips: Always smoke and cool the mustard oil for the dough; skipping this leaves an aggressive raw bitterness in the crust.
The pinch of sugar is not for sweetness — it balances the mustard pungency the way Bengali cooks season most savoury dishes.
Leftover filling makes an excellent stuffing for a quick paneer-kalonji toastie the next morning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Bengali way with begun bhaja (crisp fried aubergine slices), a smear of kasundi mustard and thin-sliced cucumber.

variations.name: Kerala Masala Paneer Paratha
variations.description: A Malabar-inspired crossover where the paneer filling is folded with fresh grated coconut, curry leaves and black pepper, and the paratha is roasted in cold-pressed coconut oil. It eats softer and subtly sweeter than northern versions, with a tropical fragrance in every bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The soft emmer dough laminates beautifully with coconut oil for a Malabar-style layered edge

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed coconut oil perfumes the crust with the unmistakable warmth of a Kerala kitchen

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and about 0.75 cup water until soft and elastic, then rest the dough for 15 minutes under a damp cloth.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds until they finish crackling, then add 12 torn curry leaves, 2 chopped green chillies and 4 finely sliced shallots and saute 2 minutes until the shallots turn translucent.
Stir in 0.5 cup fresh grated coconut and 0.25 tsp turmeric and toast on low heat for 2 minutes until the coconut smells nutty but has not browned.
Remove from heat, cool 5 minutes, then mix in 250 g crumbled paneer, 1 tsp coarsely ground black pepper and 0.5 tsp salt; the filling should be moist but hold together when pressed.
Shape the dough into 6 balls, fill each with 3 tbsp of the coconut-paneer mixture, seal the openings tightly and roll out into 7-inch discs with light, even strokes.

Roast on a medium tava with 1 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil per side, flipping once the underside shows golden freckles, about 2 minutes per side, until both faces are crisp at the edges yet soft in the middle.
tips: Use only fresh or frozen grated coconut; desiccated coconut turns the filling dry and sawdusty.
Cool the coconut mixture fully before adding paneer, or the residual steam will make the filling wet and hard to seal.
Freshly cracked pepper, not pre-ground, carries this dish — grind it just before mixing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a small bowl of coconut chutney and sweet mango pickle, or alongside a fried egg for a hearty Malabar-style breakfast plate.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Beetroot Paratha
variations.description: A fiery take on the beetroot paratha where green chillies, black pepper and red chilli powder work in three registers — fresh heat, warm bite and lingering burn. The beet's natural sweetness keeps the fire pleasurable rather than punishing. Roasted crisp in ghee, it is the paratha to wake up a sleepy palate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Wholegrain emmer's gentle sweetness tempers the triple-chilli filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee's richness rounds the heat — the traditional antidote built into the bread itself

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with about 3/4 cup water into a supple dough; cover and rest for 20 minutes.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium in a kadhai and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then fry 1 inch grated ginger and 3 finely chopped green chillies for 1 minute until sharp-smelling.
Add 2 grated, tightly squeezed beetroots with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1/4 tsp turmeric and sauté 6 minutes until the mixture dries out.
Grind 1 tsp black pepper coarsely and stir it in with 3 tbsp chopped coriander during the last minute, then spread the filling to cool completely.
Divide the dough into 8 balls; stuff each with 2 tbsp of the chilli-beet filling, pleat closed and press flat between floured palms.
Roll each into a 6-7 inch round with light pressure so no chilli fleck punctures the dough.
Cook on a hot tava on medium-high about 1 minute per side until browned in spots, then crisp both sides with the remaining Anveshan Ghee for another 30 seconds each.
tips: Deseed one or two of the green chillies if serving children — the pepper and chilli powder still carry plenty of heat.
Coarse-cracked pepper added at the end keeps its punch; pre-ground pepper cooked long goes flat.
A spoon of curd worked into leftover filling makes a quick spicy beet raita for the same meal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a big bowl of plain chilled curd and cucumber slices — the deliberate blandness beside the bread is what makes the heat addictive.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Beetroot Paratha
variations.description: Guntur red chillies — sun-dried, seeds and all — are pounded into a coarse karam that laces this beet filling with Andhra's famous slow-building fire. Curry leaves and a whisper of tamarind pulp round it out like a good vepudu. Groundnut oil on the tava is the Andhra home-kitchen finish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its rustic chew stands firm under the assertive Guntur karam

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed peanut oil, the workhorse fat of Andhra kitchens, deepens the roasted chilli flavour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A final gloss of ghee is how Andhra homes soften a ferociously spicy dish

steps: Make a soft dough from 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and roughly 3/4 cup water; knead well and rest 20 minutes.
Dry-roast 4 Guntur chillies on low heat for 2 minutes until brittle, then pound them with 4 garlic cloves and 1/2 tsp salt into a coarse, rust-red karam paste.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then crackle the leaves of 1 curry sprig for 15 seconds.
Add 2 grated and squeezed beetroots with 1/4 tsp turmeric and cook 5 minutes until dry, then work in the pounded karam and 2 tsp tamarind pulp and fry 2 minutes more. Cool the filling fully.
Divide the dough into 8 balls and stuff each with 2 tbsp of the karam-beet mixture, sealing the pleats with a firm pinch.
Roll into 6-inch rounds and roast on a hot tava about 1 minute per side until dark spots bloom, brushing with the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil.
Off the tava, brush each paratha with a little of the 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and top with the second sprig's curry leaves fried crisp in the last of the oil.
tips: Guntur chillies deliver heat that builds over seconds — start with 3 pods if you are unfamiliar with them and add the fourth next time.
Pound the karam in a mortar rather than a mixer; the uneven texture is what makes each bite different.
Tamarind pulp should be thick like honey — watery pulp will loosen the filling and tear the paratha.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a katori of chilled sadda perugu (plain curd) and a slice of raw onion; Andhra tables would add a spoon of avakaya on the side for the brave.

variations.name: Assamese Spicy Beetroot Paratha
variations.description: A tiny amount of bhut jolokia — the ghost pepper of Assam — is all this paratha needs; it perfumes the beet filling with a fruity, smoky heat unlike any other chilli. Mustard oil and a scatter of black sesame keep it firmly in the Brahmaputra valley. The heat is real, so the recipe respects it with careful quantities.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Dense wholegrain crumb that buffers the ghost pepper's intensity

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Kachi ghani mustard oil is the backbone fat of Assamese cooking and loves chilli heat

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt and about 3/4 cup water into a soft dough, working in 1 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil at the end; rest 20 minutes covered.
Wearing gloves, mince 1/2 pod bhut jolokia as finely as possible and set aside — do not touch your face while handling it.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai to a light smoke, cool briefly, then fry 1 small sliced onion and 1 inch julienned ginger on medium for 3 minutes until soft.

Add 2 grated, squeezed beetroots, the minced bhut jolokia, 1/2 tsp salt and 1/2 tsp turmeric; cook 6 minutes until dry, then fold in 2 tsp black sesame seeds and 3 tbsp chopped coriander and cool fully.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, cup and fill each with 2 tbsp of the ghost-pepper beet mixture, then pleat, seal and flatten.
Roll gently into 6-inch rounds and cook on a medium-hot tava about 75 seconds per side until blistered brown.
Finish with the remaining Anveshan Mustard Oil brushed over both faces and a final 20-second roast so the crust gleams.
tips: Half a bhut jolokia serves four sensible adults; add the second half only if your table regularly eats Naga-style food.
Gloves are not optional — the pepper's oils cling to skin for hours and a stray eye-rub is a bad evening.
Toast the black sesame separately for 1 minute if you want a stronger nutty note against the heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Assamese way with a cooling bowl of plain doi or a khar-style mild dal on the side, and slices of cucumber to reset the palate between bites.

variations.name: Karnataka Spicy Beetroot Paratha
variations.description: Modelled on Karnataka's beetroot palya and the tang of gojju, this filling balances byadgi-style chilli heat with a thick tamarind reduction and a spoon of jaggery — the classic bisi-bele flavour triangle. Fresh curry leaves and coconut ground the spice in the Deccan. It is hot, sour and just faintly sweet, all at once.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Sturdy emmer dough holds the moist tamarind-laced filling without tearing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Karnataka's festive breads are ghee-roasted; it mellows the gojju-style tang

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Balances tamarind sourness exactly as in a traditional gojju

steps: Prepare the dough with 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 3/4 cup water; knead until smooth and rest 20 minutes.
Melt 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium heat; pop 1 tsp mustard seeds, then fry 2 tsp chana dal until golden, about 90 seconds, and crackle in 1 sprig of curry leaves.
Add 2 grated and squeezed beetroots with 1/2 tsp salt and 1.5 tsp byadgi chilli powder and sauté 5 minutes until nearly dry.
Pour in 1 tbsp thick tamarind pulp and 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, then cook 2-3 minutes until the mixture turns glossy and thick like a gojju. Stir in 3 tbsp grated coconut and cool completely.
Shape 8 balls from the dough, fill each with 2 tbsp of the tangy filling, seal well and flatten with care.
Roll into 6-inch rounds, patching any thin spots with dry atta, and roast on a hot tava about 1 minute per side until spotted.
Crisp both sides with the remaining Anveshan Ghee for 30 seconds each until the edges crackle.
tips: Byadgi chilli gives colour and fragrance with moderate heat; if using ordinary chilli powder, cut the quantity to 1 tsp.
Cook the tamarind-jaggery stage until a spoon dragged through the filling leaves a clean trail — wetter than that and rolling gets messy.
The chana dal must be fully golden before the beet goes in, or it stays hard inside the paratha.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a dollop of fresh curd and Mysore-style coconut chutney; a side of sliced banana is a very Karnataka way to cool the spice.

variations.name: Kumaoni Spicy Beetroot Paratha
variations.description: Jakhya — the wild mustard of the Uttarakhand hills — crackles louder and nuttier than any cultivated seed, and it is the soul of this pahadi paratha. The beet is cooked jhol-free and dry, spiked with hill-style red chilli and finished with crushed coriander stems. Simple mountain food with an unmistakable crunch in every bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Closest match to the hardy hill wheats stone-ground in Kumaon's gharat watermills

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Pahadi kitchens finish breads with ghee from hill cattle; bilona ghee recreates that richness

steps: Knead a soft dough from 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 3/4 cup water, then let it rest 20 minutes under a damp cloth.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai on medium-high and tip in 1.5 tsp jakhya seeds — they should crackle loudly within 15 seconds; immediately add 3 crushed garlic cloves and 2 chopped green chillies.
Lower to medium, add 2 grated and squeezed beetroots with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tsp pahadi chilli powder and 1/4 tsp turmeric, and cook 6 minutes until dry and fragrant.
Fold in 4 tbsp finely chopped coriander stems and leaves off the heat — the stems carry the flavour in hill cooking — and cool the filling completely.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, pack 2 tbsp of the jakhya-beet filling into each, pleat shut and press flat.
Roll into 6-inch rounds and roast on a hot tava for about 1 minute per side until well-browned spots appear.
Glaze with the remaining Anveshan Ghee and give each side a last 30 seconds so the crust turns crisp while the jakhya inside stays crunchy.
tips: Jakhya must hit properly hot ghee to crackle; lukewarm fat leaves it bitter and sandy.
No jakhya outside the hills? Use kalonji for looks but know the true nutty pop is jakhya's alone — it is worth mail-ordering.
Do not chop the coriander stems too early; they blacken and lose their pine-fresh hill aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Eat pahadi-style with bhang ki chutney or plain dahi and a raw radish, ideally with the paratha torn by hand while still steaming.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Mixed Veg Paratha
variations.description: For those who like their breakfast with a kick, this paratha loads the vegetable filling with fresh green chillies, cracked black pepper and a double dose of red chilli powder. The heat is layered rather than one-note, brightened with ginger and finished in cooling bilona ghee. Khapli atta's natural sweetness keeps the fire pleasurable instead of punishing.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The gentle malty sweetness of emmer flour is the built-in coolant for this chilli-heavy filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee's fat carries capsaicin evenly so the heat blooms slowly instead of burning

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and about 0.75 cups water for 5 minutes until soft and stretchy; rest under a damp cloth for 20 minutes.
Boil 2 potatoes, 1 diced carrot and 0.5 cups peas for 10-12 minutes until a fork meets no resistance; drain fully and mash while warm.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds until they darken and smell nutty.

Add 4 finely chopped green chillies and 1 inch grated ginger, fry 1 minute, then stir in 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp black pepper, 0.5 tsp turmeric and immediately add the mash so the powders do not scorch.
Season with 1 tsp salt and cook the filling 3-4 minutes until dry, then fold in 3 tbsp chopped coriander. Cool completely and divide into 6 balls of about 3 tbsp each.
Stuff 6 dough balls, seal and roll into 7-inch rounds. Roast on a medium-hot tava roughly 2 minutes per side, painting with the remaining Anveshan Ghee until crisp golden spots cover both faces.
tips: Chop the green chillies fine and fry them well; large raw pieces create harsh hot spots in the filling.
Black pepper added along with red chilli builds a slower, deeper heat than chilli alone.
Serve within 10 minutes of roasting — the pepper aroma is at its peak while the crust is still crackly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Cool the fire the classic way: a big bowl of plain chilled curd, a drizzle of honey over it if you like, and lemon-pickled onions on the side.

variations.name: Assamese Spicy Mixed Veg Paratha
variations.description: Bhut jolokia, Assam's legendary ghost pepper, headlines this paratha for serious chilli devotees. A tiny, carefully measured amount of the smoky pepper is worked into a mustard-oil-fried filling of potato and beans with the clean simplicity typical of Assamese home food. The result is fierce, fruity heat with the unmistakable smokiness only bhut jolokia carries.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: A softly sweet emmer dough is essential armour around the ghost pepper's intensity

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Assamese kitchens fry nearly everything in pungent mustard oil, which stands up to bhut jolokia

steps: Prepare the dough by kneading 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil, 0.5 tsp salt and about 0.75 cups water for 5 minutes; it should be soft but not tacky. Rest 20 minutes.
Wearing gloves, deseed and mince 0.5 of a bhut jolokia as finely as possible; wash the knife and board immediately afterwards.
Boil 3 potatoes and 0.75 cups chopped beans for 10-12 minutes until fully soft, then drain and mash them together.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it releases a thin smoke, let it settle for 30 seconds, then fry 1 chopped onion with 1 inch grated ginger over medium heat for 3-4 minutes until translucent and golden-edged.

Add the minced bhut jolokia, fry 20 seconds, then fold in the mash with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt. Cook 3 minutes until dry, brighten with 1 tbsp lemon juice and 4 tbsp coriander, and cool completely before portioning into 6 balls.
Stuff, seal and roll 6 parathas to about 7 inches, then roast each on a medium tava for 2 minutes per side, dabbing the surface with the leftover mustard oil until charred-gold blisters form.
tips: Half a bhut jolokia already feeds four heat-lovers; taste a rice-grain-sized bit of filling before adding more.
Always mince the pepper in gloves and avoid touching your face; ghost pepper oils cling for hours.
Lemon juice and fresh coriander are your safety rails — they lift the fruity side of the chilli above the burn.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve Assamese-style with a plate of raw sliced cucumber and a small bowl of sweet curd, or a spoon of mashed roasted tomato (bilahi pitika) to trade fire for tang.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Mixed Veg Paratha
variations.description: Sun-dried Guntur chillies pounded with garlic form the karam-style base of this scorching Andhra rendition. The vegetables are seared in wood-pressed groundnut oil with curry leaves until every cube is coated in brick-red spice. It is the paratha equivalent of an Andhra podi lunch — direct, fiery and completely addictive.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Nutty khapli flour absorbs the fierce Guntur karam and gives each bite a mellow landing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Andhra spice pastes are traditionally seared in groundnut oil, whose high smoke point keeps them from bittering

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, 0.5 tsp salt and around 0.75 cups water into a smooth, yielding dough; rest it 20 minutes while the karam comes together.
Toast 5 Guntur chillies and 2 tsp coriander seeds in a dry pan over low heat for 2 minutes until crackly and fragrant. Cool, then grind coarsely with 6 garlic cloves into a dry red pound.
Steam 2 potatoes, 1 cup small cauliflower florets and 0.5 cups peas for 12 minutes until soft; mash coarsely, leaving some texture.
In a kadhai, heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium-high, crisp 12 curry leaves for 15 seconds, then sear the chilli-garlic pound for about 1 minute until the garlic no longer smells raw.
Add the mashed vegetables with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt and fry 4-5 minutes, scraping the pan, until the mixture turns brick-toned and dry. Cool and shape into 6 portions.

Fill 6 dough balls, seal the seams and roll to 7-inch rounds. Cook each on a hot tava about 2 minutes a side until deeply blistered, wiping the surface with the remaining groundnut oil as it finishes.
tips: Grinding the karam coarse and dry — never into a wet paste — is what gives the filling its podi-like cling.
Steaming rather than boiling the cauliflower keeps the filling dry enough for thin rolling.
If the heat overshoots, a teaspoon of ghee stirred into the finished filling tames it without dulling flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Plate with a mound of cold curd rice or majjiga (thin spiced buttermilk) — the traditional Andhra pairing that resets your palate between fiery bites.

variations.name: Rajasthani Spicy Mixed Veg Paratha
variations.description: Modelled on the fierce lal maas school of Rajasthani spicing, this paratha uses whole dried Mathania-style red chillies soaked and ground with garlic and yoghurt-tang amchur. The filling glows brick red and delivers dry desert heat rather than sharp freshness. Ghee-laminated and crisped hard on the tava, it is bold food for bold appetites.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Robust khapli grain matches the assertive chilli paste the way bajra breads do in Rajasthan

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rajasthani heat is always mounted on ghee, which mellows the dried chillies into warmth

steps: Soak 6 dried red chillies in 0.25 cups hot water for 15 minutes, then grind with 8 garlic cloves and a spoon of the soaking water into a thick scarlet paste.
Meanwhile knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 0.5 tsp ajwain, 0.5 tsp salt and about 0.75 cups water into a supple dough; rest it 20 minutes.
Boil 3 potatoes for 12 minutes until tender, peel and mash them coarsely.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then brown 1 chopped onion for 4 minutes until golden.

Fry the chilli-garlic paste for 2-3 minutes until the ghee separates and the raw smell is gone, then work in the potato mash, 2 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp amchur and 1 tsp salt. Cook 3 minutes until dry, cool, and divide into 6 portions.
Stuff and seal 6 dough balls, roll to 7-inch rounds and roast on a medium tava around 2 minutes per side, ladling on the remaining ghee and pressing until the crust turns a crackly reddish-gold.
tips: Frying the chilli paste until ghee visibly separates is the Rajasthani marker that the heat has cooked from raw to round.
Deseed half the chillies before soaking for colour-forward, medium heat instead of full fire.
These parathas travel superbly; the dry garlic-chilli filling keeps them tasty at room temperature for a full day.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a Marwari traveller would eat it: with cool dahi, raw onion rings and a piece of gud (jaggery) at the end to close the heat.

variations.name: Telangana Spicy Mixed Veg Paratha
variations.description: Telangana's love of tamarind and fierce chilli meets in this tangy-hot paratha, its filling sharpened with thick chintapandu pulp and red chilli in sesame oil. Onion and potato mellow the sourness while curry leaves add the southern perfume. It recalls the pulusu-style balance of sour, spicy and earthy that defines Deccan plateau cooking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The wholegrain sweetness of khapli rounds off tamarind's sharp sourness beautifully

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Nuvvula noone — sesame oil — is the traditional Telangana fat, adding a toasty depth to the tangy filling

steps: Mix 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and 0.5 tsp salt, then knead in about 0.75 cups water for 5 minutes to a soft, elastic dough. Rest it, covered, for 20 minutes.
Boil 2 potatoes and 0.5 cups chopped beans for 10-12 minutes until soft; drain thoroughly and mash roughly.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadhai on medium and pop 1 tsp mustard seeds, about 30 seconds, before adding 10 curry leaves and 2 slit green chillies to sizzle for 15 seconds.
Brown 1 finely chopped onion in the tempering for 3-4 minutes, then add 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp turmeric followed immediately by the vegetable mash so the chilli toasts without burning.
Pour in 2 tbsp tamarind pulp and 1 tsp salt and fry the filling 4-5 minutes until it thickens, darkens and pulls away from the pan sides. Cool fully and divide into 6 balls.

Stuff 6 dough portions, pinch them closed and roll into 7-inch rounds. Roast each about 2 minutes per side on a medium-hot tava, glossing with the last of the sesame oil until the surface bubbles deep brown.
tips: Cook the tamarind into the filling until it stops smelling raw; undercooked pulp turns the paratha soggy and harsh.
Thick, seedless tamarind pulp works best; watery extract will loosen the filling beyond rolling.
A pinch of jaggery is welcome if your tamarind is very sour — Telangana cooks balance, they do not eliminate, the tang.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a spoon of fiery Telangana pachi pulusu or simple onion-tomato perugu pachadi (curd relish), and finish with buttermilk poured over crushed ice.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Paneer Paratha
variations.description: A fiery upgrade of the everyday paneer paratha, where green chillies, black pepper and red chilli powder layer three kinds of heat into a creamy paneer filling. The khapli wheat crust roasted in bilona ghee keeps the fire pleasurable rather than punishing.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat's mild sweetness tempers the triple-chilli filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee's richness coats the palate and carries the chilli heat evenly instead of letting it spike

steps: Combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, rubbing the fat in until sandy, then knead with about 0.75 cup water into a soft, pliable dough. Rest covered for 15 minutes.

Crumble 250 g paneer until fine and fluffy, then work in 3 minced green chillies, 1 tsp grated ginger, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.75 tsp black pepper, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp salt and 3 tbsp chopped coriander.
Divide dough and filling into 6 portions each. Flatten a dough ball into a small bowl, mound in 3 tbsp of the spicy filling, gather the edges to the centre and pinch shut so no filling peeks through.
Roll each stuffed ball on a lightly floured surface into a 7-inch round, using gentle outward strokes so the chilli-flecked filling spreads to the edges without bursting.

Roast on a medium-hot tava for about 1 minute until bubbles rise, then flip, brush with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee, and cook each side a further 2 minutes, pressing gently, until crisp brown patches cover the surface.
Rest the cooked parathas under a cloth for 2 minutes before serving; the brief steam softens the crust just enough to fold without cracking.
tips: Deseed one of the three green chillies if serving children — the pepper and chilli powder still carry plenty of warmth.
Mix the filling just before stuffing; chillies and salt sitting together draw out water and make sealing difficult.
A pinch of amchur added to the filling brightens the heat if your chillies taste flat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Cool the fire with a bowl of boondi raita and a glass of chaas; a spoon of sweet mixed-fruit chutney on the side makes a lovely contrast.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Paneer Paratha
variations.description: Andhra Pradesh brings its famed Guntur chillies to the party, blended into a fiery garlic-chilli paste that stains the paneer a bold brick red. Curry leaves and a hint of tang from tamarind-free amchur keep the heat aromatic rather than flat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The wholegrain nuttiness of khapli grounds the blazing Guntur chilli paste

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the traditional frying medium of Andhra kitchens and takes high heat without breaking

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and about 0.75 cup water into a smooth, soft dough; cover and set aside for 15 minutes.
Soak 4 dried Guntur chillies in 3 tbsp hot water for 10 minutes until leathery-soft, then drain, reserving the soaking water.

Toast 1 tsp coriander seeds in a dry pan on low heat for 1 minute until fragrant, then grind them with the soaked chillies, 6 garlic cloves and 1 tsp of the soaking water into a coarse, brick-red paste.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium, crackle 10 curry leaves for 15 seconds, add the chilli-garlic paste and fry 2 to 3 minutes, stirring, until the raw garlic smell disappears and oil beads at the edges.
Cool the paste for 5 minutes, then knead it into 250 g crumbled paneer with 0.5 tsp amchur, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt until the paneer is uniformly tinted red.

Stuff 6 dough balls with 3 tbsp filling each, seal firmly, roll into 7-inch rounds, and roast on a medium tava with 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil per side until deeply blistered, about 2 minutes a side.
tips: Guntur chillies vary wildly in heat — taste a tiny piece after soaking and drop to 3 chillies if it makes your eyes water.
Frying the paste until oil separates is essential; undercooked garlic-chilli paste turns the filling harsh and raw-tasting.
The chilli paste keeps a week refrigerated and doubles as a base for Andhra-style stir-fried vegetables.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a generous ladle of chilled curd rice on the side or a katori of thick perugu (Andhra curd) — the classic coolant for Guntur heat.

variations.name: Rajasthani Spicy Paneer Paratha
variations.description: Desert cooking loves dried red chillies, whole coriander and a math of pantry spices over fresh produce, and this paratha follows suit. A Mathania-style dried chilli crush, kasuri methi and ajwain give it a rustic, sun-baked heat, all roasted in plenty of ghee.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Hardy emmer wheat mirrors the rustic millet-and-wheat rotis of Rajasthani thalis

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: In water-scarce Rajasthan, ghee is the cooking medium of honour — be generous while roasting

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, 0.5 tsp ajwain seeds bloomed for 20 seconds in 1 tbsp hot Anveshan Ghee, and about 0.75 cup water into a soft dough; rest it for 15 minutes.
Dry-roast 4 dried red chillies, 2 tsp coriander seeds and 1 tsp fennel seeds in a heavy pan on low heat for 2 to 3 minutes, tossing constantly, until the chillies darken slightly and smell smoky.
Cool the roasted spices, then pound them in a mortar into a coarse, flaky crush — Rajasthani cooks keep it gritty, never a fine powder.
Crumble 250 g paneer and mix in the spice crush, 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi, 1 tsp amchur, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt until every crumb is dusted red-gold.
Stuff 6 rested dough balls with 3 tbsp filling apiece, seal by pleating and pinching the edges, and roll each into a 7-inch round with steady, light pressure.
Roast on a medium tava, spooning 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee over each side, until crusty and mottled deep brown, about 2 minutes per side; press the edges with a spatula so they crisp too.
tips: The coarse pounded spice crush is the identity of this paratha — a mixer-ground fine powder will taste dull in comparison.
These keep well for travel, as desert food should: wrap in foil and they stay good for 8 to 10 hours without refrigeration.
If Mathania chillies are available, use them — their fruity, moderate heat is the authentic choice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Do it thali-style: serve with garlicky lehsun chutney, a wedge of raw onion and a bowl of chhaas spiked with roasted cumin.

variations.name: Tamil Spicy Paneer Paratha
variations.description: Heat here comes the Tamil way — a milagai-and-pepper masala tempered with curry leaves, mustard seeds and urad dal in wood-pressed sesame oil. The filling has the toasty depth of a Chettinad-style spice base, and the crust picks up gingelly oil's caramel aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The dense emmer crumb soaks up gingelly oil like a good Tamil parotta layer

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil is Tamil Nadu's soul fat; its caramel note defines this variation

steps: Make the dough by kneading 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and roughly 0.75 cup water until soft and stretchy; rest it 15 minutes under a damp cloth.
Dry-roast 1 tsp black peppercorns and 3 dried red chillies on low heat for 2 minutes until the chillies crisp, then cool and grind to a coarse powder.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadai on medium; pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, add 1 tsp urad dal and fry until the dal turns biscuit-gold, about 45 seconds, then toss in 15 curry leaves and 5 sliced shallots.
Saute the shallots 2 to 3 minutes until soft and lightly browned, stir in the pepper-chilli powder and 0.25 tsp turmeric, fry 30 seconds, and take off the heat.
Once the tempering is warm rather than hot, fold in 250 g crumbled paneer and 0.5 tsp salt, mashing lightly so the toasted spices streak through the cheese.
Stuff 6 dough balls with 3 tbsp filling each, roll into 7-inch rounds, and roast on a medium tava with 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil per side until crisp and burnished, about 2 minutes per side.
tips: Fry the urad dal only to biscuit-gold; a shade darker and it turns bitter through the whole filling.
Coarse-cracked pepper gives bright top-note heat, so do not grind it to dust.
For a Chettinad accent, add 0.5 tsp fennel seeds to the dry roast.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve rolled around a spoon of coconut chutney like a kathi roll, or with sambar for dunking and a tumbler of filter coffee to finish.

variations.name: Assamese Spicy Paneer Paratha
variations.description: The Northeast's legendary bhut jolokia lends this paratha a slow-building, fruity inferno, softened by fresh coriander, ginger and a squeeze of lemon in the filling. True to Assamese restraint, there is almost no powdered masala — just chilli, herb and pungent mustard oil.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli's gentle sweetness is welcome relief against the ghost pepper's slow burn

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Kachi ghani mustard oil is the default fat of Assamese kitchens and doubles the pungent kick

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it lightly smokes, cool it 2 minutes, then knead it into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt and about 0.75 cup water; rest the soft dough for 15 minutes.
Wearing gloves, mince 0.5 bhut jolokia as finely as possible — start with a quarter if you are new to ghost peppers, since the heat blooms over minutes rather than instantly.

Warm 1 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a small pan on medium, soften 3 sliced spring onion whites with 2 tsp grated ginger for about 2 minutes, then stir in the minced bhut jolokia and switch off after 20 seconds.

Cool the tempering, then combine with 250 g crumbled paneer, the spring onion greens, 4 tbsp chopped coriander, 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder, 2 tsp lemon juice and 0.5 tsp salt, mixing until evenly herb-flecked.
Divide the dough into 6 balls, encase 3 tbsp of filling in each, seal carefully and roll into 7-inch rounds, dusting sparingly with dry atta.
Roast each paratha on a medium tava with 1 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil per side until crisp and freckled brown, about 2 minutes a side, letting the mustard oil's aroma sharpen as it cooks.
tips: Wash hands, knife and board immediately after handling bhut jolokia, and never touch your face mid-prep.
The lemon juice is a heat regulator — its acidity clips the ghost pepper's peak and keeps flavours bright.
Substitute 3 green chillies plus a pinch of chilli flakes if bhut jolokia is unavailable, though the fruity aroma will differ.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve Assamese-style with a cooling cucumber-curd salad and a wedge of lemon; a side of mashed potato aloo pitika makes it a full meal.

variations.name: Classic Stuffed Dal Paratha
variations.description: The everyday North Indian dal paratha: spiced, mashed toor dal tucked inside a whole-grain khapli shell and roasted until flaky. Roasted cumin, ginger and coriander keep the filling homely and deeply savoury.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Slow-milled emmer gives the shell a rustic, wheaty depth refined atta cannot

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee turns the surface lacquered and crisp in seconds

steps: Bring 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta together with 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 0.75 cup water; knead 5 minutes to a soft, springy dough and rest it, covered, for 15 minutes.
Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium and sauté 1 tsp grated ginger for 30 seconds until it stops smelling raw.

Add 1 cup thick cooked toor dal along with 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt; mash and cook until dry and dough-like, 5-6 minutes.
Cool the filling fully, fold in 2 tbsp chopped coriander leaves, and divide it into 8 equal portions of roughly 2 tbsp each.
Flatten each of 8 dough balls into a small bowl shape, enclose one portion of filling, twist off the excess dough at the top and roll out gently to a 6-7 inch circle.

Roast on a hot tava over medium-high heat, about 1 minute per side until brown-spotted, then crisp both faces with the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, pressing the edges with a spatula until they flake.
tips: Match dough and filling softness: a stiff dough over a soft filling always tears, so knead the dough slightly softer than chapati dough.
Cook the paratha plain first and add ghee only on the second flip; this sets the surface so the ghee crisps instead of soaking in.
Stack finished parathas in a cloth-lined box, not on an open plate, to keep them supple for tiffin.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best with a bowl of whisked salted curd, mango pickle and sliced onions sprinkled with chaat masala.

variations.name: Punjabi Stuffed Dal Paratha
variations.description: A dhaba-style paratha built on nutty chana dal, kasuri methi and a knob of white butter melting on top. It is rolled thicker than usual and double-roasted so the crust shatters while the filling stays plush, pure Amritsar energy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Hearty emmer matches the dhaba habit of thick, satisfying parathas

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Punjabi tava work demands a ghee that stays fragrant at high heat

steps: Knead a soft dough from 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and roughly 0.75 cup water; let it relax for 20 minutes so it can hold a generous filling.
Melt 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium heat and soften 1 finely chopped onion with 2 minced green chillies until translucent and lightly golden, 3-4 minutes.
Add 1 cup thick cooked chana dal, 0.5 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp anardana powder and 0.5 tsp salt; mash coarsely and fry until the mixture balls up on the spoon, about 5 minutes.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi between your palms into the warm filling, mix well and cool it to room temperature before portioning into 8 mounds.
Stuff each of 8 dough balls with a mound of filling, seal, and roll to a deliberately thick 5-6 inch round so the paratha bakes up pillowy.

Roast on a medium tava for 90 seconds per side, then raise the heat, spoon over the remaining 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and fry each face again until the crust is crackly and mahogany-spotted, about 45 seconds more per side.
tips: Anardana is the dhaba secret; if unavailable, use 1 tsp amchur, but do not skip the sour note that cuts the rich dal.
Cook chana dal until a grain mashes between two fingers yet is not mushy; al dente dal punctures the dough while rolling.
The second high-heat roast is what creates the signature shattering crust, so do not rush it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Top with the 2 tbsp white butter while blistering hot and serve alongside a tall glass of salted lassi and tangy onion-chilli laccha.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Stuffed Dal Paratha
variations.description: Modelled on puran-poli technique but savoury, this paratha carries a tur dal filling seasoned with goda masala, that smoky-sweet Maharashtrian blend of dagad phool and coconut. Sesame seeds on the crust add a Puneri finishing touch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli wheat is a Maharashtra heritage grain, making this pairing historically apt

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Goda masala blooms fully only in a good, grainy ghee

steps: Prepare the dough with 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and around 0.75 cup water; knead until silky and rest 15 minutes.
Toast 2 tbsp grated dry coconut in a dry pan on low heat until it turns biscuit-brown and nutty, about 2 minutes, and set aside.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium, add 2 tsp goda masala, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 0.25 tsp turmeric, and stir for just 20 seconds until the spices darken a shade and release their smoky scent.
Immediately add 1 cup thick cooked tur dal, the toasted coconut and 0.5 tsp salt; mash and cook until the filling pulls away from the pan, 4-5 minutes, then cool completely.
Stuff 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp filling each, seal, then press the sealed side into 1 tbsp sesame seeds before rolling gently to 6 inches so the seeds stud the crust.
Roast seed-side down first on a medium tava for about 1 minute, flip, and finish both sides with the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until golden with charred sesame flecks, 2-3 minutes total.
tips: Goda masala scorches fast; 20 seconds in ghee is enough, and burnt goda turns the whole filling bitter.
If your goda masala is homemade and coconut-heavy, cut the added kopra to 1 tbsp to keep the filling from crumbling.
Rolling with seeds on the underside keeps them anchored; rolling seeds on top scatters them across the board.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a dollop of homemade curd and the classic Maharashtrian pairing of thecha, the fiery green-chilli garlic crush, on the side.

variations.name: Gujarati Stuffed Dal Paratha
variations.description: In true Gujarati fashion this paratha balances heat with sweetness: the moong dal filling is rounded off with jaggery powder and a whisper of cinnamon, echoing the flavours of vedhmi. Every bite lands sweet, spiced and gently tangy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer's natural sweetness harmonises with the jaggery-kissed filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Gujarati farsan cooks swear by ghee for its caramel-friendly roasting

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Chemical-free jaggery melts evenly into the dal without gritty lumps

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and close to 0.75 cup water into a soft dough; rest 15 minutes while you cook the filling.
Sauté 1 tsp grated ginger and 2 finely chopped green chillies in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat for about 45 seconds until aromatic.
Add 1 cup thick cooked moong dal with 0.5 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp amchur; mash smooth and cook until the moisture cooks off, about 4 minutes on medium.
Lower the flame, stir in 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.25 tsp cinnamon, and keep stirring 2 minutes as the jaggery melts and the filling turns glossy; cool it fully so it firms up.
Enclose 2 tbsp of the sweet-spiced filling in each of 8 dough balls, seal the pleats and roll delicately to 6-inch rounds, since jaggery fillings leak faster than savoury ones.
Cook on a medium (not high) tava about 75 seconds per side, then gild both faces with the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until amber-spotted; the sugar browns quickly, so keep the parathas moving.
tips: Always cool a jaggery filling before stuffing; while warm it is molten and will tear through the dough on the pin.
Keep the tava at medium throughout; high heat blackens the jaggery spots before the wheat cooks through.
A pinch more amchur rescues the balance if your jaggery batch runs extra sweet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve Gujarati thali-style with a bowl of kadhi and crunchy chhundo pickle; the sweet-sour trio is the whole point.

variations.name: Odia Stuffed Dal Paratha
variations.description: Odisha's beloved panch phoron, the five-seed blend of cumin, mustard, fennel, fenugreek and nigella, is bloomed in mustard oil to season this masoor dal filling. It has the clean, temple-kitchen simplicity of Odia cooking with a big aromatic payoff.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The unrefined grain suits Odisha's tradition of wholesome, minimally processed food

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Panch phoron demands mustard oil; wood-pressed keeps its wild pungency intact

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Odia homes finish flatbreads with ghee even when the tadka is mustard oil

steps: Make a supple dough from 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 tsp salt and about 0.75 cup water with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee rubbed in; rest 15 minutes under a damp cloth.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it shimmers and just smokes, then take it off the heat for 20 seconds to mellow before returning to a medium flame.
Crackle 1.5 tsp panch phoron with 2 torn dried red chillies in the hot oil for about 30 seconds until the fenugreek seeds turn reddish and the fennel smells sweet.
Add 1 tsp grated ginger, stir 20 seconds, then add 1 cup thick cooked masoor dal, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt; mash and fry until dry enough to shape, 5 minutes, and cool completely.
Fill each of 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp of the panch phoron dal, seal tightly and roll out to even 6-inch rounds on a floured board.
Roast on a medium-hot tava, roughly 1 minute per side until blistered, and finish both sides with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee for a glossy, fragrant crust.
tips: Fenugreek seeds in panch phoron turn bitter past reddish-brown, so pull the tempering the moment they colour.
Buy or blend panch phoron with equal parts of all five seeds except fenugreek, which should be halved for a filling this concentrated.
This filling doubles as a topping for dahi-baigana or plain rice if you have extra.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with Odia-style dahi baigana (yoghurt-dressed aubergine) or simply thick curd whisked with a pinch of roasted cumin.

variations.name: Classic Stuffed Methi Paratha
variations.description: Unlike kneaded-in versions, this paratha hides a proper filling: methi leaves sautéed in ghee with paneer, ginger and roasted spices, sealed inside soft khapli dough. Rolling it thin without bursting the parcel is the craft, and the reward is a molten, herby centre inside a ghee-crisped shell. This is the celebratory weekend format of the methi paratha family.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Extensible enough to stretch around a generous filling without tearing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Sautéing the methi filling in ghee removes rawness and binds it with rich aroma

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about ¾ cup water into a soft, smooth dough; cover and rest 20 minutes while you make the filling.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over medium flame, sizzle the minced ginger and green chillies for 30 seconds, then add 2½ cups chopped methi and cook 3 to 4 minutes, stirring, until the leaves are fully wilted and their moisture has evaporated.

Stir in 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp coriander powder, ½ tsp red chilli powder, ½ tsp turmeric and ½ tsp salt, cook 1 more minute, then remove from heat, cool completely and fold in ¾ cup crumbled paneer.

Divide the dough into 8 balls and the filling into 8 portions of about 2 tbsp each; flatten a ball into a 4-inch cup, seat one portion of filling in the centre, gather the edges over it and pinch shut.
Rest the stuffed balls seam-down for 5 minutes, then roll each gently to a 6-inch round with light, even strokes, dusting with flour and never pressing the centre hard.

Cook on a medium-hot tava about 2 minutes until blistered underneath, flip, apply ½ tsp Anveshan Ghee, and press the edges until both faces are golden with dark freckles, roughly 2 minutes more per paratha.
tips: The filling must be bone-dry and completely cool before stuffing; warm or wet filling steams inside and blows the paratha open on the tava.
Resting the stuffed balls before rolling lets the dough relax around the filling, halving the blowout rate.
If a paratha does tear while rolling, dab the breach with dry flour rather than water and roll on; flour seals, water glues the pin.
variations.servingSuggestion: Slice into quarters and serve with chilled boondi raita and lime pickle; these also pack brilliantly for lunch since the sealed filling keeps them moist.

variations.name: Odia Stuffed Methi Paratha
variations.description: Odisha's beloved panch phoron, the five-spice blend of fenugreek, nigella, cumin, fennel and mustard seeds, is bloomed in mustard oil and folded through a potato-methi filling in this eastern take. The fennel's sweetness against fenugreek's bitterness is textbook Odia balance. The paratha itself is toasted in mustard oil for a rustic, temple-town character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its earthy flavour sits naturally beside panch phoron's whole-spice rusticity

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Odia home cooking runs on pungent mustard oil; here it blooms the five-spice blend

steps: Make the dough first: knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and about ¾ cup water until soft and stretchy, then rest it covered for 20 minutes.
Heat 1½ tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it shimmers and mellows, about 90 seconds on medium, then add 1½ tsp panch phoron and let all five seeds crackle for 30 seconds.
Add the chopped onion and green chillies, fry 2 minutes until the onion softens, then add the methi leaves and cook 3 minutes until wilted and dry.
Mix in the 2 mashed potatoes, ½ tsp turmeric, ½ tsp red chilli powder and ½ tsp salt, mash everything together over low heat for 1 minute, and cool the filling completely.
Portion the dough into 8 balls and the filling into 8 lots of 2 tbsp; cup each ball, enclose the filling, pinch the seams shut and roll gently into 6-inch rounds.

Toast on a medium tava, about 2 minutes per side, brushing each face with ½ tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and pressing the rim until deep golden patches appear and the panch phoron aroma lifts off the pan.
tips: Panch phoron must hit properly hot oil; if the mustard seeds do not pop within seconds, the fenugreek seeds in the blend will stew and turn bitter.
Mash the potatoes while still warm for a lump-free filling; cold potatoes mash grainy and poke holes during rolling.
A day-old filling actually tastes better as the fennel infuses; refrigerate it and bring to room temperature before stuffing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with dahi baigana (Odia yoghurt-eggplant relish) or simply thick curd and a green chilli; a mug of black tea completes the coastal-morning picture.

variations.name: Tamil Stuffed Methi Paratha
variations.description: Here the stuffing thinks like a South Indian poriyal: methi and grated carrot tossed with urad dal, curry leaves and mustard seeds crackled in sesame oil. Gingelly (sesame) oil, Tamil Nadu's heritage cooking fat, both flavours the filling and toasts the paratha, lending its distinctive toasted-nut fragrance. Light, aromatic and less heavy-handed with chilli than its northern cousins.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Slow-milled wheat takes on the gingelly oil's nuttiness beautifully at the tava stage

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed gingelly oil is the soul of Tamil tempering and crisps the crust without smoking

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and roughly ¾ cup water into a soft dough; set it aside under a damp cloth for 20 minutes.

Heat 1½ tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadai on medium, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds fully, then add 2 tsp urad dal and fry until pale gold, about 45 seconds, before tossing in 12 curry leaves and the 2 torn dried chillies.

Add the grated carrot and stir 2 minutes, then the methi leaves for another 3 minutes until the mixture is wilted and dry; finish with ½ tsp turmeric, ½ tsp salt and 3 tbsp grated coconut, cook 1 minute and cool completely.
