Divide the dough into 8 balls and the poriyal-style filling into 8 portions of about 2 tbsp; enclose each portion inside a flattened ball, sealing the gathered edge firmly.
Roll each parcel softly into a 6-inch round, letting flecks of carrot and curry leaf show through without breaking the surface.
Cook on a medium tava about 2 minutes a side, brushing on ½ tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil per face and pressing gently until the crust turns golden brown with a toasted-sesame scent.
tips: Fry the urad dal only to pale gold in the tempering; it continues to darken in the residual heat and turns bitter past amber.
Grate the carrot on the fine side of the grater; coarse shreds pierce the dough while rolling.
Fresh curry leaves make or break this; if yours are dried, crisp them in the oil a few extra seconds to revive their aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and a small tumbler of sambar for dipping, filter coffee after; cut into wedges these also make an excellent tiffin-box lunch.

variations.name: Kashmiri Stuffed Methi Paratha
variations.description: A Valley-inspired paratha where the methi filling is enriched with paneer, fennel powder and dry ginger, the twin pillars of Kashmiri spicing, and perfumed with genuine saffron bloomed in warm milk. The saffron is brushed over the ghee-roasted crust at the end so its aroma arrives first. Elegant, gently sweet-spiced and unlike any plains paratha.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: A soft, tight crumb that carries the saffron brush without turning soggy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: GI-grade Pampore threads; a quarter teaspoon perfumes all eight parathas

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The neutral richness of bilona ghee lets the saffron and fennel lead

steps: Steep ¼ tsp Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside for 15 minutes until the milk turns a deep marigold; meanwhile knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about ¾ cup water into a soft dough and rest it covered.

Melt 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat and cook the methi leaves for 3 to 4 minutes until wilted and dry, then stir in 1½ tsp fennel powder, ¾ tsp dry ginger powder, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and ½ tsp salt for 1 minute.
Take the pan off the heat, cool fully, then fold in ½ cup crumbled paneer, 2 tbsp chopped cashews and 1 tsp of the saffron milk to bind the filling loosely.
Stuff 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp of filling each, pinching the seams closed, resting them 5 minutes, and rolling each into a 6-inch round with a featherlight hand.
Roast each round on a medium tava about 2 minutes per side, spreading ½ tsp Anveshan Ghee on each face and pressing until evenly gold with amber blisters.
Off the heat, brush the top of every hot paratha with the remaining saffron milk so it soaks into the crust, and serve within minutes while the perfume is at its peak.
tips: Never add saffron threads directly to the dough; only a warm-milk steep releases their full colour and fragrance.
Fennel and dry ginger are the Kashmiri signature; measure them exactly, as doubling either tips the filling medicinal.
The saffron-milk brush must go on hot parathas; on cool ones it sits on the surface instead of soaking in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a bowl of Kashmiri-style dahi sweetened with a little honey, or alongside kahwa tea in the afternoon; walnuts on the side echo the Valley's table.

variations.name: Malwa Stuffed Methi Paratha
variations.description: From Madhya Pradesh's Malwa plateau, where peanuts thicken and enrich everything, comes a stuffing of methi with coarsely crushed roasted peanuts, sesame and jaggery-kissed spice. The nutty crunch inside the soft parcel is the whole point, echoing the region's poha-and-sev love of texture. Toasted in groundnut oil for a doubled peanut register.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The plateau's wheat-eating heartland deserves a true heritage grain wrapper

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed from the same crop that stars in the filling, doubling the peanut aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A Malwa-style sweet counterpoint that rounds out the peanut-methi bitterness

steps: Prepare the dough by kneading 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and about ¾ cup water until smooth and yielding; rest 20 minutes under a plate.
Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium and sauté the minced green chillies for 20 seconds, then add the methi leaves and cook 3 to 4 minutes until collapsed and dry.

Stir in ½ cup crushed roasted peanuts, 1 tbsp toasted sesame, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp coriander powder, 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and ½ tsp salt; cook 1 minute so the jaggery melts through, then cool the filling completely.
Fill 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp of the peanut-methi mixture apiece, gather and twist the tops shut, and press each gently flat before resting them 5 minutes.
Roll every parcel into a 6-inch round with slow, even strokes, flouring as needed; the peanut bits will dimple the surface, which is fine as long as nothing pokes through.
Roast on a medium tava, roughly 2 minutes per side with ½ tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil brushed on each face, pressing until the crust is a toasty brown and smells of warm peanuts.
tips: Crush the peanuts to gravel, not powder; the crunch inside the soft paratha is this variation's signature.
Melting the jaggery into the warm filling distributes the sweetness evenly; sprinkled in cold it stays in pockets.
These reheat superbly on a dry tava the next day, as the peanut filling holds moisture better than plain greens.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with green coriander chutney and a bowl of plain curd, or in true Malwa spirit alongside a morning plate of poha and cutting chai.

variations.name: Classic Stuffed Palak Paratha
variations.description: A North Indian breakfast staple where a spiced, sautéed spinach filling is sealed inside soft khapli wheat dough and roasted until blistered. The filling is cooked dry so the paratha rolls out without tearing, giving you clean green layers in every bite. Nutty emmer wheat and slow-churned ghee make it taste like a village kitchen classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Stone-ground emmer wheat gives this paratha a naturally sweet, nutty crumb that stays soft for hours

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee for kneading, sautéing the filling and roasting — its caramel aroma defines the classic paratha

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and about 0.75 cup water into a soft, non-sticky dough; knead 6-7 minutes until smooth, cover and rest 15 minutes.
Wash and finely chop 250 g spinach, then squeeze it firmly in a clean cloth to press out as much water as possible so the filling stays dry.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then sauté 1 finely chopped small onion, 1 inch grated ginger and 1 minced green chilli until the onion turns light golden, about 3 minutes.

Add the chopped spinach with 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp salt; cook on medium-high, stirring, until every trace of moisture evaporates and the mixture looks dry and glossy, about 5 minutes. Cool completely.

Divide the dough into 8 balls, flatten each into a 3-inch cup, place 2 tbsp of the cooled spinach filling in the centre, pinch the edges shut and roll gently into a 6-inch round using dry flour for dusting.

Roast each paratha on a hot tava on medium-high heat for about 1 minute per side, then brush both sides with a little of the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and press with a spatula until deep golden-brown spots appear on both faces.
tips: Squeezing the spinach dry is the single most important step — a wet filling will burst through the dough while rolling.
The cooked filling keeps refrigerated for 2 days, so you can prep it the night before for a 15-minute breakfast.
If a paratha tears while rolling, dab the tear with dry atta and roll only on that side with light pressure.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot off the tava with a bowl of thick curd whisked with a pinch of roasted cumin, and a wedge of lime pickle on the side.

variations.name: Punjabi Stuffed Palak Paratha
variations.description: The dhaba version from Punjab's wheat belt: a robust ajwain-scented dough, a garlicky spinach filling with crumbled paneer, and a slick of white butter melting on top. It is rolled slightly thicker than usual so the crust crisps while the inside stays pillowy. This is the paratha you eat with a tall glass of lassi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli wheat mimics the coarse desi atta Punjabi dhabas swear by, with a deeper roasted flavour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Punjabi parathas are generous with fat — bilona ghee crisps the crust without any greasy heaviness

steps: Rub 0.5 tsp ajwain seeds and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, add 0.5 tsp salt and roughly 0.75 cup water, and knead 7-8 minutes to a soft, elastic dough. Rest it under a damp cloth for 20 minutes.
Blanch 250 g spinach in boiling water for 90 seconds, plunge into cold water, then squeeze bone-dry and chop very fine.

Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium flame and fry 4 minced garlic cloves and 2 chopped green chillies until the raw smell disappears, about 1 minute; tip in the spinach with 0.5 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp garam masala and dry it out over medium-high heat for 4 minutes.
Off the heat, crumble in 100 g paneer, mix well and let the filling cool fully so the paneer firms back up.

Shape the dough into 8 portions, cup each one, stuff with a heaped 2 tbsp of the paneer-spinach mixture, seal the pleats and roll to a 6-inch round about 0.5 cm thick — Punjabi style is thicker than everyday parathas.
Cook on a medium-hot tava for 90 seconds per side, then spoon over the remaining 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in stages, pressing the edges with a cloth until the surface is crisp and mottled deep brown.
Top each hot paratha with 0.5 tbsp white butter just before it leaves the kitchen so it melts into the crust.
tips: Blanching instead of raw-sautéing keeps the filling emerald green — the Punjabi giveaway of a well-made palak paratha.
Crumble the paneer only after the spinach cools, otherwise it turns rubbery in the residual heat.
Leftover parathas revive perfectly on a dry tava for 1 minute per side; never microwave them or the crust turns leathery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with sweet lassi and a raw onion salad sprinkled with chaat masala — the classic Amritsar dhaba plate.

variations.name: Bengali Stuffed Palak Paratha
variations.description: Bengal reimagines the palak paratha with pungent kachi ghani mustard oil, kalonji and a whisper of sugar balancing the greens. The filling gets a signature hit of grated ginger and green chilli paste, echoing the flavours of shaak bhaja. The mustard oil is heated to smoking first, which mellows its bite into a warm, nose-tingling aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The wholegrain khapli base stands up beautifully to mustard oil's sharpness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed kachi ghani mustard oil brings the authentic jhaanj — the pungent kick Bengali cooking is built on

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A final brush of bilona ghee rounds off the mustard oil's edge, the way Bengali kitchens finish parathas

steps: Make the dough by working 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and 0.5 tsp salt into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, then adding about 0.75 cup water; knead until supple, roughly 7 minutes, and rest for 15 minutes covered.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pan until it just begins to smoke, then lower the flame and let it cool for 30 seconds — this tames its raw pungency.
Crackle 0.5 tsp kalonji in the tempered oil for 15 seconds, add 1 inch grated ginger and 2 slit green chillies, and stir for 1 minute until fragrant.

Add 250 g finely chopped, well-squeezed spinach with 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp sugar; cook on medium-high for 5 minutes until completely dry, then cool the filling to room temperature.
Portion the dough into 8 balls, stuff each with 2 tbsp of the kalonji-spinach filling, pinch closed and roll into thin 6-inch discs with gentle, even strokes.
Griddle each paratha on medium heat for about 75 seconds per side until freckled brown, then brush lightly with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee divided across all parathas and serve immediately.
tips: Always smoke the mustard oil first and let it settle — skipping this leaves an aggressive raw bitterness in the filling.
The pinch of sugar is not optional in the Bengali version; it lifts the greens the way Bengali shaak dishes are seasoned.
Kalonji burns fast, so keep the flame low and have the ginger ready to go in within 15 seconds.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with begun bhaja (crisp fried aubergine slices) and a spoon of kasundi mustard relish for a fully Bengali plate.

variations.name: Kerala Stuffed Palak Paratha
variations.description: A Malabar-inspired take where the spinach filling is folded with fresh grated coconut, curry leaves and crushed black pepper, then cooked in cold-pressed coconut oil. The coconut keeps the stuffing moist and faintly sweet, a thoran-style contrast to the earthy greens. Roasting the paratha in a mix of coconut oil and ghee gives it a delicate tropical fragrance.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat's gentle sweetness pairs naturally with coconut in this southern rendition

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed from fresh copra, it perfumes the thoran-style filling exactly like a Kerala home kitchen

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A touch of bilona ghee on the tava deepens the browning that coconut oil alone cannot give

steps: Combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and 0.5 tsp salt, pour in about 0.75 cup water and knead for 7 minutes into a soft, pliable dough; rest 15 minutes under a damp cloth.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadhai on medium, pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds for 20 seconds, then fry 12 curry leaves and 4 sliced shallots until the shallots turn translucent, about 2 minutes.
Stir in 250 g chopped and firmly squeezed spinach with 0.5 tsp salt and cook on medium-high until dry, around 4 minutes, tossing frequently so nothing catches.
Fold in 0.5 cup fresh grated coconut and 0.5 tsp crushed black pepper, cook just 1 minute more so the coconut stays juicy, then spread the filling on a plate to cool completely.
Divide the dough into 8 equal balls, fill each with 2 tbsp of the coconut-spinach mixture, seal firmly and roll into 6-inch rounds, dusting sparingly with dry atta.
Roast on a medium-hot tava for about 80 seconds per side, finishing each paratha with a thin smear of the 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until golden freckles cover the surface.
tips: Add the coconut at the very end of cooking — long frying dries it out and robs the filling of its fresh sweetness.
Frozen grated coconut works if thawed and squeezed, but reduce salt slightly as it concentrates flavour.
Tear the curry leaves in half before frying to release more of their citrusy oil into the filling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and sweet mango pickle, or alongside a soft-boiled egg sprinkled with pepper for a Malabar-style breakfast.

variations.name: Malwa Stuffed Palak Paratha
variations.description: From the Malwa plateau of Madhya Pradesh comes a rustic paratha whose spinach filling is thickened with coarsely crushed roasted peanuts and sesame. The nuts soak up the greens' moisture and add a toasty crunch reminiscent of the region's beloved sev-and-peanut street snacks. Roasted coriander and a squeeze of lime keep it bright and earthy at once.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Central India's wheat-eating heartland deserves this heritage emmer grain with real rotli-like softness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil doubles down on the peanut theme, tying the filling and the roast together

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Malwa homes finish flatbreads with ghee — this bilona version adds a granular, nutty richness

steps: Work 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and 0.5 tsp salt into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, add close to 0.75 cup water and knead about 7 minutes until the dough is soft yet springy; cover and rest 15 minutes.
Toast 1 tbsp sesame seeds in a dry pan on low heat for 2 minutes until they turn pale gold and smell nutty, then set aside.
In the same pan, heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium and wilt 250 g chopped, well-squeezed spinach with 0.5 tsp salt, cooking about 5 minutes until no liquid remains in the pan.

Take the pan off the heat and mix in 0.33 cup crushed roasted peanuts, the toasted sesame, 1 tsp roasted coriander powder, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp lime juice; cool the filling fully before stuffing.
Split the dough into 8 balls, load each with 2 tbsp of the peanut-spinach filling, gather the edges into a tight seal and roll out to a 6-inch circle with steady, light pressure.
Cook each round on a medium-hot tava, about 90 seconds per side, spreading a little of the 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over both faces and pressing until crunchy brown patches develop.
tips: Crush the peanuts coarsely, not to a powder — you want pebbly bits that stay crunchy inside the soft paratha.
Add the lime juice only off the heat, or its brightness dulls and the greens discolour.
This filling also makes an excellent stuffing for baati or litti if you have extra.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of dahi tempered with mustard seeds and a side of spicy garlic chutney, Malwa dhaba style.

variations.name: Classic Stuffed Pyaaz Paratha
variations.description: The everyday North Indian breakfast paratha, stuffed generously with a sharp, spiced onion filling and roasted in slow-churned bilona ghee. Khapli wheat gives the crust a nutty depth and a softer bite than regular atta, while squeezing the salted onions keeps the filling dry so the paratha never tears.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Stone-milled emmer wheat kneads into a naturally soft dough that stays pliable even after cooling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee has a high smoke point, so the parathas crisp on the tava without burning

steps: Knead the dough: combine 3 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then work in about 1.25 cups water a little at a time. Knead for 8 minutes until the dough is soft, smooth and does not stick to your palm, then cover and rest for 20 minutes.

Finely chop 4 medium onions and 2 green chillies, toss with 0.5 tsp salt and set aside for 10 minutes. Squeeze the onions firmly in your fist to press out all their water, otherwise the filling will turn soggy and tear the dough.
Mix the squeezed onions with 1.5 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric powder and 3 tbsp chopped coriander until every piece is evenly coated a warm ochre colour.

Divide the rested dough into 8 equal balls. Flatten one ball into a 4-inch cup, place 2 tbsp of onion filling in the centre, gather the edges over the top and pinch firmly to seal so no filling peeks through.
Dust the stuffed ball lightly with atta and roll it out gently into a 7-inch round, using even pressure from the centre outward so the onions do not burst the seams.

Heat a tava on medium-high until a drop of water sizzles instantly. Cook the paratha for about 1 minute until small bubbles rise, flip, brush with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee, flip again and press the edges with a spatula until both sides show deep golden-brown spots, about 3 minutes total.
Repeat with the remaining balls, brushing each side with Anveshan Ghee, and stack the finished parathas loosely covered so they stay soft.
tips: Salting and squeezing the onions is the single most important step; skip it and the filling weeps water within minutes of rolling.
If a paratha tears while rolling, dab the tear with dry atta and roll only over that spot with feather-light pressure.
The dough can be kneaded up to a day ahead and refrigerated; bring it back to room temperature for 20 minutes before stuffing.
Roll from the centre outward and rotate the paratha a quarter turn after every stroke to keep the filling evenly distributed.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot off the tava with a bowl of chilled dahi, a wedge of aam ka achar and sliced raw onion rings sprinkled with chaat masala.

variations.name: Bengali Stuffed Pyaaz Paratha
variations.description: A Kolkata-style take where pungent kachi ghani mustard oil does double duty, seasoning the onion filling and crisping the crust. Nigella seeds and a touch of green chilli give the paratha the unmistakable aroma of a Bengali breakfast table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The wholegrain emmer base stands up beautifully to the sharpness of mustard oil

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed kachi ghani oil brings the peppery pungency that defines this Bengali version

steps: Make a soft dough with 3 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and roughly 1.25 cups water; knead a full 8 minutes until supple and rest it under a damp cloth for 20 minutes.

Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a small pan on medium heat until it just begins to smoke, then take it off the flame and let it cool for 2 minutes; this mellows its raw bite while keeping the aroma.

Finely chop 4 medium onions, salt them with 0.5 tsp salt, rest 10 minutes and squeeze dry. Stir in the cooled mustard oil, 1 tsp kalonji, 3 minced green chillies, 1 tsp grated ginger, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder and 2 tbsp coriander.
Portion the dough into 8 balls, cup each one open in your palm, spoon in 2 tbsp of the mustard-scented filling, pleat the edges shut and pinch off any excess dough at the seal.
Roll each stuffed ball into a 7-inch disc with gentle, even strokes, flouring lightly whenever the surface feels tacky.
Cook on a medium-hot tava, drizzling 1 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil around the edges of each paratha; fry about 90 seconds per side, pressing gently, until blistered with crisp bronze patches.
tips: Briefly heating and cooling the mustard oil is a Bengali trick that softens its sting; never add fully raw oil to the filling.
Kalonji burns quickly, so keep the tava at medium rather than high once the first paratha goes on.
For an even more Bengali plate, roll these slightly thicker and smaller, like a triangular porota, and fry with a little extra oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with alur dom or simply a smear of kasundi mustard and cucumber slices, with sweet milky cha to finish the meal.

variations.name: Kerala Stuffed Pyaaz Paratha
variations.description: Inspired by Malabar kitchens, this version folds fresh grated coconut and curry leaves into the onion masala and cooks the paratha in cold-pressed coconut oil. The filling is briefly sautéed, so it tastes like a thoran tucked inside soft khapli wheat layers.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its gentle sweetness echoes the coconut in the filling instead of fighting it

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed from fresh copra, it perfumes both the sautéed filling and the crust

steps: Knead 3 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and about 1.25 cups water into a soft, elastic dough; rest it covered for 20 minutes while you cook the filling.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds for about 30 seconds, then drop in 12 curry leaves and 2 slit green chillies and let them sputter and turn glossy.
Add 4 finely chopped onions with 0.5 tsp salt and sauté for 6 to 7 minutes until translucent and lightly golden at the edges, then stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp black pepper powder.
Fold in 0.5 cup fresh grated coconut, cook 2 more minutes until the mixture smells toasty and looks completely dry, then spread it on a plate and cool fully before stuffing.
Shape 8 dough balls, fill each with 2 tbsp of the cooled coconut-onion masala, seal the pleats tightly and roll into 7-inch rounds with a light hand.
Roast each paratha on a medium tava, spooning 1 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil over each side, for about 3 minutes total until freckled deep gold and crisp at the rim.
tips: Cool the sautéed filling completely; warm filling steams inside the dough and makes the paratha gummy.
Frozen grated coconut works if thawed and squeezed dry, but fresh coconut gives a sweeter, juicier crumb.
Tear a couple of extra curry leaves straight into the dough water for an aromatic crust.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and a small bowl of Kerala-style moru curry, or roll around a spoon of spicy mango pickle for a lunchbox wrap.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Stuffed Pyaaz Paratha
variations.description: Goda masala, the smoky-sweet Maharashtrian blend with dagad phool and coconut, transforms the humble onion filling into something deep and earthy. Roasted peanut coarse powder adds crunch, making each bite taste like a cross between paratha and thecha-topped bhakri.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat's rustic flavour suits the earthy goda masala better than refined flour ever could

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil doubles down on the peanut notes already in the filling

steps: Work 3 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil with about 1.25 cups water into a smooth, soft dough; knead 8 minutes and rest under a damp cloth for 20 minutes.
Dry-toast 1 tbsp sesame seeds in a small pan over low heat for about 2 minutes until they turn pale gold and start to pop, then tip them into a mixing bowl.
Finely chop 4 medium onions, mix with 0.5 tsp salt, wait 10 minutes and wring out every drop of moisture with your hands.

Combine the squeezed onions with the toasted sesame, 2 tsp goda masala, 3 tbsp roasted peanut powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 3 tbsp coriander; the mixture should hold together loosely when pressed.
Divide the dough into 8 portions, stuff each with 2 tbsp of the goda masala filling, seal firmly and roll into 7-inch discs, dusting sparingly with atta.
Fry each paratha on a medium-hot tava with 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil per side for about 90 seconds a side, pressing the centre so it puffs and blisters into mottled brown spots.
tips: Goda masala loses its aroma fast once opened, so store it airtight and use within three months for this recipe to shine.
The peanut powder absorbs onion moisture, so this filling is more forgiving to roll than most; still, do not skip squeezing the onions.
No goda masala on hand? Toast 1 clove, half an inch of cinnamon, 1 tsp coriander seeds and 1 tbsp dry coconut, then grind fine for a quick substitute.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve khandeshi-style with a dollop of homemade white butter, green chilli thecha on the side and a glass of spiced chaas.

variations.name: Rajasthani Stuffed Pyaaz Paratha
variations.description: A desert-style paratha where whole dried red chillies are bloomed in ghee and pounded into the onion filling along with tangy amchur and crushed coriander seeds. It is fiery, rustic and built to be eaten with garlic chutney the way roadside dhabas across Marwar serve it.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Sturdy khapli dough tolerates the coarse, chunky Rajasthani filling without tearing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Chilli heat blooms in bilona ghee, carrying its smoky flavour through the whole filling

steps: Prepare the dough by kneading 3 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and around 1.25 cups water for 8 minutes until soft and springy; rest it 20 minutes under a cloth.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan on low, add 4 whole dried red chillies, 2 tsp coriander seeds and 1 tsp fennel seeds and toast for about 2 minutes until the chillies darken a shade and smell smoky, then cool and pound coarsely in a mortar.
Finely chop 4 onions, salt them with 0.5 tsp salt, rest 10 minutes and squeeze bone-dry; combine with the pounded chilli-spice mix, 1 tsp amchur, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 2 tbsp coriander leaves.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, load each with 2 tbsp of the fiery filling, gather and pinch the edges shut, then rest the stuffed balls 5 minutes so the seams relax.
Roll each ball into a 7-inch round, keeping the pressure light over the centre where the chilli flecks sit close to the surface.
Roast on a medium tava for 1 minute, flip, spread 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee, flip again and cook, pressing the edges, until both faces are crisped with dark golden patches, about 3 minutes per paratha.
tips: Blooming the whole chillies in ghee before pounding is essential; raw crushed chillies taste harsh and dusty in comparison.
Adjust fire by seed count: shake the seeds out of two chillies for medium heat, keep all seeds for true Marwari punch.
These parathas keep well for travel; wrap in foil while warm and they stay soft for 6 to 8 hours, just like Rajasthani road food.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Marwari way with lehsun ki chutney, a spoon of churned white makkhan melting on top and a tall glass of salted chaas.

variations.name: Classic Dhaba-style Lauki
variations.description: The lauki you get at highway dhabas across North India: soft cubes of bottle gourd simmered in a rustic onion-tomato masala that clings to every piece. Slow-cooked in Anveshan Ghee with kasuri methi crushed in at the end, it turns a humble gourd into something you mop up greedily with tandoori roti.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Slow-churned bilona ghee gives the masala its signature dhaba-style nutty richness

steps: Peel 500 g bottle gourd, halve it lengthwise, scoop out any mature seeds and cut it into 2 cm cubes; finely chop 2 medium onions and 2 medium tomatoes and keep everything ready by the stove.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai on medium heat until it shimmers, then add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle and darken a shade, about 30 seconds.

Add the chopped onions with a pinch of the salt and sauté on medium heat for 6-7 minutes until deep golden at the edges, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 1 minute until the raw smell disappears.

Tip in the chopped tomatoes along with 2 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining salt; cook for 4-5 minutes, mashing with the back of the ladle, until the masala thickens and ghee beads at the sides.
Add the lauki cubes, toss to coat them in the masala, splash in 0.25 cup water, cover and cook on low heat for 15-18 minutes, stirring twice, until the gourd is fork-tender and translucent.

Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi between your palms straight into the pan, sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala, simmer uncovered for 2 minutes so extra moisture evaporates, then finish with 3 tbsp chopped fresh coriander.
tips: Taste a raw sliver of the lauki before cooking; if it is even slightly bitter, discard it, as bitterness intensifies when cooked.
Lauki releases a lot of water, so resist adding more than 0.25 cup; a runny sabzi is the most common way this dish goes wrong.
The masala can be made a day ahead and refrigerated; just reheat it, add the freshly cut lauki and finish cooking for weekday speed.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve straight from the kadhai with hot tandoori roti or phulkas, a wedge of lime, sliced onions sprinkled with chaat masala, and a tall glass of salted chaas on the side.

variations.name: Bengali Dhaba-style Lauki
variations.description: In Bengal, lau is treated gently but the highway version turns up the pungency with a hot Anveshan Mustard Oil base, kalonji and slit green chillies. A pinch of sugar balances the sharpness, giving you the sweet-heat contrast that defines roadside Bengali cooking on the Kolkata-Durgapur route.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed kachi ghani mustard oil brings the sinus-clearing pungency Bengali lau depends on

steps: Peel and dice 500 g bottle gourd into slim 1.5 cm batons, slice 1 medium onion thinly, chop 1 tomato, and slit 3 green chillies down their length.
Pour 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil into a kadhai and heat it on medium-high until it just reaches smoking point and the raw sharpness mellows, about 2 minutes, then lower the flame.
Scatter in 0.5 tsp kalonji and 2 of the slit green chillies; the seeds should sputter within 10 seconds, releasing a peppery aroma.
Add the sliced onion and fry on medium heat for 4-5 minutes until soft and lightly bronzed, then stir in 1 tsp grated ginger and the chopped tomato and cook for 3 minutes until pulpy.
Add the lauki batons, 0.5 tsp turmeric powder and 1 tsp salt, toss well, then cover and cook on low heat for 12-14 minutes; the gourd should steam in its own juices until soft but not mushy.
Uncover, sprinkle 0.5 tsp sugar and the last slit chilli, raise the heat for 2 minutes to dry the pan juices into a light glaze, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Always let mustard oil reach its smoking point once and then cool slightly; skipping this leaves an acrid raw-oil taste in the finished dish.
The 0.5 tsp sugar is not for sweetness but to round off the mustard's bite, so do not leave it out.
For a classic lau-er torkari touch, stir in a handful of tiny fried bori (sun-dried lentil dumplings) during the last 5 minutes of cooking.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle over steaming gobindobhog or any short-grain rice with a drizzle of the pan glaze, and pair with masoor dal and a slice of lime for a proper Bengali lunch plate.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Dhaba-style Lauki
variations.description: Dudhi bhopla the Deccan way: bottle gourd braised with goda masala, that smoky-sweet Maharashtrian blend of dagad phool and coconut, plus crushed roasted peanuts for body. Cooked in Anveshan Groundnut Oil, it is earthier and darker than its North Indian cousin, with no tomato tang to distract.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil doubles down on the nutty peanut notes central to Maharashtrian bhaji

steps: Cut 500 g peeled bottle gourd into small 1 cm dice so it cooks quickly and absorbs the goda masala; finely chop 1 medium onion and coarsely crush 0.25 cup roasted peanuts in a mortar.
Warm 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai over medium heat, drop in 1 tsp mustard seeds and wait until they pop vigorously, about 20-30 seconds, then add 8 curry leaves and let them crisp.
Sauté the chopped onion for 4-5 minutes on medium heat until translucent and just starting to colour at the edges.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp goda masala, fry the spices in the oil for 30 seconds, then immediately add the diced lauki and 1 tsp salt before they scorch.
Add 0.25 cup water, cover and simmer on low heat for 12-14 minutes, stirring midway, until the gourd is completely tender and stained a deep earthy brown.
Fold in the crushed peanuts and 2 tbsp grated coconut, cook uncovered for 2-3 minutes so the peanuts thicken the pan juices slightly, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Goda masala burns fast because of its coconut content, so never let it fry alone for more than 30 seconds before adding the vegetable.
Crush the peanuts coarse, not to a powder; you want pebbly bits that give the soft gourd some crunch.
If you cannot find goda masala, toast 1 tsp sesame seeds, 1 tsp coriander seeds and a small piece of dagad phool and grind them as a quick stand-in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft jowar or bajra bhakri, a spoonful of thecha on the side for heat lovers, and plain varan-bhaat to complete a Maharashtrian thali.

variations.name: Kerala Dhaba-style Lauki
variations.description: A thoran-style dry lauki where the gourd is steamed with a fresh coconut-cumin-green chilli crumble and tempered in Anveshan Coconut Oil with curry leaves. It is light, fragrant and barely spiced, letting the sweetness of the churakka shine the way Kerala home cooking intends.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil is the non-negotiable soul of a Kerala thoran temper

steps: Peel 500 g bottle gourd and chop it into tiny 0.5 cm dice, the traditional thoran cut that lets the coconut coat every piece; thinly slice 4 shallots.

Pulse 0.5 cup grated fresh coconut with 2 small green chillies, 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp turmeric powder in a mixer for just 2-3 short bursts to make a coarse, moist crumble; do not grind it to a paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a wide pan on medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds fully, about 20 seconds, then add 2 whole dried red chillies torn in half and 10 curry leaves.
Add the sliced shallots and sauté for 2-3 minutes until soft and fragrant but not browned, keeping the heat at medium.
Add the diced lauki and 0.75 tsp salt, toss, sprinkle 2 tbsp water, then cover and steam on low heat for 8-10 minutes until the gourd is just tender yet still holds its shape.
Scatter the coconut crumble over the gourd, mix gently, cover again for 3 minutes so the coconut steams through, then cook uncovered for 2 minutes until the pan is dry and aromatic.
tips: The fine 0.5 cm dice is what makes a thoran a thoran; large chunks will steam unevenly and reject the coconut coating.
Frozen grated coconut works if thawed fully, but squeeze out excess water or the dish turns soggy.
Never brown the coconut crumble; it should only steam through, staying white and sweet against the pale green gourd.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with red matta rice, a tangy pulissery or sambar, and pappadam crushed over the top; a few slices of ripe banana on the plate is a very Kerala touch.

variations.name: Rajasthani Dhaba-style Lauki
variations.description: On the Jaipur-Bikaner highway, lauki gets the desert treatment: a fiery tadka of whole dried Mathania-style red chillies in Anveshan Ghee, a yogurt-based gravy in place of tomatoes, and warming fennel and coriander. The curd keeps it cooling even as the chillies bring serious colour and heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Desert kitchens cook almost everything in ghee; bilona ghee keeps the yogurt gravy silky and rich

steps: Cut 500 g peeled bottle gourd into thick 3 cm chunks that can hold their own in a gravy, and whisk 0.75 cup yogurt with 1 tsp besan until completely smooth; the besan will stop the curd from splitting.

Melt 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy-bottomed pan on medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1 tsp fennel seeds, and once they sizzle, drop in 4 whole dried red chillies and fry for 30 seconds until they deepen to mahogany.
Add the julienned ginger and the lauki chunks and sear them in the ghee for 3-4 minutes, turning so the edges pick up light golden spots.
Lower the heat, stir in 2 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt with 2 tbsp water so the spices bloom without burning, about 1 minute.
Take the pan off the heat, whisk in the yogurt-besan mixture in a slow stream while stirring continuously, then return to low heat and bring to a gentle simmer without letting it boil hard.
Cover partially and simmer on low for 15-18 minutes, stirring every few minutes, until the lauki is soft and the gravy has thickened to a pale-gold curry that coats the back of a spoon.
tips: Add the yogurt off the heat and keep stirring until it returns to a simmer; a hard boil at this stage will curdle the gravy.
Searing the lauki chunks first in ghee stops them from disintegrating in the yogurt gravy.
If your dried chillies are very hot, slit one and shake out the seeds; Rajasthani red comes from chilli skin, not raw heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot bajra rotis smeared with more ghee, a side of lasan ki chutney, and raw onion rings; in true Rajasthani style, follow with a piece of churma if you have it.

variations.name: Classic Garlic Onion Paratha
variations.description: The everyday North Indian breakfast paratha, taken up a notch with a punchy garlic-onion filling folded into nutty khapli wheat dough. The onions are salted and squeezed so the filling stays dry, which keeps every paratha crisp-edged yet soft inside. Roasted in bilona ghee, it needs nothing more than a bowl of curd.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat gives this dough a naturally sweet, nutty base that browns beautifully on the tava

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee both enriches the dough and crisps the paratha without any greasy aftertaste

steps: Knead 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 1 cup water into a soft, pliable dough that springs back when pressed. Cover and rest for 20 minutes so the emmer bran hydrates fully.

Finely chop 3 medium onions, toss them with 0.5 tsp salt and set aside for 10 minutes, then squeeze out every drop of released moisture with your hands. This single step is what stops the parathas from tearing.

Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan on medium heat and sizzle 8 minced garlic cloves and 2 chopped green chillies for about 1 minute until the raw smell disappears and the garlic turns pale gold. Pour this over the squeezed onions.

Mix in 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric powder and 3 tbsp chopped coriander to make a dry, crumbly filling. Divide it into 8 equal portions of roughly 2 tbsp each.

Divide the dough into 8 balls, flatten each into a small cup, place one 2 tbsp portion of filling inside, pinch the edges shut and roll gently into a 6-7 inch round, dusting lightly with flour as needed.

Heat a tava on medium-high until a drop of water sizzles instantly, then cook each paratha for about 2 minutes per side, brushing both sides with a total of 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, until deep golden-brown spots appear and the surface blisters.
Press the edges with a folded cloth while cooking so they crisp evenly, then stack the parathas in a cloth-lined box to keep them soft until serving.
tips: Salting and squeezing the onions is non-negotiable; wet filling makes the dough tear the moment you roll.
If a paratha springs a leak while rolling, dab the spot with dry atta and roll from the edges instead of the centre.
The dough and filling both keep overnight in the fridge separately, so you can stuff and roast fresh parathas in 15 minutes the next morning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot off the tava with thick chilled curd, a wedge of lime pickle and sliced radish sprinkled with chaat masala.

variations.name: Bengali Garlic Onion Paratha
variations.description: In Kolkata homes the paratha meets pungent kachhi ghani mustard oil, which perfumes both the filling and the tava. Nigella seeds and a hint of sugar balance the sharp garlic-onion mix, giving that unmistakable sweet-hot Bengali edge. The result is darker, glossier and more aromatic than its northern cousin.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The wholegrain emmer stands up well to mustard oil's assertive flavour without turning bitter

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed kachhi ghani mustard oil delivers the sinus-tingling pungency this Bengali paratha is built around

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A final brush of ghee softens the mustard heat and adds a festive gloss

steps: Rub 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil into 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, then add about 1 cup water gradually and knead for 8 minutes until you have a smooth, supple dough. Rest it under a damp cloth for 20 minutes.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai on medium-high until it just begins to smoke, then lower the heat and crackle 1 tsp nigella seeds for 20 seconds.

Add 10 sliced garlic cloves and 3 slit green chillies and fry for 1 minute until fragrant, then tip in 3 finely chopped onions with 0.5 tsp salt. Saute for 6-7 minutes until the onions turn translucent and their edges caramelise light brown.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric powder and 0.5 tsp sugar, cook for 1 more minute, then spread the mixture on a plate to cool completely; a warm filling will steam and soften the dough.
Portion the dough into 8 balls and the cooled filling into 8 mounds of about 2 tbsp each. Stuff each ball, seal the pleats firmly and roll into a 6 inch disc with light, even strokes.
Cook on a medium-hot tava for about 2 minutes per side, drizzling the remaining 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil around the edges, until the surface puffs in spots and turns speckled mahogany-brown.
Brush each finished paratha with a little of the 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee while still hot so the mustard sharpness mellows into a rounded, buttery finish.
tips: Always let mustard oil reach its smoking point once before adding anything; this tames its raw bitterness.
Cooking the onions before stuffing makes this version more forgiving to roll, so it is a good one for beginners.
Leftover parathas crisp up beautifully next day on a dry tava; do not microwave them or they turn leathery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with begun bhaja (crisp fried aubergine slices) and a smear of kasundi mustard for a proper Kolkata-style plate.

variations.name: Kerala Garlic Onion Paratha
variations.description: A Malabar-inspired take where fresh grated coconut and curry leaves join the garlic-onion filling, and virgin coconut oil does the roasting. The coconut keeps the filling juicy and faintly sweet, while black pepper supplies the heat instead of chilli powder. It tastes like a stuffed cousin of the Kerala tea-shop paratha.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli wheat lends a wholesome chew that pairs surprisingly well with sweet coconut

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil roasts the paratha with a delicate tropical aroma that ties the whole dish to the Malabar coast

steps: Combine 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, then work in roughly 1 cup water to form a soft dough. Knead for 6-8 minutes and rest it, covered, for 20 minutes.

Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan over medium heat and pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds for about 30 seconds until they sputter, then add the leaves from 2 curry sprigs and let them crisp for a few seconds.
Add 8 sliced shallots, 2 chopped medium onions and 8 crushed garlic cloves with 0.5 tsp salt, and saute for 5-6 minutes until soft and lightly golden at the edges.

Fold in 0.5 cup fresh grated coconut, 1 tsp crushed black pepper and 0.25 tsp turmeric powder, and toast the mixture for 2 minutes until the coconut smells nutty. Cool the filling fully before stuffing.
Shape the dough into 8 balls, cup each one in your palm, tuck in 2 tbsp of the coconut-onion filling, seal tightly and roll out to a 6 inch round without pressing hard over the centre.
Roast on a medium tava for around 2 minutes each side, spooning the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil over both faces, until freckled golden-brown and puffed in patches.
Rest the cooked parathas for 2 minutes under a cloth; the coconut filling settles and slices cleanly without spilling.
tips: Use freshly grated coconut, not desiccated; dried coconut turns the filling sawdusty and dry.
Crush the pepper coarsely just before cooking for sharp bursts of heat rather than a flat background spice.
This filling doubles as a stuffing for steamed rice-flour balls if you have extra left over.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coconut-milk vegetable stew or simply with sweetened black tea, the classic Malabar tea-shop pairing.

variations.name: Kumaoni Garlic Onion Paratha
variations.description: From the Uttarakhand hills comes this rustic version tempered with jakhya, the wild mustard seed that crackles louder and tastes nuttier than regular rai. The filling is coarse, smoky and gently spiced, meant to fuel a cold mountain morning. Roasted low and slow in ghee, it develops an almost biscuit-like crust.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Hill kitchens prize hardy heritage wheats, and khapli's rustic bite is true to that tradition

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Slow-roasting in bilona ghee builds the flaky, biscuity crust that defines a pahadi paratha

steps: Make a firm-yet-soft dough from 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 1 cup water, kneading a full 8 minutes. Set it aside under a plate for 20 minutes.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in an iron kadhai over medium flame and crackle 1 tsp jakhya seeds with 2 torn dried red chillies for about 30 seconds until the seeds pop noisily and smell nutty.
Slide in 10 roughly chopped garlic cloves, fry for 45 seconds until golden, then add 3 coarsely chopped onions with 0.5 tsp salt and cook for 6 minutes until the onions slump and pick up brown edges.
Season with 1 tsp coriander powder and 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, cook 1 minute more, then stir in 2 tbsp chopped coriander leaves and cool the filling on a wide plate.
Divide dough into 8 balls and filling into 8 portions of 2 tbsp. Stuff, pleat and seal each ball, then roll into a slightly thick 5-6 inch round; hill parathas are rolled fatter than plains ones.
Cook on a tava over medium-low heat for a patient 3 minutes per side, coating with the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, until the crust turns crunchy and deeply bronzed rather than merely spotted.
Tap the surface; it should sound faintly hollow and crisp. Stack them upright in a basket so the crusts stay crackly.
tips: If you cannot find jakhya, black mustard seeds work, but toast them a few seconds longer for a similar nutty depth.
Low heat is the secret here; rushing on a high flame browns the outside while leaving the thick round doughy inside.
These sturdy parathas travel well, making them ideal trek or tiffin food even 8 hours later.
variations.servingSuggestion: Eat the pahadi way with bhang-seed chutney or plain curd whipped with a pinch of rock salt and a glass of hot milky tea.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Garlic Onion Paratha
variations.description: Here the filling is seasoned with goda masala, the coconut-and-stone-flower spice blend unique to Maharashtra, plus a scatter of roasted peanut coarse powder for crunch. Cooked in wood-pressed groundnut oil, it has a warm, faintly sweet spice profile utterly different from a Punjabi paratha. Think of it as thecha's gentler sibling wrapped in bread.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat mirrors the coarse jowar-bhakri textures Maharashtrian palates love

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil echoes the peanut notes in the filling and is the default fat of Deccan kitchens

steps: Bring together 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and close to 1 cup water into a smooth, elastic dough; knead 7-8 minutes and rest for 20 minutes under a damp cloth.
In a pan, heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium and fry 8 minced garlic cloves with 2 chopped green chillies for about 1 minute until pale gold and aromatic.

Add 3 finely chopped onions with 0.5 tsp salt and cook 5-6 minutes until soft and lightly browned, then sprinkle in 2 tsp goda masala and 0.5 tsp turmeric powder and toast for 1 minute so the masala blooms.
Take the pan off the heat and mix in 3 tbsp roasted peanut coarse powder and 3 tbsp chopped coriander; the peanuts soak up moisture and make the filling easy to handle. Cool completely.
Stuff 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp filling apiece, pinch shut, and roll each into a 6 inch circle using gentle outward strokes so the peanut bits do not pierce the dough.
Roast on a medium-hot tava for roughly 2 minutes a side with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil drizzled around the rim, until crisp golden patches bloom across the surface.
Press the centre briefly with a spatula in the final 30 seconds so the thickest part cooks through and the paratha exhales a puff of spiced steam.
tips: Goda masala scorches fast, so always add it to the onions off a high flame and toast only briefly.
Pulse the peanuts coarse, not to a paste; you want gravelly crunch, not peanut butter.
A spoon of dry filling rubbed into the dough itself makes even the edges taste seasoned.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside a bowl of mattha (spiced thin buttermilk) and a fiery green-chilli thecha for the full Deccan experience.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Bhindi
variations.description: The everyday North Indian dry okra stir-fry, where crisp-edged bhindi is tossed with a fiery onion-tomato masala sharpened with green chillies and cracked black pepper. Cooking the okra uncovered on medium heat keeps it completely slime-free, so every piece stays glossy and slightly charred rather than sticky.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil has a high smoke point and nutty depth that lets the okra crisp without turning greasy

steps: Wash 500 g okra, pat each piece completely dry with a kitchen towel, then trim the crowns and cut into 2 cm pieces; any moisture left on the okra will make it slimy, so this drying step is essential.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a wide kadai on medium-high heat until it shimmers, add the okra in a single layer and stir-fry uncovered for 8-10 minutes, tossing every 2 minutes, until the pieces are blistered at the edges and no longer sticky; transfer to a plate.

Add the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil to the same kadai on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then sauté 2 finely chopped onions with 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 3 slit green chillies for 5-6 minutes until the onions turn deep golden.

Stir in 2 finely chopped tomatoes with ½ tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 4-5 minutes, mashing occasionally, until the tomatoes break down and the masala releases oil at the sides.

Return the fried okra to the pan, sprinkle ½ tsp freshly ground black pepper, and toss gently on medium heat for 3-4 minutes so every piece is coated in masala; keep the pan uncovered so the bhindi stays dry and crisp.
Turn off the heat, scatter 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander over the bhindi and give it one final gentle toss before serving hot.
tips: Dry the okra thoroughly and never cover the pan while it cooks — steam is the number one cause of slimy bhindi.
If the okra still feels sticky midway, add 1 tsp lemon juice while stir-frying; the acidity cuts the mucilage instantly.
This dish reheats best in an open pan on medium heat for 3-4 minutes rather than in a microwave, which softens the crisp edges.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulkas, a bowl of boondi raita and sliced onions sprinkled with chaat masala for a complete weekday thali.

variations.name: Bengali Spicy Bhindi (Bhindi Bhaja Style)
variations.description: Inspired by Bengal's love of pungent mustard oil and light spicing, this take fries the okra in smoking Anveshan Mustard Oil with nigella seeds instead of cumin. The finished dish carries a sharp, wasabi-like heat from the oil, mellowed by a whisper of sugar and slit green chillies — minimal masala, maximum character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed kachi ghani mustard oil delivers the authentic pungent Bengali jhanj that refined oil simply cannot replicate

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A pinch of unrefined jaggery is the classic Bengali counterpoint that rounds off the mustard oil's sharp bite

ingredients.name: Mustard seeds, ground to paste with water

steps: Wash and thoroughly dry 500 g okra, then slit each pod lengthwise without cutting through, keeping the pods whole so they hold their shape while frying.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai on high heat until it just begins to smoke and turns pale, about 2 minutes — this step tames the raw pungency — then lower the flame to medium.

Crackle ½ tsp nigella seeds in the hot oil for 20 seconds, add 4 slit green chillies, and immediately slide in the whole slit okra; fry on medium heat for 8-9 minutes, turning occasionally, until the pods blister and turn deep green with browned patches.

Whisk 1 tbsp mustard paste and 2 tbsp poppy seed paste with 4 tbsp water, ½ tsp turmeric, ½ tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, pour it over the okra and cook uncovered for 4-5 minutes until the paste thickens and clings to each pod.
Sprinkle 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder over the pan, toss for 1 minute until it melts into the masala, then check that the okra is fork-tender but not mushy.
Finish with a final ½ tsp drizzle of raw Anveshan Mustard Oil off the heat for the signature Bengali aroma, and rest the dish for 2 minutes before serving.
tips: Always heat mustard oil until it smokes lightly before adding anything — under-heated mustard oil tastes harshly bitter.
Soak the poppy seeds in warm water for 15 minutes before grinding to get a smooth, cream-like paste.
The raw mustard oil drizzle at the end is non-negotiable in Bengali homes; add it only after the flame is off so its pungency stays intact.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with steamed gobindobhog rice, a wedge of lime and plain masoor dal — Bengalis eat this as a first course before the dal, not alongside it.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Bhindi (Bendakaya Vepudu)
variations.description: A ferociously hot Andhra-style vepudu where okra is fried till crisp and tossed with a coarse roasted powder of Guntur red chillies, chana dal and garlic. The dry, gritty spice coating and curry-leaf tempering make this the spiciest, crunchiest bhindi on any South Indian table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil is the traditional Andhra frying medium; its toasty flavour amplifies the roasted chilli podi

steps: Dry-roast 5 Guntur red chillies, 2 tbsp chana dal, 1 tbsp urad dal and 1 tsp cumin seeds in a pan on low heat for 4-5 minutes until the dals turn golden and the chillies crisp up and smell smoky; cool completely.
Grind the roasted mixture with 3 garlic cloves and ½ tsp salt into a coarse, sand-like podi — do not over-grind, as the texture should stay gritty against the soft okra.

Wash, dry and cut 500 g okra into 2.5 cm pieces, then fry them in 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil on medium-high heat for 9-10 minutes, stirring every couple of minutes, until crisp-edged and completely non-sticky.

Push the okra to one side, add the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds for 30 seconds, then add 12 curry leaves and 3 crushed garlic cloves and fry for 1 minute until the leaves turn glossy and the garlic smells toasty.
Sprinkle ¼ tsp turmeric and the remaining ½ tsp salt over the okra, toss everything together on medium heat for 2 minutes so the tempering coats every piece evenly.
Turn the flame to low, scatter the ground chilli-dal podi over the okra and toss for 2-3 minutes until each piece wears a rough, rust-red spice crust; serve immediately while crunchy.
tips: Make double the podi and store it in an airtight jar for up to a month — it lifts any stir-fried vegetable instantly.
Reduce the Guntur chillies to 3 for a family-friendly heat level without losing the smoky flavour.
Add the podi only on low heat in the final minutes; on high heat the ground dal burns and turns bitter within seconds.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the vepudu beside hot steamed rice with a spoon of Anveshan Ghee and a ladle of thin rasam — the ghee tempers the Guntur heat beautifully.

variations.name: Kerala Spicy Bhindi (Vendakka Thoran Style)
variations.description: A coastal reinterpretation where okra is stir-fried in coconut oil and finished with a fresh coconut-shallot crumble spiked with green chillies and curry leaves. The dish is gentler than northern versions, with the sweetness of coconut cushioning a clean, bright chilli heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil gives the thoran its unmistakable Malabar fragrance that refined oils flatten out

steps: Pulse ¾ cup fresh grated coconut with 4 green chillies, 4 shallots and ½ tsp turmeric in a mixer for just 3-4 short pulses to make a coarse, crumbly mixture — it should look like damp breadcrumbs, not a paste.
Wash and dry 500 g okra thoroughly, then slice it into thin 1 cm rounds so the pieces cook quickly and catch the coconut crumble in their ridges.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a wide pan on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds for 30 seconds, then add 2 torn dried red chillies, 15 curry leaves and the remaining 4 sliced shallots and fry for 2 minutes until the shallots soften and turn light gold.
Add the okra rounds with 1 tsp salt and stir-fry uncovered on medium heat for 8-9 minutes, tossing every 2 minutes, until the rounds lose their stickiness and develop light golden edges.

Scatter the coconut-chilli crumble over the okra, sprinkle ½ tsp crushed black pepper, and toss on low heat for 3-4 minutes until the coconut smells toasted and every okra round is flecked with the mixture.
Cover the pan, switch off the heat and let the thoran steam in its own residual warmth for 2 minutes so the coconut perfumes the okra before serving.
tips: Use freshly grated coconut, not desiccated — the natural moisture is what binds the crumble to the okra.
Thin rounds are key here; thick okra chunks will not pick up the coconut mixture properly.
Leftover thoran makes an excellent filling for a wrap with a smear of coconut chutney the next day.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle beside Kerala matta rice and a tangy pulissery, with pappadam crumbled over the thoran for crunch in the traditional Onam-style spread.

variations.name: Rajasthani Spicy Bhindi (Besan Wali Bhindi)
variations.description: A robust desert-style preparation where okra is tossed with roasted gram flour, crushed dried red chillies and a generous tadka of whole spices bloomed in Anveshan Ghee. The besan forms a savoury, nutty crust on each piece — a trick Rajasthani kitchens use to stretch flavour where fresh produce is scarce.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee is the backbone of Rajasthani cooking; its caramel notes toast the besan coating to a deep nutty finish

steps: Dry-roast 4 tbsp besan in a heavy pan on low heat for 5-6 minutes, stirring constantly, until it darkens a shade and smells nutty like roasted peanuts; tip it onto a plate so it stops cooking.
Wash, dry and slit 500 g okra lengthwise into quarters, keeping the strips long so the besan can cling along their inner surfaces.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat until fully melted and aromatic, then bloom 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 tsp fennel seeds and ½ tsp ajwain for 40 seconds until they crackle and darken slightly.

Add 4 crushed dried red chillies and immediately follow with the okra strips; stir-fry uncovered on medium heat for 9-10 minutes, tossing every 2 minutes, until the strips soften and their edges brown.

Sprinkle 2 tsp coriander powder, ½ tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt over the okra, toss for 1 minute, then dust the roasted besan evenly over the pan and toss gently for 3-4 minutes until every strip wears a golden, sandy crust.
Finish with 1 tsp amchur off the heat, tossing once so the sourness wakes up the roasted besan, and serve straight from the kadai while the coating is crisp.
tips: Roasting the besan separately before adding is essential — raw besan added to the pan turns gummy and tastes chalky.
If the coating looks dry, drizzle 1 extra tsp of melted Anveshan Ghee at the end rather than water, which would ruin the crust.
Crushed dried chillies give bursts of heat; swap in ½ tsp Kashmiri chilli powder if you prefer even, milder warmth.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot bajra rotis, a spoon of garlic chutney and chilled chaas on the side, the way it is eaten across rural Rajasthan at lunch.

variations.name: Classic Stuffed Paneer Paratha
variations.description: The definitive North Indian breakfast: soft khapli wheat discs hiding a crumbly, gently spiced paneer filling, roasted until blistered and brushed generously with bilona ghee. The khapli atta gives the crust a nutty sweetness that regular wheat cannot match, while the paneer stays moist and milky inside.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat kneads into a naturally soft dough that rolls thin without tearing over the paneer filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: One spoon goes into the dough for flake, the rest roasts each paratha to a golden, aromatic crust

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 1/2 tsp salt and about 3/4 cup water into a soft, non-sticky dough; knead 5 minutes until smooth, cover and rest 15 minutes.

Crumble 250 g paneer finely with your fingertips so no lumps remain, then mix in 1 finely chopped small onion, 2 minced green chillies, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1/2 tsp salt and 3 tbsp chopped coriander.

Divide the dough into 8 equal balls and the filling into 8 portions of about 2 tbsp each. Flatten a ball into a 4-inch cup, place one filling portion in the centre, gather the edges over the top and pinch to seal completely.
Dust the stuffed ball lightly with khapli atta and roll gently with even pressure into a 6-inch round, rotating a quarter turn after every few strokes so the filling spreads evenly without bursting.

Heat a tava over medium heat until a pinch of flour browns in 10 seconds. Cook the paratha 1 minute until small bubbles appear, flip, then brush 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee over each side and roast, pressing the edges with a spatula, until both faces carry deep golden-brown spots, about 3 minutes total.
Repeat with the remaining balls, re-greasing the tava with a little Anveshan Ghee between parathas, and stack the finished ones in a cloth-lined box so they stay soft and steamy.
tips: Squeeze the crumbled paneer in a muslin cloth if it feels wet; a dry filling is the single biggest guard against tearing while rolling.
Salt the filling only just before stuffing — onion and salt together weep water within 10 minutes and make sealing difficult.
The stuffed balls can be shaped and refrigerated up to 4 hours ahead; roll and roast straight from the fridge for a quick breakfast.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve two per plate with a bowl of chilled salted curd, a wedge of lime pickle and sweet milky chai for the full dhaba experience.

variations.name: Punjabi Stuffed Paneer Paratha
variations.description: The Amritsari-style indulgence where the paratha is roasted crisp in ghee, then crowned with a melting slick of white butter the moment it leaves the tava. Kasuri methi and ajwain in the dough give it that unmistakable highway-dhaba aroma, and the filling is punchier with ginger and anardana.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The high protein of emmer wheat holds the generous Punjabi-size filling without splitting at the seams

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Punjabi parathas are shallow-roasted, not brushed — bilona ghee crisps the crust without smoking

steps: Rub 1/2 tsp ajwain and 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then knead with roughly 3/4 cup water into a supple dough; rest it covered for 20 minutes.

Grate 250 g paneer on the large holes of a box grater and season with 1 tbsp grated ginger, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp anardana powder, 3/4 tsp red chilli powder, 1/2 tsp garam masala and 1/2 tsp salt, tossing lightly so the shreds stay fluffy.

Shape the dough into 8 balls. Cup each ball in your palm, pack in a heaping 2 tbsp of the paneer mixture, twist the gathered edge shut and press flat between your palms before rolling into a thick 6-inch round.

Set a heavy tava over medium-high heat. Lay a paratha on, wait 45 seconds until the underside sets, flip, then spoon 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee around the edges and shallow-roast each side, pressing firmly with a flat spatula, until crackly and mottled deep brown, about 4 minutes per paratha.
As each paratha comes off the tava, immediately top it with 1/2 tbsp white butter so it melts into the crisp surface while you cook the next one.
Stack the parathas loosely rather than airtight so the ghee-crisped crust stays crunchy at the edges the Punjabi way.
tips: Grating rather than crumbling the paneer is the Punjabi trick — the shreds knit together and never spill out when you bite in.
If you cannot find anardana, stir in 1 tsp of dried mango powder for the same sour lift against the rich butter.
Press the edges hard during roasting; the rim is the thickest part and undercooked edges taste doughy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a tall glass of sweet lassi and a spoon of gajar or gobhi pickle; in winter, add a bowl of sarson ka saag alongside for a true Punjabi thali.

variations.name: Bengali Stuffed Paneer Paratha
variations.description: A Kolkata-leaning take where the filling is sautéed in pungent mustard oil with nigella seeds and green chilli, echoing the flavours of chhanar dalna. The mustard oil is heated to its smoking point first, mellowing it into a fruity sharpness that clings to the soft paneer.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its faint earthiness stands up to mustard oil the way Bengali whole-wheat porota flour should

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed kachi ghani sharpness is the soul of this filling — smoke it briefly to tame the raw bite

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A final ghee roast gives the mustard-scented porota its glossy Bengali finish

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil, 1/2 tsp salt and about 3/4 cup water into a smooth, elastic dough and rest it under a damp cloth for 15 minutes.

Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai over medium-high heat until it just begins to smoke and turns pale, about 1 minute, then lower the heat and crackle 1/2 tsp nigella seeds for 20 seconds.

Add 1 tbsp grated ginger and 3 slit green chillies, stir 30 seconds until fragrant, then tumble in 250 g crumbled paneer with 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1/2 tsp sugar and 1/2 tsp salt; sauté 3 minutes until the paneer looks dry and pale gold, and cool completely with 2 tbsp chopped coriander folded through.
Divide dough and filling into 8 portions each, allowing 2 tbsp filling per ball. Stuff, seal by pleating the edges together, and roll each into a 6-inch round with gentle, even strokes.

Roast on a medium-hot tava for 1 minute per side until speckled, then brush both faces with a little of the 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and cook a further 2 minutes, flipping once, until the spots deepen to mahogany and the edges crisp.
Rest the porotas 2 minutes under a cloth before serving so the mustard aroma settles into the crumb.
tips: Do not skip smoking the mustard oil; raw kachi ghani oil tastes acrid, but 60 seconds of heat turns it nutty and fruity.
The pinch of sugar is classic Bengali seasoning, not sweetness — it rounds the mustard's pungency.
Cool the sautéed filling fully before stuffing or the steam will make the dough gummy and hard to seal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with begun bhaja (crisp fried aubergine slices) and a smear of kasundi mustard relish, finishing the meal with a piece of nolen gur sandesh if you can find it.

variations.name: Kerala Stuffed Paneer Paratha
variations.description: A Malabar-inspired crossover: the paneer is folded with fresh grated coconut, curry leaves and black pepper, then the paratha is roasted in coconut oil for a toasty, tropical crust. It eats like a cousin of the erachi-stuffed Malabar porotta but keeps the wholesome khapli wheat base.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Swaps Malabar maida for slow-digesting emmer wheat while keeping the porotta-soft layers

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed from fresh copra, it perfumes the crust with genuine Malabar toastiness

steps: Make the dough by kneading 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, 1/2 tsp salt and about 3/4 cup water until soft and stretchy; rest 15 minutes under a damp towel.

Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan over medium heat, pop 1/2 tsp mustard seeds until they sputter, then fry 2 sprigs of curry leaves and 4 sliced shallots for 2 minutes until the shallots turn translucent and lightly golden.

Add 2 chopped green chillies, 1/2 cup grated coconut and 1/4 tsp turmeric; toast 2 minutes until the coconut smells nutty, then fold in 200 g crumbled paneer, 3/4 tsp black pepper powder and 1/2 tsp salt, cook 1 minute more and cool completely.
Portion the dough into 8 balls and the coconut-paneer mixture into 8 lots of 2 tbsp each; stuff each ball, pinch the seam closed and roll softly into a 6-inch disc, flouring as needed.
Cook on a medium tava, drizzling 1/2 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil per side, for about 3 minutes per paratha, flipping twice, until both sides are freckled golden and the coconut aroma rises.
Scrunch each hot paratha gently between your palms, Malabar style, to loosen the layers before stacking.
tips: Use fresh or thawed frozen coconut, never desiccated — dry coconut robs the filling of its juicy sweetness.
Crushing the curry leaves slightly before frying releases far more of their citrusy oil into the filling.
Black pepper, not chilli powder, should lead the heat here; taste the cooled filling and add a pinch more if it whispers instead of warms.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coconut-milk vegetable stew or a sharp tomato-onion chammanthi, and cut the richness with slices of fresh pineapple on the side.

variations.name: Kashmiri Stuffed Paneer Paratha
variations.description: Inspired by the Valley's love of saffron and fennel, this version scents the paneer with bloomed Anveshan saffron, ground fennel and dry ginger — the signature warmth of Kashmiri wazwan cooking. The result is a pale-gold, faintly floral paratha that tastes celebratory rather than fiery.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its wheaty sweetness lets the delicate saffron perfume come through instead of fighting it

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Kashmiri cooking blooms saffron in warm fat — bilona ghee carries the strands' colour deepest

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: A dozen genuine Kashmiri threads steeped in warm milk stain the whole filling sunset gold

steps: Steep 1/4 tsp Anveshan Saffron strands in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside 10 minutes until the milk turns deep amber.
Meanwhile knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 1/2 tsp salt and about 3/4 cup water into a soft dough; rest it covered while you build the filling.

Toast 8 roughly chopped cashews in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee over low heat for 2 minutes until pale gold, then combine them with 250 g crumbled paneer, 1 tbsp raisins, 1 tsp fennel powder, 1/2 tsp dry ginger powder, 1/2 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1/2 tsp salt.
Pour the saffron milk over the filling and mix until every crumb is tinted gold; the mixture should hold together when pressed but not feel wet.
Stuff 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp filling apiece, seal the pleats firmly and roll each into a 6-inch round, dusting minimally so the pale colour shows.

Roast on a medium tava, brushing each side with the remaining Anveshan Ghee, for about 3 minutes per paratha until softly golden with light brown freckles — keep the heat moderate so the saffron does not scorch and turn bitter.
tips: Crush the saffron strands between your fingers before steeping; broken threads release twice the colour and aroma.
Fennel and dry ginger are the Kashmiri backbone — do not substitute garam masala or the profile collapses into generic North Indian.
These reheat beautifully wrapped in foil in a low oven for 8 minutes, making them ideal for festive make-ahead breakfasts.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sweetened saffron kahwa tea and a dollop of thick curd whisked with a pinch of fennel; for a festive brunch, add a bowl of warm dum aloo alongside.

variations.name: Classic Cheesy Onion Paratha
variations.description: A kid-favourite crossover where sharp raw onion meets molten cheese inside a wholegrain khapli shell. The onions are squeezed dry and the cheese grated fine, so the two knit into a gooey, savoury core that pulls into strings when you tear the paratha. Ghee-roasting gives the outside a lacy, golden crunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The nutty emmer flour balances the richness of melted cheese so the paratha never feels heavy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee browns the crust to a lacy crisp that contrasts the molten cheese centre

steps: Knead 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 1 cup water into a soft, smooth dough. Cover and let it relax for 20 minutes so it rolls thin without fighting back.
Finely chop 2 medium onions, mix with 0.25 tsp salt, wait 10 minutes, then squeeze them firmly in your fist to expel all the juice; cheese and watery onions are a recipe for burst parathas.

Toss the squeezed onions with 1 cup grated mozzarella, 0.5 cup grated processed cheese, 2 minced green chillies, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp chilli flakes and 3 tbsp chopped coriander until evenly combined.
Divide the dough into 8 balls and the filling into 8 loose mounds of about 3 tbsp each; the cheese compresses as you seal, so a generous mound is fine.
Flatten each ball into a bowl shape, pack in one mound of filling, gather the edges into a tight topknot and roll gently to a 6 inch round, keeping the pressure light over the middle.
Cook on a medium tava for about 2 minutes per side, brushing on a total of 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, until both faces are freckled deep gold and you can hear the cheese sizzling at any tiny gaps.
Rest each paratha for 1 minute before cutting; the molten cheese thickens just enough to stretch instead of gushing out.
tips: Mixing stretchy mozzarella with salty processed cheese gives both pull and flavour; either alone falls short.
Roll the stuffed ball with the sealed side down so the pleats fuse shut against the board.
Assemble only when ready to cook; cheese filling weeps if the stuffed balls sit for more than 15 minutes.
variations.servingSuggestion: Cut into wedges like a quesadilla and serve with tomato-garlic chutney and a tall glass of masala chaas.

variations.name: Punjabi Cheesy Onion Paratha
variations.description: The dhaba treatment: a thicker paratha, an ajwain-scented dough, and a filling where cheese melts into buttery onions softened with kasuri methi.
