It is finished the only way Punjab knows, with a knob of white butter melting over the hot crust. Rich, hearty and unapologetically indulgent.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Stone-ground khapli mimics the coarse chakki atta that gives dhaba parathas their rustic body

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Dhaba-style shallow roasting demands a fat that can take high tava heat, and bilona ghee does it with a caramel aroma

steps: Work 1 tsp ajwain and 1 tsp salt into 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, add 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then knead with roughly 1 cup water into a supple dough. Rest 20 minutes under a damp towel.
Melt 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat and soften 3 finely chopped onions with 0.25 tsp salt for 6-7 minutes until they turn glossy and pale gold at the edges.
Crush in 1 tbsp kasuri methi between your palms, add 1 tsp garam masala and 1 tsp red chilli powder, stir for 45 seconds, then cool the onion masala completely on a plate.
Fold 1.25 cups grated cheese into the cooled onions to make a rich, clumping filling, and divide it into 8 portions of about 3 tbsp.
Stuff 8 dough balls with the portions, seal the pleats and roll each to a thick 6 inch round; Punjabi parathas are rolled fat so the inside stays plush and molten.
Roast on a medium-hot tava for 2-3 minutes per side with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, pressing the edges with a spatula until both sides carry dark golden blisters.
Top each hot paratha with a quarter of the 2 tbsp white butter and let it melt into the crust before serving.
tips: Cooking the onions first sweetens them and removes moisture, so this version almost never leaks.
Crush ajwain lightly between your palms before kneading to release its thymol punch into the dough.
If the cheese firms up in the fridge, let the filling sit at room temperature for 10 minutes before stuffing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve dhaba-style with a bowl of dahi sprinkled with roasted jeera, sliced onions and a strong cup of adrak chai.

variations.name: Tamil Cheesy Onion Paratha
variations.description: A South-meets-cheese mashup where the filling gets a proper Tamil tadka of mustard seeds, urad dal and fresh curry leaves fried in wood-pressed sesame oil. Curry-leaf perfume cutting through molten cheese is a revelation, with sambar powder adding an earthy back-note. It eats like a cheese uttapam in paratha form.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer's mild sweetness plays the role rice batter does in an uttapam, grounding the sharp tadka flavours

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil is the soul of Tamil griddle cooking and gives the crust a toasty, nutty finish

steps: Knead 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and about 1 cup water for 7 minutes into a soft, stretchy dough, then rest it for 20 minutes.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a small kadhai on medium; crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds for 30 seconds, add 1 tsp urad dal and fry until it turns biscuit-gold, about 40 seconds.
Drop in the leaves of 2 curry sprigs and 2 chopped green chillies, sizzle 20 seconds, then add 2 finely chopped onions with 0.25 tsp salt and saute 5 minutes until translucent.
Sprinkle 1.5 tsp sambar powder over the onions, toast 1 minute until fragrant, then spread on a plate to cool. Mix in 1.25 cups grated mozzarella only once fully cool.
Portion the dough into 8 balls, stuff each with about 3 tbsp of the tadka-cheese filling, twist the gathered edges shut and roll softly into 6 inch rounds.
Griddle on medium heat for about 2 minutes per side, spooning the remaining 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil around the edges, until the crust turns a toasty brown with darker spots.
Slide each finished paratha onto a rack for a minute so the base stays crisp instead of steaming soft.
tips: Fry the urad dal only to biscuit-gold; a shade darker and it turns bitter through the whole filling.
Tear the curry leaves as they hit the oil to release maximum aroma into the filling.
A pinch of sambar powder dusted on the outside during roasting makes a fragrant, masala-crusted variant.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and a shot of hot filter coffee; the bitter coffee cuts the cheese richness perfectly.

variations.name: Andhra Cheesy Onion Paratha
variations.description: Fierce Guntur red chillies meet cooling cheese in this Andhra-style firecracker. The onions are cooked down with a dry-roasted Guntur chilli-garlic paste, so every cheesy bite arrives with a slow, smoky burn. It is the paratha for people who order everything extra-spicy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The wholegrain flour's earthy depth stands firm against Guntur chilli heat instead of disappearing under it

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Andhra kitchens fry their chilli pastes in groundnut oil, and this wood-pressed one adds a clean roasted-peanut note

steps: Prepare the dough with 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and around 1 cup water; knead until smooth and rest 20 minutes.

Dry-roast 4 Guntur chillies and 1 tsp coriander seeds on a low flame for 2 minutes until darkened a shade and smoky, then grind them with 6 garlic cloves and a splash of water into a coarse red paste.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium, crisp the leaves of 1 curry sprig for 15 seconds, then fry the chilli-garlic paste for 2 minutes until the oil separates at the edges.
Add 3 finely chopped onions, 0.25 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp turmeric powder and cook 6 minutes until the onions collapse into the fiery masala. Cool completely, then fold in 1.25 cups grated mozzarella.
Divide dough into 8 balls, stuff each with 3 tbsp of the chilli-cheese filling, seal the pleats firmly and roll out to 6 inch rounds with a light hand.
Roast on a medium-hot tava about 2 minutes per side with the remaining 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, until fierce red-flecked golden blisters cover the surface.
Let the parathas stand 2 minutes; the heat mellows fractionally and the cheese sets to a stretchy pull.
tips: Scale the Guntur chillies down to 2 for a family-friendly version; the smoky flavour survives even at lower heat.
Grinding the paste coarse leaves little chilli flecks that look stunning against the white cheese.
Keep a bowl of sweet curd on the table; it is the only thing that genuinely tames Guntur fire.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with chilled sweetened curd and thin onion rings soaked in lime juice, the classic Andhra heat-relief duo.

variations.name: Kerala Cheesy Onion Paratha
variations.description: Grated coconut and cheese might sound unlikely, but together they make a filling that is creamy, faintly sweet and irresistibly rich. Shallots, curry leaves and black pepper keep it firmly Malabari, while virgin coconut oil on the tava scents the whole kitchen. A tea-shop snack reimagined for cheese lovers.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli's gentle sweetness bridges the coconut and cheese so neither dominates the bite

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil perfumes both filling and crust with an unmistakable Malabar aroma

steps: Mix 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, then knead in about 1 cup water until soft and elastic. Rest the dough for 20 minutes under a wet cloth.
Warm 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil over medium heat and fry 12 sliced shallots, 2 chopped green chillies and 1 inch of minced ginger for 5 minutes until the shallots turn blond and sweet.
Add the torn leaves of 2 curry sprigs and 0.5 cup fresh grated coconut and toast 2 minutes until the coconut smells nutty, then season with 1 tsp crushed black pepper and 0.25 tsp salt.
Cool the coconut-shallot mixture fully, then work in 1 cup grated mozzarella so the filling holds together in soft clumps.
Shape 8 dough balls, load each with roughly 3 tbsp filling, gather and twist the edges closed, and roll gently into 6 inch rounds.
Cook on a medium tava for about 2 minutes each side, brushing with the remaining 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, until golden-brown patches spread across the surface and the edges crisp.
Stand the parathas on their edges in a rack for a minute so trapped steam escapes and the crust stays snappy.
tips: Shallots are worth the peeling effort; their concentrated sweetness is half the character of this filling.
Toast the coconut only until nutty and still white; browned coconut turns the filling grainy.
Freshly crushed pepper added at the end keeps its bite; pre-ground pepper fades into the cheese.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a sharp tomato-onion chutney or Kerala-style lime pickle, plus cardamom tea to round off the coastal mood.

variations.name: Classic Cheesy Paneer Paratha
variations.description: A kid-favourite double-dairy paratha: crumbled paneer for body and grated melting cheese for stretch, wrapped in nutty khapli wheat and roasted in bilona ghee. Cut it open hot and the cheese pulls in ribbons while the paneer keeps every bite substantial rather than greasy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat's gentle gluten stretches around the molten cheese core without springing leaks

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasting in bilona ghee browns the crust before the cheese inside can overheat and turn oily

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 1/2 tsp salt and about 3/4 cup water into a soft, pliable dough; work it 5 minutes until smooth, then rest covered for 15 minutes.

Crumble 150 g paneer finely and toss with 100 g grated mozzarella, 1 finely chopped small onion, 2 minced green chillies, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder, 1/2 tsp black pepper and 1/4 tsp salt plus 3 tbsp chopped coriander.
Divide the dough into 8 balls and the cheesy mixture into 8 portions of about 2 tbsp each; flatten each ball into a cup, tuck in one portion, gather the edges over the filling and pinch shut.
Roll each stuffed ball gently into a 6-inch round on a floured board, easing off pressure near the centre so the cheese does not squeeze through.

Roast on a medium-hot tava: 1 minute untouched until bubbles rise, flip, brush 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee on each side and cook about 3 minutes total, pressing lightly, until both faces show crisp golden-brown patches.
Rest each paratha 1 minute before cutting so the molten cheese thickens enough to pull rather than pour.
tips: Keep the cheese-to-paneer ratio at 2:3; more cheese than that liquefies on the tava and bursts the seams.
Chill the mixed filling 10 minutes before stuffing — cold cheese rolls far more forgivingly than room-temperature cheese.
If a paratha springs a cheese leak on the tava, dust the spot with dry atta and flip immediately; it will seal itself as it sets.
variations.servingSuggestion: Slice into wedges pizza-style and serve with a smoky tomato chutney and a glass of masala chaas — the tang cuts the double-dairy richness perfectly.

variations.name: Punjabi Cheesy Paneer Paratha
variations.description: The dhaba blockbuster made naughtier: a ginger-and-anardana spiked paneer-cheese filling inside an ajwain-scented crust, shallow-roasted in ghee and finished with a knob of white butter melting over the top. This is the paratha that draws a crowd off the highway.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Sturdy emmer dough shoulders a dhaba-generous double-dairy stuffing without tearing on the roll

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Spooned around the edges tava-style so every layer fries crisp the way Amritsar likes it

steps: Work 1/2 tsp ajwain, 1/2 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, then knead with about 3/4 cup water into a supple dough and rest 20 minutes under a damp cloth.

Grate 150 g paneer and 100 g cheddar together, then fold in 1 tbsp grated ginger, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp anardana powder, 1/2 tsp garam masala, 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi and 1/4 tsp salt, keeping the mixture light and shredded.
Divide the dough into 8 balls and pack each with a heaping 2 tbsp of filling; twist the gathered top shut, flatten between your palms and roll into a thick 6-inch disc.

Heat a heavy tava on medium-high until water droplets skitter. Cook each paratha 45 seconds until set underneath, flip, spoon 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee around the rim and roast both sides, pressing with the spatula, until crackly and deep brown, about 4 minutes each.
Crown every paratha straight off the tava with 1/2 tbsp white butter so it melts down into the cheese-scented crust.
Serve immediately in batches rather than stacking long — the cheddar centre is at its stretchy best in the first five minutes.
tips: Sharp cheddar stands up to garam masala better than mozzarella; use mozzarella only if you want stretch over flavour.
The anardana's sourness keeps the double-dairy filling from tasting flat — do not omit it, or substitute 1 tsp amchur.
Rope in a helper: one person rolling while another roasts keeps the tava at full temper and the parathas crispest.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a whole green chilli fried in ghee, a mound of shredded-carrot pickle and a tall sweet lassi for a proper GT Road breakfast.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Cheesy Paneer Paratha
variations.description: Goda masala — that smoky, coconut-and-stone-flower blend unique to Maharashtra — transforms the cheese-paneer filling into something deeply savoury and faintly sweet. Roasted peanut crush adds the crunch a Puneri home cook would insist on.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer's rustic flavour mirrors the bhakri-loving Deccan palate while staying roll-out soft

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed peanut oil doubles down on the filling's roasted-peanut theme as it crisps the crust

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Just a spoon in the dough for tenderness, letting groundnut oil lead on the tava

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 1/2 tsp salt and roughly 3/4 cup water until soft and springy, then rest the dough 15 minutes.

Coarsely crush 3 tbsp roasted peanuts in a mortar — pebbly, not powdery — and mix them with 150 g crumbled paneer, 100 g grated processed cheese, 2 tsp goda masala, 2 minced green chillies, 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1/4 tsp salt and 3 tbsp chopped coriander.
Shape 8 dough balls, stuff each with 2 tbsp of the peanut-cheese mixture, seal the pleats and roll out gently to 6-inch rounds, dusting with atta as needed.

Roast on a medium tava for 1 minute until the first side blisters, flip, then drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil per side and cook about 3 minutes total, pressing the edges, until nut-brown spots cover both faces.
Let each paratha sit 1 minute off the heat so the cheese binds the peanut crunch instead of running.
Repeat with the remaining rounds, wiping crumbs off the tava between batches so stray peanuts do not scorch and turn bitter.
tips: Goda masala loses its aroma fast once opened — store it frozen and it will perfume this filling for months.
Crush the peanuts just before mixing; pre-ground peanut powder turns pasty against the melting cheese.
If goda masala is unavailable, dry-roast 1 tsp sesame, 1 tsp coconut and 1/2 tsp cumin and grind — close enough to save the dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a katori of spiced buttermilk (mattha) and a spoonful of thecha on the side for those who like the Maharashtrian chilli kick.

variations.name: Andhra Cheesy Paneer Paratha
variations.description: Fiery Guntur chillies meet cooling cheese in this Andhra-style rendition, where the filling is laced with a garlicky red-chilli podi and curry-leaf crunch. The cheese is not a gimmick here — it is the buffer that lets you enjoy Guntur heat at full volume.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The wheat's subtle sweetness tempers Guntur fire the way jowar roti does in Rayalaseema homes

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Nuvvula nune is Andhra's frying fat of choice — its toasty depth belongs beside chilli podi

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, 1/2 tsp salt and about 3/4 cup water into a soft dough; cover and rest 15 minutes.

Make a quick podi: dry-roast 4 Guntur chillies, 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1 tsp coriander seeds on low heat for 3 minutes until the chillies deepen and crackle, cool, then grind coarsely with 6 garlic cloves and 1/4 tsp salt.

Fry 2 sprigs of curry leaves in 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil for 30 seconds until glassy and crisp, crumble them, and mix with 150 g crumbled paneer, 100 g grated mozzarella, the ground podi and 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
Divide dough into 8 balls, stuff each with 2 tbsp of the fiery filling, seal well and roll into 6-inch rounds with a light hand so the cheese stays put.
Roast each paratha on a medium-hot tava, drizzling 1/2 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil per side, for about 3 minutes until both faces carry dark toasted freckles and the podi smells smoky.
Rest 1 minute before serving so the molten cheese and chilli oil settle into a cohesive, scoopable centre.
tips: Roast the Guntur chillies low and slow; scorched chillies turn acrid instead of smoky-hot.
Grinding the podi coarse leaves little chilli flecks that hit intermittently — much more exciting than uniform heat.
Scale the chillies down to 2 for children; the recipe survives, the fireworks just dim.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sweetened curd and a wedge of lime; Andhra households would add a spoon of ghee-drizzled avakaya pickle for the brave.

variations.name: Tamil Cheesy Paneer Paratha
variations.description: A Chennai tiffin-room fantasy: the paneer-cheese filling is tempered with mustard seeds, urad dal and a shower of crisped curry leaves, tasting like the best parts of a masala dosa filling folded into a wheat paratha. Black pepper and ginger keep it bright rather than heavy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Brings chapati-soft wholesomeness to a tiffin-style filling usually trapped inside refined-flour breads

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Tamil tiffin rooms finish everything on the dosa kal with ghee — this paratha is no exception

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: The tempering blooms in gingelly oil first, exactly as a Tamil kitchen would start it

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, 1/2 tsp salt and about 3/4 cup water into a smooth, soft dough; rest it 15 minutes under a damp cloth.

Heat the remaining Anveshan Sesame Oil in a small pan over medium heat, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds fully, then brown 1 tsp urad dal for 30 seconds until biscuit-gold and crisp 3 sprigs of curry leaves in the same oil.

Off the heat, stir in 1 tbsp grated ginger and 2 chopped green chillies for 20 seconds, then pour this tempering over 150 g crumbled paneer mixed with 100 g grated mozzarella, 3/4 tsp black pepper and 1/4 tsp salt; toss and cool.
Stuff 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp filling each, pleat closed, and roll into 6-inch rounds, keeping the pressure feather-light over the centre.
Cook on a medium tava like a dosa-master: 1 minute dry, flip, then 1/2 tsp Anveshan Ghee smeared per side and about 3 minutes more until lacy brown spots cover both faces.
Stack under a cloth for 2 minutes; the trapped steam relaxes the crust so it folds like a soft parotta.
tips: Let the urad dal turn truly golden — pale dal stays chalky, and its nutty crunch is half the point of this variation.
Fresh curry leaves only; dried ones smell of hay and vanish against the cheese.
A pinch of asafoetida in the tempering deepens the tiffin-room authenticity if you have it on hand.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and a small tumbler of sambar for dipping, followed by strong filter coffee poured frothy from a dabara set.

variations.name: Classic Carrot Paratha
variations.description: Sweet winter carrots are grated fine, squeezed, and kneaded straight into khapli atta dough along with warm spices, so every layer of the paratha carries a faint orange blush. Because the carrot is in the dough rather than stuffed, it rolls easily and never leaks. Roasted in bilona ghee, it is the easiest way to get vegetables into a fussy eater's breakfast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat absorbs the carrot's moisture without turning gummy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Carrots and ghee are natural partners; the ghee blooms their sweetness on the tava

steps: Grate 1.5 cups carrot on the fine side of the grater, sprinkle with 0.25 tsp of the salt, rest 5 minutes, then squeeze firmly over a bowl and reserve the orange juice for kneading.

In a wide bowl mix 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with the squeezed carrot, grated 1 inch ginger, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric powder, 0.5 tsp ajwain, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp chopped coriander.
Add 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and knead, using the reserved carrot juice plus up to 0.5 cup water added little by little, into a soft dough that yields under a fingertip; rest it covered for 15 minutes.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, dust each with dry atta and roll into 6-inch rounds of even thickness, rotating the disc a quarter turn between strokes so it stays circular.
Cook each paratha on a hot tava over medium-high heat for about 1 minute until small bubbles rise, flip, and cook 1 minute more until brown freckles appear on both sides.
Brush both sides with a share of the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and roast 30 seconds per side, pressing lightly with a spatula, until the surface crisps and smells toasty.
tips: Squeezing the carrot is non-negotiable; unsqueezed carrot releases water on the tava and makes the paratha limp.
Knead with the reserved carrot juice first for deeper colour and flavour before touching plain water.
The dough keeps refrigerated for a day; the parathas actually roll better after an overnight rest.
variations.servingSuggestion: Plate with fresh homemade white butter and a spoon of green chilli pickle; for kids, a drizzle of honey over the hot paratha is magic.

variations.name: Gujarati Carrot Paratha
variations.description: In classic Gujarati fashion, this carrot paratha balances sweet, tangy and spicy in one bite: jaggery melts into the carrot dough while lemon and green chilli keep it lively. Sesame seeds pressed onto the surface toast against the tava for a nutty finish. It sits somewhere between a thepla and a paratha, and disappears fast at tea time.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its gentle wheatiness lets the jaggery-lemon interplay lead the flavour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Chemical-free jaggery dissolves evenly into the dough for the signature Gujarati sweetness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the traditional Gujarati roasting fat for theplas and parathas

steps: Squeeze 1.5 cups grated carrot well and toss it with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder; let it sit 5 minutes so the jaggery dissolves into a light glaze over the shreds.

Combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with the glazed carrot, 2 minced green chillies, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp salt and 1 tbsp lemon juice, mixing until the flour looks evenly speckled orange.
Add 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and knead with up to 0.5 cup water, added a splash at a time, into a soft, slightly glossy dough; cover and rest 15 minutes.
Shape into 8 balls, press each ball into 1 tbsp sesame seeds spread on a plate so the seeds stud one face, then roll seed-side up into thin 6.5-inch rounds.
Roast on a medium-hot tava for about 45 seconds until the underside sets, flip, and cook 1 minute until light brown spots show; jaggery browns fast, so keep the flame at medium.
Spoon a little of the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil around the edges and over the top, and roast each side another 30 seconds until the sesame turns golden and aromatic.
tips: Keep the flame no higher than medium; the jaggery in the dough caramelises and can scorch before the paratha cooks through.
These stay soft for two days, making them ideal travel food in true thepla tradition; stack in foil once fully cool.
Add 1 tbsp fine besan to the dough if your carrots are very juicy; it quietly absorbs the extra moisture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve rolled up with chhundo (sweet mango pickle) and a cup of masala chai, or pack with plain curd sweetened with a pinch of jaggery.

variations.name: Tamil Carrot Paratha
variations.description: This southern take tempers mustard seeds, chana dal and a fistful of curry leaves in sesame oil, then folds the crackling tadka into the carrot dough itself. The chana dal gives tiny toasty bites through the soft flatbread, an idea borrowed from Tamil carrot poriyal. Roasted in wood-pressed sesame oil, it has that unmistakable nallennai depth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: A sturdy yet tender base that carries the sesame oil tadka without cracking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil gives the authentic Tamil nallennai aroma to both tadka and tava

steps: Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a small pan on medium heat; add 1 tbsp chana dal and fry about 90 seconds until pale gold, then add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop for 20 seconds.

Drop in 2 torn dried red chillies, 15 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp hing; the leaves will crackle and turn glassy in about 15 seconds. Tip in 1.5 cups squeezed grated carrot and sauté 3 minutes until barely tender, then cool completely.
Pour the cooled carrot tadka, oil and all, over 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp coarsely crushed black pepper, and rub through the flour with your fingers.
Knead with up to 0.5 cup water, adding it in stages, into a supple dough that holds a thumbprint; rest covered for 15 minutes so the dal softens slightly in the dough.
Divide into 8 balls and roll each into a 6-inch disc, rolling gently so the chana dal bits do not puncture the surface.

Cook on a hot tava at medium-high for about 1 minute per side until blistered, then drizzle a share of the remaining 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil around each paratha and roast 30 seconds more per side until the edges crisp and the curry-leaf aroma lifts off the pan.
tips: Fry the chana dal patiently until fully golden; underdone dal stays chalky even after the paratha cooks.
Cool the tadka before it touches the flour, or the hot oil will make the dough greasy and hard to knead.
A pinch of sugar in the dough is a quiet Tamil hotel trick that deepens the browning on the tava.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and a small bowl of sambar for dunking, or with curd rice on a banana leaf for a full Tamil lunch.

variations.name: Rajasthani Carrot Paratha
variations.description: A desert-style paratha where the carrot dough is fired up with a coarse paste of dried red chillies and garlic, echoing Rajasthan's lahsun chutney. Kasuri methi and a hint of amchur give it that dry, savoury depth Marwari kitchens are famous for. It is rolled thick, roasted slowly, and finished with plenty of ghee, as the desert demands.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Hearty emmer flour suits Rajasthan's thick, slow-roasted paratha style

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Desert cooking finishes everything with ghee; it tempers the fierce chilli-garlic paste

steps: Soak 4 dried red chillies in 3 tbsp hot water for 10 minutes, then pound them with 6 garlic cloves and 0.25 tsp salt in a mortar into a coarse, brick-red paste.
Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan over medium heat and fry the chilli-garlic paste for about 2 minutes until the raw garlic smell fades and the ghee stains red; cool it down.

Mix 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1.5 cups squeezed grated carrot, the cooled chilli-garlic ghee, 2 tbsp crushed kasuri methi, 0.75 tsp amchur, 1 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder and 0.75 tsp salt.
Knead with up to 0.5 cup water, added gradually, into a firm yet pliable dough, then rest it under a damp cloth for 15 minutes.
Divide into 6 thick balls and roll each into a 5.5-inch round about 0.5 cm thick; Rajasthani parathas are rolled stout, not thin.

Roast on a medium-low tava for 2 minutes per side so the thick disc cooks through, then raise the heat, slather both sides using the remaining 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, and cook 45 seconds per side until the crust is burnished and crisp.
tips: Frying the chilli-garlic paste in ghee first removes its raw pungency and stops it from tasting harsh in the dough.
Roll these thicker than normal parathas; thin rolling dries them out during the slow roast.
Swap 2 of the dried chillies for Kashmiri chillies if you want the deep red colour with less heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Marwari way with a katori of chaas, a smear of extra lahsun chutney, and a piece of onion-tomato kachumber to cool the palate.

variations.name: Kashmiri Carrot Paratha
variations.description: A gently royal version where the carrot dough is scented with saffron steeped in warm milk, ground fennel and dry ginger, the twin pillars of Kashmiri spicing. The paratha turns a deep marigold on the tava, its aroma closer to a festive bread than an everyday flatbread. Slivered almonds kneaded in give it a delicate, celebratory crunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Soft emmer crumb shows off the saffron's colour like a canvas

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: GI-tagged Pampore threads bloom into a marigold hue and honeyed aroma in warm milk

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee-roasting carries the saffron and fennel fragrance into every layer

steps: Crush 0.25 tsp Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron threads between your fingers into 0.5 cup warm milk and let them steep for 10 minutes until the milk turns a deep amber.
Toss 1.5 cups finely grated, well-squeezed carrot with 1.5 tsp fennel powder, 0.75 tsp dry ginger powder and 0.25 tsp cardamom powder so the spice coats every shred.

Combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, the spiced carrot, 3 tbsp slivered almonds, 0.75 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then knead with the saffron milk, topping up with at most 0.25 cup water, into a soft golden dough; rest 15 minutes.
Divide into 8 balls and roll each into a 6-inch round, dusting sparingly with atta so the saffron colour stays bright on the surface.
Cook on a medium tava for about 1 minute per side until pale gold spots form; the milk in the dough browns quickly, so watch the heat.
Brush both sides with a share of the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and roast a final 30 seconds per side until the paratha glows amber and the fennel aroma rises.
tips: Steep the saffron a full 10 minutes; rushed steeping wastes half its colour and fragrance.
Keep the tava at medium; the milk-kneaded dough scorches faster than a water dough.
For a festive brunch, sprinkle the hot parathas with 1 tsp of extra jaggery powder and a few saffron threads before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with sweetened saffron curd or a cup of kahwa; for a savoury table, serve alongside Kashmiri dum aloo for a stunning contrast.

variations.name: Classic Sattu Paratha
variations.description: The everyday pride of eastern Indian kitchens: nutty roasted gram sattu moistened with ghee, lemon and green chilli, wrapped in a soft khapli wheat shell. The filling stays slightly crumbly, so each bite releases a puff of toasty gram aroma. It is protein-rich, deeply satisfying and best eaten straight off the tava.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Stone-ground emmer wheat rolls thin without tearing, essential for a crumbly sattu filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Slow-roasted chana sattu with a fresh, nutty aroma that packaged supermarket sattu rarely has

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Moistens the dry sattu filling and gives the roasted crust its golden sheen

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 3/4 cup water into a soft, pliable dough that does not stick to your fingers. Cover with a damp cloth and rest for 20 minutes.

In a wide bowl, mix 1 cup Anveshan Sattu with 1 finely chopped small onion, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric powder, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder, 1/2 tsp salt and 2 tbsp chopped coriander.

Drizzle in 1 tbsp melted Anveshan Ghee and 1 tbsp lemon juice, then sprinkle 2-3 tbsp water a spoon at a time, rubbing with your fingertips until the sattu just clumps when pressed but is not wet or pasty.
Divide the dough into 8 balls and the sattu mix into 8 portions of about 2 tbsp each. Flatten each ball into a 4-inch cup, fill with one portion, pull the edges together and pinch the seam closed.
Rest the stuffed balls seam-side down for 5 minutes, then roll each into a 6-7 inch round with light, even pressure, dusting sparingly with dry atta.

Roast on a hot tava over medium heat for about a minute until the base shows brown spots, flip, apply 1/2 tsp Anveshan Ghee, and cook the second side likewise; give each side one more ghee-roasted minute until golden and blistered.
Tap each finished paratha lightly between your palms to loosen the filling, which makes it fluffier, and keep wrapped in cloth until serving.
tips: The filling should hold together only when squeezed; over-wetting it produces a dense, doughy centre instead of a crumbly one.
Rub the filling mixture between your palms for a minute before stuffing, an old Bihari trick that distributes the ghee and deepens the roasted flavour.
Leftover parathas revive perfectly when dry-toasted for two minutes; avoid the microwave, which turns them leathery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with baingan chokha, a spoon of mustard-laced mango pickle and chilled sweet lassi for the full eastern-India experience.

variations.name: Bihari Sattu Paratha
variations.description: The homeland original, eaten from Patna to Bhagalpur, where the sattu is famously seasoned with mustard oil, ajwain and chopped pickle masala scraped from the achaar jar. The raw kick of kachi ghani mustard oil against tangy pickle spices is what separates a true Bihari sattu paratha from every imitation. Robust, rustic and unapologetically pungent.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: In Bihar the sattu must taste freshly roasted; this stone-milled version delivers that warm gram fragrance

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: The defining Bihari ingredient; its sharp pungency seasons the filling raw and crisps the crust

ingredients.name: Ajwain seeds
ingredients.note: Bloomed briefly in hot mustard oil before mixing so they never taste raw

ingredients.name: Mango pickle masala
ingredients.note: The oily spice paste scraped from a jar of aam ka achaar

steps: Bring 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to a light smoke in a small pan, drop in 1 tsp ajwain and 1/2 tsp kalonji, let them sizzle for 20 seconds off the heat, and set this tempered oil aside to cool.
Knead the dough: combine 2 cups khapli atta, 1/2 tsp salt and about 3/4 cup water, working it for 5 minutes into a soft, springy mass; rest covered for 20 minutes.
In a bowl, toss 1 cup Anveshan Sattu with 4 minced garlic cloves, grated 1 inch ginger, 3 chopped green chillies, 1 tbsp mango pickle masala and 1/2 tsp salt.
Pour the cooled tempered mustard oil and 1 tbsp lemon juice over the sattu, then sprinkle 2 tbsp water gradually and rub everything together until the mixture holds a loose ball when squeezed.
Shape 8 dough balls, stuff each with roughly 2 tbsp of the sattu masala, seal the gathers firmly and roll into 6-inch rounds, keeping them a touch thick in the Bihari style.

Roast on a medium-hot tava for about 90 seconds per side until spotted, then smear 1/2 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil on each face and cook until the crust turns deep golden and smells sharply nutty, about 4 minutes per paratha in total.
Crush each hot paratha slightly between your palms before serving so the steam escapes and the filling loosens.
tips: The pickle masala varies in salt, so taste the filling before adding the full half teaspoon of salt.
If serving to guests unused to raw mustard oil, temper all of it rather than reserving any raw; the flavour stays but the bite mellows.
These are traditionally eaten torn, not cut, so the crumbly filling can be scooped up with the crust.
variations.servingSuggestion: Present the Bihari way with a trio of chokhas — roasted eggplant, tomato and boiled potato — plus green chilli and a raw mango achaar on the side.

variations.name: Punjabi Sattu Paratha
variations.description: Punjab treats every stuffed paratha as a canvas for dairy, and this one is no exception: the sattu is enriched with white butter, kasuri methi and pomegranate seeds for tang. Rolled thicker, roasted in ghee until shatteringly crisp, and crowned with another knob of butter at the table. It is richer and more indulgent than the eastern original.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Sturdy enough to hold a butter-enriched filling without going soggy on the tava

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Its clean roasted-gram flavour stands up well to the richness of butter and ghee

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Punjabi parathas demand a lavish ghee roast for that dhaba-style crackle

steps: Prepare a soft dough from 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and approximately 3/4 cup water, kneading a full 6-7 minutes for the gluten to develop; rest 20 minutes under a damp towel.
Finely chop 1 medium onion, sprinkle with a pinch of salt, wait 5 minutes, then squeeze out its juice firmly; this stops the filling from turning watery.
Combine 1 cup Anveshan Sattu with the squeezed onion, 2 minced green chillies, 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi, 1 tsp anardana powder, 1/2 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder and 1/2 tsp salt.
Work 2 tbsp softened white butter into the sattu with your fingertips until the mix resembles damp sand and clumps when pressed; add a spoon of water only if it refuses to hold.
Make 8 balls of dough, load each with 2 tbsp of the buttery sattu, seal well and roll to a thickish 6-inch round so the paratha stays plush at the centre.

Roast each on a medium-hot tava, 1 minute per side dry, then with 1/2 tsp Anveshan Ghee per side until both faces are richly browned and crisp at the edges, about 4 minutes total; press the rim with a cloth so it cooks evenly.
Top each hot paratha with a small knob of the remaining white butter just before it leaves the kitchen.
tips: Squeezing the onion is the single most important step; skipping it guarantees leaky parathas.
Anardana gives a fruity tang that lemon cannot mimic here, and it keeps the filling dry, so seek it out.
For a true dhaba finish, crisp the finished paratha directly over a low open flame for ten seconds per side.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a tall glass of salted lassi, sliced radish and onion rings, and a bowl of dahi whipped with a pinch of black salt.

variations.name: Odia Sattu Paratha
variations.description: Odisha stamps its identity on this paratha with panch phoron, the five-seed blend of cumin, mustard, fennel, kalonji and fenugreek, bloomed in hot oil and folded through the sattu. Grated fresh ginger and a hint of jaggery nod to the temple-state's love of gentle sweet-savoury balance. The result is aromatic and mellow rather than fiery.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Fresh-roasted sattu carries the panch phoron aroma beautifully without any bitterness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Coastal Odia kitchens fry in pungent mustard oil; it is the backbone of the panch phoron tempering

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A discreet Odia-style sweet note that rounds off the bitter fenugreek in the five-spice

ingredients.name: Panch phoron
ingredients.note: Always bloomed in hot oil first, never mixed in raw

steps: Mix 2 cups khapli atta with 1/2 tsp salt and knead with about 3/4 cup water into a smooth, medium-soft dough; set aside covered for 20 minutes.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a small kadhai until it shimmers, lower the flame, and bloom 2 tsp panch phoron for 30-40 seconds until the mustard seeds pop and the fenugreek darkens a shade, then add 8 curry leaves and switch off.
Pour this sizzling tempering, oil and all, over 1 cup Anveshan Sattu in a wide bowl and stir while it is still warm so the seeds distribute evenly.

Season the sattu with 1 tbsp grated ginger, 2 chopped green chillies, 1/4 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1/2 tsp salt and 2 tsp lemon juice, then sprinkle 2 tbsp water and rub until the mix clumps softly in your fist.
Portion the dough into 8 balls, stuff each with 2 tbsp of the tempered sattu, seal and roll gently into 6-7 inch circles, rotating after each stroke for an even round.

Cook on a medium tava, allowing about a minute per bare side, then brush each side with 1/2 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and roast until crisp, deep-gold patches cover both faces, roughly 4 minutes per paratha.
tips: Watch the fenugreek seeds closely during blooming; a shade past golden they turn bitter enough to spoil the whole batch.
Warm tempering poured directly over sattu toasts it a second time, so do not wait for the oil to cool.
If your panch phoron is heavy on fenugreek, add an extra pinch of the jaggery powder to compensate.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside dalma or a simple tomato khatta chutney, with a piece of chhena poda for dessert if you want the full Odia thali feel.

variations.name: Kerala Sattu Paratha
variations.description: A Malabar-inspired crossover where the sattu filling meets fresh grated coconut, curry leaves and crushed black pepper, all brought together with wood-pressed coconut oil. The coconut keeps the stuffing moist and faintly sweet, while pepper supplies the warmth Kerala has traded on for centuries. Softer and more fragrant than its northern cousins.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its gentle sweetness pairs naturally with fresh coconut in the filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Roasted gram and coconut are old south-Indian companions, as any puttu-podi lover knows

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed from fresh copra, it perfumes both filling and crust with true Malabar character

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and around 3/4 cup water into a soft, silky dough, then rest it covered for 20 minutes.

Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil over medium heat and pop 1/2 tsp mustard seeds fully, about 30 seconds. Add 5 sliced shallots, 12 curry leaves and 2 chopped green chillies and saute until the shallots edge toward gold, 2-3 minutes.
Stir in 1/2 cup fresh grated coconut and toast for 2 minutes until it smells nutty and loses its raw wetness, then switch off the heat.

Fold in 1 cup Anveshan Sattu, 1 tsp crushed black pepper, 1/4 tsp turmeric powder and 1/2 tsp salt; the residual warmth binds the mix, but sprinkle 1-2 tbsp water if it will not clump when squeezed. Cool fully.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, fill each with 2 tbsp of the coconut-sattu mixture, pinch the seams shut and roll into soft 6-7 inch rounds.

Roast on a medium tava for about a minute per side until freckled, then anoint each side with 1/2 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and cook until golden with crisp edges, around 4 minutes per paratha; the kitchen should smell of toasted coconut.
tips: Frozen grated coconut works if thawed and squeezed dry, but toast it a minute longer to drive off extra moisture.
Crush the peppercorns coarsely at home; pre-ground pepper loses the bright, citrusy heat this filling depends on.
These parathas taste even better ten minutes after cooking, once the coconut oil aroma settles into the crumb.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a coconut-coriander chutney and sweet milky chaya, or serve alongside a simple moru curry for a light Kerala lunch.

variations.name: Classic Dhaba-style Aloo Matar
variations.description: The highway-dhaba original: potatoes and sweet green peas simmered in a rustic onion-tomato masala that clings to every cube. Slow-browned onions and a final flourish of kasuri methi give it that smoky roadside depth you can never quite get from a restaurant curry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed groundnut oil takes high dhaba-style heat without smoking, so the onions brown deeply instead of burning

steps: Peel 3 medium potatoes and cut them into 2 cm cubes; finely chop 2 medium onions and 3 medium tomatoes and keep everything within reach of the stove.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a heavy kadai on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 20 seconds until they darken a shade and smell nutty.

Add the chopped onions with a pinch of the salt and sauté on medium heat for 8-10 minutes, stirring often, until they turn a deep golden brown; stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute more until the raw smell disappears.

Tip in the chopped tomatoes along with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, and cook on medium for 6-7 minutes until the masala thickens and oil beads appear at the edges.

Add the potato cubes, 1 cup green peas, 1.25 tsp salt and 1.5 cups hot water; bring to a boil, then cover and simmer on low for 14-15 minutes until a knife slides through the potatoes without resistance.
Crush 1 tsp kasuri methi between your palms into the pan, sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala, and simmer uncovered for 2 minutes so the gravy turns glossy and coats the vegetables.
Switch off the heat, scatter 3 tbsp chopped fresh coriander leaves over the curry and let it rest, covered, for 5 minutes so the flavours settle before serving.
tips: Mash 3-4 potato cubes against the side of the kadai in the last 5 minutes to thicken the gravy naturally without any cream or cornflour.
If using frozen peas, add them only in the final 5 minutes of simmering so they stay bright green and sweet.
The masala base can be made a day ahead and refrigerated; just reheat, add potatoes, peas and water, and finish fresh.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle into a deep bowl with tandoori roti or jeera rice, a wedge of lime and sliced onions sprinkled with chaat masala on the side, dhaba style.

variations.name: Punjabi Dhaba-style Aloo Matar
variations.description: The Amritsar truck-stop version, where the masala is bhuno-ed hard in ghee and finished with a knob of butter and a swirl of cream. Ginger juliennes and extra kasuri methi make it rich, punchy and unapologetically indulgent.

ingredients.name: Anveshan A2 Cow Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee gives the bhuno-ed masala its signature Punjabi dhaba aroma and a nutty, caramelised finish

steps: Cube 4 medium potatoes into bite-sized pieces, slit 2 green chillies lengthwise, and cut a 1 inch piece of ginger into fine matchsticks for garnishing later.

Melt 3 tbsp Anveshan A2 Cow Ghee in a kadai over medium-high heat, sizzle 1 tsp cumin seeds until aromatic, then add 3 finely chopped onions and fry for 10-12 minutes, stirring, until they are a rich mahogany brown.
Stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the slit green chillies and fry for 90 seconds, then pour in 1 cup tomato puree with 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder.
Bhuno the masala on medium heat for 8-10 minutes, scraping the base each time it catches, until the ghee separates and the paste turns brick red and jammy.
Add the potatoes, 1.25 cups green peas, 1.25 tsp salt and 1.75 cups hot water; cover and cook on low for 15 minutes until the potatoes are completely tender but still hold their shape.
Crush 2 tsp kasuri methi over the curry, stir in 3 tbsp fresh cream and 1 tbsp butter, and simmer gently for 2-3 minutes until the gravy is silky and coats the back of a spoon.
Top with the ginger juliennes and serve piping hot straight from the kadai for the full dhaba experience.
tips: Do not rush the onion browning; the deep colour of the gravy comes almost entirely from those 10-12 minutes of patient frying.
Add the cream off direct high heat and stir constantly, or it may split in the acidic tomato base.
For a smoky dhungar touch, place a small steel bowl with a hot coal in the pan, drizzle a few drops of ghee on it, cover for 2 minutes and remove.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with hot butter-brushed lachha paratha and a tall glass of salted lassi; a side of pickled green chillies completes the Punjabi dhaba spread.

variations.name: Bengali Dhaba-style Aloo Matar
variations.description: A Kolkata line-hotel take built on pungent mustard oil, bay leaf and slit green chillies, with a whisper of jaggery to round the tomatoes. The gravy is lighter and sharper than its Punjabi cousin, letting the winter peas taste of themselves.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Heated to smoking then cooled slightly, this kachi ghani mustard oil mellows into the sharp, fruity backbone every Bengali curry depends on

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A touch of unrefined jaggery balances the mustard oil's bite and the tomatoes' acidity the way Bengali kitchens always finish a jhol

steps: Cut 3 medium potatoes into thick wedges, chop 2 onions and 2 tomatoes, and slit 3 green chillies down the middle so they perfume the gravy without making it fiery.
Pour 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil into a kadai and heat on high until it just begins to smoke, about 2 minutes; lower the flame and wait 30 seconds so the raw pungency softens.

Drop in 1 bay leaf and 1 tsp cumin seeds, let them sputter for 15 seconds, then fry the potato wedges with 0.25 tsp of the turmeric for 4-5 minutes until their edges turn pale gold; lift them out and set aside.
In the same oil, cook the chopped onions for 6-7 minutes until translucent and lightly bronzed, then add 1 tbsp ginger paste and stir for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes, remaining 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 1.5 tsp cumin powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook on medium for 5 minutes until the tomatoes collapse into a soft pulp.

Return the fried potatoes with 1 cup green peas, the slit green chillies, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1.5 cups hot water; cover and simmer on low for 12 minutes until the potatoes are fork-tender.
Finish with 0.5 tsp garam masala, give the jhol one gentle stir, and rest it off the heat for 5 minutes so the mustard notes settle into the gravy.
tips: Smoking the mustard oil first is non-negotiable; skipping it leaves an acrid rawness in the finished curry.
Frying the potatoes before simmering keeps their edges intact and adds a toasty layer the slow-cooked version lacks.
This curry tastes even better the next day; thin it with 2-3 tbsp hot water when reheating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over steaming gobindobhog or any short-grain rice with a wedge of gondhoraj or ordinary lime and crisp fried papad on the side.

variations.name: Kerala Dhaba-style Aloo Matar
variations.description: Aloo matar rerouted through a Malabar toddy-shop kitchen: mustard seeds and curry leaves crackled in coconut oil, black pepper for warmth, and thick coconut milk stirred in at the end. The gravy turns ivory, gently sweet and fragrant rather than tomato-red.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil carries the curry-leaf tempering and gives this curry its unmistakable Malabar fragrance

steps: Halve 10 small shallots, crush a 1 inch piece of ginger with 4 garlic cloves into a coarse paste, slit 3 green chillies, and cube 3 medium potatoes into 2 cm pieces.

Warm 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a deep pan on medium heat and pop 1 tsp mustard seeds until they finish crackling, about 30 seconds, then add 2 sprigs of curry leaves and let them turn glossy and crisp.
Add the shallots and fry for 4-5 minutes until soft and light gold, then stir in the crushed ginger-garlic and slit green chillies and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add 1 chopped tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder and 2 tsp coriander powder and sauté for 3-4 minutes on medium until the tomato breaks down completely.
Tip in the potatoes, 1 cup green peas, 1 tsp salt and 1.25 cups hot water; cover and simmer on low for 13-14 minutes until the potatoes are soft enough to crush with a spoon.
Reduce the heat to its lowest, pour in 1 cup thick coconut milk and 1 tsp black pepper powder, and warm through for 3 minutes without letting it boil so the milk stays smooth and ivory.
Take the pan off the heat, tear a few extra curry leaves over the top and keep it covered for 5 minutes before serving so the coconut and pepper mingle.
tips: Never boil the curry after adding coconut milk or it will curdle; tiny bubbles at the edge are your stop signal.
Shallots are worth the peeling time here; regular onions make the gravy heavier and less sweet.
For a toddy-shop kick, crush 0.5 tsp extra black peppercorns coarsely and add with the coconut milk.
variations.servingSuggestion: Spoon over Kerala matta rice or scoop up with flaky Malabar parotta; a sharp mango pickle on the side cuts the creamy coconut beautifully.

variations.name: Gujarati Dhaba-style Aloo Matar
variations.description: A Kathiyawadi roadside rendition where the masala leans sweet-sour: jaggery melts into the tomato base, lemon sharpens it at the end, and a hing-mustard tadka opens the dish. It is homely, bright and quietly addictive with hot rotli.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Saurashtra kitchens run on groundnut oil; its clean nuttiness lets the sweet-sour masala shine without any heaviness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Chemical-free jaggery powder dissolves evenly into the gravy, giving the classic Gujarati sweet note without refined sugar

steps: Dice 3 medium potatoes into small 1.5 cm cubes so they cook quickly, finely chop 1 onion and 3 tomatoes, and squeeze 1 tbsp lemon juice ready for the finish.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium and crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds fully, about 30 seconds, then add 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let it foam for 5 seconds.
Sauté the chopped onion for 4-5 minutes until soft and translucent, then add 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and stir for 45 seconds until the sharp smell mellows.
Add the tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander-cumin powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 5-6 minutes on medium until pulpy and glistening.
Stir in the potato cubes, 1 cup green peas and 1.5 cups hot water; cover and simmer on low heat for 12-13 minutes until the potatoes crush easily against the pan wall.
Melt 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder into the simmering gravy and cook uncovered for 3 minutes until it turns lightly glossy with a gentle sweet-sour balance.
Turn off the flame, add 1 tbsp lemon juice and 3 tbsp chopped fresh coriander leaves, and stir once; taste and adjust the sweet-sour balance before serving.
tips: Always add lemon juice off the heat; boiling it turns the brightness bitter.
If your tomatoes are very tangy, hold back half the lemon juice and add only after tasting.
Kathiyawadi cooks often add 2 tbsp crushed peanuts with the tomatoes for body; it works wonderfully here too.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulka rotli, a katori of kadhi and a spoon of chhundo on the thali; it also makes an excellent filling for thepla rolls the next morning.

variations.name: Classic Home-style Aloo Matar
variations.description: The everyday weeknight curry of North Indian homes: potatoes and peas in a light, soupy tomato gravy tempered in ghee. No cream, no heavy bhuno, just clean flavours that come together in one pot in half an hour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan A2 Cow Ghee
ingredients.note: Home-style jhol curries are traditionally tempered in ghee; bilona ghee adds a grassy sweetness that store ghee simply lacks

steps: Peel and cube 3 medium potatoes into 2 cm pieces, finely chop 1 onion and roughly chop 2 tomatoes while a pressure cooker or deep pan warms on the stove.
Melt 2 tbsp Anveshan A2 Cow Ghee on medium heat and let 1 tsp cumin seeds sizzle for about 20 seconds until they release their toasty aroma.
Add the chopped onion and cook for 5-6 minutes, stirring now and then, until light golden; stir in 2 tsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 1 minute until the raw edge is gone.
Add the tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, and cook for 4-5 minutes on medium until they soften into a loose masala.

Add the potatoes, 1 cup green peas, 1 tsp salt and 2 cups hot water; if using a pressure cooker, close the lid and cook for 2 whistles, or cover and simmer in a pan for 15 minutes until the potatoes are completely tender.
Open the pan, lightly crush a couple of potato pieces with the ladle to give the thin gravy some body, and simmer uncovered for 2-3 minutes until it looks just slightly thickened.
Sprinkle 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander leaves, stir gently once and serve hot while the gravy is still loose and spoonable.
tips: Keep the gravy on the thinner side; this curry is meant to be mixed into rice, not scooped like a restaurant dish.
A pinch of amchur or a squeeze of lime at the end wakes up the whole pot if your tomatoes were bland.
Leftovers thicken overnight; loosen with 0.5 cup hot water and a tiny pinch of salt when reheating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best with plain steamed rice and a dollop of extra ghee on top, or with soft phulkas, sliced cucumber and a bowl of curd for a complete homely thali.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Home-style Aloo Matar
variations.description: A Pune-style rassa bhaji where goda masala brings its warm, faintly sweet stone-flower depth and roasted peanut powder thickens the gravy. Dry coconut toasted with the onions gives the curry a nutty, distinctly Maharashtrian character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Peanut-country cooking calls for groundnut oil; wood-pressed retains the roasty aroma that ties into the peanut powder in this rassa

steps: Cube 3 medium potatoes, slice 2 onions thinly, chop 2 tomatoes, and keep 3 tbsp grated dry coconut and 3 tbsp roasted peanut powder measured out beside the stove.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium; pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, then add 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them fizz for 10 seconds.
Fry the sliced onions with the grated dry coconut for 7-8 minutes, stirring frequently, until both turn an even chocolate brown; this toasted base is the soul of the rassa.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, cook for 1 minute, then add the tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder and 1 tsp red chilli powder and mash them down over 4-5 minutes until soft.
Stir in 2 tsp goda masala and the potato cubes, coat well for 1 minute, then add 1 cup green peas, 1 tsp salt and 2 cups hot water; cover and simmer on low for 14-15 minutes until fork-tender.
Mix 3 tbsp roasted peanut powder into the gravy and simmer uncovered for 3 minutes, stirring, until the rassa thickens to a spoon-coating consistency with a faint sheen of oil on top.
Rest the curry off the heat for 5 minutes; the goda masala blooms as it sits, so taste and add a small pinch of salt only after resting.
tips: Goda masala scorches quickly; always add it with the potatoes or later, never into hot bare oil.
If you cannot find goda masala, use 1.5 tsp garam masala plus 0.5 tsp toasted sesame powder as a stopgap, though the flavour will be simpler.
Brown the onion-coconut mixture properly; underdone, the gravy tastes raw and pale rather than deep and nutty.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft ghadichi poli or bhakri, a wedge of lime and a sliced-onion koshimbir; it also pairs beautifully with plain varan-bhaat on the side.

variations.name: Rajasthani Home-style Aloo Matar
variations.description: A desert-kitchen curry built without a drop of tomato: whisked sour curd forms the tangy gravy while whole dried red chillies and hing bloom in hot ghee. It is rustic, fiery-fragrant and proof of how Rajasthan makes magic from a spare pantry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan A2 Cow Ghee
ingredients.note: Rajasthani curries begin and end with ghee; slow-churned bilona ghee stands up to the whole dried chillies without turning acrid

steps: Whisk 1 cup sour curd with 1 tsp besan, 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder until completely smooth; the besan will keep the curd from splitting later.
Cube 3 medium potatoes into 2 cm pieces and grate a 1 inch knob of ginger; keep 3 whole dried red chillies wiped clean and stemmed.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan A2 Cow Ghee in a heavy pan on medium, sizzle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then add the 3 dried red chillies and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and fry for 30 seconds until the chillies darken and smell smoky.
Add the grated ginger and the potato cubes and fry for 4-5 minutes, tossing, until the potato edges pick up light golden spots.

Lower the flame fully, pour in the whisked curd mixture in a thin stream while stirring continuously in one direction, and keep stirring for 3-4 minutes until it comes to a gentle simmer without curdling.

Add 1 cup green peas, 1 tsp salt and 1.25 cups hot water; cover partially and simmer on low for 14-15 minutes, stirring every few minutes, until the potatoes are soft and the gravy is pale gold and lightly thickened.
Finish with 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander leaves and rest for 5 minutes; the tang deepens pleasantly as it sits.
tips: Stir constantly and keep the flame low while adding curd; heat plus stillness is what makes yogurt gravies split.
Use curd that is at least a day old for genuine khatta flavour; fresh sweet curd makes the gravy taste flat.
Break one fried dried chilli into the finished curry if you want proper Rajasthani heat rather than just aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Eat with hot bajra or wheat rotis smeared with ghee and a side of lehsun ki chutney; raw onion rings and a piece of gud round off the desert thali.

variations.name: Tamil Home-style Aloo Matar
variations.description: Urulai-pattani masala the way a Chettinad-leaning home kitchen makes it: gingelly oil tempering with mustard, urad dal and plenty of curry leaves, plus freshly crushed fennel and pepper. The gravy is thin, peppery and made for ladling over hot rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Nallennai is the default fat of Tamil home cooking; wood-pressed sesame oil brings the deep, toasty base note this pepper-fennel masala needs

steps: Cube 3 medium potatoes, slice 2 onions fine, chop 2 tomatoes and crush 5 garlic cloves lightly with the flat of a knife so they stay in rustic pieces.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil in a kadai over medium heat; crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds, add 1 tsp urad dal and fry until the dal turns pale gold, about 40 seconds, then throw in 2 sprigs of curry leaves.
Add the sliced onions and crushed garlic and sauté for 6-7 minutes until the onions turn golden at the edges and the garlic smells sweet.
Stir in the tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, and cook for 5 minutes on medium until the mixture is soft and the oil shows at the sides.
Add the potatoes, 1 cup green peas, 1 tsp salt and 1.75 cups hot water; cover and simmer on low heat for 14-15 minutes until a spoon crushes a potato cube with no resistance.
Sprinkle 1 tsp crushed fennel seeds and 1 tsp black pepper powder over the curry, stir, and simmer uncovered for 2-3 minutes so the pepper heat threads through the thin gravy.
Take it off the flame and tuck a few fresh curry leaves on top; the residual heat crisps them lightly and scents the whole pot.
tips: Crush the fennel just before using; pre-ground fennel loses the anise brightness that defines this curry.
Do not skip the urad dal in the tempering; those tiny golden crunches are a signature Tamil texture.
For a Chettinad-strength version, dry-roast and grind 2 dried chillies with the fennel and pepper.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over steaming ponni rice with a spoon of extra gingelly oil, or as the side to soft idlis and crisp dosas at breakfast; appalam completes the meal.

variations.name: Odia Home-style Aloo Matar
variations.description: A gentle Odia tarkari opened with panch phoron, the five-seed tempering that defines the state's kitchens, in pungent mustard oil. Grated ginger and a spoon of jaggery keep the gravy light, aromatic and faintly sweet, closer to a temple-style bhoga than a rich curry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Odia panch phoron tempering only sings in raw-pressed mustard oil; its sharpness carries all five seeds through the mild gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Odia tarkaris finish on a soft sweet note; unrefined jaggery powder does it cleanly without the caramel heaviness of sugar

steps: Cut 3 medium potatoes into thick batons rather than cubes, chop 1 onion and 2 tomatoes, and grate a 1 inch piece of ginger fresh for the gravy.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil in a kadai on high until faint wisps of smoke appear, then lower the flame and let it stand for 20 seconds to tame the raw bite.
Add 1.5 tsp panch phoron, 1 bay leaf and 2 whole dried red chillies; let the five seeds crackle and pop for about 30 seconds until the fenugreek grains just turn brown.
Sauté the chopped onion for 4-5 minutes until soft and blond, then add the grated ginger and cook for 45 seconds until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes, 0.75 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp cumin powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 4 minutes on medium heat until the tomatoes slump into the oil.
Slide in the potato batons and 1 cup green peas with 1.75 cups hot water; cover and simmer on low for 15 minutes until the potatoes are soft all the way through.
Stir in 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer 2 minutes more until the gravy tastes gently sweet-savoury, then finish with 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander leaves off the heat.
tips: Panch phoron burns fast because of the fenugreek in it; have the onions ready to add the moment the seeds finish crackling.
Batons instead of cubes are traditional in Odia tarkari and soak up the tempering along their length.
For a no-onion bhoga-style pot, skip the onion, double the ginger and add 0.25 tsp extra cumin powder.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle beside plain rice and dalma for a proper Odia plate, or eat with soft chakuli pitha; a spoon of tomato khatta alongside is the classic pairing.

variations.name: Classic Home-style Lauki
variations.description: The everyday lauki ki sabzi of North Indian homes: lightly spiced, gently stewed, and made for daily rotis rather than showing off. Cooked in Anveshan Sunflower Oil with just cumin, turmeric and a soft tomato base, it is the comforting, easy-to-digest sabzi grandmothers prescribe on a hot afternoon.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: Light wood-pressed sunflower oil keeps this daily sabzi delicate instead of greasy

steps: Peel 500 g bottle gourd and cut it into 2 cm cubes; finely chop 1 medium onion and 2 medium tomatoes so the base cooks down quickly.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sunflower Oil in a pressure cooker or deep pan on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 20 seconds until aromatic.
Add the chopped onion and cook for 4-5 minutes until soft and pale gold, then stir in 1 tsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 40-50 seconds until it no longer smells raw.

Add the tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt; cook for 4 minutes on medium, pressing the tomatoes down until they collapse into a soft masala.
Stir in the lauki cubes with 0.25 cup water; if using a pressure cooker, cook for 2 whistles on medium, or cover a pan and simmer on low for 15 minutes until the gourd yields easily to a spoon.
Open the lid, simmer uncovered for 2-3 minutes to reduce the pan juices to a loose coating, and stir through 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander before serving.
tips: Cut the cubes evenly; mixed sizes leave you with some pieces mushy and others undercooked.
This sabzi thickens as it sits, so leave the gravy slightly looser than you want at the table.
For a sick-day version, skip the onion and chilli and add 0.5 tsp crushed black pepper instead; it becomes gentle enough for upset stomachs.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best with soft phulkas, plain toor dal and a bowl of cucumber raita; a simple mango pickle on the side wakes the mild flavours right up.

variations.name: Gujarati Home-style Lauki
variations.description: Dudhi nu shaak the Gujarati way, balancing gentle heat with the warm caramel sweetness of Anveshan Jaggery Powder and a bright lemon finish. Tempered with mustard, ajwain and asafoetida in groundnut oil, it hits the sweet-sour-spicy triangle that defines a Kathiyawadi weeknight table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Gujarati shaak is traditionally built on peanut oil; this wood-pressed one adds a toasty depth

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Chemical-free jaggery gives the authentic gud-sweetness Gujarati dudhi shaak is loved for

steps: Dice 500 g peeled bottle gourd into 1.5 cm pieces, chop 2 small green chillies finely and grate 1 tsp ginger; Gujarati shaak skips onion and garlic entirely, so prep is quick.
Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai over medium heat, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds completely, then add 0.25 tsp ajwain and 0.25 tsp hing and let them fizz for 10 seconds.

Add the green chillies and grated ginger, stir for 30 seconds, then tip in the lauki along with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and toss until every piece is yellow-stained.
Add 0.5 cup water, cover the kadhai, and cook on low heat for 14-16 minutes, stirring once halfway, until the gourd is soft enough to crush against the side of the pan.
Stir in 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and simmer uncovered for 2-3 minutes until it melts into the pan juices and they turn glossy.
Switch off the heat, squeeze in 2 tsp lemon juice and shower over 2 tbsp chopped coriander; taste and adjust so the sweet and sour sit in balance.
tips: Always add lemon juice off the heat; boiling it turns the shaak bitter and kills its brightness.
The jaggery should whisper, not shout; start with 2 tsp and add more only after tasting with the lemon in.
Leftovers make a great stuffing for thepla dough the next morning; just mash and knead in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulka rotlis, a katori of Gujarati kadhi and steamed rice; finish the thali with a spoon of chhundo pickle for the full sweet-sour experience.

variations.name: Tamil Home-style Lauki
variations.description: A Tamil suraikkai poriyal where bottle gourd is simmered with sambar powder, tempered in Anveshan Sesame Oil with urad dal, mustard and a generous handful of curry leaves, then finished with fresh coconut. Nutty gingelly oil and crisped dal give every spoonful texture that the soft gourd alone cannot.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil is the traditional cooking fat of Tamil poriyals, adding a deep nutty base

steps: Peel 500 g bottle gourd and cut it into small 1 cm cubes, the standard poriyal size that cooks through in minutes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a wide pan on medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 2 tsp urad dal and fry for 40-60 seconds until the dal turns biscuit gold.
Break in 2 dried red chillies, add 12 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp hing, and let the leaves crackle and turn glossy for about 15 seconds.
Add the cubed gourd with 0.25 tsp turmeric powder and 0.75 tsp salt and stir-fry for 2 minutes so the pieces are coated in the fragrant oil.
Sprinkle 2 tsp sambar powder and 3 tbsp water, cover and cook on low heat for 10-12 minutes, stirring once, until the gourd is tender but the pan stays fairly dry.
Turn off the heat and fold in 0.33 cup grated fresh coconut, letting the residual warmth release its aroma without cooking it.
tips: Watch the urad dal closely; it should be golden, as even slightly burnt dal turns the whole poriyal bitter.
Homemade or fresh sambar powder makes a visible difference here since it is the only masala in the dish.
If the gourd releases too much water, uncover and cook on high for the last 2 minutes; a poriyal should never be wet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Spoon alongside hot rice, ghee and paruppu (plain cooked toor dal) as a first course, or serve as the vegetable with curd rice and sun-dried vathal for a light Tamil lunch.

variations.name: Punjabi Home-style Lauki
variations.description: Ghiya sabzi the way Punjabi households actually cook it on a Tuesday: bottle gourd melted down with tomatoes, plenty of Anveshan Ghee, julienned ginger and a spoon of ghee-toasted ajwain that aids digestion. It is rustic, homely and unapologetically rich for such a light vegetable.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A generous hand of bilona ghee is what separates Punjabi ghiya from every other lauki

steps: Peel and cube 500 g bottle gourd, roughly chop 1 large onion and 3 medium tomatoes, and cut 1.5 inch ginger into fine matchsticks, reserving a third of the ginger for garnish.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan over medium heat; when it melts and smells nutty, sizzle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.5 tsp ajwain together for 20 seconds.
Add the chopped onion with most of the ginger juliennes and 1 slit green chilli and fry for 5-6 minutes until the onion turns a rich golden brown.

Add the tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt and cook on medium for 6-7 minutes, mashing steadily, until the ghee separates and pools at the edges of the masala.
Add the lauki cubes and stir to coat, then cover and cook on low heat for 15 minutes without adding water; the tomatoes and gourd release enough moisture to stew it, so just stir every 5 minutes.
Mash a few of the softest pieces against the pan for a homely half-crushed texture, dust with 0.5 tsp garam masala, and finish with 3 tbsp coriander and the reserved raw ginger juliennes on top.
tips: Not adding water is the secret; slow tomato-steamed ghiya has a concentrated flavour that watery versions never reach.
The raw ginger garnish is not optional in a Punjabi kitchen; it lifts the soft, mellow sabzi with sharp fresh heat.
Leftover ghiya mashed with a boiled potato makes an excellent paratha stuffing the next day.
variations.servingSuggestion: Eat with hot phulkas dabbed with white butter, a bowl of boondi raita and shakkar-onion salad; on a cold day, pair it with stiff makki rotis instead.

variations.name: Odia Home-style Lauki
variations.description: A lau tarkari from Odisha built on panch phoron, the five-seed temper of fenugreek, nigella, cumin, fennel and mustard bloomed in pungent Anveshan Mustard Oil. Potato chunks cook alongside the gourd, and the finish is a bare scatter of green chilli and coriander, spare and deeply aromatic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Kachi ghani mustard oil is the default fat of Odia tarkari, sharp enough to carry the five-spice temper

steps: Peel 400 g bottle gourd and 1 large potato and cut both into similar 2 cm chunks so they finish cooking together.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai on medium-high until it shimmers and its raw edge fades, about 90 seconds, then reduce the heat to medium.
Add 1.5 tsp panch phoron, 1 bay leaf and 1 dried red chilli; the fenugreek in the mix should turn light brown and the seeds should crackle within 20-30 seconds.
Add the potato chunks first and fry for 3-4 minutes until their edges look lightly toasted, then add the gourd, 1 tsp grated ginger, 0.5 tsp turmeric powder and 1 tsp salt.
Pour in 0.5 cup water, add 2 slit green chillies, cover and simmer on low heat for 14-16 minutes until both vegetables are completely soft and the liquid has reduced to a few glossy spoonfuls.
Crush one or two potato pieces into the juices to thicken them naturally, check the salt, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander.
tips: Panch phoron scorches quickly because of the fenugreek; have the potatoes ready to add the moment it crackles.
The dish should be moist, not gravied; Odia lau tarkari sits between dry and curried.
A spoon of grated coconut stirred in at the end is a lovely coastal-Odisha touch if you have it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice and a wedge of lime, or with soft rotis; it also pairs beautifully with dalma and a crisp badi chura sprinkle on the side.

variations.name: Classic Masala Baingan Bharta
variations.description: The definitive smoky mashed eggplant, fire-roasted until the skin blackens and the flesh collapses, then folded into a well-browned onion-tomato masala. A generous spice base of coriander, chilli and garam masala makes this the 'masala' version — bolder and more layered than everyday bharta.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The clean, nutty body of wood-pressed groundnut oil carries the smoky eggplant without competing with it

steps: Rub 2 large eggplants with a few drops of oil, prick them all over with a fork, and roast directly over a medium gas flame for 12-15 minutes, turning every 3 minutes with tongs, until the skin is charred black and the flesh feels completely collapsed when pressed.
Rest the eggplants covered in a bowl for 5 minutes so the steam loosens the skin, then peel away the charred skin, discard the stems and roughly mash the smoky flesh with a fork.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then sauté 2 finely chopped onions for 6-7 minutes until they turn a deep golden brown at the edges.

Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 2 chopped green chillies and fry for 1 minute until the raw smell disappears, then stir in 3 finely chopped tomatoes with ½ tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt.
Cook the masala for 6-7 minutes on medium heat, mashing the tomatoes as they soften, until the mixture thickens and oil beads appear at the edges of the pan.

Fold in the mashed eggplant and cook for 6-8 minutes, stirring and pressing with the back of the spoon, until the bharta darkens slightly and stops tasting watery; finish with 1 tsp garam masala and 3 tbsp chopped coriander stirred through in the last minute.
tips: Choose light-for-their-size eggplants with taut, glossy skin — they have fewer seeds and mash into a silkier bharta.
For extra smokiness without a gas flame, drop a piece of hot charcoal in a steel bowl set on the bharta, add a few drops of oil, and cover for 3 minutes.
