Bharta tastes even better the next day; reheat it in a pan with 1 tsp oil rather than a microwave to revive the roasted aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Scoop up with hot tandoori rotis smeared with Anveshan Ghee, alongside sliced red onions and a wedge of lime for squeezing over.

variations.name: Punjabi Masala Baingan Bharta
variations.description: The dhaba-legend version from Punjab, where the smoked eggplant is cooked down in a rich masala and finished with a swirl of white butter and slivered ginger. Whole garlic cloves roasted inside the eggplant give it that unmistakable highway-dhaba depth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Slow-churned bilona ghee replaces the dhaba's butter mountain with a cleaner, richer finish

steps: Make 8 small slits in 2 large eggplants and tuck a peeled garlic clove into each slit, so the garlic roasts to a sweet paste inside the flesh while the eggplant chars.

Roast the stuffed eggplants over a medium open flame for 14-16 minutes, rotating every 3 minutes, until the skin is uniformly blackened and a knife slides through the thickest part with no resistance; cool, peel and mash along with the softened garlic.

Melt 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadai on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add 3 finely chopped onions and fry for 8-9 minutes, stirring often, until they are richly browned — Punjabi bharta demands onions darker than golden.

Add half the ginger juliennes and 3 chopped green chillies, fry for 1 minute, then tip in 3 finely chopped tomatoes with 1½ tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1 tbsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 7-8 minutes until the masala turns glossy and pulls away from the pan.
Add the garlicky mashed eggplant and cook on medium-low for 8-10 minutes, stirring every couple of minutes and letting it catch very slightly at the base — those toasty bits are the dhaba signature.
Finish by stirring in 1 tbsp white butter until it melts into the bharta, then top with the remaining ginger juliennes and 3 tbsp chopped coriander just before taking it off the heat.
tips: Do not skip stuffing the garlic into the eggplant; roasted-inside garlic tastes mellow and sweet, completely unlike garlic fried in the pan.
Letting the bharta catch lightly at the bottom of the kadai, then scraping it back in, builds the toasted depth dhabas are famous for.
A pinch of kasuri methi crushed between your palms at the end adds another authentic Punjabi layer if you have it on hand.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter-brushed laccha paratha, a whole green chilli fried in ghee for the daring, and a tall glass of salted lassi.

variations.name: Bengali Masala Baingan Bharta (Begun Pora Style)
variations.description: Modelled on Bengal's beloved begun pora, this bharta skips the long-cooked masala entirely: the smoky flesh is folded with raw shallots, green chillies, coriander and a bold lick of pungent mustard oil. It is bracing, fresh and comes together in minutes once the eggplant is roasted.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Raw kachi ghani mustard oil is the soul of begun pora — its sharp pungency is the dish's main seasoning

steps: Slit 2 large eggplants, push 4 whole garlic cloves into the slits, and char them with 1 whole tomato over a medium flame — the tomato needs only 4-5 minutes, the eggplants 13-15 minutes with regular turning — until both are blistered and collapsed.

Rest the roasted vegetables under a covered bowl for 5 minutes, then peel off the charred skins, and mash the eggplant flesh, roasted garlic and tomato together with a fork into a rustic, slightly chunky mixture.

Warm 1 tbsp of the Anveshan Mustard Oil in a small pan on high heat for about 90 seconds until it just smokes, then cool it for a minute — this softens its raw edge while keeping the signature nose-tingling aroma.

Fold 6 finely chopped shallots, 4 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp salt and ½ tsp roasted cumin powder into the warm mash, mixing with a light hand so the shallots keep their crunch against the silky eggplant.

Pour the warmed mustard oil plus the remaining 1½ tbsp raw Anveshan Mustard Oil over the mixture and stir well; the mash should glisten and smell sharply pungent, which mellows as it sits for 2-3 minutes.
Finish with 2 tsp lime juice and 4 tbsp chopped coriander, taste for salt, and serve at room temperature rather than piping hot, as Bengali households do.
tips: The shallots must go in raw — cooking them would turn this into an ordinary bharta and lose the begun pora character.
If raw mustard oil feels too assertive at first, start with 1½ tbsp total and build up; its pungency softens noticeably after 10 minutes of resting.
Char the eggplant a little longer than usual for this recipe; with so few cooked ingredients, the smokiness has to do the heavy lifting.
variations.servingSuggestion: Traditionally eaten mounded beside steaming rice and a bowl of thin musur dal, with an extra green chilli on the rim of the plate.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Masala Baingan Bharta (Vangyache Bharit)
variations.description: The khandeshi-style bharit of Maharashtra, where smoked eggplant meets the warm, faintly sweet complexity of goda masala and crushed roasted peanuts. Spring onion greens stirred in at the end give it a fresh bite that sets it apart from every northern bharta.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Maharashtra cooks bharit in groundnut oil by tradition; the wood-pressed version doubles down on the dish's peanut notes

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A small spoon of pure jaggery powder balances the goda masala the way Maharashtrian home cooks intend

steps: Roast 2 large eggplants over a medium flame for 13-15 minutes, turning every 3 minutes, until the skin blackens completely and the flesh sags; cool briefly, peel and mash coarsely, keeping some texture rather than a smooth purée.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds for 30 seconds, then add 5 crushed garlic cloves and 3 chopped green chillies and fry for 1 minute until the garlic turns pale gold.
Add 2 finely chopped onions and sauté for 5-6 minutes until translucent and lightly golden — bharit onions stay softer and lighter than the deep-brown Punjabi style.

Stir in ½ tsp turmeric, 2 tsp goda masala and 1 tsp salt, fry the spices for 30 seconds, then fold in the mashed eggplant and cook on medium-low for 7-8 minutes, stirring occasionally so it thickens without sticking.
Mix in ⅓ cup coarsely crushed roasted peanuts and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook for 2 more minutes until the jaggery dissolves and the bharit turns aromatic, nutty and faintly sweet.
Take the pan off the heat and stir through ½ cup chopped spring onion greens so they wilt only slightly and keep their fresh crunch in the finished bharit.
tips: Goda masala scorches fast, so never fry it longer than 30 seconds before the eggplant goes in.
Crush the peanuts coarsely with a rolling pin instead of grinding; the uneven nubs are essential to the khandeshi texture.
In Jalgaon this bharit is often made with extra oil and eaten at room temperature — it keeps well for a picnic tiffin.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the traditional way with soft bhakri or hot jowar rotis, a raw onion wedge and a smear of thecha for those who want extra fire.

variations.name: Andhra Masala Baingan Bharta (Vankaya Pachadi Style)
variations.description: A fiery Andhra rendition that treats the smoked eggplant like a pachadi: mashed with a tempering of Guntur chillies, garlic and curry leaves, then brightened with tamarind. It is hotter, tangier and more rustic than any North Indian bharta, built to be eaten with mounds of rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Toasty wood-pressed gingelly oil is the default fat of Andhra pachadis and stands up to the Guntur chilli heat

steps: Char 2 large eggplants over a medium flame for 13-15 minutes, turning every 3 minutes until the skin is ash-black and the flesh is fully soft; peel while warm and mash roughly with a fork, leaving a few silky strands intact.
Soak 1½ tbsp tamarind pulp in 3 tbsp warm water for 5 minutes, then squeeze and strain to get a thick, smooth extract with no fibres.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadai on medium heat, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds for 30 seconds, then add 1 tbsp chana dal and fry for about a minute until the dal turns biscuit-gold.
Tear 4 Guntur red chillies into the oil along with 8 lightly crushed garlic cloves and 12 curry leaves, and fry for 90 seconds until the chillies deepen to a brick red and the garlic edges brown.

Add 1 finely chopped onion with ¼ tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt and sauté for 4-5 minutes until soft, then pour in the tamarind extract and simmer for 2 minutes until it thickens slightly and smells tangy-sweet.
Fold in the mashed eggplant and cook on medium-low for 5-6 minutes, stirring and pressing, until the pachadi comes together glossy and thick; finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and serve warm.
tips: Adjust Guntur chillies between 2 and 5 depending on your heat tolerance — 4 gives an honest Andhra-level burn.
The tamarind should be tasted before adding fully; some blocks are far sourer than others, so start with two-thirds and adjust.
This keeps in the fridge for 3 days and, like most pachadis, tastes deeper on day two once the tamarind mellows.
variations.servingSuggestion: Mound it over hot steamed rice with a spoonful of melted Anveshan Ghee mixed in — the classic Andhra way to soften the chilli blaze — with fryums on the side.

variations.name: Classic Masala Pyaaz Paratha
variations.description: The everyday North Indian breakfast hero: a soft khapli wheat paratha stuffed with a boldly spiced onion masala. Salting and squeezing the onions keeps the filling dry, so the paratha rolls out thin without tearing and blisters into crisp, ghee-lacquered layers on the tava.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat absorbs a touch more water than regular atta and gives these parathas a nutty flavour and softer bite

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee goes into the dough for softness and onto the tava for that classic toasted aroma

steps: Knead 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 1 cup water into a soft, non-sticky dough; it should spring back slowly when pressed. Cover and rest for 20 minutes.
Finely chop 3 medium onions, toss with 0.5 tsp salt and set aside for 10 minutes, then squeeze out every drop of moisture with your hands so the filling stays dry.

Mix the squeezed onions with 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 2 minced green chillies and 0.25 cup chopped coriander leaves.
Divide the dough into 8 balls. Flatten one ball into a 4-inch cup, place 2 tbsp of the onion filling in the centre, pleat the edges over to seal, and pinch off any excess dough.
Dust with dry atta and roll each stuffed ball gently into a 7-inch round, rotating as you roll so the filling spreads evenly without bursting through.

Heat a tava on medium-high until a drop of water sizzles instantly. Cook the paratha for about 1 minute until bubbles rise, flip, brush with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Ghee, and cook each side another 1 to 2 minutes until deep golden spots appear.
Press the edges with a spatula so they cook through, then stack the finished parathas in a cloth-lined box to keep them soft while you cook the rest.
tips: Squeezed onion juice is flavour gold; knead it into the dough instead of plain water for an extra layer of onion sweetness.
If a paratha tears while rolling, patch the hole with a pinch of dry dough and dust generously with atta before continuing.
The filling can be mixed up to 4 hours ahead, but salt the onions only at the last minute or they will weep and make sealing impossible.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot off the tava with a bowl of thick curd whisked with a pinch of black salt, a wedge of lime pickle, and cutting chai on the side.

variations.name: Punjabi Masala Pyaaz Paratha
variations.description: The dhaba original from Amritsar's Lawrence Road, where pyaaz parathas are rolled thick, cooked slowly on iron tavas and crowned with a melting spoon of white butter. Ajwain and anardana in the filling give the classic sour-carom punch that defines Punjabi stuffed parathas.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its extra gluten stretch lets you roll these generously stuffed Punjabi parathas thick without cracking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Punjabi dhabas are famously generous with ghee; use it lavishly on the tava for shatteringly crisp edges

steps: Make the dough first: work 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee into 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, then knead with roughly 1 cup water for 5 minutes until supple. Rest it under a damp cloth for 20 minutes.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan on medium, crackle 1 tsp ajwain for 20 seconds until fragrant, then pour this tempering over 4 finely chopped, salted and squeezed onions.
Stir 2 tsp anardana powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp garam masala, 1 inch grated ginger and 2 minced green chillies into the onions; the filling should smell tangy and sharp.
Portion the dough into 8 balls and stuff each with a heaped 2 tbsp of filling, gathering the edges into a tight topknot before flattening between your palms.
Roll each ball into a slightly thick 6-inch round; Punjabi parathas are meant to be hearty, not paper thin, so do not press hard.
Cook on a medium-hot tava for 2 minutes per side, drizzling 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee around the edges each time you flip, until both faces are mottled deep brown and the surface crisps audibly.
Smash each hot paratha lightly between your palms to open the layers, then top with 1 tbsp white butter so it melts into the cracks before serving.
tips: No anardana? Stir in 1 tsp amchur for the same tang, but add it just before stuffing so the onions do not turn watery.
Blooming the ajwain in hot ghee rather than adding it raw keeps the seeds from tasting bitter and sharp in the filling.
For true dhaba character, finish the cooked paratha directly over a low open flame for 10 seconds per side to char the edges.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a tall glass of salted lassi and a smoky baingan bharta; in winter, Punjabi households add a jaggery cube on the side to end the meal.

variations.name: Bengali Masala Pyaaz Paratha
variations.description: Inspired by Kolkata's street-side porota griddles, this take fries the paratha in pungent mustard oil and perfumes the onion filling with kalonji and green chillies. The mustard oil's sharp bite against the sweet onions is unmistakably Bengali, best chased with a smear of kasundi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Stone-ground emmer gives the porota a rustic chew that stands up to assertive mustard oil

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed kachi ghani mustard oil delivers the nose-tingling pungency this Bengali version is built around

steps: Rub 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil into 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt until sandy, then knead with about 1 cup water into a smooth, pliable dough. Rest 20 minutes under a damp cloth.
Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a small pan until it just begins to smoke, take it off the heat, and crackle 1 tsp kalonji in the hot oil for 15 seconds.

Pour the kalonji tempering over 3 finely chopped, salted and squeezed onions, then mix in 3 minced green chillies, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp sugar and 0.25 cup coriander leaves.
Shape the dough into 8 balls, cup each into a small bowl, spoon in 2 tbsp of the mustard-scented filling, and twist the top closed like a modak.
Roll each parcel out to a 7-inch disc with light, even strokes, flouring the board whenever the dough starts to grab.
Fry on a medium tava with 1 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil per paratha, about 90 seconds a side, until the surface bubbles into golden-brown blisters and the kitchen smells sharply of mustard.
Rest each porota for a minute on a rack rather than a plate so the base stays crisp instead of steaming soft.
tips: Always heat mustard oil to its smoking point once before using; this mellows the raw bitterness while keeping its signature pungency.
The pinch of sugar is not optional in a Bengali kitchen; it rounds out the mustard's heat and makes the onions taste sweeter.
Leftover filling makes an excellent instant salad; squeeze in half a lime and pile it onto the hot porota.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a spoon of sharp kasundi mustard, sliced cucumber, and sweet milky cha; on weekends, add a runny-yolk fried egg on top Kolkata-cabin style.

variations.name: Kerala Masala Pyaaz Paratha
variations.description: A Malabar-leaning paratha where fresh grated coconut and curry leaves are folded into the onion masala and the layers are toasted in virgin coconut oil. The coconut turns lightly caramelised inside, giving each bite a sweet, tropical depth that is completely different from the northern original.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli wheat brings wholegrain nuttiness that flatters the sweetness of toasted coconut

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed virgin coconut oil perfumes the tava and echoes the coconut in the filling for a true Malabar finish

steps: Knead 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and close to 1 cup water into a soft dough that does not stick to your fingers, then rest it for 20 minutes.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadhai on medium, pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds for 20 seconds, then add 2 sprigs of curry leaves and let them crackle and turn glossy.
Add 3 finely chopped onions, 3 slit green chillies and 1 inch julienned ginger; sauté for 4 to 5 minutes until the onions soften and pick up light golden edges.
Stir in 0.5 cup grated coconut, 0.5 tsp black pepper powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt; toast for 2 minutes until the coconut smells nutty, then cool the filling completely.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, stuff each with 2 tbsp of the cooled coconut-onion masala, seal firmly and roll into 6-inch rounds with gentle pressure.
Toast on a medium tava for about 2 minutes per side, brushing with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil at each flip, until freckled golden brown and crisp at the rim.
Rest the parathas under a clean cloth for 2 minutes; the coconut filling settles and slices cleanly instead of spilling.
tips: Cool the sautéed filling fully before stuffing; warm coconut steams the dough from inside and makes the paratha gummy.
Frozen grated coconut works if thawed and squeezed dry, but toast it 1 minute longer to drive off the extra moisture.
Tearing the curry leaves before adding releases far more aroma than dropping them in whole.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a small bowl of coconut chutney and sweet black chukku kaapi (dry-ginger coffee), or alongside a fried-egg roast for a full Malabar breakfast.

variations.name: Rajasthani Masala Pyaaz Paratha
variations.description: Built for the desert palate: the onion filling is toasted with crushed dried red chillies, coriander seeds and a spoon of besan, which soaks up moisture and adds a roasted gram savouriness. Cooked with generous ghee until sturdy and crisp, it keeps well for hours, just like a traveller's paratha should.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The hardy emmer grain mirrors Rajasthan's rustic wheat rotis and stays soft even after the paratha cools

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: In water-scarce Rajasthan ghee is the cooking medium of honour; it crisps the crust and carries the chilli aroma

steps: Combine 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp salt and 1 tbsp melted Anveshan Ghee, then knead with about 1 cup water into a firm yet pliable dough. Rest for 20 minutes.
Dry-roast 4 dried red chillies, 2 tsp coriander seeds and 1 tsp fennel seeds in a pan on low heat for 2 to 3 minutes until fragrant and brittle, then pound them coarsely in a mortar.
In the same pan, toast 2 tbsp besan in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on low for 3 minutes, stirring constantly, until it darkens a shade and smells nutty.
Mix 3 finely chopped, salted and squeezed onions with the pounded spices, toasted besan, 1 tsp amchur and 0.25 tsp turmeric; the besan will bind the filling into a crumbly masala.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, fill each with 2 tbsp masala, seal the pleats tightly and roll into 6-inch rounds, keeping the pressure light over the centre.
Roast on a medium tava for 2 minutes a side, spooning 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee over each flip, until the crust turns a deep russet brown with crisp, blistered patches.
Let the parathas sit for 2 minutes before serving; the besan-bound filling firms up and the layers turn flaky rather than doughy.
tips: Crushing the roasted chillies coarsely, not to a powder, gives the authentic Rajasthani flecks of smoky heat in every bite.
These parathas travel exceptionally well; wrap them in a muslin cloth and they stay good without refrigeration for a full day.
If the filling feels moist, toast another 1 tbsp besan and fold it in rather than adding dry flour, which would dull the flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Marwari way with a dollop of churned white makkhan, garlic-chilli lehsun chutney, and a katori of tangy kadhi or plain chaas.

variations.name: Classic Masala Tori
variations.description: Ridge gourd stewed in a proper onion-tomato masala until it turns silky and soaks up every spice. Cooked in Anveshan Ghee with cumin, coriander and a garam masala finish, this is the definitive North Indian tori that converts even the gourd-sceptics at the table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee rounds off the ridge gourd's grassy edge with a warm, nutty base

steps: Peel the tough ridges of 500 g ridge gourd with a peeler, leaving strips of green skin for texture, and cut it into 1.5 cm thick half-moons; finely chop 2 medium onions and 2 medium tomatoes.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds until they darken slightly and smell toasty, about 20-30 seconds.
Add the onions and sauté for 5-6 minutes until golden brown at the edges, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 1 minute more, stirring so it does not stick.

Stir in the tomatoes with 2 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt; cook for 4-5 minutes, mashing occasionally, until the masala turns jammy and the fat separates.
Add the ridge gourd, mix well, cover and cook on low heat for 12-14 minutes without any added water; the gourd releases plenty of its own juice as it softens.
Uncover and cook on medium for 3-4 minutes so the extra liquid evaporates into a thick coating, then sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala and 2 tbsp chopped coriander and take it off the heat.
tips: Never add water to tori; it is over 90 percent water itself and will drown the masala.
Peel only the hard ridges, not all the skin; the green strips keep the pieces from collapsing entirely.
If the sabzi still looks watery at the end, a final 2 minutes on high heat with constant stirring tightens it right up.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with phulkas and a katori of whisked dahi; it also makes a surprisingly good filling for a toasted pav with a slice of onion.

variations.name: Andhra Masala Tori
variations.description: Beerakaya kura from Andhra kitchens: ridge gourd cooked down with fiery Guntur chilli powder and a coarse roasted peanut-sesame podi that thickens the masala. Made in Anveshan Groundnut Oil, it delivers the trademark Andhra one-two of serious heat followed by nutty depth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed peanut oil is the workhorse fat of Andhra kura and echoes the peanut podi

steps: Dry-roast 1 tbsp sesame seeds in a small pan for 1-2 minutes until they pop, then grind them with 3 tbsp roasted peanuts into a coarse podi and set aside.
Peel the ridges off 500 g ridge gourd and slice it into 1.5 cm pieces; chop 1 medium onion and crush 3 garlic cloves.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then fry 2 tsp chana dal for about 45 seconds until golden and add 10 curry leaves.
Add the onion and crushed garlic and sauté for 4-5 minutes until the onion browns lightly and the garlic smells sweet rather than sharp.

Add the ridge gourd, 0.25 tsp turmeric powder, 1.5 tsp Guntur chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, toss well, then cover and cook on low heat for 12 minutes, stirring twice, until the gourd is soft and glossy.
Stir in the peanut-sesame podi and cook uncovered on medium for 3 minutes; the podi will absorb the pan juices and cling to the gourd like a thick masala crust.
tips: Guntur chilli is genuinely hot; drop to 1 tsp if your household prefers medium heat, since the podi does not mute it much.
Grind the podi coarse like breadcrumbs, not fine like flour, or it will turn pasty in the pan.
This kura thickens beautifully overnight and tastes even better the next day mixed straight into hot rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Andhra way: with steamed rice, a spoon of extra podi on the side, a dollop of curd to tame the heat, and crisp appadam broken over the top.

variations.name: Goan Masala Tori
variations.description: A coastal take where ridge gourd simmers in a light coconut-milk gravy soured with kokum petals, Goa's signature dried garcinia. Tempered in Anveshan Coconut Oil with garlic and green chilli, it is tangy, gently sweet and made for pouring over rice on a monsoon evening.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil ties the temper to the coconut-milk gravy in true Konkan style

steps: Soak 4 kokum petals in 3 tbsp warm water for 10 minutes while you peel and slice 500 g ridge gourd into chunky 2 cm pieces, slice 1 onion and 4 garlic cloves, and slit 2 green chillies.

Melt 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a wide pan over medium heat, crackle 0.75 tsp mustard seeds, then add 8 curry leaves, the sliced garlic and green chillies and fry for 1 minute until the garlic edges turn pale gold.
Add the sliced onion and cook for 3-4 minutes until soft and translucent without letting it brown, which would muddy the pale gravy.
Add the ridge gourd with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, stir, cover and cook on low for 10 minutes until it starts turning tender.
Pour in the kokum with its soaking water and 0.75 cup thick coconut milk, then simmer very gently, uncovered, for 5-6 minutes; never let the coconut milk come to a rolling boil or it will split.
Check that the gourd is soft and the gravy lightly thickened, fish out the kokum petals if you prefer a milder tang, and serve warm.
tips: Kokum keeps souring the dish as it sits, so remove the petals before storing leftovers.
Add coconut milk only in the last few minutes and keep the flame low; a hard boil breaks it into grainy curds.
A fresh grating of nutmeg over the finished gravy is an old Goan Hindu-kitchen flourish worth trying.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over steamed ukda (Goan red) rice with a crisp fried papad, or with soft sannas to soak up the tangy coconut gravy.

variations.name: Kumaoni Masala Tori
variations.description: From the Uttarakhand hills, where tori is stir-fried with jakhya, the wild mustard seed that crackles louder and tastes nuttier than any cultivated spice. Cooked simply in Anveshan Ghee with hill-style red chillies and coriander, this is minimalism that lets the crackly temper do the talking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Pahadi kitchens prize pure ghee; bilona ghee gives the sparse temper its full richness

steps: Lightly peel 500 g ridge gourd, keeping some green skin on for the rustic hill texture, and slice it into thin 1 cm rounds that will fry rather than stew.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in an iron kadhai over medium-high heat until fully melted and fragrant, then add 1 tsp jakhya seeds and let them crackle noisily for 15-20 seconds.
Add 2 whole dried red chillies broken in half and 4 chopped garlic cloves and fry for 45-60 seconds until the garlic is golden and the chillies smell smoky.
Tip in the tori rounds with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp salt and toss on medium-high heat for 2 minutes so the slices sear rather than sweat.
Reduce the heat to low, cover and cook for 8-10 minutes, tossing every few minutes instead of stirring, until the gourd is tender with lightly browned patches.
Finish uncovered on high for 1-2 minutes to crisp the edges slightly, then squeeze over 1 tsp lemon juice and scatter 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Jakhya is prized precisely because it stays crunchy; do not grind it or substitute regular mustard without expecting a different dish.
An iron kadhai gives the authentic slightly-charred pahadi flavour; keep the pieces in a single layer as much as possible.
If you cannot source jakhya, use half cumin and half mustard seeds, though the crackle will be gentler.
variations.servingSuggestion: Eat pahadi-style with thick mandua (finger millet) rotis or plain parathas and a bowl of jhwai (spiced buttermilk); a smear of bhang chutney alongside is the full Kumaon experience.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Masala Tori
variations.description: Dodka bhaji from Marathi homes: ridge gourd braised with goda masala and thickened with roasted peanut crush, tempered in Anveshan Groundnut Oil with mustard and hing. The goda masala's stone flower and coconut notes make it darker, sweeter and smokier than any North Indian tori.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Marathi bhaji is built on peanut oil; the wood-pressed version deepens the dish's nutty backbone

steps: Scrape the ridges off 500 g dodka and chop it into 1.5 cm chunks, keeping a little skin for bite; finely chop 1 medium onion and 2 small green chillies.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds fully, then add 0.25 tsp hing and the chopped green chillies and stir for 15 seconds.
Fry the onion for 4 minutes until soft and lightly coloured, then sprinkle in 0.5 tsp turmeric powder and 2 tsp goda masala and stir for just 20-30 seconds so the delicate masala does not scorch.
Immediately add the dodka chunks and 1 tsp salt, coat them in the dark spiced oil, then cover and cook on low heat for 10-12 minutes; the gourd will stew in its own released juices.
Fold in 3 tbsp coarse roasted peanut powder and cook uncovered for 3 minutes on medium, letting it drink up the liquid and bind into a thick, clingy bhaji.
Turn off the flame and finish with 2 tbsp grated fresh coconut and 2 tbsp chopped coriander stirred through while the pan is still hot.
tips: Peanut powder added too early turns gluey; it goes in only after the gourd is fully cooked.
Goda masala is aromatic, not hot; keep the green chillies in even for a mild version or the bhaji tastes flat.
The same template works for zucchini when dodka is out of season, though reduce the covered cooking to 8 minutes.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft chapatis or jowar bhakri, a katori of plain amti-dal and rice, and a wedge of lime; it also pairs well with steaming hot varan for a weekday Marathi thali.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Dal Paratha
variations.description: A North Indian breakfast staple where leftover chana dal is reborn as a fiery, well-spiced stuffing inside a khapli wheat flatbread. The dal is mashed with green chillies, ginger and black pepper, so every bite has warmth without being one-note hot. Roasted slowly in bilona ghee, the crust turns crisp and blistered while the centre stays soft.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat gives the dough natural stretch, so the dal stuffing does not tear through while rolling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee both enriches the dough and crisps the crust; its nutty aroma flatters earthy chana dal

ingredients.name: Cooked chana dal
ingredients.note: Pressure-cooked fully soft and drained well

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 3/4 cup water into a soft, non-sticky dough; it should spring back slowly when pressed. Cover and rest for 20 minutes so the emmer wheat hydrates fully.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 30 seconds until fragrant. Add grated 1 inch ginger and 2 chopped green chillies and sizzle for another 30 seconds.

Tip in 1 cup drained cooked chana dal along with 1/2 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1/2 tsp black pepper powder and 1/2 tsp salt. Mash and cook on low heat for 3-4 minutes until the mixture is dry enough to hold a ball shape, then cool and fold in 3 tbsp chopped coriander and 2 tsp lemon juice.

Divide the dough into 8 equal balls and the filling into 8 portions of about 2 tbsp each. Flatten a ball into a 4-inch cup, place one portion of filling in the centre, gather the edges over it and pinch to seal.
Dust the stuffed ball lightly with khapli atta and roll gently into a 7-inch round, using even pressure so the dal does not burst out at the edges.

Cook on a hot tava on medium heat for about 1 minute per side until pale brown spots appear, then spread 1/2 tsp Anveshan Ghee on each side and roast for another minute per side, pressing the edges with a spatula until both faces are golden and crisp.
Repeat with the remaining balls, stacking the finished parathas in a cloth-lined box so they stay soft and warm.
tips: If your cooked dal is watery, dry it out in the pan for a few extra minutes; a wet filling will make the paratha tear while rolling.
The filling can be made a day ahead and refrigerated; bring it to room temperature before stuffing so the dough does not turn clammy.
For extra heat, add 1/4 tsp crushed black peppercorns to the dough itself, not just the filling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve two parathas per person with a bowl of thick beaten curd sprinkled with roasted cumin, a wedge of lime pickle and sliced raw onion rings.

variations.name: Bengali Spicy Dal Paratha
variations.description: Inspired by Kolkata's motor dal-stuffed kachori-parathas, this version fills the bread with yellow pea dal perfumed with kalonji and green chilli. Pungent mustard oil replaces most of the fat, giving the crust the sharp, appetising bite Bengalis prize. A whisper of sugar balances the heat in true Bengali fashion.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed kachi ghani pungency is the soul of this Bengali take; it flavours both filling and crust

ingredients.name: Cooked yellow matar dal
ingredients.note: Boiled soft and mashed smooth, the classic Bengali koraishutir-style base

ingredients.name: Cumin powder
ingredients.note: Roasted and ground, safe to mix straight into the filling

steps: Make the dough by rubbing 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil into 2 cups khapli atta with 1/2 tsp salt, then adding roughly 3/4 cup water in stages. Knead for 5 minutes to a supple, non-sticky ball and rest it under a damp cloth for 20 minutes.

Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai on medium heat until it just begins to smoke, then lower the flame and let it calm for 20 seconds to mellow the raw pungency. Crackle 1/2 tsp kalonji seeds in it for about 20 seconds.

Add 2 tsp grated ginger and 3 chopped green chillies, fry for 30 seconds, then stir in 1 cup mashed matar dal, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric powder, 1/2 tsp sugar and 1/2 tsp salt. Cook for 4-5 minutes on low, stirring, until the mixture leaves the sides of the pan, then cool completely and mix in 2 tbsp coriander.

Portion the dough into 8 balls and the dal into 8 lots of 2 tbsp each. Cup each dough ball in your palm, tuck in one lot of filling, seal the pleats firmly and rest the stuffed balls for 5 minutes so the seams set.
Roll each ball into a 6-7 inch disc with light strokes, turning it a quarter after every roll so the filling spreads evenly rather than pooling at the centre.

Roast on a medium-hot tava for 60-90 seconds per side until brown freckles appear, then drizzle 1/2 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil around the edges and fry each side another minute until the crust is deep golden with a faint mustard sharpness.
tips: Always heat mustard oil to smoking point once and let it cool slightly before tempering; skipping this leaves the filling bitter and raw-tasting.
Matar dal should be boiled with just enough water to go soft; excess moisture is the main reason stuffed parathas leak.
Bengali households add the pinch of sugar not for sweetness but to round off the chilli heat, so do not skip it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a quick tomato-khejur chutney or aloo dum and finish the meal with a hot cup of milky cha, the way Kolkata breakfast stalls do.

variations.name: Rajasthani Spicy Dal Paratha
variations.description: A desert-style paratha that channels the flavours of dal baati: moong dal cooked down with fiery Mathania-style dried red chillies, ajwain and hing. The stuffing is intensely spiced because Rajasthani food was built to be eaten with plenty of ghee, and this one is finished with a generous ladle of it. Expect a rustic, crackly crust and a slow-building chilli warmth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its coarse, wholesome character suits rustic Rajasthani breads better than refined flour ever could

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rajasthani dal parathas are unapologetically ghee-laden; it tempers the dried chilli heat beautifully

ingredients.name: Cooked moong dal
ingredients.note: Yellow moong pressure-cooked soft and mashed dry

ingredients.name: Dried red chillies
ingredients.note: Mathania-style if you can find them, soaked and pounded to a coarse paste

steps: Soak 4 dried red chillies in 1/4 cup hot water for 15 minutes, then pound or grind them to a coarse red paste with a spoon of their soaking water.
Meanwhile knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp ajwain, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 3/4 cup water into a firm yet pliable dough; rest it covered for 20 minutes.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium flame, crackle the remaining 1/2 tsp ajwain for 20 seconds, then add 1/4 tsp hing and the pounded chilli paste. Fry for 1 minute until the ghee turns brick red and aromatic.

Add 1 cup mashed moong dal, 2 tsp coriander powder, 1/2 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp amchur and 1/2 tsp salt; cook and stir for 4 minutes until the mixture is thick, crumbly and pulls away from the pan. Cool it fully before stuffing.
Shape 8 dough balls, stuff each with 2 tbsp of the moong mixture, pinch shut and roll into thickish 6-inch rounds; Rajasthani parathas are kept slightly sturdy, not paper-thin.

Roast on a medium tava for about 90 seconds per side until dry spots form, then smear 1/2 tsp Anveshan Ghee per side and cook until both faces are crusty and deeply browned, pressing gently so the centre cooks through.
Brush each finished paratha with a little more melted Anveshan Ghee while still hot so it soaks into the crust.
tips: Amchur does the job lemon would, without adding moisture to the filling, so resist substituting fresh lime here.
If the pounded chilli paste feels too fierce, deseed two of the chillies before soaking; the colour stays, the burn softens.
These parathas keep well for a day wrapped in cloth, making them ideal travel food just as they were for desert journeys.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with kachumber salad, a spoon of garlic-chilli chutney and chilled chaas whisked with roasted cumin to cool the palate between bites.

variations.name: Tamil Spicy Dal Paratha
variations.description: This southern rendition packs the bread with toor dal mashed into a paruppu-style filling, seasoned with curry leaves, mustard seeds and a spoon of sambar powder. Cold-pressed sesame oil, the everyday fat of Tamil kitchens, gives the crust its distinctive nutty depth. It eats like a portable version of paruppu sadam with all the tempering built in.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed nallennai is the traditional Tamil frying medium; its toasty note ties the whole paratha together

ingredients.name: Cooked toor dal
ingredients.note: Pressure-cooked completely soft, like the base for sambar

steps: Combine 2 cups khapli atta, 1/2 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, then work in about 3/4 cup water to form a smooth, soft dough. Knead for 5 minutes and let it rest under a wet cloth for 20 minutes.

For the tempering, heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pan on medium heat and pop 1 tsp mustard seeds fully, about 30-40 seconds. Add 12 curry leaves, 1/8 tsp hing, 2 slit green chillies and 6 finely chopped shallots, and fry until the shallots turn translucent, around 2 minutes.

Stir in 1 cup mashed toor dal, 2 tsp sambar powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric powder and 1/2 tsp salt. Cook on low for 4 minutes, mashing as you go, until the paruppu mixture is thick and scoopable; cool it completely.
Divide the dough into 8 balls; flatten each into a small bowl shape, spoon in 2 tbsp of the dal mixture, gather the edges and twist off the excess dough at the seal.
Roll each stuffed ball gently into a 6-7 inch circle on a dusted board, patching any small tears with a pinch of dry atta.

Cook on a hot tava over medium flame for a minute per side until speckled, then drizzle 1/2 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil on each side and roast until golden brown with crisp lacy edges, about 1 more minute per side.
tips: Crush the curry leaves lightly in your palm before adding; bruising releases their oils and doubles the aroma.
Homemade or fresh sambar powder makes a real difference here since it is the primary spice; stale powder tastes flat.
Any leftover filling doubles as a superb side for hot rice with a spoon of ghee.
variations.servingSuggestion: Cut into wedges and serve with coconut chutney and a small tumbler of sweet-sour pineapple rasam for a full Tamil-style spread.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Spicy Dal Paratha
variations.description: Borrowing its soul from puran-less puranpoli technique and everyday chana dal usal, this paratha carries a filling scented with goda masala, the smoky-sweet Maharashtrian blend of dagad phool and coconut. Roasted peanut coarse powder adds crunch and body, while wood-pressed groundnut oil keeps the flavours firmly rooted in the Deccan. It is warming rather than sharp, with layered spice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli wheat is an old Maharashtra-grown emmer, making it the most authentic flour possible for this regional bread

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the workhorse fat of Maharashtrian kitchens and echoes the peanuts in the filling

ingredients.name: Cooked chana dal
ingredients.note: Boiled soft, drained and roughly mashed

steps: Work 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and 1/2 tsp salt into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, then knead with roughly 3/4 cup water until soft and elastic. Rest the dough covered for 20 minutes while you build the filling.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai over medium heat and crackle 1/2 tsp mustard seeds until they finish popping, about 30 seconds. Toss in 8 curry leaves and 2 chopped green chillies and fry for 20 seconds.

Add 1 cup mashed chana dal, 2 tsp goda masala, 1/2 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp grated jaggery and 1/2 tsp salt, and cook on low for 3-4 minutes until dry and fragrant. Off the heat, mix in 3 tbsp roasted peanut powder and 2 tbsp grated dry coconut, then cool.
Split the dough into 8 balls and pack each with a generous 2 tbsp of filling, sealing the pleats tightly and flattening lightly between your palms.
Roll out each ball to a 6-7 inch round with soft, even strokes, dusting with atta only as needed so the surface stays supple.

Griddle on a medium-hot tava for about 1 minute until the underside is freckled, flip, spread 1/2 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, and repeat on the other side, cooking until both faces are toasty brown, roughly 3-4 minutes total per paratha.
tips: Goda masala scorches quickly, so always add it with the dal rather than into hot oil alone.
The teaspoon of jaggery is traditional balance, not sweetness; it lifts the smoky dagad phool notes in the masala.
Peanut powder absorbs stray moisture, so if your filling ever feels loose, an extra spoon of it is the easiest rescue.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a dollop of homemade white butter, spicy thecha on the side and a glass of masala taak spiked with ginger and coriander.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Pyaaz Paratha
variations.description: A fire-forward cousin of the everyday pyaaz paratha: the onion filling gets a double hit of green chillies and freshly cracked black pepper, so the heat builds slowly and lingers. Emmer wheat dough and a ghee-glossed tava finish keep the crust flaky enough to temper the burn.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Slow-digesting khapli wheat gives a sturdy yet tender wrap that carries this fiery filling without tearing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee's sweetness is the perfect counterweight to the chilli-pepper heat, brushed on generously at every flip

steps: Knead 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and roughly 1 cup water for 5 minutes into a soft, smooth dough, then rest it covered for 20 minutes.
Finely chop 3 medium onions, sprinkle with 0.5 tsp salt, wait 10 minutes, then squeeze them firmly in your fist until no more liquid drips out.

Toss the onions with 4 minced green chillies, 1 tsp coarsely cracked black pepper, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.25 cup coriander leaves and 2 tsp lemon juice.
Divide the dough into 8 equal balls, hollow each into a cup, pack in 2 tbsp of the spicy filling and pleat the edges shut, pressing out any trapped air.
Roll each ball on a floured board into a 7-inch round, easing off the pressure near the centre so no chilli-flecked filling breaks through.
Cook on a medium-hot tava for about 90 seconds per side, brushing each face with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Ghee, until crisp bronze spots cover the surface and the edges puff.
Press the paratha gently with a folded cloth while it cooks so the layers separate, then move to a wire rack for a minute before serving.
tips: Crack the peppercorns coarsely in a mortar rather than using pre-ground pepper; the little bursts of heat are the whole point.
Deseed half the green chillies if serving children, keeping the flavour but halving the fire.
The lemon juice brightens the heat; add it only after squeezing the onions or the filling turns soggy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Cool the palate with a bowl of boondi raita and a slice of raw onion soaked in vinegar; sweet mango pickle on the side plays beautifully against the pepper.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Pyaaz Paratha
variations.description: An unapologetically hot take powered by sun-dried Guntur chillies, the pride of Andhra Pradesh. The chillies are toasted in groundnut oil and ground with garlic into a rustic paste that stains the onion filling brick-red, delivering deep, fruity heat rather than a one-note burn.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Wholegrain emmer's earthy sweetness stands up to Guntur chilli heat better than refined flour ever could

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the everyday fat of Andhra kitchens and adds a subtle roasted-peanut base note

steps: Knead 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and about 1 cup water into a supple dough; rest it for 20 minutes while you build the chilli paste.

Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a small pan on low, toast 5 Guntur chillies and 1 tsp coriander seeds for 2 minutes until the chillies puff and darken slightly, then add 1 sprig curry leaves for the last 20 seconds.
Grind the toasted chillies and leaves with 6 garlic cloves, 1 tsp tamarind paste and 0.5 tsp salt into a coarse, brick-red paste, adding a teaspoon of water only if the grinder struggles.
Fold the paste and 0.25 tsp turmeric through 3 finely chopped, salted and squeezed onions until every shred is stained red.
Shape 8 dough balls, stuff each with 2 tbsp of the fiery filling, seal well and roll into 6-inch rounds with a light, steady hand.
Roast on a medium tava, about 2 minutes per side, drizzling 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil around the rim at each flip, until charred crimson-brown spots develop and the paratha smells smoky.
Stack the parathas in a cloth for 3 minutes before serving so the residual steam softens the crumb while the crust stays crisp.
tips: Wipe the chillies with a damp cloth instead of washing them; wet chillies spit violently in hot oil.
Swap 2 of the Guntur chillies for byadgi if you want the same deep red colour with gentler heat.
A spoon of the leftover chilli-garlic paste whisked into curd makes an instant Andhra-style dip for the same paratha.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as they do in Guntur homes with thick, chilled curd, a wedge of raw onion and a drop of ghee on the first bite to soften the blow.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Spicy Pyaaz Paratha
variations.description: This version borrows the soul of kanda bhaji and thecha: onions tossed with warm, smoky goda masala and crushed roasted peanuts. Goda masala's cinnamon-coconut sweetness rides under the chilli heat, giving the paratha a layered, almost caramel spice that is unique to Maharashtra.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli wheat is an old Maharashtra-grown emmer, making it the most authentic flour possible for this regional paratha

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed groundnut oil doubles down on the peanut notes already in the filling, a very Deccan pairing

steps: Make a soft dough from 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and about 1 cup water; knead 5 minutes and rest 20 minutes under a damp cloth.
Dry-toast 1 tbsp sesame seeds in a pan on low heat for about 1 minute until they turn pale gold and start to pop, then tip them out to cool.
Pound 0.33 cup roasted peanuts to a coarse rubble in a mortar; you want gritty pieces, not peanut butter.
Combine 3 finely chopped, salted and squeezed onions with the peanuts, sesame, 2 tsp goda masala, 3 minced green chillies, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.25 cup coriander leaves.
Stuff 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp filling each, seal the pleats and roll gently into 6-inch rounds; the peanut bits will show through as a pretty speckle.
Cook on a medium tava for around 2 minutes a side with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil brushed on per face, until nutty-smelling and freckled deep brown.
Cool for 2 minutes on a rack; the peanut filling crisps slightly as it settles, giving each bite a gentle crunch.
tips: Goda masala scorches quickly, so never toast it; folding it raw into the squeezed onions preserves its sweet spice.
If goda masala is unavailable, simmer nothing and substitute nothing fancy: use garam masala plus 1 tsp toasted grated dry coconut for a close cousin.
Pound the peanuts just before mixing; pre-ground peanuts lose their aroma within hours.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a fiery green-chilli thecha, a katori of mattha (spiced buttermilk), and a few slices of guava sprinkled with chilli salt for a true Deccan spread.

variations.name: Kumaoni Spicy Pyaaz Paratha
variations.description: From the Uttarakhand hills, where jakhya seeds are the tempering of choice: their crackly, nuttier-than-mustard pop transforms the onion filling. Finished with hemp-free hill staples like coarse coriander and hill garlic, this paratha tastes of woodsmoke kitchens in Kumaon villages.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its rustic, wholegrain character matches the coarse mountain wheat traditionally ground at Kumaoni gharats (watermills)

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Hill households prize pahadi ghee; slow-churned bilona ghee recreates that grassy richness on the tava

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: A spoon of pungent kachi ghani oil is the classic Kumaoni medium for crackling jakhya seeds

steps: Knead 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt and about 1 cup water into a soft dough, working in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee at the end; rest 20 minutes.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a small pan until it shimmers and just smokes, then crackle 1.5 tsp jakhya seeds for 15 to 20 seconds until they pop like tiny fireworks.
Add 5 sliced garlic cloves to the same oil and fry for 30 seconds until pale gold, then pour the whole tempering over 3 finely chopped, salted and squeezed onions.
Coarsely crush 2 tsp coriander seeds in a mortar and mix into the onions with 3 minced green chillies, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.25 tsp turmeric.
Fill 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp of the jakhya-scented masala each, seal tightly, and roll out to 6-inch rounds on a floured board.
Roast on a medium tava for 2 minutes per side, brushing on 0.5 tsp Anveshan Ghee at each turn, until the crust is crisp and scattered with dark toasted patches.
Serve straight off the tava; jakhya's crackle is at its best in the first few minutes while the paratha is piping hot.
tips: Jakhya must hit properly hot oil; in lukewarm oil the seeds turn bitter instead of nutty and crunchy.
No jakhya in your pantry? Use half mustard and half sesame seeds; the texture will be close though the flavour is milder.
Kumaoni cooks add a pinch of crushed hemp seed (bhang jeera) when available; toasted white sesame is the easy stand-in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Eat the hill way with bhang-free pahadi aloo ke gutke, a spoon of hot bhatt ki churkani or simply fresh curd, and finish with a piece of bal mithai if you can find it.

variations.name: Odia Spicy Pyaaz Paratha
variations.description: Odisha's beloved five-spice blend, panch phoron, is bloomed whole in mustard oil and folded through the onions, so every bite lands a different seed: fennel's sweetness, fenugreek's bitter edge, cumin's warmth. A little grated ginger and green chilli keep it bright and firmly spicy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The emmer's gentle sweetness lets each of the five panch phoron seeds register clearly on the palate

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Odia tempering is unthinkable without pungent mustard oil; wood-pressed keeps its raw sharpness intact

steps: Work 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and 1 tsp salt into 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, then knead with close to 1 cup water into a smooth, elastic dough; rest 20 minutes.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pan until it just smokes, lower the heat, and crackle 2 tsp panch phoron with 2 torn dried red chillies for 20 to 30 seconds until the fenugreek turns golden, not brown.

Tip in 3 finely chopped onions and sauté on medium for 4 minutes until translucent with golden edges, then stir in 1 inch grated ginger, 3 minced green chillies and 0.5 tsp turmeric for a final minute.
Cool the mixture completely, then fold in 0.25 cup chopped coriander leaves and 0.5 tsp salt to finish the filling.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, encase 2 tbsp of cooled filling in each, and roll into 6-inch discs, dusting with atta as needed.
Cook on a medium tava for roughly 2 minutes per side, brushing 0.5 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil on each face, until deeply blistered and aromatic.
Rest under a cloth for 2 minutes so the five-spice perfume settles evenly through the layers before serving.
tips: Watch the fenugreek seeds in the panch phoron like a hawk; the moment they turn from golden to brown, the whole batch tastes bitter.
Cooking the onions (unlike raw fillings elsewhere) is deliberate here; it mellows them into a jammy base that carries the whole spices.
Mix your own panch phoron in equal parts cumin, fennel, kalonji, mustard and just half a part fenugreek for a friendlier balance.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a spoon of Odia tomato-khajuri khatta (date-tomato chutney) and plain dahi; the sweet-sour chutney is the classic foil for panch phoron.

variations.name: Classic Stuffed Matar Paratha
variations.description: A winter-morning North Indian favourite where sweet green peas are cooked down with ginger and spices, then sealed inside soft khapli atta dough. The filling stays moist and slightly coarse, so every bite has pops of pea against the ghee-crisped crust. Roasting in slow-churned bilona ghee gives the paratha its signature nutty aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat's low gluten keeps the stuffed paratha tender, not chewy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: 1 tbsp goes into the dough, 1 tbsp for the filling, 2 tbsp for roasting

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 0.75 tsp salt and about 0.75 cup water, adding the water gradually, until you have a soft, non-sticky dough; cover and rest it for 15 minutes.
Pulse 2 cups green peas in a mixer to a coarse crumble, or crush them with a masher; do not make a smooth paste or the filling will turn pasty inside the paratha.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 20 seconds until fragrant, then add grated 1 inch ginger and 2 minced green chillies and stir for 30 seconds.

Add the crushed peas with 0.5 tsp salt, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric powder and 0.5 tsp garam masala; cook on medium heat for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring, until the mixture looks dry and holds together when pressed. Stir in 3 tbsp chopped coriander and cool completely.

Divide the dough into 8 balls and the filling into 8 portions of about 2 tbsp each. Flatten each ball into a 3-inch cup, place one portion of filling in the centre, gather the edges to seal, then roll gently into a 6-inch round, dusting lightly with atta.

Roast each paratha on a hot tava on medium-high heat for about 1 minute per side until brown spots appear, then brush both sides with a total of 0.75 tsp Anveshan Ghee and cook another 30 seconds per side until golden and crisp at the edges.
tips: Cook the pea filling until it is completely dry; even slightly wet filling will tear the dough while rolling.
If a paratha springs a leak on the tava, dab the spot with a little dry atta and press gently with the spatula to seal it.
The filling can be made a day ahead and refrigerated; bring it to room temperature before stuffing so it spreads easily.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot off the tava with a bowl of thick curd whisked with a pinch of roasted cumin, and a wedge of lime on the side.

variations.name: Punjabi Stuffed Matar Paratha
variations.description: The dhaba-style rendition from Punjab, where the pea filling gets a tangy lift from anardana and ajwain, and the finished paratha is crowned with a melting pat of white butter. It is rolled slightly thicker than usual so the crust shatters while the inside stays pillowy. This is unapologetically rich breakfast food, best eaten straight off the tava.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its wholesome, slightly sweet wheat flavour stands up to the rich butter finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Punjabi parathas are shallow-roasted generously; bilona ghee will not smoke on the tava

steps: Mix 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp ajwain, 0.75 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then knead in roughly 0.75 cup water bit by bit to form a supple dough that springs back slowly when pressed; rest under a damp cloth for 15 minutes.
Warm 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan over medium flame, add grated 1 inch ginger and 2 finely chopped green chillies, and let them sizzle for about 30 seconds until the raw smell disappears.

Tip in 2 cups coarsely crushed green peas along with 0.5 tsp salt and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder; sauté for 5 minutes on medium heat until every trace of moisture is gone and the peas smell sweet and toasty.
Take the pan off the heat and work in 1 tsp anardana powder and 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi; spread the filling on a plate to cool fully, then divide into 8 equal mounds of about 2 tbsp each.
Shape the dough into 8 balls, cup each one, tuck in a mound of filling, pinch shut and roll to a slightly thick 5.5-inch disc so the crust develops that dhaba-style bite.

Cook each paratha on a hot tava for about 90 seconds per side on medium-high heat, pressing the edges with a spatula, then drizzle a total of 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee per paratha and flip twice more until deeply blistered and crisp. Top each hot paratha with 1 tbsp white butter just before serving so it melts into the crust.
tips: Anardana gives the authentic dhaba tang; if unavailable, use 0.5 tsp amchur but add it off the heat to keep it bright.
Press the paratha edges firmly while roasting; the rim is the thickest part and needs direct contact to crisp.
Rub the kasuri methi between your palms before adding to release its aroma into the warm filling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a tall glass of salted lassi and spicy mango pickle; in true Punjabi style, add a raw onion half smacked open with the palm.

variations.name: Bengali Stuffed Matar Paratha
variations.description: Inspired by Bengal's beloved koraishutir kochuri, this paratha carries a silky pea filling perfumed with roasted fennel, ginger and a whisper of hing, all bound in pungent mustard oil. The kalonji-flecked dough turns delicately crisp, and the mustard oil's sharpness balances the natural sweetness of winter peas. It tastes like a Kolkata winter morning.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Stone-ground emmer gives the kochuri-style crust its rustic, flaky texture

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed kachi ghani pungency is the soul of this Bengali filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A final ghee brush on the hot paratha softens the mustard's bite

steps: Combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 tsp kalonji, 0.75 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil, rubbing the oil in until the flour feels sandy, then knead with about 0.75 cup water into a smooth, soft dough and rest for 20 minutes.
Grind 2 cups green peas with 3 green chillies and 1.5 inch ginger into a coarse, thick paste without adding any water; a few whole peas left in the mix add nice texture.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai until it just begins to smoke, then lower the flame, add 0.25 tsp hing and 1 tsp fennel seeds and let them sputter for 15 seconds until aromatic.

Add the pea paste with 0.5 tsp salt and cook on medium heat for 6 to 7 minutes, stirring continuously, until the mixture leaves the sides of the pan and turns a shade darker. Finish with 1 tsp roasted cumin powder and cool completely before dividing into 8 portions of about 2 tbsp.
Split the dough into 8 balls, hollow each into a cup, enclose one portion of pea filling, seal the pleats and roll gently into a 6-inch round, patching any thin spots with a dusting of atta.

Roast on a medium-hot tava for about 1 minute per side until pale gold spots form, then brush each paratha with a little of the 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and give both sides 30 more seconds until flecked deep brown and crisp.
tips: Heating mustard oil to its smoking point once, then cooling slightly, mellows its raw sharpness while keeping the aroma.
Grind the peas cold from the fridge; warm peas release water and make the filling loose.
Leftover filling makes an excellent toast topping the next morning, warmed with a spoon of ghee.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Bengali way with a light aloo'r dom or simply a smear of kasundi mustard and thin-sliced cucumber.

variations.name: Kerala Stuffed Matar Paratha
variations.description: A coastal spin where the pea stuffing is folded with fresh grated coconut, curry leaves and cracked black pepper, then toasted in virgin coconut oil. The coconut keeps the filling juicy and faintly sweet, while pepper brings gentle warmth instead of chilli heat. The aroma of curry leaves hitting hot coconut oil is worth making this for on its own.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Ancient emmer wheat rolls thin without tearing around the moist coconut filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed virgin coconut oil ties the filling and the roasting into one clean flavour

steps: Work 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and 0.75 tsp salt into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, then knead with close to 0.75 cup water for 5 minutes into a soft, elastic dough; rest it covered for 15 minutes.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan on medium flame, pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds for about 20 seconds, then add 12 torn curry leaves, 4 sliced shallots and grated 1 inch ginger and fry for 1 minute until the shallots turn translucent.
Add 1.5 cups coarsely mashed green peas, 0.25 tsp turmeric powder and 0.5 tsp salt; cook for 4 minutes on medium heat, stirring, until the peas dry out and smell sweet.

Stir in 0.5 cup fresh grated coconut and 1 tsp coarsely cracked black pepper and toast for 2 more minutes until the coconut loses its raw smell; cool the filling fully, then portion into 8 mounds of about 2 tbsp each.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, flatten each into a small bowl shape, fill with one coconut-pea mound, pinch closed and roll into a gentle 6-inch circle without pressing hard.

Cook on a hot tava over medium heat for around 1 minute per side until speckled brown, then spoon a little of the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil over each side and roast 30 seconds more until the crust turns crisp and fragrant.
tips: Use fresh or frozen grated coconut, not desiccated; dry coconut will pull moisture out of the filling and turn it crumbly.
Crack the pepper coarsely in a mortar rather than using fine powder so you get warm bursts of spice.
These parathas stay soft in a lunchbox because coconut oil does not stiffen the crumb; stack them with butter paper in between.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a quick coconut-curd chutney or a spoon of Kerala-style mango pickle and sliced banana on the side for a true southern breakfast plate.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Stuffed Matar Paratha
variations.description: Here the pea filling meets goda masala, the smoky-sweet Maharashtrian spice blend, along with roasted peanut crush and sesame for body. The result is earthier and more complex than the North Indian version, with a gentle caramel note from the toasted coconut in the masala. It is hearty enough to be a full lunch with just curd alongside.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli's nutty depth mirrors the roasted notes of goda masala beautifully

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed peanut oil doubles down on the filling's roasted peanut crunch

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasting the paratha in ghee rounds off the goda masala's smokiness

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, 0.75 tsp salt and about 0.75 cup water into a pliable dough that does not stick to your fingers; set aside under a damp cloth for 15 minutes.

Dry-toast 1 tbsp white sesame seeds in a small pan over low heat for about 2 minutes until they turn pale gold and jump, then tip them out. Pound 0.25 cup roasted peanuts to a coarse crush in a mortar.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium flame and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then add 2 chopped green chillies and stir briefly.

Add 2 cups roughly crushed green peas, 0.5 tsp salt and 2 tsp goda masala; cook on medium heat for 5 minutes, stirring often, until the mixture is dry and deeply fragrant. Fold in the toasted sesame, peanut crush and 3 tbsp chopped coriander, then cool and divide into 8 portions of roughly 2 tbsp.
Portion the dough into 8 balls, open each into a cup, seat one mound of filling inside, gather and seal, and roll softly into a 6-inch round on a lightly floured board.

Roast each paratha on a medium-hot tava for about 1 minute per side until brown patches bloom, then brush with a share of the 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and cook a further 30 seconds per side until crisp and lacquered.
tips: Goda masala scorches quickly; always add it with the peas rather than into hot oil alone.
The peanut crush should be gravel-coarse, not powder, so the filling keeps its trademark crunch.
If you cannot find goda masala, toast 1 tsp coriander seeds, 2 cloves and 1 tbsp dry coconut, and grind them as a stand-in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a katori of thecha-spiked curd or simple varan on the side, and finish the meal with a piece of jaggery in the Maharashtrian tradition.

variations.name: Classic Dry Baingan Bharta
variations.description: A drier, more concentrated cousin of the saucy bharta: the fire-roasted eggplant is cooked down hard with minimal tomato until every trace of moisture evaporates and the mash turns deeply browned and almost spreadable. Perfect for rolling inside rotis or packing into tiffins without leaking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A sturdy wood-pressed oil that lets the mash fry and brown rather than stew, which is the whole point of the dry style

steps: Prick 2 large eggplants all over and roast them on a medium open flame for 12-15 minutes, turning every 3 minutes, until the skin is charred to flakes and the flesh has fully slumped; peel, discard stems and mash well.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a wide, heavy kadai on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds until they darken and release their aroma.
Add 2 finely chopped onions and fry for 7-8 minutes until deeply golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 2 chopped green chillies and cook for another minute until fragrant.

Add just 1 finely chopped tomato with ½ tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and fry for 4-5 minutes until the tomato disintegrates and the masala looks dry and clumpy rather than saucy.

Tip in the mashed eggplant and cook uncovered on medium heat for 10-12 minutes, stirring every 2 minutes and spreading the mash across the pan, until all the moisture cooks off and the bharta darkens and starts leaving the sides cleanly.
Once the mixture holds together in a thick, scoopable mass, switch off the heat and fold in 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander; the finished bharta should mound on a spoon without slumping.
tips: Use only one tomato — extra tomato is the most common reason a dry bharta ends up soggy.
Spreading the mash thin across the pan and letting it sizzle before stirring speeds up evaporation and adds toasty flavour.
Cooled completely, this bharta works beautifully as a sandwich or kathi-roll filling and keeps for 3 days refrigerated.
variations.servingSuggestion: Roll inside warm khapli-atta phulkas with pickled onions for a lunchbox wrap, or serve as a side with dal-chawal on a weeknight thali.

variations.name: Rajasthani Dry Baingan Bharta
variations.description: A desert-style bharta fried in Anveshan Ghee with crushed dried red chillies, fennel and a sour flourish of amchur — no tomatoes at all, in true arid-region fashion. The result is rustic, hot and tangy, tasting of woodsmoke and toasted spice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: In tomato-scarce Rajasthani kitchens, bilona ghee provides the richness that binds this spartan bharta together

steps: Roast 2 large eggplants over a medium flame for 13-15 minutes, rotating every 3 minutes, until the skin turns papery black and the flesh yields completely to a knife; peel while warm and mash coarsely.

Melt 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadai on medium heat until it smells nutty, then bloom 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1 tsp fennel seeds together for 40 seconds until they sputter and turn a shade darker.
Add 6 sliced garlic cloves and fry for about a minute until the edges brown, then add 4 crushed dried red chillies and stir for 20 seconds so they stain the ghee a rusty orange without burning.
Add 2 finely chopped onions with 1 tsp salt and fry for 7-8 minutes on medium heat until they brown deeply — the onions must carry the flavour that tomatoes would normally provide.

Sprinkle 2 tsp coriander powder and ½ tsp turmeric, stir for 30 seconds, then add the mashed eggplant and fry uncovered for 9-10 minutes, stirring and pressing, until the bharta is thick, dry and browned in patches.
Dust 1½ tsp amchur over the pan off the heat and fold it through; taste and adjust the sourness so it clearly cuts through the ghee's richness before serving.
tips: Amchur burns and turns bitter on direct heat, so always add it after the flame is off.
For a village-style touch, crush the dried chillies by hand rather than in a grinder so you get irregular flakes and seeds.
This bharta is intentionally rich; pair it with plain rotis rather than parathas to keep the meal balanced.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot bajra or missi roti, a raw onion smashed with the heel of your palm, and chilled chaas seasoned with roasted cumin — a complete Marwari lunch.

variations.name: Tamil Dry Baingan Bharta (Kathirikai Masiyal Style)
variations.description: Based on the Tamil kathirikai masiyal, this version tempers the smoked eggplant mash with mustard seeds, urad dal, curry leaves and sambar powder in fragrant sesame oil. A squeeze of lemon at the end keeps it light and tangy, closer to a warm relish than a heavy sabzi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Nallennai, as Tamil kitchens call wood-pressed sesame oil, is inseparable from masiyal and gives it a warm toasted base

steps: Flame-roast 2 large eggplants on medium heat for 12-14 minutes, giving them a quarter turn every 3 minutes, until the skins are blistered black all over and the pods collapse; peel once cool enough to handle and mash the flesh smooth.
Heat 2½ tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadai on medium heat, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds for 30 seconds, then add 2 tsp urad dal and fry for about a minute until the dal turns golden and smells biscuity.
Add 2 torn dried red chillies, 2 slit green chillies and 15 curry leaves and let them crackle for 30 seconds, keeping a lid handy as the leaves spit in hot oil.
Add 8 chopped shallots with 1 tsp salt and sauté for 4-5 minutes until soft and pale gold; shallots, not big onions, give masiyal its gentle sweetness.

Lower the heat, stir in 2 tsp sambar powder and ¼ tsp turmeric for 20 seconds, then add the mashed eggplant and cook for 7-8 minutes, stirring often, until the mash absorbs the tempering and turns thick enough to hold a spoon upright.
Switch off the flame, squeeze in 1 tbsp lemon juice and mix well; the masiyal should taste tangy, gently spicy and smoky all at once.
tips: Fry the urad dal to a true golden brown before anything else goes in — underdone dal stays chalky in the finished dish.
Sambar powder varies in salt and heat between brands, so start with 1½ tsp if yours is a strong one.
Masiyal thickens as it cools; loosen leftovers with a spoon of hot water and a fresh drizzle of sesame oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rice and a spoon of Anveshan Ghee mashed in, or as a side to soft idlis at breakfast the way Madurai messes do.

variations.name: Odia Dry Baingan Bharta (Baigana Bharta with Panch Phoron)
variations.description: Odisha's five-spice signature transforms this bharta: panch phoron bloomed in pungent mustard oil laces the smoky mash with fenugreek, fennel and nigella. Green chillies and raw onion folded in at the end keep it bright and homely, the way it is served beside pakhala in Odia homes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Odia bharta lives on the sharp bite of kachi ghani mustard oil, used both for tempering and as a raw finishing drizzle

steps: Char 2 large eggplants over a medium flame for 12-15 minutes, turning every 3 minutes, until the skin flakes black and the flesh is soft to the core; peel, remove stems and mash roughly, keeping a few strands whole.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai on medium-high heat for about 90 seconds until it pales and just begins to smoke, then reduce the flame to medium.
Add 1½ tsp panch phoron and let the five spices crackle for 30-40 seconds until the fenugreek darkens slightly and the fennel smells sweet — pull back the heat if the methi threatens to burn.

Add 5 crushed garlic cloves and 1 finely chopped onion and fry for 5-6 minutes until light golden, then add 1 chopped tomato with ½ tsp turmeric, ½ tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 3-4 minutes until pulpy.
Fold in the mashed eggplant and cook uncovered on medium heat for 8-9 minutes, stirring every couple of minutes, until the bharta dries out, deepens in colour and starts leaving the pan's sides.
Off the heat, stir in the second finely chopped raw onion, 3 slit green chillies, 3 tbsp chopped coriander and the remaining ½ tbsp raw Anveshan Mustard Oil for the authentic pungent Odia finish.
tips: Panch phoron's fenugreek seeds turn bitter past golden-brown, so keep the tempering under 40 seconds.
The raw onion added at the end is traditional and non-negotiable in Odia homes; it gives the soft mash its crunch.
This bharta is deliberately medium-hot; add a pinch more red chilli powder rather than extra green chillies to keep the flavour balance.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve beside a bowl of pakhala (fermented rice water) on a hot day, or with plain steamed rice, roasted papad and a wedge of lime.

variations.name: Kerala Dry Baingan Bharta (Coconut Vazhuthananga Style)
variations.description: A Malabar-leaning bharta where the smoked eggplant is dry-fried with golden coconut slivers, shallots and curry leaves in cold-pressed coconut oil. The toasted coconut lends nutty sweetness and gentle texture, making this the mellowest and most fragrant take of the set.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil ties the toasted coconut and curry leaves into one seamless Malabar aroma

ingredients.name: Fresh coconut, cut into thin slivers

steps: Roast 2 large eggplants over a medium flame for 12-14 minutes, quarter-turning every 3 minutes, until charred and collapsed; peel and mash the flesh coarsely once cool enough to handle.

Heat 2½ tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a wide pan on medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds for 30 seconds, then add ½ cup thin coconut slivers and fry for 3-4 minutes, stirring steadily, until they turn an even golden brown.
Add 10 sliced shallots, 3 slit green chillies, 1 inch chopped ginger and 15 curry leaves and sauté for 4-5 minutes until the shallots soften and pick up golden edges.

Sprinkle ½ tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, stir for 20 seconds, then add the mashed eggplant and cook uncovered on medium heat for 8-9 minutes, folding regularly, until the mash dries into a thick, cohesive mass streaked with coconut.
Grind ¾ tsp black pepper coarsely and stir it in during the final 2 minutes so its sharpness stays fresh against the sweet coconut.
