Cook uncovered on medium-high for 7-8 minutes, tossing every minute, so the mushroom moisture releases and evaporates while the pieces brown against the coconut base.
Sprinkle 2 tsp goda masala and the crushed roasted peanuts, and stir-fry for 2-3 minutes more until the sukka is dry, nutty and clumping lightly together.
Take off the heat, shower with 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander leaves and serve warm rather than piping hot, as the flavours read best that way.
tips: Add goda masala only near the end; its delicate dagad phool aroma dies in prolonged high heat.
Toast the dry coconut with genuine patience; that browned coconut is what separates a Deccan sukka from a generic stir-fry.
A squeeze of lime at the table brightens the earthy-nutty finish without breaking tradition.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside jowar or bajra bhakri with thecha and a raw onion wedge; it also works as a dry side with varan-bhaat and toop.

variations.name: Tamil Dry Mushroom
variations.description: Kalan milagu varuval: mushrooms roasted hard in gingelly oil with freshly crushed black pepper, fennel and a double dose of curry leaves. Peppery, glistening and almost black at the edges, it is the vegetarian answer to a Chettinad pepper fry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: A milagu varuval demands gingelly oil; wood-pressed sesame oil gives the pepper fry its authentic dark, toasty gloss

steps: Slice 450 g mushrooms thickly, slice 2 onions, smash 6 garlic cloves and coarsely crush 2 tsp black peppercorns with 1 tsp fennel seeds in a mortar.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil in a heavy kadai on medium; crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds, add 1 tsp urad dal and fry until it turns biscuit gold, about 40 seconds, then add 2 sprigs of curry leaves.
Fry the sliced onions and smashed garlic for 6-7 minutes until the onions brown deeply and the garlic edges caramelise.

Add the mushroom slices with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, and roast uncovered on medium-high for 8-9 minutes, tossing every minute, until all moisture is gone and the slices are browned and slightly shrunken.
Lower the heat, sprinkle the crushed pepper-fennel mixture over the pan and toss continuously for 90 seconds so the pepper toasts in the hot oil without burning.
Tear the last sprig of curry leaves directly into the pan, toss for 30 seconds until they crisp, and switch off the flame.
Squeeze 2 tsp lemon juice over the varuval while it is still hot and give it one final toss before plating.
tips: Crush the pepper coarsely, never powder it; the little cracked bits popping on the tongue are the point of a milagu varuval.
Add the pepper only after the mushrooms are dry, or it steams instead of toasting and loses its punch.
This dish is intentionally borderline over-roasted; trust the dark edges, they carry the flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a side with sambar or rasam rice and appalam, or pile onto curd rice for the classic Tamil contrast of cool and fiery.

variations.name: Rajasthani Dry Mushroom
variations.description: A ghee-roasted, curd-marinated take inspired by Jodhpuri sookha subzi: mushrooms tossed with whole dried red chillies, crushed coriander seeds and hing, finished with amchur for that dry desert tang. No tomato, no water, all flavour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan A2 Cow Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasting in bilona ghee is what gives this desert-style sookha subzi its regal, nutty backbone in place of any gravy

steps: Halve 450 g mushrooms and whisk 0.5 cups thick curd with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp of the salt; fold the mushrooms through and marinate for 15 minutes.
Meanwhile slice 1 onion thin, grate a 1 inch piece of ginger and crush 2 tsp coriander seeds coarsely in a mortar.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan A2 Cow Ghee in a heavy kadai on medium, sizzle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then add 4 whole dried red chillies and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and fry for 30 seconds until the chillies puff and darken.
Add the sliced onion and grated ginger and fry for 4-5 minutes until the onion is golden and beginning to crisp at the edges.

Tip in the marinated mushrooms with every scrap of the curd coating and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, and cook on medium-high for 10-12 minutes, stirring every couple of minutes, until the curd dries down and clings to the mushrooms as a spiced crust.
Sprinkle the crushed coriander seeds and cook 2 minutes more so they toast against the pan, releasing a citrusy aroma.
Turn off the heat, dust with 1 tsp amchur, scatter 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander leaves and toss well before serving.
tips: Use thick, well-hung curd; watery curd extends the drying stage and can make the ghee splutter aggressively.
The dish is done when the pan bottom shows toasted spice sticking lightly; scrape those bits over the mushrooms, they are gold.
Break one fried dried chilli and toss it through if serving to heat-lovers; leave whole for milder tables.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with hot bajra roti, a smear of white butter and green-chilli pickle; it also sits perfectly on a Rajasthani thali next to gatte ki sabzi and khichdi.

variations.name: Kumaoni Dry Mushroom
variations.description: A hill-kitchen stir-fry from Uttarakhand tempered with jakhya, the wild mustard-like seed that crackles louder and tastes nuttier than anything in the plains pantry. Cooked in mustard oil with minimal spices, it lets mountain simplicity speak.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Pahari kitchens fry jakhya in pungent mustard oil; this kachi ghani pressing mirrors the hill-village original exactly

steps: Tear 450 g mushrooms by hand into rough halves and quarters, hill style, rather than slicing; slice 1 onion, chop 6 garlic cloves and slit 2 green chillies.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil in a kadai on high until it just smokes, then reduce to medium and let it sit for 20 seconds so the sharpness mellows.
Add 1.5 tsp jakhya seeds and let them crackle furiously for about 20 seconds until the popping slows, then add 2 whole dried red chillies and the chopped garlic and fry for 30 seconds until golden.
Add the sliced onion and slit green chillies and sauté for 3-4 minutes on medium until the onion softens without fully browning.

Add the torn mushrooms with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook uncovered on medium-high for 8-9 minutes, tossing often, until the moisture is gone and the pieces are browned and tender.
Taste a piece for salt, then finish with 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander leaves and 2 tsp lemon juice squeezed over the hot pan.
Serve immediately, while the jakhya still has its fresh-popped crunch scattered through the dish.
tips: Jakhya must be fried until the popping nearly stops; underdone seeds taste raw and grassy.
If you cannot source jakhya, cumin is the usual stand-in, but halve the quantity as it is stronger in aroma.
Hand-torn mushrooms grip the tempering better than knife-cut slices and look pleasingly rustic.
variations.servingSuggestion: Eat the pahari way with steamed rice and a bowl of thick pahadi dal, or wrap in a hot mandua or wheat roti with a spoon of bhang-seed or coriander chutney.

variations.name: Classic Dry Tori
variations.description: A no-gravy ridge gourd stir-fry where the vegetable is cooked hot and fast in Anveshan Ghee so its juices evaporate as they release, leaving spice-crusted, lightly caramelised slices. Minimal tomato, maximum cumin-coriander, and a texture that stays firm instead of stewy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: High-heat-stable bilona ghee lets the tori sear and caramelise without a gravy to hide behind

steps: Peel the ridges off 500 g ridge gourd and cut it into thickish 2 cm half-moons; thick pieces survive high-heat cooking, thin ones dissolve. Slice 1 medium onion and chop 1 small tomato.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide, heavy pan on medium-high until shimmering, then crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 20 seconds until fragrant and a shade darker.
Add the sliced onion and fry for 3-4 minutes until golden at the edges, then stir in 2 tsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 45 seconds until the raw smell lifts.
Add the chopped tomato with 2 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 2-3 minutes until it breaks down into a rough, dryish masala.
Add the tori and toss to coat, then cook uncovered on medium-high for 10-12 minutes, tossing every 2 minutes; the moisture should evaporate as fast as it releases, letting the slices brown lightly.
When the pieces are tender with caramelised patches and the pan looks dry, sprinkle 0.5 tsp amchur, toss for 30 seconds, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: The wide pan matters more than any ingredient here; a crowded small kadhai steams the tori instead of searing it.
Salt draws water out, so if you want extra browning, add the salt only in the last 5 minutes.
Amchur added at the end keeps its sharp fruitiness; cooked long, it just disappears.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile into hot phulkas as a roll with sliced onion and green chutney, or serve alongside dal-chawal where its dry, spiced texture is the perfect contrast.

variations.name: Bengali Dry Tori
variations.description: Jhinge posto's dry cousin: ridge gourd tossed in pungent Anveshan Mustard Oil with kalonji and green chillies, finished with a coarse poppy-seed paste that clings to each piece like a nutty crumb. Quietly hot, faintly sweet, and utterly Bengali in its restraint.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Kachi ghani mustard oil and posto are an inseparable Bengali pairing; no other oil tastes right here

steps: Soak 3 tbsp poppy seeds in 3 tbsp hot water for 10 minutes, then grind them with 1 green chilli into a coarse, gritty paste; do not make it silky smooth.
Peel and slice 500 g ridge gourd into 1.5 cm pieces and thinly slice 1 small onion; slit the remaining 2 green chillies lengthwise.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai on medium-high until it just smokes and mellows, about 90 seconds, then drop the flame to medium and scatter in 0.5 tsp kalonji.
When the kalonji sputters, add the sliced onion and slit chillies and fry for 3 minutes until the onion softens without much colour.
Add the jhinge with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder and 1 tsp salt, toss, cover and cook on low for 8-10 minutes until tender; the gourd's own water is all the moisture this dish needs.
Stir in the poppy paste and 0.5 tsp sugar and cook uncovered on medium for 3-4 minutes, scraping the pan, until the posto dries into a pale nubbly coating on every piece.
tips: Grinding posto with a splash of its soaking water and a chilli in a small mixie jar works far better than a big jar, where it just flies around.
The dish is done when the posto starts sticking lightly to the kadhai; those scraped-up bits are the best part.
A final half-spoon of raw mustard oil drizzled off the heat is a classic Bengali finishing move for extra pungency.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Bengali way as a first course with plain steamed rice, a drizzle of the pan oil and a whole green chilli to bite between mouthfuls; musur dal alongside completes the meal.

variations.name: Tamil Dry Tori
variations.description: Peerkangai varuval: ridge gourd sliced thin and fried crisp-edged in Anveshan Sesame Oil with urad dal, curry leaves and cracked pepper, finished with fresh coconut. The gingelly oil's nuttiness and the fried dal's crunch turn a watery gourd into something you keep stealing off the pan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil gives varuval its trademark deep, toasty Tamil flavour

steps: Peel 500 g peerkangai lightly and slice it into thin 0.75 cm rounds; thin slices are essential so they fry dry instead of stewing.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a wide iron pan over medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 1 tbsp urad dal and fry for about 1 minute until evenly golden.
Add 3 dried red chillies torn into pieces, 12 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp hing, letting the leaves crackle and crisp for 15 seconds.
Lay in the gourd rounds with 0.25 tsp turmeric powder and 0.75 tsp salt and spread them out; cook uncovered on medium heat for 6 minutes without stirring so the bottom layer browns.
Toss, then continue cooking uncovered for another 6-8 minutes, tossing every 2 minutes, until the slices are tender with golden, slightly crisped edges and the pan is dry.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp coarsely crushed black pepper and 0.25 cup grated coconut, toss on the heat for a final 1 minute, and serve immediately while the edges still crackle.
tips: Resist stirring in the first 6 minutes; the undisturbed contact with the hot iron pan is what creates the varuval crust.
Crush the pepper coarsely in a mortar rather than using powder; the sharp bursts of pepper are the dish's signature.
This turns soggy on standing, so time it to come off the pan just as everyone sits down.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as the crisp counterpoint to rasam sadam or sambar rice, or tuck it into a curd-rice lunch box where the pepper heat cuts the cool yogurt beautifully.

variations.name: Rajasthani Dry Tori
variations.description: A desert-style dry tori seared in Anveshan Ghee with a whole-spice tadka of dried red chillies, fennel and coriander seeds, then dusted with besan that toasts into a savoury crumb around each piece. The gram-flour trick is a classic Marwari way of turning watery vegetables hearty.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rajasthani cooking runs on ghee; here it toasts the besan coating into a nutty golden crumb

steps: Peel and cut 500 g ridge gourd into 2 cm pieces and pat them dry with a kitchen towel; dry surfaces are crucial for the besan to toast rather than clump.
Dry-roast 3 tbsp besan in a small pan on low heat for 3-4 minutes, stirring constantly, until it smells nutty and darkens a shade; set aside.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium, crackle 0.75 tsp cumin seeds and 1 tsp fennel seeds, then add 3 whole dried red chillies and 1.5 tsp crushed coriander seeds and fry for 30 seconds until deeply aromatic.

Add the tori with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt and toss well, then cook uncovered on medium heat for 10-12 minutes, tossing occasionally, until tender and mostly dry.
Sprinkle the roasted besan evenly over the gourd, drizzle 1 tbsp of the ghee from the pan edges back over the top, and toss gently for 3-4 minutes until the flour coats every piece in a golden crumb.
Dust with 0.75 tsp amchur, give one final toss for 30 seconds, and serve hot before the coating softens.
tips: Roasting the besan separately first is non-negotiable; raw gram flour sprinkled into the pan tastes chalky no matter how long you cook it.
If the besan starts sticking, add ghee rather than water; water is the enemy of this dish.
The same besan-crumb technique upgrades bhindi and capsicum, so keep roasted besan in a jar.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot bajra or wheat rotis, a big spoon of dahi, and a raw onion smashed with salt on the side, dhaba style; it also travels well in tiffins as it contains no gravy.

variations.name: Odia Dry Tori
variations.description: A janhi bhaja from coastal Odisha: ridge gourd tossed with panch phoron in sharp Anveshan Mustard Oil, cooked dry with garlic and green chilli, and finished with a scatter of grated coconut. The five-seed temper's fennel and fenugreek give it a bittersweet edge no single spice can copy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Odia bhaja demands the bold bite of kachi ghani mustard oil under its five-spice temper

steps: Peel 500 g janhi lightly, leaving thin green streaks, and cut it into 1.5 cm thick diagonal slices that give more searing surface; smash 5 garlic cloves with the flat of a knife.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai on medium-high until it shimmers and loses its raw prickle, roughly 90 seconds, then lower to medium.
Add 1.5 tsp panch phoron and 1 dried red chilli; within 20-30 seconds the mustard should pop and the fenugreek turn light brown, at which point add the smashed garlic and 2 slit green chillies.
Fry the garlic for about 1 minute until its edges colour, then add the sliced gourd with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder and 0.75 tsp salt.
Cook uncovered on medium heat for 10-12 minutes, turning the slices every 2-3 minutes, letting the released moisture cook off so the pieces soften and pick up brown-edged spots.
Fold in 3 tbsp grated coconut, toss on the heat for 1 minute so it toasts faintly, then finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and serve.
tips: Cook the fenugreek in the panch phoron only to light brown; dark brown fenugreek turns the whole bhaja bitter.
Diagonal slices are more than looks; the larger cut face browns better against the kadhai.
Some Odia homes add a spoon of crushed badi (sun-dried lentil nuggets) at the end for crunch; fry them in the oil first if you have them.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with pakhala (fermented rice) and roasted tomato chutney for a true Odia summer meal, or simply with dal-bhaat where its mustardy edge cuts through the comfort.

variations.name: Classic Garlic Mooli Paratha
variations.description: Radish and garlic are natural allies — the garlic's sweetness rounds off mooli's peppery bite. Here golden-fried garlic is folded through squeezed radish shreds, the paratha roasted in bilona ghee until the whole kitchen smells of toasted garlic and warm wheat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The dense emmer crumb traps the fried-garlic aroma inside each pocket as it roasts

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Garlic fried gently in bilona ghee turns sweet and crisp instead of acrid

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 1/2 tsp salt and about 3/4 cup water into a soft, non-sticky dough; rest it covered for 15 minutes.
Grate 400 g radish, toss with 1/2 tsp salt, rest 15 minutes, then wring it bone-dry in a muslin cloth — the drier the shreds, the crisper the paratha.
Slice 10 garlic cloves thinly and fry them in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over low-medium heat for about 2 minutes until uniformly pale gold; lift them out the second they colour, saving the garlicky ghee.
Mix the squeezed radish with the fried garlic, its ghee, 2 minced green chillies, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric and 3 tbsp chopped coriander.
Stuff 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp filling each, pleat the tops closed and roll gently into 6-inch rounds, dusting with dry atta as needed.
Roast on a medium-hot tava, 1 minute dry per side, then brush 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee on each face and cook about 3 minutes total, pressing the edges, until golden-brown spots bloom all over.
tips: Pull the garlic at pale gold — it keeps darkening off the heat, and burnt garlic will bitter the entire filling.
Slice, do not mince, the garlic; slices stay sweet and crisp while mince tends to scorch in pockets.
Rub the rolling pin with a drop of ghee if the dough drags — smoother rolling means fewer filling blowouts.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thick curd whisked with a pinch of roasted cumin, and a sharp green-chilli pickle to spar with the sweet garlic.

variations.name: Bengali Garlic Mooli Paratha
variations.description: Garlic and mustard oil are the twin engines of Bengali home cooking, and both roar here: the radish is sautéed with slivered garlic in smoked kachi ghani oil with nigella seeds. The cooked, jammy filling gives this porota an almost-sweet depth against the mustard's punch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its wholegrain nuttiness anchors the loud garlic-mustard filling like a good atta porota should

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Garlic slivers fried in pungent wood-pressed mustard oil are pure Bengali kitchen perfume

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A light ghee gloss at the end softens the mustard bite into something rounded

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil, 1/2 tsp salt and roughly 3/4 cup water into a supple dough; rest under a damp cloth for 15 minutes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai until it just smokes and turns pale, about a minute, then reduce the heat and crackle 1/2 tsp nigella seeds for 20 seconds.

Fry 10 slivered garlic cloves in the same oil for 90 seconds until the edges gild, add 3 slit green chillies, then 400 g grated radish with 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1/2 tsp salt and 1/2 tsp sugar; sauté 8 minutes until the shreds are dry, glossy and faintly caramelised. Cool fully with 2 tbsp coriander folded in.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, tuck 2 tbsp of the garlicky mulo into each, seal and roll to 6-inch rounds with light, even strokes.
Roast each porota on a medium tava for 1 minute per side, then brush both faces with a share of the 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and cook 2 minutes more, flipping once, until mottled deep brown.
Rest the finished porotas under a cloth for 2 minutes so the garlic-mustard steam soaks back into the crumb.
tips: Smoke the mustard oil before anything touches it; the raw oil would bulldoze even 10 cloves of garlic.
The half-teaspoon of sugar is a Bengali balancing move, not a sweetener — it tames both radish and mustard.
This cooked filling freezes well for a month; thaw, squeeze off any thawed moisture, and stuff.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with aloo posto or simply a smear of kasundi and cucumber slices; end with a cup of milky Darjeeling for the full Kolkata morning.

variations.name: Tamil Garlic Mooli Paratha
variations.description: A poriyal-inspired take: the radish is tempered with mustard seeds, urad dal, garlic and a storm of curry leaves in gingelly oil, so the filling tastes like a beloved Tamil side dish tucked inside wheat. Black pepper carries the heat, keeping it warm rather than fiery.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: A wholegrain wrapper worthy of a poriyal filling — hearty where maida parottas are hollow

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed gingelly oil is the default Tamil tempering fat, and garlic loves its toastiness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A restrained finishing brush, the way a Tamil grandmother tops hot rice

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, 1/2 tsp salt and about 3/4 cup water into a soft dough; cover and rest 15 minutes.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadhai over medium heat, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds fully, then brown 1 tsp urad dal to biscuit-gold with 2 torn dried red chillies, about 40 seconds.

Add 8 chopped garlic cloves and 3 sprigs of curry leaves; fry 1 minute until the garlic turns pale gold and the leaves crisp, then tip in 400 g grated radish with 1/2 tsp salt and sauté 8 minutes until dry and sweet. Stir in 3/4 tsp black pepper and cool completely.
Shape 8 dough balls, fill each with 2 tbsp of the tempered radish, pleat shut and roll into 6-inch rounds without pressing hard over the centre.
Cook on a medium tava for about 3 minutes per paratha, flipping twice and brushing a thin film of Anveshan Ghee on each side, until lacy brown spots appear and the curry-leaf aroma lifts.
Stack briefly under a cloth so the crust relaxes to a soft, foldable finish.
tips: The urad dal must reach true gold — its crunch against the soft radish is the textural heart of this version.
Reserve a few fried curry leaves to crumble over the curd you serve alongside.
If the filling tastes flat once cooled, a pinch more black pepper fixes it faster than salt will.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and a small bowl of pepper rasam for sipping between bites, with filter coffee to close.

variations.name: Malwa Garlic Mooli Paratha
variations.description: From the wheat-rich Malwa plateau of Madhya Pradesh, where crushed roasted peanuts thicken and sweeten vegetable fillings. Garlic is pounded with the peanuts into a coarse rubble that gives every bite of radish a rich, nutty backbone — sturdy farmhouse food for cold plateau mornings.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Malwa is India's wheat bowl — heritage emmer honours the region's grain pride

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed peanut oil echoes the crushed-peanut filling from crust to core

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: One spoon in the dough keeps the farmhouse crumb short and tender

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 1/2 tsp salt and about 3/4 cup water into a soft dough and rest it 15 minutes.
Grate 400 g radish, salt with 1/2 tsp salt for 15 minutes, then squeeze it thoroughly dry in a cloth.
Pound 10 garlic cloves, 3 green chillies and 4 tbsp roasted peanuts in a mortar into a coarse, oily rubble — texture, not paste, is the goal.

Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan over medium heat and fry the pounded mixture for 2 minutes until the garlic loses its raw edge and smells toasty, then toss with the squeezed radish, 1 tsp coriander powder, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder and 1/2 tsp amchur.

Stuff 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp filling apiece, seal firmly and roll into 6-inch rounds; roast each on a medium tava with 1/2 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil drizzled per side for about 3 minutes until the crust is freckled deep gold.
Cool 1 minute before serving so the peanut rubble sets from molten to pleasantly fudgy.
tips: Keep the peanut pound coarse; a fine grind soaks up the radish moisture and turns pasty on the tava.
Frying the garlic-peanut rubble before mixing removes any raw-garlic burn that would overpower the mooli.
These are hearty — count on two per adult and roll the rest of the dough into plain ghee-smeared triangles for lighter eaters.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of plain curd, a spoon of spicy garlic chutney and jaggery shavings on the side, the way Malwa farm kitchens balance heat with sweetness.

variations.name: Andhra Garlic Mooli Paratha
variations.description: Garlic gets the full vellulli karam treatment: pounded with roasted Guntur chillies into a fiery red paste that stains the radish shreds crimson. This is the hottest paratha in the family, tempered only by the sweetness the radish develops on the griddle.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The mellow emmer crumb is the only thing standing between you and full Guntur voltage

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Andhra karam pastes are always loosened with gingelly oil — it deepens as it fries

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, 1/2 tsp salt and around 3/4 cup water into a soft dough; rest 15 minutes covered.
Grate 400 g radish, salt it with 1/2 tsp salt, rest 15 minutes and squeeze completely dry in a muslin cloth.

Dry-roast 5 Guntur chillies and 1 tsp cumin seeds over low heat for 3 minutes until the chillies turn glossy and brittle, then pound them with 12 garlic cloves, 1 tsp tamarind paste and 1/4 tsp salt into a coarse crimson karam.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, crisp 2 sprigs of curry leaves for 30 seconds, add the karam and fry 2 minutes until the raw garlic smell gives way to a deep roasted aroma; mix this paste through the squeezed radish with 1/4 tsp turmeric.

Stuff 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp of the red-stained filling, seal well and roll into 6-inch rounds, then roast on a medium tava with 1/2 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil per side for about 3 minutes each until darkly freckled.
Let each paratha stand 1 minute; the karam mellows noticeably in that time and the flavours knit together.
tips: Frying the karam paste is essential — raw pounded garlic and chilli would taste harsh and one-dimensional.
The teaspoon of tamarind is the Andhra signature that keeps this from being merely hot; do not skip it.
Halve the chillies to soften the blow for a mixed table, but keep all 12 garlic cloves — they carry the dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a big spoon of thick, cold curd and thin onion rings soaked in lime juice — the traditional Andhra coolants against karam heat.

variations.name: Classic Garlic Sattu Paratha
variations.description: Roasted gram flour meets a double dose of garlic — half sizzled in ghee until golden, half raw-minced for bite — inside a soft khapli wheat crust. The cooked garlic turns sweet and mellow while the raw shreds keep their punch, so the filling has real depth. A weekday paratha that smells like a feast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The sturdy emmer dough traps the garlic aroma inside instead of letting it bake away

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Fresh roasted-gram sattu is mild enough to let the double garlic lead

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Garlic fried in bilona ghee turns nutty-sweet, the flavour heart of this recipe

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and around 3/4 cup water into a soft, springy dough; cover and rest 20 minutes.

Mince 10 garlic cloves and split them in half. Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium-low and fry one half of the garlic for about 90 seconds until pale gold and sweet-smelling, watching closely so it never browns past amber.

Combine 1 cup Anveshan Sattu with the fried garlic and its ghee, the reserved raw garlic, 2 minced green chillies, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric powder, 2 tbsp coriander and 1/2 tsp salt.
Add 1 tbsp lemon juice and sprinkle 2-3 tbsp water gradually, rubbing the mixture until it clumps when squeezed yet crumbles when poked.
Portion the dough into 8 balls, cup each one, tuck in 2 tbsp of the garlic-sattu filling, twist the seam shut and roll gently into 6-7 inch rounds.

Roast on a medium-hot tava for about a minute per bare side until freckled, then crisp each side with 1/2 tsp Anveshan Ghee until deep golden, roughly 4 minutes per paratha; the garlic perfume will tell you when it is done.
tips: Golden garlic is sweet; brown garlic is bitter. Pull the pan off the heat a shade early because it keeps cooking in the hot ghee.
Crushing the fried garlic slightly into the sattu spreads its flavour further than leaving the bits whole.
The filling can be doubled and frozen dry; thaw and add lemon juice and water only on the day of cooking.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain whipped curd, a fried green chilli and sliced tomatoes with black salt; the mild sides let the garlic do the talking.

variations.name: Bengali Garlic Sattu Paratha
variations.description: Garlic and mustard oil are a devastating pair in Bengali cooking, and this paratha leans all the way in: the sattu is bound with smoking-hot kachi ghani mustard oil in which garlic and dried red chilli have been crackled. Kalonji in the dough adds the familiar radhuni-adjacent aroma of a Kolkata paratha stall. Pungent, garlicky and completely addictive.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Drinks up the garlicky mustard oil tempering without turning pasty

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed pungency that garlic loves; together they define this Bengali take

steps: Work 1/2 tsp kalonji and 1/2 tsp salt into 2 cups khapli atta, then knead with about 3/4 cup water and 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil into a smooth, elastic dough; rest under a damp cloth for 20 minutes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a small kadhai until it just smokes, then reduce the flame and let it settle for 20 seconds so the harsh edge cooks off.
Slide in 8 sliced garlic cloves and 2 torn dried red chillies and fry on low for about 2 minutes until the garlic is straw-gold and the chillies darken and smell smoky.

Pour this tempering over 1 cup Anveshan Sattu and season with 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1/2 tsp sugar, 1/2 tsp salt and 2 tsp lemon juice; sprinkle 2 tbsp water and rub to a soft, clumping crumble.
Divide the dough into 8 balls and stuff each with 2 tbsp of the garlic mixture, pinching the pleats closed before rolling into 6-7 inch discs with a light hand.

Griddle on medium heat, a minute per side dry, then a further minute per side with 1/2 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until the surface blisters mahogany-gold and the mustard-garlic scent fills the kitchen.
tips: The half teaspoon of sugar is a classic Bengali counterweight to mustard pungency, so keep it even if it seems odd.
Fry the dried chillies until genuinely dark; their smokiness is meant to read clearly in the filling.
Leftover tempering oil, if any, is liquid gold drizzled over the finished paratha.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with begun bhaja and a smear of kasundi mustard, plus thin-sliced cucumber to cool the palate between pungent bites.

variations.name: Kumaoni Garlic Sattu Paratha
variations.description: From the Uttarakhand hills comes jakhya, a wild mustard-like seed that crackles louder and nuttier than cumin, here bloomed in ghee with mountain garlic. The sattu filling is kept simple and warming, the way Kumaoni food is, with green chilli and hill coriander doing the seasoning. A rare regional gem that tastes of woodsmoke and high passes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Old-variety wheat suits this heritage hill recipe far better than modern refined flour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Roasted gram is a hill-country staple, carried on treks for its keeping quality

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Pahari kitchens finish almost everything in ghee; it softens the sharp jakhya crackle

ingredients.name: Jakhya seeds
ingredients.note: Always crackled in hot fat first; substitute brown mustard seeds if unavailable

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt and roughly 3/4 cup water into a soft mountain-style dough, working it 5 minutes; rest covered for 20 minutes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp jakhya seeds for 30-40 seconds until they pop and smell nutty, like louder mustard seeds.
Add 8 finely chopped garlic cloves and 2 tsp grated ginger to the popping jakhya and fry for about 90 seconds until the garlic edges turn golden.

Take the pan off the heat and fold in 1 cup Anveshan Sattu, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp coriander powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric powder, 3 tbsp chopped coriander and 1/2 tsp salt, sprinkling 2-3 tbsp water until the warm mixture presses into soft clumps.
Shape the dough into 8 balls, fill each with 2 tbsp of the jakhya-garlic sattu, seal the seams and roll into slightly thick 6-inch rounds, hill style.

Roast on a medium tava, about 90 seconds per dry side, then finish each side with 1/2 tsp Anveshan Ghee until crusty and browned, pressing the centre so it cooks through, roughly 4 minutes per paratha.
tips: Jakhya should sound like tiny fireworks in the ghee; if it stays silent, your fat was not hot enough and the seeds will taste raw.
This paratha is traditionally rolled thicker for cold mountain mornings, so resist rolling it thin.
Brown mustard seeds plus a pinch of sesame come closest if jakhya is impossible to find.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bhang ki chutney or a simple tomato-hemp seed dip, hot ghee drizzled on top, and sweet milky pahadi chai.

variations.name: Telangana Garlic Sattu Paratha
variations.description: Telangana's fondness for tamarind and garlic — the backbone of its famous chintapandu pachadis — reshapes this paratha into something tangy and fierce. Garlic is pounded with tamarind and red chilli into a sticky sour-hot paste that laces the sattu. Sesame oil on the tava ties it to the Deccan table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Its dry roasted body soaks up the sticky tamarind-garlic paste and stays stuffable

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil, the traditional Telangana medium for anything tamarind-based

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: Seedless pulp, soaked and reduced thick

steps: Soak 2 tbsp tamarind pulp in 1/4 cup hot water for 10 minutes, then mash, strain and boil the extract down for 3-4 minutes to a thick, spoon-coating paste.
Meanwhile knead 2 cups khapli atta with 1/2 tsp salt and about 3/4 cup water into a soft, even dough and rest it for 20 minutes under a damp cloth.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil on medium, pop 1/2 tsp mustard seeds completely, then fry 10 roughly crushed garlic cloves and 10 curry leaves for about 2 minutes until the garlic turns blond and sticky.
Stir the tamarind paste, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp grated jaggery and 1/4 tsp turmeric powder into the pan, cook for 1 minute until glossy, then remove from the heat.
Combine this hot tangy masala with 1 cup Anveshan Sattu, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder and 1/2 tsp salt, rubbing until it forms moist clumps; cool completely before stuffing.

Stuff 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp filling each, seal firmly, roll to 6-inch rounds and roast on a medium tava with 1/2 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil per side until both faces are crisp and deeply bronzed, about 4 minutes per paratha.
tips: Crush the garlic rather than mincing it; bigger sticky pieces are characteristic of Telangana pachadi texture.
The filling should taste assertively sour-hot on its own because the wheat wrapper mutes it by half.
A dry filling day-two makes an excellent podi for hot rice with a spoon of sesame oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with cooling perugu pachadi, thin onion rings soaked in vinegar, and finish with a small glass of buttermilk seasoned with curry leaves.

variations.name: Assamese Garlic Sattu Paratha
variations.description: A tiny amount of bhut jolokia — the ghost pepper of Assam — transforms this garlic-sattu filling into a slow-burning, fruity firecracker. Mustard oil and fresh coriander keep it grounded in Northeast home cooking, where the pepper is respected, not overused. Handle the chilli with care and the reward is extraordinary aroma with manageable heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The wholesome wheat sweetness makes a soothing frame for the ghost pepper's burn

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Its starchy roasted body diffuses the bhut jolokia heat evenly through the filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Assamese kitchens run on pungent mustard oil; it carries the ghost-pepper fruitiness beautifully

ingredients.name: Bhut jolokia
ingredients.note: Deseeded and minced fine; wear gloves and never touch your face

steps: Knead a soft dough from 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 tsp salt and about 3/4 cup water, working it until smooth; rest for 20 minutes under a damp cloth.
Wearing gloves, deseed and mince 1/2 small bhut jolokia; set it aside on its own plate so it touches nothing else.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to a light smoke, cool it for 20 seconds off the flame, then fry 8 sliced garlic cloves and 2 tsp grated ginger on low for about 2 minutes until golden and mellow.
Add the minced bhut jolokia to the warm pan for just 15 seconds — enough to bloom its fruity aroma — then pour everything over 1 cup Anveshan Sattu in a bowl.

Season with 1 finely chopped small red onion, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric powder, 3 tbsp coriander leaves, 1/2 tsp salt and 1 tbsp lemon juice, then sprinkle 2 tbsp water and rub to a clumping crumble.

Stuff 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp of filling each, seal well and roll into 6-7 inch rounds, then roast on a medium tava with 1/2 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil per side until blistered deep gold, about 4 minutes apiece.
tips: Half a deseeded bhut jolokia serves four; doubling it is a decision your guests should get a vote on.
Blooming the pepper briefly in warm oil unlocks its apricot-like fruitiness, which raw mincing alone never shows.
Keep milk or curd within reach at the table; water spreads capsaicin instead of calming it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Assamese way with a khar-style raw papaya mash or plain dahi, sliced onions and a wedge of lime; end with a spoon of curd and jaggery.

variations.name: Classic Home-style Aloo Gobi
variations.description: The gentle, weeknight aloo gobi of North Indian homes: no cream, no fuss, just a soft onion-tomato base, everyday spices and vegetables steamed tender in their own moisture under a tight lid. Comfort in its purest sabzi form, finished with fresh coriander.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A neutral yet nutty wood-pressed oil that lets the simple home spices speak clearly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: One finishing teaspoon of bilona ghee, the way mothers gloss a sabzi just before the dabba is packed

steps: Cut 3 medium potatoes into 1-inch cubes and separate 1 medium cauliflower into bite-size florets; rinse and drain them well so extra water does not stew the masala.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a heavy kadhai on medium and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 20 seconds until they darken a shade and smell toasty.
Add 1 finely chopped large onion and sauté for 4 to 5 minutes until soft and light golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes, 2 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp salt; cook 4 minutes, mashing gently, until the tomatoes melt and the oil separates at the rim.

Fold in the potatoes and florets until every piece wears the masala, sprinkle 3 tbsp water, cover tightly and cook on low for 15 to 18 minutes, stirring gently twice, until the potatoes yield to a spoon.
Uncover, raise the heat for 1 minute to dry any pooled liquid, then finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and 0.25 cup chopped coriander leaves folded through off the heat.
tips: A heavy-bottomed kadhai with a snug lid lets the vegetables steam in their own moisture; thin pans scorch before they soften.
Stir with a flat spatula from underneath, lifting rather than churning, so the florets stay whole.
Add 0.5 tsp amchur with the coriander leaves if your tomatoes are too sweet; home cooks adjust sourness at the end.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulkas, plain dal, and a katori of dahi; leftovers rolled into a paratha with a smear of green chutney make tomorrow's breakfast.

variations.name: Kumaoni Home-style Aloo Gobi
variations.description: The Uttarakhand hills cook their aloo-gobi as a rustic gutke: vegetables tossed over wood-fire heat with crackling jakhya seeds in mustard oil, coloured with turmeric and little else. Jakhya's nutty pop replaces cumin entirely and changes the dish's whole personality.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Pahadi kitchens fry their gutke in pungent mustard oil; the kachi ghani pressing keeps that mountain sharpness

steps: Cut 3 potatoes into thick half-moons and 1 cauliflower into medium florets; parboil the potatoes only, in salted water for 5 minutes, then drain.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in an iron kadhai until it just smokes, lower the heat, and crackle 2 tsp jakhya seeds with 3 torn dried red chillies for 15 to 20 seconds until the seeds pop like tiny sparks.
Add 6 roughly crushed garlic cloves and 2 slit green chillies and fry for 40 seconds until the garlic edges turn gold.
Tip in the florets first and toss on medium-high for 4 minutes so they blister, then add the parboiled potatoes, 0.75 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1.5 tsp salt.
Cover and cook on low for 10 to 12 minutes, lifting the lid to toss every 4 minutes, until the vegetables are tender with crusty golden patches where they touched the iron.
Finish uncovered on high for 2 minutes to crisp the edges, then scatter 0.25 cup coriander leaves and serve straight from the kadhai.
tips: Jakhya is never ground; its entire charm is the crackly whole-seed texture, so buy seeds not powder.
An iron kadhai builds the signature crust; if using steel, extend the final high-heat toss by 2 minutes.
Pahadi cooks keep spicing minimal on purpose; resist adding garam masala, which buries the jakhya.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the mountain way with thick bhang-jeera chutney or plain nimbu-salt, hot mandua (ragi) rotis, and a glass of buttermilk after a morning walk.

variations.name: Kerala Home-style Aloo Gobi
variations.description: A thoran-inspired rework: the potatoes and gobi are steamed with turmeric, then tumbled with a fresh coconut-cumin-shallot crumble and curry leaves crackled in coconut oil. Light, faintly sweet and green-flecked, it is aloo gobi wearing a Kerala mundu.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Virgin cold-pressed coconut oil perfumes the tempering and doubles the coconut character of the thoran crumble

steps: Cut 3 potatoes into small 0.5-inch cubes and 1 cauliflower into small florets; steam or simmer them with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 6 to 8 minutes until just tender, then drain thoroughly.
Pulse 0.75 cup grated coconut with 8 shallots, 3 green chillies and 1 tsp cumin seeds into a coarse, damp crumble; three or four short pulses is enough, it must not become a paste.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a wide pan on medium, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds for 20 seconds, then crackle 2 torn dried red chillies and 2 sprigs of curry leaves until glossy.
Add the coconut crumble and sauté gently for 2 to 3 minutes until it smells sweet and loses its raw edge without browning.
Fold in the steamed vegetables and 0.5 tsp salt, tossing lightly so the crumble coats every piece; cook uncovered for 4 to 5 minutes on medium-low.
Cover, switch off the heat, and let it stand 3 minutes so the coconut steam finishes the florets; fluff once before serving.
tips: Drain the steamed vegetables really well; a wet thoran turns pasty instead of fluffy.
The coconut should only warm through and soften; browning it changes the dish from thoran to podi.
Frozen coconut works if fully thawed; squeeze it lightly and add 30 seconds to the sauté.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with matta rice, a ladle of moru curry (spiced buttermilk), and pappadam; it also fits perfectly beside an Onam-style sadya spread.

variations.name: Rajasthani Home-style Aloo Gobi
variations.description: Desert-style home cooking: no tomatoes at all, sourness from amchur, heat from whole dried Mathania-style chillies, and a curd-whisked masala that clings like a dry kadhi. Cooked in ghee with fennel and hing, it tastes of Jodhpur courtyards rather than any dhaba.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: In Rajasthan's dairy-rich, water-poor kitchens ghee is the default sabzi fat; bilona ghee restores that heritage note

steps: Cut 3 potatoes into wedges and 1 cauliflower into medium florets; whisk 0.5 cup yogurt smooth with 2 tsp coriander powder and 0.5 tsp turmeric and keep beside the stove.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1.5 tsp fennel seeds for 30 seconds, then add 0.25 tsp hing and 4 whole dried red chillies for 15 seconds until they puff.
Add 1 inch julienned ginger and fry 30 seconds, then add the potatoes and florets with 1.5 tsp salt and toss for 3 to 4 minutes until glossed with ghee.
Lower the heat fully, pour in the spiced yogurt while stirring constantly, and keep stirring for 2 minutes so it coats the vegetables without splitting.
Cover and cook on the lowest flame for 15 minutes, stirring gently every 5 minutes, until the vegetables are tender and the curd has reduced to a clinging, pale-gold masala.
Sprinkle 1 tsp amchur, toss uncovered on medium for 1 minute to dry the surface, and rest 3 minutes before serving so the fennel perfume settles.
tips: Room-temperature, well-whisked curd added on low heat will not split; cold curd straight from the fridge will.
Fennel and hing together are the unmistakable Marwari signature; do not drop either.
This sabzi is intentionally tomato-free; if you crave more tang, raise the amchur to 1.5 tsp rather than adding tomato.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot bajre ki roti and a spoon of lehsun chutney, or tuck alongside dal-baati; a glass of thin chaas balances the ghee richness.

variations.name: Telangana Home-style Aloo Gobi
variations.description: A homely Telangana kura where tamarind pulp and sesame-peanut powder wrap the vegetables in a nutty, tangy masala. Tempered with curry leaves and dried chillies in groundnut oil, it sits somewhere between a dry fry and a thick pulusu, made for mounds of rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Deccan kuras are cooked in groundnut oil; the wood-pressed version deepens the dish's sesame-peanut base

steps: Dry-toast 2 tbsp sesame seeds on low for about 1 minute until pale gold, then grind with 3 tbsp roasted peanuts into a coarse powder and set aside.
Cut 3 potatoes into cubes and 1 cauliflower into medium florets; dissolve 2 tsp tamarind paste in 0.5 cup warm water.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds for 20 seconds, then fry 3 torn dried red chillies and 2 sprigs of curry leaves until crisp.
Add 1 sliced large onion and sauté 4 minutes until golden, stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then add the vegetables with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp salt.
Toss 3 minutes, pour in the tamarind water, cover and simmer on low for 12 to 14 minutes until the vegetables are tender and only a thick tangy glaze remains.
Sprinkle the sesame-peanut powder over the kura, fold through gently, and cook uncovered 2 minutes until the powder swells into a nutty coating; rest 3 minutes before serving.
tips: Toast sesame only until pale gold; darker sesame turns the whole powder bitter.
Add the nut powder at the end, never with the water, or it drinks the tamarind and turns the kura pasty.
For a Hyderabadi-leaning bowl, finish with a few drops of the tempering oil spooned over the top at the table.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rice and a drizzle of ghee, plus a fried papad; it also partners beautifully with jowar roti and raw onion the village way.

variations.name: Classic Home-style Baingan Bharta
variations.description: The gentle everyday bharta made in Indian homes on a weeknight: lightly spiced, softly cooked and letting the fire-roasted eggplant do most of the talking. Fewer chillies and no heavy garam masala keep it comforting enough for children and elders alike.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A light wood-pressed oil that keeps this everyday bharta gentle instead of heavy

steps: Prick 2 large eggplants all over with a fork and roast them over a medium flame for 12-14 minutes, turning every 3 minutes, until the skin blackens evenly and the flesh feels soft when pressed with tongs; rest covered for 5 minutes, then peel and mash.
Heat 2½ tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 30 seconds until they sizzle and release their aroma.
Sauté 2 finely chopped onions for 5-6 minutes until soft and lightly golden, then add 2 tsp ginger-garlic paste and 1 chopped green chilli and cook for another minute.
Add 2 finely chopped tomatoes with ½ tsp turmeric, ½ tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 5-6 minutes until the tomatoes soften completely into a loose masala.

Fold in the mashed eggplant and simmer on medium-low for 7-8 minutes, stirring now and then, until the bharta is soft, homogenous and no longer watery — home-style bharta stays moister than the dhaba kind.
Turn off the heat and stir in 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander, letting the residual warmth wilt the leaves into the mash.
tips: For a milder family version, deseed the green chilli or leave it whole so it flavours without much heat.
If the eggplant tastes bitter, sprinkle the mash with ¼ tsp salt and rest it for 5 minutes before cooking, then drain any dark liquid.
This bharta doubles as a great toast topping the next morning with a fried egg on top.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulkas, plain toor dal and a katori of curd — the simple weekday trio it was made for.

variations.name: Kumaoni Home-style Baingan Bharta (Jakhya Tadka)
variations.description: From the hill kitchens of Uttarakhand, where the tempering of choice is jakhya — tiny wild mustard-family seeds that pop into a crackly, nutty crunch no cumin can match. Cooked simply with hill garlic and finished in ghee, this bharta tastes of woodsmoke and the Kumaon winter hearth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Hill households finish nearly every sabzi in ghee; bilona ghee brings that pahadi warmth to the plains

steps: Roast 2 large eggplants over a medium flame for 12-14 minutes, turning every 3 minutes, until the skins are charred and the pods deflate; peel once cool and mash coarsely, keeping some texture the way hill homes prefer.

Melt 2½ tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat until it smells nutty, then add 1½ tsp jakhya seeds and let them crackle vigorously for 30-40 seconds — they pop louder than mustard, so keep a lid nearby.
Add 2 torn dried red chillies and 6 crushed garlic cloves and fry for about a minute until the garlic edges turn golden and the chillies deepen in colour.

Add 1 finely chopped onion and 2 slit green chillies and sauté for 4-5 minutes until soft and pale gold, then stir in 1 chopped tomato with ½ tsp turmeric, 1 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 3-4 minutes until pulpy.
Fold in the mashed eggplant and cook on medium-low for 7-8 minutes, stirring every couple of minutes, until the bharta thickens and takes on the toasty jakhya aroma throughout.
Finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander off the heat, and serve while the jakhya seeds still have their trademark crunch.
tips: Jakhya must be bloomed in properly hot fat to crisp; lukewarm ghee leaves the seeds chewy and raw-tasting.
If you cannot find jakhya, brown mustard seeds plus a pinch of celery seeds give a distant approximation, though pahadi cooks would protest.
This bharta is deliberately light on masala — resist adding garam masala, which would bury the jakhya's delicate nuttiness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thick mandua (finger millet) rotis or plain rice and a bowl of bhatt ki churkani for a true Kumaoni winter meal.

variations.name: Haryanvi Home-style Baingan Bharta (Ghee aur Hara Dhania)
variations.description: A dairy-belt version from Haryana's villages where the bharta is cooked entirely in generous bilona ghee, with browned onions, coarse black pepper and no tomatoes — the tang comes from a final squeeze of lime instead. Rich, rustic and built to accompany stacks of fresh rotis after a day in the fields.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: In Haryana's dairy country the bharta swims in ghee; slow-churned bilona ghee makes that abundance worth savouring

steps: Char 2 large eggplants over a medium flame for 12-15 minutes, giving them a quarter turn every 3 minutes, until the skin blackens completely and the flesh collapses; peel while warm and mash well.

Melt 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadai on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add 6 chopped garlic cloves and 1½ inch chopped ginger and fry for a minute until golden and fragrant.
Add 3 sliced onions and fry patiently for 8-9 minutes, stirring often, until they brown deeply and turn sweet — with no tomatoes in this bharta, the onions carry the entire base.
Add 3 chopped green chillies, 2 tsp coriander powder, ½ tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, and fry the spices in the oniony ghee for 1 minute until the raw smell disappears.
Fold in the mashed eggplant and cook on medium for 8-9 minutes, stirring every 2 minutes, until the bharta absorbs the ghee and turns glossy with browned flecks throughout.
Finish off the heat with 1 tsp coarsely pounded black pepper, 1 tbsp lime juice, 4 tbsp chopped coriander and the final ½ tbsp Anveshan Ghee melted over the top.
tips: Pound the pepper coarsely in a mortar rather than using fine powder; the uneven bite is central to this village-style bharta.
Do not rush the onion browning — with no tomato, under-browned onions leave the dish tasting flat.
The lime juice goes in strictly off the heat so its brightness survives to the table.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rotis dripping with more Anveshan Ghee, a whole spring onion and a tall glass of buttermilk, as Haryanvi farm lunches demand.

variations.name: Telangana Home-style Baingan Bharta (Chintapandu Style)
variations.description: A rustic Telangana rendition soured with tamarind and warmed with a dried-chilli-curry-leaf tempering in nutty sesame oil. The tangy-hot balance is designed for mixing straight into hot rice, exactly how it is eaten across the Deccan countryside.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Deccan home cooking leans on toasty gingelly oil, which deepens the tamarind's tang in this bharta

steps: Roast 2 large eggplants over a medium flame for 12-14 minutes, rotating every 3 minutes, until charred and fully softened; peel, discard the stems and mash the flesh coarsely.
Soak 1½ tbsp tamarind pulp in 4 tbsp warm water for 5 minutes, then squeeze and strain to get a smooth, thick extract.

Heat 2½ tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadai on medium heat, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds and ½ tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add 3 torn dried red chillies and 12 curry leaves and fry for 30 seconds until the leaves crisp and the chillies darken.
Add 5 crushed garlic cloves, 2 slit green chillies and 2 finely chopped onions and sauté for 5-6 minutes until the onions soften and pick up golden edges.
Sprinkle ¼ tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, pour in the tamarind extract, and simmer for 2 minutes until the raw sourness mellows and the mixture thickens slightly.
Fold in the mashed eggplant and cook on medium-low for 6-7 minutes, stirring regularly, until the bharta is thick, tangy and stained golden by the tempering; finish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Balance is everything: the tamarind should make the bharta pleasantly tart, not puckering — add the extract in two goes and taste.
Letting the dried chillies darken well in the oil adds a faint smokiness that suits the roasted eggplant.
This tastes best warm rather than piping hot, once the tamarind and smoke have had a few minutes to settle together.
variations.servingSuggestion: Mix into hot steamed rice with a spoon of Anveshan Ghee, with roasted papad and a raw onion wedge alongside, Deccan-village style.

variations.name: Delhi-style Home-style Baingan Bharta (Chatpata Garam Masala)
variations.description: The chatpata city version from Delhi's home kitchens: a punchy garam-masala-forward bharta brightened with amchur and finished with chaat-style touches of ginger juliennes and green chilli. It borrows the capital's street-food instinct — every bite a little spicy, a little sour, a little warm.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Old Delhi homes still favour pungent kachi ghani mustard oil for bharta; it gives the chatpata masala its edge

steps: Char 2 large eggplants over a medium flame for 12-15 minutes, turning every 3 minutes, until the skin flakes black and the flesh is soft to the centre; rest covered, then peel and mash.
Heat 2½ tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai on medium-high for about 90 seconds until it pales and lightly smokes, then lower to medium and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds.
Fry 5 minced garlic cloves and half the ginger juliennes for 1 minute, then add 2 finely chopped onions and 2 chopped green chillies and sauté for 6-7 minutes until golden-brown.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes with 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, ½ tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 5-6 minutes, mashing as you go, until the masala thickens and the mustard oil beads at the edges.
Fold in the mashed eggplant and cook on medium for 7-8 minutes, stirring every couple of minutes, until thick and cohesive with a few toasty patches.
Off the heat, stir in 1½ tsp garam masala and 1 tsp amchur, then top with the remaining ginger juliennes, 1 slit green chilli and 3 tbsp chopped coriander for the chatpata finish.
tips: Adding both garam masala and amchur after the flame is off keeps their aromas sharp — heat dulls them within a minute.
For extra Delhi flair, add a pinch of chaat masala on the plated bharta just before serving.
If mustard oil is new to your palate, use 2 tbsp mustard oil and finish with 1 tsp ghee for a softer landing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot khapli-atta parathas, sliced radish and lime pickle, the way it lands on winter dinner tables across Delhi.

variations.name: Classic Home-style Mushroom
variations.description: The gentle weeknight mushroom curry of North Indian homes: a light ghee-tempered onion-tomato base, everyday spices and a loose gravy that comes together in twenty-five minutes. Nothing fancy, everything comforting.

ingredients.name: Anveshan A2 Cow Ghee
ingredients.note: A modest two spoons of bilona ghee is all a home-style jhol needs; its aroma does the work heavier fats can't

steps: Wipe 400 g mushrooms clean and slice them thickly; finely chop 1 onion and 2 tomatoes while the pan heats.
Melt 2 tbsp Anveshan A2 Cow Ghee in a deep pan over medium heat and sizzle 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 20 seconds until nutty and fragrant.
Cook the chopped onion for 5-6 minutes until light golden, then stir in 2 tsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 1 minute until the rawness lifts.
Add the chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 4-5 minutes until soft and saucy.

Add the sliced mushrooms and stir over medium-high for 3-4 minutes as they release their juices, then pour in 1 cup hot water and simmer uncovered on low for 8 minutes until the gravy loosely coats a spoon.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala and 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander leaves, stir once and rest the pan off the heat for a few minutes before serving.
tips: Slice mushrooms thick; thin slices vanish into the gravy and lose their bite.
This gravy is deliberately light, so serve it the same day; mushrooms turn spongy if the curry sits refrigerated too long.
A teaspoon of extra ghee stirred in at the end gives the simple jhol a lovely gloss and aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with phulkas and a katori of plain curd, or over steamed rice with roasted papad for the simplest satisfying dinner.

variations.name: Kashmiri Home-style Mushroom
variations.description: A saffron-scented dum curry in the Kashmiri Pandit style: no onion, no garlic, just yogurt, fennel powder, dry ginger and ghee, crowned with saffron steeped in warm milk. The gravy is pale gold, aromatic and quietly luxurious.

ingredients.name: Anveshan A2 Cow Ghee
ingredients.note: Kashmiri Pandit cooking is built on ghee in place of onion-garlic; a bilona ghee base gives the dum gravy its rounded richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: A few threads of genuine Pampore saffron steeped in warm milk paint the gravy gold and perfume every spoonful

steps: Steep 0.25 tsp Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron threads in 3 tbsp warm milk and set aside for 10 minutes until the milk turns amber.
Halve 400 g mushrooms and whisk 1 cup thick curd with 1 tsp besan until perfectly smooth; the besan will hold the curd together over heat.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan A2 Cow Ghee in a heavy pan on medium, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add 3 cloves, 3 cardamom pods and a 1 inch cinnamon stick and fry for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the halved mushrooms and sauté for 5-6 minutes on medium-high until lightly browned and their moisture has mostly cooked away.
Sprinkle 2 tsp fennel powder, 1 tsp dry ginger powder, 1 tsp Kashmiri red chilli powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric powder and 1 tsp salt, and toss for 1 minute so the powders toast against the ghee.
Drop the flame to its lowest, pour in the whisked curd in a slow stream while stirring continuously, and keep stirring for 3-4 minutes until it simmers gently without splitting.
Add 0.5 cups hot water, cover and cook on low dum for 8-10 minutes, then swirl in the saffron milk and simmer 2 minutes more until the gravy is pale gold and softly thick.
Rest covered for 5 minutes off the heat so the saffron and fennel perfume settle before you lift the lid at the table.
tips: Keep the flame at minimum while the curd goes in and never stop stirring; that is the entire trick to a silky yogurt gravy.
Fennel and dry ginger are the Kashmiri backbone; do not substitute garam masala, which flattens the profile.
Save a few saffron strands to lay on top at serving; the visual gold is half the pleasure.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed long-grain rice and a Kashmiri walnut chutney; the gentle gravy also pairs beautifully with plain kulchas at a festive lunch.

variations.name: Tamil Home-style Mushroom
variations.description: Kalan kuzhambu the way a Kongunad home cook makes it: gingelly-oil tempering, shallots, tomato and a spoonful of sambar-style ground spices, simmered loose enough to soak into rice. Curry leaves go in twice, once in the tadka and once at the end.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Kuzhambu built in nallennai tastes rooted in Tamil soil; the wood-pressed sesame depth rounds the tamarind-free tang of tomato

steps: Quarter 400 g mushrooms, peel and halve 12 shallots, smash 5 garlic cloves and chop 3 tomatoes roughly.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil in a kadai on medium; pop 1 tsp mustard seeds, add 0.25 tsp fenugreek seeds and fry just 15 seconds until they turn a shade darker, then crackle 1 sprig of curry leaves.
Fry the shallots and smashed garlic for 5-6 minutes until the shallots blister golden and smell sweet.

Add the tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 2 tsp sambar powder, 1 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 5-6 minutes on medium, mashing, until the tomatoes melt into a thick, tangy base.
Add the quartered mushrooms, toss for 2-3 minutes, then pour in 1.25 cups hot water and simmer uncovered on low for 10 minutes until the kuzhambu is loose but no longer watery.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp black pepper powder, tear the second sprig of curry leaves into the pan and simmer 1 minute more so the leaves wilt and perfume the gravy.
Finish with 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander leaves and let the kuzhambu stand 5 minutes; it thickens slightly and tastes more settled.
tips: Fenugreek burns to bitterness fast; 15 seconds in the oil is genuinely all it needs.
Shallots, not big onions, give the kuzhambu its gentle sweetness; halve them so they stay visible in the gravy.
If your sambar powder is very hot, drop the pepper to 0.25 tsp and adjust at the table.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pour over hot rice with a spoon of gingelly oil and serve with a beans poriyal and appalam; it is also excellent with soft idlis the next morning.

variations.name: Odia Home-style Mushroom
variations.description: Chhatu besara territory: mushrooms simmered in a mustard-seed and garlic paste gravy, opened with panch phoron in pungent mustard oil. The besara is sharp, rustic and tastes of monsoon kitchens along the Mahanadi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: A besara doubles the mustard: ground seed paste in the gravy and this sharp kachi ghani oil in the pan, exactly as Odia homes do

steps: Soak 2 tbsp mustard seeds in warm water for 10 minutes, then grind with 3 garlic cloves, 1 green chilli and 3 tbsp water into a smooth besara paste.
Halve 400 g mushrooms, slice 1 onion, chop 1 tomato, slit the remaining 2 green chillies and roughly chop the remaining 3 garlic cloves.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil in a kadai on high until it barely smokes, lower the flame, then crackle 1 tsp panch phoron with 2 whole dried red chillies for about 25 seconds.
Add the chopped garlic and sliced onion and fry for 4-5 minutes until pale gold, then add the tomato with 0.75 tsp turmeric powder and cook for 3 minutes until soft.
Add the mushrooms with 1 tsp salt and sauté on medium-high for 4-5 minutes until their released water has mostly evaporated.
Lower the heat, stir in the mustard paste with 1 cup hot water and the slit green chillies, and simmer gently for 6-7 minutes; do not boil hard or the mustard will turn bitter.
Take the besara off the heat when the gravy lightly coats the mushrooms, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander leaves.
tips: Soaking the mustard seeds before grinding and simmering gently are the two guards against bitterness in a besara.
A pinch of salt and a green chilli ground with the mustard also sweetens the paste; never grind mustard alone.
This gravy is meant to be assertive; balance it at the table with plain rice rather than toning down the paste.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Odia way with steamed rice, a wedge of lime and crisp badi chura sprinkled on top; a bowl of pakhala on a hot day is its truest companion.

variations.name: Gujarati Home-style Mushroom
variations.description: A sweet-tangy shaak in the Kathiyawadi home register: mushrooms in a tomato base rounded with jaggery, sharpened with lemon and warmed by a mustard-ajmo tadka in groundnut oil. Mild enough for the whole family, bright enough to be interesting.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The default fat of every Gujarati shaak; wood-pressed groundnut keeps this one light and lets the sweet-sour finish stay clean

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The gentle gud sweetness that defines a Kathiyawadi shaak, dissolving evenly where block jaggery would clump

steps: Slice 400 g mushrooms thickly and chop 3 tomatoes fine; squeeze 1 tbsp lemon juice and keep it aside for the very end.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium; crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds fully, then add 0.25 tsp ajwain and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them fizz for 10 seconds.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and stir for 30 seconds, then tip in the chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander-cumin powder and 1 tsp salt.
Cook the tomatoes for 5-6 minutes on medium, mashing as they soften, until the base is pulpy and the oil winks at the edges.
Fold in the sliced mushrooms and cook uncovered for 6-7 minutes, stirring now and then, letting their juices loosen the shaak into a medium gravy without any added water.
Melt 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder into the pan and simmer for 2-3 minutes until the gravy tastes balanced between tang and gentle sweetness.
Switch off, stir in 1 tbsp lemon juice and 3 tbsp chopped fresh coriander leaves, and serve while the brightness is at its peak.
tips: No added water is the trick; mushroom juices plus tomato make exactly the right shaak consistency.
Ajwain is small but loud here; do not exceed 0.25 tsp or it will dominate the sweet-sour balance.
Taste after the jaggery melts and before the lemon goes in, so you adjust each against the other rather than guessing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulka rotli and a bowl of Gujarati kadhi; leftovers folded into a thepla wrap with chhundo make a superb lunchbox.

variations.name: Classic Masala Mushroom
variations.description: Plump button mushrooms seared first for a golden crust, then folded into a robust onion-tomato masala. The two-stage cooking keeps the mushrooms meaty instead of rubbery, and the gravy stays thick enough to scoop with roti.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Its high smoke point lets you sear the mushrooms hard for a golden crust before they meet the masala

steps: Wipe 400 g button mushrooms clean with a damp cloth and quarter them; finely chop 2 onions and 3 tomatoes and keep them in separate bowls.

Heat 1 tbsp of the Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a wide pan on high and sear the mushrooms in a single layer for 4-5 minutes, tossing only twice, until their edges are golden and any released water has evaporated; remove and set aside.
Add the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to the same pan on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Sauté the chopped onions for 7-8 minutes until golden brown, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute more until the sharp smell fades.

Add the tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt; cook for 6-7 minutes, mashing occasionally, until the masala thickens and oil separates at the edges.
Return the seared mushrooms with 0.75 cups hot water, stir to coat, and simmer uncovered on low for 6-7 minutes until the gravy is thick and clings to the mushroom pieces.
Dust with 0.5 tsp garam masala, scatter 3 tbsp chopped fresh coriander leaves and serve within a few minutes while the mushrooms are still bouncy.
tips: Never wash mushrooms under running water just before cooking; they absorb it and then steam instead of searing.
Crowding the pan is the main reason mushrooms go rubbery, so sear in two batches if your pan is small.
This gravy thickens fast on standing; keep 0.25 cup hot water handy to loosen it just before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Scoop up with hot tawa parathas or pile over buttered pav; a squeeze of lime and pickled onions on the side sharpen the earthy mushrooms.

variations.name: Punjabi Masala Mushroom
variations.description: Mushroom masala the way Punjabi dhabas serve it after dark: a deeply bhuno-ed ghee-onion base, tomato puree cooked to brick red, then butter, cream and a heavy hand of kasuri methi. Rich enough to pass for a restaurant dish, honest enough to be dinner.

ingredients.name: Anveshan A2 Cow Ghee
ingredients.note: The long bhuno that defines Punjabi mushroom masala needs a stable, aromatic fat; slow-churned bilona ghee delivers both

steps: Halve 450 g button mushrooms, keeping the small ones whole, and slit 2 green chillies; chop 3 onions as finely as you can so they melt into the gravy.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan A2 Cow Ghee in a kadai over medium-high, sizzle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then fry the onions for 10-12 minutes, stirring steadily, until deep brown and jammy.
Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste with the slit green chillies and fry for 1 minute, then pour in 1 cup tomato puree, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder.
Bhuno the masala on medium for 8-9 minutes, scraping the pan floor whenever it sticks, until it turns brick red and the ghee pools at the edges.
Tumble in the mushrooms with 1.25 tsp salt, toss to coat, and cook uncovered on medium-high for 5-6 minutes; the mushrooms will first weep and then reabsorb the masala as the liquid cooks off.
Add 0.5 cups hot water, lower the heat, and simmer for 5 minutes until the gravy is thick and glossy; stir in 3 tbsp fresh cream and 1 tbsp butter and warm gently for 2 minutes without boiling.
Crush 2 tsp kasuri methi over the pan, dust with 0.75 tsp garam masala, stir once and serve immediately while the surface still shines with butter.
tips: Letting the mushrooms weep and re-absorb in the open pan concentrates their flavour into the gravy; do not cover at that stage.
Toast the kasuri methi on a dry tawa for 20 seconds before crushing for double the aroma.
Swap a third of the mushrooms for paneer cubes to turn this into a crowd-pleasing mushroom-paneer masala.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with garlic naan or thick lachha paratha, laccha onions and a chilled glass of masala chaas to cut the richness.

variations.name: Andhra Masala Mushroom
variations.description: A fiery Guntur-style kura where the heat comes layered: Guntur chilli powder in the masala, whole dried chillies in the tadka and green chillies in the base. Curry leaves and a final flare of crushed roasted cumin keep it aromatic rather than merely hot.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Andhra kuras are traditionally built on gingelly oil; its toasty depth stands up to Guntur chilli heat instead of disappearing under it

steps: Quarter 400 g mushrooms after wiping them clean, slice 2 onions, chop 2 tomatoes and slit 2 green chillies lengthwise.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil in a kadai on medium-high; pop 1 tsp mustard seeds fully, then add 3 whole dried Guntur chillies and 2 sprigs of curry leaves and fry for 20 seconds until the leaves crisp.
Add the sliced onions and slit green chillies and sauté for 6-7 minutes until the onions brown at the edges, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for another minute.

Add the chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 1.5 tsp Guntur red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt; cook on medium for 5-6 minutes until the masala turns deep red and pulls away from the pan.
Add the mushrooms and toss on high heat for 3 minutes so they sear against the spicy masala, then reduce to low, cover and cook for 6-7 minutes in their own juices until tender.
Uncover, raise the heat and dry off the extra moisture for 2-3 minutes, stirring, until the masala coats each mushroom in a thick red jacket.
Sprinkle 1 tsp roasted cumin powder and 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander leaves, toss once and take it off the flame.
tips: Guntur chilli brings real heat; start with 1 tsp of the powder and work up if you are unsure of your tolerance.
Cooking the mushrooms covered in their own juices, then drying the pan out, gives the kura its signature clingy masala.
A spoon of thick curd stirred in at the table is the traditional Andhra rescue if the heat runs away from you.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a spoon of ghee melted on top, Andhra style, or tuck into soft chapatis; a cooling cucumber perugu pachadi on the side balances the fire.

variations.name: Kerala Masala Mushroom
variations.description: Mushroom ularthiyathu-meets-curry: mushrooms roasted with crushed pepper and fennel in coconut oil, then bathed in a short coconut-milk gravy stacked with curry leaves and fried coconut slivers. Earthy, gently sweet and unmistakably Malabari.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Roasting mushrooms and coconut slivers in cold-pressed coconut oil layers the same fat twice, the secret of Kerala's deepest curries

steps: Thickly slice 400 g mushrooms, halve 12 small shallots, mince a 1 inch piece of ginger with 4 garlic cloves, and slit 2 green chillies.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a heavy pan on medium; crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds, then fry 3 tbsp fresh coconut slivers for about 2 minutes until golden brown and lift half of them out for garnish.
Add 3 sprigs of curry leaves and the shallots to the pan and fry for 5-6 minutes until the shallots are soft and browned at the edges.
Stir in the minced ginger-garlic and slit green chillies for 1 minute, then add 0.5 tsp turmeric powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder and toast the powders for 30 seconds without letting them scorch.
Add the sliced mushrooms with 1 tsp salt and roast on medium-high for 6-7 minutes, tossing often, until their moisture cooks off and the edges catch appetising brown spots.
