Sprinkle 1.5 tsp crushed black pepper and 0.75 tsp crushed fennel seeds, toss for 30 seconds, then lower the heat fully and pour in 0.75 cups thick coconut milk, warming it gently for 3 minutes without boiling.
Finish with the reserved fried coconut slivers scattered on top and serve while the gravy is still loose; it thickens as it cools.
tips: The dish works two ways: skip the coconut milk entirely and roast 3 minutes longer for a dry ularthiyathu-style side.
Crush pepper coarsely in a mortar; powdered pepper turns the gravy grey and one-note.
Fried coconut slivers go from golden to bitter in seconds, so pull them the moment they colour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with Kerala parotta or over red matta rice; a tangy lime pickle and papadam alongside make it a full toddy-shop-style spread.

variations.name: Bengali Masala Mushroom
variations.description: A Kolkata-style mushroom kosha in pungent mustard oil, sweetened by slow-fried onions, warmed with Bengali garam masala and lifted at the end by slit green chillies. The tight, dark gravy is made for spooning over plain rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: A kosha's dark, clingy gravy starts with properly smoked kachi ghani mustard oil; nothing else gives that sharp-sweet Bengali base

steps: Halve 400 g mushrooms, slice 2 onions into thin half-moons, chop 2 tomatoes and slit 3 green chillies from tip to stem.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil in a kadai on high until it shimmers and just smokes, about 2 minutes, then drop the flame to medium and add 1 bay leaf, 2 green cardamom pods and a 1 inch cinnamon stick for 20 seconds.
Fry the sliced onions for 8-9 minutes, stirring patiently, until they collapse into a sweet golden-brown tangle that will colour the whole kosha.

Add 1 tbsp ginger paste and 1 tsp garlic paste, cook 1 minute, then add the tomatoes with 0.75 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp cumin powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 5 minutes until thick.
Add the mushrooms and the slit green chillies and koshano-fry on medium-high for 8-9 minutes, stirring every minute, letting the mushroom liquid release and cook back down into the masala.
Splash in 0.25 cups hot water only if the masala threatens to stick, and continue until the gravy is dark, tight and coats the mushrooms like a glaze.
Dust with 0.5 tsp Bengali garam masala, cover, switch off the heat and rest for 5 minutes so the cardamom-cinnamon warmth settles in.
tips: Koshano means patient frying; the repeated release-and-reduce of moisture is what builds the signature dark gravy, so do not rush with extra water.
Bengali garam masala is just cardamom, cinnamon and clove ground together; make a small fresh batch for the truest flavour.
A 0.5 tsp pinch of sugar with the onions speeds their caramelising, a common Kolkata kitchen trick.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steaming white rice and a wedge of lime, or with luchis on a Sunday morning; sliced cucumber with black salt is all the side it needs.

variations.name: Classic Masala Sattu Paratha
variations.description: A bolder, spice-forward cousin of the plain sattu paratha, where the roasted gram filling is layered with garam masala, coriander powder and amchur for a proper masala punch. Every element is toasted or roasted, so the flavour is deep rather than raw-hot. Ghee-crisped khapli wheat holds it all together with a wholesome, wheaty sweetness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat's nutty base note keeps the heavy masala from tasting harsh

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Freshly stone-milled roasted gram absorbs the spice blend evenly instead of clumping

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Blooms the ground spices and gives the paratha its glossy, crackly finish

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and roughly 3/4 cup water for 5-6 minutes to a soft, elastic dough; rest it covered for 20 minutes.

Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee gently in a small pan on low heat and stir in 1 tsp garam masala, 2 tsp coriander powder and 3/4 tsp red chilli powder for just 20 seconds until fragrant, then remove from the heat immediately so nothing scorches.
Pour the spiced ghee over 1 cup Anveshan Sattu and add 1 minced small onion, 2 minced green chillies, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp amchur, 1/4 tsp turmeric powder and 1/2 tsp salt.
Rub the mixture between your fingers, sprinkling 2-3 tbsp water gradually, until it resembles damp crumbs that hold together when pressed into a ball.
Divide dough and filling into 8 portions each, using about 2 tbsp filling per ball; enclose the masala sattu inside each flattened dough cup and seal the pleats with a firm twist.

Roll each stuffed ball into a 6-7 inch disc with light strokes, then roast on a medium-hot tava for a minute per side dry, followed by 1/2 tsp Anveshan Ghee per side, cooking until both faces carry deep golden-brown patches, about 4 minutes each.
tips: Blooming the ground spices in warm ghee before mixing is what separates a masala paratha from a merely spiced one; never skip that 20-second step.
Amchur adds tang without moisture, which keeps the crumbly filling rollable, so prefer it to lemon here.
If making for children, halve the chilli but keep the garam masala; the aroma matters more than the heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with cucumber raita and a smoky tomato chutney; a mug of adrak chai alongside turns it into a complete monsoon breakfast.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Masala Sattu Paratha
variations.description: Here the masala means goda masala, Maharashtra's smoky-sweet blend built on dagad phool, sesame and dry coconut. Folded through sattu with toasted sesame seeds and a hint of jaggery, the filling tastes uncannily like a dry bhaji from a Pune kitchen. Wood-pressed groundnut oil on the tava seals the regional signature.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli is heritage Maharashtra wheat, so this pairing is historically spot-on

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Its roasted-gram body mimics the besan base of many Maharashtrian dry masala dishes

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The everyday Deccan cooking fat, wood-pressed for a full peanut aroma

steps: Make a soft dough from 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and about 3/4 cup water; knead well and rest for 20 minutes under a damp cloth.
Dry-toast 1 tbsp sesame seeds and 2 tbsp grated dry coconut in a pan on low heat for 2-3 minutes until pale gold and nutty-smelling, then tip onto a plate.
In the same pan heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 1/2 tsp mustard seeds for 30 seconds, then add 8 curry leaves and 2 minced green chillies and fry for 20 seconds more.

Off the heat, stir in 2 tsp goda masala and 1/2 tsp turmeric powder, then combine this tempering with 1 cup Anveshan Sattu, the toasted sesame-coconut, 1 tsp grated jaggery and 1/2 tsp salt; sprinkle 2 tbsp water and rub until the filling clumps softly.
Stuff 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp filling apiece, sealing carefully, and roll each into a 6-7 inch round with gentle, even pressure.

Roast on a medium tava for about a minute per side until speckled, then apply 1/2 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil per side and cook to a deep, toasty brown, pressing the edges so they crisp, roughly 4 minutes per paratha.
tips: Goda masala burns fast, so it always goes in off the flame; scorched dagad phool tastes acrid.
Toasted sesame is a texture insurance policy: it keeps the filling loose even if you slightly over-wet it.
A batch of this filling, minus the water, keeps a week in the fridge as an instant masala base.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with green chilli thecha, a spoon of sweet lime pickle and a steel tumbler of solkadhi or spiced buttermilk.

variations.name: Andhra Masala Sattu Paratha
variations.description: Andhra's famous Guntur chillies drive this version, ground with garlic into a fierce red karam that laces the sattu filling. Curry leaves and a squeeze of lime keep the heat bright rather than brutal, and the paratha is roasted in nutty wood-pressed sesame oil, the fat of choice across Telugu kitchens. Strictly for chilli lovers.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: The neutral roasted-gram canvas lets the Guntur karam shine at full volume

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed nuvvula noone, the traditional Andhra medium that tames Guntur fire with its nuttiness

ingredients.name: Dried Guntur red chillies
ingredients.note: Soaked and ground with garlic into the signature karam paste

steps: Soak 4 dried Guntur chillies in hot water for 15 minutes, then grind them with 6 garlic cloves and a teaspoon of the soaking water into a thick red karam paste.
While the chillies soak, knead 2 cups khapli atta with 1/2 tsp salt and about 3/4 cup water into a supple dough and rest it, covered, for 20 minutes.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pan on medium, fry 10 curry leaves for 15 seconds until glassy, then add the karam paste and cook for 2-3 minutes until the raw garlic smell disappears and the oil stains red.

Take the pan off the heat and mix in 1 cup Anveshan Sattu, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp coriander powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric powder, 1/2 tsp salt and 1 tbsp lime juice, rubbing until the mixture holds together when squeezed; add a spoon of water only if needed.
Divide the dough into 8 balls and tuck 2 tbsp of the fiery filling into each, sealing the seams tightly before rolling into 6-7 inch rounds.
Roast each paratha on a medium-hot tava for a minute per bare side, then with 1/2 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil per side until crisp, deeply browned and smelling of toasted sesame, about 4 minutes apiece.
tips: Cooking the karam paste until the oil turns red is essential; undercooked garlic-chilli paste tastes raw and harsh.
Deseed half the Guntur chillies for a version that is warm rather than blazing, without losing the trademark colour.
Keep a bowl of curd on the table; Andhra meals always balance karam with cooling dairy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thick curd rice on the side or a simple onion-tomato pachadi, and finish with a piece of jaggery the traditional Telugu way.

variations.name: Karnataka Masala Sattu Paratha
variations.description: Modelled on North Karnataka's beloved tamarind-laced fillings, this paratha folds a tangy puli concentrate, curry leaves and rasam-style spicing into the sattu. The sweet-sour tamarind against earthy roasted gram recalls the flavours of gojju, and a groundnut-oil roast gives it a Hubli-dhaba crust. Bright, tangy and moreish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Robust emmer flour stands up to the moist tamarind filling without going gummy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Absorbs the tamarind pulp neatly, keeping the tangy filling rollable

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: North Karnataka's staple shenga oil, wood-pressed for genuine rustic flavour

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: Seedless pulp soaked and reduced to a thick paste

steps: Soak 2 tbsp tamarind pulp in 1/4 cup hot water for 10 minutes, mash, strain and simmer the extract in a small pan for 3-4 minutes until it thickens to a glossy paste.
Knead the dough from 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and roughly 3/4 cup water; rest it 20 minutes while the flavours come together.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium, crackle 1/2 tsp mustard seeds fully, then add 10 curry leaves, 1/8 tsp hing and 2 minced green chillies and sizzle for 20 seconds.

Off the flame, stir in the tamarind paste, 2 tsp rasam powder, 2 tsp grated jaggery, 1/4 tsp turmeric powder and 1/2 tsp salt, then work in 1 cup Anveshan Sattu until you get a moist, clumping crumble; it should taste boldly sweet-sour.
Cool the filling, divide dough and stuffing into 8 portions each with about 2 tbsp filling per ball, seal well and roll into 6-inch rounds, going gently since this filling is moister than most.
Roast on a medium tava, a minute per side plain, then 1/2 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil per side until crusty and mahogany-spotted, around 4 minutes per paratha.
tips: Reduce the tamarind extract properly; runny pulp is the difference between a tangy filling and a torn paratha.
Rasam powder brands vary in heat, so taste the filling before deciding whether the green chillies stay or go.
If the filling turns too wet, a tablespoon of extra sattu fixes it faster than any other flour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a dollop of unsalted white butter melting on top and a side of shenga chutney pudi mixed with a little oil, Hubli style.

variations.name: Gujarati Masala Sattu Paratha
variations.description: Gujarat's love of sweet-savoury balance shapes this take: the masala sattu is mellowed with jaggery powder, sesame and a dhana-jeera backbone, echoing the flavours of methi thepla and sukhdi in one bread. Green chilli-ginger paste supplies gentle warmth instead of raw heat. It is the most balanced, tiffin-friendly paratha of the family.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Rolls thin and stays soft for hours, exactly what a Gujarati tiffin bread needs

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Its roasted note plays the role besan does in classic Gujarati farsan

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The honest gol sweetness that defines Gujarati masala balance, replacing refined sugar entirely

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A ghee-roasted finish keeps the sweet-spiced filling tasting festive

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1/4 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 3/4 cup water into a soft thepla-style dough; rest 20 minutes covered.
Toast 1 tbsp sesame seeds in a dry pan on low heat for about 2 minutes until they turn pale gold and start to pop, then tip them into a mixing bowl.

Add 1 cup Anveshan Sattu, 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 tbsp green chilli-ginger paste, 2 tsp dhana-jeera powder, remaining 1/4 tsp turmeric powder, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder, 1/2 tsp salt and 3 tbsp chopped coriander to the bowl.
Moisten with 1 tbsp lemon juice, 1 tbsp melted Anveshan Ghee and 2 tbsp water sprinkled gradually, rubbing until the filling presses into a soft, faintly sweet crumble.
Shape 8 dough balls, stuff each with 2 tbsp of filling, seal the gathered edges and roll into thin 7-inch rounds; Gujarati parathas are rolled finer than most.
Cook on a medium-hot tava for about 45 seconds per plain side, then roast each side with 1/2 tsp Anveshan Ghee until amber-spotted and pliable-crisp, roughly 3 minutes per paratha.
tips: Roll these thinner than a standard stuffed paratha; the jaggery caramelises best in a fine layer.
The filling should taste slightly over-seasoned on its own since the mild wheat wrapper dilutes it.
These keep soft for a full day, making them ideal travel and tiffin food, just like thepla.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pack with chundo or kesar mango pickle and a small pot of sweetened curd; at home, serve with kadhi for a comforting Gujarati dinner.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Aloo Gobi
variations.description: A no-gravy, high-heat aloo gobi where the florets are pan-seared first so they stay nutty and never turn to mush. Green chillies, black pepper and a sharp ginger-garlic base give it a clean, assertive burn, all carried on the roasted depth of wood-pressed mustard oil.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil sears the gobi hard and fast, adding a smoky pungency refined oil cannot

steps: Cut 3 medium potatoes into 1-inch cubes and break 1 medium cauliflower into similar-sized florets; soak the florets in warm salted water for 10 minutes, then drain and pat completely dry.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a wide kadhai until it just smokes, lower to medium-high, and sear the florets and potato cubes in a single layer for 5 to 6 minutes until they pick up golden-brown edges; remove to a plate.
Add the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then sauté 2 sliced onions with 4 slit green chillies for 4 minutes until deep golden.

Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until the raw smell disappears, then add 2 chopped tomatoes, 2 tsp coriander powder, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp salt; cook 4 to 5 minutes until the masala releases oil at the edges.
Return the seared vegetables, toss to coat every piece, sprinkle 2 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 10 to 12 minutes, stirring once halfway, until a knife slides easily through the potato.
Finish uncovered on high heat for 2 minutes to evaporate any moisture, then grind 0.5 tsp black pepper over the top and toss once more before switching off.
tips: Drying the florets thoroughly is the difference between a seared, nutty gobi and a steamed, soggy one.
Resist stirring during the covered stage more than once; frequent tossing breaks the florets into crumbs.
For extra fire without changing the flavour, slit the green chillies but leave them whole so eaters can dodge or devour them.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulkas, a cooling cucumber raita, and lemon wedges; it also makes an outstanding filling for a next-day toastie.

variations.name: Bengali Spicy Aloo Gobi
variations.description: Modelled on the winter classic phulkopir dalna, this version blooms kalonji and whole green chillies in smoking mustard oil, then simmers the gobi in a light ginger-tomato gravy sweetened with a pinch of sugar. It is gently saucy, warmly spiced with Bengali garam masala, and made for steamed rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: No phulkopir dalna is authentic without pungent kachi ghani mustard oil smoking in the kadai first

steps: Halve 3 medium potatoes lengthwise and cut into thick wedges; separate 1 cauliflower into large florets and rub them with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it smokes lightly, then fry the florets on medium-high for 4 to 5 minutes until blotched golden; set aside, and fry the potato wedges 5 minutes in the same oil until crusted.
Add the last 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil, temper 1 tsp kalonji, 2 bay leaves and 4 slit green chillies for 30 seconds until the kalonji crackles and the chillies blister.
Add 1 tbsp ginger paste and 2 chopped tomatoes, cook 4 minutes until pulpy, then stir in 1.5 tsp cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp sugar and 1 tsp salt.
Return the potatoes with 1 cup hot water, cover and simmer on low for 8 minutes, then slip in the florets and simmer covered another 7 to 8 minutes until both are tender and the gravy clings loosely.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp Bengali garam masala, cover, and rest off the heat for 5 minutes so the cardamom-cinnamon perfume seeps into the vegetables.
tips: Frying the florets before simmering is the Bengali trick that keeps them intact and sweet in the gravy.
The teaspoon of sugar is seasoning, not dessert; it balances the mustard oil exactly as Kolkata kitchens intend.
Add a handful of green peas with the florets in winter for the full seasonal dalna experience.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle over steaming gobindobhog or basmati rice with a wedge of gondhoraj lime; on cold evenings it pairs beautifully with hot luchis instead.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Aloo Gobi
variations.description: A dry-roast vepudu treatment for aloo gobi: the vegetables are tossed in a fierce Guntur chilli-garlic paste, tempered with curry leaves in groundnut oil, and finished with a tamarind edge. It is intensely hot, faintly sour, and utterly addictive with curd rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil takes Andhra-level heat without breaking down and adds a roasted nuttiness to the vepudu

steps: Dry-toast 6 Guntur chillies on low heat for 2 minutes until puffed and brittle, then grind them with 8 garlic cloves, 1.5 tsp tamarind paste and 0.5 tsp salt into a coarse red paste.
Cut 3 potatoes into thick fingers and 1 cauliflower into medium florets; parboil both in salted water for 4 minutes, drain well and spread out to steam-dry.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a wide pan on medium, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tbsp chana dal for 40 seconds until the dal turns golden, then crisp 2 sprigs of curry leaves in the oil.
Add 2 sliced onions and sauté 4 minutes until golden at the edges, then fry the chilli-garlic paste for 2 minutes until the oil turns brick red and the raw garlic smell fades.

Add the parboiled vegetables, 2 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt; toss to coat and roast uncovered on medium for 12 to 14 minutes, turning every 3 minutes, until the edges crisp and char in spots.
Taste and adjust the salt, then rest the vepudu for 3 minutes off the heat so the tamarind and chilli settle into the potatoes.
tips: Parboiling then dry-roasting is the vepudu method; skipping the parboil leaves the potato fingers raw inside before the outside burns.
The chana dal in the tempering is for crunch; do not let it darken past golden or it turns bitter.
Keep a spoon of ghee-laced curd nearby when serving; it is the traditional Andhra fire extinguisher.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside mudda pappu (plain thick dal) and hot rice with a spoon of ghee, or tuck into curd rice with a roasted papad for the classic Andhra meal arc.

variations.name: Kashmiri Spicy Aloo Gobi
variations.description: Ghee-fried gobi and potatoes simmered with Kashmiri signatures: fennel powder, dry ginger, whole cloves and a saffron-stained yogurt gravy. The heat comes from vibrant Kashmiri chillies that colour more than they burn, so the dish glows deep red while staying aromatic and regal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Kashmiri wazwan cooking is built on ghee; bilona ghee gives the gravy its glossy, rounded richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: A few threads of GI-tagged Kashmiri kesar bloomed in warm milk turn the yogurt gravy golden and haunting

steps: Soak 0.25 tsp Anveshan Saffron threads in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside for at least 10 minutes until the milk turns marigold.
Cut 3 potatoes into thick rounds and 1 cauliflower into large florets; fry them in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat for 6 to 7 minutes until golden all over, then lift out onto a plate.
In the same kadhai, add the last 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, 3 cloves and 3 bruised cardamom pods for 30 seconds until fragrant.

Whisk 0.75 cup yogurt smooth with 2 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 2 tsp fennel powder and 1 tsp dry ginger powder; lower the heat fully and stir the yogurt in gradually, whisking for 2 to 3 minutes so it never splits.
Return the fried vegetables with 0.75 cup hot water and 1.5 tsp salt, cover and simmer gently for 12 to 15 minutes until tender and the gravy coats the back of a spoon.
Swirl in the saffron milk, simmer uncovered for 2 final minutes, and rest covered for 5 minutes so the kesar aroma blooms through the dish.
tips: Always add yogurt off a rolling boil and whisk continuously; a split gravy cannot be rescued.
Fennel plus dry ginger is the Kashmiri flavour spine; do not substitute garam masala or the dish loses its identity.
Crush the saffron threads between warm fingers before soaking to release twice the colour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a Kashmiri walnut chutney; a few strands of saffron on top and warm kahwa after the meal complete the Valley experience.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Spicy Aloo Gobi
variations.description: A rassa-style aloo gobi from Maharashtra: goda masala's smoky sweetness, crushed peanuts for body, and a whisper of jaggery to round the chilli. The masala clings thick and dark to every floret, tasting of home kitchens in Pune more than any restaurant.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the Maharashtrian default fat and reinforces the crushed-peanut body of the rassa

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The traditional Maharashtrian pinch of gul balances goda masala's warmth without making the dish sweet

steps: Cube 3 potatoes and cut 1 cauliflower into bite-size florets; soak the florets in warm salted water for 10 minutes, then drain and pat dry.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds for 20 seconds, then add 1 sprig curry leaves and 2 finely chopped onions and fry 4 to 5 minutes until golden brown.
Add 1 chopped tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp salt; mash and cook 3 minutes until soft and pulpy.
Stir in the potatoes and florets, coat well in the masala, add 0.5 cup hot water, cover and cook on low for 12 minutes, stirring gently once at the halfway mark.
Sprinkle 2 tsp goda masala, 3 tbsp roasted peanut powder and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder; fold through and cook uncovered 3 to 4 minutes until the masala thickens and coats every piece darkly.
Finish with 2 tbsp grated coconut folded in off the heat, and let the dish stand for 3 minutes so the peanut powder swells and binds the masala.
tips: Add goda masala near the end of cooking; long boiling dulls its delicate stone-flower aroma.
Peanut powder thickens fast, so loosen with a splash of hot water if the masala tightens before the gobi is tender.
A squeeze of lime at the table lifts the goda masala's sweetness beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft ghadichi poli (layered chapati) or jowar bhakri, sliced onion and a wedge of lime; a katori of solkadhi alongside makes it a proper Maharashtrian thali.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Baingan Bharta
variations.description: A heat-forward bharta built for chilli lovers: the smoky roasted eggplant is loaded with green chillies, extra red chilli powder and a finishing crack of black pepper. The three-way heat — fresh, powdered and peppery — layers over the char instead of masking it.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Its neutral nuttiness keeps the spotlight on the triple-chilli heat while standing up to hard frying

steps: Prick 2 large eggplants with a fork and roast them over a medium flame for 12-15 minutes, rotating every 3 minutes, until the skin is charred crisp and the flesh has gone completely limp; cover for 5 minutes, then peel and mash.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds until aromatic and a shade darker.
Fry 2 finely chopped onions for 6-7 minutes until golden-brown, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste with 5 chopped green chillies and cook for 90 seconds until the chillies blister and smell sharp.

Add 2 finely chopped tomatoes, 1½ tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder, ½ tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 5-6 minutes, mashing the tomatoes down, until the masala thickens and oil separates at the rim.
Fold in the mashed eggplant and cook on medium for 8-10 minutes, stirring every 2 minutes, until the bharta thickens, darkens and starts leaving the sides of the pan.
Finish with ¾ tsp freshly cracked black pepper and 3 tbsp chopped coriander stirred through in the last 30 seconds, so the pepper stays bright and pungent on top of the slower chilli burn.
tips: Slit-and-deseed two of the five green chillies if you want strong flavour with slightly less fire.
Cracking the pepper fresh and adding it at the very end preserves its sharp top note; cooked pepper turns dull.
Keep a bowl of plain curd on the table — it is the traditional counterweight to this bharta's heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft khapli-atta rotis, a katori of chilled plain curd and lime-pickled onions to cool and cut through the heat.

variations.name: Assamese Spicy Baingan Bharta (Bhut Jolokia Pura)
variations.description: Assam's take on mashed roasted eggplant is minimalist and volcanic: a mere sliver of bhut jolokia, raw shallots and mustard oil folded into the warm mash. There is no long-cooked masala at all — just smoke, ferocious chilli and pungent oil, the way pitika-style dishes are eaten in the Brahmaputra valley.

ingredients.name: Bhut jolokia (ghost chilli), fresh or brined
Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Assamese pitika depends on raw kachi ghani mustard oil for its pungent backbone; there is no substitute

steps: Slit 2 large eggplants and tuck 4 garlic cloves inside, then roast over a medium flame for 13-15 minutes, turning every 3 minutes, until blackened outside and butter-soft within; peel and mash the flesh with the roasted garlic while still warm.

Hold ¼ of a bhut jolokia with a fork and toast it over the flame for 20-30 seconds until it blisters and smells fruity-hot, then mince it as finely as possible — wash your hands and the board immediately afterwards.
Fold the minced bhut jolokia into the warm mash a little at a time, tasting between additions, until the heat is fierce but the eggplant's smokiness still comes through.
Add 6 finely chopped raw shallots, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger and 1 tsp salt, and mix with a fork so the shallots stay crunchy inside the soft mash.
Pour 2 tbsp raw Anveshan Mustard Oil over the mixture and beat it in for a full minute; the mash should glisten and carry the oil's sharp, sinus-clearing aroma throughout.
Finish with 1 tbsp lime juice and 4 tbsp chopped coriander, rest for 5 minutes for the heat to bloom evenly, and serve at room temperature as Assamese homes do.
tips: Bhut jolokia is among the world's hottest chillies — quarter of one pod is genuinely enough for four people; never touch your eyes while handling it.
No bhut jolokia available? Use 1 whole fresh red bird's-eye chilli, toasted the same way, for a tamer but similar fruity heat.
The dish must never go back on the heat after mixing; cooking the shallots and raw oil would erase its pitika character.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside plain steamed joha rice and a simple boiled-potato mash, letting the mild sides act as relief between fiery bites.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Baingan Bharta (Guntur Kaaram)
variations.description: This Rayalaseema-style bharta gets its firepower from a coarse fried paste of Guntur chillies and garlic stirred through the smoked eggplant. Curry leaves crisped in hot gingelly oil and a touch of tamarind finish a dish that is unapologetically hot, tangy and rustic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil deepens the roasted chilli-garlic kaaram exactly as Rayalaseema kitchens intend

steps: Roast 2 large eggplants over a medium flame for 13-15 minutes, turning every 3 minutes, until the skin is fully charred and the flesh is soft through; peel and mash coarsely, saving any smoky juices.
Soak 1 tbsp tamarind pulp in 3 tbsp warm water for 5 minutes, then squeeze out and strain a thick extract.

Fry 6 Guntur red chillies and 10 garlic cloves in 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil on low heat for 3-4 minutes until the chillies puff and crisp and the garlic softens, then pound or pulse them with 1 tsp salt into a coarse, fiery kaaram paste.

Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in the same kadai on medium, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then crisp 14 curry leaves in the oil for another 30 seconds.
Add 1 finely chopped onion with ¼ tsp turmeric and sauté for 4-5 minutes until golden, then stir in the chilli-garlic kaaram and fry for 1 minute until the oil turns a deep red.

Fold in the mashed eggplant and the tamarind extract, and cook on medium-low for 6-8 minutes, stirring and pressing, until the bharta is thick, brick-toned and glossy with red-stained oil at the edges.
tips: Frying the chillies and garlic before pounding, rather than using powders, is what gives kaaram dishes their toasty depth.
Cut the Guntur chillies down to 4 for medium heat; the flavour of the paste survives even at lower quantities.
The bharta should look slightly oily and stained red at the end — that chilli oil is where the flavour lives, so do not blot it away.
variations.servingSuggestion: Eat it the Rayalaseema way: mixed into hot rice with a generous spoon of Anveshan Ghee, with curd rice waiting as the cooling final course.

variations.name: Karnataka Spicy Baingan Bharta (Badanekayi Gojju Style)
variations.description: Borrowing from Karnataka's gojju tradition, this bharta balances chilli heat against tamarind's sourness and a hint of jaggery, with a rasam-powder warmth running underneath. It is the only take here that is hot, sweet and sour in the same spoonful — pure Kannadiga flavour logic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: North Karnataka cooks reach for groundnut oil for gojju; the wood-pressed version adds its own gentle nuttiness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Unrefined jaggery is the sweet corner of the gojju triangle, playing against tamarind and chilli

ingredients.name: White sesame seeds, roasted and ground

steps: Flame-roast 2 large eggplants for 12-15 minutes on medium heat, turning every 3 minutes, until charred all over and collapsed; peel, de-stem and mash the smoky flesh well.

Soak 2 tbsp tamarind pulp in ¼ cup warm water for 5 minutes and squeeze out a thick, strained extract; dry-roast 1 tbsp white sesame seeds for 2 minutes until they pop, then grind them to a coarse powder.

Heat 2½ tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds for 30 seconds, then add 12 curry leaves and 2 slit green chillies and fry for 30 seconds until the leaves crisp.
Sauté 1 finely chopped onion for 4-5 minutes until golden, then add ¼ tsp turmeric, 2 tsp rasam powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt and fry for 30 seconds until the spices smell toasty.
Pour in the tamarind extract with 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and simmer for 2-3 minutes until the raw sourness cooks off and the mixture turns syrupy at the edges.

Fold in the mashed eggplant and cook on medium-low for 6-8 minutes, stirring often, until thick and glossy, then finish with the ground sesame stirred through in the final minute for body and nutty aroma.
tips: Taste the gojju balance at the end: it should hit sour first, then sweet, then a slow chilli warmth — adjust tamarind or jaggery by the half-teaspoon.
The ground sesame both thickens the gojju and rounds the sharp edges; do not skip it.
This keeps for 4 days refrigerated and, like all gojjus, improves as the sweet-sour flavours marry overnight.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft jolada rotti or steamed rice, plus a simple kosambari salad, in true North Karnataka thali fashion.

variations.name: Goan Spicy Baingan Bharta (Kokum and Coconut)
variations.description: A Konkan-coast spin where the smoked eggplant is simmered briefly with kokum petals, toasted coconut and a red-chilli-garlic masala. The kokum brings a wine-dark, plummy sourness completely unlike tamarind or tomato, marking this bharta unmistakably as Goan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil anchors the Konkan flavour trio of coconut, kokum and chilli in this bharta

steps: Roast 2 large eggplants over a medium flame for 12-15 minutes, turning every 3 minutes, until the skin chars to a crisp shell and the flesh softens completely; peel and mash coarsely.
Soak 5 kokum petals in ¼ cup warm water for 10 minutes until the water turns deep pink, then tear the softened petals into small pieces and reserve both petals and soaking water.
Grind 4 soaked Kashmiri red chillies with 3 garlic cloves, 1 tsp cumin seeds and 2 tbsp water into a smooth, brick-red masala paste.

Heat 2½ tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, fry the remaining 3 sliced garlic cloves for 1 minute until golden, then add 2 finely chopped onions and sauté for 5-6 minutes until soft and lightly browned.

Add the ground chilli paste with ½ tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt and fry for 2-3 minutes until the paste thickens and the oil turns red, then toast ½ cup grated coconut in the masala for 2 minutes until it smells nutty.

Fold in the mashed eggplant, the kokum petals and their pink soaking water, and simmer on low for 6-7 minutes until thick and fragrant; finish with ½ tsp crushed black pepper and 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Kokum sourness builds as it simmers, so add the petals with their water in one go and taste after 5 minutes before deciding on more.
Kashmiri chillies give the vivid Goan-red colour with moderate heat; add 1 hot dried chilli to the grind if you want real fire.
This bharta pairs unusually well with seafood mains, which is exactly how Goan homes serve their vegetable sides.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed ukda (red) rice or crusty Goan poi bread, and a simple cucumber-coconut salad to cool the palate.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Cabbage Paratha
variations.description: Finely shredded cabbage, wilted first in ghee with green chilli and cracked pepper, folds into khapli atta dough for a flatbread that is spicy, savoury and never watery. Pre-cooking the cabbage concentrates its natural sweetness against the double dose of heat. It is a clever way to turn half a leftover cabbage into a breakfast people fight over.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer's forgiving gluten rolls thin around cabbage shreds without tearing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Wilting the cabbage in bilona ghee removes its raw sulphur note completely

steps: Shred 2.5 cups cabbage as finely as you can, keeping the shreds short so they fold into the dough without poking holes.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium flame, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then add 3 minced green chillies and grated 1 inch ginger and fry 30 seconds.

Add the cabbage with 0.5 tsp salt, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 0.25 tsp turmeric powder and sauté on medium-high for 5 minutes until it wilts to half its volume and the pan is dry; stir in 1 tsp cracked black pepper and cool completely.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with the cooled cabbage, 3 tbsp chopped coriander, 0.5 tsp salt and up to 0.5 cup water, added a little at a time, into a soft dough; rest for 15 minutes.
Divide into 8 balls and roll each on a floured board into a 6-inch round, re-flouring whenever a cabbage shred sticks to the pin.
Cook on a hot tava at medium-high for about 1 minute per side until brown-spotted, then brush both sides using the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and toast 30 seconds more per side until crisp-edged.
tips: Wilting the cabbage first is the whole trick; raw cabbage weeps water on the tava and makes limp parathas.
If the dough feels wet after resting, knead in a tablespoon of dry atta rather than adding flour while rolling.
Add the cracked pepper off the heat so it stays punchy instead of turning bitter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tomato-garlic chutney and a bowl of plain curd; these also make excellent kathi-style rolls around scrambled paneer.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Cabbage Paratha
variations.description: Cabbage meets Guntur fire in this Andhra version, where the shreds are tossed with a roasted red-chilli and garlic karam podi and the paratha is crisped in wood-pressed groundnut oil. Curry leaves fried in the same oil thread through the dough. It is aggressive, aromatic and exactly what Andhra food lovers expect.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: A robust flour that carries karam-podi heat without falling apart

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The wood-pressed nuttiness is the traditional base for Andhra podi cooking

steps: Dry-roast 4 Guntur chillies, 1 tbsp coriander seeds and 1 tbsp chana dal on low heat for 3 to 4 minutes until the dal turns gold, then cool and grind with 5 garlic cloves and 0.25 tsp salt into a coarse karam podi.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai over medium heat, pop 0.75 tsp mustard seeds for 20 seconds, then crisp 12 curry leaves in the oil for 15 seconds.

Add 2.5 cups finely shredded cabbage with 0.25 tsp turmeric powder and 0.5 tsp salt and stir-fry 5 minutes on medium-high until wilted and dry, then toss through the karam podi and switch off; cool completely.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with the podi-cabbage, 0.25 tsp salt and up to 0.5 cup water into a soft, red-flecked dough and let it rest, covered, for 15 minutes.
Shape into 8 balls and roll each to a 6-inch disc with light pressure so the cabbage shreds stay embedded.

Roast on a medium-hot tava for about 1 minute per side until deeply spotted, then spoon the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over the batch and crisp each side a further 30 seconds until the podi toasts fragrant.
tips: Grind the podi coarse; a fine powder disappears into the dough while coarse bits deliver bursts of heat.
Chana dal in the podi is the Andhra thickener that also keeps the cabbage mixture dry.
Scale the Guntur chillies down to 2 for a family-friendly version without losing the podi's aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with chilled sour curd and a wedge of lime; a side of gun-powder-dusted ghee idli makes it a full Andhra tiffin spread.

variations.name: Goan Spicy Cabbage Paratha
variations.description: Goa's souring agent of choice, kokum, is steeped and kneaded into this cabbage paratha along with a home-style recheado-inspired paste of red chilli, garlic and a touch of jaggery. The kokum's plummy tang cuts the heat the way vinegar does in Goan curries. Coconut oil on the tava seals the coastal character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its gentle sweetness balances kokum's sharp, winey tang

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil grounds the recheado spicing firmly on the Konkan coast

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Goan masalas always carry a whisper of jaggery against the sourness

steps: Soak 6 kokum petals in 0.25 cup hot water for 15 minutes, then squeeze and chop the softened petals fine, reserving the deep pink soaking liquid for the dough.

Soak 3 dried red chillies in the same window, then grind them with 5 garlic cloves, 1 tsp cumin seeds, 0.5 tsp black pepper, 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.25 tsp salt into a thick recheado-style paste.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadhai on medium flame, fry the spice paste for 2 minutes until it darkens and smells roasted, then add 2.5 cups shredded cabbage, the chopped kokum, 0.25 tsp turmeric powder and 0.5 tsp salt and sauté 5 minutes until dry; cool fully.

Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with the cooled cabbage masala, 0.25 tsp salt, the kokum water and enough plain water (0.5 cup total liquid at most) to form a soft blush-tinted dough; rest 15 minutes.
Divide into 8 balls and roll each to a 6-inch round on a floured surface, working gently since the tangy dough is slightly delicate.

Cook on a medium tava for about 75 seconds per side until mottled brown, then drizzle the remaining 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil across the batch and toast each side 30 seconds until crisp and glossy.
tips: Rinse kokum petals before soaking to remove surface salt, or the dough may end up over-seasoned.
Fry the spice paste until the oil separates at the edges; undercooked paste tastes raw and harsh in the dough.
A day-old batch revives perfectly on a hot pan with a few drops of coconut oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling coconut-curd raita and a simple tomato salad; in Goa these would flank a fried fish for a full plate.

variations.name: Tamil Spicy Cabbage Paratha
variations.description: Borrowing from Tamil cabbage poriyal and milagai podi, this paratha layers gingelly-oil-fried curry leaves, urad dal and crushed black pepper through wilted cabbage. The urad dal toasts into tiny crunchy nubs inside the bread. It is the taste of a Tamil mess hall folded into a flatbread.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer flour takes on the gingelly oil's aroma like a seasoned dosa pan

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Nallennai, wood-pressed sesame oil, is the defining fat of Tamil tempering

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadhai on medium heat, fry 1.5 tbsp urad dal for about 90 seconds until biscuit-gold, then pop 1 tsp mustard seeds alongside for 20 seconds.
Add 3 torn dried red chillies, 15 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp hing and let everything crackle for 15 seconds until the leaves turn glassy.

Tip in 2.5 cups finely shredded cabbage with 0.25 tsp turmeric powder and 0.5 tsp salt and stir-fry 5 minutes on medium-high until wilted, dry and faintly caramelised; finish with 1 tsp coarsely crushed black pepper and cool completely.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with the cooled poriyal mixture, 0.5 tsp salt and up to 0.5 cup water into a soft dough studded with dal and leaves; rest it 15 minutes.
Divide into 8 balls and roll each into a 6-inch circle with steady, light strokes so the crunchy dal bits stay seated in the dough.

Roast on a hot tava at medium-high for about 1 minute per side until brown-blistered, then anoint each side with a little of the remaining 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and crisp 30 seconds more until the edges snap.
tips: Fry the urad dal to a true golden brown; pale dal stays hard and chalky inside the paratha.
Crush the pepper coarse in a mortar for the poriyal-style pops of heat.
These parathas love company on the tava; keep the flame steady and cook them back to back so the pan stays seasoned.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and a small tumbler of filter coffee for breakfast, or with rasam rice for a comforting Tamil lunch.

variations.name: Kumaoni Spicy Cabbage Paratha
variations.description: From the Uttarakhand hills, this paratha tempers cabbage with jakhya, the wild mustard-like seed Kumaoni cooks prize for its incomparable crackle, along with hill garlic and dried red chilli. Jakhya's nutty pop is unlike cumin or mustard and defines every bite. Roasted in ghee, it tastes of woodsmoke kitchens in the mountains.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Hill kitchens swear by hardy heritage wheats; khapli fits right in

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Pahadi cooking finishes vegetables and breads alike in pure ghee

steps: Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp jakhya seeds for about 20 seconds; they should pop and crackle audibly, the sign they are ready.
Add 2 torn dried red chillies, 4 sliced garlic cloves and 2 chopped green chillies and fry 45 seconds until the garlic edges turn gold.

Add 2.5 cups finely shredded cabbage, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric powder and 0.5 tsp salt and sauté 5 minutes on medium-high until the shreds wilt and dry out; fold in 2 tbsp chopped coriander and cool completely.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with the cooled jakhya-cabbage, 0.5 tsp salt and up to 0.5 cup water into a soft, speckled dough; rest for 15 minutes under a cloth.
Divide into 8 balls and roll each into a 6-inch round, dusting minimally so the tempered seeds stay visible on the surface.

Cook on a hot tava for about 1 minute per side at medium-high until spotted deep brown, then brush both faces with the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee shared across the batch and toast 30 seconds per side until crisp.
tips: Jakhya must go into hot ghee and crackle fully; raw jakhya tastes grassy and bitter.
If you cannot source jakhya, mustard seeds plus a pinch of sesame come closest, though hill cooks would protest.
Slice the garlic instead of crushing it; the golden slivers are part of the pahadi character.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the mountain way with bhang ki chutney or plain lime-spiked curd, and a hot glass of buransh squash in season.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Carrot Paratha
variations.description: A fiery everyday paratha where sweet grated carrot is tamed by a double hit of green chilli and freshly cracked black pepper worked right into the dough. The carrot's sugars caramelise against the hot tava while the pepper burns slow and clean. It is the paratha for people who reach for the pickle jar before the curd.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer's mellow sweetness is the perfect foil to the chilli-pepper heat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries capsaicin beautifully, spreading the heat evenly instead of in spikes

steps: Grate 1.5 cups carrot finely, salt it with 0.25 tsp of the salt, wait 5 minutes and squeeze hard, keeping the pressed-out juice aside for kneading.

Mix 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with the squeezed carrot, 3 minced green chillies, grated 1 inch ginger, 1 tsp coarsely cracked black pepper, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric powder, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp chopped coriander.
Work in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then knead with the carrot juice topped up with at most 0.5 cup water into a soft dough that does not crack at the edges; rest 15 minutes under a damp cloth.
Cut the dough into 8 pieces, round them, and roll each on a floured board into a 6-inch disc of even thickness.
Cook on a hot tava at medium-high for about 1 minute until bubbles lift the surface, flip, and give the second side 1 minute until spotted brown.
Paint both sides with a share of the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and roast a final 30 seconds per side, pressing with a spatula, until crisp with charred flecks.
tips: Crack the pepper fresh in a mortar; pre-ground pepper gives dusty heat instead of a clean burn.
Deseed one of the chillies if serving children, or keep all seeds in for full fire.
A squeeze of lemon on the hot paratha lifts both the sweetness of the carrot and the chilli's edge.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling bowl of plain curd whisked smooth and a wedge of lemon; the contrast of hot and cold is half the pleasure.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Carrot Paratha
variations.description: Built around Guntur chilli, Andhra's pride, this paratha layers a roasted chilli-garlic podi through the carrot dough and gets shallow-roasted in wood-pressed groundnut oil. The heat is upfront and honest, softened only slightly by a pinch of jaggery in the podi, the classic Andhra balance. Keep water nearby; that is the point.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: A wholegrain base sturdy enough for Guntur-strength spicing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Andhra kitchens roast their podis and breads in groundnut oil; wood-pressed keeps it nutty

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A pinch of pure jaggery rounds the Guntur chilli's blaze, Andhra-style

steps: Dry-roast 4 Guntur chillies, 1 tbsp coriander seeds and 1 tsp cumin seeds in a pan on low heat for about 3 minutes until the chillies puff and darken slightly, then cool and grind with 5 garlic cloves, 0.25 tsp salt and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder into a coarse podi.
Fry 10 curry leaves in 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat for about 20 seconds until crisp and translucent, then crumble them into the podi.
Combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1.5 cups squeezed grated carrot, the chilli podi, 0.25 tsp turmeric powder and 0.75 tsp salt, tossing until the flour turns brick-flecked.
Knead with up to 0.5 cup water, added in stages, into a soft, cohesive dough, then rest it covered for 15 minutes so the podi hydrates evenly.
Divide into 8 balls and roll each into a 6-inch round, dusting lightly; the dough is tender, so use short, gentle strokes.

Roast on a medium-hot tava for about 1 minute per side until spotted, then drizzle the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil across the batch and crisp each side 30 seconds more until the podi smells toasted.
tips: Roast the chillies on low heat with the fan on; rushing them on high flame turns the podi acrid.
If Guntur chillies are unavailable, use 3 ordinary dried red chillies plus 0.5 tsp cayenne for comparable fire.
The podi recipe doubles well; the extra keeps a month in a jar and is superb over ghee rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Andhra way with a bowl of chilled curd, a spoon of avakaya pickle for the brave, and thin onion rings soaked in lemon water.

variations.name: Bengali Spicy Carrot Paratha
variations.description: Green chilli heat meets mustard's nose-tingling pungency in this Bengali rendition, where the carrot is sautéed with kalonji and slit chillies in smoking kachi ghani mustard oil before joining the dough. The spice here is aromatic rather than scorching, the kind that builds over three bites. A ghee finish softens the landing.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer flour crisps into a delicate, kochuri-like crust with mustard oil

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: The signature Bengali pungency comes from smoking wood-pressed mustard oil

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The classic Bengali one-two: cook in mustard oil, finish with ghee

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai until it just smokes, drop the flame to medium, and sputter 0.75 tsp kalonji with 0.25 tsp hing for 15 seconds.
Add 4 slit green chillies and grated 1.5 inch ginger, fry 30 seconds, then tip in 1.5 cups grated carrot with 0.5 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp sugar and sauté 4 minutes until the carrot dries and glistens.
Dust in 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, toss once, and spread the mixture on a plate to cool to room temperature.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with the cooled carrot mixture, 0.5 tsp salt, the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and up to 0.5 cup water into a soft dough; rest 15 minutes.
Divide into 8 portions, roll into balls, and flatten each into a 6-inch round, flouring lightly so the chilli-flecked dough releases cleanly.

Cook on a hot tava for about 1 minute per side over medium-high until brown-spotted, then gloss both sides with a little of the 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and toast 30 seconds per side until crisp and fragrant.
tips: The 0.5 tsp sugar is not for sweetness; it is the Bengali trick that balances mustard oil's bite.
Slit the chillies rather than chopping if you want aroma with moderate heat; chop them fine for full fire.
Let the sautéed carrot cool fully before kneading or the dough will turn slack and sticky.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with begun bhaja (crisp fried eggplant slices) and a dab of kasundi; a cup of sweet milky cha alongside is non-negotiable in Bengal.

variations.name: Karnataka Spicy Carrot Paratha
variations.description: Modelled on Karnataka's tamarind-laced spice pastes, this paratha folds a tangy-hot huli-style masala of tamarind, byadgi chilli and roasted sesame into the carrot dough. The tamarind keeps the heat bright and mouth-watering instead of heavy. Roasted in sesame oil, it tastes like a cross between a paratha and a chapati smeared with gojju.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its nutty wholegrain body holds the tangy masala without going soggy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed sesame oil is the traditional partner for tamarind-chilli masalas in Karnataka

steps: Dry-roast 3 byadgi chillies, 1 tbsp coriander seeds and 1.5 tbsp sesame seeds on low heat for about 3 minutes until the sesame turns gold and pops, then cool and grind to a coarse powder.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pan on medium flame, crackle 0.75 tsp mustard seeds for 20 seconds, add 10 curry leaves, then stir in 1.5 cups grated carrot with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder and 0.5 tsp salt and sauté 3 minutes.
Add 1.5 tbsp thick tamarind pulp and the ground spice powder, cook 2 minutes until the mixture turns jammy and pulls away from the pan, then cool completely.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with the cooled tangy carrot masala, 0.5 tsp salt and up to 0.5 cup water into a soft, faintly sticky dough; rest 15 minutes and it will firm up.
Roll the dough into 8 balls and flatten each to a 6-inch disc on a well-floured board, since tamarind dough grips the pin slightly.

Roast each paratha on a medium tava for about 75 seconds per side until deep brown patches form, then trickle a share of the remaining 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil over each side and crisp 30 seconds more.
tips: Use thick tamarind pulp, not watery extract; excess liquid ruins the dough's texture.
Byadgi chillies give colour with moderate heat; add a pinch of cayenne if you want it fiercer.
Tamarind doughs brown faster, so keep the flame at medium and flip promptly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a dollop of fresh curd and kosambari salad; in Karnataka homes a smear of butter over the hot tangy crust is the finishing touch.

variations.name: Assamese Spicy Carrot Paratha
variations.description: A dare of a paratha built around bhut jolokia, the ghost pepper of Assam, used the traditional way: a small amount, mashed with garlic and lime for aroma as much as fire. The carrot's sweetness and a mustard-oil temper keep the burn rolling instead of flat. This is heat with fragrance, the Assamese speciality.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Sweet emmer wheat cushions the ghost pepper's legendary burn

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Assamese kitchens run on pungent mustard oil; wood-pressed keeps it authentic

steps: Wearing gloves, mash 0.5 small bhut jolokia with 4 garlic cloves, 0.25 tsp salt and 1 tbsp lime juice into a loose chutney; even half a pod carries serious fire, so do not be tempted to add more on the first try.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to its smoking point in a kadhai, reduce to medium, and crackle 1 tsp panch phoron for about 20 seconds until nutty-smelling.

Add grated 1 inch ginger, stir 30 seconds, then tip in 1.5 cups grated carrot with 0.25 tsp turmeric powder and 0.5 tsp salt and sauté 4 minutes until dry; stir in the ghost-pepper chutney, cook 1 minute more, and cool fully.

Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with the cooled fiery carrot, 3 tbsp chopped coriander, 0.25 tsp salt, the last 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and up to 0.5 cup water into a soft dough; rest 15 minutes.
Divide into 8 balls and roll each into a thin 6-inch round, flouring your hands as well as the board; wash hands thoroughly afterwards.
Cook on a hot tava at medium-high for about 1 minute per side until blistered brown, pressing the edges with a folded cloth, until the paratha crisps and the chilli aroma blooms off the pan.
tips: Always handle bhut jolokia with gloves and never touch your face; its oils linger on skin for hours.
Cooking the ghost pepper briefly in the carrot mash mellows its rawest edge while keeping the fruity aroma.
Serve milk or sweet curd alongside; water spreads capsaicin instead of calming it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve Assamese-style with a plate of plain curd, a boiled egg and thin-sliced red onion; a spoon of honey-drizzled curd rescues anyone who overestimates their tolerance.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Palak Paratha
variations.description: A vivid green paratha where blanched spinach is pureed straight into the khapli dough, so every layer carries the leafy goodness instead of hiding it in a pocket. Green chillies, crushed black pepper and ginger give it a clean, sharp heat. Ghee-roasted, it emerges emerald-edged with a crackly, blistered surface.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer wheat's nutty depth keeps the spinach dough tasting hearty rather than grassy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee-roasting spinach dough coaxes out a toasted, almost saag-like aroma from the greens

steps: Blanch 3 cups of washed spinach in boiling water for exactly 60 seconds, plunge into cold water to lock the colour, squeeze dry and blend with 3 green chillies and 1 inch of ginger into a thick puree.
Add the puree to 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1.25 tsp salt, 1 tsp crushed pepper, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee.
Knead into a soft green dough, adding up to 0.25 cup water only if it feels dry; the spinach carries most of the moisture. Rest, covered, for 20 minutes.
Divide the dough into 8 balls and roll each into a 6-7 inch round on a lightly floured board, keeping an even thickness so the colour cooks uniformly.
Heat a tava on medium-high until water droplets dance, then cook each paratha for about 90 seconds per side until pale spots appear and it puffs in patches.
Brush both faces with the remaining 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, flip once more for 30 seconds per side, and look for a crackled surface with deep-green and gold blisters.
Stack in a cloth-lined box; the residual steam softens them to a perfect pliable-crisp balance in 2 minutes.
tips: The 60-second blanch and cold plunge is the difference between emerald parathas and khaki ones.
Squeeze the blanched spinach hard; wet puree forces extra flour and dilutes both colour and flavour.
Dough keeps 24 hours refrigerated, though the green dulls slightly by day two.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of spiced boondi raita and lime pickle; the cool raita against the peppery heat is the whole point.

variations.name: Bengali Spicy Palak Paratha
variations.description: Bengal treats greens with mustard, and this paratha follows suit: spinach dough perfumed with kachhi ghani mustard oil, nigella seeds and fiery chopped green chillies. The mustard oil's pungency wakes up the mellow palak the way it does in a classic shaak. Dark-blistered and sharp, it is worlds apart from the ghee-mild northern version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The robust emmer grain carries mustard oil's punch the way Bengal's whole-wheat ruti does

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed kachhi ghani oil brings the nose-tingling sharpness that defines Bengali greens

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A last-second ghee gloss rounds the mustard bite into something festive

steps: Blanch 3 cups spinach for 1 minute, shock in cold water, squeeze firmly and blend with 4 green chillies and 6 garlic cloves into a coarse green paste.

Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, cool for a minute, then pour it over 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta along with 1 tsp nigella seeds, 1.25 tsp salt, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp sugar.
Add the spinach paste and knead into a soft, deep-green dough, splashing in up to 0.25 cup water only if needed. Rest 20 minutes under a damp cloth.
Portion into 8 balls and roll each into a 6 inch round, flouring lightly; the nigella seeds should speckle the surface like poppy seeds on a kulcha.
Cook on a medium-hot tava for about 90 seconds per side until the first pale blisters rise across the green surface.
Drizzle the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil around the edges, flip and press for 30 seconds per side until the blisters darken to a burnished brown.
Finish each paratha with a thin brushing from the 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee while piping hot so the pungent and the mellow meet.
tips: Smoking the mustard oil once before kneading removes rawness while keeping the signature pungency.
The 0.5 tsp sugar is not optional in a Bengali kitchen; it rounds the bitterness of the greens.
These pair unusually well with scrambled eggs for a Kolkata-style breakfast.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with aloo posto or simply thick curd and kasundi mustard for dipping the crisp edges.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Palak Paratha
variations.description: Andhra's answer to palak paratha borrows from gongura logic: greens plus serious chilli. A roasted Guntur chilli-garlic paste is kneaded into the spinach dough itself, staining it a deep jade-red and building slow, smoky heat. Cooked in groundnut oil, it is the spiciest and boldest paratha of this family.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The earthy heritage grain anchors Guntur chilli heat instead of letting it dominate

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the traditional Andhra frying medium for chilli pastes and griddle breads alike

steps: Dry-roast 4 Guntur chillies, 1 tsp coriander seeds and the leaves of 1 curry sprig on low heat for 2 minutes until smoky, then grind with 8 garlic cloves into a coarse red paste.
Blanch 3 cups spinach for 60 seconds, cool in iced water, squeeze thoroughly and blend to a thick puree.

Combine 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with the chilli-garlic paste, spinach puree, 1.25 tsp salt, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tbsp sesame seeds and 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, kneading into a firm-soft dough with up to 0.25 cup water. Rest 20 minutes.
Divide into 8 balls and roll each to a 6 inch round; the dough will look mottled green-red, which is exactly right.
Cook on a medium-high tava for about 90 seconds a side until blisters begin to lift the surface.
Spoon the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over both faces and roast another 30-40 seconds per side until the crust crisps to a dark, spice-flecked bronze.
Rest 2 minutes before serving so the smoky heat spreads evenly rather than striking all at once.
tips: Dry-roasting the chillies is what converts raw heat into smoky depth; do not skip to plain chilli powder.
Sesame seeds in the dough toast on the tava and add a nutty crunch that offsets the fire.
Halve the chillies to 2 and the flavour survives at a family-friendly heat level.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve Andhra-style with chilled sweetened curd rice on the side or a spoon of avakaya pickle for the truly fearless.

variations.name: Kumaoni Spicy Palak Paratha
variations.description: In the Kumaon hills, greens are tempered with jakhya, the crackling wild mustard seed, and cooked slow in ghee over wood fires. This paratha channels that tradition: spinach dough studded with a jakhya-red chilli tadka, rolled thick and roasted patiently to a biscuity crust. Rustic mountain food, honest and warming.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Heritage hill wheats were always coarse and hardy; khapli brings that exact mountain character

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Slow ghee-roasting over moderate heat builds the thick, biscuity crust of a true pahadi paratha

steps: Blanch 3 cups spinach for a minute, refresh in cold water, squeeze hard and chop very fine rather than pureeing; hill kitchens like visible flecks of green.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan on medium and crackle 1 tsp jakhya seeds with 3 torn dried red chillies for 30 seconds until they pop loudly and smell nutty, then fry 6 minced garlic cloves for 45 seconds until golden.

Pour this tadka over 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, add the chopped spinach, 1.25 tsp salt, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp crushed pepper and 0.5 tsp turmeric, and knead into a firm green-flecked dough with up to 0.25 cup water. Rest 20 minutes.
Divide into 8 balls and roll each into a slightly thick 5-6 inch round; thin rolling would rob it of the doughy hill-bread heart.
Roast on a tava over medium-low heat for a full 3 minutes per side, unhurried, until the crust sets firm and takes on deep bronze patches.
Coat both faces with the remaining 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in two stages, letting each side fry another 30 seconds until crunchy at the edges.
Cool upright in a basket for 2 minutes; the crust crisps further as steam escapes.
tips: Chopped spinach, not puree, is the pahadi way; the flecks toast against the tava for extra flavour.
Jakhya must crackle fully in the ghee or it stays gritty in the dough.
These thick parathas reheat perfectly over a direct low flame for 20 seconds a side.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with pahadi aloo ke gutke and cucumber raita, or in true Kumaoni style with just ghee and a hot glass of tea.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Spicy Palak Paratha
variations.description: Modeled on the beloved palak thalipeeth, this version seasons the spinach dough with goda masala, sesame and crushed peanuts, then roasts it in wood-pressed groundnut oil. It is nubbly, nutty and gently sweet-spiced, with crisp edges that beg to be dunked in curd. A Pune breakfast in paratha form.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Stone-ground emmer echoes the multigrain heartiness of a traditional bhajani thalipeeth

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Thalipeeth is always crisped in groundnut oil, and this wood-pressed one adds a clean roasted aroma

steps: Blanch 3 cups spinach for 60 seconds, cool it fast in cold water, squeeze dry and grind with 3 green chillies and 1 inch of ginger into a thick paste.
Mix 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 2 tsp goda masala, 3 tbsp crushed roasted peanuts, 1 tbsp sesame seeds, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt.
Knead in the spinach paste and 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil to form a nubbly green dough, adding up to 0.25 cup water if it resists coming together. Rest 20 minutes.
Shape 8 balls and roll each to a 6 inch round; small peanut bumps in the surface are part of its thalipeeth charm.
Cook on a medium tava for about 2 minutes on the first side until set and freckled, then flip.
Drizzle the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil around and over the parathas and roast each side another minute until the sesame toasts golden and the edges crisp like a thalipeeth's.
Press a small dimple in the centre with a spoon while roasting, the traditional trick to crisp the middle evenly.
tips: Crushed peanuts should be coarse gravel, not powder, for authentic crunch.
Goda masala's stone-flower smokiness fades if overheated, so keep the tava at medium.
Leftovers make an excellent breakfast crumbled into curd like a savoury thalipeeth bowl.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with white butter or thick curd and a smear of green-chilli thecha, plus sweet chai to balance the spice.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Tori
variations.description: Ridge gourd for people who think gourds are boring: a double-heat build of slit green chillies cooked into the masala and coarse black pepper cracked over at the end. The Anveshan Ghee base carries the chilli heat evenly so it warms rather than burns, while the tomato keeps everything juicy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee spreads capsaicin evenly through the dish, giving deep warmth instead of raw sting

steps: Peel the hard ridges from 500 g ridge gourd and slice it into 2 cm half-moons; chop 2 medium onions and 2 medium tomatoes, and slit 3 green chillies down the middle.
Warm 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then add the slit green chillies and let them blister for 30 seconds.
Add the onions and fry for 5-6 minutes until deep golden, stirring often, then mix in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute more until fragrant.

Add the tomatoes with 2 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt; cook for 4-5 minutes on medium, mashing, until the masala is thick and the ghee glistens at its edges.
Fold in the tori, cover and cook on low heat for 12 minutes, stirring twice, until the gourd is soft and steeped in the chilli-red masala; do not add water.
Finish uncovered on medium for 2-3 minutes to thicken the juices, then crack 0.75 tsp coarse black pepper over the top and scatter 2 tbsp chopped coriander before serving.
tips: Blistering the green chillies in ghee before the onions mellows their sharpness while keeping the burn.
Add black pepper only at the end; long cooking turns its floral heat flat and bitter.
If someone at the table cannot take heat, fish out the slit chillies from their portion; most of their fire stays in the pods.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best with cooling sides: soft phulkas, a big bowl of boondi raita and kachumber salad; a squeeze of lime just before eating brightens the heat.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Tori
variations.description: Beerakaya fry at full Andhra volume: ridge gourd seared in Anveshan Groundnut Oil, loaded with Guntur chilli powder and finished with a garlic-red-chilli karam crushed in a mortar. Tamarind at the end adds the sour spike that makes the heat moreish instead of exhausting.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Sturdy wood-pressed peanut oil stands up to Guntur chilli without turning acrid

steps: Pound 6 garlic cloves with 3 dried red chillies in a mortar into a rough karam paste; peel 500 g beerakaya and cut it into 2 cm chunks, and slice 1 medium onion.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds, fry 2 tsp chana dal for 45 seconds until golden, then add 10 curry leaves and let them crisp.
Add the garlic-chilli karam and fry for 1 minute on medium-low, stirring, until the garlic loses its rawness and the oil turns brick red.
Add the onion and cook for 3-4 minutes until soft, then tip in the gourd with 0.25 tsp turmeric powder, 2 tsp Guntur chilli powder and 1 tsp salt and toss thoroughly.
Cover and cook on low heat for 10 minutes, stirring midway, until the beerakaya is tender and stained deep red by the chilli oil.
Stir in 1 tbsp tamarind pulp, cook uncovered on medium for 3 minutes until the sourness cooks in and the pan juices reduce to a clinging glaze.
tips: Frying the crushed garlic-chilli karam in oil first is the flavour engine of this dish; do not skip it for plain chilli powder.
Tamarind burns and turns muddy on long cooking, so it goes in only for the final 3 minutes.
Serve with a spoon of plain curd on the plate; in Andhra, curd is not a side but a heat-management tool.
variations.servingSuggestion: Mound over hot steamed rice with a spoon of ghee melted on top and mudda pappu on the side; a raw onion wedge and curd complete the classic Andhra plate.

variations.name: Assamese Spicy Tori
variations.description: A north-eastern scorcher where ridge gourd meets a sliver of bhut jolokia, the ghost chilli of Assam, bloomed carefully in Anveshan Mustard Oil. Beyond the fire, the dish stays true to Assamese simplicity: kalonji, a hint of ginger, and almost nothing else in the way of masala.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Assamese kitchens cook almost exclusively in mustard oil; its pungency frames the ghost chilli's fruity fire

steps: Wearing care around your eyes, slice 0.25 of a bhut jolokia into the thinnest possible slivers and wash your hands immediately; peel and cube 500 g ridge gourd and 1 medium potato into 2 cm pieces, and slice 1 onion.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai on medium-high until it shimmers and its sharpness softens, about 90 seconds, then reduce to medium and sputter 0.5 tsp kalonji for 10 seconds.
Add the sliced onion and 1 inch julienned ginger and fry for 3 minutes until the onion is soft and translucent with light gold edges.
Add the potato cubes and cook for 4 minutes, tossing, so they get a head start; then add the ridge gourd, 0.5 tsp turmeric powder and 1 tsp salt.
Slip in the ghost chilli slivers, cover and cook on low heat for 10-12 minutes, stirring twice, until the potato is cooked through and the gourd is silky; the vegetables' own moisture is enough.
Uncover, raise the heat for 2 minutes to dry the pan juices slightly, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander; warn the table about the innocent-looking chilli threads.
tips: A quarter chilli is genuinely enough for four people; bhut jolokia measures over one million Scoville units, so treat it like a spice, not a vegetable.
Handle the chilli with a fork and knife or gloves; capsaicin at this level transfers painfully from fingers to eyes hours later.
No bhut jolokia? Use 1 whole fresh red chilli plus a pinch of chilli flakes; the dish becomes tamer but keeps its character.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain rice and masor tenga-style tangy fish curry if you eat fish, or simply with dal and a lemon wedge; a bowl of chilled curd on the table is non-negotiable insurance.

variations.name: Kerala Spicy Tori
variations.description: A peechinga ularthiyathu-style dish where ridge gourd is braised with crushed black pepper, green chilli and shallots in Anveshan Coconut Oil, then finished with toasted coconut slivers. Kerala's heat here comes from pepper more than chilli, warm and resinous rather than sharp.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil gives the ularthu its glossy finish and unmistakable Kerala aroma

steps: Peel 500 g peechinga and cut it into chunky 2 cm pieces; slice 8 shallots, crush 4 garlic cloves, slit 3 green chillies, and cut 0.25 cup thin slivers from a piece of fresh coconut.

Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a cheena chatti or wok on medium, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds fully, then add 12 curry leaves and the coconut slivers and fry for 1-2 minutes until the slivers turn light brown and toasty.
Add the shallots, garlic and green chillies and sauté for 3-4 minutes until the shallots soften and pick up golden edges.
Add the gourd with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp salt and half of the 1.5 tsp crushed pepper; toss until every piece glistens with the spiced oil.
Cover and cook on low heat for 10-12 minutes, stirring twice, letting the gourd soften completely in its own steam without any added water.
Uncover, sprinkle the remaining crushed pepper, and stir-fry on medium-high for 2-3 minutes until the pieces look glossy and lightly browned, the true ularthu finish.
tips: Pepper goes in twice: cooked in for body heat, and raw at the end for the bright top note; skipping either flattens the dish.
The toasted coconut slivers must go in early with the temper so they stay crunchy against the soft gourd.
Shallots, not big onions, make this taste authentically Malayali; their sweetness against the pepper is the point.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with Kerala matta rice and a simple moru curry (spiced buttermilk), or alongside appam for a heat-and-soft contrast; a few banana chips on the plate never hurt.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Spicy Tori
variations.description: Dodka bhaji cranked to Kolhapur intensity: ridge gourd cooked in Anveshan Groundnut Oil with a fresh-ground green chilli-garlic thecha stirred through the masala and goda masala for its smoky base. The result is bold, rustic heat with the peanutty depth Maharashtrian food does best.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed peanut oil is the traditional base for fiery western-Maharashtra bhajis

steps: Dry-roast 4 green chillies and 6 garlic cloves in a bare pan for 2-3 minutes until blistered, then pound them with a pinch of the salt into a coarse thecha; peel and chop 500 g dodka into 1.5 cm pieces and dice 1 onion.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds, then crackle 0.5 tsp cumin seeds for 15 seconds.
Fry the diced onion for 4 minutes until lightly browned, then add the pounded thecha and fry for 1 minute, keeping your face back from the chilli fumes.
Add 0.5 tsp turmeric powder and 1.5 tsp goda masala, stir for 20 seconds, then immediately add the dodka and 1 tsp salt and coat the pieces in the dark, hot oil.
