Push the okra to one side, add the last 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, and fry 1 sliced large onion with 2 slit green chillies in the cleared space for 3 to 4 minutes until golden.

Combine everything, then sprinkle 2 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp salt; toss on medium for 2 to 3 minutes so the spices toast on the okra rather than steam.
Switch off, dust with 1.5 tsp amchur, toss once, and serve straight away while the frilled edges are still crisp.
tips: Crowding is the killer; if your pan is small, fry the okra in two batches rather than piling it up.
Salt and amchur both go in late; early salt sweats the okra and early amchur makes it gluey.
Leftovers re-crisp beautifully spread on a tray in a hot oven for 5 minutes; never microwave them.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as the crisp counterpoint to a soft meal: dal-chawal or kadhi-chawal, with roasted papad and a raw onion ring salad on the side.

variations.name: Kumaoni Dry Bhindi
variations.description: In Uttarakhand's hill kitchens this would be bhindi ke gutke: okra seared in mustard oil with crackling jakhya seeds, crushed garlic and whole dried chillies, and nothing else to blur the picture. Jakhya's poppy-seed crunch against the crisp pods is the entire event.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Pahadi gutke demand pungent mustard oil heated to smoking; the kachi ghani press keeps that raw mountain bite

steps: Wash and towel-dry 500 g okra thoroughly, then slice into 1-inch diagonal pieces so more surface meets the hot iron pan.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in an iron kadhai until it just begins to smoke, drop the heat to medium, and crackle 2 tsp jakhya seeds for 15 to 20 seconds until they pop in rapid bursts.
Add 3 torn dried red chillies and 6 roughly crushed garlic cloves and fry for 30 to 40 seconds until the garlic edges turn gold and the chillies darken.
Tip in the okra, toss to coat in the seeded oil, and fry uncovered on medium-high for 10 to 12 minutes, turning every 3 minutes, until the pieces are browned, dry and crisp-edged.
Season with 1.5 tsp salt, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp coriander powder only in the final 2 minutes, tossing so the spices cling without burning.
Finish off the heat with 3 tbsp chopped coriander leaves and 1 tbsp lemon juice flicked over the top just before it reaches the table.
tips: Jakhya needs genuinely hot oil to pop; lukewarm oil leaves the seeds sandy and raw-tasting.
An iron kadhai gives the charred patches that define gutke; add 2 extra minutes if using stainless steel.
No jakhya? A half-half mix of sesame and mustard seeds is the accepted plains substitute.
variations.servingSuggestion: Eat pahadi-style with mandua rotis and a bowl of jhwai (buttermilk curry), or simply tucked into hot rice with a spoon of ghee melting through.

variations.name: Tamil Dry Bhindi
variations.description: Vendakkai poriyal from a Thanjavur kitchen: okra rounds roasted in gingelly oil with a mustard-urad-chana tempering, curry leaves and sambar powder, then showered with fresh coconut at the end. Crisp pods, crunchy dal bits and sweet coconut in every spoonful.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Nutty wood-pressed gingelly oil is the traditional poriyal fat and browns the okra with a toasty depth

steps: Wash 500 g okra, dry each pod fully, and slice into thin 0.5-inch rounds; thin rounds crisp faster and hold the tempering better.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a wide kadai on medium, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds for 20 seconds, then add 1 tbsp urad dal, 1 tbsp chana dal and 2 torn dried red chillies and fry 40 seconds until the dals turn biscuit gold.
Add 0.25 tsp hing and 2 sprigs of curry leaves and let them crackle for 15 seconds until the leaves turn glossy and translucent.
Add the okra rounds, toss well, and roast uncovered on medium for 12 to 14 minutes, stirring every 3 minutes, until the rounds shrink, dry out and brown at the edges.
Sprinkle 2 tsp sambar powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp salt and toss for 2 minutes so the spices toast onto the okra.
Switch off the heat and fold in 0.33 cup grated coconut, letting the residual warmth soften it without browning; serve warm.
tips: The dals must stay golden, not brown; pull the pan off the heat for a few seconds if they colour too fast.
Coconut always goes in off the heat in a poriyal; cooked coconut loses its fresh sweetness.
A drizzle of raw gingelly oil over the finished poriyal is an old Thanjavur flourish worth trying.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as part of a South Indian lunch beside sambar rice or rasam rice with appalam; it also pairs surprisingly well inside a curd rice bowl.

variations.name: Gujarati Dry Bhindi
variations.description: Bhinda nu shaak with the Kathiyawadi sweet-heat signature: okra tossed in a sesame-flecked masala where jaggery melts against chilli and hing-scented oil. A final besan dusting toasts onto the pods, adding a savoury crumb that keeps everything perfectly dry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Gujarat's own oilseed pressed the slow way; it fries the besan coating golden without any greasiness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The gentle gol sweetness that defines a Kathiyawadi shaak, melting into the chilli-sesame masala

steps: Wash, dry completely and cut 500 g okra into 1-inch pieces; dry-roast 3 tbsp besan in a small pan on low for 3 to 4 minutes, stirring constantly, until it darkens a shade and smells nutty, then set aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a wide kadhai on medium, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then add 0.25 tsp hing and 1 tbsp sesame seeds and let them pop for 15 seconds.
Add the okra, toss in the seeded oil, and fry uncovered on medium-high for 10 to 12 minutes, turning every 3 minutes, until dry, browned and no longer sticky.
Lower the heat and season with 2 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp salt, tossing for 1 minute so nothing scorches.
Sprinkle the roasted besan and 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder over the okra and toss for 2 to 3 minutes; the besan will toast into a savoury crumb while the jaggery glazes the pods.
Finish off the heat with 1 tbsp lemon juice tossed through, and rest 2 minutes so the sweet, sour and nutty notes knit together.
tips: Pre-roasting the besan is essential; raw besan added to the pan tastes chalky and steals the crunch.
Jaggery burns fast, so it always follows the besan and gets no more than 3 minutes on heat.
For a true Kathiyawadi table, serve with a green chilli fried whole in the same oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulka rotli, kadhi and steamed rice as a Gujarati thali corner, or with bajra rotla and a spoon of white butter in winter.

variations.name: Chhattisgarhi Dry Bhindi
variations.description: Borrowing the rice-country logic of Chhattisgarh, the okra here is tossed in seasoned rice flour before hitting the pan, so each piece fries up with a delicate, crackly crust. Garlic, dried chillies and a mustard-oil tempering keep it rustic and firmly of the region.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Central-eastern village kitchens fry in pungent mustard oil; it crisps the rice-flour crust with a savoury sharpness

steps: Wash 500 g okra, dry meticulously, and slice into 0.5-inch rounds; the drier the rounds, the crisper the crust.
Toss the rounds with 4 tbsp rice flour, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt until each piece wears a thin, even dusting; shake off the excess in a sieve.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a wide pan until it just smokes, lower to medium-high, and lay the coated okra in a single layer; fry undisturbed for 3 minutes until the underside sets golden.
Turn and continue frying for 8 to 10 minutes, tossing every 2 to 3 minutes, until the rice-flour crust is crisp and speckled deep brown all over; lift onto a plate.

Add the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then fry 6 sliced garlic cloves and 3 torn dried red chillies for 40 seconds until the garlic is golden and the chillies glossy.
Return the crisp okra to the pan with 1 tsp salt, toss on high for 1 minute, then finish off the heat with 1 tsp amchur and 3 tbsp chopped coriander leaves.
tips: Coat the okra just before frying; if it sits, the rice flour draws moisture and turns gummy.
Do not cover the pan at any point, and serve within 15 minutes; the crust is at its crackly best fresh.
The same rice-flour method rescues slightly older, larger okra that would otherwise be fibrous.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a crunchy side with dal-rice or, the local way, beside a bowl of hot bore-basi style rice and a raw mango pickle; it also works as a beer-time snack with lemon wedges.

variations.name: Classic Garlic Beetroot Paratha
variations.description: Grated beetroot is sauteed with golden garlic until its earthiness turns sweet and jammy, then wrapped in khapli wheat for a paratha that blushes fuchsia at every tear. Cumin and garam masala keep it firmly savoury despite the beet's natural sugar. It is as striking on the plate as it is gentle on the palate — a favourite for lunchboxes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The emmer dough takes on a pink marbling from the beet filling without turning gummy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Sauteing beetroot in bilona ghee caramelises its sugars and rounds off the earthiness

ingredients.name: Beetroot
ingredients.note: Peeled and finely grated

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 3/4 cup water into a soft, pliable dough; cover and rest for 20 minutes.
Grate 2 medium peeled beetroots on the fine side of the grater, then squeeze the shreds firmly in a cloth, reserving the juice for the dough of your next batch or a drink.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then fry 8 minced garlic cloves and 2 minced green chillies for about a minute until the garlic smells sweet and turns pale gold.
Add the squeezed beetroot with 1/2 tsp red chilli powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric powder and 1/2 tsp salt and saute on medium for 5-6 minutes until the shreds soften, darken and look jammy rather than wet.
Stir in 1/2 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp amchur and 2 tbsp chopped coriander, cook one more minute, then spread the filling on a plate to cool completely.
Stuff 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp of the beet mixture each, pinch the pleats closed and roll gently into 6-7 inch rounds, dusting with atta as the pink shows through.

Roast on a medium tava for about a minute per bare side, then a minute per side with 1/2 tsp Anveshan Ghee until crisp, with the pink interior peeking through golden-brown spots, roughly 4 minutes per paratha.
tips: Squeezing the grated beet is non-negotiable; its juice content is deceptively high and will shred your dough.
The reserved beet juice can replace part of the kneading water next time for an all-pink dough.
Cook the filling until genuinely jammy; underdone beet stays crunchy and tastes raw-earthy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with mint-coriander raita and papad; the pink-and-green plate practically markets itself to reluctant vegetable eaters.

variations.name: Bengali Garlic Beetroot Paratha
variations.description: Bengal cooks beetroot into its winter chorchoris with mustard oil and panch-style whole spices, and this paratha borrows that exact playbook. Kalonji and green chilli crackled in pungent kachi ghani oil frame the sweet beet, while garlic slices fried till chestnut-brown add crunch and depth. A pinch of sugar, as always in Bengal, ties it together.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Its wasabi-like pungency is the classic Bengali counterpoint to sweet root vegetables

ingredients.name: Beetroot
ingredients.note: Grated and squeezed dry

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: Thinly sliced, not minced, for crisp brown chips through the filling

steps: Combine 2 cups khapli atta, 1/2 tsp salt and 1/4 tsp kalonji, then knead with 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and roughly 3/4 cup water into a smooth dough; rest 20 minutes under a damp cloth.

Bring 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to a light smoke in a kadhai, ease the flame down, and fry 8 thinly sliced garlic cloves for about 2 minutes until they turn crisp and chestnut-brown; lift half out to a plate for later.
Into the same oil crackle the remaining 1/2 tsp kalonji for 20 seconds, add 3 slit green chillies and 2 tsp grated ginger, and sizzle for 30 seconds more.

Tumble in the squeezed grated beetroot from 2 medium beets with 1/4 tsp turmeric powder, 1/2 tsp sugar and 1/2 tsp salt; cook on medium for 6 minutes, stirring, until dry, glossy and deeply pink-brown.
Mix in 1 tsp roasted cumin powder and the reserved garlic chips, cool the filling fully, then stuff it into 8 dough balls at 2 tbsp apiece, sealing the seams well.

Roll each into a 6-7 inch round and roast on a medium tava, a minute per plain side, then a minute per side with 1/2 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until blistered deep gold with the mustard aroma rising, about 4 minutes each.
tips: Fry the garlic slices to true chestnut, not blond; the bitter-sweet chips are the signature texture of this version.
The pinch of sugar mirrors how Bengali chorchoris treat sweet vegetables — seasoning, not dessert.
If the mustard oil pungency feels strong, smoke it a few seconds longer during the first fry; heat mellows it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a spoon of kasundi, cucumber slices and dal-er bora if you are feeling ambitious; sweet mishti doi closes the meal properly.

variations.name: Kerala Garlic Beetroot Paratha
variations.description: Kerala's beetroot thoran is the template here: grated beet steamed open with coconut, garlic, curry leaves and mustard seeds, all glossed with wood-pressed coconut oil. The coconut lightens the beet's density and adds a tropical sweetness that needs no sugar at all. The paratha tastes like the thoran and the Malabar porotta had a very happy child.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Wholegrain sturdiness that holds the moist coconut-beet thoran filling neatly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed from copra, it gives the filling its unmistakable Kerala fragrance

ingredients.name: Beetroot
ingredients.note: Finely grated and squeezed

steps: Knead a soft dough from 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and about 3/4 cup water; rest it for 20 minutes while the thoran-style filling cooks.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil on medium and pop 3/4 tsp mustard seeds completely, about 30 seconds, then add 12 curry leaves, 6 crushed garlic cloves, 4 sliced shallots and 2 chopped green chillies and fry for 90 seconds until fragrant and just golden.
Add the squeezed grated beetroot from 2 medium beets with 1/4 tsp turmeric powder and 1/2 tsp salt; cover and cook on low for 4 minutes so the beet steams tender in its own moisture.
Uncover, stir in 1/2 cup fresh grated coconut and cook another 3 minutes, tossing, until the mixture is dry, fluffy and vividly magenta; cool it completely on a plate.
Fill 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp of the thoran mixture each, gather and pinch the seams, and roll softly into 6-7 inch rounds.

Cook on a medium tava for about a minute per dry side, then crisp each side with 1/2 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil until golden-freckled and smelling faintly of toasted coconut, around 4 minutes per paratha.
tips: Covering the pan for the first few minutes steams the beet tender exactly as a thoran does; skipping it leaves crunchy shreds.
The coconut must be added late and toasted dry, or its milkiness makes the filling paste-like.
Frozen coconut works if squeezed well; desiccated coconut does not, as it turns sawdusty against the beet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a sharp lime pickle and cooling moru (spiced buttermilk); for a fuller meal, add a fried papadam and a wedge of steamed nendran banana.

variations.name: Goan Garlic Beetroot Paratha
variations.description: Kokum, Goa's beloved sour fruit, is the twist: its floral tang slices straight through beetroot's sweetness the way it does in a Goan solkadhi. Garlic is fried generously in coconut oil, and a touch of crushed black pepper nods to the spice-trading coast. The result is a sweet-sour-pungent paratha unlike anything north of the Konkan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its mild wheat sweetness lets the kokum's sour perfume stay in focus

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: The Konkan coast's cooking fat, wood-pressed so the coconut aroma survives the tava

ingredients.name: Beetroot
ingredients.note: Grated fine and squeezed dry

ingredients.name: Kokum petals
ingredients.note: Soaked in warm water and chopped fine; the defining Goan souring agent

steps: Soak 4 kokum petals in 3 tbsp warm water for 15 minutes until soft and wine-dark, then chop them fine, reserving the soaking liquid.
Meanwhile knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and roughly 3/4 cup water into a supple dough; rest 20 minutes covered.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil on medium, crackle 3/4 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then fry 8 minced garlic cloves and 2 minced green chillies for about a minute until the garlic is pale gold and sweet-smelling.
Add the squeezed grated beetroot from 2 medium beets with 1/4 tsp turmeric powder and 1/2 tsp salt, and saute on medium for 5 minutes until soft and jammy.

Stir in the chopped kokum with 1 tbsp of its soaking liquid and 3/4 tsp crushed black pepper; cook 2 more minutes until the tang and sweetness fuse and the pan looks dry, then cool with 2 tbsp coriander folded through.

Stuff 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp filling apiece, seal firmly and roll into 6-7 inch rounds, then roast on a medium tava with 1/2 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil per side until crisply bronzed, about 4 minutes per paratha.
tips: Add the kokum only after the beet has softened; cooked too long, its perfume fades into plain sourness.
Taste the filling before sealing — kokum batches vary wildly in sourness, and a pinch of extra salt balances a sharp one.
Dried amchur is an emergency substitute, but it loses the floral note that makes this version special.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with chilled solkadhi to double down on the kokum theme, or a simple coconut-garlic chutney and sliced raw mango in season.

variations.name: Punjabi Garlic Beetroot Paratha
variations.description: The Punjabi treatment turns the beet filling into something worthy of a Ludhiana winter breakfast: ajwain in the dough, ginger-garlic sizzled in ghee, kasuri methi and anardana in the filling, and a bold butter finish. The beet's sweetness against fenugreek's savoury bitterness is a surprisingly classic pairing. Hearty, warming and unmistakably northern.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Strong emmer gluten shoulders a moist root-vegetable filling the Punjabi way — rolled thick

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: From tempering to tava to the final drizzle, ghee is the through-line of this dhaba-style paratha

ingredients.name: Beetroot
ingredients.note: Grated and squeezed hard

ingredients.name: Ajwain seeds
ingredients.note: Kneaded into the dough, where the tava's heat toasts them fully

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 3/4 tsp ajwain, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 3/4 cup water into a soft, elastic dough; rest it 20 minutes so the ajwain perfumes the crumb.
Melt 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium heat and fry 8 minced garlic cloves with 1 tbsp grated ginger for about 90 seconds until golden and toasty.
Add the squeezed beetroot from 2 medium beets and 1/2 tsp salt, and bhuno on medium for 6-7 minutes, scraping the pan, until the shreds collapse into a thick, dark-pink masala.
Crush in 1 tbsp kasuri methi, then add 3/4 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp anardana powder and 2 minced green chillies; cook 1 more minute and cool the filling completely.
Stuff 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp filling each and roll into thickish 6-inch rounds, the sturdy style a Punjabi tandoor would approve of.

Roast on a medium tava, about 90 seconds per plain side, then a minute per side with 1/2 tsp Anveshan Ghee, pressing the edges until deep brown and crisp, roughly 5 minutes per paratha, and top each with a curl of white butter.
tips: Bhuno-ing the beet properly — until it darkens and smells roasted — is what separates this from a boiled-vegetable paratha.
Anardana keeps the tang dry; lemon juice would loosen the filling and fight the rolling pin.
These parathas love a hot tava but a patient flame; rushing on high heat browns the outside before the thick centre warms through.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve dhaba-style with dahi, a stab of aam ka achaar and a glass of namkeen lassi; winter mornings call for a mooli salad alongside.

variations.name: Classic Masala Dal Paratha
variations.description: A thrifty North Indian classic that turns leftover chana dal into a spiced, crumbly stuffing scented with garam masala, ginger and bloomed cumin. The dal is cooked soft, then dried out in ghee so it packs like damp sand and never leaks. Ghee-roasted khapli crust plus earthy dal makes it a complete protein-rich meal in one flatbread.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: High-fibre emmer pairs with dal for a genuinely sustaining paratha

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Drying the dal in bilona ghee gives the filling its rich, halwai-style aroma

steps: Rinse 0.75 cup chana dal, then pressure-cook it with 1.5 cups water, 0.25 tsp turmeric powder and 0.25 tsp salt for 3 whistles until fully soft but not mushy; drain thoroughly in a colander for 10 minutes.
Meanwhile knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 0.75 tsp salt and roughly 0.75 cup water into a soft, pliable dough; rest it covered for 15 minutes.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium flame and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then fry grated 1 inch ginger and 2 minced green chillies for 30 seconds until fragrant.

Add the drained dal with 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp garam masala and 0.25 tsp salt, mashing coarsely with the back of the spoon, and cook 4 to 5 minutes until the mixture is dry and holds a shape; stir in 0.75 tsp amchur off the heat and cool fully.
Divide the dough into 8 balls and the filling into 8 portions of about 2 tbsp; cup each ball, seat a portion inside, pleat closed and roll gently into a 6-inch round.

Roast on a hot tava at medium-high for about 1 minute per side until brown spots appear, then brush both sides with the remaining 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee across the batch and crisp 30 seconds more per side.
tips: Drain the cooked dal really well; even a little cooking liquid makes the filling paste-like and hard to roll.
Mash the dal only coarsely so the stuffing keeps a pleasant grainy bite.
Both dough and filling can be made a day ahead; assembled parathas also freeze well between sheets of parchment.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thick curd, a sharp lemon pickle and sliced onions; a bowl of plain kadhi alongside turns it into a proper lunch.

variations.name: Bihari Masala Dal Paratha
variations.description: Bihar's answer to the stuffed paratha, close cousin to the dal puri of Chhath season: chana dal ground with garlic, fennel and fiery dried chilli, bound in dough kneaded with pungent mustard oil. The kachi ghani sharpness against the sweet fennel is unmistakably Bihari. It is rustic, sturdy travel food that tastes even better at room temperature.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Hardy wholegrain in the spirit of Bihar's litti-and-sattu tradition

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: The kneading fat and tempering fat of every Bihari kitchen worth its salt

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A ghee gloss at the end, just as dal puris get on festival days

steps: Pressure-cook 0.75 cup rinsed chana dal with 1.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric powder and 0.25 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft; drain very well and let it steam-dry in the colander for 10 minutes.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil, 0.5 tsp ajwain, 0.75 tsp salt and close to 0.75 cup water into a firm-soft dough; rest 15 minutes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai until it lightly smokes, drop to medium, and sizzle 1.5 tsp fennel seeds with 3 torn dried red chillies for 25 seconds until the fennel turns golden.

Add 5 minced garlic cloves and grated 1 inch ginger, fry 45 seconds until the garlic edges colour, then add the drained dal with 0.25 tsp salt and cook 5 minutes, mashing coarsely, until the mixture is dry and crumbly like damp sand; cool completely.
Split the dough into 8 balls, stuff each with about 2 tbsp of the dal mixture, pinch the seams shut and roll patiently into a 6-inch round, sealing any small tears with a dab of dry atta.
Cook on a medium-hot tava for around 75 seconds per side until deeply freckled, then finish with the 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee brushed thin across the batch and toast 30 seconds per side until crisp.
tips: Fennel is the soul of Bihari dal stuffing; toast it until golden but never brown.
Smoking the mustard oil once tames its rawness while keeping the trademark pungency.
These keep for a day without refrigeration, which is why they are Bihar's favourite train journey food.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with aloo chokha, a roasted tomato chutney and green chillies, exactly as a Bihari household would on a Sunday morning.

variations.name: Rajasthani Masala Dal Paratha
variations.description: Drawing on the dal of dal-baati, this desert version loads the stuffing with a ghee-fried chilli-garlic paste, kasuri methi and hing, flavours built to carry without fresh produce. The paratha is rolled thick and slow-roasted so the crust turns almost baati-like. Finished with more ghee, because in Rajasthan there is no other way.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its dense, nutty crumb evokes a baati crust when slow-roasted

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rajasthani dal dishes are defined by their unapologetic ghee tadka

steps: Cook 0.75 cup rinsed chana dal in a pressure cooker with 1.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric powder and 0.25 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft right through; drain thoroughly.
Soak 4 dried red chillies in 3 tbsp hot water for 10 minutes and pound with 6 garlic cloves into a coarse red paste.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 0.75 tsp salt and about 0.75 cup water into a firm, smooth dough and rest it for 15 minutes.

Melt 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat, add 0.25 tsp hing, then fry the chilli-garlic paste for 2 minutes until the ghee stains brick-red; add the drained dal, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 0.25 tsp salt and cook 5 minutes, mashing coarsely, until crumbly-dry. Off the heat, work in 2 tbsp crushed kasuri methi and 0.75 tsp amchur, then cool.
Divide the dough into 6 balls for thick parathas, stuff each with about 2.5 tbsp filling, seal firmly and roll into stout 5.5-inch rounds.

Roast on a medium-low tava for 2 minutes per side so the thick discs cook through, then raise the flame, bathe both sides with the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee across the batch, and crisp 45 seconds per side until the crust turns deep gold.
tips: Fry the chilli-garlic paste until the ghee separates; undercooked paste tastes raw and harsh against the dal.
Thick rolling plus a slow first roast is what creates the baati-like crust; do not rush the tava.
The filling keeps for three days refrigerated and doubles as a stuffing for baati or bharwa mirchi.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a katori of chaas, garlic chutney and a spoon of churma on the side for the full dal-baati-churma echo.

variations.name: Gujarati Masala Dal Paratha
variations.description: Modelled on the sweet-sour dal of a Gujarati thali, the stuffing balances jaggery's caramel warmth against lemon and green chilli, with sesame adding nutty crunch. The dough is kneaded with wood-pressed groundnut oil, thepla-style, so the parathas stay soft for hours. Every bite lands sweet first, then tangy, then gently hot, in proper Gujarati order.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: A soft-yet-strong wrapper that stays pliable, thepla-fashion, for tiffins

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Chemical-free jaggery gives the dal its authentic Gujarati sweet spine

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The everyday wood-pressed fat of Gujarat, from vaghar to tava

steps: Pressure-cook 0.75 cup rinsed chana dal with 1.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric powder and 0.25 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft; drain well and let it sit 10 minutes to dry.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, 0.75 tsp salt and nearly 0.75 cup water into a soft, smooth dough; rest under a damp cloth for 15 minutes.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium flame, pop 0.75 tsp mustard seeds for 20 seconds, then add 10 curry leaves, 3 chopped green chillies and 1.5 tbsp sesame seeds and fry 30 seconds until the sesame turns pale gold.

Add the drained dal with 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.25 tsp salt, mash coarsely, and cook 4 to 5 minutes until the jaggery melts through and the mixture turns dry and glossy; brighten with 1.5 tbsp lemon juice off the heat and cool completely.
Shape the dough into 8 balls, tuck about 2 tbsp of the sweet-sour dal into each, seal the pleats and roll gently to a 6-inch round.

Cook on a medium tava for about 75 seconds per side until golden-spotted, keeping the flame moderate since jaggery browns fast, then drizzle the last 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over the batch and crisp each side 30 seconds.
tips: Add the lemon juice only off the heat; boiling it dulls the tang the jaggery needs for balance.
Keep the tava at medium throughout, as the jaggery in the filling can scorch before the crust cooks.
These taste wonderful at room temperature, making them ideal Gujarati-style travel and tiffin fare.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with chhundo, a bowl of plain curd and fried green chillies dusted with salt, thali-style; masala chai on the side is compulsory.

variations.name: Tamil Masala Dal Paratha
variations.description: The dal here is treated like a paruppu usili: cooked chana dal crumbled into a gingelly-oil tadka of mustard, urad dal, curry leaves and red chilli, with a whisper of hing. The result is a dry, savoury, faintly smoky stuffing that Tamil Brahmin kitchens would recognise instantly. Sesame oil on the tava completes the nallennai signature.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Wholegrain emmer takes to gingelly oil like a well-seasoned dosa kal

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed nallennai is the defining aroma of a Tamil usili tadka

steps: Pressure-cook 0.75 cup rinsed chana dal with 1.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric powder and 0.25 tsp salt for 3 whistles until tender; drain completely and crumble the dal with a fork while still warm.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, 0.75 tsp salt and about 0.75 cup water into a supple dough; rest it 15 minutes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadhai over medium heat, fry 1 tbsp urad dal for about 90 seconds until biscuit-gold, then pop 1 tsp mustard seeds for 20 seconds.

Add 3 torn dried red chillies, 15 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp hing, let them crackle 15 seconds, then tip in the crumbled dal with 0.25 tsp salt and roast 5 minutes, tossing, until dry and sandy; finish with 0.75 tsp coarsely crushed black pepper and cool fully.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, fill each with roughly 2 tbsp of the usili-style dal, seal the openings and roll softly to a 6-inch circle.

Roast on a hot tava for about 1 minute per side at medium-high until brown-freckled, then trickle the remaining 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil over the batch and toast each side another 30 seconds until crisp and aromatic.
tips: Crumble the dal while warm; cold chana dal firms up and resists breaking into the sandy usili texture.
The urad dal must reach a true golden colour for its nutty crunch; pale dal tastes raw inside the filling.
A pinch of extra hing over the filling just before stuffing deepens the classic Tam-Brahm aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and a tumbler of neer mor (spiced thin buttermilk); alongside a simple vetha kuzhambu it becomes a full Tamil feast.

variations.name: Classic Masala Matar Paratha
variations.description: A winter favourite across North India: sweet green peas steamed, coarsely crushed and seasoned with ginger, garam masala and roasted cumin, then sealed inside nutty khapli dough. The filling stays jade-green and slightly chunky so every bite pops with pea sweetness against the spice. A ghee roast turns the crust golden and fragrant.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The gently sweet emmer grain is a natural partner for green peas, echoing their flavour in the crust

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The pea masala is sauteed and the paratha roasted in bilona ghee, layering its caramel aroma twice over

steps: Knead 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 1 cup water into a soft, springy dough; rest it covered for 20 minutes.
Steam 2.5 cups green peas for 6-7 minutes until they crush easily between your fingers, then pulse or mash them coarse, not to a paste.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then fry 1 inch of grated ginger and 2 minced green chillies for 45 seconds until fragrant.

Add the crushed peas with 1 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp amchur and 0.5 tsp salt, and saute 3-4 minutes until the mixture turns dry and clumps together. Cool fully, then mix in 3 tbsp chopped coriander.
Divide the dough into 8 balls and the pea masala into 8 portions of about 2.5 tbsp. Stuff each ball, gather and pinch the edges shut, and roll gently into a 6 inch round.
Roast on a medium-hot tava for about 2 minutes per side, brushing on the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, until golden-brown spots deepen and the surface puffs in patches.
Rest the parathas in a cloth-lined box for 2 minutes so the crust settles to a tender crisp before serving.
tips: Saute the pea mash until visibly dry; peas hold hidden moisture that will otherwise tear the dough while rolling.
Frozen peas work beautifully here and need only 4 minutes of steaming.
Amchur brightens the pea sweetness; a squeeze of lime into the cooled filling does the same job.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thick curd, a sharp green-chilli pickle and hot adrak chai for a proper winter-morning spread.

variations.name: Bengali Masala Matar Paratha
variations.description: Inspired by Bengal's iconic koraishutir kochuri, this version cooks the pea filling in pungent kachhi ghani mustard oil with ginger and a whisper of sugar. The mustard sharpness against sweet winter peas is a beloved Kolkata pairing, and roasting in the same oil deepens it further. A brush of ghee at the end makes peace between the two.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Where kochuris use maida, this wholegrain emmer keeps the same soft bite with far more substance

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Kachhi ghani mustard oil against sweet peas is the classic koraishuti flavour of a Kolkata winter

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing brush of ghee mellows the mustard punch into festive richness

steps: Rub 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and 1 tsp salt into 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, then knead with about 1 cup water into a smooth, supple dough. Rest 20 minutes under a damp cloth.
Steam 2.5 cups green peas for 6 minutes until soft, then grind them coarsely with 1.5 inches of ginger and 3 green chillies, keeping the paste rough and textured.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to a light smoke in a kadhai, lower the flame and crackle 1 tsp nigella seeds for 20 seconds.

Add the pea paste with 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp sugar and 0.5 tsp salt, and stir over medium heat for 4-5 minutes until the mixture leaves the sides of the pan in a dry mass. Cool completely.
Portion the dough into 8 balls and the pea filling into 8 mounds of 2.5 tbsp. Stuff, seal the pleats into a topknot and roll softly into 6 inch rounds.
Griddle on medium heat for roughly 2 minutes per side, trickling the remaining 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil around the edges, until amber-brown blisters spread over both faces.
Brush each hot paratha with a little of the 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee so the pungent and the sweet settle into balance.
tips: Grind the peas with ginger and chilli in one go; the aromatics distribute far more evenly than when mixed later.
Letting the mustard oil smoke once and cool briefly removes its raw edge without losing pungency.
The filling is a straight koraishutir kochuri stuffing; leftover portions deep-fry into wonderful kochuris.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve Kolkata-style with a light aloor dom or simply tomato-khejur chutney and a hot cup of milky cha.

variations.name: Malwa Masala Matar Paratha
variations.description: In the Malwa belt of Madhya Pradesh, crunch is king, so this pea filling gets coarsely crushed roasted peanuts and popped coriander seeds folded through it. Roasted in wood-pressed groundnut oil, the paratha tastes doubly nutty, with the peas supplying sweetness between crunchy bites. It is hearty farmhand food from India's wheat bowl.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Grown-from-heritage-seed wheat honours Malwa's identity as the country's wheat heartland

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil reinforces the peanut crunch in the filling with its clean roasted flavour

steps: Knead 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and roughly 1 cup water into a pliant dough; cover and rest for 20 minutes.
Steam 2.5 cups green peas for 6-7 minutes until tender, then crush them coarsely with a masher, leaving plenty of half-broken peas for texture.

Warm 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat and sizzle 1.5 tsp crushed coriander seeds for 30 seconds, then fry 6 minced garlic cloves and 2 chopped green chillies for a minute until golden.

Add the crushed peas, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt, and saute 3-4 minutes until dry. Off the heat, fold in 0.5 cup crushed roasted peanuts and 3 tbsp chopped coriander, then cool fully.
Divide dough into 8 balls, tuck 2.5 tbsp of the peanut-pea filling into each, twist the tops closed and roll into 6 inch rounds with gentle strokes so peanut bits do not pierce through.
Roast on a medium tava for about 2 minutes per side, painting on the remaining 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, until crisp golden-brown patches bubble up across the crust.
Rest 2 minutes before cutting so the chunky filling firms enough to hold neat wedges.
tips: Add the peanuts off the heat; frying them inside the wet filling softens their crunch.
Crush coriander seeds in a mortar for the citrusy pop that powder cannot replicate.
These sturdy parathas hold their crunch for hours, perfect for tiffins and road trips.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve Indore-style with sweetened dahi, a spoon of spicy peanut chutney and a scatter of sev over everything.

variations.name: Rajasthani Masala Matar Paratha
variations.description: Desert kitchens season sweet peas with a coarse paste of soaked mathania-style dried red chillies and garlic, fried in ghee until the fat runs red. Ajwain in the dough and a lavish final ghee pour make this a bold, keep-well bread in the tradition of Rajasthani travel food. Fiery, garlicky and gorgeous against the green peas.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: A hardy heritage grain for a hardy desert bread that must survive a day's journey unspoiled

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rajasthan finishes its breads with poured ghee, and bilona ghee gives that ritual its full nutty glory

steps: Knead 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp ajwain, 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 1 cup water into a slightly firm dough; rest for 20 minutes.
Soak 4 dried red chillies in hot water for 15 minutes, then grind them with 8 garlic cloves into a coarse brick-red paste.
Steam 2.5 cups green peas for 6-7 minutes until soft and mash them roughly with a fork.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium flame and fry the chilli-garlic paste for 2-3 minutes until the ghee stains red and separates at the edges. Add the mashed peas, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp amchur and 0.5 tsp salt, cook 3 minutes until dry, then cool and mix in 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
Portion into 8 dough balls and 8 mounds of about 2.5 tbsp filling. Stuff, seal the pleats securely and roll into slightly thick 6 inch rounds.
Roast over a medium flame for a patient 2-3 minutes per side, spooning over the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, until the crust turns a burnished red-brown and crisps at the rim.
Serve hot, or cool fully and stack for travel; like all Marwari breads they keep beautifully for a day.
tips: Soaked-and-ground dried chillies give colour and rounded heat that chilli powder cannot match.
Swap half the chillies for Kashmiri ones to keep the dramatic red while dialling down the fire.
Fry the paste until the ghee visibly separates; underdone chilli paste tastes raw through the peas.
variations.servingSuggestion: Eat with lehsun ki chutney, a slab of white butter and a tumbler of jeera chhaas, the classic Marwari trio.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Masala Matar Paratha
variations.description: Peas seasoned the Puneri way, with smoky goda masala, toasted sesame and a soft back-note of unrefined jaggery, all sauteed in wood-pressed groundnut oil. The sweet-earthy spice blend flatters green peas the way it does a classic matar usal. Every bite lands warm, faintly sweet and quietly smoky.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer's rustic crumb recalls the wholegrain bhakris that anchor a Maharashtrian thali

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The Deccan's everyday wood-pressed oil crisps this paratha with a gentle roasted-nut finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A pinch of unrefined jaggery is the traditional counterweight to goda masala's smokiness

steps: Work 2.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil into a dough with about 1 cup water; knead 7 minutes and rest 20 minutes under a damp cloth.
Steam 2.5 cups green peas for 6-7 minutes until tender and crush them coarsely, keeping some peas whole for pops of sweetness.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium, toast 1 tbsp white sesame seeds for 30 seconds until they turn pale gold and pop, then fry 1 inch of grated ginger and 2 chopped green chillies for 45 seconds.

Add the crushed peas with 2 tsp goda masala, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.5 tsp salt; saute over low heat for 3-4 minutes until the mixture dries and smells smoky-sweet. Cool, then fold in 3 tbsp chopped coriander.
Shape 8 dough balls, cradle 2.5 tbsp of filling in each, pleat the edges shut and roll gently into 6 inch rounds.
Cook on a medium tava about 2 minutes per side, brushing with the remaining 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, until the crust freckles deep gold and the sesame flecks toast fragrant.
Rest briefly under a cloth; goda masala's stone-flower aroma blooms noticeably in those two minutes.
tips: Marry the goda masala with the peas over the lowest flame; high heat turns its delicate spices bitter.
Jaggery here should whisper, not shout; 1.5 tsp balances without making the filling sweet.
The filling doubles as a quick matar usal with a squeeze of lime if you make extra.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with green-chilli thecha, a bowl of mattha and a wedge of lime, the way a Pune lunch home would.

variations.name: Classic Masala Onion Paratha
variations.description: The bolder sibling of the plain onion paratha: the squeezed onions are dressed in a full masala wardrobe — garam masala, coriander powder, roasted cumin and amchur — so the filling tastes like the topping of a perfect pav bhaji tucked into wheat. Ghee-roasting caramelises the spiced onion right through the khapli crust.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer's forgiving stretch rolls smoothly over a heavily spiced raw-onion filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The masala blooms against the hot tava only when carried in a proper ghee film

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 1/2 tsp salt and about 3/4 cup water into a soft, non-sticky dough; cover and rest 15 minutes.
Chop 3 medium onions very finely, toss with 1/2 tsp salt, stand 10 minutes and squeeze hard in a muslin cloth until the shreds feel nearly dry.

Dress the onions with 1 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1/2 tsp amchur, 3/4 tsp red chilli powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric and 3 tbsp chopped coriander, mixing until every shred is coated russet.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, cup each around 2 tbsp of the masala onion, pinch the pleats firmly shut and roll gently into a 6-inch round, dusting with atta as needed.

Roast on a medium-hot tava for 1 minute until the base sets, flip, brush 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee on each side and cook about 3 minutes total, pressing the edges, until both faces carry deep golden-brown patches and the spices smell toasted.
Serve in cooking order — the spiced onion softens the crust faster than most fillings, so hot off the tava is best.
tips: Use only roasted, not raw, cumin powder here; the filling is never cooked long enough to tame raw spice dust.
Mix the masala into the onions just before stuffing — spiced onions weep within minutes and sog the dough.
A quarter-teaspoon of kasuri methi crushed in at the end deepens the masala noticeably.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with cool boondi raita and a wedge of lime; a smear of green chutney inside a folded quarter turns leftovers into a terrific roadside-style roll.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Masala Onion Paratha
variations.description: The kanda-bhaji flavour map redrawn as a paratha: onions tossed with smoky goda masala, crushed roasted peanuts and a garlicky tempering in wood-pressed groundnut oil. Goda's stone-flower and caramel notes make this the most fragrant onion paratha of the lot.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its rustic wholegrain body suits the Deccan table where bhakri once ruled

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Kanda bhaji's home fat — wood-pressed peanut oil doubles the filling's nutty theme

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A single spoon in the dough keeps the crumb short while peanut oil rules the tava

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 1/2 tsp salt and roughly 3/4 cup water into a soft dough; rest 15 minutes under a damp cloth.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai, fry 4 sliced garlic cloves and 2 chopped green chillies for 1 minute until the garlic edges gild, then add 3 thin-sliced onions with 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1/2 tsp salt and sweat 6 minutes until soft and light gold.
Stir 2 tsp goda masala through the hot onions and cook 30 seconds to bloom the spice, then cool completely and fold in 3 tbsp coarsely crushed roasted peanuts and 3 tbsp chopped coriander.
Stuff 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp of the goda-onion mixture each, seal the gathers and roll softly into 6-inch rounds.
Roast on a medium tava, drizzling 1/2 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil per side, about 3 minutes per paratha until both faces blister nut-brown and the goda aroma turns smoky-sweet.
Rest each round a minute so the peanut rubble settles into the jammy onion before slicing.
tips: Bloom the goda masala in the hot onions for those 30 seconds — unbloomed goda tastes dusty rather than caramel-smoky.
Crush the peanuts pebble-coarse and add them only after cooling, or they soften and vanish.
The cooked filling holds 2 days refrigerated; it also makes a superb topping for jowar bhakri.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with dry lasun chutney and a glass of salted mattha; in true Maharashtrian style, add a raw onion quarter and a lime wedge to the plate.

variations.name: Rajasthani Masala Onion Paratha
variations.description: Marwar's pyaaz kachori spirit in paratha form: onions cooked down with whole dried red chillies, coriander and fennel seeds bloomed in ghee, finished with amchur and a pinch of asafoetida. The fennel-forward, fiercely tangy masala is unmistakably Rajasthani street fare.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Hardy emmer stands in beautifully for the rugged wheats of desert griddles

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Marwari cooking blooms its whole spices in ghee first — and roasts in it after

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 1/2 tsp salt and about 3/4 cup water into a firm-soft dough and rest it 15 minutes.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai over low heat and bloom 3 broken dried red chillies, 2 tsp coriander seeds and 1.5 tsp fennel seeds for about 90 seconds until deeply fragrant; lift out and crush coarsely in a mortar.
In the same ghee, drop 1/4 tsp asafoetida, then add 3 finely chopped onions with 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1/2 tsp salt; cook 7 minutes over medium heat until soft and golden at the edges.
Stir the crushed spice rubble and 1 tsp amchur through the onions, cook 1 minute more until the masala clings dry, then cool fully with 2 tbsp chopped coriander folded in.

Stuff 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp of the kachori-style filling each, seal and roll to 6-inch rounds, then roast on a medium tava with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee brushed per side for about 3 minutes each until russet-spotted and crisp.
Cool 2 minutes before serving; like pyaaz kachori, the fennel flavour blooms as the filling settles.
tips: Bloom-then-crush is the Marwari method — ground fennel from a packet cannot match the burst of cracked bloomed seeds.
Cook the filling until it looks dry and clumping; wet onion masala breaches seams on the tava.
Roasted an extra minute per side, these keep half a day unrefrigerated — proper desert travel food.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with fiery lehsun ki chutney and a katori of kadhi for dipping; a few slices of raw onion with lime complete the Marwari roadside plate.

variations.name: Hyderabadi Masala Onion Paratha
variations.description: A nod to the Nizami kitchen: birista-style browned onions folded with saffron steeped in warm milk, mint and a whisper of garam masala — the flavour spine of a good Hyderabadi biryani, sealed inside khapli wheat. Golden, perfumed and quietly regal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: A wholesome stand-in for the sheermal-soft breads of the old city

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Onions brown into true birista only in patient, medium-hot ghee

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Steeped strands gild the browned onions the way saffron milk crowns a dum biryani

steps: Steep 1/4 tsp Anveshan Saffron strands in 2 tbsp warm milk for 10 minutes until the milk turns deep amber; meanwhile knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 1/2 tsp salt and about 3/4 cup water into a soft dough and rest it covered.

Slice 3 medium onions thin and even, then brown them in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat for 10 to 12 minutes, stirring constantly toward the end, until deep amber and sweet — proper birista colour, never black.

Off the heat, stir in 1 tbsp grated ginger, 2 minced green chillies and 1/2 tsp garam masala, then the saffron milk; cook 1 minute until the liquid is absorbed and cool completely with 3 tbsp chopped mint and 2 tsp lemon juice folded through.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, tuck 2 tbsp of the saffron-onion mixture into each, pinch the seams and roll gently into 6-inch rounds, keeping the dusting light so the golden tint shows.

Roast on a medium tava, brushing each side with a share of the remaining Anveshan Ghee, about 3 minutes per paratha until softly gold with light brown freckles — moderate heat protects the saffron from scorching bitter.
Rest under a cloth for 2 minutes; the saffron perfume settles into the crumb as it steams.
tips: Brown the onions to amber, not mahogany — past that point they turn bitter and fight the saffron.
Crush the saffron strands between your fingers before steeping to double the colour they release.
Mint added only after cooling stays green and bright; stirred into hot onions it blackens within a minute.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of mirchi ka salan or a simple dahi ki chutney whisked with mint; finish with a small cup of warm sheer khurma on festive mornings.

variations.name: Assamese Masala Onion Paratha
variations.description: From the land of the world's fiercest chilli: a restrained shard of bhut jolokia is cooked into mustard-oil-sweated onions so its smoky, floral fire threads through without scorching the palate. Ginger, coriander and a squeeze of lime keep it fresh and distinctly Assamese.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its calm, nutty crumb is the buffer bhut jolokia heat needs

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Assamese kitchens sweat onions in pungent mustard oil — wood-pressed keeps the bite alive

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A final ghee gloss cools the jolokia's edges into a warm, rounded burn

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil, 1/2 tsp salt and roughly 3/4 cup water into a soft, elastic dough; rest 15 minutes under a damp cloth.
Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai until it just smokes and pales, about 1 minute, then lower the heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds.

Add 1 tbsp grated ginger and a quarter of a small bhut jolokia, minced vanishingly fine (wear gloves), then 3 thin-sliced onions with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1/2 tsp salt; sweat 8 minutes until soft, golden and jammy.
Cool the filling completely, then brighten it with 2 tsp lime juice and 3 tbsp chopped coriander.

Stuff 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp of the fiery onion jam each, seal the pleats and roll into 6-inch rounds; roast on a medium tava for about 3 minutes per paratha, brushing both sides with a share of the 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, until mottled deep gold.
Rest 2 minutes before serving — the jolokia's heat integrates and mellows noticeably as the paratha stands.
tips: Respect the quarter-chilli measure on first cooking; bhut jolokia is 100 times hotter than a green chilli and you can always add, never subtract.
Wear gloves to mince the jolokia and wash the board immediately — its oils linger for hours.
No bhut jolokia at hand? Two fresh red bird's-eye chillies plus a drop of liquid smoke gets surprisingly close.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Assamese way with a cooling khar-style mashed banana-stem salad or simply thick curd, plus red rice kheer to douse the embers afterwards.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Aloo Matar
variations.description: Aloo matar built for chilli lovers: golden-fried potatoes and sweet peas in a hot, clingy masala layered with slit green chillies, black pepper and a punchy ginger-garlic base. Cooked in Anveshan Ghee, the heat comes through rounded and warming rather than raw, with the peas as sweet relief.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee mellows the double chilli hit into a rounded, lingering warmth

steps: Peel 4 medium potatoes and cut them into 2 cm cubes; chop 2 medium onions and 2 tomatoes, slit 3 green chillies, and measure out 1 cup shelled peas.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then blister the slit green chillies in the hot fat for 30 seconds.
Fry the potato cubes for 5 minutes, turning until pale gold on several faces, then push them to the edges and brown the chopped onion in the centre for 5-6 minutes.

Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and stir for 1 minute, then tip in the tomatoes with 2 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 1.25 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 4 minutes until pulpy and glossy.
Fold in the peas with 0.33 cup water, cover and simmer on low heat for 10 minutes, stirring once, until a knife slips through the potatoes and the masala hugs them thickly.
Finish uncovered on medium for 2 minutes to tighten the coating, then crack over 0.5 tsp black pepper and shower with 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Frying the potatoes before the masala goes in keeps them intact and gives the finished dish caramelised depth.
The three heat sources are staggered on purpose: chilli powder for base, green chilli for sharp bite, pepper for the finish; drop one, not all, to reduce heat.
A spoon of cream stirred into any leftover portion turns it into an entirely respectable second-day gravy dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with pillowy phulkas or jeera rice, a cooling bowl of boondi raita, and lime wedges; scooped into pav with chopped onion, it makes a fiery evening snack too.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Aloo Matar
variations.description: Bangaladumpa-batani kura at full Guntur strength: fried potatoes and peas turned in a garlic-forward masala with fiery Guntur chilli powder and curry leaves in Anveshan Groundnut Oil, sharpened with tamarind. This is Andhra's blueprint of heat first, tang second, comfort third.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Robust wood-pressed peanut oil carries Guntur chilli's heat without turning bitter

steps: Cube 4 peeled medium potatoes into 2 cm pieces, crush 6 garlic cloves roughly, and slice 1 large onion; have 1 cup peas and 1 tbsp tamarind pulp standing by.

Warm 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium heat, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds, then fry 2 tsp chana dal to a deep gold, about 45 seconds, before adding 10 curry leaves and the crushed garlic.
When the garlic edges brown, about 1 minute, add the sliced onion and fry for 4-5 minutes until it softens and colours lightly.
Add the potato cubes with 0.25 tsp turmeric powder and sear for 4-5 minutes, tossing occasionally, so they pick up golden patches before any liquid arrives.

Sprinkle 2 tsp Guntur chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, stir for 30 seconds, then add the peas and 0.5 cup water; cover and cook on low for 9-10 minutes until the potatoes are tender.
Stir in 1 tbsp tamarind pulp and simmer uncovered for 3 minutes until the gravy reduces to a fierce red glaze clinging to every piece.
tips: Bloom the Guntur chilli in the oil for only 30 seconds before liquid goes in; longer and it scorches into bitterness.
The tamarind is the safety valve of Andhra heat; taste at the end and add a little more pulp if the chilli overwhelms.
Cold rice mixed with leftovers of this kura and a spoon of ghee is a beloved next-morning Andhra breakfast.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile beside hot steamed rice with a big spoon of ghee and mudda pappu, curd on the side as a fire extinguisher, and a roasted appadam to crumble over the top.

variations.name: Rajasthani Spicy Aloo Matar
variations.description: A Marwari-style sukhi sabzi where potatoes and peas cook in Anveshan Ghee under a tadka of whole dried red chillies, fennel, and coriander seeds, finished with amchur instead of tomato. The desert pantry's whole-spice heat is drier, smokier and more fragrant than powder-based versions.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: In water-scarce Rajasthan, ghee does the work of gravy; it is the body of this dry sabzi

steps: Cut 4 peeled medium potatoes into slim wedges rather than cubes; the extra surface lets the ghee-spice crust develop. Crush 2 tsp coriander seeds coarsely in a mortar.

Melt 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1 tsp fennel seeds for 20 seconds, then fry 4 whole dried red chillies until they puff and darken, about 30 seconds.
Add the crushed coriander seeds and 1.5 tsp grated ginger, stir for 30 seconds, then lay in the potato wedges and sear for 6-7 minutes, turning every 2 minutes, until golden-edged.
Season with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt and toss so the wedges wear the spices evenly.
Add 1 cup peas and 3 tbsp water, cover and cook on low heat for 8-10 minutes, shaking the pan rather than stirring, until the potatoes are tender through.
Uncover, crisp everything on medium-high for 2 minutes, then dust with 1 tsp amchur and 2 tbsp chopped coriander and toss once before serving.
tips: Shaking the covered pan instead of stirring keeps the wedges whole and the crust intact.
Puffed whole chillies are flavouring, not garnish; nibbling them alongside bites of potato is the intended experience.
No tomato is deliberate; amchur delivers the sourness without adding moisture that would ruin the dry texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra rotis, a katori of dahi whisked with roasted cumin, and onion-chilli salad; it is also a classic partner to dal-baati leftovers the next day.

variations.name: Kerala Spicy Aloo Matar
variations.description: Potatoes and peas given the pepper-fry treatment of Kerala's toddy-shop kitchens: braised with crushed black pepper, shallots, ginger and curry leaves in Anveshan Coconut Oil until dark and glossy. The heat is resinous and slow-building, from pepper rather than chilli, in true Malabar style.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil gives the pepper fry its glossy dark finish and Malabar aroma

steps: Cut 4 peeled medium potatoes into 2 cm cubes and parboil them in salted water for 6-7 minutes until barely tender, then drain well; slice 10 shallots, 4 garlic cloves and 1 inch of ginger into fine strips.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a wok or cheena chatti on medium, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 15 curry leaves and let them crackle for 10 seconds.
Fry the shallots, garlic and ginger together for 4-5 minutes until the shallots turn a deep golden brown and smell sweet.
Add the drained potatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp salt and half the 2 tsp crushed pepper, and fry on medium-high for 5-6 minutes, tossing, until the cubes brown at the edges.
Add 1 cup peas with 2 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 5 minutes until the peas are just tender and the pan nearly dry.
Finish uncovered on high for 2 minutes with the remaining crushed pepper and 0.5 tsp garam masala, tossing until everything is dark, glossy and fragrant.
tips: Parboiling first means the potatoes can brown hard in the wok without staying raw inside.
Crush the peppercorns coarsely just before cooking; pre-ground pepper has lost the oils that make this dish sing.
Ten shallots may seem excessive, but their caramelised sweetness is the counterweight to 2 tsp of pepper; do not halve them.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with Kerala parotta or matta rice and a thin moru curry; in toddy-shop spirit, it also works as a standalone starter with lime wedges and sliced raw onion.

variations.name: Bihari Spicy Aloo Matar
variations.description: A Bihari chokha-adjacent fry where potatoes and peas are cooked in smoking Anveshan Mustard Oil with garlic, whole red chillies and a final tempering of raw mustard oil stirred through off the heat. The double mustard hit plus green chilli gives it the rustic sharpness of a Patna winter kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Bihari cooking uses mustard oil twice, as cooking fat and raw finish; kachi ghani pungency is essential for both

steps: Cut 4 peeled medium potatoes into 2 cm chunks, chop 6 garlic cloves and 2 green chillies, and slice 1 large onion; set aside 2 tsp of the measured Anveshan Mustard Oil for the raw finish.

Heat the remaining Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai on medium-high until it smokes lightly and mellows, about 90 seconds, then lower to medium and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds with 3 whole dried red chillies for 25 seconds.
Add the chopped garlic and fry for 45 seconds to pale gold, then the sliced onion and green chillies, cooking 4-5 minutes until browned at the edges.
Add the potato chunks with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and fry for 5 minutes, tossing, so the spice coats and toasts on the surfaces.
Stir in 1 cup peas with 0.33 cup water, cover and cook on low heat for 9-10 minutes until the potatoes crush easily against the pan wall.
Take the kadhai off the heat, drizzle over the reserved 2 tsp raw Anveshan Mustard Oil, lightly crush a few potato pieces into the juices, and fold in 3 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: The off-heat drizzle of raw mustard oil is the signature move; it delivers the wasabi-like top note that cooking destroys.
Half-crushing some potatoes at the end thickens the scant juices into a rustic, chokha-like coating.
This dish loves smoke; if you have a gas flame, char one of the dried chillies directly on it before adding for extra depth.
variations.servingSuggestion: Eat with hot rotis or crisp-edged parathas and a raw onion wedge, or serve alongside dal-bhaat; it is also the perfect gutsy companion to sattu paratha and green chutney.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Lauki
variations.description: Bottle gourd shakes off its mild reputation in this chilli-charged version, where the cubes simmer in a hot masala of green chillies, red chilli powder and cracked black pepper. Because lauki drinks up flavour like a sponge, every translucent cube carries the full three-tier heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A sturdy wood-pressed oil that carries the triple-chilli masala deep into the mild gourd

steps: Peel 600 g bottle gourd, remove any mature seeds and cut into 2 cm cubes; taste a raw sliver first and discard the gourd entirely if it is bitter.
Heat 2½ tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then fry 2 finely chopped onions for 6-7 minutes until golden-brown.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 4 chopped green chillies and fry for 90 seconds until the chillies blister and the raw paste smell disappears.

Stir in 2 finely chopped tomatoes with 1½ tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder, ½ tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 5-6 minutes, mashing occasionally, until the masala thickens and the oil separates at the edges.

Add the lauki cubes, toss for 2 minutes to coat them in the fiery masala, then cover and cook on low for 12-14 minutes, stirring twice, until the cubes turn translucent and yield easily to a knife — the gourd's own moisture forms the gravy.
Uncover and reduce on medium heat for 2-3 minutes until the gravy clings to the cubes, then finish with ¾ tsp freshly cracked black pepper and 2 tbsp chopped coriander stirred through off the heat.
tips: Add no water at all; extra liquid washes the chilli heat out of the masala and leaves the lauki bland.
Deseed two of the four green chillies for strong flavour with a slightly gentler burn.
The cracked pepper must go in last — its sharp top note is what separates this from an ordinary lauki sabzi.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft khapli-atta phulkas and a cooling bowl of plain curd, which tames the heat between bites.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Lauki (Sorakaya Kura)
variations.description: A Deccan scorcher where the gourd simmers with a fried Guntur chilli-garlic paste in toasty gingelly oil, finished with curry leaves and a whisper of tamarind. This is sorakaya cooked the Rayalaseema way — the mildest vegetable in the market carrying the state's proudest heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil is the traditional Andhra base that makes the Guntur chilli paste taste toasted, not raw

steps: Peel 600 g bottle gourd and cut into 2 cm cubes; soak 1 tbsp tamarind pulp in 3 tbsp warm water for 5 minutes, then squeeze and strain a thick extract.

Fry 5 Guntur red chillies and 8 garlic cloves in 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil on low heat for 3-4 minutes until the chillies puff and crisp and the garlic softens, then pound them with ½ tsp salt into a coarse, brick-red paste.
Heat the remaining 1½ tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in the same kadai on medium, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds and ½ tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then crisp 12 curry leaves in the oil for another 30 seconds.
Sauté 1 finely chopped onion with ¼ tsp turmeric for 4-5 minutes until golden, then add the pounded chilli-garlic paste and fry for 1 minute until the oil takes on a deep red stain.
Add the gourd cubes with the remaining ½ tsp salt, toss well, cover and cook on low for 12-13 minutes, stirring twice, until translucent and tender in their own juices.
Pour in the tamarind extract, simmer uncovered for 2-3 minutes until the gravy thickens and turns glossy, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Frying the whole chillies and garlic before pounding is the flavour engine here; powders cannot replicate that toasted depth.
Drop to 3 Guntur chillies for a medium version — the paste keeps its character even at lower heat.
The finished kura should look slightly oily and red at the rim; that stained oil is where the flavour concentrates.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot steamed rice with a spoon of Anveshan Ghee mashed in, and curd rice as the traditional cooling finale.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Spicy Lauki (Goda Masala Bhopla Style)
variations.description: The gourd meets Maharashtra's haunting goda masala — a roasted blend with dagad phool and coconut that is warm and faintly sweet rather than sharply hot — backed by crushed peanuts and a jaggery flicker. It tastes unmistakably of a Pune home kitchen, layered rather than merely fiery.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is Maharashtra's default cooking fat and knits the goda masala and peanuts into one nutty whole

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The classic Maharashtrian pinch of jaggery that lets the goda masala's sweetness bloom

steps: Peel 600 g bottle gourd and dice into 1.5 cm cubes so they cook evenly and catch the coarse peanut crumbs.

Heat 2½ tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds for 30 seconds, then add ¼ tsp hing, 4 crushed garlic cloves and 3 slit green chillies and fry for about a minute until the garlic turns pale gold.
Add 1 chopped tomato with ½ tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 3-4 minutes until soft and pulpy.
Add the gourd cubes, toss to coat, cover and cook on low heat for 11-13 minutes, stirring twice, until translucent and just tender to a knife point.
Lower the flame, sprinkle 2 tsp goda masala and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder over the pan and stir for 2 minutes so the roasted spices bloom in the moist heat without scorching.
Fold in 4 tbsp coarsely crushed roasted peanuts, cook uncovered for 2 more minutes until the gravy thickens and turns nubbly, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander off the heat.
tips: Goda masala loses its perfume on high heat, so it always goes in late and on a low flame.
Hand-crush the peanuts to uneven bits; a mixer grinds them to powder and the texture disappears.
If your goda masala is coconut-heavy, cut the jaggery to half a teaspoon to keep the dish savoury.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft chapatis or jowar bhakri, a wedge of lime and a spoon of thecha on the side for extra fire, Pune-thali style.

variations.name: Rajasthani Spicy Lauki (Sukhi Marwari Style)
variations.description: A dry, assertive Marwari preparation with no tomatoes: the gourd is fried in Anveshan Ghee with crushed dried red chillies, fennel and ajwain, then sharpened with amchur. The result is a rustic sukhi sabzi with toasty edges, big whole-spice bursts and a clean sour finish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee is the desert kitchen's answer to missing tomatoes, giving this spartan sabzi its richness

steps: Peel 600 g bottle gourd and cut into slightly larger 3 cm chunks that can fry and brown without collapsing.

Melt 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadai on medium heat until nutty-smelling, then bloom 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 tsp fennel seeds and ½ tsp ajwain together for 40 seconds until they sputter and darken a shade.
Add 5 sliced garlic cloves and fry for 1 minute until the edges brown, then add 4 crushed dried red chillies and stir for 20 seconds so they toast and tint the ghee without burning.
Add the gourd chunks with 2 tsp coriander powder, ½ tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, and toss for 2-3 minutes on medium heat so every chunk is slicked with the spiced ghee.
Cover and cook on low for 10-12 minutes, stirring twice, until the chunks are tender, then uncover and fry on medium-high for 3-4 minutes until their edges catch golden-brown, dry patches.
Dust 1 tsp amchur over the pan off the heat and toss once so the sourness brightens the toasty spice crust just before serving.
tips: The final uncovered fry is essential — it is what turns a steamed gourd into a proper sukhi sabzi with browned edges.
Hand-crush the dried chillies for irregular flakes; the uneven bursts of heat are part of the Marwari character.
Amchur added on the flame turns bitter, so keep it strictly for after the heat is off.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra rotis, a smear of garlic chutney and chilled chaas dusted with roasted cumin — a lean, honest Marwari lunch.

variations.name: Kerala Spicy Lauki (Churakka Coconut Ularthiyathu)
variations.description: The Malabar answer to a spicy gourd: churakka stir-fried in cold-pressed coconut oil with a crushed coconut-shallot-pepper masala and a shower of crisped curry leaves. Black pepper, not chilli powder, drives the heat, so the burn is aromatic and quick rather than lingering.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil is inseparable from an ularthiyathu; it perfumes both the tempering and the finish

steps: Peel 600 g bottle gourd and dice into 1.5 cm cubes, then crush ¾ cup grated coconut with 5 shallots, 1½ tsp black peppercorns and 3 green chillies in a mortar or with 3-4 mixer pulses into a coarse, damp crumble.

Heat 2½ tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a wide kadai on medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds for 30 seconds, then add 2 torn dried red chillies and 16 curry leaves and fry for 30 seconds until the leaves crackle and crisp.
Add the remaining 5 sliced shallots and sauté for 3-4 minutes until soft and golden at the edges.
Add the gourd cubes with ½ tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, toss well, then cover and cook on low heat for 9-10 minutes, stirring twice, until the cubes are just tender and translucent.
Uncover, scatter the crushed coconut-pepper masala over the pan and stir-fry on medium heat for 4-5 minutes until the coconut smells toasted and clings to every cube in golden flecks.
Rest the dish covered off the heat for 2 minutes so the pepper heat and coconut aroma settle into the gourd before serving warm.
tips: Crush the peppercorns coarsely with the coconut rather than using powder; the sharp bursts define an ularthiyathu.
Keep the coconut masala moving in the final fry — it browns from fragrant to burnt within a minute if left alone.
Fresh coconut is essential; frozen works if thawed fully, but desiccated coconut turns sawdusty here.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve beside Kerala matta rice and a tart moru curry, with a pappadam crumbled over the top in true Malabar style.

variations.name: Classic Masala Mix Veg
variations.description: The restaurant-adjacent mixed vegetable curry made honest: carrots, beans, cauliflower, peas and potato in a proper bhuno-ed onion-tomato masala. Each vegetable goes in by cooking time, so nothing turns to mush and nothing stays raw.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A sturdy cold-pressed oil that carries the masala through a long bhuno without masking the garden-fresh vegetables

steps: Cut 1 potato and 1 carrot into 1.5 cm dice, chop 0.75 cups french beans into short lengths, break 1 cup cauliflower into small florets, and finely chop 2 onions and 3 tomatoes.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a kadai over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 20 seconds until aromatic.
Fry the onions for 7-8 minutes until golden brown, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and stir for 1 minute until the raw smell goes.
Add the tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1.25 tsp salt, and cook for 6-7 minutes, mashing, until thick and oil-streaked.
Add the potato and carrot first with 1.25 cups hot water, cover and simmer on low for 6 minutes, then add the beans and cauliflower and cook covered for 7-8 minutes more.
Stir in 0.5 cups green peas and simmer uncovered for 4-5 minutes until every vegetable yields to a knife tip and the gravy is medium-thick.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala, stir gently so the florets stay whole, and rest the curry for 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Staggering the vegetables by hardness is the whole recipe; dumping them together guarantees mushy peas and raw carrots.
Cut everything roughly the same size so each spoonful carries a bit of every vegetable.
A splash of 2 tbsp milk at the end softens the acidity if your tomatoes were very sharp.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tawa parathas or jeera rice, a bowl of boondi raita and lime wedges; it also fills a thali nicely beside dal fry.

variations.name: Punjabi Masala Mix Veg
variations.description: The wedding-shamiana mix veg: vegetables folded into a rich ghee-onion gravy finished with butter, cream and hand-crushed kasuri methi. It is glossy, mildly sweet from slow-browned onions, and built to make plain naan disappear.

ingredients.name: Anveshan A2 Cow Ghee
ingredients.note: Slow-churned bilona ghee browns the onion base to wedding-caterer depth without a hint of greasiness

steps: Dice 1 potato and 1 carrot small, break 1 cup cauliflower into florets, cube 100 g paneer, slit 2 green chillies and chop 3 onions very fine.
Melt 3 tbsp Anveshan A2 Cow Ghee in a heavy kadai on medium-high, sizzle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then brown the onions patiently for 10-12 minutes until deep mahogany.

Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the slit chillies for 1 minute, pour in 1 cup tomato puree with 1.25 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, and bhuno for 8-9 minutes until brick red with ghee at the edges.
Add the potato and carrot with 1.5 cups hot water and 1.25 tsp salt, cover and simmer on low for 7 minutes to give the hard vegetables a head start.
Add the cauliflower and 0.5 cups green peas, cover again and cook for 8 minutes until everything is tender but intact.
