Slide in the paneer cubes, 3 tbsp fresh cream and 1 tbsp butter over the lowest flame and warm through for 2-3 minutes without boiling.
Crush 2 tsp kasuri methi over the pan, stir once and serve immediately while the gravy still has its buttery sheen.
tips: Pan-sear the paneer cubes in 1 tsp ghee for 2 minutes first if you like golden edges that hold in the gravy.
The onions must go past golden into mahogany; that darkness is what caterers' gravies taste of.
Balance a too-rich pot with 1 tsp lemon juice rather than more salt.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with butter naan or lachha paratha and sliced onions in vinegar; a bowl of masala papad on the side makes it a proper Punjabi spread.

variations.name: Kerala Masala Mix Veg
variations.description: An avial-inspired curry where the vegetables simmer with crushed coconut, green chilli and cumin, then get finished with beaten curd and a raw drizzle of coconut oil with curry leaves. Tangy, herbal and completely unlike a North Indian mix veg.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Avial is finished with raw cold-pressed coconut oil off the heat; this pressing keeps the fragrance a refined oil would lose

steps: Cut 1 carrot, 1 raw banana, 1 cup ash gourd and 1 drumstick into finger-length batons and chop 0.75 cups beans the same way; avial vegetables are always cut long, never diced.
Coarsely crush 1 cup grated fresh coconut with 3 green chillies and 1 tsp cumin seeds in a mixer using pulse mode, keeping the mixture rubbly rather than smooth.
Put the raw banana, drumstick and carrot in a wide pan with 1 cup water, 0.5 tsp turmeric powder and 1 tsp salt; cover and simmer on medium for 6-7 minutes.
Add the beans and ash gourd and continue simmering covered for 6-7 minutes until every vegetable is just tender and most of the water has been absorbed.
Spread the crushed coconut mixture over the vegetables, fold gently, cover and cook on low for 4-5 minutes so the coconut steams through without frying.
Take the pan off the heat, wait 2 minutes, then fold in 0.75 cups beaten thick curd until it coats everything in a pale, tangy dressing.
Drizzle 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil raw over the top, scatter 2 sprigs of torn curry leaves, cover for 5 minutes and serve warm, not hot.
tips: Add curd only off the boil; residual warmth is enough, and boiling would split it instantly.
The raw coconut-oil finish is non-negotiable avial grammar; do not cook the oil in.
Slightly sour day-old curd gives the authentic tang; fresh sweet curd needs a squeeze of lime to help it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve beside red matta rice and a simple thoran as part of a sadya-style spread, or with hot rice and pappadam for a light weekday lunch.

variations.name: Bengali Masala Mix Veg
variations.description: A chorchori-style pot from a Kolkata home: vegetables cooked down in smoked mustard oil with panch phoron until they slump into a soft, faintly sweet tangle with charred edges and almost no gravy. Humble ingredients, startling depth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: A chorchori is unimaginable without pungent kachi ghani mustard oil; it seasons the vegetables as they slowly collapse

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The whisper of sweetness every Bengali torkari hides; unrefined jaggery rounds the mustard-bitter edges cleanly

steps: Cut 1 potato, 1.5 cups pumpkin and 1 brinjal into slim wedges, chop 0.5 cups beans, grate a 1 inch piece of ginger and slit 3 green chillies.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil in a wide kadai on high until it just smokes, then lower the flame and rest it 20 seconds before adding 1.5 tsp panch phoron, 1 bay leaf and 2 whole dried red chillies.
When the five seeds finish crackling, about 25 seconds, add the potato wedges and fry on medium for 4 minutes until their edges colour.
Add the pumpkin, brinjal and beans with the grated ginger, 0.75 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp cumin powder and 1 tsp salt, and toss until every wedge is stained yellow.
Splash in just 0.5 cups water, tuck the slit green chillies on top, cover and cook on low for 12-14 minutes, stirring only twice, until the vegetables are collapsing and the pan is nearly dry.
Uncover, raise the heat and let the underside catch very lightly for 2 minutes; those toasty bits are the chorchori's signature.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, scrape the caught bits through the tangle and switch off; rest 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Stir as little as possible once the lid goes on; a chorchori should slump, not turn into a stir-fry.
The light catching at the bottom is deliberate, but keep your nose on duty; toasty is the goal, burnt is a restart.
Pumpkin is essential for the soft sweetness that balances the mustard oil; do not swap it out.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a dollop of ghee, or the classic way beside dal and rice as the second course of a Bengali lunch; fried papad alongside adds crunch.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Masala Mix Veg
variations.description: A bhaji in the goda masala register: vegetables simmered with toasted dry coconut, crushed peanuts and that unmistakable warm, stone-flower-scented spice blend. It tastes of Pune lunch homes, mildly sweet and deeply nutty.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The peanut-forward fat of the Deccan; wood-pressed, it links the tadka to the crushed groundnuts thickening this bhaji

steps: Dice 1 potato and 1 carrot, string and chop 1 cup flat beans, slice 2 onions, chop 2 tomatoes and crush 3 tbsp roasted peanuts coarsely.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium; pop 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 1 sprig of curry leaves for 10 seconds.
Fry the sliced onions with 3 tbsp grated dry coconut for 6-7 minutes until both are toasted deep brown, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute.
Add the tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt, and cook for 4-5 minutes until pulpy.
Add the potato, carrot and beans with 1.5 cups hot water, cover and simmer on low for 10 minutes, then add 0.5 cups green peas and cook 5 minutes more until all the vegetables are tender.
Stir in 2 tsp goda masala and the crushed peanuts and simmer uncovered for 3 minutes until the gravy thickens to a rustic, spoon-coating bhaji.
Rest off the heat for 5 minutes; goda masala blooms as it sits, so taste for salt only after resting.
tips: Goda masala always goes in near the end; long boiling dulls its dagad phool perfume.
The onion-coconut browning stage sets the bhaji's colour and nuttiness, so give it the full 7 minutes.
Swap the peas for diced flat val papdi in winter for a truly Puneri version.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft polis or bhakri, a wedge of lime and sliced-cucumber koshimbir; it also sits well next to varan-bhaat with a spoon of toop.

variations.name: Classic Pyaaz Paratha
variations.description: The onion paratha every North Indian home knows: finely chopped onions salted, squeezed and tossed with green chilli, coriander and roasted spices, then sealed inside khapli wheat and ghee-roasted till the onions inside turn sweet and translucent. Done right, the filling stays juicy without ever tearing the bread. Simple ingredients, big payoff.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Emmer's forgiving gluten copes with onion's moisture better than refined flour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Onions roasted against ghee-slicked wheat turn sweet and jammy — the whole point of this paratha

ingredients.name: Onions
ingredients.note: Chopped fine, salted and squeezed bone-dry

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 3/4 cup water into a soft, smooth dough; rest it covered for 20 minutes.
Chop 3 medium onions as finely as your knife allows, toss with 1/2 tsp salt and set aside for 10 minutes; the salt will pull out their water.
Squeeze the onions hard in a muslin cloth or between your palms until no more juice drips out; this single step decides whether the paratha rolls cleanly or tears.

Mix the squeezed onion with 2 minced green chillies, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp coriander powder, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp amchur and 3 tbsp chopped coriander; do not add more salt now.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, flatten each into a 4-inch cup, pack in 2 tbsp of the onion mixture, gather the pleats and pinch the seam shut, then rest the balls 5 minutes.
Roll each into a 6-7 inch round with light, even strokes, and roast on a medium-hot tava for about a minute per bare side until freckled.
Finish each side with 1/2 tsp Anveshan Ghee, pressing gently with a spatula until both faces are golden-crisp and the onions inside smell sweet, about 4 minutes per paratha.
tips: Mix the spices into the onion only at the last minute; a rested spiced filling weeps and wrecks the dough.
Amchur goes in instead of lemon precisely to keep the filling dry — resist improving it.
If an onion shred pierces the dough while rolling, press a pinch of dry atta over the spot and carry on.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with plain dahi, mango pickle and a few extra raw onion rings dressed in lemon; nothing else is needed.

variations.name: Punjabi Pyaaz Paratha
variations.description: The Amritsari kulcha's country cousin: onions mixed with anardana, kasuri methi and ajwain, stuffed generously, rolled thick and blistered in ghee till the edges crackle. A slick of white butter melts over the crust at the table, dhaba-style. It is the most indulgent, breakfast-defining member of this family.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Kneads into the strong, plush dough a kulcha-style onion stuffing demands

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A lavish ghee roast is the line between a paratha and a Punjabi paratha

ingredients.name: Onions
ingredients.note: Fine-chopped, salted, squeezed completely dry

ingredients.name: Ajwain seeds
ingredients.note: Worked into the dough where the hot tava toasts them through

steps: Make the dough with 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 3/4 tsp ajwain, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and roughly 3/4 cup water, kneading a full 6-7 minutes until plush; rest 20 minutes.
Fine-chop 3 medium onions, salt them with 1/2 tsp and leave 10 minutes, then wring them out in a cloth until they feel almost dry to the touch.
Toss the onions with 1.5 tsp anardana powder, 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi, 3/4 tsp garam masala, 3 minced green chillies and 2 tsp grated ginger just before stuffing.
Divide the dough into 8 balls and press a generous 2 tbsp of the onion masala into each flattened cup; pleat, twist off the topknot of excess dough and flatten gently between your palms.
Roll each into a thickish 6-inch round — Punjabi parathas carry their stuffing proudly, so do not chase thinness.

Roast on a medium tava for 90 seconds per plain side, then a minute per side with 1/2 tsp Anveshan Ghee, pressing the rim until the whole face is crisply bronzed, about 5 minutes per paratha; slide a curl of white butter onto each before serving.
tips: Anardana's dry, fruity sourness is the authentic kulcha note; amchur is flatter, lemon is wetter — hunt down the real thing.
Kasuri methi should be crushed over the bowl between your palms so its oils land in the filling, not on the counter.
For a tandoor illusion, finish the roasted paratha directly on a low flame for ten seconds per side until it blisters.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with chhole or simply dahi and pickle, plus a tall sweet lassi; on winter mornings add a bowl of sarson ka saag for the full Punjab spread.

variations.name: Bengali Pyaaz Paratha
variations.description: Modelled on the beloved pyaaz-pur porota of Kolkata's telebhaja lanes, this version seasons its onions with kalonji, green chilli and a scatter of crisp mustard-oil-fried garlic. The dough itself is enriched with pungent kachi ghani oil, so every layer tastes faintly of mustard. A little sugar in the filling caramelises against the tava — pure Bengal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Kachi ghani pungency in the dough, the tempering and on the tava — the Bengali trifecta

ingredients.name: Onions
ingredients.note: Chopped fine, salted and squeezed hard

steps: Knead 2 cups khapli atta with 1/2 tsp salt, 1/4 tsp kalonji, 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and about 3/4 cup water into a supple dough; rest it 20 minutes under a damp cloth.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to a light smoke, ease off the flame, then fry 5 sliced garlic cloves with the remaining 1/2 tsp kalonji for about 90 seconds until the garlic chips turn crisp and brown; cool on a plate.
Chop 3 medium onions fine, salt with 1/2 tsp, rest 10 minutes and squeeze them dry in a cloth until they stop dripping entirely.
Combine the onions with the cooled garlic-kalonji crisp, 3 minced green chillies, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1/2 tsp sugar, 1/4 tsp turmeric powder and 3 tbsp coriander leaves.
Stuff 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp of the mixture each, pleat and pinch the seals, then roll into 6-7 inch rounds with light, quick strokes.

Roast on a medium-hot tava, about a minute per plain side, then a minute per side with 1/2 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until the crust turns lacy, deep gold and sharply fragrant, roughly 4 minutes per paratha.
tips: The half teaspoon of sugar caramelises the onion edges on the tava; it reads as depth, not sweetness.
Cool the fried garlic fully before it meets the raw onion, or it softens and loses its crunch.
Kolkata stalls serve these slightly charred, so let the last thirty seconds run a shade darker than instinct suggests.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with ghugni or simply kasundi and sliced cucumber; finish with a small bhaar of mishti doi for the full para-r dokan experience.

variations.name: Odia Pyaaz Paratha
variations.description: Odisha stamps the onion paratha with panch phoron, its five-seed signature, bloomed whole in mustard oil until the fenugreek turns amber. Grated ginger and green chilli keep the filling bright, and a small spoon of jaggery powder gives the gentle sweet backbone Odia home food is known for. Subtler than the Punjabi take, and quietly addictive.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its rustic, nutty crumb suits the temple-state's understated flavour palette

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: The default fat of Odia kitchens and the only right medium for blooming panch phoron

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A restrained guda sweetness that tames raw onion sharpness the Odia way

ingredients.name: Onions
ingredients.note: Fine-chopped, salted and squeezed dry

ingredients.name: Panch phoron
ingredients.note: Bloomed whole in hot oil before it touches the filling

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt and about 3/4 cup water into a soft, even dough; cover and rest for 20 minutes.

Warm 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it shimmers, lower the heat and bloom 2 tsp panch phoron for 30-40 seconds until the mustard seeds pop and the fenugreek darkens to amber; add 8 curry leaves for the last 10 seconds and switch off.
Chop 3 medium onions finely, salt with 1/2 tsp, wait 10 minutes and squeeze them firmly in a cloth until no juice remains.
Pour the warm tempering over the onions and add 1 tbsp grated ginger, 2 minced green chillies, 1/4 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 2 tbsp coriander; toss just before stuffing.
Fill 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp of the seeded onion mixture each, seal the pleats with a firm twist and roll gently into 6-7 inch rounds.
Cook on a medium tava, about a minute per bare side until freckled, then a minute per side with 1/2 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until crisp and burnished, roughly 4 minutes per paratha.
tips: Fenugreek is the tripwire in panch phoron; past amber it turns bitter, so pull the pan early.
Pouring the tempering warm lightly wilts the onion, which softens its bite without cooking it away.
The jaggery powder is seasoning, not sweetener — its job is to round the onion, and one teaspoon is exactly enough.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with dalma or a tomato-date khatta, and a glass of chaas; a piece of chhena poda afterwards completes the Odia meal.

variations.name: Andhra Pyaaz Paratha
variations.description: Onions meet Guntur fire: a coarse karam of dried red chillies and garlic is tossed through the squeezed onion filling, with curry leaves fried in wood-pressed sesame oil lending their unmistakable Telugu aroma. A squeeze of lime at the end keeps the heat bright instead of heavy. This is the paratha for people who ask for extra podi with everything.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The wholesome wheat sweetness gives the Guntur heat something to land on

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil, the traditional Andhra partner for anything karam-laced

ingredients.name: Onions
ingredients.note: Chopped fine, salted, squeezed until dry

ingredients.name: Dried Guntur red chillies
ingredients.note: Soaked and ground coarse with garlic into karam

steps: Soak 3 dried Guntur chillies in hot water for 15 minutes, then grind coarsely with 5 garlic cloves and a teaspoon of the soaking water into a rough karam paste.
While the chillies soak, knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt and roughly 3/4 cup water into a soft dough and rest it, covered, for 20 minutes.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil on medium, pop 1/2 tsp mustard seeds fully, crisp 12 curry leaves for 15 seconds, then fry the karam paste for 2-3 minutes until the oil stains brick-red and the raw garlic smell fades; cool completely.
Chop 3 medium onions fine, salt with 1/2 tsp, wait 10 minutes and wring them dry in a cloth, then fold in the cooled karam, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric powder and 2 tsp lime juice.
Stuff 8 dough balls with 2 tbsp of the red-flecked onion filling each, seal the pleats tightly and roll into 6-7 inch rounds with a light hand.

Roast on a medium-hot tava, a minute per plain side, then a minute per side with 1/2 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil until deeply bronzed and crisp, about 4 minutes per paratha; the sesame-curry leaf aroma announces it is done.
tips: Cool the karam fully before it meets the onions; a warm paste sweats them and undoes all the careful squeezing.
Two chillies instead of three tames it to a family-friendly warmth without losing the red glow.
Any spare karam keeps a week refrigerated and doubles as an instant side for dosa or curd rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with cooling perugu (thick curd) and a spoon of avakaya if you dare; buttermilk with ginger and curry leaves is the proper thirst-quencher alongside.

variations.name: Classic Dry Mix Veg
variations.description: A no-gravy sukhi sabzi where diced carrot, beans, cauliflower, potato and peas steam-fry in their own moisture with everyday ground spices. The vegetables stay distinct and lightly caramelised at the edges, the way a good tiffin sabzi should.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: A light, neutral cold-pressed oil that lets each vegetable in the dry toss keep its own flavour

steps: Dice 1 potato and 1 carrot into small 1 cm cubes, chop 0.75 cups beans into short pieces, break 1 cup cauliflower into small florets and chop 1 onion; grate a 1 inch piece of ginger.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sunflower Oil in a wide kadai on medium and sizzle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds until they crackle and smell toasty.
Sauté the onion for 3-4 minutes until translucent, add the grated ginger for 30 seconds, then add the potato and carrot cubes and fry for 4 minutes, tossing.
Add the beans, cauliflower florets, 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1.25 tsp salt, and toss until the spices coat everything evenly.
Sprinkle 3 tbsp water over the pan, cover tightly and steam-fry on low for 10-12 minutes, lifting the lid to toss just twice, until the potato cubes are tender.
Add 0.5 cups green peas, cook covered for 3 minutes more, then uncover and raise the heat for 2 minutes so any moisture dries and the edges take colour.
Finish with 0.5 tsp amchur and 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander leaves tossed through the hot sabzi.
tips: The 3 tbsp of water is deliberate; more turns steam-frying into boiling and the florets go soggy.
Toss with a flat spatula from the pan floor upward so the potato cubes brown instead of breaking.
This sabzi packs beautifully in tiffins; add the amchur just before packing to keep it tasting fresh at lunchtime.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with phulkas, dal and rice as the dry sabzi of a weekday thali, or roll into a paratha with green chutney for a lunchbox wrap.

variations.name: Gujarati Dry Mix Veg
variations.description: A shaak in the Surti register: vegetables steam-tossed with a mustard-ajmo-hing tadka, finished with jaggery, lemon and a flourish of sesame seeds and fresh coconut. Sweet, tangy and nubbly with seeds, it is the taste of a Gujarati tiffin.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Gujarat's everyday shaak oil; its clean nutty base carries the sweet-sour finish without weighing it down

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The soft gud note that makes a shaak taste Gujarati; the powder melts evenly through a dry toss where block gud cannot

steps: Dice 1 potato and 1 carrot small, chop 0.75 cups beans, shred 1 cup cabbage and keep 0.5 cups green peas ready; a Gujarati shaak likes its pieces dainty.

Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium; crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds fully, then add 0.25 tsp ajwain, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 2 tsp sesame seeds and let them fizz golden for 15 seconds.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste for 30 seconds, then add the potato and carrot and toss for 3-4 minutes on medium.
Add the beans, cabbage and peas with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 2 tsp coriander-cumin powder and 1.25 tsp salt, tossing until the shreds glisten with tadka.
Sprinkle 3 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 10-11 minutes, stirring twice, until the potato is tender and the cabbage has wilted but kept a slight bite.
Uncover, melt 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder through the shaak and toss on medium for 2 minutes until every piece is lightly glazed.
Turn off the heat, squeeze over 1 tbsp lemon juice and shower with 2 tbsp grated fresh coconut before serving.
tips: Sesame seeds burn quickly; they should go golden in the tadka, not brown.
Keep the cabbage's slight crunch; it is the textural signature of a Surti-style dry shaak.
Taste the sweet-sour balance after the lemon; different jaggery batches vary, so adjust with a pinch more if needed.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with warm phulka rotli, a katori of dal and khichdi to complete the Gujarati square meal; it is equally at home stuffed into a thepla roll.

variations.name: Tamil Dry Mix Veg
variations.description: A poriyal in the true Tamil sense: vegetables steamed just tender, then tossed with a mustard-urad-curry leaf tadka in gingelly oil and folded through fresh grated coconut off the heat. Light, clean and green-tasting, it is the everyday side of the Tamil table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Nallennai gives the poriyal tadka its rounded, toasty base; a refined oil leaves the same dish tasting hollow

steps: Dice 2 carrots and 1 cup beans very fine, poriyal-size, shred 1 cup cabbage, chop 1 onion and slit 2 green chillies.
Steam or simmer the carrot, beans and 0.5 cups peas with 0.25 tsp turmeric powder and 0.25 cups water in a covered pan for 6-7 minutes until just tender, then drain any remaining water.

Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil in a kadai on medium; pop 1 tsp mustard seeds, add 1.5 tsp urad dal and 2 whole dried red chillies and fry for about 40 seconds until the dal turns biscuit gold.
Add 2 sprigs of curry leaves, the chopped onion and slit green chillies and sauté for 3-4 minutes until the onion softens without browning.
Add the shredded cabbage and toss on medium for 3 minutes until it wilts but keeps a whisper of crunch.
Fold in the steamed vegetables with 1 tsp salt and toss for 2-3 minutes until everything is hot, dry and speckled with tadka.
Switch off the flame, fold in 0.5 cups grated fresh coconut and serve; the coconut should taste fresh, never fried.
tips: Coconut always goes in off the heat; cooking it turns a poriyal greasy and flat.
Fine, even dicing is half the dish; large chunks steam unevenly and shrug off the tadka.
Frozen grated coconut works if thawed fully and squeezed of excess water first.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as the poriyal beside sambar or vatha kuzhambu rice, or spoon over curd rice; it even works cold, tucked into a lunchbox with lemon rice.

variations.name: Rajasthani Dry Mix Veg
variations.description: A ghee-roasted sookhi subzi with the desert pantry's bold strokes: whole dried red chillies, coarsely crushed coriander seeds, hing and a final dusting of amchur. No tomato and barely any water, just spice-crusted vegetables with toasted edges.

ingredients.name: Anveshan A2 Cow Ghee
ingredients.note: Rajasthani sookhi subzis are roasted in ghee, not oil; bilona ghee gives the spice crust its regal, nutty finish

steps: Cut 2 potatoes and 1 carrot into thick batons, break 1.5 cups cauliflower into medium florets, grate a 1 inch piece of ginger and coarsely crush 2 tsp coriander seeds in a mortar.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan A2 Cow Ghee in a heavy kadai on medium; sizzle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then add 4 whole dried red chillies and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and fry 30 seconds until the chillies puff and darken.
Add the potato batons and fry for 5-6 minutes, turning occasionally, until they pick up golden patches on most sides.
Add the carrot, cauliflower and grated ginger with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt, and toss until the ghee-stained spices coat every piece.
Sprinkle 2 tbsp water, cover and roast on low for 10-12 minutes, tossing twice, until the potatoes are tender and the florets are browned at the tips.
Add 0.5 cups green peas and the crushed coriander seeds and cook uncovered for 3-4 minutes so the seeds toast fragrant against the pan.
Finish off the heat with 1 tsp amchur and 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander leaves tossed through the hot, spice-crusted vegetables.
tips: Coarse-crushed coriander seeds, not powder, give the crunchy spice-crust this subzi is loved for.
Resist stirring too often during the covered roast; contact with the hot kadai is what browns the florets.
Crumble one of the fried dried chillies over the finished dish for heat-lovers; leave them whole for aroma only.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra rotis, a bowl of kadhi and lehsun chutney for a desert-style meal; it also partners perfectly with dal-baati as the dry vegetable.

variations.name: Odia Dry Mix Veg
variations.description: A santula-leaning dry curry from Odisha: vegetables tossed with panch phoron and garlic in pungent mustard oil, kept deliberately light on ground spice so the produce leads. A final flutter of grated coconut nods to the coastal kitchens of Puri.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Panch phoron only opens fully in sharp kachi ghani mustard oil, the everyday fat of the Odia kitchen

steps: Cut 1 potato, 1 cup pumpkin and 1 carrot into slim batons, chop 0.75 cups beans, slice 1 onion, crush 5 garlic cloves and slit 2 green chillies.

Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil in a kadai on high until the first wisp of smoke, then lower the flame and rest 20 seconds before adding 1.5 tsp panch phoron and 2 whole dried red chillies.
When the seeds finish their 25-second crackle, add the crushed garlic and sliced onion and fry for 3-4 minutes until pale gold and sweet-smelling.
Add the potato and carrot batons and toss for 4 minutes on medium, then add the pumpkin, beans and slit green chillies with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp cumin powder and 1 tsp salt.
Sprinkle 3 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 10-11 minutes, tossing gently twice, until the pumpkin is soft and the potato tender while the batons still hold shape.
Uncover and dry the pan on medium-high for 2 minutes so the vegetables finish glossy rather than wet.
Turn off the heat and fold in 3 tbsp grated fresh coconut, letting the residual warmth release its aroma before serving.
tips: Pumpkin cooks faster than potato; the baton sizes can be slightly larger for pumpkin to keep them finishing together.
Keep ground spices minimal; santula's charm is vegetables tasting of themselves under the panch phoron.
For the temple-style variant, drop the onion and garlic and add 0.5 tsp grated ginger with the vegetables.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside dalma and steamed rice for a full Odia plate, or with pakhala bhata on a summer afternoon; roasted badi crumbled on top adds the classic crunch.

variations.name: Classic Dhaba-style Gajar Matar
variations.description: The winter sabzi of highway dhabas across North India, where sweet red carrots and green peas are cooked hard on a big iron tawa until their edges catch and caramelise. A rustic onion-tomato masala scented with kasuri methi clings to every piece instead of drowning it in gravy. It is homely food with truck-stop swagger.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil takes dhaba-level high heat without smoking and adds a nutty depth to the masala

steps: Peel 4 medium carrots and cut them into thick 1-inch batons; shell or thaw 1 cup green peas. Finely chop 2 medium onions and 2 medium tomatoes and keep everything within reach of the stove.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a heavy kadhai on medium-high heat until it shimmers. Crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 30 seconds, then add the chopped onions and fry until deep golden at the edges, 6 to 7 minutes.

Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute until the raw smell disappears. Add the chopped tomatoes with 1 tsp salt and cook on medium heat, mashing occasionally, until the masala turns jammy and oil beads at the sides, about 6 minutes.

Sprinkle in 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, and fry the spices for 45 seconds so they lose their rawness. Add the carrot batons and toss to coat every piece in the masala.

Add the 1 cup green peas and a splash of about 3 tbsp water, cover, and cook on low heat for 12 to 14 minutes, stirring twice, until a knife slides through the carrots but they still hold their shape.

Uncover, raise the heat to high and stir-fry for 2 minutes so any moisture evaporates and the carrot edges catch slightly. Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi between your palms over the pan, dust with 0.5 tsp garam masala, toss, and finish with 3 tbsp chopped fresh coriander.
tips: Use red Delhi winter carrots if you can find them; they are sweeter and stay firmer than pale orange ones.
If the sabzi releases too much water, finish it uncovered on high heat while stirring so the masala re-coats the vegetables instead of pooling.
The dish reheats beautifully; make it a few hours ahead and warm it on a tawa for an even smokier dhaba character.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile it onto a steel thali with hot tandoori roti, a wedge of raw onion, a green chilli and a bowl of dahi on the side, dhaba style.

variations.name: Punjabi Dhaba-style Gajar Matar
variations.description: The Amritsar-highway version, doubled down on richness: the vegetables are braised in bilona ghee and mounted with white butter at the end. Ginger julienne and slit green chillies give it the sharp bite Punjabi dhabas are famous for. The masala is darker, butterier and unapologetically indulgent.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Slow-churned bilona ghee gives this Punjabi braise its signature nutty aroma that refined butter cannot match

steps: Cut 4 medium carrots into chunky half-moons and keep 1 cup green peas ready. Slice half of the 2-inch ginger into fine julienne for garnish, and crush the rest with 6 garlic cloves into a coarse paste; slit 2 green chillies lengthwise.

Melt 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat until fragrant, then pop 1 tsp cumin seeds. Tip in 2 large chopped onions and fry patiently for 8 to 9 minutes, stirring often, until they turn a deep brown that will colour the whole dish.

Add the crushed ginger-garlic and slit green chillies and sizzle for 1 minute. Follow with 3 chopped tomatoes and 1 tsp salt, and bhuno on medium heat for 7 to 8 minutes, pressing with the back of the ladle, until the ghee separates in glossy streaks.
Work in 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder and fry for 30 seconds. Add the carrots, stir for 2 minutes to sear them in the masala, then add the peas with 0.25 cup hot water.
Cover and simmer on low for 13 to 15 minutes, stirring midway, until the carrots are butter-soft but not mushy and the gravy has thickened to a coating consistency.

Turn off the heat and stir in 2 tbsp white butter, 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi and 0.5 tsp garam masala until the butter melts into a glossy sheen. Scatter the reserved ginger julienne on top just before serving.
tips: Browning the onions properly is the whole game here; stop too early and the sabzi tastes flat rather than dhaba-dark.
Stir the white butter in off the heat so it emulsifies into the masala instead of splitting into an oily layer.
Swap half the peas for cubed potatoes in peak winter, as many Punjabi dhabas do, adding them along with the carrots.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter-brushed lachha paratha and a tall glass of salted lassi; a few pickled green chillies on the side cut through the richness.

variations.name: Bengali Dhaba-style Gajar Matar
variations.description: A Kolkata-line-hotel take where pungent mustard oil, panch phoron and a paste of mustard seeds transform the gentle carrot-pea duo. There is no onion or garlic here; green chillies and a whisper of sugar do the balancing, niramish style. The finished sabzi is sharp, faintly sweet and unmistakably Bengali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Cold wood-pressed kachi ghani mustard oil carries the sharp jhaanj that defines Bengali vegetable cookery

steps: Soak 2 tbsp yellow mustard seeds in 3 tbsp warm water for 15 minutes, then grind them with 1 green chilli and a pinch of salt into a smooth, pale paste. Meanwhile cut 4 medium carrots into small dice and keep 1 cup green peas ready.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai on medium-high until it just reaches smoking point and the raw pungency mellows, about 1 minute. Lower the heat, add 1 dried red chilli and 1 tsp panch phoron, and let the five seeds crackle for 20 to 30 seconds.

Add 1 tsp ginger paste and 2 slit green chillies and stir for 30 seconds until aromatic. Tip in the diced carrots with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder and 1 tsp salt and sauté on medium heat for 4 minutes so the edges glisten yellow.
Add the green peas and 0.5 cup water, cover, and cook on low heat for 8 to 10 minutes until the carrots are tender when pressed with a spoon but the dice still hold their corners.
Stir in the ground mustard paste and 0.5 tsp sugar, and simmer uncovered on low for 3 to 4 minutes, stirring gently, until the sauce thickens and coats the vegetables without tasting raw or bitter.
Check the salt, finish with 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander and a few drops of raw Anveshan Mustard Oil drizzled over the top, then take it off the heat before the mustard paste can overcook.
tips: Never boil the mustard paste hard; aggressive heat turns it bitter, so keep the final simmer at the gentlest bubble.
Soaking the mustard seeds well and adding a green chilli while grinding keeps the paste creamy and tames its harshness.
If you like the Bengali dhaba shorshe punch stronger, add 0.5 tsp kasundi at the end instead of extra paste.
variations.servingSuggestion: Eat it the Kolkata way with steamed rice and a squeeze of gondhoraj or regular lime, or fold leftovers into a roll paratha for breakfast.

variations.name: Kerala Dhaba-style Gajar Matar
variations.description: Carrots and peas go south in this thoran-inspired stir-fry, tumbled with fresh grated coconut, curry leaves and mustard seeds popped in coconut oil. Shallots replace the heavy onion-tomato base, keeping the vegetables bright and the coconut centre stage. It is light, aromatic and ready in under half an hour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed coconut oil ties the tempering and the fresh coconut together with one clean, tropical aroma

steps: Chop 4 medium carrots into small, even 0.5-inch cubes so they cook quickly, and keep 1 cup green peas ready. Slice 8 shallots thin, slit 3 green chillies and finely chop 1 inch of ginger.

Pulse 0.75 cup fresh grated coconut with the chopped ginger, 1 slit green chilli, 0.25 tsp turmeric powder and 0.5 tsp cumin powder just two or three times, so it stays a coarse, fluffy crumble rather than a paste.
Warm 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a wide pan over medium heat and pop 1 tsp mustard seeds, about 30 seconds. Add the curry leaves from 2 sprigs and let them crisp and splutter for a few seconds.
Add the sliced shallots and remaining 2 green chillies and sauté for 3 minutes until the shallots turn translucent and lightly pink at the edges, not browned.
Add the carrot cubes, peas and 1 tsp salt with 0.25 cup water, cover, and steam on low heat for 8 to 9 minutes, shaking the pan once, until the carrots are just tender with a slight bite.

Scatter the spiced coconut crumble over the vegetables, toss well, and cook uncovered on low for 3 minutes so the coconut warms through and absorbs the juices without toasting brown. Serve straight from the pan while the curry leaves are still fragrant.
tips: Keep the coconut mixture coarse; over-grinding releases oil and makes the thoran heavy instead of fluffy.
Frozen grated coconut works well if thawed fully and squeezed of excess water before pulsing.
A teaspoon of raw coconut oil stirred in off the heat right before serving lifts the aroma noticeably.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside steamed matta rice and a tangy moru curry or simple dal, with pappadam crumbled over for crunch.

variations.name: Gujarati Dhaba-style Gajar Matar
variations.description: On the Ahmedabad-Rajkot highway this sabzi turns gently sweet and tangy, with jaggery and lemon playing against a hing-and-sesame tempering. There is no onion or garlic; the shaak relies on green chilli-ginger paste and a khichdi-friendly soft texture. Every bite lands sweet first, then sour, then warm.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed white sesame oil is the traditional Kathiyawadi cooking fat and deepens the shaak's nutty sweetness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Chemical-free jaggery powder dissolves evenly, giving the classic Gujarati gol sweetness without refined sugar

steps: Dice 4 medium carrots into small 0.5-inch pieces and measure out 1 cup green peas. Mix 1 tbsp green chilli-ginger paste and keep the spices lined up, because the tempering moves fast.

Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadhai on medium heat, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds for about 30 seconds, then add 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 1 tbsp white sesame seeds and let the sesame turn pale gold, roughly 20 seconds.
Add the green chilli-ginger paste and stir for 30 seconds, then tip in the diced carrots and peas with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder and 1 tsp salt, tossing until every piece is stained yellow.
Pour in 0.5 cup water, cover, and cook on low heat for 10 to 12 minutes, stirring once, until the carrots are soft enough to crush easily against the side of the pan.
Stir in 2 tsp coriander-cumin powder and 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook uncovered for 3 minutes, letting the jaggery melt into a light glaze that clings to the vegetables.
Switch off the heat, squeeze in 1 tbsp lemon juice and shower with 3 tbsp chopped fresh coriander; taste and balance so the sweet and the tang land evenly.
tips: Add the jaggery only after the carrots are fully cooked; sugar added early slows vegetable softening.
The lemon must go in off the heat or its brightness dulls; kachri or amchur can replace it in winter.
This shaak tastes even better slightly warm rather than piping hot, as Gujarati thali houses serve it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair it with soft phulka rotli, kadhi and steamed rice for a proper Gujarati thali, or spoon it over thepla for a travel-day meal.

variations.name: Classic Dry Kaddu
variations.description: The everyday North Indian sookhi kaddu ki sabzi: cubes of yellow pumpkin cooked down with onion, tomato and earthy coriander powder until the edges caramelise and the masala clings dry. Slow, covered cooking in wood-pressed groundnut oil gives the pumpkin a soft, jammy centre without turning it to mush.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold wood-pressed groundnut oil has a nutty depth that stands up to slow, dry roasting of pumpkin

steps: Peel 500 g pumpkin, scoop out the seeds and cut it into 2 cm cubes; finely chop 1 large onion and 1 large tomato and keep everything within reach of the stove.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a heavy kadai on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 20 seconds until they darken a shade and smell toasty.
Add the chopped onion with 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and saute on medium heat for 5-6 minutes, stirring often, until the onion turns golden at the edges and the raw garlic smell disappears.

Stir in the chopped tomato, 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt; cook for 3-4 minutes until the tomato collapses and the oil beads at the sides of the masala.

Tip in the pumpkin cubes, toss to coat every piece in masala, then cover and cook on low heat for 15-18 minutes, stirring gently every 5 minutes, until a knife slides through a cube with no resistance.

Uncover, raise the heat to medium-high and cook for 2-3 minutes, tossing once or twice, so any moisture evaporates and the pumpkin edges catch light brown spots; finish with 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander.
tips: Choose mature yellow pumpkin with deep orange flesh; pale green-fleshed pumpkin releases more water and stays bland in a dry sabzi.
Resist stirring vigorously after the pumpkin softens or the cubes will break; use a flat spatula and fold from the bottom.
If the pumpkin releases too much water, cook uncovered for the last 5 minutes on medium-high until the masala turns dry and glossy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with phulkas, a katori of plain curd and a wedge of lime; it also makes an excellent filling for lunchbox parathas the next day.

variations.name: Rajasthani Dry Kaddu
variations.description: Rajasthan's khatta-meetha kaddu leans on whole dried red chillies, fennel and a sharp hit of amchur instead of tomato, a desert-kitchen trick from days when fresh produce was scarce. The result is a punchy sweet-sour pumpkin with a rustic, coarse masala that clings to every cube.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed kachi ghani mustard oil brings the pungent kick Rajasthani kaddu is built on

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Chemical-free jaggery powder gives the authentic meetha counterpoint to amchur without refined sugar

steps: Cut 500 g peeled pumpkin into slightly large 3 cm chunks so they hold shape through the sweet-sour braise, and break 3 dried red chillies into halves, shaking out some seeds if you prefer milder heat.
Pour 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil into a kadai and heat on high until it just begins to smoke, about 90 seconds, then lower the flame so the raw pungency mellows without burning.
Drop in the broken dried red chillies, 1 tsp fennel seeds and 0.25 tsp fenugreek seeds; let them sizzle for 30 seconds until the chillies deepen in colour and the fennel smells sweet.
Add the pumpkin chunks with 1 slit green chilli, 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt; toss for 2 minutes on medium heat so the spices coat the cubes evenly.
Sprinkle 2 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 15 minutes, stirring twice, until the pumpkin is fork-tender but the chunks still hold their corners.

Stir in 1 tsp amchur and 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, mash 3-4 cubes lightly against the pan to thicken, and cook uncovered for 2 minutes until the jaggery melts into a glossy coating; garnish with 2 tbsp fresh coriander.
tips: Heating mustard oil to smoking point once, then cooling slightly, removes its raw bitterness; skipping this step leaves an acrid edge.
Balance is everything here: taste after adding jaggery and amchur, and adjust in quarter-teaspoon steps until sweet and sour hit equally.
This sabzi tastes even better after 2-3 hours as the fennel and jaggery mellow together, so it is a great make-ahead dish for travel.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with hot puris or bajra rotis and a side of five-lentil panchmel dal for a classic Rajasthani thali spread.

variations.name: Bengali Dry Kaddu
variations.description: In Bengali homes this is kumro bhaja-chorchori territory: pumpkin cooked in pungent mustard oil with panch phoron's five-seed crackle and a whisper of green chilli. The mustard oil's sharpness against the pumpkin's natural sweetness is the whole point of the dish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Kachi ghani mustard oil is non-negotiable in Bengali cooking; its wasabi-like sharpness defines this chorchori

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A small spoon of pure jaggery powder gives the classic Bengali misti finish that rounds off mustard oil's bite

steps: Cut 500 g peeled pumpkin into thin 1 cm-thick slices rather than cubes; thinner pieces char slightly and half-melt, which is the texture a Bengali chorchori wants.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a wide pan on high heat until faint wisps of smoke appear, roughly 1 minute, then reduce the flame to medium.
Add 1.5 tsp panch phoron, 1 whole dried red chilli and 1 bay leaf; the five seeds should crackle and pop within 20-30 seconds, releasing a nutty-bitter aroma.
Slide in the pumpkin slices with 2 slit green chillies, 1 tsp grated ginger, 0.5 tsp turmeric powder and 1 tsp salt, and toss on medium heat for 3 minutes so every slice glistens yellow.
Cover and cook on low heat for 12-15 minutes, lifting the lid to fold gently twice, until the slices are soft enough to crush against the pan with the back of a spoon.

Uncover, add 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 2 tbsp grated coconut, and cook on medium heat for 3 minutes, mashing about a third of the pumpkin, until the mixture is a rough, glossy jumble of soft and chunky pieces.
tips: Do not substitute panch phoron with plain cumin; the fenugreek and nigella in the blend give the faint bitterness that balances the sweet pumpkin.
Bengalis deliberately let some pumpkin catch lightly on the pan bottom; those caramelised bits carry the best flavour, so scrape them in.
If you find raw mustard oil too assertive, smoke it well in step 2 and add a teaspoon extra at the end off the heat for aroma instead of more during cooking.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a first course with steamed rice and a drizzle of the pan oil, followed by dal; it also sits beautifully beside luchis at a weekend breakfast.

variations.name: Kerala Dry Kaddu
variations.description: A mathanga thoran-style take where pumpkin is steam-tossed with a crushed paste of fresh coconut, cumin and green chilli, then finished with a curry-leaf tempering in coconut oil. It is lighter and fresher than the North Indian version, with the coconut keeping every bite juicy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed coconut oil carries a fresh copra aroma that ties the thoran's tempering and coconut paste together

steps: Dice 500 g peeled pumpkin into small 1.5 cm cubes; small dice matters here because the pumpkin steams quickly and stays intact instead of collapsing.
Coarsely crush 0.5 cup grated fresh coconut with 2 green chillies, 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 2 garlic cloves in a mixer using 2-3 short pulses; the paste should stay rubbly, not smooth.

Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a wide pan on medium heat, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds for about 20 seconds, then add 1 dried red chilli, 12 curry leaves and 4 sliced shallots and fry for 2 minutes until the shallots turn light gold.

Add the pumpkin cubes, 0.25 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp salt and 3 tbsp water; stir once, cover tightly and steam on low heat for 10-12 minutes until the cubes yield easily to a spoon but still hold their shape.

Scatter the crushed coconut mixture over the pumpkin, fold it through gently, then cover again and cook on the lowest flame for 3-4 minutes so the coconut steams through and smells sweet rather than raw.
Open the lid, raise the heat for 1 minute to dry off any remaining moisture, tossing lightly, and take it off the heat while the coconut is still snow-white with only a few golden flecks.
tips: Pulse the coconut paste briefly; over-grinding releases oil and makes the thoran greasy instead of fluffy.
Fresh curry leaves fried till just translucent perfume the whole dish; dried leaves lose most of their aroma, so avoid them here.
Frozen grated coconut works if thawed fully and squeezed lightly; excess water will steam the thoran soggy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside matta rice, a tangy pulissery and pappadam for a simple Kerala lunch line-up; a teaspoon of raw coconut oil drizzled at the table is customary.

variations.name: Kumaoni Dry Kaddu
variations.description: In Uttarakhand's Kumaon hills, pumpkin is stir-fried with jakhya, a wild mustard-family seed that crackles louder and nuttier than cumin, and finished simply with hill red chillies and coriander. Cooked in pure ghee, it is a spare, smoky dish that lets the mountain tempering do all the talking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee's high smoke point lets the jakhya seeds crackle hard without burning, the way Pahari kitchens do it

steps: Halve, deseed and peel 500 g pumpkin, then cut it into rustic 2.5 cm wedges; Kumaoni cooks keep the pieces chunky so they blister rather than stew.
Melt 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in an iron kadai over medium-high heat until it shimmers, then add 1.5 tsp jakhya seeds and let them crackle noisily for 20-30 seconds until the popping slows.
Add 2 whole dried red chillies, 4 sliced garlic cloves and 1 inch julienned ginger; fry for about 1 minute until the garlic edges turn pale gold and the chillies darken.

Tumble in the pumpkin wedges with 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, and stir-fry on medium heat for 4-5 minutes so the wedges pick up light char marks.
Cover and cook on low for 12-14 minutes without adding water, shaking the pan every few minutes instead of stirring, until the wedges are tender at the centre when pierced.
Finish uncovered on high heat for 2 minutes so the ghee re-coats the blistered wedges, then shower with 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander and serve straight from the kadai.
tips: If jakhya is unavailable, use a mix of 1 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin, though the signature loud crunch will be milder.
An iron kadai gives the faint smokiness Pahari food is known for; avoid non-stick pans, which never let the pumpkin blister.
Shake, do not stir, once the pumpkin softens; the wedges are delicate and shaking preserves their charred faces.
variations.servingSuggestion: Eat it the hill way: with thick mandua (finger millet) rotis or steamed rice, a spoon of bhang chutney or any tangy hemp-seed or coriander chutney on the side.

variations.name: Classic Kadai Rajma
variations.description: A dhaba-style take on rajma where soft pressure-cooked kidney beans are tossed in a rustic, freshly pounded kadai masala with charred capsicum and onion petals. The gravy clings thickly to the beans instead of drowning them, with smoky coriander-and-chilli notes from spices toasted right in the pan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Slow-churned bilona ghee gives the kadai masala its nutty, restaurant-style depth when the spices bloom in it

steps: Drain the soaked rajma, add it to a pressure cooker with 3 cups fresh water and 1 tsp salt, and cook on medium heat for 5-6 whistles, about 20 minutes. A bean should squash completely between two fingers with no chalky centre.

While the beans cook, make the kadai masala: dry-roast 1.5 tbsp coriander seeds, 3 dried red chillies and 1 tsp cumin seeds in a kadai on low heat for 2-3 minutes until fragrant and a shade darker, then cool and pound to a coarse powder.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in the same kadai on medium-high. Sear the onion petals and capsicum squares for 2 minutes until blistered at the edges but still crisp, then remove and set aside.
In the remaining Anveshan Ghee, saute 2 chopped onions for 6-7 minutes until deep golden. Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 1 minute until the raw smell disappears.
Stir in the tomato puree, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and the pounded kadai masala. Cook on medium heat for 6-8 minutes, stirring, until the masala thickens and ghee beads at the edges.
Add the cooked rajma with 1 cup of its cooking liquid and remaining 0.5 tsp salt. Simmer uncovered for 8-10 minutes, mashing a spoonful of beans against the pan to thicken the gravy.
Return the seared capsicum and onion petals, sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala, swirl in 2 tbsp cream and simmer for 2 minutes more before taking off the heat.
tips: If you forgot to soak the rajma, cover it with boiling water for 1 hour, then pressure-cook with 2 extra whistles.
Pound the roasted kadai masala coarse, not fine - the gritty texture on the beans is the signature of this dish.
The gravy thickens as it rests; loosen leftovers with a splash of hot water and a small spoon of ghee before reheating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle into a bowl, top with a thin swirl of cream and julienned ginger, and serve with tandoori roti or steamed basmati rice and a wedge of lime.

variations.name: Bengali Kadai Rajma
variations.description: Kidney beans meet Bengal's pungent mustard-oil kitchen in this take, where the oil is smoked to its flash point before panch-style whole spices crackle in it. A paste of ginger and green chilli replaces heavy garlic, and a pinch of sugar rounds the gravy the Kolkata way.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed kachi ghani mustard oil carries the sharp, nose-tingling pungency that defines this Bengali gravy

steps: Pressure-cook the drained, soaked rajma with 3 cups water and 1 tsp salt for 5-6 whistles on medium heat, roughly 20 minutes, until the beans crush easily with no resistance at the core.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai on high until it just begins to smoke and turns a paler yellow, about 1 minute; this mellows its raw edge while keeping the pungency.
Lower the heat to medium and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, 2 bay leaves and 2 dried red chillies in the hot oil for 30 seconds until aromatic.
Add the sliced onions and fry for 7-8 minutes until browned at the edges. Stir in 1 tbsp ginger paste and the slit green chillies and cook for 1 minute more.

Add the chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1 tsp cumin powder and 0.5 tsp sugar. Cook for 5-6 minutes on medium, mashing the tomatoes, until the oil separates and the masala turns glossy.
Tip in the cooked rajma with 1.25 cups of its stock and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt. Simmer for 10 minutes, partially covered, until the gravy coats the back of a spoon.
Finish with 0.5 tsp Bengali garam masala and a final few drops of raw Anveshan Mustard Oil stirred in off the heat for that classic sharp aroma.
tips: Smoking the mustard oil first is essential - skipping it leaves the gravy tasting raw and bitter.
The half teaspoon of sugar is not for sweetness; it balances the mustard's bite and deepens the onion colour.
Swap one green chilli for a slit gondhoraj-style lime leaf at the end if you can find it, for a fragrant twist.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steaming plain rice and a wedge of lime, alongside crisp fried potato slices (aloo bhaja) for a proper Kolkata-style lunch plate.

variations.name: Kerala Kadai Rajma
variations.description: Rajma simmered the Malabar way in a roasted-coconut masala, with curry leaves and black pepper crackled in coconut oil. Grinding browned coconut into the gravy gives it a deep, toasty sweetness closer to a varutharacha curry than a North Indian dal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold wood-pressed coconut oil ties the roasted-coconut gravy together with a clean, fresh coconut aroma

steps: Cook the drained soaked rajma in a pressure cooker with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 5-6 whistles on medium heat, about 20 minutes, until completely tender.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadai on medium. Roast 0.75 cup grated coconut with 1 tbsp coriander seeds, 1 tsp peppercorns and 3 dried red chillies for 6-7 minutes, stirring constantly, until the coconut turns an even deep brown.
Cool the roasted mixture, then grind it with the chopped ginger, 4 garlic cloves and 0.5 cup water to a smooth, thick brown paste.

Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in the kadai on medium. Pop 1 tsp mustard seeds for 30 seconds, then add the sliced shallots and 1 sprig curry leaves and fry for 4-5 minutes until the shallots are golden.
Add the chopped tomatoes and cook for 4 minutes until they collapse. Stir in the ground coconut paste and fry for 3-4 minutes until it smells toasty and oil films the surface.
Add the cooked rajma with 1 cup of its stock and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt. Simmer gently for 10 minutes, stirring now and then, until the gravy is thick and clinging.
Turn off the heat and crackle the second sprig of curry leaves in a spoon of hot coconut oil, pouring this tempering over the curry just before serving.
tips: Roast the coconut low and slow to an even chestnut brown - pale coconut makes a flat gravy, burnt coconut makes it bitter.
The gravy thickens fast because of the coconut; keep extra bean stock handy to adjust before serving.
For a Thalassery touch, add 0.25 tsp fennel powder to the coconut while grinding.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with Kerala red-rice matta choru or lacy appams, with a sharp mango pickle on the side to cut the richness.

variations.name: Andhra Kadai Rajma
variations.description: A fiery Rayalaseema-inspired version built on Guntur chillies fried in groundnut oil, with tamarind pulling the gravy sharp and bright. Roasted ground coriander and a garlic-heavy tadka give it the aggressive, rustic character of an Andhra kura.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil stands up to the fierce Guntur chilli heat with its own earthy, nutty backbone

ingredients.name: Tamarind, soaked in 0.25 cup warm water

steps: Pressure-cook the drained rajma with 3 cups water and 1 tsp salt on medium heat for 5-6 whistles, about 20 minutes, until a bean mashes to a paste under your thumb.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium-high. Crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then fry 4 whole Guntur chillies and 1 sprig curry leaves for another 30 seconds until the chillies darken and puff.
Add 8 crushed garlic cloves and fry for 1 minute until golden at the edges, then add the chopped onions and cook for 6-7 minutes until well browned.
Stir in the tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp Guntur chilli powder and 2 tsp roasted coriander powder. Cook for 5-6 minutes on medium until the masala darkens and oil pools at the sides.
Squeeze and strain the soaked tamarind, adding its extract to the pan. Simmer for 2 minutes so the raw tang cooks off.
Add the rajma with 1 cup of its cooking liquid and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt. Simmer for 10-12 minutes, uncovered, until the gravy reduces to a thick, brick-red coat on the beans.
Scatter 3 tbsp chopped coriander leaves over the top and rest the curry for 5 minutes off the heat so the tamarind and chilli settle into balance.
tips: Guntur chillies bring real heat - halve the powder to 0.75 tsp for a family-friendly version without losing the flavour.
Frying the garlic before the onions, Andhra-style, gives the gravy its signature toasted-garlic base note.
A day's rest in the fridge makes this curry noticeably better as the tamarind mellows into the beans.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the traditional way with hot steamed rice, a spoon of extra groundnut oil drizzled on top, and cooling curd or majjiga (buttermilk) alongside.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Kadai Rajma
variations.description: Rajma folded into a Kolhapur-leaning gravy of goda masala, roasted peanut crush and jaggery, balancing sweet, nutty and warmly spiced notes. The black-masala aroma of dagad phool and coconut in goda masala makes this taste unmistakably of a Marathi kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Maharashtrian home gravies are built on groundnut oil; the wood-pressed version doubles the peanutty depth of the masala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A traditional pinch of chemical-free jaggery rounds the goda masala's warmth exactly as Marathi households do

steps: Cook the soaked, drained rajma in a pressure cooker with 3 cups water and 1 tsp salt for 5-6 whistles over medium heat, around 20 minutes, until the beans are butter-soft.
Warm 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat. Pop 1 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add 0.25 tsp asafoetida.
Fry the chopped onions for 6-7 minutes until golden brown, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder and cook for 5 minutes on medium, mashing them down, until the mixture turns jammy and the oil separates.
Stir in 2 tsp goda masala and the 0.25 cup crushed roasted peanuts and fry for 2 minutes; the masala should smell warmly of coconut and stone flower, not raw spice.

Add the rajma with 1.25 cups of its stock, 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt. Simmer for 10 minutes until the gravy is medium-thick and glossy with peanut bits suspended in it.
Garnish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and rest, covered, for 5 minutes so the jaggery and goda masala knit together.
tips: Add goda masala late and never over high heat - its coconut content scorches quickly and turns bitter.
Crush the peanuts coarse; a fine powder makes the gravy pasty instead of pleasantly textured.
No goda masala on hand? Dry-roast 1 tsp sesame seeds, 1 tbsp grated dry coconut and 0.5 tsp garam masala as a quick stand-in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft chapatis or jowar bhakri, a raw onion wedge and a squeeze of lime - and a papad on the side for the full Maharashtrian thali feel.

variations.name: Classic Masala Malai Kofta
variations.description: The restaurant favourite done right at home: pillowy paneer-potato koftas bound with khapli atta, fried until golden and dropped into a silky onion-tomato-cashew gravy. The masala base is simmered until the ghee beads on the surface, giving the curry its deep, glossy body. A final swirl of cream and kasuri methi makes every bite rich without being heavy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: This heirloom emmer wheat binds the koftas without the gumminess of maida, so they stay soft inside with a crisp shell

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Slow-churned bilona ghee builds the masala base and gives the gravy its glossy, nutty finish

steps: Boil, peel and mash 2 medium potatoes, then grate 200 g paneer into the same bowl. Add 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta and 0.5 tsp salt and knead into a smooth, crack-free dough.
Divide the mixture into 12 equal balls, about 2 tbsp each, rolling them tight between your palms so they hold together in the hot fat.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide non-stick pan on medium heat and shallow-fry the koftas in two batches, turning every 2 minutes until evenly golden on all sides, about 6 minutes per batch. Drain on a plate.

In the same pan, melt the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then sauté 2 sliced onions, 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 4 chopped tomatoes and 12 cashews until the tomatoes collapse, about 8 minutes. Cool and blend to a completely smooth paste.

Return the paste to the pan with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp salt and 1 cup water. Simmer on medium-low, stirring occasionally, until the ghee separates at the edges, about 10 minutes.
Stir in 0.25 cup cream and 1 tsp garam masala, simmer gently for 2 minutes, then slide in the fried koftas and switch off the heat within 1 minute so they do not break apart.
tips: Add the koftas only at serving time; if they sit in the gravy longer than 10 minutes they soak up liquid and turn mushy.
If the kofta dough feels wet, work in 1 extra tsp of Anveshan Khapli Atta rather than refrigerating, which stiffens the paneer.
The blended gravy can be made 2 days ahead and refrigerated; loosen with 2 tbsp warm water when reheating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle into a shallow bowl, halve one kofta on top to show the soft centre, and serve with butter naan and thin-sliced onion rings soaked in lemon juice.

variations.name: Awadhi Masala Malai Kofta
variations.description: Lucknow's courtly answer to malai kofta: an ivory gravy of yogurt, cashew and fried onion paste, perfumed at the last moment with kewra water. The spicing is deliberately gentle, letting cardamom and mace whisper instead of shout. It is the version to make when you want elegance on the table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The stone-ground emmer flour gives these delicate koftas structure while keeping the crumb tender, true to Awadhi finesse

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Awadhi bawarchis cook only in ghee; this bilona ghee carries the cardamom and mace without masking them

steps: Soak 15 cashews in 0.5 cup hot water for 15 minutes, then grind to a fine, white paste with the soaking water.
Mash 2 boiled potatoes with 200 g grated paneer, 0.5 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, then shape into 12 smooth ovals of about 2 tbsp each, the traditional Awadhi kofta shape.
Shallow-fry the ovals in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat, rolling them gently every 2 minutes until pale gold rather than deep brown, about 5 minutes, and set aside.

Slice 3 onions thin and fry them in the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium heat until light golden and crisp at the edges, about 10 minutes, then blend with 3 tbsp water into a smooth boiled-onion style paste.
Return the onion paste to the pan with 4 bruised cardamom pods and 1 blade of mace, cook 2 minutes, then lower the heat and whisk in 0.5 cup yogurt one spoon at a time so it never splits.
Add the cashew paste, 0.5 tsp white pepper, 1 tsp salt and 1 cup water and simmer gently for 8 minutes until the gravy coats the back of a spoon like thin custard.
Finish with 3 tbsp cream and exactly 1 tsp kewra water off the heat, then nestle in the koftas and rest the pan, covered, for 3 minutes before serving.
tips: Kewra is potent; measure it with a spoon rather than pouring from the bottle, as even 0.5 tsp extra makes the dish taste soapy.
Whisk the yogurt smooth and keep the flame at its lowest while adding it, or the white gravy will curdle and turn grainy.
For a true dawat-style finish, strain the gravy through a sieve before adding cream for a porcelain-smooth texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a shallow copper bowl with warm sheermal or roomali roti, and scatter a few slivered pistachios and rose petals over the ivory gravy.

variations.name: Bengali Masala Malai Kofta
variations.description: Bengal reroutes malai kofta through its beloved kosha style: koftas seared in pungent mustard oil, then simmered in a ginger-forward tomato gravy sweetened with a pinch of jaggery. The mustard oil's sharp aroma mellows into a warm, almost smoky depth. Green chillies slit lengthwise ride on top for fragrance more than fire.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Wholegrain khapli flour binds the kofta crumb firmly enough to survive the kosha-style simmering

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed kachi ghani mustard oil is the soul of Bengali cooking; heat it to smoking once to tame its bite

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: That whisper of cane sweetness Bengalis add to balance mustard's pungency, minus refined sugar

steps: Knead 200 g grated paneer with 2 mashed boiled potatoes, 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta and 0.5 tsp salt, then roll into 12 tight rounds of roughly 2 tbsp each.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just smokes and its raw smell fades, about 90 seconds, then lower the heat to medium.
Fry the koftas in the hot mustard oil, turning every 2 minutes until they take on a deep amber crust, about 6 minutes total, and lift them out with a slotted spoon.
In the same fragrant oil, brown 1 finely chopped large onion for 5 minutes, then add 1.5 tbsp ginger paste and cook 1 minute until it no longer smells raw.
Add 3 chopped tomatoes, 1.5 tsp cumin powder, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1 tsp salt and bhuno on medium heat, mashing the tomatoes down, until the oil rises to the surface, about 8 minutes.
Pour in 1.25 cups warm water with 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 3 slit green chillies, and simmer for 5 minutes until the gravy thickens to a coating consistency.
Slide in the koftas, swirl in 3 tbsp cream and 0.5 tsp Bengali garam masala, and let everything sit off the heat for 2 minutes so the flavours knit together.
tips: Smoking the mustard oil first is non-negotiable; skipping it leaves an acrid rawness in the finished gravy.
Bengali garam masala is just cardamom, cinnamon and clove ground together; make a small fresh batch for the cleanest aroma.
The gravy should be slightly loose when you switch off the heat, as the koftas drink up liquid in the resting time.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with steamed gobindobhog rice and a wedge of gondhoraj or regular lime; the citrus lifts the mustard oil beautifully.

variations.name: Kerala Masala Malai Kofta
variations.description: Malai kofta goes to the Malabar coast: the cream is replaced by thick coconut milk, the tempering crackles with curry leaves in coconut oil, and black pepper does the warming. The result is a lighter, aromatic ishtu-style gravy that hugs the golden koftas. It tastes of a toddy-shop lunch reimagined for a vegetarian feast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The nutty emmer flour holds the koftas together even in the thin, coconut-milk gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil fries the koftas and blooms the curry leaves the way every Kerala kitchen does

steps: Combine 200 g grated paneer, 2 mashed boiled potatoes, 0.25 cup grated coconut, 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta and 0.5 tsp salt, and press into 12 firm balls of about 2 tbsp each.

Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a heavy pan over medium heat and fry the koftas, turning every couple of minutes, until crusty and golden brown all over, about 6 minutes; drain on a banana leaf or plate.
Grind 6 shallots, 1 inch ginger, 2 green chillies and 0.5 tsp fennel seeds to a coarse paste with 2 tbsp water.
Heat the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, crackle 1 sprig curry leaves for 20 seconds, then fry 4 sliced shallots until their edges brown, about 3 minutes.
Add the ground paste with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt and sauté on medium heat until its raw smell disappears and the oil glistens, about 5 minutes.
Pour in 0.75 cup water, simmer 4 minutes, then lower the flame fully before stirring in 1 cup thick coconut milk and 1 tsp black pepper powder; never let it reach a rolling boil.
Add the koftas and the second sprig of curry leaves, warm gently for 2 minutes until the gravy lightly coats the koftas, and switch off.
tips: Coconut milk splits at a hard boil; keep it below a simmer after adding and the gravy stays silky.
Crush the pepper coarsely at home instead of using fine store powder for a brighter, more floral heat.
Leftover gravy thickens overnight; thin with 0.25 cup warm water and refresh with a few new curry leaves fried in 1 tsp coconut oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with lacy appams or Kerala matta rice, plus a sharp mango pickle on the side to cut the coconut richness.

variations.name: Kashmiri Masala Malai Kofta
variations.description: Inspired by the Valley's wazwan, this take simmers koftas in a blushing yogurt gravy scented with fennel, dry ginger and true saffron. There is no onion or garlic, just Kashmiri chillies for colour and warmth. Each strand of saffron blooms in warm milk, streaking the curry gold and perfuming the whole pot.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The ancient-grain binder keeps these paneer-rich koftas intact through the long yogurt simmer

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Kashmiri gravies bloom their spice powders directly in hot ghee; bilona ghee does it without burning

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Genuine Kashmiri saffron strands steeped in milk give the dish its signature golden threads and aroma

steps: Steep 0.25 tsp Anveshan Saffron strands in 3 tbsp warm milk and set aside for at least 15 minutes until the milk turns deep gold.
Knead 250 g grated paneer with 1 large mashed boiled potato, 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta and 0.5 tsp salt, then shape into 12 elongated koftas of about 2 tbsp each, wazwan style.
Brown the koftas in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat, turning them every 2 minutes until russet on all sides, roughly 6 minutes, then set them aside on a warm plate.
Whisk 1 cup yogurt with 0.5 cup water until pourable and completely lump-free; this prevents curdling later.

Heat the last 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with 3 cardamom pods, 3 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon for 30 seconds, then take the pan off the heat and stir in 2 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder so it releases colour without scorching.
Return the pan to low heat, add the whisked yogurt in a thin stream while stirring constantly, and cook 5 minutes until it comes to a gentle, unified simmer.
Stir in 2 tsp fennel powder, 1 tsp dry ginger powder and 1 tsp salt, add the koftas and half the saffron milk, and simmer covered on low for 8 minutes until the gravy turns pale terracotta.
Drizzle the remaining saffron milk over the top just before serving so its perfume arrives first at the table.
tips: Stir the yogurt in one direction only over low heat until it boils once; changing direction or rushing the flame is what splits it.
Fennel and dry ginger are the backbone here, so use freshly ground fennel if you can for a sweeter, cleaner note.
Real saffron stains your fingers yellow when rubbed damp; if the strands bleed instantly and taste bitter, they are dyed fakes.
variations.servingSuggestion: Present over steamed long-grain rice with a few extra saffron strands on top, alongside a cooling walnut-mint chutney in the Kashmiri manner.

variations.name: Classic Masala Sem
variations.description: The everyday North Indian way with sem phali, where tender broad beans soak up a slow-cooked onion-tomato masala. Cooking the beans covered on a low flame keeps them jade-green outside while the masala clings to every pod. A final flourish of garam masala and fresh coriander makes it the definitive weeknight sabzi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil has a clean, nutty base note that lets the sem's grassy sweetness shine

steps: String 500 g broad beans by snapping the tip and pulling down the seam, then cut them into 1-inch diagonal pieces; finely chop 2 medium onions and 2 medium tomatoes.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds until they darken a shade and smell toasty, about 30 seconds.
Add the chopped onions and saute on medium heat for 6-7 minutes until the edges turn golden brown, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until the raw smell fades.

Tip in the chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt; cook on medium for 5-6 minutes until the tomatoes collapse and oil beads at the edges.
Fold in the cut beans so every piece is coated in masala, sprinkle 2 tbsp water, cover and cook on low heat for 12-15 minutes, stirring twice, until a bean bends easily but does not mush.
Turn off the heat, dust over 0.5 tsp garam masala and 3 tbsp chopped fresh coriander, toss once and let the sabzi sit covered for 2 minutes so the aroma settles in.
tips: Always string the beans on both seams; even one fibrous strand left behind makes the whole bite chewy.
If the masala starts catching before the beans are done, add water only 1 tbsp at a time so the sabzi stays dry, not soupy.
Slightly older, bumpy pods take 4-5 minutes longer; test the thickest piece, not the thinnest.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with phulkas, a katori of dal and a wedge of lime; it also packs beautifully into a lunchbox with jeera rice.

variations.name: Punjabi Masala Sem
variations.description: A dhaba-inspired take from Punjab where the beans are braised in a robust ghee-and-butter tempered masala with extra tomatoes. The finish of white butter melting over the hot sabzi gives it that unmistakable roadside-dhaba richness. Kasuri methi rubbed in at the end adds the smoky-sweet signature of Punjabi kitchens.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee browns the onions to a deep caramel that anchors this Punjabi masala

steps: De-string 500 g broad beans and slice into 1.5-inch batons; slit 2 green chillies lengthwise and grate 3 medium tomatoes into a pulp, discarding the skins.
Melt 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai over medium flame and let 1 tsp cumin seeds sputter for about 30 seconds until fragrant and a shade darker.
Brown 2 large chopped onions in the ghee for 8-9 minutes on medium heat until deeply golden, then add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the slit green chillies and fry 90 seconds more.

Pour in the grated tomato pulp with 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt; bhuno on medium-high for 7-8 minutes, scraping the base, until the masala thickens and ghee separates in glossy streaks.
Add the beans, toss to coat, splash in 3 tbsp water, then cover and simmer on low for 12-14 minutes until the pods yield to a spoon's edge but keep their shape.
Crush 1 tsp kasuri methi between your palms over the sabzi, add 0.5 tsp garam masala, and stir through 1 tbsp white butter off the heat until it melts into a light gloss.
