tips: Grating rather than chopping the tomatoes gives the smooth, clingy gravy dhabas are known for.
Do not rush the onion browning; the deep colour at 8-9 minutes is what separates Punjabi masala from a pale home curry.
Leftovers taste even better rolled into a paratha with a smear of green chutney the next morning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile it beside tandoori roti with sliced onions soaked in vinegar and a glass of salted lassi for the full dhaba spread.

variations.name: Bengali Masala Sem
variations.description: In Bengali homes sheem is beloved through winter, cooked pungent and hot in mustard oil with kalonji and green chillies. A spoon of ground mustard paste stirred in at the end gives the beans a sharp, nose-tingling edge that defines the region's vegetable cookery. It is a leaner, sharper dish than the North Indian version, with no garam masala at all.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Kachi-ghani pungency is the soul of Bengali sheem; heat it to smoking so it mellows just enough

steps: Soak 2 tsp yellow mustard seeds with 2 green chillies in 3 tbsp warm water for 10 minutes, then grind to a smooth paste with a pinch of salt.
String 500 g sheem and cut into 1-inch pieces; peel 1 medium potato and cut it into thin half-moon slices so it cooks in step with the beans.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai until it just smokes and the raw pungency lifts, about 2 minutes on high, then lower the flame and crackle 0.5 tsp kalonji with 2 slit green chillies for 20 seconds.
Add the potato slices and fry on medium for 3-4 minutes until their edges turn pale gold, then add the beans, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt and toss for 2 minutes.
Stir in 1 tsp ginger paste, sprinkle 4 tbsp water, cover and cook on low heat for 10-12 minutes until both potato and beans are fork-tender.
Mix the ground mustard paste with 0.5 tsp sugar, fold it into the sabzi and simmer uncovered for exactly 2 minutes so the mustard stays sharp, then finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Never boil the mustard paste longer than 2 minutes or it turns bitter instead of pungent.
Heating the mustard oil to its smoking point first is non-negotiable; under-heated oil tastes raw and acrid.
For an authentic touch, add a few fresh sheem seeds from mature pods; Bengalis prize their nutty bite.
variations.servingSuggestion: Eat it the Bengali way: with steaming white rice, a drizzle of the pan juices, and a slit green chilli pressed into the rice.

variations.name: Kerala Masala Sem
variations.description: A thoran-style rendition from Kerala where the beans are chopped fine and steamed open-pan with a fresh coconut-cumin-garlic crumble. Coconut oil and curry leaves perfume every strand, and the dish stays light, dry and green. It is the coastal opposite of a heavy onion-tomato masala.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil doubles the fresh-coconut aroma that defines a Kerala thoran

steps: Chop 500 g strings-removed broad beans into fine 0.5 cm rounds; the small cut is essential so they steam through quickly without turning soggy.
Pulse 0.75 cup grated coconut with 3 garlic cloves, 2 green chillies, 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp turmeric to a coarse, damp crumble; do not grind it to a paste.

Warm 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a wide kadhai on medium heat, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds, then brown 1 tsp urad dal with 2 torn dried red chillies for about 45 seconds until the dal is biscuit-coloured.
Add 6 sliced shallots and 2 sprigs of curry leaves and fry 2 minutes until the shallots soften and the leaves crisp at the edges.
Tumble in the chopped beans with 1 tsp salt, sprinkle 3 tbsp water, cover and steam on low for 8-9 minutes, tossing once, until the beans are just tender with a slight squeak.
Scatter the coconut crumble over the beans, cover for 2 minutes on the lowest flame so it steams fragrant, then toss everything well and switch off before the coconut colours.
tips: The coconut must go in at the end and only steam briefly; if it fries and browns, the thoran loses its fresh sweetness.
Frozen grated coconut works if thawed fully and squeezed of excess water first.
A teaspoon of raw coconut oil drizzled over the finished thoran is a Kerala home trick worth stealing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as part of a rice plate with sambar or moru curry; it is also lovely tucked inside a soft appam for breakfast.

variations.name: Gujarati Masala Sem
variations.description: Gujarat's beloved winter shaak treatment: beans simmered with ajwain-scented oil, then balanced with jaggery and lemon into the region's classic sweet-tangy-hot triangle. Toasted sesame seeds folded through at the end add nutty crunch. It tastes nothing like its North Indian cousin, and that is the point.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the traditional Gujarati shaak fat; wood-pressed keeps its peanut aroma intact

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Chemical-free jaggery powder dissolves evenly, giving the shaak its gentle Gujarati sweetness without syrupy patches

steps: String 500 g broad beans and snap them into 1-inch lengths; dry-toast 1 tbsp sesame seeds in a small pan for about 2 minutes until they turn pale gold and start to pop, then set aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium, crackle 0.5 tsp ajwain for 20 seconds, then stir in 0.25 tsp hing so it blooms in the hot oil without burning.
Add the beans straight to the tempering with 1 tbsp green chilli-ginger paste, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, tossing for 2 minutes so the ajwain oil coats every pod.
Sprinkle 0.25 cup water, cover the kadhai and cook on low heat for 12-14 minutes, stirring midway, until the beans are tender and the water has evaporated.
Stir in 2 tsp dhana-jeeru, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook uncovered for 2-3 minutes until the jaggery melts and lightly glazes the beans.
Finish off the heat with 1 tbsp lemon juice, the toasted sesame seeds and 2 tbsp chopped coriander, tossing so the shaak glistens sweet, tangy and nutty in the same bite.
tips: Add the jaggery only after the beans are fully tender; sugar in the pot early makes some varieties stubborn.
Taste before adding lemon: the shaak should sit exactly between sweet and sour, leaning neither way.
This shaak is served at Gujarati weddings with valor papdi; swap in half papdi beans in deep winter for authenticity.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rotli, a katori of Gujarati kadhi and steamed rice; a spoon of chhundo on the side completes the thali.

variations.name: Classic Punjabi Paneer
variations.description: The dhaba-style paneer curry of Punjab: soft paneer cubes folded into a slow-cooked onion-tomato masala enriched with cream and finished with crushed kasuri methi. Cooking the base in Anveshan Ghee gives the gravy its signature nutty depth and glossy sheen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee browns the onions evenly and gives this gravy its dhaba-style richness

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add 2 finely chopped onions and saute until deep golden brown, about 8 minutes.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute until the raw smell disappears, then add 3 pureed tomatoes and cook on medium heat until the mixture thickens and darkens, about 6 minutes.
Add 0.5 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1.25 tsp salt; fry the masala on low heat, stirring constantly, until ghee beads at the edges, about 4 minutes.
Pour in 1 cup water, bring to a gentle simmer, and cook uncovered for 5 minutes so the gravy turns smooth and coats the back of a spoon.
Slide in 400 g paneer cubes and simmer gently for 4 minutes on low heat so the paneer soaks up the masala without turning rubbery.
Stir in 0.25 cup fresh cream and 1 tsp garam masala, crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi between your palms into the pan, and cook 2 minutes until the gravy looks glossy.
Finish with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee swirled over the top just before taking the kadhai off the heat, so the aroma stays fresh and buttery.
tips: Soak paneer cubes in warm salted water for 10 minutes before adding; they stay pillowy even after simmering.
If the gravy tastes sharp, add 1 tsp cream extra and simmer 2 more minutes rather than adding sugar.
The base masala can be made 2 days ahead and refrigerated; add paneer, cream and kasuri methi only when reheating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a copper handi with butter naan and laccha onions dressed in lemon juice; a chilled glass of salted lassi rounds out the meal.

variations.name: Bengali Punjabi Paneer
variations.description: A Kolkata-style rework where the paneer is lightly pan-seared in pungent Anveshan Mustard Oil and simmered with a panch-phoron-scented tomato gravy. Green chillies and a hint of sweetness give it the balanced heat typical of Bengali home cooking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed kachi ghani mustard oil delivers the sharp pungency Bengali gravies are known for

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A touch of unrefined jaggery balances the mustard oil's bite the way Bengali kitchens do

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai on medium-high until it just reaches smoking point, then lower the heat; this mellows the oil while keeping its signature pungency.
Rub 400 g paneer cubes with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.25 tsp salt, sear them in the hot oil for 2 minutes per side until pale gold at the edges, and set aside on a plate.

Add the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to the same kadhai, crackle 1 tsp panch phoron for 30 seconds until the fenugreek darkens slightly, then add 1 sliced onion and fry until translucent, about 4 minutes.

Stir in 2 tsp ginger paste and 2 slit green chillies, cook 1 minute, then add 3 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1 tsp salt; cook until the tomatoes collapse into a jammy mass, about 6 minutes.
Pour in 1 cup water and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer 4 minutes, then return the seared paneer and cook gently for 5 minutes until the gravy clings to each cube.
Take off the heat, scatter 2 tbsp chopped coriander and 1 slit green chilli on top, cover and rest 3 minutes so the mustard aroma settles into the gravy.
tips: Always let mustard oil reach its smoking point once before cooking in it; skipping this leaves a raw bitterness.
Do not sear the paneer longer than 2 minutes per side or it turns chewy in the gravy.
For a river-fish-style twist, add 0.5 tsp nigella seeds along with the panch phoron.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with steamed gobindobhog rice and a wedge of gondhoraj lime; a simple cucumber-onion salad on the side keeps the pungent gravy in balance.

variations.name: Kerala Punjabi Paneer
variations.description: A coastal reinvention that simmers paneer in a coconut-milk gravy tempered with curry leaves and Anveshan Coconut Oil. The masala keeps its North Indian backbone of onion and tomato, but the finish is unmistakably Malabar: creamy, gently spiced and fragrant.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold wood-pressed coconut oil carries the curry-leaf tempering with a clean tropical aroma

steps: Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a deep pan over medium heat, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds for 30 seconds, then add 1 sprig curry leaves and 2 slit green chillies and let them sputter for 20 seconds.
Add 2 thinly sliced onions and saute until soft and lightly golden at the edges, about 6 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute more.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1.25 tsp salt; cook on medium heat until the tomatoes break down completely and the oil surfaces, about 5 minutes.
Grind 0.25 cup grated coconut with 3 tbsp water to a fine paste, add it to the pan and simmer 3 minutes until the raw coconut smell fades and the gravy thickens slightly.
Lower the heat, pour in 1 cup thick coconut milk, add 400 g paneer cubes and simmer very gently for 5 minutes; never let it boil hard or the coconut milk will split.
Sprinkle 1 tsp freshly crushed black pepper, then finish with a tempering of 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil heated with the second sprig of curry leaves poured sizzling over the curry.
tips: Add coconut milk only on low heat and stir in one direction to keep the gravy silky and unbroken.
Fresh curry leaves make a real difference here; dried ones lose the citrusy top note.
For a Thattukada-style version, toss the paneer with 0.5 tsp pepper and pan-fry it before adding.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle over Kerala matta rice or serve with lacy appams; a sharp mango pickle on the side cuts the creaminess beautifully.

variations.name: Kashmiri Punjabi Paneer
variations.description: Inspired by the Valley's chaman kaliya, this take simmers golden-fried paneer in a yoghurt-fennel gravy stained amber with Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron. There is no onion or garlic, so the sweetness of fennel, dry ginger and saffron carries the dish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Kashmiri kaliya gravies are built entirely on ghee, and slow-cultured bilona ghee keeps them fragrant, never greasy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: Pampore saffron strands bloomed in warm milk give the gravy its amber hue and honeyed aroma

steps: Soak 0.25 tsp Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron strands in 0.25 cup warm milk and set aside for 15 minutes until the milk turns deep gold.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide pan over medium heat and fry 400 g paneer batons for about 3 minutes, turning once, until pale golden on two sides; drain onto a plate.

In the same ghee, crackle 4 cardamom pods, 3 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon for 40 seconds on low heat until fragrant, then stir in 1 cup water with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp fennel powder and 1 tsp dry ginger powder and simmer 3 minutes.

Take the pan off the flame, whisk in 1 cup yoghurt in a slow stream while stirring continuously, then return to low heat and stir until the gravy is smooth and just steaming, about 4 minutes; boiling now would curdle it.
Add 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1.25 tsp salt and the fried paneer, and simmer gently for 5 minutes so the batons drink in the fennel-scented gravy.
Pour in the saffron milk, stir once, and cook 2 minutes more until the surface glistens amber; finish with the last 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee spooned over before serving.
tips: Whisk the yoghurt with 1 tsp of the hot gravy first to temper it and prevent splitting.
Cut the paneer into thick batons rather than cubes; that is the traditional chaman shape and it holds better.
Crush half the saffron strands between your fingers before soaking for deeper colour from fewer strands.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed long-grain rice and a spoon of walnut chutney; in true Kashmiri wazwan fashion, offer kahwa tea to close the meal.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Punjabi Paneer
variations.description: A rustic Deccan version built on goda masala, the sweet-smoky Maharashtrian blend of dagad phool and coconut. Roasted peanut powder thickens the gravy in place of cream, and Anveshan Groundnut Oil ties the nutty flavours together.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil echoes the roasted-peanut base of this Deccan gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Maharashtrian gravies finish with a whisper of jaggery, and this unrefined powder melts in instantly

steps: Dry-roast 2 tbsp grated coconut in a kadhai on low heat, stirring constantly, until it turns biscuit brown, about 3 minutes; tip it out and reserve.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in the same kadhai over medium heat, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds for 30 seconds, then fry 2 chopped onions until golden brown, about 7 minutes.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute, then stir in 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt and cook until pulpy, about 5 minutes.
Add 2 tsp goda masala, 1 tsp red chilli powder, the roasted coconut and 3 tbsp peanut powder; fry the masala on low heat for 3 minutes until it smells toasty and the oil separates at the edges.
Pour in 1.25 cups water and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer 5 minutes until the gravy thickens to a coating consistency with a rustic, grainy texture.
Add 400 g paneer cubes and simmer 4 minutes on low heat so they absorb the smoky-sweet masala, then scatter 2 tbsp chopped coriander over the top before serving.
tips: Goda masala scorches fast; keep the flame low once it goes in and stir without pausing.
If you cannot find goda masala, roast 1 tsp sesame seeds with 0.5 tsp caraway and a small piece of dagad phool and grind them as a stand-in.
The peanut powder thickens further as it rests, so loosen leftovers with 2 tbsp hot water when reheating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best mopped up with soft jowar or bajra bhakri and a raw onion wedge; a squeeze of lime just before eating lifts the earthy goda notes.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Karela
variations.description: The North Indian everyday karela sabzi at its fiery best: salt-cured bitter gourd rings pan-roasted in wood-pressed groundnut oil with a punchy onion-tomato masala. Curing tames the bitterness while green chillies and crushed black pepper build a clean, layered heat that clings to every crisp-edged slice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil has a high smoke point that crisps the karela rings without turning acrid

steps: Scrape the ridged skin of 500 g bitter gourd lightly, slice into 1 cm rings, scoop out mature seeds, and toss the rings with 1 tsp salt; set aside for 25 minutes until they release their bitter juices, then squeeze firmly and pat dry.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a heavy kadhai on medium-high heat until it shimmers, add the squeezed karela rings in a single layer, and pan-fry for 8-10 minutes, turning occasionally, until the edges turn deep golden and blistered. Lift them out onto a plate.
In the same kadhai on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add 2 sliced onions and sauté for 5-6 minutes until they turn golden brown at the edges.

Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 3 slit green chillies and fry for 1 minute until the raw smell disappears, then add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, and 2 tsp coriander powder.
Cook the masala on medium heat for 4-5 minutes, mashing the tomatoes with the back of the spoon, until the oil beads at the sides and the mixture looks glossy.
Return the fried karela to the pan, sprinkle 0.5 tsp crushed black pepper, toss well, and cook uncovered on low heat for 5 minutes so the rings soak up the masala while staying slightly crisp.
tips: Do not skip squeezing the salted karela; trapped juice steams the rings and makes them soggy instead of crisp.
If the dish still tastes too bitter for your table, a squeeze of lime at the end balances it without adding sweetness.
The fried rings can be prepped a day ahead and refrigerated; just toss them into the hot masala for 5 minutes before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside phulkas with a bowl of cool boondi raita and sliced onions dressed in lime; the raita softens the pepper heat beautifully.

variations.name: Bengali Spicy Karela (Jhaal Ucche)
variations.description: In Bengali homes, ucche is prized for its bitterness, not hidden from it. Here the gourd is fried in pungent mustard oil with nigella seeds and finished with a sharp mustard-green chilli paste, giving the dish the wasabi-like heat that defines shorshe cooking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed kachi ghani mustard oil gives ucche its signature nose-tingling pungency

steps: Soak 2 tbsp yellow mustard seeds in 3 tbsp warm water for 15 minutes, then grind with 2 green chillies and a pinch of salt into a smooth, sharp paste.
Slice 500 g bitter gourd into thin half-moons, rub with 0.5 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp turmeric, and rest for 15 minutes before squeezing out the released liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai on high until it just begins to smoke and its raw sharpness mellows, about 1 minute, then lower to medium heat.
Scatter in 0.5 tsp nigella seeds, let them sizzle for 20 seconds, then add 1 finely sliced onion and fry for 4 minutes until translucent with golden edges.
Add the karela slices and fry on medium heat for 8-10 minutes, stirring every couple of minutes, until they shrink and pick up brown, crisp patches.
Pour in the mustard paste with 0.5 cup water and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, slit the last 2 green chillies over the top, and simmer on low for 5 minutes until the gravy thickly coats the gourd.
Finish with 2 tbsp grated coconut folded through, and take the pan off the heat while the sauce is still loose enough to spoon over rice.
tips: Never boil the mustard paste hard; aggressive boiling turns it bitter in an unpleasant, acrid way rather than pleasantly sharp.
Grinding the mustard with a green chilli and salt prevents the paste from splitting and tasting harsh.
For an authentic touch, drizzle a few drops of raw mustard oil over the finished dish just before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle over steaming hot gobindobhog or any short-grain rice as the traditional bitter first course of a Bengali meal, followed by dal and a fish curry.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Karela (Kakarakaya Vepudu)
variations.description: A ferociously hot Andhra-style dry fry where crisp karela coins meet a coarse podi of Guntur red chillies, garlic, and roasted peanuts. Sesame oil deepens the roast while a pinch of jaggery powder rounds off the chilli burn the way Andhra kitchens always do.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed sesame oil gives the vepudu its nutty, toasty Andhra depth

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A whisper of unrefined jaggery powder rounds off the fierce Guntur chilli heat

steps: Cut 500 g bitter gourd into thin 0.5 cm coins, salt them with 0.5 tsp salt for 20 minutes, then squeeze dry so they fry crisp instead of stewing.

Dry-roast 6 Guntur red chillies, 3 tbsp peanuts, and 1 tsp cumin seeds in a pan on low heat for 4-5 minutes until the peanuts turn golden and smell toasty, then cool and pound coarsely with 4 garlic cloves and 0.5 tsp salt into a rough podi.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a wide kadhai on medium-high heat, add the karela coins in one layer, and fry for 10-12 minutes, turning now and then, until deeply browned and crisp at the edges.
Push the karela aside, drop in the remaining 4 garlic cloves, lightly crushed, with 12 curry leaves, and let them sputter and turn fragrant for about 1 minute.
Add 1 finely chopped onion and 0.5 tsp turmeric and sauté on medium heat for 4 minutes until the onion softens and browns lightly.

Sprinkle the pounded chilli-peanut podi and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder over the pan, toss everything vigorously for 2 minutes on low heat so the coarse spice mixture coats every coin, and switch off before the podi darkens.
tips: Pound the podi coarse, not fine; the gritty texture against the crisp gourd is the point of a vepudu.
Reduce the Guntur chillies to 3 if you are new to Andhra heat levels; the flavour stays intact.
Leftovers make an excellent rice mix the next day: crush the karela slightly and stir through hot rice with a spoon of the same sesame oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with mudda pappu (plain mashed toor dal), hot rice, and a spoonful of ghee, letting the bland dal cushion the podi's fire.

variations.name: Kerala Spicy Karela (Pavakka Thoran)
variations.description: A coastal thoran that softens karela's edge with a moist mantle of fresh grated coconut, green chilli, and shallots, all tempered in coconut oil with mustard seeds and curry leaves. Black pepper, Kerala's own spice, supplies the warmth instead of relentless chilli powder.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed coconut oil carries the fresh, faintly sweet aroma that defines a Kerala thoran

steps: Finely chop 400 g bitter gourd into small dice, mix with 0.5 tsp salt, rest for 15 minutes, then squeeze hard to press out the bitter liquid.
Pulse 1 cup grated coconut with 2 green chillies, 3 shallots, and 0.5 tsp turmeric just two or three times so it stays a coarse, fluffy crumble rather than a paste.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a cheena chatti or kadhai on medium heat, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds for about 30 seconds, then add 15 curry leaves and let them crackle.
Add the remaining 5 sliced shallots and 1 slit green chilli and sauté for 3 minutes until the shallots turn soft and lightly pink at the edges.
Tip in the squeezed karela with the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, sprinkle 0.25 cup water, cover, and cook on low heat for 8-10 minutes, stirring twice, until the gourd is tender but not mushy.

Scatter the coconut mixture and 0.75 tsp coarsely ground black pepper over the karela, toss well, and cook uncovered for 3 minutes on low so the coconut warms through and absorbs the flavours without browning.
tips: Chop the karela small; big pieces stay assertively bitter while fine dice mellows quickly under the coconut.
Add the coconut only at the end and never let it fry to brown, or the thoran loses its fresh, moist character.
A teaspoon of raw coconut oil stirred in off the heat lifts the aroma dramatically.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as part of a Kerala lunch with matta rice, moru curry (spiced buttermilk), and pappadam crumbled over the top for crunch.

variations.name: Gujarati Spicy Karela (Khatta-Meetha Karela)
variations.description: Gujarat answers bitterness with its beloved sweet-sour equation: karela simmered with jaggery powder, tangy amchur, and a gentle sesame-fennel crunch. The result is a glossy, caramel-edged sabzi where sweet, sour, bitter, and hot land in a single balanced bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: Light wood-pressed sunflower oil lets the jaggery glaze shine without competing flavours

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Chemical-free jaggery powder melts into the classic Gujarati gor glaze that tames the karela

steps: Slice 500 g karela into thin rounds, rub with 1 tsp salt, rest 25 minutes, then rinse briefly and squeeze until quite dry.
Warm 3 tbsp Anveshan Sunflower Oil in a kadhai over medium heat, add 1 tsp fennel seeds, and toast them for 30 seconds until they smell sweetly aniseed-like.
Add 1 thinly sliced onion and cook for 4-5 minutes until soft and pale gold, then slide in the karela rounds.
Fry the karela on medium heat for 10-12 minutes, stirring every 2-3 minutes, until the rounds are browned and cooked through with lightly crisp rims.
Lower the heat and stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, and 2 tsp coriander powder, coating the gourd for 1 minute so the spices bloom in the oil without scorching.

Sprinkle 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1.5 tsp amchur over the pan with 2 tbsp water, and toss on low heat for 3-4 minutes until the jaggery melts into a sticky glaze that lacquers every slice.
Turn off the heat and shower 2 tsp sesame seeds over the top, tossing once so they stick to the glaze and add a nutty crunch.
tips: Add the jaggery only after the karela is fully cooked; sugar added early makes the gourd stubbornly firm.
If the glaze turns too thick and sticky, loosen it with a teaspoon of hot water rather than more oil.
This sabzi keeps for 3 days refrigerated and tastes even better the next day as the sweet-sour flavours settle in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Roll it up in warm khapli atta rotlis with a side of kadhi and steamed rice for a proper Gujarati thali experience.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Mix Veg
variations.description: The everyday North Indian sabzi that turns humble carrots, beans, cauliflower and peas into a fiery, masala-coated medley. Green chillies and crushed black pepper give it a clean, sharp heat, while slow-cooked onion-tomato masala in wood-pressed groundnut oil keeps it rustic and deeply savoury.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed and nutty, it stands up to high-heat sautéing without turning acrid

ingredients.name: Mixed vegetables (carrot, beans, cauliflower, peas, potato)

steps: Dice 2 medium potatoes' worth of your 4 cups mixed vegetables into even 1-inch pieces so everything cooks at the same pace; finely chop 2 onions and 3 tomatoes and keep them in separate bowls.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a heavy kadhai over medium heat until it shimmers, then add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle and darken a shade, about 30 seconds.

Add the chopped onions with a pinch of the salt and sauté on medium heat until the edges turn golden brown, 6 to 7 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry until the raw smell disappears, about 1 minute.

Tip in the chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder; cook on medium-low, mashing occasionally, until the masala thickens and oil beads appear at the edges, 5 to 6 minutes.

Add the 4 cups mixed vegetables, 3 slit green chillies and the remaining salt, toss to coat every piece in masala, then cover and cook on low heat for 12 to 15 minutes, stirring twice, until a knife slides easily into the carrot.
Uncover, raise the heat to medium-high and stir-fry for 2 minutes to evaporate excess moisture, then finish with 0.5 tsp crushed black pepper and 3 tbsp chopped coriander leaves and toss well.
tips: Par-boil harder vegetables like carrot and cauliflower for 3 minutes if you want to cut the covered cooking time in half.
If the masala sticks to the pan before the tomatoes soften, splash in 2 tbsp hot water and scrape up the browned bits for extra flavour.
Crush the black pepper just before adding; pre-ground pepper loses the citrusy bite that defines this sabzi.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with phulkas and a bowl of chilled boondi raita to temper the heat; a wedge of lime on the side brightens the whole plate.

variations.name: Bengali Spicy Mix Veg
variations.description: A pungent Kolkata-style charchari where the vegetables cook in sharp mustard oil with nigella seeds and green chillies. The mustard oil is deliberately smoked to mellow its bite, leaving behind a wasabi-like warmth that clings to soft potatoes and pumpkin.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed kachi ghani pungency is the backbone of this charchari; refined oil cannot replicate it

steps: Cut 2 potatoes, 1.5 cups pumpkin and 1 brinjal into chunky 1.5-inch batons and snap 1 cup flat beans in half; keep the brinjal in salted water so it does not blacken while you prep.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a wide kadhai on high until it just begins to smoke and its raw sharpness softens, about 90 seconds, then reduce the flame to medium.
Scatter in 1 tsp nigella seeds and 4 slit green chillies and let them sizzle for 20 seconds until the chillies blister and the kalonji releases its oniony aroma.
Add the drained vegetables with 0.75 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp grated ginger and 1.25 tsp salt, and toss on medium heat for 3 minutes so every piece is stained yellow and glossy.
Pour in 0.5 cup hot water, cover and cook on low for 15 to 18 minutes, stirring gently once, until the pumpkin collapses at the edges and the potato is fork-tender.

Uncover, sprinkle 0.5 tsp sugar and cook on medium heat for 4 to 5 minutes, letting the bottom catch very slightly for the signature charchari char, then rest off the heat for 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Smoking the mustard oil properly is non-negotiable; under-heated oil tastes raw and bitter rather than pleasantly pungent.
The slight sticking at the bottom in the final step is intentional — those caramelised bits are the best part, so scrape them into the sabzi.
Add 1 tsp of the mustard oil raw over the finished dish if you love a sharper Bengali kick.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with steamed gobindobhog rice and a spoon of masoor dal; Bengalis eat this as a first course mixed into hot rice with an extra green chilli on the side.

variations.name: Kerala Spicy Mix Veg
variations.description: A thoran-style dry stir-fry from Malabar kitchens where the vegetables steam under a blanket of fresh grated coconut, curry leaves and crushed cumin. Coconut oil and mustard seeds give it that unmistakable temple-feast fragrance, with green chilli heat rather than powdered spice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed from fresh coconuts, it carries the sweet aroma that defines a true thoran

ingredients.name: Mixed vegetables (carrot, beans, cabbage, green peas)

steps: Finely dice 4 cups of carrot, beans and cabbage into small 0.5-inch bits — thoran vegetables must be cut fine so they cook through by steam alone in minutes.

Pulse 1 cup grated coconut with 3 chopped green chillies, 3 garlic cloves, 0.5 tsp crushed cumin and 0.5 tsp turmeric in a mixer for just 2 short pulses to make a coarse, moist crumble; do not grind it to a paste.

Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadhai over medium heat, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds until they finish spluttering, about 30 seconds, then add 2 dried red chillies and 2 sprigs of curry leaves and fry for 15 seconds until crisp and fragrant.
Add 8 sliced shallots and sauté for 2 to 3 minutes on medium until translucent and lightly pink at the edges, without letting them brown.
Stir in the diced vegetables and 1 tsp salt, sprinkle 3 tbsp water over the top, then cover and steam on low heat for 8 to 10 minutes until the carrot is just tender but still bright.

Spread the coconut crumble over the vegetables, cover again for 3 minutes on the lowest flame so the coconut warms through and perfumes the pan, then toss everything together and switch off before the coconut browns.
tips: Frozen grated coconut works if thawed fully, but squeeze out excess water or the thoran turns soggy instead of fluffy.
Never stir the coconut in over high heat; toasted coconut changes the dish's character from fresh to nutty.
Leftovers make an excellent filling for a khapli-atta wrap with a swipe of coconut chutney.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside matta rice and a tangy pulissery, or as the vegetable course on a banana leaf with pappadam crushed over the top.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Mix Veg
variations.description: A ferociously spiced vepudu built on sun-dried Guntur chillies, the pride of Andhra Pradesh. Sesame oil, tamarind and a roasted chilli-garlic pounded masala coat the vegetables in a brick-red, tangy-hot glaze that demands a mound of rice alongside.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil is the traditional Andhra frying medium; its earthy depth tames the Guntur fire

ingredients.name: Mixed vegetables (potato, beans, brinjal, cluster beans)

steps: Dry-roast 5 Guntur chillies on a low flame for 2 minutes until glossy and brittle, cool them, then pound coarsely with 6 garlic cloves and 0.25 tsp of the salt in a mortar into a rough, fiery paste.
Cut 4 cups of potato, beans, brinjal and cluster beans into finger-length pieces and soak 2 tbsp tamarind pulp from a lime-sized ball in 0.25 cup warm water.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadhai over medium heat; add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tbsp chana dal and fry until the dal turns golden and the seeds pop, about 45 seconds, then add 1 sprig curry leaves.
Add 2 sliced onions and sauté for 5 to 6 minutes on medium heat until deep golden at the edges, then stir in the pounded chilli-garlic paste and fry for 1 minute until the raw garlic smell fades.
Add the vegetables, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt; toss for 2 minutes, then cover and cook on low for 12 minutes, stirring midway, until the potato yields to a spoon.
Pour in the strained tamarind water, raise the heat to medium-high and cook uncovered for 4 to 5 minutes, tossing often, until the liquid reduces to a sticky red glaze that coats every piece.
tips: Guntur chillies vary in heat batch to batch; taste a tiny bit of the pounded paste and drop to 3 chillies if it makes your eyes water instantly.
The pounded (not blended) texture is key — coarse chilli flecks toast in the oil and give the authentic roadside-mess character.
A spoon of the finished tamarind glaze stirred into plain curd makes a quick pachadi-style side.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steaming white rice, a generous spoon of Anveshan Ghee melted on top, and cooling curd rice to finish the meal the Andhra way.

variations.name: Kashmiri Spicy Mix Veg
variations.description: Inspired by the vegetarian wazwan tradition, this take simmers vegetables in a fennel-and-dry-ginger scented yogurt gravy stained gold with genuine Kashmiri saffron. It is aromatic and warming rather than sharply hot, with whole spices blooming in ghee.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee gives the gravy its glossy sheen and carries the saffron aroma the way Kashmiri cooks intend

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: GI-tagged Pampore strands bloomed in warm milk turn the gravy a deep amber no food colour can imitate

ingredients.name: Mixed vegetables (potato, carrot, turnip, peas, cauliflower)

steps: Soak 0.25 tsp Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk and set aside for 15 minutes until the milk turns a deep marigold colour.
Cut 4 cups of potato, carrot, turnip and cauliflower into large 2-inch pieces; Kashmiri gravies use big chunks that hold together during simmering.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot over medium heat and bloom 3 cloves, 3 cardamom pods and a 1-inch cinnamon stick for 30 seconds until they puff and smell sweet.
Add the vegetables and fry on medium-high for 5 to 6 minutes, turning gently, until the potato edges pick up light golden spots.

Lower the flame fully, stir 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 2 tsp fennel powder and 1 tsp dry ginger powder into 1 cup whisked curd, then pour it in while stirring continuously for 2 minutes so the curd does not split.
Add 1 cup hot water and 1.25 tsp salt, cover and simmer on low for 18 to 20 minutes until the turnip is completely tender and the gravy has thickened to a coating consistency.
Swirl in the saffron milk, simmer uncovered for 2 more minutes until the surface glistens amber, and rest for 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Whisk the curd until completely smooth and always add it off a rolling boil; curdled gravy cannot be rescued once split.
Fennel and dry ginger replace onion and garlic here — resist adding either, that restraint is what makes it taste Kashmiri.
Crush the saffron strands lightly between your fingers before soaking to release double the colour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle over steamed long-grain rice with a Kashmiri walnut chutney on the side; a few extra saffron strands on top make it festive enough for guests.

variations.name: Classic Dhaba-style Arbi
variations.description: Highway-dhaba flavour comes from dark-browned onions, a hard-bhuno-ed masala and a generous finish of ghee and hand-crushed kasuri methi. Fried colocasia is simmered in the rich gravy just long enough to soak up the smoke. It is the robust, restaurant-style arbi you mop up with buttered roti.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil browns the onions deep for that dhaba-style base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a generous finishing swirl for the rich, glossy sheen dhaba food is loved for

steps: Pressure-cook 500 g arbi for 2 whistles, cool, peel and halve the pieces.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a heavy kadai on medium-high and fry the arbi for about 8 minutes until deep golden, then lift out.
Crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds in the same oil, add 2 finely chopped onions and fry until dark golden brown, about 9 minutes for that dhaba depth.
Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, cook for 2 minutes, then add 2 chopped tomatoes and cook until fully pulpy and the oil separates, about 6 minutes.
Add 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.25 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder with 3 tbsp water and bhuno the masala hard for 3 minutes until it darkens and glistens.
Fold the arbi back in with 1.25 tsp salt and 1 tsp garam masala, add 0.25 cup water and simmer on low for 6 minutes so the masala coats richly.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the top, swirl in 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, scatter 2 tbsp coriander and serve.
tips: Dhaba flavour comes from browning the onions really dark and bhuno-ing the masala hard; do not rush these two stages.
Crush the kasuri methi between your palms before adding to release its aroma far better than dropping it in whole.
The generous finish of Anveshan Ghee is what gives dhaba food its rich, glossy sheen.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter-smeared tandoori roti or lachha paratha and a raw onion-lemon salad for the full highway-dhaba experience.

variations.name: Bengali Kochu Kalia
variations.description: A kalia is a richer, festive Bengali preparation, and here colocasia simmers in a fragrant gravy tempered with bay leaf, cardamom and cinnamon in smoked mustard oil. Onions and ginger build depth while a touch of jaggery mellows the spice. The finish is glossy and just a little sweet.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked lightly to give the festive kalia its deep, aromatic Bengali base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the Bengali signature that rounds the whole-spice gravy into a mellow richness

steps: Pressure-cook 500 g kochu for 2 whistles, cool, peel and halve.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to a light smoke, then fry the arbi on medium for 7 minutes until golden and set aside.
In the same oil temper 1 bay leaf, 2 cardamom pods, 1 inch cinnamon and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds until fragrant.
Add 2 finely chopped onions and fry until richly golden, about 8 minutes, then add 1.5 tbsp ginger paste and 1 chopped tomato and cook until pulpy, about 5 minutes.
Add 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt with a splash of water and bhuno for 2 minutes, then return the arbi with 0.5 cup water and simmer covered on low for 8 minutes.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.75 tsp garam masala, simmer 2 minutes and serve in the glossy kalia gravy.
tips: Whole garam spices tempered in mustard oil give the kalia its festive, aromatic base.
A touch of Anveshan Jaggery is the Bengali signature that rounds the spice into a mellow richness.
Let the gravy reduce to a thick coat rather than a thin curry for the true kalia texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with luchi or steamed rice at a Sunday lunch, finishing with a little raw mustard oil drizzled on top.

variations.name: Kerala Chembu Roast
variations.description: This rich Kerala roast browns onions dark, then loosens the masala with coconut milk so colocasia glazes in a semi-dry, fennel-scented gravy. Kashmiri chilli lends deep colour without fierce heat while black pepper adds warmth. Curry leaves and coconut oil keep it firmly coastal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: roasts the onions and arbi with the coastal aroma the roast depends on

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a touch to balance the pepper and lift the coconut-milk gravy

steps: Boil 500 g chembu until tender, cool, peel and halve.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil on medium, splutter 0.5 tsp fennel seeds and 2 sprigs curry leaves, then fry the arbi for 6 minutes until golden and push it aside.
Add 2 sliced onions and fry until deep brown, about 8 minutes, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 1 chopped tomato and cook until soft, about 4 minutes.
Add 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 0.5 tsp black pepper and 1 tsp salt, and roast the masala for 3 minutes until dark and fragrant.
Pour in 0.5 cup coconut milk, return the arbi and simmer uncovered on low for 6 minutes until the gravy thickens and clings as a roast.
Finish with 0.75 tsp garam masala and 0.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer 2 minutes and serve as a semi-dry roast.
tips: Kashmiri chilli gives a deep red colour without fierce heat, letting the coconut milk shine.
Add the coconut milk on low heat and do not boil it hard, or it will split.
Browning the onions really dark is key to the deep roast colour and flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with appam, malabar parotta or ghee rice for a rich Kerala-style spread.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Alu Chi Rassa Bhaji
variations.description: This richer Maharashtrian version simmers colocasia in a thin, brothy rassa built on a dark roasted-coconut and onion paste, the kala-masala approach. Goda masala, tamarind and jaggery give the trademark sweet-sour-hot depth. It is meant to be ladled generously over rice or bhakri.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the staple Maharashtrian oil that carries the dark roasted-coconut rassa base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: with the tamarind it delivers the sweet-sour-hot balance of a Maharashtrian rassa

steps: Boil 500 g arbi until tender, cool, peel and halve.
Dry-roast 3 tbsp grated dry coconut until deep golden, then grind with 1 sliced onion into a coarse dark paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, add the remaining chopped onion and fry until golden, about 5 minutes.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the roasted coconut-onion paste and bhuno for 4 minutes until dark and aromatic.
Add 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 2 tsp goda masala and 1 tsp salt with 1 cup water, bring to a simmer, then add the arbi and cook on low for 8 minutes.
Stir in 1 tsp tamarind pulp and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer 3 minutes into a thin spiced rassa and finish with 2 tbsp coriander.
tips: The dark roasted-coconut paste is what gives this rassa its signature Maharashtrian colour and depth.
Goda masala with tamarind and Anveshan Jaggery create the classic sweet-sour-spicy gravy.
Keep the gravy thin and brothy; it is meant to be spooned generously over rice or bhakri.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri or steamed rice, with a wedge of lime and raw onion on the side.

variations.name: Punjabi Makhani Arbi
variations.description: The Punjabi dhaba take goes rich and buttery, simmering fried colocasia in a tomato-heavy makhani gravy softened with cream and finished with plenty of ghee. Kasuri methi and garam masala give it the familiar restaurant warmth. It is indulgent, glossy and made for tandoori breads.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: fries the arbi golden before it goes into the buttery makhani gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the makhani richness comes from a generous finish of ghee swirled through the gravy

steps: Pressure-cook 500 g arbi for 2 whistles, cool, peel and halve, then fry in 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil for 7 minutes until golden and set aside.
Blanch 4 tomatoes, blend to a smooth puree, and separately grind 1 onion to a paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, add the onion paste and 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook until pale gold, about 6 minutes.
Pour in the tomato puree with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt, and simmer on low for 12 minutes until it thickens and the ghee floats to the surface.
Fold in the fried arbi with 0.5 cup water and simmer for 6 minutes so it soaks up the gravy, then stir in 3 tbsp cream and 1 tsp garam masala.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the top, simmer 2 minutes and serve rich and glossy.
tips: Cook the tomato gravy long and slow until the fat separates; that slow simmer is what makes a makhani taste luxurious.
Add the cream on low heat right at the end so it stays silky and does not split.
For a smoother finish you can strain the tomato puree before cooking.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or lachha paratha and a side of sirka onions for an indulgent Punjabi meal.

variations.name: Classic Dhaba-style Capsicum
variations.description: Chunky capsicum cooked down in a robust, oil-glossed onion-tomato masala with kasuri methi and garam masala, the way roadside dhabas turn a humble pepper into something crave-worthy. Semi-dry, smoky and generously spiced.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The generous slick of nutty oil is what gives dhaba capsicum its glossy, indulgent finish.

steps: Deseed 3 large capsicums and cut into thick 1.5-inch chunks, finely chop 2 onions, and chop 3 tomatoes for a robust dhaba-style base.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a kadhai over medium until it shimmers, then crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for around 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add the onion and fry for 6 to 7 minutes until deep golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook a minute until the raw aroma fades.
Add the tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, and cook 8 minutes until the masala thickens and the oil pools at the edges.
Tip in the capsicum chunks with 1 tsp salt, toss to coat, cover and cook on medium-low for 8 minutes until softened but still holding shape.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the pan and add 1 tsp garam masala, stirring 2 minutes to bloom the aroma.
Uncover, raise the heat for a minute to dry the masala, then finish with 2 tbsp fresh coriander.
tips: Cut the capsicum into big chunks so it holds up to the longer dhaba-style cooking without disintegrating.
For the signature smoky note, give it a quick charcoal dhungar for two minutes at the end.
Let the masala fry until the oil separates before the capsicum goes in; that is the dhaba secret.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with buttery tandoori roti and a raw onion salad splashed with lemon and chaat masala.

variations.name: Punjabi Dhaba-style Capsicum
variations.description: The indulgent Amritsari version, where capsicum bathes in a ghee-and-butter masala finished with cream and extra kasuri methi. Rich, glossy and pure highway-dhaba comfort.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee is the base of the buttery Punjabi masala that makes this version so rich.

steps: Deseed and cube 3 capsicums into 1.5-inch pieces, grate 2 onions, and blend 3 tomatoes into a smooth puree for a velvety gravy.
Melt 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and let 1 tsp cumin seeds sizzle for 15 to 20 seconds until they release their toasty aroma.
Add the grated onion and cook 7 minutes until richly browned, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry a minute until glossy.
Pour in the tomato puree with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, and simmer 9 minutes until the ghee floats clear.
Add the capsicum with 1 tsp salt, stir to coat, cover and cook 7 to 8 minutes until tender but not collapsed.
Crush 1.5 tbsp kasuri methi over the pan, add 2 tbsp cream and 1 tsp garam masala, and simmer 3 minutes until the sauce turns luscious.
Melt 1 tbsp butter over the top just before serving for a glossy dhaba finish.
tips: Grate rather than chop the onion for the smoothest, most restaurant-like gravy.
Add the cream off the boil so it blends without splitting.
A pinch of crushed dried fenugreek added right at the end lifts the whole dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with laccha paratha or naan and a wedge of lemon to balance the richness.

variations.name: Rajasthani Dhaba-style Capsicum
variations.description: A fiery desert version where capsicum is smothered in a garlicky soaked-red-chilli paste and cooked in pungent mustard oil, with besan added to bind the masala the Marwari way. Bold, dry and deeply spiced.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Smoked and cooled, its sharpness stands up to the aggressive dried-chilli and garlic paste.

steps: Soak 6 dried red chillies in warm water for 15 minutes and grind with 8 garlic cloves into a coarse paste, while you cube 3 capsicums and chop 2 onions and 2 tomatoes.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until it just smokes, lower the flame, and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds with 0.25 tsp asafoetida for 15 seconds.
Add the chopped onion and fry 6 minutes until golden, then add the chilli-garlic paste and cook 3 minutes until the raw garlic mellows into a roasted aroma.
In a dry corner of the pan, roast 1.5 tbsp besan for a minute until nutty, then mix it into the masala with the chopped tomato, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 2 tsp coriander powder.
Cook 5 minutes until the tomato breaks down and the besan thickens the masala into a clinging coat.
Add the capsicum with 1 tsp salt, toss well, cover and cook on low for 8 minutes until softened yet still firm.
Uncover and stir on high for 2 minutes to dry the masala before serving hot.
tips: Roasting the besan first is essential; raw besan tastes pasty and dulls the masala.
Use milder Kashmiri or byadgi chillies if you want the colour without punishing heat.
This travels well as a dry sabzi and actually tastes better after an hour of resting.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra or missi roti and a glass of chaas to cool the desert heat.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Dhaba-style Capsicum
variations.description: A Vidarbha-style capsicum sabzi darkened with fragrant goda masala and a nutty peanut-coconut kut, balanced with a little jaggery. Earthy, warm and distinctly Maharashtrian.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The everyday oil of Maharashtra, it carries goda masala's dark, sweet-spiced aroma perfectly.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The gentle sweet note that completes the classic goda-masala flavour balance.

steps: Deseed and cube 3 capsicums, chop 2 onions and 2 tomatoes, and keep 2 tbsp peanut powder and 3 tbsp grated coconut ready for the kut.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.75 tsp cumin seeds and 10 curry leaves for about 20 seconds.
Add the onion and fry 6 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook a minute until aromatic.
Mix in the tomato with 1.5 tbsp goda masala and cook 6 minutes until the tomato softens and the masala turns dark and glossy.
Add the capsicum, grated coconut, peanut powder and 1 tsp salt, splash in a little hot water, cover and cook on medium-low for 8 minutes until tender.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook 2 minutes so the sweet-savoury balance settles.
Rest a couple of minutes off the heat and serve garnished with extra coconut.
tips: Freshly ground goda masala makes an enormous difference to the depth of this dish.
The peanut-coconut kut thickens as it sits, so add a splash of water when reheating.
Keep the capsicum slightly firm so it contrasts with the soft, nutty masala.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri or soft chapati and a spoon of plain yoghurt on the side.

variations.name: Bengali Dhaba-style Capsicum
variations.description: A Bengali spin on the dhaba pepper, tempered in mustard oil with panch phoron and finished with a mustard-poppy paste for a sharp, aromatic gravy. Pungent, slightly sweet and unmistakably from the east.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Essential for the pungent bite that carries the mustard-poppy paste in Bengali cooking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The gentle sweetness Bengalis use to soften the mustard paste's edge.

steps: Grind 1 tbsp mustard seeds with 1 tbsp poppy seeds and 3 green chillies into a smooth paste, then cube 3 capsicums, chop 1 onion and 2 tomatoes.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until it lightly smokes, cool briefly, then temper 1 tsp panch phoron with 1 bay leaf until the seeds crackle.
Add the chopped onion and fry on medium for 5 minutes until soft and golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger paste and cook a minute.
Mix in the tomato with 0.75 tsp turmeric and cook 4 to 5 minutes until it breaks down into the oil.
Add the capsicum with 1 tsp salt, splash in half a cup of hot water, cover and simmer on low for 8 minutes until tender.
Lower the heat and fold in the mustard-poppy paste with 0.75 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, cooking gently for 3 minutes so the mustard warms without turning bitter.
Rest off the heat and serve with a raw drizzle of mustard oil for aroma.
tips: Soak the mustard seeds before grinding and add a pinch of salt to the paste to keep it from turning bitter.
Never boil the mustard paste hard; keep the flame low the moment it goes in.
Poppy seeds thicken the gravy naturally, so hold back on extra water once the paste is in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice and a wedge of lime for a classic Bengali lunch.

variations.name: Classic Dhaba-style Karela
variations.description: Crisp-fried bitter gourd folded into a bold, oil-glossed onion-tomato masala with kasuri methi and garam masala, the way a highway dhaba would serve it. Robust, semi-dry and surprisingly craveable once the bitterness mellows.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The generous nutty oil is what gives the dhaba masala its glossy, robust body.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Balances the bitterness against the tangy tomato masala in true dhaba fashion.

steps: Slice 500 g bitter gourd into rings, rub with 1 tsp salt, rest 20 minutes, then squeeze out the juices and pat dry.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a kadhai over medium and shallow-fry the rings for 9 minutes until crisp and golden, then set them aside.
In the same oil crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 15 seconds, add 2 chopped onions, and fry 6 to 7 minutes until deep golden.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, cook a minute, then add 3 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, cooking 8 minutes until the oil separates.
Return the fried karela with 0.5 tsp remaining salt, toss to coat, cover and cook on low for 6 minutes so the masala soaks in.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the pan, add 1 tsp garam masala and 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, and stir 2 minutes to bloom the flavours.
Uncover, raise the heat for a minute to dry the masala, and serve hot.
tips: Fry the karela to a real crisp before it meets the masala so it holds up in the gravy.
The 20-minute salting is essential to tame the sharpest bitterness.
A quick charcoal dhungar at the end lends the authentic smoky dhaba note.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with buttered tandoori roti and a raw onion-lemon salad on the side.

variations.name: Punjabi Dhaba-style Karela
variations.description: The indulgent Punjabi dhaba version, bitter gourd bathed in a ghee-and-butter onion-tomato masala with extra kasuri methi and a swirl of cream. Rich, glossy and full of highway comfort.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee builds the buttery Punjabi masala that turns bitter gourd indulgent.

steps: Slice 500 g bitter gourd into rings, rub with 1 tsp salt, rest 20 minutes, then squeeze dry to draw off the bitterness.
Melt 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium and fry the karela rings for 9 minutes until crisp and browned, then lift them out.
In the same ghee crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, add 2 grated onions, and fry 7 minutes until richly browned, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook a minute.
Add 3 pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, and simmer 9 minutes until the ghee floats clear on top.
Return the karela with 0.5 tsp remaining salt, cover and cook on low for 6 minutes so the rings absorb the masala.
Crush 1.5 tbsp kasuri methi over the pan and stir in 2 tbsp cream, simmering 3 minutes until luscious.
Melt 1 tbsp butter over the top just before serving for a glossy dhaba finish.
tips: Grate the onions for a smoother, richer gravy that clings to the karela.
Add the cream off the boil so it blends in without splitting.
The richness here mellows the bitterness, making this a good gateway karela for sceptics.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with laccha paratha or naan and a wedge of lemon to cut the richness.

variations.name: Bengali Dhaba-style Karela
variations.description: A Bengali-inflected dhaba karela tempered in mustard oil with panch phoron and finished with a mustard paste, the bitterness set against sharp, aromatic pungency. Sweet-sharp and quite unlike the North Indian norm.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Its pungency is the traditional Bengali foil to bitter gourd, carrying the mustard paste.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The Bengali sweetness that softens both the mustard's bite and the karela's bitterness.

steps: Slice 500 g bitter gourd into rings, rub with 0.75 tsp salt, rest 15 minutes, then squeeze dry, and blend 1.5 tbsp mustard with 3 green chillies into a paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until it lightly smokes, cool briefly, then fry the karela rings for 8 minutes until crisp and set them aside.
In the same oil temper 1 tsp panch phoron with 1 bay leaf until the seeds crackle, then add 1 sliced large onion and fry 5 minutes until golden.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger paste, then add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.75 tsp turmeric and cook 5 minutes until the tomato breaks down.
Return the karela with 0.5 tsp remaining salt, cover and cook on low for 6 minutes so the rings soften into the masala.
Lower the heat and fold in the mustard paste and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, cooking gently 3 minutes so the mustard warms without turning bitter.
Serve with a raw drizzle of mustard oil for the full aroma.
tips: Never boil the mustard paste hard or it turns bitter; keep the flame low once it goes in.
Add a pinch of salt to the mustard while grinding to keep it mellow.
The double bitterness of karela and mustard is balanced by the jaggery, so taste and adjust.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice and a wedge of lime for a classic Bengali plate.

variations.name: Rajasthani Dhaba-style Karela
variations.description: A fiery Marwari-style dhaba karela cooked in mustard oil with a garlicky soaked-red-chilli paste and a tangy amchur finish. Bold, dry and built for the desert palate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Smoked and cooled, its sharpness stands up to the aggressive chilli-garlic paste.

steps: Slice 500 g bitter gourd into rings, rub with 1 tsp salt, rest 20 minutes, then squeeze dry, and grind 5 soaked dried red chillies with 8 garlic cloves into a coarse paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until it just smokes, lower the flame, and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds with 0.25 tsp asafoetida for 15 seconds.
Add 2 chopped onions and fry 6 minutes until golden, then add the chilli-garlic paste and cook 3 minutes until the raw garlic mellows.
Add the squeezed karela rings with 2 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp remaining salt, and stir-fry on medium for 10 minutes until browned and tender.
Cook uncovered a further 3 minutes, stirring, so the dry masala clings to the rings.
Sprinkle 1.5 tsp amchur and 0.75 tsp garam masala and toss 2 minutes for a bright, tangy finish.
Rest briefly and serve, the heat settling into a rounded warmth.
tips: Use Kashmiri or byadgi chillies for colour with less searing heat if you prefer.
Keep this dry and dark; a splash of water would dull the desert-style masala.
Amchur added at the end keeps its bright sourness against the deep chilli heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra or missi roti and a glass of buttermilk to cool the palate.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Dhaba-style Karela
variations.description: A Vidarbha-style dhaba karela darkened with goda masala and a nutty peanut-coconut kut, the bitterness balanced by jaggery. Earthy, warm and distinctly Maharashtrian in its sweet-spiced depth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The everyday Maharashtrian oil that carries goda masala's dark, sweet-spiced aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Essential to the goda-masala balance and to softening the karela's bitterness.

steps: Slice 500 g bitter gourd into rings, rub with 1 tsp salt, rest 20 minutes, then squeeze dry to remove the bitter juices.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium and fry the karela rings for 9 minutes until crisp, then lift them out.
In the same oil splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.75 tsp cumin seeds and 10 curry leaves, then add 2 chopped onions and fry 6 minutes until golden.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, add 2 chopped tomatoes with 1.5 tbsp goda masala, and cook 6 minutes until the masala turns dark and glossy.
Return the karela with the peanut powder, grated coconut and 0.5 tsp remaining salt, splash in a little hot water, cover and cook on low for 6 minutes.
Stir in 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook 2 minutes so the sweet-savoury balance settles.
Rest off the heat and serve garnished with a little extra coconut.
tips: Freshly ground goda masala makes a marked difference to the depth of this dish.
The peanut-coconut kut thickens as it stands, so loosen with water when reheating.
Frying the karela first keeps it from going mushy in the nutty masala.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri or soft chapati and a spoon of plain yoghurt.

variations.name: Classic Dhaba-style Mix Veg
variations.description: The roadside-dhaba favourite where cauliflower, carrot, beans, peas and potato simmer in a glossy onion-tomato masala loosened with kasuri methi. A generous slick of wood-pressed groundnut oil and a smoky final tadka give it that unmistakable highway-truck-stop richness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Its nutty depth is the backbone of dhaba flavour; do not substitute a bland refined oil.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A whisper of it rounds off the sharp tomato tang the way dhaba cooks use a pinch of sugar.

steps: Cut 500 g mixed vegetables into even bite-sized pieces, keeping harder potato and carrot slightly smaller so everything cooks at the same rate; finely chop 2 onions and puree 3 tomatoes.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium until it shimmers, then crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 20 seconds until fragrant and lightly darkened.

Add the chopped onion and fry on medium-high for 6 to 7 minutes, stirring often, until deep golden at the edges, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until the raw smell disappears.
Pour in the tomato puree with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, and cook on medium for 8 to 10 minutes until the oil separates and pools at the sides.
Tip in the mixed vegetables with 1.25 tsp salt, toss to coat in the masala, add a splash of hot water, cover and cook on low for 12 to 15 minutes until fork-tender but not mushy.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi between your palms and sprinkle it in with 1 tsp garam masala and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, stirring gently for 2 minutes so the flavours bloom.
Finish with 3 tbsp chopped fresh coriander, cover off the heat for 5 minutes, and serve hot.
tips: Blanch the cauliflower and beans in salted boiling water for 2 minutes first if you want the sabzi ready faster and evenly cooked.
For a smoky dhaba edge, place a small steel bowl in the pan, add a live piece of charcoal with a few drops of oil, cover for 2 minutes, then remove.
Leftovers thicken overnight; loosen with a splash of hot water rather than more oil when reheating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile into a steel thali alongside laccha paratha, a raw onion-and-lemon salad and a bowl of boondi raita for the full highway-dhaba experience.

variations.name: Punjabi Dhaba-style Mix Veg
variations.description: The full-fat Amritsari treatment: the same medley of vegetables cooked in ghee and finished with a knob of butter for a velvety, restaurant-style sheen. Extra kasuri methi and a cream swirl make it the richest version on the menu.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee gives this Punjabi version its signature buttery aroma and golden colour.

steps: Chop 500 g mixed vegetables into neat cubes, grate or finely chop 2 onions, and blend 3 tomatoes into a smooth puree so the gravy turns silky rather than chunky.
Melt 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan over medium heat and let 1 tsp cumin seeds sizzle for 15 to 20 seconds until they release their toasty aroma.
Fry the onion for 7 to 8 minutes until richly browned, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, and cook another minute until glossy and no longer raw-smelling.
Stir in the tomato puree along with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, then simmer 10 minutes until the ghee floats clear on top.
Fold in the vegetables and 1.25 tsp salt, splash in half a cup of hot water, cover and cook gently for 12 to 14 minutes until just tender.
Crush 1.5 tbsp kasuri methi over the pan, add 1 tsp garam masala and 2 tbsp cream, and simmer 3 minutes until the sauce clings to the vegetables.
Slide 1 tbsp butter over the top just before serving and let it melt into a glossy finish.
tips: Grating the onion instead of chopping gives the smoother, ghee-laced texture Punjabi dhabas are known for.
Add the cream off the boil to stop it splitting, and hold back a little to swirl on top at the table.
Skip the butter and cream and this doubles as a lighter everyday sabzi without losing the ghee aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter-brushed tandoori roti or jeera rice, and a wedge of lemon to cut through the richness.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Dhaba-style Mix Veg
variations.description: A Vidarbha-style rendition where fragrant goda masala and a handful of roasted peanuts and coconut transform the mix veg into something sweet, dark and nutty. Wood-pressed groundnut oil keeps it earthy and true to the region.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the everyday cooking fat of Maharashtra and marries beautifully with goda masala.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The gentle sweetness is essential to the classic Maharashtrian goda-masala balance.

steps: Dice 500 g mixed vegetables, finely chop 2 onions and 2 tomatoes, and keep 2 tbsp roasted peanut powder and 3 tbsp grated coconut within reach for the masala.
Warm 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds followed by 1 tsp cumin seeds until they pop, about 20 seconds.
Add the onion and saute for 6 minutes until soft and golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook a further minute until aromatic.
Mix in the chopped tomato with 1.5 tbsp goda masala, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder, and cook for 6 to 7 minutes until the tomato collapses and the masala turns dark and glossy.
Add the vegetables, grated coconut, peanut powder and 1.25 tsp salt, pour in half a cup of hot water, cover and simmer on low for 14 minutes until tender and the gravy thickens.
Stir in 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and let it cook for 2 minutes so the sweet-savoury balance settles.
Rest covered for 5 minutes off the heat and serve garnished with a little extra coconut.
tips: Toast and grind your own goda masala fresh if you can; its dark, clove-and-sesame notes are what set this apart.
Use fresh grated coconut for body, or desiccated coconut soaked in a spoon of warm water in a pinch.
This sabzi tastes even better the next day once the goda masala has fully permeated the vegetables.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with jowar bhakri or soft phulka and a dollop of plain yoghurt to temper the warm spice.

variations.name: Rajasthani Dhaba-style Mix Veg
variations.description: A fiery desert-highway version built on soaked whole dried red chillies and a garlic-forward paste, using yoghurt to carry the heat where water is scarce. Bold, smoky and unapologetically spicy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Heated to smoking then cooled slightly, its pungency stands up to the aggressive chilli heat.

steps: Soak 6 dried red chillies in warm water for 15 minutes, then grind them with 8 garlic cloves into a coarse red paste while you dice 500 g vegetables and chop 2 onions and 2 tomatoes.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until it just begins to smoke, lower the flame, and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 15 seconds to mellow the oil's sharpness.
Fry the onion for 6 minutes until golden, then add the chilli-garlic paste and cook on medium for 3 minutes until the raw garlic smell gives way to a deep roasted aroma.
Add the chopped tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 2 tsp coriander powder and cook 6 minutes until pulpy, then lower the heat and whisk in 0.5 cup yoghurt slowly so it does not curdle.
Stir in the vegetables and 1.25 tsp salt, add a small splash of water, cover and cook on low for 14 minutes until tender and coated in the fiery masala.
Sprinkle 1 tsp garam masala, simmer 2 minutes, then scatter 2 tbsp fresh coriander over the top.
Rest 5 minutes before serving so the heat settles into a rounded warmth.
tips: Use Kashmiri-type dried chillies for colour with milder heat, or byadgi for a deep red without scorching your palate.
Whisk the yoghurt smooth and add it off the boil, stirring constantly, to keep the gravy from splitting.
A spoon of the chilli-garlic paste stirred into leftover dal makes an excellent next-day meal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra roti and a cooling side of sliced cucumber and raw onion to balance the punch.

variations.name: Bengali Dhaba-style Mix Veg
variations.description: Inspired by the beloved chhanchra and labra tradition, this version is tempered in pungent mustard oil with panch phoron and finished with a smear of mustard paste. Sweet, sharp and deeply aromatic in the Bengali way.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Non-negotiable here; its nose-tingling pungency defines authentic Bengali vegetable cooking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The characteristic Bengali touch of sweetness that offsets the mustard's bite.

steps: Cut 500 g mixed vegetables into fingers, chop 1 onion and 2 tomatoes, and make a smooth paste of 1 tbsp mustard with 2 slit green chillies and a pinch of salt.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until it smokes lightly, cool for 10 seconds, then temper 1 tsp panch phoron with 2 dried red chillies and 1 bay leaf until the seeds crackle.
Add the chopped onion and fry on medium for 5 minutes until soft and pale gold, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger paste and cook a minute until fragrant.
Mix in the tomato with 0.75 tsp turmeric and cook 5 minutes until it breaks down, then add the vegetables and 1.25 tsp salt and stir to coat.
Splash in half a cup of hot water, cover and cook on low for 13 to 15 minutes until the vegetables are tender and most of the liquid has reduced.
Lower the heat and fold in the mustard paste and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, cooking gently for 3 minutes so the mustard warms without turning bitter.
Rest 5 minutes off the heat and serve with a raw drizzle of mustard oil on top for authentic aroma.
tips: Never boil mustard paste hard or it turns bitter; keep the flame low once it goes in.
A classic labra uses pumpkin, radish and sweet potato in the mix; add them for a more traditional Bengali profile.
The raw mustard-oil drizzle at the end is what Bengali households swear by, so do not skip it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice and a squeeze of lime, or alongside khichuri on a rainy day.

variations.name: Classic Dry Arbi
variations.description: Boiled colocasia is flattened and shallow-fried until genuinely crisp, then dusted with dry spices and amchur so nothing turns soggy. Ajwain and cumin in the oil keep it savoury and easy on the stomach. This is the crunchy, no-gravy version made to be eaten with dal and rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil crisps the flattened arbi to a clean, non-greasy crunch

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: drizzled over the crisp arbi at the very end for aroma and a final glossy sheen

steps: Boil 500 g arbi until just tender, cool, peel and gently flatten each piece with your palm so it fries crisp.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a wide pan on medium and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.5 tsp ajwain until fragrant.
Lay the flattened arbi in a single layer and shallow-fry undisturbed for 4 minutes, then flip and fry another 4 minutes until both sides are golden and crisp.
Lower the heat and sprinkle 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt evenly over the arbi.
Toss gently for 3 minutes so the spices toast and cling without breaking the crisp pieces, adding 1 tsp amchur in the last minute.
Drizzle 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the top, toss once, scatter 2 tbsp coriander and serve immediately while crunchy.
tips: Flattening the boiled arbi before frying dramatically increases the crisp surface; it is the beloved trick for dry arbi.
Add the dry spices only after the arbi is crisp; adding them earlier makes them burn and the arbi go soft.
Serve straight away, as dry arbi loses its crunch as it sits.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a crisp dry side with dal-rice and yogurt, or pile into a roll with mint chutney for a quick snack.

variations.name: Bengali Kochu Bhaja
variations.description: A Bengali bhaja treats colocasia like a crisp fry, tossing thin coins in smoked mustard oil with nigella and dried red chilli. Ginger and green chilli lend a fresh bite while the finish stays completely dry. It is meant to open a rice meal, eaten with the first few mouthfuls.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked lightly to mellow its bite, it gives the bhaja its unmistakable Bengali aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a whisper of sweetness that offsets the pungent mustard oil in the dry bhaja

steps: Boil 500 g kochu until tender, cool, peel and slice into thin coins so they crisp fast.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, then lower to medium so its bite mellows.
Temper 0.5 tsp nigella seeds and 2 dried red chillies for about 15 seconds, then add 1 tsp grated ginger and 2 slit green chillies.
Add the arbi coins and fry uncovered, turning often, for about 12 minutes until deeply golden and crisp at the edges.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt and toss for 2 minutes to coat.
Finish with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder for a whisper of sweetness, toss once and serve dry and hot.
tips: Slice the coins thin and keep the bhaja moving so they crisp evenly without sticking.
A light smoke on the mustard oil is what gives Bengali bhaja its signature aroma.
