Keep it bone-dry; this is meant to be eaten with the first mouthfuls of rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a crisp opener over hot rice with a drizzle of raw mustard oil and a green chilli on the side.

variations.name: Kerala Chembu Mezhukkupuratti
variations.description: Mezhukkupuratti means oil-coated, and this Kerala stir-fry glazes colocasia fingers in coconut oil with a rough crush of shallot, garlic and pepper. Curry leaves and mustard seeds crackle in first, then everything is slow-tossed until glossy and dry. It has no gravy, just a warm, peppery shine.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: glazes the arbi and gives the mezhukkupuratti its glossy Kerala finish and aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a touch to round the pepper heat and lift the shallot-garlic glaze

steps: Boil 500 g chembu until just done, cool, peel and cut into thick fingers.
Crush 6 shallots and 4 garlic cloves coarsely with 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp black pepper into a rough rub.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil on medium, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 2 dried red chillies and 2 sprigs curry leaves.
Add the arbi fingers and 1 tsp salt and fry for 6 minutes until the edges turn golden.
Add the crushed shallot-spice rub and stir-fry on low for about 8 minutes, letting it coat and glaze the arbi as the coconut oil shimmers.
Finish with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, toss and serve glossy and dry.
tips: Mezhukkupuratti means oil-coated; keep the flame low so the masala glazes rather than burns.
The shallot-garlic crush, not a fine paste, gives the dish its rustic Kerala character.
Coconut oil solidifies as it cools, so serve warm for the best glossy finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with rice and moru curry, or as a dry side to a plate of sambar-rice.

variations.name: Andhra Chama Dumpa Vepudu
variations.description: Chama dumpa is the Telugu name for colocasia, and this vepudu coats it in rice flour before frying for an extra-crisp shell. A tempering of toasted chana and urad dal, garlic and curry leaves sets the base, then Guntur chilli brings the fire. It is crackling, red-hot and made for rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil takes the heat for a crackling-crisp Andhra vepudu

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: rounds the fierce Guntur heat so the fry is fiery but not one-dimensional

steps: Boil 500 g chama dumpa until tender, cool, peel and cut into thick slices, then toss with 1 tbsp rice flour and 0.5 tsp turmeric to coat.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium and shallow-fry the coated arbi for about 8 minutes until crisp and golden, then push to one side of the pan.
In the same oil temper 1 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, 1 tbsp chana dal and 1 tbsp urad dal until the dals brown.
Add 5 crushed garlic cloves and 2 sprigs curry leaves and let them crackle for 20 seconds.
Toss the crisp arbi back through the tempering with 1.5 tsp Guntur red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt for 3 minutes until fiery red and coated.
Add 0.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder to round the heat, toss once and serve crackling hot.
tips: The rice-flour coat is the secret to an extra-crisp vepudu that stays crunchy longer.
Toast the chana and urad dal well; their nutty crunch defines the tempering.
Guntur chilli is very hot, so adjust to taste and let the Anveshan Jaggery soften the edge.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rice, a spoon of ghee and a bowl of pappu, or as a fierce side to curd rice.

variations.name: Gujarati Sukhi Arbi
variations.description: Gujarat keeps this dry version light and nutty, tossing pan-fried colocasia in a coarse peanut-sesame crush spiked with a little jaggery and lemon. Ajwain and green chilli keep it fresh and digestible. It stays dry but glistens with a mildly sweet, savoury coat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the classic Gujarati oil, light enough to keep this dry sabzi from feeling heavy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a small spoon for the gentle sweet edge Gujarati sabzis are known for

steps: Pressure-cook 500 g arbi for 2 whistles, cool, peel and cut into thick slices.
Dry-roast 3 tbsp peanuts and 1 tbsp sesame seeds until nutty, then crush coarsely together.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp ajwain, then add 2 slit green chillies.
Add the arbi slices and shallow-fry for 8 minutes until golden and crisp at the edges.
Lower the heat, add 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp salt, the crushed peanut-sesame mix and 0.75 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, and toss for 3 minutes to coat.
Switch off, squeeze in 1 tbsp lemon juice, toss once and serve dry and warm.
tips: Roast and crush the peanuts and sesame just before using so the coat stays fragrant and crunchy.
Add the lemon off the heat so its freshness is not cooked away.
A pinch of ajwain keeps this bean-and-tuber sabzi light on the stomach.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulka and a bowl of chaas, or as a dry sabzi in a Gujarati thali with dal and rice.

variations.name: Classic Dry Karela
variations.description: A simple dry-fry of salted bitter gourd tossed with onions and a light dusting of spices until crisp and caramelised. Minimal masala, maximum crunch, with a touch of jaggery to round the bitter edge.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Its high smoke point crisps the karela rings evenly for the best dry-fry texture.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Just enough to soften the bitterness without turning the dry sabzi sweet.

steps: Slice 500 g bitter gourd into thin rings, rub with 1 tsp salt, rest 20 minutes, then squeeze firmly and pat dry to remove the bitter juices.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium and shallow-fry the rings for 9 to 10 minutes until golden and crisp, then push to one side.
In a clear patch of the pan crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 15 seconds, add 2 sliced onions, and fry 6 minutes until browned and sweet.
Lower the heat and dust in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder with 0.5 tsp remaining salt, tossing to coat the karela and onions.
Cook uncovered for 4 minutes, stirring, so the spices toast on without any liquid.
Sprinkle 0.75 tsp amchur and 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, toss for 2 minutes until glossy and balanced.
Serve hot while the rings still have their crunch.
tips: Squeeze the salted karela really well; excess moisture is the enemy of a crisp dry-fry.
Slice the onions thin so they caramelise in the same time as the karela.
Add the jaggery and amchur only at the end so they glaze rather than burn.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a crunchy side with dal-rice and a spoon of ghee over the rice.

variations.name: Punjabi Dry Karela
variations.description: A ghee-rich Punjabi dry karela with plenty of caramelised onion, ground fennel and a squeeze of amchur. Robust, aromatic and cooked till the rings turn sweet and jammy at the edges.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee caramelises the onions and karela into a rich, jammy Punjabi dry sabzi.

steps: Slice 500 g bitter gourd thin, rub with 1 tsp salt, rest 20 minutes, then squeeze dry to draw out the bitterness.
Melt 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and fry the karela rings for 9 minutes until crisp and browned, then lift out.
In the same ghee crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, add 3 thinly sliced onions, and cook 8 minutes until deeply caramelised and jammy.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook a minute, then add 1 tbsp fennel powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder off the direct heat.
Return the karela with 0.5 tsp remaining salt, toss well, and cook uncovered on low for 5 minutes so the spices meld.
Sprinkle 1 tsp amchur and toss for a minute to add a bright tang.
Rest briefly and serve, when the onions and karela have melded into a sweet-savoury tangle.
tips: Caramelising the onions slowly is what gives this its rich, almost jammy Punjabi character.
Ground fennel adds a warm sweetness that pairs beautifully with the bitter karela.
Keep it dry; if it looks wet, raise the heat for a minute before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tandoori roti or plain paratha and a dollop of thick yoghurt.

variations.name: Bengali Dry Karela
variations.description: A minimalist Bengali korola bhaja, the rings shallow-fried in mustard oil with just turmeric and salt until crackling crisp, then tempered with nigella. Sharp, clean and eaten first to open the appetite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Mustard oil gives korola bhaja its signature pungent crackle and golden crust.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A mere whisper of sweetness, the restrained Bengali touch against the deliberate bitterness.

steps: Slice 500 g bitter gourd into thin rounds, rub with 0.75 tsp salt and 1 tsp turmeric, and rest 15 minutes before squeezing out the juices.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until it just smokes, cool for 10 seconds, then temper 0.75 tsp nigella seeds with 2 slit green chillies for 15 seconds.
Add the karela rounds and spread them in a single layer, frying on medium for 10 minutes and turning occasionally until deeply crisp and browned.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp remaining salt and toss for a minute so they cling to the crackling rings.
Add 0.75 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and toss 1 minute just until it melts and lightly glazes.
Turn off the heat and let the karela rest for 2 minutes to firm up further.
Serve with a raw drizzle of mustard oil for the true Bengali aroma.
tips: Fry patiently in a single layer; crowding the pan steams the karela instead of crisping it.
Keep it deliberately sharp and bitter, using only a hint of jaggery.
Traditionally the first bite of a Bengali meal, served with a little plain rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at the start of the meal with steamed rice and a spoon of ghee.

variations.name: Andhra Dry Karela
variations.description: A fiery Andhra kakarakaya vepudu, the bitter gourd stir-fried in sesame oil and coated in a roasted Guntur-chilli and sesame podi. Hot, nutty and boldly spiced in the coastal Andhra style.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Sesame oil lends the earthy nuttiness Andhra vepudu is known for and crisps the karela.

steps: Slice 500 g bitter gourd thin, rub with 1 tsp salt, rest 20 minutes, then squeeze dry, and grind 2 tbsp roasted sesame seeds coarse for the podi.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil over medium and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 1 tsp urad dal with 12 curry leaves until the dal turns golden.
Add 6 crushed garlic cloves and the karela rings and stir-fry on medium for 10 minutes until crisp and browned.
Lower the heat, sprinkle in 1.5 tsp Guntur red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp remaining salt, and toss for 2 minutes so the spices toast onto the karela.
Add the ground sesame podi and toss for 2 minutes until it clings in a dry, nutty crust.
Cook uncovered a final minute so no moisture remains.
Serve hot straight from the pan while the podi is crisp.
tips: Guntur chilli is intensely hot; scale it back to 1 tsp if you are unsure.
Roast the sesame fresh and cool it before grinding so the podi stays dry and loose.
A splash more sesame oil at the end deepens the nutty flavour if you like it richer.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rice, a spoon of ghee and a bowl of pappu charu to balance the heat.

variations.name: Gujarati Dry Karela
variations.description: A crisp, sweet-and-sour Gujarati kadva marcha style karela sambharo, coated in sesame and jaggery with a lemony finish. Crunchy, glossy and gently sweet in the classic Kathiawadi manner.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The classic Gujarati oil that crisps the karela and carries the sesame beautifully.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Delivers the pronounced sweet-sour Gujarati balance that makes bitter gourd so moreish.

steps: Slice 500 g bitter gourd thin, rub with 1 tsp salt, rest 20 minutes, then squeeze out the bitter juices and pat dry.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 2 tbsp sesame seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida for 15 seconds until the sesame pops.
Add the karela rings and stir-fry on medium for 10 minutes until golden and crisp at the edges.
Lower the heat, dust in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp coriander-cumin powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp remaining salt, and toss to coat evenly.
Cook uncovered for 3 minutes, stirring, so the spices toast on without moisture.
Stir in 2.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and toss for 2 minutes until it melts into a glossy sweet coating.
Switch off the heat, squeeze in 1 tbsp lemon juice, toss and serve.
tips: The sesame toasted into the oil gives a lovely nutty backbone, so do not skip it.
Gujarati taste runs sweet-sour, so balance the jaggery and lemon to your liking.
This stays crisp for hours, making it a great addition to a travel tiffin.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft rotli and a bowl of plain dal, or as a crunchy relish alongside khichdi.

variations.name: Classic Home-style Arbi
variations.description: The gentlest, quickest arbi, lightly fried and tossed in a mild onion-tomato masala so the tuber's own nutty flavour stays forward. Amchur adds a soft tang and a spoon of ghee rounds it off. This is the unfussy weekday sabzi that pairs with anything.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a light wood-pressed oil that keeps this everyday sabzi clean and unheavy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoon stirred in at the end for gentle homely richness and aroma

steps: Pressure-cook 500 g arbi for 2 whistles until tender, cool, peel and cut into thick rounds.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium and lightly fry the arbi for 6 minutes until golden at the edges, then set aside.
Crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds in the same oil, add 1 chopped onion and saute until soft and pale gold, about 5 minutes.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 1 chopped tomato and cook until the tomato softens, about 4 minutes.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder with a splash of water and cook for 1 minute.
Return the arbi with 1 tsp salt and 0.75 tsp amchur, toss gently and cook uncovered on low for 5 minutes until everything comes together.
Finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 2 tbsp coriander and serve warm with rotis.
tips: This is deliberately mild and quick; keep the masala light so the arbi's own nutty flavour comes through.
A gentle fry, not a deep crisp, suits this everyday version and keeps the pieces soft.
Leftovers make a lovely dry filling for a paratha roll the next day.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulkas and a bowl of moong dal, or with curd and rice for a simple weekday lunch.

variations.name: Bengali Kochu Ghonto
variations.description: A ghonto is a soft, home-style mash-down, and here colocasia and potato are cooked together with panch phoron and mustard oil until they collapse into a comforting, spoonable sabzi. A bay leaf and dried chilli scent the base. A pinch of jaggery rounds the everyday Bengali flavour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked lightly to give the humble ghonto its everyday Bengali fragrance

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the gentle sweetness that finishes a soft Bengali ghonto against the mustard oil

steps: Pressure-cook 500 g kochu for 2 whistles, cool, peel and cut into small cubes, and dice 1 potato small.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to a light smoke, lower the heat and temper 0.75 tsp panch phoron, 1 bay leaf and 2 dried red chillies.
Add the potato cubes and fry for 4 minutes, then add the arbi and 2 slit green chillies and fry for 4 minutes more.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger paste, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, and toss for 2 minutes.
Add 0.5 cup water, cover and cook on low for 8 minutes until the potato and arbi are soft and the mixture turns dry-ish and mashed at the edges.
Mash a few pieces lightly against the pan, stir in 0.75 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook 2 minutes to a soft ghonto texture.
tips: A ghonto is meant to be soft and slightly mashed; press a few pieces to thicken it naturally.
Panch phoron in mustard oil is the everyday Bengali flavour base, so keep it central and simple.
Add the green chillies whole for aroma rather than fierce heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rice and a drizzle of raw mustard oil, as a homely first course before dal.

variations.name: Kerala Chembu Thoran
variations.description: A simple home-style thoran binds cubed colocasia with a coarse crush of coconut, shallot and green chilli, kept pale and moist rather than browned. Mustard seeds and curry leaves in coconut oil set the aromatic base. It is the light, everyday Kerala side stirred through with rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday Kerala fat that gives even a simple thoran its coastal aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a small spoon to lift the coconut and gently sweeten the everyday thoran

steps: Boil 500 g chembu until just tender, cool, peel and cut into small cubes.
Coarsely crush 0.75 cup grated coconut with 5 shallots, 3 green chillies, 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 0.5 tsp turmeric, keeping it textured rather than a paste.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil on medium, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 2 sprigs curry leaves.
Add the arbi cubes and 1 tsp salt and saute for 5 minutes until lightly golden.
Fold in the crushed coconut mixture and cook on low for 6 minutes, stirring, until the coconut smells toasted and coats the arbi.
Finish with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, toss and serve while moist and fragrant.
tips: A home-style thoran should stay pale and moist, so do not over-brown the coconut.
Crush the coconut and aromatics together so the flavours meld before they hit the pan.
Any leftover thoran is delicious stirred into hot rice with a spoon of coconut oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a light side with rice, sambar and buttermilk, the everyday Kerala way.

variations.name: Gujarati Arbi Bataka nu Shaak
variations.description: Gujarat pairs colocasia with potato in a light, homely shaak lifted by a fresh green chilli-ginger paste and a mild sweet-sour finish. Mustard and cumin crackle in the oil while jaggery and tamarind round it out. It is soft, comforting and made for phulka.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday Gujarati oil, light enough for a soft homely shaak

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: brings the gentle sweet note that defines a Gujarati shaak against the tamarind

steps: Pressure-cook 400 g arbi for 2 whistles, cool, peel and halve, and cube 1 potato small.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp cumin seeds.
Add a crushed paste of 2 green chillies and 1 inch ginger and sizzle for 30 seconds, then add the potato and fry for 4 minutes.
Add the arbi, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and saute for 4 minutes.
Add 0.75 tbsp tamarind pulp, 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.5 cup water, cover and simmer on low for 8 minutes until the potato is soft and the shaak is lightly sweet-sour.
Reduce any excess liquid for 2 minutes, scatter 2 tbsp coriander and serve.
tips: The gentle sweet-sour note from Anveshan Jaggery and tamarind is the hallmark of a Gujarati shaak.
Cut the potato small so it cooks in the same time as the arbi.
This shaak tastes even better reheated, once the flavours have settled.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with phulka or thepla and a bowl of plain khichdi, or as part of a Gujarati thali with kadhi.

variations.name: Haryanvi Ghee Arbi
variations.description: Haryana's rustic kitchen keeps arbi simple and generous, cooking it almost entirely in ghee with just cumin, ginger and green chilli so the tuber tastes rich and clean. There is no onion or tomato, only a bright hit of amchur at the end. It is a plain, ghee-forward sabzi meant for fresh chapatis.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the heart of this Haryanvi sabzi, arbi is cooked almost entirely in ghee for a clean richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a small spoon balances the tang of amchur in this plain ghee sabzi

steps: Pressure-cook 500 g arbi for 2 whistles, cool, peel and gently flatten each piece.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds until fragrant.
Add 1 inch julienned ginger and 3 slit green chillies and saute for 30 seconds, then slide in the arbi.
Fry the arbi in the ghee, turning gently, for 8 minutes until golden and crisp at the edges.
Lower the heat, add 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, and toss for 3 minutes to coat.
Add 1 tsp amchur and 0.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, toss for a minute, finish with 2 tbsp coriander and serve.
tips: Cooking arbi in ghee rather than oil gives this rustic sabzi its clean, rich flavour, so do not skimp.
Skipping onion and tomato keeps it light and lets the arbi and ghee shine.
Flatten the boiled arbi for more crisp surface in the ghee.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot ghee-smeared chapatis and a glass of chaas for a rustic Haryanvi lunch.

variations.name: Classic Home-style Capsicum
variations.description: A fuss-free everyday shimla mirch sabzi: capsicum tossed with onion and a light onion-tomato masala so it stays crisp and vivid. Quick enough for a weeknight tiffin and cooked in clean wood-pressed groundnut oil.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A light oil that keeps this simple capsicum sabzi clean-tasting and lunchbox-friendly.

steps: Deseed 3 capsicums and cut into thin strips, finely chop 1 onion and 1 tomato for a light everyday base.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium and let 1 tsp cumin seeds crackle for around 15 seconds until fragrant.
Add the onion and fry for 4 minutes until soft, then stir in 1 tsp ginger-garlic paste and cook a minute until the raw smell fades.
Add the tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, and cook 3 to 4 minutes until it softens into the oil.
Raise the heat, add the capsicum strips with 1 tsp salt, and stir-fry for 6 minutes until just tender with a little crunch left.
Toss on high for a final minute to dry off any moisture and lightly char the edges.
Finish with 2 tbsp fresh coriander and serve warm.
tips: Slice the capsicum thin so it cooks quickly and stays bright rather than dull and soft.
Keep the pan hot and uncrowded so the capsicum sears instead of stewing.
A squeeze of lemon at the end brightens the whole dish for barely any effort.
variations.servingSuggestion: Roll into a chapati with a smear of green chutney, or serve as a light side with dal-chawal.

variations.name: Gujarati Home-style Capsicum
variations.description: The beloved besan-wali marcha nu shaak: capsicum coated in roasted gram flour with a sweet-sour lift from jaggery and lemon. Nutty, crumbly and gently sweet in true Gujarati style.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil helps toast the besan to a nutty crumb without any heaviness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Gives the characteristic Gujarati sweet-sour finish that offsets the earthy besan.

steps: Deseed 4 capsicums and cut into 1-inch pieces, and keep 4 tbsp besan measured out for coating.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, 1 tbsp sesame seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida for 15 seconds.
Add the capsicum with 1 tsp salt and stir-fry on medium-high for 5 minutes until it begins to soften at the edges.
Lower the heat and sprinkle in the besan along with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp coriander-cumin powder and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, tossing well to coat every piece.
Cook uncovered on low for 6 to 7 minutes, stirring often, until the besan turns golden, nutty-smelling and no longer raw.
Stir in 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook a minute until it melts through the crumbly coating.
Switch off the heat, squeeze in 1 tbsp lemon juice, toss, and serve.
tips: Roast the besan patiently on low; raw gram flour tastes bitter and pasty and ruins the shaak.
Keep tossing so the besan coats the capsicum evenly instead of clumping at the bottom.
Add the lemon off the heat so its brightness balances the jaggery without cooking away.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulka or thepla and a bowl of plain moong dal for a homely Gujarati thali.

variations.name: Kerala Home-style Capsicum
variations.description: A capsicum thoran-style stir-fry bound in a fresh coconut-cumin mixture and tempered in coconut oil with mustard and curry leaves. Light, fragrant and barely spiced so the coconut leads the way.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil is the fragrant heart of any Kerala thoran and lifts the fresh coconut.

steps: Deseed 3 capsicums and chop finely, and crush 0.75 cup grated coconut with 0.5 tsp cumin, 2 green chillies and 0.5 tsp turmeric into a coarse, still-textured mix.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil over medium and splutter 0.75 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tsp urad dal and 2 dried red chillies until the dal turns golden.
Add 12 curry leaves and 5 sliced shallots and fry for 3 minutes until the shallots soften and smell sweet.
Add the chopped capsicum with 1 tsp salt, stir well, sprinkle over a spoon of water, cover and steam-cook on low for 6 minutes until nearly tender.
Uncover and fold in the coconut mixture, tossing gently so it coats the capsicum without turning pasty.
Cook uncovered on low for 4 minutes, stirring, until the coconut smells toasty and the moisture dries off.
Drizzle a little raw coconut oil over the top off the heat and serve.
tips: Keep the coconut mix coarse so the thoran stays dry and crumbly, never gravy-like.
Chop the capsicum small so it cooks fast in the light steam-and-toss method.
Shallots bring a sweetness regular onion cannot, so use them if available.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as part of a rice meal with sambar and rasam, or alongside curd rice.

variations.name: Kashmiri Home-style Capsicum
variations.description: A delicate Valley-style capsicum simmered in a saffron-scented yoghurt gravy warmed with fennel and dry ginger, no onion or garlic in sight. Aromatic, mellow and pale gold in the classic Kashmiri manner.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries the saffron and fennel warmth that defines gentle Kashmiri gravies.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Steeped in warm milk, it lends the golden hue and floral scent of the Valley.

steps: Steep a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk, deseed and cube 3 capsicums, and whisk 0.5 cup yoghurt until completely smooth.
Melt 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and gently fry 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, 3 cloves and 2 crushed cardamom pods for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Lower the flame and stir in 1 tsp Kashmiri red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp turmeric for a few seconds without letting them burn.
Whisk in the yoghurt off the boil, stirring constantly, then add 1.5 tsp fennel powder and 0.75 tsp dry ginger powder to build the aromatic gravy.
Fold in the capsicum with 1 tsp salt, add half a cup of hot water, cover and simmer on low for 12 minutes until tender in a pale-red sauce.
Pour in the saffron milk, stir gently, and cook uncovered 3 minutes until the colour deepens and the aroma blooms.
Rest covered for 5 minutes off the heat before serving.
tips: Skip the onion and garlic; the fennel and dry ginger are what make this authentically Kashmiri.
Bloom the saffron in warm milk, not water, for a richer colour and scent.
Add the yoghurt off the boil and keep stirring to stop the gravy splitting.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice, the Valley staple, and a spoon of Kashmiri pickle.

variations.name: Punjabi Home-style Capsicum
variations.description: A homely Punjabi shimla mirch cooked in ghee with a soft onion-tomato masala and a lift of kasuri methi. Comforting and fragrant without the heaviness of its dhaba cousin.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon of bilona ghee gives this everyday capsicum sabzi its comforting home aroma.

steps: Deseed and cube 3 capsicums, finely chop 1 large onion, and chop 2 tomatoes for a soft home-style masala.
Melt 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and let 1 tsp cumin seeds sizzle for around 15 seconds until golden and fragrant.
Add the onion and cook 5 minutes until soft and light brown, then stir in 1 tsp ginger-garlic paste and fry a minute.
Add the tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, and cook 4 to 5 minutes until thick and glossy.
Add the capsicum with 1 tsp salt, stir to coat, cover and cook on medium-low for 6 to 7 minutes until just tender.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the pan and add 0.5 tsp garam masala, stirring 2 minutes to release the aroma.
Rest briefly off the heat and serve warm.
tips: Cook the masala until the ghee just separates for the deepest homely flavour.
Leave the capsicum a touch firm so it does not turn soft and lose its shape.
A spoon of yoghurt with the tomatoes makes it a little richer without any cream.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulka or ajwain paratha and a side of pickle and curd.

variations.name: Classic Home-style Karela
variations.description: The everyday North Indian bitter gourd sabzi, where thin karela rings are salted, rested and shallow-fried until crisp before being tossed in a light onion-tomato masala. Amchur and a whisper of jaggery balance the natural bitterness into a savoury, tangy dry sabzi. It is deliberately simple, the kind that shows up beside dal-chawal on a weekday.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil stands up to high heat for crisping the karela without a greasy aftertaste

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a single spoon rounds the sharp bitterness of karela without making the sabzi sweet

steps: Scrape the rough ridges off 500 g karela, slice into thin rounds and discard the hard mature seeds. Rub with 1 tsp salt and 0.25 tsp of the turmeric and rest for 30 minutes to draw out the bitter juices, then squeeze firmly and rinse lightly.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a heavy kadai on medium and add the squeezed karela. Shallow-fry, stirring often, until the edges turn golden and crisp, about 8 to 10 minutes, then lift out and set aside.
In the same oil crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds until fragrant, then add 2 finely sliced onions and saute on medium until soft and golden, about 6 minutes.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute until the raw smell goes, then add 1 chopped tomato and cook until it breaks down and the oil separates, about 4 minutes.
Lower the heat and add the remaining 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder with a splash of water so they do not burn, cooking for 1 minute until aromatic.

Return the fried karela, add the remaining 0.25 tsp salt, 1 tsp amchur and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder to round the bitterness, then toss and cook uncovered on low for 5 minutes until the masala clings.
Finish with 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander, toss once and serve hot.
tips: The salt-and-rest step is the single biggest trick to tame karela; do not skip the 30-minute rest or the firm squeeze.
Fry the karela in two batches if your pan is small, so the slices crisp rather than steam and go soggy.
A teaspoon of Anveshan Jaggery Powder plus the amchur gives the classic sweet-sour-bitter balance; add the jaggery a little at a time to taste.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile alongside dal-chawal with a dollop of chilled plain yogurt, or tuck into a folded ajwain paratha for a lunchbox that holds its flavour for hours.

variations.name: Bengali Uchche Bhaja
variations.description: In Bengal, bitter gourd is called uchche and is eaten as the very first course of a meal to open the appetite. Here it is fried bone-dry in smoked mustard oil with nigella seeds and slivers of potato, so bitterness and pungency play off each other. The result is a crisp, nutty bhaja rather than a saucy sabzi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: brought to a light smoke first so its sharp pungency mellows into the nutty base a Bengali bhaja needs

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a pinch at the end softens the bitter edge and balances the pungent mustard oil

steps: Slice 500 g karela into thin half-moons and cut 1 potato into fine matchsticks. Rub the karela with 1 tsp salt and 0.25 tsp of the turmeric and leave for 20 minutes, then press out the bitter juices.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just smokes and turns pale, which tames its raw sharpness, then lower the flame to medium.
Temper 0.5 tsp nigella seeds and 2 dried red chillies in the oil for about 20 seconds until they sizzle and smell nutty.

Slide in the potato matchsticks and fry for 4 minutes, then add the squeezed karela and 2 slit green chillies and fry uncovered, tossing often, for 12 to 14 minutes until both are browned and crisp at the edges.
Sprinkle the remaining 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.25 tsp salt and toss for 2 minutes so the spices coat everything evenly.
Finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, tossing for a final minute until the bitterness is rounded and the bhaja looks glossy and completely dry.
tips: Bringing the mustard oil to a light smoke before tempering is essential; raw mustard oil tastes harsh in a dry bhaja.
Slice the karela and potato thin and uniform so they crisp at the same rate.
Keep the bhaja bone-dry and never cover the pan, or the steam will soften the crunch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as the traditional opening bite of a Bengali meal, over the first few spoonfuls of hot steamed rice before moving on to dal and fish curry.

variations.name: Kerala Pavakka Thoran
variations.description: Pavakka is the Malayalam name for bitter gourd, and a thoran pairs it with a coarse, moist mix of grated coconut, shallots and green chilli. Everything is stir-fried in coconut oil with mustard seeds and curry leaves until the coconut turns lightly toasted. It stays dry and fluffy, sweet-bitter and deeply fragrant.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: non-negotiable here as it sets the whole Kerala character and aroma of the thoran

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a spoon tempers the bitter gourd and marries it to the sweetness of the coconut

steps: Slice 500 g pavakka into fine thin pieces, rub with 1 tsp salt and 0.25 tsp of the turmeric, rest for 20 minutes, then squeeze out the dark bitter liquid.
Coarsely crush 1 cup grated coconut with 6 shallots, 2 green chillies and the remaining 0.25 tsp turmeric to a moist, still-textured mix, taking care not to make a smooth paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a heavy pan on medium, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 2 dried red chillies and 2 sprigs curry leaves and let them crackle for 20 seconds.
Add the squeezed pavakka, cover and cook on low for 10 minutes, stirring twice, until the pieces soften and lose their raw edge.

Fold in the crushed coconut mixture, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, and stir-fry uncovered on medium for 6 to 7 minutes until the coconut turns lightly toasted and fragrant.
Taste for salt, give a final toss and switch off the heat while the thoran is still moist and flecked green.
tips: A thoran should be dry and fluffy, not oily; keep the coconut just-toasted and never let it brown dark.
Crush the coconut coarsely by pulsing so it keeps a bite instead of turning pasty.
Squeeze the salted pavakka really hard; the drier it is going in, the crisper the finished thoran.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a side in a Kerala sadya-style spread with rice, sambar and a spoon of thick curd, or alongside kanji for a light supper.

variations.name: Gujarati Karela nu Shaak
variations.description: Gujarat leans into contrast, coating fried bitter gourd in a deliberately sweet-sour masala thickened with a spoon of besan and a nutty peanut-sesame crush. Jaggery and tamarind do the heavy lifting, turning the karela mellow and moreish. It is the sabzi that famously converts karela-haters.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the traditional Gujarati cooking fat, its clean nuttiness suits the sweet-sour masala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the star of a Gujarati shaak, it carries the signature sweet note against the tamarind

steps: Cut 500 g karela into thin rounds, rub with 1 tsp salt and 0.25 tsp of the turmeric, rest for 30 minutes and squeeze firmly to remove the bitterness.
Dry-roast 3 tbsp peanuts and 1 tbsp sesame seeds separately until they smell nutty, then coarsely crush them together, keeping some texture.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium, splutter 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add the squeezed karela and saute for 10 minutes until softened and lightly golden.
Sprinkle in the remaining 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tbsp besan, and stir-fry for 3 minutes so the gram flour toasts and coats the karela.

Add the crushed peanut-sesame mix, 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 tbsp tamarind pulp and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt with a splash of water, then cook covered on low for 6 minutes until the shaak turns glossy and sweet-sour.
Uncover and dry off any excess moisture over 2 minutes, then serve warm.
tips: Balance the Anveshan Jaggery and tamarind to your taste, adding a little more jaggery if the shaak feels too sharp.
The spoon of besan soaks up excess oil and helps the masala cling to every slice.
This shaak keeps beautifully for two days and the flavour actually deepens overnight.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulka rotis and a bowl of moong dal, or as the sweet-savoury counterpoint on a Gujarati thali beside kadhi and rice.

variations.name: Andhra Kakarakaya Fry
variations.description: Kakarakaya vepudu from Andhra is unapologetically fiery, built on Guntur chilli, plenty of garlic and a tempering of toasted chana and urad dal for crunch. The bitter gourd is fried until genuinely crisp, which tames its bitterness, then coated in a deep red spice mix. It is a rice-and-ghee dish that wakes up the whole plate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the classic Andhra frying fat, it crisps the karela and carries the fierce chilli cleanly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a spoon keeps the fierce Guntur heat from turning one-note and rounds the bitterness

steps: Slice 500 g kakarakaya thin, rub with the 1 tsp salt and 0.25 tsp of the turmeric, rest for 25 minutes and squeeze out the bitter juices.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium and temper 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 tbsp chana dal and 1 tbsp urad dal until the dals turn golden and nutty, about 1 minute.
Add 6 crushed garlic cloves and 1 sprig curry leaves, let them crackle, then add 2 finely chopped onions and fry until deep golden, about 7 minutes.
Slide in the squeezed karela and stir-fry uncovered on medium for about 12 minutes until the pieces are browned and crisp.
Lower the heat and add 1.5 tsp Guntur red chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander powder, the remaining 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, tossing for 3 minutes until the fry turns a deep fiery red.
Round the heat with 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, toss for a final minute and serve blazing hot.
tips: Guntur chilli is seriously hot; start with less and build up, and let the pinch of Anveshan Jaggery keep the heat balanced.
Toasting the chana and urad dal in the tempering gives the fry its signature Andhra crunch and aroma.
Fry the karela until genuinely crisp; a soft, underfried karela always tastes far more bitter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rice and a spoon of ghee, or as a fierce dry side to plain curd rice that cools the palate between bites.

variations.name: Classic Home-style Mix Veg
variations.description: The everyday sabzi that turns up in tiffins across North India: seasonal vegetables lightly sauteed with onion, tomato and a modest spice hand so each vegetable still tastes of itself. Quick, wholesome and cooked in wood-pressed groundnut oil for clean flavour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A light, clean-tasting oil that lets the individual vegetables shine in a homely everyday sabzi.

steps: Chop 500 g mixed vegetables into small even pieces, finely dice 1 large onion, and chop 2 tomatoes so they soften quickly into the base.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a pan over medium heat and let 1 tsp cumin seeds crackle for about 15 seconds until aromatic.
Add the onion and saute for 5 minutes until translucent and pale gold, then stir in 1 tsp ginger-garlic paste and cook a minute to remove its raw edge.
Add the tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, and cook 5 to 6 minutes until the tomato softens and the oil glistens.
Tip in the vegetables with 1 tsp salt, stir to coat, add a small splash of water, cover and cook on low for 12 to 14 minutes until just tender.
Uncover, raise the heat for a minute to dry off excess moisture, then fold in 2 tbsp fresh coriander.
Rest for 3 minutes off the heat so the flavours settle before serving.
tips: Keep the pieces small and uniform so a mixed medley cooks evenly without any single vegetable turning to mush.
For a drier tiffin-friendly sabzi, cook uncovered in the last few minutes to evaporate all the moisture.
Swap in whatever is seasonal, from tinda to bottle gourd, keeping the total weight around 500 g.
variations.servingSuggestion: Roll into a phulka with a smear of ghee for a lunchbox wrap, or serve with dal and rice for a simple thali.

variations.name: Gujarati Home-style Mix Veg
variations.description: A gently sweet Gujarati shaak where jaggery and a little lemon give the classic sweet-sour balance, lifted with a green chilli-ginger paste rather than heavy spice. Light, bright and typical of a Kathiawadi kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the classic frying medium of Gujarati kitchens and keeps the shaak light.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The heart of a Gujarati shaak; it gives the gentle sweetness that defines the region's cooking.

steps: Dice 500 g mixed vegetables small, chop 2 tomatoes, and keep 1 tbsp green chilli-ginger paste ready so the tempering can move quickly.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, then add 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 10 curry leaves and let them crackle for 15 seconds.
Stir in the green chilli-ginger paste and fry for 30 seconds until fragrant, then add the tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp coriander-cumin powder.
Cook the tomato for 4 to 5 minutes until pulpy, then add the vegetables with 1 tsp salt and toss to coat in the yellow masala.
Add a small splash of water, cover and simmer on low for 12 to 14 minutes until the vegetables are tender but still hold their shape.
Stir in 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook 2 minutes until it dissolves, then switch off the heat and squeeze in 1 tbsp lemon juice.
Scatter 2 tbsp fresh coriander over the top and serve warm.
tips: Add the lemon only after switching off the heat so its brightness is not cooked away.
Gujarati shaak leans sweeter than most; adjust the jaggery up or down to your taste.
A tablespoon of roasted crushed peanuts stirred in at the end adds a lovely Kathiawadi crunch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulka or thepla and a bowl of plain kadhi for a classic Gujarati lunch.

variations.name: Kerala Home-style Mix Veg
variations.description: A thoran-inspired stir-fry where the vegetables are bound in a coarse coconut-cumin paste and tempered in coconut oil with mustard and curry leaves. Fresh, fragrant and barely spiced so the coconut leads.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil is the soul of Kerala tempering and perfumes the whole thoran as it heats.

steps: Chop 500 g mixed vegetables finely so they cook fast in the dry stir-fry style, and pulse 0.75 cup grated coconut with 0.5 tsp cumin, 2 green chillies and 0.5 tsp turmeric into a coarse, still-textured paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil over medium and splutter 0.75 tsp mustard seeds with 2 dried red chillies until they pop, about 20 seconds.
Add 12 curry leaves and 6 thinly sliced shallots and fry for 3 minutes until the shallots turn soft and lightly golden.
Tip in the chopped vegetables with 1 tsp salt, stir well, sprinkle over a couple of tablespoons of water, cover and steam-cook on low for 8 to 10 minutes until almost tender.
Uncover and fold in the coarse coconut paste, mixing gently so it coats every piece without turning pasty.
Cook uncovered on low for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring now and then, until the coconut smells toasty and the moisture has dried off.
Finish with a fresh drizzle of coconut oil off the heat for extra aroma and serve.
tips: Keep the coconut paste coarse, not smooth, so the thoran stays dry and crumbly rather than gravy-like.
Beans, cabbage and carrot are the most authentic mix for a thoran, but any firm vegetable works.
A final drizzle of raw coconut oil is a Kerala signature that lifts the whole dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as part of a rice-based meal with sambar and rasam, or alongside plain curd rice.

variations.name: Kashmiri Home-style Mix Veg
variations.description: A delicate Valley-style preparation coloured and perfumed with saffron and Kashmiri chilli, warmed with fennel and dry ginger instead of onion-garlic. Aromatic, mellow and a world apart from the fiery North Indian norm.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Kashmiri cooking leans on ghee for its warmth, carrying the saffron and fennel aromas beautifully.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: A few strands steeped in warm milk give the signature golden hue and floral perfume of the Valley.

steps: Steep a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside, while you dice 500 g mixed vegetables into neat pieces and whisk 0.5 cup yoghurt until smooth.
Melt 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and gently fry 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, 3 cloves and 2 crushed cardamom pods for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Lower the flame and stir in 1 tsp Kashmiri red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp turmeric for a few seconds, taking care not to burn the spices.
Add the whisked yoghurt off the boil, stirring continuously, then mix in 1.5 tsp fennel powder and 0.75 tsp dry ginger powder to build the aromatic gravy.
Fold in the vegetables and 1 tsp salt, add half a cup of hot water, cover and simmer on low for 14 to 16 minutes until tender and coated in the pale-red sauce.
Pour in the saffron milk, stir gently, and cook uncovered for 3 minutes until the colour deepens and the aroma blooms.
Rest covered for 5 minutes off the heat so the fennel and saffron settle before serving.
tips: Kashmiri cuisine traditionally skips onion and garlic here, relying on fennel and dry ginger for depth, so resist the urge to add them.
Bloom the saffron in warm milk rather than water for a rounder, richer colour and scent.
Keep the yoghurt whisked and the flame low when it goes in to prevent the gravy from curdling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice, the Valley's staple, and a side of Kashmiri pickle.

variations.name: Punjabi Home-style Mix Veg
variations.description: The comforting ghar-ka version from a Punjabi kitchen: a soft onion-tomato masala enriched with ghee and finished with kasuri methi, hearty but simpler than its dhaba cousin. Homely, fragrant and endlessly adaptable.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon of bilona ghee lends this everyday Punjabi sabzi its homely, comforting aroma.

steps: Chop 500 g mixed vegetables into small cubes, finely chop 1 large onion, and chop 2 tomatoes ready for a soft everyday masala.
Melt 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and let 1 tsp cumin seeds sizzle for around 15 seconds until they turn fragrant and golden.
Add the onion and cook for 6 minutes until soft and light brown, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry a minute until the raw smell fades.
Add the tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, and cook 5 to 6 minutes until the masala turns thick and glossy.
Stir in the vegetables with 1 tsp salt, splash in a little hot water, cover and cook on low for 12 to 14 minutes until tender.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the pan and add 0.75 tsp garam masala, stirring for 2 minutes to let the aromas develop.
Finish with 2 tbsp fresh coriander and rest a few minutes before serving.
tips: Cook the masala until the ghee just separates for the deepest homely flavour before adding the vegetables.
This forgiving base works with almost any vegetable, so use up whatever is in the fridge.
A spoon of yoghurt stirred in with the tomatoes makes it a touch richer without any cream.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulka or ajwain paratha and a side of pickle and curd for a satisfying home meal.

variations.name: Classic Masala Arbi
variations.description: Colocasia is boiled, peeled and shallow-fried to kill its slipperiness, then folded into a bhuno-ed onion-tomato masala until every piece is coated. Amchur and garam masala give it the familiar North Indian tang and warmth. A finish of ghee lends the semi-dry sabzi its glossy, homely richness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil fries the boiled arbi golden without a heavy, greasy coat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: swirled in at the end for a glossy, restaurant-style richness over the masala

steps: Pressure-cook 500 g arbi with water for 2 whistles until just fork-tender, cool, peel and halve each piece lengthwise.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium-high and shallow-fry the arbi halves for about 8 minutes until golden and no longer slimy, then lift out and set aside.
In the same oil crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, add 2 finely chopped onions and fry until golden brown, about 7 minutes.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for a minute, then add 2 chopped tomatoes and cook until pulpy and the oil separates, about 5 minutes.
Add 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder with 2 tbsp water and cook the masala for 2 minutes until it darkens and smells roasted.
Fold the fried arbi back in with 1.25 tsp salt, 1 tsp amchur and 0.75 tsp garam masala, toss to coat and cook uncovered on low for 5 minutes so the masala clings.
Finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 2 tbsp chopped coriander, swirl through and serve hot.
tips: Boiling the arbi first then frying is the trick to kill its slipperiness; never add water once the arbi hits the frying pan.
Choose arbi of even size so the pieces cook uniformly; overcooked arbi turns mushy and sticky.
A spoon of Anveshan Ghee stirred in at the end gives the masala a glossy, restaurant-style finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulkas or jeera rice and a side of onion rings soused in lemon; it also makes a fine dry curry for a festive thali.

variations.name: Bengali Kochu Masala
variations.description: Kochu is the Bengali name for colocasia, and here it is glazed in smoked mustard oil tempered with panch phoron and dried red chilli. Ginger and a single tomato keep it light, while a touch of jaggery lends the gentle sweetness Bengali cooking loves. It cooks down to a dry, spice-slicked sabzi rather than a gravy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: warmed to a light smoke so its raw pungency softens into the nutty backbone of the dish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the small Bengali sweetness that rounds the pungent mustard oil and panch phoron

steps: Pressure-cook 500 g kochu for 2 whistles, cool, peel and cut into thick rounds.
Warm 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it lightly smokes and mellows, then bring it down to medium heat.
Temper 1 tsp panch phoron and 2 dried red chillies for about 20 seconds until the mix turns aromatic, then add 1 chopped onion and fry until soft, about 5 minutes.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger paste and 1 chopped tomato and cook until the tomato collapses, about 4 minutes.
Add the arbi rounds, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, 2 slit green chillies and 1 tsp salt, toss to coat, then cook covered on low for 8 minutes.
Uncover, add 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and stir-fry for 3 minutes until the masala dries down and glazes the arbi.
tips: Panch phoron and mustard oil are what make this taste distinctly Bengali; keep both front and centre.
Let the mustard oil reach a light smoke first so its raw pungency softens into a nutty warmth.
Cook the arbi covered but lift the lid to stir, releasing steam so it glazes rather than stews.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice and a wedge of lime, following the Bengali habit of eating a dry shaak early in the meal.

variations.name: Kerala Chembu Masala
variations.description: Chembu, the Malayalam word for colocasia, is simmered in a freshly ground coconut masala pointed up with black pepper. Shallots, curry leaves and coconut oil build a sweet, roasted base that clings to each cube. Black pepper rather than chilli powder gives the warm, rounded heat that suits coconut.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: gives the masala its unmistakable Kerala aroma and marries with the ground coconut

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a spoon lifts the coconut masala with a gentle sweetness against the pepper

steps: Boil 500 g chembu until fork-tender, cool, peel and cut into bite-sized cubes.
Grind 0.75 cup grated coconut with 4 of the shallots, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp turmeric to a coarse, moist paste.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil on medium, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 2 dried red chillies, 2 sprigs curry leaves and the remaining 4 sliced shallots, and fry until the shallots turn golden.
Add the arbi cubes and 1 tsp salt and saute for 5 minutes until the edges catch a little colour.
Stir in the ground coconut paste and 0.5 tsp black pepper powder and cook on low for 6 minutes, stirring so the coconut toasts evenly and coats the arbi.
Finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, toss for 2 minutes and take off the heat while still moist.
tips: Freshly ground coconut paste beats desiccated here; it clings to the arbi and gives a sweet, roasted depth.
Black pepper, not just chilli, is the traditional Kerala heat and suits the coconut far better.
Keep the flame low once the coconut goes in so it toasts golden without turning bitter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as part of a rice-based Kerala meal with rasam and pappadam, or alongside plain curd rice.

variations.name: Gujarati Arbi nu Shaak
variations.description: This Gujarati take glazes halved colocasia in a sweet-sour sauce of jaggery and tamarind, thickened with a coarse peanut-sesame crush. A fresh green chilli-ginger paste keeps it bright rather than heavy. The finish is a shiny, mildly sweet sabzi that clings to soft rotis.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday Gujarati kitchen fat, its clean flavour lets the sweet-sour glaze shine

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: carries the sweet half of the classic Gujarati sweet-sour glaze against the tamarind

steps: Pressure-cook 500 g arbi for 2 whistles, cool, peel and halve the pieces.
Coarsely pound 2 tbsp roasted peanuts and 1 tbsp roasted sesame seeds, and separately crush 2 green chillies with 1 inch ginger to a rough paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add the green chilli-ginger paste and sizzle for 30 seconds.
Add the arbi with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and saute for 6 minutes until lightly golden.
Stir in the peanut-sesame crush, 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tbsp tamarind pulp with a splash of water, and simmer covered on low for 6 minutes into a sweet-sour glaze.
Uncover, reduce any liquid for 2 minutes, scatter 2 tbsp coriander and serve.
tips: The Gujarati sweet-sour balance rests on the Anveshan Jaggery and tamarind; taste and tilt it to your liking.
Keep the peanut-sesame crush coarse, not a powder, so it gives body and texture to the glaze.
Use small, firm arbi so the halves hold their shape in the sauce.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thin bajra rotla or phulka and a bowl of plain khichdi for a homely Gujarati lunch.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Goda Masala Arbi
variations.description: Maharashtra flavours its colocasia with goda masala, a dark, sweet-smoky blend of clove, cinnamon and roasted coconut quite unlike garam masala. Peanuts add crunch while tamarind and jaggery bring the region's beloved sweet-sour-hot balance. The bhaji cooks down dark, dry and deeply aromatic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the staple Maharashtrian frying oil, it carries the dark goda masala without masking it

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: with the tamarind it delivers the classic Maharashtrian sweet-sour-hot finish

steps: Boil 500 g arbi until tender, cool, peel and cut into thick slices.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium and temper 1 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 1 sprig curry leaves until they splutter.
Add 1 chopped onion and 2 tbsp peanuts and fry until the onion is golden and the peanuts crisp, about 5 minutes.
Add the arbi, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp goda masala, and toss for 3 minutes until the dark, fragrant masala coats every piece.
Stir in 2 tbsp dry grated coconut, 1 tsp tamarind pulp, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp salt with 3 tbsp water, and simmer covered on low for 6 minutes.
Uncover and cook off the moisture for 2 minutes until the bhaji is dark, dry and aromatic.
tips: Goda masala is the soul of this dish; its clove-and-coconut warmth is quite different from garam masala, so do not substitute.
The pinch of tamarind with Anveshan Jaggery is the classic Maharashtrian sweet-sour-hot signature.
Dry-roast the grated coconut before adding if you have a minute, to deepen the flavour further.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri or soft chapati and a bowl of varan-bhaat for an everyday Maharashtrian meal.

variations.name: Classic Masala Karela
variations.description: Bitter gourd rings salted to tame their edge, then cooked down with a spiced onion-tomato masala until the bitterness mellows into a savoury, deeply satisfying sabzi. A little jaggery rounds it off the way home cooks always do.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A sturdy oil that stands up to the longer cooking bitter gourd needs to mellow properly.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The classic counterweight to karela's bitterness that makes the sabzi so moreish.

steps: Scrape 500 g bitter gourd lightly, slice into thin rings, rub with 1 tsp salt and set aside for 20 minutes, then squeeze out the bitter juices and pat dry.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium and shallow-fry the karela rings for 8 to 10 minutes until browned and crisp at the edges, then lift out and set aside.
In the same oil crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 15 seconds, add 2 chopped onions and fry 6 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook a minute.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, and cook 6 minutes until the masala thickens and the oil separates.
Return the fried karela to the pan with 0.5 tsp remaining salt, toss to coat, cover and cook on low for 6 to 7 minutes so the flavours soak in.
Sprinkle 0.75 tsp amchur, 1 tsp garam masala and 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, stirring 2 minutes until the sweet-tangy balance settles.
Rest a few minutes off the heat and serve, when the bitterness has softened to a pleasant edge.
tips: The 20-minute salting step is non-negotiable if you want to tame the sharpest bitterness.
Frying the karela separately before the masala keeps the rings crisp instead of soggy.
Save the scraped peel to fry into a crunchy garnish rather than throwing it away.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulka and a cooling bowl of boondi raita to offset the gentle bitterness.

variations.name: Gujarati Masala Karela
variations.description: The quintessential Gujarati karela nu shaak, where a generous hand of jaggery and a besan-sesame coating turns bitter gourd sweet, nutty and utterly addictive. The most jaggery-forward version of the lot.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The classic Gujarati frying fat that crisps the besan coating on the karela.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Gujarati karela leans generously sweet; the jaggery is the star that balances the bitter.

steps: Slice 500 g bitter gourd into thin rings, rub with 1 tsp salt, rest 20 minutes, then squeeze out the juices and pat thoroughly dry.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 1.5 tbsp sesame seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida for 15 seconds.
Add the karela rings and stir-fry on medium for 8 minutes until they soften and colour lightly.
Lower the heat, sprinkle in 3 tbsp besan with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp coriander-cumin powder and 1 tsp red chilli powder, and toss so the besan coats every ring.
Cook uncovered on low for 6 to 7 minutes, stirring often, until the besan turns golden and nutty and loses its raw smell.
Stir in 3 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 0.5 tsp remaining salt and cook 2 minutes until it melts into a glossy sweet coat.
Switch off, squeeze in 1 tbsp lemon juice, toss and serve.
tips: Roast the besan fully on low heat; undercooked besan tastes raw and spoils the shaak.
Gujarati palates like this quite sweet, so taste and add more jaggery if you wish.
A handful of crushed roasted peanuts stirred in at the end adds lovely extra crunch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft rotli and a bowl of khichdi-kadhi for a comforting Gujarati meal.

variations.name: Bengali Masala Karela
variations.description: A Bengali korola treatment tempered in pungent mustard oil with nigella seeds, the bitterness embraced rather than hidden. Sharp, clean and often eaten first in the meal to whet the appetite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Its pungency is the traditional Bengali partner to bitter gourd, sharpening the whole dish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A restrained touch of sweetness, just enough to soften the karela's sharp edge the Bengali way.

steps: Slice 500 g bitter gourd thin, rub with 0.75 tsp salt, rest 15 minutes, then squeeze out the juices and pat dry.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until it just smokes, cool for 10 seconds, then temper 0.75 tsp nigella seeds with 3 slit green chillies for 15 seconds.
Add 1 sliced large onion and fry on medium for 5 minutes until soft and pale gold.
Add the karela with 1 tbsp ginger paste, 0.75 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, and stir-fry for 8 minutes until the rings brown and crisp at the edges.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp remaining salt, cover and cook on low for 5 minutes so the karela softens through.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook uncovered 2 minutes until the sabzi turns glossy and just slightly sweet.
Serve with a raw drizzle of mustard oil for the full Bengali aroma.
tips: Bengalis keep this fairly dry and bitter, so go easy on the jaggery.
Fry the karela long enough to crisp the edges, which mellows the sharpest bitterness.
It is traditionally eaten at the start of the meal with plain rice as an appetite opener.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as the first course with hot steamed rice and a drizzle of ghee.

variations.name: Punjabi Masala Karela
variations.description: A hearty Punjabi bharwa-style karela, the rings stuffed with a spiced onion masala and slow-cooked in ghee until sweetly caramelised. Rich, robust and worlds away from a plain bitter sabzi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee slow-caramelises the stuffed karela into a rich Punjabi treat.

steps: Scrape 500 g bitter gourd, slit each lengthwise keeping one side intact, rub inside and out with 1 tsp salt, and rest 25 minutes before squeezing dry.

For the filling, grind 1 tbsp fennel seeds coarse, then mix with 3 finely chopped onions sauteed in 1 tbsp of the ghee until golden, along with 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 2 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp amchur and 0.5 tsp salt.
Pack about 2 tbsp of this cooked masala firmly into each karela and tie loosely with thread so they hold together.
Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide pan over medium and place the stuffed karela in a single layer.
Cook covered on low for 18 to 20 minutes, turning gently every few minutes, until the karela is tender and caramelised on all sides.
Uncover, sprinkle 1 tsp garam masala, and cook 2 minutes to crisp the edges.
Remove the threads and rest 5 minutes before serving whole or halved.
tips: Cook the stuffing fully before packing, since raw spice seeds inside would stay harsh.
Tie the karela loosely with thread so the filling stays put during the long cooking.
These keep beautifully for two days and taste even better as the masala matures.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot ajwain paratha and a glass of lassi for a filling Punjabi lunch.

variations.name: Rajasthani Masala Karela
variations.description: A tangy, long-keeping Marwari karela cooked in mustard oil with a bold dried-red-chilli and amchur masala, no onion or tomato so it stores for days in the desert heat. Sour, spicy and travel-proof.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Mustard oil acts as a natural preserver, key to the no-onion Marwari style that keeps for days.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Balances the sharp amchur sourness into the sweet-sour Rajasthani profile.

steps: Slice 500 g bitter gourd thin, rub with 1 tsp salt, rest 20 minutes, then squeeze out the juices and pat dry.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until it just smokes, lower the heat, and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 tsp fennel seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida with 4 broken dried red chillies for 15 seconds.
Add the karela rings and stir-fry on medium for 9 to 10 minutes until deeply browned and crisp.
Lower the heat and add 2 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp remaining salt, tossing so the dry spices coat the rings.
Cook uncovered for 4 minutes, stirring, so the spices toast onto the karela without any moisture.
Sprinkle 1.5 tsp amchur and 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and toss for 2 minutes until the sweet-sour glaze clings.
Cool fully before storing; it keeps for three to four days without refrigeration.
tips: The absence of onion and tomato is deliberate; it is what lets this keep for days unrefrigerated.
Fry the karela until really crisp so the dry masala has something to cling to.
Pack into a clean dry jar with a spoon of extra mustard oil on top to extend its life.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra roti and a smear of white butter, ideal as a travel-friendly sabzi.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Arbi
variations.description: This is the fiery cousin of everyday arbi, layering slit green chillies and freshly ground black pepper over the usual onion masala for a clean, building heat. Fried colocasia stays firm under the spicy coat while amchur sharpens the finish. A swirl of ghee at the end keeps the burn balanced and rich.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil fries the arbi firm so it holds up under the spicy masala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: swirled in at the end to carry the heat and give the fiery sabzi a rich sheen

steps: Pressure-cook 500 g arbi for 2 whistles, cool, peel and halve the pieces.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium-high and fry the arbi for 7 minutes until golden, then remove and keep aside.
In the same oil crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, add 1 chopped onion and 4 slit green chillies and fry until the onion softens, about 5 minutes.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute, then add 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder with a splash of water for 1 minute.
Return the arbi with 1 tsp salt, 0.75 tsp black pepper powder and 1 tsp amchur, and toss on medium for 5 minutes until the fiery masala grips each piece.
Swirl in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, scatter 2 tbsp coriander and serve piping hot.
tips: The double hit of green chilli and freshly ground black pepper gives a clean, building heat rather than just red-chilli burn.
Fry the arbi well before adding it back so it stays firm under the spicy masala.
Add the amchur at the end; its tang lifts and sharpens the heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with cooling boondi raita and phulkas, or over plain rice with a squeeze of lemon.

variations.name: Bengali Kochu Jhal
variations.description: Jhal means hot in Bengali, and this one gets its punch from a freshly ground mustard paste that makes the nose tingle. Colocasia simmers in a loose, pungent mustard gravy sharpened with green chilli and nigella. A pinch of jaggery keeps the sharpness from tipping into bitterness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked lightly, it deepens the pungent jhal and pairs naturally with the mustard paste

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a pinch keeps the sharp mustard gravy from turning bitter

steps: Boil 500 g kochu until tender, cool, peel and cut into rounds.
Grind 1.5 tbsp mustard seeds with 2 of the green chillies and a little water into a smooth, pungent paste and set aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to a light smoke, lower the flame and temper 0.5 tsp nigella seeds and the remaining 2 slit green chillies.
Add the arbi, 1 tsp grated ginger, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, and saute for 5 minutes.
Stir in the mustard paste with 0.5 cup water and simmer covered on low for 8 minutes until the arbi drinks in the sharp jhal gravy.
Balance with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer 2 more minutes and serve with the loose mustard gravy.
tips: Grind the mustard with a green chilli and a pinch of salt to stop it turning bitter.
Bengali jhal is meant to make your nose tingle; go easy the first time and build up the mustard.
Never boil the mustard gravy hard or it turns acrid; a gentle simmer keeps it fragrant.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plenty of plain steamed rice to carry the pungent mustard gravy.

variations.name: Kerala Chembu Ularthiyathu
variations.description: Ularthiyathu is a dry pepper roast, and here colocasia is stir-fried with coconut slivers, shallots and a heavy hand of freshly crushed black pepper. Coconut oil, mustard seeds and curry leaves ground it firmly in Kerala. Fried coconut bits add sweet, toasty pops through the peppery heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the defining Kerala fat that carries the pepper roast and toasts the coconut slivers

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a touch to round the sharp pepper and echo the sweetness of the toasted coconut

steps: Boil 500 g chembu until fork-tender, cool, peel and cut into cubes.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil on medium, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then fry 3 tbsp coconut slivers and 2 sprigs curry leaves until the coconut turns golden.
Add 6 sliced shallots and 1 inch julienned ginger and saute for 3 minutes until soft.
Add the arbi, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, and stir-fry for 6 minutes until the edges brown.
Sprinkle 1 tsp freshly crushed black pepper and toss on low for 4 minutes so the pepper coats and perfumes the arbi.
Round off with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, toss once and serve dry and peppery.
tips: Freshly crushed black pepper added at the end gives ularthiyathu its warm heat; pre-ground loses its punch.
Frying the coconut slivers golden before the arbi adds sweet, toasty pops throughout.
Keep it dry; this pepper fry should have no gravy at all.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with rice and rasam, or as a peppery dry side to a Kerala meal on a rainy day.

variations.name: Rajasthani Chatpati Arbi
variations.description: Rajasthan brings smoky heat to colocasia with whole dried red chillies soaked and ground with garlic and fennel, then bound in a little yogurt so the fire has body. The masala turns bright red and clings to the fried arbi. A pinch of jaggery tempers the chilli in true desert-kitchen balance.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil fries the arbi and blooms the ground chilli paste to a deep red

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: tempers the fierce dried-chilli heat in the classic Rajasthani balance

steps: Pressure-cook 500 g arbi for 2 whistles, cool, peel and halve.
Soak 4 dried red chillies in warm water for 10 minutes, then grind with 6 garlic cloves, 1 tsp coriander seeds and 0.5 tsp fennel seeds into a coarse paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium-high and fry the arbi for 7 minutes until golden, then set aside.
In the same oil crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, add the ground chilli-garlic paste and fry for 3 minutes until the oil turns bright red and the raw smell lifts.
Whisk 3 tbsp yogurt with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder, lower the heat and stir it in slowly so it does not split, cooking for 2 minutes.
Return the arbi with 1 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, toss and simmer on low for 5 minutes until the fiery masala clings.
tips: Soaking and grinding whole dried chillies gives a deeper, smokier heat than chilli powder alone.
Add the yogurt off the boil and stir constantly so it melds into a glossy masala instead of curdling.
The pinch of Anveshan Jaggery tempers the fierce chilli in true Rajasthani balance.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra roti and a blob of white butter, or with steamed rice and a raw onion salad.

variations.name: Andhra Chama Dumpa Kaaram
variations.description: Kaaram means spice-hot in Telugu, and this Andhra fry pushes colocasia into blazing territory with Guntur chilli and a garlicky dal tempering. Onions fried golden give it a savoury base under the heat. It is a bold, dry side built to be cut with cooling curd rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the classic Andhra frying fat that crisps the arbi and carries the fierce kaaram cleanly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a spoon mellows the blazing Guntur heat without dulling it

steps: Pressure-cook 500 g chama dumpa for 2 whistles, cool, peel and cut into thick slices.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium and temper 1 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tbsp chana dal and 1 tbsp urad dal until the dals turn golden.
Add 6 crushed garlic cloves, 2 sprigs curry leaves and 1 chopped onion, and fry until the onion is golden, about 5 minutes.
Slide in the arbi slices and stir-fry on medium for about 8 minutes until browned and crisp at the edges.
Lower the heat, add 1.5 tsp Guntur red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, and toss for 3 minutes until blazing red and coated.
Round the heat with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, toss once and serve fiery hot.
tips: Guntur chilli brings serious heat; add it gradually and let the Anveshan Jaggery mellow it.
The toasted chana-urad dal tempering is essential for the authentic Andhra crunch and aroma.
Fry the arbi until crisp at the edges so it stands up to the fierce coating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rice and ghee, or as a bold dry side to a bowl of cooling curd rice.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Capsicum
variations.description: A quick, punchy stir-fry of crisp-tender capsicum tossed in a coarse onion-tomato masala sharpened with green chillies and cracked black pepper. It stays deliberately dry and peppery so the capsicum's sweetness plays against the heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Its high smoke point is ideal for the quick high-heat toss that keeps the capsicum crisp.

steps: Deseed 3 large capsicums and cut into 1-inch squares, finely chop 1 large onion, slit 3 green chillies, and chop 2 tomatoes so everything is prepped for a fast stir-fry.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on medium-high until shimmering, then crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for around 15 seconds until aromatic.
Add the onion and slit chillies and fry for 4 minutes until the onion softens, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook a minute to lose the raw smell.
Mix in the tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, and cook 4 to 5 minutes until pulpy and the oil separates.
Raise the heat, add the capsicum with 1 tsp salt, and toss briskly for 6 to 7 minutes so it chars slightly at the edges yet stays crunchy.
Sprinkle 0.75 tsp black pepper powder and stir for a minute so its warmth coats every piece.
Finish with 2 tbsp fresh coriander and serve immediately while the capsicum still has bite.
tips: Keep the flame high and the pan uncrowded so the capsicum sears rather than steams and goes soggy.
Add the black pepper at the end, not the start, so its sharp aroma survives to the plate.
A mix of green, red and yellow capsicum makes the dish look as vibrant as it tastes.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a dry side with dal-rice, or stuff into a soft roti roll with a smear of mint chutney.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Capsicum
variations.description: A blazing Andhra take built on fiery Guntur red chillies and a roasted sesame-peanut podi that clings to the capsicum. Sesame oil deepens the nuttiness for a dish that is proudly, gloriously hot.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Andhra cooking prizes sesame oil for the earthy nuttiness it lends to fiery podi-based dishes.
