steps: Dry-grind 2 tbsp roasted sesame seeds and 2 tbsp roasted peanuts into a coarse podi, then deseed and cube 3 capsicums and slice 1 onion and 6 garlic cloves.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil over medium and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds with 12 curry leaves for about 20 seconds.
Add the sliced garlic and onion and fry for 4 minutes until the garlic is golden and the onion turns soft.
Lower the flame, sprinkle in 1.5 tsp Guntur red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp turmeric, and stir for 15 seconds so the spices bloom without scorching.
Raise the heat, add the capsicum with 1 tsp salt, and stir-fry for 6 to 7 minutes until it takes on a slight char but stays firm.
Scatter in the sesame-peanut podi and toss for 2 minutes until it coats the capsicum in a dry, nutty crust.
Serve hot, straight from the pan, so the podi stays crisp against the capsicum.
tips: Guntur chilli is seriously hot, so start with 1 tsp and build up if you are unsure of your tolerance.
Roast the sesame and peanuts fresh and cool them fully before grinding, or the podi turns oily and clumps.
The podi keeps for a week in a jar, so make a double batch for quick fiery stir-fries.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with plain rice and a spoon of ghee, or serve alongside curd rice to tame the Guntur heat.

variations.name: Punjabi Spicy Capsicum
variations.description: A robust Punjabi rendition where capsicum meets a ghee-fried onion-tomato masala, kasuri methi and a bold chilli hit. Slightly saucier than the classic, with the round richness ghee always brings.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee gives the masala a rounded Punjabi richness that balances the fiery chilli.

steps: Deseed and cube 3 capsicums, grate or finely chop 1 large onion, slit 3 green chillies, and puree 3 tomatoes for a smoother Punjabi-style base.
Melt 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and let 1 tsp cumin seeds crackle for about 15 seconds until they turn aromatic.
Add the onion and green chillies and fry for 6 minutes until deep golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook a minute until fragrant.
Pour in the tomato puree with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.25 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, and simmer 7 to 8 minutes until the ghee separates.
Add the capsicum with 1 tsp salt, stir to coat, and cook on medium for 6 to 7 minutes until just tender with a little bite left.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the top and sprinkle 0.75 tsp garam masala, cooking 2 minutes so the aromas meld.
Rest briefly off the heat and serve warm with the masala clinging to each piece.
tips: Pureeing the tomatoes gives a silkier masala that coats the capsicum better than chopped tomato.
For extra richness, stir in a tablespoon of cream or malai with the kasuri methi.
Do not overcook the capsicum; a slight crunch keeps this from turning into a soft gravy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tandoori roti or lachha paratha and a side of sliced onions dusted with chaat masala.

variations.name: Bengali Spicy Capsicum
variations.description: A capsicum stir-fry given the Bengali kalo jeere kacha lanka treatment: tempered in pungent mustard oil with nigella seeds and green chillies, finished with a whisper of sugar. Sharp, aromatic and light.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Its sharp pungency is the classic Bengali partner for capsicum and green chilli.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A trace of sweetness is the Bengali counterpoint that rounds out the mustard oil's bite.

steps: Deseed and cut 3 capsicums into thin strips, slice 1 onion, slit 4 green chillies, and finely chop 1 tomato for a light, quick-cooking base.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until it just smokes, cool for 10 seconds, then temper 0.75 tsp nigella seeds with the slit green chillies for 15 seconds.
Add the sliced onion and fry on medium for 4 minutes until soft and pale gold, then stir in 1 tsp ginger paste and cook 30 seconds.
Mix in the chopped tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and cook 3 to 4 minutes until it softens into the oil.
Raise the heat, add the capsicum strips with 1 tsp salt, and toss for 6 minutes until the edges blister but the strips stay crisp.
Stir in 0.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook a minute so the sweetness melts into the sharp masala.
Scatter 2 tbsp fresh coriander over the top and serve hot with a raw drizzle of mustard oil.
tips: Nigella seeds are bitter if burnt, so temper them only briefly once the oil has cooled slightly.
Keep the capsicum in thin strips for the delicate Bengali torkari texture.
Leave a few whole slit green chillies in for the aroma without all their heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot steamed rice and a dab of ghee, or as a sharp side to a simple dal.

variations.name: Kerala Spicy Capsicum
variations.description: A coconut-rich Kerala stir-fry where capsicum simmers in a roasted coconut-and-chilli masala perfumed with curry leaves and coconut oil. Spicy, glossy and layered with the toasty depth of browned coconut.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil ties the roasted coconut masala together with its unmistakable Kerala fragrance.

steps: Dry-roast 0.5 cup grated coconut with 4 dried red chillies in a pan until golden-brown and fragrant, then grind with 1 inch ginger and a splash of water into a coarse masala.
Deseed and cube 3 capsicums and thinly slice 6 shallots while the roasted coconut cools.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil over medium and splutter 0.75 tsp mustard seeds with 12 curry leaves until they pop, about 20 seconds.
Add the sliced shallots and fry for 3 minutes until soft, then stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp coriander powder for a few seconds.
Add the capsicum with 1 tsp salt and stir-fry on medium-high for 6 minutes until it softens at the edges but keeps its shape.
Fold in the ground roasted-coconut masala with a splash of water and cook for 4 to 5 minutes until it thickens and clings to the capsicum.
Finish with a fresh drizzle of coconut oil off the heat and serve warm.
tips: Roast the coconut slowly to a deep golden brown, not black, for a sweet-nutty depth without bitterness.
Grind the masala coarse rather than smooth so the stir-fry keeps a pleasant texture.
Shallots give a rounder sweetness than regular onion here, so use them if you can find them.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with appam, Malabar parotta or plain rice and a bowl of moru curry.

variations.name: Classic Butter Dum Aloo
variations.description: The dhaba-style favourite: golden fried baby potatoes simmered slowly in a silky onion-tomato-cashew gravy enriched with butter and cream. The dum (slow steam) cooking lets the potatoes drink up the buttery masala until they turn glossy and rich.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil gives the fried potatoes a clean, nutty crust without greasiness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoon of bilona ghee stirred in at the end lifts the gravy with a warm dairy aroma

steps: Boil 500 g baby potatoes in salted water for about 10 minutes until just fork-tender, then drain, cool slightly and peel; prick each one all over with a toothpick so it soaks up the gravy.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat and shallow-fry the potatoes for 5 to 6 minutes, turning often, until they are golden and lightly blistered; lift them out and set aside.
In the same oil crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then add 2 chopped onions and 12 cashews and saute on medium heat for 7 to 8 minutes until the onions turn deep golden.
Stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 3 chopped tomatoes and cook for 6 minutes until pulpy and softened, then cool and blend to a smooth paste with a splash of water.
Return the paste to the pan, add 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and simmer on low for 8 to 10 minutes until the oil shimmers at the edges.
Slide in the fried potatoes and about half a cup of water, cover and dum-cook on low for 8 minutes, then stir in 2 tbsp butter, 3 tbsp cream, 0.75 tsp garam masala and 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi.
Finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, cook uncovered for 2 more minutes until glossy, and rest 5 minutes before serving so the potatoes settle into the masala.
tips: Parboil the potatoes only until just tender; over-boiled potatoes break apart during the dum stage and cloud the gravy.
For a restaurant-smooth finish, strain the blended onion-tomato paste through a coarse sieve before simmering.
The gravy thickens as it rests, so keep it a touch looser than you want; loosen with hot water, never cold, when reheating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle into a copper handi and swirl an extra ribbon of cream on top with a pinch of kasuri methi; pair with butter naan or laccha paratha and a side of pickled onions.

variations.name: Bengali Butter Dum Aloo
variations.description: A Bengali reading of dum aloo where pungent mustard oil and a whiff of sugar reframe the classic. The potatoes are browned in smoking mustard oil and finished with a gentle sweetness, giving a sharp, aromatic gravy quite unlike the North Indian version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil, smoked to its point first, is the backbone of the Bengali pungency here

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a teaspoon of jaggery gives the signature Bengali sweet-savoury balance without refined sugar

steps: Boil 500 g baby potatoes for 10 minutes until just tender, drain, peel and prick them, then rub with 0.25 tsp turmeric and a little salt so they colour evenly.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just begins to smoke and the raw pungency mellows, then fry the potatoes on medium for 5 minutes until golden brown and set aside.
In the same oil temper 1 bay leaf, 2 dried red chillies and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds until they crackle and release aroma.
Add 2 finely chopped onions and saute for 6 minutes until soft and pale gold, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger paste and cook another minute until the raw smell fades.
Mix in 2 chopped tomatoes with the remaining 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1 tsp cumin powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook on medium for 6 minutes until the masala leaves the oil.
Return the potatoes with three-quarters of a cup of water, cover and simmer on low for 10 minutes until they are cooked through and the gravy clings.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 0.5 tsp garam masala and 1 tbsp butter, simmer for 2 minutes and serve hot.
tips: Always heat mustard oil to smoking and let it cool for a few seconds before frying; this removes the raw bite Bengalis avoid in the final dish.
Keep the gravy on the thinner side, as this version is traditionally eaten soupy with plain rice.
A pinch of roasted bhaja masala (dry-roasted cumin and chilli) sprinkled at the end deepens the Bengali character.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed gobindobhog or basmati rice and a wedge of lime, or alongside luchi for a weekend brunch; a side of tomato chutney rounds out the meal.

variations.name: Kashmiri Butter Dum Aloo
variations.description: Inspired by the Kashmiri dum aloo tradition, this take skips onion and garlic and builds colour and warmth from fennel, dry ginger and a bloom of saffron. The result is a fragrant, ruby-tinted yoghurt gravy that coats the potatoes without any heaviness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee is the authentic frying and cooking fat for Kashmiri dum aloo, giving a rounded richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Kashmiri saffron steeped in warm milk lends the gravy its glow and floral perfume

steps: Soak 0.25 tsp Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside to bloom while you prepare the potatoes.
Boil 500 g baby potatoes for 10 minutes until just tender, peel, and prick them deeply so the yoghurt gravy can penetrate.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan and fry the potatoes on medium for 5 to 6 minutes until an even golden brown, then remove them.
In the same ghee add a pinch of asafoetida, 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, 3 cloves, 3 cardamom and 1 inch cinnamon, and let them sizzle for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Lower the heat, whisk 0.75 cup curd with 1.5 tsp fennel powder, 1 tsp dry ginger powder and 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, then pour it in slowly while stirring so it does not split.
Add 1 tsp salt and 1 cup water, bring to a gentle simmer, return the potatoes and cook covered on low for 12 minutes until the gravy thickens and clings.
Stir in the saffron milk, simmer for 2 more minutes and rest before serving so the colour deepens.
tips: Whisk the curd until completely smooth and add it off the boil on low heat; high heat is the main reason yoghurt gravies curdle.
Fennel and dry ginger powder are the defining Kashmiri spices here, so do not substitute garam masala for them.
Make it a few hours ahead; this gravy tastes markedly better once the potatoes have steeped in the spiced yoghurt.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed basmati rice or a soft sheermal, and offer a bowl of chilled boondi raita to balance the fennel-forward warmth.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Butter Dum Aloo
variations.description: A Maharashtrian spin built on goda masala, the region's fragrant blend of roasted sesame, coconut and warm spices. It brings a dark, slightly sweet and nutty depth to the potatoes that sets it apart from the creamy northern style.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: groundnut oil is the everyday Maharashtrian cooking fat and carries the goda masala beautifully

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a hint of jaggery rounds off the goda masala in the classic Maharashtrian sweet-savoury balance

steps: Boil 500 g baby potatoes for 10 minutes until just tender, peel and prick them all over so they absorb the masala.
Dry-roast 3 tbsp desiccated coconut in a pan on low for 3 minutes until golden and fragrant, then set aside to grind later with a little water into a paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai and fry the potatoes on medium for 5 minutes until golden, then remove them.
In the same oil crackle 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 10 curry leaves for 20 seconds, then add 2 chopped onions and saute for 7 minutes until deep brown.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 2 chopped tomatoes, 2 tsp goda masala, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 6 minutes until the oil separates.
Add the roasted coconut paste and 1 cup water, bring to a simmer, then return the potatoes and cook covered on low for 10 minutes.
Finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer for 2 minutes until glossy and serve garnished with fresh coriander.
tips: Goda masala scorches quickly, so add it with the tomatoes and wet masala rather than into dry hot oil.
Roast the coconut until just golden, not brown, to keep the gravy sweet-nutty rather than bitter.
This masala base freezes well; make a double batch and freeze half for a fast weeknight curry.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with soft jowar or bajra bhakri and a spoon of raw onion and lime, or serve with steamed rice topped with a trickle of ghee.

variations.name: Gujarati Butter Dum Aloo
variations.description: The Gujarati version leans into the beloved sweet-sour-spicy triad, with jaggery for mellow sweetness and a squeeze of lemon for lift. A lighter, brighter gravy that stays true to Gujarat's love of gentle heat balanced by sweetness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil is the traditional Gujarati kitchen fat and keeps the gravy light

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery delivers the signature Gujarati sweetness that offsets the tang of tomato and lemon

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of ghee softens the sweet-sour edge and adds aroma

steps: Boil 500 g baby potatoes for 10 minutes until just tender, peel and prick them so they take on the tangy gravy.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai and shallow-fry the potatoes on medium for 5 minutes until lightly golden, then lift them out.
In the same oil crackle 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 8 curry leaves for 20 seconds until they splutter.
Add 1 chopped onion and saute for 4 minutes until translucent, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and 3 chopped tomatoes and cook for 6 minutes until pulpy.
Mix in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander-cumin powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 3 minutes until the oil rises.
Pour in 1 cup water, return the potatoes, cover and simmer on low for 10 minutes until they are cooked through and coated.
Stir in 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, simmer for 2 minutes and serve.
tips: Balance is everything here; taste after adding jaggery and lemon and adjust so no single note dominates.
Add the lemon juice off the heat to keep its brightness from turning dull and bitter.
For extra body without cream, mash two of the boiled potatoes into the gravy before adding the rest.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulka or thepla and a bowl of plain curd; a side of sweet-and-spicy chundo pickle plays up the Gujarati flavour profile.

variations.name: Classic Dry Sem
variations.description: A homestyle dry stir-fry of tender broad beans (sem) sauteed until they lose their raw bite and turn glossy with masala. Cooked without any gravy, each bean stays separate and lightly caramelised at the edges. A pinch of jaggery rounds off the earthy legume flavour.

ingredients.name: Broad beans (sem), stringed and diagonally sliced
Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil gives the beans a clean nutty sheen without greasiness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a small pinch balances the mild bitterness of broad beans

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a heavy kadai on medium heat until it shimmers, then add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle and darken for about 20 seconds.
Add the finely chopped onion and saute on medium heat until soft and pale gold, about 5 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute until the raw smell disappears.
Add the chopped tomato along with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, and cook for 4-5 minutes until the tomato collapses and oil beads at the edges.

Tip in the 400 g sliced broad beans and 1 tsp salt, toss to coat every piece in masala, then cover and cook on low heat for 12-14 minutes, stirring every few minutes, until the beans are fork-tender but still bright.
Uncover, raise the heat to medium and stir-fry for 2-3 minutes so any moisture evaporates and the beans catch a little colour.
Sprinkle in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.5 tsp garam masala, toss for 1 minute, then finish with 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander and serve.
tips: String the beans thoroughly and slice them thin and diagonally so they cook evenly and stay tender-crisp.
If the beans are stubbornly firm, sprinkle 2 tbsp hot water, cover and steam for another 3 minutes rather than adding more oil.
This sabzi tastes even better after resting 10 minutes, as the masala settles into the beans.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pack it into a lunchbox with hot phulkas and a wedge of lemon, or serve alongside dal-rice with a spoon of plain yoghurt on the side.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Dry Sem
variations.description: A Pune-style preparation where broad beans are perfumed with warm, dusky goda masala and finished with fresh grated coconut. The masala's clove-cinnamon-sesame depth makes this take unmistakably Maharashtrian. A whisper of jaggery is traditional to counter the goda masala's heat.

ingredients.name: Broad beans (sem), stringed and cut into pieces
Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the traditional cooking fat of Maharashtrian kitchens, letting goda masala bloom cleanly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the classic Maharashtrian sweet note that tames goda masala's warmth

steps: Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and wait for them to pop, then add 0.5 tsp cumin, a pinch of asafoetida and 10 curry leaves and let them splutter for 15 seconds.
Stir in the chopped onion and cook for 4-5 minutes until translucent, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for a minute until fragrant.
Lower the heat and add 1.5 tsp goda masala, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder, stirring quickly for 20-30 seconds so the spices bloom without scorching.
Add the 400 g broad beans and 1 tsp salt, toss well, sprinkle in 3 tbsp water, then cover and cook on low for 12-14 minutes until the beans turn tender, stirring occasionally.
Uncover and stir in 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, cooking on medium for 2 minutes until the jaggery melts and glazes the beans.
Fold in 3 tbsp fresh grated coconut, cook for a final minute and take off the heat while the coconut is still moist.
tips: Goda masala scorches fast, so always add it on low heat and follow immediately with the beans.
For a drier, roasted finish, stir-fry uncovered for an extra 2-3 minutes before adding the coconut.
No goda masala on hand? A blend of garam masala with a pinch of ground sesame and dry coconut approximates its flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri and a dollop of white butter, or pair with varan-bhaat for a comforting Maharashtrian thali.

variations.name: Bengali Dry Sem
variations.description: A pungent, pared-back sem chorchori where broad beans are cooked in sharp, unrefined mustard oil and tempered with panch phoron. The mustard oil's bite and the five-spice aroma give this take its distinctly Bengali soul. A touch of green chilli and sugar keeps the flavour bright and balanced.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: heated to smoking point first to mellow its sharpness the Bengali way

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai on medium-high until it just begins to smoke, then lower the heat to let it cool slightly and shed its raw pungency.
Add 1 tsp panch phoron, 2 dried red chillies and 1 bay leaf, letting them crackle and turn aromatic for about 20 seconds.
Stir in 1 tsp ginger paste and 2 slit green chillies and fry for 30 seconds, then add 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp red chilli powder off the direct flame so they do not burn.
Add the 400 g broad beans, 1 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp sugar, toss to coat, then sprinkle 3 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 12-14 minutes until the beans are soft.
Uncover and stir-fry on medium heat for 3-4 minutes so the beans dry out and take on the mustard oil's glossy finish.
Scatter 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander over the top, give a final toss and serve.
tips: Always bring mustard oil to smoking point before cooking; raw mustard oil tastes harsh and overpowering.
Panch phoron is a whole-spice mix, so it must be tempered in hot oil first and never added to the beans raw.
For an authentic chorchori texture, keep the dish nearly dry with just the oil clinging to the beans.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot as a first course with steamed gobindobhog rice and a drizzle of raw mustard oil, followed by dal and fish.

variations.name: Kerala Dry Sem
variations.description: A Malabar-style thoran where broad beans are chopped fine and tossed with a coarse coconut-cumin paste, cooked entirely in fragrant coconut oil. Curry leaves and a mustard temper make it aromatic, while the fresh coconut keeps it moist and sweet. This is the everyday green vegetable of a Kerala sadya spread.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed coconut oil is the defining aroma of a Kerala thoran

steps: Coarsely crush together 0.5 cup grated coconut, 0.5 tsp cumin, 3 garlic cloves, 2 green chillies and 0.5 tsp turmeric in a mortar or pulse briefly in a mixer, keeping it dry and textured.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal and let them splutter and turn golden, about 30 seconds.
Add 2 dried red chillies, 12 curry leaves and 4 sliced shallots, frying for 2 minutes until the shallots soften.
Add the 400 g finely chopped broad beans and 1 tsp salt, sprinkle 3 tbsp water, then cover and steam on low for 10-12 minutes until the beans turn tender, stirring once midway.
Add the crushed coconut mixture and toss thoroughly to coat the beans, cooking uncovered on low for 3-4 minutes so the coconut warms and dries slightly.
Increase the heat for a final minute to drive off any moisture, then take off the flame while the thoran is still moist and fragrant.
tips: Chop the beans small and uniform, as thoran cooks best with finely cut vegetables.
Do not brown the coconut; it should stay pale and just heated through for the right sweet-nutty taste.
A final drizzle of raw coconut oil off the heat deepens the classic Kerala aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as part of a rice meal with sambar and rasam, or alongside curd rice for a light, coconut-scented lunch.

variations.name: Rajasthani Dry Sem
variations.description: A fiery, rustic Marwari take where broad beans are cooked in a smoky paste of soaked dried red chillies and garlic, with no tomato in sight. The chillies lend deep red colour and heat rather than sharpness, mellowed by a spoon of ghee finish. It is a bold, water-thrifty sabzi built for desert kitchens.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a neutral wood-pressed base that lets the chilli paste stay the star

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of bilona ghee rounds off the chilli heat with richness

steps: Soak 5 dried red chillies in warm water for 15 minutes, then grind them with 6 garlic cloves and a splash of the soaking water into a smooth red paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and a pinch of asafoetida and let them sizzle for 15 seconds.
Add the chopped onion and fry for 4-5 minutes until golden, then add the ground chilli-garlic paste and cook on low for 3-4 minutes until the oil separates and the raw smell fades.
Stir in 2 tsp coriander powder and 0.5 tsp turmeric, fry for 30 seconds, then add the 400 g broad beans and 1 tsp salt and toss to coat in the deep red masala.
Sprinkle 3 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 13-15 minutes until the beans are tender, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking.
Uncover, stir in 0.5 tsp amchur and finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, tossing for a minute so the ghee coats the beans glossily before serving.
tips: Use mild Mathania or Kashmiri chillies for colour without punishing heat, or blend with hotter chillies to taste.
Soaking and grinding the chillies rather than using powder gives the authentic smoky-smooth Marwari base.
Keep the sabzi nearly dry; Rajasthani cooking traditionally uses little water, relying on oil and ghee instead.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra roti and a side of raw onion and green chilli, or tuck into a khoba roti with extra ghee.

variations.name: Classic Handi Chana Masala
variations.description: Slow-simmered chickpeas in a sealed handi where whole spices and a smooth onion-tomato base marry into a deep, glossy gravy. The clay-pot method keeps the chana plump and lets the masala cling to every kernel. A restaurant-style dhaba favourite you can build entirely from scratch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Its nutty depth stands up to a long handi simmer without turning heavy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of bilona ghee rounds off the tang and adds handi aroma

steps: Pressure-cook the soaked 1.5 cups chickpeas with 0.5 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 5-6 whistles on medium heat until they crush easily between two fingers, then reserve the cooking liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a handi over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds with the whole spices for about 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the 2 chopped onions and saute for 7-8 minutes until deep golden, then stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute until the raw smell lifts.
Pour in the tomato puree with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp salt, and simmer on medium for 8-10 minutes until the oil separates at the edges.
Tip in the cooked chickpeas with 1 cup of their reserved liquid, cover the handi and simmer gently for 12-15 minutes until the gravy thickens and coats the chana.
Finish with 1 tsp garam masala, 2 tbsp cream and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, and cook uncovered for 2 more minutes until glossy.
tips: Add a black tea bag or a piece of dried amla to the cooking water to deepen the chana to a natural dark brown.
Lightly mash a handful of cooked chickpeas into the gravy to thicken it without any flour or cornstarch.
The dish tastes better the next day once the masala fully seeps into the chana, so make it ahead when you can.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in the handi itself with kulcha, sliced red onion rings, lemon wedges and a green chilli on the side for a dhaba-style spread.

variations.name: Punjabi Handi Chana Masala
variations.description: The buttery Amritsari take, where a knob of white butter and a heavy hand with kasuri methi turn the handi rich and unmistakably Punjabi. The gravy is thick, tangy and clings like a pindi chana. Best mopped up with hot lachha paratha.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee gives the Amritsari gravy its signature buttery backbone

steps: Pressure-cook the soaked 1.5 cups chickpeas with 0.5 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 5-6 whistles until soft enough to mash, then keep the cooking liquid aside.
Melt 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a handi over medium heat and pop 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds until they sizzle and turn aromatic.
Fry the 2 chopped onions for 8-9 minutes until richly browned, add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until the raw edge disappears.
Add the chopped tomatoes with 1.25 tsp red chilli, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp salt, mashing them down over medium heat for 9-10 minutes until pulpy and oil-flecked.
Stir in the cooked chickpeas with 1 cup reserved liquid and 1.5 tsp chana masala powder, then simmer covered for 12 minutes until thick.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi between your palms into the pot, swirl in 2 tbsp white butter and 3 tbsp cream, and cook 2 minutes until velvety.
tips: Toast the kasuri methi on a dry pan for 20 seconds before crushing to intensify its meadow-like aroma.
For a darker Amritsari colour, add half a teaspoon of deggi mirch along with the regular chilli powder.
If the gravy tightens on standing, loosen it with a splash of warm chana stock rather than plain water to keep the flavour intact.
variations.servingSuggestion: Top with extra butter shavings and julienned ginger, and pair with amritsari kulcha or bhatura and a glass of salted lassi.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Handi Chana Masala
variations.description: A Puneri-style handi built on freshly ground goda masala and coconut, giving the chana a warm, slightly sweet, dusky flavour quite unlike the North Indian version. Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the authentic cooking fat here. Earthy, aromatic and deeply comforting.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The traditional Maharashtrian cooking fat that carries goda masala beautifully

steps: Pressure-cook the soaked 1.5 cups chickpeas with 0.5 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 5-6 whistles until tender, then set aside with their liquid.
Dry-roast 3 tbsp grated coconut in a handi over low heat for 3-4 minutes until golden and nutty, then grind it with the 2 chopped tomatoes into a smooth paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Saute the 2 chopped onions for 7 minutes until golden brown, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute, then stir in the coconut-tomato paste with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli.
Add 2 tsp goda masala and 0.75 tsp salt, and fry the masala for 6-7 minutes on medium until it darkens and the oil rises to the surface.
Fold in the cooked chickpeas with 1 cup reserved liquid and 1 tsp grated jaggery, simmer covered for 12 minutes, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Goda masala scorches fast because of its coconut content, so keep the flame at medium and stir constantly once it goes in.
A squeeze of lime at the table brightens the dusky goda notes and balances the touch of jaggery.
Grind the roasted coconut while still warm for the smoothest paste and the deepest colour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft jowar bhakri or steamed rice topped with a spoon of raw groundnut oil and a wedge of lime, Puneri style.

variations.name: Kashmiri Handi Chana Masala
variations.description: A regal handi bloomed with saffron and Kashmiri chilli for colour without fierce heat, scented with fennel and dry ginger in place of onion-garlic. The gravy turns a deep ruby red and eats mild, fragrant and festive. A Pandit-style treatment usually reserved for feast days.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee is the classic Kashmiri fat that carries saffron and fennel aromatics

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: A saffron steep gives the ruby glow and delicate perfume central to this dish

steps: Soak 0.25 tsp Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 3 tbsp warm water and set aside to bloom while you cook the chana.
Pressure-cook the soaked 1.5 cups chickpeas with 0.5 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 5-6 whistles until tender, then reserve the liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a handi over medium heat, add the cinnamon, cloves and cardamom with 0.25 tsp asafoetida, and let them sizzle for 30 seconds.
Lower the heat, stir in 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder followed quickly by the tomato puree, and cook for 6-7 minutes until the ghee floats red on top.
Whisk in the 0.5 cup curd off the heat to prevent splitting, then add 2 tsp fennel powder, 1 tsp dry ginger and 0.75 tsp salt and simmer 3 minutes.
Add the chickpeas with 1 cup reserved liquid and the bloomed saffron water, cover and simmer gently for 12-15 minutes until the gravy is ruby-red and fragrant.
tips: Always take the pot off the flame before adding curd and stir continuously as it warms back up to stop it from curdling.
Fennel and dry ginger replace onion and garlic here, so do not be tempted to add them or you lose the clean Pandit character.
Bloom the saffron in warm, not boiling, water to protect its delicate aroma and full colour release.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed basmati rice and a bowl of Kashmiri dum aloo alongside, finished with a few saffron strands on top for a wazwan-style plate.

variations.name: Bengali Handi Chana Masala
variations.description: Kolkata's Sunday-morning cholar-style handi, pungent with wood-pressed mustard oil and a whole-spice bloom, brightened with a hint of sugar and slit green chillies. The mustard oil gives the chana an addictive sharp edge that pairs with luchi. Comfort food from a Bengali winter kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Pungent kachi ghani mustard oil is the soul of a Bengali chana handi

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A whisper of jaggery gives the classic Bengali sweet-savoury balance

ingredients.name: Bay leaf and dried red chilli

steps: Pressure-cook the soaked 1.5 cups chickpeas with 0.5 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 5-6 whistles until soft, then keep aside with the liquid.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil in a handi over medium-high until it just begins to smoke, then lower the heat to temper 1 tsp cumin seeds, the bay leaf and dried red chilli for 30 seconds.
Add the chopped onion and fry for 6-7 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger paste and cook 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli and 0.75 tsp salt, and cook for 8 minutes on medium until the tomatoes collapse and oil separates.
Tip in the cooked chickpeas with 1 cup reserved liquid, add the 3 slit green chillies and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, and simmer covered for 12 minutes.
Sprinkle 0.75 tsp Bengali garam masala over the top, cook uncovered for 2 more minutes and rest 5 minutes before serving so the mustard flavour settles.
tips: Heat the mustard oil until it wisps and loses its raw bite before adding spices, otherwise the gravy tastes harsh.
Bengali garam masala is a lighter blend of cinnamon, cardamom and clove only, so avoid the cumin-heavy North Indian mix here.
The single spoon of jaggery is meant to be barely detectable, just enough to round the mustard's pungency.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with luchi or steamed gobindobhog rice, and add a slit green chilli and a drizzle of raw mustard oil on top for authentic bite.

variations.name: Classic Home-style Kaddu
variations.description: The everyday North Indian khatta-meetha pumpkin that turns up in tiffins and thali corners across the Hindi belt. Soft cubes of kaddu are collapsed into a jammy onion-tomato base, balanced by a whisper of jaggery and a squeeze of tang so it never tastes flat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: its clean nutty base lets the pumpkin's sweetness lead instead of masking it

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melts into the masala to give the signature khatta-meetha rounding without refined sugar

steps: Peel 600 g pumpkin, scoop out the seeds and cut into rough 2 cm cubes, keeping the skin on a few pieces for texture if you like. Finely chop the onion and tomatoes and keep aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 20 seconds until they sizzle and smell toasty.
Add the chopped onion and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and saute on medium heat for 4 to 5 minutes until the onion turns soft and pale gold at the edges.
Stir in the tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, then cook 4 to 5 minutes until the tomatoes break down and oil beads at the sides.
Tip in the pumpkin cubes with 1 tsp salt, toss to coat, add a splash of about 3 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 12 to 15 minutes, stirring twice, until the pieces mash easily against the pan.
Add 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.75 tsp amchur, mash roughly a third of the pumpkin for a jammy body, and cook uncovered 2 minutes. Finish with 2 tbsp fresh coriander.
tips: For a drier tiffin-style sabzi, mash less and cook uncovered an extra 3 minutes so the surface caramelises slightly.
If your pumpkin is very sweet, cut the jaggery to 2 tsp and push the amchur up to 1 tsp to keep the sweet-sour balance.
This keeps well for two days and the flavour deepens; loosen with a spoon of hot water when reheating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile it beside plain phulkas with a bowl of thick curd and a wedge of lemon; it also makes a surprisingly good stuffing for a folded paratha roll.

variations.name: Gujarati Home-style Kaddu
variations.description: Gujarat leans fully into the khatta-meetha instinct, building a shining sweet-sour pumpkin shaak spiked with peanuts and a warm jaggery finish. Sesame and a little kokum-like tang from lemon make it glossy and moreish, meant to be eaten with soft rotli.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: gives the shaak its characteristic Gujarati toasty aroma and pairs with the peanuts

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the signature Gujarati sweetness that lacquers the pumpkin as it dissolves

steps: Cut 600 g peeled pumpkin into 2 cm cubes and slit 2 green chillies lengthwise. Coarsely crush 3 tbsp roasted peanuts so some texture remains.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadai on medium heat and add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds; when they pop after about 20 seconds add 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida.
Drop in the slit green chillies and the pumpkin cubes with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, toss to coat well in the fragrant oil for 2 minutes.
Add 1.5 tsp coriander-cumin powder and the crushed peanuts, splash in about 4 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 12 to 14 minutes until the pumpkin is fork-tender.
Stir in 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and let it melt for 2 minutes, gently mashing a few cubes so the shaak turns glossy and clings together.
Switch off the heat, mix in 1 tbsp lemon juice and 2 tbsp fresh coriander, and taste to check the sweet, sour and salty notes are balanced.
tips: Add the lemon juice only off the heat so its brightness stays sharp against the jaggery.
For a festive version, fold in 1 tbsp fresh grated coconut with the coriander at the end.
The crushed peanuts should stay slightly chunky; if you pre-grind them fine the shaak turns pasty.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with phulka rotli and a spoon of aam ras or plain chaas on the side; it also rounds out a Gujarati thali next to kadhi and rice.

variations.name: Bengali Home-style Kaddu
variations.description: This is kumro chokka in spirit, where pumpkin is tempered in pungent mustard oil and panch phoron, then finished with a hint of sugar and roasted spice. The five-seed tempering and the bite of mustard oil give it a distinctly Bengali sweetness-forward, aromatic character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: heated to smoking then cooled slightly, its sharp pungency is the backbone of Bengali pumpkin

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the gentle Bengali sweetness that offsets the mustard oil's edge

steps: Cut 600 g peeled pumpkin into 2.5 cm cubes. Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just smokes, then lower the heat to take off the raw pungency.
Temper 1 tsp panch phoron, 2 dried red chillies and 1 bay leaf in the hot oil for about 20 seconds until the seeds crackle and turn fragrant.
Add 1 tsp ginger paste and the pumpkin cubes with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, tossing to coat, and fry uncovered for 3 to 4 minutes so the edges catch a little colour.
Sprinkle in 1 tsp cumin powder and 2 slit green chillies, add about 4 tbsp water, cover and steam on low for 12 to 14 minutes until the pumpkin is soft and glossy.
Add 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, mash a few cubes lightly to thicken, and cook uncovered 2 minutes until the mixture pulls away from the pan.
Finish by dusting over 0.5 tsp roasted bhaja masala and stir once; the smoky note should hit you as you serve.
tips: Always smoke the mustard oil first; using it raw leaves a harsh nose that overpowers the dish.
For a heartier chokka, add a handful of soaked chana or fried bori (lentil dumplings) along with the pumpkin.
Make the bhaja masala by dry-roasting cumin and dried chilli, then grinding; a pinch added at the very end lifts everything.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best scooped up with hot luchi or steamed rice as the first course of a Bengali lunch, with a wedge of lime alongside.

variations.name: Rajasthani Home-style Kaddu
variations.description: A fiery, tangy desert-style pumpkin where whole dried red chillies and fennel do the talking and amchur keeps it bright. With almost no onion or tomato, it relies on smoky chilli-tempered mustard oil and dry spice, the way it is cooked in Marwari kitchens where fresh produce was once scarce.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the traditional Marwari cooking fat that carries the dried-chilli smoke through the dish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: balances the aggressive dried chilli heat with a mellow desert sweetness

steps: Cut 600 g peeled pumpkin into 2 cm cubes. Snap 4 dried red chillies in half and shake out most of the seeds if you want less heat.

Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it smokes, lower the flame, then add the broken dried chillies, 1 tsp cumin, 1 tsp fennel, 0.25 tsp methi seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida, frying 20 seconds until the chillies darken.
Add the pumpkin with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt and stir-fry on medium heat for 4 minutes so the cubes take on the smoky chilli oil.
Sprinkle in 2 tsp coriander powder, add about 3 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 10 to 12 minutes until the pumpkin softens but still holds its shape.
Uncover, add 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp amchur, and toss on medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes until the masala coats the cubes and turns glossy.
Taste and adjust; it should land sharp, sweet and smoky all at once, with the dried chillies still visible in the sabzi.
tips: Keeping the pumpkin slightly firm is authentic here; do not mash it as you would a North Indian kaddu.
The whole fried chillies are meant to be eaten by the brave; leave them in for looks and warn milder eaters.
A pinch of kasuri methi crushed in at the end deepens the desert-kitchen aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with bajra or wheat rotla brushed with ghee and a dollop of white butter to tame the heat, plus raw onion rings on the side.

variations.name: Kerala Home-style Kaddu
variations.description: Inspired by mathanga erissery, this Kerala pumpkin is simmered soft then folded into a fresh coconut-cumin paste and crowned with a curry-leaf and coconut tempering in fragrant coconut oil. It is mellow, nutty and lightly sweet, a temple-style comfort dish with no onion or tomato.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the defining Kerala tempering fat that perfumes the curry leaves and toasted coconut

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: just a teaspoon to lift the natural sweetness of pumpkin the Kerala way

steps: Cut 600 g peeled pumpkin into 2 cm cubes, place in a pan with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp salt and about half a cup of water, cover and simmer 12 minutes until soft.
Meanwhile grind 0.75 cup grated coconut with 1 tsp cumin seeds and 2 green chillies to a coarse paste using a splash of water.
Stir the coconut paste into the cooked pumpkin along with 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, mash lightly and simmer on low for 4 to 5 minutes until thick and well blended.
For the tempering, heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan and pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds until they splutter.
Add 2 dried red chillies and 12 curry leaves and fry 20 seconds until the leaves go crisp and the oil smells nutty and fragrant.
Pour the sizzling tempering over the pumpkin, stir once gently, and cover for a minute so the aroma settles into the dish before serving.
tips: For a truly authentic erissery, dry-roast 2 extra tbsp coconut until golden and add it into the tempering.
Do not over-grind the coconut; a slightly coarse paste gives the right rustic body.
It thickens as it sits, so keep it a touch loose if you plan to serve it later.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot Kerala matta rice with a spoon of extra coconut oil drizzled on top, alongside a tangy pachadi or pappadam.

variations.name: Classic Kadai Chole
variations.description: Kadai chole is a semi-dry, wok-tossed chickpea dish built on a freshly pounded kadai masala of roasted coriander seeds and dried red chilli. Chunky onion petals and capsicum stay slightly crisp while the chickpeas take on a smoky, coarse-ground coating rather than a pool of gravy. It is finished in a screaming-hot kadai so the masala clings to every bean.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil gives this kadai a clean, nutty base that stands up to the coarse roasted masala.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon of bilona ghee stirred in at the very end rounds off the sharp roasted-chilli edge.

steps: Soak 1.5 cups kabuli chickpeas overnight in plenty of water, then pressure cook them with 1.25 tsp salt and 3 cups fresh water for 5 to 6 whistles until they crush easily between two fingers.

Dry roast 1 tbsp coriander seeds, 4 dried red chillies and 1 tsp cumin seeds in a hot kadai over medium heat until fragrant and a shade darker, about 2 minutes, then cool and coarsely pound into a gritty kadai masala.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in the same kadai on medium-high, add 2 diced onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, and fry until the onions turn deep golden at the edges, about 6 minutes.
Stir in 3 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder, and cook until the tomatoes collapse and the oil rims the pan, roughly 7 to 8 minutes.
Add 1 large cubed capsicum and the pounded kadai masala, then toss over high heat for 2 minutes so the peppers stay crunchy and the spices turn smoky.
Tip in the drained chickpeas with about 0.5 cup of their cooking water and simmer uncovered for 8 minutes, mashing a few chickpeas against the pan so the coating thickens and clings.
Finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 0.5 tsp garam masala and 3 tbsp chopped coriander, toss once and serve while the masala still hugs each chickpea.
tips: For a dhaba-style smoky note, rest a live charcoal ember in a small steel bowl on top of the finished chole, drizzle a few drops of ghee over it and cover for 2 minutes to trap the smoke.
Add the capsicum late and keep the heat high so it holds a slight bite against the soft chickpeas.
Double the roasted kadai masala and store it in an airtight jar for up to two weeks to cut weeknight cooking time in half.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve straight from a copper kadai with butter-laminated laccha paratha, lemon-soaked onion rings and a wedge of lime for a full dhaba-style plate.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Kadai Chole
variations.description: This Konkani-leaning take swaps standard garam masala for goda masala, a dark roasted blend of sesame, dry coconut and stone flower that turns the chickpeas almost mahogany. Roasted peanuts and coconut make it nutty, while a small spoon of Anveshan Jaggery Powder gives the gentle sweet-earthy balance Maharashtrian kitchens love. It is warming and mellow rather than fiery.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the everyday cooking fat of the Deccan and carries goda masala beautifully.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A teaspoon of jaggery powder rounds the smoky goda masala without turning the dish sweet.

steps: Pressure cook 1.5 cups soaked kabuli chickpeas with 1.25 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 5 to 6 whistles, then keep them and their cooking liquid aside.

Dry roast 3 tbsp grated coconut and 2 tbsp peanuts in a pan over low heat until the coconut smells toasty and turns light brown, about 4 minutes, then cool and grind to a coarse paste with a splash of water.
Warm 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin and 10 curry leaves, then add 2 chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and saute until browned, about 7 minutes.
Mix in 2 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp goda masala, and cook until the raw smell lifts and the oil separates, around 6 minutes.
Stir in the ground coconut-peanut paste and fry for 2 minutes until it darkens and smells nutty and deep.
Add the chickpeas with 1 cup of their cooking water and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, then simmer for 10 minutes until the gravy thickens to a coating consistency.
Scatter 2 tbsp chopped coriander over the top and rest the dish covered for 5 minutes so the goda masala settles before serving.
tips: Toast the coconut low and slow; if it scorches it turns bitter and there is no rescuing goda masala gravy afterwards.
No goda masala on hand? Approximate it with a pinch each of cinnamon, clove and roasted sesame stirred into your garam masala.
This gravy deepens overnight, so it makes an excellent make-ahead dish for a weekend thali.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with soft jowar bhakri or steamed rice and a side of raw onion, and add a spoon of thick curd on the side to cool the earthy spice.

variations.name: Gujarati Kadai Chole
variations.description: The Gujarati version leans into the region's signature sweet-savoury-sour triangle, using Anveshan Jaggery Powder against tomatoes and a squeeze of lemon. The masala is lighter and less oily, meant to be a little souped so it soaks into soft rotli. Ground peanut and a hint of green chilli keep it homely and comforting.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Gujarati homes favour a lighter hand with wood-pressed groundnut oil so the sweetness of the gravy shines.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery powder is the heartbeat of Gujarati gravies, balancing the tomato tang into a gentle sweet-sour finish.

steps: Pressure cook 1.5 cups soaked chickpeas with 1 tsp salt and 3 cups water for about 6 whistles until very soft, then lightly mash a quarter of them with the back of a ladle.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds until they sizzle and float, then add 1 finely chopped onion and 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and cook until translucent, about 4 minutes.
Add 3 pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander-cumin powder, and simmer until the mixture thickens and the oil floats, roughly 8 minutes.
Stir in 2 tbsp roasted peanut powder and cook for 2 minutes so it thickens the gravy and adds a nutty body.
Add the chickpeas along with 1.5 cups of their cooking water and 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, then simmer gently for 12 minutes until slightly soupy and glossy.
Switch off the heat, stir through 1 tbsp lemon juice and 2 tbsp coriander, and taste to balance the sweet, sour and salt before serving.
tips: Add the lemon juice only off the heat so its brightness is not cooked away.
Keep the gravy a touch thin; it is meant to be mopped up with rotli and will thicken as it stands.
For a festive version, temper an extra pinch of asafoetida in ghee and pour it over just before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thin phulka rotli or steamed rice, a bowl of plain chhaas and a spoon of sweet-hot chundo pickle on the side.

variations.name: Bengali Kadai Chole
variations.description: Cooked entirely in pungent Anveshan Mustard Oil and tempered with panch phoron, this Bengali interpretation reads more like a robust chholar-inspired curry than a North Indian kadai. Slit green chillies and a bay leaf give it a fragrant, gently sweet-hot character. The mustard oil brings the unmistakable nasal warmth that defines eastern cooking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil is the soul of this curry, giving the sharp, warming pungency Bengali cooking is built on.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A final teaspoon of ghee softens the bite of raw mustard oil and adds a nutty aroma.

steps: Pressure cook 1.5 cups soaked chickpeas with 1.25 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 whistles until tender, then reserve them with their liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just begins to smoke and lightens in colour, then lower the flame and add 1 tsp panch phoron and 1 bay leaf, letting them splutter for 30 seconds.
Add 2 finely chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger paste and fry over medium heat until soft and pale gold, about 6 minutes.
Stir in 2 chopped tomatoes, 0.75 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1 tsp cumin powder, and cook until the masala thickens and the mustard oil surfaces, about 7 minutes.
Slide in the chickpeas with 1 cup of their water and 3 slit green chillies, then simmer for 10 minutes so the panch phoron flavour seeps into the beans.
Finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and 2 tbsp coriander, stir gently and rest for 3 minutes before serving.
tips: Always heat mustard oil to the smoking point first and then cool it slightly; this tames its raw sharpness and prevents a bitter aftertaste.
Keep the green chillies whole and slit so they perfume the curry without making it unbearably hot.
A pinch of sugar can be added with the tomatoes if you want the subtle sweetness typical of Bengali home cooking.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with luchi or steamed gobindobhog rice, and offer a wedge of lime and a few extra slit green chillies on the side.

variations.name: Kerala Kadai Chole
variations.description: This Malabar-style version is simmered in fresh coconut milk and finished with a fragrant tempering of curry leaves and shallots in Anveshan Coconut Oil. Ground roasted coconut gives the gravy a silky, nutty body and a mild, soothing heat. It sits closer to a Kerala chana curry than a dry kadai, meant to be spooned over rice or appam.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil gives the tempering its distinctive Malabar aroma and rounds the whole curry.

steps: Pressure cook 1.5 cups soaked chickpeas with 1.25 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 whistles until soft, then set aside with their liquid.
Dry roast 0.5 cup grated coconut with 0.5 tsp fennel seeds over low heat until deep golden and fragrant, about 5 minutes, then grind to a smooth paste with a little water.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil on medium, add 8 sliced shallots and 10 curry leaves, and fry until the shallots turn light brown, about 4 minutes.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 1 chopped tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, and cook until the tomato breaks down, about 5 minutes.
Stir in the roasted coconut paste and the chickpeas with 0.5 cup of their water, then simmer for 8 minutes until thick and glossy.
Pour in 1 cup coconut milk, warm through on the lowest flame for 3 minutes without boiling, and finish with a fresh tempering of the remaining curry leaves crackled in a little coconut oil.
tips: Never let the curry boil after adding coconut milk or it will split; keep it at the barest simmer.
Roasting the coconut to a deep gold is what gives this curry its signature nutty depth, so do not stop at pale.
Shallots are worth the peeling here as they are sweeter and more aromatic than large onions in Kerala gravies.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle over steamed red rice, appam or lacy idiyappam, with a side of thoran or crisp banana chips for texture.

variations.name: Classic Kadai Kofta
variations.description: Soft mixed-vegetable dumplings bathed in a semi-dry, capsicum-flecked kadai gravy built on freshly pounded coriander and red chilli. The koftas stay pillowy inside while the masala clings thick and glossy, carrying the smoky char of a well-seasoned iron kadai.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: nutty khapli flour binds the koftas without turning them dense like maida

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: high smoke point keeps the koftas crisp and golden while deep-frying

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of bilona ghee rounds out the tang and lifts the aroma

steps: Mash the 2 boiled potatoes while still warm, then mix in 0.5 cup grated carrot, 0.25 cup green peas, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta until a soft, non-sticky dough forms that holds its shape.
Roll into 10 walnut-sized balls and deep-fry in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil heated to a medium 170C, turning gently until evenly golden brown, about 4 minutes; drain on paper.

In 2 tbsp of the same oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then saute 2 finely chopped onions over medium heat until light golden, about 6 minutes, and stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for another minute until raw smell fades.

Add 3 pureed tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tbsp kadai masala and 0.75 tsp salt; cook on medium heat until the oil separates at the edges and the masala darkens, about 8 minutes.
Toss in 1 cubed capsicum and cook 2 minutes so it stays crunchy, then pour in 0.5 cup hot water and simmer the gravy for 4 minutes until it thickens to a clinging coat.
Stir in 3 tbsp cream and slide in the fried koftas, spooning gravy over them; simmer gently for 3 minutes so they soak up flavour without breaking.
Finish with 1 tsp garam masala and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, swirl through, and rest off the heat for 2 minutes before serving so the koftas plump up.
tips: Add the koftas only just before serving; sitting too long in gravy turns them soggy, so keep fried koftas and gravy separate until the last minute.
If the kofta dough feels sticky, add khapli atta one teaspoon at a time rather than flour, which keeps the dumplings light.
Dry-roast whole coriander, cumin and Kashmiri chilli and grind fresh for the kadai masala; the coarse texture is what defines an authentic kadai.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in the same iron kadai for drama, showered with julienned ginger and a crushed dried fenugreek pinch, alongside butter-brushed laccha paratha and a kachumber salad.

variations.name: Bengali Kadai Kofta
variations.description: A Bengali reimagining where the koftas and gravy are cooked in pungent Anveshan Mustard Oil and lifted with a nutty panch phoron temper. A whisper of mustard paste gives the kadai a sharp, sinus-tingling edge quite unlike the northern version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: holds the soft cabbage-potato mix together for a tender bite

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked to its haze first so the koftas fry with a clean, sharp bengali pungency

steps: Mash the 2 boiled potatoes with 0.5 cup grated cabbage, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta into a firm dough that just holds together.
Heat Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until it hazes and the raw smell mellows, then lower to medium and deep-fry 10 lime-sized koftas until russet-brown, about 5 minutes; set aside.
In 3 tbsp of the mustard oil, splutter 1 tsp panch phoron for 30 seconds until the fennel turns fragrant, then add 2 sliced onions and fry over medium heat until deep golden, about 7 minutes.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.75 tsp salt; cook until the tomatoes collapse and oil beads out, about 6 minutes.
Whisk 1 tbsp mustard paste into 0.5 cup water and pour in with 3 slit green chillies and cubed capsicum; simmer 4 minutes so the mustard loses its rawness but keeps its bite.
Slip in the fried koftas and 0.5 tsp garam masala, spooning the thin, sharp gravy over them, and simmer gently for 3 minutes.
Rest off heat for 2 minutes, drizzle with a teaspoon of raw mustard oil, and serve while the pungent aroma is at its peak.
tips: Always heat mustard oil to smoking point once and cool slightly before frying; this tames the bitterness and gives the classic Bengali flavour.
Soak the mustard seeds for the paste with a pinch of salt and a green chilli before grinding to stop it turning bitter.
Keep the gravy deliberately thin and pourable here, as Bengali koftas are meant to be enjoyed spooned over steaming rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle over a mound of hot gobindobhog rice with a wedge of lime and a fried green chilli on the side for a true Bengali lunch.

variations.name: Kerala Kadai Kofta
variations.description: Coconut runs through every layer of this Malabar-style kadai, from the coconut-oil fry to a silky coconut-milk finish and a crackle of curry leaves. Warm with roasted spice yet mellow and sweet, it trades the northern cream for the tropical richness of fresh coconut.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: binds the starchy plantain-potato koftas so they hold in the coconut gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: lends the unmistakable Kerala aroma to both the fried koftas and the tempering

steps: Combine 2 mashed boiled potatoes with 0.5 cup grated raw banana, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, kneading into a soft dough that shapes cleanly into balls.
Deep-fry 10 koftas in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil over medium heat until golden and firm, about 4 minutes, and drain; the coconut oil perfumes them beautifully.
In 3 tbsp coconut oil, pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 1 sprig curry leaves for 20 seconds, then saute 2 sliced onions until soft and pale gold, about 6 minutes.
Dry-roast 0.5 cup grated coconut in a separate pan until nut-brown, blend to a paste with a splash of water, and add to the pan with 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, cooking 2 minutes.
Stir in 2 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tbsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp salt; cook until the coconut masala turns glossy and thick, about 7 minutes.
Add cubed capsicum and 0.75 cup coconut milk, bring to the gentlest simmer without boiling, then lower in the koftas and cook 3 minutes so they drink up the gravy.
Finish with a second sprig of curry leaves crisped in a teaspoon of coconut oil and rest 2 minutes before serving.
tips: Never boil the gravy hard once coconut milk goes in, or it will split; keep it at a bare tremble for a silky finish.
Roasting the grated coconut to a deep brown is essential for the toasty, nutty depth typical of Malabar cooking.
Raw banana koftas hold together better than pure potato and add an earthy sweetness that suits the coconut base.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with Kerala red matta rice or soft appams, with a side of thinly sliced shallots in coconut oil to echo the tropical notes.

variations.name: Rajasthani Kadai Kofta
variations.description: A fiery, ghee-rich Marwari take built on a paste of soaked Mathania dried red chillies and thick yogurt in place of tomatoes. The gravy is deep crimson and smoky-hot, clinging to koftas fried in pure Anveshan Ghee for a decadent, desert-style richness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: binds the potato-paneer koftas so they stay tender in the spicy gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee both fries the koftas and enriches the Marwari gravy in true royal style

steps: Mash 2 boiled potatoes with 0.5 cup crumbled paneer, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta into a firm dough, and shape into 10 small koftas.
Shallow-fry the koftas in 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat until golden on all sides, about 5 minutes, and set aside on a plate.
Soak 8 dried red chillies in warm water for 15 minutes, then blend with 2 onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste to a smooth crimson paste.
In the remaining 3 tbsp ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, add the chilli-onion paste and fry over medium heat until it thickens and the ghee separates, about 9 minutes.
Lower the heat, whisk 1 cup yogurt with 1 tbsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt, and add slowly while stirring constantly so it does not curdle; simmer 5 minutes.
Pour in 0.5 cup water, slide in the koftas and simmer gently for 4 minutes until the gravy turns thick and glossy and coats each kofta.
Finish with 1 tsp garam masala, rest for 2 minutes, and serve while the ghee glistens on top.
tips: Deseed some of the dried chillies if you want the deep colour without punishing heat; Mathania chillies give red without excessive fire.
Always add whisked yogurt off a rolling boil and stir continuously to prevent it from splitting in the hot ghee.
Make the chilli paste a day ahead and refrigerate; the flavour deepens and the koftas soak it up even better.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra roti smeared with white butter and a side of sliced onions and green chilli, desert-thali style.

variations.name: Kashmiri Kadai Kofta
variations.description: Inspired by the Valley's wazwan, this gentle kadai skips onion and garlic in favour of fennel and dry ginger, with strands of Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron steeped in warm milk for colour and perfume. Mustard oil and a Kashmiri chilli base give it a rose-red hue and a fragrant, aromatic warmth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: keeps the delicate potato koftas intact in the aromatic saffron gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the traditional Kashmiri cooking fat that carries the fennel and chilli beautifully

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk for the signature golden-red bloom and floral aroma

steps: Mash 3 boiled potatoes with 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta into a smooth, firm dough and roll into 10 oval koftas.
Steep 1 pinch Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside to bloom while you fry the koftas.
Deep-fry the koftas in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil, pre-heated to its haze and cooled slightly, over medium heat until golden, about 4 minutes; drain and reserve.
In 3 tbsp of the mustard oil, crackle 3 cardamom, 3 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon for 20 seconds, then add 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder off the heat so it blooms without burning.
Whisk 1 cup yogurt with 1.5 tbsp fennel powder, 1 tsp dry ginger powder and 0.75 tsp salt, and stir into the pan on low heat, cooking gently for 6 minutes until the gravy is smooth and rust-red.
Add 0.75 cup water and the saffron milk, slip in the koftas, and simmer very gently for 5 minutes so they absorb the fragrant gravy.
Rest off heat for 2 minutes, letting the saffron and fennel aromas settle, before serving.
tips: Bloom the Kashmiri chilli powder off the heat in warm oil; direct high heat scorches it and dulls the prized red colour.
Fennel and dry ginger powder are the backbone of Kashmiri gravies, so use them fresh and generously in place of onion-garlic.
Keep the flame low throughout after adding yogurt to keep the koftas soft and the gravy from curdling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed Kashmiri rice and a spoon of the saffron milk drizzled on top, alongside a cooling walnut chutney.

variations.name: Classic Masala Aloo Tamatar
variations.description: The everyday North Indian comfort curry: boiled potatoes broken into a tangy onion-tomato masala loosened with plenty of gravy. Cumin, coriander and a final flourish of garam masala make it the perfect no-fuss companion to puri or rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Clean wood-pressed groundnut oil lets the tomato tang stay bright

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon of ghee stirred in at the end rounds the sharp tomato edge

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds until they darken and smell toasty.
Add 2 finely chopped onions and fry until golden, 6 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in the puree of 3 tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt; cook 8 minutes until the oil separates.
Add the 4 boiled cubed potatoes and lightly mash a few pieces against the pan so they thicken the gravy naturally.
Pour in 1.5 cups hot water, bring to a boil and simmer on low for 8 minutes so the potatoes drink up the masala.
Stir in 0.5 tsp garam masala and 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee, simmer 1 minute, then finish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander before serving.
tips: Slightly mashing a few potato cubes is the trick to a body-rich gravy without any cream.
Use day-old boiled potatoes if you can; they hold their shape better and soak up flavour more evenly.
For a runnier puri-shop consistency, add an extra half cup of water and a pinch more salt.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot with fluffy pooris and a wedge of lemon, the classic North Indian weekend breakfast.

variations.name: Bengali Aloo Tamatar
variations.description: A Kolkata niramish-style potato curry cooked in mustard oil and tempered with panch phoron, finished with a sweet-tart balance. The mustard oil and whole-spice temper give this humble dish a distinctly Bengali soul.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Pungent wood-pressed mustard oil defines Bengali niramish cooking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A little jaggery is the classic Bengali balance to the mustard sharpness

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, then reduce the flame and let it settle for 20 seconds to soften its bite.
Temper 1 tsp panch phoron, 1 bay leaf and 2 dried red chillies for 20 seconds until the seeds pop and perfume the oil.
Add the 4 cubed potatoes and fry on medium heat for 5 minutes until their edges turn golden and lightly blistered.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger paste, 3 chopped tomatoes, 0.75 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp cumin powder, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt; cook 6 minutes until the tomatoes collapse.
Pour in 2 cups hot water, cover and simmer on low for 12 minutes until the potatoes are fork-tender and the gravy thickens.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and simmer 2 minutes until the sweet-sour balance settles, then serve steaming.
tips: Frying the raw potatoes directly in the mustard oil, rather than boiling first, gives this curry its rustic Bengali texture.
Keep the curry light on garlic-onion; the authentic niramish version is cooked without them.
Panch phoron should be added whole and never ground, so each seed bursts fresh in the hot oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot luchi or plain steamed rice, Bengali style, with a green chilli on the side.

variations.name: Andhra Aloo Tamatar
variations.description: A fiery Rayalaseema-style potato curry that leans on Guntur red chillies and a garlic-heavy tempering in groundnut oil, with tamarind sharpening the tomato. This one is proudly hot, tangy and built for rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the everyday cooking fat of Andhra

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds until they crackle.
Add 12 curry leaves and 8 crushed garlic cloves and fry for 1 minute until the garlic turns pale gold and aromatic.
Tip in the 4 cubed potatoes and saute 5 minutes on medium heat until their surfaces firm up and colour lightly.
Add 3 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp Guntur red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt; cook 6 minutes until the tomatoes break down.
Pour in 1.5 cups hot water along with 1 tsp tamarind paste, cover and simmer on low for 12 minutes until the potatoes are soft.
Uncover and cook 2 minutes more to concentrate the gravy into a thick, fiery-red coating on the potatoes.
tips: Guntur chilli powder is intense; start with 1 tsp and build up if you want the authentic Andhra burn.
Tamarind is the essential tang that balances the heat; add it after the potatoes have softened so it stays bright.
Crushing the garlic rather than mincing it releases a bolder aroma that stands up to the chilli.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot steamed rice topped with a spoon of ghee, or alongside ragi mudde for a Rayalaseema meal.

variations.name: Kerala Aloo Tamatar
variations.description: A coconut-rich Malabar potato curry simmered with fresh coconut paste and tempered in coconut oil with curry leaves and mustard. Mildly spiced and creamy, it carries the gentle sweetness of the Kerala coast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed coconut oil carries the true fragrance of Kerala cooking

steps: Grind 0.75 cup grated fresh coconut with 0.5 tsp fennel seeds and 0.25 cup water into a smooth white paste and set aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds for 15 seconds, then add 14 curry leaves and let them crisp.
Add 6 sliced shallots and 2 slit green chillies and fry until the shallots soften and turn golden, about 4 minutes.
Add the 4 cubed potatoes, 2 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, stir well, then pour in 1.5 cups hot water.
Cover and simmer on low for 12 minutes until the potatoes are tender and the tomatoes have melted into the broth.
Stir in the ground coconut paste and simmer gently for 3 minutes without boiling hard, until the gravy thickens to a creamy, pale curry.
tips: Do not let the curry boil vigorously after adding coconut paste or it can turn grainy; a gentle simmer keeps it silky.
Shallots (kunjulli) give a deeper sweetness than regular onions and are worth seeking out for authenticity.
A final drizzle of raw coconut oil off the heat intensifies the Kerala aroma beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with appam, idiyappam or Kerala red rice to soak up the creamy coconut gravy.

variations.name: Gujarati Aloo Tamatar
variations.description: A lightly sweet, tangy Gujarati-style raswala aloo where jaggery and lemon lift a gentle cumin-coriander gravy. Kept low on chilli, it is the mild, homely curry that suits a full thali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the backbone fat of the Gujarati kitchen

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery brings the gentle sweetness that marks Gujarati gravies

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 15 seconds, then add 0.25 tsp asafoetida for 5 seconds.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and fry for 30 seconds until fragrant and no longer raw.
Add the puree of 3 tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp coriander-cumin powder and 1 tsp salt; cook 6 minutes until glossy and thick.
Add the 4 boiled cubed potatoes, lightly mashing a couple of pieces to thicken the curry.
Pour in 2 cups hot water, bring to a gentle boil and simmer on low for 7 minutes so the flavours meld.
Stir in 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tbsp lemon juice, simmer 1 minute until sweet and sour balance, then finish with 3 tbsp coriander.
tips: The gravy should be thin and rasa-like rather than thick; it is meant to be spooned generously over rice or roti.
Add jaggery and lemon together at the end and taste; the two must balance so neither dominates.
Asafoetida stands in for onion and garlic here, keeping the dish suitable for Jain-style eating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as part of a Gujarati thali with phulka, steamed rice and a spoon of plain curd on the side.

variations.name: Classic Masala Tinda
variations.description: The everyday North Indian home version of tinda where peeled apple gourd is simmered in a onion-tomato masala until it turns silky and soaks up the spices. A gentle, comforting sabzi that lets the mild sweetness of the gourd shine through a warm cumin-and-coriander base.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: its clean, nutty base lets the tinda's mild flavour come through without heaviness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of bilona ghee rounds off the masala with a homely aroma

steps: Peel the 500 g apple gourd, quarter each piece, and finely chop the 2 onions and 2 tomatoes so everything cooks evenly.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds until they sizzle and turn fragrant, about 30 seconds.
Add the chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and sauté on medium for 6 to 7 minutes until soft and light golden at the edges.
