Stir in the tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, then cook for 5 minutes until the oil separates and the masala looks glossy.
Add the quartered tinda and 1 tsp salt, toss to coat, then cover and cook on low for 15 to 18 minutes, stirring occasionally, until a knife slides through easily.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala and finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee, tossing gently so every piece glistens.
Garnish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander leaves and take off the heat.
tips: Choose small, firm tinda that feel heavy for their size; large ones turn seedy and spongy.
If the masala catches before the gourd is tender, splash in 2 to 3 tbsp hot water and keep the lid on.
Make it a day ahead; the tinda absorbs the masala overnight and tastes even better reheated.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a shallow bowl with a wedge of lemon and hot phulkas, alongside a cooling boondi raita to balance the spice.

variations.name: Punjabi Masala Tinda
variations.description: A rich Punjabi treatment where tinda is cooked in ghee with a robust onion-tomato masala and a whisper of kasuri methi. The gourd turns buttery-soft and the gravy clings thick, meant to be scooped up with a hot tandoori roti.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: Punjabi kitchens cook tinda in generous ghee for its signature buttery richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a splash alongside the ghee keeps the masala from browning too fast

steps: Peel and quarter the 500 g tinda, finely chop the 2 onions, and puree the 3 tomatoes to a smooth pulp for a clinging gravy.
Melt 2 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee with 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on medium and let 1 tsp cumin seeds and the 1 bay leaf splutter for about 30 seconds.
Add the onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 7 to 8 minutes until deep golden, stirring so they colour evenly.
Pour in the tomato puree with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, then simmer for 6 minutes until the ghee floats on top.
Fold in the tinda and 1 tsp salt, cover, and cook on low for 16 to 18 minutes until the pieces are fork-tender and coated in thick masala.
Crush 1 tsp kasuri methi between your palms and add it with 0.75 tsp garam masala, then swirl in 2 tbsp fresh cream and cook uncovered for 2 minutes to a silky gravy.
Scatter 2 tbsp coriander leaves over the top and serve piping hot.
tips: Pureeing the tomatoes rather than chopping gives the thicker, restaurant-style gravy Punjabi tinda is known for.
Toast the kasuri methi in a dry pan for ten seconds before crushing to amplify its aroma.
For a party version, stir in 2 tbsp fresh cream in the last minute for a silkier finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with butter-brushed tandoori rotis and a side of sliced onions splashed with lemon and a sprinkle of chaat masala.

variations.name: Bengali Masala Tinda
variations.description: A Bengali-style tinda tempered in pungent mustard oil with nigella seeds and slit green chillies, then rounded with a touch of jaggery for the region's beloved sweet-savoury balance. Light, glossy and fragrant, it eats beautifully with plain rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: heated to smoking then cooled slightly, it gives the dish its authentic Bengali pungency

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a spoon of jaggery is the classic Bengali counterpoint to mustard's sharpness

steps: Peel and cube the 500 g tinda, thinly slice the 1 onion, chop the 1 tomato, and slit the 3 green chillies lengthwise.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until it just begins to smoke, then lower the flame and let it cool for 20 seconds to mellow its bite.
Temper 0.5 tsp nigella seeds and the slit green chillies for about 20 seconds until aromatic, then add the sliced onion and fry for 4 minutes until translucent.
Stir in 1 tsp ginger paste, the tomato, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, cooking for 4 minutes until the tomato collapses.
Add the tinda cubes with 1 tsp salt, cover, and steam-cook on low for 14 to 16 minutes until tender, stirring once or twice.
Sprinkle in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook uncovered for 2 minutes so it melts and glazes the gourd.
Finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander leaves and serve warm.
tips: Always smoke the mustard oil first; raw mustard oil tastes harsh and overpowers the delicate gourd.
Keep the green chillies whole and slit so they perfume the dish without making it fiery.
A pinch more jaggery rescues the balance if your tomatoes turn out especially tart.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle over a mound of steamed gobindobhog or any short-grain rice with a wedge of lime and a few extra fried green chillies on the side.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Masala Tinda
variations.description: A Maharashtrian rendition built on aromatic goda masala, roasted peanuts and a hint of jaggery, giving the tinda a warm, subtly sweet, coconut-and-clove depth. The crushed peanuts add body and a gentle crunch to every spoonful.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the traditional cooking fat of Maharashtra that carries the goda masala beautifully

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a small amount lifts the goda masala with the region's signature gentle sweetness

steps: Peel and dice the 500 g tinda, finely chop the 2 onions and 1 tomato, and coarsely pound the 3 tbsp roasted peanuts into a gritty powder.
Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on medium and pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds followed by 0.5 tsp cumin seeds until they crackle, about 20 seconds.
Add the onions and fry for 6 minutes until golden, then stir in the tomato, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder and cook for 3 minutes.
Mix in 1.5 tsp goda masala and the crushed peanuts, sauté for 1 minute until the roasted aroma rises from the pan.
Tip in the tinda and 1 tsp salt, cover, and cook on low for 15 to 17 minutes until soft, adding a splash of water if it sticks.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 2 tbsp grated coconut and simmer uncovered for 2 minutes to marry the flavours.
Garnish with 2 tbsp coriander leaves and serve hot.
tips: Good goda masala is key; if yours is mild, add an extra half teaspoon rather than more chilli.
Pound the peanuts coarsely, not to a paste, so they thicken the sabzi while keeping a bit of texture.
Fresh grated coconut beats desiccated here; if using dry, soak it in 1 tbsp warm water first.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft jowar bhakri or steamed rice and a dollop of plain yoghurt to offset the warm goda spice.

variations.name: Rajasthani Masala Tinda
variations.description: A fiery desert-style tinda built on smoky whole dried red chillies and a ghee tempering, with yoghurt lending body in place of the region's scarce fresh tomatoes. Bold, rustic and deeply aromatic, it is made to stand up to bajra rotis.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee is the fat of choice across Rajasthan and mellows the punch of the dried chillies

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: a teaspoon adds a rustic sharpness typical of the region's everyday cooking

steps: Peel and quarter the 500 g tinda, finely chop the 1 large onion, and whisk the 0.5 cup yoghurt smooth with the 2 tsp coriander powder to stop it splitting.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee with 1 tsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil on medium and break the 4 dried red chillies into the fat, frying for 20 seconds until they darken and smell smoky.
Add 1 tsp cumin seeds and the onion, sautéing for 6 minutes until soft, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for another minute.
Lower the flame and pour in the spiced yoghurt with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder, stirring constantly for 3 minutes until it thickens without curdling.
Fold in the tinda and 1 tsp salt, cover, and cook on low for 16 to 18 minutes until tender and coated in the tangy masala.
Uncover and cook for 2 minutes to reduce any excess liquid to a clinging sauce.
Finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander leaves and serve hot.
tips: Whisk the yoghurt with a little flour or the coriander powder before adding, and keep the flame low, to prevent it from splitting.
For extra desert smokiness, use round Mathania chillies if you can find them.
This sabzi keeps well for travel as it uses yoghurt rather than perishable fresh tomato.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best mopped up with hot bajra or makki rotis and a side of raw onion rings and green chilli pickle.

variations.name: Classic Punjabi Mushroom Matar
variations.description: The dhaba-style favourite from Punjab: button mushrooms and green peas simmered in a glossy onion-tomato masala scented with kasuri methi and garam masala. A splash of cream rounds the tang into that unmistakable creamy-rustic finish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil gives the base a clean, nutty backbone

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A ghee finish lifts the gravy to true dhaba richness

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 20 seconds until they sizzle and smell toasty.
Add 2 finely chopped onions and saute on medium heat until deep golden, 6-7 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until the raw smell fades.
Pour in the puree of 3 tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt; cook 8-10 minutes until the oil separates and the masala looks glossy.
Slide in 300 g quartered mushrooms and 1 cup green peas, raise the heat briefly and stir-fry 3 minutes until the mushrooms release their water and shrink slightly.
Add about 0.75 cup hot water, cover and simmer on low for 8 minutes until the peas are tender and the mushrooms are cooked through.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi between your palms into the pan, stir in 3 tbsp cream, 0.5 tsp garam masala and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, and simmer 2 minutes until the gravy turns silky.
tips: Do not add salt to the mushrooms too early elsewhere; salting them only once they hit the masala keeps them plump rather than rubbery.
If the gravy tastes sharp, an extra 1 tsp cream or a pinch of sugar balances the tomato acidity.
Make the onion-tomato masala a day ahead and refrigerate; the flavour deepens and weeknight assembly takes ten minutes.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with butter-brushed tandoori roti or lachha paratha and a side of sliced onions splashed with lemon and chaat masala.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Mushroom Matar
variations.description: A Puneri rassa spin where fragrant goda masala, its dark warmth built from stone flower and sesame, replaces garam masala. Coconut and a mustard-cumin tempering give the mushrooms and peas a smoky-sweet Deccan character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The Maharashtrian pantry runs on wood-pressed groundnut oil

steps: Dry-roast 3 tbsp desiccated coconut in a pan over low heat until it turns nutty brown, about 3 minutes, then set aside to cool.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds until they pop.
Add 2 chopped onions and fry until golden brown, 6 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the roasted coconut and cook 1 minute more.
Mix in 2 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tbsp goda masala and 1 tsp salt; cook 6-7 minutes until the masala darkens and the oil beads at the edges.
Add 300 g sliced mushrooms and 1 cup peas, stir-fry 3 minutes on high until the mushrooms wilt, then pour in 1 cup hot water.
Cover and simmer on low for 10 minutes until the rassa thickens slightly and the peas soften, adjusting salt before serving.
tips: Goda masala can taste flat if old; buy small and store airtight, as its stone-flower aroma fades within months.
Roasting the coconut is essential for the signature smoky note; raw coconut makes the gravy taste milky instead.
For a thinner Puneri-style rassa, add an extra half cup of water and simmer two minutes longer.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri or steamed rice and a spoon of fresh coconut chutney on the side.

variations.name: Gujarati Mushroom Matar
variations.description: The Gujarati love of the sweet-savoury balance shines here: a lightly spiced gravy nudged with Anveshan jaggery and a squeeze of lemon. It stays gentle on heat, letting the mushrooms and peas taste bright and homely.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the defining cooking fat of Gujarati kitchens

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A touch of jaggery gives the classic Gujarati sweet-savoury lilt

steps: Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat and temper 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds until fragrant and lightly darkened.
Add 1 chopped onion and saute until soft and pale gold, 4 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and cook 30 seconds.
Pour in the puree of 3 tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp coriander-cumin powder and 1 tsp salt; simmer 6-7 minutes until thickened and glossy.
Add 300 g quartered mushrooms and 1 cup peas, stir 3 minutes on medium-high until the mushrooms soften and colour lightly.
Pour in 0.75 cup hot water, cover and simmer on low for 8 minutes until the peas are tender.
Stir in 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tbsp lemon juice, simmer 1 minute to balance sweet and tart, then finish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Add the jaggery only near the end; boiling it long can turn the gravy cloyingly dark.
Taste as you balance; the dish should land sweet, sour and salty at once, never sugary.
Keep the heat mild here so the delicate sweet-sour profile is not overwhelmed by chilli.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulka rotli and a bowl of plain khichdi with a dollop of ghee for a comforting Gujarati thali.

variations.name: Kashmiri Mushroom Matar
variations.description: Inspired by Wazwan gravies, this take blooms Kashmiri chilli and saffron in ghee for a deep-red, aromatic sauce thickened with curd and fennel. It is warming and fragrant rather than fiery, perfect for cold evenings.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Kashmiri gravies are traditionally built on ghee for their rich body

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: A saffron bloom lends the signature colour and Wazwan perfume

steps: Soak 1 pinch Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm water and set aside to steep into a golden infusion.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and crackle 3 cardamom pods, 3 cloves and a 1-inch cinnamon stick for 30 seconds until aromatic.
Lower the heat, add 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and stir for 10 seconds, then quickly pour in 0.5 cup whisked curd, stirring constantly so it does not split.
Add 1.5 tsp fennel powder, 0.5 tsp dry ginger powder and 1 tsp salt, then cook the gravy 4 minutes until the ghee floats to the top.
Slide in 300 g halved mushrooms and 1 cup peas, stir 2 minutes, then add 1 cup hot water along with the saffron infusion.
Cover and simmer on low for 12 minutes until the mushrooms are tender and the gravy is a deep glowing red, adjusting salt to taste.
tips: Whisk the curd smooth and add it off high heat, stirring nonstop, to prevent the gravy from curdling.
Fennel and dry ginger, not garam masala, define authentic Kashmiri flavour; do not substitute them.
The gravy tastes even better reheated the next day as the saffron and fennel mellow into the sauce.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed basmati rice or a soft Kashmiri girda bread to soak up the fragrant red gravy.

variations.name: Bengali Mushroom Matar
variations.description: A Kolkata-style rendition cooked in pungent mustard oil and tempered with panch phoron, finished with a hint of Bengali sweetness. The mustard oil gives the mushrooms and peas an unmistakable sharp, earthy edge.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil is the soul of any Bengali gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A whisper of jaggery is the classic Bengali counterpoint to mustard heat

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, then lower the flame and let it cool for 20 seconds to tame the pungency.
Temper 1 tsp panch phoron and 1 bay leaf in the oil for 20 seconds until the seeds crackle and smell nutty.
Add 2 sliced onions and fry until soft and golden, 5 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger paste and cook 1 minute.
Mix in 2 chopped tomatoes, 0.75 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt; cook 6 minutes until the masala loosens its oil.
Add 300 g quartered mushrooms and 1 cup peas, stir-fry 3 minutes, then pour in 1 cup hot water and simmer covered on low for 9 minutes.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer 1 minute until the sweetness melts in and balances the sharp mustard oil, then serve hot.
tips: Always heat mustard oil to smoking first; this removes its raw bite and leaves a mellow, nutty pungency.
Panch phoron must not be ground; the whole five-seed blend is what gives the dish its Bengali stamp.
A tiny amount of jaggery is traditional and rounds the mustard oil; leave it out and the gravy tastes harsher.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice and a wedge of lime, or tuck into soft luchi for a weekend Bengali brunch.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Sem
variations.description: A hot, tongue-tingling version of dry broad beans loaded with green chilli, black pepper and red chilli for layered heat. The beans stay crisp-tender while a peppery masala clings to every piece. Built for those who like their sabzi with a real kick.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a robust wood-pressed oil that carries the layered chilli heat cleanly

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat until it shimmers, then crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add the chopped onion and 3 chopped green chillies and fry for 5 minutes until the onion turns golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for a minute.
Add the chopped tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, cooking for 4-5 minutes until the tomato breaks down and oil surfaces.
Add the 400 g sliced broad beans and 1 tsp salt, toss thoroughly, then cover and cook on low for 12-14 minutes, stirring now and then, until the beans are tender.
Uncover, sprinkle in 0.75 tsp coarsely crushed black pepper and stir-fry on medium for 3 minutes so the beans dry and the pepper perfumes the dish.
Finish with 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander, toss once and serve piping hot.
tips: Crush the black pepper fresh and add it near the end so its aroma stays sharp and does not turn dull.
Adjust the green chillies up or down; they bring brightness distinct from the deeper red chilli heat.
A squeeze of lemon at the table lifts all the heat and keeps the dish refreshing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with cooling boondi raita and hot tawa rotis, or alongside jeera rice to balance the pepper punch.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Sem
variations.description: A blazing Rayalaseema-style sem where fiery Guntur red chilli powder and a garlic-heavy tempering define the heat. Sesame oil deepens the earthy, roasted quality typical of Andhra vegetable fries. This is not for the faint-hearted, with heat balanced only by a final burst of curry leaves.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed gingelly oil is the classic Andhra base and stands up to the Guntur heat

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadai on medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal and let them splutter and turn golden, about 30 seconds.
Add 0.5 tsp cumin, 6 crushed garlic cloves and 12 curry leaves, frying for a minute until the garlic turns pale gold and fragrant.

Add the chopped onion and cook for 4-5 minutes until soft, then lower the heat and add 2 tsp Guntur red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, stirring for 20 seconds so the chilli does not scorch.
Add the 400 g broad beans and 1 tsp salt, toss well to coat in the red masala, then sprinkle 3 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 13-15 minutes until tender.
Stir in 1 tsp tamarind pulp and cook uncovered on medium for 3-4 minutes so the sourness melds and the beans dry out with a roasted edge.
Taste, adjust salt and serve while the sesame-garlic aroma is at its peak.
tips: Guntur chilli is intensely hot, so start with less and build up if you are unsure of your tolerance.
Crushing the garlic rather than mincing it releases more aroma into the sesame oil.
A spoon of tamarind is essential here; it rounds off the aggressive chilli heat with a tangy backnote.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or with pesarattu for a hearty Andhra breakfast plate.

variations.name: Rajasthani Spicy Sem
variations.description: A rugged Marwari-style spicy sem built on whole dried red chillies tempered until smoky, with no onion or tomato to soften the heat. Amchur brings a dry tang while ghee gives the fire a mellow finish. It is the kind of bold, minimal-water sabzi that suits the desert palate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee tempers the whole-chilli heat with a nutty desert richness

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat, then add 4 whole dried red chillies and let them darken and turn smoky for 15-20 seconds without burning.
Add 1 tsp cumin, 0.5 tsp ajwain and a pinch of asafoetida, followed by 5 crushed garlic cloves, and fry for a minute until the garlic is golden.
Lower the heat and stir in 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 0.5 tsp turmeric with a splash of water to keep the spices from burning, cooking for 30 seconds.
Add the 400 g broad beans and 1 tsp salt, toss to coat in the spice-ghee mixture, then cover and cook on low for 13-15 minutes until the beans are tender, stirring occasionally.
Uncover and stir-fry on medium for 3 minutes so the beans dry and the whole chillies release their smoky heat into the dish.
Sprinkle 0.75 tsp amchur, toss for a minute to spread the tang and serve hot.
tips: Break the dried chillies slightly if you want more heat, or leave them whole for aroma with milder fire.
Ajwain aids digestion and cuts the heaviness of ghee, so do not skip it in this rich preparation.
Keep the flame moderate when tempering chillies in ghee, as ghee browns faster than oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thick bajra rotis smeared with ghee and a raw onion salad, the Marwari way.

variations.name: Bengali Spicy Sem
variations.description: A sharp, pungent take where broad beans are cooked in smoking mustard oil and a paste of green chilli and mustard, giving the signature Bengali kasundi-like bite. The heat here is nasal and bright rather than deep red. Slit green chillies and a mustard-paste finish keep it fiery yet fresh.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked first, then paired with a mustard paste for a double hit of pungency

steps: Grind 1.5 tsp soaked yellow mustard seeds and 1 tsp poppy seeds with 2 green chillies and a splash of water into a smooth, slightly grainy paste and set aside.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai on medium-high until it smokes, then reduce the heat and add 0.5 tsp nigella seeds and 2 slit green chillies, letting them sizzle for 20 seconds.
Add the 400 g broad beans with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, tossing well to coat, then sprinkle 4 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 12-14 minutes until tender.
Stir in the ground mustard-poppy paste and 0.5 tsp sugar, mixing so the paste coats the beans evenly.
Cook uncovered on low for 3-4 minutes, being careful not to let the mustard paste boil hard or it will turn bitter.
Drizzle a teaspoon of raw mustard oil over the top, give a gentle toss and serve.
tips: Never overheat the mustard-seed paste; a hard boil makes it bitter, so keep the flame low once it goes in.
Soak the mustard seeds for 20 minutes before grinding to cut their bitterness and get a smoother paste.
A pinch of sugar is traditional and offsets the twin sharpness of mustard oil and mustard paste.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice as the opening course of a Bengali meal, with a wedge of lime alongside.

variations.name: Assamese Spicy Sem
variations.description: A clean, ferociously hot Assamese preparation where a whisper of bhut jolokia lends smoky, fruity fire to lightly cooked broad beans. The masala is minimal, letting the ghost chilli and fresh garlic shine. A drizzle of mustard oil and a squeeze of lime keep it bright and simple.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday Assamese cooking fat, its pungency matching the ghost chilli heat

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai on medium-high until it smokes, then lower the heat and add 0.5 tsp panch phoron, letting it crackle for 15 seconds.
Add 5 crushed garlic cloves, 1 inch julienned ginger and half a deseeded bhut jolokia, frying gently for a minute so the chilli perfumes the oil without scorching.
Add the sliced onion and cook for 4-5 minutes until translucent and lightly golden.
Add the 400 g broad beans, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, tossing to coat, then sprinkle 3 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 12-14 minutes until the beans are tender.
Uncover and stir-fry on medium for 3 minutes so the beans dry out and absorb the smoky chilli heat.
Take off the heat, squeeze in 1 tbsp lime juice, toss and serve.
tips: Handle bhut jolokia with gloves and deseed it; even half a chilli delivers formidable heat.
Add the ghost chilli whole and remove it before serving if you want aroma with more controllable heat.
The lime at the end is essential to balance and refresh the intense chilli fire.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft steamed joha rice and a plate of fresh cucumber to cool the palate between bites.

variations.name: Classic Butter Aloo Tamatar
variations.description: A rich restaurant-style potato curry in a velvety butter-tomato gravy, mildly sweet and glossy with cream. Baby potatoes soak up the makhani-inspired sauce, making it a crowd-pleasing, kid-friendly favourite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee deepens the makhani base beyond what plain butter delivers

steps: Boil 1 chopped onion, 4 pureed tomatoes and 10 cashews with 1 cup water for 8 minutes until soft, then cool and blend to a smooth paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with 2 tbsp butter over medium heat, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in the blended tomato-cashew paste with 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1 tsp salt; cook 8 minutes, stirring, until the ghee floats to the surface.
Prick the 500 g boiled baby potatoes lightly with a fork and add them to the gravy, coating each one well.
Pour in 1 cup hot water, cover and simmer on low for 8 minutes so the potatoes absorb the buttery sauce.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the pan, stir in 3 tbsp cream and 0.5 tsp garam masala, and simmer 2 minutes until glossy and rich.
tips: Straining the blended gravy through a sieve gives the ultra-smooth restaurant texture, though it is optional at home.
Pricking the potatoes helps them drink up the makhani gravy instead of staying bland inside.
Balance the tomato tartness with a pinch of sugar if your tomatoes are sharp; the dish should taste mellow.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or jeera rice and a scatter of cream swirled on top for a party-style presentation.

variations.name: Kashmiri Butter Aloo Tamatar
variations.description: A dum-style aloo where saffron and Kashmiri chilli tint the buttery curd gravy a glowing red, perfumed with fennel and dry ginger. Rich yet aromatic, it echoes the elegance of a Wazwan dish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee is the traditional cooking fat for Kashmiri dum gravies

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: Saffron gives the buttery gravy its glowing colour and delicate perfume

steps: Soak 1 pinch Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside to release its colour and aroma.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with 1 tbsp butter over medium heat and shallow-fry the 500 g boiled baby potatoes until golden all over, about 4 minutes, then remove them.
In the same fat, crackle 3 cardamom, 3 cloves and a 1-inch cinnamon stick for 30 seconds until aromatic.
Lower the heat, add 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, stir for 10 seconds, then whisk in 0.75 cup curd slowly so it does not split.
Add 2 tsp fennel powder, 0.5 tsp dry ginger powder, 1 tsp salt and the saffron milk, then return the fried potatoes and pour in 1 cup hot water.
Cover and simmer on very low heat for 15 minutes, dum-style, until the gravy is deep red and the potatoes are infused through.
tips: Frying the potatoes before simmering gives them the firm, flavour-soaked texture of authentic Kashmiri dum aloo.
Add the curd off high heat and whisk continuously to keep the gravy smooth rather than curdled.
Fennel and dry ginger are the true Kashmiri seasonings; skipping them leaves the curry tasting generic.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed basmati rice or Kashmiri pulao and a side of walnut chutney.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Butter Aloo Tamatar
variations.description: A Puneri twist on buttery potatoes where goda masala and roasted peanut-coconut paste replace the usual garam masala. The result is nutty, dark and mildly sweet, a Deccan take on comfort curry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the classic Maharashtrian cooking medium

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A ghee finish adds the buttery richness this dish is named for

steps: Dry-roast 3 tbsp peanuts and 3 tbsp desiccated coconut separately until golden, about 3 minutes each, then grind them with a little water into a coarse paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds for 15 seconds until they pop.
Add 2 chopped onions and fry until golden brown, 6 minutes, then add 3 chopped tomatoes and cook until soft, 5 minutes.
Stir in the peanut-coconut paste, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tbsp goda masala and 1 tsp salt; cook 4 minutes until the oil separates.
Add the 500 g boiled halved potatoes with 1.5 cups hot water, cover and simmer on low for 8 minutes.
Finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee stirred through and simmer 1 minute so the gravy turns glossy and nutty-dark.
tips: Grind the peanuts and coconut only coarsely; a little texture is what makes the Maharashtrian gravy special.
Goda masala carries the whole flavour here, so use a fresh, aromatic batch for the best result.
For extra body, mash a couple of the boiled potatoes into the gravy before simmering.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar or bajra bhakri, or with plain rice and a spoon of the peanut-thickened gravy on top.

variations.name: Rajasthani Butter Aloo Tamatar
variations.description: A bold Marwari-style curry that builds heat from dried red chillies soaked and ground into a smoky paste, richened with ghee and curd instead of water. Fiery, rustic and deeply flavoured for the desert palate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee is the defining fat of Rajasthani cooking where water is scarce

steps: Soak 5 dried red chillies in hot water for 15 minutes, then grind them with a splash of water into a smooth, fiery-red paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 3 cloves for 20 seconds until aromatic.
Add 2 chopped onions and fry until deep golden, 7 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Add the red chilli paste, 2 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt; fry 3 minutes until the ghee separates and the paste darkens.
Lower the heat and whisk in 0.75 cup curd slowly, stirring continuously so it does not split, then add the 500 g boiled potatoes.
Pour in 1 cup hot water, cover and simmer on low for 10 minutes until the gravy clings thickly to the potatoes.
tips: Mathania or Kashmiri-type dried chillies give brilliant colour with manageable heat; adjust the count to taste.
Soaking and grinding the chillies rather than using powder gives the authentic glossy Rajasthani gravy.
Add the curd off the boil and stir without stopping to keep the sauce from breaking.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra roti and a dollop of white butter, or with steamed rice for a hearty Marwari meal.

variations.name: Goan Butter Aloo Tamatar
variations.description: A coastal xacuti-leaning potato curry where kokum lends a gentle tang and roasted spices with coconut build a warm, aromatic sauce. Tangy, mildly spicy and fragrant, it brings the Konkan coast to a humble aloo.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil grounds this curry firmly on the Goan coast

steps: Dry-roast 1 tbsp coriander seeds, 3 dried red chillies and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds until fragrant, 2 minutes, then grind with 0.5 cup grated coconut and water into a paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil over medium heat and fry 2 chopped onions until golden, about 6 minutes.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes and 0.5 tsp turmeric and cook 4 minutes until the tomatoes soften and break down.
Stir in the ground coconut-spice masala and 1 tsp salt, and fry 4 minutes until the oil separates and the paste smells roasted.
Add the 500 g boiled potatoes and 4 kokum petals with 1.5 cups hot water, cover and simmer on low for 10 minutes.
Uncover and cook 2 minutes more until the gravy thickens and turns a warm reddish-brown, adjusting salt before serving.
tips: Kokum gives a rounded, fruity sourness quite different from tamarind or lemon; do not substitute if you can find it.
Roast the spices just until fragrant, not dark, or the masala turns bitter.
Discard the softened kokum petals before serving so no one bites into a sour piece.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with Goan pao, steamed rice, or soft neer dosa to mop up the tangy coconut gravy.

variations.name: Classic Butter Malai Kofta
variations.description: Melt-in-the-mouth paneer koftas stuffed with nuts and raisins, resting in a pale, buttery cashew-cream gravy. Mildly sweet and luxuriously smooth, this is the banquet centrepiece that defines Indian vegetarian indulgence.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: wholegrain binder that keeps the stuffed koftas soft and crack-free

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: clean, high-smoke-point oil for frying the delicate koftas golden

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon that deepens the buttery aroma of the white gravy

steps: Mash 2 boiled potatoes with 1.5 cups grated paneer, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta into a smooth dough, then flatten portions and stuff each with a little chopped cashew and raisin before sealing into 10 balls.
Deep-fry the koftas in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat, lowering them gently, until pale gold, about 4 minutes; drain carefully as they are delicate.
Boil 2 chopped onions with 3 cardamom for 8 minutes, cool, and blend to a smooth white paste, keeping it pale for the classic look.
In 2 tbsp butter, saute 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for a minute without browning, then add the onion paste and cook gently for 4 minutes.
Stir in 4 tbsp cashew paste and 2 tbsp melon seed paste with 0.75 tsp salt and 1 cup hot water, and simmer 5 minutes to a silky, ivory gravy, stirring so it does not catch.
Add 5 tbsp cream, 1 tsp sugar and 0.5 tsp garam masala, and warm through for 2 minutes without boiling hard.
Finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, place the koftas in just before serving, and spoon the pale gravy over them so they stay whole.
tips: Keep the gravy pale by boiling rather than frying the onions and avoiding turmeric or red chilli.
Stuff and seal the koftas well so the nuts do not spill and cause the koftas to break while frying.
Add koftas only at serving time; a long soak turns these soft dumplings to mush.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or saffron pulao, garnished with a cream drizzle, slivered pistachios and a single rose petal for elegance.

variations.name: Kashmiri Butter Malai Kofta
variations.description: A Valley-inspired malai kofta glowing with Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron and warmed by fennel and dry ginger. The white gravy takes on a golden blush and a delicate floral aroma, richer and more perfumed than the everyday version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: binds the koftas softly for the fragrant saffron gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the koftas and forms the rich base, as in Kashmiri kitchens

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm milk for the golden colour and signature aroma

steps: Mash 2 boiled potatoes with 1.5 cups grated paneer, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta into a smooth dough and shape into 10 oval koftas.
Fry the koftas in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat until pale gold, about 4 minutes, and steep 1 pinch Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk.
Boil 2 onions with 4 cardamom for 8 minutes, then blend to a smooth pale paste.
In the remaining 3 tbsp ghee, add the onion paste with 1 tbsp fennel powder and 0.75 tsp dry ginger powder, and cook gently for 4 minutes without browning.
Stir in 4 tbsp cashew paste and 1 cup hot water with 0.75 tsp salt, simmer 4 minutes, then lower the heat and whisk in 0.5 cup yogurt slowly so it does not split.
Add the saffron milk and 3 tbsp cream, warm through for 3 minutes, and let the gravy turn a pale gold.
Slip the koftas in just before serving and spoon the fragrant gravy over them; rest 2 minutes so the saffron perfume settles.
tips: Fennel and dry ginger are the aromatic heart of Kashmiri gravies, so grind them fresh for the best fragrance.
Add yogurt only on low heat with constant stirring to keep the pale gravy smooth.
Reserve a few saffron strands to float on top for colour and a luxurious look.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with Kashmiri pulao studded with dry fruit, and drizzle a little extra saffron milk over the koftas at the table.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Butter Malai Kofta
variations.description: A Maharashtrian spin where the creamy kofta meets the smoky warmth of goda masala and a whisper of roasted coconut. Cooked in wood-pressed groundnut oil, it balances the malai richness with a dark, aromatic spice note unique to the Deccan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: binds the koftas so they hold up to the robust goda masala gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the classic Maharashtrian oil for frying and building the masala

steps: Mash 2 boiled potatoes with 1.5 cups grated paneer, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta into a soft dough and shape into 10 koftas.
Fry the koftas in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat until golden, about 4 minutes, and drain.
Dry-roast 3 tbsp coconut until deep brown, then blend with 2 onions and 1 chopped tomato to a smooth paste.
In 3 tbsp oil, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the coconut-onion paste, and cook over medium heat until it darkens and oil separates, about 8 minutes.
Add 1.5 tbsp goda masala, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.75 tsp salt, fry for a minute, then stir in 3 tbsp cashew paste and 1 cup hot water and simmer 5 minutes.
Add 3 tbsp cream and warm the gravy to a glossy, medium-thick consistency, about 2 minutes.
Place the koftas in just before serving, spoon the smoky gravy over, and rest 2 minutes.
tips: Roast the coconut to a rich brown for the deep, nutty character that defines Maharashtrian gravies.
Goda masala carries a natural sweetness, so go easy on any added sugar here.
Toast the goda masala for just a few seconds in the oil to bloom its aroma without burning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft chapati or masala bhaat, garnished with fresh coriander and a light dusting of goda masala.

variations.name: Bengali Butter Malai Kofta
variations.description: A Bengali malai kofta where paneer koftas rest in a delicate poppy-seed and coconut gravy cooked in Anveshan Mustard Oil. Gently sweet with a faint mustard warmth, it echoes the refined shorshe-narkel flavours of a Kolkata feast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: binds the koftas softly for the poppy-coconut gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked first so it lends a gentle Bengali pungency to the gravy

steps: Mash 2 boiled potatoes with 1.5 cups grated paneer, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta into a smooth dough and roll into 10 koftas.
Heat Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil to its haze, cool slightly, and fry the koftas over medium heat until pale gold, about 4 minutes; drain.
In 3 tbsp of the mustard oil, splutter 0.5 tsp nigella seeds, then add 2 finely chopped onions and cook to soft and translucent, about 6 minutes, keeping them pale.
Add 1 tbsp ginger paste and 0.5 tsp turmeric, fry for a minute, then stir in 3 tbsp poppy seed paste and 3 tbsp coconut paste with 0.75 tsp salt.
Pour in 1 cup water and simmer 5 minutes until the gravy is creamy and the poppy seeds lose their rawness, then add 3 slit green chillies and 0.75 tsp sugar.
Stir in 2 tbsp cream and warm gently for 2 minutes without boiling hard.
Add the koftas just before serving, spoon the pale gravy over, drizzle a teaspoon of raw mustard oil, and rest 2 minutes.
tips: Soak poppy seeds in warm water before grinding for a smooth, lump-free white paste.
Keep the onions pale rather than browned so the gravy stays light-coloured and delicate.
The touch of sugar is essential to the mellow Bengali balance against the mustard sharpness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with luchi or steamed rice, with a wedge of lime and a few extra slit green chillies alongside.

variations.name: Kerala Butter Malai Kofta
variations.description: A tropical malai kofta where the creamy koftas rest in a coconut-milk gravy tempered with curry leaves and Anveshan Coconut Oil. Lighter and gently sweet, it swaps the northern cashew-cream for the mellow richness of fresh coconut.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: binds the koftas so they stay whole in the coconut gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: gives the koftas and tempering their signature Kerala aroma

steps: Mash 2 boiled potatoes with 1.5 cups grated paneer, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta into a smooth dough and roll into 10 koftas.
Fry the koftas in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil over medium heat until golden and firm, about 4 minutes, and drain.
In 3 tbsp coconut oil, pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 1 sprig curry leaves, then add 2 sliced onions and 3 slit green chillies and cook to soft gold, about 6 minutes.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 0.5 tsp turmeric, fry a minute, then add 2 tbsp cashew paste and 0.5 cup water and simmer 3 minutes.
Pour in 1 cup coconut milk with 0.75 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp black pepper, and bring to the gentlest simmer without boiling.
Lower in the koftas and simmer softly for 3 minutes so they soak up the sweet, fragrant gravy.
Crisp the second curry-leaf sprig in a teaspoon of coconut oil, pour over the top, and rest 2 minutes before serving.
tips: Add thick coconut milk at the end and keep the flame gentle so it does not split.
Black pepper rather than heavy chilli gives the warm Malabar note to this gravy.
Toast the cashew paste briefly so it thickens the gravy without a raw taste.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft appams, malabar parotta or matta rice, with a side of coconut-shallot chutney.

variations.name: Classic Butter Paneer
variations.description: The velvety paneer makhani that defined Indian restaurant menus worldwide, built on a smooth tomato-cashew gravy enriched with butter and cream. It is mildly sweet, subtly smoky and glossy, the paneer cubes bathed in a sauce you will want to mop up to the last streak.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: used to bhuno the tomato base, adding a nutty depth beneath the butter

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a natural swap for white sugar that balances the tomato tang the makhani way

steps: Roughly chop 5 tomatoes and 1 onion and simmer them with 15 cashews, 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and about a cup of water for 12 minutes until everything is very soft.
Cool slightly, blend to a completely smooth puree, then strain through a sieve for that signature silky makhani texture.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with 2 tbsp butter in a pan, add 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder off the heat, then pour in the strained puree carefully as it will splutter.
Simmer the gravy on low for 10 minutes, stirring often, until it thickens, deepens in colour and the fat floats to the surface.
Add 1 tsp salt and 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, then slide in 300 g cubed paneer and simmer 4 minutes so it softens into the sauce.
Finish with 4 tbsp cream, 0.75 tsp garam masala, 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi and the last tbsp of butter, swirling gently just before serving.
tips: Straining the puree is the single biggest step towards restaurant-smooth makhani; do not skip it.
For a smoky dhaba touch, place a hot charcoal in a bowl set in the gravy, drizzle with ghee, and cover for two minutes.
Balance is everything here; if too tangy add a little more jaggery, if too sweet a squeeze of lemon.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or jeera rice, a swirl of extra cream on top and a scatter of julienned ginger for the full restaurant presentation.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Butter Paneer
variations.description: This version swaps the sweet makhani profile for the dark, fragrant complexity of goda masala, giving the buttery paneer a Maharashtrian soul. Dry coconut and toasted spices lend an earthy, slightly smoky depth that sets it apart from any North Indian gravy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the staple Maharashtrian frying oil that carries the goda masala's roasted notes

steps: Dry-roast 3 tbsp desiccated coconut in a pan on low until golden, about 3 minutes, then set aside to cool.

In 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil fry 2 chopped onions with 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 6 minutes until browned, add 2 chopped tomatoes and cook 4 minutes, then blend with the roasted coconut to a smooth paste.
Heat the remaining 1 tbsp oil with 2 tbsp butter, add the blended paste and fry on medium for 5 minutes until it darkens and the oil separates.
Stir in 2 tsp goda masala, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder and cook 1 minute so the toasted spice aroma blooms.
Pour in about a cup of water with 1 tsp salt, bring to a gentle simmer, then add 300 g cubed paneer and cook 5 minutes until it absorbs the dark masala.
Swirl in 2 tbsp cream, simmer 1 minute, and finish with 2 tbsp fresh coriander over the top.
tips: Roasting the coconut until just golden, not brown, keeps the gravy nutty rather than bitter.
Goda masala varies by brand; start with less and add more, as some blends are intensely aromatic.
A teaspoon of jaggery can be added if your goda masala leans very savoury, in true Maharashtrian style.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft jowar bhakri or ghee-brushed chapati, alongside a cooling koshimbir salad of cucumber and peanuts.

variations.name: Kerala Butter Paneer
variations.description: A coconut-forward southern spin where the buttery paneer meets a coconut-milk gravy tempered with curry leaves and warm spices. Coconut oil replaces the usual base, and the sauce turns silky and mildly sweet, more Kerala stew than Punjabi makhani.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the defining Kerala fat that perfumes the curry leaves and marries with coconut milk

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil with 1.5 tbsp butter and fry 15 curry leaves and 2 slit green chillies for 15 seconds until fragrant.
Add 2 finely sliced onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and saute 6 minutes until soft and pale gold.
Add 1 chopped tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp fennel powder and cook 4 minutes until pulpy and the raw smell disappears.
Pour in half a cup of water with 1 tsp salt and simmer 3 minutes, then slide in 300 g cubed paneer and cook 4 minutes.
Lower the heat and stir in 1 cup thick coconut milk, warming it through gently for 3 to 4 minutes without letting it boil, or it will split.
Finish with 0.75 tsp garam masala, taste for salt, and serve while the gravy is silky and just steaming.
tips: Never boil the dish hard after the coconut milk goes in; a bare simmer keeps it smooth.
Add a second tempering of curry leaves in hot coconut oil on top for a fragrant finish.
A squeeze of lime just before serving brightens the mellow coconut sweetness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with appam, Malabar parotta or ghee rice to soak up the coconut gravy, with pappadam on the side.

variations.name: Rajasthani Butter Paneer
variations.description: A robust desert-style butter paneer where soaked dried red chillies build a deep red, smoky heat and a curd base replaces the tomato-heavy makhani. Cooked in ghee with warming whole spices, it is richer, spicier and closer to a Marwari laal maas in attitude.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the classic Rajasthani cooking fat that carries the soaked-chilli paste and whole spices

steps: Soak 8 dried Mathania red chillies in hot water for 15 minutes, then grind with 10 garlic cloves to a smooth red paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with 1 tbsp butter and crackle 4 cloves, 3 cardamom pods and 1 bay leaf for 20 seconds.
Add 2 finely chopped onions and fry on medium for 7 minutes until deep golden brown, the base of the dish's colour and flavour.
Add the chilli-garlic paste with 1.5 tsp coriander powder and fry 3 minutes until the ghee separates and the raw garlic smell disappears.
Lower the heat, whisk in 0.75 cup curd a spoon at a time so it does not split, add 1 tsp salt and about half a cup of water, and simmer 5 minutes into a glossy red gravy.
Slide in 300 g cubed paneer and simmer gently for 6 minutes until it soaks up the fiery masala and turns tinted red.
tips: Mathania or Kashmiri chillies give colour without unbearable heat; adjust the count to your tolerance.
Whisk the curd smooth and add it off the boil to avoid curdling in the hot ghee.
This tastes even better the next day once the chilli mellows into the curd.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra roti and a dollop of white butter, or with steamed rice and thin buttermilk to temper the heat.

variations.name: Kashmiri Butter Paneer
variations.description: A fragrant Kashmiri interpretation where saffron and fennel scent a mild, glowing red gravy set off by ghee and butter. Skipping onion and garlic in the Wazwan tradition, it leans on dry ginger and warm whole spices for a delicate, aromatic richness quite unlike the usual makhani.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the base fat that blooms the fennel and dry ginger central to Kashmiri gravies

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk to give the buttery gravy its glow and gentle perfume

steps: Steep a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk. Cut 300 g paneer into cubes.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with 2 tbsp butter and crackle 3 cardamom pods and 1 inch cinnamon for 20 seconds.
Off the heat add 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1.5 tsp fennel powder and 0.75 tsp dry ginger powder, stirring 15 seconds so they bloom without scorching.
Whisk 0.75 cup curd smooth, add it off the flame while stirring constantly, then return to low heat with about half a cup of water and 1 tsp salt and simmer 5 minutes.
Pour in the saffron milk, slide in the paneer cubes, and simmer very gently for 6 minutes until the gravy turns a warm glowing red.
Finish with 2 tbsp cream stirred through, and rest the dish for 5 minutes so the saffron aroma settles.
tips: Blooming the spice powders in hot fat off the heat prevents the fennel from turning bitter.
Add the curd gradually and off the boil; a rushed pour will split it into the ghee.
A few slivered almonds fried in ghee make an elegant, traditional garnish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sheermal or a saffron-flecked pulao, and a small kachumber of radish and walnut for a Kashmiri flourish.

variations.name: Classic Butter Rajma
variations.description: A luxuriously rich rajma finished with a generous knob of butter and a splash of cream for a silky, restaurant-style gravy. The kidney beans stay soft and coated in a glossy tomato masala that eats indulgent yet familiar. Rajma dressed up for a special dinner.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee starts the base with a nutty depth before the butter finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A little wood-pressed oil keeps the onions from browning too fast

ingredients.name: Dried red kidney beans, soaked overnight

steps: Pressure-cook the soaked 1.5 cups kidney beans with 0.5 tsp salt and 3.5 cups water for 7-8 whistles until fully soft, then keep them in their liquid.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the 2 chopped onions and fry for 8 minutes until golden, then stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until the raw smell lifts.
Pour in the tomato puree with 1 tsp red chilli, 2 tsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp salt, and cook 10 minutes until thick and the fat separates.
Add the beans with their liquid, mash a quarter of them, and simmer covered for 15 minutes until the gravy is thick and creamy.
Stir in 3 tbsp butter, 3 tbsp cream, 1 tsp garam masala and crushed kasuri methi, and simmer 3 minutes until silky and glossy.
tips: Add the butter only towards the end so it emulsifies into a glossy finish rather than cooking off.
For extra silkiness, blend a ladle of the gravy smooth and stir it back before adding the cream.
Balance the richness with a squeeze of lemon at the table if the gravy feels too heavy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or jeera rice, a swirl of cream on top and a side of pickled onions.

variations.name: Kashmiri Butter Rajma
variations.description: A gentler, aromatic butter rajma drawing on the Kashmiri palate: saffron, fennel and Kashmiri chilli for a ruby colour and mellow heat, enriched with butter and curd instead of a heavy cream. Elegant, fragrant and lightly festive. A meeting of Pandit spicing and modern richness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries the fennel and saffron aromatics of a Kashmiri gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: Saffron lends the ruby hue and delicate perfume that define this take

ingredients.name: Dried red kidney beans, soaked overnight

steps: Soak 0.25 tsp Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 3 tbsp warm water and set aside to bloom.
Pressure-cook the soaked 1.5 cups kidney beans with 0.5 tsp salt and 3.5 cups water for 8 whistles until soft, then keep them in their liquid.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat, add the whole cloves, cardamom and cinnamon with 0.25 tsp asafoetida, and sizzle 30 seconds.
Lower the flame, stir in 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli and immediately the tomato puree, cooking 7 minutes until the ghee floats red, then whisk in the 0.5 cup curd off the heat.
Return to low heat, add 2 tsp fennel powder, 1 tsp dry ginger and 0.75 tsp salt, then add the beans with their liquid and the bloomed saffron water.
Simmer covered 15 minutes, stir in 2 tbsp butter until it melts into a glossy ruby gravy, and rest 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Take the pan off the flame before the curd goes in and stir steadily as it reheats to prevent splitting.
Fennel and dry ginger do the aromatic work here, so keep onion and garlic out to honour the Kashmiri style.
Bloom the saffron in warm water, never boiling, to protect its colour and fragrance.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed basmati and a bowl of plain curd, scattered with a few saffron strands and slivered almonds.

variations.name: Bengali Butter Rajma
variations.description: A playful east-meets-north rajma where a pungent wood-pressed mustard oil base meets a mellowing finish of butter, brightened with slit green chillies and a touch of sugar. The mustard sharpness and buttery smoothness make an unexpectedly moreish gravy. Not traditional, but thoroughly delicious.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Mustard oil gives a pungent Bengali base that the butter later softens

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A pinch of jaggery brings the Bengali sweet-savoury balance

ingredients.name: Dried red kidney beans, soaked overnight
Bay leaf and dried red chilli

steps: Pressure-cook the soaked 1.5 cups kidney beans with 0.5 tsp salt and 3.5 cups water for 7-8 whistles until soft, then keep them in their liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil in a pan over medium-high until it smokes, then lower the heat and temper 1 tsp cumin seeds, the bay leaf and dried red chilli for 30 seconds.
Add the chopped onion and fry 6-7 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger paste and cook 1 minute.
Pour in the tomato puree with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli and 0.75 tsp salt, and cook 8 minutes until the oil separates.
Add the beans with their liquid, the 3 slit green chillies and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, mash a few beans, and simmer covered 15 minutes.
Stir in 2 tbsp butter and 0.75 tsp Bengali garam masala, simmer 2 minutes until the gravy turns smooth, and rest 5 minutes.
tips: Smoke the mustard oil first so its raw pungency mellows before the butter later smooths the gravy.
Add the butter at the very end so its dairy sweetness balances the mustard rather than cooking away.
Keep the green chillies whole and slit for aroma without overwhelming heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice or hot parathas, a drizzle of raw mustard oil and extra slit green chillies on top.

variations.name: Andhra Butter Rajma
variations.description: A bold southern reworking that layers fiery Guntur chilli and a garlic-heavy base under a smoothing finish of butter, with curry leaves in the tempering. The result is a rajma that hits with heat then softens with dairy. For those who want their comfort food to fight back.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the Andhra base fat that tempers the raw chilli

ingredients.name: Dried red kidney beans, soaked overnight

steps: Pressure-cook the soaked 1.5 cups kidney beans with 0.5 tsp salt and 3.5 cups water for 7-8 whistles until soft, then keep them in their liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a pan over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and the curry leaves for 30 seconds, then fry the 8 crushed garlic cloves until pale gold.
Add the 2 chopped onions with the minced ginger and saute 7 minutes until browned, guarding the garlic from burning.
Pour in the tomato puree with 2 tsp Guntur chilli, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp salt, and cook 8 minutes until the oil rises red.
Add the beans with their liquid, mash a quarter of them, and simmer covered 15 minutes until thickened.
Swirl in 2 tbsp butter off the heat until it melts into a glossy layer that tames the chilli, and rest 5 minutes.
tips: Guntur chilli is searing, so treat the stated amount as a firm starting point and let the butter carry the balance.
Frying the garlic before the onions builds the deep pungent base that marks an Andhra gravy.
A squeeze of lime alongside the butter finish keeps the heat lively rather than flat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain rice and papad, a bowl of curd to cool the palate and extra butter for those who need it.

variations.name: Gujarati Butter Rajma
variations.description: A softer, sweeter butter rajma leaning into the Gujarati khatta-meetha style, where jaggery and a hint of tamarind meet a buttery, coriander-cumin gravy tempered with curry leaves. Lighter and rounder than the North Indian version. Comforting with phulka and rice alike.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The everyday Gujarati cooking fat that lets the sweet-sour notes shine

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery brings the signature Gujarati sweetness balancing the tamarind

ingredients.name: Dried red kidney beans, soaked overnight

steps: Pressure-cook the soaked 1.5 cups kidney beans with 0.5 tsp salt and 3.5 cups water for 7-8 whistles until soft, then keep them in their liquid.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a pan over medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard and cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then add the curry leaves.
Add the chopped onion and saute 5 minutes until soft, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and cook 1 minute.
Pour in the tomato puree with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp coriander-cumin powder and 0.75 tsp salt, and simmer 8 minutes until the oil separates.
Add the beans with their liquid, 1 tbsp tamarind pulp and 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, mash a few beans, and simmer covered 14 minutes.
Swirl in 2 tbsp butter, adjust the sweet-sour balance, and simmer 2 minutes until the gravy turns smooth and glossy.
tips: Build the khatta-meetha slowly, tasting after each addition of tamarind and jaggery to land the right balance.
The butter here softens the edges of the tang, so add it near the end for a rounded finish.
Keep the gravy medium-thick so it works equally with phulka and rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft ghee-brushed phulka or plain rice, a side of kachumber and sweet mango chunda.

variations.name: Classic Butter Soya Chunk
variations.description: A vegetarian riff on butter masala, where tender soya chunks bathe in a silky tomato-cashew gravy enriched with ghee, cream and crushed kasuri methi. The chunks are boiled and squeezed so they soak up the mildly sweet, buttery sauce. It is rich, smooth and endlessly crowd-pleasing.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee stands in for butter here, giving the makhani gravy its glossy richness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A little jaggery powder replaces refined sugar to give the makhani its signature gentle sweetness.

steps: Boil 1.5 cups soya chunks in salted water for 5 minutes, then drain, rinse in cold water and squeeze each chunk dry.
Simmer 5 chopped tomatoes, 1 chopped onion, 12 cashews, 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 2 cardamom in 1 cup water for 12 minutes until soft, then cool and blend to a silky puree and strain.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium, add 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder off the heat for colour, then pour in the strained puree and cook for 10 minutes until it thickens and the ghee rims the pan.
Add the squeezed soya chunks with 1 cup hot water and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, then simmer for 8 minutes so the chunks drink in the gravy.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi between your palms and stir it in along with 0.5 tsp garam masala, cooking for 2 minutes.
Swirl in 3 tbsp cream, warm through for 1 minute without boiling, and serve with an extra drizzle of cream on top.
tips: Straining the blended gravy is the secret to that restaurant-smooth makhani texture.
Soak the cashews in warm water for 10 minutes before blending for an even silkier sauce.
Balance is everything here; adjust the jaggery and salt until the sweet, tangy and savoury notes sing together.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan, tandoori roti or jeera rice, finishing with a swirl of cream and a sprinkle of kasuri methi.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Butter Soya Chunk
variations.description: A Deccan twist on the creamy classic, where the smooth tomato-cashew base is deepened with goda masala and a hint of roasted coconut. Cooked in wood-pressed groundnut oil and finished with ghee, it is nuttier and darker than the usual makhani. Jaggery keeps the sweet-smoky balance the region loves.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil grounds the creamy base in an earthy Deccan flavour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of ghee brings the richness expected of a butter-style curry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery powder balances the smoky goda masala in place of refined sugar.

steps: Boil 1.5 cups soya chunks in salted water for 5 minutes, then drain, rinse and squeeze them completely dry.
Dry roast 2 tbsp grated coconut until golden, about 3 minutes, then simmer it with 4 tomatoes, 1 onion and 10 cashews in 1 cup water for 12 minutes and blend to a smooth puree.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 2 tsp goda masala, and fry for 1 minute until fragrant, then pour in the puree with 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder.
Cook the gravy for 10 minutes until it thickens and the oil separates at the edges, stirring so the goda masala does not catch.
Add the squeezed soya chunks with 1 cup hot water and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, and simmer for 8 minutes until the chunks are plump and coated.
Finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 2 tbsp cream, warm through for a minute, and serve.
tips: Toast the coconut just to golden; any darker and it will turn the smooth gravy bitter.
Goda masala is potent, so start with 2 tsp and add more only after tasting.
This gravy tastes richer the next day as the goda masala deepens overnight.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft naan or steamed rice, with a wedge of lime and sliced onion to cut the richness.

variations.name: Gujarati Butter Soya Chunk
variations.description: The creamy soya curry taken in a lighter, sweeter Gujarati direction, with a jaggery-kissed tomato gravy and a smooth cashew-melon-seed base. It is milder on spice and rounded with lemon in the classic sweet-sour style. Comforting and family-friendly, it pairs beautifully with soft rotli.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A gentle amount of groundnut oil keeps this butter-style curry light and homely.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery powder gives this gravy its signature Gujarati sweetness against the tangy tomato.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A drop of ghee at the finish lends the creamy body of a butter curry.

steps: Boil 1.5 cups soya chunks in salted water for 5 minutes, then drain, rinse and squeeze them dry.
Simmer 4 tomatoes, 1 onion, 10 cashews and 1 tbsp melon seeds in 1 cup water for 12 minutes, then cool and blend to a smooth, pale puree.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, add 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and cook for 1 minute, then pour in the puree with 0.75 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder.
Simmer the gravy for 10 minutes until it thickens and the oil floats to the surface.
Add the squeezed soya chunks with 1 cup hot water and 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, then simmer for 8 minutes until the chunks are soft and coated.
Turn off the heat, stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and 1 tbsp lemon juice, and balance the sweet-sour finish before serving.
tips: Melon seeds and cashews together give a creamy body without needing much dairy.
Add lemon only off the heat so its freshness stays bright against the jaggery.
Keep the chilli gentle here; this curry is meant to be mild and sweet-leaning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulka or peas pulao, a bowl of chhaas and a spoon of sweet pickle.

variations.name: Bengali Butter Soya Chunk
variations.description: A Bengali-style creamy soya curry that starts with a mustard-oil base and finishes with a smooth cashew-poppy seed paste for body. Slit green chillies and a touch of sweetness give it the sweet-hot character of eastern cooking. The mustard oil brings a warmth you do not get in a standard makhani.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil gives this creamy curry a warm, pungent Bengali base.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of ghee rounds the mustard oil into a mellow, buttery richness.

steps: Boil 1.5 cups soya chunks in salted water for 5 minutes, then drain, rinse and squeeze them dry.
Soak 10 cashews and 1 tbsp poppy seeds in warm water for 10 minutes, then grind to a smooth white paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it smokes and pales, then add 2 chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger paste and fry until golden, about 7 minutes.
Add 3 pureed tomatoes with 0.75 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, and cook until the mustard oil surfaces, about 8 minutes.
Stir in the cashew-poppy paste and cook for 3 minutes, then add the squeezed soya chunks, 3 slit green chillies and 1.5 cups hot water and simmer for 8 minutes.
Finish with 0.5 tsp garam masala and 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee, warm through for a minute, and serve.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to smoking to soften its raw pungency before building the gravy.
The cashew-poppy paste gives the creaminess of a butter curry without any cream.
Keep the green chillies whole and slit for aroma with a controlled level of heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice, luchi or pulao, with a wedge of lime and a spoon of tomato chutney on the side.

variations.name: Kerala Butter Soya Chunk
variations.description: A coconut-forward take on the creamy curry, where coconut milk replaces cream and a shallot tempering fried in Anveshan Coconut Oil perfumes the pot. Ground cashew and roasted coconut give a plush, silky body with a gentle sweetness. It is a mild, aromatic bridge between makhani comfort and Kerala flavour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil gives the tempering its warm, sweet Kerala fragrance.

steps: Boil 1.5 cups soya chunks in salted water for 5 minutes, then drain, rinse and squeeze them dry.
Soak 12 cashews in warm water for 10 minutes and grind to a smooth paste with 3 tomatoes and 0.5 tsp fennel.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, fry 10 sliced shallots and 10 curry leaves until light brown, about 4 minutes, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste.
Pour in the tomato-cashew paste with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, and cook for 10 minutes until thick and the oil separates.
Add the squeezed soya chunks with 0.5 cup hot water, then simmer for 8 minutes until the chunks are plump and coated.
Lower the flame, pour in 1 cup coconut milk with 0.5 tsp garam masala, warm for 3 minutes without boiling, and finish with the last curry leaves crackled in coconut oil.
tips: Never boil the curry after the coconut milk goes in or it will split into grains.
The cashew paste plus coconut milk gives a double creaminess that stands in for butter and cream.
Small shallots melt into a sweeter, silkier base than large onions here.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with appam, ghee rice or steamed red rice, with pappadam and a coconut chutney on the side.

variations.name: Classic Dhaba-style Sem
variations.description: A rustic highway-dhaba rendition of broad beans, cooked in a bold bhuna masala finished with crushed kasuri methi and a smoky garam masala. The beans are cooked semi-dry so the thick masala clings richly to each piece. It carries the unmistakable robust, slightly charred flavour of roadside cooking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a generous pour of wood-pressed oil gives the bhuna masala its dhaba richness

steps: Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a heavy kadai on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds until aromatic.
Add 2 chopped onions and fry for 7-8 minutes until deep golden brown, then add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 2 minutes until the raw edge is gone.
Pour in the 2 pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, and bhuna on medium for 6-7 minutes until the oil separates and the masala darkens.
Add the 400 g broad beans and 1 tsp salt, toss to coat well, then cover and cook on low for 13-15 minutes until the beans are tender, stirring a few times.
Uncover and stir-fry on medium-high for 3-4 minutes so the masala thickens and clings and the beans catch a little colour.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi between your palms and sprinkle it in along with 1 tsp garam masala, cook for a minute, then finish with 2 tbsp fresh coriander and serve.
tips: Deep-brown the onions patiently; this is what gives dhaba food its signature robust base.
Dry-roast the kasuri methi lightly before crushing to intensify its aroma.
Keep the dish semi-dry with a thick clinging masala rather than a runny gravy for authentic dhaba texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter-laden tandoori roti or laccha paratha and a side of sliced onions with green chutney.

variations.name: Punjabi Dhaba-style Sem
variations.description: A rich Punjabi dhaba take where the broad beans simmer in a buttery onion-tomato masala and are finished with a knob of ghee instead of the usual white butter. Kasuri methi and a touch of cream-like richness make it indulgent. This is comfort food with a highway soul.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee replaces dhaba white butter and lends a deeper nutty richness

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat and let 1 tsp cumin seeds sizzle and turn fragrant for 20 seconds.
Add 2 chopped onions and fry for 7 minutes until golden, then stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 2 minutes.
Add the 2 pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.25 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, and cook on medium for 6-7 minutes until the ghee floats on top.
Add the 400 g broad beans and 1 tsp salt, mix well, then cover and cook on low for 13-15 minutes until tender.
Uncover, stir in 2 tbsp fresh cream and cook on low for 2 minutes so the gravy turns silky and clings to the beans.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the top, add 0.75 tsp garam masala, simmer for a minute and serve hot.
tips: Finishing with ghee rather than butter gives a rounder, nuttier flavour that does not turn greasy on cooling.
For a lighter version, swap the cream for 2 tbsp whisked yoghurt added off the heat to avoid splitting.
A pinch of sugar can balance the tomatoes if they are too tart.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot naan or missi roti and a glass of salted lassi for a true Punjabi dhaba meal.

variations.name: Haryanvi Dhaba-style Sem
variations.description: A hearty, ghee-forward Haryanvi version where broad beans are cooked simply in plenty of pure ghee with a rustic onion masala and a hit of home-ground garam masala. Farmhouse cooking here leans on ghee and buttermilk rather than cream. The result is earthy, wholesome and deeply satisfying.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Haryanvi kitchens cook vegetables generously in ghee for a rich farmhouse taste

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin and a pinch of asafoetida and let them crackle for 15 seconds.
Add 2 chopped onions and fry for 6-7 minutes until golden, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for a minute until aromatic.
Add the chopped tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.25 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, and cook for 5 minutes until the tomato softens and the ghee separates.
Add the 400 g broad beans and 1 tsp salt, toss well in the ghee masala, then cover and cook on low for 13-15 minutes until the beans are tender.
Lower the heat, stir in 3 tbsp buttermilk and cook gently for 2-3 minutes so it blends in without curdling.
Sprinkle 1 tsp garam masala, stir-fry for a minute to concentrate the masala and serve hot.
tips: Add the buttermilk on low heat and keep stirring so it does not split into curds.
Do not stint on the ghee here; it is the defining richness of Haryanvi home cooking.
Home-ground garam masala with extra black cardamom deepens the rustic flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thick hand-rolled rotis, a bowl of extra buttermilk and a knob of white butter on top.

variations.name: Awadhi Dhaba-style Sem
variations.description: A refined Lucknowi interpretation where broad beans are slow-cooked in a fragrant, mildly spiced onion masala scented with kewra water and a hint of mace. The dhaba robustness is softened into something aromatic and courtly. Fried onion garnish adds a subtle sweetness typical of Awadhi cooking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee is the heart of Awadhi cooking, carrying the delicate kewra aroma

steps: Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat, add 0.75 tsp cumin, 3 green cardamom pods and 1 blade of mace, letting them release their perfume for 20 seconds.
Add the onion paste (from 2 onions) and fry patiently for 8-9 minutes until pale gold, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 2 minutes.
Lower the heat and stir in 3 tbsp whisked yoghurt gradually, followed by 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, cooking for 3-4 minutes until the ghee surfaces.
Add the 400 g broad beans and 1 tsp salt, mix well, then cover and cook on very low for 15 minutes until the beans are meltingly tender.
Uncover and simmer for 2-3 minutes to thicken the masala to a soft coating consistency.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp kewra water and 2 tbsp crushed fried onions, cover and rest off the heat for 3 minutes before serving so the aroma settles.
tips: Add kewra water only at the very end and sparingly, as its floral aroma turns overpowering if cooked.
Whisk the yoghurt well and add it on low heat to prevent it from splitting into the ghee.
Resting the dish covered after cooking lets the Awadhi aromatics infuse the beans fully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sheermal or rumali roti and a saffron-scented pulao for an elegant Awadhi spread.

variations.name: Kashmiri Dhaba-style Sem
variations.description: A Kashmiri-inflected dhaba sem coloured and perfumed with saffron and dry ginger, using fennel and Kashmiri chilli in place of onion-garlic in the traditional style. The gravy is warmly spiced yet gentle, glowing red-gold from saffron and mild chilli. Yoghurt gives it a soft, comforting body.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the base fat for Kashmiri wazwan-style vegetables, mild and rich

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk to lend the signature glow and aroma of Kashmiri cooking

steps: Steep a pinch of Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside to bloom while you cook.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat and add 3 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon, letting them crackle for 20 seconds.
