Lower the heat and add 1.5 tsp Kashmiri red chilli powder with a splash of water to stop it burning, then whisk in 4 tbsp yoghurt slowly and cook for 3-4 minutes until the ghee floats.
Stir in 1.5 tsp fennel powder and 0.75 tsp dry ginger powder, then add the 400 g broad beans and 1 tsp salt and toss to coat in the red-gold masala.
Add 0.5 cup water, cover and simmer on low for 15 minutes until the beans are soft and the gravy has reduced to a light coating.
Pour in the saffron milk, simmer uncovered for 2 minutes so the colour and aroma spread through, then serve.
tips: Fennel and dry ginger replace onion and garlic in the classic Kashmiri Pandit style, so keep them prominent.
Bloom the saffron in warm milk rather than water for a richer colour and rounder aroma.
Whisk the yoghurt smooth and add on low heat to keep the gravy from curdling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a dollop of extra ghee, alongside a simple Kashmiri haakh for balance.

variations.name: Classic Dhaba-style Tinda
variations.description: A rustic highway-dhaba tinda cooked in a robust onion-tomato masala finished with crushed kasuri methi and a charcoal-smoke touch. Bold, smoky and generously spiced, it captures the unfussy, ladle-clanging flavour of a roadside kadhai.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: dhabas cook in generous oil on a fierce flame for that signature bhuna depth

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoon stirred in at the end gives the rich dhaba-style finish

steps: Peel and quarter the 500 g tinda, finely chop the 3 onions, and puree the 3 tomatoes for a thick clinging masala.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on medium-high and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add the onions and 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry hard for 8 minutes until deep golden brown.
Pour in the tomato puree with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, and bhuna on medium for 7 minutes until the oil pools at the edges.
Add the tinda and 1 tsp salt, cover, and cook on low for 16 to 18 minutes until tender, then uncover and stir-fry for 3 minutes to thicken.
Crush 1.5 tsp kasuri methi over the pan, add 1 tsp garam masala and 1 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee, and toss for 2 minutes.
For the dhaba touch, place a small heated piece of charcoal in a steel bowl set in the pan, drizzle a few drops of oil over it, cover for 2 minutes, then remove.
Garnish with 3 tbsp coriander leaves and serve hot.
tips: Brown the onions really well; the deep colour is what gives dhaba food its characteristic robust base.
The charcoal dhungar step is optional but delivers the unmistakable smoky roadside aroma.
Rest for 10 minutes with the lid on after smoking so the flavour penetrates the gourd.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with buttered tandoori rotis or lachha paratha, sliced onions and a green chilli on the side.

variations.name: Punjabi Dhaba-style Tinda
variations.description: The quintessential Punjabi dhaba tinda swimming in a thick, buttery onion-tomato masala with plenty of ginger juliennes and a ghee finish. Hearty and full-flavoured, it is the kind of sabzi that anchors a truckers' thali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: Punjabi dhabas ladle in ghee for the rich, glossy masala they are famous for

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: added with the ghee to keep the onions from catching over the high dhaba flame

steps: Peel and quarter the 500 g tinda, finely chop the 3 onions, puree the 3 tomatoes, and cut the 2 inch ginger into fine juliennes, saving some for garnish.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee with 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on medium-high and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and the 1 bay leaf for 20 seconds.
Add the onions, half the ginger juliennes and the 6 crushed garlic cloves, frying for 8 minutes until richly golden.
Pour in the tomato puree with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder and bhuna for 7 minutes until the ghee separates.
Fold in the tinda and 1 tsp salt, cover, and cook on low for 16 to 18 minutes until soft and coated in the thick masala.
Crush 1.5 tsp kasuri methi and add with 1 tsp garam masala, then stir in 2 tbsp fresh cream and cook uncovered for 2 minutes.
Top with the reserved ginger juliennes and 3 tbsp coriander leaves and serve hot.
tips: Raw ginger juliennes scattered on top are the classic Punjabi dhaba flourish, so keep some back.
For an even richer plate, stir in 2 tbsp fresh cream along with the garam masala.
A generous knob of white butter melting on top just before serving is very dhaba-authentic.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot lachha parathas, a raw onion-and-lemon salad and a tall glass of salted lassi.

variations.name: Rajasthani Dhaba-style Tinda
variations.description: A highway-dhaba tinda from the Rajasthan road, smoky with roasted dried chillies and finished in mustard oil and ghee, with yoghurt for body instead of heavy tomato. Rustic, fiery and deeply savoury, built for the desert traveller.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: the fat of choice on the Rajasthan highway that carries the smoky chilli heat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: a spoon adds the pungent, rustic backbone of a desert dhaba

steps: Peel and quarter the 500 g tinda, finely chop the 2 onions, and whisk the 0.5 cup yoghurt smooth with the 2 tsp coriander powder to keep it from splitting.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee with 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil on medium and roast the 5 broken dried red chillies with 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds until smoky.
Add the onions and 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 7 minutes until golden brown.
Lower the flame, pour in the spiced yoghurt with 0.5 tsp turmeric, and stir constantly for 3 minutes until thickened and glossy.
Fold in the tinda and 1 tsp salt, cover, and cook on low for 16 to 18 minutes until tender.
Crush 1 tsp kasuri methi, add with 1 tsp garam masala, and stir-fry uncovered for 2 minutes to reduce.
Garnish with 2 tbsp coriander leaves and serve hot.
tips: Roast the dried chillies just until they darken and smell smoky; burnt ones turn the whole dish bitter.
Keep the flame low while the yoghurt cooks and stir without stopping to avoid curdling.
The yoghurt base makes this sabzi hold up for hours, true to its travel-food roots.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot bajra or missi roti, a spoon of garlic chutney and thick chaas alongside.

variations.name: Haryanvi Dhaba-style Tinda
variations.description: A ghee-rich Haryanvi dhaba tinda cooked simply with plenty of pure ghee, green chillies and a light tomato masala, letting fresh dairy fat do the heavy lifting. Wholesome and mildly spiced, it is farmhouse comfort food from the fields of Haryana.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: Haryana's dairy-rich kitchens use ghee lavishly, and it defines this sabzi's flavour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a touch alongside the ghee raises the smoke point for the initial frying

steps: Peel and quarter the 500 g tinda, finely chop the 2 onions and 2 tomatoes, grate the 1 inch ginger, and slit the 3 green chillies.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee with 1 tsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on medium and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.5 tsp ajwain for about 20 seconds.
Add the onions, grated ginger and slit green chillies and fry for 6 minutes until soft and pale gold.
Stir in the tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 2 tsp coriander powder and cook for 5 minutes until the ghee glistens on top.
Add the tinda and 1 tsp salt, cover, and cook on low for 16 to 18 minutes until meltingly tender.
Sprinkle 0.75 tsp garam masala and stir-fry uncovered for 2 minutes so the ghee coats every piece.
Garnish with 2 tbsp coriander leaves and serve hot.
tips: The ajwain aids digestion and cuts the richness of all that ghee, so do not leave it out.
Use good bilona ghee since it is the star flavour here, not a background fat.
Keep the spicing gentle; this is meant to be a comforting, ghee-forward everyday sabzi.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thick bajra khichdi topped with more ghee, or hot phulkas and a glass of fresh chaas.

variations.name: Awadhi Dhaba-style Tinda
variations.description: A refined Lucknawi take on the dhaba tinda, gently perfumed with kewra water, fried-onion paste and warm whole spices for a subtle, aromatic richness. Fragrant and mellow rather than fiery, it brings a touch of Awadhi finesse to the roadside classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: Awadhi cooking favours ghee for its perfumed, dum-style richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: used to fry the onions crisp for the birista paste base

steps: Peel and quarter the 500 g tinda, and thinly slice the 3 onions, then fry them in 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on medium for 8 minutes until crisp and golden, and grind to a smooth paste with a splash of water.
In the same pan add 2 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee on medium and crackle the 3 cardamom pods, 3 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the fried-onion paste and cook for 3 minutes until it deepens in colour.
Lower the flame, whisk in the 0.5 cup yoghurt with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, and stir for 3 minutes until the ghee separates.
Fold in the tinda and 1 tsp salt, cover, and cook on low for 16 to 18 minutes until tender in the silky gravy.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp kewra water, cover, and rest off the heat for 3 minutes so the aroma infuses.
Stir gently to keep the pieces intact and serve warm while the kewra perfume is at its peak.
tips: Kewra is potent, so measure it carefully; a few drops too many will overwhelm the dish.
The fried-onion (birista) paste gives a natural sweetness and body without needing tomato.
Finish with a rest under the lid, the Awadhi dum touch, to let the perfume settle in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with warm rumali roti or a saffron pulao and a side of sliced cucumber and mint raita.

variations.name: Classic Dry Tinda
variations.description: A no-gravy sukhi tinda where diced apple gourd is stir-fried with a dry masala until the edges caramelise and each piece stays separate and glossy. Quick, lunchbox-friendly and mildly spiced, it celebrates the gourd's clean flavour without any sauce to hide behind.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: its light body helps the diced tinda fry dry and take on golden edges

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing drizzle gives the dry sabzi a homely, roasted aroma

steps: Peel the 500 g tinda and dice into small 2 cm cubes, and finely chop the 1 onion so the sabzi stays dry and quick-cooking.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on medium and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add the onion and 1 tsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 4 minutes until softened but not browned.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder for 30 seconds, then add the diced tinda and 1 tsp salt and toss well.
Cover and cook on low for 14 to 16 minutes, uncovering to stir every few minutes, until the pieces are tender and dry with lightly caramelised edges.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp amchur powder and drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee, tossing on high for 1 minute to crisp the edges.
Garnish with 2 tbsp coriander leaves and serve.
tips: Cut the tinda evenly and small so it cooks through by the time the surface catches colour.
Do not add water; cover and let the gourd steam in its own moisture to keep the sabzi dry.
Add the amchur only at the end so its tang stays bright rather than cooking away.
variations.servingSuggestion: Roll into a hot ghee-smeared paratha with a smear of green chutney for a satisfying lunchbox wrap.

variations.name: Gujarati Dry Tinda
variations.description: A Gujarati dry sabzi where tinda is stir-fried with a sweet-and-tangy masala, jaggery and crushed peanuts, delivering the classic khatta-mithu balance of the region. The peanuts add nutty crunch while sesame and coconut lend a soft aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: groundnut oil is the everyday Gujarati cooking fat and complements the peanuts

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the essential sweet note that defines Gujarati khatta-mithu sabzis

steps: Peel and dice the 500 g tinda into small cubes, slit the 2 green chillies, and coarsely crush the 3 tbsp roasted peanuts.
Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on medium and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds with 1 tbsp sesame seeds for about 20 seconds until they pop.
Add the slit green chillies and 0.5 tsp turmeric, then tip in the tinda cubes with 1 tsp salt and toss to coat in the tempering.
Stir in 2 tsp coriander-cumin powder and the crushed peanuts, cover, and cook on low for 14 to 16 minutes until the gourd is tender.
Add 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook uncovered for 2 minutes until it melts and lightly glazes the cubes.
Turn off the heat and mix in 1 tbsp lemon juice, 2 tbsp grated coconut and 2 tbsp coriander leaves for the sweet-sour-fresh finish.
Toss gently and serve warm or at room temperature.
tips: Balance is everything; taste and adjust jaggery and lemon so neither the sweet nor the sour dominates.
Add the lemon off the heat to keep its tang lively.
This sabzi travels well and tastes great cold, making it ideal for a Gujarati thali dabba.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as part of a thali with soft phulkas, a spoon of plain khichdi and a wedge of lime pickle.

variations.name: Kerala Dry Tinda
variations.description: A Kerala-style thoran-inspired dry tinda where the gourd is cooked with fresh grated coconut, curry leaves and a coconut-oil tempering of mustard seeds and urad dal. Light, fragrant and pale green, it is the gentlest, most coconut-forward take in the family.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: coconut oil is non-negotiable for an authentic Kerala thoran aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: a final teaspoon deepens the roasted-coconut fragrance beautifully

steps: Peel and finely dice the 500 g tinda, thinly slice the 4 shallots, and pulse the 0.5 cup grated coconut with the 2 green chillies, 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 0.5 tsp turmeric to a coarse crumble.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil on medium and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, then 1 tsp urad dal until golden, about 30 seconds.
Add the 12 curry leaves and sliced shallots and fry for 2 minutes until the shallots soften.
Tip in the diced tinda with 1 tsp salt, toss, cover, and cook on low for 10 to 12 minutes until just tender, sprinkling a little water only if it sticks.
Add the coconut crumble, mix gently, and cook uncovered on low for 4 to 5 minutes until the coconut is warmed through and fragrant but not browned.
Drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee over the top and toss once.
Take off the heat and serve while fragrant.
tips: Keep the flame low once the coconut goes in so it stays fresh and pale rather than toasting dark.
Shallots (small onions) give a sweeter, more authentic base than regular onions here.
Pulse the coconut only to a coarse crumble, never a paste, to keep the thoran texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a side with steamed matta rice, sambar and a spoon of tangy mango pickle for a classic Kerala sadya plate.

variations.name: Andhra Dry Tinda
variations.description: A punchy Andhra vepudu where tinda is stir-fried in sesame oil with fiery Guntur chilli powder, garlic and a curry-leaf tadka until the cubes turn dry and roasted at the edges. Bold, garlicky and unapologetically hot, it is built for rice and ghee.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: gingelly sesame oil is the classic Andhra frying fat that carries the Guntur heat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon tames the Guntur chilli just enough and adds richness

steps: Peel and dice the 500 g tinda into small cubes and crush the 6 garlic cloves coarsely so they melt into the oil.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil on medium and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 1 tsp urad dal until the dal turns golden, about 30 seconds.
Add the crushed garlic and 12 curry leaves and fry for 40 seconds until the garlic is fragrant and pale gold.
Tip in the tinda with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, toss, cover, and cook on low for 12 to 14 minutes until tender.
Uncover, add 1.5 tsp Guntur red chilli powder and 1 tsp coriander powder, and stir-fry on medium-high for 4 to 5 minutes until the cubes turn dry and roasted.
Drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee and toss for a final minute to coat.
Serve hot straight from the pan while the roasted edges are still crisp and fragrant.
tips: Add the Guntur chilli powder only after the gourd is cooked, so it roasts without burning and stays vivid red.
Dial the chilli down to 1 tsp for a milder plate; Guntur chilli is genuinely fierce.
A final splash of ghee over hot rice with this vepudu is the classic Andhra way to eat it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile over hot steamed rice with a spoon of ghee and a papad, or serve alongside a bowl of thin pappu charu.

variations.name: Kashmiri Dry Tinda
variations.description: An elegant Kashmiri-inspired dry tinda scented with saffron, fennel and dry ginger, and gently spiced with Kashmiri chilli for colour rather than fierce heat. Warm, aromatic and delicately floral, it is the most fragrant take in the family.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: Kashmiri cooking leans on ghee, which carries the saffron and fennel aromas gently

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: a few threads bloomed in warm milk give the signature Kashmiri colour and floral scent

steps: Peel and quarter the 500 g tinda, and soak 1 pinch Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk for 10 minutes until the milk turns deep gold.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee on medium and lightly crackle 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, the 2 cardamom pods and 2 cloves for about 30 seconds.
Add the tinda pieces with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp Kashmiri red chilli powder and toss to coat in the aromatic ghee.
Stir in 1 tsp fennel powder and 0.5 tsp dry ginger powder with 1 tsp salt, then cover and cook on low for 14 to 16 minutes until tender.
Pour over the saffron milk and cook uncovered on low for 3 to 4 minutes until the liquid dries up and glazes the pieces.
Toss gently so every quarter takes on the golden saffron colour.
Rest off the heat for 2 minutes before serving so the aroma settles.
tips: Kashmiri chilli powder is for colour, not heat, so do not swap in regular chilli powder or the balance is lost.
Blooming the saffron in warm milk draws out far more colour and fragrance than adding it dry.
Fennel and dry ginger powder are the aromatic backbone of Kashmiri vegetable dishes; keep them fresh for best scent.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice or soft phulkas and a bowl of Kashmiri-style yoghurt whisked with a little dry mint.

variations.name: Classic Handi Aloo Tamatar
variations.description: A slow-cooked handi curry where whole spices perfume potatoes simmered in a thick onion-tomato masala under a sealed lid. The dum method deepens the flavour, giving a homely dish restaurant-worthy aroma and body.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A clean wood-pressed oil carries the whole-spice aroma without competing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A ghee finish gives the slow-cooked handi its rich, rounded depth

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a handi over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 bay leaf, 3 cardamom, 4 cloves and a 1-inch cinnamon stick for 30 seconds.
Add 2 finely chopped onions and fry until deep golden, 7 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Pour in the puree of 3 tomatoes with 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook 8 minutes until the oil separates from the masala.
Add the 4 boiled cubed potatoes, mashing a couple gently, and toss until each piece is coated in the fragrant masala.
Pour in 1.5 cups hot water, cover the handi tightly and simmer on very low heat for 12 minutes, dum-style, without stirring.
Uncover, stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and simmer 2 minutes until the gravy is glossy and the whole spices have infused through.
tips: Sealing the handi lid, even with a simple dough rope, traps the whole-spice aroma for the true dum effect.
Resist stirring during the dum stage; letting it steam undisturbed builds the layered flavour.
Fish out the whole cardamom, clove and cinnamon before serving, or warn diners they are there.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jeera rice or soft rumali roti and a side of kachumber salad.

variations.name: Awadhi Handi Aloo Tamatar
variations.description: A Lucknawi handi with royal refinement: a smooth ivory gravy of fried onion and cashew paste scented with kewra water and mace. Fragrant, mild and elegant, it turns the humble potato into nawabi fare.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee is the fat of Awadhi dum cooking, essential to its richness

steps: Soak 12 cashews in warm water for 10 minutes, then grind with the fried onions and 0.25 cup water into a smooth pale paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and crackle 4 cardamom pods for 20 seconds until aromatic.
Add 1 tbsp ginger paste and fry 1 minute, then lower the heat and add the onion-cashew paste, cooking 5 minutes without letting it brown.
Whisk in 0.5 cup curd slowly off the boil, stirring nonstop, then add 0.5 tsp white pepper, 0.25 tsp mace powder and 1 tsp salt.
Add the 4 boiled cubed potatoes with 1 cup hot water, cover and simmer on very low heat for 12 minutes so the potatoes drink in the fragrant gravy.
Finish with 0.5 tsp kewra water stirred in off the heat, keeping the lid on 2 minutes to trap the perfume before serving.
tips: Keep the gravy pale; browning the onion-cashew paste ruins the ivory Awadhi look and flavour.
Kewra water is potent, so measure carefully; a few extra drops can overwhelm the whole dish.
White pepper instead of red chilli keeps the heat gentle and the colour clean, as nawabi cooking intends.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sheermal or a delicate saffron pulao for an elegant Awadhi spread.

variations.name: Kashmiri Handi Aloo Tamatar
variations.description: A handi dum aloo in the Kashmiri idiom, its curd-based gravy glowing red from Kashmiri chilli and saffron, warmed with fennel and dry ginger. Aromatic rather than fiery, it is a cold-weather comfort in a pot.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee builds the rich body typical of Kashmiri handi gravies

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: Saffron lends the warm colour and unmistakable Kashmiri aroma

steps: Soak 1 pinch Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside to steep.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and shallow-fry the 4 boiled potato cubes until golden, about 4 minutes, then remove them.
In the same ghee, crackle 4 cloves, 3 cardamom and a 1-inch cinnamon stick for 30 seconds, then lower the heat and add 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder for 10 seconds.
Whisk in 0.75 cup curd slowly, stirring constantly so it stays smooth, then add 2 tsp fennel powder, 0.5 tsp dry ginger and 1 tsp salt.
Return the fried potatoes with the saffron milk and 1 cup hot water, cover the handi and simmer on very low heat for 15 minutes.
Uncover and cook 2 minutes to thicken, by which time the gravy should be a deep glowing red clinging to the potatoes.
tips: Frying the potatoes first gives them the firm, flavour-soaked bite of true Kashmiri dum aloo.
Add the curd off high heat and never stop stirring to prevent the gravy from splitting.
Fennel and dry ginger are non-negotiable Kashmiri seasonings; garam masala would make it taste ordinary.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed basmati rice or Kashmiri girda bread and a bowl of chilled curd.

variations.name: Malwa Handi Aloo Tamatar
variations.description: A Malwi handi from Madhya Pradesh thickened with roasted peanuts, giving a nutty, earthy body quite unlike a cream gravy. Mildly spiced and rustic, it reflects the peanut-loving kitchens of the Malwa plateau.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil doubles down on the peanut character of Malwa cooking

steps: Grind 4 tbsp roasted peanuts with a splash of water into a coarse, thick paste and set aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a handi over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds until toasty.
Add 2 chopped onions and fry until golden, 6 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Add 3 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt; cook 6 minutes until pulpy.
Stir in the peanut paste and fry 2 minutes, then add the 4 boiled potatoes with 1.5 cups hot water.
Cover and simmer on low for 10 minutes until the gravy thickens into a nutty, earthy sauce clinging to the potatoes.
tips: Do not grind the peanuts too fine; a slightly coarse paste gives the gravy its rustic Malwi texture.
The peanuts can thicken quickly, so keep an eye on the water and loosen with a splash if needed.
A pinch of jaggery balances the earthy peanut flavour if the tomatoes run too tart.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulka or bajra roti and a wedge of lemon to cut the richness.

variations.name: Bengali Handi Aloo Tamatar
variations.description: A Bengali handi where potatoes slow-cook in mustard oil with a panch phoron temper and a whisper of sweetness, finished with a fresh ground mustard-poppy paste. Pungent and distinctive, it is the aloo dish of a Bengali winter table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil is the heart of Bengali handi cooking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A little jaggery is the classic Bengali counterweight to mustard heat

steps: Soak 1 tbsp poppy seeds and 1 tsp mustard seeds in warm water for 10 minutes, then grind them into a smooth paste with 2 slit green chillies.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, then lower the flame and rest it 20 seconds to soften.
Temper 1 tsp panch phoron and 1 bay leaf for 20 seconds, then add the 4 cubed potatoes and fry 5 minutes until golden at the edges.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes, 0.75 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, and cook 5 minutes until the tomatoes soften.
Stir in the mustard-poppy paste with 1.5 cups hot water, cover the handi and simmer on low for 12 minutes until the potatoes are tender.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and simmer 2 minutes to settle the sweet-pungent balance before serving.
tips: Grind the mustard with green chillies and a pinch of salt to keep the paste from turning bitter.
Always smoke the mustard oil first so its raw sharpness mellows into a nutty pungency.
The poppy-mustard paste can catch quickly, so keep the flame low once it goes in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice, Bengali style, with a green chilli and a wedge of lime on the side.

variations.name: Classic Handi Chole
variations.description: Handi chole is a slow-simmered chickpea curry cooked in a narrow-mouthed clay handi so the whole spices and steam stay locked in. Cardamom, cinnamon and black cardamom perfume a deep onion-tomato gravy that clings to plump chickpeas. The handi finish gives an earthy, dum-cooked roundness you cannot rush in a kadai.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil carries the whole-spice aromatics without overpowering the slow-cooked gravy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon of bilona ghee stirred in during the dum stage gives the handi its rich, rounded aroma.

steps: Pressure cook 1.5 cups soaked chickpeas with 1.25 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 whistles until soft enough to smash, and keep the cooking liquid.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a clay handi or heavy pot, add 1 tsp cumin, 4 green cardamom, 1 black cardamom, 1 inch cinnamon and 4 cloves, and let them crackle and release their fragrance for about 40 seconds.
Add 3 finely chopped onions with 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry patiently until deep brown, about 10 minutes, as this colour sets the depth of the gravy.
Stir in 3 pureed tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, and cook until the masala thickens and oil pools at the edges, roughly 9 minutes.
Add the chickpeas with 1.5 cups of their cooking water, mash a handful against the side, and bring to a gentle simmer.
Stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, cover the handi tightly, and let it dum on the lowest flame for 12 minutes so the whole spices infuse deeply.
Uncover, discard the black cardamom and cinnamon if you like, scatter 3 tbsp coriander over the top and serve piping hot from the handi.
tips: If you have a clay handi, soak it in water for 20 minutes before first use so it does not crack on the flame.
Browning the onions fully is non-negotiable here; a pale masala gives a flat, watery handi.
The dish tastes even better the next day once the whole spices have had time to bloom fully into the gravy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve from the handi with hot tandoori roti or steamed basmati, a raw onion-and-green-chilli salad and a dab of pickle.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Handi Chole
variations.description: Here the slow handi is scented with goda masala and finished with a roasted coconut-onion paste in the Malvani style. A restrained spoon of Anveshan Jaggery Powder tempers the dark, smoky spice blend. The long simmer lets the nutty masala settle into a thick, comforting curry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the classic Deccan fat and lets the goda masala stay the star of the handi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery powder mellows the pungent goda masala into a warm, balanced handi gravy.

steps: Boil 1.5 cups soaked chickpeas with 1.25 tsp salt and 3 cups water in a pressure cooker for 6 whistles, then reserve them with the stock.
Dry roast 4 tbsp grated coconut with 1 sliced onion over medium heat until both turn a rich brown, about 6 minutes, then grind to a coarse paste, which the Malvani cooks call kaap.
Warm 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a handi, splutter 1 tsp cumin and 12 curry leaves, then add the 2 remaining chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and brown for 8 minutes.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.25 tsp red chilli powder and 2.5 tsp goda masala, and fry until the oil separates and the masala smells deep and smoky, about 7 minutes.
Fold in the roasted coconut-onion paste and cook for 3 minutes until it darkens further and thickens the base.
Add the chickpeas with 1.5 cups stock and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, cover, and dum on low for 12 minutes.
Finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and let the handi rest, covered, for 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Roast the coconut-onion kaap to a genuine brown; the colour is what gives Malvani gravies their signature depth.
Increase the chilli powder if you want the fiery Kolhapuri edge, or keep it as written for a gentler Konkani style.
This handi freezes well, so make a double batch and reheat with a splash of hot water.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar or bajra bhakri, a spoon of thecha and sliced cucumber to cool the palate.

variations.name: Gujarati Handi Chole
variations.description: A softer, sweeter handi that follows Gujarat's beloved balance of jaggery, tomato and lemon, kept light and slightly soupy. Anveshan Jaggery Powder and roasted peanuts give body while whole spices scent the slow simmer. It is a homely one-pot curry built for mopping up with soft rotli.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A modest amount of wood-pressed groundnut oil keeps this handi light, the way Gujarati kitchens prefer.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery powder gives this handi its gentle sweet-sour Gujarati signature against the tomato.

steps: Cook 1.5 cups soaked chickpeas with 1 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 whistles until very tender, and keep the liquid for the gravy.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a handi, crackle 1 tsp cumin, 1 inch cinnamon and 3 cloves, then add 2 chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and soften for 5 minutes.
Add 3 pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 2 tsp coriander-cumin powder, and simmer until thick and glossy, about 8 minutes.
Stir in 2 tbsp roasted peanut powder and cook for 2 minutes to thicken and enrich the base.
Add the chickpeas with 2 cups of their cooking water and 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, cover the handi, and simmer gently for 12 minutes until lightly soupy.
Turn off the heat, stir in 1 tbsp lemon juice and 2 tbsp coriander, and balance the sweet-sour-salt to taste before serving.
tips: Keep this handi on the thinner side; the peanut powder will thicken it further as it rests.
Add the lemon at the end so its freshness is not dulled by the long simmer.
A pinch of asafoetida with the cumin makes the whole curry easier to digest and more aromatic.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thin phulka, steamed rice and a bowl of cool chhaas, finishing with a little sweet chundo on the side.

variations.name: Bengali Handi Chole
variations.description: This eastern handi is built on pungent Anveshan Mustard Oil and a whole-spice tempering of bay leaf, dried red chilli and cardamom. Slit green chillies and a hint of sweetness echo the Bengali chholar dal tradition. The slow dum lets the mustard oil mellow into a warm, rounded curry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil brings the sharp, warming pungency that anchors this Bengali-style handi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing teaspoon of ghee balances the mustard oil and gives the dum a fragrant lift.

steps: Pressure cook 1.5 cups soaked chickpeas with 1.25 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 whistles until soft, and set aside with the liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a handi until it just smokes and pales, lower the heat, and temper 1 tsp cumin, 2 bay leaves, 2 dried red chillies and 3 green cardamom for about 40 seconds.
Add 2 chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger paste and fry over medium heat until golden brown, about 8 minutes.
Stir in 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.75 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, and cook until the mustard oil surfaces and the masala thickens, roughly 8 minutes.
Add the chickpeas with 1.5 cups water and 3 slit green chillies, cover, and dum on the lowest flame for 12 minutes so the spices infuse the beans.
Finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and 2 tbsp coriander, stir gently, and rest covered for 4 minutes before serving.
tips: Bring the mustard oil to a smoke first; heating it fully removes the raw bitterness and leaves a clean pungency.
A small pinch of sugar with the tomatoes brings the classic Bengali sweet undertone if you like it.
Keep the green chillies whole so they scent the handi without overwhelming the heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with fluffy luchi or steamed rice, a wedge of lime and a simple cucumber-onion salad dressed with mustard oil.

variations.name: Kerala Handi Chole
variations.description: A coastal handi finished in coconut milk and a shallot-curry leaf tempering fried in Anveshan Coconut Oil. Roasted coconut and fennel give it the mellow, aromatic depth of a Kerala kadala curry. The slow simmer draws the coconut sweetness deep into the chickpeas.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil gives the shallot tempering its unmistakable Kerala fragrance.

steps: Pressure cook 1.5 cups soaked chickpeas with 1.25 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 whistles until soft, then keep them with their stock.
Dry roast 0.5 cup grated coconut with 0.5 tsp fennel over low heat until deep brown and fragrant, about 5 minutes, then grind to a smooth paste with a little water.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a handi, add 10 sliced shallots, 1 inch cinnamon and 10 curry leaves, and fry until the shallots caramelise to golden, about 5 minutes.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 1 chopped tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, and cook until the tomato melts down, about 5 minutes.
Stir in the roasted coconut paste and the chickpeas with 0.5 cup stock, cover, and simmer on low for 12 minutes so the flavours meld.
Pour in 1 cup coconut milk, warm gently for 3 minutes without letting it boil, and finish with the remaining curry leaves crackled in a spoon of coconut oil.
tips: Add coconut milk only at the end and never boil it, or the gravy will curdle and turn grainy.
Deeply roasted coconut is the key to that dark Kerala kadala colour and nutty aroma.
Small shallots give a sweeter, more authentic base than regular onions, so seek them out.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with puttu, appam or steamed red rice, and add crisp pappadam and a coconut thoran on the side.

variations.name: Classic Handi Dum Aloo
variations.description: Cooked and served in an earthen handi, this version leans on whole spices and slow steam to build a deep, layered gravy around fried baby potatoes. Sealing the handi traps the aroma, so every potato emerges soaked in fragrant, mildly creamy masala.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil crisps the potatoes and carries the whole-spice aroma through the slow dum

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoon of bilona ghee drizzled before sealing the handi perfumes the whole dish during dum

steps: Boil 500 g baby potatoes for 10 minutes until just tender, peel and prick them all over so they drink up the gravy.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a handi and fry the potatoes on medium for 5 minutes until golden, then remove; in the same oil fry 10 cashews for a minute and set aside to grind into a paste.
Temper 1 bay leaf, 3 cardamom, 4 cloves, 1 inch cinnamon and 1 tsp cumin in the oil for 30 seconds until fragrant, then add 2 chopped onions and saute for 7 minutes until deep golden.
Stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, then 3 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 7 minutes until the oil separates.
Add the cashew paste and 1 cup water, bring to a simmer, then slide in the fried potatoes and stir to coat well.
Drizzle 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the top, cover the handi tightly and dum-cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes so the potatoes steam through.
Uncover, swirl in 3 tbsp cream, simmer for 2 minutes and rest 5 minutes before serving straight from the handi.
tips: Seal the handi lid with a strip of dough or a heavy weight to trap the steam and aroma during the dum stage.
Fried cashew paste gives body without heavy cream, so add cream only for the final gloss.
Keep the heat at its lowest during dum; too high and the gravy catches at the base of the handi.
variations.servingSuggestion: Bring the sealed handi to the table and crack it open for aroma, serving with saffron pulao or garlic naan and a kachumber salad.

variations.name: Kashmiri Handi Dum Aloo
variations.description: A no-onion, no-garlic handi built the Kashmiri way on fennel, dry ginger and a bloom of saffron, slow-steamed in a yoghurt gravy. The sealed handi concentrates the floral saffron and warm spice into a ruby, aromatic curry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee is the authentic fat for a Kashmiri handi and rounds out the yoghurt gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Kashmiri saffron bloomed in warm milk gives the sealed handi its glow and perfume

steps: Bloom 0.25 tsp Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside while you prepare the potatoes.
Boil 500 g baby potatoes for 10 minutes until just tender, peel and prick them deeply so the yoghurt gravy seeps in.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a handi and fry the potatoes on medium for 6 minutes until evenly golden, then remove them.
In the same ghee add 0.25 tsp asafoetida, 4 cloves, 3 green cardamom, 1 black cardamom and 1 inch cinnamon, and let them sizzle for 20 seconds.

Off the boil, whisk 0.75 cup curd with 1.5 tsp fennel powder, 1 tsp dry ginger powder, 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, then pour it into the handi on low heat while stirring so it stays smooth.
Add 1 cup water and the potatoes, cover the handi and dum-cook on the lowest heat for 15 minutes until the gravy thickens and clings.
Stir in the saffron milk, cook uncovered for 2 minutes and rest before serving so the colour and aroma settle.
tips: Add the whisked curd only on low heat and keep stirring; the sealed dum works best when the gravy has not split at the start.
Fennel and dry ginger are non-negotiable here and replace the usual onion-garlic base entirely.
This handi tastes even better reheated, as the saffron and spices bloom further overnight.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed basmati, sheermal or a plain naan, alongside a cooling walnut or boondi raita to offset the warm spices.

variations.name: Odia Handi Dum Aloo
variations.description: An Odisha-style handi tempered with panch phoron, the five-spice blend that defines eastern-Indian cooking. The whole-seed tempering and a light, mustard-oil-kissed gravy give an earthy, aromatic curry with gentle heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil is the everyday Odia cooking fat and pairs naturally with panch phoron

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoon of ghee stirred in at the end softens the mustard-oil sharpness and adds aroma

steps: Boil 500 g baby potatoes for 10 minutes until just tender, peel and prick them, then rub with a little turmeric and salt.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a handi until it just smokes, then fry the potatoes on medium for 5 minutes until golden and set aside.
In the same oil temper 1 tsp panch phoron, 1 bay leaf and 2 dried red chillies for 30 seconds until the seeds crackle and turn aromatic.
Add 2 chopped onions and saute for 6 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook a minute until the raw smell fades.
Mix in 2 chopped tomatoes, the remaining 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp cumin powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 6 minutes until the oil separates.
Add 1 cup water, return the potatoes, cover the handi and dum-cook on low for 12 minutes until the potatoes are cooked through and coated.
Stir in 0.5 tsp garam masala and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, simmer for 2 minutes and serve garnished with coriander.
tips: Temper the panch phoron until you can smell the fenugreek turning nutty, but pull it off before it darkens or it will taste bitter.
Keep this gravy light and pourable, the way Odia homes serve it with rice.
A cracked tomato mashed into the gravy adds body without needing any cream.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a wedge of lime, or with soft rotis; a side of dalma or a simple dal completes the Odia thali.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Handi Dum Aloo
variations.description: A handi seasoned with goda masala and roasted coconut, giving the slow-steamed potatoes a dark, nutty, faintly sweet depth. This kala-masala style curry is bolder and earthier than the creamy northern handi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: groundnut oil is the classic Maharashtrian fat and carries goda masala without masking it

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery balances the goda masala with the gentle sweetness typical of Maharashtrian gravies

steps: Dry-roast 4 tbsp desiccated coconut on low for 3 minutes until golden and nutty, then grind to a paste with a splash of water.
Boil 500 g baby potatoes for 10 minutes until just tender, peel and prick them, then fry in 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium for 5 minutes until golden and set aside.
In the same oil crackle 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin and 10 curry leaves for 20 seconds, then add 2 chopped onions and saute for 7 minutes until deep brown.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 2 chopped tomatoes, 2 tsp goda masala, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 6 minutes until the oil separates.
Add the roasted coconut paste and 1 cup water, bring to a simmer, then return the potatoes to the handi.
Cover and dum-cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes so the potatoes absorb the dark masala.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer for 2 minutes and serve topped with fresh coriander.
tips: Add the goda masala with the wet tomato mixture rather than the dry tempering, as it burns and turns bitter in hot oil.
Roast the coconut only to a light gold; a darker roast overpowers the delicate goda spices.
The gravy tastes best after resting, when the goda masala mellows into the coconut.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri or plain rice, a spoon of raw onion and a lemon wedge, in true Maharashtrian home style.

variations.name: Malwa Handi Dum Aloo
variations.description: From the Malwa plateau of Madhya Pradesh comes a handi thickened with roasted peanuts, giving a creamy, nutty body without any dairy. Earthy and satisfying, it reflects the region's fondness for groundnut in everyday cooking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil echoes and deepens the roasted peanut base of this Malwa handi

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of ghee lifts the earthy peanut gravy with a warm aroma

steps: Grind 0.5 cup roasted peanuts to a coarse powder, reserving a spoonful for garnish, and blend the rest with a little water into a smooth paste.
Boil 500 g baby potatoes for 10 minutes until just tender, peel and prick them, then fry in 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium for 5 minutes until golden and set aside.
In the same oil crackle 1 tsp cumin and 8 curry leaves for 20 seconds, then add 2 chopped onions and saute for 7 minutes until golden brown.
Stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 2 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 6 minutes until the oil separates.
Add the peanut paste and 1.25 cups water, stir well and bring to a simmer, then return the potatoes to the handi.
Cover and dum-cook on low for 12 minutes until the gravy thickens to a creamy, nutty consistency and the potatoes are cooked through.
Finish with 0.5 tsp garam masala and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, simmer 2 minutes and serve sprinkled with the reserved crushed peanuts.
tips: Roast the peanuts until deeply golden before grinding; a good roast is what gives the gravy its sweet, nutty backbone.
The peanut paste thickens fast, so keep a little hot water handy to adjust the consistency.
Simmer gently after adding the peanut paste, as it can catch and scorch at the base of the handi.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain rotis or steamed rice and a sharp lime pickle; a crunchy peanut and onion salad on the side echoes the nutty theme.

variations.name: Classic Handi Kofta
variations.description: Vegetable koftas slow-simmered in a clay handi under a sealed lid so the whole-spice gravy turns deeply aromatic and mellow. The earthenware traps steam and lets the masala breathe, giving a rounder, dum-cooked flavour you never get from a flat pan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: wholegrain khapli soaks up the gourd's moisture and binds the koftas cleanly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: fries the koftas crisp and gives the handi masala a clean, nutty base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: brushed on before sealing the handi so the dum steam carries its aroma through

steps: Squeeze 1 cup grated bottle gourd dry, then mix with 2 mashed potatoes, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta to a firm dough that rolls into 10 neat balls.
Deep-fry the koftas in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat until golden brown and set, about 4 minutes, and drain well.
In a clay handi with 3 tbsp of the oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin, 2 bay leaves, 4 cardamom, 4 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon for 30 seconds until fragrant.

Add 3 sliced onions and cook over medium heat until deep golden, about 9 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 3 pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.75 tsp salt.
Cook the masala until the oil separates and it turns glossy, about 8 minutes, then add 1 cup hot water and bring to a simmer.
Gently lower in the fried koftas, stir in 3 tbsp cream and 1 tsp garam masala, and brush 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the surface.
Seal the handi with a tight lid or dough rim and cook on the lowest heat for 8 minutes of dum, then rest 3 minutes before opening at the table.
tips: Squeezing the bottle gourd thoroughly is the difference between koftas that hold and ones that disintegrate in the gravy.
If you do not have a clay handi, any heavy pot with a tight lid works; the key is trapping steam on the lowest flame.
Open the sealed handi only at the table so the built-up aroma releases in front of your guests.
variations.servingSuggestion: Present the whole handi with a swirl of cream and a scatter of mint, paired with sheermal or garlic naan to scoop up the koftas.

variations.name: Punjabi Handi Kofta
variations.description: A rich dhaba-style handi finished with butter and crushed kasuri methi, where the koftas swim in a velvety onion-tomato gravy. Slow dum in the pot gives it that unmistakable Punjabi depth, buttery and faintly smoky at once.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: binds the potato-paneer koftas so they stay soft under the buttery gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the dhaba fat that fries the koftas and gives the handi its rich Punjabi body

steps: Mash 3 boiled potatoes with 0.5 cup grated paneer, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, and roll into 10 firm koftas.
Shallow-fry the koftas in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat until golden all around, about 5 minutes, and keep warm.
In the handi, heat the remaining 2 tbsp ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin, and cook 3 sliced onions until soft and golden, about 8 minutes, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste.
Add 4 pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.75 tsp salt, and cook until the oil rises, about 8 minutes, then stir in 3 tbsp cashew paste for a silky body.
Pour in 1 cup hot water, add 4 tbsp cream and 1 tsp garam masala, and simmer 4 minutes until the gravy is smooth and clings.
Slide in the koftas, crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi between your palms over the pot, and dot 2 tbsp butter on top.
Cover and dum on the lowest heat for 7 minutes, then rest 3 minutes so the butter melts into a glossy sheen before serving.
tips: Roast the kasuri methi lightly in a dry pan before crushing to release its full aroma into the gravy.
Soak the cashews in hot water for 15 minutes before grinding for a lump-free, restaurant-smooth paste.
Add the koftas at the very end and dum briefly so they plump up without going mushy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or laccha paratha and a raw onion-lachha salad dusted with chaat masala for a true Punjabi spread.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Handi Kofta
variations.description: A Vidarbha-inspired handi built on smoky goda masala and a roasted peanut-coconut paste that gives the gravy a dark, sweet-savoury depth. Cooked in wood-pressed groundnut oil, it is warmly spiced with the distinctive black masala of Maharashtra.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: binds the mixed-veg koftas for the robust goda masala gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday Maharashtrian frying fat that suits the peanut base perfectly

steps: Mix 2 mashed potatoes with 0.5 cup grated carrot, 0.25 cup peas, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta into a firm dough and shape into 10 koftas.
Fry the koftas in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat until crisp and golden, about 4 minutes, and drain.
Dry-roast 3 tbsp peanuts and 3 tbsp dry coconut until dark and fragrant, then blend to a coarse paste with a little water.
In the handi with 3 tbsp oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin, add 3 sliced onions and fry over medium heat to a deep brown, about 10 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste.

Add 2 chopped tomatoes, 2 tbsp goda masala, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt, and cook 5 minutes, then mix in the peanut-coconut paste and cook until oil separates, about 5 minutes.
Pour in 1.5 cups hot water for a slightly thin, spicy gravy and simmer 5 minutes, then lower in the koftas.
Cover and dum on low heat for 7 minutes so the koftas absorb the black masala, then rest 3 minutes before serving.
tips: Roast the peanuts and dry coconut separately and watch them closely; the dark colour is the source of the gravy's signature depth.
Goda masala is sweeter and smokier than garam masala, so do not swap the two if you want the authentic Vidarbha taste.
Keep the gravy thin and rustic here, the way it is served across Maharashtrian households with bhakri.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri or steamed rice and a sprinkle of fresh coriander, with a wedge of lime to cut the richness.

variations.name: Gujarati Handi Kofta
variations.description: The characteristic Gujarati sweet-savoury balance shines here, with Anveshan Jaggery Powder rounding a mildly spiced tomato gravy. Koftas laced with a hint of besan simmer in a smooth, slightly sweet handi that pairs beautifully with soft rotli.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: teams with besan to bind the soft koftas without heaviness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the classic Gujarati kitchen oil for frying koftas and the gravy base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the signature sweet note that balances the tomato and chilli, Gujarati style

steps: Squeeze 0.75 cup grated cabbage dry and mix with 2 mashed potatoes, 2 tbsp besan, 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta and 0.75 tsp salt into a soft dough, then shape into 10 koftas.
Fry the koftas in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat until golden, about 4 minutes, and drain.
In the handi with 3 tbsp oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin, add 2 chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, and cook until soft and pale gold, about 6 minutes.
Add 3 pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tbsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp salt, and cook until the masala thickens and glistens, about 7 minutes.
Stir in 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1.25 cups hot water, and simmer 5 minutes until the sweet-savoury gravy comes together.
Gently add the koftas, spoon gravy over them, and cover the handi.
Dum on the lowest heat for 6 minutes, then rest 3 minutes so the koftas soak up the balanced gravy before serving.
tips: Taste and adjust the jaggery last; the sweetness should be subtle and just balance the tomato, not dominate.
A little besan in the koftas gives a pleasant graininess typical of Gujarati muthiya-style dumplings.
Keep the chilli gentle so the sweet-savoury contrast, the hallmark of Gujarati food, stays in focus.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulka rotli and a bowl of plain kadhi, finishing the thali with a spoon of sweet chundo pickle.

variations.name: Andhra Handi Kofta
variations.description: A blazing Andhra handi powered by fiery Guntur red chillies and finished in nutty Anveshan Sesame Oil. The gravy is thin, tangy and unapologetically hot, with a garlicky punch that defines Rayalaseema-style cooking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: binds the koftas so they survive the thin, fiery Andhra gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: gingelly oil gives the earthy, nutty base typical of Andhra cooking

steps: Mash 3 boiled potatoes with 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta into a firm dough and roll into 10 small koftas.
Fry the koftas in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil over medium heat until golden and firm, about 4 minutes, and drain.
Soak 8 Guntur chillies in warm water for 15 minutes, then grind with 10 garlic cloves and 1 inch ginger to a coarse red paste.
In the handi with 3 tbsp sesame oil, splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tsp cumin and 1 sprig curry leaves, then add 2 chopped onions and fry to golden, about 7 minutes.

Add the chilli-garlic paste with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tbsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp salt, and fry until the raw smell goes and oil separates, about 6 minutes, then add 3 chopped tomatoes and cook 5 minutes.
Pour in 1.5 cups hot water for a thin, spicy gravy, simmer 5 minutes, and slide in the koftas.
Cover and dum on low heat for 6 minutes, crisp the second curry-leaf sprig in a little sesame oil on top, and rest 3 minutes before serving.
tips: Adjust the number of Guntur chillies to your tolerance; they bring searing heat, so start low and build up.
Gingelly sesame oil has a strong flavour that is essential here, so do not substitute a neutral oil.
A splash of tamarind water at the end brightens the gravy and cuts the heat pleasantly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a dollop of ghee, or with pesarattu, and keep plenty of curd on hand to temper the heat.

variations.name: Classic Handi Paneer
variations.description: A slow-simmered handi paneer where whole spices bloom in fat before a creamy onion-tomato-cashew gravy comes together, then finishes under a gentle dum. Cooking in the narrow-necked handi traps the aroma, giving a richer, rounder curry than a quick stovetop version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: carries the whole-spice tempering that defines the handi's deep aroma

steps: Soak 12 cashews in warm water for 15 minutes, then grind to a smooth paste. Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a handi and crackle 1 bay leaf, 3 cardamom pods, 4 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon for 20 seconds.
Add 2 finely chopped onions and 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry on medium for 6 minutes until golden brown.
Add 3 pureed tomatoes with 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, and cook 7 minutes until the masala thickens and the ghee separates.
Stir in the cashew paste with 1 tsp salt and about half a cup of water, and simmer 4 minutes until the gravy turns rich and glossy.
Slide in 300 g cubed paneer, cover the handi tightly, and cook on very low dum for 8 minutes so the paneer drinks in the spice.
Uncover, swirl in 3 tbsp cream and 0.75 tsp garam masala, and rest covered for 5 minutes before serving.
tips: The low dum at the end is what separates a handi from a stir-fried paneer; do not rush it.
Soaking and grinding cashews smooth gives body without needing extra cream.
If your gravy tightens too much during dum, loosen with a splash of hot water, not cold.
variations.servingSuggestion: Bring the handi to the table sealed and open it at the table for the aroma, serving with rumali roti or saffron pulao.

variations.name: Awadhi Handi Paneer
variations.description: A courtly Lucknawi handi perfumed with kewra water and a white, onion-cashew korma base kept deliberately pale by skipping tomato and red chilli. Slow dum cooking and a saffron-kewra finish make it delicate, floral and fit for a Nawabi dastarkhwan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the refined Awadhi cooking fat that keeps the korma pale and fragrant

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk to lend the Awadhi korma its subtle glow and aroma

steps: Boil 3 sliced onions for 6 minutes until soft, drain, then grind with 15 cashews and 1 tbsp melon seeds to a smooth pale paste. Steep a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a handi and gently crackle 4 cardamom pods and 1 blade of mace for 20 seconds without browning them.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry 1 minute, then add the onion-cashew paste and cook on low for 6 minutes, stirring so it stays white and does not catch colour.
Whisk 0.5 cup curd smooth and add it off the heat, stirring constantly, then return to low with 1 tsp salt, 0.5 tsp white pepper and about half a cup of water and simmer 4 minutes.
Slide in 300 g cubed paneer, cover the handi, and cook on gentle dum for 8 minutes so the korma stays silky and the paneer softens.
Pour in the saffron milk and 0.5 tsp kewra water, stir once, and rest covered for 5 minutes so the floral aroma settles in.
tips: Keep the flame low throughout so the korma stays ivory-white, the mark of an Awadhi handi.
Kewra is potent; half a teaspoon is plenty, and more can overwhelm the dish.
Boiling the onions before grinding removes their sharpness and keeps the gravy sweet and pale.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sheermal or a delicate zafrani pulao, garnished with slivered pistachios and a few rose petals for a Nawabi table.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Handi Paneer
variations.description: A handi built on the dark, roasted intensity of goda masala and a kala masala-style onion-coconut base, slow-cooked to draw out earthy depth. Where the classic is creamy and mild, this one is smoky, robust and distinctly Maharashtrian in its spicing.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the classic Maharashtrian oil that toasts the coconut-onion masala for the handi

steps: Dry-roast 4 tbsp desiccated coconut in a pan until deep golden, about 4 minutes, then grind with a splash of water to a paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a handi and crackle 3 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon for 20 seconds, then add 3 sliced onions and 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry 7 minutes until well browned.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and cook 5 minutes until pulpy and the oil separates.
Stir in the roasted coconut paste and 2.5 tsp goda masala with 1 tsp salt and fry on medium for 4 minutes until the masala turns dark and intensely fragrant.
Add about three-quarters of a cup of water to make a thick gravy, bring to a simmer, then slide in 300 g cubed paneer.
Cover the handi and cook on low dum for 8 minutes, then finish with 2 tbsp fresh coriander stirred through.
tips: Roast the coconut to a deep gold for the smoky kala-masala character; pale coconut leaves it flat.
Goda masala and roasted coconut are both strong, so taste before adding any extra chilli.
A small piece of jaggery melted in balances the heat in true Maharashtrian fashion.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft bhakri or vade, with a wedge of lemon and raw onion, and a spoon of thecha for heat lovers.

variations.name: Kerala Handi Paneer
variations.description: A coconut-milk handi that simmers paneer stew-style with whole spices, curry leaves and ginger, all rounded in fragrant coconut oil. Kept pale and silky like a Kerala ishtu, it is gently spiced and aromatic, a world away from the creamy North Indian handi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the essential Kerala fat that ties the curry leaves and coconut milk together

steps: Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a handi and crackle 3 cardamom pods, 3 cloves, 1 inch cinnamon and 0.5 tsp peppercorns for 20 seconds.
Add 15 curry leaves, 2 sliced onions, 1.5 inch julienned ginger and 3 slit green chillies, and saute on medium for 6 minutes until the onions turn soft and translucent, not browned.
Pour in 1 cup thin coconut milk with 1 tsp salt, bring to a gentle simmer, and cook 4 minutes to build the base.
Slide in 300 g cubed paneer, cover the handi, and simmer on low for 8 minutes so the paneer takes on the spiced coconut flavour.
Lower the heat right down and stir in 1 cup thick coconut milk, warming it for 3 minutes without letting it boil so it stays silky.
Switch off, add a final tempering of curry leaves fried in a teaspoon of coconut oil, and rest 3 minutes before serving.
tips: Keep the onions pale, not golden, to preserve the ivory Kerala-stew look.
Add the thick coconut milk only at the very end and never boil it, or it will curdle.
A squeeze of lime just before eating brightens the mellow coconut base.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with lacy appam, idiyappam or Malabar parotta, letting the fragrant coconut gravy soak in.

variations.name: Andhra Handi Paneer
variations.description: A fiery Andhra handi where a roasted Guntur chilli and garlic masala is slow-simmered in sesame oil until deep and pungent. Bold, tangy with tamarind and finished with a curry-leaf tempering, it turns the gentle handi format into a spice lover's centrepiece.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: the weighty Andhra oil that holds up to the roasted Guntur chilli masala

steps: Dry-roast 7 Guntur chillies, 1 tbsp coriander seeds and 1 tsp cumin on low for 2 minutes, then grind with 12 garlic cloves to a coarse paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a handi, pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 18 curry leaves for 15 seconds, then add 2 chopped onions and fry 6 minutes until browned.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric and cook 4 minutes to a pulp, then stir in the roasted chilli-garlic paste and fry on medium for 4 minutes until the sesame oil separates.
Add 1 tsp salt, 1.5 tsp tamarind pulp and about three-quarters of a cup of water, and simmer 4 minutes into a thick fiery gravy.
Slide in 300 g cubed paneer, cover the handi, and cook on low dum for 8 minutes so the paneer absorbs the pungent masala.
Uncover, simmer 2 minutes to tighten the gravy, and serve while it glistens red with sesame oil.
tips: Deseed a few chillies to keep the deep colour while making the heat manageable.
The dum step lets the tamarind and chilli mellow into the paneer, so keep the flame very low.
Serve with plenty of curd or a coconut chutney to balance the deliberate fire.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or with ragi sangati, and cool mor (spiced buttermilk) alongside.

variations.name: Classic Handi Rajma
variations.description: Kidney beans slow-cooked in a sealed handi with whole spices, letting the masala infuse the beans without a heavy hand of cream. The clay pot keeps the gravy earthy and the beans whole yet tender. A rustic, smoky-edged take on everyday rajma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Its nutty depth withstands the long handi simmer without turning greasy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of bilona ghee gives the handi its comforting aroma

ingredients.name: Dried red kidney beans, soaked overnight
Bay leaf, cinnamon, cloves and black cardamom

steps: Pressure-cook the soaked 1.5 cups kidney beans with 0.5 tsp salt and 3.5 cups water for 7-8 whistles until soft, then keep them in their liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a handi over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds with the whole spices for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the 2 chopped onions and fry 8 minutes until deep golden, then stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until the raw aroma fades.
Pour in the tomato puree with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli, 2 tsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp salt, and cook 10 minutes until the oil separates.
Tip in the beans with their liquid, cover the handi and simmer very gently for 18-20 minutes, mashing a few beans to thicken, until the masala soaks in.
Stir in 1 tsp garam masala and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, cover and rest off the heat for 5 minutes so the flavours settle.
tips: The slow, sealed simmer is the point of a handi, so resist stirring too often and let the beans steep in the masala.
Black cardamom adds the faint smokiness that sets a handi rajma apart, so do not swap it for green.
A piece of charcoal smoked over the finished pot for two minutes gives a lovely dhungar aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve straight from the handi with jeera rice or tandoori roti, sliced onions and a wedge of lime.

variations.name: Punjabi Handi Rajma
variations.description: The handi meets the dhaba: kidney beans slow-simmered with whole spices then enriched with white butter and kasuri methi for a thick, buttery Amritsari finish. Richer and rounder than the plain handi version. Made for a leisurely rajma-chawal feast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee gives the handi its buttery dhaba-style richness

ingredients.name: Dried red kidney beans, soaked overnight

steps: Pressure-cook the soaked 1.5 cups kidney beans with 0.5 tsp salt and 3.5 cups water for 7-8 whistles until very soft, then keep them in their liquid.
Melt 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a handi over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds with the whole spices for 30 seconds.
Fry the 2 chopped onions 9 minutes until richly browned, then add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until the raw edge goes.
Pour in the tomato puree with 1.25 tsp red chilli, 2 tsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp salt, and cook 11 minutes until thick and the ghee floats.
Add the beans with their liquid, mash a third of them, cover the handi and simmer gently 18 minutes until luxuriously thick.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the pot, swirl in 2 tbsp white butter and 1 tsp garam masala, and cook 2 minutes until glossy.
tips: The extra tomato and longer mash give this its signature dhaba thickness, so do not rush the reduction.
Toast the kasuri methi briefly before crushing to draw out its full fragrance.
Loosen any leftover gravy with warm bean stock rather than water to preserve the buttery flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a final knob of white butter melting on top, plus a crunchy onion-tomato salad.

variations.name: Kashmiri Handi Rajma
variations.description: The revered Kashmiri rajma given the handi treatment: beans slow-cooked with fennel, dry ginger, Kashmiri chilli and a saffron steep into a ruby, onion-and-garlic-free gravy. Mild, fragrant and quietly regal. This is how the valley eats its rajma-chawal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee is the traditional Kashmiri fat carrying fennel and saffron notes

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: Saffron gives the ruby glow and gentle perfume of a valley rajma

ingredients.name: Dried red kidney beans, soaked overnight

steps: Soak 0.25 tsp Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 3 tbsp warm water and set aside to bloom.
Pressure-cook the soaked 1.5 cups kidney beans with 0.5 tsp salt and 3.5 cups water for 8-9 whistles until very soft, then keep them in their liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a handi over medium heat, add the whole cloves, green and black cardamom and cinnamon with 0.25 tsp asafoetida, and sizzle 30 seconds.
Lower the flame, stir in 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli then quickly the tomato puree, and cook 8 minutes until the ghee floats bright red.
Add 2 tsp fennel powder, 1 tsp dry ginger and 0.75 tsp salt, then tip in the beans with their liquid and the bloomed saffron water.
Cover the handi and simmer gently 18-20 minutes, mashing a few beans to thicken, and finish with 0.5 tsp garam masala.
tips: The small dark Kashmiri beans hold shape while turning creamy, so cook low and slow rather than fast.
Keep this strictly onion and garlic free, letting fennel and dry ginger define the aroma.
Stir the tomato in the instant the chilli hits the ghee so it colours deep red without burning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice and a bowl of curd, garnished with a pinch of saffron strands.

variations.name: Kerala Handi Rajma
variations.description: An inventive Malabar-style handi where kidney beans simmer in a roasted-coconut gravy finished with a coconut-oil and curry-leaf tempering. The toasty coconut and warm fennel turn the rajma dark, nutty and unmistakably southern. A coastal twist on a northern staple.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil gives the distinct Malabar aroma

ingredients.name: Dried red kidney beans, soaked overnight

steps: Pressure-cook the soaked 1.5 cups kidney beans with 0.5 tsp salt and 3.5 cups water for 7-8 whistles until soft, then keep them in their liquid.
Dry-roast 0.5 cup grated coconut with 1 tsp fennel seeds over low heat 5-6 minutes until deep golden, then grind with a little water to a smooth dark paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a handi over medium heat, saute the 8 sliced shallots 5 minutes, then add the chopped tomatoes and cook 3 minutes until pulpy.
Add 2 tsp coriander powder, 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt, fry 2 minutes, then stir in the roasted coconut paste and cook 4 minutes.
Tip in the beans with their liquid, cover the handi and simmer gently 15 minutes until the gravy turns thick and dark.
Heat the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a small pan, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds and the curry leaves, and pour this sizzling tempering over the rajma.
tips: Roast the coconut to a rich brown for depth but pull it off the heat before it scorches and turns bitter.
Shallots melt into a sweeter base than onions, so use them for the authentic Malabar note.
Add the raw coconut-oil tempering just before serving to keep its aroma bright and fresh.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed matta rice or appam, with a wedge of lime and extra curry-leaf tempering on top.

variations.name: Rajasthani Handi Rajma
variations.description: A robust desert-style handi built on whole dried red chillies pounded into a smoky paste, with plenty of garlic and no tomato-heavy sweetness. The gravy is fiery, deep red and rugged, matched to the bold Marwari palate. Rajma for a hearty thali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee is the traditional Rajasthani cooking fat for a rich handi

ingredients.name: Dried red kidney beans, soaked overnight

steps: Soak the 6 whole dried red chillies in hot water for 15 minutes, then grind them with the 10 garlic cloves into a smooth fiery paste.
Pressure-cook the soaked 1.5 cups kidney beans with 0.5 tsp salt and 3.5 cups water for 7-8 whistles until soft, then keep them in their liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a handi over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Fry the 2 chopped onions 8 minutes until browned, add the minced ginger and the chilli-garlic paste, and cook 3 minutes until the raw smell burns off.
Add the chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp salt, and cook 7 minutes until pulpy and the ghee floats red.
Tip in the beans with their liquid, cover the handi and simmer gently 18 minutes, mash a few to thicken, and finish with 1 tsp garam masala.
tips: Deseed the dried chillies before grinding if you want the smoky colour with a little less blazing heat.
Grinding whole soaked chillies rather than using powder gives the gravy its characteristic rugged texture.
A dollop of curd on the side is the classic Marwari way to temper the fire.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra roti and a spoon of ghee, or with steamed rice and sliced raw onion for a rustic Rajasthani thali.

variations.name: Classic Home-style Tinda
variations.description: The unhurried everyday tinda most North Indian homes make, lightly spiced and cooked in its own moisture so the gourd stays soft and juicy. Simple, wholesome and quick, it is the kind of sabzi that appears on the table any ordinary weekday.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a light everyday oil that keeps this simple sabzi easy on the stomach

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: a small finishing spoon gives the homely aroma of a mother's kitchen

steps: Peel and dice the 500 g tinda, finely chop the 1 onion and 2 tomatoes, grate the 1 inch ginger, and slit the 2 green chillies.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on medium and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add the onion, grated ginger and green chillies and sauté for 4 minutes until the onion softens.
Stir in the tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder and cook for 5 minutes until the tomato breaks down.
Add the tinda and 1 tsp salt, toss, cover, and cook on low for 15 to 17 minutes, letting the gourd steam in its own juices until soft.
Uncover, mash a few pieces lightly against the pan to thicken, and finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee.
Garnish with 2 tbsp coriander leaves and serve warm.
tips: Mashing a few cooked pieces gives a natural, lightly thick masala without any extra effort.
Cover and cook low so the tinda releases its water and you need barely any extra liquid.
Keep the spicing gentle; this sabzi is about the fresh, clean taste of the gourd.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulkas, a spoon of ghee and a simple dal for a comforting everyday meal.

variations.name: Gujarati Home-style Tinda
variations.description: A light Gujarati household tinda with a gentle sweet-sour note from jaggery and lemon, a tempering of sesame and a soft green-chilli-ginger warmth. Mild, glossy and a little sweet, it is a comforting everyday shaak from a Gujarati kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the default oil in Gujarati homes, mild enough for a delicate shaak

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a gentle sweetness that marks almost every Gujarati vegetable

steps: Peel and dice the 500 g tinda and finely chop the 1 tomato.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on medium and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 1 tbsp sesame seeds for about 20 seconds until they pop.
Add 1 tbsp green chilli-ginger paste and the tomato and cook for 3 minutes until the tomato softens.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric and 2 tsp coriander-cumin powder, then add the tinda and 1 tsp salt and toss to coat.
Cover and cook on low for 14 to 16 minutes until the gourd is tender, adding 2 tbsp water only if needed.
Add 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook uncovered for 2 minutes until it dissolves and glazes the pieces.
Take off the heat, stir in 1 tbsp lemon juice and 2 tbsp coriander leaves, and serve warm.
tips: The coriander-cumin powder (dhana-jeera) is the Gujarati pantry staple that flavours this shaak; keep it handy.
Add the lemon at the very end so its brightness is not lost to the heat.
Adjust jaggery to taste; the sweetness should be a whisper, not a dessert.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft rotli brushed with ghee, a bowl of plain moong dal and a spoonful of chundo pickle.

variations.name: Bengali Home-style Tinda
