variations.description: A homely Bengali tinda tempered in mustard oil with panch phoron and a slit green chilli, kept light and mildly sweet in the everyday Bengali way. Fragrant with five spices and finished simply, it is a gentle niramish sabzi for a rice plate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the defining aroma of a Bengali home kitchen, smoked before use

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the customary pinch of sweetness that rounds a Bengali vegetable

steps: Peel and dice the 500 g tinda and slit the 2 green chillies lengthwise.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until it just smokes, then lower the flame and temper 1 tsp panch phoron, the 1 bay leaf and the slit green chillies for about 20 seconds until the seeds crackle.
Add 1 tsp ginger paste and stir for 30 seconds, then add 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp cumin powder with a splash of water and cook for 1 minute.
Tip in the tinda and 1 tsp salt, toss, cover, and cook on low for 14 to 16 minutes until tender, stirring once.
Uncover and stir-fry for 2 minutes to dry off any excess moisture.
Sprinkle 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook for 1 minute until it melts into the sabzi.
Garnish with 2 tbsp coriander leaves and serve with rice.
tips: Panch phoron is a whole-seed blend, so let it crackle fully in hot oil to release its aroma.
Keep this sabzi light and slightly sweet; it is meant as a gentle start to a Bengali rice meal.
Smoke the mustard oil first to soften its raw bite before the seeds go in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as the first course of a Bengali lunch with steamed rice and a wedge of lime, before the dal and fish.

variations.name: Tamil Home-style Tinda
variations.description: A Tamil-home poriyal-style tinda cooked with a mustard-and-urad-dal tadka, curry leaves and a finish of fresh grated coconut. Light, mildly spiced and aromatic with curry leaf, it is the gentle South Indian everyday take on the gourd.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: gingelly oil is the traditional Tamil cooking fat that suits a light poriyal

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: a small finishing spoon deepens the aroma of the curry leaves and coconut

steps: Peel and finely dice the 500 g tinda, chop the 1 onion, and finely chop the 2 green chillies.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil on medium and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal until the dal turns golden, about 30 seconds.
Add 1 pinch asafoetida, the 15 curry leaves, chopped onion and green chillies and fry for 3 minutes until the onion softens.
Add the diced tinda, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, toss, cover, and cook on low for 12 to 14 minutes until tender, sprinkling a little water only if needed.
Uncover and stir-fry for 2 minutes to dry out any moisture so the poriyal stays crumbly.
Mix in 3 tbsp grated coconut and cook for 1 minute until warmed and fragrant, then drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee.
Toss once and serve warm while the curry leaves and coconut are still fragrant.
tips: Add the coconut at the very end and cook only briefly so it stays fresh and soft.
Keep the pieces small and the sabzi dry for a proper crumbly poriyal texture.
Fry the urad dal to a nutty gold; it gives the tadka its signature South Indian crunch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a side with sambar rice or curd rice and a crisp appalam for a comforting Tamil meal.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Home-style Tinda
variations.description: A simple Maharashtrian ghar-style tinda bhaji with a mustard-cumin tadka, a spoon of goda masala and a little jaggery and coconut for balance. Warm, gently sweet and everyday-easy, it brings the household flavour of a Marathi kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the staple Maharashtrian cooking oil that carries goda masala well

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the gentle sweetness typical of an everyday Marathi bhaji

steps: Peel and dice the 500 g tinda and finely chop the 1 onion.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on medium and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, then add the 8 curry leaves for a few seconds.
Add the chopped onion and fry for 4 minutes until soft and pale gold.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp goda masala for 30 seconds, then add the tinda and 1 tsp salt and toss well.
Cover and cook on low for 14 to 16 minutes until the gourd is tender, stirring once midway.
Add 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 2 tbsp grated coconut and cook uncovered for 2 minutes to bring the flavours together.
Garnish with 2 tbsp coriander leaves and serve warm.
tips: A little goda masala goes a long way; start with a teaspoon and add more only if you like it stronger.
The jaggery-and-coconut finish is what makes this taste like home-cooked Marathi food.
Fresh coconut is best, but soak desiccated coconut in a spoon of warm water if that is all you have.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft jowar or bajra bhakri and a spoon of thecha, or with plain varan-bhaat.

variations.name: Classic Kadai Aloo Tamatar
variations.description: A semi-dry restaurant-style kadai curry where potatoes and capsicum are tossed in a freshly pounded coriander-chilli kadai masala. Chunky, aromatic and clinging with a thick tomato masala, it is all about that just-ground spice fragrance.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A neutral wood-pressed oil lets the freshly pounded kadai masala shine

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon of ghee at the finish rounds the sharp kadai spices

steps: Dry-roast 1.5 tbsp coriander seeds with 3 dried red chillies until fragrant, about 2 minutes, then coarsely pound them into a fresh kadai masala.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai over medium-high heat and stir-fry 2 cubed onions and 1 cubed capsicum for 3 minutes until charred at the edges, then remove.
In the same oil, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry 1 minute, then add 3 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt and cook 6 minutes until pulpy.
Stir in the pounded kadai masala and cook 2 minutes until the oil separates and the spices smell toasty.
Add the 4 boiled cubed potatoes and the reserved onion-capsicum, tossing to coat, then add 0.5 cup hot water and cook 4 minutes.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the pan and stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, cooking 1 minute until the masala clings thickly to every piece.
tips: Freshly pounding the coriander and chilli, rather than using ready powder, is the single biggest flavour difference in kadai dishes.
Keep the capsicum slightly crunchy by adding it back only near the end.
This dish is meant to be semi-dry; do not flood it with water or it loses its kadai character.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tandoori roti or laccha paratha and a side of onion rings dusted with chaat masala.

variations.name: Rajasthani Kadai Aloo Tamatar
variations.description: A smoky Marwari-style kadai where soaked dried red chillies ground to a paste bring fierce colour and heat, and ghee replaces oil for desert-kitchen richness. Bold and rustic, it swaps subtlety for full-throttle spice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee is the traditional cooking fat across water-scarce Rajasthan

steps: Soak 5 dried Mathania chillies in hot water for 15 minutes, then grind them into a smooth, vivid red paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds until aromatic.
Add 2 chopped onions and fry until deep golden, 7 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Add the chilli paste, 3 chopped tomatoes, 2 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt; cook 8 minutes until the ghee separates and the gravy turns glossy red.
Toss in the 4 boiled potatoes and 1 cubed capsicum with 0.75 cup hot water and simmer 5 minutes.
Cook uncovered 2 minutes more so the fiery masala thickens and clings to the potatoes and capsicum.
tips: Mathania chillies give the signature Rajasthani red with a heat you control by the number soaked.
The capsicum here is kept softer than in a classic kadai, blending into the robust gravy.
A spoon of curd stirred in at the end tempers the heat if it turns too fierce for your table.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra roti smeared with white butter, or steamed rice and a raw onion on the side.

variations.name: Andhra Kadai Aloo Tamatar
variations.description: A blistering Andhra kadai driven by Guntur chilli powder and a garlic-forward tempering in groundnut oil, with curry leaves and a hint of tamarind. Semi-dry and punchy, it is built for those who chase the heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the everyday frying medium of Andhra kitchens

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds for 15 seconds, then add 12 curry leaves and 8 crushed garlic cloves.
Fry the garlic 1 minute until pale gold, then add 2 cubed onions and 1 cubed capsicum and stir-fry 3 minutes on high until charred at the edges.
Add 3 chopped tomatoes, 1.5 tsp Guntur chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt; cook 6 minutes until the tomatoes collapse into a thick masala.
Stir in 0.75 tsp tamarind paste dissolved in 0.5 cup hot water and cook 2 minutes to brighten the gravy.
Add the 4 boiled potatoes, tossing until every cube wears the fiery red masala.
Cook uncovered on medium heat for 3 minutes until semi-dry and the oil glistens at the edges.
tips: Guntur chilli is genuinely hot; start with 1 tsp if serving those who prefer milder food.
The tamarind is what stops the heat from feeling flat, so do not skip that quick sour lift.
Crush the garlic coarsely for a bolder aroma that survives the strong chilli.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and ghee, or with ragi mudde and a bowl of thin rasam alongside.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Kadai Aloo Tamatar
variations.description: A Puneri kadai take where goda masala and a roasted coconut-sesame paste give the potatoes and capsicum a dark, nutty depth. Smoky and mildly sweet, it trades North Indian brightness for Deccan warmth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the base of everyday Maharashtrian cooking

steps: Dry-roast 3 tbsp desiccated coconut and 1 tbsp sesame seeds together until golden, about 3 minutes, then grind coarsely.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds for 15 seconds until they pop.
Add 2 chopped onions and fry until golden, 6 minutes, then add 1 cubed capsicum and cook 2 minutes.
Stir in 2 chopped tomatoes, the coconut-sesame paste, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tbsp goda masala and 1 tsp salt; cook 5 minutes until the oil separates.
Add the 4 boiled potatoes and 0.5 cup hot water, tossing to coat, and cook 4 minutes.
Continue on medium heat 2 minutes until semi-dry and the masala turns a rich, nutty brown.
tips: Roasted sesame adds a subtle bitterness that balances the sweetness of goda masala; do not skip it.
Keep the paste coarse for the pleasant grainy texture typical of Maharashtrian gravies.
A squeeze of lemon at the table lifts the deep, dark flavours beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bhakri or steamed rice and a fresh koshimbir salad of cucumber and peanuts.

variations.name: Bihari Kadai Aloo Tamatar
variations.description: A rustic Bihari kadai cooked in sharp mustard oil and tempered with panch phoron, the potatoes deliberately pan-charred for a smoky bite. Earthy and pungent, it carries the plain-spoken flavours of a Bihar kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Pungent mustard oil is the everyday cooking fat across Bihar

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, then lower the flame and rest it 20 seconds to soften the pungency.
Fry the 4 cubed potatoes on medium-high heat for 5 minutes until their edges are charred and golden, then remove them.
Temper 1 tsp panch phoron and 6 crushed garlic cloves in the same oil for 30 seconds until they crackle and turn fragrant.
Add 2 chopped onions and fry until golden, 5 minutes, then add 3 chopped tomatoes, 0.75 tsp turmeric, 1.25 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt; cook 6 minutes.
Return the charred potatoes with 1 cubed capsicum and 0.75 cup hot water, tossing to coat.
Cook uncovered on medium heat for 4 minutes until semi-dry and the potatoes are cooked through and smoky.
tips: Charring the raw potatoes in mustard oil first gives a smoky depth that boiled potatoes cannot match.
Always smoke the mustard oil before use to mellow its raw sharpness.
Panch phoron should stay whole in the temper; grinding it loses the distinct five-seed aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain rice and a spoon of raw mustard oil and green chilli, or with hot litti on the side.

variations.name: Classic Kadai Dum Aloo
variations.description: Baby potatoes and charred capsicum tossed in a semi-dry, coarsely spiced gravy built on freshly pounded kadai masala. The hallmark is the crushed coriander-chilli blend and the smoky bite of peppers cooked hot and fast in an iron kadai.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil stands up to the high kadai heat and keeps the masala tasting clean

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of bilona ghee gives the semi-dry masala a glossy, aromatic coat

steps: Dry-roast 1.5 tbsp coriander seeds, 3 dried red chillies and 0.5 tsp of the cumin on low for 2 minutes until fragrant, then coarsely crush them into a rough kadai masala.
Boil 500 g baby potatoes for 10 minutes until just tender, peel and prick them, then shallow-fry in 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium for 5 minutes until golden and set aside.
In the same oil, on high heat, toss 1 large diced capsicum for 2 minutes until edges char, then remove; add the remaining 0.5 tsp cumin and let it crackle.
Add 2 chopped onions and saute for 6 minutes until golden, then stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook a minute until the raw smell disappears.
Mix in 3 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, the crushed kadai masala and 1 tsp salt, and cook on medium for 7 minutes until the oil separates.
Return the potatoes with half a cup of water, cover and simmer on low for 8 minutes, then fold in the charred capsicum and 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi.
Swirl in 2 tbsp cream and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, cook uncovered for 2 minutes to a semi-dry, glossy finish and serve.
tips: Crush the roasted kadai masala coarsely rather than powdering it; the uneven texture is what defines a true kadai dish.
Cook the capsicum separately on high heat so it stays crunchy and smoky instead of stewing soft in the gravy.
Keep the finish semi-dry; if it dries out too much, loosen with a splash of hot water rather than more cream.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve sizzling from the kadai with laccha paratha or tandoori roti, scattered with julienned ginger and a wedge of lemon.

variations.name: Rajasthani Kadai Dum Aloo
variations.description: A fiery desert-style kadai where whole dried red chillies, soaked and ground, give both a deep red colour and a bold heat. Built without much tomato and thickened with curd, it echoes the robust, water-thrifty cooking of Rajasthan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rajasthani kitchens cook liberally in ghee, and it tempers the fierce chilli heat with richness

steps: Soak 6 dried red chillies in hot water for 15 minutes, then grind them with a splash of water into a smooth, bright red paste.
Boil 500 g baby potatoes for 10 minutes until just tender, peel and prick them all over so they carry the chilli gravy.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai and fry the potatoes on medium for 5 minutes until golden, then remove them.
In the same ghee temper 1 tsp cumin, 3 cloves, 1 black cardamom and 1 bay leaf for 20 seconds, then add 2 chopped onions and saute for 7 minutes until deep brown.
Stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, the red chilli paste, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 2 tsp coriander powder, and cook on medium for 5 minutes until the ghee separates and the colour turns rich.
Lower the heat, whisk 0.5 cup curd smooth and stir it in slowly with 1 tsp salt, cooking gently for 3 minutes so it does not split.
Add three-quarters of a cup of water, return the potatoes, cover and simmer on low for 10 minutes, then finish with 0.5 tsp garam masala and serve.
tips: Use a mild Kashmiri-type chilli for the paste if you want the deep colour without punishing heat; the seeds carry most of the fire.
Temper the curd on the lowest heat and keep stirring, as this tomato-free gravy relies on it entirely for body.
This curry deepens overnight, making it an ideal make-ahead dish for a spread.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra roti and a dollop of white butter, or with steamed rice and a cooling side of sliced cucumber and onion.

variations.name: Andhra Kadai Dum Aloo
variations.description: A searing Andhra-style kadai powered by Guntur red chillies, famed for their heat and colour. A coarse guntur-forward spice paste and a hit of curry leaves and sesame make this the boldest, spiciest reading of the dish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed sesame oil is the classic Andhra cooking fat and stands up to the Guntur heat

steps: Dry-roast 1 tbsp sesame seeds and 5 Guntur red chillies separately on low until the seeds pop and the chillies darken, then grind both to a coarse paste with a little water.
Boil 500 g baby potatoes for 10 minutes until just tender, peel and prick them, then fry in 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil on medium for 5 minutes until golden and set aside.
In the same oil crackle 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tsp cumin and 15 curry leaves for 30 seconds until they splutter and turn crisp.
Add 2 chopped onions and saute for 7 minutes until browned, then stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook a minute until aromatic.
Mix in 2 chopped tomatoes, the sesame-chilli paste, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook on medium for 6 minutes until the oil separates and the gravy turns brick red.
Add 1 tbsp tamarind pulp and 1 cup water, return the potatoes, cover and simmer on low for 10 minutes until they soak up the fiery masala.
Uncover and cook 2 more minutes to a thick, clinging finish, then serve garnished with a few fried curry leaves.
tips: Toast the Guntur chillies gently and keep the window open; the fumes are sharp but this is where the signature aroma comes from.
Roasted sesame paste both thickens and tempers the heat, so do not skip it even if you shorten other steps.
Balance the fire with the tamarind and adjust salt at the end, as Guntur chillies can vary widely in intensity.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or with pesarattu; a bowl of thick curd on the side is almost essential to tame the heat.

variations.name: Kerala Kadai Dum Aloo
variations.description: A coastal reimagining where roasted coconut and coconut oil replace cream, giving a nutty, aromatic gravy flecked with curry leaves. Warm spices and a coconut-milk finish make this the mellowest, most fragrant version in the family.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil gives the unmistakable Kerala aroma the moment it hits the pan

steps: Dry-roast 0.5 cup grated coconut on low for 4 minutes until golden brown and fragrant, then grind to a coarse paste with a little water.
Boil 500 g baby potatoes for 10 minutes until just tender, peel and prick them, then fry in 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil on medium for 5 minutes until golden and set aside.
In the same oil crackle 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp fennel seeds and 15 curry leaves for 30 seconds until they release their aroma.
Add 2 sliced onions and saute for 7 minutes until soft and golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook a minute.
Mix in 1 chopped tomato, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook on medium for 5 minutes until the raw spice smell fades.
Add the roasted coconut paste and 1 cup water, return the potatoes, cover and simmer on low for 10 minutes until cooked through.
Pour in 0.5 cup coconut milk, warm through on low for 2 minutes without boiling, and serve topped with a final tempering of curry leaves in coconut oil.
tips: Roast the grated coconut slowly and evenly; a golden, not dark, colour keeps the gravy sweet and prevents bitterness.
Add the coconut milk at the very end and do not let it boil, or it will split and turn grainy.
For a deeper coastal flavour, finish with a fresh tempering of mustard seeds and curry leaves in a spoon of coconut oil poured over the top.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with appam, malabar parotta or steamed red rice, and a side of thin buttermilk to complete the Kerala meal.

variations.name: Bengali Kadai Dum Aloo
variations.description: A Bengali-inflected kadai that swaps the usual oil for pungent mustard oil and folds in a hint of sugar and a bhaja masala finish. Sharp, aromatic and lighter on cream, it carries the unmistakable eastern-India character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked wood-pressed mustard oil gives the kadai its signature Bengali pungency

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a touch of jaggery lends the sweet undertone Bengali cooking loves against the sharp mustard oil

steps: Dry-roast 1 tbsp coriander seeds, 0.5 tsp of the cumin and 2 dried red chillies on low for 2 minutes, then grind coarsely into a rough bhaja-style masala.
Boil 500 g baby potatoes for 10 minutes until just tender, peel and prick them, then rub with a little turmeric and salt.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, then fry the potatoes on medium for 5 minutes until golden and remove them.
In the same oil toss 1 diced capsicum on high for 2 minutes until charred at the edges and set aside, then crackle the remaining 0.5 tsp cumin.

Add 2 chopped onions and saute for 6 minutes until golden, stir in 1 tbsp ginger paste, 2 chopped tomatoes, 0.75 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook 6 minutes until the oil surfaces.
Add the crushed roasted masala and half a cup of water, return the potatoes, cover and simmer on low for 8 minutes, then fold in the charred capsicum.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, cook uncovered for 2 minutes to a semi-dry finish and serve.
tips: Bring the mustard oil to a wisp of smoke before frying so the finished dish smells nutty rather than raw and harsh.
The freshly crushed roasted masala is what carries the Bengali flavour, so grind it just before cooking.
Keep the capsicum crisp by adding it back only in the last few minutes.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with luchi or plain paratha, or spoon over steamed rice with a squeeze of lime and a few slit green chillies on the side.

variations.name: Classic Kadai Malai Kofta
variations.description: Creamy paneer koftas meet the bold, coarse-ground spice of a kadai masala studded with charred capsicum and onion. The result marries malai richness with the smoky, peppery bite of a classic kadai for the best of both worlds.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: wholegrain binder that keeps the koftas soft in the spicy kadai gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: high smoke point for frying the koftas and building the kadai masala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon that rounds the coarse kadai spice with a mellow richness

steps: Mash 2 boiled potatoes with 1.5 cups grated paneer, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta into a smooth dough and shape into 10 koftas.
Deep-fry the koftas in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat until golden, about 4 minutes, and drain gently.
In 3 tbsp of the oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin, add 2 chopped onions and cook to golden, about 6 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste.
Add 3 pureed tomatoes, 2 tbsp coarsely ground kadai masala, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.75 tsp salt, and cook until the oil separates, about 8 minutes.
Toss in 1 cubed capsicum and cook 2 minutes so it keeps its crunch, then pour in 0.75 cup hot water and simmer 4 minutes to a clinging gravy.
Stir in 4 tbsp cream and 0.5 tsp garam masala, and warm through for 2 minutes to a glossy, medium-thick sauce.
Add 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, slide in the koftas just before serving, and spoon the gravy over so they stay whole; rest 2 minutes.
tips: Grind the kadai masala coarse rather than fine; the rustic texture is what sets a kadai gravy apart.
Add the capsicum late so it stays crunchy and bright against the creamy koftas.
Balance the cream and kadai spice by tasting at the end; the malai should soften, not smother, the heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in an iron kadai topped with ginger juliennes and a cream swirl, alongside laccha paratha or tandoori roti.

variations.name: Rajasthani Kadai Malai Kofta
variations.description: A robust Marwari kadai finished in pure Anveshan Ghee with a smoky base of soaked dried red chillies. The creamy koftas take on a fiery crimson coat, balancing desert-style heat against a luxurious malai finish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: binds the koftas so they hold up to the fiery ghee gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the royal fat that fries the koftas and carries the Mathania chilli flavour

steps: Mash 2 boiled potatoes with 1.5 cups grated paneer, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta into a firm dough and roll into 10 koftas.
Shallow-fry the koftas in 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat until golden on all sides, about 5 minutes, and set aside.
Soak 8 dried red chillies in warm water for 15 minutes, then blend with 2 onions and 2 tomatoes to a smooth crimson paste.
In the remaining 3 tbsp ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the chilli paste, and fry over medium heat until thick and oil separates, about 9 minutes.
Add 1 tbsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt, then lower the heat and whisk in 0.5 cup yogurt slowly, stirring so it does not curdle; simmer 4 minutes.
Pour in 0.5 cup water and 3 tbsp cream, and simmer to a glossy, fiery-red gravy, about 3 minutes.
Slide the koftas in just before serving, coat them in the gravy, and rest 2 minutes while the ghee glistens on top.
tips: Deseed some chillies for deep red colour without overwhelming heat, using Mathania chillies if you can find them.
Whisk the yogurt smooth and add it off a rolling boil so it blends into the ghee without splitting.
A pinch of dried fenugreek crushed at the end lends the classic Rajasthani aromatic finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra or missi roti and a side of sliced onion, green chilli and lime for a hearty desert-thali feel.

variations.name: Andhra Kadai Malai Kofta
variations.description: A searing Andhra kadai built on Guntur red chillies and nutty Anveshan Sesame Oil, where the creamy koftas provide a cooling counterpoint to the heat. Tangy, garlicky and boldly spiced, it channels the fire of Rayalaseema cooking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: binds the koftas so they survive the fiery, tangy gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: gingelly oil gives the earthy, nutty Andhra base

steps: Mash 2 boiled potatoes with 1.5 cups grated paneer, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta into a smooth dough and roll into 10 koftas.
Fry the koftas in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil over medium heat until golden, about 4 minutes, and drain.
Soak 8 Guntur chillies in warm water for 15 minutes, then grind with 8 garlic cloves to a coarse red paste.
In 3 tbsp sesame oil, splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tsp cumin and 1 sprig curry leaves, then add 2 chopped onions and fry to golden, about 6 minutes.
Add the chilli-garlic paste with 1 tbsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt, fry until oil separates, about 6 minutes, then add 3 pureed tomatoes and cook 5 minutes.
Pour in 0.75 cup water and simmer 4 minutes, then stir in 3 tbsp cream to temper the heat into a glossy gravy.
Slide the koftas in just before serving, crisp the second curry-leaf sprig in a little sesame oil on top, and rest 2 minutes.
tips: Control the Guntur chillies to your tolerance; they bring both fierce heat and a deep red colour.
The cream is what makes this malai version approachable, so add enough to round the fiery edge.
A squeeze of tamarind at the end lifts the gravy with the sour note typical of Andhra food.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice topped with ghee, or with pesarattu, and keep a bowl of curd nearby to cool the palate.

variations.name: Gujarati Kadai Malai Kofta
variations.description: A milder, sweet-savoury kadai in the Gujarati manner, with Anveshan Jaggery Powder rounding the tomato and capsicum masala. The creamy koftas sit in a gently spiced gravy that balances warmth and sweetness in the regional way.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: binds the soft koftas for the sweet-savoury kadai gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday Gujarati kitchen oil for frying and the masala base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the signature sweet note balancing the tomato and chilli, Gujarati style

steps: Mash 2 boiled potatoes with 1.5 cups grated paneer, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta into a soft dough and shape into 10 koftas.
Fry the koftas in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat until golden, about 4 minutes, and drain.

In 3 tbsp of the oil, splutter 1 tsp cumin, 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 1 sprig curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida, then add 2 chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, and cook to soft gold, about 6 minutes.
Add 3 pureed tomatoes, 1.5 tbsp kadai masala, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt, and cook until the masala thickens and glistens, about 7 minutes.
Toss in 1 cubed capsicum and cook 2 minutes, then stir in 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.75 cup water and simmer 4 minutes.
Add 3 tbsp cream and warm through to a smooth, balanced gravy, about 2 minutes.
Add the koftas just before serving, spoon the sweet-savoury gravy over them, and rest 2 minutes.
tips: Add the jaggery last and taste; the sweetness should just balance the tomato, not lead the dish.
Keep the chilli gentle so the characteristic Gujarati sweet-savoury contrast stays in focus.
The koftas can be pan-fried in less oil for a lighter, everyday version.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulka or methi thepla and a bowl of buttermilk to complete a Gujarati thali.

variations.name: Kerala Kadai Malai Kofta
variations.description: A coastal kadai where roasted coconut and curry leaves meet the coarse kadai spice, all cooked in Anveshan Coconut Oil. The creamy koftas soak up a toasty, faintly sweet gravy with the unmistakable aroma of Malabar.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: binds the koftas so they hold in the coconut kadai gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: gives the koftas and tempering the signature Kerala aroma

steps: Mash 2 boiled potatoes with 1.5 cups grated paneer, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta into a smooth dough and roll into 10 koftas.
Fry the koftas in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil over medium heat until golden, about 4 minutes, and drain.
Dry-roast 3 tbsp coconut until nut-brown, then blend to a coarse paste with a splash of water.
In 3 tbsp coconut oil, pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 1 sprig curry leaves, then add 2 sliced onions and cook to soft gold, about 6 minutes, and stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes, 1.5 tbsp kadai masala, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.75 tsp salt, and cook 6 minutes, then mix in the coconut paste and cook until glossy, about 4 minutes.
Toss in 1 cubed capsicum and 0.75 cup water, simmer 4 minutes so the capsicum stays crisp, then lower in the koftas and cook 3 minutes.
Crisp the second curry-leaf sprig in a teaspoon of coconut oil, pour over the top, and rest 2 minutes before serving.
tips: Roast the coconut to a deep brown for the toasty depth typical of Malabar gravies.
Grind the kadai masala coarse to keep the rustic texture of a true kadai dish.
Add the capsicum late so it stays bright and crunchy against the creamy koftas.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with malabar parotta or steamed matta rice, with a side of thinly sliced shallots in coconut oil.

variations.name: Classic Kadai Paneer
variations.description: The bold, semi-dry kadai paneer built around a freshly pounded coriander-chilli kadai masala and chunky peppers. Unlike a creamy gravy, this one is all about the coarse roasted spice clinging to paneer and capsicum, finished with a quick toss so everything stays crisp-edged and fragrant.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a clean high-heat oil ideal for the fast, hot tossing that defines kadai cooking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoon added at the finish gives the dhaba-style richness kadai paneer is known for

steps: Dry-roast 1.5 tbsp coriander seeds, 4 dried red chillies and 1 tsp cumin seeds on low for 2 minutes until fragrant, then pound coarsely to make the kadai masala.

Cube 1 large capsicum and 1 onion into 2 cm pieces. Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai and stir-fry the capsicum and onion cubes on high for 2 minutes until charred at the edges, then remove.
In the same oil add 1 finely chopped onion and 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry 4 minutes, then add 3 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric and cook 6 minutes to a thick masala.
Stir in most of the pounded kadai masala with 1 tsp salt and fry 2 minutes until the oil separates and the spice smells toasty.
Add 300 g cubed paneer and the charred peppers and onion, tossing on high for 3 minutes so everything is coated but the vegetables stay crunchy.
Crush in 1 tbsp kasuri methi, add 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and the remaining kadai masala, toss once more, and finish with 2 tbsp fresh coriander.
tips: Pounding your own kadai masala fresh makes all the difference; ready-made powder tastes flat here.
Char the peppers on high and keep them slightly crunchy for the signature kadai texture.
For a semi-gravy version, add a quarter cup of water with the tomatoes and simmer a little longer.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve sizzling from a cast-iron kadai with tandoori roti or lachha paratha and a squeeze of lemon over the top.

variations.name: Andhra Kadai Paneer
variations.description: An incendiary Andhra version where the kadai masala is amplified with Guntur chillies and a garlic-heavy roasted paste, cooked down in sesame oil. Fiery, tangy with a touch of tamarind and pungent with curry leaves, it turns the familiar kadai into something unapologetically spicy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: the heavy nutty Andhra oil that stands up to Guntur chilli and garlic

steps: Dry-roast 6 Guntur chillies, 1.5 tbsp coriander seeds and 1 tsp cumin on low for 2 minutes, then pound coarsely with 10 garlic cloves into a rough Andhra kadai masala.
Cube 1 capsicum and 1 onion. Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and stir-fry the capsicum and onion cubes on high for 2 minutes until blistered, then set aside.
In the same oil add 15 curry leaves and 1 chopped onion and fry 4 minutes, then add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric and cook 5 minutes to a pulp.
Add the pounded chilli-garlic masala and fry on medium for 3 minutes until the raw garlic smell goes and the sesame oil separates.
Add 1 tsp salt, 1 tsp tamarind pulp and a splash of about 3 tbsp water, then fold in 300 g cubed paneer and the charred peppers and onion.
Toss on high for 3 to 4 minutes until the fiery masala coats every piece and the dish glistens with sesame oil.
tips: Deseed a few of the Guntur chillies to keep the vivid colour while easing the heat.
The tamarind is what balances the chilli; without it the dish reads flat and harsh.
Keep a bowl of curd nearby, as this is genuinely fiery in the authentic Andhra style.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice topped with ghee, or with pulka, and a cooling raita of onion and curd on the side.

variations.name: Bengali Kadai Paneer
variations.description: A Bengali-accented kadai where mustard oil and a nigella-tempered base bring pungent warmth, and slit green chillies replace the usual dried-chilli heat. The peppers and paneer are tossed in a lighter, sharper masala that carries the unmistakable bite of sarson ka tel.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked first, its pungency gives the kadai a distinct Bengali sharpness

steps: Dry-roast 1 tbsp coriander seeds on low for 90 seconds and pound coarse. Cube 1 capsicum and 1 onion.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, lower the heat, then stir-fry the capsicum and onion cubes on high for 2 minutes until they blister, and remove.
In the same oil temper 0.5 tsp nigella seeds and 2 slit green chillies for 15 seconds, then add 1 chopped onion and 1 tbsp ginger paste and fry 4 minutes.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.75 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp cumin powder and cook 5 minutes until pulpy, then stir in the pounded coriander with 1 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp sugar.
Fold in 300 g cubed paneer, the charred peppers and 2 more slit green chillies, tossing on medium for 3 minutes so the sharp masala coats everything.
Drizzle over 1 tsp raw mustard oil for that Bengali kick and finish with 2 tbsp fresh coriander.
tips: Smoke the mustard oil before cooking to soften its raw pungency into a pleasant sharpness.
The green chillies carry the heat here, so adjust their number rather than adding chilli powder.
A final raw drizzle of mustard oil is what marks this out as a Bengali kadai.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulka or luchi and a side of thinly sliced onion soaked in lime, letting the mustard sharpness shine.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Kadai Paneer
variations.description: This kadai takes on a Maharashtrian character with dark, aromatic goda masala and a scatter of roasted peanuts and dry coconut in the spice mix. Earthy and lightly sweet-savoury, it is a warmly spiced cousin of the classic, distinct from any northern preparation.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday Maharashtrian oil that toasts the peanuts and coconut in the masala

steps: Dry-roast 2 tbsp desiccated coconut, 2 tbsp peanuts and 1 tbsp coriander seeds on low for 3 minutes until golden, then pound to a coarse powder.
Cube 1 capsicum and 1 onion. Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and stir-fry the cubes on high for 2 minutes until charred, then set aside.

In the same oil fry 1 chopped onion with 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 4 minutes, then add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder and cook 5 minutes to a thick masala.
Stir in 2 tsp goda masala and the roasted peanut-coconut powder with 1 tsp salt and fry 2 minutes until the aroma turns deep and toasty.
Add a splash of about 4 tbsp water to bind the masala, then fold in 300 g cubed paneer and the charred peppers and onion.
Toss on medium for 3 minutes until the dark, nutty masala clings to every piece and the paneer is warmed through.
tips: Roast the coconut and peanuts only to golden; taking them too dark turns the masala bitter.
Goda masala brings its own warmth, so hold back on extra garam masala.
A squeeze of lime at the end lifts the earthy, nutty flavours beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar or bajra bhakri and a spoon of thecha on the side for those who want extra heat.

variations.name: Rajasthani Kadai Paneer
variations.description: A rugged Marwari kadai where soaked dried red chillies build a smoky crimson heat and ghee carries the whole spices. With minimal tomato and a hit of amchur for tang, it is drier, fierier and more spice-forward, the way a Rajasthani kitchen would toss paneer over a wood fire.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the traditional Rajasthani fat that blooms the soaked-chilli paste and whole spices

steps: Soak 6 dried Mathania chillies in hot water for 15 minutes, then grind with 8 garlic cloves to a coarse red paste. Separately pound 1.5 tbsp coriander seeds and 1 tsp cumin.
Cube 1 capsicum and 1 onion. Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and stir-fry the cubes on high for 2 minutes until charred, then remove.
In the same ghee add the pounded coriander-cumin and fry 20 seconds, then add 1 chopped onion and fry 5 minutes until golden.
Add the chilli-garlic paste with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 chopped tomato and fry on medium for 4 minutes until the ghee separates and the colour deepens to crimson.
Add 1 tsp salt and 0.75 tsp amchur, then fold in 300 g cubed paneer and the charred peppers and onion, tossing on high for 3 minutes.
Crush in 1 tbsp kasuri methi, toss once more, and serve while the smoky chilli aroma is at its peak.
tips: Mathania chillies give a smoky red without excessive heat; use fewer if you prefer milder food.
Keep this one on the drier side, as Rajasthani kadai is meant to coat rather than pool.
A little more amchur perks up the dish if it tastes too rich from the ghee.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with ghee-smeared bajra roti and sliced onions, with a glass of chilled chaas to cool the chilli.

variations.name: Classic Masala Mushroom Matar
variations.description: Meaty button mushrooms and sweet green peas simmered in a spiced onion-tomato masala finished with a touch of cream. The mushrooms are seared first so they stay firm and soak up the gravy rather than turning watery.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil sears the mushrooms cleanly and builds a nutty base gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of bilona ghee lifts the masala with a warm, buttery aroma

steps: Wipe 300 g mushrooms clean and quarter them, then sear in 1 tbsp of the Anveshan Groundnut Oil on high for 3 minutes until golden at the edges and set aside.
In the remaining 2 tbsp oil crackle 1 tsp cumin for 20 seconds, then add 2 chopped onions and saute for 7 minutes until deep golden.
Stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for a minute, then add 3 chopped tomatoes and cook for 6 minutes until pulpy and softened.
Mix in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 3 minutes until the oil separates.
Add 1 cup green peas and 1 cup water, cover and simmer on medium for 6 minutes until the peas are tender.
Fold in the seared mushrooms and dum-cook covered on low for 5 minutes so they absorb the masala.
Stir in 3 tbsp cream, 0.75 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, simmer 2 minutes and serve.
tips: Sear the mushrooms on high heat in a single layer so they brown instead of stewing and releasing water.
If using frozen peas, add them in the last 4 minutes so they stay bright and sweet.
Add the mushrooms late so they keep their bite; overcooking makes them rubbery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jeera rice or tandoori roti and a swirl of cream, garnished with fresh coriander and julienned ginger.

variations.name: Kerala Masala Mushroom Matar
variations.description: A coconut-rich coastal version where roasted coconut and coconut milk replace cream, and curry leaves and fennel scent the gravy. The mushrooms and peas simmer into a mellow, fragrant curry with the unmistakable aroma of coconut oil.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil delivers the signature Kerala aroma from the first sizzle

steps: Dry-roast 0.5 cup grated coconut on low for 4 minutes until golden and nutty, then grind to a coarse paste with a little water.
Quarter 300 g mushrooms and sear in 1 tbsp of the Anveshan Coconut Oil on high for 3 minutes until golden, then set aside.
In the remaining 2 tbsp oil crackle 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp fennel seeds and 15 curry leaves for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 2 sliced onions and saute for 7 minutes until soft and golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 1 chopped tomato and cook for 4 minutes.
Mix in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, then add the roasted coconut paste, 1 cup peas and 1 cup water.
Cover and simmer on medium for 6 minutes until the peas soften, then fold in the seared mushrooms and cook 4 minutes more.
Pour in 0.5 cup coconut milk, warm through on low for 2 minutes without boiling, and serve.
tips: Roast the grated coconut only until golden, not brown, to keep the gravy sweet and free of bitterness.
Add coconut milk at the end off a rolling boil so it does not split.
A last tempering of mustard seeds and curry leaves in coconut oil poured over the top deepens the coastal aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with appam, malabar parotta or steamed red rice and a small bowl of thin buttermilk on the side.

variations.name: Andhra Masala Mushroom Matar
variations.description: A fiery Andhra reading built on Guntur red chillies and a roasted sesame paste, with curry leaves and tamarind for a sour-hot edge. This is the boldest, spiciest mushroom matar in the family, cooked in aromatic sesame oil.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed sesame oil is the classic Andhra fat and stands up to the Guntur heat

steps: Dry-roast 1 tbsp sesame seeds and 5 Guntur red chillies separately on low until the seeds pop and the chillies darken, then grind both together to a coarse paste with a little water.
Quarter 300 g mushrooms and sear in 1 tbsp of the Anveshan Sesame Oil on high for 3 minutes until golden, then set aside.
In the remaining 2 tbsp oil crackle 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tsp cumin and 15 curry leaves for 30 seconds until they splutter.
Add 2 chopped onions and saute for 7 minutes until browned, then stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 2 chopped tomatoes and cook for 5 minutes.
Mix in the sesame-chilli paste, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 4 minutes until the oil surfaces and the gravy turns brick red.
Add 1 cup peas, 1 tbsp tamarind pulp and 1 cup water, cover and simmer on medium for 6 minutes until the peas are tender.
Fold in the seared mushrooms, simmer uncovered for 4 minutes to a thick clinging gravy and serve garnished with fried curry leaves.
tips: Roast the Guntur chillies gently with the window open; that toasted aroma is the heart of the dish.
The roasted sesame paste both thickens the gravy and tames the fierce heat, so do not skip it.
Balance the fire with the tamarind and adjust salt at the end, since Guntur chillies vary in strength.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot steamed rice topped with a spoon of ghee, or with pesarattu, and keep a bowl of thick curd close to cool the heat.

variations.name: Bengali Masala Mushroom Matar
variations.description: A Bengali-style curry cooked in smoked mustard oil and tempered with panch phoron, finished with a whisper of jaggery. The pungent oil and five-spice give the mushrooms and peas an earthy, aromatic character quite distinct from the northern masala.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked wood-pressed mustard oil gives the curry its signature Bengali pungency

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a touch of jaggery gives the gentle sweet undertone Bengali gravies balance against sharp mustard oil

steps: Quarter 300 g mushrooms, heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, then sear the mushrooms on high for 3 minutes until golden and set aside.
In the same oil temper 1 tsp panch phoron and 2 dried red chillies for 30 seconds until the seeds crackle and turn aromatic.
Add 2 chopped onions and saute for 6 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger paste and cook a minute until the raw smell fades.
Mix in 2 chopped tomatoes, 0.75 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1 tsp cumin powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 6 minutes until the masala leaves the oil.
Add 1 cup peas and 1 cup water, cover and simmer on medium for 6 minutes until the peas soften.
Fold in the seared mushrooms and cook covered on low for 4 minutes so they take on the spice.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.5 tsp garam masala, simmer for 2 minutes and serve.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to a wisp of smoke before cooking so the finished dish tastes nutty rather than raw.
Temper the panch phoron until the fenugreek smells nutty but pull it before it browns, or it turns bitter.
Keep the gravy on the lighter side, the way it is served with rice in Bengali homes.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a wedge of lime, or with luchi, alongside a simple cucumber and onion salad.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Masala Mushroom Matar
variations.description: A kala-masala style curry built on goda masala and roasted coconut, giving the mushrooms and peas a dark, nutty, gently sweet depth. Earthier and more robust than the creamy northern version, it reflects Maharashtra's love of goda and groundnut.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: groundnut oil is the everyday Maharashtrian fat and carries goda masala without masking it

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery balances the goda masala with the gentle sweetness typical of Maharashtrian gravies

steps: Dry-roast 4 tbsp desiccated coconut on low for 3 minutes until golden and nutty, then grind to a paste with a splash of water.
Quarter 300 g mushrooms and sear in 1 tbsp of the Anveshan Groundnut Oil on high for 3 minutes until golden, then set aside.
In the remaining 2 tbsp oil crackle 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin and 10 curry leaves for 20 seconds, then add 2 chopped onions and saute for 7 minutes until deep brown.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 2 chopped tomatoes, 2 tsp goda masala, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 6 minutes until the oil separates.
Add the roasted coconut paste, 1 cup peas and 1 cup water, cover and simmer on medium for 6 minutes until the peas soften.
Fold in the seared mushrooms and cook covered on low for 4 minutes so they absorb the dark masala.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer 2 minutes and serve topped with fresh coriander.
tips: Add goda masala with the wet tomato mixture, never into dry hot oil, as it scorches and turns bitter quickly.
Roast the coconut to a light gold so it does not overpower the delicate goda spices.
The curry tastes best after a short rest, when the goda masala melds into the coconut.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar or bajra bhakri and a spoon of raw onion with lime, or with plain rice topped with a trickle of ghee.

variations.name: Classic Masala Paneer
variations.description: The restaurant-style semi-dry masala paneer every home cook falls back on, with soft cubes coated in a glossy onion-tomato masala that clings rather than pools. A finishing touch of cream and garam masala rounds the tang into something rich and dinner-worthy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a neutral wood-pressed base that lets the masala's spices stay sharp and clear

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: stirred in at the finish for a nutty richness that says home-cooked

steps: Cut 300 g paneer into 2 cm cubes and keep in warm water so they stay soft. Finely chop 2 onions and puree 3 tomatoes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add the chopped onion and 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and saute 5 to 6 minutes until deep golden, then add the tomato puree with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder.
Cook the masala on medium for 6 to 7 minutes until it thickens and the oil separates and rims the pan, a sign it is properly bhuno-ed.
Add the drained paneer with 1 tsp salt and a splash of about 4 tbsp water, and simmer gently for 3 to 4 minutes so the cubes soak up the masala without breaking.
Stir in 3 tbsp cream, 0.75 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, cook 1 minute more, and scatter 2 tbsp fresh coriander over the top.
tips: Soaking paneer in warm water for ten minutes before cooking keeps it pillowy; skip this and it can turn rubbery.
For a thicker restaurant-style coat, reduce the water and mash a spoon of the masala before adding paneer.
Crush the kasuri methi between your palms as you add it to release maximum aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or lachha paratha and a side of sliced onions dusted with chaat masala for a classic North Indian dinner spread.

variations.name: Bengali Masala Paneer
variations.description: A Bengali reimagining that trades the heavy cream base for pungent mustard oil, a nubby mustard-poppy seed paste and slit green chillies, echoing the region's beloved shorshe treatment. The result is sharp, aromatic and lighter, with the paneer standing in for the usual fish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked first, it delivers the unmistakable Bengali shorshe pungency the dish is built on

steps: Soak 1.5 tbsp mustard seeds and 1 tbsp poppy seeds in warm water for 15 minutes, then grind with 2 green chillies and a pinch of salt to a smooth paste.
Cut 300 g paneer into thick fingers. Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, then lightly fry the paneer 1 minute a side until pale gold and set aside.
In the same oil temper 0.5 tsp nigella seeds and 2 slit green chillies for 15 seconds, then add the finely chopped onion and fry 4 minutes until soft.
Add 1 chopped tomato and 0.75 tsp turmeric, cook 3 minutes until pulpy, then stir in the mustard-poppy paste and fry gently for 2 minutes; do not let it boil hard or the mustard turns bitter.
Pour in about half a cup of water with 1 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp sugar, slide in the fried paneer, and simmer on low for 5 minutes until the gravy thickens and coats the pieces.
Drizzle over 1 tsp raw mustard oil for authentic pungency, scatter 2 tbsp coriander, and rest 2 minutes before serving.
tips: Add a pinch of salt while grinding the mustard seeds; it stops the paste from turning bitter.
Keep the heat gentle after the mustard paste goes in, as high heat makes the shorshe sharp and acrid.
The final drizzle of raw mustard oil is traditional and non-negotiable for that Bengali kick.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice and a wedge of lime; the mustard gravy is meant to be mixed into the first few mouthfuls of rice by hand.

variations.name: Kashmiri Masala Paneer
variations.description: A regal Kashmiri version coloured deep red with soaked chillies and perfumed with saffron, fennel and dry ginger instead of onion and garlic. Cooked in ghee and finished with a saffron-milk swirl, it is aromatic, mildly warming and closer to a Wazwan-style paneer than a Punjabi one.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the traditional Kashmiri cooking fat that carries the fennel and dry ginger aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk to lend the colour and delicate perfume central to Kashmiri cooking

steps: Steep a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk and set aside. Cut 300 g paneer into triangles.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan on medium and lightly fry the paneer triangles for 1 minute until just golden, then lift out.
Into the same ghee add 3 cardamom pods, 3 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon and let them sizzle for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Lower the heat, add 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1.5 tsp fennel powder, 0.75 tsp dry ginger powder and 0.5 tsp turmeric, and stir 15 seconds so the spices bloom without burning.
Whisk 0.5 cup curd smooth and add it off the heat, stirring constantly, then return to low heat with about half a cup of water and 1 tsp salt and simmer 4 minutes until it thickens.
Slide in the fried paneer, pour in the saffron milk, and simmer very gently for 6 to 7 minutes until the gravy turns a glowing red and the paneer is infused with aroma.
tips: Add the curd off the flame and stir non-stop to stop it from splitting into the gravy.
Use true Kashmiri chilli for colour without harsh heat; ordinary chilli powder will make it too fiery.
Resting the dish for ten minutes before serving lets the saffron and fennel bloom fully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with warm sheermal or plain basmati rice, and a small bowl of Kashmiri-style radish salad to cut the richness.

variations.name: Andhra Masala Paneer
variations.description: A blazing Andhra take that leans on fiery Guntur red chillies and a coarse roasted spice paste for its trademark heat and depth. Sesame oil and a curry-leaf tempering ground it in coastal Andhra flavour, making a paneer bold enough to hold its own against the region's meat curries.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: the classic Andhra cooking oil whose nutty weight stands up to Guntur chilli heat

steps: Dry-roast 6 Guntur dried red chillies, 1 tbsp coriander seeds and 1 tsp cumin seeds on low for 2 minutes until fragrant, then grind with 8 garlic cloves and a splash of water to a coarse paste.
Cut 300 g paneer into cubes. Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and sear the paneer for 1 minute until edges catch colour, then remove.
In the same oil pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 15 curry leaves for 15 seconds, then add 2 finely chopped onions and fry 5 minutes until browned.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes and 0.5 tsp turmeric, cook 4 minutes until soft, then stir in the roasted chilli-garlic paste and fry on medium for 4 minutes until the raw smell goes and oil separates.
Pour in about half a cup of water with 1 tsp salt and 1 tsp tamarind pulp, simmer 3 minutes, then return the paneer and coat it in the thick fiery masala.
Cook 3 to 4 minutes more on low until the gravy clings tightly to each cube and glistens with sesame oil.
tips: Deseed some of the Guntur chillies to keep the colour while dialling the heat down for family meals.
Grinding the roasted spices coarse, not smooth, gives the rustic Andhra texture.
The tamarind is essential; its sourness is what balances the aggressive chilli.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or with ragi mudde, and keep plain curd handy to cool the palate.

variations.name: Gujarati Masala Paneer
variations.description: Gujarat softens the masala paneer with its signature sweet-sour hand, folding jaggery and a little lemon into a lighter tomato base warmed with dhana-jeeru. It is gentle, glossy and family-friendly, the kind of subji that rounds out a thali beside dal and rotli.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday Gujarati kitchen oil, light enough to let the sweet-sour notes shine

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melts into the tomato base to create the signature Gujarati khatta-meetha balance

steps: Cut 300 g paneer into cubes and keep in warm water. Finely chop 1 onion and puree 3 tomatoes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 0.75 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida for 15 seconds, then add the onion and 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and fry 4 minutes until soft.
Add the tomato puree with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp dhana-jeeru and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, and cook 6 minutes until the masala thickens and darkens.
Stir in 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp salt, letting the jaggery melt into the gravy for 1 minute.
Add about half a cup of water and the drained paneer, and simmer on low for 4 to 5 minutes so the cubes plump up in the sweet-sour masala.
Turn off the heat, stir in 1 tbsp lemon juice and 2 tbsp coriander, and taste to check the sweet, sour and salt sit in gentle balance.
tips: Add the lemon only after switching off the heat to keep its freshness lively.
For a smoother thali-style gravy, blend the cooked masala before adding the paneer.
A tablespoon of cream can be swirled in for guests, though the classic home version stays light.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with phulka rotli or thepla and a bowl of moong dal; the mild sweetness makes it a favourite with children.

variations.name: Classic Masala Rajma
variations.description: Creamy red kidney beans simmered until melting in a smooth onion-tomato masala, thickened by mashing some of the beans right into the gravy. Warmly spiced with cumin, coriander and garam masala, it is the ultimate rajma-chawal comfort bowl. Homely, hearty and endlessly satisfying.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Its clean nutty note lets the rajma masala stay front and centre

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of bilona ghee gives the gravy a homely richness

ingredients.name: Dried red kidney beans, soaked overnight

steps: Pressure-cook the soaked 1.5 cups kidney beans with 0.5 tsp salt and 3.5 cups water for 7-8 whistles on medium until they mash easily, then keep them in their cooking liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a pan over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds until they sizzle and darken slightly.
Add the 2 chopped onions and fry for 8 minutes until golden brown, then stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until the raw aroma fades.
Pour in the tomato puree with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli, 2 tsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp salt, and cook 9-10 minutes until the masala thickens and oil separates.
Tip in the cooked rajma with all its liquid, mash roughly a quarter of the beans against the pan, and simmer covered for 15 minutes until the gravy turns thick and creamy.
Stir in 1 tsp garam masala and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, simmer 2 minutes, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Soaking the beans a full 8 hours is non-negotiable, as under-soaked rajma stays hard no matter how long you cook it.
Mashing a portion of the beans is what gives authentic rajma its naturally thick, clingy gravy without any cream.
The dish deepens overnight, so leftovers make an even better rajma-chawal the next day.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over steamed basmati rice with a spoon of ghee, sliced onions, a green chilli and a dab of mango pickle on the side.

variations.name: Punjabi Masala Rajma
variations.description: The dhaba-style Pindi rajma, made unctuous with white butter and a bloom of kasuri methi and a heavier tomato base. The gravy is thick, buttery and deeply savoury, meant to be eaten with rice till you can barely move. Peak Punjabi comfort food.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee builds the rich, buttery dhaba-style base

ingredients.name: Dried red kidney beans, soaked overnight

steps: Pressure-cook the soaked 1.5 cups kidney beans with 0.5 tsp salt and 3.5 cups water for 7-8 whistles until very soft, then keep them in their liquid.
Melt 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan over medium heat and pop 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Fry the 2 chopped onions for 9 minutes until deeply browned, then add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until the raw edge disappears.
Pour in the tomato puree with 1.25 tsp red chilli, 2 tsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp salt, and simmer 11-12 minutes until the base is thick and the ghee floats on top.
Add the rajma with its liquid, mash a third of the beans into the gravy, and simmer covered for 15 minutes until luxuriously thick.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the pot, swirl in 2 tbsp white butter, 2 tbsp cream and 1 tsp garam masala, and cook 2 minutes until glossy.
tips: A longer, slower simmer is the dhaba secret, so give the beans the full time to break down into a silky gravy.
Toast the kasuri methi for 20 seconds before crushing to release its full aroma into the buttery base.
If the gravy over-thickens, loosen with warm bean stock rather than water to keep the richness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jeera rice and a swirl of extra white butter on top, alongside a crisp onion-cucumber salad and lemon.

variations.name: Kashmiri Masala Rajma
variations.description: The famed rajma of the Kashmiri Pandit kitchen, where the small Bhaderwah beans are simmered with fennel, dry ginger and Kashmiri chilli into a mild, ruby-red gravy scented with saffron. No onion or garlic, yet unforgettably aromatic. This is rajma at its most elegant.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries the fennel and dry-ginger aromatics central to Pandit rajma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: A saffron steep lends the ruby glow and subtle perfume of a wazwan dish

ingredients.name: Dried red kidney beans, soaked overnight

steps: Soak 0.25 tsp Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 3 tbsp warm water and set aside while the beans cook.
Pressure-cook the soaked 1.5 cups kidney beans with 0.5 tsp salt and 3.5 cups water for 8-9 whistles until very soft, then keep them in their liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat, add the cinnamon, cloves and cardamom with 0.25 tsp asafoetida, and let them sizzle for 30 seconds.
Lower the flame, stir in 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and immediately add the tomato puree, cooking 7-8 minutes until the ghee floats bright red on top.
Add 2 tsp fennel powder, 1 tsp dry ginger and 0.75 tsp salt, then tip in the beans with their liquid and the bloomed saffron water.
Simmer covered for 15-18 minutes, mashing a few beans to thicken, and finish with 0.5 tsp garam masala for a fragrant ruby gravy.
tips: Kashmiri rajma is prized for staying whole yet creamy, so cook it low and long rather than rushing on high heat.
The dish is deliberately onion and garlic free, so lean on fennel and dry ginger for all its aroma.
Add the chilli powder off high heat and stir in the tomato fast so it colours without scorching.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice in true Kashmiri style, with a bowl of curd and a sprinkle of saffron strands over the gravy.

variations.name: Bengali Masala Rajma
variations.description: A Kolkata-kitchen rajma tempered in pungent wood-pressed mustard oil with a whole-spice bhaja, brightened by slit green chillies and a whisper of sugar. The mustard oil gives the beans a sharp, distinctive character rarely found in a rajma. A niramish-style vegetarian treat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Kachi ghani mustard oil gives the rajma its signature Bengali pungency

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A pinch of jaggery lends the classic Bengali sweet-savoury balance

ingredients.name: Dried red kidney beans, soaked overnight
Bay leaf and dried red chilli

steps: Pressure-cook the soaked 1.5 cups kidney beans with 0.5 tsp salt and 3.5 cups water for 7-8 whistles until soft, then keep them in their liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil in a pan over medium-high until it just smokes, then reduce the heat and temper 1 tsp cumin seeds, the bay leaf and dried red chilli for 30 seconds.
Add the chopped onion and fry for 6-7 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger paste and cook 1 minute until aromatic.
Add the chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli and 0.75 tsp salt, and cook 8 minutes until they collapse and the oil separates.
Tip in the beans with their liquid, add the 3 slit green chillies and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, mash a few beans, and simmer covered 15 minutes.
Sprinkle 0.75 tsp Bengali garam masala over the top, cook 2 minutes uncovered, and rest 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Always heat the mustard oil to smoking first to burn off its raw sharpness before it meets the spices.
Use the lighter cinnamon-clove-cardamom Bengali garam masala rather than a cumin-heavy blend to keep the character true.
The teaspoon of jaggery should sit just below the surface of the flavour, balancing rather than sweetening.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a drizzle of raw mustard oil, or with hot luchi for a Sunday-brunch Bengali plate.

variations.name: Gujarati Masala Rajma
variations.description: A Kathiawadi rajma tuned to the Gujarati love of khatta-meetha, with jaggery and tamarind rounding a lighter, spiced gravy tempered with mustard, curry leaves and a coriander-cumin blend. Softer and more soupy than its North Indian cousin. Lovely with phulka or khichdi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the daily cooking fat across Gujarati homes

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery gives the signature Gujarati sweetness that offsets the tamarind

ingredients.name: Dried red kidney beans, soaked overnight

steps: Pressure-cook the soaked 1.5 cups kidney beans with 0.5 tsp salt and 3.5 cups water for 7-8 whistles until soft, then keep them in their liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a pan over medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard and cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then add the curry leaves.
Add the chopped onion and saute for 5 minutes until soft, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and cook 1 minute.
Pour in the tomato puree with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp coriander-cumin powder and 0.75 tsp salt, and simmer 7-8 minutes until the oil separates.
Add the beans with their liquid, 1 tbsp tamarind pulp and 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, mash a few beans, and simmer covered 14 minutes.
Taste and adjust the sweet-sour balance, simmer 2 more minutes uncovered, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Add jaggery and tamarind gradually and keep tasting, since the ideal khatta-meetha point is a matter of a spoon either way.
Keep this rajma looser than a Punjabi one so it spoons nicely over rice or soaks into phulka.
A pinch of cinnamon-clove powder in the tempering rounds out the Kathiawadi warmth.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft ghee-brushed phulka or plain rice, kachumber salad and a spoon of sweet chunda on the side.

variations.name: Classic Masala Soya Chunk
variations.description: A homely everyday curry where spongy soya chunks are simmered in a straightforward onion-tomato masala until they soak up every bit of flavour. The chunks are first boiled and squeezed so they turn tender and drink in the gravy like little sponges. It is high-protein comfort food that comes together on a weeknight.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil gives this everyday masala a clean, nutty base.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of bilona ghee rounds the masala and adds a homely aroma.

steps: Boil 1.5 cups soya chunks in 4 cups water with 0.5 tsp salt for 5 minutes until spongy, then drain, rinse in cold water and squeeze each chunk firmly to remove the water.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium, crackle 1 tsp cumin, then add 2 chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry until golden, about 6 minutes.
Add 3 pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, and cook until the oil separates and the masala thickens, about 8 minutes.
Tip in the squeezed soya chunks and toss for 2 minutes so they take on the masala colour all over.
Pour in 1.5 cups hot water, cover, and simmer for 8 minutes until the chunks plump up and the gravy clings to them.
Stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 0.5 tsp garam masala and 3 tbsp coriander, then rest for 3 minutes before serving.
tips: Always squeeze the boiled soya chunks well; trapped water dilutes the gravy and mutes the spice.
Boiling the chunks first removes the raw, beany smell that puts many people off soya.
For extra flavour, boil the chunks in leftover vegetable stock instead of plain water.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulka or jeera rice, a spoon of curd and a crunchy onion-cucumber salad.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Masala Soya Chunk
variations.description: The soya chunks meet the dark, roasted depth of goda masala and a nutty coconut-peanut paste in this Deccan version. A touch of Anveshan Jaggery Powder balances the smoky spice. It is earthy and satisfying, tasting far more special than its humble weeknight roots.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the everyday Maharashtrian fat that carries goda masala well.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery powder rounds off the smoky goda masala without turning the curry sweet.

steps: Boil 1.5 cups soya chunks in salted water for 5 minutes, then drain, rinse and squeeze them dry thoroughly.
Dry roast 3 tbsp grated coconut and 2 tbsp peanuts over low heat until the coconut smells toasty and browns, about 4 minutes, then grind to a coarse paste with a little water.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp cumin and 10 curry leaves, then add 2 chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and brown for 6 minutes.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.25 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp goda masala, and cook until the oil separates, about 6 minutes.
Stir in the coconut-peanut paste and fry for 2 minutes until it darkens and smells nutty, then add the squeezed soya chunks and coat well.
Pour in 1.5 cups hot water and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer for 8 minutes until thick, and finish with 2 tbsp coriander.
tips: Roast the coconut gently; scorched coconut turns the whole gravy bitter.
No goda masala? Blend a pinch each of clove, cinnamon and roasted sesame into your garam masala.
The chunks soak up flavour overnight, making this an excellent make-ahead lunchbox curry.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri or steamed rice and a spoon of thecha, with sliced raw onion on the side.

variations.name: Gujarati Masala Soya Chunk
variations.description: A light, slightly sweet gravy in the Gujarati style, where soya chunks simmer in a tomato base balanced with Anveshan Jaggery Powder and lemon. Roasted peanut gives it body while ginger and green chilli keep it fresh. It is gentle, wholesome and made for soaking into soft rotli.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A light hand with wood-pressed groundnut oil keeps this soya curry homely and clean.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery powder brings the signature Gujarati sweet-sour balance against the tomato.

steps: Boil 1.5 cups soya chunks in salted water for 5 minutes, then drain, rinse and squeeze out all the water firmly.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin, then add 1 chopped onion and 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and soften for 4 minutes.
Add 3 pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander-cumin powder, and simmer until thick and glossy, about 8 minutes.
Stir in 2 tbsp roasted peanut powder and the squeezed soya chunks, tossing for 2 minutes so they colour evenly.
Add 1.5 cups hot water and 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, cover, and simmer for 8 minutes until the chunks are plump and the gravy is slightly soupy.
Off the heat, stir in 1 tbsp lemon juice and 2 tbsp coriander, then balance the sweet, sour and salt before serving.
tips: Add the lemon after the flame is off to keep its brightness intact.
Keep the gravy a little thin as the peanut powder thickens it on standing.
A pinch of asafoetida in the tempering makes the soya easier to digest.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulka or steamed rice, a glass of chhaas and a spoon of sweet chundo pickle.

variations.name: Bengali Masala Soya Chunk
variations.description: Known affectionately as soya-r dalna, this Bengali curry cooks the chunks in pungent Anveshan Mustard Oil with a panch phoron and bay leaf tempering. Potatoes and slit green chillies join the pot in true dalna style. It is warming, aromatic and gently sweet-hot.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil gives this dalna its unmistakable Bengali pungency.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A final teaspoon of ghee softens the raw mustard edge and lifts the aroma.

steps: Boil 1.5 cups soya chunks in salted water for 5 minutes, drain, rinse and squeeze dry, then set aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it smokes and pales, then fry 2 cubed potatoes until golden on the edges, about 5 minutes, and remove.
In the same oil, temper 1 tsp panch phoron and 2 bay leaves for 30 seconds, then add 2 chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger paste and fry until golden, about 6 minutes.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.75 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1 tsp cumin powder, and cook until the mustard oil surfaces, about 7 minutes.
Return the potatoes, add the squeezed soya chunks and 3 slit green chillies, and pour in 2 cups hot water, then cover and simmer for 12 minutes until the potatoes are tender.
Finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and 2 tbsp coriander, and rest for 3 minutes before serving.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to smoking first so its raw sharpness mellows into a clean warmth.
Frying the potatoes before simmering keeps them from breaking apart in the gravy.
A pinch of sugar with the tomatoes adds the subtle sweetness Bengali dalnas are known for.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice or luchi, a wedge of lime and a few extra slit green chillies on the side.

variations.name: Kerala Masala Soya Chunk
variations.description: A coconut-rich soya curry finished in creamy coconut milk with a shallot-curry leaf tempering fried in Anveshan Coconut Oil. Ground roasted coconut and fennel give it the mellow, aromatic body of a Kerala stew. The soya chunks turn plump and soak up the gentle, fragrant gravy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil gives the tempering its warm Malabar aroma.

steps: Boil 1.5 cups soya chunks in salted water for 5 minutes, then drain, rinse and squeeze out all the water.
Dry roast 0.5 cup grated coconut with 0.5 tsp fennel over low heat until deep golden, about 5 minutes, then grind to a smooth paste with a little water.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, fry 10 sliced shallots and 10 curry leaves until the shallots turn light brown, about 4 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste.
Add 1 chopped tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, and cook until the tomato breaks down, about 5 minutes.
Add the roasted coconut paste and the squeezed soya chunks with 1 cup hot water, then simmer for 8 minutes until the chunks plump up.
Lower the flame, pour in 1 cup coconut milk, warm for 3 minutes without boiling, and finish with the remaining curry leaves crackled in coconut oil.
tips: Keep the heat low after adding coconut milk to stop the gravy from splitting.
Roast the coconut to a rich brown for that authentic Kerala depth and colour.
