Small shallots give a sweeter base than large onions and are worth the extra peeling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with appam, steamed red rice or idiyappam, with crisp pappadam alongside.

variations.name: Classic Punjabi Chana Masala
variations.description: The definitive Amritsari chana: dark, tangy chickpeas simmered with a brewed tea for colour, a punchy chana masala blend and a generous finish of butter and kasuri methi. Thick enough to scoop with bhatura yet soupy enough for rice. This is the version that anchors every Punjabi Sunday lunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee gives the gravy its rich Amritsari-dhaba body

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A little wood-pressed oil raises the smoke point so onions brown evenly

steps: Pressure-cook the soaked 1.5 cups chickpeas with 0.5 tsp salt, 3 cups water and the tea bag tied in muslin for 5-6 whistles until soft and deep brown, then remove the tea bag and reserve the liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a pan over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds until aromatic.
Add the 2 chopped onions and fry for 8-9 minutes until deep golden, then stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until the raw smell goes.
Pour in the tomato puree with 1.25 tsp red chilli, 2 tsp chana masala powder and 0.75 tsp salt, and cook for 9-10 minutes on medium until thick and oil-flecked.
Add the cooked chickpeas with 1.5 cups reserved liquid and simmer covered for 12-15 minutes, mashing a few chana against the side to thicken the gravy.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the top, swirl in 2 tbsp white butter and cook 2 minutes until glossy and rich.
tips: The tea bag is the secret to the natural dark colour, so do not skip it and never use extra chilli to fake the shade.
For bhatura-style thickness, mash more chana; for a rice-friendly gravy, add extra chana stock instead.
Rest the finished chana for 15 minutes before serving so the masala penetrates each chickpea fully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with fluffy bhatura or kulcha, sliced onions dusted with chaat masala, green chilli pickle and a wedge of lemon.

variations.name: Gujarati Punjabi Chana Masala
variations.description: A Kathiawadi reinterpretation where jaggery and a hint of tamarind give the chana the sweet-sour-spicy khatta-meetha profile Gujaratis love. The gravy stays lighter and more soupy, scented with a whole-spice tempering. Perfect with soft phulka or khichdi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the everyday cooking fat of the Gujarati kitchen

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery delivers the signature Gujarati sweetness that balances the tamarind

steps: Pressure-cook the soaked 1.5 cups chickpeas with 0.5 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 5-6 whistles until tender, then keep aside with their liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a pan over medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard and cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then add the curry leaves and let them crackle.
Add the chopped onion and saute for 5-6 minutes until soft and pale gold, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and cook 1 minute.
Pour in the tomato puree with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli, 1.5 tsp coriander-cumin powder and 0.75 tsp salt, and simmer 7-8 minutes until the oil separates.
Add the chickpeas with 1.5 cups reserved liquid, 1 tbsp tamarind pulp and 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, and simmer covered for 12 minutes until the flavours meld.
Taste and adjust the sweet-sour balance, then simmer uncovered 2 more minutes until the gravy is lightly thickened but still pourable.
tips: Balance is everything here, so add tamarind and jaggery a little at a time and taste until the khatta-meetha feels even.
Keep the gravy thinner than a Punjabi version, as Gujaratis prefer to spoon it over rice or dunk phulka.
A pinch of ground cinnamon and clove in the tempering deepens the Kathiawadi aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft ghee-brushed phulka or plain rice, a side of kachumber salad and a spoon of sweet mango chunda.

variations.name: Kerala Punjabi Chana Masala
variations.description: A Malabar kadala-style chana simmered in a roasted coconut gravy and tempered in coconut oil with curry leaves, giving it the dark, toasty depth of a Kerala breakfast curry. Fresh grated coconut and fennel lend sweetness and warmth. Traditionally the partner to puttu.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil gives the unmistakable Malabar aroma

steps: Pressure-cook the soaked 1.5 cups chickpeas with 0.5 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 5-6 whistles until tender, then reserve the liquid.
Dry-roast 0.5 cup grated coconut with 1 tsp fennel seeds in a pan over low heat for 5-6 minutes until deep golden-brown, then grind with a little water into a smooth dark paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil over medium heat, saute the 8 sliced shallots for 5 minutes until soft, add the chopped tomato and cook 3 minutes until pulpy.
Add 2 tsp coriander powder, 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt, and fry the masala for 2 minutes, then stir in the roasted coconut paste and cook 4 minutes.
Tip in the cooked chickpeas with 1.5 cups reserved liquid and simmer covered for 12-15 minutes until the gravy turns thick and dark.
In a small pan heat the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds and the curry leaves, and pour this sizzling tempering over the curry.
tips: Roast the coconut slowly to a chocolate-brown for the authentic Malabar depth, but pull it off the heat before it turns bitter.
Kerala shallots are milder and sweeter than onions, so use them if you can find them for the true kadala flavour.
Finish with the raw coconut-oil tempering right before serving so the aroma stays bright.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the classic way with steaming puttu, or with appam and idiyappam for a full Kerala breakfast spread.

variations.name: Andhra Punjabi Chana Masala
variations.description: A fiery Andhra take that swaps the mild North Indian heat for pounded Guntur red chillies and a garlic-forward tempering. The gravy is thin, blazing red and unapologetically hot, cut only by a squeeze of lime. Built for those who chase serious spice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the backbone fat of Andhra cooking and tames raw chilli heat

steps: Pressure-cook the soaked 1.5 cups chickpeas with 0.5 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 5-6 whistles until soft, then keep aside with their liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a pan over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and the curry leaves for 30 seconds, then add the 8 crushed garlic cloves and fry until pale gold.
Add the 2 chopped onions with the minced ginger and saute for 7 minutes until browned, keeping the garlic from burning.
Add the chopped tomatoes with 2 tsp Guntur chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp salt, and cook 8 minutes until the tomatoes break down and oil rises red.
Tip in the chickpeas with 1.5 cups reserved liquid and simmer covered for 12 minutes, keeping the gravy thin and pourable in the Andhra style.
Finish with 1 tbsp lime juice off the heat, stir once and rest 5 minutes so the heat mellows just slightly before serving.
tips: Guntur chilli is intensely hot, so start with the stated amount and add more only if your table can take the burn.
The lime at the end is essential to cut the chilli, so never leave it out even if you love heat.
Frying the garlic first builds the deep pungent base that defines an Andhra gravy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice and a dollop of ghee to temper the heat, with raw onion and extra lime on the side.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Punjabi Chana Masala
variations.description: A Puneri-style chana in a roasted-coconut and goda masala gravy that eats warm, dusky and gently sweet. Wood-pressed groundnut oil and a jaggery finish are true to the regional palate. Unlike the buttery Amritsari original, this one is earthy and aromatic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The traditional Maharashtrian fat that carries goda masala without masking it

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A touch of jaggery is classic to round the dusky goda notes

steps: Pressure-cook the soaked 1.5 cups chickpeas with 0.5 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 5-6 whistles until tender, then reserve the liquid.
Dry-roast 4 tbsp grated coconut over low heat for 4 minutes until golden, then grind with the 2 chopped tomatoes into a smooth paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds until aromatic.
Fry the 2 chopped onions for 7 minutes until golden, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute, then add the coconut-tomato paste with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli.
Stir in 2 tsp goda masala and 0.75 tsp salt and fry for 6 minutes on medium until the masala darkens and oil separates at the edges.
Add the chickpeas with 1.5 cups reserved liquid and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer covered 12 minutes, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Stir constantly once the goda masala goes in because its coconut content catches and burns quickly on high heat.
Roast the coconut for the gravy just to golden, not brown, so the dish stays warm-sweet rather than bitter.
A finishing squeeze of lime lifts the whole pot and balances the jaggery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar or bajra bhakri and a spoon of thecha, or over hot rice topped with a drizzle of raw groundnut oil.

variations.name: Classic Punjabi Chole
variations.description: The definitive Pindi-Amritsari chole, stained dark by tea decoction and amla and finished with crushed kasuri methi. The chickpeas are boiled with whole spices and a tea bag so they turn a deep brown before meeting a robust onion-tomato masala. It is tangy, spicy and unmistakably restaurant-style.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee gives Punjabi chole its rich, glossy body and classic dhaba aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A little jaggery powder rounds the tang of amla and tomato without masking the spice.

steps: Pressure cook 1.5 cups soaked chickpeas with 1.25 tsp salt, 3 cups water, 2 tea bags and 2 dried amla pieces for 6 to 7 whistles until soft and deep brown, then remove the tea bags and amla.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan, crackle 1 tsp cumin, then add 3 finely chopped onions and 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry until dark golden, about 10 minutes.
Add 3 pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tbsp chole masala, and cook until the ghee separates and the masala turns glossy and dark, about 9 minutes.
Pour in the boiled chickpeas along with 1.5 cups of their dark cooking liquid and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, then simmer for 12 minutes, mashing a few chickpeas to thicken the gravy.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi between your palms and stir it in, cooking for a further 2 minutes until fragrant.
Finish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander, adjust salt and tang, and serve hot with a ghee sheen on top.
tips: The tea and amla are what give authentic chole its dark colour and sourness, so do not skip them.
For a smokier, spicier finish, top with julienned ginger and a slit green chilli just before serving.
Mashing a small handful of chickpeas thickens the gravy naturally without any cream or flour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with fried bhatura or kulcha, a mound of sliced onions, green chillies and lemon, and a side of tangy mango pickle.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Punjabi Chole
variations.description: A Deccan reworking of the Punjabi favourite, where goda masala and a roasted coconut paste replace the usual chole masala. Cooked in wood-pressed groundnut oil, it turns nutty and dark with a gentle sweetness from jaggery. It keeps the hearty spirit of chole but with a distinctly Maharashtrian soul.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the honest Deccan fat that lets goda masala lead.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery powder softens the smoky goda masala and rounds the tomato tang.

steps: Pressure cook 1.5 cups soaked chickpeas with 1.25 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 whistles until tender, and reserve the stock.
Dry roast 4 tbsp grated coconut with 1 sliced onion until deep brown and fragrant, about 6 minutes, then grind to a coarse paste with a splash of water.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp cumin and 12 curry leaves, then add the 2 remaining chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and brown for 8 minutes.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.25 tsp red chilli powder and 2.5 tsp goda masala, and cook until the oil separates, about 7 minutes.
Stir in the roasted coconut paste and fry for 3 minutes until it darkens and thickens the base.
Add the chickpeas with 1.5 cups stock and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer for 12 minutes, and finish with 2 tbsp coriander before serving.
tips: Grind the roasted coconut coarse rather than silky for the rustic Malvani texture.
Bump up the red chilli powder for a fiery Kolhapuri version, or keep it mild for a Konkani feel.
Let the curry sit for 10 minutes off the heat so the goda masala blooms fully into the gravy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft jowar bhakri or steamed rice, a spoon of thecha and a wedge of lime.

variations.name: Gujarati Punjabi Chole
variations.description: This gentler take dresses the Punjabi classic in Gujarat's sweet-sour palette, replacing the dark tea decoction with a bright tomato-jaggery-lemon base. Anveshan Jaggery Powder and roasted peanut give it a rounded, homely character. It is lighter and slightly soupy, made for soaking into rotli.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A light hand with wood-pressed groundnut oil keeps this chole homely, not heavy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery powder is the sweet counterweight to tomato and lemon in this Gujarati gravy.

steps: Pressure cook 1.5 cups soaked chickpeas with 1 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 whistles until very soft, then lightly mash a quarter of them.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin, then add 2 chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and cook until translucent, about 5 minutes.
Add 3 pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander-cumin powder, and simmer until thick and the oil floats, about 8 minutes.
Stir in 2 tbsp roasted peanut powder and cook for 2 minutes to give the gravy a nutty body.
Add the chickpeas with 1.5 cups of their water and 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, then simmer gently for 12 minutes until lightly soupy.
Off the heat, stir in 1 tbsp lemon juice and 2 tbsp coriander, and balance the sweet, sour and salt before serving.
tips: Add lemon only after switching off the flame so its brightness stays lively.
The peanut powder both thickens the gravy and echoes the nuttiness Gujarati cooks love.
Keep it slightly thin, as it firms up considerably once it cools.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thin phulka or jeera rice, a glass of chhaas and a spoon of sweet chundo pickle.

variations.name: Bengali Punjabi Chole
variations.description: The Punjabi chole reimagined through a Bengali lens, cooked in sharp Anveshan Mustard Oil with a panch phoron tempering and slit green chillies. It trades the dark amla tang for the pungent warmth of mustard and a whisper of sweetness. The result is bold, aromatic and distinctly eastern.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil gives this chole its signature Bengali pungency and depth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing touch of ghee tempers the raw edge of the mustard oil beautifully.

steps: Pressure cook 1.5 cups soaked chickpeas with 1.25 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 whistles until soft, and keep the stock.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it smokes and turns pale, lower the flame, and temper 1 tsp panch phoron and 2 bay leaves for about 30 seconds.
Add 2 chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger paste and fry over medium heat until golden, about 7 minutes.
Stir in 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.75 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1 tsp cumin powder, and cook until the mustard oil rises to the top, about 8 minutes.
Add the chickpeas with 1.5 cups stock and 3 slit green chillies, then simmer for 12 minutes so the panch phoron perfumes the beans.
Finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and 2 tbsp coriander, stir gently, and rest for 3 minutes before serving.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to smoking first; this single step removes its raw bitterness.
A pinch of sugar with the tomatoes gives the gentle sweetness typical of Bengali gravies.
Slit the green chillies rather than chopping them so they flavour without dominating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with luchi or steamed rice, a squeeze of lime and a few slit green chillies alongside.

variations.name: Kerala Punjabi Chole
variations.description: A South Indian coastal spin on Punjabi chole, simmered in coconut milk and tempered with shallots and curry leaves in Anveshan Coconut Oil. Ground roasted coconut and fennel bring a mellow, kadala-curry sweetness in place of the usual tang. It is creamy, aromatic and gentle on heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil lends the tempering its warm, sweet Kerala aroma.

steps: Pressure cook 1.5 cups soaked chickpeas with 1.25 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 whistles until soft, then keep them with their stock.
Dry roast 0.5 cup grated coconut with 0.5 tsp fennel over low heat until dark golden, about 5 minutes, then grind to a smooth paste with a little water.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, fry 10 sliced shallots and 10 curry leaves until the shallots caramelise, about 5 minutes, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste.
Add 1 chopped tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, and cook until the tomato melts, about 5 minutes.
Stir in the roasted coconut paste and the chickpeas with 0.5 cup stock, then simmer for 10 minutes until thick and glossy.
Pour in 1 cup coconut milk with 0.5 tsp garam masala, warm gently for 3 minutes without boiling, and finish with the last curry leaves crackled in coconut oil.
tips: Do not boil the curry once the coconut milk goes in or it will split.
Roast the coconut to a genuine deep gold for the authentic kadala-curry colour and flavour.
Use small shallots rather than onions for the natural sweetness this gravy relies on.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with puttu, appam or steamed red rice, with crisp pappadam and banana chips for crunch.

variations.name: Classic Punjabi Dum Aloo
variations.description: The full-bodied Punjabi classic: fried baby potatoes simmered in a rich onion-tomato-cashew gravy finished with cream, kasuri methi and a knob of butter. It is generously spiced and deeply comforting, the kind of curry made for soaking up with naan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil fries the potatoes to a clean golden crust and builds the base gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoon of bilona ghee finishes the gravy with the rich aroma Punjabi cooking is known for

steps: Boil 500 g baby potatoes for 10 minutes until just tender, peel and prick them all over so they soak up the gravy.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai and fry the potatoes on medium for 5 minutes until golden, then remove; fry 12 cashews for a minute and reserve to grind into a paste.
Crackle 1 tsp cumin in the oil for 20 seconds, add 2 chopped onions and saute for 8 minutes until deep golden, then stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook a minute.

Add 3 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 7 minutes until the oil separates; cool and blend with the cashews to a smooth paste.
Return the paste to the pan with 1 cup water and simmer on low for 6 minutes, then slide in the fried potatoes and stir to coat.
Cover and dum-cook on low for 8 minutes, then add 2 tbsp butter, 3 tbsp cream, 0.75 tsp garam masala and 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi.
Finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, simmer uncovered for 2 minutes until glossy and rest before serving.
tips: Blending the fried onion-tomato base with cashews gives the signature Punjabi smoothness, so do not skip the blend.
Crush the kasuri methi between your palms before adding to release its full aroma.
If the gravy turns too thick after resting, loosen only with hot water to keep the richness intact.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or laccha paratha, a swirl of cream on top and a side of sirke wale pyaaz (vinegar onions).

variations.name: Kashmiri Punjabi Dum Aloo
variations.description: The Punjabi richness reworked the Kashmiri way, dropping onion and garlic for fennel, dry ginger and a saffron bloom in a smooth yoghurt gravy. The saffron lends both a warm glow and a delicate floral aroma to the fried potatoes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee is the traditional Kashmiri cooking fat and enriches the yoghurt gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: saffron steeped in warm milk gives the gravy its signature colour and perfume

steps: Steep 0.25 tsp Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside to bloom.
Boil 500 g baby potatoes for 10 minutes until just tender, peel and prick them deeply so the gravy penetrates.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and fry the potatoes on medium for 6 minutes until golden all over, then remove them.
Temper 0.25 tsp asafoetida, 0.5 tsp cumin, 4 cloves, 3 cardamom and 1 inch cinnamon in the ghee for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Off the heat, whisk 0.75 cup curd with 1.5 tsp fennel powder, 1 tsp dry ginger powder, 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, then stir it in on low so it does not curdle.
Add 1 cup water and the potatoes, cover and simmer on low for 12 minutes until the gravy thickens and clings.
Stir in the saffron milk, cook 2 more minutes and rest before serving so the colour deepens.
tips: Take the pan off the boil before adding the whisked curd, then return it to low heat while stirring to prevent splitting.
Bloom the saffron in warm, not hot, milk to draw out its colour without scorching the delicate threads.
Fennel powder is the defining spice here, so grind fresh fennel if your powder has lost its aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed basmati or a soft sheermal and a bowl of chilled cucumber raita to balance the fennel warmth.

variations.name: Bengali Punjabi Dum Aloo
variations.description: A Bengali crossover that trades the creamy Punjabi base for a mustard-oil gravy brightened with a touch of sugar and a bhaja masala finish. Sharper and lighter, it keeps the fried potatoes but reframes the whole flavour eastward.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked wood-pressed mustard oil gives the dish its unmistakable Bengali pungency

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery gives the gentle sweet undertone Bengali gravies balance against the sharp mustard oil

steps: Boil 500 g baby potatoes for 10 minutes until just tender, peel and prick them, then rub with 0.25 tsp turmeric and a little salt.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, then fry the potatoes on medium for 5 minutes until golden and set aside.
In the same oil temper 1 bay leaf, 2 dried red chillies and 1 tsp cumin for 20 seconds until they crackle.
Add 2 chopped onions and saute for 6 minutes until pale gold, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger paste and cook a minute.
Mix in 2 chopped tomatoes, the remaining 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1 tsp cumin powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 6 minutes until the masala leaves the oil.
Add three-quarters of a cup of water, return the potatoes, cover and simmer on low for 10 minutes until cooked through.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.5 tsp garam masala, simmer for 2 minutes and serve.
tips: Smoke the mustard oil first so the finished gravy tastes nutty and mellow rather than raw.
A pinch of roasted bhaja masala at the very end deepens the Bengali signature.
Keep this one soupier than the Punjabi original, as it is meant to be eaten with rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and lime, or with luchi for a festive brunch, alongside a sweet tomato chutney.

variations.name: Gujarati Punjabi Dum Aloo
variations.description: A lighter, sweeter cousin where the Punjabi cream gives way to a tangy tomato gravy balanced with jaggery and lemon. It keeps mild heat and a bright finish, echoing Gujarat's signature sweet-sour-spicy harmony.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil is the classic Gujarati kitchen fat and keeps this version light

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery brings the signature Gujarati sweetness that offsets the tomato and lemon tang

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of ghee rounds off the sweet-sour gravy with a warm aroma

steps: Boil 500 g baby potatoes for 10 minutes until just tender, peel and prick them so they take on the tangy gravy.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai and shallow-fry the potatoes on medium for 5 minutes until lightly golden, then set aside.
In the same oil crackle 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin and 8 curry leaves for 20 seconds until they splutter.
Add 1 chopped onion and saute for 4 minutes until translucent, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and 3 chopped tomatoes and cook for 6 minutes until pulpy.
Mix in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander-cumin powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 3 minutes until the oil rises.
Add 1 cup water, return the potatoes, cover and simmer on low for 10 minutes until cooked through and coated.
Stir in 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, simmer 2 minutes off the boil and serve.
tips: Taste and adjust jaggery and lemon together so the sweet and sour stay in balance without cream to soften them.
Add the lemon juice off the heat to keep its fresh brightness.
Mash a couple of the boiled potatoes into the gravy for natural body in place of the Punjabi cashew-cream base.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulka or methi thepla and a bowl of plain curd; sweet chundo pickle on the side plays up the Gujarati profile.

variations.name: Rajasthani Punjabi Dum Aloo
variations.description: A desert-bold take that trades the Punjabi cream for a fiery ground red-chilli paste and a curd gravy cooked in ghee. Onion-light and intensely red, it brings the robust, spice-forward character of Rajasthani kitchens to the dish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rajasthani cooking is generous with ghee, which tempers the intense chilli with richness

steps: Soak 6 dried red chillies in hot water for 15 minutes, then grind to a smooth, bright red paste with a splash of water.
Boil 500 g baby potatoes for 10 minutes until just tender, peel and prick them all over.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai and fry the potatoes on medium for 5 minutes until golden, then remove them.
Temper 1 tsp cumin, 3 cloves, 1 black cardamom and 1 bay leaf in the ghee for 20 seconds, then add 1 chopped onion and saute for 6 minutes until browned.
Stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, the red chilli paste, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 2 tsp coriander powder, and cook for 5 minutes until the ghee separates and the colour turns rich.
Lower the heat and whisk in 0.5 cup curd with 1 tsp salt, cooking gently for 3 minutes so it does not split.
Add three-quarters of a cup of water, return the potatoes, cover and simmer on low for 10 minutes, finish with 0.5 tsp garam masala and serve.
tips: Use milder Kashmiri-type dried chillies for colour and deseed a few if you want less heat.
Add the curd on the lowest heat and stir constantly, as this near onion-free gravy depends on it for body.
This curry only improves overnight, making it a great prepare-ahead dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra roti and white butter, or with jeera rice and a cooling onion-cucumber salad to offset the heat.

variations.name: Classic Punjabi Kofta
variations.description: The quintessential Punjabi kofta: soft paneer-and-potato dumplings in a luscious onion-tomato-cashew gravy scented with kasuri methi. Buttery, mildly sweet and glossy, it is the dish that anchors every North Indian celebration table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: wholegrain binder that keeps the paneer koftas soft yet intact

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee fries the koftas golden and enriches the classic Punjabi gravy

steps: Mash 2 boiled potatoes with 1 cup grated paneer, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta until a smooth, pliable dough forms that rolls without cracking.
Shape into 10 koftas and shallow-fry in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat, rolling for even colour, until golden all over, about 5 minutes; drain.
In the remaining 2 tbsp ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin, add 3 finely chopped onions and cook to a soft gold, about 8 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for a minute.
Add 4 pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.75 tsp salt, and cook until the ghee separates and the masala deepens, about 8 minutes.
Stir in 3 tbsp cashew paste and 1 cup hot water, simmer 4 minutes to a silky gravy, then add 4 tbsp cream and 1 tsp garam masala.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the pot and simmer 2 minutes, then gently place the koftas in just before serving.
Spoon warm gravy over the koftas, rest 2 minutes so they soften slightly, and serve immediately.
tips: Grate the paneer very fine and knead the dough well; any lumps cause the koftas to crack while frying.
Keep koftas and gravy apart until serving so the dumplings stay soft rather than dissolving.
A teaspoon of sugar or a splash of cream balances the tomato tang for the classic mild Punjabi profile.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or jeera rice, garnished with a swirl of cream, slivered almonds and coriander for a festive finish.

variations.name: Bengali Punjabi Kofta
variations.description: A Bengali crossover where the familiar kofta meets pungent Anveshan Mustard Oil and a nutty poppy-seed paste in place of cashew. The gravy turns golden and gently sharp, finished with slit green chillies for a distinctly eastern character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: binds the koftas so they hold in the mustard-poppy gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked to its haze so the koftas and gravy carry a clean Bengali pungency

steps: Mash 3 boiled potatoes with 0.5 cup grated paneer, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta into a firm dough and roll into 10 koftas.
Heat Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil to its haze, cool slightly, and deep-fry the koftas over medium heat until golden, about 4 minutes; drain.
In 3 tbsp of the mustard oil, splutter 0.5 tsp nigella seeds for 20 seconds, then add 2 sliced onions and fry over medium heat to a light brown, about 6 minutes.
Add 1 tbsp ginger paste and 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 0.75 tsp salt, and cook until the tomatoes break down, about 5 minutes.
Stir in 3 tbsp poppy seed paste and 0.75 cup water, then simmer 4 minutes until the gravy thickens to a pale gold and the poppy seeds lose their rawness.
Add 4 slit green chillies, 0.5 tsp sugar and the koftas, spooning the sharp gravy over them, and simmer gently for 3 minutes.
Finish with a teaspoon of raw mustard oil, rest 2 minutes, and serve while pungent and fragrant.
tips: Soak poppy seeds in warm water for 20 minutes before grinding to a smooth, creamy paste without grit.
The pinch of sugar is traditional in Bengali gravies and balances the sharp mustard beautifully.
Do not skip heating the mustard oil to smoking point first, as it removes the raw bitterness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over steamed rice with a wedge of lime and a fried green chilli, ending the meal with a little tomato chutney.

variations.name: Hyderabadi Punjabi Kofta
variations.description: A regal Hyderabadi rendition finished on dum with Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron and fried-onion birista folded through a fragrant, mildly nutty gravy. Slow steam in a sealed pot lends the koftas a delicate, perfumed richness fit for a Nizami table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: keeps the koftas soft through the long dum cooking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the royal fat for frying koftas and enriching the dum gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk for the golden hue and floral perfume of Nizami cooking

steps: Mash 2 boiled potatoes with 1 cup grated paneer, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, and roll into 10 smooth koftas.
Fry the koftas in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat until golden, about 5 minutes, and steep 1 pinch Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk.
In the remaining 2 tbsp ghee, fry 3 thinly sliced onions to a deep brown birista, about 12 minutes, then remove half for garnish and blend the rest to a paste.
Return the onion paste with 4 cardamom and 4 cloves, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 3 tbsp cashew paste, and cook over medium heat for 4 minutes.
Lower the heat and whisk in 0.75 cup yogurt slowly with 0.75 tsp salt, stirring constantly to prevent curdling, then simmer 5 minutes to a smooth ivory gravy.
Add 0.75 cup water, the saffron milk and the koftas, sprinkle 1 tsp garam masala, and scatter the reserved birista on top.
Seal the pot and dum on the lowest heat for 8 minutes, then rest 3 minutes before opening so the saffron aroma floods out.
tips: Fry the birista slowly and evenly to a deep brown, not black, as burnt onions turn the gravy bitter.
Always add yogurt on low heat while stirring so the delicate dum gravy stays smooth.
Reserve some crisp birista and saffron milk to garnish at the table for the full Hyderabadi effect.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sheermal or bagara khana rice, garnished with the reserved fried onions and a few saffron strands.

variations.name: Kerala Punjabi Kofta
variations.description: A coastal twist that swaps cream for coconut milk and fries the koftas in fragrant Anveshan Coconut Oil, tempered with mustard and curry leaves. The gravy is lighter and subtly sweet, carrying the unmistakable aroma of a Malabar kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: binds the koftas so they stay whole in the coconut gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: gives the koftas and tempering their signature Kerala aroma

steps: Mash 2 boiled potatoes with 0.75 cup grated paneer, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, and roll into 10 koftas.
Fry the koftas in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil over medium heat until golden and firm, about 4 minutes, and drain.
In 3 tbsp coconut oil, pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 1 sprig curry leaves, then add 2 sliced onions and cook to soft gold, about 6 minutes.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tbsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp salt, cooking until glossy, about 6 minutes.
Pour in 0.75 cup coconut milk and 0.5 cup water, and bring to the gentlest simmer without letting it boil, about 3 minutes.
Lower in the koftas and simmer softly for 3 minutes so they soak up the sweet, fragrant gravy.
Crisp the second curry-leaf sprig in a teaspoon of coconut oil, pour over the top, and rest 2 minutes before serving.
tips: Keep the flame gentle after the coconut milk goes in to stop it from splitting.
Add thick coconut milk at the very end for the richest flavour and smoothest texture.
A pinch of crushed black pepper at the finish gives the warm Malabar edge without extra chilli.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft appams, malabar parotta or steamed rice, with a side of coconut-shallot chutney.

variations.name: Rajasthani Punjabi Kofta
variations.description: A desert-style reworking where the koftas are fried in pure Anveshan Ghee and simmered in a smoky, yogurt-based gravy of soaked dried red chillies. Fiery and crimson, it trades the mild Punjabi cream for the bold Marwari love of chilli and ghee.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: binds the koftas so they hold in the fiery ghee gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the royal fat that fries the koftas and carries the dried chilli flavour

steps: Mash 2 boiled potatoes with 1 cup grated paneer, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta into a firm dough and roll into 10 koftas.
Shallow-fry the koftas in 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat until golden all around, about 5 minutes, and set aside.
Soak 8 dried red chillies in warm water for 15 minutes, then blend with 2 onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste to a smooth crimson paste.
In the remaining 3 tbsp ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin, add the chilli-onion paste and fry over medium heat until thick and the ghee separates, about 9 minutes.
Lower the heat and whisk 1 cup yogurt with 1 tbsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt, then add slowly while stirring so it does not curdle, and simmer 5 minutes.
Pour in 0.5 cup water and slide in the koftas, simmering gently for 4 minutes until the gravy thickens and coats each one.
Finish with 1 tsp garam masala, rest 2 minutes, and serve while the ghee glistens on top.
tips: Deseed some chillies for colour without punishing heat, using Mathania chillies where possible.
Add whisked yogurt off a rolling boil and stir constantly so it blends smoothly into the ghee.
The chilli paste can be made ahead and refrigerated; the flavour deepens overnight.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra roti and white butter, with sliced onion and green chilli on the side for a desert-thali feel.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Tinda
variations.description: A boldly spiced tinda where the mild gourd meets a double hit of green chillies and freshly cracked black pepper over a peppy onion-tomato base. The heat is layered, not just fiery, with pepper warmth building behind the chilli kick.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a neutral base that lets the pepper and green chilli heat stay sharp and clean

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: finishing with ghee softens the sharp heat into a rounder warmth

steps: Peel and dice the 500 g tinda, finely chop the 2 onions and 2 tomatoes, and slit the 4 green chillies lengthwise.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on medium and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and the slit green chillies for about 30 seconds.

Add the onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 6 minutes until golden, then add the tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder and cook for 5 minutes until pulpy.
Tip in the tinda and 1 tsp salt, toss, cover, and cook on low for 15 to 17 minutes until tender.
Uncover, add 1 tsp freshly cracked black pepper, and stir-fry on medium for 3 minutes to dry out the masala and toast the pepper.
Finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee and toss to gloss the pieces.
Garnish with 2 tbsp coriander leaves and serve hot.
tips: Crack the peppercorns fresh in a mortar just before adding for a sharper, more aromatic heat than pre-ground pepper.
For milder eaters, deseed the green chillies but keep the count so the flavour stays.
A squeeze of lime at the table brightens all that layered heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with cool cucumber raita and hot jeera rice to balance the pepper-and-chilli heat.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Tinda
variations.description: The hottest take in the family, an Andhra kaaram-style tinda blazing with Guntur red chilli, garlic and a sesame-oil tadka of curry leaves. Searing, savoury and deeply garlicky, it is tempered only by a final spoon of ghee.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: gingelly oil stands up to the fierce Guntur chilli the way Andhra cooking demands

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: a final spoon rounds the searing heat into something you can actually savour

steps: Peel and dice the 500 g tinda, finely chop the 1 onion, and crush the 8 garlic cloves to a rough paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil on medium and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, then add the 15 curry leaves and crushed garlic and fry for 1 minute until golden.
Add the onion and cook for 4 minutes until soft, then stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric and the diced tinda with 1 tsp salt.
Cover and cook on low for 13 to 15 minutes until the gourd is tender, stirring once midway.
Uncover, add 2 tsp Guntur red chilli powder and 1 tsp tamarind pulp, and stir-fry on medium for 4 minutes until the masala coats the pieces and turns glossy red.
Finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee and toss for a final minute.
Serve blazing hot with plenty of rice so the fierce chilli has something to lean on.
tips: The tamarind is essential; its sourness balances the Guntur chilli and stops the dish from being one-note heat.
Reduce the chilli to 1 tsp for a family-friendly version without losing the Andhra character.
Rest the dish for 10 minutes before serving so the garlic and chilli mellow and marry.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rice, a dollop of ghee and a bowl of plain curd on the side to cool the palate.

variations.name: Rajasthani Spicy Tinda
variations.description: A smoky, desert-hot tinda built on whole dried red chillies and a mathania-style chilli paste, tempered in ghee and mustard oil for rustic depth. Fiery yet fragrant, it carries the bold, tomato-light character of Rajasthani home cooking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee carries the smoky dried-chilli heat the way desert kitchens intend

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: a spoonful lends the sharp, rustic edge typical of Rajasthani sabzis

steps: Peel and quarter the 500 g tinda, finely chop the 1 large onion, and soak the 6 dried red chillies in hot water for 10 minutes, then grind to a coarse paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee with 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil on medium and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds.
Add the onion and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 6 minutes until golden, then stir in the ground chilli paste and cook for 2 minutes until the raw smell goes.
Add 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1.5 tsp red chilli powder with a splash of water and fry for 2 minutes until the ghee separates.
Fold in the tinda and 1 tsp salt, cover, and cook on low for 16 to 18 minutes until tender and coated in the smoky masala.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp amchur powder and stir-fry uncovered for 2 minutes to concentrate the flavours.
Garnish with 2 tbsp coriander leaves and serve hot.
tips: Soaking and grinding the dried chillies gives a smoky depth that chilli powder alone cannot match.
The amchur stands in for fresh tomato and gives the trademark tang of desert cooking.
Use fewer whole chillies and deseed them for a milder but still smoky result.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot bajra rotis, a knob of white butter and sliced raw onion for a true Rajasthani plate.

variations.name: Kolhapuri Spicy Tinda
variations.description: A Kolhapuri-style tinda fired up with a freshly roasted-and-ground kanda-lasun masala of dry coconut, chillies and warm spices. Dark, intensely aromatic and seriously hot, it brings western Maharashtra's most famous spice blend to the humble gourd.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Kolhapuri cooking uses generous groundnut oil to roast the masala and coconut

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon smooths the fierce Kolhapuri heat

steps: Peel and dice the 500 g tinda and finely chop the 2 onions, setting one chopped onion aside for the masala.

Dry-roast the 3 tbsp dry coconut, 4 dried red chillies, 1 tbsp coriander seeds, 1 tbsp sesame seeds, 1 tsp cumin seeds and 6 garlic cloves in a pan on low for 4 minutes until fragrant and golden, then grind to a coarse dark masala.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on medium and fry the remaining chopped onion for 6 minutes until deep golden.
Add the ground Kolhapuri masala and 0.5 tsp turmeric and roast for 2 minutes with a splash of water until the oil separates and the aroma turns nutty.
Fold in the tinda and 1 tsp salt, cover, and cook on low for 15 to 17 minutes until tender and coated in the dark masala.
Uncover and stir-fry for 2 minutes to thicken, then finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee.
Garnish with 2 tbsp coriander leaves and serve hot.
tips: Roast the coconut and spices low and slow; scorching them turns the masala bitter.
Grind the masala coarse rather than fine so it clings to the gourd and gives texture.
The freshly ground blend keeps for a week in the fridge, so double it for a quick second meal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft jowar bhakri or ghee rice and a wedge of lemon; a bowl of thin buttermilk on the side helps with the heat.

variations.name: Bengali Spicy Tinda
variations.description: A Bengali jhal preparation where tinda is cooked in smoking mustard oil with a bold mustard-and-green-chilli paste, delivering the sinus-clearing pungency the cuisine loves. Sharp, glossy and fiercely aromatic, it needs nothing more than steamed rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the double dose of mustard oil drives the sharp jhal heat this dish is built on

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: just a hint tempers the fierce mustard without dulling the heat

steps: Peel and cube the 500 g tinda and thinly slice the 1 onion, then soak the 1 tbsp mustard seeds for 10 minutes and grind with 3 of the green chillies to a smooth paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until it just smokes, then lower the flame and temper 0.5 tsp nigella seeds and the 2 remaining slit green chillies for 20 seconds.
Add the sliced onion and fry for 4 minutes until soft, then stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder.
Add the tinda cubes and 1 tsp salt, toss, cover, and cook on low for 12 to 14 minutes until nearly tender.
Stir in the mustard-chilli paste with 3 tbsp water, cover, and cook for 4 more minutes until the raw pungency mellows and the gourd is fully soft.
Add 0.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, stir, and simmer uncovered for 1 minute to balance the sharpness.
Garnish with 2 tbsp coriander leaves and serve with rice.
tips: Do not overcook the mustard paste or it turns bitter; add it near the end and cook just until the raw smell fades.
Grinding the mustard with green chillies rather than water alone keeps it from going bitter.
The tiny bit of jaggery is a Bengali trick to round the mustard, so do not skip it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot steamed rice with a drizzle of raw mustard oil and an extra green chilli on the side.

variations.name: Classic Butter Chana Masala
variations.description: A creamy, buttery cousin of Punjabi chole, where soft chickpeas swim in a smooth tomato-cashew gravy enriched with butter and finished with cream. Milder and silkier than dhaba chole, it is the makhani treatment applied to chana, glossy and instantly comforting.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: used to bhuno the tomato base for a nutty depth beneath the butter

steps: Soak 1.5 cups chickpeas overnight and pressure-cook with 1 tsp salt for 6 to 7 whistles until completely soft, reserving the liquid.
Simmer 4 tomatoes, 2 onions, 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 15 cashews in a cup of water for 12 minutes, cool, blend smooth and strain for a silky base.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with 2 tbsp butter, add 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder off the heat, then carefully pour in the strained puree.
Simmer the gravy on low for 10 minutes, stirring often, until it thickens, darkens and the fat floats to the top.
Add the cooked chickpeas with about a cup of their liquid and 0.25 tsp salt, and simmer 8 minutes, mashing a ladleful of chana to thicken the gravy.
Finish with 4 tbsp cream, 0.75 tsp garam masala, 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi and the last tbsp of butter, swirling gently before serving.
tips: Straining the puree gives the smooth makhani-style body that sets this apart from rustic chole.
Mash some chickpeas into the gravy so it clings and turns velvety without extra cream.
Balance a too-tangy gravy with a teaspoon of jaggery, or a too-sweet one with a squeeze of lemon.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or laccha paratha, a swirl of cream and julienned ginger on top, alongside a kachumber salad.

variations.name: Kashmiri Butter Chana Masala
variations.description: A fragrant Kashmiri buttered chana glowing red from soaked chillies and perfumed with saffron, fennel and dry ginger, in the Wazwan style that skips onion and garlic. Cooked in ghee and butter with a curd base, it is aromatic and mild-hot rather than creamy-sweet.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the base fat that blooms the fennel and dry ginger central to Kashmiri cooking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk to give the buttery chana its glow and gentle perfume

steps: Soak 1.5 cups chickpeas overnight and pressure-cook with 1 tsp salt for 6 to 7 whistles until soft, reserving the liquid. Steep a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with 2 tbsp butter and crackle 3 cardamom pods and 3 cloves for 20 seconds.
Off the heat add 2 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1.5 tsp fennel powder, 0.75 tsp dry ginger powder and 0.5 tsp turmeric, stirring 15 seconds so they bloom without burning.
Whisk 0.75 cup curd smooth, add it off the flame while stirring constantly, then return to low heat and cook 4 minutes into a glossy red gravy.
Add the cooked chickpeas with about a cup of their liquid and 0.25 tsp salt, pour in the saffron milk, and simmer 10 minutes, mashing a few chickpeas to thicken.
Rest the dish covered for 5 minutes so the saffron and fennel aromas settle fully before serving.
tips: Bloom the spice powders in hot fat off the heat to keep the fennel from turning bitter.
Add the curd gradually and off the boil so it blends in without splitting.
A handful of ghee-fried almond slivers makes a beautiful traditional garnish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with warm sheermal or a saffron pulao, with a Kashmiri radish-walnut salad on the side.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Butter Chana Masala
variations.description: A buttered chana carrying the dark, roasted soul of goda masala and a toasted-coconut base, giving it an earthy, smoky-sweet depth. Richer than a plain usal yet distinctly Maharashtrian, it is a warmly spiced departure from northern buttered chole.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the staple Maharashtrian oil that toasts the coconut-onion masala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a small spoon of natural sweetness balances the goda masala the Maharashtrian way

steps: Soak 1.5 cups chickpeas overnight and pressure-cook with 1 tsp salt for 6 to 7 whistles until soft, reserving the liquid.
Dry-roast 4 tbsp desiccated coconut until deep golden, about 4 minutes, then grind with a splash of water to a paste.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil with 2 tbsp butter, fry 2 chopped onions and 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 7 minutes until browned, then add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and cook 5 minutes.
Stir in the roasted coconut paste and 2.5 tsp goda masala with 1 tsp salt and fry on medium for 4 minutes until the masala darkens and smells toasty.
Add the cooked chickpeas with about a cup of their liquid and 0.25 tsp salt, and simmer 10 minutes, mashing a few to thicken the gravy.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder to balance, cook 2 minutes, and finish with 2 tbsp fresh coriander.
tips: Roast the coconut only to golden, not brown, to keep the gravy nutty rather than bitter.
Goda masala is potent, so taste before reaching for extra garam masala.
The teaspoon of jaggery is the classic Maharashtrian counterpoint to the dark spice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri or ghee-brushed chapati and a cooling koshimbir of cucumber and roasted peanuts.

variations.name: Andhra Butter Chana Masala
variations.description: Butter meets fire in this Andhra chana, where a roasted Guntur chilli and garlic paste brings blazing heat that the butter only just tempers. Tangy with tamarind and pungent with a curry-leaf and sesame temper, it is bold, glossy and unapologetically spicy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: the weighty Andhra oil that stands up to Guntur chilli and garlic

steps: Soak 1.5 cups chickpeas overnight and pressure-cook with 1 tsp salt for 6 to 7 whistles until soft, reserving the liquid.
Dry-roast 6 Guntur chillies, 1 tbsp coriander seeds and 1 tsp cumin on low for 2 minutes, then grind with 10 garlic cloves to a coarse paste.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil with 1.5 tbsp butter, pop 15 curry leaves, then fry 2 chopped onions for 6 minutes until browned; add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric and cook 4 minutes.
Stir in the roasted chilli-garlic paste and fry on medium for 4 minutes until the raw smell goes and the sesame oil separates.
Add the cooked chickpeas with about a cup of their liquid, 0.25 tsp salt and 1.5 tsp tamarind pulp, and simmer 10 minutes, mashing a few to thicken.
Swirl in the last 1 tbsp butter to round the heat, simmer 2 minutes, and serve glistening red and fiery.
tips: Deseed a few Guntur chillies to keep the colour while easing the ferocious heat.
The butter softens the chilli edge but does not tame it, so keep curd on the table.
Tamarind is essential here; its sourness is what keeps the heat balanced.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice topped with ghee, or with pulka, and a cooling onion raita alongside.

variations.name: Bengali Butter Chana Masala
variations.description: A Bengali-leaning buttered chana that starts with a pungent mustard-oil and nigella temper, then softens into a lightly sweet, buttery gravy finished with roasted bhaja masala. It marries sarson ka tel sharpness with a rich butter body, quite unlike either Punjabi chole or plain ghugni.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked first, its pungency gives the buttered chana a distinct Bengali sharpness

steps: Soak 1.5 cups chickpeas overnight and pressure-cook with 1 tsp salt for 6 to 7 whistles until soft, reserving the liquid.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it smokes, lower the heat, add 2 tbsp butter, then temper 0.5 tsp nigella seeds and 1 bay leaf for 15 seconds.
Add 2 finely chopped onions and 1.5 tbsp ginger paste and fry 6 minutes until golden, then add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.75 tsp turmeric and 2 tsp cumin-coriander powder and cook 5 minutes.
Add the cooked chickpeas with about a cup of their liquid, 0.25 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp sugar, and simmer 10 minutes, mashing a few to thicken the buttery gravy.
Stir in 1 tsp roasted bhaja masala and the last 1 tbsp butter, cooking 2 minutes so the smoky aroma runs through.
Finish with a small drizzle of raw mustard oil for the traditional Bengali kick before serving.
tips: Smoke the mustard oil first so its raw pungency mellows before the butter goes in.
The pinch of sugar is Bengali balance rather than sweetness, so do not leave it out.
Bhaja masala added right at the end keeps its smoky aroma sharp and fresh.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot luchi or soft parathas, with a wedge of lime and thin onion rings on the side.

variations.name: Classic Butter Chole
variations.description: A rich, creamy take on chole where soft-cooked chickpeas swim in a buttery tomato-cashew gravy, mellowed with cream and kasuri methi. Less tangy than street-style chana and altogether more indulgent, it eats like a bean version of a makhani curry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee deepens the buttery makhani base beyond plain butter alone

steps: Pressure-cook the 1.5 cups soaked chickpeas with 0.75 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 5-6 whistles until completely soft, then reserve the liquid.
Boil 1 chopped onion, 4 pureed tomatoes and 12 cashews with 1 cup water for 8 minutes, then cool and blend to a smooth paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with 2 tbsp butter over medium heat, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in the tomato-cashew paste with 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 0.5 tsp salt; cook 8 minutes until the ghee floats to the surface.
Add the cooked chickpeas with 1.5 cups reserved liquid, mashing a handful to thicken, and simmer on low for 12 minutes.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the pan, stir in 3 tbsp cream and 0.5 tsp garam masala, and simmer 2 minutes until glossy and rich.
tips: Straining the blended gravy gives the ultra-smooth restaurant texture, though it is optional at home.
Mash a handful of chickpeas into the gravy for a thicker body that hugs every bean.
Balance any tomato sharpness with a pinch of sugar so the curry stays mellow and buttery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or jeera rice, with a swirl of cream and a scatter of coriander on top.

variations.name: Kashmiri Butter Chole
variations.description: A regal Kashmiri spin on buttery chole where saffron and Kashmiri chilli glow through a curd-and-ghee gravy scented with fennel and dry ginger. Rich yet aromatic, it lends the humble chickpea Wazwan grandeur.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee is the traditional fat behind every rich Kashmiri gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: Saffron gives the buttery gravy its glowing colour and perfume

steps: Pressure-cook the 1.5 cups soaked chickpeas with 0.75 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 5-6 whistles until soft, then reserve the liquid.
Soak 1 pinch Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside to steep.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with 1 tbsp butter over medium heat and crackle 3 cardamom, 3 cloves and a 1-inch cinnamon stick for 30 seconds.
Lower the heat, add 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder for 10 seconds, then whisk in 0.75 cup curd slowly, and add 2 tsp fennel powder, 0.5 tsp dry ginger and 0.5 tsp salt.
Add the cooked chickpeas with 1.5 cups reserved liquid and the saffron milk, and simmer on low for 12 minutes.
Uncover and cook 3 minutes to thicken the gravy into a deep glowing red that coats every chickpea.
tips: Add the curd off high heat and whisk continuously so the buttery gravy stays smooth.
Fennel and dry ginger define authentic Kashmiri flavour; do not swap in garam masala.
This chole deepens overnight as the saffron and fennel meld into the beans.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed basmati rice or Kashmiri pulao and a side of walnut chutney.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Butter Chole
variations.description: A Puneri twist on buttery chole where goda masala and a roasted peanut-coconut paste give the chickpeas a dark, nutty richness. Smoky and mildly sweet, it trades the North Indian cream note for Deccan depth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the base of everyday Maharashtrian cooking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A ghee finish adds the buttery richness this dish is named for

steps: Pressure-cook the 1.5 cups soaked chickpeas with 0.75 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 5-6 whistles until soft, then reserve the liquid.
Dry-roast 3 tbsp peanuts and 3 tbsp desiccated coconut separately until golden, about 3 minutes each, then grind into a coarse paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds for 15 seconds until they pop.
Add 2 chopped onions and fry until golden, 6 minutes, then add 3 chopped tomatoes and cook until soft, 5 minutes.
Stir in the peanut-coconut paste, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tbsp goda masala and 0.5 tsp salt; cook 4 minutes until the oil separates.
Add the cooked chickpeas with 1.5 cups reserved liquid, simmer on low for 12 minutes, then finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee stirred through.
tips: Grind the peanuts and coconut only coarsely; a little texture is what defines the Maharashtrian gravy.
Use a fresh, aromatic goda masala since it carries the whole flavour of the dish.
A squeeze of lemon at the table brightens the deep, nutty gravy beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bhakri or steamed rice and a fresh koshimbir salad of cucumber and peanuts.

variations.name: Kerala Butter Chole
variations.description: A coconut-milk chickpea curry in the Kerala kadala idiom, tempered in coconut oil with curry leaves and finished with a roasted coconut-fennel paste. Creamy, fragrant and gently spiced, it echoes the beloved breakfast kadala curry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed coconut oil is essential to authentic Kerala kadala

steps: Pressure-cook the 1.5 cups soaked chickpeas with 0.75 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 5-6 whistles until soft, then reserve the liquid.
Dry-roast 0.5 cup grated coconut with 0.5 tsp fennel seeds until deep golden, about 4 minutes, then grind with a splash of water into a paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds for 15 seconds, then add 14 curry leaves and 6 sliced shallots.
Fry the shallots until golden, about 4 minutes, then add 2 tsp coriander powder and 0.5 tsp turmeric and stir for 20 seconds.
Add the cooked chickpeas with 1.5 cups reserved liquid and the roasted coconut paste, and simmer on low for 10 minutes.
Lower the heat, pour in 1 cup coconut milk and warm gently for 3 minutes without boiling, until the gravy turns thick and creamy.
tips: Roasting the coconut dark is what gives kadala curry its signature toasty brown gravy.
Do not boil after the coconut milk goes in, or the curry can split; a gentle warm-through keeps it silky.
Shallots give a deeper sweetness than regular onions and are traditional to Kerala cooking.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with puttu, appam or steamed rice for the classic Kerala kadala breakfast.

variations.name: Andhra Butter Chole
variations.description: A fiery Andhra rendition of buttery chole where Guntur chilli and a garlic-forward tempering in groundnut oil bring serious heat, tamed just slightly by a ghee finish. Bold, tangy with tamarind, and built for those who love the burn.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the everyday frying medium of Andhra kitchens

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A ghee finish softens the Guntur heat into a rounder richness

steps: Pressure-cook the 1.5 cups soaked chickpeas with 0.75 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 5-6 whistles until soft, then reserve the liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat and crackle 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, then add 12 curry leaves and 8 crushed garlic cloves.
Fry the garlic 1 minute until pale gold, then add 2 chopped onions and cook until golden, 6 minutes.
Add 3 chopped tomatoes, 1.5 tsp Guntur chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 0.5 tsp salt; cook 6 minutes until the tomatoes collapse.
Add the cooked chickpeas with 1.5 cups reserved liquid and 1 tsp tamarind paste, and simmer on low for 12 minutes.
Finish with 1 tbsp hot Anveshan Ghee poured over the chole, simmering 1 minute so the fiery gravy turns glossy.
tips: Guntur chilli is genuinely hot; begin with 1 tsp and build up to the authentic Andhra burn.
Tamarind keeps the heat from tasting flat, so add it once the beans have softened.
The ghee finish is deliberate here, rounding the sharp heat into a fuller, buttery flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and extra ghee, or with hot pooris and a cooling raita on the side.

variations.name: Classic Butter Kofta
variations.description: Soft paneer-and-vegetable koftas in a luscious buttery tomato-cashew gravy, the malai-kofta style everyone loves at celebrations. Mildly sweet, silky and rich, with the koftas added at the last moment to stay tender. Pure indulgence on a plate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: High-smoke and neutral, it fries the koftas to an even gold

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee deepens the buttery richness of the malai gravy

steps: Mix 1 cup grated paneer with 0.5 cup mashed potato, 3 tbsp cornflour and 0.5 tsp salt into a smooth, firm dough that holds a ball.
Roll into 12 balls and deep-fry in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil at medium heat 3-4 minutes until golden all over, then drain on paper.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat, fry the 2 chopped onions 7 minutes until soft and pale gold, add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Add the tomato puree with 1 tsp red chilli and 1 tsp salt and cook 9 minutes, then stir in 4 tbsp cashew paste and cook 3 minutes until the gravy turns glossy.
Loosen with 1 cup hot water, simmer 5 minutes, then swirl in 3 tbsp butter, 4 tbsp cream and crushed kasuri methi for a velvety malai gravy.
Gently place the koftas in the gravy just 2-3 minutes before serving so they soften slightly but keep their shape.
tips: Cornflour binds the soft paneer koftas better than besan here, giving a smoother, more delicate ball.
Fry a test kofta first; if it cracks, add a spoon more cornflour before frying the rest.
Keep the gravy slightly sweet and mild to let the buttery cashew richness shine.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or jeera rice, a swirl of cream, a few crushed cashews and a sprinkle of kasuri methi on top.

variations.name: Awadhi Butter Kofta
variations.description: A nawabi butter kofta in a pale ivory korma of cashew, curd and fried onion, richly buttered yet delicately perfumed with kewra and mace. Where the classic is red-buttery, this is white, aromatic and courtly. Fit for a Lucknawi dawat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Fries the koftas and keeps the white gravy pale and clean

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee gives the buttery richness expected of a nawabi korma

steps: Mix 1 cup grated paneer with 0.5 cup mashed potato, 3 tbsp cornflour and 0.5 tsp salt into a firm dough, roll into 12 balls and deep-fry in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil at medium heat 3-4 minutes until pale gold.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over low-medium heat, add the crushed cardamom and mace, and let them perfume the fat 30 seconds without browning.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 3 tbsp fried onion paste and cook 2 minutes on low, keeping everything pale.
Whisk in the 0.5 cup curd off the heat, return to low heat, add 5 tbsp cashew paste, 0.5 tsp white pepper and 1 tsp salt, and cook gently 4 minutes.
Loosen with 1 cup hot water and simmer 6 minutes on low into a smooth ivory gravy, never letting it boil hard.
Slip in the koftas and 0.5 tsp kewra water 2-3 minutes before serving so they warm through and the perfume stays fresh.
tips: Keep the flame low the whole time so the korma stays pale ivory rather than browning.
Add kewra water in the tiniest amount at the end, as too much makes the dish taste soapy.
The extra cashew paste is what gives this korma its buttery body without any tomato.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with warm sheermal or rumali roti, garnished with slivered pistachios and a few saffron strands.

variations.name: Kashmiri Butter Kofta
variations.description: Buttery koftas in a Kashmiri ruby gravy bloomed with saffron and Kashmiri chilli, spiced with fennel and dry ginger and softened with curd and butter, all without onion or garlic. Mild, red and perfumed with valley warmth. A festive, elegant kofta.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Fries the koftas crisp for the ruby gravy to coat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: Saffron lends the ruby glow and delicate wazwan perfume

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries the fennel and saffron aromatics of a Kashmiri gravy

steps: Soak 0.25 tsp Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 3 tbsp warm water and set aside to bloom.

Mix 1 cup grated paneer with 0.5 cup mashed potato, 3 tbsp cornflour and 0.5 tsp salt into a firm dough, roll into 12 balls and deep-fry in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil at medium heat 3-4 minutes until golden.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat, add the cloves, cardamom and cinnamon, and sizzle 30 seconds, then lower the heat and stir in 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli followed quickly by the tomato puree.
Cook 7 minutes until the ghee floats red, whisk in the 0.5 cup curd off the heat, then return to low heat and add 2 tsp fennel powder, 1 tsp dry ginger and 1 tsp salt.
Loosen with 1 cup hot water and the bloomed saffron water, simmer 6 minutes, then swirl in 2 tbsp butter for a glossy ruby gravy.
Slip the koftas in gently 2-3 minutes before serving so they soak up the fragrant gravy without breaking.
tips: Add the curd off the heat and stir as it warms to keep the ruby gravy from splitting.
Keep it onion and garlic free, letting fennel and dry ginger define the aroma.
Bloom the saffron in warm water only to protect its colour and delicate scent.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice or a soft roti, finished with saffron strands and slivered almonds.

variations.name: Gujarati Butter Kofta
variations.description: A softer, sweeter butter kofta tuned to the Gujarati palate, where jaggery and a hint of tamarind round a buttery coriander-cumin gravy tempered with curry leaves. Gentler and more khatta-meetha than the North Indian malai kofta. Comforting with phulka or rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The everyday Gujarati fat, high-smoke for frying the koftas

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery brings the signature Gujarati sweetness balancing the tamarind

steps: Mix 1 cup grated paneer with 0.5 cup mashed potato, 3 tbsp cornflour and 0.5 tsp salt into a firm dough, roll into 12 balls and deep-fry in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil at medium heat 3-4 minutes until golden, then drain.
In a separate pan heat 3 tbsp of the frying oil over medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard and cumin seeds 20 seconds, then add the curry leaves.
Add the chopped onion and saute 5 minutes until soft, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and cook 1 minute.
Pour in the tomato puree with 2 tsp coriander-cumin powder and 1 tsp salt, and simmer 8 minutes until the oil separates.
Loosen with 1 cup hot water, add 1 tbsp tamarind pulp and 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, and simmer 5 minutes, then swirl in 2 tbsp butter.
Taste and adjust the sweet-sour balance, then slip in the koftas 2-3 minutes before serving so they stay soft.
tips: Build the khatta-meetha gradually, tasting after the tamarind and jaggery to land the right balance.
Add the koftas at the very end, since the tangy gravy will soften them faster than a plain one.
A pinch of cinnamon-clove powder in the tempering deepens the Kathiawadi warmth.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft ghee-brushed phulka or plain rice, a side of kachumber and sweet mango chunda.

variations.name: Andhra Butter Kofta
variations.description: A bold southern butter kofta where fiery Guntur chilli and a garlic-forward tomato gravy are smoothed with butter and a curry-leaf tempering. The heat hits first, then the butter rounds it off. Comfort food with a serious kick.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The Andhra base fat, high-smoke for frying and taming raw chilli

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee rounds the fiery gravy and adds a rich finish

steps: Mix 1 cup grated paneer with 0.5 cup mashed potato, 3 tbsp cornflour and 0.5 tsp salt into a firm dough, roll into 12 balls and deep-fry in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil at medium heat 3-4 minutes until golden.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and the curry leaves 30 seconds, then fry the 8 crushed garlic cloves until pale gold.
Add the 2 chopped onions and saute 7 minutes until browned, guarding the garlic from burning.
Pour in the tomato puree with 2 tsp Guntur chilli, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook 9 minutes until the oil rises red.
Loosen with 1 cup hot water and simmer 5 minutes, then swirl in 2 tbsp butter off the heat to tame the chilli into a glossy gravy.
Slip the koftas in gently 2-3 minutes before serving so they soak up the fiery-buttery sauce without breaking.
tips: Guntur chilli is intense, so treat the amount as a firm starting point and let the butter balance the heat.
Fry the garlic before the onions to build the deep pungent base of an Andhra gravy.
A squeeze of lime at the table keeps the heat lively rather than flat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain rice and papad, a bowl of curd to cool the palate and extra butter on the side.

variations.name: Classic Butter Mushroom Matar
variations.description: A rich, buttery take on mushroom matar with a smooth tomato-cashew gravy, mellow spice and a glossy cream-and-butter finish. Seared mushrooms and sweet peas make it a crowd-pleasing, mildly indulgent curry in the makhani spirit.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil sears the mushrooms cleanly before the buttery gravy takes over

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoon of bilona ghee deepens the makhani richness alongside the butter

steps: Quarter 300 g mushrooms and sear in 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on high for 3 minutes until golden, then set aside.
In the same pan add 2 roughly chopped onions, 4 chopped tomatoes, 15 cashews and 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste with half a cup of water, and simmer covered for 12 minutes until everything is soft.
Cool the mixture, blend to a very smooth puree and strain it through a coarse sieve for a silky gravy.
Melt 3 tbsp butter in the pan, add the strained puree with 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and simmer on low for 8 minutes until it thickens and the butter surfaces.
Add 1 cup peas and half a cup of water, cover and cook on medium for 6 minutes until the peas are tender.
Fold in the seared mushrooms and simmer covered on low for 4 minutes so they soak up the buttery gravy.
Stir in 4 tbsp cream, 0.5 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, simmer 2 minutes and serve.
tips: Straining the puree is the single biggest step toward a smooth, restaurant-style makhani gravy.
Balance any tomato tartness with a small pinch of jaggery rather than more cream.
Add the mushrooms near the end so they stay firm and do not weep water into the gravy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or a soft kulcha, finished with a swirl of cream and a scatter of crushed kasuri methi.

variations.name: Kashmiri Butter Mushroom Matar
variations.description: A regal, saffron-scented version that builds warmth from fennel and dry ginger in a smooth yoghurt-and-cashew gravy without onion or garlic. The saffron gives a soft golden hue and a floral aroma to the buttery mushrooms and peas.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee is the authentic Kashmiri fat and enriches the yoghurt gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: saffron bloomed in warm milk lends the gravy its golden hue and floral perfume

steps: Soak 0.25 tsp Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk, and separately soak 12 cashews in hot water for 10 minutes, then grind the cashews to a smooth paste.
Quarter 300 g mushrooms and sear in 1 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee on high for 3 minutes until golden, then set aside.
In the remaining 2 tbsp ghee temper 3 cardamom, 3 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Off the heat, whisk 0.5 cup curd with 1.5 tsp fennel powder, 1 tsp dry ginger powder, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, then stir it in on low so it does not split.
Add the cashew paste and 1 cup water, bring to a gentle simmer, then add 1 cup peas and cook covered on medium for 6 minutes until tender.
Fold in the seared mushrooms and simmer covered on low for 4 minutes so they take on the spiced gravy.
Stir in the saffron milk, cook 2 minutes and rest before serving so the colour and aroma settle.
tips: Whisk the curd smooth and add it only on low heat while stirring to keep the gravy from curdling.
The cashew paste gives a buttery body without heavy cream, keeping the dish rich but elegant.
Fennel and dry ginger are the defining spices here, so grind them fresh if your powders have faded.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a soft sheermal or plain naan and a bowl of chilled walnut raita to echo the Kashmiri table.

variations.name: Gujarati Butter Mushroom Matar
variations.description: A lighter, sweeter version where the makhani richness is softened with jaggery and a squeeze of lemon for the classic Gujarati sweet-sour-spicy balance. Mild heat and a bright tomato gravy make it fresh and approachable.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil is the classic Gujarati kitchen fat and keeps the gravy light

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery brings the signature Gujarati sweetness that offsets the tomato and lemon tang

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of ghee rounds off the sweet-sour gravy with warmth

steps: Quarter 300 g mushrooms and sear in 1 tbsp of the Anveshan Groundnut Oil on high for 3 minutes until golden, then set aside.
In the remaining 2 tbsp oil crackle 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin and 8 curry leaves for 20 seconds until they splutter.
Add 1 chopped onion and saute for 4 minutes until translucent, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and 3 chopped tomatoes and cook for 6 minutes until pulpy.
Mix in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander-cumin powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 3 minutes until the oil rises.
Add 1 cup peas and 1 cup water, cover and simmer on medium for 6 minutes until the peas soften.
Fold in the seared mushrooms and cook covered on low for 4 minutes so they absorb the tangy gravy.
Stir in 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, simmer 2 minutes off the boil and serve.
