tips: Taste after adding jaggery and lemon and adjust together so the sweet and sour stay balanced.
Add the lemon juice off the heat to keep it fresh and bright.
For a little more body without cream, blend one of the cooked tomatoes into the gravy before adding the peas.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulka or methi thepla and a bowl of plain curd; sweet chundo pickle on the side plays up the Gujarati profile.

variations.name: Rajasthani Butter Mushroom Matar
variations.description: A bolder desert-style version where a ground red-chilli paste and a curd gravy replace the makhani cream, all cooked in ghee. Onion-light and intensely red, it brings robust Rajasthani heat to the mushrooms and peas.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rajasthani cooking is generous with ghee, which tempers the fierce chilli with richness

steps: Soak 6 dried red chillies in hot water for 15 minutes, then grind to a smooth, bright red paste with a splash of water.
Quarter 300 g mushrooms and sear in 1 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee on high for 3 minutes until golden, then set aside.
In the remaining 2 tbsp ghee temper 1 tsp cumin, 3 cloves and 1 black cardamom for 20 seconds, then add 1 chopped onion and saute for 6 minutes until browned.
Stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, the red chilli paste, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 2 tsp coriander powder, and cook for 5 minutes until the ghee separates and the colour turns rich.
Lower the heat and whisk in 0.5 cup curd with 1 tsp salt, cooking gently for 3 minutes so it does not split.
Add 1 cup peas and 1 cup water, cover and simmer on medium for 6 minutes until the peas are tender.
Fold in the seared mushrooms, cook covered on low for 4 minutes, finish with 0.5 tsp garam masala and serve.
tips: Use milder Kashmiri-type chillies and deseed a few if you want the deep colour without extreme heat.
Add the curd on the lowest heat and stir constantly, as this near onion-free gravy relies on it for body.
This curry deepens in flavour overnight and reheats beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra roti and a dab of white butter, or with jeera rice and a cooling onion-cucumber salad.

variations.name: Kerala Butter Mushroom Matar
variations.description: A coastal reworking where roasted coconut and coconut milk stand in for cream and butter, scented with curry leaves and fennel. The mushrooms and peas simmer into a mellow, aromatic curry carried by the perfume of coconut oil.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil gives the unmistakable Kerala aroma from the first sizzle

steps: Dry-roast 0.5 cup grated coconut on low for 4 minutes until golden and nutty, then grind to a coarse paste with a little water.
Quarter 300 g mushrooms and sear in 1 tbsp of the Anveshan Coconut Oil on high for 3 minutes until golden, then set aside.
In the remaining 2 tbsp oil crackle 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp fennel seeds and 15 curry leaves for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 2 sliced onions and saute for 7 minutes until soft and golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 1 chopped tomato and cook for 4 minutes.
Mix in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, then add the roasted coconut paste, 1 cup peas and 1 cup water.
Cover and simmer on medium for 6 minutes until the peas soften, then fold in the seared mushrooms and cook 4 minutes more.
Pour in 0.5 cup coconut milk, warm through on low for 2 minutes without boiling, and serve.
tips: Roast the grated coconut only to golden, not brown, to keep the gravy sweet and free of bitterness.
Add the coconut milk at the very end off a boil so it stays smooth and does not split.
Finish with a fresh tempering of mustard seeds and curry leaves in coconut oil for an extra coastal lift.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with appam, malabar parotta or steamed red rice and a small bowl of thin buttermilk alongside.

variations.name: Classic Dhaba-style Kaddu
variations.description: A robust roadside-dhaba pumpkin cooked in a deeply browned onion-tomato masala with kasuri methi and a smoky charcoal finish, sitting between the familiar khatta-meetha and a full-blown spicy sabzi. Bold, rustic and generously spiced for a truckers' thali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: dhabas cook in generous oil over a fierce flame for that deep bhuna base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoon at the end delivers the rich, glossy dhaba finish

steps: Peel and deseed the 500 g pumpkin and cut into 3 cm chunks, finely chop the 3 onions, and puree the 3 tomatoes.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on medium-high and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add the onions and 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry hard for 8 minutes until deep golden brown.
Pour in the tomato puree with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder and bhuna for 7 minutes until the oil separates.
Add the pumpkin and 1 tsp salt, cover, and cook on low for 14 to 16 minutes until soft, then mash a few chunks to thicken the masala.
Crush 1.5 tsp kasuri methi and add with 1 tsp garam masala and 0.75 tsp amchur powder, stir-frying uncovered for 3 minutes.
For the dhaba touch, set a small heated piece of charcoal in a steel bowl in the pan, drizzle a few drops of oil over it, cover for 2 minutes, then remove; stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee.
Garnish with 3 tbsp coriander leaves and serve hot.
tips: Brown the onions really deeply; that colour is the whole secret to dhaba-style robustness.
The charcoal dhungar is optional but gives the genuine smoky roadside aroma.
The amchur keeps this from tipping into dessert-sweet while still tasting rich.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with buttered tandoori rotis or lachha paratha, sliced onions and a green chilli on the side.

variations.name: Punjabi Dhaba-style Kaddu
variations.description: A hearty Punjabi dhaba pumpkin in a thick, ghee-rich onion-tomato masala with ginger juliennes and a good hit of kasuri methi. Full-bodied and comforting, it eats like the vegetable cousin of a dhaba dal, made for mopping up with roti.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: Punjabi dhabas ladle in ghee for the rich, glossy masala they are known for

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: added with the ghee to keep the onions from scorching on the high flame

steps: Peel and deseed the 500 g pumpkin and cut into 3 cm chunks, finely chop the 3 onions, puree the 3 tomatoes, and cut the 2 inch ginger into fine juliennes, saving some for garnish.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee with 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on medium-high and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and the 1 bay leaf for 20 seconds.
Add the onions, half the ginger juliennes and the 6 crushed garlic cloves and fry for 8 minutes until richly golden.
Pour in the tomato puree with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder and bhuna for 7 minutes until the ghee floats.
Add the pumpkin and 1 tsp salt, cover, and cook on low for 14 to 16 minutes until soft, mashing a few pieces to thicken.
Crush 1.5 tsp kasuri methi and add with 1 tsp garam masala, then swirl in 2 tbsp fresh cream and cook uncovered for 2 minutes.
Top with the reserved ginger juliennes and 3 tbsp coriander leaves and serve hot.
tips: Reserve some raw ginger juliennes for the top; it is the classic Punjabi dhaba flourish.
For a richer plate, swirl in 2 tbsp fresh cream with the garam masala.
A knob of white butter melting on top just before serving makes it truly dhaba-style.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot lachha parathas, a raw onion-and-lemon salad and a tall glass of salted lassi.

variations.name: Awadhi Dhaba-style Kaddu
variations.description: A refined Lucknawi pumpkin gently perfumed with kewra, fried-onion paste and warm whole spices in a silky yoghurt gravy. Fragrant and mellow rather than fiery, it lends Awadhi finesse to the rugged dhaba format.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: Awadhi cooking favours ghee for its perfumed, dum-style richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: used to fry the onions crisp for the birista paste base

steps: Peel and deseed the 500 g pumpkin and cut into 3 cm chunks, and thinly slice the 3 onions, then fry them in 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on medium for 8 minutes until crisp and golden, and grind to a smooth paste with a little water.
In the same pan add 2 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee and crackle the 3 cardamom pods, 3 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon for 30 seconds.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the fried-onion paste and cook for 3 minutes until it deepens in colour.
Lower the flame and whisk in the 0.5 cup yoghurt with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, stirring for 3 minutes until the ghee separates.
Fold in the pumpkin and 1 tsp salt, cover, and cook on low for 14 to 16 minutes until soft in the silky gravy.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala and 0.5 tsp kewra water, cover, and rest off the heat for 3 minutes so the aroma infuses.
Stir gently to keep the soft pumpkin from breaking and serve warm while fragrant.
tips: Kewra is potent, so measure carefully; a few drops too many will overwhelm the dish.
The fried-onion birista paste gives natural sweetness and body without needing tomato.
Finish with a rest under the lid, the Awadhi dum touch, to let the perfume settle.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with warm rumali roti or a saffron pulao and a side of sliced cucumber and mint raita.

variations.name: Rajasthani Dhaba-style Kaddu
variations.description: A desert-highway pumpkin smoky with roasted dried red chillies and finished in mustard oil and ghee, with yoghurt for body and amchur for a savoury-sour lift. Rustic, fiery and full-flavoured, built for a traveller's plate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: the fat of choice on the Rajasthan highway, carrying the smoky chilli heat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: a spoon adds the pungent, rustic backbone of a desert dhaba

steps: Peel and deseed the 500 g pumpkin and cut into 3 cm chunks, finely chop the 2 onions, and whisk the 0.5 cup yoghurt smooth with the 2 tsp coriander powder to keep it from splitting.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee with 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil on medium and roast the 5 broken dried red chillies with 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds until smoky.
Add the onions and 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 7 minutes until golden brown.
Lower the flame, pour in the spiced yoghurt with 0.5 tsp turmeric, and stir constantly for 3 minutes until thickened and glossy.
Fold in the pumpkin and 1 tsp salt, cover, and cook on low for 14 to 16 minutes until soft, mashing a few chunks to thicken.
Add 1 tsp amchur powder, crush in 1 tsp kasuri methi with 1 tsp garam masala, and stir-fry uncovered for 2 minutes.
Garnish with 2 tbsp coriander leaves and serve hot.
tips: Roast the dried chillies just until they darken; burnt ones make the whole dish bitter.
Keep the flame low while the yoghurt cooks and stir without stopping to avoid curdling.
The yoghurt base makes this sabzi hold up for hours, true to its travel-food roots.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot missi roti, a spoon of garlic chutney and thick chaas alongside.

variations.name: Haryanvi Dhaba-style Kaddu
variations.description: A ghee-lavished Haryanvi dhaba pumpkin cooked simply with green chillies, ajwain and a light tomato masala, letting fresh dairy fat lead the flavour. Wholesome, gently spiced farmhouse food from the fields of Haryana.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: Haryana's dairy-rich kitchens use ghee lavishly, and it defines this sabzi

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a touch alongside the ghee raises the smoke point for the initial frying

steps: Peel and deseed the 500 g pumpkin and cut into 3 cm chunks, finely chop the 2 onions and 2 tomatoes, grate the 1 inch ginger, and slit the 3 green chillies.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee with 1 tsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on medium and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.5 tsp ajwain for about 20 seconds.
Add the onions, grated ginger and slit green chillies and fry for 6 minutes until soft and pale gold.
Stir in the tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 2 tsp coriander powder and cook for 5 minutes until the ghee glistens on top.
Add the pumpkin and 1 tsp salt, cover, and cook on low for 14 to 16 minutes until meltingly soft, mashing a few pieces to thicken.
Crush 1 tsp kasuri methi and add with 0.75 tsp garam masala, stir-frying uncovered for 2 minutes so the ghee coats every piece.
Garnish with 2 tbsp coriander leaves and serve hot.
tips: The ajwain aids digestion and cuts the richness of all that ghee, so keep it in.
Use good bilona ghee since it is the star flavour here, not a background fat.
Keep the spicing gentle so the pumpkin and ghee stay the heroes of the plate.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thick bajra khichdi topped with more ghee, or hot phulkas and a glass of fresh chaas.

variations.name: Classic Dry Gajar Matar
variations.description: A quick, dry stir-fry of diced carrots and peas cooked until just tender with a light cumin tempering and minimal masala. The carrots keep a slight bite and their sweetness stays front and centre. It is the fuss-free everyday sabzi that comes together in minutes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a light wood-pressed oil keeps this dry sabzi clean and non-greasy

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add 2 chopped green chillies and 1 inch grated ginger, frying for 30 seconds until aromatic.
Add the 3 diced carrots and 1 cup peas, then sprinkle 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, tossing to coat evenly.
Cover and cook on low for 12-14 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the carrots are just tender and the peas are soft.
Uncover and stir-fry on medium-high for 3 minutes so any moisture evaporates and the edges catch a little colour.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp amchur, toss for a minute, then finish with 2 tbsp fresh coriander and serve.
tips: No onion or tomato is needed here; keeping it dry lets the carrots' sweetness shine.
Add a pinch of sugar if the carrots are not very sweet to boost their flavour.
Amchur added at the end keeps the tang bright rather than dull.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot chapatis and a bowl of curd, or pack it into a tiffin with rice.

variations.name: Gujarati Dry Gajar Matar
variations.description: A sweet-savoury Gujarati sambharo-style sabzi where shredded carrots and peas are quickly tossed with a mustard tempering, jaggery and lemon. It stays slightly crunchy and bright, striking the classic khatta-mitha balance. A warm-weather favourite eaten fresh off the stove.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the traditional Gujarati oil for a quick, light sambharo

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the signature sweetness that balances the tang in a Gujarati sambharo

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop, then add a pinch of asafoetida, 8 curry leaves and 2 slit green chillies.
Once the tempering splutters for 15 seconds, add the 1 cup green peas and cook for 3 minutes until they soften.
Add the thickly grated carrots along with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, tossing well to coat.
Cook uncovered on medium-high for 4-5 minutes, stirring often, so the carrots soften slightly but keep a fresh crunch.
Lower the heat, stir in 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook for a minute until it melts into the carrots.
Turn off the heat, squeeze in 1 tbsp lemon juice, toss and serve immediately while crisp.
tips: Grate the carrots thick, not fine, so they hold a little crunch in this quick-cooked sambharo.
Serve it fresh; the crunch fades if it sits too long.
Balance jaggery and lemon by taste so the dish is neither too sweet nor too sour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a side with thepla and chai, or alongside khichdi for a light supper.

variations.name: Rajasthani Dry Gajar Matar
variations.description: A bold, dry Marwari sabzi where carrots and peas are cooked in ghee with whole dried red chillies and a punch of coriander and amchur. There is no onion or tomato, keeping it desert-style dry and intense. The ghee tempers the chilli heat into something warm and rounded.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee softens the whole-chilli heat with a nutty desert richness

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat, then add 3 whole dried red chillies and let them darken and turn smoky for 15 seconds.
Add 1 tsp cumin, 0.5 tsp ajwain and a pinch of asafoetida, letting them crackle for 15 seconds.
Lower the heat and add 2 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp turmeric with a splash of water so they do not burn, cooking for 30 seconds.
Add the 3 diced carrots and 1 cup peas with 1 tsp salt, toss to coat in the spiced ghee, then cover and cook on low for 12-14 minutes until tender.
Uncover and stir-fry on medium-high for 3 minutes so the vegetables dry and take on a roasted edge.
Sprinkle 0.75 tsp amchur, toss for a minute to spread the tang and serve hot.
tips: Break the dried chillies for more heat, or keep them whole for smoky aroma with milder fire.
Ajwain balances the ghee and aids digestion, so keep it in even though the quantity is small.
This travels well and tastes good at room temperature, making it a good tiffin choice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra or missi roti and a dollop of ghee, with sliced onions on the side.

variations.name: Odia Dry Gajar Matar
variations.description: A homely Odia-style dry sabzi tempered with panch phoron in mustard oil and lightly scented with crushed garlic. The carrots stay soft and sweet, carrying the gentle five-spice aroma. It is the simple, everyday vegetable of an Odia rice plate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday Odia fat, its gentle pungency lifting the sweet carrots

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai on medium-high until it smokes, then reduce the heat and add 1 tsp panch phoron and 2 dried red chillies, crackling for 20 seconds.
Add 4 crushed garlic cloves and 2 slit green chillies, frying for 30 seconds until the garlic is fragrant.
Add the 3 diced carrots and 1 cup peas, then sprinkle 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp cumin powder and 1 tsp salt, tossing to coat.
Add 4 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 12-14 minutes until the carrots are soft, stirring once midway.
Uncover and stir-fry on medium for 3 minutes so the vegetables dry and glisten with the mustard oil.
Garnish with 2 tbsp fresh coriander and serve warm.
tips: Temper the panch phoron whole in hot oil; it should never go in raw or unbloomed.
Crushed garlic in the tadka is characteristic of Odia cooking, so add it generously.
A little extra green chilli suits the mild carrots if you like more heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rice, a spoon of ghee and a tangy tomato khatta on the side.

variations.name: Kumaoni Dry Gajar Matar
variations.description: A rustic Pahari sabzi from the Kumaon hills, tempered with jakhya seeds that pop and crackle for a nutty crunch. Cooked in mustard oil with barely any spice, it celebrates the sweetness of hill-grown carrots. Honest, minimal mountain cooking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the staple Kumaoni cooking fat, a natural match for jakhya

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai on medium-high until it smokes, then lower the heat and add 1 tsp jakhya seeds, letting them crackle and pop for about 20 seconds.
Add 2 dried red chillies, 4 crushed garlic cloves and 2 slit green chillies, frying for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the 3 diced carrots and 1 cup peas, then sprinkle 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, tossing to coat.
Add 4 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 12-14 minutes until the carrots are tender, stirring occasionally.
Uncover and stir-fry on medium for 3 minutes so the vegetables dry and the jakhya aroma comes through.
Garnish with 2 tbsp fresh coriander and serve warm.
tips: Let the jakhya crackle fully before adding anything; that popping is the essence of the tempering.
If you cannot find jakhya, cumin works but you will lose the signature nutty crunch.
Keep the masala minimal so the sweet hill carrots and jakhya stay in the foreground.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with mandua roti or plain rice and a bowl of gahat (horse gram) dal for a hearty Pahari meal.

variations.name: Classic Handi Malai Kofta
variations.description: Creamy paneer koftas slow-steamed in a sealed clay handi with whole spices and a cashew-cream gravy. The dum method rounds every flavour into a mellow, aromatic richness, letting the koftas drink up the perfumed sauce.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: wholegrain binder that keeps the koftas soft through the long dum

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: clean oil for frying the delicate koftas golden

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: brushed on before sealing so the dum steam carries its aroma

steps: Mash 2 boiled potatoes with 1.5 cups grated paneer, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta into a smooth dough and roll into 10 koftas.
Deep-fry the koftas in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat until pale gold, about 4 minutes, and drain gently.
Boil 2 onions for 8 minutes, cool, and blend to a smooth pale paste, keeping it light for the classic look.
In a handi with 3 tbsp oil, crackle 2 bay leaves, 4 cardamom, 4 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the onion paste and cook 4 minutes without browning.
Stir in 4 tbsp cashew paste with 0.75 tsp salt and 1 cup hot water, and simmer 5 minutes to a silky ivory gravy.
Add 5 tbsp cream, 1 tsp sugar and 0.5 tsp garam masala, place the koftas in, and brush 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the surface.
Seal the handi and dum on the lowest heat for 7 minutes, then rest 3 minutes before opening at the table.
tips: Boil the onions instead of frying to keep the gravy pale and the flavour delicate.
Handle the fried koftas gently and add them near the end so the dum plumps them without breaking.
A tight seal traps the aroma; open the handi only in front of your guests for maximum effect.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the whole handi with a cream swirl and slivered almonds, alongside saffron pulao or butter naan.

variations.name: Awadhi Handi Malai Kofta
variations.description: A Lucknawi korma-style handi scented with kewra water and finished on gentle dum in Anveshan Ghee. Fried-onion birista and a nut paste give the koftas a regal, faintly floral richness in the true Awadhi tradition.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: binds the koftas softly for the delicate korma gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the fat that fries the koftas and the birista, as in Lucknawi kitchens

steps: Mash 2 boiled potatoes with 1.5 cups grated paneer, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta into a smooth dough and roll into 10 koftas.
Fry the koftas in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat until pale gold, about 4 minutes, and set aside.
In the remaining 3 tbsp ghee, fry 3 thinly sliced onions to a deep golden birista, about 12 minutes, then blend to a smooth paste with a little water.
Return the onion paste to the handi with 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 4 cardamom and 1 blade mace, and cook gently for 4 minutes without browning.
Stir in 3 tbsp cashew paste, then lower the heat and whisk in 0.5 cup yogurt slowly with 0.75 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp white pepper, simmering 5 minutes to a smooth ivory gravy.
Add 0.75 cup water, 3 tbsp cream and the koftas, then sprinkle 0.5 tsp kewra water over the top.
Seal the handi and dum on the lowest heat for 8 minutes, then rest 3 minutes so the kewra aroma settles before serving.
tips: Use kewra water sparingly; a few drops perfume the whole handi, while too much turns it soapy.
White pepper keeps the korma pale and lends gentle heat without the colour of red chilli.
Fry the birista slowly to golden, not brown, so the gravy stays light and never bitter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sheermal or ultra-thin rumali roti, garnished with a few strands of fried onion and slivered pistachio.

variations.name: Kashmiri Handi Malai Kofta
variations.description: A fragrant Valley handi coloured with Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron and warmed by fennel and dry ginger, cooked in mustard oil. Slow dum lets the koftas soak up a golden, floral gravy quite unlike any northern korma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: binds the koftas for the fragrant saffron dum gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the traditional Kashmiri fat that carries the fennel and saffron

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm milk for the golden hue and floral aroma

steps: Mash 2 boiled potatoes with 1.5 cups grated paneer, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta into a smooth dough and roll into 10 koftas.
Fry the koftas in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil, pre-heated to its haze and cooled slightly, over medium heat until golden, about 4 minutes; drain.
Steep 1 pinch Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk while you build the gravy.
In 3 tbsp of the mustard oil, crackle 4 cardamom and 3 cloves, then add 1.5 tbsp fennel powder and 1 tsp dry ginger powder off the heat so they bloom without burning.
Lower the heat and whisk in 0.75 cup yogurt with 3 tbsp cashew paste and 0.75 tsp salt, stirring constantly, then simmer 5 minutes to a smooth rust-gold gravy.
Add 0.75 cup water, the saffron milk, 2 tbsp cream and the koftas to the handi.
Seal and dum on the lowest heat for 7 minutes, then rest 3 minutes so the saffron and fennel aromas mingle before serving.
tips: Fennel and dry ginger define Kashmiri gravies, so use them fresh and do not substitute garam masala.
Add yogurt only on low heat with steady stirring to keep the delicate gravy from splitting.
Float a few saffron strands on top at serving for colour and fragrance.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed Kashmiri rice and a spoon of saffron milk drizzled over, with a cooling walnut chutney on the side.

variations.name: Kerala Handi Malai Kofta
variations.description: A coastal handi where the creamy koftas dum-cook in a coconut-milk gravy fragrant with curry leaves and Anveshan Coconut Oil. Lighter and subtly sweet, it brings the aroma of a Malabar kitchen to the malai kofta.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: binds the koftas so they stay whole through the dum

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: gives the koftas and tempering their signature Kerala aroma

steps: Mash 2 boiled potatoes with 1.5 cups grated paneer, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta into a smooth dough and roll into 10 koftas.
Fry the koftas in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil over medium heat until golden and firm, about 4 minutes, and drain.
In a handi with 3 tbsp coconut oil, pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 1 sprig curry leaves, then add 2 sliced onions and 3 slit green chillies and cook to soft gold, about 6 minutes.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 0.5 tsp turmeric, fry for a minute, then add 2 tbsp cashew paste and 0.5 cup water and simmer 3 minutes.
Pour in 1 cup coconut milk with 0.75 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp black pepper, and bring to the gentlest simmer without boiling.
Lower in the koftas, cover the handi, and dum on the lowest heat for 6 minutes so they soak up the sweet, fragrant gravy.
Crisp the second curry-leaf sprig in a teaspoon of coconut oil, pour over the top, and rest 3 minutes before serving.
tips: Add thick coconut milk last and keep the heat gentle so it never splits.
Black pepper rather than heavy chilli gives the warm Malabar character to this gravy.
A short dum is enough; over-steaming softens the koftas too much in the thin coconut gravy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with appams, malabar parotta or steamed matta rice, with a side of coconut-shallot chutney.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Handi Malai Kofta
variations.description: A Deccan handi where the creamy koftas dum-cook in a smoky goda masala gravy deepened by roasted peanuts and coconut. Cooked in wood-pressed groundnut oil, it layers the malai richness with the dark, aromatic spice of Maharashtra.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: binds the koftas for the robust goda masala dum gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the classic Maharashtrian oil for frying and building the masala

steps: Mash 2 boiled potatoes with 1.5 cups grated paneer, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta into a soft dough and roll into 10 koftas.
Fry the koftas in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat until golden, about 4 minutes, and drain.
Dry-roast 3 tbsp peanuts and 2 tbsp dry coconut until dark and fragrant, then blend with 1 chopped tomato to a coarse paste.
In a handi with 3 tbsp oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin, add 3 sliced onions and fry over medium heat to deep brown, about 10 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste.
Add 1.5 tbsp goda masala, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.25 tsp red chilli powder and 0.75 tsp salt, fry a minute, then mix in the peanut-coconut paste and cook until oil separates, about 5 minutes.
Pour in 1 cup hot water and 2 tbsp cream, simmer 4 minutes to a glossy gravy, then place the koftas in.
Cover and dum on the lowest heat for 7 minutes so the koftas absorb the black masala, then rest 3 minutes before serving.
tips: Roast the peanuts and coconut to a rich brown for the deep, nutty base that defines the gravy.
Goda masala is smoky-sweet, so avoid adding sugar and let it carry the flavour.
Keep a little cream aside to swirl on top, balancing the smoky spice with malai softness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft chapati or masala bhaat, garnished with fresh coriander and a light dusting of goda masala.

variations.name: Classic Handi Mushroom Matar
variations.description: Cooked and served in an earthen handi, this version leans on whole spices and slow steam to build a deep, layered gravy around seared mushrooms and sweet peas. Sealing the handi traps the aroma so every bite is fragrant and mildly creamy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil sears the mushrooms and carries the whole-spice aroma through the slow dum

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoon of bilona ghee drizzled before sealing the handi perfumes the dish during dum

steps: Quarter 300 g mushrooms and sear in 1 tbsp of the Anveshan Groundnut Oil on high for 3 minutes until golden, then set aside; fry 10 cashews in the same oil for a minute and reserve to grind into a paste.
In the remaining 2 tbsp oil temper 1 bay leaf, 3 cardamom, 4 cloves, 1 inch cinnamon and 1 tsp cumin for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 2 chopped onions and saute for 7 minutes until deep golden, then stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook a minute.
Add 3 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 7 minutes until the oil separates.
Add the cashew paste, 1 cup peas and 1 cup water, cover and simmer on medium for 6 minutes until the peas are tender.
Fold in the seared mushrooms, drizzle 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the top, cover the handi tightly and dum-cook on the lowest heat for 8 minutes.
Uncover, swirl in 3 tbsp cream, simmer for 2 minutes and rest 5 minutes before serving straight from the handi.
tips: Seal the handi lid with a strip of dough or a heavy weight to trap the steam and aroma during dum.
Fried cashew paste gives body without heavy cream, so add cream only for the final gloss.
Keep the heat at its lowest during dum or the gravy catches at the base of the handi.
variations.servingSuggestion: Bring the sealed handi to the table and crack it open for aroma, serving with saffron pulao or garlic naan and a kachumber salad.

variations.name: Kashmiri Handi Mushroom Matar
variations.description: A no-onion, no-garlic handi built the Kashmiri way on fennel, dry ginger and a bloom of saffron, slow-steamed in a yoghurt-cashew gravy. The sealed handi concentrates the floral saffron and warm spice into a golden, aromatic curry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee is the authentic fat for a Kashmiri handi and rounds out the yoghurt gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Kashmiri saffron bloomed in warm milk gives the sealed handi its glow and perfume

steps: Bloom 0.25 tsp Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk, and separately soak 12 cashews in hot water for 10 minutes, then grind the cashews to a smooth paste.
Quarter 300 g mushrooms and sear in 1 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee on high for 3 minutes until golden, then set aside.
In the remaining 2 tbsp ghee add 0.25 tsp asafoetida, 4 cloves, 3 cardamom and 1 inch cinnamon, and let them sizzle for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Off the heat, whisk 0.5 cup curd with 1.5 tsp fennel powder, 1 tsp dry ginger powder, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, then stir it into the handi on low so it does not split.
Add the cashew paste, 1 cup peas and 1 cup water, cover and simmer on medium for 6 minutes until the peas soften.
Fold in the seared mushrooms, cover the handi and dum-cook on the lowest heat for 8 minutes so they take on the spiced gravy.
Stir in the saffron milk, cook uncovered for 2 minutes and rest before serving so the colour and aroma settle.
tips: Add the whisked curd only on low heat while stirring, as the sealed dum works best when the gravy has not split at the start.
Fennel and dry ginger replace the onion-garlic base entirely, so do not swap in garam masala.
This handi tastes even better reheated, when the saffron and spices bloom further.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed basmati or a soft sheermal and a cooling walnut or boondi raita to offset the warm spices.

variations.name: Odia Handi Mushroom Matar
variations.description: An Odisha-style handi tempered with panch phoron, the five-spice blend of eastern India, and cooked in mustard oil. The whole-seed tempering and light gravy give the mushrooms and peas an earthy, aromatic character with gentle heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil is the everyday Odia fat and pairs naturally with panch phoron

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoon of ghee at the end softens the mustard-oil sharpness and adds aroma

steps: Quarter 300 g mushrooms, heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a handi until it just smokes, then sear the mushrooms on high for 3 minutes until golden and set aside.
In the same oil temper 1 tsp panch phoron, 1 bay leaf and 2 dried red chillies for 30 seconds until the seeds crackle and turn aromatic.
Add 2 chopped onions and saute for 6 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook a minute until the raw smell fades.
Mix in 2 chopped tomatoes, 0.75 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp cumin powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 6 minutes until the oil separates.
Add 1 cup peas and 1 cup water, cover and simmer on medium for 6 minutes until the peas are tender.
Fold in the seared mushrooms, cover the handi and dum-cook on low for 6 minutes so they take on the spice.
Stir in 0.5 tsp garam masala and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, simmer for 2 minutes and serve garnished with coriander.
tips: Temper the panch phoron until the fenugreek smells nutty but pull it before it darkens, or it turns bitter.
Keep the gravy light and pourable, the way Odia homes serve it with rice.
Mash a cracked tomato into the gravy for body without needing any cream.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a wedge of lime, or with soft rotis; a side of dalma or simple dal completes the Odia thali.

variations.name: Kerala Handi Mushroom Matar
variations.description: A coastal handi where roasted coconut and coconut milk replace cream, scented with curry leaves and fennel and slow-steamed to meld the flavours. The mushrooms and peas turn mellow and fragrant, carried by the aroma of coconut oil.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil delivers the signature Kerala aroma from the first sizzle

steps: Dry-roast 0.5 cup grated coconut on low for 4 minutes until golden and nutty, then grind to a coarse paste with a little water.
Quarter 300 g mushrooms and sear in 1 tbsp of the Anveshan Coconut Oil on high for 3 minutes until golden, then set aside.
In the remaining 2 tbsp oil crackle 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp fennel seeds and 15 curry leaves for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 2 sliced onions and saute for 7 minutes until soft and golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 1 chopped tomato and cook for 4 minutes.
Mix in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, then add the roasted coconut paste, 1 cup peas and 1 cup water.
Cover the handi and simmer on medium for 6 minutes until the peas soften, then fold in the seared mushrooms and dum-cook on low for 5 minutes.
Pour in 0.5 cup coconut milk, warm through on low for 2 minutes without boiling, and serve with a final tempering of curry leaves in coconut oil.
tips: Roast the grated coconut only to golden, not brown, to keep the gravy sweet and free of bitterness.
Add the coconut milk at the very end off a boil so it stays smooth and does not split.
A last tempering of mustard seeds and curry leaves in coconut oil poured over the top deepens the coastal aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with appam, malabar parotta or steamed red rice and a small bowl of thin buttermilk on the side.

variations.name: Rajasthani Handi Mushroom Matar
variations.description: A desert-bold handi where a ground red-chilli paste and a curd gravy cooked in ghee replace the cream, slow-steamed to let the mushrooms drink up the fiery masala. Onion-light and intensely red, it brings robust Rajasthani heat to the dish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rajasthani cooking is generous with ghee, which tempers the fierce chilli with richness

steps: Soak 6 dried red chillies in hot water for 15 minutes, then grind to a smooth, bright red paste with a splash of water.
Quarter 300 g mushrooms and sear in 1 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee on high for 3 minutes until golden, then set aside.
In the remaining 2 tbsp ghee temper 1 tsp cumin, 3 cloves, 1 black cardamom and 1 bay leaf for 20 seconds, then add 1 chopped onion and saute for 6 minutes until browned.
Stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, the red chilli paste, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 2 tsp coriander powder, and cook for 5 minutes until the ghee separates and the colour turns rich.
Lower the heat and whisk in 0.5 cup curd with 1 tsp salt, cooking gently for 3 minutes so it does not split, then add 1 cup peas and 1 cup water.
Cover the handi and simmer on medium for 6 minutes until the peas soften, then fold in the seared mushrooms and dum-cook on low for 6 minutes.
Finish with 0.5 tsp garam masala, simmer 2 minutes and serve straight from the handi.
tips: Use milder Kashmiri-type chillies and deseed a few for deep colour without punishing heat.
Add the curd on the lowest heat and stir constantly, as this near onion-free gravy relies on it for body.
This curry deepens overnight, making it an ideal make-ahead dish for a spread.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra roti and a dab of white butter, or with jeera rice and a cooling onion-cucumber salad.

variations.name: Classic Handi Soya Chunk
variations.description: A slow-simmered soya curry cooked in a narrow-mouthed clay handi so the whole spices and steam stay sealed in. Cardamom, cinnamon and cloves perfume a deep, browned onion-tomato gravy that soaks into the plump chunks. The dum finish gives an earthy roundness a quick fry cannot match.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil carries the whole-spice aromatics through the long dum.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon of bilona ghee stirred in during the dum gives the handi its rich aroma.

steps: Boil 1.5 cups soya chunks in salted water for 5 minutes, then drain, rinse and squeeze each chunk dry.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a clay handi, add 1 tsp cumin, 4 green cardamom, 1 inch cinnamon, 4 cloves and 1 bay leaf, and let them crackle and release fragrance for about 40 seconds.
Add 3 finely chopped onions and 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry patiently until deep brown, about 10 minutes, as this colour sets the gravy's depth.
Stir in 3 pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, and cook until the oil pools at the edges, about 8 minutes.
Add the squeezed soya chunks with 1.5 cups hot water, stir well, then add 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, cover the handi and dum on the lowest flame for 12 minutes.
Uncover, fold in 3 tbsp coriander, and let it rest for 5 minutes so the whole spices settle before serving.
tips: Soak a new clay handi in water for 20 minutes before first use so it does not crack on the flame.
Brown the onions fully; a pale masala gives a flat, watery handi with no depth.
The chunks soak up more flavour overnight, making this even better as a next-day meal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve from the handi with tandoori roti or steamed basmati, a raw onion salad and a dab of pickle.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Handi Soya Chunk
variations.description: A slow handi scented with goda masala and finished with a roasted coconut-onion paste in the Malvani style. Wood-pressed groundnut oil and a spoon of jaggery give the dark, smoky-sweet balance of the Konkan. The long dum draws the nutty masala deep into the soya chunks.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the classic Deccan fat that lets goda masala lead the handi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery powder mellows the pungent goda masala into a warm, rounded handi.

steps: Boil 1.5 cups soya chunks in salted water for 5 minutes, then drain, rinse and squeeze them dry.
Dry roast 4 tbsp grated coconut with 1 sliced onion until both turn deep brown, about 6 minutes, then grind to a coarse Malvani-style paste.
Warm 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a handi, splutter 1 tsp cumin and 12 curry leaves, then add the 2 remaining chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and brown for 8 minutes.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.25 tsp red chilli powder and 2.5 tsp goda masala, and cook until the oil separates, about 7 minutes.
Fold in the roasted coconut paste and cook for 3 minutes, then add the squeezed soya chunks with 1.5 cups hot water and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder.
Cover the handi and dum on low for 12 minutes, then finish with 2 tbsp coriander and rest covered for 5 minutes.
tips: Roast the coconut-onion paste to a real brown for the signature Malvani depth.
Push up the chilli powder for a fiery Kolhapuri handi, or keep it mild for a Konkani style.
This handi freezes well; reheat gently with a splash of hot water.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri or steamed rice, a spoon of thecha and sliced cucumber.

variations.name: Gujarati Handi Soya Chunk
variations.description: A softer, sweeter handi following Gujarat's sweet-sour tradition, kept light and slightly soupy. Anveshan Jaggery Powder and roasted peanut give body while whole spices scent the slow simmer. It is a homely one-pot curry made for soaking into soft rotli.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A modest amount of wood-pressed groundnut oil keeps this handi light, the Gujarati way.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery powder gives this handi its gentle Gujarati sweet-sour signature.

steps: Boil 1.5 cups soya chunks in salted water for 5 minutes, then drain, rinse and squeeze them dry.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a handi, crackle 1 tsp cumin, 1 inch cinnamon and 3 cloves, then add 2 chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and soften for 5 minutes.
Add 3 pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 2 tsp coriander-cumin powder, and simmer until thick and glossy, about 8 minutes.
Stir in 2 tbsp roasted peanut powder and cook for 2 minutes to thicken and enrich the base.
Add the squeezed soya chunks with 2 cups hot water and 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, cover the handi, and simmer gently for 10 minutes until lightly soupy.
Off the heat, stir in 1 tbsp lemon juice and 2 tbsp coriander, and balance the sweet-sour-salt before serving.
tips: Keep this handi on the thinner side; the peanut powder thickens it as it rests.
Add lemon at the end so its freshness survives the long simmer.
A pinch of asafoetida with the cumin makes the whole curry lighter and more fragrant.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thin phulka, steamed rice and a bowl of cool chhaas, with a little chundo on the side.

variations.name: Bengali Handi Soya Chunk
variations.description: An eastern handi built on pungent Anveshan Mustard Oil and a whole-spice tempering of bay leaf, dried red chilli and cardamom. Fried potatoes and slit green chillies join the pot in true dalna style. The slow dum lets the mustard oil mellow into a warm, rounded curry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil brings the sharp, warming pungency that anchors this handi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing teaspoon of ghee balances the mustard oil and lifts the dum aroma.

steps: Boil 1.5 cups soya chunks in salted water for 5 minutes, then drain, rinse and squeeze them dry.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a handi until it smokes and pales, fry 2 cubed potatoes until golden, about 5 minutes, and set them aside.
In the same oil, temper 1 tsp cumin, 2 bay leaves, 2 dried red chillies and 3 green cardamom for 30 seconds, then add 2 chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger paste and fry until golden, about 7 minutes.
Stir in 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.75 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, and cook until the mustard oil surfaces, about 8 minutes.
Return the potatoes, add the squeezed soya chunks, 3 slit green chillies and 2 cups hot water, then cover and dum on low for 12 minutes until the potatoes are tender.
Finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee, rest covered for 4 minutes, and serve.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to smoking first so its raw bitterness mellows into clean warmth.
Fry the potatoes before the dum so they hold their shape rather than crumbling.
A pinch of sugar with the tomatoes gives the subtle sweetness typical of a dalna.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice or luchi, a wedge of lime and extra slit green chillies on the side.

variations.name: Kerala Handi Soya Chunk
variations.description: A coastal handi finished in coconut milk with a shallot-curry leaf tempering fried in Anveshan Coconut Oil. Roasted coconut and fennel give the soya chunks the mellow, aromatic depth of a Kerala stew. The slow simmer draws the coconut sweetness deep into the chunks.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil gives the shallot tempering its unmistakable Kerala fragrance.

steps: Boil 1.5 cups soya chunks in salted water for 5 minutes, then drain, rinse and squeeze them dry.
Dry roast 0.5 cup grated coconut with 0.5 tsp fennel over low heat until deep brown, about 5 minutes, then grind to a smooth paste with a little water.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a handi, add 10 sliced shallots, 1 inch cinnamon and 10 curry leaves, and fry until the shallots caramelise, about 5 minutes.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 1 chopped tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, and cook until the tomato melts, about 5 minutes.
Stir in the roasted coconut paste and the squeezed soya chunks with 1 cup hot water, cover, and simmer on low for 12 minutes.
Pour in 1 cup coconut milk, warm gently for 3 minutes without boiling, and finish with the last curry leaves crackled in coconut oil.
tips: Add coconut milk only at the end and keep it below a boil so it does not split.
Deeply roasted coconut gives the dark, nutty Kerala colour and aroma.
Small shallots melt into a sweeter base than large onions, so use them if you can.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with puttu, appam or steamed red rice, with crisp pappadam and a coconut thoran.

variations.name: Classic Home-style Sem
variations.description: The everyday sem sabzi cooked the way it is in most North Indian homes, gently spiced and simmered until soft rather than crisp. A light onion-tomato base lets the beans stay the focus, with just enough masala to make them comforting. Quick, wholesome and lunchbox-friendly.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a light wood-pressed oil keeps this everyday sabzi clean and digestible

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a tiny bit softens the everyday masala without making it sweet

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add the chopped onion and cook for 4-5 minutes until soft and pale, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for a minute.
Add the chopped tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, cooking for 4 minutes until the tomato turns pulpy.
Add the 400 g broad beans and 1 tsp salt, mix well, then sprinkle 4 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 14-16 minutes until the beans are soft, stirring occasionally.
Uncover and cook on medium for 2 minutes to dry off any excess water.
Stir in 0.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, finish with 2 tbsp fresh coriander and serve warm.
tips: Cook the beans a touch softer than a stir-fry for a mellow, home-style texture.
A splash of water and a covered simmer is all it takes; avoid deep-frying the masala.
Leftovers make a great paratha stuffing when mashed lightly with a little extra garam masala.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulkas and a bowl of moong dal, with a spoon of pickle on the side.

variations.name: Gujarati Home-style Sem
variations.description: A gently sweet-and-spicy Gujarati sem where jaggery and a squeeze of lemon create the classic khatta-mitha balance. The masala is light, the beans soft, and a pinch of sugar-like jaggery rounds every bite. It is the kind of everyday shaak served in a Gujarati thali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: groundnut oil is the traditional Gujarati cooking medium for everyday shaak

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the signature sweet note that defines the Gujarati khatta-mitha balance

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop, then add 0.5 tsp cumin, a pinch of asafoetida, 8 curry leaves and 2 slit green chillies.
Once the tempering splutters for 15 seconds, add the 400 g broad beans and toss to coat in the oil.
Sprinkle in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp coriander-cumin powder and 1 tsp salt, mixing well so the spices coat the beans.
Add 4 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 13-15 minutes until the beans are soft, stirring once or twice.
Uncover and stir in 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, cooking on low for 2 minutes until it melts and glazes the beans.
Take off the heat, squeeze in 1 tbsp lemon juice, toss and serve.
tips: Balance is everything here; taste and adjust jaggery and lemon so neither dominates.
Dhana jeeru (coriander-cumin powder) is the Gujarati pantry staple that gives this its familiar flavour.
Keep the beans just soft, not mushy, for the best home-style shaak texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as part of a thali with rotli, dal-bhaat and a spoon of chhundo pickle.

variations.name: Tamil Home-style Sem
variations.description: A simple Tamil poriyal where broad beans are steamed soft and tossed with a curry-leaf and mustard tempering, brightened with fresh coconut. Cooked in sesame oil, it is light, aromatic and everyday. A pinch of urad dal in the tadka adds a subtle nutty crunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed gingelly oil gives Tamil poriyal its characteristic earthy aroma

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadai on medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop, then add 1 tsp urad dal and 1 tsp chana dal and fry until golden, about 30 seconds.
Add 2 dried red chillies, 12 curry leaves and 2 chopped green chillies, sizzling for 15 seconds until aromatic.
Add the 400 g finely chopped broad beans, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, tossing to coat in the tempering.
Sprinkle 4 tbsp water, cover and steam on low for 12-14 minutes until the beans are soft, stirring once midway.
Uncover and cook on medium for 2 minutes to evaporate any water left in the pan.
Turn off the heat, fold in 3 tbsp fresh grated coconut and serve while fragrant.
tips: Chop the beans small so they steam quickly and evenly in the classic poriyal style.
Add the coconut off the heat to keep it fresh and moist rather than toasted.
The twin dals in the tempering are what give poriyal its signature nutty crunch, so do not skip them.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a side with sambar rice and rasam, or with curd rice for a light, cooling meal.

variations.name: Odia Home-style Sem
variations.description: A homely Odia sem bhaja-torkari lightly spiced with panch phoron and a fresh grind of garlic. The beans cook in mustard oil until soft, with a subtle sweetness and a mustard-seed aroma. It is the unfussy everyday vegetable of an Odia meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday Odia cooking fat, lending gentle pungency to the soft beans

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai on medium-high until it smokes, then lower the heat and add 1 tsp panch phoron and 2 dried red chillies, letting them crackle for 20 seconds.
Add 4 crushed garlic cloves and the chopped onion, frying for 4-5 minutes until the onion is soft and lightly golden.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp cumin powder off the direct flame so they do not scorch.
Add the 400 g broad beans and 1 tsp salt, toss to coat, then add 4 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 13-15 minutes until soft.
Uncover and stir-fry on medium for 2-3 minutes so the beans dry and take on a light glaze.
Scatter 2 tbsp fresh coriander over the top and serve warm.
tips: Panch phoron must be tempered whole in hot oil first; never stir it raw into the beans.
Crushed garlic in the tempering is a hallmark of Odia home cooking, so add it generously.
Keep the sabzi soft and lightly moist rather than dry-fried for the true home-style feel.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rice, a dollop of ghee and a side of dalma for a comforting Odia meal.

variations.name: Kumaoni Home-style Sem
variations.description: A rustic Pahari sem from the Kumaon hills, tempered with jakhya seeds that crackle and pop for a nutty, sesame-like crunch. Cooked simply in mustard oil with minimal spices, it lets the hill-grown beans and jakhya shine. Wholesome mountain cooking at its most honest.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the staple cooking fat of Kumaoni kitchens, pairing perfectly with jakhya

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai on medium-high until it smokes, then reduce the heat and add 1 tsp jakhya seeds, letting them crackle and pop for about 20 seconds.
Add 2 dried red chillies and 4 crushed garlic cloves, frying for 30 seconds until the garlic is fragrant.
Add the chopped onion and cook for 4-5 minutes until soft and golden at the edges.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, then add the 400 g broad beans and 1 tsp salt and toss well.
Add 4 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 13-15 minutes until the beans are tender, stirring occasionally.
Uncover, cook on medium for 2 minutes to dry off, garnish with 2 tbsp fresh coriander and serve.
tips: Wait for the jakhya to crackle fully before adding anything else; that pop is the whole point of the tempering.
If jakhya is unavailable, cumin gives a different but pleasant tempering, though the nutty crunch will be missed.
Keep the spicing minimal so the hill-grown beans and jakhya aroma stay in the foreground.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with mandua (finger millet) roti and a bowl of bhatt ki churkani for an authentic Kumaoni plate.

variations.name: Classic Kadai Chana Masala
variations.description: A semi-dry kadai chana built around a freshly pounded coriander-chilli kadai masala and chunky charred peppers. The chickpeas stay coated in a coarse, aromatic masala rather than a gravy, making it bolder and more textured than everyday chole.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a clean high-heat oil suited to the fast, hot tossing kadai cooking needs

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon adds the dhaba-style richness the kadai is known for

steps: Soak 1.5 cups chickpeas overnight and pressure-cook with 1 tsp salt for 6 to 7 whistles until soft, then drain, keeping the liquid.
Dry-roast 1.5 tbsp coriander seeds, 4 dried red chillies and 1 tsp cumin on low for 2 minutes, then pound coarsely to make the kadai masala.
Cube 1 capsicum and 1 onion; heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and stir-fry the cubes on high for 2 minutes until charred, then set aside.

In the same oil fry 1 chopped onion with 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 4 minutes, add 3 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric and cook 6 minutes to a thick masala, then stir in most of the pounded kadai masala with 0.25 tsp salt and fry 2 minutes.
Add the cooked chickpeas with about half a cup of their liquid, and simmer 6 minutes, mashing a spoonful to bind, until the masala coats them.
Fold in the charred peppers and onion, crush in 1 tbsp kasuri methi, add 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and the remaining kadai masala, and toss on high for 2 minutes; finish with 2 tbsp coriander.
tips: Pound the kadai masala fresh for the best aroma; pre-ground powder tastes noticeably flatter.
Keep the peppers charred yet crunchy for the signature kadai bite.
For a semi-gravy version, add a little more of the chickpea cooking liquid and simmer briefly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve sizzling from the kadai with tandoori roti or laccha paratha and a squeeze of lemon over the top.

variations.name: Andhra Kadai Chana Masala
variations.description: A blistering Andhra kadai where the spice mix is loaded with roasted Guntur chillies and garlic and cooked down in sesame oil. Tangy with tamarind and fragrant with curry leaves, it turns the familiar semi-dry chana into a fierce, deeply savoury plate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: the heavy nutty Andhra oil that stands up to Guntur chilli and garlic

steps: Soak 1.5 cups chickpeas overnight and pressure-cook with 1 tsp salt for 6 to 7 whistles until soft, then drain, keeping the liquid.
Dry-roast 6 Guntur chillies, 1.5 tbsp coriander seeds and 1 tsp cumin on low for 2 minutes, then pound coarsely with 10 garlic cloves.
Cube 1 capsicum and 1 onion; heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and stir-fry the cubes on high for 2 minutes until blistered, then remove.

In the same oil pop 15 curry leaves, add 1 chopped onion and fry 4 minutes, then add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric and cook 5 minutes; stir in the roasted chilli-garlic masala and fry 3 minutes until the oil separates.
Add the cooked chickpeas with about half a cup of their liquid, 0.25 tsp salt and 1.5 tsp tamarind pulp, and simmer 6 minutes, mashing a few to bind the masala.
Fold in the charred peppers and onion, toss on high for 3 minutes until fiery red and glistening with sesame oil.
tips: Deseed a few chillies to preserve the colour while making the heat family-friendly.
Tamarind is what balances the aggressive chilli, so do not leave it out.
Keep curd or a coconut chutney on the table to cool the deliberate fire.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and ghee, or with ragi mudde, and a bowl of spiced buttermilk alongside.

variations.name: Rajasthani Kadai Chana Masala
variations.description: A rugged Marwari kadai chana where soaked dried red chillies build a smoky crimson heat and ghee carries the whole spices. With amchur for tang and almost no tomato, it is drier and more spice-forward, the way a desert kitchen would toss chana over a fire.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the traditional Rajasthani fat that blooms the soaked-chilli paste and whole spices

steps: Soak 1.5 cups chickpeas overnight and pressure-cook with 1 tsp salt for 6 to 7 whistles until soft, then drain, keeping the liquid. Soak 6 Mathania chillies in hot water 15 minutes and grind with 8 garlic cloves to a coarse paste.
Dry-roast 1.5 tbsp coriander seeds and 1 tsp cumin on low for 90 seconds and pound coarse. Cube 1 capsicum and 1 onion.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and stir-fry the capsicum and onion cubes on high for 2 minutes until charred, then set aside.

In the same ghee fry the pounded coriander-cumin 20 seconds, add 1 chopped onion and fry 5 minutes until golden, then add the chilli-garlic paste with 1 chopped tomato and 0.5 tsp turmeric and fry 4 minutes until the ghee separates.
Add the cooked chickpeas with about half a cup of their liquid and 0.25 tsp salt, and simmer 6 minutes, mashing a few to bind the smoky masala.
Fold in the charred peppers and onion, stir in 1 tsp amchur and 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi, and toss on high for 2 minutes before serving.
tips: Mathania chillies give a smoky red without unbearable heat; adjust the number to taste.
Keep this one drier than a gravy chana, as Rajasthani kadai is meant to coat and cling.
A little extra amchur perks up the dish if the ghee makes it taste too rich.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with ghee-smeared bajra roti and sliced raw onion, with chilled chaas to cool the chilli.

variations.name: Bengali Kadai Chana Masala
variations.description: A Bengali-accented kadai chana where mustard oil and a nigella temper bring pungent warmth and slit green chillies carry the heat instead of dried chilli. Finished with roasted bhaja masala, the chickpeas and charred peppers take on the unmistakable sharpness of sarson ka tel.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked first, its pungency gives the kadai a distinct Bengali sharpness

steps: Soak 1.5 cups chickpeas overnight and pressure-cook with 1 tsp salt for 6 to 7 whistles until soft, then drain, keeping the liquid. Dry-roast 1 tbsp coriander seeds on low for 90 seconds and pound coarse.
Cube 1 capsicum and 1 onion. Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it smokes, lower the heat, then stir-fry the cubes on high for 2 minutes until blistered, and remove.
In the same oil temper 0.5 tsp nigella seeds and 2 slit green chillies for 15 seconds, add 1 chopped onion and 1 tbsp ginger paste and fry 4 minutes.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.75 tsp turmeric and cook 5 minutes to a pulp, then stir in the pounded coriander with 0.25 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp sugar.
Add the cooked chickpeas with about half a cup of their liquid and simmer 6 minutes, mashing a few to bind the masala.
Fold in the charred peppers, onion and 2 more slit green chillies, sprinkle over 1 tsp bhaja masala, and finish with a drizzle of raw mustard oil for the Bengali kick.
tips: Smoke the mustard oil before cooking so its raw pungency softens into fragrant sharpness.
The green chillies carry the heat here, so adjust their number rather than adding chilli powder.
Bhaja masala and raw mustard oil added at the end are what mark this as a Bengali kadai.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot luchi or phulka and thin onion rings soaked in lime, letting the mustard sharpness shine.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Kadai Chana Masala
variations.description: This kadai chana takes on a Maharashtrian character with dark goda masala and a roasted peanut-coconut spice mix. Earthy, smoky and lightly sweet-savoury, it is a warmly spiced departure from the northern kadai, with the chickpeas soaking up all that toasty depth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday Maharashtrian oil that toasts the peanuts and coconut in the masala

steps: Soak 1.5 cups chickpeas overnight and pressure-cook with 1 tsp salt for 6 to 7 whistles until soft, then drain, keeping the liquid.
Dry-roast 2 tbsp desiccated coconut, 2 tbsp peanuts and 1 tbsp coriander seeds on low for 3 minutes until golden, then pound to a coarse powder.
Cube 1 capsicum and 1 onion; heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and stir-fry the cubes on high for 2 minutes until charred, then set aside.

In the same oil fry 1 chopped onion with 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 4 minutes, add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder and cook 5 minutes; stir in 2 tsp goda masala and the peanut-coconut powder with 0.25 tsp salt and fry 2 minutes.
Add the cooked chickpeas with about half a cup of their liquid, and simmer 6 minutes, mashing a few to bind the dark nutty masala.
Fold in the charred peppers and onion, toss on medium for 3 minutes until everything is coated, and serve warm.
tips: Roast the coconut and peanuts only to golden; taking them darker turns the masala bitter.
Goda masala carries its own warmth, so go easy on any extra garam masala.
A squeeze of lime at the end brightens the earthy, nutty flavours.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar or bajra bhakri and a spoon of thecha for those who want extra heat.

variations.name: Classic Kadai Mushroom Matar
variations.description: Seared mushrooms, sweet peas and charred capsicum tossed in a coarse, freshly pounded kadai masala. The crushed coriander-chilli blend and smoky peppers cooked hot in an iron kadai give it a bold, semi-dry character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil takes the high kadai heat and keeps the coarse masala tasting clean

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of bilona ghee gives the semi-dry masala a glossy, aromatic coat

steps: Dry-roast 1.5 tbsp coriander seeds, 3 dried red chillies and 0.5 tsp of the cumin on low for 2 minutes until fragrant, then coarsely crush into a rough kadai masala.
Quarter 300 g mushrooms and sear in 1 tbsp of the Anveshan Groundnut Oil on high for 3 minutes until golden, then set aside; in the same oil char 1 diced capsicum for 2 minutes and remove.
In the remaining 2 tbsp oil crackle the other 0.5 tsp cumin, add 2 chopped onions and saute for 6 minutes until golden, then stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook a minute.
Add 3 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, the crushed kadai masala and 1 tsp salt, and cook on medium for 7 minutes until the oil separates.
Add 1 cup peas and half a cup of water, cover and simmer on medium for 6 minutes until the peas are tender.
Fold in the seared mushrooms and charred capsicum with 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi and cook uncovered on medium for 3 minutes.
Swirl in 2 tbsp cream and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, cook 2 minutes to a semi-dry, glossy finish and serve.
tips: Crush the roasted kadai masala coarsely rather than powdering it; the texture is what defines a kadai dish.
Char the capsicum separately on high heat so it stays crunchy and smoky instead of stewing soft.
Keep the finish semi-dry and loosen with hot water, not more cream, if it dries out too far.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve sizzling from the kadai with laccha paratha or tandoori roti, scattered with julienned ginger and a lemon wedge.

variations.name: Andhra Kadai Mushroom Matar
variations.description: A fiery Andhra kadai driven by Guntur red chillies and a roasted sesame paste, with curry leaves and tamarind adding a sour-hot edge. Cooked in aromatic sesame oil, it is the spiciest reading of the dish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed sesame oil is the classic Andhra fat and holds up to the Guntur heat

steps: Dry-roast 1 tbsp sesame seeds and 5 Guntur red chillies separately on low until the seeds pop and the chillies darken, then grind both to a coarse paste with a little water.
Quarter 300 g mushrooms and sear in 1 tbsp of the Anveshan Sesame Oil on high for 3 minutes until golden, then set aside; char 1 diced capsicum in the same oil for 2 minutes and remove.
In the remaining 2 tbsp oil crackle 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tsp cumin and 15 curry leaves for 30 seconds until they splutter.
Add 2 chopped onions and saute for 7 minutes until browned, then stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 2 chopped tomatoes and cook for 5 minutes.
Mix in the sesame-chilli paste, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 4 minutes until the oil surfaces and the gravy turns brick red.
Add 1 cup peas, 1 tbsp tamarind pulp and 1 cup water, cover and simmer on medium for 6 minutes until the peas soften.
Fold in the seared mushrooms and charred capsicum, simmer uncovered for 3 minutes to a thick clinging gravy and serve.
tips: Roast the Guntur chillies gently with a window open; that toasted aroma is central to the dish.
The roasted sesame paste thickens the gravy and softens the heat, so do not leave it out.
Balance the fire with tamarind and adjust salt at the end, since Guntur chillies vary in strength.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rice topped with ghee or with pesarattu, and keep thick curd close by to cool the heat.

variations.name: Bengali Kadai Mushroom Matar
variations.description: A Bengali kadai cooked in smoked mustard oil with a coarse home-roasted bhaja masala and a whisper of jaggery. The pungent oil and freshly crushed spices give the mushrooms, peas and capsicum a sharp, aromatic eastern character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked wood-pressed mustard oil gives the kadai its signature Bengali pungency

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a touch of jaggery lends the sweet undertone Bengali cooking balances against the sharp mustard oil

steps: Dry-roast 1 tbsp coriander seeds, 0.5 tsp of the cumin and 2 dried red chillies on low for 2 minutes, then crush coarsely into a rough bhaja masala.
Quarter 300 g mushrooms, heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, then sear the mushrooms on high for 3 minutes until golden and set aside.
In the same oil char 1 diced capsicum for 2 minutes and remove, then crackle the remaining 0.5 tsp cumin for 15 seconds.

Add 2 chopped onions and saute for 6 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger paste, 2 chopped tomatoes, 0.75 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook 6 minutes until the oil surfaces.
Add the crushed roasted masala, 1 cup peas and 1 cup water, cover and simmer on medium for 6 minutes until the peas soften.
Fold in the seared mushrooms and charred capsicum and cook uncovered on medium for 3 minutes.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, cook 2 minutes to a semi-dry finish and serve.
tips: Bring the mustard oil to a wisp of smoke before cooking so the finished dish tastes nutty, not raw.
Grind the roasted bhaja masala just before cooking, as its aroma is what carries the Bengali flavour.
Add the capsicum back only in the last few minutes to keep it crisp.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with luchi or plain paratha, or over steamed rice with a squeeze of lime and slit green chillies.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Kadai Mushroom Matar
variations.description: A kadai seasoned with goda masala and roasted coconut for a dark, nutty, faintly sweet depth. The coarse spice base and coconut make this earthier and more robust than the North Indian kadai.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: groundnut oil is the everyday Maharashtrian fat and carries goda masala without masking it

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery balances the goda masala with the gentle sweetness typical of Maharashtrian gravies

steps: Dry-roast 4 tbsp desiccated coconut on low for 3 minutes until golden and nutty, then grind to a paste with a splash of water.
Quarter 300 g mushrooms and sear in 1 tbsp of the Anveshan Groundnut Oil on high for 3 minutes until golden, then set aside; char 1 diced capsicum in the same oil for 2 minutes and remove.
In the remaining 2 tbsp oil crackle 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin and 10 curry leaves for 20 seconds, then add 2 chopped onions and saute for 7 minutes until deep brown.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 2 chopped tomatoes, 2 tsp goda masala, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 6 minutes until the oil separates.
Add the roasted coconut paste, 1 cup peas and 1 cup water, cover and simmer on medium for 6 minutes until the peas soften.
Fold in the seared mushrooms and charred capsicum and cook covered on low for 4 minutes so they absorb the dark masala.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer 2 minutes and serve topped with fresh coriander.
tips: Add goda masala with the wet tomato mixture, not into dry hot oil, or it scorches and turns bitter.
Roast the coconut to a light gold so it does not overpower the goda spices.
Let the curry rest a few minutes before serving so the goda masala melds into the coconut.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri and a spoon of raw onion with lime, or with plain rice and a trickle of ghee.

variations.name: Malwa Kadai Mushroom Matar
variations.description: From the Malwa plateau of Madhya Pradesh, a kadai thickened with roasted peanuts for a creamy, nutty body without dairy. Earthy and hearty, it reflects the region's fondness for groundnut in everyday cooking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil echoes and deepens the roasted peanut base of this Malwa kadai

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of ghee lifts the earthy peanut gravy with a warm aroma

steps: Grind 0.5 cup roasted peanuts to a coarse powder, reserving a spoonful for garnish, and blend the rest with a little water into a smooth paste.
Quarter 300 g mushrooms and sear in 1 tbsp of the Anveshan Groundnut Oil on high for 3 minutes until golden, then set aside; char 1 diced capsicum in the same oil for 2 minutes and remove.
In the remaining 2 tbsp oil crackle 1 tsp cumin and 8 curry leaves for 20 seconds, then add 2 chopped onions and saute for 7 minutes until golden brown.
Stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 2 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 6 minutes until the oil separates.
Add the peanut paste, 1 cup peas and 1.25 cups water, stir well and simmer covered on medium for 6 minutes until the peas soften and the gravy turns creamy.
Fold in the seared mushrooms and charred capsicum and cook covered on low for 4 minutes.
Finish with 0.5 tsp garam masala and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, simmer 2 minutes and serve sprinkled with the reserved crushed peanuts.
tips: Roast the peanuts until deeply golden before grinding, as this gives the gravy its sweet, nutty backbone.
The peanut paste thickens fast, so keep hot water handy to adjust the consistency.
Simmer gently after adding the peanut paste, since it can catch and scorch at the base.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain rotis or steamed rice and a sharp lime pickle; a crunchy peanut-onion salad echoes the nutty theme.

variations.name: Classic Kadai Soya Chunk
variations.description: A semi-dry, wok-tossed soya curry built on a freshly pounded kadai masala of roasted coriander and dried red chilli. Cubed capsicum and onion petals stay slightly crisp while the boiled soya chunks soak up the coarse, smoky spice. It clings to the chunks rather than pooling as gravy, exactly as a kadai should.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil gives the kadai a clean, nutty base for the coarse masala.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of bilona ghee softens the sharp roasted-chilli edge of the kadai masala.

steps: Boil 1.5 cups soya chunks in 4 cups salted water for 5 minutes, then drain, rinse in cold water and squeeze each chunk firmly dry.
Dry roast 1 tbsp coriander seeds, 4 dried red chillies and 1 tsp cumin in a hot kadai for 2 minutes until fragrant, then cool and coarsely pound into a gritty kadai masala.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in the kadai on medium-high, add 2 diced onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, and fry until golden at the edges, about 6 minutes.
Stir in 3 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder, and cook until they collapse and the oil rims the pan, about 7 minutes.
Add 1 large cubed capsicum and the pounded kadai masala, tossing over high heat for 2 minutes so the peppers stay crisp and the spices smell smoky.
Add the squeezed soya chunks with 1 cup hot water and simmer uncovered for 8 minutes until the chunks plump up and the masala clings tightly.
Finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 0.5 tsp garam masala and 3 tbsp coriander, toss once, and serve hot.
tips: Squeeze the boiled soya chunks thoroughly so they act like sponges for the dry masala.
Add the capsicum late over high heat so it keeps a fresh crunch against the soft chunks.
Double the pounded kadai masala and jar it for up to two weeks of quick cooking.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve straight from the kadai with laccha paratha or tandoori roti, sliced onions and a wedge of lemon.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Kadai Soya Chunk
variations.description: The kadai gets a Deccan makeover with goda masala and a roasted coconut-peanut paste that turns it dark and nutty. Wood-pressed groundnut oil and a touch of jaggery give the smoky-sweet balance of a Malvani kitchen. The soya chunks carry the bold, earthy masala beautifully.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the honest Deccan fat that lets goda masala shine in the kadai.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery powder rounds the smoky goda masala into a warm, balanced kadai.

steps: Boil 1.5 cups soya chunks in salted water for 5 minutes, then drain, rinse and squeeze them dry.
Dry roast 3 tbsp grated coconut and 2 tbsp peanuts over low heat until toasty and brown, about 4 minutes, then grind to a coarse paste with a little water.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 10 curry leaves, then add 2 chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and brown for 6 minutes.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.25 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp goda masala, and cook until the oil separates, about 6 minutes.
