Stir in the coconut-peanut paste and 1 cubed capsicum, fry for 2 minutes, then add the squeezed soya chunks and toss to coat.
Pour in 1 cup hot water with 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer for 8 minutes until thick and clinging, and finish with 2 tbsp coriander.
tips: Roast the coconut low and slow, as scorched coconut turns the whole kadai bitter.
Keep the capsicum slightly crunchy to contrast the soft chunks and rich paste.
Add more red chilli powder for a fiery Kolhapuri edge if you like real heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri or steamed rice, a spoon of thecha and sliced raw onion.

variations.name: Gujarati Kadai Soya Chunk
variations.description: A lighter, sweeter kadai in the Gujarati mould, with capsicum and soya chunks in a tomato base rounded by Anveshan Jaggery Powder and lemon. Roasted peanut adds body while the spice stays gentle and homely. It is a little more moist than a typical kadai, made for scooping with rotli.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A light hand with groundnut oil keeps this kadai homely and clean-tasting.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery powder delivers the classic Gujarati sweet-sour balance against the tomato.

steps: Boil 1.5 cups soya chunks in salted water for 5 minutes, then drain, rinse and squeeze them dry.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin, then add 1 chopped onion and 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and soften for 4 minutes.
Add 3 pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander-cumin powder, and simmer until thick, about 8 minutes.
Stir in 2 tbsp roasted peanut powder and 1 cubed capsicum, cooking for 2 minutes so the peppers just soften.
Add the squeezed soya chunks with 1 cup hot water and 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, then simmer for 8 minutes until the chunks are plump.
Off the heat, stir in 1 tbsp lemon juice and finish with fresh coriander, balancing the sweet, sour and salt.
tips: Add the lemon after switching off the flame to keep its brightness.
Leave a little moisture in the pan; the peanut powder thickens it as it stands.
A pinch of asafoetida in the tempering makes the soya lighter on the stomach.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulka or jeera rice, a glass of chhaas and a spoon of sweet chundo.

variations.name: Bengali Kadai Soya Chunk
variations.description: The kadai reworked in pungent Anveshan Mustard Oil with a panch phoron tempering and slit green chillies. Capsicum and soya chunks take on the warm, sharp character of eastern cooking with a whisper of sweetness. Mustard oil gives it a nasal warmth no ordinary kadai has.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil anchors this kadai in sharp, warming Bengali pungency.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing teaspoon of ghee tempers the raw mustard edge and lifts the aroma.

steps: Boil 1.5 cups soya chunks in salted water for 5 minutes, then drain, rinse and squeeze them dry.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes and pales, then lower the flame and temper 1 tsp panch phoron for 30 seconds until it splutters.
Add 2 chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger paste and fry over medium heat until golden, about 6 minutes.
Stir in 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.75 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1 tsp cumin powder, and cook until the mustard oil surfaces, about 7 minutes.
Add 1 cubed capsicum and the squeezed soya chunks with 3 slit green chillies, tossing for 2 minutes, then pour in 1 cup hot water and simmer for 8 minutes.
Finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and 2 tbsp coriander, and rest for 3 minutes before serving.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to smoking first to strip away its raw bitterness.
Slit rather than chop the green chillies so they perfume without overwhelming.
A pinch of sugar with the tomatoes brings the gentle Bengali sweetness if you like it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice or luchi, a wedge of lime and a few extra green chillies.

variations.name: Kerala Kadai Soya Chunk
variations.description: A coastal kadai finished in coconut milk with a shallot-curry leaf tempering fried in Anveshan Coconut Oil. Roasted coconut and fennel give the soya chunks and capsicum a mellow, nutty coating rather than a dry masala. It sits between a kadai and a Kerala stew, gentle and fragrant.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil gives the tempering its warm Malabar aroma.

steps: Boil 1.5 cups soya chunks in salted water for 5 minutes, then drain, rinse and squeeze them dry.
Dry roast 0.5 cup grated coconut with 0.5 tsp fennel over low heat until deep golden, about 5 minutes, then grind to a smooth paste with a little water.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, fry 10 sliced shallots and 10 curry leaves until light brown, about 4 minutes, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste.
Add 1 chopped tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, and cook until the tomato breaks down, about 5 minutes.
Stir in the roasted coconut paste, 1 cubed capsicum and the squeezed soya chunks with 0.75 cup hot water, then simmer for 8 minutes.
Lower the flame, pour in 0.75 cup coconut milk, warm for 3 minutes without boiling, and finish with the last curry leaves crackled in coconut oil.
tips: Do not boil after adding coconut milk, or the gravy will split.
Roast the coconut to a deep gold for the true Kerala nuttiness and colour.
Add the capsicum with the soya so it stays just tender, not mushy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with appam, steamed red rice or idiyappam, with crisp pappadam alongside.

variations.name: Classic Masala Chana Masala
variations.description: The dhaba-dark Punjabi chole where chickpeas are pressure-cooked with tea and whole spices, then folded into a deeply bhuno-ed onion-tomato masala spiked with anardana and chole masala. It is tangy, robust and almost black, the definitive way to eat chana across North India.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a sturdy wood-pressed base for the long bhuno the dark chole masala needs

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: spooned over at the finish for a glossy dhaba-style richness

steps: Soak 1.5 cups dried chickpeas overnight, then pressure-cook them with 1 tea bag tied in muslin, 1 tsp salt and enough water for 6 to 7 whistles until completely soft; discard the tea bag.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then add 3 finely chopped onions and 2 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry 8 minutes until deep brown.
Add 3 pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tbsp chole masala, and bhuno on medium for 8 minutes until the masala is thick and the oil separates.
Tip in the cooked chickpeas along with a cup of their cooking liquid and 0.25 tsp more salt, and mash a ladleful of chana against the pan to thicken the gravy.
Simmer uncovered for 10 minutes so the chickpeas soak up the masala and the gravy turns dark and glossy, stirring now and then.
Stir in 1 tsp anardana powder and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, and finish with a scatter of ginger julienne over the top.
tips: The tea bag deepens the colour without altering the taste, the classic dhaba trick for dark chole.
Mashing a spoonful of chickpeas thickens the gravy naturally without any flour.
Rest the chole an hour before serving; the flavour deepens noticeably as it sits.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with fluffy bhature or kulcha, sliced onions, green chillies and a lemon wedge for the full Punjabi chole experience.

variations.name: Bengali Masala Chana Masala
variations.description: This is chana treated like Bengali ghugni, tempered in mustard oil with whole cumin and bay leaf and finished with roasted bhaja masala and a hint of sugar. Lighter and sweeter than Punjabi chole, it carries the pungent warmth of sarson ka tel and a fresh coconut garnish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked first, its sharpness gives the ghugni its unmistakable Bengali character

steps: Soak 1.5 cups chickpeas overnight, then pressure-cook with 1 tsp salt for 6 to 7 whistles until fully soft, and keep the cooking liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it smokes, lower the heat, then temper 1 tsp cumin seeds, 2 bay leaves and 2 dried red chillies for 20 seconds.
Add 2 finely chopped onions and 1.5 tbsp ginger paste and fry 6 minutes until golden, then add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.75 tsp turmeric and 2 tsp cumin-coriander powder and cook 5 minutes to a pulp.
Add the cooked chickpeas with about a cup of their liquid, 0.25 tsp salt and 0.75 tsp sugar, and simmer 10 minutes, lightly mashing a few to thicken the ghugni.
Stir in 1 tsp roasted bhaja masala and cook 2 minutes more so the smoky aroma runs through.
Finish with 2 tbsp fresh grated coconut and a small drizzle of raw mustard oil for the traditional Bengali kick.
tips: Smoke the mustard oil before use so its raw bite mellows into fragrant sharpness.
The pinch of sugar is authentic Bengali balance, not sweetness; do not skip it.
Fresh coconut on top is classic ghugni; toasted coconut adds an even nuttier note.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a breakfast or evening snack with luchi or fried puris, or spooned over muri (puffed rice) as Kolkata street-style ghugni.

variations.name: Gujarati Masala Chana Masala
variations.description: Gujarat sweetens and softens the chana into a light, khatta-meetha stew scented with dhana-jeeru and finished with jaggery and lemon. Thinner and gentler than Punjabi chole, it leans on a sesame temper and a touch of coconut for a homely thali-style curry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: the toasty Gujarati kitchen oil that frames the sweet-sour spicing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melts into the broth for the signature Gujarati khatta-meetha finish

steps: Soak 1.5 cups chickpeas overnight and pressure-cook with 1 tsp salt for 6 to 7 whistles until soft, reserving the liquid.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, then add 0.5 tsp cumin and 0.25 tsp asafoetida for 15 seconds.
Add 1 finely chopped onion and 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and fry 4 minutes, then add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 2 tsp dhana-jeeru and cook 5 minutes to a soft masala.
Add the cooked chickpeas with about a cup and a half of their liquid and 0.25 tsp salt, and simmer 10 minutes to a light, brothy curry, mashing a few chickpeas to lightly thicken it.
Stir in 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and let it dissolve over 2 minutes so the curry turns gently sweet-sour.
Switch off the heat, mix in 1 tbsp lemon juice and 2 tbsp fresh coriander, and check that the sweet, sour and salt are in balance.
tips: Keep this curry loose and brothy rather than thick, the way a Gujarati thali chana is served.
Add the lemon off the heat so it stays bright against the jaggery.
A tablespoon of fresh coconut stirred in at the end makes it more festive.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft rotli or over steamed rice, with a side of chaas, as part of a homestyle Gujarati thali.

variations.name: Kerala Masala Chana Masala
variations.description: Modelled on Kerala kadala curry, this simmers chickpeas in a dark roasted-coconut gravy scented with fennel and finished with a mustard and curry-leaf temper in coconut oil. Earthy, nutty and aromatic, it is the classic partner to puttu and worlds apart from northern chole.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the defining Kerala fat that carries the mustard and curry-leaf tempering

steps: Soak 1.5 cups chickpeas overnight and pressure-cook with 1 tsp salt for 6 to 7 whistles until soft, reserving the liquid.
Dry-roast 0.75 cup grated coconut with 1 tsp fennel seeds in a pan on low until deep golden brown, about 5 minutes, then grind with 4 shallots and a splash of water to a dark smooth paste.
In a pot warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, add 4 sliced shallots and fry 3 minutes, then add 2 tsp coriander powder, 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 0.5 tsp turmeric and fry 30 seconds.
Add the roasted coconut paste and the cooked chickpeas with about a cup of their liquid and 0.25 tsp salt, and simmer 10 minutes until the gravy turns thick and dark.
In a small pan heat the remaining 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, then add 2 dried red chillies and 15 curry leaves until crackling.
Pour the sizzling tempering over the curry, stir once, and cover for 2 minutes so the aroma soaks in.
tips: Roast the coconut to a genuine deep brown; this dark paste is what gives kadala curry its signature colour.
Shallots (cheriya ulli) give a sweeter, more authentic base than regular onions here.
It thickens as it cools, so keep a little cooking liquid aside to loosen before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the classic way with steamed puttu, or with appam or red rice, for a traditional Kerala breakfast.

variations.name: Rajasthani Masala Chana Masala
variations.description: A rustic Marwari chana cooked without tomato, leaning on a curd base, soaked dried red chillies and a hearty dose of ghee for its bold, tangy heat. Warming whole spices and amchur give it a dry-land intensity quite different from the tomato-rich Punjabi version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the traditional Rajasthani fat that blooms the soaked-chilli paste and whole spices

steps: Soak 1.5 cups chickpeas overnight and pressure-cook with 1 tsp salt for 6 to 7 whistles until soft. Soak 6 Mathania chillies in hot water 15 minutes and grind to a smooth paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and crackle 1 tsp cumin, 3 cloves and 1 bay leaf for 20 seconds, then add 2 finely chopped onions and 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry 7 minutes until golden.
Add the soaked-chilli paste with 2 tsp coriander powder and fry on medium for 3 minutes until the ghee separates and the red deepens.
Lower the heat and whisk in 0.75 cup curd a spoon at a time, stirring constantly so it does not split, then cook 3 minutes into a glossy red gravy.
Add the cooked chickpeas with about a cup of their liquid and 0.25 tsp salt, and simmer 10 minutes, mashing a few to thicken.
Stir in 1 tsp amchur and 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi, cook 2 minutes, and serve while the ghee glistens on top.
tips: Add the curd off the boil and stir non-stop to keep it from curdling in the hot ghee.
Mathania chillies give the deep Rajasthani red; adjust the number to control the heat.
A generous hand with ghee is traditional here and gives the dish its characteristic richness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra roti and a dollop of white butter, or with steamed rice and thin chaas to balance the heat.

variations.name: Classic Masala Chole
variations.description: The Punjabi Sunday classic: soaked chickpeas pressure-cooked soft, then simmered in a dark, tangy masala of onion, tomato and toasted chole spices. Amchur and a tea-bag boil give the signature deep colour and mouth-puckering tang.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A clean wood-pressed oil lets the toasted chole masala dominate

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A ghee tempering poured over at the end gives dhaba-style richness

steps: Pressure-cook the 1.5 cups soaked chickpeas with 1 tea bag, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 5-6 whistles until completely soft, then discard the tea bag and reserve the cooking liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds until toasty.
Add 2 finely chopped onions and fry until deep golden brown, 8 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Pour in the puree of 3 tomatoes with 2 tbsp chole masala, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp salt; cook 8 minutes until the oil separates and the masala darkens.
Add the cooked chickpeas with 1.5 cups of their reserved liquid, mashing a handful to thicken, and simmer on low for 12 minutes.
Stir in 1 tsp amchur, then heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee till hot and pour it sizzling over the chole before serving.
tips: The tea bag in the cooking water is the classic trick for the deep brown colour without any artificial help.
Mashing a handful of chickpeas thickens the gravy naturally and helps it cling to every bean.
Chole tastes better the next day; the masala penetrates the chickpeas fully once rested overnight.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with fluffy bhature or kulcha, sliced onions, green chilli and a wedge of lemon.

variations.name: Bengali Masala Chole
variations.description: A Bengali-style chana cooked in mustard oil with a panch phoron temper and a gentle sweetness, closer to the festive cholar-style bean dish. The mustard oil and whole-spice temper set it apart from the Punjabi original.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Pungent wood-pressed mustard oil gives the chana its Bengali character

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A touch of jaggery is the classic Bengali balance to the mustard sharpness

steps: Pressure-cook the 1.5 cups soaked chickpeas with 0.75 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 5-6 whistles until fully soft, then reserve the liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, then lower the flame and rest it 20 seconds to soften the pungency.
Temper 1 tsp panch phoron, 1 bay leaf and 2 dried red chillies for 20 seconds until the seeds pop.
Add 1 tbsp ginger paste and 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.75 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp cumin powder and 0.5 tsp salt; cook 6 minutes until the tomatoes break down.
Add the cooked chickpeas with 1.5 cups reserved liquid and simmer on low for 12 minutes so the beans absorb the flavour.
Stir in 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.5 tsp garam masala, simmer 2 minutes until the sweet-pungent balance settles, then serve.
tips: Always smoke the mustard oil first to mellow its raw bite into a nutty warmth.
Keep the whole panch phoron seeds intact; grinding them loses the characteristic Bengali aroma.
A little jaggery is traditional and rounds the mustard heat; leaving it out makes the dish taste harsher.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with luchi or steamed rice for a festive Bengali-style bean dish.

variations.name: Andhra Masala Chole
variations.description: A fiery Andhra senagalu-inspired chickpea curry driven by Guntur chilli and a garlic-heavy tempering in groundnut oil, sharpened with tamarind and curry leaves. Proudly hot, tangy and unapologetically bold.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the everyday cooking fat of Andhra

steps: Pressure-cook the 1.5 cups soaked chickpeas with 0.75 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 5-6 whistles until soft, then reserve the liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds for 15 seconds, then add 12 curry leaves and 8 crushed garlic cloves.
Fry the garlic 1 minute until pale gold, then add 2 chopped onions and cook until golden, 6 minutes.
Add 3 chopped tomatoes, 1.5 tsp Guntur chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 0.5 tsp salt; cook 6 minutes until the tomatoes collapse into a thick masala.
Add the cooked chickpeas with 1.5 cups reserved liquid and 1 tsp tamarind paste, and simmer on low for 12 minutes.
Uncover and cook 3 minutes more to concentrate the fiery-red gravy so it coats the beans thickly.
tips: Guntur chilli is genuinely hot; start with 1 tsp and build up to the authentic Andhra burn.
Tamarind is what keeps the heat from tasting flat, so add it once the beans have softened.
Crush the garlic coarsely for a bolder aroma that stands up to the strong chilli.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and ghee, or with hot pooris and a bowl of thin rasam alongside.

variations.name: Gujarati Masala Chole
variations.description: A milder, sweet-tart Gujarati chana where jaggery and lemon balance a gentle cumin-coriander gravy. Light on chilli and easy on the palate, it is the sort of homely bean curry that fits a full thali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the backbone fat of the Gujarati kitchen

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery brings the gentle sweetness typical of Gujarati gravies

steps: Pressure-cook the 1.5 cups soaked chickpeas with 0.75 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 5-6 whistles until soft, then reserve the liquid.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 15 seconds, then add 0.25 tsp asafoetida for 5 seconds.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and fry 30 seconds, then add the puree of 3 tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp coriander-cumin powder and 0.5 tsp salt.
Cook the masala 6 minutes until thick and glossy and the oil begins to separate.
Add the cooked chickpeas with 1.5 cups reserved liquid, mashing a handful, and simmer on low for 12 minutes.
Stir in 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tbsp lemon juice, simmer 1 minute, then finish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Balance the jaggery and lemon at the end so the curry lands sweet, sour and salty at once.
Keep the gravy loose and rasa-like; it is meant to be spooned over rice rather than scooped thick.
Asafoetida stands in for onion and garlic, keeping the dish suitable for Jain-style eating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as part of a Gujarati thali with phulka, steamed rice and a bowl of curd.

variations.name: Kashmiri Masala Chole
variations.description: A Kashmiri-style chana in a curd gravy tinted red by Kashmiri chilli and saffron, warmed with fennel and dry ginger rather than garam masala. Fragrant and gently spiced, it wraps the chickpeas in Wazwan-style perfume.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee is the traditional fat that gives Kashmiri gravies their body

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: Saffron lends the glowing colour and Kashmiri fragrance

steps: Pressure-cook the 1.5 cups soaked chickpeas with 0.75 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 5-6 whistles until soft, then reserve the liquid.
Soak 1 pinch Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside to steep.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and crackle 3 cloves, 3 cardamom and a 1-inch cinnamon stick for 30 seconds.
Lower the heat, add 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder for 10 seconds, then whisk in 0.75 cup curd slowly so it stays smooth, and add 2 tsp fennel powder, 0.5 tsp dry ginger and 0.5 tsp salt.
Add the cooked chickpeas with 1.5 cups reserved liquid and the saffron milk, and simmer on low for 12 minutes.
Uncover and cook 3 minutes to thicken the gravy into a deep glowing red clinging to the beans.
tips: Whisk the curd smooth and add it off high heat, stirring nonstop, so the gravy does not split.
Fennel and dry ginger are the true Kashmiri seasonings; garam masala would make it taste ordinary.
The dish deepens overnight as the saffron and fennel meld into the chickpeas.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed basmati rice or soft Kashmiri girda bread and a side of chilled curd.

variations.name: Classic Masala Gajar Matar
variations.description: A vibrant dry sabzi of diced carrots and green peas cooked in a warm, well-rounded onion-tomato masala. The natural sweetness of carrots plays against garam masala and a touch of tang. It is a quick, colourful everyday dish that brightens any thali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: clean wood-pressed oil lets the natural sweetness of carrots come through

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add the chopped onion and fry for 4-5 minutes until golden, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for a minute until the raw smell fades.
Add the chopped tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, cooking for 4 minutes until the tomato softens and oil surfaces.
Add the 3 diced carrots and 1 cup green peas with 1 tsp salt, toss to coat, then cover and cook on low for 12-14 minutes until the carrots are just tender.
Uncover and stir-fry on medium for 3 minutes so the vegetables dry and the masala clings tightly.
Sprinkle 0.75 tsp garam masala, toss for a minute, then finish with 2 tbsp fresh coriander and serve.
tips: Dice the carrots evenly and slightly small so they cook in the same time as the peas.
If using frozen peas, add them halfway through so they do not turn mushy.
A squeeze of lemon at the end lifts the carrots' sweetness beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulkas and dal, or stuff the leftovers into a grilled sandwich for a quick snack.

variations.name: Punjabi Masala Gajar Matar
variations.description: A rich Punjabi take where carrots and peas simmer in a ghee-based masala finished with kasuri methi and a hint of cream. The ghee deepens the carrots' sweetness into something almost buttery. This is the festive, indulgent version of the everyday sabzi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee turns the carrots' sweetness rich and buttery, the Punjabi way

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat and let 1 tsp cumin seeds sizzle for 20 seconds until aromatic.
Add the chopped onion and fry for 5 minutes until golden, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for a minute.
Add the pureed tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, cooking for 4-5 minutes until the ghee separates.
Add the 3 diced carrots and 1 cup peas with 1 tsp salt, mix well, then cover and cook on low for 12-14 minutes until the carrots are tender.
Uncover, stir in 2 tbsp fresh cream and crushed 1 tbsp kasuri methi, cooking on low for 2 minutes so the masala turns glossy.
Sprinkle 0.75 tsp garam masala, toss for a minute and serve hot.
tips: Crush the kasuri methi between your palms just before adding to release maximum aroma.
Swap cream for a spoon of malai or thick yoghurt for a homelier richness.
Do not overcook the carrots into mush; they should hold a slight bite for the best texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with laccha paratha or jeera rice and a side of onion-lachha salad.

variations.name: Kashmiri Masala Gajar Matar
variations.description: A fragrant Kashmiri version where carrots and peas take on a saffron glow and the warmth of fennel and dry ginger, in the onion-garlic-free Pandit style. The saffron plays gorgeously against the sweet carrots. Yoghurt gives a soft, gently spiced body.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the base fat of Kashmiri vegetable dishes, mild and aromatic

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk to gild the sweet carrots with colour and aroma

steps: Steep a pinch of Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside to bloom.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat and crackle 3 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon for 20 seconds.
Lower the heat, add 1.5 tsp Kashmiri red chilli powder with a splash of water so it does not burn, then whisk in 3 tbsp yoghurt slowly and cook for 3 minutes until the ghee floats.
Stir in 1.5 tsp fennel powder and 0.75 tsp dry ginger powder, then add the 3 diced carrots and 1 cup peas with 1 tsp salt and toss to coat.
Add 0.5 cup water, cover and simmer on low for 13-15 minutes until the carrots are tender and the gravy has reduced to a light coating.
Pour in the saffron milk, simmer uncovered for 2 minutes to spread the colour and aroma, then serve.
tips: Fennel and dry ginger stand in for onion and garlic here, so keep them prominent for authenticity.
Bloom the saffron in warm milk, never cold water, for a fuller colour and scent.
Add the yoghurt on low heat and whisk it smooth first to stop the gravy from curdling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed basmati rice and a spoon of extra ghee, alongside a simple cucumber raita.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Masala Gajar Matar
variations.description: A Pune-style rendition where carrots and peas are dusted with dusky goda masala and finished with fresh coconut. The warm, sweetish masala complements the carrots naturally, while a pinch of jaggery ties it together. It carries the distinctive aroma of a Maharashtrian kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday Maharashtrian fat that lets goda masala bloom cleanly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the classic sweet note that rounds off goda masala's warmth

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop, then add 0.5 tsp cumin, a pinch of asafoetida and 10 curry leaves.
Add the chopped onion and fry for 4-5 minutes until translucent and soft.
Lower the heat and add 1.5 tsp goda masala and 0.5 tsp turmeric, stirring for 20 seconds so the spices bloom without scorching.
Add the 3 diced carrots and 1 cup peas with 1 tsp salt, toss well, then add 4 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 12-14 minutes until the carrots are tender.
Uncover, stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook on medium for 2 minutes until it melts and glazes the vegetables.
Fold in 3 tbsp fresh grated coconut, cook for a final minute and serve warm.
tips: Goda masala burns quickly, so add it on low heat and follow at once with the vegetables.
Keep the coconut fresh and moist by adding it right at the end off the heat if you prefer.
A splash of water helps the carrots steam soft without needing extra oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri and a spoon of thecha, or with varan-bhaat for a wholesome Maharashtrian meal.

variations.name: Bengali Masala Gajar Matar
variations.description: A gentle Bengali gajor-motorshuti chchechki tempered with panch phoron in mustard oil, where the carrots' sweetness meets a whisper of sugar and green chilli. The five-spice aroma and mustard oil give it an unmistakable Bengali character. Light, slightly sweet and everyday.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked first to mellow its bite, then paired with panch phoron the Bengali way

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai on medium-high until it smokes, then lower the heat and add 1 tsp panch phoron, 2 dried red chillies and 1 bay leaf, crackling for 20 seconds.
Add 1 tsp ginger paste and 2 slit green chillies and fry for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp cumin powder off the direct flame, then add the 3 diced carrots and 1 cup peas.
Add 1 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp sugar, toss well, then add 4 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 13-15 minutes until the carrots turn tender.
Uncover and stir-fry on medium for 3 minutes so the vegetables dry and glisten with the mustard oil.
Taste and adjust salt or sugar, then serve while warm.
tips: The pinch of sugar is traditional and heightens the carrots' natural sweetness against the mustard oil.
Bring the mustard oil to smoking point first to shed its raw pungency.
Keep the dish lightly dry (chchechki style), with the spices just clinging to the vegetables.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with warm steamed rice and a dal, or with luchi for a slightly festive Bengali breakfast.

variations.name: Classic Masala Kaddu
variations.description: The beloved khatta-meetha kaddu of North Indian kitchens, where soft red pumpkin is cooked down with fennel, amchur and a little jaggery until it half-melts into a sweet-sour-spicy mash. Comforting and quick, it is the classic partner to hot pooris.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a clean oil that lets the sweet-sour pumpkin flavours come forward

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the meetha half of khatta-meetha kaddu, melting into the pumpkin

steps: Peel the 500 g pumpkin, remove the seeds, and cut into rough 3 cm chunks; it will break down as it cooks.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on medium and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 tsp fennel seeds, 0.25 tsp fenugreek seeds and the 2 dried red chillies for about 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder and stir for 15 seconds, then tip in the pumpkin and 1 tsp salt.
Toss to coat, cover, and cook on low for 15 to 18 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the pumpkin is completely soft.
Mash about half the pumpkin against the side of the pan to give the classic part-chunky, part-pulpy texture.
Add 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp amchur powder and cook uncovered for 3 minutes until glossy and jammy.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala and 2 tbsp coriander leaves, stir, and serve hot.
tips: Choose deep-orange, ripe pumpkin; it is naturally sweeter and cooks to a softer mash.
Balance the amchur and jaggery to taste so the dish lands squarely between sweet and sour.
Leftovers thicken as they sit and make a delicious filling for a paratha the next day.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the traditional way with hot, puffy pooris and a few slices of raw onion on the side.

variations.name: Bengali Masala Kaddu
variations.description: A Bengali kumro chokka where pumpkin is tempered in mustard oil with panch phoron and a slit chilli, then simmered soft with a light sweet-savoury balance. Fragrant with five spices and gently sweet, it is a homely niramish favourite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked first, it gives kumro chokka its unmistakable Bengali pungency

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the customary sweetness that balances the mustard and five spices

steps: Peel and deseed the 500 g pumpkin and cut into 3 cm chunks, and slit the 2 green chillies.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until it just smokes, lower the flame, and temper 1 tsp panch phoron, the 1 bay leaf and the slit chillies for about 20 seconds until the seeds crackle.
Add 1 tsp ginger paste and stir for 30 seconds, then add 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp cumin powder with a splash of water.
Tip in the pumpkin and 1 tsp salt, toss, cover, and cook on low for 14 to 16 minutes until very soft.
Mash lightly so the pumpkin holds together as a soft, part-broken mass.
Add 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook uncovered for 2 minutes until it melts and glazes the pumpkin.
Garnish with 2 tbsp coriander leaves and serve warm.
tips: Let the panch phoron crackle fully in the hot oil so all five seeds release their aroma.
Kumro chokka is meant to be soft and slightly sweet, so do not rush the mashing step.
It tastes even better the next day once the five spices have had time to mingle.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with luchi (Bengali pooris) or plain steamed rice and a dab of extra mustard oil.

variations.name: Gujarati Masala Kaddu
variations.description: A Gujarati kolu nu shaak where pumpkin is cooked with a sesame tempering, green chilli-ginger and a pronounced sweet-sour finish of jaggery and lemon. Silky, glossy and lightly sweet, it is a soothing everyday shaak with a gentle warmth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday Gujarati oil, mild enough for a delicate pumpkin shaak

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the sweet backbone of a Gujarati kolu shaak

steps: Peel and deseed the 500 g pumpkin and cut into 3 cm chunks.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on medium and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 1 tbsp sesame seeds for about 20 seconds until they pop.
Add 1 tbsp green chilli-ginger paste and stir for 30 seconds, then add 0.5 tsp turmeric and 2 tsp coriander-cumin powder.
Tip in the pumpkin and 1 tsp salt, toss, cover, and cook on low for 14 to 16 minutes until soft, adding 2 tbsp water only if needed.
Mash a little so the shaak turns soft and part-pulpy.
Add 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook uncovered for 2 minutes until it dissolves and glazes the pumpkin.
Take off the heat, stir in 1 tbsp lemon juice, 2 tbsp grated coconut and 2 tbsp coriander leaves, and serve warm.
tips: The sesame seeds add a subtle nutty aroma that is characteristic of Gujarati tempering.
Add the lemon off the heat so its tang stays fresh against the jaggery.
Ripe, deep-orange pumpkin needs less jaggery, so taste before adding the full amount.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft ghee-brushed rotli, a bowl of thin kadhi and steamed rice for a classic Gujarati thali.

variations.name: Rajasthani Masala Kaddu
variations.description: A spicier desert version where pumpkin meets smoky dried red chillies, fennel and a ghee tempering, with amchur sharpening the sweetness of the ripe gourd. Bold and warming yet still touched with jaggery, it balances desert heat with mellow sweetness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee is the desert kitchen's fat and mellows the smoky dried chillies

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a touch of sweetness that tempers the fiery chilli in true Rajasthani balance

steps: Peel and deseed the 500 g pumpkin and cut into 3 cm chunks, finely chop the 1 onion, and break the 4 dried red chillies in half.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee on medium and add 1 pinch asafoetida, 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 tsp fennel seeds, 0.25 tsp fenugreek seeds and the dried chillies, frying for 30 seconds until smoky and fragrant.

Add the chopped onion and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and sauté for 5 minutes until golden, then stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder for 15 seconds and tip in the pumpkin and 1 tsp salt.
Toss, cover, and cook on low for 15 to 18 minutes until the pumpkin is completely tender.
Mash about half the chunks to give a rustic, part-pulpy body.
Add 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp amchur powder and cook uncovered for 3 minutes until glossy and jammy.
Garnish with 2 tbsp coriander leaves and serve hot.
tips: The pinch of asafoetida and fenugreek gives the distinctive Rajasthani aroma, so do not skip them.
Fry the dried chillies only until they darken; burnt chillies make the whole dish bitter.
Keep the sweet-sour-hot balance in check by tasting before serving and adjusting amchur or jaggery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot bajra rotis, a knob of ghee and a side of green chilli pickle for a hearty desert plate.

variations.name: Odia Masala Kaddu
variations.description: An Odia kakharu bhaja-style pumpkin tempered with panch phoron and finished with a whisper of roasted-spice powder, kept light and gently sweet from the pumpkin itself. Simple, homely and fragrant, it is the everyday Odia way with kaddu.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday oil of Odia kitchens, giving kakharu its earthy base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a small spoon lifts the pumpkin's natural sweetness the Odia way

steps: Peel and deseed the 500 g pumpkin and cut into 3 cm chunks, and lightly crush the 4 garlic cloves.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until it just smokes, lower the flame, and temper 1 tsp panch phoron and the 2 broken dried red chillies for about 20 seconds until crackling.
Add the crushed garlic and fry for 40 seconds until pale gold, then add 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder.
Tip in the pumpkin and 1 tsp salt, toss, cover, and cook on low for 14 to 16 minutes until very soft.
Mash lightly so the pumpkin holds as a soft, rustic mass.
Add 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp roasted cumin powder and cook uncovered for 2 minutes to bring the flavours together.
Garnish with 2 tbsp coriander leaves and serve warm.
tips: The roasted cumin powder added at the end gives a warm, nutty aroma distinct to Odia cooking.
Crushed garlic in the tempering deepens the flavour; use it generously if you like.
Keep it soft and lightly sweet, letting the pumpkin's own sugar shine through.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a spoon of dalma, or tuck it into a dosa for a quick Odia-style snack.

variations.name: Classic Masala Kofta
variations.description: Golden fried vegetable koftas of grated mixed vegetables and paneer bound with besan, bathed in a smooth spiced onion-tomato gravy just before serving so they stay soft inside and hold shape. A crowd-pleasing restaurant classic. Comforting, saucy and satisfying.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Its high smoke point fries the koftas crisp and clean for deep-frying

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee starts the gravy with a nutty richness under the tomato

steps: Squeeze the moisture out of 2 cups grated mixed vegetables, then mix with 0.5 cup paneer, 4 tbsp besan, 0.5 tsp salt and 0.25 tsp garam masala into a firm dough that holds a ball.
Roll into 12 walnut-sized balls and deep-fry in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil heated to medium-high, 5-6 at a time, for 3-4 minutes until evenly golden, then drain on paper.
In a separate pan heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds until fragrant.

Add the 2 chopped onions and fry 8 minutes until golden, then stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute, followed by the tomato puree with 1 tsp red chilli, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt.
Simmer the gravy 10 minutes until the ghee separates, then add 1 cup hot water and 0.75 tsp garam masala and cook 5 minutes into a smooth sauce.
Stir in 2 tbsp cream, then gently slip in the koftas just 3-4 minutes before serving so they soak up the gravy without breaking apart.
tips: Squeeze the grated vegetables really dry, because excess water is the main reason koftas fall apart in hot oil.
Add the koftas to the gravy only at the last minute; soaking them too long turns them mushy.
If the mix feels loose, add a spoon more besan rather than adding water, to keep the koftas firm.
variations.servingSuggestion: Arrange the koftas in a shallow bowl, pour the gravy over just before serving, and finish with a cream swirl and coriander alongside naan.

variations.name: Punjabi Masala Kofta
variations.description: The rich dhaba-style kofta, where fried veg-and-paneer balls sit in a buttery tomato gravy laced with kasuri methi and cream. Indulgent, glossy and unmistakably Punjabi. A wedding-menu favourite you can make at home.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Neutral and high-smoke, it fries the koftas to an even gold

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee deepens the buttery Amritsari base of the gravy

steps: Squeeze 2 cups grated vegetables dry and mix with 0.75 cup paneer, 4 tbsp besan and 0.5 tsp salt into a firm, pliable dough.
Shape into 12 balls and deep-fry in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil at medium-high for 3-4 minutes until deep golden, then rest on paper.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat, fry the 2 chopped onions 8 minutes until golden, then add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Add the tomato puree with 1.25 tsp red chilli, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook 11 minutes until thick and the ghee floats on top.
Pour in 1 cup hot water with 3 tbsp cashew paste, crush in 1 tbsp kasuri methi and simmer 5 minutes, then stir in 2 tbsp butter and 4 tbsp cream for a velvety gravy.
Slip the koftas in gently just 3-4 minutes before serving so they warm through and soak up the buttery sauce without collapsing.
tips: A little extra paneer in the mix makes softer, more luxurious koftas suited to this rich gravy.
For a smoother restaurant finish, blend the cooled onion-tomato base before adding water and cream.
Toast the kasuri methi for 20 seconds before crushing to release its full aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or laccha paratha, an extra drizzle of cream and a sprinkle of crushed kasuri methi on top.

variations.name: Awadhi Masala Kofta
variations.description: A Lucknawi nawabi kofta in a pale, fragrant white gravy of cashew, curd and fried onion paste, delicately perfumed with kewra water and a whisper of mace. Mild, aromatic and elegant rather than fiery. Banquet food from the courts of Awadh.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Fries the koftas crisp and cooks the delicate white gravy without colour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee lends the refined richness expected of a nawabi korma

ingredients.name: Grated mixed vegetables (potato, bottle gourd, paneer)

steps: Squeeze 2 cups grated vegetables dry, mix with 4 tbsp besan and 0.5 tsp salt into a firm dough, roll into 12 balls and deep-fry in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil at medium-high 3-4 minutes until pale gold.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over low-medium heat, add the crushed cardamom and mace, and let them perfume the fat for 30 seconds without browning.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 3 tbsp fried onion paste and cook 2 minutes on low, keeping the colour pale.
Whisk in the 0.5 cup curd off the heat to stop it splitting, return to low heat, add 4 tbsp cashew paste, 0.5 tsp white pepper and 1 tsp salt, and cook gently 4 minutes.
Loosen with 1 cup hot water and simmer 6 minutes on low into a smooth, ivory gravy, taking care it never boils hard.
Slip in the koftas and 0.5 tsp kewra water 3-4 minutes before serving so they warm through and the delicate perfume stays fresh.
tips: Keep the flame low throughout so the gravy stays pale ivory, the mark of a true Awadhi korma.
Add kewra water only at the very end and in tiny amounts, as too much turns the dish soapy.
Whisk the curd smooth and add it off the heat to keep the white gravy from curdling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with warm sheermal or rumali roti, garnished with slivered almonds and a few saffron strands for a nawabi table.

variations.name: Kashmiri Masala Kofta
variations.description: Koftas in a Kashmiri-style ruby gravy bloomed with saffron and Kashmiri chilli, spiced with fennel and dry ginger rather than onion and garlic, and thickened with curd. Mild, red and fragrant with a wazwan elegance. A festive treatment of the humble veg kofta.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Fries the koftas crisp for the ruby gravy to cling to

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: Saffron gives the ruby glow and delicate wazwan perfume

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries the fennel and saffron aromatics of a Kashmiri gravy

steps: Soak 0.25 tsp Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 3 tbsp warm water and set aside to bloom.
Squeeze 2 cups grated vegetables dry, mix with 4 tbsp besan and 0.5 tsp salt, roll into 12 balls and deep-fry in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil at medium-high 3-4 minutes until golden.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat, add the cloves, cardamom and cinnamon with 0.25 tsp asafoetida, and sizzle 30 seconds.
Lower the heat, stir in 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli then quickly the tomato puree, and cook 7 minutes until the ghee floats red, then whisk in the 0.5 cup curd off the heat.
Return to low heat, add 2 tsp fennel powder, 1 tsp dry ginger, 1 tsp salt and the bloomed saffron water, loosen with 1 cup hot water, and simmer 6 minutes into a ruby gravy.
Slip the koftas in gently 3-4 minutes before serving so they soak up the fragrant gravy without breaking.
tips: Take the pan off the flame before the curd goes in and stir as it reheats to prevent splitting.
Keep the gravy onion and garlic free, letting fennel and dry ginger carry the aroma.
Bloom the saffron in warm, not boiling, water to protect its colour and scent.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice or a soft roti, scattered with saffron strands and slivered almonds.

variations.name: Bengali Masala Kofta
variations.description: A niramish-style kofta where the balls are fried and simmered in a pungent wood-pressed mustard oil gravy with a whole-spice bhaja, slit green chillies and a touch of sugar. The mustard sharpness gives the koftas a distinctly Bengali bite. Sunday-lunch comfort with an eastern accent.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Mustard oil both fries the koftas and gives the gravy its Bengali pungency

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A pinch of jaggery brings the classic Bengali sweet-savoury balance

ingredients.name: Bay leaf and dried red chilli

steps: Squeeze 2 cups grated vegetables dry, mix with 4 tbsp besan, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt, roll into 12 balls and deep-fry in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil at medium-high 3-4 minutes until golden, then drain.
Pour off all but 3 tbsp of the mustard oil, reheat until it smokes, then lower the heat and temper 1 tsp cumin seeds, the bay leaf and dried red chilli for 30 seconds.
Add the chopped onion and fry 6-7 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger paste and cook 1 minute.
Add the tomato puree with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli and 1 tsp salt, and cook 9 minutes until the oil separates.
Pour in 1 cup hot water, add the 3 slit green chillies and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, and simmer 6 minutes into a smooth gravy.
Sprinkle 0.75 tsp Bengali garam masala over the top, slip in the koftas 3-4 minutes before serving, and rest briefly so the mustard flavour settles.
tips: Fry the koftas first, then reuse a little of the same mustard oil so the gravy carries the roasted flavour through.
Heat the mustard oil to smoking before the tempering to soften its raw pungency.
Use the lighter cinnamon-clove-cardamom Bengali garam masala for the authentic finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a drizzle of raw mustard oil, or with luchi and a slit green chilli on the side.

variations.name: Classic Punjabi Aloo Tamatar
variations.description: The dhaba-style Punjabi potato curry: cubed aloo in a robust onion-tomato masala finished with butter and kasuri methi. Hearty and full-flavoured, it is the everyday sabzi that turns a simple roti meal into something satisfying.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil gives the base a clean, nutty foundation

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A ghee finish delivers the dhaba richness this dish is known for

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds until they darken and smell toasty.
Add 2 finely chopped onions and fry until deep golden, 6-7 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in the puree of 3 tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt; cook 8 minutes until the oil separates.
Add the 4 boiled cubed potatoes and lightly mash a few pieces against the pan to thicken the gravy.
Pour in 1.5 cups hot water, bring to a boil and simmer on low for 8 minutes so the potatoes soak up the masala.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the pan, stir in 1 tbsp butter, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 0.5 tsp garam masala, and simmer 2 minutes until glossy.
tips: Kasuri methi crushed between the palms just before adding releases far more aroma than crumbling it in whole.
Mashing a couple of potatoes is the no-cream trick to a thick, clinging Punjabi gravy.
The masala base freezes well; make a double batch and you have a weeknight curry ready in minutes.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter-brushed tandoori roti or lachha paratha and sliced onions with lemon.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Aloo Tamatar
variations.description: A Puneri rassa-style potato curry built on goda masala and a roasted coconut paste, tempered with mustard seeds. Dark, nutty and mildly sweet, it swaps the Punjabi butter finish for Deccan warmth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the everyday cooking fat of Maharashtra

steps: Dry-roast 3 tbsp desiccated coconut over low heat until nutty brown, about 3 minutes, then grind coarsely with a splash of water.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds.
Add 2 chopped onions and fry until golden, 6 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the roasted coconut and cook 1 minute.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tbsp goda masala and 1 tsp salt; cook 6 minutes until the oil beads at the edges.
Add the 4 boiled potatoes with 1.5 cups hot water, stirring to coat, then cover and simmer on low for 8 minutes.
Uncover and simmer 2 minutes to thicken the rassa into a dark, aromatic gravy, adjusting salt to taste.
tips: Roasting the coconut until brown is what gives the smoky depth; raw coconut makes it taste milky.
Goda masala is the signature here; buy a fresh, aromatic batch for the truest Puneri flavour.
Loosen with extra water for a thinner rassa to spoon generously over rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri or steamed rice and a spoon of coconut chutney on the side.

variations.name: Gujarati Aloo Tamatar
variations.description: A mild, sweet-tart Gujarati potato rasa where jaggery and lemon lift a gentle cumin-coriander gravy, kept low on chilli. It is the homely, thali-friendly curry meant to be spooned generously over rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the defining cooking fat of Gujarat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery gives the gentle sweetness that marks Gujarati gravies

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 15 seconds, then add 0.25 tsp asafoetida for 5 seconds.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and fry 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the puree of 3 tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp coriander-cumin powder and 1 tsp salt; cook 6 minutes until thick and glossy.
Add the 4 boiled cubed potatoes, mashing a couple to thicken the rasa.
Pour in 2 cups hot water, bring to a gentle boil and simmer on low for 7 minutes.
Stir in 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tbsp lemon juice, simmer 1 minute, then finish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Keep this rasa thin and pourable rather than thick; it is meant to flood over rice and roti.
Balance jaggery and lemon at the end so the dish lands sweet, sour and salty at once.
Asafoetida stands in for onion and garlic, keeping the curry suitable for Jain-style meals.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as part of a Gujarati thali with phulka, plain rice and a bowl of curd.

variations.name: Kerala Aloo Tamatar
variations.description: A coconut-milk potato stew in the Kerala style, tempered in coconut oil with curry leaves and mustard, gently spiced with green chilli and fennel. Creamy, fragrant and soothing, it carries the mild sweetness of the coast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed coconut oil carries the true aroma of a Kerala stew

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp fennel seeds for 15 seconds until fragrant.
Add 14 curry leaves, 6 sliced shallots and 3 slit green chillies and fry until the shallots soften, about 4 minutes.
Add the 4 cubed potatoes, 2 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, stir, then pour in 1.5 cups hot water.
Cover and simmer on low for 12 minutes until the potatoes are tender and the tomatoes have melted in.
Lower the heat and pour in 1 cup coconut milk, warming gently for 3 minutes without letting it boil.
Finish with a drizzle of raw coconut oil off the heat to intensify the aroma before serving.
tips: Never boil the coconut milk hard or it will split; a gentle warm-through keeps the stew silky.
Shallots give a deeper sweetness than regular onions and are worth seeking out.
Add the green chillies whole and slit for fragrance and mild heat without overpowering the coconut.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with appam, idiyappam or steamed Kerala red rice to soak up the creamy stew.

variations.name: Kashmiri Aloo Tamatar
variations.description: A Kashmiri-style potato curry glowing red from Kashmiri chilli and saffron, its curd gravy warmed by fennel and dry ginger. Aromatic and comforting rather than fiery, it brings Wazwan elegance to a simple aloo.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee gives Kashmiri gravies their traditional richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: Saffron lends the signature colour and Kashmiri perfume

steps: Soak 1 pinch Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside to steep.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and crackle 3 cloves, 3 cardamom and a 1-inch cinnamon stick for 30 seconds.
Lower the heat, add 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder for 10 seconds, then whisk in 0.75 cup curd slowly so it stays smooth.
Add 2 tsp fennel powder, 0.5 tsp dry ginger powder, 1 tsp salt and the saffron milk, and cook 4 minutes until the ghee floats up.
Add the 4 boiled cubed potatoes with 1 cup hot water, cover and simmer on low for 10 minutes.
Uncover and cook 2 minutes to thicken the gravy into a deep glowing red clinging to the potatoes.
tips: Whisk the curd smooth and add it off high heat, stirring constantly, so the gravy does not split.
Fennel and dry ginger define authentic Kashmiri flavour; do not swap in garam masala.
The curry tastes even better the next day as the saffron and fennel deepen into the sauce.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed basmati rice or a soft Kashmiri girda bread to soak up the fragrant gravy.

variations.name: Classic Punjabi Malai Kofta
variations.description: The dhaba-favourite malai kofta: nut-stuffed paneer dumplings in a rich onion-tomato-cashew gravy finished with butter and kasuri methi. Creamy, mildly sweet and deeply aromatic, it is the showpiece of every Punjabi vegetarian spread.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: wholegrain binder that keeps the stuffed koftas soft and crack-free

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee fries the koftas and enriches the classic dhaba gravy

steps: Mash 2 boiled potatoes with 1.5 cups grated paneer, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta into a smooth dough, then stuff each portion with chopped cashew and raisin and seal into 10 koftas.
Shallow-fry the koftas in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat until golden all over, about 5 minutes, and drain gently.
In the remaining 2 tbsp ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin, add 3 chopped onions and cook to soft gold, about 8 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste.
Add 3 pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.75 tsp salt, and cook until the ghee separates, about 8 minutes.
Stir in 4 tbsp cashew paste and 1 cup hot water, simmer 4 minutes to a silky gravy, then add 4 tbsp cream, 1 tsp sugar and 1 tsp garam masala.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the pot, dot 2 tbsp butter in, and simmer 2 minutes to a glossy finish.
Place the koftas in just before serving, spoon the gravy over so they stay whole, and rest 2 minutes.
tips: Seal the nut stuffing well so the koftas do not burst while frying.
Keep koftas and gravy separate until serving so the dumplings stay soft rather than soggy.
A teaspoon of sugar and a splash of cream give the signature mild, balanced Punjabi profile.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or jeera rice, garnished with a cream swirl, slivered almonds and coriander.

variations.name: Kashmiri Punjabi Malai Kofta
variations.description: A Valley-scented version glowing with Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron and warmed by fennel and dry ginger. The creamy koftas take on a golden blush and a delicate floral aroma, more perfumed and gentler than the dhaba original.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: binds the koftas softly for the fragrant saffron gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the koftas and forms the rich Kashmiri base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm milk for the golden colour and floral aroma

steps: Mash 2 boiled potatoes with 1.5 cups grated paneer, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta into a smooth dough and roll into 10 oval koftas.
Fry the koftas in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat until pale gold, about 4 minutes, and steep 1 pinch Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk.
Boil 2 onions with 4 cardamom for 8 minutes, then blend to a smooth pale paste.
In the remaining 3 tbsp ghee, add the onion paste with 1 tbsp fennel powder and 0.75 tsp dry ginger powder, and cook gently for 4 minutes without browning.
Stir in 4 tbsp cashew paste and 1 cup hot water with 0.75 tsp salt, simmer 4 minutes, then lower the heat and whisk in 0.5 cup yogurt slowly so it does not split.
Add the saffron milk and 3 tbsp cream, warm through 3 minutes, and let the gravy turn a pale gold.
Slip the koftas in just before serving, spoon the fragrant gravy over, and rest 2 minutes so the saffron perfume settles.
tips: Grind fennel and dry ginger fresh, as they are the aromatic heart of Kashmiri gravies.
Add yogurt on low heat with constant stirring to keep the pale gravy smooth.
Reserve a few saffron strands to float on top for colour and a luxurious look.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with Kashmiri pulao studded with dry fruit and drizzle a little extra saffron milk over the koftas.

variations.name: Bengali Punjabi Malai Kofta
variations.description: A Bengali crossover where the creamy koftas rest in a poppy-seed and coconut gravy cooked in Anveshan Mustard Oil. Gently sweet with a faint mustard warmth, it lends the malai kofta a refined shorshe-narkel character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: binds the koftas softly for the poppy-coconut gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked first for a gentle Bengali pungency in the gravy

steps: Mash 2 boiled potatoes with 1.5 cups grated paneer, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta into a smooth dough and roll into 10 koftas.
Heat Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil to its haze, cool slightly, and fry the koftas over medium heat until pale gold, about 4 minutes; drain.
In 3 tbsp of the mustard oil, splutter 0.5 tsp nigella seeds, then add 2 finely chopped onions and cook to soft and translucent, about 6 minutes, keeping them pale.
Add 1 tbsp ginger paste and 0.5 tsp turmeric, fry a minute, then stir in 3 tbsp poppy seed paste and 3 tbsp coconut paste with 0.75 tsp salt.
Pour in 1 cup water and simmer 5 minutes until the gravy turns creamy and the poppy seeds lose their rawness, then add 3 slit green chillies and 0.75 tsp sugar.
Stir in 2 tbsp cream and warm gently 2 minutes without boiling hard.
Add the koftas just before serving, spoon the pale gravy over, drizzle a teaspoon of raw mustard oil, and rest 2 minutes.
tips: Soak poppy seeds in warm water before grinding for a smooth, grit-free paste.
Keep the onions pale so the gravy stays light and delicate.
The touch of sugar is key to the mellow Bengali balance against the mustard sharpness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with luchi or steamed rice, with a wedge of lime and a few slit green chillies alongside.

variations.name: Rajasthani Punjabi Malai Kofta
variations.description: A bold Marwari take that fries the creamy koftas in Anveshan Ghee and bathes them in a smoky, yogurt-based dried-red-chilli gravy. Fiery crimson and ghee-rich, it swaps the mild Punjabi cream for the desert's love of chilli.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: binds the koftas so they hold in the fiery ghee gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the royal fat that fries the koftas and carries the Mathania chilli

steps: Mash 2 boiled potatoes with 1.5 cups grated paneer, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta into a firm dough and roll into 10 koftas.
Shallow-fry the koftas in 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat until golden all around, about 5 minutes, and set aside.
Soak 8 dried red chillies in warm water for 15 minutes, then blend with 2 onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste to a smooth crimson paste.
In the remaining 3 tbsp ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin, add the chilli-onion paste and fry over medium heat until thick and the ghee separates, about 9 minutes.
Lower the heat and whisk 1 cup yogurt with 1 tbsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt, then add slowly while stirring so it does not curdle, and simmer 5 minutes.
Pour in 0.5 cup water and 2 tbsp cream, slide in the koftas, and simmer gently 4 minutes until the gravy thickens and coats each one.
Finish with 1 tsp garam masala, rest 2 minutes, and serve while the ghee glistens on top.
tips: Deseed some chillies for deep colour without punishing heat, using Mathania chillies if available.
Whisk the yogurt smooth and add off a rolling boil so it blends into the ghee without splitting.
The small amount of cream here softens the fire just enough while keeping the Marwari boldness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra or missi roti and a side of sliced onion, green chilli and lime, desert-thali style.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Punjabi Malai Kofta
variations.description: A Deccan twist where the creamy koftas meet the smoky warmth of goda masala and a roasted peanut-coconut paste. Cooked in wood-pressed groundnut oil, it balances malai richness with the dark, aromatic spice of Maharashtra.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: binds the koftas so they hold in the robust goda masala gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the classic Maharashtrian oil for frying and the masala base

steps: Mash 2 boiled potatoes with 1.5 cups grated paneer, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta into a soft dough and roll into 10 koftas.
Fry the koftas in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat until golden, about 4 minutes, and drain.
Dry-roast 3 tbsp peanuts and 2 tbsp dry coconut until dark and fragrant, then blend with 1 chopped tomato to a coarse paste.
In 3 tbsp oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin, add 2 sliced onions and fry to deep brown, about 9 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste.
Add 1.5 tbsp goda masala, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.25 tsp red chilli powder and 0.75 tsp salt, fry a minute, then mix in the peanut-coconut paste and cook until oil separates, about 5 minutes.
Pour in 1 cup hot water and 2 tbsp cream, and simmer 4 minutes to a glossy, medium-thick gravy.
Place the koftas in just before serving, spoon the smoky gravy over them, and rest 2 minutes.
tips: Roast the peanuts and coconut to a rich brown for the deep, nutty base of the gravy.
Goda masala is smoky-sweet, so skip added sugar and let it lead the flavour.
Swirl the cream on at the end to soften the smoky spice without dulling it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft chapati or masala bhaat, garnished with fresh coriander and a dusting of goda masala.

variations.name: Classic Punjabi Rajma
variations.description: The quintessential Punjabi rajma-chawal: dark red beans slow-simmered in a browned onion-tomato masala, finished with butter and kasuri methi for that unmistakable homestyle depth. Thick, clingy and soul-warming. The Sunday lunch that defines a Punjabi kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee lays down the homely, rounded base of a Punjabi rajma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A little wood-pressed oil helps the onions brown without scorching

ingredients.name: Dried red kidney beans, soaked overnight

steps: Pressure-cook the soaked 1.5 cups kidney beans with 0.5 tsp salt and 3.5 cups water for 7-8 whistles until they mash easily, then keep them in their liquid.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds until aromatic.
Add the 2 chopped onions and fry 9 minutes until deep golden brown, then stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until the raw smell lifts.
Pour in the tomato puree with 1.25 tsp red chilli, 2 tsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp salt, and cook 10-11 minutes until thick and oil-flecked.
Add the beans with their liquid, mash a third of them into the gravy, and simmer covered 15 minutes until thick and creamy.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the pot, swirl in 2 tbsp butter and 1 tsp garam masala, and cook 2 minutes until glossy.
tips: The colour comes from properly browned onions and ripe tomatoes, so give both the time they need rather than adding food colour.
Mashing part of the beans is what thickens an authentic Punjabi rajma without any cream.
It tastes even better reheated the next day once the masala fully penetrates the beans.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over steamed rice with a spoon of ghee, sliced onions, green chilli and a dab of mango pickle.

variations.name: Kashmiri Punjabi Rajma
variations.description: The Punjabi bean meets the valley's spicing: a ruby, saffron-scented gravy built on fennel, dry ginger and Kashmiri chilli, without onion or garlic. Milder and more perfumed than the Amritsari original, yet still hearty. A fragrant, festive rajma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries the fennel and saffron aromatics of a Pandit-style gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: Saffron gives the ruby colour and gentle perfume of the valley

ingredients.name: Dried red kidney beans, soaked overnight

steps: Soak 0.25 tsp Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 3 tbsp warm water and set aside to bloom.
Pressure-cook the soaked 1.5 cups kidney beans with 0.5 tsp salt and 3.5 cups water for 8 whistles until soft, then keep them in their liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat, add the whole cloves, cardamom and cinnamon with 0.25 tsp asafoetida, and sizzle 30 seconds.
Lower the flame, stir in 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli then quickly the tomato puree, and cook 7-8 minutes until the ghee floats bright red.
Add 2 tsp fennel powder, 1 tsp dry ginger and 0.75 tsp salt, then add the beans with their liquid and the bloomed saffron water.
Simmer covered 16 minutes, mashing a few beans to thicken, and finish with 0.5 tsp garam masala for a perfumed ruby gravy.
tips: Cook the beans low and long so they turn creamy inside while holding their shape.
Resist adding onion or garlic; the clean fennel-forward aroma is the whole point of this take.
Bloom the saffron in warm water only, as boiling water dulls both its colour and scent.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain basmati rice and a bowl of curd, finished with a scatter of saffron strands.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Punjabi Rajma
variations.description: A Puneri spin on the Punjabi bean, simmered in a roasted-coconut and goda masala gravy that eats warm, dusky and gently sweet. Wood-pressed groundnut oil and a jaggery lift replace the butter and cream. Earthy and aromatic where the original is rich.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The traditional Maharashtrian fat that carries goda masala cleanly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A touch of jaggery rounds the dusky goda notes in true Puneri style

ingredients.name: Dried red kidney beans, soaked overnight

steps: Pressure-cook the soaked 1.5 cups kidney beans with 0.5 tsp salt and 3.5 cups water for 7-8 whistles until soft, then keep them in their liquid.
Dry-roast 4 tbsp grated coconut over low heat 4 minutes until golden, then grind with the 2 chopped tomatoes into a smooth paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds until aromatic.
Fry the 2 chopped onions 7 minutes until golden, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute, then add the coconut-tomato paste with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli.
Stir in 2 tsp goda masala and 0.75 tsp salt and fry 6 minutes on medium until the masala darkens and oil separates.
Add the beans with their liquid and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, mash a few beans, simmer covered 15 minutes, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Keep stirring once the goda masala goes in, since its coconut base catches and burns easily on high heat.
Roast the coconut only to golden for a warm-sweet gravy rather than a bitter one.
A finishing squeeze of lime lifts the dusky goda and jaggery beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri and thecha, or over hot rice with a drizzle of raw groundnut oil.

variations.name: Gujarati Punjabi Rajma
variations.description: The Punjabi bean tuned to the Gujarati khatta-meetha palate, with jaggery and a hint of tamarind rounding a lighter, coriander-cumin gravy tempered with mustard and curry leaves. Softer and more soupy than the Amritsari style. A gentle, sweet-savoury rajma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The daily Gujarati cooking fat that lets the sweet-sour notes shine

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery gives the signature Gujarati sweetness balancing the tamarind

ingredients.name: Dried red kidney beans, soaked overnight

steps: Pressure-cook the soaked 1.5 cups kidney beans with 0.5 tsp salt and 3.5 cups water for 7-8 whistles until soft, then keep them in their liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard and cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then add the curry leaves.
Add the chopped onion and saute 5 minutes until soft, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and cook 1 minute.
Pour in the tomato puree with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp coriander-cumin powder and 0.75 tsp salt, and simmer 8 minutes until the oil separates.
Add the beans with their liquid, 1 tbsp tamarind pulp and 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, mash a few beans, and simmer covered 14 minutes.
Taste and adjust the sweet-sour balance, simmer 2 minutes uncovered, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Add tamarind and jaggery in small increments and keep tasting to land the ideal khatta-meetha point.
Keep this rajma looser than a Punjabi one so it spoons over rice or soaks into phulka.
A pinch of cinnamon-clove powder in the tempering deepens the Kathiawadi warmth.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft ghee-brushed phulka or plain rice, kachumber salad and a spoon of sweet chunda.

variations.name: Bengali Punjabi Rajma
variations.description: The Punjabi bean given a Kolkata accent: tempered in pungent wood-pressed mustard oil with a whole-spice bhaja, slit green chillies and a whisper of sugar. The mustard oil lends a sharp bite quite unlike the buttery original. An east-Indian rajma with real character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Kachi ghani mustard oil gives the sharp, distinctive Bengali edge

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A pinch of jaggery brings the classic Bengali sweet-savoury balance

ingredients.name: Dried red kidney beans, soaked overnight
Bay leaf and dried red chilli

steps: Pressure-cook the soaked 1.5 cups kidney beans with 0.5 tsp salt and 3.5 cups water for 7-8 whistles until soft, then keep them in their liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil over medium-high until it just smokes, then lower the heat and temper 1 tsp cumin seeds, the bay leaf and dried red chilli for 30 seconds.
Add the chopped onion and fry 6-7 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger paste and cook 1 minute.
Add the chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli and 0.75 tsp salt, and cook 8 minutes until they collapse and oil separates.
Tip in the beans with their liquid, the 3 slit green chillies and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, mash a few beans, and simmer covered 15 minutes.
Sprinkle 0.75 tsp Bengali garam masala over the pot, cook 2 minutes uncovered, and rest 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Smoke the mustard oil first to burn off its raw pungency before the spices go in.
Use the lighter cinnamon-clove-cardamom Bengali garam masala rather than a cumin-heavy blend.
Keep the jaggery subtle, just balancing the mustard's sharpness rather than sweetening the dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a drizzle of raw mustard oil, or with hot luchi for a Bengali brunch.

variations.name: Classic Punjabi Soya Chunk
variations.description: A hearty Punjabi-style soya masala, where boiled chunks simmer in a robust browned-onion and tomato gravy lifted with crushed kasuri methi. Ghee, a cashew paste and a touch of cream give it the full-bodied dhaba richness of a paneer or chana dish. It is spicy, aromatic and deeply satisfying.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee replaces the usual butter, giving this Punjabi gravy its glossy, rich body.

steps: Boil 1.5 cups soya chunks in salted water for 5 minutes, then drain, rinse and squeeze each chunk firmly dry.
Soak 10 cashews in warm water for 10 minutes and grind to a smooth paste, then set it aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin, then add 3 finely chopped onions and 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry until dark golden, about 10 minutes.
Add 3 pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, and cook until the ghee separates and the masala turns glossy, about 9 minutes.
Stir in the cashew paste and cook for 2 minutes, then add the squeezed soya chunks with 1.5 cups hot water and simmer for 8 minutes.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi into the pan, add 0.5 tsp garam masala and 2 tbsp cream, warm for 2 minutes, and finish with 3 tbsp coriander.
tips: Brown the onions properly for a dark, restaurant-style gravy rather than a pale one.
The cashew paste gives body and a subtle sweetness that balances the spice.
Crush the kasuri methi between your palms just before adding to release its full aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan, laccha paratha or jeera rice, finished with julienned ginger and a swirl of cream.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Punjabi Soya Chunk
variations.description: The rich Punjabi soya masala reworked with the dark, roasted depth of goda masala and a coconut-onion paste. Cooked in wood-pressed groundnut oil and rounded with jaggery, it trades the creamy finish for a nutty, smoky Malvani character. Bold and earthy, it tastes far from ordinary.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the honest Deccan fat that lets goda masala take centre stage.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery powder softens the smoky goda masala and rounds the tomato tang.

steps: Boil 1.5 cups soya chunks in salted water for 5 minutes, then drain, rinse and squeeze them dry.
Dry roast 4 tbsp grated coconut with 1 sliced onion until deep brown, about 6 minutes, then grind to a coarse paste with a little water.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp cumin and 12 curry leaves, then add the 2 remaining chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and brown for 8 minutes.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.25 tsp red chilli powder and 2.5 tsp goda masala, and cook until the oil separates, about 7 minutes.
Stir in the roasted coconut paste and fry for 3 minutes, then add the squeezed soya chunks with 1.5 cups hot water and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder.
