Simmer for 8 minutes until the gravy thickens and coats the chunks, then finish with 2 tbsp coriander.
tips: Grind the roasted coconut coarse for the rustic Malvani texture.
Increase the chilli powder for a fiery Kolhapuri edge if you like real heat.
Rest the curry for 10 minutes off the heat so the goda masala blooms fully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri or steamed rice, a spoon of thecha and a wedge of lime.

variations.name: Gujarati Punjabi Soya Chunk
variations.description: The rich Punjabi soya curry taken in a lighter, sweeter Gujarati direction, with a jaggery-kissed tomato gravy and a smooth cashew base. It is milder on spice, rounded with lemon in the classic sweet-sour style. Comforting and family-friendly, it loves a plate of soft rotli.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A light hand with groundnut oil keeps this curry homely rather than heavy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery powder is the sweet counterweight to tomato and lemon in this Gujarati gravy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A drop of ghee at the finish lends a little of the richness of a Punjabi gravy.

steps: Boil 1.5 cups soya chunks in salted water for 5 minutes, then drain, rinse and squeeze them dry.
Simmer 4 tomatoes, 1 onion and 10 cashews in 1 cup water for 12 minutes, then cool and blend to a smooth puree.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin, add 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, then pour in the puree with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander-cumin powder.
Simmer the gravy for 10 minutes until it thickens and the oil floats to the top.
Add the squeezed soya chunks with 1 cup hot water and 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, then simmer for 8 minutes until the chunks are soft and coated.
Off the heat, stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and 1 tbsp lemon juice, and balance the sweet-sour finish before serving.
tips: Add the lemon after switching off the flame so its brightness stays lively.
The cashew puree keeps this mild curry smooth without needing cream.
Keep the chilli gentle, as this version is meant to lean sweet and soft.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulka or peas pulao, a glass of chhaas and a spoon of sweet pickle.

variations.name: Bengali Punjabi Soya Chunk
variations.description: The Punjabi soya curry reimagined through a Bengali lens, cooked in sharp Anveshan Mustard Oil with a whole-spice tempering and a cashew-poppy paste for body. Slit green chillies and a whisper of sweetness give the sweet-hot balance of eastern cooking. The mustard oil brings a warmth no creamy Punjabi gravy has.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil gives this curry its signature Bengali pungency and warmth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing teaspoon of ghee rounds the mustard oil into a mellow richness.

steps: Boil 1.5 cups soya chunks in salted water for 5 minutes, then drain, rinse and squeeze them dry.
Soak 8 cashews and 1 tbsp poppy seeds in warm water for 10 minutes, then grind to a smooth white paste.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it smokes and pales, temper 2 bay leaves and 3 green cardamom for 30 seconds, then add 2 chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger paste and fry until golden, about 7 minutes.
Stir in 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.75 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, and cook until the mustard oil surfaces, about 8 minutes.
Add the cashew-poppy paste and cook for 3 minutes, then add the squeezed soya chunks, 3 slit green chillies and 1.5 cups hot water and simmer for 8 minutes.
Finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee, rest for 3 minutes, and serve.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to smoking first to remove its raw bitterness.
The cashew-poppy paste gives a silky body without any cream.
A pinch of sugar with the tomatoes brings the gentle Bengali sweetness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice, luchi or pulao, with a wedge of lime and tomato chutney on the side.

variations.name: Kerala Punjabi Soya Chunk
variations.description: A South Indian coastal spin on the rich Punjabi curry, simmered in coconut milk and tempered with shallots and curry leaves in Anveshan Coconut Oil. Ground cashew and roasted coconut give a plush body with a gentle sweetness in place of cream. It is mild, aromatic and soothing.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil lends the tempering its warm, sweet Kerala aroma.

steps: Boil 1.5 cups soya chunks in salted water for 5 minutes, then drain, rinse and squeeze them dry.
Dry roast 0.25 cup grated coconut with 0.5 tsp fennel until golden, about 4 minutes, then grind with 10 soaked cashews and 2 tomatoes to a smooth paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, fry 10 sliced shallots and 10 curry leaves until light brown, about 4 minutes, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste.
Pour in the coconut-cashew-tomato paste with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, and cook for 10 minutes until thick and the oil separates.
Add the squeezed soya chunks with 0.5 cup hot water, then simmer for 8 minutes until the chunks are plump and coated.
Lower the flame, pour in 1 cup coconut milk, warm for 3 minutes without boiling, and finish with the last curry leaves crackled in coconut oil.
tips: Never boil the curry after the coconut milk goes in, or it will split.
Cashew and coconut together give the plush body of a Punjabi gravy without any cream.
Small shallots melt into a sweeter, silkier base than large onions.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with appam, ghee rice or steamed red rice, with pappadam and a coconut chutney.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Gajar Matar
variations.description: A fiery version of the carrot-and-pea sabzi loaded with green chilli, black pepper and red chilli so the sweetness of carrots is offset by real heat. The vegetables stay firm while a peppery masala coats them. A punchy dry sabzi for chilli lovers.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a robust wood-pressed oil that carries the layered chilli heat cleanly

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add the chopped onion and 3 chopped green chillies, frying for 4-5 minutes until the onion turns golden, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for a minute.
Lower the heat and add 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, stirring for 20 seconds with a splash of water so they do not burn.
Add the 3 diced carrots and 1 cup peas with 1 tsp salt, toss well, then cover and cook on low for 12-14 minutes until the carrots are just tender.
Uncover, sprinkle 0.75 tsp coarsely crushed black pepper and stir-fry on medium-high for 3 minutes so the vegetables dry and the pepper perfumes them.
Finish with 2 tbsp fresh coriander, toss and serve hot.
tips: Crush the black pepper fresh and add it late so its aroma stays sharp.
The carrots' sweetness balances the heat, so this can take more chilli than you might expect.
A squeeze of lemon at the table keeps the heat refreshing rather than heavy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with cooling cucumber raita and hot rotis, or with plain rice and a bowl of dal.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Gajar Matar
variations.description: A blazing Andhra fry where carrots and peas take on the fierce heat of Guntur red chilli and a garlic-forward sesame-oil tempering. A touch of tamarind rounds off the fire with tang. The carrots' sweetness only makes the chilli hit harder and more addictive.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed gingelly oil is the classic Andhra base that stands up to Guntur heat

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadai on medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal and let them splutter and turn golden, about 30 seconds.
Add 6 crushed garlic cloves and 12 curry leaves, frying for a minute until the garlic is pale gold and fragrant.

Add the chopped onion and cook for 4-5 minutes until soft, then lower the heat and add 2 tsp Guntur red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, stirring for 20 seconds so the chilli does not scorch.
Add the 3 diced carrots and 1 cup peas with 1 tsp salt, toss to coat, then add 4 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 12-14 minutes until tender.
Stir in 1 tsp tamarind pulp and cook uncovered on medium for 3-4 minutes so the sourness melds and the vegetables dry with a roasted edge.
Taste, adjust salt and serve while the sesame-garlic aroma is fresh.
tips: Guntur chilli is intensely hot; start with less if you are unsure and build up.
Crush the garlic rather than mince it so it releases more aroma into the sesame oil.
The spoon of tamarind is essential to balance the aggressive chilli with tang.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or as a fiery side to curd rice.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Spicy Gajar Matar
variations.description: A Kolhapuri-style fiery take where carrots and peas are cloaked in dark, spicy kanda-lasun-inspired masala with goda masala and plenty of red chilli. The heat is deep and complex rather than sharp, cut with fresh coconut. This is Maharashtra at its spiciest.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday Maharashtrian fat that carries a bold Kolhapuri masala well

steps: Dry-roast 3 tbsp grated dry coconut in a hot pan until golden and fragrant, about 2 minutes, then set aside.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin and let them splutter, then add 10 curry leaves.
Add the chopped onion and fry for 5 minutes until golden, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for a minute.
Lower the heat and add 1 tsp goda masala, 2 tsp Kolhapuri red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp turmeric with a splash of water so the chilli does not burn, cooking for 30 seconds.
Add the 3 diced carrots and 1 cup peas with 1 tsp salt, toss well, then cover and cook on low for 12-14 minutes until the carrots are tender.
Uncover, stir in the roasted coconut and stir-fry on medium for 3 minutes until the masala clings dark and dry, then serve.
tips: Roasting the dry coconut first adds a smoky depth that defines Kolhapuri-style spice.
Kolhapuri chilli is very hot; adjust the quantity to your tolerance.
Goda masala and chilli both scorch easily, so keep the flame low when they go in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri and raw onion, or with plain rice and a spoon of ghee to temper the heat.

variations.name: Rajasthani Spicy Gajar Matar
variations.description: A rugged Marwari dry sabzi where carrots and peas are fried in ghee with whole dried red chillies and a heavy hand of coriander and chilli powder. There is no onion or tomato, keeping the heat bold and direct. Amchur adds a dry tang that suits the desert palate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee rounds off the whole-chilli heat with desert richness

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat, then add 4 whole dried red chillies and let them darken and turn smoky for 15 seconds.
Add 1 tsp cumin, 0.5 tsp ajwain and a pinch of asafoetida, letting them crackle for 15 seconds.
Lower the heat and add 2 tsp coriander powder, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp turmeric with a splash of water so they do not burn, cooking for 30 seconds.
Add the 3 diced carrots and 1 cup peas with 1 tsp salt, toss to coat in the spiced ghee, then cover and cook on low for 12-14 minutes until tender.
Uncover and stir-fry on medium-high for 3 minutes so the vegetables dry and the chillies release their smoky heat.
Sprinkle 0.75 tsp amchur, toss for a minute and serve hot.
tips: Break the dried chillies for extra fire or leave them whole for aroma with milder heat.
The splash of water when adding powders keeps the ghee from scorching the spices.
This keeps well and tastes good at room temperature, ideal for a spicy tiffin.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra roti and a dollop of ghee, with sliced raw onion and green chilli alongside.

variations.name: Assamese Spicy Gajar Matar
variations.description: A clean, ferociously hot Assamese fry where a sliver of bhut jolokia lends smoky, fruity fire to sweet carrots and peas. The spicing is minimal, letting the ghost chilli and garlic dominate. A drizzle of mustard oil and a squeeze of lime keep it bright.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday Assamese fat whose pungency matches the ghost chilli heat

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai on medium-high until it smokes, then lower the heat and add 0.5 tsp panch phoron, letting it crackle for 15 seconds.
Add 5 crushed garlic cloves, 1 inch julienned ginger and half a deseeded bhut jolokia, frying gently for a minute so the chilli perfumes the oil without scorching.
Add the sliced onion and cook for 4-5 minutes until translucent and lightly golden.
Add the 3 diced carrots and 1 cup peas with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, tossing to coat, then add 4 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 12-14 minutes until tender.
Uncover and stir-fry on medium for 3 minutes so the vegetables dry and absorb the smoky chilli heat.
Take off the heat, squeeze in 1 tbsp lime juice, toss and serve.
tips: Handle bhut jolokia with gloves and deseed it; even half delivers formidable heat.
Add the ghost chilli whole and fish it out before serving if you want aroma with controllable heat.
The lime at the end is essential to balance and refresh the intense fire.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft steamed joha rice and a plate of fresh cucumber to cool the palate.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Kaddu
variations.description: A savoury, chilli-forward twist on pumpkin that trades the usual sweetness for green chillies, black pepper and a sharp amchur edge. The pumpkin's natural mellowness plays against real heat, making a punchy sabzi that wakes up the plate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a clean base that keeps the pepper and chilli heat crisp and clear

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon rounds the sharp heat into a warmer glow

steps: Peel and deseed the 500 g pumpkin and cut into 2.5 cm chunks, finely chop the 1 onion, and slit the 4 green chillies.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on medium and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and the slit green chillies for about 30 seconds.
Add the onion and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 5 minutes until golden, then stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder.
Add the pumpkin and 1 tsp salt, toss, cover, and cook on low for 14 to 16 minutes until tender but still holding some shape.
Uncover, add 1 tsp freshly cracked black pepper and 0.75 tsp amchur powder, and stir-fry on medium for 3 minutes to dry the masala and toast the pepper.
Finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee and toss to coat.
Garnish with 2 tbsp coriander leaves and serve hot.
tips: Do not mash the pumpkin here; keep the chunks intact so this savoury version stays a proper sabzi.
Crack the pepper fresh for a brighter, sharper heat than pre-ground.
The amchur, not jaggery, is what keeps this version savoury rather than sweet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulkas and a cooling boondi raita, or alongside plain dal-chawal to balance the heat.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Kaddu
variations.description: A fiery Andhra gummadikaya version where pumpkin is cooked in sesame oil with searing Guntur chilli, garlic and a curry-leaf tadka, then sharpened with tamarind. Hot, tangy and garlicky, it turns the mild gourd into something bold and rice-ready.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: gingelly oil stands up to the fierce Guntur chilli in true Andhra style

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: a final spoon softens the Guntur heat just enough to savour

steps: Peel and deseed the 500 g pumpkin and cut into 2.5 cm chunks, and crush the 8 garlic cloves coarsely.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil on medium and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 1 tsp urad dal until the dal turns golden, about 30 seconds.
Add the crushed garlic and 15 curry leaves and fry for 1 minute until the garlic is golden and fragrant.
Add the pumpkin with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, toss, cover, and cook on low for 12 to 14 minutes until tender but holding shape.
Uncover, add 2 tsp Guntur red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp tamarind pulp, and stir-fry on medium for 4 minutes until the masala clings and turns glossy.
Finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee and toss for a final minute.
Serve blazing hot with rice so the searing Guntur heat has a soft base to land on.
tips: The tamarind is essential to balance the Guntur chilli; without it the dish is flat heat.
Cut the pumpkin a little larger so it survives the vigorous stir-fry without turning to mush.
Rest for 10 minutes before serving so the garlic and chilli mellow and marry.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot steamed rice, a spoon of ghee and a bowl of plain curd to temper the fire.

variations.name: Rajasthani Spicy Kaddu
variations.description: A smoky, hot desert pumpkin built on roasted dried red chillies, fennel and a ghee-mustard tempering, with amchur cutting through for a savoury-sour edge. Bold and rustic, it keeps the sweetness low and the fire high.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee carries the smoky dried-chilli heat the desert way

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: a spoon lends the sharp, rustic edge typical of Rajasthani cooking

steps: Peel and deseed the 500 g pumpkin and cut into 2.5 cm chunks, and break the 5 dried red chillies in half.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee with 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil on medium and add 1 pinch asafoetida, 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 tsp fennel seeds and the dried chillies, frying for 30 seconds until smoky.
Add 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder with a splash of water and stir for 30 seconds.
Tip in the pumpkin and 1 tsp salt, toss, cover, and cook on low for 14 to 16 minutes until tender but still chunky.
Uncover and stir-fry on medium for 3 minutes to dry off the masala so it clings.
Add 1 tsp amchur powder and cook for 1 minute to sharpen the flavour.
Garnish with 2 tbsp coriander leaves and serve hot.
tips: Keep the pumpkin chunky and cook it just to tender so it does not collapse into a mash.
Roast the whole chillies only until darkened for smoky depth without bitterness.
The amchur keeps this version savoury; skip any jaggery to let the heat lead.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot bajra roti, a knob of white butter and sliced onions splashed with lemon.

variations.name: Bengali Spicy Kaddu
variations.description: A Bengali jhal kumro fired up with a pungent mustard-and-green-chilli paste over a mustard-oil tempering, giving the pumpkin a sinus-clearing sharpness. Hot, glossy and fiercely aromatic, it is the bold end of the Bengali repertoire.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: a double dose drives the sharp jhal heat this dish is built on

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: just a hint keeps the fierce mustard in check without dulling the heat

steps: Peel and deseed the 500 g pumpkin and cut into 2.5 cm chunks, then soak the 1 tbsp mustard seeds for 10 minutes and grind with 3 of the green chillies to a smooth paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until it just smokes, lower the flame, and temper 0.5 tsp nigella seeds and the 2 remaining slit green chillies for about 20 seconds.
Add 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp cumin powder with a splash of water and stir for 30 seconds.
Add the pumpkin and 1 tsp salt, toss, cover, and cook on low for 12 to 14 minutes until nearly tender.
Stir in the mustard-chilli paste with 3 tbsp water, cover, and cook for 4 more minutes until the raw pungency mellows and the pumpkin is soft.
Add 0.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and simmer uncovered for 1 minute to round the sharpness.
Garnish with 2 tbsp coriander leaves and serve with rice.
tips: Grind the mustard with green chillies rather than water alone to stop it turning bitter.
Add the mustard paste near the end and cook only until the raw smell fades.
The tiny bit of jaggery is a Bengali balancing trick, so do not leave it out.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot steamed rice with a drizzle of raw mustard oil and an extra green chilli on the side.

variations.name: Kerala Spicy Kaddu
variations.description: A Kerala erissery-inspired spicy pumpkin simmered with a coarse coconut-cumin paste and finished with a fiery coconut-oil tadka of curry leaves and red chillies. Creamy from the coconut yet properly hot, it is the richest of the spicy takes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: coconut oil is essential to the erissery aroma and the roasted-coconut tadka

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon deepens the roasted coconut and curry-leaf fragrance

steps: Peel and deseed the 500 g pumpkin and cut into 2.5 cm chunks, and grind 0.4 cup of the grated coconut with 1 tsp cumin seeds and the 3 green chillies to a coarse paste, saving the rest of the coconut for the tadka.
Place the pumpkin in a pot with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp salt and 0.5 cup water, cover, and cook on medium for 10 to 12 minutes until soft.
Stir in the coarse coconut paste and simmer on low for 4 minutes, mashing lightly so it thickens into a creamy mass.

In a small pan heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, then add the 3 broken dried red chillies, 15 curry leaves and the reserved coconut, frying for 2 minutes until the coconut turns golden.
Pour this sizzling tadka over the pumpkin and stir it through.
Drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee and mix once.
Serve hot with steamed rice, letting the creamy coconut base carry the chilli heat.
tips: Roast the tadka coconut to a proper golden brown; that toasty note defines erissery.
Grind the coconut paste coarse, not smooth, so the dish keeps a pleasant texture.
For extra heat leave the dried red chillies whole in the tadka rather than breaking them.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed matta rice and a spoon of tangy pickle, or as part of a larger South Indian meal.

variations.name: Classic Home-style Gajar Matar
variations.description: This is the everyday North Indian carrot-and-pea sabzi that shows up on weeknight thalis, cooked dry so the sweet carrots keep a little crunch. A cumin-scented onion-tomato base holds it together, kept light and homely rather than rich. It is the version most families cook without a recipe.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: its nutty warmth suits the sweet carrots without overpowering them

steps: Peel and dice the carrots into 1 cm cubes and keep the peas ready; finely chop the onion and tomatoes so they melt evenly into the base.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds until they sizzle and smell toasty, about 20 seconds.
Add the chopped onion with 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and saute on medium for 5 to 6 minutes until the onion turns soft and pale gold at the edges.
Stir in the tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, and cook for 4 to 5 minutes until the oil just begins to separate at the sides.
Add the diced carrots, peas and 1 tsp salt, toss to coat, then cover and cook on low for 10 to 12 minutes, stirring once, until the carrots are tender but still hold a slight bite.
Uncover, sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala, raise the heat for a minute to dry off any moisture, then fold through 3 tbsp chopped coriander and serve.
tips: Do not add water; the moisture from the tomatoes and covered carrots is enough to cook them without turning the sabzi mushy.
For a sweeter, more restaurant-style finish, grate a small handful of the carrots instead of dicing them all so they dissolve into the masala.
Leftovers make an excellent paratha stuffing the next morning; mash lightly and add a pinch of extra garam masala.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piled beside dal and phulka, with a spoon of thick curd and a wedge of lemon on the side to cut the sweetness.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Home-style Gajar Matar
variations.description: In Maharashtrian kitchens this sabzi turns fragrant and dark with goda masala, the roasted-coconut-and-spice blend that gives Puneri cooking its sweet-woody depth. A whisper of jaggery rounds the carrots off, echoing the region's love of a sweet-savoury balance. It eats beautifully with soft jowar bhakri.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the traditional frying fat of Maharashtrian everyday sabzis

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: dissolves fast to give the gentle sweetness central to this goda style

steps: Dice the carrots small and keep the peas ready; finely chop the onion so it softens quickly into the tempering.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on medium and add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds; when they pop, add 0.5 tsp cumin and let it sizzle for 10 seconds.
Add the chopped onion and saute for 4 minutes until translucent, then stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and cook for 30 seconds so the spices bloom.
Tip in the carrots and peas with 1 tsp salt, toss well, then cover and cook on low for 10 minutes until the carrots are just tender.
Sprinkle 1.5 tsp goda masala and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder over the vegetables and stir for 2 minutes so the masala coats everything and smells deeply roasted.
Fold in 3 tbsp grated coconut and 2 tbsp coriander, cook for another minute, and take off the heat while the coconut is still fresh and moist.
tips: Goda masala scorches easily, so add it near the end and keep the flame low once it goes in.
If you cannot find fresh coconut, use 2 tbsp desiccated coconut soaked in a spoon of warm water for a minute.
This sabzi tastes even better after resting 15 minutes, which lets the goda masala settle into the carrots.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with jowar or bajra bhakri and a spoon of thecha, or tuck it into a soft pav for a quick Pune-style snack.

variations.name: Gujarati Home-style Gajar Matar
variations.description: The Gujarati version leans openly sweet, with jaggery melting into a light, almost glossy masala lifted by lemon at the end. Green chilli and ginger keep it from cloying, giving that signature sweet-hot-tangy Gujarati balance. It is a gentle, everyday shaak meant for soft rotli and dal-bhaat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: groundnut oil is the staple cooking fat across Gujarati homes

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: gives the shaak its characteristic mellow sweetness without any bitterness

steps: Dice the carrots into small even cubes, keep the peas ready, and crush the ginger with the green chillies into a coarse paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on medium, add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and let them splutter, then add 0.5 tsp cumin and 0.25 tsp asafoetida for a few seconds until fragrant.
Stir in the ginger-chilli paste and fry for 30 seconds, then add 0.5 tsp turmeric and immediately follow with the carrots and peas so the turmeric does not burn.
Add 1 tsp salt and 2 tbsp water, cover, and cook on low for 10 to 12 minutes until the carrots turn tender and slightly glossy.
Sprinkle 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder over the shaak and stir for 2 minutes until it dissolves and lightly glazes the vegetables.
Turn off the heat, squeeze in 1 tbsp lemon juice, scatter 2 tbsp coriander, and toss so the flavours brighten just before serving.
tips: Add the lemon only after switching off the flame; boiling it turns the tang flat and slightly bitter.
Adjust jaggery to your carrots' natural sweetness; winter carrots may need only 1 tsp.
Keep the chillies coarsely crushed rather than finely minced so guests can push them aside if they prefer it milder.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thin phulka rotli brushed with ghee and a bowl of Gujarati kadhi for a classic light lunch.

variations.name: Bengali Home-style Gajar Matar
variations.description: Bengal reworks the sabzi into a pungent, aromatic style using nose-tingling mustard oil and a five-spice panch phoron tempering. The carrots stay lightly sweet while the mustard oil and fennel notes give it an unmistakable eastern character. It is comforting spooned over hot steamed rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: heated to smoking then cooled slightly for the authentic sharp Bengali aroma

steps: Dice the carrots small, keep the peas ready, and finely chop the tomato so it breaks down into the masala.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until it just begins to smoke, lower the heat, then add 1 tsp panch phoron, 2 dried red chillies and 1 bay leaf and let them crackle for 20 seconds.
Add the chopped tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp cumin powder, and cook for 3 minutes until the tomato softens and the raw smell lifts.
Tip in the carrots and peas with 1 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp sugar, stir to coat, then add 3 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 10 minutes.
Uncover and stir-fry on medium for 3 to 4 minutes until the carrots are tender and the masala clings dry to the vegetables.
Finish with 0.5 tsp ghee stirred through off the heat for a glossy, aromatic sheen and serve warm.
tips: Always let raw mustard oil reach smoking point first; this mellows its harshness and gives the true Bengali flavour.
Panch phoron should stay whole, so add it to hot oil and never grind it for this dish.
A pinch of sugar is traditional here and balances the pungency rather than making the dish sweet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over a mound of steaming gobindobhog or any short-grain rice, with a slice of lime and a green chilli on the side.

variations.name: Kerala Home-style Gajar Matar
variations.description: This is a thoran-style take, where the carrots and peas are tossed with a coarse coconut-cumin mix and finished with a coconut-oil tempering of mustard seeds and curry leaves. It stays dry and fresh, the sweet carrots meeting toasty coconut. It rounds out a Kerala sadya-style meal beautifully.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: essential for the true fragrance of a Kerala thoran

steps: Grate or finely chop the carrots, keep the peas ready, and pulse the grated coconut with 0.5 tsp cumin, the green chillies and 0.5 tsp turmeric into a coarse, dry mix.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil on medium and add 1 tsp mustard seeds; when they pop, add 1 tsp urad dal and 2 dried red chillies and fry until the dal turns golden.
Throw in 12 curry leaves, let them crackle for 5 seconds, then add the carrots and peas with 1 tsp salt and toss well.
Sprinkle over 2 tbsp water, cover, and steam on low for 8 to 10 minutes until the carrots are just tender.
Add the coconut-cumin mix, stir gently to combine, then cook uncovered on low for 3 to 4 minutes until the coconut is warmed through and lightly toasted.
Turn off the heat while the thoran is still moist and vivid, and serve without letting it dry out further.
tips: Keep the coconut mix coarse and dry; a smooth wet paste makes the thoran gluey rather than fluffy.
Grating the carrots instead of dicing gives the classic fine thoran texture and cooks faster.
Add the coconut only in the last few minutes so it stays fresh and does not brown into a paste.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as one of several sides with rice and sambar, or alongside curd rice for a cooling contrast.

variations.name: Classic Masala Dum Aloo
variations.description: Baby potatoes are fried until their skins blister, then slow-simmered dum-style in a smooth onion-tomato-cashew gravy so they soak up every bit of masala. The sauce is glossy, mildly spiced and finished with cream and garam masala. This is the crowd-pleasing restaurant-style version that works with both roti and rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for shallow-frying the potatoes to a crisp golden skin

steps: Boil the baby potatoes for 10 minutes until just fork-tender, peel them, and prick each one a few times so it drinks up the gravy.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on medium and shallow-fry the potatoes for 5 to 6 minutes, turning, until the skins are golden and blistered, then set aside.

In the same oil crackle 1 tsp cumin, add the chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, and saute for 6 minutes until deep golden; add the tomatoes and cashews and cook 5 minutes until pulpy, then cool and blend to a smooth paste.
Return the paste to the pan with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, and cook on medium for 5 to 6 minutes until the oil separates at the edges.
Add 1 cup water and 1.25 tsp salt, slip in the fried potatoes, cover and simmer on low for 10 minutes so the potatoes absorb the masala in true dum style.
Stir in 3 tbsp cream and 0.75 tsp garam masala, simmer 2 more minutes, then scatter 2 tbsp coriander and serve hot.
tips: Pricking the boiled potatoes is the secret to dum aloo; unpricked potatoes stay bland inside no matter how long they simmer.
For a deeper colour without extra heat, use Kashmiri red chilli powder in place of some of the regular chilli.
The gravy thickens as it rests, so loosen with a splash of hot water before serving leftovers.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or jeera rice and a side of sliced onions tossed in lemon and chaat masala.

variations.name: Kashmiri Masala Dum Aloo
variations.description: The true Kashmiri dum aloo skips onion and tomato entirely, building its brick-red gravy on yogurt, fennel and dry ginger with saffron for perfume. The result is tangy, warmly spiced and aromatic rather than sweet. This is the temple-and-wedding classic of the valley.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the defining fat of Kashmiri cooking, giving the gravy its sharp pungency

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm water for the signature colour and aroma of valley dum aloo

steps: Boil the baby potatoes for 10 minutes until just tender, peel, and prick them all over so they absorb the yogurt gravy.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the flame, and fry the potatoes for 5 minutes until browned; lift them out and reserve.
In the same oil add 3 cloves, 2 cardamom pods, 1 inch cinnamon and 0.25 tsp asafoetida, and let them sizzle for 20 seconds until fragrant.

Whisk 1 cup yogurt smooth with 2 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 2 tsp fennel powder and 1 tsp dry ginger, then pour it in off the heat and stir continuously so it does not split as you return it to a low flame.
Add the potatoes, 1.25 tsp salt and 1 cup water, cover and simmer on low for 12 to 15 minutes until the gravy thickens and clings to the potatoes.
Stir in the steeped Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron with its water, simmer 2 more minutes, and serve once the surface shows a ring of red oil.
tips: Always whisk the yogurt smooth and add it off the heat while stirring, or it will curdle into grainy lumps.
Fennel and dry ginger powder are non-negotiable here; they, not onion, carry the whole flavour.
The dish tastes better the next day once the potatoes have fully absorbed the spiced yogurt.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice as part of a Kashmiri meal, alongside a simple haakh saag for contrast.

variations.name: Bengali Masala Dum Aloo
variations.description: The Bengali aloor dum is a lighter, homelier braise, potatoes simmered in a mustard-oil gravy scented with a whole-spice bhaja masala and a little sugar for that classic sweet-savoury edge. It is the potato dish that partners luchi at weekend breakfasts. Warming, gently spiced and deeply comforting.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: gives the aloor dum its unmistakable sharp Bengali base

steps: Boil the baby potatoes for 10 minutes until tender, peel, and prick each so the gravy soaks in.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the heat, and fry the potatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric and a pinch of salt for 5 minutes until golden; remove them.
In the same oil temper 1 tsp cumin, 2 bay leaves and 2 dried red chillies for 15 seconds, then add 1 tbsp ginger paste and the chopped tomatoes and cook 5 minutes to a pulp.
Stir in 1.5 tsp cumin powder and 1 tsp coriander powder with a splash of water and fry for 2 minutes until the masala smells roasted and the oil surfaces.
Return the potatoes with 1.25 tsp salt, 0.75 tsp sugar and 1.5 cups water, cover, and simmer on low for 12 minutes until the gravy reduces to a light coating consistency.
Finish with 0.5 tsp garam masala, simmer 1 minute, and serve warm with the gravy just clinging to each potato.
tips: The pinch of sugar rounds the mustard oil's bite and is what makes it taste authentically Bengali.
Keep the gravy on the thinner side, as aloor dum is meant to be a touch runny for mopping up with luchi.
For extra aroma, dry-roast and crush a little cumin and dried chilli to sprinkle over at the end.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with luchi or radhaballavi for breakfast, or with plain parathas and a wedge of lime.

variations.name: Gujarati Masala Dum Aloo
variations.description: This Gujarati take turns the gravy sweet, tangy and light, balancing jaggery against tomato and a hint of yogurt, with no cream in sight. Warm spices stay gentle so the sweet-sour character leads. It is the kind of everyday shaak that makes soft rotli disappear fast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday cooking oil of Gujarati kitchens, mild enough to let the sweet-sour gravy shine

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melts into the tomato gravy for the classic Gujarati sweet-sour balance

steps: Boil the baby potatoes for 10 minutes until tender, peel, prick them, and blend the tomatoes to a smooth puree.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on medium, add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin, and when they splutter add 0.25 tsp asafoetida.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and the tomato puree with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp coriander-cumin powder and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, and cook 6 minutes until thick and glossy.
Whisk the 0.5 cup yogurt smooth, lower the flame, stir it in gradually so it does not split, and cook 2 minutes until the gravy looks creamy.
Add the potatoes, 1.25 tsp salt and 1 cup water, cover, and simmer on low for 10 minutes until the potatoes take on the masala.
Stir in 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer 2 minutes until it dissolves into a sweet-sour glaze, and serve warm.
tips: Balance is everything here; taste after adding jaggery and adjust with a squeeze of lemon if the tomatoes were mild.
Add yogurt on a low flame while stirring so the gravy stays smooth and does not curdle.
This shaak reheats well and the sweet-sour flavour deepens overnight.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulka rotli or thepla and a bowl of plain khichdi for a homely Gujarati meal.

variations.name: Andhra Masala Dum Aloo
variations.description: This is a fiery Andhra rendering built on smoky Guntur red chillies and a sesame-peanut paste that thickens the gravy with earthy body. Curry leaves and garlic in the tempering make it aromatic and bold. It is potatoes for those who like real heat with their rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: nallennai is the traditional cooking oil of Andhra, adding a nutty depth to the spicy gravy

steps: Boil the baby potatoes for 10 minutes until tender, peel and prick them, and dry-roast the peanuts and sesame seeds separately until fragrant, then grind with 5 Guntur chillies and the garlic to a coarse paste with a little water.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil on medium and fry the potatoes for 5 minutes until browned; lift them out and reserve.
In the same oil crackle 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 12 curry leaves, add the chopped onions, and saute for 6 minutes until deep golden.
Stir in the ground peanut-sesame-chilli paste with 0.5 tsp turmeric and cook on low for 4 to 5 minutes until the raw smell goes and the oil surfaces.
Add the potatoes, 1 tbsp tamarind pulp, 1.25 tsp salt and 1.5 cups water, cover, and simmer on low for 12 minutes until the gravy thickens.
Uncover, simmer 2 more minutes to concentrate the flavour, and serve once the gravy coats the potatoes richly.
tips: Toast the peanuts and sesame just until they colour; over-roasting makes the gravy bitter.
Adjust the number of Guntur chillies to your tolerance, as they bring serious heat and a smoky aroma.
The tamarind is what stops the dish being one-dimensionally hot, so do not skip it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or with ragi mudde for a rustic Andhra plate.

variations.name: Classic Butter Methi Matar Malai
variations.description: A silky North Indian restaurant favourite where fresh fenugreek leaves and sweet green peas swim in a pale cashew-and-cream gravy. The faint bitterness of methi is balanced by butter, malai and a whisper of jaggery, giving a mild, luxurious curry that never fights the palate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the nutty bilona ghee carries the mild gravy and blooms the cumin

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: rounds off the methi bitterness far more gently than refined sugar

steps: Wash the 2 cups fenugreek leaves well, sprinkle over 0.5 tsp salt, rest for 10 minutes, then squeeze out the dark liquid to tame the bitterness before cooking.
Boil the 2 chopped onions and 12 cashews in 1 cup water for 8 minutes until soft, cool, then blend to a smooth ivory paste with a splash of the cooking water.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 20 seconds until fragrant and lightly darkened.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 2 slit green chillies, saute for 1 minute, then pour in the onion-cashew paste and cook on low for 6 minutes until it thickens and smells sweet.
Stir in the squeezed methi and 1 cup green peas with 0.5 tsp salt, cover and simmer for 6 minutes until the peas are tender and the leaves collapse.
Lower the heat, add 0.5 cup milk and 0.5 cup cream in a slow stream while stirring so the gravy stays velvety and does not split, about 3 minutes.
Finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 0.5 tsp garam masala and 1 tbsp butter, swirl for 2 minutes until glossy and serve hot.
tips: Salting and squeezing the methi is the single biggest trick to a mild, non-bitter gravy; skip it and the curry turns sharp.
If the gravy splits after adding cream, whisk in 1 tbsp cold milk off the heat to bring it back together.
The gravy tastes even better the next day; loosen with a splash of warm milk when reheating gently.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle into a copper handi and pair with butter naan or lachha paratha; a side of pickled onion rings cuts the richness beautifully.

variations.name: Bengali Butter Methi Matar Malai
variations.description: Bengal reworks this creamy classic with the pungent bite of raw mustard oil and a gentle sweetness typical of the region's cooking. A finishing dab of Kashmiri chilli and a hint of jaggery gives the pale gravy a warm-golden edge without heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked to remove its raw edge, it gives the malai a distinctly Bengali pungency

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the trademark Bengali touch of sweetness that offsets the mustard oil's sharpness

steps: Soak 2 tbsp poppy seeds in warm water for 15 minutes, then grind with 2 green chillies to a smooth white paste that will thicken the gravy Bengali-style.
Rinse the 2 cups methi, rub in 0.5 tsp salt, leave 10 minutes and squeeze firmly to drain the bitter juices.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just wisps smoke, then cool for 30 seconds so it loses its raw pungency.
Fry the 2 sliced onions in the mustard oil over medium heat for 6 minutes until soft and pale gold, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger paste for another minute.
Add the poppy-seed paste and 0.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, cook on low for 4 minutes until the raw smell lifts and the oil beads at the edges.
Fold in the squeezed methi, 1 cup peas, 1 slit green chilli and 0.5 tsp salt, splash in 0.5 cup water, cover and simmer for 7 minutes.
Lower the flame, stir in 0.5 cup cream, 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.5 tsp sugar, simmer 3 minutes until the gravy is glossy and gently sweet, then serve.
tips: Always heat mustard oil to smoking first; raw mustard oil tastes acrid and overpowers the delicate peas.
Grind the poppy seeds with a little milk instead of water for an even silkier, whiter gravy.
Balance is key here: taste after adding jaggery and add a pinch more only if the mustard bite still dominates.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steaming Gobindobhog rice or fluffy luchis, and a wedge of lime on the side to lift the sweetness.

variations.name: Gujarati Butter Methi Matar Malai
variations.description: The Gujarati kitchen leans into its love of sweet-savoury balance, folding melted jaggery straight into the creamy peas-and-fenugreek gravy. Wood-pressed groundnut oil and a tempering of curry leaves give it a homely, faintly nutty character quite unlike the Punjabi original.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the traditional wood-pressed cooking fat of Gujarat, sweetly nutty and light

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the signature Gujarati sweetness melted right into the gravy

steps: Blend 2 chopped tomatoes with 10 cashews to a smooth puree that will lend body and a mild tang to the Gujarati gravy.
Rub 0.5 tsp salt into the 2 cups methi, rest 10 minutes, then squeeze out the bitter dark liquid before cooking.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds with 10 curry leaves until they splutter, about 20 seconds.
Add 1 finely chopped onion and saute for 4 minutes until translucent, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and 0.25 tsp turmeric for a minute.
Pour in the tomato-cashew puree and cook on low for 6 minutes until it darkens and the oil separates at the sides.
Add the squeezed methi, 1 cup peas and 0.5 tsp salt with 0.5 cup water, cover and simmer for 7 minutes until the peas are soft.
Stir in 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.4 cup cream, simmer gently for 3 minutes until the sweet-savoury gravy turns glossy, then serve warm.
tips: Gujaratis prefer the sweetness pronounced; taste and add a little extra jaggery if your tomatoes are very sour.
Adding curry leaves to the tempering is essential here for the homely western-Indian aroma.
For a make-ahead version, cook up to the peas stage and stir in cream and jaggery only when reheating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best mopped up with soft phulka rotis or thepla, alongside a cooling boondi raita and a spoon of sweet mango chutney.

variations.name: Kerala Butter Methi Matar Malai
variations.description: Kerala swaps dairy cream for velvety coconut milk and cooks everything in fragrant wood-pressed coconut oil, turning the northern classic into a mellow, tropical curry. Freshly ground coconut and a curry-leaf tempering make it lighter yet deeply aromatic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed and intensely aromatic, it is the soul of any Kerala gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a small spoon rounds the coconut gravy the way Malabar cooks favour

steps: Grind 0.75 cup grated coconut with 2 green chillies and 1 inch ginger to a smooth paste using a little water, the fragrant base of this Kerala version.
Rub 0.5 tsp salt into the 2 cups methi, rest 10 minutes and squeeze out the dark bitter juices thoroughly.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadai over medium heat, splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds with 12 curry leaves for 15 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 sliced onion and 1 slit green chilli, saute for 4 minutes until soft, then stir in the ground coconut paste and 0.25 tsp turmeric.
Cook the paste on low for 4 minutes until the raw coconut smell fades and it turns pale gold, stirring so it does not catch.
Add the squeezed methi, 1 cup peas and 0.5 tsp salt with 0.5 cup water, cover and simmer for 7 minutes until the peas soften.
Reduce the heat to low, pour in 0.75 cup thick coconut milk and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, warm through for 2 minutes without boiling, then serve.
tips: Never boil the dish hard after adding coconut milk or it will curdle; keep it at a bare simmer.
A final drizzle of raw coconut oil just before serving intensifies the classic Kerala aroma.
Use the second, thinner pressing of coconut milk to cook the peas and reserve the thick milk for finishing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Wonderful with appam, Kerala red rice or a stack of malabar parottas; add a papadam for crunch.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Butter Methi Matar Malai
variations.description: This version borrows the smoky, complex warmth of homemade goda masala, Maharashtra's signature spice blend of roasted coconut, sesame and stone flower. Cooked in wood-pressed groundnut oil with a touch of jaggery, it is earthier and more aromatic than the creamy northern take.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday wood-pressed oil of Maharashtrian kitchens, mild and nutty

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the customary sweet note that offsets goda masala's dark spice

steps: Dry-roast 3 tbsp desiccated coconut in a hot pan for 2 minutes until golden and nutty, then blend with 2 chopped onions to a coarse paste.
Rub 0.5 tsp salt into the 2 cups methi, rest 10 minutes and squeeze out the bitter liquid before use.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds until aromatic.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the roasted coconut-onion paste, cook for 6 minutes until deep golden and the oil surfaces.
Stir in 1.5 tsp goda masala, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, roast for 1 minute until intensely fragrant.
Add the squeezed methi, 1 cup peas and 0.5 tsp salt with 0.5 cup water, cover and simmer for 7 minutes until the peas are tender.
Lower the heat, stir in 0.4 cup cream and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer for 3 minutes until the dark, glossy gravy comes together, then serve.
tips: Goda masala scorches quickly; add it to a slightly cooled pan and keep the flame low.
Roasting the coconut before grinding is what gives this version its signature smoky depth.
No goda masala on hand? A pinch of cinnamon, clove and stone flower ground together is a fair stand-in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri or steamed rice and a dollop of homemade white butter, with a lemon wedge alongside.

variations.name: Classic Jeera Rice
variations.description: The everyday North Indian cumin rice served in homes and dhabas alike, where long-grain basmati is toasted in ghee-bloomed jeera until every grain stands separate and perfumed. Warm whole spices and a sizzle of cumin do all the flavouring, making it the ideal quiet partner for dals and curries.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee blooms the cumin and gives the rice its signature nutty aroma

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati rice under cold water until it runs clear, then soak for 20 minutes and drain in a colander so the grains stay firm and separate while cooking.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot over medium heat, then add 1 bay leaf, 3 green cardamom pods, 4 cloves and a 1 inch cinnamon stick and fry for 30 seconds until fragrant and gently sizzling.
Add 1.5 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle for about 15 seconds, then add 1 thinly sliced medium onion and saute over medium heat until golden, about 6 minutes.
Tip in the drained rice and toss gently for 2 minutes until the grains turn glossy and smell nutty, taking care not to break them.
Pour in 2.25 cups hot water with 1.25 tsp salt, stir once, and bring to a rolling boil over high heat.
Cover with a tight lid, lower the heat to minimum and steam for 12 minutes, then rest off the heat for 5 minutes; fluff with a fork and scatter 2 tbsp chopped coriander before serving.
tips: Do not skip the 20 minute soak; it lets the grains elongate and keeps them from snapping when you stir.
Bloom the cumin only until it darkens a shade and smells toasty, as burnt jeera turns the whole pot bitter.
For guaranteed separate grains, spread the cooked rice on a wide plate for a minute before piling it into a serving bowl.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a shallow bowl with a wedge of lemon and thin onion rings on the side, alongside dal tadka or a bowl of cooling boondi raita.

variations.name: Punjabi Jeera Rice
variations.description: The buttery dhaba-style rendition from Punjab, finished with a knob of butter that melts into each grain for a glossy richness beyond plain ghee. It leans indulgent, meant to soak up thick makhani gravies and creamy dals.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The base ghee carries the cumin while butter is layered on top for dhaba-style richness

steps: Wash 1.5 cups basmati rice in three changes of water, soak for 20 minutes and drain thoroughly so the grains cook up long and loose.
Warm 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide pan over medium heat and drop in 1 bay leaf, 3 cloves and 6 black peppercorns, frying for 20 seconds until they release their warm scent.
Scatter in 1.5 tsp cumin seeds and let them sputter for 10 seconds, then add 1 finely sliced onion and 1 slit green chilli and cook until the onion is deep golden, roughly 7 minutes.
Fold in the drained rice and stir gently for 2 minutes so each grain is coated in the spiced fat.
Add 2.25 cups hot water and 1.25 tsp salt, bring to a brisk boil, then cover and steam on the lowest heat for 12 minutes until the water is absorbed.
Rest for 5 minutes, dot 1 tbsp butter over the hot rice so it melts through, then fluff and finish with 2 tbsp coriander before serving.
tips: Add the butter only after cooking so it stays creamy and glossy rather than frying away.
A single slit green chilli adds Punjabi warmth without real heat; leave it whole to lift out later if serving children.
This reheats beautifully with a teaspoon of water and a fresh dab of butter in a covered pan.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile into a brass bowl beside dal makhani or paneer butter masala, with sliced cucumber and a squeeze of lime to cut the richness.

variations.name: Bengali Jeera Rice
variations.description: A Bengali take that swaps the cooking fat for pungent wood-pressed mustard oil, lending the rice a sharp, earthy backbone quite unlike the ghee version. A whisper of sugar and a scatter of fried onions echo the sweet-savoury balance loved across Bengal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil is heated to smoking first to mellow its bite and give the rice a Bengali sharpness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A final spoon of ghee rounds off the pungent mustard oil for balance

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain well while you prepare the tempering.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat until it just begins to smoke, then lower the flame to take the raw edge off the oil.
Drop in 2 bay leaves and 2 dried red chillies, follow with 1.5 tsp cumin seeds, and let everything crackle for 20 seconds until deeply aromatic.
Add 1 thinly sliced onion with 0.5 tsp sugar and fry over medium heat until the onion turns a rich brown, about 8 minutes.
Stir in the drained rice for 2 minutes, then pour in 2.25 cups hot water and 1.25 tsp salt and bring to a boil over high heat.
Cover and steam on the lowest heat for 12 minutes, rest for 5 minutes, then swirl in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee, fluff, and top with 2 tbsp coriander.
tips: Always heat mustard oil to smoking point first; this tames its sharpness and prevents a raw, bitter taste.
The pinch of sugar is not for sweetness but to deepen the onions to a Bengali mahogany brown.
Fish out the bay leaves and whole chillies before serving so no one bites into them.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside a light cholar dal or aloo bhaja, with a wedge of lime and a few extra fried onion slivers scattered on top.

variations.name: Kashmiri Jeera Rice
variations.description: An aromatic Valley-style version tinted gold with saffron and warmed by a Kashmiri whole-spice blend heavy on fennel and cardamom. The saffron milk stains alternate grains sunset-orange, turning a humble side into something fit for a wazwan spread.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries the fennel and cardamom and helps the saffron colour bloom evenly through the rice

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Kashmiri saffron threads are steeped in warm milk to paint the grains gold and add a floral top note

steps: Soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes and drain; meanwhile steep 0.25 tsp Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside to bloom.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot over medium heat and lightly fry 2 tbsp slivered almonds until pale gold, about 1 minute, then lift them out for garnish.
Into the same ghee add 4 green cardamom pods, 3 cloves and a 1 inch cinnamon stick, then 1.5 tsp cumin seeds and 0.5 tsp fennel seeds, and let them crackle for 20 seconds until floral and toasty.
Add the drained rice and toss gently for 2 minutes to coat each grain, then pour in 2.25 cups hot water and 1.25 tsp salt and bring to a boil.
Cover and steam on the lowest heat for 12 minutes until the water is absorbed and the grains are tender.
Drizzle the saffron milk over the hot rice, rest for 5 minutes, then fluff so the colour streaks through and top with the fried almonds.
tips: Steep the saffron in warm, not hot, milk so it releases colour slowly without turning bitter.
Fennel is the signature Kashmiri note here; keep it to half a teaspoon so it perfumes rather than dominates.
Drizzle the saffron milk at the end and fold only once for a marbled look rather than a uniform yellow.
variations.servingSuggestion: Present alongside a rich rogan josh or a paneer yakhni, garnished with a few extra saffron threads and a scatter of pomegranate seeds for colour.

variations.name: Kerala Jeera Rice
variations.description: A coastal reimagining where wood-pressed coconut oil replaces ghee and fresh grated coconut is toasted into the rice for a mild, tropical sweetness. Curry leaves and a bright coconut aroma make it a natural companion to Kerala's tangy curries.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil gives the rice its unmistakable Kerala fragrance and a silky finish

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain in a colander while you set up the tempering.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pot over medium heat and fry 2 tbsp cashews until golden, about 1 minute, then scoop them out to garnish later.

Add 1.5 tsp cumin seeds and 12 curry leaves to the oil and let them splutter for 15 seconds, then add 1 sliced onion, 1 chopped green chilli and 1 inch julienned ginger and cook until the onion softens, about 5 minutes.
Stir in 0.25 cup grated coconut and toast for 2 minutes until it smells sweet and turns pale gold at the edges.
Add the drained rice and fold gently for 2 minutes, then pour in 2.25 cups hot water and 1.25 tsp salt and bring to a boil over high heat.
Cover and steam on the lowest heat for 12 minutes, rest for 5 minutes, then fluff and crown with the fried cashews.
tips: Toast the grated coconut just to pale gold; letting it brown fully will make the rice taste scorched.
Fresh or thawed frozen coconut both work, but squeeze out excess moisture from thawed coconut first.
A final teaspoon of raw coconut oil drizzled over the hot rice deepens the coastal aroma if you love it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a Kerala-style vegetable stew or fish moilee, a papadum on the side and a spoon of coconut chutney to double down on the flavour.

variations.name: Classic Dhuli Moong Fry
variations.description: A comforting North Indian everyday dal of skinned split green gram cooked soft, then dressed with a fragrant ghee-cumin tadka of garlic, onion and tomato. The finish is silky and buttery rather than watery, meant to be scooped up with roti. This is the version most Indian homes make on a weekday when they want something light yet satisfying.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee gives this simple dal its nutty, restaurant-style richness.

steps: Rinse 1 cup dhuli moong dal in 2 to 3 changes of water until it runs clear, then pressure-cook it with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft and creamy.
While the dal cooks, finely chop 1 onion, 2 tomatoes, 1 inch ginger and 6 garlic cloves so the tadka comes together quickly.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds until they sizzle and turn fragrant, about 20 seconds.
Add the garlic and ginger and fry for 30 seconds, then add the onion and cook until soft and pale gold, about 4 minutes.
Stir in the tomatoes, remaining 0.75 tsp salt and 1 tsp red chilli powder and cook until the tomatoes collapse into a thick masala and ghee separates at the edges, about 6 minutes.
Pour the cooked dal into the tadka, add half a cup of hot water to loosen it, and simmer on low for 5 minutes so the flavours marry.
Finish with a spoon of Anveshan Ghee and a scatter of fresh coriander, and serve hot with steamed rice or roti.
tips: For a smoother dal, whisk it briskly with a ladle after simmering; for a rustic texture leave it as is.
If the dal thickens on standing, loosen with hot water rather than cold so the silky finish stays intact.
A pinch of asafoetida added with the cumin makes this light dal much easier to digest.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a warm bowl with a wedge of lemon on the side and a plate of crisp jeera rice or hot phulkas; a spoon of extra ghee melted on top just before eating makes it feel indulgent.

variations.name: Bengali Dhuli Moong Fry
variations.description: In Bengal, moong dal is dry-roasted before boiling and then tempered in pungent mustard oil, giving it a golden aroma and gentle sweetness quite unlike the North Indian version. Whole panch-phoron-style cumin and green chilli keep it fresh, while a light hand with onion lets the roasted dal shine. It is the everyday bhaja moong dal served with steamed rice and a squeeze of lime.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Kachi-ghani mustard oil gives the roasted dal its unmistakable Bengali pungency.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A final spoon of ghee rounds off the sharp mustard oil beautifully.

steps: Dry-roast 1 cup dhuli moong dal in a heavy pan on medium-low heat, stirring constantly, until it turns golden and smells nutty, about 5 minutes.
Rinse the roasted dal gently, then pressure-cook it with 3.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft but still holding a little shape.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pan until it just begins to smoke, then lower the heat so it loses its raw sharpness.
Crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 bay leaf and 2 dried red chillies in the oil for about 20 seconds until fragrant, then add 1 inch grated ginger and fry for 30 seconds.
Pour in the boiled dal, add the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, 0.5 tsp sugar and 2 slit green chillies, and simmer on low for 6 minutes so the mustard aroma soaks in.
Finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and chopped coriander, stir once, and serve hot with plain steamed rice.
tips: Roasting the dal first is the key Bengali step; do not skip it, as it gives the dish its signature aroma.
Keep the green chillies whole and slit so they perfume the dal without making it fiery.
A squeeze of lime just before serving brightens the roasted, mustardy flavours.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle over a mound of hot gobindobhog or short-grain rice with a side of aloo bhaja and a wedge of lime; it also pairs beautifully with a simple begun bhaja.

variations.name: Gujarati Dhuli Moong Fry
variations.description: Gujarat's moong dal leans sweet-and-tangy, balancing jaggery and lime against a gentle ghee tadka of cumin, curry leaves and a hint of green chilli. It is thinner and more soupy than the North Indian fry, meant to be sipped alongside rice, and carries the region's signature triple note of sweet, sour and mild heat. This is the dal that appears on a Gujarati thali beside kadhi and shaak.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries the curry-leaf tadka that defines this Gujarati dal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Organic jaggery gives the signature sweet-sour Gujarati balance without refined sugar.

steps: Rinse 1 cup dhuli moong dal well, then pressure-cook it with 3.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 3 whistles until very soft, then whisk smooth and keep it slightly loose.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium heat and add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds; when they pop, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them sizzle for 15 seconds.
Add 10 curry leaves, 2 slit green chillies and 1 inch grated ginger and fry for 30 seconds until the leaves turn crisp and aromatic.
Pour the whisked dal into the tadka along with 1 cup hot water and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, then bring to a gentle simmer.
Stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and simmer on low for 6 minutes until it dissolves and the dal turns glossy and pourable.
Turn off the heat, stir in 1 tbsp lemon juice and chopped coriander, and serve hot in a bowl to sip alongside rice.
tips: Add the lemon juice off the heat so its brightness is not cooked away.
Keep this dal thin and pourable; it is meant to be sipped, not scooped like a thick North Indian dal.
Adjust jaggery and lemon together until you taste a clear sweet-sour balance.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as part of a thali with soft phulka, steamed rice, a dry sabzi and a spoon of pickle; the sweet-sour dal is also lovely simply poured over rice with a dollop of ghee.

variations.name: Andhra Dhuli Moong Fry
variations.description: Andhra turns up the heat with fiery Guntur red chillies, garlic and a sesame-oil tadka, making a bold, garlicky moong fry that is drier and hotter than its northern cousins. The dal is cooked just soft enough to hold together, then coated in a rasping garlic-chilli masala. It is built to be eaten with rice and a spoon of ghee to tame the fire.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed sesame oil is the authentic Andhra cooking fat and stands up to the chillies.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of ghee mellows the Guntur heat on the plate.

steps: Rinse 1 cup dhuli moong dal and pressure-cook it with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 2 whistles only, so the grains stay soft but distinct rather than mushy.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pan on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds with 4 broken Guntur red chillies for about 20 seconds until the chillies darken.
Add 10 crushed garlic cloves and 12 curry leaves and fry until the garlic turns golden and intensely fragrant, about 1 minute.
Add 1 finely chopped onion and cook until soft and browning at the edges, about 5 minutes, then stir in 1 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.75 tsp salt.
Fold in the drained cooked dal and toss on medium-high heat for 4 minutes so it soaks up the garlicky masala and turns slightly dry.
Finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and chopped coriander, and serve hot with rice, papad and a cooling curd.
tips: Under-cooking the dal slightly keeps this a fry rather than a soupy dal, which is how Andhra kitchens serve it.
Crush the garlic rather than mincing it so it browns into fragrant nuggets.
Reduce the Guntur chillies to two if cooking for children, and keep extra ghee on the table to temper the heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile onto hot rice with a puddle of extra ghee, crisp appadam and a spoon of thick yogurt; it also works as a spicy side with plain curd rice.

variations.name: Kerala Dhuli Moong Fry
variations.description: Kerala's take, cherupayar-style, wraps soft moong in a fresh coconut and curry-leaf masala finished in fragrant coconut oil. Ground coconut with cumin and green chilli gives it a creamy, mildly sweet body, while the mustard-and-curry-leaf tempering adds that unmistakable Malayali aroma. It is a moist, coconutty upperi eaten with rice or red matta rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil is the soul of Kerala tempering and lifts the whole dish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A little ghee at the end deepens the coconut sweetness.

steps: Rinse 1 cup dhuli moong dal and pressure-cook it with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 2 to 3 whistles until soft but not broken, then drain any excess water.
Coarsely grind 0.5 cup grated coconut with 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 2 green chillies to a moist, textured paste using just a splash of water.
Gently fold the coconut paste into the warm cooked dal with the remaining 0.5 tsp salt and warm through on low heat for 3 minutes.
In a small pan heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil on medium heat and pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and the remaining 0.5 tsp cumin seeds.
Add 6 sliced shallots, 1 slit green chilli and 12 curry leaves and fry until the shallots turn golden and the curry leaves crisp, about 2 minutes.
Pour the sizzling tempering over the coconut dal, add 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, fold once and serve warm with rice.
tips: Grind the coconut coarse, not smooth, so the dal keeps a pleasant grainy bite.
Add the coconut paste off high heat to keep it fresh-tasting and prevent it from turning oily.
Fresh coconut gives the best result, but thawed frozen grated coconut works well too.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside red matta rice with a spoon of mango pickle and pappadam, or pair with plain rice and a tangy rasam for a full Kerala meal.

variations.name: Classic Lauki Chana Dal Punjabi
variations.description: The everyday Punjabi comfort dal where nutty bengal gram and soft bottle gourd melt into a golden, ghee-glossed gravy. A late crush of kasuri methi and a spoon of butter give it that unmistakable homestyle roundness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee gives this Punjabi dal its glossy finish and cumin-blooming aroma.

steps: Rinse 0.75 cup bengal gram until the water runs clear, then pressure-cook it with the 400 g diced bottle gourd, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 2.5 cups water for 4 to 5 whistles until the dal is soft enough to smear between two fingers.
While the dal cooks, heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 20 seconds until they turn fragrant and slightly darker.

Add the minced garlic and grated ginger and stir for 40 seconds until raw-smelling steam gives way to a mellow aroma, then tip in the chopped onion and fry for 5 to 6 minutes until soft and pale gold.
Stir in the chopped tomato with 0.25 tsp salt and 1 tsp red chilli powder, cover, and cook for 6 to 7 minutes until the tomato collapses and ghee beads at the edges of the masala.

Pour the cooked lauki-dal into the masala, add 0.5 cup hot water to loosen it to a pourable consistency, and simmer gently for 8 minutes so the flavours marry, mashing a few pieces against the pan for body.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi between your palms and scatter it in, swirl through 1 tbsp butter, and finish with the chopped coriander just before serving.
tips: If the dal thickens on standing, loosen it with a splash of hot water rather than cold, which dulls the ghee's shine.
Under-cooked chana dal stays grainy; if a piece resists mashing, pressure-cook for one extra whistle before adding the tadka.
For a richer restaurant feel, reserve a teaspoon of the cumin tadka in ghee and drizzle it over each bowl at the table.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a brass katori alongside jeera rice and a raw onion-and-lemon salad, with hot tawa phulkas to scoop up the last of the gravy.

variations.name: Bengali Lauki Chana Dal with Mustard Oil
variations.description: A Bengali reading of the dish where pungent mustard oil and a scatter of whole spices replace the usual ghee tadka, giving a sharper, earthier gravy. A pinch of sugar and slit green chillies keep it in classic Bengali sweet-hot balance.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Kachi ghani mustard oil brings the sharp, nose-tingling pungency that defines a Bengali dal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A whisper of jaggery rounds the mustard oil's bite in true Bengali sweet-savoury balance.

steps: Pressure-cook 0.75 cup rinsed bengal gram with the 400 g diced bottle gourd, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 2.5 cups water for 4 to 5 whistles until the grains are tender but still hold a faint shape.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai over medium-high until it just begins to smoke and the raw pungency mellows, about 1 minute, then lower the heat to medium.
Drop in 1 bay leaf, 2 dried red chillies and 0.75 tsp cumin seeds and let them sizzle for 20 to 30 seconds until the chillies darken and the kitchen smells nutty.
Add the grated ginger and chopped tomato with 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and cook for 5 minutes, pressing the tomato until it softens into a rough paste and the oil separates.
Slide in the cooked lauki-dal along with 0.5 cup hot water and the slit green chillies, then simmer uncovered for 8 to 10 minutes so the mustard oil perfumes the whole pot.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and the remaining 0.25 tsp salt, taste for the signature sweet-hot balance, and finish with chopped coriander off the heat.
tips: Always heat mustard oil to smoking point first; raw mustard oil tastes bitter and overpowers the dal.
Bengali cooks keep the lauki slightly firm, so release the cooker pressure a touch early if you want distinct pieces.
A final teaspoon of raw mustard oil swirled in off the heat deepens the pungency for those who love it sharp.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with plain steamed gobindobhog or short-grain rice and a wedge of lime, letting the mustard-sharp dal shine as the first course of a Bengali thali.

variations.name: Gujarati Lauki Chana Dal with Jaggery
variations.description: The Gujarati version leans gently sweet-and-sour, with jaggery and a squeeze of lime balancing the earthy chana dal. A curry-leaf and mustard-seed tadka in ghee keeps it light and fragrant rather than heavy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries the curry leaf and mustard tadka that gives this Gujarati dal its lift.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery is the heart of the Gujarati sweet-sour balance, dissolving smoothly into the warm dal.

steps: Pressure-cook 0.75 cup rinsed bengal gram with the diced 400 g bottle gourd, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 2.75 cups water for 5 whistles, then whisk lightly so the dal turns creamy but the lauki stays visible.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat and add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds; when they pop after about 20 seconds, add 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and let them foam.
Toss in 10 curry leaves, 0.25 tsp asafoetida, the minced green chilli and grated ginger, standing back as the curry leaves crackle for 15 seconds and release their citrusy scent.
Pour this tadka straight into the cooked dal, add 0.75 cup hot water to keep it soupy, and bring it to a gentle simmer for 6 minutes.
Stir in 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder until it fully melts, then simmer another 4 minutes so the sweetness settles into the dal.
Turn off the heat, mix in 1 tbsp lime juice and the remaining 0.25 tsp salt, and scatter chopped coriander over the top before serving.
tips: Add the jaggery only after the dal is cooked; boiling it too long can turn the flavour flat and overly molasses-like.
Keep this dal thinner than a Punjabi one, as Gujarati dal is meant to be sipped almost like a broth.
Balance is everything here, so adjust jaggery and lime a little at a time until the sweet and sour meet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle over a mound of steamed rice with a spoon of extra ghee, or serve as a light dal course beside soft rotli and a crisp kachumber.

variations.name: Kerala Lauki Chana Dal with Coconut
variations.description: A South Indian take thickened with fresh coconut paste and finished with a coconut-oil tadka of curry leaves and dried chilli. The result is creamy, faintly sweet and deeply aromatic, closer to a lauki-and-kadala erissery.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil gives the tempering its sweet, unmistakably Kerala fragrance.

steps: Pressure-cook 0.75 cup rinsed bengal gram with the 400 g diced bottle gourd, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt, the slit green chillies and 2.5 cups water for 4 to 5 whistles until soft.
Grind 0.5 cup grated coconut with 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 3 tablespoons water to a smooth paste using a little more water only if needed.
Stir the coconut paste into the cooked dal and simmer over low heat for 6 to 7 minutes, stirring often so the coconut thickens the gravy without catching at the base.
In a small pan, heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and the remaining 0.25 tsp cumin for about 20 seconds.
Add the sliced shallots, 2 dried red chillies and 12 curry leaves and fry for 3 to 4 minutes until the shallots turn golden-brown at the edges and the curry leaves crisp.
Pour the sizzling coconut-oil tadka over the dal, fold it through with the remaining 0.25 tsp salt, and cover for 2 minutes so the aromas settle before serving.
tips: Fry the shallots until genuinely browned; their sweetness is what balances the coconut and lifts the whole dal.
Grind the coconut with warm water for a silkier paste that blends seamlessly into the gravy.
This dal thickens noticeably as it cools, so keep it a little loose if you plan to reheat it later.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with red parboiled matta rice and a side of pappadam, or pair with plain rice and a spoonful of thick curd for a cooling contrast.

variations.name: Andhra Lauki Chana Dal with Guntur Chilli
variations.description: A fiery Andhra rendition built on smoky Guntur red chillies and a groundnut-oil tempering, with a tang of tamarind cutting through the heat. It is bold, garlicky and unapologetically spicy, made to be mixed into rice with a spoon of ghee.
