ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the traditional Andhra cooking fat that carries the Guntur chilli heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of ghee tames the Guntur fire and rounds the dal for mixing into rice.

steps: Pressure-cook 0.75 cup rinsed bengal gram with the 400 g diced bottle gourd, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 2.5 cups water for 4 to 5 whistles until the dal is soft and just breaking down.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 0.75 tsp cumin for 20 seconds until they crackle.
Add 4 broken Guntur red chillies and the crushed garlic and fry for about 1 minute until the garlic turns pale gold and the chillies smell smoky and toasted.
Tip in the chopped onion with 10 curry leaves and cook for 5 minutes until the onion softens and picks up the deep red colour of the chillies.
Add the cooked lauki-dal, 1 tbsp tamarind pulp and 0.5 cup hot water, then simmer for 8 minutes so the sourness balances the heat and the gravy thickens slightly.
Finish with the remaining 0.25 tsp salt and swirl in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee off the heat to soften the sharp edges before serving.
tips: Deseed a couple of the Guntur chillies if you want the deep colour and smokiness without the full punishing heat.
Add the tamarind only towards the end, as long boiling can make it taste unpleasantly metallic.
This dal is meant to be intense; a mound of plain rice and extra ghee are the traditional way to temper each bite.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot rice pressed into a well with a nub of ghee, alongside a cooling tomato pachadi and crisp appadam to offset the chilli.

variations.name: Classic Masoor Dal Home-style
variations.description: The everyday North Indian masoor dal, where whole red lentils cook down to a silky, sunset-orange pot and get lifted by a fragrant cumin-and-garlic tadka in ghee. It is the quick weeknight dal that needs nothing more than steamed rice and a squeeze of lemon. Comfort food at its most honest.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: grassy bilona ghee for the finishing tadka gives this plain dal its restaurant aroma

steps: Rinse 1 cup red lentils in three changes of water until the water runs clear, then pressure-cook them with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp of the salt for 3 whistles on medium heat until completely soft and creamy.
While the dal cooks, finely chop 1 large onion, 2 tomatoes and 6 garlic cloves, keeping them in separate piles so they go into the pan at the right moment.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds until they sizzle and turn a shade darker, about 30 seconds.
Add the chopped garlic and fry until pale gold, then add the onion and cook until soft and translucent, about 5 minutes, stirring so it does not catch.
Stir in the tomatoes with the remaining 0.5 tsp salt and 1 tsp red chilli powder and cook until the tomatoes collapse and the ghee separates at the edges, about 6 minutes.
Pour this tadka into the cooked dal, add up to 0.5 cup hot water to loosen it, and simmer gently for 5 minutes so the flavours marry into a pourable, glossy dal.
Turn off the heat, fold in 3 tbsp chopped coriander, and serve steaming hot.
tips: For a smoky dhaba edge, hold a piece of live charcoal over the finished dal in a small steel bowl, drizzle a few drops of ghee on it and cover for 2 minutes.
If the dal thickens on standing, whisk in hot water a splash at a time rather than cold water, which dulls the flavour.
A pinch of sugar balances very tangy tomatoes without making the dal sweet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a copper katori with a wedge of lemon, thinly sliced raw onion rings and a hot tawa roti, letting each person squeeze lemon to taste.

variations.name: Bengali Masoor Dal Home-style
variations.description: In Bengali kitchens this everyday masoor is called masoor dal and is tempered in pungent mustard oil with nigella seeds and slit green chillies, giving it a sharp, mustardy warmth entirely unlike the North Indian version. It is deliberately thin and soupy, meant to be mixed into the first mound of rice with a little ghee. Simple, nostalgic, quietly addictive.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed kachi ghani mustard oil gives the authentic sharp Bengali tadka; heat it to smoking first to mellow it

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a teaspoon stirred in at the end is the classic Bengali finish that rounds out the mustard sharpness

steps: Rinse 1 cup red lentils well and pressure-cook with 3.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 3 whistles until very soft, then whisk the dal smooth and keep it slightly thin.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai over high heat until it just begins to smoke and loses its raw pungency, then lower the heat to medium.
Add 0.5 tsp nigella seeds and 3 slit green chillies and let them crackle for about 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 finely chopped small onion and fry until it turns light brown at the edges, about 4 minutes, then add 1 chopped tomato and cook until pulpy, about 3 minutes.
Pour in the cooked dal along with the remaining 0.5 tsp salt and 0.25 tsp sugar, and simmer uncovered for 6 minutes so the tempering infuses the thin dal.
Finish by stirring in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee off the heat, which softens the mustard bite and adds a nutty gloss.
tips: Always heat mustard oil to smoking point before adding spices, otherwise the dal tastes raw and bitter.
Bengalis keep this dal loose and pourable, so add extra hot water if it sets thick while resting.
A quartered boiled egg or fried bori (lentil dumplings) dropped in turns it into a light meal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle over a mound of hot gobindobhog or short-grain rice with a wedge of lime and a few pieces of aloo bhaja (crisp potato slivers) on the side.

variations.name: Kerala Masoor Dal Home-style
variations.description: This coastal take simmers red lentils into a coconut-rich, curry-leaf-scented dal finished with a coconut-oil tempering that smells of the backwaters. Fresh grated coconut and a whisper of coconut milk make it creamy and gently sweet, a world away from the tomato-heavy northern dal. It pairs beautifully with red matta rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil for the tadka carries the unmistakable Kerala aroma; do not substitute

steps: Rinse 1 cup red lentils and pressure-cook with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 slit green chillies and 1 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft and mushy.
Grind 0.5 cup grated coconut with a splash of water to a coarse paste, then stir it into the cooked dal and simmer for 4 minutes to thicken and sweeten the base.
Pour in 0.5 cup coconut milk, warm through on low heat for 2 minutes without boiling so it does not split, and switch off.
For the tadka, heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan over medium heat until it shimmers, then add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop.
Add 2 broken dried red chillies, 6 thinly sliced shallots and 2 sprigs curry leaves, and fry until the shallots turn golden brown and the leaves crisp, about 3 minutes.
Pour this sizzling tempering over the dal, stir once, and cover for a minute to trap the aroma before serving.
tips: Add coconut milk only at the end and never let it boil hard, or the dal will look curdled.
Sliced shallots fried to deep gold give a sweetness that ordinary onions cannot match here.
For a Sunday version, temper a few cashews along with the shallots for richness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed red matta rice and a spoon of tangy mango pickle, or ladle over appams for a lighter supper.

variations.name: Gujarati Masoor Dal Home-style
variations.description: The Gujarati kitchen tips the balance toward sweet, sour and spicy all at once, dissolving jaggery into the lentils with tamarind, ginger and a curry-leaf tadka. The result is a thin, drinkable dal with the region's signature khatti-meethi character. It is meant to be sipped alongside rice, ghee and a vegetable.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: organic jaggery powder dissolves instantly and gives the clean caramel sweetness that defines Gujarati dal

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil is the traditional Gujarati cooking fat for the tempering

steps: Rinse 1 cup red lentils and pressure-cook with 3.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 3 whistles, then whisk to a thin, smooth consistency.
Set the dal on low heat and stir in 1 tbsp tamarind pulp, 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and a grated 1 inch piece of ginger, simmering for 5 minutes until the sweet-sour balance rounds out.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a small pan over medium heat until it shimmers.
Add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and let them splutter, then add 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, 1 pinch asafoetida, 1 sprig curry leaves and 2 slit green chillies and fry for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Pour the tempering into the simmering dal, stir well, and let it bubble gently for another 4 minutes so the sweetness and spice settle in.
Taste and adjust jaggery or tamarind to reach the classic khatti-meethi balance before serving hot.
tips: Add jaggery only after the dal is cooked, as cooking lentils with jaggery can keep them from softening.
Keep this dal deliberately thin and pourable, almost like a spiced broth.
A few peanuts fried in the tadka add a Kathiawadi crunch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice topped with a nub of ghee, or sip it warm from a bowl before a thali of rotli and shaak.

variations.name: Andhra Masoor Dal Home-style
variations.description: Fiery and unapologetic, the Andhra version leans on smoky Guntur red chillies and a garlic-heavy tempering in sesame oil for a dal that bites back. Tamarind adds the sour counterpoint typical of the region, and a final flourish of pounded garlic keeps it pungent. Serve with rice and a dollop of ghee to tame the heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed gingelly oil is the classic Andhra fat and stands up to the aggressive chilli tadka

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a final teaspoon of ghee mellows the Guntur heat and rounds the sour edge

steps: Rinse 1 cup red lentils and pressure-cook with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft, then stir in 1 tbsp tamarind pulp and keep warm on low heat.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadai over medium heat until it shimmers and gives off its nutty aroma.
Add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop, then add 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, 4 broken Guntur red chillies and 1 sprig curry leaves and fry for 20 seconds until the chillies darken and smoke lightly.
Add 8 crushed garlic cloves and 1 finely chopped onion and fry until the garlic is golden and the onion softens, about 5 minutes.
Tip the entire tempering into the tamarind-laced dal, add 0.25 cup hot water, and simmer for 6 minutes so the heat and sourness meld.
Finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee stirred in off the heat to soften the fierce chilli edge before serving.
tips: Guntur chillies are intensely hot, so deseed a couple if you want colour without full firepower.
Crushing the garlic rather than mincing it releases a stronger pungency that suits this dal.
Serve with a bowl of plain curd on the side to cool the palate between bites.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile over hot rice with a spoon of ghee and a papad, and keep sliced onion and extra curd nearby for the heat.

variations.name: Classic Mixed Dal Tadka
variations.description: The everyday North Indian comfort bowl where five lentils cook down to a creamy, self-thickening base and a sizzling cumin-garlic tempering is poured over at the table. The sputter of ghee hitting the dal is half the pleasure, and the finish is soft, rounded and gently spiced rather than fiery.

ingredients.name: Mixed lentils (toor, masoor, chana, moong, urad)
Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Nutty bilona ghee carries the tadka aroma into every spoonful of dal

steps: Rinse 1 cup mixed lentils in three changes of water, then pressure-cook with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp of the salt for 4 whistles until completely soft and creamy, about 15 minutes.
Open the cooker once pressure drops, whisk the dal briskly for 30 seconds so it turns smooth and pourable, then keep it warm on a low flame.
For the tadka, heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan over medium heat and add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 2 dried red chillies; let them crackle and darken for about 30 seconds until fragrant.

Add 0.25 tsp asafoetida, 6 sliced garlic cloves and 1 inch grated ginger, and fry until the garlic turns pale gold, about 1 minute, then stir in 1 finely chopped onion and cook until soft and light brown, roughly 4 minutes.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes, 1 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.75 tsp salt, and cook until the tomatoes collapse and the ghee separates at the edges, about 5 minutes.
Pour the sizzling tadka into the warm dal, simmer together for 5 minutes so the flavours marry, then fold in 3 tbsp chopped coriander and serve hot.
tips: If the dal thickens too much on standing, loosen it with a splash of hot water rather than cold, which would dull the flavour.
Reserve a spoon of the raw tadka to swirl on top at serving so guests get that fresh-fried aroma.
A little extra Anveshan Ghee stirred in just before serving gives the classic glossy sheen and rounded taste.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle into a copper katori with a wedge of lemon on the rim and serve alongside jeera rice and thin phulka, with sliced onion and green chilli on the side.

variations.name: Punjabi Mixed Dal Tadka
variations.description: A richer, dhaba-inspired version from Punjab where the dal is finished with butter and a crushed kasuri methi flourish. It is deeper in colour, glossier and slightly smoky from a double tempering, built to be scooped up with hot buttered rotis.

ingredients.name: Mixed lentils (toor, masoor, chana, moong, urad)
Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Used for the final tadka so the kasuri methi blooms in fragrant bilona ghee

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed mixed lentils with 3.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 5 whistles until very soft, then mash lightly so the dal is thick and homogenous.
Melt 2 tbsp butter in a heavy pan over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them foam and sizzle for 20 seconds until nutty.
Stir in 7 minced garlic cloves and 1 inch grated ginger, fry for 1 minute, then add 1 large finely chopped onion and cook slowly until deep golden, about 6 minutes.
Add 3 chopped tomatoes, 1 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.75 tsp salt, and cook down to a thick pulpy masala until the fat pools, roughly 7 minutes.
Tip the cooked dal into the masala with a little hot water to reach a creamy consistency and simmer for 8 minutes, stirring so the bottom does not catch.

In a small pan heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, switch off the flame and crush in 1 tsp kasuri methi and 0.5 tsp garam masala, then pour this over the dal and fold through with 3 tbsp coriander before serving.
tips: Crushing the kasuri methi between your palms before it hits the ghee releases far more of its haunting aroma.
For a smokier dhaba note, place a live coal in a small bowl on the dal, drizzle with ghee and cover for two minutes to catch the smoke.
Cook the onions low and slow; their caramelised sweetness is what balances the tang of three tomatoes.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a kadai with a melting knob of butter on top, laccha onion rings, green chilli and warm tandoori roti brushed with ghee.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Mixed Dal Tadka
variations.description: A Deccan take built on goda masala, the sweet-warm blend of dry coconut, sesame and stone flower that defines Maharashtrian kitchens. It carries a faint sweetness and a dark, roasted depth quite unlike the North Indian original, brightened with a squeeze of lemon.

ingredients.name: Mixed lentils (toor, masoor, chana, moong, urad)
Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the everyday cooking fat of Maharashtra and toasts the goda masala beautifully

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon stirred in at the end softens the sharp edges of the goda masala

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed mixed lentils with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 4 whistles until soft, then whisk smooth and keep warm.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 0.75 tsp cumin seeds for about 20 seconds until they pop.

Add 5 crushed garlic cloves and 1 chopped onion and saute until the onion is soft and pink-gold, about 4 minutes, then dry-toast 2 tbsp grated dry coconut in with them for 1 minute until it smells nutty.
Stir in 1 chopped tomato, 1.5 tsp goda masala, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.75 tsp salt, and cook for 3 minutes until the masala turns dark and glossy.
Pour in the cooked dal along with a little hot water, simmer for 6 minutes so the goda masala infuses fully, then finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 2 tbsp coriander.
Squeeze in a little lemon just before serving to lift the sweet-earthy masala and check the salt once more.
tips: Goda masala can turn bitter if scorched, so add it with the tomato and never straight into smoking oil.
A pinch of jaggery instead of lemon gives the more traditional Vidarbha sweet-savoury balance.
Toasting the dry coconut is worth the extra minute; raw coconut leaves the dal tasting flat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or with bhakri and a side of raw onion and papad for a rustic Maharashtrian thali.

variations.name: Gujarati Mixed Dal Tadka
variations.description: The signature sweet-sour-spicy Gujarati register, where jaggery, a hint of tamarind and a curry-leaf tempering turn the dal light and almost drinkable. It is thinner than the North Indian version by design, meant to be sipped alongside rice, with peanuts adding welcome bite.

ingredients.name: Mixed lentils (toor, masoor, chana, moong, urad)
Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries the curry-leaf and mustard tempering that defines a Gujarati dal

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Melts in to give the gentle sweetness that balances the tamarind sourness

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed mixed lentils with 3.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 2 tbsp soaked peanuts for 4 whistles until the peanuts are tender and the dal is soft.
Whisk the dal thin and pourable, then stir in 1 tbsp tamarind pulp, 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 chopped tomato and 1.25 tsp salt and simmer gently for 8 minutes.
Meanwhile heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan over medium heat and add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds; when they pop after about 20 seconds add 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida.
Drop in 10 curry leaves, 2 slit green chillies and 1 inch julienned ginger and let them crackle for 30 seconds until the curry leaves turn translucent and aromatic.
Pour this tempering into the simmering dal, stir well and let it bubble for another 3 minutes so the sweet, sour and spicy notes settle into balance.
Taste and adjust the jaggery-tamarind balance, then finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and serve hot.
tips: Keep this dal deliberately thin; Gujaratis pour it over rice like a light broth rather than eating it thick.
Add the jaggery only after the tamarind so you can tune the sweet-sour balance to taste in small steps.
Soaking the peanuts for an hour before cooking guarantees they turn soft rather than staying stubbornly hard.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot steamed rice with a spoon of ghee, khichdi, or as the dal course of a Gujarati thali with kadhi and a vegetable shaak.

variations.name: Bengali Mixed Dal Tadka
variations.description: A Bengali reimagining tempered in pungent mustard oil with panch phoron, the five-spice mix of cumin, fennel, fenugreek, nigella and radhuni. The mustard oil lends a sharp, warming bite and the fennel a gentle sweetness, making the dal fragrant and distinctly eastern.

ingredients.name: Mixed lentils (toor, masoor, chana, moong, urad)
Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil gives the pungent kick that is the soul of a Bengali tempering

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A final drizzle of ghee rounds off the sharpness of the mustard oil

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed mixed lentils with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 4 whistles until soft, then whisk to a smooth, medium-thick consistency.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pan over medium-high until it just reaches smoking point and turns pale, about 1 minute, which mellows its raw pungency.
Lower the heat and add 1 tsp panch phoron, 2 dried red chillies and 1 bay leaf, letting them crackle for 30 seconds until the fenugreek turns a shade darker and the spices smell toasty.

Add 1 finely chopped onion and 1 inch grated ginger and fry until the onion is soft and golden, about 4 minutes, then stir in 1 chopped tomato, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 0.75 tsp salt and cook for 4 minutes until pulpy.
Pour in the cooked dal with a little hot water, add 0.25 tsp sugar to round the flavour, and simmer for 6 minutes so the panch phoron perfumes the whole pot.
Finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and 2 tbsp chopped coriander, and serve piping hot.
tips: Always heat mustard oil to smoking first, then cool it slightly; raw mustard oil tastes harsh and bitter.
Do not grind the panch phoron; the whole seeds are meant to be bitten into for little bursts of flavour.
The tiny pinch of sugar is traditional and quietly lifts every other spice without making the dal sweet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed gobindobhog or plain rice, a wedge of lime, a fried papad and a side of aloo bhaja for a classic Bengali lunch.

variations.name: Classic Toor Dal Dhaba-style
variations.description: The rich, smoky yellow dal you get at a highway dhaba, built on soft-simmered pigeon pea lentils and a generous ghee tempering. Kasuri methi and a whisper of jaggery round out the tang of tomatoes for that unmistakable roadside depth. A final coal-smoked finish gives it the aroma that keeps travellers coming back.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee gives the dhaba dal its glossy sheen and nutty aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a pinch to soften the tomato tang the way dhaba cooks do

steps: Rinse 1 cup toor dal until the water runs clear, then pressure-cook it with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 4 to 5 whistles on medium heat until the lentils are completely soft and collapse when pressed.
While the dal cooks, heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 20 seconds until they turn fragrant and float.
Add 6 finely chopped garlic cloves and 1 inch grated ginger, frying for 40 seconds until pale gold, then tip in 1 large finely chopped onion and cook for 6 to 7 minutes until deep golden brown.
Stir in 2 chopped tomatoes, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp jaggery powder, cover and cook for 5 minutes until the tomatoes turn pulpy and the ghee separates at the edges.

Pour the mashed cooked dal into the masala along with 0.5 cup hot water, add 1 tsp salt and simmer gently for 8 minutes, stirring so the base does not catch, until it thickens to a pourable, creamy consistency.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi between your palms and scatter it in with 0.5 tsp garam masala, simmer 2 more minutes, then garnish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander before serving.
tips: For a true dhaba aroma, place a small heated piece of natural charcoal in a steel bowl set on the dal, drizzle a few drops of ghee over it and cover for 2 minutes to trap the smoke.
If the dal thickens too much on standing, loosen it with a splash of hot water rather than cold, so the creamy texture stays intact.
Browning the onion properly to a deep gold is what separates a dhaba dal from a home dal, so do not rush this step.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a steel katori with a swirl of extra ghee on top, alongside tandoori roti, sliced raw onion rings and a wedge of lemon for the full roadside experience.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Toor Dal Dhaba-style
variations.description: This varan-amti inspired take swaps the northern spice box for fragrant goda masala, giving the toor dal a warm, coconut-and-clove sweetness. Groundnut oil and a spoon of jaggery build the signature Maharashtrian sweet-savoury balance, lifted by a bright curry-leaf tempering. It is comforting, aromatic and quite unlike any dhaba dal from the north.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil is the traditional cooking fat across Maharashtra

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the defining sweet note of a Maharashtrian amti

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed toor dal with 3 cups water and 0.5 tsp turmeric for 4 to 5 whistles, then whisk it smooth with a ladle while still warm.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, followed by 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 10 curry leaves, frying for 20 seconds until aromatic.
Add 1 finely chopped onion and saute for 4 minutes until soft and translucent, then stir in 1 chopped tomato and cook 3 minutes until it breaks down.
Sprinkle in 1.5 tsp goda masala and 2 tbsp grated coconut, frying gently for 1 minute so the spice blooms without burning and releases its clove-cinnamon aroma.

Pour in the whisked dal with 0.5 cup water, then add 1 tsp jaggery powder, 1 tsp tamarind pulp and 1 tsp salt, and simmer for 8 to 10 minutes on low heat until the flavours meld and the dal turns silky.
Taste and adjust the sweet-sour balance, then finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander just before serving.
tips: Goda masala can scorch quickly, so always add it after the tomatoes have softened and the pan has cooled slightly from the added moisture.
For a thinner amti to pour over rice, add an extra half cup of hot water at the final simmer and check the salt again.
A teaspoon of freshly roasted and ground peanuts stirred in at the end deepens the nutty Maharashtrian character.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle over a mound of hot steamed rice with a spoon of ghee and a papad on the side, or pair with soft jowar bhakri for an everyday Maharashtrian thali.

variations.name: Gujarati Toor Dal Dhaba-style
variations.description: A classic Gujarati dal that plays sweet, sour and spicy all at once, thickened just enough to sip. Jaggery and a squeeze of tamarind meet peanuts, curry leaves and a hint of cinnamon for the trademark khatti-meethi flavour. Ghee tempering ties it together into a light, almost drinkable dal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee tempering carries the sweet-sour Gujarati dal beautifully

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the signature sweetness that defines a Gujarati dal

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed toor dal with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 2 tbsp raw peanuts for 5 whistles so the peanuts soften alongside the lentils, then whisk until smooth.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a deep pan over medium heat and add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds; once they pop, add 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, 1 inch cinnamon, 2 cloves, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 10 curry leaves and fry for 20 seconds.
Stir in 1 inch julienned ginger and 2 slit green chillies, sizzling for 30 seconds until the raw edge fades.
Pour in the whisked dal along with 0.5 cup hot water to loosen it, then add 1.5 tbsp jaggery powder, 1.5 tsp tamarind pulp and 1 tsp salt.
Simmer uncovered on low heat for 10 minutes, stirring often, until the dal turns light, frothy and the sweet-sour flavours settle into balance.
Finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and serve piping hot.
tips: Keep this dal thin and sippable; if it reduces too much, add hot water as it should coat the back of a spoon, not cling to it.
Taste for the khatti-meethi balance at the end and adjust jaggery or tamarind a little at a time until it sings.
Adding the peanuts into the cooker with the dal saves a step and lets them turn creamy-soft rather than crunchy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as part of a Gujarati thali with plain rice, a wedge of lime, and soft phulka, letting the sweet dal counter the spicier shaak on the plate.

variations.name: Bengali Toor Dal Dhaba-style
variations.description: Pungent mustard oil and a five-spice panch phoron tempering turn everyday toor dal into a fragrant Bengali arhar dal. The mustard oil is smoked to mellow its sharpness before slit green chillies and dried red chilli go in. A finishing spoon of ghee lends the traditional round, comforting aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil gives the dal its authentic Bengali pungency

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon for the classic Bengali aroma

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed toor dal with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 4 to 5 whistles until soft, then whisk lightly to a pourable consistency.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai over medium-high heat until it just begins to smoke, then lower the heat to let its sharpness mellow for 30 seconds.
Add 1 tsp panch phoron, 2 dried red chillies and 1 bay leaf, letting them crackle for about 20 seconds until the fennel in the mix turns fragrant.
Stir in 1 inch grated ginger and 1 chopped tomato, cooking for 4 minutes until the tomato softens, then add 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp sugar.
Pour in the cooked dal with 2 slit green chillies, adjust salt, and simmer gently for 6 to 8 minutes so the panch phoron aroma infuses through the lentils.
Turn off the heat, drizzle in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and scatter 2 tbsp coriander, then cover for a minute before serving.
tips: Always heat mustard oil to smoking point first; this removes its raw bite and leaves behind a clean, nutty pungency.
The tiny pinch of sugar is authentic to Bengali cooking and rounds the mustard sharpness rather than making the dal sweet.
Toast the panch phoron only until you smell fennel and cumin, as burnt fenugreek in the mix will turn the dal bitter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed gobindobhog rice and a piece of aloo bhaja on the side, keeping the dal loose enough to mix into the rice by hand.

variations.name: Andhra Toor Dal Dhaba-style
variations.description: A fiery Andhra kandi pappu that leans on smoky Guntur red chillies, garlic and tangy tamarind for its bold punch. Nutty sesame oil is the traditional tempering fat, its aroma deepening the roasted-chilli heat. A touch of jaggery keeps the fire in check without dulling the spice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: gingelly sesame oil is the classic tempering fat of Andhra kitchens

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a small amount to temper the ferocious Guntur chilli heat

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed toor dal with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 chopped tomato and 4 crushed garlic cloves for 5 whistles, then mash coarsely with a wooden masher.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadhai over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds for 15 seconds.

Add 4 broken Guntur red chillies, the remaining 4 sliced garlic cloves, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 12 curry leaves, frying for 40 seconds until the garlic turns golden and the chillies darken and smell smoky.
Tip in 1 finely chopped onion and cook for 5 minutes until soft and lightly browned at the edges.
Pour in the mashed dal with 2 tsp tamarind pulp, 1 tsp jaggery powder and 1 tsp salt, add 0.5 cup hot water, and simmer for 8 minutes until thick and glossy.
Finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and serve while the tempering aroma is still lively.
tips: For extra depth, roast the Guntur chillies in the dry pan for 20 seconds before adding oil, but keep the window open as the fumes are strong.
Cooking half the garlic inside the dal and frying the rest gives two layers of flavour, one mellow and one sharp.
This dal is meant to be thick and clingy so it can be mixed into rice, so hold back on extra water.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot rice topped with a spoon of raw sesame oil and a fried papad, with a side of avakaya mango pickle to complete the Andhra meal.

variations.name: Classic Butter Veg Korma
variations.description: This is the indulgent, buttery cousin of the everyday korma, where mixed vegetables bathe in a mildly sweet tomato-cashew gravy enriched with ghee, butter and cream. The sauce is velvety and pale orange, gently spiced so the richness leads. It is the dish that turns a simple dinner into a celebration.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee brings the deep buttery aroma this korma is named for

steps: Dice and steam the mixed vegetables for 8 minutes until just tender, then set aside so they hold their shape.
Boil the chopped tomatoes, sliced onion and 16 cashews with 1 cup water for 8 minutes until very soft, cool, blend smooth, and strain for a silky gravy.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with 2 tbsp butter on medium, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, and fry for 1 minute until the raw smell goes.
Pour in the strained tomato-cashew puree with 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, and simmer on low for 8 minutes, stirring, until it thickens and turns glossy.
Add 1 cup water and 1.25 tsp salt, fold in the steamed vegetables, and simmer gently for 5 minutes so they soak up the buttery gravy.
Stir in 4 tbsp cream, 0.5 tsp garam masala and 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi, simmer 2 minutes, and serve rich and hot.
tips: Straining the gravy is the single step that gives it a restaurant-smooth, luxurious finish.
Crush the kasuri methi between your palms before adding to release its full aroma.
If the gravy tastes sharp, a teaspoon of sugar or a splash more cream balances the tomatoes.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or laccha paratha, finishing each plate with a swirl of cream and a dot of butter.

variations.name: Punjabi Butter Veg Korma
variations.description: The Punjabi makhani-style korma is unapologetically rich, its tomato-butter gravy smoky from a charcoal dhungar and rounded with cream and honey. Kasuri methi perfumes the whole pan. It is dhaba comfort food built for cold nights and hot tandoori roti.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the foundation fat of Punjabi makhani gravies

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: a spoon of raw honey replaces sugar to round the tangy tomato gravy

steps: Dice and steam the mixed vegetables for 8 minutes until tender, then keep them aside.
Simmer the chopped tomatoes with 14 cashews and 1 cup water for 10 minutes until pulpy, cool, blend to a smooth puree, and strain.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry 1 minute, then pour in the tomato-cashew puree with 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder.
Simmer the gravy on low for 10 minutes, stirring often, until it darkens, thickens and the ghee floats to the top.
Add 1 cup water and 1.25 tsp salt, fold in the steamed vegetables, and cook 5 minutes; stir in 2 tbsp butter, 4 tbsp cream, 1 tsp Anveshan Honey and 1.5 tsp crushed kasuri methi.
For a dhaba aroma, place a lit piece of charcoal in a small bowl set in the pan, drizzle a little ghee over it, cover for 2 minutes to smoke, then remove and serve.
tips: The dhungar smoking step is optional but gives that unmistakable tandoori-style aroma at home.
Add honey off a rolling boil so its delicate flavour and aroma are not cooked away.
Simmer the tomato gravy long and slow; rushing it leaves a raw, sour edge.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tandoori roti, garlic naan or jeera rice, topped with a final swirl of cream and a pinch of kasuri methi.

variations.name: Hyderabadi Butter Veg Korma
variations.description: The Hyderabadi shahi korma is a royal affair, its butter-and-cream gravy scented with saffron, cardamom and a fried-onion birista paste. It is fragrant, mildly sweet and jewelled with nuts. This is the korma that belongs on a Nizami dastarkhan beside biryani.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: carries the shahi aroma of the saffron and whole spices

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk for the perfume and colour of a Nizami korma

steps: Dice and steam the mixed vegetables for 8 minutes until tender, and soak the pinch of Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk.

Thinly slice the onions and fry them in 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium for 8 minutes until deep golden birista, then reserve half for garnish and grind the rest with 12 cashews and 10 almonds to a smooth paste.
In the same ghee add 4 cardamom pods and 1 inch cinnamon, let them sizzle for 20 seconds, then add the fried-onion-nut paste and cook on low for 4 minutes.
Whisk the 0.5 cup yogurt smooth with 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, lower the flame, and stir it in slowly so it does not split.
Add 1 cup water and 1.25 tsp salt, fold in the steamed vegetables, and simmer gently for 6 minutes until the gravy is thick and creamy.
Stir in 3 tbsp cream and the saffron milk, simmer 2 minutes, and serve topped with the reserved birista.
tips: Frying the onions to an even deep gold, not brown, keeps the gravy sweet rather than bitter.
Blanch and peel the almonds before grinding for the palest, smoothest shahi gravy.
Add the saffron milk near the end so its aroma stays bright on the plate.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sheermal, rumali roti or a plain zafrani pulao, scattered with fried onions and slivered almonds.

variations.name: Bengali Butter Veg Korma
variations.description: This is a niramish-inspired korma, a gentle Bengali-style vegetable braise where mustard oil and a whole-spice temper meet a mild cashew-yogurt gravy softened with butter. Ginger and a touch of sugar define it, with no onion or garlic. It is festive-day cooking, subtle and aromatic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the pungent base that makes the mild gravy taste distinctly Bengali

steps: Dice and steam the mixed vegetables for 8 minutes until tender, and grind 14 cashews to a smooth paste with a little water.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the heat, and temper 1 tsp cumin, 2 bay leaves and 3 cardamom pods for 20 seconds.
Add 1.5 tbsp ginger paste with 0.5 tsp turmeric and fry for 1 minute until the raw smell lifts and the mixture is fragrant.
Stir in the cashew paste and cook on low for 4 minutes, then whisk the 0.5 cup yogurt smooth and add it off the heat, stirring, so it does not split.
Return to a low flame, add 1 cup water, 1.25 tsp salt and 1 tsp sugar, fold in the vegetables, and simmer 6 minutes until the gravy thickens gently.
Melt in 1.5 tbsp butter off the heat for a glossy finish and serve warm.
tips: Skipping onion and garlic keeps this true to niramish cooking; the ginger and whole spices carry it.
Heat the mustard oil fully before lowering the flame to temper, so its sharpness mellows.
The pinch of sugar is characteristic and balances the mustard oil rather than sweetening the dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with luchi, plain pulao or steamed rice, garnished with a slit green chilli.

variations.name: Gujarati Butter Veg Korma
variations.description: A lighter, sweeter korma in the Gujarati mould, where jaggery and a mild yogurt-cashew gravy meet a fragrant ginger-chilli paste. It is buttery but bright, with lemon lifting the finish. This is a festive shaak that pairs happily with puri and pulao.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: gives the shaak a gentle buttery richness Gujarati festive food loves

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the signature sweet note balancing the tangy yogurt gravy

steps: Dice and steam the mixed vegetables for 8 minutes until tender, grind 14 cashews to a smooth paste, and puree the tomatoes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium, crackle 1 tsp cumin, then add 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and fry for 30 seconds.
Pour in the tomato puree with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 2 tsp coriander-cumin powder, and cook 5 minutes until thick and the ghee shows at the edges.
Stir in the cashew paste, cook 3 minutes, then whisk the 0.5 cup yogurt smooth and add it on a low flame, stirring so it stays creamy.
Add 1 cup water and 1.25 tsp salt, fold in the vegetables, and simmer 6 minutes until the gravy is silky.
Stir in 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer 2 minutes, turn off the heat, add 1 tbsp lemon juice and 2 tbsp coriander, and serve.
tips: Add the lemon only after switching off the flame so the tang stays fresh.
Taste before serving and tune the jaggery and lemon to hit the sweet-sour Gujarati balance.
Keep the chilli gentle; this korma is meant to be mild and fragrant rather than hot.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with puri, soft rotli or a simple peas pulao, with a bowl of sweet boondi on the side.

variations.name: Classic Peas Pulao
variations.description: The beloved North Indian matar pulao, where sweet green peas and long basmati grains are cooked together in ghee-bloomed whole spices. It is fragrant, lightly spiced and comforting, the default one-pot rice for a weeknight dinner or a simple gathering.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee blooms the whole spices and carries the sweetness of the peas through the rice

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati rice until the water runs clear, soak for 20 minutes and drain so the grains stay firm and separate.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot over medium heat and add 1 bay leaf, 3 green cardamom pods, 4 cloves and a 1 inch cinnamon stick, then 1.5 tsp cumin seeds, frying for 20 seconds until aromatic.
Add 1 sliced onion and 1 inch julienned ginger and saute over medium heat until the onion is golden, about 6 minutes.
Stir in 1 cup green peas and cook for 2 minutes, then add the drained rice and toss gently for another 2 minutes.
Pour in 2.25 cups hot water with 1.25 tsp salt, stir once, and bring to a rolling boil over high heat.
Cover with a tight lid, lower the heat to minimum and steam for 13 minutes, then rest for 5 minutes and fluff so the peas stay whole.
tips: If using frozen peas, add them straight from the freezer so they stay bright green and do not turn mushy.
Fresh winter peas may need a couple of extra minutes of sauteing before the rice goes in.
Fluff with a fork from the edges inward to keep the delicate grains and peas intact.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of cool boondi raita and a wedge of lemon, or beside a simple dal and pickle for an easy dinner.

variations.name: Punjabi Peas Pulao
variations.description: The rich Punjabi matar pulao finished with butter, where the peas and rice glisten with dhaba-style indulgence. A touch of green chilli and extra ghee-fried onions make it hearty enough to headline a simple meal with just raita alongside.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee builds the base flavour while butter is layered on top for Punjabi richness

steps: Wash 1.5 cups basmati rice in three changes of water, soak for 20 minutes and drain well.
Warm 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide pot over medium heat and add 1 bay leaf, 3 cloves and 6 black peppercorns, then 1.5 tsp cumin seeds, frying for 20 seconds.
Add 1 sliced onion and 1 slit green chilli and cook until the onion is deep golden, about 7 minutes.
Stir in 1 cup green peas for 2 minutes, then fold in the drained rice and toss gently for 2 minutes.
Add 2.25 cups hot water and 1.25 tsp salt, bring to a boil, then cover and steam on the lowest heat for 13 minutes.
Rest for 5 minutes, dot 1 tbsp butter over the hot pulao so it melts through, then fluff and serve.
tips: Fold in the butter at the end so it stays glossy rather than frying away into the pot.
Deep-golden onions give the pulao its dhaba sweetness, so do not rush the frying.
Leftovers reheat well with a splash of water and a fresh dab of butter under a lid.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a thick cucumber raita and a side of masala onions, letting the buttery pulao be the star of a quick dinner.

variations.name: Kashmiri Peas Pulao
variations.description: An aromatic Valley-style matar pulao coloured with saffron and warmed by fennel, cardamom and a scatter of nuts. The saffron milk marbles the grains gold against the green peas, turning a homely pulao into a fragrant showpiece.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries the fennel and cardamom and helps the saffron colour bloom through the pulao

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Saffron steeped in warm milk paints the grains gold and adds a floral note to match the sweet peas

steps: Soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes and drain; meanwhile steep 0.25 tsp Anveshan Saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk until it glows.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot over medium heat and fry 2 tbsp slivered almonds until pale gold, about 1 minute, then lift them out for garnish.
Add 4 green cardamom pods and 3 cloves to the ghee, then 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.5 tsp fennel seeds, and let them crackle for 20 seconds until floral.
Stir in 1 cup green peas for 2 minutes, then add the drained rice and toss gently for 2 minutes.
Pour in 2.25 cups hot water and 1.25 tsp salt, bring to a boil, then cover and steam on the lowest heat for 13 minutes.
Drizzle the saffron milk over the hot pulao, rest for 5 minutes, then fluff so the colour streaks through and top with the fried almonds.
tips: Steep the saffron in warm rather than hot milk to draw out colour without bitterness.
Fennel is the signature Kashmiri note; half a teaspoon perfumes without overwhelming the peas.
Fold the saffron milk in only once for a marbled gold-and-green look rather than a uniform yellow.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside a paneer yakhni or a simple dum aloo, garnished with a few saffron threads and pomegranate seeds for colour.

variations.name: Bengali Peas Pulao
variations.description: A Bengali-style ghugni-inspired pulao built on pungent wood-pressed mustard oil with a whisper of sugar, giving the peas and rice a sweet-sharp character. Bay leaves and dried chillies in mustard oil lend it the unmistakable aroma of a Bengali kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil is heated to smoking to give the pulao its sharp Bengali backbone

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of ghee rounds off the pungent mustard oil

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain well and set aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pot over medium-high heat until it just smokes, then lower the flame to mellow it.
Add 2 bay leaves and 2 dried red chillies, then 1.5 tsp cumin seeds, and let them crackle for 20 seconds until deeply aromatic.
Add 1 sliced onion with 0.5 tsp sugar and fry until the onion turns rich brown, about 8 minutes, then stir in 1 cup green peas for 2 minutes.
Fold in the drained rice for 2 minutes, then pour in 2.25 cups hot water and 1.25 tsp salt and bring to a boil.
Cover and steam on the lowest heat for 13 minutes, rest for 5 minutes, then swirl in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and fluff gently.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to smoking point first so its raw sharpness softens into a pleasant pungency.
The pinch of sugar deepens the onions to a Bengali mahogany and balances the mustard oil.
Remove the whole bay leaves and chillies before serving so no one bites into them.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a light cholar dal or a simple aloo dum, with a wedge of lime to lift the sweet-sharp flavours.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Peas Pulao
variations.description: A Puneri-style vatana bhaat where goda masala lends its dark, smoky-sweet depth to the peas and rice. Tempered with mustard and curry leaves and finished with fresh coconut, it eats almost like a light masale bhaat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the traditional Maharashtrian fat and lets the goda masala shine

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of ghee softens the smoky goda masala

steps: Wash and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain and keep aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pot over medium heat, add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and when they pop add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 10 curry leaves.
Add 1 chopped onion and cook until soft and pale gold, about 5 minutes, then stir in 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp goda masala for 20 seconds until smoky.
Add 1 cup green peas and saute for 2 minutes, then fold in the drained rice for 2 minutes.
Pour in 2.25 cups hot water and 1.25 tsp salt, bring to a boil, then cover and steam on the lowest heat for 13 minutes.
Rest for 5 minutes, swirl in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee, then fluff and garnish with 2 tbsp grated fresh coconut.
tips: Goda masala is darker and sweeter than garam masala, so do not swap them or the flavour will be off.
Toast the goda masala only briefly since it is already roasted and scorches quickly.
A handful of roasted peanuts folded in adds the crunch typical of Maharashtrian rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with plain yoghurt, a wedge of lime and a fried papad, the classic partners to a Maharashtrian pulao.

variations.name: Classic Veg Pulao
variations.description: A fragrant one-pot rice where long-grain basmati is tempered with whole spices in ghee, then steamed with mixed vegetables so every grain stays separate and glossy. It is mildly spiced, letting the aroma of cumin, bay leaf and cardamom lead rather than heat. This is the go-to pulao for a quick weeknight dinner or an everyday lunchbox.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee coats each grain and carries the whole-spice aroma through the pulao.

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati rice until the water runs clear, then soak it for 20 minutes and drain well.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 bay leaf, 3 cardamom pods, 4 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon for about 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 sliced large onion and saute until golden, about 5 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger garlic paste and 2 slit green chillies and cook for 1 minute.
Add 1.5 cups mixed vegetables, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt and saute for 3 minutes so the vegetables take on the spice.
Add the drained rice and toss very gently for 2 minutes until each grain is coated in ghee and lightly toasted.
Pour in 2.5 cups hot water, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes until the water is absorbed and the rice is fluffy.
Rest covered for 5 minutes, then fluff with a fork, garnish with coriander and serve hot with raita.
tips: Soaking the rice and toasting it in ghee are the two secrets to separate, non-sticky grains.
Resting the pulao covered off the heat lets the grains firm up so they do not break when fluffed.
Use a 1:1.65 rice-to-water ratio for soaked basmati; adjust slightly for older rice which drinks more.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of cool boondi raita, a wedge of lemon and a crunchy papad; a simple dal or paneer curry on the side turns it into a full meal.

variations.name: Kashmiri Veg Pulao
variations.description: A festive, jewel-toned pulao where saffron, whole garam spices and dry fruits transform plain rice into something regal, the way it is served at a Kashmiri wazwan-style feast. Saffron lends colour and a honeyed aroma while fried nuts and a hint of fennel add richness. It is aromatic, gently sweet and studded with colour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee fries the nuts and blooms the whole spices for this festive Kashmiri rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: Saffron gives the pulao its golden streaks and unmistakable honeyed perfume.

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain; warm 3 tbsp milk and steep 0.25 tsp Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in it to release its colour.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot on medium heat and fry 3 tbsp cashews and 2 tbsp raisins until the cashews are golden and the raisins plump, then scoop them out and reserve.
In the same ghee crackle 1 bay leaf, 4 cardamom pods and 1 inch cinnamon for 30 seconds, then add 1 cup mixed vegetables and saute for 3 minutes.
Stir in 0.5 tsp fennel powder, 0.5 tsp dry ginger powder and 1.25 tsp salt, then add the drained rice and toss gently for 2 minutes.
Pour in 2.5 cups hot water and the saffron milk, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes until the water is absorbed.
Rest covered for 5 minutes, then fluff gently and fold in the fried cashews and raisins.
Serve hot, mounded on a platter, as the centrepiece of a festive meal.
tips: Steeping saffron in warm milk draws out more colour and aroma than adding the strands dry.
Fry the nuts before the spices so they stay crisp and do not burn later in the cooking.
Fennel and dry ginger are the quiet Kashmiri signatures here; keep them subtle.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a wide platter garnished with extra fried nuts and saffron strands, paired with a cooling walnut or cucumber raita and a tangy pickle.

variations.name: Awadhi Veg Pulao
variations.description: The Lucknowi kitchen builds a delicate, perfumed pulao using kewra water, a spiced stock and the slow dum method, so the rice drinks up aroma rather than masala. It stays pale and elegant, scented with rose, kewra and a bouquet garni of whole spices tied in muslin. This is the refined pulao of Awadhi dastarkhwan spreads.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee gives the Awadhi pulao its silky mouthfeel and refined aroma.

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain; loosely tie 2 bay leaves, 1 black cardamom, 4 green cardamoms, 5 cloves and 1 mace blade in a small muslin pouch.
Bring 2.5 cups water to a boil with the spice pouch and 1.25 tsp salt, simmer for 5 minutes to make an aromatic stock, then discard the pouch.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot on medium heat, add 1 thinly sliced large onion and fry until golden brown and crisp, about 7 minutes, then remove half for garnish.
Add 1 tsp shahi jeera to the ghee, let it crackle for 15 seconds, then add 1.25 cups mixed vegetables and saute for 3 minutes.
Add the drained rice and toss gently for 2 minutes, then pour in the hot spiced stock and bring to a boil.
Cover tightly, cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes, then drizzle 1 tsp kewra water and 2 tbsp milk over the top, cover again and rest on dum for 6 minutes.
Fluff gently, top with the reserved fried onions, and serve hot.
tips: A muslin spice pouch flavours the stock cleanly and is lifted out before the rice cooks, keeping the pulao pale.
Kewra water is potent, so a single teaspoon is enough to perfume the whole pot.
Sealing the pot for dum lets the aromas settle evenly into every grain.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve garnished with crisp fried onions and a few rose petals, alongside a subz korma or a mint raita for an elegant Awadhi table.

variations.name: Gujarati Veg Pulao
variations.description: Gujarat's pulao carries a signature sweet-savoury note from a touch of jaggery and warming spice, often lightened with peas, potato and a squeeze of lime. It is milder and gently sweet, reflecting the region's love of the sweet-sour-spicy balance, and pairs naturally with kadhi. This is a comforting everyday pulao with a distinctly Gujarati soul.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee gives the pulao a soft richness that balances the jaggery and lime.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A little jaggery brings the sweet-savoury note typical of Gujarati cooking.

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain well.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 inch cinnamon and 3 cloves for about 20 seconds.
Add 1 inch grated ginger and 2 slit green chillies and fry for 30 seconds, then add 1.5 cups mixed vegetables, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt and saute for 3 minutes.
Add the drained rice and toss gently for 2 minutes until glossy, then stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder.
Pour in 2.5 cups hot water, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes until the water is absorbed.
Rest covered for 5 minutes, then drizzle 1 tbsp lemon juice, fluff gently and fold in chopped coriander.
Serve hot with a bowl of Gujarati kadhi on the side.
tips: The jaggery should be barely perceptible, just enough to round the spice, not sweeten the rice.
Add lemon juice after cooking so its freshness is not lost to the heat.
Diced potato and green peas are the classic vegetables for this gently sweet pulao.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with warm Gujarati kadhi poured over, a spoon of sweet chundo pickle and crisp papad; a bowl of plain yogurt also pairs well.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Veg Pulao
variations.description: Known as masale bhaat in spirit, this pulao is darkened and deepened with goda masala, giving the rice a smoky, aromatic warmth quite different from a mild North Indian pulao. Goda masala plus a generous tempering and a handful of peanuts create the region's signature layered flavour. It is a robust, festive-tasting rice made for gatherings.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee blooms the goda masala and gives masale-bhaat-style rice its glossy finish.

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain well.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot on medium heat and pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, then add 1 tsp cumin seeds, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 10 curry leaves and let them crackle for 20 seconds.
Add 3 tbsp roasted peanuts and fry for 30 seconds, then add 1.5 cups mixed vegetables and saute for 3 minutes.
Lower the heat and add 2 tsp goda masala, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt, stirring for 30 seconds until the ghee turns dark and fragrant.
Add the drained rice and toss gently for 2 minutes until each grain is coated in the dark masala.
Pour in 2.5 cups hot water, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes until the water is absorbed.
Rest covered for 5 minutes, then fluff and garnish with 2 tbsp grated coconut and chopped coriander before serving.
tips: Add goda masala on low heat so it darkens without scorching, which would turn it bitter.
A garnish of fresh grated coconut is traditional and balances the smoky spice.
Diced brinjal or tendli alongside the usual vegetables makes this taste like authentic masale bhaat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve topped with grated coconut and coriander, with a bowl of plain yogurt or a simple koshimbir salad and a spoon of ghee melted over the top.

variations.name: Classic Dal Makhani Fry
variations.description: A brisker, more forward-flavoured cousin of the slow makhani, where the cooked black dal is fried hard into a bhuna onion-tomato masala so the fat and spices coat every bean. Butter and ghee keep it rich while the vigorous frying builds a deeper, roasted taste. It is dal makhani with attitude, ready in half the time.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee is the frying fat that gives this fried makhani its roasted, bhuna aroma

steps: Soak 1 cup black urad and 0.25 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 6 whistles until soft, and drain, reserving the liquor.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with 2 tbsp butter in a wide kadai over medium-high heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds until fragrant.
Add a paste of 8 garlic cloves and 1.5 inch ginger, fry 1 minute, then add 2 chopped onions and fry until deep golden brown, about 8 minutes.
Add 3 chopped tomatoes with 1 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt and fry hard until the masala is thick, dark and the fat separates, about 9 minutes.
Add the drained beans and fry them into the masala for 5 minutes, mashing some, then add the reserved liquor a little at a time and simmer 15 minutes to a thick, glossy dal.
Stir in 0.75 tsp garam masala, 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi and 2 tbsp cream, cook 3 minutes more, and serve hot.
tips: Frying the beans into the masala before adding liquid is what gives this version its roasted depth.
Add the cooking liquor gradually so you control the final thickness.
A final knob of butter melted on top makes it glisten like a restaurant serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or laccha paratha, sliced onions and a green chilli, with a swirl of cream on top.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Dal Makhani Fry
variations.description: This Deccan version fries the creamy black dal with earthy goda masala, its dagad-phool and roasted-coconut notes giving a dark, faintly sweet complexity. Groundnut oil and a coconut garnish anchor it firmly in Maharashtra. The familiar makhani turns rustic and aromatic, unlike anything from a Punjabi kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil is the everyday Maharashtrian fat and marries with goda masala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of ghee balances the dark, earthy goda masala

steps: Soak 1 cup black urad and 0.25 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 6 whistles until soft; drain and reserve the liquor.
Dry-roast 3 tbsp grated coconut in the kadai until golden and set aside, then heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds.
Add 6 crushed garlic cloves and 2 chopped onions and fry until deep golden, about 8 minutes, then add 2 chopped tomatoes and 1 tsp red chilli powder and fry until pulpy, about 7 minutes.
Sprinkle in 2 tsp goda masala and fry for 1 minute until its dark aroma blooms and the oil turns rich brown.
Add the drained beans, fry them into the masala for 5 minutes while mashing some, then add reserved liquor gradually and simmer 15 minutes to a thick dal.
Finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and the roasted coconut stirred in, and serve hot.
tips: Roasting the coconut first deepens the nutty note that defines this Deccan version.
Fry goda masala only briefly; scorching it turns the dal bitter.
A little jaggery is a common Maharashtrian touch to round the tomato acidity.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri or steamed rice and a wedge of lemon, topped with extra roasted coconut.

variations.name: Tamil Dal Makhani Fry
variations.description: A southern spin where the fried black dal is finished with a sesame-oil tempering of mustard, curry leaves and dried chillies and a whisper of tamarind for brightness. Ground pepper and shallots replace the North's garam masala, giving a fragrant, slightly tangy makhani. Rich yet refreshing, it eats beautifully with rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed gingelly oil defines the Tamil tempering and adds warm nuttiness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of ghee softens the pepper heat and gives a glossy finish

steps: Soak 1 cup black urad and 0.25 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 6 whistles until soft; drain and reserve the liquor.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop, then add 2 broken dried red chillies and 2 sprigs curry leaves.
Add 10 sliced shallots and 6 sliced garlic cloves and fry until deep golden, about 6 minutes, then add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and cook until pulpy, about 6 minutes.
Add the drained beans and fry into the masala for 5 minutes, mashing some, then stir in 1 tsp tamarind pulp and 0.5 tsp black pepper powder.
Pour in the reserved liquor gradually and simmer for 15 minutes until thick and glossy, adjusting the remaining 0.5 tsp salt.
Finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee stirred through and serve hot.
tips: Black pepper, not garam masala, gives the warmth here in true Tamil style.
Fry the shallots to deep gold for a subtle sweetness that balances the tamarind.
Keep the tamarind gentle so it brightens rather than sours the rich dal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot rice with a crisp appalam and a spoon of ghee, or alongside soft parottas.

variations.name: Rajasthani Dal Makhani Fry
variations.description: Bold and desert-rustic, this version fries the black dal with whole dried Mathania chillies and a garlic-heavy ghee tadka, skipping cream for a leaner, punchier body. Dry spices and a touch of amchur supply tang where fresh tomato is minimal. It is smoky, fiery and built to stand up to bajra roti.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee is used generously in Rajasthani cooking to carry spice where fresh produce is scarce

steps: Soak 1 cup black urad and 0.25 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 6 whistles until soft; drain and reserve the liquor.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 4 broken dried red chillies and fry until the chillies darken and smell smoky, about 40 seconds.
Add 1 pinch asafoetida and 10 crushed garlic cloves and fry until golden, then add 2 chopped onions and cook until well browned, about 8 minutes.
Add 1 chopped tomato, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp amchur and fry until the masala is thick and the ghee separates, about 6 minutes.
Add the drained beans and fry into the masala for 5 minutes while mashing some, then add reserved liquor gradually and simmer 15 minutes to a robust dal.
Adjust the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, ladle with the fried chillies on top, and serve piping hot.
tips: Amchur provides the tang that fresh tomatoes would, keeping it true to the arid Rajasthani larder.
Skipping cream here is deliberate; the dal stays lean, smoky and bean-forward.
Fry the whole chillies only until they puff, as burnt chillies turn the ghee bitter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra roti and a dollop of ghee, plus raw onion and green chilli to match its rustic fire.

variations.name: Kerala Dal Makhani Fry
variations.description: A coastal reimagining where the fried black dal is enriched with ground coconut and coconut milk and lifted by a coconut-oil tadka of mustard, curry leaves and shallots. Green chilli and ginger keep it fresh while the coconut lends a mellow, creamy sweetness in place of dairy. It is a lighter, aromatic take on the heavy classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil is essential to the Kerala flavour and cannot be substituted

steps: Soak 1 cup black urad and 0.25 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 6 whistles until soft; drain and reserve the liquor.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop, then add 8 sliced shallots, 6 sliced garlic cloves, 2 slit green chillies, a grated 1 inch piece of ginger and 2 sprigs curry leaves.
Fry until the shallots are deep golden, about 6 minutes, then add 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and stir for 15 seconds.
Grind 0.5 cup grated coconut to a paste and add it along with the drained beans, frying the mixture for 5 minutes while mashing some beans.
Add the reserved liquor gradually and simmer for 12 minutes until thick, then stir in 0.5 cup coconut milk and warm through on low heat for 3 minutes without boiling.
Adjust the remaining 0.5 tsp salt and serve warm with the coconut aroma fresh.
tips: Ground coconut plus coconut milk gives a creaminess that replaces dairy entirely here.
Do not boil after adding coconut milk or the dal will split and look grainy.
Deep-golden fried shallots are essential to the sweetness of this version.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed red rice or appams and a spoon of tangy mango pickle to cut the richness.

variations.name: Classic Dal Makhani Home-style
variations.description: The unfussy home version of dal makhani, made with a pressure cooker and a modest amount of butter and cream so it stays comforting rather than indulgent. Black urad and a little rajma cook into a creamy, family-friendly dal finished with a simple ghee tadka. It is the weekday makhani that still tastes like a treat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a simple ghee tadka gives the home-style dal its cosy, nutty finish without restaurant heaviness

steps: Soak 1 cup black urad and 0.25 cup rajma for at least 6 hours, then pressure-cook with 5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 6 whistles until the beans mash easily.
Heat 2 tbsp butter in a pot over medium heat, add a paste of 6 garlic cloves and 1 inch ginger and fry 1 minute, then add 1 chopped onion and cook until golden, about 6 minutes.
Add 3 pureed tomatoes with 1 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt and cook until the masala thickens and fat separates, about 8 minutes.
Add the cooked beans with their liquor, mash a portion against the pot, and simmer uncovered on low heat for 20 minutes, stirring so it does not stick.
Stir in 0.5 tsp garam masala and 2 tbsp cream and simmer 4 minutes until smooth and creamy.
Finish with a tadka of 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee heated with 1 tsp cumin seeds until fragrant, poured sizzling over the dal before serving.
tips: Mashing some of the beans against the pot thickens the dal naturally so you need less cream.
If short on time, skip overnight soaking and give the cooker a few extra whistles.
A splash of milk during the simmer keeps the colour soft and the texture plush.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulka or jeera rice, a little butter on top and a simple onion-cucumber salad on the side.

variations.name: Kashmiri Dal Makhani Home-style
variations.description: A gently perfumed home version scented with saffron, fennel and dry ginger in the Kashmiri Pandit style, made without onion or garlic for a clean, aromatic dal. Ghee carries the fragile spices while saffron milk tints it a warm amber. It is soothing and fragrant, an unexpected twist on the everyday makhani.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Kashmiri saffron bloomed in warm milk gives the home dal its floral aroma and amber tint

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee carries the delicate fennel and saffron in this onion-free Pandit-style dal

steps: Soak 1 cup black urad and 0.25 cup rajma for 6 hours, then pressure-cook with 5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 6 whistles until soft; soak 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot over medium heat and add 3 crushed cardamom pods and 2 cloves, frying until fragrant, about 30 seconds.
Add 2 pureed tomatoes and 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and cook until the ghee separates, about 8 minutes, then lower the heat and stir in 1 tsp fennel powder and 0.5 tsp dry ginger for 20 seconds.
Add the cooked beans with their liquor, mash a portion, and simmer uncovered on low heat for 20 minutes until creamy.
Pour in the saffron milk and 2 tbsp cream and simmer 5 minutes until the dal glows amber and smells floral.
Rest covered for 3 minutes so the spices settle, then serve warm.
tips: Cook the onion-free base gently so the tomatoes and ghee stay pale enough for the saffron colour to show.
Add saffron milk near the end to preserve its aroma.
Fennel and dry ginger are the signature here, so resist adding garam masala.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed basmati or soft rotis and a cooling bowl of curd to let the saffron aroma stand out.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Dal Makhani Home-style
variations.description: This home take flavours the creamy black dal with earthy goda masala and a groundnut-oil tempering of mustard and curry leaves, with a scatter of fresh coconut. Its dark, faintly sweet spice sets it apart from the Punjabi version. Rustic and fragrant, it suits an everyday Maharashtrian table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil is the everyday Maharashtrian fat that suits goda masala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of ghee balances the dark goda masala

steps: Soak 1 cup black urad and 0.25 cup rajma for 6 hours, then pressure-cook with 5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 6 whistles until soft enough to mash.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pot over medium heat, add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and let them splutter, then add 0.5 tsp cumin and 1 sprig curry leaves.
Add 5 crushed garlic cloves and 1 chopped onion and fry until golden, about 6 minutes, then add 2 chopped tomatoes and 1 tsp red chilli powder and cook until pulpy, about 6 minutes.
Sprinkle in 1.5 tsp goda masala and fry for 1 minute until its dark aroma blooms.
Add the cooked beans with their liquor, mash a portion, and simmer uncovered on low heat for 20 minutes until creamy.
Finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 3 tbsp fresh grated coconut stirred in, and serve warm.
tips: Fry goda masala only briefly, as overcooking makes it bitter.
A teaspoon of jaggery is a common home touch to soften the tomato acidity.
Use freshly grated coconut rather than desiccated for the right moist finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri or steamed rice, a wedge of lemon and a little extra coconut scattered on top.

variations.name: Gujarati Dal Makhani Home-style
variations.description: The Gujarati home cook tips the creamy black dal toward the region's khatta-metha balance, melting in jaggery against tomato tang and tempering with mustard, curry leaves and asafoetida in groundnut oil. Milder and a touch sweet, it is a gentle, family-friendly makhani. It sits happily on a simple thali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: organic jaggery powder gives the mild caramel sweetness of the Gujarati khatta-metha balance

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil is the traditional Gujarati tempering fat

steps: Soak 1 cup black urad and 0.25 cup rajma for 6 hours, then pressure-cook with 5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 6 whistles until soft enough to mash.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pot over medium heat, add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and let them splutter, then add 0.5 tsp cumin, 1 pinch asafoetida and 1 sprig curry leaves.
Add 1 chopped onion with a grated 1 inch piece of ginger and 2 slit green chillies and fry until soft and golden, about 6 minutes.
Add 3 pureed tomatoes and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and cook until the masala thickens and oil separates, about 8 minutes.
Add the cooked beans with their liquor, mash a portion, stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, and simmer uncovered on low heat for 20 minutes.
Taste and adjust the sweet-tangy balance, then serve warm and creamy.
tips: Add jaggery toward the end so it dissolves smoothly without scorching.
Keep the chilli gentle; this version is about balance, not heat.
A last drizzle of raw groundnut oil adds a glossy, authentic finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulka rotis or steamed rice and a crunchy kachumber salad for a homely Gujarati meal.

variations.name: Bengali Dal Makhani Home-style
variations.description: A Bengali home twist that finishes the creamy black dal with a pungent mustard-oil tadka of nigella and green chillies and a rounding spoon of ghee. Lighter on cream and sharper in aroma, it swaps Punjabi butteriness for the bright, homely signature of a Bengali kitchen. Simple and quietly different.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil heated to smoking builds the sharp Bengali base and tadka

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of ghee mellows the mustard sharpness in the Bengali style

steps: Soak 1 cup black urad and 0.25 cup rajma for 6 hours, then pressure-cook with 5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 6 whistles until soft enough to mash.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pot over high heat until it smokes, lower to medium, then add a paste of 5 garlic cloves and 1 inch ginger and fry 1 minute.
Add 1 chopped onion and fry until golden, about 6 minutes, then add 2 chopped tomatoes and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and cook until pulpy, about 7 minutes.
Add the cooked beans with their liquor, mash a portion, and simmer uncovered on low heat for 18 minutes until creamy, then stir in 1 tbsp cream.
Make a tadka by heating 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackling 0.5 tsp nigella seeds and 3 slit green chillies for 20 seconds, and pour it sizzling over the dal.
Adjust the remaining 0.5 tsp salt and serve warm.
tips: Smoke the mustard oil before frying so the dal is nutty rather than raw.
Nigella seeds, not cumin, give this the distinctive Bengali aroma.
Keep the cream light so the mustard and nigella stay forward.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rice or luchi and a quick cucumber salad to balance the mustard warmth.

variations.name: Classic Dal Makhani Punjabi
variations.description: The full-dress Punjabi dal makhani, slow-simmered with butter, cream and kasuri methi until it turns dark, silky and luxurious. Whole black urad and rajma are cooked for hours, then finished with a ghee tadka for that unmistakable dhaba richness. This is the celebratory dal Punjab is famous for.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee for the finishing tadka delivers the nutty depth that defines Punjabi makhani

steps: Soak 1 cup black urad and 0.3 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 7 whistles until the beans crush easily.
Heat 4 tbsp butter in a heavy pot over medium heat, add a paste of 8 garlic cloves and 1.5 inch ginger, fry 1 minute, then add 1 chopped onion and cook until golden, about 7 minutes.
Add 4 pureed tomatoes with 1 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, and cook down until thick and glossy with fat pooling, about 12 minutes.
Add the cooked beans with their liquor, mash a good portion, and simmer uncovered on very low heat for a full 50 minutes, stirring often, until dark and velvety.
Stir in 0.5 tsp garam masala, 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi and 4 tbsp cream and simmer 8 minutes more until luxuriously smooth.
Finish with a tadka of 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee heated with 1 tsp cumin seeds until fragrant, poured sizzling over the dal before serving.
tips: The long, slow simmer is what gives authentic makhani its body; do not rush it.
A tablespoon of milk added during simmering keeps the colour rich but not muddy.
It tastes even better the next day, reheated gently with a fresh spoon of butter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or laccha paratha, a swirl of cream, a nub of butter and julienned ginger over the top.

variations.name: Delhi-style Dal Makhani Punjabi
