variations.description: The Delhi restaurant style leans on a ground cashew paste and whole warm spices for a glossy, mildly sweet, almost gravy-like makhani that clings to a spoon. Bay leaf, black cardamom and cinnamon perfume the buttery base while cashews replace some of the cream for silkiness. This is the dal of Old Delhi's iconic eateries.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee tadka adds the restaurant-style richness Delhi makhani is known for

steps: Soak 1 cup black urad and 0.3 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 5 cups water and 1 tsp salt for 7 whistles until soft; meanwhile soak 15 cashews in hot water for 15 minutes and grind to a smooth paste.

Heat 4 tbsp butter in a pot over medium heat, add 1 bay leaf, 1 crushed black cardamom and 1 inch cinnamon and fry until fragrant, then add a paste of 8 garlic cloves and 1.5 inch ginger and cook 1 minute.

Add 1 chopped onion and fry until golden, about 7 minutes, then add 4 pureed tomatoes with 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt and cook until thick and deep red, about 12 minutes.
Add the cooked beans with their liquor, mash a portion, stir in the cashew paste, and simmer uncovered on low heat for 30 minutes until rich and glossy.
Stir in 1 tsp garam masala and 4 tbsp cream and simmer 6 minutes for a smooth, mildly sweet restaurant-style finish.
Finish with a tadka of 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee heated until fragrant, poured sizzling over the dal before serving.
tips: The cashew paste is the Delhi restaurant secret that makes the gravy glossy without a flood of cream.
Fish out the whole bay leaf and cardamom before serving so no one bites into them.
Blend a ladle of the dal smooth and stir it back in for an even silkier texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with garlic naan or missi roti, a generous swirl of cream and a slick of melted butter over the top.

variations.name: Malwa Dal Makhani Punjabi
variations.description: From the Malwa plateau comes a nutty reinterpretation, where roasted peanuts are ground into the creamy black dal for body and a toasty sweetness. A groundnut-oil tempering and a hint of extra chilli give it a warm, rustic character. The peanut richness stands in for some of the dairy, making it distinctly central Indian.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil echoes the roasted peanut theme of this Malwa version

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of ghee lends the toasty peanut dal a rounded richness

steps: Soak 1 cup black urad and 0.3 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 7 whistles until soft.
Grind 0.33 cup roasted peanuts to a coarse paste with a little water and set aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pot over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add a paste of 6 garlic cloves and 1 inch ginger and fry 1 minute.
Add 1 chopped onion and fry until golden, about 6 minutes, then add 3 pureed tomatoes, 1.25 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp coriander powder and cook until the oil separates, about 9 minutes.
Add the cooked beans with their liquor and the peanut paste, mash a portion, and simmer uncovered on low heat for 25 minutes until thick and nutty.
Finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee stirred through, adjust the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, and serve warm.
tips: Grind the peanuts coarse rather than fine for a pleasant texture in the dal.
The peanut paste thickens as it simmers, so keep a little hot water handy to loosen it.
Toasting the peanuts a shade darker deepens the nutty flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rotis or steamed rice and a sprinkle of crushed roasted peanuts on top for crunch.

variations.name: Kerala Dal Makhani Punjabi
variations.description: A coastal reworking where the creamy black dal is enriched with ground coconut and coconut milk and finished with a coconut-oil tadka of mustard, curry leaves and shallots. Green chilli and ginger keep it fresh while coconut replaces the dairy, giving a mellow, fragrant sweetness. It is a light, aromatic answer to the heavy Punjabi classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil is the soul of the Kerala tadka and cannot be substituted

steps: Soak 1 cup black urad and 0.3 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 7 whistles until soft.
Grind 0.5 cup grated coconut to a smooth paste and set aside.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pot over medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop, then add 2 broken dried red chillies, 8 sliced shallots, 2 slit green chillies, a grated 1 inch piece of ginger and 2 sprigs curry leaves.
Fry until the shallots are deep golden, about 6 minutes, then add 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and stir for 15 seconds.
Add the cooked beans with their liquor and the coconut paste, mash a portion, and simmer uncovered on low heat for 22 minutes until thick.
Stir in 0.5 cup coconut milk, warm on low heat for 3 minutes without boiling, adjust the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, and serve warm.
tips: Ground coconut plus coconut milk gives a creaminess that fully replaces dairy here.
Never boil after adding coconut milk or the dal will split and turn grainy.
Deep-golden shallots are essential to the gentle sweetness of this version.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed red rice or soft appams and a spoon of lime pickle to cut the coconut richness.

variations.name: Bengali Dal Makhani Punjabi
variations.description: A Bengali-accented makhani where the rich black dal meets a pungent mustard-oil tadka of nigella and slit green chillies, softened by a final spoon of ghee. Lighter on cream and brighter in spice, it trades Punjabi butteriness for the sharp, homely aroma of a Bengali kitchen. A surprising but deeply satisfying twist.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil heated to smoking builds the sharp Bengali base and tadka

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of ghee mellows the mustard sharpness in the Bengali style

steps: Soak 1 cup black urad and 0.3 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 7 whistles until soft.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pot over high heat until it smokes, lower to medium, then add a paste of 6 garlic cloves and 1 inch ginger and fry 1 minute.
Add 1 chopped onion and fry until golden, about 6 minutes, then add 3 chopped tomatoes and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and cook until pulpy and the oil separates, about 8 minutes.
Add the cooked beans with their liquor, mash a portion, and simmer uncovered on low heat for 30 minutes until creamy, then stir in 2 tbsp cream.
Make a tadka by heating 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackling 0.5 tsp nigella seeds and 3 slit green chillies for 20 seconds, and pour it sizzling over the dal.
Adjust the remaining 0.5 tsp salt and serve warm.
tips: Smoke the mustard oil before frying so the dal tastes nutty rather than raw.
Nigella seeds, not cumin, give this its distinctive Bengali fragrance.
Keep the cream light so the mustard and nigella stay in the foreground.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rice or luchi and a quick cucumber salad to balance the mustard warmth.

variations.name: Classic Dal Makhani Tadka
variations.description: The iconic Punjabi dal makhani, where whole black urad and rajma are simmered low and slow until creamy, then enriched with tomato, butter and ghee and crowned with a final sizzling tadka. Hours of gentle cooking give it its velvet body without any cream shortcuts. This is the celebratory dal that anchors every North Indian feast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee for the finishing tadka gives dal makhani its signature nutty richness

steps: Soak 1 cup black urad and 0.25 cup rajma together overnight, then pressure-cook them with 5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 6 whistles until the beans mash easily between two fingers.
Heat 3 tbsp butter in a heavy pot over medium heat, add a paste of 8 garlic cloves and 1.5 inch ginger and fry 1 minute, then add 1 finely chopped onion and cook until golden, about 7 minutes.
Add 3 pureed tomatoes with 1 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, and cook down until the masala thickens and fat pools at the edges, about 10 minutes.
Tip in the cooked beans with their liquor and mash a portion against the pot; simmer uncovered on low heat for at least 40 minutes, stirring often, until thick and glossy.
Stir in 0.5 tsp garam masala and 3 tbsp cream and simmer for 5 more minutes until the dal turns silky and dark.
For the tadka, heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until nearly smoking, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 2 dried red chillies, and pour the sizzling ghee over the dal just before serving.
tips: The longer and slower the final simmer, the creamier the dal; a smashed handful of beans thickens it naturally without extra cream.
A splash of milk during simmering keeps the colour pale and the texture plush.
Made a day ahead and reheated with a fresh ghee tadka, it tastes even better.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with naan or jeera rice, a swirl of extra cream, a nub of butter and a scatter of julienned ginger on top.

variations.name: Kashmiri Dal Makhani Tadka
variations.description: This aromatic version perfumes the creamy black-dal base with saffron, fennel and dry ginger in the Kashmiri manner, giving a floral, warmly spiced makhani with a delicate amber tint. Ghee carries the fragile spices while saffron-infused milk deepens both colour and scent. It is an elegant, festive spin on the robust classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Kashmiri saffron bloomed in warm milk lends the makhani its floral aroma and amber glow

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee both cooks the base and finishes the dal, carrying the delicate fennel and saffron notes

steps: Soak 1 cup black urad and 0.25 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 6 whistles until fully soft; meanwhile soak 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot over medium heat, add 3 crushed cardamom pods, then 1 finely chopped onion and fry until soft and pale gold, about 7 minutes, keeping it from browning too dark.
Add 2 pureed tomatoes and 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and cook until the fat separates, about 8 minutes, then lower the heat and stir in 1 tsp fennel powder and 0.5 tsp dry ginger for 20 seconds.
Add the cooked beans with their liquor, mash a portion, and simmer uncovered on low heat for 35 minutes, stirring so it does not stick.
Pour in the saffron milk and 3 tbsp cream and simmer for 6 minutes until the dal turns amber and creamy.
Finish with a tadka of the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee heated until fragrant and poured over the dal just before serving.
tips: Keep the onions pale rather than deeply browned so the saffron colour reads clearly.
Add saffron milk near the end so its fragrance is not cooked away.
Fennel and dry ginger give the Kashmiri character; do not swap in garam masala.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with saffron pulao or soft rotis and a light kachumber, letting the floral aroma of the dal lead the meal.

variations.name: Bengali Dal Makhani Tadka
variations.description: A Bengali-inflected makhani where the creamy black dal meets a pungent mustard-oil tadka of nigella and green chillies, then a rounding spoon of ghee. Lighter on cream and brighter in spice, it swaps Punjabi butteriness for the sharp, aromatic signature of a Bengali kitchen. Unexpected, but deeply satisfying.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil heated to smoking builds the sharp Bengali base and tadka

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of ghee rounds off the mustard sharpness in the Bengali style

steps: Soak 1 cup black urad and 0.25 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 6 whistles until soft enough to mash.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pot over high heat until it smokes, lower to medium, then add a paste of 6 garlic cloves and 1 inch ginger and fry for 1 minute.
Add 1 chopped onion and fry until golden, about 6 minutes, then add 2 chopped tomatoes and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and cook until pulpy and the oil separates, about 8 minutes.
Add the cooked beans with their liquor, mash a portion against the pot, and simmer uncovered on low heat for 30 minutes until thick and creamy.
Stir in 2 tbsp cream and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt and simmer 4 minutes more.
Make a tadka by heating 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackling 0.5 tsp nigella seeds and 3 slit green chillies for 20 seconds, then pour it sizzling over the dal and serve.
tips: Smoke the mustard oil before use so the dal is nutty rather than raw and bitter.
Nigella seeds, not cumin, give this version its distinctive Bengali aroma.
Keep the cream light so the mustard and nigella stay in the foreground.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rice or luchi and a side of quick cucumber salad to balance the mustard heat.

variations.name: Andhra Dal Makhani Tadka
variations.description: A fiery Deccan reworking of the mellow classic, where smoky Guntur chillies and a garlic-loaded sesame-oil tadka bring aggressive heat to the creamy black dal. Curry leaves and a squeeze of tamarind lend a southern tang the Punjabi original never has. Rich yet blazing, it is tamed only by a final spoon of ghee.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed gingelly oil stands up to the fierce Guntur tadka and adds Andhra depth

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of ghee softens the aggressive Guntur heat and adds gloss

steps: Soak 1 cup black urad and 0.25 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 6 whistles until soft, then stir in 1 tsp tamarind pulp.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pot over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 4 broken Guntur chillies and fry until the chillies darken and smoke lightly, about 30 seconds.
Add 10 crushed garlic cloves and 1 sprig curry leaves and fry until the garlic is golden, then add 1 chopped onion and cook until browned, about 6 minutes.
Add 2 pureed tomatoes and 1 tsp red chilli powder and cook until the masala thickens and the oil separates, about 8 minutes.
Add the cooked beans with their liquor, mash a portion, and simmer uncovered on low heat for 30 minutes until creamy and fiery.
Finish with a spoon of 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee stirred through to round the heat, then serve very hot.
tips: Guntur chillies are searing; deseed a couple if you want the colour without full fire.
The tamarind is subtle here, just enough to lift the richness with a southern tang.
Serve a bowl of chilled curd alongside to cool the palate.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over ghee rice with a papad and plenty of curd, or with plain rotis for those who want to temper the heat.

variations.name: Gujarati Dal Makhani Tadka
variations.description: The Gujarati hand brings a gentle sweetness to the creamy black dal, melting in jaggery against tomato tang for the region's beloved khatta-metha balance. A groundnut-oil tempering with whole spices and curry leaves keeps it fragrant and homely rather than heavy. Milder and sweeter than the Punjabi original, it charms a family table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: organic jaggery powder gives the mild caramel sweetness of the Gujarati khatta-metha balance

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil is the traditional Gujarati cooking fat for the base and tadka

steps: Soak 1 cup black urad and 0.25 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 6 whistles until soft enough to mash.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pot over medium heat, add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and let them splutter, then add 0.5 tsp cumin, 1 pinch asafoetida and 1 sprig curry leaves.
Add 1 chopped onion with a grated 1 inch piece of ginger and 2 slit green chillies and fry until soft and golden, about 6 minutes.
Add 3 pureed tomatoes and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and cook until the masala thickens and the oil separates, about 9 minutes.
Add the cooked beans with their liquor, mash a portion, stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, and simmer uncovered on low heat for 30 minutes.
Taste and adjust the sweet-tangy balance, then serve warm and creamy.
tips: Add jaggery toward the end so it dissolves smoothly without scorching the base.
Keep the chilli gentle; this version is about balance rather than heat.
A last drizzle of raw groundnut oil or a spoon of ghee adds a glossy finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulka rotis or steamed rice and a crunchy kachumber salad for a comforting Gujarati-style meal.

variations.name: Classic Dhuli Moong Dhaba-style
variations.description: Smoky, buttery and unapologetically rich, this is the moong dal of highway dhabas, built on a deep bhuna masala, kasuri methi, garam masala and a charcoal-smoke finish. The dal is cooked till creamy, then given a second ghee tadka poured over at the table. It is meant to be eaten hot with tandoori roti smeared in butter.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A double ghee tadka gives this dal its true dhaba-style depth and shine.

steps: Rinse 1 cup dhuli moong dal and pressure-cook it with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 3 whistles until creamy, then whisk smooth.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add 1 inch grated ginger and 7 minced garlic cloves and fry for 40 seconds.
Add 2 finely chopped onions and cook until deep golden brown, about 8 minutes, then add 2 chopped tomatoes and 1 tsp red chilli powder and bhuno until the ghee separates, about 7 minutes.
Pour in the whisked dal with the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, then simmer on low for 8 minutes, adding hot water to keep it creamy.
Crush 1 tsp kasuri methi over the dal, add 0.75 tsp garam masala and simmer 2 more minutes.
For the smoky finish, place a small bowl on the dal, add a piece of glowing charcoal, drizzle with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, cover for 1 minute, then discard the coal.
Finish with chopped coriander and serve hot with buttered tandoori roti.
tips: Browning the onions well and slowly is the backbone of true dhaba flavour, so do not rush this step.
The charcoal smoke is optional but gives that unmistakable dhaba aroma; skip it safely if unsure.
Keep a little hot water handy, as this dal thickens fast and should stay creamy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter-laden tandoori roti or laccha paratha, sliced onions dusted with chaat masala, and a green chilli pickle for the full highway-dhaba feast.

variations.name: Delhi-style Dhuli Moong Dhaba-style
variations.description: Delhi's version amps up the garam masala and adds a bright dhania-jeera masala with a squeeze of lemon, giving a punchy, aromatic dal that leans street-food bold. Freshly powdered garam masala stirred in at the end, plus a green-chilli-ginger julienne garnish, keeps it lively. It is the moong dal of Old Delhi eateries, served with kulcha or rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee blooms the freshly ground garam masala that defines this Delhi-style dal.

steps: Rinse 1 cup dhuli moong dal and pressure-cook it with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft, then whisk lightly.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add half the 1.5 inch ginger grated and 6 minced garlic cloves and fry 40 seconds.
Add 1 large chopped onion and cook until golden, about 6 minutes, then add 2 chopped tomatoes, 1 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp red chilli powder and cook until pulpy, about 6 minutes.
Pour in the whisked dal with the remaining 0.5 tsp salt and 0.5 cup hot water and simmer on low for 6 minutes.
Stir in 1 tsp garam masala and simmer 2 more minutes so the spice blooms through the dal.
Turn off the heat and stir in 1 tbsp lemon juice, then garnish with the remaining ginger cut into fine juliennes, 2 slit green chillies and chopped coriander.
Serve hot with kulcha, roti or steamed rice.
tips: Add lemon juice off the heat so the dal stays bright and tangy.
Ginger juliennes and slit green chilli on top give the Delhi-eatery look and a fresh bite.
Freshly ground garam masala makes a noticeable difference over a stale packet blend.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot amritsari kulcha or tandoori roti, a raw onion-lemon salad and a spoon of green chutney for a bustling Delhi-style plate.

variations.name: Karnataka Dhuli Moong Dhaba-style
variations.description: Karnataka brings a tangy-sweet spin with tamarind, jaggery and a coconut-tempered tadka, turning the moong into a saaru-like dal with layered flavour. A dry-roasted spice powder of coriander and chana dal deepens it, while curry leaves and coconut oil give the southern lift. It is comforting, tangy and lovely poured over rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil gives the tempering its unmistakable South Indian fragrance.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery balances the tamarind for the sweet-sour Karnataka saaru profile.

steps: Soak 1 tbsp tamarind in 0.5 cup warm water for 10 minutes, then squeeze and strain to get a smooth pulp.
Rinse 1 cup dhuli moong dal and pressure-cook it with 3.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft, then whisk it smooth.

Add the tamarind pulp, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 3 tbsp grated coconut, 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt to the dal and simmer on low for 8 minutes until tangy and rounded.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan on medium heat and pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, then add 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, 2 broken dried red chillies and 0.25 tsp asafoetida.
Add 12 curry leaves and let them crisp for 15 seconds until fragrant, then pour the sizzling tempering over the simmering dal.
Stir once, finish with chopped coriander, and serve hot.
Pour generously over steamed rice with a spoon of ghee for a comforting Karnataka-style meal.
tips: Balance the tamarind and jaggery until you taste a clear sweet-sour note, adjusting either as needed.
Add the coconut-oil tempering last so its aroma stays fresh and bright.
For extra body, grind the grated coconut with a little water into a paste before adding.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot rice with a dollop of ghee and a crisp sandige or papad; it also pairs well with soft set dosa or plain rice and a vegetable palya.

variations.name: Kerala Dhuli Moong Dhaba-style
variations.description: This coastal version simmers the moong in a coconut-milk gravy scented with garam masala and fennel, closer to a moong dal curry than a dry dal. Coconut milk gives it a mellow, creamy body while a coconut-oil tadka of shallots and curry leaves crowns it. It is rich yet fragrant, perfect with appam or ghee rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil ties the shallot tadka to the coconut-milk gravy for a true Kerala taste.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of ghee adds richness over the coconut-milk base.

steps: Rinse 1 cup dhuli moong dal and pressure-cook it with 2.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft, keeping it slightly loose.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan on medium heat and pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, then add 8 sliced shallots, 1 inch julienned ginger and 2 slit green chillies.
Fry until the shallots turn golden, about 3 minutes, then add 14 curry leaves and let them crisp for 15 seconds.
Stir in 0.5 tsp fennel powder and 0.5 tsp garam masala for 15 seconds, then add the cooked dal and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt.
Pour in 1 cup coconut milk and simmer on very low heat for 5 minutes, stirring gently, without letting it boil hard so the milk does not split.
Finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and chopped coriander, and serve warm.
Serve with appam, ghee rice or steamed matta rice to soak up the creamy gravy.
tips: Add coconut milk on low heat and avoid a rolling boil to keep the gravy from curdling.
Shallots give a sweeter, more authentic base than regular onions here.
Thin with a little warm water if the gravy tightens after resting.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside lacy appam or fragrant ghee rice with a wedge of lime; a simple beetroot thoran on the side completes the Kerala plate.

variations.name: Goan Dhuli Moong Dhaba-style
variations.description: Goa lends a coastal tang with kokum and a coconut-coriander masala, making a light, souring moong dal that cuts through humid days. Kokum petals steep in the dal for a gentle purple-tinged sourness quite unlike tamarind, while a coconut-oil tadka keeps it aromatic. It is a breezy, everyday Goan dal for rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil is the classic Goan cooking fat and complements the kokum beautifully.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A little jaggery softens the sharp sourness of the kokum.

steps: Rinse 1 cup dhuli moong dal and pressure-cook it with 3.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft, then whisk lightly.
Rinse 4 kokum petals and soak them in 3 tbsp warm water for 10 minutes to soften.
Grind 3 tbsp grated coconut with 1 tsp coriander powder and a splash of water to a coarse paste.
Add the coconut paste, the soaked kokum with its water, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt to the dal and simmer on low for 8 minutes until gently sour.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan on medium heat and crackle 0.75 tsp cumin seeds, then add 6 crushed garlic cloves, 2 slit green chillies and 10 curry leaves.
Fry until the garlic is golden and the leaves crisp, about 1 minute, then pour the tempering over the dal and stir once.
Finish with chopped coriander and serve hot with steamed rice.
tips: Remove the kokum petals before serving if you prefer a smoother dal; they have done their souring work.
Kokum gives a milder, fruitier sourness than tamarind, so do not substitute one for the other blindly.
Balance with a touch more jaggery if the kokum makes the dal too tart.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot par-boiled Goan red rice with a fried papad and a simple raw mango salad; it also works as a light dal with soft rice and a coconut chutney.

variations.name: Classic Dhuli Moong Home-style
variations.description: This is the unfussy weeknight moong dal cooked in most Indian homes: skinned green gram simmered soft, then finished with a quick ghee-cumin-garlic tadka and a handful of coriander. It is light on spice and heavy on comfort, sitting somewhere between a soup and a stew. The whole thing comes together in half an hour with pantry staples.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A generous ghee tadka turns plain boiled dal into something homely and rich.

steps: Rinse 1 cup dhuli moong dal until the water runs clear, then pressure-cook it with 3.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft and creamy.
Lightly whisk the cooked dal with a ladle so it turns smooth, adding a little hot water if it looks too thick.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds until they sizzle and smell toasty, about 20 seconds.
Add 5 sliced garlic cloves and 2 slit green chillies and fry until the garlic turns pale gold, then add 1 chopped onion and cook 3 minutes until soft.
Stir in 1 chopped tomato and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and cook until the tomato softens and the ghee glistens, about 4 minutes.
Pour the tadka over the whisked dal, add the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, and simmer on low for 5 minutes before finishing with chopped coriander.
Serve hot with roti or rice, with an extra drizzle of ghee if you like.
tips: Whisking the boiled dal before tempering gives the classic smooth, homely consistency.
Keep the tadka on medium heat so the garlic flavours the ghee without burning.
Leftovers thicken overnight; loosen with hot water and a fresh pinch of salt when reheating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle into bowls and serve with phulka, a simple cucumber salad and a spoon of lime pickle; a bowl of plain rice on the side makes it a complete comforting meal.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Dhuli Moong Home-style
variations.description: Maharashtra folds in fragrant goda masala, a warm blend of sesame, coconut and stone flower, giving this moong dal a dark, aromatic sweetness quite distinct from a plain tadka dal. Goda masala plus a mustard-and-curry-leaf tempering and a touch of jaggery create the region's classic sweet-savoury balance. It is a soulful everyday dal served with soft bhakri or rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee blooms the goda masala and rounds out its smoky notes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A little jaggery is the classic Maharashtrian counterpoint to the spicy goda masala.

steps: Rinse 1 cup dhuli moong dal and pressure-cook it with 3.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft, then whisk lightly.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium heat and pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, then add 0.75 tsp cumin seeds and 10 curry leaves and let them crackle for 20 seconds.
Add 1 finely chopped onion and saute until soft and translucent, about 4 minutes.
Lower the heat and add 1.5 tsp goda masala and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, stirring for 30 seconds until the ghee turns aromatic and dark; do not let the masala scorch.
Pour in the whisked dal with 1 cup hot water and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, and simmer on low for 6 minutes.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder until it dissolves, finish with chopped coriander, and serve hot.
Serve with jowar bhakri or steamed rice and a spoon of ghee for a true Maharashtrian meal.
tips: Add goda masala on low heat so its delicate coconut-and-stone-flower notes bloom without burning.
The jaggery should whisper, not shout; add just enough to soften the spice, not sweeten the dal.
If you cannot find goda masala, a mix of garam masala with a pinch of ground sesame and coconut is a fair stand-in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with warm jowar or bajra bhakri, a raw onion wedge and a dab of thecha; over rice, a spoonful of ghee and a papad round it off.

variations.name: Odia Dhuli Moong Home-style
variations.description: Odia kitchens temper this moong dal with panch phoron, the five-spice mix of cumin, fenugreek, mustard, nigella and fennel, giving it a distinctive sweet-savoury aroma. Roasting the dal first, then finishing it with panch phoron in ghee and a bay leaf, makes it fragrant and light. It is the everyday dal that anchors an Odia thali beside rice and a fry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries the panch phoron tempering that defines this Odia dal.

steps: Dry-roast 1 cup dhuli moong dal in a pan on medium-low heat until golden and nutty, about 5 minutes, then rinse it gently.
Pressure-cook the roasted dal with 3.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft, then whisk it lightly smooth.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium heat and add 1 tsp panch phoron, 1 bay leaf and 2 dried red chillies; let them crackle for about 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 inch grated ginger and 1 chopped tomato and cook until the tomato turns pulpy, about 4 minutes.
Pour in the whisked dal with the remaining 0.5 tsp salt and 2 slit green chillies, and simmer on low for 6 minutes so the five-spice aroma infuses.
Finish with chopped coriander and a little extra ghee, and serve hot with steamed rice.
For the classic Odia touch, keep the dal medium-thin so it coats the rice rather than sitting thick.
tips: Do not grind the panch phoron; the whole seeds are meant to crackle and stay whole in the tadka.
Roasting the dal deepens the aroma and helps it hold a little shape after cooking.
A pinch of sugar can be added to underline the gentle sweetness typical of Odia dals.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot rice with a wedge of lime, a dry aloo bhaja and a spoon of tomato khatta on the side for a balanced Odia plate.

variations.name: Rajasthani Dhuli Moong Home-style
variations.description: The desert version leans on whole dried red chillies, garlic and a smoky ghee tadka, with no tomato and very little water, giving a robust, rustic dal built for a land of few fresh vegetables. Ground coriander and a hint of amchur bring earthy warmth and tang. It is hearty, spicy and made to be mopped up with bajra roti.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A bold ghee tadka is essential in Rajasthani cooking where fresh produce is scarce.

steps: Rinse 1 cup dhuli moong dal and pressure-cook it with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft, keeping the dal on the thicker side.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium heat and add 0.25 tsp asafoetida followed by 1 tsp cumin seeds and 4 broken dried red chillies; let them crackle for 20 seconds.
Add 8 crushed garlic cloves and fry until deep golden and aromatic, about 1 minute.
Lower the heat and add 1 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, stirring for 20 seconds so the spices bloom in the ghee.
Pour in the cooked dal, add half a cup of hot water only if needed, and simmer on low for 6 minutes until thick and glossy.
Stir in 0.5 tsp amchur powder and chopped coriander off the heat, and serve hot.
Serve with bajra or wheat roti and a raw onion for a true Rajasthani meal.
tips: Keep this dal thick and robust; the desert style is not meant to be soupy.
Add amchur off the heat so its sharp tang stays bright.
Crush the garlic coarsely so it browns into flavourful bits rather than dissolving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best mopped up with hot bajra roti smeared with ghee, alongside sliced onions and a green chilli; it also pairs well with plain steamed rice and papad.

variations.name: Tamil Dhuli Moong Home-style
variations.description: The Tamil paruppu keeps things gentle: soft moong mashed with turmeric, then finished with a sesame-oil tadka of mustard, curry leaves and dried chilli. A spoon of ghee and a squeeze of lime at the end make it silky and comforting, the everyday dal that becomes paruppu sadam when mixed into rice. It is mild, fragrant and endlessly soothing.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil is the traditional Tamil tempering fat and adds a nutty depth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon of ghee stirred in at the end makes the paruppu silky and rich.

steps: Rinse 1 cup dhuli moong dal and pressure-cook it with 3.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 3 to 4 whistles until very soft, then mash it smooth with the back of a ladle.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a small pan on medium heat and pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, then add 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 2 broken dried red chillies.
Add 0.25 tsp asafoetida, 6 sliced shallots and 12 curry leaves and fry until the shallots turn golden and the leaves crisp, about 2 minutes.
Pour the tempering into the mashed dal along with the remaining 0.5 tsp salt and 0.5 cup hot water, and simmer on low for 4 minutes.
Stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until it melts into the dal and turns it glossy.
Turn off the heat, stir in 1 tbsp lemon juice, and serve warm.
Ladle over hot rice or serve as a side to sambar rice for a comforting Tamil meal.
tips: Mash the dal well; a smooth paruppu is characteristic of the Tamil home style.
Add lemon juice only after switching off the heat to keep its fresh sourness.
Mixed straight into hot rice with a little extra ghee, this becomes classic paruppu sadam.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over steamed rice with a teaspoon of ghee, a papad and a spoon of avakkai pickle; it also makes a gentle side for rasam rice.

variations.name: Classic Dhuli Moong Punjabi
variations.description: The dhaba-loved Punjabi moong dal is rich with a double tadka of ghee, ginger-garlic and tomato, rounded off with crushed kasuri methi and a knob of butter. It is thicker and more indulgent than a plain home dal, with a deep golden colour and a buttery sheen. This is the version you crave with hot tandoori roti on a cold evening.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee gives this Punjabi dal its signature dhaba-style richness.

steps: Rinse 1 cup dhuli moong dal and pressure-cook it with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft, then whisk lightly and keep thick.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then add 1 inch grated ginger and 6 minced garlic cloves and fry 40 seconds.
Add 1 finely chopped onion and cook until golden, about 5 minutes, then add 2 chopped tomatoes and cook until pulpy and the ghee separates, about 6 minutes.
Stir in 1 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, then pour in the cooked dal with 0.5 cup hot water and simmer on low for 6 minutes.
Crush 1 tsp kasuri methi between your palms and add it with 0.5 tsp garam masala, simmering another 2 minutes so the aromas bloom.
Finish with 1 tbsp butter and chopped coriander, letting the butter melt into a glossy sheen before serving.
Serve hot with tandoori roti, naan or jeera rice.
tips: Crushing the kasuri methi between your palms releases far more aroma than adding it whole.
For a richer dhaba finish, add a small piece of glowing charcoal in a bowl over the dal, drizzle ghee and cover for a minute to smoke it.
Keep this dal thick; loosen only slightly with hot water if it sets on standing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter-brushed tandoori roti or lachha paratha, a raw onion and lemon salad, and a green chilli on the side for the full dhaba experience.

variations.name: Kashmiri Dhuli Moong Punjabi
variations.description: This regal take perfumes the moong dal with saffron, fennel and dry ginger, the aromatics of a Kashmiri kitchen, and skips onion and garlic in the Pandit tradition. Saffron gives a golden hue and honeyed aroma while ground fennel and a whisper of clove keep it warming. It is delicate, fragrant and unlike any everyday dal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee is the only fat in this onion-and-garlic-free Kashmiri Pandit style dal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: A few strands of Kashmiri saffron give the dal its golden colour and honeyed aroma.

steps: Soak 0.25 tsp Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm water and set aside to bloom into a golden liquid.
Rinse 1 cup dhuli moong dal and pressure-cook it with 3.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft, then whisk lightly.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, 2 cloves and 2 lightly crushed cardamom pods for 20 seconds.
Lower the heat and add 1 tsp fennel powder, 0.5 tsp dry ginger powder and 1 tsp Kashmiri red chilli powder, stirring for 15 seconds until fragrant but not burnt.
Pour in the whisked dal with the remaining 0.5 tsp salt and the bloomed saffron water, and simmer on low for 6 minutes so the aromatics infuse.
Finish with chopped coriander and a drizzle of ghee, and serve hot.
Serve with steamed rice or a soft roti to let the saffron and fennel aromas shine.
tips: Bloom the saffron in warm water first so its colour and aroma spread evenly through the dal.
Kashmiri chilli powder is for colour, not heat, so use it generously without fear.
Fennel and dry ginger are the defining Kashmiri notes; keep them balanced so neither dominates.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over plain steamed rice with a side of Kashmiri haakh or a simple yogurt, letting the delicate saffron aroma lead the plate.

variations.name: Malwa Dhuli Moong Punjabi
variations.description: From the Malwa plateau comes a nutty twist, with roasted peanuts and a groundnut-oil tadka lending crunch and earthiness to the moong dal. A little groundnut paste thickens the dal while whole peanuts add texture, balanced by a mild tomato masala. It is a rustic, protein-rich dal that eats well with roti or rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil echoes the peanuts and gives an authentic Malwa nuttiness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of ghee balances the earthy groundnut oil.

steps: Coarsely grind half of the 0.33 cup roasted peanuts to a rough powder and keep the rest whole for texture.
Rinse 1 cup dhuli moong dal and pressure-cook it with 3.25 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft, then whisk lightly.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add 6 minced garlic cloves and fry until golden, about 1 minute.
Add 1 chopped onion and cook until soft, then stir in 1 chopped tomato, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp coriander powder and cook until pulpy, about 5 minutes.
Pour in the whisked dal with the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, the ground peanut powder and the whole peanuts, and simmer on low for 6 minutes until nutty and thick.
Finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and chopped coriander, and serve hot.
Serve with wheat roti or steamed rice, keeping some whole peanuts on top for crunch.
tips: Grinding half the peanuts thickens the dal while leaving the rest whole keeps a pleasant crunch.
Add the peanut powder only after the dal is simmering so it does not clump.
Toast raw peanuts in a dry pan until spotty brown if you do not have ready-roasted ones.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulka and a raw onion salad, or over rice topped with extra roasted peanuts and a squeeze of lime for a rustic Malwa meal.

variations.name: Kumaoni Dhuli Moong Punjabi
variations.description: The hill kitchens of Kumaon temper this dal with jakhya, tiny wild mustard-family seeds that pop like fireworks and add a nutty crunch found nowhere else. A simple ghee tadka with jakhya, garlic and dried chilli keeps the dal light and mountain-fresh, with no heavy masala to mask its clean flavour. It is the everyday pahadi dal eaten with rice or mandua roti.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee lets the jakhya seeds crackle and toast without turning bitter.

steps: Rinse 1 cup dhuli moong dal and pressure-cook it with 3.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft, then whisk lightly.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium heat until hot, then add 1 tsp jakhya seeds and 2 broken dried red chillies and let them crackle and pop for about 20 seconds.
Add 6 sliced garlic cloves and 1 inch grated ginger and fry until the garlic turns golden and nutty, about 1 minute.
Add 1 chopped small onion and cook 3 minutes until soft, then stir in 1 chopped small tomato and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and cook until pulpy, about 4 minutes.
Pour in the whisked dal with the remaining 0.5 tsp salt and 0.5 cup hot water, and simmer on low for 6 minutes.
Finish with chopped coriander and a little extra ghee, and serve hot.
Serve with steamed rice or mandua (finger millet) roti for an authentic Kumaoni plate.
tips: Wait until the ghee is properly hot before adding jakhya so the seeds pop and release their nutty aroma.
Jakhya needs no grinding; its charm is the tiny crackle it keeps in the finished dal.
Keep the masala minimal so the clean, hill-fresh flavour of the dal comes through.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot rice with a side of bhang ki chutney and a wedge of lime, or with mandua roti for a hearty mountain meal.

variations.name: Bihari Dhuli Moong Punjabi
variations.description: Bihar cooks this moong dal with a sharp mustard-oil tadka, plenty of garlic and whole dried chillies, giving it a pungent, rustic character that stands up to litti and rice alike. The dal is kept medium-thick and finished with a raw-garlic-and-mustard-oil chhaunk for an extra hit of aroma. It is bold, garlicky and deeply satisfying.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Pungent kachi-ghani mustard oil gives this Bihari dal its bold, rustic character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon of ghee at the end softens the sharpness of the mustard oil.

steps: Rinse 1 cup dhuli moong dal and pressure-cook it with 3.25 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft, then whisk lightly.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pan until it just smokes, then lower the heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds with 3 broken dried red chillies for 20 seconds.
Add 7 minced garlic cloves and fry until golden, then add 1 chopped onion and cook until soft and light brown, about 5 minutes.
Stir in 1 chopped tomato, 1 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt and cook until the tomato breaks down, about 4 minutes.
Pour in the whisked dal with 0.5 cup hot water and simmer on low for 6 minutes until medium-thick.
For the finishing chhaunk, heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil with the remaining 3 crushed garlic cloves until golden, then pour the sizzling oil over the dal.
Stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and chopped coriander, and serve hot with rice or litti.
tips: Always heat mustard oil to smoking first, then cool slightly, to tame its raw pungency.
The second raw-garlic chhaunk poured over the top is what gives this dal its signature Bihari aroma.
Keep it medium-thick so it clings to rice or can be scooped with litti.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with baked litti and a dollop of ghee, or over steamed rice with a raw onion, green chilli and a wedge of lime for a classic Bihari spread.

variations.name: Classic Festive Jeera Rice
variations.description: A dressed-up cumin rice for celebrations, studded with fried cashews, raisins and extra whole spices so it feels special beside a festive spread. The grains stay long and separate but glisten with ghee and carry a gentle sweetness from the plumped raisins.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A generous pour of bilona ghee fries the nuts and gives festive richness to every grain

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati rice until clear, soak for 20 minutes and drain so the grains stay whole and firm.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot over medium heat and fry 3 tbsp cashews and 2 tbsp raisins until the nuts are gold and the raisins plump, about 1 minute, then lift them out.
Into the same ghee add 1 bay leaf, 4 green cardamom pods, 4 cloves and a 1 inch cinnamon stick, then 1.5 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle for 20 seconds.
Add 1 sliced onion and cook until golden, about 6 minutes, then fold in the drained rice and toss gently for 2 minutes.
Pour in 2.25 cups hot water with 1.25 tsp salt, bring to a boil, then cover and steam on the lowest heat for 12 minutes.
Rest for 5 minutes, then fluff and fold in most of the fried cashews and raisins, scattering the rest on top for a festive finish.
tips: Fry the nuts and raisins first and set them aside so they stay crisp and do not turn soggy in the steam.
Reserve a spoon of the ghee-fried nuts to crown the platter just before serving for a glossy look.
Use aged basmati for the longest, most impressive grains on a celebration table.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a wide platter beside a paneer curry and dal, garnished with fried onions and a few extra cashews for a festive centrepiece.

variations.name: Hyderabadi Festive Jeera Rice
variations.description: A Nizami-style festive rice perfumed with saffron and cooked dum-style so the aroma is trapped within, borrowing the fragrance of Hyderabadi biryani without the meat. Saffron-stained grains, fried onions and a whisper of rose make it a showpiece for feasts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries the whole spices and helps the saffron milk seep evenly during the dum finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Saffron steeped in warm milk lends the rice its Nizami gold streaks and floral aroma

steps: Soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, drain, and steep 0.25 tsp Anveshan Saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk until it glows deep orange.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot over medium heat and add 4 green cardamom pods, 4 cloves and a 1 inch cinnamon stick, then 1.5 tsp cumin seeds, frying for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add the drained rice and toss gently for 2 minutes, then pour in 2.25 cups hot water and 1.25 tsp salt and bring to a boil over high heat.
Once the water is nearly absorbed and craters form, drizzle over the saffron milk and 0.5 tsp rose water and scatter 3 tbsp fried onions on top.
Cover with a tight lid, place the pot on a tawa over the lowest heat and dum-cook for 10 minutes so the perfume is sealed in.
Rest for 5 minutes, then fluff so the saffron streaks marble through and finish with the remaining fried onions.
tips: Dum-cooking over a tawa spreads the heat gently and stops the base from catching while the aroma builds.
Add the saffron milk and rose water only after the water has mostly cooked off so they perfume rather than dilute.
Reserve a spoon of saffron milk to drizzle at the table for extra colour and drama.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a mirchi ka salan or a bowl of dahi ki chutney, with a dish of sliced onions and lemon on the side as at a Hyderabadi feast.

variations.name: Gujarati Festive Jeera Rice
variations.description: A subtly sweet Gujarati festive rice where a touch of jaggery balances the warm spices, echoing the sweet-savoury love of a Gujarati thali. Cumin and cloves keep it grounded while the jaggery rounds off the edges for a gently comforting side.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee is central to Gujarati festive cooking and mellows the jaggery into the rice

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A spoon of jaggery powder brings the signature Gujarati sweet-savoury balance

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain and set aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot over medium heat and add 1 bay leaf, 3 cloves and a 1 inch cinnamon stick, then 1.5 tsp cumin seeds, frying for 20 seconds until aromatic.
Add 1 sliced onion and 1 slit green chilli and cook until the onion is soft and golden, about 6 minutes.
Stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and let it melt into the ghee for 30 seconds until it smells caramel-like but does not darken.
Fold in the drained rice for 2 minutes, then add 2.25 cups hot water and 1.25 tsp salt and bring to a boil over high heat.
Cover and steam on the lowest heat for 12 minutes, rest for 5 minutes, then fluff and garnish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Let the jaggery just melt without browning; over-caramelised jaggery turns the rice bitter rather than sweet.
Keep the sweetness gentle at one tablespoon so the rice is balanced, not dessert-like.
The slit green chilli is important to counter the jaggery, so keep it in even if you like mild food.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as part of a Gujarati thali beside kadhi and a dry shaak, with a spoon of chundo pickle to complete the sweet-savoury balance.

variations.name: Malwa Festive Jeera Rice
variations.description: A rustic Madhya Pradesh festive rice enriched with roasted peanuts that add crunch and a nutty warmth beloved across the Malwa plateau. The peanuts are fried in ghee until blistered, then folded through the cumin rice for texture in every mouthful.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee is used to blister the peanuts and enrich the rice in true Malwa style

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain and keep aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot over medium heat and fry 0.33 cup raw peanuts until blistered and crunchy, about 3 minutes, then lift out half for garnish.
To the remaining peanuts and ghee add 1 bay leaf, 3 cloves and 2 dried red chillies, then 1.5 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle for 15 seconds.
Add 1 sliced onion with 0.25 tsp turmeric and cook until golden, about 6 minutes.
Fold in the drained rice for 2 minutes, then pour in 2.25 cups hot water and 1.25 tsp salt and bring to a boil over high heat.
Cover and steam on the lowest heat for 12 minutes, rest for 5 minutes, then fluff, fold through half the reserved peanuts and scatter the rest with 2 tbsp coriander on top.
tips: Fry the peanuts on medium heat so they crisp evenly; too high and the outsides burn before the centres cook.
Adding half the peanuts at garnish keeps some crunch intact while the rest soften into the rice.
Skinless peanuts look neater, but keeping the skins on adds extra rustic colour and flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of plain yoghurt or a Malwa-style dal bafla accompaniment, with lemon wedges to brighten the nutty rice.

variations.name: Delhi-style Festive Jeera Rice
variations.description: The Old Delhi banquet version, where a final dusting of freshly ground garam masala and a scatter of fried onions lift plain jeera rice to wedding-hall standard. Warm, deeply spiced and glossy, it is built to sit beside rich Mughlai gravies.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee gives the banquet-style richness and blooms the finishing garam masala

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain thoroughly.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot over medium heat and add 1 bay leaf, 1 black cardamom, 3 green cardamom pods and 4 cloves, then 1.5 tsp cumin seeds, frying for 20 seconds.
Add 1 sliced onion and cook until deep golden, about 7 minutes, so it lends a banquet-style sweetness.
Fold in the drained rice for 2 minutes, then add 2.25 cups hot water and 1.25 tsp salt and bring to a boil over high heat.
Cover and steam on the lowest heat for 12 minutes, then rest for 5 minutes off the heat.
Sprinkle 0.75 tsp garam masala over the hot rice, fluff so it blooms through the grains, and finish with 3 tbsp crisp fried onions.
tips: Add the garam masala at the very end so its volatile aroma perfumes the rice rather than cooking away.
One black cardamom is enough to give the smoky Old Delhi note; more will overpower the dish.
Homemade or freshly ground garam masala makes a noticeable difference in a dish this simple.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a shahi paneer or dal makhani, topped with extra fried onions and a lemon wedge for a proper banquet plate.

variations.name: Classic Festive Peas Pulao
variations.description: A celebration-worthy matar pulao dressed up with ghee-fried cashews, paneer cubes and extra whole spices so it can hold its own on a feast table. Sweet peas, golden nuts and soft paneer give every forkful something special.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A generous pour of bilona ghee fries the nuts and paneer and gives festive richness

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati rice until clear, soak for 20 minutes and drain so the grains stay firm.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot over medium heat and fry 150 g cubed paneer and 3 tbsp cashews until both are golden, about 3 minutes, then lift them out.
Into the same ghee add 4 green cardamom pods, 4 cloves and a 1 inch cinnamon stick, then 1.5 tsp cumin seeds, frying for 20 seconds.
Add 1 sliced onion and cook until golden, about 6 minutes, then stir in 1 cup green peas for 2 minutes.
Fold in the drained rice for 2 minutes, then pour in 2.25 cups hot water with 1.25 tsp salt and bring to a boil.
Cover and steam on the lowest heat for 13 minutes, rest for 5 minutes, then fold through the fried paneer and cashews, saving a few to scatter on top.
tips: Fry the paneer and nuts first and set them aside so they stay golden and do not break up in the steam.
Soak the fried paneer cubes in warm salted water for a minute if you like them extra soft.
Reserve a spoon of nuts and paneer to crown the platter for a festive finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a wide platter beside a rich paneer curry and dal, garnished with fried onions and a few extra cashews as a centrepiece.

variations.name: Hyderabadi Festive Peas Pulao
variations.description: A Nizami-style festive matar pulao perfumed with saffron and cooked dum so the aroma stays sealed within, borrowing the fragrance of a Hyderabadi biryani. Saffron-gold grains, sweet peas and fried onions make it a showpiece for feasts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries the whole spices and helps the saffron milk seep in during the dum finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Saffron steeped in warm milk lends the pulao its Nizami gold streaks and floral aroma

steps: Soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, drain, and steep 0.25 tsp Anveshan Saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk until it glows deep orange.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot over medium heat and add 4 green cardamom pods, 4 cloves and 1.5 tsp cumin seeds, frying for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Stir in 1 cup green peas for 2 minutes, then fold in the drained rice for 2 minutes.
Pour in 2.25 cups hot water with 1.25 tsp salt and bring to a boil; when the water is nearly absorbed and craters form, drizzle over the saffron milk and scatter 3 tbsp fried onions and 2 tbsp mint.
Cover with a tight lid, set the pot on a tawa over the lowest heat and dum-cook for 10 minutes so the perfume is sealed in.
Rest for 5 minutes, then fluff so the saffron marbles through and finish with the remaining fried onions.
tips: Dum-cooking over a tawa spreads the heat gently and stops the base from catching as the aroma builds.
Add the saffron milk only after the water has mostly cooked off so it perfumes rather than dilutes.
Reserve a spoon of saffron milk to drizzle at the table for extra colour and drama.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with mirchi ka salan or a bowl of dahi ki chutney, with sliced onions and lemon on the side as at a Hyderabadi feast.

variations.name: Awadhi Festive Peas Pulao
variations.description: A regal Lucknowi matar pulao scented with kewra and a delicate blend of mace and cardamom, cooked gently so the perfume clings to each grain. Restrained yet luxurious, it borrows the aromatic subtlety of Awadhi pulaos rather than shouting with chilli.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rich bilona ghee is essential to the Awadhi style, carrying the mace and kewra perfume

steps: Soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes and drain gently to keep the long grains intact.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot over medium heat and add 1 bay leaf, 1 blade of mace, 4 green cardamom pods and 3 cloves, frying for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1.5 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle, then add 1 thinly sliced onion and cook slowly to a soft pale gold, about 6 minutes.
Stir in 1 cup green peas for 2 minutes, then fold in the drained rice for 2 minutes.
Pour in 2.25 cups hot water with 1.25 tsp salt, bring to a boil, then cover and steam on the lowest heat for 13 minutes.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp kewra water over the hot pulao, rest for 5 minutes, then fluff and top with 3 tbsp crisp fried onions.
tips: Kewra is potent; measure it by the half teaspoon and add at the end so the aroma is not cooked away.
Cook the onions low and slow to a soft gold rather than dark brown to keep the pulao delicate and pale.
Layer fried onions and a few drops of extra kewra between servings for a dum-style finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as an elegant side to a korma or shahi paneer, garnished with fried onions and pomegranate seeds for a courtly touch.

variations.name: Gujarati Festive Peas Pulao
variations.description: A subtly sweet Gujarati festive pulao where a touch of jaggery balances the warm spices and the natural sweetness of the peas, echoing the sweet-savoury love of a Gujarati thali. Gentle and comforting, it rounds off a celebratory meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee is central to Gujarati festive cooking and mellows the jaggery into the pulao

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A spoon of jaggery powder brings the signature Gujarati sweet-savoury balance

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain and set aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot over medium heat and add 1 bay leaf, 3 cloves and a 1 inch cinnamon stick, then 1.5 tsp cumin seeds, frying for 20 seconds.
Add 1 sliced onion and 1 slit green chilli and cook until soft and golden, about 6 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and let it melt for 30 seconds until caramel-like.
Add 1 cup green peas for 2 minutes, then fold in the drained rice for 2 minutes.
Pour in 2.25 cups hot water with 1.25 tsp salt, bring to a boil, then cover and steam on the lowest heat for 13 minutes.
Rest for 5 minutes and fluff gently so the peas stay whole and the sweetness spreads evenly.
tips: Let the jaggery just melt without browning, as over-caramelised jaggery turns the pulao bitter.
Keep the sweetness gentle at one tablespoon so the dish stays balanced, not dessert-like.
The slit green chilli is important to counter the jaggery, so keep it in even if you like mild food.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as part of a Gujarati thali beside kadhi and a dry shaak, with a spoon of chundo pickle to complete the balance.

variations.name: Malwa Festive Peas Pulao
variations.description: A rustic Madhya Pradesh festive pulao enriched with ghee-blistered peanuts that add crunch and a nutty warmth beloved across the Malwa plateau. The peanuts play against the soft peas, giving texture in every mouthful.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee is used to blister the peanuts and enrich the pulao in true Malwa style

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain and keep aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot over medium heat and fry 0.33 cup raw peanuts until blistered, about 3 minutes, then lift out half for garnish.
To the remaining peanuts and ghee add 1 bay leaf, 3 cloves and 2 dried red chillies, then 1.5 tsp cumin seeds, and let them crackle for 15 seconds.
Add 1 sliced onion with 0.25 tsp turmeric and cook until golden, about 6 minutes, then stir in 1 cup green peas for 2 minutes.
Fold in the drained rice for 2 minutes, then pour in 2.25 cups hot water with 1.25 tsp salt and bring to a boil.
Cover and steam on the lowest heat for 13 minutes, rest for 5 minutes, then fluff, fold in half the reserved peanuts and scatter the rest on top.
tips: Fry the peanuts on medium heat so they crisp evenly without the outsides burning.
Adding half the peanuts at garnish keeps some crunch while the rest soften into the pulao.
Keeping the peanut skins on adds extra rustic colour and a deeper nutty flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain yoghurt or a Malwa-style dal, with lemon wedges to brighten the nutty, peppery pulao.

variations.name: Classic Festive Veg Pulao
variations.description: A celebration-worthy pulao layered with saffron, fried onions, cashews and paneer, richer and more aromatic than an everyday version yet still elegantly balanced. The rice is cooked with a whole-spice ghee base and finished with saffron milk and a dum rest for that special-occasion aroma. This is the pulao that anchors a festive vegetarian spread.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A generous ghee base makes this pulao taste rich and celebratory.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: Saffron steeped in milk gives the festive pulao its golden streaks and aroma.

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain; warm 3 tbsp milk and steep 0.25 tsp Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in it.
Heat 3.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot on medium heat and fry 3 tbsp cashews and 0.75 cup cubed paneer until golden, then remove and reserve.
In the same ghee crackle 1 bay leaf, 4 cardamoms, 4 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon for 20 seconds, add 1 sliced large onion and fry until golden, about 6 minutes, then remove half for garnish.
Add 1 tbsp ginger garlic paste to the pot and cook for 1 minute, then add 1.25 cups mixed vegetables and 1.25 tsp salt and saute for 3 minutes.
Add the drained rice and toss gently for 2 minutes, then pour in 2.5 cups hot water and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes, then drizzle the saffron milk over the top, scatter the fried paneer and cashews, cover again and rest on dum for 6 minutes.
Fluff gently, garnish with the reserved fried onions and chopped mint, and serve hot.
tips: Fry the paneer and nuts first so they stay golden and do not soften in the steam.
Layering the saffron milk on top rather than mixing it gives the pretty streaked look.
A short dum rest lets all the festive aromas settle evenly into the rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a large platter topped with fried onions, paneer and a few saffron strands, with a rich vegetable korma and a boondi raita alongside.

variations.name: Kashmiri Festive Veg Pulao
variations.description: The grand Kashmiri modur pulao is a sweet festive rice, tinted gold with saffron and warmed with cinnamon, fennel and a touch of sugar, then loaded with fried nuts and dry fruit. It is gently sweet rather than savoury, meant for celebrations and served alongside spicy dishes. Fennel and dry ginger give it that distinctive valley aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee fries the nuts and carries the sweet spices of this festive modur pulao.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: Saffron is the heart of modur pulao, colouring and perfuming every grain.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery gives the traditional gentle sweetness without refined sugar.

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain; warm 3 tbsp milk and steep 0.3 tsp Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron to make a golden liquid.
Heat 3.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot on medium heat and fry 3 tbsp cashews, 3 tbsp slivered almonds and 2 tbsp raisins until golden, then scoop out and reserve.
In the same ghee crackle 4 cardamoms, 1 inch cinnamon and 3 cloves for 20 seconds, then stir in 0.5 tsp fennel powder and 0.5 tsp dry ginger powder for 15 seconds.
Add the drained rice and toss gently for 2 minutes, then pour in 2.5 cups hot water, the saffron milk, 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.75 tsp salt and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes until the water is absorbed and the rice is tender and golden.
Rest covered for 6 minutes so the sweetness sets, then fluff very gently to keep the grains whole.
Fold in most of the fried nuts and raisins, scatter the rest on top, and serve warm.
tips: Keep the salt low here; modur pulao is meant to be sweet, not savoury.
Fluff extra gently as the sweet, ghee-rich grains are more fragile than in a savoury pulao.
Serve it alongside a spicy dish so the sweet-savoury contrast shines, as is traditional in Kashmir.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as part of a festive spread beside a spicy rajma or dum aloo, letting the sweet saffron rice balance the heat of the mains.

variations.name: Awadhi Festive Veg Pulao
variations.description: A refined Lucknowi celebration rice, the subz pulao is cooked in a fragrant spiced stock and finished with kewra, rose and a slow dum so the pale grains carry deep perfume without heavy spice. Fried onions, a bouquet of whole spices and a hint of saffron keep it elegant. It is the graceful centrepiece of an Awadhi dawat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee gives the Awadhi pulao its silky, luxurious mouthfeel.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: A little saffron adds subtle colour and depth to this refined festive rice.

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain; steep 0.2 tsp Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk.
Tie 2 bay leaves, 1 black cardamom, 4 green cardamoms, 5 cloves and 1 mace blade in muslin, simmer in 2.5 cups water with 1.25 tsp salt for 5 minutes to make a stock, then discard the pouch.
Heat 3.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot on medium heat, fry 1 thinly sliced large onion until golden and crisp, then remove half for garnish.
Add 1 tsp shahi jeera to the ghee, let it crackle for 15 seconds, then add 1.25 cups mixed vegetables and saute for 3 minutes.
Add the drained rice and toss gently for 2 minutes, then pour in the hot spiced stock and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes, then drizzle the saffron milk, 1 tsp kewra water and 0.5 tsp rose water over the top, cover and rest on dum for 7 minutes.
Fluff gently, top with the reserved fried onions, and serve hot.
tips: Add kewra and rose water only at the dum stage so their delicate aromas are not boiled away.
The muslin spice pouch perfumes the stock while keeping the finished rice clean and pale.
Use rose and kewra sparingly; they are meant to whisper, not overpower.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve garnished with crisp fried onions and rose petals, paired with a subz shahi korma and a burani raita for an elegant Awadhi feast.

variations.name: Bengali Festive Veg Pulao
variations.description: The Bengali basanti pulao is a golden, gently sweet festive rice tinted with turmeric, scented with ghee and whole garam spices, and jewelled with cashews and raisins. Unlike savoury pulaos it leans sweet, with jaggery balancing the warm spice, and is served at weddings and pujas. Its short, fragrant grains and glossy sheen make it unmistakable.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee is essential to basanti pulao, giving its glossy sheen and rich aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery lends the traditional gentle sweetness that defines this Bengali pulao.

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati rice, soak for 20 minutes, drain, then spread on a cloth for 10 minutes to dry and toss with 0.75 tsp turmeric and 1 tbsp of the ghee until each grain is coated yellow.
Heat the remaining 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot on medium heat and fry 3 tbsp cashews and 3 tbsp raisins until golden, then scoop out and reserve.
In the same ghee crackle 2 bay leaves, 4 cardamoms, 4 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon for 20 seconds, then add 1 inch grated ginger and fry for 30 seconds.
Add the turmeric-coated rice and toss very gently for 3 minutes until the grains smell toasty and turn glossy.
Pour in 2.5 cups hot water, add 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.75 tsp salt, and bring to a gentle boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes until the water is absorbed and the rice is golden and fluffy.
Rest for 6 minutes, fold in most of the fried nuts and raisins, scatter the rest on top, and serve warm.
tips: Coating the drained rice in turmeric and ghee before cooking gives the signature even golden colour.
Keep the salt modest and let the jaggery lead, as basanti pulao is meant to be sweet.
Handle the cooked grains gently; the short, ghee-rich grains break easily if stirred hard.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm alongside a Bengali cholar dal or aloor dum, the sweet golden rice playing off the savoury sides in classic puja-feast fashion.

variations.name: Malwa Festive Veg Pulao
variations.description: From central India comes a hearty festive pulao enriched with roasted peanuts, a groundnut-oil and ghee base and warm whole spices, giving a nutty depth rarely found in northern pulaos. Crunchy peanuts and fried onions run through soft, spiced grains for a rustic celebration rice. It is filling, earthy and made for large family gatherings.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil deepens the nutty character of the peanuts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee rounds out the earthy groundnut oil and enriches the festive rice.

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain well.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a heavy pot on medium heat and fry 0.33 cup roasted peanuts for 1 minute until glossy, then scoop out and reserve.
Add 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee to the pot and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 bay leaf, 4 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon for 20 seconds, then add 1 sliced large onion and fry until golden, about 6 minutes.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger garlic paste, then lower the heat and add 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt for 20 seconds.
Add 1.5 cups mixed vegetables and saute for 3 minutes, then add the drained rice and toss gently for 2 minutes.
Pour in 2.5 cups hot water, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes until absorbed.
Rest for 5 minutes, fold in most of the fried peanuts, scatter the rest with chopped coriander on top, and serve hot.
tips: Frying the peanuts first in groundnut oil keeps them crunchy against the soft grains.
Reserve a handful of peanuts for the top so the garnish stays crisp.
A squeeze of lime just before serving lifts the earthy, nutty flavours.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a garlicky yogurt raita and a spicy sev-tomato curry, keeping extra roasted peanuts and lime wedges on the table for a rustic Malwa feast.

variations.name: Classic Handi Methi Matar Malai
variations.description: Slow-simmered in a sealed clay handi so the whole spices perfume every spoonful, this is the most fragrant version of the creamy peas-and-fenugreek curry. The dum method keeps the malai silky and lets the methi mellow into a rounded, dinner-party-worthy gravy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: essential for a handi; it carries the whole-spice aroma deep into the gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: balances the methi bitterness in the slow-cooked gravy

steps: Boil 2 chopped onions with 14 cashews in 1 cup water for 8 minutes, cool and blend to a smooth ivory paste.
Rub 0.5 tsp salt into the 2 cups methi, rest 10 minutes and squeeze out the bitter juices.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a handi over medium heat and gently crackle 3 cardamom, 1 inch cinnamon and 4 cloves for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and saute 1 minute, then pour in the onion-cashew paste and cook on low for 7 minutes until it thickens and smells sweet.
Stir in the squeezed methi, 1 cup peas and 0.5 tsp salt with 0.5 cup water, cover and simmer 8 minutes until the peas are tender.
Add 0.5 cup milk, 0.5 cup cream and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, stirring slowly so the gravy stays smooth, about 3 minutes.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala, seal the handi lid with a little dough and cook on the lowest flame for 6 minutes of dum, then open at the table and serve.
tips: Sealing the handi with dough traps the whole-spice aroma; if you have no handi, a heavy pot with a tight lid works.
Fish out the whole spices before serving if you prefer not to bite into them.
Rest the sealed handi off the heat for five minutes before opening so the flavours settle.
variations.servingSuggestion: Bring the sealed handi to the table and open it for guests; serve with sheermal or warm naan to soak up the perfumed gravy.

variations.name: Awadhi Handi Methi Matar Malai
variations.description: Lucknow's royal kitchens perfume the handi with kewra water and a delicate white korma base, keeping the gravy pale, floral and refined. Cooked on slow dum, it is the most aristocratic reading of methi matar malai, meant for a nawabi spread.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the fragrant fat at the heart of every Awadhi dum dish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a barely-there sweetness that keeps the korma gentle and refined

steps: Soak 12 cashews and 2 tbsp melon seeds in warm water 15 minutes, then grind to a pure white paste for the korma base.
Fry 2 sliced onions in a little ghee until pale golden, then blend to a smooth paste, taking care not to brown them so the gravy stays white.
Rub 0.5 tsp salt into the 2 cups methi, rest 10 minutes and squeeze out the bitter juices.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a handi over low heat, crackle 3 cardamom and 1 blade of mace for 20 seconds, then add 1 tbsp ginger paste and the boiled onion paste and cook 5 minutes without colouring.
Lower the heat and whisk in 0.5 cup curd a spoon at a time, then add the cashew-melon paste and cook gently 4 minutes until the raw smell lifts.
Add the squeezed methi, 1 cup peas, 0.5 tsp salt and 0.5 cup water, cover and simmer 8 minutes until the peas turn tender.
Stir in 0.4 cup cream, 0.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp kewra water, seal the handi and give it 6 minutes of dum before serving.
tips: Keep every stage pale; brown onions or dark spices will ruin the ivory Awadhi look.
Add kewra water only at the end and sparingly, as it turns soapy if overdone.
Beat the curd smooth and add off the boil to prevent the korma from splitting.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with warm sheermal, ulte tawe ka paratha or saffron pulao for a full Lucknawi dawat.

variations.name: Kashmiri Handi Methi Matar Malai
variations.description: The valley tints its handi a warm gold with hand-picked saffron and rounds it with fennel and dry ginger in the Kashmiri manner. Curd replaces some of the cream for a light tang, giving a fragrant, saffron-scented curry unlike any plains version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the base fat for Kashmiri wazwan-style slow cooking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Kashmiri Mongra strands steeped in warm milk give the handi its golden hue

steps: Steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside so it blooms into a deep golden liquid.
Soak 10 cashews 15 minutes and grind to a smooth paste to thicken the gravy without heavy cream.
Rub 0.5 tsp salt into the 2 cups methi, rest 10 minutes and squeeze out the bitter juices.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a handi over low heat, crackle 3 cardamom and 3 cloves for 20 seconds, then whisk in 0.75 cup curd off the boil so it does not split.
Stir in 1 tsp fennel powder, 0.5 tsp dry ginger powder and the cashew paste, cook gently 4 minutes until the raw smell lifts and the ghee glistens.
Add the squeezed methi, 1 cup peas, 0.5 tsp salt and 0.5 cup water, cover and simmer 8 minutes until the peas are soft.
Pour in the saffron milk and 0.3 cup cream, seal the handi and dum for 6 minutes until fragrant and golden, then serve.
tips: Fennel and dry ginger are the Kashmiri signature; do not swap them for garam masala or you lose the valley flavour.
Bloom the saffron in warm, not hot, milk to draw out colour without bitterness.
Keep the flame low throughout so the curd-based gravy stays smooth and never boils hard.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with Kashmiri saffron pulao or plain basmati rice and a side of walnut chutney.

variations.name: Kerala Handi Methi Matar Malai
variations.description: A Malayali handi where coconut milk carries the peas and fenugreek and everything is slow-cooked in fragrant coconut oil. Whole spices and curry leaves give a gentle, tropical warmth, and a final drizzle of raw coconut oil seals in the aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
