ingredients.note: cold-pressed and aromatic, it is what makes a handi taste of Kerala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a spoon of jaggery to round the coconut in the Malabar style

steps: Rub 0.5 tsp salt into the 2 cups methi, rest 10 minutes and squeeze out the bitter juices before cooking.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a handi over medium heat, crackle 0.5 tsp fennel seeds, 1 inch cinnamon and 3 cloves with 14 curry leaves for 20 seconds.
Add 2 sliced onions, 3 slit green chillies and 1 inch julienned ginger, saute 5 minutes until the onions soften and turn pale gold.
Stir in 0.25 tsp turmeric and cook 1 minute, then add the squeezed methi and 1 cup peas with 0.5 cup water and 0.5 tsp salt.
Cover and simmer on low for 8 minutes until the peas are tender and most of the water has gone.
Lower the flame, pour in 1 cup thick coconut milk and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and warm through for 3 minutes without letting it boil.
Seal the handi and rest off the heat for 4 minutes, then finish with a drizzle of raw coconut oil and serve.
tips: Coconut milk must never boil hard or it splits; keep the handi on the gentlest flame.
The raw coconut oil finish is traditional and doubles the aroma, so do not skip it.
Use fresh peas if you can; they hold up better against the mild coconut gravy than frozen.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with appam, idiyappam or ghee rice, and a crisp banana chip on the side.

variations.name: Bengali Handi Methi Matar Malai
variations.description: Bengal cooks its handi in smoked mustard oil with a whole-spice tempering and a poppy-seed thickening, keeping the gravy pale, nutty and faintly sweet. The pungency of the oil against the sweet peas gives a distinctly eastern-Indian character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked to soften its bite, it defines the Bengali handi's aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the customary Bengali sweetness balancing the sharp mustard oil

steps: Soak 2 tbsp poppy seeds 15 minutes and grind with 2 green chillies to a smooth pale paste that thickens the gravy the Bengali way.
Rub 0.5 tsp salt into the 2 cups methi, rest 10 minutes and squeeze out the bitter juices.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a handi until it just smokes, cool 30 seconds, then temper 1 bay leaf and 2 dried red chillies for 15 seconds.
Add 2 sliced onions and fry 6 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger paste and 0.25 tsp turmeric for a minute.
Add the poppy-seed paste and cook on low for 5 minutes until the raw smell lifts and the oil beads at the edges.
Fold in the squeezed methi, 1 cup peas, 1 slit green chilli, 0.5 tsp salt and 0.5 cup water, cover and simmer 8 minutes.
Stir in 0.4 cup cream, 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp Bengali garam masala, seal the handi and dum 5 minutes, then serve.
tips: Smoke the mustard oil fully before tempering, or its raw sharpness will dominate.
Grind the poppy seeds with a splash of milk for a whiter, silkier gravy.
Bengali garam masala is sweeter and lighter; add it at the end so it stays fragrant.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed Gobindobhog rice or luchi, and a wedge of gondhoraj lime to lift the dish.

variations.name: Classic Handi Veg Korma
variations.description: Handi korma is slow-cooked in a heavy clay or steel pot sealed with dough, so the vegetables steam gently in a whole-spice cashew gravy and turn meltingly soft. The dum method keeps every aroma trapped inside until you break the seal at the table. It is unhurried, fragrant, festive cooking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the dum method relies on ghee to carry the whole-spice aromas through slow cooking

steps: Dice the mixed vegetables and blend the tomatoes with 14 cashews to a smooth puree; keep 0.5 cup whisked yogurt ready.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a handi on medium, add 1 black and 3 green cardamom, 4 cloves, 1 inch cinnamon and 2 bay leaves, and let them crackle for 20 seconds.
Add the finely chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and saute 6 minutes until golden, then pour in the tomato-cashew puree and cook 6 minutes until thick and glossy.
Lower the flame, stir in the whisked yogurt gradually so it does not split, then add the diced vegetables, 1.25 tsp salt and 0.5 cup water and mix gently.
Cover the handi, seal the rim with a strip of stiff dough or a tight lid, and cook on the lowest heat over a tawa for 18 to 20 minutes so the vegetables steam in their own aroma.
Break the seal at the table, fold in 0.5 tsp garam masala, and serve straight from the handi.
tips: Cook the dum over a tawa or heat diffuser so the base does not scorch during the long slow steam.
Cut the vegetables a little larger than usual since they cook fully in the sealed handi.
If you lack a handi, any heavy pot with a well-fitting lid weighed down will hold the steam.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve straight from the handi with sheermal or rumali roti, scattered with a few fried cashews.

variations.name: Awadhi Handi Veg Korma
variations.description: The Awadhi dum-pukht korma is the aristocrat of the family, a pale, delicate gravy of fried-onion paste, yogurt and nuts perfumed with kewra and rose. Nothing is browned harshly; everything is coaxed slowly under a sealed lid. It is Lucknawi refinement on a plate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the soul of dum-pukht cooking, giving the pale gravy its richness

steps: Dice and steam the mixed vegetables for 7 minutes until just tender, and soak 12 cashews and 1 tbsp melon seeds in warm water for 15 minutes, then grind to a smooth paste.
Thinly slice the onions and fry them in 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium for 8 minutes to a pale golden birista, then drain and grind to a paste with a little water.
In the same ghee add 4 cardamom pods and 1 blade of mace, let them sizzle for 20 seconds, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry gently without colouring.
Add the fried-onion paste and the nut paste, cook on very low for 5 minutes, then whisk the 0.75 cup yogurt smooth and stir it in off the heat so the gravy stays pale.
Return to a low flame, add the steamed vegetables, 1.25 tsp salt, 0.5 tsp white pepper and 0.5 cup water, cover, seal the handi, and dum for 15 minutes.
Uncover, drizzle in 0.5 tsp kewra water, fold through gently, and serve the fragrant pale korma at once.
tips: Keep everything pale; do not let the onions or spices brown, as Awadhi korma prizes a light golden colour.
White pepper instead of red chilli keeps the gravy elegant and the colour clean.
Add kewra at the very end and sparingly, as it is potent and easily overpowers the dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sheermal, warqi paratha or a delicate zafrani pulao for a Lucknawi feast.

variations.name: Hyderabadi Handi Veg Korma
variations.description: A Nizami handi korma rich with fried-onion birista, saffron and a sesame-peanut paste that gives the gravy a nutty, tangy depth. It is dum-cooked so the flavours meld under the seal. Fragrant and jewelled, it belongs beside a bagara khana or biryani.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: carries the saffron and birista aromas of Nizami dum cooking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk for the perfume and colour of a shahi korma

steps: Dice and steam the mixed vegetables for 7 minutes until just tender, soak the pinch of Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk, and dry-roast 2 tbsp peanuts and 1.5 tbsp sesame seeds, then grind to a paste.
Thinly slice the onions and fry in 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium for 8 minutes to golden birista, reserving half for garnish and grinding the rest to a paste.
In the same ghee add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, fry 1 minute, then add the fried-onion paste and the peanut-sesame paste and cook on low for 4 minutes.
Stir in 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp tamarind pulp, then whisk the 0.5 cup yogurt smooth and add it off the heat, stirring so it does not split.
Return to a low flame, add the steamed vegetables, 1.25 tsp salt and 0.75 cup water, cover, seal the handi, and dum for 15 minutes.
Uncover, fold in the saffron milk and 0.5 tsp garam masala, and serve topped with the reserved birista and 2 tbsp coriander.
tips: The sesame-peanut paste is what gives Hyderabadi korma its signature nutty, slightly tangy body.
Fry the onions evenly to deep gold, not brown, so the gravy does not taste bitter.
A little tamarind is essential to balance the richness the Hyderabadi way.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bagara khana, ghee rice or rumali roti, garnished with fried onions and mint.

variations.name: Kerala Handi Veg Korma
variations.description: A coconut-milk handi korma from Kerala, where the vegetables simmer slowly in a fragrant ground-coconut and fennel gravy finished with thick first-press coconut milk. Curry leaves and a coconut-oil temper crown it. It is mild, creamy and sweetly aromatic, made for appam.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the defining fat of Kerala cooking, deepening the coconut gravy

steps: Dice the mixed vegetables and grind 0.5 cup grated coconut with 1 tsp fennel seeds, the ginger and 3 green chillies to a smooth paste.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a handi on medium, add 12 curry leaves and the sliced onion, and saute 6 minutes until soft and pale.
Add 0.5 tsp turmeric and the ground coconut paste and cook on low for 4 minutes until fragrant and the raw smell lifts.
Add the diced vegetables with 1.25 tsp salt and 0.75 cup water, cover, seal the handi, and dum on the lowest heat for 15 minutes until the vegetables are tender.
Uncover, pour in 1 cup thick coconut milk and 0.5 tsp garam masala, and warm gently for 3 minutes without letting it boil so the milk does not curdle.
Take off the heat while the gravy is creamy and glossy and serve at once.
tips: Never boil the dish after adding thick coconut milk, or it will split and turn oily.
Grinding fresh coconut into the base as well as adding milk gives a double coconut depth.
Add the green chillies to the paste for aroma and gentle heat rather than sharp spice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with lacy appam, idiyappam or ghee rice, with a wedge of lime alongside.

variations.name: Gujarati Handi Veg Korma
variations.description: This Gujarati handi is gently sweet and tangy, the vegetables dum-cooked in a light yogurt-tomato gravy sweetened with jaggery and brightened by a ginger-chilli paste. It is milder and homelier than the northern versions. A festive shaak that partners puri and pulao.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a modest amount of ghee enriches the light dum gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the signature sweetness balancing the tangy yogurt-tomato gravy

steps: Dice the mixed vegetables, puree the tomatoes, and grind 10 cashews to a smooth paste with a little water.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a handi on medium, crackle 1 tsp cumin and 3 cloves, then add 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and fry 30 seconds.
Add the tomato puree with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 2 tsp coriander-cumin powder, and cook 5 minutes until thick, then stir in the cashew paste and cook 2 minutes.
Whisk the 0.5 cup yogurt smooth, lower the flame, and stir it in gradually so it stays creamy.
Add the diced vegetables with 1.25 tsp salt and 0.75 cup water, cover, seal the handi, and dum on the lowest heat for 15 minutes.
Uncover, stir in 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer 2 minutes until it melts into a sweet-sour glaze, scatter 2 tbsp coriander, and serve.
tips: Taste at the end and balance jaggery against the tomato's tang with a squeeze of lemon if needed.
Keep the spice gentle, as this korma is meant to be mild, sweet and fragrant.
Sealing the handi lets the vegetables soak up the sweet-sour gravy without extra stirring.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with puri, soft rotli or peas pulao and a bowl of chaas on the side.

variations.name: Classic Kadai Methi Matar Malai
variations.description: A rustic kadai spin on the creamy classic, built on a coarsely pounded coriander-and-chilli kadai masala and finished with charred capsicum and onion. The peas and fenugreek stay bright against a semi-dry, spice-forward gravy rather than the usual velvety malai.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: gives the kadai masala a rich toasted base you cannot get from plain oil

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a small spoon tames the tomato acidity in the kadai gravy

steps: Dry-roast 2 tbsp coriander seeds with 4 dried red chillies over low heat for 2 minutes until fragrant, cool and pound coarsely to make the kadai masala.
Rub 0.5 tsp salt into the 2 cups methi, rest 10 minutes and squeeze out the bitter liquid before cooking.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over medium-high heat, add 1 diced onion and 1 diced capsicum and sear for 3 minutes until edges char, then remove and set aside.
In the same ghee add 1 chopped onion and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, saute 4 minutes, then add 3 chopped tomatoes and 0.25 tsp turmeric and cook 6 minutes to a pulpy masala.
Stir in the pounded kadai masala and cook for 2 minutes until the oil separates and the kitchen smells deeply of roasted coriander.
Add the squeezed methi, 1 cup peas, 0.5 tsp salt and 0.5 cup water, cover and simmer 8 minutes until the peas are tender.
Fold the charred capsicum and onion back in with 0.4 cup cream, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi, simmer 3 minutes and serve.
tips: Pound the kadai masala coarse, not fine; the gritty texture clinging to the peas is the whole point of a kadai dish.
Keep the capsicum slightly crunchy by adding it back only at the end.
For a drier kadai finish, skip half the cream and let it reduce two minutes longer.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve sizzling in a cast-iron kadai with tandoori roti or missi roti and a raw onion-lemon salad.

variations.name: Rajasthani Kadai Methi Matar Malai
variations.description: The desert kitchen turns up the heat with whole dried Mathania red chillies for a smoky crimson gravy, and cooks it in wood-pressed groundnut oil the way water-scarce Rajasthan always did. Cream tempers the fire while the fenugreek stays boldly aromatic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the hardy wood-pressed oil of Marwar kitchens, sturdy against high heat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: eases the searing chilli heat the way Rajasthani cooks balance their laal maas

steps: Soak 6 dried red chillies in warm water for 15 minutes, then grind to a smooth crimson paste that gives this version its fiery colour.
Rub 0.5 tsp salt into the 2 cups methi, rest 10 minutes and squeeze out the dark bitter juices.
Whisk 0.5 cup curd smooth and keep ready so it does not curdle when it hits the hot gravy later.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, add 2 chopped onions and fry 6 minutes until deep brown.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, the red chilli paste and 1 tbsp coriander powder, saute 2 minutes, then add 2 chopped tomatoes and cook 5 minutes until pulpy.
Lower the heat and stir in the whisked curd a spoon at a time so it blends smoothly, then add the squeezed methi, 1 cup peas, 0.5 tsp salt and 0.5 cup water and simmer 8 minutes.
Finish with 0.3 cup cream and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer 2 minutes until the crimson gravy glistens, then serve hot.
tips: Deseed some of the chillies if you want the colour without the full desert-level heat.
Add the curd only on low heat and keep stirring, or it will split in the hot masala.
The gravy thickens as it sits; loosen with a little water rather than more cream when reheating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with bajra roti and a smear of white butter, or with steamed rice and a cooling glass of chaas.

variations.name: Bengali Kadai Methi Matar Malai
variations.description: A Bengali kadai reading built on pungent mustard oil and a whole-spice bhaja masala, with a poppy-seed thickening that keeps the gravy pale and nutty. The result is aromatic and gently sweet, a world away from the fiery northern kadai.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked first, it delivers the unmistakable sharp warmth of Bengali cooking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the customary Bengali sweetness that mellows the mustard and spice

steps: Soak 2 tbsp poppy seeds 15 minutes and grind with 2 green chillies to a smooth pale paste to thicken the gravy the Bengali way.
Rub 0.5 tsp salt into the 2 cups methi, rest 10 minutes and squeeze out the bitter juices.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, cool 30 seconds, then sear 1 diced capsicum for 2 minutes until blistered and set aside.
In the same oil fry 2 sliced onions for 6 minutes until golden, add 1 tbsp ginger paste and 0.25 tsp turmeric and cook 1 minute.
Add 1 chopped tomato and the poppy-seed paste, cook on low for 5 minutes until the raw smell lifts and the oil beads at the edges.
Fold in the squeezed methi, 1 cup peas, 1 slit green chilli, 0.5 tsp salt and 0.5 cup water, cover and simmer 8 minutes until the peas soften.
Return the capsicum with 0.4 cup cream, 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp Bengali garam masala, simmer 3 minutes and serve.
tips: Bengali garam masala is milder and sweeter than the Punjabi blend; a mix of cardamom, cinnamon and clove works if you have none.
Heat the mustard oil to smoking every time to strip its raw acridity.
Grind the poppy seeds with a couple of cashews for extra silkiness without changing the flavour much.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft luchi or plain steamed rice, finishing the plate with a squeeze of gondhoraj lime.

variations.name: Andhra Kadai Methi Matar Malai
variations.description: Andhra brings its trademark fire with fiery Guntur red chillies and a punchy garlic-heavy tempering in wood-pressed sesame oil. The malai is thinned so the peas and fenugreek carry a bold, tangy heat rather than a soothing creaminess.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: the nutty wood-pressed gingelly oil that anchors most Andhra gravies

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a touch of sweetness Andhra cooks use to round out searing Guntur heat

steps: Soak 5 Guntur red chillies and 1 tsp tamarind in warm water 15 minutes, then grind together to a fiery, tangy paste.
Rub 0.5 tsp salt into the 2 cups methi, rest 10 minutes and squeeze out the bitter juices.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds with 12 curry leaves and 8 crushed garlic cloves for 30 seconds until aromatic.
Add 2 chopped onions and fry 6 minutes until golden, then add 2 chopped tomatoes and cook 5 minutes until softened.
Stir in the chilli-tamarind paste and 1 tbsp coriander powder, cook 3 minutes on low until the oil floats and the smell turns pungent.
Add the squeezed methi, 1 cup peas, 0.5 tsp salt and 0.5 cup water, cover and simmer 8 minutes until the peas are tender.
Swirl in 0.3 cup cream and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer 2 minutes to soften the edge of the heat, then serve blazing hot.
tips: Guntur chillies are intense; start with three if you are heat-shy and build up.
The tamarind is essential for the tangy backbone that defines Andhra gravies.
A extra teaspoon of raw sesame oil drizzled at the end deepens the nutty Andhra character.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or with pesarattu, and keep plenty of curd on hand to cool the palate.

variations.name: Gujarati Kadai Methi Matar Malai
variations.description: Gujarat softens the robust kadai with its beloved sweet-sour balance, folding jaggery and a little tomato tang into a lighter groundnut-oil gravy. The kadai masala is kept mild so the sweetness and the fresh fenugreek shine through.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the sweet-nutty wood-pressed oil that defines everyday Gujarati cooking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the signature Gujarati sweetness melted into the kadai gravy

steps: Dry-roast 1.5 tbsp coriander seeds for 2 minutes until fragrant and pound coarse for a mild Gujarati-style kadai masala.
Rub 0.5 tsp salt into the 2 cups methi, rest 10 minutes and squeeze out the bitter liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat, add 10 curry leaves and 1 diced capsicum, sear 2 minutes until blistered and set aside.
In the same oil saute 1 chopped onion for 4 minutes, add 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and 0.25 tsp turmeric and cook 1 minute.
Add 3 chopped tomatoes and the pounded coriander, cook 6 minutes until pulpy and the oil separates.
Fold in the squeezed methi, 1 cup peas, 0.5 tsp salt and 0.5 cup water, cover and simmer 8 minutes until the peas are soft.
Return the capsicum with 0.4 cup cream and 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer 3 minutes until the sweet-savoury gravy turns glossy, then serve.
tips: Keep the coriander masala coarse and mild; Gujaratis want the jaggery and methi, not the chilli, to lead.
If your tomatoes are sweet, add a small squeeze of lemon at the end to keep the sweet-sour balance.
The dish reheats well; add the cream fresh each time for the best texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulka or methi thepla and a side of sweet-sour chundo pickle.

variations.name: Classic Kadai Veg Korma
variations.description: Kadai korma is the semi-dry, boldly spiced cousin of the creamy korma, built on a freshly pounded kadai masala of roasted coriander seeds and dried chillies with charred capsicum and onion. The gravy clings tight to the vegetables rather than pooling. It is smoky, peppery and made for scooping with roti.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: handles the high heat needed to sear the capsicum and onion

steps: Dice and steam the mixed vegetables for 7 minutes until nearly tender, and cut the capsicum and one onion into 2 cm chunks for searing.
Dry-roast 1.5 tbsp coriander seeds with 3 dried red chillies on low until fragrant and deep brown, cool, and grind to a coarse kadai masala.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on high, sear the capsicum and onion chunks for 2 minutes until charred at the edges, then remove and reserve.
Lower the heat, add the finely chopped second onion with 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, saute 5 minutes until golden, add the chopped tomatoes and 0.5 tsp turmeric, and cook 5 minutes to a thick masala.

Stir in the ground kadai masala and cook 2 minutes, then add the steamed vegetables, seared capsicum and onion, 1.25 tsp salt and 0.5 cup water, and toss on medium for 4 minutes so the masala coats everything.
Crush in 1 tsp kasuri methi, swirl through 2 tbsp cream, scatter 2 tbsp coriander, and serve semi-dry and glossy.
tips: Freshly pounding the coriander and chilli, rather than using ready powder, is what makes kadai masala taste vivid.
Sear the capsicum on high heat and add it late so it stays crunchy with a smoky edge.
Keep the dish semi-dry; add water by the spoon only if the masala catches.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a small kadai or bowl with tandoori roti or laccha paratha and sliced onions dressed in lemon.

variations.name: Rajasthani Kadai Veg Korma
variations.description: This desert-style kadai leans hot and rustic, its gravy built on soaked whole dried red chillies ground to a fiery paste with garlic, and yogurt standing in for the scarce fresh tomato. Smoky and lean, it is finished with a ghee tempering. It is bold cooking that keeps well in a hot climate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the classic Rajasthani cooking fat that softens the fierce chilli heat

steps: Dice and steam the mixed vegetables for 7 minutes until nearly tender, and soak 6 dried red chillies in hot water for 15 minutes, then grind with the garlic to a smooth red paste.
Cut the capsicum into chunks, sear it in a dry-hot pan for 2 minutes until blistered, and set aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium, crackle 1 tsp cumin, add the finely chopped onions, and saute 6 minutes until deep golden.
Add the red chilli-garlic paste with 2 tsp coriander powder and 0.5 tsp turmeric, and fry on low for 4 minutes until the ghee separates and the raw chilli smell goes.
Whisk the 0.75 cup yogurt smooth, lower the flame, stir it in gradually so it does not split, then add the steamed vegetables, seared capsicum, 1.25 tsp salt and 0.5 cup water.
Simmer semi-dry on medium for 5 minutes until the fiery gravy clings to the vegetables, and serve hot.
tips: Use a milder Kashmiri-Mathania chilli for the colour and only a couple of hot chillies if you want less fire.
Whisk and add the yogurt off the heat, stirring, so it blends smoothly into the chilli gravy.
A little extra ghee stirred in at the end tames the heat and adds a glossy richness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra roti or plain paratha and a cooling side of sliced onion and buttermilk.

variations.name: Karnataka Kadai Veg Korma
variations.description: This southern kadai borrows the tangy backbone of Udupi cooking, thickening the gravy with a roasted-gram and coconut masala and sharpening it with tamarind. Curry leaves in a coconut-oil temper set it apart from the northern original. It is nutty, tangy and comforting over rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday cooking oil of coastal Karnataka, tying the masala together

steps: Dice and steam the mixed vegetables for 7 minutes until nearly tender, and cut the capsicum into chunks.
Grind 0.5 cup grated coconut, 2 tbsp roasted gram and 3 dried red chillies with 1 tbsp tamarind pulp and a little water to a smooth masala.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil on medium, crackle 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 12 curry leaves, then add the sliced onion and capsicum and saute 5 minutes until softened.
Add 0.5 tsp turmeric and the ground coconut-tamarind masala, and cook on low for 5 minutes until the raw smell lifts and the oil surfaces.
Pour in 1 cup water with 1.25 tsp salt, bring to a simmer, then fold in the steamed vegetables and cook 5 minutes until the gravy thickens around them.
Simmer 2 more minutes to a semi-dry coating consistency and serve warm.
tips: Roasted gram thickens the gravy and adds a nutty body without needing cream.
Balance the tamarind with a small pinch of jaggery if the gravy tastes too sharp.
Add the capsicum with the onion so it softens but keeps a little crunch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with neer dosa, set dosa or plain steamed rice and a spoon of ghee.

variations.name: Bengali Kadai Veg Korma
variations.description: A Bengali reworking of the kadai, where mustard oil and a whole-spice garam masala replace the northern kadai powder, and a little poppy-seed paste lends body. It stays semi-dry, pungent and aromatic with a gentle sweetness. It eats well with rice or roti alike.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the pungent base that redefines the kadai in the Bengali style

steps: Dice and steam the mixed vegetables for 7 minutes until nearly tender, cut the capsicum into chunks, and soak 1.5 tbsp poppy seeds in warm water for 10 minutes, then grind to a smooth paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the heat, and temper 1 tsp cumin and 2 bay leaves for 15 seconds.
Add the chopped onion and 1 tbsp ginger paste, saute 5 minutes until golden, then add the chopped tomatoes and 0.5 tsp turmeric and cook 4 minutes to a pulp.
Stir in the poppy-seed paste and cook on low for 3 minutes until it thickens and smells nutty, then add the capsicum and fry 2 minutes.
Fold in the steamed vegetables with 1.25 tsp salt, 0.5 tsp sugar and 0.5 cup water, and cook semi-dry on medium for 5 minutes.
Sprinkle 0.75 tsp garam masala, toss for a minute, and serve while the mustard aroma is bright.
tips: Poppy-seed paste gives a Bengali-style body without cream, but grind it smooth so it does not turn gritty.
Bring the mustard oil to smoking point first to round off its raw sharpness.
The pinch of sugar and a homemade garam masala together give the classic Bengali finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a wedge of lime, or with soft rotis for a lighter meal.

variations.name: Kashmiri Kadai Veg Korma
variations.description: This valley-style kadai swaps the usual heat for aroma, its brick-red gravy coloured by Kashmiri chilli and perfumed with saffron, fennel and dry ginger. Ghee and yogurt make it mellow and fragrant rather than fiery. It is an elegant, semi-dry take fit for a festive plate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: carries the saffron and fennel aromas central to Kashmiri cooking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm water for the signature perfume and colour

steps: Dice and steam the mixed vegetables for 7 minutes until nearly tender, cut the capsicum into chunks, and soak the pinch of Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm water.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium, add 3 cardamom pods and 3 cloves, and let them puff for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Sear the capsicum chunks in the ghee for 2 minutes until blistered, then lift out and reserve.
Lower the flame and add 2 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1.5 tsp fennel powder and 0.75 tsp dry ginger, frying for 20 seconds so they bloom without burning.
Whisk the 0.75 cup yogurt smooth, stir it in off the heat, return to a low flame, add 0.75 cup water and 1.25 tsp salt, and simmer 3 minutes until glossy.
Fold in the steamed vegetables, seared capsicum and the saffron water, simmer semi-dry for 5 minutes, and serve fragrant and red.
tips: Bloom the chilli and fennel only briefly in warm ghee off high heat, or they scorch and turn bitter.
Fennel and dry ginger are the flavour backbone here, so use them fresh and generously.
Keep the yogurt on a gentle flame while stirring to hold the gravy together.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with saffron pulao or plain rice and a side of Kashmiri onion salad.

variations.name: Classic Lauki Chana Dal Dhaba-style
variations.description: This is the rustic highway-dhaba version, cooked dark and robust with a double tadka and a hit of garam masala. A quick charcoal smoking at the end lends the roadside dhungar aroma that sets it apart from a homestyle dal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A generous pour of ghee builds the dark, glossy masala base that defines dhaba dal.

steps: Soak 0.75 cup bengal gram for 20 minutes, then pressure-cook it with the 400 g diced bottle gourd, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 2.5 cups water for 5 whistles until fully soft.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai over medium-high heat and let 1 tsp cumin seeds sizzle and darken for 20 seconds.
Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 45 seconds until the raw smell disappears, then add both chopped onions and cook for 8 minutes, stirring, until deep golden-brown.
Pour in the tomato puree with 1.25 tsp red chilli powder and 0.25 tsp salt and fry on medium heat for 8 to 9 minutes until the ghee splits out and the masala turns thick and glossy.
Tip in the cooked lauki-dal with 0.75 cup hot water, mash a few spoonfuls against the pan, and simmer for 10 minutes so it turns rich and slightly thick.

Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the top, stir in 0.75 tsp garam masala, and finish with chopped coriander; for the dhaba touch, set a lit charcoal piece in a small bowl on the dal, drizzle with ghee and cover for 2 minutes to smoke.
tips: Browning the onions properly is the single biggest step; pale onions give a flat, un-dhaba-like colour and taste.
Skip the charcoal smoking if unavailable, but a pinch of extra garam masala at the end helps mimic the depth.
Make it a day ahead if you can, as this dal deepens in flavour overnight and reheats beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with buttered tandoori roti or laccha paratha, sliced onions, green chillies and a lemon wedge, exactly as it comes at a roadside dhaba.

variations.name: Bengali Lauki Chana Dal Dhaba-style with Mustard Oil
variations.description: A Bengali spin on the dhaba dal, swapping ghee for smoking-hot mustard oil and whole spices for a sharper backbone. Slit green chillies and a hint of sugar keep it recognisably Bengali while retaining the robust dhaba body.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Smoked-hot mustard oil replaces ghee to give this dhaba dal a pungent Bengali edge.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A restrained touch of jaggery softens the mustard-oil sharpness the Bengali way.

steps: Pressure-cook 0.75 cup rinsed bengal gram with the 400 g diced bottle gourd, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 2.5 cups water for 5 whistles until tender.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai over high heat until it smokes and loses its raw edge, roughly 1 minute, then lower to medium.
Add 1 bay leaf and 1 tsp panch phoron and let the five spices splutter for about 25 seconds until fenugreek turns a shade darker and smells toasty.

Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the sliced onions and fry for 7 minutes until the onions soften and colour to a light brown, then add the chopped tomato with 1 tsp red chilli powder and cook 6 minutes until pulpy.
Pour in the cooked lauki-dal with the slit green chillies and 0.75 cup hot water, then simmer uncovered for 9 minutes so the mustard oil and panch phoron perfume the pot.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and the remaining 0.25 tsp salt, adjust for a gentle sweet-hot balance, and scatter coriander over the top before serving.
tips: Panch phoron must be added to hot oil whole and never ground, or the fennel and fenugreek can turn bitter.
Keep the green chillies slit but whole for aroma without turning the dal fiercely hot.
A last drizzle of raw mustard oil off the heat amplifies the signature pungency if you love it strong.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best with steamed rice and a side of aloo bhaja, or mopped up with a coarse jowar roti for a rustic Bengali-meets-dhaba plate.

variations.name: Gujarati Lauki Chana Dal Dhaba-style with Jaggery
variations.description: A Gujarati-leaning dhaba dal that keeps the robust masala base but tips it sweet-sour with jaggery, lime and a fragrant curry-leaf tadka. It is a little lighter and brighter than the classic, without losing its hearty character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee anchors the fragrant curry-leaf tadka that brightens this Gujarati dhaba dal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery brings the gentle Gujarati sweetness that offsets the dhaba masala's heat.

steps: Pressure-cook 0.75 cup rinsed bengal gram with the 400 g diced bottle gourd, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 2.75 cups water for 5 whistles, then stir to a creamy consistency.
Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat and pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 0.75 tsp cumin, adding 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 12 curry leaves once they crackle for 15 seconds.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and the chopped onion and fry for 6 minutes until the onion is soft and translucent with lightly golden edges.
Stir in the chopped tomato with 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and cook for 6 minutes until the tomato breaks down and the masala smells rounded.
Add the cooked lauki-dal and 0.75 cup hot water and simmer for 7 minutes, then stir in 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder until it dissolves completely.
Simmer 3 more minutes, turn off the heat, and finish with 1 tbsp lime juice and the remaining 0.25 tsp salt for the classic sweet-sour close.
tips: Dissolve the jaggery fully before serving so no gritty bits remain in the smooth gravy.
This dal tastes best a touch runnier than the classic dhaba style, so add extra hot water if it tightens.
Taste and re-balance with a few drops more lime if the sweetness starts to dominate.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulka or steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, rounded off with a plate of fried papad and mango pickle.

variations.name: Kerala Lauki Chana Dal Dhaba-style with Coconut
variations.description: This version reimagines the dhaba dal through a Kerala lens, folding in a roasted coconut paste for body and finishing with a coconut-oil and shallot tadka. It is thick, nutty and aromatic, with a warmth that comes from browned coconut rather than heavy masala.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil gives the final shallot tadka its authentic Kerala sweetness.

steps: Pressure-cook 0.75 cup rinsed bengal gram with the 400 g diced bottle gourd, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 2.5 cups water for 5 whistles until soft.
In a dry pan, roast 0.5 cup grated coconut with 0.5 tsp cumin over medium heat for 4 to 5 minutes until golden and fragrant, then grind with 4 tablespoons water to a coarse paste.
Stir the roasted coconut paste into the cooked dal with the minced ginger and simmer over low heat for 8 minutes, stirring so the gravy thickens evenly.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds for 20 seconds until they pop.
Add the sliced shallots, 3 broken dried red chillies and 12 curry leaves and fry for 4 to 5 minutes until the shallots are deep golden and crisp at the edges.
Pour the tadka over the dal, stir in the remaining 0.25 tsp salt, and rest it covered for 2 minutes so the roasted-coconut aroma settles before serving.
tips: Roasting the coconut before grinding gives a deeper, nuttier flavour than a raw coconut paste.
Fry the shallots slowly and fully, as their caramelised sweetness is what balances the roasted coconut.
Thin with hot water at serving time, since the roasted coconut makes this dal thicken fast as it sits.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with matta rice and a crisp pappadam, or serve alongside appam for a heartier South Indian spread.

variations.name: Andhra Lauki Chana Dal Dhaba-style with Guntur Chilli
variations.description: A dhaba dal turned up to full Andhra heat with smoky Guntur chillies, plenty of garlic and a groundnut-oil tadka. Tamarind lends a sour lift that keeps the robust, fiery gravy from feeling heavy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the Andhra fat of choice for carrying searing Guntur chilli heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A closing spoon of ghee mellows the Guntur fire for mixing into rice.

steps: Pressure-cook 0.75 cup rinsed bengal gram with the 400 g diced bottle gourd, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 2.5 cups water for 5 whistles until the dal is soft and creamy.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai over medium heat and crackle 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 0.75 tsp cumin for about 20 seconds.
Add 5 broken Guntur chillies and the crushed garlic and fry for 1 minute until the garlic is golden and the chillies deepen to a smoky brick-red.
Add the chopped onion with 12 curry leaves and cook for 6 minutes until the onion softens and takes on the chilli's colour.
Stir in the cooked lauki-dal, 1.5 tbsp tamarind pulp and 0.75 cup hot water, then simmer for 9 minutes so the sourness and heat come into balance and the gravy thickens.
Season with the remaining 0.25 tsp salt and swirl in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee off the heat to soften the sharp chilli edge before serving.
tips: Toast the Guntur chillies just until fragrant; letting them blacken turns the whole dal acrid.
Stir the tamarind pulp in near the end so its brightness survives rather than boiling flat.
Serve with extra rice on the side, as this dal is deliberately fierce and best eaten in small, well-diluted portions.
variations.servingSuggestion: Spoon over hot rice with a dab of ghee and a fried papad, adding a cooling cucumber raita to temper the Guntur heat.

variations.name: Classic Lauki Chana Dal Fry
variations.description: A restaurant-style dal fry where boiled bengal gram and bottle gourd are cooked into a well-browned onion-tomato masala so everything fuses into a thick, glossy bowl. Nuttier and heartier than a tadka version, the chana dal keeps its bite while the lauki melts into the fried gravy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Frying the masala in bilona ghee gives the dal its rich, rounded body

steps: Soak 0.75 cup bengal gram for 30 minutes, then pressure-cook with 2 cups diced bottle gourd, 2.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 5 whistles until soft but the grains stay intact.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add 7 minced garlic cloves, 1 inch grated ginger and 2 chopped green chillies, fry 1 minute, then add 2 finely chopped onions and cook until richly golden brown, about 7 minutes.
Stir in 2 chopped tomatoes with 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander powder and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, and cook until the masala is thick and the ghee separates, about 6 minutes.
Tip the cooked dal and lauki into the masala with a little hot water and fry-simmer for 8 minutes, stirring gently so the dal soaks up the browned masala without breaking the grains.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala and 3 tbsp coriander, stir through and serve hot with a drizzle of ghee.
tips: Brown the onions properly; pale onions leave the fry tasting raw and flat.
Stir gently once the dal goes in so the tender chana grains stay whole rather than mashing.
Pick a young, firm bottle gourd and taste a raw sliver first to be sure it is not bitter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a kadai topped with ginger juliennes and a swirl of ghee, with jeera rice, tandoori roti and a kachumber salad.

variations.name: Punjabi Lauki Chana Dal Fry
variations.description: A richer Punjabi dhaba-style fry finished with butter, kasuri methi and garam masala, the bottle gourd and bengal gram simmered into a deep, glossy gravy. It is fuller-bodied and slightly smoky, made to be scooped up with hot buttered rotis.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee blooms the kasuri methi in the final tempering

steps: Soak 0.75 cup bengal gram for 30 minutes, then pressure-cook with 2 cups diced bottle gourd, 2.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 5 whistles until soft but intact.
Melt 2 tbsp butter in a heavy pan over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them foam for 20 seconds until nutty.
Add 7 minced garlic cloves and 1.5 inch grated ginger, fry 1 minute, then add 2 finely chopped onions and cook until deep golden, about 7 minutes.
Stir in 3 chopped tomatoes with 1 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, and cook to a thick pulpy masala until the fat pools, about 7 minutes.
Add the cooked dal and lauki with a little hot water and simmer for 8 minutes, stirring gently so the chana stays whole.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, take it off the heat and crush in 1 tsp kasuri methi and 0.5 tsp garam masala, pour over the dal, fold in 3 tbsp coriander and serve hot.
tips: Crush the kasuri methi between your palms before it hits the ghee to release its full aroma.
Cook the onions low and slow; their caramel sweetness balances three tomatoes.
For a smoky dhaba note, smoke the dal with a hot coal and a drizzle of ghee under a lid for two minutes.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a kadai with a melting knob of butter, laccha onion and green chilli, alongside warm tandoori roti brushed with ghee.

variations.name: Kerala Lauki Chana Dal Fry
variations.description: A coconut-rich southern fry where ground coconut and a coconut-oil tempering turn the bottle gourd and bengal gram mellow and creamy, close to a lauki erissery. Curry leaves, shallots and a little black pepper give it a coastal fragrance far from the tomato-heavy northern version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed coconut oil gives the unmistakable Kerala aroma to the tempering

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A last spoon of ghee deepens the coconut and pepper finish

steps: Rinse and soak 0.75 cup bengal gram for 30 minutes, then pressure-cook it with 2 cups diced bottle gourd, 2.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 5 whistles until tender yet whole.
Grind 0.5 cup grated coconut with 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 4 garlic cloves to a coarse paste with a splash of water, and set aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds with 2 dried red chillies and 12 curry leaves for 20 seconds.
Add 8 sliced shallots and fry until soft and golden, about 4 minutes, then stir in the coconut paste and 0.5 tsp black pepper and fry for 2 minutes until the raw smell disappears.
Add the cooked dal and lauki with the remaining 0.5 tsp salt and a little hot water, and simmer for 7 minutes until creamy, mashing a little of the lauki to thicken.
Finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee, check the salt and serve hot.
tips: Grind the coconut coarse so you still get little bursts of texture through the creamy dal.
Shallots give a natural sweetness that ordinary onions cannot match, so seek them out.
Add the coconut paste on low heat; boiling it hard can make the coconut split and turn grainy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with matta red rice and a spoon of coconut oil, pappadam and a tart mango pickle on the side.

variations.name: Karnataka Lauki Chana Dal Fry
variations.description: A Karnataka version with the gentle sweet-sour balance of tamarind and a pinch of jaggery, close to a hurali-style saaru in spirit. A coconut-oil tempering and rasam-style spicing make it tangy and aromatic, the lauki and chana carrying a bright, appetising finish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil gives the coastal Karnataka fragrance to the tempering

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A little jaggery rounds the tamarind sourness in classic Karnataka style

steps: Soak 0.75 cup bengal gram for half an hour, then pressure-cook with 2 cups diced bottle gourd, 2.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 5 whistles until the gram softens but keeps its shape.
Stir 1 tbsp tamarind pulp, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 chopped tomato, 1 tsp rasam powder and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt into the dal and simmer for 8 minutes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds until popping.
Add 2 dried red chillies, 12 curry leaves, 4 crushed garlic cloves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and fry for 30 seconds until the garlic is golden and the leaves crisp.
Pour the tempering into the simmering dal, stir well and let it bubble for 3 minutes so the sweet-sour-spiced flavours settle.
Taste for the tamarind-jaggery balance, finish with 2 tbsp coriander and serve hot.
tips: Add the tamarind before the jaggery so you can dial in the sour-sweet balance a little at a time.
Toast the rasam powder for a few seconds in the tempering oil to wake up its aroma.
Mash a little of the softened lauki to thicken the gravy while keeping the chana grains whole.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over steaming rice with a spoon of ghee and a crisp sandige, with a dry vegetable palya on the side.

variations.name: Kashmiri Lauki Chana Dal Fry
variations.description: An aromatic Kashmiri interpretation gilded with saffron and warm ground fennel and dry ginger, giving the bottle gourd and bengal gram a floral, festive character. Kashmiri chilli lends deep red colour without harsh heat, making it gentle, fragrant and elegant.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Kashmiri cooking leans on ghee, which carries the saffron and fennel beautifully

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Saffron bloomed in warm milk gives the dal its floral aroma and golden glow

steps: Soak a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside to release its colour while you cook.
Pressure-cook 0.75 cup bengal gram, soaked for 30 minutes first, with 2 cups diced bottle gourd, 2.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 5 whistles until soft yet intact.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat and add 1 tsp cumin seeds, 2 cardamom pods and 2 cloves, letting them sizzle for 30 seconds until fragrant.

Add 1 finely chopped onion and fry until soft and pale gold, about 5 minutes, then stir in 1 tsp fennel powder, 0.5 tsp ginger powder and 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder off the heat so they do not scorch.
Return to the heat, add 1 chopped tomato and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, cook for 4 minutes, then add the cooked dal and lauki with a little hot water and simmer for 8 minutes.
Stir in the saffron milk, simmer 2 more minutes, and finish with 2 tbsp coriander so the floral aroma stays bright.
tips: Bloom saffron in warm milk, not water, for a rounder colour and mellower aroma.
Toast the ground fennel and dry ginger only briefly so they stay sweet rather than bitter.
Use Kashmiri chilli for ruby colour without heat, adding fresh chilli separately only if you want a kick.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice or a mild pulao, finishing the plate with a thread of saffron milk for aroma.

variations.name: Classic Lauki Chana Dal Tadka
variations.description: A wholesome North Indian one-pot where nutty bengal gram and soft bottle gourd cook together, then take a sizzling cumin-garlic ghee tempering. The chana dal holds its bite while the lauki melts into the gravy, giving a comforting contrast of textures under a fragrant tadka.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee crackles the cumin and garlic tadka that finishes this dal

steps: Soak 0.75 cup bengal gram for 30 minutes, then pressure-cook it with 2 cups diced bottle gourd, 2.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 5 whistles until the dal is soft but still holds its shape.
Open the cooker, lightly mash a quarter of the dal against the side to thicken the gravy while keeping most grains whole, and keep warm.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 2 dried red chillies with 0.25 tsp asafoetida for 30 seconds.
Add 6 sliced garlic cloves and 1 inch grated ginger, fry until pale gold for about 1 minute, then add 1 chopped onion and cook until soft and golden, roughly 4 minutes.
Stir in 2 chopped tomatoes with 1 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, and cook until pulpy and the ghee separates, about 5 minutes.
Pour the sizzling tadka into the dal, simmer together for 5 minutes so the lauki soaks up the flavour, then finish with 3 tbsp coriander and serve hot.
tips: Do not over-soak or over-cook the chana dal; it should stay just tender so it contrasts with the soft lauki.
Choose a young, pale bottle gourd; older ones can taste bitter, so taste a sliver of the raw flesh first.
Mash only a little of the dal to thicken the gravy, keeping most of the nutty grains intact.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or with hot phulkas and a wedge of lemon and sliced onion.

variations.name: Gujarati Lauki Chana Dal Tadka
variations.description: The Gujarati sweet-sour treatment, where jaggery and a squeeze of tamarind lift the earthy chana dal and lauki, tempered with mustard and curry leaves. It is lighter and gently sweet, the bottle gourd soaking up a balanced blend of sweet, sour and mild spice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries the mustard and curry-leaf tempering that defines a Gujarati dal

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Balances the tamarind sourness with a gentle warmth

steps: Soak 0.75 cup bengal gram for 30 minutes, then pressure-cook with 2 cups diced bottle gourd, 2.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 5 whistles until soft but intact.
Stir 1 tbsp tamarind pulp, 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 chopped tomato and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt into the dal and simmer gently for 8 minutes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan over medium heat and add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds; when they pop after 20 seconds add 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida.
Drop in 10 curry leaves, 2 slit green chillies and 1 inch julienned ginger and let them crackle for 30 seconds until the curry leaves turn translucent.
Pour the tempering into the simmering dal, stir well and let it bubble for 3 minutes so the sweet, sour and spiced notes settle into balance.
Taste and adjust the jaggery-tamarind balance, finish with 2 tbsp coriander and serve hot.
tips: Add jaggery after the tamarind so you can fine-tune the sweet-sour balance a little at a time.
Keep this dal on the looser side; the lauki releases water, so adjust with hot water as needed.
A young bottle gourd is essential, as an older bitter one will throw off the delicate sweet-sour balance.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot rice with a spoon of ghee, or as part of a Gujarati thali with rotli, kadhi and a dry shaak.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Lauki Chana Dal Tadka
variations.description: A Deccan version scented with goda masala and a groundnut-oil tempering, giving the chana dal and lauki a dark, roasted, faintly sweet depth. Toasted dry coconut adds nuttiness and a squeeze of lemon keeps it bright, quite distinct from the North Indian tadka.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the everyday Maharashtrian fat and toasts goda masala well

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon softens the sharp edge of the goda masala

steps: Rinse and soak 0.75 cup bengal gram for 30 minutes, then pressure-cook it with 2 cups diced bottle gourd, 2.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 5 whistles until the gram is tender but not mushy.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard and 0.75 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds until popping.
Add 5 crushed garlic cloves and 1 chopped onion and fry until soft and golden, about 4 minutes, then toast 2 tbsp grated dry coconut in with them for 1 minute until nutty.
Stir in 1 chopped tomato, 1.5 tsp goda masala, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, and cook for 3 minutes until dark and glossy.
Pour in the cooked dal with a little hot water and simmer for 6 minutes so the goda masala infuses the lauki and chana.
Finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 2 tbsp coriander and a squeeze of lemon, then serve hot.
tips: Add goda masala with the tomato, never into smoking oil, or it will turn bitter.
Toast the dry coconut properly; raw coconut leaves the dal tasting flat and dull.
A pinch of jaggery instead of lemon gives the sweeter Vidarbha-style balance if you prefer it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and ghee, or with jowar bhakri, raw onion and a papad for a rustic Maharashtrian plate.

variations.name: Bengali Lauki Chana Dal Tadka
variations.description: A Bengali-style lau chholar dal cousin, tempered in smoking mustard oil with panch phoron and a faint sweetness. The five-spice crackle and pungent oil give the bottle gourd and bengal gram an aromatic eastern character, mild, comforting and fragrant.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil gives the pungent kick that is the soul of a Bengali tempering

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A final drizzle of ghee rounds off the sharpness of the mustard oil

steps: Soak 0.75 cup bengal gram for half an hour, then pressure-cook with 2 cups diced bottle gourd, 2.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 5 whistles until the dal turns soft while still holding its shape.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pan over medium-high until it lightens and just smokes, about 1 minute, to mellow the raw pungency.
Lower the heat and add 1 tsp panch phoron, 2 dried red chillies and 1 bay leaf, letting them crackle for 30 seconds until the fenugreek darkens and smells toasty.
Add 1 inch grated ginger and 1 chopped tomato with 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and cook for 4 minutes until the tomato breaks down.
Pour in the cooked dal with the remaining 0.5 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp sugar, add a little hot water, and simmer for 6 minutes so the panch phoron perfumes the pot.
Finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and 2 tbsp coriander, and serve hot.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to smoking then cool slightly; raw mustard oil tastes harsh and bitter.
The touch of sugar echoes the Bengali cholar dal tradition and gently rounds the spices.
Leave the panch phoron whole so you get little bursts of fennel and nigella in each spoonful.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice, a fried papad and a slice of lime, or with soft luchi for a festive Bengali touch.

variations.name: Andhra Lauki Chana Dal Tadka
variations.description: A fiery Andhra rendition where Guntur red chillies and a garlic-heavy sesame-oil tempering bring bold heat to the mellow bottle gourd. Curry leaves make it aromatic and the chana dal soaks up the spice, a robust dal that begs for a mound of rice and ghee.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed sesame oil is the classic Andhra frying fat and carries the Guntur heat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of ghee makes the ferocious Guntur heat pleasurable

steps: Pressure-cook 0.75 cup bengal gram, soaked for 30 minutes beforehand, with 2 cups diced bottle gourd, 2.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 5 whistles until soft but still whole.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadai over medium heat, splutter 0.5 tsp mustard and 1 tsp cumin seeds, then snap in 4 Guntur chillies and 12 curry leaves and fry 30 seconds until crackling.
Add 8 crushed garlic cloves and fry until pale gold, about 1 minute, then add 1 chopped onion and cook until light brown, roughly 5 minutes.
Stir in 1 chopped tomato with 1 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, and cook until the masala darkens and the oil separates, about 5 minutes.
Add the cooked dal with a splash of hot water and simmer for 7 minutes so the Guntur heat works through the lauki and chana.
Finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee to gentle the fire and scatter 2 tbsp coriander before serving.
tips: Guntur chillies are intensely hot, so deseed a couple for colour and aroma without full firepower.
The spoon of ghee at the end is what makes the ferocious heat pleasurable rather than punishing.
Fry the curry leaves crisp so they shatter into the dal and release their full citrus aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plenty of steamed rice, a dollop of ghee, fried papad and a cooling raita to balance the heat.

variations.name: Classic Masala Veg Korma
variations.description: A restaurant-style mixed-vegetable korma in a silky onion-tomato-cashew gravy, mildly spiced and finished with cream so every vegetable tastes luxurious. The masala is smooth and lightly sweet, letting the medley of beans, carrot, potato and peas stay the star. It is the reliable party-menu korma everyone reaches for.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a clean-tasting base fat that lets the cashew gravy stay delicate

steps: Dice the mixed vegetables into even pieces and steam or boil them for 8 minutes until just tender but not mushy, then drain and set aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on medium, crackle 1 tsp cumin, add the chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, and saute 6 minutes until soft and pale gold.
Add the tomatoes and 14 cashews and cook for 5 minutes until pulpy, then cool and blend to a very smooth paste with a little water.
Return the paste to the pan with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, and cook on medium for 6 minutes until the oil separates and the raw smell lifts.
Add 1 cup water and 1.25 tsp salt, bring to a simmer, then fold in the cooked vegetables and cook gently for 5 minutes so they soak up the gravy.
Stir in 4 tbsp cream and 0.75 tsp garam masala, simmer 2 minutes, garnish with 2 tbsp coriander, and serve.
tips: Blend the cashew gravy while warm and strain it once for a truly velvety, hotel-style texture.
Steam the vegetables separately rather than boiling them in the gravy so they keep their colour and shape.
A teaspoon of sugar rounds off overly tangy tomatoes if your gravy tastes sharp.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan, laccha paratha or fragrant ghee rice, with a wedge of lemon alongside.

variations.name: Kerala Masala Veg Korma
variations.description: This is the fragrant coconut korma of Kerala, where a freshly ground coconut-and-roasted-spice paste replaces cashew cream for a naturally rich, aromatic gravy. Curry leaves and a coconut-oil temper make it unmistakably southern. It is the classic partner to appam and idiyappam.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the heart of Kerala cooking, tying the coconut gravy together

steps: Dice the mixed vegetables and simmer them with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.25 tsp salt and 1.5 cups water for 10 minutes until nearly tender.
Meanwhile grind 1 cup grated coconut with 1 tsp fennel seeds, 8 cashews, the ginger and 3 green chillies to a smooth white paste using a little warm water.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil on medium, add 12 curry leaves and the sliced onion, and saute 6 minutes until the onion is soft and translucent.
Pour the ground coconut paste into the softened vegetables, stir well, and simmer gently on low for 6 to 7 minutes, stirring so the coconut does not catch.
Add 0.5 tsp garam masala, adjust the consistency with a splash of hot water to a pourable gravy, and cook 2 minutes more until it smells sweet and aromatic.
Pour the fried onion and curry-leaf tempering over the korma, fold through, and take off the heat before the coconut turns oily.
tips: Never boil the coconut paste hard; keep it on a low flame or the gravy will split and turn grainy.
Grind the coconut with warm water for the whitest, smoothest paste.
A final drizzle of raw coconut oil off the heat deepens the aroma the Kerala way.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with lacy appam, idiyappam or Malabar parotta, with a bowl of pickle on the side.

variations.name: Kashmiri Masala Veg Korma
variations.description: A regal, saffron-scented korma where yogurt and a whisper of fennel replace tomato, giving a pale golden gravy perfumed with cardamom and saffron. It is mild, aromatic and elegant rather than fiery. This is the vegetarian showpiece of a Kashmiri wazwan-style spread.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee gives the korma its rich, festive aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk for the signature colour and fragrance

steps: Dice and steam the mixed vegetables for 8 minutes until just tender, and soak the pinch of Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk.
Boil the sliced onion with 12 cashews for 5 minutes, drain, cool, and blend to a smooth pale paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium, add 3 cardamom pods, 3 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon, and let them puff up for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add the onion-cashew paste with 1 tsp fennel powder and 0.5 tsp dry ginger, and cook on low for 5 minutes without letting it brown, keeping the gravy pale.
Whisk the 0.75 cup yogurt smooth, lower the flame, and stir it in gradually so it does not split, then add 1 cup water and 1.25 tsp salt and simmer 4 minutes.
Fold in the steamed vegetables and the saffron milk, simmer gently for 5 minutes, and serve once the gravy is glossy and golden.
tips: Keep the onions from browning during boiling and frying so the gravy stays elegant and pale.
Add yogurt only on low heat while stirring continuously to keep the korma smooth.
Steeping saffron in warm milk rather than water draws out more colour and aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with saffron pulao or soft rumali roti for a festive spread, garnished with a few fried cashews.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Masala Veg Korma
variations.description: This korma carries the smoky, roasted-coconut depth of goda masala and a freshly ground kala masala paste that turns the gravy dark and intensely aromatic. It is spicier and earthier than the creamy northern version. A little jaggery keeps the balance true to Maharashtrian taste.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday frying oil that carries goda masala's roasted notes

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: balances the fiery goda masala the way Maharashtrian cooks intend

steps: Dice and steam the mixed vegetables for 8 minutes until just tender, and dry-roast 3 tbsp dry coconut on low until deep brown, then grind it with the sliced onion to a coarse dark paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on medium, crackle 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 30 seconds.
Add the roasted coconut-onion paste and cook on medium for 6 to 7 minutes until it turns rich brown and the oil begins to leave the sides.
Stir in the chopped tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp goda masala, and cook 4 minutes until the tomato collapses and the masala smells roasted.
Pour in 1.5 cups water with 1.25 tsp salt, bring to a simmer, then add the steamed vegetables and cook 6 minutes so they absorb the dark gravy.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer 2 minutes, scatter 2 tbsp coriander, and serve hot.
tips: Roast the dry coconut slowly to a deep brown for the authentic smoky kala-masala colour, but stop before it burns.
Goda masala varies in heat between brands, so add the chilli powder gradually and taste as you go.
This gravy tastes best a little thin, as it thickens noticeably on standing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri or steamed rice topped with a spoon of the spicy gravy and a raw onion wedge.

variations.name: Andhra Masala Veg Korma
variations.description: A bold, chilli-forward korma from Andhra, thickened with a roasted poppy-seed and coconut paste and lit up by smoky Guntur red chillies. Sesame oil and curry leaves ground it firmly in the south. It is rich and fiery at once, made for mopping up with rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: traditional nallennai adds nutty depth to the fiery gravy

steps: Dice and steam the mixed vegetables for 8 minutes until just tender, and soak 1 tbsp poppy seeds in warm water for 10 minutes.
Grind the soaked poppy seeds with 0.5 cup grated coconut and 4 Guntur chillies to a smooth paste using a little water.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil on medium, crackle 1 tsp cumin and 12 curry leaves, add the chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, and saute 6 minutes until golden.
Add the poppy-coconut-chilli paste with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 2 tsp coriander powder, and cook on low for 5 minutes until the oil surfaces and the raw smell disappears.
Pour in 1.5 cups water and 1.25 tsp salt, bring to a simmer, then add the steamed vegetables and cook 6 minutes until the gravy thickens around them.
Simmer 2 more minutes to marry the flavours and serve piping hot with the red oil pooling on top.
tips: Soaking the poppy seeds first makes them grind into a silky paste that thickens the gravy naturally.
Guntur chillies bring heat and colour, so deseed a couple if you want the aroma with less fire.
Toast the coconut lightly before grinding for an extra layer of nutty flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or with ragi sangati for a rustic Andhra meal.

variations.name: Classic Masoor Dal Dhaba-style
variations.description: This is the smoky, robust dal you get at a highway dhaba, with a dark onion-tomato bhuna masala, garam masala, crushed kasuri methi and a charcoal-smoked finish. It is deliberately rustic and heavy on ghee, meant to be mopped up with a thick tandoori roti. The dhungar smoking is what sets it apart from a home dal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: generous bilona ghee delivers the rich, heavy mouthfeel expected of dhaba dal

steps: Rinse 1 cup red lentils and pressure-cook with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft and creamy, then whisk lightly.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadai over medium-high heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds until dark and fragrant.
Add a paste of 8 garlic cloves and 1 inch ginger, fry 30 seconds, then add 2 chopped onions and fry until deep brown, about 9 minutes, for the essential dhaba bhuna base.
Add 3 chopped tomatoes, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, and cook down hard until the masala is jammy and the ghee separates, about 9 minutes.
Pour in the dal with 0.5 cup hot water, add 1 tsp garam masala and 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi, and simmer 8 minutes until thick and glossy.
For the dhungar, place a hot piece of charcoal in a small bowl set on the dal, pour the remaining 1 tbsp ghee over it, cover for 3 minutes to smoke, then remove the bowl and stir in 3 tbsp coriander.
tips: The onions must be browned far darker than for a home dal; that colour is the backbone of dhaba flavour.
If you skip the charcoal, a tiny pinch of smoked paprika in the tadka gives a faint smoky hint.
Keep it on the thicker side so it clings to roti rather than running off.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter-brushed tandoori roti or laccha paratha, sliced onions, green chilli and a lemon wedge, dhaba-style on a steel plate.

variations.name: Odia Masoor Dal Dhaba-style
variations.description: The Odia table brings its signature panch phoron, a five-seed blend of fenugreek, nigella, cumin, mustard and fennel, crackled in ghee for a uniquely aromatic tadka. The dal stays light and slightly sweet with a hint of tomato, letting the whole-spice fragrance lead. It is the everyday dalma-adjacent comfort of coastal Odisha.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee is the traditional medium for crackling panch phoron and carries its five-seed aroma beautifully

steps: Rinse 1 cup red lentils and pressure-cook with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft, then whisk to a smooth, medium consistency.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat and add 1 whole bay leaf, 1 tsp panch phoron and 2 broken dried red chillies, letting the seeds crackle and release their aroma, about 30 seconds.
Add 4 sliced garlic cloves and 1 chopped onion and fry until golden, about 5 minutes.
Add 1 chopped tomato and 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and cook until the tomato softens into the masala, about 4 minutes.
Pour in the cooked dal with 0.25 cup hot water and simmer gently for 7 minutes so the panch phoron flavour permeates the lentils.
Taste for salt, rest covered for 2 minutes, and serve warm.
tips: Do not grind the panch phoron; the whole seeds crackling in ghee are the point of this dal.
Keep the heat moderate so the fenugreek seeds do not brown too far and turn bitter.
A few chunks of pumpkin or brinjal simmered in turn this into a light dalma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a drizzle of raw ghee, alongside a simple aloo bharta for a homely Odia meal.

variations.name: Kerala Masoor Dal Dhaba-style
variations.description: A coconut-forward coastal take where ground coconut thickens the dal and a coconut-oil tadka of mustard, curry leaves and shallots crowns it. Green chilli and ginger keep it fresh while coconut milk lends body and a mellow sweetness. It trades the smoky heaviness of the dhaba for the bright, aromatic ease of the backwaters.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil in the tadka is the soul of any Kerala dal and cannot be swapped

steps: Rinse 1 cup red lentils and pressure-cook with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 slit green chillies, a grated 1 inch piece of ginger and 1 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft.
Grind 0.5 cup grated coconut to a smooth paste with a little water and stir it into the dal, simmering for 4 minutes to thicken.
Add 0.5 cup coconut milk and warm on low heat for 2 minutes without letting it boil, then switch off.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan over medium heat and add 1 tsp mustard seeds, letting them pop.
Add 2 broken dried red chillies, 6 sliced shallots and 2 sprigs curry leaves and fry until the shallots are deep golden and the leaves crisp, about 3 minutes.
Pour the tempering over the dal, cover for a minute to lock in the aroma, and serve warm.
tips: Grinding coconut into the dal, rather than only using milk, gives a fuller texture and richer taste.
Never boil the dal after adding coconut milk or it will split and look grainy.
Deep-golden shallots are essential; pale ones leave the dal flat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice or soft appams and a spoonful of lime pickle to cut the richness of the coconut.

variations.name: Gujarati Masoor Dal Dhaba-style
variations.description: The Gujarati version turns the hearty dhaba dal sweet, sour and spicy at once, melting jaggery and tamarind into a thin dal with ginger, curry leaves and a groundnut-oil tempering. Whole spices and a pinch of asafoetida keep it fragrant while the sweetness balances the chilli. It is a light, sippable dal that anchors a Gujarati thali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: organic jaggery powder gives the clean caramel sweetness central to the Gujarati khatti-meethi profile

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil is the classic Gujarati tempering fat

steps: Rinse 1 cup red lentils and pressure-cook with 3.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 3 whistles, then whisk to a thin, smooth dal.
Set the dal on low heat and stir in 1 tbsp tamarind pulp, 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, a grated 1 inch piece of ginger and 2 slit green chillies, simmering 5 minutes.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a small pan over medium heat until it shimmers.
Add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and let them splutter, then add 0.5 tsp cumin, 2 cloves, 1 inch cinnamon, 1 pinch asafoetida and 1 sprig curry leaves and fry for 25 seconds until fragrant.
Pour the whole-spice tempering into the dal and simmer for another 5 minutes so the sweet-sour balance rounds out.
Taste and fine-tune jaggery or tamarind, then serve hot and pourable.
tips: Add jaggery only after the lentils are fully cooked, as it can otherwise hinder softening.
Whole cloves and cinnamon in the tadka give the fragrance; fish them out before serving if you prefer.
Keep this dal thin enough to drink; it is meant to be light against a rich thali.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and ghee, or sip warm alongside rotli, kadhi and a dry shaak for a complete Gujarati thali.

variations.name: Bengali Masoor Dal Dhaba-style
variations.description: The Bengali take swaps ghee-heavy richness for a pungent mustard-oil tadka with nigella seeds and slit green chillies, keeping the dal thin, bright and homely. A late spoon of ghee softens the mustard bite in the classic Bengali way. It is worlds apart from the heavy dhaba style, favouring sharpness and simplicity.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil heated to smoking gives the sharp, authentic Bengali tadka

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing teaspoon of ghee is the traditional Bengali touch that mellows the mustard sharpness

steps: Rinse 1 cup red lentils and pressure-cook with 3.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 3 whistles until very soft, then whisk to a thin dal.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai over high heat until it just smokes and loses its raw edge, then reduce to medium.
Add 0.5 tsp nigella seeds, 3 slit green chillies and 2 broken dried red chillies and let them crackle for 20 seconds.
Add 1 chopped small onion and fry until lightly browned, about 4 minutes, then add 1 chopped tomato and cook until pulpy, about 3 minutes.
Pour in the cooked dal with the remaining 0.5 tsp salt and 0.25 tsp sugar and simmer for 6 minutes so the mustard tadka infuses.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee off the heat and serve the dal thin and warm.
tips: Smoking the mustard oil first is non-negotiable, or the dal will taste raw and bitter.
Keep the dal loose; Bengalis pour it over rice rather than scoop it thick.
Drop in a few fried bori for a traditional crunchy garnish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot rice with a wedge of lime and crisp aloo bhaja on the side for a classic Bengali first course.

variations.name: Classic Masoor Dal Punjabi
variations.description: The Punjabi masoor is richer and more robust than the everyday version, built on a slow-cooked onion-tomato masala, crushed kasuri methi and a double tadka of ghee. It carries the buttery, deeply spiced character of Punjab's home kitchens where dal is never an afterthought. Ladled over rice or scooped with roti, it eats like a treat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee used generously here is what gives Punjabi dal its glossy, buttery body

steps: Rinse 1 cup red lentils thoroughly and pressure-cook with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft and creamy, then whisk lightly.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds until fragrant, about 30 seconds.
Add a paste of 6 garlic cloves and 1 inch ginger, fry for 30 seconds, then add 2 finely chopped onions and cook until deep golden, about 8 minutes.
Add 3 chopped tomatoes with 1 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, and cook down until the masala is thick and the ghee separates, about 8 minutes.
Pour in the cooked dal with 0.5 cup hot water, add 0.5 tsp garam masala and 1 tbsp kasuri methi crushed between your palms, and simmer for 8 minutes until rich and pourable.
Heat the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee till nearly smoking and pour it sizzling over the dal as a second tadka, then scatter 3 tbsp chopped coriander and serve.
tips: The second hot-ghee tadka poured just before serving is the trick that gives dhaba-style aroma at home.
Toast the kasuri methi in a dry pan for 10 seconds before crushing to intensify its fragrance.
Make it a day ahead; Punjabi dal deepens in flavour overnight and only needs a fresh tadka to revive.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jeera rice or laccha paratha, a side of sliced onions, green chilli and a lump of white butter melting on top.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Masoor Dal Punjabi
variations.description: This version reimagines the dal through a Maharashtrian lens, swapping garam masala for aromatic goda masala with its notes of dagad phool, sesame and coconut. The masala's dark, faintly sweet warmth turns a familiar dal into something earthy and distinctive. Groundnut oil and a coconut garnish complete the Deccan character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil is the everyday Maharashtrian cooking fat and complements goda masala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of ghee balances the dark spice of goda masala
