steps: Rinse 1 cup red lentils and pressure-cook with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft, then whisk smooth.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai over medium heat and add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds; when they pop add 0.5 tsp cumin, 1 pinch asafoetida and 1 sprig curry leaves.
Add 1 finely chopped large onion and fry until golden, about 6 minutes, then stir in 2 chopped tomatoes and cook until soft and pulpy, about 5 minutes.
Sprinkle in 1.5 tsp goda masala and fry for 1 minute until its dark aroma blooms and the oil takes on a rich brown colour.
Pour in the cooked dal with 0.25 cup hot water and simmer for 8 minutes so the goda masala infuses the lentils fully.
Finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee stirred in and garnish with 2 tbsp fresh grated coconut just before serving.
tips: Goda masala can turn bitter if scorched, so fry it only for a minute on moderate heat.
A teaspoon of jaggery is a common Maharashtrian touch that offsets the tomato's acidity.
Freshly grated coconut on top, not desiccated, gives the authentic moist finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or with bhakri and a wedge of lemon for a rustic Maharashtrian meal.

variations.name: Tamil Masoor Dal Punjabi
variations.description: A South Indian reinterpretation where the lentils become a paruppu-style dal, tempered with mustard, curry leaves and dried chillies in sesame oil and brightened with tamarind. It is soft, comforting and meant to be mashed into rice with a spoon of ghee. The curry-leaf-forward tadka gives it an unmistakably Tamil fragrance.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed gingelly oil is the defining Tamil tempering fat and lends a warm nuttiness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoon of ghee stirred into the finished paruppu is the classic Tamil serving touch

steps: Rinse 1 cup red lentils and pressure-cook with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 3 whistles until very soft, then mash lightly with the back of a ladle.
Stir 1 tbsp tamarind pulp into the dal and simmer for 3 minutes on low heat to cook out the raw sourness.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pan over medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them splutter fully.
Add 2 broken dried red chillies, 1 pinch asafoetida, 8 halved shallots, 4 sliced garlic cloves and 2 sprigs curry leaves, and fry until the shallots turn golden, about 4 minutes.
Add 1 chopped tomato to the tempering and cook until it softens, about 3 minutes, then pour the whole mixture into the dal.
Simmer the combined dal for 5 minutes, finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee, and serve warm.
tips: Frying the shallots slowly until deep gold is what gives this dal its subtle sweetness.
Keep the tamarind gentle so the dal stays comforting rather than sharply sour.
Leftovers thicken into a lovely paste that is delicious mixed with hot rice and ghee.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot rice with a spoon of ghee and a crisp appalam, alongside a simple poriyal for a homestyle Tamil plate.

variations.name: Kashmiri Masoor Dal Punjabi
variations.description: The Kashmiri rendition is aromatic and elegant, coloured with saffron and Kashmiri chilli, and perfumed with fennel and dried ginger in the Pandit style that avoids onion and garlic. Ghee carries the delicate spices and saffron lends both fragrance and a warm amber hue. It is a refined, gently spiced dal unlike the robust Punjabi original.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: a pinch of Kashmiri saffron bloomed in warm milk gives the dal its signature fragrance and amber colour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee is essential to carry the delicate fennel and saffron notes in this Pandit-style dal

steps: Soak 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside to bloom while you cook the dal.
Rinse 1 cup red lentils and pressure-cook with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft, then whisk smooth.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat and add 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, 2 cloves and 2 lightly crushed cardamom pods, frying until fragrant, about 30 seconds.
Lower the heat and add 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1 tsp fennel powder and 0.5 tsp dry ginger powder, stirring for 15 seconds so they bloom without burning.
Pour in the cooked dal with 0.25 cup hot water and the bloomed saffron milk, and simmer gently for 8 minutes until the colour deepens to amber and the aroma turns floral.
Rest the dal covered for 5 minutes so the spices settle, then serve warm.
tips: Blooming saffron in warm milk rather than water gives a rounder colour and aroma.
The dish is traditionally cooked without onion or garlic, so lean on fennel and ginger for depth.
Do not overload the chilli powder; Kashmiri chilli is for colour and mild warmth, not fierce heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice and a side of Kashmiri haakh or a simple yoghurt to let the saffron aroma shine.

variations.name: Rajasthani Masoor Dal Punjabi
variations.description: Built for the desert, this dal is bold and smoky, dominated by whole dried Mathania chillies and a garlic-forward tadka in ghee, with no fresh tomato to soften it. It leans on dry spices and a hint of amchur for tang, giving a punchy, rustic dal that stands up to bajra roti. A drama of red chillies floats on top as both garnish and warning.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee is used liberally in Rajasthani cooking where fresh vegetables are scarce and fat carries the spice

steps: Rinse 1 cup red lentils and pressure-cook with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft, then whisk to a medium-thick consistency.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 4 broken dried red chillies, and fry until the chillies darken and smell smoky, about 40 seconds.
Add 1 pinch asafoetida and 8 crushed garlic cloves and fry until the garlic is deep golden, about 2 minutes, then add 1 finely chopped onion and cook until browned, about 5 minutes.
Lower the heat and add 1 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp amchur, stirring for 20 seconds so they bloom in the ghee without scorching.
Pour in the cooked dal with 0.25 cup hot water and simmer for 8 minutes so the smoky, tangy masala saturates the lentils.
Ladle into bowls with the whole fried chillies on top and serve piping hot.
tips: Amchur stands in for fresh tomato here and keeps the dal true to the arid Rajasthani style.
Fry the whole chillies just until they puff and darken; burnt chillies turn the ghee bitter.
This dal reheats beautifully and is even punchier the next day.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra or makki roti and a dollop of ghee, plus raw onion and green chilli to match its rustic heat.

variations.name: Classic Masoor Dal Tadka
variations.description: Quick-cooking red lentils turn creamy in minutes and take beautifully to a fragrant ghee tadka of cumin, garlic and dried red chilli. Asafoetida keeps it light while the tempering delivers all the aroma. It is the fastest weeknight dal that still tastes like a treat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the ghee tadka poured over sizzling hot is the heart of this dal

steps: Rinse 1 cup masoor dal until the water runs clear, then pressure-cook it with 2.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 inch grated ginger and 0.5 tsp salt for 2 to 3 whistles until soft and creamy.
Whisk the cooked dal lightly and keep it warm on a low flame, loosening with hot water if it has thickened.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a tadka pan over medium heat until it shimmers, then add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them sizzle for 15 seconds until golden.
Add 5 sliced garlic cloves and 2 halved dried red chillies, frying 40 seconds until the garlic is golden, then stir in 0.25 tsp asafoetida.
Add 1 chopped onion and cook 4 minutes until soft, then add 1 chopped tomato, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp salt, and cook 3 minutes until pulpy.
Pour the sizzling tadka over the warm dal, simmer together 2 minutes, and finish with 2 tbsp coriander.
tips: Masoor dal cooks much faster than other lentils, so check after 2 whistles to keep it from turning to mush.
Pour the tadka over the dal just before serving so the tempering stays aromatic and pronounced.
A final drizzle of ghee with a pinch of red chilli powder on top makes it look restaurant-worthy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jeera rice or plain rice and a dollop of ghee, with papad and a simple salad on the side.

variations.name: Bengali Masoor Dal Tadka
variations.description: Bengali masoor dal, or musur dal, is an everyday favourite tempered in pungent mustard oil with kalonji and dried red chilli. Slit green chillies and a light body make it soothing rather than heavy. A finishing spoon of ghee gives it a comforting round aroma over rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil gives musur dal its true Bengali character

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon for the classic comforting aroma

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed masoor dal with 2.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 2 to 3 whistles until soft, then whisk to a smooth, pourable dal.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai over medium-high heat until it just smokes, then lower the flame to mellow its sharpness.
Add 0.5 tsp nigella seeds and 2 dried red chillies, letting them crackle for 15 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 finely chopped onion and fry 3 minutes until soft, then add 1 chopped tomato and cook 3 minutes until it breaks down.
Pour in the whisked dal with 2 slit green chillies and 0.5 tsp sugar, adjust salt, and simmer gently for 6 minutes.
Turn off the heat, drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee, garnish with 2 tbsp coriander, and serve warm.
tips: Nigella seeds, not cumin, are the classic tempering for Bengali musur dal and give a distinct oniony aroma.
Smoke the mustard oil first so its raw pungency softens into a clean, nutty flavour.
Keep the dal thin so it can be poured generously over rice in Bengali fashion.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice, a wedge of lime and a piece of aloo bhaja or fried fish on the side.

variations.name: Gujarati Masoor Dal Tadka
variations.description: A Gujarati-style masoor dal that plays sweet, sour and spicy with jaggery, tamarind and a ghee tempering of curry leaves and warm whole spices. The quick-cooking lentils turn light and frothy, perfect for sipping. Peanuts add a gentle bite to the smooth body.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee tempering rounds the sweet-sour Gujarati flavours

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the signature sweetness of a Gujarati dal

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed masoor dal with 2.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 2 tbsp raw peanuts for 3 whistles until the peanuts soften, then whisk smooth.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a deep pan over medium heat and add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds; when they pop, add 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, 1 inch cinnamon, 2 cloves, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 10 curry leaves.
Add 1 inch julienned ginger and 2 slit green chillies, frying 30 seconds until aromatic.
Pour in the whisked dal with 0.5 cup hot water, then stir in 1 tbsp jaggery powder, 1 tsp tamarind pulp and 1 tsp salt.
Simmer uncovered on low for 8 minutes, stirring often, until light and frothy with a settled sweet-sour balance.
Finish with 2 tbsp coriander and serve warm.
tips: Cook the peanuts with the dal so they turn creamy-soft rather than crunchy.
Balance jaggery and tamarind at the end, tasting until the sweet and sour notes are even.
Keep this dal thin and sippable, loosening with hot water if it thickens on standing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain rice and a wedge of lime, or as part of a Gujarati thali to balance spicier dishes.

variations.name: Kerala Masoor Dal Tadka
variations.description: A South Indian take that enriches red lentils with a smooth ground-coconut paste for a mellow, creamy body. Coconut oil tempering with mustard seeds, shallots and curry leaves lends the aroma of a Kerala kitchen. Gentle and subtly sweet, it pairs beautifully with rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil gives the dal its true Kerala fragrance

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed masoor dal with 2.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 2 slit green chillies for 2 to 3 whistles until soft, then mash lightly.
Grind 0.5 cup grated coconut with 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 3 garlic cloves to a smooth paste using a little water.
Stir the coconut paste into the cooked dal with 1 tsp salt and simmer 5 minutes on low heat until creamy and the raw coconut smell fades.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds until they pop.
Add 2 halved dried red chillies, 12 curry leaves and 5 sliced shallots, frying 4 minutes until the shallots turn deep golden.
Pour this tempering over the dal, stir once, cover for a minute to trap the aroma, and serve.
tips: Use freshly ground coconut rather than desiccated for the smoothest, sweetest body.
Fry the shallots slowly to a deep gold, as they carry much of the tempering's flavour.
Keep this dal on the thicker side so it can be mashed into rice with a spoon of ghee.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over matta or white rice with a drizzle of raw coconut oil and a spoon of ghee, followed by sambar and pickle.

variations.name: Andhra Masoor Dal Tadka
variations.description: A fiery Andhra rendition that heats up mild red lentils with smoky Guntur chillies and generous garlic in a sesame-oil tempering. Tomato and tamarind bring the signature tang while the roasted chillies bring the heat. Nutty and bold, it is dal with real character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: gingelly oil deepens the smoky Guntur-chilli flavour of Andhra dal

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed masoor dal with 2.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 chopped tomato and 4 garlic cloves for 3 whistles, then mash to a thick consistency.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadhai over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds for 15 seconds.
Add 4 broken Guntur chillies, the remaining 4 crushed garlic cloves, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 12 curry leaves, frying 40 seconds until the garlic is golden and the chillies smell smoky.
Add 1 finely chopped onion and cook 4 minutes until soft and lightly browned.
Fold in the mashed dal with 1 tsp tamarind pulp, 1 tsp salt and 0.5 cup hot water, then simmer 6 minutes until thick and tangy.
Finish with 2 tbsp coriander and serve hot.
tips: Cooking half the garlic in the dal and frying the rest gives both mellow sweetness and a sharp aromatic hit.
Adjust the Guntur chillies to taste, as they are far hotter than ordinary dried red chillies.
Keep the dal thick so it can be mixed into hot rice with a spoon of sesame oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice, a spoon of ghee and a fried papad, with mango pickle for the classic Andhra combination.

variations.name: Classic Mixed Dal Dhaba-style
variations.description: The smoky, robust dal of highway dhabas, slow-cooked in a heavy pot and finished with a live-coal smoking that gives it its signature roadside aroma. Kasuri methi, garam masala and a double ghee tempering make it bold, rich and unapologetically hearty.

ingredients.name: Mixed lentils (toor, masoor, chana, moong, urad)
Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A generous hand of bilona ghee gives dhaba dal its rich body and glossy top

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed mixed lentils with 3.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 5 whistles until very soft, then mash lightly to a thick creamy base.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadai over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds until golden and fragrant.
Add 8 minced garlic cloves, 1.5 inch grated ginger and 2 chopped green chillies, fry 1 minute, then add 2 chopped onions and cook until deep brown, about 8 minutes.

Stir in 3 chopped tomatoes with 1 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.75 tsp salt, cook until thick and the ghee separates, about 8 minutes, then add the cooked dal with hot water and simmer 10 minutes.

Sprinkle 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi and 0.75 tsp garam masala, then place a small steel bowl on the dal, add a red-hot coal to it, drizzle 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the coal and cover for 2 minutes to catch the smoke.
Lift out the coal bowl, stir the smoke through, finish with 3 tbsp coriander and serve piping hot.
tips: The coal smoking is what makes it taste like a dhaba, so do not skip it if you can manage it safely.
Cook the dal a little longer than usual; dhaba dal is prized for its slow-simmered, melt-in body.
A splash of hot water at the end keeps it pourable, as it thickens fast once off the heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a lohe ki kadai with a knob of butter, sliced onion, green chilli and lemon, alongside tandoori roti or laccha paratha.

variations.name: Andhra Mixed Dal Dhaba-style
variations.description: A fiery Andhra dhaba version stoked with Guntur red chillies and a garlicky gunpowder heat, tempered in sesame oil. It is scorching, deeply savoury and aromatic with curry leaves, built for eating with a generous mound of rice and a cooling side.

ingredients.name: Mixed lentils (toor, masoor, chana, moong, urad)
Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed sesame oil is the classic Andhra frying fat and stands up to the Guntur heat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of ghee makes the ferocious Guntur heat pleasurable

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed mixed lentils with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 4 whistles until soft, then whisk smooth and keep warm.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadai over medium heat, splutter 0.5 tsp mustard and 1 tsp cumin seeds, then snap in 5 Guntur chillies and 15 curry leaves and fry 30 seconds until crackling.
Add 10 crushed garlic cloves and fry until deep gold, about 90 seconds, then add 1 large chopped onion and cook until browned, roughly 6 minutes.
Stir in 2 chopped tomatoes with 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.75 tsp salt, and cook until the masala is dark and the oil separates, about 6 minutes.
Pour in the cooked dal with a splash of hot water and simmer for 8 minutes so the Guntur heat penetrates the whole pot.
Finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee to round the fire and scatter 2 tbsp coriander before serving.
tips: Guntur chilli heat builds, so start with fewer if unsure; you can always add more chilli powder later.
The ten cloves of garlic here are deliberate, giving the dal its pungent Andhra backbone.
Serve with something cooling like curd rice on the side to balance the intensity.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a big helping of steamed rice, ghee, a fried papad and cucumber raita to temper the heat.

variations.name: Bengali Mixed Dal Dhaba-style
variations.description: A Bengali roadside rendition tempered in smoking mustard oil with panch phoron and green chilli, sharper and more aromatic than the North Indian dhaba dal. The five-spice crackle and pungent oil give it an unmistakable eastern character, finished with a touch of ghee.

ingredients.name: Mixed lentils (toor, masoor, chana, moong, urad)
Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil gives the pungent kick that defines Bengali tempering

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A drizzle of ghee at the end rounds the sharpness of the mustard oil

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed mixed lentils with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 4 whistles until soft, then whisk to a smooth medium-thick dal.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai over medium-high until it lightens and just smokes, about 1 minute, to mellow the raw bite.
Lower the heat and add 1 tsp panch phoron, 1 bay leaf and 3 slit green chillies, letting them crackle for 30 seconds until the fenugreek darkens and smells toasty.

Add 7 crushed garlic cloves, 1 inch grated ginger and 1 large chopped onion and fry until golden, about 6 minutes, then stir in 2 chopped tomatoes, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.75 tsp salt and cook 5 minutes.
Pour in the cooked dal with a little hot water, add 0.25 tsp sugar to round the flavour, and simmer for 7 minutes so the panch phoron perfumes the pot.
Finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and 2 tbsp coriander, and serve hot.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to smoking then cool slightly; raw mustard oil tastes harsh and bitter.
Leave the panch phoron whole for little bursts of aroma; grinding it flattens the effect.
The pinch of sugar is a Bengali habit that quietly lifts the spices without sweetening the dal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice, a wedge of lime, aloo bhaja and a fried papad for a comforting Bengali-style meal.

variations.name: Gujarati Mixed Dal Dhaba-style
variations.description: A Gujarati sweet-sour take on the hearty dhaba dal, mellowed with jaggery and tamarind and lifted by a curry-leaf tempering. Lighter and more rounded than the fiery northern original, it balances warmth with a gentle sweetness and a whisper of peanut crunch.

ingredients.name: Mixed lentils (toor, masoor, chana, moong, urad)
Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries the curry-leaf and mustard tempering of a Gujarati dal

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Melts in to give the gentle sweetness that balances the tamarind

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed mixed lentils with 3.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 2 tbsp soaked peanuts for 4 whistles until the peanuts are tender and the dal soft.
Whisk the dal thin, then stir in 1 tbsp tamarind pulp, 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 chopped tomato and 1.25 tsp salt and simmer gently for 8 minutes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan over medium heat and add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds; when they pop after 20 seconds add 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida.
Drop in 10 curry leaves, 2 slit green chillies and 1 inch julienned ginger and let them crackle for 30 seconds until the leaves turn translucent.
Pour the tempering into the simmering dal, stir well and let it bubble for 3 minutes so the sweet-sour-spiced flavours settle into balance.
Taste and adjust the jaggery-tamarind balance, finish with 2 tbsp coriander and serve hot.
tips: Keep it thinner than a typical dhaba dal; Gujaratis pour it over rice like a light broth.
Add jaggery after the tamarind so you can tune the sweet-sour balance in small steps.
Soak the peanuts for an hour so they cook soft rather than staying hard in the dal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot rice with a spoon of ghee, or as the dal course of a Gujarati thali with kadhi, rotli and a vegetable shaak.

variations.name: Kumaoni Mixed Dal Dhaba-style
variations.description: A Kumaoni hill-station version tempered with jakhya, the tiny wild mustard-like seeds of Uttarakhand that crackle and pop with a nutty crunch. Cooked simply in ghee with garlic and dried chilli, it is rustic, aromatic and warming, the way it is eaten in the mountains.

ingredients.name: Mixed lentils (toor, masoor, chana, moong, urad)
Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Pahadi kitchens temper jakhya in pure ghee for the best crackle and aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: A little wood-pressed mustard oil gives the earthy mountain note typical of Kumaon

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed mixed lentils with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 4 whistles until soft, then whisk to a smooth medium consistency.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pan over medium heat until shimmering, about 1 minute.
Add 1 tsp jakhya seeds and 2 dried red chillies and let them crackle and pop for about 30 seconds until they smell nutty and toasted.
Add 6 crushed garlic cloves and 1 inch grated ginger, fry for 1 minute, then add 1 chopped onion and cook until golden, about 5 minutes.
Stir in 1 chopped tomato, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander powder and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, and cook for 4 minutes until pulpy.
Pour in the cooked dal with a little hot water, simmer for 6 minutes, finish with 2 tbsp coriander and serve hot.
tips: Jakhya must crackle fully in hot fat to release its signature nutty crunch, so wait for the popping to peak.
If you cannot find jakhya, a mix of cumin and a few mustard seeds approximates the texture, though not the flavour.
Keep the spicing simple and let the jakhya and mountain ghee be the stars of this rustic dal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice, a hill-style bhang ki chutney and a simple green vegetable, or with plain roti and ghee.

variations.name: Classic Mixed Dal Fry
variations.description: Where tadka dal is tempered at the end, dal fry cooks the boiled lentils right into a well-browned onion-tomato masala so the flavours fuse into a thicker, restaurant-style bowl. The result is a homogenous, deeply savoury dal with a glossy sheen and none of the split-tempering separation.

ingredients.name: Mixed lentils (toor, masoor, chana, moong, urad)
Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Frying the masala in bilona ghee gives dal fry its signature rich, rounded body

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed mixed lentils with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 4 whistles until soft, then mash lightly so the dal is thick but still spoonable.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds until fragrant and golden.
Add 7 minced garlic cloves, 1 inch grated ginger and 2 chopped green chillies, fry for 1 minute, then add 2 finely chopped onions and cook until richly golden brown, about 7 minutes.
Stir in 2 chopped tomatoes with 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander powder and the remaining 0.75 tsp salt, and cook until the masala is thick and the ghee separates, about 6 minutes.
Tip the cooked dal into the masala, add a little hot water to loosen, and let it fry-simmer for 8 minutes, stirring often so the dal soaks up the browned masala.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala and 3 tbsp coriander, stir through and serve hot with a final drizzle of ghee.
tips: The key to dal fry is browning the onions properly; pale onions give a raw, flat masala.
Keep stirring once the dal goes in, as the thick mixture catches and scorches easily on the base.
Leftover dal fry thickens overnight and makes an excellent stuffing loosened with a little water for parathas.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a kadai topped with fried ginger juliennes and a swirl of ghee, with jeera rice, tandoori roti and a kachumber salad.

variations.name: Andhra Mixed Dal Fry
variations.description: A fiery Andhra rendition powered by Guntur red chillies, which bring searing heat and a bright crimson colour. Curry leaves and a garlic-heavy tempering make it aromatic as well as hot, the kind of dal that demands a mound of rice and a spoon of ghee to tame it.

ingredients.name: Mixed lentils (toor, masoor, chana, moong, urad)
Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed sesame oil is the classic frying fat of Andhra cooking and stands up to the Guntur heat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Stirred in at the end to mellow the ferocious Guntur chilli heat

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed mixed lentils with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 4 whistles until soft, then whisk to a smooth medium-thick dal.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadai over medium heat, splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp cumin seeds, then snap in 4 Guntur red chillies and 12 curry leaves and fry for 30 seconds until crackling and fragrant.
Add 8 crushed garlic cloves and fry until pale gold, about 1 minute, then add 1 chopped onion and cook until soft and light brown, roughly 5 minutes.
Stir in 2 chopped tomatoes, 1 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.75 tsp salt, and cook until the masala darkens and the oil separates, about 6 minutes.
Add the cooked dal with a splash of hot water and simmer for 8 minutes so the Guntur heat works right through the dal.
Finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee to gentle the spice and scatter 2 tbsp coriander before serving.
tips: Guntur chillies are intensely hot, so deseed a couple if you want colour and aroma without full firepower.
The spoon of ghee at the end is not optional here; it is what makes the ferocious heat pleasurable.
Fry the curry leaves until crisp so they shatter into the dal and release their full citrusy aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plenty of steamed rice, a dollop of ghee, fried papad and a cooling cucumber raita to balance the fire.

variations.name: Kerala Mixed Dal Fry
variations.description: A coconut-rich southern version where freshly grated coconut and coconut oil soften the dal into something mellow and creamy. Curry leaves, shallots and a whisper of black pepper give it a coastal fragrance, worlds away from the tomato-heavy northern fry.

ingredients.name: Mixed lentils (toor, masoor, chana, moong, urad)
Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed coconut oil gives the unmistakable Kerala aroma to the tempering

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A last spoon of ghee deepens the coconut and pepper finish

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed mixed lentils with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 4 whistles until soft, then whisk lightly and keep warm.
Grind 0.5 cup grated coconut with 4 garlic cloves and a splash of water to a coarse paste, and set it aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan over medium heat, splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds with 2 dried red chillies and 12 curry leaves for 20 seconds until they crackle.
Add 8 sliced shallots and fry until soft and golden, about 4 minutes, then add 1 chopped tomato and cook for 3 minutes until it breaks down.
Stir in the coconut-garlic paste and 0.5 tsp black pepper and fry for 2 minutes until the raw smell disappears and the mixture smells sweet and nutty.
Add the cooked dal with a little hot water, simmer for 6 minutes until creamy, then finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and check the salt before serving.
tips: Grind the coconut coarse, not smooth, so you still get little bursts of texture in the finished dal.
Shallots dissolve into a natural sweetness that ordinary onions cannot match, so seek them out for this one.
Add the coconut paste on low heat; boiling it hard can make the coconut split and turn grainy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with matta red rice, a spoon of extra coconut oil, and pappadam, with a tart mango pickle on the side.

variations.name: Kashmiri Mixed Dal Fry
variations.description: An aromatic Kashmiri interpretation gilded with saffron and warm ground fennel, ginger and Kashmiri chilli for colour without harsh heat. It is fragrant, faintly floral and a deep red, the kind of gentle, festive dal that pairs with a Wazwan spread.

ingredients.name: Mixed lentils (toor, masoor, chana, moong, urad)
Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Kashmiri cooking leans on ghee, and it carries the saffron and fennel beautifully

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: A saffron pinch bloomed in warm milk gives the dal its floral aroma and golden glow

steps: Soak a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside so it releases its colour and aroma while you cook.
Cook 1 cup rinsed mixed lentils in the pressure cooker with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 4 whistles, then release the pressure and whisk to a smooth, medium-thick base.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat and add 1 tsp cumin seeds, 2 cardamom pods and 2 cloves, letting them sizzle for 30 seconds until fragrant.

Add 1 finely chopped onion and fry until soft and pale gold, about 5 minutes, then stir in 1 tsp fennel powder, 0.5 tsp ginger powder and 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder off the heat so they do not burn.
Return to the heat, add 1 chopped tomato and 0.75 tsp salt, and cook for 4 minutes until the masala is soft, then pour in the cooked dal with a little hot water and simmer for 8 minutes.
Stir in the saffron milk, simmer for 2 more minutes, and finish with 2 tbsp coriander so the floral aroma stays bright.
tips: Blooming saffron in warm milk rather than water gives a rounder colour and a mellower, less bitter aroma.
Ground fennel and dry ginger are the backbone of Kashmiri masala; toast them only briefly to keep them sweet.
Use Kashmiri chilli for that ruby colour without heat, and add fresh chilli separately only if you want a kick.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice, a Kashmiri haakh or a mild yakhni, finishing the plate with a thread of saffron milk for aroma.

variations.name: Odia Mixed Dal Fry
variations.description: An Odia-style dal fry tempered with panch phoron and finished with a whisper of roasted cumin, keeping it light, homely and fragrant. A tempering of dried chilli and garlic in mustard oil gives it eastern warmth without heaviness, the way it is cooked in everyday Odisha kitchens.

ingredients.name: Mixed lentils (toor, masoor, chana, moong, urad)
Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil gives the earthy sharpness typical of Odia tempering

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A final spoon of ghee with roasted cumin is the classic Odia finishing touch

steps: Boil 1 cup rinsed mixed lentils with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt in a pressure cooker for 4 whistles until tender, then whisk the dal smooth and keep it warm.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pan over medium-high until it lightens and just smokes, about 1 minute, to take off the raw bite.
Lower the heat, add 1 tsp panch phoron and 2 dried red chillies, and let them crackle for 30 seconds until the fenugreek darkens slightly and smells nutty.
Add 6 crushed garlic cloves and 1 chopped onion and fry until golden, about 5 minutes, then stir in 1 chopped tomato, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 0.75 tsp salt and cook for 4 minutes until soft.
Add the cooked dal with a little hot water and let it fry-simmer for 7 minutes so the panch phoron flavour steeps through.
Finish by heating 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee with 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder and pouring it over, then scatter 2 tbsp coriander and serve.
tips: Roast the cumin for the finish in a dry pan until dark and fragrant, then grind it fresh for the best aroma.
Keep the dal on the thinner side; Odia dal is meant to mix easily into hot rice.
Bite-sized bursts of whole panch phoron are the point, so resist grinding the mix.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice, a spoon of ghee and a fried brinjal or potato bhaja, with a lime wedge on the side.

variations.name: Classic Mixed Dal Home-style
variations.description: The unfussy weeknight dal that most Indian homes cook on autopilot, softer and lighter than the restaurant fry, with a simple single tempering and no heavy masala. It is gently spiced, quick and forgiving, meant to be comforting rather than showy.

ingredients.name: Mixed lentils (toor, masoor, chana, moong, urad)
Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A simple cumin-garlic tadka in bilona ghee is all this homely dal needs

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed mixed lentils with 3.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 chopped tomato, 1 inch grated ginger and 0.75 tsp salt for 4 whistles until soft.
Open the cooker, whisk the dal to a smooth, slightly loose consistency, and keep it warm on a low flame.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds with 0.25 tsp asafoetida for about 20 seconds.
Add 5 crushed garlic cloves and 1 slit green chilli and fry until the garlic is golden, about 1 minute, then add 1 chopped onion and cook until soft, roughly 4 minutes.
Stir in the second chopped tomato, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, and cook for 3 minutes until pulpy.
Pour the tempering into the dal, simmer together for 5 minutes, then finish with 2 tbsp coriander and serve hot.
tips: Cooking one tomato inside the cooker with the dal saves a step and gives a gentle background tang.
This dal is meant to be light; add extra hot water freely if it thickens as it sits.
A squeeze of lemon at the table brightens the whole bowl without changing the simple character.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice, a spoon of ghee and a simple sabzi, or with hot phulkas for an easy everyday meal.

variations.name: Tamil Mixed Dal Home-style
variations.description: A Tamil household version tempered with curry leaves, mustard and a hint of black pepper, closer in spirit to a paruppu than a North Indian dal. Fresh curry leaves and a garlicky sesame-oil tempering give it a distinct southern fragrance, soft and comforting over rice.

ingredients.name: Mixed lentils (toor, masoor, chana, moong, urad)
Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil is the everyday tempering fat of Tamil homes

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon of ghee stirred into hot dal is a beloved Tamil finishing habit

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed mixed lentils with 3.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 4 whistles until soft, then mash smooth and keep warm.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pan over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds until they pop.
Add 2 dried red chillies, 15 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them crackle for 15 seconds until the curry leaves crisp up and smell fragrant.
Add 6 sliced shallots and 5 crushed garlic cloves and fry until soft and golden, about 4 minutes, then stir in 1 chopped tomato and 0.5 tsp black pepper and cook for 3 minutes.
Pour in the cooked dal with the remaining 0.5 tsp salt and a little hot water, and simmer for 6 minutes so the tempering flavours the dal.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee just before serving for the traditional finishing aroma.
tips: Black pepper rather than heavy chilli is what gives this dal its gentle Tamil warmth, so do not overdo the red chilli.
Fry the curry leaves until they turn crisp so they crumble into the dal and release their full aroma.
Shallots melt into a natural sweetness; if using regular onion, cook it a couple of minutes longer.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot rice with a spoon of ghee and a fried appalam, alongside a dry poriyal and a piece of lime pickle.

variations.name: Karnataka Mixed Dal Home-style
variations.description: A Karnataka-style dal with the gentle sweet-sour balance of tamarind and a pinch of jaggery, close to a light saaru in character. A coconut-oil tempering and a hint of rasam-style spicing make it aromatic and tangy rather than rich, easy to drink over rice.

ingredients.name: Mixed lentils (toor, masoor, chana, moong, urad)
Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil gives the coastal Karnataka fragrance to the mustard-curry leaf tempering

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A little jaggery rounds the tamarind sourness in classic Karnataka style

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed mixed lentils with 3.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 4 whistles until soft, then whisk to a thin, pourable dal.
Stir 1 tbsp tamarind pulp, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 chopped tomato, 1 tsp rasam powder and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt into the dal and simmer gently for 8 minutes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds until popping.
Add 2 dried red chillies, 12 curry leaves, 4 crushed garlic cloves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and fry for 30 seconds until the garlic is golden and the leaves crisp.
Pour the tempering into the simmering dal, stir well and let it bubble for 3 more minutes so the sweet-sour-spiced flavours settle.
Taste for the tamarind-jaggery balance, finish with 2 tbsp coriander and serve hot.
tips: Add the tamarind before the jaggery so you can dial in the sour-sweet balance a little at a time.
Keep this dal loose and soup-like; it is meant to be mixed generously into hot rice.
A store-bought rasam powder works well here, but toast it for a few seconds in the tempering oil to wake it up.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over steaming rice with a spoon of ghee and a crisp sandige or papad, with a dry vegetable palya on the side.

variations.name: Bihari Mixed Dal Home-style
variations.description: A rustic Bihari version tempered in pungent mustard oil with garlic, dried chilli and a generous crackle of cumin, the way it accompanies litti or plain rice in Bihar. The mustard oil gives it a bold, earthy sharpness, and it is kept simple, thick and satisfying.

ingredients.name: Mixed lentils (toor, masoor, chana, moong, urad)
Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil gives the bold, sharp tempering typical of Bihari kitchens

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A final spoon of ghee softens the pungency of the mustard oil tadka

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed mixed lentils with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 4 whistles until soft, then whisk to a thick, homely consistency.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pan over medium-high until it lightens and just smokes, about 1 minute, to mellow the raw pungency.
Add 1 tsp cumin seeds, 3 dried red chillies and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them crackle for 30 seconds until dark and aromatic.
Add 7 crushed garlic cloves and 1 inch grated ginger and fry for 1 minute, then add 1 chopped onion and cook until deep golden, about 5 minutes.
Stir in 1 chopped tomato, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, and cook for 4 minutes until the masala thickens and the oil edges out.
Pour in the cooked dal with a little hot water, simmer for 6 minutes, then finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and 2 tbsp coriander before serving.
tips: Get the mustard oil properly hot first; under-heated mustard oil leaves a raw, bitter aftertaste.
Bihari dal is generous with garlic, so do not be shy with the seven cloves; it is central to the flavour.
Keep it thicker than a tadka dal so it stands up well to litti or a coarse rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with baati or litti crushed into it with extra ghee, or with plain rice, raw onion and a green chilli.

variations.name: Malwa Mixed Dal Home-style
variations.description: A Malwa-region dal from the Madhya Pradesh heartland, given nutty body and crunch with roasted peanuts and a simple ghee tempering. The peanuts, coarsely crushed, thicken the dal and lend a gentle sweetness, making it hearty and distinctly central-Indian.

ingredients.name: Mixed lentils (toor, masoor, chana, moong, urad)
Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee toasts the peanuts and carries the cumin tempering in true Malwa style

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A little wood-pressed groundnut oil echoes and deepens the peanut flavour

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed mixed lentils with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 4 whistles until soft, then whisk smooth and keep warm.
Coarsely crush 3 tbsp roasted peanuts in a mortar, leaving some texture, and set aside for the finish.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, 2 dried red chillies and 0.25 tsp asafoetida for 30 seconds.

Add 5 crushed garlic cloves and 1 chopped onion and fry until golden, about 5 minutes, then stir in 1 chopped tomato, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander powder and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt and cook for 4 minutes.
Pour in the cooked dal with a little hot water, add most of the crushed peanuts, and simmer for 7 minutes so the peanuts soften and thicken the dal.
Finish with 2 tbsp coriander and the reserved crushed peanuts sprinkled on top for crunch, then serve hot.
tips: Reserve a spoon of crushed peanuts to scatter at the end so you keep some crunch against the soft dal.
Roast the peanuts a shade darker than usual for a deeper, sweeter nuttiness through the dal.
If the peanuts thicken it too much, loosen with hot water; they keep absorbing liquid as it stands.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar or bajra roti and a spoon of ghee, or with plain rice and a raw onion-tomato salad for a Malwa-style meal.

variations.name: Classic Mixed Dal Punjabi
variations.description: The full-bodied Punjabi mixed dal, slow-simmered and finished with butter, kasuri methi and garam masala for that unmistakable dhaba richness. Creamy, mildly smoky and deeply savoury, it is built around a well-browned onion-tomato-ginger-garlic base and a double dose of good fat.

ingredients.name: Mixed lentils (toor, masoor, chana, moong, urad)
Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee gives the base its rich, rounded dhaba character

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed mixed lentils with 3.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 5 whistles until very soft, then mash lightly so the dal is thick and creamy.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadai over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds until golden.
Add 8 minced garlic cloves, 1.5 inch grated ginger and 2 chopped green chillies, fry for 1 minute, then add 2 finely chopped onions and cook slowly until deep golden brown, about 8 minutes.
Stir in 3 chopped tomatoes with 1 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.75 tsp salt, and cook down to a thick pulpy masala until the ghee separates, about 8 minutes.
Tip in the cooked dal with a little hot water and simmer for 8 minutes, stirring so the base does not catch, until the dal is glossy and unified.
Melt 2 tbsp butter with 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi and 0.75 tsp garam masala, pour over the dal, fold in 3 tbsp coriander and serve hot.
tips: Deeply browned onions are non-negotiable here; they give the caramel sweetness that defines the dish.
Crush the kasuri methi between your palms before adding to release its full aroma into the butter.
For a dhaba-style smokiness, finish with a quick coal smoking under a covered lid for two minutes.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a kadai with a melting cube of butter, laccha onion and lemon, alongside butter naan or jeera rice.

variations.name: Rajasthani Mixed Dal Punjabi
variations.description: A desert-state take that swaps the fresh onion-tomato gravy for a bold ghee tempering of whole dried red chillies and a yogurt-based tang, the way water-scarce Rajasthani kitchens once cooked. It is smoky, ghee-rich and gently sour, robust enough to eat with baati.

ingredients.name: Mixed lentils (toor, masoor, chana, moong, urad)
Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rajasthani dal is famously generous with ghee, which carries the whole-chilli tadka

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed mixed lentils with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 4 whistles until soft, then whisk smooth and keep warm.
Whisk 0.25 cup yogurt with 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder to a smooth spiced slurry and set aside.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat and add 1 tsp cumin seeds, 3 cloves, 1 bay leaf and 0.25 tsp asafoetida, letting them sizzle for 30 seconds.
Add 4 whole dried red chillies, 6 crushed garlic cloves and 1 inch grated ginger and fry for 1 minute until the chillies darken and the garlic is golden.
Lower the heat and pour in the yogurt slurry, stirring continuously for 3 minutes so it does not split, until the ghee separates and the masala smells cooked.
Add the cooked dal with the remaining 0.5 tsp salt and a little hot water, simmer for 6 minutes, then finish with 2 tbsp coriander and serve hot.
tips: Add the yogurt on low heat and keep stirring so it thickens the dal instead of curdling into lumps.
This dal is meant to be ghee-forward, so resist cutting the quantity if you want the authentic taste.
Whole dried chillies give smoky aroma more than heat, so leave them whole and lift them out if serving to children.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with ghee-soaked baati crushed into the dal, or with steamed rice and a side of garlic chutney.

variations.name: Goan Mixed Dal Punjabi
variations.description: A Goan coastal spin brightened with kokum and coconut, giving the dal a tangy-sweet edge and a mellow richness unlike any northern version. A coconut-oil tempering of curry leaves and dried chilli makes it fragrant and summery, the sourness coming from kokum rather than tomato.

ingredients.name: Mixed lentils (toor, masoor, chana, moong, urad)
Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed coconut oil is the defining cooking fat of Goan kitchens

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of ghee balances the tang of kokum

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed mixed lentils with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 4 whistles until soft, then whisk to a smooth medium consistency.
Soak 4 kokum petals in a little warm water, then add them with their soaking liquid to the dal along with 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and simmer for 8 minutes.
Grind 0.33 cup grated coconut to a smooth paste with a splash of water, stir it into the dal and simmer for 3 more minutes until it turns creamy.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds.
Add 2 dried red chillies, 10 curry leaves, 5 crushed garlic cloves and 1 chopped small onion and fry until golden, about 4 minutes.
Pour the tempering into the dal, add the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, simmer for 2 minutes, finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and 2 tbsp coriander, then serve.
tips: Kokum gives a fruity sourness quite different from tamarind; start with four petals and add more only if needed.
Grind the coconut smooth for a creamy body, or leave it coarse if you prefer a more textured dal.
Remove the softened kokum petals before serving so no one bites into a sharply sour piece.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice, a Goan sol kadhi on the side, and a fried fish or a simple potato bhaji.

variations.name: Hyderabadi Mixed Dal Punjabi
variations.description: A regal Hyderabadi treatment perfumed with saffron and a hint of green cardamom, richer and more fragrant than the everyday dal. Fried onions and a saffron-milk finish give it a Nizami elegance, mildly spiced and aromatic rather than fiery.

ingredients.name: Mixed lentils (toor, masoor, chana, moong, urad)
Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee fries the onions and carries the cardamom aroma in this Nizami-style dal

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Saffron bloomed in warm milk gives the dal its fragrance and golden tint

steps: Soak a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside to release its colour while you cook.
Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed mixed lentils with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 4 whistles until soft, then whisk smooth and keep warm.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 3 lightly crushed cardamom pods, and fry for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add 2 thinly sliced onions and fry patiently until deep golden and almost crisp, about 8 minutes, then add 6 minced garlic cloves and 1 inch grated ginger and fry for 1 minute.
Stir in 1 chopped tomato, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.75 tsp salt, cook for 4 minutes, then add the cooked dal with a little hot water and simmer for 6 minutes.
Stir in the saffron milk and 0.5 tsp garam masala, simmer 2 minutes, finish with 2 tbsp coriander and serve fragrant and hot.
tips: Fry the onions slowly to a deep gold; their sweetness and slight crispness define the Nizami character.
Bloom saffron in warm milk, not water, for a rounder colour and gentler aroma.
Bruise the cardamom pods just enough to open them so they perfume without turning the dal bitter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed basmati or a mild pulao, a wedge of lime and a crisp onion salad, garnished with a few saffron threads.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Mixed Dal Punjabi
variations.description: A Deccan reworking that trades the Punjabi butter for goda masala and a coconut-groundnut tempering, giving a dark, sweet-warm depth. It carries the roasted, faintly sweet signature of Maharashtrian spicing and a bright lemon finish, distinctly different from the creamy northern original.

ingredients.name: Mixed lentils (toor, masoor, chana, moong, urad)
Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the everyday Maharashtrian fat and toasts the goda masala well

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon stirred in at the end softens the goda masala's sharp edge

steps: Boil 1 cup rinsed mixed lentils in a pressure cooker with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 4 whistles until tender, then whisk to a smooth, pourable dal and keep warm.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan over medium heat, splutter 0.5 tsp mustard and 0.75 tsp cumin seeds with 10 curry leaves for 20 seconds until popping.
Add 5 crushed garlic cloves and 1 chopped onion, fry until soft and golden for about 4 minutes, then dry-toast 2 tbsp grated dry coconut in with them for 1 minute until nutty.
Stir in 1 chopped tomato, 1.5 tsp goda masala, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.75 tsp salt, and cook for 3 minutes until dark and glossy.
Pour in the cooked dal with a little hot water and simmer for 6 minutes so the goda masala infuses fully.
Finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 2 tbsp coriander and a squeeze of lemon to lift the sweet-earthy flavour, then serve.
tips: Add goda masala with the tomato, never into smoking oil, or it turns bitter.
Toasting the dry coconut with the onions deepens the flavour; raw coconut leaves the dal tasting flat.
A pinch of jaggery in place of lemon gives the sweeter Vidarbha-style balance if you prefer it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or with jowar bhakri, raw onion and papad for a rustic Maharashtrian plate.

variations.name: Classic Moong Dal Dhaba-style
variations.description: Roadside dhaba moong dal is smoky, robust and full of char-grilled aroma from a live coal finish. A deeply browned onion-tomato masala with garam masala and kasuri methi gives it a rustic, no-frills punch. This is the dal that tastes best eaten off a charpai with hot tandoori roti.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee gives the dhaba dal its glossy body and carries the smoky finish

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 3 to 4 whistles until soft, then keep aside lightly mashed.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add 6 chopped garlic cloves, 1 inch grated ginger and 2 slit green chillies and fry 40 seconds.
Add 2 finely chopped onions and cook for 8 minutes until deep golden brown, the crucial step for the dhaba flavour.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes with 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp coriander powder, and cook 6 minutes until pulpy and the ghee separates at the edges.
Fold in the cooked dal with 0.5 cup hot water and 0.5 tsp salt, simmer 8 minutes, then crush in 1 tbsp kasuri methi and 0.5 tsp garam masala.
For the dhungar finish, rest a red-hot coal in a small bowl on the dal, pour a few drops of ghee over it, cover for 2 minutes, remove the coal, garnish with 2 tbsp coriander and serve.
tips: The coal smoking step is what makes it taste like a real dhaba, so do not skip it if you can manage a live coal.
Deeply browned onions are essential; a pale saute will never give the rustic depth this dal needs.
Keep the dal medium-thick so the smoky masala clings rather than washing out in a watery base.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tandoori roti or laccha paratha, sliced onions, green chilli and a wedge of lemon for the full highway-dhaba plate.

variations.name: Punjabi Moong Dal Dhaba-style
variations.description: A richer Amritsari-style rendering that turns the dhaba dal creamy and buttery, finished with fresh cream and a foaming butter tadka. Tomato puree and kasuri methi give it a smooth, makhani-like body. It is indulgent, silky and made for mopping up with naan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee builds the base before a butter finish for classic Punjabi richness

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 4 whistles until very soft, then whisk into a smooth, creamy dal.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1 crushed black cardamom, then add 6 grated garlic cloves and 1 inch grated ginger and fry 40 seconds.
Add 1 large finely chopped onion and cook 6 minutes until golden, then add 3 pureed tomatoes with 1 tsp red chilli powder and simmer 8 minutes until thick and the ghee separates.
Pour in the whisked dal with 0.5 cup hot water and 0.5 tsp salt, stir in 2 tbsp cashew paste, and simmer on low for 8 minutes, stirring, until glossy and velvety.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the dal, stir in 3 tbsp cream and 0.5 tsp garam masala, and cook 2 minutes on low.
Melt 2 tbsp butter until foaming, pour it over the dal, garnish with 2 tbsp coriander, and serve hot.
tips: Pureeing the tomatoes rather than chopping gives the smooth, makhani-style body this version is known for.
Add the cream on gentle heat and avoid a hard boil afterwards so it does not split.
For extra richness, finish with a small pat of white butter melting on top at the table.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or garlic naan and a side of pickled onions, with an extra swirl of cream and butter on top.

variations.name: Gujarati Moong Dal Dhaba-style
variations.description: A Gujarati twist that lightens the dhaba dal into a sweet-sour, sippable version with jaggery, tamarind and peanuts. A ghee tempering of mustard, curry leaves and warm whole spices replaces the heavy garam masala. It is bright, gently spiced and easy to drink alongside rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee tempering carries the light sweet-sour Gujarati flavours

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the signature sweetness of a Gujarati dal

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 2 tbsp raw peanuts for 4 whistles until the peanuts soften, then whisk smooth.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a deep pan over medium heat and add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds; when they pop, add 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, 1 inch cinnamon, 2 cloves, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 10 curry leaves.
Add 1 inch julienned ginger and 2 slit green chillies, frying for 30 seconds until aromatic.
Pour in the whisked dal with 0.5 cup hot water, then stir in 1.5 tbsp jaggery powder, 1.5 tsp tamarind pulp and 1 tsp salt.
Simmer uncovered on low for 10 minutes, stirring often, until light and frothy with a settled sweet-sour balance.
Finish with 2 tbsp coriander and serve warm.
tips: Cook the peanuts with the dal so they turn creamy-soft rather than staying crunchy.
Adjust jaggery and tamarind at the end until the khatti-meethi flavour is even and bright.
Keep it thin and pourable, adding hot water if the dal thickens on standing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain rice and a wedge of lime, or as part of a Gujarati thali to balance spicier dishes on the plate.

variations.name: Bengali Moong Dal Dhaba-style
variations.description: A Bengali interpretation where the dal is roasted for a nutty depth then tempered in pungent mustard oil with panch phoron and bay leaf. It swaps the North Indian coal-smoke for the aroma of five-spice and smoked mustard oil. A finishing spoon of ghee gives it a comforting round finish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil brings the authentic Bengali pungency

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon for the classic roasted-moong aroma

steps: Dry-roast 1 cup moong dal over medium heat for 4 to 5 minutes until nutty and golden, rinse quickly, then pressure-cook with 3 cups water and 0.5 tsp turmeric for 3 whistles.
Whisk the roasted cooked dal to a smooth, pourable consistency and set aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai over medium-high heat until it lightly smokes, lower the flame, then add 1 tsp panch phoron, 1 bay leaf and 2 dried red chillies and crackle 20 seconds.
Stir in 1 inch grated ginger and 1 chopped tomato, cook 4 minutes until soft, then add 0.5 tsp cumin powder and fry 30 seconds.
Pour in the roasted dal with 2 slit green chillies, 0.5 tsp sugar and 1 tsp salt, and simmer 6 minutes until the smoky flavour infuses.
Turn off the heat, drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee, garnish with 2 tbsp coriander, and serve.
tips: Roasting the dal gives the depth that the classic dhaba version gets from coal smoke.
Heat the mustard oil to smoking first to strip its raw bite before tempering.
Toast the panch phoron only until the fennel is fragrant, since burnt fenugreek turns it bitter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and aloo bhaja, or with luchi for a festive Bengali spread.

variations.name: Andhra Moong Dal Dhaba-style
variations.description: A fiery Andhra-style dhaba dal built on smoky Guntur chillies, generous garlic and a sesame-oil tempering. Tamarind lends the signature tang while roasted chillies bring serious heat. Thick and bold, it is a dal for those who want their roadside meal to bite back.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: gingelly oil deepens the smoky Guntur-chilli heat of Andhra dal

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 chopped tomato and 4 garlic cloves for 3 whistles, then mash to a thick consistency.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadhai over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds for 15 seconds.
Add 4 broken Guntur chillies, the remaining 4 crushed garlic cloves, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 12 curry leaves, frying 40 seconds until the garlic is golden and the chillies smell smoky.
Add 1 finely chopped onion and cook 5 minutes until soft and lightly caramelised.
Fold in the mashed dal with 2 tsp tamarind pulp, 1 tsp salt and 0.5 cup hot water, then simmer 6 minutes until thick and glossy.
Finish with 2 tbsp coriander and serve hot.
tips: Cook half the garlic in the dal and fry the rest for a double layer of mellow and sharp garlic notes.
Adjust the Guntur chillies to your heat tolerance, as they are far hotter than ordinary dried chillies.
Keep the dal thick so it clings to rice in true Andhra style.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot rice with a spoon of raw sesame oil and a fried papad, adding avakaya pickle for the full Andhra effect.

variations.name: Classic Moong Dal Fry
variations.description: Unlike a light tadka dal, moong dal fry has a properly bhuna-ed onion-tomato masala cooked in ghee until the fat separates, then the boiled dal is folded in and reduced thick. The frying step gives it a deeper, restaurant-style flavour and a richer colour. It is hearty enough to be the centrepiece of a rice plate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the masala is fried in ghee until it separates for that rich fry-style body

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed split moong dal with 2.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft, then set aside without whisking so it keeps some texture.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 15 seconds, then add 6 minced garlic cloves and 1 inch grated ginger and fry for 40 seconds.
Add 2 finely chopped onions and 2 slit green chillies, cooking for 7 to 8 minutes until the onions turn a deep golden brown, which builds the fry-style base.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes with 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp coriander powder, and cook for 6 minutes until the tomatoes break down and the ghee separates and pools at the sides.
Fold in the cooked dal along with 0.5 cup hot water and 0.5 tsp salt, then simmer for 6 minutes, stirring, until thick and glossy and the masala clings to the dal.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala and 2 tbsp chopped coriander, cook 1 more minute, and serve.
tips: The key to fry dal is patience with the onions; deep golden onions give the sweetness and colour that a pale saute cannot.
Keep this dal thick and scoopable rather than soupy, adding water only a little at a time.
Cook the tomatoes until you clearly see the ghee separating, which is the signal the masala is fully done.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot tandoori roti or laccha paratha and a raw onion salad, topping the dal with a final drizzle of ghee for shine.

variations.name: Punjabi Moong Dal Fry
variations.description: The Punjabi dhaba take makes moong dal fry extra rich with a butter finish, a handful of kasuri methi and a creamy consistency. The dal is simmered longer so it turns luxuriously smooth before the buttery tadka goes in. A coal-smoke finish gives it that beloved dhaba aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee builds the base while butter finishes it for the classic Punjabi richness

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 4 whistles until very soft, then whisk it into a smooth, creamy dal.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add 6 grated garlic cloves and 1 inch grated ginger and fry for 40 seconds until aromatic.
Add 2 finely chopped onions and cook for 7 minutes to a rich golden brown, then add 2 pureed tomatoes with 1 tsp red chilli powder and simmer 6 minutes until thick and glossy.
Pour in the whisked dal with 0.5 cup hot water and 0.5 tsp salt, then simmer for 8 minutes on low heat, stirring, until velvety.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the dal, stir in 2 tbsp fresh cream and 0.5 tsp garam masala, and cook 2 more minutes.
Melt 2 tbsp butter in a small pan until foaming, pour it over the dal, garnish with 2 tbsp coriander and serve.
tips: For dhaba smokiness, rest a red-hot coal in a bowl on the dal, drip ghee over it and cover for 2 minutes before the butter finish.
Whisking the dal well after cooking is what gives the Punjabi version its signature smooth, creamy body.
Add the cream on low heat and avoid boiling hard afterwards, or it may split and turn grainy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or jeera rice, with an extra knob of butter melting on top and a side of pickled onions.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Moong Dal Fry
variations.description: This version fries the dal masala with warming goda masala and a scatter of roasted peanuts for crunch and body. Groundnut oil is the authentic fat, and a spoon of jaggery balances the earthy spice. The result is a nutty, gently sweet fry dal quite distinct from its northern cousin.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil is the everyday cooking fat of Maharashtra

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: balances the earthy goda masala the Maharashtrian way

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 2.5 cups water and 0.5 tsp turmeric for 3 whistles, then keep it aside lightly mashed but still textured.
Coarsely crush 3 tbsp roasted peanuts and set aside for stirring in later.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 10 curry leaves for 20 seconds.
Add 1 large finely chopped onion and fry for 6 minutes until golden, then add 1 chopped tomato and cook 3 minutes until pulpy.
Lower the heat, sprinkle in 1.5 tsp goda masala and the crushed peanuts, and fry gently for 1 minute until the spice blooms and smells fragrant.
Fold in the cooked dal with 0.5 cup water, 1 tsp jaggery powder and 1 tsp salt, simmer for 6 minutes until thick, then finish with 2 tbsp coriander.
tips: Add goda masala on lowered heat after the tomato, as its delicate cinnamon-clove notes burn easily on high flame.
Crushed roasted peanuts thicken the dal and add crunch, so add them coarse rather than powdered.
A final squeeze of lime brightens the goda masala and peanut richness if you find it too heavy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or scoop it up with jowar or bajra bhakri alongside a raw onion wedge.

variations.name: Kerala Moong Dal Fry
variations.description: A South Indian spin where the fried dal masala is built on shallots, coconut and curry leaves in fragrant coconut oil. Roasted coconut slivers add a toasty depth that sets it apart from creamy northern fry dals. It is aromatic, lightly spiced and deeply comforting over rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil carries the toasty Kerala aroma through the dal

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 2.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 2 slit green chillies for 3 whistles, then mash coarsely and keep aside.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadhai over medium heat and roast 0.33 cup grated coconut for 3 minutes until golden and toasty, then remove and set aside.
In the same pan add the remaining 1.5 tbsp coconut oil, splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, then add 3 broken dried red chillies and 14 curry leaves and let them crisp for 20 seconds.
Add 6 sliced shallots and 5 crushed garlic cloves, frying for 5 minutes until deep golden, then add 1 chopped tomato and cook 3 minutes until soft.
Fold in the mashed dal with the roasted coconut, 0.5 cup hot water and 1 tsp salt, and simmer for 6 minutes until thick and fragrant.
Drizzle over a teaspoon of raw coconut oil off the heat and serve warm.
tips: Roasting the coconut separately first keeps it from burning and gives a toasty depth you cannot get by adding it raw.
Shallots, not regular onions, give the authentic sweet-savoury base of Kerala cooking, so use them if you can.
A final drizzle of raw coconut oil off the heat is a Kerala hallmark that lifts the whole dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with red matta rice and a simple thoran, or scoop it up with kerala parotta for a satisfying meal.

variations.name: Rajasthani Moong Dal Fry
variations.description: A robust desert-style dal fry that relies on whole dried red chillies and a heavy hand with garlic, built without tomatoes in true Marwari fashion. Ghee, cumin and dry spices do all the work, giving a smoky, intense dal. Kasuri methi and a chilli-ghee tempering on top seal the bold flavour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee is the sole cooking fat in this water-scarce desert dal tradition

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 2.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft, then keep aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida, then add 8 crushed garlic cloves and fry for 40 seconds until golden.

Add 1 finely chopped onion and cook for 6 minutes until browned, then lower the heat and add 1 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp red chilli powder, frying for 20 seconds with a splash of water so the spices do not burn.
Fold in the cooked dal with 0.5 cup hot water, 0.5 tsp amchur and 0.5 tsp salt, and simmer for 6 minutes until thick and full-bodied.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the top and stir it through the dal.
For the finishing tadka, heat the remaining 1 tbsp ghee, fry 4 dried red chillies until they darken, pour over the dal, garnish with 2 tbsp coriander and serve.
tips: The absence of tomato is intentional and traditional, so lean on amchur for the necessary tang instead.
Fry the whole dried red chillies in the final tadka only until they puff and darken, not blacken, for a smoky aroma.
This dal keeps well and tastes even better the next day as the garlic and chilli deepen overnight.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra roti and a dollop of white butter, or with steamed rice and a side of Rajasthani gatte for a hearty desert meal.

variations.name: Classic Moong Dal Home-style
variations.description: The unfussy, wholesome dal that simmers in Indian kitchens on an ordinary weeknight, cooked soft and finished with a modest ghee tadka. There is no heavy masala here, just cumin, garlic and turmeric letting the sweet moong flavour shine. Light, quick and easy to digest, it is comfort in a bowl.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a modest home-style tadka of ghee to keep the dal light and comforting

steps: Rinse 1 cup split moong dal and pressure-cook it with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 inch grated ginger and 0.5 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft and mashable.
Whisk the dal lightly to your preferred consistency, adding a little hot water if needed, and keep it warm.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan over medium heat and add 1 tsp cumin seeds, letting them sizzle for 15 seconds until golden and fragrant.
Add 4 sliced garlic cloves and 1 chopped green chilli, frying for 30 seconds until the garlic turns pale gold.
Add 1 small chopped onion and cook for 3 minutes until soft, then add 1 small chopped tomato and 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and cook 3 minutes until pulpy.
Pour this tadka into the warm dal, add the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, simmer together for 3 minutes, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Keep the seasoning gentle so the natural sweetness of moong comes through; this is meant to be an easy everyday dal.
If cooking for someone unwell or for a child, skip the chilli powder and green chilli and keep just the cumin-garlic tadka.
A squeeze of lemon at the table brightens the dal without needing tomato or extra spice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulka or plain steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, with a simple sabzi and yogurt to round out a homely meal.

variations.name: Bengali Moong Dal Home-style
variations.description: An everyday Bengali moog dal tempered in mustard oil with cumin, bay leaf and dried red chilli, kept light and slightly sweet. Unlike the roasted festive version, this weekday dal stays pale and soothing. A finishing touch of green chilli and coriander keeps it fresh.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil gives even a simple weekday dal its Bengali soul

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft, then whisk to a smooth, pourable dal.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai over medium-high heat until it shimmers and just smokes, then lower the flame to soften its bite.
Add 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 bay leaf and 2 dried red chillies, letting them crackle for 20 seconds until aromatic.
Stir in 1 inch grated ginger and fry for 30 seconds, then pour in the whisked dal along with 2 slit green chillies.
Add 0.5 tsp sugar and adjust salt, then simmer gently for 6 minutes so the mustard-cumin aroma infuses through.
Finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and a few drops of raw mustard oil, then serve warm.
tips: Smoking the mustard oil before tempering is non-negotiable for a clean flavour without raw pungency.
The small amount of sugar is a Bengali habit that balances rather than sweetens, so do not skip it.
Keep this dal thin so it can be mixed into the first course of rice with a squeeze of lime.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a wedge of lime as the opening course of a Bengali meal, followed by a vegetable and fish.

variations.name: Gujarati Moong Dal Home-style
variations.description: A homely Gujarati moong dal that is gently sweet and sour, tempered in ghee with mustard, curry leaves and a whisper of jaggery. It is thinner and lighter than northern dals, meant to be sipped or poured over rice. A squeeze of lime keeps the sweetness bright and clean.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee tempering rounds out the light sweet-sour Gujarati dal

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a gentle sweetness typical of daily Gujarati cooking

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 3 cups water and 0.5 tsp turmeric for 3 whistles until soft, then whisk smooth and thin with a little hot water.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat and add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds; when they splutter, add 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 10 curry leaves.
Add 2 slit green chillies and 1 inch julienned ginger, frying for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Pour in the whisked dal, then stir in 1 tsp jaggery powder and 1 tsp salt until the jaggery dissolves.
Simmer gently for 8 minutes on low heat until the dal turns light and frothy and the sweet-savoury balance settles.
Switch off the heat, add 1 tbsp lime juice and 2 tbsp coriander, and serve warm.
tips: Add the lime only off the heat so it stays fresh and does not turn bitter.
This dal is deliberately thin; if it thickens on standing, loosen it with hot water before serving.
For a fuller flavour, add a couple of curry leaves fried extra crisp on top just before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as part of a Gujarati thali with plain rice, a spicy shaak and soft rotli, or enjoy warm on its own as a light dal.

variations.name: Tamil Moong Dal Home-style
variations.description: A comforting Tamil paruppu where soft moong dal is mashed with garlic and finished with a fragrant curry-leaf tempering in sesame oil. A little cooked tomato and cumin keep it light, and a squeeze of lime lifts it. This is the everyday dal that starts a Tamil rice meal with a spoon of ghee.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: gingelly sesame oil is the everyday tempering fat of Tamil homes

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 chopped tomato for 3 whistles, then mash smooth with a wooden masher and add 1 tsp salt.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a small pan over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds until they pop.
Add 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, 2 broken dried red chillies, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 14 curry leaves, frying for 20 seconds until the curry leaves crisp.
Add 5 crushed garlic cloves and 4 sliced shallots, frying for 3 minutes until golden and sweet.
Pour this tempering into the mashed dal, simmer together for 4 minutes on low heat so the flavours combine.
Switch off the heat, stir in 1 tbsp lime juice and 2 tbsp coriander, and serve.
tips: Mash the dal well with the cooked tomato so it turns silky, which is how paruppu is traditionally served.
Crushed garlic fried in sesame oil is the heart of this dal, so let it turn properly golden.
Reserve a spoon of the crisp tempering to spoon over the top of each serving for aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot rice with a spoon of ghee and a wedge of lime as the first course, followed by sambar and rasam in the Tamil meal sequence.

variations.name: Andhra Moong Dal Home-style
variations.description: A everyday Andhra pesara pappu with a homely edge, spiked with a few smoky Guntur chillies and plenty of garlic in a sesame-oil tempering. Tomato and tamarind bring a gentle tang while keeping it lighter than the restaurant version. It stays thick and rice-friendly with a lively kick.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: gingelly oil deepens the garlic and roasted-chilli notes of Andhra dal
