variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a simple chokha or a bowl of dal, with a wedge of lime and a green chilli on the side for a rustic Bihari meal.

variations.name: Classic Quick Peas Pulao
variations.description: A one-pot pressure-cooker matar pulao that skips the soaking and lands on the table in under half an hour. Frozen peas and rinsed basmati cook together with ghee-bloomed whole spices for a fuss-free weeknight rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee blooms the whole spices instantly for a quick but fragrant one-pot pulao

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati rice in two changes of water and drain; there is no need to soak for this quick method.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pressure cooker over medium heat and add 1 bay leaf, 3 green cardamom pods, 3 cloves and a 1 inch cinnamon stick, then 1.5 tsp cumin seeds, frying for 20 seconds.
Add 1 sliced onion and 1 slit green chilli and saute for 4 minutes until the onion softens and turns pale gold.
Stir in 1 cup green peas and the rinsed rice and toss gently for 1 minute, then add 2.5 cups water and 1.25 tsp salt.
Close the lid and pressure cook on medium for 2 whistles, then turn off the heat and let the pressure release naturally.
Open the cooker, fluff the pulao gently with a fork and let it sit uncovered for 2 minutes before serving.
tips: Skipping the soak means the rice needs a touch more water, so keep to the 2.5 cup measure for firm grains.
Let the pressure drop naturally rather than forcing it, which keeps the grains from breaking.
Add frozen peas straight from the freezer so they stay bright green in the quick cook.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve straight from the cooker with a bowl of curd, a spoon of pickle and a papad for a fast, complete meal.

variations.name: Tamil Quick Peas Pulao
variations.description: A quick South Indian matar pulao tempered with mustard, curry leaves and coconut milk, giving the peas and rice a light, fragrant richness. A pressure cooker and coconut oil get it done fast without losing the coastal character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil gives the quick pulao its authentic South Indian aroma

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati rice and drain; no soaking is needed for this quick cooker method.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pressure cooker over medium heat, add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and when they pop add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 12 curry leaves.
Add 1 sliced onion, 1 inch julienned ginger and 1 chopped green chilli and saute for 4 minutes until the onion softens.
Stir in 1 cup green peas and the rinsed rice for 1 minute, then add 0.5 cup coconut milk, 2 cups water and 1.25 tsp salt.
Close the lid and pressure cook on medium for 2 whistles, then let the pressure release naturally.
Open the cooker, fluff gently and rest uncovered for 2 minutes so the coconut aroma settles before serving.
tips: Coconut milk counts as part of the liquid, so use 2 cups water rather than the usual 2.5 to avoid mush.
Add the coconut milk with the water, not earlier, so it does not split over direct heat.
Fresh curry leaves added whole give the best aroma, so scatter them generously.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a simple tomato pachadi or plain curd and an appalam, or pack it into a lunchbox where it travels well.

variations.name: Malwa Quick Peas Pulao
variations.description: A quick, rustic Madhya Pradesh matar pulao where ghee-blistered peanuts add instant crunch and nutty warmth to a one-pot cooker rice. It delivers the Malwa plateau's love of peanuts without any slow simmering.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee blisters the peanuts and enriches the quick pulao in true Malwa style

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati rice and drain; no soaking is needed for this quick method.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pressure cooker over medium heat and fry 0.33 cup raw peanuts until blistered, about 3 minutes, then lift out half for garnish.
To the remaining peanuts and ghee add 3 cloves and 2 dried red chillies, then 1.5 tsp cumin seeds, and let them crackle for 15 seconds.
Add 1 sliced onion with 0.25 tsp turmeric and saute for 4 minutes until pale gold, then stir in 1 cup green peas and the rinsed rice for 1 minute.
Add 2.5 cups water and 1.25 tsp salt, close the lid and pressure cook on medium for 2 whistles, then let the pressure release naturally.
Open the cooker, fluff gently, fold in half the reserved peanuts and scatter the rest with 2 tbsp coriander on top.
tips: Fry the peanuts on medium heat so they crisp through without the outsides scorching.
Reserving half the peanuts for garnish keeps some crunch after the pressure cook softens the rest.
Let the pressure release naturally to keep the delicate grains whole.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain yoghurt and lemon wedges, or a simple dal, to round out the nutty, rustic pulao.

variations.name: Delhi-style Quick Peas Pulao
variations.description: A fast Old Delhi matar pulao lifted by a finishing dusting of garam masala and a scatter of fried onions, giving one-pot rice a banquet-style depth. Warm, spiced and quick, it is built to sit beside a rich gravy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee gives banquet-style richness and blooms the finishing garam masala

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati rice and drain; skip the soak for this quick cooker method.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pressure cooker over medium heat and add 1 bay leaf, 1 black cardamom and 3 cloves, then 1.5 tsp cumin seeds, frying for 20 seconds.
Add 1 sliced onion and 1 tsp ginger garlic paste and saute for 4 minutes until golden and the raw smell fades.
Stir in 1 cup green peas and the rinsed rice for 1 minute, then add 2.5 cups water and 1.25 tsp salt.
Close the lid and pressure cook on medium for 2 whistles, then let the pressure release naturally.
Open the cooker, sprinkle 0.75 tsp garam masala over the hot pulao, fluff so it blooms through, and finish with 3 tbsp fried onions.
tips: Add the garam masala at the end so its aroma perfumes the pulao rather than cooking away.
One black cardamom gives the smoky Old Delhi note; more will overpower the dish.
Freshly ground garam masala makes a real difference in a quick dish like this.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a shahi paneer or dal makhani, topped with extra fried onions and a lemon wedge for a banquet feel.

variations.name: Bihari Quick Peas Pulao
variations.description: A quick Bihari matar pulao finished in pungent wood-pressed mustard oil with nigella and garlic for an earthy, rustic bite. The sharp oil gives a one-pot cooker rice a distinctly eastern character in minutes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil gives the quick pulao its earthy Bihari sharpness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of ghee rounds off the pungent mustard oil

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati rice and drain; no soaking is needed for this quick method.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pressure cooker over medium-high heat until it just smokes, then lower the flame to soften its bite.
Add 1 tsp cumin seeds, 0.5 tsp nigella seeds and 2 dried red chillies and let them crackle for 15 seconds, then add 4 sliced garlic cloves and fry until golden.
Add 1 sliced onion with 0.25 tsp turmeric and saute for 4 minutes, then stir in 1 cup green peas and the rinsed rice for 1 minute.
Add 2.5 cups water and 1.25 tsp salt, close the lid and pressure cook on medium for 2 whistles, then let the pressure release naturally.
Open the cooker, fold in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and fluff gently before serving.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to smoking first, always, or the pulao will carry a raw, harsh taste.
Nigella seeds add the signature Bihari earthiness, so do not swap them for more cumin.
Slice the garlic thin so it turns golden quickly in the short cooking time.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a simple aloo chokha or a bowl of dal, with a wedge of lime and a green chilli on the side for a rustic Bihari meal.

variations.name: Classic Spiced Jeera Rice
variations.description: A bolder cousin of everyday jeera rice, where the cumin is joined by a rounded masala of coriander, pepper and a hint of garam masala for a fuller, restaurant-style flavour. It stays fragrant and grain-separate but carries enough spice to be eaten almost on its own with a spoon of yoghurt.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee blooms the ground spices so their oils coat every grain evenly

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati rice until the water runs clear, soak for 20 minutes and drain so the grains stay firm.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot over medium heat, add 1 bay leaf and 1.5 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle for 15 seconds until aromatic.
Add 1 sliced onion and 1 tsp ginger garlic paste and saute over medium heat until golden and the raw smell disappears, about 6 minutes.
Lower the heat and stir in 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp garam masala and 0.25 tsp turmeric for 20 seconds, just until the spices smell toasted but not burnt.
Add the drained rice and fold gently for 2 minutes, then pour in 2.25 cups hot water and 1.25 tsp salt and bring to a rolling boil.
Cover and steam on the lowest heat for 12 minutes, rest for 5 minutes, then fluff and scatter 2 tbsp coriander leaves over the top.
tips: Add the ground spices off a high flame; a few seconds too long over high heat and they scorch and turn bitter.
Keep the turmeric to a quarter teaspoon so it tints without making the rice taste medicinal.
A spoon of thick yoghurt stirred in at the table turns this into a light one-bowl meal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a simple cucumber-tomato raita and roasted papad, or alongside a dry aloo sabzi for a fuss-free weekday plate.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Spiced Jeera Rice
variations.description: This version leans on goda masala, the dark Maharashtrian blend of stone flower, sesame and dried coconut, giving the rice a smoky, faintly sweet depth. It is the kind of masale bhaat-adjacent rice served at Puneri weddings, hearty enough to anchor a simple thali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the traditional Maharashtrian cooking fat and lets the goda masala shine

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of ghee softens the smoky goda masala edge

steps: Wash and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain thoroughly and keep aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pot over medium heat and add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds; when they pop after about 10 seconds, add 1.5 tsp cumin seeds and 10 curry leaves.
Add 1 finely chopped onion and cook until soft and pale gold, about 5 minutes, then stir in 0.25 tsp turmeric.
Lower the heat and add 1.5 tsp goda masala, stirring for 20 seconds until the blend smells smoky and toasted.
Fold in the drained rice for 2 minutes, then add 2.25 cups hot water and 1.25 tsp salt and bring to a boil over high heat.
Cover and steam on the lowest heat for 12 minutes, rest for 5 minutes, then swirl in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee, fluff and garnish with 2 tbsp grated fresh coconut.
tips: Goda masala is much darker and sweeter than garam masala, so do not swap the two or the flavour will be wrong.
Toast the goda masala only briefly; it is already roasted and burns faster than raw spice powders.
A handful of roasted peanuts folded in at the end adds the crunch typical of Maharashtrian rice dishes.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a bowl of plain yoghurt, a wedge of lime and a fried papad, the classic accompaniments to Maharashtrian spiced rice.

variations.name: Andhra Spiced Jeera Rice
variations.description: A fiery southern version built on fierce Guntur red chillies and a garlicky tempering that turns cumin rice into something with real heat. Toasted and coarsely pounded chillies coat the grains a rusty red, making this a bold partner to cooling curd rice or a plain omelette.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed sesame oil is the classic Andhra fat and stands up to the fierce Guntur chilli heat

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain well and set aside.
Dry roast 4 Guntur red chillies in a pan over low heat for 1 minute until crisp and fragrant, then pound them coarsely with 6 garlic cloves in a mortar.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pot over medium heat, add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 1.5 tsp cumin seeds and let them splutter for 15 seconds, then add 12 curry leaves.
Add 1 sliced onion and the pounded chilli-garlic paste and fry until the onion softens and the mixture smells toasty, about 5 minutes, then stir in 0.25 tsp turmeric.
Fold in the drained rice for 2 minutes, then pour in 2.25 cups hot water and 1.25 tsp salt and bring to a boil over high heat.
Cover and steam on the lowest heat for 12 minutes, rest for 5 minutes, then fluff gently and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Deseed the Guntur chillies before pounding if you want the colour and flavour with less ferocious heat.
Pound the chillies and garlic coarsely rather than to a paste so you get little bursts of heat in the rice.
A spoon of thick curd on the side is the traditional Andhra rescue if the heat catches you off guard.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of cooling perugu annam or plain curd, a papad and a slice of raw onion to temper the chilli fire.

variations.name: Awadhi Spiced Jeera Rice
variations.description: A regal Lucknowi rendition scented with kewra water and a delicate blend of mace and cardamom, cooked gently so the perfume clings to each grain. Restrained yet luxurious, it borrows the aromatic restraint of Awadhi pulaos rather than shouting with chilli.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rich bilona ghee is essential to the Awadhi style, carrying the mace and kewra perfume

steps: Soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes and drain gently, taking care to keep the long grains intact.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot over medium heat and add 1 bay leaf, 1 blade of mace, 4 green cardamom pods and 3 cloves, frying for 30 seconds until the kitchen fills with perfume.
Add 1.5 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle for 15 seconds, then add 1 thinly sliced onion and cook slowly to a soft pale gold, about 6 minutes.
Fold in the drained rice and toss for 2 minutes so each grain glistens with the spiced ghee.
Pour in 2.25 cups hot water and 1.25 tsp salt, bring to a boil, then cover and steam on the lowest heat for 12 minutes.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp kewra water over the hot rice, rest covered for 5 minutes, then fluff and top with 3 tbsp crisp fried onions.
tips: Kewra is potent; measure it by the half teaspoon and add at the end so the aroma is not cooked away.
Cook the onions low and slow to a soft gold rather than dark brown to keep the dish delicate and pale.
Layer the fried onions and a few drops of extra kewra between servings for a dum-style finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as an elegant side to a korma or shahi paneer, garnished with fried onions and a sprinkle of pomegranate seeds for a courtly touch.

variations.name: Odia Spiced Jeera Rice
variations.description: An eastern take tempered with panch phoron, the five-seed Odia-Bengali blend of cumin, fennel, fenugreek, nigella and mustard that gives the rice a unique bittersweet, aniseed lift. Gentle and homely, it mirrors the simple, aromatic rice dishes of coastal Odisha.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil is the everyday Odia fat and the natural bed for panch phoron

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A closing spoon of ghee balances the pungent mustard oil

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain and keep aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pot over medium-high heat until it just smokes, then lower the flame to mellow it.
Add 1 tsp panch phoron, 1 tsp cumin seeds, 2 dried red chillies and 1 bay leaf and let them crackle for 20 seconds until the fennel and nigella turn fragrant.
Add 1 sliced onion and 0.25 tsp turmeric and fry over medium heat until the onion is golden, about 6 minutes.
Stir in the drained rice for 2 minutes, then pour in 2.25 cups hot water and 1.25 tsp salt and bring to a boil.
Cover and steam on the lowest heat for 12 minutes, rest for 5 minutes, then fold in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee, fluff and finish with 2 tbsp coriander.
tips: Do not grind the panch phoron; the seeds are meant to stay whole so each delivers a distinct pop of flavour.
Fenugreek in the blend can turn bitter if over-fried, so add the rice as soon as the seeds are fragrant.
Heating the mustard oil to smoking point first is essential to soften its raw pungency.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a light dalma or a simple aloo-tomato jhol, with a wedge of lime and a spoon of mango pickle on the side.

variations.name: Classic Spiced Peas Pulao
variations.description: A bolder matar pulao where a rounded masala of coriander, garam masala and ginger-garlic joins the sweet peas for a fuller, restaurant-style flavour. It stays grain-separate and fragrant but carries enough spice to be eaten with just a bowl of curd.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee blooms the ground spices so their oils coat every grain and pea

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati rice until clear, soak for 20 minutes and drain so the grains stay firm.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot over medium heat, add 1 bay leaf and 1.5 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle for 15 seconds.
Add 1 sliced onion and 1 tsp ginger garlic paste and saute until golden, about 6 minutes, then add 1 chopped small tomato and cook 2 minutes until soft.
Lower the heat and stir in 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp garam masala and 0.25 tsp turmeric for 20 seconds until fragrant but not scorched.
Add 1 cup green peas for 2 minutes, then fold in the drained rice for 2 minutes, and pour in 2.25 cups hot water with 1.25 tsp salt.
Bring to a boil, then cover and steam on the lowest heat for 13 minutes, rest for 5 minutes and fluff gently.
tips: Add the ground spices off a high flame; a moment too long and they scorch and turn bitter.
Cook the tomato down fully before the rice goes in, or the grains can turn sticky.
A spoon of thick yoghurt at the table turns this spiced pulao into a light one-bowl meal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cucumber-tomato raita and roasted papad, or beside a dry aloo sabzi for a satisfying weekday plate.

variations.name: Andhra Spiced Peas Pulao
variations.description: A fiery southern matar pulao built on fierce Guntur red chillies and a garlicky tempering that gives the sweet peas a real chilli kick. Coarsely pounded roasted chillies stain the grains rusty red, making a bold counterpoint to the tender peas.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed sesame oil is the classic Andhra fat and stands up to the fierce Guntur chilli heat

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain and set aside.
Dry roast 4 Guntur red chillies over low heat for 1 minute until crisp, then pound them coarsely with 6 garlic cloves in a mortar.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pot over medium heat, add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 1.5 tsp cumin seeds and let them splutter for 15 seconds, then add 12 curry leaves.
Add 1 sliced onion and the pounded chilli-garlic paste and fry until the onion softens, about 5 minutes, then stir in 0.25 tsp turmeric.
Add 1 cup green peas for 2 minutes, then fold in the drained rice for 2 minutes and pour in 2.25 cups hot water with 1.25 tsp salt.
Bring to a boil, cover and steam on the lowest heat for 13 minutes, rest for 5 minutes and fluff gently so the peas stay whole.
tips: Deseed the Guntur chillies before pounding for the colour and flavour with less ferocious heat.
Pound the chillies and garlic coarsely so you get little bursts of heat rather than uniform fire.
A bowl of thick curd on the side is the traditional Andhra cooler if the heat catches you out.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain curd or a light perugu pachadi and a papad, with sliced raw onion to temper the chilli fire.

variations.name: Rajasthani Spiced Peas Pulao
variations.description: A robust desert-style matar pulao tempered with whole dried red chillies and asafoetida for a smoky, garlicky heat that suits Rajasthan's bold palate. Pantry spices and sweet peas balance the fire, making it a hearty partner to dal or kadhi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee tempers the dried chillies and gives the desert-style pulao its rich base

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain and keep aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot over medium heat, add 3 cloves and 3 broken dried red chillies and fry for 20 seconds until the chillies darken and smell smoky.
Add 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 1.5 tsp cumin seeds, then 1 sliced onion, and cook until the onion is golden, about 6 minutes.
Lower the heat and stir in 1 tsp coriander powder and 0.25 tsp red chilli powder for a few seconds to bloom their colour without burning.
Add 1 cup green peas for 2 minutes, fold in the drained rice for 2 minutes, then pour in 2.25 cups hot water with 1.25 tsp salt.
Bring to a boil, cover and steam on the lowest heat for 13 minutes, rest for 5 minutes and fluff gently.
tips: Break the dried chillies so their seeds toast and release smoky heat into the ghee.
Bloom the chilli powder off a high flame; it colours the pulao but scorches in seconds.
Asafoetida stands in for onions and garlic in a stricter Marwari kitchen, so keep it generous.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with Rajasthani kadhi or panchmel dal and a dollop of plain curd to balance the smoky heat.

variations.name: Kerala Spiced Peas Pulao
variations.description: A coastal matar pulao cooked in wood-pressed coconut oil with toasted coconut, curry leaves and a hint of garam masala for a mild, tropical warmth. The sweetness of peas and coconut plays against a fragrant southern tempering.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil gives the pulao its unmistakable Kerala fragrance

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain in a colander.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pot over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds, 0.5 tsp fennel seeds and 12 curry leaves and let them splutter for 15 seconds.
Add 1 sliced onion and 1 chopped green chilli and cook until the onion softens, about 5 minutes, then stir in 0.25 cup grated coconut and toast for 2 minutes until pale gold.
Stir in 0.5 tsp garam masala for 15 seconds, then add 1 cup green peas and saute for 2 minutes.
Fold in the drained rice for 2 minutes, then pour in 2.25 cups hot water with 1.25 tsp salt and bring to a boil.
Cover and steam on the lowest heat for 13 minutes, rest for 5 minutes and fluff gently.
tips: Toast the grated coconut only to pale gold; browning it fully makes the pulao taste scorched.
Fennel and coconut together give the Kerala character, so keep both even if you simplify elsewhere.
A final teaspoon of raw coconut oil drizzled over the hot pulao deepens the coastal aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a Kerala vegetable stew or a tangy tomato pachadi, with a papadum on the side for crunch.

variations.name: Odia Spiced Peas Pulao
variations.description: An eastern matar pulao tempered with panch phoron, the five-seed blend whose fennel and nigella give the peas and rice a bittersweet, aniseed lift. Gentle and homely, it mirrors the simple aromatic rice dishes of coastal Odisha.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil is the everyday Odia fat and the natural bed for panch phoron

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A closing spoon of ghee balances the pungent mustard oil

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain and keep aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pot over medium-high heat until it just smokes, then lower the flame to mellow it.
Add 1 tsp panch phoron, 2 dried red chillies and 1 bay leaf and let them crackle for 20 seconds until the fennel and nigella turn fragrant.
Add 1 sliced onion and 0.25 tsp turmeric and fry until golden, about 6 minutes, then stir in 1 cup green peas for 2 minutes.
Fold in the drained rice for 2 minutes, then pour in 2.25 cups hot water with 1.25 tsp salt and bring to a boil.
Cover and steam on the lowest heat for 13 minutes, rest for 5 minutes, then fold in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and finish with 2 tbsp coriander.
tips: Do not grind the panch phoron; the whole seeds are meant to pop and deliver distinct bursts of flavour.
Add the rice as soon as the seeds are fragrant so the fenugreek does not over-fry and turn bitter.
Heating the mustard oil to smoking point first is essential to soften its raw pungency.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a light dalma or an aloo-tomato jhol, with a wedge of lime and a spoon of mango pickle on the side.

variations.name: Classic Spiced Veg Pulao
variations.description: A bolder, masaledar cousin of the everyday pulao, built on a fried onion base and a full spread of ground spices so the rice carries real punch, not just aroma. Ginger, garlic, garam masala and a hint of yogurt give it body while the grains stay separate. This is the pulao you make when you want the rice itself to be the star of the plate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee gives the masala base its richness and keeps the spiced grains glossy.

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain; whisk 3 tbsp yogurt smooth and keep aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 bay leaf and 3 cardamom pods for 20 seconds.
Add 1 thinly sliced large onion and fry until deep golden, about 7 minutes, then add 1 tbsp ginger garlic paste and cook for 1 minute.

Lower the heat, add 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp garam masala and stir for 20 seconds, then add the whisked yogurt and cook until the ghee separates, about 3 minutes.
Add 1.5 cups mixed vegetables and 1.25 tsp salt and saute for 3 minutes, then add the drained rice and toss gently for 2 minutes.
Pour in 2.25 cups hot water, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes until the water is absorbed.
Rest covered for 5 minutes, then fluff and fold in chopped mint before serving hot.
tips: Add the yogurt on low heat and whisked smooth so it does not split into the masala.
Frying the onions to a deep gold is what gives this spiced pulao its rich colour and depth.
Because the masala adds moisture, use slightly less water than for a plain pulao.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a thick cucumber-mint raita, a wedge of lemon and sliced onions, or pair with a paneer or soya curry to make it a hearty main.

variations.name: Andhra Spiced Veg Pulao
variations.description: Fiery and fragrant, this pulao gets its punch from Guntur red chillies and a freshly ground spice paste of green chilli, mint and coriander, in the style of an Andhra vegetable bhath. A sesame-oil and ghee base carries the heat while curry leaves add southern aroma. It is bold, herby and unapologetically spicy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed sesame oil is the classic Andhra base and stands up to the Guntur heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee softens the fiery masala and finishes the rice with a rich sheen.

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain; grind 0.5 cup mint, 0.5 cup coriander and 3 green chillies to a coarse green paste with a splash of water.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pot on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, 4 broken Guntur red chillies and 12 curry leaves for 20 seconds until the chillies darken.
Add 1 sliced large onion and fry until golden, about 6 minutes, then add 1 tbsp ginger garlic paste and cook for 1 minute.
Stir in the ground green paste and 1.25 tsp salt and cook for 3 minutes until the raw smell goes and the oil surfaces.
Add 1.25 cups mixed vegetables and saute for 3 minutes, then add the drained rice and toss gently for 2 minutes.
Pour in 2.25 cups hot water, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes until absorbed.
Rest for 5 minutes, drizzle 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the top, fluff gently and serve hot.
tips: Grind the herb paste coarse so it flecks the rice green rather than dyeing it fully.
Reduce the Guntur chillies to two for a milder version without losing the aroma.
The finishing ghee is not optional here; it tames the heat and rounds the flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a large bowl of cooling onion-tomato raita, fried papad and extra ghee on the side to balance the fire.

variations.name: Rajasthani Spiced Veg Pulao
variations.description: A robust desert pulao leaning on whole dried red chillies, cloves and a smoky bhuna base, with hardy vegetables and no fresh herbs, reflecting a cuisine built for a dry land. It is deeply spiced and warming, often studded with fried cashews and a hint of amchur for tang. This is a rustic, festive rice that stands up to bold curries.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A generous amount of ghee suits the rich Rajasthani style where fresh produce is scarce.

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain well.
Heat 3.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot on medium heat and fry 3 tbsp cashews until golden, then scoop them out and reserve.
In the same ghee crackle 4 broken dried red chillies, 1 tsp cumin seeds, 4 cloves, 1 black cardamom and 1 inch cinnamon for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 sliced large onion and fry until deep golden, about 7 minutes, then lower the heat and add 1 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt and stir for 20 seconds.
Add 1.5 cups mixed vegetables and saute for 3 minutes, then add the drained rice and toss gently for 2 minutes.
Pour in 2.5 cups hot water, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes until the water is absorbed.
Rest for 5 minutes, sprinkle 0.5 tsp amchur powder, fluff gently, top with the fried cashews and serve hot.
tips: Use sturdy vegetables like carrot, beans, potato and peas that hold their shape in this robust rice.
Sprinkle amchur after cooking so its tang stays sharp and does not cook out.
Deeply browned onions and whole dried chillies give the smoky desert character.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of garlicky ker sangri or a spicy gatte ki sabzi and a plain raita; sliced onions and papad round out the Rajasthani thali.

variations.name: Tamil Spiced Veg Pulao
variations.description: This South Indian pulao, in the spirit of a Tamil-style vegetable biryani, is fragrant with curry leaves, star anise and a coconut-milk cook, giving soft, aromatic grains with gentle heat. A ground paste of ginger, garlic and green chilli plus a sesame-oil base carries the regional flavour. It is comforting, herby and pairs beautifully with a simple raita.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil is the traditional Tamil cooking fat and deepens the aroma of the spices.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee added with the tempering gives the rice its festive fragrance.

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain well.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil with 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot on medium heat and crackle 1 star anise, 1 inch cinnamon, 3 cloves and 14 curry leaves for 30 seconds.
Add 1 sliced large onion and fry until golden, about 6 minutes, then add 1 tbsp ginger garlic paste and 3 slit green chillies and cook for 1 minute.
Add 1.25 cups mixed vegetables, 3 tbsp chopped mint and 1.25 tsp salt and saute for 3 minutes.
Add the drained rice and toss gently for 2 minutes, then pour in 1.5 cups hot water and 0.75 cup coconut milk and bring to a gentle boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes until the liquid is absorbed and the rice is fluffy.
Rest covered for 5 minutes, then fluff gently and serve hot with raita.
tips: Count the coconut milk as part of the liquid so the total stays right and the rice does not turn mushy.
Keep the heat low once the coconut milk goes in so it does not scorch at the base.
Star anise is assertive, so a single pod is plenty to flavour the whole pot.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling onion raita and a South Indian style vegetable kurma or a simple potato roast for a satisfying Tamil-style meal.

variations.name: Kerala Spiced Veg Pulao
variations.description: A Malabar-inspired pulao where the rice is cooked with coconut milk and warm spices, then crowned with a coconut-oil tempering of shallots, cashews and raisins. It is mildly sweet, deeply aromatic and studded with nuts, echoing the festive rice of Kerala's Muslim kitchens. Fennel and a bay leaf give it that distinct coastal fragrance.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil binds the shallot-and-nut tempering to the coconut-milk rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee toasts the spices and gives the festive rice its richness.

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain well.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot on medium heat and crackle 1 bay leaf, 3 cardamom pods and 1 inch cinnamon for 20 seconds, then add 6 of the sliced shallots and 2 slit green chillies.
Fry the shallots until golden, about 3 minutes, then stir in 0.5 tsp fennel powder and add 1.25 cups mixed vegetables and 1.25 tsp salt, sauteing for 3 minutes.
Add the drained rice and toss gently for 2 minutes, then pour in 1.5 cups hot water and 0.75 cup coconut milk and bring to a gentle boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes until the liquid is absorbed and the grains are tender.
Meanwhile heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan and fry 3 tbsp cashews, 2 tbsp raisins and the remaining 2 sliced shallots until golden.
Rest the rice for 5 minutes, fluff gently, top with the coconut-oil-fried nuts and shallots, and serve hot.
tips: Frying extra shallots for the topping adds sweetness and a crisp finish typical of Malabar rice.
Count coconut milk as part of the total liquid to keep the rice fluffy rather than sticky.
A pinch of sugar can underline the gentle sweetness if you like it more festive.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a tangy pineapple pachadi or a vegetable ishtu and pappadam; a squeeze of lime over the top brightens the coconut richness.

variations.name: Classic Toor Dal Fry
variations.description: Dal fry differs from a simple tadka in its thick, well-fried onion-tomato masala into which the cooked lentils are folded and sauteed until glossy. This is the restaurant staple, rich and slightly chunky, finished with a hit of garam masala and coriander.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: frying the masala in bilona ghee gives dal fry its rich, glossy body

steps: Rinse 1 cup toor dal and pressure-cook with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 4 to 5 whistles until soft, then whisk lightly, keeping some texture.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 15 seconds until fragrant.
Add 6 crushed garlic cloves, 1 inch grated ginger and 2 slit green chillies, saute 1 minute, then add 2 finely chopped onions and fry 6 minutes until golden brown.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes with 1 tbsp coriander powder, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp salt, cook 6 minutes until the masala is thick and the ghee separates.
Tip the cooked dal into the fried masala and stir well to coat, adding a little hot water to reach a thick, spoonable consistency.
Simmer the dal fry for 6 minutes, stirring often, so the lentils take on the fried masala flavour.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala and 2 tbsp chopped coriander, cook 1 minute more and serve hot.
tips: Fry the onions to a proper golden brown; this deep base is what makes dal fry richer than dal tadka.
Leave a little texture in the dal rather than whisking it fully smooth for the classic dal fry mouthfeel.
A squeeze of lemon at the end brightens the whole dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jeera rice or butter roti, sliced onions and a green chilli, the way roadside dhabas plate it.

variations.name: Punjabi Toor Dal Fry
variations.description: The Punjabi version doubles down on richness with white butter and toasted kasuri methi folded into the fried dal, plus a smoky dhungar of ghee-doused charcoal. It is the indulgent, buttery dal fry you find in Amritsari dhabas.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: used both to fry the masala and for the smoky dhungar finish

steps: Rinse 1 cup toor dal and pressure-cook with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 5 whistles until soft, then whisk lightly.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 2 chopped onions and fry 6 minutes to deep gold.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes, 1 tbsp coriander powder, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp salt, cook 6 minutes until the masala is thick and glossy.
Fold in the cooked dal with a little hot water and simmer 6 minutes, then crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over it and stir in 0.5 tsp garam masala.
For the dhungar, heat 1 piece charcoal on the flame until red-hot and place it in a small steel bowl set on top of the dal.
Pour the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the hot charcoal, immediately cover the pan and let the smoke infuse for 2 minutes.
Remove the charcoal bowl, swirl in 1.5 tbsp white butter until it melts and serve at once.
tips: The charcoal dhungar gives a subtle tandoor smokiness; skip it only if you cannot manage the charcoal safely.
Toast the kasuri methi on a dry pan before crushing to release its full aroma.
Finish with the white butter off the heat so it melts into a glossy sheen rather than boiling away.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with laccha paratha or naan, a wedge of white butter on top and sirke wale pyaaz alongside.

variations.name: Kerala Toor Dal Fry
variations.description: A coconut-forward southern dal fry where the lentils are folded into a coconut-oil masala and finished with a splash of coconut milk. A mustard-and-curry-leaf tempering and green chillies keep it fragrant and gently creamy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil gives the fried dal a distinct Malabar fragrance

steps: Rinse 1 cup toor dal and pressure-cook with 2.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 5 whistles until soft, then mash lightly.
Coarsely crush 0.5 cup grated coconut with 3 green chillies to a rough paste for the Kerala masala.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan over medium heat, add 1 sliced onion and saute 4 minutes until soft.
Add the crushed coconut paste and 1 chopped tomato, fry 4 minutes until the raw coconut smell fades and the mix turns pale gold.
Tip in the cooked dal and 0.5 cup thin coconut milk, simmer gently 6 minutes without boiling hard so the coconut milk does not split.
In a separate pan heat the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 2 dried red chillies, 6 sliced shallots and 14 curry leaves until the shallots are golden.
Pour this fragrant tempering over the dal, stir once and serve hot.
tips: Crush the coconut coarsely rather than grinding to a paste for a more rustic Kerala texture.
Keep the flame low after the coconut milk goes in so the dal stays smooth.
Fried shallots in the tempering add a sweetness that ordinary onions cannot match.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with Kerala matta rice or steamed rice and a stir-fried thoran, with a papadam for crunch.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Toor Dal Fry
variations.description: Maharashtra frames its dal fry around smoky goda masala and a touch of jaggery, cooked in wood-pressed groundnut oil with a peanut-thickened body. It carries a warm sweet-spicy depth quite unlike the buttery northern versions.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday wood-pressed oil of Maharashtrian kitchens, nutty and light

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the customary sweet counterpoint to smoky goda masala

steps: Rinse 1 cup toor dal and pressure-cook with 3 cups water, 2 tbsp raw peanuts, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 5 whistles until soft, then whisk lightly.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin and 10 curry leaves for 20 seconds.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 1 chopped onion, fry 5 minutes until golden, then add 2 chopped tomatoes and cook 4 minutes to a pulp.
Stir in 1.5 tsp goda masala, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp salt and roast on low 1 minute until deeply fragrant.
Fold in the cooked peanut-dal with a little hot water and simmer 6 minutes so the goda masala infuses the lentils.
Stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and let it dissolve, then simmer 2 minutes to balance the sweet and spicy.
Taste, adjust salt and serve hot with a scattering of extra curry leaves fried crisp if you like.
tips: Add goda masala to a low flame as it burns quickly and turns bitter.
The peanuts pressure-cooked with the dal give a subtle nutty thickness typical of the region.
Balance is everything here; taste after the jaggery and adjust so neither sweet nor spice dominates.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or with jowar bhakri and a raw onion wedge.

variations.name: Kashmiri Toor Dal Fry
variations.description: The valley perfumes its dal fry with saffron, fennel and dry ginger, skipping onion and garlic in the traditional Kashmiri Pandit manner. Gently spiced and golden, it is aromatic rather than fiery, finished with a bloom of saffron milk.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the base fat for Kashmiri Pandit cooking, which uses no onion or garlic

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Kashmiri Mongra strands bloomed in warm milk tint the dal a delicate gold

steps: Steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside to bloom into a golden liquid.
Rinse 1 cup toor dal and pressure-cook with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 5 whistles until soft, then whisk smooth.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, 3 cloves, 2 cardamom and 0.25 tsp asafoetida for 20 seconds.
Add 2 finely chopped tomatoes and cook 5 minutes until they collapse into a thick pulp.
Stir in 1 tsp fennel powder, 0.5 tsp dry ginger powder and 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, roast 1 minute until the ghee turns deep red and fragrant.
Fold in the cooked dal with 0.5 tsp salt and a little hot water, simmer 7 minutes so the fennel and ginger perfume the lentils.
Swirl in the saffron milk, simmer 2 minutes until golden and aromatic, then serve.
tips: Fennel and dry ginger define the Kashmiri flavour, so measure them properly and do not substitute garam masala.
Kashmiri chilli powder is used mainly for its colour; add more only if you want real heat.
Bloom the saffron in warm milk, not boiling, to draw out its colour without bitterness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain basmati rice or a Kashmiri saffron pulao and a side of nadru or haakh.

variations.name: Classic Toor Dal Home-style
variations.description: The unfussy everyday dal cooked in kitchens across India, thin enough to pour over rice and gently spiced so it never tires the palate. A single light tadka of ghee, cumin and garlic is all it needs to feel like a warm home-cooked meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a modest spoon of bilona ghee is all a homely dal needs to taste comforting

steps: Rinse 1 cup toor dal and pressure-cook with 3.5 cups water, 1 chopped tomato, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 5 whistles until soft and creamy.
Whisk the dal smooth and loosen with a little hot water so it is thin enough to pour over rice.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida for 15 seconds.
Add 5 crushed garlic cloves and 1 slit green chilli, fry 30 seconds until the garlic turns pale gold and fragrant.
Add 1 finely chopped small onion and saute 3 minutes until soft, then stir in 0.5 tsp red chilli powder off the heat so it does not scorch.
Pour this tadka into the simmering dal with 0.5 tsp salt and cook together 5 minutes so the flavours settle.
Garnish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and serve hot over rice.
tips: This dal is meant to be thin and pourable, so keep adding hot water until it is the consistency you like.
Cooking the tomato inside the cooker saves a step and gives a smoother base.
A single spoon of ghee stirred in at the end lifts even the plainest dal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over steaming rice with a wedge of lime, a spoon of ghee and a simple stir-fried vegetable on the side.

variations.name: Gujarati Toor Dal Home-style
variations.description: The classic sweet-sour Gujarati dal made at home daily, thin as a broth and balanced with jaggery, kokum and a peanut crunch. A curry-leaf tempering in groundnut oil and a hint of ginger make it light, warming and quietly addictive.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the clean-tasting wood-pressed oil of the Gujarati everyday kitchen

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the defining sweetness of a homely Gujarati dal

steps: Rinse 1 cup toor dal and pressure-cook with 3.5 cups water, 3 tbsp raw peanuts, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 5 whistles until very soft.
Whisk the dal thin, adding about 1 cup hot water so it is broth-like and pourable.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin, 0.25 tsp asafoetida, 1 inch cinnamon, 2 cloves and 12 curry leaves for 20 seconds.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and saute 30 seconds until fragrant.
Pour in the whisked dal with 3 pieces kokum and 0.5 tsp salt, bring to a boil and simmer 8 minutes so the sourness infuses.
Stir in 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and let it dissolve fully, then simmer 3 minutes and taste to balance sweet against sour.
Loosen with a little hot water if needed and serve hot with the peanuts running through.
tips: Keep this dal thin and drinkable; a thick Gujarati dal is considered a mistake.
Kokum gives a gentle, fruity sourness; substitute a squeeze of lemon added off the heat if unavailable.
Whole cinnamon and clove in the tempering give the subtle warmth that sets Gujarati dal apart.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain rice and a spoon of ghee as part of a thali, or sip it warm from a bowl before the meal.

variations.name: Bengali Toor Dal Home-style
variations.description: A homely Bengali arhar dal tempered with panch phoron and smoked mustard oil, kept light and faintly sweet. The whole five-spice crackle and a couple of green chillies give it all its character with barely any masala.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked first, it gives this simple dal its characteristic Bengali warmth

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the gentle Bengali sweetness that balances the mustard oil

steps: Rinse 1 cup toor dal and pressure-cook with 3.5 cups water, 1 inch grated ginger, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 5 whistles until soft.
Whisk the dal smooth and loosen with about 0.75 cup hot water to a light, pourable consistency.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, then cool for 20 seconds to soften its raw bite.
Temper 1 tsp panch phoron, 2 dried red chillies and 1 bay leaf in the oil for 20 seconds until the seeds crackle and smell fragrant.
Add 2 slit green chillies and fry 15 seconds, then carefully pour the tempering into the simmering dal.
Add 0.5 tsp salt and simmer the dal 6 minutes so the panch phoron perfume soaks in.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer 2 minutes until balanced and serve hot.
tips: Use whole panch phoron, never ground, so each seed crackles and releases its aroma.
Smoke the mustard oil fully before tempering to remove its raw sharpness.
This dal is meant to be light; resist the urge to add onion or tomato to it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice, a wedge of lime and a simple aloo bhaja on the side.

variations.name: Karnataka Toor Dal Home-style
variations.description: A tovve-style Karnataka dal made soft and mild, brought alive with a tamarind tang and a fragrant coconut-oil tempering of mustard, curry leaves and dried chilli. Simple and soothing, it is the daily dal of many Kannadiga homes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: coastal Karnataka tempers its everyday dal in fragrant coconut oil

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a small spoon balances the tamarind tang the Karnataka way

steps: Rinse 1 cup toor dal and pressure-cook with 3 cups water, 1 chopped tomato, 2 slit green chillies and 0.5 tsp turmeric for 5 whistles until very soft, then mash smooth.
Soak 1.5 tsp tamarind in 3 tbsp warm water and squeeze out the pulp.
Add the tamarind pulp, 0.5 tsp salt and a little hot water to the dal and simmer gently 5 minutes so the sourness blends in.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin, 2 dried red chillies, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 14 curry leaves for 20 seconds.
Pour the fragrant coconut-oil tempering into the simmering dal and stir it through.
Add 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and simmer 3 minutes to round the tang.
Adjust with hot water to a soft, spoonable consistency and serve warm.
tips: A tovve is meant to be mild and comforting, so keep the chilli gentle and let the tamarind lead.
Coconut oil in the tempering is what marks this as coastal Karnataka; do not swap it for ghee.
Add the jaggery a little at a time and taste, as it should only just balance the tamarind.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot rice with a spoon of ghee and a side of crisp happala, or with ragi mudde.

variations.name: Rajasthani Toor Dal Home-style
variations.description: The desert home cooks a robust dal fired up with whole dried red chillies and a garlic-forward ghee tadka, using minimal water-heavy vegetables. It is punchy and warming, the kind of dal that pairs with bajra roti on a cold Marwari night.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: generous ghee is the Rajasthani way to enrich a dal where vegetables are scarce

steps: Rinse 1 cup toor dal and pressure-cook with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 5 whistles until soft, then whisk smooth.
Loosen the dal with a little hot water and 0.5 tsp salt and keep it at a gentle simmer.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, 4 broken dried red chillies and 0.25 tsp asafoetida for 20 seconds.
Add 8 crushed garlic cloves and fry 40 seconds until deep golden and aromatic.
Take the pan off the heat and stir in 1 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder so they bloom in the hot ghee without burning.
Pour this fiery tadka into the simmering dal and cook together 6 minutes so the garlic and chilli infuse.
Garnish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and serve hot.
tips: Break the dried chillies so they release more heat into the ghee, or leave whole for a milder finish.
Bloom the ground spices off the heat in the hot ghee to avoid the acrid taste of scorched chilli powder.
Rajasthanis keep this dal fairly thick to scoop up with bajra roti, so go easy on the water.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra or missi roti and a dollop of white butter, or with plain rice and a green chilli.

variations.name: Classic Toor Dal Tadka
variations.description: The definitive dhaba-style dal, where soft-cooked pigeon pea lentils get a dramatic two-stage tadka of ghee, cumin, garlic and dried red chilli poured over sizzling at the table. Simple, smoky and deeply comforting, it is the dal every Indian kitchen falls back on.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the nutty bilona ghee is what gives the tadka its signature aroma and shine

steps: Rinse 1 cup toor dal well and pressure-cook with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 4 to 5 whistles until completely soft and creamy.
Whisk the cooked dal smooth with a ladle, add a little hot water if it is too thick and keep it at a gentle simmer.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan over medium heat, crackle 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida for 15 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 chopped onion and half the garlic, saute 4 minutes until golden, then add 2 chopped tomatoes and 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and cook 4 minutes to a pulp.
Pour this masala into the simmering dal with 0.5 tsp salt and simmer together for 6 minutes so the flavours marry.
For the second tadka, heat the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 0.5 tsp cumin, the rest of the garlic sliced and 3 dried red chillies until the garlic is golden.
Pour the sizzling second tadka over the dal, cover for 1 minute to trap the aroma, garnish with 2 tbsp coriander and serve.
tips: The second tadka poured on at the end is what separates a great dal tadka from an ordinary one, so do not skip it.
Whisk the dal well after cooking for the creamy, homogenous texture dhabas are known for.
A knob of ghee stirred in just before serving makes the dal taste richer than any amount of cream.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jeera rice or tandoori roti, a raw onion salad and a green chilli on the side.

variations.name: Gujarati Toor Dal Tadka
variations.description: Gujarat's everyday dal is famously sweet, sour and thin, balancing jaggery against kokum or lemon and studded with peanuts and curry leaves. Cooked light in groundnut oil, it drinks like a spiced soup and could not be more different from the thick northern dal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the light wood-pressed oil Gujarati kitchens use for a clean-tasting dal

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the defining sweet note of a true Gujarati dal, balanced against the sourness

steps: Rinse 1 cup toor dal and pressure-cook with 3.5 cups water, 3 tbsp raw peanuts, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 5 whistles until very soft.
Whisk the dal thin and smooth, adding about 1 cup hot water so it has a pourable, soup-like consistency.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat, splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 12 curry leaves for 20 seconds.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and 1 chopped tomato, saute 3 minutes until the tomato softens.
Pour in the whisked dal with 3 pieces kokum and 0.5 tsp salt, bring to a boil and simmer 8 minutes so the sourness infuses.
Stir in 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and let it dissolve, then simmer 3 minutes and taste to balance the sweet and sour.
Adjust with a little hot water if it thickens, then serve piping hot with the peanuts bobbing through.
tips: The dal should be thin and drinkable, not thick; add hot water freely to get there.
Kokum gives a rounder sourness than lemon, but a squeeze of lime works if you have none.
Pressure-cooking the peanuts with the dal softens them perfectly and thickens the base slightly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or ladle into bowls to sip alongside a Gujarati thali.

variations.name: Tamil Toor Dal Tadka
variations.description: In Tamil Nadu this becomes a paruppu-style dal, mashed soft and finished with a fragrant sesame-oil tarka of mustard, curry leaves and dried chilli. Bright, garlicky and lemon-lifted, it is the everyday comfort dal of the south.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: the nutty gingelly oil that gives a Tamil tarka its unmistakable aroma

steps: Rinse 1 cup toor dal and pressure-cook with 3 cups water and 0.5 tsp turmeric for 5 whistles until completely soft, then mash smooth with the back of a ladle.
Add 0.5 tsp salt and about 0.5 cup hot water to the mashed dal and keep it at a gentle simmer.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin, 3 dried red chillies and 0.25 tsp asafoetida for 20 seconds.
Add 15 curry leaves and 6 crushed garlic cloves, fry 30 seconds until the garlic is golden and fragrant.
Add 1 chopped onion and saute 4 minutes until soft, then add 1 chopped tomato and cook 3 minutes until pulpy.
Pour the tarka into the simmering dal with 0.5 tsp salt and cook together 6 minutes so the flavours meld.
Turn off the heat, stir in 1 tbsp lemon juice and serve immediately while the curry leaves are still fragrant.
tips: Sesame oil is key to the southern character; ghee will taste north Indian instead.
Add the lemon juice off the heat so it stays bright and does not turn bitter.
Crush rather than chop the garlic so it melts into the tarka and perfumes the whole dal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot steamed rice with a teaspoon of sesame oil and a crisp appalam, or alongside rasam and poriyal.

variations.name: Bengali Toor Dal Tadka
variations.description: Bengal tempers its dal with a fragrant panch phoron and smoked mustard oil, adding a whisper of sugar for the region's signature balance. Light and aromatic, it leans on the five-spice crackle rather than heavy garlic for its personality.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked first, it lends the dal the sharp warmth Bengalis prize

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the subtle Bengali sweetness that balances the mustard-oil tarka

steps: Rinse 1 cup toor dal and pressure-cook with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 inch grated ginger for 5 whistles until soft, then whisk smooth.
Loosen the dal with about 0.5 cup hot water and 0.5 tsp salt and keep it at a gentle simmer.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, then cool for 20 seconds to soften its raw edge.
Temper 1 tsp panch phoron, 2 dried red chillies and 1 bay leaf in the oil for 20 seconds until the seeds crackle and smell fragrant.
Add 1 chopped tomato and 2 slit green chillies, saute 3 minutes until the tomato breaks down.
Pour the tempering into the simmering dal with 0.5 tsp salt and cook together 6 minutes so the panch phoron perfumes the dal.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer 2 minutes until balanced and serve hot.
tips: Do not grind the panch phoron; the whole seeds crackling in mustard oil are the whole point.
Smoke the mustard oil fully before tempering to strip its acrid raw taste.
A couple of whole green chillies simmered in add fragrance without much heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a wedge of lime, or with luchi for a lazy Bengali weekend lunch.

variations.name: Andhra Toor Dal Tadka
variations.description: Andhra turns up the fire with fiery Guntur chillies and a garlic-heavy sesame tarka, plus a tang of tamarind that nods to the region's beloved pappu. It is bold, spicy and tangy, a dal that stands up to plenty of rice and ghee.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: the wood-pressed gingelly oil that anchors Andhra tarkas

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a small spoon rounds the searing Guntur heat and tamarind tang

steps: Rinse 1 cup toor dal and pressure-cook with 3 cups water, 1 chopped tomato and 0.5 tsp turmeric for 5 whistles until very soft, then mash smooth.
Soak 1 tsp tamarind in 3 tbsp warm water and squeeze out the pulp, then stir it into the mashed dal with 0.5 tsp salt and a little hot water.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin, 4 Guntur chillies and 12 curry leaves for 20 seconds.
Add 8 crushed garlic cloves and fry 30 seconds until golden and pungent.
Add 1 chopped onion and saute 4 minutes until soft and lightly browned.
Pour the tarka into the tamarind dal with 0.5 tsp salt and simmer together 7 minutes so the heat and sourness settle in.
Stir in 0.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder to round the edges, simmer 2 minutes and serve hot.
tips: Start with three Guntur chillies if you are heat-shy; they are far hotter than ordinary dried red chillies.
Cooking the tomato inside the cooker with the dal gives a smoother, tangier base.
Keep the garlic generous and crush it coarse for the authentic pappu character.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over steamed rice with a spoon of ghee, an avakaya pickle and a papad.

variations.name: Classic Dal Makhani Dhaba-style
variations.description: The smoky, unctuous makhani ladled at highway dhabas, cooked over a slow flame with plenty of butter, ghee and a charcoal smoking for that signature roadside aroma. Kasuri methi and a robust bhuna masala give it depth while a charcoal dhungar seals the deal. It is dal makhani at its most indulgent and aromatic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: generous ghee plus a charcoal dhungar delivers the smoky, heavy dhaba character

steps: Soak 1 cup black urad and 0.3 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 7 whistles until the beans crush easily.

Heat 4 tbsp butter with 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot over medium heat, add a paste of 10 garlic cloves and 1.5 inch ginger, fry 1 minute, then add 1 chopped onion and cook until deep golden, about 8 minutes.
Add 4 pureed tomatoes with 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt and cook down hard until dark and the fat separates, about 12 minutes.
Add the cooked beans with their liquor, mash a good portion, and simmer uncovered on very low heat for 45 minutes, stirring often, until thick and velvety.
Stir in 1 tsp garam masala, 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi and 4 tbsp cream and simmer 8 minutes more.

For the dhaba finish, place a hot piece of charcoal in a small bowl on the dal, pour the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over it, cover for 3 minutes to smoke, then remove the bowl and stir once before serving.
tips: The charcoal dhungar is what gives that unmistakable roadside smokiness; do not skip it if you can help it.
Brown the onions darker than usual for the deep dhaba masala base.
It reheats beautifully and tastes richer the next day with a fresh spoon of butter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter-laden tandoori roti or naan, sliced onions, green chilli and a swirl of cream on a steel plate.

variations.name: Kashmiri Dal Makhani Dhaba-style
variations.description: This version perfumes the rich smoky dal with saffron, fennel and dry ginger in the Kashmiri manner, giving a floral, warmly spiced makhani with an amber glow. Ghee carries the delicate spices while saffron milk deepens colour and scent. It marries dhaba richness with the elegance of a Kashmiri kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Kashmiri saffron bloomed in warm milk lends the dal its floral aroma and amber colour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee carries the fennel and saffron notes that define this Kashmiri-style makhani

steps: Soak 1 cup black urad and 0.3 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 7 whistles until soft; soak 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot over medium heat, add 3 crushed cardamom pods and 2 cloves, then 1 chopped onion and fry until soft and light gold, about 7 minutes.

Add 3 pureed tomatoes and 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and cook until the ghee separates, about 10 minutes, then lower the heat and stir in 1 tsp fennel powder and 0.5 tsp dry ginger for 20 seconds.
Add the cooked beans with their liquor, mash a portion, and simmer uncovered on low heat for 40 minutes until thick and creamy.
Pour in the saffron milk and 3 tbsp cream and simmer 6 minutes until the dal turns amber and smells floral.
Rest covered for 3 minutes so the spices settle, then serve warm.
tips: Keep the onions pale rather than deep brown so the saffron colour reads through.
Add the saffron milk near the end to preserve its fragrance.
Kashmiri chilli is for colour and mild warmth; lean on fennel and dry ginger for depth.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with saffron pulao or soft rotis and a light kachumber to let the floral aroma shine.

variations.name: Andhra Dal Makhani Dhaba-style
variations.description: A fiery southern take that arms the smoky black dal with Guntur chillies and a garlic-loaded sesame-oil tadka, plus a squeeze of tamarind for a tangy edge. It keeps the dhaba richness but blazes with Andhra heat the Punjabi version never has. A final spoon of ghee is the only thing that tames it.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed gingelly oil stands up to the fierce Guntur tadka and adds Andhra depth

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of ghee softens the aggressive Guntur heat and adds gloss

steps: Soak 1 cup black urad and 0.3 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 7 whistles until soft, then stir in 1 tsp tamarind pulp.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pot over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 5 broken Guntur chillies and fry until the chillies darken and smoke lightly, about 30 seconds.
Add 12 crushed garlic cloves and 1 sprig curry leaves and fry until golden, then add 1 chopped onion and cook until well browned, about 7 minutes.
Add 3 pureed tomatoes and 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and cook until the masala thickens and the oil separates, about 10 minutes.
Add the cooked beans with their liquor, mash a portion, and simmer uncovered on low heat for 35 minutes until rich, creamy and fiery.
Finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee stirred through to round the heat, adjust the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, and serve very hot.
tips: Guntur chillies are searing, so deseed a couple for colour without the full firepower.
The tamarind is subtle, just enough to lift the richness with a tang.
Serve chilled curd alongside to cool the palate between bites.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over ghee rice with a papad and plenty of curd, or with plain rotis for those who want to temper the heat.

variations.name: Gujarati Dal Makhani Dhaba-style
variations.description: The Gujarati hand rounds the smoky black dal with jaggery against tomato tang for the region's khatta-metha balance, tempered with mustard, curry leaves and asafoetida in groundnut oil. Milder and gently sweet, it softens the heavy dhaba style into something homely. It sits beautifully on a Gujarati thali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: organic jaggery powder gives the mild caramel sweetness of the Gujarati khatta-metha balance

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil is the traditional Gujarati tempering fat

steps: Soak 1 cup black urad and 0.3 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 7 whistles until soft enough to mash.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pot over medium heat, add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and let them splutter, then add 0.5 tsp cumin, 1 pinch asafoetida and 1 sprig curry leaves.
Add 1 chopped onion with a grated 1 inch piece of ginger and 2 slit green chillies and fry until golden, about 6 minutes.
Add 3 pureed tomatoes and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and cook until the masala thickens and oil separates, about 9 minutes.
Add the cooked beans with their liquor, mash a portion, stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, and simmer uncovered on low heat for 35 minutes.
Taste and adjust the sweet-tangy balance, then serve warm and creamy.
tips: Add jaggery toward the end so it dissolves smoothly without scorching.
Keep the chilli gentle; this version is about balance, not heat.
A final drizzle of raw groundnut oil adds a glossy, authentic finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulka rotis or steamed rice and a crunchy kachumber salad for a homely Gujarati meal.

variations.name: Tamil Dal Makhani Dhaba-style
variations.description: A southern reinterpretation where the smoky black dal is finished with a sesame-oil tempering of mustard, curry leaves and dried chillies, brightened with tamarind and warmed by black pepper instead of garam masala. Fried shallots lend a gentle sweetness. Rich yet fragrant, it carries an unmistakably Tamil signature.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed gingelly oil defines the Tamil tempering and adds warm nuttiness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of ghee softens the pepper heat and gives a glossy finish

steps: Soak 1 cup black urad and 0.3 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 7 whistles until soft.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pot over medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop, then add 2 broken dried red chillies and 2 sprigs curry leaves.
Add 10 sliced shallots and 8 sliced garlic cloves and fry until deep golden, about 7 minutes, then add 2 chopped tomatoes and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and cook until pulpy, about 7 minutes.
Add the cooked beans with their liquor, mash a portion, stir in 1 tsp tamarind pulp and 0.5 tsp black pepper powder, and simmer uncovered on low heat for 35 minutes until thick.
Adjust the remaining 0.5 tsp salt and simmer 3 more minutes to meld the flavours.
Finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee stirred through and serve hot.
tips: Black pepper, not garam masala, provides the warmth in true Tamil style.
Fry the shallots to deep gold for a subtle sweetness that balances the tamarind.
Keep the tamarind gentle so it brightens rather than sours the rich dal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot rice with a crisp appalam and a spoon of ghee, or alongside soft parottas.

variations.name: Classic Dhuli Moong Tadka
variations.description: A light, quick-cooking dal of skinned split green gram, simmered soft and finished with a fragrant ghee tadka of cumin, garlic and dried red chilli. Delicate and easy to digest, it is the everyday comfort dal of North Indian homes.

ingredients.name: Dhuli moong dal (skinned split green gram)
Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries the cumin-garlic tadka that defines this delicate moong dal.

steps: Rinse 1 cup dhuli moong dal until the water runs clear, then pressure-cook with the grated ginger, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 2.5 cups water for 2 to 3 whistles until just soft, as moong cooks fast.
Open the cooker, whisk the dal lightly to a smooth, thin consistency, and keep it warm on a low flame with the chopped tomato stirred in.
Simmer the dal for 4 minutes so the tomato softens and blends in, adjusting with 0.5 cup hot water to keep it pourable.
For the tadka, heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan over medium-high heat and add 1 tsp cumin seeds, letting them sizzle and darken for 20 seconds.

Add the sliced garlic and 2 broken dried red chillies and fry for about 1 minute until the garlic is golden and the chillies puff, then switch off and stir in 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 0.5 tsp red chilli powder.
Pour the sizzling tadka over the dal, cover for 30 seconds to trap the aroma, and finish with chopped coriander before serving.
tips: Moong dal cooks quickly, so stop at 2 to 3 whistles to keep it from turning gluey.
Bloom the chilli powder in the off-heat ghee so it colours the tadka without burning.
A squeeze of lemon at the table brightens this mild dal beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or with soft phulkas and a simple salad for a light, restorative meal.

variations.name: Bengali Dhuli Moong Tadka with Mustard Oil
variations.description: A Bengali-style moong dal, ideally with the dal lightly roasted first, tempered in smoking mustard oil with panch phoron. Slit chillies and a hint of jaggery give it the gentle sweet-hot character loved across Bengal.

ingredients.name: Dhuli moong dal (skinned split green gram)
Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Smoking mustard oil gives this roasted moong dal its pungent Bengali aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A pinch of jaggery balances the mustard oil in the Bengali sweet-hot style.

steps: Dry-roast 1 cup dhuli moong dal in a pan over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes until it smells nutty and turns a shade darker, then rinse it well.
Pressure-cook the roasted dal with the grated ginger, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 2.5 cups water for 3 whistles until soft, then whisk to a smooth consistency.
Loosen the dal with 0.5 cup hot water, drop in the slit green chillies, and keep it warm on a low flame.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a small pan over high heat until it smokes and mellows, about 1 minute, then lower to medium.
Add 1 bay leaf, 1 tsp panch phoron and 2 broken dried red chillies and let them crackle for 25 seconds until the fenugreek darkens and the mix smells toasty.
Pour the tadka into the dal, stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder until it melts, and serve once the sweet-hot balance tastes right.
tips: Roasting the moong before cooking is the Bengali touch that gives the dal its distinctive nutty aroma.
Bring the mustard oil to smoking point first so its flavour is aromatic rather than raw.
Keep panch phoron whole in the hot oil to avoid any bitterness from grinding it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice, a wedge of lime and a side of aloo bhaja for a classic light Bengali lunch.

variations.name: Gujarati Dhuli Moong Tadka with Jaggery
variations.description: A thin, sippable Gujarati moong dal gently sweetened with jaggery and brightened by lime, finished with a curry-leaf and mustard-seed ghee tadka. It is soothing, mildly spiced and everyday-friendly.

ingredients.name: Dhuli moong dal (skinned split green gram)
Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries the mustard-and-curry-leaf tadka that scents this Gujarati moong dal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery lends the mild Gujarati sweetness that defines this sweet-sour dal.

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed dhuli moong dal with the grated ginger, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 2.75 cups water for 3 whistles until soft, then whisk to a thin, smooth consistency.
Stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and the minced green chilli and simmer for 3 minutes until the jaggery dissolves.
In a small pan, heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, adding 0.5 tsp cumin once they splutter for 15 seconds.
Add 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 10 curry leaves and let them crackle for 15 seconds until the leaves release their citrus fragrance.
Pour the tadka into the dal and stir it through so the aroma spreads evenly.
Take the dal off the heat, mix in 1 tbsp lime juice for the sweet-sour close, and serve warm.
tips: Keep this dal thin enough to sip, adding hot water if it thickens on standing.
Add the jaggery and lime near the end so both flavours stay bright and balanced.
A pinch more asafoetida deepens the comforting Gujarati aroma if you enjoy it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle over steamed rice with a spoon of ghee, or serve as a light dal beside soft rotli and a spoon of sweet chundo pickle.

variations.name: Kerala Dhuli Moong Tadka with Coconut
variations.description: A Kerala-style cherupayar parippu made creamy with a fresh coconut-cumin paste and finished with a coconut-oil, shallot and curry-leaf tempering. It is mellow, nutty and comforting, a staple across Kerala kitchens.

ingredients.name: Dhuli moong dal (skinned split green gram)
Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil gives the shallot tadka its sweet, authentic Kerala scent.

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed dhuli moong dal with the slit green chillies, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 2.5 cups water for 3 whistles until soft.
Grind 0.5 cup grated coconut with 0.5 tsp cumin and 3 tablespoons water to a smooth paste.
Stir the coconut paste into the cooked dal and simmer for 6 minutes on low heat, stirring, until creamy and just thickened.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and the remaining 0.25 tsp cumin for 20 seconds.
Add the sliced shallots, 2 dried red chillies and 12 curry leaves and fry for 3 to 4 minutes until the shallots turn golden and crisp.
Pour the coconut-oil tadka over the dal, stir it in, and rest covered for 2 minutes before serving warm.
tips: Simmer gently after adding coconut paste and stir often so it does not split or catch.
Fry the shallots to a proper golden for the sweetness that lifts the coconut base.
Add hot water at serving time, since the coconut thickens the dal as it stands.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with red matta rice and pappadam, or with plain rice and a side of thoran for a homely Kerala plate.

variations.name: Andhra Dhuli Moong Tadka with Guntur Chilli
variations.description: A spicy Andhra pesara pappu with a punchy garlic-and-Guntur-chilli tadka in groundnut oil and a touch of tamarind. The mild moong turns fiery and rustic, made for mixing into hot rice with ghee.

ingredients.name: Dhuli moong dal (skinned split green gram)
Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the Andhra fat for a garlicky Guntur chilli tadka.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of ghee softens the Guntur heat for mixing into rice.

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed dhuli moong dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 2.5 cups water for 3 whistles until soft, then whisk lightly.
Stir 0.75 tbsp tamarind pulp into the dal and simmer for 4 minutes so the sourness works through, adjusting with a splash of hot water.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a small pan over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 0.75 tsp cumin for 20 seconds.
Add 4 broken Guntur chillies, the crushed garlic and 10 curry leaves and fry for 1 minute until the garlic is golden and the chillies smell smoky.
Add the chopped onion and cook 4 minutes until soft and reddened, then pour this tadka into the dal and simmer together 3 minutes.
Adjust salt to taste and swirl in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee off the heat to round the chilli before serving.
tips: Deseed a Guntur chilli or two for the smoky flavour with a little less heat.
Add tamarind before the tadka so it melds into the dal rather than sitting sharp.
This pappu is meant to be fiery, so serve it with plenty of rice and a spoon of ghee.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot rice pressed with a nub of ghee and fried papad, adding a cooling curd on the side to temper the Guntur heat.

variations.name: Classic Masoor Dal Fry
variations.description: Masoor dal fry builds a well-browned onion-tomato masala in ghee until the fat separates, then folds in the quick-cooked red lentils and reduces it thick. The frying gives a deeper, dhaba-style flavour than a simple tadka dal. Hearty and satisfying, it holds its own on a rice plate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the masala is fried in ghee until it separates for a rich fry-style body
