steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed masoor dal with 2.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 2 to 3 whistles until soft, then set aside without whisking so it keeps some body.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add 6 minced garlic cloves and 1 inch grated ginger and fry 40 seconds.
Add 2 finely chopped onions and 2 slit green chillies, cooking 7 to 8 minutes until the onions are deep golden brown, which builds the fry-style base.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes with 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp coriander powder, and cook 6 minutes until the tomatoes break down and the ghee separates.
Fold in the cooked dal with 0.5 cup hot water and 0.5 tsp salt, then simmer 6 minutes, stirring, until thick and the masala clings to the dal.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala and 2 tbsp coriander, cook 1 more minute, and serve.
tips: Brown the onions patiently to a deep gold, as this gives the sweetness and colour a fry dal needs.
Keep the dal thick and scoopable rather than soupy, adding water only a little at a time.
Cook the tomatoes until the ghee visibly separates, the signal that the masala is fully done.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tandoori roti or laccha paratha and a raw onion salad, topping the dal with a final drizzle of ghee.

variations.name: Punjabi Masoor Dal Fry
variations.description: The Punjabi dhaba version makes masoor dal fry rich and creamy with a butter finish, kasuri methi and a swirl of cream. The lentils are simmered until velvety before the buttery tadka goes in. A coal-smoke finish adds the beloved dhaba aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee builds the base while butter finishes it for Punjabi richness

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed masoor dal with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 3 whistles until very soft, then whisk into a smooth, creamy dal.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add 6 grated garlic cloves and 1 inch grated ginger and fry 40 seconds.
Add 2 finely chopped onions and cook 7 minutes to a rich golden brown, then add 2 pureed tomatoes with 1 tsp red chilli powder and simmer 6 minutes until the ghee separates.
Pour in the whisked dal with 0.5 cup hot water and 0.5 tsp salt, and simmer on low 8 minutes, stirring, until velvety.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the dal, stir in 2 tbsp cream and 0.5 tsp garam masala, and cook 2 minutes.
Melt 2 tbsp butter until foaming, pour it over the dal, garnish with 2 tbsp coriander, and serve.
tips: For dhaba smokiness, rest a hot coal in a bowl on the dal, drip ghee over it and cover 2 minutes before the butter finish.
Whisk the dal thoroughly after cooking for the smooth, creamy Punjabi body.
Add cream on low heat and avoid a hard boil afterwards, or it may split.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or jeera rice, with an extra knob of butter on top and a side of pickled onions.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Masoor Dal Fry
variations.description: This version fries the masoor masala with warming goda masala and roasted peanuts, cooked in groundnut oil. Its coconut-clove aroma and gentle jaggery balance set it apart from northern fry dals. Nutty, fragrant and lightly sweet, it is a comforting Maharashtrian plate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil is the everyday cooking fat of Maharashtra

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: balances the earthy goda masala the Maharashtrian way

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed masoor dal with 2.5 cups water and 0.5 tsp turmeric for 2 to 3 whistles, then keep aside lightly mashed but still textured.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 10 curry leaves for 20 seconds.
Add 1 large finely chopped onion and fry 6 minutes until golden, then add 1 chopped tomato and cook 3 minutes until soft.
Lower the heat and add 1.5 tsp goda masala, 2 tbsp grated coconut and 3 tbsp coarsely crushed roasted peanuts, frying 1 minute until fragrant.
Fold in the dal with 0.5 cup water, 1 tsp jaggery powder and 1 tsp salt, and simmer 6 minutes until thick and nutty.
Finish with 2 tbsp coriander and a squeeze of lime, then serve.
tips: Add goda masala only on lowered heat, as its delicate spices scorch and turn bitter easily.
Crushed roasted peanuts thicken the dal and add crunch, so keep them coarse rather than powdered.
A final squeeze of lime brightens the goda masala and peanut richness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or scoop it up with jowar bhakri and a raw onion wedge.

variations.name: Bengali Masoor Dal Fry
variations.description: A Bengali-style fried masoor dal tempered in pungent mustard oil with nigella seeds and dried red chilli, then simmered with a lightly fried onion-tomato base. The mustard oil gives it a sharp, distinctive aroma quite unlike a North Indian fry dal. A finishing spoon of ghee softens the edges.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil gives the fry dal its distinctive Bengali pungency

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon to round the sharp mustard-oil edge

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed masoor dal with 2.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 2 to 3 whistles, then keep aside lightly mashed.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai over medium-high heat until it lightly smokes, lower the flame, then add 0.5 tsp nigella seeds and 2 dried red chillies and crackle 15 seconds.
Add 2 finely chopped onions and fry 6 minutes until golden, then add 1 inch grated ginger and 1 chopped tomato and cook 3 minutes until soft.
Add 0.5 tsp cumin powder and 0.5 tsp red chilli powder with a splash of water, frying 30 seconds so the spices do not burn.
Fold in the dal with 2 slit green chillies, 0.5 tsp sugar, 0.5 tsp salt and 0.5 cup hot water, then simmer 6 minutes until thick.
Turn off the heat, drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee, garnish with 2 tbsp coriander, and serve.
tips: Nigella seeds give this fry dal its distinct Bengali aroma, so avoid substituting cumin seeds here.
Smoke the mustard oil first to soften its raw pungency into a clean, nutty flavour.
The pinch of sugar balances the mustard sharpness without sweetening the dal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a piece of aloo bhaja, or with roti and a wedge of lime on the side.

variations.name: Kerala Masoor Dal Fry
variations.description: A South Indian fry dal where the masala is built on shallots, garlic and toasted coconut in fragrant coconut oil. Roasted coconut slivers and curry leaves give a toasty depth that sets it apart from creamy northern fry dals. Aromatic and lightly spiced, it is deeply comforting over rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil carries the toasty Kerala aroma through the dal

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed masoor dal with 2.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 2 slit green chillies for 2 to 3 whistles, then mash coarsely and keep aside.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadhai over medium heat and roast 0.33 cup grated coconut for 3 minutes until golden and toasty, then remove and set aside.
In the same pan add the remaining 1.5 tbsp coconut oil, splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, then add 3 broken dried red chillies and 14 curry leaves and crisp them 20 seconds.
Add 6 sliced shallots and 5 crushed garlic cloves, frying 5 minutes until deep golden, then add 1 chopped tomato and cook 3 minutes until soft.
Fold in the mashed dal with the roasted coconut, 0.5 cup hot water and 1 tsp salt, and simmer 6 minutes until thick and fragrant.
Drizzle over a teaspoon of raw coconut oil off the heat and serve warm.
tips: Roast the coconut separately first so it turns toasty without burning in the masala.
Use shallots rather than regular onions for the authentic sweet-savoury Kerala base.
A final drizzle of raw coconut oil off the heat lifts the whole dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with red matta rice and a simple thoran, or scoop it up with kerala parotta for a hearty meal.

variations.name: Classic Punjabi Veg Korma
variations.description: This is the hearty Punjabi korma, a robust onion-tomato-cashew gravy enriched with ghee, cream and crushed kasuri methi that clings to a medley of vegetables. It is fuller-bodied and more assertively spiced than the delicate southern kormas. A true dhaba-style vegetarian centrepiece.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the backbone of Punjabi gravies, giving richness and aroma

steps: Dice and steam the mixed vegetables for 8 minutes until just tender, then set aside.
Boil the chopped onions, tomatoes and 14 cashews with 1 cup water for 8 minutes until soft, cool, and blend to a smooth gravy.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium, crackle 1 tsp cumin, add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, and fry 1 minute until the raw smell goes.
Pour in the blended gravy with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, and cook on medium for 8 minutes until the ghee separates and floats on top.
Add 1 cup water and 1.25 tsp salt, fold in the steamed vegetables, and simmer 5 minutes so they take on the masala.
Stir in 4 tbsp cream, 0.75 tsp garam masala and 1.5 tsp crushed kasuri methi, simmer 2 minutes, and serve rich and hot.
tips: Boiling the onions before blending, rather than frying, gives a smoother gravy without a raw bite.
Roast and crush the kasuri methi in your palm just before adding for maximum aroma.
A teaspoon of sugar balances the tomatoes if the gravy tastes too tangy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan, laccha paratha or jeera rice, finished with a swirl of cream and a pinch of kasuri methi.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Punjabi Veg Korma
variations.description: This take swaps the creamy Punjabi base for the dark, smoky depth of goda masala and roasted dry coconut, giving the korma an earthy, spicy character. A touch of jaggery keeps the flavours in balance. It is a rustic, aromatic reinvention of the familiar dish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday oil that carries goda masala's roasted aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: balances the fiery goda masala as Maharashtrian cooks prefer

steps: Dice and steam the mixed vegetables for 8 minutes until just tender, and dry-roast 3 tbsp dry coconut on low until deep brown, then grind with the sliced onions to a coarse dark paste.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on medium, crackle 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, and fry 30 seconds.
Add the coconut-onion paste and cook on medium for 7 minutes until it turns rich brown and the oil leaves the sides.
Stir in the chopped tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp goda masala, and cook 4 minutes until the tomato collapses.
Add 1.5 cups water and 1.25 tsp salt, bring to a simmer, then fold in the steamed vegetables and cook 6 minutes so they absorb the dark gravy.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer 2 minutes, scatter 2 tbsp coriander, and serve.
tips: Roast the dry coconut slowly to a deep even brown, stopping just before it burns, for the true kala-masala colour.
Goda masala heat varies, so add the chilli powder gradually and taste.
Keep the gravy a touch thin as it thickens on standing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri or steamed rice and a raw onion wedge with lemon.

variations.name: Bengali Punjabi Veg Korma
variations.description: A Bengali rendition where pungent mustard oil, a whole-spice temper and a poppy-and-cashew paste replace the cream, giving a mild, nutty gravy with a gentle sweetness. Ginger leads in place of garlic-heavy Punjabi masala. It is a softer, aromatic take that suits both rice and luchi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the pungent base that reshapes the korma in the Bengali idiom

steps: Dice and steam the mixed vegetables for 8 minutes until just tender, and soak 1.5 tbsp poppy seeds and 10 cashews in warm water for 15 minutes, then grind to a smooth white paste.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the heat, and temper 1 tsp cumin, 2 bay leaves and 3 cardamom pods for 20 seconds.
Add 1.5 tbsp ginger paste and the chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, and cook 5 minutes until the tomatoes soften to a pulp.
Stir in the poppy-cashew paste and cook on low for 4 minutes until it thickens and smells nutty, keeping the gravy pale.
Add 1 cup water, 1.25 tsp salt and 0.75 tsp sugar, fold in the steamed vegetables, and simmer 6 minutes.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala, simmer 1 minute, and serve while the mustard aroma is fresh.
tips: Grind the poppy and cashew very smooth so the gravy is silky rather than grainy.
Heat the mustard oil to smoking first to tame its raw pungency.
The pinch of sugar and the ginger together give the characteristic Bengali balance.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice, luchi or plain pulao and a slit green chilli.

variations.name: Kerala Punjabi Veg Korma
variations.description: Here the north Indian korma is reimagined with a ground coconut-fennel paste and coconut milk, tempered with curry leaves in coconut oil for an unmistakably southern fragrance. It is mild, creamy and lightly sweet from the coconut. A gentle bridge between two very different korma traditions.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: essential for the true fragrance of a Kerala coconut gravy

steps: Dice the mixed vegetables and simmer them with 0.75 cup thin coconut milk, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt for 8 minutes until nearly tender.
Grind 0.75 cup grated coconut with 1 tsp fennel seeds, 8 cashews, the ginger and 3 green chillies to a smooth paste using a little warm water.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil on medium, add 12 curry leaves and the sliced onion, and saute 6 minutes until soft and pale.
Add the ground coconut paste to the onions and cook on low for 4 minutes until fragrant, stirring so it does not catch.
Fold the coconut base into the simmering vegetables, add a splash of hot water for a pourable gravy, and cook gently for 5 minutes.
Stir in 0.5 tsp garam masala, warm 1 minute without boiling hard, and serve creamy and aromatic.
tips: Simmer gently once the coconut goes in, as a hard boil splits the gravy.
Grind the coconut with warm water for the smoothest, whitest paste.
Finish with a few drops of raw coconut oil off the heat for extra fragrance.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with appam, idiyappam or Malabar parotta and a spoon of tangy pickle.

variations.name: Kashmiri Punjabi Veg Korma
variations.description: This version trades the tomato-heavy Punjabi base for a pale, saffron-scented yogurt gravy built on fennel, dry ginger and cardamom. It is aromatic and mild, the vegetables glowing gold under a slick of ghee. A refined, festive reinterpretation of the everyday korma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: gives the korma its rich, festive Kashmiri aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk for the signature colour and fragrance

steps: Dice and steam the mixed vegetables for 8 minutes until just tender, soak the pinch of Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk, and boil the sliced onion with 12 cashews for 5 minutes, then blend to a smooth pale paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium, add 3 cardamom pods, 3 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon, and let them puff for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add the onion-cashew paste with 1.5 tsp fennel powder and 0.75 tsp dry ginger, and cook on low for 5 minutes without browning, keeping it pale.
Whisk the 0.75 cup yogurt smooth, lower the flame, and stir it in gradually so it does not split.
Add 1 cup water and 1.25 tsp salt, fold in the steamed vegetables and the saffron milk, and simmer gently for 6 minutes.
Cook 1 more minute until the gravy is glossy and golden, and serve garnished with a few fried cashews.
tips: Keep the onions from browning so the gravy stays pale and elegant.
Add the yogurt on a low flame while stirring continuously to keep the korma smooth.
Fennel and dry ginger carry the flavour here, so use them fresh.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with saffron pulao or soft rumali roti for a festive spread.

variations.name: Classic Toor Dal Punjabi
variations.description: The rich Punjabi rendition of arhar dal, slow-simmered with a buttery onion-tomato masala, crushed kasuri methi and a final flourish of white butter. Thick, creamy and mildly spiced, it is the dal that anchors a hearty North Indian thali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee gives the buttery Punjabi dal its rich, rounded base

steps: Rinse 1 cup toor dal and pressure-cook with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 5 whistles until soft and creamy, then whisk smooth.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 15 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 2 finely chopped onions, fry 7 minutes until deep golden, the base of a good Punjabi dal.
Add 3 chopped tomatoes, 1 tbsp coriander powder, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp salt, cook 6 minutes until the masala is thick and the ghee separates.
Fold the whisked dal into the masala with a little hot water and simmer 8 minutes, stirring, so the lentils turn creamy and rich.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi between your palms and stir it in with 0.5 tsp garam masala.
Swirl in 1.5 tbsp white butter off the heat until it melts, garnish with 2 tbsp coriander and serve hot.
tips: Frying the onions properly to deep gold is the secret to the rich body of a Punjabi dal.
Toast the kasuri methi lightly before crushing to bring out its full aroma.
Keep this dal thicker than a home-style dal; it should coat the back of a spoon.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with laccha paratha, jeera rice or naan, topped with an extra knob of white butter and sirke wale pyaaz.

variations.name: Kashmiri Toor Dal Punjabi
variations.description: The valley recasts the buttery Punjabi dal in its own aromatic idiom, swapping onion and garlic for fennel, dry ginger and a bloom of saffron. Gently golden and fragrant rather than heavy, it shows how the same lentil transforms across regions.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the base fat of onion-free Kashmiri Pandit cooking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Kashmiri Mongra strands bloomed in warm milk lend a delicate golden aroma

steps: Steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside to bloom into a golden liquid.
Rinse 1 cup toor dal and pressure-cook with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 5 whistles until soft, then whisk smooth.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, 3 cloves, 2 cardamom and 0.25 tsp asafoetida for 20 seconds.
Add 2 finely chopped tomatoes and cook 5 minutes until they collapse into a thick pulp.
Stir in 1 tsp fennel powder, 0.5 tsp dry ginger powder and 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, roast 1 minute until the ghee turns deep red and fragrant.
Fold in the whisked dal with 0.5 tsp salt and a little hot water, simmer 7 minutes so the fennel and ginger perfume the lentils.
Swirl in the saffron milk, simmer 2 minutes until golden and serve hot.
tips: Fennel and dry ginger are the signature Kashmiri spices; do not replace them with garam masala.
Kashmiri chilli powder is chosen for its colour more than its heat, so it can be used generously.
Bloom the saffron in warm, never boiling, milk to draw out colour without bitterness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain basmati or a Kashmiri saffron pulao and a side of haakh greens.

variations.name: Tamil Toor Dal Punjabi
variations.description: The buttery North Indian dal is reimagined southern-style, mashed soft and finished with a sesame-oil tarka of mustard, curry leaves and dried chilli. A squeeze of lemon and plenty of garlic give it the bright, comforting character of Tamil paruppu.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: the nutty gingelly oil that gives a Tamil tarka its unmistakable aroma

steps: Rinse 1 cup toor dal and pressure-cook with 3 cups water, 1 chopped tomato and 0.5 tsp turmeric for 5 whistles until soft, then mash smooth with a ladle.
Add 0.5 tsp salt and a little hot water to the dal and keep it at a gentle simmer.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin, 3 dried red chillies and 0.25 tsp asafoetida for 20 seconds.
Add 15 curry leaves and 7 crushed garlic cloves, fry 30 seconds until the garlic turns golden.
Add 1 chopped onion and saute 4 minutes until soft and lightly coloured.
Pour the tarka into the simmering dal with 0.5 tsp salt and cook together 6 minutes so the flavours meld.
Turn off the heat, stir in 1 tbsp lemon juice and serve immediately while the tarka is fragrant.
tips: Sesame oil gives the true southern character, so resist swapping it for ghee here.
Add the lemon juice off the heat so it stays fresh and does not turn bitter.
Crush the garlic rather than chopping so it melts into the tarka and perfumes the dal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot rice with a teaspoon of sesame oil and a crisp appalam, or alongside a vegetable poriyal.

variations.name: Gujarati Toor Dal Punjabi
variations.description: Gujarat softens the robust Punjabi dal into its signature sweet-sour style, melting jaggery against kokum and lightening it with a curry-leaf tempering in groundnut oil. The result is gentler, thinner and quietly addictive.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the light wood-pressed oil of the everyday Gujarati kitchen

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the defining sweetness of a Gujarati-style dal

steps: Rinse 1 cup toor dal and pressure-cook with 3.5 cups water, 2 tbsp raw peanuts, 1 chopped tomato and 0.5 tsp turmeric for 5 whistles until very soft.
Whisk the dal thin, adding about 1 cup hot water so it turns light and pourable.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 12 curry leaves for 20 seconds.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and saute 30 seconds until fragrant.
Pour in the whisked dal with 3 pieces kokum and 0.5 tsp salt, bring to a boil and simmer 8 minutes so the sourness infuses.
Stir in 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and let it dissolve, then simmer 3 minutes and taste to balance sweet against sour.
Loosen with hot water if needed and serve warm with the peanuts running through.
tips: Keep this dal thin and drinkable, the hallmark of a Gujarati preparation.
Kokum lends a gentle fruity sourness; a squeeze of lemon off the heat works in its place.
The peanuts cooked with the dal add a subtle crunch and body without any extra thickener.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain rice and ghee as part of a thali, or sip it warm before the meal.

variations.name: Andhra Toor Dal Punjabi
variations.description: Andhra fires up the mellow Punjabi dal with pungent Guntur chillies, a garlic-heavy sesame tarka and a tang of tamarind that nods to the region's pappu. Bold, spicy and tangy, it turns the buttery original on its head.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: the wood-pressed gingelly oil that anchors every Andhra tarka

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a small spoon rounds the searing Guntur heat and tamarind tang

steps: Rinse 1 cup toor dal and pressure-cook with 3 cups water, 1 chopped tomato and 0.5 tsp turmeric for 5 whistles until very soft, then mash smooth.
Soak 1 tsp tamarind in 3 tbsp warm water, squeeze out the pulp and stir it into the dal with 0.5 tsp salt and a little hot water.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin, 4 Guntur chillies and 12 curry leaves for 20 seconds.
Add 8 crushed garlic cloves and fry 30 seconds until golden and pungent.
Add 1 chopped onion and saute 4 minutes until soft and lightly browned.
Pour the tarka into the tamarind dal with 0.5 tsp salt and simmer together 7 minutes so the heat and sourness settle.
Stir in 0.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder to round the edges, simmer 2 minutes and serve hot.
tips: Guntur chillies are fierce; start with three if you prefer a milder dal.
The tamarind gives the tangy backbone that defines Andhra pappu, so do not omit it.
Keep the garlic generous and crush it coarse for the authentic pungent character.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over steamed rice with a spoon of ghee, an avakaya pickle and a papad.

variations.name: Classic Lauki Chana Dal Home-style
variations.description: The unfussy everyday lauki chana dal cooked in most North Indian homes, lighter and simpler than the restaurant fry, with a single cumin-garlic ghee tadka. The bottle gourd melts gently into the nutty bengal gram, gently spiced and quick, comfort food at its most honest.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A simple cumin-garlic tadka in bilona ghee is all this homely dal needs

steps: Soak 0.75 cup bengal gram for 30 minutes, then pressure-cook with 2 cups diced bottle gourd, 2.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 chopped tomato, 1 inch grated ginger and 0.75 tsp salt for 5 whistles until soft.
Open the cooker, lightly mash a little of the dal against the side to thicken the gravy, and keep it warm on a low flame.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds with 0.25 tsp asafoetida for about 20 seconds.
Add 5 crushed garlic cloves and 1 slit green chilli and fry until the garlic is golden, about 1 minute, then add 1 chopped onion and cook until soft, roughly 4 minutes.
Stir in the second chopped tomato, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, and cook for 3 minutes until pulpy.
Pour the tempering into the dal, simmer together for 5 minutes, then finish with 2 tbsp coriander and serve hot.
tips: Cooking one tomato inside the cooker with the dal saves a step and gives a gentle background tang.
Keep this dal light and add hot water freely if it thickens as it stands.
Taste a raw sliver of the bottle gourd first; an older bitter one can spoil the whole pot.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or with hot phulkas and a simple salad for an easy everyday meal.

variations.name: Tamil Lauki Chana Dal Home-style
variations.description: A Tamil household version tempered with curry leaves, mustard and black pepper in gingelly oil, closer to a sorakkai paruppu than a northern dal. The fragrant tempering and a spoon of ghee at the end make the bottle gourd and bengal gram soft, aromatic and soothing over rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil is the everyday tempering fat of Tamil homes

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon of ghee stirred into hot dal is a beloved Tamil finishing habit

steps: Soak 0.75 cup bengal gram for 30 minutes, then pressure-cook with 2 cups diced bottle gourd, 2.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 5 whistles until soft, and mash a little to thicken.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pan over medium heat and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds until they pop.
Add 2 dried red chillies, 15 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them crackle for 15 seconds until the curry leaves crisp and smell fragrant.
Add 6 sliced shallots and 5 crushed garlic cloves and fry until soft and golden, about 4 minutes, then stir in 1 chopped tomato and 0.5 tsp black pepper and cook 3 minutes.
Pour in the cooked dal and lauki with the remaining 0.5 tsp salt and a little hot water, and simmer for 6 minutes so the tempering flavours the pot.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee just before serving for the traditional finishing aroma.
tips: Black pepper rather than heavy chilli gives this dal its gentle Tamil warmth, so keep the red chilli light.
Fry the curry leaves crisp so they crumble into the dal and release their aroma.
Shallots melt into a natural sweetness; if using regular onion, cook it a couple of minutes longer.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot rice with a spoon of ghee and a fried appalam, alongside a dry poriyal and a piece of lime pickle.

variations.name: Bihari Lauki Chana Dal Home-style
variations.description: A rustic Bihari version tempered in pungent mustard oil with garlic, dried chilli and a generous crackle of cumin, kept thick and hearty. The bold mustard oil gives the bottle gourd and bengal gram an earthy sharpness, the kind of dal eaten with litti or coarse rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil gives the bold, sharp tempering typical of Bihari kitchens

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A final spoon of ghee softens the pungency of the mustard oil tadka

steps: Soak 0.75 cup bengal gram for 30 minutes, then pressure-cook with 2 cups diced bottle gourd, 2.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 5 whistles until soft, then mash a little to thicken.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pan over medium-high until it lightens and just smokes, about 1 minute, to mellow the raw pungency.
Add 1 tsp cumin seeds, 3 dried red chillies and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them crackle for 30 seconds until dark and aromatic.
Add 7 crushed garlic cloves and 1 inch grated ginger, fry 1 minute, then add 1 chopped onion and cook until deep golden, about 5 minutes.
Stir in 1 chopped tomato, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, and cook for 4 minutes until the masala thickens and the oil edges out.
Pour in the cooked dal and lauki with a little hot water, simmer for 6 minutes, finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and 2 tbsp coriander and serve.
tips: Get the mustard oil properly hot first; under-heated mustard oil leaves a raw, bitter aftertaste.
Bihari dal is generous with garlic, so do not be shy with the seven cloves.
Keep it thick so it stands up well to litti or a coarse rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with baati or litti crushed into it with extra ghee, or with plain rice, raw onion and a green chilli.

variations.name: Malwa Lauki Chana Dal Home-style
variations.description: A Malwa-region dal from the Madhya Pradesh heartland, given nutty body and crunch with roasted peanuts and a simple ghee tempering. Coarsely crushed peanuts thicken the bottle gourd and bengal gram and lend a gentle sweetness, making it hearty and distinctly central-Indian.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee toasts the peanuts and carries the cumin tempering in true Malwa style

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A little wood-pressed groundnut oil echoes and deepens the peanut flavour

steps: Soak 0.75 cup bengal gram for half an hour, then pressure-cook it with 2 cups diced bottle gourd, 2.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 5 whistles until soft, and mash a little against the side to thicken.
Coarsely crush 3 tbsp roasted peanuts in a mortar, leaving some texture, and set aside for the finish.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, 2 dried red chillies and 0.25 tsp asafoetida for 30 seconds.

Add 5 crushed garlic cloves and 1 chopped onion and fry until golden, about 5 minutes, then stir in 1 chopped tomato, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander powder and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt and cook 4 minutes.
Pour in the cooked dal and lauki with a little hot water, add most of the crushed peanuts, and simmer for 7 minutes so the peanuts soften and thicken the dal.
Finish with 2 tbsp coriander and the reserved crushed peanuts scattered on top for crunch, then serve hot.
tips: Reserve a spoon of crushed peanuts to scatter at the end so you keep some crunch against the soft dal.
Roast the peanuts a shade darker for a deeper, sweeter nuttiness through the dal.
The peanuts keep absorbing liquid, so loosen with hot water if it thickens too much on standing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar or bajra roti and a spoon of ghee, or with plain rice and a raw onion-tomato salad.

variations.name: Odia Lauki Chana Dal Home-style
variations.description: An Odia-style dalma-inspired bowl where bottle gourd and bengal gram are tempered with panch phoron and finished with a whisper of roasted cumin and ghee. Light, homely and fragrant, it carries the gentle eastern warmth of the five-spice crackle without any heaviness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee with roasted cumin is the classic Odia dalma finishing touch

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: A little wood-pressed mustard oil gives the earthy base note typical of Odia cooking

steps: Soak 0.75 cup bengal gram for 30 minutes, then pressure-cook with 2 cups diced bottle gourd, 2.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 inch grated ginger and 0.75 tsp salt for 5 whistles until soft.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil with 1 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat until shimmering, about 1 minute.
Add 1 tsp panch phoron and 2 dried red chillies and let them crackle for 30 seconds until the fenugreek darkens and smells nutty.
Add 5 crushed garlic cloves and fry 1 minute, then stir in 1 chopped tomato, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tbsp grated coconut and cook for 3 minutes until the tomato softens.
Pour in the cooked dal and lauki with the remaining 0.5 tsp salt and a little hot water, and simmer for 7 minutes so the panch phoron steeps through.
Heat the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder, pour it over, scatter 2 tbsp coriander and serve hot.
tips: Roast the cumin for the finish in a dry pan until dark, then grind it fresh for the best aroma.
The grated coconut is a signature dalma touch that adds subtle sweetness, so do not skip it.
Leave the panch phoron whole for little bursts of fennel and nigella in each spoonful.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or with plain roti, a fried papad and a lime wedge on the side.

variations.name: Classic Quick Veg Pulao
variations.description: A fuss-free pressure-cooker pulao that puts a fragrant, vegetable-studded rice on the table in about half an hour, perfect for busy weeknights. A quick whole-spice ghee tempering, a handful of vegetables and a single whistle do all the work. It is mild, comforting and endlessly adaptable to whatever vegetables are in the fridge.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee delivers full whole-spice aroma even in this speedy one-pot method.

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati rice well and soak it for 10 minutes while you chop the vegetables, then drain.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pressure cooker on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 bay leaf, 3 cardamoms, 3 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon for 20 seconds.
Add 1 sliced onion and saute until light golden, about 4 minutes, then add 1 tbsp ginger garlic paste and 2 slit green chillies and cook for 1 minute.
Add 1.5 cups mixed vegetables and 1.25 tsp salt and saute for 2 minutes, then add the drained rice and toss gently for 1 minute.
Pour in 2.25 cups hot water, stir once, close the lid and cook on medium heat for 1 whistle, then turn off the heat.
Let the pressure release naturally for 8 minutes, then open, fluff gently with a fork and fold in chopped coriander.
Serve hot with a bowl of chilled raita or a quick pickle on the side.
tips: A short 10-minute soak is enough for a quick pulao; drain well so the grains stay separate.
Let the pressure drop on its own rather than forcing it, so the grains do not break.
Frozen mixed vegetables work perfectly here and cut the prep time further.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a fast cucumber-onion raita and a papad, or a spoon of ready pickle; it also makes an easy lunchbox rice with a boiled egg or paneer cube on the side.

variations.name: Delhi-style Quick Veg Pulao
variations.description: This speedy version borrows Delhi's love of garam masala and chaat-style tang, finishing a quick one-pot pulao with a bright sprinkle of garam masala, chaat masala and lemon. It is punchy and street-food-ish yet ready in under half an hour. A scatter of fresh onion and coriander at the end keeps it lively.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee blooms the garam masala for a quick pulao with real Delhi punch.

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 10 minutes, then drain well.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pressure cooker on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1 bay leaf for 15 seconds, then add 1 sliced onion and fry until golden, about 4 minutes.
Add 1 tbsp ginger garlic paste and 1 chopped tomato and cook for 2 minutes, then add 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt.
Add 1.5 cups mixed vegetables and saute for 2 minutes, then add the drained rice and toss gently for 1 minute.
Pour in 2.25 cups hot water, close the lid and cook on medium heat for 1 whistle, then turn off the heat.
After the pressure releases naturally for 8 minutes, open and sprinkle 1 tsp garam masala and 0.5 tsp chaat masala over the rice.
Drizzle 1 tbsp lemon juice, fold in chopped coriander, fluff gently and serve hot.
tips: Add garam masala and chaat masala at the end so their aroma stays sharp and fresh.
A squeeze of lemon lifts the whole dish with a street-food style tang.
Top with thin raw onion rings dusted with chaat masala for an extra Delhi touch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a tangy mint raita and lemon wedges, or pair with quick chana masala from a can for a filling weeknight plate.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Quick Veg Pulao
variations.description: A fast weeknight take on masale bhaat, this quick pulao gets its distinctive smoky warmth from goda masala and a mustard-curry-leaf tempering, all done in one pot. Goda masala plus a few peanuts deliver big regional flavour without a long cook. It is aromatic, comforting and comes together in under half an hour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee blooms the goda masala quickly for a fast one-pot masale bhaat.

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 10 minutes, then drain well.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pressure cooker on medium heat and pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, then add 1 tsp cumin seeds, 0.25 tsp asafoetida, 10 curry leaves and 3 tbsp peanuts and fry for 30 seconds.
Add 1 sliced onion and saute until soft, about 3 minutes, then lower the heat and add 2 tsp goda masala, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt and stir for 20 seconds.
Add 1.5 cups mixed vegetables and saute for 2 minutes, then add the drained rice and toss gently for 1 minute until coated in the dark masala.
Pour in 2.25 cups hot water, close the lid and cook on medium heat for 1 whistle, then turn off the heat.
Let the pressure release naturally for 8 minutes, then open and fluff gently.
Garnish with 2 tbsp grated coconut and serve hot.
tips: Add goda masala on low heat so it does not scorch during the fast tempering.
A garnish of fresh grated coconut is the classic finishing touch for masale bhaat.
Diced brinjal added with the vegetables makes this taste closer to the traditional dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of plain yogurt or a quick koshimbir salad and a spoon of ghee melted on top, with a papad on the side.

variations.name: Kerala Quick Veg Pulao
variations.description: A speedy coconut-scented pulao where the rice cooks in coconut milk with a coconut-oil tempering of shallots and curry leaves, delivering big Kerala flavour fast. It is mild, fragrant and faintly sweet, ready in one pot in under half an hour. Fennel and a bay leaf give it that unmistakable coastal aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil delivers instant Kerala aroma and ties into the coconut-milk rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon of ghee finishes the rice with a little richness.

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 10 minutes, then drain well.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pressure cooker on medium heat and pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, then add 1 bay leaf, 2 cardamoms, 8 sliced shallots, 2 slit green chillies and 12 curry leaves.
Fry until the shallots turn golden, about 3 minutes, then stir in 0.5 tsp fennel powder and add 1.5 cups mixed vegetables and 1.25 tsp salt, sauteing for 2 minutes.
Add the drained rice and toss gently for 1 minute, then pour in 1.25 cups hot water and 0.75 cup coconut milk and stir once.
Close the lid and cook on medium heat for 1 whistle, then turn off the heat.
Let the pressure release naturally for 8 minutes, then open, drizzle 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the rice and fluff gently.
Serve hot with a simple raita or pickle.
tips: Count the coconut milk as part of the total liquid so the quick pulao does not turn soggy.
Shallots give a sweeter, more authentic base than regular onions in this coastal rice.
Add the ghee at the end so its aroma stays fresh over the coconut.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling raita and a quick vegetable stew, or simply with pappadam and a wedge of lime for an easy Kerala-style meal.

variations.name: Bihari Quick Veg Pulao
variations.description: This brisk one-pot pulao carries Bihar's love of pungent mustard oil and garlic, giving a bold, rustic rice that comes together fast yet tastes anything but plain. A sharp mustard-oil tempering with whole chillies and garlic infuses every grain. It is hearty, aromatic and pairs naturally with a simple curd or chokha.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Pungent mustard oil gives this quick pulao its bold, rustic Bihari character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of ghee softens the sharp mustard oil.

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 10 minutes, then drain well.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pressure cooker until it just smokes, then lower the heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 bay leaf and 2 broken dried red chillies for 20 seconds.
Add 8 sliced garlic cloves and fry until golden, then add 1 sliced onion and cook until soft and light brown, about 4 minutes.
Add 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt, then add 1.5 cups mixed vegetables and saute for 2 minutes.
Add the drained rice and toss gently for 1 minute, then pour in 2.25 cups hot water and stir once.
Close the lid and cook on medium heat for 1 whistle, then turn off and let the pressure release naturally for 8 minutes.
Open, drizzle 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, fold in chopped coriander, fluff gently and serve hot.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to smoking first, then cool it slightly, to mellow its raw pungency.
Plenty of golden-fried garlic is what gives this pulao its bold Bihari aroma.
Finish with ghee to round off the sharpness of the mustard oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of cold curd, a spoon of aloo-tomato chokha and a raw onion, or a simple green chilli pickle for a rustic Bihari meal.

variations.name: Classic Masala Methi Matar Malai
variations.description: A silky North Indian favourite where slightly bitter fenugreek leaves and sweet green peas swim in a pale, mildly sweet cashew-and-cream gravy. The white gravy is barely spiced so the methi and malai lead, with a hint of green chilli for warmth. It is restaurant comfort food at its most elegant.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: keeps the white gravy rich without darkening its delicate colour

steps: Chop 2 cups fenugreek leaves, sprinkle with a little salt for 10 minutes, then squeeze out the bitter juices; boil the onions with 14 cashews for 5 minutes and blend to a smooth white paste with the ginger and green chillies.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium, crackle 1 tsp cumin and 2 cardamom pods, then add the onion-cashew paste and cook on low for 5 minutes without letting it brown.
Add the squeezed fenugreek leaves and saute for 3 minutes until they wilt and their aroma turns mellow.
Stir in the green peas with 0.5 cup milk and 0.5 cup water, add 1 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp sugar, and simmer on low for 8 minutes until the peas are tender.
Pour in 4 tbsp cream and cook gently for 2 minutes so the gravy turns glossy and thick, keeping it pale.
Adjust the consistency with a splash of hot milk if needed and serve warm and creamy.
tips: Salting and squeezing the fenugreek removes its harsh bitterness while keeping the pleasant edge.
Never brown the onion-cashew paste; the whole appeal is the pale, ivory gravy.
Use fresh green peas in season, or thaw frozen peas so they stay sweet and bright.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan, tandoori roti or a mild jeera pulao, with a swirl of cream on top.

variations.name: Kashmiri Masala Methi Matar Malai
variations.description: This regal take gilds the creamy methi-matar with saffron and a whisper of fennel and cardamom, turning the pale gravy a soft gold. It is fragrant and mildly sweet, the saffron lifting the fenugreek's earthiness. A festive reinvention worthy of a celebration table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: carries the saffron and cardamom aroma through the delicate gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk for the golden colour and perfume of a festive gravy

steps: Chop 2 cups fenugreek leaves, salt them for 10 minutes and squeeze out the bitter juice; soak the pinch of Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk.
Boil the sliced onion with 12 cashews for 5 minutes, cool, and blend to a smooth pale paste with the green chillies.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium, add 3 cardamom pods, let them puff for 15 seconds, then add the onion-cashew paste and 0.75 tsp fennel powder and cook on low for 5 minutes without browning.
Add the squeezed fenugreek leaves and saute 3 minutes until wilted and fragrant.
Stir in the green peas with 0.75 cup milk and 0.5 cup water, add 1 tsp salt, and simmer on low for 8 minutes until the peas are tender.
Pour in 3 tbsp cream and the saffron milk, warm gently for 2 minutes until the gravy turns pale gold, and serve.
tips: Steep the saffron in warm milk, not water, to draw out both colour and fragrance for this pale gravy.
Keep the flame low throughout so the milk and cream do not split.
A pinch of fennel powder echoes Kashmiri cooking and pairs beautifully with fenugreek.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with saffron pulao or soft rumali roti, garnished with a few saffron strands and slivered almonds.

variations.name: Gujarati Masala Methi Matar Malai
variations.description: The Gujarati version leans into a sweeter, tangier profile, balancing the fenugreek with jaggery and a squeeze of lemon in a lighter milk-thickened gravy. Ginger and green chilli keep it lively. It is a gentle, homely shaak rather than a heavy restaurant dish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a light touch of ghee enriches the milk-based gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the signature sweetness that balances the fenugreek's edge

steps: Chop 2 cups fenugreek leaves, salt them for 10 minutes and squeeze out the bitter juice; soak 10 cashews in warm water for 10 minutes, then grind to a smooth paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium, crackle 1 tsp cumin, then add 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and 0.25 tsp turmeric and fry for 30 seconds.
Add the squeezed fenugreek leaves and saute 3 minutes until wilted and mellow.
Stir in the cashew paste and green peas, then pour in 0.75 cup milk and 0.5 cup water, add 1 tsp salt, and simmer on low for 8 minutes until the peas are tender.
Stir in 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 2 tbsp cream and cook 2 minutes until the gravy is creamy and lightly sweet.
Turn off the heat, add 1 tbsp lemon juice, stir, and serve with the bright sweet-sour finish.
tips: Add the lemon only after switching off the flame so the tang stays fresh.
Balance the jaggery and lemon at the end to hit the classic Gujarati sweet-sour note.
Keep this gravy lighter and more pourable than the rich Punjabi original.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulka rotli or thepla and a bowl of plain khichdi.

variations.name: Hyderabadi Masala Methi Matar Malai
variations.description: A shahi Hyderabadi take enriched with fried-onion birista and a melon-seed paste, scented with saffron and cardamom for a fragrant, layered gravy. It is a little tangy from yogurt and jewelled with nuts. Refined dum-style cooking suited to a Nizami spread.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the base for frying the birista and carrying the saffron aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk for the perfume of a shahi gravy

steps: Chop 2 cups fenugreek leaves, salt them for 10 minutes and squeeze out the bitter juice; soak the pinch of Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and soak 1.5 tbsp melon seeds and 10 cashews in warm water, then grind to a smooth paste.
Thinly slice the onions and fry in 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium for 8 minutes to golden birista, reserving half for garnish and grinding the rest with the green chillies to a paste.
In the same ghee add 3 cardamom pods, let them sizzle 15 seconds, then add the fried-onion paste and the melon-cashew paste and cook on low for 4 minutes without browning.
Whisk the 0.5 cup yogurt smooth and stir it in off the heat, then return to a low flame and add the squeezed fenugreek and green peas.
Pour in 1 cup water with 1 tsp salt, cover, and simmer on low for 10 minutes until the peas are tender and the gravy thickens.
Stir in 2 tbsp cream and the saffron milk, simmer 2 minutes, and serve topped with the reserved birista.
tips: Fry the onions to an even deep gold for sweetness; browning them makes the gravy bitter.
Melon-seed paste gives a delicate body and pale colour prized in shahi gravies.
Add yogurt off the heat and stir it in slowly to prevent curdling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sheermal, rumali roti or a light zafrani pulao, scattered with fried onions and mint.

variations.name: Bengali Masala Methi Matar Malai
variations.description: A Bengali-inflected version where a whole-spice temper in mustard oil and a poppy-seed paste give the creamy methi-matar an eastern accent, softened with a little sugar. The pungency of the oil is balanced by the mild poppy gravy. A gentle, aromatic crossover dish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: brings the distinct Bengali pungency to the mild creamy base

steps: Chop 2 cups fenugreek leaves, salt them for 10 minutes and squeeze out the bitter juice; soak 2 tbsp poppy seeds and 8 cashews in warm water for 15 minutes, then grind to a smooth white paste with the green chillies.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the heat, and temper 0.75 tsp cumin and 1 bay leaf for 15 seconds.
Add 1 tbsp ginger paste and fry 30 seconds, then add the squeezed fenugreek leaves and saute 3 minutes until wilted.
Stir in the poppy-cashew paste and cook on low for 4 minutes until it thickens and smells nutty, keeping the gravy pale.
Add the green peas, 0.5 cup milk and 0.5 cup water with 1 tsp salt and 0.75 tsp sugar, and simmer on low for 8 minutes until the peas are tender.
Cook 1 more minute until the gravy is creamy, then serve while the mustard aroma is fresh.
tips: Bring the mustard oil to smoking point first so its raw sharpness mellows into the mild gravy.
Grind the poppy and cashew very smooth so the gravy stays silky.
The pinch of sugar is characteristic and rounds the mustard oil without sweetening the dish much.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with luchi, plain pulao or steamed rice and a slit green chilli.

variations.name: Classic Coconut Rice
variations.description: The definitive South Indian thengai sadam, where cooled cooked rice is folded into a fragrant coconut tempering of dals, cashews and curry leaves. Each grain stays separate and glistening, mildly nutty and comforting rather than spicy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the authentic tempering fat that deepens the fresh-coconut aroma of the dish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon that makes the grains glossy and rounds the nuttiness

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati and cook with 2.5 cups water and 0.5 tsp salt until just tender, then spread on a plate to cool so the grains firm up and stay separate.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil on medium and fry 12 cashews until pale gold, about 2 minutes, then lift them out and reserve.
In the same oil crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 1 tbsp chana dal and 1 tbsp urad dal and fry until the dals turn reddish-gold, about 90 seconds.
Add 2 torn dried red chillies, 2 slit green chillies, grated 1 inch ginger and 15 curry leaves and let them splutter for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Lower the heat, tip in 0.75 cup grated coconut and toast gently for 3 minutes until it smells sweet and just begins to colour at the edges.
Fold in the cooled rice, the fried cashews and 0.75 tsp salt with a light hand so the grains coat evenly without breaking.
Finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, toss once more, and let it rest covered for 3 minutes before serving warm.
tips: Use rice cooked a few hours ahead and fully cooled, as warm rice turns the dish mushy.
Toast the coconut only to the edge of colour; browning it makes the rice taste burnt.
For a make-ahead lunchbox, keep the temper and rice separate and toss just before packing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a crisp potato roast and a bowl of thick curd, or pack with lemon pickle for a fragrant travel meal.

variations.name: Tamil Nadu Coconut Rice
variations.description: The Kovil-style thengai sadam served as temple prasadam, built on a generous curry-leaf and coconut temper with peppery warmth. It is aromatic and lightly peppery rather than chilli-hot, meant to be eaten at room temperature.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the temple-kitchen fat that carries the curry-leaf perfume through the rice

steps: Cook 1.5 cups sona masoori with 3 cups water and 0.5 tsp salt until soft but not sticky, then cool it on a wide plate for 20 minutes.
Coarsely crush 0.5 tsp black pepper with 2 of the dried chillies in a mortar so they release a warm, sharp aroma.
Warm 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and fry 15 cashews to gold, about 2 minutes, then set them aside to stay crunchy.
In the same oil pop 1 tsp mustard seeds, add 1.5 tbsp urad dal, 1 tbsp chana dal and the last whole red chilli, and fry until the dals are golden, about 1 minute.
Scatter in 25 curry leaves, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and the crushed pepper mix and let them sizzle for 20 seconds until intensely fragrant.
Add 1 cup grated coconut and roast on low for 4 minutes until it turns pale gold and smells toasty, stirring so it does not catch.
Gently mix in the cooled rice, fried cashews and 0.75 tsp salt, then rest off the heat for 5 minutes so the flavours settle before serving.
tips: A double handful of curry leaves is what defines this version, so do not skimp on them.
Crushing rather than powdering the pepper gives little bursts of warmth in every mouthful.
It tastes better an hour after making, once the coconut oil has perfumed the rice fully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature with fried appalam and a spoon of mango thokku, the way it is offered at temple annadanam.

variations.name: Kerala Coconut Rice
variations.description: A Malabar thenga choru where the rice is enriched with thick coconut milk as well as grated coconut, giving it a soft, creamy body. Warm with cardamom and shallots, it leans richer and more festive than the dry South Indian temper style.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Kerala's defining fat, layering coconut on coconut for a rounded richness

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups jeerakasala rice and soak for 20 minutes, then drain well in a colander.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and fry 12 cashews and 1 tbsp raisins until the cashews gild and the raisins puff, then scoop them out.
In the same oil sizzle 4 cracked cardamom pods, 3 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon for 20 seconds, then saute 8 sliced shallots for 4 minutes until soft and golden.
Add the drained rice with 0.5 cup grated coconut and 15 curry leaves and toast gently for 3 minutes until the grains look glossy.
Pour in 1 cup thick coconut milk plus 1.5 cups water and 1.25 tsp salt, and bring to a gentle boil without stirring too much.
Cover, drop the heat to its lowest and steam undisturbed for 12 minutes until the liquid is absorbed and the grains are tender.
Rest off the heat for 5 minutes, then fluff with a fork and scatter the fried cashews and raisins over the top before serving.
tips: Add the thick coconut milk with the water at the start so it does not split during the long steam.
Keep the flame at its lowest under a heavy lid so the creamy grains cook without sticking.
A short-grain jeerakasala or kaima rice gives the authentic soft, aromatic Malabar texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a Kerala-style egg roast or a tangy pineapple pachadi to cut the richness of the coconut milk.

variations.name: Andhra Coconut Rice
variations.description: A fiery Andhra kobbari annam where roasted Guntur chillies lend blazing heat and colour to the coconut temper. Sharp, garlicky and hot, it is the boldest coconut rice on the table, made for those who like their food to bite back.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the robust Andhra oil that stands up to roasted Guntur chilli and garlic

steps: Cook 1.5 cups sona masoori with 3 cups water and 0.5 tsp salt until just done, then cool it fully so the grains do not clump.
Dry-roast 5 Guntur chillies for 90 seconds until they darken, then grind them coarse with 6 garlic cloves and 0.75 cup grated coconut.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and roast 3 tbsp peanuts until they crackle and brown, about 3 minutes, then set them aside.
In the same oil splutter 1 tsp mustard and 1 tsp cumin seeds, add 1 tbsp urad dal and 15 curry leaves and fry until the dal is golden.
Tip in the ground chilli-garlic-coconut paste with 0.25 tsp turmeric and roast on medium for 5 minutes until the raw garlic smell disappears and the oil separates.
Fold in the cooled rice, the roasted peanuts and 0.75 tsp salt, mixing thoroughly so every grain glows red.
Cover and rest on the lowest heat for 3 minutes so the chilli heat mellows slightly into the rice before serving.
tips: Roasting the Guntur chillies before grinding deepens the colour and tames the raw throat-catch.
Grind the coconut with the chillies so its sweetness cushions the heat from within.
Keep thick curd or a banana on hand, as this version is genuinely fiery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling perugu (curd) pachadi and crisp fryums, with an extra wedge of lime to temper the heat.

variations.name: Bengali Coconut Rice
variations.description: A Bengali narkel bhat perfumed with a pungent mustard-oil and panch-phoron temper, lightly sweetened the way Bengal likes its festive rice. It is fragrant, gently sweet and mustard-sharp, quite distinct from the peppery southern styles.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked first, its pungency gives narkel bhat its unmistakable Bengali edge

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the gentle nolen-style sweetness that Bengal folds into festive rice

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups gobindobhog gently and soak for 15 minutes, then drain so the fragile grains do not break.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, lower the flame, and fry 10 cashews and 1 tbsp raisins until golden, then lift them out.
In the same oil temper 1 tsp panch phoron, 2 bay leaves, 3 cracked cardamom pods and 2 dried chillies for 20 seconds until the seeds pop and smell nutty.
Add grated 1 inch ginger and 0.75 cup grated coconut and roast on low for 3 minutes until the coconut turns pale gold.
Stir in the drained rice and toast gently for 2 minutes, then pour in 2.25 cups hot water with 1 tsp salt and 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes until the water is absorbed and the grains are separate and tender.
Fold in the fried cashews and raisins, rest covered for 4 minutes, and fluff lightly before serving warm.
tips: Smoke the mustard oil first so its raw bite softens into a mellow warmth in the rice.
Gobindobhog is delicate, so soak only briefly and stir as little as possible while cooking.
The jaggery should be barely perceptible, a rounding note rather than an outright sweetness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as part of a festive thala with cholar dal and a mixed-vegetable chorchori, ending with a spoon of chutney.

variations.name: Classic Corn Pulao
variations.description: A gentle, everyday pulao where sweet corn kernels burst against fluffy separate grains of basmati. Whole spices bloomed in nutty bilona ghee perfume the rice without any heavy masala, letting the corn's natural sweetness lead. This is the reassuring one-pot dinner every North Indian kitchen falls back on.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee gives the whole spices a rounded, nutty aroma that plain oil cannot.

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati rice until the water runs clear, then soak it in fresh water for 20 minutes and drain well in a colander.

Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot over medium heat until it shimmers, then add 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 bay leaf, 3 cardamom pods, 4 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon and let them sizzle for about 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 large thinly sliced onion and saute on medium heat for 5 to 6 minutes, stirring often, until the edges turn light golden.
Stir in 1 cup sweet corn kernels and 0.5 tsp turmeric powder and fry for 2 minutes so the corn takes on a glossy coat.
Add the drained rice and fold gently for 1 minute, taking care not to break the grains, until each grain looks coated in ghee.
Pour in 2.5 cups water and 1 tsp salt, bring to a rolling boil, then lower the heat to a whisper, cover tightly and cook for 12 to 14 minutes until the water is absorbed and the grains are tender.
Turn off the heat and rest covered for 5 minutes, then fluff with a fork and scatter 2 tbsp chopped coriander leaves before serving.
tips: Do not skip the 20-minute soak; it lets the grains elongate and stay separate instead of clumping.
Use frozen or fresh corn, but if using tinned corn, drain and rinse it so the pulao does not turn watery.
For guaranteed separate grains, spread the cooked pulao on a wide plate for a minute before serving so residual steam escapes.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a shallow bowl with a side of cool boondi raita and a wedge of lime, plus a spoon of extra Anveshan Ghee melted over the top for a festive gloss.

variations.name: Punjabi Corn Pulao
variations.description: The Punjabi table loves richness, so this pulao finishes with a knob of white butter melting into ghee-laced rice. Garam masala and a little kasuri methi deepen the corn's sweetness into something buttery and full. It eats like a comforting dhaba plate you would mop up with the last grain.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries the garam masala and kasuri methi far better than butter alone in this rich take.

steps: Wash 1.5 cups basmati rice thoroughly, soak for 20 minutes, then drain so the grains are ready to cook evenly.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide pot on medium flame and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 20 seconds until they turn a shade darker.
Add 1 large sliced onion and fry for 6 minutes until deep golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute until the raw smell disappears.
Tip in 1 cup sweet corn, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi, and saute for 2 minutes until the kitchen smells toasty.
Fold in the drained rice and 0.5 tsp garam masala for 1 minute, coating every grain without mashing them.
Pour in 2.5 cups water and 1 tsp salt, boil hard once, then cover and cook on the lowest heat for 13 minutes until fluffy and dry.
Rest for 5 minutes, dot the top with 1 tbsp white butter so it melts in, fluff gently and finish with 2 tbsp coriander leaves.
tips: Crush the kasuri methi between your palms before adding so its aroma releases fully into the ghee.
Let the butter melt from residual heat rather than stirring it in cold, which keeps the grains glossy not greasy.
This reheats beautifully next day; sprinkle a teaspoon of water and warm covered to revive the fluff.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a bowl of thick dahi, sliced onions dressed in lemon and a spoon of mango pickle for a true Punjabi thali feel.

variations.name: Bengali Corn Pulao
variations.description: Bengal swaps the frying medium for pungent Anveshan wood-pressed mustard oil and leans on the sweet-savoury balance the region adores. A whisper of sugar, whole garam and a final drizzle of raw mustard oil give the corn a sharp, aromatic lift. It is closer to the gentle mishti pulao served at Bengali celebrations.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil is heated to smoking first to mellow its bite into the classic Bengali pungency.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of bilona ghee rounds the sharp mustard oil for the signature sweet-savoury Bengali balance.

steps: Soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, drain, and spread it on a cloth so the surface dries slightly.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pot until it just begins to smoke, then lower the flame and let it cool for 30 seconds to tame the sharpness.
Add 2 bay leaves, 4 cardamom pods, 4 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon and let them puff up for 20 seconds, then add 1 sliced medium onion and fry for 4 minutes until soft and pale gold.
Stir in 1 cup sweet corn, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp sugar, cooking for 2 minutes until the sugar dissolves and the corn glistens.
Add the drained rice and toss gently for 1 minute so every grain is coated in the golden oil.
Pour in 2.5 cups water and 1 tsp salt, bring to a boil, then cover and steam on very low heat for 13 minutes until the grains are cooked through.
Rest 5 minutes, drizzle 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the top, fluff lightly and serve warm.
tips: Always smoke the mustard oil first; raw wood-pressed mustard oil can taste bitter if added cold.
Keep the sugar subtle, it should round the corn's sweetness rather than turn the pulao dessert-like.
Whole garam masala is meant to be pushed aside while eating, so keep the pieces large and easy to spot.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside cholar dal or a light aloo dum, with a few fried cashews scattered over the rice for a Bengali festive touch.

variations.name: Kerala Corn Pulao
variations.description: Kerala reimagines the pulao with fresh coconut, curry leaves and the deep aroma of Anveshan wood-pressed coconut oil. Grated coconut cooked into the rice makes it moist and faintly sweet, while a temper of mustard and curry leaves brings the coast to the plate. It is fragrant, mellow and unmistakably southern.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed coconut oil gives the tempering an authentic Kerala fragrance that refined oil flattens.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon of bilona ghee stirred in at the end lends richness that balances the light coconut.

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain thoroughly.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pot on medium flame, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and wait for them to splutter, about 20 seconds.
Add 12 curry leaves, 2 slit green chillies and 1 inch julienned ginger and fry for 30 seconds until the leaves crisp and smell fragrant.
Stir in 1 sliced medium onion and cook for 4 minutes until translucent, then add 1 cup sweet corn and 0.5 cup grated coconut and saute for 3 minutes until the coconut turns light gold.
Add the drained rice and 0.5 tsp turmeric and fold gently for 1 minute so the grains glow yellow.
Pour in 2.5 cups water and 1 tsp salt, boil once, then cover and cook on low heat for 13 minutes until tender and dry.
Rest 5 minutes, drizzle 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, fluff with a fork and serve hot.
tips: Toast the grated coconut just to light gold; browning it too far makes the pulao taste bitter.
Fresh coconut is best, but if using desiccated, soak it in 2 tbsp warm water first so it does not dry the rice.
Slit the green chillies rather than chopping so heat lovers can eat them and others can set them aside.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling cucumber pachadi and papadam, finishing with a light dusting of extra grated coconut over the rice.

variations.name: Kashmiri Corn Pulao
variations.description: This regal version borrows the Kashmiri love of saffron, dry fruit and warm whole spice. Strands of Anveshan Kashmiri saffron steeped in warm milk stain the rice gold and lend a floral perfume, while fried cashews and almonds add festive crunch. Sweet corn plays soft against the nutty, aromatic backdrop.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Generous bilona ghee is essential here to fry the nuts and carry the saffron aroma through the rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Kashmiri saffron steeped in warm milk gives the pulao its royal colour and floral fragrance.

steps: Soak a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside so the colour bleeds out while you cook.
Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain well.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot on medium heat and fry 10 cashews and 10 almonds for 2 minutes until golden, then lift them out and reserve.
In the same ghee crackle 4 cardamom pods, 4 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon for 20 seconds, then add 1 cup sweet corn and 0.5 tsp fennel powder and saute for 2 minutes.
Fold in the drained rice for 1 minute until glossy, then pour in 2.5 cups water and 1 tsp salt and bring to a boil.
Stir in the saffron milk, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 13 minutes until the grains are gold-streaked and fluffy.
Rest 5 minutes, then fluff and top with the fried cashews and almonds before serving.
tips: Steep the saffron in warm, not hot, milk to draw out colour without scorching the delicate strands.
Fry the nuts on gentle heat; ghee browns them fast and they turn bitter if rushed.
For a deeper festive aroma, add a single strand of mace along with the whole spices.
variations.servingSuggestion: Present on a platter with a dollop of thick yogurt raita studded with pomegranate seeds, ideal for a celebratory spread.

variations.name: Classic Curd Rice
variations.description: The comforting South Indian thayir sadam, where soft-cooked rice is mashed creamy with fresh curd and a splash of milk, then crowned with a fragrant tempering. It is cooling, tangy and gently spiced, the kind of everyday meal that soothes after a fiery curry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee gives the tempering a nutty aroma that lifts the plain curd base.

steps: Rinse 1 cup sona masoori rice until the water runs clear, then pressure-cook it with 3 cups water for 4 whistles on medium heat so the grains turn soft and slightly overcooked.
Tip the hot rice into a wide bowl and mash it gently with the back of a ladle while still warm, then let it cool for 10 minutes until just above room temperature.
Stir in 2 cups plain curd, 0.5 cup whole milk and 1 tsp salt, mixing until the mixture is creamy and loose; it will thicken as it sits, so keep it slightly runny.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan over medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them crackle for about 30 seconds, then add 1 tsp urad dal and 1 tsp chana dal and fry until golden.
Drop in 2 dried red chillies, 2 slit green chillies, 1 inch finely grated ginger, 12 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida, and sauté for 20 seconds until the leaves turn crisp and aromatic.
Pour the sizzling tempering over the curd rice, fold it through gently, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and 3 tbsp pomegranate seeds before serving.
tips: If you plan to pack it for later, keep the mixture extra loose and hold back a little curd, since chilled rice absorbs moisture and stiffens over a few hours.
For the softest texture use freshly cooked warm rice; day-old fridge rice stays grainy and never turns creamy no matter how much you mash it.
Slightly sour curd works beautifully here, but if yours is very tangy, increase the milk to 0.75 cup to mellow it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled in summer with a spoon of mango or lime pickle on the side and a few crisp papadums for contrast.

variations.name: Tamil Nadu Thayir Sadam
variations.description: The temple-style Tamil curd rice, kept deliberately plain and pristine so the cooling curd shines. A double tempering of mustard, urad dal and dried red chilli in ghee, plus grated raw mango, gives it the tang and crunch that defines a Chennai lunchbox.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A ghee tempering is the traditional finish for thayir sadam, carrying the hing aroma into every grain.

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed rice with 3.5 cups water for 5 whistles so it emerges mushy and soft, which is exactly the texture temple curd rice needs.
Mash the warm rice thoroughly to a smooth paste-like consistency, then cool it for 10 minutes so the heat does not curdle the yogurt when mixed.
Whisk 2.5 cups curd with 0.5 cup milk and 1 tsp salt, then fold it into the mashed rice until glossy and spoonable rather than stiff.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium flame, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds for 30 seconds, then add 1.5 tsp urad dal, 1 tbsp roasted gram and 3 thinly sliced shallots and toast until deep golden and nutty.
Add 3 broken dried red chillies, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 15 curry leaves and a generous 0.5 tsp asafoetida, frying for 20 seconds until intensely fragrant.
Fold the hot tempering and 3 tbsp grated raw mango through the rice, then rest it for 15 minutes so the flavours settle before serving at room temperature.
tips: When raw mango is out of season, swap in 2 tbsp finely chopped seedless grapes for the same sweet-tart pop.
A pinch of extra hing added straight to the curd, not just the tempering, deepens the classic Tamil aroma.
This packs into a stainless tiffin beautifully; keep it looser than you think, as it firms up by lunchtime.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a fiery vathal or a nub of Andhra avakkai pickle so the cooling rice balances the heat.

variations.name: Bengali Doi Bhaat
variations.description: A Bengali reading of curd rice where a whisper of pungent Anveshan Mustard Oil in the tempering meets panch-phoron-inspired warmth. The curd is sweetened just barely, echoing the Bengali love of a sweet-savoury balance, and finished with fried cashews.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil brings the sharp kick that makes this tempering unmistakably Bengali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon of ghee rounds off the mustard oil's bite and fries the cashews to gold.

steps: Cook 1 cup rinsed short-grain rice with 2.75 cups water until very soft, then mash lightly and cool for 10 minutes.
Beat 2 cups curd with 0.5 cup milk, 0.75 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp sugar until smooth, then combine with the cooled rice into a loose, creamy bhaat.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan and fry 12 cashews over medium heat until golden, about 2 minutes, then lift them out and set aside.
In the same pan add 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and heat until it just shimmers and loses its raw smell, which takes about 1 minute.
Crackle 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp nigella seeds for 20 seconds, then add 2 dried red chillies, 2 slit green chillies and 10 curry leaves and fry for another 20 seconds until crisp.
Pour the pungent tempering over the doi bhaat, fold gently, scatter the fried cashews on top and serve cool.
tips: Always heat mustard oil to smoking point and let it cool slightly before tempering; raw mustard oil tastes harsh in a delicate curd dish.
Gobindobhog rice adds a floral aroma, but any soft short-grain rice works if you cook it a touch extra.
Make it a few hours ahead and add the fried cashews only at serving so they stay crunchy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside a small bowl of tomato-date chutney to lean into the Bengali sweet-and-tangy table.

variations.name: Kerala Thengai Thayir Sadam
variations.description: Kerala folds fresh grated coconut and a coconut-oil tempering into curd rice, giving it a mellow sweetness and tropical fragrance. Curry leaves and whole red chilli fried in Anveshan Coconut Oil make it distinctly Malayali, cooling yet aromatic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil is the soul of a Kerala tempering, perfuming the curd with a nutty sweetness.

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed rice with 3 cups water for 4 whistles until soft, then mash while warm and cool for 10 minutes.
Coarsely crush 0.33 cup fresh grated coconut with 2 slit green chillies and 1 inch ginger to a rough paste that will melt into the curd.
Mix 2 cups curd, 0.5 cup milk and 1 tsp salt into the rice, then stir in the coconut paste until the whole is creamy and pale green-flecked.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil over medium flame, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal, and fry for 40 seconds until the dal is golden and the oil smells sweet.
Toss in 2 dried red chillies, 15 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida, letting them crackle for 15 seconds until the leaves crisp up.
Fold the fragrant tempering through the coconut curd rice and rest for 10 minutes so the flavours meld before serving.
tips: Use unsweetened fresh or frozen coconut, not desiccated, which stays dry and gritty in the soft rice.
A single crushed shallot added to the tempering deepens the Kerala character without overpowering the curd.
Coconut oil solidifies when chilled, so serve this one at cool room temperature rather than straight from the fridge.
variations.servingSuggestion: Delicious with a spoon of Kerala inji puli (ginger-tamarind relish) and crisp banana chips alongside.

variations.name: Gujarati Meethu Dahi Bhaat
variations.description: Gujarat leans into its signature sweet-savoury palate, stirring a little Anveshan Jaggery Powder into the curd for a gentle caramel warmth against the tang. A ghee tempering with peanuts and a squeeze of lemon keeps it bright and moreish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A spoon of jaggery powder gives the Gujarati sweet-savoury lilt that white sugar cannot match.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries the peanut and mustard tempering that defines this western-style dahi bhaat.

steps: Cook 1 cup rinsed rice with 3 cups water until very soft, mash gently while warm, and cool for 10 minutes.
Whisk 2 cups curd with 0.5 cup milk, 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp salt until the jaggery fully dissolves and the curd tastes sweet-tangy.
