Fold the sweetened curd into the rice along with 1 tsp lemon juice to keep the balance lively rather than cloying.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and fry 3 tbsp raw peanuts for 2 minutes until they turn crunchy and spotted brown.
Add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and let them splutter for 20 seconds, then add 2 slit green chillies, 12 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and fry briefly until aromatic.
Pour the peanut tempering over the rice, fold through, and garnish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander before serving.
tips: Dissolve the jaggery powder into the curd rather than the hot rice so it stays smooth and does not clump.
Toast the peanuts until fully crisp before the seeds go in; half-cooked peanuts turn chewy once mixed into the moist rice.
Balance is everything here, so taste after mixing and nudge with a little more lemon if the sweetness dominates.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thin khakhra or fryums and a dollop of chundo (sweet mango relish) for a full Gujarati thali touch.

variations.name: Classic Gajar Halwa
variations.description: The definitive North Indian winter dessert, where red Delhi carrots are grated and simmered in full-fat milk until every strand drinks up the dairy and turns jammy. Finished with ghee, cardamom and fried nuts, it is glossy, deeply carroty and warming, the smell of it cooking synonymous with January in the plains.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: used to saute the carrots and fry the nuts, giving the halwa its glossy richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined sugar swapped for white sugar, sweetening without dulling the carrot flavour

steps: Wash, peel and grate 1 kg red carrots finely so they cook down evenly and quickly.
Bring the grated carrots and 1 litre full-fat milk to a boil in a heavy kadhai, then simmer on medium for 30 minutes, stirring often until the milk has nearly all evaporated.
Add 0.33 cup Anveshan Ghee and saute the carrots on medium-low for 8 minutes until they deepen in colour and smell caramelised.
Stir in 0.75 cup Anveshan Khandsari; it will loosen the mixture, so keep cooking 6 minutes until the released liquid dries up again.
Crumble in 0.5 cup khoya with 0.75 tsp cardamom powder and cook 4 minutes until it melts in and the halwa turns thick and glossy.
Fry 12 almonds, 12 cashews, 10 pistachios and 2 tbsp raisins in a spoon of ghee until golden, fold most in, and cook 2 minutes more until the ghee separates.
Garnish with the reserved nuts and serve hot.
tips: Choose the red winter Delhi carrots over orange ones for the sweetest colour and least fibre.
Grate rather than food-process the carrots so the strands stay distinct and do not turn watery.
This halwa keeps for a week refrigerated; reheat with a splash of milk to bring back the moisture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot with a scoop of vanilla ice cream for the beloved hot-cold contrast, or top with extra khoya for a festive spread.

variations.name: Gujarati Gajar Halwa
variations.description: Gujarat trades white sugar for jaggery, giving this carrot halwa a burnished bronze colour and a mellow molasses sweetness. Cooked a little drier and scented with nutmeg, it carries the homely, wholesome character typical of Kathiawadi mithai.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: sautes the carrots and stops the jaggery from turning sticky as it melts

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the Gujarati sweetener that lends a bronze colour and deep molasses warmth

steps: Peel and finely grate 1 kg red carrots and set them aside in a bowl.
Simmer the grated carrots with 0.75 litre full-fat milk in a heavy pan for 28 minutes on medium, stirring until the milk dries down almost completely.
Add 0.33 cup Anveshan Ghee and roast the carrots 8 minutes until they turn a rich reddish-brown and smell sweet.
Turn the flame to low and stir in 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder, cooking 5 minutes as it melts and then dries back to a thick mass.
Mix in 0.5 tsp cardamom, 0.25 tsp nutmeg and 2 tbsp charoli seeds, and cook 3 minutes until the halwa glistens.
Fold in slivered almonds and 2 tbsp raisins, cook a final 2 minutes until the ghee beads at the edges, and remove from heat.
Serve warm with a light dusting of extra charoli on top.
tips: Add jaggery only on low heat and after the milk has dried, otherwise the dairy left in the pan can curdle.
Nutmeg is the quiet Gujarati signature here, so grate it fresh for the best aroma.
Keep this version slightly drier than the sugar one, as jaggery holds more moisture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as prasad during Uttarayan, or pair with a wedge of thepla-style shortbread for a rustic Gujarati sweet plate.

variations.name: Kashmiri Gajar Halwa
variations.description: The Kashmiri rendition perfumes carrot halwa with saffron and crowns it lavishly with walnuts and almonds, echoing the valley's love of dry fruit. Its colour glows a deeper orange from the saffron, and a hint of dry ginger gives a warming lift ideal for the mountain cold.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: carries the saffron through the carrots and toasts the walnuts to a deep aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm milk to deepen the halwa's colour and lend a honeyed valley fragrance

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined sugar that sweetens gently without overpowering the saffron

steps: Grate 1 kg red carrots finely and steep 0.5 tsp Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 3 tbsp of warm milk taken from the litre.
Boil the carrots with the remaining full-fat milk in a heavy kadhai and simmer 32 minutes on medium, stirring until the milk reduces to a thick coating.
Add 0.33 cup Anveshan Ghee and saute 8 minutes until the carrots turn glossy and darken.
Pour in the bloomed saffron milk, then stir in 0.66 cup Anveshan Khandsari and cook 6 minutes until the liquid dries and the colour deepens.
Add 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp dry ginger powder, cook 3 minutes, and fold in the coarsely broken walnuts.
Fry the blanched almonds in a little ghee until pale gold, stir most through the halwa, and cook 2 minutes until the ghee separates.
Scatter the remaining almonds over the top and serve hot.
tips: Toast the walnuts lightly before adding them to remove any bitterness from the skins.
Steep the saffron in warm milk rather than water so it blends seamlessly into the dairy.
A pinch of dry ginger is the authentic Kashmiri warming note; do not overdo it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot in copper bowls with a final flourish of chopped walnuts and a saffron strand, perfect after a Wazwan-style meal.

variations.name: Kerala Gajar Halwa
variations.description: Kerala reimagines the northern classic with coconut at its heart, sauteing the carrots in fragrant coconut oil and folding in thick coconut milk for a tropical, faintly nutty sweetness. Studded with fried cashews and coconut slivers, it is lighter than the milk-heavy original yet lusciously creamy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the wood-pressed Kerala fat that sautes the carrots and lends an unmistakable coconut aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: unrefined sweetener that echoes the earthy sweetness of Kerala's coconut sweets

steps: Peel and grate 1 kg red carrots, then simmer them with 1 cup full-fat milk for 20 minutes until softened and the milk is mostly absorbed.
Push the carrots aside, add 0.25 cup Anveshan Coconut Oil, and saute them 8 minutes until glossy and fragrant with coconut.
Pour in 1.5 cups thick coconut milk and cook 8 minutes on medium, stirring until it thickens and clings to the carrots.
Lower the flame and stir in 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder, cooking 5 minutes until it melts in and the mixture dries to a thick halwa.
Add 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.33 cup fresh coconut slivers, cooking 3 minutes until aromatic.
Fry 15 cashews and 2 tbsp raisins in a spoon of coconut oil until golden, fold them through, and cook 2 minutes more.
Serve warm topped with a few toasted coconut slivers.
tips: Add the coconut milk after the dairy has reduced so it does not split during the long cook.
Toast the coconut slivers separately until pale gold for a nuttier finish and prettier garnish.
Use thick first-press coconut milk for the creamiest texture, thinning only if it tightens too fast.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm in banana-leaf cups at a sadya-style feast, or chilled with a scoop of tender coconut ice cream.

variations.name: Awadhi Gajar Halwa
variations.description: Lucknow's version is a refined, khoya-rich halwa scented with kewra and rosewater, cooked until dense and spoonable. Delicate and aromatic rather than rustic, it carries the perfumed elegance of nawabi dessert tables and finishes with a shimmer of silver leaf.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the nawabi fat that sautes the carrots and binds the kewra fragrance into the halwa

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined sugar chosen so the delicate kewra and rose aromas are not masked

steps: Finely grate 1 kg red carrots and simmer them with 0.75 litre full-fat milk for 30 minutes until the milk reduces to a thick coating.
Add 0.33 cup Anveshan Ghee and saute the carrots 8 minutes until they turn rich and glossy.
Crumble in 0.75 cup khoya and cook 4 minutes until it melts smoothly into the mixture.
Lower the heat and stir in 0.75 cup Anveshan Khandsari with 0.5 tsp cardamom, cooking 6 minutes until the released moisture dries and the halwa thickens.
Fry 12 cashews in a little ghee until golden and fold them through the halwa.
Switch off the flame and stir in 1 tsp kewra water and 1 tsp rosewater so their perfume is preserved.
Smooth into a dish, lay silver leaf on top, and serve warm.
tips: Add kewra and rosewater only after the pan is off the heat, as high heat drives the aroma away.
Fresh khoya gives the best melt; if using firm mawa, grate it before adding.
Keep the halwa dense and spoonable rather than loose, which suits its refined character.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in small silver bowls to round off an Awadhi dawat of biryani and korma, with a scatter of rose petals.

variations.name: Classic Ghee Rice
variations.description: The definitive ghee rice: long-grain basmati toasted in nutty Anveshan bilona ghee, perfumed with whole garam masala and crowned with deep-golden fried onions and cashews. Every grain stays separate, glossy and fragrant, making it the perfect companion to any curry or dal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The grassy, caramel aroma of bilona ghee is the backbone of this pilaf; do not swap for refined oil.

steps: Rinse 2 cups basmati under cold water until the water runs clear, then soak for 20 minutes and drain thoroughly in a colander so the grains stay firm and separate.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot over medium heat and fry 2 tbsp cashews until golden, about 2 minutes, then lift them out and reserve for garnish.
Into the same ghee add 1 tsp cumin seeds, 2 bay leaves, 4 cardamom pods, 4 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon and let them sizzle for 30 seconds until the kitchen smells fragrant.
Add 2 thinly sliced onions and cook over medium heat, stirring often, until deep golden brown, about 9 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until the raw smell fades.
Tip in the drained rice and toast gently for 2 minutes until every grain glistens with ghee, then pour in 3 cups hot water and 1.25 tsp salt and taste the water for a pleasant saltiness.

Bring to a rolling boil, cover tightly, drop the heat to its lowest setting and steam for 12 minutes, then rest off the heat for 5 minutes; fluff with a fork and scatter over the fried cashews and 2 tbsp torn mint.
tips: Draining the soaked rice really well is the single biggest trick to non-sticky grains; let it sit in the colander for a full 10 minutes if you can.
If the base ever catches, lift the pot off the flame and set it on a cold, damp cloth for a minute before fluffing to stop further scorching.
Fry a double batch of onions and cashews and freeze half; they crisp back up in a warm pan and cut ten minutes off your next pot.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve mounded in a wide bowl with a cooling boondi raita, a wedge of lime and a spoon of tangy mango pickle on the side for contrast.

variations.name: Kerala Coconut Ghee Rice
variations.description: Kerala's celebrated neychoru, where short-grain jeerakasala or basmati is simmered in coconut milk with Anveshan ghee and a whisper of Anveshan wood-pressed coconut oil. Sweet shallots, curry leaves and toasted cashews give it the mellow, festive character served at Malabar weddings.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries the coconut sweetness here; stir a final teaspoon through the cooked rice for gloss.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: A spoon of cold-pressed coconut oil deepens the Malabar aroma that ghee alone cannot give.

steps: Wash 2 cups basmati until clear, soak for 20 minutes and drain, then combine 1 cup coconut milk with 2 cups water so your cooking liquid is ready and measured.

Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil with 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot over medium heat and fry 2 tbsp cashews and 1 tbsp raisins until the cashews turn pale gold and the raisins plump, about 90 seconds, then scoop them out.
Crackle 0.5 tsp fennel seeds, 4 cardamom pods, 4 cloves, 1 inch cinnamon and a sprig of curry leaves in the same fat for 20 seconds until they release a sweet, woody aroma.
Add 12 thinly sliced shallots and fry over medium heat until soft and light gold, about 6 minutes, keeping them paler than usual so the coconut flavour stays forward.
Fold in the drained rice and toast for 2 minutes, then pour in the coconut milk mixture with 1.25 tsp salt and bring to a gentle boil, stirring once so nothing sticks.
Cover, cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes and rest 5 minutes off the flame, then fluff and finish with the fried cashews and raisins.
tips: Coconut milk scorches faster than water, so keep the flame genuinely low and resist lifting the lid before the 12-minute mark.
Jeerakasala (kaima) rice is the authentic grain; if using it, reduce total liquid to 2.5 cups as it drinks less than basmati.
A pinch of crushed fried shallot stirred in at the end doubles the sweetness without any extra cooking.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a spicy Kerala chicken or vegetable ishtu (stew) and thin coconut-onion pachadi to echo the coconut notes.

variations.name: Bengali Basanti Ghee Rice
variations.description: West Bengal's golden mishti pulao, tinted with turmeric and gently sweetened with Anveshan jaggery powder. A quick bloom of Anveshan mustard oil under the ghee lends the unmistakable Bengali pungency, while cashews and raisins make it a Durga Pujo table favourite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bengali sweet pulao leans almost entirely on ghee for its glossy, festive richness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Just one spoon, smoked to faint pungency, gives the pulao its subtle Bengali edge.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Replaces refined sugar for the signature sweet-savoury balance of basanti pulao.

steps: Rinse and soak 2 cups basmati for 20 minutes, drain, then toss the damp grains with 0.5 tsp turmeric and a teaspoon of ghee so each grain takes on an even saffron-gold colour.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pot over medium-high until it just wisps smoke, then lower the flame and add 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee to temper the pungency.
Fry 2 tbsp cashews and 2 tbsp raisins until golden and plumped, about 1 minute, remove them, then crackle 2 bay leaves, 4 cardamom, 4 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon for 30 seconds.
Add the turmeric-coated rice and toast gently for 3 minutes so it dries slightly and smells nutty, taking care not to break the delicate coloured grains.
Pour in 3 cups water, 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, the remaining 1 tbsp ghee and 1 tsp salt, then bring to a boil and taste for a gentle sweet-salt balance.
Cover, steam on the lowest heat for 12 minutes, rest 5 minutes, then fluff and fold the fried cashews and raisins back through.
tips: Coating the raw rice in turmeric and ghee before cooking keeps the colour even; adding turmeric to the water alone gives patchy grains.
Keep the sweetness restrained: basanti pulao should taste faintly sweet against a spicy kosha mangsho, never like a dessert.
Whole spices are left in for aroma but warn diners, or fish out the cinnamon and bay before serving to guests.
variations.servingSuggestion: Traditionally served alongside a rich Bengali mutton kosha or chholar dal, with a few extra fried cashews showered on top.

variations.name: Kashmiri Saffron Ghee Rice
variations.description: A regal pilaf scented with Anveshan Kashmiri saffron steeped in warm milk, studded with almonds, walnuts and jewel-like pomegranate. Fennel and dry ginger give the gentle warmth of a Kashmiri wazwan, all carried on fragrant Anveshan ghee.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee is the neutral, aromatic base that lets the saffron and dry fruits shine through.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: Bloom the threads in warm milk for ten minutes to draw out maximum colour and aroma.

steps: Soak a pinch of Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk and set aside for at least 10 minutes so it blooms into a deep amber; rinse and soak 2 cups basmati separately, then drain.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot over medium heat and lightly toast 2 tbsp slivered almonds and 2 tbsp walnut pieces until fragrant and golden, about 2 minutes, then remove.
Add 1 tsp fennel seeds, 4 cardamom pods, 3 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon to the ghee and let them crackle for 30 seconds until the fennel smells sweet.
Stir in 0.5 tsp dry ginger powder for just 10 seconds, then add the drained rice and toast for 2 minutes so the grains coat evenly in the spiced ghee.
Pour in 3 cups water and 1.25 tsp salt, bring to a boil, then drizzle over the saffron milk in swirls so the pulao cooks up mottled gold and white.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes, rest 5 minutes, then fluff and top with the toasted nuts and 3 tbsp fresh pomegranate seeds.
tips: Do not stir the saffron milk in fully; the marbled gold-and-white look is the hallmark of a Kashmiri pulao.
Add the pomegranate only at the very end so the seeds stay crisp and jewel-bright rather than bleeding into the rice.
Dry ginger can turn bitter if it browns, so add it off the boil and move straight to the rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Beautiful as the centrepiece of a vegetarian spread with dum aloo Kashmiri and a bowl of chilled mint yoghurt.

variations.name: Gujarati Sweet-Savoury Ghee Rice
variations.description: A homely Gujarati pilaf balancing the region's beloved sweet-and-spicy note: Anveshan jaggery powder against green chilli and ginger, finished with a bright squeeze of lemon. Cooked in Anveshan ghee and wood-pressed groundnut oil with sweet peas, it is comfort food from a Kathiawadi kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee rounds off the sweet-spicy tug and keeps the grains glossy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the everyday Gujarati cooking fat and adds a faint nutty base note.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Unrefined jaggery gives the characteristic gentle sweetness without the harshness of white sugar.

steps: Rinse and soak 2 cups basmati for 20 minutes and drain; meanwhile finely chop 2 green chillies and grate 1 inch ginger so your aromatics are ready.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil with 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat, then add 1 tsp cumin seeds, 3 cloves, 3 cardamom and 1 inch cinnamon and let them sizzle 30 seconds until aromatic.
Add the chopped chilli and grated ginger and fry for 40 seconds until the raw sharpness softens, then stir in 0.5 cup green peas and cook 1 minute.
Fold in the drained rice and toast for 2 minutes, then sprinkle over 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and stir until it melts and coats the grains.
Pour in 3 cups water and 1 tsp salt, taste for a balanced sweet-salt-heat, then bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes, rest 5 minutes, then fluff and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and the juice of 1 lemon.
tips: Add the lemon only after cooking; heating it makes the juice turn bitter and dulls the fresh lift Gujarati food loves.
Melt the jaggery directly onto the hot rice rather than into the water so it caramelises slightly and clings to each grain.
For a fuller one-dish meal, stir in a handful of boiled chana or diced boiled potato with the peas.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a bowl of thin kadhi and crisp papad, letting the sweet rice play against the tangy yoghurt curry.

variations.name: Classic Masala Khichdi
variations.description: The comforting one-pot khichdi that every North Indian home cook falls back on, where soft basmati and yellow moong dal collapse into a spoonable, gently spiced porridge. A tempering of whole spices and a generous finish of nutty ghee lift it from plain sickbed food to a soul-warming weeknight meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Stir 2 tbsp into the pot and drizzle the last spoon raw on top for the classic aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Used with the ghee for the tempering so the whole spices bloom without the ghee scorching.

steps: Rinse 1 cup basmati rice and 0.5 cup yellow moong dal together in 2-3 changes of water until it runs clear, then soak for 15 minutes and drain in a colander.

In a pressure cooker, heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium and add 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 bay leaf, 3 cloves and 2 green cardamom pods; let them sizzle and turn fragrant for about 30 seconds.
Add 1 finely sliced medium onion and sauté on medium heat until soft and pale gold, about 4 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for another minute until the raw smell lifts.
Add 1 chopped tomato, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 cup mixed vegetables, and cook for 3 minutes until the tomato softens and the masala looks glossy.
Tip in the drained rice and dal, sauté gently for 2 minutes so the grains coat in the masala, then pour in 4 cups hot water and 1.25 tsp salt and stir well.
Close the lid and pressure cook on medium for 3 whistles, then let the pressure drop naturally; the khichdi should be soft, thick and spoonable.
Open the cooker, fluff lightly, and finish with the reserved 1 tbsp raw Anveshan Ghee drizzled over the top just before serving.
tips: If the khichdi thickens too much on standing, loosen it with a splash of hot water and a little extra salt, since the dal keeps drinking up liquid as it sits.
For a lighter grain-forward texture reduce the water to 3.5 cups; for a wetter, soupy khichdi push it to 4.5 cups.
Dry-roasting the moong dal in a pan until faintly nutty before rinsing deepens the flavour and helps it hold a little shape.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in deep bowls with a spoonful of cool boondi raita, a wedge of lime pickle and a papad crushed over the top for crunch.

variations.name: Bengali Masala Khichdi
variations.description: Bengal's bhuni khichuri is a rainy-day ritual, built on pungent mustard oil and moong dal that is dry-roasted until it smells like toasted nuts. The grains stay slightly separate and the whole pot carries the warm sweetness of ghee-roasted spices, a world away from the mushy North Indian style.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Heat it until it just wisps and loses its raw bite before tempering, the signature Bengali base.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Swirled in at the end for the rich finish that balances the sharp mustard oil.

steps: Dry-roast 0.75 cup moong dal in a hot kadhai on medium heat for 4-5 minutes, stirring constantly until it deepens to golden and smells toasty, then rinse it with the 1 cup rice and drain.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in the kadhai until it shimmers and just begins to wisp, which tames its raw pungency, then lower the heat to medium.
Fry the cauliflower florets in the hot mustard oil for 3-4 minutes until their edges catch golden spots, then lift them out and set aside.
Into the same oil add 2 bay leaves, 2 dried red chillies, 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1 inch cinnamon and let them crackle for 20-30 seconds until aromatic.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger paste, 0.75 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp cumin powder, cook for a minute, then add the rice-dal, the fried cauliflower and 0.5 cup peas and toss for 2 minutes.
Pour in 4 cups hot water with 1.25 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp sugar, bring to a boil, then cover and simmer on low for about 18 minutes until soft but with the grains still distinct.
Turn off the heat and fold in 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, letting it melt through the hot khichuri before serving.
tips: Roasting the moong dal is non-negotiable here, as it is what gives bhuni khichuri its nutty backbone and keeps the grains from turning to paste.
Bengalis serve this with beguni (batter-fried eggplant), so slice an eggplant thin and shallow-fry it alongside while the khichuri simmers.
A pinch of sugar is authentic and rounds out the mustard oil, so do not skip it even if you keep your food savoury.
variations.servingSuggestion: Plate it hot with crisp beguni, a wedge of lime, and a small mound of aam-tel (mango pickle in oil) on the side for a true Bengali monsoon thali.

variations.name: Gujarati Masala Khichdi
variations.description: Gujarat's khichdi leans soft and soothing, with a whisper of jaggery sweetness that is unmistakably regional and a lighter hand on the chilli. It is traditionally served swimming in a ladle of ghee and paired with kadhi, making it the ultimate gentle comfort supper.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Half goes into the tempering and half is poured over each hot bowl, the Gujarati way.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A small spoon melted in for the gentle sweet-savoury balance typical of Gujarati cooking.

steps: Rinse 1 cup rice with 0.5 cup moong dal until the water clears, soak for 15 minutes and drain well in a sieve.
In a pressure cooker heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium and add 1 tsp cumin seeds, 3 cloves, 2 cardamom pods and 0.25 tsp asafoetida, letting them sizzle for about 20 seconds until fragrant.
Stir in 1 tbsp green chilli-ginger paste and cook for 30 seconds, just until the raw edge softens and the kitchen smells sharp and fresh.
Add 0.5 cup peas and 0.5 cup diced bottle gourd with 0.5 tsp turmeric and toss for 2 minutes to coat the vegetables in the tempering.
Add the drained rice and dal, 4 cups water, 1.25 tsp salt and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, and stir until the jaggery dissolves evenly.
Seal and pressure cook on medium for 3 whistles, then let the pressure release naturally so the khichdi turns soft, thick and almost creamy.
Ladle into bowls and pour the remaining 1.5 tbsp warm Anveshan Ghee generously over each serving.
tips: This khichdi is meant to be soft and moist, so if it looks stiff after cooking, mash it lightly with the back of a ladle and stir in a little hot water.
The touch of jaggery is what marks it as Gujarati, but keep it subtle so the dish stays savoury with just a rounded backnote.
Cook it a shade wetter than you think, because it firms up noticeably as it sits and the diners wait.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of hot Gujarati kadhi to pour over, a spoon of chundo (sweet mango pickle) and thin crisp papad for the classic khichdi-kadhi comfort plate.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Masala Khichdi
variations.description: This Maharashtrian khichdi gets its dark, brooding character from goda masala, the region's sweet-savoury spice blend of roasted coconut, sesame and stone flower. Studded with peanuts for crunch, it is heartier and more aromatic than a plain khichdi and stands up beautifully on its own.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The everyday Maharashtrian cooking fat that carries the goda masala and peanuts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Finished on top so the goda masala aroma blooms in warm ghee.

steps: Rinse 1 cup rice with 0.5 cup moong dal, soak for 15 minutes, then drain thoroughly so the grains are damp but not dripping.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a heavy pot on medium and add 0.33 cup raw peanuts, frying for 2-3 minutes until they turn glossy and crisp, then scoop half of them out for garnish.
To the same oil add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp cumin, and when they crackle add 1 sliced onion and 4 crushed garlic cloves, sautéing 4 minutes until golden.
Stir in 1.5 tbsp goda masala, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder and cook for 45 seconds, taking care not to burn the masala as it darkens and turns intensely fragrant.
Add the drained rice and dal and toss for 2 minutes, then pour in 3.75 cups hot water with 1.25 tsp salt and bring to a rolling boil.
Cover and simmer on low heat for about 18 minutes until the water is absorbed and the khichdi is soft yet still has body.
Finish with 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee stirred through, then scatter the reserved fried peanuts over the top before serving.
tips: Goda masala scorches fast because of its coconut and sesame, so keep the heat moderate and have the water ready to add the moment it smells done.
If you cannot find goda masala, a mix of garam masala with a pinch of ground roasted sesame and desiccated coconut gets you close.
Reserving half the fried peanuts for the top keeps that crunch intact, since peanuts left in the pot soften as the khichdi steams.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of cool plain yogurt whisked with salt, a spoon of thecha (green chilli-garlic relish) and crisp papad for a proper Maharashtrian spread.

variations.name: Kerala Masala Khichdi
variations.description: A South Indian reimagining where the khichdi is finished in fragrant coconut oil and enriched with thick coconut milk, giving it a silky, faintly sweet body. Curry leaves and a mustard-seed tempering pull it firmly into Kerala territory, turning humble rice and dal into something coastal and luxurious.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: The defining Kerala fat, used for the tempering so the curry leaves crackle in coconut aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A small finishing spoon to round the coconut richness with nutty warmth.

steps: Rinse 1 cup rice with 0.5 cup moong dal, soak for 15 minutes and drain, then keep 0.75 cup thick coconut milk ready near the stove.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pot on medium and splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 15 curry leaves and 2 dried red chillies and let them crackle for 15 seconds.
Add 6 sliced shallots and 1 tbsp minced ginger and sauté for 3 minutes until the shallots turn soft and translucent with golden edges.
Stir in 1 cup diced carrot and beans with 0.5 tsp turmeric and cook for 2 minutes so the vegetables take on the tempering.
Add the drained rice and dal, 3 cups hot water and 1.25 tsp salt, bring to a boil, then cover and simmer on low for 16 minutes until nearly soft.
Pour in the 0.75 cup thick coconut milk, stir gently and cook uncovered on low for 3-4 more minutes until creamy, never letting it hit a hard boil so the milk does not split.
Turn off the heat, swirl in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and rest covered for 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Add the coconut milk only at the end and keep the flame low, because boiling it hard will curdle the milk and turn the khichdi grainy.
Kerala shallots (small onions) have a sweeter, deeper flavour than regular onions and are worth seeking out for this dish.
For extra fragrance, warm a little Anveshan Coconut Oil with a few fresh curry leaves and pour it over just before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a tangy tomato-shallot pachadi or a simple raw mango pickle, and a poppadom crushed over the top for a coastal Kerala touch.

variations.name: Classic Sattu Ladoo
variations.description: The everyday North Indian sattu ladoo built on wood-roasted Bengal gram flour, browned slowly in ghee until it smells like toasted biscuits. Jaggery keeps them earthy rather than cloyingly sweet, while gond adds a light, brittle crunch inside a dense, nutty bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: wood-roasted Bengal gram sattu is already cooked, so it toasts to a nutty aroma in minutes

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee both roasts the sattu and binds the ladoos as it cools

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: dissolves evenly into warm sattu, replacing refined sugar for a mineral-rich sweetness

steps: Warm 2 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadai on low heat and fry the 2 tbsp edible gum for about 1 minute until each piece puffs up white and turns crisp, then lift out and crush coarsely.
Add the remaining Anveshan Ghee to the same kadai and stir in the 2 cups Anveshan Sattu, roasting on low heat for 12 to 15 minutes until it darkens a shade and gives off a deep, biscuity aroma.
Scatter in the 3 tbsp almonds, 3 tbsp cashews, 2 tbsp melon seeds and 2 tbsp raisins and roast for 2 minutes more until the nuts are pale gold and the raisins swell.

Switch off the heat and let the mixture cool for 5 minutes, then mix in the 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 tsp cardamom, 0.25 tsp nutmeg, the crushed gum and a pinch of salt while still warm, so the jaggery softens without turning molten.
While the mix is warm enough to handle comfortably, scoop 2 tbsp portions and press each firmly between your palms into a tight round ladoo, making about 12.
Rest the shaped ladoos on a tray for 20 minutes to firm up completely before serving.
tips: If the warm mixture crumbles instead of holding, drizzle in 1 tbsp extra warm ghee and press again; if it feels greasy, dust in a spoon of extra roasted sattu.
Always fold jaggery powder in off the heat — added to a hot pan it melts and the cooled ladoos set stone-hard.
Stored in an airtight jar they keep for 3 weeks, and the cardamom flavour rounds out beautifully after the first day.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve one with a warm glass of milk as an after-school snack, or tuck a couple into a travel tin as a slow-release energy bite for long journeys.

variations.name: Kashmiri Sattu Ladoo
variations.description: A cold-weather ladoo from the Valley, perfumed with saffron bloomed in warm milk and warmed through with dry ginger and fennel. Walnuts, the everyday Kashmiri nut, replace cashews and give a slightly bitter, resinous depth against the honeyed jaggery.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: roasted gram sattu carries the saffron and dry ginger without turning pasty

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee carries the fat-soluble saffron colour and aroma deep into the ladoo

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: its molasses note flatters the earthy walnuts better than white sugar

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Kashmiri saffron steeped in milk perfumes and gently tints the whole batch

steps: Crush the pinch of Anveshan Saffron with your fingers and soak it in the 2 tbsp warm milk for 10 minutes until the liquid turns a bright amber.
Melt the 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over low heat and roast the 2 cups Anveshan Sattu for 12 to 14 minutes, stirring without pause, until it smells toasty and loses its raw edge.
Toss in the 4 tbsp walnuts and 3 tbsp almonds along with 1 tsp fennel seeds and roast for 2 minutes until the fennel is fragrant and the nuts crisp.

Take the pan off the heat, cool for 4 minutes, then stir in the 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 tsp cardamom, 0.5 tsp dry ginger, a pinch of salt and the saffron milk, mixing until the colour streaks evenly through.
Once the warm mass just holds together when pressed, roll firm 2 tbsp balls between your palms to shape roughly 12 ladoos.
Leave them uncovered for 25 minutes so the saffron milk sets and the surface dries before storing.
tips: Add the saffron milk one spoon at a time — too much moisture stops the ladoos binding and they will slump.
Toast the walnuts a touch darker than almonds; their oils turn sweet and remove any raw bitterness.
This one is best eaten within 10 days, as the milk shortens its shelf life compared with a dry ladoo.
variations.servingSuggestion: Offer alongside kahwa or a cup of noon chai on a winter evening, the saffron in the ladoo echoing the brew.

variations.name: Kerala Sattu Ladoo
variations.description: A coastal reworking where roasted coconut and a spoon of wood-pressed coconut oil braid a tropical sweetness through the nutty sattu. Cardamom and toasted sesame nod to Kerala's temple-sweet tradition, giving a softer, more fragrant ladoo than the northern original.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: the roasted gram base balances the richness of coconut and coconut oil

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a smaller amount of ghee here leaves room for the coconut oil flavour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed coconut oil to bloom the grated coconut and deepen the coastal aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: unrefined jaggery pairs naturally with coconut in Kerala sweets

steps: Heat the 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadai on low and roast the 0.75 cup desiccated coconut for 3 to 4 minutes, stirring, until it turns pale gold and smells nutty, then set it aside.
Add the 0.33 cup Anveshan Ghee to the pan and roast the 2 cups Anveshan Sattu for 12 minutes on low heat until it deepens in colour and gives a warm, toasted scent.
Stir in the 3 tbsp cashews and 1 tbsp sesame seeds and roast for 2 minutes until the cashews colour and the sesame begins to pop.
Turn off the heat, return the roasted coconut, and after 4 minutes fold in the 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 2 tbsp raisins, 1 tsp cardamom and a pinch of salt while the mix is still warm.
Press 2 tbsp portions firmly into rounds between your palms, shaping about 12 ladoos; the coconut oil helps them hold.
Set them aside for 20 minutes to firm before serving or storing.
tips: Roast the coconut only to pale gold — pushed to brown it turns bitter and dominates the ladoo.
In humid coastal weather use desiccated rather than fresh coconut so the ladoos do not spoil within days.
For a festive finish, roll the warm ladoos in a little extra desiccated coconut for a snowy coating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a naivedyam-style sweet after a South Indian meal, or with filter coffee where the coconut and cardamom sing together.

variations.name: Malwa Sattu Ladoo
variations.description: A rustic ladoo from the Malwa plateau of Madhya Pradesh, where crushed roasted peanuts and sesame do the heavy lifting alongside sattu. Poppy seeds and dry ginger give it the same warming, winter-food character as the region's beloved peanut chikki, but in a soft ladoo form.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: sattu stretches the peanuts and keeps the ladoo light rather than dense

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee rounds off the assertive peanut and sesame flavours

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery and peanuts are the classic Malwa winter pairing

steps: Dry-roast the 0.5 cup peanuts in a kadai on low heat for 4 minutes until the skins loosen, then rub them off, coarsely crush the peanuts and set aside.
In the same pan dry-roast the 2 tbsp sesame and 1 tbsp poppy seeds for about 2 minutes until they turn golden and pop, and tip them out with the peanuts.
Add the 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee and roast the 2 cups Anveshan Sattu on low heat for 12 to 15 minutes until it colours evenly and smells nutty and toasted.
Take the pan off the heat, rest for 5 minutes, then work in the crushed peanuts, sesame, poppy seeds, 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 tsp cardamom, 0.5 tsp dry ginger and a pinch of salt while warm.
Shape firm 2 tbsp balls by pressing between your palms, making roughly 12 sturdy ladoos.
Cool them on a plate for 20 minutes until they set into a solid, chikki-like bite.
tips: Crush the peanuts coarsely, not to a paste, so you keep pockets of crunch through the ladoo.
Keep the heat low while roasting sattu with all these oil-rich seeds around, as they scorch fast.
These travel exceptionally well and stay good for a month in an airtight tin.
variations.servingSuggestion: A classic winter tiffin sweet — eat one mid-morning with masala chai when the plateau turns cold.

variations.name: Awadhi Sattu Ladoo
variations.description: A refined Lucknawi take, lightly sweetened with khandsari rather than dark jaggery and perfumed with a whisper of kewra water and mace. Pistachios and chironji make it delicate and dinner-party pretty, a world away from the rustic village ladoo.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: the mild roasted gram base lets the kewra and mace come through cleanly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: generous ghee gives this ladoo its melt-in-the-mouth Awadhi richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined khandsari keeps the sweetness pale and clean so the perfume shows

steps: Melt the 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over low heat and roast the 2 cups Anveshan Sattu for 12 to 14 minutes, stirring steadily, until it turns a light gold and smells gently toasted.
Add the 3 tbsp pistachios, 2 tbsp chironji and 2 tbsp almonds and roast for 2 minutes until the chironji swells and the nuts are fragrant.
Take the pan off the heat and let it cool for 5 minutes so the khandsari will not melt.
Fold in the 1 cup Anveshan Khandsari, 1 tsp cardamom, 0.25 tsp mace and a pinch of salt, then sprinkle over the 1 tsp kewra water and mix so the fragrance is evenly distributed.
Press 2 tbsp portions into neat rounds between your palms, shaping about 12 dainty ladoos.
Rest them for 20 minutes until firm, keeping them uncovered so the kewra aroma settles rather than turning sharp.
tips: Kewra is potent — 1 tsp is plenty for the whole batch, and more will make the ladoos taste soapy.
Reserve a few chopped pistachios to press onto the top of each ladoo for an elegant finish.
Because khandsari is less hygroscopic than jaggery, these stay pleasantly crumbly for up to 3 weeks.
variations.servingSuggestion: Plate on a silver thali as part of a festive mithai spread, or serve after a rich Awadhi biryani when a light, perfumed sweet is welcome.

variations.name: Classic Festive Atta Ladoo
variations.description: The wholemeal ladoo that appears on every North Indian festive thali, built on slow-roasted whole-wheat flour bound with ghee and unrefined jaggery. Edible gum and mixed nuts give it a celebratory crunch, while cardamom and nutmeg perfume every warm, crumbly bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Nutty ancient-wheat flour that roasts to a deep aroma and keeps these ladoos wholesome

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee is the roasting medium and the binder; keep a spoon extra for shaping

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Stirred in off the heat so it sweetens without hardening into candy

steps: Warm 2 tablespoons of the Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadai on medium heat and fry the 3 tablespoons edible gum in batches until each piece puffs up white and crisp, about 40 seconds each, then lift out, cool and crush coarsely.

Add the remaining Anveshan Ghee to the same pan and roast the 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta on low heat, stirring constantly, until it turns deep golden and smells toasty and nutty, about 18 to 20 minutes.
Toss in the chopped almonds, cashews and 2 tablespoons melon seeds and roast for 2 more minutes until the nuts are fragrant and lightly coloured, then take the pan off the heat.

Let the mixture cool for 5 minutes until just warm, then mix in 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder, the crushed gond, 1 teaspoon cardamom powder, 1/4 teaspoon grated nutmeg and a pinch of salt until evenly combined.
While the mixture is still warm and holds together when pressed, scoop 2 tablespoons at a time and roll firmly between your palms into 12 smooth ladoos.
Rest the ladoos on a tray for 20 minutes to firm up before serving or storing.
tips: If the mixture feels too dry to bind, drizzle in 1 to 2 tablespoons of warm melted ghee, not water, and press again.
Fry the gond on genuinely low heat; if the ghee is too hot the pieces brown outside while staying raw and chewy inside.
Roast the atta a shade darker than you think, as under-roasted flour tastes raw and dulls the festive aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile them in a brass thali lined with a banana leaf for Diwali or Karva Chauth, and offer a warm glass of saffron milk alongside to cut the richness.

variations.name: Punjabi Panjiri Festive Atta Ladoo
variations.description: A postnatal-turned-festive Punjabi treat where the atta is loaded with panjiri spices, gond, phool makhana and generous ghee. Warming ginger powder and edible gum make it the winter ladoo served in Punjabi homes through Lohri and the cold months.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Roasted long and slow to give the panjiri its signature grainy, sandy texture

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Punjabi panjiri is deliberately ghee-rich; it fries the gond and carries the warmth

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Replaces boora sugar for a deeper, mineral-rich sweetness suited to winter

steps: Heat 3 tablespoons of the Anveshan Ghee in a wide kadai and fry the 1/4 cup edible gum in small batches on low heat until the pieces balloon and turn crisp, roughly 40 seconds each, then crush them coarsely once cool.
In the same ghee, fry the 1 cup phool makhana on medium-low heat until they feel light and crunchy, about 4 minutes, then break them into small bits.
Pour in the rest of the Anveshan Ghee and roast the 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta on low heat, stirring without pause, until it is sandy, deep gold and richly fragrant, about 20 minutes.

Stir in the chopped almonds, 3 tablespoons melon seeds, 1 tablespoon fennel seeds and 1 teaspoon dry ginger powder and roast for 2 minutes until the spices release their aroma, then remove from the heat.
Cool for about 6 minutes to just warm, then fold in 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 teaspoon cardamom powder, the crushed gond and makhana until the mixture clumps when squeezed.
Shape 2 tablespoons at a time into 12 firm round ladoos while the mix is warm, and let them set on a plate for 15 minutes.
tips: Keep the finished panjiri loose in a jar if you prefer; it doubles as a spoonable winter energy mix when you skip shaping.
The dry ginger and fennel are what make this Punjabi and warming, so do not swap them for plain cardamom alone.
Use warm ghee, never cold, to loosen a stiff batch, as water will make the ladoos spoil within days.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve one warmed ladoo at breakfast during Lohri with a tumbler of hot masala milk, the traditional Punjabi way to start a winter morning.

variations.name: Rajasthani Dry-Fruit Festive Atta Ladoo
variations.description: In water-scarce Rajasthan, festive ladoos lean on ghee, jaggery and a lavish hand of dry fruits to stay rich and long-keeping. This version folds in poppy seeds and a whisper of dry ginger, giving a coarse, opulent crumb favoured at Marwari weddings and Teej.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Coarse ancient-wheat flour holds the heavy dry-fruit load without turning dense

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A generous pour is the Marwari signature, keeping the ladoos moist for weeks

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Desert kitchens prefer jaggery over sugar for its earthy depth

ingredients.name: Anveshan Dry Fruit Paak
ingredients.note: A ready ghee-cooked dry-fruit conserve that deepens the richness in one spoon

steps: Dry roast the 2 tablespoons poppy seeds and 2 tablespoons chironji in a hot kadai for about 90 seconds until they crackle and smell toasted, then set aside.
Melt the Anveshan Ghee in the same kadai and roast the 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta on low heat, stirring steadily, until it is deep golden and nutty, about 18 minutes.
Add the chopped almonds and pistachios and roast for 2 minutes until glossy and fragrant, then stir in 1/3 cup Anveshan Dry Fruit Paak and mix for a minute until it loosens into the flour.

Take the pan off the heat and cool for 5 minutes to just warm, then mix in 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder, the toasted poppy seeds and chironji, 1/2 teaspoon dry ginger powder and 1 teaspoon cardamom powder.
When the mixture binds on pressing, roll 2 tablespoons at a time into 12 generous ladoos, pressing firmly so the dry fruits stay embedded.
Let them rest for 20 minutes so the ghee sets and the ladoos hold their shape.
tips: The dry fruit paak already carries ghee and sweetness, so taste before adding all the jaggery and adjust down if needed.
These keep beautifully for up to three weeks in an airtight tin, which is exactly why desert kitchens make them ahead of festivals.
Press a whole blanched almond on top of each ladoo for a classic Marwari wedding-mithai finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Present them in small silver foil cups as part of a Teej sweet box, paired with thandai for a true Rajasthan festive spread.

variations.name: Kashmiri Saffron Festive Atta Ladoo
variations.description: A regal ladoo tinted and scented with Kashmiri saffron and finished with slivered walnuts, the valley's beloved nut. Gentle sweetness from jaggery lets the floral saffron and toasted walnut lead, making this the ladoo for Navreh and wedding feasts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its mellow wheat flavour is the perfect quiet backdrop for saffron

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Carries the fat-soluble saffron colour and aroma through the whole batch

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: Bloomed in warm milk so its colour and honeyed aroma bleed through every ladoo

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Kept modest so the saffron and walnut stay in the foreground

steps: Soak 1/2 teaspoon Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tablespoons warm milk and set it aside for 10 minutes until the liquid turns a deep amber.
Melt the Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan and roast the 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta on low heat, stirring without stopping, until pale gold and fragrant, about 16 minutes.
Add the chopped walnuts and almonds and roast for 3 minutes until the walnuts smell toasty and turn a touch darker, then remove from the heat.
Stir the bloomed saffron milk into the warm flour and mix well so the colour streaks evenly through, letting the residual heat cook off the moisture for a minute.
Cool for 5 minutes, then fold in 3/4 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 teaspoon cardamom powder and the crushed dried rose petals until the mixture holds together.
Shape 2 tablespoons at a time into 12 ladoos and press a walnut half onto each before they set for 20 minutes.
tips: Bloom the saffron in warm, not boiling, milk so its delicate aroma is coaxed out rather than scorched.
Add the saffron milk only a spoon at a time; too much liquid shortens the shelf life and softens the crumb.
Toast the walnuts well, as raw walnut can taste faintly bitter and muddy the saffron.
variations.servingSuggestion: Offer these on a walnut-wood platter with kahwa, the saffron green tea of Kashmir, for an elegant end to a Navreh meal.

variations.name: Awadhi Kewra Festive Atta Ladoo
variations.description: Lucknow's nawabi kitchens perfume their festive ladoos with kewra water and a hint of rose, layering in khoya for a soft, melt-in-mouth finish. It is a refined, fragrant ladoo built for Eid and wedding dastarkhwans.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Roasted golden to give body to the soft khoya-enriched ladoo

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The fragrant fat that defines Awadhi mithai and blooms the kewra

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A softer sweetness that lets the kewra and rose perfume shine

steps: Crumble the 3/4 cup khoya into a dry pan and roast on low heat for about 5 minutes, stirring, until it softens and smells milky and sweet, then set aside.
Melt the Anveshan Ghee in a kadai and roast the 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta on low heat, stirring constantly, until it is even gold and nutty, about 17 minutes.
Add the chopped pistachios and 2 tablespoons charoli and roast for 2 minutes until fragrant, then fold the roasted khoya into the warm flour and mix for a minute.
Take the pan off the heat, cool for 5 minutes, then sprinkle in 1 teaspoon kewra water and 1/2 teaspoon rose water and mix so the perfume spreads evenly.
Add 3/4 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 teaspoon cardamom powder and combine until the mixture is soft yet holds a shape when pressed.
Roll 2 tablespoons at a time into 12 smooth ladoos and press a small square of silver leaf onto each before they rest for 15 minutes.
tips: Kewra water is potent, so measure the single teaspoon carefully; an extra splash quickly turns perfumed into soapy.
Because of the fresh khoya these ladoos are best eaten within four days and kept refrigerated.
If the khoya makes the mix too soft to roll, chill it for 15 minutes before shaping.
variations.servingSuggestion: Arrange on a fine china plate with a scatter of rose petals as part of an Eid dessert spread, alongside cups of cardamom chai.

variations.name: Classic Festive Sattu Ladoo
variations.description: The celebration version of the humble sattu ladoo, loaded with four kinds of nuts, crisp fried gond and a shimmer of edible silver leaf for Diwali and weddings. Richer with ghee and studded with fruit, it is meant to look and taste like an occasion.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: roasted gram sattu gives a festive ladoo body without deep-frying

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a generous hand of bilona ghee makes these ladoos rich and glossy for the occasion

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery keeps even this indulgent ladoo grounded and less sugary

steps: Warm 3 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on low heat and fry the 3 tbsp gond in batches for about 1 minute each until they balloon and crisp, then crush them to a coarse rubble.
Pour the remaining Anveshan Ghee into the pan and roast the 2 cups Anveshan Sattu on low heat for 14 to 16 minutes until it turns a rich golden-brown and smells intensely nutty.
Add the 4 tbsp almonds, 4 tbsp cashews, 3 tbsp pistachios and 3 tbsp melon seeds and roast for 3 minutes until every nut is toasted and glossy with ghee.

Take the pan off the heat, cool for 5 minutes, then mix in the 1.25 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder, the crushed gond, 0.33 cup chopped dates, 1.5 tsp cardamom and a pinch of salt while still warm so it all binds.
Roll generous 2 tbsp portions into large, tightly packed ladoos, shaping about 12 to 14.
Press a torn square of silver leaf onto the top of each ladoo and rest them for 25 minutes until firm.
tips: Fry the gond in small batches — a crowded pan traps steam and the pieces fry chewy instead of crisp.
Chop the dates fine and toss them in a little roasted sattu so they do not clump while mixing.
For gifting, set each finished ladoo in a paper cup; they hold their shape for up to 3 weeks.
variations.servingSuggestion: Arrange on a brass platter as part of a Diwali mithai box, or offer one with a small cup of masala doodh to guests during festivities.

variations.name: Kashmiri Festive Sattu Ladoo
variations.description: A wedding-table ladoo from Kashmiri kitchens, lavish with saffron, walnuts and dried apricots and warmed by dry ginger for the cold season celebrations. The saffron is doubled here so each ladoo glows a deep gold worthy of a feast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: the roasted gram base anchors a rich, saffron-heavy festive mix

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: extra ghee dissolves the doubled saffron and enriches the celebration ladoo

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery deepens the colour and complements walnuts and apricot

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: a festive double dose of Kashmiri saffron for a glowing gold ladoo

steps: Steep the 0.5 tsp Anveshan Saffron in the 3 tbsp warm milk for 10 minutes until it releases a deep amber colour and heady aroma.
Melt the 0.66 cup Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on low heat and roast the 2 cups Anveshan Sattu for 14 minutes, stirring constantly, until richly golden and fragrant.
Fold in the 5 tbsp walnuts, 4 tbsp almonds and 1 tsp fennel and roast for 3 minutes until the nuts crisp and the fennel perfumes the pan.

Off the heat, cool for 4 minutes, then stir in the 1.25 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 0.33 cup chopped dried apricots, 1.5 tsp cardamom, 0.5 tsp dry ginger, a pinch of salt and the saffron milk until the colour runs evenly through.
Shape big 2 tbsp ladoos by pressing firmly, making about 12 to 14, richly speckled with saffron.
Leave them uncovered for 25 minutes so the surface dries to a set, jewelled finish.
tips: Snip the apricots small and soft; large pieces make the ladoos hard to roll into a smooth ball.
Reserve a few saffron strands to press onto each ladoo top for a visible festive flourish.
The added milk means these are best enjoyed within a week, so make them close to the celebration.
variations.servingSuggestion: Present on a walnut-wood platter at a winter wedding, each glowing ladoo echoing the saffron in the accompanying kahwa.

variations.name: Kerala Festive Sattu Ladoo
variations.description: An Onam-worthy ladoo where roasted coconut, coconut oil and jaggery meet the nutty sattu, finished with fried cashews and a coconut-flake coating. It carries the fragrance of a Kerala payasam kitchen rolled into a handheld sweet.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: roasted gram keeps this coconut-rich festive ladoo from turning too heavy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee for frying the cashews to the golden Kerala-sweet standard

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed coconut oil roasts the coconut and defines the festive aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery and coconut are the backbone of every Kerala festive sweet

steps: Heat the 0.33 cup Anveshan Ghee and fry the 5 tbsp cashews and 3 tbsp raisins on low for 2 minutes until the cashews are golden and the raisins puff, then lift them out, leaving the ghee behind.
Add the 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil to the same pan and roast 0.75 cup of the desiccated coconut for 4 minutes until pale gold and fragrant, keeping the remaining 0.25 cup aside for coating.
Stir the 2 cups Anveshan Sattu into the pan and roast on low heat for 12 minutes until it colours and smells deeply toasted.

Off the heat, cool for 4 minutes, then mix in the 1.25 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder, the fried cashews and raisins, 2 tbsp toasted sesame, 1.5 tsp cardamom, 0.25 tsp dry ginger and a pinch of salt while warm.
Press generous 2 tbsp portions into rounds, shaping about 12 to 14 ladoos.
Roll each warm ladoo in the reserved desiccated coconut for a snowy festive coating and rest for 20 minutes to set.
tips: Fry cashews only to light gold; carried over on the hot ghee they darken further off the heat.
Coat the ladoos while still slightly warm so the coconut clings without needing any syrup.
In festive quantities, use desiccated rather than fresh coconut so a big batch keeps for two weeks.
variations.servingSuggestion: Set out during Onam sadya as a finishing sweet, the coconut and cardamom rounding off the banana-leaf feast.

variations.name: Malwa Festive Sattu Ladoo
variations.description: The Sankranti ladoo of the Malwa plateau, heaped with roasted peanuts, sesame and jaggery in the same spirit as the region's til-gul sweets. Warming dry ginger and a hint of nutmeg make it a proper cold-festival indulgence.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: sattu keeps this peanut-and-sesame festive ladoo from turning claggy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a festive measure of ghee to enrich the rustic peanut base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery, peanut and sesame make the classic Sankranti flavour trio

steps: Dry-roast the 0.66 cup peanuts on low heat for 4 to 5 minutes until the skins crack, rub them off and crush the peanuts coarsely.
In the same pan toast the 3 tbsp sesame, 2 tbsp poppy seeds and 0.25 cup dry coconut for 2 to 3 minutes until golden and aromatic, then set aside with the peanuts.
Add the 0.66 cup Anveshan Ghee and roast the 2 cups Anveshan Sattu on low heat for 14 minutes until deep gold and richly fragrant.

Off the heat, rest 5 minutes, then combine the crushed peanuts, toasted seeds and coconut, 1.25 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1.5 tsp cardamom, 0.5 tsp dry ginger, 0.25 tsp nutmeg and a pinch of salt while warm.
Press firm, generous 2 tbsp ladoos, shaping about 12 to 14 hearty rounds.
Cool for 20 minutes until they set solid and hold a satisfying crunch.
tips: Roll a few of the ladoos in extra toasted sesame for a til-gul look that suits Sankranti.
Keep the peanut crush coarse so the festive ladoo stays chunky and textured, not smooth.
These sturdy ladoos are ideal for gifting and keep for a full month in a sealed tin.
variations.servingSuggestion: Share during Makar Sankranti with the customary greeting, alongside cups of hot jaggery tea against the winter chill.

variations.name: Awadhi Festive Sattu Ladoo
variations.description: A courtly Lucknawi festive ladoo, delicately sweetened with khandsari and layered with rose, kewra and mace for an Eid or Shab-e-Baraat spread. Pistachios, chironji and a rose-petal garnish make it as fragrant as it is elegant.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: the gentle roasted gram base keeps the floral perfumes centre stage

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: rich ghee gives this festive ladoo its signature Awadhi softness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: pale khandsari keeps the sweetness refined so the rose and kewra shine

steps: Melt the 0.66 cup Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on low heat and roast the 2 cups Anveshan Sattu for 13 to 15 minutes until it is light gold and gently toasted in aroma.
Add the 4 tbsp pistachios, 3 tbsp chironji and 3 tbsp almonds and roast for 3 minutes until the chironji plumps and the nuts smell fragrant.
Take the pan off the heat and cool for 5 minutes so the khandsari will fold in without melting.
Mix in the 1.25 cups Anveshan Khandsari, 1.5 tsp cardamom, 0.25 tsp mace and a pinch of salt, then sprinkle over the 1 tbsp rose water and 1 tsp kewra water and blend evenly.
Shape neat, generous 2 tbsp ladoos by pressing firmly, making about 12 to 14 delicate rounds.
Press a few pistachio slivers and dried rose petals onto each ladoo and rest for 20 minutes until set.
tips: Add the rose and kewra waters last and sparingly; layered together they can quickly overwhelm the ladoo.
Crush the rose petals lightly for the garnish so they scatter prettily rather than sitting in whole flakes.
Khandsari keeps these crumbly and fragrant for up to 3 weeks, making them ideal to prepare a day ahead of the festival.
variations.servingSuggestion: Offer on a fine china plate after an Eid feast, the rose and kewra ladoo pairing beautifully with a cup of cardamom qahwa.

variations.name: Classic Roasted Atta Ladoo
variations.description: The everyday atta ladoo boiled down to its honest essentials: whole-wheat flour patiently roasted in ghee until nutty, then bound with jaggery and cardamom. No frills, just a warm, crumbly, wholesome sweet that keeps for a fortnight.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The whole soul of this ladoo; roast it low and slow for a deep nutty flavour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Both the roasting fat and the binder that holds the crumb together

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Added off the heat so it sweetens without melting into hard toffee

steps: Melt the Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadai on low heat and add the 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, stirring continuously so it toasts evenly.
Keep roasting on low for about 18 to 20 minutes until the flour turns deep golden, loosens in the ghee and smells distinctly nutty.
Stir in the chopped almonds and cashews and roast for 2 more minutes until the nuts colour lightly, then pull the pan off the heat.
Let the mixture cool for 5 minutes to just warm, then mix in 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 teaspoon cardamom powder and a pinch of salt until fully combined.
When the warm mixture clumps on pressing, scoop 2 tablespoons at a time and roll firmly into 12 round ladoos.
Rest the ladoos for 20 minutes so the ghee sets before you serve or store them.
tips: If the mix will not bind, add 1 to 2 tablespoons of extra warm ghee rather than any water.
Never add jaggery to a hot pan, or it melts and sets the ladoos rock hard as they cool.
Sift the roasted flour if you want a finer, smoother crumb before mixing in the jaggery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Keep a jar on the counter for a quick after-meal sweet, and warm one for 10 seconds to bring back that fresh-roasted aroma.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Besan-Atta Roasted Ladoo
variations.description: Maharashtrian kitchens marry roasted wheat with gram flour for a two-grain ladoo that is nuttier and grainier than plain atta. A pinch of nutmeg and coarse rava give it the sandy, melt-in-mouth texture prized at Ganesh Chaturthi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The wheat half of the two-grain base, roasted for body and nuttiness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasts both flours and gives the ladoo its rich Maharashtrian aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The traditional gul that sweetens Marathi festive ladoos

steps: Melt the Anveshan Ghee in a kadai and first roast the 1/2 cup besan on low heat for about 8 minutes, stirring, until it darkens and smells cooked, not raw.
Add the 1.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta and 1/4 cup rava and roast together on low for a further 12 minutes until the whole mix is golden and grainy.
Stir in the chopped cashews and 2 tablespoons raisins and roast for 2 minutes until the cashews turn pale gold and the raisins plump, then take off the heat.
Cool for 6 minutes to just warm, then mix in 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 teaspoon cardamom powder and 1/4 teaspoon grated nutmeg.
Once the mixture binds when pressed, roll 2 tablespoons at a time into 12 firm ladoos.
Let them set for 20 minutes so the besan-atta crumb firms into shape.
tips: The besan must be roasted until its raw smell fully disappears, or the whole batch will taste floury.
Roasting the rava separately for a minute first keeps the crumb sandy rather than pasty.
A tiny pinch of nutmeg is the Maharashtrian signature here; do not skip it for authentic flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as prasad after Ganpati aarti, wrapped singly in butter paper so guests can carry one home.

variations.name: Gujarati Sukhadi Roasted Atta Ladoo
variations.description: Sukhadi, also called gol papdi, is Gujarat's four-ingredient miracle of atta cooked in ghee and jaggery. Rolled into ladoos here, it is chewy-soft, deeply caramel and traditionally offered to guests and gods with equal reverence.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Roasted just to golden so the sukhadi stays soft rather than crumbly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Sukhadi is famously ghee-forward; it fries the atta and melts the jaggery

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Melted into the hot flour to give sukhadi its chewy caramel character

steps: Melt the Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan on low heat and roast the 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, stirring constantly, until it turns golden and aromatic, about 12 minutes.
Lower the flame to the minimum and quickly stir in 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder so it melts into the hot flour within a minute without hardening.
As soon as the jaggery has just melted and coated the flour, take the pan off the heat and mix in 1 teaspoon cardamom powder.
Working fast while the mixture is hot and pliable, scoop 2 tablespoons at a time and roll into 12 ladoos, protecting your palms with a little ghee.
Press a few sesame seeds and chopped almonds onto each ladoo while they are still warm so they stick.
Let the ladoos cool completely for 25 minutes to set into their signature soft-chewy bite.
tips: Speed matters: jaggery sukhadi stiffens quickly, so shape the ladoos while the mixture is genuinely hot.
Melt the jaggery on the lowest heat and for the shortest time, as overcooking turns the ladoos hard and bitter.
For the classic barfi format, press the hot mixture into a greased tray and cut into diamonds instead of rolling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Cut a few pieces into diamonds and serve alongside the rolled ladoos on a festive Gujarati thali next to a bowl of shrikhand.

variations.name: Malwi Peanut Roasted Atta Ladoo
variations.description: From the Malwa plateau comes a rustic ladoo where roasted peanuts are ground into the wheat, lending a groundnut-butter richness and a satisfying grit. Groundnut oil and jaggery make it a hardy, travel-friendly sweet of central India.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The wheat base that carries the ground-peanut richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Echoes the peanut flavour and is the everyday cooking fat of the Malwa region

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rounds out the groundnut oil and binds the crumb into ladoos

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The rustic sweetener of central India, added off the heat

steps: Dry roast the 1 cup raw peanuts in a hot kadai for about 6 minutes until the skins loosen and blister, then rub them off, cool and pulse to a coarse powder.
Warm the Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil and Anveshan Ghee together in the kadai and roast the 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta on low heat, stirring, until deep golden, about 16 minutes.
Add the coarse peanut powder and 2 tablespoons sesame seeds and roast for 3 minutes until everything smells richly nutty, then remove from the heat.
Cool for 5 minutes to just warm, then mix in 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 teaspoon cardamom powder and a pinch of salt until the mixture binds.
Roll 2 tablespoons at a time into 12 sturdy ladoos, pressing firmly so the coarse peanut crumb holds.
Rest for 20 minutes to let the ladoos firm up for the road or the tin.
tips: Keep the ground peanuts coarse, not pasty, or their released oil makes the mixture greasy and hard to shape.
The pinch of salt sharpens the peanut and jaggery contrast, which is central to the Malwi character.
These are famously sturdy travel sweets and hold up for two weeks in a cool, dry tin.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pack a couple into a journey tiffin with a flask of masala tea, the way Malwa families send them along on long train rides.

variations.name: Kashmiri Walnut Roasted Atta Ladoo
variations.description: A cold-country ladoo enriched with the valley's abundant walnuts and warmed by dry ginger and cinnamon. Roasted wheat, jaggery and toasted walnut come together into a hearty, warming sweet eaten through the long Kashmiri winter.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Hearty wheat that stands up to the bold walnut and spice

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Warming fat that roasts the flour and carries the winter spices

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Its warmth pairs naturally with dry ginger and cinnamon

steps: Dry roast the 3/4 cup walnuts in a hot pan for about 3 minutes until fragrant and a shade darker, then cool and chop coarsely.
Melt the Anveshan Ghee in a kadai and roast the 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta on low heat, stirring steadily, until deep golden and nutty, about 17 minutes.
Stir in the chopped walnuts, 3 tablespoons raisins, 1 teaspoon dry ginger powder and 1/2 teaspoon cinnamon powder and roast for 2 minutes until aromatic, then take off the heat.
Cool for 5 minutes to just warm, then mix in 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 teaspoon cardamom powder until the mixture holds together.
Shape 2 tablespoons at a time into 12 ladoos, pressing firmly so the walnut pieces stay embedded.
Let them rest for 20 minutes to set before serving warm.
tips: Roast the walnuts only briefly, as overtoasting makes them bitter and overpowers the jaggery.
The dry ginger and cinnamon make this a warming winter ladoo, so keep both prominent.
Store in a cool, dry jar; walnut-rich ladoos can turn if kept somewhere warm and humid.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a hot cup of noon chai, the pink salt tea of Kashmir, for a warming winter afternoon pairing.

variations.name: Classic Roasted Moong Dal Halwa
variations.description: The wedding-season heirloom of North Indian kitchens, where soaked yellow moong dal is ground and then patiently roasted in ghee until it turns deep gold and releases a nutty, almost fudgy aroma. This slow-roasted halwa is grainy yet melting, rich with milk and cardamom, and famously demands an unhurried arm at the pan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the roasting medium that toasts the dal grain by grain and gives this halwa its signature grainy sheen

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined raw sugar swapped for white sugar, dissolving into a clean caramel sweetness

steps: Rinse 1 cup split yellow moong dal, soak it in water for 3 hours, drain well, then grind to a coarse, slightly grainy paste using barely any water.
Warm 2 cups full-fat milk with 0.5 cup water and 10 saffron strands in a separate pan and keep it hot on the lowest flame.

Melt 0.75 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai, add the ground dal and roast on low heat, stirring constantly for 25 to 30 minutes until it breaks from a lump into loose golden grains and smells deeply nutty.
Ladle the hot saffron milk into the roasted dal a little at a time, stirring hard after each addition to keep it lump-free, and cook 6 to 8 minutes until it thickens and absorbs the liquid.
Stir in 0.75 cup Anveshan Khandsari and 0.75 tsp cardamom powder, and keep cooking 5 minutes until the sugar melts and the halwa glistens and pulls away from the sides.
Fry 12 almonds, 12 cashews and 2 tbsp raisins in a spoon of ghee until golden, fold most of them in, and cook a final 2 minutes until the ghee separates at the edges.
Garnish with the remaining fried nuts and serve warm.
tips: Do not rush the dal roasting; if it stays pale the halwa tastes raw and pasty, so hold your nerve until it is uniformly golden.
If the halwa turns dense on standing, loosen it with a splash of hot milk and a teaspoon of ghee over low heat.
Grind the dal coarse rather than smooth to keep the traditional grainy bite that defines this halwa.
variations.servingSuggestion: Spoon into small brass katoris while warm and top with a few extra saffron strands and slivered pistachios for a festive Holi or Diwali dessert.

variations.name: Gujarati Roasted Moong Dal Halwa
variations.description: Gujarat sweetens its moong dal halwa with earthy jaggery instead of sugar, lending a molasses warmth that pairs beautifully with the toasted dal. Often called moong dal sheera in Kathiawadi homes, it is a touch softer and darker, perfumed with nutmeg alongside cardamom.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the dal and later keeps the jaggery from seizing into a hard mass

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the Gujarati sweetener of choice, giving a deep molasses note that white sugar cannot

steps: Soak 1 cup split yellow moong dal for 3 hours, drain thoroughly, and grind to a coarse paste with minimal water so it stays thick.
Dissolve 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 0.25 cup warm water to make a syrup, strain out any grit, and set it aside off the heat.
Heat 0.75 cup Anveshan Ghee in a thick-bottomed pan, add the dal paste, and roast on low for about 28 minutes, stirring without pause until it is grainy, golden and fragrant.
Pour in 2 cups warm full-fat milk gradually, whisking to avoid lumps, and simmer 6 minutes until the mixture drinks up the milk and thickens.
Lower the flame fully before stirring in the strained jaggery syrup so it does not curdle, then cook 4 to 5 minutes until glossy and thick.
Mix in 0.5 tsp cardamom, 0.25 tsp nutmeg and 2 tbsp charoli seeds, cook 2 more minutes until the ghee beads at the sides, and fold through slivered almonds and pistachios.
Rest for five minutes off the heat to let the flavours settle, then serve warm.
tips: Always add jaggery on the lowest heat and after the milk has been absorbed, or the dairy can split.
Charoli seeds are the classic Gujarati garnish here; toast them lightly for a richer aroma.
A pinch of nutmeg rounds out the jaggery beautifully, so do not leave it out.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm alongside a glass of cold masala milk, or offer it as prasad in leaf donas during Navratri celebrations.

variations.name: Kashmiri Roasted Moong Dal Halwa
variations.description: The Kashmiri table gives this halwa a regal turn with generous saffron and a wash of rosewater, its pale gold deepening to sunset amber. Crowned with blanched almonds and a hint of dry ginger, it is fragrant, luxurious and made for cold-weather feasting.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: carries the saffron oils through the dal and gives the halwa its rich Kashmiri finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk to bloom its colour and honeyed aroma through the halwa

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined sugar that keeps the delicate saffron flavour from being masked

steps: Soak 1 cup split yellow moong dal for 3 hours, drain, and grind coarsely with as little water as possible.
Warm 2 cups full-fat milk and steep 0.5 tsp Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in it for ten minutes until the milk glows deep amber.
In a heavy pan melt 0.75 cup Anveshan Ghee and roast the ground dal on low heat for 26 to 30 minutes, stirring steadily until it loosens into golden grains and smells toasted.
Add the saffron milk in small ladles, stirring firmly each time, and cook 7 minutes until the dal thickens and absorbs the liquid.
Stir in 0.75 cup Anveshan Khandsari with 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp dry ginger powder, and simmer 5 minutes until glossy and thickened.
Fold in half the blanched almonds and pistachios, cook 2 minutes until the ghee separates, then finish with 1 tsp rosewater off the heat.
Scatter the remaining nuts over the top and serve warm.
