tips: Bloom the saffron in warm, not boiling, milk to protect its aroma and draw out maximum colour.
Add rosewater only after switching off the flame, since heat drives away its perfume.
Dry ginger is the quiet Kashmiri touch that warms the palate; a pinch is plenty.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in shallow bowls with a final drizzle of warm saffron milk and a few rose petals for a wintry Kashmiri feast finale.

variations.name: Awadhi Roasted Moong Dal Halwa
variations.description: From the nawabi kitchens of Lucknow comes this delicately perfumed halwa, scented with kewra and a whisper of screwpine that lingers on the palate. Slow-roasted and enriched with khoya, it is silkier and more aromatic than its rustic cousins, the kind of sweet served at the close of a dawat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the nawabi cooking fat that roasts the dal and marries the kewra perfume into the halwa

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined sugar that keeps the sweetness clean so the kewra aroma stays centre stage

steps: Soak 1 cup split yellow moong dal for 3 hours, drain fully, and grind to a coarse paste using minimal water.
Crumble 0.5 cup khoya and keep it ready, and warm 1.5 cups full-fat milk in a small pan.
Melt 0.75 cup Anveshan Ghee in a broad kadhai and roast the dal paste on low heat for around 28 minutes, stirring constantly until deep golden and nutty.
Add the warm milk gradually while stirring, cook 5 minutes, then mix in the crumbled khoya and cook 3 minutes until it melts smoothly into the halwa.
Stir in 0.75 cup Anveshan Khandsari with 0.5 tsp cardamom and cook 5 minutes on low until the mixture thickens and the ghee glistens at the edges.
Fry 15 cashews and 2 tbsp raisins in a little ghee, fold them in, and finish with 1 tsp kewra water once the pan is off the flame.
Smooth into a dish, lay a sheet of silver leaf on top, and serve warm.
tips: Kewra is potent, so measure a level teaspoon; too much turns the halwa soapy.
Adding khoya makes this version richer, but grate it fresh so it melts without lumps.
For a true dawat finish, apply the silver leaf with the back of a spoon so it does not tear.
variations.servingSuggestion: Present in a shallow silver thali cut into diamonds, garnished with rose petals, to close a nawabi-style meal of biryani and kebabs.

variations.name: Malwa Roasted Moong Dal Halwa
variations.description: The Malwa plateau of Madhya Pradesh folds roasted peanuts into its moong dal halwa, giving a rustic crunch and a deep groundnut warmth found nowhere else. Sweetened with jaggery and finished with a scatter of crushed peanuts, it is homely, sturdy and made for winter afternoons.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the dal and the peanuts together so their aromas mingle into the halwa

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the Malwa sweetener whose molasses depth suits the earthy peanuts perfectly

steps: Soak 1 cup split yellow moong dal for 3 hours, drain, and grind coarse with barely any water.
Coarsely crush 0.5 cup roasted peanuts, keeping 2 tbsp aside for garnish, and dissolve 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 0.25 cup warm water into a strained syrup.
Heat 0.66 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan and roast the ground dal on low for about 27 minutes, stirring throughout until it turns golden and grainy.
Tip in the crushed peanuts and 3 tbsp dry coconut slivers, roast 2 minutes more, then add 2 cups warm milk in stages and cook 6 minutes until thick.
Reduce the flame to its lowest, pour in the jaggery syrup with 0.5 tsp cardamom, and cook 5 minutes until glossy and pulling from the sides.
Fold in slivered almonds, cook a final 2 minutes until the ghee separates, and take off the heat.
Top with the reserved crushed peanuts and serve warm.
tips: Use freshly roasted peanuts and rub off their skins for a cleaner, sweeter crunch.
Crush the peanuts coarse rather than powder them so you keep the signature texture.
If the jaggery makes the halwa sticky, a spoon of extra ghee restores its glossy grain.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a side of roasted makhana or pair with kadak masala chai on a cold Malwa evening.

variations.name: Classic Spiced Coconut Rice
variations.description: A masala-forward take on coconut rice where a freshly ground coconut-spice paste coats each grain with warmth from cumin, pepper and roasted dal. Bolder and more aromatic than plain thengai sadam, yet still balanced and family-friendly.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: carries the ground coconut-spice paste evenly through the warm rice

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing drizzle that lifts the roasted-spice aroma

steps: Cook 1.5 cups basmati with 2.5 cups water and 0.5 tsp salt until just tender, then spread it out to cool so the grains stay loose.
Dry-roast 1.5 tbsp chana dal, 1 tsp cumin, 0.75 tsp pepper and 3 dried chillies on low for 2 minutes, then grind with 1 cup grated coconut to a coarse paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and fry 12 cashews until pale gold, about 2 minutes, then remove and reserve.
In the same oil crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds and 15 curry leaves for 20 seconds until they splutter and smell fragrant.
Add the ground coconut-spice paste and roast on medium for 4 minutes, stirring, until it dries slightly and turns aromatic.
Fold in the cooled rice, the fried cashews and 0.75 tsp salt, mixing gently so the masala coats every grain.
Drizzle over 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, toss once, and rest covered for 3 minutes before serving warm.
tips: Grinding the spices fresh with the coconut is what makes this version far more aromatic than a simple temper.
Roast the dal-spice mix only until fragrant; over-roasting turns the pepper harsh.
Leftovers reheat well with a splash of water and a fresh curry-leaf tempering.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a crisp okra fry and cucumber raita, or alongside a peppery rasam for a comforting South Indian plate.

variations.name: Karnataka Coconut Rice
variations.description: A Bangalore-style coconut chitranna where tamarind sharpness meets a fragrant coconut temper, giving a tangy-nutty balance. Bright and slightly sour, it is the lunchbox favourite of Karnataka homes, livelier than the mild classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday Karnataka oil that carries the tamarind-coconut temper

steps: Cook 1.5 cups sona masoori with 3 cups water and 0.5 tsp salt until fluffy, then cool it on a plate so the grains separate.
Loosen 2 tsp tamarind pulp in 3 tbsp warm water and keep it ready beside the stove.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and roast 3 tbsp peanuts until crunchy and browned, about 3 minutes, then set aside.
In the same oil pop 1 tsp mustard seeds, then fry 1.5 tbsp chana dal, 1 tbsp urad dal and 3 slit green chillies until the dals turn golden.
Add 15 curry leaves, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 0.5 tsp turmeric, then pour in the tamarind water and simmer 2 minutes until it thickens.
Stir in 0.75 cup grated coconut and roast 2 minutes until it just colours and soaks up the tangy temper.
Fold in the cooled rice, roasted peanuts and 0.75 tsp salt, mixing well, and rest 3 minutes so the tamarind settles evenly through the grains.
tips: Cook the tamarind down until the raw sourness mellows before the coconut goes in.
The crunchy peanuts are essential for the classic chitranna texture, so add them generously.
It tastes even better the next day, making it a perfect prepare-ahead lunchbox rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a dollop of thick curd and a fried papad, or pack with a spoon of majjige menasu for a tangy meal.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Coconut Rice
variations.description: A Maharashtrian coconut rice built on the dark, roasted depth of goda masala with a hint of jaggery for balance. Earthy and warmly sweet-spiced, it carries the signature smoky-sweet character of Maharashtra's masala box.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the staple Maharashtrian oil that toasts the goda masala without masking it

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the small sweet counterpoint that goda masala always leans on

steps: Cook 1.5 cups basmati with 2.5 cups water and 0.5 tsp salt until just done, then cool it fully so the grains hold their shape.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and roast 3 tbsp peanuts until crisp and golden, about 3 minutes, then remove them.
In the same oil crackle 1 tsp mustard and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, then add 2 slit green chillies and 12 curry leaves and let them splutter 20 seconds.
Add 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 0.5 tsp turmeric, then tip in 0.75 cup grated coconut and toast for 2 minutes until pale gold.
Sprinkle in 2 tsp goda masala and roast on low for 90 seconds until its dark, smoky aroma blooms into the oil.
Fold in the cooled rice, the roasted peanuts, 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.75 tsp salt, mixing so the masala coats evenly.
Cover and rest on the lowest heat for 3 minutes so the goda masala perfume runs through before serving.
tips: Add goda masala on low heat, as its delicate roasted spices scorch quickly on a high flame.
The jaggery is a rounding note against the earthy masala, not meant to make the rice sweet.
A squeeze of lime at the table brightens the deep, smoky flavours beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of dahi and a spicy thecha, or alongside a simple varan for a homely Maharashtrian meal.

variations.name: Andhra Coconut Rice
variations.description: An extra-spiced Andhra kobbari annam where a coarse Guntur-chilli podi is stirred through the coconut rice for lingering heat. Pungent, garlicky and unmistakably hot, this is coconut rice for chilli lovers.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: the heavy Andhra oil that anchors the fierce Guntur-chilli podi

steps: Cook 1.5 cups sona masoori with 3 cups water and 0.5 tsp salt until tender, then cool it so the grains do not stick together.
Dry-roast 6 Guntur chillies, 1 tbsp coriander seeds and 1 tsp cumin for 2 minutes, then grind coarse with 8 garlic cloves into a fiery podi.
Warm 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and roast 0.75 cup grated coconut on low for 3 minutes until golden, then scoop it out.
In the same oil pop 1 tsp mustard seeds, add 1 tbsp urad dal and 15 curry leaves, and fry until the dal is reddish-gold.
Stir in the ground chilli-garlic podi with 0.25 tsp turmeric and roast on medium for 3 minutes until the garlic smell fades and the oil separates.
Return the roasted coconut, then fold in the cooled rice and 0.75 tsp salt so every grain turns deep red.
Cover and rest on the lowest heat for 4 minutes so the heat settles into the rice before serving hot.
tips: Toast the coconut separately so it stays sweet against the aggressive chilli podi.
Deseed a couple of the Guntur chillies if you want the colour without the full ferocity.
The podi keeps for a week, so make a double batch for quick fiery rice on busy days.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a thick curd pachadi and a fried boiled egg, with sliced raw onion to cool the palate between bites.

variations.name: Tamil Nadu Coconut Rice
variations.description: A Chettinad-inflected spiced coconut rice where a roasted fennel, pepper and star-anise blend deepens the curry-leaf temper. Fragrant and warmly spiced, it carries the perfumed complexity Chettinad cooking is loved for.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the Chettinad kitchen fat that binds the fennel-pepper masala to the coconut

steps: Cook 1.5 cups seeraga samba with 3 cups water and 0.5 tsp salt until tender, then cool it on a plate so the small grains loosen.
Dry-roast 1 tsp fennel, 0.75 tsp pepper, 1 star anise and 3 dried chillies for 90 seconds, then grind them to a fragrant coarse powder.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and fry 12 cashews to gold, about 2 minutes, then lift them out to keep crunchy.
In the same oil crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds, add 1 tbsp urad dal and 20 curry leaves, and fry until the dal is golden and the leaves crisp.
Add 0.75 cup grated coconut and the ground Chettinad spice powder and roast on low for 3 minutes until deeply aromatic.
Fold in the cooled rice, the fried cashews and 0.75 tsp salt, tossing so the perfumed masala clings to every grain.
Rest the rice covered off the heat for 4 minutes so the fennel and pepper settle before serving warm.
tips: Seeraga samba's tiny grains soak up the Chettinad masala better than long basmati.
Grind the star anise sparingly, as too much can overpower the delicate coconut.
A pinch of the spice powder saved aside makes a lovely finishing dust before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a Chettinad-style egg roast or a bowl of thin pepper rasam and crisp vadagam fritters.

variations.name: Classic Spiced Corn Pulao
variations.description: A bolder cousin of the everyday corn pulao, built on a fragrant base of ginger, garlic and a rounded garam masala. The corn stays sweet but now sits against warm cumin, coriander and a gentle chilli hum. It is the pulao you make when plain rice feels too quiet for the table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee blooms the ground spices so their aroma coats every grain of rice.

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati rice until clear, soak for 20 minutes and drain in a colander.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot over medium flame and add 1 tsp cumin seeds, letting them crackle for about 20 seconds.
Add 1 large sliced onion and fry for 6 minutes until golden brown, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Lower the heat and add 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp turmeric, stirring for 20 seconds so the spices do not burn.
Add 1 cup sweet corn and saute for 2 minutes, then fold in the drained rice and 0.5 tsp garam masala for 1 minute until evenly coated.
Pour in 2.5 cups water and 1 tsp salt, boil once, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 13 minutes until the grains are tender and separate.
Rest 5 minutes, fluff with a fork and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander leaves.
tips: Add the ground spices off the boil and on low heat, since dry spices scorch in seconds and turn bitter.
For extra depth, dry-roast the garam masala whole spices and grind them fresh the morning you cook.
If you like a little tang, squeeze half a lime over the finished pulao just before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a garlicky burani raita and a crisp roasted papad, letting the cool yogurt offset the warm spice.

variations.name: Andhra Spiced Corn Pulao
variations.description: Andhra brings the heat with fiery Guntur red chillies and a robust ginger-garlic base cooked in Anveshan wood-pressed groundnut oil. The corn's sweetness becomes a deliberate counterpoint to the searing chilli, and a curry-leaf temper keeps it grounded in the south. This is not a shy pulao.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil stands up to the fierce Guntur chilli the way southern kitchens intend.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of bilona ghee softens the chilli's edge without dulling the heat.

steps: Soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain thoroughly.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pot on medium flame, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop for 20 seconds.
Add 3 broken Guntur red chillies and 12 curry leaves and fry for 15 seconds until the chillies darken and smell smoky.
Stir in 1 large sliced onion and cook for 5 minutes until golden, then add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 1 minute.
Add 1 cup sweet corn, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder and saute for 2 minutes, then fold in the drained rice for 1 minute.
Pour in 2.5 cups water and 1 tsp salt, boil once, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 13 minutes until fluffy.
Rest 5 minutes, drizzle 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the top and fluff gently before serving.
tips: Break the Guntur chillies rather than powdering them so the heat stays fragrant and not overwhelming.
Fry the dry chillies for only a few seconds; overcooking releases acrid smoke that can sting the throat.
Balance the fire at the table with a spoon of thick curd rather than reducing the chilli in the pot.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of cooling perugu (spiced curd) and a fried appadam, the classic Andhra way to temper a spicy rice.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Spiced Corn Pulao
variations.description: The soul of this pulao is goda masala, the sweet-dark Maharashtrian spice blend of stone flower, sesame and coconut. It wraps the corn in an earthy, faintly sweet warmth quite unlike garam masala. A scatter of peanuts adds the crunch that Maharashtrian rice dishes are known for.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the everyday Maharashtrian cooking fat and pairs naturally with goda masala.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon of bilona ghee at the finish lifts the dark goda masala into something fragrant.

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain well.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pot on medium heat and fry 3 tbsp peanuts for 2 minutes until they turn ruddy, then scoop them out and reserve.
In the same oil add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin, let them splutter for 20 seconds, then add 10 curry leaves and 1 large sliced onion and fry for 5 minutes until golden.
Lower the heat and stir in 1.5 tsp goda masala and 0.5 tsp turmeric for 20 seconds so the blend blooms without scorching.
Add 1 cup sweet corn and saute for 2 minutes, then fold in the drained rice for 1 minute until evenly darkened by the masala.
Pour in 2.5 cups water and 1 tsp salt, boil once, cover and cook on very low heat for 13 minutes until tender.
Rest 5 minutes, drizzle 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then fluff and scatter the fried peanuts on top.
tips: Goda masala can taste raw if under-bloomed, so give it a full 20 seconds in the hot oil before the rice goes in.
Add the peanuts only at the end so they keep their crunch instead of softening in the steam.
If you cannot find goda masala, a mix of garam masala with a pinch of ground sesame is a fair stand-in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of koshimbir (cucumber-peanut salad) and a wedge of lime for a homely Maharashtrian lunch.

variations.name: Rajasthani Spiced Corn Pulao
variations.description: Rajasthan cooks with what the desert offers, so this pulao leans on whole dried red chillies, cumin and a bold ghee temper. The chillies fried in bilona ghee give a smoky, dry heat rather than a wet gravy burn, and the corn keeps everything from turning too fierce. It is rustic, aromatic and built to eat with bajra roti.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Desert cooking relies on generous bilona ghee to fry the dried chillies to a smoky depth.

steps: Soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain in a colander.
Lightly crush 1 tsp coriander seeds and 4 cloves in a mortar so they release aroma but stay coarse.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot on medium flame, add 4 broken dried red chillies and 1 tsp cumin, and fry for 20 seconds until the chillies deepen and smell smoky.
Add the crushed coriander-clove mix and 1 cracked black cardamom, stir for 10 seconds, then add 1 large sliced onion and fry for 6 minutes until deep golden.
Add 1 cup sweet corn and 0.5 tsp turmeric and saute for 2 minutes, then fold in the drained rice for 1 minute.
Pour in 2.5 cups water and 1 tsp salt, boil once, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 13 minutes until dry and fluffy.
Rest 5 minutes, then fluff gently, discarding the whole chillies if you prefer a milder plate.
tips: Toasting and crushing the whole seeds fresh gives a far more aromatic pulao than using ready powders.
Fry the dried chillies just until fragrant; a few seconds too long and the ghee turns acrid.
This pulao keeps its flavour well in a tiffin, since the dry-spiced grains do not go soggy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of garlic-tempered kadhi and a piece of bajra roti for an authentic Marwari meal.

variations.name: Karnataka Spiced Corn Pulao
variations.description: This Karnataka take stirs a whisper of tamarind and coconut into the corn, giving the pulao a signature tang the region loves in its rice dishes. A temper of urad dal, mustard and curry leaves in Anveshan wood-pressed coconut oil sets the southern tone. Sweet, sour and nutty meet in one fragrant pot.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed coconut oil ties the tamarind and coconut together in the classic Karnataka way.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of bilona ghee rounds the tamarind's tang with a mellow richness.

steps: Soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain, and separately dissolve 1 tsp tamarind paste in 3 tbsp warm water.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pot on medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal and fry for 30 seconds until the dal turns golden.
Add 12 curry leaves and 2 slit green chillies and fry for 15 seconds, then add 1 sliced medium onion and cook for 4 minutes until soft.
Stir in 1 cup sweet corn, 0.25 cup grated coconut and 0.5 tsp turmeric and saute for 3 minutes until the coconut smells toasty.
Fold in the drained rice for 1 minute, then pour in the tamarind water, 2.5 cups water and 1 tsp salt and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 13 minutes until the grains are tender and the tang has settled in.
Rest 5 minutes, drizzle 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then fluff gently and serve warm.
tips: Keep the tamarind to a single teaspoon; too much makes the rice sticky and overwhelms the corn.
Frying the urad dal to golden is what gives the temper its signature nutty crunch, so do not rush it.
Reduce the total water slightly if your tamarind water is generous, to keep the grains separate.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of plain curd and a crisp sandige (fryum), letting the mild dairy balance the tangy rice.

variations.name: Classic Spiced Curd Rice
variations.description: A boldly tempered take on curd rice, where cracked black pepper and extra green chilli push the everyday thayir sadam into pleasantly warming territory. The cooling curd still leads, but each spoon carries a slow heat that builds gently on the tongue.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee tempers the peppercorns without burning them, releasing a warm, fragrant heat into the curd.

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed rice with 3 cups water for 4 whistles until soft, then mash while warm and cool for 10 minutes.
Coarsely crush 1 tsp black peppercorns in a mortar so they release aroma but still give the odd sharp bite.
Stir 2 cups curd, 0.5 cup milk and 1 tsp salt into the rice until creamy, keeping it loose enough to fall off a spoon.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin, then add 1 tsp urad dal and the crushed pepper and fry for 40 seconds until fragrant.
Add 3 slit green chillies, 2 dried red chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 15 curry leaves and 0.5 tsp asafoetida, sautéing 20 seconds until the leaves crisp.
Fold the peppery tempering through the curd rice, garnish with 2 tbsp coriander and rest for 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Crush the pepper fresh rather than using pre-ground powder; whole cracked corns give bursts of heat instead of a flat background burn.
If the dish turns too spicy, an extra spoon of chilled curd stirred in at the end cools it instantly.
The pepper heat intensifies as it sits, so go lighter if making it several hours ahead.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling cucumber-mint raita on the side and plain steamed appalam to offset the pepper.

variations.name: Tamil Nadu Milagu Thayir Sadam
variations.description: This Tamil version turns up the black pepper and dried chilli, a style often eaten during colds and monsoon days for its warming quality. The double tempering in ghee is aggressive and aromatic, yet the mashed curd rice underneath stays soft and soothing.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A generous ghee tempering is the traditional carrier for the pepper-heavy milagu style.

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed rice with 3.5 cups water for 5 whistles until very soft, then mash to a smooth mush and cool for 10 minutes.
Whisk 2.5 cups curd with 0.5 cup milk and 1 tsp salt, then blend into the rice along with 2 tbsp fresh grated coconut until spoonable and creamy.
Pound 1.5 tsp peppercorns coarsely with 2 of the dried red chillies and 1 tbsp roasted gram to make a rough, slightly thickening hot-spice blend.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 1.5 tsp urad dal and 3 sliced shallots and toast for 45 seconds until deeply golden.

Add the crushed pepper-chilli-gram mix, the remaining 2 dried red chillies, 1.5 inch grated ginger, 20 curry leaves and 0.5 tsp asafoetida, frying for 20 seconds until the leaves are crisp and the kitchen smells sharp.
Fold the fiery tempering through the curd rice and rest 15 minutes so the pepper warmth infuses evenly before serving.
tips: This pepper-forward style is meant to clear the sinuses, so do not shy from the full quantity if you are chasing that effect.
Grate the ginger finely so it disperses; large shreds clump and taste raw against the smooth curd.
Leftovers reheat poorly, but the dish keeps well cool for a day if you hold back some curd to refresh it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best with a smear of tangy tomato thokku and a hot cup of rasam alongside on a rainy afternoon.

variations.name: Bengali Kasundi Doi Bhaat
variations.description: A spicy Bengali spin using Anveshan Mustard Oil and a hint of mustard paste heat to echo kasundi, the region's pungent condiment. Green chilli and nigella seeds sharpen it further, making a curd rice with a bracing, nose-tingling edge.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Pungent wood-pressed mustard oil doubles down on the kasundi character of this spicy doi bhaat.

steps: Cook 1 cup rinsed short-grain rice with 2.75 cups water until soft, mash lightly and cool for 10 minutes.
Loosen 1 tsp mustard paste with a spoon of water so it will disperse smoothly rather than sit in bitter lumps.
Beat 2 cups curd with 0.5 cup milk, 0.75 tsp salt and the loosened mustard paste, then fold into the rice for a sharp, tangy base.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes and mellows, about 1 minute, then lower the heat to medium.
Crackle 0.75 tsp nigella seeds for 15 seconds, then add 4 slit green chillies, 2 dried red chillies, 1 inch julienned ginger and 10 curry leaves and fry for 30 seconds until pungent.
Pour the tempering over the doi bhaat, fold thoroughly, and rest 10 minutes so the mustard heat blooms before serving.
tips: Use only a teaspoon of mustard paste and mix it well; too much or poorly dispersed paste turns the dish bitter.
Slit the green chillies rather than chopping them so you get aroma and gentle heat without overwhelming raw pungency.
Heat the mustard oil properly to tame its raw bite before it ever touches the delicate curd.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with crisp begun bhaja (fried aubergine) and a wedge of lime for a punchy Bengali plate.

variations.name: Andhra Guntur Perugu Annam
variations.description: Andhra brings its trademark fire with fierce Guntur red chillies powdered into the tempering, plus garlic and curry leaves fried in sesame oil. It is curd rice for those who like a serious kick, the yogurt tempering just enough of the Guntur heat to keep it edible.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed sesame oil is the classic Andhra frying fat, standing up to the fierce Guntur chilli.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of ghee softens the Guntur heat and rounds the sharp sesame edge.

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed rice with 3.5 cups water for 5 whistles until soft, mash while warm and cool for 10 minutes.
Dry-roast 4 Guntur red chillies in a pan for 1 minute until they darken slightly, then crush them coarsely for maximum bite.
Mix 2.5 cups curd, 0.5 cup milk and 1 tsp salt into the rice until thick and creamy, which helps buffer the coming heat.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil over medium flame, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal, then fry 4 sliced garlic cloves until golden, about 1 minute.
Add the crushed Guntur chillies, 15 curry leaves and 0.5 tsp asafoetida, frying for 20 seconds until the oil turns fiery red and fragrant.
Fold the tempering and a finishing 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee through the curd rice, then rest 10 minutes so the flavours settle before serving.
tips: Keep the extra-thick curd base for this one; a watery mix cannot carry the Guntur heat and turns sharp.
Deseed the Guntur chillies if you want the smoky flavour with less scorch.
The garlic is best sliced, not minced, so it fries evenly to gold rather than burning into bitterness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a scoop of cooling plain curd and steamed rice on the side for anyone who finds the heat too much.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Goda Dahi Bhaat
variations.description: Maharashtra stirs its aromatic goda masala into a curd rice, lending sweet-woody notes of dagad phool and dry coconut against the tang. A peanut-and-ghee tempering rounds it out, making a spiced curd rice quite unlike its southern cousins.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee blooms the goda masala, coaxing out its dark, woody aroma into the curd rice.

steps: Cook 1 cup rinsed rice with 3 cups water until soft, mash gently while warm and cool for 10 minutes.
Stir 2 cups curd, 0.5 cup milk and 1 tsp salt into the rice for a smooth, creamy base.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and fry 3 tbsp peanuts for 2 minutes until crunchy and browned.
Add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin and let them splutter for 20 seconds, then add 2 slit green chillies, 12 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida.
Lower the heat, sprinkle in 1 tsp goda masala and fry for just 10 seconds so it blooms without scorching, then take the pan off the flame.
Fold the aromatic tempering through the curd rice, garnish with 2 tbsp coriander, and rest 10 minutes before serving.
tips: Add the goda masala at the very end of tempering off a low flame, as its delicate flowers and coconut burn in seconds.
Good goda masala varies in strength, so start with a teaspoon and add more only after tasting the mixed rice.
A pinch of jaggery in the curd underlines the sweet-woody profile that Maharashtrians love in goda dishes.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a crunchy koshimbir (cucumber-peanut salad) and lime pickle for a proper Maharashtrian touch.

variations.name: Classic Spiced Ghee Rice
variations.description: A bolder, deeply aromatic ghee rice built on a full whole-spice tempering plus a hit of warming garam masala and black pepper. Anveshan ghee toasts the basmati to a nutty gloss while browned onions and a red-chilli edge give it real backbone against robust curries.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee tames the heavier spicing here and stops the pepper from turning harsh.

steps: Rinse 2 cups basmati until the water runs clear, soak 20 minutes and drain well so the grains cook up firm and distinct.

Melt 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot over medium heat, then add 1 tsp cumin, 0.5 tsp peppercorns, 1 star anise, 4 cardamom, 5 cloves, 1 inch cinnamon and 2 bay leaves and fry 40 seconds until they crackle and perfume the ghee.
Add 2 thinly sliced onions and cook until richly golden-brown, about 10 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until fragrant.
Lower the heat and sprinkle in 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp garam masala, stirring for 20 seconds off the boil so the ground spices bloom without scorching.
Add the drained rice and toast for 2 minutes until glossy, then pour in 3 cups hot water and 1.25 tsp salt and bring to a strong boil.
Cover, reduce to the lowest heat and steam 12 minutes, then rest 5 minutes off the flame and fluff gently with a fork so the grains separate.
tips: Blooming the chilli and garam masala off the boil for only 20 seconds keeps them fragrant; leave them longer and they turn acrid.
For extra-separate grains, spread the fluffed rice on a wide plate for two minutes to let residual steam escape.
A teaspoon of ghee stirred through just before serving revives the aroma if the rice has been sitting.
variations.servingSuggestion: Excellent under a thick dal makhani or paneer butter masala, with sliced onions soaked in vinegar and green chilli alongside.

variations.name: Andhra Guntur Chilli Ghee Rice
variations.description: Fiery by design, this Andhra pilaf leans on smoky Guntur red chilli and gingelly-scented Anveshan wood-pressed sesame oil under the ghee. Curry leaves and a garlic-forward tempering make it a punchy partner for a simple pappu or yoghurt.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee softens the aggressive Guntur heat so the rice stays fragrant rather than raw-hot.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil is the classic Andhra fat and grounds the chilli with a toasty depth.

steps: Wash and soak 2 cups basmati for 20 minutes, then drain thoroughly while you smash 6 garlic cloves and slice 1 large onion.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil with 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin, 3 cloves, 3 cardamom and 1 inch cinnamon for 30 seconds.
Add the smashed garlic and a sprig of curry leaves and fry until the garlic is golden and aromatic, about 1 minute, then add the sliced onion and cook 8 minutes to deep gold.
Pull the pot off the heat and stir in 1 tsp Guntur red chilli powder for 15 seconds so it turns glossy red without burning to bitterness.
Return to the flame, add the drained rice and toast 2 minutes, then pour in 3 cups water and 1.25 tsp salt and bring to a rolling boil.
Cover, cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes, rest 5 minutes and fluff, leaving the fried garlic and curry leaves in for bursts of flavour.
tips: Guntur chilli is intensely hot; start with 0.75 tsp if cooking for children and build up from there.
Adding the chilli powder off the heat is essential, as its high pigment scorches in seconds on a live flame.
A spoon of thick curd on the side is the traditional coolant and completes the meal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a plain tempered yoghurt (perugu) and a fried papad to balance the chilli's smoky heat.

variations.name: Odia Panch Phoron Ghee Rice
variations.description: From Odisha's kitchens, this pilaf is tempered with panch phoron, the five-seed blend of cumin, fennel, fenugreek, nigella and mustard, bloomed in Anveshan mustard oil and ghee. Earthy and lightly pungent, it is a fragrant everyday rice with quiet regional character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee mellows the mustard oil and carries the earthy panch phoron aroma through the rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: The pungent kick of mustard oil is authentic to eastern-Indian tempering.

steps: Rinse and soak 2 cups basmati for 20 minutes, then drain well while you thinly slice 1 onion.
Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pot over medium-high until it faintly smokes, then reduce the heat and add 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee.
Tip in 1 tsp panch phoron and 2 dried red chillies and let them splutter for 30 seconds until the mustard and fenugreek seeds pop and turn fragrant.
Add 2 bay leaves, 3 cardamom, 1 inch cinnamon and the sliced onion and fry 7 minutes until the onion is soft and golden at the edges.
Stir in 0.25 tsp turmeric for 10 seconds, add the drained rice and toast 2 minutes, then pour in 3 cups water and 1.25 tsp salt and bring to a boil.
Cover, cook on the lowest heat 12 minutes, rest 5 minutes, then fluff gently and remove the whole red chillies if you prefer a milder plate.
tips: Panch phoron must splutter fully in the hot fat first; the whole fenugreek turns bitter if it does not toast through.
Keep the turmeric low, at a quarter teaspoon, so the rice takes a pale gold rather than a strong yellow.
This rice reheats beautifully with a splash of water and makes a fine base for a next-day fried rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with an Odia-style dalma (dal with vegetables) and a spoon of tomato khatta for a complete regional plate.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Goda Masala Ghee Rice
variations.description: Maharashtra's aromatic masala bhaat spirit in a ghee-rice form, its warmth coming from goda masala, the state's dark, faintly sweet spice blend built on stone flower and toasted coconut. Cooked in Anveshan ghee and wood-pressed groundnut oil, it is earthy, mellow and comforting.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee lends the roundness that balances goda masala's smoky, slightly sweet edge.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the staple Maharashtrian cooking fat and adds a gentle nuttiness.

steps: Rinse and soak 2 cups basmati for 20 minutes and drain, then dry-roast 2 tbsp grated dry coconut in a pan until pale gold and set aside.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil with 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds; when they crackle, add 1 tsp cumin, 3 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon.
Add 1 sliced onion and fry 7 minutes until soft and golden, then stir in 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp goda masala and cook 30 seconds off the boil until dark and fragrant.
Fold in the roasted coconut and the drained rice and toast for 2 minutes so the grains take on the masala's colour.
Pour in 3 cups water and 1.25 tsp salt, bring to a boil and taste the liquid for a deep, savoury-sweet warmth.
Cover, steam on the lowest heat 12 minutes, rest 5 minutes, then fluff and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Toasting the dry coconut separately keeps it from burning in the spice base and adds a nutty crunch through the rice.
Goda masala brands vary in salt and heat, so add the last quarter teaspoon only after tasting.
A handful of soaked cashews or fried peanuts fried in with the onion nudges this closer to a festive masala bhaat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of thin varan (plain toor dal), a wedge of lime and a dollop of extra ghee stirred in at the table.

variations.name: Rajasthani Red Chilli Ghee Rice
variations.description: A rustic Marwari pilaf built for the desert palate, whole dried red chillies and coarse-cracked spices bloomed in generous Anveshan ghee. With no onion and only pantry spices, it is the frugal, intensely aromatic rice of a Rajasthani thali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rajasthani cooking is generous with ghee; here it carries the whole-chilli heat and the aroma of the desert kitchen.

steps: Rinse and soak 2 cups basmati for 20 minutes and drain; lightly crack 1 tsp coriander seeds and 1 black cardamom with the flat of a knife to release their oils.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot over medium heat and add 4 whole dried red chillies, frying 20 seconds until they darken and swell but do not blacken.
Add 1 tsp cumin, the cracked coriander, 4 cloves, 3 green cardamom, the black cardamom, 1 inch cinnamon and 2 bay leaves and let everything crackle 30 seconds until deeply aromatic.
Tip in the drained rice and toast for 3 minutes over medium heat so the grains absorb the spiced ghee and smell toasty.
Pour in 3 cups water and 1.25 tsp salt, bring to a boil and give one gentle stir to distribute the whole spices.
Cover, cook on the lowest heat 12 minutes, rest 5 minutes, then fluff and lift out the softened whole chillies before serving if you want it milder.
tips: Frying the whole chillies just to a darker red, never black, gives a smoky aroma without overwhelming bitterness.
The extra ghee is intentional and traditional; it keeps this onion-free rice moist and rich.
Serve the fried whole chillies on top for those who like to crush one into their plate for a fierce kick.
variations.servingSuggestion: The classic partner is a bowl of panchmel dal and a spoon of garlic-red-chilli chutney, with buttermilk to cool the palate.

variations.name: Classic Spiced Masala Khichdi
variations.description: A bolder, more assertively spiced take on everyday khichdi, where a full masala base of onion, tomato and ground spices coats every grain. It eats like a light pulao-khichdi hybrid, hearty enough to be a meal on its own yet still soft and forgiving.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Two spoons for the masala and one drizzled raw over the finished pot for aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Blended with ghee so the onions can fry to a deep gold without burning.

steps: Rinse 1 cup rice with 0.5 cup moong dal until clear, soak 15 minutes and drain in a colander.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium and crackle 1 tsp cumin, 6 peppercorns and 3 cloves for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 large finely sliced onion and fry for 5 minutes until deep golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook a further minute.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.25 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp garam masala, and cook for 4 minutes until the oil separates and the masala looks jammy.
Fold in 1 cup mixed vegetables and the drained rice-dal, sauté for 2 minutes, then add 4 cups hot water and 1.25 tsp salt.
Pressure cook on medium for 3 whistles and let the pressure fall naturally, giving a soft, well-spiced khichdi.
Fluff gently and finish with the reserved 1 tbsp raw Anveshan Ghee before serving hot.
tips: Frying the onions properly to deep gold is what gives this spiced version its depth, so do not rush that step.
Add the garam masala with the other powders rather than at the end so it cooks into the base and does not taste raw.
Leftovers thicken overnight into a lovely tikki mixture; shape into patties and pan-fry in a little ghee.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a garlicky tomato chutney and a bowl of chilled cucumber raita to cut the spice.

variations.name: Rajasthani Spiced Masala Khichdi
variations.description: From the desert kitchens of Rajasthan comes a robust khichdi built on whole dried red chillies, plenty of ghee and a garlicky heat that suits the arid climate. Often made with bajra or coarse grains and finished with a fiery chilli-garlic tempering, it is unapologetically bold and warming.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rajasthan uses ghee lavishly; reserve 2 tbsp for the fierce chilli-garlic tadka on top.

steps: Rinse 1 cup rice with 0.5 cup chilka moong dal, soak for 15 minutes and drain well.
In a pressure cooker heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium, add 1 tsp cumin, 0.25 tsp asafoetida, 3 cloves and 1 bay leaf, and let them foam and turn fragrant for 20 seconds.
Add 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp red chilli powder, stir for 15 seconds off the direct heat so the powders do not scorch.
Tip in the drained rice and dal, toss for 2 minutes, then pour in 4.25 cups hot water with 1.25 tsp salt.
Seal and pressure cook on medium for 4 whistles, then let the pressure release naturally into a soft, thick khichdi.

For the tadka, heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan and fry 8 sliced garlic cloves with 4 whole dried red chillies until the garlic is golden and the chillies darken, about 2 minutes.
Pour the sizzling chilli-garlic ghee over the opened khichdi and fold it through just before serving.
tips: The whole dried red chillies are meant to perfume the ghee rather than blow your head off, so use the milder Mathania type if you want colour over fierce heat.
Chilka (split green) moong dal holds its shape better than yellow dal and gives this desert khichdi a more rustic, textured bite.
Keep it on the wetter side, as Rajasthani khichdi is traditionally eaten loose with an extra pool of ghee spooned over.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the classic way with a bowl of Rajasthani kadhi, garlic-red chilli chutney and a dollop of white butter melting on top.

variations.name: Andhra Spiced Masala Khichdi
variations.description: This is khichdi with an Andhra temper: searing Guntur red chilli, gingelly oil and a curry-leaf tadka that make it closer to a spicy pongal than a mild comfort bowl. Toasted cashews and a hit of black pepper round out a dish that is fiery, fragrant and deeply satisfying.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil is the Andhra base, giving the khichdi its earthy, nutty depth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Used to toast the cashews and pepper for the finishing tadka.

steps: Rinse 1 cup rice with 0.5 cup moong dal, soak for 15 minutes and drain, keeping everything ready by the stove.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pot on medium and crackle 1 tsp cumin, then add 1 tbsp minced ginger and 2 slit green chillies and fry for a minute.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp Guntur red chilli powder off the flame for a few seconds so the fierce chilli blooms without burning, then return to the heat.
Add the drained rice and dal, toss for 2 minutes, then pour in 4 cups hot water with 1.25 tsp salt and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on low for about 18 minutes until soft and thick, mashing it lightly for a pongal-like texture.
In a small pan, heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and fry 0.25 cup cashews with 1 tsp crushed pepper and 15 curry leaves until the cashews are golden and the leaves crisp, about 90 seconds.
Pour this fragrant ghee tadka over the khichdi and fold it in just before serving.
tips: Guntur chilli is genuinely hot, so start with 1 tsp if you are heat-shy and build up, since you can always add more in the tadka.
Crushing the peppercorns coarsely rather than powdering them gives little bursts of heat that are characteristic of Andhra pongal-style dishes.
A squeeze of lime at the table brightens all that chilli and oil and keeps the dish from feeling heavy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling coconut chutney or thick set curd and a spoonful of gongura pickle for a true Andhra flavour contrast.

variations.name: Tamil Spiced Masala Khichdi
variations.description: A Tamil Nadu spin that borrows the soul of ven pongal, tempered heavily with curry leaves, cumin and whole black pepper in gingelly oil and ghee. It is soft, peppery and soothing, the kind of khichdi served warm at temples and family breakfasts alike.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ven pongal style relies on generous ghee for its silky richness and aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: A spoon of gingelly oil in the tempering adds the earthy Tamil backbone.

steps: Dry-roast 0.5 cup moong dal in a pan for 3 minutes until it smells nutty, then rinse it with 1 cup rice and drain.
Pressure cook the rice and dal with 4.25 cups water, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt for 4 whistles until very soft, then mash lightly to a creamy pongal-like consistency.
In a separate pan heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil on medium until warm and fragrant.
Add 0.25 cup cashews and fry for a minute until golden, then add 1.5 tsp cumin, 1.5 tsp whole peppercorns and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them crackle.
Toss in 20 curry leaves, 1 tbsp grated ginger and 2 slit green chillies, frying for 30 seconds until the leaves go crisp and the kitchen fills with pepper aroma.
Pour this entire ghee tempering over the mashed rice and dal and fold it through thoroughly.
Cook together on low for 2 minutes so the flavours meld, adding a splash of hot water if it stiffens, then serve warm.
tips: Whole peppercorns give the authentic ven-pongal pop, but crack them lightly if you prefer the heat more evenly spread.
This dish is meant to be soft and almost creamy, so cook the dal fully and do not skimp on the ghee.
Make the tempering last and pour it over while sizzling, as that is when the curry leaves and pepper are at their most fragrant.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot with coconut chutney and a small bowl of tangy gothsu (tamarind-brinjal sauce) in the classic Tamil breakfast pairing.

variations.name: Kashmiri Spiced Masala Khichdi
variations.description: An aromatic, saffron-kissed khichdi inspired by Kashmiri Pandit cooking, gently warmed with fennel, dry ginger and a bloom of pure saffron. Pale gold and delicately spiced rather than fiery, it carries the floral, regal character that defines the valley's kitchens.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Kashmiri cooking is ghee-rich; some tempers the spices and some finishes the pot.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Bloomed in 2 tbsp warm milk to give the khichdi its golden hue and floral aroma.

steps: Soak 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside to steep into a deep gold liquor while you prep the rest.
Rinse 1 cup rice with 0.5 cup moong dal, soak 15 minutes and drain in a sieve.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pressure cooker on medium and add 1 tsp cumin, 3 cloves, 3 cardamom pods and 1 inch cinnamon, letting them puff and perfume the ghee for 30 seconds.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Kashmiri red chilli powder, 1 tsp fennel powder and 0.5 tsp dry ginger powder for 15 seconds, keeping the heat gentle so the aromatic powders do not brown.
Add the drained rice and dal, toss for 2 minutes, then pour in 4 cups hot water with 1.25 tsp salt.
Pressure cook on medium for 3 whistles and allow natural release, then open and pour in the bloomed saffron milk, folding it through for colour and fragrance.
Finish with the remaining 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee melted over the top and rest covered for 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Kashmiri red chilli is prized for its ruby colour and mild heat, so it is what keeps this khichdi vivid without making it hot.
Fennel and dry ginger are the signature Kashmiri Pandit spice pair, giving a warm, slightly sweet note quite unlike Punjabi khichdi.
Bloom the saffron in warm rather than boiling milk to draw out its colour and aroma without dulling the delicate threads.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of Kashmiri dum aloo or a simple yogurt-walnut chutney and a scatter of fried onions for a festive valley-style plate.

variations.name: Classic Atta Ladoo
variations.description: A wholesome winter staple where nutty khapli whole-wheat atta is slow-roasted in ghee until golden and toasty, then bound with jaggery into satisfying, energy-dense ladoos. The ancient khapli wheat gives an earthier, more robust flavour than regular atta, making these both nourishing and deeply comforting.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Ancient khapli wheat roasted slowly for a nutty, wholesome ladoo base.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasts the atta to a deep gold and binds the ladoos with richness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Stirred into the cooled roasted atta so it melds without hardening.

steps: Melt 0.75 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai on low, take 1 tbsp aside and fry 2 tbsp edible gum in it until it puffs into white balls, then crush and reserve.
Add 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta to the remaining ghee and roast on low heat, stirring constantly for 15-18 minutes, until it turns deep golden and smells warmly nutty.
Stir in 0.25 cup chopped almonds and 0.25 cup chopped cashews and roast for 2 more minutes until fragrant.
Turn off the heat, add the crushed fried gond, 1 tsp cardamom powder and a pinch of salt, and cool the mixture until just warm.
Mix in 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder into the warm atta until it binds into a soft, pliable dough; adding it to hot atta would make the ladoos hard.
Take 2 tbsp portions and roll firmly between your palms into smooth round ladoos.
Rest for an hour to firm up, then store in an airtight container.
tips: Khapli atta needs a slightly longer, gentler roast than maida-style flours to lose its raw edge, so keep the heat low and be patient.
The fried edible gum (gond) adds a lovely crunch and makes these a warming winter and post-partum ladoo, but it can be left out for a smoother version.
If the dough won't bind, drizzle in a spoon of warm melted ghee; if it feels greasy, let it cool a little more before rolling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these rustic ladoos with a glass of warm milk on cold mornings as a nourishing start to the day.

variations.name: Kashmiri Atta Ladoo
variations.description: A valley-style whole-wheat ladoo warmed with saffron, walnuts and a hint of dry ginger, marrying the earthy khapli atta with the region's beloved nut and spice. Golden-hued and gently floral, it is a nourishing winter sweet with a regal aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Nutty ancient wheat that stands up to the saffron and walnuts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasts the atta and dissolves the saffron for even golden colour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Caramel sweetness folded into the cooled atta to bind the ladoos.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Bloomed in warm ghee to lend colour and a honeyed aroma.

steps: Melt 0.75 cup Anveshan Ghee on low, steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 1 tsp of the warm ghee, and add 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta to the rest.
Roast the atta on low, stirring constantly for 15-18 minutes, until deep golden and warmly nutty.
Add 0.5 cup chopped walnuts and roast for 2 minutes until they toast lightly and smell fragrant.
Off the heat, stir in the saffron ghee, 1 tsp cardamom powder, 0.25 tsp dry ginger powder and a pinch of salt, then cool until just warm.
Mix in 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder until the saffron-tinted atta binds into a soft dough.
Roll into firm 2 tbsp ladoos and press a walnut piece onto each top.
Let them set for an hour before storing in a tin.
tips: Dry ginger gives a warming kick that suits these winter ladoos and aids digestion, a classic North Indian pairing with jaggery.
Bloom the saffron in warm ghee rather than adding it dry so its colour runs right through the atta.
Toast the walnuts only briefly at the end, since the residual heat of the atta will continue to cook them.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with saffron-infused warm milk or kahwa for a comforting valley-style winter treat.

variations.name: Kerala Atta Ladoo
variations.description: A coastal whole-wheat ladoo where nutty khapli atta meets toasted coconut, ghee-fried cashews and a crackle of coconut oil for a tropical spin. It echoes the coconut-jaggery soul of Kerala sweets while keeping the wholesome heartiness of an atta ladoo.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The wholesome nutty base that carries the coconut beautifully.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Fries the cashews and roasts the atta alongside the coconut oil.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Lends the signature Kerala coconut fragrance to the roasted atta.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The coconut-friendly sweetener folded into the cooled atta.

steps: Dry-roast 0.75 cup grated coconut on low for 5 minutes until pale golden and toasty, then set aside.
Melt 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee with 0.25 cup Anveshan Coconut Oil on low and fry 0.33 cup chopped cashews until golden, then lift them out.
Add 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta to the fat and roast on low, stirring, for 15-18 minutes until deep golden and nutty.
Stir in the toasted coconut and fried cashews and roast together for 2 minutes.
Off the heat, add 1 tsp cardamom powder and a pinch of salt, then cool the mixture until just warm.
Fold in 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder until the coconut-flecked atta binds into a soft dough.
Roll into 2 tbsp ladoos, coat lightly in extra toasted coconut, and set for an hour.
tips: Roast the coconut only to pale gold, as taking it too dark makes the ladoos dry and faintly bitter.
Fresh coconut shortens shelf life, so refrigerate these and enjoy within four to five days.
The coconut oil is what makes these taste distinctly Kerala, so do not swap it out entirely for ghee.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a banana leaf rolled in toasted coconut, a lovely wholesome sweet after a South Indian meal.

variations.name: Malwa Atta Ladoo
variations.description: A rustic Madhya Pradesh whole-wheat ladoo loaded with crushed roasted peanuts and sesame, giving nutty crunch and groundnutty depth over the earthy khapli atta base. Hearty and filling, it is the kind of energy-rich sweet made in big batches through the plateau's cold months.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The wholesome base that pairs naturally with the peanuts of the region.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasts the atta deep and gold and binds the crunchy mixture.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Earthy caramel sweetener that suits the roasted peanuts and sesame.

steps: Coarsely crush 0.66 cup roasted peanuts and toast 3 tbsp sesame seeds until they pop; keep both aside.
Melt 0.75 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai on low, add 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta and roast, stirring, for 15-18 minutes until deep golden and nutty.
Add the crushed peanuts and toasted sesame and roast together for 2 minutes so their flavours marry.
Off the heat, stir in 1 tsp cardamom powder and a pinch of salt, then cool the mixture until just warm.
Mix in 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder until the crunchy atta binds into a firm dough.
Press 2 tbsp portions firmly into rustic ladoos so the peanut and sesame pieces hold together.
Rest for an hour, then store in an airtight jar.
tips: Leave the peanuts coarse for that signature Malwa crunch rather than grinding them fine.
Toast the sesame just until it pops and turns aromatic; browning it makes the ladoos taste bitter.
Press these ladoos firmly, as the crunchy peanut mixture needs a good squeeze to stay bound.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these filling ladoos with warm jaggery tea or plain milk as a winter energy snack.

variations.name: Awadhi Atta Ladoo
variations.description: A refined Lucknowi whole-wheat ladoo perfumed with rose, kewra and pistachio, dressing the earthy khapli atta in Nawabi elegance. Floral and delicate yet wholesome, it bridges rustic winter comfort and courtly festive polish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The nutty wheat base that grounds the delicate florals.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasts the atta and carries the rose and kewra aromas evenly.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A gentle caramel base that lets the florals come through.

steps: Melt 0.75 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan on low, add 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta and roast, stirring, for 15-18 minutes until deep golden and nutty.
Add half the 0.33 cup slivered pistachios and roast for a minute, reserving the rest for garnish.
Turn off the heat, stir in 1 tsp cardamom powder and a pinch of salt, then cool the mixture until just warm.
Sprinkle in 0.5 tsp kewra water and 1 tsp rose water and fold quickly so the delicate aromas fold in without evaporating.
Mix in 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder to form a soft, fragrant dough.
Roll into smooth 2 tbsp ladoos and press the reserved pistachios and dried rose petals onto the tops.
Rest for an hour so the flavours settle before serving or storing.
tips: Add the kewra and rose water only off the heat, as their volatile perfume cooks away quickly on a hot pan.
Kewra is strong, so keep to half a teaspoon or the ladoos will taste medicinal.
For a Nawabi flourish, finish a few ladoos with edible silver leaf before plating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Present on a rose-strewn tray with cups of warm cardamom or saffron milk for an elegant Awadhi festive close.

variations.name: Classic Besan Barfi
variations.description: The melt-in-the-mouth gram flour fudge of North Indian mithai shops, built on besan roasted low and slow in ghee until it turns deep gold and floods the kitchen with a nutty aroma. Bound with a one-string sugar syrup and cardamom, it sets into dense, grainy squares that crumble tenderly on the tongue.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the roasting fat that toasts the besan grain by grain, the single most important step for barfi

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined sugar cooked to a one-string syrup, swapped for white sugar to bind the barfi

steps: Melt 1 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai, add 2 cups coarse gram flour, and roast on low heat for 18 to 20 minutes, stirring without pause until it turns deep golden and smells richly nutty.
Sprinkle in 2 tbsp milk while stirring; it will bubble and make the besan grainy, then keep roasting 3 minutes more until the froth settles.
Take the roasted besan off the heat to cool slightly while you make the syrup.
In another pan dissolve 1.5 cups Anveshan Khandsari in 0.5 cup water and boil until it reaches a one-string consistency, about 6 minutes.
Pour the hot syrup into the warm besan with 0.75 tsp cardamom and stir briskly for 2 minutes until the mixture thickens and starts leaving the sides.
Working quickly, pour into a greased tray, level the top, and press slivered almonds and pistachios over the surface.
Cool for 30 minutes until just set, then cut into squares or diamonds and lift out once firm.
tips: Adding a splash of milk during roasting gives the classic grainy, porous texture, so do not skip it.
Test the syrup by pressing a drop between thumb and finger; a single thread means it is ready.
Cut the barfi while it is still slightly warm, as it crumbles if you wait until fully hard.
variations.servingSuggestion: Arrange the diamonds in a mithai box lined with butter paper, or serve on a festive platter with a bowl of warm rabri.

variations.name: Gujarati Besan Barfi
variations.description: Gujarat sweetens its besan barfi with jaggery, giving a bronze colour and mellow molasses depth in place of the usual sugar sharpness. Coarser besan and a hint of nutmeg make it the earthy, wholesome mithai of Kathiawadi festivals.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the besan deeply and keeps the jaggery pliable as it binds the barfi

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the Gujarati sweetener that lends a bronze colour and molasses depth to the barfi

steps: Melt 1 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan, add 2 cups coarse gram flour, and roast on low for 18 to 20 minutes, stirring constantly until deep golden and nutty.
Take the roasted besan off the heat and let it cool for a few minutes so the jaggery will not seize.
In a separate pan dissolve 1.25 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 0.33 cup water and simmer 5 minutes to a soft, sticky syrup, then strain out any grit.
Pour the warm jaggery syrup into the besan with 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp nutmeg, stirring briskly for 2 minutes until it thickens and leaves the sides.
Mix in 2 tbsp charoli seeds, then quickly pour into a greased tray and level the surface.
Press slivered almonds over the top while it is still warm.
Cool 35 minutes until set, then cut into squares and lift out once firm.
tips: Let the besan cool a little before adding jaggery syrup, as very hot besan can make the jaggery grainy.
Strain the jaggery syrup so the barfi stays smooth and free of impurities.
Jaggery holds more moisture, so give this barfi a slightly longer setting time.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the bronze squares at a Diwali gathering alongside a glass of chilled thandai.

variations.name: Kashmiri Besan Barfi
variations.description: The Kashmiri barfi is perfumed with saffron and topped generously with slivered almonds, its pale gold turning a warm amber. A whisper of dry ginger gives the warming lift characteristic of the valley's winter sweets.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the besan and carries the saffron oils through the barfi

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk to lend the barfi its amber glow and honeyed valley aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined sugar cooked to a one-string syrup that keeps the saffron flavour clear

steps: Steep 0.5 tsp Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside to bloom.
Melt 1 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai, add 2 cups coarse gram flour, and roast on low for 18 to 20 minutes, stirring until deep golden and fragrant.
Stir the saffron milk into the roasted besan along with 0.25 tsp dry ginger, then take it off the heat to cool slightly.
In a separate pan dissolve 1.5 cups Anveshan Khandsari in 0.5 cup water and boil to a one-string syrup, about 6 minutes.
Pour the hot syrup into the besan with 0.5 tsp cardamom and stir briskly for 2 minutes until it thickens and leaves the sides.
Pour into a greased tray, level the top, and cover the surface with slivered blanched almonds.
Cool 30 minutes until set, then cut into diamonds and lift out once firm.
tips: Bloom the saffron in warm milk, not water, so it blends richly into the besan.
Dry ginger is the quiet valley warmth here; a pinch is enough.
Cut while slightly warm for clean edges, as the barfi crumbles once fully cold.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the amber diamonds with a cup of kahwa for an elegant Kashmiri sweet course.

variations.name: Kerala Besan Barfi
variations.description: Kerala folds fresh coconut into the roasted besan and finishes it in fragrant coconut oil, giving a chewy, tropical twist to the classic fudge. Toasted coconut on top makes each square distinctly coastal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the wood-pressed Kerala fat that roasts the besan and layers in a warm coconut aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined sugar cooked to a one-string syrup that binds the coconut barfi

steps: Heat 0.75 cup Anveshan Coconut Oil in a heavy pan, add 2 cups coarse gram flour, and roast on low for 16 minutes, stirring until golden and nutty.
Add 0.75 cup grated fresh coconut and roast 4 minutes more until the coconut dries out and smells toasty.
Take the pan off the heat to cool slightly while you prepare the syrup.
In a separate pan dissolve 1.5 cups Anveshan Khandsari in 0.5 cup water and boil to a one-string syrup, about 6 minutes.
Pour the hot syrup into the besan-coconut mixture with 0.5 tsp cardamom and stir briskly for 2 minutes until it thickens and leaves the sides.
Pour into a greased tray, level the surface, and scatter chopped cashews on top.
Cool 35 minutes until set, then cut into squares and lift out once firm.
tips: Dry the grated coconut well by roasting it with the besan, or the barfi will not set firm.
Use fresh, not desiccated, coconut for the chewy texture that defines this version.
Watch the syrup closely, as it moves fast from one-string to hard once it starts.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the coconut squares with a small cup of filter coffee for a coastal tea-time sweet.

variations.name: Malwa Besan Barfi
variations.description: The Malwa version studs the roasted besan with crushed peanuts and sweetens it with jaggery, giving a nutty crunch and rustic caramel warmth. It is the sturdy, homely barfi of Madhya Pradesh winter kitchens.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the besan and the peanuts so their toasted aromas combine in the barfi

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the Malwa sweetener whose caramel depth complements the roasted peanuts

steps: Melt 1 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan, add 2 cups coarse gram flour, and roast on low for 18 minutes, stirring until deep golden and nutty.
Coarsely crush 0.5 cup roasted peanuts, keeping 2 tbsp aside, add the rest to the besan with 2 tbsp dry coconut slivers, and roast 3 minutes more.
Take the pan off the heat to cool slightly while you make the syrup.
In a separate pan dissolve 1.25 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 0.33 cup water and simmer 5 minutes to a sticky syrup, then strain.
Pour the warm jaggery syrup into the besan with 0.5 tsp cardamom and stir briskly for 2 minutes until it thickens and leaves the sides.
Pour into a greased tray, level the top, and scatter the reserved crushed peanuts over the surface.
Cool 35 minutes until set, then cut into squares and lift out once firm.
tips: Skin the peanuts and crush them coarse to keep the plateau crunch in every bite.
Let the besan cool slightly before adding the jaggery syrup so it does not turn grainy.
Press the surface peanuts in gently while warm so they stick once the barfi sets.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the peanut-studded squares with masala chai on a cold Malwa evening.

variations.name: Classic Besan Ladoo
variations.description: The quintessential Indian sweet: gram flour slow-roasted in ghee until it turns deep golden and intensely nutty, then bound with jaggery and cardamom into melt-in-the-mouth balls. Getting the roast right is everything, giving these ladoos their signature grainy, fudgy bite and shelf-life of weeks.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The roasting medium that carries the besan to a deep gold and gives the ladoos their richness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Added to the cooled roasted besan so it melds without turning the ladoos hard.

steps: Melt 0.75 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai on low heat, then add 2 cups gram flour and stir to a thick, sandy paste.
Roast the besan on low, stirring continuously for 18-22 minutes, until it loosens, turns a rich golden brown and smells deeply nutty; rushing this on high heat leaves a raw taste.
Stir in 0.25 cup chopped almonds, 0.25 cup chopped cashews and 2 tbsp melon seeds and roast for another 2 minutes until the nuts are fragrant.
Turn off the heat, mix in 1 tsp cardamom powder and a pinch of salt, and let the mixture cool until just warm to the touch, about 10 minutes.
Add 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder to the warm besan and mix thoroughly so it melts evenly into a soft, pliable dough; adding it while piping hot would make the ladoos rock-hard.
Take 2 tbsp of the mixture at a time and roll firmly between your palms into smooth round ladoos.
Rest the ladoos for an hour to firm up before storing them in an airtight jar.
tips: The single biggest mistake is under-roasting the besan, so keep going on low heat until it visibly darkens and the raw smell is completely gone.
If the mixture feels too dry to bind, work in a tablespoon of warm melted ghee; if too loose, cool it a few more minutes before rolling.
Using coarse (ladoo) besan instead of fine gives a more traditional grainy texture that many prefer.
variations.servingSuggestion: Present on a festive platter dusted with a few saffron strands and slivered pistachios, ideal alongside evening chai during Diwali.

variations.name: Kashmiri Besan Ladoo
variations.description: A regal valley version perfumed with saffron and studded with walnuts, the Kashmiri pantry's favourite nut, over the classic ghee-roasted besan base. The saffron lends both a honeyed aroma and a warm amber colour that makes these ladoos feel especially festive.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasts the besan and dissolves the saffron so its colour spreads evenly.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Folded into the cooled besan for a caramel sweetness that suits the saffron.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Warmed in a little ghee to release its colour and aroma before mixing through.

steps: Melt 0.75 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan on low, take out 1 tsp of the warm ghee into a small bowl and steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in it to bloom.
Add 2 cups gram flour to the remaining ghee and roast on low, stirring without pause for 18-22 minutes, until deep golden and richly fragrant.
Add 0.5 cup chopped walnuts and 0.5 tsp lightly crushed fennel seeds and roast for 2 more minutes so the walnuts toast lightly.
Switch off the heat and stir in the saffron ghee, 1 tsp cardamom powder and a pinch of salt, letting the colour streak through, then cool until just warm.
Mix in 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder into the warm mixture until it comes together into a soft dough that holds its shape.
Scoop 2 tbsp portions and roll into firm, smooth ladoos, pressing a walnut piece onto the top of each if you like.
Let them set for an hour before storing in an airtight tin.
tips: Blooming the saffron in warm ghee rather than sprinkling it dry spreads both its colour and perfume far more evenly through the ladoos.
Lightly crushing the fennel seeds releases their sweet aroma, a subtle Kashmiri touch that pairs beautifully with saffron.
Walnuts can turn bitter if over-toasted, so add them near the end of the roast and watch them closely.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these amber ladoos with kahwa, the saffron-almond Kashmiri tea, for a matched valley-style sweet course.

variations.name: Kerala Besan Ladoo
variations.description: A coastal reimagining where roasted besan meets toasted fresh coconut and a fragrant crackle of coconut oil, giving the ladoos a tropical sweetness and a moist, tender crumb. It borrows the coconut-forward soul of Kerala sweets like a besan-unni-appam hybrid.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The main roasting fat for the besan, giving richness under the coconut.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Added to the roast for the unmistakable Kerala coconut aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Mixed into the cooled base for a deep caramel sweetness that loves coconut.

steps: Dry-roast 0.75 cup fresh grated coconut in a pan on low for 4-5 minutes until it turns pale golden and smells toasty, then set aside.
In the same pan melt 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee with 0.25 cup Anveshan Coconut Oil on low heat.
Add 2 cups gram flour and roast on low, stirring constantly for about 18 minutes, until deep golden and nutty with the coconut oil perfuming the kitchen.
Stir in 0.33 cup chopped cashews and the toasted coconut and roast together for 2 more minutes.
Turn off the heat, mix in 1 tsp cardamom powder and a pinch of salt, and cool the mixture until just warm.
Fold in 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder until the mixture binds into a soft, coconut-flecked dough.
Roll into 2 tbsp ladoos and, if you like, coat each in a little extra toasted coconut before setting for an hour.
tips: Roast the coconut only until pale gold, as browning it too far turns the ladoos dry and slightly bitter.
Because fresh coconut adds moisture, these ladoos are best eaten within four to five days unless refrigerated.
For a firmer set in humid weather, use half fresh and half desiccated coconut.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve rolled in toasted coconut on a banana leaf for a South Indian festive touch, wonderful after an Onam sadya.

variations.name: Malwa Besan Ladoo
variations.description: From the peanut-rich Malwa belt of Madhya Pradesh comes a rustic ladoo where roasted crushed peanuts join the besan for extra crunch and a groundnutty depth. Heartier and more textured than the smooth classic, it is a farmer's-market kind of sweet.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasts both the besan and the peanuts to a deep, aromatic gold.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The earthy caramel sweetener that pairs naturally with roasted peanuts.

steps: Coarsely crush 0.75 cup roasted peanuts, leaving some texture, and dry-toast 2 tbsp sesame seeds until they pop; keep both aside.
Melt 0.75 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai on low, add 2 cups gram flour and roast, stirring constantly, for 18-22 minutes until golden brown and nutty.
Add the crushed peanuts and toasted sesame seeds and roast together for 2 minutes so their flavours marry with the besan.
Turn off the heat, stir in 1 tsp cardamom powder and a pinch of salt, and let the mixture cool until just warm.
Mix in 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder until the dough is soft, crunchy with peanuts and holds together when pressed.
Roll 2 tbsp portions into slightly rustic ladoos, pressing firmly so the peanut pieces stay bound.
Allow to set for an hour, then store in an airtight container.
tips: Leave the peanuts coarse rather than powdered, since the little crunchy bits are the whole point of this Malwa version.
Toast the sesame just until it pops for a nutty aroma, and stop before it browns or it turns bitter.
If the peanuts release oil and the dough feels greasy, cool it a little longer before rolling and it will firm up.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these hearty ladoos with a glass of warm turmeric or plain milk as a wholesome winter snack.

variations.name: Awadhi Besan Ladoo
variations.description: A refined Lucknowi rendition scented with kewra and rose, dressed with slivered pistachios and a hint of edible camphor in the classic Nawabi mithai tradition. Delicate and floral, it turns the humble besan ladoo into something fit for a royal dessert tray.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The rich roasting fat that carries the delicate kewra and rose aromas.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Mixed into the cooled base for a mellow sweetness beneath the florals.

steps: Melt 0.75 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan on low, add 2 cups gram flour and roast steadily for 18-22 minutes, stirring, until deep golden and aromatic.
Add half the 0.33 cup slivered pistachios and roast for a minute, reserving the rest for garnish.
Turn off the heat and stir in 1 tsp cardamom powder and a pinch of salt, then let the mixture cool until just warm.
Sprinkle in 0.5 tsp kewra water and 1 tsp rose water, mixing quickly so the delicate aromas fold in without evaporating.
Add 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder to the warm mixture and combine into a soft, fragrant dough.
Roll into smooth 2 tbsp ladoos and press the reserved pistachio slivers and a few dried rose petals onto the tops.
Let the ladoos rest for an hour so the flavours settle before serving or storing.
tips: Add the kewra and rose water only after the pan is off the heat, as their volatile aromas cook off quickly on a hot flame.
Kewra is strong, so stick to half a teaspoon; too much makes the ladoos taste medicinal rather than floral.
For a true Nawabi look, roll a few ladoos in edible silver leaf (vark) before plating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Arrange on a silver tray scattered with rose petals and slivered pistachios, a fragrant finish to an Awadhi dawat.

variations.name: Classic Coconut Ladoo
variations.description: The five-minute festive favourite: grated coconut simmered with condensed milk and ghee until it clumps, then rolled and dusted in more coconut. Soft, milky and fragrant with cardamom, it is the ladoo every Indian household makes when guests arrive unannounced.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Keeps the coconut from catching and lends a glossy richness to the ladoo

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A spoon of unrefined sweetness deepens the flavour beyond flat condensed-milk sugar
