steps: Set aside 1/2 cup of the desiccated coconut for rolling, and dry roast the remaining 2.5 cups in a pan on low heat for 2 minutes just until warm and fragrant, not browned.
Add the 2 tablespoons Anveshan Ghee and the chopped cashews and stir for a minute until the cashews turn pale gold.
Pour in the 1 cup condensed milk and 3 tablespoons Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook on low heat, stirring constantly, for about 6 minutes until the mixture thickens and leaves the sides of the pan.
Stir in 1 teaspoon cardamom powder and, if the mix looks dry, 2 tablespoons of milk to keep it pliable, then take the pan off the heat.
Cool for 5 minutes until warm enough to handle, then roll 2 tablespoons at a time into 14 balls and coat each in the reserved coconut.
Chill the ladoos for 20 minutes so they firm up and hold their round shape.
tips: Do not overcook after adding the condensed milk, or the ladoos turn dry and chewy once cooled.
If the mixture is too soft to roll, chill it for 15 minutes and it will firm up enough to shape.
These keep for four to five days refrigerated in an airtight box.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled straight from the fridge on a hot day, arranged on a coconut-shell plate for a playful festive touch.

variations.name: Kerala Nariyal Ladoo with Coconut Oil
variations.description: Kerala doubles down on the coconut, using fresh grated coconut cooked in aromatic wood-pressed coconut oil and jaggery instead of condensed milk. Toasted cashews and a hint of cardamom make it closer to a soft coconut-jaggery halwa rolled into balls.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: The soul of Kerala cooking; it amplifies the coconut aroma tenfold

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Replaces condensed milk entirely for a darker, more traditional Kerala sweetness

steps: Warm 1 tablespoon Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a kadai and fry the 1/3 cup cashews and 2 tablespoons raisins until the cashews are golden and the raisins swell, then set aside.
In the same pan melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 3 tablespoons water on low heat, stirring, until it dissolves into a thick syrup, about 4 minutes.
Add the 3 cups fresh grated coconut and the remaining coconut oil and cook on low heat, stirring often, for about 10 minutes until the mixture thickens and pulls away from the sides.
Mix in 1 teaspoon cardamom powder, 1/4 teaspoon dry ginger powder and the fried cashews and raisins, then cook for a final minute and remove from the heat.
Cool for 6 minutes until warm, then roll 2 tablespoons at a time into 14 firm ladoos.
Let them set for 20 minutes; they firm up as the coconut oil resolidifies at room temperature.
tips: Fresh coconut carries moisture, so cook until the mixture genuinely leaves the pan or the ladoos will not hold.
The tiny bit of dry ginger is a classic Kerala touch that keeps the sweetness from feeling heavy.
In a cool kitchen the coconut oil sets the ladoos beautifully; in summer, refrigerate them to keep their shape.
variations.servingSuggestion: Offer with a small cup of strong Malabar filter coffee, the way these are handed out at Kerala house gatherings.

variations.name: Gujarati Kopra Pak Coconut Ladoo
variations.description: Gujarat's kopra pak turns coconut and milk into a fudgy, saffron-tinged sweet set with ghee and cardamom. Rolled into ladoos, it is denser and richer than the everyday version, a mithai-shop classic offered during Diwali and weddings.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Enriches the kopra pak and gives it a glossy, fudgy set

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: Unrefined golden sugar that sets the pak cleanly while staying wholesome

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: Bloomed in warm milk to tint the pak a festive gold

steps: Soak 1/4 teaspoon Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tablespoons of the warm milk and leave it for 10 minutes to release its colour.
Heat the remaining milk with the 1/2 cup crumbled khoya in a kadai on low heat, stirring, until it forms a smooth thick paste, about 5 minutes.
Add the 3 cups desiccated coconut and 3 tablespoons Anveshan Ghee and cook on low, stirring, for 6 minutes until the mixture is thick and comes together.
Stir in 3/4 cup Anveshan Khandsari Sugar and the saffron milk and keep cooking for about 6 more minutes until the sugar melts and the mass leaves the sides of the pan.
Mix in 1 teaspoon cardamom powder, take off the heat and cool for 5 minutes until warm and pliable.
Roll 2 tablespoons at a time into 14 ladoos and press sliced pistachios onto each before they set for 20 minutes.
tips: Cook the khandsari only until the mixture leaves the pan; overcooking sets the ladoos grainy and hard.
Adding the khoya gives the authentic mithai-shop density, but you can skip it for a lighter ladoo.
Bloom the saffron rather than adding it dry so its colour spreads evenly through the pale pak.
variations.servingSuggestion: Present in a Diwali mithai box lined with butter paper, alternating with rows of kaju katli for contrast.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Ole Naral Ladoo
variations.description: A wedding-and-festival favourite from Maharashtra using fresh coconut and jaggery cooked to a soft, sticky mass scented with nutmeg. Slightly coarse and gloriously fragrant, ole naaralache ladoo are made fresh and eaten within a couple of days.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The gul that gives Marathi coconut ladoo its caramel depth

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Keeps the coconut-jaggery mass from sticking and adds a soft sheen

steps: Dry roast the 2 tablespoons poppy seeds in a hot pan for about 90 seconds until they turn fragrant and set them aside for rolling.
Melt the 2 tablespoons Anveshan Ghee in a kadai, add the 3 cups fresh grated coconut and the chopped cashews and stir on low heat for 3 minutes until warmed through.
Add 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 2 tablespoons milk and cook on low, stirring often, for about 10 minutes until the jaggery melts and the mixture thickens into a sticky mass.
Stir in 1 teaspoon cardamom powder and 1/4 teaspoon grated nutmeg, cook for one more minute, then remove from the heat.
Cool for 6 minutes to a workable warmth, then roll 2 tablespoons at a time into 14 ladoos and dust each with the roasted poppy seeds.
Rest for 15 minutes to set; because they use fresh coconut, eat them within two days.
tips: Fresh coconut with jaggery spoils faster than the condensed-milk version, so make only what you will eat in two days.
Cook the jaggery just until the mixture holds; too long and the ladoos become hard and dry.
Nutmeg is the defining Maharashtrian note here, so grate it fresh for the best aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as part of a Marathi festive naivedya thali beside puran poli, dusted with an extra pinch of poppy seeds.

variations.name: Awadhi Malai Coconut Ladoo
variations.description: A soft, milky Lucknawi ladoo where coconut is bound with reduced milk and khoya, then perfumed with rose and kewra. Pale, delicate and lightly sweet, it is the coconut ladoo dressed up for a nawabi dessert table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Enriches the milky base and blooms the delicate rose and kewra

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: A clean, mild sweetness that lets the floral perfumes stay in front

steps: Melt the 2 tablespoons Anveshan Ghee in a kadai, add the 1 cup crumbled khoya and 1/2 cup milk and cook on low heat, stirring, until smooth and thick, about 5 minutes.
Reserve 1/2 cup coconut for coating and add the remaining 2.5 cups desiccated coconut to the pan, cooking on low for 5 minutes until the mixture comes together.
Stir in 1/2 cup Anveshan Khandsari Sugar and cook for about 5 minutes until it melts and the mass thickens and leaves the sides of the pan.
Take off the heat, cool for 3 minutes, then mix in 1 teaspoon cardamom powder, 1/2 teaspoon rose water and 1/2 teaspoon kewra water so the perfume spreads evenly.
Cool for 5 more minutes to a workable warmth, then roll 2 tablespoons at a time into 14 ladoos and coat each in the reserved coconut.
Press a few slivered almonds on top and chill for 25 minutes to set the soft, milky crumb.
tips: Add the rose and kewra off the heat so their fragile aromas are not cooked away.
The fresh khoya makes these perishable; refrigerate and finish within three days.
If the mixture stays too soft to roll, chill it briefly and it will hold its shape.
variations.servingSuggestion: Arrange on a mirrored tray scattered with dried rose petals for an elegant close to an Awadhi dinner.

variations.name: Classic Dry Fruit Ladoo
variations.description: A no-cook-sugar ladoo bound entirely by a sticky date paste and a spoon of honey, packed with four nuts and rolled in coconut. It is the modern healthy mithai of choice — naturally sweet, protein-dense and quick to make for fasting days or lunchboxes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee softens the dates into a paste and stops the ladoos drying out

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: a spoon of honey binds the nut mix without needing any refined sugar

steps: Pit and finely chop the 1.5 cups dates, then warm 1 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee in a pan and cook the dates on low heat for 4 to 5 minutes, mashing, until they melt into a soft, sticky paste.
Meanwhile dry-roast the 0.5 cup almonds, 0.5 cup cashews and 0.25 cup walnuts on low heat for 4 minutes until crisp, then cool and pulse to a coarse rubble.
In the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, toast the 0.25 cup pistachios and 2 tbsp melon seeds for about 1 minute until the pistachios smell fresh and green.

Take the pan off the heat, mix the date paste, nut rubble, pistachios and melon seeds with 1 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp nutmeg, then drizzle in the 1 tbsp Anveshan Honey and knead into a stiff, holdable dough.
Grease your palms with a little ghee and roll 2 tbsp portions into about 14 firm balls, then roll each in the desiccated coconut to coat.
Chill the ladoos for 20 minutes so the date paste sets and they hold their shape.
tips: If the mixture is too sticky to roll, work in a spoon more of the roasted nut rubble; if it crumbles, mash in one or two extra dates.
Use soft, fresh dates — dry, hard ones will not form a paste and the ladoos will not bind.
Stored in the fridge in an airtight box these keep for 2 weeks; bring to room temperature before eating for the best texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Perfect as a Navratri vrat sweet or a post-workout energy bite, served straight from the fridge with a glass of milk.

variations.name: Kashmiri Dry Fruit Ladoo
variations.description: A luxurious Valley ladoo built on dates and dried figs, heavy with walnuts and perfumed with saffron bloomed in ghee. Fennel and dry ginger give it the warming quality Kashmiris prize in winter dry-fruit sweets.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee blooms the saffron and melts the figs and dates together

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Kashmiri saffron bloomed in warm ghee tints and scents the whole ladoo

steps: Finely chop the 1 cup dates and 0.5 cup dried figs, then warm 1 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee and cook them together on low heat for 5 minutes, mashing, until they form one sticky mass.
In a separate small pan warm the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crush the pinch of Anveshan Saffron and stir it in for 30 seconds until the ghee turns golden and fragrant.
Dry-roast the 0.66 cup walnuts, 0.33 cup almonds and 1 tsp fennel on low heat for 4 minutes until crisp, then cool and crush to a coarse rubble.
Take everything off the heat and knead the fruit mass, nut rubble, saffron ghee, 0.5 tsp dry ginger and 1 tsp cardamom into a firm, fragrant dough.
Grease your palms and roll 2 tbsp portions into about 14 balls, then press chopped pistachios onto each for a green speckle.
Rest the ladoos for 20 minutes until the fig and date paste sets firm.
tips: Blooming the saffron in ghee rather than milk keeps these dairy-free and longer-keeping.
Figs add natural stickiness, so if the dough feels wet, add a little more crushed walnut to balance it.
Toast the walnuts until just fragrant to remove any raw bitterness against the sweet figs.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a winter evening with kahwa, the saffron in the ladoo mirroring the saffron in the cup.

variations.name: Kerala Dry Fruit Ladoo
variations.description: A coastal dry-fruit ladoo where roasted coconut and wood-pressed coconut oil wrap the dates and cashews in a tropical fragrance. Toasted in coconut oil rather than ghee alone, it tastes of the Kerala sweet-shop counter.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed coconut oil roasts the coconut and defines the coastal aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoon of ghee to fry the cashews to a Kerala-sweet gold

steps: Warm the 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and fry the 0.5 cup cashews and 0.25 cup raisins on low heat for 2 minutes until the cashews are golden and the raisins swell, then lift them out.
Add the 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil to the pan and roast 0.75 cup of the desiccated coconut for 4 minutes until pale gold, keeping the remaining 0.25 cup aside for coating.
Pit and chop the 1.5 cups dates, add them to the roasted coconut and cook on low for 4 to 5 minutes, mashing, until they form a sticky mass.
Off the heat, mix in the fried cashews and raisins, 2 tbsp toasted sesame, 1 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp dry ginger, kneading into a firm coconut-rich dough.
Roll 2 tbsp portions into about 14 balls and roll each in the reserved desiccated coconut.
Rest for 20 minutes so the coconut and date paste sets before serving.
tips: Roast the coconut only to pale gold; browned too far it turns bitter against the sweet dates.
Coat the ladoos while just warm so the desiccated coconut sticks without any syrup.
Use desiccated rather than fresh coconut so the ladoos keep for two weeks even in humid weather.
variations.servingSuggestion: Offer after a South Indian meal with filter coffee, the coconut and cardamom rounding off the plate.

variations.name: Malwa Dry Fruit Ladoo
variations.description: A hearty plateau ladoo that stretches the dry fruit with roasted peanuts and sesame, sweetened further with a little jaggery in the region's til-gul spirit. Rustic and filling, it is winter energy food from Madhya Pradesh.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee melts the dates and rounds off the assertive peanut flavour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a little jaggery deepens the peanut-and-sesame Malwa flavour

steps: Dry-roast the 0.75 cup peanuts on low heat for 4 minutes until the skins loosen, rub them off and crush the peanuts coarsely with the 0.33 cup almonds.
In the same pan toast the 3 tbsp sesame and 2 tbsp poppy seeds for 2 minutes until they pop and turn golden, then set aside.
Pit and chop the 1 cup dates, warm 1 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee and cook the dates on low for 4 minutes until they form a paste, then stir in the 0.33 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder until it melts.
Off the heat, add the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, the crushed peanuts and almonds, toasted seeds, 1 tsp cardamom and 0.5 tsp dry ginger, kneading into a firm, coarse dough.
Press 2 tbsp portions hard into about 12 sturdy ladoos.
Cool for 20 minutes until they set into a dense, chikki-like bite.
tips: Keep the peanut crush coarse so the ladoo stays chunky and textured rather than smooth.
Melt the jaggery only until liquid; boiling it hard will make the cooled ladoos set too firm.
These sturdy ladoos travel well and keep for three weeks in a sealed tin.
variations.servingSuggestion: Share around Sankranti with hot jaggery tea, the peanut and sesame echoing the season's til-gul treats.

variations.name: Gujarati Dry Fruit Ladoo
variations.description: A Gujarati winter tonic ladoo in the gaund-paak tradition, where dates and nuts are enriched with jaggery, fried edible gum and warming dry ginger. Dense, restorative and mildly medicinal, it is the ladoo made for new mothers and cold mornings.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: plenty of ghee to fry the gum and carry the warming spices

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery is the traditional sweetener of Gujarati winter gaund ladoo

steps: Warm 3 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee on low heat and fry the 3 tbsp gond in batches for about 1 minute each until the pieces puff up and crisp, then crush them coarsely.
In the same ghee lightly roast the 0.33 cup almonds and 0.33 cup cashews for 3 minutes until golden, then crush them coarsely and toast the 0.33 cup grated dry coconut for 1 minute.
Pit and chop the 1 cup dates, add the remaining ghee and cook them on low for 4 minutes into a paste, then stir in the 0.5 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder until it melts smoothly.
Off the heat, combine the date-jaggery mass with the crushed gum, nuts, coconut, 1 tsp dry ginger, 1 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp black pepper into a firm, warming dough.
Grease your palms and press 2 tbsp portions into about 12 dense, round ladoos.
Rest for 25 minutes until the gum-set ladoos firm up completely.
tips: Fry the gond in small batches so each piece puffs crisp; crowded, it stays chewy in the centre.
The dry ginger and pepper are traditional and warming — keep them in for the authentic gaund-ladoo character.
These restorative ladoos keep for a month and are meant to be eaten one a day through winter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve one each cold morning with warm milk, in the Gujarati tradition of winter strength-building sweets.

variations.name: Classic Lemon Rice
variations.description: The everyday South Indian chitranna: cooked rice tossed in a bright turmeric tempering of mustard, dals, peanuts and curry leaves, then lifted with fresh lemon. Cooked in Anveshan wood-pressed sesame oil and finished with ghee, it is tangy, nutty and endlessly comforting.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil is the traditional base for the tempering and gives lemon rice its authentic toasty depth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon of ghee folded in at the end rounds the sharp lemon and enriches the grains.

steps: Spread 3 cups cooked rice on a wide plate to cool and separate the grains with a fork so they stay firm and non-sticky.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil in a wide pan over medium heat and fry 3 tbsp raw peanuts until crisp and golden, about 3 minutes, then scoop them out.
Into the same oil add 1 tsp mustard seeds and, once they pop, add 1 tsp urad dal and 1 tsp chana dal and fry until golden, about 40 seconds.

Add 2 dried red chillies, 2 slit green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 2 sprigs curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and crackle for 20 seconds, then stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric off the heat for 10 seconds.
Add the cooled rice, the fried peanuts and 1 tsp salt and toss gently over low heat for 2 minutes until every grain turns an even pale yellow.
Turn off the heat, squeeze in the juice of 2 lemons, fold in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and toss once so the tang is bright and evenly distributed.
tips: Always add the lemon juice off the heat; cooking it makes the rice turn bitter and dull instead of fresh and zingy.
Cooled, slightly dry rice absorbs the tempering best, so day-old rice or rice spread to cool works far better than piping-hot rice.
Taste and adjust lemon at the very end, as lemons vary widely in sourness from one to the next.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pack it for a lunchbox with a fried papad and a spoon of tangy tomato thokku, or serve with plain curd for a light meal.

variations.name: Karnataka Tamarind-Lemon Rice
variations.description: A Karnataka twist on chitranna, layering a whisper of tamarind under the fresh lemon for a deeper, rounded sourness, plus toasted dry coconut. Cooked in Anveshan wood-pressed groundnut oil with a ghee finish, it is the tangy rice of a Bengaluru tiffin room.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the everyday Karnataka cooking fat and gives the temper a mild nutty base.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee softens the double sourness of tamarind and lemon into a mellow finish.

steps: Spread 3 cups cooked rice to cool and loosen the grains; dissolve 1 tsp tamarind paste in 2 tbsp warm water and keep it ready.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat and fry 3 tbsp peanuts until golden, about 3 minutes, then remove and dry-toast 2 tbsp grated coconut in the pan until pale gold.
In the same oil pop 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 1 tsp urad dal and 1 tsp chana dal and fry to a golden colour, about 40 seconds.
Add 2 slit green chillies, 2 sprigs curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida, crackle 20 seconds, then pour in the tamarind water and 0.5 tsp turmeric and simmer 1 minute until it thickens slightly.
Add the cooled rice, the fried peanuts, toasted coconut and 1 tsp salt and toss gently over low heat for 2 minutes until evenly coated.
Turn off the heat, add the juice of 1 lemon and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and fold through so the tamarind depth and lemon brightness balance.
tips: Simmer the tamarind briefly to cook off its raw edge, but keep the lemon raw and added last for a fresh top note.
Toasting the dry coconut separately stops it burning in the temper and adds a sweet, nutty layer.
Balance is everything here: if the tamarind makes it too sour, a pinch of jaggery rounds it back out.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a dollop of thick curd and crisp sandige (fryums) for the full Karnataka tiffin experience.

variations.name: Andhra Guntur Lemon Rice
variations.description: A fiery Andhra lemon rice charged with smoky Guntur red chilli and extra garlic in the tempering, cooked in Anveshan wood-pressed sesame oil. Sharp, hot and citrusy, it is the bold pulihora-style rice that stands up to a spoon of plain curd.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil grounds the fierce Guntur heat with its toasty, grounding aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A ghee finish takes the raw edge off the chilli while keeping the citrus bright.

steps: Spread 3 cups cooked rice to cool and fork it loose; lightly crush 4 garlic cloves and finely slice 1 small onion.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil over medium heat and fry 3 tbsp peanuts until crisp and golden, about 3 minutes, then remove.

Pop 1 tsp mustard seeds and 0.25 tsp fenugreek seeds in the oil, add 1 tsp urad dal and fry to golden, then add the crushed garlic, sliced onion and 2 dried red chillies and fry 3 minutes until the onion softens and turns golden.
Add 2 sprigs curry leaves, then pull the pan off the heat and stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp Guntur red chilli powder for 15 seconds so they bloom without scorching.
Return to low heat, add the cooled rice, fried peanuts and 1 tsp salt and toss for 2 minutes until deep yellow-red and evenly hot.
Turn off the heat, squeeze in the juice of 2 lemons, fold in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 2 tbsp coriander, tossing once to balance the heat with citrus.
tips: Guntur chilli is fierce, so add it off the heat and start with 0.5 tsp if you are sensitive to spice.
The fried garlic is what sets this apart from a standard lemon rice; keep it in for little bursts of flavour.
A generous spoon of thick, cold curd on the side is the traditional Andhra coolant.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain set curd and a fried appalam, with a wedge of extra lemon for those who like it sharper.

variations.name: Kerala Coconut Lemon Rice
variations.description: A Malabar-style lemon rice enriched with fresh grated coconut and tempered in Anveshan wood-pressed coconut oil for a sweet, mellow roundness against the citrus. Curry leaves and a ghee finish make it a soft, fragrant plate from a Kerala kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil is the defining Kerala fat and echoes the fresh coconut folded through the rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee balances the coconut sweetness and softens the lemon into a gentle tang.

steps: Spread 3 cups cooked rice to cool and fork the grains loose so they stay separate.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil over medium heat and fry 2 tbsp cashews until golden, about 90 seconds, then remove.
Pop 1 tsp mustard seeds in the oil, add 1 tsp urad dal and fry to golden, then add 2 dried red chillies, 2 slit green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger and 2 sprigs curry leaves and crackle 20 seconds.
Off the heat stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric for 10 seconds, then add 0.33 cup grated fresh coconut and warm it through for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the cooled rice, the fried cashews and 1 tsp salt and toss gently over low heat for 2 minutes until pale gold and flecked with coconut.
Turn off the heat, squeeze in the juice of 2 lemons and fold in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee so the coconut, citrus and ghee marry.
tips: Warm the fresh coconut only briefly; overcooking dries it out and loses the sweet, moist contrast to the lemon.
Use fresh or frozen grated coconut rather than desiccated, which will drink up the moisture and turn the rice dry.
A final drizzle of raw coconut oil over the top deepens the unmistakable Kerala aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coconut-onion pachadi and thin banana chips for a light, coastal-style meal.

variations.name: Gujarati Sweet-Sour Lemon Rice
variations.description: A Gujarati take that plays the region's signature sweet-and-sour note, balancing bright lemon with a touch of Anveshan jaggery powder. Tempered in ghee and wood-pressed groundnut oil with peanuts, it is a gentle, crowd-pleasing citrus rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee harmonises the sweet jaggery and sour lemon into a rounded, mellow finish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the classic Gujarati tempering fat and complements the peanuts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A teaspoon of jaggery gives the sweet-sour Gujarati balance without refined sugar.

steps: Spread 3 cups cooked rice to cool and loosen the grains with a fork.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat and fry 3 tbsp peanuts until crisp and golden, about 3 minutes, then remove.
Pop 1 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin in the oil, then add 2 slit green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 2 sprigs curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and crackle for 20 seconds.
Off the heat stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, returning the pan to low heat until the jaggery just melts, about 30 seconds.
Add the cooled rice, fried peanuts and 1 tsp salt and toss gently for 2 minutes until the grains are evenly yellow and glossy.
Turn off the heat, squeeze in the juice of 2 lemons, fold in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 2 tbsp coriander so the sweet, sour and savoury come together.
tips: Melt the jaggery into the warm oil before the rice goes in so it disperses evenly rather than forming sticky lumps.
The jaggery should only round the edges, not sweeten the dish; a single teaspoon is enough for three cups of rice.
This mild, balanced version is especially good for children who find plain lemon rice too sharp.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of cool chaas and a handful of crunchy sev sprinkled over the top just before eating.

variations.name: Classic Moong Dal Halwa
variations.description: The definitive North Indian winter halwa, where soaked yellow moong dal is roasted slowly in ghee for nearly half an hour until it turns grainy, golden and nutty. Enriched with milk and khoya and lightly sweetened with khandsari, it is patient, luxurious comfort food.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the long, low roast of dal in bilona ghee is what gives this halwa its aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined khandsari sweetens the halwa cleanly in place of white sugar

steps: Rinse the 1 cup moong dal and soak it for 3 hours, then drain well and grind to a thick, coarse, slightly grainy paste with just 2 tbsp water.

Heat the 0.75 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadai and add the dal paste, then roast on low-medium heat for 25 to 30 minutes, stirring almost constantly, until it breaks from a sticky lump into loose golden grains and releases the ghee.
Meanwhile warm the 1 cup milk with the 0.5 cup water together until steaming but not boiling.

Pour the hot milk-water into the roasted dal a little at a time, standing back as it splutters, and stir for about 5 minutes until fully absorbed, then mix in the 0.25 cup grated khoya and cook 3 minutes.
Add the 0.75 cup Anveshan Khandsari and stir for 6 to 8 minutes; the halwa will loosen, then thicken and start leaving ghee at the sides of the pan.
Fold in the 1 tsp cardamom, fry the 3 tbsp almonds, 3 tbsp cashews and 2 tbsp raisins in a little ghee until golden, stir most through and garnish, then serve hot.
tips: Grind the dal coarse, never to a smooth batter — the grainy texture is what makes moong dal halwa, not a paste.
The 25-minute roast is the whole dish; stop too early and the halwa will taste raw and beany, so keep going until it smells nutty and the colour deepens.
Add the milk hot, not cold, or the roasted dal will seize into lumps that never smooth out.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot on a cold evening with an extra scatter of slivered almonds, ideally alongside a small glass of warm saffron milk.

variations.name: Kashmiri Moong Dal Halwa
variations.description: A saffron-rich Valley version where the roasted moong dal is steeped in saffron milk and studded with walnuts rather than cashews. Warmed with a whisper of dry ginger, it glows deep gold and tastes of a Kashmiri winter feast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee carries the fat-soluble saffron colour deep into the halwa

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: pale khandsari keeps the sweetness clean so the saffron colour shows

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Kashmiri saffron steeped in warm milk tints the whole halwa a deep gold

steps: Rinse the 1 cup moong dal, soak for 3 hours, drain and grind to a thick, coarse paste with 2 tbsp water.
Steep the 0.5 tsp Anveshan Saffron in the 1.5 cups warm milk for 10 minutes until the milk turns a rich amber.
Heat the 0.75 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadai, add the dal paste and roast on low-medium heat for 25 to 30 minutes, stirring constantly, until it turns golden, grainy and releases the ghee.
Pour the hot saffron milk into the roasted dal in stages, standing back from the splutter, and stir for about 6 minutes until absorbed and the colour runs evenly gold.
Add the 0.75 cup Anveshan Khandsari and 0.25 tsp dry ginger and cook for 6 to 8 minutes until the halwa thickens and leaves ghee at the sides.
Fold in the 1 tsp cardamom, fry the 4 tbsp walnuts and 3 tbsp almonds in a little ghee until fragrant, stir through and serve hot.
tips: Toast the walnuts only until fragrant so their oils turn sweet against the saffron rather than bitter.
Grind the saffron with a pinch of the khandsari before steeping; it disperses far more evenly through the milk.
This halwa reheats beautifully with a splash of warm milk, and the saffron colour deepens overnight.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm after a Kashmiri wazwan, the saffron in the halwa echoing the kahwa poured alongside.

variations.name: Gujarati Moong Dal Halwa
variations.description: A Gujarati take that swaps refined sugar for earthy jaggery, giving the halwa a darker colour and a caramel, almost sheera-like depth. Nutmeg alongside cardamom makes it warmer and more festive, in the region's sweet-loving spirit.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee roasts the dal and balances the strong jaggery flavour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery gives this Gujarati halwa its dark colour and caramel depth

steps: Rinse the 1 cup moong dal, soak for 3 hours, drain and grind to a thick, coarse paste with 2 tbsp water.
Heat the 0.75 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadai and roast the dal paste on low-medium heat for 25 to 30 minutes, stirring constantly, until golden, grainy and releasing the ghee.
Warm the 1 cup milk with the 0.5 cup water, then add it to the roasted dal in stages, standing back from the splutter, and stir for 5 minutes until absorbed, then mix in the 0.33 cup khoya.
Take the pan off direct high heat and stir in the 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder on low heat so it melts without curdling the milk, cooking for 5 to 6 minutes until thick.
Fold in the 1 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp nutmeg and cook 2 minutes more until the halwa turns glossy and leaves ghee at the sides.
Fry the 3 tbsp cashews and 2 tbsp charoli in a little ghee until golden, stir most through and garnish, then serve hot.
tips: Add the jaggery on low heat and after the milk has been absorbed, so the acidity does not split the dairy.
Jaggery darkens the halwa naturally, so do not mistake the deeper colour for burning.
Charoli is the traditional Gujarati garnish here and adds a gentle almond-like crunch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as part of a Gujarati festive thali, the jaggery halwa rounding off a meal of dhokla and shaak.

variations.name: Awadhi Moong Dal Halwa
variations.description: A courtly Lucknawi rendition, pale and delicate with khandsari, perfumed with kewra and mace and finished in silver leaf. Pistachios and chironji make it as elegant as the Awadhi dastarkhwan it belongs to.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: an extra-generous hand of ghee gives this halwa its Awadhi richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: pale khandsari keeps the halwa light so the kewra and mace lead

steps: Rinse the 1 cup moong dal, soak for 3 hours, drain and grind to a thick, coarse paste with 2 tbsp water.
Heat the 0.8 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadai and roast the dal paste on low heat for 28 to 32 minutes, stirring patiently, until pale gold, grainy and glistening with released ghee.
Warm the 1.25 cups milk and add it to the roasted dal in stages, standing back from the splutter, stirring for about 6 minutes until fully absorbed.
Add the 0.75 cup Anveshan Khandsari and 0.25 tsp mace and cook for 6 to 8 minutes until the halwa thickens and leaves ghee at the sides.
Fold in the 1 tsp cardamom and 3 tbsp pistachios, then sprinkle over the 1 tsp kewra water and stir gently so the perfume spreads without cooking off.
Fry the 2 tbsp chironji in a little ghee until golden, scatter over the halwa, lay torn silver leaf on top and serve warm.
tips: Keep the roast on low and stop at pale gold — an Awadhi halwa is meant to look delicate, not deeply browned.
Add the kewra at the very end off strong heat, or its fragrance will simply evaporate.
Apply the silver leaf just before serving with the tip of a dry knife so it does not crumple.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in small silver bowls after an Awadhi biryani, the kewra-scented halwa a refined close to the meal.

variations.name: Kerala Moong Dal Halwa
variations.description: A coastal reimagining closer to a parippu payasam set thick, where the roasted moong dal is simmered in coconut milk and jaggery and finished with coconut-oil-fried cashews. Fragrant with cardamom and dry ginger, it bridges halwa and payasam.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee roasts the dal to a nutty base before the coconut milk goes in

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed coconut oil fries the cashews and adds coastal aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery and coconut are the backbone of a Kerala parippu sweet

steps: Rinse the 1 cup moong dal, soak for 3 hours, drain and grind to a thick, coarse paste with 2 tbsp water.
Heat the 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadai and roast the dal paste on low-medium heat for 25 minutes, stirring constantly, until golden, grainy and releasing the ghee.
Melt the 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with the 0.5 cup water into a syrup, strain out any grit, then stir it into the roasted dal and cook for 4 minutes until absorbed.
Lower the heat and pour in the 1 cup thick coconut milk with the 0.5 tsp dry ginger, stirring gently for 6 to 8 minutes until the halwa thickens without letting the coconut milk boil hard.
Fold in the 1 tsp cardamom and cook 2 minutes more until glossy and leaving a little fat at the sides.
Fry the 4 tbsp cashews and 3 tbsp coconut slivers in the 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil until golden, pour over the halwa and serve warm.
tips: Add the coconut milk on low heat and do not let it come to a rolling boil, or it will split and turn grainy.
Melt and strain the jaggery into a syrup first so any impurities do not end up in the halwa.
For a looser, payasam-like texture, stir in a little extra warm coconut milk just before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm or at room temperature after a Kerala sadya, where its coconut-and-jaggery character sits naturally among the other sweets.

variations.name: Classic Paneer Pulao
variations.description: Soft cubes of paneer lightly browned in bilona ghee fold into fragrant basmati for a protein-rich one-pot meal. Whole spices and a gentle masala keep it homely rather than heavy, letting the paneer stay the star. It is the reliable pulao that turns a simple evening into a satisfying dinner.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee browns the paneer to a soft gold and blooms the whole spices for the rice.

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati rice until clear, soak for 20 minutes and drain, then cut 250 g paneer into 2 cm cubes.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot on medium heat and fry the paneer cubes for 2 minutes, turning until pale gold, then lift them out and reserve.
In the same ghee add 1 tsp cumin, 1 bay leaf, 3 cardamom pods, 4 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon and let them sizzle for 20 seconds.
Add 1 large sliced onion and fry for 6 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add 0.5 tsp turmeric and the drained rice and fold gently for 1 minute until the grains glisten.
Pour in 2.5 cups water and 1 tsp salt, boil once, then cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes.
Scatter the fried paneer over the rice, cover again for 3 minutes off the heat, then fluff and finish with 2 tbsp coriander leaves.
tips: Fry the paneer only until pale gold; over-frying makes it rubbery and dry inside the pulao.
Add the paneer near the end so it stays soft and does not break apart while the rice steams.
If your paneer is firm, soak the fried cubes in warm water for 5 minutes before adding to keep them tender.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cool mint raita and a squeeze of lemon, plus a spoon of extra Anveshan Ghee melted over the paneer for richness.

variations.name: Punjabi Paneer Pulao
variations.description: The Punjabi version is unapologetically rich, with paneer and rice finished in butter and warmed by garam masala and kasuri methi. The paneer soaks up a buttery, herby depth that feels straight from a dhaba kitchen. It is hearty comfort food meant to be eaten hot and generous.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee fries the paneer and carries the kasuri methi deeper than butter can alone.

steps: Soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, drain, and cut 250 g paneer into 2 cm cubes.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot on medium heat and fry the paneer for 2 minutes until light golden, then remove and reserve.
In the same ghee crackle 1 tsp cumin for 15 seconds, add 1 large sliced onion and fry for 6 minutes until deep gold, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute.
Lower the heat and add 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi, stirring for 20 seconds.
Add the drained rice and 0.5 tsp garam masala and fold for 1 minute until evenly coated.
Pour in 2.5 cups water and 1 tsp salt, boil once, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes.
Scatter the fried paneer and dot with 1 tbsp white butter, cover off the heat for 3 minutes, then fluff and top with 2 tbsp coriander leaves.
tips: Crush the kasuri methi between your palms to release its full aroma into the rich base.
Let the butter melt over the paneer from residual heat so it glazes rather than greases the rice.
For an even more dhaba flavour, stir a tablespoon of tomato puree in with the ginger-garlic paste.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of thick dahi, a raw onion salad dressed in lemon and a spoon of mixed pickle for a full Punjabi plate.

variations.name: Bengali Paneer Pulao
variations.description: Bengal treats paneer gently, cooking it in pungent Anveshan wood-pressed mustard oil with a pinch of sugar for the beloved sweet-savoury balance. Whole garam and a soft dum give the paneer a delicate, aromatic character close to the festive mishti pulao. It is refined and fragrant rather than fiery.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil, smoked first, lends the paneer its characteristic Bengali pungency.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of bilona ghee balances the sharp mustard oil for the sweet-savoury Bengali note.

steps: Soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, drain, and cut 250 g paneer into 2 cm cubes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pot until it just smokes, then lower the flame and fry the paneer for 2 minutes until pale gold, and remove.
To the same oil add 2 bay leaves, 4 cardamom pods, 4 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon and let them puff for 20 seconds.
Add 1 sliced medium onion and fry for 4 minutes until soft, then stir in 1 tsp sugar and 0.5 tsp turmeric until the sugar dissolves.
Add the drained rice and fold gently for 1 minute, then pour in 2.5 cups water and 1 tsp salt and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on very low heat for 11 minutes, then scatter the fried paneer over the top and steam covered for 3 more minutes.
Rest 3 minutes off the heat, drizzle 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then fluff gently and serve.
tips: Smoke the mustard oil before frying the paneer, or its raw sharpness will dominate the delicate rice.
Keep the sugar subtle so the pulao stays balanced and never crosses into dessert territory.
Add the paneer late and steam it briefly so it stays pillowy soft against the aromatic grains.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a light cholar dal or aloo dum and a scatter of fried cashews for a Bengali festive touch.

variations.name: Kashmiri Paneer Pulao
variations.description: A regal pulao where paneer meets saffron, dry fruit and warm Kashmiri whole spice. Strands of Anveshan Kashmiri saffron steeped in milk stain the rice gold, while fennel and dry ginger lend the cool, aromatic signature of the valley. Fried nuts and soft paneer make it a celebration on a plate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Generous bilona ghee fries the paneer and nuts and carries the saffron through the rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Kashmiri saffron steeped in warm milk gives the pulao its golden colour and floral aroma.

steps: Soak a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside to release its colour.
Soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, drain, and cut 250 g paneer into 2 cm cubes.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot on medium heat, fry 10 cashews and 10 almonds for 2 minutes until golden and reserve, then fry the paneer for 2 minutes and reserve.
In the same ghee crackle 4 cardamom pods and 4 cloves for 20 seconds, then add 0.5 tsp fennel powder and 0.25 tsp dry ginger powder and stir for 10 seconds.
Add the drained rice and fold for 1 minute, then pour in 2.5 cups water and 1 tsp salt and bring to a boil.
Stir in the saffron milk, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 11 minutes, then scatter the paneer on top and steam 3 more minutes.
Rest 3 minutes, then fluff gently and crown with the fried cashews and almonds.
tips: Fennel and dry ginger are the quiet Kashmiri signatures, so do not swap them for regular garam masala.
Steep the saffron in warm milk, never boiling, to draw colour without dulling the aroma.
Fry the paneer and nuts on gentle heat, as ghee browns them quickly and they can turn bitter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a platter with a bowl of yogurt raita studded with pomegranate seeds, perfect for a celebratory spread.

variations.name: Kerala Paneer Pulao
variations.description: Kerala reinvents paneer pulao with fresh coconut, curry leaves and the aroma of Anveshan wood-pressed coconut oil. Grated coconut cooked into the rice keeps it moist and faintly sweet, while a mustard-and-curry-leaf temper anchors it to the coast. Soft paneer against the fragrant coconut rice makes for a mellow southern comfort.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed coconut oil gives the temper and paneer an authentic Kerala fragrance.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon of bilona ghee at the finish adds richness that balances the light coconut.

steps: Soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, drain, and cut 250 g paneer into 2 cm cubes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pot on medium heat and fry the paneer for 2 minutes until pale gold, then remove and reserve.
To the same oil add 1 tsp mustard seeds and wait for them to splutter, then add 12 curry leaves, 2 slit green chillies and 1 inch julienned ginger and fry for 20 seconds.
Add 1 sliced medium onion and cook for 4 minutes until soft, then stir in 0.5 cup grated coconut and 0.5 tsp turmeric and saute for 3 minutes until the coconut is light gold.
Add the drained rice and fold for 1 minute, then pour in 2.5 cups water and 1 tsp salt and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on low for 11 minutes, then scatter the paneer over the rice and steam covered for 3 more minutes.
Rest 3 minutes, drizzle 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then fluff gently and serve hot.
tips: Toast the coconut only to light gold; taking it darker turns the whole pulao bitter.
If using desiccated coconut, soak it in 2 tbsp warm water first so it does not dry out the rice.
Slit the green chillies rather than chopping so heat lovers can eat them and others can set them aside.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling cucumber pachadi and crisp papadam, finished with a light dusting of fresh coconut.

variations.name: Classic Rava Kesari
variations.description: The glossy, saffron-golden semolina sweet that appears at every South Indian celebration and temple prasad counter, where roasted rava swells in sweetened water and sets into a soft, ghee-laden mass. Fragrant with saffron and cardamom and studded with fried cashews and raisins, it is quick, forgiving and endlessly comforting.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the rava to a nutty aroma and gives the kesari its glistening, non-sticky finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm water to give the classic golden colour and honeyed fragrance

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined sugar swapped for white sugar, dissolving into a clean glossy sweetness

steps: Steep 0.5 tsp Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp of warm water and set aside to bloom.
Heat 2 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai and fry 15 cashews and 2 tbsp raisins until golden, then remove and reserve them.
In the same ghee, roast 1 cup fine semolina on low for 6 minutes until it smells nutty and turns a shade darker without browning.
In a separate pan bring 2.5 cups water to a rolling boil with the bloomed saffron and its soaking water.
Lower the flame under the rava and pour in the boiling saffron water in a steady stream while stirring hard to keep it lump-free, then cook 4 minutes until the water is absorbed.
Add 1.25 cups Anveshan Khandsari with 0.5 tsp cardamom; the mixture will loosen, so keep stirring 4 minutes until it thickens again.
Drizzle in the remaining ghee, fold in most of the fried cashews and raisins, and cook 2 minutes until glossy and leaving the sides; garnish with the rest and serve warm.
tips: Always pour boiling water into the roasted rava, never cold, or the kesari turns lumpy.
Keep stirring continuously as you add the water to prevent any raw semolina pockets.
If it stiffens on cooling, sprinkle a little hot water and a spoon of ghee, then reheat gently.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as prasad on a banana leaf, or pair a scoop with hot upma for the classic Tamil chow-chow bath breakfast.

variations.name: Kerala Rava Kesari
variations.description: Kerala's version enriches the semolina sweet with coconut, roasting the rava in coconut oil and folding in coconut milk for a fragrant, tropical richness. Fried coconut slivers replace some of the nuts, giving a chewy sweetness that sets it apart from the classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the wood-pressed Kerala fat that roasts the rava and layers in a warm coconut aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined sugar that sweetens cleanly and lets the coconut flavour shine

steps: Heat 2 tbsp of the Anveshan Coconut Oil and fry 0.33 cup coconut slivers, 12 cashews and 2 tbsp raisins until golden, then set them aside.
In the same oil, roast 1 cup fine semolina on low for 6 minutes until aromatic and lightly toasted.
Bring 1.5 cups thin coconut milk and 1 cup water to a gentle boil in a separate pan.
Lower the flame under the rava and pour in the hot coconut liquid gradually while stirring vigorously, then cook 4 minutes until absorbed.
Stir in 1.25 cups Anveshan Khandsari with 0.5 tsp cardamom and cook 4 minutes as it loosens and then thickens.
Drizzle in the remaining coconut oil, fold in most of the fried coconut and nuts, and cook 2 minutes until glossy.
Garnish with the reserved coconut slivers and serve warm.
tips: Use thin, not thick, coconut milk so it does not split during the vigorous cooking.
Fry the coconut slivers just to pale gold, as they darken fast and can turn bitter.
Watch the flame after adding coconut milk, keeping it gentle to protect the delicate dairy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm at a Kerala sadya as part of the sweet course, alongside a small cup of payasam.

variations.name: Gujarati Rava Kesari
variations.description: Gujarat sweetens its rava sheera with jaggery instead of sugar, giving a caramel-brown colour and mellow molasses depth. Enriched with a splash of milk and scented with nutmeg, it is the sheera offered as prasad on festival mornings.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the rava richly and keeps the jaggery from turning sticky in the sheera

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the Gujarati sweetener giving the sheera its bronze colour and molasses warmth

steps: Dissolve 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 1 cup warm water, strain out any grit, and keep the syrup ready.
Heat 2 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee and fry 12 slivered almonds and 2 tbsp charoli seeds until golden, then reserve them.
In the same ghee, roast 1 cup fine semolina on low for 6 minutes until it smells nutty.
Bring 1.5 cups full-fat milk to a gentle boil, lower the flame under the rava, and pour in the hot milk while stirring hard, cooking 4 minutes until absorbed.
Reduce the heat fully and pour in the strained jaggery syrup with 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp nutmeg, stirring 4 minutes until it thickens.
Drizzle in the remaining ghee, fold in most of the fried almonds and charoli, and cook 2 minutes until glossy.
Garnish with the reserved nuts and serve warm.
tips: Add the jaggery syrup on the lowest flame and after the milk is absorbed so the dairy does not split.
Strain the jaggery syrup to remove impurities for a smooth, clean sheera.
A pinch of nutmeg is the classic Gujarati touch that rounds out the jaggery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as prasad in leaf bowls during Satyanarayan puja, or with a wedge of Gujarati fried puri.

variations.name: Malwa Rava Kesari
variations.description: The Malwa kitchen folds roasted peanuts into its rava kesari, giving a nutty crunch and groundnut warmth uncommon in the southern classic. Sweetened with jaggery and finished with crushed peanuts, it is a rustic, hearty take on the semolina sweet.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the rava and the peanuts so their toasted aromas blend into the kesari

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the Malwa sweetener whose caramel depth suits the earthy roasted peanuts

steps: Dissolve 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 1 cup of the water, strain, and keep the syrup aside.
Coarsely crush 0.5 cup roasted peanuts and keep 2 tbsp aside for garnish.
Heat 2 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee and fry 10 slivered almonds and 3 tbsp dry coconut slivers until golden, then reserve.
In the same ghee, roast 1 cup fine semolina on low for 6 minutes, then stir in the crushed peanuts and roast 2 minutes more.
Bring the remaining 1.5 cups water to a boil, lower the flame under the rava, and pour it in while stirring hard, cooking 4 minutes until absorbed.
Reduce the heat and add the strained jaggery syrup with 0.5 tsp cardamom, stirring 4 minutes until thick and glossy.
Drizzle in the remaining ghee, fold in the fried nuts, and serve warm topped with the reserved crushed peanuts.
tips: Skin the roasted peanuts and crush them coarse to keep the signature crunch.
Add jaggery syrup on low heat so it blends smoothly without seizing.
Roast the peanuts with the rava briefly to marry their flavours before the liquid goes in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with masala chai as a filling tea-time sweet, or press into a tray and cut into rustic squares.

variations.name: Awadhi Rava Kesari
variations.description: Lucknow refines the semolina sweet with kewra and rosewater, its saffron rava perfumed like a nawabi dessert and enriched with a little khoya. Delicate and aromatic, it trades rustic heft for perfumed elegance and a shimmer of silver leaf.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the rava and carries the kewra and rose perfume through the sweet

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined sugar chosen so the delicate kewra and rose aromas remain forward

steps: Heat 2 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee and fry 12 slivered pistachios until pale gold, then set them aside.
In the same ghee, roast 1 cup fine semolina on low for 6 minutes until nutty and lightly toasted.
Bring 2.5 cups water to a rolling boil, lower the flame under the rava, and pour it in while stirring hard, cooking 4 minutes until absorbed.
Crumble in 0.33 cup khoya and stir 2 minutes until it melts into the rava.
Add 1.25 cups Anveshan Khandsari with 0.5 tsp cardamom and cook 4 minutes until the mixture thickens and turns glossy.
Drizzle in the remaining ghee, then switch off the flame and stir in 1 tsp kewra water and 1 tsp rosewater.
Fold in most of the pistachios, smooth into a dish, lay silver leaf on top, and serve warm.
tips: Add kewra and rosewater off the heat so their perfume is not cooked away.
Fresh khoya melts best; grate firm mawa before adding it to the rava.
Keep the kesari a touch softer here to match its delicate, refined character.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in small silver bowls with a scatter of rose petals to close a nawabi meal on a fragrant note.

variations.name: Classic Tahri
variations.description: The homely Uttar Pradesh one-pot tahri, a turmeric-golden rice studded with potatoes and seasonal vegetables, tempered generously with cumin in ghee. Comforting and lightly spiced, it is the everyday khichdi-adjacent meal of North Indian kitchens.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the base fat that blooms the cumin and gives tahri its homely richness

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati, soak for 20 minutes and drain, and dice 2 potatoes into bite-sized cubes.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and crackle 1.5 tsp cumin, 2 bay leaves, 3 cardamom pods and 3 cloves for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 sliced large onion and 2 slit green chillies and fry for 6 minutes until the onion turns golden.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, the potato cubes and 1.5 cups mixed vegetables, and saute 4 minutes so the edges catch a little colour.
Add 0.75 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1.5 tsp salt, and stir for a minute until the vegetables are well coated.
Add the drained rice, toast gently for 2 minutes, then pour in 2.5 cups hot water and bring to a rolling boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 14 minutes until the water is absorbed and the potatoes are tender, then rest 5 minutes and fluff.
tips: Soak the rice so the grains cook evenly with the vegetables and stay separate.
Cut the potatoes to match the rice cooking time so they turn tender at the same moment.
Rest the tahri off the heat before opening the lid so the steam finishes the grains.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a bowl of cool boondi raita, a spoon of mango pickle and a crisp papad.

variations.name: Awadhi Tahri
variations.description: A refined Lucknawi tahri cooked on dum and perfumed with kewra, mace and saffron, in the courtly style of Awadhi kitchens. Delicate and aromatic, it turns the humble vegetable rice into something fit for a dawat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the Awadhi dum fat that carries kewra and mace gently into the rice

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati, soak 20 minutes and drain, and warm 3 tbsp milk with a crushed blade of mace to set aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and sizzle 4 cardamom pods and 1 inch cinnamon for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 2 diced potatoes and 1 cup mixed vegetables and saute for 5 minutes until lightly golden.
Lower the heat, whisk in 0.5 cup curd with 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1.5 tsp salt, and cook 3 minutes until the masala thickens.
Add the drained rice, toast 2 minutes, then pour in 2.5 cups hot water and bring to a boil until most of it is absorbed.
Drizzle over 0.5 tsp kewra water and the mace milk, scatter half the fried onions, then seal the lid with dough and cook on the lowest dum for 14 minutes.
Rest 5 minutes, fluff gently, and finish with the remaining birista before serving.
tips: Add the curd off the boil and stir steadily so it blends in without splitting.
A dough seal keeps the kewra and mace steam trapped for the true dum aroma.
Fry the onions to a deep even gold for the subtle sweetness Awadhi rice depends on.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a mint-coriander raita and a sharp onion-lachcha salad, with lime wedges on the side.

variations.name: Bengali Tahri
variations.description: A Bengali-style vegetable tahri tempered in pungent mustard oil with panch phoron and a hint of jaggery. Sharp, warm and gently sweet, it swaps the northern cumin base for the unmistakable flavours of a Bengal kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked first, it gives the tahri its distinct Bengali pungency

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the gentle sweet balance Bengal folds into its vegetable rice

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups gobindobhog gently and soak 15 minutes, then drain, and dice 2 potatoes into cubes.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, lower the flame, and shallow-fry the potato cubes and 1 cup cauliflower for 5 minutes until golden at the edges, then remove.
In the same oil temper 1 tsp panch phoron, 2 bay leaves and 2 dried chillies for 20 seconds until the seeds pop.
Add 1 tbsp ginger paste, 0.75 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp cumin powder, and stir for a minute until fragrant.
Return the fried vegetables with 0.5 cup peas, the drained rice, 1.5 tsp salt and 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, and toss for 2 minutes.
Pour in 2.5 cups hot water, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on the lowest heat for 13 minutes until the water is absorbed.
Rest 5 minutes off the heat, then fluff the fragrant grains gently before serving.
tips: Frying the potatoes and cauliflower first in mustard oil deepens their flavour and keeps them intact.
Gobindobhog is delicate, so handle it lightly and avoid over-stirring once the water is in.
The jaggery is a Bengali rounding note, so keep it subtle rather than sweet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a plain tomato-date chutney and fried papad, or a bowl of cooling curd on the side.

variations.name: Hyderabadi Tahri
variations.description: A saffron-scented Hyderabadi vegetable tahri layered with mint, fried onions and a spiced curd marinade, cooked on dum. Rich and aromatic, it borrows the biryani kitchen's technique for a fragrant one-pot rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the dum fat that seals in the saffron and mint aromas

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk to give the tahri its golden streaks and perfume

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati, soak 20 minutes and drain, and steep a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk.
Marinate 2 diced potatoes and 1.5 cups mixed vegetables in 0.5 cup curd with 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 1 tsp garam masala and 1 tsp salt for 10 minutes.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and fry the marinated vegetables with 3 slit green chillies for 6 minutes until the masala coats and thickens.
Add the drained rice and 0.5 tsp salt, toss for 2 minutes, then pour in 2.5 cups hot water and bring to a boil.
When most of the water is absorbed, scatter over 0.25 cup mint, half the fried onions and the saffron milk.
Seal the lid with dough and cook on the lowest dum heat for 14 minutes so the aromas steam through the rice.
Rest 5 minutes, fluff gently, and finish with the remaining birista before serving.
tips: Marinating the vegetables in spiced curd first gives the tahri its layered biryani-like depth.
Drizzle the saffron milk over the top so it streaks the rice in gold rather than dyeing it evenly.
Keep the dum heat as low as possible, using a tawa under the pot if needed, to avoid catching.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a mirchi ka salan or a simple raita and a squeeze of lime for the full Hyderabadi table.

variations.name: Rajasthani Tahri
variations.description: A rustic Rajasthani tahri fired up with whole dried red chillies and a robust dry-spice temper, made without much onion in the desert style. Bold, smoky and warming, it leans on pantry spices rather than fresh vegetables for its punch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the desert-kitchen fat that fries the whole red chillies for a smoky base

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati, soak 20 minutes and drain, and cut 2 potatoes into thick cubes.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and fry 4 whole Mathania chillies for 20 seconds until they darken and smell smoky, then add 1.5 tsp cumin, 3 cloves and 2 bay leaves.
Add 0.5 tsp asafoetida and the potato cubes and saute for 4 minutes until the potatoes take on a little colour.
Stir in 2 tsp coriander powder, 0.75 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp salt with a splash of water, and cook 2 minutes into a dry masala.
Add the drained rice and 0.75 cup peas, toss gently for 2 minutes so the grains take on the spice colour.
Pour in 2.5 cups hot water, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on the lowest heat for 14 minutes.
Rest 5 minutes off the heat, then fluff the smoky, golden rice before serving.
tips: Mathania chillies give deep red colour with moderate heat, so use Kashmiri chilli if you cannot find them.
The generous asafoetida stands in for the missing onion and garlic in the desert style.
Fry the whole chillies only briefly, as they turn acrid if they blacken fully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of plain curd, a dollop of ghee and Rajasthani garlic chutney on the side.

variations.name: Classic Til Ladoo
variations.description: The winter and Makar Sankranti staple: nutty sesame seeds roasted till they pop, then bound in molten jaggery scented with cardamom. Warming, crunchy and just sweet enough, til ladoo are the sweet that traditionally carries the message let us be sweet to one another.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Melted to the soft-ball stage; it is the binder and the soul of til ladoo

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Melts with the jaggery and greases the palms for shaping the hot mixture

steps: Dry roast the 1.5 cups white sesame seeds in a kadai on low heat, stirring constantly, until they turn light golden and start popping, about 5 minutes, then transfer to a plate.

In the same pan melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 3 tablespoons water and 1 tablespoon of the Anveshan Ghee on low heat, stirring, until it reaches the soft-ball stage, when a drop set in cold water forms a firm pliable ball, about 6 minutes.
Quickly stir the roasted sesame, 2 tablespoons chopped peanuts and 1 teaspoon cardamom powder into the molten jaggery until evenly coated.
Take the pan off the heat and let it cool for just 2 minutes until warm enough to touch but still soft.
Grease your palms with the remaining ghee and roll 1.5 tablespoons at a time into 16 firm balls, working fast before the jaggery sets.
Rest the ladoos on a greased plate for 15 minutes until they harden completely.
tips: The soft-ball stage is make-or-break: undercook and the ladoos will not bind, overcook and they turn into brittle chikki.
Shape the ladoos while the mixture is warm; once it cools it becomes too hard to roll.
Grease your palms well or dip your fingers in cold water between rolls to handle the hot jaggery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Share a boxful on Makar Sankranti with the customary words til-gul ghya, god god bola, alongside cups of masala chai.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Tilgul
variations.description: Tilgul is the tiny, dry Maharashtrian sesame ladoo exchanged on Makar Sankranti, made with roasted sesame, crushed roasted peanuts and grated dry coconut in jaggery. Small enough to pop whole, it is the definitive Sankranti sweet of the Deccan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Cooked to soft-ball stage to bind the classic Sankranti tilgul

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Melts with the jaggery and eases the shaping of these tiny balls

steps: Dry roast the 1 cup sesame seeds on low heat until golden and popping, about 5 minutes, then roast the 1/2 cup desiccated coconut for 2 minutes until light gold and set both aside.
Coarsely crush the 1/2 cup roasted peanuts, then combine them with the sesame, coconut, 1 teaspoon cardamom powder and 1/4 teaspoon grated nutmeg in a bowl.
Melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 3 tablespoons water and 1 tablespoon Anveshan Ghee on low heat until it reaches the soft-ball stage, about 6 minutes.
Tip the sesame mixture into the molten jaggery and stir quickly until everything is evenly coated, then take off the heat.
Cool for 2 minutes, grease your palms with the remaining ghee and roll 1 tablespoon at a time into 20 small, firm tilgul.
Set them on a greased plate for 15 minutes until hard and dry.
tips: Keep these ladoos small and firm; tilgul are meant to be bite-sized and dry, not large and soft.
Crush the peanuts fine so the little balls hold together neatly.
Stored dry, tilgul last for two to three weeks, perfect for making a big Sankranti batch ahead.
variations.servingSuggestion: Present in small paper boxes to give away to neighbours and friends on Sankranti morning, the Maharashtrian custom.

variations.name: Gujarati Til Sankdi Ladoo
variations.description: Gujarat makes its til ladoo softer and lighter by folding in a little roasted gram flour and a hint of ghee, giving a melt-in-mouth crumb rather than a hard crunch. Cardamom and a touch of dry ginger warm it for the Uttarayan kite festival.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Cooked to soft-ball stage to bind the sesame and besan crumb

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasts the besan and softens the ladoo to a Gujarati melt-in-mouth texture

steps: Dry roast the 1.5 cups sesame seeds on low heat until golden and popping, about 5 minutes, and set aside.
Melt 2 tablespoons of the Anveshan Ghee in the pan and roast the 1/4 cup besan on low heat for about 5 minutes until it darkens and smells cooked, then mix it with the sesame and chopped almonds.
In the same pan melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 3 tablespoons water on low heat until it reaches the soft-ball stage, about 6 minutes.
Stir the sesame-besan mixture, 1 teaspoon cardamom powder and 1/2 teaspoon dry ginger powder into the molten jaggery until evenly combined, then take off the heat.
Cool for 2 minutes, grease your palms with the remaining ghee and roll 2 tablespoons at a time into 16 ladoos while warm.
Rest for 15 minutes until set; the besan keeps them softer than a plain til ladoo.
tips: Roast the besan until its raw smell is gone, or the whole batch tastes floury.
The dry ginger is a warming Gujarati winter touch that also aids digestion of the sesame.
These stay soft for about a week in an airtight jar, unlike the harder plain version.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on the terrace during the Uttarayan kite festival with hot masala chai and chikki for a classic Gujarati winter spread.

variations.name: Rajasthani Til Ladoo with Dry Fruits
variations.description: The desert version enriches the sesame with chopped almonds, cashews and melon seeds for an opulent, long-keeping winter ladoo. A little extra ghee and jaggery make it richer than the everyday til ladoo, fit for Marwari winter feasts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Cooked to soft-ball stage to hold the heavy dry-fruit load

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A generous Marwari pour keeps these ladoos rich and moist for weeks

steps: Dry roast the 1.5 cups sesame seeds on low heat until golden and popping, about 5 minutes, and set aside.
Melt 1 tablespoon of the Anveshan Ghee and toast the chopped almonds, cashews and 3 tablespoons melon seeds for 2 minutes until fragrant, then mix with the sesame.
In the same pan melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 3 tablespoons water and 1 tablespoon ghee on low heat to the soft-ball stage, about 6 minutes.
Stir the sesame and dry-fruit mixture and 1 teaspoon cardamom powder into the molten jaggery until well coated, then remove from the heat.
Cool for 2 minutes, grease your palms with the remaining ghee and roll 2 tablespoons at a time into 16 generous ladoos.
Rest on a greased plate for 15 minutes until firm.
tips: Chop the dry fruits small so the ladoos bind without falling apart at the crunchy bits.
The extra ghee is deliberate; it keeps these desert ladoos soft and edible for up to three weeks.
For a festive finish, press a slivered almond on top of each ladoo before it sets.
variations.servingSuggestion: Offer as part of a Marwari winter sweet box beside gajak, with a glass of warm badam milk.

variations.name: Malwi Til-Peanut Ladoo
variations.description: Central India pairs sesame with a generous amount of roasted peanuts and a base of groundnut oil, creating a rustic, protein-packed winter ladoo. Coarser and crunchier than a plain til ladoo, it is Malwa comfort food for the cold months.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Cooked to soft-ball stage to bind the sesame and peanut crunch

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The Malwa cooking fat that reinforces the roasted peanut flavour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rounds the groundnut oil and greases the palms for shaping

steps: Dry roast the 1 cup raw peanuts for about 6 minutes until the skins blister, rub them off, cool and crush coarsely.
Dry roast the 1 cup sesame seeds on low heat until golden and popping, about 5 minutes, then mix with the crushed peanuts and 1 teaspoon cardamom powder.
Melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 3 tablespoons water, the 1 tablespoon Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil and 1 tablespoon Anveshan Ghee on low heat to the soft-ball stage, about 6 minutes.
Stir the sesame-peanut mixture into the molten jaggery until evenly coated, then take the pan off the heat.
Cool for 2 minutes until warm, grease your palms and roll 2 tablespoons at a time into 16 sturdy ladoos.
Rest for 15 minutes until firm and crunchy.
tips: Keep the peanuts coarse for a satisfying crunch that defines this Malwi version.
Roll quickly while warm; the peanut-heavy mix stiffens fast as it cools.
These hardy ladoos keep for two weeks and make an excellent winter energy snack.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a mid-morning winter snack with jaggery tea, the way farming families across Malwa fuel a cold day.

variations.name: Classic Tomato Rice
variations.description: A fragrant one-pot tomato rice where basmati soaks up a tangy, spiced tomato-onion masala cooked in ghee. Comforting and lunchbox-friendly, it strikes the everyday balance of tart tomato, gentle warmth and fluffy, separate grains.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee gives the tomato masala a rich, rounded base and keeps the grains glossy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A teaspoon of jaggery rounds off the tomatoes' acidity the way a pinch of sugar traditionally would.

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati rice until the water runs clear and soak it for 20 minutes, then drain in a colander.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin, 1 bay leaf and 1 inch cinnamon and let them sizzle for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add 2 finely sliced onions and 2 slit green chillies and sauté for 6 minutes until the onions turn soft and golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute.
Add 4 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1.25 tsp salt, and cook for 8 minutes until the tomatoes collapse into a thick, oil-glistening masala.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder to balance the tartness, then fold in the drained rice and toast it gently for 2 minutes so each grain is coated.
Pour in 1.75 cups hot water, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes; rest off the heat for 5 minutes, fluff with a fork and garnish with 3 tbsp coriander.
tips: Toasting the drained rice in the masala before adding water is the secret to separate, non-mushy grains.
Use ripe, red tomatoes for natural sweetness; pale winter tomatoes need a little extra jaggery to taste right.
Let the rice rest covered for five minutes after cooking so the steam finishes the grains evenly before you fluff.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a bowl of cooling boondi raita and a crisp papad, or pack it with a boiled egg for lunch.

variations.name: Tamil Nadu Thakkali Sadam
variations.description: The classic Tamil thakkali sadam, where a curry-leaf-heavy tempering and a freshly ground spice paste give the tomato rice its distinctive South Indian aroma. Cooked in sesame oil and finished with ghee, it is tangy, nutty and deeply savoury.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed sesame oil is the traditional Tamil cooking fat, lending a nutty depth to the tomato base.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of ghee rounds the tang and adds aroma to the thakkali sadam.

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups rice for 20 minutes, then drain; separately grind 3 dried red chillies, 1 tsp fennel and 2 tbsp coconut with a splash of water into a coarse paste.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pot over medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 1 tsp urad dal, 1 tsp chana dal and 20 curry leaves and fry until the dals turn golden.
Add 1 sliced onion and sauté for 5 minutes until soft, then stir in the ground spice paste and fry for 2 minutes until the raw smell disappears.
Add 5 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp sambar powder and 1.25 tsp salt, and cook for 10 minutes until the mixture thickens into a glossy masala.
Fold in the drained rice and toast for 2 minutes, then pour in 1.75 cups hot water and bring to a rolling boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes, rest 5 minutes off the heat, then drizzle 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the top and fluff gently.
tips: Grinding the coconut-fennel paste fresh is what separates thakkali sadam from an ordinary tomato rice, so do not skip it.
Sesame oil can taste bitter if smoked, so heat it only until it shimmers before tempering.
This rice tastes even better after an hour as the sambar-powder flavours deepen, making it ideal for tiffins.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with crisp appalam and a spoon of thick, set curd on the side to balance the tang.

variations.name: Andhra Guntur Tomato Rice
variations.description: Andhra fires up tomato rice with pounded Guntur red chillies and garlic, cooked down in sesame oil to a searing, tangy masala. Bold and unapologetically hot, it is the kind of tomato rice that needs a bowl of curd to keep pace.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Sesame oil stands up to the fierce Guntur chilli and gives the Andhra masala its authentic depth.

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups rice for 20 minutes, then drain; meanwhile pound 5 Guntur chillies with 6 garlic cloves into a coarse fiery paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pot over medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard, 1 tsp cumin and 1 tsp urad dal, then add 15 curry leaves and fry until crisp.
Add 1 sliced onion and sauté for 5 minutes until golden, then stir in the Guntur-garlic paste and fry for 2 minutes until the raw pungency softens.
Add 5 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt, and cook for 10 minutes until the masala turns thick and deep red with oil surfacing.
Fold in the drained rice, toast for 2 minutes, then pour in 1.75 cups hot water and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes, rest 5 minutes, then fluff and garnish with 3 tbsp coriander.
tips: Pound the chillies and garlic rather than blend them; the coarse texture gives bursts of heat typical of Andhra cooking.
For serious heat lovers, keep the Guntur seeds in; for a smokier, milder version, shake them out first.
A cooling spoon of thick curd stirred in at the table tames the fire without dulling the flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a generous scoop of plain curd and a fried papad to balance the Guntur heat.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Goda Tomato Bhaat
variations.description: Maharashtra stirs its aromatic goda masala into tomato rice, adding dark, sweet-woody notes and a scatter of peanuts for crunch. Cooked in ghee with a hint of jaggery, it carries the distinctive sweet-spicy balance of Maharashtrian masale bhaat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee blooms the goda masala and toasts the peanuts for this western-style tomato bhaat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery underlines the sweet-woody profile that goda masala dishes are known for.

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati for 20 minutes, then drain thoroughly.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot over medium heat and fry 3 tbsp peanuts for 2 minutes until crunchy, then remove and set aside.
