In the same ghee splutter 1 tsp mustard and 0.5 tsp cumin, add 12 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida, then sauté 1 sliced onion for 5 minutes until golden.

Add 4 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt, and cook for 8 minutes until pulpy, then stir in 1.5 tsp goda masala and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and fry for 1 minute.
Fold in the drained rice and the fried peanuts, toast for 2 minutes, then pour in 1.75 cups hot water and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes, rest 5 minutes, then fluff and garnish with 3 tbsp coriander.
tips: Add the goda masala after the tomatoes have cooked down so its delicate flowers and coconut do not scorch.
Reserve the fried peanuts and stir them in with the rice so they keep some crunch rather than softening in the masala.
Goda masala brands vary in intensity, so taste and adjust rather than adding the full amount blindly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling koshimbir salad and a spoon of thick curd for a classic Maharashtrian plate.

variations.name: Bengali Tomato Bhaat
variations.description: A Bengali tomato rice tempered in pungent Anveshan Mustard Oil with panch phoron, the five-spice blend that defines the region's cooking. Lightly sweet and gently spiced, it is a fragrant one-pot bhaat quite distinct from its southern relatives.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Sharp wood-pressed mustard oil gives the bhaat its unmistakable Bengali pungency.

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups rice for 20 minutes, then drain.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pot until it just smokes and mellows, then lower to medium and add 1 tsp panch phoron, 1 bay leaf and 2 dried red chillies and let them crackle for 20 seconds.
Add 1 sliced onion and 1 inch grated ginger and sauté for 5 minutes until soft and lightly golden.
Add 4 chopped tomatoes, 2 slit green chillies, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp sugar and 1.25 tsp salt, and cook for 8 minutes until the tomatoes break down into a glossy masala.
Fold in the drained rice and toast for 2 minutes, then pour in 1.75 cups hot water and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes, rest 5 minutes, then fluff and garnish with 3 tbsp coriander.
tips: Do not skip smoking the mustard oil first, as its raw sharpness would otherwise overpower the delicate bhaat.
Panch phoron is used whole and left in; warn diners about the fenugreek seeds, which are bitter if bitten.
The teaspoon of sugar balances the tomato acidity in true Bengali style, so keep it in for authenticity.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a simple aloo bhaja and a wedge of lime, or alongside a light fish jhol for a Bengali meal.

variations.name: Classic Festive Besan Ladoo
variations.description: A celebration-grade besan ladoo enriched with khoya and a lavish mix of dry fruits, making it richer and more indulgent than the everyday version. The mawa keeps the ladoos moist and gives them a deeper, milky sweetness perfect for Diwali and wedding trays.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasts the besan deep and gold and enriches the mawa-laden mixture.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Stirred into the cooled base for a festive caramel sweetness.

steps: Melt 0.75 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai on low, add 2 cups gram flour and roast, stirring without stopping, for about 20 minutes until deep golden and nutty.
Push the besan to one side, add 0.5 cup grated khoya to the pan and roast it for 3-4 minutes until it softens and smells milky, then mix it into the besan.
Stir in 0.25 cup almonds, 0.25 cup cashews and 2 tbsp pistachios and roast for 2 minutes until the nuts are fragrant.
Turn off the heat, add 1 tsp cardamom powder, 0.25 tsp nutmeg and a pinch of salt, and cool the mixture until just warm.
Mix in 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder thoroughly, working it into a soft, rich dough that holds together.
Roll firm 2 tbsp ladoos, pressing well so the mawa-enriched mixture binds smoothly.
Let them set for an hour; because of the khoya, refrigerate if keeping beyond three days.
tips: Roast the khoya separately for a few minutes before mixing in, as this cooks off its raw dairy note and prevents the ladoos spoiling fast.
Mawa adds moisture, so you may need slightly less jaggery; taste the warm mixture and adjust before rolling.
These are richer than plain besan ladoos, so roll them a touch smaller for an elegant festive platter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Garnish each with a sliver of pistachio and a dab of edible silver leaf, and box them as a homemade Diwali gift.

variations.name: Kashmiri Festive Besan Ladoo
variations.description: A festive valley besan ladoo layered with saffron, chironji and walnuts, carrying the warm floral signature of Kashmiri sweets. The saffron infuses both a golden glow and a delicate honeyed scent that lifts these ladoos above the ordinary.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasts the besan and dissolves the saffron for an even amber colour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Folded into the cooled mixture for a caramel base beneath the saffron.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Steeped in a spoon of warm ghee so its colour and aroma spread through the dough.

steps: Melt 0.75 cup Anveshan Ghee on low, spoon 1 tsp into a bowl and steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in it to release its colour.
Add 2 cups gram flour to the pan and roast on low, stirring for about 20 minutes, until deep golden and richly aromatic.
Add 0.33 cup chopped walnuts, 2 tbsp chironji and 0.5 tsp crushed fennel and roast for 2 minutes until the nuts toast lightly.
Turn off the heat, mix in the saffron ghee, 1 tsp cardamom powder and a pinch of salt so amber streaks run through, then cool until just warm.
Add 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and combine into a soft, saffron-tinted dough.
Roll into smooth 2 tbsp ladoos and press a piece of walnut into each top.
Rest for an hour before storing in an airtight tin.
tips: Chironji seeds are a hallmark of North Indian festive mithai and add a subtle almond-like note, so include them if you can find them.
Steeping saffron in warm ghee draws far more colour than adding the threads dry to the dough.
Toast the walnuts only briefly, since over-roasting turns them bitter and spoils the delicate saffron balance.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these golden ladoos with kahwa or warm saffron milk as a matched Kashmiri festive dessert.

variations.name: Kerala Festive Besan Ladoo
variations.description: A festive coastal ladoo where roasted besan is enriched with toasted coconut, ghee-fried cashews and a crackle of coconut oil for a tropical, celebratory sweetness. It captures the coconut-and-jaggery heart of Kerala festival sweets in a moist, tender ladoo.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The base roasting fat and the medium for frying the cashews golden.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Lends the distinct Kerala coconut fragrance to the roasted besan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The traditional coconut-friendly sweetener folded into the cooled base.

steps: Dry-roast 1 cup grated coconut on low for 5 minutes until pale gold and fragrant, then set aside.
Melt 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee with 0.25 cup Anveshan Coconut Oil on low and fry 0.33 cup halved cashews until golden, then lift them out.
Add 2 cups gram flour to the fat and roast on low, stirring, for about 20 minutes until deep golden and nutty.
Stir in the toasted coconut and fried cashews and roast together for 2 minutes to bring the flavours together.
Turn off the heat, add 1 tsp cardamom powder, 0.25 tsp dry ginger powder and a pinch of salt, and cool until just warm.
Mix in 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder until the coconut-flecked mixture binds into a soft dough.
Roll into 2 tbsp ladoos, coat in a little reserved toasted coconut, and set for an hour.
tips: A pinch of dry ginger is a Kerala jaggery-sweet trick that deepens the flavour and aids digestion after a heavy festive meal.
Since fresh coconut makes these moist, keep them refrigerated and enjoy within four days for the best texture.
Fry the cashews until just golden in the coconut-ghee blend, as they crisp further while cooling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a banana leaf rolled in extra toasted coconut, a fitting sweet to close an Onam or Vishu feast.

variations.name: Malwa Festive Besan Ladoo
variations.description: A festive Malwi ladoo where roasted besan, crushed peanuts and puffed makhana come together for a crunchy, celebratory sweet with real heft. Rooted in the peanut-growing plateau of Madhya Pradesh, it is rustic yet generous, made in big batches for weddings and fairs.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasts the besan and crisps the makhana to a festive crunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The earthy sweetener that binds the peanut-and-makhana mixture.

steps: Melt 2 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai and roast 1 cup makhana on low for 5 minutes until crisp, then cool and crush coarsely.
Add the remaining Anveshan Ghee to the pan, tip in 2 cups gram flour and roast on low, stirring, for about 20 minutes until deep golden.
Add 0.75 cup crushed roasted peanuts and 2 tbsp sesame seeds and roast for 2 minutes until aromatic.
Mix in the crushed makhana, then turn off the heat, add 1 tsp cardamom powder and a pinch of salt, and cool until just warm.
Work in 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder until the crunchy mixture binds into a firm dough.
Press 2 tbsp portions firmly into ladoos so the peanut and makhana pieces hold together.
Let them set for an hour, then store in an airtight jar.
tips: Crushing the crisped makhana coarsely keeps a pleasant crunch while still letting the ladoos bind.
Press these ladoos more firmly than usual, since the peanut and makhana pieces need a good squeeze to stay together.
This mixture scales up well for large festive batches, so double it confidently for a crowd.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these crunchy ladoos with masala chai at a winter get-together or pack them for a festival food stall.

variations.name: Awadhi Festive Besan Ladoo
variations.description: An opulent Lucknowi festive ladoo perfumed with rose, kewra and a hint of saffron, gilded with pistachios and edible silver leaf in the grand Nawabi mithai style. Floral, delicate and dressed for celebration, it is the centrepiece of a festive sweet tray.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The rich fat that carries the rose, kewra and saffron aromas evenly.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A gentle caramel sweetness that lets the florals shine through.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Bloomed in warm ghee for a whisper of colour and royal aroma.

steps: Melt 0.75 cup Anveshan Ghee on low, steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 1 tsp of the warm ghee, and roast 2 cups gram flour in the rest for about 20 minutes until deep golden.
Add half the 0.33 cup slivered pistachios and roast for a minute, keeping the rest for garnish.
Turn off the heat and stir in the saffron ghee, 1 tsp cardamom powder and a pinch of salt, then cool until just warm.
Sprinkle in 0.5 tsp kewra water and 1 tsp rose water and fold quickly so the aromas stay locked in.
Mix in 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder to form a soft, fragrant, faintly golden dough.
Roll into elegant 2 tbsp ladoos and press the reserved pistachios and dried rose petals onto the tops.
Rest for an hour, then finish with a dab of edible silver leaf before presenting.
tips: Fold in the rose and kewra water only off the heat, or their delicate perfume will simply cook away.
A single pinch of saffron alongside the florals gives a Nawabi glow without overpowering the rose.
Keep these ladoos small and neat, as this style of mithai is meant to look jewel-like on the tray.
variations.servingSuggestion: Present on a mirrored tray strewn with rose petals and silver leaf, a regal close to an Awadhi festive dawat.

variations.name: Classic Festive Coconut Ladoo
variations.description: The dressed-up festive version of the coconut ladoo, enriched with khoya, saffron and a shower of chopped nuts. Soft, milky and gently spiced, it is the centrepiece coconut sweet on Diwali and wedding thalis across the country.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Fries the nuts and gives the festive ladoo its glossy richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: Bloomed in warm milk to lend a festive golden hue and floral aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A spoon of unrefined depth to lift the flat sweetness of condensed milk

steps: Soak 1/4 teaspoon Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tablespoons warm milk and set it aside for 10 minutes to draw out its colour.
Set aside 1/2 cup coconut for rolling, melt the 2 tablespoons Anveshan Ghee in a kadai and fry the 1/2 cup mixed nuts until golden, then remove and reserve half.
Add the remaining 2.5 cups coconut and 1/2 cup crumbled khoya to the pan and stir on low heat for 4 minutes until the khoya melts in.
Pour in the 1 cup condensed milk and 3 tablespoons Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook, stirring, for about 6 minutes until the mixture thickens and leaves the sides.
Stir in the saffron milk, 1 teaspoon cardamom powder and the remaining fried nuts, then take the pan off the heat and cool for 5 minutes.
Roll 2 tablespoons at a time into 14 ladoos, coat in the reserved coconut, press a few reserved nuts on top and chill for 20 minutes to set.
tips: Do not overcook once the condensed milk goes in, or the festive ladoos turn dry and dense.
Bloom the saffron in warm milk so its colour and aroma disperse through the pale coconut.
Refrigerate and enjoy within four days, as the khoya makes them more perishable.
variations.servingSuggestion: Set them out in decorative foil cups on a Diwali sweet platter with a scatter of saffron strands on top.

variations.name: Bengali Narkel Naru
variations.description: Narkel naru is Bengal's festive coconut ladoo, made every Lakshmi and Durga Puja by cooking fresh coconut with nolen gur date-palm jaggery until sticky and deeply caramel. Small, dark and intensely coconut, they are offered to the goddess and then shared.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Stands in for nolen gur to give naru its dark, caramel Bengali character

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A traditional Bengali touch to grease the pan and the palms for rolling

steps: Melt 1 tablespoon Anveshan Ghee in a kadai, drop in the bay leaf and add the 3 cups fresh grated coconut, stirring on low heat for 3 minutes until warmed and fragrant.
Add 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 3 tablespoons milk and cook on low, stirring steadily, for about 12 minutes until the jaggery melts and the mixture turns thick, dark and sticky.
Fold in 2 tablespoons raisins and 1 teaspoon cardamom powder and cook for a final 2 minutes until the mass clumps together and leaves the sides of the pan.
Discard the bay leaf, take the pan off the heat and let the mixture cool for 5 minutes until warm enough to handle.
Rub the remaining ghee on your palms and roll 1.5 tablespoons at a time into 16 small, firm naru.
Set them on a plate to cool completely for 20 minutes; they harden as they cool.
tips: Roll while the mixture is warm; once fully cool it becomes too stiff to shape smoothly.
Cook the jaggery until the mixture genuinely leaves the pan, or the naru stay soft and will not hold.
Naru made with fresh coconut keep for three to four days at room temperature in a dry jar.
variations.servingSuggestion: Offer as bhog on the Lakshmi Puja plate with batasha and fruit, then hand out to family the Bengali way.

variations.name: Kashmiri Saffron Coconut Ladoo
variations.description: A festive coconut ladoo perfumed generously with valley saffron and studded with slivered almonds and walnuts. Milky and pale gold, its restrained sweetness lets the saffron and dry-fruit shine at Kashmiri celebrations.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Carries the fat-soluble saffron colour into the whole batch

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: A generous bloom so the ladoo is unmistakably saffron-forward

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: A gentle unrefined sweetness that keeps the saffron in focus

steps: Warm the 3/4 cup milk and soak 1/2 teaspoon Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in it for 10 minutes until it turns deep gold.
Melt the 2 tablespoons Anveshan Ghee in a kadai and lightly toast the slivered almonds and chopped walnuts for 2 minutes, then reserve half for topping.
Add the 3 cups desiccated coconut and 1/2 cup crumbled khoya to the pan and stir on low heat for 4 minutes until the khoya melts through.
Pour in the saffron milk and 1/2 cup Anveshan Khandsari Sugar and cook, stirring, for about 8 minutes until the sugar melts and the mixture thickens and leaves the sides.
Stir in 1 teaspoon cardamom powder and the remaining toasted nuts, then take off the heat and cool for 5 minutes.
Roll 2 tablespoons at a time into 14 ladoos, press the reserved nuts on top and chill for 20 minutes to set.
tips: Use enough saffron for a real presence; this ladoo is meant to taste and smell of it, not just hint.
Cook the khandsari until the mixture leaves the pan so the ladoos hold once chilled.
Keep refrigerated and eat within four days because of the fresh khoya and milk.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a walnut-wood platter with kahwa for a festive Kashmiri spread that plays saffron in both sweet and cup.

variations.name: Gujarati Kopra Pak Festive Ladoo
variations.description: The festive kopra pak of Gujarat, cooked richer with khoya and jaggery for a fudgy, celebratory ladoo garnished with pistachio and charoli. Denser and more luxurious than the everyday coconut ladoo, it is a Diwali mithai-box staple.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Enriches the pak and gives it its signature fudgy, glossy set

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Deepens the pak with earthy caramel notes over plain sugar

steps: Warm the 3/4 cup milk with the 3/4 cup crumbled khoya in a kadai on low heat, stirring, until it forms a smooth paste, about 5 minutes.
Add the 3 cups desiccated coconut and 3 tablespoons Anveshan Ghee and cook on low, stirring, for 7 minutes until the mixture is thick and cohesive.
Stir in 3/4 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook for about 7 more minutes until the jaggery melts and the mass pulls cleanly from the sides of the pan.
Mix in 1 teaspoon cardamom powder, 1/4 teaspoon grated nutmeg and 2 tablespoons charoli, then take off the heat and cool for 5 minutes.
Roll 2 tablespoons at a time into 14 fudgy ladoos while warm and pliable.
Press sliced pistachios onto each and let them set for 20 minutes.
tips: Jaggery browns the pak, so do not expect the pale colour of the sugar version; that deeper hue is the point.
Stop cooking the moment the mass leaves the pan; a minute too long turns the ladoos grainy.
These keep for five days refrigerated and taste even richer on day two.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pack into a Diwali mithai box between rows of magas ladoo for a classic Gujarati festive assortment.

variations.name: Kerala Festive Nariyal Ladoo
variations.description: Kerala's festive coconut ladoo fries fresh coconut in wood-pressed coconut oil with jaggery, toasted cashews and a scatter of curry-leaf-warmed spice. Aromatic and rustic, it is the sweet made for Onam and temple offerings.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: The defining Kerala fat that deepens the coconut aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The traditional sweetener for Onam coconut sweets

steps: Warm 1 tablespoon Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a kadai and fry the 1/3 cup cashews and 3 tablespoons raisins until golden and plump, then set aside.
Melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 1/4 cup water in the same pan on low heat, stirring, until it forms a thick syrup, about 5 minutes.
Add the 3 cups fresh grated coconut and the remaining coconut oil and cook on low, stirring often, for about 10 minutes until thick and leaving the sides.
Stir in 1 teaspoon cardamom powder, 1/4 teaspoon dry ginger powder and the fried cashews and raisins, then cook for a final minute and take off the heat.
Cool for 6 minutes to a workable warmth, then roll 2 tablespoons at a time into 14 firm ladoos.
Rest for 20 minutes; the coconut oil resets and firms the ladoos as they cool.
tips: Cook the fresh coconut until the mixture truly leaves the pan so the ladoos are not damp inside.
The dry ginger keeps the rich sweetness light, a hallmark of Kerala festival sweets.
In warm weather, refrigerate to help the coconut oil hold the ladoos together.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a fresh banana leaf as part of an Onam sadya sweet course with a cup of strong filter coffee.

variations.name: Classic Festive Coconut Rice
variations.description: A celebration version of coconut rice, cooked in ghee with whole spices, saffron and a shower of ghee-fried dry fruits. Richer and more perfumed than everyday thengai sadam, it is meant for feast-day thalis.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the festive fat that fries the dry fruits and enriches every grain

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk to gild the rice and add a celebratory perfume

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati, soak for 20 minutes and drain, and steep a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and fry 15 cashews, 10 sliced almonds and 2 tbsp raisins until gold, then lift the dry fruits out and reserve.
In the same ghee sizzle 4 cardamom pods, 3 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add 0.75 cup grated coconut and toast on medium for 3 minutes until it turns pale gold and smells sweet.
Stir in the drained rice and toast 2 minutes, then pour in 2.5 cups hot water with 1.25 tsp salt and the saffron milk.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes until the liquid is absorbed and each grain is fluffy and golden.
Scatter the ghee-fried dry fruits over the top, rest covered for 5 minutes, and fluff gently before serving.
tips: Steep the saffron in warm, not hot, milk to draw out colour without dulling its aroma.
Fry the dry fruits first and add them at the end so they stay crunchy against the soft rice.
For a party, layer the rice and dry fruits in a dish and steam on dum for a few extra minutes.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as the centrepiece of a festive thali with a rich paneer korma and a cooling boondi raita.

variations.name: Kashmiri Festive Coconut Rice
variations.description: A Kashmiri-style festive coconut rice glowing with saffron and perfumed with fennel and dry ginger, studded with walnuts in the Wazwan spirit. Delicate, floral and mildly sweet, it skips onion and garlic for a pure aromatic profile.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the Wazwan fat that blooms the fennel and dry ginger central to Kashmiri rice

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: the heart of Kashmiri cooking, steeped to give the rice its amber glow

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati, soak 20 minutes and drain, and steep a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and toast 10 roughly chopped walnuts for 90 seconds until fragrant, then set them aside.
In the same ghee crackle 4 cardamom pods, 3 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon for 20 seconds until their aroma rises.
Off the heat stir in 1 tsp fennel powder and 0.5 tsp dry ginger powder for 15 seconds so they bloom without scorching.
Add 0.5 cup grated coconut and the drained rice and toast on medium for 3 minutes until the grains glisten.
Pour in 2.5 cups hot water with 1.25 tsp salt and the saffron milk, and bring to a gentle boil.
Cover, cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes, then rest 5 minutes and fold in the toasted walnuts before serving.
tips: Bloom the fennel and dry ginger off the flame so they perfume the ghee without turning bitter.
Walnuts, not cashews, give the authentic Kashmiri character and a pleasant slight bitterness.
A few extra saffron strands scattered on top just before serving make it look truly festive.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a Kashmiri dum aloo or a mild yakhni, with a walnut-and-radish salad on the side.

variations.name: Awadhi Festive Coconut Rice
variations.description: A Lucknawi-style coconut rice cooked on dum and finished with kewra water and rose, giving it a courtly floral fragrance. Delicate and perfumed, it brings the refined aromas of Awadhi kitchens to a coconut base.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the Awadhi dum fat that carries kewra and rose gently into the grains

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati, soak 20 minutes and drain, and warm 2 tbsp milk with a crushed pinch of mace to keep aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and fry 12 cashews to gold, about 2 minutes, then remove them for the garnish.
In the same ghee sizzle 4 cardamom pods and 1 bay leaf for 20 seconds until fragrant, then add 0.5 cup grated coconut and toast 2 minutes.
Stir in the drained rice and toast 2 minutes, then pour in 2.5 cups hot water with 1.25 tsp salt and bring to a boil.
When most of the water is absorbed, drizzle over 0.5 tsp kewra water, 0.5 tsp rose water and the mace milk, and scatter half the fried onions.
Seal the pot with a tight lid or dough and cook on the lowest dum heat for 12 minutes so the aromas steam into the rice.
Rest 5 minutes, then fluff and top with the fried cashews and remaining birista before serving.
tips: Add kewra and rose water sparingly and late, as their perfume fades fast if boiled hard.
A dough seal traps the delicate floral steam far better than a loose lid.
Homemade birista adds a subtle sweetness that store-bought fried onions rarely match.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a creamy shahi paneer or navratan korma and a mint raita, garnished with a few rose petals.

variations.name: Gujarati Festive Coconut Rice
variations.description: A Gujarati festive coconut rice with the region's beloved sweet-savoury balance, gently sweetened with jaggery and warmed with a clove-cinnamon temper. Soft, mildly sweet and aromatic, it suits a celebratory Gujarati thali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the festive fat that softens the jaggery and warms the whole spices

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the signature Gujarati sweetness folded gently into celebratory rice

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati, soak 20 minutes and drain thoroughly in a colander.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and fry 12 cashews and 2 tbsp raisins until the cashews gild and the raisins swell, then remove them.
In the same ghee crackle 4 cardamom pods, 4 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add 0.75 cup grated coconut and toast on medium for 3 minutes until it just turns gold and smells sweet.
Stir in the drained rice, toast 2 minutes, then pour in 2.5 cups hot water with 0.75 tsp salt and cook covered on low for 12 minutes.
When the rice is tender, gently fold in 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.25 tsp nutmeg so the jaggery melts through without mashing the grains.
Top with the fried cashews and raisins, rest 4 minutes, and fluff lightly before serving warm.
tips: Fold the jaggery in at the end off high heat so it melts evenly without making the rice sticky.
Keep the salt low here, as the balance leans towards the gentle sweetness.
A pinch of extra nutmeg or a strand of saffron dresses it up nicely for a festival table.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as part of a Gujarati thali with kadhi and a spicy sambharo to balance the sweet notes.

variations.name: Kerala Festive Coconut Rice
variations.description: A Kerala sadya-style festive coconut rice cooked in coconut milk and ghee, layered with cashews, raisins and a whisper of cardamom. Creamy, faintly sweet and aromatic, it echoes the celebratory rice of a Malabar feast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the Kerala fat that deepens the coconut-milk richness of festive rice

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon that fries the cashews and adds feast-day gloss

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups jeerakasala rice and soak 20 minutes, then drain it well.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and fry 15 cashews and 2 tbsp raisins until golden and plump, then lift them out to garnish.
Add 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil to the pan, crackle 5 cardamom pods and 3 cloves, then saute 6 sliced shallots with 12 curry leaves for 4 minutes.
Stir in 0.5 cup grated coconut and the drained rice and toast for 3 minutes until the grains look glossy.
Pour in 1 cup thick coconut milk with 1.5 cups water and 1.25 tsp salt, and bring to a gentle boil without over-stirring.
Cover and steam on the lowest heat for 12 minutes until the coconut milk is absorbed and the rice is soft and fragrant.
Rest 5 minutes, then fluff and crown with the ghee-fried cashews and raisins before serving.
tips: Add the coconut milk with the water from the start so it does not curdle over long heat.
Fry the cashews in ghee rather than the rice pot to keep them crisp for the garnish.
A short-grain aromatic rice like jeerakasala gives the soft, festive Malabar texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at a sadya alongside a mild vegetable stew and pappadam, finishing with a spoon of banana payasam.

variations.name: Classic Festive Corn Pulao
variations.description: Dressed up for a celebration, this pulao layers sweet corn with fried onions, whole garam and a shower of toasted cashews. The rice is cooked in extra bilona ghee so each grain glistens, and a saffron-milk finish gives it a golden, party-ready glow. It is the corn pulao you bring out when guests arrive.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A festive pulao wants generous bilona ghee to fry the onions crisp and the nuts golden.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Saffron steeped in warm milk gives the celebration rice its signature golden streaks.

steps: Soak a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside to bloom.
Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain thoroughly.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot on medium heat and fry 12 cashews for 90 seconds until golden, then remove them and reserve.
In the same ghee fry 2 thinly sliced onions for 8 minutes until crisp and deep brown, then lift out half for garnish.
To the remaining onions add 4 cardamom pods, 4 cloves, 1 inch cinnamon and 1 bay leaf, sizzle for 20 seconds, then add 1 cup sweet corn and saute for 2 minutes.
Fold in the drained rice for 1 minute, pour in 2.5 cups water and 1 tsp salt, stir in the saffron milk and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 13 minutes, rest 5 minutes, then fluff and crown with the reserved fried onions and cashews.
tips: Fry the onions slowly and evenly to a true brown; pale onions will not give the sweet crunch a festive plate needs.
Reserve half the fried onions and all the nuts for the top so the garnish stays crisp against the soft rice.
The saffron milk can be made an hour ahead; a longer steep gives a deeper colour and aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a large platter with a bowl of pineapple raita and a mint chutney, ideal as the centrepiece of a vegetarian feast.

variations.name: Awadhi Festive Corn Pulao
variations.description: The Lucknawi kitchen prizes delicate perfume over heat, so this pulao is scented with kewra water, mace and a slow dum finish. The corn turns silky against rice steamed under a sealed lid, absorbing every trace of the floral aroma. It is elegant, restrained and fit for a nawabi dastarkhwan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Awadhi dum cooking depends on pure bilona ghee to carry the kewra and mace through the sealed rice.

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain gently to keep the long grains intact.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot on medium flame and add 1 blade mace, 4 cardamom pods, 4 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon, sizzling for 20 seconds until aromatic.
Add 1 large thinly sliced onion and fry for 6 minutes until light gold, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute.
Add 1 cup sweet corn and saute for 2 minutes, then fold in the drained rice for 1 minute so the grains are silky with ghee.
Pour in 2.5 cups water and 1 tsp salt, bring to a boil, then reduce to the lowest heat.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp kewra water over the surface, seal the lid with a tight cover or foil and cook undisturbed on dum for 14 minutes.
Rest 5 minutes off the heat, then lift the lid, fluff very gently and serve the fragrant rice at once.
tips: Kewra is potent, so measure it carefully; a few extra drops will make the rice taste soapy.
Seal the pot well for the dum stage, as escaping steam takes the delicate aroma with it.
Rest the pulao fully before opening; the trapped fragrance settles into the grains as it cools slightly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a smooth shahi paneer or a bowl of burhani raita, in the layered nawabi style where the rice is the quiet star.

variations.name: Gujarati Festive Corn Pulao
variations.description: Gujarat loves the interplay of sweet and savoury, so this festive pulao is gently sweetened with Anveshan jaggery powder and warmed with a mild masala. The corn's natural sugar and the jaggery meet a whisper of chilli, creating the balanced, celebratory rice served at Gujarati gatherings. Toasted cashews and raisins seal its festive spirit.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee frays into the jaggery to give the pulao its glossy, festive sheen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery powder brings the signature Gujarati sweet-savoury balance in place of refined sugar.

steps: Soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain well.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot on medium heat and fry 10 cashews and 2 tbsp raisins for 1 minute until the nuts are golden and the raisins plump, then remove and reserve.
In the same ghee crackle 1 tsp cumin, 3 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon for 20 seconds, then add 1 sliced medium onion and 1 slit green chilli and fry for 4 minutes until soft.
Add 1 cup sweet corn and 0.5 tsp turmeric and saute for 2 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and let it melt for 30 seconds.
Fold in the drained rice for 1 minute until the grains glisten with the sweet ghee.
Pour in 2.5 cups water and 1 tsp salt, boil once, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 13 minutes until tender.
Rest 5 minutes, then fluff and scatter the reserved cashews and raisins over the top.
tips: Melt the jaggery only briefly with the corn; boiling it hard can make the rice sticky.
Keep the chilli whole and slit so the gentle sweetness stays in the foreground.
For a deeper festive note, add a pinch of ground clove along with the jaggery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of kadhi and a spoon of tangy chhundo pickle, the sweet-sour partners a Gujarati table expects.

variations.name: Malwa Festive Corn Pulao
variations.description: From the Malwa plateau of Madhya Pradesh comes a hearty pulao rich with roasted peanuts and a rustic spice temper. The peanuts, fried in Anveshan wood-pressed groundnut oil, give the corn a toasty, filling crunch beloved at regional feasts. It is earthy and satisfying, the kind of rice made in big pots for a crowd.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil deepens the roasted peanut flavour central to Malwa cooking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon of bilona ghee at the end lends festive richness to the rustic rice.

steps: Soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain thoroughly.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pot on medium heat and fry 4 tbsp peanuts for 2 minutes until crisp and ruddy, then remove and reserve half for garnish.
To the oil add 1 tsp cumin and 2 broken dried red chillies and fry for 20 seconds until fragrant, then add 1 large sliced onion and cook for 6 minutes until golden.
Lower the heat and add 1 tsp coriander powder and 0.5 tsp turmeric for 20 seconds, then stir in 1 cup sweet corn and the peanuts kept in the pot and saute for 2 minutes.
Fold in the drained rice and 0.5 tsp garam masala for 1 minute until well coated.
Pour in 2.5 cups water and 1 tsp salt, boil once, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 13 minutes until fluffy.
Rest 5 minutes, drizzle 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then fluff and top with the reserved fried peanuts.
tips: Roast the peanuts until they smell nutty and their skins loosen for the fullest toasty flavour.
Keeping half the peanuts back for garnish preserves a crunchy contrast against the soft grains.
A squeeze of lemon at the table brightens the earthy peanut-heavy rice nicely.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of spiced buttermilk (chaas) and a fried papad for a filling plateau-style meal.

variations.name: Hyderabadi Festive Corn Pulao
variations.description: The Deccan royal kitchens give this pulao a dum finish scented with saffron, mint and fried onions. Sweet corn sits in fragrant rice steamed under a sealed lid, soaking up the perfume of Anveshan Kashmiri saffron and warm spice. It borrows the drama of biryani while staying a gentle, celebratory pulao.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Dum cooking in the Hyderabadi style needs plenty of bilona ghee to fry the onions and seal in aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Kashmiri saffron in warm milk gives the dum pulao its royal Deccan colour and scent.

steps: Soak a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk, and separately soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes before draining.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot on medium heat and fry 2 sliced onions for 8 minutes until crisp and brown, then remove half for garnish.
To the pot add 4 cardamom pods, 4 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon, sizzle for 20 seconds, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute.
Stir in 1 cup sweet corn and 2 tbsp chopped mint and saute for 2 minutes, then fold in the drained rice for 1 minute.
Pour in 2.5 cups water and 1 tsp salt, bring to a boil, then drizzle the saffron milk over the surface.
Scatter the reserved fried onions and remaining 1 tbsp mint on top, seal the lid tightly and cook on dum on the lowest heat for 14 minutes.
Rest 5 minutes, then open, fluff very gently and serve the fragrant layered rice.
tips: Reserve the crispest fried onions for the dum layer so their sweetness perfumes the whole pot.
Do not stir during the dum stage; layering and steaming undisturbed is what gives the biryani-like aroma.
Warm the serving plates so the delicate saffron fragrance lingers as the pulao is eaten.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of mirchi ka salan or a simple raita, plated so the golden saffron grains show against the white rice.

variations.name: Classic Festive Curd Rice
variations.description: A celebration-worthy curd rice dressed up with ghee-fried cashews, jewel-like pomegranate and a fragrant tempering. Often prepared as prasadam and for feasts, it is richer and prettier than the everyday bowl yet keeps that soothing, cooling heart.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Extra ghee here fries the cashews and enriches the curd for a festive, celebratory feel.

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed rice with 3 cups water for 4 whistles until soft, mash while warm and cool for 10 minutes.
Stir 2 cups curd, 0.75 cup milk and 1 tsp salt into the rice until luxuriously creamy and loose.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and fry 15 cashews for 2 minutes until golden, then scoop half of them out for garnish.
Into the same ghee add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal and let them splutter and turn golden, about 40 seconds.
Add 2 slit green chillies, 2 dried red chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 15 curry leaves and 0.5 tsp asafoetida, frying 20 seconds until crisp and fragrant.
Fold the tempering with its cashews through the curd rice, then crown with the reserved cashews, 4 tbsp pomegranate and 2 tbsp coriander before serving.
tips: Fry the cashews first and set some aside whole; softening them into the rice would waste their festive crunch.
Add pomegranate only just before serving so the seeds stay bright and do not bleed pink into the white curd.
For a banquet, mound the rice on a platter and arrange the garnishes in rings for a striking presentation.
variations.servingSuggestion: Present alongside sweet-tangy mango pickle and a small cup of payasam to round out a festive South Indian spread.

variations.name: Kashmiri Kesar Doon Chaman Dahi
variations.description: A regal Kashmiri-inspired curd rice bloomed with Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron and a scatter of walnuts, giving it a golden hue and honeyed aroma. Mild and fragrant rather than fiery, it channels the delicate, dry-fruit-rich cooking of the valley.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: A pinch of Kashmiri saffron steeped in warm milk turns the curd rice pale gold and deeply aromatic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee fries the walnuts and carries the gentle spice tempering of this valley-style dish.

steps: Warm the 0.75 cup milk gently and steep 0.25 tsp Anveshan Saffron in it for 10 minutes until the milk turns deep amber.
Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed basmati with 3 cups water for 4 whistles until soft, mash lightly and cool for 10 minutes.
Whisk 2 cups curd, the saffron milk and 1 tsp salt together, then fold into the rice for a golden, fragrant base.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and fry 3 tbsp walnut pieces for 90 seconds until they smell toasty, then lift out half for garnish.
Crackle 0.75 tsp cumin and 3 lightly crushed cardamom pods in the ghee for 20 seconds, then add 1 slit green chilli and 8 curry leaves and fry briefly.
Fold the delicate tempering with its walnuts through the rice, then scatter the reserved walnuts and 1 tbsp dried rose petals on top before serving.
tips: Steep the saffron in warm, not boiling, milk to draw out colour and aroma without turning it bitter.
Keep the tempering restrained here; this is a fragrant, delicate dish, not a fiery one.
Toast the cardamom only lightly so it perfumes the ghee rather than dominating the saffron.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in shallow copper bowls with a side of stewed apricots or a spoon of quince preserve for a valley-style feast.

variations.name: Awadhi Kewra Dahi Chawal
variations.description: The Lucknawi kitchen perfumes curd rice with kewra water and a hint of honey, layering it with fried onions and dry fruits in the nawabi tradition. It is subtle, floral and faintly sweet, a festive bowl that feels straight out of a Dastarkhwan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: A drizzle of raw honey lends the gentle sweetness that balances the floral kewra in nawabi style.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee crisps the onions and carries the whole-spice tempering of this Awadhi bowl.

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed basmati with 3 cups water for 4 whistles until soft, mash gently and cool for 10 minutes.
Whisk 2 cups curd with 0.5 cup milk, 1 tbsp Anveshan Honey, 1 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp kewra water until smooth and lightly perfumed.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and fry 1 thinly sliced onion for 6 minutes until golden and crisp, then remove half for garnish.
In the same ghee toast 3 tbsp mixed raisins and slivered almonds for 1 minute until the raisins plump, then set aside with a slotted spoon.
Crackle 0.75 tsp cumin, 3 crushed cardamom pods and 2 cloves in the ghee for 20 seconds, add 1 slit green chilli, then fold this tempering and the honeyed curd into the rice.
Top with the reserved fried onions and dry fruits, rest 10 minutes so the kewra settles, and serve at cool room temperature.
tips: Kewra is potent, so measure it carefully; even a few extra drops can make the dish taste soapy.
Fry the onions slowly to an even gold, as scorched onions turn the delicate curd bitter.
Stir the honey into the curd, never the hot rice, to keep its floral aroma and raw goodness intact.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling mint raita and warm sheermal, or alongside a rich korma for a nawabi table.

variations.name: Kerala Sadya Thengai Thayir
variations.description: The curd rice that closes a Kerala sadya, enriched with fresh coconut, a coconut-oil tempering and the crunch of fried curry leaves. Cooling and faintly sweet, it is the traditional last course served on a banana leaf before dessert.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil gives the sadya its signature aroma and fries the curry leaves crisp.

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed rice with 3 cups water for 4 whistles until very soft, mash while warm and cool for 10 minutes.
Grind 0.5 cup fresh coconut with 2 green chillies and 1 inch ginger to a coarse paste that will melt creamily into the curd.
Mix 2 cups curd, 0.5 cup milk and 1 tsp salt into the rice, then fold in the coconut paste until pale and fragrant.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil over medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard and 1 tsp urad dal, then fry 2 sliced shallots for 1 minute until golden.
Add 2 dried red chillies and 20 curry leaves and fry for 20 seconds until the leaves go crisp and the oil smells sweet and nutty.
Fold the tempering through the coconut curd rice, reserving a few crisp curry leaves for the top, and serve cool.
tips: Fry a handful of curry leaves until fully crisp and crumble them over the top for a festive, aromatic finish.
Kerala matta rice gives an earthy, traditional flavour, but soft-cooked sona masoori is a fine everyday substitute.
Serve at cool room temperature, since coconut oil firms up and dulls the flavour when fridge-cold.
variations.servingSuggestion: Spoon onto a banana leaf beside sweet mango pachadi and crunchy sharkara varatti chips for a true sadya finish.

variations.name: Gujarati Utsav Meethu Dahi Bhaat
variations.description: A festive Gujarati dahi bhaat, sweetened with Anveshan Jaggery Powder and studded with pomegranate, roasted peanuts and coriander. The signature sweet-savoury balance is dialled up for celebrations, bright and joyful against the cooling curd.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery powder brings a festive caramel sweetness that defines the celebratory Gujarati dahi bhaat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee toasts the peanuts and carries the mustard-cumin tempering for this feast bowl.

steps: Cook 1 cup rinsed rice with 3 cups water until soft, mash gently while warm and cool for 10 minutes.
Whisk 2 cups curd with 0.5 cup milk, 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp salt until the jaggery dissolves into a sweet-tangy curd.
Fold the sweetened curd into the rice until creamy and evenly combined.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and fry 3 tbsp peanuts for 2 minutes until crunchy and golden-spotted.
Add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin and splutter for 20 seconds, then add 2 slit green chillies, 12 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and fry briefly.
Fold the peanut tempering through the rice and finish with 3 tbsp pomegranate and 2 tbsp coriander just before serving.
tips: Dissolve the jaggery fully in the curd before mixing, so no gritty crystals remain in the finished bowl.
The pomegranate adds festive colour and a juicy pop, so add it last to keep the seeds intact.
For a celebration platter, serve in a wide dish and border it with concentric rings of peanuts and pomegranate.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with crisp methi thepla and a spoon of sweet chundo for a proper Gujarati festive plate.

variations.name: Classic Festive Dry Fruit Ladoo
variations.description: The showpiece dry-fruit ladoo for Diwali and weddings, thick with five nuts and dried berries, gently sweetened with honey and finished in silver leaf. Denser and more jewelled than the everyday version, it is meant to headline a mithai box.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a festive measure of ghee gives the ladoos a rich sheen and soft bite

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: honey binds the loaded nut mix and adds a floral festive note

steps: Pit and finely chop the 1.5 cups dates, then warm 2 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee and cook them on low heat for 5 minutes, mashing, until they form a glossy, sticky paste.
Dry-roast the 0.5 cup almonds, 0.5 cup cashews, 0.33 cup pistachios and 0.33 cup walnuts on low for 5 minutes until crisp, then cool and crush to a coarse rubble.
In the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, toast the 3 tbsp melon seeds and 0.25 cup dried cranberries for 1 minute until the seeds puff.
Off the heat, knead the date paste, nut rubble, melon seeds, cranberries, 1.5 tsp cardamom and the 2 tbsp Anveshan Honey into a firm, richly studded dough.
Grease your palms and roll generous 2 tbsp portions into about 14 large ladoos.
Press a torn square of silver leaf onto each ladoo and rest for 20 minutes until set.
tips: Chop the cranberries so no single ladoo gets an overly tart pocket; distribute them evenly through the dough.
Apply silver leaf with the tip of a dry knife rather than your fingers, which make it crumple and stick.
For gifting, seat each ladoo in a foil cup; they hold for two weeks refrigerated.
variations.servingSuggestion: Present in a Diwali mithai box with an assortment of ladoos, or serve one on a small plate with masala doodh to festive guests.

variations.name: Kashmiri Festive Dry Fruit Ladoo
variations.description: A wedding-grade Kashmiri dry-fruit ladoo lavish with walnuts, figs, apricots and a doubled hit of saffron. Warmed with fennel and dry ginger, it is the opulent cold-season sweet of Valley celebrations.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: generous ghee blooms the doubled saffron and enriches the festive mix

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: a festive double dose of Kashmiri saffron for glow and aroma

steps: Finely chop the 1 cup dates, 0.5 cup figs and 0.33 cup apricots, then warm 2 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee and cook them on low for 6 minutes, mashing, into a single glossy mass.
Warm the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crush the 0.5 tsp Anveshan Saffron into it and let it bloom for 30 seconds until the ghee is a deep amber.
Dry-roast the 0.66 cup walnuts, 0.5 cup almonds and 1 tsp fennel for 5 minutes until crisp and fragrant, then crush to a coarse rubble.
Off the heat, knead the fruit mass, nut rubble, saffron ghee, 0.5 tsp dry ginger and 1.5 tsp cardamom into a firm, saffron-streaked dough.
Roll generous 2 tbsp portions into about 14 balls and press chopped pistachios onto each for a jewelled top.
Rest the ladoos for 20 minutes until the rich fruit paste sets.
tips: Snip the apricots and figs small so the loaded dough rolls into smooth balls without splitting.
Reserve a few saffron strands to lay on top of each ladoo for a visible festive flourish.
The high dried-fruit content keeps these moist and good for two weeks refrigerated.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at a winter wedding on a walnut-wood platter, each glowing ladoo paired with saffron kahwa.

variations.name: Kerala Festive Dry Fruit Ladoo
variations.description: An Onam-worthy dry-fruit ladoo where dates, cashews and raisins are bound with double-roasted coconut and coconut oil, then rolled in coconut flakes. It carries the fragrance of a festive Kerala payasam in a handheld sweet.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed coconut oil for roasting the coconut to a festive gold

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee to fry the cashews to a rich festive sheen

steps: Warm the 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and fry the 0.66 cup cashews and 0.33 cup raisins on low heat for 2 minutes until the cashews are golden and the raisins swell, then lift out.
Add the 4 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and roast 1 cup of the desiccated coconut for 5 minutes to a deep festive gold, reserving 0.25 cup for coating.
Pit and chop the 1.5 cups dates plus the extra 0.25 cup, add to the coconut and cook on low for 5 minutes, mashing, into a thick sticky mass.
Off the heat, mix in the fried cashews and raisins, 3 tbsp toasted sesame, 1.5 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp dry ginger into a firm coconut-rich dough.
Roll generous 2 tbsp portions into about 14 balls and roll each in the reserved desiccated coconut.
Rest for 20 minutes so the festive coconut ladoos set firm.
tips: Roast the larger batch of coconut to a deeper gold for festive flavour, but keep the coating coconut raw and white for contrast.
Coat the ladoos while just warm so the coconut clings evenly for a snowy finish.
Use desiccated coconut for a big festive batch so it keeps two weeks even in humid weather.
variations.servingSuggestion: Set out during the Onam sadya as a finishing sweet, the coconut and cardamom closing the banana-leaf feast.

variations.name: Malwa Festive Dry Fruit Ladoo
variations.description: A festive Sankranti dry-fruit ladoo where dates and nuts meet a generous heap of roasted peanuts, sesame and jaggery in the region's til-gul spirit. Warming, chunky and celebratory, it is winter-festival food from Madhya Pradesh.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a festive measure of ghee to enrich the rustic peanut base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery, peanut and sesame make the celebratory Sankranti trio

steps: Dry-roast the 0.75 cup peanuts on low heat for 5 minutes until the skins crack, rub them off and crush the peanuts coarsely with the 0.5 cup almonds.
In the same pan toast the 4 tbsp sesame, 2 tbsp poppy seeds and 0.33 cup grated dry coconut for 3 minutes until golden and fragrant, then set aside.
Pit and chop the 1 cup dates, warm 2 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee and cook them on low for 4 minutes into a paste, then stir in the 0.5 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder until it melts.
Off the heat, add the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, the crushed peanuts and almonds, toasted seeds and coconut, 1.5 tsp cardamom and 0.5 tsp dry ginger, kneading into a firm chunky dough.
Press generous 2 tbsp portions hard into about 14 sturdy festive ladoos.
Cool for 20 minutes until they set into a dense, satisfying bite.
tips: Roll a few finished ladoos in extra toasted sesame for a classic til-gul festive look.
Keep the peanut and almond crush coarse so the celebration ladoo stays chunky and textured.
These robust ladoos are ideal for gifting and keep for a full month in a sealed tin.
variations.servingSuggestion: Share during Makar Sankranti with the customary greeting, alongside hot jaggery tea against the winter cold.

variations.name: Gujarati Festive Dry Fruit Ladoo
variations.description: A festive gaund-paak style Gujarati ladoo, richer than the everyday tonic version, loaded with fried gum, five nuts and jaggery and warmed with dry ginger and pepper. It is the celebratory winter mithai served at Gujarati gatherings and to new mothers.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: generous ghee to fry a festive quantity of gum and carry the spices

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery is the traditional sweetener of festive Gujarati gaund ladoo

steps: Warm 4 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee on low heat and fry the 4 tbsp gond in batches for about 1 minute each until they puff and crisp, then crush them coarsely.
In the same ghee roast the 0.5 cup almonds, 0.5 cup cashews and 0.25 cup pistachios for 4 minutes until golden, crush coarsely, then toast the 0.5 cup grated dry coconut for 2 minutes.
Pit and chop the 1 cup dates, add the remaining ghee and cook on low for 4 minutes into a paste, then stir in the 0.66 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder until it melts smoothly.
Off the heat, knead the date-jaggery mass with the crushed gum, nuts, coconut, 1 tsp dry ginger, 1.5 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp black pepper into a firm festive dough.
Grease your palms and press generous 2 tbsp portions into about 14 dense round ladoos.
Rest for 25 minutes until the gum-set festive ladoos firm up completely.
tips: Fry the gond in small batches so every piece puffs crisp, giving the festive ladoo its signature crackle.
Keep the dry ginger and pepper generous; they define the warming, restorative gaund-ladoo character.
These rich ladoos keep for a month and make a thoughtful festive gift for winter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at a Gujarati winter gathering with warm saffron milk, in the tradition of celebratory strength-building sweets.

variations.name: Classic Festive Gajar Halwa
variations.description: A shahi, celebration-grade carrot halwa where the milk is first infused with whole cardamom, clove and cinnamon before the carrots go in, then enriched heavily with mawa and a generous handful of mixed dry fruit. It is denser, more perfumed and more indulgent than an everyday halwa, built for a Diwali or wedding thali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the whole spices, sautes the carrots and fries the dry fruit for a festive richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined sugar replacing white sugar, sweetening the halwa cleanly for a festive spread

steps: Bring 1.25 litre full-fat milk to a boil with 5 crushed cardamom pods, 3 cloves and a 1 inch cinnamon stick, and let it infuse on low for 5 minutes.
Add 1.25 kg finely grated red carrots to the spiced milk and simmer 32 minutes on medium, stirring often until the milk reduces to a thick clinging mass.
Fish out the whole spices, add 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee, and saute the carrots 10 minutes until deep red and glossy.
Crumble in 1 cup mawa and cook 5 minutes until it melts and coats every strand.
Lower the heat and stir in 1 cup Anveshan Khandsari with 0.75 tsp cardamom powder, cooking 7 minutes until the released liquid dries and the halwa turns thick.
Fry 0.75 cup mixed nuts and 3 tbsp raisins in a little ghee until golden, fold most through, and cook 3 minutes until the ghee separates.
Garnish generously with the reserved fried nuts and serve hot.
tips: Infusing the milk with whole spices first is what lifts this from everyday to festive; strain them before adding sugar.
Mawa can catch quickly, so keep the flame low and stir continuously once it goes in.
Make it a day ahead, as the flavours deepen overnight; just reheat gently with a spoon of ghee.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile into a decorative copper handi, blanket with slivered pistachios and silver leaf, and serve as the centrepiece sweet of a festive dinner.

variations.name: Kashmiri Festive Gajar Halwa
variations.description: A saffron-drenched celebration halwa from the valley, lavished with walnuts, almonds and a warming trace of dry ginger and fennel. The saffron turns it a jewel-like amber, and the abundance of dry fruit reflects the Kashmiri festive habit of not holding back.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: carries the saffron and toasts the walnuts for a festive Kashmiri depth

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk to flood the halwa with amber colour and a honeyed festive aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined sugar that sweetens without dulling the prized saffron

steps: Steep 0.75 tsp Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 4 tbsp of warm milk taken from the litre and set aside to bloom.
Simmer 1.25 kg grated red carrots with the rest of the full-fat milk for 33 minutes on medium until the milk cooks down to a thick coating.
Add 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee and saute the carrots 10 minutes until they turn glossy and deeply coloured.
Crumble in 0.75 cup mawa, cook 4 minutes, then pour in the bloomed saffron milk and stir until the halwa glows amber.
Reduce the flame and add 1 cup Anveshan Khandsari with 0.5 tsp fennel powder and 0.25 tsp dry ginger, cooking 7 minutes until thick.
Toast 0.5 cup walnuts and 0.33 cup almonds in a little ghee, fold most through, and cook 3 minutes until the ghee separates.
Finish with the reserved nuts and serve hot.
tips: Fennel powder is the distinctive valley touch here; grind it fresh for a brighter aroma.
Do not boil the saffron directly, as gentle steeping in warm milk gives a truer colour and scent.
Break the walnuts coarse so you get pockets of crunch throughout the halwa.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm in walnut-wood bowls with an extra pinch of saffron on top to close a Kashmiri festive meal.

variations.name: Awadhi Festive Gajar Halwa
variations.description: The nawabi festive halwa is all fragrance and finesse, its carrots slow-cooked in reduced milk then lifted with kewra, rose and a touch of screwpine. Richly studded with chironji and pistachio and finished in silver leaf, it is the perfumed sweet that closes a Lucknawi celebration.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the nawabi fat that sautes the carrots and locks in the kewra and rose aromas

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined sugar chosen so the delicate festive perfumes stay in the foreground

steps: Simmer 1.25 kg finely grated red carrots with 1 litre full-fat milk for 32 minutes on medium until the milk reduces to a thick mass.
Add 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee and saute the carrots 10 minutes until glossy and rich in colour.
Crumble in 1 cup mawa and cook 5 minutes until it melts fully into the halwa.
Turn the heat low and stir in 1 cup Anveshan Khandsari, cooking 7 minutes until the moisture dries and the mixture thickens.
Fry 3 tbsp chironji seeds and half the pistachios in a little ghee until pale gold and fold them through.
Switch off the flame, then stir in 1.5 tsp kewra water and 1 tsp rosewater to keep their perfume intact.
Spread into a tray, lay silver leaf and the remaining pistachios on top, and serve warm.
tips: Both kewra and rose are strong, so add them off the heat and taste before adding more.
Chironji seeds are the nawabi signature garnish; a light fry deepens their nutty flavour.
Keep this halwa thick and set enough to cut into diamonds for an elegant presentation.
variations.servingSuggestion: Cut into diamonds on a silver platter, dot with rose petals, and serve as the closing sweet after a royal Awadhi feast.

variations.name: Malwa Festive Gajar Halwa
variations.description: The Malwa festive table folds roasted peanuts and jaggery into its carrot halwa, giving a rustic crunch and a deep caramel warmth. Heartier and less dairy-heavy than northern versions, it reflects the plateau's love of groundnut in celebration sweets.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: sautes the carrots and roasts the peanuts so their aromas meld into the halwa

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the Malwa festive sweetener whose caramel depth complements the roasted peanuts

steps: Simmer 1.25 kg grated red carrots with 0.75 litre full-fat milk for 28 minutes on medium until the milk dries down and clings to the carrots.
Add 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee and saute the carrots 10 minutes until they turn glossy and sweet-smelling.
Coarsely crush 0.66 cup roasted peanuts, keep 3 tbsp aside, and roast the rest with 0.33 cup dry coconut slivers in the pan for 3 minutes.
Crumble in 0.75 cup mawa and cook 4 minutes until melted through.
Lower the flame and stir in 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 0.75 tsp cardamom, cooking 6 minutes until the halwa thickens and glistens.
Fold in 0.33 cup slivered almonds, cook 3 minutes until the ghee separates, and take off the heat.
Top with the reserved crushed peanuts and serve hot.
tips: Rub the skins off the roasted peanuts for a cleaner taste and prettier golden colour.
Add jaggery on low heat only, so the mawa and dairy do not split.
Keep the peanuts coarsely crushed to preserve the signature Malwa crunch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm in earthen bowls with a cup of masala chai, a hearty festive sweet for cold plateau nights.

variations.name: Gujarati Festive Gajar Halwa
variations.description: Gujarat's festive carrot halwa leans on jaggery and a hint of nutmeg, cooked drier and denser to set into soft squares for the sweet box. Studded with charoli and almond, it carries the wholesome, homely elegance of Kathiawadi celebration mithai.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: sautes the carrots and keeps the jaggery pliable so the halwa sets smooth

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the festive Gujarati sweetener that gives a bronze colour and molasses richness

steps: Simmer 1.25 kg grated red carrots with 0.75 litre full-fat milk for 30 minutes on medium until the milk is almost fully absorbed.
Add 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee and roast the carrots 10 minutes until they turn a rich reddish-brown.
Crumble in 0.75 cup mawa and cook 4 minutes until it blends smoothly into the mixture.
Lower the flame and stir in 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder, cooking 7 minutes until the released liquid dries and the halwa is thick enough to hold shape.
Mix in 0.5 tsp cardamom, 0.25 tsp nutmeg and 3 tbsp charoli seeds, cooking 3 minutes until fragrant.
Fold in 0.33 cup slivered almonds, cook 2 minutes until the ghee separates, and remove from heat.
Press into a greased tray, cool slightly, and cut into squares to serve.
tips: Cook this version drier than usual so it firms up enough to slice into festive squares.
Add jaggery only after the dairy has reduced to prevent curdling.
Freshly grated nutmeg makes all the difference against the jaggery's depth.
variations.servingSuggestion: Cut into neat squares, dust with charoli, and arrange in a festive sweet box alongside other Gujarati mithai.

variations.name: Classic Festive Ghee Rice
variations.description: A celebration-scale ghee rice made lavish with extra Anveshan ghee, a shower of golden fried onions and a generous mix of cashews, almonds and raisins. Cooked for a crowd, each grain is fragrant, glossy and rich enough to anchor a full festive spread.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A festive pot is generous with bilona ghee; it fries the nuts, browns the onions and glosses every grain.

steps: Rinse 3 cups basmati until clear, soak 20 minutes and drain thoroughly so the larger batch still cooks up light and separate.
Heat 5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a large heavy pot and fry 3 tbsp cashews, 2 tbsp almonds and 2 tbsp raisins in batches until golden, about 2 minutes, then remove and reserve.
In the same ghee crackle 1.5 tsp cumin, 3 bay leaves, 6 cardamom, 6 cloves and 2 inch cinnamon for 40 seconds until the pot is intensely fragrant.
Add 3 thinly sliced onions and fry over medium heat until deep golden brown, about 12 minutes, then stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute more.
Add the drained rice and toast for 3 minutes until glossy, then pour in 4.5 cups hot water and 2 tsp salt and bring to a vigorous boil.
Cover, cook on the lowest heat 14 minutes, rest 8 minutes off the heat, then fluff and fold through the fried nuts, raisins and 3 tbsp torn mint.
tips: For a crowd, cook in the widest pot you have so the deeper rice bed still steams evenly without the base compacting.
Reserve a few of the crispest onions and nuts to scatter on top at the table for a generous festive look.
The rice holds well covered for 30 minutes; a warm oven at its lowest setting keeps it fluffy without drying.
variations.servingSuggestion: Present as the centrepiece with a rich korma, a raita studded with pomegranate, and lime wedges around the platter.

variations.name: Awadhi Kewra Ghee Rice
variations.description: Lucknow's refined moti pulao, its perfume built on kewra water and a delicate whole-spice potli, cooked in Anveshan ghee for a courtly softness. Understated and elegant, it is the fragrant white rice of an Awadhi dawat, meant to let the aroma speak.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Awadhi cooking prizes ghee for its clean richness that never masks the kewra perfume.

steps: Rinse 3 cups basmati until clear, soak 20 minutes and drain; loosely tie 5 cardamom, 5 cloves, 2 inch cinnamon, 1 black cardamom, 1 mace blade and 2 bay leaves in a small muslin potli.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide pot and fry 3 tbsp cashews to a pale gold, about 90 seconds, then lift them out for the garnish.
Fry 2 thinly sliced onions in the ghee until just golden, about 8 minutes, keeping them soft rather than crisp so the pulao stays pale and elegant.
Add the drained rice and toast gently 3 minutes, then pour in 4.5 cups water, drop in the spice potli and add 2 tsp salt and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 14 minutes until the water is absorbed, then remove the potli and rest the pot 8 minutes off the heat.
Sprinkle 1 tsp kewra water over the surface, fluff very gently and top with the fried cashews just before serving.
tips: The spice potli lets you perfume the rice then remove every hard whole spice, giving the clean grain Awadhi cooks want.
Kewra is potent; a single teaspoon added at the end is plenty, and more will turn the rice soapy.
Fluff with a flat spatula and a light hand, as long basmati grains snap easily when hot.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a mild shahi paneer or murgh korma and a saffron-flecked boondi raita to match its courtly restraint.

variations.name: Hyderabadi Saffron Ghee Rice
variations.description: A dum-style festive rice from the Deccan, layered with Anveshan Kashmiri saffron milk, fried onions and mint, then sealed and steamed so the aromas mingle. Rich with ghee and warm spice, it carries the ceremony of a Hyderabadi kitchen without a full biryani's effort.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee drizzled between the layers is what gives dum rice its glossy, festive richness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: Steeped in warm milk, it streaks the rice gold and lends the signature Deccan aroma.

steps: Soak a pinch of Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 4 tbsp warm milk for 10 minutes; rinse and soak 3 cups basmati 30 minutes, then drain.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide pot and fry 3 thinly sliced onions until deep brown and crisp, about 14 minutes, then lift out half onto paper for layering.
To the remaining onions and ghee add 1 tsp shahi jeera, 5 cardamom, 5 cloves and 2 inch cinnamon and let them sizzle 30 seconds.
Boil 5 cups water with 2 tsp salt in a separate pan, add the drained rice and cook 6 minutes until 70 percent done, then drain the parboiled rice.
Layer the parboiled rice over the spiced onions, scatter the reserved fried onions and 4 tbsp mint, and drizzle the saffron milk and a little extra ghee over the top.
Cover with a tight lid, cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes to steam on dum, then rest 8 minutes and fold gently from the bottom to reveal the streaks of gold.
tips: Parboiling then steaming on dum is what gives each grain its length; do not let the rice cook past 70 percent in the water.
Seal the lid with a strip of dough or a heavy weight if it does not fit tightly, so no steam escapes.
Fold, never stir, the finished rice so the saffron stays in dramatic streaks rather than colouring everything uniformly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a tangy mirchi ka salan and a cucumber-onion raita, the classic Hyderabadi accompaniments.

variations.name: Malwa Peanut Ghee Rice
variations.description: A hearty festive pilaf from the Malwa plateau of Madhya Pradesh, crunchy with roasted peanuts and cooked in Anveshan ghee and wood-pressed groundnut oil. Earthy and satisfying, the double dose of groundnut gives it a distinct nutty richness for a celebratory thali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee rounds out the earthy peanut base and keeps the festive rice glossy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil doubles down on the peanut theme central to Malwa cooking.

steps: Rinse and soak 3 cups basmati for 20 minutes and drain; heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil and roast 0.5 cup raw peanuts until crisp and golden, about 4 minutes, then set aside.
Add 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee to the same pot and crackle 1.5 tsp cumin, 5 cloves, 4 cardamom and 2 inch cinnamon for 40 seconds until fragrant.
Add 2 sliced onions and 2 slit green chillies and fry 10 minutes until the onions are golden and sweet.
Stir in 0.25 tsp turmeric for 10 seconds, then add the drained rice and toast 3 minutes so the grains glisten with the spiced fat.
Pour in 4.5 cups water and 2 tsp salt, stir in half the roasted peanuts and bring to a rolling boil.
Cover, cook on the lowest heat 14 minutes, rest 8 minutes, then fluff and finish with the remaining peanuts and 3 tbsp coriander for crunch.
tips: Roasting the peanuts first in groundnut oil keeps them crisp; raw peanuts added to the water turn soft and lose their bite.
Splitting the peanuts between the pot and the garnish gives both an infused nuttiness and a fresh crunch on top.
Skins-on peanuts add colour and rustic character, but rub them off after roasting if you prefer a cleaner look.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a Malwi-style dal bafla or a simple kadhi, with a spoon of green chilli-garlic chutney on the side.

variations.name: Goan Kokum Ghee Rice
variations.description: A coastal festive rice with a gentle tang from kokum and the sweetness of Anveshan wood-pressed coconut oil alongside ghee. Curry leaves and green chilli give it a Konkan brightness, making it a refreshing, slightly sour counterpoint on a celebration table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee balances the sour kokum and rounds the coconut oil into a mellow festive base.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil brings the coastal Goan character that ghee alone cannot provide.

steps: Rinse and soak 3 cups basmati for 20 minutes and drain; soak 4 kokum petals in 3 tbsp warm water for 10 minutes to soften and release their tang.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil with 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat, add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and, once they pop, add 1 tsp cumin, 4 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon.
Toss in a sprig of curry leaves and 2 slit green chillies for 20 seconds, then add 2 sliced onions and fry 9 minutes until golden.
Add the drained rice and toast 3 minutes, then tuck in the softened kokum petals with their soaking water.
Pour in 4.5 cups water and 2 tsp salt, bring to a boil and taste for a faint, pleasant sourness balanced by salt.
Cover, cook on the lowest heat 14 minutes, rest 8 minutes, then fluff and remove the spent kokum petals before serving.
tips: Kokum lends a clean, fruity tang without the fibre of tamarind; four petals is enough for a subtle sourness across three cups of rice.
Remove the softened petals before serving so no one bites into a very sour piece.
A last drizzle of warm coconut oil over the fluffed rice deepens the coastal aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a Goan-style prawn or vegetable curry and a solkadhi (kokum-coconut cooler) to complete the Konkan theme.

variations.name: Classic Festive Lemon Rice
variations.description: A celebration-scale lemon rice made generous with fried cashews, extra peanuts and a double tempering, all brightened with plenty of fresh lemon. Cooked in Anveshan wood-pressed sesame oil and finished with ghee, it is the festive tangy rice for a large gathering.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil gives the big-batch tempering its authentic toasty backbone.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Extra ghee at the finish makes this festive version richer and glossier than an everyday plate.

steps: Spread 4.5 cups cooked rice on a large tray to cool and separate the grains thoroughly with a fork so the big batch tosses freely.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil in a large pan and fry 3 tbsp cashews and 4 tbsp peanuts in turn until golden, about 3 minutes total, then remove.
Pop 1.5 tsp mustard seeds in the oil, add 1.5 tsp urad dal and 1.5 tsp chana dal and fry until golden, about 45 seconds.
Add 3 slit green chillies, 3 dried red chillies, 1.5 inch grated ginger, 3 sprigs curry leaves and 0.5 tsp asafoetida, crackle 20 seconds, then take off the heat and stir in 0.75 tsp turmeric.
Return to low heat, add the cooled rice, the fried nuts and 1.5 tsp salt and toss gently for 3 minutes until every grain is an even bright yellow.
Turn off the heat, squeeze in the juice of 3 lemons and fold in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, tossing so the tang and richness spread evenly through the large batch.
tips: Use the widest pan you have so the deeper bed of rice heats and coats evenly without the grains crushing.
Fry the cashews and peanuts separately, as cashews colour faster and can burn while the peanuts are still raw.
For a party, keep the lemon slightly under and set wedges on the table so guests can sharpen their own portion.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as part of a festive tiffin spread with coconut chutney, medu vada and a pot of thick curd.

variations.name: Kerala Festive Coconut Lemon Rice
variations.description: A festive Malabar lemon rice lush with fresh grated coconut, fried cashews and raisins, all tempered in Anveshan wood-pressed coconut oil. Sweet, tangy and fragrant, it is the kind of citrus rice served at a Kerala sadya-style celebration.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil doubles the coconut theme and gives the festive rice its Kerala soul.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee enriches the celebration version and balances the coconut sweetness with the lemon.

steps: Spread 4.5 cups cooked rice to cool and separate the grains with a fork.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a large pan and fry 3 tbsp cashews and 2 tbsp raisins until the cashews are golden and the raisins plump, about 90 seconds, then remove.

Pop 1.5 tsp mustard seeds in the oil, add 1.5 tsp urad dal and fry to golden, then add 3 slit green chillies, 2 dried red chillies, 1.5 inch grated ginger and 3 sprigs curry leaves and crackle 20 seconds.
Off the heat stir in 0.75 tsp turmeric, then add 0.5 cup grated fresh coconut and warm through on low heat for 40 seconds until fragrant.
Add the cooled rice, the fried cashews and raisins and 1.5 tsp salt and toss gently for 3 minutes until evenly pale gold and flecked with coconut.
Turn off the heat, squeeze in the juice of 3 lemons and fold in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee so the coconut, nuts and citrus come together.
tips: Warm the fresh coconut only briefly so it keeps its sweet, moist bite against the tang.
The raisins add festive pops of sweetness; leave them out for a more savoury plate if you prefer.
A last drizzle of raw coconut oil over the top intensifies the Kerala aroma for guests.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a spiced Kerala vegetable stew and banana chips for a celebratory sadya-style meal.

variations.name: Karnataka Festive Chitranna
variations.description: A festive Karnataka chitranna with a deeper sourness from tamarind layered under the lemon, toasted coconut and a fragrant sesame-coconut spice powder. Cooked in Anveshan wood-pressed groundnut oil with ghee, it is the celebratory tangy rice of a Mysore feast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
