ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the everyday Karnataka fat and carries the tamarind temper well.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee mellows the tamarind-lemon sourness into a festive richness.

steps: Spread 4.5 cups cooked rice to cool; dry-roast 3 tbsp grated coconut with 1 tbsp sesame seeds until golden, then grind to a coarse powder and set aside.
Dissolve 1.5 tsp tamarind paste in 3 tbsp warm water; heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil and fry 4 tbsp peanuts until golden, about 3 minutes, then remove.
Pop 1.5 tsp mustard seeds, add 1.5 tsp urad dal and 1.5 tsp chana dal and fry to golden, then add 3 slit green chillies, 3 sprigs curry leaves and 0.5 tsp asafoetida and crackle 20 seconds.
Pour in the tamarind water with 0.75 tsp turmeric and simmer 2 minutes until it thickens to a glaze.
Add the cooled rice, fried peanuts, the coconut-sesame powder and 1.5 tsp salt and toss gently for 3 minutes until deeply coated and aromatic.
Turn off the heat, squeeze in the juice of 2 lemons and fold in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee so the tamarind depth and lemon lift both shine.
tips: The roasted coconut-sesame powder is what makes a festive chitranna special; grind it coarse for texture.
Cook the tamarind to a glaze so its raw sourness mellows, then add lemon last for a fresh finish.
This keeps and travels beautifully, so it is a fine make-ahead dish for a celebration.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of majjige huli (Karnataka yoghurt curry) and crisp happala for a full festive plate.

variations.name: Kashmiri Saffron Lemon Rice
variations.description: An opulent festive lemon rice tinted with Anveshan Kashmiri saffron and studded with almonds and walnuts, its citrus tang balanced by warm fennel. Cooked in Anveshan ghee, it is a fragrant, jewel-toned celebration rice for a special table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee is the clean, rich base that lets the saffron and lemon perfume the festive rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: Bloomed in warm milk, it streaks the rice gold and adds a luxurious festive aroma.

steps: Soak a pinch of Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk for 10 minutes; spread 4.5 cups cooked rice to cool and fork it loose.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a large pan and lightly toast 3 tbsp slivered almonds and 2 tbsp walnuts until golden, about 2 minutes, then remove.
Add 1 tsp fennel, 1 tsp cumin and 3 lightly crushed cardamom pods to the ghee and let them crackle 30 seconds until sweetly fragrant.
Add 2 slit green chillies and fry 20 seconds, then take off the heat and stir in 0.25 tsp turmeric so the rice takes a soft gold rather than a strong yellow.
Return to low heat, add the cooled rice and 1.5 tsp salt and toss for 2 minutes, then drizzle over the saffron milk and toss gently so it streaks the grains.
Turn off the heat, squeeze in the juice of 2 lemons and fold through the toasted nuts, keeping the saffron in visible streaks.
tips: Keep the turmeric minimal so the saffron colour is not muddied; the gold streaks should show clearly.
Toast the nuts gently and add them last so they stay crunchy against the soft rice.
This delicate, fragrant version pairs best with mild dishes that will not overpower the saffron.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a mild yoghurt-based dum aloo and a scatter of pomegranate seeds for a jewelled festive look.

variations.name: Gujarati Festive Sweet Lemon Rice
variations.description: A festive Gujarati lemon rice balancing bright citrus with Anveshan jaggery powder and a shower of pomegranate and coriander. Tempered in ghee and wood-pressed groundnut oil with peanuts, it is a bright, sweet-sour rice for a celebration thali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee harmonises the sweet jaggery and sharp lemon into a festive balance.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the Gujarati staple and complements the roasted peanuts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery gives the signature Gujarati sweet-sour lift in place of white sugar.

steps: Spread 4.5 cups cooked rice to cool and fork it loose.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a large pan and fry 4 tbsp peanuts until crisp, about 3 minutes, then remove.
Pop 1.5 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp cumin, then add 3 slit green chillies, 1.5 inch grated ginger, 3 sprigs curry leaves and 0.5 tsp asafoetida and crackle 20 seconds.
Off the heat stir in 0.75 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, then return to low heat until the jaggery melts, about 30 seconds.
Add the cooled rice, fried peanuts and 1.5 tsp salt and toss gently for 3 minutes until evenly yellow and glossy.
Turn off the heat, squeeze in the juice of 3 lemons, fold in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then scatter 3 tbsp pomegranate seeds and 3 tbsp coriander over the top.
tips: Melt the jaggery into the warm oil so it disperses evenly through the large batch without clumping.
Add the pomegranate only at the end so the seeds stay crisp and jewel-bright for a festive look.
Keep the jaggery restrained so it merely balances the lemon rather than sweetening the whole dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of cool sweetened shrikhand and crisp fried papad for a complete Gujarati festive plate.

variations.name: Classic Festive Masala Khichdi
variations.description: A celebratory, dressed-up khichdi meant for festival tables, enriched with ghee-fried cashews, raisins and a fragrant whole-spice base. Softer and richer than the everyday version, it turns a humble rice-and-dal dish into something worthy of a Sankranti or Navratri spread.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Festive khichdi is generous with ghee, some for frying nuts and some to finish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Blended with ghee to fry the onions to a deep festive gold without scorching.

steps: Rinse 1 cup rice with 0.5 cup moong dal, soak 15 minutes and drain thoroughly.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot on medium and fry 0.25 cup cashews until golden, then add 2 tbsp raisins and fry for 15 seconds until they plump; scoop both out for garnish.
Add 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil to the same pot with 1 tsp cumin, 4 cloves, 3 cardamom pods and 1 inch cinnamon, and let them crackle for 30 seconds.
Add 1 large sliced onion and fry for 5 minutes until deep gold, then stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp garam masala for 20 seconds.
Add 1.25 cups mixed vegetables and the drained rice-dal, toss for 2 minutes, then pour in 4 cups hot water and 1.25 tsp salt.
Cover and simmer on low for 18 minutes until soft and fragrant, or pressure cook for 3 whistles with natural release.
Finish with the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and scatter the fried cashews and raisins over the top before serving.
tips: Fry the cashews and raisins first and reserve them, since stirring them in early makes the nuts soggy and the raisins dissolve.
For a festive golden colour, use a large onion fried patiently to a deep caramel rather than pale.
This khichdi reheats beautifully with a splash of milk or water, so it is ideal to make ahead for a gathering.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a festive thali with pineapple raita, a sweet-tangy tomato chutney and crisp fried papad.

variations.name: Awadhi Festive Masala Khichdi
variations.description: A regal Lucknowi take that treats khichdi like a light pulao, perfumed with kewra water, saffron and warm garam whole spices in the dum tradition. Delicate, floral and lavishly ghee-rich, it is the sort of refined khichdi that graced Nawabi tables.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Nawabi cooking is rich with ghee, layered through the spices and the dum finish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Steeped in warm milk to lend the khichdi its golden Awadhi elegance.

steps: Soak 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside; rinse 1 cup rice with 0.5 cup moong dal, soak 15 minutes and drain.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot on medium and add 1 tsp cumin, 1 black cardamom, 3 green cardamom, 4 cloves and 1 mace blade, letting them release their perfume for 30 seconds.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and half the fried onions, sauté for a minute, then stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric.
Add the drained rice and dal and toss gently for 2 minutes to coat every grain in the fragrant ghee.
Pour in 3.75 cups hot water with 1.25 tsp salt, bring to a boil, then drizzle in the saffron milk and 0.5 tsp kewra water.
Cover with a tight lid, lower the heat to the minimum and cook on dum for 18 minutes, then rest undisturbed for 5 minutes.
Open gently, fold in the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, and garnish with the rest of the fried onions before serving.
tips: Kewra water is potent, so measure it carefully; even half a teaspoon perfumes the whole pot and more can turn it soapy.
Cooking on true dum with a tight lid traps the floral aromas, so seal the lid with a little atta dough if it does not fit snugly.
Keep the water slightly lower than a regular khichdi so the grains stay separate and pulao-like rather than mushy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling burani raita of whisked yogurt and garlic, and a side of sheermal or ulte tawe ka paratha for a Nawabi feast.

variations.name: Kashmiri Festive Masala Khichdi
variations.description: A festive valley khichdi glowing with saffron and warmed by fennel, dry ginger and Kashmiri chilli for colour without fire. Studded with walnuts, a Kashmiri pantry staple, it is fragrant, golden and celebratory in the understated, aromatic style of the region.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Layered through the spices and finished on top in the ghee-rich Kashmiri manner.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Bloomed in warm milk for the signature golden hue and honeyed aroma.

steps: Steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk; rinse 1 cup rice with 0.5 cup moong dal, soak 15 minutes and drain.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot on medium and toast 0.33 cup chopped walnuts for a minute until fragrant, then lift out and reserve for the garnish.

In the same ghee crackle 1 tsp cumin, 3 cardamom pods and 3 cloves for 30 seconds, then add 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli, 1 tsp fennel powder and 0.5 tsp dry ginger, stirring gently for 15 seconds.
Add the drained rice and dal and toss for 2 minutes to coat, then pour in 4 cups hot water with 1.25 tsp salt.
Bring to a boil, cover and simmer on low for 18 minutes until soft, then fold in the saffron milk for colour and scent.
Drizzle over the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and rest the covered pot for 5 minutes off the heat.
Scatter the toasted walnuts over the top and serve the khichdi warm and golden.
tips: Toasting the walnuts before garnishing removes any raw bitterness and adds a lovely festive crunch to each spoonful.
Use genuine Kashmiri chilli for its deep red colour, since regular chilli powder would make the dish hot rather than merely vibrant.
The fennel and dry ginger duo is what gives this its unmistakable Kashmiri warmth, so do not substitute garam masala here.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside a tangy Kashmiri radish-walnut chutney (muji chetin) and a bowl of yogurt to complete the festive valley meal.

variations.name: Odia Festive Masala Khichdi
variations.description: Modelled on the sacred temple khechudi of Puri, this Odia festive khichdi is tempered with panch phoron, the five-spice blend, and gently sweetened by whole spices and ghee. It is the very bhog offered to Lord Jagannath, soft and mildly spiced with a soulful, ritual simplicity.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Temple khechudi is famously ghee-laden, layered through the pot and the tadka.

steps: Rinse 1 cup rice with 0.5 cup moong dal, soak 15 minutes and drain in a colander.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot on medium and add 1 tbsp panch phoron, 2 bay leaves and 2 dried red chillies, letting the five seeds crackle and pop for about 30 seconds.
Add 1 tbsp grated ginger, 3 cardamom pods and 1 inch cinnamon and sauté for a minute, then stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp cumin powder.
Add the drained rice and dal along with 0.25 cup grated coconut and 2 tbsp cashews, tossing for 2 minutes so everything is glossed in the tempering.
Pour in 4.25 cups hot water and 1.25 tsp salt, bring to a boil, then cover and simmer on low for 18 minutes until soft and thick.
Warm the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and pour it over the cooked khechudi, folding it through for the temple-style richness.
Rest covered for 5 minutes so the aromas settle, then serve warm as bhog.
tips: Panch phoron must be added whole to hot ghee and never ground here, so it can crackle and release its fenugreek-fennel-nigella fragrance.
The grated coconut is traditional to Puri khechudi and gives a subtle sweetness, so use fresh coconut if you can.
Keep the dish soft and moist like temple bhog rather than dry, adding a little hot water if it firms up while resting.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Puri way with dalma, saga bhaja (stir-fried greens) and a spoon of tomato khajur chutney for a complete Jagannath bhog thali.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Festive Masala Khichdi
variations.description: A festive Maharashtrian khichdi built on the deep, sweet-savoury goda masala and enriched with cashews, coconut and a little extra ghee for special occasions. Darker and more aromatic than the everyday bowl, it is the kind of khichdi made for family feasts and satyanarayan pujas.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The regional base fat that carries the goda masala and fries the cashews.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Added generously at the end for a festive richness over the spiced khichdi.

steps: Rinse 1 cup rice with 0.5 cup moong dal, soak 15 minutes and drain in a colander.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a heavy pot on medium and fry 0.25 cup cashews for a minute until golden, then scoop out and reserve for the garnish.
In the same oil crackle 1 tsp cumin and 3 cloves for 20 seconds, add 1 sliced onion and fry for 4 minutes until golden.
Stir in 1.5 tbsp goda masala, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder and cook for 45 seconds, watching closely as the coconut-rich masala darkens fast.
Add 1 cup mixed vegetables, 0.25 cup grated coconut and the drained rice-dal, toss for 2 minutes, then pour in 3.75 cups hot water with 1.25 tsp salt.
Cover and simmer on low for 18 minutes until soft and fragrant, or pressure cook for 3 whistles with natural release.
Fold in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and scatter the fried cashews over the top before serving.
tips: Goda masala carries coconut and sesame that scorch quickly, so keep the heat moderate and add the water promptly once it smells done.
Fresh grated coconut in the body of the khichdi deepens the festive Maharashtrian character, so use it if you can.
Reserve the fried cashews for the top, since cashews stirred in early lose their crunch in the steam.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a festive thali with a bowl of sweet-sour tomato saar, thecha and crisp papad for a Maharashtrian celebration meal.

variations.name: Classic Festive Paneer Pulao
variations.description: Dressed up for a celebration, this paneer pulao layers golden-fried cubes with crisp onions, whole garam and toasted cashews. The rice is cooked in extra bilona ghee and finished with a saffron-milk glow for a party-ready sheen. It is the paneer rice you make when the table calls for something special.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A festive pulao wants generous bilona ghee to fry the paneer, onions and nuts to gold.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Saffron steeped in warm milk gives the celebration rice its golden streaks and aroma.

steps: Soak a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk, and separately soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes before draining, then cut 250 g paneer into 2 cm cubes.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot on medium heat, fry 12 cashews for 90 seconds until golden and reserve, then fry the paneer for 2 minutes until pale gold and reserve.
In the same ghee fry 2 sliced onions for 8 minutes until crisp and deep brown, then lift out half for garnish.
To the remaining onions add 4 cardamom pods, 4 cloves, 1 inch cinnamon and 1 bay leaf, sizzle 20 seconds, then add the drained rice and fold for 1 minute.
Pour in 2.5 cups water and 1 tsp salt, stir in the saffron milk and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes, then scatter the fried paneer and steam covered off the heat for 3 minutes.
Fluff gently and crown with the reserved fried onions and cashews before serving.
tips: Fry the onions slowly to a true brown; pale onions will not give the sweet crunch a festive plate needs.
Reserve half the onions and all the nuts for the top so the garnish stays crisp against the soft rice.
Make the saffron milk an hour ahead for a deeper colour and a stronger fragrance.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a large platter with pineapple raita and mint chutney, as the centrepiece of a vegetarian feast.

variations.name: Awadhi Festive Paneer Pulao
variations.description: The Lucknawi kitchen prizes perfume over heat, scenting this paneer pulao with kewra water, mace and a slow dum. The paneer turns silky against rice steamed under a sealed lid, drinking in every trace of the floral aroma. It is elegant and restrained, fit for a nawabi dastarkhwan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Awadhi dum cooking depends on pure bilona ghee to carry the kewra and mace through the rice.

steps: Soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, drain, and cut 250 g paneer into 2 cm cubes.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot on medium heat and fry the paneer for 2 minutes until pale gold, then remove and reserve.
To the ghee add 1 blade mace, 4 cardamom pods, 4 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon and sizzle for 20 seconds, then add 1 large sliced onion and fry for 6 minutes until light gold.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then lower the heat and add 3 tbsp whisked yogurt, stirring for 1 minute until smooth.
Add the drained rice and fold for 1 minute, then pour in 2.25 cups water and 1 tsp salt and bring to a boil.
Tuck the fried paneer into the rice, sprinkle 0.5 tsp kewra water over the surface, seal the lid tightly and cook on dum on the lowest heat for 13 minutes.
Rest 5 minutes off the heat, then lift the lid, fluff very gently and serve the fragrant rice.
tips: Measure the kewra carefully; a few extra drops will make the rice taste soapy rather than floral.
Whisk the yogurt smooth and add it on low heat so it enriches the base without curdling.
Seal the pot well for the dum stage, as escaping steam carries the delicate aroma away.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a smooth shahi paneer or burhani raita, in the layered nawabi style where the rice is the quiet star.

variations.name: Gujarati Festive Paneer Pulao
variations.description: Gujarat loves the play of sweet and savoury, so this festive paneer pulao is gently sweetened with Anveshan jaggery powder and warmed with a mild masala. The soft paneer and the jaggery meet a whisper of chilli for the balanced, celebratory rice served at Gujarati gatherings. Cashews and raisins seal its festive spirit.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee frays into the jaggery to give the pulao its glossy, festive sheen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery powder brings the signature Gujarati sweet-savoury balance in place of refined sugar.

steps: Soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, drain, and cut 250 g paneer into 2 cm cubes.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot on medium heat, fry 10 cashews and 2 tbsp raisins for 1 minute until golden and plump and reserve, then fry the paneer for 2 minutes and reserve.
In the same ghee crackle 1 tsp cumin, 3 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon for 20 seconds, then add 1 sliced medium onion and 1 slit green chilli and fry for 4 minutes until soft.
Add 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and let it melt for 30 seconds, then add the drained rice and fold for 1 minute.
Pour in 2.5 cups water and 1 tsp salt, boil once, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes.
Scatter the fried paneer over the top and steam covered off the heat for 3 minutes.
Fluff gently and finish with the reserved cashews and raisins before serving.
tips: Melt the jaggery only briefly with the onions; boiling it hard can make the rice sticky.
Keep the chilli whole and slit so the gentle sweetness stays in the foreground.
A pinch of ground clove added with the jaggery deepens the festive aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of kadhi and a spoon of tangy chhundo pickle, the sweet-sour partners a Gujarati table expects.

variations.name: Malwa Festive Paneer Pulao
variations.description: From the Malwa plateau of Madhya Pradesh comes a hearty paneer pulao rich with roasted peanuts and a rustic spice temper. The peanuts, fried in Anveshan wood-pressed groundnut oil, give the soft paneer a toasty, filling crunch loved at regional feasts. It is earthy, generous food made for a crowd.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil deepens the roasted peanut flavour central to Malwa cooking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon of bilona ghee at the end lends festive richness to the rustic rice.

steps: Soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, drain, and cut 250 g paneer into 2 cm cubes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pot on medium heat, fry 4 tbsp peanuts for 2 minutes until crisp and reserve half, then fry the paneer for 2 minutes and reserve.
To the oil add 1 tsp cumin and 2 broken dried red chillies and fry for 20 seconds, then add 1 large sliced onion and cook for 6 minutes until golden.
Lower the heat and add 1 tsp coriander powder and 0.5 tsp turmeric for 20 seconds, then add the drained rice and 0.5 tsp garam masala and fold for 1 minute.
Pour in 2.5 cups water and 1 tsp salt, boil once, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes.
Scatter the fried paneer and the peanuts left in the pot, steam covered off the heat for 3 minutes.
Drizzle 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, fluff gently and top with the reserved fried peanuts.
tips: Roast the peanuts until their skins loosen and they smell nutty for the fullest flavour.
Keep half the peanuts back for garnish so a crunchy contrast survives against the soft grains.
A squeeze of lemon at the table brightens the earthy, peanut-heavy rice nicely.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of spiced buttermilk (chaas) and a fried papad for a filling plateau-style meal.

variations.name: Hyderabadi Festive Paneer Pulao
variations.description: The Deccan royal kitchens give this paneer pulao a dum finish scented with saffron, mint and fried onions. Soft paneer rests in fragrant rice steamed under a sealed lid, soaking up the perfume of Anveshan Kashmiri saffron and warm spice. It borrows the drama of biryani while staying a gentle celebratory pulao.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Dum cooking in the Hyderabadi style needs plenty of bilona ghee to fry the onions and seal in aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Kashmiri saffron in warm milk gives the dum pulao its royal Deccan colour and scent.

steps: Soak a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk, soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes and drain, then cut 250 g paneer into 2 cm cubes.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot on medium heat, fry 2 sliced onions for 8 minutes until crisp and brown, then remove half for garnish.
Fry the paneer in the same ghee for 2 minutes until pale gold and reserve, then add 4 cardamom pods, 4 cloves and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute.
Lower the heat and stir in 3 tbsp whisked yogurt and 2 tbsp chopped mint for 1 minute, then add the drained rice and fold for 1 minute.
Pour in 2.25 cups water and 1 tsp salt, bring to a boil, then tuck in the fried paneer and drizzle the saffron milk over the surface.
Scatter the reserved fried onions and remaining 1 tbsp mint, seal the lid tightly and cook on dum on the lowest heat for 13 minutes.
Rest 5 minutes, then open, fluff very gently and serve the fragrant layered rice.
tips: Whisk the yogurt smooth and add it on low heat so it enriches the base without splitting.
Reserve the crispest fried onions for the dum layer so their sweetness perfumes the whole pot.
Do not stir during the dum stage; layering and steaming undisturbed gives the biryani-like aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with mirchi ka salan or a simple raita, plated so the golden saffron grains show against the white rice.

variations.name: Classic Festive Rava Kesari
variations.description: A shahi, celebration-grade kesari where the cooking water is infused with whole cardamom and a hint of edible camphor, the rava enriched with khoya and lavished with a full medley of fried dry fruit. Cooked slightly firmer so it can be cut into glossy saffron diamonds, it is the version reserved for weddings and grand pujas.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the rava, fries the dry fruit and gives the festive kesari its firm glossy set

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: generously bloomed to flood the festive kesari with deep golden colour and aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined sugar swapped for white sugar, giving a clean sweetness that sets firm

steps: Bloom 0.75 tsp Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 3 tbsp warm water and lightly crush 5 cardamom pods.
Heat 3 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee and fry 0.75 cup mixed nuts and 3 tbsp raisins until golden, then set them aside.
In the same ghee, roast 1.5 cups fine semolina on low for 7 minutes until it turns nutty and a shade deeper.
Boil 3.5 cups water with the crushed cardamom, the bloomed saffron and a pinch of edible camphor, then pour it into the rava in a stream while stirring hard, cooking 5 minutes until absorbed.
Crumble in 0.5 cup khoya and stir 3 minutes until it melts smoothly into the rava.
Add 2 cups Anveshan Khandsari and cook 5 minutes, stirring as it loosens and then thickens to a heavy, glossy mass.
Drizzle in the remaining ghee, fold in most of the fried nuts, cook 2 minutes until it leaves the sides, then spread in a greased tray and garnish with the rest before cutting into diamonds.
tips: Edible camphor is potent, so use a single small pinch, or the kesari will taste medicinal.
Cook it a little firmer than everyday kesari so it holds a clean cut once cooled.
Grease the tray and your knife with ghee for neat, non-sticking festive pieces.
variations.servingSuggestion: Arrange the saffron diamonds on a silver thali with slivered pistachios and silver leaf as a centrepiece festive sweet.

variations.name: Kerala Festive Rava Kesari
variations.description: Kerala's festive kesari is lush with coconut, the rava roasted in coconut oil and cooked in thick coconut milk for a creamy, tropical richness. Fried coconut chips and cashews crown it, making a celebration sweet that tastes distinctly of the coast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the wood-pressed Kerala fat that roasts the rava and deepens the festive coconut aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined sugar that sweetens cleanly and lets the rich coconut come through

steps: Heat 3 tbsp of the Anveshan Coconut Oil and fry 0.5 cup coconut chips, 0.33 cup cashews and 3 tbsp raisins until golden, then reserve them.
In the same oil, roast 1.5 cups fine semolina on low for 7 minutes until aromatic and lightly toasted.
Warm 2 cups thick coconut milk with 1.5 cups water to just below a boil in a separate pan.
Lower the flame under the rava and pour in the hot coconut liquid gradually while stirring vigorously, then cook 5 minutes until absorbed.
Stir in 2 cups Anveshan Khandsari with 0.75 tsp cardamom and cook 5 minutes as it loosens and thickens.
Drizzle in the remaining coconut oil, fold in most of the fried coconut and nuts, and cook 3 minutes until glossy.
Garnish with the reserved coconut chips and serve warm.
tips: Keep the flame gentle after the coconut milk goes in so it does not split under the heat.
Toast the coconut chips only to pale gold, as they crisp and brown very quickly.
Thick first-press coconut milk gives the richest festive body, thinned only if it tightens fast.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm at a festive sadya, or set in a tray, cut into squares, and pack into the sweet box.

variations.name: Gujarati Festive Rava Kesari
variations.description: The Gujarati festive sheera is jaggery-sweetened and milk-enriched, cooked dense enough to mound generously on the puja thali. Fragrant with nutmeg and studded with charoli and almond, it is the celebratory sheera of festival mornings.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the rava richly and keeps the festive jaggery sheera glossy, not sticky

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the Gujarati festive sweetener that lends a deep bronze colour and molasses richness

steps: Dissolve 1.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 1.5 cups warm water, strain, and keep the syrup ready.
Heat 3 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee and fry 0.33 cup slivered almonds and 3 tbsp charoli until golden, then set aside.
In the same ghee, roast 1.5 cups fine semolina on low for 7 minutes until nutty and fragrant.
Bring 2 cups full-fat milk to a gentle boil, lower the flame under the rava, and pour it in while stirring hard, cooking 5 minutes until absorbed.
Reduce the heat fully and pour in the strained jaggery syrup with 0.75 tsp cardamom and 0.33 tsp nutmeg, stirring 5 minutes until thick.
Drizzle in the remaining ghee, fold in most of the fried almonds and charoli, and cook 3 minutes until glossy and mounding.
Garnish with the reserved nuts and serve warm.
tips: Add jaggery syrup on the lowest flame after the milk is absorbed to keep the dairy from splitting.
Strain the jaggery well for a smooth sheera free of grit.
Cook it dense enough to hold a generous mound on the puja thali.
variations.servingSuggestion: Offer warm as prasad in leaf donas during festival puja, alongside crisp fried puris.

variations.name: Awadhi Festive Rava Kesari
variations.description: The nawabi festive kesari is perfumed and opulent, its saffron rava scented with kewra and rose, enriched with khoya and heaped with chironji and pistachio. Finished in silver leaf and cut into elegant pieces, it is the refined semolina sweet of a Lucknawi celebration.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the rava and binds the festive kewra and rose perfumes into the sweet

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed for a golden hue that sets off the nawabi kewra and rose aromas

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined sugar chosen so the delicate festive perfumes stay in the foreground

steps: Bloom 0.5 tsp Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 3 tbsp warm water and set aside.
Heat 3 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee and fry 3 tbsp chironji and half the pistachios until pale gold, then reserve.
In the same ghee, roast 1.5 cups fine semolina on low for 7 minutes until nutty.
Boil 3.5 cups water with the bloomed saffron, pour it into the rava while stirring hard, and cook 5 minutes until absorbed.
Crumble in 0.5 cup khoya, stir 3 minutes until melted, then add 2 cups Anveshan Khandsari and cook 5 minutes until thick and glossy.
Drizzle in the remaining ghee, switch off the flame, and stir in 1.5 tsp kewra water and 1 tsp rosewater.
Spread into a greased tray, top with silver leaf and the reserved nuts, cool slightly, and cut into pieces to serve.
tips: Add kewra and rose only off the heat, tasting as you go since both are strong.
Chironji lightly fried is the nawabi garnish; do not let it darken past gold.
Grease the knife with ghee so the perfumed pieces cut cleanly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the cut pieces on a silver platter dotted with rose petals to close a royal Awadhi feast.

variations.name: Malwa Festive Rava Kesari
variations.description: The Malwa festive kesari brings roasted peanuts and jaggery to the semolina sweet, giving a hearty crunch and caramel warmth. Enriched with dry coconut and cooked to a sturdy set, it is the celebration sweet of the Madhya Pradesh plateau.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the rava and peanuts together so their aromas mingle in the festive kesari

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the Malwa festive sweetener whose caramel depth complements roasted peanuts

steps: Dissolve 1.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 1.5 cups of the water, strain, and keep the syrup ready.
Coarsely crush 0.66 cup roasted peanuts, keeping 3 tbsp aside for garnish.
Heat 3 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee and fry 0.33 cup slivered almonds and 0.33 cup dry coconut slivers until golden, then reserve.
In the same ghee, roast 1.5 cups fine semolina on low for 7 minutes, add the crushed peanuts, and roast 2 minutes more.
Boil the remaining 2 cups water, pour it into the rava while stirring hard, and cook 5 minutes until absorbed.
Reduce the heat and add the strained jaggery syrup with 0.75 tsp cardamom, stirring 5 minutes until thick and sturdy.
Drizzle in the remaining ghee, fold in the fried nuts and coconut, and serve warm topped with the reserved peanuts.
tips: Skin the peanuts and crush them coarse to keep the festive crunch intact.
Add jaggery syrup on low heat so it melts in smoothly without seizing.
Cook it to a sturdy set so it can be cut into hearty squares for a crowd.
variations.servingSuggestion: Cut into generous squares and serve warm with masala chai at a plateau festival gathering.

variations.name: Classic Festive Tahri
variations.description: A celebratory tahri cooked in ghee with saffron, whole spices and a crown of fried dry fruits and paneer. Richer and more perfumed than the weekday version, it is the vegetable rice brought out for guests and festivals.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the festive fat that fries the paneer and dry fruits and enriches the grains

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk to give the festive rice its golden threads

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati, soak 20 minutes and drain, and steep a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk.
Heat 3.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and fry 150 g cubed paneer to gold, then 12 cashews and 2 tbsp raisins, lifting each out as it colours.
In the same ghee sizzle 4 cardamom pods and 1 inch cinnamon, then fry 1 sliced onion for 6 minutes until golden.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 1 diced potato and 1.5 cups mixed vegetables and saute 4 minutes, then stir in 1 tsp garam masala and 1.5 tsp salt.
Add the drained rice, toast 2 minutes, then pour in 2.5 cups hot water with the saffron milk and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 14 minutes until the water is absorbed and the grains are fluffy.
Rest 5 minutes, then fold in the fried paneer and crown with the cashews and raisins before serving.
tips: Fry the paneer and dry fruits first so they stay crisp against the soft festive rice.
Steep saffron in warm milk to draw its colour out fully before it goes into the pot.
For a party, finish the rice on a low dum for five extra minutes to marry the aromas.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a festive centrepiece with a rich paneer korma and a boondi raita, garnished with mint.

variations.name: Awadhi Festive Tahri
variations.description: A courtly Lucknawi festive tahri layered with birista, kewra and rose and cooked on a sealed dum. Delicate and floral, it treats the vegetable rice with the same care Awadh gives its finest biryanis.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the dum fat that seals the kewra and rose perfume into the rice

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati, soak 20 minutes and drain, and warm 3 tbsp milk with a crushed blade of mace.
Heat 3.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and sizzle 4 cardamom pods, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 2 diced potatoes and 1.5 cups vegetables and saute 5 minutes.
Lower the heat, whisk in 0.5 cup curd with 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1.5 tsp salt, and cook 3 minutes until thickened.
Add the drained rice, toast 2 minutes, then pour in 2.5 cups hot water and cook until most of it is absorbed.
Scatter half the birista over the rice and drizzle with 0.5 tsp kewra water, 0.5 tsp rose water and the mace milk.
Seal the pot with a tight lid or dough and cook on the lowest dum heat for 14 minutes so the floral steam settles in.
Rest 5 minutes, fluff gently, and finish with the remaining fried onions before serving.
tips: Add the kewra and rose water late and lightly, since hard boiling drives their perfume off.
A dough seal traps the delicate aromas far better than an ordinary lid.
Deep, evenly fried birista adds a sweetness that is central to the Awadhi character.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a shahi paneer or navratan korma and a cooling mint raita, dressed with a few rose petals.

variations.name: Kashmiri Festive Tahri
variations.description: A Kashmiri festive tahri rich with saffron, fennel and dry ginger and studded with walnuts, made in the meat-free Wazwan spirit. Floral, warming and mildly hot, it skips onion and garlic to let the aromatics shine.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the Wazwan fat that blooms fennel and dry ginger and toasts the walnuts

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: the soul of Kashmiri cooking, steeped for the rice's amber glow

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati, soak 20 minutes and drain, and steep a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk.
Heat 3.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and toast 10 chopped walnuts for 90 seconds until fragrant, then set them aside.
In the same ghee crackle 4 cardamom pods and 3 cloves, then off the heat stir in 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1.5 tsp fennel powder and 0.75 tsp dry ginger powder for 15 seconds.
Whisk in 0.5 cup curd off the flame, return to low heat, add 2 diced potatoes, 1.5 cups vegetables and 1.5 tsp salt, and cook 4 minutes.
Add the drained rice, toast 2 minutes, then pour in 2.25 cups hot water with the saffron milk and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 14 minutes until the liquid is absorbed and the grains are tender.
Rest 5 minutes, then fold in the toasted walnuts and fluff the red-gold rice before serving.
tips: Bloom the spice powders off the flame so the fennel keeps its sweetness and does not turn bitter.
Walnuts give the true Kashmiri richness, so choose them over cashews here.
Add the curd gradually and off the boil so it enriches the rice without curdling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a Kashmiri dum aloo and a walnut-radish salad, with extra saffron milk drizzled on top.

variations.name: Gujarati Festive Tahri
variations.description: A Gujarati festive tahri with the region's gentle sweet-savoury balance, jaggery-kissed and warmed with a clove-cinnamon temper, dotted with paneer and dry fruits. Soft, mildly sweet and aromatic, it suits a celebratory thali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the festive fat that softens the jaggery and warms the whole spices

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the signature Gujarati sweetness folded into celebratory rice

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati, soak 20 minutes and drain in a colander.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and fry 120 g cubed paneer and 12 cashews to gold, then lift them out to garnish.
In the same ghee crackle 4 cardamom pods, 4 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon, then add 2 slit green chillies.
Add 1 diced potato and 1.5 cups mixed vegetables with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt, and saute 4 minutes.
Add the drained rice, toast 2 minutes, then pour in 2.5 cups hot water and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 14 minutes until the water is absorbed and the grains are soft.
Rest 5 minutes, gently fold in 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and the fried paneer and cashews, and fluff before serving.
tips: Fold the jaggery in off the heat so it melts through without turning the rice sticky.
Keep the salt gentle so it balances rather than fights the mild sweetness.
A strand of saffron or a pinch of nutmeg dresses this up beautifully for a festival.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as part of a Gujarati thali with kadhi and a spicy sambharo to offset the sweetness.

variations.name: Bengali Festive Tahri
variations.description: A Bengali festive tahri in the niramish bhog style, cooked in ghee and mustard oil with whole garam masala, ginger and a hint of sugar, finished with fried cashews. Fragrant and gently sweet, it echoes the no-onion-no-garlic feast rice of Bengali pujas.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the bhog fat that enriches the niramish festive rice

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: a smoked spoon that lends the traditional Bengali sharpness beneath the ghee

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups gobindobhog gently, soak 15 minutes and drain, then dice 2 potatoes into cubes.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, add 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, and fry 12 cashews to gold, then remove.
Shallow-fry the potatoes and 1 cup cauliflower in the same fat for 5 minutes until golden, then lift them out.
Temper 2 bay leaves, 4 cardamom pods, 4 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon for 20 seconds, then add 1 tbsp ginger paste, 1.5 tsp cumin powder and 0.5 tsp turmeric.
Return the fried vegetables with 0.5 cup peas, the drained rice, 1.5 tsp salt and 1 tsp sugar, and toss 2 minutes.
Pour in 2.5 cups hot water, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on the lowest heat for 13 minutes.
Rest 5 minutes, scatter the fried cashews on top, and fluff the fragrant rice gently before serving.
tips: The niramish style skips onion and garlic, so ginger and whole garam masala carry the aroma.
A little mustard oil under the ghee keeps the traditional Bengali sharpness alive.
The teaspoon of sugar is festive Bengali balance, not meant to sweeten the rice outright.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as puja bhog with cholar dal and a tomato chutney, ending with a spoon of mishti.

variations.name: Classic Festive Til Ladoo
variations.description: A festive upgrade of the humble sesame ladoo, enriched with khoya, saffron and slivered dry fruits for a softer, more luxurious bite. Warm with cardamom and studded with nuts, it dresses the winter til ladoo up for Diwali and weddings.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Cooked to soft-ball stage to bind the sesame and enriched khoya

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasts the khoya and softens the festive ladoo to a richer crumb

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: Bloomed in warm milk to lend a festive golden hue and aroma

steps: Soak 1/4 teaspoon Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tablespoons warm milk for 10 minutes to release its colour.
Dry roast the 1.5 cups sesame seeds on low heat until golden and popping, about 5 minutes, and set aside.
Melt 2 tablespoons of the Anveshan Ghee and roast the 1/2 cup crumbled khoya on low heat for 4 minutes until soft and fragrant, then mix in the chopped mixed nuts.

In the same pan melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tablespoons water to the soft-ball stage, about 5 minutes, then stir in the sesame, khoya-nut mixture, saffron milk and 1 teaspoon cardamom powder.
Take the pan off the heat, cool for 2 minutes, grease your palms with the remaining ghee and roll 2 tablespoons at a time into 16 ladoos while warm.
Rest for 15 minutes to set; the khoya keeps them softer and richer than a plain til ladoo.
tips: Because of the fresh khoya, keep these refrigerated and eat within four days.
Bloom the saffron in warm milk so its colour streaks through the pale sesame mix.
If the khoya makes the mixture too soft to roll, chill it briefly before shaping.
variations.servingSuggestion: Arrange on a festive thali with a scatter of saffron and slivered pistachios for a Diwali dessert course.

variations.name: Kashmiri Saffron-Walnut Til Ladoo
variations.description: The valley perfumes its festive sesame ladoo with saffron and folds in its prized walnuts, warmed by dry ginger and cinnamon. Hearty and aromatic, it is a winter celebration sweet built to fortify against the cold.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Cooked to soft-ball stage to bind sesame and walnut

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Carries the saffron colour and greases the palms for shaping

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: A generous bloom for an unmistakably saffron-scented ladoo

steps: Soak 1/2 teaspoon Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tablespoons warm milk for 10 minutes until deeply coloured.
Dry roast the 1.5 cups sesame seeds on low heat until golden and popping, about 5 minutes, then roast the 1/2 cup walnuts for 2 minutes and chop them coarsely.
Combine the sesame, chopped walnuts, 1/2 teaspoon dry ginger powder and 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon powder in a bowl.
Melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 3 tablespoons water to the soft-ball stage, about 6 minutes, then stir in the sesame-walnut mixture and the saffron milk until coated.
Take off the heat, cool for 2 minutes, grease your palms with the 2 tablespoons Anveshan Ghee and roll 2 tablespoons at a time into 16 ladoos.
Rest the ladoos on a greased plate for 15 minutes until firm and set.
tips: Toast the walnuts only briefly so they do not turn bitter and overpower the saffron.
Add the saffron milk sparingly; too much liquid softens the set and shortens shelf life.
The dry ginger and cinnamon make this a warming winter ladoo, so keep both present.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cup of kahwa, doubling the saffron note across the sweet and the tea.

variations.name: Awadhi Kewra Til Ladoo
variations.description: Lucknow lends its nawabi perfume to the sesame ladoo, scenting it with kewra and rose and softening it with khoya for an elegant, melt-in-mouth festive sweet. Fine, fragrant and lightly sweet, it belongs on a dastarkhwan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A softer sweetness that lets the kewra and rose perfume lead

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasts the khoya and blooms the delicate floral waters

steps: Dry roast the 1.5 cups sesame seeds on low heat until golden and popping, about 5 minutes, and set aside.
Melt 2 tablespoons of the Anveshan Ghee and roast the 3/4 cup crumbled khoya on low heat for 5 minutes until soft and milky, then stir in the chopped pistachios.
In the same pan melt 3/4 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tablespoons water to the soft-ball stage, about 5 minutes, then mix in the sesame, khoya-pistachio mixture and 1 teaspoon cardamom powder.
Take the pan off the heat, cool for 2 minutes, then sprinkle in 1 teaspoon kewra water and 1/2 teaspoon rose water and mix so the perfume spreads.
Grease your palms with the remaining ghee and roll 2 tablespoons at a time into 16 soft ladoos.
Rest for 15 minutes to set; refrigerate as they contain fresh khoya.
tips: Add the kewra and rose off the heat so their delicate aromas are not cooked away.
Measure the kewra carefully; a heavy hand quickly turns perfumed into soapy.
These khoya-rich ladoos are best within three days and should be kept chilled.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on fine china with a scatter of rose petals to close an Awadhi feast, alongside cardamom chai.

variations.name: Bengali Tiler Naru
variations.description: Tiler naru is Bengal's festive sesame ball, made at Lakshmi Puja by cooking roasted til with jaggery to a sticky mass scented with cardamom and a bay leaf. Small, dark and deeply caramel, they are offered as bhog and shared warm.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Stands in for nolen gur to give the naru its dark, caramel character

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The Bengali touch for greasing the pan and palms while rolling

steps: Dry roast the 1.5 cups sesame seeds on low heat until golden and popping, about 5 minutes, then lightly roast the 1/4 cup desiccated coconut for a minute and set both aside.
Melt 1 tablespoon Anveshan Ghee in a kadai, drop in the bay leaf, then add 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 3 tablespoons water and cook on low, stirring, to a thick sticky syrup, about 6 minutes.
Discard the bay leaf, add the roasted sesame, coconut and 1 teaspoon cardamom powder and stir quickly until the mixture clumps together.
Take the pan off the heat and cool for 2 minutes until warm enough to touch but still pliable.
Rub the remaining ghee on your palms and roll 1.5 tablespoons at a time into 18 small naru.
Set them on a plate to cool for 15 minutes until firm.
tips: Roll the naru while warm, as they stiffen and crack once the jaggery cools fully.
Cook the jaggery to a thick sticky syrup, not the hard-crack stage, so the naru stay soft inside.
Tiler naru keep three to four days in a dry jar at room temperature.
variations.servingSuggestion: Place on the Lakshmi Puja bhog plate with narkel naru and fruit, then share warm with the family.

variations.name: Kerala Ellu-Coconut Til Ladoo
variations.description: Kerala marries sesame with roasted coconut and its own wood-pressed coconut oil for a tropical twist on the festive til ladoo. Jaggery and a hint of dry ginger bind it into a fragrant, rustic sweet for temple festivals.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The traditional sweetener that binds the sesame and coconut

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Deepens the coconut aroma in the Malabar style

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rounds the coconut oil and greases the palms for rolling

steps: Warm the 1 tablespoon Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil and fry the 3 tablespoons cashews until golden, then set aside.
Dry roast the 1 cup sesame seeds on low heat until golden and popping, about 5 minutes, then roast the 1 cup fresh grated coconut for 4 minutes until light gold and dry.

Melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 3 tablespoons water to a thick sticky syrup, about 6 minutes, then stir in the sesame, roasted coconut, fried cashews, 1/4 teaspoon dry ginger powder and 1 teaspoon cardamom powder.
Take the pan off the heat and cool for 2 minutes until warm and pliable.
Grease your palms with the 1 tablespoon Anveshan Ghee and roll 2 tablespoons at a time into 16 ladoos.
Rest the ladoos on a greased plate for 15 minutes until firm and set.
tips: Roast the fresh coconut until dry, or its moisture will keep the ladoos from setting.
The dry ginger keeps the sweetness light, a hallmark of Kerala festival sweets.
Eat within four days as the fresh coconut shortens the shelf life.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a banana leaf at a temple festival with strong Malabar filter coffee.

variations.name: Classic Festive Tomato Rice
variations.description: A celebration-grade tomato rice enriched with ghee-fried cashews, golden raisins and whole aromatic spices, closer to a light pulao than an everyday bowl. Fragrant, festive and colourful, it is dressed up for a special-occasion table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A generous pour of ghee fries the nuts and gives this festive pulao its rich, glossy finish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A hint of jaggery balances the tomato tang and lends a festive rounded sweetness.

steps: Rinse, soak and drain 1.5 cups basmati; heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and fry 15 cashews and 2 tbsp raisins for 2 minutes until golden and plump, then remove.
In the same ghee add 1 tsp cumin, 4 cardamom, 4 cloves, 1 inch cinnamon and 1 star anise and let them sizzle for 30 seconds.
Add 2 sliced onions and sauté for 6 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute.
Add 4 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt, cook for 8 minutes until pulpy, then stir in 0.75 tsp garam masala and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder.
Fold in the drained rice and toast for 2 minutes, then pour in 1.75 cups hot water and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes, rest 5 minutes, then fluff, fold in the fried nuts and raisins, and garnish with 3 tbsp mint.
tips: Fry the cashews and raisins first and reserve them so their crunch and sweetness survive to the final dish.
Whole spices are meant to perfume, not be eaten, so warn guests or fish out the larger pieces before serving.
A few drops of rosewater sprinkled at the resting stage lends an extra festive fragrance.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a platter garnished with fried onions and pomegranate, alongside a rich mixed-vegetable raita.

variations.name: Hyderabadi Zafrani Tomato Rice
variations.description: A Hyderabadi festive tomato rice glowing with Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron and layered with fried onions in the biryani tradition. Saffron milk, mint and whole spices give it a regal aroma, making it a fitting centrepiece for celebrations.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Kashmiri saffron steeped in warm milk gives the rice its golden streaks and regal aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee fries the onions to a deep gold and enriches this biryani-style tomato rice.

steps: Steep 0.25 tsp Anveshan Saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk for 10 minutes; separately rinse, soak and drain 1.5 cups basmati.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and fry 2 thinly sliced onions for 8 minutes until deep golden, then remove half for garnish.
To the remaining onions add 1 tsp shahi jeera, 4 cardamom, 4 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon and sizzle for 20 seconds, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 2 slit green chillies.
Add 4 chopped tomatoes, 0.25 cup whisked yogurt, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt, and cook for 8 minutes until the masala is thick and glossy.
Fold in the drained rice and 3 tbsp mint, toast for 2 minutes, then pour in 1.75 cups hot water and bring to a boil.
Drizzle over the saffron milk, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes, rest 5 minutes, then fluff and top with the reserved fried onions and 1 tbsp mint.
tips: Steep saffron in warm rather than hot milk to coax out maximum colour and fragrance without bitterness.
Whisk the yogurt smooth and add it off a high boil so it enriches the masala without splitting.
Reserve half the fried onions for the top; their sweetness and crunch are the signature Hyderabadi finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling mirchi ka salan or a simple raita and a wedge of lemon for a festive Hyderabadi spread.

variations.name: Awadhi Kewra Tomato Pulao
variations.description: A Lucknawi festive tomato pulao perfumed with kewra water and a touch of honey, layered with fried onions and dry fruits in nawabi style. Subtle, floral and gently sweet, it channels the refined dum cooking of Awadh.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee crisps the onions and dry fruits and gives the pulao its nawabi richness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: A drizzle of raw honey lends the delicate sweetness that balances the floral kewra.

steps: Rinse, soak and drain 1.5 cups basmati; heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and fry 2 sliced onions for 8 minutes until golden, then remove half for garnish.
Toast 3 tbsp almonds and raisins in the same ghee for 1 minute until the raisins swell, then set aside.
Add 1 tsp cumin, 4 cardamom, 3 cloves, 1 inch cinnamon and 1 mace blade to the ghee and sizzle for 20 seconds, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste.
Add 4 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt, and cook for 8 minutes until the masala turns soft and glossy.
Fold in the drained rice, toast for 2 minutes, then pour in 1.75 cups hot water mixed with 1 tbsp Anveshan Honey and bring to a boil.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp kewra water, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes, rest 5 minutes, then fluff and top with the fried onions and dry fruits.
tips: Kewra is intense, so add just half a teaspoon; overdoing it turns the pulao perfumey and soapy.
Stir the honey into the cooking water rather than the hot ghee so its aroma stays intact.
Fry the onions slowly to an even gold, as any scorching adds bitterness to this delicate dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a saffron-flecked burhani raita and warm sheermal for a true Awadhi feast.

variations.name: Gujarati Utsav Tomato Bhaat
variations.description: A festive Gujarati tomato bhaat with the signature sweet-savoury lift of Anveshan Jaggery Powder, brightened with peanuts, green peas and a squeeze of lemon. Colourful and celebratory, it captures the joyful balance of the Gujarati table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee toasts the peanuts and carries the mustard-cumin tempering of this festive bhaat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery gives the celebratory Gujarati sweet-savoury balance against the tangy tomato.

steps: Rinse, soak and drain 1.5 cups basmati; heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and fry 3 tbsp peanuts for 2 minutes until crunchy, then remove.
In the same ghee splutter 1 tsp mustard and 0.5 tsp cumin, add 12 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida, then sauté 1 sliced onion and 2 slit green chillies for 5 minutes until soft.
Add 4 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 cup green peas, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt, and cook for 8 minutes until the tomatoes soften and the peas turn tender.
Stir in 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, then fold in the drained rice and the fried peanuts and toast for 2 minutes.
Pour in 1.75 cups hot water, bring to a boil, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes.
Rest 5 minutes, then fold in 1 tbsp lemon juice, fluff, and garnish with 3 tbsp coriander before serving.
tips: Add the lemon juice only after cooking, since boiling dulls its brightness and can turn it faintly bitter.
Keep the peanuts crunchy by frying them first and folding them in with the rice, not the masala.
Taste for the sweet-savoury-tangy balance after mixing and nudge with jaggery or lemon as needed.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with cool boondi kadhi or plain curd and crisp fryums for a festive Gujarati thali.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Masale Tomato Bhaat
variations.description: A festive Maharashtrian masale bhaat built around tomatoes, goda masala and a generous scatter of cashews and peanuts. Ghee-rich and aromatic with dark, sweet-woody spice, it is a celebration dish served at weddings and feasts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee blooms the goda masala and fries the nuts for a festive, aromatic masale bhaat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery deepens the sweet-woody goda character typical of Maharashtrian feast rice.

steps: Rinse, soak and drain 1.5 cups basmati; heat 3.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and fry 12 cashews and 3 tbsp peanuts for 2 minutes until golden, then remove.
In the same ghee splutter 1 tsp mustard and 0.5 tsp cumin, add 3 cloves, 1 inch cinnamon, 12 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and sizzle for 20 seconds.
Add 1 sliced onion and sauté for 5 minutes until golden, then add 4 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt and cook for 8 minutes until pulpy.
Lower the heat, stir in 2 tsp goda masala and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and fry gently for 1 minute so the masala blooms without scorching.
Fold in the drained rice and the fried nuts, toast for 2 minutes, then pour in 1.75 cups hot water and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes, rest 5 minutes, then fluff and garnish with 3 tbsp coriander.
tips: Add goda masala on a low flame after the tomatoes cook down, as its dry coconut and flowers burn in seconds.
Fry the cashews and peanuts first and fold them in late so they stay crunchy in the finished bhaat.
A spoon of grated fresh coconut folded in at the end deepens the traditional Maharashtrian flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling tomato saar or plain curd and a crisp papad, wedding-feast style.

variations.name: Classic Quick Coconut Rice
variations.description: A fifteen-minute coconut rice built for leftover rice, using desiccated coconut and a fast one-pan temper. Light, nutty and fuss-free, it turns yesterday's rice into a fragrant meal in the time it takes to boil water.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the quick-temper fat that revives desiccated coconut with fresh aroma

steps: Fluff 4 cups of cooked, cooled rice with a fork so the grains loosen and no lumps remain.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and fry 10 cashews for 90 seconds until pale gold, then set them aside.
In the same oil pop 1 tsp mustard seeds, add 1 tbsp urad dal and 2 torn dried chillies, and fry until the dal is golden.
Toss in 2 slit green chillies and 12 curry leaves and let them crackle for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add 0.5 cup desiccated coconut and toast on low for 2 minutes until it smells sweet and just colours.
Fold in the rice, the fried cashews and 0.75 tsp salt, tossing gently for a minute so everything warms through evenly and serve at once.
tips: Sprinkle a teaspoon of water over dry leftover rice before tossing to keep the grains soft.
If using desiccated coconut, toast it low and slow so it does not turn dry and bitter.
A squeeze of lime at the end brightens the whole dish in seconds.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a quick fried papad and a spoon of any pickle for an easy weeknight plate.

variations.name: Tamil Nadu Quick Coconut Rice
variations.description: A speedy Tamil-style thengai sadam heavy on curry leaves and a quick roasted-gram temper, ready in minutes. Aromatic and lightly peppery, it captures the temple-rice character without the long cooling.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the quick fat that lets the curry-leaf perfume bloom fast

steps: Fluff 4 cups of cooked, cooled rice and keep it ready in a wide bowl.
Coarsely crush 0.5 tsp black pepper with 2 dried chillies so they will release a sharp warmth.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 2 tbsp roasted gram and fry 30 seconds until it smells nutty.
Throw in 20 curry leaves, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and the crushed pepper mix and let them sizzle 20 seconds until intensely fragrant.
Add 0.75 cup grated coconut and toast on low for 2 minutes until pale gold, stirring so it does not catch.
Fold in the rice and 0.75 tsp salt, toss for a minute so the coconut coats every grain, and serve warm.
tips: Roasted gram gives an instant nutty crunch without needing to fry raw dals.
A big handful of curry leaves is the shortcut to authentic temple-rice aroma.
Fresh coconut beats desiccated here, so grate it while the rice reheats if you can.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a quick potato fry and a bowl of curd, or pack warm into a lunchbox with lime pickle.

variations.name: Bengali Quick Coconut Rice
variations.description: A fast Bengali narkel bhat with a quick mustard-oil and panch-phoron temper and a touch of jaggery. Fragrant, mustard-sharp and gently sweet, it brings Bengal's festive rice to a weeknight in minutes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked briefly, it lends the quick rice its unmistakable Bengali sharpness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a gentle sweet note stirred in the Bengali way

steps: Fluff 4 cups of cooked, cooled rice and set it aside in a wide bowl.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, lower the flame, and fry 10 cashews to gold, then remove them.
In the same oil temper 1 tsp panch phoron, 2 dried chillies and 1 bay leaf for 20 seconds until the seeds pop.
Add grated 1 inch ginger and 0.75 cup grated coconut and toast on low for 2 minutes until pale gold.
Fold in the rice, the fried cashews, 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.75 tsp salt, tossing so the jaggery melts through.
Warm everything together for a minute so the mustard aroma runs through the grains, then serve at once.
tips: A quick smoke of the mustard oil is enough to soften its raw edge for a fast dish.
Keep the jaggery light, as it is meant only to round the mustard sharpness.
Panch phoron must pop before anything else goes in, or the temper will taste raw.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a simple aloo bhaja and a wedge of lime, or with a bowl of cholar dal for a fuller meal.

variations.name: Karnataka Quick Coconut Rice
variations.description: A quick coconut chitranna from Karnataka using ready tamarind paste for instant tang and a crunchy peanut temper. Bright, sour-nutty and lunchbox-ready, it comes together faster than a fresh chitranna.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the fast-frying Karnataka oil that crisps the peanuts and carries the tamarind

steps: Fluff 4 cups of cooked, cooled rice and keep it in a wide bowl ready to toss.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and roast 3 tbsp peanuts for 3 minutes until crunchy, then scoop them out.
In the same oil pop 1 tsp mustard seeds, add 1 tbsp chana dal and 2 slit green chillies, and fry until the dal turns golden.
Add 12 curry leaves and 0.5 tsp turmeric, then stir in 1.5 tsp tamarind paste loosened with 2 tbsp water and simmer 1 minute.
Add 0.5 cup grated coconut and toast for a minute until it soaks up the tangy temper.
Fold in the rice, the roasted peanuts and 0.75 tsp salt, tossing for a minute so the tamarind coats evenly, and serve warm.
tips: Ready tamarind paste cuts out the soaking, but simmer it briefly to lose the raw sharpness.
Add the peanuts last so they keep their crunch against the soft rice.
This one only improves after resting, so it is ideal to make ahead for tiffin.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thick curd and a fried sandige, or pack cold with a slit green chilli for a tangy office lunch.

variations.name: Andhra Quick Coconut Rice
variations.description: A quick, fiery Andhra coconut rice using a spoon of ready chilli powder and a garlic temper for instant heat. Hot, garlicky and fast, it delivers the Andhra kick without grinding a fresh podi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: the sturdy Andhra oil that carries the quick garlic-chilli heat

steps: Fluff 4 cups of cooked, cooled rice and keep it ready in a wide bowl.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, pop 1 tsp mustard and 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add 1 tbsp urad dal and fry to golden.
Add 6 crushed garlic cloves and 15 curry leaves and fry for 40 seconds until the garlic turns pale and aromatic.
Lower the heat, sprinkle in 1.5 tsp Guntur chilli powder and 0.25 tsp turmeric, and stir for 15 seconds so they bloom without burning.
Add 0.75 cup grated coconut and toast for a minute until it just colours and takes on the chilli.
Fold in the rice and 0.75 tsp salt, tossing for a minute until every grain glows red, and serve hot.
tips: Add the chilli powder off high heat so it colours the oil without scorching bitter.
Crushed fresh garlic gives far more punch here than paste.
Balance the heat at the table with a spoon of cool curd or a slice of banana.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling onion-curd raita and a fried papad to temper the chilli heat.

variations.name: Classic Quick Corn Pulao
variations.description: A weeknight rescue that skips the long soak and comes together in one pot in half an hour. A short 10-minute soak and a hot ghee temper still deliver fluffy grains studded with sweet corn. It is the fastest way to turn plain rice into something that feels cooked with care.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee gives a fast pulao instant aroma without any long marination or dum.

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati rice well and soak it for just 10 minutes while you chop the vegetables, then drain.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pressure cooker or pot on high heat and add 1 tsp cumin, 1 bay leaf and 3 cloves, letting them crackle for 15 seconds.
Add 1 sliced medium onion and fry for 3 minutes on high until the edges brown, then stir in 1 tsp ginger-garlic paste for 30 seconds.
Add 1 cup sweet corn and 0.5 tsp turmeric and saute for 1 minute, then fold in the drained rice for 30 seconds.
Pour in 2.5 cups water and 1 tsp salt and bring to a rolling boil.
Cover and cook on low for 12 minutes if using a pot, or pressure cook for 2 whistles and let the pressure release naturally.
Fluff with a fork and scatter 2 tbsp coriander leaves before serving.
tips: A short soak plus hot ghee is the trick to fluffy grains when you have no time for the full 20-minute rest.
If pressure cooking, reduce the water to 2.25 cups since less evaporates under pressure.
Keep frozen corn on hand; it goes straight in from the freezer and needs no thawing for a quick pulao.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a quick boondi raita stirred together in minutes and a store-bought pickle for an easy weeknight plate.

variations.name: Punjabi Quick Corn Pulao
variations.description: This speedy version keeps the Punjabi love of butter and garam masala but trims every slow step. A knob of butter melts into ghee-cooked rice for that dhaba richness in under half an hour. It is comfort food fast enough for the busiest evening.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee delivers the rich dhaba base instantly, no long cooking required.

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 10 minutes, then drain while the pot heats.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot on high heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin for 15 seconds.
Add 1 sliced medium onion and fry for 3 minutes until golden, then add 1 tsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 30 seconds.
Stir in 1 cup sweet corn and 0.5 tsp turmeric and saute for 1 minute, then fold in the drained rice and 0.5 tsp garam masala for 30 seconds.
Pour in 2.5 cups water and 1 tsp salt and bring to a hard boil.
Cover and cook on low for 12 minutes until the water is absorbed and the grains are tender.
Dot the top with 1 tbsp white butter, let it melt for a minute, then fluff and finish with 2 tbsp coriander leaves.
tips: Add the garam masala with the rice, not the onions, so its aroma stays fresh in a quick cook.
Let the butter melt from the heat of the rice rather than stirring it in, keeping the grains glossy.
Salted butter works in a pinch; just cut the added salt to three-quarters of a teaspoon.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sliced onion rings, a green chilli and a dollop of dahi for a fast, hearty dhaba-style plate.

variations.name: Tamil Quick Corn Pulao
variations.description: A brisk southern spin where a crackling temper of mustard, curry leaves and green chilli does the flavouring in seconds. Cooked in Anveshan wood-pressed sesame oil, the corn takes on a nutty, peppery lift with almost no effort. It is a quick pulao that tastes like a Tamil tiffin.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed sesame oil gives the quick temper its authentic nutty Tamil aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon of bilona ghee at the end rounds the sharp sesame oil into something mellow.

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 10 minutes, then drain.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pot on high heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal and fry for 30 seconds until the dal turns golden.
Add 12 curry leaves, 2 slit green chillies and 1 inch julienned ginger and let them crackle for 15 seconds.
Stir in 1 sliced medium onion and fry for 3 minutes until soft, then add 1 cup sweet corn and 0.5 tsp turmeric and saute for 1 minute.
Fold in the drained rice for 30 seconds, then pour in 2.5 cups water and 1 tsp salt and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on low for 12 minutes until the grains are tender and separate.
Rest 3 minutes, drizzle 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then fluff and serve hot.
tips: Fry the urad dal to golden before anything else; that nutty crunch is the heart of a Tamil temper.
Sesame oil has a strong flavour, so a single tablespoon of ghee at the end is enough to soften it.
Add a pinch of asafoetida with the mustard seeds for an even more authentic tiffin aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of thick curd and a spoon of tomato thokku, the way a Tamil quick meal is rounded off.

variations.name: Bengali Quick Corn Pulao
variations.description: A fast take on Bengal's gently sweet pulao, cooked in pungent Anveshan wood-pressed mustard oil with a pinch of sugar. Whole garam and a quick temper give the corn that sweet-savoury balance in a fraction of the usual time. It carries the spirit of a festive Bengali rice without the fuss.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil, smoked briefly, gives the fast pulao its signature Bengali pungency.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of bilona ghee balances the sharp mustard oil in the sweet-savoury Bengali way.

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 10 minutes, then drain.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pot until it just smokes, then lower the flame for 20 seconds to soften its bite.
Add 1 bay leaf, 3 cardamom pods and 3 cloves and let them puff for 15 seconds, then add 1 sliced medium onion and fry for 3 minutes until pale gold.
Stir in 1 cup sweet corn, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp sugar and saute for 1 minute until the sugar dissolves.
Fold in the drained rice for 30 seconds, then pour in 2.5 cups water and 1 tsp salt and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on low for 12 minutes until the grains are tender and lightly sweet.
Rest 3 minutes, drizzle 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then fluff gently and serve warm.
tips: Even in a hurry, smoke the mustard oil first; skipping this leaves a raw, bitter edge.
The sugar should be barely detectable, just enough to lift the corn, so measure it level.
Push the whole spices to the side of the pot before serving so no one bites into a clove.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a simple aloo bhaja (crisp potato fries) and a wedge of lime for a quick Bengali-style supper.

variations.name: Gujarati Quick Corn Pulao
variations.description: This fast Gujarati version leans on the region's love of a light sweet note from Anveshan jaggery powder against a mild masala. The corn's sweetness and the jaggery come together with a quick temper in under half an hour. It is gentle, homely and quick enough for a busy tiffin.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee melts into the jaggery for a quick sweet-savoury Gujarati base.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery powder brings the gentle Gujarati sweetness in place of refined sugar, no extra step needed.

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 10 minutes, then drain.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot on high heat, add 1 tsp cumin and 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and let them splutter for 20 seconds.
Add 8 curry leaves and 1 slit green chilli, fry for 10 seconds, then add 1 sliced medium onion and cook for 3 minutes until soft.
Stir in 1 cup sweet corn and 0.5 tsp turmeric and saute for 1 minute, then add 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and let it melt for 20 seconds.
Fold in the drained rice for 30 seconds, then pour in 2.5 cups water and 1 tsp salt and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on low for 12 minutes until the grains are tender and faintly sweet.
Rest 3 minutes, then fluff gently and serve warm.
tips: Add the jaggery just before the rice so it coats the corn without caramelising too hard.
A single slit green chilli keeps the mild sweet-savoury balance that defines Gujarati home cooking.
This travels well in a tiffin box as the gentle sweetness holds up even when the rice cools.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of plain chaas and a spoon of sweet chhundo for a light, quick Gujarati meal.

variations.name: Classic Quick Curd Rice
variations.description: A five-minute curd rice for busy days, built on warm leftover rice mashed with fresh curd and finished with a fast, single-pan tempering. It keeps the soul of thayir sadam while skipping the wait, ideal for a speedy lunchbox or a light dinner.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A quick ghee tempering is all this fast bowl needs to taste freshly made.

steps: Tip 3 cups warm cooked rice into a bowl and mash it lightly with a ladle for about 1 minute until softened.
Add 2 cups curd, 0.5 cup milk and 1 tsp salt and mix into a smooth, loose curd rice.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan over medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal and fry for 40 seconds until golden and spluttering.
Toss in 2 slit green chillies, 1 dried red chilli, 12 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and fry for 15 seconds until aromatic.
Pour the hot tempering over the curd rice and fold it through evenly.
Fold in 2 tbsp roasted peanuts, garnish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and 3 tbsp pomegranate seeds, and serve straight away or pack for lunch.
tips: Warm the leftover rice for 30 seconds first; cold fridge rice will not soften or turn creamy however hard you mash it.
If the rice was salted already, taste before adding the full teaspoon of salt to the curd.
Keep it loose, as even a quick curd rice thickens noticeably within the hour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a spoon of lime pickle and a couple of microwave-crisped papads for an instant, satisfying meal.

variations.name: Tamil Nadu Quick Thayir Sadam
variations.description: The classic Chennai lunchbox curd rice, streamlined for speed with a swift ghee tempering of mustard, urad dal and dried chilli. Grated carrot goes in for colour and a little crunch, keeping it fresh and travel-friendly.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee makes the quick tempering taste rich and traditional despite the speed.

steps: Mash 3 cups warm cooked rice in a bowl for a minute until soft and lump-free.
Fold in 2.5 cups curd, 0.5 cup milk, 1 tsp salt and 0.25 cup grated carrot for a loose, colourful base.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 1 tsp urad dal and fry until golden, about 40 seconds.
Add 2 dried red chillies, 1 chopped green chilli, 0.5 inch grated ginger, 12 curry leaves and 0.5 tsp asafoetida and fry for 15 seconds.
Pour the tempering over the curd rice and mix well so the carrot and spices spread evenly.
Serve immediately or pack into a tiffin for a ready lunch.
tips: The grated carrot needs no cooking; its slight crunch is exactly what a quick lunchbox curd rice wants.
Add a little extra curd if packing for lunch, as it firms up considerably by midday.
A pinch of hing straight into the curd, beyond the tempering, boosts the classic aroma in seconds.
variations.servingSuggestion: Tuck a small portion of tangy narthangai (citron) pickle beside it in the tiffin for the authentic school-lunch taste.

variations.name: Kerala Quick Thengai Thayir
variations.description: A speedy Malayali curd rice where grated coconut is folded straight in and a fast coconut-oil tempering brings instant fragrance. No grinding, no waiting, just soft rice, cool curd and that unmistakable Kerala aroma in ten minutes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
