This mild version is a good pick for children who find sharper lemon rice too sour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a glass of cool chaas and a scatter of sev over the top for crunch.

variations.name: Delhi Quick Masala Lemon Rice
variations.description: A North Indian quick lemon rice with a warming pinch of garam masala and browned onion in the ghee temper, lifted with fresh lemon. Robust and fast, it gives leftover rice a Delhi-kitchen character in ten minutes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee blooms the garam masala and browns the onion for a warm North Indian base.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A little groundnut oil lets the onion fry without the ghee browning too fast.

steps: Fork through 3 cups cooked rice to loosen the grains.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 15 seconds.
Add 1 sliced onion, 2 slit green chillies and 1 inch grated ginger and fry until the onion is golden, about 5 minutes.
Lower the heat and stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp garam masala and 0.25 tsp red chilli powder for 15 seconds so they bloom without burning.
Add the loosened rice and 1 tsp salt and toss for 2 minutes until the grains take on an even warm colour.
Turn off the heat, squeeze in the juice of 2 lemons and fold in 2 tbsp coriander so the citrus lifts the masala.
tips: Bloom the ground spices off a fierce boil for just 15 seconds so they perfume the rice without scorching.
Brown the onion well for sweetness; pale onion leaves the quick rice tasting raw.
A spoon of curd folded in at the end turns this into a mild, creamy masala rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling mint raita and thin onion rings dressed in lemon and chaat masala.

variations.name: Classic Masala Dosa
variations.description: The definitive Udupi-style crepe: a lacy, golden-crisp fermented rice-and-urad dosa wrapped around a soft, turmeric-yellow potato masala studded with a mustard-curry-leaf tempering. Crisp at the edges, pillowy where the filling sits, and built to be torn and dunked into chutney.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil crisps the dosa edges without any greasy aftertaste.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A brush of bilona ghee down the centre gives the classic nutty aroma and crackle.

steps: Boil 4 medium potatoes until fork-tender, about 15 minutes, then peel and coarsely crush them so a few soft lumps remain.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai over medium heat and splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds for 20 seconds, then add 0.25 tsp asafoetida, 12 curry leaves, 2 slit green chillies and grated 1 inch ginger and fry until fragrant.
Add 1 thinly sliced large onion and cook until soft and translucent, about 4 minutes, then stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp salt.
Fold in the crushed potatoes with a splash of water and cook 3 minutes until the masala is moist and holds together; keep it warm.
Heat a flat tava until a droplet of water skitters, wipe it with a halved onion, then pour a ladle of dosa batter and spread it thin in a spiral from the centre outward.
Drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and a little Anveshan Ghee around the edges and cook until the base is deep golden and crisp, about 2 minutes, without flipping.
Place 3 tbsp potato masala along the centre, fold the dosa over it and slide onto a plate to serve hot.
tips: For the crispest dosa, the tava must be hot enough that batter sizzles on contact but not smoking; sprinkle a few drops of water and wipe before each dosa to reset the temperature.
Leftover potato masala keeps 2 days refrigerated and makes an excellent stuffing for parathas or a quick sandwich.
If your batter is too thick to spread, loosen it with a tablespoon of water at a time until it flows like thin cream.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a trio of coconut chutney, tomato-onion chutney and a bowl of piping sambar, with an extra dish of Anveshan Ghee on the side for drizzling.

variations.name: Kerala Coconut Masala Dosa
variations.description: A Malabar-inflected dosa where the potato filling turns lush with fresh grated coconut and is cooked entirely in fragrant coconut oil. The coconut rounds the spice and lends a sweet, tropical depth you notice in the first bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil is the soul of this dosa, perfuming both the tempering and the crust.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A final smear of ghee balances the coconut sweetness with a savoury edge.

steps: Pressure-cook 4 medium potatoes for 3 whistles, cool, peel and break them into rough chunks.
Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan and pop 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 15 curry leaves, 3 slit green chillies and julienned 1 inch ginger and let them crackle for 30 seconds.
Slide in 1 sliced large onion and saute until glassy, about 5 minutes, then scatter in 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 cup fresh grated coconut and stir for a minute until the coconut smells toasty.
Add the potato chunks and 1.5 tsp salt, mash lightly with a splash of water and simmer 3 minutes so the coconut melds into the filling.
Heat a tava, splash and wipe it, then ladle batter and spread it into a thin round with the back of the ladle.
Trickle 1 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and a little Anveshan Ghee at the rim and cook undisturbed until lacy and browned, about 2 minutes.
Spoon a generous 3 tbsp of coconut potato masala over one half, fold, and serve immediately while crisp.
tips: Use only fresh or frozen-thawed grated coconut; desiccated coconut turns the filling dry and grainy.
Coconut oil solidifies below 24C, so warm the bottle in a bowl of hot water if it has set before you start.
A pinch of freshly cracked pepper stirred into the masala at the end deepens the Malabar character without adding raw heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a coconut-heavy green chutney and a small bowl of Kerala-style sambar spiked with drumstick, finishing the plate with a wedge of lime.

variations.name: Mysore Tamarind Masala Dosa
variations.description: The Karnataka classic, smeared inside with a fiery red garlic chutney and paired with a tangy-sweet tamarind potato masala mellowed by jaggery. Sweet, sour and hot land together, making it the most layered dosa on the menu.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery rounds off the tamarind's sourness for the signature Mysore sweet-sour balance.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil fries the red chutney and crisps the dosa evenly.

steps: Boil 4 medium potatoes until soft, peel and crush them coarsely, and soak 1 tbsp tamarind in 3 tbsp warm water, then squeeze out the pulp.
For the red chutney, fry 8 garlic cloves and 5 dried red chillies in 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil until deep red, then grind to a thick paste with a pinch of salt.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds with 12 curry leaves, then add 1 sliced onion and cook until golden, about 5 minutes.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric, the tamarind pulp, 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1.5 tsp salt, simmer 2 minutes, then fold in the crushed potatoes and cook until glossy.
Heat the tava, wipe it, spread a thin dosa, then smear 1 tsp of the red garlic chutney across the surface with the ladle.
Drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil at the edges and cook until the base is crisp and rust-red from the chutney, about 2 minutes.
Mound 3 tbsp tamarind potato masala down the middle, fold into a triangle and serve hot.
tips: Make the red garlic chutney in a bigger batch; it keeps a week refrigerated and instantly upgrades plain dosas and idlis.
Add the jaggery gradually and taste, as tamarind sourness varies and you want a gentle sweet finish, not a syrupy one.
Spread the chutney only after the batter has just set, or it will scorch before the dosa crisps.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve Mysore-style with a dollop of white coconut chutney alongside the red one, letting the two colours and temperatures contrast on the plate.

variations.name: Bengali Mustard Masala Dosa
variations.description: An East-Indian reimagining where the dosa is cooked in pungent mustard oil and the potato filling carries the sharp, sinus-clearing hit of kasundi-style mustard. It marries the Bengali love of shorshe with the Southern crepe for a bold, unexpected bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Kachi ghani mustard oil delivers the authentic Bengali pungency in both filling and crust.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A touch of ghee at the end tames the mustard oil's raw bite with mellow richness.

steps: Boil 4 medium potatoes until tender, peel and crush them, and loosen 1.5 tbsp mustard paste with 2 tbsp water so it is spreadable.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, then lower the heat and crackle 0.5 tsp nigella seeds with 3 slit green chillies and julienned 1 inch ginger for 30 seconds.
Add 1 sliced onion and fry until soft and lightly browned, about 5 minutes, then stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric and the loosened mustard paste and cook 1 minute until the raw smell lifts.
Tip in the crushed potatoes with 1.5 tsp salt and a splash of water, mixing until the mustard coats every piece; keep warm.
Heat the tava, wipe with a cloth dipped in Anveshan Mustard Oil, then ladle and spread the batter thinly.
Drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and finish with a little Anveshan Ghee, cooking until the underside is golden and crisp, about 2 minutes.
Lay 3 tbsp mustard potato masala across the centre, roll the dosa into a cylinder and serve hot.
tips: Always heat mustard oil until it just smokes and then cool it slightly before tempering; this mellows its harshness and prevents a bitter filling.
Soak the mustard paste with a pinch of sugar and salt for ten minutes to curb any bitterness before it goes into the pan.
Keep the chilli count high here, as mustard and green chilli are the traditional Bengali pairing that makes the dish sing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Break the regional rulebook and serve with a cooling cucumber-yoghurt raita alongside the usual coconut chutney to offset the mustard heat.

variations.name: Andhra Guntur Masala Dosa
variations.description: A blazing coastal-Andhra version dusted inside with karam podi built on fiery Guntur red chillies, then finished with nutty sesame oil. It is unapologetically hot, gingelly-scented and made for those who chase the burn.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil stands up to the high heat needed to crisp this fiery dosa.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly sesame oil, drizzled to finish, gives the toasty aroma Andhra cooks prize.

steps: Boil 4 medium potatoes, peel and crush them coarsely, and dry-roast 1 tbsp chana dal with 6 Guntur red chillies until the dal is golden and the chillies darken.
Grind the roasted dal and chillies with 6 garlic cloves and a pinch of salt into a coarse karam podi.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds with 12 curry leaves, then add 1 sliced onion and cook until soft, about 4 minutes.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric, half the karam podi and 1.5 tsp salt, then fold in the crushed potatoes with a splash of water and cook 3 minutes.
Heat the tava, wipe it, spread a thin dosa, then dust 1 tsp karam podi over the surface and drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil.
Cook until the base is crisp and flecked red, about 2 minutes, adding a little Anveshan Groundnut Oil at the edges for extra crunch.
Pile 3 tbsp spicy potato masala down the centre, fold over and serve hot with the remaining podi on the side.
tips: Guntur chillies are seriously hot, so deseed a few before roasting if you want the flavour without the full firepower.
The karam podi stores for a month in an airtight jar and doubles as a sprinkle over idli, rice and ghee.
Finish with sesame oil off the heat rather than cooking it in, so its delicate toasted aroma survives.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling glass of buttermilk and a mild coconut chutney; the dairy is essential to balance the Guntur heat.

variations.name: Classic Moong Dal Cheela
variations.description: The everyday North Indian protein pancake made from freshly ground split green gram, cooked thin and lacy on a hot tava. This definitive version keeps the flavour clean and savoury so the nutty dal and toasted edges shine.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Wood-Pressed Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed groundnut oil greases the tava without any raw smell, letting the cheela crisp evenly.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: A final brush of grassy bilona ghee gives the folded cheela its glossy, aromatic finish.

steps: Rinse 1 cup split green gram in two changes of water, then soak in plenty of fresh water for 3 hours until the grains swell and split easily, and drain thoroughly.
Blend the drained dal with 1 inch ginger, 2 green chillies and about 0.75 cup water into a smooth, pourable batter the thickness of thin cream, stopping before it turns watery.

Stir in 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, a pinch of asafoetida and 1 tsp salt, then fold through 1 finely chopped onion and 3 tbsp coriander and rest the batter for 15 minutes.
Set a flat tava over medium heat and grease it lightly with a few drops of Anveshan Groundnut Wood-Pressed Oil, wiping the surface with a halved onion until evenly filmed and shimmering.

Pour a ladleful of batter into the centre and spread it in a widening spiral into a 7-inch round, then drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Wood-Pressed Oil around the rim and cook until the underside is golden and lacy, about 3 minutes.
Flip and cook the second side for 2 minutes until set with light brown freckles, brush the top with Anveshan Bilona Ghee, fold into a half-moon and serve hot.
tips: Grinding freshly soaked dal gives the lightest cheela; if the batter thickens on standing, loosen it with a spoon of water so it still spreads thin.
Keep the tava on steady medium heat and wait until the top looks dry before flipping, which guarantees crisp lacy edges instead of a soft, torn cheela.
The batter can be ground the night before and refrigerated; bring it back to room temperature and re-season before cooking.
variations.servingSuggestion: Plate with a cooling mint-coriander chutney and a bowl of whisked curd, adding a lime wedge on the side to brighten each nutty bite at breakfast.

variations.name: Bengali Moong Dal Cheela
variations.description: A Bengali reading of the cheela where pungent wood-pressed mustard oil and a scatter of nigella seeds lend the batter its unmistakable kick and colour. Sharper and earthier than the North Indian version, it eats beautifully with a chilli-lime kasundi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Wood-Pressed Oil
ingredients.note: Kachi ghani mustard oil, heated to smoking first, delivers the signature Bengali pungency that defines this cheela.

steps: Soak 1 cup split green gram for 3 hours until plump, drain, and grind with 1 inch ginger and 3 green chillies plus roughly 0.75 cup water to a smooth batter that just falls off the ladle in a ribbon.
Season the batter with 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, then fold in 2 chopped spring onions and 3 tbsp coriander and let it rest for 15 minutes.
Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Wood-Pressed Oil in a small pan until it just begins to smoke, cool for thirty seconds, then stir it into the batter to tame its raw sharpness while keeping the aroma.
Heat a tava over medium heat, film it with a little more Anveshan Mustard Wood-Pressed Oil, and scatter a few nigella seeds directly onto the greased surface so they toast and stick to the pancake.
Ladle batter over the seeds and spread into a thin 7-inch round, drizzle the edges with mustard oil, and cook until the base is deep golden and crisp, about 3 to 4 minutes.
Flip and press gently with a spatula, cook for another 2 minutes until cooked through, then fold and serve while the mustard aroma is still lively.
tips: Always heat mustard oil to smoking point before adding it to the batter; this mellows the bite while preserving the nutty, sinus-clearing fragrance Bengalis prize.
Nigella seeds toast fast, so lay them on the oiled tava only moments before pouring the batter to avoid scorching.
For a fuller meal, tuck grated coconut and slit green chilli into the fold just before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside a spoon of tangy kasundi mustard and thin cucumber slices, letting the sharp condiment echo the mustard oil in the batter.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Moong Dal Cheela
variations.description: This Maharashtrian take folds warm, clove-and-cinnamon-scented goda masala into the batter for a mildly sweet, deeply aromatic pancake. It carries the coastal-Deccan love of coconut and a whisper of jaggery in the accompaniment.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Wood-Pressed Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the classic Maharashtrian cooking fat and keeps the goda-spiced cheela earthy and light.

steps: Soak 1 cup split green gram for 3 hours, drain, and blend with 1 inch ginger, 2 green chillies and about 0.75 cup water into a smooth, spoon-coating batter.
Whisk 1.5 tsp goda masala, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder and 1 tsp salt into the batter until the warm spices are evenly distributed and the mix smells fragrant.
Fold in 3 tbsp grated fresh coconut and 3 tbsp chopped coriander, then rest the batter for 15 minutes so the goda masala blooms and softens.
Heat a tava over medium heat and rub it with a thin film of Anveshan Groundnut Wood-Pressed Oil until the surface shimmers evenly.

Pour a ladle of batter and spread into a 7-inch round, drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Wood-Pressed Oil around the edge, and cook until the base is golden brown and the coconut flecks caramelise, about 3 minutes.
Flip and cook the second side for 2 minutes until firm and speckled, then fold into a triangle and serve hot.
tips: Goda masala varies by household, so start with 1.5 tsp and add more only after tasting a test cheela, since it can turn bitter if overdone.
Toast the grated coconut for a minute in a dry pan if using frozen, which revives its sweetness and stops the batter from weeping.
The batter keeps for a day refrigerated; the goda flavour actually deepens overnight.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a dollop of jaggery-sweetened coconut chutney and hot filter coffee for a satisfying Deccan-style tiffin.

variations.name: Rajasthani Moong Dal Cheela
variations.description: Built for the desert palate, this fiery version leans on soaked dried red chillies pounded into the batter and a smoky ghee finish. It is robust, rustic and made to be scooped with a garlicky chutney.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: Cooking these cheela in nutty bilona ghee gives the Rajasthani richness that stands up to the chillies.

steps: Soak 1 cup split green gram and 4 dried red chillies together for 3 hours until both soften, then drain, reserving the plump chillies.
Grind the dal with the soaked chillies, 5 garlic cloves, 1 inch ginger and about 0.75 cup water into a smooth, brick-red batter with visible chilli flecks.
Stir in 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, fold in 1 finely chopped onion and 3 tbsp coriander, and rest for 15 minutes.
Heat a tava over medium heat and grease it with a little Anveshan Bilona Ghee, letting it melt into a fragrant, shimmering film.
Ladle the batter and spread into a slightly thick 6-inch round, spoon 1 tsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee around the edges, and cook until the base is deep golden and crisp, about 4 minutes.
Flip, press with the spatula, and cook 2 more minutes until cooked through and blistered, then serve straight off the tava.
tips: Soaking the dried chillies with the dal both softens their heat and stains the batter a warm red without any raw powder harshness.
For a milder plate, deseed the chillies before soaking while keeping their smoky flavour intact.
Slightly thicker cheela here holds up to the robust chutney without tearing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a pungent garlic-red chilli chutney and a glass of buttermilk to balance the heat, desert-thali style.

variations.name: Gujarati Moong Dal Cheela
variations.description: The Gujarati palate loves a sweet-savoury balance, so this cheela carries a touch of mellow jaggery against green chilli and ginger heat. Soft, thin and gently sweet, it is a classic farsan-style breakfast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Wood-Pressed Oil
ingredients.note: Light wood-pressed sunflower oil keeps this delicate cheela soft without masking the jaggery sweetness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A spoon of mineral-rich jaggery powder gives the signature Gujarati sweet-savoury edge.

steps: Soak 1 cup split green gram for 3 hours, drain, and grind with about 0.75 cup water into a smooth, thin, pourable batter.
Dissolve 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder in the lemon juice, then whisk it into the batter along with 1.5 tsp ginger-green chilli paste, 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt.
Fold in 3 tbsp chopped coriander and rest the batter for 15 minutes, letting the jaggery fully dissolve for an even sweetness.
Heat a tava over medium-low heat and grease it thinly with Anveshan Sunflower Wood-Pressed Oil until it just glistens.
Pour a ladle of batter and spread into a thin 7-inch round, drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Sunflower Wood-Pressed Oil around the rim, and cook gently until the base is pale gold, about 3 minutes.
Flip and cook for 2 minutes more until soft-set and lightly spotted, keeping the heat low so the jaggery does not burn, then fold and serve warm.
tips: Keep the flame on the lower side because the jaggery in the batter can catch and brown too fast over high heat.
Dissolving the jaggery in lemon juice first prevents gritty undissolved bits in the finished cheela.
Balance is key; taste and add a pinch more salt if the sweetness feels forward.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with fresh green chutney and a cup of masala chai, or roll it around a spoon of thick curd for a lunchbox treat.

variations.name: Classic Rava Dosa
variations.description: The lacy, glass-crisp instant dosa of South Indian tiffin counters, made from a thin semolina-and-rice-flour batter that needs no fermenting. Poured rather than spread, it sets into a paper-thin net of golden holes that shatters at the first bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: an ancient-wheat swap for the usual maida that keeps the lace crisp with a gentle nutty edge

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil for greasing and drizzling that fries the edges to a clean, non-greasy crisp

steps: In a large bowl whisk 1 cup fine semolina, 0.5 cup rice flour, 0.25 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta and 1 tsp salt, then pour in 3 cups water a little at a time to make a thin, lump-free batter the consistency of buttermilk.

Stir in 1 tsp cumin seeds, 0.5 tsp coarsely crushed peppercorns, 2 finely chopped green chillies, 1 tbsp grated ginger, 12 torn curry leaves and 2 tbsp chopped coriander, then rest the batter for 15 minutes so the semolina swells.
Heat a flat iron tava over medium-high until a drop of water skitters and evaporates, then rub it with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil using a halved onion.
Stir the settled batter well and pour it in a thin stream from the outer edge inward, letting small holes form naturally; never spread it with the ladle or the lace collapses.
Drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil around the rim and cook undisturbed on medium-high for 3 to 4 minutes until the base is deep golden and the edges lift on their own.
Fold the dosa in half, press for 10 seconds until crisp, and slide onto a plate; whisk the batter again before every fresh pour.
tips: The batter must be watery, not pourable-thick; if the first dosa comes out solid instead of lacy, thin it with 2 to 3 tbsp more water.
Always stir just before ladling because the semolina and rice flour sink fast and the holes depend on an even mix.
Keep the tava on the hotter side of medium-high throughout; a cool griddle gives a pale, soggy dosa instead of a shattering one.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve immediately with coconut chutney and a bowl of sambar, standing the folded dosa upright in a steel plate so it stays crisp to the table.

variations.name: Bengali Rava Dosa
variations.description: West Bengal reimagines the crisp rava dosa with the sharp, warming pungency of Anveshan Mustard Oil and a scatter of nigella seeds. The result carries the unmistakable ghaani-oil bite of a Kolkata kitchen against the delicate semolina lace.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: stands in for maida and echoes the wholesome atta Bengali homes favour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked to its first wisp so its raw pungency mellows into the classic Bengali kick

steps: Whisk 1 cup fine semolina, 0.5 cup rice flour, 0.25 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta and 1 tsp salt together, then loosen with 3 cups water added gradually until the batter runs off the whisk like thin buttermilk.
Fold in 0.75 tsp nigella seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin, 3 slit green chillies, 1 tbsp julienned ginger and 3 tbsp chopped coriander, then let the batter stand 15 minutes to soften the grains.
Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a small pan until it just smokes, cool it slightly to tame the sharpness, and stir 1 tbsp of it into the rested batter.
Heat a tava on medium-high and wipe it with a few drops of the remaining Anveshan Mustard Oil so the surface glistens without pooling.
Pour the stirred batter from the edges inward in a lacy ring, leave the gaps untouched, and drizzle 1 tsp of the mustard oil around the border.
Cook undisturbed for 3 to 4 minutes until the underside is mahogany-gold and crackly, then fold and lift; stir the batter before each new dosa.
tips: Heating the mustard oil to first smoke is essential; raw mustard oil in the batter tastes bitter and overpowering.
Nigella can turn acrid if scorched, so keep the heat at a steady medium-high rather than letting the tava overheat.
A pinch more rice flour crisps the dosa further if your semolina is on the coarser side.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a green coconut-coriander chutney and a wedge of lime; the mustard bite is lovely alongside a simple aloo bhaja on the side.

variations.name: Kerala Rava Dosa
variations.description: Kerala folds fresh grated coconut into the batter and cooks the dosa in fragrant Anveshan Coconut Oil, giving the lace a sweet, tropical richness. Curry leaves and coconut oil together carry the coastal Malabar aroma into every crisp bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: replaces maida while keeping the batter light enough for a crisp lace

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil for cooking that doubles the coconut aroma the Kerala way

steps: Combine 1 cup fine semolina, 0.5 cup rice flour, 0.25 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta and 1 tsp salt in a bowl, then whisk in 3 cups water bit by bit to a thin, flowing batter.
Stir through 0.5 cup fresh grated coconut, 1 tsp cumin, 0.5 tsp crushed pepper, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tbsp grated ginger and 15 torn curry leaves, and rest for 15 minutes.
Set a tava over medium-high heat and grease it with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil rubbed on with a folded cloth until the surface shines.
Give the batter a brisk stir and pour it in a thin lacy circle from the outer rim inward, leaving the natural holes intact for maximum crunch.
Trickle 1 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil around and over the dosa and cook it undisturbed for 3 to 4 minutes until deeply golden and lifting at the edges.
Fold into a half-moon, hold for 10 seconds to crisp, and serve; remember to stir in a little water if the coconut settles and thickens the mix.
tips: Use fresh or thawed frozen coconut, never desiccated, or the batter drinks up moisture and loses its lacy flow.
Coconut in the batter browns faster, so watch the base and pull the dosa the moment it turns rich gold.
If the batter thickens as it rests, the coconut is to blame; thin it back with a splash of warm water.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a coconut-and-roasted-gram chutney and a small ladle of Kerala-style sambar spiked with drumstick.

variations.name: Andhra Rava Dosa
variations.description: Andhra Pradesh turns up the heat with fiery Guntur red chilli and cooks the dosa in nutty Anveshan Sesame Oil, the region's beloved nuvvula nune. Bold, blistering and aromatic, it is a rava dosa built for those who love their tiffin with a kick.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: an earthy whole-grain swap for maida that stands up to the bold Guntur spice

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed til oil, the classic Andhra cooking fat, for its warm nutty backbone

steps: Whisk 1 cup fine semolina, 0.5 cup rice flour, 0.25 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp salt and 0.25 tsp asafoetida, then add 3 cups water gradually to a thin lace-ready batter.
Beat in 1.5 tsp Guntur red chilli powder, 1 tsp cumin, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tbsp minced ginger and 12 torn curry leaves, then rest the batter 15 minutes so the rava plumps.
Heat a tava on medium-high until it radiates heat, then season it with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil wiped across with a cloth.
Stir the batter thoroughly and pour it from the edges toward the centre in a thin, hole-studded ring without smoothing it over.
Drizzle a generous 1.5 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil around the perimeter and let it fry undisturbed for 3 to 4 minutes until rust-gold and crackling.
Fold and press the dosa for a few seconds, lift it crisp, and stir the batter well before ladling the next one.
tips: Guntur chilli is intense, so start with 1 tsp if serving children and build up on later dosas.
Sesame oil browns beautifully but can smoke fast, so keep the flame steady at medium-high, not full blast.
A pinch of asafoetida in the batter deepens the savoury Andhra flavour and eases digestion of the semolina.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling tomato-onion pachadi and a dollop of thick curd to temper the Guntur fire.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Rava Dosa
variations.description: Maharashtra laces the crisp dosa with dark, fragrant goda masala and a handful of crushed roasted peanuts for crunch. The toasted-coconut warmth of goda masala gives this instant dosa an earthy, festive character all its own.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: a nutty whole-wheat swap for maida that suits the roasted goda masala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday Maharashtrian frying oil that lifts the goda masala's roasted notes

steps: Whisk 1 cup fine semolina, 0.5 cup rice flour, 0.25 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta and 1 tsp salt, then work in 3 cups water slowly to a thin, easily pourable batter.
Stir in 2 tsp goda masala, 3 tbsp coarsely crushed roasted peanuts, 1 tsp cumin, 2 chopped green chillies, 12 torn curry leaves and 2 tbsp coriander, then rest 15 minutes.
Heat a tava on medium-high and grease it with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil rubbed in with a halved onion until it just shimmers.
Stir the batter to redistribute the peanuts, then pour it in a lacy ring from the outer edge inward, keeping the holes open for crunch.
Drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil around the dosa and cook undisturbed for 3 to 4 minutes until the base turns dark gold and releases cleanly.
Fold the dosa over, press briefly to set the crisp, and stir the batter before starting the next.
tips: Add the goda masala only after the batter is smooth so it disperses evenly and doesn't clump.
Crush the peanuts coarsely rather than to a powder so you get pockets of crunch in the lace.
Goda masala varies by brand; taste and add a pinch more if you want a deeper, smokier note.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a garlic-peanut thecha or a coconut chutney and a glass of buttermilk for a true Maharashtrian breakfast spread.

variations.name: Classic Sattu Cheela
variations.description: The everyday Bihari-style savoury pancake made from roasted gram flour beaten into a smooth batter with onion, ginger and green chilli. Cooked in Anveshan wood-pressed groundnut oil and finished with ghee, it is protein-rich, nutty and crisp at the edges with a soft, tender centre.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Stone-ground roasted Bengal gram sattu is the whole star here, lending its signature toasty, protein-dense body to every cheela.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil greases the tava cleanly and lets the cheela crisp without soaking up excess fat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A brush of ghee at the end gives the classic cheela its glossy sheen and roasted aroma.

steps: In a wide bowl whisk 1.5 cups Anveshan Sattu with 1 tsp salt, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp ajwain, then pour in 1.5 cups water a little at a time, beating out every lump into a smooth, pourable batter the consistency of thin cream.

Finely chop 1 medium onion, 2 green chillies, 1 inch ginger, 3 garlic cloves and 3 tbsp coriander and stir them through the batter, then rest it for 10 minutes so the sattu hydrates fully; add a splash more water if it thickens too much.

Heat a flat tava over medium heat until a drop of water skitters and evaporates in 2 seconds, then rub the surface with a few drops of Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil using a halved onion or paper towel.

Pour a full ladle of batter into the centre and spread it outward in a gentle spiral into a 7-inch round, then drizzle about 0.5 tsp groundnut oil around the edges and cook undisturbed for 2 to 3 minutes until the underside is golden and lacy.
Flip the cheela with a flat spatula, press lightly so the centre cooks through, and cook the second side for 1 to 2 minutes until brown spots appear and the edges turn crisp.
Brush the top with a little Anveshan Ghee, fold into a half-moon and serve hot; repeat with the remaining batter, re-greasing the tava lightly before each one.
tips: Rest the batter for at least 10 minutes but no longer than 30, as sattu keeps drinking water and you may need to loosen it again before the last few cheela.
Keep the flame at medium, not high; sattu browns fast and a scorched underside will taste bitter rather than nutty.
For a softer cheela add 2 tbsp curd to the batter, which also helps the edges crisp more evenly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of coriander-mint chutney and a wedge of lemon, with plain curd on the side for a filling breakfast or light dinner.

variations.name: Bihari Mustard-Oil Sattu Cheela
variations.description: The authentic Magadh-belt version where the batter is bound with the pungency of raw mustard oil and a pop of kalonji, the way sattu is eaten across Bihar. Cooked in Anveshan wood-pressed mustard oil, it is sharp, earthy and unapologetically rustic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Bihari sattu is the heart of this cheela, giving the batter its dense, roasted-gram backbone.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Mustard oil is non-negotiable in Bihar and gives the cheela its signature sharp, warming bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A final smear of ghee tempers the mustard heat and adds a village-kitchen richness.

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups Anveshan Sattu with 1 tsp salt, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp kalonji, then gradually beat in 1.5 cups water to a smooth, lump-free pouring batter.

Stir 1 tbsp raw Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil, 1 tbsp mashed pickle masala, 1 finely chopped onion, 3 chopped green chillies, 4 minced garlic cloves and 3 tbsp coriander into the batter and rest it 10 minutes for the sattu to swell.
Set a tava over medium heat until hot, then smear it with a few drops of mustard oil and let the oil just begin to shimmer so its raw pungency mellows.
Ladle the batter on and spread it into a 7-inch round, drizzle 0.5 tsp mustard oil around the rim, and cook for 2 to 3 minutes until the base is deep golden and pulls away cleanly.
Flip and cook the second side for about 2 minutes, pressing gently, until brown blistered spots form and the cheela smells sharp and toasty.
Finish with a light brush of Anveshan Ghee, fold, and serve straight off the tava while the mustard aroma is at its peak.
tips: Heat the mustard oil until it just shimmers before greasing; this cooks off the harsh raw note while keeping the characteristic bite.
The spoon of pickle masala is the Bihari shortcut to depth; use whatever mango or chilli pickle masala you have, mashing it fine first.
Leftover batter keeps overnight in the fridge and the flavours deepen, though you will need to thin it with a little water before cooking.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with green chilli-garlic chokha or a raw onion salad dressed with mustard oil and lemon for a true Bihari plate.

variations.name: Kerala Coconut Sattu Cheela
variations.description: A Malabar-inspired reimagining that folds fresh grated coconut and a curry-leaf tempering into the sattu batter, cooked in Anveshan wood-pressed coconut oil. Mellow, fragrant and gently sweet against the roasted gram, it bridges North Indian sattu with a coastal soul.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Sattu carries the protein and nuttiness while the coconut softens it into a coastal-style cheela.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil is the defining Kerala fat and echoes the fresh coconut in the batter.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A ghee finish rounds the coconut sweetness and adds a warm gloss.

steps: Heat 1 tsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a small pan, splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, then add 2 sprigs curry leaves and 4 finely sliced shallots and fry until the shallots turn soft and golden, about 3 minutes; cool this tempering.

Whisk 1.5 cups Anveshan Sattu with 1 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp turmeric, beat in 1.5 cups water to a smooth pouring batter, then fold in the cooled tempering, 0.33 cup grated coconut, 2 chopped green chillies and 1 inch grated ginger and rest 10 minutes.
Heat a tava over medium heat and grease it with a few drops of coconut oil until the surface just glistens.
Pour a ladle of batter and spread into a 7-inch round, drizzle 0.5 tsp coconut oil around the edge, and cook for 2 to 3 minutes until the base is golden and freckled with coconut.
Flip carefully and cook the second side for about 2 minutes until set and lightly crisp, taking care the coconut does not scorch.
Brush with Anveshan Ghee, fold, and serve hot so the coconut aroma stays lively.
tips: Use fresh or frozen grated coconut, never desiccated, which will dry the batter and rob it of its moist, sweet flecks.
Cook these on medium-low rather than high, because the coconut in the batter catches and browns faster than plain sattu.
A pinch of crushed black pepper in the tempering deepens the Malabar character without adding chilli heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut-based kadala curry or a simple coconut chutney and a cup of filter coffee for a cross-regional breakfast.

variations.name: Gujarati Sweet-Savoury Sattu Cheela
variations.description: A Gujarati take that leans into the region's beloved sweet-and-savoury balance, tempering the roasted-gram batter with a touch of Anveshan jaggery powder and a green chilli-ginger paste. Cooked in wood-pressed groundnut oil, it is soft, mildly sweet and thoroughly moreish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Sattu gives structure and nuttiness that stands up to the gentle jaggery sweetness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the classic Gujarati cooking fat and keeps the cheela light.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A spoon of jaggery gives the signature Gujarati sweet-savoury lift without refined sugar.

steps: Dissolve 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 0.25 cup warm water and set aside; crush 3 green chillies and 1 inch ginger to a coarse paste.
Whisk 1.5 cups Anveshan Sattu with 1 tsp salt, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.25 tsp asafoetida, then beat in the jaggery water and enough of the remaining 1.25 cups water to make a smooth, pourable batter.
Fold the chilli-ginger paste, 1 tbsp sesame seeds, 3 tbsp coriander and 1 tbsp lemon juice into the batter and rest it 10 minutes to balance sweet, sour and heat.
Heat a tava over medium heat and grease lightly with Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil until it shimmers faintly.
Ladle on the batter, spread into a 7-inch round, drizzle 0.5 tsp groundnut oil around the rim, and cook 2 to 3 minutes until the base is golden and the sesame seeds toast.
Flip and cook the second side about 2 minutes until set and speckled, then fold and serve warm.
tips: Dissolve the jaggery in water first so it disperses evenly rather than leaving sticky patches that burn on the tava.
The lemon juice is essential to stop the batter tasting flatly sweet; it sharpens the whole cheela.
Keep the sweetness subtle at 1.5 tbsp jaggery for three cups of batter, just enough to round the roasted-gram edge.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a tangy green chutney and a bowl of chaas, or with sweet-hot chundo pickle for a full Gujarati contrast.

variations.name: Andhra Guntur Sattu Cheela
variations.description: A fiery Andhra version charged with smoky Guntur red chilli, garlic and a sesame-oil temper that gives the roasted-gram cheela a serious kick. Cooked in Anveshan wood-pressed sesame oil, it is hot, garlicky and built for those who love their breakfast bold.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Sattu's toasty body is the perfect canvas for the aggressive Guntur chilli heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly sesame oil is the Andhra base fat and its toasty depth grounds the fierce chilli.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A ghee finish takes the raw edge off the Guntur chilli while keeping the cheela glossy.

steps: Heat 1 tsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil in a small pan, crackle 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, then fry 6 crushed garlic cloves and 2 sprigs curry leaves for 1 minute until aromatic and just golden; cool this temper.
Whisk 1.5 cups Anveshan Sattu with 1 tsp salt, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp Guntur red chilli powder, then beat in 1.5 cups water to a smooth pouring batter.
Fold the cooled garlic temper, 1 finely chopped onion and 3 tbsp coriander into the batter and rest 10 minutes so the chilli heat blooms through.
Heat a tava over medium heat and grease with a little sesame oil until it shimmers.
Pour a ladle of batter, spread into a 7-inch round, drizzle 0.5 tsp sesame oil around the edge, and cook 2 to 3 minutes until the base is a deep red-gold and crisp.
Flip and cook the second side about 2 minutes, then brush with Anveshan Ghee, fold and serve blazing hot.
tips: Guntur chilli is intensely hot, so start with 0.75 tsp if you are spice-shy and build up in later batches.
Frying the garlic before it goes into the batter stops it turning acrid on the tava and keeps its sweetness.
A spoon of thick cold curd on the side is the traditional Andhra coolant against the chilli.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain set curd and a fried appalam, with an extra sprinkle of Guntur chilli for those who want it hotter.

variations.name: Classic Crispy Aloo Tikki
variations.description: The definitive North Indian street-cart tikki, with a shatteringly crisp golden crust giving way to a soft, spiced potato centre. A double coat of breadcrumbs and a rest in the fridge are the two tricks that guarantee crunch instead of sog.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: high smoke point wood-pressed oil that shallow-fries the tikkis to a clean, non-greasy crunch

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: whole-wheat khapli dredge replaces cornflour to lock the crust and stop the tikki cracking in the pan

steps: Boil 4 medium potatoes until a knife slides through easily, about 15 minutes, then peel and grate them while still warm so no wet lumps remain.

Mix the grated potato with 1 finely chopped onion, 2 minced green chillies, 3 tbsp coriander, 1 inch grated ginger, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt until it holds together like soft dough.
Work in 0.5 cup bread crumbs to firm the mixture, then divide into 8 equal balls and flatten each into a 1 cm thick disc with clean, lightly oiled palms.
Dust each tikki in 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, then press both faces into the remaining 0.5 cup bread crumbs for a double crust and chill the tikkis for 15 minutes to set.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a heavy pan over medium heat until it shimmers, then slide in the tikkis without crowding.
Shallow-fry 4 to 5 minutes per side without moving them early, until deep golden and audibly crisp, then lift onto paper to drain.
Serve straight away while the crust still crackles, with mint chutney and sweet tamarind chutney on the side.
tips: Grate the potatoes a day ahead and refrigerate uncovered so surface moisture evaporates, which is the single biggest factor in crispness.
If the mixture feels sticky and refuses to hold, add breadcrumbs a tablespoon at a time rather than more flour, which would toughen the centre.
Fry on steady medium heat, not high, or the crust browns before the inside heats through and turns pasty.
variations.servingSuggestion: Plate on a bed of whisked chilled yoghurt, scatter pomegranate arils and fine sev, and finish with a zigzag of both chutneys for a quick tikki chaat.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Crispy Aloo Tikki
variations.description: A Pune-style tikki built around dark, aromatic goda masala, whose roasted coconut and sesame notes make the potato taste smoky and sweet-warm rather than sharp. Crushed roasted peanuts through the mix add a distinctly Maharashtrian crunch inside the crust.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: nutty wood-pressed groundnut oil echoes the peanut flavour Maharashtra loves and fries the crust crisp

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a whisper of jaggery balances the pungent goda masala the way Maharashtrian kitchens traditionally do

steps: Pressure-cook 4 medium potatoes for 3 whistles, cool, peel and mash them coarsely so a little texture stays in the mix.
Toast 3 tbsp peanuts in a dry pan until they crackle, then crush them roughly and stir them into the potato with 1.5 tsp goda masala and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder.
Fold in 1 chopped onion, 2 minced green chillies, 3 tbsp coriander, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, then bind with 0.5 cup bread crumbs until the dough is firm and shapeable.
Divide into 8 portions and pat each into a thick round, then coat all over in the remaining 0.5 cup bread crumbs and rest 15 minutes so the goda masala perfumes the potato.
Warm 4 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a griddle pan over medium heat until a crumb sizzles on contact.
Fry the tikkis 4 to 5 minutes each side, pressing gently once, until the crust is a rich mahogany-gold and crackly, then drain on paper.
Serve hot with a dry garlic-peanut chutney and thick beaten curd for a true Pune-cart plate.
tips: Toast your own goda masala spices if you can, as pre-ground packs lose the roasted coconut aroma that defines this tikki within weeks.
Keep the peanuts coarse, not powdered, so you get little pops of crunch against the soft potato.
These reheat beautifully on a dry tava; avoid the microwave, which steams the crust soft.
variations.servingSuggestion: Tuck a hot tikki into a soft pav smeared with green chutney and fried onions for a Maharashtrian tikki-pav that eats like a light vada pav.

variations.name: Bengali Crispy Aloo Tikki
variations.description: A Kolkata-footpath aloor chop cousin, shallow-fried in pungent mustard oil that gives the crust its unmistakable sharp aroma. A hint of Bengali garam masala and a mustard kick set it apart from every North Indian version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: sharp kachi ghani mustard oil is the soul of any Bengali chop and gives the crust its signature bite

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli flour whisked into a thin slurry helps the breadcrumbs cling for an extra-crisp chop shell

steps: Boil 4 medium potatoes until soft, about 15 minutes, then peel and mash them smooth while warm.

Heat 1 tbsp of the Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until it just smokes, cool slightly, then fry 1 chopped onion, 2 slit green chillies and 1 inch grated ginger until soft and golden, about 4 minutes.

Mix the fried aromatics into the mashed potato with 1 tsp Bengali garam masala, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, 3 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp salt, then firm the mixture with 0.5 cup bread crumbs.
Shape into 8 oval croquettes, dip each in a thin slurry of 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta and water, then roll in the remaining 0.5 cup bread crumbs.
Heat the remaining 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil in a pan over medium heat until the raw pungency mellows.
Shallow-fry the chops 4 to 5 minutes each side until the shell is deep golden and crisp, then rest on paper.
Serve hot with kasundi mustard and thin rings of raw onion, the classic Bengali way.
tips: Always heat mustard oil to smoking once and let it cool a touch before frying, which tames the raw bite while keeping the aroma.
Shape ovals rather than discs to stay true to the aloor chop form and to get more crunchy surface area.
A pinch of sugar in the potato mix rounds off the mustard oil's edge without making the chop sweet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a monsoon-evening snack with muri (puffed rice) tossed through, a wedge of lime, and hot cha in a clay cup.

variations.name: Rajasthani Crispy Aloo Tikki
variations.description: A fiery desert-style tikki that leans on whole dried red chillies soaked and ground to a coarse paste for deep red colour and slow-building heat. Crushed dried mint and a dusting of amchur give the arid, tangy edge Rajasthan is known for.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: sturdy wood-pressed groundnut oil stands up to the fierce chilli paste and fries a robust crust

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli dredge gives these desert tikkis a rustic, extra-firm coat that carries the heat

steps: Soak 4 dried red chillies in warm water for 15 minutes, then grind to a coarse paste with a splash of the soaking water.
Boil and mash 4 medium potatoes, then beat in the red chilli paste, 1 tsp amchur, 1 tsp crushed dried mint, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt.
Stir through 1 finely chopped onion and 2 tbsp coriander, then bind with 0.5 cup bread crumbs into a firm, deep-red dough.
Divide into 8 thick discs, dust each in 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta and press into the remaining 0.5 cup bread crumbs, then chill 15 minutes.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat until a breadcrumb sizzles briskly.
Fry the tikkis 4 to 5 minutes per side until the crust is fiery red-gold and crisp, then drain on paper.
Serve hot with garlic-red chilli chutney and a cooling glass of chaas to temper the burn.
tips: Deseed the dried chillies before soaking if you want the colour and flavour without punishing heat.
Grind the chilli paste coarse so flecks of skin catch in the crust and blister slightly when fried.
The amchur can be swapped for a squeeze of lime stirred in just before shaping if you prefer fresh tang.
variations.servingSuggestion: Break the tikkis over a plate of spiced chana and top with onion, chilli chutney and sev for a Rajasthani-style aloo tikki chaat.

variations.name: Kerala Crispy Aloo Tikki
variations.description: A coastal reinvention bound with freshly grated coconut and tempered with curry leaves and mustard seeds crackled in coconut oil. The coconut keeps the centre moist and faintly sweet while the crust fries up light and shatter-crisp.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil both tempers the spices and fries the tikkis, doubling the coastal coconut aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli slurry helps the crumb coat grip the moist, coconut-rich potato mixture

steps: Boil and mash 4 medium potatoes, keeping the mash on the drier side so the coconut moisture can be absorbed.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil, crackle 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 15 curry leaves for 30 seconds, then add 2 minced green chillies and 1 inch grated ginger and fry 1 minute.
Tip the tempering into the mashed potato along with 0.5 cup grated coconut, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, and mix until evenly green-flecked.
Bind with 0.5 cup bread crumbs, shape into 8 discs, coat in a thin 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta slurry and roll in the remaining 0.5 cup bread crumbs.
Heat the remaining 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a pan over medium heat until it flows freely and shimmers.
Fry the tikkis 4 to 5 minutes each side until pale gold and crisp, taking care as coconut in the mix browns fast, then drain.
Serve warm with a fresh coconut-coriander chutney and a wedge of lime.
tips: Use fresh or frozen grated coconut rather than desiccated, which draws moisture out and dries the centre.
Fry a shade lighter than other tikkis because the coconut sugars catch and darken quickly.
Crush the curry leaves lightly before adding so their aroma spreads through the whole mixture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside a small bowl of coconut-milk stew or with steamed appam for a South-coast-inspired brunch plate.

variations.name: Classic Crispy Corn Cutlet
variations.description: The definitive teatime corn tikki: sweet American corn coarsely crushed for texture, bound with soft boiled potato and rolled in a golden bread-crumb crust. It shatters crisp on the outside and stays creamy-sweet within, the way street-side stalls in every Indian city serve it.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: roasted and used as the binder so the tikkis hold without maida or cornflour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for deep-frying; its high smoke point keeps the crust clean and non-greasy

steps: Pulse 1.5 cups of the sweet corn in a grinder to a coarse crush, leaving the remaining 0.5 cup whole for bite, then tip both into a large bowl.

Warm 1 tbsp of the Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a pan over medium heat and saute the chopped onion, green chillies and grated ginger for 3 minutes until the onion turns soft and translucent, then cool completely.

Add the mashed potato, sauteed aromatics, chopped coriander, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt to the corn, then mix in the 3 tbsp roasted Anveshan Khapli Atta until the mixture binds into a firm, non-sticky dough.
Divide into 10 equal portions, roll each into a ball and flatten to a 2 cm-thick tikki, then press both faces firmly into the bread crumbs for an even coating.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to 180C (a crumb should sizzle up at once) and slide in 3-4 tikkis at a time, frying 3 minutes per side until deep golden and crisp.
Lift out with a slotted spoon and rest on a wire rack or paper towel so steam escapes and the crust stays shatteringly crisp.
tips: Chill the shaped tikkis for 20 minutes before frying so they firm up and never break apart in the oil.
If the mixture feels wet and refuses to hold, stir in another tablespoon of roasted khapli atta rather than more bread crumbs, which can turn the centre dense.
Roast the khapli atta on a dry tava until it smells nutty before adding it; raw flour leaves a pasty taste.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile them on a banana leaf with a ramekin of coriander-mint chutney and a second of sweet tamarind chutney, and tuck a few lemon wedges alongside for squeezing at the table.

variations.name: Punjabi Makhani Crispy Corn Cutlet
variations.description: Punjab loves its corn rich and buttery, so here the tikkis are shallow-fried in nutty Anveshan Ghee instead of oil and finished with a glossy ghee baste that stands in for the classic makhan. Kasuri methi and a touch of garam masala give it that tandoor-side dhaba warmth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: roasted binder that keeps the buttery tikkis firm on the tava

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: shallow-fries the tikkis and doubles as the finishing baste in place of butter

steps: Coarsely crush 1.5 cups of the corn and keep 0.5 cup whole, then combine both in a mixing bowl.

Melt 1 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat and fry the onion, green chillies and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 4 minutes until the raw smell lifts and the mix turns pale gold, then cool.

Fold the mashed potato, cooled masala, 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi, chopped coriander, 1 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt into the corn, then bind with the 3 tbsp roasted Anveshan Khapli Atta into a pliable dough.
Shape 10 thick tikkis and press each into the bread crumbs, coating both flat sides evenly.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee on a flat tava over medium heat and shallow-fry the tikkis in batches for about 4 minutes a side until richly browned and crusted.
Just before serving, brush the hot tikkis with the last spoon of melted Anveshan Bilona Ghee so they glisten and carry that unmistakable makhani aroma.
tips: Keep the tava on steady medium heat; ghee browns faster than oil and will scorch the crust if the flame is high.
A pinch of amchur folded into the mix cuts the richness and brightens the sweet corn.
These reheat beautifully in an air fryer at 180C for 5 minutes without losing the ghee-crisp edge.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a brass thali with pickled onion rings, a swirl of mint raita and hot masala chai for a proper Amritsari evening snack.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Goda Masala Crispy Corn Cutlet
variations.description: This Pune-style tikki carries the dusky, faintly sweet warmth of goda masala with its dagad phool and roasted coconut notes. Crushed roasted peanuts run through the mix for crunch, and a curry-leaf tempering perfumes the corn before it is crumbed and fried crisp.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: nutty roasted binder that suits the earthy goda masala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for tempering and deep-frying, echoing Maharashtra's love of groundnut oil

steps: Grind 1.5 cups corn to a coarse paste and reserve 0.5 cup whole kernels, combining both in a bowl.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a pan, splutter the 12 curry leaves for 20 seconds, then add the onion and green chillies and cook 3 minutes until softened; stir in the 1.5 tsp goda masala for 30 seconds until fragrant and take off the heat to cool.

Mix the mashed potato, tempered masala, 3 tbsp crushed roasted peanuts, chopped coriander, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt into the corn, then work in the 3 tbsp roasted Anveshan Khapli Atta until it comes together firmly.
Roll into 10 tikkis and coat each thoroughly in bread crumbs.
Bring the remaining Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to 180C and deep-fry the tikkis 3-4 at a time for 3 minutes a side until dark gold and crackling.
Drain on a rack so the peanuts inside stay crunchy and the crust does not steam soft.
tips: Toast the peanuts fresh and crush them coarse, not fine, so you get little pockets of crunch in every bite.
Goda masala scorches quickly, so add it off a fierce flame and stir for only half a minute.
The mixture can be made a day ahead and refrigerated; the goda masala deepens overnight.
variations.servingSuggestion: Offer them Pune-style with a dab of thecha and a wedge of lime, alongside cutting chai for the full Maharashtrian nashta experience.

variations.name: Bengali Sorshe Crispy Corn Cutlet
variations.description: Bengal's chop-shop tradition inspires this version, where the corn is fried in pungent Anveshan Mustard Oil and lifted with a whisper of mustard-paste heat and beguni-style crisp. A hint of Bengali garam masala and green chilli keeps it aromatic rather than fiery.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: roasted binder that soaks up the mustard-oil flavour without going pasty

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked to its peak first so its sharp pungency mellows into the classic Bengali chop aroma

steps: Crush 1.5 cups of the corn coarsely and leave 0.5 cup whole, then gather both in a bowl.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until it just smokes, lower the flame and fry the onion and green chillies for 3 minutes until glossy, then stir in the 1 tsp mustard paste and 0.75 tsp Bengali garam masala for 30 seconds and cool.

Combine the mashed potato, mustard tempering, chopped coriander, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp sugar and 1 tsp salt with the corn, then bind using the 3 tbsp roasted Anveshan Khapli Atta into a firm mass.
Form 10 oval croquette-style cutlets, a nod to the Bengali chop, and roll them in bread crumbs to coat.
Reheat the remaining Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil to 180C and fry the cutlets for 3 minutes per side until mahogany-gold and crisp.
Rest them on paper so the surface dries and the interior keeps its soft, mustard-scented sweetness.
tips: Always heat mustard oil to smoking point once, then cool slightly; this tames the raw bite that can overwhelm the corn.
The pinch of sugar is essential Bengali balance against the mustard's sharpness, so do not skip it.
Shape them oval rather than round to echo the classic Kolkata vegetable chop.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot with kasundi mustard, thin onion rings and a few cucumber slices, the way a Kolkata para tea-stall would plate a chop.

variations.name: Andhra Guntur Crispy Corn Cutlet
variations.description: For heat-seekers, this fiery take leans on fierce Guntur red chilli and a curry-leaf-and-sesame tempering typical of Andhra kitchens. The corn's natural sweetness is the only thing standing between you and a blazing, deeply savoury crunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: roasted binder that stands up to the bold Guntur spicing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for the sesame-curry-leaf tempering and deep-frying, standard Andhra frying fat

steps: Coarsely crush 1.5 cups corn, keep 0.5 cup whole, and set both aside in a bowl.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil, crackle the 1 tbsp sesame seeds and 15 curry leaves for 20 seconds, add the onion and 1 tbsp garlic and fry 3 minutes until golden, then stir in the 1.5 tsp Guntur chilli powder off the heat so it blooms without burning.
Mix the mashed potato, the fiery tempering, chopped coriander, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt into the corn, then bring it together with the 3 tbsp roasted Anveshan Khapli Atta into a stiff dough.
Shape 10 firm tikkis and press each into the bread crumbs for full coverage.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to 180C and fry the tikkis for 3 minutes a side until the crust is a deep red-gold and audibly crisp.
Drain on a rack and dust with an extra pinch of Guntur chilli if you want the full Andhra kick.
tips: Bloom the Guntur chilli off the flame; it is potent and turns bitter the instant it scorches.
A spoon of thick curd folded into the mix tempers the burn while keeping the tikkis tender inside.
Toast the sesame seeds just until they pop for a nuttier depth against the chilli.
variations.servingSuggestion: Plate them with cooling coconut chutney and a mound of sliced onions dusted in more Guntur chilli, with cold buttermilk on the side to douse the fire.

variations.name: Classic Crispy Pakora
variations.description: The definitive tea-time onion pakora, where thinly sliced onions weep into a spiced besan batter and fry into lacy, shatter-crisp clusters. A little rice flour and khapli atta in the coating is the trick that keeps them crunchy long after they leave the oil, never soggy or bready.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: stirred into the coating for a nutty bite and an extra-crisp shell that shatters

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil heated to 180C so the pakoras fry crisp and clean without turning greasy

steps: Thinly slice 2 onions, finely chop 3 green chillies and grate 1 inch ginger, toss with 3 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt, and rest 10 minutes until the onions soften and release their moisture.
Add 1.5 cups besan, 0.25 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta, 3 tbsp rice flour, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp ajwain, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder, tossing so every strand is coated.
Sprinkle in only 4 to 5 tbsp water and bring it to a thick, just-clinging batter that mounds on a spoon, keeping it stiff so the fritters stay lacy rather than flat.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C, until a pinch of batter dropped in rises steadily to the surface within 4 seconds.
Drop in loose, craggy clusters with your fingers and fry in batches over medium-high heat for 4 to 5 minutes, turning once, until deep golden and audibly crisp.
Lift onto a wire rack, dust with a little chaat masala while hot, and if you like them extra crunchy return them for a 1 minute second fry just before serving.
tips: Keep the batter thick and add water by the tablespoon; a runny batter spreads and fries greasy instead of crisp.
Resting the salted onions draws out water so you need barely any added liquid, giving a shatter-crisp result.
Fry in small batches so the oil temperature never crashes, which is what makes pakoras soak up oil and go limp.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile into a bowl with mint-coriander chutney and imli chutney, add fried green chillies on the side, and serve with steaming masala chai on a rainy evening.

variations.name: Punjabi Crispy Pakora
variations.description: A robust dhaba-style pakora scented with ajwain and garam masala, finished the Punjabi way with a brush of melted butter and a dusting of amchur the moment it comes out of the oil. Ginger-garlic in the batter gives it a warm, savoury depth that stands up to strong pickle and thick chutney.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: gives the thick dhaba-style coating body and a sturdy crunch that holds the butter finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the deep-frying medium that carries the ajwain aroma and fries the batter to a sturdy golden crust

steps: Slice 2 onions and mix with 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 3 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt, resting 8 minutes so the mix turns juicy.
Fold in 1.5 cups besan, 0.25 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp garam masala, 0.75 tsp ajwain, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp turmeric until thickly coated.
Splash in 5 to 6 tbsp water gradually to form a stiff, spoon-clinging batter, keeping it heavy so the pakoras fry dense and crunchy like a roadside dhaba.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C and slide in rough clusters, frying over medium-high for 5 minutes until mahogany-golden and firm.
Drain on a rack, then immediately brush the hot pakoras with 2 tbsp melted butter and dust with 0.5 tsp amchur so it clings and sizzles.
Serve at once while the butter is glossy and the crust is loud and crisp under the spoon.
tips: Brush the butter the second they leave the oil so it melts into the crust rather than sitting greasy on top.
Add the amchur only after frying; heating it in the batter dulls its bright, sour edge.
For a hotter dhaba kick, slit and toss two extra green chillies in the leftover oil and serve them alongside.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a steel plate with thick garlic chutney, sliced onion rings and a wedge of lemon, and a pot of tandoori chai to round out the roadside feel.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Crispy Pakora
variations.description: Kanda bhaji as it is fried across Maharashtra, with plenty of rice flour for glassy crispness and the warm, clove-and-cinnamon fragrance of goda masala. No ginger-garlic here; just onion, chilli and that dark house masala, fried until each strand crackles.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: a spoonful in the batter deepens the crunch and the earthy note that suits goda masala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the classic Maharashtrian frying fat that gives kanda bhaji its clean, light crunch

steps: Slice 3 onions lengthwise and mix with 3 chopped green chillies, 3 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt, then rest 10 minutes until glossy and wet.

Sprinkle over 1.25 cups besan, 0.5 cup rice flour, 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1.5 tsp goda masala, 1 tbsp white sesame seeds, 0.5 tsp sugar, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder, tossing to coat every sliver.
Add just 3 to 4 tbsp water, only enough to bind, so the mix clumps loosely and fries into open, crackly lace rather than solid fritters.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C until a shred of batter sizzles up briskly in 3 to 4 seconds.
Drop in small ragged handfuls and fry over medium-high for 4 to 5 minutes, separating them once, until pale gold turns to deep crisp brown.
Drain on paper, scatter a pinch more goda masala over the hot bhaji, and serve straight away for maximum crunch.
tips: The high rice-flour ratio is what makes Maharashtrian kanda bhaji glass-crisp, so do not swap it all for besan.
Keep the water minimal; the onions release enough moisture to bring the batter together on their own.
Warm goda masala in a dry pan for 20 seconds before mixing to wake up its clove and dagad-phool aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with dry garlic-peanut chutney (lasun khobra) and fried green chillies, and a cutting chai, exactly as it is sold at Pune tapris.

variations.name: Gujarati Crispy Pakora
variations.description: Kanda bhajiya with the unmistakable Gujarati sweet-savoury balance, where a spoon of jaggery and a squeeze of lemon lift the spiced besan. The batter is loosened with a little oil for a softer-shelled, gently sweet fritter that pairs beautifully with fried chillies and hot tea.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: dissolved into the batter for the signature Gujarati sweet edge against the chilli and lemon

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday Gujarati wood-pressed frying oil, plus a spoon stirred hot into the batter for softness

steps: Slice 2 onions and mix with 3 chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 3 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt, resting 8 minutes until juicy.
Stir 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tbsp lemon juice into 3 tbsp water until dissolved, then pour over the onions.

Add 1.5 cups besan, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, plus 1 tbsp hot Anveshan Groundnut Oil, mixing to a thick, glossy batter with a little extra water if needed.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 175C, slightly gentler than usual so the sweetened batter browns evenly without scorching.
Drop in rounded spoonfuls and fry over medium heat for 4 to 5 minutes, turning, until golden with crisp, ruffled edges.
Drain on paper and serve warm, when the sweet-tart flavour is at its most rounded.
tips: Fry a touch cooler than plain pakora; the jaggery browns faster and can catch if the oil is too hot.
Dissolve the jaggery in the lemon water first so it disperses evenly instead of leaving sweet pockets.
A pinch of baking soda in the batter makes these bhajiya especially light and puffy if you prefer them airy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve Gujarati-style with fried salted green chillies, sweet-hot chutney and a cup of masala chai, or tuck into soft pav for a monsoon bhajiya-pav.

variations.name: Bengali Crispy Pakora
variations.description: Peyaji, the Bengali onion fritter, fried in pungent mustard oil and freckled with nigella seeds for that unmistakable Kolkata-street aroma. Sharper and more savoury than its northern cousins, it leans on the bite of raw mustard oil and green chilli rather than a heavy spice mix.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: adds grip to the coating so the thin-sliced onions hold together and fry extra crisp

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil brought to smoking point first, the pungent heart of Bengali peyaji

steps: Slice 3 onions very thinly and mix with 4 slit green chillies, 0.75 tsp nigella seeds, 2 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt, resting 8 minutes until they wilt.
Add 1.25 cups besan, 0.25 cup rice flour, 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, tossing to a thick coating.
Sprinkle in just 3 to 4 tbsp water to bind into a stiff mix that barely holds, so the onion strands stay separate and lacy.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, then lower the flame to medium and let it settle for a minute to mellow the sharpness.
Drop in small flattened clusters and fry for 4 to 5 minutes, turning once, until crisp and deep golden with the mustard aroma clinging.
Drain on paper and serve hot, when the nigella crackle and mustard bite are most pronounced.
tips: Always heat mustard oil to smoking first, then cool slightly; this tames the raw pungency and prevents a bitter edge.
Slice the onions paper-thin so they cook through and crisp in the same time the batter browns.
A handful of these peyaji stirred into hot khichuri is the classic Bengali monsoon pairing if any are left over.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with muri (puffed rice), extra slit green chillies and a wedge of lemon, or alongside khichuri and begun bhaja on a rainy Kolkata afternoon.

variations.name: Classic Festive Besan Barfi
variations.description: The definitive Diwali besan barfi: coarsely ground gram flour slow-roasted in ghee until it smells like toasted hazelnuts, then bound with a fragrant cardamom syrup and set into melt-in-the-mouth fudge squares. The grainy, sandy crumb is the mark of a barfi roasted with patience rather than rushed on high heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the roasting fat that carries the toasted-besan aroma through every square

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined cane sugar for a cleaner, less cloying sweetness than white sugar

steps: Warm 1 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy-bottomed kadhai on low heat until it melts and just shimmers, about 2 minutes, then tip in 2 cups coarse besan mixed with 2 tbsp fine semolina.

Roast on low-medium heat, stirring without pause, until the besan turns deep honey-gold and smells nutty, about 18 minutes; drizzle in 3 tbsp milk halfway through and keep stirring so the mixture forms a loose, sandy crumb.
While it roasts, dissolve 1 cup Anveshan Khandsari in 0.5 cup water in a separate pan and simmer to a one-string consistency, about 6 minutes, then stir in 1 tsp cardamom powder and a pinch of salt.
Pull the roasted besan off the heat, pour in the hot syrup in a steady stream and beat hard for 2 minutes until the mass thickens and pulls cleanly from the sides of the pan.
Spread into a ghee-greased tray to a 1 cm thickness, level the top with a spatula, and scatter over 15 slivered almonds and 12 chopped pistachios, pressing them in gently.
Cool undisturbed for 30 minutes until just set but still slightly warm, then cut into 16 diamonds with a greased knife and let firm up fully before lifting out.
tips: If the barfi turns out crumbly and won't hold, the syrup was under-cooked; melt the crumbs back with 1 tbsp warm ghee and press again.
Roast the besan on genuinely low heat: rushing it on high scorches the outside while the centre stays raw and pasty.
For a coarser, halwai-style grain, rub 2 tbsp of the ghee into the dry besan before roasting to make a loose paste (mohan).
variations.servingSuggestion: Stack the diamonds on a brass thali lined with a banana leaf and tuck a few in a decorated mithai box with silver vark for gifting during Diwali.

variations.name: Gujarati Festive Besan Barfi
variations.description: A Gujarati Diwali version sweetened entirely with earthy jaggery instead of sugar, giving the barfi a deep caramel-brown colour and a mineral molasses note that plays against warm nutmeg. Gujarati halwais keep the grain slightly coarser and the ghee generous, so it stays soft for days.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: keeps the jaggery barfi soft and glossy rather than brittle

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melts into a caramel syrup that colours and sweetens the whole batch

steps: Heat 1 cup Anveshan Ghee in a thick kadhai over low flame until melted, then add 2 cups coarse besan and fold it through so every grain is coated.
Roast steadily on low heat for about 16 minutes, stirring in 3 tbsp milk once the mix darkens, until the besan is a rich brown and gives off a deep roasted-chickpea scent.

In a small pan, melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 0.33 cup water over low heat and simmer just until it forms a thick, sticky syrup that coats a spoon, about 5 minutes, then strain out any grit.
Take the besan off the heat, stir in a pinch of salt, 1 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp grated nutmeg, then pour in the warm jaggery syrup and beat for 2 minutes until glossy and pulling together.
Fold in 15 broken cashews and 1 tbsp charoli, then scrape the mixture into a greased tray and smooth it to a 1 cm slab while still warm.
Rest for 25 minutes until set but yielding, then slice into 16 squares; jaggery barfi stays deliberately softer than the sugar version.
tips: Never boil jaggery syrup to a hard stage or the barfi sets rock-hard; a thick coating consistency is all you need.
Taste your jaggery first: if it is very sharp, add an extra tablespoon of ghee to round the flavour.
This one keeps well for a week in an airtight tin as the jaggery holds moisture better than refined sugar.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve slightly warmed alongside a cup of masala chai on Bestu Varas, or crumble a piece over vanilla shrikhand for a quick festive dessert.

variations.name: Kashmiri Festive Besan Barfi
variations.description: A jewel-toned barfi bloomed with Kashmiri saffron and rosewater, its pale-gold crumb flecked with crushed pistachio in the Wazwan dessert tradition. The saffron is steeped in warm milk so its colour and honeyed aroma soak evenly through the fudge rather than sitting in streaks.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: carries the saffron's fat-soluble aroma into every bite

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: its pale colour lets the saffron gold show through undimmed
