Keep the added salt low since cheese brings plenty; taste the batter before cooking to be sure.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tomato ketchup for the kids and a sharp green chutney for the adults, cut into wedges like a quesadilla.

variations.name: Punjabi Amritsari Cheesy Sattu Cheela
variations.description: A rich Punjabi dhaba-style cheela brushed generously with butter and layered with cheese and a tandoori-masala kick. Cooked and finished in Anveshan ghee for that unmistakable buttery Amritsari indulgence, it is hearty, smoky and outrageously satisfying.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Sattu keeps this rich, buttery cheela grounded with protein and a nutty backbone.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Punjabi cooking leans on ghee, and here it cooks and finishes the cheela with a dhaba-style richness.

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups Anveshan Sattu with 0.75 tsp salt, 1 tsp tandoori masala, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi, then beat in 1.5 cups water to a smooth pouring batter.
Fold 1 chopped onion, 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 2 chopped green chillies and 3 tbsp coriander into the batter and rest 10 minutes.
Heat a tava over medium heat and grease it generously with Anveshan Ghee until it foams slightly.
Ladle on the batter, spread into a 7-inch round, drizzle 1 tsp ghee around the rim, and cook 2 to 3 minutes until the base is deep golden.
Scatter 3 tbsp grated cheese over one half, dot with a little butter, fold the bare half over and cook on low 2 minutes until the cheese melts into the buttery layer.
Brush the top with more Anveshan Ghee, press once on the tava for a crisp finish, and serve hot straight off the griddle.
tips: The kasuri methi is what gives this its dhaba aroma; crush it between your palms to release the oils before adding.
Do not rush the ghee-cooking on high heat; a slow golden base is what makes it taste like an Amritsari treat.
Add a spoon of grated paneer along with the cheese for an even richer, more North Indian filling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a dollop of white butter, pickled onions and mint chutney, dhaba-style, with a tall glass of lassi.

variations.name: Delhi Street-Style Cheesy Sattu Cheela
variations.description: Inspired by Delhi's cheela carts, this version pumps up the garam masala and chaat elements, topping the cheesy cheela with onion, chaat masala and a squeeze of lemon. Cooked in Anveshan wood-pressed groundnut oil and finished with ghee, it is a full street-food experience.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Sattu is the classic Delhi street-cheela base, filling and protein-rich for a quick meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the workhorse fat of Delhi thela cooking and crisps the cheela fast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A ghee finish gives that indulgent street-stall sheen and aroma.

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups Anveshan Sattu with 0.75 tsp salt, 1 tsp garam masala and 0.5 tsp turmeric, then beat in 1.5 cups water to a smooth pouring batter.
Fold 2 chopped green chillies and 3 tbsp coriander into the batter and rest 10 minutes; keep 1 finely chopped onion and 1 small chopped tomato ready for topping.
Heat a tava over medium heat and grease with a little Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil until it shimmers.
Ladle on the batter, spread into a 7-inch round, drizzle 0.5 tsp oil around the rim, and cook 2 to 3 minutes until the base is golden.
Scatter 3 tbsp grated cheese, a spoon of chopped onion and tomato over the top, cover for 1 minute so the cheese melts, then sprinkle 0.25 tsp chaat masala and a few drops of lemon.
Brush the edges with Anveshan Ghee, fold in half or leave open like an uttapam, and serve hot with the toppings glistening.
tips: Add the chaat masala and lemon only at the end so their tang stays fresh and sharp.
Leaving it open-faced like an uttapam shows off the melty cheese and chopped toppings, true to the street style.
A drizzle of green and tamarind chutney over the top turns this into a full cheela chaat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve open-faced with green chutney and sweet tamarind chutney drizzled across, topped with a little more raw onion.

variations.name: Haryanvi Desi Ghee Cheesy Sattu Cheela
variations.description: A rustic Haryanvi cheela cooked lavishly in desi ghee, the pride of the region's dairy kitchens, with a simple homely spicing and a generous cheese fold. Rich, wholesome and unfussy, it tastes of a farmhouse breakfast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Sattu and ghee are both Haryanvi staples, and together they make a filling farmhouse cheela.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Generous desi ghee is the whole point of a Haryanvi cheela, cooking and finishing it richly.

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups Anveshan Sattu with 0.75 tsp salt, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp ajwain and 0.5 tsp turmeric, then beat in 1.5 cups water to a smooth pouring batter.
Fold 1 chopped onion, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger and 3 tbsp coriander into the batter and rest 10 minutes.
Heat a tava over medium heat and grease it well with Anveshan Ghee until it foams lightly.
Ladle on the batter, spread into a 7-inch round, drizzle 1 tsp ghee around the rim, and cook 2 to 3 minutes until the base is a rich golden brown.
Scatter 3 tbsp grated cheese over one half, fold the bare half over, and cook on low 2 minutes until the cheese melts through.
Brush the top with more Anveshan Ghee, press once for crispness, and serve hot with the ghee aroma filling the kitchen.
tips: Do not skimp on the ghee here; the generous fat is exactly what defines the Haryanvi style.
Ajwain aids digestion of the heavy sattu-and-ghee combination and is traditional in this region.
A glass of fresh chaas alongside cuts the richness and is the authentic Haryanvi accompaniment.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with homemade white butter, a raw onion and green chilli, and a tall glass of salted buttermilk.

variations.name: Malwa Peanut Cheesy Sattu Cheela
variations.description: A Malwa-region take that folds crushed roasted peanuts into the cheesy cheela for a nutty crunch against the melting cheese, a nod to the peanut-rich cooking of central India. Cooked in Anveshan wood-pressed groundnut oil and finished with ghee, it is crunchy, cheesy and moreish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Sattu and peanuts stack up the protein and give this cheela a doubly nutty character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil echoes the peanuts and is the natural fat of the Malwa kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A ghee finish binds the nutty, cheesy flavours with a warm richness.

steps: Coarsely crush 0.33 cup roasted peanuts so some crunch remains, keeping a spoonful aside for garnish.
Whisk 1.5 cups Anveshan Sattu with 0.75 tsp salt, 0.75 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp amchur and 1 tbsp sesame seeds, then beat in 1.5 cups water to a smooth pouring batter.
Fold most of the crushed peanuts, 1 chopped onion, 2 chopped green chillies and 3 tbsp coriander into the batter and rest 10 minutes.
Heat a tava over medium heat and grease with a little Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil until it shimmers.
Ladle on the batter, spread into a 7-inch round, drizzle 0.5 tsp oil around the rim, and cook 2 to 3 minutes until the base is golden.
Scatter 3 tbsp grated cheese and the reserved peanuts over one half, fold over, cook on low 2 minutes to melt the cheese, then brush with Anveshan Ghee and serve hot.
tips: Keep the peanut crush coarse for texture; a fine powder disappears into the batter and loses the crunch.
Roast raw peanuts fresh and rub off the skins for a cleaner, sweeter flavour if you have the time.
A pinch of amchur in the batter adds a tangy central-Indian note that cuts the cheese richness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a garlic-peanut chutney and a bowl of curd, with extra crushed peanuts scattered on top for crunch.

variations.name: Classic Cheesy Vegetable Appe
variations.description: An indulgent, kid-friendly paniyaram where each vegetable dumpling hides a molten cube of cheese at its heart. Cooked in an appe pan with Anveshan wood-pressed groundnut oil and ghee, they are crisp and golden outside with a soft, cheese-filled centre that pulls into strings.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil crisps the shell so it holds while the cheese melts inside.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A few drops of ghee in each mould give the cheesy appe a rich golden base.

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 1 chopped onion, 0.33 cup grated carrot, 0.33 cup finely chopped capsicum and 2 chopped green chillies and saute 3 minutes; cool the mixture.
Fold the cooled vegetables and 3 tbsp coriander into 2 cups dosa batter with 0.5 tsp salt, keeping the batter thick; keep the salt light because the cheese is salty.
Add 0.5 tsp Eno just before cooking and fold until the batter is light and bubbly.
Heat an appe pan over medium heat, put a few drops of groundnut oil and Anveshan Ghee in each mould, and spoon batter to half-fill each cavity.
Press a small cube of mozzarella into the centre of each, cover with a little more batter to seal, then cover the pan and cook 3 to 4 minutes until golden underneath.
Flip each appe carefully and cook 2 to 3 minutes more until golden all over and the cheese is molten inside; serve immediately.
tips: Seal the cheese fully inside the batter or it will leak out and stick to the pan as it melts.
Cook on medium, not high, so the centre heats through and the cheese melts before the shell over-browns.
Cut the mozzarella into small cubes; too large a piece will not melt in time and stays rubbery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with tomato ketchup for the children and a sharp green chutney for the adults, straight from the pan.

variations.name: Punjabi Amritsari Cheesy Vegetable Appe
variations.description: A rich Punjabi-styled paniyaram with a buttery tandoori-masala batter and a cheese-filled heart, finished with a brush of butter for dhaba-style indulgence. Cooked in Anveshan ghee, these dumplings are hearty, smoky and outrageously cheesy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Punjabi cooking leans on ghee, and here it greases the moulds and finishes the appe richly.

steps: Heat 1 tbsp butter in a pan, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 1 chopped onion and fry 2 minutes, then add 0.33 cup chopped capsicum, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp tandoori masala and 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi and saute 2 minutes; cool the mixture.
Fold the cooled masala and 3 tbsp coriander into 2 cups dosa batter with 0.5 tsp salt, keeping the salt light for the salty cheese.
Add 0.5 tsp Eno just before cooking and fold until light and bubbly.
Heat an appe pan over medium heat, put a few drops of Anveshan Ghee in each mould, and half-fill each cavity with batter.
Press a small cube of cheese into each centre, top with a little more batter to seal, cover and cook 3 to 4 minutes until golden underneath.
Flip each appe, brush the tops with more Anveshan Ghee, and cook 2 to 3 minutes more until golden and the cheese is molten; serve hot.
tips: Crush the kasuri methi between your palms before adding to release its dhaba aroma.
Add a spoon of grated paneer alongside the cheese for an even richer, more North Indian centre.
A slow golden cook in ghee is what gives these their Amritsari richness, so resist turning up the heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with pickled onions, mint chutney and a dollop of white butter, dhaba-style, with a glass of lassi.

variations.name: Delhi Street-Style Cheesy Vegetable Appe
variations.description: Inspired by Delhi's chaat carts, these cheese-filled dumplings are dusted with chaat masala and garam masala and finished with a squeeze of lemon. Cooked in Anveshan wood-pressed groundnut oil and ghee, they are a fun cross between a paniyaram and a cheesy street snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the workhorse fat of Delhi street cooking and crisps the appe fast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A little ghee in the moulds gives that indulgent street-stall sheen and aroma.

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 1 chopped onion and 2 chopped green chillies and saute 2 minutes; stir in 1 tsp garam masala and cool the mixture.
Fold the cooled mixture and 3 tbsp coriander into 2 cups dosa batter with 0.5 tsp salt, keeping the salt light for the cheese.
Add 0.5 tsp Eno just before cooking and fold until light and bubbly.
Heat an appe pan over medium heat, put a few drops of groundnut oil and Anveshan Ghee in each mould, and half-fill each cavity with batter.
Press a small cube of cheese into each centre, seal with a little more batter, cover and cook 3 to 4 minutes until golden underneath.
Flip each appe and cook 2 to 3 minutes more until golden, then sprinkle 1 tsp chaat masala and a few drops of lemon over the hot appe and serve at once.
tips: Add the chaat masala and lemon only at the end so their tang stays sharp and fresh.
Toss the hot appe in a bowl with the chaat masala for even coating, street-cart style.
A drizzle of green and tamarind chutney turns these into a full cheesy appe chaat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve skewered with toothpicks, drizzled with green and sweet tamarind chutney and a scatter of raw onion.

variations.name: Haryanvi Desi Ghee Cheesy Vegetable Appe
variations.description: A rustic Haryanvi paniyaram cooked lavishly in desi ghee, the pride of the region's dairy kitchens, with a homely spicing and a molten cheese centre. Rich, wholesome and unfussy, these taste of a generous farmhouse table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Generous desi ghee is the whole point of a Haryanvi dish, greasing and finishing the appe richly.

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 0.5 tsp ajwain, then add 1 chopped onion, 0.33 cup grated carrot, 2 chopped green chillies and 1 inch grated ginger and saute 3 minutes; cool the mixture.
Fold the cooled vegetables and 3 tbsp coriander into 2 cups dosa batter with 0.5 tsp salt, keeping the salt light for the cheese.
Add 0.5 tsp Eno just before cooking and fold until light and bubbly.
Heat an appe pan over medium heat, put a few drops of Anveshan Ghee in each mould, and half-fill each cavity with batter.
Press a small cube of cheese into each centre, seal with a little more batter, cover and cook 3 to 4 minutes until golden underneath.
Flip each appe, brush the tops with more Anveshan Ghee, and cook 2 to 3 minutes more until golden and the cheese is molten; serve hot.
tips: Do not skimp on the ghee, as the generous fat is exactly what defines the Haryanvi style.
Ajwain aids digestion of the rich ghee-and-cheese combination and is traditional in the region.
A glass of fresh chaas alongside cuts the richness in the authentic Haryanvi way.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with homemade white butter, a green chilli-garlic chutney and a tall glass of salted buttermilk.

variations.name: Hyderabadi Saffron Cheesy Vegetable Appe
variations.description: A shahi Hyderabadi-styled paniyaram where the batter is enriched with an Anveshan saffron infusion and warm garam spices, cradling a molten cheese centre. Cooked in Anveshan ghee, these dumplings are fragrant, mildly regal and lightly golden with saffron.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee greases the moulds and carries the shahi richness typical of Hyderabadi cooking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: A saffron infusion lends a gentle regal colour and aroma to the batter, the Hyderabadi shahi touch.

steps: Warm 2 tbsp milk and steep 0.25 tsp Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in it for 10 minutes until the milk turns deep gold and fragrant.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 1 chopped onion and fry 2 minutes, then add 2 chopped green chillies and 0.5 tsp garam masala and saute 1 minute; cool the mixture.
Fold the cooled mixture, the saffron milk, 2 tbsp mint and 2 tbsp coriander into 2 cups dosa batter with 0.5 tsp salt, keeping the salt light for the cheese.
Add 0.5 tsp Eno just before cooking and fold until light and bubbly.
Heat an appe pan over medium heat, put a few drops of Anveshan Ghee in each mould, half-fill each cavity, press a small cube of cheese into each centre and seal with a little more batter.
Cover and cook 3 to 4 minutes until golden underneath, then flip each appe and cook 2 to 3 minutes more until golden and the cheese is molten; serve hot.
tips: Steep the saffron in warm milk rather than water for a rounder colour and aroma that suits the shahi style.
A little chopped mint is what gives these their Hyderabadi character, so do not leave it out.
Keep the spicing gentle so the saffron fragrance comes through against the melting cheese.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a mint-coriander raita and a wedge of lemon, plated on a bed of fried onions for a shahi touch.

variations.name: Classic Adai
variations.description: The protein-packed Tamil breakfast crepe, made from a coarsely ground mix of chana, toor, urad and moong dals with rice, studded with dried red chilli and cumin. Thicker and nuttier than a dosa, with crisp lacy holes and a satisfying, hearty bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil gives adai its trademark crisp, golden lace.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A drizzle of ghee on each adai is the classic Tamil finishing touch.

steps: Rinse and soak the chana, toor, urad and moong dals with 1 cup raw rice together for 3 hours, then drain well.
Grind the soaked dals and rice with 4 dried red chillies, 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida to a coarse batter, adding water sparingly so it stays thick and spoonable.
Stir in 1.5 tsp salt, 15 torn curry leaves and 1 finely chopped medium onion; the batter should be thick, not pourable like dosa batter.
Heat a tava over medium heat, grease lightly with Anveshan Groundnut Oil, then spread a ladle of batter into a thick round about 7 inches wide, leaving it slightly heavier than a dosa.
Poke a hole in the centre and drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil around and into it, cooking until the underside is deep golden and crisp, about 3 minutes.
Flip and cook the second side until browned and cooked through, about 2 minutes, then drizzle with a little Anveshan Ghee.
Serve the adai hot off the tava while the edges are shatteringly crisp.
tips: Grind the batter coarse, not smooth, as that grainy texture is exactly what gives adai its characteristic bite.
Adai batter needs no fermentation, so you can grind and cook the same day, though an hour's rest deepens the flavour.
The centre hole is not just tradition; it lets oil reach the middle so the thick adai crisps evenly rather than staying doughy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Tamil way with avial and a knob of butter, or simply with jaggery and extra ghee for a sweet-savoury contrast.

variations.name: Kerala Coconut Adai
variations.description: A Malabar version enriched with coarse coconut bits ground into the batter and cooked in coconut oil, giving the adai a sweet, tropical richness. It pairs the lentil heartiness with the unmistakable perfume of the Kerala coast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil deepens the coconut in the batter and perfumes the crust.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A little ghee at the finish balances the sweet coconut with savoury depth.

steps: Soak the chana, toor and urad dals with 1 cup raw rice for 3 hours, then drain.
Grind the soaked mix with 4 dried red chillies and 1 tsp fennel seeds to a coarse batter, then pulse in 0.5 cup grated coconut so flecks remain visible.
Stir in 1.5 tsp salt, 15 curry leaves and 6 finely chopped shallots to make a thick, spoonable batter.
Heat a tava over medium heat, grease with Anveshan Coconut Oil, and spread a ladle of batter into a thick 7-inch round.
Make a hole in the centre and drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil around it, cooking until the base is golden and crisp, about 3 minutes.
Flip and cook the second side until browned, about 2 minutes, then finish with a little Anveshan Ghee.
Serve the coconut adai hot while fragrant and crisp.
tips: Pulse the coconut in only at the end so it stays in coarse flecks rather than dissolving into the batter.
Shallots, not regular onions, give the authentic Kerala sweetness, so use them if you can find them.
Warm solidified coconut oil in a bowl of hot water before greasing the tava for an even coat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coconut-heavy avial and a dab of jaggery on the side, the classic Kerala accompaniment to adai.

variations.name: Andhra Guntur Adai
variations.description: A fiery Andhra adai where extra Guntur red chillies and garlic are ground into the lentil batter and it is cooked in sesame oil. Robust, garlicky and blazing, it turns a humble protein crepe into a fierce coastal treat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly sesame oil gives the toasty, nutty base Andhra cooks prefer for adai.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing touch of ghee softens the aggressive Guntur heat.

steps: Soak the chana, toor and urad dals with 1 cup raw rice for 3 hours, then drain.
Grind the soaked mix with 6 Guntur red chillies, 6 garlic cloves and 1 tsp cumin seeds to a coarse, fiery batter, adding water sparingly.
Stir in 1.5 tsp salt, 15 curry leaves and 1 finely chopped onion to a thick batter.
Heat a tava over medium heat, grease with Anveshan Sesame Oil, and spread a ladle of batter into a thick 7-inch round.
Make a central hole and drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil around it, cooking until the base is crisp and red-flecked, about 3 minutes.
Flip and cook until browned through, about 2 minutes, then finish with a little Anveshan Ghee.
Serve the Guntur adai searing hot, straight off the tava while the edges are crisp.
tips: Grinding the garlic straight into the batter mellows its bite as the adai cooks, unlike raw garlic which would taste sharp.
Deseed a couple of the Guntur chillies if you want the flavour and colour without the full firepower.
Sesame oil can smoke fast, so keep the tava at steady medium heat rather than high.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling coconut chutney and a small bowl of curd, the essential Andhra counterpoint to this much heat.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Peanut Goda Adai
variations.description: A Deccan-style adai where crushed roasted peanuts and warm goda masala are worked into the lentil batter for a sweet-woody, crunchy crepe. Cooked in groundnut oil, it tastes like a Maharashtrian thalipeeth crossed with a South Indian adai.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil echoes the peanut in the batter and crisps the adai evenly.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A hint of jaggery balances the goda masala in true Maharashtrian style.

steps: Soak the chana, toor and urad dals with 1 cup raw rice for 3 hours, then drain, and dry-roast 0.33 cup peanuts until spotty and crush coarsely.
Grind the soaked mix with 3 dried red chillies to a coarse batter, adding water sparingly to keep it thick.
Stir in 1.5 tsp salt, 1.5 tsp goda masala, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, the crushed peanuts, 1 chopped onion and 3 tbsp chopped coriander.
Heat a tava over medium heat, grease with Anveshan Groundnut Oil, and spread a ladle of batter into a thick 7-inch round.
Make a central hole and drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil around it, cooking until golden and crisp, about 3 minutes.
Flip and cook the second side until browned and cooked through, about 2 minutes.
Serve the peanut goda adai hot with its crunchy edges intact.
tips: Leave the roasted peanuts coarse for pockets of crunch in every bite rather than grinding them to a paste.
Goda masala strength varies, so start with less and adjust, as some blends are far more intense than others.
The jaggery should just round the spice, not sweeten the adai, so keep it to the stated amount.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a fresh coconut-coriander chutney and a spoon of thecha for those who want an extra Maharashtrian kick.

variations.name: Karnataka Tamarind Adai
variations.description: A tangy Mysore-region adai where tamarind and a touch of jaggery are folded into the batter for a sweet-sour lentil crepe. The tamarind brightens the earthy dals, making it lighter and more refreshing than the classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery balances the tamarind for the signature Karnataka sweet-sour note.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil crisps the tangy batter into lacy edges.

steps: Soak the chana, toor and urad dals with 1 cup raw rice for 3 hours, then drain, and soak 1 tbsp tamarind in 3 tbsp warm water, squeezing out the pulp.
Grind the soaked mix with 4 dried red chillies and 1 tsp cumin seeds to a coarse batter, adding water sparingly.
Stir in the tamarind pulp, 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1.5 tsp salt, 15 curry leaves and 1 chopped onion to a thick, tangy batter.
Heat a tava over medium heat, grease with Anveshan Groundnut Oil, and spread a ladle of batter into a thick 7-inch round.
Make a central hole and drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil around it, cooking until golden and crisp, about 3 minutes.
Flip and cook the second side until browned through, about 2 minutes.
Serve the tamarind adai hot while crisp.
tips: Add the tamarind pulp gradually and taste, since sourness varies and you want a gentle tang, not a mouth-puckering one.
The jaggery and tamarind should balance each other; if it tastes too sour after resting, stir in a little more jaggery.
Because the batter is loosened with tamarind water, hold back on extra water so the adai still crisps.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling mint chutney and a bowl of thin buttermilk, which offsets the tamarind tang beautifully.

variations.name: Classic Besan Cheela
variations.description: The quickest savoury pancake in the Indian kitchen, made from gram flour whisked with water and gentle spices, needing no soaking or grinding. This definitive version is thin, soft-centred and lightly crisp, ready in minutes for a wholesome breakfast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Wood-Pressed Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil films the tava cleanly and gives the besan cheela its light golden crisp.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing brush of bilona ghee adds a nutty, glossy aroma to the folded cheela.

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups gram flour with 1.5 cups water in a steady stream into a smooth, lump-free batter the consistency of thin cream, roughly a one-to-one flour-to-water ratio.
Stir in 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, a pinch of asafoetida and 1 tsp salt until evenly coloured.
Fold in 1 finely chopped onion, 1 chopped tomato, 2 minced green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger and 3 tbsp coriander, then rest the batter for 10 minutes.
Heat a flat tava over medium heat and grease it with a film of Anveshan Groundnut Wood-Pressed Oil, wiping evenly until the surface shimmers.
Pour a ladle of batter and spread it in a spiral into a thin 7-inch round, drizzle 1 tsp groundnut oil around the rim, and cook until the underside is golden and the top looks dry, about 3 minutes.
Flip and cook the second side for 2 minutes until set with brown spots, brush with Anveshan Bilona Ghee, fold into a half-moon and serve hot.
tips: Whisk the batter well and rest it briefly so the gram flour hydrates fully, which prevents a raw, pasty taste.
If the batter thickens on standing, thin it with a spoon of water; besan absorbs liquid as it sits.
Spread the first cheela thin as a test and adjust the batter consistency before cooking the rest.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a fresh mint-coriander chutney and a cup of masala chai, or roll it around grated paneer for a heartier plate.

variations.name: Bengali Besan Cheela
variations.description: A Bengali gram-flour cheela sharpened with pungent wood-pressed mustard oil and studded with nigella seeds, close in spirit to a besan-based pakora batter. Earthy, sharp and deeply aromatic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Wood-Pressed Oil
ingredients.note: Smoked kachi ghani mustard oil is what gives this besan cheela its distinct Bengali pungency.

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups gram flour with 1.5 cups water into a smooth, pourable batter free of lumps.
Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Wood-Pressed Oil until it just smokes, cool for thirty seconds, and whisk it into the batter to soften its raw sharpness while keeping the aroma.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder and 1 tsp salt, then fold in 3 minced green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 2 chopped spring onions and 3 tbsp coriander and rest 10 minutes.
Heat a tava over medium heat, film it with more Anveshan Mustard Wood-Pressed Oil, and scatter a pinch of nigella seeds onto the greased surface to toast.
Pour a ladle of batter over the seeds and spread into a thin 7-inch round, drizzle mustard oil around the rim, and cook until the base is deep golden and crisp, about 3 to 4 minutes.
Flip and cook 2 minutes more until cooked through, then fold and serve while the mustard fragrance is bright.
tips: Always smoke the mustard oil first; besan batter amplifies any raw bitterness in unheated kachi ghani oil.
Nigella toasts fast, so scatter it on the tava only just before pouring the batter.
A pinch of sugar in the batter balances the mustard pungency the classic Bengali way.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a spoon of kasundi and thin cucumber slices, letting the mustard condiment mirror the oil in the batter.

variations.name: Rajasthani Besan Cheela
variations.description: Gram flour is the heart of Rajasthani cooking, and this cheela leans into it with soaked dried red chillies, ajwain and a rich ghee cook. Robust and warming, it is desert comfort food.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: Nutty bilona ghee gives these gram-flour cheela their signature Rajasthani richness and browns the base deeply.

steps: Soak 4 dried red chillies in warm water for 15 minutes until soft, then pound them with 5 garlic cloves into a coarse paste.
Whisk 1.5 cups gram flour with 1.5 cups water into a smooth batter, then beat in the chilli-garlic paste, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt.

Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee, crackle 0.5 tsp ajwain in it for ten seconds until fragrant, cool, and stir the tempering into the batter along with 1 chopped onion and 3 tbsp coriander, then rest 10 minutes.
Heat a tava over medium heat and grease it with a little Anveshan Bilona Ghee until it melts into a shimmering film.
Ladle the batter and spread into a slightly thick 6-inch round, spoon 1 tsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee around the rim, and cook until the base is deep golden and crisp, about 4 minutes.
Flip, press with the spatula, and cook 2 minutes more until blistered and cooked through, then serve straight off the tava.
tips: Blooming the ajwain in ghee first is essential; raw carom seeds in besan batter taste harsh and medicinal.
Soaked dried chillies give a smoky, rounded heat that dry chilli powder cannot match.
Cook these a touch thicker so they stand up to a robust garlic chutney without tearing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a fiery lehsun chutney and a bowl of salted chaas, thali style, to round out the desert flavours.

variations.name: Gujarati Besan Cheela
variations.description: The Gujarati puda, a soft gram-flour cheela with a gentle jaggery sweetness against ginger-chilli heat and a hint of curd for tang. Thin, tender and characteristically sweet-savoury.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Wood-Pressed Oil
ingredients.note: Light wood-pressed sunflower oil keeps the puda soft and lets the jaggery sweetness read clearly.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A spoon of jaggery powder gives the classic Gujarati sweet-savoury note that defines a puda.

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups gram flour with 0.25 cup whisked curd and 1.25 cups water into a smooth, thin, pourable batter.
Stir in 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1.5 tsp ginger-green chilli paste, 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, mixing until the jaggery fully dissolves.
Fold in 3 tbsp coriander and rest the batter for 10 minutes so the curd and jaggery meld.
Heat a tava over medium-low heat and grease it thinly with Anveshan Sunflower Wood-Pressed Oil until it just glistens.
Pour a ladle of batter and spread into a thin 7-inch round, drizzle 1 tsp oil around the rim, and cook gently until the base is pale gold, about 3 minutes.
Flip and cook 2 minutes more until soft-set and lightly spotted, keeping the heat low so the jaggery does not catch, then fold and serve warm.
tips: The spoon of curd makes the puda especially soft and adds a subtle tang that balances the jaggery.
Keep the flame low, since the jaggery in the batter browns and can burn quickly over high heat.
Taste the batter and adjust salt so the sweetness sits gently in the background.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coriander-chilli chutney and a bowl of thick curd, or pack it warm into a tiffin where it stays tender.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Besan Cheela
variations.description: The Maharashtrian besan cheela, or dhirde, spiced with warm goda masala and brightened with fresh coriander and coconut. Softly spiced and comforting, it is a staple quick tiffin.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Wood-Pressed Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the everyday Maharashtrian fat and keeps the goda-spiced dhirde earthy and light.

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups gram flour with 1.5 cups water into a smooth, lump-free batter of thin-cream consistency.
Beat in 1.5 tsp goda masala, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder and 1 tsp salt until the warm spices are evenly blended.
Fold in 3 tbsp grated coconut, 2 minced green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger and 3 tbsp coriander, then rest the batter for 10 minutes so the goda masala softens.
Heat a tava over medium heat and grease it with a film of Anveshan Groundnut Wood-Pressed Oil until it shimmers.
Ladle the batter and spread into a 7-inch round, drizzle 1 tsp groundnut oil around the rim, and cook until the base is golden and the coconut flecks toast, about 3 minutes.
Flip and cook 2 minutes more until firm and speckled, then fold into a triangle and serve hot.
tips: Add goda masala to taste, starting at 1.5 tsp, as its intensity varies widely between brands and homes.
Toast frozen coconut in a dry pan for a minute to revive its sweetness and keep the batter from weeping.
The batter is best used within a couple of hours; besan can turn sour if left too long in warmth.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a jaggery-tamarind chutney and hot filter coffee for a classic Maharashtrian tiffin plate.

variations.name: Classic Nariyal Barfi
variations.description: The everyday coconut barfi of Indian home kitchens: fresh grated coconut simmered with milk and sugar until it thickens into a soft, snowy fudge, scented simply with green cardamom. It sets in under an hour and captures the pure, milky sweetness of good coconut.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the pan and enriches the coconut mass so it does not stick

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined sugar for a clean sweetness that keeps the barfi white

steps: Warm 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide non-stick pan on low heat, then add 3 cups fresh grated coconut and toss for 3 minutes until it smells fragrant but stays white.
Pour in 1 cup whole milk and 1 cup Anveshan Khandsari, raise to medium heat and cook, stirring often, until the mixture comes together and the milk reduces, about 12 minutes.
Sprinkle in 0.5 cup milk powder and a pinch of salt and keep stirring for another 6 minutes until the mass thickens and pulls away from the sides of the pan.
Stir in 1 tsp cardamom powder and 12 chopped cashews, cooking one more minute until the mixture holds its shape on the spoon.
Scrape into a ghee-greased tray, press to a 1.5 cm slab with a spatula and scatter 10 slivered almonds over the top, pressing them in.
Cool for 30 minutes until set, then cut into 16 squares with a greased knife; the barfi should be soft but hold a clean edge.
tips: Do not let the coconut brown in the ghee or you will lose the pale, snowy colour of a classic nariyal barfi.
If the mixture stays loose, cook a few minutes longer; it must leave the pan sides cleanly before setting.
Fresh coconut gives the best texture, but frozen grated coconut, thawed and squeezed, works well too.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile the white squares in a bright silver katori for pooja prasad, or serve after dinner with a few strands of saffron laid on top.

variations.name: Gujarati Nariyal Barfi
variations.description: A Gujarati kopra pak sweetened with jaggery rather than sugar, turning the coconut fudge a warm golden-brown with a mellow molasses depth. A little nutmeg and a generous hand with ghee make it soft and festive.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: keeps the jaggery coconut mass soft and prevents it turning grainy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: colours the coconut golden and adds a mellow caramel note

steps: Melt 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide pan on low heat and toast 3 cups grated coconut for 3 minutes until fragrant, keeping the colour light for now.
Add 0.75 cup whole milk and cook on medium heat for about 8 minutes, stirring, until the coconut plumps and most of the milk is absorbed.
Lower the heat, stir in 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and let it melt into the coconut over about 6 minutes until the whole mass turns golden-brown and glossy.
Mix in 0.5 cup milk powder, a pinch of salt, 1 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp nutmeg, cooking another 5 minutes until it leaves the pan sides.
Fold in 1 tbsp charoli, then press into a greased tray to a 1.5 cm slab and smooth the top while warm.
Cool for 30 minutes until set but soft, then cut into 16 squares that glow amber-gold from the jaggery.
tips: Add the jaggery only after the milk has mostly reduced, or the acidity can make the milk split.
Keep the flame low once the jaggery is in so it melts smoothly instead of hardening.
This barfi stays soft for days because jaggery holds moisture; store it airtight at room temperature.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm at a Gujarati wedding sweet counter, or pair a square with a shot of unsweetened masala chai to balance the caramel.

variations.name: Kashmiri Nariyal Barfi
variations.description: A saffron-gilded coconut barfi in the Kashmiri manner, the white fudge tinted pale gold and perfumed with rosewater, then showered with slivered almonds and pistachios. Delicate and aromatic, it is a barfi built for a wedding thali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: carries the saffron colour evenly into the coconut

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: keeps the base pale so the saffron gold shows clearly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk to gild and perfume the coconut

steps: Steep a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 1 cup warm whole milk for 10 minutes until the milk glows deep gold.
Melt 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide pan on low heat and toss 3 cups grated coconut for 3 minutes, keeping it white.
Pour in the saffron milk with 1 cup Anveshan Khandsari and cook on medium heat for about 12 minutes, stirring, until the coconut turns pale gold and the milk reduces.
Add 0.5 cup milk powder, a pinch of salt and 1 tsp cardamom and cook 5 minutes more until the mass thickens and leaves the pan; stir in 1 tsp rosewater off the heat.
Press into a greased tray to a 1.5 cm slab and shower the top with 3 tbsp slivered pistachios and almonds, pressing them lightly in.
Cool for 30 minutes until set, then cut into 16 diamonds that gleam gold at every edge.
tips: Reserve a few saffron threads to lay on top so the finished barfi looks as saffron-rich as it tastes.
Stir rosewater in only after the heat is off so its perfume is preserved.
Keep the coconut from browning to protect the pale-gold saffron colour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Arrange on a silver tray with a dusting of dried rose petals for a wedding sweet course, served with warm kahwa.

variations.name: Awadhi Nariyal Barfi
variations.description: A Lucknawi coconut barfi scented with kewra and a breath of screwpine-sweet mace, kept pale and soft in the nazakat tradition. The fragrance arrives before the sweetness, a hallmark of Awadhi mithai.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: mild and clean so the kewra perfume stays in front

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: a delicate sweetness suited to a fragrance-led barfi

steps: Melt 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide pan on low heat and warm 3 cups grated coconut for 3 minutes without colouring it.
Add 1 cup whole milk and 1 cup Anveshan Khandsari and cook on medium heat, stirring, for about 12 minutes until the milk reduces into the coconut.
Stir in 0.5 cup milk powder, a pinch of salt, 1 tsp cardamom and 0.125 tsp mace and cook 5 minutes more until the mass thickens and pulls away from the pan.
Take the pan off the heat and gently stir in 1.5 tsp kewra water so its volatile perfume is not cooked off.
Press into a greased tray to a 1.5 cm slab, scatter 2 tbsp slivered almonds over the surface and smooth gently.
Cool for 30 minutes until set, then cut into 16 delicate squares with a clean, lightly greased knife.
tips: Measure the kewra sparingly; too much turns a fragrant barfi soapy in an instant.
Keep everything pale, as a courtly Awadhi sweet should look as soft as it tastes.
Mace is stronger than nutmeg, so an eighth of a teaspoon is plenty for the whole batch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on fine china after an Awadhi meal, each square resting on a small silver-edged doily beside cups of scented tea.

variations.name: Malwa Nariyal Barfi
variations.description: A rustic Malwa version where grated coconut meets crushed roasted peanuts and jaggery, giving the barfi a double nuttiness and a sturdy, chewy bite. It is a plateau harvest sweet, generous and unfussy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: binds coconut and peanut together into a chewy slab

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the warming sweetener that ties into the roasted peanuts

steps: Melt 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide pan on low heat and toast 3 cups grated coconut for 4 minutes until lightly golden and fragrant.
Add 0.5 cup whole milk and cook on medium heat for about 7 minutes until the coconut absorbs it and turns tender.
Lower the heat and melt in 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder over about 6 minutes until it coats the coconut in a golden syrup.
Stir in 0.33 cup milk powder, a pinch of salt, 1 tsp cardamom and 0.5 tsp dried ginger, cooking 4 minutes until thick, then fold in 0.75 cup crushed roasted peanuts off the heat.
Press firmly into a greased tray to a 2 cm slab so the chunky mixture packs together well.
Cool for 30 minutes until firm, then cut into 16 sturdy squares that show peanut and coconut in every piece.
tips: Fold the peanuts in off the heat to keep their crunch against the soft coconut.
Press the slab well; the peanut chunks need firm packing so the squares hold together.
A wedge of this travels well in a tiffin without melting, unlike softer milk barfis.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pack squares for a winter journey or Sankranti hamper, or crumble one over warm jaggery-sweetened milk for a filling nightcap.

variations.name: Classic Onion Uttapam
variations.description: The thick, spongy cousin of the dosa, poured fat and studded with sweet chopped onions pressed into its surface. Soft and pillowy within with a lacy golden underside, it is South India's answer to a savoury pancake breakfast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil for cooking that crisps the onion-studded underside without heaviness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee dotted on to finish, giving each uttapam a fragrant, glossy top

steps: Loosen 2.5 cups fermented dosa batter with a little water if needed so it is thick but still spreadable, then stir in 0.5 tsp salt and 1 tsp cumin seeds.
Finely chop 2 onions, 1 tomato, 2 green chillies and 3 tbsp coriander and keep them together in a bowl for topping.
Heat a tava on medium until a drop of water sizzles gently, then grease it with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil wiped across with a cloth.
Pour a ladle of batter and spread it into a thick round about 5 inches wide, keeping it far thicker than a dosa so it stays spongy.
Scatter a generous handful of the onion topping and a few curry leaves over the surface, press gently with the ladle, and drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil around the edge.
Cover and cook for 3 minutes until the base is golden, flip and cook the topping side for 2 minutes, then dot with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Ghee and serve.
tips: Cook uttapam on medium, never high, so the thick centre cooks through before the base burns.
Press the onions in firmly so they embed and cook into the batter rather than falling off on the flip.
If your batter is very sour, a pinch of jaggery or a rest at room temperature softens the tang.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and sambar, or a simple tomato-onion chutney for a lighter weekday breakfast.

variations.name: Tamil Onion Uttapam
variations.description: Tamil Nadu crowns the uttapam with a fragrant curry-leaf and mustard tempering poured over the onions, the classic tiffin-shop flourish. A hit of ginger and green chilli in the mola-podi style gives it that unmistakable Kongunadu aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed gingelly oil, the Tamil tiffin standard, for cooking and the tempering

steps: Stir 0.5 tsp salt into 2.5 cups fermented dosa batter and adjust with a splash of water so it holds a thick, spreadable consistency.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal until the dal turns golden, then add 20 curry leaves and 1 tbsp minced ginger and switch off.
Finely chop 2 onions and 2 green chillies and toss them with 3 tbsp coriander and half the warm tempering.
Heat a tava on medium and grease it with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, then pour a ladle of batter into a thick 5-inch round.
Press a handful of the tempered onion mix over the top, drizzle 1 tsp sesame oil around the edge, cover and cook 3 minutes until the base is deep gold.
Flip and cook the topping side 2 minutes, spoon over a little of the reserved tempering, and serve hot.
tips: Gingelly sesame oil is central to Tamil tiffin flavour, so use it for both the temper and the tava.
Fry the urad dal to a proper golden colour in the tempering for a nutty crunch against the soft uttapam.
Keep half the tempering back to spoon over at the end so the curry-leaf aroma stays fresh and bright.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coconut-roasted gram chutney and a peppery Tamil-style rasam to sip alongside.

variations.name: Bengali Onion Uttapam
variations.description: Bengal lends its pungent Anveshan Mustard Oil and a nigella-seed crackle to the onion uttapam, so each bite carries that sharp Kolkata edge. Slit green chillies and mustard oil give the humble tiffin a distinctly eastern personality.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked to first wisp so its pungency mellows into the classic Bengali kick

steps: Stir 0.5 tsp salt into 2.5 cups fermented dosa batter, loosening with a little water so it stays thick yet spreadable.
Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to its first smoke, cool slightly, then stir 1 tbsp of it into the batter along with 0.75 tsp nigella seeds.
Finely chop 2 onions, 3 green chillies, 1 tomato and 1 tbsp ginger and mix with 3 tbsp coriander for the topping.
Heat a tava on medium and wipe it with a few drops of the smoked mustard oil, then pour a ladle of batter into a thick 5-inch round.
Press a handful of the onion topping into the surface, drizzle 1 tsp mustard oil around the edge, cover and cook 3 minutes until golden underneath.
Flip and cook the topping side for 2 minutes until the onions char lightly at the edges, then serve piping hot.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to smoking before it goes into the batter, or its raw bitterness lingers.
Nigella seeds add the signature Bengali note; a scant three-quarter teaspoon is plenty as they are potent.
Let the onions catch a little colour on the flipped side for a smoky-sweet contrast to the mustard sharpness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coconut-coriander chutney and a side of lime-pickled onions to lean into the eastern flavours.

variations.name: Kerala Onion Uttapam
variations.description: The Malabar uttapam folds fresh coconut and curry leaves into the topping and cooks it in fragrant Anveshan Coconut Oil. Sweet coconut against sharp onion, all perfumed with coconut oil, makes for a soft, aromatic coastal breakfast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil for cooking that layers coconut aroma into every bite

steps: Stir 0.5 tsp salt into 2.5 cups fermented dosa batter, adjusting with water so it stays thick and spreadable.
Finely chop 2 onions, 2 green chillies and 1 tbsp ginger, then combine with 0.33 cup grated coconut, 15 chopped curry leaves and 3 tbsp coriander for the topping.
Heat a tava on medium and grease it with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil wiped across until it shines.
Pour a ladle of batter and spread it into a thick 5-inch round, keeping it spongy rather than thin.
Press a generous handful of the coconut-onion topping into the surface, drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil around the edge, cover and cook 3 minutes.
Flip and cook the topping side 2 minutes until the coconut toasts golden and fragrant, then serve warm.
tips: Use fresh grated coconut so the topping toasts sweet on the flip; desiccated turns dry and dusty.
Coconut oil sets solid when cool, so keep it gently warm for easy greasing between uttapams.
Press the topping in firmly, as loose coconut tends to scatter when you turn the uttapam over.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a roasted coconut chutney and a small ladle of drumstick sambar for a true Kerala tiffin.

variations.name: Andhra Onion Uttapam
variations.description: Andhra fires up the onion uttapam with a Guntur-chilli and garlic topping cooked in nutty Anveshan Sesame Oil. Bold, garlicky and blistering, it eats like a spicy Vijayawada tiffin, the soft batter tempering a serious heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed til oil, the Andhra staple, carrying the garlic and Guntur heat

steps: Stir 0.5 tsp salt and 1 tsp cumin seeds into 2.5 cups fermented dosa batter, loosening with water to a thick, spreadable mix.
Finely chop 2 onions and mince 4 garlic cloves, then toss them with 1.5 tsp Guntur red chilli powder, 15 chopped curry leaves and 3 tbsp coriander.
Heat a tava on medium and season it with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil rubbed across the surface.
Pour a ladle of batter into a thick 5-inch round, keeping it far thicker than a dosa so the centre stays soft.
Press a handful of the fiery onion-garlic topping into the surface, drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil around the edge, cover and cook 3 minutes.
Flip and cook the topping side 2 minutes until the garlic crisps and the onions char at the edges, then serve hot.
tips: Mix the Guntur chilli into the raw onions so it coats them and mellows slightly as the uttapam cooks.
Mince the garlic fine so it crisps rather than burns when the topping side hits the tava.
Keep plenty of curd on hand; the Guntur chilli makes this a genuinely hot tiffin.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling onion-tomato pachadi and a bowl of thick set curd to balance the heat.

variations.name: Classic Peanut Chikki
variations.description: The definitive Indian peanut brittle: roasted peanuts locked into a glassy jaggery caramel, rolled thin and snapped into shards. The trick is cooking the jaggery to the hard-crack stage so the chikki shatters crisply instead of turning sticky or chewy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: cooked to hard-crack so the chikki sets glassy and crisp

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the caramel, rolling pin and board so the chikki does not stick

steps: Warm 2 cups roasted, skinned peanuts in a dry pan and keep them hot on the side, and grease a marble board, rolling pin and spatula with a little of the 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee.
Melt 1.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan on medium heat, stirring, until it liquefies and starts to bubble, about 6 minutes.

Cook the jaggery to the hard-crack stage: drop a little into cold water and it should form a brittle thread that snaps cleanly, about 4 more minutes, then stir in 0.5 tsp cardamom, 0.25 tsp salt and 0.125 tsp baking soda for a lighter snap.
Working fast, tip in the warm peanuts and stir for 20 seconds until every nut is coated, then pour the mass onto the greased board.
Scatter 2 tbsp toasted sesame seeds over the top and roll out to a 5 mm thick sheet with the greased pin while still hot and pliable, moving quickly before the caramel hardens.
Score into 12 rectangles while warm with a greased knife, then let cool 15 minutes until fully hard and snap along the lines.
tips: The hard-crack test is everything: undercook and the chikki stays chewy, overcook and it tastes burnt.
Keep the peanuts warm before adding them, or a cold nut will seize the caramel before you can roll it.
Work quickly once the peanuts go in; jaggery caramel sets fast, so have your board greased and ready.
variations.servingSuggestion: Stack the shards in a glass jar for a Makar Sankranti snack table, or crush a piece over vanilla ice cream for instant peanut praline.

variations.name: Kerala Peanut Chikki
variations.description: A coastal chikki where toasted coconut chips join the peanuts in the jaggery caramel and a whisper of coconut oil scents the brittle. The coconut adds a second crunch and a tropical fragrance quite distinct from the plain version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted to hard-crack to set the coconut-peanut brittle crisp

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: scents the caramel with an unmistakable Kerala coconut aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the board and pin so the sticky sheet lifts cleanly

steps: Toast 0.75 cup coconut chips in a dry pan for 3 minutes until pale gold, warm 1.5 cups roasted peanuts alongside, and grease a board and pin with the 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee.
Melt 1.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water and 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a heavy pan on medium heat, stirring, until it bubbles, about 6 minutes.
Cook to hard-crack, testing that a drop snaps brittle in cold water, about 4 minutes more, then stir in 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp salt.
Quickly fold in the warm peanuts and toasted coconut chips, stirring 20 seconds until coated, then turn the mass out onto the greased board.
Roll to a 5 mm sheet with the greased pin while hot, working fast before the coconut-studded caramel firms.
Score into 12 pieces while warm, cool 15 minutes until hard and snap apart along the lines.
tips: Use thin coconut chips rather than fine desiccated coconut, which can scorch in the hot caramel.
The coconut oil aroma is delicate; keep the jaggery from cooking too dark so it survives.
Store airtight with a bay leaf, as the coconut can go soft in humid weather.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cup of strong Malabar coffee, or crumble over sliced banana and coconut yoghurt for a tropical dessert.

variations.name: Kashmiri Peanut Chikki
variations.description: A luxe chikki where the peanut caramel is perfumed with saffron and enriched with slivered walnuts, giving the brittle a floral aroma and an extra layer of orchard-nut crunch. Pale gold saffron threads gleam through the amber caramel.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: cooked to hard-crack to hold the saffron caramel crisp

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: crushed into the hot caramel to perfume and gild the brittle

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the surfaces and carries the saffron aroma into the caramel

steps: Crush a pinch of Anveshan Saffron and stir it into 1 tbsp of the 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, warm 1.5 cups peanuts, and grease a board and pin with the remaining ghee.
Melt 1.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water in a heavy pan on medium heat, stirring, until it liquefies and bubbles, about 6 minutes.
Cook to hard-crack, checking a drop snaps in cold water, about 4 minutes more, then stir in the saffron ghee, 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp salt.
Working fast, fold in the warm peanuts and 0.5 cup slivered walnuts, stirring 20 seconds until coated, then pour onto the greased board.
Roll to a 5 mm sheet with the greased pin while hot, before the nut-heavy caramel sets.
Score into 12 pieces while warm, cool 15 minutes until hard and break along the lines; saffron threads should show in the amber.
tips: Blooming saffron in a little warm ghee draws out both colour and aroma into the caramel.
Toast the walnuts briefly first so they do not taste raw in the finished brittle.
Keep the caramel from going too dark so the saffron gold still reads against it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Offer the saffron shards on a festive tray with dried figs and apricots, alongside cups of warm kahwa.

variations.name: Rajasthani Peanut Chikki
variations.description: A bold Rajasthani sweet-heat chikki where a hint of dried red chilli and black salt cuts through the jaggery, giving a moreish sweet-savoury-spicy brittle in the desert style of pairing gud with warming spice. The chilli is roasted and ground so it perfumes the caramel without raw bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: cooked to hard-crack to set the sweet-heat brittle crisp

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the chilli powder and greases the rolling surfaces

steps: Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan and gently bloom 0.5 tsp roasted red chilli powder in it for 20 seconds until fragrant, then set aside; keep 2 cups peanuts warm.
Grease a board and pin with the second tbsp of Anveshan Ghee, then melt 1.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water in a heavy pan on medium heat until bubbling, about 6 minutes.
Cook to hard-crack, testing a drop snaps in cold water, about 4 minutes more, then stir in the chilli ghee, 0.5 tsp black salt, 0.5 tsp crushed fennel and 0.5 tsp cardamom.
Working fast, tip in the warm peanuts and stir 20 seconds until every nut is coated in the spiced caramel, then pour onto the greased board.
Roll to a 5 mm sheet with the greased pin while hot and pliable, moving quickly before it hardens.
Score into 12 pieces while warm, cool 15 minutes until crisp and snap apart; each bite should be sweet first, then gently warming.
tips: Bloom the chilli in ghee first; adding raw chilli powder to caramel tastes harsh and dusty.
Start with half a teaspoon of chilli and increase next time; it should tickle, not burn.
Black salt is key to the sweet-savoury balance, so do not swap it for plain salt.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a cocktail-hour nibble with masala chai, where the gentle heat makes each shard surprisingly moreish.

variations.name: Awadhi Peanut Chikki
variations.description: A refined Lucknawi chikki scented with kewra and studded with slivered pistachios, its jaggery caramel kept a touch lighter so the perfume carries. It brings Awadhi fragrance to a humble peanut brittle.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: cooked to hard-crack but kept lighter so the kewra survives

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the surfaces and rounds the caramel for a courtly finish

steps: Warm 1.75 cups roasted peanuts and grease a board and pin with 1 tbsp of the 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee.
Melt 1.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan on medium heat, stirring, until it bubbles, about 6 minutes.
Cook just to hard-crack, testing a drop snaps in cold water, about 4 minutes more, then take the pan off the heat and stir in 1 tsp kewra water, 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp salt.
Working fast, fold in the warm peanuts and 0.33 cup slivered pistachios, stirring 20 seconds until coated, then pour onto the greased board.
Roll to a 5 mm sheet with the greased pin while hot, moving quickly before it sets.
Score into 12 pieces while warm, cool 15 minutes until crisp and snap apart along the lines.
tips: Add kewra off the heat at the very end so its delicate perfume is not boiled away.
Keep the caramel a shade lighter than usual so the floral note is not buried under deep toffee.
Green pistachios make it look as refined as it smells, so slice them thin and even.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve small shards on a doily-lined plate with cups of rose sherbet after an Awadhi meal.

variations.name: Classic Vegetable Appe
variations.description: The beloved South Indian paniyaram: fluffy little steamed-fried dumplings made from fermented dosa batter studded with colourful vegetables and a mustard-curry-leaf tempering. Cooked in an appe pan with Anveshan wood-pressed sesame oil and ghee, they are golden and crisp outside, soft and airy within.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly sesame oil tempers the spices and greases the moulds for that authentic Tamil-Kannada aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A few drops of ghee in each mould crisps the base of the appe to a deep gold.

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil in a small pan over medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 1 tsp chana dal and fry until golden, about 40 seconds.

Add 1 finely chopped onion, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 2 sprigs curry leaves, 0.33 cup grated carrot, 0.25 cup green peas and 0.33 cup finely chopped capsicum and saute for 3 minutes until the vegetables soften; cool this mixture completely.
Stir the cooled vegetables and 3 tbsp coriander into 2 cups dosa batter with 0.5 tsp salt; the batter should be thick and dropping, not runny, so add a splash of water only if too stiff.
Just before cooking, sprinkle 0.5 tsp Eno over the batter and fold gently until it turns light and bubbly, which keeps the appe fluffy.
Heat an appe pan over medium heat, put a few drops of sesame oil and Anveshan Ghee in each mould, then spoon batter into each cavity until three-quarters full.
Cover and cook 3 to 4 minutes until the edges set and the bottoms are golden, then flip each ball with a skewer or spoon and cook 2 to 3 minutes more until golden and cooked through all over.
tips: Use slightly sour, well-fermented dosa batter for the best flavour and lift; fresh unfermented batter gives dense appe.
If you skip Eno, a well-fermented batter rested at room temperature will still puff nicely, so do not overdo the fruit salt.
Keep the flame at medium and covered so the insides steam through before the outsides over-brown.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with coconut chutney and a small bowl of sambar, or with a spicy tomato-garlic chutney for dipping.

variations.name: Kerala Coconut Vegetable Appe
variations.description: A Malabar-style kuzhi paniyaram enriched with fresh grated coconut and cooked in Anveshan wood-pressed coconut oil for a sweet, rounded coastal aroma. Soft-centred and fragrant, these little dumplings taste of a Kerala tea-time snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil is the defining Kerala fat and doubles the coconut flavour in every appe.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A little ghee in each mould crisps the base against the soft coconut crumb.

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a small pan, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 5 finely sliced shallots, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger and 2 sprigs curry leaves and fry 3 minutes until the shallots turn soft and golden; cool it.
Stir the cooled tempering, 0.33 cup grated fresh coconut and 3 tbsp coriander into 2 cups dosa batter with 0.5 tsp salt, keeping the batter thick and dropping.
Just before cooking, fold in 0.5 tsp Eno until the batter turns airy and bubbly.
Heat an appe pan over medium heat and put a few drops of coconut oil and Anveshan Ghee into each mould.
Spoon batter into each cavity to three-quarters full, cover and cook 3 to 4 minutes until the edges set and the bottoms are golden.
Flip each appe with a skewer and cook 2 to 3 minutes more until golden all over and springy to the touch, then serve hot.
tips: Use fresh or frozen grated coconut rather than desiccated, which soaks up moisture and dries out the appe.
Shallots (small onions) give a sweeter, more authentic Kerala flavour than regular onion here.
A final drizzle of raw coconut oil over the hot appe deepens the unmistakable Malabar aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coconut-shallot chutney and hot filter coffee for a classic Kerala evening snack.

variations.name: Karnataka Tamarind Vegetable Appe
variations.description: A Karnataka-style paniyaram where a whisper of tamarind and a chana-dal crunch give the vegetable dumplings a tangy, textured lift, in the spirit of a Udupi tiffin. Cooked in Anveshan wood-pressed groundnut oil and ghee, they are savoury, tangy and satisfying.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the everyday Karnataka tiffin fat and keeps the appe light.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee in each mould crisps the base and softens the tamarind tang.

steps: Soak 1.5 tbsp chana dal in water for 20 minutes and drain; dissolve 1 tsp tamarind paste in 1 tbsp warm water.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, add the drained chana dal and fry until golden, then add 1 chopped onion, 2 chopped green chillies, 2 sprigs curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and saute 3 minutes; cool it.
Stir the cooled tempering, the tamarind water and 3 tbsp coriander into 2 cups dosa batter with 0.5 tsp salt, keeping it thick and dropping.
Fold in 0.5 tsp Eno just before cooking until the batter turns light and bubbly.
Heat an appe pan over medium heat, put a few drops of groundnut oil and Anveshan Ghee in each mould, and spoon batter to three-quarters full.
Cover and cook 3 to 4 minutes until the bottoms are golden, then flip each appe and cook 2 to 3 minutes more until golden all over, and serve hot.
tips: Keep the tamarind gentle at 1 tsp; it should tang and round the flavour, not sour the appe.
The soaked chana dal must stay slightly crunchy, so fry it just to golden and no further.
A pinch of jaggery in the batter balances the tamarind into the classic Karnataka sweet-sour note.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coconut-chana-dal chutney and a bowl of rasam for a wholesome Udupi-style tiffin.

variations.name: Tamil Curry-Leaf Vegetable Appe
variations.description: The classic Chettinad kuzhi paniyaram, fragrant with a heavy curry-leaf and urad-dal tempering and a hint of pepper, cooked in Anveshan wood-pressed sesame oil. Crisp-shelled and soft-hearted, these are the definitive Tamil tiffin dumplings.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly sesame oil is the true Chettinad paniyaram fat and gives its toasty edge.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee in the moulds crisps the shell and rounds the sharp sesame note.

steps: Coarsely crush 0.5 tsp black peppercorns; heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil and splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then fry 1.5 tbsp urad dal until golden.
Add 3 sprigs curry leaves, the crushed pepper, 0.25 tsp asafoetida, 1 chopped onion, 2 chopped green chillies and 1 inch grated ginger and saute 3 minutes until fragrant; cool completely.
Stir the cooled tempering and 3 tbsp coriander into 2 cups dosa batter with 0.5 tsp salt, keeping it thick and dropping.
Fold in 0.5 tsp Eno just before cooking until the batter is light and bubbly.
Heat an appe pan over medium heat, put a few drops of sesame oil and Anveshan Ghee in each mould, and spoon batter to three-quarters full.
Cover and cook 3 to 4 minutes until the bottoms are deep golden, then flip each appe and cook 2 to 3 minutes more until crisp and golden all over; serve hot.
tips: Fry the urad dal to a proper golden colour for a nutty crunch in every bite, a Chettinad hallmark.
Crushed fresh pepper rather than chilli powder keeps the heat warm and aromatic, true to the style.
Leftover appe reheat well in the same pan with a drop of ghee, crisping up almost like fresh.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and a fiery kara chutney, with an extra sprinkle of gingelly oil over the top.

variations.name: Gujarati Sweet-Sour Vegetable Appe
variations.description: A Gujarati twist that turns the paniyaram into a soft, khaman-inspired snack with a sweet-sour balance from Anveshan jaggery and lemon, cooked in wood-pressed groundnut oil. Fluffy, mildly sweet and studded with vegetables, it is a crowd-pleasing tea-time bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the classic Gujarati fat and keeps these appe light and clean.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A spoon of jaggery gives the signature Gujarati sweet-sour lift without refined sugar.

steps: Dissolve 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 2 tbsp warm water and set aside; heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil and splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tbsp sesame seeds.
Add 0.33 cup grated carrot, 0.25 cup peas, 2 chopped green chillies and 1 inch grated ginger and saute 3 minutes until the vegetables soften; cool it.
Stir the cooled vegetables, the jaggery water, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 3 tbsp coriander into 2 cups dosa batter with 0.5 tsp salt, keeping the batter thick and dropping.
Fold in 0.5 tsp Eno just before cooking until the batter turns airy and bubbly.
Heat an appe pan over medium heat, put a few drops of groundnut oil in each mould, and spoon batter to three-quarters full.
Cover and cook 3 to 4 minutes until the bottoms are golden, then flip each appe and cook 2 to 3 minutes more until golden all over; serve warm.
tips: Dissolve the jaggery before adding so it spreads evenly rather than leaving sticky pockets that burn.
The lemon is essential to keep the sweetness from tasting flat, giving the true Gujarati sweet-sour balance.
These are especially good for children who find plain spicy appe too sharp.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coriander-mint chutney and sweet tamarind-date chutney, with a cup of masala chai alongside.

variations.name: Classic Crispy Hara Bhara Kebab
variations.description: The restaurant-style green kebab everyone loves: blanched spinach and mashed green peas bound with potato, spiced gently and rolled in bread crumbs for a crackling crust. Vivid green within, golden and crisp outside, with a soft cashew tucked in the centre.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for deep-frying; its high smoke point crisps the crust while keeping the kebab green inside

steps: Blanch the spinach in boiling water for 1 minute, plunge into ice water to lock the colour, then squeeze out every drop of moisture and chop fine.

Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil and saute the green chillies and 1 tbsp ginger for 1 minute, then add the chopped spinach and cook 3 minutes until the excess water dries off, and cool.

Combine the dry spinach, mashed peas, mashed potato, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp chaat masala, 0.75 tsp garam masala and 1 tsp salt, then work in the 3 tbsp roasted gram flour until the mixture is firm and no longer sticky.
Divide into 10 portions, press a cashew half into the centre of each and seal into a smooth patty, then coat all over in bread crumbs.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to 180C and fry the kebabs 3-4 at a time for 2-3 minutes until the crust is golden and crisp.
Drain on a rack so the crumb crust stays crisp and the interior keeps its bright green colour.
tips: Squeezing the blanched spinach bone-dry is the single most important step; wet spinach makes the kebabs fall apart.
Roasted gram flour binds and removes any raw-bean taste, unlike raw besan.
Chill the shaped kebabs for 15 minutes so they hold firm and do not crack in the oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a bed of onion rings with mint-yogurt chutney and lemon wedges, garnished with a dusting of chaat masala.

variations.name: Punjabi Makhani Crispy Hara Bhara Kebab
variations.description: A dhaba-rich version shallow-fried in nutty Anveshan Ghee instead of butter, with kasuri methi and a soft paneer centre that melts as you bite. The ghee gives it a deep, tandoori-adjacent aroma over the fresh green base.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: shallow-fries the kebabs with the buttery richness Punjab loves, in place of makhan

steps: Blanch the spinach 1 minute, shock in ice water, then squeeze completely dry and chop fine.
Melt 1 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee and fry the green chillies and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, add the chopped spinach and cook 3 minutes until dry, then cool.

Mix the dry spinach, mashed peas, mashed potato, crumbled paneer, 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi, 1 tsp garam masala, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, then bind with the 3 tbsp roasted gram flour into a firm mixture.
Shape 10 patties and coat each in bread crumbs, pressing so the crust adheres.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee on a tava over medium heat and shallow-fry the kebabs 3 minutes a side until golden, spooning ghee around the edges.
Brush the tops with the remaining ghee just before serving for a glossy, aromatic finish.
tips: Fold the paneer in gently so it stays in soft pockets rather than blending into the mix.
Cook in ghee over steady medium heat, as it browns faster than oil.
Crush kasuri methi warm between your palms so it perfumes the ghee as they fry.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with pudina chutney and pickled onions, with a wedge of lemon and hot chai, dhaba-style.

variations.name: Kashmiri Kesar Crispy Hara Bhara Kebab
variations.description: An aromatic, softly regal kebab scented with Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron, fennel and dry ginger, the warm Wazwan spices. The saffron gives a faint golden glow and a floral perfume against the green spinach and pea base.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in 1 tbsp warm milk to lend colour and the signature Kashmiri aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the traditional Kashmiri cooking fat, smoked first, for deep-frying

steps: Steep the 20 strands of Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 1 tbsp warm milk for 10 minutes until deep amber.
Blanch the spinach 1 minute, shock in ice water, squeeze dry and chop fine.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the flame, fry the green chillies for 1 minute, add the spinach with the 1 tsp fennel powder and 0.5 tsp dry ginger and cook 3 minutes until dry, then cool.
Combine the spinach, mashed peas, mashed potato, the saffron milk, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, then bind with the 3 tbsp roasted gram flour into a firm, faintly golden mixture.
Shape 10 patties, coat each in bread crumbs and rest 10 minutes so the saffron colour spreads.
Reheat the remaining Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil to 180C and fry the kebabs for 3 minutes until pale gold and crisp, then drain.
tips: Steep saffron in warm, not boiling, milk to draw out both colour and its delicate aroma.
Fennel and dry ginger are the heart of Kashmiri warmth; grind them fresh for the best fragrance.
Use mild Kashmiri chilli so the saffron perfume is not overpowered.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a saffron-yogurt dip and a pot of kahwa for an elegant Kashmiri-inspired platter.

variations.name: Andhra Guntur Crispy Hara Bhara Kebab
variations.description: A fiery southern twist where the green kebab meets blazing Guntur red chilli and a curry-leaf-garlic tempering. The spinach sweetness barely tempers the heat, making it a bold, savoury kebab for chilli lovers.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for the curry-leaf-garlic tempering and deep-frying, the Andhra frying staple

steps: Blanch the spinach 1 minute, shock in ice water, squeeze bone-dry and chop fine.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil, crackle the 15 curry leaves, fry the 1.5 tbsp garlic for 1 minute, add the spinach and cook 3 minutes until dry, then stir in the 1.5 tsp Guntur chilli powder off the heat and cool.
Mix the spicy spinach, mashed peas, mashed potato, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder and 1 tsp salt, then bind with the 3 tbsp roasted gram flour into a firm mixture.
Shape 10 patties and coat each thoroughly in bread crumbs.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to 180C and fry the kebabs for 2-3 minutes until the crust is deep red-gold and crisp.
Drain on a rack and dust with a little extra Guntur chilli for the full Andhra kick.
tips: Add the Guntur chilli off the flame; it scorches and turns bitter almost instantly.
A spoon of thick curd in the mix softens the heat and keeps the kebabs moist.
Fry a few curry leaves till crisp and crumble them over the top for aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with cooling coconut chutney and cold buttermilk to balance the fierce heat.

variations.name: Bengali Sorshe Crispy Hara Bhara Kebab
variations.description: Inspired by Bengal's chop tradition, this green kebab is fried in pungent Anveshan Mustard Oil and lifted with a whisper of mustard paste and green chilli. Shaped like a Kolkata chop and crumbed crisp, it is aromatic with a gentle sweet-sharp edge.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked first, for that unmistakable Bengali chop pungency and deep-frying

steps: Blanch the spinach 1 minute, shock in ice water, squeeze dry and chop fine.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the flame, fry the green chillies for 1 minute, add the spinach and cook 3 minutes until dry, then stir in the 1 tsp mustard paste and 0.75 tsp Bengali garam masala and cool.
Combine the spinach, mashed peas, mashed potato, 0.5 tsp sugar and 1 tsp salt, then bind with the 3 tbsp roasted gram flour into a firm mixture.
Shape 10 oval croquette-style kebabs, a nod to the Bengali chop, and coat them in bread crumbs.
