Reheat the remaining Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil to 180C and fry the kebabs for 3 minutes until mahogany-gold and crisp.
Rest on paper so the crust dries and the mustard-scented interior stays soft.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to smoking once, then cool slightly to tame its raw bite.
The pinch of sugar is the classic Bengali balance to the mustard's sharpness.
Shape them oval rather than round to echo the Kolkata vegetable chop.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with kasundi mustard, thin onion rings and cucumber, the way a Kolkata para stall would.

variations.name: Classic Crispy Veg Cutlet
variations.description: The tea-time cutlet of Indian bakeries and railway platforms, a soft mash of carrot, beans, peas and potato in a golden double-crumbed shell. A cornflour-free khapli slurry and a firm chill give it a crust that stays crackly long after frying.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: high smoke point wood-pressed groundnut oil deep-fries a clean, crackly crust without greasiness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: whole-wheat khapli slurry replaces cornflour as the glue that binds the crumb coat

steps: Boil 2 potatoes until soft and steam 1 cup diced carrot, 0.5 cup chopped beans and 0.5 cup peas until just tender, about 8 minutes, then mash everything together dry.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil and saute 1 chopped onion, 2 minced green chillies and 1 inch grated ginger for 3 minutes, then mix into the mash.
Season with 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp garam masala, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, then firm with 0.5 cup bread crumbs into a shapeable dough.
Divide into 10 portions and pat each into an oval cutlet about 1.5 cm thick.
Whisk 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta with water into a thin slurry, dip each cutlet, then coat all over in the remaining 1 cup bread crumbs and chill 15 minutes.
Heat the remaining 4 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a pan over medium heat and shallow-fry the cutlets 3 to 4 minutes per side until deep golden and crisp, then drain.
Serve hot with tomato ketchup and mint chutney.
tips: Steam rather than boil the vegetables and mash them dry, since watery mash is the main cause of soggy, bursting cutlets.
Chilling the crumbed cutlets sets the coat so it doesn't slide off in the hot oil.
Double-crumb any cutlet that looks patchy, as bare spots are where oil seeps in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a doily-lined plate with ketchup and a pot of chai for a proper Indian bakery snack, or tuck into a bun as a cutlet pav.

variations.name: Bengali Crispy Veg Cutlet
variations.description: The famous vegetable chop of Kolkata, a beetroot-tinged mash of winter vegetables rolled in crumbs and fried crisp in mustard oil. A hint of Bengali garam masala and roasted peanuts inside give it the sweet-earthy character of a Park Street chop.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: pungent mustard oil is the defining fat of a Kolkata vegetable chop, sharp and aromatic

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli slurry binds the crumb shell around the sweet beetroot mash for a true chop crust

steps: Boil 2 potatoes and 1 cup grated beetroot with 0.5 cup carrot and 0.5 cup peas until soft, then drain very well and mash dry.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until it just smokes, cool slightly, then fry 1 inch grated ginger and 2 minced green chillies for 1 minute and mix into the mash.
Season with 1 tsp Bengali garam masala, 0.5 tsp sugar, 1 tsp salt and 3 tbsp coarsely crushed roasted peanuts, then bind with 0.5 cup bread crumbs.
Shape into 10 long, tapering chops, dip in a thin slurry of 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta and water, and roll in the remaining 1 cup bread crumbs.
Chill the chops 15 minutes so the deep-pink mash firms up.
Heat the remaining 4 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil over medium heat until mellowed, then fry the chops 3 to 4 minutes per side until crisp and dark, and drain.
Serve hot with kasundi mustard and cucumber-onion salad.
tips: Drain the boiled beetroot thoroughly and even squeeze it in a cloth, as its water is what makes chops fall apart.
Shape the chops long and tapering, the classic Kolkata form, for more crunchy surface.
The half-teaspoon of sugar is traditional and balances the earthy beetroot and sharp mustard oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a rainy-evening snack with a wedge of lime, kasundi and a cup of milky Kolkata cha.

variations.name: Kerala Crispy Veg Cutlet
variations.description: The beloved Kerala bakery cutlet, its vegetable mash brightened with grated coconut, curry leaves and a warm hit of black pepper and garam masala. Fried in coconut oil, it is crisp outside, fragrant and faintly sweet within.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil both tempers the aromatics and fries the cutlet, the true Kerala bakery fat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli slurry glues the crumb coat onto the moist, coconut-rich mash

steps: Boil 2 potatoes and steam 0.75 cup diced carrot and 0.5 cup chopped beans until tender, then mash dry.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil, crackle 15 curry leaves, then fry 6 sliced shallots and 1 inch grated ginger for 3 minutes until soft.
Mix the temper into the mash with 0.5 cup grated coconut, 0.75 tsp crushed black pepper, 0.75 tsp garam masala and 1 tsp salt.
Bind with 0.5 cup bread crumbs, shape into 10 round cutlets, dip in a thin 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta slurry and coat in the remaining 1 cup bread crumbs.
Chill the cutlets 15 minutes to firm the coconut mash.
Heat the remaining 4 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil over medium heat and fry the cutlets 3 to 4 minutes per side until golden and crisp, taking care as coconut browns fast, then drain.
Serve hot with a coconut-chilli chutney and thin tomato ketchup.
tips: Black pepper, not just chilli, is the Kerala signature here, so crush it fresh for maximum fragrance.
Fry a shade lighter than usual because the coconut in the mash catches quickly in the hot oil.
Squeeze any excess moisture from the steamed vegetables so the coconut can bind the mash firmly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at tea time with strong Kerala chai, or plate alongside a bowl of kadala curry for a heartier spread.

variations.name: Andhra Crispy Veg Cutlet
variations.description: A fiery Andhra take where Guntur chilli and a garlic-curry-leaf temper turn a mild vegetable cutlet into something bold and pungent. The crust fries up bright red-gold, with heat that builds steadily behind the crunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil is the Andhra everyday fat and carries the Guntur heat cleanly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli slurry seals the crumb coat over the fiery, garlicky mash

steps: Boil 2 potatoes and steam 0.75 cup carrot and 0.5 cup peas until tender, then mash dry.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil, crackle 15 curry leaves and 6 crushed garlic cloves for 1 minute, then add 1 chopped onion and fry 3 minutes.
Mix the temper into the mash with 2 tsp Guntur red chilli powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for a vivid red mixture.
Bind with 0.5 cup bread crumbs, shape into 10 oval cutlets, dip in a thin 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta slurry and coat in the remaining 1 cup bread crumbs.
Chill the crumbed cutlets for 15 minutes so the coat sets firmly before frying.
Heat the remaining 4 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat and fry the cutlets 3 to 4 minutes per side until red-gold and crisp, then drain.
Serve scorching hot with a cooling onion raita and lime.
tips: Guntur chilli is potent, so begin with the stated 2 tsp and add more only to taste.
Fry the garlic in the temper gently; scorched garlic turns bitter and dominates the cutlet.
A tablespoon of curd in the mash tempers the burn without dulling the red colour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with curd rice and a smear of gongura pickle for a full Andhra-style plate that tames the heat.

variations.name: Gujarati Crispy Veg Cutlet
variations.description: A lightly sweet-savoury Gujarati cutlet where jaggery, lime and green chilli meet the classic khatta-mitha-teekha balance. Sweetcorn and coriander keep it fresh and juicy against the mellow jaggery warmth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery powder gives the gentle Gujarati sweetness that balances the lime and green chilli

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil is Gujarat's staple frying oil for a crisp, clean cutlet crust

steps: Boil 2 potatoes and steam 0.5 cup carrot and 0.5 cup peas until tender, then mash with 0.75 cup lightly crushed sweetcorn.
While warm, mix in 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tbsp lime juice so the jaggery dissolves evenly.
Add 2 tsp green chilli-ginger paste, 3 tbsp coriander, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, then bind with 0.5 cup bread crumbs into a soft dough.
Shape into 10 round cutlets and coat all over in the remaining 1 cup bread crumbs.
Chill the cutlets 15 minutes so the sweetcorn mash firms up.
Heat 5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat and fry the cutlets 3 to 4 minutes per side until golden and crisp, watching closely as the jaggery browns them faster, then drain.
Serve warm with a sweet-sour date-tamarind chutney.
tips: Taste the mash and adjust jaggery, lime and chilli until the sweet-sour-hot balance feels even.
Keep the sweetcorn kernels only lightly crushed so they pop juicily inside the crust.
Because jaggery colours quickly, hold the flame at medium and pull the cutlets at first golden.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a spoon of sweet Gujarati chundo and fresh green chutney for the full khatta-mitha spread.

variations.name: Classic Festive Nariyal Barfi
variations.description: A richer, celebration-grade coconut barfi that folds fresh khoya into the grated coconut for a dense, milky fudge, layered with cardamom and crowned with silver vark and mixed nuts. This is the version made for Raksha Bandhan and Diwali trays, more luxurious than the everyday nariyal barfi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: enriches the khoya-coconut mass and keeps it from sticking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined sugar keeping the festive barfi pale and clean-sweet

steps: Melt 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide heavy pan on low heat and toast 3 cups grated coconut for 3 minutes until fragrant but still pale.
Add 1.5 cups grated khoya and 0.5 cup milk and cook on medium heat, stirring, for about 8 minutes until the khoya melts and blends smoothly into the coconut.
Stir in 1.25 cups Anveshan Khandsari and a pinch of salt and keep cooking for about 12 minutes until the sugar dissolves and the mixture thickens into a heavy mass.
Add 1.5 tsp cardamom powder and 2 tbsp charoli and cook a final 4 minutes until the fudge pulls cleanly from the pan and mounds on the spoon.
Press into a greased tray to a 1.5 cm slab, scatter 0.33 cup chopped mixed nuts across the top and lay 2 sheets of silver vark over the surface.
Cool for 35 minutes until firmly set, then cut into 20 festive squares with a greased knife.
tips: Use fresh, soft khoya; hard or dry khoya makes the barfi crumbly rather than dense and fudgy.
Cook the sugar in fully before judging thickness, as the mass loosens when sugar first melts.
For a cleaner cut, chill the set slab for 20 minutes before slicing into squares.
variations.servingSuggestion: Lay the vark-topped squares in a partitioned mithai box with a few rose petals for a Diwali gift, or serve on a festive thali beside jalebi.

variations.name: Gujarati Festive Nariyal Barfi
variations.description: A festive kopra pak from Gujarat, jaggery-sweetened and enriched with khoya so it turns a deep golden-brown with a fudgy, almost caramel-toffee density. Nutmeg, clove and charoli give it the warmth expected at a Gujarati celebration.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: keeps the jaggery-khoya fudge soft and glossy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: deepens the festive barfi to a caramel-gold with a molasses edge

steps: Melt 5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide pan on low heat and toast 3 cups grated coconut for 3 minutes until fragrant.
Add 1.5 cups grated khoya with 0.33 cup milk and stir on medium heat for about 8 minutes until the khoya softens and coats the coconut evenly.
Lower the heat, add 1.25 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder and let it melt into the mixture over about 7 minutes, turning it a rich golden-brown and glossy.
Season with a pinch of salt, 1.5 tsp cardamom, 0.25 tsp nutmeg and 0.125 tsp clove, then cook 5 minutes more until the fudge leaves the pan sides.
Fold in 2 tbsp charoli, press into a greased tray to a 1.5 cm slab and smooth the warm surface.
Cool for 30 minutes until set but soft, then cut into 20 caramel-gold squares.
tips: Add the jaggery only after the khoya has melted, or the mixture can turn grainy.
Keep the heat low once jaggery is in so it does not seize into hard threads.
The warming spices bloom overnight, so this barfi is even better made a day ahead.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm at a Diwali get-together with a scoop of chilled shrikhand alongside for a hot-cold contrast.

variations.name: Kashmiri Festive Nariyal Barfi
variations.description: A festive coconut barfi gilded with saffron and rosewater and enriched with khoya, then studded generously with walnuts and pistachios in the lavish Kashmiri wedding-sweet style. Pale gold and heavily perfumed, it is made to impress.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: spreads the saffron colour through the khoya-coconut mass

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: keeps the base pale for the saffron gold to shine

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm milk to gild and perfume this festive barfi

steps: Steep a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 0.5 cup warm milk for 10 minutes until the milk turns deep gold.
Melt 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide pan on low heat, toast 3 cups grated coconut for 3 minutes, then stir in 1.5 cups grated khoya and the saffron milk.
Cook on medium heat for about 9 minutes, stirring, until the khoya melts and the mass turns pale gold, then add 1.25 cups Anveshan Khandsari and a pinch of salt.
Continue cooking about 10 minutes until the sugar dissolves and the fudge thickens and leaves the pan, then stir in 1.5 tsp cardamom and 1 tsp rosewater off the heat.
Press into a greased tray to a 1.5 cm slab and press 0.5 cup chopped walnuts and pistachios evenly over the top.
Cool for 35 minutes until set, then cut into 20 saffron-gold diamonds, laying a saffron thread on each if you like.
tips: Reserve some saffron milk to brush over the top for an even deeper gold finish.
Toast the walnuts briefly so they do not taste raw against the sweet fudge.
Add rosewater off the heat so its fragrance survives into the finished barfi.
variations.servingSuggestion: Present on an engraved silver tray at a wedding sweet table, served with cups of saffron kahwa.

variations.name: Awadhi Festive Nariyal Barfi
variations.description: A Lucknawi festive coconut barfi perfumed with kewra and rose, kept pale and dense with khoya, and finished with silver vark. It carries the fragrance-first nazakat of Awadhi dessert-making into a coconut sweet.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: clean and mild to let the kewra and rose lead

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: a delicate sweetness matched to a perfume-forward barfi

steps: Melt 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide pan on low heat and toast 3 cups grated coconut for 3 minutes without letting it colour.
Add 1.5 cups grated khoya and 0.5 cup milk and cook on medium heat for about 8 minutes until the khoya melts into a smooth, pale mass.
Stir in 1.25 cups Anveshan Khandsari and a pinch of salt and cook about 11 minutes until the sugar dissolves and the fudge thickens and leaves the pan.
Take the pan off the heat and stir in 1.5 tsp kewra water, 1 tsp rosewater and 1.5 tsp cardamom so the perfumes stay bright.
Press into a greased tray to a 1.5 cm slab, scatter 0.33 cup slivered almonds and pistachios and lay 2 sheets of silver vark over the top.
Cool for 35 minutes until set, then cut into 20 delicate squares with a clean, greased knife.
tips: Add kewra and rosewater together off the heat; both are delicate and boil away quickly.
Keep the coconut and khoya pale for the refined Awadhi look.
Rest the barfi an hour before serving so the floral notes settle and marry.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on fine porcelain at a festive dawat, each square beside a small cup of rose-scented sherbet.

variations.name: Punjabi Festive Nariyal Barfi
variations.description: A generous, ghee-rich Punjabi festive coconut barfi loaded with khoya and a lavish hand of nuts, finished with a spoon of extra ghee for gloss and shine. It is the hearty, indulgent style beloved at Punjabi weddings and Lohri.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: used generously through the barfi and a final spoon for a glossy Punjabi richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined sugar rounding out the rich khoya without over-sweetening

steps: Melt 5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide heavy pan on low heat and toast 3 cups grated coconut for 3 minutes until aromatic.
Add 2 cups grated khoya and 0.5 cup milk and cook on medium heat for about 9 minutes, stirring, until the khoya melts into a rich, thick mass.
Stir in 1.25 cups Anveshan Khandsari and a pinch of salt and cook about 11 minutes until the sugar dissolves and the fudge pulls from the pan sides.
Add 1.5 tsp cardamom, half the chopped nuts and 2 tbsp melon seeds, then finish with a final 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee stirred in for gloss.
Press into a greased tray to a 2 cm slab and cover the top with the remaining chopped nuts, pressing them firmly in.
Cool for 35 minutes until set, then cut into 20 generous squares thick with nuts.
tips: Use plenty of khoya for the dense, indulgent texture Punjabi barfi is known for.
The final spoon of ghee gives the signature shine; stir it in only at the very end.
Toast the melon seeds briefly so they pop with crunch in the finished barfi.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve big squares at a Lohri bonfire gathering with hot masala doodh, or box them up richly for a wedding return gift.

variations.name: Classic Festive Peanut Chikki
variations.description: A dressed-up festive chikki that keeps peanuts at the heart but folds in almonds, melon seeds and a sheet of silver vark for a gift-worthy brittle. Cooked to a clean hard-crack, it shatters into glossy, nut-packed shards fit for a Sankranti or Diwali platter.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: cooked to hard-crack to bind the loaded festive brittle crisp

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the surfaces and gives the festive chikki a glossy sheen

steps: Warm 1.5 cups peanuts, 0.5 cup slivered almonds and 3 tbsp melon seeds together in a dry pan, and grease a board and pin with 1 tbsp of the 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee.
Melt 1.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan on medium heat, stirring, until liquid and bubbling, about 6 minutes.
Cook to hard-crack, checking that a drop snaps brittle in cold water, about 4 minutes more, then stir in 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp salt.
Working fast, add the warm nut-and-seed mix and stir 20 seconds until everything is caramel-coated, then pour onto the greased board.
Roll to a 6 mm sheet with the greased pin while hot, then lay 1 sheet of silver vark over the top and press gently.
Score into 14 pieces while warm, cool 15 minutes until hard and snap along the lines into glossy, nut-studded shards.
tips: Warm all the nuts and seeds together so none chills the caramel when added.
Apply the vark right after rolling while the surface is still tacky so it adheres.
For a thicker festive bar, roll to 8 mm and cut into smaller squares instead.
variations.servingSuggestion: Layer the vark-topped shards in a decorated tin between sheets of butter paper as a Diwali gift box.

variations.name: Kashmiri Festive Peanut Chikki
variations.description: A festive saffron chikki heavy with walnuts and a scatter of pistachio, the caramel perfumed with saffron and a drop of rosewater in the lavish Kashmiri manner. Rich, aromatic and studded with the valley's favourite nuts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: cooked to hard-crack to hold the nut-laden saffron brittle

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm ghee to gild and perfume the festive caramel

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: carries the saffron and greases the rolling surfaces

steps: Crush a pinch of Anveshan Saffron into 1 tbsp warm Anveshan Ghee to bloom, and warm 1.25 cups peanuts with 0.66 cup broken walnuts; grease a board and pin with the second tbsp of ghee.
Melt 1.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water in a heavy pan on medium heat, stirring, until it bubbles, about 6 minutes.
Cook to hard-crack, testing a drop snaps in cold water, about 4 minutes more, then stir in the saffron ghee, 0.5 tsp cardamom, 0.25 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp rosewater off the heat.
Working fast, fold in the warm peanuts, walnuts and 0.33 cup slivered pistachios, stirring 20 seconds until coated, then pour onto the greased board.
Roll to a 6 mm sheet with the greased pin while hot, before the nut-heavy caramel firms.
Score into 14 pieces while warm, cool 15 minutes until hard and break apart; saffron should gild the amber and pistachios flash green.
tips: Add rosewater and bloomed saffron off the heat so their fragrance is not cooked away.
Break the walnuts coarsely, not fine, so they stay meaty in the brittle.
Keep the caramel from darkening too much to protect the saffron colour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Present on a carved walnut-wood tray with dried apricots and kahwa for a festive Kashmiri spread.

variations.name: Kerala Festive Peanut Chikki
variations.description: A festive coastal chikki loaded with toasted coconut chips and cashews alongside the peanuts, the caramel scented with coconut oil and cardamom. Two crunches and a tropical perfume make it a celebration brittle for Onam and Vishu.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: cooked to hard-crack to set the coconut-cashew brittle

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: perfumes the festive caramel with fresh coconut

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the board and pin for a clean release

steps: Toast 0.75 cup coconut chips and 0.5 cup cashews in a dry pan until pale gold, warm 1.25 cups peanuts alongside, and grease a board and pin with the 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee.
Melt 1.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water and 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a heavy pan on medium heat, stirring, until bubbling, about 6 minutes.
Cook to hard-crack, checking a drop snaps in cold water, about 4 minutes more, then stir in 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp salt.
Working fast, fold in the warm peanuts, cashews and toasted coconut chips, stirring 20 seconds until coated, then turn onto the greased board.
Roll to a 6 mm sheet with the greased pin while hot, before the coconut-rich caramel firms up.
Score into 14 pieces while warm, cool 15 minutes until crisp and snap apart into coconut-flecked shards.
tips: Toast coconut and cashews only to pale gold, as they darken further in the hot caramel.
Keep the jaggery lighter so the coconut oil fragrance is not overwhelmed.
Store airtight in humid climates, as coconut chips soften if exposed to air.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a banana leaf at an Onam sadya sweet course, or crumble over coconut ice cream for a festive dessert.

variations.name: Rajasthani Festive Peanut Chikki
variations.description: A festive desert chikki that layers peanuts with sesame and a warming whisper of dried red chilli and dry ginger, in the Rajasthani love of gud paired with warming spice for the cold season. Sweet, nutty and gently fiery.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: cooked to hard-crack to bind the sweet-heat festive brittle

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the chilli and ginger and greases the surfaces

steps: Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and bloom 0.5 tsp roasted red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp dried ginger in it for 20 seconds until fragrant, then set aside; warm 1.5 cups peanuts and 0.5 cup toasted sesame.
Grease a board and pin with the second tbsp of Anveshan Ghee, then melt 1.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water in a heavy pan on medium heat until bubbling, about 6 minutes.
Cook to hard-crack, testing a drop snaps in cold water, about 4 minutes more, then stir in the spiced ghee, 0.5 tsp black salt and 0.5 tsp cardamom.
Working fast, fold in the warm peanuts and sesame, stirring 20 seconds until every piece is coated in the spiced caramel, then pour onto the greased board.
Roll to a 6 mm sheet with the greased pin while hot and pliable, moving quickly before it hardens.
Score into 14 pieces while warm, cool 15 minutes until crisp and snap apart; each shard is sweet, nutty, then gently warming.
tips: Bloom chilli and ginger in ghee first so they perfume the caramel instead of tasting raw.
Sesame toasts fast, so watch it and pull it off the moment it smells nutty.
This sweet-heat chikki suits cold weather; the dry ginger is warming and settling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a winter snack with hot masala chai, or pack squares for a Rajasthan road trip.

variations.name: Awadhi Festive Peanut Chikki
variations.description: A festive Lucknawi chikki perfumed with kewra and rose, dotted with pistachio and finished with silver vark for a refined nazakat brittle. Fragrance leads, then the peanut crunch follows.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: cooked to a lighter hard-crack so the kewra perfume survives

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: rounds the caramel and greases the surfaces for a courtly finish

steps: Warm 1.5 cups peanuts and grease a board and pin with 1 tbsp of the 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee.
Melt 1.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan on medium heat, stirring, until it bubbles, about 6 minutes.
Cook just to a light hard-crack, testing a drop snaps in cold water, about 4 minutes more, then take off the heat and stir in 1 tsp kewra water, 0.5 tsp rosewater, 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp salt.
Working fast, fold in the warm peanuts and 0.5 cup slivered pistachios, stirring 20 seconds until coated, then pour onto the greased board.
Roll to a 6 mm sheet with the greased pin while hot, then lay 1 sheet of silver vark over the top and press gently.
Score into 14 pieces while warm, cool 15 minutes until crisp and snap apart along the lines.
tips: Add both kewra and rose off the heat and measure carefully, as they overpower easily.
Cook the caramel a touch lighter so the toffee note does not bury the perfume.
Lay the vark while the surface is still tacky so it clings without sliding.
variations.servingSuggestion: Arrange the vark-topped shards on porcelain with rose sherbet for a refined Awadhi festive table.

variations.name: Classic Masala Adai
variations.description: A spiced-up adai where warm garam masala and coriander powder are ground into the four-dal batter for a more aromatic, hearty crepe. The extra spice layer over the nutty lentils makes this a filling one-dish meal on its own.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil crisps the spiced batter into lacy, golden edges.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee drizzled over the adai amplifies the warm garam-masala aroma.

steps: Soak the chana, toor, urad and moong dals with 1 cup raw rice for 3 hours, then drain well.
Grind the soaked mix with 3 dried red chillies and grated 1 inch ginger to a coarse batter, adding water sparingly to keep it thick.
Stir in 1 tsp garam masala, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 1.5 tsp salt, 15 curry leaves and 1 chopped onion, folding the spices through evenly.
Heat a tava over medium heat, grease with Anveshan Groundnut Oil, and spread a ladle of batter into a thick 7-inch round.
Make a central hole and drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil around it, cooking until the base is deep golden and crisp, about 3 minutes.
Flip and cook the second side until browned through, about 2 minutes, then drizzle with a little Anveshan Ghee.
Serve the masala adai hot while the edges crackle.
tips: Fold the ground spices in after grinding rather than adding them to the grinder, so their aroma stays bright.
Since the batter is thick, spread it a little thinner than a plain adai so the added spices cook through fully.
A rest of 30 minutes lets the spices bloom into the batter and improves the flavour noticeably.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling coconut chutney and a bowl of jaggery for dipping, the traditional sweet foil to a spiced adai.

variations.name: Kerala Coconut Masala Adai
variations.description: The spiced masala adai enriched with coarse coconut and fennel, cooked in coconut oil for a fragrant Malabar depth. The coconut softens the garam-masala warmth into something rounded and comforting.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil ties the coconut batter to a fragrant coastal crust.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A little ghee grounds the sweet coconut with savoury richness.

steps: Soak the chana, toor and urad dals with 1 cup raw rice for 3 hours, then drain.
Grind the soaked mix with 3 dried red chillies and 1 tsp fennel seeds to a coarse batter, then pulse in 0.5 cup grated coconut so flecks remain.
Stir in 1 tsp garam masala, 1.5 tsp salt, 15 curry leaves and 6 chopped shallots to a thick batter.
Heat a tava over medium heat, grease with Anveshan Coconut Oil, and spread a ladle of batter into a thick 7-inch round.
Make a central hole and drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil around it, cooking until golden and crisp, about 3 minutes.
Flip and cook the second side until browned, about 2 minutes, then finish with a little Anveshan Ghee.
Serve the coconut masala adai hot and fragrant.
tips: Fennel and coconut are the Kerala signature here, so do not skip the fennel even though it is a small amount.
Pulse the coconut in last so it stays coarse and does not turn the batter watery.
Shallots caramelise more sweetly than onions, reinforcing the coconut's natural sweetness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with avial and a spoon of coconut chutney, plating it as a wholesome Kerala tiffin.

variations.name: Bengali Mustard Masala Adai
variations.description: An East-Indian crossover where the spiced adai batter is finished in pungent mustard oil with nigella seeds for a sharp, warming edge. The mustard oil against the four-dal earthiness gives it a bold, unexpected character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Kachi ghani mustard oil gives the sharp Bengali pungency that defines this adai.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing dab of ghee mellows the mustard oil's raw bite.

steps: Soak the chana, toor and urad dals with 1 cup raw rice for 3 hours, then drain.
Grind the soaked mix with 3 green chillies and grated 1 inch ginger to a coarse batter, adding water sparingly.
Stir in 1 tsp garam masala, 0.5 tsp nigella seeds, 1.5 tsp salt, 1 chopped onion and 3 tbsp chopped coriander to a thick batter.
Heat a tava over medium heat and grease with Anveshan Mustard Oil that has been heated until smoking once and cooled, so its harshness is tamed.
Spread a ladle of batter into a thick 7-inch round, make a central hole and drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil around it, cooking until crisp and golden, about 3 minutes.
Flip and cook the second side until browned, about 2 minutes, then finish with a little Anveshan Ghee.
Serve the mustard masala adai hot, while the pungent aroma and crisp edges are at their best.
tips: Pre-smoke the mustard oil before greasing the tava so the adai carries a clean pungency rather than a raw bite.
Nigella seeds go straight into the batter and cook through on the tava, giving a subtle oniony aroma.
Keep the green chillies generous, as mustard and chilli are the classic Bengali pairing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling cucumber raita instead of the usual chutney, a refreshing counter to the mustard heat.

variations.name: Andhra Guntur Masala Adai
variations.description: A fierce Andhra masala adai where Guntur chillies and garlic join the garam masala in the batter, all cooked in gingelly sesame oil. It is smoky, garlicky and blazing, a protein crepe for serious spice lovers.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly sesame oil lends the toasty Andhra base and stands up to the heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A little ghee at the finish tames the Guntur fire.

steps: Soak the chana, toor and urad dals with 1 cup raw rice for 3 hours, then drain.
Grind the soaked mix with 6 Guntur red chillies, 6 garlic cloves and 1 tsp cumin seeds to a coarse, fiery batter.
Stir in 1 tsp garam masala, 1.5 tsp salt, 1 chopped onion and 15 curry leaves to a thick batter.
Heat a tava over medium heat, grease with Anveshan Sesame Oil, and spread a ladle of batter into a thick 7-inch round.
Make a central hole and drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil around it, cooking until crisp and red-flecked, about 3 minutes.
Flip and cook the second side until browned through, about 2 minutes, then finish with a little Anveshan Ghee.
Serve the Guntur masala adai searing hot.
tips: Grinding the garlic into the batter lets it cook through and lose its raw edge as the adai fries.
Deseed some of the Guntur chillies to keep the colour while dialling back the punishing heat.
Keep the tava at steady medium heat, since sesame oil scorches quickly on high.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain curd and a mild coconut chutney, the classic Andhra way to enjoy fire without overwhelming the palate.

variations.name: Rajasthani Lal Mirch Masala Adai
variations.description: A desert-inspired masala adai coloured deep red with a smoky dried-chilli and garlic paste, cooked in ghee for Marwari richness. It borrows the laal maas palette to turn the humble adai into something regal and warming.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee carries the red-chilli richness at the heart of Rajasthani cooking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A little groundnut oil raises the smoke point so the ghee-rich adai crisps cleanly.

steps: Soak the chana, toor and urad dals with 1 cup raw rice for 3 hours, then drain, and soak 6 dried red chillies in warm water for 15 minutes.
Grind the drained chillies with 6 garlic cloves into a smooth red paste, then coarsely grind the soaked dals and rice separately.
Combine the batters and stir in the red paste, 1 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp coriander powder, 1.5 tsp salt, 1 chopped onion and 3 tbsp coriander leaves.
Heat a tava over medium heat, grease with a mix of Anveshan Ghee and Anveshan Groundnut Oil, and spread a ladle of batter into a thick 7-inch round.
Make a central hole and drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee around it, cooking until crisp and rust-coloured, about 3 minutes.
Flip and cook the second side until browned through, about 2 minutes.
Serve the laal masala adai hot and glistening.
tips: Use Kashmiri or Mathania chillies for a vivid red with gentle heat, adding a hotter variety only if you want real fire.
Grinding the chilli-garlic paste smooth and the dals coarse keeps the adai's signature grainy texture intact.
This ghee-rich adai is best served fresh, as it firms up as it cools.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling mint-yoghurt dip and lime-dressed onion rings, a Rajasthani-thali touch that cuts the richness.

variations.name: Classic Masala Aloo Tikki
variations.description: A fully spiced tikki where garam masala and coriander powder are layered with a stuffing of spiced peas, giving two textures in one bite. It is the halwai-style tikki that anchors North Indian chaat counters, aromatic and generously masaledar.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil fries a crisp shell and sautes the masala peas stuffing cleanly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli dredge seals the stuffed tikki so the pea filling never bursts out in the pan

steps: Boil and grate 4 medium potatoes, mix with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp of the coriander powder and 0.5 tsp salt, then bind with 0.5 cup bread crumbs into a smooth dough.
For the filling, heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil and saute 1 chopped onion, 2 minced green chillies and 1 inch grated ginger for 3 minutes until soft.
Add 0.5 cup peas, 1 tsp garam masala, the remaining 1 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp salt, mash lightly and cook 4 minutes into a dry stuffing, then cool.
Flatten a portion of dough, spoon 1 tbsp of the pea masala into the centre, seal and pat into a disc; repeat to make 8 stuffed tikkis.
Dust each in 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, press into the remaining 0.5 cup bread crumbs and chill 15 minutes.
Heat the remaining 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat and fry the tikkis 4 to 5 minutes per side until golden and crisp, then drain.
Serve hot with green chutney and sweet tamarind chutney for that halwai-counter finish.
tips: Cook the pea filling until properly dry, as any moisture inside will steam and split the tikki open while frying.
Seal the stuffing with damp fingertips so no filling peeks through the crust to leak.
Make the filling a day ahead; the masala deepens and shaping goes faster.
variations.servingSuggestion: Set a tikki on chilled yoghurt, layer both chutneys, red chilli, roasted cumin and sev for a classic Delhi-style aloo tikki chaat.

variations.name: Punjabi Masala Aloo Tikki
variations.description: The rich dhaba-style tikki finished in ghee for that unmistakable golden, buttery crust Punjab loves. Kasuri methi and a generous garam masala give it a deep, tandoor-adjacent aroma without any butter at all.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee gives the buttery Punjabi crust and aroma traditionally got from white butter, without the butter

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli coat crisps richly in ghee and keeps the soft dhaba-style tikki intact

steps: Boil and mash 4 medium potatoes, then crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi between your palms and mix it in while the mash is warm to release its aroma.
Beat in 1.5 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 inch grated ginger and 1 tsp salt for a deep, fragrant mix.
Stir through 1 finely chopped onion and 2 minced green chillies, then bind with 0.5 cup bread crumbs into a firm dough.
Shape into 8 thick discs, dust each in 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, press into the remaining 0.5 cup bread crumbs and rest 15 minutes.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan over medium heat until it is clear and fragrant.
Fry the tikkis 4 to 5 minutes per side, basting with the hot ghee, until burnished gold and crisp, then drain briefly.
Serve hot with pudina chutney and sirka onions, dhaba style.
tips: Rub the kasuri methi to a coarse powder before adding so it perfumes the whole mash evenly.
Ghee gives colour fast, so keep the flame at medium and rely on the crust turning deep gold as your cue.
A spoonful of the same ghee brushed over the hot tikkis just before serving amplifies the buttery aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve stuffed into a hot kulcha with sliced onion and mint chutney for a Punjabi tikki-kulcha that eats like a meal.

variations.name: Gujarati Masala Aloo Tikki
variations.description: A gently sweet-savoury tikki in the Gujarati mould, where jaggery, lime and green chilli meet in the tell-tale khatta-mitha-teekha balance. Crushed roasted peanuts and coriander keep it light and fresh against the mellow sweetness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: chemical-free jaggery powder gives the signature Gujarati sweet edge that balances the lime and chilli

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil is Gujarat's staple frying oil and complements the peanut in the mix

steps: Boil and mash 4 medium potatoes, then while warm mix in 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tbsp lime juice so the jaggery melts evenly.
Crush 3 tbsp roasted peanuts coarsely and add them with 2 tsp green chilli-ginger paste, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt.
Fold in 3 tbsp coriander, then bind with 0.5 cup bread crumbs into a soft, faintly sweet dough.
Shape into 8 discs, press each into the remaining 0.5 cup bread crumbs and rest 15 minutes.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat until it shimmers.
Fry the tikkis 4 to 5 minutes per side until golden and crisp, watching closely as the jaggery makes them colour a touch faster, then drain.
Serve warm with a sweet-sour date-tamarind chutney that echoes the Gujarati flavour.
tips: Balance is everything here; taste the mash and adjust jaggery, lime and chilli until no single note dominates.
Because jaggery browns quickly, keep the flame at a steady medium and pull the tikkis at first deep gold.
Keep the peanuts coarse for texture, and toast them fresh for the best nutty aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of sweet-and-spicy Gujarati chunda or a spoon of fresh green chutney and a wedge of lime.

variations.name: Odia Masala Aloo Tikki
variations.description: An eastern tikki tempered with panch phoron, the five-seed blend whose fennel and nigella notes perfume the potato from the first bite. A finish of roasted panch phoron powder and mustard oil gives it the earthy character of Odia street food.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: pungent mustard oil is the everyday Odia frying fat and lifts the panch phoron temper

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli coat crisps up around the seed-tempered mix and keeps the tikki firm

steps: Boil and mash 4 medium potatoes and set aside to cool.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until it just smokes, cool a little, then crackle 1 tsp panch phoron for 20 seconds until the seeds pop and turn fragrant.
Add 1 chopped onion, 4 crushed garlic cloves and 2 minced green chillies to the tempering and fry 4 minutes until golden.
Mix the temper into the potato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp salt, then bind with 0.5 cup bread crumbs.
Shape into 8 discs, dust in 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, press into the remaining 0.5 cup bread crumbs and rest 15 minutes.
Heat the remaining 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil over medium heat until mellowed, then fry the tikkis 4 to 5 minutes per side until golden and crisp, and drain.
Serve hot with a raw onion and green chilli salad and a wedge of lime.
tips: Never add panch phoron raw to the mash; the whole seeds must be crackled in hot oil first or they taste harsh.
Toast and grind a little extra panch phoron to dust over the finished tikkis for a stronger aroma.
Let the tempered onions cool before mixing so they don't make the mash sticky.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside ghuguni (spiced yellow peas) topped with onion and coriander for a Cuttack-style evening snack.

variations.name: Malwa Masala Aloo Tikki
variations.description: An Indori-style tikki loaded with crushed roasted peanuts and finished with a sharp sev-and-chaat crunch. Ground peanuts through the potato give a nutty body that carries the bustling masala of Malwa's famous street stalls.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil deepens the peanut character central to Indori tikki

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli dredge holds the peanut-heavy mix together for a sturdy, crunchy shell

steps: Boil and mash 4 medium potatoes and let them cool slightly.
Coarsely crush 0.33 cup roasted peanuts and mix two-thirds into the potato, saving the rest to garnish.
Add 1 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 chopped onion, 2 minced green chillies and 1 tsp salt to the mash and combine.
Bind with 0.5 cup bread crumbs, shape into 8 discs, dust in 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta and press into the remaining 0.5 cup bread crumbs, then rest 15 minutes.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat until a crumb sizzles at once.
Fry the tikkis 4 to 5 minutes per side until golden and crisp, then drain on paper.
Dust hot with 1 tsp chaat masala and scatter the reserved crushed peanuts and sev before serving.
tips: Reserve a third of the peanuts for garnishing so you get both a nutty body and a crunchy top.
Sprinkle the chaat masala only once the tikkis are out of the pan, so its tang stays bright.
Keep peanuts coarsely crushed, never powdered, to stay true to the Indori texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile the tikkis with chopped onion, tomato, sev, coriander and both chutneys for a loaded Indori-style tikki chaat.

variations.name: Classic Masala Besan Cheela
variations.description: A fully loaded gram-flour cheela with a complete masala base of garam masala, coriander and cumin whisked into the batter and a fresh vegetable topping pressed on top. It doubles as a savoury pancake and a light meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Wood-Pressed Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil crisps the masala batter cleanly and carries the spice without heaviness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing brush of bilona ghee rounds off the sharp masala with a nutty warmth.

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups gram flour with 1.5 cups water into a smooth, lump-free batter of thin-cream consistency.

Beat in 1 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt until uniformly spiced, then fold in 3 tbsp coriander and rest 10 minutes.
Finely chop 1 onion, 1 tomato, 0.5 capsicum and 2 green chillies and keep the topping ready in a bowl.
Heat a tava over medium heat and grease it with a film of Anveshan Groundnut Wood-Pressed Oil until it shimmers.
Ladle the batter and spread into a 7-inch round, immediately scatter the chopped vegetables over the wet top and press lightly so they embed as the base cooks golden, about 3 minutes.
Drizzle 1 tsp oil around the rim, flip to sear the topping for 2 minutes, brush with Anveshan Bilona Ghee, fold and serve hot.
tips: Press the topping into the wet batter before flipping so the vegetables stay put when you fold the cheela.
Rest the batter only 10 to 15 minutes, since besan thickens and may need a splash of water to spread thin again.
Chop the capsicum fine so it softens in the short griddle time rather than staying raw.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve open-faced with green chutney drizzled over the topping and a side of pickled onions for crunch.

variations.name: Andhra Masala Besan Cheela
variations.description: Andhra heat runs through this gram-flour cheela with searing Guntur chilli and a curry-leaf tempering in sesame oil. Bold, garlicky and fierce, it is a spice-lover's breakfast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Wood-Pressed Oil
ingredients.note: Nutty wood-pressed sesame oil is the classic Andhra fat and stands up to the fierce Guntur chilli.

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups gram flour with 1.5 cups water into a smooth, lump-free batter.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Wood-Pressed Oil until hot, crackle 12 curry leaves and 5 crushed garlic cloves for twenty seconds until fragrant, then cool and stir the tempering into the batter.
Beat in 1.5 tsp Guntur red chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, fold in 1 chopped onion and 3 tbsp coriander, and rest 10 minutes.
Heat a tava over medium heat and coat it thinly with Anveshan Sesame Wood-Pressed Oil until it shimmers.
Ladle the fiery-red batter and spread into a 7-inch round, drizzle 1 tsp sesame oil around the rim, and cook until the base is deep red-gold and crisp, about 3 to 4 minutes.
Flip and cook 2 minutes more until firm and blistered, then fold and serve at once with a cooling side.
tips: Frying the garlic and curry leaves in sesame oil first is what gives this cheela its authentic Andhra aroma.
Guntur chilli is intensely hot; drop to 1 tsp for a milder plate while keeping the vivid colour.
A spoon of curd whisked into the batter softens both the heat and the texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thick set curd and raw onion rings, the classic Andhra counter to a chilli-forward breakfast.

variations.name: Kerala Masala Besan Cheela
variations.description: A Malabar-style gram-flour cheela enriched with fresh coconut, shallots and curry leaves, finished in fragrant coconut oil. Lush, mildly spiced and unmistakably coastal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil gives the cheela its unmistakable Kerala aroma and a delicate crisp edge.

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups gram flour with 1.5 cups water into a smooth, pourable batter.
Stir in 0.5 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder and 1 tsp salt until evenly blended.
Fold in 4 tbsp grated coconut, 4 sliced shallots, 12 chopped curry leaves and 2 minced green chillies, then rest the batter for 10 minutes so the coconut hydrates.
Heat a tava over medium heat and grease it with Anveshan Coconut Oil until the surface glistens and smells sweetly of coconut.
Ladle the batter and spread into a 7-inch round, drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil around the rim, and cook until the base is golden with toasted coconut flecks, about 3 minutes.
Flip and cook 2 minutes more until set and lightly crisp, then fold and serve hot.
tips: Use fresh or frozen grated coconut rather than desiccated, which dries the batter and toughens the cheela.
Sliced shallots sweeten as they cook and are worth the extra chopping over a plain onion.
Warm solidified coconut oil before greasing so it spreads into an even film.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coconut-green-chilli chutney and a small bowl of sambar for a full Malabar breakfast.

variations.name: Bengali Masala Besan Cheela
variations.description: This Bengali masala cheela threads panch phoron warmth and pungent mustard oil through the gram-flour batter. Aromatic, mustard-sharp and quietly layered.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Wood-Pressed Oil
ingredients.note: Smoked kachi ghani mustard oil brings the sharp Bengali pungency that lifts the whole masala.

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups gram flour with 1.5 cups water into a smooth, pourable batter.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Wood-Pressed Oil until it smokes, add 1 tsp panch phoron and let it splutter for twenty seconds until fragrant, then cool and tip the whole tempering into the batter.

Stir in 0.5 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, fold in 1 chopped onion, 2 minced green chillies and 3 tbsp coriander, and rest 10 minutes.
Heat a tava over medium heat and film it with more Anveshan Mustard Wood-Pressed Oil until it shimmers.
Pour a ladle of batter, spread into a thin 7-inch round, drizzle mustard oil around the rim, and cook until the base is deep golden and crisp, about 3 to 4 minutes.
Flip and cook 2 minutes more until cooked through, then fold and serve while the mustard aroma is at its peak.
tips: Temper the panch phoron in hot mustard oil so the whole fenugreek and fennel release flavour and lose their raw edge.
Do not skip smoking the mustard oil, as raw kachi ghani can taste harshly bitter in a besan batter.
A pinch of sugar balances the mustard sharpness the Bengali way without making it sweet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a spoon of kasundi and a simple aloo bhaja on the side for a homestyle Bengali breakfast.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Masala Besan Cheela
variations.description: Goda masala gives this gram-flour cheela its dark, sweet-smoky depth, while crushed peanuts add a Puneri crunch. Warming and aromatic, it is a hearty tiffin.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Wood-Pressed Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the everyday Maharashtrian fat and pairs naturally with the roasted peanuts and goda masala.

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups gram flour with 1.5 cups water into a smooth, lump-free batter of thin-cream consistency.
Coarsely crush 3 tbsp roasted peanuts and beat them in with 1.5 tsp goda masala, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder and 1 tsp salt.
Fold in 2 minced green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger and 3 tbsp coriander, then rest the batter for 10 minutes so the goda masala blooms.
Heat a tava over medium heat and coat it with a thin film of Anveshan Groundnut Wood-Pressed Oil until it shimmers.
Ladle the batter and spread into a 7-inch round, drizzle 1 tsp groundnut oil around the rim, and cook until the base is golden and the peanuts toast, about 3 minutes.
Flip and cook 2 minutes more until firm and speckled, then fold into a triangle and serve hot.
tips: Crush the peanuts coarsely rather than powdering them to keep a pleasant crunch in every bite.
Goda masala scorches easily, so hold the flame at steady medium and avoid an overheated dry tava.
Leftover batter makes excellent thick mini-cheela for lunchboxes the next day.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a jaggery-tamarind chutney and a wedge of lime to echo the sweet-sour notes Maharashtrians love with goda masala.

variations.name: Classic Masala Corn Cutlet
variations.description: The fully spiced version, layered with garam masala and roasted coriander powder so every bite tastes seasoned right through, not just hot. Sweet corn and potato carry the aromatic masala, and a light dusting gives a thin crisp shell over the soft, fragrant middle.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: roasted, to bind the mix and dust the tikkis for a thin crackly crust

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for shallow-frying to an even golden crust

steps: Coarsely crush 1.5 cups of the corn and keep 0.5 cup whole, then combine both in a mixing bowl.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil and fry the onion, green chillies and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 4 minutes until softened and the raw smell disappears, then stir in the 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp garam masala for 30 seconds and cool.

Add the mashed potato, the toasted masala, chopped coriander, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt to the corn, then bind with 3 tbsp of the roasted Anveshan Khapli Atta into a firm dough.
Shape into 10 tikkis and dust each with the remaining 1 tbsp roasted Anveshan Khapli Atta.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a wide pan over medium heat and shallow-fry the tikkis 4 minutes a side until golden and crisp.
Drain on a rack so the masala crust stays crisp and does not steam soft.
tips: Toasting the whole spice powders in oil before mixing is what gives the deep, rounded masala flavour.
Add garam masala last and off the heat so its volatile aroma is not cooked away.
Rest the dough 10 minutes so the flavours meld and the atta firms the mix for easy shaping.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a tangy tamarind-date chutney and thinly sliced onions dusted with chaat masala.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Kala Masala Corn Cutlet
variations.description: Built on the smoky depth of goda (kala) masala, this tikki tastes of roasted coconut, sesame and dagad phool, the dark aromatic blend of Vidarbha kitchens. Crushed peanuts add crunch and a dry-coconut coat crisps up beautifully in the pan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: roasted binder that complements the earthy kala masala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Maharashtra's staple frying oil, for toasting the masala and shallow-frying

steps: Grind 1.5 cups corn to a coarse crush and reserve 0.5 cup whole, combining both in a bowl.

Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil and fry the onion and green chillies for 3 minutes, then add the 3 tbsp grated dry coconut and toast for 2 minutes until it smells nutty; stir in the 2 tsp goda masala off the heat and cool.

Fold the mashed potato, the coconut-goda masala, 3 tbsp crushed peanuts, chopped coriander, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt into the corn, then bind with the 3 tbsp roasted Anveshan Khapli Atta into a stiff mixture.
Shape 10 firm tikkis, packing them tight so the peanuts and coconut hold.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat and shallow-fry the tikkis 4 minutes a side until the copra-flecked crust turns dark gold.
Rest on a rack so the crunchy bits inside stay crisp.
tips: Toasting the dry coconut before adding goda masala doubles the roasted, smoky depth.
Goda masala varies by household; start with less and taste, as some blends are intensely aromatic.
Crush peanuts coarse for texture that contrasts the soft corn.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a fiery thecha and lime wedges, alongside kokum sharbat to cool the palate, Vidarbha-style.

variations.name: Andhra Karam Masala Corn Cutlet
variations.description: A blazing masala tikki where Guntur red chilli meets a homemade karam-style blend of roasted coriander, cumin and garlic. The heat is upfront but layered, and a curry-leaf tempering keeps it fragrant beneath the fire.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: roasted binder that stands up to the bold Andhra karam spicing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for the curry-leaf tempering and shallow-frying

steps: Coarsely crush 1.5 cups corn and keep 0.5 cup whole, then set both in a bowl.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil, crackle the 15 curry leaves, then fry the onion and 1.5 tbsp garlic for 4 minutes until golden; stir in the 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1.5 tsp Guntur chilli powder off the heat so they bloom without burning, and cool.

Mix the mashed potato, the karam tempering, chopped coriander, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt into the corn, then bind with 3 tbsp of the roasted Anveshan Khapli Atta into a firm dough.
Shape 10 tikkis and dust them with the remaining 1 tbsp roasted Anveshan Khapli Atta.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat and shallow-fry 4 minutes a side until the crust is a deep red-gold.
Drain on a rack and finish with a squeeze of lime to balance the karam heat.
tips: Bloom the Guntur chilli and coriander powder off the flame; they turn bitter if scorched.
A spoonful of thick curd in the mix keeps the tikkis moist against the drying heat.
Fry a few extra curry leaves till crisp and crumble them over the top for aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with cooling coconut chutney and gongura pickle on the side for a true Andhra-style snack plate.

variations.name: Odia Panch Phoron Masala Corn Cutlet
variations.description: Odisha's five-spice panch phoron, fennel, cumin, mustard, fenugreek and nigella, is bloomed in mustard oil to perfume this gently spiced tikki. It is aromatic rather than hot, with a faint sweetness and the earthy tang typical of an Odia snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: roasted binder that keeps the panch-phoron mix from breaking apart

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the classic eastern-Indian fat, for blooming the panch phoron and shallow-frying

steps: Crush 1.5 cups of the corn coarsely and keep 0.5 cup whole, then combine both in a bowl.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the flame and crackle the 1.5 tsp panch phoron for 20 seconds until the mustard pops and the fenugreek darkens, then add the onion, green chillies and 1 tbsp ginger and fry 4 minutes until soft; cool the tempering.

Fold the mashed potato, the panch-phoron tempering, chopped coriander, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt into the corn, then bind with the 4 tbsp roasted Anveshan Khapli Atta into a firm dough.
Shape into 10 neat tikkis and let them rest 10 minutes so the aromas settle in.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil over medium heat and shallow-fry the tikkis 4 minutes a side until golden and fragrant.
Drain on paper and serve warm to catch the panch-phoron aroma at its best.
tips: Let the fenugreek in the panch phoron just darken, not blacken, or it will turn the whole mix bitter.
Do not grind the panch phoron; the whole bloomed seeds give little bursts of flavour and texture.
Smoke the mustard oil once before frying to soften its pungency into a mellow warmth.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a light tomato-date khajuri chutney, an Odia favourite, and a cup of ginger tea.

variations.name: Haryanvi Ghee Masala Corn Cutlet
variations.description: Rustic and hearty in true Haryanvi style, these tikkis are cooked entirely in nutty Anveshan Ghee, which gives a rich, almost tandoori depth. A generous hit of garam masala, kasuri methi and green chilli keeps them bold and homely.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: roasted binder that suits the rich ghee-cooked masala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: cooks the masala and shallow-fries the tikkis for a deep, rustic Haryanvi richness

steps: Coarsely crush 1.5 cups corn and keep 0.5 cup whole, combining both in a bowl.

Melt 2 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee and fry the onion, green chillies and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 4 minutes until golden, then add the 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1.5 tsp garam masala and stir 30 seconds off the heat; cool.

Mix the mashed potato, the ghee-fried masala, 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi, 0.75 tsp amchur, chopped coriander, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt into the corn, then bind with the 4 tbsp roasted Anveshan Khapli Atta into a firm dough.
Shape 10 thick, rustic tikkis, patting them a little uneven for a homely look.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee on a flat tava over medium heat and shallow-fry the tikkis 4-5 minutes a side until richly browned and crusted; ghee browns faster, so watch the flame.
Drain briefly and serve hot while the ghee aroma is at its fullest.
tips: Cook on steady medium heat; ghee scorches quicker than oil and can darken the crust too fast.
Crush kasuri methi between your palms before adding so its aroma bursts through the ghee.
A spoon of ghee brushed on just before serving deepens the rustic richness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with white butter (makkhan), fresh onion rings and a glass of lassi for a hearty Haryanvi spread.

variations.name: Classic Masala Hara Bhara Kebab
variations.description: The fully spiced green kebab, layered with garam masala and roasted coriander so the spinach-and-pea base tastes seasoned right through. Rolled in bread crumbs and fried crisp, it is vivid green within and deeply aromatic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: roasted binder that firms the spiced mix without a raw-flour taste

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for toasting the masala and deep-frying to a crisp crust

steps: Blanch the spinach 1 minute, plunge into ice water, then squeeze completely dry and chop fine.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil and fry the onion with 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 4 minutes until golden, then add the 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp garam masala and toast 30 seconds; add the spinach and cook 3 minutes until dry, and cool.
Combine the masala spinach, mashed peas, mashed potato, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, then bind with the 3 tbsp roasted Anveshan Khapli Atta into a firm mixture.
Shape 10 patties and coat each in bread crumbs, pressing so the crust adheres.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to 180C and fry the kebabs for 2-3 minutes until golden and crisp.
Drain on a rack so the masala crust stays crisp over the green centre.
tips: Toast the coriander powder in oil before adding spinach for a deeper, rounded masala flavour.
Add garam masala off the heat so its volatile aroma is not cooked away.
Squeeze the spinach bone-dry so the kebabs bind and fry crisp.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tamarind-date chutney and onions dusted with chaat masala.

variations.name: Punjabi Makhani Masala Hara Bhara Kebab
variations.description: A dhaba-rich masala kebab shallow-fried in nutty Anveshan Ghee, with kasuri methi, garam masala and a soft paneer centre that melts as you bite. The ghee lends a butter-like, tandoori-adjacent depth over the green base.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: roasted binder that firms the rich, paneer-studded mix

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: shallow-fries the kebabs with the buttery makhani richness Punjab loves

steps: Blanch the spinach 1 minute, shock in ice water, squeeze dry and chop fine.

Melt 1 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee and fry 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, add the spinach with the 1.5 tsp garam masala and cook 3 minutes until dry, then fold in the 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi and cool.
Mix the spinach, mashed peas, mashed potato, crumbled paneer, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, then bind with the 3 tbsp roasted Anveshan Khapli Atta into a firm mixture.
Shape 10 patties and coat each in bread crumbs.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee on a tava over medium heat and shallow-fry the kebabs 3 minutes a side until golden, spooning ghee around the edges.
Brush the tops with the last of the ghee just before serving for a glossy finish.
tips: Fold the paneer in gently so it stays in soft melting pockets.
Cook in ghee over medium heat, as it browns faster than oil.
Crush kasuri methi warm so it perfumes the ghee as the kebabs fry.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with pudina chutney and pickled onions, with lemon and hot chai, dhaba-style.

variations.name: Gujarati Gud Masala Hara Bhara Kebab
variations.description: Gujarat's sweet-hot-tangy balance runs through this masala kebab, where Anveshan Jaggery Powder rounds off the spice and a squeeze of lemon keeps it lively. Soft and faintly sweet inside, crisp outside, it is the green kebab reimagined as farsan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted in for the signature Gujarati sweet-spicy balance in place of sugar

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday Gujarati frying fat, for a light golden deep-fry

steps: Blanch the spinach 1 minute, shock in ice water, squeeze dry and chop fine.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil and fry 1.5 tbsp green chilli-ginger paste for 1 minute, add the spinach and cook 3 minutes until dry, then cool.

Mix the spinach, mashed peas, mashed potato, 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 tbsp lemon juice, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt until the jaggery dissolves evenly, then bind with the 3 tbsp roasted gram flour into a soft mixture.
Shape 10 patties, wetting your palms lightly so the sweet mix does not cling, and coat each in bread crumbs.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to 180C and fry the kebabs for 2-3 minutes until golden; watch closely as the jaggery browns faster.
Drain on paper and finish with a squeeze of lemon for a bright Gujarati lift.
tips: Dissolve the jaggery powder fully into the mix for balanced sweetness, not sugary pockets.
Because jaggery caramelises fast, keep the oil at a steady 180C and do not over-fry.
A pinch of sesame in the mix adds a farsan-style crunch that suits the sweet-savoury profile.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with chunda and a scatter of thin sev for a proper Gujarati farsan plate.

variations.name: Odia Panch Phoron Masala Hara Bhara Kebab
variations.description: Odisha's five-spice panch phoron, bloomed in mustard oil, perfumes this gently spiced green kebab with fennel, cumin, mustard, fenugreek and nigella. It is aromatic rather than hot, with the earthy tang typical of an Odia snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: roasted binder that keeps the panch-phoron mix from breaking apart

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the classic eastern fat, for blooming the panch phoron and deep-frying

steps: Blanch the spinach 1 minute, shock in ice water, squeeze dry and chop fine.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the flame and crackle the 1.5 tsp panch phoron for 20 seconds until the mustard pops, then fry the onion and green chillies 4 minutes until soft; add the spinach and cook 2 minutes until dry, and cool.
Mix the spinach, mashed peas, mashed potato, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, then bind with the 3 tbsp roasted Anveshan Khapli Atta into a firm mixture.
Shape 10 patties and coat each in bread crumbs.
Reheat the remaining Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil to 180C and fry the kebabs for 2-3 minutes until golden and fragrant.
Drain on paper and serve warm to catch the panch-phoron aroma at its best.
tips: Let the fenugreek in the panch phoron just darken, not blacken, or it turns bitter.
Keep the panch phoron whole so the bloomed seeds give little bursts of flavour.
Smoke the mustard oil once before frying to mellow its pungency.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a light tomato-date khajuri chutney and a cup of ginger tea, Odia-style.

variations.name: Andhra Karam Masala Hara Bhara Kebab
variations.description: A blazing masala green kebab where Guntur red chilli meets a karam-style blend of roasted coriander, cumin and garlic. The heat is upfront but layered, with a curry-leaf tempering keeping it fragrant beneath the fire.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: roasted binder that stands up to the bold Andhra karam spicing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for the curry-leaf tempering and deep-frying, the Andhra staple

steps: Blanch the spinach 1 minute, shock in ice water, squeeze bone-dry and chop fine.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil, crackle the 15 curry leaves, fry the 1.5 tbsp garlic 1 minute, add the spinach and cook 3 minutes until dry, then stir in the 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1.5 tsp Guntur chilli powder off the heat and cool.
Mix the spicy spinach, mashed peas, mashed potato, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder and 1 tsp salt, then bind with the 3 tbsp roasted Anveshan Khapli Atta into a firm mixture.
Shape 10 patties and coat each in bread crumbs.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to 180C and fry the kebabs for 2-3 minutes until the crust is deep red-gold.
Drain on a rack and finish with a squeeze of lime to balance the karam heat.
tips: Bloom the Guntur chilli and coriander powder off the flame so they do not scorch and turn bitter.
A spoon of thick curd in the mix keeps the kebabs moist against the drying heat.
Crumble a few crisp-fried curry leaves over the top for extra aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and gongura pickle for a true Andhra snack plate.

variations.name: Classic Masala Moong Dal Cheela
variations.description: A loaded spin on the moong dal cheela where a full masala base of garam masala, coriander and cumin is built into the batter, then crowned with a fresh onion-tomato topping. It eats like a savoury pancake and a sabzi in one.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Wood-Pressed Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil crisps the masala batter cleanly and carries the spice without heaviness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing brush of bilona ghee rounds off the sharp masala with a nutty warmth.

steps: Soak 1 cup split green gram for 3 hours until swollen, drain, and grind with 2 green chillies and about 0.75 cup water into a smooth, thick-cream batter.
Beat in 1 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt until the batter is uniformly spiced.
Fold in 3 tbsp coriander and rest the batter 15 minutes; meanwhile finely chop 1 onion and 1 tomato and keep them ready for topping.
Heat a tava over medium heat and grease with a film of Anveshan Groundnut Wood-Pressed Oil until it shimmers across the surface.
Ladle batter and spread into a 7-inch round, immediately scatter the chopped onion and tomato over the wet top, and press lightly so they embed as the base cooks golden, about 3 minutes.
Drizzle 1 tsp oil around the edge, flip to sear the topping for 2 minutes, brush with Anveshan Bilona Ghee, fold and serve hot.
tips: Pressing the topping into the wet batter before flipping locks the vegetables in so they do not fall off when you fold the cheela.
Roast whole cumin and coriander and grind fresh for the masala if you can; the aroma outclasses pre-ground packets.
Rest the batter no longer than 30 minutes at room temperature so it stays lively and does not ferment in warm weather.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve open-faced, topping-side up, with green chutney drizzled across and a side of pickled onions for crunch.

variations.name: Andhra Masala Moong Dal Cheela
variations.description: Andhra heat takes over here with fiery Guntur red chilli and a curry-leaf tempering stirred into the masala batter. It is bold, garlicky and unapologetically hot, made for spice lovers.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Wood-Pressed Oil
ingredients.note: Nutty wood-pressed sesame oil is the classic Andhra fat and stands up to the fierce Guntur chilli.

steps: Soak 1 cup split green gram for 3 hours, drain, and grind with 5 garlic cloves and about 0.75 cup water into a smooth, thick batter.
In a small pan, heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Wood-Pressed Oil until hot and crackle 12 curry leaves for ten seconds until fragrant, then cool and stir the entire tempering into the batter.

Mix in 1.5 tsp Guntur red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, then fold in 1 finely chopped onion and rest 15 minutes.
Heat a tava over medium heat and coat it thinly with Anveshan Sesame Wood-Pressed Oil until it just begins to shimmer.
Pour a ladle of the fiery batter, spread into a 7-inch round, drizzle 1 tsp sesame oil around the rim, and cook until the base is deep red-gold and crisp, about 3 to 4 minutes.
Flip and cook the second side for 2 minutes until firm and blistered, then fold and serve at once with a cooling side.
tips: Blooming the curry leaves in hot sesame oil first releases their aroma properly instead of leaving them raw and papery in the batter.
Guntur chilli is intensely hot; dial it to 1 tsp for a milder plate without losing the bright red colour.
A spoon of curd whisked into the batter tempers the heat while keeping the cheela soft.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thick set curd and a wedge of raw onion, the classic Andhra way to cool a chilli-forward tiffin.

variations.name: Kerala Masala Moong Dal Cheela
variations.description: A coconut-rich Malabar interpretation where fresh grated coconut and a coconut-oil finish make the masala cheela lush and fragrant. Curry leaves and shallots deepen the coastal character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil gives the cheela its unmistakable Kerala aroma and a delicate crisp edge.

steps: Soak 1 cup split green gram for 3 hours, drain, and grind with 2 green chillies and about 0.75 cup water to a smooth batter.
Pulse in 4 tbsp grated fresh coconut just to combine, then stir in 0.5 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt.
Fold through 4 finely sliced shallots and 12 chopped curry leaves, then rest the batter for 15 minutes to let the coconut hydrate.
Heat a tava over medium heat and grease it with Anveshan Coconut Oil until the surface glistens and smells sweetly of coconut.
Ladle the batter and spread into a 7-inch round, drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil around the edges, and cook until the base is golden with toasted coconut flecks, about 3 minutes.
Flip and cook for 2 minutes until set and lightly crisp, then fold and serve hot off the pan.
tips: Use fresh or frozen grated coconut rather than desiccated, which can dry out the batter and turn the cheela tough.
Sliced shallots soften and sweeten as they cook; do not swap them for a large onion, which lacks the same depth.
Coconut oil solidifies in cool kitchens, so warm the bottle briefly before greasing the tava.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coconut-and-green-chilli chutney and a small bowl of sambar for a full Malabar breakfast plate.

variations.name: Bengali Masala Moong Dal Cheela
variations.description: This Bengali version swaps the usual oil for pungent wood-pressed mustard oil and threads panch phoron warmth through the masala. The result is aromatic, mustard-sharp and quietly complex.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Wood-Pressed Oil
ingredients.note: Smoked-off kachi ghani mustard oil brings the sharp Bengali pungency that lifts the whole masala.

steps: Soak 1 cup split green gram for 3 hours, drain, and grind with 2 green chillies and about 0.75 cup water into a smooth, pourable batter.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Wood-Pressed Oil until it smokes, add 1 tsp panch phoron and let it splutter for twenty seconds until fragrant, then cool and tip the whole tempering into the batter.
Stir in 0.5 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, fold in 1 chopped onion and 3 tbsp coriander, and rest 15 minutes.
Heat a tava over medium heat and film it with a little more Anveshan Mustard Wood-Pressed Oil until it shimmers.
Pour a ladle of batter, spread into a thin 7-inch round, drizzle mustard oil around the rim, and cook until the base is deep golden and crisp, about 3 to 4 minutes.
Flip and cook 2 minutes more until cooked through, then fold and serve while the mustard aroma is at its peak.
tips: Tempering the panch phoron in hot mustard oil is essential, as the whole fenugreek and fennel need heat to release flavour and lose their raw edge.
Do not skip smoking the mustard oil first; raw kachi ghani oil can taste harshly bitter in the batter.
A pinch of sugar balances the mustard sharpness the Bengali way without making the cheela sweet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a spoon of kasundi and a simple aloo bhaja on the side for a homestyle Bengali breakfast.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Masala Moong Dal Cheela
