variations.description: Goda masala replaces the standard garam masala here, lending its dark, sweet-smoky depth to the batter, while peanuts add a Puneri crunch. It is warming, aromatic and distinctly Maharashtrian.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Wood-Pressed Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the everyday Maharashtrian fat and pairs naturally with the roasted peanuts and goda masala.

steps: Soak 1 cup split green gram for 3 hours, drain, and grind with 1 inch ginger, 2 green chillies and about 0.75 cup water into a smooth batter.
Coarsely crush 3 tbsp roasted peanuts and stir them in along with 1.5 tsp goda masala, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt.
Fold through 3 tbsp coriander and rest the batter for 15 minutes so the goda masala blooms and the peanuts soften slightly.
Heat a tava over medium heat and coat it with a thin film of Anveshan Groundnut Wood-Pressed Oil until it shimmers.
Ladle the batter and spread into a 7-inch round, drizzle 1 tsp groundnut oil around the edge, and cook until the base is golden and the peanuts toast, about 3 minutes.
Flip and cook the second side for 2 minutes until firm and speckled, then fold into a triangle and serve hot.
tips: Crushing rather than powdering the peanuts keeps a pleasant crunch in every bite of the finished cheela.
Goda masala can taste bitter if scorched, so keep the flame steady at medium and avoid a dry, overheated tava.
Leftover batter makes excellent thick mini-cheela for lunchboxes the next morning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a jaggery-tamarind chutney and a wedge of lime, echoing the sweet-sour notes Maharashtrians love with goda masala.

variations.name: Classic Masala Onion Uttapam
variations.description: A spiced-up onion uttapam where garam masala and coriander powder are folded into the batter and a warm onion-tomato masala tops each round. Thicker and more robust than the plain version, it eats almost like a savoury spiced pancake.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil for the masala saute and for crisping the uttapam base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee to finish each uttapam with a fragrant, glossy top

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin, add 2 finely chopped onions, 2 chopped green chillies and 1 tbsp ginger, and fry until the onions soften and turn pale gold.
Stir in 1 chopped tomato, 1 tsp coriander powder and 0.5 tsp garam masala, cook 3 minutes to a thick masala, then set aside.
Stir 0.75 tsp salt and the remaining 0.5 tsp garam masala into 2.5 cups fermented dosa batter, loosening with water to a thick, spreadable mix.
Heat a tava on medium, grease with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, and pour a ladle of batter into a thick 5-inch round.
Spread 2 tbsp of the warm masala and a scatter of raw chopped onion over the top, press gently, drizzle 1 tsp oil around the edge, cover and cook 3 minutes.
Flip and cook the topping side 2 minutes until set, dot with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Ghee, and serve hot with 3 tbsp coriander scattered over.
tips: Cook the masala until fairly dry so it sits on the uttapam without making the batter soggy.
Adding some raw onion alongside the cooked masala gives a sweet crunch against the soft spiced base.
Keep the tava at a steady medium so the thick uttapam cooks through before the base over-browns.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and sambar, or a tangy tomato chutney for a heartier brunch plate.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Masala Onion Uttapam
variations.description: Maharashtra spices the masala uttapam with dark, roasted goda masala and a peanut crunch, giving it an earthy, festive depth. The toasted-coconut warmth of goda masala sets this apart from any North Indian spicing.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the classic Maharashtrian oil for the goda masala saute and the tava

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds, add 2 chopped onions, 2 green chillies and 12 curry leaves, and saute until the onions go glassy.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp goda masala and 3 tbsp crushed roasted peanuts, cook 2 minutes into a fragrant dry masala, and set aside.
Season 2.5 cups fermented dosa batter with 0.75 tsp salt, loosening with a splash of water to a thick, spreadable consistency.
Heat a tava on medium, grease with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, and spread a ladle of batter into a thick 5-inch round.
Press 2 tbsp of the goda-peanut masala and a little chopped raw onion into the surface, drizzle 1 tsp oil around the edge, cover and cook 3 minutes.
Flip and cook the topping side 2 minutes until the peanuts toast, scatter 3 tbsp coriander over, and serve warm.
tips: Toast the goda masala briefly in the oil so its roasted aroma blooms before it hits the batter.
Keep the peanut pieces coarse for crunch; a fine powder disappears into the masala.
A squeeze of lime over the finished uttapam lifts the earthy goda notes beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a fiery green thecha and coconut chutney, with hot filter coffee alongside.

variations.name: Gujarati Masala Onion Uttapam
variations.description: Gujarat gives the masala uttapam its trademark sweet-savoury balance, tempering the spice with Anveshan Jaggery in the batter. Mildly sweet, gently spiced and soft, it captures the hallmark khatta-mitha character of a Gujarati kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil, the everyday Gujarati cooking fat, for the masala and the tava

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the natural sweetener that gives Gujarati batters their signature gentle sweetness

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 12 curry leaves, add 2 chopped onions, 2 green chillies and 1 tbsp ginger, and fry until soft.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp coriander powder, cook 2 minutes to a light masala, and set aside.
Dissolve 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder in a spoon of warm water and stir it into 2.5 cups fermented dosa batter with 0.75 tsp salt, loosening to a thick, spreadable mix.
Heat a tava on medium, grease with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, and spread a ladle of the sweetened batter into a thick 5-inch round.
Press 2 tbsp of the onion masala and a little raw chopped onion into the top, drizzle 1 tsp oil around the edge, cover and cook 3 minutes.
Flip and cook the topping side 2 minutes until golden, scatter 3 tbsp coriander over, and serve warm.
tips: Dissolve the jaggery first so it blends smoothly rather than leaving sweet lumps in the batter.
The sweetness should be subtle; two teaspoons of jaggery balances the spice without turning the uttapam dessert-like.
Jaggery makes the base brown faster, so keep the heat at a gentle medium and watch the underside.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a sweet-and-spicy date-tamarind chutney and a cooling coconut chutney to play up the khatta-mitha theme.

variations.name: Andhra Masala Onion Uttapam
variations.description: Andhra loads the masala uttapam with a fiery Guntur-chilli onion masala and a garlic-sesame temper, cooked in nutty Anveshan Sesame Oil. It is bold and blistering, the kind of spicy tiffin that Vijayawada breakfast stalls are famous for.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed til oil, the Andhra staple, for the fiery masala and the tava

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard and 0.5 tsp cumin, add 2 chopped onions, 5 minced garlic cloves and 15 curry leaves, and fry until the onions caramelise at the edges.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp Guntur red chilli powder off direct heat, cook 2 minutes into a fiery masala, and set aside.
Season 2.5 cups fermented dosa batter with 0.75 tsp salt, loosening with water to a thick, spreadable consistency.
Heat a tava on medium, season with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, and spread a ladle of batter into a thick 5-inch round.
Press 2 tbsp of the Guntur masala and a little raw onion into the surface, drizzle 1 tsp sesame oil around the edge, cover and cook 3 minutes.
Flip and cook the topping side 2 minutes until the garlic crisps, scatter 3 tbsp coriander over, and serve blazing hot.
tips: Add the Guntur chilli powder away from full heat so it colours the oil without scorching bitter.
Mince the garlic fine so it melts into the masala and crisps on the flip rather than staying raw.
Serve with generous curd, as the Guntur heat in the masala is deliberately fierce.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling onion raita and a gunpowder podi loosened in sesame oil for dipping.

variations.name: Bengali Masala Onion Uttapam
variations.description: Bengal spices its masala uttapam with a pungent Anveshan Mustard Oil temper and a nigella crackle over the onion masala. The sharp mustard-oil bite against the soft spiced batter gives this tiffin an unmistakable Kolkata soul.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked to first wisp so its pungency softens into the classic Bengali kick

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to first smoke, cool slightly, then crackle 0.75 tsp nigella seeds and add 2 chopped onions, 3 slit green chillies and 1 tbsp ginger.
Fry until the onions soften, stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp coriander powder and 1 chopped tomato, and cook 3 minutes into a thick masala.
Season 2.5 cups fermented dosa batter with 0.75 tsp salt and 1 tbsp of the smoked mustard oil, loosening to a thick, spreadable mix.
Heat a tava on medium, wipe with a little mustard oil, and spread a ladle of batter into a thick 5-inch round.
Press 2 tbsp of the mustard masala and a little raw onion into the top, drizzle 1 tsp mustard oil around the edge, cover and cook 3 minutes.
Flip and cook the topping side 2 minutes until the onions catch colour, scatter 3 tbsp coriander over, and serve hot.
tips: Smoke the mustard oil fully before using so its raw bitterness cooks off and only the warm sharpness stays.
Nigella is potent, so three-quarters of a teaspoon is enough to flavour the whole batch.
Cook the masala until quite dry so it sits on the uttapam without seeping into the batter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coconut-coriander chutney and lime-pickled onions to echo the Bengali mustard theme.

variations.name: Classic Masala Pakora
variations.description: A fully spiced pakora where garam masala and coriander powder are worked right into the besan, so every bite carries a rounded, aromatic warmth rather than just chilli heat. Crisp-edged and deeply seasoned, it is the pakora that needs no chutney but welcomes one anyway.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: grounds the heavily spiced batter with a nutty crunch that stays crisp

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed frying oil that crisps the spiced batter cleanly without masking the masala

steps: Slice 2 onions, chop 3 green chillies and grate 1 inch ginger, mixing with 3 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt, then rest 10 minutes until juicy.

Add 1.5 cups besan, 0.25 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1.25 tsp garam masala, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp fennel seeds, 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder, tossing to coat.
Bind with only 4 to 5 tbsp water into a thick, clinging batter so the fritters stay open and crackly under the heavy spicing.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C until a scrap of batter surfaces steadily in 4 seconds.
Fry ragged clusters over medium-high for 4 to 5 minutes, turning, until deep golden and fragrant with masala.
Drain on a rack and serve hot, when the toasted-spice aroma is at its fullest.
tips: Add the powdered spices to the dry besan first so they distribute evenly before any water goes in.
A fresh, home-ground garam masala transforms this pakora; stale masala just tastes dusty when fried.
If the batter tastes flat before frying, it usually needs salt, not more chilli.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with green chutney, a sprinkle of chaat masala and sliced onions, alongside adrak chai for a classic evening snack.

variations.name: Punjabi Masala Pakora
variations.description: The dhaba masala pakora, thick-coated and butter-finished, with ginger-garlic and a bold hand of garam masala. Richer and heftier than the classic, it is brushed with butter and dusted with amchur so it eats almost like a chaat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: thickens the coating for a hearty dhaba-style fritter that soaks up the butter finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the deep-frying medium that builds the sturdy golden crust a dhaba pakora needs

steps: Slice 2 onions and mix with 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 3 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt, resting 8 minutes until wet.

Fold in 1.5 cups besan, 0.25 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1.5 tsp garam masala, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp anardana, 0.5 tsp black salt, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp turmeric to a thick coating.
Add 5 to 6 tbsp water to a stiff, heavy batter so the pakoras fry dense and satisfying like the roadside version.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C and fry rough clusters over medium-high for 5 minutes until deep golden and firm.
Drain on a rack, brush the hot pakoras with 2 tbsp melted butter and dust with 0.5 tsp amchur so it sizzles into the crust.
Serve immediately while the butter gleams and the masala aroma is strong.
tips: The double dose of garam masala and coriander powder is what marks this out from a plain pakora, so do not skimp.
Brush butter and dust amchur only after frying so the flavours stay bright and do not scorch.
Leftover pakoras crisp up beautifully in a hot air fryer or oven for a few minutes; skip the microwave.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve dhaba-style with thick garlic chutney, onion rings and lemon, or chopped into a quick pakora chaat with curd and chutneys.

variations.name: Delhi-style Masala Pakora
variations.description: The chaat-corner masala pakora of Delhi, where the fried fritters are tossed hot in a punchy garam-masala and chaat-masala mix so the spice clings to every crag. Sharp, tangy and street-loud, it is engineered to be scooped up with green and sweet chutneys.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: keeps the fritters crunchy enough to hold the spice toss without going soft

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: fries the potato-onion fritters to a crisp shell ready for the chaat-masala toss

steps: Grate 1 potato, slice 1 onion and grate 1 inch ginger, mix with 3 chopped green chillies, 3 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt, resting 5 minutes so the potato softens.
Add 1.5 cups besan, 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp turmeric, tossing to coat.
Bind with 4 to 5 tbsp water into a thick batter, keeping 1.5 tsp chaat masala aside for finishing.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C and fry ragged clusters over medium-high for 5 minutes until crisp and deep golden.
Drain briefly, then while still hot toss the pakoras in a bowl with 1.5 tsp chaat masala until every crag is coated.
Scatter over 3 tbsp fresh pomegranate seeds and serve at once, when the tangy chaat masala is fragrant and the crust is loud and crisp.
tips: Grated potato adds a soft, chaat-like centre against the crisp shell that Delhi snackers love.
Toss in chaat masala only after frying; its amchur and black salt lose their zing if heated in the oil.
Serve the moment they are tossed, as the salt in chaat masala will slowly soften the crust if they sit.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a quick chaat with green chutney, sweet tamarind chutney, a drizzle of curd and a shower of sev and pomegranate.

variations.name: Kerala Masala Pakora
variations.description: A coconut-rich pakora in the Malabar spirit, where grated fresh coconut and crackled curry leaves go into the besan and the frying is done in fragrant coconut oil. Sweet, nutty and warm with pepper, it is the tea-shop bhaji of Kerala evenings.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed coconut oil that fries the bhaji with the sweet Malabar aroma no other oil gives

steps: Slice 2 onions and mix with 0.5 cup grated coconut, 20 torn curry leaves, 3 chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger and 1.25 tsp salt, resting 8 minutes.
Add 1.5 cups besan, 1 tsp coarse black pepper, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder, tossing to a thick coating.
Bind with 4 to 5 tbsp water into a stiff batter so the coconut-flecked clusters fry crisp and open.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Coconut Oil to 175C, a touch gentler as coconut oil browns quickly, until a drop rises in 4 seconds.
Fry rough clusters over medium heat for 4 to 5 minutes, turning, until golden, crisp and fragrant with coconut.
Drain on paper and serve hot, when the sweet coconut and curry-leaf aroma is strongest.
tips: Use fresh grated coconut, not desiccated, for the moisture and sweetness that define this bhaji.
Coconut oil smokes lower than groundnut oil, so keep the flame at medium to avoid a burnt taste.
Toss in a few extra curry leaves in the last minute of frying for a crisp, aromatic garnish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and a glass of sulaimani or strong Kerala tea, as sold at roadside tea shops across Malabar.

variations.name: Bihari Masala Pakora
variations.description: A rustic Bihari pakora fried in sharp mustard oil, with garlic, ajwain and a good hit of garam masala for a bold, earthy flavour. The mustard oil gives it a pungent backbone that carries the spice, a proper winter-evening fritter of the Gangetic plains.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: adds a hearty crunch that stands up to the pungent mustard-oil frying

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil heated to smoking, the pungent base flavour of Bihari frying

steps: Slice 2 onions and mix with 5 crushed garlic cloves, 3 chopped green chillies, 0.75 tsp ajwain and 1.25 tsp salt, resting 8 minutes.
Add 1.5 cups besan, 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1.25 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder, tossing to coat.
Bind with 4 to 5 tbsp water into a thick, clinging batter that mounds on the spoon.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, then lower to medium and rest a minute to mellow the sharpness.
Fry rough clusters for 4 to 5 minutes, turning once, until deep golden and crisp with the mustard aroma clinging.
Drain on paper and serve hot, when the garlic and mustard notes are at their most vivid.
tips: Crush the garlic rather than mincing it so it perfumes the batter without burning in the oil.
Heat the mustard oil to smoking first; this removes the raw pungency and any bitterness.
These are excellent stuffed into a chura-dahi plate or eaten with a raw onion and green chilli on the side.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sattu-stuffed litti or plain rice-dal, alongside a raw onion, green chilli and a wedge of lemon for a rustic Bihari spread.

variations.name: Classic Masala Rava Dosa
variations.description: The crisp semolina lace of a rava dosa wrapped around a soft, golden potato masala, uniting shatter and comfort in one plate. Garam masala and coriander powder in the batter lift it beyond the plain version into full tiffin-house indulgence.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: an ancient-wheat swap for maida that keeps the batter crisp under the heavy filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil for both the masala tempering and drizzling the dosa crisp

steps: Boil 4 potatoes until fork-tender, peel and roughly mash them, keeping a few chunks for texture.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin, add 2 sliced onions, 2 slit green chillies and 12 curry leaves, and fry until the onions soften and turn pale gold.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric, then the mashed potato and 1 tsp salt, mash together for 3 minutes until warm and cohesive, and set the masala aside.

Whisk 1 cup semolina, 0.5 cup rice flour, 0.25 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp coriander powder and 0.5 tsp cumin, then thin with 3 cups water to a lacy batter and rest 15 minutes.
Heat a tava on medium-high, grease it with a little Anveshan Groundnut Oil, stir the batter and pour it edge-to-centre in a holey ring, then drizzle 1 tsp oil around it.
Cook for 3 to 4 minutes until deep gold and crisp, spoon 3 tbsp potato masala down the middle, fold over and serve hot.
tips: Cook the masala until it holds together but stays moist; a dry filling makes the folded dosa crack.
Blooming the mustard and cumin in hot oil first is essential, as raw seeds in the filling would taste harsh.
Keep the masala warm in a covered pan so it spreads easily when you fill each freshly poured dosa.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney, a spicy red garlic chutney and a bowl of sambar for dipping the crisp folds.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Masala Rava Dosa
variations.description: The potato filling here is perfumed with dark goda masala and studded with roasted peanuts, a distinctly Maharashtrian twist on the tiffin classic. Earthy, mildly sweet-spiced and hearty, it eats like a Pune breakfast counter special.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: a wholesome swap for maida matching the rustic goda-masala filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the classic Maharashtrian oil for tempering the masala and frying the lace

steps: Pressure-cook 4 potatoes until soft, peel and mash them coarsely, and crush 3 tbsp roasted peanuts to a rough rubble.
Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds, add 2 sliced onions, 2 slit green chillies and 12 curry leaves, and saute until the onions go glassy and soft.
Sprinkle in 0.5 tsp turmeric and 2 tsp goda masala, let them toast for 30 seconds, then fold in the mashed potato, crushed peanuts, 1 tsp salt and 3 tbsp coriander and cook 3 minutes.
Separately whisk 1 cup semolina, 0.5 cup rice flour, 0.25 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta and 0.5 tsp salt with 3 cups water to a thin batter and rest it 15 minutes.
Grease a hot tava with Anveshan Groundnut Oil, stir the batter, and pour it in a lacy ring from the rim inward before drizzling 1 tsp oil around the edge.
Fry for 3 to 4 minutes until crackling gold, lay 3 tbsp of the goda-peanut masala along the centre, fold and lift onto the plate.
tips: Toast the goda masala briefly in the oil before adding potato so its roasted aroma blooms fully.
Keep some peanut pieces coarse for bite; grinding them fine loses the signature Maharashtrian crunch.
If the masala tastes flat, a squeeze of lemon at the end brightens the earthy goda notes.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a fiery green thecha and coconut chutney, and a side of hot filter coffee to complete the Maharashtrian table.

variations.name: Bengali Masala Rava Dosa
variations.description: A Kolkata-leaning masala dosa where the potato filling is tempered in pungent Anveshan Mustard Oil with nigella seeds and green chilli. The batter itself carries a mustard-oil edge, giving the whole dosa an unmistakable Bengali sharpness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: swaps out maida for a heartier grain the Bengali kitchen favours

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked first to soften its bite, then used to fry the aloo and crisp the dosa

steps: Boil 4 potatoes until soft, peel and break them into rough chunks rather than a fine mash.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to first smoke, cool slightly, then splutter 1 tsp nigella seeds, add 2 sliced onions, 3 slit green chillies and 1 tbsp julienned ginger and fry until golden.
Add 0.75 tsp turmeric, the potato chunks and 1 tsp salt, toss for 3 minutes so the aloo takes on the mustard-oil pungency, then finish with 3 tbsp coriander.
Whisk 1 cup semolina, 0.5 cup rice flour, 0.25 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta and 0.5 tsp salt with 3 cups water, stir in 1 tbsp smoked mustard oil, and rest 15 minutes.
Wipe a hot tava with Anveshan Mustard Oil, stir the batter, and pour it edge-to-centre in a lace ring, drizzling 1 tsp oil around the rim.
Cook 3 to 4 minutes to a crackling mahogany crisp, spoon 3 tbsp of the mustard aloo down the middle, fold and serve.
tips: Always heat mustard oil to smoking before use so its raw bitterness cooks off and only the warm pungency stays.
Leaving the potato in chunks rather than mashing keeps the Bengali aloo texture rustic and satisfying.
Nigella scorches quickly, so add it just as the oil settles from its smoke, not while it is still ripping hot.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coconut-coriander chutney and a side of quick-pickled onions in lime to echo the mustard sharpness.

variations.name: Kerala Masala Rava Dosa
variations.description: The Malabar rendition tucks a coconut-oil potato masala fragrant with curry leaves into a coconut-laced dosa. Everything is cooked in Anveshan Coconut Oil, so the whole plate hums with the sweet, nutty aroma of the Kerala coast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: a light whole-grain swap for maida that keeps the coconut dosa crisp

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil for the masala and the tava, layering coconut on coconut

steps: Boil 4 potatoes until tender, peel and mash them lightly, keeping some texture.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds and 15 curry leaves, add 2 sliced onions, 2 slit green chillies and 1 tbsp grated ginger, and fry until the onions soften.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric, the mashed potato and 1 tsp salt, cook 3 minutes, then set the fragrant coconut-oil masala aside.
Whisk 1 cup semolina, 0.5 cup rice flour, 0.25 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta and 0.5 tsp salt with 3 cups water, fold in 0.5 cup grated coconut, and rest 15 minutes.
Grease a hot tava with Anveshan Coconut Oil, stir the batter well, and pour it in a lacy ring from the edge inward, drizzling 1 tsp oil around it.
Cook 3 to 4 minutes to a golden crisp, place 3 tbsp of the potato masala along the centre, fold and serve while the coconut aroma is at its peak.
tips: Fresh coconut in the batter thickens it as it stands, so keep a little warm water handy to loosen the mix.
Coconut oil gives the truest Kerala flavour when it is unrefined and cold-pressed rather than deodorised.
Fry the curry leaves until just crackling, not brown, so they perfume the masala without turning bitter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a roasted coconut chutney and Kerala sambar, and a small banana on the side as they do in Malabar tiffin shops.

variations.name: Andhra Masala Rava Dosa
variations.description: Andhra fires up the masala dosa with a Guntur-chilli potato filling and a til-oil temper, all built on nutty Anveshan Sesame Oil. It is bold, blistering and unapologetically spicy, the way Rayalaseema tiffin stalls serve it.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: an earthy swap for maida that stands up to the bold Guntur spicing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed til oil for the temper and tava, the backbone of Andhra tiffin

steps: Boil 4 potatoes until soft, peel and mash them coarsely, and crush 4 garlic cloves to a paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard and 0.5 tsp cumin, add 2 sliced onions, the crushed garlic and 15 curry leaves, and fry until the onions caramelise at the edges.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp Guntur red chilli powder off direct heat, then add the potato and 1 tsp salt and mash together for 3 minutes into a fiery masala.
Whisk 1 cup semolina, 0.5 cup rice flour, 0.25 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta and 0.5 tsp salt with 3 cups water to a lacy batter and rest 15 minutes.
Season a hot tava with Anveshan Sesame Oil, stir the batter, pour it edge-to-centre in a hole-filled ring, and drizzle 1.5 tsp oil around it.
Fry 3 to 4 minutes until rust-gold and crisp, spoon 3 tbsp of the Guntur masala down the middle, fold and serve blazing hot.
tips: Add the Guntur chilli powder away from full heat so it colours the oil without scorching to bitterness.
Sesame oil deepens as it warms, so temper the seeds gently and let the garlic mellow before the potato goes in.
Serve with plenty of curd; the Guntur heat is intense and the yoghurt keeps it enjoyable.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with gunpowder podi mixed into a little sesame oil for dipping, and a cooling onion raita alongside.

variations.name: Classic Masala Sabudana Vada
variations.description: A fully spiced sabudana vada where garam masala and coriander powder are bloomed into the sago-and-peanut base for a rounded, aromatic warmth. Crisp outside and soft within, this is the everyday masala version that eats well as a snack rather than a plain fasting fritter.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: used to soften the onion and bloom the cumin, garam masala and coriander powder into the mix

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil at 180C that fries the masala vadas crisp without masking the spice

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup sago in just enough water for 5 to 6 hours until soft, then drain thoroughly.
Boil and mash 3 potatoes, and coarsely crush 0.5 cup roasted peanuts.
Soften 1 chopped onion in 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee for 2 minutes, add 1 tsp cumin, then 1.25 tsp garam masala and 1 tsp coriander powder off the heat for 15 seconds.
Combine the drained sago, mashed potato, crushed peanuts, the onion-masala ghee, 3 chopped green chillies, 3 tbsp coriander, 0.5 tsp chaat masala, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 1 tsp salt into a firm dough.
Shape into 12 patties and heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C until a crumb sizzles up briskly.
Fry over medium-high for 3 to 4 minutes per batch, turning, until crisp and deep golden, then drain and serve hot.
tips: Cooking the onion in ghee first removes its raw sharpness so it blends smoothly into the vada.
Bloom the powdered spices off the heat for a few seconds; direct heat scorches garam masala fast.
Since this version has onion, it is not for strict fasting days; keep the classic vada for those.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with green chutney and a sprinkle of chaat masala, or with sweet tamarind chutney for a masala-vada chaat.

variations.name: Punjabi Masala Sabudana Vada
variations.description: A hearty Punjabi-style masala sabudana vada, richer and bolder, finished with a brush of butter and an amchur dusting like a dhaba tikki. Ginger-garlic and a generous garam masala give it a robust, north-Indian flavour quite unlike the delicate Maharashtrian original.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: cooks the ginger-garlic and blooms the garam masala for a rich dhaba-style base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the deep-frying oil that builds a sturdy golden crust for the butter finish

steps: Soak 1 cup rinsed sago in just enough water for 5 to 6 hours until soft, then drain thoroughly.
Boil and mash 3 potatoes, and coarsely crush 0.5 cup roasted peanuts.
Cook 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste in 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee for 1 minute, add 1 tsp cumin, then 1.5 tsp garam masala and 1 tsp coriander powder off the heat for 15 seconds.
Mix the drained sago, mashed potato, crushed peanuts, the ginger-garlic ghee, 2 chopped green chillies, 3 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp salt into a firm dough.
Shape into 12 patties and fry in 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil at 180C over medium-high for 3 to 4 minutes per batch until crisp and golden.
Drain, brush the hot vadas with 1.5 tbsp melted butter and dust with 0.5 tsp amchur, then serve at once.
tips: Cook the ginger-garlic paste until its raw smell goes so it does not turn harsh inside the vada.
Brush butter and dust amchur only after frying so both stay bright and do not scorch.
A little grated boiled potato extra helps bind if the dough feels loose after adding the wet masala.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve dhaba-style with thick garlic chutney and onion rings, or chopped into a quick chaat with curd and chutneys.

variations.name: Hyderabadi Masala Sabudana Vada
variations.description: A fragrant Hyderabadi masala vada perfumed with saffron and a mild spice blend, echoing the aromatics of a royal dum kitchen. Saffron milk and warm garam masala give it a delicate, festive character rather than raw heat, with a golden, aromatic crumb.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk and mixed in for a golden hue and gentle royal perfume

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the cumin and garam masala so the mild aromatics infuse the mix

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the neutral frying oil that lets the saffron and mint aromatics shine through

steps: Soak 1 cup rinsed sago in just enough water for 5 to 6 hours until soft, then drain thoroughly, and steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk.
Boil and mash 3 potatoes, and coarsely crush 0.5 cup roasted peanuts.
Bloom 1 tsp cumin in 1.5 tbsp hot Anveshan Ghee for 15 seconds, then add 1 tsp garam masala off the heat for 10 seconds until fragrant.
Combine the drained sago, mashed potato, crushed peanuts, the ghee-masala, the saffron milk, 3 chopped green chillies, 2 tbsp mint, 2 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp salt into a firm, golden dough.
Shape into 12 patties and heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C.
Fry over medium-high for 3 to 4 minutes per batch, turning, until crisp and pale golden, then drain and serve warm.
tips: Steep the saffron in warm, not boiling, milk to coax out its colour and aroma without dulling it.
Fresh mint is key to the Hyderabadi fragrance here, so add it chopped rather than dried.
Keep the spice mild; this vada is about perfume and subtlety, not chilli heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a mint-yoghurt dip and thin sliced onions, as an elegant starter before a Hyderabadi biryani spread.

variations.name: Tamil Masala Sabudana Vada
variations.description: A South Indian masala vada style, the sago base studded with soaked urad dal, curry leaves and pepper for a masala-vadai crunch, fried in toasty sesame oil. It bridges the North Indian sabudana vada and the Tamil paruppu vadai for a nutty, aromatic bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: crisps the curry leaves and blooms the cumin and pepper for the mix

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed gingelly oil that fries the vadas with a toasty Tamil nallennai aroma

steps: Soak 1 cup rinsed sago in just enough water for 5 to 6 hours until soft, then drain; separately soak 3 tbsp urad dal for 30 minutes, drain and coarsely crush.
Boil and mash 2 potatoes, and coarsely crush 0.33 cup roasted peanuts.
Crisp 20 torn curry leaves in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee for 20 seconds, add 1 tsp cumin and 1 tsp coarse black pepper off the heat for 10 seconds.
Combine the drained sago, mashed potato, crushed peanuts, crushed urad dal, the curry-leaf ghee, 3 chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 2 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp salt into a firm dough.
Shape into 12 patties and heat 3 cups Anveshan Sesame Oil to 175C, gentler as sesame oil browns quickly.
Fry over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes per batch, turning, until crisp and golden, then drain and serve hot.
tips: Soaked, crushed urad dal gives the crunchy, dal-studded texture of a Tamil masala vadai.
Sesame oil has a low smoke point, so hold the flame at medium to keep it from turning bitter.
Use a little less potato here since the urad dal also helps bind the dough.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and filter coffee, or alongside a bowl of rasam for a Tamil tiffin-style snack.

variations.name: Odia Masala Sabudana Vada
variations.description: An Odisha-inflected masala vada tempered with panch phoron, the five-spice blend of cumin, fennel, mustard, fenugreek and nigella that defines eastern Indian cooking. Its layered, seedy aroma gives the familiar sabudana vada a fragrant, gently bitter-sweet complexity.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: used to temper the panch phoron so all five seeds crackle and perfume the mix

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil, the eastern Indian frying fat that suits the panch phoron aromatics

steps: Soak 1 cup rinsed sago in just enough water for 5 to 6 hours until soft, then drain thoroughly.
Boil and mash 3 potatoes, and coarsely crush 0.5 cup roasted peanuts.
Temper 1.25 tsp panch phoron in 1.5 tbsp hot Anveshan Ghee over medium for 20 seconds until all five seeds crackle, then stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder off the heat.
Combine the drained sago, mashed potato, crushed peanuts, the panch phoron ghee, 3 chopped green chillies, 3 tbsp coriander, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 1 tsp salt into a firm dough.
Shape into 12 patties, heat 3 cups Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, then lower to medium.
Fry over medium for 3 to 4 minutes per batch, turning, until crisp and deep golden, then drain and serve hot.
tips: Let all five seeds of the panch phoron crackle before adding the powders, or the fenugreek can taste raw and bitter.
Heat the mustard oil to smoking first to mellow its pungency before frying.
The fenugreek in panch phoron is faintly bitter, so the lemon juice is important to keep the balance.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coconut-mustard chutney or plain green chutney, alongside puffed rice for an Odia evening tiffin.

variations.name: Classic Masala Sattu Cheela
variations.description: A fully spiced roasted-gram pancake where the batter is loaded with garam masala, coriander powder and a fistful of aromatics for a punchy, complete-meal cheela. Cooked in Anveshan wood-pressed groundnut oil and finished with ghee, it is savoury, layered and deeply satisfying.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Roasted-gram sattu forms the protein-rich base that soaks up the masala without going soggy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil crisps the masala cheela cleanly and carries the spices well.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A ghee finish blooms the ground spices and rounds the whole cheela.

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups Anveshan Sattu with 1 tsp salt, 1 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp red chilli powder into a dry mix, then beat in 1.5 cups water gradually to a smooth pouring batter.

Finely chop 1 onion, 1 small tomato, 2 green chillies and 3 tbsp coriander and fold them into the batter along with 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, then rest 10 minutes so the sattu swells and the spices hydrate.
Heat a tava over medium heat until hot and grease it with a few drops of Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil, wiping off the excess.
Ladle on the batter and spread into a 7-inch round, drizzle 0.5 tsp oil around the rim, and cook for 2 to 3 minutes until the underside is a rich golden brown and lifts cleanly.
Flip and cook the second side for about 2 minutes, pressing gently so the tomato and onion inside soften and the centre sets.
Brush the top with Anveshan Ghee, fold, and serve hot; regrease the tava lightly before pouring each fresh cheela.
tips: Squeeze excess juice from the chopped tomato before adding it, or the batter will loosen and the cheela may tear when flipped.
Toast your garam masala for a few seconds in a dry pan before mixing it in for a noticeably deeper aroma.
If the batter thickens between batches, whisk in a tablespoon of water at a time to keep it spreadable.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with garlic-tomato chutney and a side of pickled onions, or roll it around a spoon of curd for a quick handheld meal.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Goda Masala Sattu Cheela
variations.description: A Maharashtrian spin built on fragrant goda masala, the sweet-warm blend of the Deshastha kitchen, giving the roasted-gram cheela a distinctive coconut-and-clove perfume. Cooked in Anveshan wood-pressed groundnut oil and finished with ghee, it is aromatic and gently sweet-spiced.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Sattu's nuttiness complements the roasted-coconut notes of goda masala beautifully.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the everyday Maharashtrian fat and keeps the masala clean and light.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee blooms the goda masala and rounds its warm, sweet spice.

steps: Dry-roast 2 tbsp grated dry coconut in a pan over low heat until pale gold and fragrant, about 2 minutes, then set aside to cool.
Whisk 1.5 cups Anveshan Sattu with 1 tsp salt, 1.5 tsp goda masala, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, then beat in 1.5 cups water to a smooth pouring batter.
Fold the toasted coconut, 1 finely chopped onion, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger and 3 tbsp coriander into the batter and rest 10 minutes.
Heat a tava over medium heat and grease it with a little Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil until it just glistens.
Ladle on the batter and spread into a 7-inch round, drizzle 0.5 tsp oil around the edge, and cook 2 to 3 minutes until the base is golden and the goda masala smells sweet and toasty.
Flip and cook about 2 minutes more, then brush with Anveshan Ghee, fold and serve warm.
tips: Goda masala varies by household; taste your blend and start with 1 tsp if it is a strong, clove-heavy one.
Toasting the dry coconut separately mirrors how goda masala itself is built and layers in extra nuttiness.
This cheela tastes even better with a spoon of freshly grated coconut folded in just before cooking if you have it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coconut-coriander chutney and a bowl of solkadhi for a distinctly Maharashtrian pairing.

variations.name: Bengali Mustard Sattu Cheela
variations.description: A Bengali reinterpretation where the masala batter is sharpened with a kasundi-style mustard kick and a panch-phoron-free simplicity, cooked in Anveshan wood-pressed mustard oil. Pungent, bright and unmistakably eastern in character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Sattu gives a hearty roasted-gram base that carries the pungent mustard well.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Mustard oil is the soul of the Bengali kitchen and drives this cheela's sharp, bright flavour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A ghee finish balances the mustard sharpness with a mellow richness.

steps: Soak and grind 1 tbsp mustard seeds with 1 green chilli and a pinch of salt to a smooth paste, or use ready mustard paste, keeping it fresh so it does not turn bitter.
Whisk 1.5 cups Anveshan Sattu with 1 tsp salt, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp nigella seeds, then beat in 1.5 cups water to a smooth pouring batter.
Fold the mustard paste, 1 finely chopped onion, 2 chopped green chillies and 3 tbsp coriander through the batter and rest 10 minutes.
Heat a tava over medium heat, grease with a little Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil and let it shimmer to mellow the raw pungency.
Ladle on the batter, spread into a 7-inch round, drizzle 0.5 tsp mustard oil around the rim, and cook 2 to 3 minutes until the base is golden and pulls away cleanly.
Flip and cook about 2 minutes more, then brush with Anveshan Ghee, fold and serve immediately while the mustard aroma is sharp.
tips: Grind the mustard paste just before using and add a slit green chilli to the grinder, which keeps it from developing a bitter edge.
Do not overcook the batter side with the mustard paste on high heat, as scorched mustard turns acrid.
A little grated raw mango folded in when it is in season gives a lovely Bengali sweet-sour lift.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a kasundi mustard dip and a plate of jhuri aloo bhaja for a true Bengali breakfast spread.

variations.name: Rajasthani Red Chilli Sattu Cheela
variations.description: A robust Marwari version built around soaked dried red chillies and garlic ground into a rustic red paste, in the spirit of Rajasthan's lal maas heat. Cooked in Anveshan wood-pressed groundnut oil and finished with ghee, it is smoky, garlicky and desert-bold.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Sattu is a Rajasthani staple and its roasted body stands up to the fiery red-chilli paste.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil suits the arid Rajasthani kitchen and carries the smoky chilli cleanly.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee softens the fierce dried-chilli heat and lends a festive richness.

steps: Soak 5 dried red chillies in hot water for 15 minutes, then grind them with 6 garlic cloves to a coarse red paste.
Heat 1 tsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil, crackle 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, add the red-chilli paste and fry for 2 minutes until it darkens and smells smoky, then cool it.

Whisk 1.5 cups Anveshan Sattu with 1 tsp salt, 1 tsp coriander powder and 0.5 tsp turmeric, beat in 1.5 cups water to a smooth pouring batter, then fold in the cooled chilli paste, 1 chopped onion and 3 tbsp coriander and rest 10 minutes.
Heat a tava over medium heat and grease with a little groundnut oil until it shimmers.
Ladle on the batter, spread into a 7-inch round, drizzle 0.5 tsp oil around the edge, and cook 2 to 3 minutes until the base is a deep brick-red and crisp.
Flip and cook about 2 minutes more, brush with Anveshan Ghee, fold and serve hot with the smoky aroma intact.
tips: Use Mathania or Kashmiri dried chillies for colour with moderate heat, or add a couple of hotter chillies if you want it truly fiery.
Frying the chilli-garlic paste before it goes into the batter removes any raw, harsh taste and deepens the smokiness.
A spoon of curd whisked into the batter tames the heat and keeps the cheela soft.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with garlic chutney and a dollop of white butter, alongside a glass of buttermilk to cut the heat.

variations.name: Tamil Curry-Leaf Sattu Cheela
variations.description: A South Indian-styled cheela perfumed with a curry-leaf and urad-dal tempering and a hint of asafoetida, cooked in Anveshan wood-pressed sesame oil for that unmistakable gingelly aroma. Crisp-edged, fragrant and a clever bridge to a Tamil breakfast plate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Sattu gives this a protein boost that a plain rice adai lacks, while staying light.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly sesame oil is the classic Tamil tava fat and gives the cheela its toasty edge.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A ghee finish adds gloss and mellows the sharp sesame note.

steps: Heat 1 tsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil, splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, then fry 1 tsp urad dal, 2 dried red chillies and 3 sprigs curry leaves until the dal turns golden, about 1 minute, and stir in 0.25 tsp asafoetida; cool this temper.
Whisk 1.5 cups Anveshan Sattu with 1 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp turmeric, then beat in 1.5 cups water to a smooth pouring batter.
Fold the cooled temper, 2 chopped green chillies and 1 inch grated ginger into the batter and rest 10 minutes so the curry-leaf aroma infuses.
Heat a tava over medium heat and grease with a little sesame oil until it just smokes faintly.
Ladle on the batter, spread into a 7-inch round, drizzle 0.5 tsp sesame oil around the rim, and cook 2 to 3 minutes until the base is golden and crisp with the dal freckled through.
Flip and cook about 2 minutes more, brush with Anveshan Ghee, fold and serve hot off the tava.
tips: Let the curry leaves crisp fully in the tempering; brittle leaves release far more aroma than limp ones.
A tablespoon of grated coconut in the batter pushes this even closer to a Tamil adai in spirit.
Spread the batter a touch thinner than usual for a crispier, dosa-like cheela that shatters at the edge.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and a small bowl of sambar, with a smear of extra ghee and jaggery for the traditional sweet-savoury bite.

variations.name: Classic Masala Veg Cutlet
variations.description: A fully spiced vegetable cutlet built on a fragrant garam-masala and coriander-powder base, with a little roasted besan folded in for a nutty, bind-tight mash. It is the aromatic, masaledar cutlet that eats as a light meal rather than a plain snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil sautes the masala base and fries a crisp, clean cutlet crust

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli slurry replaces cornflour as the glue that fixes the crumb coat

steps: Boil 2 potatoes and steam 0.75 cup carrot, 0.5 cup beans and 0.5 cup peas until tender, then mash dry.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil, fry 1 chopped onion and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 3 minutes, then stir in 1 tsp garam masala, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp red chilli powder and cook 1 minute until fragrant.
Fold the masala into the mash with 2 tbsp roasted besan and 1 tsp salt, mixing until the besan tightens the mixture.
Bind with 0.5 cup bread crumbs, shape into 10 oval cutlets, dip in a thin 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta slurry and coat in the remaining 1 cup bread crumbs.
Chill the cutlets 15 minutes so the coat sets firmly.
Heat the remaining 4 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat and fry the cutlets 3 to 4 minutes per side until deep golden and crisp, then drain.
Serve hot with green chutney and sweet tamarind chutney.
tips: Roast the besan in a dry pan until it smells nutty before adding, as raw besan tastes bitter and pasty.
Cook the whole spices into the onion base rather than adding them raw, so the cutlet tastes rounded, not sharp.
The besan also helps mop up any residual moisture, keeping the cutlet from splitting in the oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve two cutlets over spiced ragda with onion, chutneys and sev for a filling masala-cutlet chaat plate.

variations.name: Malwa Masala Veg Cutlet
variations.description: An Indori-style cutlet loaded with crushed roasted peanuts and finished with a bright chaat-masala and sev crunch. The ground peanut gives the vegetable mash a rich, nutty body that carries Malwa's busy street-stall masala.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil deepens the peanut character central to Indori street food

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli slurry holds the peanut-heavy mash together for a sturdy, crunchy shell

steps: Boil 2 potatoes and steam 0.5 cup carrot and 0.5 cup peas until tender, then mash dry.
Coarsely crush 0.33 cup roasted peanuts and mix two-thirds into the mash, reserving the rest to garnish.
Add 1 chopped onion, 2 minced green chillies, 1 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt and combine.
Bind with 0.5 cup bread crumbs, shape into 10 oval cutlets, dip in a thin 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta slurry and coat in the remaining 1 cup bread crumbs.
Chill the crumbed cutlets for 15 minutes so the coat sets firmly before frying.
Heat the remaining 4 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat and fry the cutlets 3 to 4 minutes per side until golden and crisp, then drain.
Dust the hot cutlets with 1 tsp chaat masala and scatter the reserved crushed peanuts and sev before serving.
tips: Reserve a third of the peanuts for the garnish so you get both a nutty body and a crunchy top.
Sprinkle the chaat masala only after frying so its tang stays bright and lively.
Keep the peanuts coarsely crushed, never powdered, to hold the Indori texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile the cutlets with chopped onion, tomato, coriander, sev and both chutneys for a loaded Indori-style cutlet chaat.

variations.name: Odia Masala Veg Cutlet
variations.description: An eastern cutlet tempered with panch phoron, whose fennel and nigella notes perfume the vegetable mash from the first bite. A finish of mustard oil and roasted panch phoron powder gives it the earthy, aromatic stamp of Odia street food.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: pungent mustard oil is the everyday Odia frying fat and lifts the panch phoron temper

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli slurry crisps around the seed-tempered mash and keeps the cutlet firm

steps: Boil 2 potatoes and steam 0.5 cup carrot, 0.5 cup beans and 0.5 cup peas until tender, then mash dry.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until it just smokes, cool slightly, then crackle 1 tsp panch phoron for 20 seconds until the seeds pop.
Add 1 chopped onion, 4 crushed garlic cloves and 2 minced green chillies to the tempering and fry 4 minutes until golden, then mix into the mash.
Season with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, then bind with 0.5 cup bread crumbs.
Shape into 10 oval cutlets, dip in a thin 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta slurry, coat in the remaining 1 cup bread crumbs and chill 15 minutes.
Heat the remaining 4 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil over medium heat until mellowed, then fry the cutlets 3 to 4 minutes per side until golden and crisp, and drain.
Serve hot with a raw onion salad, a dust of roasted panch phoron powder and lime.
tips: Never stir raw panch phoron into the mash; the whole seeds must be crackled in hot oil first.
Toast and grind a little extra panch phoron to dust over the cutlets for a stronger finishing aroma.
Cool the tempered onions before mixing so they don't turn the mash sticky and hard to shape.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside ghuguni topped with onion and coriander for a Cuttack-style evening cutlet plate.

variations.name: Gujarati Masala Veg Cutlet
variations.description: A gently sweet-savoury masala cutlet in the Gujarati mould, balancing jaggery, lime and green chilli with a fragrant dhana-jeera spice base. Fresh coriander and methi keep it herby and bright against the mellow sweetness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery powder gives the gentle Gujarati sweetness that balances the lime and chilli

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil is Gujarat's staple frying oil for a crisp, clean cutlet

steps: Boil 2 potatoes and steam 0.5 cup carrot and 0.5 cup peas until tender, then mash dry.
Chop and wilt 0.5 cup fresh methi leaves in 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil for 2 minutes to take off the bitterness, then mix into the mash.

While warm, add 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tbsp lime juice so the jaggery dissolves, then season with 1.5 tsp dhana-jeera powder, 2 tsp green chilli-ginger paste, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt.
Bind with 0.5 cup bread crumbs, shape into 10 round cutlets and coat all over in the remaining 1 cup bread crumbs.
Chill the cutlets 15 minutes so the herby mash firms up.

Heat the remaining 4 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat and fry the cutlets 3 to 4 minutes per side until golden and crisp, watching closely as the jaggery browns them faster, then drain.
Serve warm with a sweet-sour date-tamarind chutney.
tips: Wilt the methi briefly first to mellow its bitterness before it goes into the sweet-savoury mash.
Taste and adjust jaggery, lime and chilli until the sweet-sour-hot balance feels even.
Keep the flame steady at medium since the jaggery makes these colour quickly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a spoon of sweet Gujarati chundo and fresh green chutney for the full khatta-mitha spread.

variations.name: Kerala Masala Veg Cutlet
variations.description: A coconut-and-pepper masala cutlet in the Kerala bakery tradition, the vegetable mash spiced with a garam-masala and black-pepper blend and tempered with curry leaves in coconut oil. Grated coconut keeps it moist and toasty within a crisp crust.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil tempers the aromatics and fries the cutlet, the true Kerala bakery fat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli slurry glues the crumb coat onto the moist, coconut-rich masala mash

steps: Boil 2 potatoes and steam 0.5 cup carrot and 0.5 cup beans until tender, then mash dry.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil, crackle 15 curry leaves, then fry 6 sliced shallots and 1 inch grated ginger for 3 minutes until soft.
Mix the temper into the mash with 0.5 cup grated coconut, 0.75 tsp crushed black pepper, 1 tsp garam masala and 1 tsp salt.
Bind with 0.5 cup bread crumbs, shape into 10 round cutlets, dip in a thin 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta slurry and coat in the remaining 1 cup bread crumbs.
Chill 15 minutes to firm the coconut mash.
Heat the remaining 4 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil over medium heat and fry the cutlets 3 to 4 minutes per side until golden and crisp, taking care as coconut browns fast, then drain.
Serve hot with a coconut-chilli chutney and thin ketchup.
tips: Black pepper is the Kerala signature here alongside garam masala, so crush it fresh for full fragrance.
Fry a shade lighter than usual, as the coconut in the mash catches and darkens quickly.
Squeeze the steamed vegetables dry so the coconut can bind the masala mash firmly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at tea time with strong Kerala chai, or plate alongside kadala curry for a heartier spread.

variations.name: Classic Masala Vegetable Appe
variations.description: A fully spiced version of the South Indian paniyaram, where fermented dosa batter is loaded with vegetables, garam masala and coriander powder for a punchy, North-meets-South dumpling. Cooked in an appe pan with Anveshan wood-pressed groundnut oil and ghee, they are golden, fragrant and satisfying.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil tempers the masala and greases the moulds cleanly for a crisp shell.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A little ghee in each mould blooms the ground spices and deepens the golden base.

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 1 chopped onion and fry 2 minutes until the raw smell goes.

Add 0.33 cup grated carrot, 0.33 cup chopped capsicum, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp garam masala and saute 3 minutes until the vegetables soften and the spices smell toasty; cool completely.
Stir the cooled masala vegetables and 3 tbsp coriander into 2 cups dosa batter with 0.5 tsp salt, keeping the batter thick and dropping.
Fold in 0.5 tsp Eno just before cooking until the batter turns light and bubbly.
Heat an appe pan over medium heat, put a few drops of groundnut oil and Anveshan Ghee in each mould, and spoon batter to three-quarters full.
Cover and cook 3 to 4 minutes until the bottoms are golden, then flip each appe and cook 2 to 3 minutes more until golden and cooked through; serve hot.
tips: Cook the ground spices into the vegetables first rather than adding them raw to the batter, so they bloom and never taste dusty.
Grate the carrot fine and chop the capsicum small so the vegetables set inside the little dumplings without leaving hollows.
Well-fermented, slightly sour batter carries the masala best and gives the fluffiest appe.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a tangy tomato-onion chutney and mint raita, or with tomato ketchup for a kid-friendly evening snack.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Goda Masala Vegetable Appe
variations.description: A Maharashtrian paniyaram perfumed with fragrant goda masala and a hint of roasted coconut, giving the vegetable dumplings a sweet-warm Deshastha character. Cooked in Anveshan wood-pressed groundnut oil and ghee, they are aromatic and comforting.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the everyday Maharashtrian fat and keeps the appe clean and light.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee in the moulds blooms the goda masala and crisps the base.

steps: Dry-roast 2 tbsp grated dry coconut over low heat until pale gold and fragrant, about 2 minutes, and set aside.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, then add 1 chopped onion, 0.33 cup grated carrot and 2 chopped green chillies and saute 3 minutes.
Stir in 1.5 tsp goda masala and the toasted coconut, cook 1 minute until aromatic, then cool the mixture completely.
Fold the cooled mixture and 3 tbsp coriander into 2 cups dosa batter with 0.5 tsp salt, then add 0.5 tsp Eno just before cooking until light and bubbly.
Heat an appe pan over medium heat, put a few drops of groundnut oil and Anveshan Ghee in each mould, and spoon batter to three-quarters full.
Cover and cook 3 to 4 minutes until golden underneath, then flip each appe and cook 2 to 3 minutes more until golden all over; serve hot.
tips: Goda masala strength varies by brand, so start with 1 tsp if yours is clove- and cinnamon-heavy.
Toasting the dry coconut mirrors how goda masala is built and adds a nutty depth to the dumplings.
A spoon of crushed roasted peanuts folded in gives an extra Maharashtrian crunch if you like.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coconut-coriander chutney and a bowl of thin solkadhi for a distinctly Maharashtrian snack.

variations.name: Bengali Mustard Vegetable Appe
variations.description: A Bengali reimagining tempered with panch phoron and a sharp mustard note, cooked in Anveshan wood-pressed mustard oil for a pungent, eastern-Indian character. Fluffy inside with a mustardy bite, these dumplings are an inventive fusion tiffin.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Mustard oil is the soul of Bengali cooking and gives these appe their signature pungency.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A little ghee in each mould softens the mustard sharpness and crisps the base.

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until it just shimmers to mellow its rawness, then splutter 1 tsp panch phoron until the seeds pop.
Add 1 chopped onion, 0.33 cup grated carrot, 2 chopped green chillies and 0.5 tsp turmeric and saute 3 minutes until the vegetables soften; cool it.
Stir the cooled tempering, 1 tbsp fresh mustard paste and 3 tbsp coriander into 2 cups dosa batter with 0.5 tsp salt, keeping the batter thick and dropping.
Fold in 0.5 tsp Eno just before cooking until the batter is light and bubbly.
Heat an appe pan over medium heat, put a few drops of mustard oil and Anveshan Ghee in each mould, and spoon batter to three-quarters full.
Cover and cook 3 to 4 minutes until the bottoms are golden, then flip each appe and cook 2 to 3 minutes more until golden all over; serve hot.
tips: Grind the mustard paste fresh with a slit green chilli to stop it turning bitter.
Heat the mustard oil to shimmering before the tempering to cook off the harsh raw pungency while keeping the bite.
Panch phoron adds a lovely fennel-and-fenugreek fragrance, so do not swap it for plain cumin here.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a kasundi mustard dip and a cooling cucumber raita to balance the pungent mustard.

variations.name: Andhra Guntur Vegetable Appe
variations.description: A fiery Andhra paniyaram spiked with smoky Guntur red chilli and a garlic-heavy sesame temper, cooked in Anveshan wood-pressed sesame oil. Hot, garlicky and golden, these dumplings pack a serious punch for chilli lovers.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly sesame oil is the Andhra base fat and grounds the fierce Guntur chilli.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee in the moulds takes the raw edge off the Guntur heat and crisps the base.

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil, crackle 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, then fry 6 crushed garlic cloves and 2 sprigs curry leaves for 1 minute until golden.
Add 1 chopped onion and 0.33 cup grated carrot, saute 3 minutes, then stir in 1 tsp Guntur red chilli powder off the heat so it blooms without scorching; cool the mixture.
Fold the cooled mixture and 3 tbsp coriander into 2 cups dosa batter with 0.5 tsp salt, keeping the batter thick and dropping.
Add 0.5 tsp Eno just before cooking and fold until light and bubbly.
Heat an appe pan over medium heat, put a few drops of sesame oil and Anveshan Ghee in each mould, and spoon batter to three-quarters full.
Cover and cook 3 to 4 minutes until the bottoms are deep red-gold, then flip each appe and cook 2 to 3 minutes more until cooked through; serve hot.
tips: Guntur chilli is fierce, so scale back to 0.5 tsp if you want warmth rather than a serious burn.
Adding the chilli powder off the heat keeps it from turning black and bitter in the hot oil.
Serve with plenty of cold curd on the side, the classic Andhra way to balance the heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a spicy tomato-garlic chutney and a bowl of plain curd, with extra curry leaves fried in sesame oil on top.

variations.name: Malwa Peanut Vegetable Appe
variations.description: A central-Indian Malwa take that folds crushed roasted peanuts and a mild masala into the vegetable dumplings for a nutty crunch, cooked in Anveshan wood-pressed groundnut oil. Hearty, crunchy and gently spiced, they suit a Malwa tea-time table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil echoes the peanuts and is the natural fat of the Malwa kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee in the moulds binds the nutty flavours and crisps the base.

steps: Coarsely crush 0.33 cup roasted peanuts, keeping a spoonful aside for garnish.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 1 chopped onion, 0.5 cup shredded cabbage and 2 chopped green chillies and saute 3 minutes.
Stir in 0.5 tsp amchur, cook 1 minute, then cool the mixture and fold it with most of the crushed peanuts and 3 tbsp coriander into 2 cups dosa batter with 0.5 tsp salt.
Add 0.5 tsp Eno just before cooking and fold until light and bubbly.
Heat an appe pan over medium heat, put a few drops of groundnut oil and Anveshan Ghee in each mould, and spoon batter to three-quarters full.
Cover and cook 3 to 4 minutes until golden underneath, then flip, scatter the reserved peanuts, and cook 2 to 3 minutes more until golden all over; serve hot.
tips: Keep the peanut crush coarse for a proper crunch; a fine powder melts into the batter and is lost.
The amchur adds a tangy central-Indian brightness that lifts the nutty, mild masala.
Rub the skins off freshly roasted peanuts for a cleaner, sweeter flavour if you have the time.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a garlic-peanut chutney and plain curd, with the reserved crushed peanuts sprinkled over for extra crunch.

variations.name: Classic Roasted Nariyal Barfi
variations.description: This barfi puts the coconut through a proper roast first, toasting the gratings to a golden-brown before the milk goes in, so the finished fudge tastes nutty and caramelised rather than milky-white. The deeper toast gives a firmer, chewier bite and a warm amber colour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the fat that lets the coconut toast evenly to golden-brown

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: balances the toasted coconut without masking its caramel note

steps: Melt 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide pan on medium-low heat, add 3 cups grated coconut and roast steadily for about 8 minutes, stirring, until the gratings turn an even golden-brown and smell toasty.
Pour in 1 cup whole milk and 1 cup Anveshan Khandsari and cook on medium heat for about 12 minutes, stirring, until the milk reduces and the coconut plumps.
Add 0.5 cup milk powder and a pinch of salt and keep cooking for 6 minutes until the mass thickens and pulls from the pan sides.
Stir in 1 tsp cardamom and 12 chopped cashews, cooking one more minute until the fudge holds firm on the spoon.
Press into a greased tray to a 1.5 cm slab, scatter 10 slivered almonds over the top and smooth the amber surface with an oiled spatula.
Cool for 30 minutes until set, then cut into 16 squares that are noticeably chewier and darker than an unroasted coconut barfi.
tips: Roast the coconut on medium-low and stir constantly; it goes from golden to burnt quickly at the edges.
If your coconut is very moist, roast a couple of minutes longer to drive off water before the milk goes in.
The toasted version keeps a little longer than white coconut barfi because the roast reduces moisture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the amber squares with strong filter coffee, whose roast echoes the toasted coconut.

variations.name: Gujarati Roasted Nariyal Barfi
variations.description: A Gujarati toasted kopra pak where golden-roasted coconut meets jaggery for a deep, double-caramel barfi, warmed with nutmeg. The roast and the gud together give it an almost butterscotch character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: toasts the coconut and keeps the jaggery fudge soft

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: layers a molasses caramel over the toasted coconut

steps: Melt 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide pan on medium-low heat and roast 3 cups grated coconut for about 8 minutes until deep golden and toasty.
Add 0.75 cup whole milk and cook on medium heat for about 7 minutes until the coconut absorbs it and softens.
Lower the heat and melt in 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder over about 6 minutes until the mass turns a dark, glossy amber.
Stir in 0.5 cup milk powder, a pinch of salt, 1 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp nutmeg and cook 5 minutes until it thickens and leaves the pan.
Fold in 1 tbsp charoli, press into a greased tray to a 1.5 cm slab and smooth the top while warm.
Cool for 30 minutes until set, then cut into 16 butterscotch-toned squares.
tips: Roast the coconut a shade darker than usual to stand up to the jaggery's own colour.
Add jaggery on low heat so it melts smoothly instead of hardening into threads.
A pinch of flaky salt on top before setting sharpens the butterscotch effect.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside a small cup of unsweetened cutting chai, letting the barfi carry all the sweetness.

variations.name: Kashmiri Roasted Nariyal Barfi
variations.description: Golden-roasted coconut meets saffron and walnuts in this Kashmiri barfi, where the toasty base and the floral saffron play off each other and the walnuts nod to the valley's orchards. Warm amber shot through with saffron gold.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: toasts the coconut and carries the saffron aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: keeps the sweetness clean so saffron and roast both show

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk to streak the toasted coconut with gold

steps: Steep a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 1 cup warm milk for 10 minutes until deeply golden.
Melt 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide pan on medium-low heat and roast 3 cups grated coconut for about 7 minutes until golden-brown and fragrant.
Pour in the saffron milk with 1 cup Anveshan Khandsari and cook on medium heat for about 12 minutes, stirring, until the milk reduces and colour deepens.
Add 0.5 cup milk powder, a pinch of salt and 1 tsp cardamom and cook 5 minutes until the mass thickens and leaves the pan, then fold in 0.33 cup chopped walnuts.
Press into a greased tray to a 1.5 cm slab and smooth the amber-and-gold surface.
Cool for 30 minutes until set, then cut into 16 diamonds flecked with walnut and streaked with saffron.
tips: Toast the walnuts lightly so they stay crisp inside the fudge.
Keep some saffron milk to brush over the top for extra colour against the toasted base.
Bloom saffron in warm rather than boiling milk to keep its aroma sweet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a cold evening with hot noon chai, the salted pink tea whose savoury note frames the sweet.

variations.name: Malwa Roasted Nariyal Barfi
variations.description: The Malwa plateau roasts both coconut and peanuts, then binds them with jaggery for a rugged, deeply toasty barfi with a double crunch. A touch of dried ginger keeps it warming, a true cold-season sweet.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the coconut and binds the peanut-jaggery mass

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the plateau sweetener that unites both roasts

steps: Melt 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide pan on medium-low heat and roast 3 cups grated coconut for about 8 minutes until golden-brown and toasty.
Add 0.5 cup whole milk and cook on medium heat for about 6 minutes until the coconut softens and takes it up.
Lower the heat and melt in 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder over about 6 minutes until it coats the coconut in dark syrup.
Stir in 0.33 cup milk powder, a pinch of salt, 1 tsp cardamom and 0.5 tsp dried ginger, cook 4 minutes until thick, then fold in 0.75 cup crushed roasted peanuts off the heat.
Press firmly into a greased tray to a 2 cm slab so the chunky mixture packs together.
Cool for 30 minutes until firm, then cut into 16 rugged squares crunchy with peanut and toasted coconut.
tips: Roast coconut and peanuts separately so each reaches the right toast without one scorching.
Fold peanuts in off the heat to protect their crunch.
Press the slab hard; this chunky barfi needs firm packing to hold its shape.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pack chunks for a winter trek or Sankranti box, or serve with hot gud-sweetened milk on a cold night.

variations.name: Awadhi Roasted Nariyal Barfi
variations.description: An unusual Awadhi barfi that lightly toasts the coconut for warmth, then veils it in kewra and rose so the toasty and floral notes weave together. Silver vark and a delicate cut keep it courtly despite the roast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: gives a gentle toast while keeping the perfume clean

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: a light sweetness that lets kewra lead over the roast

steps: Melt 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide pan on medium-low heat and lightly roast 3 cups grated coconut for about 5 minutes to a pale gold, stopping before it browns deeply.
Add 1 cup whole milk and 1 cup Anveshan Khandsari and cook on medium heat for about 12 minutes, stirring, until the milk reduces.
Stir in 0.5 cup milk powder, a pinch of salt and 1 tsp cardamom and cook 5 minutes until the mass thickens and leaves the pan.
Take the pan off the heat and stir in 1.5 tsp kewra water and 0.5 tsp rosewater so their fragrance is preserved.
Press into a greased tray to a 1.5 cm slab, scatter 2 tbsp slivered pistachios and lay 1 sheet of silver vark over the surface.
Cool for 30 minutes until set, then cut into 16 delicate squares.
tips: Keep the roast gentle here; a light gold, not deep brown, so the perfume is not overpowered.
Add kewra and rose off the heat, and go easy, as both are potent.
Rest the barfi an hour so the toast and floral notes settle into balance.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a fine plate with a scatter of rose petals after an Awadhi meal, beside cardamom tea.

variations.name: Classic Roasted Peanut Chikki
variations.description: This version starts from raw peanuts roasted fresh in the pan until the skins blister and slip, giving a deeper, warmer nut flavour than pre-roasted peanuts. Folded into hard-crack jaggery caramel, it makes the toastiest possible brittle.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: cooked to hard-crack to lock the freshly roasted peanuts into a crisp sheet

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the board and pin and adds a nutty richness to the caramel

steps: Dry-roast 2 cups raw peanuts in a heavy pan on medium heat for about 8 minutes, stirring, until the skins blister and the nuts smell deeply toasty, then cool briefly and rub off the skins.
Grease a board, rolling pin and spatula with 1 tbsp of the 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and keep the skinned peanuts warm nearby.
Melt 1.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan on medium heat, stirring, until it liquefies and bubbles, about 6 minutes.
Cook to hard-crack, testing that a drop snaps brittle in cold water, about 4 minutes more, then stir in 0.5 tsp cardamom, 0.25 tsp salt and 0.125 tsp baking soda for a lighter texture.
Working fast, tip in the warm roasted peanuts and stir 20 seconds until coated, scatter 2 tbsp toasted sesame seeds over the top, pour onto the greased board and roll to a 5 mm sheet while hot.
Score into 12 pieces while warm, cool 15 minutes until fully hard and snap along the lines into deeply toasty shards.
tips: Roasting raw peanuts fresh gives a far deeper flavour, but let them cool a minute so the skins rub off cleanly.
Keep the roasted nuts warm; a cold nut seizes the caramel before you can roll it.
If bits of skin remain, sieve them out; they can taste bitter in the finished chikki.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the toasty shards with a glass of cold milk as an after-school snack, or crush over kulfi for peanut praline.

variations.name: Kerala Roasted Peanut Chikki
variations.description: Fresh-roasted peanuts meet pan-toasted coconut in this coastal chikki, the caramel finished with coconut oil so the whole brittle smells of the Malabar coast. A double roast, of nut and coconut, gives it real depth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: cooked to hard-crack to set the double-roasted brittle crisp

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: finishes the caramel with the aroma of fresh coconut

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the surfaces for a clean lift

steps: Dry-roast 1.5 cups raw peanuts on medium heat for about 8 minutes until skins blister, cool briefly and rub off the skins, then toast 0.75 cup coconut chips for 3 minutes until pale gold.
Grease a board and pin with the 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and keep the peanuts and coconut warm.
Melt 1.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water and 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a heavy pan on medium heat, stirring, until bubbling, about 6 minutes.
Cook to hard-crack, checking a drop snaps in cold water, about 4 minutes more, then stir in 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp salt.
Working fast, fold in the warm peanuts and toasted coconut, stirring 20 seconds until coated, then pour onto the greased board and roll to a 5 mm sheet while hot.
Score into 12 pieces while warm, cool 15 minutes until crisp and snap apart into coconut-flecked shards.
tips: Roast the peanuts first and the coconut second, since coconut chips scorch far faster.
Keep the caramel a shade light so the coconut oil aroma comes through.
Store airtight, as coconut draws moisture and can soften the chikki in humid weather.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with filter coffee at teatime, or crumble over sliced mango and coconut yoghurt for a coastal dessert.

variations.name: Kashmiri Roasted Peanut Chikki
