variations.description: Freshly roasted peanuts and broken walnuts bound in a saffron-scented caramel, a chikki with the orchard richness and floral aroma of a Kashmiri sweet. The deeper peanut roast stands up beautifully to the walnuts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: cooked to hard-crack to hold the walnut-peanut saffron brittle

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm ghee to gild and scent the caramel

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: carries the saffron and greases the rolling surfaces

steps: Dry-roast 1.5 cups raw peanuts for about 8 minutes until skins blister, cool briefly and rub them off, then crush a pinch of Anveshan Saffron into 1 tbsp warm Anveshan Ghee to bloom.
Grease a board and pin with the second tbsp of ghee and warm the peanuts with 0.5 cup broken walnuts.
Melt 1.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water in a heavy pan on medium heat, stirring, until bubbling, about 6 minutes.
Cook to hard-crack, testing a drop snaps in cold water, about 4 minutes more, then stir in the saffron ghee, 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp salt.
Working fast, fold in the warm peanuts and walnuts, stirring 20 seconds until coated, pour onto the greased board and roll to a 5 mm sheet while hot.
Score into 12 pieces while warm, cool 15 minutes until hard and snap apart; saffron should gleam through the deep amber.
tips: Blooming saffron in warm ghee releases both its colour and aroma into the caramel.
Toast the walnuts a minute in the peanut pan so they are not raw.
Do not overcook the jaggery to very dark, or it will hide the saffron gold.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a wooden board with dried apricots and a pot of kahwa for a Kashmiri winter tea.

variations.name: Rajasthani Roasted Peanut Chikki
variations.description: Fresh-roasted peanuts in a jaggery caramel spiked with roasted red chilli and black salt, the Rajasthani sweet-heat brittle that balances desert warmth against gud sweetness. The deep peanut roast makes the sweet-savoury contrast even bolder.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: cooked to hard-crack to bind the sweet-heat brittle

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the chilli and greases the board and pin

steps: Dry-roast 2 cups raw peanuts for about 8 minutes until skins blister, cool briefly and rub them off, keeping the nuts warm.
Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and bloom 0.5 tsp roasted red chilli powder in it for 20 seconds until fragrant, then grease a board and pin with the second tbsp of ghee.
Melt 1.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water in a heavy pan on medium heat, stirring, until bubbling, about 6 minutes, then cook to hard-crack, about 4 minutes more.
Stir the chilli ghee, 0.5 tsp black salt, 0.5 tsp crushed fennel and 0.5 tsp cardamom into the caramel once it snaps brittle in a cold-water test.
Working fast, tip in the warm peanuts, stir 20 seconds until coated in the spiced caramel, pour onto the greased board and roll to a 5 mm sheet while hot.
Score into 12 pieces while warm, cool 15 minutes until crisp and snap apart; each shard is sweet, deeply nutty, then warming.
tips: Bloom the chilli in ghee so it perfumes the caramel rather than tasting raw and dusty.
Adjust the chilli to your taste; it should warm the throat gently, not scald.
Fennel and black salt make it moreish, so do not skip them for the full Rajasthani effect.
variations.servingSuggestion: Offer as a spicy-sweet teatime nibble with kadak chai, or set out at a Diwali card party for guests to graze.

variations.name: Awadhi Roasted Peanut Chikki
variations.description: Fresh-roasted peanuts folded into a kewra-scented jaggery caramel with slivered pistachios, a fragrant Lucknawi brittle where the deep nut roast is balanced by delicate perfume. Refined enough for a dawat, humble enough for every day.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: cooked to a lighter hard-crack so the kewra note carries

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: rounds the caramel and greases the rolling surfaces

steps: Dry-roast 1.75 cups raw peanuts for about 8 minutes until skins blister, cool briefly and rub them off, keeping the nuts warm.
Grease a board and pin with 1 tbsp of the 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and set the pistachios ready.
Melt 1.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan on medium heat, stirring, until bubbling, about 6 minutes.
Cook just to a light hard-crack, testing a drop snaps in cold water, about 4 minutes more, then take off the heat and stir in 1 tsp kewra water, 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp salt.
Working fast, fold in the warm peanuts and 0.33 cup slivered pistachios, stir 20 seconds until coated, pour onto the greased board and roll to a 5 mm sheet while hot.
Score into 12 pieces while warm, cool 15 minutes until crisp and snap apart along the lines.
tips: Add kewra off the heat so its delicate scent survives into the finished chikki.
Keep the caramel light so the deep peanut roast and the perfume stay in balance.
Slice the pistachios thin so they scatter evenly and look jewel-like in each shard.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve small shards after an Awadhi meal with cups of cardamom tea or chilled rose sherbet.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Adai
variations.description: A fiery take on the Tamil protein crepe, its four-dal batter loaded with green chillies and coarsely crushed black pepper. The peppery heat builds through the nutty lentils for a warming, robust adai that eats like a meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil crisps the spicy batter while the heat stays lively.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee drizzled on top mellows the pepper burn with buttery richness.

steps: Soak the chana, toor, urad and moong dals with 1 cup raw rice for 3 hours, then drain, and coarsely crush 1.5 tsp black pepper in a mortar.
Grind the soaked mix with 5 green chillies and grated 1 inch ginger to a coarse batter, adding water sparingly.
Stir in the crushed pepper, 1.5 tsp salt, 15 curry leaves and 1 chopped onion to a thick batter.
Heat a tava over medium heat, grease with Anveshan Groundnut Oil, and spread a ladle of batter into a thick 7-inch round.
Make a central hole and drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil around it, cooking until deep golden and crisp, about 3 minutes.
Flip and cook the second side until browned through, about 2 minutes, then drizzle with a little Anveshan Ghee.
Serve the spicy adai hot while the pepper aroma is at its peak.
tips: Crush the pepper fresh just before mixing; the coarse cracks give bursts of heat that pre-ground pepper cannot.
The pepper cooks through on the tava, so it loses its raw sting and turns fragrant and warming.
Serve with plenty of cooling chutney rather than reducing the chillies, to keep the character intact.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cold glass of buttermilk and coconut chutney, the dairy pairing that tames the pepper between bites.

variations.name: Andhra Guntur Spicy Adai
variations.description: The hottest adai in the range, its batter fired up with Guntur red chillies and garlic and cooked in gingelly sesame oil. Robust, garlicky and blazing, it is coastal-Andhra spice in its most uncompromising crepe form.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly sesame oil gives the toasty Andhra base and holds up to intense heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing touch of ghee softens the Guntur fire.

steps: Soak the chana, toor and urad dals with 1 cup raw rice for 3 hours, then drain.
Grind the soaked mix with 7 Guntur red chillies, 6 garlic cloves, 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.5 tsp black pepper to a coarse, fiery batter.
Stir in 1.5 tsp salt, 1 chopped onion and 15 curry leaves to a thick batter.
Heat a tava over medium heat, grease with Anveshan Sesame Oil, and spread a ladle of batter into a thick 7-inch round.
Make a central hole and drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil around it, cooking until crisp and deeply red, about 3 minutes.
Flip and cook the second side until browned through, about 2 minutes, then finish with a little Anveshan Ghee.
Serve the Guntur spicy adai blisteringly hot.
tips: Grinding both garlic and chilli into the batter lets them cook through so the heat is deep rather than raw.
Keep chilled buttermilk handy, as it neutralises the capsaicin far better than water.
Deseed a couple of chillies for a more manageable burn while keeping the vivid colour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with curd rice on the side, the traditional Andhra cool-down that lets you enjoy the fire without regret.

variations.name: Kerala Pepper Coconut Spicy Adai
variations.description: A Malabar-style spicy adai where whole-plantation black pepper and coarse coconut meet in the batter, all cooked in coconut oil. The pepper heat is rounded by coconut sweetness for a fragrant, coastal warmth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil rounds the pepper heat with coastal aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A little ghee balances the coconut sweetness against the pepper.

steps: Soak the chana, toor and urad dals with 1 cup raw rice for 3 hours, then drain, and coarsely crush 1.5 tsp black pepper.
Grind the soaked mix with 3 green chillies to a coarse batter, then pulse in 0.5 cup grated coconut so flecks remain.
Stir in the crushed pepper, 1.5 tsp salt, 15 curry leaves and 6 chopped shallots to a thick batter.
Heat a tava over medium heat, grease with Anveshan Coconut Oil, and spread a ladle of batter into a thick 7-inch round.
Make a central hole and drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil around it, cooking until golden and crisp, about 3 minutes.
Flip and cook the second side until browned, about 2 minutes, then finish with a little Anveshan Ghee.
Serve the pepper coconut adai hot and aromatic.
tips: Pepper and coconut is a signature Kerala pairing, so let the pepper stay coarse for the fullest aroma.
Pulse the coconut in last to keep it in flecks rather than making the batter watery.
Warm the coconut oil in hot water if it has solidified before greasing the tava.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coconut chutney and a small bowl of jaggery, letting the sweetness offset the pepper for a true Kerala plate.

variations.name: Assamese Bhut Jolokia Spicy Adai
variations.description: A Northeastern extreme where a trace of the ghost chilli is ground into the lentil batter over pungent mustard oil and fresh herbs. The heat is ferocious but the aroma is fruity and floral, unlike any conventional adai.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Pungent mustard oil is the Assamese base that stands up to the ghost chilli.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing dab of ghee softens the extreme heat with richness.

steps: Soak the chana, toor and urad dals with 1 cup raw rice for 3 hours, then drain, and finely mince a quarter of a deseeded bhut jolokia wearing gloves.
Grind the soaked mix with 2 green chillies and grated 1 inch ginger to a coarse batter.
Stir in the minced ghost chilli very carefully, then add 1.5 tsp salt, 1 chopped onion and 3 tbsp chopped coriander to a thick batter.
Heat a tava over medium heat and grease with Anveshan Mustard Oil that has been heated to smoking once and cooled.
Spread a ladle of batter into a thick 7-inch round, make a central hole and drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil around it, cooking until crisp and golden, about 3 minutes.
Flip and cook the second side until browned, about 2 minutes, then finish with a little Anveshan Ghee.
Serve the ghost-chilli adai hot and with caution.
tips: Bhut jolokia is one of the world's hottest chillies, so use even less than stated and taste before committing more.
Wear gloves throughout, keep away from your eyes, and wash the board and knife immediately.
The fresh coriander lifts the searing heat with a cool, green aroma that is characteristically Assamese.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice and a wedge of lime, the local way to stretch and soothe such intense heat.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Thecha Spicy Adai
variations.description: A rustic Deccan spicy adai smeared with fiery green thecha of pounded chillies, garlic and peanuts, and cooked in groundnut oil. Sharp, garlicky and coarse, it channels the roadside dhaba energy of western Maharashtra.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil roasts the thecha and crisps the adai in true Maharashtrian style.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A little ghee at the finish tempers the aggressive thecha.

steps: Soak the chana, toor and urad dals with 1 cup raw rice for 3 hours, then drain, and dry-roast 3 tbsp peanuts until spotty.
For the thecha, saute 6 green chillies and 8 garlic cloves in 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil until blistered, then pound coarsely with the roasted peanuts, 1 tsp cumin and a pinch of salt.
Grind the soaked dals and rice to a coarse batter and stir in 1.5 tsp salt, 1 chopped onion and 3 tbsp coriander.
Heat a tava over medium heat, grease with Anveshan Groundnut Oil, and spread a ladle of batter into a thick 7-inch round, then smear 1 tbsp thecha across the surface.
Make a central hole and drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil around it, cooking until crisp and golden, about 3 minutes.
Flip and cook the second side until browned through, about 2 minutes, then finish with a little Anveshan Ghee.
Serve the thecha adai hot with extra thecha on the side.
tips: Saute the chillies and garlic before pounding so the thecha tastes roasted and deep rather than raw and harsh.
The coarsely pounded peanuts give the thecha body and crunch, so do not grind it to a smooth paste.
Leftover thecha keeps a week refrigerated and lifts any plain rice, roti or adai.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a spoon of thick curd and raw onion wedges, the classic Maharashtrian foil to fiery thecha.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Aloo Tikki
variations.description: A boldly seasoned tikki that turns up the heat with coarse black pepper, extra red chilli and a green chilli paste worked right through the potato. The crust stays crisp while every bite carries a clean, building warmth rather than one-note spice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: neutral wood-pressed groundnut oil fries a firm crust that holds up to the heavy spicing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli dredge seals in the fiery mix and keeps the tikki from cracking as it fries

steps: Boil 4 medium potatoes until tender, about 15 minutes, then peel and grate them warm for a smooth, lump-free base.

Grind 3 green chillies with 1 inch ginger to a rough paste and beat it into the potato with 1 tsp freshly crushed black pepper, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt.
Fold in 1 finely chopped onion and 3 tbsp coriander, then bind with 0.5 cup bread crumbs until the spiced dough holds a shape.
Divide into 8 discs, dust each in 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, press into the remaining 0.5 cup bread crumbs and chill for 15 minutes.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat until it shimmers and a crumb sizzles at once.
Shallow-fry the tikkis 4 to 5 minutes per side until deep golden and crisp, then drain on paper.
Serve piping hot with cooling mint-yoghurt dip to balance the heat.
tips: Crush the black pepper coarsely just before mixing so its aroma stays sharp and doesn't fade into the potato.
Serve a yoghurt dip alongside rather than sweet chutney, so the tikki reads spicy rather than sweet-hot.
Taste a pinch of the raw mix on your fingertip and adjust chilli before shaping, since frying mutes heat slightly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Split a tikki, stuff it into a toasted bun with sliced onion and a smear of chilli-garlic mayo for a spicy aloo tikki burger.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Aloo Tikki
variations.description: An unapologetically hot tikki powered by Guntur red chillies, whose bright red heat defines Andhra cooking. A garlic-heavy paste and a curry-leaf temper give it a pungent, savoury depth beneath the fire.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil is the everyday Andhra frying fat and carries the Guntur heat cleanly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli coat gives a sturdy shell that holds against the very moist garlic-chilli mix

steps: Boil and mash 4 medium potatoes, then set aside to cool to room temperature.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil, crackle 15 curry leaves and 6 crushed garlic cloves for 1 minute until fragrant but not browned.
Stir the garlic-curry temper into the potato with 2 tsp Guntur red chilli powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for a vivid red, garlicky mix.
Add 1 chopped onion and 2 tbsp coriander, bind with 0.5 cup bread crumbs, then shape into 8 firm discs.
Dust each disc in 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, press into the remaining 0.5 cup bread crumbs and rest 15 minutes.
Heat the remaining 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat and fry the tikkis 4 to 5 minutes each side until fiery red-gold and crisp, then drain.
Serve scorching hot with a cooling onion-tomato pachadi and plenty of curd rice on the side.
tips: Guntur chilli is intense; start with the stated amount and scale up only once you know your tolerance.
Fry the garlic gently in the temper, as burnt garlic turns the whole mix bitter under the heat.
A spoon of curd worked into the mash softens the burn without dulling the Guntur colour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over a mound of curd rice with a smear of Andhra gongura pickle for a full-on Southern spice plate.

variations.name: Kashmiri Spicy Aloo Tikki
variations.description: A saffron-scented tikki where the heat comes from mild, deep-red Kashmiri chilli and warmth from fennel and dry ginger, the backbone of Kashmiri Pandit cooking. Saffron steeped in warm milk turns the potato golden and gently perfumed.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: a pinch of hand-picked Kashmiri saffron bloomed in warm milk colours and perfumes the potato from within

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee frying carries the saffron and fennel aromas the way traditional Kashmiri kitchens intend

steps: Steep a pinch of Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk for 10 minutes until the milk turns deep amber.
Boil and mash 4 medium potatoes, then beat in the saffron milk along with 1.5 tsp Kashmiri red chilli powder, 1 tsp fennel powder, 0.5 tsp dry ginger powder and 1 tsp salt.
Mix in 2 minced green chillies and 2 tbsp coriander, then bind with 0.5 cup bread crumbs into a soft golden dough.
Shape into 8 discs, press each into the remaining 0.5 cup bread crumbs and rest 15 minutes so the saffron colour deepens.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat until it is clear and gently foaming.
Fry the tikkis 4 to 5 minutes each side until pale gold and crisp, basting once with the hot ghee, then drain.
Serve warm with a saffron-yoghurt dip and thin walnut chutney for a Kashmiri touch.
tips: Never boil saffron; a warm-milk steep releases far more colour and aroma than direct heat.
Fennel and dry ginger define this tikki, so keep the chilli mild and let those warm notes lead.
Ghee browns faster than oil, so hold the heat at medium and pull the tikkis at the first deep gold.
variations.servingSuggestion: Arrange on a platter dusted with slivered almonds and a drizzle of saffron yoghurt for a festive Kashmiri high-tea snack.

variations.name: Bengali Spicy Aloo Tikki
variations.description: A mustard-forward chop turned up in heat, with a raw mustard paste and green chillies giving a sinus-clearing sharpness on top of pungent mustard oil. The double dose of mustard makes it distinctly, fiercely Bengali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: kachi ghani mustard oil doubles down on the mustard heat that makes a Bengali chop sing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli slurry helps the crumb shell grip for a crackly, sharp-smelling chop

steps: Boil and mash 4 medium potatoes and let them cool to room temperature.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until it just smokes, cool slightly, then crackle 0.5 tsp nigella seeds and fry 1 chopped onion until golden, about 4 minutes.
Beat the fried onion into the potato with 1.5 tsp mustard paste, 3 minced green chillies, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt for a sharp, pungent mix.
Fold in 2 tbsp coriander, bind with 0.5 cup bread crumbs, then shape into 8 oval chops.
Dip each chop in a thin 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta slurry and roll in the remaining 0.5 cup bread crumbs.
Heat the remaining 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil over medium heat until mellowed, then fry the chops 4 to 5 minutes each side until deep golden and crisp, and drain.
Serve blistering hot with kasundi and raw onion rings for a proper Kolkata footpath feel.
tips: Soak and grind your own mustard for the paste with a pinch of salt to keep it from turning bitter.
The raw mustard paste is what sets this apart from the crispy version, so don't cook it out; add it to the cooled mash.
Balance the sharpness with a tiny pinch of sugar rather than reducing the mustard.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of ghugni (spiced yellow peas) spooned over and a squeeze of lime for a hearty Bengali street plate.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Spicy Aloo Tikki
variations.description: A tikki fired up with kolhapuri-style heat, layering goda masala's roasted depth with a hot red kanda-lasun chilli paste. The result is smoky and searing at once, echoing the fierce misal-belt flavours of western Maharashtra.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil is the classic Maharashtrian frying medium and balances the fiery masala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a touch of jaggery rounds the searing kanda-lasun heat the way Kolhapuri kitchens do

steps: Boil and mash 4 medium potatoes coarsely, leaving a little texture, and cool.
Pound 5 garlic cloves to a rough paste and mix into the potato with 1 tsp goda masala, 1.5 tsp kanda lasun masala, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt.
Stir in 1 finely chopped onion and 2 tbsp coriander, then bind with 0.5 cup bread crumbs into a smoky red dough.
Shape into 8 thick discs, press into the remaining 0.5 cup bread crumbs and rest 15 minutes so the masalas bloom.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat until a crumb sizzles vigorously.
Fry the tikkis 4 to 5 minutes per side until dark red-gold and crisp, then lift onto paper.
Serve fiery hot with beaten curd and a sprinkle of raw onion and coriander.
tips: Kanda lasun masala already carries salt and heat, so taste before adding the full teaspoon of salt.
The jaggery is essential to round the burn; skip it and the tikki tastes harsh rather than deep.
Rest the shaped tikkis so the dry masalas absorb moisture and don't taste raw after frying.
variations.servingSuggestion: Crown a bowl of spicy misal usal with a broken tikki, farsan and onion for a Maharashtrian misal-tikki mashup.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Besan Cheela
variations.description: A deliberately hot gram-flour cheela driven by fresh green chillies and cracked black pepper worked into the batter. Bright, sharp and quick, it is for anyone who finds the plain version too tame.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Wood-Pressed Oil
ingredients.note: Neutral wood-pressed groundnut oil lets the green chilli and pepper heat lead without competing flavours.

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups gram flour with 1.5 cups water into a smooth, lump-free batter of thin-cream consistency.
Stir in 1 tsp freshly cracked black pepper, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt until evenly spiced.
Fold in 4 minced green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 1 finely chopped onion and 3 tbsp coriander, then rest the batter 10 minutes.
Heat a tava over medium heat and grease it with a film of Anveshan Groundnut Wood-Pressed Oil until it shimmers.
Pour a ladle of batter and spread into a thin 7-inch round, drizzle 1 tsp groundnut oil around the rim, and cook until the base is golden and crisp, about 3 minutes.
Flip and cook 2 minutes more until firm and freckled, then fold and serve hot with a cooling accompaniment.
tips: Cracking the pepper fresh gives bursts of heat and a far livelier aroma than fine pre-ground powder.
Mince the green chillies finely so the heat spreads evenly rather than landing in one fiery bite.
Keep whisked curd handy, since the pepper-chilli combination builds a slow, warming heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a thick garlic-curd dip and cucumber sticks to temper the heat, plus a lime wedge for brightness.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Besan Cheela
variations.description: Andhra pushes the gram-flour cheela to its fiery limit with blazing Guntur chilli, heavy garlic and a sesame-oil finish. Searing and unforgettable, it is heat with real depth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Wood-Pressed Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed sesame oil is the backbone Andhra fat and gives the fiery batter a rounded, nutty base.

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups gram flour with 1.5 cups water into a smooth, lump-free batter.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Wood-Pressed Oil until hot, crackle 12 curry leaves and 6 crushed garlic cloves for twenty seconds until fragrant, then cool and stir the tempering into the batter.
Beat in 2 tsp Guntur red chilli powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, fold in 1 chopped onion and 3 tbsp coriander, and rest 10 minutes.
Heat a tava over medium heat and coat it thinly with Anveshan Sesame Wood-Pressed Oil until it shimmers.
Ladle the blazing-red batter and spread into a 7-inch round, drizzle 1 tsp sesame oil around the rim, and cook until the base is deep red-gold and crisp, about 4 minutes.
Flip and cook 2 minutes more until firm and blistered, then fold and serve immediately with a cooling side.
tips: Guntur chilli is extreme; scale back to 1 tsp for a heat most people can enjoy while keeping the vivid colour.
Frying the garlic and curry leaves in sesame oil first builds the authentic Andhra fragrance.
Serve with plenty of set curd, the traditional Andhra counter to a chilli-heavy plate.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a mound of curd rice and raw onion rings to cut through the intense Guntur heat.

variations.name: Rajasthani Spicy Besan Cheela
variations.description: The desert version relies on soaked dried red chillies, ajwain and pungent garlic pounded into the gram-flour batter, then a rich ghee cook. Smoky, robust and rustic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: Rich bilona ghee gives these robust cheela their desert-thali depth and carries the smoky chilli beautifully.

steps: Soak 5 dried red chillies in warm water for 15 minutes until soft, then pound them with 6 garlic cloves into a coarse paste.
Whisk 1.5 cups gram flour with 1.5 cups water into a smooth batter, then beat in the chilli-garlic paste, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt.

Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee, crackle 0.5 tsp ajwain in it for ten seconds until fragrant, cool, and stir the tempering into the batter with 1 chopped onion and 3 tbsp coriander, then rest 10 minutes.
Heat a tava over medium heat and grease it with a little Anveshan Bilona Ghee until it melts into a shimmering film.
Ladle the batter and spread into a slightly thick 6-inch round, spoon 1 tsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee around the rim, and cook until the base is deep golden and crisp, about 4 minutes.
Flip, press with the spatula, and cook 2 minutes more until blistered and cooked through, then serve straight off the tava.
tips: Bloom the ajwain in ghee first, since raw carom seeds in besan batter taste harsh and medicinal.
Soaked whole chillies give a smoky, rounded heat far mellower than raw chilli powder.
Deseed a couple of the chillies for colour and flavour with less ferocity.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a punchy garlic-red chilli chutney and a tall glass of salted chaas to balance the fire, thali style.

variations.name: Bengali Spicy Besan Cheela
variations.description: Here the heat comes wrapped in mustard: pungent wood-pressed mustard oil, green chilli and nigella build a sharp, sinus-clearing gram-flour cheela. Fierce but layered rather than one-note.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Wood-Pressed Oil
ingredients.note: Pungent kachi ghani mustard oil, smoked first, layers its own heat over the green chillies for a sharp Bengali bite.

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups gram flour with 1.5 cups water into a smooth, pourable batter.
Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Wood-Pressed Oil until it just smokes, cool briefly, and whisk it into the batter to soften its pungency while keeping the aroma.

Stir in 0.5 tsp cracked black pepper, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder and 1 tsp salt, fold in 4 minced green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger and 2 chopped spring onions, and rest 10 minutes.
Heat a tava over medium heat, film it with more Anveshan Mustard Wood-Pressed Oil, and scatter a pinch of nigella seeds onto the greased surface to toast.
Pour the batter over the seeds and spread into a thin 7-inch round, drizzle mustard oil around the rim, and cook until the base is deep golden and crisp, about 3 to 4 minutes.
Flip and cook 2 minutes more until cooked through, then fold and serve while the mustard heat is bright.
tips: Smoking the mustard oil before it touches the batter is essential for taming the raw bite while keeping the punch.
Nigella toasts quickly, so add it to the tava only just before the batter goes in.
A squeeze of lime at the table lifts the mustard-and-chilli combination beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling cucumber raita and a spoon of kasundi for those who want even more mustard heat.

variations.name: Kerala Spicy Besan Cheela
variations.description: A coastal firecracker where crushed black pepper, green chilli and curry leaves meet mellow coconut and coconut oil. The coconut sweetness keeps the aggressive pepper heat in check.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil rounds the sharp pepper heat with its sweet Kerala aroma.

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups gram flour with 1.5 cups water into a smooth, pourable batter.
Stir in 1.5 tsp freshly cracked black pepper, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder and 1 tsp salt until evenly spiced.
Fold in 3 tbsp grated coconut, 3 minced green chillies, 4 sliced shallots and 12 chopped curry leaves, then rest the batter 10 minutes to let the coconut hydrate.
Heat a tava over medium heat and grease it with Anveshan Coconut Oil until the surface glistens and smells of coconut.
Ladle the batter and spread into a 7-inch round, drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil around the rim, and cook until the base is golden with toasted coconut, about 3 minutes.
Flip and cook 2 minutes more until set and lightly crisp, then fold and serve hot.
tips: Cracked pepper delivers a cleaner, more fragrant heat here than chilli powder, and it pairs naturally with coconut.
Warm solidified coconut oil gently before greasing so it spreads into an even film.
Toast frozen coconut for a minute to revive its sweetness and stop the batter weeping.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coconut chutney spiked with extra pepper and a small bowl of rasam for a warming coastal breakfast.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Corn Cutlet
variations.description: A pepper-forward corn tikki built for people who find the usual version too mild. Coarsely cracked black pepper and green chilli cut clean through the sweetness of the corn, and a light khapli-atta dust gives a thin, crackly crust when shallow-fried.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: roasted, used both to bind the mix and to dust the tikkis for a thin crisp crust

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for shallow-frying; clean-tasting so the black pepper stays the star

steps: Pulse 1.5 cups of the corn to a coarse crush and keep 0.5 cup whole, combining both in a large bowl.
Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil and saute the onion, green chillies and 1 tbsp grated ginger for 3 minutes until soft, then cool the mixture completely.

Add the mashed potato, sauteed aromatics, chopped coriander, 1.5 tsp cracked black pepper, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt to the corn, then bind with 3 tbsp of the roasted Anveshan Khapli Atta into a firm dough.
Shape 10 tikkis and dust each all over with the remaining 1 tbsp roasted Anveshan Khapli Atta for a light crust.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a wide pan over medium heat and shallow-fry the tikkis for 4 minutes a side until golden and crisp at the edges.
Drain on a rack and crack a little extra black pepper over the top while they are still hot.
tips: Crack the pepper fresh rather than using fine pepper powder; the coarse grind gives bursts of heat and aroma.
Keep the flame at medium so the thin khapli crust crisps without the pepper turning acrid.
If the dough feels loose, rest it 10 minutes so the atta absorbs moisture before shaping.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling hung-curd dip whipped with mint, which soothes the pepper heat between bites.

variations.name: Kerala Nadan Spicy Corn Cutlet
variations.description: A coastal reinvention where fresh grated coconut and a curry-leaf-coconut-oil tempering wrap around the corn, with black pepper and green chilli bringing the Malabar heat. Fried in fragrant Anveshan Coconut Oil, these smell exactly like a Kerala tea-shop at four in the afternoon.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: roasted binder that keeps the coconut-rich mix from falling apart

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: for tempering and shallow-frying, carrying the unmistakable Kerala aroma

steps: Crush 1.5 cups of the corn coarsely and keep 0.5 cup whole, then place both in a bowl.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil and splutter the 15 curry leaves, then fry the sliced shallots, green chillies and 1 tbsp ginger for 4 minutes until the shallots turn golden and sweet; cool the tempering.

Mix the mashed potato, 0.5 cup grated coconut, the coconut-oil tempering, 1.5 tsp cracked black pepper, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt into the corn, then bind with the 4 tbsp roasted Anveshan Khapli Atta into a shapeable dough.
Form 10 round tikkis, pressing them firm so the coconut does not crumble at the edges.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a pan over medium heat and shallow-fry the tikkis 4 minutes a side until deep golden and the coconut caramelises at the rim.
Lift onto paper and serve warm while the coconut-oil fragrance is at its peak.
tips: Use fresh, not desiccated, coconut; desiccated draws moisture and makes the mix dry and crumbly.
Shallots (kunjulli) give a sweeter, more authentic base than regular onion here.
Fry gently, as coconut oil browns the coconut quickly and can taste burnt on high heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a spoon of coconut chutney and a small cup of strong Kerala chai or sulaimani for a true nadan snack spread.

variations.name: Rajasthani Laal Spicy Corn Cutlet
variations.description: Inspired by the fiery red palette of Marwari cooking, whole dried red chillies are bloomed and coarsely pounded into the corn for a smoky, brick-red heat. A garlic-heavy tempering and a pinch of amchur give it the punchy, tangy edge of a Rajasthani snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: roasted binder suited to the arid, robust Marwari spicing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for blooming the chillies and shallow-frying to a crisp finish

steps: Coarsely crush 1.5 cups corn, reserve 0.5 cup whole, and set both aside in a bowl.

Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil and fry the 4 dried red chillies for 30 seconds until they darken and smell smoky, then add the onion and 1.5 tbsp garlic and cook 4 minutes until deep golden; cool, then pound the softened chillies into a coarse paste with the masala.

Fold the mashed potato, the smoky chilli-garlic paste, 1 tsp cracked black pepper, 1 tsp amchur, chopped coriander, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt through the corn, then bind with the 4 tbsp roasted Anveshan Khapli Atta into a firm dough.
Shape 10 tikkis, pressing them tight so the coarse chilli bits stay embedded.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat and shallow-fry the tikkis 4 minutes a side until a deep brick-red crust forms.
Rest on a rack and scatter a few fried curry leaves or extra amchur over the top for tang.
tips: Deseed the dried chillies for colour and smokiness without pushing the heat too far.
The amchur is what gives that classic Rajasthani sweet-sour bite, so add it generously.
Pound the bloomed chillies coarse, not to a smooth paste, for rustic texture and visible flecks.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside garlic-red-chilli chutney and a glass of chaas, the way these would appear on a Jodhpur snack platter.

variations.name: Gujarati Gud Spicy Corn Cutlet
variations.description: Gujarat's signature sweet-hot-tangy balance runs through this tikki, where Anveshan Jaggery Powder rounds off the black-pepper heat and a squeeze of lemon keeps it lively. Soft, faintly sweet within and crisp outside, it is the corn cutlet reimagined as farsan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted into the mix for the signature Gujarati sweet-spicy balance in place of sugar

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: roasted binder that keeps the soft, jaggery-sweetened mix intact

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday Gujarati frying fat, for a light golden shallow-fry

steps: Crush 1.5 cups of the corn coarsely and keep 0.5 cup whole, then combine both in a bowl.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil and saute the onion with 1.5 tbsp green chilli-ginger paste for 3 minutes until soft and aromatic, then cool.

Stir the mashed potato, sauteed paste, 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 tsp cracked black pepper, 1 tbsp lemon juice, chopped coriander, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt into the corn until the jaggery dissolves evenly, then bind with the 4 tbsp roasted Anveshan Khapli Atta into a soft dough.
Shape 10 slightly flattened tikkis, wetting your palms lightly so the sticky sweet mix does not cling.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat and shallow-fry the tikkis 4 minutes a side until evenly golden; watch closely as the jaggery browns faster.
Drain on paper and finish with a final squeeze of lemon for that bright Gujarati lift.
tips: Dissolve the jaggery powder fully into the warm mix so you get balanced sweetness, not sugary pockets.
Because jaggery caramelises fast, keep the heat at medium and turn the tikkis gently.
A pinch of sesame in the dough adds a farsan-style crunch that suits the sweet-savoury profile.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with chunda (sweet mango pickle) and thin sev sprinkled on top for a proper Gujarati farsan plate.

variations.name: Kashmiri Kesar Spicy Corn Cutlet
variations.description: An aromatic, gently regal take scented with Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron, ground fennel and dry ginger, the warm masalas of a Wazwan kitchen. Fried in pungent mustard oil as Kashmir prefers, the tikkis glow faintly golden and taste of pepper, fennel and that unmistakable saffron perfume.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in 1 tbsp warm milk to release colour and the signature Kashmiri aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: roasted binder that carries the delicate saffron mix without masking it

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked first, the traditional Kashmiri cooking fat that deepens the warm masalas

steps: Steep the 20 strands of Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 1 tbsp warm milk for 10 minutes until it turns deep amber.
Coarsely crush 1.5 cups corn and keep 0.5 cup whole, then combine both in a bowl.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the flame and fry the onion for 4 minutes until golden, then stir in the 1 tsp fennel powder, 0.5 tsp dry ginger and 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder for 30 seconds and cool.

Mix the mashed potato, the warm-spiced onion, the saffron milk, 1 tsp cracked black pepper, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt into the corn, then bind with the 4 tbsp roasted Anveshan Khapli Atta into a firm dough.
Shape 10 neat tikkis and let them rest 10 minutes so the saffron colour spreads through the mix.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil over medium heat and shallow-fry the tikkis 4 minutes a side until pale gold and fragrant, then drain.
tips: Steep saffron in warm milk, never boiling liquid, to draw out colour and aroma without dulling it.
Fennel and dry ginger are the backbone of Kashmiri warmth, so grind them fresh if you can.
Keep the chilli Kashmiri (mild, red) rather than hot so the saffron stays the hero note.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a saffron-flecked yogurt dip and a pot of noon chai or kahwa for an elegant Kashmiri-inspired platter.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Hara Bhara Kebab
variations.description: A bolder green kebab where coarsely cracked black pepper and extra green chilli push through the sweetness of spinach and peas. Bound with roasted khapli atta and shallow-fried, it stays vivid green inside with a peppery, savoury bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: roasted, binds the mix and dusts the kebabs for a thin crisp shell

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for shallow-frying; clean-tasting so the black pepper stays forward

steps: Blanch the spinach 1 minute, plunge into ice water to hold the colour, then squeeze completely dry and chop fine.
Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil and saute the green chillies and 1 tbsp ginger for 1 minute, add the spinach and cook 3 minutes until the moisture dries off, then cool.

Combine the dry spinach, mashed peas, mashed potato, 1.5 tsp cracked black pepper, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp chaat masala and 1 tsp salt, then bind with 3 tbsp of the roasted Anveshan Khapli Atta into a firm mixture.
Shape 10 patties and dust each with the remaining 1 tbsp roasted Anveshan Khapli Atta for a light crust.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a wide pan over medium heat and shallow-fry the kebabs 3 minutes a side until golden and crisp at the edges.
Drain on a rack and crack a little more black pepper over the top while hot.
tips: Crack the pepper fresh and coarse for bursts of heat rather than an even background warmth.
Squeeze the spinach bone-dry so the peppery kebabs hold together and crisp well.
Rest the mix 10 minutes so the khapli atta absorbs moisture before shaping.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling mint-curd dip that offsets the black-pepper heat.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Goda Spicy Hara Bhara Kebab
variations.description: The green kebab meets the smoky, faintly sweet warmth of goda masala with its roasted coconut and dagad phool notes. Crushed peanuts add crunch and a curry-leaf tempering perfumes the spinach for a distinctly Maharashtrian bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: roasted binder that complements the earthy goda masala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for the curry-leaf tempering and shallow-frying, the Maharashtrian staple oil

steps: Blanch the spinach 1 minute, shock in ice water, squeeze dry and chop fine.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil, splutter the 12 curry leaves and green chillies, add the spinach and cook 3 minutes until dry, then stir in the 1.5 tsp goda masala off the heat and cool.
Mix the spiced spinach, mashed peas, mashed potato, 3 tbsp crushed peanuts, 1 tsp cracked black pepper and 1 tsp salt, then bind with 3 tbsp of the roasted Anveshan Khapli Atta into a firm mixture.
Shape 10 patties and dust each with the remaining 1 tbsp roasted Anveshan Khapli Atta.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat and shallow-fry the kebabs 3 minutes a side until golden with the peanuts toasted inside.
Drain on a rack so the crushed peanuts stay crunchy against the soft green centre.
tips: Add goda masala off a fierce flame, as it scorches and turns bitter in seconds.
Crush the peanuts coarse for pockets of crunch through the soft kebab.
The mix can be made a day ahead; the goda masala deepens overnight.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with fiery thecha and lime, alongside kokum sharbat, for a Maharashtrian snack spread.

variations.name: Kerala Nadan Spicy Hara Bhara Kebab
variations.description: A coastal green kebab where fresh grated coconut and a shallot-curry-leaf tempering in coconut oil meet spinach and peas. Black pepper brings the Malabar warmth, and the whole thing smells of a Kerala tea-shop afternoon.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: roasted binder that holds the coconut-rich green mix together

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: for the tempering and shallow-frying, carrying the coastal Kerala aroma

steps: Blanch the spinach 1 minute, shock in ice water, squeeze dry and chop fine.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil, splutter the 15 curry leaves, fry the shallots and green chillies for 3 minutes until golden, add the spinach and cook 2 minutes until dry, then cool.
Mix the spinach tempering, mashed peas, mashed potato, 0.5 cup grated coconut, 1.5 tsp cracked black pepper and 1 tsp salt, then bind with the 4 tbsp roasted Anveshan Khapli Atta into a firm mixture.
Shape 10 round patties, pressing firm so the coconut holds at the edges.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil over medium heat and shallow-fry the kebabs 3-4 minutes a side until golden and the coconut caramelises at the rim.
Serve warm while the coconut-oil fragrance is at its peak.
tips: Use fresh coconut, not desiccated, so the kebabs stay moist and do not crumble.
Fry gently, as coconut on the surface browns fast on high heat.
Shallots give a sweeter, more authentic Kerala base than regular onion.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with coconut chutney and a cup of strong sulaimani chai for a nadan snack spread.

variations.name: Rajasthani Laal Spicy Hara Bhara Kebab
variations.description: A desert-bold green kebab bloomed with whole dried red chillies for a smoky, brick-red heat, sharpened with garlic and amchur. The spinach sweetness barely holds back the fierce Marwari fire.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: roasted binder suited to the robust, arid Marwari spicing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for blooming the chillies and shallow-frying to a crisp finish

steps: Blanch the spinach 1 minute, shock in ice water, squeeze bone-dry and chop fine.

Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil, fry the 4 dried red chillies for 30 seconds until smoky-dark, add the 1.5 tbsp garlic and cook 1 minute, then add the spinach and cook 3 minutes until dry; cool and pound the chillies coarsely into the mix.

Combine the smoky spinach, mashed peas, mashed potato, 1 tsp amchur, 1 tsp cracked black pepper, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, then bind with the 4 tbsp roasted Anveshan Khapli Atta into a firm mixture.
Shape 10 patties, packing them tight so the coarse chilli flecks stay embedded.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat and shallow-fry the kebabs 3-4 minutes a side until a deep brick-red crust forms.
Drain on a rack and scatter a little extra amchur over the top for tang.
tips: Deseed the dried chillies for a deep red colour without runaway heat.
Pound the bloomed chillies coarse for rustic, visible smoky flecks.
Amchur gives the classic Rajasthani sweet-sour edge, so use it generously.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with garlic-red-chilli chutney and cool chaas to offset the desert heat.

variations.name: Haryanvi Ghee Spicy Hara Bhara Kebab
variations.description: Rustic and hearty, this green kebab is cooked entirely in nutty Anveshan Ghee, which lends a deep, almost tandoori richness. Black pepper, green chilli and kasuri methi keep it bold and homely in true Haryanvi style.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: roasted binder that suits the rich, ghee-cooked kebab

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: cooks the spinach and shallow-fries the kebabs for a deep, rustic Haryanvi richness

steps: Blanch the spinach 1 minute, shock in ice water, squeeze dry and chop fine.

Melt 2 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee and fry the green chillies and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, add the spinach and cook 3 minutes until dry, then stir in the 1 tsp garam masala and 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi off the heat and cool.
Mix the ghee-cooked spinach, mashed peas, mashed potato, 1.5 tsp cracked black pepper and 1 tsp salt, then bind with the 4 tbsp roasted Anveshan Khapli Atta into a firm mixture.
Shape 10 thick, rustic patties, patting them a little uneven for a homely look.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee on a tava over medium heat and shallow-fry the kebabs 3-4 minutes a side until richly browned, spooning ghee at the edges.
Baste the tops with a final touch of ghee and serve hot.
tips: Cook on steady medium heat; ghee browns faster than oil and can darken the crust too quickly.
Rub kasuri methi warm between your palms to release its aroma into the ghee.
A final ghee baste before serving deepens the rustic richness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with white butter, onion rings and a glass of lassi for a hearty Haryanvi plate.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Masala Dosa
variations.description: A dosa for heat-seekers, its potato filling loaded with slit green chillies and a bold hit of freshly crushed black pepper. The peppery warmth builds slowly while the crisp crust and cooling chutney keep it moreish rather than punishing.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: High-smoke-point groundnut oil crisps the dosa while the filling stays fiery.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee tempers the pepper burn with a mellow, buttery finish.

steps: Boil 4 medium potatoes until soft, peel and crush them coarsely, and coarsely crush 1 tsp black pepper in a mortar so the heat stays lively.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds with 12 curry leaves, 5 slit green chillies and julienned 1 inch ginger for 30 seconds.
Add 1 sliced onion and cook until soft, about 4 minutes, then stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric and the crushed pepper.
Fold in the potatoes and 1.5 tsp salt with a splash of water and cook 3 minutes until the pepper aroma perfumes the masala.
Heat the tava, wipe it, and spread a thin dosa in an outward spiral.
Drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and brush a little Anveshan Ghee at the edges, cooking until deep golden and crisp, about 2 minutes.
Fill with 3 tbsp spicy potato masala, fold and serve hot.
tips: Crush the pepper fresh just before cooking; pre-ground pepper loses its punch and gives only a flat heat.
Balance the burn by serving with a generous, cooling coconut chutney rather than reducing the chillies.
For an even hotter version, leave the green chilli seeds in; to soften it, scrape them out before slicing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with an ice-cold glass of buttermilk and coconut chutney, letting the dairy tame the pepper between bites.

variations.name: Andhra Guntur Spicy Masala Dosa
variations.description: The spiciest dosa of them all, built on searing Guntur red chillies pounded into the filling and a finish of nutty sesame oil. This is coastal-Andhra heat in its purest, most gingelly-scented form.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil holds up to the high heat this fiery filling demands.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly sesame oil drizzled at the end gives the toasty Andhra signature.

steps: Boil 4 medium potatoes, peel and crush them, and grind 7 Guntur red chillies with 6 garlic cloves and a pinch of salt into a coarse red paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds with 12 curry leaves for 20 seconds.
Add 1 sliced onion and cook until soft, about 4 minutes, then stir in the chilli-garlic paste, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp crushed black pepper and fry 2 minutes until the raw smell lifts.
Fold in the crushed potatoes and 1.5 tsp salt with a splash of water and simmer 3 minutes until fiery and glossy.
Heat the tava, wipe it, and spread a thin dosa.
Drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and a little Anveshan Groundnut Oil at the edges, cooking until crisp and red-flecked, about 2 minutes.
Fill with 3 tbsp Guntur potato masala, fold and serve blisteringly hot.
tips: Fry the chilli-garlic paste thoroughly until it stops smelling raw, or the filling will taste harsh rather than deep.
Keep a glass of chilled buttermilk within reach; it neutralises capsaicin far better than water.
Deseed a couple of the Guntur chillies to dial the heat back a notch while keeping the colour and flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain curd rice on the side, the traditional Andhra antidote that lets you enjoy the fire without regret.

variations.name: Rajasthani Lal Mirch Spicy Masala Dosa
variations.description: Inspired by the crimson laal maas of Marwar, this dosa uses a smoky dried-red-chilli paste for colour and controlled heat, cooked in ghee for a desert-rich finish. It is fiery yet rounded, with a deep red hue that stains the crust.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee is central to Rajasthani cooking and carries the red-chilli richness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A little groundnut oil raises the smoke point so the ghee-rich dosa can crisp without burning.

steps: Boil 4 medium potatoes, peel and crush them, and soak 6 dried red chillies in warm water for 15 minutes, then grind with 6 garlic cloves into a smooth red paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and splutter 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 sliced onion and cook until golden, about 5 minutes, then stir in the red-chilli paste, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp coriander powder and fry 2 minutes until the ghee separates at the edges.
Fold in the crushed potatoes and 1.5 tsp salt with a splash of water and simmer 3 minutes until deep red and unctuous.
Heat the tava, wipe it, and spread a thin dosa.
Drizzle a mix of 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and Anveshan Groundnut Oil at the edges and cook until crisp and rust-coloured, about 2 minutes.
Fill with 3 tbsp laal potato masala, fold and serve hot.
tips: Use Kashmiri or Mathania dried chillies for a vivid red colour with moderate heat, adding a hotter variety only if you want real fire.
Frying the chilli paste until the ghee separates is what removes the raw edge and builds the laal maas depth.
This rich filling is best served fresh and hot, as the ghee firms up when it cools.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling mint-yoghurt dip and thin onion rings dressed in lime, a Rajasthani-thali touch that cuts the richness.

variations.name: Assamese Bhut Jolokia Spicy Masala Dosa
variations.description: A Northeastern dare, this dosa laces the filling with a mere trace of the ghost chilli, bhut jolokia, layered over mustard oil and fresh herbs. The heat is extreme but the aroma is fruity and floral, unlike any other spicy dosa.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Pungent mustard oil is the Assamese base that stands up to the ghost chilli.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing dab of ghee softens the extreme heat with richness.

steps: Boil 4 medium potatoes, peel and crush them, and finely mince just a quarter of a deseeded bhut jolokia, handling it with gloves.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it smokes, cool slightly, then crackle 2 slit green chillies with julienned 1 inch ginger for 30 seconds.
Add 1 sliced onion and cook until soft, about 5 minutes, then stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric and the minced ghost chilli very carefully.
Fold in the crushed potatoes and 1.5 tsp salt with a splash of water, cook 3 minutes, then stir through 3 tbsp chopped coriander leaves off the heat.
Heat the tava, wipe it, and spread a thin dosa.
Drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and a little Anveshan Ghee at the edges, cooking until crisp and golden, about 2 minutes.
Fill with 3 tbsp fiery potato masala, fold and serve hot with caution.
tips: Bhut jolokia is one of the world's hottest chillies, so start with an even smaller amount than stated and taste before adding more.
Wear gloves while handling the chilli and never touch your eyes; wash the board and knife immediately after.
The fresh coriander added at the end lifts the heat with a cool, green aroma that is very Assamese.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of plain steamed rice and a wedge of lime, the local way to stretch and soothe such intense heat.

variations.name: Kolhapuri Spicy Masala Dosa
variations.description: Channeling the notorious fire of Kolhapur, this dosa filling is spiked with a home-ground kanda-lasun tarri masala and finished in groundnut oil. Smoky, garlicky and relentlessly hot, it is western Maharashtra on a crepe.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil roasts the Kolhapuri masala and crisps the dosa without masking the spice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A little ghee at the finish rounds the aggressive garlic and chilli.

steps: Boil 4 medium potatoes, peel and crush them, and dry-roast 5 dried red chillies, 2 tbsp dry coconut and 1 tsp coriander seeds until the coconut turns golden.
Grind the roasted mix with 8 garlic cloves into a coarse, dark Kolhapuri masala.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and fry 1 sliced onion until deep golden, about 6 minutes, then stir in the ground masala and 0.5 tsp turmeric and cook 2 minutes.
Fold in the crushed potatoes and 1.5 tsp salt with a splash of water and simmer 3 minutes until smoky and rich.
Heat the tava, wipe it, and spread a thin dosa.
Drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and a little Anveshan Ghee at the edges, cooking until crisp and dark-flecked, about 2 minutes.
Fill with 3 tbsp Kolhapuri potato masala, fold and serve hot.
tips: Roasting the dry coconut until golden is what gives Kolhapuri masala its characteristic smoky depth, so do not rush it.
The ground masala keeps a fortnight refrigerated and turns any potato sabzi into a Kolhapuri feast.
If it is too hot for the table, stir a spoon of thick curd into the filling to mellow it without losing flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of thin, spicy tarri on the side for dunking and a raw onion wedge, true to Kolhapuri custom.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Moong Dal Cheela
variations.description: A deliberately fiery cheela driven by fresh green chillies and cracked black pepper worked right into the batter. It is bright, sharp and built for anyone who thinks the standard version needs more punch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Wood-Pressed Oil
ingredients.note: Neutral wood-pressed groundnut oil lets the green chilli and pepper heat lead without competing flavours.

steps: Soak 1 cup split green gram for 3 hours until soft, drain, and grind with 4 green chillies, 1 inch ginger and about 0.75 cup water into a smooth, thick batter.
Stir in 1 tsp freshly cracked black pepper, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt until evenly spiced.
Fold in 1 finely chopped onion and 3 tbsp coriander, then rest the batter for 15 minutes to mellow the raw chilli edge slightly.
Heat a tava over medium heat and grease it with a film of Anveshan Groundnut Wood-Pressed Oil until it shimmers evenly.
Pour a ladle of batter and spread into a 7-inch round, drizzle 1 tsp groundnut oil around the rim, and cook until the base is golden and crisp, about 3 minutes.
Flip and cook the second side for 2 minutes until firm and freckled, then fold and serve hot with something cooling alongside.
tips: Cracking the pepper fresh rather than using fine powder gives bursts of heat and a far livelier aroma.
Resting the batter tames the sharpest raw-chilli bite; grind the chillies coarsely if you like visible green flecks.
Keep a bowl of curd handy, since the pepper-chilli combination builds a slow, warming heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a thick garlic-curd dip and cucumber sticks to temper the heat, plus a lime wedge for brightness.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Moong Dal Cheela
variations.description: Andhra turns up the fire with searing Guntur red chilli and a garlic-heavy batter finished in nutty sesame oil. This is one of the hottest cheela on the map, and gloriously so.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Wood-Pressed Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed sesame oil is the backbone Andhra fat and gives the fiery batter a rounded, nutty base.

steps: Soak 1 cup split green gram for 3 hours, drain, and grind with 6 garlic cloves and about 0.75 cup water into a smooth, thick batter.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Wood-Pressed Oil until hot, crackle 12 curry leaves for ten seconds, cool, and stir the tempering into the batter.
Beat in 2 tsp Guntur red chilli powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, then fold in 1 chopped onion and 3 tbsp coriander and rest 15 minutes.
Heat a tava over medium heat and coat it thinly with Anveshan Sesame Wood-Pressed Oil until it shimmers.
Ladle the blazing-red batter and spread into a 7-inch round, drizzle 1 tsp sesame oil around the edge, and cook until the base is deep red-gold and crisp, about 4 minutes.
Flip and cook 2 minutes more until firm and blistered, then fold and serve immediately with a cooling accompaniment.
tips: Guntur chilli is extreme; scale back to 1 tsp for a heat level most people can enjoy while keeping the vivid colour.
Frying the curry leaves in sesame oil first is what gives the batter its authentic Andhra fragrance.
Serve with plenty of set curd, the traditional Andhra counter to a chilli-heavy plate.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a mound of thick curd rice on the side and raw onion rings to cut through the intense Guntur heat.

variations.name: Rajasthani Spicy Moong Dal Cheela
variations.description: The desert version relies on soaked dried red chillies and pungent raw garlic pounded into the batter, then a rich ghee cook. Smoky, robust and rustic, it is built to be torn and dunked.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: Rich bilona ghee gives these robust cheela their desert-thali depth and carries the smoky chilli beautifully.

steps: Soak 1 cup split green gram together with 5 dried red chillies for 3 hours until both soften, then drain and keep the plumped chillies.
Grind the dal with the soaked chillies, 6 garlic cloves and about 0.75 cup water into a smooth, brick-red batter flecked with chilli skins.
Stir in 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, fold in 1 chopped onion and 3 tbsp coriander, and rest 15 minutes.
Heat a tava over medium heat and grease it with a little Anveshan Bilona Ghee until it melts into a shimmering film.
Ladle the batter and spread into a slightly thick 6-inch round, spoon 1 tsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee around the rim, and cook until the base is deep golden and crisp, about 4 minutes.
Flip, press with the spatula, and cook 2 minutes more until blistered and cooked through, then serve straight off the tava.
tips: Soaking the whole dried chillies with the dal draws out a smoky, mellow heat far rounder than raw chilli powder.
Deseed a couple of the chillies if you want the colour and flavour with less ferocity.
Cook these a touch thicker so they hold up to being dunked in a robust chutney.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a punchy lehsun (garlic) chutney and a tall glass of salted chaas to balance the fire, thali style.

variations.name: Bengali Spicy Moong Dal Cheela
variations.description: Here the heat comes wrapped in mustard: pungent wood-pressed mustard oil, green chilli and a scatter of nigella build a sharp, sinus-clearing cheela. It is fierce but layered, not one-note.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Wood-Pressed Oil
ingredients.note: Pungent kachi ghani mustard oil, smoked first, layers its own heat over the green chillies for a sharp Bengali bite.

steps: Soak 1 cup split green gram for 3 hours, drain, and grind with 4 green chillies and 1 inch ginger plus about 0.75 cup water into a smooth batter.
Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Wood-Pressed Oil until it just smokes, cool briefly, and whisk it into the batter to soften its pungency while keeping the aroma.
Mix in 0.5 tsp cracked black pepper, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder and 1 tsp salt, fold in 2 chopped spring onions, and rest 15 minutes.
Heat a tava over medium heat, film it with more Anveshan Mustard Wood-Pressed Oil, and scatter a pinch of nigella seeds onto the greased surface to toast.
Pour the batter over the seeds and spread into a thin 7-inch round, drizzle mustard oil around the rim, and cook until the base is deep golden and crisp, about 3 to 4 minutes.
Flip and cook 2 minutes more until cooked through, then fold and serve while the mustard heat is bright.
tips: Smoking the mustard oil before it touches the batter is non-negotiable for taming the raw bite while keeping the punch.
Nigella toasts quickly, so add it to the tava only just before the batter goes in.
A squeeze of lime at the table lifts the mustard-and-chilli combination beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of cooling cucumber raita and a spoon of kasundi for those who want even more mustard heat.

variations.name: Kerala Spicy Moong Dal Cheela
variations.description: A coastal firecracker where crushed black pepper, green chilli and curry leaves meet mellow coconut and coconut oil. The sweetness of coconut keeps the aggressive pepper heat from overwhelming the palate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil rounds the sharp pepper heat with its sweet Kerala aroma.

steps: Soak 1 cup split green gram for 3 hours, drain, and grind with 3 green chillies and about 0.75 cup water into a smooth batter.
Pulse in 3 tbsp grated coconut, then stir in 1.5 tsp freshly cracked black pepper, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder and 1 tsp salt.
Fold in 4 sliced shallots and 12 chopped curry leaves, then rest the batter for 15 minutes to let the coconut hydrate and the flavours settle.
Heat a tava over medium heat and grease it with Anveshan Coconut Oil until the surface glistens and smells of coconut.
Ladle the batter and spread into a 7-inch round, drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil around the edge, and cook until the base is golden with toasted coconut, about 3 minutes.
Flip and cook 2 minutes more until set and lightly crisp, then fold and serve hot.
tips: Cracked pepper delivers a cleaner, more fragrant heat here than red chilli powder, and it pairs naturally with coconut.
Warm solidified coconut oil gently before greasing so it spreads into an even film.
Toast the coconut for a minute if frozen to revive its sweetness and stop the batter weeping.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coconut chutney spiked with extra pepper and a small bowl of rasam for a warming coastal breakfast.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Onion Uttapam
variations.description: A fiery take on the soft onion uttapam, loaded with green chilli, crushed pepper and a sharp ginger note. The thick, spongy batter carries the heat gently while the golden onion crust delivers it in every bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil for cooking that crisps the spicy onion crust cleanly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee dotted on to finish, rounding off the pepper heat with richness

steps: Stir 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tsp cumin and 1.5 tsp coarsely crushed peppercorns into 2.5 cups fermented dosa batter, loosening with water to a thick, spreadable mix.
Finely chop 2 onions, 4 green chillies and 1.5 tbsp ginger, and toss them with 12 chopped curry leaves and 3 tbsp coriander for the topping.
Heat a tava on medium and grease it with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil wiped across until it shimmers.
Pour a ladle of batter and spread it into a thick 5-inch round, keeping the centre spongy rather than thin.
Press a generous handful of the chilli-onion topping into the surface, drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil around the edge, cover and cook 3 minutes.
Flip and cook the topping side 2 minutes until the onions char lightly, dot with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Ghee, and serve hot.
tips: Crush the pepper coarse and fresh so it gives warm bursts rather than an even dusty heat.
Press the chillies and onions in firmly so they cook into the batter and do not scatter on the flip.
A finishing dot of ghee balances the pepper burn and adds a lovely aroma to each uttapam.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling coconut-curd chutney and a bowl of rasam to sip alongside the heat.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Onion Uttapam
variations.description: Andhra takes the spice to its limit with a Guntur-chilli and garlic onion topping over a pepper-spiked batter, all cooked in nutty Anveshan Sesame Oil. This is a tiffin for true chilli lovers, blistering and deeply aromatic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed til oil, the Andhra staple, deepening the garlic and Guntur heat

steps: Stir 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tsp cumin and 1 tsp coarsely crushed pepper into 2.5 cups fermented dosa batter, loosening with water to a thick, spreadable mix.
Finely chop 2 onions and mince 5 garlic cloves, then toss them with 2 tsp Guntur red chilli powder, 15 chopped curry leaves and 3 tbsp coriander.
Heat a tava on medium and season it with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil rubbed across the surface.
Pour a ladle of batter and spread it into a thick 5-inch round, keeping the centre soft and spongy.
Press a handful of the fiery onion-garlic topping into the surface, drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil around the edge, cover and cook 3 minutes.
Flip and cook the topping side 2 minutes until the garlic crisps and the onions char, then serve blazing hot.
tips: Toss the Guntur chilli into the raw onions so it clings and softens as the uttapam cooks.
Mince the garlic finely so it crisps on the flip rather than staying pungent and raw.
Keep thick curd on the table; this uttapam is built to be seriously hot.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling cucumber-onion raita and a spoon of gunpowder podi in sesame oil for the brave.

variations.name: Bengali Spicy Onion Uttapam
variations.description: Bengal layers its pungent Anveshan Mustard Oil and a nigella crackle over a green-chilli onion topping, adding sinus-clearing sharpness to the heat. The mustard bite and pepper together give this uttapam a fierce Kolkata character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked to first wisp so its sharp heat mellows into the classic Bengali kick

steps: Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to first smoke, cool slightly, and stir 1 tbsp of it into 2.5 cups fermented dosa batter with 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tsp crushed pepper and 1 tsp nigella seeds.
Finely chop 2 onions, 5 green chillies and 1.5 tbsp ginger and mix them with 3 tbsp coriander for the topping.
Heat a tava on medium and wipe it with a few drops of the smoked mustard oil until it glistens.
Pour a ladle of batter and spread it into a thick 5-inch round, keeping the centre soft.
Press a handful of the chilli-onion topping into the surface, drizzle 1 tsp mustard oil around the edge, cover and cook 3 minutes.
Flip and cook the topping side 2 minutes until the onions catch a smoky colour, then serve hot.
tips: Smoke the mustard oil fully before it touches the batter, or the uttapam turns bitter and raw-tasting.
Leave the chillies whole-chopped rather than deseeded for the full Bengali kaancha lanka heat.
Nigella scorches fast, so keep the tava at a steady medium between uttapams.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coriander-green chilli chutney and a wedge of lime, with crisp aloo bhaja on the side.

variations.name: Rajasthani Spicy Onion Uttapam
variations.description: Rajasthan brings smoky dried red chillies and a garlic temper to the spicy uttapam, bloomed first in Anveshan Groundnut Oil so the heat is roasted and round. It carries the bold, sun-baked character of a desert kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil used to bloom the dried chillies and crisp the uttapam

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and bloom 4 broken dried red chillies with 5 crushed garlic cloves and 1 tsp cumin until the chillies darken and smell smoky, about 1 minute.
Cool the tempering slightly, then stir it into 2.5 cups fermented dosa batter with 0.5 tsp salt and 0.75 tsp crushed pepper, loosening to a thick, spreadable mix.
Finely chop 2 onions and mix with 10 chopped curry leaves and 3 tbsp coriander for the topping.
Heat a tava on medium and grease it with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil until it just shimmers.
Spread a ladle of the chilli batter into a thick 5-inch round, press a handful of the onion topping in, drizzle 1 tsp oil around the edge, cover and cook 3 minutes.
Flip and cook the topping side 2 minutes until the onions colour, then serve hot with extra coriander.
tips: Blooming the whole chillies first gives a smoky roasted heat rather than the raw bite of chilli powder.
Shake some seeds from the dried chillies if you want the flavour without the fiercest heat.
Let the tempering cool a little before it hits the batter so it does not start cooking the mix unevenly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a garlic-tomato chutney and a bowl of plain curd, with chopped raw onion on the side.

variations.name: Kerala Spicy Onion Uttapam
variations.description: Kerala balances the heat with sweet coconut, folding fresh gratings and crushed pepper into a curry-leaf onion topping cooked in Anveshan Coconut Oil. Malabar black pepper and coconut make a warm, fragrant heat rather than a sharp one.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil for cooking that softens the pepper heat with its aroma

steps: Stir 0.5 tsp salt and 1.5 tsp coarsely crushed peppercorns into 2.5 cups fermented dosa batter, loosening with water to a thick, spreadable mix.
Finely chop 2 onions, 3 green chillies and 1 tbsp ginger, then combine with 0.33 cup grated coconut, 18 chopped curry leaves and 3 tbsp coriander.
Heat a tava on medium and grease it with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil wiped across until it shines.
Pour a ladle of batter and spread it into a thick 5-inch round, keeping the centre spongy.
Press a generous handful of the coconut-pepper topping into the surface, drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil around the edge, cover and cook 3 minutes.
Flip and cook the topping side 2 minutes until the coconut toasts golden, then serve warm.
tips: Coconut mellows the pepper, so this eats warm and fragrant rather than sharply hot.
Use fresh coconut so it toasts sweet on the flip; desiccated turns dry and dusty.
Keep the coconut oil gently warm for easy greasing, as it sets solid when it cools.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a roasted coconut chutney and a light drumstick sambar for a coastal breakfast.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Pakora
variations.description: A fiery version of the onion pakora built for chilli lovers, where coarsely crushed black pepper and extra green chilli cut through the besan for a proper nose-tingling heat. Crisp on the outside and packed with pepper warmth inside, it is the fritter you reach for with a cold evening and a strong cup of tea.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: sharpens the crunch so the crust holds up against the juicy, heavily spiced onion

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: high-smoke-point wood-pressed oil that fries the peppery batter crisp without dulling the heat

steps: Slice 2 onions, finely chop 4 green chillies and grate 1 inch ginger, mixing with 3 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt, then rest 10 minutes until wet and glossy.
Add 1.5 cups besan, 0.25 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1.5 tsp coarse black pepper, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, tossing to coat.
Bind with only 4 to 5 tbsp water into a thick, clinging batter, keeping it stiff so the fritters stay open and crisp under all that spice.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C until a scrap of batter surfaces briskly in about 4 seconds.
Drop in ragged clusters and fry over medium-high for 4 to 5 minutes, turning, until deep golden and crackling.
Drain on a rack, crack over a little more black pepper while hot, and serve at once for the sharpest bite.
tips: Crush the peppercorns coarsely just before mixing so you get pockets of aromatic heat rather than flat, dusty spice.
Balance the fire with a cooling mint-yoghurt dip rather than reducing the chilli, which keeps the fritters lively.
A final crack of pepper on the hot pakoras hits the nose far more than pepper hidden in the batter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling mint-yoghurt raita, sliced onions and lemon, and plenty of hot chai to chase the pepper heat.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Pakora
variations.description: A blistering Andhra-style pakora coloured deep red by Guntur chilli, which brings a searing, smoky heat quite unlike ordinary chilli powder. Curry leaves and a whisper of garlic go into the batter, making a fritter that is unapologetically hot and fragrant.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: steadies the fiery batter with a firm crunch that carries the Guntur chilli heat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the frying oil, with a spoon used to crisp the curry leaves that flavour the batter

steps: Fry 15 curry leaves in 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil for 20 seconds until crisp, then crush them coarsely to release their aroma into the batter.
Slice 2 onions and mix with 3 chopped green chillies, 4 crushed garlic cloves, 2 tbsp coriander, the crushed curry leaves and 1.25 tsp salt, resting 8 minutes.
Add 1.5 cups besan, 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, 2 tsp Guntur red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, tossing to a bright red coating.
Bind with 4 to 5 tbsp water into a thick batter, then heat the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C until a drop sizzles up in 4 seconds.
Fry rough clusters over medium-high for 4 to 5 minutes, turning once, until crisp and darkened to a deep brick red.
