tips: Add goda masala off a fierce flame, as it scorches and turns bitter in seconds.
Crush the peanuts coarse for pockets of crunch through the soft kebab.
The mix can be made a day ahead; the goda masala deepens overnight.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with fiery thecha and lime, alongside kokum sharbat, for a Maharashtrian snack spread.

variations.name: Classic Tava Pakora
variations.description: A lighter, low-oil take on the pakora, where the spiced besan-and-onion mix is shaped into flat tikkis and shallow-fried on a hot tava instead of deep-fried. You get crisp, golden edges and a soft, well-seasoned centre with a fraction of the oil, perfect for an everyday snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: binds the tikki mix and crisps the edges beautifully on the dry tava

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: drizzled around the tikkis on the tava so they shallow-fry crisp with far less oil than deep-frying

steps: Slice 2 onions, chop 3 green chillies and grate 1 inch ginger, mixing with 3 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt, then rest 10 minutes until the onions weep.

Add 1.5 cups besan, 0.25 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp ajwain, 1 tbsp white sesame seeds, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder, mixing to a thick dough with only 2 to 3 tbsp water.
Divide the mix and press into flat tikkis about 2 inches wide and half an inch thick so they cook through on the griddle.
Heat a flat tava on medium, drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil per tikki, and lay them on to cook for 3 to 4 minutes until the underside is set and golden.
Flip carefully, drizzle a little more oil around the edges and press down gently, cooking another 3 to 4 minutes until both sides are crisp and deep golden.
Transfer to a plate and serve hot, the edges shatter-crisp and the centre soft and spiced.
tips: Keep the mix stiff, almost like a dough, so the tikkis hold their shape on the tava instead of spreading.
Press the tikkis thin and even for a higher crisp-to-soft ratio and quicker, uniform cooking.
A well-seasoned cast-iron tava needs less oil and gives a better crust than a non-stick pan.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with mint-coriander chutney and a cup of masala chai, or tuck a tikki into a pav with chutney for a lighter vada-pav style bite.

variations.name: Haryanvi Tava Pakora
variations.description: A ghee-fried tava pakora in the hearty Haryanvi style, where the tikkis are shallow-fried in generous desi ghee for a rich, roasted aroma and a golden, almost paratha-like crust. Ajwain and green chilli keep it rustic and warming, the way it is made in village kitchens.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the tikkis are shallow-fried in bilona ghee for a nutty, roasted richness unique to Haryanvi cooking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: a handful worked into the mix gives the ghee-fried tikkis a sturdy, wheaty bite

steps: Slice 2 onions and mix with 3 chopped green chillies, 0.75 tsp ajwain, 3 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt, resting 8 minutes until softened.
Add 1.5 cups besan, 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder, mixing to a stiff dough with 2 to 3 tbsp water.
Shape into thick tikkis about 2 inches wide so they stay juicy inside while the ghee crisps the outside.
Heat a tava on medium and melt 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, lay on the tikkis and cook 3 to 4 minutes until the base is golden and set.
Flip, add another spoon of Anveshan Ghee around each tikki and press gently, cooking 3 to 4 minutes more until both sides are deep golden and crisp.
Lift off and serve piping hot, when the ghee aroma is at its most fragrant.
tips: Do not rush the flame; medium heat lets the ghee roast the tikkis slowly for that signature aroma.
Spoon a little extra ghee around the edges as they cook so the sides crisp as well as the faces.
These stay good for a few hours and reheat well on the tava with a touch more ghee.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with white butter (safed makkhan) and a jaggery piece on the side, or with garlic chutney and buttermilk for a full Haryanvi snack.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Tava Pakora
variations.description: A tava-fried kanda bhaji tikki carrying the dark, aromatic warmth of goda masala, shallow-fried for a lighter finish than the deep-fried original. Rice flour keeps the edges brittle-crisp while the centre stays soft and heavily spiced.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: drizzled on the tava to shallow-fry the goda-spiced tikkis crisp with minimal oil

steps: Slice 3 onions and mix with 3 chopped green chillies, 3 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt, resting 10 minutes until juicy.
Add 1.25 cups besan, 0.5 cup rice flour, 1.5 tsp goda masala, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder, mixing to a stiff mass with 2 to 3 tbsp water.
Press into flat tikkis about half an inch thick so the rice-flour crust can crisp evenly on the griddle.
Heat a tava on medium, drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil per tikki, and cook 3 to 4 minutes until the base is crisp and golden.
Flip, drizzle more oil around the edges and press gently, cooking 3 to 4 minutes more until both faces are brittle and deep golden.
Serve hot with a final pinch of goda masala dusted over, when the clove-and-cinnamon aroma is strongest.
tips: The rice flour is essential here for the glassy Maharashtrian crunch, even on a tava, so keep the ratio high.
Warm the goda masala briefly in a dry pan first to release its layered aroma before mixing.
Serve with dry garlic-peanut chutney to echo the classic kanda-bhaji-and-chutney pairing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with dry lasun-khobra chutney and cutting chai, or slip a tikki into a pav with green chutney for a lighter bhaji-pav.

variations.name: Gujarati Tava Pakora
variations.description: A soft, sweet-savoury tava pakora in the Gujarati mould, the tikkis flecked with jaggery and lemon and shallow-fried until the edges caramelise gently. Lighter than deep-fried bhajiya, it has a lovely balance of sweet, tang and warm spice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: kneaded into the tikki mix for the gentle Gujarati sweetness that caramelises on the tava

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: drizzled on the tava so the sweetened tikkis shallow-fry to a caramelised, crisp edge

steps: Slice 2 onions and mix with 3 chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 1 tbsp lemon juice, 3 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt, resting 8 minutes.
Add 1.5 cups besan, 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder, mixing to a stiff dough with 2 to 3 tbsp water.
Shape into flat tikkis about half an inch thick so the sweet edges can catch and caramelise.
Heat a tava on medium, drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil per tikki, and cook 3 to 4 minutes until the base is golden with darkened edges.
Flip gently, add a little oil around the edges and cook 3 to 4 minutes more until both sides are crisp and caramelised without burning.
Serve warm, when the sweet-tart-spice balance is at its most rounded.
tips: Keep the flame at medium; the jaggery caramelises fast and will scorch on a fierce tava.
Dissolve the jaggery into the lemon and onion moisture first so it spreads evenly through the mix.
A pinch of baking soda makes these tikkis softer and fluffier if you like a more cake-like centre.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sweet-and-spicy chhundo or a green chutney and hot masala chai, Gujarati tea-time style.

variations.name: Tamil Tava Pakora
variations.description: A South Indian tava pakora scented with crackled curry leaves and pepper, shallow-fried in sesame oil (nallennai) for a distinctly Tamil aroma. The tikkis are studded with curry leaves and a little urad dal for a nutty crunch reminiscent of a masala vadai.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed gingelly oil drizzled on the tava for the toasty Tamil nallennai aroma

steps: Soak 2 tbsp urad dal in water for 20 minutes, then drain and coarsely crush for a nutty bite in the tikkis.
Slice 2 onions and mix with 20 torn curry leaves, 3 chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 2 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt, resting 8 minutes.
Add 1.5 cups besan, the crushed urad dal, 1 tsp coarse black pepper, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder, mixing to a stiff dough with 2 to 3 tbsp water.
Shape into flat tikkis and heat a tava on medium, drizzling 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil per tikki.
Cook 3 to 4 minutes per side, drizzling a little more oil around the edges and pressing gently, until both faces are crisp and deep golden.
Serve hot, when the sesame oil and curry-leaf aroma are at their most fragrant.
tips: Soaked, crushed urad dal gives these tikkis the crunchy, dal-studded texture of a masala vadai.
Sesame oil has a low smoke point, so keep the tava on medium to avoid a bitter, burnt note.
Tear the curry leaves rather than leaving them whole so their aroma releases into every bite.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and filter coffee, or alongside a bowl of rasam for a comforting South Indian evening snack.

variations.name: Classic Tava Sabudana Vada
variations.description: A lighter, low-oil sabudana vada shaped into thin tikkis and shallow-fried on a hot tava instead of deep-frying. You still get crisp golden faces and a soft, peanut-studded centre, but with a fraction of the oil, making it a guilt-free fasting-day snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: used to bloom the cumin and crisp the curry leaves, since the tikkis are not deep-fried

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: drizzled around the tikkis on the tava to shallow-fry them crisp with minimal oil

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup sago in just enough water for 5 to 6 hours until soft and squashable, then drain thoroughly.
Boil and mash 3 potatoes, and coarsely crush 0.5 cup roasted peanuts.

Bloom 1 tsp cumin seeds and 10 curry leaves in 1 tbsp hot Anveshan Ghee for 15 seconds, then combine with the sago, potato, peanuts, 3 chopped green chillies, 3 tbsp coriander, 0.5 tsp chaat masala, 0.5 tsp amchur, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 1 tsp rock salt into a firm dough.
Shape into 12 flat tikkis about half an inch thick so they cook through evenly on the griddle.
Heat a tava on medium, drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil per tikki, and cook 4 to 5 minutes until the base is crisp and golden.
Flip, drizzle a little more oil around the edges and press gently, cooking 4 to 5 minutes more until both faces are crisp and deep golden, then serve hot.
tips: Press the tikkis thin and even so the centre cooks through before the faces over-brown.
A well-seasoned cast-iron tava needs less oil and gives a crisper crust than non-stick.
Drain the soaked sago really well, or the tikkis will steam and stick instead of crisping.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with cooling peanut-curd chutney or a green chutney, ideal for a lighter Navratri fasting snack.

variations.name: Haryanvi Tava Sabudana Vada
variations.description: A ghee-rich tava sabudana vada in the hearty Haryanvi manner, the tikkis shallow-fried in generous desi ghee for a nutty, roasted crust almost like a paratha. Simple, warming and rustic, it leans on good ghee and green chilli rather than a complex spice mix.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the tikkis are shallow-fried in bilona ghee for a roasted, paratha-like crust and rich aroma

steps: Soak 1 cup rinsed sago in just enough water for 5 to 6 hours until soft, then drain thoroughly.
Boil and mash 3 potatoes, and coarsely crush 0.5 cup roasted peanuts.

Bloom 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.75 tsp ajwain in 1 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee for 15 seconds, then combine with the sago, potato, peanuts, 3 chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 1 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi, 3 tbsp coriander, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 1 tsp rock salt into a firm dough.
Shape into 12 thick tikkis so they stay soft inside while the ghee crisps the outside.
Heat a tava on medium and melt 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, lay on the tikkis and cook 4 to 5 minutes until the base is golden.
Flip, add another spoon of Anveshan Ghee around each tikki and press gently, cooking 4 to 5 minutes more until both faces are deep golden and crisp, then serve piping hot.
tips: Keep the flame at medium so the ghee slowly roasts the tikkis for that signature nutty aroma.
Spoon a little extra ghee around the edges as they cook so the sides crisp along with the faces.
These reheat well on the tava with a touch more ghee if made ahead.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with white butter (safed makkhan) and a green chutney, or with sweetened curd for a rich Haryanvi fasting snack.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Tava Sabudana Vada
variations.description: A tava-fried Pune-style sabudana tikki warmed with a hint of goda masala and a heavy hand of crushed peanuts. Shallow-frying keeps it lighter than the deep-fried vada while the goda masala lends its clove-and-cinnamon depth to the soft, nutty centre.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the cumin and warms the goda masala so it perfumes the tikki mix

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: drizzled on the tava to shallow-fry the goda-spiced tikkis crisp with little oil

steps: Soak 1 cup rinsed sago in just enough water for 5 to 6 hours until soft, then drain thoroughly.
Boil and mash 3 potatoes, and coarsely crush 0.75 cup roasted peanuts for a pronounced crunch.
Bloom 1 tsp cumin in 1.5 tbsp hot Anveshan Ghee for 15 seconds, then stir in 1 tsp goda masala off the heat for 10 seconds until fragrant.

Combine the sago, potato, peanuts, the ghee-masala, 1 tbsp white sesame seeds, 0.5 tsp sugar, 3 chopped green chillies, 3 tbsp coriander, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 1 tsp salt into a firm dough and shape into 12 flat tikkis.
Heat a tava on medium, drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil per tikki, and cook 4 to 5 minutes until the base is crisp and golden.
Flip, drizzle more oil around the edges and press gently, cooking 4 to 5 minutes more until both faces are crisp, then serve hot with a final pinch of goda masala.
tips: Add the goda masala off the heat so it warms without scorching and turning bitter.
The extra peanuts give this tikki its Maharashtrian crunch, so crush them coarse.
If the dough feels loose from the lemon juice, mash in a spoon of extra crushed peanuts to firm it up.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with dry roasted-peanut chutney (danyachi chutney) and hot chai, Pune tapri style.

variations.name: Kerala Tava Sabudana Vada
variations.description: A Malabar-style tava sabudana tikki flecked with fresh coconut and crackled curry leaves, shallow-fried in fragrant coconut oil. The coconut and curry-leaf aroma with a warm pepper heat gives this griddled vada a distinctly South Indian, tea-shop character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: crisps the curry leaves and blooms the cumin and pepper for the mix

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: drizzled on the tava to shallow-fry the tikkis with the sweet Malabar coconut aroma

steps: Soak 1 cup rinsed sago in just enough water for 5 to 6 hours until soft, then drain thoroughly.
Boil and mash 3 potatoes, and coarsely crush 0.33 cup roasted peanuts.
Crisp 20 torn curry leaves in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee for 20 seconds, add 1 tsp cumin and 1 tsp coarse black pepper off the heat for 10 seconds.
Combine the sago, potato, peanuts, 0.5 cup grated coconut, the curry-leaf ghee, 3 chopped green chillies, 2 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp salt into a firm dough and shape into 12 tikkis.
Heat a tava on medium, drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil per tikki, and cook 4 to 5 minutes until the base is golden.
Flip, drizzle a little more coconut oil around the edges and cook 4 to 5 minutes more until both faces are crisp and coconut-fragrant, then serve hot.
tips: Use fresh grated coconut for moisture and sweetness; desiccated turns dry and gritty on the tava.
The coconut adds moisture, so drain the sago extra well to keep the dough firm enough to shape.
Keep the flame at medium as coconut oil browns and smokes faster than other oils.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and a glass of sulaimani tea, as at a Malabar roadside tea shop.

variations.name: Gujarati Tava Sabudana Vada
variations.description: A soft, sweet-savoury Gujarati farali tikki, the sago base kissed with jaggery and lemon and shallow-fried on the tava until the edges caramelise gently. Lighter than the deep-fried vada, it carries the region's beloved balance of sweet, tang and mild spice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: mashed into the mix for the signature Gujarati sweetness that caramelises on the tava

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the cumin so its warmth balances the jaggery in the mix

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: drizzled on the tava so the sweetened tikkis shallow-fry to a caramelised, crisp edge

steps: Soak 1 cup rinsed sago in just enough water for 5 to 6 hours until soft, then drain thoroughly.
Boil and mash 3 potatoes, and coarsely crush 0.5 cup roasted peanuts.
Bloom 1 tsp cumin in 1 tbsp hot Anveshan Ghee for 15 seconds, then mash 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 1 tbsp lemon juice until dissolved.

Combine the sago, potato, peanuts, the ghee-cumin, the jaggery-lemon paste, 3 chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 1 tbsp raisins, 3 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp rock salt into a firm dough and shape into 12 tikkis.
Heat a tava on medium, drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil per tikki, and cook 4 to 5 minutes until the base is golden with darkened edges.
Flip gently, add a little oil around the edges and cook 4 to 5 minutes more until both sides are crisp and caramelised without burning, then serve warm.
tips: Keep the flame at medium; the jaggery caramelises fast and can scorch on a fierce tava.
Dissolve the jaggery in lemon juice first so the sweetness spreads evenly through the dough.
Drain the sago well so the sweetened, moist dough still holds together neatly when shaped.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sweetened farali curd or a green chutney and a wedge of lemon for a Gujarati fasting-day platter.

variations.name: Classic Tava Veg Cutlet
variations.description: A lighter, oil-shy vegetable cutlet cooked flat on an iron tava until the crumbed surface turns lacquered and crisp. Griddling instead of deep-frying keeps it wholesome while still delivering a satisfying golden crunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: just a brush of wood-pressed groundnut oil crisps the cutlet on the tava without deep-frying

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli atta worked into the mash stiffens it so the cutlet holds shape while griddling

steps: Boil 2 potatoes and steam 0.75 cup carrot, 0.5 cup beans and 0.5 cup peas until tender, then mash dry.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil and saute 1 chopped onion, 2 minced green chillies and 1 inch grated ginger for 3 minutes, then mix into the mash.
Season with 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp garam masala, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, then work in 0.5 cup bread crumbs and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta until firm.
Shape into 10 flat patties and press each face into the remaining 0.5 cup bread crumbs for a rough crust.
Heat a flat tava over medium heat and brush with 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil until it glistens.
Griddle the cutlets 5 to 6 minutes per side, drizzling a little oil around each and pressing occasionally, until deeply browned and crisp-edged, then remove.
Serve hot with tomato ketchup and mint chutney.
tips: Mash the vegetables dry and add the khapli atta, since a stiff mixture is what lets a tava cutlet hold together without deep-frying.
Let a proper crust form before flipping, or the cutlet will tear on the griddle.
Keep the patties a little thicker than deep-fried cutlets so they stay moist over the longer griddle time.
variations.servingSuggestion: Slide two hot cutlets into a plate of ragda, top with onion, chutneys and sev for a lighter ragda-cutlet.

variations.name: Bengali Tava Veg Cutlet
variations.description: A griddled vegetable chop shallow-cooked in mustard oil until the edges frill and crisp, carrying that sharp Bengali aroma throughout. Slow-fried onions and a whisper of jaggery give it the sweet-savoury balance of a Kolkata chop, without deep-frying.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: sharp mustard oil brushed on the tava gives the chop its unmistakable Bengali edge

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a whisper of jaggery replaces refined sugar for the sweet-savoury balance of a Bengali chop

steps: Boil 2 potatoes with 0.75 cup grated beetroot, 0.5 cup carrot and 0.5 cup peas until soft, then drain very well and mash dry.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until it just smokes, cool slightly, then fry 2 sliced onions until deep golden, about 6 minutes, and reserve half.
Mix the remaining fried onions into the mash with 1 tsp Bengali garam masala, 1 inch grated ginger, 2 minced green chillies, 0.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp salt.
Bind with 0.5 cup bread crumbs, shape into 10 flat ovals and press into the remaining 0.5 cup bread crumbs.
Heat a tava over medium heat and brush with 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until the raw smell fades.
Griddle the chops 5 to 6 minutes per side, drizzling a little oil around the edges, until crisp and deep pink-brown, then lift off.
Serve hot topped with the reserved fried onions, kasundi and lime.
tips: Drain and even squeeze the boiled beetroot, as its water will otherwise make the chops fall apart on the tava.
Fry the onions low and slow to a true golden brown for the caramel sweetness this chop needs.
Shape flat, wide ovals for maximum crisp surface against the griddle.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as an evening tea-time snack with muri, a green chilli and a cup of milky Kolkata cha.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Tava Veg Cutlet
variations.description: A tava cutlet in the usal-plate tradition, spiced with goda masala and a crackled mustard-cumin temper, then griddled flat until browned and sturdy. It is built to sit under a ladle of spicy usal without falling apart.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil both tempers the seeds and griddles the cutlet, the Maharashtrian staple fat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery rounds the pungent goda masala the way Maharashtrian home cooks balance their spice

steps: Boil 2 potatoes and steam 0.5 cup carrot, 0.5 cup beans and 0.5 cup peas until tender, then mash dry.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil and crackle 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then fry 1 chopped onion and 2 minced green chillies for 4 minutes.
Stir the temper into the mash with 1.5 tsp goda masala, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt.
Work in 0.5 cup bread crumbs, shape into 10 flat sturdy patties and press into the remaining 0.5 cup bread crumbs.
Heat a tava over medium heat and brush with 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil until it shimmers.
Griddle the cutlets 5 to 6 minutes per side, pressing occasionally and drizzling a little oil, until dark and crusty, then remove.
Serve hot, drowned in spicy matki usal with onion and farsan.
tips: Whole mustard and cumin must be crackled in oil first; never stir raw seeds into the mash.
Keep the patties flat and firm so they hold once the usal gravy soaks in.
Toast the goda masala for a few seconds in the hot oil before the onion to wake up its aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Plate as cutlet-usal: the griddled cutlet under hot usal with onion, coriander, farsan and a lime wedge.

variations.name: Rajasthani Tava Veg Cutlet
variations.description: A rugged desert-style tava cutlet coloured deep red with a soaked dried-chilli and garlic paste, sharpened with amchur. Griddled slow in ghee, it develops a robust, blistered crust suited to Rajasthan's bold palate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee brushed on the tava gives a rich, blistered desert-style crust and carries the chilli aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli atta gives these rustic cutlets a firm, hearty body suited to griddling

steps: Soak 4 dried red chillies in warm water for 15 minutes, then grind with 5 garlic cloves to a coarse red paste.
Boil 2 potatoes and steam 0.5 cup carrot and 0.5 cup peas until tender, then mash dry and beat in the chilli-garlic paste.
Season with 1 tsp amchur, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 chopped onion and 1 tsp salt, then work in 0.5 cup bread crumbs and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta.
Shape into 10 flat patties and press each into the remaining 0.5 cup bread crumbs.
Heat a tava over medium heat and brush with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until fragrant.
Griddle the cutlets 5 to 6 minutes per side, brushing with more ghee and pressing occasionally, until the crust is deep red and blistered, then remove.
Serve hot with a fiery garlic-chilli chutney and cooling chaas.
tips: Deseed a couple of the dried chillies if you want the red colour without the full desert heat.
Ghee on the tava can smoke if too hot, so keep the flame at medium and brush little and often.
A squeeze of lime at the end brightens the amchur tang if the mash tastes flat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steaming bajra khichdi and a dollop of white butter for a rustic Rajasthani winter plate.

variations.name: Andhra Tava Veg Cutlet
variations.description: A fiery Andhra griddle cutlet driven by Guntur chilli and a garlic-curry-leaf temper, cooked flat on the tava until the red crust blisters. It carries steady heat and a savoury, garlicky depth with far less oil than a fried cutlet.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil tempers the aromatics and griddles the cutlet, the Andhra everyday fat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli atta firms the fiery, garlicky mash so it griddles cleanly without spreading

steps: Boil 2 potatoes and steam 0.5 cup carrot and 0.5 cup peas until tender, then mash dry.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil, crackle 15 curry leaves and 6 crushed garlic cloves for 1 minute, then fry 1 chopped onion for 3 minutes.
Mix the temper into the mash with 2 tsp Guntur red chilli powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for a vivid red mixture.
Work in 0.5 cup bread crumbs and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, shape into 10 flat patties and press into the remaining 0.5 cup bread crumbs.
Heat a tava over medium heat and brush with 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil until it shimmers.
Griddle the cutlets 5 to 6 minutes per side, drizzling a little oil and pressing occasionally, until the crust is red-gold and blistered, then remove.
Serve scorching hot with a cooling onion raita and lime.
tips: Guntur chilli is potent, so start with the stated amount and scale up only to taste.
Fry the garlic gently in the temper; burnt garlic turns the whole cutlet bitter.
A spoon of curd in the mash softens the burn without dulling the red colour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with curd rice and a smear of gongura pickle for a full Andhra-style plate that tames the heat.

variations.name: Classic Crispy Sabudana Vada
variations.description: The beloved Maharashtrian fasting fritter, crisp-shelled sabudana vada made from well-soaked sago, mashed potato and coarsely crushed roasted peanuts. A light coat of bread crumbs is the secret to a shatter-crisp crust that never turns chewy, while cumin bloomed in ghee gives it a fragrant, nutty depth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: used to bloom the cumin seeds and crisp the curry leaves so they release their aroma into the mix

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil heated to 180C so the vadas fry crisp without soaking up grease or bursting

steps: Rinse 1 cup sago until the water runs clear, then soak in just enough water to cover for 5 to 6 hours until each pearl is soft and squashes easily between your fingers, and drain thoroughly.
Boil 3 potatoes until tender, peel and mash smooth, then coarsely crush 0.5 cup roasted peanuts leaving some texture.
Bloom 1 tsp cumin seeds and 10 curry leaves in 1 tbsp hot Anveshan Ghee for 15 seconds until fragrant and crackling, then tip over the mash.
Combine the drained sago, mashed potato, crushed peanuts, 3 chopped green chillies, 3 tbsp coriander, 0.5 tsp sugar, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 1 tsp rock salt into a firm, non-sticky dough.
Shape into 12 flat patties, press each lightly in 3 tbsp bread crumbs to coat, and heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C.
Fry in batches over medium-high for 3 to 4 minutes, turning once, until deep golden and crisp, then drain on a rack and serve hot.
tips: Drain the soaked sago really well; excess water makes the vadas absorb oil and burst in the pan.
The bread-crumb coat is what keeps these extra crisp, distinguishing them from a plain sabudana vada.
Fry a test vada first; if it falls apart, mash in a spoon of the crushed peanuts or a little more potato to bind.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with cooling peanut-curd chutney (danyachi amti-style) or a green coriander chutney, ideal for a Navratri fast or a rainy-day snack.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Crispy Sabudana Vada
variations.description: The Pune-style sabudana vada elevated with a hint of goda masala for a warm, clove-scented backbone, and a heavier hand of crushed peanuts for crunch. This everyday (non-fasting) version leans savoury and aromatic, fried crisp and served with a nutty amti chutney.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the cumin and warms the goda masala so it perfumes the vada mix evenly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the classic Maharashtrian frying fat that gives the vada a clean, light crunch

steps: Soak 1 cup rinsed sago in just enough water for 5 to 6 hours until soft and squashable, then drain thoroughly in a colander.
Boil and mash 3 potatoes, and coarsely crush 0.75 cup roasted peanuts for a pronounced crunch.
Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, bloom 1 tsp cumin seeds for 15 seconds, then stir in 1 tsp goda masala off the heat for 10 seconds until fragrant.
Mix the drained sago, mashed potato, crushed peanuts, the ghee-spice tempering, 3 chopped green chillies, 3 tbsp coriander, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 1 tsp salt into a firm dough.
Shape into 12 patties, coat lightly in 3 tbsp bread crumbs, and heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C.
Fry over medium-high for 3 to 4 minutes per batch, turning, until crisp and deep golden, then drain and serve hot.
tips: Add the goda masala off the heat so it warms without scorching and turning bitter.
The extra peanuts give this version its signature crunch, so crush them coarse, not fine.
Keep the flame steady at medium-high; a crashing oil temperature makes the vadas greasy and pale.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with danyachi chutney (roasted peanut chutney) and a cup of kokum sherbet or chai, Pune tapri style.

variations.name: Gujarati Crispy Sabudana Vada
variations.description: A khatta-meetha Gujarati farali vada that plays the region's signature sweet-savoury-tangy chord: Anveshan Jaggery Powder for gentle sweetness, lemon for tang, and a nutty sesame-peanut crust in place of bread crumbs. Fresh mint and coriander keep it bright, and a whole crop of crushed peanuts gives it real crunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: dissolved in lemon juice for the signature Gujarati khatta-meetha balance against the chilli

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the cumin and grated ginger so their warmth balances the jaggery sweetness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday Gujarati frying oil, kept at 175C so the sweetened, sesame-crusted vada browns without scorching

steps: Rinse 1 cup sago until the water runs clear, soak in just enough water for 5 to 6 hours until each pearl squashes easily, then drain very well in a colander.
Boil 3 potatoes until tender, peel and mash smooth, then coarsely crush 0.75 cup roasted peanuts, keeping half aside to mix into the sesame coating.
Bloom 1 tsp cumin seeds in 1 tbsp hot Anveshan Ghee for 15 seconds, add 1 tsp grated ginger for another 10 seconds until fragrant, then take off the heat.

Dissolve 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 1.5 tbsp lemon juice, then combine with the drained sago, mashed potato, half the crushed peanuts, the ghee-cumin, 2 chopped green chillies, 2 tbsp mint, 3 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp rock salt into a firm, non-sticky dough.
Mix 3 tbsp white sesame seeds with the reserved crushed peanuts, shape the dough into 12 flat patties and press each firmly into this sesame-peanut coat.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 175C and fry the vadas in batches over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes, turning once, until golden with a toasted sesame crust, then drain and serve warm.
tips: Dissolve the jaggery in lemon juice first so the sweetness spreads evenly instead of leaving sticky pockets.
Fry a touch cooler than usual, around 175C, as both the jaggery and sesame brown quickly and can scorch.
The sesame-peanut crust replaces bread crumbs here, so press it on firmly and re-coat any bald patches before frying.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sweetened farali curd (dahi) topped with a little jaggery, and a bright coriander-mint chutney, for a Gujarati fasting-day platter.

variations.name: Rajasthani Crispy Sabudana Vada
variations.description: A fiery, drier Marwari tikki built on a smoky soaked dried-red-chilli paste and the sour bite of amchur, with no lemon or bread crumbs in sight. Roasted khapli atta binds the mix into a firm, spice-crusted patty, and crackled ajwain gives it that rugged desert-kitchen warmth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: roasted on a dry tava and worked in as the binder in place of bread crumbs for a firm, dry tikki

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: used to bloom the cumin and ajwain and to cook the red-chilli paste so its smoky heat loses any raw edge

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the deep-frying oil that crisps the drier, spicier vadas to a firm red-gold shell

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup sago in just enough water for 5 to 6 hours until soft, then drain thoroughly so the dough stays dry.
Soak 5 dried red chillies in hot water for 15 minutes, then grind to a coarse, smoky paste with a splash of the soaking water.
Boil 3 potatoes until tender, peel and mash, and coarsely crush 0.5 cup roasted peanuts for texture.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.5 tsp ajwain for 15 seconds, add 1 tsp grated ginger and the red-chilli paste and cook 1 minute over medium heat until the raw smell lifts and the ghee turns glossy red.

Roast 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta on a dry tava until nutty, then bind the drained sago, mashed potato, crushed peanuts, the chilli tempering, 1 tsp amchur, 3 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp rock salt into a firm, dry dough.
Shape into 12 flat, thin tikkis and heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C, then fry in batches over medium-high for 3 to 4 minutes, turning, until crisp and deep red-gold, and drain on a rack.
tips: Grind the soaked chillies to a coarse, not smooth, paste so you get little bursts of smoky heat throughout.
Amchur replaces the lemon here and keeps the dough dry, which is what makes this tikki crisp rather than soft.
Roast the khapli atta before binding; raw flour leaves a pasty taste and does not grip the sago as well.
If the dough feels loose, work in another spoon of roasted khapli atta rather than adding water.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with cooling mint-curd raita and a scatter of thin onion rings, alongside a glass of chaas to temper the desert heat.

variations.name: Kashmiri Crispy Sabudana Vada
variations.description: An aromatic sabudana vada perfumed with saffron and fennel in the Kashmiri manner, mild-warm rather than fiery, with a delicate golden hue. Steeped saffron milk works into the crumb and a whisper of dry ginger gives it a gentle, fragrant heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk and worked into the mix for a golden hue and gentle perfume

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the cumin and fennel so the Kashmiri aromatics infuse the mix

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the neutral frying oil that lets the saffron and fennel aromatics shine

steps: Soak 1 cup rinsed sago in just enough water for 5 to 6 hours until soft, then drain well, and steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk.
Boil and mash 3 potatoes, and coarsely crush 0.5 cup roasted peanuts.
Bloom 1 tsp cumin seeds in 1 tbsp hot Anveshan Ghee for 15 seconds, then add 0.75 tsp fennel powder and 0.5 tsp dry ginger powder off the heat for 10 seconds.
Combine the drained sago, mashed potato, crushed peanuts, the ghee-spice tempering, the saffron milk, 2 chopped green chillies, 3 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp rock salt into a firm, golden dough.
Shape into 12 patties, coat in 3 tbsp bread crumbs, and heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C.
Fry over medium-high for 3 to 4 minutes per batch, turning, until crisp and pale golden, then drain and serve warm.
tips: Steep the saffron in warm, not hot, milk to draw out its colour and aroma without dulling it.
Toast the fennel powder briefly to deepen its sweet, aniseed note before it goes into the mix.
This gentler vada suits guests who find the classic too plain and the Rajasthani too fiery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a walnut-curd chutney and pink noon chai, or as an aromatic starter before a Kashmiri fasting meal.

variations.name: Classic Aloo Paratha
variations.description: The definitive Punjabi breakfast paratha: a soft Anveshan Khapli Atta dough wrapped around a fragrant spiced-potato filling and griddled in Anveshan Ghee until blistered and golden. Nutty khapli wheat gives a heartier, more wholesome bite than refined atta, and the ghee makes the crust irresistibly crisp.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Ancient emmer-wheat atta kneaded into the dough for a nutty flavour and softer, gut-friendly paratha.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: One spoon worked into the dough and the rest for roasting the parathas to a golden, crisp finish.

steps: Knead 3 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and about 1.25 cups water into a soft, non-sticky dough, then cover and rest 20 minutes.
Boil 4 medium potatoes until fork-tender, peel while warm and mash smooth with no lumps.
Mix the mash with 2 finely chopped green chillies, a grated 1-inch piece of ginger, 1.5 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp amchur, 4 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp salt.
Divide dough and filling into 8 balls each; flatten a dough ball, place 2 tbsp filling in the centre, gather the edges over the top and seal, then dust and roll gently into a 7-inch round.
Roast on a hot tava for about 1 minute until bubbles appear, flip, and brush with 0.5 tsp ghee; cook each side 1-2 minutes, pressing lightly, until golden-brown spots form.
Repeat with the rest, stacking the cooked parathas under a cloth so they stay soft and warm.
tips: Use roasted cumin powder rather than raw seeds so the filling is aromatic and never has a raw crunch.
Mash the potatoes while still warm; cold potato turns gluey and is harder to spread evenly.
If the filling feels wet, cool it fully and add a spoon of roasted besan to stop the parathas tearing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a bowl of thick set curd, a spoon of mango pickle and a knob of white butter melting on top.

variations.name: Masala Aloo Paratha
variations.description: A more richly spiced version where the potato filling is built on garam masala, coriander powder and a tangy amchur-anardana lift, giving a deeper, chaat-like flavour. The Anveshan Khapli Atta dough and ghee-roasted crust keep it wholesome while the masala does the talking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Kneaded into a supple dough; its nutty depth stands up to the bolder masala filling.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon in the dough and the rest brushed on while roasting for a fragrant golden crust.

steps: Knead 3 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and about 1.25 cups water into a soft dough; cover and rest 20 minutes.
Boil 4 medium potatoes until soft, peel and mash while warm until completely smooth.

Finely chop 1 small onion and squeeze out its moisture, then mix into the mash with 1 tsp garam masala, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp anardana powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 4 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp salt.
Divide dough and filling into 8 portions; encase 2 tbsp filling in each dough ball, seal well and roll gently to a 7-inch round, dusting with atta as needed.
Roast on a hot tava for 1 minute until the surface puffs, flip and brush with 0.5 tsp ghee, cooking each side 1-2 minutes until deep golden with crisp spots.
Stack the finished parathas wrapped in a cloth so the steam keeps them soft.
tips: Squeeze the chopped onion dry before mixing, or its water will make the filling ooze and tear the paratha.
Anardana adds a fruity tang; if unavailable, use an extra teaspoon of amchur instead.
Toast the garam masala for 10 seconds in a dry pan to intensify its aroma before mixing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling boondi raita and a wedge of lemon to play off the tangy masala filling.

variations.name: Spicy Aloo Paratha
variations.description: For those who like a fiery breakfast: the potato filling is loaded with green chillies, crushed black pepper and extra red chilli for a genuine slow-building heat. The nutty Anveshan Khapli Atta dough and ghee crust give a mellow, wholesome base that carries the spice beautifully.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Forms the soft, nutty dough that balances the fiery filling within.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: Worked into the dough and brushed on the tava to crisp the parathas and cool the palate slightly.

steps: Knead 3 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and about 1.25 cups water into a soft dough; rest, covered, for 20 minutes.
Boil 4 medium potatoes until tender, peel and mash smooth while warm.

Coarsely crush 1 tsp peppercorns and mix into the mash with 4 finely chopped green chillies, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, a grated 1-inch piece of ginger, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 2 tbsp thick curd, 4 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp salt.
Divide dough and filling into 8 each; stuff 2 tbsp filling into each dough ball, seal, and roll gently to a 7-inch round with a light atta dusting.
Roast on a hot tava for 1 minute, flip, brush with 0.5 tsp ghee and cook each side 1-2 minutes until golden with crisp brown spots.
Keep the cooked parathas warm under a cloth while you finish the rest.
tips: Crush the pepper fresh for a sharper, more aromatic heat than pre-ground powder.
For a milder batch, deseed the green chillies but keep the count for flavour.
A spoon of thick curd mixed into the filling tempers the heat while keeping it moist.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plenty of cold curd and a sliced cucumber salad to cool the fire, plus a glass of chaas.

variations.name: Garlic Aloo Paratha
variations.description: A punchy, garlic-forward paratha where sauteed garlic and a garlicky green paste run right through the potato filling for a savoury, aromatic hit. Ghee-roasting on the tava toasts the garlic edges while the Anveshan Khapli Atta keeps the whole thing hearty and wholesome.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Kneaded into the dough; its wholegrain nuttiness pairs well with the robust garlic filling.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: Used to saute the garlic and to roast the parathas, deepening the toasty garlic aroma.

steps: Knead 3 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and about 1.25 cups water into a soft dough; cover and rest 20 minutes.
Finely chop 10 garlic cloves and saute in 1 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee over medium heat for 1-2 minutes until pale golden and fragrant, then cool.
Boil and mash 4 medium potatoes while warm, then mix with the sauteed garlic, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 4 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp salt.
Divide dough and filling into 8 each; stuff 2 tbsp filling into each ball, seal, and roll gently to a 7-inch round, dusting with atta.
Roast on a hot tava for 1 minute, flip, brush with 0.5 tsp ghee and cook each side 1-2 minutes until golden with toasty brown spots.
Stack under a cloth to stay soft while the rest cook.
tips: Sauteing the garlic first tames its raw sharpness and gives a mellow, sweet-savoury depth.
Leave a few cloves slightly coarse for little bursts of garlic in every bite.
A pinch of kasuri methi in the filling rounds out the garlic beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a garlicky tomato chutney and plain curd, or alongside a simple dal for a comforting meal.

variations.name: Cheesy Aloo Paratha
variations.description: A kid-friendly favourite where grated cheese melts into the mildly spiced potato filling for a gooey, stretchy centre. The Anveshan Khapli Atta dough griddled in ghee gives a crisp, golden shell that gives way to a molten cheese-and-potato core.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The nutty wholegrain dough that crisps around the molten cheese-potato filling.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon in the dough and the rest for roasting to a crisp, golden, cheese-friendly crust.

steps: Knead 3 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and about 1.25 cups water into a soft dough; cover and rest 20 minutes.
Boil 3 medium potatoes until tender, peel and mash smooth while warm, then let cool to room temperature.
Mix the cooled mash with 1 cup grated cheese, 1 finely chopped green chilli, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp black pepper powder, 3 tbsp coriander and 0.5 tsp salt.
Divide dough and filling into 8 each; encase 2 tbsp filling in each ball, seal well and roll gently to a 6-inch round so the cheese stays contained.
Roast on a medium-hot tava for 1-2 minutes per side, brushing with 0.5 tsp ghee, until golden and crisp and the cheese has melted inside.
Serve immediately while the centre is still molten and stretchy.
tips: Let the mash cool before adding cheese, or the cheese melts prematurely and makes the filling greasy.
Roll these a little smaller and thicker so the cheese doesn't burst through the seams.
A mix of processed and mozzarella cheese gives the best flavour-plus-stretch combination.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with tomato ketchup for the kids and a tangy schezwan chutney for the grown-ups.

variations.name: Classic Aloo Tamatar
variations.description: The everyday comfort curry of soft potato chunks in a light, tangy tomato gravy, cooked without onion or garlic in the true vrat-friendly style. The potatoes are lightly mashed so they thicken the sauce and drink up the tang. Simple, quick and endlessly reassuring with hot pooris.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee gives this simple no-onion curry its homely, rounded richness

steps: Boil 4 potatoes until soft, peel, and break them into rough chunks with your hands, lightly mashing a few so they thicken the gravy.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 inch grated ginger and 2 slit green chillies and saute for 30 seconds, then add 4 pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder.
Cook the tomato masala on medium heat until it thickens and the ghee separates at the edges, about 8 minutes.
Add the potato chunks with 2 cups water and 1.25 tsp salt, stir well, and bring to a gentle boil.
Simmer uncovered for 8 to 10 minutes so the potatoes absorb the tang and the gravy thickens to a light coating.
Finish with 0.5 tsp garam masala and 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander stirred through the curry.
tips: Mashing a few potato chunks is the trick to a naturally thick gravy without any flour.
For a vrat version, skip the coriander powder and garam masala and use rock salt instead.
A pinch of amchur or a squeeze of lemon at the end brightens the tomato tang beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot with pooris or kachoris and a side of pickle, the classic combination for a festive or travel breakfast.

variations.name: Masala Aloo Tamatar
variations.description: A fierier southern take where roasted coriander powder and a garlic-red-chilli base give the potato curry real heat and depth. A curry-leaf tempering and a hint of tamarind lift the tomato tang into something sharper. Bold, spicy and made to wake up a plain rice plate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil carries the fiery southern tempering cleanly

steps: Boil 4 potatoes until soft, peel, and cut into bite-sized cubes.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, then add 10 curry leaves and 6 crushed garlic cloves and fry for 30 seconds until fragrant.

Add 1 chopped onion and fry for 5 minutes until soft, then dry-roast 2.5 tsp coriander powder separately for 40 seconds and add it with 3 pureed tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp red chilli powder.
Cook the masala on medium heat until the oil separates and it turns glossy, about 8 minutes.
Add the potato cubes with 2 cups water and 1.25 tsp salt, stir gently, and simmer for 8 minutes so the potatoes soak up the spicy gravy.
Stir in 1 tsp tamarind pulp and cook 3 more minutes for a sharp, tangy finish.
Garnish with 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander before serving.
tips: Crush the garlic rather than chopping it for a stronger, more pungent southern base.
Adjust the tamarind to taste; it should sharpen the tomato without overpowering it.
Toast the coriander powder fresh to give the fiery gravy its earthy backbone.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot steamed rice with a spoon of ghee and a crisp appalam, or with dosa for a spicy southern breakfast.

variations.name: Kadai Aloo Tamatar
variations.description: A kadai-style potato curry where cubed potatoes and charred capsicum are tossed with a coarse hand-pounded coriander-chilli masala into a thick, clinging sauce. The tomato stays chunky rather than pureed, keeping the dish rustic and textured. Smoky, punchy and quick.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked wood-pressed mustard oil gives the kadai its sharp, robust base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon rounds the mustard oil and glazes the potatoes

steps: Boil 4 potatoes until just tender, peel, and cut into thick cubes; cut 1 large capsicum into wedges.
Dry-roast 2 tbsp coriander seeds and 3 dried red chillies for 2 minutes until fragrant, cool, and pound to a coarse kadai masala.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until hazy, lower the heat, and fry 2 diced onions for 6 minutes until softened.
Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then 3 chopped tomatoes and 0.5 tsp turmeric and cook until pulpy but still chunky, about 6 minutes.
Stir in most of the pounded masala and the potato cubes with 0.75 cup water and 1.25 tsp salt, and toss on medium-high heat for 6 minutes until the thick gravy coats them.
Add the capsicum wedges and toss on high heat for 3 to 4 minutes so they char yet stay crunchy.
Crush 1 tsp kasuri methi over the pan, swirl in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and the reserved masala, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Keep the potatoes firm, not fully soft, so they hold their cubes in the tossed dish.
Leave the tomato slightly chunky for the rustic kadai texture.
Add the capsicum at the end so it keeps its bite and bright colour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve from the kadai with tandoori roti or ajwain paratha and a side of sliced onion and green chilli.

variations.name: Handi Aloo Tamatar
variations.description: A slow handi potato curry from the eastern belt, scented with whole spices bloomed in ghee and a smoky black cardamom. The potatoes steam under a sealed lid in a light tomato gravy, taking on a deep, homely aroma. Gentle, warming and perfect with plain rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: whole spices bloom in bilona ghee and their aroma steams into the potatoes on dum

steps: Peel 4 potatoes and cut into thick cubes; there is no need to pre-boil them for this slow dum.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a handi and bloom 1 inch cinnamon, 1 black cardamom, 4 cloves, 1 bay leaf and 1 tsp cumin seeds until fragrant, about 40 seconds.
Add 1 chopped onion and fry for 6 minutes until golden, then stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute.
Add 4 pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and cook until the ghee separates, about 8 minutes.
Add the raw potato cubes with 2 cups water and 1.25 tsp salt, stir to coat, and bring to a gentle simmer.
Cover the handi tightly, lower the heat to minimum, and dum-cook for 18 to 20 minutes until the potatoes are tender and infused with the spice aroma.
Uncover, discard the bay leaf and black cardamom skin, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander.
tips: Cooking raw potatoes slowly in the gravy lets them absorb far more flavour than pre-boiled ones.
Bruise the black cardamom so it lends its smoky note without dominating the pot.
Remove the whole spices before serving so no one bites into a clove or cardamom.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or with litti or sattu paratha for an authentic Bihari meal.

variations.name: Punjabi Aloo Tamatar
variations.description: A richer Punjabi version where the potato curry gets a smooth onion-tomato gravy finished with cream and crushed kasuri methi, with butter swapped for bilona ghee. Fuller and more indulgent than the everyday curry, with a mellow buttery-fenugreek aroma. Dhaba comfort on a plate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: replaces butter to give the gravy a lush body and nutty bilona aroma

steps: Boil 4 potatoes until soft, peel, and break into rough chunks, mashing a few lightly.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then fry 2 chopped onions for 8 minutes until golden and add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute.
Add 3 pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder and cook until the ghee separates, about 8 minutes.
Add the potato chunks with 2 cups water and 1.25 tsp salt, stir, and simmer for 8 minutes so they soak up the gravy and it thickens.
Lower the heat, stir in 3 tbsp cream and 0.75 tsp garam masala, and warm through for 2 minutes without boiling.
Crush 1.5 tsp kasuri methi between your palms over the pan and stir it in.
Simmer 1 more minute until the gravy turns glossy and clings to the potatoes.
tips: Mash a few potato chunks to thicken the gravy naturally before the cream goes in.
Keep the flame low once cream is added so it does not split.
A pinch of jaggery balances the tomato if the gravy tastes too sharp.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or laccha paratha, topped with a cream swirl and kasuri methi, alongside a raw onion salad.

variations.name: Classic Arbi
variations.description: The comforting North Indian arbi sabzi where boiled colocasia is crisped in a pungent tempering and folded through a light onion-tomato masala. The trick is getting the arbi golden and non-slimy, so it holds its shape while soaking up cumin, coriander and a bright hit of amchur.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: its sharpness cuts arbi's natural sliminess and crisps it beautifully

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: drizzled at the finish for a rounded, nutty aroma over the crisp arbi

steps: Boil 500 g colocasia until just fork-tender, about 15 minutes, then cool, peel, and cut into 1/2-inch thick slices.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the flame, and shallow-fry the arbi slices for 8 minutes until golden and crisp, then lift out.
In the same oil crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, add 2 chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, and saute 5 minutes until golden.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, cooking 4 minutes until pulpy and the oil separates.
Return the fried arbi with 1 tsp salt, toss gently to coat, and cook uncovered on medium for 5 minutes so it absorbs the masala without breaking.
Finish with 1 tsp amchur and a drizzle of 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee, tossing off the heat until fragrant.
tips: Boil the arbi only until just tender; overcooked colocasia turns gluey and impossible to crisp.
Do not cover the pan after the arbi goes back in, as trapped steam brings back the sliminess.
Frying the slices well before adding to the masala is the single biggest step for a non-sticky sabzi.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot puris or plain parathas and a side of mint chutney for a classic weekend brunch plate.

variations.name: Masala Arbi
variations.description: A Delhi-style arbi masala with a thicker, spicier onion-tomato base rounded off with garam masala. The colocasia is fried until crusty, then simmered briefly so the edges stay crisp while the centre turns creamy, giving a richer, more festive take than the everyday sabzi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: gives a clean crisp fry and a neutral base for the layered masala

steps: Boil, cool and peel 500 g colocasia, then halve the pieces and flatten each lightly with your palm so more surface crisps up.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and fry the arbi for 8 minutes until a deep golden crust forms, then remove and set aside.
In the same oil crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds with 1 bay leaf, add 3 chopped onions and 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, and fry 7 minutes until browned.
Add 3 pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.25 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, cooking 8 minutes until the masala is thick and the oil floats.
Fold in the fried arbi with 1 tsp salt and a splash of water, simmering 5 minutes so it soaks up the masala while keeping crisp edges.
Sprinkle 1 tsp garam masala and 2 tbsp chopped coriander, stir gently, and cook a final minute before serving.
tips: Flattening the boiled pieces before frying creates more crusty surface area for the masala to grip.
Keep the simmer short; long cooking in the wet masala softens the crisp fry you worked for.
For a restaurant-style sheen, add the garam masala in warm oil rather than dry over the top.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with laccha paratha or jeera rice, garnished with ginger juliennes and a lemon wedge on the side.

variations.name: Spicy Pepper Arbi
variations.description: A dry, fiery arbi fry from the eastern heartland, tossed with slit green chillies, coarse black pepper and curry leaves. There is no gravy at all, just crisp colocasia catching heat and a garlicky tadka, making it a bold, snacky side that eats almost like a roast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: its nutty depth suits the dry, peppery roast-style finish

steps: Boil 500 g colocasia until just tender, peel, and cut into thick 1/2-inch rounds.
Coarsely crush 1.5 tsp black pepper and 8 garlic cloves together in a mortar into a rough paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 12 curry leaves and 4 slit green chillies and fry for 30 seconds.
Stir in the crushed pepper-garlic and cook for a minute until raw garlic smell fades, then add the arbi with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt.
Stir-fry uncovered on medium-high for 10 minutes, pressing the pieces down so they crisp and brown on all sides.
Dust in 0.5 tsp red chilli powder in the last 2 minutes, toss well, and serve hot and crackling.
tips: Give the arbi space in the pan and let it sit undisturbed for a minute at a time to get a proper crust.
Fresh curry leaves and freshly crushed pepper make all the difference to this simple dry fry.
If the pieces stick, add a teaspoon more oil rather than water, which would make them soggy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a crunchy side with sambar rice or plain dal-chawal, or offer it as a spicy tea-time nibble.

variations.name: Dhaba-style Arbi
variations.description: A robust, semi-dry arbi in a clinging onion-tomato masala scented with kasuri methi and garam masala. The colocasia is fried crisp then coated in a thick, glossy gravy, giving that hearty roadside richness while the crisp edges peek through the masala.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the pungent base fat behind the bold dhaba masala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: stirred in at the end for the glossy, buttery dhaba finish

steps: Boil and peel 500 g colocasia, cut into thick slices, and shallow-fry in 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil for 8 minutes until crisp and golden, then set aside.
In the same oil fry 3 chopped onions with 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 8 minutes until deeply caramelised.
Add 2 pureed tomatoes with 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, and cook 7 minutes until thick and glossy with oil separating.
Fold in the fried arbi with 1 tsp salt and 3 tbsp water, simmering 5 minutes so the masala coats each piece.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the top with 0.75 tsp garam masala and stir for a minute until fragrant.
Finish by stirring in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, cooking 1 minute until the gravy turns rich and clinging.
tips: Keep the gravy thick and coating rather than soupy so the arbi does not turn slippery.
Caramelising the onions deeply is the secret to a masala that tastes like a highway dhaba.
Warm the kasuri methi briefly before crushing to draw out its full aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Scoop it up with butter naan or missi roti, with a raw onion-and-lemon salad alongside.

variations.name: Ajwain Arbi Fry
variations.description: The simplest Punjabi home fry where boiled arbi is smashed lightly and shallow-fried with ajwain and carom-scented spices until crackling crisp. No onion, no tomato, just golden colocasia, carom and amchur, the kind of quick sabzi that disappears straight off the tawa.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: enough to shallow-fry the smashed arbi to a proper crackling crust

steps: Boil 500 g colocasia until just tender, peel, and flatten each piece gently with your palm to about half its thickness.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a wide pan and lower the flame, then add 1 tsp ajwain and let it sizzle for 15 seconds.
Lay the flattened arbi in a single layer and fry undisturbed for 4 minutes per side until deeply golden and crisp.
Sprinkle over 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp coriander powder with 1 tsp salt, tossing gently for 3 minutes to coat.
Raise the heat for the last 2 minutes to crisp the edges further and drive off any moisture.
Turn off the heat, dust with 1.5 tsp amchur, and scatter 2 tbsp chopped coriander over the top.
tips: Flatten the boiled pieces before frying for maximum crunch and even browning.
Do not crowd the pan; fry in batches if needed so each piece crisps instead of steaming.
Ajwain aids digestion and cuts arbi's heaviness, so do not skimp on it here.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve straight from the pan with dal makhani and roti, or as a crisp accompaniment to rajma-chawal.

variations.name: Classic Baingan Bharta
variations.description: The definitive smoky bharta where a whole eggplant is charred over an open flame until the skin blisters and the flesh turns silky, then mashed into a cumin-and-tomato masala. That fire-roasted smokiness is the soul of the dish. Rustic, deeply savoury and best mopped up with hot roti.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Its pungency is the traditional partner to smoky roasted eggplant across the north.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing teaspoon softens the mustard oil's edge and rounds the smoke.

steps: Rub 1 large eggplant with a little oil, prick it in a few places and roast it directly over a medium gas flame for 12 to 15 minutes, turning often, until the skin is fully charred and the flesh feels collapsed and soft.
Cool the eggplant, peel off all the blackened skin, discard the stem and mash the smoky flesh coarsely with a fork.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai on medium-high until it shimmers, then crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds with 0.5 tsp ajwain for 15 seconds.
Add 2 finely chopped onions, 2 chopped green chillies and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 7 minutes until the onions turn golden.
Stir in 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 6 minutes until pulpy and the oil separates.
Fold in the mashed eggplant and cook uncovered on medium for 6 to 7 minutes, stirring, until thick and glossy, then finish with 0.5 tsp amchur powder, 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and 3 tbsp coriander.
tips: Choose a large, light eggplant that feels hollow; heavy dense ones are full of seeds and roast unevenly.
Roast directly on the flame for real smokiness; an oven-baked eggplant tastes cleaner but loses the signature char.
Mash coarsely rather than pureeing, since a little texture is what makes a bharta feel homemade.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot bajra or wheat rotis, a knob of white butter and sliced onions rubbed with lemon.

variations.name: Masala Baingan Bharta
variations.description: A Bengali-leaning bharta, locally close to begun pora, where the roasted eggplant is enriched with a warm garam masala and a touch more onion for a fuller, spiced body. Mustard oil keeps it rooted in the east. Fragrant, hearty and a little indulgent.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Central to eastern cooking, its bite carries the roasted eggplant and garam masala.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The garam masala is bloomed in ghee to deepen the aroma without harshness.

steps: Char 1 large eggplant over a medium flame for 12 to 15 minutes until the skin blackens and the inside turns completely soft, then cool, peel and mash the flesh.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai until shimmering, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds with a 1 inch piece of cinnamon, 3 green cardamoms and 3 cloves, then add 3 chopped onions, 2 green chillies and 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste.
Fry the onions for 9 minutes until deep golden and jammy, the base of this richer bharta.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 6 minutes until thick.
Fold in the mashed eggplant and cook uncovered on medium for 7 minutes, mashing further, until the bharta pulls together and looks glossy.
Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, stir 1.25 tsp garam masala into it for 10 seconds, then fold it through with 3 tbsp coriander and take off the heat.
tips: Cook the onions well past soft to a proper golden for the deeper, richer character this version needs.
Blooming the garam masala in ghee at the end keeps its aroma bright rather than dull and cooked-out.
A spoon of this bharta stirred into hot khichuri makes a wonderful next-day meal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a wedge of lime, or with soft luchis for a weekend spread.

variations.name: Spicy Baingan Bharta
variations.description: A Kerala-style spin where slit green chillies and crushed black pepper meet a fragrant crackle of curry leaves and coconut oil, giving the smoky eggplant a coastal, peppery warmth. The pepper heat builds gently and lingers. Aromatic, fiery and distinctly southern.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: The unmistakable base of Kerala cooking, its sweetness balances the pepper heat.

steps: Roast 1 large eggplant over a medium flame for 12 to 15 minutes until fully charred and soft, then peel and mash the smoky flesh.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadhai on medium, splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, then add 12 curry leaves and 4 slit green chillies and let them crackle for 20 seconds.
Add 2 chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and saute for 6 minutes until soft and pale gold.
Stir in 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 5 minutes until pulpy.
Fold in the mashed eggplant and cook uncovered on medium for 6 minutes until it thickens and the coconut oil glistens through.
Crush 1 tsp black pepper coarsely, stir it in with 3 tbsp coriander and cook for a final minute so the pepper warmth infuses the bharta.
tips: Add the crushed black pepper near the end so its aromatic heat stays sharp instead of turning flat.
Curry leaves must go into hot oil to release their fragrance, so do not rush the tempering.
If coconut oil's aroma feels strong, use slightly less and finish with a few drops of fresh lime to lighten it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with Kerala red rice or appams and a small bowl of thin buttermilk to cool the palate.

variations.name: Dhaba-style Baingan Bharta
variations.description: A hearty dhaba bharta with a herby kasuri-methi finish and extra onion browned deep for that highway-kitchen richness. The smoky eggplant is folded into a thick, glossy masala and rounded off with ghee. Robust, aromatic and made to disappear fast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A generous pour to brown the onions into a proper dhaba masala.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Kasuri methi is crushed into warm ghee at the end for the signature dhaba aroma.

steps: Char 1 large eggplant over a medium flame for 12 to 15 minutes until blackened and soft, then peel and mash the flesh coarsely.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add 3 chopped onions, 2 green chillies and 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste.
Fry the onions for 9 to 10 minutes until deep brown and richly caramelised, the heart of a dhaba masala.
Add 3 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 7 minutes until thick and the oil separates.
Fold in the mashed eggplant and cook uncovered on medium for 6 minutes until glossy and well combined.
Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi into it, pour over with 1 tsp garam masala and 3 tbsp coriander, and fold through before serving.
tips: The deep-browned onions are what give this bharta its dhaba character, so do not stop at golden.
Crush kasuri methi between your palms before adding to release its full herbal fragrance.
For a smokier hit, drop a lit piece of charcoal in a small bowl set in the pan, add a drop of ghee and cover for two minutes to infuse.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot butter naan or laccha paratha and a raw onion salad dressed with chaat masala.

variations.name: Home-style Baingan Bharta
variations.description: An everyday Andhra household bharta cooked without roasting on flame, where the eggplant is instead sauteed soft in the pan with a tangy tamarind edge and a simple tempering. Quick, mild and tangy, it is the practical version made on busy days. Homely and comforting.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: The nutty gingelly oil beloved across Andhra kitchens gives this simple bharta its depth.

steps: Chop 3 medium eggplants into small cubes and drop them into salted water for 5 minutes to stop them browning, then drain.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadhai on medium, splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, then add 10 curry leaves.
Add 1 chopped onion and saute for 4 minutes until soft, keeping the heat moderate.
Add the eggplant cubes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, cover and cook on low for 12 minutes, stirring twice, until the eggplant is very soft.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes and 1 tsp tamarind pulp, mash everything together with the back of the ladle and cook uncovered for 5 minutes until thick and tangy.
Stir in 2 tbsp coriander, adjust salt and serve warm.
tips: Soaking the cut eggplant in salted water keeps it from discolouring and draws out any bitterness.
Mash the softened eggplant right in the pan for a quick bharta texture without flame-roasting.
The tamarind is key to this southern version, so add it in stages and taste to get the tang you like.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or with dosas for an easy tiffin.

variations.name: Classic Beetroot Paratha
variations.description: A jewel-pink paratha made by kneading cooked beetroot puree straight into a khapli-atta dough, so the colour and gentle sweetness run all the way through. Soft, faintly earthy and lightly spiced with cumin, it is as pretty as it is wholesome. A Kerala-kitchen favourite for sneaking vegetables into children's plates.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Nutty emmer wheat takes on the beetroot's rosy hue and keeps the paratha soft

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon in the dough and the rest for roasting to a tender, golden finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: A Kerala touch that lends a subtle sweetness suited to the beetroot

steps: Boil 1 medium beetroot until fork-tender, peel and blend to a smooth 0.5 cup puree, then let it cool to room temperature.

In a bowl combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric, minced green chilli, grated ginger, coriander, 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil and the beetroot puree.
Knead the mixture, adding only about 0.25 cup water a little at a time, into a soft, non-sticky pink dough, then cover and rest for 15 minutes.
Divide into 6 balls, dust with atta and roll each out to a 7-inch round of even thickness.
Place on a hot tava over medium heat and cook for about 1 minute until small bubbles appear on the surface.
Flip, brush with Anveshan Ghee, then turn again and press with a spatula, roasting each side 1 to 2 minutes until golden spots form and it smells toasty.
tips: Because beetroot puree adds moisture, hold back the water and add it by the spoonful so the dough does not turn sticky.
Let the puree cool fully before kneading; warm puree makes the dough slack and hard to roll.
The dough can be kneaded a day ahead and refrigerated, which actually deepens the colour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with thick coconut curd, a wedge of lemon and a spoon of coconut chutney for a Kerala-style plate.

variations.name: Masala Beetroot Paratha
variations.description: A Karnataka-style stuffed paratha with a cooked beetroot filling perfumed with garam masala and roasted coriander, so the sweetness is wrapped in warm, savoury spice. The beetroot is grated and sauteed until dry, keeping the paratha from turning soggy. Rich, aromatic and a shade more grown-up than the plain version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Sturdy emmer crumb holds the spiced beetroot filling without tearing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Used to saute the filling dry and to roast the parathas golden

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 0.75 cup water into a soft dough and rest, covered, for 15 minutes.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat and crackle 0.75 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then add the chopped onion and fry until soft.

Stir in the 1.5 cups grated beetroot with 1 tsp garam masala, 1.5 tsp roasted coriander powder, 0.75 tsp red chilli, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt, and cook 6 to 8 minutes until completely dry, then mix in the coriander and cool.
Cup each dough ball, spoon in 2 tbsp of the cooled beetroot masala, seal the pleats over the top and flatten gently.
Roll out to a 7-inch round with light, even pressure so the moist filling stays sealed.
Roast on a medium-hot tava, brushing both sides with Anveshan Ghee, for 1 to 2 minutes each until deep golden blisters form.
tips: Cook the grated beetroot until it looks dry and glossy; any residual moisture will tear the paratha as you roll.
Cooling the filling completely before stuffing prevents the dough from going slack.
The masala filling keeps for two days refrigerated and doubles as a quick sandwich stuffing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of cucumber raita and a spoon of lemon pickle, with extra ghee melting on top.

variations.name: Spicy Beetroot Paratha
variations.description: An Andhra-inspired paratha that plays the beetroot's natural sweetness against sharp green chilli and freshly cracked black pepper for a bold, sinus-clearing heat. Wood-pressed sesame oil in the dough adds a toasty Andhra note. Vivid in colour and fierce in flavour, it is for those who want their vegetables with attitude.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Wholegrain emmer stands up to the punchy chilli-pepper beetroot

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: A classic Andhra fat that gives the dough a nutty, toasted backbone

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: For roasting the parathas crisp and golden

steps: Rub 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, then knead with roughly 0.75 cup water to a supple dough and rest 15 minutes.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, add the chopped curry leaves and grated garlic, and fry 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add the 1.5 cups grated beetroot, minced green chilli, 1 tsp cracked black pepper and 0.5 tsp salt, and saute 6 to 7 minutes until dry and glossy, then cool.
Fill each flattened dough ball with 2 tbsp of the spicy beetroot, gather and pinch the edges shut, and pat into a thick disc.
Dust and roll out to a 7-inch round, easing gently from the centre so the fiery filling does not break through.
Cook on a medium-hot tava, brushing with Anveshan Ghee, for 1 to 2 minutes a side until crisp brown spots appear and the pepper smells fragrant.
tips: The mustard-and-curry-leaf tempering is what turns this from a plain spicy paratha into an unmistakably Andhra one.
Reduce the beetroot moisture fully on the heat; wet filling and high chilli together make sealing very tricky.
Serve with something cooling, as the black pepper heat builds with each paratha.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a bowl of plain curd or a coconut-based pachadi to temper the heat, plus a wedge of lime.

variations.name: Garlic Beetroot Paratha
