variations.description: A Telangana-style paratha where a generous hit of garlic, toasted in ghee, plays off the sweet earthiness of beetroot for a deeply savoury filling. The garlic caramelises as the paratha roasts, filling the kitchen with an irresistible aroma. Comforting, colourful and full of character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The nutty emmer base complements the toasted garlic beautifully

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: For toasting the garlic and roasting the parathas to a golden crust

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 0.75 cup water to a soft dough and rest, covered, for 15 minutes.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and toast the grated garlic for 40 seconds until pale gold, then add the chopped onion and cook until soft.

Tip in the 1.5 cups grated beetroot with 0.75 tsp red chilli, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, crushed kasuri methi and 0.5 tsp salt, and saute 6 to 8 minutes until dry, then fold in the coriander and cool.
Hollow each dough ball, load 2 tbsp of the garlic beetroot, pinch the seam closed and flatten into a disc.
Roll out to a 7-inch round with gentle pressure so the filling stays neatly enclosed.
Roast on a medium tava, brushing both faces with Anveshan Ghee, for 1 to 2 minutes each until golden and the garlic smells sweet and nutty.
tips: Stop toasting the garlic while it is still pale gold; browned garlic turns bitter against the sweet beetroot.
Squeeze the grated beetroot lightly before cooking if it seems very juicy, to speed up the drying.
This filling makes a fantastic wrap stuffing with a smear of curd the next day.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with garlic pickle and plain curd, or alongside a simple tomato dal for a complete meal.

variations.name: Cheesy Beetroot Paratha
variations.description: A fun, family-pleasing paratha where sweet cooked beetroot is bound with melting cheese for a pink-and-golden surprise inside. The cheese mellows the earthiness and the whole thing turns gooey and comforting on the tava. A colourful way to win over reluctant vegetable eaters.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Wholegrain emmer keeps the cheesy beetroot paratha from feeling too rich

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: To saute the beetroot dry and roast the parathas to a golden crust

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and around 0.75 cup water into a soft dough and rest it, covered, for 15 minutes.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, saute the chopped onion and minced green chilli until soft, then add the 1.25 cups grated beetroot with 1 tsp roasted cumin powder and 0.25 tsp salt and cook 6 minutes until dry, and cool completely.
Mix the cooled beetroot with 1 cup grated cheese, 0.5 tsp crushed black pepper and the coriander until evenly combined.
Flatten each dough ball, place 2 tbsp of the cheesy beetroot in the centre, seal the edges over the top and pat into a disc.
Roll out slowly to a 7-inch round so the soft cheese filling stays sealed inside.
Cook on a medium tava, brushing with Anveshan Ghee, for 1 to 2 minutes a side until golden and the cheese is just melting at the seams.
tips: Cool the beetroot fully before adding cheese, or the cheese will melt prematurely and make the mix hard to handle.
Chill the assembled filling briefly so it firms up and seals more easily inside the dough.
Serve straight away while the cheese is still stretchy and molten.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with tomato ketchup or a tangy mint chutney, ideal as an after-school snack or light dinner.

variations.name: Classic Bhindi
variations.description: The clean, dry everyday bhindi where okra is sauteed uncovered on brisk heat so it stays firm and never turns slimy. A light onion-tomato masala clings to each piece, brightened with coriander and a finish of ghee. Simple, non-sticky and quick enough for any weeknight.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A generous amount lets the okra fry dry and crisp instead of stewing in its own gum.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing teaspoon gives the plain sabzi a warm, rounded aroma.

steps: Wash 500 g okra, wipe every piece completely dry with a cloth, then top-and-tail and cut into 2 cm rounds; any water left on the skin makes the sabzi sticky.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a wide kadhai on medium-high, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds with 0.5 tsp ajwain, then add the okra and fry uncovered for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the pieces firm up and lose their sliminess.
Push the okra to the side, add 2 sliced onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste in the centre and saute for 5 minutes until the onions soften and turn light gold.
Add 1 chopped tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 4 minutes until the tomato collapses.
Fold everything together and cook uncovered on medium for another 4 to 5 minutes so the masala coats the okra and any moisture cooks off.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp amchur powder, drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and scatter 2 tbsp coriander, then toss once and serve straight away.
tips: Never cover the pan while cooking bhindi; trapped steam is the single biggest cause of slimy okra.
Wipe the okra dry hours ahead and leave it out so the surface is bone-dry before it hits the oil.
Add the amchur only at the end, as its acidity also helps cut any lingering stickiness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulkas and a bowl of moong dal, or roll it into a chapati with a smear of pickle for lunch.

variations.name: Masala Bhindi
variations.description: A Jharkhand-style masala bhindi where the okra is tossed in a fragrant garam-masala onion base for a warmer, spicier profile than the plain version. The garam masala is bloomed late so it perfumes rather than muddies. Rich, aromatic and full-flavoured.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Fries the okra dry first so the masala later clings instead of sliding off.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The garam masala is bloomed in ghee at the end for its full warm aroma.

steps: Wipe 500 g okra bone-dry, trim the ends and slice into 2 cm rounds, keeping the pieces uniform for even frying.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium-high and fry the okra uncovered for 9 minutes until firm and no longer slippery, then lift it out onto a plate.

In the same pan crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds with a 1 inch piece of cinnamon, 3 green cardamoms and 3 cloves, then add 3 chopped onions and 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 8 minutes until golden brown.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 5 minutes until the masala thickens and the oil glistens.
Return the fried okra, fold gently and cook uncovered on medium for 4 minutes so it soaks up the masala without going soft.
Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee separately, stir 1.25 tsp garam masala into it for 10 seconds, pour over the bhindi with 3 tbsp coriander and toss to finish.
tips: Frying and removing the okra first keeps it firm while you build a proper browned masala without overcooking the vegetable.
Blooming garam masala in warm ghee off the heat gives a far more fragrant result than sprinkling it dry.
If the masala turns too thick, loosen it with a tablespoon of hot water rather than adding more oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pairs beautifully with jeera rice and a cucumber-mint raita, or with hot tawa parathas.

variations.name: Spicy Bhindi
variations.description: A fiery Maharashtrian-leaning bhindi where slit green chillies and crushed black pepper drive the heat, sharpened further by a nutty crackle of mustard oil. The okra stays crisp-edged and the pepper gives a lingering warmth. Bold, bright and unapologetically spicy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Its sharp pungency amplifies the green-chilli and pepper heat in this fiery sabzi.

steps: Wipe 500 g okra completely dry, trim and cut into 2 cm rounds, and slit 4 green chillies lengthways.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai on medium-high until it shimmers and the raw smell fades, then crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 15 seconds.
Add the okra and fry uncovered on high for 9 to 10 minutes, stirring now and then, until firm, browned at the edges and non-sticky.
Push the okra aside, add 2 sliced onions, the slit green chillies and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and saute for 5 minutes until the onions soften.
Add 1 chopped tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 4 minutes until pulpy, then fold in the okra.
Crush 1 tsp black pepper coarsely, sprinkle over with 3 tbsp coriander and toss on high for a final 2 minutes so the pepper heat coats every piece.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to shimmering first so its raw bite mellows into a clean, nutty pungency.
Crushing the peppercorns fresh gives a far more aromatic heat than pre-ground pepper.
Keep the pan uncovered throughout; the high, dry heat both keeps the okra crisp and concentrates the chilli flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot bajra bhakri and a cooling spoon of plain curd to balance the fire.

variations.name: Dhaba-style Bhindi
variations.description: A Gujarat-highway dhaba bhindi with a herby kasuri-methi lift and a whisper of jaggery that rounds the spice, the way western dhabas love a sweet-savoury edge. The okra is folded into a glossy onion-tomato masala and finished in ghee. Comforting, aromatic and slightly sweet-hot.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Builds the glossy browned masala the okra folds into.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A teaspoon melts into the masala for the gentle sweet-savoury balance typical of western dhabas.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The kasuri methi is crushed into warm ghee at the end for the classic dhaba aroma.

steps: Wipe 500 g okra dry, trim and cut into 2 cm rounds, then fry them in 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium-high for 9 minutes until firm and set aside.
In the same pan crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, add 3 chopped onions and 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 8 minutes until deep golden.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 5 minutes until the oil separates.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and let it melt for a minute, then return the fried okra and fold to coat in the masala.
Cook uncovered on medium for 4 minutes so the okra absorbs the flavours while staying firm.
Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi into it, pour over with 1 tsp garam masala and 3 tbsp coriander, and toss well before serving.
tips: Let the jaggery fully melt into the masala before the okra returns, so the sweetness distributes evenly.
Crush the kasuri methi between your palms to wake up its aroma before it hits the ghee.
This version holds well in a tiffin because the jaggery-rounded masala keeps the okra tasting fresh even when cool.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with methi thepla or soft phulkas and a spoon of sweet mango chhundo on the side.

variations.name: Home-style Bhindi
variations.description: A minimalist Rajasthani home bhindi cooked with barely any onion, leaning on the vegetable's own flavour with just turmeric, chilli and a lift of amchur for tang. Slow, dry frying gives it a lovely toasted edge. Frugal, honest and endlessly comforting.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: The classic Rajasthani choice, its pungency stands in for the missing onion and spice.

steps: Wipe 500 g okra completely dry, trim and slice into 2 cm rounds so no surface moisture remains.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai on medium-high until shimmering, then crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.5 tsp ajwain with 1 inch grated ginger for 20 seconds.
Add the okra and fry uncovered on medium-high for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until firm, dry and lightly browned.
Add 1 finely chopped onion and cook for 4 minutes until softened, keeping the pan open the whole time.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and toss for 4 minutes so the spices toast onto the okra.
Finish with 0.75 tsp amchur powder and 2 tbsp coriander, toss for a minute and serve hot.
tips: Ajwain here aids digestion and cuts any heaviness, a classic touch in desert-region cooking.
With so little masala, the dryness of the okra is everything, so keep the flame high enough to keep it frying rather than steaming.
A pinch more amchur at the end brightens the whole dish if it tastes flat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra roti smeared with white butter and a side of raw onion and green chilli.

variations.name: Classic Cabbage Paratha
variations.description: A light, everyday paratha stuffed with finely shredded cabbage that is salted, squeezed and briefly sauteed so the filling stays dry and just-tender. Cabbage turns mild and faintly sweet once cooked, making this an easy family favourite. Ghee-griddled to a spotty gold, it is quick, wholesome and never heavy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: wraps the soft cabbage filling in a tender crust that stays light, never dense

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: wilts the shredded cabbage and bastes the paratha to a golden finish

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with a little salt and about 0.75 cup water for 6 minutes into a soft dough, cover, and rest it 15 minutes.
Toss 2 cups shredded cabbage with 0.5 tsp salt, wait 10 minutes, and squeeze out the water so the filling will not turn soggy.

Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, add 1 tsp ginger-chilli paste and the squeezed cabbage, and saute on medium 3 minutes with 1 tsp roasted cumin, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 3 tbsp coriander and remaining salt until just tender; cool it.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, flatten one, place 2 tbsp of the cabbage filling in the centre, pleat the edges shut, and press flat.
Dust with khapli atta and roll into a 6-inch round with gentle strokes so the light filling stays enclosed.
Cook on a medium tava, brushing both sides with Anveshan Ghee, flipping until golden-brown spots appear, about 3 minutes per paratha.
tips: Salting and squeezing the cabbage is essential, as raw cabbage releases a surprising amount of water.
Keep the saute brief; overcooked cabbage smells strong and loses its fresh sweetness.
Shred the cabbage as fine as possible so it packs neatly and does not tear the rolled paratha.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with plain curd and a spoon of green-chilli pickle; a bowl of tomato saar or thin dal alongside makes it a full meal.

variations.name: Masala Cabbage Paratha
variations.description: A Goan-style cabbage paratha where the filling is warmed with garam masala and coriander powder and finished with fresh grated coconut for a coastal sweetness. Cooked in wood-pressed coconut oil, it carries an unmistakable seaside aroma. The coconut keeps the mild cabbage moist and flavourful.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: the nutty flour pairs naturally with coconut and holds the spiced cabbage filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed coconut oil lends the paratha its coastal Goan fragrance as it griddles

steps: Bring 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta together with salt and roughly 0.75 cup water, kneading 6 minutes into a pliable dough; rest it covered 15 minutes.
Salt 2 cups shredded cabbage, rest 10 minutes, and squeeze out the moisture thoroughly.

Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, saute 2 minced green chillies and the cabbage 3 minutes, then add 0.33 cup grated coconut, 1 tsp garam masala, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and remaining salt, cook 2 minutes, finish with 1 tbsp lemon juice, and cool it.
Split the dough into 8 balls, cup one, spoon in 2 tbsp of the coconut-cabbage filling, seal the edges over the top, and press flat.
Roll into a 6-inch round on a floured board, working gently so the filling stays centred.
Griddle on a medium tava, brushing both faces with Anveshan Coconut Oil, flipping until golden and freckled, about 3 minutes per paratha.
tips: Use fresh grated coconut for the best moisture and aroma; soak desiccated coconut in warm milk if using it.
Stir the lemon juice in off the heat so its brightness is not lost.
Cook the cabbage only until wilted, keeping a slight crunch for texture in the filling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a tangy tomato-coconut chutney and a bowl of sol kadhi or plain buttermilk to complete the coastal mood.

variations.name: Spicy Cabbage Paratha
variations.description: A warming Kashmiri-inspired cabbage paratha for cold weather, the filling spiked with slit green chillies, cracked black pepper and a hint of fennel and dry ginger. Wood-pressed mustard oil, the valley's staple fat, gives it a pungent backbone. Robust and gently fiery, it makes a comforting winter breakfast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: the hearty flour suits a warming winter paratha and grips the spiced cabbage

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the valley's signature pungent oil deepens the filling and crisps the crust

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with salt and about 0.75 cup water for 6 minutes into a soft dough, cover, and rest it 15 minutes.
Salt 2 cups shredded cabbage, rest 10 minutes, and wring out the water so the filling stays dry.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, lower the heat, add 4 chopped green chillies and the cabbage, and saute 3 minutes with 1 tsp cracked pepper, 1 tsp fennel powder, 0.5 tsp dry ginger and remaining salt; cool it.
Roll the dough into 8 balls, flatten one, mound 2 tbsp filling in the centre, close and pinch the edges, and press flat.
Dust and roll into a 6-inch round, patching any spot where a chilli piece threatens to poke through.
Cook on a medium-high tava, brushing both faces with Anveshan Mustard Oil, turning until deep golden and blistered, about 3 minutes per paratha.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to smoking point first to mellow its sharpness before the cabbage goes in.
Fennel and dry ginger give this its Kashmiri character, so keep both in even if you reduce the chilli.
Serve extra hot, as this warming filling is best on a cold day.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with Kashmiri-style salted yogurt whisked with roasted cumin, and a side of walnut chutney.

variations.name: Garlic Cabbage Paratha
variations.description: A Himachali hill-style cabbage paratha threaded with garlic browned in ghee until sweet and nutty. The garlic lifts the mild cabbage into something deeply savoury and warming. Sturdy and comforting, it is the sort of food hill kitchens make to keep out the chill.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: gives a filling hill-style paratha with a soft, satisfying chew

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: browns the garlic to a sweet gold and wilts the cabbage down

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with salt and roughly 0.75 cup water for 6 minutes into a soft dough, then rest it covered 15 minutes.
Salt 2 cups shredded cabbage, rest 10 minutes, and squeeze out the water thoroughly.

Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, fry 2 tbsp minced garlic on low for 2 minutes until pale gold, then add the cabbage and saute 3 minutes with 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander powder, 3 tbsp coriander and remaining salt; cool it.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, cup one, place 2 tbsp of the garlicky cabbage inside, seal the edges together, and flatten gently.
Roll into a 6-inch round on a dusted board, easing the pin outward so the filling spreads evenly.
Cook on a medium tava, brushing both sides with Anveshan Ghee, flipping until golden and fragrant with garlic, about 3 minutes per paratha.
tips: Fry the garlic only to pale gold before the cabbage goes in, or it turns bitter.
Mince the garlic finely so no one bites into a raw-tasting chunk.
The garlic-cabbage filling can be made a day ahead and refrigerated; drain any liquid before stuffing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thick curd, a knob of butter and a spoon of red-chilli garlic chutney.

variations.name: Cheesy Cabbage Paratha
variations.description: A crowd-pleasing version from Odisha's cafe scene, folding grated cheese through the shredded cabbage so it turns rich and gooey. The cheese binds the cabbage into a soft, sliceable core that children adore. It is the easiest way to get a plate of greens into a reluctant eater.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: wraps the soft cheesy cabbage core in a sturdy yet tender crust

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: crisps the paratha to a golden shell while keeping the cheesy filling molten

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.75 tsp salt and about 0.75 cup water for 6 minutes into a soft dough, cover, and rest it 15 minutes.
Salt 1.5 cups shredded cabbage, rest 10 minutes, squeeze out the water, and pat it dry so the filling is not wet.
Mix the drained cabbage with 0.75 cup grated mozzarella, 0.5 tsp black pepper, 0.5 tsp chilli flakes and 0.5 tsp mixed herbs so the cheese coats the shreds.
Divide the dough into 6 balls, roll one into a 4-inch disc, spoon 3 tbsp of the cheesy cabbage in the middle, seal the edges over, and press flat.
Roll out gently to a 6-inch round, keeping the seam side down so the cheese stays enclosed.
Cook on a medium tava, brushing both sides with Anveshan Ghee and pressing gently, until golden and crisp with a melting centre, about 3 minutes per paratha.
tips: Squeeze and dry the cabbage well; extra moisture is the main reason a cheesy paratha turns soggy.
Serve immediately, as reheated cheesy parathas lose the stretch that makes them fun.
Use raw squeezed cabbage rather than sauteed here, so it keeps a light crunch against the cheese.
variations.servingSuggestion: Cut into strips and serve with ketchup or a herby yogurt dip, alongside a simple carrot-cucumber salad.

variations.name: Classic Capsicum
variations.description: The everyday North Indian shimla mirch sabzi in which crisp-tender capsicum is tossed through a quick, glossy onion-tomato masala. It stays slightly crunchy and forward with cumin and coriander, a fifteen-minute stir-fry that turns a plain bell pepper into a proper accompaniment for hot phulkas.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: its clean, nutty body lets the peppers stay bright without greasiness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: swirled in at the end for a nutty aroma that lifts the finished sabzi

steps: Deseed 3 capsicums and cut them into 1-inch squares, then finely chop 2 onions and 2 tomatoes and keep them ready.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds until they sizzle and turn fragrant, about 20 seconds.
Add the onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and sauté for 5 minutes until soft and pale gold at the edges.
Stir in the tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, cooking 4 minutes until the tomatoes collapse and the oil beads at the sides.
Add the capsicum squares and 1 tsp salt, toss to coat, then cover and cook on low for 6 minutes so they turn tender but keep a slight bite.
Uncover, sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala, swirl in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander tossed through off the heat.
tips: Keep the flame lively while the capsicum cooks; low slow steaming makes it soggy and dull instead of crisp-tender.
Choose thick-walled, glossy peppers as they hold their shape and stay juicier than thin, wrinkled ones.
A pinch of sugar or jaggery smooths any sharpness if your tomatoes are very tart.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile it beside a bowl of yellow dal and cucumber raita, with soft phulkas fresh off the tawa for a light weekday thali.

variations.name: Besan Masala Capsicum
variations.description: A beloved UP home preparation where roasted gram flour coats the capsicum in a dry, savoury crust flecked with garam masala and amchur. The besan soaks up the masala and clings to each piece, giving a nutty, almost crumbly texture that is completely unlike the usual gravy sabzi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: its pungency is the traditional backbone of this dry UP-style besan sabzi

steps: Deseed 4 capsicums and slice them into thin long strips so they cook quickly and hold the besan coating.
Dry-roast 4 tbsp besan in a pan on low for 3 minutes until it smells toasty and turns a shade darker, then tip it onto a plate and set aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just begins to smoke, lower the flame, and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1 tsp fennel seeds for 20 seconds.
Add the capsicum strips with 1 tsp salt and stir-fry uncovered on medium-high for 5 minutes until they soften and pick up light char spots.
Sprinkle in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp coriander powder, tossing for a minute so the spices coat every strip.
Scatter the roasted besan over the capsicum and keep tossing on low for 4 minutes until it turns dry and grainy, then finish with 0.75 tsp garam masala and 1 tsp amchur.
tips: Roast the besan properly before adding it or the sabzi will taste raw and pasty rather than nutty.
Keep tossing constantly once the besan goes in so it toasts evenly instead of forming lumps.
Make it ahead for tiffins as this dry sabzi holds beautifully for hours without turning watery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Roll it into a hot ajwain paratha with a smear of white butter, or serve alongside dal and rice for a satisfying vegetarian spread.

variations.name: Spicy Pepper Capsicum
variations.description: A fiery Malwa-style stir-fry that leans on slit green chillies and coarsely crushed black pepper rather than gravy for its heat. Crushed peanuts add a rustic crunch and the whole thing stays dry, smoky and unapologetically hot, meant to wake up a simple bajra roti.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday Malwa cooking fat that carries the pepper and chilli heat cleanly

steps: Cut 3 capsicums into thick strips, slit 4 green chillies lengthwise, and coarsely crush 1 tsp black pepper in a mortar.
Dry-roast 3 tbsp peanuts in a kadai until spotty and fragrant, then crush them roughly and set aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add 6 sliced garlic cloves and the slit green chillies and fry for a minute until aromatic.
Add 1 sliced onion and sauté on high for 3 minutes until it softens and takes on golden edges.
Tip in the capsicum with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, the crushed black pepper and 1 tsp salt, stir-frying on high for 6 minutes until charred at the edges but still crunchy.
Fold through the crushed peanuts, cook a final minute, and finish with 1 tsp lemon juice squeezed over off the heat.
tips: Crush the pepper fresh just before cooking; pre-ground powder loses the sharp fragrance this dish depends on.
For extra heat leave the green chilli seeds in, or deseed them for a milder but still peppery result.
Add the peanuts only at the end so they keep their crunch instead of going soft in the pan.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot with bajra or jowar rotla and a dollop of plain curd to temper the black-pepper heat.

variations.name: Dhaba-style Capsicum
variations.description: A rich, semi-dry roadside-style capsicum with a clinging onion-tomato masala perfumed by crushed kasuri methi and garam masala. A knob of butter and a splash of cream round it into something indulgent, the peppers glossy and coated rather than dry, exactly as a highway dhaba would ladle it out.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the base frying fat that gives the dhaba masala its robust body

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a small dhaba-style swap for sugar to round the tomato tang in the masala

steps: Cut 3 capsicums into 1-inch pieces, finely chop 2 onions, and puree 3 tomatoes to a smooth paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, add the onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, and fry on medium for 6 minutes until deep golden.
Pour in the tomato puree with 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, and cook 8 minutes until the masala thickens and the oil separates at the edges.
Add the capsicum pieces with 1 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, cover, and cook on low for 5 minutes until just tender.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi between your palms and sprinkle it in with 0.75 tsp garam masala, stirring for a minute to release its aroma.
Finish with 1 tbsp butter and 2 tbsp cream swirled through gently, letting it simmer one minute until glossy and rich.
tips: Roasting the kasuri methi briefly on your palm before crushing amplifies its signature dhaba fragrance.
Keep the masala semi-dry and clinging; add only a splash of water if it catches, as too much loosens the coating.
For a smoky note, give the finished dish a quick charcoal dhungar under a covered lid for two minutes.
variations.servingSuggestion: Mop it up with butter-brushed tandoori roti or laccha paratha, with sliced onions and a lemon wedge on the side.

variations.name: Dry Aloo Capsicum
variations.description: A no-onion, no-tomato Bihari everyday sabzi where cubed potato and capsicum are stir-fried together in pungent mustard oil and finished with amchur. It is dry, rustic and lunchbox-friendly, the potato lending body while the capsicum keeps its fresh snap, seasoned simply so the mustard oil shines.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the defining pungent fat of Bihari dry sabzis, essential to this recipe's character

steps: Peel and cube 3 potatoes into 1/2-inch pieces and cut 2 capsicums into similar-sized chunks.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it smokes lightly, then lower the flame and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds with 2 broken dried red chillies.
Add the potato cubes with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, cover, and cook on low for 10 minutes, stirring twice, until nearly tender.
Uncover and add the capsicum with 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp coriander powder, tossing on medium-high for 6 minutes until both vegetables are cooked with browned edges.
Raise the heat for the last 2 minutes to crisp the potatoes lightly and dry off any moisture in the pan.
Turn off the heat, dust over 1 tsp amchur, and toss well so the tang coats everything evenly.
tips: Cut the potatoes small and even so they cook through in the same time the capsicum needs.
Always heat mustard oil to smoking point first to mellow its raw sharpness before the tempering goes in.
Add amchur off the heat; cooking it dulls the bright sourness that lifts this simple sabzi.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pack it with plain parathas and mango pickle for a classic Bihari tiffin, or serve with dal-bhaat at home.

variations.name: Classic Carrot Paratha
variations.description: A naturally sweet, sunny-orange paratha where grated carrot is lightly sauteed to drive off its moisture and then kneaded straight into the khapli dough. Cooking the carrot first concentrates its sweetness and keeps the dough from turning wet. Soft and mildly spiced, it is a gentle, colourful way to slip more vegetables onto the plate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: takes on the grated carrot into a soft, sweet-tinged dough that stays pliable

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: softens the grated carrot as it cooks and bastes the paratha to a golden finish

steps: Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and saute 1.5 cups grated carrot with 1 tsp ginger-chilli paste on medium for 4 minutes until softened and dry, then cool it fully.
In a bowl combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, the cooked carrot, 1 tsp roasted cumin, 0.5 tsp ajwain, 3 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp salt.
Knead in about 0.5 cup water a little at a time for 6 minutes into a soft, non-sticky dough; cover and rest it 15 minutes.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, dust with khapli atta, and roll each into a 6-inch round of even thickness.
Heat a tava on medium and cook the first side 45 seconds until faint bubbles rise, then flip and brush with Anveshan Ghee.
Turn once more, ghee the second side, and press until golden-brown spots cover both faces, about 3 minutes per paratha.
tips: Sauteing the carrot first is what keeps the dough dry; raw grated carrot weeps water as it rests.
Grate the carrot fine so it blends into the dough without leaving hard shreds.
The dough's natural sweetness makes these a hit with children, especially cut into small rounds.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a bowl of plain curd and a spoon of lemon or mixed pickle; they also pack beautifully into a lunchbox with a smear of butter.

variations.name: Masala Carrot Paratha
variations.description: A Karnataka-style carrot paratha lifted with garam masala, coriander powder and a curry-leaf tempering that gives it a distinctly South Indian character. The warm spices play against the carrot's sweetness for a savoury, aromatic result. Cooked in wood-pressed groundnut oil, it eats like a hearty tiffin.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: gives a wholesome, sturdy dough that carries the spiced carrot and curry leaves

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: tempers the curry leaves and griddles the paratha with a mellow South Indian warmth

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 12 curry leaves for 20 seconds, then add 1.5 cups grated carrot and the minced green chilli and saute 4 minutes until dry; cool it.
In a bowl mix 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with the tempered carrot, 1 tsp garam masala, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt.
Knead in roughly 0.5 cup water in stages for 6 minutes into a soft, pliable dough; rest it covered for 15 minutes.
Shape the dough into 8 balls and roll each on a floured board into a 6-inch round of even thickness.
Warm a tava on medium-high, lay a paratha down, and cook 40 seconds until the surface turns matte.
Flip, brush with Anveshan Groundnut Oil, turn again, oil the second side, and press until both faces are deep golden, about 3 minutes per paratha.
tips: Crush the curry leaves lightly as they crackle to release more of their aroma into the carrot.
Cook the carrot until it looks glossy and dry before mixing, or the masala dough turns slack.
These reheat well, so make a double batch of dough for the next day's breakfast.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and a small bowl of sambar for dipping, the way a Karnataka tiffin plate would frame it.

variations.name: Spicy Carrot Paratha
variations.description: An Andhra-hot carrot paratha where the vegetable's sweetness is deliberately set against the fire of green chillies and cracked black pepper. The contrast of sweet and searing is what makes it addictive. Cooked in wood-pressed sesame oil, it carries a toasty depth true to Andhra kitchens.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: balances the fiery seasoning with a grounding, wholesome chew

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed gingelly oil adds the deep toasted note that defines Andhra cooking

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, add 4 minced green chillies and 1.5 cups grated carrot, and saute on medium 4 minutes until the carrot softens and dries; cool it fully.
Combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with the spicy carrot, 1 tsp cracked black pepper, 1 tsp roasted cumin, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt.
Knead in about 0.5 cup water in stages for 6 minutes into a soft dough; cover and rest it 15 minutes.
Divide into 8 balls and roll each into a 6-inch round, dusting lightly so the dough releases cleanly.
Cook on a medium-high tava for 40 seconds until the surface dulls, then flip and brush with Anveshan Sesame Oil.
Turn again, oil the second face, and press until charred-gold and blistered, about 3 minutes per paratha.
tips: Deseed the green chillies if you want the aroma without the full Andhra heat.
Add the cracked pepper to the dough rather than the pan so its perfume survives the griddling.
A spoon of curd worked into the dough tempers the heat and softens the finished paratha.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with cooling tomato pachadi and thick curd to balance the heat, with sliced raw onion and lime alongside.

variations.name: Garlic Carrot Paratha
variations.description: A Telangana-style paratha marrying sweet carrot with garlic browned in ghee until nutty, a pairing that turns the mild vegetable deeply savoury. The garlic rounds out the sweetness into something wholly moreish. Rustic and comforting, it needs little beyond a bowl of curd.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: holds the garlicky carrot dough together with a soft, wholesome bite

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: browns the garlic to a mellow sweetness and cooks the carrot down

steps: Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and fry 2 tbsp minced garlic on low for 2 minutes until pale gold, then add 1.5 cups grated carrot and cook 4 minutes until soft and dry; cool it.
In a bowl combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with the garlicky carrot, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander powder, 3 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp salt.
Knead in roughly 0.5 cup water in stages for 6 minutes into a soft dough; cover and rest it 15 minutes.
Roll the dough into 8 balls and flatten each into a 6-inch round, dusting so it does not stick.
Cook on a medium tava for 45 seconds until faint bubbles form, flip, and brush with Anveshan Ghee.
Turn again, ghee the second side, and press until golden and heady with garlic, about 3 minutes per paratha.
tips: Brown the garlic only to pale gold before the carrot goes in, or it will taste bitter.
Mince the garlic fine so its sweetness spreads through every bite of the dough.
Reserve a spoon of the garlic-ghee to brush over the hot paratha for an extra aromatic finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with curd tempered with mustard seeds and curry leaves, and a side of tomato-garlic pachadi.

variations.name: Cheesy Carrot Paratha
variations.description: A playful stuffed version popular in Bihar's small-town cafes, where the sweet carrot dough encases a molten cheese core so bright orange gives way to a stretchy centre. The carrot's sweetness balances the salty cheese beautifully. It is an easy win for fussy young eaters.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: forms a pliable carrot dough that seals cleanly around the melting cheese

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: crisps the orange crust to gold while keeping the cheese inside molten

steps: Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and saute 1.5 cups grated carrot on medium for 4 minutes until soft and dry, then cool it completely.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with the cooked carrot, 0.75 tsp salt and about 0.4 cup water for 6 minutes into a soft dough; rest it 15 minutes.
Mix 1 cup grated mozzarella with 0.5 cup grated processed cheese, 0.5 tsp black pepper and 0.5 tsp chilli flakes for the filling.
Divide the dough into 6 balls, roll one into a 4-inch disc, place 3 tbsp of the cheese mix in the centre, gather the edges over, and seal.
Dust and roll gently into a 6-inch paratha, keeping the pressure even so the cheese stays enclosed.
Cook on a medium tava, brushing both sides with Anveshan Ghee and pressing the centre, until golden and crisp with a molten core, about 3 minutes per paratha.
tips: Cook and cool the carrot before it goes into the dough, so the cheese does not sit in a wet crumb.
Serve straight off the tava while the cheese still pulls into strings.
A firmer mozzarella-heavy blend stretches better than a soft, watery one.
variations.servingSuggestion: Cut into wedges and serve with a smoky tomato-chilli dip or ketchup for children, and a cooling mint raita for the adults.

variations.name: Classic Chana Masala
variations.description: The definitive Delhi-style chana masala: nutty kabuli chickpeas simmered in a glossy onion-tomato gravy sharpened with amchur and a whisper of jaggery. The chickpeas stay whole but turn creamy inside, and the gravy clings to every one. This is the version that anchors every dhaba thali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil gives the base a clean, nutty backbone without masking spices

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoon of bilona ghee stirred in at the end rounds off the tang and adds aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a small pinch balances the amchur and tomato acidity without turning the gravy sweet

steps: Soak 1.5 cups kabuli chana in plenty of water overnight, then pressure-cook with 3 cups fresh water, 0.5 tsp salt and a pinch of turmeric for 5 to 6 whistles until a chickpea crushes easily between two fingers.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a heavy kadai over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds until they sizzle and turn fragrant, about 30 seconds.

Add 2 finely chopped onions and fry over medium heat, stirring often, until deep golden brown, roughly 8 to 10 minutes; then stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute until the raw smell lifts.
Add 3 pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, and cook on medium heat until the oil separates and beads at the edges, about 8 minutes.
Tip in the drained chickpeas along with 1.25 cups of their cooking liquid, add the remaining 0.75 tsp salt, and simmer uncovered for 12 to 15 minutes until the gravy thickens and darkens.
Mash a ladleful of chickpeas against the side of the pan and stir back in to naturally thicken the gravy to a coating consistency.
Finish with 1 tsp amchur powder, 0.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 0.75 tsp garam masala and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, simmer 2 more minutes, and garnish with 3 tbsp chopped fresh coriander.
tips: For an even darker dhaba colour, drop a used tea bag or a small muslin of tea leaves into the pressure cooker with the chana and remove before making the gravy.
If the gravy tastes flat, it usually needs salt or a touch more amchur rather than more chilli; add a pinch at a time and taste.
This reheats beautifully the next day; loosen with a splash of hot water as the chickpeas keep drinking up the gravy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with fluffy bhature or a stack of kulchas, a raw onion-and-lemon salad, and a green chilli on the side for the full Chole-Bhature experience.

variations.name: Masala Chana Masala
variations.description: A Gujarati-leaning take built on a generous hand of freshly roasted coriander powder, which gives the gravy an earthy, citrusy warmth rather than heat. A light finish of jaggery nods to the region's sweet-savoury palate. The masala is thinner and more soupy, made to be scooped up with rotli.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the classic Gujarati cooking fat; its mild nuttiness suits the coriander-forward masala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the signature gentle sweetness of a Gujarati gravy, added to round the coriander and tomato

steps: Pressure-cook 1.5 cups soaked kabuli chana with 3 cups water and 0.5 tsp salt for 5 to 6 whistles until soft, and keep the cooking liquid aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan on medium heat and temper 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds until they pop, then add 8 curry leaves and let them crackle for 10 seconds.
Add 1 large finely chopped onion and saute for 5 to 6 minutes until soft and pale gold, then stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and cook 1 minute.

Dry-roast 2.5 tsp coriander powder in a small pan for 40 seconds until fragrant, then add it along with 4 pureed tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, cooking on medium heat until the oil floats to the top, about 7 minutes.
Add the cooked chickpeas with 1.5 cups of their liquid and the remaining 0.75 tsp salt, and simmer this deliberately thinner gravy for 10 minutes.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and simmer 2 minutes more until it dissolves and the flavours meld into a mellow sweet-savoury balance.
Turn off the heat and finish with 3 tbsp chopped fresh coriander stirred through the hot gravy.
tips: Roasting the coriander powder fresh is what defines this version; skip it and the gravy loses its signature earthiness.
Keep this gravy loose and spoonable rather than thick, as it is traditionally eaten with soft phulka rotli.
A squeeze of lemon at the table brightens the sweetness if it leans too mellow for your taste.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with soft ghee-brushed rotli and a bowl of plain curd, or spoon over steamed rice with a wedge of lime for a light weekday lunch.

variations.name: Kadai Chana Masala
variations.description: A semi-dry kadai treatment where chickpeas meet charred capsicum and a coarse, freshly pounded kadai masala of coriander seeds and dried red chillies. The gravy is thick and clingy rather than soupy, with the crunch of onion and pepper wedges left visible. Bold, smoky and built for scooping with roti.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil heated to smoking gives the kadai its characteristic pungent edge

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: swirled in at the end to soften the mustard oil's bite and add a glossy finish

steps: Pressure-cook 1.5 cups soaked kabuli chana with 3 cups water and 0.5 tsp salt for 5 to 6 whistles until tender, then drain and reserve the liquid.
Make the kadai masala: dry-roast 2 tbsp coriander seeds and 3 dried red chillies in a pan over medium heat until deeply fragrant, about 2 minutes, then cool and pound to a coarse powder.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just begins to smoke, lower the heat, and add 2 diced onions, frying for 5 minutes until they soften at the edges.
Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute, then add 2 chopped tomatoes and 0.5 tsp turmeric and cook until pulpy and the oil separates, about 6 minutes.

Stir in most of the pounded kadai masala and the drained chickpeas, add just 0.5 cup of the reserved liquid and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, and cook on medium-high heat for 8 minutes until thick and clinging.
Add 1 large capsicum cut into thick wedges and toss on high heat for 3 to 4 minutes so it stays crunchy and lightly charred at the edges.
Crush 1 tsp kasuri methi between your palms over the pan, swirl in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and the last of the kadai masala, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander.
tips: Pound the kadai masala coarse, not fine; the little gritty flecks of coriander seed are the whole point of the texture.
Add the capsicum only in the last few minutes so it keeps its snap and doesn't turn soggy.
For a smokier finish, char the capsicum wedges separately in a dry pan before folding them in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve straight from the kadai with butter naan or laccha paratha and a side of sliced cucumber and radish to cut the richness.

variations.name: Handi Chana Masala
variations.description: A slow handi-cooked chana where whole spices are bloomed in ghee and the chickpeas are sealed under a lid to steam in their own aromatic steam. There is no ground masala here; the flavour comes entirely from cinnamon, cardamom, cloves and bay leaf infusing the gravy. Rustic, deeply perfumed and gently spiced.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: whole spices bloom best in bilona ghee, which carries their aroma into every chickpea

steps: Pressure-cook 1.5 cups soaked kabuli chana with 3 cups water and 0.5 tsp salt for 5 to 6 whistles until soft, reserving the liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a deep handi over medium heat and bloom 1 inch cinnamon, 4 cardamom pods, 4 cloves, 1 bay leaf and 8 peppercorns until they swell and turn fragrant, about 40 seconds.
Add 2 sliced onions and fry gently for 8 to 10 minutes until golden and jammy, letting the whole spices infuse the ghee all the while.

Stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then add 3 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and cook until the tomatoes collapse and the ghee glistens on top, about 8 minutes.
Add the drained chickpeas and 1 cup of the reserved liquid with the remaining 0.75 tsp salt, stir once, and bring to a gentle simmer.
Cover the handi with a tight lid, lower the heat to minimum, and let it dum-cook undisturbed for 15 minutes so the whole-spice aroma penetrates the chickpeas.
Uncover, mash a few chickpeas to thicken the gravy, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander, discarding the bay leaf before serving.
tips: Warn diners about the whole spices, or fish out the cinnamon, cloves and bay leaf before serving to avoid a surprise bite.
The longer and slower the dum, the deeper the aroma; resist lifting the lid to peek in the first 10 minutes.
No garam masala is needed here because the whole spices do that job; adding powder would muddy the clean, perfumed flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle into a warm bowl and serve with jeera rice and a raita of whisked curd, roasted cumin and mint to echo the aromatic spicing.

variations.name: Punjabi Chana Masala
variations.description: The rich, restaurant-style Punjabi chana: a smooth onion-tomato gravy enriched with cream and finished with crushed kasuri methi, its butter swapped for aromatic bilona ghee. It is fuller and more luxurious than the dhaba version, with a mellow, buttery depth. This is the one you make for a special Sunday lunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: used in place of butter for the same richness plus a nutty bilona aroma

steps: Pressure-cook 1.5 cups soaked kabuli chana with 3 cups water and 0.5 tsp salt for 5 to 6 whistles until very soft, and set aside with the liquid.
Soak 10 cashews in warm water for 15 minutes, then blend with 2 boiled onions to a silky paste for the creamy base.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add the onion-cashew paste and fry for 5 minutes until it thickens and no longer smells raw.

Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute, then stir in 3 pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder and cook until the ghee separates, about 8 minutes.
Add the drained chickpeas with 1 cup reserved liquid and the remaining 0.75 tsp salt, and simmer gently for 12 minutes so the gravy turns thick and velvety.
Lower the heat, stir in 3 tbsp cream and 0.75 tsp garam masala, and simmer 2 minutes without letting it boil hard.
Crush 1.5 tsp kasuri methi between your palms, sprinkle it over the top, and give one final gentle stir before serving.
tips: The cashew-onion paste is what makes this gravy restaurant-smooth; blend it well and strain if you want it silkier.
Add cream on low heat and never let it come to a rolling boil, or it can split and turn grainy.
Make the gravy base a day ahead and add chickpeas and cream just before serving for an easy dinner-party dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter-ghee laccha paratha or saffron pulao, topped with a swirl of cream and thin ginger juliennes for a festive presentation.

variations.name: Classic Amritsari Chole
variations.description: The dark, robust Amritsari-Pindi chole where chickpeas are boiled with tea and whole spices until almost black, then tossed in a dry-roasted chole masala sharpened with anardana. There is barely any gravy; the masala clings tight to each glossy chickpea. Punchy, tangy and built for bhature.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil gives Amritsari chole its bold, pungent Punjabi character

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a final spoon of bilona ghee glazes the dark, dry masala and lifts the aroma

steps: Soak 1.5 cups kabuli chana overnight, then pressure-cook with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp salt and 2 tsp black tea tied in a muslin for 6 whistles until soft and darkened; discard the tea bundle.
Dry-roast 1 tbsp coriander seeds, 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1.5 tsp anardana until deeply fragrant, about 2 minutes, then grind to a coarse chole masala.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it smokes, lower the heat, and fry 2 finely chopped onions for 9 minutes until deep brown.
Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder and cook until the oil separates, about 7 minutes.
Stir in most of the ground chole masala, then add the drained chickpeas with just 0.75 cup of their dark cooking liquid and the remaining 0.75 tsp salt.
Cook on medium-high heat for 10 minutes, mashing a few chickpeas, until the masala turns almost dry and clings to each one.
Swirl in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and the reserved masala, and top with 1 tbsp fresh ginger juliennes before serving.
tips: The tea bundle is what gives Amritsari chole its signature dark colour without any artificial help.
Anardana is essential for the authentic sour note; if unavailable, use amchur but the flavour shifts.
Keep this nearly dry rather than saucy, as it is meant to sit thick on the plate beside bhature.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot puffed bhature, a raw onion-and-lemon salad, sliced green chillies and a mango pickle for the full Punjabi chole-bhature plate.

variations.name: Masala Chole
variations.description: A coastal-leaning chole where roasted coriander powder and a coconut-tomato base soften the usual Punjabi punch into something mellower and more aromatic. The gravy is thicker and rounder, with a gentle sweetness from onions cooked slow. Fragrant, saucy and easy on the palate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed coconut oil gives the coastal base its rounded, aromatic sweetness

steps: Pressure-cook 1.5 cups soaked kabuli chana with 3 cups water and 0.5 tsp salt for 6 whistles until soft, reserving the liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, then add 10 curry leaves and let them crackle for 10 seconds.
Add 2 chopped onions and fry gently for 8 minutes until soft and sweet, then stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute.

Dry-roast 2.5 tsp coriander powder and 3 tbsp grated coconut together for 1 minute until golden, then add with 3 pureed tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and cook until the oil separates, about 8 minutes.
Add the chickpeas with 1.5 cups reserved liquid and the remaining 0.75 tsp salt, and simmer for 12 minutes until the gravy thickens and turns creamy from the coconut.
Mash a ladleful of chickpeas to round out the body of the gravy.
Finish with 3 tbsp chopped fresh coriander stirred through off the heat.
tips: Roasting the coconut with the coriander gives the gravy a nutty depth, so do not skip that step.
Keep this saucier than Amritsari chole, as it is meant to be eaten with rice or soft pav.
A squeeze of lime at the end brightens the mellow, coconut-rounded gravy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice or soft pav, a wedge of lime and a fresh coconut-coriander chutney on the side.

variations.name: Kadai Chole
variations.description: A kadai chole where chickpeas meet charred capsicum and onion in a thick, coarse gravy built on hand-pounded coriander and dried red chilli. The masala clings tight and the pepper keeps its crunch. Semi-dry, smoky and bold, a punchier cousin of the saucy versions.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked wood-pressed mustard oil gives the kadai its sharp, gutsy foundation

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of bilona ghee glazes the chickpeas and softens the mustard oil

steps: Pressure-cook 1.5 cups soaked kabuli chana with 3 cups water and 0.5 tsp salt for 6 whistles until tender, then drain and reserve the liquid.
Dry-roast 2 tbsp coriander seeds and 3 dried red chillies for 2 minutes until fragrant, cool, and pound to a coarse kadai masala.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until hazy, lower the heat, and fry 2 diced onions for 6 minutes until softened at the edges.
Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then 2 chopped tomatoes and 0.5 tsp turmeric and cook until pulpy and the oil separates, about 6 minutes.
Stir in most of the pounded masala and the drained chickpeas with just 0.5 cup reserved liquid and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, and cook on medium-high heat for 8 minutes until thick and clinging.
Add 1 large capsicum in thick wedges and toss on high heat for 3 to 4 minutes so it chars but stays crunchy.
Crush 1 tsp kasuri methi over the pan, swirl in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and the reserved masala, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Pound the kadai masala coarse so the little flecks of coriander seed give texture in every bite.
Keep the dish semi-dry with minimal liquid so the masala hugs the chickpeas.
Add the capsicum last for its signature crunch and colour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve straight from the kadai with laccha paratha or tandoori roti and a side of pickled onions.

variations.name: Handi Chole
variations.description: A slow handi chole scented purely with whole spices bloomed in ghee, the chickpeas sealed under a lid to steam in their own aromatic gravy. Cinnamon, black cardamom and cloves perfume the pot in place of any spice powder. Rustic, deeply fragrant and gently spiced.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: whole spices bloom in bilona ghee and infuse the chickpeas as they dum-cook

steps: Pressure-cook 1.5 cups soaked kabuli chana with 3 cups water and 0.5 tsp salt for 6 whistles until soft, keeping the liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a deep handi and bloom 1 inch cinnamon, 1 black cardamom, 3 green cardamoms, 4 cloves and 1 bay leaf until swollen and fragrant, about 40 seconds.
Add 2 sliced onions and fry slowly for 9 minutes until golden, letting the whole spices steep in the ghee.
Stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then 3 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and cook until the ghee glistens on top, about 8 minutes.
Add the drained chickpeas with 1 cup reserved liquid and the remaining 0.75 tsp salt, and bring to a gentle simmer.
Cover the handi tightly, lower the heat to minimum, and dum-cook undisturbed for 18 minutes so the whole-spice aroma soaks into the chickpeas.
Uncover, mash a few chickpeas to thicken, discard the bay leaf and black cardamom skin, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Bruise the black cardamom before adding so it lends a smoky depth without taking over.
The long, low dum is what layers the aroma, so resist opening the lid too soon.
Remove the larger whole spices before serving so no one bites into a clove or cardamom pod.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jeera rice or soft phulka and a cumin-mint raita to balance the warm, aromatic spicing.

variations.name: Punjabi Chole
variations.description: The plush restaurant-style Punjabi chole: a smooth onion-tomato gravy enriched with a cashew paste and finished with cream and crushed kasuri methi, its butter swapped for bilona ghee. Fuller and silkier than the dhaba version, with a mellow buttery-fenugreek finish. Made for a special spread.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: replaces butter for the same rich body plus a nutty bilona aroma

steps: Pressure-cook 1.5 cups soaked kabuli chana with 3 cups water and 0.5 tsp salt for 6 whistles until very soft, reserving the liquid.
Soak 12 cashews in warm water for 15 minutes, then blend with 2 boiled onions to a smooth, pourable paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add the onion-cashew paste and fry for 6 minutes until thickened and no longer raw-smelling.
Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then 3 pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder and cook until the ghee separates, about 8 minutes.
Add the chickpeas with 1 cup reserved liquid and the remaining 0.75 tsp salt, and simmer for 12 minutes until the gravy turns thick and velvety.
Lower the heat, stir in 3 tbsp cream and 0.75 tsp garam masala, and warm through for 2 minutes without boiling.
Crush 1.5 tsp kasuri methi between your palms over the pan and stir it in just before serving.
tips: Strain the cashew-onion paste for the smoothest, most restaurant-style gravy.
Keep the flame low once the cream goes in so it does not split.
Make the gravy base ahead and add chickpeas and cream just before serving for an easy dinner-party dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or saffron pulao, topped with a swirl of cream, kasuri methi and fine ginger juliennes for a festive finish.

variations.name: Classic Crispy Bread Roll
variations.description: The definitive tea-time crispy bread roll, where spiced mashed-potato filling is rolled snugly inside dampened bread, coated and deep-fried to a shatteringly crisp golden shell. The outside crackles while the inside stays soft and steamy. A make-anytime snack that vanishes off the plate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Its high smoke point fries the rolls evenly gold without turning greasy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Blooms the cumin and enriches the potato filling with a nutty aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Whisked into a slurry it seals each roll so no oil seeps into the filling

steps: Boil 4 potatoes until fork-tender, peel and mash them smooth while still warm so no lumps remain, about 15 minutes.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then add the chopped onion and 2 green chillies and saute 3 minutes until soft and translucent.
Add the mashed potato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt, cook 4 minutes stirring, then fold in 3 tbsp coriander and cool the filling completely.
Trim the crusts from 10 bread slices, dip each briefly in water and press gently between your palms to squeeze out excess, place 2 tbsp filling and roll into a tight sealed cylinder.
Whisk 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta with 4 tbsp water into a thin slurry, coat each roll all over, then roll it in 1 cup bread crumbs pressing lightly so they stick.
Deep-fry in hot Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil at 180C, 3-4 rolls at a time for 3-4 minutes until deep golden and crisp, then drain on paper.
tips: Cool the potato filling fully before rolling, as warm filling makes the bread soggy and hard to seal.
Squeeze the dampened bread firmly; too much water inside causes the rolls to burst in the oil.
Fry on medium-high heat, since low heat lets the bread drink oil and turn heavy instead of crisp.
variations.servingSuggestion: Slice each roll on the diagonal to show the golden filling and serve with mint-coriander chutney and sweet tamarind chutney alongside masala chai.

variations.name: Punjabi Crispy Bread Roll
variations.description: A robust Amritsari-style bread roll where the potato filling is warmed with garam masala, ginger-garlic and tangy anardana, then the fried rolls are brushed with butter for that dhaba richness. Bolder and more buttery than the everyday version. Made for hearty appetites.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Fries the stuffed rolls crisp before the buttery finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Carries the garam masala and ginger-garlic through the Punjabi filling

steps: Boil and mash 4 potatoes smooth, then keep aside while you build the tempering, about 15 minutes total.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat, splutter 1 tsp cumin seeds, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the chopped onion, and fry 4 minutes until golden and aromatic.
Stir in the mashed potato, 1 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp anardana powder, 1 tsp red chilli, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt, cook 4 minutes, then mix in 3 tbsp coriander and cool.
Trim and lightly dampen 10 bread slices, flatten each, spoon in 2 tbsp filling and roll into firm cylinders, sealing the seam well.
Dip each roll in a thin flour-water batter, roll in 1 cup bread crumbs, and deep-fry in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil at 180C for 3-4 minutes until crisp and deep gold.
Drain the rolls and immediately brush them with 2 tbsp softened butter so it melts into the hot crust.
tips: Anardana gives the tangy Amritsari edge; if unavailable, use half a teaspoon of amchur instead.
Brush the butter while the rolls are piping hot so it seeps in rather than sitting on top.
Make the filling a day ahead and refrigerate, as chilled filling rolls even more neatly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile onto a platter with rings of raw onion, a wedge of lemon and a bowl of pudina raita for a proper Punjabi tea spread.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Crispy Bread Roll
variations.description: A Pune-style bread roll perfumed with dark, aromatic goda masala and studded with coconut and roasted peanut, finished with a whisper of jaggery for the classic sweet-savoury Maharashtrian balance. Earthy and fragrant where the classic is plain. A batata-vada cousin in roll form.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The everyday Maharashtrian frying fat that keeps the shell light

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A pinch rounds the goda masala with the signature gentle sweetness

steps: Boil and mash 4 potatoes and keep ready, taking about 15 minutes for them to cook through.
Heat 2 tbsp of the groundnut oil in a pan over medium heat, splutter 0.5 tsp mustard and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then saute the onion and 2 green chillies 3 minutes.
Add the mashed potato with 1.5 tsp goda masala, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1.25 tsp salt, then fold in 3 tbsp coconut, 2 tbsp peanut powder and 3 tbsp coriander and cool.
Trim and dampen 10 bread slices, press out the water, place 2 tbsp filling on each and roll into tight sealed logs.
Coat the rolls in a thin flour-water slurry followed by 1 cup bread crumbs, pressing so the crumbs cling.
Deep-fry in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil at 180C for 3-4 minutes until crisp and evenly browned, then drain on paper.
tips: Goda masala can taste raw if under-cooked, so let it fry a full minute with the potato before stuffing.
Use fresh grated coconut for moisture; desiccated coconut can dry the filling.
Keep the jaggery to a single teaspoon, just enough to lift the spices without making it sweet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with dry garlic-peanut chutney and a mug of kadak chai for an authentic Puneri snack.

variations.name: Bengali Crispy Bread Roll
variations.description: A Kolkata-inspired bread roll where the potato is tempered in pungent mustard oil with panch phoron and roasted bhaja masala, giving the sharp, warming aroma of a Bengali aloor chop. The mustard oil hits the nose before the crunch hits the teeth. Perfect with a cup of cha.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Its sharp pungency defines the Bengali flavour and fries the rolls deep gold

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Makes the sealing slurry that locks in the mustard-scented filling

steps: Boil and mash 4 potatoes and set aside, allowing about 15 minutes to cook them soft.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil in a pan to smoking, cool it slightly, then crackle 1 tsp panch phoron for 20 seconds and add the ginger and 2 green chillies.
Add the chopped onion, fry 3 minutes, then stir in the mashed potato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli, 1 tsp bhaja masala and 1.25 tsp salt, cook 4 minutes and fold in coriander.
Cool the filling, trim and dampen 10 bread slices, press out the water, add 2 tbsp filling each and roll into firm sealed cylinders.
Whisk 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta with 4 tbsp water, coat each roll, then roll it in 1 cup bread crumbs.
Deep-fry in the remaining Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil at 180C for 3-4 minutes until crisp and richly browned, then drain.
tips: Always heat mustard oil to smoking then cool a little before tempering, which mellows its raw bite.
Panch phoron must only splutter briefly; burnt fenugreek in it turns the filling bitter.
Sprinkle a little extra bhaja masala over the drained rolls for a stronger roasted aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with kasundi mustard and beetroot-onion salad, the classic Bengali telebhaja accompaniments.

variations.name: Andhra Crispy Bread Roll
variations.description: A fiery southern bread roll where the potato is loaded with Guntur red chilli, crushed garlic and a crackling curry-leaf tempering, delivering serious heat under the crisp crust. Where the classic is mild, this one bites back. A snack for chilli lovers.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The Andhra base fat, high-smoke for frying and for taming raw chilli

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rounds the fierce Guntur chilli and carries the garlic-curry leaf tadka

steps: Boil and mash 4 potatoes and keep aside, which takes about 15 minutes on a rolling boil.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 12 curry leaves for 20 seconds, then fry the 6 crushed garlic cloves until pale gold.
Add the chopped onion and 2 green chillies, saute 3 minutes, then stir in the mashed potato with 2 tsp Guntur chilli, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt and cook 4 minutes.
Fold in 3 tbsp coriander, cool the filling, then trim and dampen 10 bread slices, squeeze out the water and roll 2 tbsp filling into each into tight logs.
Coat the rolls in a thin flour-water slurry and 1 cup bread crumbs, pressing them on firmly.
Deep-fry in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil at 180C for 3-4 minutes until crisp and deep golden, then drain on paper.
tips: Guntur chilli is intense, so start with the stated amount and let the ghee soften its edge.
Fry the garlic before the onion so it turns nutty rather than acrid in the finished roll.
A squeeze of lime over the drained rolls keeps the heat lively instead of flat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with cooling coconut chutney and a bowl of thick curd to balance the Guntur heat.

variations.name: Classic Crispy Moong Dal Pakora
variations.description: The quintessential monsoon fritter, made from coarsely ground soaked moong dal beaten light and studded with onion, chilli and coriander, then fried into shatteringly crisp golden nuggets. Crunchy outside, soft and savoury within. Best eaten hot off the kadhai.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: High-smoke and neutral, it fries the pakoras crisp without greasiness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon of hot ghee beaten into the batter gives an extra-crisp, light crumb

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup split green gram in water for 3 hours until swollen, then drain it well.
Grind the dal with the 2 green chillies and 1 tbsp ginger to a coarse, thick batter, using as little water as possible so it stays scoopable.
Beat the batter briskly for 2 minutes until it lightens, then fold in the onion, 3 tbsp coriander, 1 tsp cumin seeds, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli, 2 tbsp rice flour and 1.25 tsp salt.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until hot and beat it into the batter to make the pakoras extra crisp and light.
Heat Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to 180C and gently drop rough spoonfuls, frying 8-10 at a time without crowding.
Fry 3-4 minutes, turning, until deep golden and crisp, then lift out and drain on paper.
tips: Grind the dal coarse, not smooth, so the pakoras stay light and crunchy rather than dense.
Beating air into the batter is the real secret to fluffy-crisp pakoras, so do not skip it.
Add rice flour just before frying for maximum crunch; it softens if the batter sits too long.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile hot into a bowl and serve with mint chutney and a cup of adrak chai on a rainy afternoon.

variations.name: Punjabi Crispy Moong Dal Pakora
variations.description: A hearty Punjabi pakora where the moong dal batter is spiced with garam masala, ajwain and ginger-garlic, fried in ghee-rich oil for a deep dhaba flavour. Fuller and more robust than the plain fritter. Made for cold-weather cravings.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Fries the spiced pakoras crisp and golden

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Beaten into the batter it brings the rich, nutty dhaba aroma

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup split green gram 3 hours, then drain and grind coarse with the 2 green chillies using minimal water.
Beat the batter 2 minutes until light, then fold in the onion, 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 1 tsp garam masala, 0.5 tsp ajwain, 1 tsp red chilli, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 tbsp rice flour and 1.25 tsp salt.
Rub the ajwain between your fingers as you add it so its aroma releases into the batter, then mix in 3 tbsp coriander.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until hot and beat it into the batter for a crisp, rich crumb.
Heat Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to 180C and drop rough spoonfuls, frying 8-10 at a time without crowding.
Fry 3-4 minutes, turning, until deep golden and crunchy, then drain on paper.
tips: Ajwain not only flavours but also makes the fried dal easier to digest.
Keep the batter thick so the pakoras stay craggy and crisp rather than flat.
Fry a tester first and adjust salt and garam masala before frying the whole batch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with pudina-onion chutney and a wedge of lemon, dhaba-style with hot chai.

variations.name: Bengali Crispy Moong Dal Pakora
variations.description: A Kolkata-style moong dal fritter fried in pungent mustard oil and seasoned with nigella and green chilli, echoing the crisp dal bora of Bengali kitchens. Sharp, aromatic and golden. A classic rainy-day telebhaja.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Its pungency gives the pakoras their unmistakable Bengali character

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon beaten into the batter lightens and crisps the bora

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup split green gram 3 hours, then drain and grind coarse with the 3 green chillies and 1 tbsp ginger using minimal water.
Beat the batter 2 minutes until fluffy, then fold in 0.5 tsp nigella seeds, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp bhaja masala, 2 tbsp rice flour, 3 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until hot and beat it in for a lighter, crisper bora.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil to smoking, cool slightly, then top up the kadhai and bring to 180C for frying.
Drop rough spoonfuls into the hot mustard oil, frying 8-10 at a time without crowding the pan.
Fry 3-4 minutes, turning, until deep golden and crisp, then drain on paper.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to smoking then let it cool a little so its raw bite softens before frying.
Nigella adds the signature Bengali aroma, so add it whole rather than grinding it in.
Serve immediately; mustard-oil pakoras taste best fresh and lose their edge as they cool.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with kasundi mustard and puffed muri, the classic Bengali monsoon combination.

variations.name: Andhra Crispy Moong Dal Pakora
variations.description: A fiery Andhra fritter where the moong dal batter is loaded with Guntur red chilli, garlic and crackling curry leaves, fried to a searing crisp. The heat is upfront and unapologetic. A pakora with serious southern fire.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The Andhra base fat, high-smoke for frying and taming raw chilli

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Beaten in, it rounds the fierce Guntur chilli and crisps the crumb

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup split green gram 3 hours, then drain and grind coarse with the 2 green chillies using minimal water.

Beat the batter 2 minutes until light, then fold in 2 tsp Guntur chilli, 6 crushed garlic cloves, 14 chopped curry leaves, the onion, 1 tsp cumin, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 tbsp rice flour, 3 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until hot and beat it into the batter to crisp the crumb and soften the chilli edge.
Heat Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to 180C and drop rough spoonfuls, frying 8-10 at a time.
Fry 3-4 minutes, turning, until deep golden and crunchy with the curry leaves crisped through.
Drain on paper and sprinkle with a little extra salt while still hot.
tips: Guntur chilli is intense, so treat 2 tsp as a starting point and let the ghee soften the heat.
Crush the garlic rather than mincing it, so it fries into fragrant nuggets in each pakora.
Chop the curry leaves so they distribute evenly and crisp up inside the fritter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with cooling coconut chutney and thick curd to balance the Guntur heat.

variations.name: Kerala Crispy Moong Dal Pakora
variations.description: A Malabar-style moong dal fritter fried in fragrant coconut oil with curry leaves, coconut slivers and black pepper for a coastal, gently sweet crunch. Nutty and aromatic in true Kerala fashion. A tea-shop parippu vada cousin.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Its coconut aroma defines Kerala frying and perfumes every fritter

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon in the batter adds richness and an extra-crisp finish

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup split green gram 3 hours, then drain and grind coarse with the 3 green chillies and 1 tbsp ginger using minimal water.
Beat the batter 2 minutes until fluffy, then fold in 3 tbsp coconut slivers, 14 chopped curry leaves, 1 tsp crushed pepper, 4 chopped shallots, 2 tbsp rice flour, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until hot and beat it into the batter for a crisp, rich crumb.
Heat Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil to 180C and drop rough spoonfuls, frying 8-10 at a time.
Fry 3-4 minutes, turning, until deep golden with the coconut slivers toasted and crisp.
Drain on paper and serve while hot and crunchy.
tips: Use fresh coconut slivers, not desiccated, so they toast to a sweet crunch in the oil.
Shallots give a sweeter, more authentic Kerala base than regular onion here.
Keep coconut oil hot and steady, as it firms up quickly when the temperature drops.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut-curry leaf chutney and strong Kerala chai for a chaya-kada evening.

variations.name: Classic Crispy Onion Bhaji
variations.description: The definitive tea-time fritter: thinly sliced onions bound in a light besan batter sharpened with a little rice flour so the edges shatter like glass. Salting the onions first draws out just enough moisture to hold the batter together with barely any added water, giving a lacy, open crunch rather than a dense pakora.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: For deep-frying; its high smoke point keeps the batter crisp and clean-tasting instead of greasy.
