steps: Slice 3 large onions as thin as you can, put them in a bowl with 1 tsp salt, and toss well; leave for 10 minutes until they soften and release their own moisture.

Add 1.5 cups gram flour, 3 tbsp rice flour, 2 finely chopped green chillies, 3 tbsp coriander, 1 tsp cumin seeds, 0.5 tsp ajwain, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder to the onions and mix with your fingertips.
Sprinkle in only 2-3 tbsp water and mix to a thick, clinging batter that just coats the onions; it should look shaggy, not runny, so the fritters stay lacy.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a kadai over medium-high heat to about 180C, until a pinch of batter dropped in rises and sizzles at once.
Slide in loose spoonfuls of the mixture, 5-6 at a time, and fry for 3-4 minutes, turning once, until deep golden and crisp all over.
Lift the bhajis out with a slotted spoon and drain on a wire rack or paper so they stay crunchy rather than steaming soft.
tips: Fry in small batches; crowding the kadai drops the oil temperature and makes the bhajis soak up oil and go limp.
The rice flour is the secret to the crunch, so don't skip it; at a pinch, 2 tbsp fine semolina works too.
If the batter turns watery from the onions, stiffen it with an extra tablespoon of besan rather than more water.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile them in a newspaper cone with a wedge of lemon and a bowl of coriander-mint chutney, alongside a pot of adrak chai on a rainy evening.

variations.name: Punjabi Crispy Onion Bhaji
variations.description: A dhaba-style rendition where the fried bhajis are tossed the moment they leave the oil in a knob of nutty Anveshan Ghee laced with kasuri methi and a pinch of garam masala. The ghee glazes the crisp edges and carries a buttery aroma that plain oil never delivers.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The frying medium; keeps the crust crisp so the ghee finish adds flavour, not heaviness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: Melted over the hot bhajis at the end for that unmistakable dhaba butter-ghee glaze.

steps: Thinly slice 3 large onions, salt them with 1 tsp salt, and rest for 10 minutes so they wilt and weep their moisture.
Mix in 1.5 cups besan, 2 chopped green chillies, a grated 1-inch piece of ginger, 3 tbsp coriander, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp turmeric, adding just 2-3 tbsp water for a thick batter.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to 180C and fry spoonfuls in batches for 3-4 minutes until golden and crisp, then drain on a rack.
In a small pan, warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee over low heat, crush in 1 tbsp kasuri methi between your palms and add 0.5 tsp garam masala, letting it sizzle for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Tip the hot bhajis into a bowl, pour over the fragrant ghee and toss quickly so every fritter catches the buttery, herby glaze.
Serve at once while the ghee coating is still glossy and the crust is crackling.
tips: Crush the kasuri methi to a coarse powder before adding it; whole leaves can taste raw and stalky.
Toss the bhajis in the ghee only just before serving, or the crust softens as it sits.
For a richer dhaba flavour, brown a teaspoon of the ghee first until it smells nutty before adding the methi.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a steel thali with pickled onions, a dollop of white butter and a glass of salted lassi for a true roadside-dhaba spread.

variations.name: Bengali Crispy Onion Bhaji (Peyaji)
variations.description: Kolkata's beloved peyaji, fried in pungent Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil that gives the fritters their characteristic sharp, sinus-clearing edge. Nigella seeds and a touch of green chilli keep the batter minimal so the onion and the mustard oil do all the talking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Heated to smoking then cooled slightly before frying; its pungency is the soul of an authentic peyaji.

steps: Slice 3 large onions thinly, salt with 1 tsp salt and rest 10 minutes until softened and juicy.

Add 1.25 cups besan, 2 tbsp rice flour, 1 tsp nigella seeds, 3 slit-and-chopped green chillies, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tbsp coriander, mixing with only 2 tbsp water into a thick, sticky batter.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just begins to smoke, then lower the flame to medium so the raw pungency mellows.
Drop in flattened spoonfuls of batter and fry for 3-4 minutes, turning once, until the peyaji are deep golden and crisp at the frilled edges.
Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper; the fritters will smell sharply of mustard oil, exactly as they should.
Fry the remaining batter in batches, letting the oil return to temperature between each round.
tips: Always heat mustard oil to smoking point once and let it cool a little before frying; this tames the raw bite while keeping the aroma.
Keep the batter thin and the onions dominant; peyaji is meant to be more onion than gram flour.
A pinch of extra nigella seeds sprinkled on top just before frying deepens the smoky-nutty note.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside steaming rice and a bowl of yellow moong dal, or as the classic evening jhalmuri companion with a cup of milky cha.

variations.name: Gujarati Crispy Onion Bhaji
variations.description: A Kathiawadi twist that plays the region's signature sweet-hot-sour balance: a whisper of Anveshan Jaggery Powder in the batter rounds off the heat while lemon keeps it bright. The fritters stay crisp but carry a gentle caramel edge that pairs beautifully with fiery green chutney.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the traditional Gujarati frying fat, lending a subtle sweetness that suits this bhaji.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Dissolved into the batter for the signature Gujarati sweet-savoury balance without turning the fritters sticky.

steps: Thinly slice 3 large onions, toss with 1 tsp salt and 1 tbsp lemon juice, and set aside for 10 minutes to soften.
Stir 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder into 3 tbsp warm water until dissolved, then pour it over the onions along with a grated 1-inch piece of ginger.
Add 1.5 cups besan, 2 tbsp rice flour, 2 chopped green chillies, 3 tbsp coriander, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder, mixing to a thick batter that clings to the onions.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to 180C until a drop of batter surfaces immediately with a lively sizzle.
Fry loose spoonfuls in batches for 3-4 minutes, turning once, until golden-brown with crisp lacy edges, then drain on a rack.
Repeat with the rest of the batter, letting the oil reheat between batches so each fritter stays crunchy.
tips: Dissolve the jaggery first; adding it as a lump makes the fritters brown too fast and stay soft in the middle.
The batter browns quicker because of the jaggery, so keep the flame at medium rather than high.
Balance is everything here: taste and adjust so the sweetness is a background note, not the headline.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a sharp coriander-green-chilli chutney and a side of fried green chillies to set off the gentle sweetness, Kathiawadi-style.

variations.name: Andhra Crispy Onion Bhaji
variations.description: A fiery southern take built on smoky Guntur red chilli, which brings a deep brick-red heat quite unlike ordinary chilli powder. Curry leaves and a splash of Anveshan Coconut Oil frying give the fritters a fragrant, unmistakably coastal-Andhra character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Frying in coconut oil gives the bhajis a subtle sweet-nutty aroma typical of coastal Andhra cooking.

steps: Slice 3 large onions thinly, salt with 1 tsp salt and rest 10 minutes; meanwhile crush 4 garlic cloves and roughly tear 15 curry leaves.
Add 1.5 cups besan, 3 tbsp rice flour, 2 tsp Guntur red chilli powder, the garlic, curry leaves, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp cumin and 0.5 tsp turmeric to the onions.
Mix with just 3 tbsp water into a thick, fiery red batter that coats the onions without pooling.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil to 180C until shimmering and a test drop of batter rises instantly.
Fry spoonfuls in batches for 3-4 minutes, turning once, until deep brick-red and crisp, then drain on a rack.
Toss a few extra curry leaves into the hot oil for the last batch and scatter them over the drained bhajis for aroma.
tips: Guntur chilli is genuinely hot; start with 1.5 tsp and build up if you want the full Andhra fire.
Frying the extra curry leaves crisp makes an edible, fragrant garnish that intensifies the aroma.
Coconut oil solidifies as it cools, so serve these fritters hot for the best texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a spoon of tangy tomato-garlic pachadi and plain curd rice to temper the Guntur heat.

variations.name: Classic Dal Dhaba-style
variations.description: The smoky, robust dal of highway dhabas, where toor lentils are cooked with a bold garam-masala tomato base and given a final charcoal dhungar for that signature roadside smokiness. Mustard oil and a generous ghee tadka make it earthy and full-throated. This is dal with dust-on-the-boots character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The final ghee tadka gives the dhaba dal its glossy, aromatic finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Pungent mustard oil is the backbone of authentic dhaba flavour

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed toor dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 4 to 5 whistles until soft, then whisk lightly.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 15 seconds.
Add the 2 chopped onions and fry 7 minutes until deep golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Add the tomatoes with 1 tsp red chilli, 1 tsp coriander powder and 0.5 tsp salt and cook 7 minutes until pulpy and the oil separates, then add the dal with 1 cup hot water and simmer 8 minutes.
For the dhungar, set a small heated piece of charcoal in a steel bowl on the dal, drizzle 0.5 tsp ghee over it, cover the pot for 2 minutes, then remove the bowl.
Heat the remaining 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, sizzle 1 tsp garam masala and crushed kasuri methi for 10 seconds and pour it over the smoked dal.
tips: The charcoal dhungar is what sets dhaba dal apart; if you skip it, add a pinch of smoked paprika instead.
Fry the onions until genuinely deep golden for that characteristic robust base.
Let the smoked dal rest covered for a few minutes so the smokiness settles in evenly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tandoori roti or laccha paratha, raw onion rings, green chilli and a squeeze of lemon.

variations.name: Moong Dal Dhaba-style
variations.description: A lighter dhaba dal using split yellow moong, given the same bold onion-tomato base and smoky garam-masala finish so it eats hearty despite the gentle lentil. An Assam-style hint of extra ginger keeps it warming. Roadside flavour, weeknight ease.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The ghee-and-garam-masala finish gives even light moong a robust edge

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Pungent mustard oil builds the dhaba-style base

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp salt and 2.75 cups water for 3 whistles until soft, then whisk smooth.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 15 seconds.
Add the chopped onion, grated ginger and minced garlic and fry 5 minutes until golden and fragrant.
Stir in the tomatoes with 0.75 tsp red chilli and 0.5 tsp salt and cook 6 minutes until pulpy, then add the dal with 0.75 cup hot water and simmer 6 minutes.
Heat the remaining 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, sizzle 0.75 tsp garam masala and crushed kasuri methi for 10 seconds.
Pour the aromatic ghee over the dal, cover 1 minute to lock in the scent, and serve hot.
tips: Smoke the mustard oil first so its sharpness mellows into a rounded pungency.
The extra ginger gives an Assam-style warmth that suits the light moong.
Keep the dal a touch loose, as moong thickens quickly off the heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice or tandoori roti and a side of sliced onions and green chilli.

variations.name: Masoor Dal Dhaba-style
variations.description: A gutsy dhaba dal with quick-cooking red masoor that soaks up a smoky, garam-masala-heavy base and turns rich brick-red. Extra garlic and a robust ghee tadka give it real roadside swagger. Bold, fast and deeply satisfying.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A garlicky ghee tadka gives the masoor its dhaba punch

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Pungent mustard oil builds the smoky, robust base

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed masoor dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp salt and 2.75 cups water for 3 whistles until soft, then whisk smooth.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 15 seconds.
Add the 2 chopped onions and minced garlic and fry 6 minutes until deep golden.
Stir in the tomatoes with 1 tsp red chilli, 1 tsp coriander powder and 0.5 tsp salt and cook 6 minutes until the fat separates, then add the dal with 1 cup hot water and simmer 6 minutes.
Heat the remaining 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, sizzle 1 tsp garam masala and crushed kasuri methi for 10 seconds until fragrant.
Pour the sizzling ghee tadka over the dal, cover briefly, and serve piping hot.
tips: Fry the garlic right along with the onions for a deeper, roasted flavour in the base.
Masoor cooks fast, so three whistles keep it from going gluey.
A squeeze of lemon at the table cuts through the rich, smoky base.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tandoori roti or jeera rice, raw onion rings and a green chilli on the side.

variations.name: Chana Dal Dhaba-style
variations.description: A hearty dhaba take on chana dal where the nutty grains stay firm in a smoky, garam-masala base, given a Bengali touch of warm whole spices in the tadka. Substantial and full of texture, it eats almost like a rustic curry. Roadside comfort with a regional twist.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries the warm whole-spice tadka over the sturdy chana dal

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: The quintessential Bengali oil for a robust, pungent base

steps: Pressure-cook the soaked 1 cup chana dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 to 7 whistles until tender but holding shape.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the heat and fry the bay leaf and cinnamon with 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds.
Add the chopped onion and fry 6 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Add the tomatoes with 0.75 tsp red chilli and 0.5 tsp salt and cook 6 minutes until pulpy, then add the chana dal with 1 cup of its liquid and simmer 8 minutes.
Heat the remaining 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, sizzle 1 tsp garam masala and crushed kasuri methi for 10 seconds.
Pour the fragrant ghee over the dal, cover 1 minute, and serve warm.
tips: The whole bay leaf and cinnamon give a Bengali warmth; fish them out before serving.
Keep the chana dal grains firm and separate rather than mashing them.
Loosen with hot water when reheating, as this dal thickens a lot on standing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with luchi or steamed rice and a side of pickled green chilli for a rustic Bengali-dhaba plate.

variations.name: Palak Dal Dhaba-style
variations.description: A smoky dhaba dal palak from the Punjab heartland where toor lentils and fresh spinach meet a bold garam-masala base and a robust ghee tadka. The greens stay vibrant against the earthy, mustard-oil-rich masala. Hearty, colourful and unmistakably roadside.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The ghee tadka lifts the spinach and ties the smoky dal together

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Pungent mustard oil is the earthy base of this dhaba dal

steps: Pressure-cook 0.75 cup rinsed toor dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp salt and 2.5 cups water for 4 whistles until soft, then whisk smooth.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 15 seconds.
Add the chopped onion and slit green chillies and fry 5 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Add the tomatoes with 0.75 tsp red chilli and 0.5 tsp salt, cook 5 minutes until pulpy, then stir in the 3 cups spinach and saute 3 minutes until just wilted.
Add the cooked dal with 0.75 cup hot water and simmer 6 minutes until the flavours meld.
Heat the remaining 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, sizzle 0.75 tsp garam masala and crushed kasuri methi for 10 seconds, pour over the dal, finish with 1 tbsp lemon juice and serve while green.
tips: Add the spinach late and cook briefly so the dal stays bright rather than dull.
Smoke the mustard oil first to mellow its raw bite into a rounded pungency.
A squeeze of lemon at the end keeps the greens tasting fresh.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tandoori roti or steamed rice, raw onion rings and a wedge of lemon.

variations.name: Classic Dal Fry
variations.description: Unlike a tadka poured on top, dal fry builds its flavour by simmering the boiled dal right into a well-bhunoed onion-tomato masala until thick and glossy. Toor dal is the go-to here, turning rich and homely with cumin, ginger-garlic and a whisper of garam masala. The everyday dal that tastes like a proper meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee gives the fried masala base its rounded, homely richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A clean wood-pressed oil to fry the onions golden without heaviness

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed toor dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 4 to 5 whistles until soft, then mash lightly and set aside.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds.
Add the 2 chopped onions and fry 7 minutes until deep golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until the raw smell lifts.
Add the tomatoes with 0.75 tsp red chilli, 1 tsp coriander powder and 0.5 tsp salt and fry 7 minutes until the masala is thick and the fat glistens at the edges.
Tip in the mashed dal with 1 cup hot water, stir well and simmer 8 minutes, letting it fry into the masala until thick and glossy.
Finish with the remaining 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 0.5 tsp garam masala, stir through the coriander and serve hot.
tips: The key to dal fry is bhunoing the onion-tomato base properly until the fat separates, so do not rush this step.
Mash the dal only lightly so a little texture remains in the finished dish.
Drizzle the finishing ghee off the heat so its aroma stays fresh on the plate.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed basmati rice or laccha paratha and a side of kachumber salad.

variations.name: Moong Dal Fry
variations.description: A quick, light dal fry using split yellow moong that cooks in minutes and fries into a smooth, mellow masala. This Himachali-style version keeps things gentle with ginger and a single green chilli, so the dal stays soothing rather than heavy. Perfect for a fuss-free weekday dinner.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee keeps this light dal fry tasting rich despite its simplicity

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A neutral wood-pressed oil to sweat the onions gently

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp salt and 2.75 cups water for 3 whistles until soft, then stir smooth.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds.
Add the chopped onion, grated ginger and minced green chilli and fry 5 minutes until the onion is soft and pale gold.
Stir in the tomato with 0.5 tsp red chilli and 0.5 tsp salt and cook 4 minutes until the tomato breaks down.
Pour in the cooked dal with 0.75 cup hot water and simmer 6 minutes, stirring, until it thickens to a smooth, pourable dal.
Swirl in the remaining 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, scatter the coriander and serve at once.
tips: Yellow moong needs no soaking and cooks fast, so watch it does not catch at the base while simmering.
Keep the masala gentle here; heavy spicing overwhelms the delicate moong.
A pinch of crushed kasuri methi at the end adds a lovely aroma if you like.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft rotis or plain rice and a simple cucumber-tomato salad for a light meal.

variations.name: Masoor Dal Fry
variations.description: A punchy Delhi-style dal fry with split red masoor that cooks fast and fries into a deeply savoury, brick-red masala. Extra garlic and a good hit of coriander powder give it a street-corner boldness. Robust, quick and thoroughly satisfying.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee rounds out the bold garlic-and-chilli masala of this dal fry

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Its pungency builds a robust, street-style onion base

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed masoor dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp salt and 2.75 cups water for 3 whistles until soft, then stir to a smooth pour.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until smoking, lower the heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 15 seconds.
Add the 2 chopped onions and minced garlic and fry 6 minutes until deep golden and fragrant.
Stir in the tomatoes with 1 tsp red chilli, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 0.5 tsp salt and fry 6 minutes until thick and the oil separates.
Add the cooked dal with 1 cup hot water and simmer 6 minutes, letting it fry down into a thick, brick-red dal.
Finish with 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee stirred in off the heat and a shower of fresh coriander.
tips: Heating the mustard oil to smoking first mellows its raw sharpness into a pleasant pungency.
Masoor turns mushy quickly, so keep the pressure cooking to three whistles.
Finish with a squeeze of lemon to cut through the richness of the fried base.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jeera rice or hot tandoori roti, sliced onions and a green chilli on the side.

variations.name: Chana Dal Fry
variations.description: A textured Maharashtrian dal fry with nutty chana dal that holds its shape and soaks up a fragrant goda-style masala. Fried into a thick, spice-laden base with onion and tomato, it eats almost like a dry curry. Wholesome, chewy and full of character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee enriches the substantial chana dal and its aromatic masala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A staple Maharashtrian oil to fry the onion base golden

steps: Pressure-cook the soaked 1 cup chana dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 whistles until tender but intact.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds.
Add the 2 chopped onions and fry 6 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Add the tomatoes with 0.75 tsp red chilli, 1 tsp goda masala and 0.5 tsp salt and fry 7 minutes until thick and aromatic.
Tip in the cooked chana dal with 0.75 cup of its liquid and simmer 8 minutes so the grains absorb the masala.
Fold in the grated coconut and remaining 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, scatter coriander and serve warm.
tips: Goda masala and a little coconut are what mark this out as Maharashtrian; garam masala can stand in at a pinch.
Keep the dal slightly thick so it clings to rice or bhakri like a semi-dry curry.
Soaked chana dal cooks more evenly and is far less likely to stay hard in the centre.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri or steamed rice, a wedge of lime and a spoon of thecha for heat.

variations.name: Palak Dal Fry
variations.description: A Telangana-style dal fry where toor dal and spinach are cooked together and fried into a tangy, garlic-rich masala with a squeeze of tamarind. The sourness and the greens make it lively and distinctly southern. Comforting yet bright, it turns a simple dal into something memorable.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee rounds the tangy, garlicky spinach dal beautifully

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: A classic southern oil that stands up to tamarind and garlic

steps: Pressure-cook 0.75 cup rinsed toor dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp salt and 2.5 cups water for 4 whistles until soft, then mash lightly.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and the curry leaves for 20 seconds.
Add the minced garlic and chopped onion and fry 5 minutes until golden, then add the tomato and cook 3 minutes until soft.
Stir in the 3 cups chopped spinach with 0.75 tsp red chilli and 0.5 tsp salt and saute 3 minutes until just wilted.
Add the mashed dal, 1 tbsp tamarind pulp and 0.75 cup hot water, and simmer 6 minutes until tangy and thick.
Finish with 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee drizzled over the top and serve while the spinach is still green.
tips: Add the tamarind only after the dal is cooked; acid slows down the softening of lentils.
Cook the spinach briefly so it stays green rather than turning dull and khaki.
Adjust the tamarind to taste; the dal should be pleasantly sour, not sharp.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a spoon of extra ghee, or with hot phulkas and a papad on the side.

variations.name: Classic Dal Home-style
variations.description: The unshowy everyday dal cooked in most Indian homes: toor dal simmered soft with turmeric, then finished with a single, simple ghee tempering of cumin, garlic and a pinch of asafoetida. No heavy masala, just clean, honest flavour that pairs with anything. This is the pot that quietly holds a household together.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A simple ghee tadka is the soul of this plain, comforting dal

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A little wood-pressed oil keeps the tempering from browning too fast

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed toor dal with the chopped tomato, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 4 to 5 whistles until soft, then whisk smooth.
Set the dal on a low simmer with a little hot water to reach a comfortable pouring consistency.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a small pan until hot.
Crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then add the crushed garlic and fry until pale gold and fragrant.
Off the heat stir in 0.25 tsp asafoetida and the broken dried red chilli so they sizzle without burning.
Pour the tempering over the simmering dal, cover for 1 minute, then stir through the coriander and serve.
tips: Cooking the tomato right along with the dal saves a step and gives a gentle tang throughout.
Keep the tempering simple; the beauty of a home-style dal is its restraint.
A knob of extra ghee stirred in at the table makes it taste even more comforting.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot steamed rice, a spoon of ghee and a simple aloo sabzi or papad on the side.

variations.name: Moong Dal Home-style
variations.description: A featherlight everyday moong dal from the hills, cooked soft and given the gentlest tempering of cumin and ginger. Nothing heavy interferes with the sweet, clean taste of the yellow lentils. This is the dal you reach for when you want something nourishing and easy on the stomach.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee makes even this plainest of dals taste rich and nurturing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A neutral wood-pressed oil so the gentle tempering does not scorch

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, half the grated ginger, 1 tsp salt and 2.75 cups water for 3 whistles until soft, then stir smooth.
Loosen the dal with a little hot water and keep it simmering gently on low heat.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil until hot.
Crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then add the remaining ginger and the slit green chilli and fry 30 seconds until aromatic.
Stir in 0.25 tsp asafoetida off the heat so it blooms without burning.
Pour the tempering over the dal, cover 1 minute, then finish with the coriander and serve warm.
tips: Moong dal thickens as it stands, so keep it looser than you want it to end up.
This dal is ideal for anyone unwell or wanting a gentle meal; skip the chilli entirely if you like.
A squeeze of lemon brightens the mild moong without adding heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft plain rice or khichdi and a dollop of ghee, with a little curd on the side.

variations.name: Masoor Dal Home-style
variations.description: A quick, everyday masoor dal with a southern accent, given a mustard-and-curry-leaf tempering that crackles with flavour. The red lentils cook down soft and take the tangy tomato and the fragrant tadka beautifully. Simple weeknight food with a lively, homely character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee finishes the dal while the oil carries the southern tempering

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: A traditional southern oil ideal for a mustard-and-curry-leaf tadka

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed masoor dal with the chopped tomato, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 2.75 cups water for 3 whistles until soft, then stir smooth.
Keep the dal simmering gently on low heat with a splash of hot water to loosen it.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil until hot and splutter 0.75 tsp mustard seeds until they pop.
Add 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, the curry leaves, crushed garlic and 2 dried red chillies and fry 30 seconds until the garlic is golden.
Pour the crackling tempering over the dal and cover for 1 minute to trap the aroma.
Stir in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee for a rich finish and serve piping hot.
tips: Let the mustard seeds fully pop before adding the curry leaves, or the tadka will taste raw.
Masoor cooks in minutes, so three whistles keep it from turning to mush.
Stand back when the curry leaves hit the hot oil as they splutter sharply.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or with hot rotis and a slice of lime.

variations.name: Chana Dal Home-style
variations.description: A Gujarati-style everyday chana dal with the region's signature gentle sweet-sour balance, finished with a little jaggery and a squeeze of lemon. The nutty lentils stay tender and separate in a lightly spiced, slightly sweet broth. Homely, distinctive and a lovely change from savoury-only dals.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries the cumin tempering and rounds the sweet-sour dal

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The characteristic Gujarati sweetness comes from natural jaggery, not sugar

steps: Pressure-cook the soaked 1 cup chana dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 whistles until tender but still holding shape.
Set the dal to simmer gently with the chopped tomato and a little hot water for 5 minutes until the tomato softens.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, then add 1 tsp cumin seeds, the curry leaves and slit green chillies and fry 30 seconds.
Pour this tempering into the dal and stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder until it dissolves.
Simmer 4 minutes so the sweet, tangy and savoury notes come together, adjusting water for a light consistency.
Finish with 1 tbsp lemon juice and the coriander, and serve warm.
tips: Balance is everything here; taste and tweak the jaggery and lemon until it is gently sweet and sour.
Keep the dal thinner than a Punjabi dal, as Gujarati dal is meant to be sippable.
Soaked chana dal cooks evenly and keeps its lovely nutty bite.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a papad, or as part of a Gujarati thali with rotli and shaak.

variations.name: Mixed Dal Home-style
variations.description: A comforting panchmel-style dal from central India that blends five lentils for a fuller, more complex flavour than any single dal. Each lentil adds its own texture, from creamy to firm, brought together by a warm cumin-and-garlic tempering. A wholesome, protein-rich pot that eats like a treat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee ties the five lentils together with its nutty tempering

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A clean oil to fry the aromatics without overpowering the mixed dals

ingredients.name: Mixed lentils (toor, moong, masoor, chana, urad), rinsed

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed mixed lentils with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 3.25 cups water for 5 to 6 whistles until all the lentils are soft, then whisk lightly.
Heat 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds.
Add the chopped onion and crushed garlic and fry 5 minutes until golden and fragrant.
Stir in the tomato with 0.75 tsp red chilli, 1 tsp coriander powder and 0.25 tsp salt and cook 5 minutes until pulpy.
Pour in the cooked mixed dal with a little hot water and simmer 8 minutes so the flavours settle.
Finish with the remaining 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee stirred in and a generous scatter of coriander.
tips: Give the mixed lentils an extra whistle or two, as the firmer chana and urad take longer than the rest.
The blend of lentils makes this naturally creamy, so only a light whisk is needed.
It thickens a lot on standing; loosen with hot water when reheating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice, a spoon of ghee and a tangy pickle, or with baati for a rustic central-Indian meal.

variations.name: Classic Dal Paratha
variations.description: A protein-rich paratha stuffed with cooked chana dal that is pressure-cooked soft, then dried on the stove with cumin and ginger into a firm, crumbly filling that stuffs without leaking. The dal turns nutty and savoury as it dries out. Ghee-griddled to a spotty gold, it makes a filling, wholesome meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: wraps the dry dal filling in a soft crust that keeps this protein-rich paratha tender

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: tempers the dal filling and bastes the paratha to a rich, nutty gold

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup chana dal until fully soft, drain off any excess water, and mash it coarsely so it holds together as a thick paste.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with a little salt and about 0.75 cup water for 6 minutes into a soft dough, cover, and rest it 15 minutes.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, add 1 tbsp grated ginger and 2 minced green chillies, then stir in the mashed dal with 1 tsp amchur, 0.5 tsp turmeric and remaining salt and cook on medium 6 minutes until dry and crumbly; cool it fully.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, flatten one, place 2 tbsp of the dal filling in the centre, pleat the edges shut, and press flat.
Dust with khapli atta and roll into a 6-inch round with gentle strokes so the crumbly filling stays enclosed.
Cook on a medium tava, brushing both sides with Anveshan Ghee, flipping until deep golden spots appear, about 3 minutes per paratha.
tips: Cook the dal until it is completely soft and then dry it out well; a wet dal filling tears the paratha.
If the filling feels loose, add a spoon of roasted besan to bind it into a firm, stuffable mass.
The dried dal filling keeps two days refrigerated and doubles as a quick stuffing for kachoris.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a bowl of thick curd, a spoon of mango pickle and a pat of white butter; a side of aloo sabzi turns it into a hearty thali.

variations.name: Masala Dal Paratha
variations.description: A hearty Haryanvi version where the cooked dal filling is deepened with garam masala and coriander powder for a warm, rounded spice profile suited to a farmhouse breakfast. Cooked in wood-pressed groundnut oil, it takes on a nutty, homely aroma. Robust and filling, it powers a long working morning.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: gives a robust, rustic crust that stands up to the spiced dal filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil tempers the dal and crisps the paratha with a hearty nuttiness

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup toor dal until fully soft, drain well, and mash it into a thick paste that will dry easily.
Bring 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta together with salt and roughly 0.75 cup water, kneading 6 minutes into a pliable dough; rest it covered 15 minutes.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, saute the chopped onion 3 minutes until soft, then add the dal with 1 tsp garam masala, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and remaining salt and cook 6 minutes until dry; cool it.
Split the dough into 8 balls, cup one, spoon in 2 tbsp of the masala dal filling, seal the edges over the top, and press flat.
Roll into a 6-inch round on a floured board, working gently so the filling stays put.
Griddle on a medium tava, brushing both faces with Anveshan Groundnut Oil, turning until richly spotted, about 3 minutes per paratha.
tips: Saute the onion until fully soft, since any crunch left in it will pierce the rolled paratha.
Dry the dal until it leaves the sides of the pan, so the masala filling is firm enough to stuff.
This dough and filling both keep overnight, making it an easy make-ahead breakfast.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with homemade white butter and a green-chilli pickle, with a tall glass of salted chaas on the side.

variations.name: Spicy Dal Paratha
variations.description: A Delhi street-style dal paratha with real bite, the cooked dal filling fired up with green chillies and cracked black pepper and given the trademark chatpata tang with amchur. It is the kind of robust, spicy stuffing you find at a busy Purani Dilli breakfast stall. Bold and satisfying, it needs only curd alongside.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: the wholesome flour carries the bold, spicy dal filling with a satisfying chew

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: tempers the dal and griddles the paratha crisp, mellowing the chilli heat

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup chana dal until fully soft, drain off the excess liquid, and mash it into a thick paste.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with salt and about 0.75 cup water for 6 minutes into a soft dough, then rest it covered 15 minutes.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, add 4 minced green chillies, then stir in the dal with 1 tsp cracked pepper, 1 tsp amchur and remaining salt and cook on medium 6 minutes until dry and crumbly; cool it.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, open one into a 4-inch cup, load 2 tbsp of the spicy dal, seal the top, and press flat.
Roll into a 6-inch round, dusting well and patching any spot where the filling shows through.
Cook on a medium-high tava, brushing both sides with Anveshan Ghee, flipping until golden and blistered, about 3 minutes per paratha.
tips: Add the cracked pepper towards the end so its aroma stays lively in the filling.
Deseed the green chillies for a milder version that keeps the tang without the full heat.
Finish the hot paratha with a sprinkle of chaat masala for extra street-style flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with cold, thick dahi and a fiery red-chilli achar, the classic Dilli nashta pairing, plus sliced onion and lime.

variations.name: Garlic Dal Paratha
variations.description: A Telangana-style dal paratha where the cooked dal filling is deepened with garlic browned in ghee until sweet and nutty, plus a hit of dried red chilli. The garlic transforms the mild dal into something intensely savoury. Hearty and full-flavoured, it is a satisfying one-dish meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: carries the rich garlic-dal filling with a soft, wholesome crumb

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: browns the garlic sweet and tempers the dal with a nutty richness

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup chana dal until fully soft, drain, and mash it into a thick paste that dries readily.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with salt and roughly 0.75 cup water for 6 minutes into a soft dough, cover, and rest it 15 minutes.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, fry 2 tbsp minced garlic and 2 broken dried red chillies on low for 2 minutes until the garlic is pale gold, then add the dal with 1 tsp coriander powder and remaining salt and cook 6 minutes until dry; cool it.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, flatten one, place 2 tbsp of the garlicky dal inside, gather and seal the edges, and press down.
Roll into an even 6-inch round on a dusted board so the filling stays enclosed.
Cook on a medium tava, brushing both faces with Anveshan Ghee, turning until deep golden and aromatic, about 3 minutes per paratha.
tips: Fry the garlic and dried chilli only to pale gold, since both turn bitter if browned too far.
Dry the dal until crumbly so the garlicky filling holds its shape when stuffed.
A spoon of the garlic-ghee brushed over the finished paratha deepens the aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with curd tempered with mustard seeds and curry leaves, and a fiery garlic-red chilli chutney.

variations.name: Cheesy Dal Paratha
variations.description: A modern, protein-packed twist gaining popularity in Jharkhand's towns, pairing a spiced cooked dal filling with grated cheese for a rich, gooey centre. The cheese binds the dal into a soft, sliceable core that appeals to children. Wholesome and indulgent at once, it is a clever way to serve lentils.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: wraps the soft cheesy dal core in a sturdy yet tender crust

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: crisps the paratha to a golden shell while keeping the cheesy dal centre molten

steps: Pressure-cook 0.75 cup chana dal until fully soft, drain thoroughly, and mash it into a dry, thick paste.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 0.75 tsp cumin seeds, add the mashed dal with 0.5 tsp black pepper and 0.5 tsp chilli flakes, and cook on medium 5 minutes until dry; cool it completely.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.75 tsp salt and about 0.75 cup water for 6 minutes into a soft dough; rest it 15 minutes.
Fold 0.75 cup grated mozzarella into the cooled dal so the cheese binds it into a soft filling.
Divide the dough into 6 balls, roll one into a 4-inch disc, mound 3 tbsp of the cheesy dal in the centre, seal the edges over, and flatten gently.
Cook on a medium tava, brushing both sides with Anveshan Ghee and pressing the middle, until golden and crisp with a molten centre, about 3 minutes per paratha.
tips: Dry the dal well before adding cheese, since a wet filling will not hold the molten centre.
Serve straight off the tava while the cheese still stretches, as it firms up on cooling.
Stir the cheese into the dal only once it has cooled, or it will melt prematurely and turn oily.
variations.servingSuggestion: Cut into wedges and serve with a tangy tomato dip or ketchup for kids, and a cooling mint raita for the adults.

variations.name: Classic Dal Punjabi
variations.description: A rich, restaurant-style Punjabi dal where soft toor lentils are simmered in a buttery tomato masala and finished with cream and a fistful of crushed kasuri methi. The butter and dried fenugreek give it that unmistakable dhaba perfume, while ghee rounds out the depth. Indulgent, aromatic and made for a special dinner.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee deepens the buttery Punjabi base with a nutty richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A clean oil to fry the onion base before the butter finish

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed toor dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 4 to 5 whistles until soft, then whisk creamy.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds.
Add the chopped onion and fry 6 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in the tomato puree with 1 tsp red chilli and 0.5 tsp salt and cook 8 minutes until thick and the fat separates.
Add the cooked dal with 1 cup hot water and simmer 8 minutes, then stir in 2 tbsp butter, 2 tbsp cream and crushed kasuri methi.
Finish with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 0.75 tsp garam masala, simmer 2 minutes until glossy and serve.
tips: Crush the kasuri methi between your palms before adding it to release its full aroma.
Add the cream on a low flame so it enriches without splitting.
A pinch of sugar balances the tomato if the puree tastes sharp.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or jeera rice, a swirl of cream on top and a side of pickled onions.

variations.name: Moong Dal Punjabi
variations.description: A lighter Punjabi-style dal that swaps heavy lentils for split yellow moong, giving a silky, golden dal that still carries the butter-and-kasuri-methi richness. It feels indulgent yet sits easy, making it a clever midweek take on the dhaba classic. Smooth, buttery and quick to the table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee lends the light moong dal a satisfying Punjabi richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A neutral oil to build the onion-tomato base

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp salt and 2.75 cups water for 3 whistles until soft, then whisk to a silky pour.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds.
Add the chopped onion and fry 5 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Add the chopped tomatoes with 0.75 tsp red chilli and 0.5 tsp salt and cook 6 minutes until soft and jammy.
Pour in the cooked moong dal with 0.75 cup hot water and simmer 6 minutes, then stir in 2 tbsp butter and crushed kasuri methi.
Finish with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 0.5 tsp garam masala and serve hot.
tips: Moong keeps the dish lighter, so a little butter goes a long way here.
Do not over-thicken; this dal is best silky and just pourable.
A squeeze of lemon at the end keeps the richness from feeling heavy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulkas or jeera rice and a crisp kachumber salad on the side.

variations.name: Masoor Dal Punjabi
variations.description: A robust Punjabi-style dal built on quick-cooking red masoor, which drinks up the buttery tomato masala and turns beautifully thick. The kasuri methi and a good hit of garam masala make it taste far grander than its short cooking time suggests. Deeply savoury and satisfying.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee enriches the thick, masala-heavy masoor dal

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: A robust oil that stands up to the bold Punjabi masala

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed masoor dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp salt and 2.75 cups water for 3 whistles until soft, then whisk smooth.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the heat, add 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 15 seconds.
Add the chopped onion and fry 6 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Pour in the tomato puree with 1 tsp red chilli and 0.5 tsp salt and cook 8 minutes until thick and glossy.
Add the cooked masoor with 1 cup hot water and simmer 6 minutes, then stir in 2 tbsp butter and crushed kasuri methi.
Finish with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 0.75 tsp garam masala and serve piping hot.
tips: Smoke the mustard oil first to tame its sharpness before building the masala.
Masoor thickens fast, so keep hot water handy to adjust the consistency.
Let it rest five minutes off the heat so the kasuri methi perfume settles in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tandoori roti or steamed rice, sliced onions and a wedge of lemon.

variations.name: Chana Dal Punjabi
variations.description: A festive Punjabi-Rajasthani dal where nutty chana lentils hold their shape in a rich, buttery tomato gravy fragrant with kasuri methi. The firm grains and the indulgent masala make it hearty enough to be the star of the table. Rustic yet celebratory.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee gives the sturdy chana dal its rich, festive character

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A clean oil to fry the onion base for this heavier dal

steps: Pressure-cook the soaked 1 cup chana dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 to 7 whistles until tender but intact.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds.
Add the chopped onion and fry 6 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Add the finely chopped tomatoes with 1 tsp red chilli and 0.5 tsp salt and cook 8 minutes until pulpy and the fat glistens.
Add the cooked chana dal with 1 cup of its liquid and 0.5 tsp amchur powder, and simmer 8 minutes so the grains soak up the tangy gravy, then stir in 2 tbsp butter and crushed kasuri methi.
Finish with the remaining 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 0.75 tsp garam masala, scatter the coriander and serve hot.
tips: Soaking is essential so the chana dal turns tender without disintegrating in the rich gravy.
Keep the grains a little firm; their bite is what makes this dal special.
Loosen with hot water before serving, as chana dal thickens sharply on standing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot laccha paratha or steamed rice and a spoon of mango pickle.

variations.name: Palak Dal Punjabi
variations.description: A wholesome Punjabi-style dal palak where toor lentils and fresh spinach meet a buttery tomato masala and a whisper of kasuri methi. The greens keep it vibrant while the butter and ghee lend the signature dhaba richness. Nourishing comfort food that looks as good as it tastes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee ties the spinach and buttery masala together richly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A light oil to wilt the spinach and fry the base

steps: Pressure-cook 0.75 cup rinsed toor dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp salt and 2.5 cups water for 4 whistles until soft, then whisk smooth.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds.
Add the chopped onion and slit green chillies and fry 5 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Add the tomatoes with 0.75 tsp red chilli and 0.5 tsp salt, cook 5 minutes until pulpy, then stir in the 3 cups spinach and saute 3 minutes until just wilted.
Pour in the cooked dal with 0.75 cup hot water and simmer 6 minutes, then stir in 2 tbsp butter and crushed kasuri methi.
Finish with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 0.5 tsp garam masala, scatter the coriander and serve while vividly green.
tips: Add the spinach late and cook briefly so the dal stays bright rather than dull.
For a smoother finish, puree half the wilted spinach before adding the dal.
A squeeze of lemon lifts the greens and balances the butter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or jeera rice and a swirl of cream, with a side of pickled onions.

variations.name: Classic Dal Tadka
variations.description: The restaurant favourite: soft yellow toor dal simmered creamy, then crowned with a sizzling ghee tadka of cumin, garlic and dried red chilli poured over at the table. The double hit of aromatics and the final smoky chilli give it that unmistakable dhaba fragrance. Comforting, buttery and endlessly moppable with roti.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The pourable finishing tadka depends on ghee for that glossy, nutty aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A clean wood-pressed oil to soften the onion base without masking the dal

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed toor dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 4 to 5 whistles until completely soft, then whisk it smooth and creamy.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a pan over medium heat, add the chopped onion and fry 5 minutes until golden, then add the tomatoes and cook 5 minutes until pulpy.
Stir in 0.75 tsp red chilli and 0.5 tsp salt, then pour in the cooked dal with a little hot water to loosen and simmer gently for 8 minutes until thick.
For the tadka, heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan until shimmering and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds.
Add the sliced garlic and fry until pale gold, then take off the heat and stir in 0.25 tsp asafoetida and the 2 dried red chillies broken in half so they sizzle.
Pour the hot ghee tadka over the simmering dal, cover for 1 minute to trap the aroma, then stir through the coriander and serve.
tips: Whisk the cooked dal well before the final simmer; it is what gives that smooth, restaurant-style body.
Pour the tadka over the dal at the very last moment so the garlic and chilli stay fragrant and audible.
Add hot water, never cold, when loosening the dal so the simmer is not interrupted.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jeera rice or hot phulka, a wedge of lemon and a side of thinly sliced onion and green chilli.

variations.name: Moong Dal Tadka
variations.description: A lighter, quick-cooking tadka made with split green moong dal that turns silky and pale gold, gently spiced and easy on the stomach. This mountain-style version keeps the tempering simple with cumin, ginger and a hint of dry ginger powder for warmth. Soothing comfort food for any day.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries the gentle ginger tempering that defines this light dal

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A neutral wood-pressed oil to sweat the aromatics without heaviness

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, half the grated ginger, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 3 whistles until soft, then whisk lightly.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat, add the chopped tomato and slit green chillies, and cook 4 minutes until the tomato collapses.
Pour in the cooked dal with a splash of hot water, add 0.5 tsp salt and simmer 6 minutes until it looks silky and pourable.
For the tadka, heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan until hot and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds.
Off the heat, stir in the remaining grated ginger, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 0.25 tsp dry ginger powder so they bloom in the residual heat.
Pour the fragrant tadka over the dal, cover 1 minute, then fold in the coriander and serve hot.
tips: Moong dal thickens noticeably as it sits, so keep it a touch looser than you think off the heat.
The pinch of dry ginger powder gives a warming, easy-to-digest quality perfect for a light supper.
Skim off any froth while the dal cooks for a cleaner, brighter colour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice and a dollop of ghee, or with soft khichdi-style comfort in mind.

variations.name: Masoor Dal Tadka
variations.description: A rustic Haryanvi tadka with split red masoor dal that cooks quickly into a soft, faintly sweet base and takes a bold garlic-and-chilli tempering beautifully. The dal turns a warm golden-brown and the smoky tadka gives it real depth. Everyday food with a satisfying punch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: For the assertive garlic tadka that this quick-cooking dal soaks up

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: A pungent Haryanvi touch to build the onion-tomato base

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed masoor dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 3 whistles until soft, then whisk lightly to a smooth pour.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the heat, add the chopped onion and fry 5 minutes until golden.
Add the tomatoes with 1 tsp red chilli, 1 tsp coriander powder and 0.5 tsp salt and cook 6 minutes until pulpy and the oil separates.
Pour in the cooked dal with a little hot water and simmer 6 minutes until it thickens to a comforting consistency.
For the tadka, heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, add the crushed garlic and fry until deep golden and nutty.
Slip in the 2 dried red chillies for the last 10 seconds, pour the tadka over the dal, cover briefly, then finish with coriander.
tips: Masoor dal breaks down fast, so three whistles are plenty; overcooking turns it gluey.
Fry the garlic to a deep gold for a smoky, almost roasted flavour in the tadka.
A squeeze of lemon at the end lifts the earthy masoor beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a raw onion salad, or with hot tandoori roti for a fuller plate.

variations.name: Chana Dal Tadka
variations.description: A hearty Punjabi tadka made with nutty chana dal that stays in distinct, tender grains rather than melting away, giving a wonderful bite. The robust dal takes a rich ghee tempering of cumin, garlic and ginger, rounded out with garam masala. Substantial, wholesome and full of texture.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee gives the sturdy chana dal its rich, festive-tasting tadka

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: To build the onion base for this heavier dal without weighing it down

steps: Pressure-cook the soaked 1 cup chana dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 to 7 whistles until tender but still holding shape.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat, fry the chopped onion 5 minutes until golden, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Add the tomatoes, 0.75 tsp red chilli and 0.5 tsp salt and cook 6 minutes until soft and jammy.
Tip in the cooked chana dal with its liquid and simmer 8 minutes so the grains soak up the masala.
For the tadka, heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds until fragrant, then stir in 0.75 tsp garam masala off the heat.
Pour the aromatic ghee over the dal, cover 1 minute to lock in the scent, then stir through the coriander and serve.
tips: Soaking the chana dal for an hour cuts the cooking time and keeps the grains from splitting.
Do not over-whisk this dal; the charm of chana dal is its firm, separate grains.
It thickens as it cools, so loosen with hot water when reheating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rotis or jeera rice and a spoon of mango pickle for a filling everyday meal.

variations.name: Palak Dal Tadka
variations.description: A wholesome Delhi-style dal where soft toor dal is folded together with fresh spinach and finished with a bright garlic-cumin tadka. The spinach keeps the dal light and vividly green while adding an earthy sweetness. A nourishing one-pot that makes greens genuinely crave-worthy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The garlicky ghee tadka lifts the spinach and ties the dal together

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A light wood-pressed oil to wilt the spinach without dulling its colour

steps: Pressure-cook 0.75 cup rinsed toor dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp salt and 2.5 cups water for 4 whistles until soft, then whisk smooth.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil over medium heat, add the chopped tomato and slit chillies and cook 3 minutes until softened.
Add the 3 cups chopped spinach and 0.5 tsp salt and saute 3 minutes just until wilted and still bright green.
Pour in the cooked dal with a splash of hot water and simmer 6 minutes until the flavours meld.
For the tadka, heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, add the minced garlic and fry until golden, then stir in 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 0.5 tsp red chilli off the heat.
Pour the sizzling tadka over the dal, stir once, and serve while the spinach is still vivid.
tips: Add the spinach late and cook it only until just wilted to keep the dal green rather than khaki.
Blanch and refresh the spinach first if you want an even brighter colour in the finished dal.
A squeeze of lemon just before serving stops the spinach tasting flat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a wedge of lemon, or with hot phulkas and a dollop of white butter.

variations.name: Classic Dum Aloo
variations.description: Whole baby potatoes pricked, fried until blistered, then slow-cooked on dum in a spiced onion-tomato gravy so the flavour seeps right into the flesh. The skins turn glossy and the centres stay fluffy. A dish where patience, not shortcuts, makes all the difference.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil fries the potatoes and gives dum aloo its traditional pungent depth

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of bilona ghee rounds the gravy and adds a glossy sheen

steps: Boil 500 g baby potatoes until just tender, peel them, and prick each all over with a fork so they soak up the gravy.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it smokes, lower the heat, and shallow-fry the potatoes for 5 to 6 minutes until the skins blister and turn golden, then set aside.
In the same oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, add 2 chopped onions, and fry for 8 minutes until browned, then stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute.
Add 3 pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, and cook until the oil separates, about 8 minutes.
Lower the heat and whisk in 0.5 cup curd a spoon at a time so it does not curdle, then cook 2 minutes until the gravy comes together.
Return the fried potatoes with 1.25 cups water and the remaining 0.75 tsp salt, cover tightly, and dum-cook on the lowest heat for 12 to 15 minutes.
Uncover, stir in 0.75 tsp garam masala and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, and simmer 2 minutes until the gravy clings to each potato.
tips: Pricking the potatoes is essential; it is how the masala travels into the centre during the dum.
Add curd off the boil and whisk constantly, or it will split and leave the gravy grainy.
The slow dum on low heat is what defines this dish, so resist rushing it on high flame.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the glossy potatoes with jeera rice or soft phulka and a side of thin onion rings soaked in lemon to cut the richness.

variations.name: Masala Dum Aloo
variations.description: A rustic, coriander-forward dum aloo where a heavy dose of roasted coriander powder builds an earthy, tangy gravy with no cream in sight. The baby potatoes are simmered in a thinner, spicier sauce that soaks deep into their fluffy centres. Homely, robust and full of aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil fries the potatoes and keeps the coriander-led gravy clean

steps: Boil 500 g baby potatoes until just tender, peel, and prick all over with a fork so the spicy gravy can seep in.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and shallow-fry the potatoes for 5 minutes until golden and blistered, then remove and set aside.
In the same oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin and 0.5 tsp fennel seeds for 30 seconds, add 2 chopped onions, and fry for 8 minutes until golden brown.

Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then dry-roast 2.5 tsp coriander powder separately for 40 seconds and add it with 3 pureed tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp red chilli powder, cooking until the oil surfaces, about 8 minutes.
Pour in 2 cups water and the remaining 0.75 tsp salt to make a deliberately thinner gravy, and bring to a simmer.
Return the potatoes, cover, and dum-cook on low heat for 15 minutes so they drink up the tangy, coriander-rich sauce.
Uncover and finish with 3 tbsp chopped fresh coriander stirred through the gravy.
tips: The fennel seeds add a subtle sweetness that balances the tang; do not skip them in this version.
Keep the gravy loose so the potatoes can absorb it fully during the dum.
Roast the coriander powder just before use for the earthy aroma that carries this rustic dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot bajra or wheat roti and a spoon of white butter, or over plain rice with a raw onion salad and green chilli.

variations.name: Kadai Dum Aloo
variations.description: A kadai treatment where fried baby potatoes are tossed with charred capsicum and a coarse hand-pounded coriander-chilli masala into a thick, semi-dry dish. The sauce clings tightly and the pepper keeps its crunch against the soft potatoes. Bold, smoky and vibrant on the plate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked wood-pressed mustard oil gives the kadai its sharp, gutsy edge

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon glazes the potatoes and softens the mustard oil's bite

steps: Boil 500 g baby potatoes until just tender, peel, and prick with a fork all over.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until hazy, lower the heat, and fry the potatoes for 5 minutes until the skins blister and brown, then set aside.
Dry-roast 2 tbsp coriander seeds and 3 dried red chillies for 2 minutes until fragrant, cool, and pound to a coarse kadai masala.
In the same oil, fry 2 diced onions for 6 minutes, add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then 3 chopped tomatoes and 0.5 tsp turmeric and cook until the oil separates, about 7 minutes.
Stir in most of the pounded masala with just 0.75 cup water and the remaining 0.75 tsp salt, then return the potatoes and toss on medium-high heat for 6 minutes until the thick gravy coats them.
Add 1 large capsicum in thick wedges and toss on high heat for 3 to 4 minutes so it chars yet stays crunchy.
Crush 1 tsp kasuri methi over the pan, swirl in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and the reserved masala, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Keep this semi-dry, using little water so the coarse masala clings to the potatoes.
Add the capsicum near the end so it holds its crunch against the soft potatoes.
For extra smokiness, blister the boiled potatoes over an open flame before frying.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve straight from the kadai with laccha paratha or tandoori roti and a sharp mint-onion chutney on the side.

variations.name: Handi Dum Aloo
variations.description: A slow handi dum aloo scented entirely with whole spices bloomed in ghee, the potatoes sealed under a tight lid to steam in the aromatic gravy. Cinnamon, cloves and cardamom perfume every bite in place of powdered garam masala. Gentle, fragrant and deeply comforting.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: whole spices bloom in bilona ghee and their aroma steams into the potatoes on dum

steps: Boil 500 g baby potatoes until just tender, peel, and prick all over with a fork.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a handi and bloom 1 inch cinnamon, 4 cardamom pods, 4 cloves, 1 bay leaf and 8 peppercorns until fragrant and swollen, about 40 seconds.
Fry the potatoes in the spiced ghee for 4 minutes until lightly golden, then lift them out and keep aside.

Add 2 sliced onions to the same ghee, fry for 9 minutes until golden, add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then 3 pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and cook until the ghee separates, about 8 minutes.
Lower the heat and whisk in 0.5 cup curd gradually so it does not split, then cook 2 minutes until smooth.
Return the potatoes with 1 cup water and the remaining 0.75 tsp salt, cover the handi tightly, and dum-cook on minimum heat for 15 minutes.
Uncover, discard the bay leaf and cinnamon, and serve the perfumed potatoes without any powdered garam masala.
tips: Frying the potatoes in the spiced ghee first layers the whole-spice aroma right onto the skins.
Whisk the curd in off the boil to keep the gravy silky rather than curdled.
Remove the larger whole spices before serving so no one bites into a clove or peppercorn.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the fragrant potatoes with ghee rice or rumali roti and a cooling mint raita to balance the warm spicing.

variations.name: Punjabi Dum Aloo
variations.description: A rich Punjabi dum aloo where the baby potatoes rest in a cashew-smooth gravy finished with cream and crushed kasuri methi, its butter replaced by bilona ghee. Fuller and creamier than the classic, with a mellow fenugreek fragrance. A restaurant-style treat for special meals.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: swapped in for butter to give the creamy gravy a rich, nutty bilona depth

steps: Boil 500 g baby potatoes until just tender, peel, and prick all over with a fork.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan and shallow-fry the potatoes for 5 minutes until lightly golden, then remove and set aside.
Soak 12 cashews in warm water for 15 minutes, then blend with 2 boiled onions and 3 tomatoes into a smooth paste.

Crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds in the remaining ghee, add the blended paste with 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, and cook for 10 minutes until the ghee separates.
Add 1.5 cups water and the remaining 0.75 tsp salt, return the potatoes, cover, and simmer gently for 12 minutes so they soak up the creamy gravy.
Lower the heat, stir in 3 tbsp cream and 0.75 tsp garam masala, and warm through for 2 minutes without boiling.
Crush 1.5 tsp kasuri methi between your palms over the pan and stir it in just before serving.
tips: Strain the cashew paste for the smoothest, most restaurant-like gravy.
Keep the flame low after the cream goes in so it does not split and dull the sheen.
Make the gravy base ahead and add fried potatoes and cream when reheating for an easy party dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or saffron pulao, garnished with a cream swirl, kasuri methi and slivered almonds for a festive finish.

variations.name: Classic Gajar Matar
variations.description: The quintessential winter dry sabzi of sweet carrots and fresh green peas cooked together in a simple cumin tempering. Naturally sweet and cheerful, it needs little more than turmeric, chilli and a squeeze of lime, the peas keeping their pop against the tender carrot.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: its nutty richness beautifully complements the natural sweetness of carrots and peas

steps: Peel and dice 4 carrots into small 1/2-inch cubes and shell 1 cup of green peas.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add 1 inch grated ginger and 2 slit green chillies and fry for 30 seconds.
Add the diced carrots with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, tossing to coat, then cover and cook on low for 6 minutes.
Stir in the green peas with 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp coriander powder, cover, and cook another 6 minutes until both are tender.
Uncover and stir-fry on medium for 3 minutes to dry off any moisture and lightly glaze the vegetables.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala, turn off the heat, and finish with 1 tsp lime juice tossed through.
tips: Dice the carrots small and even so they cook in the same time as the peas.
Use fresh winter peas when in season for the sweetest result; frozen peas need only the last 4 minutes.
Keep it dry and glossy rather than watery so it holds well in a lunchbox.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulkas and a dab of ghee, or tuck it into a paratha roll with mint chutney.

variations.name: Masala Gajar Matar
variations.description: A UP-style version with a proper onion-tomato masala and garam masala giving the sweet carrots and peas a richer, spicier frame. The masala clings to each cube while the peas add bursts of freshness, making it fuller and more festive than the everyday dry sabzi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: its pungency balances the sweetness of the carrots and peas in the masala

steps: Dice 4 carrots into small cubes and shell 1 cup of peas, keeping them ready.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the flame, and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds.
Add 2 chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 6 minutes until golden brown.
Stir in 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, cooking 5 minutes until the oil separates.
Add the carrots and peas with 1 tsp salt, cover, and cook on low for 10 minutes until tender, stirring once.
Sprinkle 0.75 tsp garam masala and 2 tbsp chopped coriander, stir for a minute, and serve.
tips: Cook the masala until the oil visibly separates for a properly bhunoed, non-raw taste.
Add a splash of water only if the masala catches, keeping the final sabzi dry.
Frozen peas can go in with the carrots but reduce their cook time to avoid mushiness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tawa parathas and a bowl of curd, or pair with dal and rice for a fuller lunch.

variations.name: Spicy Pepper Gajar Matar
variations.description: A punchy southern-style stir-fry where sweet carrots and peas are cut through with slit green chillies, coarse black pepper and a curry-leaf tempering. The heat plays against the vegetables' natural sugar for a bold, dry poriyal-adjacent sabzi with real bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: its toasty depth is a natural base for the southern pepper tempering

steps: Dice 4 carrots small, shell 1 cup peas, and coarsely crush 1 tsp black pepper with 5 garlic cloves.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal until golden.
Add 12 curry leaves and 3 slit green chillies, let them crackle, then stir in the crushed pepper-garlic for a minute.
Add the carrots with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, cover, and cook on low for 6 minutes until half-tender.
Add the peas, cover, and cook another 6 minutes until both vegetables are just done but still bright.
Uncover and stir-fry on medium-high for 3 minutes so it dries out and the pepper coats everything.
tips: Crush the pepper fresh for the sharp fragrance that defines this southern-style dish.
Do not overcook the peas; you want them to still burst rather than turn pasty.
The urad dal adds a nutty crunch to the tempering, so fry it just to golden and no darker.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a side with steamed rice and a bowl of rasam, or alongside curd rice to balance the heat.

variations.name: Dhaba-style Gajar Matar
variations.description: A rich, semi-dry gajar matar in a clinging onion-tomato masala perfumed with kasuri methi and garam masala. A knob of butter rounds the sweet vegetables into something indulgent, the peas and carrots glossy in a hearty roadside-style coating.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the base frying fat that gives the dhaba masala its robust body

steps: Dice 4 carrots small and shell 1 cup of peas, keeping them ready.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, fry 2 chopped onions with 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 6 minutes until deep golden.
Add 2 pureed tomatoes with 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, cooking 6 minutes until thick and glossy.
Add the carrots and peas with 1 tsp salt and a splash of water, cover, and cook on low for 9 minutes until tender.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the top with 0.75 tsp garam masala and stir for a minute until fragrant.
Finish with 1 tbsp butter swirled through, cooking a final minute until the masala turns rich and clinging.
tips: Keep the masala thick and coating so it clings to the vegetables rather than pooling.
Rub the kasuri methi between your palms before adding to release its full dhaba aroma.
A pinch of jaggery can balance the tomato if it turns too tangy against the sweet vegetables.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter-brushed tandoori roti or naan and a raw onion salad on the side.

variations.name: Bengali Gajar Matar Chholar
variations.description: A gently sweet, subtly spiced version finished with coconut and a whole-spice tempering, in the light Bengali-Kerala coastal register. Bay leaf, cinnamon and a touch of jaggery give the carrots and peas a fragrant, festive edge quite unlike the North Indian sabzi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the coastal fat that echoes the coconut finish and softens the spice

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the gentle sweetness that defines this coastal-style preparation

steps: Dice 4 carrots small and shell 1 cup of peas, keeping them aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, add 1 bay leaf, 1 inch cinnamon and 1 tsp cumin seeds, letting them sizzle for 30 seconds.
Add 2 slit green chillies and the carrots with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, tossing to coat.
Pour in half a cup of water, cover, and cook on low for 8 minutes until the carrots begin to soften.
Add the peas and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, cover, and cook another 6 minutes until tender and the water dries up.
Fold in 3 tbsp grated coconut off the heat, tossing until evenly coated and fragrant.
tips: The whole spices should perfume the oil gently; keep the flame low so they do not burn.
Add the jaggery to taste, aiming for a faint sweetness rather than a dessert-like dish.
Fresh grated coconut folded in at the end keeps its sweet, delicate texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a dal, or with soft luchi for a festive coastal-style meal.

variations.name: Classic Ghee Rice
variations.description: A fragrant, buttery rice where basmati is cooked in generous ghee with whole spices and crowned with crisp fried onions. Simple yet indulgent, it is the beloved neychoru of South Indian feasts, each grain gleaming and aromatic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: this dish is all about the ghee, so nutty bilona ghee is what makes it sing

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati rice until the water runs clear, soak for 20 minutes, then drain so the grains cook long and separate.

Heat the Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot over medium heat, fry 12 cashews until golden and lift them out, then fry the thinly sliced onions for 8 minutes until deep golden and crisp and reserve half for garnish.
To the ghee and remaining onions add 4 cardamom, 4 cloves, a 1 inch cinnamon stick and 2 bay leaves, and let them bloom for 30 seconds, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Add the drained rice and toss very gently for 2 minutes so each grain is coated in the aromatic ghee.
Pour in exactly 3 cups water with 1.5 tsp salt, bring to a rolling boil, then cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes until the water is absorbed.
Rest covered for 5 minutes, then fluff with a fork and top with the reserved fried onions, fried cashews and 2 tbsp coriander.
tips: Fry the onions slowly and evenly to a deep golden birista, as they carry the dish's flavour and garnish.
