Do not skimp on the ghee here, since its richness is the whole point of ghee rice.
Reserve half the fried onions and cashews for the top so the finish looks and tastes generous.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a spicy vegetable kurma or a tangy raita, the way it is traditionally paired in Malabar homes.

variations.name: Assamese Ghee Bhat
variations.description: A pared-back Assamese ghee bhat where fragrant short-grain rice is simply anointed with ghee and a whisper of whole spice, no fried onions or nuts. It celebrates the pure aroma of good rice and pure ghee, the way Assamese thalis begin a meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: with so few ingredients, the pure nutty aroma of bilona ghee is the whole dish

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati rice until the water runs clear, soak for 20 minutes, then drain to keep the grains long and separate.
Heat the Anveshan Ghee in a pot over medium heat and add 1 tsp cumin seeds, 2 bay leaves, 2 cloves and a 1 inch cinnamon stick, letting them bloom gently for 30 seconds.
Slip in 1 slit green chilli for aroma, then add the drained rice and toss very gently for 2 minutes so each grain is coated in ghee.
Pour in exactly 3 cups water with 1.5 tsp salt, bring to a rolling boil, then cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes until the water is absorbed.
Rest covered for 5 minutes off the heat so the grains firm up, then fluff gently with a fork.
Drizzle a little extra warm ghee over the top and scatter 1 tbsp coriander just before serving for the simplest, purest finish.
tips: With so few ingredients, use the best rice and ghee you have, as there is nothing to hide behind.
Keep the whole spices whole and mild so they perfume without dominating the delicate rice.
A final drizzle of raw ghee over the hot rice is traditional and lifts the aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as the opening course of an Assamese thali with a wedge of lime and a little mashed potato, or alongside a light dal.

variations.name: Haryanvi Spiced Ghee Rice
variations.description: A robust Haryanvi twist where the buttery rice is deepened with a coarse crushed masala of pepper, coriander and cumin. It is heartier and more warming than the mild classic, built for cold-weather appetites.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee forms the rich base that carries the coarse crushed spices

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes and drain, then coarsely crush 2 tsp coriander seeds, 1 tsp cumin seeds and 10 peppercorns in a mortar.
Heat the Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and fry the sliced onions for 8 minutes until deep golden, reserving a third for garnish.
Add 3 cloves and a 1 inch cinnamon stick with the crushed spice mix, and let them bloom in the ghee for 30 seconds until intensely fragrant.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 2 slit green chillies, cook for 1 minute, then add the drained rice and toss gently for 2 minutes.
Pour in 3 cups water with 1.5 tsp salt, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on the lowest heat for 13 minutes until the water is absorbed.
Rest for 5 minutes, fluff gently, and scatter the reserved fried onions on top before serving.
tips: Crush the whole spices coarsely rather than powdering them for pockets of warmth in the rice.
Toast the crushed spices in ghee just until fragrant to avoid a bitter, burnt note.
Add a little extra pepper if you like a stronger warming heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of thick kadhi or a spiced chana masala, and a side of pickled green chillies.

variations.name: Delhi Festive Ghee Rice
variations.description: A dressed-up Delhi banquet version gilded with saffron milk, mixed nuts and rose water. The rice turns golden and perfumed, echoing the Mughlai kitchens of the old city with its rich, celebratory character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: rich bilona ghee is the base of this Mughlai-style celebratory rice

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: saffron steeped in warm milk gives the golden Mughlai colour and aroma

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, drain, and steep 0.25 tsp Anveshan Saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk.
Heat the Anveshan Ghee over medium heat, fry 10 cashews and 10 slivered almonds until golden and lift them out, then fry the sliced onions for 8 minutes until deep golden and reserve half.
Add 4 cardamom, 3 cloves and a 1 inch cinnamon stick to the ghee and bloom for 30 seconds, then add the drained rice and toss gently for 2 minutes.
Pour in 3 cups water with 1.5 tsp salt, bring to a rolling boil, then drizzle the saffron milk over the surface.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes until the water is absorbed and golden streaks run through the rice.
Rest for 5 minutes, sprinkle 0.5 tsp rose water, fluff gently, and garnish with the fried nuts and reserved onions.
tips: Add the rose water sparingly at the very end, as too much can turn the rice soapy.
Steep the saffron in warm milk for the deepest colour before drizzling it over the rice.
Fry the nuts on gentle heat so they turn evenly golden without any bitterness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at a feast with a rich navratan korma or shahi paneer, garnished with silver leaf for a banquet finish.

variations.name: Telangana Quick Ghee Rice
variations.description: A speedy Telangana-style ghee rice made in a pressure cooker with a fresh curry-leaf and green-chilli temper. It keeps all the buttery comfort of the classic while cutting the effort for a weeknight table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee delivers the full buttery aroma even in a quick cooker method

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati rice well and rest it for just 10 minutes, then drain to keep the recipe fast.
Heat the Anveshan Ghee in a pressure cooker over medium heat, add 3 cardamom, 3 cloves, 1 bay leaf and 12 curry leaves, and let them crackle for 20 seconds.
Add the sliced onion and 2 slit green chillies and fry for 5 minutes until the onion turns golden at the edges.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute, then add the drained rice and toss gently for 1 minute.
Pour in 2.5 cups water with 1.5 tsp salt, close the lid, and cook on medium heat for 2 whistles before turning off the flame.
Let the pressure release naturally for 8 minutes, then open, fluff gently, and serve hot with a drizzle of extra ghee.
tips: The curry-leaf temper gives a fresh southern aroma that sets this apart from the North Indian classic.
Use slightly less water in the cooker to keep the grains fluffy rather than sticky.
Drizzle a little extra ghee over the hot rice just before serving for a glossy finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a simple tomato pappu or a bowl of curd, adding a spoon of gongura pickle on the side.

variations.name: Classic Gobi Paratha
variations.description: A North Indian winter classic: finely grated cauliflower seasoned simply and stuffed into a soft Anveshan Khapli Atta dough, then griddled in ghee until golden and flecked with brown. The trick is squeezing the gobi bone-dry so the parathas roll without tearing and stay crisp, not soggy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Kneaded into a soft dough; the nutty emmer wheat suits the delicate cauliflower filling.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: One spoon in the dough and the rest for roasting the parathas to a crisp golden finish.

steps: Knead 3 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and about 1.25 cups water into a soft, pliable dough; cover and rest 20 minutes.
Grate 1 medium cauliflower finely, sprinkle with 0.5 tsp salt, leave 10 minutes, then squeeze out every drop of moisture in a clean cloth.
Mix the dry gobi with 2 finely chopped green chillies, a grated 1-inch piece of ginger, 1.5 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp amchur, 4 tbsp coriander and 0.5 tsp salt.
Divide dough and filling into 8 each; flatten a dough ball, place 2 tbsp filling inside, gather and seal the edges, then roll gently to a 7-inch round with light atta dusting.
Roast on a hot tava for about 1 minute until the top blisters, flip and brush with 0.5 tsp ghee, cooking each side 1-2 minutes until golden with brown spots.
Stack the parathas under a cloth to keep them soft while you finish rolling and roasting the rest.
tips: Squeezing the grated cauliflower completely dry is the single most important step; wet filling makes parathas tear.
Do not skip resting the salted gobi; it draws out water so you can wring it out properly.
Roll with a gentle hand and even pressure so the soft filling spreads without bursting through.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot with a bowl of curd, mixed pickle and a small mound of white butter melting over the top.

variations.name: Masala Gobi Paratha
variations.description: A more aromatic gobi paratha where the grated cauliflower is folded with garam masala, coriander powder and toasted spices for a warmer, restaurant-style depth. The Anveshan Khapli Atta dough and ghee crust keep it hearty while the masala lifts the mild cauliflower.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The wholegrain dough base that stands up to the bolder spiced cauliflower filling.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: Worked into the dough and brushed on while roasting for a fragrant, crisp golden crust.

steps: Knead 3 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and about 1.25 cups water into a soft dough; cover and rest 20 minutes.
Grate 1 medium cauliflower and 1 small onion finely, salt with 0.5 tsp salt, rest 10 minutes and then squeeze out all the water in a cloth.
Mix the dry vegetables with 1 tsp garam masala, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 chopped green chillies, 4 tbsp coriander and 0.5 tsp salt.
Divide dough and filling into 8 each; stuff 2 tbsp filling into each dough ball, seal, and roll gently to a 7-inch round, dusting with atta as needed.
Roast on a hot tava for 1 minute, flip, brush with 0.5 tsp ghee and cook each side 1-2 minutes until golden with crisp brown flecks.
Keep the cooked parathas warm and soft under a cloth while you finish the batch.
tips: Grate the onion with the gobi and squeeze them together; onion water is what most often makes these parathas soggy.
Toast the garam masala briefly in a dry pan to bloom its aroma before mixing it in.
If the filling still feels damp, dust in a spoon of roasted besan to soak up excess moisture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a spiced onion-tomato raita and a wedge of lemon to sharpen the masala.

variations.name: Spicy Gobi Paratha
variations.description: A hot-headed gobi paratha packed with green chillies, crushed black pepper and extra red chilli for a lingering warmth that suits cold mornings. The mild cauliflower is the perfect canvas for the heat, wrapped in a nutty Anveshan Khapli Atta crust griddled in ghee.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The soft, nutty dough that mellows and carries the fiery cauliflower filling.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: In the dough and on the tava, its richness softens the edge of the heat while crisping the crust.

steps: Knead 3 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and about 1.25 cups water into a soft dough; cover and rest 20 minutes.
Grate 1 medium cauliflower finely, salt with 0.5 tsp salt, rest 10 minutes and wring it bone-dry in a cloth.

Coarsely crush 1 tsp peppercorns and mix into the gobi with 4 finely chopped green chillies, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, a grated 1-inch piece of ginger, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp chaat masala, 4 tbsp coriander and 0.5 tsp salt.
Divide dough and filling into 8 each; stuff 2 tbsp filling into each dough ball, seal, and roll gently to a 7-inch round with an atta dusting.
Roast on a hot tava for 1 minute, flip, brush with 0.5 tsp ghee and cook each side 1-2 minutes until golden with crisp brown spots.
Stack under a cloth to stay soft and warm while the rest cook.
tips: Freshly crushed pepper gives a brighter, more aromatic heat than pre-ground pepper.
Deseed a couple of the green chillies if you want the flavour without the full burn.
Serve with something cooling; the heat builds quickly once you start eating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a generous bowl of chilled curd and a mint chutney to soothe the palate.

variations.name: Garlic Gobi Paratha
variations.description: A savoury, garlic-laced gobi paratha where sauteed garlic threads through the grated cauliflower for a deep, moreish aroma. Ghee-roasting toasts the garlic edges, and the wholesome Anveshan Khapli Atta dough gives a satisfying, nutty chew.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Kneaded into the dough; its earthy nuttiness marries perfectly with toasted garlic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: Used to saute the garlic and roast the parathas, layering in a rich toasted-garlic aroma.

steps: Knead 3 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and about 1.25 cups water into a soft dough; cover and rest 20 minutes.
Finely chop 10 garlic cloves and saute in 1 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee over medium heat for 1-2 minutes until pale gold and fragrant, then cool.

Grate 1 medium cauliflower, salt with 0.5 tsp salt, rest 10 minutes, squeeze dry, then mix with the sauteed garlic, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 4 tbsp coriander and 0.5 tsp salt.
Divide dough and filling into 8 each; stuff 2 tbsp filling into each ball, seal, and roll gently to a 7-inch round, dusting with atta.
Roast on a hot tava for 1 minute, flip, brush with 0.5 tsp ghee and cook each side 1-2 minutes until golden with toasty spots.
Stack under a cloth to keep soft while you finish the remaining parathas.
tips: Sauteing the garlic mellows its raw pungency into a sweet, nutty aroma that suits cauliflower.
Squeeze the gobi dry after the garlic has cooled so no extra moisture sneaks in.
A pinch of ajwain in the filling aids digestion and complements the garlic.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a tangy tomato-garlic chutney and a simple bowl of dal for a warming meal.

variations.name: Cheesy Gobi Paratha
variations.description: A crowd-pleasing hybrid where grated cheese melts into the mildly spiced cauliflower filling for a gooey, savoury centre. The Anveshan Khapli Atta dough griddled in ghee crisps into a golden shell that yields to soft gobi and stretchy cheese within.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The nutty wholegrain dough that crisps around the cheese-and-cauliflower filling.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon in the dough and the rest for roasting to a crisp, cheese-melting golden crust.

steps: Knead 3 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and about 1.25 cups water into a soft dough; cover and rest 20 minutes.
Grate 1 small cauliflower finely, salt with 0.5 tsp salt, rest 10 minutes and squeeze completely dry in a cloth.
Mix the dry gobi with 1 cup grated mozzarella, 1 finely chopped green chilli, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp black pepper powder, 3 tbsp coriander and 0.5 tsp salt.
Divide dough and filling into 8 each; encase 2 tbsp filling in each ball, seal well and roll gently to a 6-inch round so the cheese stays sealed in.
Roast on a medium-hot tava for 1-2 minutes per side, brushing with 0.5 tsp ghee, until golden and crisp with the cheese melted inside.
Serve straight away while the centre is molten and stretchy.
tips: Keep the gobi extra dry here; combined with cheese moisture, any excess water will split the paratha.
Roll these thicker and smaller so the cheese doesn't leak out of the edges.
Cook on medium heat so the cheese melts fully before the crust over-browns.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with tomato ketchup and a fresh coriander chutney for dipping.

variations.name: Classic Jeera Rice
variations.description: The quintessential North Indian cumin rice where basmati is cooked fluffy and tossed with ghee-bloomed jeera. Simple and aromatic, it lets the toasty perfume of cumin and the richness of ghee shine in every separate grain.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee is the soul of jeera rice, blooming the cumin into a warm, nutty aroma

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati rice until the water runs clear, soak for 20 minutes, then drain so the grains stay long and separate.
Heat the Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot over medium heat and add 2 tsp cumin seeds, letting them sizzle and darken slightly for about 30 seconds until deeply aromatic.
Drop in 1 bay leaf, 3 cloves, 2 cardamom and 1 slit green chilli, and let the whole spices crackle for 15 seconds.
Add the drained rice and toss very gently for 2 minutes so every grain glistens with the cumin ghee without breaking.
Pour in exactly 3 cups water with 1.5 tsp salt, bring to a rolling boil, then cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes until all the water is absorbed.
Rest covered for 5 minutes off the heat, then fluff with a fork and fold in 2 tbsp chopped coriander before serving.
tips: Let the cumin darken just slightly for a toasty flavour, but pull back before it burns and turns bitter.
The 1:2 rice-to-water ratio with soaked rice guarantees fluffy, separate grains.
Fluff only after a 5 minute rest so the grains firm up and do not clump.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside dal tadka or a rich paneer curry, with a wedge of lemon and sliced onions on the side.

variations.name: Awadhi Jeera Rice
variations.description: A delicate Lucknowi rendition from the kitchens of Awadh, where the cumin rice is perfumed with mace and a few drops of kewra water. Subtler and more aristocratic than the everyday version, it is finished with light golden onions rather than heavy spice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee gives this Awadhi rice its refined, aristocratic aroma

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain gently so the long grains stay unbroken.
Heat the Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and fry the thinly sliced onion for 6 minutes until pale gold and soft, then lift out half for garnish.
Add 2 tsp cumin seeds, 1 blade of mace, 3 cardamom and 3 cloves to the ghee, and let them bloom quietly for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the drained rice and toss very gently for 2 minutes so the grains glisten without any browning.
Pour in exactly 3 cups water with 1.5 tsp salt, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes until the water is absorbed.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp kewra water, rest covered for 5 minutes, then fluff gently and scatter the reserved golden onions on top.
tips: Use kewra water in tiny amounts, as its floral aroma quickly turns overpowering.
Keep the onions pale gold rather than deep brown to preserve the dish's delicate character.
A single blade of mace is enough, since too much can make the rice medicinal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a mild korma or a bowl of yogurt-based salan, garnished with a few fried onion strands for an Awadhi touch.

variations.name: Bihari Spiced Jeera Rice
variations.description: A heartier Bihari take that builds on the cumin base with fried onions, cracked black pepper and extra whole spices. The rice turns golden-flecked and boldly aromatic, closer to a light pulao than a plain cumin rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee fries the onions and blooms the cumin for a deep, homely aroma

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain and keep aside for cooking.
Heat the Anveshan Ghee over medium heat, add 2 tsp cumin seeds, 8 black peppercorns, 4 cloves, a 1 inch cinnamon stick and 2 bay leaves, and let them crackle for 30 seconds.
Add the thinly sliced onions and fry for 7 minutes until deep golden and crisp at the edges, then add julienned ginger and 2 slit green chillies and saute 1 minute.
Fold in the drained rice and toss gently for 2 minutes so the grains take on the golden onion colour and spice aroma.
Pour in 3 cups water with 1.5 tsp salt, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on the lowest heat for 13 minutes until the water is absorbed.
Rest covered for 5 minutes, then fluff gently with a fork, leaving some fried onion visible on top for garnish.
tips: Fry the onions until truly golden for a natural sweetness that balances the pepper heat.
Lightly crush the peppercorns before adding for a stronger, warming kick.
Keep some of the crisp fried onion aside to scatter over just before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pairs wonderfully with a bowl of kadhi or a spicy aloo-baingan, finished with a squeeze of lime.

variations.name: Madhya Pradesh Festive Jeera Rice
variations.description: A dressed-up festive version from Madhya Pradesh where the cumin rice is gilded with saffron milk, fried cashews and cardamom. Streaked with gold and studded with nuts, it rises to a special-occasion accompaniment.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: extra bilona ghee gives this festive rice its rich sheen and celebratory aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: saffron steeped in warm milk lends golden streaks worthy of a feast

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, drain, and steep 0.25 tsp Anveshan Saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk to draw out its colour.
Heat the Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and fry 15 cashews and 2 tbsp raisins until the cashews are golden and the raisins plump, then lift them out and set aside.
In the same ghee add 2 tsp cumin seeds, 4 cardamom and 3 cloves, and let them bloom for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the drained rice and toss gently for 2 minutes, then pour in 3 cups water with 1.5 tsp salt and bring to a rolling boil.
Drizzle the saffron milk over the surface, cover, and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes until the water is absorbed and golden streaks appear.
Rest for 5 minutes, fluff gently, and fold in most of the fried cashews and raisins, saving a few to scatter on top.
tips: Steep the saffron for at least 10 minutes in warm milk for the deepest colour and aroma.
Fry the cashews on gentle heat so they turn evenly golden without scorching.
Drizzle the saffron milk over the top rather than mixing it in for a marbled two-tone effect.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at a festive spread with shahi paneer or a creamy dal makhani, garnished with a few extra saffron strands.

variations.name: Goan Quick Jeera Rice
variations.description: A breezy Goan-style cumin rice with a coconut-oil temper and curry leaves for a coastal twist. Quick to make and lightly fragrant, it swaps the usual heavy whole spices for a fresh, southern-leaning aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed coconut oil gives this quick rice its coastal Goan fragrance

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoon of bilona ghee stirred in at the end rounds out the coconut aroma

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati rice well and rest it for just 10 minutes, then drain to keep the recipe quick.
Heat the Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pot over medium heat, add 2 tsp cumin seeds and 12 curry leaves, and let them splutter for 20 seconds.
Add julienned ginger and 2 slit green chillies and saute for 30 seconds until fragrant, being careful not to brown them.
Add the drained rice and toss gently for 1 minute, then pour in 2.75 cups water with 1.5 tsp salt and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes until the water is absorbed and the surface is dotted with steam holes.
Rest for 4 minutes, stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 2 tbsp coriander, and fluff gently before serving.
tips: Skip the soak to save time, but do rinse thoroughly so the rice does not turn sticky.
Let the curry leaves crisp in the hot oil for the best coastal aroma.
Stir the finishing ghee in while the rice is warm so it melts evenly through the grains.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coconut-based fish curry or a simple dal, adding a wedge of lime and a spoon of mango pickle.

variations.name: Classic Khatta Meetha Kaddu
variations.description: The beloved sweet-and-sour pumpkin sabzi of North Indian bhandara feasts, where soft pumpkin is cooked down with fenugreek, amchur and jaggery into a spoonable, jammy mash. It hits sweet, tangy and mildly spicy all at once and pairs magically with hot puris.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: its pungency is traditional for this bhandara-style khatta meetha kaddu

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the meetha half of khatta meetha, melting into the pumpkin for its signature sweetness

steps: Peel and dice 500 g pumpkin into rough 1-inch cubes, leaving the skin on a few pieces for texture if you like.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the flame, and add 0.5 tsp fenugreek seeds, 1 tsp cumin seeds, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 2 broken dried red chillies.
Once the fenugreek darkens slightly, add the pumpkin with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, tossing to coat.
Add a quarter cup of water, cover, and cook on low for 12 minutes until the pumpkin is completely soft and collapsing.
Mash roughly with the back of the spoon, then stir in 1.5 tsp amchur and 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder.
Cook uncovered for 4 minutes until the jaggery melts and the sabzi turns thick, glossy and jammy.
tips: Do not brown the fenugreek too far or it turns bitter; pull it back the moment it darkens.
Adjust the sweet-sour balance at the end, aiming for tangy and sweet in equal measure.
Leaving a little skin on some pieces is traditional and adds a pleasant texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with puffed puris or kachoris, the classic pairing at North Indian feasts and festival meals.

variations.name: Masala Kaddu
variations.description: A savoury pahari take where pumpkin is cooked in an onion-tomato masala rounded with garam masala, dropping the usual sweetness for a spicier, everyday sabzi. The pumpkin softens into the masala while cumin and coriander keep it grounded and warming.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the customary hill-kitchen oil that grounds this savoury version

steps: Peel and dice 500 g pumpkin into 1-inch cubes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the flame, and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds.
Add 2 chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, frying for 5 minutes until golden.
Stir in 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, cooking 4 minutes until pulpy and the oil separates.
Add the pumpkin with 1 tsp salt and a quarter cup of water, cover, and cook on low for 12 minutes until soft.
Sprinkle 0.75 tsp garam masala and 2 tbsp chopped coriander, stir gently keeping some cubes whole, and serve.
tips: Stir gently so the pumpkin stays in pieces rather than turning fully to mash.
If the pumpkin is very watery, cook uncovered at the end to thicken the masala.
A pinch of amchur brightens it without turning it into the sweet-sour version.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hand-rolled rotis and a bowl of curd, or alongside dal and rice for a hearty hill meal.

variations.name: Spicy Pepper Kaddu
variations.description: A dry, fiery pumpkin stir-fry cut through with slit green chillies and coarse black pepper, tempered eastern-style with panch phoron. The sweetness of the pumpkin plays against sharp pepper and mustard, giving a bold, brothless side that eats like a spiced roast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the pungent eastern staple that suits the panch phoron tempering

steps: Peel 500 g pumpkin and cut into thin 1/4-inch slices so they cook fast and can brown.
Coarsely crush 1.25 tsp black pepper with 6 garlic cloves into a rough paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the flame, and add 1 tsp panch phoron, letting it splutter for 20 seconds.
Add the crushed pepper-garlic and 4 slit green chillies, frying a minute, then add the pumpkin with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt.
Cover and cook on low for 8 minutes until soft, then uncover and stir-fry on medium-high for 5 minutes until the edges brown and it dries out.
Dust in 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, toss for a minute, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Slice the pumpkin thin so it browns rather than turning into a wet mash.
Panch phoron is a five-seed eastern blend; let it splutter fully to release its aroma.
Raise the heat at the end to caramelise the natural sugars in the pumpkin.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a dal, or with hot rotis for a fiery, no-fuss vegetable side.

variations.name: Dhaba-style Kaddu
variations.description: A rich, semi-dry pumpkin in a clinging onion-tomato masala scented with kasuri methi and garam masala. Browned onions and a knob of butter turn the humble kaddu hearty and savoury, the pumpkin glossy in a bold roadside-style coating rather than the usual sweet-sour mash.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the base frying fat that gives the dhaba masala its robust body

steps: Peel and dice 500 g pumpkin into 1-inch cubes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, fry 2 chopped onions with 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 6 minutes until deep golden.
Add 2 pureed tomatoes with 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, cooking 6 minutes until thick and glossy.
Add the pumpkin with 1 tsp salt and a quarter cup of water, cover, and cook on low for 12 minutes until tender.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the top with 0.75 tsp garam masala and stir for a minute until fragrant.
Finish with 1 tbsp butter swirled through, cooking a final minute until the masala is rich and clinging.
tips: Keep the masala thick and coating so it clings to the soft pumpkin.
Stir gently to keep some cubes intact rather than mashing everything.
Rub the kasuri methi between your palms before adding to release its aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or tandoori roti and a raw onion-lemon salad on the side.

variations.name: Kaddu Bhaji with Coconut
variations.description: A gently sweet coastal bhaji where pumpkin is simmered soft and finished with fresh coconut and a mustard-curry-leaf tempering. Light and fragrant with a whisper of jaggery, it balances the pumpkin's sweetness against green chilli and the nutty coconut crunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the coastal fat that echoes the fresh coconut finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a light sweetness that lifts the pumpkin the coastal way

steps: Peel and dice 500 g pumpkin into small 1/2-inch cubes so they cook quickly.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, then add 12 curry leaves and 2 slit green chillies.
Add the pumpkin with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, tossing to coat in the tempering.
Pour in a quarter cup of water, cover, and cook on low for 12 minutes until the pumpkin is soft.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and mash lightly, cooking 2 minutes until thick.
Fold in 4 tbsp grated coconut off the heat, tossing until evenly distributed.
tips: Dice the pumpkin small so it cooks fast and mashes easily for a soft bhaji.
Add the coconut at the very end so it stays fresh and does not brown.
Keep the jaggery subtle; this should be lightly sweet, not a dessert.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and dal, or alongside soft parathas for a comforting coastal-style meal.

variations.name: Classic Karela
variations.description: The homely North Indian bitter gourd sabzi where salted, sauteed karela is softened in a light onion-tomato masala until its bitterness mellows into a savoury, appetite-whetting edge. Slow cooking and a touch of amchur turn a much-feared vegetable into something you actually reach back for.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: its pungency stands up to karela's bitterness better than any bland oil

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a natural sweetener that balances the bitterness the traditional way

steps: Scrape and thinly slice 4 bitter gourds into rings, rub with 1 tsp of the salt, and rest 20 minutes, then squeeze out and discard the bitter juices.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the flame, and fry the squeezed karela rings for 8 minutes until browned and crisp, then lift out and set aside.
In the same oil crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, add 2 sliced onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, and saute 5 minutes until golden.
Stir in 1 chopped tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, cooking 4 minutes until pulpy and the oil separates.
Return the fried karela with the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, cover, and cook on low for 8 minutes so the flavours meld and the rings soften.
Finish by stirring in 1 tsp amchur and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, cooking 2 minutes until the bitterness is rounded and the sabzi is glossy.
tips: The salt-and-squeeze step is essential; skipping it leaves the karela aggressively bitter no matter how you cook it.
Frying the rings until genuinely crisp before the masala keeps them from turning mushy later.
Balance is key: taste at the end and add a touch more jaggery if the bitterness still dominates.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain paratha and a cooling boondi raita, or alongside dal-chawal where its bitter edge cuts through the richness.

variations.name: Bharwa Masala Karela
variations.description: Whole bitter gourds stuffed with a roasted spice-and-onion masala brightened by garam masala and fennel, then slow-cooked until the shells turn silky. This pahari-style stuffed karela is a festive, labour-of-love dish where the filling tames the bitterness from the inside out.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: used both to cook the filling and to shallow-fry the stuffed gourds

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: folded into the stuffing to counter bitterness with a mellow sweetness

steps: Scrape 6 small bitter gourds, slit each lengthwise keeping one edge intact, rub with 1 tsp salt, and rest 30 minutes before squeezing out the juices.
Dry-roast 2 tsp fennel and 2 tsp coriander powder for a minute, then grind coarsely for the stuffing base.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and fry 3 finely chopped onions for 8 minutes until deep brown, then mix in the ground spices, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp garam masala, 1.5 tsp amchur, 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and the remaining salt.
Cool the masala slightly and pack it firmly into each slit gourd, using about 2 tbsp filling per piece, then tie them with thread if needed.
Heat the remaining 2 tbsp mustard oil in a wide pan and lay in the stuffed gourds, cooking covered on low for 20 minutes and turning gently every 5 minutes.
Uncover and cook a final 5 minutes on medium to crisp the shells and dry any oozed filling before removing the threads to serve.
tips: Choose small, slim gourds as they stuff more easily and cook through evenly than fat ones.
Do not rush the onion browning; a deep caramelised base is what makes the stuffing taste rich rather than raw.
These keep and even improve overnight, making them a smart make-ahead dish for guests.
variations.servingSuggestion: Present the whole stuffed gourds on a platter with hot phulkas and a wedge of lemon, letting each person split one open at the table.

variations.name: Spicy Pepper Karela
variations.description: An Odia-style dry fry where crisp karela slivers meet slit green chillies and coarse black pepper for a bracing, sharp heat. There is no onion-tomato masala to hide behind, just bitterness playing against fresh chilli and pepper, finished with a squeeze of lime for a fierce, appetising side.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: its toasty warmth is a natural partner to bitter gourd in eastern cooking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a small hit of sweetness to keep the sharp heat and bitterness in check

steps: Thinly sliver 4 bitter gourds, rub with 1 tsp salt, rest 20 minutes, then squeeze firmly to release the bitter liquid.
Coarsely crush 1.5 tsp black pepper and 8 garlic cloves together in a mortar into a rough paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, add 1 tsp panch phoron, and let it splutter for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add the crushed pepper-garlic and 4 slit green chillies, frying for a minute, then tip in the karela slivers with 0.5 tsp turmeric and the remaining salt.
Stir-fry uncovered on medium-high for 12 minutes, pressing the karela against the pan so it crisps and browns at the edges.
Turn off the heat, stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 2 tsp lime juice, and toss until every sliver glistens.
tips: Slice the gourd as thin as you can so it crisps quickly and the bitterness recedes.
Crush the pepper coarsely rather than using fine powder for bursts of pungent heat throughout.
Keep the pan hot and the karela in a single layer if possible so it fries rather than steams.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a sharp, crisp side with steamed rice and a plain moong dal, or as a fiery accompaniment to curd rice.

variations.name: Dhaba-style Karela
variations.description: A rich, semi-dry karela with a clinging onion-tomato masala lifted by crushed kasuri methi and garam masala. Caramelised onions and slow browning give the bitter gourd a deep, almost sweet edge, turning a humble vegetable into a robust roadside-style treat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the robust base fat that gives the dhaba masala its punch

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: rounds the bitterness and tomato tang into a mellow dhaba-style gravy

steps: Slice 4 bitter gourds into rings, salt with 1 tsp, rest 20 minutes, and squeeze out the bitter juice.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, fry the karela rings for 8 minutes until crisp and browned, then set them aside.
In the same oil fry 3 finely sliced onions with 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 8 minutes until deeply caramelised.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes with 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, cooking 6 minutes until it forms a thick, glossy masala.
Return the fried karela with the remaining 0.5 tsp salt and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, cover, and simmer on low for 6 minutes.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the top, sprinkle 0.75 tsp garam masala, and stir for a minute until fragrant and clinging.
tips: Deep caramelisation of the onions is what gives this its dhaba richness, so let them go well past golden.
Keep the masala thick and coating rather than watery so it clings to each ring.
Rub the kasuri methi between your palms before adding to release its full aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with butter-brushed tandoori roti and a raw onion salad for a hearty, highway-style vegetarian meal.

variations.name: Dry Onion Karela
variations.description: A simple pahari everyday dry sabzi where crisped karela is tossed with a generous heap of sliced onions cooked down to sweet, golden softness. Minimal spicing lets the sweet onions naturally offset the bitterness, making this the gentlest introduction to bitter gourd.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the customary hill-kitchen oil that suits the pungent karela

steps: Slice 4 bitter gourds thinly, rub with 1 tsp salt, rest 20 minutes, and squeeze out the bitter liquid firmly.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the heat, and crackle 1 tsp fennel seeds and 0.5 tsp ajwain for 20 seconds.
Add 6 sliced garlic cloves and 4 thickly sliced onions, cooking on medium for 10 minutes until soft, sweet and golden.
Push the onions aside, add the squeezed karela with 0.5 tsp turmeric and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, and stir-fry together for 8 minutes until browned.
Sprinkle in 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and toss on medium-high for 3 minutes so everything crisps at the edges.
Turn off the heat and finish with 2 tsp lemon juice squeezed over for a gentle tang.
tips: Use plenty of onion; its natural sweetness is what makes this mild version so approachable.
Cook the onions slowly to golden rather than browning them fast for the best sweet-savoury balance.
This travels well and is a good lunchbox candidate as it has no gravy to turn watery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thick hand-rolled rotis and a bowl of curd, or as a side to a simple mandua roti pahari meal.

variations.name: Classic Vegetable Kofta
variations.description: Golden mixed-vegetable dumplings of grated bottle gourd, potato and carrot, bound with besan and fried crisp, then bathed in a smooth onion-tomato gravy. The koftas soak up just enough sauce to soften at the edges while staying tender within. A restaurant favourite made properly at home.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed sunflower oil for deep-frying gives clean, light koftas that don't turn greasy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the gravy is cooked in bilona ghee for a rich, aromatic base

steps: Grate 2 cups bottle gourd, 1 potato and 1 carrot, then squeeze out the excess water firmly with your hands and reserve that liquid for the gravy.
Mix the squeezed vegetables with 5 tbsp besan, 0.5 tsp salt, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 0.25 tsp turmeric into a stiff, shapeable dough, adding a little more besan if it feels wet.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Sunflower Oil to 170C and fry walnut-sized koftas in batches for 4 to 5 minutes until deep golden and crisp all over, then drain on a rack.
In a separate pan, heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then fry 2 chopped onions for 8 minutes until golden and add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute.
Add 3 pureed tomatoes with the remaining 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, and cook until the ghee separates, about 8 minutes.
Pour in 1.5 cups water plus the reserved vegetable water and the remaining 1 tsp salt, simmer 8 minutes, then stir in 0.75 tsp garam masala.
Gently slide the koftas into the hot gravy only 3 to 4 minutes before serving so they soften slightly but do not disintegrate.
tips: Squeeze the grated vegetables really dry, or the koftas will drink oil and fall apart while frying.
Add the koftas to the gravy at the last minute; leaving them to sit too long turns them mushy.
Fry a test kofta first, and if it breaks up, work in another spoon of besan to firm up the mix.
variations.servingSuggestion: Arrange the koftas in a shallow dish, pour the gravy around them, and top with cream and coriander; serve with tandoori roti or peas pulao.

variations.name: Masala Vegetable Kofta
variations.description: A Malwa-style kofta where a bold hand of roasted coriander powder builds an earthy, rustic gravy, and the koftas themselves are studded with crushed peanuts for texture. Less creamy and more spice-driven than the restaurant version, with a warm, nutty character throughout.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil deep-fries the koftas and echoes the peanuts inside them

steps: Grate 2 cups bottle gourd and 1 potato, squeeze out the water tightly, and mix with 3 tbsp crushed peanuts, 5 tbsp besan, 0.5 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp red chilli powder into a firm dough.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 170C and fry small koftas for 4 to 5 minutes until crisp and golden brown, then drain well.
In another pan, heat 3 tbsp of the same groundnut oil and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then fry 2 chopped onions for 8 minutes until browned and add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute.

Dry-roast 2.5 tsp coriander powder in a small pan for 40 seconds, then add it with 3 pureed tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and cook until the oil separates, about 8 minutes.
Pour in 2 cups water and the remaining 1 tsp salt and simmer this rustic, spice-forward gravy for 10 minutes until it thickens slightly.
Slide the koftas in 3 minutes before serving so they stay intact and just soak up the edges of the gravy.
Finish with 3 tbsp chopped fresh coriander scattered over the top.
tips: The crushed peanuts add crunch and a nutty depth; roast them lightly first for the best flavour.
Fresh-roasted coriander powder defines this gravy, so grind it just before cooking if you can.
Keep the gravy on the thinner side, as this rustic version is meant to be mopped up with bajra or jowar roti.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra roti and a dollop of white butter, or with plain rice and a wedge of lemon for a hearty village-style meal.

variations.name: Kadai Vegetable Kofta
variations.description: A semi-dry kadai kofta where the vegetable dumplings are tossed with charred capsicum and a coarse hand-pounded kadai masala. The thick, clinging gravy coats the koftas rather than drowning them, and the pepper stays crunchy. Bold, smoky and vividly spiced.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: neutral wood-pressed sunflower oil keeps the koftas light so the kadai masala leads

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the kadai gravy starts in bilona ghee for aroma and finishes glossy

steps: Grate 2 cups bottle gourd and 1 potato, squeeze dry, and bind with 5 tbsp besan, 0.5 tsp salt and 0.25 tsp turmeric into a stiff dough, then shape into small balls.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Sunflower Oil to 170C and fry the koftas for 4 to 5 minutes until crisp and golden, then set aside to drain.
Dry-roast 2 tbsp coriander seeds and 3 dried red chillies until fragrant, about 2 minutes, then cool and pound to a coarse kadai masala.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai, fry 2 diced onions for 6 minutes until softened, add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then 3 chopped tomatoes and the remaining 0.25 tsp turmeric and cook until the ghee separates, about 7 minutes.
Stir in most of the pounded kadai masala with 1 cup water and the remaining 1 tsp salt, and cook 6 minutes into a thick, clinging gravy.
Add 1 large capsicum in thick wedges and toss on high heat for 3 to 4 minutes so it chars lightly but stays crunchy.
Fold in the koftas for the last 2 minutes, crush 1 tsp kasuri methi over the top, and finish with the reserved kadai masala.
tips: Keep this gravy thick so it coats the koftas; a thin sauce would waterlog them in a semi-dry dish.
Toss the koftas in only at the end so they stay crisp-edged rather than soggy.
Char the capsicum wedges hard for a smokier, more authentic kadai flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve straight from the kadai with laccha paratha or butter naan, garnished with ginger juliennes and a squeeze of lemon.

variations.name: Handi Vegetable Kofta
variations.description: A slow handi kofta scented purely with whole spices bloomed in ghee, the dumplings finished under a sealed lid so they drink in the aromatic steam. No powdered garam masala goes in; cinnamon, cloves and cardamom carry the fragrance. Gentle, homely and richly perfumed.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: whole spices bloom in bilona ghee and infuse both gravy and koftas as they steam

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed sunflower oil for frying the koftas keeps them light and crisp

steps: Grate 2 cups bottle gourd and 1 potato, squeeze out the moisture, and bind with 5 tbsp besan, 0.5 tsp salt and 0.25 tsp turmeric into a firm dough shaped into balls.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Sunflower Oil to 170C and fry the koftas for 4 to 5 minutes until golden and crisp, then drain on a rack.
In a handi, heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and bloom 1 inch cinnamon, 4 cardamom pods, 4 cloves and 1 bay leaf until fragrant and swollen, about 40 seconds.

Add 2 sliced onions and fry slowly for 9 minutes until golden, stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then add 3 pureed tomatoes with the remaining 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and cook until the ghee surfaces, about 8 minutes.
Pour in 2 cups water and the remaining 1 tsp salt, bring to a gentle simmer, and taste the aromatic gravy for seasoning.
Slide in the koftas, cover the handi tightly, lower the heat to minimum, and dum-cook for 8 minutes so they absorb the whole-spice fragrance.
Uncover gently, discard the bay leaf, and serve without stirring too vigorously so the koftas stay whole.
tips: Add the koftas only for the short dum at the end; a long simmer would break these delicate dumplings.
Skip the garam masala entirely, since the bloomed whole spices already give a rounded, layered aroma.
Fish out the cinnamon, cloves and bay leaf before serving so no one bites into a hard whole spice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the koftas gently spooned over saffron pulao or with soft phulka, finished with a light drizzle of cream and fresh coriander.

variations.name: Punjabi Vegetable Kofta
variations.description: A rich Punjabi-style kofta in a cashew-smooth gravy finished with cream and crushed kasuri methi, its butter swapped for bilona ghee. The koftas are extra tender, bound with a little khapli atta, and the sauce is plush and mildly sweet. A festive, indulgent version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: replaces butter in the gravy for a lush, aromatic bilona richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed sunflower oil for frying gives clean, golden koftas

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: a spoon of nutty khapli atta binds the koftas in place of refined flour and keeps them tender

steps: Grate 2 cups bottle gourd, squeeze dry, and mix with 0.5 cup crumbled paneer, 3 tbsp besan, 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta and 0.5 tsp salt into a soft but shapeable dough.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Sunflower Oil to 170C and fry the koftas for 4 minutes until pale golden and tender, then drain gently.
Soak 12 cashews in warm water for 15 minutes, then blend with 2 boiled onions and 3 tomatoes to a smooth paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan, add the blended paste with 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 1 tsp red chilli powder, and cook for 10 minutes until the ghee separates and the base thickens.
Add 1.5 cups water and the remaining 1 tsp salt, simmer 6 minutes, then lower the heat and stir in 3 tbsp cream and 0.75 tsp garam masala.
Crush 1.5 tsp kasuri methi between your palms into the gravy and warm through for 2 minutes without boiling.
Place the koftas in a serving dish and pour the hot gravy over them just before serving so they stay soft yet intact.
tips: Pouring the gravy over the koftas at the table keeps them from soaking through and breaking.
The paneer and khapli atta make these koftas especially tender, so handle them gently while frying.
For a smoother gravy, strain the cashew paste before cooking and finish with an extra spoon of cream.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a wide bowl with the koftas half-submerged, drizzled with cream and slivered almonds, alongside butter naan or jeera rice.

variations.name: Classic Lauki
variations.description: The light everyday bottle-gourd sabzi where soft cubes of lauki simmer in a thin onion-tomato masala until they melt in the mouth. It is gentle on the stomach and quick to cook, relying on cumin and coriander for its clean flavour. A staple comfort dish for simple thalis.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A light wood-pressed oil keeps this delicate sabzi clean and easy to digest.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing teaspoon adds gentle richness without weighing down the lauki.

steps: Peel 700 g bottle gourd, halve it, scoop out any hard seeds and cut the flesh into 2 cm cubes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds with 0.5 tsp ajwain and 2 slit green chillies for 20 seconds.
Add 1 chopped onion and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and saute for 5 minutes until the onion turns soft and pale gold.
Stir in 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 4 minutes until pulpy.
Add the lauki cubes, splash in 3 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 14 to 16 minutes, stirring twice, until the pieces turn translucent and soft.
Uncover, mash a few pieces lightly for body, stir in 0.5 tsp amchur powder, finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and 2 tbsp coriander, and serve hot.
tips: Always taste a small raw piece of lauki first; a bitter gourd will ruin the dish and must be discarded.
Lauki releases plenty of its own water, so add only a little and adjust rather than drowning it.
Mashing a few cooked cubes into the masala gives the sabzi a lovely natural body without any thickener.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulkas and a spoon of yoghurt, or with plain moong dal and rice for a soothing meal.

variations.name: Masala Lauki
variations.description: A Telangana-style masala lauki lifted with warm garam masala and a slightly thicker onion-tomato base so the mild gourd carries real spice. The masala clings to each cube for a fuller, more festive feel. Fragrant, satisfying and far from bland.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Builds a slightly richer masala base that coats the mild gourd.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The garam masala is bloomed in ghee to give the sabzi its warm finish.

steps: Peel 700 g bottle gourd, deseed and cut into 2 cm cubes, keeping them uniform so they cook evenly.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds with a 1 inch piece of cinnamon, 3 green cardamoms and 3 cloves for 20 seconds.
Add 2 chopped onions and 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 7 minutes until golden.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 5 minutes until the oil separates.
Add the lauki with 3 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 15 minutes until soft and coated in a thick masala.
Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, stir 1.25 tsp garam masala into it for 10 seconds, then fold it through with 3 tbsp coriander.
tips: Keep the masala on the thicker side so the mild gourd picks up plenty of flavour.
Add the garam masala only at the finish for a fresh, fragrant lift rather than a cooked-out taste.
A tablespoon of whisked curd stirred in with the tomatoes gives an even richer, tangier gravy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jeera rice or hot rotis and a side of onion rings with lemon.

variations.name: Spicy Lauki
variations.description: A Bihari-style spicy lauki where slit green chillies and coarsely crushed black pepper cut through the gourd's mildness, tempered in pungent mustard oil for real bite. It is a bold way to make a humble vegetable exciting. Sharp, peppery and warming.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: The pungent oil of the eastern plains stands up to the pepper and green-chilli heat.

steps: Peel 700 g bottle gourd, deseed and cut into 2 cm cubes, and slit 4 green chillies lengthways.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai on medium-high until it shimmers, then crackle 1 tsp panch phoron until the seeds pop, about 20 seconds.
Add 1 chopped onion, the slit green chillies and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and saute for 5 minutes until the onion softens and the chillies blister.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 4 minutes until pulpy.
Add the lauki with 3 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 15 minutes until the pieces are soft and glossy.
Crush 1 tsp black pepper coarsely, stir it in with 3 tbsp coriander and cook uncovered for a final 2 minutes so the pepper heat blooms.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to shimmering to tame its raw sharpness before the tempering goes in.
Panch phoron adds a distinctive eastern aroma, so let all five seeds crackle before adding the onion.
Add the black pepper at the very end to keep its heat lively and aromatic.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a drizzle of raw mustard oil, or with hot litti for a Bihari spread.

variations.name: Dhaba-style Lauki
variations.description: A Madhya Pradesh dhaba lauki with the tell-tale kasuri-methi and garam-masala finish and a richer browned masala that transforms the plain gourd into something crave-worthy. A ghee tempering seals in the highway-kitchen aroma. Hearty, herby and full-bodied.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A generous pour to brown the onions into a glossy dhaba masala.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Kasuri methi crushed into warm ghee delivers the classic dhaba finish.

steps: Peel 700 g bottle gourd, deseed and cut into 2 cm cubes, then finely chop 2 onions and 3 tomatoes.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add the onions and 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste.
Fry the onions for 8 minutes until deep golden brown, the base of a good dhaba masala.
Add the tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 6 minutes until thick and the oil separates.
Add the lauki with 4 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 15 minutes until soft and coated in the masala.
Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi into it, pour over with 1 tsp garam masala and 3 tbsp coriander, and fold through.
tips: Brown the onions well past golden for the deep, rich flavour a dhaba masala needs.
Crush the kasuri methi between your palms before adding to release its herbal aroma.
For a wetter, gravy-style dish add an extra half cup of hot water and simmer two minutes longer.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter rotis or laccha paratha and a side of pickled onions.

variations.name: Home-style Lauki
variations.description: A Goan household lauki tempered with mustard seeds and curry leaves and rounded with a splash of coconut for a mild coastal sweetness. Cooked soft and light, it is the practical everyday take with a southern-western accent. Gentle, aromatic and soothing.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: The coastal fat ties the grated coconut and curry-leaf tempering together.

steps: Peel 700 g bottle gourd, deseed and cut into 1.5 cm cubes so they cook quickly and stay tender.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadhai on medium, splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, then add 10 curry leaves and 2 slit green chillies.
Add 1 chopped onion and saute for 4 minutes until soft and translucent.
Add 1 chopped tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 3 minutes until softened.
Add the lauki with 3 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 14 minutes until the pieces are soft and translucent.
Stir in 3 tbsp grated coconut and 2 tbsp coriander, cook uncovered for a final minute and serve warm.
tips: Keep the spicing gentle so the natural sweetness of the gourd and coconut comes through.
Add the grated coconut near the end so it stays fresh-tasting rather than dry.
A squeeze of lime just before serving brightens this mild, coconut-rich sabzi beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a bowl of thin dal, or with soft chapatis for a light meal.

variations.name: Classic Lemon Rice
variations.description: The bright South Indian chitranna where cooled rice is tossed with a sizzling temper of mustard, dals and curry leaves, then lit up with fresh lemon and turmeric. Tangy, nutty and sunshine-yellow, it is a lunchbox and festival staple.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed sesame oil is the authentic gingelly oil that defines South Indian lemon rice

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoon of bilona ghee added at the end rounds the tang with a mellow richness

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati rice, cook it in 3 cups water with a pinch of salt until just tender, then spread it on a plate to cool so the grains stay separate.
Heat the Anveshan Sesame Oil over medium heat and fry 3 tbsp peanuts until golden and crunchy, about 3 minutes, then lift them out and reserve.
In the same oil add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop, then add 1 tbsp chana dal and 1 tbsp urad dal and fry until the dals turn golden, about 1 minute.
Add 15 curry leaves, 2 slit green chillies and 0.25 tsp asafoetida, let them crackle for 15 seconds, then stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric and turn off the heat so it does not burn.
Add the cooled rice, the fried peanuts and 1 tsp salt, and toss gently until every grain is coated an even yellow.
Squeeze in the juice of 2 lemons, drizzle 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, and fold through so the rice is tangy and glossy before serving.
tips: Always add the lemon juice off the heat, as boiling it turns the juice bitter.
Use day-old or fully cooled rice so the grains stay separate rather than mushy.
Fry the peanuts first and add them last so they keep their crunch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature with a spoon of coconut chutney or crisp potato chips, ideal for a lunchbox or picnic.

variations.name: Chhattisgarhi Lemon Rice
variations.description: A homely central-Indian take where the tangy rice is tempered in coconut oil and finished with roasted split chickpeas and fresh coconut for a soft, sweet crunch. Milder and more rounded than the coastal classic, it carries a gentle nuttiness in every bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed coconut oil gives this central-Indian version its soft, sweet nuttiness

steps: Cook 1.5 cups rinsed basmati rice in 3 cups water until just tender, then spread it on a plate to cool and firm up.
Heat the Anveshan Coconut Oil over medium heat and lightly toast 3 tbsp grated coconut for 1 minute until fragrant, then lift it out and reserve.
In the same oil add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tbsp urad dal, let them pop and turn golden, then add 12 curry leaves, 2 slit green chillies and finely chopped ginger for 20 seconds.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric and take the pan off the heat so it does not scorch, then add the cooled rice and 1 tsp salt.
Toss gently until the rice is an even yellow, then fold in the toasted coconut and 2 tbsp roasted split chickpeas for crunch.
Squeeze in the juice of 2 lemons off the heat and mix through so the rice turns tangy, soft and nutty before serving.
tips: Roasted split chickpeas, or putana dal, add crunch without any frying, so stir them in at the very end.
Toast the coconut only until pale gold to keep its sweetness rather than a burnt edge.
Add the lemon off the heat so its brightness is not cooked away.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature with a spoon of tomato chutney or plain curd, ideal for a simple midday meal.

variations.name: Jharkhandi Spiced Lemon Rice
variations.description: A punchier, spice-forward take that layers dried red chillies, ginger and toasted sesame into the tangy rice. Warmer and more assertive than the mild classic, it suits those who like their lemon rice with real heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil stands up to the bold dried-chilli temper

steps: Cook 1.5 cups rinsed basmati rice in 3 cups water until just tender, then spread it out to cool completely.
Dry-roast 1 tbsp sesame seeds in a hot pan for 1 minute until they pop and smell nutty, then set them aside.
Heat the Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat, fry 3 tbsp peanuts until golden, remove them, then add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 3 broken dried red chillies and let them crackle.
Add finely chopped ginger, 15 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida, saute for 30 seconds, then stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric and take the pan off the heat.
Fold in the cooled rice, the fried peanuts, the roasted sesame and 1 tsp salt, tossing until the rice is evenly yellow and speckled.
Squeeze in the juice of 2 lemons off the heat and mix gently so the rice turns tangy, spicy and fragrant before serving.
tips: Break the dried chillies so their heat and aroma release fully into the oil.
Toast the sesame seeds separately so they do not burn in the busy temper.
Taste and add a little more lemon if the extra spice needs balancing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling boondi raita or plain curd to offset the heat, and a crisp fried papad.

variations.name: Punjabi Festive Lemon Rice
variations.description: A richer, festive-style lemon rice dressed with fried cashews, grated coconut and jewel-like pomegranate. Ghee and nuts give it a celebratory heft while the lemon keeps it bright, making it a colourful party rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee lends this festive version its rich aroma and gloss

steps: Cook 1.5 cups rinsed basmati rice in 3 cups water until just done, then spread it on a plate to cool and firm up.
Heat the Anveshan Ghee over medium heat, fry 12 cashews until golden and lift them out, then lightly toast 3 tbsp grated coconut for 1 minute until fragrant and reserve.
In the same ghee add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tbsp urad dal, let them pop and turn golden, then add 12 curry leaves and 2 slit green chillies for 15 seconds.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric and take the pan off the heat, then add the cooled rice and 1 tsp salt and toss until evenly yellow.
Fold in the fried cashews, toasted coconut and the juice of 2 lemons off the heat so the rice turns tangy and rich.
Scatter 3 tbsp fresh pomegranate seeds over the top just before serving for jewel-like colour and bursts of sweetness.
tips: Add the pomegranate seeds only at the end so they stay firm and do not bleed colour.
Toast the coconut gently until just golden for a sweet, nutty depth.
Balance the richness with a touch more lemon if the dish tastes too heavy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a festive platter garnished with extra pomegranate and coconut, alongside a mixed vegetable raita.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Quick Lemon Rice
variations.description: A fast, everyday Maharashtrian fodnicha bhaat style where leftover rice is revived with a brisk mustard-and-peanut temper and lemon. Minimal, tangy and ready in minutes, it is the ultimate use-it-up lunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil gives the classic Maharashtrian fodni its nutty aroma

steps: Fluff 4 cups of cooled leftover rice with a fork so the grains loosen and separate before you start.
Heat the Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat and fry 3 tbsp peanuts until golden and crunchy, then lift them out and reserve.
Add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds to the same oil and let them splutter, then add 12 curry leaves and 2 slit green chillies for 15 seconds.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric and immediately take the pan off the heat so the turmeric does not scorch.
Add the loosened rice, the fried peanuts and 1 tsp salt, and toss quickly until the rice is coated an even yellow.
Squeeze in the juice of 1.5 lemons off the heat, fold through 2 tbsp coriander, and serve straight away.
tips: This is the perfect way to use up day-old rice, which tosses better than fresh hot rice.
Keep the temper quick and take the pan off the heat before the turmeric and lemon go in.
Adjust the lemon to taste depending on how tangy the leftover rice already is.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a dollop of plain curd and a spoon of lime pickle for a fast, satisfying meal.

variations.name: Classic Malai Kofta
variations.description: The banquet-hall favourite: soft paneer-and-potato koftas hiding a cashew-raisin centre, fried golden and set in a silky, pale cashew-tomato gravy. The koftas melt at the first bite while the mildly sweet, buttery sauce coats the spoon. Rich, delicate and unapologetically festive.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed sunflower oil deep-fries the delicate koftas without weighing them down

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the white gravy is built on bilona ghee for a mellow, buttery aroma

steps: Boil and mash 2 potatoes, then knead with 1 cup grated paneer, 3 tbsp cornflour and 0.5 tsp salt into a smooth, crack-free dough.
Flatten small portions, place a few chopped cashews and raisins in the centre, seal into balls, and fry in 2 cups Anveshan Sunflower Oil at 170C for 3 to 4 minutes until pale gold, then drain.
For the gravy, boil 2 onions, 2 tomatoes and 10 cashews together for 8 minutes, cool, and blend to a completely smooth paste, then strain.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan, bloom 3 cardamom pods for 30 seconds, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then pour in the strained paste and cook for 8 minutes until it thickens and the ghee glistens.
Add 1.5 cups water and the remaining 1 tsp salt, simmer 6 minutes, then lower the heat and stir in 4 tbsp cream and 0.5 tsp garam masala.
Keep the gravy pale and silky, adding a splash of water if it thickens too much as the cream goes in.
Place the koftas in a serving dish and ladle the hot gravy over them just before serving so they stay plump and soft.
tips: Cornflour and well-mashed potato keep the koftas from cracking; if a test kofta splits, add another spoon of cornflour.
Never simmer the koftas in the gravy, as they will dissolve; combine only at serving time.
Straining the gravy is what gives malai kofta its signature glassy, restaurant-smooth finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve halved koftas cut-side up in the pale gravy, finished with a cream swirl, slivered pistachios and a few soaked saffron strands, with butter naan.

variations.name: Masala Malai Kofta
variations.description: A spicier reinvention where the usual pale gravy gives way to an earthy, coriander-heavy tomato masala, so the soft koftas sit in a bolder, more savoury sauce. Freshly roasted coriander powder does the heavy lifting, cutting the richness of the paneer dumplings. Comforting and full-flavoured rather than delicate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed sunflower oil fries the koftas light and clean before the spicy gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the masala gravy is tempered in bilona ghee for a rounded, aromatic base

steps: Boil and mash 2 potatoes, knead with 1 cup grated paneer, 3 tbsp cornflour and 0.5 tsp salt, and shape into smooth balls.
Fry the koftas in 2 cups Anveshan Sunflower Oil at 170C for 3 to 4 minutes until golden, then drain and set aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then fry 2 chopped onions for 8 minutes until browned and add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute.
Dry-roast 2.5 tsp coriander powder for 40 seconds until fragrant, then add it with 4 pureed tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder and cook until the ghee separates, about 9 minutes.
Pour in 1.5 cups water and the remaining 1 tsp salt and simmer this bold, tangy gravy for 8 minutes until it thickens.
Slide the koftas in only 2 to 3 minutes before serving so they warm through without falling apart.
Finish with 3 tbsp chopped fresh coriander stirred gently around the koftas.
tips: This spicier gravy pairs better with firmer koftas, so chill the shaped koftas for 15 minutes before frying.
Roast the coriander powder fresh; it is the backbone of this earthier, non-creamy version.
Balance the tomato tang with a pinch of jaggery if it turns too sharp for your taste.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the koftas in the deep red gravy with steamed rice or tandoori roti and a cooling boondi raita on the side.

variations.name: Kadai Malai Kofta
variations.description: A kadai spin where the soft paneer koftas meet charred capsicum and onion in a thick, coarse-textured gravy built on hand-pounded coriander and chilli. The semi-dry sauce clings to each kofta and the pepper keeps its bite. A punchy, rustic contrast to the usual creamy malai kofta.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed sunflower oil keeps the koftas neutral so the kadai masala dominates

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the kadai gravy is cooked in bilona ghee and finished glossy

steps: Boil and mash 2 potatoes, knead with 1 cup grated paneer, 3 tbsp cornflour and 0.5 tsp salt, and shape into smooth balls.
Fry the koftas in 2 cups Anveshan Sunflower Oil at 170C for 3 to 4 minutes until golden, then drain on a rack.
Dry-roast 2 tbsp coriander seeds and 3 dried red chillies for 2 minutes until fragrant, cool, and pound to a coarse kadai masala.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai, fry 2 diced onions for 6 minutes, add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then 3 chopped tomatoes and 0.5 tsp turmeric and cook until the ghee separates, about 7 minutes.
Stir in most of the pounded kadai masala with 1 cup water and the remaining 1 tsp salt and cook 6 minutes into a thick, coarse gravy.
Add 1 large capsicum in thick wedges and toss on high heat for 3 to 4 minutes so it chars but stays crunchy.
Fold in the koftas for the final 2 minutes, crush 1 tsp kasuri methi over the top, and sprinkle the reserved kadai masala before serving.
tips: Keep the gravy thick and clingy; a watery kadai will make the koftas collapse.
Add the koftas last so their soft centres do not break in the rugged sauce.
Toast the whole spices until you can smell them across the kitchen for the deepest kadai aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve from the kadai with laccha paratha or missi roti, topped with ginger juliennes and a squeeze of lemon to lift the smoky spice.

variations.name: Handi Malai Kofta
variations.description: A slow handi malai kofta scented with whole spices bloomed in ghee, the koftas resting under a sealed lid to soak up the aromatic steam. The gravy stays creamy but takes its fragrance from cinnamon, cardamom and cloves rather than powder. Elegant, perfumed and gently rich.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: whole spices bloom in bilona ghee, perfuming the creamy gravy and the koftas within

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed sunflower oil fries the koftas light and golden

steps: Boil and mash 2 potatoes, knead with 1 cup grated paneer, 3 tbsp cornflour and 0.5 tsp salt, and shape into smooth balls.
Fry the koftas in 2 cups Anveshan Sunflower Oil at 170C for 3 to 4 minutes until pale gold, then drain and reserve.
In a handi, heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and bloom 1 inch cinnamon, 4 cardamom pods, 4 cloves and 1 bay leaf until fragrant, about 40 seconds.
Boil 2 onions with 12 cashews, blend to a smooth paste, add it to the handi with 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, and cook for 8 minutes until the ghee separates.
Pour in 1.5 cups water and the remaining 1 tsp salt, simmer 5 minutes, then lower the heat and stir in 3 tbsp cream to keep the gravy pale and silky.
Slide in the koftas, cover the handi tightly, drop the heat to minimum, and dum-cook for 6 minutes so they drink in the whole-spice aroma.
Uncover gently, discard the bay leaf and cinnamon stick, and serve without stirring hard so the koftas stay whole.
tips: Keep the dum short and the flame low, as a long steam will soften the koftas past holding together.
The whole spices replace garam masala here; adding powder would cloud the clean, creamy fragrance.
Remove the cinnamon, cloves and bay leaf before serving to spare anyone a hard whole-spice bite.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the koftas in the aromatic cream gravy over saffron pulao, finished with a light dusting of crushed cardamom and rose petals for an Awadhi flourish.

variations.name: Punjabi Malai Kofta
variations.description: The plush Punjabi rendition: paneer-potato koftas in a deeply rich cashew-tomato gravy finished with cream and crushed kasuri methi, its butter swapped for bilona ghee. Fuller-bodied and more decadent than the white version, with a warm fenugreek-scented finish. The one for celebrations.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: used instead of butter for the same richness with a nutty bilona aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed sunflower oil for frying the koftas keeps them clean and golden

steps: Boil and mash 2 potatoes, knead with 1 cup grated paneer, 3 tbsp cornflour and 0.5 tsp salt, and shape into smooth balls.
Fry the koftas in 2 cups Anveshan Sunflower Oil at 170C for 3 to 4 minutes until golden, then drain and keep aside.
Boil 2 onions, 3 tomatoes and 15 cashews together for 8 minutes, cool, and blend to a rich, smooth paste.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan, add the paste with 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, and cook for 10 minutes until thick and the ghee separates at the edges.
Add 1.5 cups water and the remaining 1 tsp salt, simmer 6 minutes, then lower the heat and stir in 4 tbsp cream and 0.75 tsp garam masala.
Crush 1.5 tsp kasuri methi between your palms into the gravy and warm through for 2 minutes without boiling.
Toast 2 tbsp slivered almonds in a dry pan until golden, then arrange the koftas in a serving dish, pour the hot gravy over them just before serving, and scatter the almonds on top.
tips: Pour the gravy over the koftas at the table so they hold their shape until the first spoonful.
For an even richer sauce, replace half the water with milk and finish with an extra spoon of cream.
Toast and hand-crush the kasuri methi for the fullest fenugreek aroma before it goes in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve halved koftas in the deep gravy topped with a cream swirl, chopped cashews and kasuri methi, alongside butter naan or ghee-laced pulao.

variations.name: Classic Masala Bread Roll
variations.description: A well-spiced bread roll where the potato filling is layered with garam masala, coriander powder and a full aromatic tempering before being rolled and fried crisp. Richly flavoured and moreish, the masala carrying through every bite. The most crowd-pleasing of the bread rolls.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Fries the masala-filled rolls to an even, crisp gold

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Blooms the whole spices so the masala tastes deep, not raw

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its slurry seals the roll so the spiced filling never leaks into the oil

steps: Boil 4 potatoes until tender, peel and mash them smooth while warm, about 15 minutes.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then saute the onion and 2 green chillies 3 minutes until soft.
Add the mashed potato with 1.5 tsp garam masala, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli and 1.25 tsp salt, cook 4 minutes, then fold in 3 tbsp coriander and cool.
Trim and dampen 10 bread slices, press out the water, place 2 tbsp filling and roll into tight sealed cylinders.
Whisk 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta with 4 tbsp water into a slurry, coat each roll, then roll in 1 cup bread crumbs.
Deep-fry in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil at 180C for 3-4 minutes until crisp and golden, then drain on paper.
tips: Toast the coriander powder with the potato for a minute to deepen the masala flavour.
Use fresh garam masala; stale powder tastes dusty and flattens the whole roll.
