Add a spoon of the filling to the crumb coating for extra masala on the outside.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with green chutney and a masala tomato ketchup, garnished with chaat masala and onion slivers.

variations.name: Punjabi Masala Bread Roll
variations.description: A dhaba-rich masala roll where the spiced potato is deepened with ginger-garlic and kasuri methi, then the crisp rolls are finished with a brush of butter. Fuller and more buttery than the classic, with that unmistakable North Indian warmth. A generous, satisfying snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Fries the rolls crisp ahead of the buttery finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Carries the ginger-garlic and kasuri methi through the rich filling

steps: Boil and mash 4 potatoes and set aside, taking about 15 minutes to cook them soft.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the onion, and fry 4 minutes until golden.
Add the mashed potato with 1.5 tsp garam masala, 0.5 tsp turmeric, crushed 1 tsp kasuri methi and 1.25 tsp salt, cook 4 minutes, then fold in the 2 green chillies and 3 tbsp coriander and cool.
Trim and dampen 10 bread slices, squeeze dry, place 2 tbsp filling and roll into firm sealed logs.
Coat each roll in a thin flour-water slurry and 1 cup bread crumbs, then deep-fry in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil at 180C for 3-4 minutes until crisp and gold.
Drain the rolls and brush at once with 2 tbsp softened butter so it soaks into the hot crust.
tips: Crush the kasuri methi between your palms before adding to release its full aroma.
Brush butter only after frying, since butter in the oil would burn and darken the rolls.
Refrigerate the shaped rolls 15 minutes before frying for a neater, firmer finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with pudina raita, sliced onion and green chilli, dhaba-style with extra butter on the side.

variations.name: Kashmiri Masala Bread Roll
variations.description: An elegant masala roll bloomed with saffron and Kashmiri chilli, spiced with fennel and dry ginger for the aromatic, mild wazwan-style warmth of the valley. Gently perfumed and rosy rather than fiery, with no onion or garlic. A refined take on the humble roll.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Fries the rolls crisp and keeps the delicate saffron colour clean

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: Bloomed in warm milk it lends the rosy glow and gentle valley perfume

steps: Soak 0.25 tsp Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside to bloom while you work.
Boil and mash 4 potatoes and keep ready, allowing about 15 minutes to cook them through.
Heat 2 tbsp of the groundnut oil over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.5 tsp ground cloves-cinnamon, then add 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli and stir 10 seconds off strong heat.
Add the mashed potato with 1.5 tsp fennel powder, 1 tsp dry ginger, 0.5 tsp turmeric, the bloomed saffron milk and 1.25 tsp salt, cook 4 minutes and fold in 3 tbsp coriander.
Cool the filling, trim and dampen 10 bread slices, squeeze dry, roll 2 tbsp filling into each and coat in flour-water slurry and 1 cup bread crumbs.
Deep-fry in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil at 180C for 3-4 minutes until crisp and rosy-gold, then drain.
tips: Bloom the saffron in warm, not hot, milk to protect its colour and fragrance.
Fennel and dry ginger define this filling, so keep onion and garlic out entirely.
Kashmiri chilli is for colour more than heat, giving a rosy filling without burning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling walnut-curd chutney and a sprinkle of slivered almonds over the top.

variations.name: Tamil Masala Bread Roll
variations.description: A South Indian masala roll tempered in nutty sesame oil with mustard, urad dal and curry leaves, the potato spiced with sambar-style warmth. Aromatic and gently coconutty, with the crackle of a proper tadka. A tiffin-shop snack turned crisp roll.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Nallennai gives the earthy Tamil aroma and fries the rolls crisp

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its slurry seals each roll around the tempered filling

steps: Boil and mash 4 potatoes and keep ready, taking about 15 minutes to cook them soft.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil over medium heat, splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal until the dal turns golden, then add 14 curry leaves and 2 green chillies.
Add the onion, fry 3 minutes, then stir in the mashed potato with 1.5 tsp sambar powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt and cook 4 minutes, then fold in 3 tbsp coriander.
Cool the filling, trim and dampen 10 bread slices, squeeze dry, roll 2 tbsp filling into each into tight logs.
Whisk 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta with 4 tbsp water, coat each roll and roll it in 1 cup bread crumbs.
Deep-fry in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil at 180C for 3-4 minutes until crisp and golden, then drain on paper.
tips: Fry the urad dal until just golden for a nutty crunch; burnt dal turns the tadka bitter.
Sesame oil has a strong flavour, so let it heat fully before frying to mellow it.
Swap sambar powder for rasam powder if you want a peppery, more tangy filling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and a small bowl of sambar for dipping, tiffin-style.

variations.name: Malwa Masala Bread Roll
variations.description: A Malwi roll from the peanut-rich heart of Madhya Pradesh, where crushed roasted peanuts and garlic give the masala potato a coarse, nutty crunch and rustic depth. Heartier and more textured than the classic. A satisfying bite from central India.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The peanut-belt oil of Malwa, perfect for frying these nutty rolls

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Blooms the garlic and masala for the rustic Malwi depth

steps: Boil and mash 4 potatoes and keep ready, allowing about 15 minutes for them to cook.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, fry the 5 crushed garlic cloves until pale gold, then add the onion and 2 green chillies and saute 3 minutes.
Stir in the mashed potato with 1.5 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp amchur, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt, cook 4 minutes, then fold in 4 tbsp crushed peanuts and 3 tbsp coriander.
Cool the filling, trim and dampen 10 bread slices, squeeze dry and roll 2 tbsp filling into each into firm logs.
Coat each roll in a thin flour-water slurry and 1 cup bread crumbs, pressing them on well.
Deep-fry in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil at 180C for 3-4 minutes until crisp and deep gold, then drain.
tips: Crush the peanuts coarse, not fine, to keep the signature crunch through the soft filling.
Roast the peanuts fresh and rub off the skins for a cleaner, sweeter nutty taste.
Add the peanuts at the end so they stay crisp rather than going soft in the potato.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coarse peanut-garlic chutney and thin buttermilk on the side, Malwi-style.

variations.name: Classic Masala Moong Dal Pakora
variations.description: A fully spiced moong dal fritter where the ground dal batter is layered with garam masala, coriander powder and a bright aromatic mix before frying crisp. Deeply flavoured in every bite, the masala carrying right through. The most moreish of the pakoras.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Fries the masala-rich fritters to an even, crisp gold

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A hot spoon beaten in crisps the crumb and deepens the masala

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup split green gram 3 hours until swollen, then drain it well.
Grind the dal coarse with the 2 green chillies and 1 tbsp ginger, using minimal water so the batter stays thick.
Beat the batter 2 minutes until light, then fold in 1.5 tsp garam masala, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, the onion, 1 tsp cumin, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli, 3 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until hot and beat it into the batter for a crisp crumb and rounded masala.
Heat Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to 180C and drop rough spoonfuls, frying 8-10 at a time.
Fry 3-4 minutes, turning, until deep golden and crisp, then drain on paper.
tips: Use freshly ground garam masala; stale powder tastes flat and dusty in the fritters.
Beat the batter well to trap air so the masala pakoras stay light rather than heavy.
Fry a tester to check seasoning and adjust the masala before the full batch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with green chutney and a sprinkle of chaat masala and onion slivers over the top.

variations.name: Punjabi Masala Moong Dal Pakora
variations.description: A dhaba-rich masala fritter where the moong dal batter is deepened with ginger-garlic, kasuri methi and garam masala, fried in ghee-touched oil for hearty North Indian warmth. Fuller and more fragrant than the classic. A cold-evening favourite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Fries the rich masala fritters crisp and golden

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Beaten into the batter for the nutty dhaba aroma and crisp finish

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup split green gram 3 hours, then drain and grind coarse with the 2 green chillies using minimal water.

Beat the batter 2 minutes until light, then fold in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 1.5 tsp garam masala, crushed 1 tsp kasuri methi, the onion, 1 tsp cumin, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli, 3 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt.
Crush the kasuri methi between your palms as you add it so its aroma bursts into the batter.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until hot and beat it into the batter for a crisp, rich crumb.
Heat Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to 180C and drop rough spoonfuls, frying 8-10 at a time.
Fry 3-4 minutes, turning, until deep golden and crunchy, then drain on paper.
tips: Crush the kasuri methi before adding to release its full dried-fenugreek fragrance.
Keep the batter thick so the fritters stay craggy and crisp rather than spreading flat.
A pinch of amchur in the batter adds a subtle dhaba-style tang.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with pudina-onion chutney and hot masala chai, dhaba-style with lemon on the side.

variations.name: Kashmiri Masala Moong Dal Pakora
variations.description: A gently aromatic moong dal fritter bloomed with saffron and Kashmiri chilli, spiced with fennel and dry ginger for the mild, perfumed warmth of the valley. Rosy and fragrant rather than fiery, without onion or garlic. An elegant twist on the pakora.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Fries the fritters crisp while keeping the delicate saffron colour clean

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: Bloomed in warm milk it lends the rosy glow and gentle valley perfume

steps: Soak 0.25 tsp Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside to bloom while you work.
Rinse and soak 1 cup split green gram 3 hours, then drain and grind coarse with the 2 green chillies using minimal water.

Beat the batter 2 minutes until light, then fold in 1.5 tsp fennel powder, 1 tsp dry ginger, 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli, 1 tsp cumin, 0.5 tsp ground cloves-cinnamon, 0.5 tsp turmeric, the bloomed saffron milk, 3 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt.
Heat Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to 180C and drop rough spoonfuls, frying 8-10 at a time.
Fry 3-4 minutes, turning, until crisp and rosy-gold, keeping the heat steady for even colour.
Drain on paper and serve warm with the saffron aroma still fresh.
tips: Bloom the saffron in warm, not hot, milk to protect its colour and delicate scent.
Fennel and dry ginger carry this batter, so leave onion and garlic out completely.
Kashmiri chilli is mostly for colour, giving a rosy fritter without harsh heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling walnut-curd chutney and a scatter of slivered almonds on top.

variations.name: Gujarati Masala Moong Dal Pakora
variations.description: A sweet-savoury Gujarati fritter where the masala dal batter is lifted with jaggery, lemon and a sesame-mustard note for the beloved khatta-meetha-teekha balance. Spiced yet softly sweet, unmistakably Gujarati. A dainty farsan-style snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The staple Gujarati frying fat for a light, crisp fritter

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Brings the signature Gujarati sweetness to offset the chilli and lemon

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup split green gram 3 hours, then drain and grind coarse using minimal water.
Dry-roast 0.5 tsp mustard, 0.5 tsp cumin and 1 tsp sesame seeds until fragrant, then lightly crush them.

Beat the batter 2 minutes until light, then fold in 1.5 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, the roasted crushed seeds, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 tbsp lemon juice, 3 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt.
Heat Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to 180C and drop rough spoonfuls, frying 8-10 at a time.
Fry 3-4 minutes, turning, until deep golden and crisp with the sesame toasted through.
Drain the fritters on paper and serve warm while the sweet-sour spicing is at its brightest.
tips: Taste the batter after the jaggery and lemon to strike the sweet-sour balance you like.
Toast the sesame just until it pops for nutty aroma without bitterness.
Keep the batter thick so the sweet fritters stay crisp and do not spread in the oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sweet date-tamarind chutney and a scatter of fine sev, Gujarati farsan style.

variations.name: Malwa Masala Moong Dal Pakora
variations.description: A Malwi fritter from peanut-rich central India, where crushed roasted peanuts and garlic give the masala dal batter a coarse, nutty crunch and rustic depth. Heartier and more textured than the classic. A satisfying bite from Madhya Pradesh.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The peanut-belt oil of Malwa, ideal for frying these nutty fritters

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Beaten in, it deepens the garlic-masala base with rustic richness

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup split green gram 3 hours, then drain and grind coarse with the 2 green chillies using minimal water.

Beat the batter 2 minutes until light, then fold in 5 crushed garlic cloves, 1.5 tsp garam masala, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, the onion, 1 tsp cumin, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 3 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt.
Fold in 4 tbsp coarsely crushed roasted peanuts last so they stay crunchy through the batter.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until hot and beat it into the batter for a crisp, rich crumb.
Heat Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to 180C and drop rough spoonfuls, frying 8-10 at a time.
Fry 3-4 minutes, turning, until deep golden and crunchy, then drain on paper.
tips: Crush the peanuts coarse, not fine, to keep the signature crunch against the soft dal.
Roast the peanuts fresh and rub off the skins for a cleaner, sweeter nutty taste.
Add the peanuts last so they stay crisp rather than softening in the wet batter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coarse peanut-garlic chutney and thin buttermilk, Malwi tea-time style.

variations.name: Classic Masala Onion Bhaji
variations.description: A fuller-flavoured bhaji where a proper masala base of garam masala, roasted coriander and cumin powders turns a simple fritter into something you reach for again and again. The spices are ground and blended into the batter so every bite is evenly seasoned rather than patchy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A clean high-heat oil that lets the layered masala flavours dominate the fritter.

steps: Slice 3 large onions thinly, salt with 1 tsp salt and rest 10 minutes until they soften and give up moisture.
Add 1 tsp garam masala, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, a grated 1-inch piece of ginger and 2 chopped green chillies, tossing to coat.
Mix in 1.5 cups besan, 2 tbsp rice flour and 3 tbsp coriander leaves with just 3 tbsp water to a thick, clinging batter.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to 180C until a test drop of batter surfaces immediately.
Fry loose spoonfuls in batches for 3-4 minutes, turning once, until golden-brown and crisp, then drain on a rack.
Taste one and adjust the salt or chilli in the remaining batter before frying the next batch.
tips: Use roasted cumin powder rather than raw; the toasty note is what lifts the whole masala.
Grinding your own garam masala fresh makes a noticeable difference, but a good shop blend works too.
Rest the spiced onions for the full 10 minutes so the masala penetrates before the flour goes in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tangy tamarind-date chutney and a cup of ginger chai for a satisfying evening snack.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Masala Onion Bhaji
variations.description: Here the masala is unmistakably Maharashtrian: dark, aromatic goda masala built on roasted coconut, sesame and warm spices gives the fritter a deep, slightly sweet complexity. It is the kind of bhaji you find at a Pune snack stall, craggy and richly spiced.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The traditional Maharashtrian frying fat, mellow enough to let goda masala shine.

steps: Slice 3 large onions thinly, salt with 1 tsp salt and rest 10 minutes until softened and moist.
Add 2 tsp goda masala, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tbsp roasted peanut powder, 2 chopped green chillies, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 3 tbsp coriander, mixing to coat the onions in dark spice.
Stir in 1.5 cups besan and 2 tbsp semolina with just 3 tbsp water into a thick batter, then rest 5 minutes to hydrate the rava.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to 180C until a pinch of batter rises with a lively sizzle.
Fry rough, irregular spoonfuls in batches for 3-4 minutes, turning once, until dark golden and crisp-edged.
Drain on paper; the peanut and goda masala should give a nutty, warm-sweet depth under the heat.
tips: Roasted peanut powder adds body and a subtle sweetness that echoes the goda masala; grind it just coarse.
Goda masala can taste flat if underdosed, so don't be shy with the full 2 tsp here.
Keep the fritter shapes ragged for maximum crunchy surface area.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thecha (fiery green chilli-garlic relish) and slices of raw onion, Maharashtrian-style.

variations.name: Gujarati Masala Onion Bhaji
variations.description: A masala bhaji balanced the Gujarati way, where a spoon of Anveshan Jaggery Powder rounds off the garam masala and chilli into that beloved sweet-savoury harmony. Sesame seeds in the batter add a delicate crunch and a nutty aroma typical of Gujarati farsan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The everyday Gujarati kitchen oil; its gentle sweetness suits this balanced masala.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Dissolved into the batter to bring the classic Gujarati sweet-savoury balance to the masala.

steps: Slice 3 large onions thinly, toss with 1 tsp salt and 1 tbsp lemon juice, and rest 10 minutes.
Dissolve 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 3 tbsp warm water and pour it over the onions.

Add 1 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp coriander powder, 1.5 tbsp sesame seeds, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 chopped green chillies and 3 tbsp coriander, then mix in 1.5 cups besan to a thick batter.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to 175C, a touch lower than usual since the jaggery browns fast.
Fry spoonfuls in batches for 3-4 minutes, turning once, until golden with a slightly deeper caramel tint, then drain.
Taste and confirm the sweet-savoury balance before frying the rest, adjusting salt if needed.
tips: Toast the sesame seeds lightly before adding for an extra nutty aroma.
Keep the flame at medium; the jaggery makes these colour quicker than plain masala bhajis.
A pinch of amchur (dry mango powder) sharpens the balance if you want a tangier finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with fresh coriander-chilli chutney and a glass of chaas (spiced buttermilk) to round off the sweet heat.

variations.name: Tamil Masala Onion Bhaji (Vengaya Bajji)
variations.description: A Tamil Nadu bajji-shop favourite where curry leaves, asafoetida and a South Indian masala perfume the batter, and a pinch of rice flour delivers the shatteringly crisp coat you expect from a roadside bajji. Coconut-oil frying seals in the unmistakable southern aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Frying in coconut oil gives Tamil bajji its signature fragrance and light, crisp finish.

steps: Slice 3 large onions thinly, salt with 1 tsp salt and rest 10 minutes until they soften and weep.
Add 20 torn curry leaves, 0.25 tsp asafoetida, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 2 chopped green chillies to the onions.
Mix in 1.5 cups besan and 4 tbsp rice flour with just 3 tbsp water into a thick, crisp-forming batter.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil to 180C until a test drop rises at once with fine bubbles.
Fry spoonfuls in batches for 3-4 minutes, turning once, until deep golden and shatteringly crisp, then drain.
Crisp a few extra curry leaves in the oil and scatter over the drained bajji for aroma.
tips: The generous rice flour is what gives bajji its glassy crunch, so measure it properly.
A pinch of cooking soda in the batter makes them puff lighter, but they must be fried immediately.
Bloom the asafoetida flavour by mixing it into the wet onions early so its rawness cooks off in the fry.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and a cup of filter coffee, or tuck into pav for a South Indian bajji-bun.

variations.name: Kashmiri Masala Onion Bhaji
variations.description: An elegant, aromatic bhaji coloured and perfumed with Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron, ground fennel and dry ginger in the Kashmiri ver style. Deep Kashmiri chilli lends a glorious red hue with gentle heat, making these fritters as fragrant as they are striking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A clean frying oil that carries the saffron and fennel aromas without competing with them.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: Steeped in warm water and stirred into the batter for a golden hue and delicate floral aroma.

steps: Steep 0.25 tsp Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 3 tbsp warm water for 10 minutes until the water turns deep gold.
Slice 3 large onions thinly, salt with 1 tsp salt and rest 10 minutes, then pour over the saffron water.
Add 2 tsp Kashmiri red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp fennel powder, 0.5 tsp dry ginger powder, 0.5 tsp garam masala and 1 chopped green chilli, mixing to coat.
Stir in 1.5 cups besan and 2 tbsp rice flour into a thick, richly red batter; add a splash more water only if too dry.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to 180C and fry spoonfuls in batches for 3-4 minutes, turning once, until crisp and glowing red.
Drain on a rack; the fritters should smell faintly of saffron and fennel, the hallmark of Kashmiri spicing.
tips: Steeping the saffron in warm (not boiling) water draws out the most colour and aroma without scorching it.
Kashmiri chilli is for colour more than heat, so these stay gentle; add a hotter chilli if you want more punch.
Ground fennel is the defining Kashmiri note here, so use it fresh for the best fragrance.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling walnut chutney and a pot of pink noon chai for a refined Kashmiri tea spread.

variations.name: Classic Matar Paratha
variations.description: A Punjabi winter favourite stuffed with a coarsely crushed green pea filling that is briefly sauteed with ginger and green chilli so it stays sweet, dry and fragrant. The peas keep a little texture rather than turning to paste. Griddled generously in ghee, it is the paratha that celebrates the fresh-matar season.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: wraps the crushed pea filling in a soft crust that stays tender through a winter meal

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: cooks the pea filling and bastes the paratha to a rich, seasonal gold

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with a little salt and about 0.75 cup water for 6 minutes into a soft dough, cover, and rest it 15 minutes.
Crush 1.5 cups boiled peas coarsely with a masher, leaving some whole for texture rather than making a smooth paste.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, add 1 tbsp grated ginger and 2 minced green chillies, then stir in the crushed peas with 1 tsp amchur, 0.5 tsp garam masala and remaining salt and cook 4 minutes until dry; cool fully.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, flatten one, mound 2 tbsp of the pea filling in the centre, pleat the edges shut, and press flat.
Dust with khapli atta and roll into a 6-inch round with gentle strokes so the filling does not squeeze out.
Cook on a medium tava, brushing both sides with Anveshan Ghee, flipping until deep golden spots form, about 3 minutes per paratha.
tips: Crush the peas by hand, not in a blender; a blender turns them gummy and hard to stuff.
Fresh winter peas need only a short boil, while frozen peas can go in straight after a quick blanch.
The filling can be made a day ahead and refrigerated, ready to stuff at breakfast.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a bowl of thick curd, a spoon of mango pickle and a pat of white butter, with masala chai to match the season.

variations.name: Masala Matar Paratha
variations.description: A Maharashtrian spin where the pea filling is deepened with garam masala, coriander powder and a spoon of goda-style warmth, then brightened with fresh coconut and coriander. Cooked in wood-pressed groundnut oil, it takes on a nutty, homely aroma. The result is a more layered, aromatic matar paratha.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: its nutty body complements the coconut and holds the spiced pea filling firmly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil lends a homely Maharashtrian nuttiness as it griddles

steps: Bring 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta together with salt and roughly 0.75 cup water, kneading 6 minutes into a pliable dough; rest it covered 15 minutes.
Coarsely crush 1.5 cups boiled peas, keeping a rough texture rather than a smooth mash.

Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, saute 2 minced green chillies for 30 seconds, add the peas with 1 tsp garam masala, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.25 cup grated coconut, 3 tbsp coriander and remaining salt, and cook 4 minutes until dry; cool it.
Split the dough into 8 balls, cup one, spoon in 2 tbsp of the masala pea filling, seal the edges over the top, and flatten gently.
Roll into a 6-inch round on a floured board, easing outward so the coconut-flecked filling stays put.
Griddle on a medium tava, brushing both faces with Anveshan Groundnut Oil, turning until richly spotted, about 3 minutes per paratha.
tips: Use fresh coconut for moisture and sweetness; toast desiccated coconut lightly first if that is all you have.
Cook the filling until it just holds together, since a wet coconut mix will steam the dough.
A pinch of goda masala in place of garam masala makes this taste unmistakably Maharashtrian.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of dahi koshimbir or plain buttermilk and a spoon of green-coconut chutney.

variations.name: Spicy Matar Paratha
variations.description: A Gujarati-style pea paratha with the region's signature sweet-hot balance, the filling sparked by green chillies and black pepper and rounded with a touch of jaggery. The gentle sweetness makes the heat sing rather than sting. Rolled thin and cooked in mustard oil, it is a lunchbox favourite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: rolls thin and stays soft, ideal for a lunchbox pea paratha

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: its pungency plays against the sweet-hot filling and helps the paratha keep longer

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a Gujarati touch that softens the chilli heat and lifts the sweetness of the peas

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with salt and about 0.75 cup water for 6 minutes into a soft dough, then rest it covered for 15 minutes.
Coarsely mash 1.5 cups boiled peas with 3 finely chopped green chillies, keeping some texture in the mix.

Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the heat, add the pea mix with 0.75 tsp cracked pepper, 1 tsp roasted cumin, 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and salt, cook 4 minutes until dry, finish with 1 tbsp lemon juice, and cool it.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, open one into a 4-inch cup, load 2 tbsp of the sweet-hot pea filling, seal the top, and press flat.
Roll into a thin 6-inch round, dusting well and patching any spot where the filling shows through.
Cook on a medium tava, brushing both sides with Anveshan Mustard Oil, flipping until golden and blistered, about 3 minutes per paratha.
tips: Add the jaggery while the filling is still warm so it melts and coats the peas evenly.
Stir in the lemon juice off the heat to keep its fresh tang intact.
Roll these thin; a thinner Gujarati-style paratha keeps softer in a tiffin for longer.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sweet-and-sour chhundo pickle and a bowl of set curd, or roll around a smear of green chutney for a travel snack.

variations.name: Garlic Matar Paratha
variations.description: A Rajasthani version where the sweet pea filling is grounded by a bold amount of garlic browned in ghee, plus a hit of dried red chilli for warmth. The garlic turns the mild peas into something deeply savoury and moreish. Sturdy and full-flavoured, it is built to satisfy on a working day.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: gives a hearty crust that stands up to the robust garlic-pea filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: browns the garlic sweet and bastes the paratha with a nutty richness

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with salt and roughly 0.75 cup water for 6 minutes into a soft dough, cover, and rest it 15 minutes.
Coarsely crush 1.5 cups boiled peas, keeping a rough, textured mash.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, fry 2 tbsp minced garlic and 2 broken dried red chillies on low for 2 minutes until the garlic is pale gold, then add the peas with 1 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin and salt and cook 4 minutes until dry; cool it.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, flatten one, place 2 tbsp of the garlicky pea filling inside, gather and seal the edges, and press down.
Roll into an even 6-inch round on a dusted board so the filling stays enclosed.
Cook on a medium tava, brushing both faces with Anveshan Ghee, turning until deep golden and aromatic, about 3 minutes per paratha.
tips: Fry the garlic and dried chilli only until pale gold; over-browning turns both bitter.
Discard the dried chilli seeds before frying if you want the flavour with less heat.
A crushed clove of raw garlic worked into the dough intensifies the aroma for garlic lovers.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain set curd, a fiery garlic-red chilli chutney and a glass of chaas to cool the palate.

variations.name: Cheesy Matar Paratha
variations.description: A cafe-style favourite across Tamil Nadu's cities, pairing sweet crushed peas with a molten cheese centre for a filling that is both wholesome and indulgent. The peas keep it from feeling too heavy, while the cheese makes it irresistible to children. It oozes gently at the first bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: seals reliably around the pea-and-cheese core without tearing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: crisps the crust to gold while keeping the cheesy pea centre molten

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.75 tsp salt and about 0.75 cup water for 6 minutes into a soft dough, then rest it covered 15 minutes.
Coarsely mash 1 cup boiled peas and pat them dry, then mix with 0.5 tsp black pepper, 0.5 tsp chilli flakes and 2 tbsp coriander.
Fold in 0.75 cup grated mozzarella so the cheese binds the crushed peas into a soft filling.
Divide the dough into 6 balls, roll one into a 4-inch disc, mound 3 tbsp of the pea-cheese mix in the centre, seal the edges over it, and flatten.
Roll out gently to a 6-inch round, keeping the pressure light so the cheese stays inside.
Cook on a medium tava, brushing both sides with Anveshan Ghee and pressing the middle, until golden and crisp with a molten centre, about 3 minutes per paratha.
tips: Pat the mashed peas dry before adding cheese, since damp peas make the filling loose.
Serve immediately while the cheese still stretches, as it firms up on cooling.
Grated paneer stirred into the mix lightens the richness while keeping it soft.
variations.servingSuggestion: Cut into wedges and serve with a tomato-garlic dip or ketchup for kids, and a cucumber-mint raita for the adults.

variations.name: Classic Methi Matar Malai
variations.description: A creamy North Indian favourite where slightly bitter fresh fenugreek leaves meet sweet green peas in a white cashew-and-cream gravy. The interplay of gentle bitterness, sweetness and richness makes it irresistibly mild and elegant.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee gives the white gravy a clean, mellow richness that suits the delicate flavours

steps: Pluck 2 cups fenugreek leaves, wash well, sprinkle with a little salt for 10 minutes, then squeeze out the dark liquid to remove excess bitterness.
Boil 2 chopped onions with 12 cashews in 1 cup water for 8 minutes until soft, cool, and blend to a smooth white paste.
Heat the Anveshan Ghee over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle for 20 seconds, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 2 slit green chillies and saute 1 minute.
Add the squeezed fenugreek leaves and 1 cup green peas, and stir-fry for 4 minutes until the fenugreek wilts and smells cooked rather than raw.
Pour in the onion-cashew paste with 0.5 cup milk and 1 tsp salt, and simmer gently for 6 minutes until the gravy thickens to a creamy pale sauce.
Stir in 4 tbsp cream and 0.25 tsp garam masala, cook for 2 minutes on low heat, and serve while glossy and warm.
tips: Salting and squeezing the fenugreek is key, as it tames the bitterness without losing the herb's character.
Keep the heat low once the cashew paste goes in so the white gravy does not brown.
Use fresh peas when in season, but frozen peas work well if blanched for 2 minutes first.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter-brushed tandoori roti or plain paratha, garnished with a few whole cashews and a light drizzle of cream.

variations.name: Bengali Masala Methi Matar Malai
variations.description: A Bengali reinterpretation that warms the creamy classic with roasted coriander powder and a hint of subtle sweetness. The gravy is a touch spicier and more aromatic, echoing the Bengali love for a delicate sweet-savoury balance.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: a small amount of wood-pressed mustard oil lends the unmistakable Bengali pungency

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of bilona ghee mellows the mustard oil into a rounded richness

steps: Clean and salt 2 cups fenugreek leaves for 10 minutes, then squeeze firmly to drain the bitter juices before cooking.
Boil 2 onions with 10 cashews in 1 cup water for 8 minutes, cool, and grind to a smooth pale paste for the gravy base.
Warm the Anveshan Mustard Oil to its smoke point, then lower the heat, add 1 tbsp ginger paste and 2 slit green chillies, and saute for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the squeezed fenugreek and 1 cup peas with 1.5 tsp roasted coriander powder, and stir-fry for 4 minutes so the coriander toasts into the greens.
Add the onion-cashew paste, 0.5 cup milk and 1 tsp salt, and simmer for 6 minutes until the gravy is creamy and the coriander aroma blooms.
Finish with 3 tbsp cream and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, simmer 2 minutes, and let it rest briefly before serving.
tips: Take the mustard oil just to smoking before lowering the heat to strip its raw sharpness.
Dry-roast the coriander powder for 30 seconds before use for a nuttier, deeper flavour.
A pinch of sugar can be added to nod to the classic Bengali sweet-savoury balance.
variations.servingSuggestion: Delicious with luchi or steamed gobindobhog rice, finished with a sliver of green chilli and a drop of raw mustard oil for aroma.

variations.name: Tamil Butter Methi Matar Malai
variations.description: A South Indian butter-rich take that folds curry leaves and a coconut-milk creaminess into the fenugreek and peas. Butter and coconut milk make the gravy plush and fragrant, a gentle bridge between North Indian malai and Tamil flavours.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed coconut oil roots the dish in Tamil kitchens and complements the coconut milk

steps: Salt 2 cups fenugreek leaves for 10 minutes, then squeeze out the bitter liquid, and boil 2 onions with 10 cashews in 0.75 cup water for 8 minutes before grinding smooth.
Heat the Anveshan Coconut Oil with 1 tbsp butter over medium heat, add 12 curry leaves and 2 slit green chillies, and let them splutter for 20 seconds.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and saute for 1 minute, then add the squeezed fenugreek and 1 cup peas and stir-fry for 4 minutes until wilted.
Pour in the onion-cashew paste with 1 tsp salt and simmer for 5 minutes until the gravy thickens and the raw cashew note fades.
Lower the heat and stir in 0.5 cup coconut milk, cooking gently for 3 minutes without boiling so the coconut milk does not split.
Swirl in 2 tbsp cream and the remaining tbsp of butter, warm through for 2 minutes, and serve fragrant and hot.
tips: Add coconut milk on low heat and never boil it hard, or it will curdle and turn grainy.
Fry the curry leaves until crisp for the fullest aroma before the rest of the tempering goes in.
Balance any extra bitterness with a small pinch of jaggery stirred in at the end.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pairs beautifully with malabar parotta or ghee-roasted appam, garnished with a few crisp fried curry leaves on top.

variations.name: Kerala Kadai Methi Matar Malai
variations.description: A Kerala kadai-style version that turns the creamy classic into a semi-dry, boldly spiced dish with charred capsicum and a coarse kadai masala. Coconut oil and fresh-pounded spices give it a distinctly southern, aromatic punch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed coconut oil withstands the high-heat kadai toss and adds a Kerala aroma

steps: Dry-roast 2 tsp coriander seeds, 3 dried red chillies and 1 tsp cumin seeds for 90 seconds until fragrant, cool, and pound coarsely into a kadai masala.
Salt 2 cups fenugreek leaves for 10 minutes and squeeze dry, then cut the capsicum into thick 3 cm squares to keep them crunchy.
Heat the Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadai on high heat, add the cubed onions and capsicum, and char for 3 minutes, then lift out and reserve the capsicum.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the chopped tomatoes, and cook on high for 5 minutes until the tomatoes collapse into a thick masala.
Add the squeezed fenugreek, 1 cup peas, most of the kadai masala, 1 tsp salt and 0.5 cup water, and toss on high heat for 6 minutes until semi-dry and clingy.
Return the charred capsicum, swirl in 2 tbsp cream and the reserved kadai masala, toss once, and serve straight from the kadai.
tips: Pound the kadai masala just before cooking so the aroma stays sharp and fresh.
Keep this dish semi-dry, so add water sparingly and cook on the highest heat.
The little cream at the end softens the spice without turning it into a full gravy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulka or a spiced pulao, adding a squeeze of lime and rings of raw onion alongside.

variations.name: Karnataka Handi Methi Matar Malai
variations.description: A slow handi version from Karnataka where fenugreek and peas steam with whole spices in a sealed pot for a deeply perfumed, layered gravy. Cardamom, cloves and cinnamon infuse the malai base while keeping the fenugreek's gentle bitterness intact.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee carries the whole-spice aroma through the slow handi steaming

steps: Salt 2 cups fenugreek leaves for 10 minutes and squeeze dry, and boil 2 onions with 12 cashews in 1 cup water for 8 minutes before blending smooth.
Heat the Anveshan Ghee in a heavy handi over medium heat and bloom 3 cardamom, 3 cloves and a 1 inch cinnamon stick for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 2 slit green chillies, saute for 1 minute, then add the squeezed fenugreek and 1 cup peas and stir-fry for 4 minutes.
Pour in the onion-cashew paste with 0.5 cup milk and 1 tsp salt, stir well, and bring to a gentle simmer.
Seal the handi with a tight lid and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes so the whole spices perfume the malai gravy and the peas turn tender.
Lift the lid, stir in 3 tbsp cream, and rest covered off the heat for 4 minutes to let the aroma settle before serving.
tips: Sealing the handi traps the aromatic steam, so use a heavy lid or seal the rim with a little dough.
Fish out the whole spices before serving or alert diners so no one bites a clove.
Keep the flame very low after the milk goes in to protect the pale colour of the gravy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with ghee-laced jeera rice or soft naan, garnished with a scatter of fried cashews and a light cream swirl.

variations.name: Classic Methi Paratha
variations.description: The definitive Punjabi methi paratha, where finely chopped fresh fenugreek is kneaded straight into a khapli-wheat dough thepla-style rather than stuffed, so every bite carries that gently bitter, herby fragrance. Yogurt keeps the crumb tender while ajwain and roasted cumin round off the fenugreek's edge. Griddled with ghee to a spotty gold, it stays soft for hours in a lunchbox.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: the nutty ancient-wheat flour gives methi paratha a soft, wholesome crumb that resists drying out

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: one spoon enriches the dough, the rest bastes the paratha into a fragrant golden crust

steps: Rinse and finely chop 2 cups fenugreek leaves, toss them with a quarter of the salt, and rest for 10 minutes; then squeeze out the released water firmly so the dough will not turn slack.

In a wide bowl combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, the squeezed methi, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp ajwain, 1 tsp ginger-chilli paste and the remaining salt, mixing until the leaves are evenly coated.
Work in 3 tbsp yogurt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then add about 0.5 cup water in small splashes, kneading for 6 minutes into a soft, non-sticky dough; cover and rest 15 minutes.
Divide the dough into 8 equal balls, dust each with a little khapli atta, and roll into 6-inch rounds roughly 2 mm thick, keeping the thickness even so they puff uniformly.
Set a tava over medium heat and cook the first side for about 45 seconds until faint bubbles appear, flip, and brush the top with Anveshan Ghee.
Turn once more, smear the second side with ghee, and press the edges with a spatula until both faces show deep golden-brown spots, about 3 minutes total per paratha.
tips: Salting and squeezing the methi is the single trick that keeps the dough soft and the paratha from tearing while rolling.
The dough keeps well covered in the fridge for a day; let it come to room temperature before rolling so it does not crack.
If the fenugreek is very bitter, add a pinch of jaggery to the dough to mellow it without making the paratha sweet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Fan them out warm with a bowl of chilled boondi raita and a spoon of garlic pickle; for tiffin, roll one around a smear of white butter and cut into pinwheels.

variations.name: Masala Methi Paratha
variations.description: A Maharashtrian take that leans into a warm masala backbone of garam masala and coriander powder, with the methi folded into the dough alongside a little besan for a savoury, almost thepla-like bite. Cooked in wood-pressed groundnut oil, it carries a rounder, earthier aroma than the ghee version. It travels beautifully and needs nothing more than a chunk of jaggery and pickle.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: holds the besan and methi together into a supple thepla-style dough without going gluey

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil lends the Maharashtrian nutty warmth and crisps the edges as it griddles

steps: Wash 2 cups fenugreek leaves, chop them fine, sprinkle over a pinch of the salt, leave 10 minutes, and press out the moisture between your palms so the dough stays firm.

Tip 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta and 0.25 cup besan into a paraat, then stir through the methi, 1 tsp garam masala, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tbsp sesame seeds and the remaining salt.
Drizzle in 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and roughly 0.6 cup water, bringing everything together and kneading for 7 minutes into a smooth, pliable dough; rest it under a damp cloth for 15 minutes.
Pinch off 8 balls, flatten each in your palm, and roll on a floured board into 7-inch rounds a little under 3 mm thick so they hold up to the hearty masala.
Warm a tava on medium-high, lay a rolled paratha down, and cook 40 seconds until the surface dulls and small blisters form.
Flip, brush with Anveshan Groundnut Oil, turn again after a minute, oil the second face, and press until both sides are freckled deep brown, about 3 minutes each.
tips: Adding besan gives a savoury depth and helps soak up any lingering methi moisture, so skip it only if you want a plainer taste.
Roast these a shade darker than a plain paratha; the extra colour is what carries the garam masala aroma.
Cooled fully and wrapped in foil, they stay pliable for an 8-hour workday and can be eaten without reheating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a wedge of jaggery and a smear of thecha or green-chilli pickle, the classic Maharashtrian roadside pairing, plus a cup of hot masala chai.

variations.name: Spicy Methi Paratha
variations.description: This is the Gujarati thepla end of the methi spectrum, where crushed green chillies and black pepper bring a clean, building heat balanced by a whisper of jaggery. Rolled thin and cooked in pungent wood-pressed mustard oil, it is the classic travel food of Gujarat, meant to keep for days. The sweet-hot-herby interplay is what sets it apart.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: rolls out into the thin, durable thepla-style rounds that keep for days without going brittle

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: its sharp pungency stands up to the green chilli heat and helps the theplas keep longer

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a Gujarati touch that rounds the chilli heat and deepens the colour of the crust

steps: Finely chop 2 cups fenugreek leaves and crush 4 green chillies to a coarse paste, then mix the chillies into the leaves so their heat spreads evenly.

In a bowl gather 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, the methi-chilli mix, 0.75 tsp black pepper, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tbsp sesame seeds, 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and the salt, tossing to coat the greens.
Add 0.25 cup yogurt and 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil, then knead in just 0.3 cup water, a spoon at a time, into a stiff-ish dough that softens as it rests for 20 minutes.
Roll the dough into 9 small balls and, on a well-floured board, flatten each into a very thin 7-inch round, dusting often so the sticky methi does not grab.
Heat a tava to medium, place a thepla, and cook 30 seconds until the colour turns matte, then flip and smear with Anveshan Mustard Oil.
Flip a final time, oil the second side, and press with a folded cloth so it cooks through to crisp brown flecks, about 2.5 minutes per thepla.
tips: Keep the dough on the firmer side; a slack methi dough is impossible to roll thin enough for a true thepla.
Stacked and cooled, these keep at room temperature for two to three days, making them ideal for train journeys.
For extra fire without more chilli, add a crushed clove of raw garlic to the dough.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with sweet mango chhundo pickle and a cup of masala chai, or roll around cold set curd for a Gujarati travel breakfast.

variations.name: Garlic Methi Paratha
variations.description: A robust Rajasthani version built on a heady base of pounded garlic and dried red chilli, the sort of paratha that keeps a farmer full through a working morning. The garlic is bloomed in ghee before it meets the dough so its raw bite turns sweet and mellow. Fenugreek and garlic together give a deeply savoury, almost pickle-like aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: its sturdy crumb carries the heavy garlic-methi dough without turning dense

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: used to bloom the garlic paste and to baste, layering a nutty richness over the pungency

steps: Pound 10 garlic cloves and 3 dried red chillies to a coarse paste, then warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan and fry the paste on low for 90 seconds until it smells sweet and toasty, and cool it.
Chop 2 cups fenugreek leaves fine, salt them lightly, rest 10 minutes, and squeeze out the water so the dough does not weep.
Combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, the bloomed garlic paste, the methi, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp roasted cumin, 1 tsp coriander powder and the salt, rubbing the flavours evenly through the flour.
Pour in about 0.7 cup water in stages and knead 6 minutes into a soft dough; cover and let it rest for 15 minutes to relax the gluten.
Shape 8 balls, roll each into a 6-inch round of even thickness, and slap off the excess flour so it will not scorch on the tava.
Cook on a medium tava 45 seconds a side, brushing generously with Anveshan Ghee on each flip, until the surface is blistered deep golden and the garlic aroma fills the kitchen, about 3 minutes.
tips: Blooming the garlic first is essential; raw garlic in the dough turns harsh and bitter once griddled.
For a Rajasthani rustic finish, crush the paratha lightly between your palms straight off the tava to open its layers.
Leftover garlic-ghee paste keeps a week refrigerated and doubles as a quick tadka for dal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot with a bowl of plain set curd and a dab of ker-sangri or garlic chutney; a glass of chaas alongside tames the heat.

variations.name: Cheesy Methi Paratha
variations.description: A modern, kid-friendly riff where a molten core of grated cheese meets the herby methi dough, a format that has become a cafe favourite across Tamil Nadu's cities. The cheese tempers the fenugreek's bitterness into something mellow and moreish. Sealed and griddled in ghee, it oozes at the first tear.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: makes a pliable, forgiving dough that seals easily around the cheese without splitting

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: griddles the stuffed paratha to a crisp gold while keeping the cheese inside molten

steps: Finely chop 1.5 cups fenugreek leaves, mix in 0.75 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp roasted cumin, rest 10 minutes, and squeeze out the liquid so the dough binds cleanly.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with the drained methi and about 0.75 cup water for 6 minutes into a soft dough, then rest it covered for 15 minutes.
For the filling, toss 1 cup grated mozzarella with 0.5 cup grated processed cheese, 0.5 tsp black pepper and 0.5 tsp chilli flakes so the cheese is evenly spiced.
Divide the dough into 6 balls, roll each into a 4-inch disc, place about 3 tbsp of the cheese mix in the centre, gather the edges over the top, pinch to seal, and flatten gently.
Dust and roll the stuffed ball into a 6-inch paratha with a light hand so the cheese does not burst through the seam.
Cook on a medium tava, brushing both sides with Anveshan Ghee, pressing the middle so the cheese melts, until golden and crisp with a soft molten centre, about 3 minutes per paratha.
tips: Roll gently and evenly; too much pressure at the centre pushes the cheese to the seam where it leaks and sticks.
Serve within a few minutes, as the cheese firms up quickly and loses its pull once it cools.
A firmer mozzarella-heavy blend stretches better than a soft, watery one, so drain any excess moisture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Cut into wedges and serve with a tangy tomato-garlic dip or ketchup for children, and a fresh cucumber-mint raita for the adults.

variations.name: Classic Mix Veg
variations.description: The everyday medley of carrots, beans, cauliflower, potato and peas cooked in a light cumin-tomato masala until each vegetable is just tender yet distinct. It is the practical way to use up the crisper drawer without sacrificing flavour. Colourful, wholesome and family-friendly.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A clean wood-pressed oil lets each vegetable's flavour come through.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of ghee ties the mixed vegetables together with warm aroma.

steps: Cut 1 carrot and 12 french beans into 1 cm pieces, break 1 cup cauliflower into small florets, cube 1 potato small and keep 0.5 cup peas ready.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds with 0.5 tsp ajwain for 20 seconds.
Add 2 chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 6 minutes until golden.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 5 minutes until the oil separates.
Add all the vegetables, toss to coat, splash in 0.5 cup hot water, cover and cook on low for 14 to 16 minutes, stirring twice, until everything is just tender.
Uncover, dry off excess moisture on medium for 2 minutes, then finish with 0.5 tsp amchur powder, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 3 tbsp coriander.
tips: Cut every vegetable to a similar small size so they all cook tender at the same time.
Add the harder vegetables like carrot and potato a minute before the softer ones if you want perfect texture.
Blanch the vegetables first for a brighter colour if you are serving guests.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulkas or jeera rice and a bowl of cool boondi raita.

variations.name: Masala Mix Veg
variations.description: A Tamil-influenced masala mix veg where the vegetables are folded into a warm garam-masala base finished with fresh grated coconut for a southern accent. The coconut lends body and a mild sweetness to the medley. Fragrant, wholesome and distinctive.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: The southern fat ties the grated coconut and curry-leaf tempering to the vegetables.

steps: Cut 1 carrot and 12 french beans into 1 cm pieces, break 1 cup cauliflower into small florets and keep 0.5 cup peas ready.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadhai on medium, splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, then add 12 curry leaves.
Add 2 chopped onions and 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 6 minutes until soft and light gold.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 5 minutes until pulpy.
Add all the vegetables with 0.5 cup hot water, cover and cook on low for 15 minutes until just tender.
Stir in 4 tbsp grated coconut and 1.25 tsp garam masala, cook uncovered for 2 minutes, then finish with 3 tbsp coriander.
tips: Add the grated coconut near the end so it stays fresh-tasting rather than drying out.
Curry leaves must hit hot oil to release their aroma, so add them right after the mustard splutters.
A squeeze of lime at the table brightens the coconut-rich medley beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or with soft chapatis and thin rasam on the side.

variations.name: Spicy Mix Veg
variations.description: A Karnataka-style spicy mix veg where slit green chillies and crushed black pepper cut through the sweetness of the vegetables, tempered in nutty sesame oil. The pepper heat gives the medley a warm, lingering edge. Bold, aromatic and vibrant.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: The nutty gingelly oil of the south carries the pepper and green-chilli heat.

steps: Cut 1 carrot and 12 french beans into 1 cm pieces, break 1 cup cauliflower into florets, cube 1 potato small, keep 0.5 cup peas ready and slit 4 green chillies.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadhai on medium and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds.
Add 2 chopped onions, the slit green chillies and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 6 minutes until the onions soften and the chillies blister.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 5 minutes until pulpy.
Add all the vegetables with 0.5 cup hot water, cover and cook on low for 15 minutes until just tender, then dry off excess moisture uncovered for 2 minutes.
Crush 1 tsp black pepper coarsely, stir it in with 3 tbsp coriander and toss for a final minute so the pepper heat coats the medley.
tips: Add the crushed pepper at the end to keep its heat sharp and aromatic.
Cut the vegetables evenly so they cook through in one go without any staying crunchy.
Deseed a couple of the green chillies if you want the aroma with a little less fire.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rotis and a bowl of plain curd, or with lemon rice for a heartier plate.

variations.name: Dhaba-style Mix Veg
variations.description: An Andhra dhaba-style mix veg with a herby kasuri-methi and garam-masala finish over a deeply browned onion-tomato masala, plus a spoon of cream for that rich highway-kitchen feel. The vegetables sit in a glossy, indulgent gravy. Robust, aromatic and generous.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A generous pour browns the onions into a glossy dhaba gravy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Kasuri methi crushed into warm ghee delivers the signature dhaba finish.

steps: Cut 1 carrot and 12 french beans into 1 cm pieces, break 1 cup cauliflower into florets, cube 1 potato small and keep 0.5 cup peas ready.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add 3 chopped onions and 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste.
Fry the onions for 9 minutes until deep golden brown for a rich dhaba base.
Add 3 pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 7 minutes until thick and the oil separates.
Add all the vegetables with 0.75 cup hot water, cover and cook on low for 15 minutes until tender, then stir in 2 tbsp fresh cream.
Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi into it, pour over with 1 tsp garam masala and 3 tbsp coriander, and simmer for a final minute.
tips: Brown the onions well and cook the tomatoes fully for the glossy, rich dhaba gravy.
Add the cream on low heat and avoid a hard boil so it does not split.
Crush the kasuri methi between your palms before adding it to the ghee for the best aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or laccha paratha and a sliced onion salad with lemon.

variations.name: Home-style Mix Veg
variations.description: A Telangana home-style mix veg kept simple and dry, tempered with mustard seeds and curry leaves and cooked so each vegetable stays crisp-tender. It is the light, practical everyday version with a southern tempering. Fresh, quick and comforting.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A light hand of wood-pressed oil keeps this dry medley clean and fresh.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A last teaspoon of ghee rounds off the simple tempering.

steps: Cut 1 carrot and 12 french beans into 1 cm pieces, break 1 cup cauliflower into small florets and keep 0.5 cup peas ready.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium, splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, then add 10 curry leaves and 2 slit green chillies.
Add 1 chopped onion and saute for 4 minutes until soft and translucent.
Add 1 chopped tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 3 minutes until softened.
Add all the vegetables, splash in 3 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 13 to 15 minutes, stirring once, until crisp-tender.
Uncover and dry off any moisture on medium for 2 minutes, then finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and 2 tbsp coriander.
tips: Keep the water minimal and finish uncovered so this stays a light, dry sabzi.
Cut the vegetables small and even so they cook quickly and stay crisp-tender.
Add the mustard seeds to properly hot oil and let them splutter fully for the right southern aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or with hot phulkas and a bowl of thin dal.

variations.name: Classic Mixed Veg Paratha
variations.description: A wholesome all-in-one paratha from the Malwa heartland, stuffed with a dry, spiced mash of boiled potato, grated carrot, peas and beans. The vegetables are sauteed until every drop of moisture is gone, which is the secret to a filling that never leaks. Griddled in ghee, it is a complete meal in itself.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: its strong, elastic gluten wraps a chunky vegetable filling without cracking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: cooks the vegetable mash and bastes the paratha to a rich, even gold

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with a little salt and about 0.75 cup water for 6 minutes into a soft dough, cover, and rest it 15 minutes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then add 1 tsp ginger-chilli paste, the grated carrot and chopped beans and saute 4 minutes until softened.
Stir in the boiled peas and mashed potato with 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp amchur and remaining salt, and cook on medium 5 minutes, mashing until the mixture is completely dry; cool it fully.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, roll one into a 4-inch disc, place 2 tbsp of the vegetable filling in the centre, pleat the edges over, seal, and flatten.
Dust with khapli atta and roll into a 7-inch round with gentle, even pressure so the chunky filling stays enclosed.
Cook on a medium tava, brushing both faces with Anveshan Ghee, turning until golden-brown blisters cover both sides, about 3 minutes per paratha.
tips: Drying out the filling completely is non-negotiable; any residual moisture makes the stuffing burst mid-roll.
Grate the carrot and chop the beans small so they cook fast and never leave hard bits in the filling.
The vegetable mix keeps two days refrigerated and makes an excellent cutlet or sandwich filling too.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a bowl of thick curd, mango pickle and a pat of white butter melting on top; a mint-coriander chutney rounds out the plate.

variations.name: Masala Mixed Veg Paratha
variations.description: A Goan-inflected version where the vegetable filling is warmed with garam masala, coriander powder and a squeeze of tang, finished with fresh grated coconut for a coastal sweetness. Cooked in wood-pressed coconut oil, it carries an unmistakable seaside aroma. The coconut keeps the filling moist yet stuffable.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: the nutty flour pairs naturally with coconut and holds the spiced masala filling firmly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed coconut oil lends the paratha its coastal Goan fragrance as it griddles

steps: Bring 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta together with salt and roughly 0.75 cup water, kneading 6 minutes into a soft, pliable dough; rest it covered 15 minutes.
Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, add 2 minced green chillies and the grated carrot, and saute 3 minutes until the carrot loses its rawness.

Fold in the boiled peas, mashed potato, 0.33 cup grated coconut, 1 tsp garam masala, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 1 tbsp lemon juice and remaining salt, cooking 4 minutes on medium until dry; cool completely.
Split the dough into 8 balls, open one into a 4-inch cup, spoon in 2 tbsp of the coconut-veg filling, seal the edges over the top, and press down.
Roll the ball out to a 7-inch round on a floured board, working outward gently so the filling stays centred.
Griddle on a medium tava, brushing both sides with Anveshan Coconut Oil, flipping until golden and freckled, about 3 minutes per paratha.
tips: Use fresh, not desiccated, coconut; it keeps the filling juicy without needing extra water.
Add the lemon juice off the heat so its brightness is not cooked away.
If fresh coconut is hard to find, soak desiccated coconut in two spoons of warm milk for ten minutes first.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a tangy tomato-coconut chutney and a bowl of sol kadhi or plain buttermilk to complete the Goan mood.

variations.name: Spicy Mixed Veg Paratha
variations.description: A warming Kashmiri-style paratha for cold days, the vegetable filling lifted with slit green chillies, cracked black pepper and a hint of fennel and dry ginger in the local manner. Wood-pressed mustard oil, the fat of choice in the valley, gives it a pungent depth. Robust and gently fiery, it stands up to a hard winter.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: the hearty flour suits a warming winter paratha and grips the spiced filling well

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the valley's signature pungent oil deepens the filling and crisps the crust

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with salt and about 0.75 cup water for 6 minutes into a soft dough, cover, and let it rest for 15 minutes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, lower the heat, and fry 4 chopped green chillies with the grated carrot for 3 minutes.

Mix in the peas, mashed potato, 1 tsp cracked pepper, 1 tsp fennel powder, 0.5 tsp dry ginger and remaining salt, and cook 5 minutes on medium until the filling is dry and holds together; cool it fully.
Roll the dough into 8 balls, flatten one, mound 2 tbsp filling in the centre, close and pinch the edges, and press flat.
Dust and roll into a 7-inch round, patching any spot where a chilli piece threatens to poke through.
Cook on a medium-high tava, brushing both faces with Anveshan Mustard Oil, turning until deep golden and blistered, about 3 minutes per paratha.
tips: Heating mustard oil to smoking point first mellows its sharpness before the vegetables go in.
Fennel and dry ginger are what make this taste of Kashmir; do not skip them for the pepper alone.
Serve extra hot, as this filling is designed to warm you from the inside on a cold day.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a bowl of Kashmiri-style plain yogurt whisked with a pinch of salt and roasted cumin, and a side of walnut chutney.

variations.name: Garlic Mixed Veg Paratha
variations.description: A Himachali hill-style paratha where a generous amount of garlic, sizzled golden in ghee, threads through the mixed vegetable filling. The garlic's sweetness after cooking balances the earthy vegetables beautifully. It is the kind of sturdy, warming food that hill kitchens make to keep out the chill.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: the wholesome flour gives a filling hill-style paratha with a soft, satisfying chew

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: browns the garlic to a sweet gold and bastes the paratha with a nutty richness

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with salt and roughly 0.75 cup water for 6 minutes into a soft dough, then rest it covered for 15 minutes.
Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and fry 2 tbsp minced garlic on low for 2 minutes until pale gold, then add the grated carrot and cook 3 minutes more.
Stir in the peas, mashed potato, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander powder, 3 tbsp coriander leaves and remaining salt, and cook 4 minutes until dry; cool the filling completely.
Divide the dough into 8 balls, cup one, place 2 tbsp of the garlicky filling inside, seal the edges together, and flatten gently.
Roll into a 7-inch round on a dusted board, easing the pin outward so the filling spreads evenly.
Cook on a medium tava, brushing both sides with Anveshan Ghee, flipping until richly golden and fragrant with garlic, about 3 minutes per paratha.
tips: Fry the garlic only to pale gold; darker than that and it turns bitter in the filling.
Mince the garlic finely so it distributes evenly and no one bites into a raw-tasting chunk.
This filling freezes well in a flat pack for up to a month, ready to thaw and stuff.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of Himachali-style madra or simply thick curd, a knob of butter and a spoon of red-chilli garlic chutney.

variations.name: Cheesy Mixed Veg Paratha
variations.description: A crowd-pleasing version from Odisha's growing cafe scene, folding grated cheese through the mixed vegetable filling so it turns rich and gooey. The cheese binds the vegetables into a soft, sliceable core that children love. It is the easiest way to get a plate of vegetables into a reluctant eater.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: wraps the soft cheesy vegetable core in a sturdy yet tender crust

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: crisps the paratha to a golden shell while keeping the cheesy filling molten

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.75 tsp salt and about 0.75 cup water for 6 minutes into a soft dough, cover, and rest it 15 minutes.
In a bowl mash the boiled potato with the grated carrot and boiled peas, then season with 0.5 tsp black pepper, 0.5 tsp chilli flakes and 0.5 tsp mixed herbs.
Fold in 0.75 cup grated mozzarella so the cheese coats the cooled vegetables and binds them into a soft mass.
Divide the dough into 6 balls, roll one to a 4-inch disc, spoon 3 tbsp of the cheesy filling in the middle, seal the edges over, and press flat.
Roll out to a 6-inch round with a light touch, keeping the seam side down so the cheese stays enclosed.
Cook on a medium tava, brushing both sides with Anveshan Ghee and pressing gently, until golden and crisp with a melting centre, about 3 minutes per paratha.
tips: Make sure the boiled vegetables are cool and dry before adding cheese, or the filling turns runny.
Serve immediately; reheated cheesy parathas lose the stretch that makes them fun.
Sneak in a handful of grated beetroot for colour that turns the filling pink and delights kids.
variations.servingSuggestion: Cut into strips and serve with ketchup or a herby yogurt dip, alongside a simple carrot-cucumber salad.

variations.name: Classic Mooli Paratha
variations.description: A beloved winter paratha from the North where sharp, peppery grated radish is squeezed dry, lightly spiced and stuffed into a soft Anveshan Khapli Atta dough. The secret is wringing every drop from the mooli so the filling stays dry and the ghee-roasted parathas turn out crisp, never soggy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Kneaded into a soft dough; its nutty warmth balances the peppery bite of the radish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: One spoon in the dough and the rest for roasting the parathas to a crisp golden finish.

steps: Knead 3 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and about 1.25 cups water into a soft, pliable dough; cover and rest 20 minutes.
Grate 2 medium radishes finely, sprinkle with 0.5 tsp salt, leave 10 minutes, then squeeze out every drop of liquid in a clean cloth.
Mix the dry mooli with 2 finely chopped green chillies, a grated 1-inch piece of ginger, 0.5 tsp ajwain, 1.5 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 4 tbsp coriander and 0.5 tsp salt.
Divide dough and filling into 8 each; flatten a dough ball, place 2 tbsp filling inside, gather and seal the edges, then roll gently to a 7-inch round with an atta dusting.
Roast on a hot tava for about 1 minute until it blisters, flip and brush with 0.5 tsp ghee, cooking each side 1-2 minutes until golden with brown spots.
Stack the parathas under a cloth so they stay soft and warm while you finish the rest.
tips: Squeeze the grated radish as dry as possible; leftover water is the number one cause of tearing.
Save the drained radish water and knead it into the dough instead of plain water for extra flavour and less waste.
Add the salt to the filling only just before stuffing, or it will draw out fresh moisture again.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot with a bowl of curd, a smear of white butter and a spoon of tangy mixed pickle.

variations.name: Masala Mooli Paratha
variations.description: A punchier take where the peppery radish is folded with garam masala, coriander powder and a squeeze of amchur for a warm, tangy, well-rounded filling. The Anveshan Khapli Atta dough and ghee-roasted crust make it a hearty, flavour-packed winter meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The wholegrain dough base that stands up to the spiced, tangy radish filling.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: Worked into the dough and brushed on the tava for a fragrant, crisp golden crust.

steps: Knead 3 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and about 1.25 cups water into a soft dough; cover and rest 20 minutes.
Grate 2 medium radishes finely, salt with 0.5 tsp salt, rest 10 minutes and squeeze bone-dry in a cloth.
Mix the dry mooli with 1 tsp garam masala, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp amchur, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 4 tbsp coriander and 0.5 tsp salt.
Divide dough and filling into 8 each; stuff 2 tbsp filling into each dough ball, seal, and roll gently to a 7-inch round, dusting with atta.
Roast on a hot tava for 1 minute, flip, brush with 0.5 tsp ghee and cook each side 1-2 minutes until golden with crisp brown flecks.
Keep the cooked parathas soft and warm under a cloth as you finish the batch.
tips: Amchur balances the sharp radish and adds a pleasant tang; lemon juice works if you don't have it.
Toast the garam masala for a few seconds in a dry pan to bloom its aroma before mixing.
If the filling weeps after mixing, drain it again and dust in a spoon of roasted besan.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a spiced onion raita and a wedge of lemon to lift the tangy masala.

variations.name: Spicy Mooli Paratha
variations.description: A fiery version where the naturally peppery radish is amped up with green chillies and crushed black pepper for a warming, sinus-clearing kick, perfect for cold mornings. The nutty Anveshan Khapli Atta crust griddled in ghee mellows the heat just enough.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The soft, nutty dough that carries and balances the fiery radish filling.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: In the dough and on the tava; its richness tempers the heat while crisping the crust.

steps: Knead 3 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and about 1.25 cups water into a soft dough; cover and rest 20 minutes.
Grate 2 medium radishes finely, salt with 0.5 tsp salt, rest 10 minutes and wring completely dry in a cloth.

Coarsely crush 1 tsp peppercorns and mix into the mooli with 4 finely chopped green chillies, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, a grated 1-inch piece of ginger, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp chaat masala, 4 tbsp coriander and 0.5 tsp salt.
Divide dough and filling into 8 each; stuff 2 tbsp filling into each dough ball, seal, and roll gently to a 7-inch round with an atta dusting.
Roast on a hot tava for 1 minute, flip, brush with 0.5 tsp ghee and cook each side 1-2 minutes until golden with crisp spots.
Stack under a cloth to keep the parathas warm and soft while the rest cook.
tips: Freshly crushed pepper plays up the radish's natural peppery note for a double warmth.
Deseed a couple of chillies for a gentler heat while keeping the flavour.
Serve with plenty of curd; the heat and the raw radish both feel milder with something cooling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a big bowl of chilled curd and a fresh mint chutney to soothe the palate.

variations.name: Garlic Mooli Paratha
variations.description: A robust, garlic-forward radish paratha where sauteed garlic tames the sharpness of the mooli and adds a deep, savoury aroma. Ghee-roasting toasts the garlic edges while the wholesome Anveshan Khapli Atta gives a satisfying, nutty chew.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Kneaded into the dough; its earthy nuttiness marries well with garlic and radish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: Used to saute the garlic and roast the parathas, layering in a rich toasted-garlic aroma.

steps: Knead 3 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and about 1.25 cups water into a soft dough; cover and rest 20 minutes.
Finely chop 10 garlic cloves and saute in 1 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee over medium heat for 1-2 minutes until pale gold and fragrant, then cool.

Grate 2 medium radishes finely, salt with 0.5 tsp salt, rest 10 minutes, squeeze dry, then mix with the sauteed garlic, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 4 tbsp coriander and 0.5 tsp salt.
Divide dough and filling into 8 each; stuff 2 tbsp filling into each ball, seal, and roll gently to a 7-inch round, dusting with atta.
Roast on a hot tava for 1 minute, flip, brush with 0.5 tsp ghee and cook each side 1-2 minutes until golden with toasty brown spots.
Stack under a cloth to keep soft while you finish the remaining parathas.
tips: Sauteing the garlic mellows both its own bite and the sharpness of the raw radish.
Squeeze the mooli dry only after the garlic has cooled so no extra moisture is introduced.
A pinch of ajwain in the filling aids digestion and cuts any radish heaviness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a garlicky tomato chutney and plain curd, or alongside a bowl of dal for a hearty winter meal.

variations.name: Cheesy Mooli Paratha
variations.description: A modern, kid-friendly twist where grated cheese melts into the peppery radish filling, its creaminess taming the mooli's sharp edge into a mild, gooey centre. The Anveshan Khapli Atta dough griddled in ghee crisps into a golden shell around the molten filling.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The nutty wholegrain dough that crisps around the cheese-and-radish filling.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon in the dough and the rest for roasting to a crisp, cheese-melting golden crust.

steps: Knead 3 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and about 1.25 cups water into a soft dough; cover and rest 20 minutes.
Grate 1 medium radish finely, salt with 0.5 tsp salt, rest 10 minutes and squeeze completely dry in a cloth.
