ingredients.note: Its earthy roast tames the raw heat of the green chilli beautifully

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Worked into the dough for a tender, faintly nutty paratha

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: For roasting the parathas to a crisp, golden finish

steps: Rub 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, then knead with about 0.75 cup water to a soft dough and rest 15 minutes.

Combine 1 cup Anveshan Sattu with the minced green chilli, 1 tsp cracked black pepper, grated ginger, 1 tbsp lemon juice, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, chopped coriander and 0.5 tsp salt, adding 2 tbsp water for a just-cohesive filling.
Pinch off 6 dough balls, hollow each into a cup, load 2 tbsp of the spicy sattu, seal the pleats tightly and press flat.
Roll out carefully to a 7-inch round, keeping pressure even so the peppery filling does not tear through.
Slap onto a hot tava and cook 1 minute until the underside firms, then flip and brush generously with Anveshan Ghee.
Turn once more and roast each side 1 to 2 minutes, pressing lightly, until crisp brown blisters appear and the pepper turns fragrant.
tips: Cracking the peppercorns fresh rather than using fine powder gives bursts of aromatic heat instead of a flat burn.
Deseed one of the green chillies if you want the flavour without the full fire.
A cold cucumber raita on the side resets the palate between spicy bites.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with thick set curd, a drizzle of extra lemon and a plate of raw onion rings and cucumber.

variations.name: Garlic Sattu Paratha
variations.description: A robust Rajasthani-style paratha where plenty of garlic, both raw grated and lightly toasted, drives the flavour of the sattu filling. The garlic mellows on the tava into something deeply savoury, rounded out with a whisper of red chilli. Sturdy and satisfying, it travels well and needs little more than pickle.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Hearty emmer flour suits this rustic, garlic-forward paratha

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Absorbs the toasted garlic aroma and stays moist through cooking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Used to toast the garlic and to roast the parathas golden

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 0.75 cup water to a pliable dough, then cover and rest 15 minutes.
Heat 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and gently toast half the grated garlic for 30 seconds until pale gold and fragrant, then cool it slightly.

Mix 1 cup Anveshan Sattu with the toasted garlic, the remaining raw grated garlic, chopped onion, 1 tsp red chilli, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, crushed kasuri methi, coriander and 0.5 tsp salt, moistening with 2 tbsp water to bind.
Cup each dough ball, fill with 2 tbsp of the garlic sattu, pinch the edges closed and press into a thick disc.
Roll out to a 7-inch round with a light touch so the garlicky filling stays sealed inside.
Roast on a medium-hot tava, brushing both sides with Anveshan Ghee, for 1 to 2 minutes each until golden-brown and the garlic smells sweet and toasty.
tips: Toasting half the garlic softens its bite while the raw half keeps the punch, giving a rounder flavour.
Do not let the garlic brown past pale gold in the ghee or it will turn bitter in the filling.
These hold up for hours in a tiffin, making them ideal for travel or lunchboxes.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with garlic pickle and a bowl of plain curd, or serve alongside a simple kadhi for a fuller meal.

variations.name: Cheesy Sattu Paratha
variations.description: A playful, kid-friendly fusion where nutty sattu meets a molten core of grated cheese, finished with a curry-leaf and black-pepper tempering for a South Indian twist. The cheese melts into the earthy filling so each bite is creamy, savoury and just a little spicy. A modern favourite that turns a humble paratha into a treat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The wholegrain base keeps the rich cheesy filling from feeling heavy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Earthy roasted gram balances the melted cheese and adds protein

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: For the curry-leaf tempering and for roasting the parathas

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and around 0.75 cup water into a soft dough and rest it, covered, for 15 minutes.
Warm 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and crackle the chopped curry leaves, minced green chilli and grated ginger for 20 seconds, then stir in 0.75 tsp crushed black pepper and switch off the heat.
Cool this tempering, then fold it into a mix of 0.75 cup Anveshan Sattu, 1 cup grated cheese, coriander and 0.25 tsp salt until evenly combined.
Flatten each dough ball, place 2 tbsp of the cheesy sattu in the middle, seal the edges over the top and pat into a disc.
Roll out gently to a 7-inch round, working slowly so the soft cheese filling stays contained.
Cook on a medium tava, brushing with Anveshan Ghee, for about 1 to 2 minutes a side until golden and you can see the cheese just beginning to melt at the seams.
tips: Use a firm melting cheese and keep the heat at medium so the cheese softens without scorching the crust.
Chill the filling for ten minutes before stuffing; a firmer filling is much easier to seal.
Serve immediately while the cheese is molten, as it firms up quickly once cool.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve straight off the tava with tomato ketchup for children or a coconut chutney for a South Indian touch.

variations.name: Classic Sem
variations.description: A wholesome winter sabzi of tender broad beans simmered in a light onion-tomato masala until they turn sweet and buttery. The flat sem pods take time to soften, so this is a patient, homely dish where cumin and coriander frame the beans' fresh, grassy flavour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: its warmth suits the earthy beans and gives a traditional North Indian base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: swirled in at the end to round the earthy beans with a nutty finish

steps: String 400 g broad beans and cut them diagonally into 1-inch pieces, then rinse and drain.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the flame, and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds.
Add 2 chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and saute for 5 minutes until golden and soft.
Stir in 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, cooking 4 minutes until pulpy.
Add the beans with 1 tsp salt and half a cup of water, cover, and simmer on low for 15 minutes until the pods are tender and the water has dried up.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala, swirl in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee, and toss for a minute off the heat.
tips: Choose young, flat pods; older beans turn fibrous and need the tough strings removed carefully.
Add water sparingly and let it cook off so the sabzi stays dry and the beans do not get waterlogged.
A short rest off the heat before serving lets the beans absorb the last of the masala.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulkas and a spoon of ghee, alongside a bowl of moong dal for a light winter thali.

variations.name: Sem nu Shaak
variations.description: A Gujarati-style dry broad-bean shaak balanced between sweet, spicy and tangy, thickened lightly with a spoon of gram flour that clings to the pods. Jaggery and lemon give it that classic Kathiawadi sweet-sour lilt, while ajwain and green chilli keep it lively.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday Gujarati kitchen oil that carries the sweet-spicy shaak

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the essential sweet note in Gujarati shaak, balancing chilli and lemon

steps: String and cut 400 g broad beans into 1-inch pieces and slit 2 green chillies lengthwise.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds with 0.5 tsp ajwain and 0.25 tsp asafoetida, then add the green chillies.
Add the beans with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, tossing for 2 minutes to coat.
Pour in half a cup of water, cover, and cook on low for 15 minutes until the pods are just tender.
Sprinkle 1.5 tbsp besan evenly over the beans and stir well for 3 minutes so it toasts and thickens the moisture into a light coating.
Stir in 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook a minute, then turn off the heat and finish with 2 tsp lemon juice.
tips: Sprinkle the besan gradually while stirring so it coats the beans without forming lumps.
Taste and adjust the sweet-sour balance at the end; it should be gently tangy, sweet and spicy at once.
A pinch of asafoetida is traditional here and makes the beans easier to digest.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft bajra rotla or phulka and a dollop of white butter, Kathiawadi style.

variations.name: Spicy Pepper Sem
variations.description: A dry, fiery Marwari-style broad bean fry with slit green chillies, coarse black pepper and a garlicky tempering. Kept desert-style with no tomato and little water, the beans stay firm and smoky, the pepper and chilli giving a sharp heat that suits a bajra roti.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the staple Rajasthani cooking fat for a robust dry sabzi

steps: String and slice 400 g broad beans thinly on the diagonal so they cook fast in a dry fry.
Coarsely crush 1.5 tsp black pepper and 8 garlic cloves together into a rough paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add the crushed pepper-garlic and 4 slit green chillies and fry a minute.
Add 1 sliced onion and cook on high for 3 minutes until softened, then add the beans with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt.
Sprinkle just 3 tbsp water, cover, and cook on low for 10 minutes until the beans are tender but still firm.
Uncover, raise the heat, and stir-fry a final 4 minutes until dry, blistered and coated in the peppery masala.
tips: Slice the beans thin so they cook through with minimal water and stay dry.
Crush the pepper coarsely for pockets of sharp heat rather than an even background warmth.
Finish on high heat to blister the beans and drive off any remaining moisture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra roti and a smear of white butter, or alongside dal-baati for a Rajasthani spread.

variations.name: Dhaba-style Sem
variations.description: A rich, semi-dry broad bean preparation in a thick onion-tomato masala scented with kasuri methi and garam masala. Slow-browned onions give the beans a deep, savoury coating, turning a plain winter vegetable into a hearty, roadside-style main.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the pungent eastern kitchen oil that underpins this bold masala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a small swap for sugar to round the tomato tang in the dhaba masala

steps: String and cut 400 g broad beans into 1-inch pieces and parboil them for 6 minutes so they finish quickly in the masala.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, then fry 3 sliced onions with 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 8 minutes until deeply caramelised.
Add 2 pureed tomatoes with 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, cooking 7 minutes until thick and glossy.
Drain the beans and fold them in with 1 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, cooking covered on low for 8 minutes.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the top and sprinkle 0.75 tsp garam masala, stirring for a minute until fragrant.
Cook uncovered a final 3 minutes so the masala thickens and clings to every piece.
tips: Parboiling the beans first keeps the total cook time down and ensures they turn tender in the masala.
Let the onions caramelise fully for the signature dhaba depth.
Keep it semi-dry so the masala coats the beans rather than pooling at the bottom.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tandoori roti or laccha paratha and a side of sliced onions with lemon.

variations.name: Coconut Sem Poriyal
variations.description: A light South Indian broad bean poriyal tempered with mustard, curry leaves and urad dal, then finished with a shower of fresh grated coconut. Steamed rather than simmered in masala, the beans stay bright and crisp, the coconut lending a sweet, delicate crunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the authentic southern fat that echoes the fresh coconut garnish

steps: String and finely chop 400 g broad beans into small even pieces so they steam quickly.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 1 tsp urad dal and fry until golden.
Add 2 broken dried red chillies, 12 curry leaves and 2 slit green chillies, letting them crackle for 20 seconds.
Tip in the chopped beans with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, tossing to coat in the tempering.
Sprinkle 3 tbsp water, cover, and steam-cook on low for 12 minutes until the beans are just tender and dry.
Turn off the heat and fold in 4 tbsp grated coconut, tossing until evenly distributed.
tips: Chop the beans small so they cook through by gentle steaming without needing extra water.
Add the coconut only at the end so it stays fresh and does not brown in the pan.
Fresh grated coconut is best, but thawed frozen coconut works well for the same sweet crunch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a side with sambar rice and rasam, or alongside curd rice for a comforting South Indian meal.

variations.name: Classic Soya Chunk Masala
variations.description: The everyday restaurant-style soya chunk curry, where spongy nuggets are simmered in a smooth onion-tomato gravy until they drink up every drop of masala. A finish of cream and a spoon of ghee rounds the tang into something silky and comforting.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil gives the gravy a nutty backbone that holds up to the spice

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of bilona ghee lifts the aroma just before serving

steps: Soak the soya chunks in freshly boiled water for 10 minutes until they swell and soften, then drain and squeeze each one gently to remove the raw beany water, and keep them aside.
Heat the Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle and turn fragrant for about 20 seconds.
Add the finely chopped onions and sauté for 6 to 7 minutes until they turn deep golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for another minute until the raw smell disappears.
Add the pureed tomatoes along with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, and cook on medium heat for 8 to 10 minutes until the oil separates at the edges.
Stir in the squeezed soya chunks with 1 tsp salt and 1.5 cups water, cover and simmer for 12 minutes until the chunks are plump and have soaked up the gravy.
Swirl in 3 tbsp fresh cream, 0.5 tsp garam masala and the finishing tbsp of Anveshan Ghee, cook for 2 more minutes, then scatter 2 tbsp chopped coriander over the top.
tips: Always squeeze the soaked chunks dry, otherwise they release stored water into the pan and dilute the masala.
For a smoother restaurant finish, blend the cooled onion-tomato masala before adding the chunks.
Add a pinch of sugar if your tomatoes are very sour to balance the gravy without masking the spice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a shallow bowl with a swirl of extra cream on top, alongside butter naan and a wedge of raw onion dressed with lime and chaat masala.

variations.name: Assamese Masala Soya Chunk
variations.description: An Assam-style take that leans hard on freshly roasted coriander powder for an earthy, citrusy warmth rather than heavy cream. The gravy stays lighter and more brothy, the way rice-first Assamese kitchens prefer it.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil brings the sharp pungency that defines Assamese home cooking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a small drizzle at the end softens the mustard bite

steps: Boil the soya chunks in salted water for 5 minutes, drain, and rinse under cold water before squeezing them firmly so they cook up tender rather than rubbery.
Heat the Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just begins to smoke, then lower the flame and drop in 1 bay leaf to temper for 15 seconds so the oil loses its raw sting.
Add the sliced onions and fry on medium heat for 7 minutes until light brown, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook until the mixture smells sweet and cooked.
Toss in the chopped tomatoes with 2 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder, and stir-fry for 6 minutes until the tomatoes collapse into a thick masala.
Add the squeezed chunks, 1 tsp salt and 2 cups water, then cover and simmer for 12 to 14 minutes so the curry stays brothy and the coriander flavour deepens.
Finish with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and a handful of chopped coriander, and let it rest off the heat for 3 minutes before serving.
tips: Roast the coriander powder in a dry pan for 30 seconds before adding it to intensify the citrus note.
Keep the gravy loose, as Assamese meals pair this with plenty of steamed rice rather than bread.
A slit green chilli dropped in during the simmer adds fragrance without extra heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle over a mound of short-grain steamed rice with a side of blanched greens and a slice of lemon on the rim of the plate.

variations.name: Haryanvi Butter Soya Chunk
variations.description: A dhaba-inspired Haryanvi version where soya chunks are simmered in a rich buttery tomato gravy, glossy and mildly sweet. Generous butter and a splash of milk make it a crowd-pleaser that clings thickly to each chunk.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee stands in for part of the butter to give a cleaner, deeper richness

steps: Soak the soya chunks in hot water for 10 minutes, drain, squeeze dry, and set aside so they are ready to soak up the buttery gravy.
Boil the tomatoes, onion and 10 cashews in 1 cup water for 8 minutes until soft, cool slightly, then blend to a completely smooth puree and strain for a velvet texture.
Heat the Anveshan Ghee with 1 tbsp of the butter over medium heat, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 1 minute until fragrant and pale gold.
Pour in the strained puree with 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.25 tsp turmeric, and cook covered for 10 minutes, stirring often, until the raw tomato smell is gone and the ghee floats on top.
Add the squeezed chunks, 1 tsp salt and 0.5 cup milk, then simmer gently for 10 minutes until the gravy turns thick and glossy around the chunks.
Crush 1 tsp kasuri methi between your palms and stir it in with 0.5 tsp garam masala and the remaining tbsp of butter, cook for 2 minutes, and serve hot.
tips: Straining the puree is the secret to the smooth, dhaba-style body, so do not skip it.
Use full-fat milk rather than cream to keep the gravy rich but not cloying.
If the gravy tightens too much on standing, loosen it with a splash of warm milk before reheating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with soft laccha paratha and a bowl of boondi raita, finishing the plate with a curl of butter melting on top of the curry.

variations.name: Delhi Kadai Soya Chunk
variations.description: A punchy Delhi kadai-style dish where soya chunks and thick capsicum wedges are tossed in a coarsely pounded kadai masala. The gravy is semi-dry and clingy, built for scooping with tandoori roti and eaten piping hot from the wok.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: its high smoke point suits the fast, high-heat kadai tossing

steps: Dry-roast 2 tsp coriander seeds, 3 dried red chillies and 1 tsp cumin seeds in a hot pan for about 90 seconds until aromatic, then cool and pound coarsely into a fresh kadai masala.
Boil the soya chunks for 5 minutes, drain, squeeze dry, and cut the capsicum into thick 3 cm wedges so they stay crunchy in the toss.
Heat the Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai over high heat, add the cubed onions and sear for 3 minutes until the edges char slightly, then push them to the side.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, and cook on high for 6 minutes until the tomatoes soften and the mixture thickens.
Stir in most of the pounded kadai masala, the squeezed chunks, capsicum wedges, 1 tsp salt and 0.5 cup water, and toss on high heat for 6 minutes so the gravy coats everything and stays semi-dry.
Crush 1 tsp kasuri methi over the top, sprinkle the reserved kadai masala and 2 tbsp coriander, and give it one final toss before serving straight from the wok.
tips: Pounding the kadai masala fresh instead of using store-bought powder is what gives this dish its signature coarse crunch and aroma.
Keep the capsicum slightly crisp by adding it only in the last few minutes.
Cook on the highest heat your stove allows to get that smoky kadai character.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve sizzling in a mini iron kadai with rings of onion and lemon, and hot tandoori rotis torn straight from the tandoor.

variations.name: Telangana Handi Soya Chunk
variations.description: A slow handi-style curry from Telangana where whole spices are bloomed in oil and the soya chunks steam gently in a sealed pot. The result is a deeply aromatic, layered gravy that carries the perfume of cardamom, cloves and cinnamon in every bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed sesame oil is the traditional Telangana cooking fat and carries whole-spice aroma beautifully

steps: Soak the soya chunks in hot water for 10 minutes, drain and squeeze dry, then whisk 0.5 cup yogurt smooth so it will not split when it hits the hot pan.
Heat the Anveshan Sesame Oil in a heavy handi over medium heat and bloom 4 cardamom, 4 cloves, a 1 inch cinnamon stick and 2 bay leaves for 30 seconds until they sizzle and release their perfume.
Add the thinly sliced onions and fry patiently for 10 minutes until richly browned, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for a minute more.
Lower the heat, add the whisked yogurt with 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp turmeric, and stir continuously for 3 minutes until the masala thickens and the oil beads at the surface.
Add the chopped tomatoes, squeezed chunks, 1 tsp salt and 1 cup water, then seal the handi with a tight lid and cook on the lowest heat for 15 minutes so the spices infuse the chunks.
Lift the lid, fold in 2 tbsp chopped coriander, and let the curry sit covered off the heat for 5 minutes to settle the whole-spice aroma before serving.
tips: Do not remove the whole spices, but warn diners so they can set them aside as they eat.
A tight seal on the handi traps the aromatic steam, so use a heavy lid or press dough around the rim.
Brown the onions properly, as they provide the natural sweetness and body of this gravy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft rumali roti or a bowl of ghee rice, garnished with fried onion slivers and a few strands of fresh mint.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Bread Roll
variations.description: A pepper-forward bread roll where the mashed-potato filling is fired up with freshly crushed black pepper, green chilli and red chilli, then rolled in bread and fried crisp. Sharper and hotter than a plain roll, with warmth that builds slowly. The snack that wakes up a rainy evening.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: High-smoke frying fat that crisps the rolls without absorbing into them

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Blooms the cumin and the crushed pepper for a rounded heat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its slurry seals the rolls so the fiery filling stays put while frying

steps: Boil 4 potatoes until soft, peel and mash them while warm so the filling is lump-free, about 15 minutes.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1.5 tsp crushed black pepper for 20 seconds until fragrant, then add the onion and 3 green chillies.
Saute 3 minutes, add the mashed potato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli and 1.25 tsp salt, cook 4 minutes, then fold in 3 tbsp coriander and cool fully.
Trim and dampen 10 bread slices, press out the water, place 2 tbsp filling on each and roll into tight sealed cylinders.
Whisk 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta with 4 tbsp water into a slurry, coat each roll and roll in 1 cup bread crumbs.
Deep-fry in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil at 180C for 3-4 minutes until crisp and golden, then drain on paper.
tips: Crush the pepper fresh just before cooking for a brighter, more aromatic heat than pre-ground.
Cool the filling completely, since a hot spicy filling steams the bread and softens the crust.
For extra kick, mix a little crushed pepper into the bread crumbs too.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot with cooling mint-yoghurt dip and lemon wedges to cut the pepper heat.

variations.name: Rajasthani Spicy Bread Roll
variations.description: A desert-style spicy roll built on smoky whole dried red chillies pounded into a paste with garlic, finished with amchur for the tangy Marwari edge and enriched with ghee. Deeply red and searing, without a single onion. A bold roll from the land of lal maas.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Fries the rolls crisp while standing up to the fierce chilli paste

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The heart of Rajasthani cooking, it tames the dried chilli into a smooth heat

steps: Soak 6 dried red chillies in warm water 10 minutes, then grind with 6 garlic cloves into a smooth red paste.
Boil and mash 4 potatoes, keeping them ready while you cook the masala base, about 15 minutes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add the chilli-garlic paste and fry 2 minutes until the raw smell goes and the ghee turns red.
Stir in the mashed potato with 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp amchur and 1.25 tsp salt, cook 4 minutes, then fold in 3 tbsp coriander and cool.
Trim and dampen 10 bread slices, squeeze out the water, roll 2 tbsp filling into each into firm logs, then coat in flour-water slurry and 1 cup bread crumbs.
Deep-fry in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil at 180C for 3-4 minutes until crisp and dark gold, then drain.
tips: Deseed some of the dried chillies if you want the smoky colour with a little less heat.
Frying the chilli-garlic paste well is essential, or the filling tastes raw and harsh.
Amchur is what gives the Marwari tang, so do not swap it for lemon which thins the filling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with garlic-chilli chutney and a cooling glass of chaas to balance the desert-style heat.

variations.name: Kerala Spicy Bread Roll
variations.description: A coastal spicy roll where the potato is bound with fresh grated coconut, curry leaves and a coconut-oil tempering, spiked with black pepper and green chilli in true Malabar style. Fragrant, warm and gently nutty beneath the crunch. A tea-shop favourite reimagined.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Its coconut aroma is the soul of Kerala frying and perfumes every roll

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Forms the binding slurry that seals the coconut-rich filling

steps: Boil and mash 4 potatoes and keep them ready, allowing about 15 minutes for cooking.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil over medium heat, splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 12 curry leaves, then add the ginger and 3 green chillies.
Add the onion, fry 3 minutes, then stir in the mashed potato with 1 tsp crushed pepper, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt, cook 4 minutes and fold in 4 tbsp grated coconut.
Cool the filling, trim and dampen 10 bread slices, press out the water and roll 2 tbsp filling into each into tight cylinders.
Whisk 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta with 4 tbsp water, coat each roll and roll it in 1 cup bread crumbs.
Deep-fry in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil at 180C for 3-4 minutes until crisp and golden, then drain on paper.
tips: Add the coconut at the end and do not overcook it, so it stays fresh and moist in the filling.
Coconut oil solidifies when cool, so keep the oil hot and steady for even crisp frying.
Toast the crushed pepper for a few seconds for a deeper Malabar aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut-curry leaf chutney and strong Kerala chai for a proper chaya-kada snack.

variations.name: Gujarati Spicy Bread Roll
variations.description: A sweet-heat Gujarati roll where the fiery pepper-and-green-chilli filling is balanced by jaggery and a sesame-mustard tempering for the beloved khatta-meetha-teekha play. Spicy but softly sweet, unmistakably Gujarati. Lovely with a hot cup of masala chai.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The staple Gujarati frying fat for a light, crisp shell

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Delivers the signature Gujarati sweetness that offsets the pepper and chilli

steps: Boil and mash 4 potatoes and keep aside, taking about 15 minutes for them to soften.
Heat 2 tbsp of the groundnut oil over medium heat, splutter 0.5 tsp mustard, 0.5 tsp cumin and 1 tsp sesame seeds for 20 seconds, then add 1.5 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste.
Fry 1 minute, add the mashed potato with 1 tsp crushed pepper, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1.25 tsp salt, cook 4 minutes, then mix in 1 tbsp lemon juice and 3 tbsp coriander.
Cool the filling, trim and dampen 10 bread slices, squeeze dry and roll 2 tbsp filling into each into neat logs.
Coat in a thin flour-water slurry and 1 cup bread crumbs, pressing them on firmly.
Deep-fry in Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil at 180C for 3-4 minutes until crisp and gold, then drain on paper.
tips: Taste the filling after the jaggery and lemon to land the sweet-sour-spicy balance you like.
Sesame in the tempering adds a nutty note; toast it just until it starts to pop.
Grind fresh ginger-green chilli paste for a brighter flavour than a store-bought jar.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sweet date-tamarind chutney and thin sev sprinkled on top for a Gujarati farsan touch.

variations.name: Bihari Spicy Bread Roll
variations.description: A rustic Bihari roll where roasted sattu is folded into the spicy potato with mustard oil, ajwain and pungent mustard, echoing the beloved litti-chokha flavour. Nutty, earthy and sharp all at once. Filling enough to be a small meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Its pungency is central to Bihari cooking and fries the rolls deep gold

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Roasted gram sattu gives the nutty litti-style character and binds the filling

steps: Boil and mash 4 potatoes and keep ready while you prepare the tempering, about 15 minutes.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil to smoking, cool slightly, then crackle 0.5 tsp ajwain and fry the 5 crushed garlic cloves and 3 green chillies 1 minute.
Add the onion, fry 3 minutes, then stir in the mashed potato with 1 tsp crushed pepper, 0.5 tsp mustard powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt and cook 3 minutes.
Fold in 3 tbsp Anveshan Sattu and 3 tbsp coriander until the filling is nutty and just moist, then cool it completely.
Trim and dampen 10 bread slices, squeeze dry, roll 2 tbsp filling into each into firm logs, then coat in flour-water slurry and 1 cup bread crumbs.
Deep-fry in the remaining Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil at 180C for 3-4 minutes until crisp and browned, then drain.
tips: Add the sattu off the heat, since cooking it long makes the filling dry and crumbly.
Keep the filling just moist enough to hold, as sattu absorbs moisture and can stiffen it.
A splash of mustard oil drizzled raw over the filling deepens the authentic Bihari pungency.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tomato-garlic chokha chutney and thin onion rings, litti-chokha style.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Moong Dal Pakora
variations.description: A pepper-charged moong dal fritter where coarsely ground dal is fired up with crushed black pepper, green chilli and red chilli, fried into crackling hot nuggets. Sharper and hotter than the everyday pakora, with a slow-building warmth. The perfect stormy-evening munch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: High-smoke frying fat that crisps the fritters cleanly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A hot spoon beaten into the batter rounds the pepper heat and crisps the crumb

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup split green gram 3 hours until swollen, then drain it well.
Grind the dal coarse with the 3 green chillies and 1 tbsp ginger, using as little water as possible so it stays thick.
Beat the batter 2 minutes until light, then fold in 1.5 tsp crushed pepper, the onion, 1 tsp cumin, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli, 3 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until hot and beat it into the batter to crisp the pakoras and soften the pepper bite.
Heat Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to 180C and drop rough spoonfuls, frying 8-10 at a time without crowding.
Fry 3-4 minutes, turning, until deep golden and crisp, then drain on paper.
tips: Crush the pepper fresh for a brighter, more aromatic heat than pre-ground powder.
Keep the batter thick and craggy so the fritters trap air and stay light and crisp.
A pinch of pepper over the drained pakoras adds an extra fragrant kick.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with cooling mint-yoghurt dip and lemon wedges to temper the pepper heat.

variations.name: Rajasthani Spicy Moong Dal Pakora
variations.description: A desert-fierce moong dal fritter built on a smoky dried-red-chilli and garlic paste with amchur for a tangy Marwari heat, fried rich in ghee-touched oil. Deeply red and blistering, with no onion at all. A bold bite from Rajasthan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Fries the fritters crisp while standing up to the fierce chilli paste

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The heart of Rajasthani cooking, beaten in to smooth the dried-chilli heat

steps: Soak 6 dried red chillies in warm water 10 minutes, then grind with 6 garlic cloves into a smooth red paste.
Rinse and soak 1 cup split green gram 3 hours, then drain and grind coarse using minimal water.
Beat the dal batter 2 minutes until light, then fold in the chilli-garlic paste, 1 tsp cumin, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp amchur, 3 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until hot and beat it into the batter to crisp the crumb and mellow the raw chilli.
Heat Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to 180C and drop rough spoonfuls, frying 8-10 at a time.
Fry 3-4 minutes, turning, until deep red-gold and crisp, then drain on paper.
tips: Deseed some of the dried chillies for the smoky colour with a touch less heat.
Grind the chilli-garlic to a fine paste so it blends smoothly through every fritter.
Amchur gives the Marwari tang, so avoid swapping it for lemon which thins the batter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with garlic-chilli chutney and a cold glass of chaas to cool the desert heat.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Spicy Moong Dal Pakora
variations.description: A Puneri moong dal fritter where dark goda masala and crushed pepper meet grated coconut and a mustard-cumin lift, fried crisp for an earthy, fragrant heat. Warmly spiced and distinctly Maharashtrian. A soulful monsoon snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The everyday Maharashtrian frying fat for light, crisp fritters

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A pinch balances the goda masala with the signature gentle sweetness

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup split green gram 3 hours, then drain and grind coarse with the 2 green chillies using minimal water.
Dry-roast 0.5 tsp mustard and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds until fragrant, then crush lightly and set aside.

Beat the dal batter 2 minutes until light, then fold in 1.5 tsp goda masala, 1 tsp crushed pepper, the crushed roasted seeds, the onion, 3 tbsp coconut, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 3 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt.
Heat Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to 180C and drop rough spoonfuls, frying 8-10 at a time.
Fry 3-4 minutes, turning, until deep golden and crisp with the goda masala fragrant.
Drain on paper and serve while hot and crunchy.
tips: Roasting and crushing the seeds first deepens the earthy Maharashtrian aroma.
Fresh coconut keeps the fritters moist inside; desiccated makes them dry.
Keep the jaggery to a single teaspoon so it lifts the spice without turning sweet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with dry garlic-peanut chutney and kadak chai for a Puneri tea-time treat.

variations.name: Tamil Spicy Moong Dal Pakora
variations.description: A South Indian moong dal fritter fried in nutty sesame oil and seasoned with pepper, curry leaves and fennel, in the spirit of a Tamil paruppu vadai. Aromatic and peppery with a crackle of tadka. A tiffin-shop favourite made fresh.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Nallennai lends the earthy Tamil aroma and fries the vadai crisp

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon beaten in adds richness and a shatter-crisp finish

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup split green gram 3 hours, then drain and grind coarse with the 2 green chillies and 1 tbsp ginger using minimal water.
Beat the batter 2 minutes until light, then fold in 1.5 tsp crushed pepper, 14 chopped curry leaves, 1 tsp fennel seeds, 5 chopped shallots, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 3 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until hot and beat it into the batter for a crisp, rich crumb.
Heat Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil to 180C and drop rough spoonfuls, frying 8-10 at a time.
Fry 3-4 minutes, turning, until deep golden and crunchy with the curry leaves crisped.
Drain on paper and serve hot with a squeeze of lime.
tips: Whole fennel seeds give bursts of sweet aroma against the pepper heat, so keep them uncrushed.
Shallots fry sweeter than onion and give the authentic Tamil base.
Let the sesame oil heat fully before frying to mellow its strong raw flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and hot filter coffee for a proper Tamil tiffin snack.

variations.name: Bihari Spicy Moong Dal Pakora
variations.description: A rustic Bihari fritter where the moong dal batter is sharpened with mustard oil, ajwain and pungent mustard powder, fried into pepper-hot golden bites. Earthy and bracing like a roadside snack of the Gangetic plains. Hearty and full of character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Its pungency is central to Bihari cooking and fries the fritters deep gold

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon beaten in lightens the batter and crisps the crumb

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup split green gram 3 hours, then drain and grind coarse with the 3 green chillies using minimal water.

Beat the batter 2 minutes until light, then fold in 1.5 tsp crushed pepper, 0.5 tsp ajwain rubbed between your fingers, 0.5 tsp mustard powder, the onion, 5 crushed garlic cloves, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 3 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until hot and beat it into the batter for a crisp, light crumb.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil to smoking, cool slightly, then top up the kadhai and bring to 180C.
Drop rough spoonfuls into the hot mustard oil, frying 8-10 at a time without crowding.
Fry 3-4 minutes, turning, until deep golden and crisp, then drain on paper.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to smoking then cool it a little so its raw sharpness softens.
Rub the ajwain as you add it to release its aroma and help digestion.
Mustard powder brings a nose-tingling Bihari edge, so add it in small amounts to taste.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with green-chilli-garlic chutney and raw onion rings, roadside dhaba style.

variations.name: Classic Spicy Onion Bhaji
variations.description: A bolder cousin of the everyday bhaji, built for people who want heat you can feel: coarsely crushed black pepper and extra green chilli layer a slow, warming burn over the sweet fried onion. The besan batter stays thin and crisp so the spice, not the flour, is the star.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A neutral high-heat frying oil that lets the pepper and chilli come through cleanly.

steps: Coarsely crush 1.5 tsp black peppercorns in a mortar so you get uneven, punchy shards rather than fine powder.
Slice 3 large onions thinly, salt with 1 tsp salt and rest 10 minutes until they soften and release moisture.

Mix in 1.5 cups besan, 2 tbsp rice flour, the crushed pepper, 4 chopped green chillies, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp cumin, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 3 tbsp coriander, using just 3 tbsp water for a thick batter.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to 180C until a drop of batter sizzles up immediately.
Fry loose spoonfuls in batches for 3-4 minutes, turning once, until golden and crisp, then drain on a wire rack.
Finish with a light dusting of extra crushed pepper over the hot fritters for an aromatic hit.
tips: Crush the pepper fresh rather than using pre-ground; the volatile oils fade fast and are what make this bhaji sing.
The heat builds as you eat, so taste one before adding more chilli to the remaining batter.
A squeeze of lemon at the table brightens the pepper and stops the heat feeling flat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with cooling mint-yoghurt raita and thin cucumber slices to balance the pepper, with masala chai alongside.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Onion Bhaji
variations.description: This is heat with a pedigree: fiery Guntur red chilli and crushed pepper together create the layered, lingering burn Andhra kitchens are famous for. A garlic-heavy batter and coconut-oil frying add depth so the fritters are intense yet deeply savoury, never one-note.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: The coastal-Andhra frying fat; its sweet edge tempers the ferocious Guntur chilli.

steps: Pound 6 garlic cloves with 1 tsp black peppercorns to a coarse paste in a mortar for a pungent base.
Slice 3 large onions thinly, salt with 1 tsp salt and rest 10 minutes, then add the garlic-pepper paste.

Stir in 1.5 cups besan, 3 tbsp rice flour, 2.5 tsp Guntur red chilli powder, 15 torn curry leaves, 3 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp cumin and 0.5 tsp turmeric with just 3 tbsp water for a thick red batter.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil to 180C until it shimmers and a test drop rises at once.
Fry spoonfuls in batches for 3-4 minutes, turning once, until deep brick-red and crackling crisp.
Drain on a rack and scatter a few crisp-fried curry leaves over the top for aroma.
tips: Pounding garlic and pepper together releases more aroma than chopping and makes the heat feel rounded.
If the batch is for a mixed crowd, fry half with 1.5 tsp chilli so there's a milder option.
Coconut oil sets firm when cold, so eat these piping hot for the crispest bite.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain curd, a spoon of gongura pickle and hot rice to soak up and soften the Guntur fire.

variations.name: Kerala Spicy Onion Bhaji (Ulli Vada)
variations.description: Kerala's ulli vada reimagined with a spicy kick: freshly grated coconut folded into the batter keeps the fritters moist inside while curry leaves and crushed pepper bring the warmth. Frying in Anveshan Coconut Oil ties every element to the Malabar coast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Essential for a genuine Kerala vada; the coconut oil aroma defines the whole snack.

steps: Slice 3 large onions thinly, salt with 1 tsp salt and rest 10 minutes; crush 1 tsp peppercorns coarsely.
Add 0.5 cup fresh grated coconut, 20 torn curry leaves, 4 chopped green chillies, a grated 1-inch piece of ginger, the crushed pepper and 0.5 tsp turmeric to the onions.
Mix in 1.25 cups besan and 3 tbsp rice flour with just 3 tbsp water to a thick batter that holds together when pressed.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil to 175C until a test drop rises steadily with fine bubbles.
Shape the mixture into small flattened rounds and fry in batches for 4-5 minutes, turning once, until golden and crisp-edged.
Drain on paper and serve while the coconut inside is still warm and fragrant.
tips: Fresh coconut, not desiccated, keeps the vada juicy; if using frozen, thaw and squeeze out excess water first.
Fry at a slightly lower temperature than plain bhajis so the thicker coconut fritters cook through without burning.
Leftover batter can be shaped and shallow-fried on a tava for a lighter version the next day.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a small cup of milky South Indian filter coffee and a smear of coconut chutney for a proper Kerala tea-shop snack.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Spicy Onion Bhaji (Kanda Bhaji)
variations.description: Monsoon kanda bhaji with a spicy Maharashtrian soul: aromatic goda masala and a hit of red chilli give the fritters their signature dark, complex warmth. A pinch of rice flour and semolina in the batter make them extra crisp for that first-rain craving.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the classic Maharashtrian frying medium and complements the goda masala's warmth.

steps: Slice 3 large onions thinly, salt with 1 tsp salt and leave for 10 minutes until they wilt and release moisture.
Add 1.5 tsp goda masala, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, 3 chopped green chillies, 3 tbsp coriander and 0.5 tsp turmeric, tossing so the spices coat the onions evenly.
Mix in 1.5 cups besan, 2 tbsp semolina and 2 tbsp rice flour with just 3 tbsp water into a thick, sticky batter.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to 180C until a pinch of batter surfaces at once with a brisk sizzle.
Drop in irregular spoonfuls and fry in batches for 3-4 minutes, turning once, until dark golden and crackling crisp.
Drain on paper and taste; the goda masala should give a warm, faintly sweet-spicy finish under the heat.
tips: Let the semolina sit in the batter for 5 minutes before frying so it hydrates and crisps up rather than staying gritty.
Goda masala varies by brand, so start with 1 tsp if yours is strong and build up.
For the true monsoon experience, keep the shapes rough and craggy; smooth fritters lose the crunchy edges.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with dry garlic chutney (lasun chutney) and cutting chai as the rain comes down.

variations.name: Bengali Spicy Onion Bhaji
variations.description: A spicier peyaji fried in sharp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil, with a crushed panch-phoron edge and extra green chilli for bite. The mustard oil's natural pungency compounds the heat, making these among the most assertive of all onion fritters.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Smoked once then cooled; its pungency amplifies the chilli heat for a fierce Bengali fritter.

steps: Dry-roast 1 tsp panch phoron in a small pan for 30 seconds until fragrant, then crush it coarsely.
Slice 3 large onions thinly, salt with 1 tsp salt and rest 10 minutes until juicy and soft.

Add the crushed panch phoron, 0.5 tsp nigella seeds, 5 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 2 tbsp coriander, then mix in 1.25 cups besan and 2 tbsp rice flour with just 2 tbsp water.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until it smokes, then lower to medium so the raw edge softens.
Fry flattened spoonfuls in batches for 3-4 minutes, turning once, until deep golden and crisp at the frilled edges.
Drain on paper; the fritters will carry a sharp mustard-and-panch-phoron aroma with a real chilli kick.
tips: Roasting the panch phoron before crushing wakes up the fenugreek and fennel and stops any bitterness.
Five green chillies makes these genuinely hot; halve the count for a family-friendly batch.
Do not skip smoking the mustard oil first, or the fritters can taste raw and overly pungent.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice, a wedge of lime and a green chilli on the side, Bengali home-style.

variations.name: Classic Tava Bread Roll
variations.description: A lighter, low-oil bread roll shallow-fried on a flat tava instead of deep-frying, so the shell crisps golden while using just a few spoons of oil. The spiced potato stays soft inside a crunchy skin. A guilt-lighter version of the beloved snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Just enough drizzled on the tava to shallow-fry the rolls crisp

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Blooms the cumin and enriches the potato filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its slurry glues the roll shut so it holds shape on the open tava

steps: Boil 3 potatoes until tender, peel and mash them smooth while warm, about 15 minutes.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then saute the onion and 2 green chillies 3 minutes until soft.
Add the mashed potato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli and 1 tsp salt, cook 4 minutes, then fold in 3 tbsp coriander and cool the filling.
Trim and dampen 8 bread slices, press out the water, place 2 tbsp filling on each and roll into firm cylinders, sealing the seam with a little Anveshan Khapli Atta slurry.
Heat a flat tava over medium heat and drizzle 2 tbsp of the groundnut oil, then place the rolls seam-side down.
Shallow-fry rolling them every 1-2 minutes, adding oil as needed, for 6-7 minutes total until crisp and golden all around.
tips: Roll the logs tight and seal well, since a loose seam opens up on the flat tava.
Keep the heat medium; too high browns the bread before the roll heats through.
Press the rolls gently with the spatula to crisp all sides evenly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with green chutney and ketchup, sliced in half to show the soft filling inside the crisp skin.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Tava Bread Roll
variations.description: A tava-crisped roll carrying the dark, aromatic goda masala of Maharashtra with coconut and a touch of jaggery, shallow-fried for a lighter finish. Earthy and fragrant, the masala shining through without deep-frying. A wholesome evening snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Drizzled on the tava to shallow-fry the rolls with little oil

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A pinch balances the goda masala with the gentle Maharashtrian sweetness

steps: Boil and mash 3 potatoes and keep ready, taking about 15 minutes for them to soften.
Heat 1 tbsp of the groundnut oil over medium heat, splutter 0.5 tsp mustard and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, then saute the onion and 2 green chillies 3 minutes.
Add the mashed potato with 1.5 tsp goda masala, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp salt, cook 4 minutes, then fold in 3 tbsp coconut and 3 tbsp coriander and cool.
Trim and dampen 8 bread slices, squeeze dry, place 2 tbsp filling on each and roll into tight sealed logs.
Heat a tava on medium and drizzle 2 tbsp oil, then set the rolls seam-side down to hold their shape.
Shallow-fry turning every couple of minutes, adding oil as needed, for 6-7 minutes until crisp and evenly browned.
tips: Cook the goda masala a full minute with the potato so its roasted spices lose any raw edge.
Grate fresh coconut for moisture; desiccated will dry out the filling on the tava.
Keep the jaggery to just a teaspoon so the roll stays savoury with a hint of sweet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with dry garlic chutney and hot cutting chai for a true Maharashtrian tea-time plate.

variations.name: Bengali Tava Bread Roll
variations.description: A tava-fried Bengali roll where the potato is tempered in sharp mustard oil with panch phoron and roasted bhaja masala, shallow-crisped for a lighter aloor-chop flavour. Pungent and warming with a golden skin. Lovely alongside evening cha.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Its sharp pungency flavours the filling and crisps the rolls on the tava

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its slurry seals the rolls so they hold on the open griddle

steps: Boil and mash 3 potatoes and keep aside, allowing about 15 minutes to cook them soft.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil to smoking, cool slightly, then crackle 1 tsp panch phoron 20 seconds and add the ginger and 2 green chillies.
Add the onion, fry 3 minutes, then stir in the mashed potato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli, 1 tsp bhaja masala and 1 tsp salt, cook 4 minutes and fold in 3 tbsp coriander.
Cool the filling, trim and dampen 8 bread slices, squeeze dry, roll 2 tbsp filling into each and seal the seam with a little Anveshan Khapli Atta slurry.
Heat a tava on medium and drizzle 2 tbsp mustard oil, then place the rolls seam-side down.
Shallow-fry, turning every couple of minutes and adding oil as needed, for 6-7 minutes until crisp and browned.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to smoking then cool before tempering to soften its raw pungency.
Let the panch phoron only splutter briefly, as burnt fenugreek turns the filling bitter.
Dust the crisp rolls with extra bhaja masala for a stronger roasted aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with kasundi mustard and a quick beetroot-onion salad, Bengali telebhaja style.

variations.name: Gujarati Tava Bread Roll
variations.description: A tava-crisped Gujarati roll with a sweet-savoury potato filling lifted by jaggery, lemon and a sesame-mustard tempering. Light on oil yet full of the khatta-meetha charm of Gujarat. A dainty farsan-style snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The Gujarati kitchen staple, drizzled to shallow-fry the rolls light

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Brings the signature Gujarati sweetness to balance the lemon and chilli

steps: Boil and mash 3 potatoes and keep ready, taking about 15 minutes for them to soften.
Heat 1 tbsp of the groundnut oil over medium heat, splutter 0.5 tsp mustard, 0.5 tsp cumin and 1 tsp sesame seeds, then add 1.5 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and fry 1 minute.
Add the mashed potato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp salt, cook 4 minutes, then mix in 1 tbsp lemon juice and 3 tbsp coriander and cool.
Trim and dampen 8 bread slices, squeeze dry, place 2 tbsp filling on each and roll into firm sealed logs.
Heat a tava on medium and drizzle 2 tbsp oil, then set the rolls seam-side down to seal.
Shallow-fry, turning every couple of minutes and adding oil as needed, for 6-7 minutes until crisp and gold.
tips: Taste after the jaggery and lemon to strike the sweet-sour balance you prefer.
Toast the sesame just until it pops for a nutty aroma without bitterness.
Make the filling slightly stiff so it rolls neatly and does not spread on the tava.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sweet date-tamarind chutney and a sprinkle of fine sev, Gujarati farsan style.

variations.name: Goan Tava Bread Roll
variations.description: A coastal Goan roll fried in coconut oil, the potato brightened with tangy kokum and a coconut-onion masala for a tropical sweet-sour lilt. Shallow-crisped and fragrant with the sea breeze of Goa. A breezy tea-time bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: The everyday Goan fat, lending its aroma as the rolls crisp on the tava

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Rounds the sour kokum into the Goan sweet-sour balance

steps: Soak 4 kokum petals in 3 tbsp warm water 10 minutes, then chop them fine and reserve the tangy soaking water.
Boil and mash 3 potatoes and keep ready, taking about 15 minutes to cook them soft.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil over medium heat, splutter 0.5 tsp mustard and 0.5 tsp cumin, then saute the onion and 2 green chillies 3 minutes.

Add the mashed potato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli, the chopped kokum with its water, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp salt, cook 4 minutes, then fold in 3 tbsp coconut and 3 tbsp coriander.
Cool the filling, trim and dampen 8 bread slices, squeeze dry, roll 2 tbsp filling into each into tight sealed logs.
Heat a tava on medium, drizzle 2 tbsp coconut oil, set the rolls seam-side down and shallow-fry 6-7 minutes, turning and adding oil, until crisp and golden.
tips: Use the kokum soaking water for the tang; do not add raw kokum which can taste harsh.
Balance the sourness with the jaggery a little at a time until the sweet-sour feels right.
Keep coconut oil hot and steady, as it firms up quickly when the tava cools.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a fresh coconut-green chilli chutney and a wedge of lime, Goan seaside style.

variations.name: Classic Tava Moong Dal Pakora
variations.description: A lighter moong dal pakora shaped into flat patties and shallow-fried on a tava with just a little oil, so they crisp golden without deep-frying. Soft and savoury within, crunchy at the edges. A wholesome, low-oil take on the monsoon fritter.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Just a few spoons on the tava to shallow-fry the patties crisp

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Mixed into the batter for a richer flavour and crisper edge

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup split green gram 3 hours until swollen, then drain it very well.
Grind the dal to a thick, coarse paste with the 2 green chillies and 1 tbsp ginger, using almost no water so it holds a shape.
Mix in the onion, 3 tbsp coriander, 1 tsp cumin, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli, 3 tbsp rice flour, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 1 tsp salt into a firm, scoopable batter.
Heat a flat tava over medium heat and drizzle 2 tbsp of the groundnut oil across the surface.
Drop heaped spoonfuls and flatten each into a 1 cm thick patty, cooking 3-4 minutes until the underside is golden and crisp.
Flip, drizzle a little more oil around the edges and cook 3 minutes more until both sides are crisp and cooked through.
tips: Keep the batter thick and drain the dal well, or the patties will not hold on the tava.
The extra rice flour helps bind the patties and gives a crisper edge than deep-fried pakoras.
Press the patties thin and even so the dal cooks through before the outside over-browns.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with green chutney and ketchup, stacked warm with a side of sliced onion.

variations.name: Bengali Tava Moong Dal Pakora
variations.description: A tava-crisped Bengali dal patty tempered with nigella and green chilli and cooked in pungent mustard oil, echoing the flavour of dal bora with far less oil. Sharp, aromatic and golden-edged. A lighter telebhaja for everyday tea.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Its pungency gives the patties their Bengali character on the tava

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Mixed into the batter to lighten and crisp the patties

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup split green gram 3 hours, then drain very well and grind thick with the 3 green chillies and 1 tbsp ginger using almost no water.
Mix in 0.5 tsp nigella seeds, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp bhaja masala, 3 tbsp rice flour, 3 tbsp coriander, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 1 tsp salt into a firm batter.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil on a tava over medium heat until it just smokes, then lower the heat.
Drop heaped spoonfuls and flatten each into a 1 cm patty, cooking 3-4 minutes until the underside is crisp and golden.
Flip, drizzle a little more mustard oil around the edges, and cook 3 minutes more until both sides are crisp.
Lift onto paper and dust with a little extra bhaja masala while hot.
tips: Heat the mustard oil until it just smokes so its raw pungency mellows before cooking.
Add nigella whole for the signature Bengali aroma rather than grinding it in.
Keep the batter stiff so the patties stay neat on the open tava.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with kasundi mustard and puffed muri, a lighter take on Bengali monsoon snacking.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Tava Moong Dal Pakora
variations.description: A tava-cooked moong dal patty carrying the dark, roasted goda masala of Maharashtra with coconut and a touch of jaggery, shallow-fried for a lighter finish. Earthy, fragrant and gently sweet-savoury. A wholesome tea-time bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Drizzled on the tava to shallow-fry the patties with little oil

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A pinch balances the goda masala with the gentle Maharashtrian sweetness

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup split green gram 3 hours, then drain very well and grind thick with the 2 green chillies using almost no water.
Mix in 1.5 tsp goda masala, the onion, 3 tbsp coconut, 1 tsp cumin, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 3 tbsp rice flour, 3 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp salt into a firm batter.
Heat a tava over medium heat and drizzle 2 tbsp of the groundnut oil across it.
Drop heaped spoonfuls, flatten each into a 1 cm patty, and cook 3-4 minutes until the underside is crisp and the goda masala smells fragrant.
Flip, drizzle a little more oil at the edges, and cook 3 minutes more until both sides are golden.
Lift the patties onto paper and serve hot while the goda masala aroma is still fragrant.
tips: Cook the patties fully so the raw goda masala mellows into its deep roasted flavour.
Use fresh coconut for moisture; desiccated will dry the patties on the tava.
Keep the jaggery to a teaspoon so the patties stay savoury with just a hint of sweet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with dry garlic-peanut chutney and hot cutting chai, Maharashtrian style.

variations.name: Andhra Tava Moong Dal Pakora
variations.description: A fiery tava-cooked dal patty loaded with Guntur red chilli, garlic and crackling curry leaves, shallow-fried for a lighter yet blistering southern bite. The heat is bold and upfront. A pakora with real Andhra fire and less oil.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Drizzled on the tava to crisp the patties and tame the raw chilli

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Mixed in to round the fierce Guntur chilli and enrich the patties

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup split green gram 3 hours, then drain very well and grind thick with the 2 green chillies using almost no water.

Mix in 2 tsp Guntur chilli, 6 crushed garlic cloves, 14 chopped curry leaves, the onion, 1 tsp cumin, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 3 tbsp rice flour, 3 tbsp coriander, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 1 tsp salt into a firm batter.
Heat a tava over medium heat and drizzle 2 tbsp of the groundnut oil across it.
Drop heaped spoonfuls, flatten each into a 1 cm patty, and cook 3-4 minutes until the underside is crisp with the curry leaves toasted.
Flip, drizzle a little more oil at the edges, and cook 3 minutes more until both sides are deep golden.
Lift onto paper and sprinkle with a little salt while hot.
tips: Guntur chilli is intense, so start with 2 tsp and let the ghee soften the heat.
Crush the garlic rather than mincing it, so it flavours the patties in fragrant bits.
Cook patties fully on medium heat so the dal sets before the outside chars.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with cooling coconut chutney and thick curd to balance the Guntur heat.

variations.name: Kerala Tava Moong Dal Pakora
variations.description: A Malabar-style dal patty tava-cooked in fragrant coconut oil with curry leaves, coconut and black pepper for a coastal, gently sweet crunch. Nutty and aromatic with a golden crust and less oil. A lighter parippu vada cousin.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Its coconut aroma defines Kerala cooking and crisps the patties on the tava

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Mixed in for richness and a crisper crust

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup split green gram 3 hours, then drain very well and grind thick with the 2 green chillies and 1 tbsp ginger using almost no water.

Mix in 3 tbsp coconut, 14 chopped curry leaves, 1 tsp crushed pepper, 5 chopped shallots, 3 tbsp rice flour, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 3 tbsp coriander, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 1 tsp salt into a firm batter.
Heat a tava over medium heat and drizzle 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil across it.
Drop heaped spoonfuls, flatten each into a 1 cm patty, and cook 3-4 minutes until the underside is crisp and the coconut toasted.
Flip, drizzle a little more coconut oil at the edges, and cook 3 minutes more until both sides are golden.
Lift onto paper and serve hot and crunchy.
tips: Use fresh coconut so it toasts to a sweet crunch rather than drying out.
Shallots give a sweeter, more authentic Kerala base than regular onion.
Keep the coconut oil warm and topped up, as it firms quickly when the tava cools.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut-curry leaf chutney and strong Kerala chai for a chaya-kada evening.

variations.name: Classic Tava Onion Bhaji
variations.description: A lighter, pan-fried take on the deep-fried classic: the same spiced onion-besan mixture is shaped into flat tikkis and shallow-fried on a hot tava with just a slick of oil. You lose none of the crisp edges but use a fraction of the fat, making it an everyday-friendly bhaji.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Just enough drizzled around each tikki on the tava for a shallow-fried crisp base.

steps: Slice 3 large onions thinly, salt with 1 tsp salt and rest 10 minutes until softened and moist.

Add 1.25 cups besan, 2 tbsp rice flour, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp cumin, 0.5 tsp ajwain, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 3 tbsp coriander, mixing with just 2 tbsp water to a thick, mouldable mixture.
Heat a flat tava over medium heat and drizzle on 1 tsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil per tikki.
Place golf-ball portions on the tava and press each into a flat 1-cm-thick round with the back of a spoon.
Cook for 3-4 minutes per side, drizzling a little more oil around the edges, until deep golden and crisp on both faces.
Press the edges down as they cook so they crisp evenly, then lift off and serve hot.
tips: Keep the mixture thick enough to hold a shape; if it slumps, add a spoon more besan.
A cast-iron tava gives the best crust; let it heat fully before the first tikki goes on.
These reheat well on the tava, so make extra and crisp them up again the next day.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with green chutney and a cup of chai, or tuck a tikki into a soft pav with sliced onion for a quick bhaji-pav.

variations.name: Punjabi Tava Onion Bhaji
variations.description: A hearty Punjabi griddle version cooked in nutty Anveshan Ghee, with ginger, kasuri methi and garam masala worked through the onion mixture. The ghee gives the tikkis a rich golden crust and a dhaba-style aroma that shallow oil simply cannot match.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: Used to shallow-fry the tikkis on the tava for a rich, dhaba-style golden crust and aroma.

steps: Slice 3 large onions thinly, salt with 1 tsp salt and rest 10 minutes until they wilt.

Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi between your palms and add it with 0.75 tsp garam masala, a grated 1-inch piece of ginger, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 3 tbsp coriander.
Mix in 1.25 cups besan with just 2 tbsp water to a thick, shapeable mixture.
Heat a tava over medium heat and add 1 tsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee per tikki, letting it melt and shimmer.
Place flattened rounds on the tava and cook 3-4 minutes per side, adding a little more ghee around the edges, until deep golden and crisp.
Baste the tops with a final brush of ghee just before flipping the last time for extra richness.
tips: Don't let the ghee smoke; keep the tava at medium so the tikkis crisp slowly and evenly.
Crushing the kasuri methi first releases its aroma and prevents a stalky texture.
A pinch of amchur in the mix cuts the richness of the ghee nicely.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with mint chutney, pickled onions and a dollop of white butter for a proper Punjabi griddle snack.

variations.name: Bengali Tava Onion Bhaji
variations.description: A pan-fried peyaji cooked in pungent Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil with nigella seeds and green chilli, giving flat, crisp tikkis with that sharp Bengali mustard bite. Using the tava keeps them lighter than the deep-fried original while preserving the signature aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Drizzled onto the tava around each tikki for the sharp, authentic peyaji flavour.

steps: Slice 3 large onions thinly, salt with 1 tsp salt and rest 10 minutes until juicy.
Add 1 tsp nigella seeds, 3 chopped green chillies, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tbsp coriander, then mix in 1.25 cups besan and 2 tbsp rice flour with just 2 tbsp water.
Heat a tava over medium heat, drizzle on 1 tsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil per tikki and let it heat until it just smokes lightly.
Place spoonfuls on the tava and flatten to 1-cm rounds, cooking 3-4 minutes per side while adding a little more mustard oil at the edges.
Cook until deep golden and crisp, pressing down so the frilled edges brown evenly.
Lift off and serve hot; the tikkis will carry the unmistakable sharp mustard-oil aroma.
tips: Let the mustard oil heat until it shimmers and just wisps smoke before adding tikkis, to mellow its raw bite.
Nigella seeds are the classic peyaji spice, so don't substitute them with cumin here.
Keep the tikkis thin; a thinner peyaji crisps better on the tava than a thick one.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with muri (puffed rice) and a green chilli on the side, or as a crisp partner to a bowl of dal-bhaat.

variations.name: Rajasthani Tava Onion Bhaji
variations.description: A rustic desert-style tikki fired up with whole dried red chillies pounded coarse, plus ajwain and a hint of dried mango for that Rajasthani tang. Shallow-fried on the tava, these are robust, deeply red and built to eat with bajra roti and buttermilk.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Drizzled generously on the tava for a robust, crisp desert-style tikki.

steps: Dry-roast 4 whole dried red chillies in a hot pan for 30 seconds until they darken and smell smoky, then pound them coarse with 4 garlic cloves.
Slice 3 large onions thinly, salt with 1 tsp salt and rest 10 minutes, then add the chilli-garlic pound.
Mix in 0.75 tsp ajwain, 1 tsp amchur, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 3 tbsp coriander, then 1.25 cups besan with just 2 tbsp water to a thick mixture.
Heat a tava over medium heat and drizzle on 1.5 tsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil per tikki.
Flatten spoonfuls into thick rounds and cook 4 minutes per side, adding oil at the edges, until dark red and crisp.
Press the tikkis firmly so they brown right through, then lift off and serve hot.
tips: Roasting the dried chillies before pounding deepens their smoky flavour and softens harsh heat.
Amchur gives the Rajasthani sour note; lemon juice works if you don't have it, added to the mix.
Make these slightly thicker than usual so they stay hearty alongside a bajra roti.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with cool buttermilk (chaas), a smear of garlic chutney and hot bajra roti for a desert-thali feel.

variations.name: Kerala Tava Onion Bhaji
variations.description: A South Indian griddle tikki studded with fresh coconut, curry leaves and a whisper of black pepper, shallow-fried in fragrant Anveshan Coconut Oil. The coconut keeps the inside moist while the tava gives a crisp, golden shell with a distinctly Malabar aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Drizzled on the tava to shallow-fry the tikkis and layer in the signature Kerala coconut aroma.

steps: Slice 3 large onions thinly, salt with 1 tsp salt and rest 10 minutes; coarsely crush 0.75 tsp peppercorns.
Add 0.5 cup fresh grated coconut, 15 chopped curry leaves, 3 chopped green chillies, a grated 1-inch piece of ginger, the crushed pepper and 0.5 tsp turmeric to the onions.
Mix in 1.25 cups besan and 2 tbsp rice flour with just 2 tbsp water to a thick, shapeable mixture.
Heat a tava over medium heat and drizzle on 1 tsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil per tikki.
Flatten spoonfuls into 1-cm rounds and cook 3-4 minutes per side, adding coconut oil at the edges, until golden and crisp.
Press gently so the coconut-flecked edges brown, then lift off and serve while fragrant and hot.
tips: Use fresh coconut for moisture; desiccated will make the tikkis dry and crumbly.
Coconut oil sets on cooling, so serve straight off the tava for the best texture.
Toast a few extra curry leaves on the tava and crumble over the tikkis for more aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and a cup of filter coffee, Kerala tea-shop style.

variations.name: Classic Tinda
variations.description: A gentle North Indian apple-gourd sabzi where tender tinda pieces are simmered in a light onion-tomato masala until they turn soft and juicy. Mild and homely, it lets the vegetable's delicate flavour shine, seasoned simply with cumin, coriander and a touch of amchur.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: its pungency lifts the mild apple gourd the traditional way

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: swirled in at the finish to round the mild gourd with a nutty aroma

steps: Peel 500 g apple gourd, cut into quarters, and remove any hard seeds from mature pieces.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the flame, and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds.
Add 2 chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, frying for 5 minutes until golden.
Stir in 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, cooking 4 minutes until pulpy.
Add the tinda with 1 tsp salt and half a cup of water, cover, and simmer on low for 12 minutes until soft and the water dries up.
Finish with 1 tsp amchur and a drizzle of 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee, tossing gently off the heat.
tips: Choose small, light-green tinda; larger ones develop hard seeds and a spongy centre.
Peel thoroughly as the skin can be slightly tough and bitter on older gourds.
Do not add too much water; tinda releases its own moisture as it cooks.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulkas and a bowl of dal, or with plain rice and a spoon of ghee for a light meal.

variations.name: Masala Tinda
variations.description: A heartier Bihari take where the apple gourd is cooked into a thicker onion-tomato masala rounded with garam masala. The tinda soaks up the deeper spicing while staying juicy, giving a fuller, more robust sabzi than the delicate everyday version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the defining pungent oil of Bihari home cooking

steps: Peel and quarter 500 g apple gourd, deseeding any mature pieces.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, then crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds with 1 bay leaf.
Add 3 chopped onions and 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, frying for 7 minutes until browned.
Stir in 3 pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.25 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder, cooking 6 minutes until the oil separates.
Add the tinda with 1 tsp salt and half a cup of water, cover, and simmer on low for 12 minutes until soft and coated in thick masala.
Sprinkle 1 tsp garam masala and 2 tbsp chopped coriander, stir for a minute, and serve.
tips: Bhuno the masala until the oil separates before adding the gourd for a deep, non-raw flavour.
Mash a few cooked tinda pieces against the pan to naturally thicken the masala.
Let it rest a few minutes off the heat so the gourd absorbs the spicing fully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain parathas or steamed rice, with a side of raw onion rings and green chilli.

variations.name: Spicy Pepper Tinda
variations.description: A dry, coastal-style stir-fry where apple gourd meets slit green chillies, coarse black pepper and a garlicky, curry-leaf tempering. Kept without gravy, the tinda catches the heat and browns lightly, turning a mild vegetable into a bracing, peppery side.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the Goan coastal fat that suits the peppery, curry-leaf tempering

steps: Peel 500 g apple gourd and cut into thin wedges so they cook fast in a dry fry.
Coarsely crush 1.25 tsp black pepper with 6 garlic cloves into a rough paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 12 curry leaves and 4 slit green chillies.
Stir in the crushed pepper-garlic and cook a minute, then add the tinda wedges with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt.
Cover and cook on low for 8 minutes until the gourd softens, then uncover and stir-fry on medium-high for 5 minutes until dry and lightly browned.
Fold in 2 tbsp grated coconut off the heat and toss until evenly coated.
tips: Cut the tinda into thin wedges so it cooks through with little water and can brown.
Crush the pepper coarsely for sharp bursts of heat throughout the dish.
Uncover and raise the heat at the end to dry off moisture and get light caramelisation.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a bowl of dal, or as a spicy dry side to a fish curry meal.

variations.name: Dhaba-style Tinda
variations.description: A rich, semi-dry apple gourd in a thick onion-tomato masala scented with kasuri methi and garam masala. Deeply browned onions and a splash of cream turn the humble tinda into a hearty, roadside-style dish where the mild gourd carries a bold, savoury coating.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the pungent base fat that anchors the bold dhaba masala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a small swap for sugar to round the tomato tang in the dhaba gravy

steps: Peel and quarter 500 g apple gourd, deseeding mature pieces.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, then fry 3 chopped onions with 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 8 minutes until deeply caramelised.
Add 2 pureed tomatoes with 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, cooking 7 minutes until thick and glossy.
Add the tinda with 1 tsp salt, 0.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and half a cup of water, cover, and simmer on low for 12 minutes until tender.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the top with 0.75 tsp garam masala and stir for a minute until fragrant.
Swirl in 2 tbsp cream and cook a final minute until the masala is rich and clinging.
tips: Caramelise the onions deeply for the signature dhaba richness.
Keep the masala thick and coating so it clings to the mild gourd.
Warm the kasuri methi briefly before crushing to draw out its full aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or laccha paratha and a raw onion-lemon salad on the side.

variations.name: Bharwa Tinda
