tips: Always let mustard oil heat until it just shimmers before pouring batter, which mellows its raw bite into a nutty warmth.
Grate the vegetables finely so they cook through in the short griddling time and don't tear the thin cheela.
Make the batter an hour ahead and refrigerate; the masalas bloom and the flavour deepens noticeably.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve wedges alongside a garlicky tomato-chilli chokha and a mug of sweet-salt lassi for a filling plateau-style brunch.

variations.name: Punjabi Spicy Besan Cheela
variations.description: A fiery Punjabi-style cheela built for people who like heat first thing in the morning, with pounded green chillies and cracked black pepper running right through the batter. Cooked in Anveshan Groundnut Oil and enriched with a spoon of thick curd, it stays soft inside with crackly, blistered edges.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Clean wood-pressed groundnut oil that fries the peppery edges crisp without masking the heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: A nutty wholegrain addition that gives the spicy cheela structure and a satisfying chew.

steps: Pound 4 green chillies and a 1-inch piece of ginger to a coarse paste, and crush 1 tsp black peppercorns roughly in a mortar.

Whisk 2 cups gram flour with 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp ajwain and 1 tsp salt, then beat in 2 tbsp thick curd and about 1.75 cups water to a smooth thin batter.
Stir the chilli-ginger paste, crushed pepper and 3 tbsp coriander leaves through the batter and rest it for 10 minutes.
Heat a tava over medium-high and grease with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil until it just begins to shimmer.
Pour a ladleful and spread thin into a 7-inch round, drizzle 0.5 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil around the edge, and cook for about 2 minutes until the base blisters golden.
Flip and cook the second side for 1-2 minutes until crisp-edged and speckled, then continue with the rest of the batter.
tips: The spoon of curd keeps this fiery cheela tender inside so the heat doesn't come with a dry, cardboardy texture.
For a sharper, cleaner heat, crush the peppercorns fresh rather than reaching for pre-ground pepper.
Tame the burn for children by halving the green chillies and deseeding them while keeping the pepper for aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a cooling mint-cucumber raita and slices of ripe tomato to balance the heat, plus a glass of salted chaas.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Cheesy Besan Cheela
variations.description: A playful Pune-style cheela topped the moment it hits the tava with grated cheese, sweetcorn and spring onion so it melts into a golden, gooey blanket. The batter carries a gentle goda-masala warmth and is cooked in Anveshan Groundnut Oil for a crisp base that holds the molten topping.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Griddles the cheela base to a firm, golden crisp that supports the melting cheese topping.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Adds a wholegrain sturdiness so the loaded, cheesy cheela lifts cleanly off the tava.

steps: Beat 2 cups gram flour with 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.75 tsp goda masala, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, 0.75 tsp roasted cumin powder and 0.75 tsp salt, then add about 1.75 cups water and whisk to a smooth thin batter.
Rest the batter for 10 minutes while you grate 0.75 cup cheese and chop 3 tbsp spring onion greens.
Heat a tava over medium heat and grease with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil until a test drop of batter sets in a few seconds.
Ladle on the batter and spread into a thin 7-inch round, then immediately scatter 0.5 cup sweetcorn, the grated cheese and spring onion evenly over the wet top.
Drizzle 0.5 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil around the edge and cook covered for 3 minutes until the base is golden and the cheese has fully melted and turned glossy.
Fold in half or slide out flat, then repeat with the remaining batter and toppings.
tips: Cover the pan for the last two minutes so the cheese melts by trapped steam without the base burning.
Press the corn and cheese gently into the wet batter so they anchor and don't slide off when you fold.
A mix of processed cheese for stretch and a little mozzarella for pull gives the best gooey finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Cut into wedges and serve with a tangy tomato-garlic thecha or ketchup, ideal as an after-school snack.

variations.name: Gujarati Methi Besan Cheela
variations.description: A Kathiawadi-inspired cheela where fresh fenugreek leaves and a whisper of jaggery bring the signature Gujarati sweet-savoury balance to the gram-flour batter. Cooked in Anveshan Groundnut Oil, it is soft, herby and faintly caramelised at the edges, wonderful with a smear of white butter.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The classic Gujarati cooking fat, wood-pressed here for a clean nutty note in the herby cheela.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A spoon of chemical-free jaggery for the gentle sweet-savoury lift typical of Kathiawadi cooking.

steps: Whisk 2 cups gram flour with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp salt, then pour in about 1.75 cups water and beat to a smooth thin pouring batter.
Wash and finely chop 1 cup fresh methi leaves, then fold them into the batter with 2 chopped green chillies, a grated 1-inch piece of ginger and 1 tbsp sesame seeds.
Rest the batter for 10 minutes so the jaggery dissolves fully and the methi softens.
Set a tava over medium heat and grease with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil until it shimmers lightly.
Pour a ladle of batter and spread into a thin 7-inch round, drizzle 0.5 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil around the edges, and cook for about 2 minutes until the base is golden with caramelised spots.
Flip and cook for a further 1-2 minutes until cooked through, then repeat with the remaining batter.
tips: If fresh methi tastes too bitter, toss the chopped leaves with a pinch of salt, rest 10 minutes and squeeze out the dark juices before use.
Keep the jaggery to just two teaspoons; it should round the edges of the flavour, not make the cheela sweet.
Kasuri methi (2 tbsp, crushed) works well out of season, added straight to the batter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a knob of white butter melting on top and a side of sweet mango chhundo pickle.

variations.name: Classic Besan Ladoo
variations.description: The definitive slow-roasted gram-flour sweet, where besan is patiently cooked in ghee until it turns deep gold and gives off a nutty, almost caramel aroma. Melt-in-the-mouth and grainy in the best way, sweetened with unrefined jaggery rather than white sugar. This is the ladoo that appears on every Diwali and festival thali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The bilona ghee is what carries heat gently into the besan, giving that unmistakable roasted-gram fragrance.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Fine jaggery powder dissolves evenly into cooled besan without the graininess of chopped gud.

steps: Melt 3/4 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai on low heat, then add 2 cups besan and stir continuously so the flour toasts evenly in the fat.
Keep the flame low and roast for 18 to 20 minutes; the besan will first go thick and clumpy, then loosen into a glossy, flowing paste as the ghee separates and it smells deeply nutty.
Switch off the heat and let the roasted besan cool for 10 minutes until just warm to the touch, so the jaggery will not melt into a sticky syrup.
Stir in 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp green cardamom powder, mixing well for a minute until the mixture is uniform and holds shape when pressed in your fist.
Fold in 2 tbsp chopped almonds, 2 tbsp cashews and 1 tbsp melon seeds, then roll into 12 walnut-sized ladoos, pressing each firmly so it does not crack.
Rest the shaped ladoos on a plate for 30 minutes to firm up before storing in an airtight jar.
tips: Roast strictly on the lowest flame; rushing on high heat browns the surface while leaving a raw, bitter core even when the colour looks right.
Add the jaggery only after the besan cools to warm; mixing it into hot besan releases moisture and turns the ladoos hard and dense.
If the mixture feels too dry to bind, drizzle in 1 tbsp extra warm melted ghee; if it is too soft to roll, chill for 10 minutes first.
variations.servingSuggestion: Press a single saffron strand onto each ladoo and arrange on a brass thali for gifting; they pair beautifully with hot masala chai or a glass of cold milk.

variations.name: Rajasthani Gond Besan Ladoo
variations.description: A winter-strength Marwari version fortified with fried edible gum (gond), which puffs into airy, crunchy nuggets and gives the ladoo its characteristic warming quality. Coarse besan and extra ghee make it richer and more rustic than the everyday sweet. Traditionally made for new mothers and cold Rajasthan mornings.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: You need the extra ghee here to both fry the gum and roast the coarse besan to a crumbly texture.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Its deep mineral sweetness stands up to the earthy gond far better than plain sugar.

steps: Heat 2 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium heat and fry 1/4 cup edible gum in small batches for about 30 seconds each, until each piece puffs up white and light; lift out and cool.
Crush the fried gond coarsely with a rolling pin so you have crunchy pea-sized bits, and set aside.
In the same kadhai add the remaining ghee and 2 cups coarse besan, and roast on low heat for 20 to 22 minutes, stirring throughout, until it is sandy, golden and smells strongly of toasted gram.
Take the pan off the heat and let it cool for 12 minutes to just warm, then mix in 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 tsp cardamom powder and 1/2 tsp dry ginger powder.
Add the crushed gond, 3 tbsp chopped almonds and 2 tbsp melon seeds, folding until the mixture clumps together when squeezed.
Shape into 12 firm ladoos while warm and leave to set for 40 minutes; the gond crunch sharpens as they cool.
tips: Fry the gond on medium, never high, heat; too hot and the outside browns before the inside puffs, leaving a hard, chewy centre.
Coarse laddu besan is essential for this style; fine besan turns pasty and loses the crumbly bite that defines the Marwari version.
These keep for up to three weeks and actually taste better after a day as the sonth and cardamom mellow into the ghee.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve one warmed slightly with a glass of hot turmeric milk on cold evenings; the gond makes it a genuinely restorative winter treat.

variations.name: Gujarati Magaj Ladoo
variations.description: The Gujarati magaj uses granular ladva besan for a distinctly coarse, sandy crumb quite unlike the smooth classic, and is perfumed with freshly grated nutmeg alongside cardamom. Charoli seeds add a soft nutty bite throughout. A festive favourite made in large batches for weddings and Diwali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee coats each coarse grain so the magaj stays crumbly and never cakes into a solid block.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Chosen over powdered sugar so the magaj keeps its warm caramel colour and rounded sweetness.

steps: Rub 3 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee into 2 cups coarse ladva besan with your fingertips and rest for 10 minutes; this loose-crumb step is what gives magaj its signature grainy texture.
Warm the remaining ghee in a kadhai on low heat, add the rubbed besan and roast gently for 20 minutes, stirring, until it turns reddish-gold and releases a rich toasted aroma.
Remove from heat and cool for 10 minutes until warm, keeping the crumbly grains loose rather than pasty.
Mix in 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 tsp cardamom powder and 1/2 tsp freshly grated nutmeg until evenly combined and the mixture just holds together.
Scatter in 2 tbsp charoli seeds and 2 tbsp slivered pistachios and fold through, then press into 12 ladoos or spread in a greased tray to cut into diamonds.
Let them set for 30 minutes so the coarse grains firm around the ghee before serving.
tips: Freshly grated nutmeg is worth the effort here; the pre-ground kind is flat and misses the warm high note that defines authentic magaj.
Do not over-blend after adding jaggery or you crush the coarse grains and lose the sandy texture that separates magaj from ordinary besan ladoo.
If cutting into diamonds, press the mixture firmly and evenly into the tray while warm so the pieces do not crumble at the edges.
variations.servingSuggestion: Cut into small diamonds and layer in a steel dabba lined with butter paper; excellent after a Gujarati thali with a cardamom-spiced buttermilk.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Besan-Rava Ladoo
variations.description: A popular Maharashtrian hybrid where fine semolina is roasted alongside the besan, lending a pleasant grainy chew that plain besan ladoos lack. Poppy seeds toasted in ghee add a subtle nuttiness and a delicate speckle. Common at Ganesh Chaturthi and everyday festive occasions.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The ghee toasts both the rava and besan and binds the two different textures into one ladoo.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Balances the semolina's mild flavour with a molasses depth that white sugar cannot give.

steps: Dry-roast 2 tbsp poppy seeds in a kadhai on low heat for 2 minutes until they turn a shade darker and smell toasty, then set aside.
Add 1/4 cup of the Anveshan Ghee and roast 1/2 cup fine semolina on low heat for 8 minutes until it is pale gold and fragrant, then tip it onto a plate.
In the same pan warm the remaining ghee and roast 1.5 cups besan on low heat for 15 to 18 minutes, stirring, until it loosens and smells nutty, then mix the roasted rava back in.
Cool the mixture for 10 minutes to just warm, then stir in 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp cardamom powder until it comes together.
Fold in the toasted poppy seeds and 3 tbsp chopped cashews, then roll into 12 ladoos, pressing firmly so the grainy mixture binds.
Set aside for 30 minutes to firm; the semolina absorbs the ghee and the ladoos hold their shape cleanly.
tips: Roast the rava separately and first; it needs a gentler, shorter toast than besan and burns quickly if left in a hotter pan.
Let the rava swell for the full resting time before rolling, otherwise the ladoos can feel slightly hard and dry the next day.
A pinch of the toasted poppy seeds pressed on the outside makes the ladoos look and taste more special for festivals.
variations.servingSuggestion: Offer as naivedya at a Ganpati aarti and then share warm; the rava chew makes them especially good alongside strong filter coffee.

variations.name: Andhra Peanut Besan Ladoo
variations.description: An Andhra-leaning take that folds coarsely crushed roasted peanuts into the roasted besan, giving an earthy, groundnut-forward flavour typical of the region's love for verusenaga. A whisper of dry ginger keeps it warm and digestible. Rustic, protein-rich and deeply satisfying.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A spoon of wood-pressed groundnut oil deepens the peanut theme before the ghee rounds it off.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee finishes the roast and binds the crushed peanuts smoothly into the besan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery and peanuts are a classic Andhra pairing, echoing the region's beloved chikki.

steps: Pulse 3/4 cup roasted peanuts in a mixer to a coarse rubble with a few larger bits for bite, and keep aside.
Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil with 1/2 cup Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on low heat, then add 2 cups besan and roast for 18 minutes, stirring, until deep gold and aromatic.
Take off the heat and cool for 10 minutes until just warm so the jaggery does not melt.
Mix in 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 3/4 tsp cardamom powder and 1/2 tsp dry ginger powder until the mixture is even and cohesive.
Fold in the crushed peanuts, then shape into 12 sturdy ladoos, pressing firmly so the nutty rubble stays embedded.
Rest for 30 minutes before storing; the peanuts settle and the flavour turns rounder overnight.
tips: Crush the peanuts coarse, not to a paste; a fine grind releases oil that makes the ladoos greasy and slippery to roll.
Rub off the loose red peanut skins after roasting for a cleaner look and to avoid any faint bitterness.
The dry ginger is not just for flavour; it balances the heaviness of peanuts and ghee so the ladoo sits lighter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside strong South Indian filter coffee, or crumble one over a bowl of warm sweetened milk for an impromptu dessert.

variations.name: Classic Coconut Ladoo
variations.description: The quick, crowd-pleasing coconut ladoo where desiccated coconut simmers with condensed milk into a soft, milky dough in minutes. Fragrant with cardamom and rolled in more coconut for a snowy finish. The five-ingredient sweet everyone learns first and makes for every last-minute celebration.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A little ghee stops the coconut from sticking and adds a soft richness to the dough.

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a non-stick pan on low heat and lightly toast 3 tbsp chopped cashews for a minute until pale gold, then push them to one side.
Add 2 cups of the desiccated coconut (reserve 1/2 cup for coating) and stir on low heat for 2 minutes just to warm it without browning.
Pour in 1 cup condensed milk and 1 tsp cardamom powder, and cook on low heat for 5 to 6 minutes, stirring, until the mixture thickens and pulls away from the sides of the pan.
If it looks dry, splash in 2 tbsp milk; the dough should be soft and just moist enough to shape.
Take off the heat, cool for 5 minutes until handleable, then roll into 14 small ladoos and press them in the reserved coconut to coat.
Chill for 20 minutes so they firm up and hold their round shape.
tips: Do not let the coconut brown while cooking; the classic look is pale and snowy, and toasting it changes the flavour entirely.
If the mixture turns too sticky to roll, refrigerate it for 10 minutes and grease your palms with a drop of ghee.
These keep only three to four days refrigerated because of the condensed milk, so make them close to when you need them.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile in a white bowl and dust with extra coconut for a clean, festive look; lovely with cardamom tea or as a quick prasad.

variations.name: Bengali Narkel Naru
variations.description: The Bengali narkel naru, made with freshly grated coconut cooked down with date-palm or cane jaggery until sticky and deeply caramelised. Darker, chewier and more rustic than the condensed-milk kind, with an unmistakable molasses depth. A staple of Lakshmi Puja and Bengali festive tables.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery is the soul of naru, giving the deep caramel colour and molasses flavour that define it.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee greases the pan and stops the sticky jaggery-coconut mass from catching as it thickens.

steps: Grease a kadhai with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, add a bay leaf and 3 cups fresh grated coconut, and stir on low heat for 4 to 5 minutes to dry out excess moisture.
Add 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and stir continuously on low heat; it will melt, bubble and loosen the mixture into a glossy, sticky mass.
Keep cooking for 12 to 15 minutes, stirring so it does not stick, until the mixture thickens, deepens in colour and starts leaving the sides of the pan.
Discard the bay leaf, mix in 1 tsp cardamom powder, 2 tbsp raisins and the remaining ghee, and cook for another minute.
Cool for 5 to 6 minutes until warm enough to handle but still pliable, greasing your palms with ghee.
Roll firmly into 14 naru while warm, as the mixture hardens quickly once it cools; set aside to firm up.
tips: Roll the naru while the mixture is still warm; jaggery sets fast and a cooled mass crumbles and refuses to bind.
Cook long enough that the mixture visibly leaves the pan sides, or the naru will stay soft and lose shape.
Fresh coconut gives the authentic chew, but squeeze out excess water first or the mixture takes much longer to thicken.
variations.servingSuggestion: Offer as bhog during Lakshmi or Saraswati Puja, then serve at room temperature; the chewy, caramel bite pairs well with plain milk.

variations.name: Goan Coconut Jaggery Ladoo
variations.description: A Goan-style ladoo celebrating fresh coconut and jaggery with a warm hit of nutmeg, echoing the coastal love for these three flavours. A splash of wood-pressed coconut oil deepens the tropical aroma. Soft, aromatic and unmistakably from the Konkan coast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Coastal jaggery sweetness pairs naturally with fresh coconut in Goan sweets.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: A spoon of wood-pressed coconut oil amplifies the fresh coconut aroma the Konkan is known for.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee rounds the coconut oil and keeps the sticky mixture from catching.

steps: Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on low heat and toast 3 tbsp chopped cashews for a minute until golden.
Add 3 cups fresh grated coconut and stir on low heat for 4 minutes to dry it slightly without colouring.
Stir in 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook on low heat for 10 to 12 minutes, stirring often, until it melts, binds the coconut and thickens into a sticky mass that leaves the pan sides.
Mix in 1/2 tsp freshly grated nutmeg and 3/4 tsp cardamom powder and cook for another minute so the spices bloom.
Cool for 5 minutes until warm and pliable, then grease your palms and roll firmly into 14 ladoos.
Let them set for 20 minutes; the nutmeg aroma intensifies as they cool.
tips: Grate the nutmeg fresh right before using; its warm, resinous note fades quickly once ground and is central to the Goan flavour.
Shape while warm since the jaggery firms fast, and work in small batches so the mixture stays pliable.
For an extra-coastal touch, roll the finished ladoos in a little more fresh coconut before it dries out.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve slightly warm after a Goan fish-curry-rice meal; the nutmeg-coconut warmth is a gentle, fragrant way to finish.

variations.name: South Indian Roasted Coconut Ladoo
variations.description: A South Indian take where the coconut is deliberately roasted to a golden, toasty brown before being bound with jaggery, giving a nuttier, deeper flavour than the pale classic. Roasted sesame adds an extra layer of aroma. Fragrant, warm-toned and a little rustic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery complements the toasty roasted coconut with a matching caramel depth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee helps roast the coconut evenly to a golden brown without scorching.

steps: Dry-roast 2 tbsp sesame seeds in a kadhai on low heat for 2 minutes until they turn golden and start to pop, then remove.
Add 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 3 cups fresh grated coconut, and roast on low-medium heat for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring, until the coconut turns golden brown and deeply fragrant.
Lower the heat, add 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and stir for 8 minutes until it melts and binds the roasted coconut into a sticky, cohesive mass.
Mix in the toasted sesame, 3/4 tsp cardamom powder, 1/4 tsp dry ginger powder and 3 tbsp chopped cashews.
Cook for one more minute, then cool for 5 minutes until warm enough to handle.
Grease your palms and roll firmly into 14 ladoos while warm; set aside to firm up.
tips: Watch the coconut closely as it browns; the line between golden and burnt is quick and a scorched batch tastes acrid.
Toast the sesame just until it pops, since over-roasted seeds turn bitter and overpower the coconut.
The dry ginger is subtle but keeps the roasted, jaggery-rich ladoo from feeling heavy, so do not skip it.
variations.servingSuggestion: A fine offering for Krishna Jayanthi; serve alongside a small cup of strong filter coffee to echo the toasty notes.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Khoya Coconut Ladoo
variations.description: A festive Maharashtrian ladoo enriched with khoya, giving the coconut a creamy, fudgy body and a milky sweetness quite unlike the lighter versions. Saffron lends colour and a floral note for celebrations. Soft, rich and clearly special-occasion fare.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery keeps the rich khoya ladoo unrefined while adding warm depth to the milk.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee cooks the khoya smoothly and binds it with the coconut.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: A pinch bloomed in warm milk gives these festive ladoos their golden hue and aroma.

steps: Soak a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside to bloom into a golden liquid.
Melt 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on low heat and crumble in 1 cup khoya, cooking for 4 to 5 minutes until it softens and smells of warm milk.
Add 2 cups of the desiccated coconut (reserve 1/2 cup for coating) and stir on low heat for 3 minutes until well combined.
Mix in 3/4 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder, the saffron milk and 1 tsp cardamom powder, and cook for 5 to 6 minutes until the mixture thickens and leaves the pan sides.
Cool for 5 minutes until warm, then roll into 14 ladoos and press them into the reserved coconut and slivered pistachios.
Refrigerate for 20 minutes so the khoya firms and the ladoos hold cleanly.
tips: Use fresh soft khoya and cook it just until softened; overcooking makes it grainy and the ladoos dry.
Because of the dairy, keep these refrigerated and finish within four days.
Bloom the saffron in warm rather than hot milk to draw out colour and fragrance without dulling it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Present on a decorated thali for Diwali or Ganeshotsav, garnished with saffron strands and pistachio; rich enough to serve just one per guest.

variations.name: Classic Coconut Rice
variations.description: The fragrant South Indian thengai sadam, where fresh grated coconut is folded into fluffy rice with a nutty tempering of dals, cashews and curry leaves. Mild, aromatic and lightly crunchy, it is a temple and festival favourite that comes together in minutes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed coconut oil doubles down on the coconut aroma at the heart of this dish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon of ghee toasts the cashews to a rich golden crunch

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, cook with 3 cups water until each grain is separate, about 15 minutes, then spread on a plate to cool.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and fry 3 tbsp cashews until golden, about 2 minutes, then remove and set aside.
In the same pan add 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, then 1 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tsp urad dal and 1 tsp channa dal, frying 1 minute until the dals turn golden and the seeds splutter.
Add 2 dry red chillies, 2 slit green chillies, 15 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida, sizzling 30 seconds until aromatic.
Lower the heat, add 1 cup grated coconut and 1 tsp salt, and toast gently for 3 minutes until the coconut smells fragrant but stays white.
Fold in the cooled rice and fried cashews until evenly mixed, warm through for 2 minutes and serve.
tips: Toast the coconut only until fragrant; browning it makes the rice taste dry and dull.
Use freshly grated coconut for the best aroma, or thaw frozen coconut fully and pat it dry.
Keep the heat low once the coconut goes in so it does not burn or turn bitter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a spicy tomato thokku or a simple potato roast for a satisfying South Indian plate.

variations.name: Bihari Sweet Coconut Rice
variations.description: A gently sweet, festive coconut rice inspired by Bihar's love of jaggery and warm spices, closer to a mild pulao-kheer hybrid served at pujas. Cardamom, raisins and jaggery give it a dessert-like warmth while staying a savoury-sweet rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries the warm spices and gives this festive rice its glossy richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery replaces refined sugar for a mellow, mineral-rich sweetness

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, cook with 3 cups water until fluffy, about 15 minutes, then cool on a plate.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat, add 4 lightly crushed cardamom pods, 3 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon and let them sizzle 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 3 tbsp cashews and 2 tbsp raisins, frying until the cashews are golden and the raisins plump, about 1 minute.
Lower the heat, add 1 cup grated coconut and toast gently for 3 minutes until it smells sweet and nutty but stays pale.
Stir in 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.5 tsp salt and cook 1 minute until the jaggery melts and coats the coconut without hardening.
Fold in the cooled rice until evenly mixed and glossy, warm through for 2 minutes and serve warm.
tips: Add the jaggery on low heat and mix quickly, as high heat can make it seize and turn sticky.
Keep the salt low but present, since a pinch sharpens the sweetness beautifully.
This rice is traditionally offered warm, but it also packs well for festive tiffins.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as part of a puja thali alongside a tangy tomato chutney to balance the sweetness.

variations.name: Madhya Pradesh Peanut Coconut Rice
variations.description: A hearty central-Indian style that pairs coconut with the roasted peanuts and sesame beloved across Madhya Pradesh, cooked in wood-pressed groundnut oil. The result is a nutty, mildly spiced rice with satisfying crunch in every bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil deepens the peanut flavour central to this rice

steps: Cook 1.5 cups soaked basmati rice with 3 cups water until fluffy, about 15 minutes, then spread out to cool.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them splutter for 40 seconds.
Add 1 tbsp sesame seeds and 0.33 cup roasted peanuts, toasting 1 minute until the sesame pops and turns golden.
Stir in 3 slit green chillies, 12 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp turmeric, frying 30 seconds until aromatic.
Lower the heat, add 0.75 cup grated coconut and 1 tsp salt, and toast gently for 3 minutes until the coconut smells nutty.
Fold in the cooled rice, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 2 tbsp coriander until evenly mixed, warm 2 minutes and serve.
tips: Coarsely crush half the peanuts so their flavour spreads through while the rest stay whole for crunch.
The lemon juice brightens the nutty coconut, so add it off the heat to keep it fresh.
Toast the sesame just until it pops, as over-roasting turns it bitter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling cucumber raita and a crunchy papad to round out the nutty, textured rice.

variations.name: Goan Coconut Rice
variations.description: A coastal Goan version where the rice is cooked in coconut milk and finished with fresh coconut, green chilli and a whisper of black pepper. Creamy, fragrant and subtly sweet, it is the perfect mellow base for a fiery Goan curry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil ties the coconut-milk-cooked rice together in true Goan coastal style

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes and drain well so it cooks evenly in the coconut milk.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil over medium heat, add 1 bay leaf, 3 cloves and 0.5 tsp crushed peppercorns and sizzle 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 thinly sliced small onion, 2 slit green chillies, grated 1 inch ginger and 10 curry leaves, sautéing 4 minutes until the onion softens.
Add the drained rice and toast gently for 2 minutes, then pour in 1.5 cups coconut milk, 1 cup water and 1 tsp salt and bring to a gentle boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes until the liquid is absorbed and each grain is tender and separate.
Fold in 0.5 cup grated coconut, rest covered 5 minutes, then fluff gently with a fork and serve.
tips: Use a 1:1.5 rice-to-liquid ratio counting coconut milk plus water, since coconut milk cooks a touch heavier.
Cook on the lowest possible heat so the coconut milk does not scorch at the bottom.
Let it rest covered off the heat before fluffing to keep the grains intact.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside a spicy Goan prawn or vegetable curry, letting the creamy rice soak up the tangy gravy.

variations.name: Uttar Pradesh Awadhi Coconut Pulao
variations.description: An Awadhi-inspired coconut pulao where basmati is layered with fried onions, whole garam spices and toasted coconut for a fragrant, mildly rich rice. It carries the delicate dum-cooked aroma the region is famous for, without heavy gravy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee gives this pulao the rich Awadhi aroma associated with royal kitchens

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain thoroughly so the grains stay long and separate.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat and fry 2 thinly sliced onions for 8 minutes until deep golden and crisp, then remove half for garnish.
To the remaining onions add 4 cardamom pods, 4 cloves, 1 inch cinnamon and 1 bay leaf, sizzling 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 tbsp ginger garlic paste and 2 slit green chillies, frying 1 minute, then add 0.75 cup grated coconut and toast 3 minutes until lightly golden.
Add the drained rice and 1.25 tsp salt, toast gently 2 minutes, then pour in 2.5 cups hot water and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes, then scatter 2 tbsp mint and the reserved fried onions, rest 5 minutes and fluff before serving.
tips: Fry the onions slowly to a true golden brown for the signature Awadhi sweetness and colour.
Toast the coconut only to light gold so it perfumes the rice without dominating it.
Rest the pulao covered off the heat so the delicate aromas settle before you fluff it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling burani raita and a simple salad of onion rings and lemon for an Awadhi feast.

variations.name: Classic Curd Rice
variations.description: The comforting South Indian thayir sadam where soft-cooked rice is folded into fresh yogurt and a little milk, then crowned with a fragrant ghee tempering of mustard, urad dal and curry leaves. Cooling, gently tangy and lightly spiced, it is the traditional close to a festive meal or a soothing summer lunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee gives the tempering its nutty aroma that defines authentic curd rice

steps: Rinse 1 cup sona masoori rice until the water runs clear, then pressure-cook it with 3 cups water for 4 whistles on medium heat until the grains are very soft and slightly mushy, about 15 minutes.
Transfer the hot rice to a wide bowl and mash it gently with the back of a spoon, then let it cool for 10 minutes until just warm so the yogurt will not split.
Fold in 1.5 cups whisked yogurt, 0.5 cup milk and 1 tsp salt, mixing until the rice is loose and creamy; the milk keeps it soft even after refrigeration.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan over medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal and wait until the seeds crackle and the dal turns golden, about 1 minute.
Add 2 dry red chillies, 2 slit green chillies, grated 1 inch ginger, 12 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida, frying for 30 seconds until the leaves go crisp and aromatic.
Pour the sizzling tempering over the curd rice, scatter 2 tbsp chopped coriander and stir once; serve at room temperature or chilled.
tips: Always cool the rice to lukewarm before adding yogurt, or the heat will make the curd sour and grainy.
If serving later, hold back some milk and stir it in just before eating, as the rice keeps absorbing moisture.
For a picnic-friendly version, use slightly set curd and skip the extra milk so it does not turn watery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve mounded in a bowl topped with a spoon of tangy mango or lime pickle and a few pomegranate arils for a jewel-like South Indian finish.

variations.name: Gujarati Sweet-Tempered Curd Rice
variations.description: A Gujarati-leaning take that balances the tang of curd with a whisper of jaggery and cooling cucumber, reflecting the region's love of the sweet-savoury note. Crunchy cucumber and roasted peanuts give it texture the classic version never has.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A spoon of mineral-rich jaggery rounds the tang the Gujarati way without any refined sugar

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries the sweet-savoury tempering and adds a festive richness

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed sona masoori rice with 3 cups water for 4 whistles on medium heat until soft, about 15 minutes, then cool it in a wide bowl for 10 minutes.
Whisk 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder into 1.5 cups yogurt until it dissolves, then fold this into the cooled rice with 1 tsp salt for a gentle sweet-tangy base.
Finely dice 0.5 cup deseeded cucumber and stir it in along with 3 tbsp crushed roasted peanuts just before the tempering so they stay crunchy.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them splutter for about 40 seconds until fragrant.
Toss in 10 curry leaves, 2 slit green chillies and grated 1 inch ginger, frying 30 seconds until the leaves crisp, then pour the tempering over the rice.
Fold everything together, garnish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and serve lightly chilled.
tips: Salt the diced cucumber for five minutes and squeeze it dry to stop the rice from turning watery.
Add the peanuts at the very end so they keep their bite against the creamy rice.
Dissolve the jaggery in the yogurt rather than the hot pan so it blends evenly without clumping.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with crisp Gujarati fryums or a spoon of sweet chhundo pickle on the side to echo the sweet-savoury theme.

variations.name: Rajasthani Boondi Curd Rice
variations.description: Inspired by Rajasthan's beloved boondi raita, this version folds soaked gram-flour boondi and roasted cumin into the curd rice for a spiced, savoury bowl. The boondi soaks up the yogurt and turns pillowy, giving every bite a soft burst.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee deepens the roasted-spice tempering typical of Rajasthani kitchens

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed rice with 3 cups water for 4 whistles on medium heat until very soft, about 15 minutes, then cool it in a wide bowl for 10 minutes.
Soak 0.75 cup plain boondi in warm water for 3 minutes, then squeeze gently and set aside so it stays soft but not soggy.
Fold 1.5 cups whisked yogurt, 0.75 tsp salt, 0.5 tsp black salt and 1 tsp roasted cumin powder into the cooled rice, then stir in the softened boondi.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them sizzle for 30 seconds until they darken and smell toasty.
Add 10 curry leaves, 2 slit green chillies and 0.5 tsp red chilli powder off the heat for 10 seconds so the chilli does not burn, then pour over the rice.
Mix well, top with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and serve immediately while the boondi is still tender.
tips: Squeeze the soaked boondi lightly so it releases excess oil yet keeps its melt-in-the-mouth softness.
Add the chilli powder only after taking the pan off heat, as direct flame turns it bitter.
Make the base an hour ahead but fold in boondi just before serving so it does not dissolve completely.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with crunchy Rajasthani papad and a wedge of raw onion for a desert-thali style contrast.

variations.name: Bengali Panch Phoron Curd Rice
variations.description: A Bengali reimagining where the tempering swaps to pungent wood-pressed mustard oil and the five-spice panch phoron, lending a sharp, aromatic edge quite unlike the mild southern original. A scatter of slit green chilli keeps it bright and warming.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil gives the Bengali pungency that mustard-averse regions never use

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A final spoon of ghee softens the sharp mustard tempering

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed gobindobhog rice with 3 cups water for 3 whistles on medium heat until soft and fragrant, about 12 minutes, then cool it for 10 minutes.
Fold 1.5 cups whisked yogurt and 1 tsp salt into the cooled aromatic rice until creamy and loose.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a small pan over medium-high heat until it just begins to smoke, then lower the heat to keep it from burning.
Add 1 tsp panch phoron and 2 dry red chillies, letting the seeds crackle for about 40 seconds until deeply aromatic.
Stir in 3 slit green chillies, grated 1 inch ginger and 8 curry leaves for 20 seconds, then finish the tempering with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee off the heat.
Pour over the curd rice, fold through, garnish with 2 tbsp coriander and rest 5 minutes so the mustard mellows before serving.
tips: Heat mustard oil to smoking point first, then cool slightly, to tame its raw sharpness before tempering.
Gobindobhog rice is fragrant and short-grained; if unavailable use any soft short rice and cook it a touch softer.
Let the finished bowl rest a few minutes so the pungent oil settles into a gentle, rounded flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a fried papad and a spoon of Bengali aam kasundi on the side to double down on the mustard theme.

variations.name: Tamil Nadu Fruit Thayir Sadam
variations.description: The temple-style thayir sadam of Tamil Nadu, made luxuriously creamy with a splash of milk and studded with pomegranate and grated carrot for sweetness and colour. The classic mustard-urad tempering with ginger makes it the definitive prasadam-style curd rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee is essential for the sattvic temple-style tempering that defines this dish

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed rice with 3.5 cups water for 5 whistles on medium heat until very soft and mushy, about 16 minutes, then mash lightly and cool for 10 minutes.
Fold in 1.5 cups yogurt, 0.75 cup milk and 1 tsp salt until the mixture is loose and creamy, keeping it extra soft for temple-style texture.
Stir in 0.33 cup pomegranate arils and 0.25 cup finely grated carrot for pops of sweetness and colour.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tsp urad dal and 1 tsp bengal gram, frying until the dals turn golden, about 1 minute.
Add grated 1 inch ginger, 2 slit green chillies, 12 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida, sizzling 30 seconds until fragrant, then pour over the rice.
Fold gently to keep the arils whole and serve at room temperature as a cooling finish to the meal.
tips: Keep this batch loose and milky, since curd rice thickens noticeably as it sits.
Add pomegranate just before serving so the juice does not bleed into the white rice.
For an authentic prasadam aroma, do not skip the asafoetida and fresh curry leaves in the ghee tempering.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled in a banana-leaf-lined bowl with a dab of spicy avakai pickle to cut the coolness.

variations.name: Classic Dal Makhani
variations.description: The iconic Punjabi dhaba dal of whole black urad and a handful of rajma, simmered low and slow until the lentils turn silken and glossy. A tomato-onion masala bloomed in ghee, cream and butter give it that unmistakable velvet body and faint smokiness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bloom the cumin and finish the dal in nutty bilona ghee for the classic dhaba aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A teaspoon rounds off the tomato acidity and lends the dal its deep dhaba sweetness.

steps: Soak 1 cup black urad and 0.25 cup rajma in plenty of water for at least 8 hours or overnight, then drain and rinse until the water runs clear.

Pressure-cook the soaked lentils with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 3.5 cups fresh water for 6 to 7 whistles on medium heat, then simmer 15 minutes until the urad is completely soft and mashes between two fingers.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan on medium, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds until fragrant, then add 2 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the finely chopped large onion and fry 6 to 8 minutes until deep golden.
Stir in the 3 pureed tomatoes, 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 0.5 tsp salt and cook on medium 10 to 12 minutes until the masala thickens and ghee pools at the edges.

Pour the cooked lentils with their liquid into the masala, add 2 tbsp butter and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, and simmer uncovered on low for 30 to 40 minutes, stirring often and mashing lightly, until glossy and thick.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the pot, stir in 0.25 cup cream and 1 tsp garam masala, and simmer a final 5 minutes until the dal turns silky and rich.
tips: The longer and lower you simmer, the creamier the dal; a full hour on the lowest flame is what separates dhaba dal from an ordinary one.
If it thickens too much overnight, loosen with warm milk rather than water so the richness stays intact.
For an authentic smoky note, place a live charcoal ember in a small steel bowl over the dal, drizzle with ghee, cover for two minutes, then remove.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a copper handi with an extra swirl of cream and a cube of butter melting on top, alongside garlic naan and thin rings of raw onion tossed in lemon.

variations.name: Amritsari Smoked Dal Makhani
variations.description: The old-city Amritsar rendition leans into wood-smoke and restraint, using less cream and more slow-charred depth. A double dhungar of charcoal and ghee gives it a tandoor-like aroma that clings to every spoonful.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Used both in the tadka and poured over the smoking charcoal for the signature Amritsari dhungar.

steps: Soak 1 cup black urad and 0.3 cup rajma overnight, drain, then pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 4 cups water for 7 whistles until the beans crush easily.
While the dal cooks, grate the 2 inches ginger and crush the 8 garlic cloves to a coarse paste, and finely chop the 2 onions and 3 tomatoes separately.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium, splutter 1 tsp cumin seeds, add the ginger-garlic and slit green chillies and fry 1 minute, then add onions and cook 8 minutes to a rich brown.
Add the tomatoes, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp salt and cook 12 minutes on medium until fully broken down and jammy, then tip in the cooked dal and 0.5 cup milk.
Simmer the dal uncovered on the lowest flame for 40 minutes, mashing against the side every few minutes, until it turns thick, dark and creamy without any added cream.

For the dhungar, nestle a heated charcoal piece in a small bowl set on the dal, pour the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over it, cover tightly for 3 minutes, then remove and stir in 0.75 tsp garam masala.
tips: Amritsari style stays deliberately lean, so resist adding cream; the body should come only from long mashing of the urad.
Roast the whole cumin dry for 30 seconds before it goes into the ghee to deepen the smoky character.
A second round of dhungar just before serving makes the smoke aroma noticeably stronger for guests.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle into rustic clay bowls and pair with tandoori roti and a raw onion-cucumber salad dressed with vinegar and a pinch of salt.

variations.name: Kashmiri Wazwan-style Maa Chholiya
variations.description: In Kashmiri kitchens the black urad and rajma pairing becomes maa chholiya, perfumed with fennel and dry ginger instead of garam masala. Curd replaces cream and the fat of choice is mustard oil finished with ghee, giving a sharp, aromatic dal quite unlike the Punjabi original.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Smoked to its haze point first to tame the pungency, giving maa chholiya its distinctive Kashmiri base.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoonful stirred in at the end rounds the mustard sharpness into a mellow finish.

steps: Soak 1 cup black urad and 0.3 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt in 4 cups water for 7 whistles until meltingly soft.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pot on high until it just begins to smoke and turns pale, then lower the flame to medium to mellow its bite.
Add 1 tsp cumin seeds, 3 broken dry Kashmiri chillies, 3 cardamom pods and 4 cloves to the oil and let them crackle for 30 seconds until intensely fragrant.
Whisk 0.5 cup curd with 1 tsp dry ginger powder and 1 tsp fennel powder, then pour into the pan off the direct heat and stir constantly on low for 3 minutes so it does not split.
Add the cooked dal with its liquid and 0.5 tsp salt, and simmer gently for 25 to 30 minutes until the gravy thickens and the fennel aroma perfumes the kitchen.
Finish by swirling in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, cover for 2 minutes off the heat, then stir once so the ghee marbles through the dal.
tips: Grinding the fennel and dry ginger fresh, rather than using old powders, is what gives maa chholiya its authentic Kashmiri fragrance.
Keep the curd at room temperature and add it off the boil to prevent the gravy from curdling.
This dal deliberately skips onion, tomato and garlic in the temple-friendly wazwan tradition, so let the whole spices carry the flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed Kashmiri rice and a side of muli anchar (radish pickle) to cut the richness.

variations.name: Marwari Ghee-laden Ma-Rajma
variations.description: The Marwari version is a fasting-friendly, no-onion-no-garlic dal thick with ghee and heat from Mathania chillies. Hing and a heavy hand of ghee do the work that onions do elsewhere, making it intensely rich and pure-veg.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Marwari dal is unapologetically ghee-rich; a full four tablespoons carry the whole spices and give body without any cream.

steps: Soak 1 cup black urad and 0.25 cup rajma for 8 hours, then pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt in 4 cups water for 7 whistles until soft enough to mash.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.5 tsp hing and let them sizzle for 20 seconds until the hing smells toasty.
Add the grated 1 inch ginger and fry 30 seconds, then stir in 1.5 tsp Mathania chilli powder and 1 tbsp coriander powder off the heat so the spices do not scorch.
Return to medium heat, add the 2 chopped tomatoes and 0.5 tsp salt, and cook 8 to 10 minutes until the tomatoes collapse and the ghee separates out bright red.
Pour in the cooked dal with liquid and simmer on low for 25 minutes, mashing the urad against the pan, until the dal is thick and the surface glistens with ghee.
Stir in 0.75 tsp garam masala, simmer 3 more minutes, and serve piping hot with a final drizzle of ghee if you like.
tips: Mathania chillies give colour more than fierce heat, so use the full amount for that glowing red Marwari look.
Being onion and garlic free, this dal keeps well for two days and actually deepens in flavour, ideal for festival cooking.
If the dal tastes flat, a squeeze of lemon at the table lifts the ghee richness beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with bajra roti smeared with white butter and a side of garlic-free green chilli thecha for the full Marwari thali feel.

variations.name: Bengali Sabut Urad with Panch Phoron
variations.description: A Bengali reimagining tempers the whole black urad with panch phoron and mustard oil rather than cumin and cream. The result is lighter and more aromatic, with the five-spice fragrance and a hint of sugar that defines Bengali dal cookery.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: The defining Bengali fat; smoked first, it gives the dal its pungent, warming backbone.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A characteristic Bengali touch of sweetness that balances the mustard heat and salt.

steps: Soak 1 cup black urad and 0.25 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt in 3.5 cups water for 7 whistles until soft and creamy.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pan on high until it smokes lightly, then lower to medium and drop in 2 dry red chillies and 2 bay leaves for 20 seconds.
Add 1 tsp panch phoron and let the fennel, fenugreek and nigella seeds crackle for 30 seconds until they release a nutty, aromatic smell.
Stir in the grated 1.5 inch ginger and 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp salt, and cook 8 minutes until the tomatoes turn pulpy.
Pour in the cooked dal with its water, add 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, and simmer on low for 20 minutes until it thickens to a pourable, glossy consistency.
Taste and adjust salt, simmer 2 more minutes, and serve with the whole spices left in for their fragrance.
tips: Do not grind the panch phoron; the whole seeds tempering is essential to the Bengali character of this dal.
Keep this version looser than Punjabi dal makhani, as Bengali dals are meant to be spooned over rice rather than scooped with bread.
A few drops of raw mustard oil stirred in at the very end intensifies the signature pungency.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot steamed rice with a wedge of lime and a side of aloo bhaja (crisp fried potato matchsticks).

variations.name: Classic Moong Dal Fry
variations.description: Unlike a thin tadka dal, moong fry is thick and bhuna, where the onion-tomato masala is fried down hard in ghee before the dal joins it. The result is a robust, richly browned dal with clinging masala rather than a soupy pour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The frying fat for the bhuna masala; it browns the onions and gives the fry its deep aroma.

steps: Rinse and pressure-cook 1 cup moong dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 2.5 cups water for 3 whistles so it holds a little shape rather than turning to paste.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them splutter for 20 seconds, then add the 2 finely chopped onions.
Fry the onions for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring often, until they turn a rich golden brown, then add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 2 slit green chillies and cook 1 minute.
Add the 2 chopped tomatoes, 1 tbsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp salt and bhuna on medium 8 minutes until the masala is thick and the ghee separates.
Tip in the cooked dal, stir hard for 3 minutes so the masala coats every grain, adding just a little hot water to keep it thick rather than runny.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala, simmer 2 minutes, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: The key to a good fry is browning the onions properly; pale onions give a flat, boiled taste.
Keep this dal thick and clingy so it can be scooped with roti rather than mixed into rice.
Cook the dal only to 3 whistles so the grains stay slightly separate and give the fry its texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve thick and hot with tawa roti or jeera rice, topped with thin onion rings and a wedge of lemon.

variations.name: Punjabi Bhuna Moong Fry with Kasuri Methi
variations.description: The Punjabi dhaba fry is heavier and more perfumed, built on a well-browned masala and finished with crushed kasuri methi and a knob of butter. It clings to the spoon and carries the smoky, roasted-fenugreek aroma of North Indian roadside cooking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The base frying fat that gives the bhuna masala its dhaba richness.

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 2.5 cups water for 3 whistles, then keep aside without mashing.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with 1 tbsp butter in a kadhai on medium, splutter 1 tsp cumin seeds, then fry the 2 chopped onions for 10 minutes to a deep brown.
Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute, then add the 2 pureed tomatoes, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1 tbsp coriander powder and bhuna 8 minutes until the fat separates.
Add the cooked dal and 0.5 tsp salt, stir vigorously for 4 minutes so the masala thickly coats the grains, adding hot water sparingly to keep it dense.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi between your palms and scatter it over the dal along with 0.75 tsp garam masala, then simmer 3 minutes.
Finish with 2 tbsp coriander and an extra sliver of butter melting on top before serving.
tips: Dry-roasting the kasuri methi for a few seconds before crushing releases far more aroma.
This is a thick, ladle-clinging dal, so hold back the water and let the masala dominate.
A pinch of sugar or a splash of cream can be added if you want an even more indulgent dhaba profile.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or lachha paratha and a side of pickled green chillies for the full dhaba experience.

variations.name: Andhra Pesara Pappu Fry with Gongura Kick
variations.description: The Andhra fry turns moong into a fiery pesara pappu, tempered in sesame oil with garlic, curry leaves and a bold hit of red chilli, then sharpened with tangy gongura or tamarind. It is thick, spicy and unmistakably Telugu on the plate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: The traditional Andhra cooking oil (nuvvula nune) that carries the garlic and chilli tempering.

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 2.5 cups water for 3 whistles until soft but not fully broken down.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadhai on medium, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin and let the mustard pop for 30 seconds.
Add 4 broken dry red chillies, 0.25 tsp hing, 15 curry leaves and the 8 crushed garlic cloves and fry 1 minute until the garlic is golden and fragrant.
Add the chopped large onion and cook 5 minutes until soft, then stir in the 1 cup chopped gongura leaves and cook 3 minutes until they wilt and turn sour-smelling.
Add the cooked dal, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and a splash of hot water, and mash-fry on medium for 6 minutes until thick and the oil glistens at the edges.
Taste for salt and tang, simmer 2 minutes more, and serve hot.
tips: Gongura is intensely sour; if you cannot find it, use 1 tbsp tamarind pulp for a similar tang.
Sesame oil is central to Andhra flavour, so do not swap it out for a neutral oil here.
Keep the dal thick and coarse; pesara pappu is meant to be mixed into rice with a spoon of ghee.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve mounded over hot rice with a drizzle of ghee, a fried papad and a dab of avakaya mango pickle.

variations.name: Gujarati Sukhi Moong Fry with Jaggery
variations.description: The Gujarati sukhi moong is a nearly dry fry where the dal is steamed grainy and tossed in a light groundnut-oil tempering with ginger, green chilli and a touch of jaggery. Sweet, mild and fluffy, it eats almost like a savoury poha rather than a gravy dal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The everyday Gujarati cooking oil that keeps this dry moong light and fragrant.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The signature Gujarati sweetness that balances the green chilli and lemon.

steps: Soak 1 cup moong dal for 30 minutes, drain well, then pressure-cook with just 1.25 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 2 whistles so the grains stay separate and fluffy.
Fluff the cooked dal gently with a fork and spread it out so it does not clump; it should look like grainy, dry lentils.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan on medium, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp hing and let them sizzle for 20 seconds.
Add the grated 1 inch ginger and 2 finely chopped green chillies and fry 1 minute until fragrant, taking care not to brown them.
Add the fluffed dal, 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and a splash of hot water, and toss gently on low for 4 minutes until the jaggery melts and coats the grains.
Turn off the heat, stir in 1 tbsp lemon juice, 3 tbsp coriander and 2 tbsp grated coconut, and serve warm.
tips: The trick to fluffy sukhi moong is minimal water and only two whistles, so the grains never go mushy.
Balance is everything here; adjust jaggery, chilli and lemon until it tastes gently sweet, hot and tangy at once.
Add the lemon off the heat so its fresh brightness is not cooked away.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a light lunch with soft phulka and a bowl of chaas, or as a protein-rich side in a Gujarati thali.

variations.name: Kolhapuri Tambda Moong Fry
variations.description: This fiery Kolhapuri fry drenches the moong in a fresh coconut-and-red-chilli tambda masala, fried down in groundnut oil until dark and glossy. It is bold, hot and layered with the roasted dry-spice depth that defines western Maharashtra.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The Kolhapuri kitchen fat used to fry the fresh coconut masala until dark and aromatic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Stirred in at the finish to soften the fiery Kolhapuri heat with a nutty richness.

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 2.5 cups water for 3 whistles until soft but intact.
Dry-roast the 0.33 cup grated coconut in a pan on medium until golden brown and fragrant, about 4 minutes, then set aside.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium, splutter 1 tsp cumin, add the chopped large onion and fry 7 minutes until browned.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, the chopped tomato and the roasted coconut, and cook 4 minutes, then stir in 1.5 tbsp Kolhapuri kanda-lasun masala and 1 tsp Byadgi chilli powder off the heat.
Return to the flame, fry the masala for 3 minutes until dark and oil-slicked, then add the cooked dal and a cup of hot water and simmer 6 minutes to a thick, fiery gravy.
Swirl in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee to round the heat, scatter 2 tbsp coriander, and serve hot.
tips: Roasting the coconut deeply is what gives the tambda masala its dark colour and smoky depth.
Kolhapuri masala is very hot, so start with less and build up if you are unused to the heat.
The finishing spoon of ghee is not optional here; it tempers the fire and gives the dal a glossy sheen.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri or plain rice, a raw onion wedge and a slice of lemon to cool the palate.

variations.name: Classic Moong Dal Tadka
variations.description: The everyday comfort dal of skinned yellow moong, cooked soft and finished with a fragrant ghee tadka of cumin, garlic and dried red chilli. Light, buttery and quick, it is the dal most Indian homes cook when they want something soothing over rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The tadka fat that carries the cumin and garlic; its bilona nuttiness defines this simple dal.

steps: Rinse 1 cup yellow moong dal in two changes of water, then pressure-cook it with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 4 whistles until soft and pale gold.
Whisk the cooked dal smooth with a ladle, adding a splash of hot water if it looks too thick, and keep it simmering gently on low.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small tadka pan on medium, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp hing and let them sizzle for 20 seconds until aromatic.
Add the 5 sliced garlic cloves and 2 broken dry red chillies and fry 1 minute until the garlic turns pale gold, then add the finely chopped small onion and cook 3 minutes until soft.
Stir in the chopped tomato and 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and cook 4 minutes until the tomato melts and the ghee separates.
Pour the sizzling tadka over the simmering dal, stir once, simmer 2 minutes, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Whisking the cooked dal before the tadka gives it that smooth, restaurant-style body rather than a grainy texture.
Add the tadka at the very last moment so the cumin and garlic aromas hit the table still crackling.
A squeeze of lemon just before eating brightens the whole dal without making it sour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over a mound of steamed rice with a dollop of ghee and a side of crisp papad and mango pickle.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Varan-style Moong Tadka
variations.description: A Maharashtrian take that keeps the dal plain and gently sweet like varan, then finishes it with a phodni of mustard, curry leaves and goda masala in groundnut oil and ghee. It is soft, subtly sweet-sour and deeply homely.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The traditional Maharashtrian cooking oil for the mustard-curry leaf phodni base.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Spooned over the finished varan for the classic Maharashtrian aroma of ghee-dal.

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 4 whistles, then whisk smooth and drop in 2 pieces of kokum to steep.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a small pan on medium, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop fully for 30 seconds.
Add 0.5 tsp cumin, 0.25 tsp hing, 12 curry leaves and 2 slit green chillies and fry 30 seconds until the curry leaves crisp and turn glossy.
Stir in 1 tsp goda masala off the heat for 10 seconds so its warm, coconutty spice blooms without burning.
Pour this phodni into the simmering dal, add a splash of hot water to loosen, and simmer gently for 5 minutes so the kokum lends a mild tang.
Spoon 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the top, scatter 2 tbsp coriander, and serve warm.
tips: Goda masala is the heart of this dal; without it the phodni tastes ordinary, so seek out a good Maharashtrian blend.
Kokum gives a gentle purple-tinged tang; if unavailable, use a small piece of tamarind instead.
Maharashtrian varan is meant to be slightly sweet, so a tiny pinch of jaggery can be added if your family likes it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as varan-bhaat, poured over hot rice with a spoon of ghee and a wedge of lime, alongside a dry sabzi.

variations.name: Tamil Paruppu with Coconut Oil Tadka
variations.description: The Tamil paruppu keeps moong dal plain and soupy, mashed with a knob of ghee, then crowned with a coconut-oil tempering of mustard, urad dal and curry leaves. It is the gentle everyday dal eaten with the first course of a South Indian meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: The authentic Tamil tempering fat that gives the tadka its sweet, tropical aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Mashed into the hot dal so each spoonful is glossy and rich.

steps: Rinse and pressure-cook 1 cup moong dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt, the chopped small tomato and 3 cups water for 4 whistles until it collapses into a soft mash.
Mash the dal with the back of a ladle, stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, and keep it warm on low with a little hot water to reach a soupy consistency.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a tadka pan on medium, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal and fry until the mustard pops and the urad turns golden, about 40 seconds.
Add 2 broken dry red chillies, 0.25 tsp hing, 15 curry leaves and the 6 sliced shallots and fry 2 minutes until the shallots soften and smell sweet.
Tip the coconut-oil tadka into the mashed dal, stir well, and simmer gently for 3 minutes so the flavours meld.
Taste for salt, loosen with a little hot water if needed, and serve immediately while fragrant.
tips: Small shallots (chinna vengayam) give a sweeter, deeper flavour than regular onion in this Tamil dal.
Keep the dal loose and pourable; it is meant to be mixed with rice and ghee, not eaten thick.
Frying the urad dal until just golden adds a subtle nutty crunch, so do not let it darken too far.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as the opening paruppu-sadam course with hot rice, a teaspoon of ghee and a fried appalam on the side.

variations.name: Sindhi Moong Dal with Garlic Tadka
variations.description: The Sindhi rendition is bold and garlicky, the moong dal kept slightly grainy and finished with a fiery double tadka of pounded garlic and red chilli. A splash of tamarind water gives it the tangy edge that Sindhi cooking loves.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Used generously for the aggressive garlic tadka that defines Sindhi dal.

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 2.75 cups water for just 3 whistles so it stays soft but with a little grain, not fully mushy.
Stir 1 tbsp tamarind pulp into 0.25 cup warm water, strain, and set this tangy liquid aside.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium, add 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add the 10 crushed garlic cloves and fry 2 minutes until deep golden and intensely aromatic.
Add the chopped medium onion and 2 slit green chillies and fry 4 minutes until the onion turns brown at the edges, then add the chopped tomato and 1 tsp red chilli powder and cook 4 minutes.
Pour in the cooked dal and the tamarind water, add a splash of hot water to reach a medium consistency, and simmer on low for 6 minutes so the sourness balances the garlic.
Finish with 2 tbsp coriander and serve hot with the garlic pieces left whole for anyone who loves them.
tips: Sindhi dal is meant to taste unabashedly of garlic, so brown it well but stop before it turns bitter.
Keeping the dal a touch grainy rather than smooth is traditional and gives a better bite with rice.
Adjust the tamarind to your taste; the dal should be pleasantly tangy, not sharply sour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain rice and Sindhi-style fried aloo tuk, or scoop it up with hot phulka and sliced onions.

variations.name: Bengali Sona Moong with Ghee-Cumin Tadka
variations.description: In Bengal the moong is dry-roasted before cooking, turning it into fragrant sona moong dal with a nutty depth. A restrained tempering of whole cumin, bay leaf and dry chilli in ghee, plus a whisper of sugar, keeps it delicate and aromatic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The tempering fat for the cumin and bay; roasted moong plus ghee gives the classic Bengali sona moong perfume.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A small spoon lends the gentle sweetness typical of a Bengali moong dal.

steps: Dry-roast 1 cup moong dal in a hot pan on medium heat for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring constantly, until it turns golden and gives off a nutty aroma.
Rinse the roasted dal quickly, then pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt, the grated 1 inch ginger and 3 cups water for 4 whistles until soft but with grains still distinct.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium, add 1 tsp cumin seeds, 2 bay leaves and 2 dry red chillies and let them crackle for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 2 slit green chillies, fry 20 seconds, then pour in the cooked dal along with 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and stir well.
Simmer the dal on low for 6 to 7 minutes, adding hot water as needed, until it is smooth and lightly sweet, then stir in 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder.
Garnish with 2 tbsp coriander and serve warm as the traditional first course.
tips: Roasting the moong until golden is what turns ordinary dal into fragrant sona moong, so do not rush this step.
Keep the dal on the thinner side, as Bengali moong dal is traditionally eaten with rice at the start of the meal.
The sprinkle of roasted cumin powder at the end adds a smoky top note distinct from the whole cumin in the tadka.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at the beginning of a Bengali meal with steamed rice, a wedge of lime and crisp begun bhaja (fried aubergine).

variations.name: Classic Onion Uttapam
variations.description: The thick, soft-centred cousin of the dosa: fermented rice-and-urad batter poured into a small fat round and pressed with a generous layer of chopped onion, green chilli and coriander. Cooked slowly in Anveshan Coconut Oil, it turns golden and crisp underneath while the onions sweeten and char into the spongy top.

ingredients.name: Fermented dosa batter (rice and urad dal)
Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil that crisps the base and carries the sweet aroma of a Kerala tiffin.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing drizzle over the onions for a rich, nutty gloss that lifts the whole uttapam.

steps: Stir 3 cups fermented dosa batter to a thick, spreadable pouring consistency, adding a splash of water only if it is stiff, and mix in 0.5 tsp salt.
Finely chop 2 onions, 2 green chillies and a 1-inch piece of ginger, tear 12 curry leaves and chop 4 tbsp coriander, then keep the topping mix ready.
Heat a tava over medium heat, rub with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, then pour a ladle of batter and spread gently into a thick 5-inch round without thinning it out.
Scatter a generous handful of the onion mixture over the top and press it lightly into the wet batter with the back of the ladle.
Drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil around the edge, cover and cook for 3-4 minutes until the base is golden-crisp and the top looks set.
Flip, press gently and cook the onion side for 1-2 minutes until charred and sweet, drizzle with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee and serve, then repeat with the rest.
tips: Keep the batter thick, not runny, so the uttapam stays soft and spongy inside rather than turning into a thin dosa.
Cover the pan while the first side cooks so the thick batter sets through before you attempt the flip.
Chop the onions fine and press them in firmly, or they scatter off when you turn the uttapam.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with coconut chutney and a small bowl of sambar, or a fresh tomato-onion chutney for tang.

variations.name: Karnataka Masala Onion Uttapam
variations.description: A Mysore-inspired uttapam where garam masala and coriander powder are folded through the batter and a saute of onion, capsicum and tomato crowns the top. Cooked in Anveshan Groundnut Oil, it eats like a spiced open pancake, hearty enough to be a meal on its own.

ingredients.name: Fermented dosa batter (rice and urad dal)
Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil for sauteing the masala topping and crisping the uttapam base.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: Brushed over the masala top at the end for a fragrant, restaurant-style finish.

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and saute 2 chopped onions, half a chopped capsicum and 1 chopped tomato over medium heat for 4-5 minutes until softened, then stir in 0.75 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and cook 1 minute more; set aside.
Stir 3 cups fermented dosa batter with 0.5 tsp salt to a thick spreadable consistency.
Heat a tava over medium heat, grease with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, pour a ladle of batter and spread into a thick 5-inch round.
Spread 2 tbsp of the cooked masala over the top and press it gently into the batter with the ladle.
Drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil around the edge, cover and cook for 3-4 minutes until the underside is golden and crisp.
Flip for 1-2 minutes to lightly char the masala side, brush with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee, then repeat with the remaining batter and topping.
tips: Cook the masala until fairly dry so it doesn't make the soft uttapam soggy from the moisture.
Let the masala cool a little before topping, so it doesn't slide off the wet batter.
Scatter a few extra raw onions over the masala for a sweet char and a bit of crunch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling mint-curd chutney to balance the spiced topping, and a wedge of lime.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Onion Uttapam
variations.description: A fiery Andhra take where the onion topping is bound with pounded green chillies, crushed black pepper and a scatter of curry leaves for a genuine, building heat. Anveshan Sesame Oil crisps the base to a deep gold and lends the nutty gingelly note beloved across Andhra kitchens.

ingredients.name: Fermented dosa batter (rice and urad dal)
Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil that gives the base a nutty aroma and the deep crispness Andhra tiffins are known for.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: A small finishing drizzle to round off the sharp heat with a mellow richness.

steps: Pound 4 green chillies with a 1-inch piece of ginger to a coarse paste and crush 1 tsp peppercorns roughly.
Finely chop 2 onions and toss them with the chilli-ginger paste, crushed pepper, 15 torn curry leaves and 4 tbsp coriander to make a fiery topping.
Stir 3 cups fermented dosa batter with 0.5 tsp salt to a thick, spreadable consistency.
Heat a tava over medium heat, grease with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, pour a ladle of batter and spread into a thick 5-inch round.
Press a generous handful of the spicy onion topping into the wet surface, drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil around the rim, cover and cook 3-4 minutes until the base is deep golden and crisp.
Flip and cook the topping side 1-2 minutes until the onions char, drizzle with a little Anveshan Bilona Ghee, and repeat with the rest of the batter.
tips: For maximum heat keep the green chilli seeds in; for a gentler version deseed them but keep the pepper.
The crushed pepper delivers a warm, lingering heat quite different from chilli, so don't skip it.
Press the wet onion topping firmly so it fuses into the batter and chars evenly on the flip.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling coconut-curd chutney and a mound of plain curd rice to temper the Andhra heat.

variations.name: Telangana Cheesy Onion Uttapam
variations.description: A Hyderabad cafe-style uttapam where a layer of chopped onion is topped with grated cheese that melts into the spongy surface as it cooks. Made in Anveshan Coconut Oil with a ghee finish, the crisp base and gooey, oniony cheese top make it an irresistible snack for all ages.

ingredients.name: Fermented dosa batter (rice and urad dal)
Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil for a fragrant, crisp base that supports the melting cheese.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing drizzle over the cheese for a glossy, aromatic, cafe-style top.

steps: Stir 3 cups fermented dosa batter with 0.5 tsp salt to a thick, spreadable consistency and finely chop 2 onions and 1 green chilli.
Heat a tava over medium heat, grease with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, pour a ladle of batter and spread into a thick 5-inch round.
Scatter a handful of chopped onion and chilli over the top, then press them gently into the wet batter.

Sprinkle 3 tbsp grated cheese and a pinch of black pepper over the onions, drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil around the edge, cover and cook 3-4 minutes until the base is golden and the cheese melts.
Flip carefully for just 1 minute so the cheese sets without sticking, then turn back cheese-side up.
Drizzle with a little Anveshan Bilona Ghee and serve hot, repeating with the remaining batter and cheese.
tips: Add the cheese only after the onions so it melts into the topping rather than directly onto the tava.
Flip gently and briefly, or use the covered-steam method to melt the cheese without turning at all.
A blend of processed cheese and mozzarella gives both flavour and that satisfying stretch.
