variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tangy tomato chutney or ketchup, cut into quarters for easy sharing as a tea-time snack.

variations.name: Tamil Podi Onion Uttapam
variations.description: A Chennai mess-style uttapam where the onion top is dusted with idli-milagai podi and finished in ghee so the gunpowder toasts into the sponge. Anveshan Sesame Oil crisps the base while the podi-ghee combination delivers the salty, garlicky punch of an authentic Tamil tiffin.

ingredients.name: Fermented dosa batter (rice and urad dal)
Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Nutty wood-pressed gingelly oil, the classic Tamil tiffin fat, for a crisp golden base.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: Drizzled over the podi so the gunpowder toasts and perfumes the whole uttapam.

steps: Stir 3 cups fermented dosa batter with 0.5 tsp salt to a thick, spreadable consistency, and finely chop 2 onions with 1 green chilli.
Heat a tava over medium heat, grease with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, ladle on the batter and spread into a thick 5-inch round.
Scatter a handful of chopped onion, 1 chopped chilli, a few torn curry leaves and coriander over the top and press them into the batter.
Sprinkle 1 tbsp molagapodi over the onions and drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee across the podi so it begins to toast.
Drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil around the rim, cover and cook 3-4 minutes until the base is deep golden and crisp.
Flip for 1-2 minutes to char the onion-podi top, then serve podi-side up and repeat with the rest of the batter.
tips: Sprinkle the podi over the wet onions so it sticks and toasts rather than scattering off a dry surface.
Adjust podi to taste; a rounded tablespoon per uttapam gives the authentic mess-style kick.
Finish with an extra few drops of ghee for the glossy sheen and deeper roasted aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a mild coconut chutney to cool the podi heat, and a bowl of hot sambar for dunking.

variations.name: Classic Pakora
variations.description: The monsoon classic every Indian home craves: sliced onion and potato bound in a spiced gram-flour batter and fried into craggy, golden clusters. Crunchy at the edges and soft in the middle, these are the fritters that make rainy afternoons and cups of chai worth waiting for.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: a spoonful in the batter adds body and a longer-lasting crunch than besan alone

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for deep-frying; its high smoke point gives an even, crisp golden crust

steps: Thinly slice 2 large onions and 1 medium potato into fine half-moons and place in a bowl with 2 chopped green chillies and 3 tbsp coriander leaves.
Add 1.5 cups gram flour, 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp cumin seeds, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp carom seeds and 1.25 tsp salt directly over the vegetables.

Mix with your fingers without adding water first, letting the onions release their own moisture for 5 minutes, then sprinkle in just 3 to 4 tbsp water to form a thick, clinging batter that barely coats the slices.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a kadai to medium-hot, about 180C; a drop of batter should rise steadily to the surface within a few seconds.
Drop rough spoonfuls of the mixture into the oil, frying 5 or 6 clusters at a time, and fry for 3 to 4 minutes, turning, until deep golden and crisp all over.
Lift out with a slotted spoon and drain on a wire rack; fry the remaining batter in batches so the oil stays hot and the pakoras stay crunchy.
tips: Let the salted onions sit before adding water; their natural juices mean you need very little extra liquid and the pakoras crisp up better.
Keep the oil at a steady medium heat, as too hot browns the outside while leaving the potato raw, and too cool makes them oily.
For extra-crisp pakoras, fry them once until pale, rest 10 minutes, then fry a second time just before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile into a bowl lined with paper, sprinkle with chaat masala, and serve with green coriander chutney and a hot masala chai.

variations.name: Uttar Pradesh Crispy Pakora
variations.description: This UP bazaar-style pakora gets an extra-shattering crust from a coating of fine breadcrumbs pressed over the besan-battered vegetables. Popular at Lucknow's evening chaat carts, it stays crisp far longer than the plain version, perfect for a big family platter.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: thickens the batter so the breadcrumb layer grips firmly to each floret

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: light wood-pressed oil that fries the breadcrumb crust to an even, pale gold

steps: Parboil 1.5 cups cauliflower florets in salted water for 3 minutes until just tender, drain well and pat completely dry so the batter clings.

Whisk 1.25 cups gram flour, 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp cumin seeds, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 inch grated ginger and 1.25 tsp salt with about 0.75 cup water into a thick batter that coats the back of a spoon.
Fold 1 sliced large onion and 2 chopped green chillies into the batter along with the dried florets so everything is evenly coated.
Spread 1 cup bread crumbs on a plate, lift each battered piece and roll it in the crumbs, pressing so a dense crust forms.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sunflower Oil to medium-hot, about 175C, and slide in the coated pieces a few at a time.
Fry for 4 to 5 minutes, turning once, until the breadcrumb crust is crisp and golden and the cauliflower is soft inside; drain on a rack.
tips: Dry the parboiled cauliflower thoroughly, as any surface water will make the breadcrumb coating slide off in the oil.
Keep one hand for the wet batter and one for the dry crumbs to stop your fingers turning into a clumpy mess.
These reheat beautifully in a hot oven for 6 minutes, regaining their crunch far better than any other pakora.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a bed of shredded cabbage with a swirl of mint chutney and a bowl of spicy tomato ketchup for the kids.

variations.name: Bihar Spicy Pakora
variations.description: Bihar's roadside pakora is fierce with freshly pounded black pepper and mustard oil, giving a warmth that hits the back of the throat. The pungency of the wood-pressed mustard oil is central here, lending the fritters their earthy, nose-tingling character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: gives structure to the batter so the peppery clusters hold their craggy shape

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: heated to smoking first, then cooled slightly; its sharp pungency is the soul of this Bihari version

steps: Coarsely crush 1.5 tsp black pepper and 5 garlic cloves together in a mortar into a rough, aromatic paste.
Slice 2 large onions thinly and place in a bowl with 3 chopped green chillies, 3 tbsp coriander and the pepper-garlic paste.
Add 1.5 cups gram flour, 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp cumin seeds, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt, mix, and add about 4 tbsp water to form a thick, sticky batter.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just begins to smoke to tame its raw pungency, then lower the flame to medium and let the oil settle to about 180C.
Drop rough spoonfuls of batter into the hot mustard oil, frying 5 or 6 at a time for 3 to 4 minutes until dark golden and crisp.
Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on a rack; the fritters will carry the unmistakable sharp aroma of mustard oil and pepper.
tips: Always heat mustard oil to smoking point once before frying to mellow its raw bite, then bring it back down to a steady medium.
Crush the pepper coarse rather than powdering it, so you get little bursts of heat in every bite.
If you like extra fire, add a pinch of crushed pepper to the batter's last mix rather than to the oil, which would burn it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot with a sharp green chilli-garlic chutney and thick slices of raw onion, Bihari dhaba style.

variations.name: Madhya Pradesh Masala Pakora
variations.description: Indore's famous masala pakora is aromatic with garam masala and roasted coriander powder folded through a mixed-vegetable batter. Sold by the kilo at the city's Sarafa night market, these fritters are fragrant, festive and generously spiced.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: balances the besan and keeps the masala batter crisp rather than dense

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: clean-frying oil that lets the layered masala aroma come through

steps: Dry-roast 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 0.5 tsp fennel seeds in a pan for 30 seconds until fragrant, then crush the fennel lightly.
Chop and combine 2 cups mixed vegetables of spinach, potato and onion with 2 chopped green chillies in a large bowl.
Add 1.5 cups gram flour, 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, the roasted spices, 1 tsp garam masala, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt, and mix.
Add about 0.5 cup water gradually to make a thick, dropping batter that holds the vegetables together in loose clumps.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to medium-hot, around 180C, and drop in spoonfuls of the masala batter.
Fry 5 or 6 at a time for 3 to 4 minutes, turning, until crisp and richly golden, then drain on a wire rack.
tips: Roasting the coriander and fennel before mixing is what gives this pakora its distinctive Indore aroma.
Squeeze the chopped spinach lightly so it does not thin the batter and make the fritters flat.
Make the dry masala mix in a larger batch and store it airtight for quick pakoras on busy evenings.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a sweet-and-sour imli chutney and a sprinkle of sev on top, the way Indore's Sarafa stalls plate them.

variations.name: Goa Tava Pakora
variations.description: A Goan coastal twist that shallow-cooks flat besan fritters on a tava with coconut oil and a whisper of tangy kokum. Lighter than deep-fried pakoras, they are crisp-edged, faintly sweet from the coconut oil, and studded with curry leaves.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: helps the thin tava batter set into a firm, flippable disc

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: brushed over the tava; its coastal sweetness defines this Goan shallow-fried style

steps: Soak 3 kokum pieces in 2 tbsp warm water for 10 minutes, then finely chop them and reserve the soaking water.

In a bowl combine 1.5 cups gram flour, 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 finely chopped large onion, 2 chopped green chillies, 2 sprigs chopped curry leaves, 0.25 cup grated coconut, 1 tsp cumin seeds, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and the chopped kokum.
Add the kokum water and enough extra water, about 0.5 cup total, to make a thick spoonable batter that is not runny.
Heat a flat tava on medium and brush with 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil until it shimmers.
Place spoonfuls of batter and press each into a flat 8 cm disc, cook for 3 minutes until the underside is crisp and golden.
Flip the discs, drizzle a little more coconut oil around the edges, and cook the second side for 3 minutes until crisp; repeat with the rest of the batter.
tips: Kokum adds the signature Goan tang; if unavailable, use 1 tbsp lime juice stirred in off the heat.
Keep the discs thin so they cook through on the tava without needing the deep oil bath.
Cook on medium heat only, since coconut oil browns quickly and high heat will scorch the edges before the centre sets.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a fresh coconut-chilli chutney and steamed rice, or tuck into pao for a Goan-style fritter sandwich.

variations.name: Classic Rava Dosa
variations.description: The instant, no-ferment dosa: a very thin, buttermilk-slack batter of fine semolina and rice flour that is ladled (never spread) so it sets into a gorgeously lacy, crisp net. Toasted cumin, pepper and curry leaves flavour the batter, and Anveshan Sesame Oil crisps the holes to a shattering golden finish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: A wholegrain stand-in for the usual maida, binding the lacy batter without a refined-flour aftertaste.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil drizzled over the holes for the nutty aroma and shattering crispness typical of a good rava dosa.

steps: Toast 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.5 tsp peppercorns in a dry pan over low heat for about 1 minute until fragrant, then crush the pepper coarsely.

In a bowl combine 1 cup fine semolina, 0.5 cup rice flour, 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, the toasted cumin, crushed pepper and 1 tsp salt, then whisk in about 3.5 cups water to a very thin, watery batter that pours like buttermilk.
Stir in 12 torn curry leaves, 2 finely chopped green chillies, a grated 1-inch piece of ginger and 3 tbsp coriander, then rest the batter for 10 minutes and stir again before each dosa.
Heat a tava over medium-high until hot, then stir the batter well and ladle it from a height around the edges inward so it falls in a thin lacy layer with natural holes; do not spread it.
Drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil over the holes and cook undisturbed for 2-3 minutes until the edges lift and the base is deep golden and crisp.
Fold and remove without flipping if fully crisp, or flip for 30 seconds for extra colour, then stir and repeat with the rest of the batter.
tips: The batter must be watery like thin buttermilk; if it thickens as the semolina swells, thin it back with water or the lace won't form.
Always stir the batter just before ladling, as the semolina and rice flour settle quickly to the bottom.
Keep the tava hot and pour from a height so the batter spatters into the characteristic holes rather than a solid sheet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve straight off the tava, still crackling, with coconut chutney and a small bowl of piping tiffin sambar.

variations.name: Rajasthani Masala Rava Dosa
variations.description: A hearty Rajasthani-style rava dosa where garam masala and coriander powder are toasted into the batter and a spiced onion-tomato masala is spooned across the crisp lace before folding. Cooked in Anveshan Groundnut Oil, it eats almost like a chaat, bold and desert-kitchen warm.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Replaces maida in the batter, giving the masala dosa a nuttier, more filling wholegrain base.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil for crisping the dosa and sauteing the spiced onion masala.

steps: Toast 1 tsp cumin seeds in a dry pan for a minute until aromatic, then tip into a bowl with 1 cup semolina, 0.5 cup rice flour, 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp garam masala, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt.
Whisk in about 3.5 cups water to a thin, pourable buttermilk-like batter and rest for 10 minutes, stirring again before use.

For the masala, heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and saute 1 finely chopped onion for 3 minutes until soft, add 1 chopped tomato and cook 2 minutes more until pulpy, then season lightly and keep warm.
Heat a tava over medium-high, stir the batter and ladle it from a height around the pan so it falls in a thin lacy round with open holes.
Drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over the top and cook for 2-3 minutes until the base turns crisp and deep golden.
Spoon 2 tbsp of the onion-tomato masala across one half, fold the dosa over it and slide out, then repeat with the remaining batter and masala.
tips: Cook the onion masala until quite dry so it doesn't make the crisp dosa go soggy once folded.
Toast the garam masala into the dry mix rather than the wet batter to keep its aroma sharp.
If the first dosa comes out patchy, the tava is too cool; give it another minute to heat before the next pour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of thin garlic-tempered sambar and a dab of fiery red Rajasthani lehsun chutney on the side.

variations.name: Bengali Spicy Rava Dosa
variations.description: An eastern twist where the lacy rava dosa batter is spiked with pounded green chillies, crushed black pepper and the warm heat of grated ginger. Anveshan Mustard Oil gives it an unmistakably Bengali pungency, crisping the holes while the pepper builds a slow, mouth-tingling heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Binds the delicate lace and adds wholegrain body to the peppery batter.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Pungent wood-pressed mustard oil that gives this dosa its sharp, distinctly Bengali edge.

steps: Dry-toast 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1 tsp peppercorns for a minute until fragrant, then pound the pepper coarsely and set aside.
Pound 4 green chillies with a 1.5-inch piece of ginger to a rough paste in the same mortar.

Whisk 1 cup semolina, 0.5 cup rice flour, 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, the toasted cumin, crushed pepper, 0.5 tsp nigella seeds and 1 tsp salt with about 3.5 cups water to a very thin batter, then stir in the chilli-ginger paste, 1 finely chopped small onion and 3 tbsp coriander and rest 10 minutes.
Heat a tava over medium-high and, once hot, ladle the well-stirred batter from a height so it scatters into a thin holey round without spreading.
Drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil over the holes and cook for 2-3 minutes until the lace turns golden and crisp at the edges.
Lift out folded, or flip for 30 seconds for a deeper colour, then stir the batter and repeat for each dosa.
tips: Let the mustard oil warm on the tava until it just smokes faintly before ladling, which softens its raw sting.
Grate rather than chop the ginger so it disperses evenly through the thin batter for consistent warmth.
For extra tingle, keep the peppercorns coarsely crushed rather than powdered so you get little bursts of heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling coconut-curd chutney and a squeeze of lime to offset the mustard-oil pungency.

variations.name: Tamil Cheesy Rava Dosa
variations.description: A modern tiffin-centre favourite from Tamil Nadu where grated cheese is showered over the lacy rava dosa the instant it is poured, melting into the crisp holes for a golden, gooey net. Cooked in Anveshan Coconut Oil for a fragrant South-Indian base, it is a firm hit with children.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Wholegrain binder in place of maida, giving the cheesy dosa a sturdier lace to hold the melt.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil for that unmistakable South-Indian tiffin aroma and a crisp base.

steps: Toast 1 tsp cumin seeds in a dry pan for a minute until fragrant, then combine with 1 cup semolina, 0.5 cup rice flour, 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 tsp black pepper powder and 0.75 tsp salt.
Whisk in about 3.5 cups water to a thin, buttermilk-loose batter, add 10 torn curry leaves, 1 chopped green chilli and 3 tbsp coriander, and rest 10 minutes, stirring before use.
Heat a tava over medium-high and, once hot, ladle the stirred batter from a height so it falls into a thin lacy round with plenty of holes.
Immediately scatter 3 tbsp grated cheese over the wet dosa and drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil around the edges.
Cook covered for 2-3 minutes until the base is crisp and golden and the cheese has melted into the lace, then fold in half.
Slide out and repeat with the remaining batter and cheese, stirring the batter each time before ladling.
tips: Cover the pan briefly so the cheese melts by steam without needing to flip and risk tearing the delicate lace.
Use a firm grating cheese rather than a very soft one, which can slide off the holey surface before it melts.
Grate the cheese fine so it melts quickly in the short cook time and clings to the crisp net.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a mild coconut chutney and, for the children, a small bowl of tomato ketchup on the side.

variations.name: Karnataka Podi Rava Dosa
variations.description: A Bengaluru darshini-style rava dosa dusted generously with fiery molagapodi and finished with ghee so the gunpowder toasts into the crisp lace. The Anveshan Ghee gives a rich, aromatic sheen while the podi lends the salty, garlicky punch that makes this a Karnataka breakfast classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Wholegrain binder that keeps the lace intact under a heavy dusting of podi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: Nutty bilona ghee brushed over the podi so the gunpowder toasts and perfumes the whole dosa.

steps: Dry-toast 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.5 tsp peppercorns for a minute until fragrant, crush the pepper, and mix into 1 cup semolina, 0.5 cup rice flour, 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta and 0.75 tsp salt.
Whisk in about 3.5 cups water to a thin runny batter, stir in 12 torn curry leaves, a grated 1-inch piece of ginger and 3 tbsp coriander, and rest 10 minutes.
Heat a tava over medium-high and ladle the stirred batter from a height so it forms a thin holey round across the pan.
Sprinkle 1 tbsp molagapodi evenly over the wet dosa and drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee over the podi and holes.
Cook for 2-3 minutes until the base is crisp and golden and the ghee has toasted the podi to a fragrant crust.
Fold and lift out without flipping, then stir the batter and repeat, dusting each dosa with fresh podi.
tips: Add the podi to the wet side only, so it sticks to the batter rather than scattering off a set surface.
Adjust the podi quantity to taste; a heaping tablespoon per dosa gives the authentic darshini punch.
Brush a little extra ghee at the end for the glossy, restaurant-style finish and richer aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of thick coconut chutney and hot sambar, the podi-ghee crust needing little else.

variations.name: Classic Rava Kesari
variations.description: The definitive South Indian temple sweet: fine semolina roasted in ghee, swelled soft in saffron-scented water and turned glossy with unrefined khandsari. It scoops in soft, sunset-orange mounds that melt on the tongue, studded with ghee-fried cashews and plump raisins.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the rava to a nutty aroma and gives the finished kesari its signature glossy sheen

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined khandsari melts into a clean, floral sweetness without the harsh edge of white sugar

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm milk to lend the dish its sunset-orange colour and delicate aroma

steps: Soak 20 strands of Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside for 10 minutes, until the milk turns deep gold and fragrant.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadai on low heat, fry 2 tbsp cashews and 1 tbsp raisins until the cashews are pale gold and the raisins plump, about 2 minutes, then scoop them out and reserve.
Add 1 cup fine semolina to the same ghee and roast on low-medium heat, stirring without pause, for 6-7 minutes until it smells nutty and turns light golden; do not let it brown.

Meanwhile bring 2.5 cups water to a rolling boil and pour it into the roasted rava in a slow, steady stream while stirring hard to prevent lumps, then cook 3-4 minutes until the grains swell and drink up the water.
Stir in 0.75 cup Anveshan Khandsari and the saffron milk; the mixture will loosen as the khandsari melts, then thicken again over 4-5 minutes on low heat.
Add 0.5 tsp cardamom powder, 1 pinch salt, the reserved nuts and a final 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, and cook 2 minutes until the kesari turns glossy and pulls cleanly from the sides of the pan.
tips: If lumps form the moment you add the water, mash them against the side of the pan with the back of the ladle at once, before the rava sets and they turn stubborn.
Roast the rava patiently on low heat; a rushed high flame browns the outside while leaving a raw, grainy centre.
For a richer festive set, swap 0.5 cup of the water for hot whole milk, which gives a creamier, softer scoop.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm in scooped mounds beside a peppery upma for the classic Tamil-Karnataka 'chow-chow bath' plate; a few extra saffron strands scattered on top make it festive.

variations.name: Karnataka Pineapple Kesari Bath
variations.description: The lavish Bengaluru darshini sweet, drenched in ghee and flecked with sweet-tart pineapple. Whole cloves bloomed in ghee and a whisper of edible camphor give it a temple-tiffin fragrance you won't find in the plain version, while extra khandsari keeps it almost wet and spoonable.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: kesari bath is unapologetically ghee-rich, which gives its melt-in-mouth darshini texture

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: keeps the sweet clear and clean so the pineapple and saffron colours shine through

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: the traditional colour of kesari bath, bloomed in a spoon of warm milk

steps: Bloom 15 strands of Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk for 10 minutes, until it colours deeply.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and crackle 2 cloves for 20 seconds until fragrant, then fry 2 tbsp cashews to golden, about 2 minutes, lifting out the cashews while leaving the cloves in the ghee.
Tip in 1 cup chiroti rava and roast on low heat for 5-6 minutes until it turns light and smells toasty, taking care not to colour it.

Add 0.5 cup finely chopped pineapple and sauté 2 minutes until it releases its fragrance, then pour in 2.5 cups boiling water in a steady stream, stirring hard to avoid lumps, and cook 4 minutes until the rava is soft.
Stir in 1 cup Anveshan Khandsari, the saffron milk and 1 pinch edible camphor; the mixture loosens, then thickens over 5 minutes on low heat.
Finish with 0.5 tsp cardamom, the fried cashews and the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, cooking 2-3 minutes until glossy and it leaves the pan sides clean.
tips: Use ripe, sweet pineapple; sour fruit can split the ghee and leave the kesari watery.
The full 1 cup khandsari is what gives kesari bath its almost-wet, spoonable body, so resist trimming it or the sweet sets dry.
A single pinch of edible camphor is authentic to Bengaluru tiffin rooms, but any more will turn the dish bitter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot as one half of a 'chow chow bath' plate next to a peppery vegetable khara bath; the sweet-and-savoury contrast on one plate is the quintessential Bengaluru breakfast.

variations.name: Kerala Jaggery-Coconut Rava Kesari
variations.description: A sadhya-style semolina sweet where earthy Anveshan jaggery replaces sugar and toasted fresh coconut is folded through, giving an amber, caramel-deep flavour. A pinch of dry ginger, the Kerala signature, cuts the richness and makes it sit lightly after a heavy meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Kerala kitchens finish the rava with generous ghee for a coconut-scented richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: molten jaggery lends an earthy caramel depth that marries beautifully with coconut

steps: In 0.5 cup of the water, melt 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder over low heat until fully dissolved, about 3 minutes, then strain through a sieve to remove grit and keep the syrup warm.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai and fry 2 tbsp cashews, 2 tbsp coconut slivers and 1 tbsp raisins until golden and the coconut smells toasty, about 3 minutes, then remove and reserve.
Add 1 more tbsp Anveshan Ghee to the pan with 0.5 cup grated coconut and sauté 2 minutes until fragrant, then add 1 cup semolina and roast on low heat for 6 minutes until pale gold and nutty.
Pour the remaining 1.5 cups hot water into the rava in a thin stream while stirring vigorously to keep it lump-free, and cook 3 minutes until the grains swell soft.
Lower the heat and stir in the warm jaggery syrup, stirring 4-5 minutes as the mixture darkens to amber and thickens; adding jaggery only after the rava is cooked keeps it from turning hard.
Fold in 0.5 tsp cardamom, 0.25 tsp dry ginger powder, the reserved nuts and a final 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, cooking 2 minutes until glossy and pulling from the sides.
tips: Always cook the rava soft in water first and add jaggery last; jaggery introduced too early toughens the semolina.
Strain the melted jaggery, as unrefined blocks often carry sand and fibre that would ruin the smooth texture.
The pinch of dry ginger is a very Kerala touch that both aids digestion and stops the sweet from cloying.
variations.servingSuggestion: Offer warm as the sweet course of an Onam sadhya, just before the payasam; it also firms up overnight into fudgy squares perfect for a lunchbox.

variations.name: Andhra Roasted Cashew Kesari
variations.description: A robust, halwa-like take where coarse rava is browned a shade deeper in extra ghee until it smells almost like roasted grain. Loaded with a generous hand of cashews and a whisper of nutmeg, it is denser and more intensely nutty than the delicate southern classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Andhra cooks brown the rava in extra ghee for a deep, almost halwa-like nuttiness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: balances the toasty edge of the well-browned rava with a clean sweetness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: adds colour and aroma that stand out against the darker roasted grain

steps: Bloom 15 strands of Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk for 10 minutes until richly coloured.
In 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, fry 4 tbsp cashews and 2 tbsp raisins to deep gold over low heat, about 3 minutes, then lift them out, leaving the flavoured ghee behind.
Tip in 1 cup coarse rava and roast patiently on low-medium heat for 8-9 minutes until it turns a shade darker than usual and smells strongly nutty; this deep roast is the Andhra signature.
Stream in 2.5 cups boiling water while whisking to break any lumps, then simmer 4-5 minutes until every grain is plump and tender.
Mix in 0.75 cup Anveshan Khandsari, the saffron milk, 0.5 tsp cardamom and 1 pinch nutmeg, stirring 5 minutes on low heat as it thickens and the ghee begins to surface.
Fold the fried cashews and raisins back in with the last 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and cook 2 minutes until rich, glossy and just clumping together.
tips: The darker roast walks a fine line; pull the rava off the heat the instant it smells nutty, as a scorched grain turns the whole batch bitter.
Coarse bombay rava holds its grain far better for this robust style than fine sooji.
Rest the kesari covered for 5 minutes before serving so the grains drink up the last of the ghee and soften fully.
variations.servingSuggestion: In Andhra homes this is offered warm as festival prasadam and cut into wedges once cooled; a small bowl of plain curd on the side tempers its richness.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Banana Sheera
variations.description: The soft, milk-cooked semolina offering made for Satyanarayan puja, sweetened gently with khandsari and enriched with mashed ripe banana that caramelises into the grain. Cooking it in milk rather than water gives a wetter, more tender set than a firm kesari, with a warm hum of nutmeg.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: puja sheera is enriched with ghee for a soft, offering-worthy texture

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: dissolves smoothly into the milk for a gentle, prasad-like sweetness

steps: Warm 1.5 cups whole milk with 1 cup water together and keep it just below a simmer beside the stove.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and fry 2 tbsp cashews and 1 tbsp raisins to golden over low heat, about 2 minutes, then set them aside.
Add 1 cup fine semolina to the same ghee and roast gently for 6 minutes until pale gold and fragrant, then stir in 1 mashed ripe banana and cook 2 minutes until it smells caramelised.
Pour the hot milk-and-water into the rava in a slow stream, stirring continuously to keep it silky and lump-free, and cook 3-4 minutes until thick.
Add 0.75 cup Anveshan Khandsari, 0.5 tsp cardamom and 1 pinch nutmeg; the sheera slackens, then firms again over 4 minutes on low heat.
Finish with the fried nuts and the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, cooking 2 minutes until glossy and soft enough to fall from the spoon in ribbons.
tips: Use a very ripe, spotty banana; an under-ripe one stays fibrous and refuses to melt into the sheera.
Cooking with milk rather than only water gives the wetter, softer set that sets Maharashtrian sheera apart from a firm kesari.
Make it just before serving, as banana sheera stiffens noticeably as it cools.
variations.servingSuggestion: Share warm as prasad after the Satyanarayan puja, traditionally on a banana leaf or steel plate; a dusting of cardamom and a single cashew crowning each portion is the customary finish.

variations.name: Classic Sabudana Vada
variations.description: The beloved Maharashtrian fasting fritter: soaked sago pearls, mashed potato and coarsely crushed roasted peanuts, fried into crisp golden patties. Crunchy outside and pleasantly chewy within, these vadas are the star of any upvas thali and just as good with evening tea.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: peanuts roasted in a little bilona ghee turn nuttier and more fragrant than dry-roasted

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for deep-frying; keeps the vadas crisp and light without a heavy aftertaste

steps: Rinse 1 cup sago until the water runs clear, then soak in just enough water to cover by a finger for 5 hours until each pearl is soft and squashes easily between two fingers; drain off any excess.
Roast 0.5 cup peanuts in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee on low heat for 4 minutes until they smell nutty, cool, rub off the skins, and coarsely crush them.

Boil 2 medium potatoes until soft, peel and mash them smooth, then combine with the drained sago, crushed peanuts, 3 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp cumin seeds, 3 tbsp coriander, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 1 tsp rock salt.
Mix well and knead lightly into a soft dough that holds shape; divide into 10 portions and press each into a flat round patty about 1.5 cm thick.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to medium, around 170C, so the vadas cook through without browning too fast.
Slide in 4 or 5 vadas at a time and fry for 4 to 5 minutes, turning once, until crisp and pale gold on both sides; drain on a rack.
tips: The soaking is everything: too little water leaves hard centres, too much makes the vadas absorb oil, so soak just till a pearl mashes easily.
If the mixture cracks while shaping, mash in one more boiled potato to bind it without adding any flour.
Fry a test vada first; if it disintegrates, the mix is too wet, so rest it uncovered for 15 minutes before frying the rest.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a cooling peanut-curd chutney and a wedge of lemon, the classic Maharashtrian upvas pairing.

variations.name: Jammu & Kashmir Crispy Sabudana Vada
variations.description: This northern hill-station take rolls the sago patties in fine breadcrumbs for a bakery-crisp shell that survives the cold mountain air. A pinch of dried mint and crushed walnut give it a distinctly Kashmiri fragrance and a richer crunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: whisked into a slurry so the breadcrumbs grip the soft sago patty firmly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for deep-frying the crumb-coated vadas to an even golden brown

steps: Soak 1 cup sago in water to just cover for 5 hours until soft, then drain thoroughly.
Dry-roast 0.25 cup peanuts and 0.25 cup walnuts for 4 minutes, cool and crush them coarsely so you keep some texture.
Boil and mash 2 medium potatoes, then combine with the drained sago, crushed nuts, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp dried mint, 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1 tsp salt into a soft dough.
Shape into 10 flat patties. Whisk 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta with 6 tbsp water into a thin slurry, dip each patty in it, then press firmly into 1 cup bread crumbs.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to medium, about 170C, and lower in the coated vadas a few at a time.
Fry for 4 to 5 minutes, turning once, until the breadcrumb shell is crisp and golden; lift onto a rack to drain.
tips: Crush the walnuts only coarsely, as fine powder makes the mixture oily and heavy.
The khapli slurry must be thin enough to coat but thick enough to help crumbs stick, so adjust with a little water if needed.
Coat the vadas and chill them for 20 minutes before frying so the crust sets and does not crack in the oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a walnut-mint chutney and hot noon chai for a cosy Kashmiri winter snack.

variations.name: Himachal Pradesh Spicy Sabudana Vada
variations.description: A warming hill version laced with freshly cracked black pepper and pahadi ginger to fight the mountain chill. The pepper gives a deep, slow heat that suits the cold, and a little grated ginger cuts through the richness of the peanuts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: peanuts roasted in bilona ghee gain a toasty depth that stands up to the pepper

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for deep-frying; a neutral base that lets the pepper heat shine

steps: Soak 1 cup sago in just enough water to cover for 5 hours until soft and drain well.
Roast 0.5 cup peanuts in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee on low for 4 minutes until fragrant, cool and crush coarsely, then coarsely crack 1.5 tsp black pepper in a mortar.

Boil and mash 2 medium potatoes, then combine with the sago, crushed peanuts, cracked pepper, 1.5 inch grated ginger, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp cumin seeds, 3 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp rock salt.
Knead into a firm dough and press into 10 thick patties about 1.5 cm high.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to medium, around 170C, ready for frying.
Fry the vadas 4 or 5 at a time for 4 to 5 minutes, turning, until crisp and golden with the pepper aroma rising; drain on a rack and dust with a little extra cracked pepper.
tips: Grate the ginger finely so it melts into the mixture rather than leaving fibrous strands.
Crack the pepper fresh and coarse for pockets of warmth in every bite.
Serve straight from the pan, as pepper-spiced vadas taste best when the heat is still lively and the shell crisp.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a sharp coriander-ginger chutney and a cup of pahadi ginger chai to warm up on a cold evening.

variations.name: Uttarakhand Masala Sabudana Vada
variations.description: The Garhwali masala vada folds warm garam masala and roasted coriander powder into the sago base, along with a handful of local greens. Aromatic and festive, it turns the humble fasting fritter into a fuller-flavoured snack for family gatherings.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: used to bloom the garam masala for a rounder, more aromatic masala base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for deep-frying the spiced patties to a rich golden crust

steps: Soak 1 cup sago in just enough water for 5 hours until soft and drain thoroughly.
Dry-roast 1.5 tsp coriander powder for 30 seconds until fragrant. Warm 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan and bloom 1 tsp garam masala in it for 20 seconds until aromatic, then cool.
Dry-roast and coarsely crush 0.5 cup peanuts. Boil and mash 2 medium potatoes.

Combine the sago, mashed potato, crushed peanuts, roasted coriander powder, bloomed garam masala, 0.5 cup chopped spring onion greens, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1 tsp salt into a soft dough, then shape into 10 patties.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to medium, about 170C, and lower in the patties in batches.
Fry for 4 to 5 minutes, turning once, until crisp and deep golden; drain on a rack and serve warm.
tips: Blooming the garam masala in ghee before mixing gives a far rounder aroma than stirring it in raw.
Add the spring onion greens last so they stay green and do not release water into the mixture.
If shaping ahead, keep the patties covered with a damp cloth so the sago surface does not dry and crack.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a tangy tomato-jaggery chutney and sliced radish for a hearty Garhwali evening plate.

variations.name: Odisha Tava Sabudana Vada
variations.description: This Odia adaptation shallow-cooks the sago patties on a flat tava with mustard oil for a lighter, less-oily result. A tempering of curry leaves and mustard seeds gives the vadas an eastern coastal aroma and a delicate crisp lace at the edges.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: kneaded in as a binder so the flatter patties hold together on the tava

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: brushed over the tava for the pungent eastern-Indian aroma that defines this version

steps: Soak 1 cup sago in just enough water for 5 hours until soft, then drain well.

Heat 1 tsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil in a small pan until smoking, lower the heat, add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 2 sprigs curry leaves and let them splutter for 20 seconds, then cool this tempering.

Dry-roast and crush 0.5 cup peanuts. Boil and mash 2 medium potatoes, then combine with the sago, crushed peanuts, the cooled tempering, 2 chopped green chillies, 3 tbsp coriander, 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1 tsp salt.
Knead in 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta until the mixture is firm, then shape into 10 flat, thin patties.
Heat a tava on medium and brush with 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil, place the patties and cook for 4 minutes until the underside is crisp and lacy.
Flip, drizzle a little more mustard oil around each patty, and cook the second side for 3 to 4 minutes until golden and cooked through.
tips: Always smoke the mustard oil once before using so its raw pungency mellows into a pleasant aroma.
Keep the patties thin for the tava so they cook through without the deep-fry oil bath.
The khapli atta binder is essential here, as tava-cooked sago patties need extra structure to flip cleanly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coconut-mustard chutney and a bowl of curd rice for a light Odia-style tiffin.

variations.name: Classic Tahri
variations.description: The beloved Awadhi one-pot rice where potatoes and mixed vegetables are simmered with turmeric-tinted basmati and whole garam spices. Homely, golden and lightly spiced, tahri is the vegetarian answer to biryani, cooked in a single pot with everyday pantry staples.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee gives tahri its comforting home-style richness and toasts the whole spices

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain so the grains cook long and fluffy.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 bay leaf, 3 cardamom pods and 4 cloves and let them sizzle 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 2 sliced onions and fry 6 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger garlic paste and cook 1 minute until the raw smell fades.
Add 2 cubed potatoes, 1 diced carrot, 0.5 cup peas and 1 chopped tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp chilli powder and 1.5 tsp salt, sautéing 5 minutes until the tomato softens.
Add the drained rice and toast gently for 2 minutes, then pour in 2.5 cups hot water and bring to a rolling boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 15 minutes until the water is absorbed and the potatoes are tender, then rest 5 minutes and fluff before serving.
tips: Cut the potatoes and carrots evenly so they cook through in the same time as the rice.
Do not stir once the water goes in, or the rice will turn mushy; just fluff at the end.
A squeeze of lemon at the end brightens the earthy, turmeric-rich flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot with a bowl of cooling boondi raita and a wedge of lemon and green chilli on the side.

variations.name: Kashmiri Tahri
variations.description: A regal Kashmiri version scented with fennel, dry ginger and saffron, coloured a warm russet by Kashmiri chilli rather than turmeric. The aromatic whole spices and saffron soak give it the delicate perfume of Valley cooking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee blooms the Kashmiri whole spices and carries the saffron aroma through the rice

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: A saffron soak lends the golden hue and floral fragrance signature to Kashmiri rice

steps: Soak a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk and set aside while you rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat, add 3 green cardamom, 1 black cardamom, 4 cloves, 1 inch cinnamon and 1 bay leaf and sizzle 30 seconds until aromatic.
Add 2 cubed potatoes and fry 4 minutes until the edges turn light gold, then stir in 1 tsp fennel powder, 0.5 tsp dry ginger powder and 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder off the heat for 10 seconds.
Add the drained rice and 1.5 tsp salt, toast gently for 2 minutes, then pour in 2.5 cups hot water and bring to a boil.
Drizzle the saffron milk over the top, cover, and cook on the lowest heat for 15 minutes until the water is absorbed and the potatoes are soft.
Rest covered for 5 minutes, then fluff gently to reveal the streaks of saffron-gold rice and serve warm.
tips: Fennel and dry ginger are the backbone of Kashmiri flavour, so measure them accurately.
Bloom the saffron in warm milk, never boiling, to draw out colour without bitterness.
Kashmiri chilli gives colour with gentle heat, so do not substitute a hotter variety.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of Kashmiri-style dahi churned with walnut and mint for an authentic Valley meal.

variations.name: Himachali Rajma Tahri
variations.description: A hearty hill version from Himachal that folds soft-cooked rajma into the tahri, turning it into a wholesome single-pot meal. Cooked in wood-pressed mustard oil, it carries the rustic, warming character of Himachali pahadi kitchens.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil gives this pahadi tahri its warming, robust hill-country flavour

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes and drain; keep 1 cup pre-cooked soft rajma ready.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pot over medium-high heat until it just smokes, then lower the heat and add 1 tsp cumin seeds to splutter for 30 seconds.
Add 2 sliced onions and fry 6 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp chilli powder and 1.5 tsp salt, cooking 5 minutes until the tomatoes turn pulpy and the oil surfaces.
Add 2 cubed potatoes and the cooked rajma, toss 2 minutes, then add the drained rice and 0.5 tsp garam masala and toast gently for 2 minutes.
Pour in 2.5 cups hot water, bring to a boil, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 15 minutes, then rest 5 minutes and fluff before serving.
tips: Use fully soft-cooked rajma so it holds shape but melts pleasantly into the rice.
Smoke the mustard oil first to mellow its pungency before the tempering goes in.
Small red pahadi rajma from the hills cooks softer and sweeter if you can find it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a sharp onion-tomato cachumber and a spoon of homemade white butter melting on top.

variations.name: Uttarakhand Bhatt Tahri
variations.description: A Kumaoni-inspired tahri enriched with nutty black soybean (bhatt) and local greens, reflecting the protein-rich hill cooking of Uttarakhand. Earthy, wholesome and lightly spiced, it turns humble rice into a nourishing mountain meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Mustard oil is the everyday cooking fat of Kumaoni kitchens and anchors this earthy tahri

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes and drain; keep 0.75 cup pre-cooked black soybean ready.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it smokes, lower the heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them darken for 30 seconds.
Add 1 chopped large onion with crushed 1.5 inch ginger and 6 garlic cloves, frying 6 minutes until golden and fragrant.
Add 2 cubed potatoes, 1 cup chopped spinach, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp chilli powder and 1.5 tsp salt, sautéing 4 minutes until the spinach wilts.
Stir in the cooked black soybean and the drained rice, toast gently for 2 minutes, then pour in 2.5 cups hot water and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 15 minutes until the rice is tender and the beans are soft, then rest 5 minutes and fluff before serving.
tips: Pressure-cook the black soybean until fully tender first, as it is denser than most beans.
Add the spinach with the potatoes so it collapses into the masala and colours the rice.
A final drizzle of raw mustard oil, common in the hills, adds an authentic sharp finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of tangy bhang-jeera chutney or plain curd for a true Kumaoni-style plate.

variations.name: Odisha Ghee Tarkari Tahri
variations.description: An Odia-style tahri fragrant with the region's beloved panch phutana five-spice and finished with a generous spoon of ghee, much like the ghanta tarkari it echoes. Mild, buttery and vegetable-laden, it is temple-kitchen comfort food.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee is stirred in Jagannath-temple style to give this tahri its buttery aroma

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes and drain so it stays fluffy.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat, add 1 tsp panch phutana and 1 bay leaf and let the seeds crackle for 40 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 chopped onion, grated 1 inch ginger and 3 slit green chillies, sautéing 4 minutes until the onion softens.
Add 2 cubed potatoes, 1 cup cauliflower florets, 1 diced carrot and 0.5 cup peas with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp salt, tossing 4 minutes until glossy.
Add the drained rice, toast gently for 2 minutes, then pour in 2.5 cups hot water and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 15 minutes until the vegetables and rice are tender, rest 5 minutes, garnish with 2 tbsp coriander and serve.
tips: Panch phutana is a whole-seed mix, so bloom it fully in hot ghee to release its aroma.
Cut cauliflower into medium florets so it stays intact rather than turning to mush.
A final spoon of raw ghee stirred through at the end is the classic Odia finishing touch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling dahi-baigana or a simple tomato khajuri chutney for a comforting Odia meal.

variations.name: Classic Tomato Rice
variations.description: A tangy, one-pot South Indian tomato rice where ripe tomatoes are cooked down into a glossy masala and tossed with fluffy basmati. Bright, mildly spiced and deeply comforting, it is the quintessential lunchbox rice that tastes even better once the flavours settle.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee gives the tomato masala a rounded richness that balances the acidity

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups basmati rice, soak 20 minutes, then cook with 3 cups water until each grain is separate, about 15 minutes, and spread on a plate to cool.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide pan over medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them splutter for 40 seconds until fragrant.
Add 12 curry leaves and 1 finely sliced large onion, sautéing 5 minutes until the onion turns soft and pale gold.

Stir in 1 tbsp ginger garlic paste and cook 1 minute until the raw smell fades, then add 4 finely chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1.25 tsp salt.
Cook the masala on medium heat for 10 minutes, mashing occasionally, until the tomatoes collapse into a thick glossy paste that leaves ghee at the edges.
Fold in the cooled rice and 0.5 tsp garam masala gently until every grain is coated, warm through for 2 minutes, then garnish with 3 tbsp coriander and serve.
tips: Cool the rice before mixing so it stays fluffy and does not clump into the masala.
Cook the tomatoes until the ghee separates, as this is the sign the raw acidity has gone.
A pinch of jaggery can be added if your tomatoes are very sour, to balance without making it sweet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a bowl of cooling boondi raita and a crisp fried papad or potato chips on the side.

variations.name: Kerala Coconut Tomato Rice
variations.description: Kerala's coastal version simmers the tomato masala in fragrant coconut oil and finishes with fresh coconut and a hint of coconut milk for a mellow, silky bowl. The sweetness of coconut tempers the tomato's tang in true Malabar style.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed coconut oil is the soul of Kerala cooking and perfumes the whole dish

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, cook with 3 cups water until fluffy, about 15 minutes, then cool on a wide plate.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil over medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 15 curry leaves and let them crackle for 40 seconds until intensely aromatic.
Add 1 sliced large onion, 3 slit green chillies and grated 1 inch ginger, sautéing 5 minutes until the onion softens and turns translucent.
Stir in 4 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt, cooking 10 minutes until the masala thickens and darkens.
Add 0.5 cup grated coconut and 0.25 cup coconut milk, simmering 3 minutes until the mixture is creamy and the raw coconut smell disappears.
Fold in the cooled rice until evenly coated, warm through for 2 minutes, garnish with 3 tbsp coriander and serve.
tips: Add coconut milk on low heat and do not boil hard, or it may split and turn grainy.
Lightly toast the grated coconut first if you want a deeper, nuttier flavour.
This rice pairs beautifully with pappadam crushed over the top just before eating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a tangy Kerala-style pachadi or a simple cucumber-yogurt side to complement the coconut richness.

variations.name: Karnataka Vangi-Style Tomato Rice
variations.description: Karnataka's take borrows the fragrant home-ground masala of vangi bhath, roasting whole spices, coconut and channa dal into a nutty powder that coats the tomato rice. It is more aromatic and complex than the everyday version, with a signature roasted depth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the traditional cooking fat for Karnataka rice dishes

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of ghee lifts the roasted masala aroma

steps: Rinse, soak and cook 1.5 cups basmati rice with 3 cups water until fluffy, about 15 minutes, then spread to cool.
Dry-roast 1 tbsp coriander seeds, 4 dry red chillies, 1 tbsp channa dal, 1 inch cinnamon and 3 tbsp grated coconut on low heat for 4 minutes until golden and fragrant, then grind to a coarse powder.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat, add 12 curry leaves and 1 sliced large onion, frying 6 minutes until the onion is soft and light brown.
Add 4 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt, cooking 10 minutes until the tomatoes break down into a thick pulp.
Stir in the freshly ground masala powder and cook 3 minutes until the mixture smells deeply roasted and the oil surfaces.
Fold in the cooled rice and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until glossy and coated, warm 2 minutes, then finish with 3 tbsp coriander and serve.
tips: Roast the masala on low heat and stir constantly so the coconut and dal brown evenly without scorching.
Grind the masala slightly coarse for a pleasant texture rather than a smooth paste.
The masala powder keeps a week in an airtight jar, so make a double batch for quick weekday rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a dollop of thick curd and a fried sandige (rice crisp) for an authentic Karnataka plate.

variations.name: Andhra Fiery Tomato Rice
variations.description: A boldly spicy Andhra version built on a paste of dry red chillies, garlic and tamarind that gives it heat and a signature tang. Sesame oil and a peanut-garlic finish make it a robust, fiery bowl that stands up to strong pickles.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed sesame oil brings the earthy pungency typical of Andhra cooking

steps: Cook 1.5 cups soaked basmati rice with 3 cups water until fluffy, about 15 minutes, then cool it on a wide plate.
Grind 6 dry red chillies, 8 garlic cloves and 1 tsp tamarind paste with a splash of water into a coarse fiery paste.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil over medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tsp cumin seeds and 12 curry leaves and let them crackle for 40 seconds.
Add 1 sliced large onion and fry 5 minutes until golden, then stir in the chilli-garlic paste and cook 3 minutes until the raw garlic smell fades.
Add 5 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt, cooking 12 minutes until the masala reduces to a thick, oil-flecked paste.
Fold in the cooled rice and 3 tbsp crushed roasted peanuts until evenly coated, warm 2 minutes, garnish with 3 tbsp coriander and serve.
tips: Adjust the number of dry chillies to your heat tolerance; Byadgi chillies give colour with less burn.
The tamarind is essential to balance the heat, so do not skip it even in a hurry.
Add the peanuts last so they stay crunchy against the soft rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain thick curd and a wedge of raw onion to cool the palate between fiery bites.

variations.name: Telangana Tamarind Tomato Rice
variations.description: This Telangana-style bowl leans on tangy tamarind and roasted sesame for a rustic, earthy flavour rooted in the region's love of sour, robust food. A sesame-peanut podi stirred through at the end gives it a distinctive nutty coating.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Sesame oil doubles the nutty depth alongside the sesame podi in this Telangana bowl

steps: Cook 1.5 cups soaked basmati rice with 3 cups water until fluffy, about 15 minutes, then cool on a wide plate.
Dry-roast 2 tbsp sesame seeds and 2 tbsp roasted peanuts on low heat for 3 minutes until golden, cool, and grind to a coarse podi.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil over medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal and fry 40 seconds until the dal is golden.
Add 12 curry leaves and 1 chopped onion, sautéing 5 minutes until soft, then add 4 chopped tomatoes, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt.
Stir in 1.5 tsp tamarind paste and cook 10 minutes until the masala turns thick, glossy and tangy with the oil surfacing.
Fold in the cooled rice and the sesame-peanut podi until every grain is coated, warm 2 minutes, garnish with 3 tbsp coriander and serve.
tips: Grind the sesame podi coarse so it clings to the rice instead of turning oily and pasty.
Taste and balance the tamarind with a tiny pinch of jaggery if it becomes too sour.
The podi can be made ahead and sprinkled over plain rice with ghee for a quick meal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with fried green chillies and a spoon of thick set curd to round off the tangy, nutty flavours.

variations.name: Classic Veg Cutlet
variations.description: The tea-time favourite from every Indian household kitchen: a soft mixed-vegetable and potato core spiked with green chilli and coriander, cased in golden breadcrumbs. Crisp and shattering outside, fluffy and mildly spiced within, it is the cutlet everyone learns to make first.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: whisked with water into a slurry to help the breadcrumbs cling without any maida

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for shallow-frying; its high smoke point keeps the crust crisp and never greasy

steps: Boil 3 medium potatoes until fork-tender, about 15 minutes, then peel and mash them smooth while still warm. Steam 1.5 cups mixed vegetables until just soft, about 8 minutes, and lightly crush them.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a pan on medium and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds until fragrant, then add 1 finely chopped onion and 2 chopped green chillies and saute until the onion turns soft and pale gold, about 3 minutes.

Add the mashed potato and crushed vegetables to the pan with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt, mix well and cook on low for 4 minutes until the mixture pulls away from the sides and holds together; fold in 3 tbsp coriander leaves and cool completely.
Whisk 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta with 6 tbsp water into a smooth, thin slurry. Divide the cooled mixture into 8 portions and shape each into a flat oval tikki about 1 cm thick.
Dip each tikki into the khapli slurry, then roll it firmly in 1 cup bread crumbs to coat all sides evenly, pressing gently so the crumbs stick.

Heat the remaining Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a flat pan to medium-hot (a crumb should sizzle at once) and shallow-fry the cutlets in batches for 2 to 3 minutes per side until deep golden and crisp; drain on a rack, not paper, to stay crunchy.
tips: Make sure the potato mixture is completely cool and dry before shaping, otherwise the cutlets absorb oil and turn soggy.
If the mixture feels too wet to shape, work in 2 extra tablespoons of bread crumbs rather than more flour to keep the inside light.
You can shape and crumb the cutlets a day ahead and refrigerate on a tray; fry straight from cold for the crispest result.
variations.servingSuggestion: Stack on a platter with lemon wedges and a sprinkle of chaat masala, and serve alongside a mint-coriander chutney and sweet tamarind chutney for dipping.

variations.name: Kerala Crispy Veg Cutlet
variations.description: Kerala's bakery-style cutlet leans on coconut oil and a fistful of curry leaves for its unmistakable coastal aroma. Rolled in coarse breadcrumbs and shallow-fried till mahogany, these ovals are the ones sold hot at every Thattukada tea stall.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: makes the egg-free binding slurry that seals in the beetroot colour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the defining Kerala fat; fry in it for the sweet, nutty coconut fragrance that sets these apart

steps: Boil 3 medium potatoes until soft and mash them. Separately boil 1 grated small beetroot and 1 grated carrot for 5 minutes until tender, then squeeze out excess water so the mixture stays firm.

Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a kadai on medium, drop in 2 sprigs curry leaves and let them splutter for 15 seconds, then add 8 sliced shallots, 3 slit green chillies and 1 inch minced ginger and fry until the shallots turn glassy and gold, about 4 minutes.

Tip in the potato, beetroot and carrot with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp garam masala and 1.25 tsp salt, and cook on low for 5 minutes, stirring, until it forms a firm rose-pink dough that leaves the pan; spread on a plate to cool.
Whisk 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta with 6 tbsp water to a pouring slurry. Roll the cooled mixture into 8 equal balls and flatten each into a thick oval between your palms.
Coat each oval in the khapli slurry and press it into 1 cup coarse bread crumbs until fully jacketed, giving a second dip-and-crumb for extra crunch if you like.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil until shimmering and shallow-fry the cutlets for about 3 minutes a side until crisp and deeply browned; lift onto a wire rack to drain.
tips: Wear gloves or oil your palms when handling the beetroot mixture to avoid staining your hands pink.
Coconut oil solidifies as it cools, so keep the pan on steady medium heat to avoid the cutlets sitting in cold fat and going oily.
The double-crumb coating can be done ahead and the cutlets frozen; fry from frozen adding an extra minute per side.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve Kerala style with sliced onion rings soaked in vinegar, a wedge of lime and strong milky chai on the side.

variations.name: Karnataka Spicy Veg Cutlet
variations.description: This Bengaluru darshini-style cutlet turns up the heat with freshly crushed black pepper and a hint of roasted gram. Pepper gives a warm, lingering bite that is quite different from chilli heat, making these cutlets a favourite with filter coffee.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: used as the crumb-binding slurry, adding a nutty wholewheat backnote to the pepper

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: neutral wood-pressed oil that lets the sharp pepper flavour lead

steps: Boil and mash 3 medium potatoes. Steam 1 cup green peas and 0.5 cup sweet corn for 6 minutes, then coarsely mash the peas while leaving the corn kernels whole for texture.
Coarsely crush 1.5 tsp black pepper in a mortar so you get uneven, aromatic flecks rather than fine powder.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on medium, saute 1 finely chopped large onion and 2 chopped green chillies for 3 minutes until soft, then stir in the crushed pepper and 2 tbsp roasted gram flour and cook 1 minute until the gram smells toasty.
Add the potato, peas and corn with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt, mix into a firm mass over low heat for 4 minutes, fold through 3 tbsp coriander, and cool fully on a tray.
Whisk 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta with 6 tbsp water to a slurry, shape the mixture into 8 round patties, dip each in the slurry and roll in 1 cup bread crumbs.

Shallow-fry in hot Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil for 2 to 3 minutes per side until crisp and golden with the pepper aroma rising; drain on a rack and finish with a light dusting of extra crushed pepper.
tips: Crush the pepper fresh just before cooking; pre-ground pepper loses the fragrant heat that defines this version.
The roasted gram flour tightens the mixture, so if it feels stiff add a spoon of warm milk to keep the centre soft.
These are best served within twenty minutes; reheat leftovers in a hot oven, never a microwave, to bring back the crunch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a cooling coconut chutney and a small cup of South Indian filter coffee for the full darshini experience.

variations.name: Andhra Masala Veg Cutlet
variations.description: The Andhra take is unapologetically robust, layering garam masala and roasted coriander powder over a fiery green-chilli base. A squeeze of lime and a scatter of fried curry leaves give these masala cutlets their bold, spice-market punch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: binds the crumb crust and stands up to the heavy masala without turning gummy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: carries the deep-fried spice flavour cleanly and drains off well

steps: Boil and mash 3 medium potatoes. Steam 1 cup finely chopped cauliflower for 6 minutes, then mash it and squeeze out any moisture so the mixture is not watery.
Dry-roast 1.5 tsp coriander powder in a small pan for 30 seconds until fragrant to deepen its flavour, then set aside.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil, add 1 chopped large onion and 4 chopped green chillies and fry 3 minutes, stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until raw smell goes, then add the roasted coriander powder, 1 tsp garam masala, 0.5 tsp turmeric and cook 30 seconds.
Fold in the potato and cauliflower with 1.25 tsp salt and cook on low for 4 minutes into a firm masala dough, finish with 1 tbsp lemon juice, and spread out to cool completely.
Whisk 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta with 6 tbsp water, shape the mixture into 8 thick discs, coat each in the slurry and press into 1 cup bread crumbs.
Shallow-fry in hot Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil for 2 to 3 minutes each side until crisp and dark golden; drain on a rack and serve blazing hot.
tips: Roasting the coriander powder for just half a minute is the secret to the aromatic Andhra masala depth, so do not skip it.
Add the lemon juice off the heat; boiling it away flattens the bright, tangy lift this cutlet needs.
For a lunchbox version, shape smaller and shallow-fry a shade lighter so they hold up till midday without hardening.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a fiery Andhra gongura or tomato chutney and thin onion rings, with extra lime on the side to cut the spice.

variations.name: Telangana Tava Veg Cutlet
variations.description: A lighter, everyday Telangana version cooked on a flat tava with just a film of oil instead of deep-frying. The patties develop a lace of crisp golden edges while staying soft and moist inside, making them an easy, less-oily tiffin.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: kneaded straight into the mixture as a wholesome binder so no separate coating is needed

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: brushed onto the tava a little at a time for a light, everyday shallow-cook

steps: Boil and mash 2 medium potatoes. Grate 1 cup bottle gourd, squeeze out its water thoroughly, and steam 0.5 cup peas for 5 minutes then lightly mash them.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sunflower Oil on a tava, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then soften 1 chopped medium onion and 2 chopped green chillies for 3 minutes.
Combine the potato, squeezed bottle gourd and peas with the fried onion, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp salt and 3 tbsp coriander in a bowl.
Knead in 4 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta and 0.5 cup bread crumbs until the mixture is firm enough to shape; rest it for 5 minutes so the atta absorbs moisture, then form 8 flat patties.
Heat the tava on medium and brush with 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sunflower Oil, place the patties and cook for 4 minutes until the underside is crisp and lacy.
Flip the patties, drizzle a little more oil around the edges, and cook the second side for 3 to 4 minutes until golden and cooked through; press gently with the spatula for even browning.
tips: Squeeze the grated bottle gourd really dry, otherwise the patties will not crisp on the tava and may fall apart.
Resting the kneaded mixture lets the khapli atta swell and bind, which is what holds these together without deep-frying.
Cook on steady medium heat, not high, so the inside cooks through before the outside scorches.
variations.servingSuggestion: Slide onto a plate with a dollop of thick curd, a smear of tomato-garlic chutney, and a side of sliced cucumber for a wholesome tiffin.

variations.name: Classic Adai
variations.description: A rustic, protein-packed Tamil pancake of mixed lentils and rice, coarsely ground with dry red chillies and ginger so it fries up thick, nutty and satisfyingly crisp-edged. Unlike a dosa there is no fermenting and no fuss; a good pour of Anveshan Sesame Oil at the edges gives it that shattering golden crust.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil poured at the edges to crisp the thick adai to a deep, nutty gold.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing drizzle for aroma and the traditional richness that suits adai's earthy lentils.

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup rice, 0.5 cup toor dal, 0.5 cup chana dal and 0.25 cup urad dal together with 5 dry red chillies in plenty of water for 3 hours.
Drain and grind with a 1-inch piece of ginger and a little water to a thick, coarse batter with some grainy texture left in, then mix in 1 tsp salt and 0.25 tsp asafoetida.
Stir in 1 finely chopped onion, 12 torn curry leaves and enough water to reach a thick, spreadable consistency, and rest 20 minutes.
Heat a tava over medium heat, rub with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, pour a ladle of batter and spread into a thick 6-inch round, making a small hole in the centre.
Drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil around the edge and into the hole and cook for 3-4 minutes until the base is deep golden and crisp.
Flip and cook the second side 2 minutes until firm and browned, finish with a drizzle of Anveshan Bilona Ghee, and repeat with the remaining batter.
tips: Grind the batter coarse, not silky; that grainy texture is what gives adai its signature crunch.
The centre hole helps the thick adai cook through evenly and crisps beautifully when oil pools in it.
Cook on medium, not high heat; adai is thick and needs time for the lentils to cook without burning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a knob of jaggery-sweetened avial or the classic pairing of soft white butter and molagapodi.

variations.name: Himachali Masala Adai
variations.description: A hill-station reinvention where the lentil batter is warmed with garam masala and coriander powder and studded with grated carrot and beans for a wholesome, one-dish meal. Cooked in Anveshan Groundnut Oil, this masala adai is heartier and more aromatic than the temperate South original.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil that crisps the vegetable-loaded adai and suits the warm masala.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing drizzle to round the spices and enrich the hearty, veg-packed adai.

steps: Soak 1 cup rice, 0.5 cup toor dal, 0.5 cup chana dal and 0.25 cup urad dal with 3 dry red chillies for 3 hours, then drain.
Grind coarsely with a 1-inch piece of ginger and a little water, then mix in 1 tsp garam masala, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt.
Grate 1 small carrot, finely chop 6 french beans and fold them through the batter with 3 tbsp coriander leaves and enough water for a thick spreadable batter; rest 20 minutes.
Heat a tava over medium heat, rub with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, pour a ladle of batter and spread into a thick 6-inch round with a hole in the centre.
Drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil around the edge and cook 3-4 minutes until the base is golden and crisp.
Flip and cook 2 minutes more until the vegetables are cooked and the adai is browned, finish with Anveshan Bilona Ghee, and repeat with the rest.
tips: Grate and chop the vegetables small so they cook fully in the time the thick adai takes to crisp.
Toast the garam masala briefly in a dry pan before mixing to lift its aroma in the batter.
This adai freezes well cooked; reheat on a tava with a little oil to bring back the crispness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of thick set curd and a spoon of tangy tomato chutney for a filling one-plate lunch.

variations.name: Uttarakhand Spicy Adai
variations.description: A punchy mountain-style adai where extra dry chillies, pounded green chillies and crushed black pepper are ground through the lentils for a genuine, slow-building heat. Anveshan Mustard Oil gives it a bracing pungency that suits the cold-climate palate, crisping the edges to a fiery golden lace.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Pungent wood-pressed mustard oil that gives this hill-style adai its bracing, warming edge.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: A small finishing drizzle to temper the heat with a mellow, nutty richness.

steps: Soak 1 cup rice, 0.5 cup toor dal, 0.5 cup chana dal and 0.25 cup urad dal with 6 dry red chillies for 3 hours, then drain.
Grind coarsely with 3 green chillies, 1 tsp peppercorns and a 1.5-inch piece of ginger, keeping the batter grainy, then mix in 1 tsp salt.
Stir in 1 finely chopped onion, 12 torn curry leaves and enough water for a thick spreadable batter, and rest 20 minutes.
Heat a tava over medium heat and rub with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil, letting it shimmer to lose its raw sharpness.
Pour a ladle of batter, spread into a thick 6-inch round with a central hole, drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil around the edge and into the hole, and cook 3-4 minutes until deep golden.
Flip and cook 2 minutes until firm and browned, finish with a little Anveshan Bilona Ghee, and repeat with the remaining batter.
tips: Grind the peppercorns into the batter rather than sprinkling on top, so the heat runs all through the adai.
Heat the mustard oil until it just shimmers before each adai to soften its pungency into a warm nuttiness.
For a milder adai, cut the dry red chillies to three and deseed the green chillies before grinding.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plenty of cool set curd and a wedge of lime to take the edge off the layered heat.

variations.name: Odia Cheesy Adai
variations.description: A fusion adai for younger palates where grated cheese melts over the crisp lentil pancake, its savoury pull balancing the earthy dals beautifully. Cooked in Anveshan Coconut Oil, the crisp base and molten cheese top turn this protein-rich classic into an easy, crowd-pleasing snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil for a fragrant, crisp base that carries the melting cheese.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing drizzle to gloss the cheese and enrich the earthy lentil base.

steps: Soak 1 cup rice, 0.5 cup toor dal, 0.5 cup chana dal and 0.25 cup urad dal with 3 dry red chillies for 3 hours, then drain.
Grind coarsely with a 1-inch piece of ginger, then mix in 1 tsp salt, 0.5 tsp black pepper powder, 3 tbsp coriander and enough water for a thick spreadable batter; rest 20 minutes.
Heat a tava over medium heat, rub with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, pour a ladle of batter and spread into a thick 6-inch round.
Drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil around the edge and cook 3-4 minutes until the base is golden and crisp.
Scatter 3 tbsp grated cheese over the top, cover for 1-2 minutes until it melts, then drizzle with a little Anveshan Bilona Ghee.
Fold over or serve open once the cheese is molten, then repeat with the remaining batter and cheese.
tips: Melt the cheese under a lid rather than flipping, so the delicate cheese layer doesn't stick to the tava.
A grinding of black pepper into the batter cuts the richness of the cheese and keeps it interesting.
Serve immediately while the cheese is stretchy; adai firms up as it cools.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a mild tomato chutney or a swipe of green coriander chutney and ketchup for the little ones.

variations.name: Tamil Keerai Adai
variations.description: The much-loved greens version from Tamil kitchens where a big handful of chopped spinach or amaranth leaves is folded into the coarse lentil batter, adding colour, iron and a soft, wilted texture against the crisp edges. Anveshan Sesame Oil crisps it beautifully while a ghee finish rounds off the earthy flavours.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil to crisp the greens-flecked adai to a deep, nutty gold.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing drizzle that rounds the earthy greens and lentils with a nutty richness.

steps: Soak 1 cup rice, 0.5 cup toor dal, 0.5 cup chana dal and 0.25 cup urad dal with 4 dry red chillies for 3 hours, then drain.
Grind coarsely with a 1-inch piece of ginger, keeping the batter grainy, then mix in 1 tsp salt.
Finely chop 2 cups spinach leaves and fold them into the batter with 1 chopped onion, 3 tbsp grated coconut, 12 torn curry leaves and enough water for a thick spreadable batter; rest 20 minutes.
Heat a tava over medium heat, rub with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, pour a ladle of batter and spread into a thick 6-inch round with a central hole.
Drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil around the edge and into the hole, cooking 3-4 minutes until deep golden and crisp.
