Flip and cook 2 minutes until the greens are wilted through and the base is browned, finish with Anveshan Bilona Ghee, and repeat with the rest.
tips: Chop the greens fine so they distribute evenly and don't leave large wet patches that stop the adai crisping.
The grated coconut adds a subtle sweetness that balances the iron-rich greens; keep it in if you can.
Squeeze any washed greens dry before folding in, so extra moisture doesn't loosen the thick batter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jaggery and a spoon of soft white butter, the traditional sweet counterpoint to a savoury keerai adai.

variations.name: Classic Bread Roll
variations.description: The quick-fix party snack of Indian homes: soft bread slices wrapped tight around a spiced potato filling and fried into crisp golden logs. The contrast of the shatter-crisp crust and the warm, fluffy potato centre makes these vanish the moment they hit the plate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for deep-frying; a bit is also used to temper the filling for a clean, crisp finish

steps: Boil 4 medium potatoes until soft, peel and mash them coarsely.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a pan on medium and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then add 1 chopped onion and 2 chopped green chillies and saute 3 minutes until soft.

Add the mashed potato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.75 tsp amchur, 3 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt, cook 3 minutes until it holds together, then cool and roll into 8 oblong logs of about 2 tbsp each.
Trim the crusts from 8 bread slices, dip each slice quickly in water and press between your palms to squeeze out all the moisture so it turns pliable.
Place a potato log on the damp slice, roll the bread around it, and seal the edges firmly into a smooth cylinder with no cracks.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to medium-hot, about 180C, and deep-fry the rolls in batches for 3 to 4 minutes, turning, until crisp and deep golden; drain on a rack.
tips: Squeeze the soaked bread really dry, as any trapped water will make the roll burst open and soak up oil.
Seal every edge and crack well; unsealed rolls drink oil and fall apart in the pan.
Fry at a steady medium-hot temperature so the bread crisps quickly before it can absorb oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Slice each roll on the diagonal to show the golden filling and serve with green chutney and tomato ketchup.

variations.name: Gujarat Crispy Bread Roll
variations.description: The Gujarati version rolls the stuffed bread in a second coat of fine breadcrumbs for an extra-crunchy shell, with a lightly sweet-spiced potato filling true to the region's palate. A touch of jaggery balances the green chilli for that signature Gujarati sweet-heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a spoonful in the filling gives the gentle Gujarati sweet-heat balance against the chilli

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for deep-frying the crumb-coated rolls to a sturdy golden crust

steps: Boil and mash 4 medium potatoes, and boil 0.5 cup green peas until soft then lightly crush them.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, add 2 chopped green chillies and 1 inch grated ginger and fry 1 minute, then add the potato and peas with 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 1.25 tsp salt and cook 3 minutes.
Cool the filling and shape into 8 oblong logs of about 2 tbsp each.
Trim crusts from 8 bread slices, dip each in water and squeeze dry, place a filling log on top and roll into a sealed cylinder.
Roll each cylinder in 1 cup bread crumbs, pressing so a firm crust forms, then chill for 10 minutes.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to medium-hot, about 180C, and deep-fry the rolls for 3 to 4 minutes until crisp and golden; drain on a rack.
tips: The jaggery should just balance, not sweeten; a single teaspoon in the whole batch is plenty.
Chilling the crumbed rolls firms the coating so it does not flake off during frying.
Add the lemon juice off the heat to keep its brightness in the sweet-and-sour Gujarati filling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a sweet date-tamarind chutney and fried green chillies for a true Gujarati farsan spread.

variations.name: Rajasthan Spicy Bread Roll
variations.description: A fiery desert-style roll with coarsely cracked black pepper and pungent mustard oil worked through the potato filling. Built for Rajasthan's love of bold, warming spice, these rolls carry a deep peppery heat that lingers pleasantly.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked first, then used both to temper the filling and deep-fry for a bold desert pungency

steps: Boil and coarsely mash 4 medium potatoes. Coarsely crack 1.5 tsp black pepper and crush 6 garlic cloves in a mortar.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until it just smokes, lower the heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, add 1 chopped onion, 2 chopped green chillies and the pepper-garlic paste and fry 3 minutes.
Add the mashed potato with 1 tsp red chilli powder, 3 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt, cook 3 minutes until firm, then cool and roll into 8 oblong logs.
Trim crusts from 8 bread slices, dip each in water and squeeze dry, place a filling log on top and roll into a tightly sealed cylinder.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil to medium-hot, having smoked it once to mellow the rawness.
Deep-fry the rolls in batches for 3 to 4 minutes, turning, until crisp and golden with a sharp peppery aroma; drain on a rack.
tips: Smoke the mustard oil before frying so its raw pungency softens into a rounded sharpness.
Crush the pepper and garlic coarse for pockets of heat rather than an even, flat spice.
Keep the potato filling on the drier side so the fierce rolls seal tight and do not split.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a fiery garlic-red chilli chutney and sliced onions for a bold Rajasthani snack.

variations.name: West Bengal Masala Bread Roll
variations.description: Kolkata's beloved bread roll, cousin to the city's egg rolls, is fragrant with garam masala, roasted coriander powder and a whisper of subtle sweetness. Sold at every para tea shop, it is aromatic, lightly spiced and utterly moreish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the classic Bengali frying fat; also tempers the filling for that para tea-shop aroma

steps: Dry-roast 1.5 tsp coriander powder for 30 seconds until fragrant. Boil and mash 4 medium potatoes.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until it just smokes, lower the heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, add 1 chopped onion, 2 chopped green chillies and 1 inch grated ginger and fry 3 minutes.
Stir in the roasted coriander powder and 1 tsp garam masala for 30 seconds, then add the potato with 3 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt and cook 3 minutes; cool and shape into 8 logs.
Trim crusts from 8 bread slices, dip each in water and squeeze dry, place a filling log on top and roll into a sealed cylinder.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil to medium-hot, having smoked it once.
Deep-fry the rolls for 3 to 4 minutes, turning, until crisp and golden with a warm masala aroma; drain on a rack.
tips: Roasting the coriander powder before adding it is what gives the filling its Kolkata street-roll depth.
Smoke the mustard oil first so the finished rolls carry aroma without raw bite.
Serve with thin onion rings tossed in lemon and chilli, exactly as the city's roll shops do.
variations.servingSuggestion: Slice on the diagonal and serve with lime-and-chilli onions and a squeeze of kasundi mustard for a true Kolkata roll experience.

variations.name: Tamil Nadu Tava Bread Roll
variations.description: A lighter southern take that pan-toasts the stuffed rolls flat on a tava with sesame oil instead of deep-frying, finished with a curry-leaf tempered filling. The result is crisp and golden with far less oil, and an unmistakable South Indian fragrance.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: gingelly oil both tempers the filling and toasts the rolls, giving the South Indian aroma

steps: Boil and mash 4 medium potatoes. Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil in a pan, add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal and let them splutter and turn golden for 20 seconds.
Add 2 sprigs curry leaves, 1 chopped onion, 2 chopped green chillies and 1 inch grated ginger and fry 3 minutes until soft.
Add the potato with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt, cook 3 minutes into a firm masala, then cool and shape into 8 oblong logs.
Trim crusts from 8 bread slices, dip each in water and squeeze dry, place a filling log on top and roll into a sealed cylinder, pressing the seam closed.
Heat a flat tava on medium and brush with 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil, place the rolls seam-side down and cook 3 minutes until crisp underneath.
Keep turning the rolls every couple of minutes, drizzling a little sesame oil, until crisp and golden on all sides, about 8 minutes total.
tips: Toast the rolls seam-side down first so the join sets and the roll holds together while you turn it.
Keep the tava on steady medium heat and turn often so all sides crisp evenly without deep oil.
Gingelly sesame oil has a strong flavour, so start with less and add as needed to suit your taste.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coconut chutney and a small bowl of sambar for dipping, South Indian tiffin style.

variations.name: Classic Corn Cutlet
variations.description: A juicy, café-style cutlet built on sweet corn and mashed potato, studded with pops of whole kernel for texture. Crisp and golden on the outside, sweet and creamy within, it is the crowd-pleaser that disappears fastest at any tea party.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: whisked into a slurry as an eggless binder for the crumb coat and a little into the mix for body

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: for shallow-frying; a light oil that lets the natural sweetness of the corn come through

steps: Boil 2 cups sweet corn for 5 minutes, drain, and coarsely crush half of it in a blender while keeping the other half whole for texture.
Boil 2 medium potatoes until soft, peel and mash them, then heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sunflower Oil and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds.

Add 1 chopped medium onion and 2 chopped green chillies to the pan and saute for 3 minutes until soft, then combine with the mashed potato, all the corn, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 3 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt.
Knead in 1 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta to firm the mixture, then divide into 8 portions and shape into thick round patties.
Whisk the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta with 4 tbsp water into a slurry, dip each patty and coat evenly in 1 cup bread crumbs.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sunflower Oil in a flat pan to medium and shallow-fry the cutlets for 2 to 3 minutes per side until crisp and golden; drain on a rack.
tips: Crushing only half the corn gives the best of both worlds: a smooth binding base and sweet bursts of whole kernel.
If the mixture feels loose, chill it for 15 minutes before shaping so the patties hold their form in the pan.
Sweet corn browns fast, so keep the heat at medium to avoid dark spots before the inside heats through.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a creamy mint-yoghurt dip and a sprinkle of chaat masala, alongside tomato ketchup for children.

variations.name: Assam Crispy Corn Cutlet
variations.description: This Assamese version wraps the sweet corn core in a double coat of breadcrumbs for a robust, travel-friendly crunch, brightened with a little tangy tomato and fresh coriander. It is a favourite for tea gardens picnics where snacks must stay crisp for hours.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: makes the eggless slurry for a firm double crumb coat that stays crisp for hours

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for shallow-frying to a deep, durable golden crust

steps: Boil and coarsely crush 2 cups sweet corn, and boil and mash 2 medium potatoes.

Deseed and finely chop 1 small tomato and squeeze out its juice so the mixture stays firm, then combine with the corn, potato, 1 chopped onion, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt.
Knead the mixture until it holds, then shape into 8 oval cutlets.
Whisk 4 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta with 8 tbsp water into a slurry; dip each cutlet, roll in 1.5 cups bread crumbs, then dip and crumb a second time for a thicker shell.
Heat 1 cup Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a flat pan to medium-hot and shallow-fry the cutlets in batches.
Fry for 3 minutes per side until the double crust is crisp and deep golden, then drain on a wire rack.
tips: Squeeze the chopped tomato dry, as excess juice is the main reason corn cutlets fall apart in the pan.
Chill the double-coated cutlets for 20 minutes before frying so the crumbs bond and do not flake off.
These hold their crunch well in a lunchbox, especially if you let them cool on a rack rather than stacking them warm.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pack with a tangy tomato-chilli chutney and cucumber sticks for a tea-garden picnic, or serve warm with Assam's own strong black tea.

variations.name: Haryana Spicy Corn Cutlet
variations.description: A rustic Haryanvi cutlet that balances the corn's sweetness with a bold hit of crushed black pepper and a spoon of thick homemade curd. Hearty and warming, it reflects the region's love of dairy-rich, generously spiced dhaba food.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: kneaded in to soak up the curd's moisture and bind the peppery mix

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for shallow-frying the pepper-spiced cutlets to a crisp finish

steps: Boil and coarsely crush 2 cups sweet corn, and boil and mash 2 medium potatoes.
Coarsely crack 1.5 tsp black pepper in a mortar for uneven, fragrant flecks.
Combine the corn, potato, 3 tbsp hung curd, cracked pepper, 1 chopped onion, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp cumin seeds, 3 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt in a bowl.
Knead in 4 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta until the mixture is firm and no longer sticky, then rest it 5 minutes and shape into 8 thick patties.
Roll each patty lightly in 1 cup bread crumbs to coat, pressing gently.
Heat 1 cup Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a flat pan to medium and shallow-fry the cutlets for 3 minutes per side until crisp and golden with a peppery aroma; drain on a rack.
tips: Use thick hung curd, not runny yoghurt, or the mixture will turn too soft to shape.
The khapli atta must be kneaded in well to absorb the curd, so give the mix a good five-minute rest before frying.
Add a final crack of pepper over the hot cutlets to lift the aroma just before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a garlicky white-butter chutney and thick lassi for a true Haryanvi dhaba feel.

variations.name: Delhi Masala Corn Cutlet
variations.description: The Delhi chaat-shop cutlet is loud with garam masala, roasted coriander powder and a squeeze of lime, finished with a scatter of pomegranate for a jewel-bright topping. It is the cutlet reimagined as street-side chaat, tangy, spicy and irresistible.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: slurry binder for the crumb coat that keeps the masala cutlet crisp

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for shallow-frying the chaat-style cutlets evenly golden

steps: Dry-roast 1.5 tsp coriander powder for 30 seconds until fragrant. Boil and coarsely crush 2 cups sweet corn, and boil and mash 2 medium potatoes.
Combine the corn, potato, roasted coriander powder, 1 tsp garam masala, 1 chopped onion, 2 chopped green chillies and 1.25 tsp salt, mixing well.
Add 1 tbsp lemon juice and shape the mixture into 8 flat round patties.
Whisk 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta with 6 tbsp water into a slurry, dip each patty and coat in 1 cup bread crumbs.
Heat 1 cup Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a flat pan to medium and shallow-fry for 3 minutes per side until crisp and golden.
Drain on a rack, dust with 1 tsp chaat masala while hot, and scatter 3 tbsp pomegranate seeds over the top before serving.
tips: Add the chaat masala only after frying, as its dried mango powder burns and turns bitter in hot oil.
Keep the pomegranate for the final garnish so it stays crunchy and bright against the soft cutlet.
For a full chaat, top with a drizzle of curd, tamarind chutney and a pinch of roasted cumin powder.
variations.servingSuggestion: Plate as a chaat with curd, green and tamarind chutneys, sev and extra pomegranate for a Delhi street-food spread.

variations.name: Telangana Tava Corn Cutlet
variations.description: A lighter Telangana version griddled on a flat tava with just a brush of oil, keeping the corn's juiciness intact while crisping the edges. A tempering of curry leaves and mustard seeds gives it a distinctly southern, homely aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: kneaded in as a wholesome binder so the patties griddle without falling apart

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: brushed lightly onto the tava for an everyday low-oil griddle

steps: Boil and coarsely crush 2 cups sweet corn, and boil and mash 2 medium potatoes.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sunflower Oil on a tava, add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 2 sprigs curry leaves and let them splutter for 20 seconds, then add 1 chopped onion and 2 chopped green chillies and soften for 3 minutes.
Combine the corn, potato and the tempered onion with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 3 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp salt in a bowl.
Knead in 4 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta and 0.5 cup bread crumbs until firm, rest 5 minutes, and shape into 8 flat patties.
Heat the tava on medium and brush with 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sunflower Oil, place the patties and cook for 4 minutes until the underside is crisp.
Flip, drizzle a little oil around the edges, and cook the second side for 3 to 4 minutes until golden and cooked through.
tips: Let the tempering cool a little before mixing so it does not start cooking the corn prematurely.
Resting the kneaded mixture lets the khapli atta swell and hold the patties together on the griddle.
Cook on steady medium heat so the sweet corn caramelises gently rather than scorching.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coconut-coriander chutney and a bowl of curd for a light southern tiffin plate.

variations.name: Classic Corn Pulao
variations.description: A cheerful one-pot pulao where sweet corn kernels are cooked with fragrant basmati and whole garam spices. The natural sweetness of the corn plays against warm spices for a quick, wholesome rice that is a guaranteed hit with children and adults alike.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee toasts the whole spices and gives the pulao a fragrant, buttery base

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain so the grains cook long and separate.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 bay leaf, 3 cardamom pods, 4 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon and sizzle 30 seconds until aromatic.
Add 1 sliced large onion and 2 slit green chillies, frying 5 minutes until the onion turns soft and golden.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger garlic paste and cook 1 minute, then add 1.5 cups sweet corn, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt and sauté 3 minutes.
Add the drained rice and toast gently for 2 minutes, then pour in 2.5 cups hot water and bring to a rolling boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 15 minutes until the water is absorbed, rest 5 minutes, garnish with 3 tbsp coriander and fluff before serving.
tips: Use fresh or frozen sweet corn; if using frozen, thaw it so it does not lower the pot temperature.
Do not overcook the corn before the rice goes in, so it keeps its juicy pop.
A squeeze of lemon at the end brightens the natural sweetness of the corn.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cool mint raita and a crisp papad for an easy, crowd-pleasing weekday lunch.

variations.name: Assamese Corn Herb Pulao
variations.description: An Assamese-leaning pulao brightened with fresh coriander, spring onion and a hint of ginger, cooked in mild mustard oil as the region prefers. Light, herby and subtly pungent, it reflects Assam's fondness for fresh, understated flavours.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Mild wood-pressed mustard oil suits the fragrant joha rice of Assam

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups fragrant joha rice for 20 minutes, then drain gently as it is a delicate short grain.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, lower the heat, then add 1 bay leaf, 3 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon and sizzle 30 seconds.
Add crushed 1.5 inch ginger, 5 garlic cloves and 3 slit green chillies, frying 1 minute until fragrant, then add the white parts of 0.5 cup spring onions and sauté 3 minutes.
Stir in 1.5 cups sweet corn and 1.25 tsp salt and cook 3 minutes until the corn glistens.
Add the drained rice, toast gently for 2 minutes, then pour in 2.25 cups hot water and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes, then scatter the spring onion greens and 0.25 cup coriander, rest 5 minutes and fluff before serving.
tips: Joha rice is aromatic and cooks fast, so use slightly less water and a gentler hand.
Add most of the herbs at the end so their fresh fragrance is not lost to the heat.
If joha rice is unavailable, any short fragrant rice works with the water reduced slightly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a tangy tomato-tamarind tenga on the side to complement the light, herby pulao.

variations.name: Haryanvi Buttery Corn Pulao
variations.description: A rich, rustic Haryanvi take that celebrates the state's dairy heritage, finishing the corn pulao with white butter and a generous hit of ghee. Hearty and mildly spiced, it is farm-style comfort food built for big appetites.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A generous pour of bilona ghee reflects the dairy-rich Haryanvi kitchen

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes and drain thoroughly.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them splutter for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 sliced onion and fry 5 minutes until golden, then add 1 tbsp ginger garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Add 1 chopped tomato, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt, cooking 4 minutes until the tomato turns pulpy.
Stir in 1.5 cups sweet corn and 0.5 tsp garam masala, sauté 2 minutes, then add the drained rice and toast gently for 2 minutes.
Pour in 2.5 cups hot water, bring to a boil, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 15 minutes, then dot with 2 tbsp white butter, rest 5 minutes, garnish with 3 tbsp coriander and fluff.
tips: Stir the white butter through while the pulao is hot so it melts into a glossy coating.
Keep the spicing gentle so the sweetness of the corn and richness of the dairy shine.
For extra indulgence, serve with an additional knob of white butter melting on top.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a thick bowl of chaas and a wedge of raw onion for a true Haryanvi countryside meal.

variations.name: Delhi Corn Tikka Pulao
variations.description: A punchy Delhi street-style pulao where the corn is tossed in tandoori-style masala and yogurt before joining the rice, echoing the city's love of smoky tikka flavours. Tangy, spicy and vibrant, it eats like a corn tikka and pulao in one bowl.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee gives the tikka-spiced pulao a rich dhaba-style depth

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes and drain; whisk 1.5 cups corn with 0.33 cup thick yogurt, 1.5 tsp tandoori masala and 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and marinate 10 minutes.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1 bay leaf and sizzle 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 sliced onion and fry 5 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Add the marinated corn and 1.25 tsp salt, cooking 4 minutes until the yogurt masala thickens and coats the kernels and the raw smell fades.
Add the drained rice and crushed 1 tsp kasuri methi, toast gently for 2 minutes, then pour in 2.5 cups hot water and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 15 minutes, rest 5 minutes, garnish with 3 tbsp coriander and fluff before serving.
tips: Marinate the corn in the spiced yogurt for at least ten minutes so the flavour penetrates.
Cook the yogurt masala until it thickens and the fat separates, or the pulao may taste raw.
Crush the kasuri methi between your palms before adding to release its full aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling mint-yogurt dip and thin onion rings soaked in lemon, dhaba-style.

variations.name: Telangana Corn Gongura Pulao
variations.description: A tangy Telangana version that folds sour gongura (sorrel) leaves into the corn pulao, giving it the region's signature pucker and heat. Cooked in sesame oil with green chilli, it is a bold, zingy rice unlike any mild pulao.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Earthy sesame oil is the classic Telangana fat that balances the sour gongura

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes and drain; wash and roughly chop 2 cups gongura leaves.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil over medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tsp cumin seeds and 12 curry leaves and let them crackle for 40 seconds.
Add 1 sliced onion, 4 slit green chillies and 6 crushed garlic cloves, frying 5 minutes until the onion softens and turns golden.
Add the chopped gongura and 0.25 tsp turmeric, cooking 3 minutes until the leaves wilt and turn dark and sour-smelling.
Stir in 1.5 cups sweet corn and 1.25 tsp salt, sauté 2 minutes, then add the drained rice and toast gently for 2 minutes.
Pour in 2.5 cups hot water, bring to a boil, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 15 minutes, then rest 5 minutes and fluff before serving.
tips: Gongura is naturally very sour, so no tamarind or lemon is needed in this pulao.
If gongura is unavailable, a handful of sorrel or a little extra tamarind approximates the tang.
Adjust the green chillies to taste, as gongura pairs beautifully with a strong hit of heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain thick curd and fried papad to temper the bold sour-spicy flavours.

variations.name: Classic Dry Fruit Ladoo
variations.description: A naturally sweetened ladoo where a sticky date paste binds a generous mix of roasted nuts, with no added sugar at all. Chewy, rich and studded with almonds, cashews and pistachios in every bite. The modern favourite for anyone wanting a wholesome, refined-sugar-free treat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee softens the date paste and stops the sticky mixture from clinging to the pan and your palms.

steps: Dry-roast 1/2 cup almonds, 1/2 cup cashews, 1/4 cup pistachios and 1/4 cup walnuts in a pan on low heat for 4 to 5 minutes until fragrant, then cool and pulse to a coarse rubble.
Chop 1.5 cups deseeded dates finely; if they are dry, steam them for 2 minutes to soften.
Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on low heat, add the chopped dates and cook for 3 to 4 minutes, mashing, until they melt into a sticky, uniform paste.
Stir in the crushed nuts and 1 tsp cardamom powder and mix well until the mass comes together and pulls from the pan.
Cool for 5 minutes until warm enough to handle, then grease your palms with a little ghee.
Roll firmly into 14 ladoos while warm; they hold together as the date paste cools and sets.
tips: Keep the nuts coarse rather than powdered so each ladoo has a satisfying chew and crunch.
If your dates are very dry the paste will not bind, so steam or soak them briefly before cooking.
Being sugar-free and moist, these keep best refrigerated and stay good for up to two weeks.
variations.servingSuggestion: An ideal guilt-free energy bite for lunchboxes or post-gym; roll a few in extra crushed pistachio for a festive finish.

variations.name: Gond Dry Fruit Ladoo
variations.description: A Rajasthani winter powerhouse combining fried edible gum with dates and nuts for a warming, restorative ladoo traditionally fed to new mothers. The puffed gond adds an airy crunch amid the chewy fruit. Dense, fortifying and made in big batches for the cold months.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee is essential here to puff the gond and soften the dates for a fortifying winter ladoo.

steps: Heat 3 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium heat and fry 1/3 cup edible gum in batches for about 30 seconds each until they puff white and light, then crush coarsely.
In the same ghee roast 1/2 cup almonds and 1/3 cup cashews for 3 minutes until golden, then pulse to a coarse rubble with 3 tbsp melon seeds.
Add the remaining ghee to the pan with 1.5 cups finely chopped dates and cook on low heat for 4 minutes, mashing, until they form a sticky paste.
Stir in the crushed nuts, crushed gond, 1/2 tsp dry ginger powder and 1 tsp cardamom powder until the mixture binds.
Cool for 5 minutes until warm, greasing your palms with ghee.
Roll firmly into 14 ladoos while warm; the gond crunch sets as they cool.
tips: Fry the gond on medium heat only; too hot and it browns and hardens rather than puffing into light nuggets.
Crush the gond just before mixing so it stays crisp and does not soften in the humid date paste.
These are meant as a warming winter tonic, so eat one or two a day rather than treating them like a light snack.
variations.servingSuggestion: A traditional postnatal and cold-weather strengthener; serve one warmed slightly with a glass of hot milk.

variations.name: Anjeer Coconut Ladoo
variations.description: A luxurious fig-based ladoo where dried anjeer paste replaces most of the dates for a jammy, mildly grainy sweetness, rolled in coconut. A drizzle of wood-pressed coconut oil deepens the tropical note. Elegant enough for a mithai box yet entirely sugar-free.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed coconut oil lifts the fig paste with a soft tropical aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee balances the coconut oil and keeps the sticky fig mixture manageable.

steps: Soak 1.5 cups dried figs in warm water for 10 minutes until softened, then drain and chop finely.
Dry-roast 1/2 cup almonds and 1/3 cup pistachios on low heat for 3 minutes and pulse to a coarse rubble.
Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on low heat, add the figs and 1/2 cup chopped dates, and cook for 5 to 6 minutes, mashing, until a thick sticky paste forms.
Stir in the crushed nuts, 1 tsp cardamom powder and 3 tbsp of the desiccated coconut until the mixture holds together.
Cool for 5 minutes until warm, then roll into 14 ladoos and press each in the remaining coconut to coat.
Chill for 20 minutes so the fig paste firms and the ladoos set.
tips: Drain the soaked figs well and pat them dry; excess water keeps the paste loose and stops the ladoos from binding.
Toast the coconut for coating lightly if you prefer a nuttier finish, or leave it white for a cleaner look.
Figs have tiny seeds that add a pleasant grain, so do not over-blend the paste trying to smooth them out.
variations.servingSuggestion: A refined sugar-free mithai for gifting; arrange in mini paper cups with a pistachio sliver on top.

variations.name: Seed and Nut Energy Ladoo
variations.description: A contemporary superfood ladoo balancing dates with a big handful of roasted seeds, oats and nuts for fibre, protein and healthy fats. Less sweet and more textured than a pure dry-fruit ladoo. The gym-bag and desk-drawer bite of the moment.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A little ghee toasts the oats and seeds and binds the leaner mixture together.

steps: Warm 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on low heat and toast 1/2 cup rolled oats for 3 minutes until golden and nutty, then set aside.
In the same pan dry-roast 1/3 cup almonds, 3 tbsp pumpkin seeds, 3 tbsp sunflower seeds and 2 tbsp flax seeds for 3 minutes until they pop and smell toasty; cool and pulse coarsely.
Chop 1.5 cups deseeded dates finely and pulse them to a sticky paste in the mixer.
In a bowl combine the date paste, toasted oats, crushed seeds and nuts, and 3/4 tsp cardamom powder, and knead with your hands until it binds.
If the mix is too dry to hold, add a teaspoon of warm ghee and knead again.
Roll firmly into 14 ladoos and refrigerate for 20 minutes to set.
tips: Grind the flax seeds coarsely rather than leaving them whole so their nutrients are actually absorbed.
Toast the oats until they smell nutty for the best flavour, but stir constantly as they scorch quickly.
These are deliberately less sweet, so add two extra dates if you prefer a more dessert-like ladoo.
variations.servingSuggestion: Keep a batch in the fridge for a quick breakfast-on-the-run or a pre-workout bite with black coffee.

variations.name: Khoya Dry Fruit Ladoo
variations.description: A Punjabi wedding-season indulgence where the dry fruits are bound with khoya rather than dates, giving a milky, fudgy richness closer to a mithai. Saffron and cardamom make it unmistakably festive. Softer and more decadent than the chewy date versions.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery keeps this rich khoya ladoo unrefined while adding a warm caramel depth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee cooks the khoya smoothly and toasts the nuts for the festive base.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: A pinch bloomed in warm milk gives the ladoos their golden festive colour and aroma.

steps: Soak a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside to bloom.
Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on low heat and toast 1/2 cup almonds, 1/2 cup cashews and 1/4 cup pistachios for 3 minutes, then cool and pulse to a coarse rubble.
In the same pan crumble 1 cup khoya and cook on low heat for 5 to 6 minutes until it softens and smells of caramelised milk.
Stir in 1/2 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder, the saffron milk and 1 tsp cardamom powder, and cook for 3 minutes until it thickens and leaves the pan sides.
Fold in the crushed nuts and cook for another minute, then cool for 5 minutes until warm.
Roll into 14 ladoos and refrigerate for 20 minutes so the khoya firms and they hold cleanly.
tips: Use fresh soft khoya and cook it just until it leaves the pan; overcooking turns it grainy and the ladoos dry.
Because of the dairy, store these refrigerated and finish within four to five days.
Bloom the saffron in warm rather than hot milk to draw out full colour and fragrance.
variations.servingSuggestion: Present on a decorated tray at weddings and Diwali, garnished with saffron and slivered pistachio; rich enough to serve one per guest.

variations.name: Classic Hara Bhara Kebab
variations.description: The emerald-green vegetarian kebab of North Indian restaurant menus, built on blanched spinach, green peas and potato with a mild, herby spicing. Soft and moist inside with a lightly crisped surface, its brilliant colour and fresh flavour make it a favourite starter.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: kneaded in to bind the wet green mixture without dulling its colour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: for shallow-frying; light enough to keep the kebabs from tasting greasy

steps: Blanch 4 cups spinach in boiling water for 1 minute, then plunge into cold water to lock the green colour, squeeze out all moisture, and chop finely.
Boil 1 cup green peas and 1 large potato until soft, drain, and mash both together well.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sunflower Oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, add 2 chopped green chillies and 1 inch grated ginger and fry 1 minute, then stir in the spinach and cook 2 minutes to dry it out.

Combine the spinach, mashed peas and potato with 3 tbsp roasted gram flour, 1 tsp chaat masala, 3 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt, then knead in 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta until firm and shape into 10 round patties.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sunflower Oil in a flat pan to medium.
Shallow-fry the kebabs for 3 minutes per side until crisp at the edges and set through, keeping the heat moderate to preserve the green colour; drain on a rack.
tips: Squeeze the blanched spinach bone-dry, as excess water is the main reason these kebabs turn soggy and fall apart.
The roasted gram flour must be pre-toasted so it binds without a raw taste; cook it 2 minutes in a dry pan if unsure.
Keep the frying heat medium, not high, so the kebabs stay vividly green rather than browning too dark.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with mint chutney and thin onion rings, or press a cashew half into the centre of each kebab before frying for the classic restaurant look.

variations.name: Chhattisgarh Crispy Hara Bhara Kebab
variations.description: This Chhattisgarhi take gives the green kebab a shattering breadcrumb jacket so it holds up to the region's love of hearty, crunchy snacks. The crisp shell contrasts beautifully with the soft, herb-flecked spinach and pea centre.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: makes the eggless dipping slurry so the crumb shell grips the soft green kebab

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for shallow-frying the crumb-coated kebabs to a durable golden crust

steps: Blanch 4 cups spinach for 1 minute, refresh in cold water, squeeze completely dry and chop fine.

Boil and mash 1 cup green peas and 1 large potato together, then heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil and fry 1 tsp cumin seeds, 2 chopped green chillies and 1 inch grated ginger for 1 minute.
Add the spinach to the pan and stir-cook for 2 minutes to dry, then mix with the mashed peas and potato, 1 tsp amchur powder and 1.25 tsp salt.
Shape the mixture into 10 thick patties. Whisk 4 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta with 8 tbsp water into a slurry, dip each patty, and coat firmly in 1.5 cups bread crumbs.
Chill the coated kebabs for 15 minutes so the crust sets, then heat the remaining Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to medium-hot.
Shallow-fry for 3 minutes per side until the breadcrumb shell is crisp and deep golden; drain on a rack.
tips: Chilling the coated kebabs before frying stops the crumb layer from sliding off the moist filling.
Amchur adds a tang that cuts the richness; use lemon juice mixed into the filling if you do not have it.
Fry in small batches so the oil stays hot and the crumb crust turns crisp rather than absorbing oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a garlicky red-chilli chutney and a squeeze of lime for a hearty, crunchy starter.

variations.name: Jharkhand Spicy Hara Bhara Kebab
variations.description: A forest-region kebab with a bold kick of coarsely cracked black pepper and pungent mustard oil, reflecting Jharkhand's earthy, robust palate. The pepper's slow heat and the sharp mustard aroma turn the mild green kebab into something far punchier.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: binds the peppery green mix so the kebabs hold firm while shallow-frying

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked once then used to shallow-fry, lending the sharp, earthy pungency of the region

steps: Blanch 4 cups spinach for 1 minute, refresh, squeeze dry and chop fine. Boil and mash 1 cup green peas and 1 large potato together.
Coarsely crack 1.5 tsp black pepper and crush 5 garlic cloves in a mortar into a rough paste.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until it just smokes, lower the heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 2 chopped green chillies, add the pepper-garlic paste and fry 1 minute, then stir in the spinach and cook 2 minutes to dry.
Combine the spinach mix with the mashed peas and potato, 3 tbsp roasted gram flour, 3 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt, knead in 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, and shape into 10 patties.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil in a flat pan to medium, having smoked it first to mellow the rawness.
Shallow-fry the kebabs for 3 minutes per side until set and crisp-edged with a peppery mustard aroma; drain on a rack.
tips: Smoke the mustard oil once before frying so its raw pungency softens into a pleasant sharpness.
Crack the pepper coarse rather than powdering it for bursts of warmth through each bite.
If the mixture is loose, add another spoon of roasted gram flour instead of more atta to keep the texture light.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a raw mango-mustard chutney and sliced onions for an earthy, robust plate.

variations.name: Punjabi Masala Hara Bhara Kebab
variations.description: The Punjabi version is richer and more aromatic, layered with garam masala, roasted coriander powder and a little grated paneer for a melt-in-mouth centre. It eats like a tandoori-house starter, hearty, warmly spiced and satisfying.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: binds the masala mixture and stops the paneer moisture loosening the kebabs

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: shallow-frying in bilona ghee gives the Punjabi-style richness and a nutty aroma

steps: Blanch 4 cups spinach for 1 minute, refresh, squeeze dry and chop fine. Boil and mash 1 cup green peas and 1 large potato together, and grate 0.5 cup paneer.
Dry-roast 1.5 tsp coriander powder for 30 seconds until fragrant.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, fry 2 chopped green chillies and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, stir in the roasted coriander powder and 1 tsp garam masala, then add the spinach and cook 2 minutes to dry.
Combine the spinach mix with the mashed peas, potato and grated paneer and 1.25 tsp salt, knead in 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, and shape into 10 patties.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Ghee in a flat pan to medium.
Shallow-fry the kebabs for 3 minutes per side until golden and set, basting with a little ghee for a rich finish; drain on a rack.
tips: Grate the paneer fine so it distributes evenly and melts into a soft centre rather than leaving lumps.
Bloom the garam masala briefly in ghee before adding the greens for a deeper Punjabi aroma.
These freeze well shaped and uncooked; fry straight from the freezer adding a minute per side.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a thick mint-yoghurt raita, pickled onions and lemon wedges as a tandoori-house style starter.

variations.name: Maharashtra Tava Hara Bhara Kebab
variations.description: A lighter Maharashtrian version griddled flat on a tava with minimal oil and brightened with a goda-masala hint. The kebabs get crisp, lacy edges while staying soft and green inside, making them an easy, wholesome evening snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: kneaded in as a wholesome binder so the flat kebabs griddle cleanly without breaking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: brushed lightly over the tava for a low-oil everyday griddle

steps: Blanch 4 cups spinach for 1 minute, refresh, squeeze dry and chop fine. Boil and mash 1 cup green peas and 1 large potato together.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on a tava, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, fry 2 chopped green chillies and 1 inch grated ginger for 1 minute, add 1 tsp goda masala, then stir in the spinach and cook 2 minutes to dry.
Combine the spinach mix with the mashed peas and potato, 2 tbsp roasted gram flour, 3 tbsp coriander and 1.25 tsp salt.
Knead in 4 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta until firm, rest 5 minutes, and shape into 10 flat, thin patties.
Heat the tava on medium and brush with 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil, place the patties and cook 4 minutes until the underside is crisp and lacy.
Flip, drizzle a little oil around the edges, and cook the second side 3 minutes until golden and set through.
tips: Goda masala brings a sweet-warm Maharashtrian note; use a mild garam masala if you cannot find it.
Keep the patties thin so they cook through on the tava without needing deep oil.
Rest the kneaded mixture so the khapli atta absorbs moisture and the kebabs flip without cracking.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coconut-coriander chutney and slices of raw onion for a light Maharashtrian snack plate.

variations.name: Classic Dal Makhani Tadka
variations.description: The definitive slow-simmered black dal, where whole urad and a handful of rajma are pressure-cooked to melting softness, then mashed and cooked low for hours with tomato, butter and cream. A final sizzling tadka of cumin and garlic in Anveshan ghee, poured over at the table, is what gives it that unmistakable dhaba aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the onion-tomato base is bhuno-ed in clean wood-pressed groundnut oil before the ghee tadka goes on top

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the finishing tadka of cumin and garlic is bloomed in sizzling ghee for that signature dhaba aroma

steps: Soak 1 cup whole urad and 0.25 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook them with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 4 cups water for 6-7 whistles until completely soft and creamy when pressed.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a heavy pot, add 1 large chopped onion and sauté on medium heat for 6 minutes until golden, then stir in 2 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 2 minutes until the raw smell goes.
Add 1 cup tomato puree, 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1 tsp garam masala and bhuno for 8 minutes until the oil separates and the masala turns glossy and deep red.
Tip in the cooked dal with its water, lightly mash a portion against the side, and simmer uncovered on low heat for 30-40 minutes, stirring often, until it turns thick, dark and silky.
Stir in 3 tbsp butter, 0.25 cup cream, 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, and simmer 5 minutes more until rich and glossy.
For the tadka, heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds until fragrant, add a little chopped garlic to sizzle golden, then pour it over the dal just before serving.
tips: The long, slow simmer is non-negotiable; the dark colour and creamy body come from time, not from adding more cream.
A splash of hot water during the simmer keeps the dal from catching and lets it cook down without turning pasty.
Make it a day ahead; dal makhani deepens in flavour overnight and only needs a fresh ghee tadka to revive it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot with a swirl of cream, hot tandoori roti or jeera rice, and a side of sliced onion and green chilli for the full dhaba experience.

variations.name: Amritsari Dhaba Dal Makhani
variations.description: The garlicky, robust roadside version from Amritsar, heavier on garlic and tomato and lighter on cream than restaurant dal makhani. A double dose of tadka, one worked into the dal and one poured on top, plus a whiff of coal smoke give it its bold, no-frills dhaba character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: pungent wood-pressed mustard oil gives the Amritsari base its earthy, dhaba-style bite

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the second, top tadka of garlic and whole chilli is fried in ghee for a glossy finish

steps: Soak 1 cup urad and 0.25 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 4 cups water for 7 whistles until they collapse when pressed.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking point, then lower the flame, crackle 1 tsp cumin and 2 dried red chillies, and fry 2 tbsp chopped garlic until pale gold, about 1 minute.
Add 2 chopped onions and cook 7 minutes to deep golden, then stir in 1.5 cups tomato puree and 2 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and bhuno 8-9 minutes until thick and the oil pools at the edges.
Add the cooked dal, mash a ladleful for body, and simmer on low heat for 30 minutes with a splash of hot water as needed until dark and thick.
For the coal smoke, place a lit charcoal piece in a small bowl set on the dal, drizzle it with a little ghee, cover for 2 minutes, then remove; stir in 2 tbsp butter and the remaining salt.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, fry the remaining 1 tbsp garlic, 1 dried red chilli and the ginger juliennes until golden, and pour this second tadka sizzling over the dal.
tips: Mustard oil must be heated to smoking and then cooled slightly before use, or its raw pungency will dominate the dal.
The dhungar coal-smoking step is optional but delivers the authentic dhaba smokiness in minutes.
Keep the cream out entirely for the true Amritsari leanness; the butter and slow simmer supply all the richness needed.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle into a steel bowl topped with ginger juliennes and serve with thick tandoori laccha paratha and a raw onion-lachcha salad dressed in lemon.

variations.name: Kashmiri Dal Makhani
variations.description: A fragrant valley-style black dal cooked without onion or garlic, in the Kashmiri Pandit tradition, and seasoned instead with fennel, dry ginger and a hint of ratan jot for colour. The result is aromatic and gently spiced, quite different from the garlicky Punjabi original.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the traditional cooking fat of Kashmiri kitchens, giving the dal its authentic valley character

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the finishing tadka of cumin and Kashmiri chilli is bloomed in ghee for aroma and colour

steps: Soak 1 cup urad and 0.25 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 1 tsp salt and 4 cups water for 7 whistles until fully soft.
Warm 1 tsp ratan jot in 1 tbsp of the Anveshan Mustard Oil on low heat for 1 minute until the oil turns crimson, then strain and reserve this coloured oil.

Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, cool slightly, then crackle 3 cloves and 3 cardamom and fry 0.75 cup tomato puree with 2 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder for 7 minutes until the oil separates.
Stir in 1.5 tsp fennel powder and 1 tsp dry ginger, cook 1 minute, then add the cooked dal and simmer on low heat for 30 minutes until thick and aromatic.
Mix in 2 tbsp butter, the remaining salt and the reserved ratan jot oil for a deep red hue, simmering 5 minutes more.
For the tadka, heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin and a pinch of Kashmiri chilli, and pour it over the dal just before serving.
tips: Fennel and dry ginger replace onion and garlic here, so measure them properly; they carry the whole dish.
Ratan jot is purely for the classic red colour and is steeped in warm oil, never eaten, so strain it out before using the oil.
This dal tastes cleaner and lighter than the Punjabi version, so keep the cream out and let the spices lead.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed Kashmiri rice and a side of haakh or a simple radish salad; the fennel-scented dal is a natural partner to plain rice rather than bread.

variations.name: Hyderabadi Dal Makhani
variations.description: A spicier, tangier southern reimagining where curry leaves, a hint of tamarind and extra green chilli sharpen the rich black dal. The southern tadka of mustard seeds and curry leaves in ghee brings a fragrance you'd never find in a Punjabi dhaba.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil suits the southern-style base and tempering perfectly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the curry-leaf and mustard-seed tadka is finished in ghee for a rounded, aromatic top note

steps: Soak 1 cup urad and 0.25 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 4 cups water for 7 whistles until soft and creamy.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, sauté 1 large chopped onion with 3 slit green chillies for 6 minutes until golden, then add 2 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 2 minutes.
Add 1 cup chopped tomato and 2 tsp red chilli powder and cook 8 minutes until pulpy and the oil separates, then stir in 1 tsp tamarind pulp for a gentle southern tang.
Tip in the cooked dal, mash lightly, and simmer on low heat for 30 minutes with a little hot water until thick and dark.
Stir in 3 tbsp cream and the remaining salt and simmer 4 minutes until glossy and rounded.
For the tadka, heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil with 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 15 curry leaves until they crackle, and pour over the dal.
tips: Add the tamarind sparingly; it should brighten the dal, not turn it sour, so taste as you go.
Let the mustard seeds fully splutter before adding curry leaves, or the tadka tastes raw and bitter.
The green chillies bring the heat here rather than red chilli alone, giving a fresher, sharper spice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft rumali roti or plain steamed rice and a wedge of lime; a bowl of cooling raita balances the extra chilli and tang.

variations.name: Rajasthani Smoked Dal Makhani
variations.description: A leaner, boldly smoky desert-style black dal that leans on a double dhungar coal-smoking and dry red chilli rather than cream for its punch. Ghee, not butter, carries the richness, giving it a rustic Marwari depth suited to eating with bajra roti.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the desert-style base is cooked in wood-pressed groundnut oil for a clean, robust flavour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee replaces cream and butter here, carrying the Marwari richness and the final dry-chilli tadka

steps: Soak 1 cup urad and 0.25 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 4 cups water for 7 whistles until melting soft.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin and fry 2 tbsp crushed garlic until golden, then add 1 large chopped onion and cook 6 minutes to deep brown.
Add 1 cup tomato puree, 2 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, and bhuno 8 minutes until the masala is thick and the oil surfaces.
Add the cooked dal, mash a portion, and simmer on low heat for 35 minutes with splashes of hot water until dark and thick.
Do a first dhungar: rest a lit coal in a bowl on the dal, pour over a little ghee, cover 2 minutes, then repeat the smoking once more for the desert-deep smokiness before removing the coal.
Finish by heating 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, frying 4 whole Mathania chillies until they darken and swell, and pouring this fiery tadka over the dal with the remaining salt stirred in.
tips: Doing the dhungar twice is the trick to the pronounced smokiness that defines this desert version.
Mathania chillies are more about deep colour and aroma than raw heat, so don't be alarmed by the four whole pods.
Skipping cream keeps it lean and rustic, so let the ghee and long simmer do the enriching instead.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot bajra or makki roti smeared with white butter and a side of jaggery and sliced onion, the classic Rajasthani winter plate.

variations.name: Classic Masala Dosa
variations.description: The iconic South-Indian breakfast: a fermented rice-and-urad batter spread paper-thin and crisped on the tava, wrapped around a soft, turmeric-yellow potato masala. Cooked and finished in Anveshan Sesame Oil and ghee, the dosa shatters at the edges and stays soft where it hugs the buttery aloo.

ingredients.name: Fermented dosa batter (rice and urad dal)
Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil for tempering the masala and crisping the dosa to a golden lace.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: Brushed on the dosa as it crisps for the classic aromatic, restaurant-style sheen.

steps: Boil 4 medium potatoes until fork-tender, peel and break them into rough chunks, not a smooth mash.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal for 30 seconds, then add 2 sliced onions, 2 slit green chillies, a chopped 1-inch piece of ginger and 12 curry leaves and saute 3-4 minutes until the onions turn soft and translucent.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric and the potatoes with 1 tsp salt and a splash of water, and cook 2-3 minutes until it comes together into a moist, chunky masala; keep warm.
Heat a tava over medium-high, wipe it with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, then pour a ladle of batter at the centre and spread it outward in a spiral into a thin, even round.
Drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil around the edge, brush the top with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee, and cook for 2-3 minutes until the base is golden-brown and crisp and lifts easily.
Place 3 tbsp potato masala along the centre, fold the dosa over it into a roll or triangle, and serve hot before repeating with the rest.
tips: Break the boiled potatoes into chunks rather than mashing them, so the masala keeps texture instead of turning pasty.
The tava must be hot but not smoking; sprinkle a few drops of water and wipe with an onion half to season it before the first dosa.
Spread the batter in a single confident spiral; going back over set batter tears the thin dosa.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve open with coconut chutney, tomato chutney and a bowl of sambar for dipping the crisp corners.

variations.name: Bihari Masala Dosa
variations.description: A northern-plains reworking where the potato filling is built on garam masala, coriander powder and a hit of amchur for a tangy, spice-market depth quite unlike the mild South classic. The dosa is crisped in Anveshan Groundnut Oil and finished with ghee for a fragrant, hearty result.

ingredients.name: Fermented dosa batter (rice and urad dal)
Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil for the north-Indian style tempering and a crisp dosa base.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: Brushed on the dosa to crisp and perfume the crust in the northern manner.

steps: Boil and peel 4 medium potatoes, then break them into rough chunks.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, add 2 chopped onions and fry 3-4 minutes until golden at the edges.

Lower the heat and stir in 1 tsp garam masala, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder for 30 seconds, then fold in the potatoes, 1 tsp amchur, 1 tsp salt and a splash of water and cook 3 minutes into a tangy, chunky masala.
Heat a tava over medium-high, wipe with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, ladle the batter at the centre and spread outward into a thin round.
Drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil at the edges, brush the top with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee, and cook 2-3 minutes until crisp and golden underneath.
Spoon 3 tbsp of the masala down the centre, scatter coriander, fold over and serve, then repeat with the remaining batter.
tips: Toast the ground spices in the oil for only half a minute; any longer over high heat and they turn bitter.
Amchur gives the signature tang here, but a squeeze of lime stirred in at the end works if you have none.
For a drier filling that won't wet the dosa, cook off any extra water before spooning it in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a raw onion-and-green-chilli salad and a bowl of thin sambar for a satisfying plains-style breakfast.

variations.name: Madhya Pradesh Spicy Masala Dosa
variations.description: A bold central-Indian version where the potato masala is fired up with pounded green chillies and cracked black pepper, and a light dusting of pepper goes into the crisp dosa itself. Cooked in Anveshan Sesame Oil with a ghee finish, it is aromatic, peppery and warming from the first bite.

ingredients.name: Fermented dosa batter (rice and urad dal)
Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Nutty wood-pressed gingelly oil for tempering the fiery masala and crisping the dosa.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: Brushed on to crisp the dosa and gently soften the sharp pepper heat.

steps: Boil, peel and roughly break 4 medium potatoes, and coarsely crush 1.5 tsp peppercorns.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 3 broken dry red chillies, then add 2 chopped onions, 4 slit green chillies, a chopped 1.5-inch piece of ginger and 12 curry leaves and saute 3-4 minutes until soft.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric, half the crushed pepper and the potatoes with 1 tsp salt and a splash of water, cooking 3 minutes into a peppery, chunky masala.
Heat a tava over medium-high, wipe with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, ladle the batter and spread thin, then scatter a pinch of the remaining crushed pepper over the surface.
Drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil at the edges, brush with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee, and cook 2-3 minutes until deep golden and crisp.
Lay 3 tbsp of the spicy masala along the middle, scatter 3 tbsp coriander leaves over it, fold over and serve immediately, then repeat with the rest of the batter.
tips: Crack the peppercorns fresh for a clean, aromatic heat that layers differently from chilli powder.
Splitting the pepper between filling and dosa gives heat in both the crust and the core.
A spoon of curd served alongside quickly cools the palate between fiery bites.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling coconut-curd chutney and plenty of sambar to balance the pepper-and-chilli heat.

variations.name: Goan Cheesy Masala Dosa
variations.description: A coastal cafe-style dosa where a layer of grated cheese is melted over the crisp interior before the potato masala goes in, giving a gooey, molten cheese-and-aloo core. Cooked in Anveshan Coconut Oil for a fragrant Goan base, it is rich, indulgent and a sure-fire favourite with children.

ingredients.name: Fermented dosa batter (rice and urad dal)
Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil for a fragrant coastal base that crisps around the melting cheese.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: A brush of ghee to crisp the dosa and gloss the cheesy interior.

steps: Boil, peel and roughly break 3 medium potatoes.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, add 1 chopped onion, 2 slit green chillies and 10 curry leaves and saute 3 minutes until soft, then fold in the potatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp black pepper and 1 tsp salt and cook 2 minutes into a mild masala.
Heat a tava over medium-high, wipe with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, ladle the batter and spread thin, then drizzle 1 tsp coconut oil at the edges.
When the base is nearly crisp, scatter 3 tbsp grated cheese over the centre and brush the surface with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee, letting the cheese melt for about a minute.
Spoon 3 tbsp of the potato masala over the melted cheese, then fold the dosa over the filling.
Cook another 30 seconds until the base is deep golden, then serve hot and repeat with the remaining batter.
tips: Add the cheese only once the dosa base is set and crisp, so it melts onto the dosa and not the bare tava.
Keep the potato masala mild here, letting the cheese be the star rather than competing with heavy spice.
A mix of processed and mozzarella cheese gives both the savoury flavour and the satisfying pull.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a fresh coconut chutney and, for younger eaters, a small bowl of tomato ketchup.

variations.name: Mysore Red Masala Dosa
variations.description: The famous Karnataka dosa smeared inside with a fiery red garlic-chilli chutney before the potato masala is added, giving a signature sweet-hot base you taste in every bite. Made with Anveshan Sesame Oil and finished in ghee, the crisp dosa and spicy red layer are a Bengaluru institution.

ingredients.name: Fermented dosa batter (rice and urad dal)
Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil for frying the red chutney base and crisping the dosa.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: Brushed on generously for the rich, glossy crust a Mysore masala dosa is known for.

steps: Soak 6 dry red chillies in hot water for 10 minutes, then grind with 8 garlic cloves, 2 tbsp roasted chana dal, half a chopped onion and a little water to a thick, smooth red chutney.

Boil, peel and break 4 potatoes; heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, add the remaining 1.5 onions and 12 curry leaves, saute 3 minutes, then fold in the potatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for a chunky masala.
Heat a tava over medium-high, wipe with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, ladle the batter and spread it thin into an even round.
Spread 1 heaped tbsp of the red chutney over the surface, drizzle 1 tsp sesame oil at the edges and brush with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee.
Cook 2-3 minutes until the base is deep golden and crisp and the chutney has darkened into the dosa.
Lay 3 tbsp potato masala along the centre, fold over and serve hot, then repeat with the remaining batter and chutney.
tips: Grind the red chutney thick, not runny, so it clings to the dosa instead of soaking through and tearing it.
Make a double batch of the chutney; it keeps a week refrigerated and doubles as a sandwich spread.
Roasted chana dal thickens the chutney and rounds the garlic; don't skip it for the authentic texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with white coconut chutney and sambar so each bite balances the fiery red layer with something cool.

variations.name: Classic Masala Khichdi
variations.description: The ultimate one-pot comfort food where rice and moong dal are pressure-cooked soft with mixed vegetables and warm spices, then finished with a fragrant ghee tempering. Soothing yet flavourful, it is nourishing enough for a sick day and tasty enough for a family dinner.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee makes the finishing tarka and gives khichdi its comforting, digestible richness

steps: Rinse 1 cup rice and 0.5 cup moong dal together until the water runs clear, then soak 15 minutes and drain.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pressure cooker over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them sizzle 30 seconds.
Add 1 chopped onion, grated 1 inch ginger and 2 slit green chillies, frying 3 minutes until softened, then add 1 chopped tomato and 1 cup mixed vegetables and sauté 3 minutes.
Add the drained rice and dal, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt, stir 1 minute, then pour in 4 cups water.
Close the lid and pressure-cook for 4 whistles on medium heat, about 12 minutes, until the dal is completely soft and the mixture is porridge-like.
Release the pressure, stir in the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, adjust with hot water for a loose consistency and serve hot.
tips: Use a 2:1 rice-to-dal ratio for a khichdi that is soft but not gluey.
Khichdi thickens as it cools, so keep it looser than you think and loosen with hot water later.
A final spoon of raw ghee on top is traditional and makes it far easier to digest.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve steaming hot with a bowl of plain curd, a spoon of mango pickle and crisp papad on the side.

variations.name: Gujarati Vaghareli Khichdi
variations.description: The homely Gujarati vaghareli khichdi, softer and more porridge-like, tempered with cloves, cinnamon and a hint of sweetness. Traditionally eaten with kadhi, it is soothing everyday food that Gujarati households turn to for a light, wholesome dinner.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee makes the aromatic vaghar and is spooned over generously, Gujarati style

steps: Rinse 1 cup rice and 0.5 cup moong dal together, soak 15 minutes and drain well.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pressure cooker over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds, 3 cloves, 1 inch cinnamon and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and sizzle 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add grated 1 inch ginger and 2 slit green chillies, fry 30 seconds, then add 1 cubed potato and 0.5 cup peas and toss 2 minutes.
Add the drained rice and dal, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt, stir 1 minute, then pour in 4.5 cups water for a soft, loose texture.
Close the lid and pressure-cook for 5 whistles on medium heat, about 14 minutes, until the dal is fully soft and the khichdi is porridge-like.
Release the pressure, whisk in the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and a little hot water to keep it flowing, and serve hot.
tips: Gujarati khichdi is meant to be soft and moist, so use more water than a firm khichdi.
It pairs classically with a bowl of hot Gujarati kadhi poured right over the top.
Bloom the whole cloves and cinnamon well in ghee, as they carry the signature aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with warm Gujarati kadhi, a spoon of chunda pickle and a papad for the classic khichdi-kadhi combination.

variations.name: Rajasthani Bajra Khichdi
variations.description: A rustic Rajasthani khichdi that swaps in nutty pearl millet (bajra) alongside moong dal, cooked hearty and finished with plenty of ghee to suit the desert winter. Wholesome and grounding, it is traditionally paired with chaas and a lump of white butter.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Generous ghee warms and enriches this hearty desert-winter millet khichdi

steps: Coarsely crush 1 cup pearl millet, rinse it with 0.5 cup moong dal, then soak 30 minutes and drain, as millet needs longer to soften.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pressure cooker over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds, 3 cloves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and sizzle 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 6 crushed garlic cloves, grated 1 inch ginger and 2 slit green chillies, frying 1 minute until the garlic turns golden and fragrant.
Add the drained millet and dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt, stir 1 minute, then pour in 5 cups water.
Close the lid and pressure-cook for 7 whistles on medium heat, about 20 minutes, until the millet and dal are completely soft and blended.
Release the pressure, mash lightly, stir in the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and loosen with hot water before serving.
tips: Crush the bajra coarsely and soak it well so it cooks soft in the pressure cooker.
This khichdi is dense, so mash it a little and keep it loose with extra hot water and ghee.
It is winter food; serve it very hot as it thickens quickly in cold weather.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve Rajasthani-style with a glass of salted chaas, a spoon of white butter and a garlic-chilli chutney.

variations.name: Bengali Bhuni Khichuri
variations.description: The festive Bengali bhuni khichuri where roasted moong dal and rice are cooked with vegetables in mustard oil and a whole-spice tempering, then finished with ghee. Drier and richer than everyday khichdi, it is the beloved rainy-day and Durga Puja bhog dish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Mustard oil starts the tempering with the sharp Bengali flavour khichuri needs

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of ghee gives the bhog khichuri its festive aroma

steps: Dry-roast 0.75 cup moong dal in a pan on low heat for 4 minutes until golden and fragrant, then rinse it with 1 cup gobindobhog rice and drain.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pot until it smokes, lower the heat, and fry 1 cubed potato and 1 cup cauliflower for 4 minutes until light golden, then remove.
In the same oil add 2 bay leaves and 1 tsp cumin seeds, sizzle 30 seconds, then add grated 1.5 inch ginger and 3 slit green chillies and fry 30 seconds.
Add the roasted dal and rice with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt, stir 2 minutes, then pour in 4 cups hot water and add 0.5 cup peas.
Simmer uncovered on medium heat for 15 minutes, adding the fried vegetables halfway, until the dal is soft and the khichuri is thick but not dry.
Stir in 0.5 tsp garam masala and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, rest 5 minutes covered and serve hot.
tips: Roasting the moong dal first is essential for the nutty aroma that defines bhuni khichuri.
Keep this khichuri thicker and drier than a regular khichdi so the grains stay distinct.
Fry the vegetables separately and add them late so they keep their shape and bite.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve Durga Puja bhog style with begun bhaja (fried aubergine) and a tomato-date chutney.

variations.name: Tamil Nadu Ven Pongal Khichdi
variations.description: A South Indian ven pongal style khichdi where rice and moong dal are cooked creamy and tempered with peppercorns, cumin, ginger and cashews in ghee. Peppery, silky and deeply comforting, it is the classic temple breakfast dressed as a savoury khichdi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee fries the cashews and pepper tempering that define ven pongal

steps: Dry-roast 0.5 cup moong dal on low heat for 3 minutes until fragrant, then rinse it with 1 cup raw rice and drain.
Pressure-cook the rice and dal with 4.5 cups water and 1.25 tsp salt for 5 whistles on medium heat, about 14 minutes, until very soft, then mash lightly to a creamy mush.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat and fry 3 tbsp cashews until golden, about 2 minutes, then remove half for garnish.
To the remaining ghee add 1.5 tsp crushed black pepper, 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida, sizzling 30 seconds until aromatic.
Add grated 1.5 inch ginger, 2 slit green chillies and 12 curry leaves, frying 30 seconds until the leaves crisp.
Pour the tempering into the mashed khichdi, stir well, garnish with the reserved cashews and serve piping hot.
tips: Freshly crushed black pepper, not powder, gives ven pongal its signature warm heat.
Keep the khichdi soft and creamy, mashing it while hot and loosening with hot water as needed.
Do not skimp on ghee here, as it carries the pepper and cumin flavour through the dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and a small bowl of sambar for a temple-style South Indian breakfast.

variations.name: Classic Moong Dal Halwa
variations.description: The labour-of-love North Indian halwa where soaked split moong is ground to a paste and roasted in ghee for the better part of an hour until it turns granular, deep golden and richly aromatic. Finished with warm milk and cardamom into a glossy, ghee-laden indulgence. The showpiece dessert of winter weddings and Holi feasts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The generous ghee is non-negotiable; it roasts the raw dal paste and gives the halwa its signature richness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery lends a deeper, more wholesome sweetness than sugar and marries well with the roasted dal.

steps: Soak 1 cup split moong dal in water for 4 hours, then drain and grind to a coarse, thick paste using very little water.
Heat 3/4 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai on low-medium heat and add the dal paste, stirring to break up lumps.

Roast patiently for 30 to 35 minutes on low heat, stirring almost constantly, until the paste changes from a sticky mass to a loose, granular, deep-golden mixture that smells nutty and the ghee separates.
Meanwhile warm 1.5 cups milk with 1/2 cup water; pour it into the roasted dal in a slow stream, stirring hard to avoid lumps, and cook for 5 minutes until absorbed.
Lower the heat, stir in 3/4 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp cardamom powder, and cook for 4 to 5 minutes until glossy and thick.
Fold in 3 tbsp slivered almonds and 3 tbsp chopped cashews and serve hot.
tips: The long roast is the whole dish; rush it and the halwa tastes raw and pasty no matter how much ghee you add.
Add the jaggery only after the milk is absorbed and off high heat, since jaggery can make dairy split if boiled hard.
Keep the ground paste thick and coarse; a watery grind lengthens the roasting time dramatically and dulls the texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot in winter, topped with extra ghee and a scatter of nuts; a small bowl is plenty after a festive meal.

variations.name: Rajasthani Mawa Moong Halwa
variations.description: The regal Marwari version enriched with khoya, which makes the halwa denser, creamier and even more decadent. Saffron gives it a jewel-like colour fit for royal thalis. Slow-cooked and lavish, this is the halwa of Rajasthani wedding feasts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee roasts the dal and later helps the khoya melt into a smooth, rich body.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery deepens the milky khoya with a warm caramel note while keeping the halwa unrefined.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Saffron bloomed in warm milk gives this royal halwa its golden hue and heady aroma.

steps: Soak 1 cup split moong dal for 4 hours, drain and grind to a coarse, thick paste; soak a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp of the warm milk.
Heat 3/4 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai on low-medium heat, add the dal paste and roast for 30 to 35 minutes, stirring, until granular, deep golden and separating from the ghee.
Crumble in 3/4 cup khoya and cook together for 5 minutes on low heat until it melts and smells of caramelised milk.
Warm the remaining milk and pour it in slowly with the saffron milk, stirring hard, and cook for 5 minutes until absorbed.
Stir in 3/4 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp cardamom powder and cook for 4 to 5 minutes until thick and glossy.
Garnish with 3 tbsp slivered pistachios and serve hot.
tips: Add the khoya only after the dal is properly roasted, or its moisture stalls the roasting and the halwa turns gluey.
Use fresh soft khoya; dried mawa refuses to melt smoothly and leaves grainy lumps.
Bloom the saffron in warm milk rather than adding it dry so its colour and fragrance spread evenly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm in small silver bowls at a wedding or Teej feast, topped with a saffron strand and pistachio slivers.

variations.name: Gujarati Coarse Moong Halwa
variations.description: A quicker Gujarati-style halwa made with coarsely ground moong for a distinctly grainy, rustic texture rather than a smooth paste. Lighter on ghee and dairy, leaning on the roasted-dal flavour itself. Homely, fast and everyday-festive.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A slightly lighter hand with ghee suits this quicker, grainier home-style halwa.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery gives the coarse-grain halwa a warm, rounded sweetness.

steps: Soak 1 cup split moong dal for 3 hours, drain and grind to a coarse rava-like consistency rather than a smooth paste.
Heat 1/2 cup Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on low-medium heat, add the coarse dal and roast for 25 minutes, stirring, until sandy, golden and fragrant.
Warm 1 cup milk with 3/4 cup water and add it slowly to the roasted dal, stirring to avoid lumps; cook for 6 to 7 minutes until the grains swell and soften.
Lower the heat and stir in 3/4 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 tsp cardamom powder and 1/4 tsp freshly grated nutmeg.
Cook for 4 minutes until the halwa thickens and holds a grainy, spoonable texture.
Fold in 3 tbsp slivered pistachios and serve warm.
tips: Grind the dal coarse like semolina for the signature grainy bite; a fine paste turns this into the richer classic instead.
The coarse grains need a little more liquid, so add a splash more warm milk if the halwa stiffens too fast.
Freshly grated nutmeg gives a warm lift that suits this lighter style; add it at the end so it does not cook off.
