variations.servingSuggestion: A comforting everyday sweet after a Gujarati thali; the grainy texture pairs nicely with a spoon of cool plain yoghurt on the side.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Nutmeg Moong Halwa
variations.description: A fragrant Maharashtrian take perfumed generously with nutmeg and a bloom of whole spices in the ghee, giving the halwa a warm, aromatic complexity. Finished with a splash of milk for a soft set. Cosy, spiced and a little different from the plain classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The whole spices are bloomed in hot ghee first so their aroma infuses the entire halwa.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery underpins the warm spice profile with a molasses depth.

steps: Soak 1 cup split moong dal for 4 hours, drain and grind to a coarse, thick paste.
Heat 3/4 cup Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium heat and bloom 4 lightly crushed cardamom pods and 2 cloves for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the dal paste and roast on low heat for 30 to 35 minutes, stirring, until granular, deep golden and the ghee separates.
Warm 1.5 cups milk and pour it in slowly, stirring hard to keep it smooth, then cook for 5 minutes until absorbed.
Lower the heat and stir in 3/4 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1/2 tsp freshly grated nutmeg, cooking for 4 minutes until thick and glossy.
Fish out the whole cloves, fold in 3 tbsp chopped cashews and serve hot.
tips: Bloom the whole spices only briefly and on medium heat; burnt cloves turn the whole halwa acrid.
Remove the whole cloves before serving so no one bites into one, or tie the spices in a small muslin bundle.
Grate the nutmeg fresh and add it late so its warm aroma stays bright rather than cooking away.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm on a cold evening with an extra grating of nutmeg on top; lovely alongside a cup of masala chai.

variations.name: Almond Moong Dal Halwa
variations.description: A doubly rich Punjabi variation where a paste of soaked almonds joins the moong dal, deepening the nuttiness and giving an almost badam-halwa luxury. Slow-roasted and finished with saffron milk. Festive, fragrant and thoroughly indulgent.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee roasts both the dal and almond pastes together into a deeply nutty base.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery complements the almond richness with a warm, unrefined sweetness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Saffron bloomed in warm milk perfumes and colours the almond-rich halwa.

steps: Soak 1 cup split moong dal and 1/2 cup almonds separately for 4 hours; peel the almonds, then grind the dal and almonds each to a coarse thick paste.
Soak a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp of the warm milk and set aside.
Heat 3/4 cup Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on low-medium heat, add both pastes and roast for 32 to 38 minutes, stirring, until granular, golden and the ghee separates.
Warm the remaining milk, pour it in slowly with the saffron milk, stirring hard, and cook for 5 minutes until absorbed.
Lower the heat, stir in 3/4 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp cardamom powder, and cook for 4 to 5 minutes until glossy and thick.
Garnish with 3 tbsp chopped cashews and serve hot.
tips: The almond paste browns faster than the dal, so keep the heat low and stir continuously to roast them evenly.
Peel the soaked almonds for a smoother, paler halwa; the skins add a faint bitterness and speckle.
This version needs a touch longer roasting than the classic because of the extra almond moisture, so be patient.
variations.servingSuggestion: A luxurious close to a festive Punjabi meal; serve warm with a thin drizzle of ghee and extra saffron strands.

variations.name: Classic Smoky Dhaba Moong Dal
variations.description: The roadside dhaba moong is robust and smoky, its onion-tomato masala fried dark in ghee, spiked with garam masala and kasuri methi, and finished with a charcoal dhungar. It carries the unmistakable tandoor-smoke aroma that makes highway dal so addictive.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Used both to fry the dark dhaba masala and to pour over the smoking charcoal for the dhungar.

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 4 whistles, then whisk to a medium consistency and keep warm.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium, splutter 1 tsp cumin, then fry the 2 chopped onions for 9 minutes until deep golden brown.

Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 2 slit green chillies, cook 1 minute, then add the 2 chopped tomatoes, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tbsp coriander powder and bhuna 8 minutes until the ghee separates.
Pour in the whisked dal with a little hot water, add 0.5 tsp salt, and simmer on low for 8 minutes, then crush in 1 tbsp kasuri methi and 0.75 tsp garam masala.
For the dhungar, set a heated charcoal piece in a small bowl on the dal, pour the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over it, cover tightly for 2 minutes, then remove the bowl.
Stir the smoke through, garnish with 2 tbsp coriander, and serve hot.
tips: The charcoal dhungar is what gives dhaba dal its signature smoke, so do not skip it if you can help it.
Fry the masala until you see ghee pooling at the edges; under-cooked masala tastes raw and flat.
A knob of butter melted on top just before serving adds the final dhaba flourish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tandoori roti or laccha paratha, sliced onions, green chilli and a wedge of lemon.

variations.name: Haryanvi Desi Ghee Moong Dal
variations.description: The Haryanvi highway version is rustic and ghee-forward, thickened with a little bathua or fresh greens and finished with a heavy hand of desi ghee. It is hearty, garlicky and unpretentious, the fuel of farmers and truckers alike.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A generous pour of desi ghee is the whole point of this rustic Haryanvi dal.

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt, the grated 1 inch ginger, the 1 cup chopped bathua and 3 cups water for 5 whistles until soft.
Whisk the dal and greens together into a coarse, hearty mash and keep it simmering on low.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium, add 1 tsp cumin and 3 broken dry red chillies and let them crackle for 30 seconds.
Add the 8 crushed garlic cloves and fry 1.5 minutes until deep golden and fragrant, then add the chopped large onion and cook 6 minutes to brown.
Add the chopped tomato and 1 tsp red chilli powder and cook 4 minutes until pulpy, then pour this ghee tadka into the dal.
Simmer everything together for 5 minutes, adjust salt, and serve with the ghee glistening on top.
tips: Bathua greens are traditional and add an earthy note; spinach works well if bathua is out of season.
This is meant to be a ghee-rich dal, so do not be shy with the tadka fat.
Crush the garlic rather than mincing it, so you get soft, sweet bites of it through the dal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thick bajra or wheat roti smeared with white butter and a raw onion on the side.

variations.name: GT Road Trucker's Garlic Tadka Moong
variations.description: This is the fiery, garlic-loaded moong slapped together at Grand Trunk Road truck stops, where a second sizzling tadka is poured over the dal tableside. Sharp with garlic and whole red chilli, it is built for flavour and speed rather than finesse.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The base cooking fat for the first tadka that builds the dal's body.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Smoked and used for the fierce second garlic tadka poured over the dal at the finish.

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 4 whistles, then whisk to a medium consistency.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium, splutter 1 tsp cumin, add 6 of the crushed garlic cloves and fry 1 minute, then add the chopped onion and cook 6 minutes to golden.
Add the 2 chopped tomatoes and 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and cook 6 minutes until pulpy, then pour in the dal and simmer 6 minutes with 0.5 tsp garam masala.
Ladle the dal into a serving bowl and keep it hot while you make the second tadka.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a small pan on high until it smokes, lower the flame, add the remaining 6 crushed garlic cloves and 4 dry red chillies, and fry 1 minute until the garlic is dark gold.
Pour this fierce sizzling tadka over the dal so it crackles, scatter 2 tbsp coriander, and serve at once.
tips: The drama and flavour come from the second tadka, so pour it over piping hot for that roadside sizzle.
Use plenty of garlic; this dal is meant to be boldly, unapologetically garlicky.
Smoke the mustard oil well before the garlic goes in to soften its raw pungency.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot tandoori roti and thick onion slices, letting everyone scoop the crackling garlic tadka.

variations.name: Malwi Dhaba Moong with Amchur
variations.description: From the dhabas of Malwa in Madhya Pradesh comes this tangy moong, spiced with a coarse local garam masala and soured with dry mango powder rather than tomato. It is medium-thick, warmly spiced and pleasantly sour, distinct from the creamy Punjabi style.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Carries the coarse Malwi spice tadka and gives the dal its dhaba richness.

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 4 whistles, then whisk to a medium-thick consistency.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium, add 1 tsp cumin and 0.25 tsp hing and let them sizzle for 20 seconds.
Add the chopped large onion and fry 7 minutes until golden, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Lower the heat and add 1.25 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tbsp coriander powder, stirring for 15 seconds so they bloom, then pour in the whisked dal.
Simmer the dal on low for 7 minutes, then stir in 1 tsp amchur and 0.75 tsp garam masala and cook 3 more minutes so the tang sets in.
Adjust salt, garnish with 2 tbsp coriander, and serve hot.
tips: Amchur gives a cleaner, sharper tang than tomato and keeps the dal a lovely golden colour.
Add the amchur towards the end so its sourness stays bright rather than turning flat.
A coarsely pounded homemade garam masala suits this rustic Malwi style better than a fine store blend.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thick hand-rolled roti and a side of raw onion, or with steamed rice and a green chilli pickle.

variations.name: Awadhi Dum Moong Dal
variations.description: The Awadhi dhaba treatment finishes moong with a slow dum, sealing the pot so the whole spices and ghee perfume the dal deeply. Fragrant with green cardamom and mace, it is gentler and more aromatic than its fiery North-Indian cousins.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The aromatic base fat that carries the whole spices during the slow dum finish.

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 4 whistles, then whisk smooth and keep aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot on medium, add 1 tsp cumin, 4 cardamom pods, 4 cloves and 1 mace blade and let them release their aroma for 40 seconds.
Add the finely chopped large onion and fry 8 minutes to a soft gold, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Add the chopped tomato and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and cook 5 minutes until soft, then pour in the whisked dal and a little hot water.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp kewra water, cover the pot with a tight lid or seal with dough, and cook on the lowest flame for 10 minutes so the dal takes on a dum aroma.
Open the pot, stir gently, garnish with 2 tbsp coriander, and serve fragrant and warm.
tips: The dum stage is what sets this apart, so seal the pot well and keep the flame as low as possible.
Use kewra sparingly; a few drops perfume the whole dal but too much turns it soapy.
Fish out the whole cardamom and cloves before serving if you prefer not to bite into them.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sheermal, roomali roti or a light pulao, garnished with fried onions for an Awadhi touch.

variations.name: Classic Home-style Moong Dal
variations.description: This is the unfussy weeknight moong dal that tastes of home, cooked soft with turmeric and finished with a gentle ghee tadka of cumin, garlic and a little onion-tomato. Nothing heavy, nothing showy, just a light, nourishing dal that goes with anything.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The homely tadka fat; a modest amount keeps this dal light yet fragrant.

steps: Rinse 1 cup moong dal well and pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp turmeric, the grated 1 inch ginger, 1 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 4 whistles until soft.
Lightly whisk the dal to a smooth, medium-thick consistency, adding hot water if needed, and keep it warm on low.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan on medium, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and the 4 sliced garlic cloves and fry 1 minute until the garlic is pale gold.
Add the chopped small onion and 1 slit green chilli and cook 3 minutes until the onion softens, then add the chopped tomato and 0.5 tsp red chilli powder.
Cook the tadka 4 minutes until the tomato breaks down and the ghee just separates, then pour it over the simmering dal.
Stir, simmer 2 minutes, and finish with 2 tbsp fresh coriander.
tips: Keep the tadka light; home-style dal should not be greasy or heavily spiced.
This dal thickens as it sits, so keep a little hot water handy to loosen it before serving.
A spoon of ghee stirred in at the table makes even the plainest dal feel special.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulka, plain rice and a simple cucumber-onion salad for an easy everyday meal.

variations.name: Rajasthani No-Onion Moong Dal
variations.description: The Rajasthani home version skips onion and garlic entirely, leaning on hing, ghee and dry spices for depth. It is a light, temple-style dal that comes together in minutes yet tastes remarkably complete thanks to a generous cumin-hing tempering.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: With no onion or garlic, ghee and hing do all the flavour-building in this Rajasthani dal.

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 4 whistles, then whisk to a smooth, medium consistency.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.5 tsp hing and let them sizzle for 20 seconds until the hing turns aromatic.
Add 2 broken dry red chillies and the grated 1 inch ginger and fry 40 seconds until the chillies darken slightly.
Lower the heat, add 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp coriander powder and stir for 10 seconds so they bloom without scorching, then add the chopped tomato.
Cook the tomato 4 minutes until soft, pour in the whisked dal, and simmer on low for 6 minutes so the hing perfumes the whole pot.
Adjust salt, garnish with 2 tbsp coriander, and serve hot.
tips: Hing is doing the job of onion and garlic here, so use a good-quality one and let it bloom fully in the ghee.
This dal is ideal for fasting days and quick lunches when you have no time to chop aromatics.
Blooming the ground spices off the direct flame prevents the bitterness that comes from burnt chilli powder.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra roti and a spoon of white butter, or with plain rice and a Rajasthani ker-sangri on the side.

variations.name: Kerala Cherupayar Parippu Curry
variations.description: In Kerala homes moong becomes a soft parippu curry finished with a fragrant coconut-oil tempering of mustard, shallots and curry leaves. A little coconut milk stirred in gives it a mellow, faintly sweet richness distinct from any North Indian dal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: The essential Kerala tempering fat that gives the parippu its sweet, nutty aroma.

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 slit green chillies, 1 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 4 whistles until very soft.
Grind the 3 tbsp grated coconut with a little water to a coarse paste, stir it into the cooked dal, and simmer 3 minutes on low.
Pour in 0.5 cup coconut milk, warm through gently without boiling hard so it does not split, then keep the parippu on the lowest flame.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan on medium, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop for 30 seconds.
Add 3 broken dry red chillies, the 6 sliced shallots and 15 curry leaves and fry 2 minutes until the shallots turn golden and the leaves crisp.
Pour the sizzling coconut-oil tempering over the parippu, stir once, and serve warm.
tips: Add the coconut milk only at the end and keep the heat low, as a rolling boil will curdle it.
Kerala shallots are sweeter than onion and give the tempering its signature flavour, so use them if you can.
A pinch of jaggery can be added with the coconut milk for the gentle sweetness typical of Kerala parippu.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as parippu over hot Kerala matta rice with a spoon of ghee and a poppadom, or as part of a sadya spread.

variations.name: Bihari Ghugni-style Moong with Mustard Oil
variations.description: This rustic Bihari home dal cooks the moong slightly thick and tempers it in mustard oil with panch phoron, garlic and green chilli. Earthy and pungent, it carries the no-frills, mustard-forward character of everyday eastern kitchens.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: The pungent eastern-Indian fat that gives this home dal its earthy, sharp backbone.

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 2.75 cups water for 4 whistles so it stays a little thick, then keep aside.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pan on high until it just smokes and pales, then lower to medium.
Add 1 tsp panch phoron and 2 dry red chillies and let them crackle for 30 seconds, then add the 6 crushed garlic cloves and fry 1 minute to golden.
Add the chopped medium onion and 3 slit green chillies and cook 4 minutes until soft, then add the chopped tomato and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and cook 4 minutes.
Pour the cooked dal into the tempering, stir well, and simmer on low for 6 minutes so the mustard-oil pungency mellows into the dal.
Adjust salt, garnish with 2 tbsp coriander, and serve hot.
tips: Smoking the mustard oil first is essential to remove its raw sharpness before the tempering goes in.
Keep this dal on the thicker side, as Bihari home dals are hearty rather than soupy.
The whole panch phoron seeds should stay in the dal for their fragrance, so do not strain them out.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice, a dollop of ghee and a fiery green chilli, or mop it up with hot litti.

variations.name: Assamese Matar Dali with Lemon
variations.description: The Assamese home dal is light, thin and clean-tasting, tempered simply in mustard oil with panch phoron and finished with a bright squeeze of lemon. It is meant to be sipped and mixed with rice, letting the natural sweetness of moong shine through.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: A light hand of mustard oil keeps this Assamese dal delicate yet subtly pungent.

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, the grated 1 inch ginger, 1 tsp salt and 3.25 cups water for 4 whistles until soft and thin.
Whisk the dal light and pourable, adding hot water if needed, and keep it warm on low.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a small pan on high until it just smokes, then reduce to medium.
Add 1 tsp panch phoron, 2 dry red chillies and 1 bay leaf and let them crackle for 30 seconds until the seeds turn fragrant.
Add 2 slit green chillies, fry 20 seconds, then pour the tempering into the dal and simmer 4 minutes so the flavours settle.
Turn off the heat, stir in 1 tbsp lemon juice and 2 tbsp coriander, and serve warm and light.
tips: Assamese dal is deliberately thin and delicate, so resist the urge to thicken or over-spice it.
Add the lemon off the heat to keep its fresh sourness intact.
A small piece of ginger cooked in the dal, then mashed, adds a clean warmth without any onion or garlic.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve poured over hot rice as the first course of an Assamese meal, alongside a simple aloo pitika (mashed potato).

variations.name: Classic Punjabi Moong Dal
variations.description: The rich Punjabi treatment of humble moong, built on a well-fried onion-tomato masala, butter and cream, and rounded off with crushed kasuri methi and garam masala. It is fuller and more indulgent than an everyday tadka dal, the kind served at family feasts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The base fat for frying the Punjabi masala; its richness underpins the whole dal.

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 4 whistles, then whisk lightly and keep warm.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with 1.5 tbsp butter in a pan on medium, splutter 1 tsp cumin seeds, then fry the 2 chopped onions for 9 minutes until golden brown.
Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute, then add the 2 pureed tomatoes and 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and cook 8 minutes until the ghee separates.
Pour the whisked dal into the masala, add a little hot water to reach a medium-thick consistency, and simmer on low for 8 minutes so the flavours meld.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the dal, stir in 3 tbsp cream and 0.75 tsp garam masala, and simmer a final 3 minutes until glossy.
Finish with 2 tbsp coriander and an extra swirl of cream before serving.
tips: Browning the onions well is the single biggest factor in getting that rich Punjabi flavour.
For a lighter version, skip the cream and use a little extra whisked curd instead.
Crushing the kasuri methi between your palms before adding it releases far more aroma into the dal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or jeera rice, a raw onion-lemon salad and a spoon of extra cream on top.

variations.name: Amritsari Langar-style Moong Dal
variations.description: Modeled on the vast simmering pots of the Golden Temple langar, this version is pure, ghee-finished and free of onion and garlic. Slow cooking and a simple hing-cumin tadka give it a soulful, comforting flavour that feeds a crowd.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The langar staple fat; a generous finishing spoon gives this pure dal its comforting richness.

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, the grated 1.5 inch ginger, 2 slit green chillies, 1 tsp salt and 3.5 cups water for 4 whistles until very soft.
Whisk the dal smooth and let it simmer gently on low for 10 minutes, stirring now and then, so it develops that slow-cooked langar body.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.5 tsp hing and let them sizzle for 20 seconds until aromatic.
Add the 2 finely chopped tomatoes, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp coriander powder and cook 6 minutes until the tomatoes melt and the ghee separates.
Pour this tadka into the simmering dal, stir well, and cook a further 5 minutes so the flavours settle into the pot.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala and 2 tbsp coriander, and serve piping hot.
tips: The character of langar dal comes from unhurried simmering, so give it the full slow cook rather than rushing.
Keeping it onion and garlic free makes it satvik and gentle on the stomach, true to the temple kitchen.
A final spoon of ghee stirred in just before serving mimics the way langar sevadars finish the pot.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tandoori roti or plain rice and a bowl of kheer to echo a Golden Temple langar meal.

variations.name: Patiala Shahi Moong with Saffron
variations.description: A royal Patiala rendition that turns everyday moong into a banquet dish with a cashew-cream base and threads of saffron. Mildly spiced and luxuriously smooth, it carries the courtly richness of old Punjabi princely kitchens.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The luxurious base fat for the shahi masala, giving the dal its silky mouthfeel.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Steeped in warm milk and swirled in for the golden colour and regal aroma of a shahi dal.

steps: Soak 0.25 tsp Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside, and soak the 12 cashews in hot water for 10 minutes, then grind them to a smooth paste.
Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 4 whistles, then whisk to a smooth cream.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium, crackle 1 tsp cumin and 3 lightly crushed cardamom pods, then add the finely chopped large onion and fry 8 minutes to a soft pale gold, not brown.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute, then stir in the cashew paste and cook 3 minutes on low until it smells nutty and the ghee edges out.
Pour in the whisked dal with a little hot water, add 0.25 tsp white pepper, and simmer gently for 6 minutes to a velvety consistency.
Stir in 3 tbsp cream and the saffron milk, warm through 2 minutes without boiling hard, and serve glowing golden.
tips: Keep the onions pale, not browned, so the dal stays fair and elegant as a shahi dish should.
Steeping the saffron in warm milk draws out both its colour and aroma far better than adding it dry.
White pepper instead of chilli keeps the heat gentle and the colour pristine, true to royal kitchens.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a fine bowl with a saffron thread garnish, alongside sheermal or a delicate pulao for a festive spread.

variations.name: Pindi-style Dry Moong Bhuna
variations.description: Inspired by Rawalpindi cooking, this is a nearly dry, deeply bhuna moong where the dal is steamed grainy and tossed with a dark, spice-heavy masala. Bold with anardana and coarse spices, it eats more like a sabzi than a soupy dal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Used to bhuna the dark masala that clings to the grainy, near-dry dal.

steps: Soak 1 cup moong dal 30 minutes, drain, then pressure-cook with just 1.25 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 2 whistles so the grains stay separate.
Dry-roast 1 tbsp coriander seeds until fragrant, then crush coarsely with the 1 tsp anardana to a rough powder.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium, splutter 1 tsp cumin, then fry the 2 chopped onions for 9 minutes until dark golden.

Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 2 slit green chillies, cook 1 minute, then add the chopped tomato, 1 tsp red chilli powder and the crushed coriander-anardana and bhuna 6 minutes until thick and dark.
Fold in the grainy dal and toss on medium for 4 minutes so the dry masala coats every grain, adding barely a splash of water to keep it nearly dry.
Sprinkle 0.75 tsp garam masala and 1 tbsp ginger julienne, toss once, and serve.
tips: Anardana gives this dal its characteristic tang and dark colour, so do not skip it.
The dal must stay grainy and dry, so keep the water to an absolute minimum after cooking.
Toasting and coarsely crushing your own spices, rather than using fine powders, gives the rugged Pindi texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve dry and hot with tandoori roti or kulcha, ginger julienne on top and a wedge of lemon.

variations.name: Kashmiri Pandit Moong with Fennel
variations.description: The Kashmiri Pandit version flavours moong with fennel and dry ginger instead of onion and garlic, tempered in ghee with a bloom of Kashmiri chilli. It is aromatic, warming and gently spiced, echoing the no-onion tradition of Pandit cooking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The Pandit kitchen fat that carries the fennel and Kashmiri chilli for this onion-free dal.

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rinsed moong dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 4 whistles, then whisk to a smooth, medium consistency.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium, add 1 tsp cumin, 0.5 tsp hing, 2 cardamom pods and 3 cloves and let them sizzle for 30 seconds.
Lower the flame and add 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1 tsp fennel powder and 0.75 tsp dry ginger powder, stirring for 10 seconds so they bloom in the ghee without burning.
Add the chopped tomato and cook 4 minutes until it softens and the spices turn glossy and deep red.
Pour in the whisked dal, add a little hot water, and simmer on low for 7 minutes so the fennel aroma infuses the pot.
Adjust salt, garnish with 2 tbsp coriander, and serve warm.
tips: Fennel and dry ginger are the defining Kashmiri notes, so use them fresh for the best fragrance.
Blooming the Kashmiri chilli in ghee gives a glowing red colour without much heat.
This onion-free dal suits fasting days and pairs beautifully with plain rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a Kashmiri dum aloo, or a simple nadru (lotus stem) side.

variations.name: Classic Nariyal Barfi
variations.description: The soft, snow-white coconut fudge of festival trays, made by simmering fresh grated coconut with milk and khandsari until it thickens into a fragrant, sliceable mass. A little milk powder gives body while cardamom and a hint of saffron lift it above the everyday.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: keeps the coconut from catching and lends the barfi a soft, glossy finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: sweetens the coconut cleanly and keeps the barfi bright white

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: a few strands bloomed in warm milk add fragrance and a faint golden fleck

steps: Soak 12 strands of Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 1 tbsp warm milk and grease an 8-inch tray with a little Anveshan Ghee.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan and sauté 3 cups fresh grated coconut on low heat for 4 minutes until it smells fragrant but has not coloured.
Pour in 0.5 cup whole milk and 1.25 cups Anveshan Khandsari and cook on medium heat for 8-10 minutes, stirring often, until the coconut absorbs the liquid and the mixture thickens.
Stir in 3 tbsp milk powder, the saffron milk and 0.75 tsp cardamom, and keep cooking 4-5 minutes until the mass pulls away from the sides and leaves a clean trail.
Fold in 2 tbsp chopped cashews, then spread the mixture into the greased tray and press it flat with the back of a greased spoon.
Smooth the top, let it set for 25 minutes until firm, then cut into squares and lift out once fully cool.
tips: Fresh coconut gives the best texture, but if using desiccated, soak it in the warm milk first so the barfi doesn't turn dry.
Stop cooking the moment the mixture leaves the sides; overcooked coconut barfi turns hard and chewy as it cools.
For clean cuts, wet the knife between slices so the sticky coconut doesn't drag.
variations.servingSuggestion: Cut into neat squares or press into small moulds for Raksha Bandhan and Janmashtami thalis; they stay fresh three to four days in an airtight box.

variations.name: Goan Coconut Jaggery Barfi
variations.description: Inspired by Goan doce, this barfi swaps sugar for earthy Anveshan jaggery, turning it a warm caramel-brown with a deeper, more toffee-like flavour. Toasted cashews and a whisper of nutmeg echo the Portuguese-influenced sweets of coastal Goa.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: helps the jaggery coat the coconut evenly and stops it sticking to the pan

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: gives the Goan barfi its warm caramel colour and toffee-deep sweetness

steps: Grease an 8-inch tray with a little Anveshan Ghee and toast 1 tbsp poppy seeds in a dry pan until they smell nutty, then set aside.
Melt 1.25 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 0.25 cup water on low heat and simmer 4 minutes into a thick syrup, straining out any grit.
In another pan heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and sauté 3 cups fresh grated coconut for 4 minutes on low heat until fragrant.
Pour the jaggery syrup over the coconut and cook on medium heat for 8-9 minutes, stirring constantly, until the mixture darkens to caramel and thickens into a mass.
Stir in 0.75 tsp cardamom, 0.25 tsp nutmeg and 3 tbsp toasted cashews, cooking 2 minutes more until it leaves the sides of the pan.
Spread into the tray, scatter the toasted poppy seeds on top, press flat and cut into squares after 25 minutes once set.
tips: Strain the melted jaggery to remove sand and fibre, which are common in unrefined blocks.
Jaggery barfi sets a touch softer than the sugar version, so chill it briefly before cutting for cleaner edges.
Toast the coconut only lightly; over-browning muddies the caramel colour the jaggery provides.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these caramel squares with a cup of filter coffee or wrap them for Christmas kuswar hampers alongside other Goan sweets.

variations.name: Bengali Narkel Naru
variations.description: The hand-rolled coconut jaggery balls made across Bengal for Lakshmi Puja, where fresh coconut is cooked down with date-palm jaggery until sticky, then shaped warm into small rounds. Softer and more rustic than a set barfi, with the unmistakable smoky sweetness of nolen gur.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the palms and enriches the coconut so the naru hold their shape

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: stands in for date-palm nolen gur, giving the naru their smoky, molasses depth

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai with 1 bay leaf for 30 seconds until fragrant, then add 3 cups fresh grated coconut and sauté 4 minutes on low heat.
Pour in 0.25 cup whole milk and cook 3 minutes until the coconut softens and the milk is absorbed.
Add 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook on medium heat for 8-9 minutes, stirring constantly, until the mixture turns sticky, glossy and pulls together in a lump.
Mix in 0.5 tsp cardamom and 2 tbsp raisins, then discard the bay leaf and take the pan off the heat.
Let the mixture cool for 5 minutes until just warm enough to handle, checking that a pinch holds its shape when pressed.
Grease your palms with a little ghee and roll heaped tablespoons of the mixture into small round naru, setting them on a greased plate to firm up.
tips: Roll the naru while the mixture is warm; once it cools fully it crumbles and won't bind.
If the mixture feels too loose to roll, return it to the heat for a minute or two to drive off more moisture.
Traditional nolen gur gives the truest flavour in winter, but Anveshan jaggery powder carries the same molasses note year-round.
variations.servingSuggestion: Offer these on the bhog thali at Lakshmi Puja or serve as an after-meal sweet; they pair beautifully with a small cup of unsweetened tea.

variations.name: Madhya Pradesh Mawa Nariyal Barfi
variations.description: A richer, two-layer feeling barfi from the mithai shops of MP, where khoya melted into the coconut makes it dense, creamy and pale gold. Saffron and rose water give it a regal fragrance, finished with slivered almonds pressed into the top.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: binds the khoya and coconut into a smooth, creamy fudge

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: sweetens the mawa-rich barfi without overpowering the delicate coconut

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm milk to give a golden hue and festive perfume

steps: Soak 15 strands of Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 1 tbsp warm milk and grease an 8-inch tray with a little Anveshan Ghee.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and sauté 2.5 cups fresh grated coconut on low heat for 4 minutes until fragrant.
Add 1 cup grated khoya and stir 4-5 minutes on low heat until it melts and coats the coconut smoothly.
Mix in 1 cup Anveshan Khandsari and cook 6-7 minutes on medium heat, stirring often, until the sugar dissolves and the mixture thickens and glosses.
Stir in the saffron milk, 0.5 tsp rose water and 0.75 tsp cardamom, cooking 2 minutes until the mass pulls from the sides.
Spread into the tray, press 3 tbsp slivered almonds evenly over the top, and cut into squares after 25 minutes once firm.
tips: Use fresh, moist khoya; dry mawa makes the barfi grainy instead of creamy.
Add the rose water off the heat so its delicate fragrance isn't cooked away.
Chill these once set, as the mawa content means they keep best refrigerated for about five days.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these creamy, saffron-flecked squares at Diwali or a wedding sweet counter, chilled slightly, alongside dry-fruit mithai.

variations.name: Kashmiri Saffron Coconut Barfi
variations.description: A fragrant winter barfi in the Kashmiri style, generous with saffron and dry fruit and warmed by ground fennel, which is a signature note of the valley's sweets. Condensed milk makes it quick and creamy, with a delicate, aromatic finish quite unlike the plain white version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: carries the saffron and fennel aromas through the coconut as it cooks

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: used generously, valley-style, for a deep colour and heady aroma

steps: Bloom 25 strands of Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk for 10 minutes and grease an 8-inch tray with a little Anveshan Ghee.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and sauté 3 cups fresh grated coconut on low heat for 4 minutes until fragrant but pale.
Pour in 0.75 cup sweetened condensed milk and cook on medium heat for 6-7 minutes, stirring constantly, until it thickens and pulls together.
Stir in the saffron milk, 0.5 tsp fennel powder and 0.5 tsp cardamom, cooking 3 minutes until the mixture leaves the sides and turns glossy.
Fold in 2 tbsp chopped walnuts and 2 tbsp slivered almonds until evenly distributed.
Spread into the tray, press flat, and cut into squares after 20 minutes once firm, lifting out when cool.
tips: Condensed milk is already sweet, so taste before adding anything more; the barfi should be balanced, not sugary.
The ground fennel is subtle but essential to the Kashmiri character, so don't leave it out.
Toast the walnuts lightly first to keep them from turning soft inside the barfi.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these saffron-gold squares with kahwa or noon chai on a cold evening; the fennel and walnut make them feel distinctly of the valley.

variations.name: Classic Paneer Pulao
variations.description: A protein-rich pulao where golden pan-fried paneer cubes are folded into fragrant basmati cooked with whole garam spices. Mildly spiced and satisfying, it turns everyday paneer into a festive one-pot meal that needs little more than a bowl of raita.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee crisps the paneer edges and blooms the whole spices for a rich base

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes and drain; cut 250 g paneer into 2 cm cubes.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot over medium heat and fry the paneer cubes for 3 minutes until golden on two sides, then remove and set aside.
Add the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 bay leaf, 3 cardamom pods, 4 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon, sizzling 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 sliced onion and 2 slit green chillies, frying 5 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Add the drained rice, 0.5 tsp garam masala and 1.25 tsp salt, toast gently 2 minutes, then pour in 2.5 cups hot water and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 13 minutes, gently fold in the fried paneer, rest 5 minutes, garnish with 3 tbsp coriander and fluff before serving.
tips: Soak the fried paneer in warm salted water for a few minutes to keep it soft and spongy.
Add the paneer near the end so it stays intact and does not break into the rice.
Do not over-fry the paneer, or it turns rubbery; a light golden crust is enough.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a chilled cucumber-mint raita and a wedge of lemon for a comforting, complete meal.

variations.name: Chhattisgarhi Herb Paneer Pulao
variations.description: A rustic central-Indian pulao brightened with fresh coriander, mint and green chilli ground into a vibrant paste, cooked in wood-pressed groundnut oil. Earthy and herb-forward, it reflects Chhattisgarh's simple, ingredient-led home cooking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the everyday cooking fat across Chhattisgarh homes

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes and drain; grind 0.5 cup coriander, 0.25 cup mint and 3 green chillies into a coarse green paste.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat and fry 250 g cubed paneer for 3 minutes until light golden, then remove.
Add the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, then 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 bay leaf and 3 cloves, sizzling 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 sliced onion and fry 5 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger garlic paste and the green paste and cook 3 minutes until the raw smell fades.
Add the drained rice and 1.25 tsp salt, toast gently 2 minutes, then pour in 2.5 cups hot water and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 13 minutes, fold in the fried paneer, rest 5 minutes and fluff before serving.
tips: Grind the herb paste coarse and add it fresh so the pulao keeps its bright green fragrance.
Cook the green paste until the raw chilli smell disappears to avoid a harsh edge.
Blanch the mint briefly if you want the green colour to stay vivid after cooking.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a tangy tomato-onion salad and plain curd for a fresh, herby everyday meal.

variations.name: Jharkhandi Smoked Paneer Pulao
variations.description: A tribal-belt inspired pulao that leans on the smoky, earthy flavours of Jharkhand, finishing the dish with a dhungar charcoal smoke and a scatter of roasted peanuts. Cooked in mustard oil, it is robust, rustic and quietly dramatic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Pungent mustard oil stands up to the smoky charcoal finish of this rustic pulao

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes and drain; cut 250 g paneer into cubes.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, lower the heat, and fry the paneer for 3 minutes until golden, then remove.
In the same oil add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1 bay leaf, sizzle 30 seconds, then add 1 sliced onion and fry 5 minutes until golden.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger garlic paste, 1 chopped tomato, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt, cooking 4 minutes until pulpy.
Add the drained rice, toast gently 2 minutes, pour in 2.5 cups hot water, bring to a boil, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 13 minutes.

Fold in the fried paneer and 3 tbsp crushed peanuts, then place a hot charcoal in a small bowl on the rice, drizzle a few drops of mustard oil, cover 2 minutes to smoke, garnish with coriander and serve.
tips: For the dhungar smoke, heat the charcoal until glowing red, then work fast and cover tightly.
Skip the charcoal if unavailable and add a pinch of smoked paprika for a hint of the effect.
Add the peanuts at the end so they stay crunchy against the soft paneer and rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a sharp onion-chilli salad and a spoon of plain curd to balance the smoky richness.

variations.name: Punjabi Makhani Paneer Pulao
variations.description: A rich Punjabi-style pulao where paneer is simmered in a buttery tomato makhani masala before being layered with fragrant rice. Creamy, mildly sweet and indulgent, it brings the flavours of paneer makhani into a satisfying one-pot form.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee gives the makhani masala its signature Punjabi richness and gloss

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes and drain; boil 3 tomatoes, 1 onion and 10 cashews for 8 minutes, then cool and blend to a smooth puree.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds, sizzle 30 seconds, then add 1 tbsp ginger garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Pour in the tomato-cashew puree with 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt, and cook 8 minutes until it thickens and the ghee surfaces.
Add 250 g paneer cubes, 3 tbsp cream, 0.5 tsp garam masala and crushed 1 tsp kasuri methi, simmering 3 minutes until the paneer softens in the masala.
Meanwhile cook the drained rice with 2.5 cups water until just done, about 12 minutes, and keep it fluffy and separate.
Layer the makhani paneer and the rice gently in the pot, cover and steam on the lowest heat for 5 minutes, then fold once and serve warm.
tips: Blend the puree very smooth and strain if you want a silky, restaurant-style masala.
Layer rather than stir vigorously so the paneer stays whole and the rice does not turn mushy.
A pinch of jaggery balances the tomato tang the classic makhani way if the tomatoes are sour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a crunchy onion-lachha salad and a cool boondi raita to offset the creamy richness.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Masala Paneer Pulao
variations.description: A spicy Maharashtrian take built on fiery goda-style masala and fresh coconut, cooked in wood-pressed groundnut oil for a nutty depth. Bold, fragrant and a little sweet-hot, it channels the flavours of a Puneri masale bhaat with paneer.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil lends the nutty base typical of Maharashtrian masale bhaat

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati rice for 20 minutes and drain; cut 250 g paneer into cubes.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tsp cumin seeds and 10 curry leaves and let them crackle for 40 seconds.
Add 1 sliced onion and fry 5 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Add 1 chopped tomato, 1.5 tsp goda masala, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt, cooking 4 minutes until the tomato softens and the masala smells roasted.
Stir in the paneer cubes and 0.25 cup grated coconut for 2 minutes, then add the drained rice and toast gently 2 minutes.
Pour in 2.5 cups hot water, bring to a boil, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 13 minutes, then rest 5 minutes and fluff before serving.
tips: Goda masala is the heart of this dish; use a good roasted blend for the authentic sweet-hot aroma.
Add the coconut with the paneer so it toasts lightly and perfumes the rice.
A little grated jaggery stirred in balances the heat the Maharashtrian way if you like.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a spoon of plain curd and crisp papad, topped with extra fresh coconut and coriander.

variations.name: Classic Peanut Chikki
variations.description: The winter brittle of Indian childhoods: roasted peanuts bound in molten Anveshan jaggery cooked to the hard-crack stage, rolled thin and cut into glassy, snap-clean bars. A spoon of ghee keeps it from turning sticky and a scatter of toasted sesame adds a nutty crunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the rolling surface and enriches the jaggery so the chikki snaps clean instead of sticking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: cooked to the hard-crack stage for a glassy, crisp snap

steps: Dry-roast 2 cups raw peanuts on medium heat for 6-7 minutes until the skins darken and loosen, then cool, rub off the skins and coarsely crush half of them.
Toast 1 tbsp white sesame in the same pan for 1 minute until it smells nutty and set aside, then grease the back of a tray and a rolling pin with a little Anveshan Ghee.

Melt 1.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on low heat, then cook 5-6 minutes to the hard-crack stage, when a drop dropped into cold water sets brittle and snaps.
Working fast, switch off the heat and stir in the peanuts, sesame, 0.5 tsp cardamom and 1 pinch salt until every nut is coated.
Tip the mixture onto the greased tray and roll it out 4-5 mm thin with the greased pin before it hardens.
Score into bars while still warm, then let the chikki cool completely for 20 minutes and snap along the lines.
tips: The hard-crack test is everything: too soft and the chikki stays chewy, too long and the jaggery burns bitter.
Have the peanuts, tray and pin ready before you melt the jaggery, because you have barely a minute to roll once it is off the heat.
Store in an airtight jar with a sachet of dry rice to keep the chikki crisp through humid weather.
variations.servingSuggestion: Snap into rough shards for a Makar Sankranti platter or pack small bars as an energy-dense winter snack; it pairs well with a glass of warm milk.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Thin Shengdana Chikki
variations.description: The paper-thin Sangli-style chikki sold at every Maharashtrian shop, rolled so fine it is almost translucent and shatters at a touch. A pinch of dry ginger and nutmeg gives it a warming edge that makes it a beloved winter and Sankranti treat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: just enough to grease the surface and give the thin brittle a clean release

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: cooked to a firm hard crack so the wafer-thin chikki stays crisp

steps: Dry-roast 2 cups peanuts on medium heat for 6 minutes until fragrant and the skins flake, then cool and rub the skins off completely.
Grease a smooth stone slab or the back of a large tray and a rolling pin generously with Anveshan Ghee, keeping them within arm's reach.
Melt 1.25 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water and 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on low heat, then boil 5 minutes to a firm hard crack that snaps cleanly in cold water.
Take off the heat and immediately fold in the whole peanuts, 0.25 tsp dry ginger, 1 pinch nutmeg and 1 pinch salt.
Pour onto the greased slab and roll out as thin as possible, no more than 2-3 mm, pressing firmly so the peanuts sit in a single layer.
Mark into small squares while hot and let the wafer-thin chikki cool 15 minutes before breaking apart.
tips: Roll faster and thinner than you think you can; the hallmark of Sangli chikki is its delicate, near-transparent snap.
Keep the peanuts whole rather than crushed for this style, so each shard shows off the nuts.
If the chikki hardens before you finish rolling, warm the slab from underneath or return the mass briefly to low heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these thin shards with afternoon chai or hand them out at Makar Sankranti with the customary 'til-gul' greeting.

variations.name: Uttarakhand Til-Peanut Chikki
variations.description: A Pahari winter chikki where toasted sesame is folded in alongside peanuts, in the sesame-loving style of the hills, with a scatter of poppy seeds for extra crunch. The higher sesame content makes it nuttier and more warming, perfect against the mountain cold.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the surface and helps the sesame-heavy mix roll out smoothly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the traditional hill sweetener, cooked to hard crack for a firm snap

steps: Dry-roast 1.5 cups peanuts on medium heat for 6 minutes, cool and rub off the skins, then coarsely crush them.
In the same pan, toast 0.75 cup white sesame and 1 tbsp poppy seeds separately for about 1 minute each, just until they turn golden and pop, then set aside.
Grease a tray and rolling pin with Anveshan Ghee and keep the roasted seeds and nuts ready beside the stove.
Melt 1.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on low heat, then cook 5-6 minutes to the hard-crack stage that snaps in cold water.
Off the heat, quickly stir in the peanuts, sesame, poppy seeds and 0.25 tsp dry ginger powder until well coated.
Spread onto the greased tray, roll out 4 mm thick, score into bars while warm and break apart after cooling 20 minutes.
tips: Toast the sesame just to golden; burnt sesame turns the whole chikki bitter fast.
The generous sesame makes this chikki richer, so cut it into slightly smaller bars than a plain peanut one.
Keep it dry and airtight; sesame absorbs moisture quickly and can soften the snap.
variations.servingSuggestion: A staple of Pahari winters, serve these with hot ginger tea or carry them as trail food on a cold-weather trek.

variations.name: Odisha Coconut-Cardamom Chikki
variations.description: A softer, more fragrant chikki from the Odia coast where toasted dry coconut is folded through the peanuts and jaggery, cooked to a gentler set so it yields with a chew rather than a hard snap. Cardamom and a touch of dry ginger perfume every bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: keeps the softer-set chikki supple and easy to press flat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: cooked just to soft-ball stage for a chewier, coastal-style set

steps: Dry-roast 1.5 cups peanuts on medium heat for 6 minutes, cool, deskin and coarsely crush them.
Toast 0.5 cup grated dry coconut in the same pan for 2 minutes until pale gold and fragrant, then set aside.
Grease a tray and spatula with Anveshan Ghee and keep the nuts and coconut ready.
Melt 1.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 3 tbsp water and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on low heat, then cook 4-5 minutes only to the soft-ball stage, when a drop in cold water forms a pliable ball.
Off the heat, fold in the peanuts, toasted coconut, 0.75 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp dry ginger until evenly mixed.
Spread onto the greased tray about 6 mm thick, press flat, and cut into squares after 25 minutes while still slightly soft.
tips: Stop the jaggery at soft-ball, not hard-crack, for the signature chewy set; cook it longer and you lose the tender bite.
Because this chikki is softer, wrap individual pieces in butter paper so they don't stick together.
Use fresh dry coconut; stale coconut turns rancid and dulls the flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these chewy squares as a festival sweet during Raja Parba or with an evening cup of tea; they are gentle on the teeth for children and elders alike.

variations.name: Himachali Dry-Fruit Chikki
variations.description: A festive, loaded chikki from the apple-country hills, studded with almonds, cashews and melon seeds alongside the peanuts for a richer, more premium brittle. It is the kind of energy-dense sweet Himachali families make to see them through a hard mountain winter.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: coats the mixed nuts and stops the rich chikki from sticking as it sets

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: cooked to hard crack to bind the heavy load of nuts into a firm brittle

steps: Dry-roast 1 cup peanuts on medium heat for 6 minutes, cool and rub off the skins, then lightly toast 0.5 cup almonds, 0.5 cup cashews and 2 tbsp melon seeds until golden and fragrant.
Grease a tray and rolling pin with Anveshan Ghee and keep all the roasted nuts and seeds ready in a bowl.
Melt 1.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on low heat, then boil 5-6 minutes to the hard-crack stage that snaps brittle in cold water.
Working quickly off the heat, stir in all the nuts, melon seeds and 0.5 tsp cardamom until every piece is glossed with jaggery.
Tip onto the greased tray and roll out 5 mm thick, pressing so the nuts spread in an even layer.
Score into bars while warm and let the chikki cool for 20 minutes before snapping it apart.
tips: Toast each nut only lightly, since they will keep cooking in the hot jaggery and can turn bitter if over-browned.
This nut-heavy chikki needs a firm hard crack to hold together, so don't underboil the jaggery.
Cut it into smaller pieces than plain chikki, as it is far richer and more filling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Offer these loaded bars as a festive Lohri or Diwali treat, or pack them for high-altitude travel where a compact, energy-rich snack is welcome.

variations.name: Classic Sattu Ladoo
variations.description: A no-cook Bihari energy ladoo where roasted-gram sattu is simply bound with ghee and jaggery, needing no roasting since the flour is already toasted. High in plant protein and endlessly filling, it is the original farmer's fuel of the Gangetic plains. Earthy, nutty and ready in minutes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Stone-ground roasted-gram sattu is already cooked, so it binds into ladoos without any further roasting.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Warm ghee is the only fat that binds the dry sattu into a smooth, rollable dough.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Fine jaggery melts into the warm ghee and sweetens the sattu without any cooking.

steps: Warm 1/2 cup Anveshan Ghee gently until it is fully liquid but not hot, then take it off the heat.
Stir 3/4 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder into the warm ghee until it softens and mostly dissolves into a smooth, glossy mix.
In a large bowl combine 2 cups Anveshan Sattu, 1 tsp cardamom powder, 3 tbsp chopped pistachios and 2 tbsp melon seeds.
Pour the jaggery-ghee over the sattu and mix well; it will look crumbly at first as the fat coats the flour.
Sprinkle in up to 2 tbsp water a little at a time and knead gently until the mixture just holds together when pressed.
Roll firmly into 12 ladoos and let them set for 20 minutes so they hold their shape.
tips: Add the water in tiny amounts; sattu is thirsty but too much turns the ladoos pasty and prone to spoiling.
If the mixture will not bind, add another spoon of warm ghee rather than more water for a cleaner, longer-keeping ladoo.
Because nothing is cooked, use good fresh sattu with no musty smell, as its raw flavour comes through directly.
variations.servingSuggestion: A superb pre-workout or mid-morning ladoo with a glass of water or buttermilk; keeps well for a week in a dry jar.

variations.name: Bihari Dry-Fruit Sattu Ladoo
variations.description: A festive Bihari upgrade of the humble sattu ladoo, loaded with chopped dates, cashews and raisins so it eats almost like a fruit-and-nut bar. Richer and more indulgent while keeping the earthy roasted-gram base. Made for travellers and students who need lasting energy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: The protein-rich roasted-gram base anchors the dry fruits and keeps the ladoo filling.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee softens the chopped dates and binds the loaded mixture together.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Less jaggery is needed here since the dates bring their own natural sweetness.

steps: Warm 2 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee in a pan on low heat and saute 1/4 cup chopped cashews and 3 tbsp raisins for a minute until the cashews are golden and the raisins plump; set aside.
In the same pan add another 2 tbsp ghee and 3/4 cup chopped dates, and cook on low heat for 3 to 4 minutes, mashing, until they soften into a sticky paste.
Take off the heat, stir in the remaining ghee and 1/2 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder until it melts into the dates.
In a large bowl mix 2 cups Anveshan Sattu with 1 tsp cardamom powder, then pour in the warm date mixture and the sauteed nuts.
Knead gently while still warm until the mixture binds into a soft, cohesive dough.
Roll firmly into 12 ladoos and set aside for 20 minutes to firm up.
tips: Chop the dates finely and mash them well; large chunks make the ladoos hard to shape and roll unevenly.
Keep the jaggery modest as written, and taste the date mixture first since very sweet dates may need even less.
These are richer and denser than plain sattu ladoos, so make them slightly smaller for an ideal single portion.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pack two in a travel tin for long journeys; substantial enough to replace a light breakfast on the go.

variations.name: Coconut Sattu Ladoo
variations.description: A tribal-belt take where toasted coconut is worked into the sattu, adding a sweet, nutty chew and a coastal aroma to the earthy gram base. Lightly perfumed with cardamom. A pleasant, textured twist that feels less austere than the plain version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: The roasted-gram base gives body and protein beneath the sweet coconut.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee toasts the coconut and binds it with the sattu into a smooth dough.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery pairs naturally with the toasted coconut for a warm, rounded sweetness.

steps: Warm 2 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee in a pan on low heat and toast 3/4 cup grated dry coconut for 2 to 3 minutes until pale gold and fragrant; reserve 2 tbsp for coating.
Add the remaining ghee to the pan and warm it, then take off the heat and stir in 3/4 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder until it softens.
In a large bowl combine 2 cups Anveshan Sattu, the toasted coconut, 1 tsp cardamom powder and 3 tbsp chopped cashews.
Pour over the jaggery-ghee and mix until crumbly and evenly coated.
Add up to 2 tbsp water a little at a time and knead gently until it holds together, then roll into 12 ladoos.
Press each ladoo in the reserved toasted coconut and set aside for 20 minutes to firm up.
tips: Toast the coconut just to pale gold; darker and it turns bitter and overwhelms the mild sattu.
Reserve a little toasted coconut for rolling the finished ladoos, which makes them look and smell more appealing.
As with all sattu ladoos, add water sparingly and lean on ghee for binding to keep them from going pasty.
variations.servingSuggestion: A nice tea-time ladoo; the toasted coconut makes it feel a touch more like a treat than a plain energy ball.

variations.name: Fennel-Spiced Sattu Ladoo
variations.description: A gently spiced version fragrant with toasted fennel and a whisper of dry ginger, drawing on the digestive-spice tradition of the Awadh region. The aromatics make the earthy sattu lighter and easier on the stomach. Soothing, subtly perfumed and quietly wholesome.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: The roasted-gram base carries the toasted fennel and ginger warmth beautifully.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee blooms the fennel's aroma and binds the sattu into a soft dough.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery keeps the spiced ladoo unrefined and rounds the digestive spices.

steps: Dry-roast 1 tbsp fennel seeds in a pan on low heat for 1 to 2 minutes until fragrant, then crush them coarsely.
Warm 1/2 cup Anveshan Ghee gently, take it off the heat and stir in 3/4 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder until it softens into a smooth mix.
In a large bowl combine 2 cups Anveshan Sattu, the crushed fennel, 1/2 tsp dry ginger powder, 3/4 tsp cardamom powder and 3 tbsp chopped almonds.
Pour in the jaggery-ghee and mix until evenly moist and crumbly.
Add up to 2 tbsp water gradually and knead gently until the mixture just binds.
Roll firmly into 12 ladoos and rest for 20 minutes to set.
tips: Crush the toasted fennel rather than leaving it whole so its aroma spreads through the ladoo without a hard seed to bite.
The dry ginger and fennel together make these notably easier to digest, which is why they suit heavier meals.
Toast the fennel gently; scorched seeds turn bitter and will taint the whole batch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve one after a rich meal as a mukhwas-style digestive sweet, alongside warm water or fennel tea.

variations.name: Sattu Peanut Jaggery Ladoo
variations.description: A rustic Central Indian take that folds crushed roasted peanuts and sesame into the sattu for a chikki-like crunch and extra protein. Earthier and more textured than the smooth classic. A hardy field-and-farm ladoo built for stamina.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: The roasted-gram protein base pairs with peanuts for a genuinely sustaining ladoo.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A spoon of wood-pressed groundnut oil deepens the peanut flavour of this Central Indian style.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee rounds the groundnut oil and binds the crunchy mixture into ladoos.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery and peanuts echo the region's beloved chikki flavour.

steps: Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil with 1/3 cup Anveshan Ghee in a pan on low heat until liquid, then take off the heat.
Stir 3/4 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder into the warm fat until it softens into a smooth mix.
In a large bowl combine 2 cups Anveshan Sattu, 1/2 cup crushed roasted peanuts, 3 tbsp toasted sesame and 3/4 tsp cardamom powder.
Pour over the jaggery-fat and mix until crumbly and evenly coated.
Add up to 2 tbsp water gradually and knead gently until the mixture holds together.
Roll firmly into 12 sturdy ladoos and let them set for 20 minutes; the peanuts and sesame give a satisfying crunch.
tips: Crush the peanuts coarse for bite; a fine grind releases oil and makes the ladoos greasy.
Toast the sesame just until it pops so it adds aroma without turning bitter.
This mixture binds well thanks to the extra fat, so add water only if it still refuses to come together.
variations.servingSuggestion: A robust ladoo for long workdays; pair with buttermilk to make a genuinely filling mid-day break.

variations.name: Classic Til Ladoo
variations.description: The winter sesame ladoo where toasted til is bound with molten jaggery into crunchy, warming little spheres. Sesame and jaggery are both considered heat-giving foods, which is why this sweet crowns Makar Sankranti and cold-weather kitchens. Simple, nutty and pleasantly brittle at the edges.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery is the binder and the warming heart of the ladoo, melted just to soft-ball to set crisp.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A little ghee keeps the jaggery pliable and stops the ladoos from turning rock-hard.

steps: Dry-roast 1.5 cups white sesame seeds in a kadhai on low heat for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring, until they turn golden and pop; tip onto a plate to cool.
In the same pan warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on low heat, add 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and stir until it melts into a smooth, bubbling syrup, about 3 to 4 minutes.
Test the syrup by dropping a little into cold water; it should form a soft, pliable ball, which means it is ready to bind.
Working quickly, stir in the toasted sesame, 1/4 cup crushed roasted peanuts and 1 tsp cardamom powder until evenly coated.
Grease your palms with ghee and roll the hot mixture into 15 small ladoos, pressing firmly before it cools and sets.
Leave to firm for 15 minutes; they will crisp as they cool.
tips: Do not overcook the jaggery syrup past the soft-ball stage or the ladoos set glassy and hard enough to hurt your teeth.
Roll immediately while hot, greasing your palms often; once the jaggery cools it will not bind and the mixture crumbles.
Keep a bowl of cold water beside you for the soft-ball test and to briefly cool your fingertips while shaping the hot mix.
variations.servingSuggestion: The traditional Sankranti sweet exchanged with the words tilgul ghya, god god bola; serve with warm milk on frosty evenings.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Tilgul
variations.description: The quintessential Maharashtrian tilgul of Makar Sankranti, combining sesame with roasted peanuts and dry coconut for extra crunch and body. A little more textured and substantial than the plain til ladoo. Exchanged among friends and family as a token of sweet words and goodwill.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery binds the trio of sesame, peanut and coconut into the classic Sankranti sweet.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee keeps the jaggery supple so the loaded mixture still rolls smoothly.

steps: Dry-roast 1 cup sesame seeds on low heat for 4 minutes until golden and popping, then remove.
In the same pan toast 1/2 cup grated dry coconut for 2 minutes until pale gold, then coarsely crush 1/2 cup roasted peanuts and combine all three in a bowl.
Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on low heat, add 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook for 3 to 4 minutes to a smooth syrup that forms a soft ball in cold water.
Tip in the sesame-peanut-coconut mix and 1 tsp cardamom powder and stir fast to coat everything evenly.
With greased palms, roll the hot mixture into 15 firm ladoos before it sets.
Let them harden for 15 minutes; the peanuts and coconut give a satisfying, sturdy crunch.
tips: Crush the peanuts only coarsely; whole ones make the ladoos hard to shape and a fine powder makes them dense.
Toast the dry coconut lightly and separately, as it browns and turns bitter much faster than sesame.
Work in small batches near the warm pan so the jaggery mix stays pliable enough to roll.
variations.servingSuggestion: Wrap a few in coloured paper to gift on Sankranti; equally good crumbled over warm milk if any harden past rolling.

variations.name: Rajasthani Til Gajak Ladoo
variations.description: A Rajasthani gajak-style ladoo where the sesame is pounded with jaggery to a slightly flaky, layered crunch rather than left whole. Cooked a touch harder for that characteristic brittle snap. A winter sweet sold at every roadside stall across the desert state in the cold months.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: For gajak the jaggery is cooked slightly firmer to give the ladoo its signature brittle snap.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee greases the surface for pounding and keeps the brittle mix from cracking apart.

steps: Dry-roast 1.5 cups sesame seeds on low heat for 5 minutes until deep golden, then pulse briefly in a mixer so some seeds break for a flakier texture.
Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on low heat, add 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook for 4 to 5 minutes to a slightly firmer syrup that snaps when a drop is cooled in water.
Quickly stir in the pounded sesame, 1/2 tsp dry ginger powder, 3/4 tsp cardamom powder and 3 tbsp slivered almonds.
Turn the hot mass onto a ghee-greased surface and press it together while it is still workable.
Grease your palms and roll into 15 firm ladoos before the mixture hardens.
Cool completely for 20 minutes; the ladoos set with a distinct brittle, gajak-like crunch.
tips: Cook the jaggery a stage past soft-ball to the hard-crack feel for the true gajak snap, but not so far that it burns and turns bitter.
Pulsing part of the sesame is what gives gajak its flaky bite; leave it all whole and you simply get a standard til ladoo.
Work very fast once the sesame is in, as this firmer syrup sets even quicker than the classic version.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot masala chai on cold desert evenings; the brittle snap is meant to be enjoyed at room temperature.

variations.name: Bengali Til Naru
variations.description: The Bengali til naru pairs sesame with fresh grated coconut and jaggery for a softer, chewier ladoo than the crisp northern kind. Cooked gently so it stays tender rather than brittle. A beloved offering during Poush and Lakshmi Puja in Bengal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery cooked to a softer stage keeps the naru tender and chewy in the Bengali style.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee greases the pan and hands for the sticky coconut-sesame mixture.

steps: Dry-roast 1 cup sesame seeds on low heat for 4 minutes until golden and popping, then remove.
In the same pan dry 1 cup fresh grated coconut on low heat for 3 minutes to remove excess moisture.
Add 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and cook on low heat for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring, until it melts and binds into a soft, sticky mass.
Stir in the toasted sesame, 1 tsp cardamom powder and 2 tbsp raisins and cook for another minute.
Cool for 4 minutes until warm and pliable, then grease your palms with ghee.
Roll firmly into 15 soft naru while warm; they stay tender rather than hard as they cool.
tips: Cook the jaggery only to a soft, sticky stage, not a hard crack, so the naru stays chewy the way Bengalis prefer.
Squeeze excess water from fresh coconut before drying it, or the mixture takes much longer to come together.
Roll while warm; these soften and hold shape better than northern til ladoos but still firm up on cooling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as prasad during Poush Sankranti, at room temperature alongside other coconut naru for a Bengali festive platter.

variations.name: Black Sesame Til Ladoo
variations.description: A nutrient-dense take using black sesame, prized in South Indian kitchens for its stronger, earthier flavour and higher iron and calcium. Bound with jaggery and a touch of dry ginger for warmth. Darker, more intense and considered especially strengthening in winter.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery's minerals complement the iron-rich black sesame for a genuinely strengthening sweet.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee keeps the dark, dense mixture pliable enough to roll while warm.

steps: Dry-roast 1.5 cups black sesame seeds on low heat for 4 minutes, stirring, until they smell nutty and start crackling; because they are already dark, judge by aroma not colour.
Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on low heat, add 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook for 3 to 4 minutes to a soft-ball syrup.
Quickly stir in the roasted black sesame, 1/2 tsp dry ginger powder, 3/4 tsp cardamom powder and 3 tbsp chopped cashews.
Mix fast so every seed is coated in the warm jaggery.
Grease your palms and roll the hot mixture into 15 firm ladoos before it sets.
Let them harden for 15 minutes; the black sesame gives a deep, earthy nuttiness.
tips: Judge black sesame by smell and sound while roasting, since you cannot rely on colour to tell when it is done.
Do not overcook the syrup; black sesame ladoos turn especially hard and are easy to push too far.
The dry ginger balances the intense sesame and aids digestion, making these a favourite for cold, sluggish mornings.
variations.servingSuggestion: A wholesome winter energiser; serve one with warm turmeric milk for an iron- and calcium-rich pick-me-up.

variations.name: Classic Gajar Halwa
variations.description: The beloved winter carrot halwa where grated red carrots are simmered slowly in whole milk until it reduces to a thick, fudgy khoya clinging to every strand. Finished with ghee, cardamom and toasted nuts for a warm, deeply comforting dessert. The undisputed star of North Indian cold-weather tables.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee sautes the carrots at the start and enriches the halwa at the finish for that classic gloss.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery gives a warmer, earthier sweetness than sugar and suits the carrot beautifully.

steps: Heat 2 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai on medium heat and saute 5 cups grated red carrots for 6 to 7 minutes until they soften and smell sweet.
Pour in 3 cups full-fat milk, bring to a boil, then simmer on medium-low heat for 30 to 35 minutes, stirring often, until the milk reduces almost completely and coats the carrots thickly.
Lower the heat and stir in 3/4 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder; it will loosen the mixture as it melts, so keep cooking for 6 to 8 minutes until the halwa thickens again.
In a small pan toast 3 tbsp slivered almonds, 3 tbsp chopped cashews and 2 tbsp raisins in the remaining ghee until golden and the raisins plump.
Stir the toasted nuts and 1 tsp cardamom powder into the halwa and cook for a final 2 minutes.
Serve hot, with the ghee glistening on top.
tips: Use juicy red winter carrots (Delhi gajar) if you can; they are sweeter and give the halwa its characteristic deep colour.
Add the jaggery only after the milk has reduced, since jaggery added early can make the milk curdle.
Grate the carrots on the thicker side of the grater so they keep some bite instead of dissolving into mush.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot on a cold night, or warm with a scoop of vanilla ice cream for a modern hot-cold contrast.

variations.name: Punjabi Khoya Gajar Halwa
variations.description: The rich Punjabi halwai-style halwa where khoya is folded in to make it dense, grainy and extravagantly fudgy, well beyond the everyday version. Slow-cooked with plenty of ghee for that dhaba-counter decadence. The one piled high in glass cases across Amritsar in winter.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A generous hand with ghee gives this halwa its rich halwai-style body and gloss.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery deepens the khoya's milky sweetness while keeping the halwa unrefined.

steps: Heat 3 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai on medium heat and saute 5 cups grated carrots for 8 minutes until softened and glossy.
Add 2 cups full-fat milk and simmer on medium-low heat for 25 to 30 minutes, stirring, until the milk dries up and the carrots turn deep and jammy.
Crumble in 1 cup khoya and cook for 6 to 7 minutes on low heat, stirring, until it melts and coats the carrots richly.
Stir in 3/4 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook for 6 minutes until the halwa thickens and the ghee begins to glisten at the edges.
Mix in the remaining ghee, 1 tsp cardamom powder, 1/4 cup slivered almonds and 3 tbsp pistachios.
Cook for a final 2 minutes and serve hot, dense and glossy.
tips: Use fresh soft khoya and crumble it in only after the milk has dried, or the halwa turns loose and gluey.
This version is meant to be rich and dense, so resist adding extra milk once the khoya is in.
Leftovers reheat beautifully with a splash of milk and a knob of ghee to bring back the gloss.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm in generous bowls topped with khoya crumbles and pistachio; a true showstopper at a Punjabi winter dinner.

variations.name: Bengali Chhena Gajar Halwa
variations.description: A Bengali-inspired twist that folds soft crumbled chhena into the carrot halwa for a lighter, moist, almost sandesh-like texture. Perfumed delicately with cardamom and a hint of rosewater. Softer and less dense than the khoya-heavy northern style.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee sautes the carrots and keeps the delicate chhena from sticking as it warms through.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Nolen-style jaggery sweetness pairs naturally with fresh chhena in Bengali sweets.

steps: Heat 2 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium heat and saute 5 cups grated carrots for 6 minutes until softened.
Add 2.5 cups full-fat milk and simmer on medium-low heat for 25 minutes, stirring, until the milk reduces and thickly coats the carrots.
Lower the heat and gently fold in 1 cup crumbled fresh chhena, cooking for just 5 minutes so it stays soft and moist rather than rubbery.
Stir in 3/4 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook for 5 to 6 minutes until the halwa thickens and comes together.
Mix in the remaining ghee, 1 tsp cardamom powder and 1/2 tsp rosewater, and cook for 1 more minute.
Garnish with 3 tbsp slivered pistachios and serve warm.
tips: Add the chhena late and cook it briefly; long cooking toughens it and you lose the soft, moist texture that defines this version.
Use freshly made chhena that is soft and just drained, not pressed firm like paneer.
Add the rosewater right at the end and sparingly, since heat and a heavy hand both kill its delicate aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm or lightly chilled in the Bengali way, topped with pistachio; a gentler, moister halwa to end a rich meal.

variations.name: Rajasthani Mawa Dry-Fruit Gajar Halwa
