variations.description: A regal Marwari halwa cooked largely in reduced khoya rather than milk for a fast, intensely rich result, then loaded with dry fruits and saffron. Deep, opulent and made for lavish thalis. The dry-fruit-studded version reserved for celebrations.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee fries the carrots deeply and carries the saffron and dry-fruit richness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery grounds the opulent khoya and dry fruits with an earthy sweetness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Saffron bloomed in warm milk gives this festive halwa its royal colour and aroma.

steps: Soak a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp of the warm milk and set aside to bloom.
Heat 1/3 cup Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium heat and saute 5 cups grated carrots for 10 minutes until deeply softened and their raw smell is gone.
Add the remaining milk and cook for 12 to 15 minutes until it dries up and the carrots turn jammy.
Crumble in 1.25 cups khoya with the saffron milk and cook for 6 minutes on low heat until it melts into a rich mass.
Stir in 3/4 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 tsp cardamom powder and 1/2 cup chopped mixed dry fruits, and cook for 5 to 6 minutes until thick and glossy.
Serve hot, heaped and studded with the dry fruits.
tips: Frying the carrots longer at the start in extra ghee is what gives this halwa its deep colour and concentrated flavour.
Because it leans on khoya over milk, it comes together faster but can catch, so keep the heat moderate and stir often.
Toast the dry fruits separately for a minute if you like extra crunch amid the soft halwa.
variations.servingSuggestion: A lavish festival dessert; serve warm in small bowls with a final flourish of saffron strands and slivered almonds.

variations.name: Vegan Coconut Jaggery Gajar Halwa
variations.description: A dairy-free South Indian take where carrots are simmered in coconut milk and finished with wood-pressed coconut oil, giving a fragrant, tropical spin on the winter classic. Sweetened purely with jaggery and brightened with cashews. Light, aromatic and entirely plant-based.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed coconut oil sautes the carrots and gives this vegan halwa its fragrant tropical base.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery is the sole sweetener, its earthiness balancing the sweet coconut milk.

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadhai on medium heat and saute 5 cups grated carrots for 7 to 8 minutes until softened and fragrant.
Pour in 2 cups thick coconut milk and simmer on medium-low heat for 20 to 25 minutes, stirring often, until it reduces and clings to the carrots.
Stir in 1/3 cup desiccated coconut and cook for 3 minutes until it melds in.
Lower the heat and add 3/4 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp cardamom powder, cooking for 5 to 6 minutes until the halwa thickens.
In a small pan toast 1/4 cup chopped cashews and 2 tbsp raisins in the remaining coconut oil until golden, then stir them in.
Serve warm, fragrant with coconut and studded with the golden cashews and raisins.
tips: Stir the coconut milk often as it reduces since it catches and scorches faster than dairy milk.
Taste before adding all the jaggery; coconut milk is naturally sweet, so you may need a little less.
For a richer body, stir in a spoon of coconut cream at the very end off the heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: A lovely dairy-free dessert to close a South Indian meal; serve warm, or chill it for a coconut-forward treat in warmer months.

variations.name: Classic Dal Makhani Fry
variations.description: A bhuna-forward take on the black dal, where the onion-tomato masala is fried hard and long until deeply caramelised before the cooked urad and rajma go in. The extra frying gives a thicker, more intensely savoury dal than the simmer-only version, finished with butter and a ghee tadka.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the masala is fried hard in wood-pressed groundnut oil for the deep bhuna flavour this style is named for

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the garlic-cumin tadka is bloomed in ghee to finish the fried dal with a rich top note

steps: Soak 1 cup urad and 0.25 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 4 cups water for 7 whistles until soft enough to mash easily.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin, then fry 2 chopped onions on medium heat for 8 minutes until richly browned.

Add 2 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 2 minutes, then add 1.5 cups chopped tomato, 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp garam masala, and fry hard for 10-12 minutes until the masala is jammy and the oil separates.
Tip in the cooked dal, mash a ladleful for body, and cook on medium-low heat for 20 minutes, stirring, so the fried masala fully melds into the thick dal.
Stir in 3 tbsp butter and the remaining salt and simmer 5 minutes until glossy and rich.
For the tadka, heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, sizzle a little chopped garlic to golden, and pour it over the fried dal just before serving.
tips: The long, hard frying of the masala is the whole point here, so don't rush it; the browner the base, the deeper the dal.
Keep this version thicker than a simmered dal makhani, more scoopable than pourable.
If the masala catches while frying, deglaze with a spoon of the dal water rather than plain water to keep the flavour concentrated.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve this thick, savoury dal with butter naan or laccha paratha and pickled onions; its concentrated flavour also makes it a great filling for kathi rolls the next day.

variations.name: Delhi Restaurant Makhani
variations.description: The velvety, mildly sweet restaurant-style dal of Delhi's Moti Mahal lineage, loaded with butter, cream and a touch of tomato sweetness and blitzed silky-smooth. Slow-cooked overnight in spirit, it is the plush, indulgent version most people picture when they hear dal makhani.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: starts the tomato gravy cleanly before the lavish butter and cream take over

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a final ghee-and-kasuri-methi tadka lends the restaurant aroma over the creamy dal

steps: Soak 1 cup urad and 0.33 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 1 tsp salt and 5 cups water for 8 whistles until utterly soft, and mash roughly with a whisk.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, add 2 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute, then add 1.5 cups tomato puree and 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli and simmer 12 minutes until thick and deep red.
Add the mashed dal with 2 cups water and 4 tbsp butter and simmer very gently on low heat for 60 minutes, stirring every few minutes so it never catches, until dark and creamy.
Stir in 0.5 cup cream, 0.5 tsp sugar, 0.75 tsp garam masala and the remaining salt, and cook 10 minutes more until luxuriously smooth.
Crush 1.5 tsp kasuri methi between your palms into the dal for the restaurant fragrance.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with the last 2 tbsp butter until foaming, pour it over the dal, and swirl in a little extra cream to serve.
tips: The long, gentle cook with butter is what makes it plush; a pinch of sugar rounds the tomato just like restaurants do.
For an even silkier finish, lightly blend a ladleful of the cooked dal and stir it back in.
Don't boil hard once the cream is in, or it can split; keep it at the barest simmer.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve glossy and cream-swirled with pillowy butter naan and a wedge of onion; this is the version that shines on a festive or dinner-party table.

variations.name: Bengali-style Cholar Makhani
variations.description: An inventive Bengali reworking of the black dal, tempered in pungent mustard oil with the five-spice panch phoron and a whole dried chilli. Lighter on cream and brightened by a hint of sugar, it carries the sweet-savoury balance so typical of Bengali cooking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: sharp wood-pressed mustard oil is the backbone of Bengali tempering and defines this dal

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoon of ghee stirred in at the end mellows the mustard oil's bite

steps: Soak 1 cup urad and 0.25 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 4 cups water for 7 whistles until soft.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, cool slightly, then crackle 1 tsp panch phoron, 2 dried red chillies and 1 bay leaf for 30 seconds until aromatic.
Add 1 large chopped onion and fry 6 minutes to golden, stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger paste, then add 1 cup chopped tomato, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.75 tsp sugar and cook 8 minutes until pulpy.
Add the cooked dal, mash lightly for body, and simmer on low heat for 25 minutes with a little hot water until thick and glossy.
Season with the remaining salt and check the sweet-savoury balance, adjusting sugar or salt by a pinch as needed.
Swirl in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee just before serving to round off the mustard-oil sharpness.
tips: Let the panch phoron fully crackle so its fennel and fenugreek notes bloom; raw fenugreek turns the dal bitter.
The gentle pinch of sugar is authentically Bengali and rounds the tomato, so don't skip it.
This version stays lighter than the Punjabi one, so resist adding cream; the ghee finish is richness enough.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed gobindobhog rice and a wedge of lime, or with luchi for a weekend brunch; a side of aloo bhaja completes the Bengali spread.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Kala Masala Dal Makhani
variations.description: A Deccan twist where smoky, roasted goda-style kala masala and a little dry coconut give the black dal a warm, complex, faintly sweet-spiced depth. Fried in groundnut oil and finished with ghee, it eats richer and more aromatic than the northern original.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday cooking oil of Maharashtra, ideal for frying the coconut-masala base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the finishing tadka in ghee lifts the roasted kala masala aromas

steps: Soak 1 cup urad and 0.25 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 4 cups water for 7 whistles until fully soft.
Dry-roast 3 tbsp grated dry coconut in a pan for 2 minutes until golden and nutty, then set aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin, fry 1 large chopped onion for 6 minutes to golden, then add 2 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 2 minutes.
Add 1 cup chopped tomato, the roasted coconut, 1.5 tbsp goda masala and 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, and fry 8 minutes until dark, thick and fragrant.
Tip in the cooked dal, mash a portion, and simmer on low heat for 25 minutes until thick and the kala masala flavour permeates.
Finish with a tadka of 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee heated until fragrant and poured over, stirring in the remaining salt.
tips: Roast the dry coconut just to golden; it burns quickly and would turn the dal acrid.
Goda masala is potent and slightly sweet, so start with the measured amount and adjust only after tasting.
Keep the cream out; the roasted coconut and ghee provide all the body this Deccan version needs.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri or soft phulkas and a spoon of raw onion; a side of Maharashtrian koshimbir salad cuts the richness nicely.

variations.name: Awadhi Dum Dal Makhani
variations.description: A refined Lucknowi rendition, mild and aromatic, thickened with a cashew paste and gently perfumed with saffron, mace and rose water, then finished on slow dum. It is elegant and subtly royal, a world away from the robust dhaba style.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the whole dish is built on ghee in the Awadhi manner, from the base to the dum finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm milk to lend the royal Lucknowi fragrance and pale gold sheen

steps: Soak 1 cup urad and 0.25 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 1 tsp salt and 4 cups water for 7 whistles until soft, and bloom 15 strands of Anveshan Kashmiri Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on low heat and fry 0.5 cup onion paste for 8 minutes until pale gold, taking care not to brown it dark, in the delicate Awadhi way.
Add 2 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 2 minutes, then stir in 0.75 cup tomato puree, 3 tbsp cashew paste and 1 tsp red chilli powder and cook 8 minutes until smooth and the ghee separates.
Add the cooked dal with a little hot water and simmer gently on low heat for 25 minutes until creamy, keeping the colour light.
Stir in 0.25 cup cream, the saffron milk, 0.25 tsp mace and 0.5 tsp cardamom with the remaining salt, and simmer 5 minutes.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp rose water, cover tightly and leave on the lowest dum heat for 10 minutes so the perfumes settle before serving.
tips: Fry the onion paste only to pale gold; a dark brown base would make this dish too rustic for the Awadhi style.
Add rose water off or at the barest heat so its fragrance lingers rather than cooking away.
The cashew paste, not cream, does most of the thickening here, giving a smoother, more elegant body.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve this delicate, saffron-scented dal with sheermal or rumali roti and a mint-onion salad; it belongs on a refined Awadhi thali rather than a dhaba plate.

variations.name: Classic Home-style Dal Makhani
variations.description: The everyday home version of the black dal, easier and lighter than the restaurant kind, made in one pot with a modest amount of butter and just a swirl of cream. It skips the hours of slow cooking yet still delivers a comforting, creamy bowl through a good mash and a proper ghee tadka.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: an everyday wood-pressed oil to build the quick home-style masala base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a simple cumin-garlic tadka in ghee gives the home dal its comforting finish

steps: Soak 1 cup urad and 0.25 cup rajma for 6 hours or overnight, then pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 4 cups water for 6-7 whistles until soft and mash-able.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 0.5 tsp cumin, fry 1 large chopped onion for 6 minutes to golden, then add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 2 minutes.
Add 1 cup chopped tomato, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp garam masala, and cook 7 minutes until the tomatoes break down and the oil separates.
Add the cooked dal, mash roughly with the ladle for a creamy body, and simmer on low heat for 20 minutes with a little hot water until thick.
Stir in 2 tbsp butter, 2 tbsp cream and the remaining salt, and simmer 5 minutes until glossy.
For the tadka, heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, sizzle the remaining 0.5 tsp cumin and a little chopped garlic to golden, and pour over the dal before serving.
tips: Mashing a good ladleful of the cooked dal against the pot is the home cook's shortcut to creaminess without long simmering.
This is a weeknight-friendly version, so it stays lighter; add only as much butter and cream as you like.
Leftovers thicken overnight, so loosen with a splash of hot water and a fresh tadka when reheating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with everyday phulkas or plain steamed rice and a simple cucumber-onion salad; a dab of white butter on top makes it feel special.

variations.name: Punjabi Pind-style Dal Makhani
variations.description: The village or 'pind' way of making maa ki dal, cooked long and patient over a low flame, traditionally left overnight on dying embers to turn almost black and spoon-coating. It leans on white butter and whole spices rather than cream, for a rustic, deeply homely richness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee carries the whole pind-style dal, from the tadka to the long slow cook

steps: Soak 1 cup urad and 0.33 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 black cardamom, 1 tsp salt and 5 cups water for 8 whistles until completely broken down and creamy.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin, then fry 2 tbsp crushed garlic and 2 tbsp grated ginger for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add 1 large chopped onion and 2 chopped green chillies and cook 7 minutes to deep golden, then add 1 cup chopped tomato and 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and cook 8 minutes until pulpy.

Tip in the cooked dal, mash well, and simmer on the lowest possible heat for 90 minutes, stirring every 10 minutes and adding hot water in splashes, until it darkens to near-black and coats the spoon.
Stir in 3 tbsp white butter and the remaining salt in the last 10 minutes, letting it melt slowly into the dal.
Give it a final rest, covered, off the heat for 15 minutes so the flavours settle before serving straight from the pot.
tips: The near-black colour and thick body come purely from long, patient simmering, so give it the full time.
White butter rather than cream keeps it rustic and true to a Punjabi farmhouse kitchen.
Cooking it a day ahead and reheating gently deepens the flavour even further, just as the overnight-embers method does.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot with makki di roti and a generous knob of white butter melting on top, alongside jaggery and a glass of lassi for the full Punjabi pind meal.

variations.name: Himachali Dal Makhani
variations.description: A simpler, lighter hill version cooked the Pahari way with local spices and yogurt for a gentle tang, and no heavy cream. Warm notes of cinnamon and clove suit the cold mountain climate, giving a homely dal that sits well with rice or siddu.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil is the everyday cooking fat of the Himachali hills

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of ghee warms and rounds the lightly spiced hill dal

steps: Soak 1 cup urad and 0.25 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 4 cups water for 7 whistles until soft.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, cool slightly, then crackle 1 tsp cumin, 1 inch cinnamon and 3 cloves for 30 seconds until aromatic.
Add 1 medium chopped onion and fry 6 minutes to golden, stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, then add 0.75 cup chopped tomato and 1 tsp red chilli powder and cook 6 minutes until soft.
Lower the heat and stir in 0.33 cup whisked yogurt a spoon at a time, stirring constantly so it doesn't split, and cook 3 minutes until the masala is glossy.
Add the cooked dal, mash lightly, and simmer on low heat for 25 minutes with a little hot water until thick and the whole spices infuse.
Finish with a spoon of 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee stirred through with the remaining salt just before serving.
tips: Add the yogurt on low heat and keep stirring, or it will curdle into the dal.
The whole cinnamon and clove are meant to perfume gently, so fish them out before serving if you prefer.
This hill version stays deliberately light, so skip cream entirely and let the yogurt provide the mild tang.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice or the steamed Himachali bread siddu and a spoon of local ghee; a simple tomato chutney on the side rounds the meal.

variations.name: Sindhi Dal Makhani
variations.description: A tangy, garlic-forward Sindhi take finished with dried mango powder for a signature sour edge and a hefty garlic tadka. Robust and rustic, it trades cream for a generous ghee tempering, in the hearty spirit of Sindhi home cooking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: builds the Sindhi masala base cleanly before the big garlic-ghee tadka

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a generous garlic tadka in ghee is the finishing signature of this Sindhi dal

steps: Soak 1 cup urad and 0.25 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 4 cups water for 7 whistles until soft and creamy.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin, fry 1 large chopped onion for 6 minutes to golden, then add 1 tbsp of the sliced garlic and cook 1 minute.
Add 1 cup chopped tomato, 2 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder and cook 8 minutes until the masala thickens and the oil separates.
Tip in the cooked dal, mash a portion, and simmer on low heat for 25 minutes with hot water as needed until thick.
Stir in 1.5 tsp amchur and the remaining salt and simmer 5 minutes so the sour note melds through.
For the tadka, heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and fry the remaining 2 tbsp sliced garlic until deep golden and crisp, then pour it sizzling over the dal.
tips: Add amchur towards the end so its bright sourness stays fresh rather than cooking flat.
Fry the tadka garlic to a proper deep gold for that sweet, toasty aroma, but pull it off before it browns to bitter.
This dal is meant to be tangy and garlicky, so skip cream and let the amchur and ghee lead.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with Sindhi koki or plain phulkas and a raw onion-lemon salad; the tangy dal also pairs beautifully with plain jeera rice.

variations.name: Banarasi Dal Makhani
variations.description: A UP-style black dal from the ghats of Banaras, mellow and lightly sweet-spiced with a hint of ground fennel and a tempering of asafoetida, in the region's meat-free, no-fuss idiom. It is softer and more fragrant than the muscular Punjabi version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the Banarasi dal is cooked and finished in ghee, from the hing tadka to the last swirl

steps: Soak 1 cup urad and 0.25 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 4 cups water for 7 whistles until soft.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, add 0.5 tsp asafoetida and 1 tsp cumin with 1 bay leaf and let them sizzle for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 medium chopped onion and fry 6 minutes to golden, stir in 2 tbsp grated ginger, then add 1 cup chopped tomato and 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and cook 7 minutes until pulpy.
Stir in 1 tsp fennel powder and 0.75 tsp garam masala, cook 1 minute, then add the cooked dal and mash lightly.
Simmer on low heat for 30 minutes with hot water as needed until thick, soft and fragrant.
Finish with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee swirled in with the remaining salt just before serving.
tips: The asafoetida and fennel are what give this dal its distinct Banarasi fragrance, so add them fresh and don't overcook.
Keep it onion-light and garlic-free for the authentic UP temple-town character.
A gentle mash rather than a hard one keeps this version softer and more homely than the Punjabi style.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot puris or plain rice and a side of aloo sabzi, in the classic Banarasi vegetarian thali style; a spoon of ghee on top is customary.

variations.name: Classic Moong Dal Cheela
variations.description: A high-protein savoury pancake made from soaked and ground split green gram, cooked crisp and golden on a hot tava. Light, wholesome and naturally gluten-free, it is a beloved North Indian breakfast that comes together with just a handful of pantry staples.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil crisps the cheela edges without any refined-oil aftertaste

steps: Rinse 1 cup split green gram and soak it in plenty of water for 3 hours, then drain and grind with about 0.5 cup fresh water to a smooth, pourable batter the consistency of dosa batter.
Stir 1 tsp cumin seeds, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 1 tsp salt into the batter, then fold in grated 1 inch ginger, 2 finely chopped green chillies and 3 tbsp coriander.
Heat a flat tava over medium heat until a drop of water sizzles, then brush it with a little Anveshan Groundnut Oil and wipe off the excess.
Pour a ladle of batter in the centre and spread it in a spiral into a thin round about 18 cm wide, then drizzle 0.5 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil around the edges.
Cook for 2 minutes until the underside is golden and crisp and the top looks set, then flip and cook the other side for 1 minute.
Fold into a half-moon and repeat with the remaining batter, brushing the tava with oil between each cheela, and serve hot.
tips: Soak the dal fully so the batter grinds smooth; grainy batter gives brittle, patchy cheelas.
Keep the batter pourable but not runny, adding water a spoon at a time until it spreads easily.
Wipe the tava with a halved onion between cheelas to stop the batter from sticking.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with fresh green coriander-mint chutney and a cup of masala chai for a classic breakfast.

variations.name: Haryanvi Masala Moong Dal Cheela
variations.description: A robust Haryana-style cheela where the batter is spiced with garam masala and roasted coriander, then stuffed with a spiced potato-onion filling. Heartier than the plain version, it eats like a wholesome meal fit for a farm-country breakfast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil gives the masala cheela its crisp golden base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A brush of ghee on the finished cheela adds a rich, aromatic Haryanvi touch

steps: Soak 1 cup split green gram for 3 hours, drain, and grind with about 0.5 cup water to a smooth pourable batter, then mix in 1 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric, grated 1 inch ginger and 1 tsp salt.
Mash 2 boiled potatoes with 1 finely chopped onion, 0.5 tsp chilli powder, 0.25 tsp salt and 3 tbsp coriander to make a spiced filling, portioning about 2 tbsp per cheela.
Heat a tava over medium heat, brush with Anveshan Groundnut Oil, then pour and spread a ladle of batter into a thin round about 18 cm wide.
Drizzle 0.5 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil at the edges and cook 2 minutes until the base is golden and crisp, then flip and cook 1 minute.
Spread 2 tbsp of the potato filling over one half, fold the cheela over it and press gently to seal.
Brush the top with a little Anveshan Ghee, warm 30 seconds, then repeat with the remaining batter and filling and serve hot.
tips: Since the filling uses already-boiled potato, the garam masala can go straight in without extra cooking.
Keep the filling dry and well-mashed so it does not tear the cheela when folded.
Spread the batter thin so the stuffed cheela stays crisp rather than doughy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tangy tamarind chutney and a bowl of whisked curd for a filling, satisfying breakfast.

variations.name: Delhi Spicy Peppered Moong Cheela
variations.description: A fiery Delhi street-style cheela loaded with green chillies and freshly crushed black pepper for a real kick, finished with a squeeze of lemon. Sharp, zesty and quick, it channels the bold, no-nonsense flavours of the capital's breakfast carts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Sesame oil adds a warm nuttiness that balances the fierce pepper heat

steps: Soak 1 cup split green gram for 3 hours, drain, and grind with 4 green chillies, 1.5 inch ginger and about 0.5 cup water to a smooth, pourable batter.
Stir 1 tsp freshly crushed black pepper, 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1 tsp salt into the batter, then fold in 1 finely chopped small onion and 3 tbsp coriander.
Heat a tava over medium-high heat, brush with Anveshan Sesame Oil, then pour and spread a ladle of batter into a thin round about 18 cm wide.
Drizzle 0.5 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil around the edges and cook 2 minutes until the underside is deep golden and lacy-crisp.
Flip and cook the other side for 1 minute until set and speckled, pressing lightly for even crisping.
Squeeze a little lemon juice over the top, fold, and repeat with the remaining batter, serving each cheela hot off the tava.
tips: Crush the peppercorns coarsely just before mixing for a bright, aromatic heat rather than dull spice.
Cook these on slightly higher heat for the crisp, lacy edges typical of street-style cheelas.
Adjust the green chillies to your tolerance, as this version is meant to be genuinely spicy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling mint-yogurt dip and sliced onions to temper the pepper and chilli heat.

variations.name: Telangana Cheesy Moong Cheela
variations.description: A modern, kid-friendly twist popular in Hyderabad's cafe scene, where the moong cheela is topped with molten cheese, sweet corn and capsicum before folding. Gooey, mild and colourful, it turns the humble protein pancake into an irresistible melt.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil gives a clean crisp base that lets the melted cheese shine

steps: Soak 1 cup split green gram for 3 hours, drain, and grind with 2 green chillies and about 0.5 cup water to a smooth pourable batter, then mix in 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1 tsp salt.
Finely chop 1 small onion, 0.5 cup capsicum and stir together with 0.5 cup sweet corn and 3 tbsp coriander for the topping.
Heat a tava over medium heat, brush with Anveshan Groundnut Oil, then pour and spread a ladle of batter into a round about 18 cm wide.
Drizzle 0.5 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil at the edges and cook 2 minutes until the base is golden, then scatter a quarter of the vegetable topping and 3 tbsp grated cheese over one half.
Cover the tava for 1 minute so the cheese melts, then sprinkle a little chaat masala and fold the cheela over the melted filling.
Press gently, warm 30 seconds until the cheese oozes, then repeat with the remaining batter and toppings and serve immediately.
tips: Cover the tava briefly to melt the cheese evenly without burning the base of the cheela.
Use a good melting cheese and grate it fresh so it turns gooey rather than oily.
Serve straight away, as cheese cheelas lose their molten appeal once they cool.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tomato ketchup or a smoky red-pepper dip for a cafe-style plate kids will love.

variations.name: Andhra Pesarattu Cheela
variations.description: The iconic Andhra pesarattu, a whole green moong cheela ground with ginger, green chilli and cumin and cooked crisp with a sprinkle of onion pressed into the surface. Traditionally paired with ginger chutney, it is thinner and nuttier than the North Indian cheela.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Sesame oil is the classic Andhra fat that crisps the pesarattu edges beautifully

steps: Soak 1 cup whole green gram and 2 tbsp raw rice together for 5 hours, then drain and grind with 1.5 inch ginger, 3 green chillies and about 0.5 cup water to a slightly coarse pourable batter.
Stir 1 tsp cumin seeds, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 1 tsp salt into the batter, keeping it a touch thicker than dosa batter.
Heat a tava over medium heat, brush with Anveshan Sesame Oil, then pour a ladle of batter and spread it thin into a round about 20 cm wide.
Immediately sprinkle 2 tbsp finely chopped onion and a little coriander over the wet surface and press gently so they stick.
Drizzle 0.5 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil around the edges and cook 3 minutes until the base is deep golden and crisp, then flip and cook 1 minute.
Fold into a half-moon and repeat with the remaining batter, serving each pesarattu hot with the onion side up.
tips: Whole green moong keeps the skin on, giving pesarattu its characteristic nutty flavour and green flecks.
The spoon of rice in the batter is the secret to extra-crisp edges, so do not skip it.
Press the onion firmly into the wet batter so it roasts into the surface rather than falling off.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve Andhra-style with spicy ginger allam chutney and a bowl of upma tucked inside for MLA pesarattu.

variations.name: Classic Moong Dal Pakora
variations.description: A North Indian monsoon staple made from coarsely ground soaked moong dal, whipped light and dropped into hot oil to fry into nubbly golden fritters. Crisp outside and moist, protein-rich and lentil-sweet within, they are the pakoras that feel like a proper snack, not just a nibble.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: a single spoon in the batter gives the pakoras extra crispness without weighing them down

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for deep-frying; its high smoke point cooks the dal batter through to a crisp golden shell

steps: Soak 1.5 cups split green gram in plenty of water for 4 hours until the grains swell and soften, then drain well.
Grind the dal to a slightly coarse, thick batter using only a splash of water, then whip it vigorously with a whisk for 2 minutes until light and fluffy so the pakoras stay airy.

Fold in 3 chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 1 finely chopped onion, 3 tbsp coriander, 1 tsp cumin seeds, 0.25 tsp asafoetida, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta and 1.25 tsp salt.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a kadai to medium-hot, about 175C; a small drop of batter should rise steadily to the surface.
Drop rough teaspoons of batter into the oil, frying 6 or 7 at a time, and fry for 3 to 4 minutes, turning, until deep golden and crisp all over.
Lift out with a slotted spoon and drain on a wire rack; fry the rest in batches so the oil stays hot and the pakoras crisp.
tips: Whipping the ground dal until fluffy is the secret to light, crisp pakoras; test by dropping a little into water, and it should float.
Grind with as little water as possible, as a runny batter gives flat, oily fritters.
The deep-frying fully cooks the whole cumin in the batter; add the salt only just before frying so the batter does not turn watery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a coriander-mint chutney and a cup of ginger chai, or drop into a bowl of spiced yoghurt for instant dal kadhi.

variations.name: Kerala Crispy Moong Dal Pakora
variations.description: A Kerala parippu-vada inspired version, thicker and pattied, coated in breadcrumbs and fried in coconut oil for a nutty coastal crunch. Curry leaves and coconut slivers run through the lentil, giving these fritters their unmistakable Malabar fragrance.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the defining Kerala frying fat, lending its sweet, nutty coconut fragrance to each vada

steps: Soak 1.5 cups split green gram for 4 hours, drain, and grind to a thick, coarse paste using minimal water so it can be shaped.

Lightly crush 0.5 tsp fennel seeds, then fold into the dal along with 2 sprigs chopped curry leaves, 3 tbsp coconut slivers, 6 sliced shallots, 3 chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 1.25 tsp salt.
Shape the mixture into 10 thick flat patties and press each into 1 cup bread crumbs to coat both sides.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil to medium, about 170C, so the thick patties cook through without burning.
Fry the coated patties 4 or 5 at a time for 4 to 5 minutes, turning once, until crisp and golden.
Lift onto a wire rack to drain; the coconut oil will leave a distinct Malabar aroma.
tips: Grind the dal coarse, not smooth, so the vadas keep the grainy bite that defines the Kerala style.
Coconut oil solidifies when cool, so keep the pan on steady heat to avoid the patties sitting in cold fat.
Add the coconut slivers only when shaping so they stay in visible flecks rather than blending in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a fresh coconut chutney and hot black tea, or tuck into a banana-leaf tiffin with sambar.

variations.name: Karnataka Spicy Moong Dal Pakora
variations.description: A Bengaluru-style pakora with a bold hit of coarsely cracked black pepper and a scatter of chopped dill for a herby, warming bite. The pepper's slow heat plays against the sweet lentil, making these a favourite with evening filter coffee.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: a spoon in the batter crisps the pepper-spiced pakoras and stops them turning soft

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for deep-frying; a neutral base that lets the sharp pepper flavour lead

steps: Soak 1.5 cups split green gram for 4 hours, drain, and grind to a coarse, thick batter with minimal water, then whip for 2 minutes until light.
Coarsely crack 1.5 tsp black pepper in a mortar for uneven, aromatic flecks.

Fold the cracked pepper into the batter with 3 tbsp chopped dill, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 1 chopped onion, 1 tsp cumin seeds, 0.25 tsp asafoetida, 1 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta and 1.25 tsp salt.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to medium-hot, about 175C.
Drop teaspoons of batter into the oil, frying 6 or 7 at a time for 3 to 4 minutes until deep golden and crisp.
Drain on a wire rack and finish with a light dusting of extra cracked pepper while hot.
tips: Crack the pepper fresh and coarse just before mixing, as pre-ground pepper loses its fragrant heat.
Fresh dill can be swapped for chopped fenugreek leaves for a more bitter, equally aromatic bite.
The deep-fry cooks the cumin fully; keep the oil at steady medium-hot so the thick batter cooks inside before over-browning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling coconut chutney and a small tumbler of South Indian filter coffee.

variations.name: Andhra Masala Moong Dal Pakora
variations.description: The Andhra version is bold and aromatic, with garam masala, roasted coriander powder and a generous fistful of curry leaves and green chilli. Fiery and fragrant, these lentil fritters are made for spice-lovers and pair perfectly with strong chai.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: one spoon crisps the heavily spiced batter so the pakoras stay crunchy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for deep-frying; carries the layered masala flavour cleanly

steps: Soak 1.5 cups split green gram for 4 hours, drain, and grind to a coarse thick batter with minimal water, then whip 2 minutes until light.
Dry-roast 1.5 tsp coriander powder for 30 seconds until fragrant.

Fold the roasted coriander powder into the batter with 1 tsp garam masala, 2 sprigs chopped curry leaves, 4 chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 1 chopped onion, 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1.25 tsp salt, along with 1 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to medium-hot, about 175C.
Drop teaspoons of the spiced batter into the oil, frying 6 or 7 at a time for 3 to 4 minutes until deep golden and crisp.
Drain on a wire rack and serve blazing hot.
tips: Roast the coriander powder before folding it in for the aromatic Andhra masala depth.
For extra fire, add a few slit green chillies to fry alongside the pakoras as a spicy garnish.
The whole cumin cooks in the deep-fry; if the batter thickens as it sits, whip in a splash of water before frying the next batch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a fiery Andhra tomato-garlic chutney and thin onion rings to cool the heat.

variations.name: Telangana Tava Moong Dal Pakora
variations.description: A lighter Telangana adaptation that griddles the dal batter into flat mini-uttapam-style fritters on a tava, using far less oil. A curry-leaf and sesame tempering gives them a crisp base and a homely southern aroma, perfect for an everyday tiffin.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: brushed over the tava for a low-oil griddle and a nutty gingelly aroma

steps: Soak 1.5 cups split green gram for 4 hours, drain, and grind to a thick, spreadable batter using minimal water.
Stir into the batter 1 chopped onion, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 1 tsp cumin seeds, 3 tbsp coriander, 1 tbsp sesame seeds, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt.
Heat a flat tava on medium and brush with 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil, then scatter a few curry leaves onto the tava.
Spoon small mounds of batter over the curry leaves and spread each into a flat 7 cm disc, cooking for 3 minutes until the underside is crisp and golden.
Flip the discs, drizzle a little sesame oil around each, and cook the second side for 3 minutes until crisp and cooked through.
Repeat with the remaining batter, brushing the tava with a little oil each time; serve hot off the griddle.
tips: Keep the batter thick enough to hold its shape on the tava; if it spreads too much, stir in a spoon of the reserved ground dal.
Pressing curry leaves onto the tava first embeds them crisp into the base of each fritter.
Cook on steady medium heat so the dal cooks through before the sesame-brushed base scorches.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a spicy tomato-peanut chutney and a bowl of curd for a wholesome, low-oil tiffin.

variations.name: Classic Onion Bhaji
variations.description: The definitive onion fritter: sweet sliced onions bound in a thin, spiced gram-flour coating and fried into lacy, tangled clusters. Shatteringly crisp at the frilly edges and meltingly soft where the onion caramelises, these are the ultimate rainy-day pakoras with chai.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: a little wholewheat atta with the besan gives the bhajis a longer-lasting crunch

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for deep-frying; its high smoke point crisps the lacy edges without greasiness

steps: Thinly slice 4 large onions into fine half-moons, place in a bowl with 1.25 tsp salt, and rest for 10 minutes so they soften and release their moisture.
Add 2 chopped green chillies, 3 tbsp coriander, 1 tsp cumin seeds, 0.5 tsp carom seeds, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder to the onions and mix.
Sprinkle in 1 cup gram flour and 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta and toss with your fingers, adding only 2 to 3 tbsp water so the flour just coats the onions in a thick, clinging batter.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a kadai to medium-hot, about 180C; a strand of batter should sizzle and rise at once.
Drop loose, craggy clusters of the onion mixture into the oil, frying 5 or 6 at a time, and fry for 3 to 4 minutes, turning, until deep golden and crisp.
Lift out with a slotted spoon and drain on a wire rack; fry the rest in batches so the oil stays hot and the bhajis stay lacy and crisp.
tips: Salt the onions first and use their released juices to bind, so you need almost no water and the bhajis crisp up beautifully.
Keep the clusters loose and open rather than packing them, so the edges fry into crisp lace.
For extra crunch, fry once until pale, rest 10 minutes, then fry a second time just before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile onto a paper-lined plate, dust with chaat masala, and serve with mint chutney and a strong masala chai.

variations.name: Uttar Pradesh Crispy Onion Bhaji
variations.description: A Lucknawi bazaar-style bhaji given an extra-crunchy edge by tossing the battered onions with fine breadcrumbs before frying. The double-textured crust stays crisp for hours, making it the bhaji of choice for large evening platters and iftar spreads.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: thickens the batter so the breadcrumbs cling to every strand of onion

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: light wood-pressed oil that fries the crumb-crusted bhajis to an even pale gold

steps: Thinly slice 4 large onions, mix with 1.25 tsp salt and rest 10 minutes, then add 2 chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 1 tsp cumin seeds, 0.5 tsp lightly crushed fennel seeds and 0.5 tsp turmeric.
Add 1 cup gram flour and 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta and toss, using only 2 to 3 tbsp water so the batter thickly coats the onions.
Sprinkle 0.75 cup bread crumbs over the battered onions and toss so the crumbs cling to the strands.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sunflower Oil to medium-hot, about 175C.
Drop craggy clusters into the oil, frying 5 or 6 at a time for 4 to 5 minutes, turning, until the crumb-studded crust is crisp and golden.
Drain on a wire rack and fry the remaining clusters in batches to keep the oil hot.
tips: Add the breadcrumbs at the very end so they stay on the surface and crisp rather than getting lost in the batter.
These hold their crunch longest of all the bhajis, so they are ideal for making a little ahead of a gathering.
Reheat in a hot oven for 5 minutes to bring back the crisp if they soften.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a green coriander-mint chutney and a sweet imli chutney, Lucknawi evening-snack style.

variations.name: Bihar Spicy Onion Bhaji
variations.description: Bihar's roadside bhaji is fierce with coarsely cracked black pepper, crushed garlic and pungent mustard oil, giving a warmth that hits the back of the throat. The sharp mustard oil is central, lending these onion fritters their earthy, nose-tingling character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: gives the batter body so the peppery clusters hold their craggy shape

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoked once then used to fry; its sharp pungency is the soul of this Bihari bhaji

steps: Thinly slice 4 large onions, mix with 1.25 tsp salt and rest 10 minutes. Coarsely crack 1.5 tsp black pepper and crush 6 garlic cloves in a mortar.
Add the pepper-garlic paste to the onions with 3 chopped green chillies, 3 tbsp coriander, 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.5 tsp turmeric.
Add 1 cup gram flour and 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta and toss with 2 to 3 tbsp water into a thick clinging batter.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just begins to smoke to tame its raw pungency, then lower to medium and settle the oil to about 180C.
Drop craggy clusters into the hot mustard oil, frying 5 or 6 at a time for 3 to 4 minutes until dark golden and crisp.
Drain on a wire rack; the bhajis will carry the unmistakable sharp aroma of mustard oil and pepper.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to smoking point once before frying to mellow its raw bite, then bring it back to medium.
Crush the pepper coarse so you get little bursts of heat rather than an even flat spice.
Serve immediately, as these peppery bhajis are best when the heat is still lively and the edges crisp.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot with a sharp green chilli-garlic chutney and raw onion slices, Bihari dhaba style.

variations.name: Madhya Pradesh Masala Onion Bhaji
variations.description: Indore's masala onion bhaji is aromatic with garam masala, roasted coriander powder and crushed fennel, sold by the plateful at the city's Sarafa night market. Fragrant, festive and generously spiced, it turns the simple onion fritter into a full-flavoured indulgence.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: balances the besan and keeps the masala bhajis crisp rather than dense

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: clean-frying oil that lets the layered masala aroma come through

steps: Dry-roast 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp fennel seeds for 30 seconds until fragrant, then lightly crush the fennel.
Thinly slice 4 large onions, mix with 1.25 tsp salt and rest 10 minutes, then add the roasted spices, 1 tsp garam masala, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger and 0.5 tsp turmeric.
Add 1 cup gram flour and 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta and toss with 2 to 3 tbsp water into a thick clinging batter.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to medium-hot, about 180C.
Drop craggy clusters into the oil, frying 5 or 6 at a time for 3 to 4 minutes, turning, until crisp and richly golden.
Drain on a wire rack and fry the rest in batches.
tips: Roasting the coriander and fennel first gives these bhajis their signature Indore aroma.
Crush the fennel only lightly so you get fragrant flecks rather than a powder.
Make a big batch of the dry masala mix and store it airtight for quick bhajis on busy evenings.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a sweet-and-sour imli chutney and a sprinkle of sev, the way Indore's Sarafa stalls plate them.

variations.name: Goa Tava Onion Bhaji
variations.description: A Goan coastal twist that griddles flat onion-besan cakes on a tava with coconut oil and a whisper of tangy kokum. Lighter than deep-fried bhajis, they are crisp-edged, faintly sweet from the coconut oil, and fragrant with curry leaves.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: helps the thin tava batter set into firm, flippable cakes

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: brushed over the tava; its coastal sweetness defines this Goan shallow-cooked style

steps: Soak 3 kokum pieces in 2 tbsp warm water for 10 minutes, then finely chop and reserve the soaking water.

Thinly slice 3 large onions and mix with 1 cup gram flour, 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, 2 sprigs chopped curry leaves, 0.25 cup grated coconut, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp cumin seeds, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and the chopped kokum.
Add the kokum water and enough extra water, about 4 tbsp total, to make a thick spoonable batter that is not runny.
Heat a flat tava on medium and brush with 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil until it shimmers.
Place spoonfuls of batter and press each into a flat 8 cm cake, cooking 3 minutes until the underside is crisp and golden.
Flip the cakes, drizzle a little more coconut oil around the edges, and cook the second side 3 minutes until crisp; repeat with the rest.
tips: Kokum adds the signature Goan tang; if unavailable, use 1 tbsp lime juice stirred in off the heat.
Keep the cakes thin so they cook through on the tava without a deep oil bath.
Cook on medium heat only, as coconut oil browns quickly and high heat will scorch the edges before the centre sets.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a fresh coconut-chilli chutney and steamed rice, or tuck into pao for a Goan onion-cake sandwich.

variations.name: Classic Sattu Cheela
variations.description: A wonderfully nutty, high-protein pancake built on Anveshan Sattu, roasted Bengal-gram flour that needs no cooking to develop its toasty depth. The batter comes together in minutes, studded with onion and green chilli, and crisps in Anveshan Mustard Oil into a savoury, wholesome breakfast that keeps you full for hours.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Stone-ground roasted Bengal-gram flour that forms the protein-rich, nutty body of the cheela.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Pungent wood-pressed mustard oil for greasing the tava and crisping the edges the eastern way.

steps: Whisk 2 cups Anveshan Sattu with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp ajwain and 1 tsp salt, then slowly add about 2.5 cups water, beating out lumps into a smooth, thin pouring batter.
Stir in 1 finely chopped onion, 2 chopped green chillies, a grated 1-inch piece of ginger and 3 tbsp coriander, and rest 5 minutes as sattu thickens quickly.
Check the batter and loosen with a little water if it has stiffened, keeping it thin enough to pour and spread.
Heat a tava over medium heat, rub with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it shimmers, then pour a ladle of batter and spread into a thin 7-inch round.
Drizzle 0.5 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil around the edge and cook 2-3 minutes until the base is golden and set, as sattu browns faster than plain besan.
Flip and cook the second side 1-2 minutes until speckled and cooked through, then fold and repeat with the rest of the batter.
tips: Sattu drinks up water fast, so keep a little extra by the stove and thin the batter between cheelas.
Cook on medium heat only; roasted sattu catches and browns quickly and can turn bitter over high flame.
Add the ajwain for more than flavour: it makes this protein-dense cheela easier to digest.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a spoon of tangy tomato-chilli chokha and a bowl of set curd for a filling, gut-friendly breakfast.

variations.name: Haryanvi Masala Sattu Cheela
variations.description: A robust rural-Haryana take where the sattu batter is deepened with garam masala and coriander powder and folded with grated bottle gourd for moisture and bulk. Cooked in Anveshan Groundnut Oil, it is a filling, farm-style breakfast that pairs the nutty sattu with warm North-Indian spice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Roasted gram flour giving the cheela its protein-rich, nutty backbone under the masala.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil for a clean, crisp base that suits the hearty spiced batter.

steps: Whisk 2 cups Anveshan Sattu with 1 tsp garam masala, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt.
Grate 1 cup bottle gourd and squeeze it lightly, then mix it and its released juices into the sattu with 1 chopped onion, a grated 1-inch piece of ginger and 3 tbsp coriander.
Add about 2 cups water gradually to a smooth, thick-but-pourable batter, accounting for the moisture the gourd gives off, and rest 5 minutes.
Heat a tava over medium heat, rub with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, then pour a ladle of batter and spread into a 7-inch round.
Drizzle 0.5 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil around the edge and cook 2-3 minutes until golden and set underneath.
Flip and cook 2 minutes until the gourd is cooked and the cheela is browned, then repeat with the remaining batter.
tips: Use the liquid squeezed from the gourd as part of the water so none of its flavour or nutrients is wasted.
Because the gourd adds water, hold back some of the 2 cups and adjust as you go to avoid a runny batter.
Toast the garam masala for a few seconds in a dry pan first to sharpen the aroma against the mild gourd.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a dollop of home-churned white butter and a green chilli pickle, farmhouse-breakfast style.

variations.name: Dilliwala Spicy Sattu Cheela
variations.description: A street-smart Delhi version fired up with pounded green chillies, cracked black pepper and a squeeze of lemon for a chaat-like zing. Cooked in Anveshan Groundnut Oil, this sattu cheela is thin, crisp-edged and packs the bold, spicy punch of a Purani Dilli breakfast stall.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Roasted gram flour that turns nutty and crisp, carrying the fiery spicing well.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Clean wood-pressed groundnut oil to fry the peppery edges crisp without dulling the heat.

steps: Pound 4 green chillies with a 1-inch piece of ginger to a coarse paste and crush 1 tsp peppercorns roughly.
Whisk 2 cups Anveshan Sattu with 0.5 tsp ajwain, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, then beat in about 2.5 cups water to a smooth thin batter.
Stir in the chilli-ginger paste, crushed pepper, 1 finely chopped onion, 2 tsp lemon juice and 3 tbsp coriander, and rest 5 minutes, loosening with water if needed.
Heat a tava over medium heat, grease with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, pour a ladle of batter and spread into a thin 7-inch round.
Drizzle 0.5 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil at the edges and cook 2-3 minutes until the base is golden and crisp.
Flip and cook the second side 1-2 minutes until speckled and cooked through, then repeat with the remaining batter.
tips: Add the lemon juice to the batter for a bright, chaat-like tang that lifts the earthy sattu.
Crush the peppercorns fresh for a warm, aromatic heat distinct from the green-chilli sharpness.
Keep the batter thin so these cheelas crisp up like street-stall ones rather than turning thick and soft.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a sharp onion-lachha salad and green mint chutney, rolled up to eat on the go.

variations.name: Telangana Cheesy Sattu Cheela
variations.description: A modern city-cafe spin where grated cheese is melted over the crisp sattu cheela, its savoury pull playing off the nutty roasted-gram base for a surprisingly good match. Cooked in Anveshan Sesame Oil, it turns a wholesome high-protein breakfast into a treat kids happily ask for.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Nutty roasted gram flour whose toasty flavour stands up nicely to the melted cheese.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil for a crisp base and a gentle nuttiness beneath the cheese.

steps: Whisk 2 cups Anveshan Sattu with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp black pepper powder and 0.75 tsp salt, then beat in about 2.5 cups water to a smooth thin batter.
Stir in 1 finely chopped onion, 1 chopped green chilli and 3 tbsp coriander, and rest 5 minutes, loosening with a splash of water if it thickens.
Heat a tava over medium heat, grease with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, pour a ladle of batter and spread into a 7-inch round.
Drizzle 0.5 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil around the edge and cook 2-3 minutes until the base is golden and crisp.
Scatter 3 tbsp grated cheese over the top, cover for 1-2 minutes until melted, then fold the cheela in half.
Cook another 30 seconds to set, then serve hot and repeat with the remaining batter and cheese.
tips: Melt the cheese under a lid instead of flipping onto it, so the layer stays intact and doesn't stick.
A little black pepper in the batter cuts the richness and stops the cheese tasting flat against the sattu.
Serve at once while the cheese is molten; the cheela firms and the cheese sets as it cools.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a tangy tomato chutney and ketchup on the side, cut into wedges for easy sharing.

variations.name: Bihari Stuffed Sattu Cheela
variations.description: The definitive Bihari treatment where a punchy dry sattu masala of mustard oil, pickle spices, garlic and ajwain is spread over the cheela and folded in, echoing the beloved sattu-stuffed litti and paratha. Cooked in Anveshan Mustard Oil, it is intensely savoury, tangy and unmistakably from the Magadh kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Roasted gram flour used both in the batter and the classic Bihari dry stuffing masala.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Sharp wood-pressed mustard oil, the soul of Bihari sattu masala, for the stuffing and the tava.

steps: For the stuffing, mix 0.5 cup of the Anveshan Sattu with 6 finely minced garlic cloves, 3 chopped green chillies, 1 tbsp pickle masala, 0.5 tsp ajwain, 2 tsp lemon juice, 1 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and a pinch of salt into a moist, crumbly masala.
Whisk the remaining 1.5 cups Anveshan Sattu with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt, then beat in about 2.5 cups water to a smooth thin batter and stir in 1 chopped onion and 3 tbsp coriander.
Heat a tava over medium heat, grease with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it shimmers, pour a ladle of batter and spread into a 7-inch round.
Drizzle 0.5 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil at the edges and cook 2-3 minutes until the base is golden and set.
Spread 2 tbsp of the sattu stuffing over one half, drizzle a few drops of mustard oil on top, and fold the cheela over the filling.
Press gently and cook 1 minute more to warm the stuffing through, then serve and repeat with the rest.
tips: Keep the stuffing crumbly and just-moist, not wet, so it stays put when you fold the cheela.
Pickle masala brings the authentic tang; a spoon of the oily masala from a jar of mango pickle works perfectly.
Make the stuffing ahead as it only improves overnight, and use it for littis and parathas too.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with baigan chokha and a raw onion wedge, the classic Bihari accompaniments to anything sattu.

variations.name: Classic Vegetable Appe
variations.description: Golden little dumplings cooked in a dimpled appe pan from fermented dosa batter folded with finely chopped vegetables and a quick mustard-curry-leaf tempering. Crisp and lacquered outside, soft and fluffy within, each ball is turned in its Anveshan Sesame Oil-greased cavity to a perfect all-round gold.

ingredients.name: Fermented dosa batter (rice and urad dal)
Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil brushed into each cavity so the appe crisp and release cleanly.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: A little in the tempering for a nutty aroma that lifts the vegetable appe.

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil with 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, add 2 chopped green chillies and 12 curry leaves, then saute 1 finely chopped onion for 2 minutes until soft.
Add 1 small grated carrot and half a finely chopped capsicum, saute 2 minutes until just softened, then cool the mixture.
Fold the cooled vegetables and 3 tbsp coriander into 3 cups fermented dosa batter with 0.5 tsp salt to a thick dropping consistency.
Heat an appe pan over medium heat and brush each cavity with a few drops of Anveshan Sesame Oil, then fill each three-quarters full with batter.
Cover and cook 3-4 minutes until the tops look set and the undersides are golden, then turn each ball with a skewer or spoon.
Drizzle a little more sesame oil, cook 2-3 minutes more until crisp and golden all over, and repeat with the remaining batter.
tips: Cool the sauteed vegetables before mixing in, or the warmth deflates the airy fermented batter.
Keep the batter thick like a dropping consistency so the appe hold their round shape and don't spread.
Turn the balls only once a golden crust has formed, or they stick and tear in the cavity.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot on a platter with coconut chutney and a small bowl of molagapodi mixed with sesame oil for dipping.

variations.name: Jharkhand Masala Vegetable Appe
variations.description: A spiced-up plateau version where garam masala and coriander powder season the vegetable batter and grated beetroot lends colour and a faint earthy sweetness. Cooked in Anveshan Mustard Oil-brushed cavities, these appe carry a warm, eastern-Indian masala flavour in every fluffy bite.

ingredients.name: Fermented dosa batter (rice and urad dal)
Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Pungent wood-pressed mustard oil brushed into the cavities for a crisp, earthy-flavoured appe.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon in the tempering to round the sharp mustard oil and warm the masala.

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil with 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, add 2 chopped green chillies and 1 chopped onion and saute 2 minutes until soft.
Stir in 0.75 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp coriander powder and 0.25 tsp turmeric for 30 seconds, add half a small grated beetroot, saute 2 minutes and cool.
Fold the cooled masala and 3 tbsp coriander into 3 cups fermented dosa batter with 0.5 tsp salt to a thick dropping consistency.
Heat an appe pan over medium heat, brush each cavity with a few drops of Anveshan Mustard Oil, and fill each three-quarters full.
Cover and cook 3-4 minutes until the bases are golden, then turn each ball with a skewer.
Add a few more drops of oil, cook 2-3 minutes until crisp all over, and repeat with the remaining batter.
tips: Grate the beetroot fine so it cooks quickly and tints the appe a pretty pink without bleeding too much.
Bloom the ground spices in the hot oil before adding the beetroot so they lose any raw taste.
Let the mustard oil shimmer before brushing the cavities to mellow its pungency into a nutty note.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coriander-mint chutney and a wedge of lime, ideal as a colourful tiffin-box snack.

variations.name: Punjabi Spicy Vegetable Appe
variations.description: A fiery North-Indian twist where pounded green chillies, crushed black pepper and grated ginger heat up the vegetable batter for a bold, tingling bite. Cooked in Anveshan Groundnut Oil-brushed cavities, these appe stay soft and fluffy inside while the spice builds a satisfying, slow warmth.

ingredients.name: Fermented dosa batter (rice and urad dal)
Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Clean wood-pressed groundnut oil brushed into the cavities for a crisp, neutral base that lets the heat shine.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: A little in the tempering to soften the sharp pepper heat with a mellow richness.

steps: Pound 4 green chillies with a 1.5-inch piece of ginger to a coarse paste and crush 1 tsp peppercorns roughly.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil with 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 10 curry leaves, add 1 chopped onion and saute 2 minutes, then stir in the chilli-ginger paste and crushed pepper for 1 minute and cool.
Fold the cooled spice base and 3 tbsp coriander into 3 cups fermented dosa batter with 0.5 tsp salt to a thick dropping consistency.
Heat an appe pan over medium heat, brush the cavities with a few drops of Anveshan Groundnut Oil, and fill each three-quarters full.
Cover and cook 3-4 minutes until the bases are golden and set, then turn each ball with a skewer.
Drizzle a little more oil, cook 2-3 minutes until crisp and golden all over, and repeat with the rest of the batter.
tips: For a milder batch, deseed the green chillies but keep the crushed pepper for its aromatic warmth.
Sauteing the chilli-ginger paste briefly takes off the raw edge and deepens the flavour of the appe.
A spoon of thick curd folded into the batter tempers the heat and keeps the appe extra soft.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling mint-curd dip and cucumber sticks to balance the heat at snack time.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Cheesy Vegetable Appe
variations.description: A kid-friendly Pune-style appe where a cube of cheese is tucked into the centre of each vegetable ball so it oozes molten when you bite in. Cooked in Anveshan Sesame Oil-brushed cavities, the crisp golden shell gives way to a soft, cheesy, corn-flecked middle.

ingredients.name: Fermented dosa batter (rice and urad dal)
Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil for crisp cavities that hold the molten-cheese centres.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: A little in the tempering for a nutty aroma alongside the melting cheese.

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil with 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, add 1 chopped green chilli and 1 chopped onion and saute 2 minutes until soft, then cool.
Fold the cooled onion, 0.5 cup sweetcorn, 0.5 tsp black pepper and 3 tbsp coriander into 3 cups fermented dosa batter with 0.5 tsp salt to a thick dropping consistency.
Heat an appe pan over medium heat and brush each cavity with a few drops of Anveshan Sesame Oil.
Half-fill each cavity with batter, press a small cheese cube into the centre, then top with a little more batter to enclose it.
Cover and cook 3-4 minutes until the bases are golden, then turn each ball gently with a skewer.
Cook 2-3 minutes more until crisp and golden all over and the cheese inside has melted, then repeat with the rest.
tips: Enclose the cheese fully in batter so it melts inside rather than leaking out and burning in the cavity.
Use firm cheese cubes straight from the fridge; soft cheese melts too fast and escapes before the shell sets.
Serve these immediately, as the cheese centre is at its gooey best while piping hot.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tomato ketchup and a tangy schezwan chutney, a guaranteed hit at children's parties.

variations.name: Tamil Kuzhi Paniyaram
variations.description: The authentic Chettinad ancestor of the appe, where the fermented batter is finished with a fragrant tempering of mustard, urad dal, chopped shallots and coconut bits before being cooked in a kuzhi paniyaram pan. Anveshan Sesame Oil gives the classic crisp shell and nutty aroma that define this beloved South tiffin.

ingredients.name: Fermented dosa batter (rice and urad dal)
Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil, essential for the tempering and the crisp shell of a proper paniyaram.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: A little in the tempering for the rich aroma typical of Chettinad cooking.

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil with 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then fry 1 tsp urad dal and 1 tsp chana dal for 30 seconds until golden.
Add 10 chopped shallots, 2 chopped green chillies, a chopped 1-inch piece of ginger, 3 tbsp coconut bits and 12 curry leaves, and saute 2-3 minutes until the shallots turn soft and fragrant; cool.
Fold the cooled tempering into 3 cups fermented dosa batter with 0.5 tsp salt to a thick dropping consistency.
Heat a paniyaram pan over medium heat, brush each cavity with a few drops of Anveshan Sesame Oil, and fill each three-quarters full.
Cover and cook 3-4 minutes until the undersides are deep golden, then turn each ball with a skewer.
Drizzle a little more sesame oil, cook 2-3 minutes until crisp and evenly browned, and repeat with the remaining batter.
tips: Shallots are key to the authentic flavour; their sweetness is markedly better here than large onions.
Little bits of fresh coconut give bursts of sweetness and texture that set paniyaram apart from plain appe.
Slightly sour, day-old batter gives the best crisp shell and characteristic tang for paniyaram.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and tomato thokku, the traditional Chettinad tiffin accompaniments.

variations.name: Classic Aloo Tikki
variations.description: The definitive crisp-shelled, soft-centred potato patty of North-Indian chaat stalls, spiced with roasted cumin, amchur and green chilli and bound with a little Anveshan Sattu instead of bread crumbs for extra crunch. Shallow-fried in Anveshan Groundnut Oil, it turns a deep, shattering gold on the outside while staying pillowy within.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Roasted gram flour worked in as a wholesome binder, replacing bread crumbs for a crisper shell.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil for shallow-frying the tikkis to a deep, even golden crust.

steps: Boil 5 medium potatoes until fork-tender, peel while warm and mash them completely smooth with no lumps.

Mix the mash with 4 tbsp Anveshan Sattu, 2 finely chopped green chillies, a grated 1-inch piece of ginger, 1.5 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp amchur, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, 4 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp salt into a firm, non-sticky dough.
Divide into 8 equal portions and shape each into a smooth round patty about 2 cm thick, pressing the edges so they don't crack.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a flat pan over medium heat until it shimmers.
Slide in the tikkis in batches and shallow-fry 3-4 minutes per side, pressing lightly, until a deep golden crust forms and they lift cleanly.
Drain on a wire rack rather than paper to keep them crisp, and fry the rest with the remaining oil.
tips: Sattu binds the tikki without the sogginess bread crumbs can bring and gives a noticeably crisper crust.
Mash the potatoes while warm and avoid any water; a wet mix makes the tikkis fall apart in the pan.
Chill the shaped patties for 15 minutes before frying so they hold shape and crisp up better.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a plate of chaat topped with whisked curd, green chutney, tamarind chutney and a shower of sev.

variations.name: Rajasthani Spicy Aloo Tikki
variations.description: A desert-kitchen tikki with real bite, where coarsely cracked black pepper and extra red chilli give a warm, lingering heat quite unlike a mild chaat tikki. Bound with Anveshan Sattu and shallow-fried in Anveshan Groundnut Oil, it is crisp, fiery and made to stand up to a tangy chutney.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Roasted gram flour that binds the fiery mix and crisps the shell without any bread crumbs.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Clean wood-pressed groundnut oil that fries the peppery tikkis crisp without dulling the heat.

steps: Boil, peel and mash 5 medium potatoes smooth while still warm, and coarsely crush 1.5 tsp peppercorns in a mortar.

Finely chop 1 small onion and squeeze out its moisture, then mix the mash with 4 tbsp Anveshan Sattu, the crushed pepper, the onion, 3 finely chopped green chillies, a grated 1-inch piece of ginger, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp chaat masala, 4 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp salt into a firm dough.
Divide into 8 portions and shape into thick, smooth patties, sealing any cracks at the edges.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a flat pan over medium heat until it shimmers.
Fry the tikkis in batches for 3-4 minutes each side, pressing gently, until deep golden and crisp all over.
Drain on a wire rack and fry the remaining batch with the rest of the oil.
tips: Crack the peppercorns coarsely rather than powdering them, so you get little bursts of heat in every bite.
The pepper heat blooms as it fries, so start with 1.5 tsp and scale up only once you have tasted a test tikki.
A spoon of thick curd served alongside quickly cools the palate between fiery mouthfuls.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling boondi raita and sliced onions dusted with chaat masala to balance the pepper heat.

variations.name: Bengali Masala Aloo Tikki
variations.description: An eastern-style tikki where warming garam masala and coriander powder are folded through the potato and a fine dice of fried onion adds sweetness. Bound with Anveshan Sattu and shallow-fried in Anveshan Mustard Oil, it has the aromatic, gently spiced character of a Kolkata street-corner chop.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Roasted gram flour binder that keeps the spiced tikkis firm and crisp without bread crumbs.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Pungent wood-pressed mustard oil, the signature frying fat that gives these tikkis a Kolkata-chop character.

steps: Boil, peel and mash 5 medium potatoes smooth while warm.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and fry 1 finely chopped onion for 3 minutes until golden, then cool.

Mix the mash with 4 tbsp Anveshan Sattu, the fried onion, 1 tsp garam masala, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 2 chopped green chillies, 4 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp salt into a firm dough.
Divide into 8 portions and shape into smooth, thick patties without cracks.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a flat pan over medium heat until it just shimmers and loses its raw edge.
Fry the tikkis in batches 3-4 minutes per side, pressing gently, until deep golden and aromatic, then drain on a rack and fry the rest.
tips: Frying the onion first removes its raw sharpness and lends the tikki a subtle sweetness against the masala.
Heat the mustard oil until it just shimmers before frying so its pungency softens into a nutty warmth.
Toast the garam masala for a few seconds in a dry pan before mixing to make its aroma really sing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with kasundi mustard and a beetroot-onion salad for a genuinely Bengali chop-shop plate.

variations.name: Tava Aloo Tikki
variations.description: A lighter, less oily tikki griddled slowly on a flat tava rather than fried, so it develops a crackly crust with just a brush of fat. Cooked in Anveshan Groundnut Oil and finished with a little ghee, it stays wholesome while still delivering that irresistible crisp-outside, soft-inside contrast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Roasted gram flour binder that helps the tikkis crisp on the tava with minimal oil.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Brushed on the tava to griddle the tikkis crisp using far less fat than deep-frying.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing brush for a golden, aromatic crust on the griddled tikki.

steps: Boil, peel and mash 5 medium potatoes smooth while warm, keeping the mix dry.

Mix the mash with 4 tbsp Anveshan Sattu, 2 chopped green chillies, a grated 1-inch piece of ginger, 3 tbsp chopped spring onion, 1.5 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp amchur, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, 4 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp salt into a firm dough.
Divide into 8 portions, shape into slightly flattened patties so more surface touches the tava, and press both sides into 2 tbsp sesame seeds spread on a plate.
Heat a flat tava over medium heat and brush it with 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil until it shimmers.
Place the tikkis on and griddle 4-5 minutes per side, brushing with a little oil, until a crackly deep-golden crust forms.
Brush the tops with a little Anveshan Bilona Ghee in the last minute for aroma, then serve hot and repeat with the rest.
tips: Flatten the patties a little more than for frying so they cook through evenly on the flat tava.
Resist moving them too soon; let a crust set first or they will stick and break on the griddle.
This lighter method is ideal for a lunchbox, staying crisp longer than deep-fried tikkis.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve tucked into a soft pav with green chutney and sliced onion for a lighter tikki burger.

variations.name: Amritsari Stuffed Aloo Tikki
variations.description: The famous Amritsari tikki with a surprise inside: a spiced green-pea and paneer filling tucked into the potato shell so it steams as the tikki fries. Bound with Anveshan Sattu and shallow-fried in Anveshan Ghee, it is rich, festive and worlds apart from a plain patty.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Roasted gram flour binder for the potato shell so the stuffed tikkis hold together while frying.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: Nutty bilona ghee for shallow-frying the stuffed tikkis to a rich, festive golden crust.

steps: Boil, peel and mash 5 medium potatoes smooth, then mix with 4 tbsp Anveshan Sattu, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 4 tbsp coriander and 0.75 tsp salt into a firm shell dough.

For the filling, coarsely mash 1 cup boiled green peas and crumble in 0.5 cup paneer, then mix with 2 chopped green chillies, a grated 1-inch piece of ginger, 1 tsp garam masala, 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp amchur and 0.5 tsp salt.
Divide the potato dough into 8 balls; flatten each, place 1.5 tbsp of the pea-paneer filling in the centre, gather the edges over to seal, and press gently into a thick patty.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee in a flat pan over medium heat until it shimmers.
Shallow-fry the stuffed tikkis in batches 3-4 minutes per side, turning carefully, until deep golden and crisp with the filling steamed through.
Drain on a rack and fry the remaining tikkis with the rest of the ghee.
tips: Seal the filling well and keep the potato shell an even thickness so the tikki doesn't split and leak while frying.
Squeeze any moisture from the mashed peas so the filling stays firm and the tikki fries crisp.
Fry over steady medium heat; too hot and the shell browns before the paneer filling warms through.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sweet tamarind chutney and a spoon of thick curd, garnished with pomegranate seeds for a festive touch.

variations.name: Classic Punjabi Dal Makhani
variations.description: The archetypal Punjabi black dal, slow-simmered with butter and cream and generously scented with hand-crushed kasuri methi, which is the note that says Punjab in one whiff. Rich, dark and velvety, it is the benchmark against which every other version is measured.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the tomato base is cooked in wood-pressed groundnut oil before the butter and ghee enrich the dal

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the finishing tadka of cumin and garlic in ghee brings the classic Punjabi aroma

steps: Soak 1 cup urad and 0.25 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 4 cups water for 7 whistles until fully soft and creamy.
