Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, fry 1 large chopped onion for 6 minutes to golden, then add 2 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 2 minutes until the raw edge goes.
Add 1 cup tomato puree, 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli and 1 tsp garam masala, and bhuno 8 minutes until the oil separates and the masala is glossy red.
Add the cooked dal, mash a ladleful, and simmer on low heat for 35 minutes, stirring often with splashes of hot water, until dark and silky.
Stir in 3 tbsp butter, 0.33 cup cream and 1.5 tsp kasuri methi crushed between the palms, with the remaining salt, and simmer 5 minutes.
For the tadka, heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin and a little chopped garlic to golden, and pour it over the dal before serving.
tips: Crush the kasuri methi between your palms as you add it to release its full aroma into the dal.
The slow simmer, not extra cream, is what makes it velvety, so give it the full time.
Made a day ahead and reheated with a fresh tadka, this dal tastes even better.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a swirl of cream and butter naan or jeera rice, with sliced onions and green chilli on the side for the complete Punjabi meal.

variations.name: Patiala Shahi Dal Makhani
variations.description: The royal Patiala-court version, richer and more aristocratic, thickened with cashew and almond paste and gently perfumed with green cardamom and mace. Extravagant with butter and cream, it is the plush, princely cousin of the everyday Punjabi dal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the royal dal is built entirely on ghee, from the base to the finishing tadka

steps: Soak 1 cup urad and 0.33 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 1 tsp salt and 5 cups water for 8 whistles until completely soft.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 4 green cardamom, then fry 1 large chopped onion for 7 minutes to golden and add 2 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 2 minutes.
Add 1 cup tomato puree and 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli and cook 7 minutes, then stir in 4 tbsp cashew-almond paste and cook 4 minutes until smooth and the ghee separates.
Tip in the cooked dal, mash a portion, and simmer on low heat for 35 minutes with hot water as needed until rich and dark.
Stir in 4 tbsp butter, 0.5 cup cream, 0.25 tsp mace and 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi with the remaining salt, and simmer 8 minutes until luxuriously thick.
Cover and rest off the heat for 10 minutes so the cardamom and mace perfume settles before serving.
tips: The nut paste does much of the thickening and gives a smoother, more regal body than cream alone.
Keep the heat gentle once the cream is in so the rich gravy doesn't split.
Add mace with a light hand; it should whisper in the background, not dominate.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve this princely dal with sheermal or butter kulcha and a saffron pulao; a scatter of slivered almonds on top befits its royal pedigree.

variations.name: Ludhianvi Dhaba Dal Makhani
variations.description: The buttery, coal-smoked highway-dhaba style of the Malwa belt, finished with a shameless quantity of butter and a dhungar smoking that gives it its addictive charred aroma. Bold, glossy and unabashedly rich, it is the truckers' favourite black dal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: cooks the masala base cleanly before the heavy butter and coal smoke go in

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the ghee tadka and dhungar drizzle carry the dhaba's smoky, buttery signature

steps: Soak 1 cup urad and 0.25 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 1 tsp salt and 4 cups water for 7 whistles until melting soft.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin with 1 black cardamom, 1 inch cinnamon and 1 bay leaf, then fry 1 large chopped onion for 6 minutes to golden and add 2 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 2 minutes.
Add 1.25 cups tomato puree and 2 tsp Kashmiri chilli and bhuno 9 minutes until deep red and the oil separates.
Add the cooked dal, mash a ladleful, and simmer on low heat for 35 minutes with hot water as needed until thick and dark.

For the dhungar, rest a lit charcoal in a bowl on the dal, drizzle 1 tsp ghee over the coal, cover 2-3 minutes for that trademark smoke, then remove the coal and stir in 6 tbsp butter and 1.5 tsp crushed kasuri methi.
Finish with a tadka of the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and a little garlic sizzled golden, poured over the smoky dal with the remaining salt stirred through.
tips: The dhungar coal-smoking is what gives this style its trademark dhaba aroma, so don't skip it.
It is meant to be lavishly buttery, but you can trim the butter and still get a great smoky dal.
A last knob of butter melting on top as you serve is the classic highway-dhaba flourish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve glossy and smoky with a big knob of butter, tandoori roti or naan, and a plate of raw onion, green chilli and lemon like a real dhaba dinner.

variations.name: Malwai Rustic Dal Makhani
variations.description: The plain-spoken, cream-free version of the cotton-belt Malwa countryside, cooked lean with mustard oil, extra garlic and a good hit of red chilli. It is a working farmer's dal, hearty and direct, relying on ghee and long cooking rather than dairy for its body.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: pungent wood-pressed mustard oil gives this rustic country dal its earthy backbone

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a hearty garlic-chilli tadka in ghee replaces the cream in this lean farm-style dal

steps: Soak 1 cup urad and 0.25 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 4 cups water for 7 whistles until soft and creamy.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, cool slightly, then crackle 1 tsp cumin and fry 2 tbsp crushed garlic until pale gold.
Add 2 chopped onions and 2 chopped green chillies and cook 7 minutes to deep golden, then add 1 cup chopped tomato, 2 tsp red chilli and 1.5 tsp coriander powder and cook 8 minutes until thick.
Tip in the cooked dal, mash well for body, and simmer on low heat for 40 minutes with splashes of hot water until dark and thick.
Season with the remaining salt and simmer 5 minutes more so the flavours settle.
For the tadka, heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and fry the remaining 1 tbsp crushed garlic to golden, then pour it over the dal just before serving.
tips: Heat mustard oil to smoking and cool it slightly before cooking, to tame its raw sharpness.
This is a deliberately lean, cream-free dal, so let the long simmer and mash build the body instead.
Extra garlic and red chilli define the rustic Malwa character, so be generous with both.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thick tandoori or hand-slapped roti and raw onion, the way it is eaten in the fields; a dollop of ghee melting on top is the only garnish it needs.

variations.name: Doaba Yogurt Dal Makhani
variations.description: A Jalandhar-belt home version from the Doaba region where whisked yogurt replaces cream for a lighter, gently tangy richness, brightened with ginger juliennes. Comforting and slightly sour, it is the kind of dal made in NRI-heartland kitchens for an everyday feast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: builds the onion-tomato base before the yogurt is folded in

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a ginger-and-cumin tadka in ghee finishes this lighter, tangy Doaba dal

steps: Soak 1 cup urad and 0.25 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 4 cups water for 7 whistles until soft.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, fry 1 large chopped onion 6 minutes to golden, then add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 2 minutes.
Add 0.75 cup chopped tomato, 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli and 1 tsp garam masala, and cook 7 minutes until the oil separates.
Lower the heat and stir in 0.5 cup whisked yogurt a spoon at a time, stirring constantly so it doesn't split, and cook 3 minutes until glossy.
Add the cooked dal, mash a portion, and simmer on low heat for 25 minutes with hot water as needed until thick and lightly tangy, then add the remaining salt.
For the tadka, heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin and fry the ginger juliennes until golden, and pour it over the dal before serving.
tips: Whisk the yogurt smooth and add it on low heat while stirring, or it will curdle into the dal.
The yogurt keeps this version lighter than a cream-laden dal while still tasting rich.
Top with extra fresh ginger juliennes just before serving for a bright, aromatic lift.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with laccha paratha or plain rice and a side of mango pickle; the gentle tang of the yogurt makes it especially good on a hot day.

variations.name: Classic Chilli Paneer
variations.description: This Classic Chilli Paneer is an Indo-Chinese favourite of crisp-fried paneer cubes tossed with peppers and onions in a glossy soy-chilli-garlic sauce. It strikes the beloved balance of crunchy, spicy and umami, served semi-dry as a starter or with fried rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: its high smoke point crisps the paneer beautifully for the stir-fry

steps: Toss the 300 g paneer cubes with 3 tbsp cornflour and a pinch of salt until evenly coated for a crisp exterior.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a wok over medium-high heat and shallow-fry the paneer for 3 to 4 minutes until golden and crisp, then drain.
In 1 tbsp of the same oil, stir-fry the chopped garlic, ginger and 3 green chillies on high heat for 30 seconds until aromatic but not browned.
Add the cubed onion and capsicum and stir-fry on high for 2 minutes so they stay crunchy with a slight char.
Pour in 2 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tbsp green chilli sauce, 1 tbsp ketchup and 0.5 tsp salt, and toss for 1 minute until glossy.
Return the fried paneer, toss for 1 minute so it coats in the sauce, garnish with 3 tbsp spring onion and serve immediately.
tips: Fry the paneer just before tossing so it stays crisp, as it softens quickly once sauced.
Keep the flame high throughout the stir-fry to retain the vegetables' crunch and get a smoky wok flavour.
For a saucy gravy version, add half a cup of water mixed with 1 tsp cornflour and simmer briefly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a starter with toothpicks, or over veg fried rice or hakka noodles for a full Indo-Chinese meal.

variations.name: Gravy Chilli Paneer
variations.description: The saucy restaurant version with a thick, spicy soy-chilli gravy that clings to soft paneer and vegetables. Unlike the dry starter, this one is built to be spooned generously over noodles or fried rice, with a glossy, slurp-worthy sauce.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: a light wood-pressed oil ideal for high-heat wok frying the paneer

steps: Coat the 300 g paneer cubes in 2 tbsp cornflour and shallow-fry in 4 tbsp Anveshan Sunflower Oil for 3 minutes until golden, then drain.
In 1 tbsp of the same oil, stir-fry the finely chopped garlic and ginger on high heat for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the cubed onion and capsicum and toss on high for 2 minutes so they soften slightly but keep some bite.
Pour in 1.5 cups vegetable stock, 2 tbsp soy sauce, 1.5 tbsp red chilli sauce, 1 tsp vinegar and 0.5 tsp salt, and bring to a simmer.
Mix the remaining 2 tbsp cornflour with 4 tbsp cold water, stir it in gradually, and cook for 2 minutes until the gravy turns thick and glossy.
Add the fried paneer, simmer for 2 minutes so it softens in the sauce, garnish with 3 tbsp spring onion and serve hot.
tips: Always mix the cornflour with cold water before adding, or it will form lumps in the hot gravy.
Adjust the stock quantity to control thickness, using less for a coating gravy and more for a soupy one.
A dash of white pepper at the end gives an authentic Indo-Chinese restaurant aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle generously over Hakka noodles or steamed rice and top with extra spring onion greens.

variations.name: Schezwan Chilli Paneer
variations.description: A fiery version tossed in homemade-style Schezwan sauce packed with dry red chillies, garlic and Sichuan-pepper heat. It is bolder and spicier than the classic, with a numbing, garlicky punch that lingers pleasantly.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: withstands the high heat needed to crisp paneer and bloom the chilli paste

steps: Toss the 300 g paneer cubes in 3 tbsp cornflour and shallow-fry in 4 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil for 3 to 4 minutes until crisp and golden, then drain.
In 1 tbsp of the same oil, fry the 4 broken dry red chillies and chopped garlic on high for 30 seconds until they release their aroma.
Add the grated ginger and cubed onion and capsicum and stir-fry on high for 2 minutes to keep them crunchy.
Stir in 3 tbsp Schezwan sauce, 1 tbsp soy sauce and 0.5 tsp salt and toss for 1 minute until the vegetables are coated and glossy.
Return the fried paneer and toss on high heat for 2 minutes so every cube is coated in the fiery sauce.
Garnish with 3 tbsp chopped spring onion, give a final toss off the heat, and serve at once while crisp.
tips: Adjust the Schezwan sauce to your heat tolerance, starting with less and adding more to taste.
Fry the dry red chillies only briefly, as burnt chillies turn acrid and spoil the sauce.
A teaspoon of sugar can be added to balance the intense heat if the sauce feels too sharp.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a spicy starter with a cooling cucumber salad, or over Schezwan fried rice for a bold meal.

variations.name: Air-Fried Chilli Paneer
variations.description: A lighter take where the paneer is air-fried instead of deep-fried, then tossed in the same punchy soy-chilli sauce with a minimal-oil stir-fry. It delivers the crunch and flavour of the classic with far less oil, ideal for a guilt-free treat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: a light coating and finishing drizzle adds a nutty Indo-Chinese aroma

steps: Toss the 300 g paneer cubes with 2 tbsp cornflour, 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and a pinch of salt until evenly coated.
Air-fry the coated paneer at 200 C for 8 to 10 minutes, shaking the basket halfway, until the cubes are golden and crisp.
Heat the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a wok, add the chopped garlic, ginger and 2 green chillies and stir-fry on high for 30 seconds.
Add the cubed onion and capsicum and toss on high heat for 2 minutes so they retain their crunch.
Pour in 2 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tbsp green chilli sauce and 0.5 tsp salt and toss for 1 minute until glossy.
Add the air-fried paneer, toss for 1 minute to coat, finish with 3 tbsp spring onion and serve immediately.
tips: Preheat the air fryer so the paneer crisps evenly rather than drying out slowly.
Do not overcrowd the basket, as the cubes need space around them to turn crisp on all sides.
Toss and serve quickly, since air-fried paneer loses its crunch even faster than deep-fried.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a lighter party starter with a squeeze of lime, or alongside a clear vegetable soup.

variations.name: Classic Matar Paneer
variations.description: This Classic Matar Paneer pairs soft paneer cubes and sweet green peas in a smooth, tangy onion-tomato gravy scented with garam masala. It is a weeknight North Indian staple, quick to build yet rich enough for a Sunday lunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: gives the onion-tomato gravy a homely richness and blooms the whole spices

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle for about 20 seconds until aromatic.
Add the finely chopped onions and saute for 6 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute until the raw smell fades.
Add the pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 6 to 7 minutes until the ghee separates.
Tip in the 1 cup green peas with half a cup of water, cover and simmer for 6 minutes until the peas are tender.
Gently add the 250 g paneer cubes and simmer for 3 minutes on low so they soak up the gravy without breaking.
Crush 1 tsp kasuri methi between your palms, sprinkle it with 0.5 tsp garam masala over the curry, stir once and serve hot.
tips: Use fresh peas when in season for natural sweetness, or blanch frozen peas for 2 minutes to keep them bright green.
Pureeing the tomatoes rather than chopping gives a smoother, restaurant-like body to the gravy.
Soak firm paneer in warm water for 10 minutes before adding so it stays soft in the finished curry.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulkas or jeera rice and a side of sliced onions tossed with lemon and chaat masala.

variations.name: Punjabi Matar Paneer
variations.description: A robust Punjabi rendition with a deeply browned onion-tomato masala, extra ginger-garlic and a generous kasuri methi finish. The gravy is thicker and more full-bodied than the everyday version, built for scooping up with thick rotis.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the onion masala to a deep Punjabi brown and enriches the thick gravy

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadai over medium heat, add 1 bay leaf and 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them sizzle for 20 seconds.
Add the finely chopped onions and fry patiently for 10 to 12 minutes until deep golden brown, the hallmark of a Punjabi bhuna gravy.
Stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the slit green chillies, cook for 1 minute, then add the pureed tomatoes, 1.5 tsp chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt.
Bhuno the masala for 8 minutes on medium heat until it darkens and the ghee pools at the sides, adding a splash of water if it sticks.
Add the 1 cup peas and 1 cup hot water, cover and simmer for 7 minutes until the peas soften and the gravy thickens.
Fold in the 250 g paneer cubes, simmer 3 minutes on low, then finish with 1.5 tsp crushed kasuri methi and 0.75 tsp garam masala.
tips: Do not rush the onion browning, as the depth of a Punjabi gravy comes entirely from that slow caramelisation.
A tablespoon of the gravy blended and returned to the pan thickens it further without any cream.
Toast the kasuri methi lightly on a dry pan before crushing to intensify its aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best with tandoori roti or missi roti and a glass of salted lassi to cut the richness.

variations.name: Restaurant-style Matar Paneer
variations.description: A creamy, mildly sweet dhaba-restaurant version built on a cashew-melon-seed paste for silkiness and a smooth tomato base. The paneer is lightly fried for a soft golden crust and the gravy carries a gentle richness that appeals to every palate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: adds a smooth restaurant-style richness to the creamy cashew gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: rounds the tomato tang with a mellow sweetness typical of restaurant gravies

steps: Boil the 2 onions, 3 tomatoes and 15 cashews together in a cup of water for 8 minutes until soft, then cool and blend to a smooth pale paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan and lightly fry the 250 g paneer cubes for 2 minutes until pale gold, then remove and reserve.
In the same ghee add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and saute for 1 minute, then pour in the blended paste and 1 tsp chilli powder and cook for 8 minutes until it thickens and the ghee separates.
Add 1 cup peas with half a cup of water and 1 tsp salt, cover and simmer for 6 minutes until the peas are tender.
Lower the heat, stir in 3 tbsp cream and 0.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, and simmer 2 minutes so the gravy turns glossy without splitting.
Return the fried paneer, add 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi and 0.5 tsp garam masala, warm through for 2 minutes and serve.
tips: Boiling the base ingredients instead of frying gives the pale, smooth colour typical of restaurant matar paneer.
Always add cream on low heat and stir continuously to keep the gravy from curdling.
Fry the paneer just until pale, as over-frying makes it rubbery in the gravy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or laccha paratha and a saffron-scented pulao for a festive spread.

variations.name: No-Onion-No-Garlic Matar Paneer
variations.description: A satvik matar paneer that skips onion and garlic entirely, drawing its savoury depth from a ripe tomato base, asafoetida and freshly ground spices. Light yet flavourful, it fits fasting days and Jain kitchens without compromising on comfort.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the cumin and hing that build flavour in place of onion and garlic

steps: Blend the 4 tomatoes, 10 cashews and 2 green chillies into a smooth puree to form the base of this onion-free gravy.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them sizzle for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Pour in the tomato-cashew puree with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.75 tsp chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 8 minutes until thick and glossy.
Add the 1 cup peas with half a cup of water, cover and simmer for 6 minutes until the peas turn tender.
Gently fold in the 250 g paneer cubes and simmer for 3 minutes on low so they absorb the tangy gravy.
Finish with 0.5 tsp garam masala, stir once, and rest the curry for 5 minutes before serving so the flavours settle.
tips: Use fully ripe red tomatoes so the gravy has natural sweetness and body without onions.
The cashew paste is essential here, as it lends the creaminess that a browned onion base would otherwise provide.
A pinch of dry ginger powder can be added for extra warmth on a fasting day.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with kuttu or singhare ki puri for vrat, or with plain steamed rice for an everyday satvik meal.

variations.name: Classic Palak Paneer
variations.description: This Classic Palak Paneer is a North Indian favourite where soft paneer cubes rest in a velvety, deep-green spinach gravy. Blanching the spinach briefly keeps the colour vivid and the flavour fresh rather than bitter, while a ghee tempering of cumin, garlic and ginger lends warmth and depth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: carries the cumin and garlic tempering that flavours the whole gravy

steps: Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil, drop in the 400 g spinach for 2 minutes until just wilted and bright green, then plunge it into cold water to lock the colour.
Drain the spinach well and blend it with the 2 green chillies into a smooth, thick puree, adding only a splash of water so the gravy stays concentrated.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them splutter for about 20 seconds until fragrant.

Add the chopped garlic, ginger and onion and saute for 5 to 6 minutes until the onion turns soft and pale gold, then stir in the chopped tomato, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt and cook until the tomato collapses, about 4 minutes.
Pour in the spinach puree, lower the heat and simmer gently for 6 to 7 minutes so it loses its raw smell, stirring often to stop it catching.
Fold in 250 g paneer cubes, 0.5 tsp garam masala and 2 tbsp cream, simmer for 3 minutes on low until the paneer is heated through, and serve hot.
tips: Do not overcook the blanched spinach or overheat the finished puree, as prolonged heat is what dulls the green to olive.
If your paneer is firm, soak the cubes in warm water for 10 minutes before adding so they stay soft and spongy in the gravy.
For a smoother restaurant finish, blend the cooked onion-tomato masala before adding the spinach puree.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a shallow bowl with a swirl of cream and a cube of butter on top, alongside hot butter naan or jeera rice and a wedge of lemon.

variations.name: Dhaba-style Palak Paneer
variations.description: A rustic highway-dhaba take with a coarser, chunkier spinach texture and a bold, smoky finish from a mustard-oil tempering. The paneer is lightly pan-seared first for a golden edge, and a final charcoal-smoke dhungar gives it that unmistakable roadside aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: gives the gravy its pungent, smoky dhaba character and sears the paneer

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pan until it just smokes, then sear the 250 g paneer cubes for about 2 minutes until they catch golden edges, and set them aside.
Boil the 400 g spinach for 2 minutes, refresh in cold water, then chop it coarsely by hand instead of blending so the gravy stays rustic and textured.
In the same pan add the remaining 2 tbsp mustard oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then fry the chopped garlic, ginger and 3 green chillies until aromatic, about 1 minute.

Add the finely chopped onions and cook for 7 to 8 minutes until deep brown, then add the chopped tomatoes, 1 tsp chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and fry until the oil separates, about 5 minutes.
Stir in the chopped spinach with a splash of water and simmer uncovered for 8 minutes so it thickens and turns glossy, then crush in 1 tsp kasuri methi.
Fold in the seared paneer, place a small bowl in the centre with a live charcoal ember, drizzle a few drops of mustard oil over it, cover for 2 minutes to smoke, then serve.
tips: Always heat mustard oil to smoking point first and let it cool a touch, as this mellows its raw sharpness into a rounded pungency.
Skip the charcoal step if you like, but a pinch of smoked salt at the end gives a comparable roadside aroma.
Chopping rather than blending the spinach is what separates dhaba texture from smooth restaurant gravy, so resist the mixer.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with laccha paratha or tandoori roti, a raw onion-and-lemon salad, and a dollop of white butter melting on top.

variations.name: Restaurant-style Palak Paneer
variations.description: The silky, creamy version you get at restaurants, where the spinach is blanched with a pinch of sugar to set the colour and the gravy is enriched with cashew paste and cream. It is mild, luxurious and a uniform emerald green, ideal for guests who find the classic too sharp.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: gives the creamy gravy a rich restaurant-style aroma and gloss

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a pinch balances the spinach and deepens the colour without refined sugar

steps: Soak the 12 cashews in warm water for 15 minutes, then blend to a smooth paste and keep aside for enriching the gravy later.
Blanch the 400 g spinach for 2 minutes with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder in the water, refresh in ice water, and blend with the 2 green chillies to a silky puree.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat and saute the chopped garlic, ginger and onion for 6 minutes until soft but not browned, keeping the colour pale for a green gravy.
Cool the onion mixture slightly, blend it smooth, return it to the pan, add 0.5 tsp cumin powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 2 minutes.
Pour in the spinach puree and simmer gently for 5 minutes on low, then stir in the cashew paste and 3 tbsp cream and cook another 3 minutes until glossy and thick.
Slide in the 250 g paneer cubes, sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala, simmer 2 minutes on low so the paneer stays soft, and finish with a cream swirl.
tips: Keeping the onions pale and never browning them is the secret to the bright uniform green restaurants achieve.
Add the cashew paste and cream only on low heat, since high heat can make the gravy grainy or split.
For a make-ahead party dish, prepare the spinach and cashew bases separately and combine just before serving to protect the colour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a copper handi with garlic naan, a saffron pulao and a cooling boondi raita for a restaurant-thali feel.

variations.name: Jain Palak Paneer
variations.description: A satvik version made entirely without onion, garlic or ginger, relying instead on green chilli, asafoetida and a tomato-cashew base for body. It proves how fragrant palak paneer can be even under Jain restrictions, staying bright, mild and comforting.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the asafoetida and cumin that replace onion-garlic in this satvik gravy

steps: Blanch the 400 g spinach for 2 minutes, refresh in cold water and blend with the 3 green chillies to a smooth puree, keeping it thick.
Soak the 10 cashews for 15 minutes and blend with the 2 tomatoes into a smooth tomato-cashew paste for a satvik gravy base.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them sizzle for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Pour in the tomato-cashew paste along with 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 6 to 7 minutes until the ghee separates at the edges.
Add the spinach puree and simmer gently on low for 6 minutes so the raw taste cooks off, stirring frequently to prevent scorching.
Fold in the 250 g paneer cubes, 0.5 tsp garam masala and 2 tbsp cream, warm through for 2 minutes on low, and serve.
tips: Asafoetida bloomed in hot ghee delivers the savoury depth that onion and garlic normally provide, so do not skip it.
Use ripe red tomatoes, as their natural sweetness balances the greens without needing any sugar.
This gravy thickens as it sits, so loosen it with a splash of hot water when reheating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with phulka or plain jeera rice and a side of sabudana papad for a light satvik meal.

variations.name: Classic Paneer Bhurji
variations.description: This Classic Paneer Bhurji is crumbled paneer scrambled with onion, tomato and everyday spices into a quick, protein-packed dish. It comes together in under twenty minutes and is equally at home in a breakfast wrap or as a dry side with rotis.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the cumin and keeps the scramble moist and fragrant

steps: Grate or crumble the 300 g paneer coarsely by hand and keep it aside so it stays fluffy and does not clump.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them splutter for about 20 seconds.
Add the grated ginger, 2 green chillies and chopped onions and saute for 4 minutes until the onion softens and turns pale gold.
Stir in the chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp salt, and cook for 4 minutes until the tomato turns mushy.
Add the crumbled paneer and toss gently for 3 minutes on medium heat so it coats in the masala but stays soft and moist.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala and 2 tbsp chopped coriander, fold through, and serve immediately while hot.
tips: Do not cook the paneer for more than 3 to 4 minutes, as prolonged heat dries it out and makes it chewy.
Crumble the paneer by hand rather than grating too fine for a pleasant scramble-like texture.
A squeeze of lemon at the end lifts the whole dish if your tomatoes are not tangy enough.
variations.servingSuggestion: Roll it into a hot paratha wrap with sliced onions, or serve alongside pav and butter for a quick meal.

variations.name: Mumbai Tawa Paneer Bhurji
variations.description: The buttery, spicy paneer bhurji cooked on a sizzling tawa at Mumbai street stalls, loaded with pav bhaji masala and finished with lemon and coriander. It is scooped up with soft buttered pav for a satisfying street-style plate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: gives the tawa bhurji its rich buttery street-stall flavour

steps: Crumble the 300 g paneer coarsely and finely chop the onion, tomato and capsicum so they cook quickly on the tawa.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on a flat tawa over medium-high heat, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and saute for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the chopped onion and capsicum and cook for 4 minutes until softened, mashing lightly with the spatula as they cook.
Add the chopped tomatoes, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp pav bhaji masala and 0.75 tsp salt, and cook for 5 minutes until pulpy.
Mix in the crumbled paneer and stir-fry on the hot tawa for 3 minutes, mashing gently so it soaks up the buttery masala.
Finish with 1 tbsp lemon juice and 3 tbsp chopped coriander, give it a final toss, and serve sizzling.
tips: Keep the tawa hot and cook fast, as the street-style char and aroma come from high-heat cooking.
Add an extra spoon of ghee at the end for that unmistakable Mumbai stall richness.
Mash the vegetables lightly for a softer, bhaji-like texture that clings to the paneer.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with ghee-toasted pav, a mound of chopped onion and an extra lemon wedge on the side.

variations.name: Egg-Free Anda-style Paneer Bhurji
variations.description: A vegetarian stand-in for anda bhurji that mimics its soft, saucy scramble using paneer, a touch of besan for bind and a hit of kala namak for that eggy aroma. It is a high-protein twist that fits perfectly into wraps and toasts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a neutral wood-pressed oil that keeps the scramble light and street-style

steps: Crumble the 300 g paneer finely and mix in 0.5 tsp black salt and 0.5 tsp turmeric so it takes on a soft yellow, eggy look.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan over medium heat, add 1 tbsp besan and roast it for 1 minute until nutty and pale gold.
Add the chopped onions and 2 green chillies and saute for 4 minutes until the onion turns translucent and soft.
Stir in the chopped tomatoes, 0.75 tsp chilli powder, 0.5 tsp cumin powder and 0.5 tsp regular salt, and cook for 4 minutes until the mixture thickens.
Add the seasoned crumbled paneer and stir-fry gently for 3 minutes so the besan binds it into a soft, saucy scramble.
Garnish with 2 tbsp coriander, adjust the black salt to taste for that anda-bhurji aroma, and serve hot.
tips: Kala namak is the key to the eggy flavour, so add it in two stages and taste as you go.
Roasting the besan first removes its raw smell and gives the scramble a subtle richness.
Keep the mixture slightly moist rather than dry so it resembles a soft anda bhurji.
variations.servingSuggestion: Stuff into a toasted bun with ketchup and onions, or serve with buttered toast for a hearty breakfast.

variations.name: South Indian Paneer Bhurji
variations.description: A southern spin on paneer bhurji tempered with mustard seeds, curry leaves and urad dal, brightened with coconut and a mild chilli-ginger kick. It is aromatic and slightly nutty, a lovely change from the north Indian version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: lends the authentic South Indian aroma to the mustard-curry leaf tempering

steps: Crumble the 300 g paneer coarsely and keep it ready near the stove for quick tossing.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan over medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop, then add 1 tsp urad dal and fry until golden.
Toss in the 12 curry leaves, 2 green chillies and grated ginger and saute for 30 seconds until intensely fragrant.
Add the chopped onions and cook for 4 minutes until soft, then add the chopped tomato, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt and cook for 3 minutes.
Fold in the crumbled paneer and stir-fry gently for 3 minutes so it warms through and absorbs the tempered flavours.
Mix in 3 tbsp grated coconut, toss for 1 minute off the heat, and serve while aromatic.
tips: Let the mustard seeds pop fully before adding the dal, as this releases their true flavour.
Add the coconut at the very end so it stays fresh and does not brown or turn dry.
Fresh curry leaves make a big difference here, so use them in preference to dried.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot dosas, appams or steamed rice and a drizzle of coconut oil on top.

variations.name: Classic Paneer Do Pyaza
variations.description: This Classic Paneer Do Pyaza celebrates onions used two ways, both as a browned gravy base and as chunky sauteed petals folded in at the end. The result is a semi-dry curry where sweet, caramelised onion chunks and soft paneer share centre stage in a fragrant, lightly spiced masala.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: sautes the onion petals to a sweet gold and builds the masala base

steps: Cut 2 onions into petals by quartering and separating the layers, and finely chop the other 2 onions for the gravy base.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over medium-high heat and saute the onion petals and cubed capsicum for 3 minutes until they char lightly at the edges, then remove and reserve.
In the same kadai add the remaining 2 tbsp ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then fry the finely chopped onions for 6 minutes until golden.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 6 minutes until pulpy.
Fold in the 300 g paneer cubes with a quarter cup of water and simmer for 3 minutes so they absorb the masala.
Return the charred onion petals and capsicum, crush in 1 tsp kasuri methi and 0.5 tsp garam masala, toss for 2 minutes and serve semi-dry.
tips: Sear the onion petals on high heat briefly so they stay crunchy-sweet rather than turning fully soft.
Keep the dish semi-dry by using minimal water, as do pyaza is not meant to be a runny gravy.
Reserve a few charred petals to scatter on top for texture and visual appeal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tandoori roti or laccha paratha and a wedge of lemon to brighten the sweet onions.

variations.name: Mughlai Paneer Do Pyaza
variations.description: A richer Mughlai take where a yogurt and fried-onion gravy cradles the paneer and onion petals, perfumed with whole garam spices. It is creamier and more aromatic than the everyday version, echoing royal kitchen sensibilities.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the birista and infuses the whole spices for a Mughlai depth

steps: Slice 2 onions thin and fry in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee for 8 minutes until golden and crisp, then blend into a smooth birista paste with the 12 soaked cashews.
Cut the remaining 2 onions into petals and saute in 1 tbsp ghee for 3 minutes until lightly charred, then set aside.
Heat the last 1 tbsp ghee, add 3 cardamom pods, 1 inch cinnamon and 3 cloves and let them infuse for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and saute for 1 minute, then add the birista-cashew paste, 1 tsp chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 5 minutes.
Lower the heat and whisk in 0.5 cup yogurt gradually so it does not split, then simmer for 4 minutes until thick and glossy.
Fold in the 300 g paneer cubes and the charred onion petals, add 0.5 tsp garam masala, simmer 3 minutes and serve.
tips: Add the yogurt off the boil and stir continuously to keep the Mughlai gravy from curdling.
Fry the birista onions to an even gold, since burnt onions turn the gravy bitter.
Rest the curry for 10 minutes before serving so the whole spices perfume the paneer.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sheermal or a mild pulao and a sprinkle of fried onions on top for a regal touch.

variations.name: Kadai Paneer Do Pyaza
variations.description: A dry, spicy kadai-style version with a coarse coriander-chilli masala and chunky peppers alongside the double onions. It is more assertive and aromatic than the classic, meant to be scooped up dry with hot rotis.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a robust wood-pressed oil that suits the high-heat kadai stir-fry

steps: Dry-roast 2 tbsp coriander seeds and 4 dry red chillies for 2 minutes until fragrant, then coarsely pound into a rustic kadai masala.
Cut 2 onions into petals and 1 capsicum into chunks, and finely chop the other 2 onions for the base.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai over high heat and stir-fry the onion petals and capsicum chunks for 3 minutes until charred, then reserve.

In the same oil saute the chopped onions for 5 minutes until golden, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute, then add the chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and half the pounded masala.
Cook for 6 minutes until the tomatoes soften, then add the 300 g paneer cubes and toss on medium heat for 3 minutes.
Return the charred petals and capsicum, add the remaining kadai masala, 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi and 0.5 tsp garam masala, toss 2 minutes and serve dry.
tips: Pound the roasted spices coarse, as the rustic texture is the heart of a kadai masala.
Keep the flame high while charring the petals and capsicum for that smoky kadai edge.
Serve immediately, since this dry dish tastes best hot off the kadai before the paneer firms up.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a mini kadai with tawa roti and a side of onion rings dusted with chaat masala.

variations.name: Hyderabadi Achari Paneer Do Pyaza
variations.description: A tangy Hyderabadi-inspired version tempered with pickling spices and finished with a mustard-oil punch and a squeeze of lime. The pickle-spiced double onions give a zesty, appetising profile quite distinct from the mild classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: carries the achari pickling spices and gives the dish its tangy pungency

steps: Cut 2 onions into petals and finely chop the remaining 2 onions, keeping them separate for the two textures.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, lower the heat, then add 1 tsp fennel, 0.5 tsp nigella, 0.5 tsp mustard and 0.25 tsp fenugreek seeds and crackle for 20 seconds.
Add the onion petals and stir-fry for 2 minutes until they soften slightly with the pickling spices, then remove and reserve.

In the same oil fry the chopped onions for 5 minutes until golden, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute, then add the chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp chilli powder and 1 tsp salt and cook 6 minutes.
Lower the heat and whisk in 3 tbsp yogurt gradually so it does not split, then add the 300 g paneer cubes and simmer 3 minutes.
Return the spiced onion petals, toss for 2 minutes, finish with 1 tbsp lemon juice, and serve with the achari aroma fresh.
tips: Toast the pickling spices only briefly, as fenugreek in particular turns bitter if it browns.
Whisk the yogurt smooth and add off the heat so the achari gravy stays creamy and does not curdle.
This curry deepens in flavour as it rests, so it makes an excellent make-ahead dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with warm paratha or plain rice and a spoon of mango pickle to play up the achari notes.

variations.name: Classic Paneer Lababdar
variations.description: This Classic Paneer Lababdar is a rich Punjabi restaurant curry where paneer, both cubed and grated, swims in a buttery tomato-cashew gravy. The grated paneer melts into the sauce for a luscious body, while the smooth, mildly tangy gravy is finished with cream and kasuri methi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: builds the buttery base and rounds off the tangy tomato gravy

steps: Boil the 2 onions, 4 tomatoes and 15 cashews in a cup of water for 8 minutes until soft, then cool and blend to a smooth puree.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with 1 tbsp butter in a kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them splutter for 20 seconds.
Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and saute for 1 minute, then pour in the blended puree along with 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt.
Cook the gravy on medium heat for 10 minutes, stirring often, until it thickens and the ghee separates at the edges.
Cut 200 g of the paneer into cubes and grate the remaining 100 g, then add both with half a cup of water and simmer for 4 minutes.
Stir in 3 tbsp cream, 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi and 0.5 tsp garam masala on low heat, simmer 2 minutes, and serve.
tips: The grated paneer is what gives lababdar its characteristic thick, clinging body, so do not skip it.
Use ripe red tomatoes and Kashmiri chilli for a naturally vibrant colour without artificial dye.
Loosen the gravy with warm water when reheating, as the grated paneer thickens it further on standing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or laccha paratha and a swirl of cream with a few grated paneer flecks on top.

variations.name: Dhaba-style Paneer Lababdar
variations.description: A bolder, spicier dhaba rendition with a browned onion masala, whole spices and a mustard-oil base for punch. It trades some of the creaminess for a robust, fiery flavour that pairs perfectly with thick tandoori rotis.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: gives the dhaba gravy its bold, pungent backbone

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, then lower the heat, add 1 bay leaf, 1 black cardamom and 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle for 20 seconds.
Add the finely chopped onions and fry for 9 to 10 minutes until deep golden brown for a rich dhaba base.
Stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, cook for 1 minute, then add the pureed tomatoes blended with the 10 cashews, 1.5 tsp chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt.
Bhuno the masala for 10 minutes on medium heat until it darkens and the oil pools at the sides, adding a splash of water if it sticks.
Cube 200 g paneer and grate 100 g, add both with three-quarters of a cup of water, and simmer for 5 minutes.
Crush in 1 tsp kasuri methi and 0.75 tsp garam masala, simmer 2 minutes, and serve piping hot.
tips: Brown the onions patiently, as their caramelisation gives the deep colour and flavour of a true dhaba gravy.
Heat mustard oil to smoking first and let it cool slightly to mellow its sharp raw taste.
For extra dhaba smokiness, finish with a quick charcoal dhungar before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best with tandoori roti or missi roti, sliced onions and green chillies on the side.

variations.name: Restaurant Creamy Paneer Lababdar
variations.description: The ultra-smooth, mildly sweet restaurant version with extra cashew and cream and a whisper of honey to balance the tomato. It is pale-red, luxuriously silky and gentle on spice, perfect for guests and children alike.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: adds gloss and richness to the smooth creamy gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: balances the tomato tang with a mellow natural sweetness

steps: Boil the 2 onions, 4 tomatoes and 20 cashews together for 10 minutes until very soft, then blend smooth and strain for a silky gravy.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and saute for 1 minute without letting it brown.
Pour in the strained puree with 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, and simmer on low for 10 minutes until thick and glossy.
Cube 200 g paneer and grate 100 g, add both with half a cup of water and simmer gently for 4 minutes.
Lower the heat and stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Honey and 5 tbsp cream, simmering for 2 minutes until velvety.
Finish with 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi and 0.5 tsp garam masala, stir once, and serve with a cream swirl.
tips: Straining the puree gives the flawless, lump-free smoothness expected of a restaurant gravy.
Keep the flame low after adding cream and honey so the gravy stays silky and never splits.
For a party, make the gravy ahead and add the paneer only when reheating to keep it fresh and soft.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft butter kulcha or a mild saffron pulao for an indulgent restaurant-style meal.

variations.name: Methi Paneer Lababdar
variations.description: A winter-inspired twist folding fresh fenugreek leaves into the classic lababdar gravy for a pleasant, mildly bitter counterpoint to the creamy tomato base. The methi adds aroma and a seasonal freshness that lifts the rich curry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: sautes the fresh methi and enriches the tomato-cashew gravy

steps: Wash the 1 cup fresh methi leaves, sprinkle with a little salt, rest 10 minutes and squeeze out the bitter juices before chopping.
Boil the 2 onions, 4 tomatoes and 12 cashews for 8 minutes until soft, then cool and blend to a smooth puree.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them splutter for 20 seconds, then saute the chopped methi for 3 minutes until wilted and aromatic.
Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute, then pour in the puree with 1.5 tsp chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt.
Cook the gravy for 9 minutes on medium heat until it thickens and the ghee separates, keeping some flecks of methi visible.
Cube 200 g paneer and grate 100 g, add both with half a cup of water, stir in 3 tbsp cream and 0.5 tsp garam masala, simmer 3 minutes and serve.
tips: Salting and squeezing the methi removes excess bitterness while keeping its fragrance.
In summer, substitute 1 tbsp kasuri methi soaked in warm water when fresh leaves are unavailable.
Balance the mild bitterness with the cream and a pinch of extra chilli for a rounded flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with makki di roti or plain paratha and a dollop of white butter for a winter feast.

variations.name: Classic Paneer Tikka Masala
variations.description: This Classic Paneer Tikka Masala features char-grilled, yogurt-marinated paneer tikka simmered in a spiced onion-tomato gravy. The smoky, tandoori-marinated cubes lend a grilled depth that sets it apart from plain paneer curries, with a rich, tangy sauce clinging to every piece.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: brushes the tikka for a golden grill and enriches the finished gravy

steps: Whisk 0.5 cup yogurt with 0.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1 tsp tandoori masala and 0.5 tsp salt, then marinate the 300 g paneer and capsicum chunks for at least 20 minutes.
Thread the paneer and capsicum onto skewers and grill on a hot tawa brushed with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee for 6 minutes, turning until charred at the edges, then set aside.
Boil the 2 onions, 3 tomatoes and 12 cashews in a cup of water for 8 minutes, cool and blend to a smooth puree.
Heat the remaining 1 tbsp ghee, saute 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then add the puree, 0.5 tsp chilli powder and 0.5 tsp salt and cook 8 minutes until the fat separates.
Lower the heat, stir in 3 tbsp cream and simmer for 2 minutes until glossy, then crush in 1 tsp kasuri methi and 0.5 tsp garam masala.
Fold in the grilled paneer tikka, simmer gently for 3 minutes so the smoky cubes absorb the gravy, and serve hot.
tips: Grill the tikka on high heat for real char, and do not over-marinate beyond an hour or the paneer softens too much.
Reserve a few tikka pieces to place on top at serving for an attractive presentation.
A charcoal dhungar smoke on the finished dish deepens the tandoori aroma if you have no grill.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or laccha paratha, garnished with grilled capsicum and a swirl of cream.

variations.name: Tandoori Smoked Paneer Tikka Masala
variations.description: A deeply smoky version where the tikka gets a double dose of char and the finished curry is infused with charcoal dhungar smoke. Mustard oil in the marinade adds pungency and colour, delivering the authentic tandoor-house flavour at home.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: in the marinade it gives the tikka its authentic tandoori pungency and colour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: enriches the gravy and carries the smoky finish

steps: Roast 1 tbsp besan on a dry pan for 1 minute, then whisk it into 0.5 cup hung curd with 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil, 0.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 1 tsp chilli powder and 0.5 tsp salt.
Marinate the 300 g paneer cubes in this mixture for 30 minutes, then grill on a tawa or over an open flame for 6 minutes until well charred, and set aside.
Heat the remaining 1 tbsp mustard oil and 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, saute 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the finely chopped onions and cook for 6 minutes until golden, then add the pureed tomatoes, 1 tsp chilli powder and 0.5 tsp salt and cook 8 minutes until the oil separates.
Add half a cup of water and simmer the gravy for 4 minutes, then crush in 1 tsp kasuri methi and 0.75 tsp garam masala.
Fold in the grilled tikka, place a charcoal ember in a bowl in the centre, drizzle ghee over it, cover for 2 minutes to smoke, and serve.
tips: Hung curd clings better than regular yogurt, giving a thicker coat and better char on the tikka.
Heat the mustard oil to smoking point before cooling and using it in the marinade to tame its rawness.
The besan in the marinade prevents the yogurt from making the tikka watery on the grill.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tandoori roti and a mint-coriander chutney, with a lemon wedge to cut the smoke.

variations.name: Makhani Paneer Tikka Masala
variations.description: A buttery, mildly sweet makhani-style gravy cradles the grilled tikka here, built on a silky tomato-butter base finished with cream and a touch of honey. It is the indulgent, restaurant-favourite crossover between paneer tikka and paneer makhani.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: grills the tikka and lends the makhani gravy its rich sheen

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: gives the makhani gravy its signature gentle sweetness without refined sugar

steps: Marinate the 300 g paneer cubes in 0.5 cup yogurt with 0.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 0.5 tsp chilli powder and 0.5 tsp salt for 20 minutes.
Grill the marinated paneer on a tawa brushed with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee for 6 minutes until golden and charred, then keep aside.
Boil the 5 tomatoes and 15 cashews for 10 minutes until soft, cool, blend smooth and strain for a silky makhani base.
Heat 2 tbsp butter with the remaining 1 tbsp ghee, saute 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then add the strained puree, 1 tsp chilli powder and 0.5 tsp salt.
Simmer the gravy on low for 10 minutes, stirring often, until it thickens and turns deep red and glossy.
Stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Honey, 4 tbsp cream, 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi and 0.5 tsp garam masala, fold in the grilled tikka, simmer 3 minutes and serve.
tips: Straining the tomato-cashew puree is essential for the ultra-smooth texture of a makhani gravy.
Simmer the gravy low and slow so the tomatoes lose their raw edge and turn naturally sweet.
Add cream and honey only on low heat to keep the gravy from splitting.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with garlic naan or jeera rice, finished with a butter cube and a coriander sprig.

variations.name: Kadai Paneer Tikka Masala
variations.description: A robust kadai-style version with a coarse, freshly pounded coriander-chilli masala and chunky peppers, giving a drier, spicier profile than creamy gravies. The grilled tikka soaks up the aromatic, semi-dry masala for a bold, restaurant-kadai finish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: grills the tikka and carries the freshly pounded kadai masala

steps: Marinate the 300 g paneer in 0.25 cup yogurt with 0.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 0.5 tsp salt for 20 minutes, then grill on a ghee-brushed tawa for 6 minutes until charred.
Dry-roast 2 tbsp coriander seeds and 4 dry red chillies for 2 minutes until fragrant, then coarsely pound them into a rustic kadai masala.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the cubed onions and saute for 5 minutes until the onion softens.
Add the chunky capsicum and chopped tomatoes with half the pounded masala and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 6 minutes until the tomatoes soften but stay chunky.
Stir in the remaining kadai masala, 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi and 0.5 tsp garam masala, cooking for 2 minutes so the aroma blooms.
Fold in the grilled paneer tikka, toss for 3 minutes on medium heat so it coats in the semi-dry masala, and serve hot.
tips: Pound the roasted spices coarsely rather than grinding fine, as the texture defines a kadai masala.
Keep the onion and capsicum chunky for the signature kadai bite and appearance.
This dish is meant to be semi-dry, so avoid adding water and let the tomato provide the moisture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a mini kadai with tawa roti or missi roti and sliced raw onions dusted with chaat masala.

variations.name: Classic Shahi Paneer
variations.description: This Classic Shahi Paneer is a Mughlai-inspired royal curry where paneer bathes in a pale, cashew-cream gravy that is mildly sweet and delicately spiced. The whole spices are bloomed in ghee, the base is kept white by not browning the onions, and a whisper of cardamom lends its signature aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the whole garam spices and gives the royal gravy its silky mouthfeel

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: provides the gentle royal sweetness shahi gravy is known for without refined sugar

steps: Boil the 2 onions and 20 cashews in a cup of water for 8 minutes until soft, then cool and blend to a completely smooth, pale paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over low heat, add 3 cardamom pods, 1 inch cinnamon and 3 cloves and let them infuse for about 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and saute gently for 1 minute without browning, then pour in the onion-cashew paste and 1 tsp salt.
Cook the paste on low for 6 to 7 minutes, stirring constantly so it thickens but stays pale and never catches colour.
Pour in 0.5 cup milk and simmer for 3 minutes to loosen the gravy, then stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 4 tbsp cream on low heat.
Add the 300 g paneer cubes and 0.5 tsp garam masala, simmer gently for 3 minutes so the paneer softens, and serve warm.
tips: Keeping every step on low heat and never browning the onions is what preserves the pale, regal colour.
Strain the blended onion-cashew paste for an ultra-smooth gravy worthy of the name shahi.
If the gravy thickens too much on standing, thin it with warm milk rather than water to keep it creamy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with warm rumali roti or a fragrant saffron pulao, garnished with slivered almonds and a few rose petals.

variations.name: Mughlai Shahi Paneer
variations.description: An opulent Mughlai take enriched with a fried onion (birista) paste, poppy seeds and a hint of saffron and kewra. It is deeper and more aromatic than the classic, echoing the royal kitchens of the Nawabs with its layered, perfumed richness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the birista and carries the saffron for an authentic Mughlai perfume

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk to give the gravy its golden royal hue and aroma

steps: Soak 0.25 tsp Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and soak the 15 cashews and 1 tbsp poppy seeds separately in warm water for 15 minutes.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and fry the thinly sliced 3 onions for 8 to 10 minutes until deep golden and crisp, then drain and blend into a smooth birista paste.
Blend the soaked cashews and poppy seeds into a fine paste with a little water for the enriching base.
In the same ghee saute 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the 4 cardamom pods for 1 minute, then add the birista paste and cook for 3 minutes.
Lower the heat, whisk in 3 tbsp yogurt slowly so it does not split, add the cashew-poppy paste and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 6 minutes until thick.
Stir in the saffron milk, 3 tbsp cream, 0.5 tsp kewra water and 0.5 tsp garam masala, fold in the 300 g paneer, simmer 3 minutes on low and serve.
tips: Whisk the yogurt smooth and add it off the boil to prevent the gravy from curdling.
Fry the onions slowly and evenly, since burnt birista turns the gravy bitter rather than sweet.
A drop of kewra goes a long way, so measure it carefully or the perfume can overpower the dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sheermal or a rich zafrani pulao and a bowl of kachumber for a Nawabi dawat.

variations.name: Restaurant-style Shahi Paneer
variations.description: The bright, creamy, slightly reddish shahi paneer served across Indian restaurants, built on a tomato-cashew base with tandoori-red colour balanced by cream and honey. It is richer and tangier than the pale classic, a crowd-pleaser for parties.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: adds body and gloss to the creamy tomato-cashew restaurant gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: balances the tomato tang with a floral sweetness in place of sugar

steps: Boil the 2 onions, 3 tomatoes and 18 cashews in a cup of water for 8 minutes until soft, then blend to a smooth puree and strain for silkiness.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with 1 tbsp butter, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and saute for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder for colour, then pour in the strained puree and 1 tsp salt and cook for 8 minutes until it thickens and the fat separates.
Lower the heat and stir in 4 tbsp cream and 1 tbsp Anveshan Honey, simmering for 2 minutes until glossy and rich.
Fold in the 300 g paneer cubes and simmer gently for 3 minutes so they warm through without breaking.
Crush 1 tsp kasuri methi over the top with 0.5 tsp garam masala, stir once, and finish with a swirl of cream.
tips: Use Kashmiri chilli powder purely for a vibrant colour without adding sharp heat.
Straining the puree gives the smooth, luxurious body diners expect from restaurant shahi paneer.
Add the honey and cream only after lowering the flame so the gravy stays smooth and does not split.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or tandoori roti and a side of pickled onions for a classic restaurant plate.

variations.name: Achari Shahi Paneer
variations.description: A tangy fusion where royal shahi creaminess meets a pickling-spice tempering of fennel, nigella, mustard and fenugreek. The result is a rich yet zesty gravy with a mustard-oil edge, marrying Mughlai luxury with the punch of Indian achaar.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: gives the achari tempering its characteristic pickle-like pungency

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: finishes the gravy with richness to balance the sharp pickling spices

steps: Boil the 2 onions with 15 cashews for 8 minutes until soft, then blend to a smooth pale paste for the creamy base.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, lower the heat, then add 1 tsp fennel, 0.5 tsp nigella, 0.5 tsp mustard and 0.25 tsp fenugreek seeds and let them crackle for 20 seconds.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and saute for 1 minute, then add the onion-cashew paste, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt and cook for 6 minutes.
Lower the heat fully and whisk in 4 tbsp yogurt gradually so it blends without splitting, then simmer for 4 minutes until thick.
Stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 2 tbsp cream to round off the sharp achari spices with richness.
Fold in the 300 g paneer cubes, simmer gently for 3 minutes, and rest for 5 minutes so the pickling flavours infuse the paneer.
tips: Toast the whole pickling spices only briefly, as fenugreek in particular turns bitter if it darkens.
The finishing ghee and cream are essential to balance the mustard oil, so do not skip them.
This gravy tastes even better the next day once the achari spices have fully mellowed into the paneer.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with plain paratha or steamed rice and a spoon of mango pickle to echo the achari theme.

variations.name: Classic Karnataka Akki Roti
variations.description: A beloved Karnataka breakfast of rice-flour flatbread patted out by hand and roasted on a hot tava until crisp-edged and tender. The dough is studded with onion, green chilli, coriander and cumin, then flattened directly on the pan or a wet cloth. Cooked in ghee until golden freckles appear, it needs nothing more than a smear of butter and chutney.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Drizzled around the edges as the roti cooks, it crisps the base and carries a nutty aroma into the soft crumb

steps: In a wide bowl combine 2 cups rice flour, 1 finely chopped onion, 2 minced green chillies, 3 tbsp chopped coriander, 1 tsp cumin seeds, 3 tbsp grated coconut and 1 tsp salt, rubbing everything together.
Pour in about 1.25 cups hot water a little at a time and mix with a spoon, then knead into a soft, pliable dough once it is cool enough to handle.
Take a lemon-sized ball, place it on a greased sheet of parchment or a damp cloth, and pat it outward with wet fingers into a thin 7-inch round, poking a few holes through it.
Slide the roti off the sheet onto a medium-hot tava, or flip the cloth over onto the pan and peel it away, and drizzle 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee around the edges.
Cover and cook for 2-3 minutes until the underside turns golden with brown spots, then flip and cook the other side uncovered for 2 minutes, drizzling a little more Anveshan Ghee.
Press gently with a spatula until both faces are crisp and freckled, then repeat with the remaining dough, greasing the sheet each time.
tips: Keep your fingers wet while patting, as rice-flour dough is sticky and will tear if it dries out.
Cover the tava while the first side cooks; the trapped steam sets the thin roti so it does not crack when flipped.
Mix the dough with genuinely hot water, which partially cooks the rice flour and makes it far easier to shape.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with fresh coconut chutney and a dab of white butter, or with a spicy ennegai (stuffed brinjal) curry for a fuller meal.

variations.name: Ragi Akki Roti
variations.description: A hearty millet variation from rural Karnataka that blends finger-millet flour into the rice dough for a darker, more nourishing flatbread. The ragi lends earthy body and a satisfying chew while keeping the roti soft. Dotted with onion and dill or coriander, it is a favourite of farm kitchens for its staying power through a long morning.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: The South Indian fat of choice here, it fries the millet roti to a crisp base and complements its earthy flavour

steps: Combine 1.5 cups ragi flour, 0.5 cups rice flour, 1 finely chopped onion, 2 minced green chillies, 3 tbsp chopped dill, 1 tsp cumin, 0.5 cups grated carrot and 1 tsp salt in a bowl.
Add about 1 cup water gradually and knead into a soft, smooth dough that does not stick to your palms, resting it 5 minutes.
Grease a sheet of parchment with a little Anveshan Coconut Oil, place a ball of dough on it, and pat with wet fingers into a thin 7-inch round with a few holes poked through.
Invert the sheet onto a medium-hot tava, peel it away carefully, and drizzle 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil around the edges of the roti.
Cover and cook 3 minutes until the underside is set and speckled, then flip and cook the second side 2-3 minutes with a little more coconut oil, pressing until crisp.
Repeat with the rest of the dough, re-greasing the sheet each time, and stack the cooked rotis under a cloth to keep them soft.
tips: Ragi dough dries faster than plain rice dough, so keep it covered and re-wet your fingers frequently while patting.
Pat the ragi roti a touch thicker than white akki roti, as the millet cracks if rolled too thin.
Grated carrot or bottle gourd adds moisture that keeps the dense millet flatbread from turning dry.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a garlicky groundnut chutney or a spoon of thick curd, both of which cool and balance the earthy ragi.

variations.name: Vegetable-Loaded Akki Roti
variations.description: A colourful, protein-and-fibre-rich version where the plain rice dough is packed with grated carrot, cabbage, dill and roasted sesame. This is how many Bengaluru homes turn akki roti into a complete one-dish breakfast that hides plenty of vegetables. The extra moisture from the veg keeps the flatbread soft well after it cools.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Kneaded into the dough it adds a warm nutty backbone that pairs with the toasted sesame seeds

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasts the vegetable-packed roti to a crisp, golden base on the tava

steps: In a bowl mix 2 cups rice flour, 0.5 cups grated carrot, 0.5 cups shredded cabbage, 1 chopped onion, 2 minced green chillies, 3 tbsp dill, 1 tbsp sesame seeds and 1 tsp salt.
Drizzle in 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, then add about 1 cup hot water gradually and knead into a soft dough; the vegetables will release water, so add the last of the liquid cautiously.
Grease a parchment sheet, place a ball of dough on it, and pat outward with wet fingers into a thin 7-inch round with a few holes poked in the centre.
Flip the sheet onto a medium-hot tava, peel it off, and drizzle 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee around the edges of the roti.
Cover and cook 3 minutes until the base is golden and set, then flip, add a little more Anveshan Ghee, and roast the second side 2-3 minutes until crisp and freckled.
Press with a spatula to cook the vegetable-studded centre through, then repeat with the remaining dough.
tips: Squeeze the grated carrot and cabbage lightly before mixing so the dough does not turn too wet to shape.
Toast the sesame seeds in a dry pan for a minute before adding them; it deepens their nutty aroma.
These stay soft in a lunchbox for hours, making them ideal for packing thanks to the vegetable moisture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling cucumber raita or a coconut-mint chutney; the fresh sides balance the loaded, savoury roti.

variations.name: Stuffed Masala Akki Roti
variations.description: A richer, restaurant-style akki roti where a spiced potato-and-pea filling is sealed inside the rice dough before roasting. The soft outer shell crisps on the tava while the tangy amchur-spiked centre stays hot and fluffy. A more indulgent treatment that turns the humble breakfast bread into a satisfying meal in itself.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Blooms the tempering for the filling and crisps the stuffed roti to a golden shell

steps: Boil 3 potatoes and 0.5 cups peas for 10-12 minutes until soft, drain well, and mash while warm.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium flame, crackle 1 tsp cumin for 30 seconds, add 1 inch grated ginger and 2 minced green chillies, and fry for 1 minute until fragrant.
Fold in the mash with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp amchur, 0.5 tsp salt and 3 tbsp coriander, cook 3 minutes until dry, cool, and roll into 6 balls.
Knead 2 cups rice flour with 0.5 tsp salt and about 1.25 cups hot water into a soft dough, then flatten a portion on a greased sheet, seat a filling ball in the centre, and gather the dough over it.
Pat the stuffed ball gently with wet fingers into a thin 7-inch round, taking care not to let the filling break through, then invert it onto a medium-hot tava.
Drizzle 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee around the edges, cover and cook 3 minutes until golden, then flip, add a little more ghee, and roast until both sides are crisp and speckled.
tips: Cool the potato filling fully before stuffing; a hot filling steams the dough and makes it split while patting.
Keep the dough shell a little thicker than an unstuffed roti so the filling stays sealed on the tava.
Make extra filling and refrigerate it; the stuffed rotis come together in minutes the next morning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of chilled curd and a spoon of tangy tomato-onion chutney, tearing the roti to reveal the spiced centre.

variations.name: Classic Aloo Baingan
variations.description: This Classic Aloo Baingan is a homely dry sabzi of soft potato cubes and silky brinjal cooked together in a light onion-tomato masala. The brinjal melts into the spices while the potato holds its shape, giving a comforting, everyday North Indian side.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the traditional pungent oil that suits brinjal and deepens the dry masala

steps: Cut the 3 potatoes and 300 g brinjal into bite-sized cubes and keep the brinjal in salted water so it does not darken.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just smokes, lower the heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle for 15 seconds.
Add the finely chopped onion and saute for 4 minutes until soft, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until the raw smell fades.
Add the chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 4 minutes until pulpy.
Add the drained potato and brinjal cubes and toss well to coat in the masala for 2 minutes.
Cover and cook on low heat for 12 minutes, stirring gently every few minutes, until both vegetables are fork-tender.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala, stir once and serve hot garnished with fresh coriander.
tips: Keep the cut brinjal in salted water to stop it browning and to draw out any bitterness.
Cook covered on low heat so the vegetables steam soft without needing extra water.
Cut the potato slightly smaller than the brinjal so both finish cooking at the same time.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulkas or ajwain paratha and a side of plain curd for a satisfying home meal.

variations.name: Punjabi Aloo Baingan Masala
variations.description: A robust Punjabi rendition where the potato and brinjal simmer in a deeply bhuna onion-tomato masala enriched with kasuri methi. It is semi-dry and full-bodied, with the brinjal turning almost creamy against the spiced gravy clinging to the potato.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the onion masala to a deep Punjabi brown and enriches the semi-dry gravy

steps: Cube the 3 potatoes and 300 g brinjal and soak the brinjal in salted water while you build the masala.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them sizzle for 20 seconds.
Add the finely chopped onions and fry patiently for 8 minutes until deep golden, then stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the slit green chillies and cook 1 minute.
Add the pureed tomatoes with 1.5 tsp chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and bhuno for 7 minutes until the ghee pools at the edges.
Add the drained potato and brinjal, toss to coat, then add half a cup of hot water, cover and simmer on low for 14 minutes until tender.
Uncover and cook 2 minutes on higher heat to dry the excess moisture into a clinging masala.
Crush 1 tsp kasuri methi over the top, add 0.75 tsp garam masala, stir once and serve.
tips: Brown the onions slowly, as the depth of a Punjabi masala comes from that caramelisation.
Choose the small purple bharta brinjals which turn soft and creamy when cooked.
Mash a couple of brinjal pieces into the masala to naturally thicken the semi-dry gravy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best with thick tandoori roti or missi roti and a glass of salted lassi alongside.

variations.name: Bharwa Aloo Baingan
variations.description: A festive stuffed version where baby brinjals and small potatoes are filled with a roasted spice-and-besan masala, then slow-cooked until tender. The stuffing keeps the flavour locked inside each vegetable for a richer, celebratory take on the humble sabzi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil to slow-fry the stuffed vegetables to a tender finish

steps: Dry-roast the 3 tbsp besan on low heat for 3 minutes until nutty, then mix it with 2 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp fennel powder, 1 tsp chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp amchur and 1 tsp salt to make the dry stuffing.
Parboil the 8 baby potatoes for 6 minutes, cool and make a deep cross-slit in each without cutting through.
Slit the 8 small brinjals into a cross from the base, keeping the stem end intact.
Press the roasted spice-besan stuffing firmly into the slits of both the potatoes and brinjals.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a wide pan over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle for 15 seconds.
Arrange the stuffed vegetables in a single layer, cover and cook on low for 18 minutes, turning gently every 5 minutes so all sides brown evenly.
Sprinkle any leftover stuffing over the top, cook uncovered for 3 minutes and serve hot.
tips: Roast the besan well so the stuffing tastes nutty rather than raw and pasty.
Do not slit the vegetables all the way through, so the stuffing stays packed inside.
Cook on low and turn gently to prevent the stuffing from spilling out into the pan.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot bajra roti or phulkas and a side of plain yogurt for a rustic feast.

variations.name: No-Onion-No-Garlic Aloo Baingan
variations.description: A satvik aloo baingan that leaves out onion and garlic, relying on asafoetida, ginger and ripe tomato for its savoury base. Light and clean, it lets the natural flavours of potato and brinjal come through, ideal for fasting days and Jain kitchens.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil that keeps the satvik sabzi light and blooms the hing

steps: Cube the 3 potatoes and 300 g brinjal and keep the brinjal in salted water to prevent browning.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them sizzle for 15 seconds until fragrant.
Add the grated ginger and chopped green chillies and saute for 30 seconds, then add the chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.75 tsp chilli powder and 1 tsp salt.
Cook the tomato masala for 5 minutes until it turns pulpy and the oil separates at the edges.
Add the drained potato and brinjal cubes and toss well to coat them in the spices.
Cover and cook on low heat for 14 minutes, stirring gently a few times, until both vegetables are soft.
Uncover, cook 2 minutes to dry any moisture, then rest 5 minutes and serve with fresh coriander.
tips: Use ripe red tomatoes for natural tang and body since there is no onion base here.
The asafoetida gives a savoury depth that replaces the missing onion and garlic.
Keep the pieces uniform so they cook evenly under cover without extra water.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice or soft satvik rotis and a bowl of cucumber raita.

variations.name: Classic Aloo Beans
variations.description: The homely North Indian sookhi aloo beans: diced potatoes and finely chopped french beans tossed together with cumin, turmeric and a light onion masala until the beans stay bright green and the potato edges catch a little crust. It is a no-gravy, lunchbox-friendly sabzi that leans on good fat and correct timing rather than heavy spicing.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: Its clean, light body lets the beans keep their fresh green flavour instead of tasting heavy or fried

steps: Peel 2 medium potatoes and cut them into 1 cm cubes; string 300 g french beans and chop them into small 1 cm pieces so they match the potato and cook at the same pace.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sunflower Oil in a heavy kadhai on medium heat until it shimmers, then add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them sizzle and darken a shade, about 30 seconds.
Add 1 finely chopped onion and 2 slit green chillies and saute on medium for 4-5 minutes until the onion turns soft and pale gold at the edges.
Add the potatoes and beans with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp coriander powder, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, and toss for 2 minutes until every piece is coated in the spiced oil.
Cover the kadhai, drop the heat to low and cook for 12-14 minutes, stirring every 4 minutes, until the potatoes are fork-tender and the beans are cooked through but still bright green.
