Uncover, raise the heat to medium-high, sprinkle 0.75 tsp amchur and toss for 2-3 minutes to dry off any moisture and crisp the potato edges. Finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander leaves.
tips: Cut the potato and beans to the same small size; mismatched pieces leave you with mushy potato or raw, squeaky beans.
Cook covered on low without any water - the vegetables steam in their own moisture and stay dry rather than turning into a wet bhaji.
For extra crunch, finish the last 3 minutes uncovered on high so the potato cubes develop golden, slightly crisp faces.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with phulkas and a bowl of dal or curd; a spoon of this dry sabzi also tucks neatly into a paratha roll for a tiffin.

variations.name: Punjabi Dhaba-Style Aloo Beans
variations.description: The roadside dhaba treatment turns aloo beans richer and smokier: a ginger-garlic and tomato masala fried down in ghee, finished with kasuri methi and a pinch of garam masala so the sabzi tastes like it came off a tandoor kitchen's gas ring. The beans stay slightly firm against the soft, masala-slicked potatoes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan A2 Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee gives this dhaba sabzi its rich, roasted aroma and carries the kasuri methi beautifully

steps: Dice 2 medium potatoes into 1.5 cm cubes and chop 300 g french beans into 1.5 cm pieces; finely chop 1 large onion and 2 medium tomatoes and keep them ready by the stove.
Melt 2 tbsp Anveshan A2 Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat until fragrant, then crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds until they smell nutty.
Add the chopped onion and fry for 5-6 minutes until golden brown, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute until the raw smell lifts.

Tip in the tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook on medium for 5 minutes, mashing, until the masala turns glossy and ghee beads at the edges.
Add the potatoes and beans, toss for 2 minutes to coat, then cover and cook on low for 14-16 minutes, stirring twice, until the potatoes are soft and the beans tender.
Crush 1 tsp kasuri methi between your palms and scatter it over the sabzi with 0.5 tsp garam masala, toss on medium heat for 2 minutes, then finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Brown the onion properly to a deep gold before the tomatoes go in - this caramel base is what gives dhaba food its signature depth.
Toast the kasuri methi in your palm before crushing it in; the brief heat wakes up its aroma dramatically.
If the masala catches or dries too fast, splash in 2 tbsp hot water rather than lowering the heat, so the browning continues.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best mopped up with butter-smeared tandoori roti or laccha paratha, with a side of sliced onions, green chilli and a lemon wedge.

variations.name: South Indian Aloo Beans with Coconut
variations.description: A southern reimagining of the dish as a poriyal-style stir-fry: potatoes and beans tempered in coconut oil with mustard seeds, urad dal and curry leaves, then showered with fresh grated coconut. It is lighter and more fragrant than the northern version, with a nutty crunch from the dal and a sweetness from the coconut.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Unrefined coconut oil is the soul of a South Indian stir-fry and echoes the grated coconut finish

steps: Cut 2 medium potatoes into small 1 cm dice and chop 300 g french beans into fine 0.75 cm pieces so both cook quickly and evenly in the stir-fry.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a kadhai on medium; when hot, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and wait until they pop, about 30 seconds.

Add 1 tsp urad dal and 2 dried red chillies torn in half, and fry for 40 seconds until the dal turns golden, then throw in 12 curry leaves and 2 chopped green chillies and let them crackle for 15 seconds.

Add the potatoes and beans with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, toss well, then cover and cook on low heat for 12-14 minutes, stirring twice and sprinkling 2 tbsp water only if the base begins to stick.
When the vegetables are tender and dry, raise the heat to medium and stir uncovered for 2 minutes to evaporate any moisture and lightly crisp the potato.
Switch off the flame, fold in 4 tbsp grated fresh coconut and 2 tbsp chopped coriander, and toss so the warm coconut clings to the vegetables without browning.
tips: Fry the urad dal to a proper golden before the vegetables go in; its toasty crunch is the signature of a good poriyal.
Add the coconut only after the flame is off - cooking it dries out the coconut and dulls its sweetness.
Keep the dice small and uniform so the stir-fry cooks fast on low heat without needing extra water.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside sambar rice or curd rice as part of a South Indian plate; it also pairs beautifully with plain rasam and steamed rice.

variations.name: Jain Aloo Beans (No Onion, No Garlic)
variations.description: A satvik version made entirely without onion and garlic, relying on a hing-cumin tempering and a tang of amchur to build flavour. Ginger and green chilli bring warmth while roasted ground spices give body, proving that a bright, satisfying aloo beans needs no aromatics from the allium family.

ingredients.name: Anveshan A2 Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries the hing and cumin in this onionless sabzi and rounds out the tang of amchur

steps: Dice 2 medium potatoes into 1 cm cubes and chop 300 g french beans into 1 cm pieces so they cook evenly without any onion base to cushion them.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan A2 Ghee in a kadhai on medium, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them sizzle for 20 seconds, then add 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 2 chopped green chillies and fry for 15 seconds until fragrant.
Add the potatoes and beans with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp coriander powder, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, and toss for 2 minutes so the spices coat the vegetables in the hot ghee.
Cover and cook on low heat for 14-16 minutes, stirring every 4 minutes and adding 2 tbsp water only if the base threatens to catch, until the potatoes are soft and the beans tender.
Uncover, raise the heat to medium-high and stir for 2 minutes to dry the sabzi and lightly brown the potato edges.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder and 1 tsp amchur, toss for a minute so the tang coats everything, then finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Add the hing right after the cumin and let it bloom for only a few seconds - overheating turns it bitter and its aroma is what replaces the onion depth.
Amchur and roasted cumin at the end supply the brightness that onion and garlic would otherwise give, so do not skip either.
This sabzi keeps well for a day and its flavour deepens, making it an ideal make-ahead tiffin dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulkas or puris and a cooling bowl of plain curd; a satvik meal of jeera rice and this sabzi needs nothing more.

variations.name: Classic Aloo Chaat
variations.description: This Classic Aloo Chaat is a North Indian street favourite of crisp fried potato cubes tossed hot with tangy chaat masala, red chilli, lime and fresh coriander. Golden and crunchy outside, fluffy within, it is a fast, addictive snack drizzled with sweet tamarind chutney.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: shallow-frying the potato cubes in bilona ghee gives a rich golden crust and aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the tamarind drizzle with a deep natural note

steps: Boil the 5 potatoes until just fork-tender but still firm, peel and cut them into 2 cm cubes.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide pan over medium-high heat and shallow-fry the potato cubes for 8 to 10 minutes, turning until deeply golden and crisp on all sides.
Simmer 2 tbsp tamarind pulp with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and a splash of water for 4 minutes into a thick sweet-sour chutney.

Tip the crisp potatoes into a bowl and add chopped 2 green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 1.5 tsp chaat masala, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp black salt and 0.5 tsp salt.
Squeeze over 2 tbsp lime juice and toss well so every cube is coated in the tangy spice mix.
Drizzle with the tamarind chutney, fold through the coriander, and serve immediately while hot and crisp.
tips: Boil the potatoes only until just tender so they crisp up rather than turning mushy when fried.
Fry in a single layer without crowding the pan so each cube browns evenly and stays crisp.
Toss with the spices and lime only when ready to serve so the potatoes keep their crunch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot in a bowl or paper cone with an extra lime wedge and a sprinkle of chaat masala on top.

variations.name: Dilli Aloo Chaat
variations.description: The Old Delhi style crisps the potatoes on a large tawa in ghee and douses them in both spicy green and dark tamarind chutneys with a heavy hand of tangy masala. It is wetter, punchier and more chutney-forward than the dry classic, the way Chandni Chowk carts serve it.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: tawa-frying the potatoes in ghee mimics the aroma of Chandni Chowk chaat carts

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: gives the dark tamarind chutney its deep sweet-sour Dilli character

steps: Boil the 5 potatoes until just tender, peel and cut into bite-sized cubes.
Spread 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on a hot tawa and fry the potato cubes over medium-high heat for 10 minutes, pressing and turning until crackling crisp and browned.
Blend the soaked 4 dates and 3 tbsp tamarind with 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and simmer 5 minutes into a thick, dark sweet chutney.
Move the crisp potatoes to a bowl and sprinkle over 2 tsp chaat masala, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.75 tsp black salt and 0.5 tsp salt.
Add 4 tbsp green chutney, a generous drizzle of the date-tamarind chutney and 1 tbsp lime juice, and toss until well coated and glossy.
Garnish thickly with coriander and serve immediately while the potatoes are hot under the chutneys.
tips: Press the cubes firmly on the tawa to build the crackling crust that defines Delhi aloo chaat.
Keep both chutneys ready so you can drown the hot potatoes the moment they leave the tawa.
Add extra chaat masala at the end, as this style is meant to taste boldly tangy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a steel plate loaded with extra chutney and coriander, with masala chai alongside.

variations.name: Dahi Aloo Chaat
variations.description: A cooling version where the crisp fried potatoes are topped with chilled sweetened yogurt, tamarind chutney and sev for a creamy, tangy contrast. The soothing curd balances the spice and makes this a refreshing hot-weather chaat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: frying the potatoes in ghee gives a rich base that stands up to the cool yogurt

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens both the yogurt topping and the tamarind chutney

steps: Boil the 5 potatoes until just tender, peel and cut into bite-sized cubes.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium-high heat and shallow-fry the potatoes for 8 to 10 minutes until golden and crisp, then season with 0.5 tsp salt.
Whisk the 2 cups yogurt smooth with 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and a pinch of black salt and chill.
Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder for 4 minutes into a sweet-sour chutney and cool it.
Arrange the crisp potatoes on a plate and spoon the chilled sweetened yogurt generously over the top.
Drizzle with tamarind and green chutney, dust with 1.5 tsp chaat masala, 1 tsp roasted cumin and 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, and finish with sev and coriander.
tips: Let the fried potatoes cool for a minute before adding cold yogurt so the contrast stays sharp.
Whisk the yogurt well and chill it so it drapes smoothly over the crisp cubes.
Add the sev right at the end so it keeps its crunch against the creamy yogurt.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled as a cooling snack, finished with a final dusting of roasted cumin and red chilli powder.

variations.name: Air-Fried Aloo Chaat
variations.description: A lighter take that air-fries the potato cubes with just a light coating of oil, delivering the same crunch with a fraction of the fat. Tossed in bright chaat masala and lime, it is a guilt-free way to enjoy the street classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a light toss in wood-pressed oil helps the cubes crisp in the air fryer with minimal fat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the tamarind drizzle naturally for the lighter chaat

steps: Peel the 5 potatoes and cut into 2 cm cubes, then parboil for 4 minutes until just softened and pat completely dry.
Toss the cubes with 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, 0.5 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp red chilli powder until evenly coated.
Air-fry at 200 C for 18 to 20 minutes, shaking the basket every 6 minutes, until the cubes are deeply golden and crisp.
Simmer 2 tbsp tamarind with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder for 4 minutes into a quick sweet-sour chutney.
Tip the hot cubes into a bowl and toss with chopped green chillies, 1.5 tsp chaat masala, 1 tsp roasted cumin, 0.5 tsp black salt and 2 tbsp lime juice.
Drizzle with the tamarind chutney, fold in coriander, and serve immediately while crisp and hot.
tips: Dry the parboiled cubes thoroughly so they crisp rather than steam in the air fryer.
Do not overcrowd the basket, giving the cubes room so they brown on all sides.
Serve straight from the air fryer, as air-fried potatoes lose their crunch faster than deep-fried.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a lighter tea-time snack with a squeeze of lime and extra coriander scattered over.

variations.name: Classic Aloo Methi
variations.description: This Classic Aloo Methi is a fragrant dry sabzi of golden potato cubes tossed with fresh fenugreek leaves in a simple cumin-and-garlic tempering. The gentle bitterness of the methi balances the soft, starchy potato for a wholesome winter favourite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the cumin and garlic and mellows the slight bitterness of the methi

steps: Clean the 3 cups fenugreek leaves, wash well, chop and sprinkle with a little salt for 10 minutes, then squeeze out the bitter juices.
Peel and dice the 3 potatoes into small even cubes for quick, even cooking.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle for 15 seconds, then add the sliced garlic and green chillies and saute 30 seconds until golden.
Add the potato cubes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp salt and toss to coat.
Cover and cook on low heat for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the potatoes are almost tender.
Add the squeezed methi leaves and stir-fry uncovered on medium heat for 6 minutes until the leaves wilt and the moisture dries off.
Toss on higher heat for a final 2 minutes to lightly crisp the edges of the potato and serve hot.
tips: Salting and squeezing the methi removes excess bitterness while keeping its aroma.
Cook the sabzi uncovered at the end so the methi dries rather than stews.
Use tender young fenugreek leaves and discard thick stems for the best texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulkas and a bowl of dal, or tuck into a paratha roll with pickle.

variations.name: Punjabi Aloo Methi with Onion
variations.description: A heartier Punjabi rendition built on golden fried onions and extra garlic that round out the bitterness of the fenugreek. The potatoes soak up the onion sweetness while the methi stays vibrant, making a rich, dhaba-style dry sabzi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the onions to a sweet golden brown that balances the fenugreek

steps: Chop the 3 cups methi leaves, salt them for 10 minutes and squeeze out the bitter liquid.
Peel and dice the 3 potatoes into small cubes.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them sizzle, then add the sliced onions and fry for 7 minutes until golden brown.
Add the chopped garlic, grated ginger and green chillies and cook 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the potato cubes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, toss well, cover and cook on low for 10 minutes.
Add the squeezed methi and stir-fry uncovered for 6 minutes until the leaves wilt and the mixture turns dry.
Increase the heat for 2 minutes to crisp the potato edges, then serve hot.
tips: Fry the onions to a proper golden brown so their sweetness offsets the methi's bitterness.
Add a splash of water if the potatoes stick before they soften under cover.
Squeeze the methi well so the finished sabzi stays dry and does not turn soggy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tandoori roti or laccha paratha and a dollop of white butter on top.

variations.name: Methi Aloo Paratha Stuffing Sabzi
variations.description: A finely crumbled version where the potato is mashed and folded with chopped methi and warming spices into a dry, textured mix. It doubles beautifully as a paratha stuffing yet is delicious on its own, with the fenugreek perfuming every bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil that keeps the crumbled mix light and blooms the ajwain

steps: Boil the 4 potatoes until fully soft, peel and coarsely mash them, leaving a little texture.
Chop the 2 cups methi leaves finely, salt for 10 minutes and squeeze out the bitter liquid.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp ajwain and let them crackle for 15 seconds.
Add the grated ginger and chopped green chillies and saute for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the squeezed methi and stir-fry for 4 minutes until it wilts and loses its raw smell.
Add the mashed potato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp chilli powder and 0.75 tsp salt and mix thoroughly for 4 minutes so the methi is evenly distributed.
Sprinkle 0.75 tsp amchur, stir for a minute and serve warm or use as a paratha filling.
tips: Cook off all moisture from the methi before mixing in the potato so the stuffing binds well.
Let the mix cool fully before using it as a paratha filling to prevent tearing the dough.
Adjust amchur to taste for the right tangy lift against the earthy fenugreek.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve rolled into hot khapli-atta parathas, or as a dry side with dal and rice.

variations.name: Methi Aloo with Kasuri Methi Twist
variations.description: A satvik version that skips onion and garlic and layers fresh fenugreek with a pinch of dried kasuri methi for a double methi aroma. Asafoetida and ginger carry the savoury base, making it fasting-friendly yet deeply flavourful and dry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the cumin and hing that build savoury depth without onion or garlic

steps: Chop the 3 cups fresh methi, salt for 10 minutes and squeeze out the bitter liquid.
Peel and dice the 3 potatoes into small cubes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them sizzle for 15 seconds.
Add the grated ginger and chopped green chillies and saute for 30 seconds, then add the potato cubes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp salt.
Cover and cook on low for 10 minutes until the potatoes are almost done, stirring once or twice.
Add the squeezed fresh methi and stir-fry uncovered for 5 minutes until wilted and dry.
Crush 1 tsp kasuri methi between your palms, sprinkle over the sabzi, toss for a minute and serve hot.
tips: The dried kasuri methi deepens the fenugreek aroma without adding any bitterness.
Use asafoetida generously to make up for the missing onion and garlic depth.
Cook the potatoes covered first so they soften before the quick-cooking methi goes in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain phulkas and a bowl of curd, or with khichdi for a soothing satvik meal.

variations.name: Classic Aloo Palak
variations.description: This Classic Aloo Palak is a semi-dry sabzi of soft potato cubes simmered with fresh chopped spinach and everyday spices. The greens wilt into a light, garlicky masala that coats the potatoes, giving a nourishing, quick side that suits any weekday meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the cumin and garlic that flavour the wilted spinach

steps: Peel and dice the 3 potatoes into small cubes, and wash and finely chop the 5 cups spinach.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle for 15 seconds, then add the chopped garlic and green chillies and saute 30 seconds.
Add the finely chopped onion and cook for 4 minutes until soft, then add the chopped tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp salt and cook 3 minutes.
Add the potato cubes, toss to coat, then pour in half a cup of water, cover and cook on low for 10 minutes until nearly tender.
Add the chopped spinach and stir well, letting it wilt down into the masala for 5 minutes.
Uncover and cook on medium heat for 3 minutes so the excess moisture dries into a semi-dry sabzi.
Adjust salt, give a final toss and serve hot.
tips: Add the chopped spinach only towards the end so it stays green and does not overcook.
Use small potato cubes so they cook through quickly without extra water.
A squeeze of lemon at the end brightens the earthy spinach flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulkas or jeera rice and a bowl of plain curd on the side.

variations.name: Dhaba-style Aloo Palak
variations.description: A rustic dhaba rendition where the spinach is coarsely pureed into a thicker gravy and the potatoes are lightly fried before simmering. Mustard oil and a smoky tempering give it the bold, roadside character that pairs so well with thick rotis.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: pungent wood-pressed oil that gives the sabzi its bold dhaba character

steps: Blanch the 6 cups spinach with the 2 green chillies for 2 minutes, refresh in cold water and coarsely blend so some texture remains.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just smokes, then shallow-fry the diced 3 potatoes for 5 minutes until golden at the edges and set aside.
In the same oil add 1 tsp cumin seeds, let them crackle, then add the chopped onion and fry for 5 minutes until golden.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the chopped tomatoes with 1 tsp chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and bhuno for 6 minutes until the oil separates.
Return the fried potatoes and add the coarse spinach puree, then simmer uncovered on low for 8 minutes until the potatoes soak up the flavour.
Stir in 0.5 tsp garam masala and cook 2 minutes more to thicken the sabzi.
Finish with a spoon of raw mustard oil for that authentic dhaba pungency and serve hot.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to smoking first to mellow its sharpness before frying.
Frying the potatoes first gives them a firmer bite that holds up in the gravy.
Keep the spinach coarse rather than smooth for the rustic dhaba texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best with thick tandoori roti or makki di roti and a raw onion salad with lemon.

variations.name: Creamy Aloo Palak
variations.description: A smooth restaurant-style take where potatoes rest in a silky pureed spinach gravy softened with cashew and a swirl of cream. Milder and richer than the everyday sabzi, its glossy green gravy makes an inviting centrepiece for guests.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: adds a smooth richness that ties the cashew and cream gravy together

steps: Boil the diced 3 potatoes until just tender, about 10 minutes, and drain.
Blanch the 5 cups spinach for 2 minutes, refresh in cold water and blend with the 2 green chillies and 10 cashews into a smooth puree.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat, add 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, then the finely chopped onion and saute for 5 minutes until soft but pale.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 1 tsp coriander powder and cook 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in the spinach-cashew puree with 1 tsp salt and half a cup of water and simmer on low for 5 minutes.
Add the boiled potatoes and simmer 4 minutes so they absorb the creamy gravy.
Lower the heat fully, swirl in 3 tbsp cream and 0.5 tsp garam masala, warm 2 minutes without boiling and serve glossy and hot.
tips: Keep the onion pale and add cashews so the gravy stays soft green and creamy.
Add the cream on low heat only, stirring gently to keep the gravy from splitting.
Reserve a swirl of cream on top for a restaurant-style presentation.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or jeera rice and a saffron-scented pulao for a special dinner.

variations.name: No-Onion-No-Garlic Aloo Palak
variations.description: A satvik aloo palak that omits onion and garlic, drawing its warmth from cumin, asafoetida and ginger. The potatoes and fresh spinach cook down into a clean, light semi-dry sabzi that fits fasting days and Jain kitchens without losing comfort.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the cumin and hing that build flavour without onion or garlic

steps: Peel and dice the 3 potatoes into small cubes and finely chop the 5 cups spinach.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them sizzle for 15 seconds.

Add the grated ginger and chopped green chillies, saute 30 seconds, then add the chopped tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.75 tsp chilli powder and 0.75 tsp salt and cook 4 minutes.
Add the potato cubes, toss to coat, pour in half a cup of water, cover and cook on low for 10 minutes until nearly tender.
Add the chopped spinach and stir, letting it wilt into the masala for 5 minutes.
Uncover and cook 3 minutes on medium heat to dry the moisture into a semi-dry sabzi.
Rest for 5 minutes off heat so the satvik flavours settle, then serve.
tips: Use ripe tomato for tang since there is no onion base in this satvik version.
Add spinach near the end so it stays green and does not turn mushy.
A pinch of dry ginger powder adds extra warmth on a fasting day.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice or soft satvik rotis and a cooling boondi raita.

variations.name: Classic Aloo Shimla Mirch
variations.description: This Classic Aloo Shimla Mirch is a quick dry stir-fry of golden potato cubes and crunchy capsicum tossed in a simple cumin-and-spice tempering. The capsicum keeps its bite and fresh aroma while the potato turns tender, making a bright, everyday side.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil that keeps the stir-fry light and lets the capsicum shine

steps: Peel and dice the 3 potatoes into small even cubes and cut the 2 capsicums into similar-sized pieces.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle for 15 seconds, then add the slit green chillies.
Add the potato cubes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp salt and toss to coat.
Cover and cook on low heat for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the potatoes are almost tender.
Add the capsicum pieces and stir-fry uncovered on medium-high heat for 4 minutes so they stay crunchy and bright.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp amchur, toss for a minute to coat everything evenly.
Increase the heat for a final minute to lightly crisp the potato edges and serve hot.
tips: Add the capsicum only in the last few minutes so it retains its crunch and colour.
Cook the potatoes covered first, adding a splash of water only if they stick.
Amchur gives a tangy lift that balances the sweetness of the capsicum.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve rolled inside a hot chapati with pickle, or alongside dal and rice for lunch.

variations.name: Besan Coated Aloo Shimla Mirch
variations.description: A dhaba-style dry sabzi where roasted besan coats the potato and capsicum in a spiced, crumbly masala that clings to every piece. The gram flour soaks up the mustard oil and spices, giving a hearty, savoury dryness typical of roadside kitchens.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: pungent wood-pressed oil that gives the dhaba-style masala its earthy kick

steps: Dry-roast the 3 tbsp besan on low heat for 3 minutes until it smells nutty and turns a shade darker, then set aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just smokes, lower the heat and add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.5 tsp fennel seeds and let them crackle for 15 seconds.
Add the diced 3 potatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and toss well.
Cover and cook on low for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the potatoes are almost tender.
Add the diced 2 capsicums and stir-fry uncovered on medium-high for 4 minutes so they stay crisp.
Sprinkle the roasted besan over the vegetables and toss continuously for 3 minutes until it coats everything in a dry, spiced crumble.
Finish with 0.75 tsp amchur, stir once and serve the dhaba-style sabzi hot.
tips: Roast the besan until properly nutty so it never tastes raw or pasty in the sabzi.
Heat the mustard oil to smoking first to soften its sharp pungency.
Toss constantly after adding besan so it clings evenly without clumping.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot ajwain parathas and a spoon of plain yogurt for a rustic lunch.

variations.name: Indo-Chinese Aloo Shimla Mirch
variations.description: A fusion stir-fry where crisp potato fingers and capsicum are tossed high in a garlicky soy-chilli glaze for a sticky, savoury-sweet finish. Quick and punchy with a peppery kick, it turns the humble pairing into a wok-charred street snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: lends a nutty wok aroma that defines the Indo-Chinese stir-fry

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: balances the salty soy and chilli with a clean natural sweetness

steps: Cut the 3 potatoes into thick fingers, parboil for 5 minutes until just tender and pat dry.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a wok on high heat and shallow-fry the potato fingers for 5 minutes until golden, then set aside.
In the same oil add the chopped garlic, slit green chillies and the white parts of the spring onion and stir-fry for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the diced 2 capsicums and stir-fry on high for 2 minutes so they blister but stay crunchy.
Return the potatoes and add 1 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tbsp chilli sauce, 0.5 tsp black pepper, 1 tsp Anveshan Honey and 0.5 tsp salt, tossing for 2 minutes to coat.
Toss on high for a final minute so the glaze turns sticky and clings to the vegetables.
Garnish with the chopped spring onion greens and serve immediately while hot.
tips: Parboil and dry the potatoes well before frying so they crisp instead of steaming.
Keep the flame high throughout so the vegetables char rather than stew.
Balance the honey and chilli sauce to suit your preferred sweet-heat level.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a starter, or over fried rice or hakka noodles for a fusion meal.

variations.name: No-Onion-No-Garlic Aloo Shimla Mirch
variations.description: A satvik stir-fry that skips onion and garlic and leans on cumin, asafoetida and amchur for its savoury-tangy flavour. The potato and capsicum stay bright and crisp in a clean, light masala suited to fasting days and Jain kitchens.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil that keeps the satvik stir-fry light and blooms the hing

steps: Peel and dice the 3 potatoes into small cubes and cut the 2 capsicums into similar pieces.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them sizzle for 15 seconds.
Add the grated ginger and slit green chillies, saute 30 seconds, then add the potato cubes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp salt.
Cover and cook on low for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the potatoes are almost tender.
Add the capsicum and stir-fry uncovered on medium-high for 4 minutes so it stays crisp.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp amchur and toss for a minute to coat evenly.
Cook a final minute on high to crisp the potato edges and serve hot.
tips: Asafoetida provides the savoury depth that replaces onion and garlic here.
Add capsicum late so it keeps its crunch and vivid colour.
Adjust amchur for the right tangy balance against the sweet capsicum.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain phulkas and curd, or as a dry side with khichdi for a light meal.

variations.name: Classic Kerala Avial
variations.description: The iconic Kerala avial: a medley of vegetables cut into long batons and simmered until just tender, then bound in a coarse coconut paste ground with cumin and green chilli and loosened with thick sour curd. A raw drizzle of coconut oil and a scatter of curry leaves at the end give it its unmistakable perfume.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Drizzled raw at the end, its aroma is the signature finish that defines a true Kerala avial

steps: Cut the ash gourd, 1 raw banana, 2 carrots, 2 drumsticks, 150 g yam and 100 g french beans into uniform batons about 5 cm long and 1 cm thick so they cook evenly and look elegant.

Add the firmer vegetables - yam, drumstick, carrot and beans - to a wide pan with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.25 tsp salt and 0.75 cup water, and simmer covered on medium for 8 minutes, then add the ash gourd and raw banana and cook 6-7 minutes more until all are just tender.
While they cook, coarsely grind 1 cup grated coconut with 1 tsp cumin and 3 green chillies, using a splash of water only if needed, into a thick, gritty paste.
Fold the coconut paste into the cooked vegetables and simmer gently on low for 4-5 minutes so the raw coconut smell disappears and the paste coats every baton.
Whisk 0.75 cup thick sour curd until smooth, lower the heat to the barest flame, and stir the curd in gently off the boil so it warms through without splitting.
Switch off, drizzle 2 tbsp raw Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil over the top and scatter 15 curry leaves; cover for 5 minutes to let the aroma infuse before serving.
tips: Add vegetables in order of firmness so nothing turns mushy - yam and drumstick first, softer ash gourd and banana later.
Add the whisked curd only off the boil on the lowest heat; boiling it will curdle the avial and spoil the texture.
The raw coconut oil and curry leaves must go in at the very end without further cooking - this final aroma is the soul of avial.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as the centrepiece of an Onam sadya with rice and sambar, or alongside adai and steamed rice for an everyday Kerala meal.

variations.name: Tamil Nadu Avial with Tamarind
variations.description: The Tamil version skips curd entirely and draws its sourness from a little tamarind, making a tangier, dairy-free avial that keeps well in warm weather. The coconut paste and vegetables stay the same, but the bright acidity gives it a different, sunnier character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Raw coconut oil drizzled at the finish gives even the tamarind version its Kerala-Tamil border aroma

steps: Cut the ash gourd, 1 raw banana, 2 carrots, 2 drumsticks, 100 g french beans and 150 g snake gourd into 5 cm batons. Soak 1 tbsp tamarind in 0.25 cup warm water and squeeze out a thick extract, discarding the pulp.

Simmer the firmer vegetables - drumstick, carrot and beans - with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.25 tsp salt and 0.75 cup water covered on medium for 8 minutes, then add the ash gourd, banana and snake gourd and cook 6 minutes more until just tender.
Coarsely grind 1 cup grated coconut with 1 tsp cumin and 3 green chillies into a thick, gritty paste using minimal water.
Stir the tamarind extract into the cooked vegetables and simmer for 2 minutes so the sourness spreads evenly.
Fold in the coconut paste and cook on low for 4-5 minutes until the raw coconut smell goes and the avial thickens around the batons.
Switch off, drizzle 2 tbsp raw Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil over the top and scatter 15 curry leaves, then cover for 5 minutes to let the aroma settle in.
tips: Use only a thick tamarind extract, not watery juice, so the avial does not turn thin and soupy.
Because there is no curd, this version keeps longer and travels better in the heat.
Add the tamarind before the coconut so its tang mingles evenly through the vegetables.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or as a tangy side to adai and molagootal for a Tamil-Kerala border meal.

variations.name: Raw Mango Avial
variations.description: A summer avial that borrows its sourness from tangy raw mango instead of curd or tamarind, giving a fruity, bright acidity that cuts through the coconut. The seasonal favourite pairs the mango's tartness with the usual medley of vegetables for a fresh, sunny take on the classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: The raw coconut oil finish keeps this seasonal avial rooted in classic Kerala aroma

steps: Peel and cut 1 raw mango into 5 cm batons along with the ash gourd, 2 carrots, 2 drumsticks, 100 g beans and 1 raw banana, keeping the mango separate as it cooks fast.
Simmer the drumstick, carrot, beans and banana with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.25 tsp salt and 0.75 cup water covered on medium for 8 minutes, then add the ash gourd and cook 5 minutes more.
Add the mango batons and simmer for just 3-4 minutes until they soften but still hold their shape and lend their tartness.
Coarsely grind 1 cup grated coconut with 1 tsp cumin and 3 green chillies into a thick, gritty paste with minimal water.
Fold the coconut paste into the vegetables and mango, and cook on low for 4 minutes until the raw coconut smell goes and everything is coated.
Switch off, drizzle 2 tbsp raw Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil over the top and scatter 15 curry leaves, then cover 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Taste the mango first - if it is very sour, use a little less and skip any other souring; if mild, add an extra piece.
Add the mango late so it keeps its shape and does not dissolve into the gravy.
No curd or tamarind is needed here; the mango alone provides all the tang this avial should have.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and pappadam in summer, or as a bright side to a South Indian thali when raw mangoes are in season.

variations.name: Classic Beans Poriyal
variations.description: The everyday Tamil Nadu beans poriyal: finely chopped french beans steamed just until crisp-tender, tempered in coconut oil with mustard, urad dal and curry leaves, and crowned with fresh grated coconut. It is a light, subtly sweet dry stir-fry that turns up on almost every South Indian lunch plate beside sambar and rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Its gentle sweetness is the defining fat of a Tamil poriyal and lifts the fresh coconut finish

steps: String 400 g french beans and chop them as finely as you can into 0.5 cm pieces - the fine cut is what separates a proper poriyal from a rough stir-fry.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a kadhai on medium; add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop, about 30 seconds, then add 1 tsp urad dal and 1 tsp chana dal and fry until golden.
Add 2 dried red chillies torn in half, 0.25 tsp asafoetida, 12 curry leaves and 2 chopped green chillies, and let them crackle for 15-20 seconds until aromatic.
Add the chopped beans with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, toss well, then sprinkle in 3 tbsp water, cover and steam on low heat for 8-10 minutes until the beans are crisp-tender and bright green.
Uncover, raise the heat to medium and stir for 2-3 minutes to evaporate all the moisture so the poriyal turns completely dry.
Switch off the flame and fold in 5 tbsp grated fresh coconut, tossing until the coconut coats the beans evenly while still raw and fragrant.
tips: Chop the beans very fine - large pieces stay squeaky and refuse to soak up the coconut and tempering.
Use only a few spoons of water to steam; too much water leaves the poriyal soggy and washes out the flavour.
Add the coconut off the heat so it stays sweet and fluffy rather than drying against the hot pan.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a dry side with sambar rice, rasam rice or curd rice; a poriyal like this rounds out a simple South Indian thali perfectly.

variations.name: Andhra Beans Poriyal (Beans Vepudu)
variations.description: Andhra kitchens fry their beans hotter and drier, seasoning them with a garlicky red chilli-cumin podi and skipping the coconut in favour of a deep, roasted char. This beans vepudu is spicier and more robust, the pieces cooked down until they shrink and take on a nutty, almost caramelised edge.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Andhra vepudu needs a robust oil that can take the higher heat of a proper dry-fry without burning

steps: Chop 400 g french beans into small 0.75 cm pieces and crush 6 garlic cloves lightly so they are broken but still chunky for the tempering.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium; add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and let them splutter for 30 seconds.
Add 1 tsp urad dal and the crushed garlic and fry for 1 minute until the garlic turns golden and fragrant, then toss in 12 curry leaves for 10 seconds.
Add the beans with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, toss well, cover and cook on low for 8 minutes, stirring twice, until the beans soften while staying slightly firm.
Uncover, add 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp coriander powder, raise the heat to medium-high and stir-fry uncovered for 5-6 minutes until the beans shrink, dry out and catch a roasted edge.
Sprinkle 1 tbsp roasted cumin-chilli podi over the beans, toss for a final minute so the podi coats every piece, and switch off.
tips: Do not add coconut here - Andhra vepudu is deliberately dry and roasted, and coconut would soften that character.
The final high-heat fry is essential; that is where the beans lose moisture and develop their signature nutty char.
No podi on hand? Dry-roast 1 tsp cumin with 2 red chillies and 1 tsp chana dal and grind coarse for an instant version.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot steamed rice topped with a spoon of ghee and a bowl of pappu charu, or as a fiery dry side to curd rice.

variations.name: Chettinad Beans Poriyal
variations.description: The Chettinad kitchen grinds a fragrant fresh masala of coconut, fennel, roasted gram and red chillies and folds it through the beans at the end, so the poriyal carries the region's signature perfume of fennel and pepper. It is richer and more aromatic than the plain version, with a coarse, moist coconut coat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil grounds the fennel-scented Chettinad masala in authentic regional flavour

steps: Chop 400 g french beans finely into 0.5 cm pieces. In a mixer, pulse 4 tbsp grated coconut with 0.5 tsp fennel seeds, 1 tbsp roasted gram, 2 dried red chillies and 0.5 tsp peppercorns into a coarse, dry masala without adding water.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a kadhai on medium; add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop, then add 1 tsp urad dal and 1 remaining dried red chilli and fry until golden.
Add 12 curry leaves and let them crackle for 10 seconds, then add the chopped beans with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt and toss well.
Sprinkle in 3 tbsp water, cover and steam the beans on low heat for 8-10 minutes until crisp-tender and bright.
Uncover and stir on medium for 2 minutes to dry off any moisture in the pan.
Add the ground coconut-fennel masala and fold it through the beans, cooking on low for 2-3 minutes until the masala turns fragrant and coats every piece, then switch off.
tips: Grind the masala coarse and dry; a wet paste turns the poriyal pasty instead of leaving a fragrant, crumbly coat.
Fennel is the heart of Chettinad flavour, so measure it carefully - too much and the dish tastes medicinal.
Roasted gram thickens and binds the masala; if unavailable, use 1 tbsp of roasted peanuts ground coarse.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with Chettinad-style kuzhambu and steamed rice, or serve as an aromatic dry side to a coconut milk-based vegetable stew.

variations.name: Karnataka Beans Palya with Coconut and Jaggery
variations.description: The Kannadiga palya carries a gentle sweetness: a whisper of jaggery balances the green chilli heat and a generous handful of fresh coconut keeps it soft and moist. Cooked with a simple mustard and urad dal tempering, it is the comforting, faintly sweet beans dish of Bengaluru home kitchens.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: The traditional palya fat, its sweetness marries perfectly with the jaggery and coconut

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A Kannadiga touch - unrefined jaggery rounds the chilli heat without making the palya sweet

steps: Chop 400 g french beans finely into 0.5 cm pieces so they cook quickly and take on the palya seasoning evenly.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a kadhai on medium; add 1 tsp mustard seeds, let them pop, then add 1 tsp urad dal and fry for 40 seconds until golden.
Add 12 curry leaves, 2 chopped green chillies and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them crackle for 15 seconds until fragrant.
Add the beans with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, toss, then sprinkle in 3 tbsp water, cover and steam on low heat for 8-10 minutes until crisp-tender.
Uncover and stir on medium heat for 2 minutes until the palya dries out, then add 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and stir until it melts and coats the beans.
Switch off the flame and fold in 5 tbsp grated fresh coconut, tossing until the coconut clings evenly to the warm beans.
tips: The jaggery should only round the flavour, not sweeten the dish; a single teaspoon is enough for 400 g beans.
Melt the jaggery into the dry beans just before the coconut so it distributes evenly instead of clumping.
For a softer palya common in some homes, steam the beans a couple of minutes longer until fully tender.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot chapatis or as a side to bisi bele bath and a papad; it also goes well with plain rice and a drizzle of ghee.

variations.name: Classic Bhel Puri
variations.description: This Classic Bhel Puri is Mumbai's iconic beach-side chaat of puffed rice tossed with crushed puris, chopped potato, onion and tomato, laced with sweet tamarind and spicy green chutney. It is a riot of textures, at once light, crunchy, tangy and sweet, finished with a shower of fine sev.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: crisping the puffed rice and papdi in wood-pressed oil keeps the bhel crunchy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: gives the tamarind chutney its rounded sweet-sour depth without refined sugar

steps: Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a wide pan and toss the 4 cups puffed rice over low heat for 3 to 4 minutes until crisp and dry, then set aside to cool.
In the same pan, crisp the roasted peanuts in 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil for 2 minutes until fragrant and golden.
Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind pulp with 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and a splash of water for 5 minutes into a thick, glossy sweet-sour chutney and cool it.
In a large bowl, combine the crisp puffed rice, 1 cup crushed papdi, chopped boiled potato, onion and tomato.
Add 3 tbsp of the tamarind chutney, 4 tbsp green chutney, 1 tsp chaat masala, the crisped peanuts and 0.5 tsp salt, and toss lightly but thoroughly.
Fold in most of the sev, garnish the top with the rest along with coriander, and serve immediately while the bhel is at its crunchiest.
tips: Toss the bhel only just before serving, as the chutneys quickly soften the puffed rice.
Crisp the puffed rice fresh in a little oil if it has gone limp, and cool it fully before mixing.
Balance the chutneys to taste, adding more green for heat or more tamarind for tang.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in paper cones or bowls topped with an extra fistful of sev and a lime wedge on the side.

variations.name: Dry Bhel Puri
variations.description: A chutney-light dry bhel, or sukha bhel, that skips the wet chutneys in favour of dry masalas so it stays crackling crisp much longer. Popular as a travel-friendly namkeen, it relies on lime, chaat masala and roasted spices for its punch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: roasting the puffed rice and dals in wood-pressed oil makes a long-lasting crisp dry bhel

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a light dusting rounds the tangy dry masala with subtle sweetness

steps: Roast the 4 cups puffed rice in 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over low heat for 4 minutes until crackling crisp, then cool completely.
In 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, roast the peanuts and 3 tbsp roasted chana dal for 2 minutes until fragrant.
In a dry bowl, combine the crisp puffed rice, roasted peanuts, chana dal and finely chopped onion and green chilli.
Sprinkle over 1.5 tsp chaat masala, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.5 tsp salt and toss thoroughly.
Squeeze in 2 tbsp lime juice just before serving and toss again quickly so the mix stays crisp.
Fold in most of the thin sev, top with the rest and coriander, and serve at once as a crunchy dry snack.
tips: Keep every ingredient bone-dry, as any moisture will turn a dry bhel soggy within minutes.
Add the lime juice at the very last moment, or the puffed rice will lose its snap.
Store the roasted puffed rice airtight and assemble the dry bhel just before eating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a tea-time namkeen in a dry bowl, with extra lime wedges for those who want more zing.

variations.name: Nagpuri Tarri Bhel
variations.description: The Nagpur speciality tops a bed of bhel with a ladle of fiery spiced ragda gravy called tarri, blurring the line between bhel and misal. It is punchy, warm and messy, eaten with a spoon and beloved across central India.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: tempering the fiery tarri gravy in wood-pressed oil carries the Nagpuri chilli heat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a little sweetness tempers the sharp tarri and tamarind chutney

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup soaked white peas with 1 tsp salt and 2.5 cups water for 6 whistles until soft, then lightly mash.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, saute 1 chopped onion and 1 tbsp ginger garlic paste for 4 minutes, add the tomato, 1.5 tbsp goda masala and 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, and cook 3 minutes.
Add the cooked peas with 2 cups water and 0.5 tsp salt and simmer for 10 minutes until a thin, fiery tarri gravy floats a layer of red oil on top.
Simmer 2 tbsp tamarind with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and a splash of water for 4 minutes into a quick chutney.
In each bowl, layer 1 cup puffed rice, a spoon of tamarind chutney and a handful of chopped onion.
Ladle the hot tarri gravy over the bhel, shower generously with thin sev and coriander, and serve at once with a spoon.
tips: Skim and spoon the spicy red oil layer from the tarri over the top for authentic Nagpuri fire.
Assemble in the bowl just before pouring the tarri so the puffed rice keeps some crunch.
Adjust the chilli powder to taste, as traditional tarri is meant to be intensely spicy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft pav or plain bread on the side to mop up the fiery tarri gravy.

variations.name: Sprouts Bhel Puri
variations.description: A wholesome, protein-rich take that loads the bhel with boiled moong and matki sprouts, diced cucumber and pomegranate for freshness and crunch. Lighter on fried elements, it is a guilt-free chaat that keeps all the tangy-spicy appeal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a light toss in wood-pressed oil crisps the puffed rice for the healthy bhel

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: natural sweetness for the tamarind chutney binding the sprouts bhel

steps: Steam or boil the 1.5 cups mixed sprouts with a pinch of salt for 6 to 8 minutes until just tender but still crunchy, then cool.
Toss the 3 cups puffed rice in 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over low heat for 3 minutes until crisp and dry.
Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and a splash of water for 5 minutes into a smooth sweet-sour chutney and cool it.
In a bowl, combine the crisp puffed rice, cooked sprouts, diced cucumber and tomato and half the pomegranate.
Add 3 tbsp of the tamarind chutney, 3 tbsp green chutney, 1 tbsp lime juice, 1 tsp chaat masala and 0.5 tsp salt and toss gently.
Top with the remaining pomegranate, coriander and a little more chutney, and serve immediately while fresh and crisp.
tips: Cook the sprouts only until just tender so they keep a fresh bite and their nutrients.
Add the crunchy vegetables and pomegranate at the end so they stay crisp and juicy.
Skip or minimise the sev to keep this version light, letting the sprouts and veg shine.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a nourishing evening snack or light meal, garnished with extra pomegranate and a lime wedge.

variations.name: Classic Bisi Bele Bath
variations.description: Karnataka's beloved one-pot of rice and toor dal simmered soft with mixed vegetables, tamarind and a freshly roasted bisi bele bath masala. The name means 'hot lentil rice', and it is meant to be eaten piping hot, glossy with ghee and studded with fried cashews. A comforting, tangy-spicy porridge that eats like a full meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Stirred in at the end and used to fry the cashews, giving the bath its signature richness and shine

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed oil for roasting the masala spices without masking their aroma

ingredients.name: Mixed vegetables
ingredients.note: Carrot, beans, potato, peas and capsicum cut into 1-inch pieces

steps: Pressure cook 3/4 cup toor dal with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 2 cups water for 4 whistles until completely soft, then mash smooth. Separately cook 1 cup rice with 2.5 cups water until very soft and slightly mushy.

For the masala, dry-roast 1 tbsp chana dal, 2 tbsp coriander seeds, 5 dry red chillies, 1 inch cinnamon and 3 cloves in 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over low heat until deep golden and fragrant, about 4 minutes, add 3 tbsp grated coconut for the last minute, cool and grind to a fine paste with a splash of water.
Soak the lemon-sized tamarind ball in 1 cup hot water for 10 minutes, then squeeze and strain to extract a thick pulp.

In a large pot, simmer the 2 cups mixed vegetables with 1 cup water and 1 tsp salt over medium heat until fork-tender, about 8 minutes, then pour in the tamarind extract and boil for 3 minutes to cook off the raw sourness.
Stir in the mashed dal, the ground masala paste and 1/2 tsp more salt, and let everything bubble gently for 5 minutes so the flavours marry into a thick, tangy gravy.
Fold the cooked rice into the pot along with 1 cup hot water, mixing well to a loose, flowing porridge consistency; simmer 3 minutes, adjusting water as it thickens on standing.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan, fry 12 cashews until golden and 10 curry leaves until crisp, then pour this sizzling tempering over the bath and serve immediately while steaming hot.
tips: Bisi bele bath thickens dramatically as it cools, so keep it looser than you think while cooking and loosen with hot water before serving.
Roasting the masala on low heat is non-negotiable; scorched spices turn the whole dish bitter and no amount of tamarind will fix it.
A pinch of jaggery balances the tamarind's sharpness beautifully if your batch tastes too sour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in deep bowls topped with extra ghee, crisp boondi or potato chips on the side, and a cooling spoon of plain curd to offset the heat.

variations.name: Iyengar Temple-Style Bisi Bele Bath
variations.description: The prasadam version from Karnataka's Iyengar kitchens, made without onion or garlic and distinguished by a heady masala of marathi moggu, kapok buds and extra dried coconut. It is richer, more aromatic and slightly sweeter than the everyday version, finished with a generous ladle of ghee as befits temple food. Every spoonful carries the perfume of freshly ground spice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Temple bath is famously ghee-laden; it is both fried into the tempering and drizzled generously at the end

ingredients.name: Mixed vegetables
ingredients.note: Traditionally carrot, chow-chow, beans and drumstick cut into 1-inch pieces

ingredients.name: Marathi moggu
ingredients.note: Kapok buds, dry-roasted with the other spices for a musky temple aroma

steps: Pressure cook 1 cup toor dal with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 2.5 cups water for 5 whistles until melting soft, and separately cook 1 cup rice quite soft with 2.5 cups water; mash the dal and keep both warm.

Roast the temple masala in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over low heat: add 1.5 tbsp chana dal, 2 tbsp coriander seeds, 6 byadgi chillies, 2 marathi moggu, 1 tsp poppy seeds and 1 inch cinnamon, toasting until golden and intensely fragrant, then add 3 tbsp dry coconut for the final minute and grind to a smooth paste.
Soak the tamarind ball in 1 cup hot water, extract a thick pulp, and set aside.
Simmer the 2 cups vegetables in 1.5 cups water with 1 tsp salt until soft, about 10 minutes, then add the tamarind extract and boil 4 minutes to remove the raw edge.
Whisk in the mashed dal and the ground masala with 1/2 tsp salt, letting it simmer 6 minutes into a fragrant, thick base while you stir often to prevent catching.
Add the cooked rice with 1.5 cups hot water and mix to a soft, pongal-like consistency, cooking gently for 4 minutes so the grains soak up the masala.
In 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, fry 15 cashews golden and crisp 12 curry leaves, then pour the whole ghee tempering over the bath and serve at once as steaming prasadam.
tips: Marathi moggu is the defining temple aroma; if unavailable, a tiny pinch of grated nutmeg approximates its musky warmth.
Temple bath is deliberately soft and unctuous, so err on the side of more water and more ghee than a home version.
Grind the masala fresh each time rather than using stored powder, as the poppy seeds and coconut turn rancid quickly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a banana leaf with a mound of thick curd, crunchy sandige (fryums) and a wedge of lime, temple-thali style.

variations.name: Millet Bisi Bele Bath
variations.description: A wholesome modern reworking that swaps white rice for foxtail millet, giving the bath a nuttier bite and a lower glycemic load while keeping every bit of the classic tangy-spicy soul. The millet holds its shape better than rice, so the dish stays looser and less gluey. A nourishing one-pot for anyone chasing a healthier plate without sacrificing flavour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed oil keeps this version lighter than ghee while roasting the masala cleanly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Just a spoon stirred in at the end for aroma without weighing down the healthier bath

ingredients.name: Mixed vegetables
ingredients.note: Extra veg-heavy: carrot, beans, pumpkin, peas and capsicum in 1-inch dice

steps: Rinse 1 cup foxtail millet well and pressure cook with 2.5 cups water for 2 whistles until fluffy but tender; separately cook 3/4 cup toor dal with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 2 cups water until soft, then mash.

Dry-roast 1 tbsp chana dal, 2 tbsp coriander seeds, 5 red chillies and 1/4 tsp fenugreek in 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on low heat until golden, add 2 tbsp coconut for the last minute, cool and grind to a paste.
Soak the tamarind ball in 3/4 cup hot water for 10 minutes and squeeze out a thick extract.
Simmer the 2.5 cups vegetables in 1.5 cups water with 1 tsp salt until just tender, about 8 minutes, then stir in the tamarind extract and boil 3 minutes.
Add the mashed dal, the ground masala and 1/2 tsp salt, simmering 5 minutes into a thick, aromatic gravy that clings to a spoon.
Fold in the cooked millet with 1.5 cups hot water, mixing to a loose, spoonable consistency; simmer 3 minutes, remembering millet drinks up more liquid than rice.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, toast 3 tbsp peanuts golden and crisp 10 curry leaves, pour over the bath, finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and serve hot.
tips: Millet keeps absorbing liquid long after cooking, so serve this version promptly or loosen generously with hot water before each round.
Toasted peanuts instead of cashews add protein and a rustic crunch that suits the millet's earthy character.
Do not over-pressure the millet; two whistles keep the grains separate, while more turns them to mush.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a crisp papad, a spoon of thick set curd and a side of cucumber-carrot salad for a balanced, high-fibre meal.

variations.name: Restaurant-Style Bisi Bele Bath
variations.description: The rich darshini-hotel rendition of Bengaluru's fast-food joints, deeper in colour and heavier with masala, cashew paste and a lavish ghee finish. A touch of onion and extra byadgi chilli give it the vivid red hue and full-bodied gravy that diners expect from a plated hotel version. Indulgent, generously spiced and built to impress.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Hotel-style bath is unabashedly ghee-forward, fried into the tempering and drizzled thickly at serving

ingredients.name: Mixed vegetables
ingredients.note: Carrot, beans, potato and green peas in 1-inch pieces

ingredients.name: Byadgi red chillies
ingredients.note: Prized for deep red colour with moderate heat, the secret to hotel-style hue

ingredients.name: Cashews
ingredients.note: Half ground into the masala for body, half fried whole for garnish

steps: Pressure cook 1 cup toor dal with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 2.5 cups water until very soft and mash; cook 1.25 cups rice with 3 cups water until soft and slightly overdone. Keep both warm.

Roast the masala in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over low heat: 2 tbsp chana dal, 3 tbsp coriander seeds, 8 byadgi chillies, 1 inch cinnamon and 4 cloves until glossy and fragrant, add 1/4 cup coconut and 10 cashews for the last minute, cool and grind with water into a smooth, rich paste.
Soak the large tamarind ball in 1.25 cups hot water and extract a thick, dark pulp.

In a wide pot, warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and saute 1 finely chopped medium onion until soft and golden, about 4 minutes, then add the 2 cups vegetables and 1 cup water and cook until tender, roughly 8 minutes.
Pour in the tamarind extract and boil 4 minutes, then stir in the mashed dal, the ground cashew masala and 1 tsp salt, simmering 8 minutes into a thick, deep-red gravy.
Add the cooked rice with 2 cups hot water, stirring to a rich, flowing consistency, and simmer 4 minutes so it takes on the colour and flavour of the masala.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, fry the remaining 10 cashews golden and crisp 12 curry leaves, pour over the bath and serve piping hot with an extra ghee drizzle on top.
tips: Byadgi chillies deliver the restaurant-red colour without fierce heat; do not substitute hot guntur chillies or the balance tips.
Grinding half the cashews into the masala gives the gravy its luxurious body, a trick every darshini kitchen relies on.
This version tastes best made slightly loose, as the extra dal and cashew paste thicken it fast on standing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Plate hotel-style with crisp potato chips, a scoop of raita and a small bowl of extra tangy tamarind gravy for those who like it sharper.

variations.name: Classic Cabbage Poriyal
variations.description: The quick Tamil cabbage poriyal: finely shredded cabbage stir-fried in coconut oil with mustard, urad dal and curry leaves, then finished with fresh grated coconut so it stays sweet and just-cooked. It comes together in minutes and is the lightest, most everyday of South Indian dry sides.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil keeps this delicate stir-fry authentically South Indian and lifts the grated coconut finish

steps: Shred 500 g cabbage as finely as possible into thin ribbons - the finer the shred, the faster and more evenly the poriyal cooks.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a kadhai on medium; add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop, about 30 seconds, then add 1 tsp urad dal and 2 dried red chillies torn in half and fry until the dal turns golden.
Add 12 curry leaves, 2 chopped green chillies and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them crackle for 15 seconds until aromatic.

Add the shredded cabbage with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, toss well to coat, then cover and cook on low heat for 6-8 minutes, stirring once, until the cabbage wilts and softens but keeps a slight bite.
Uncover, raise the heat to medium and stir for 2 minutes to dry off the moisture the cabbage releases so the poriyal is not watery.
Switch off the flame and fold in 5 tbsp grated fresh coconut, tossing until the coconut coats the cabbage while still raw and sweet.
tips: Cabbage releases a lot of water, so never add any while cooking; it steams perfectly in its own moisture under a lid.
Do not overcook - cabbage poriyal should keep a fresh, slight crunch rather than turning limp and grey.
Add the coconut off the heat so it stays sweet and does not brown or dry out against the pan.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sambar rice and a papad, or as a light dry side to rasam and steamed rice for an everyday South Indian meal.

variations.name: Cabbage Paruppu Poriyal (with Moong Dal)
variations.description: This protein-rich version cooks soft moong dal into the cabbage so each mouthful has creamy little pockets of lentil against the sweet shreds. Popular in Tamil Brahmin kitchens, the paruppu poriyal is more filling and wholesome than the plain stir-fry while staying just as light on spice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil ties the soft dal and cabbage together in classic South Indian style

steps: Rinse 0.33 cup moong dal and boil it in 1.25 cups water with 0.25 tsp turmeric for about 10 minutes until just soft but not mushy, then drain any excess water and set aside.
Shred 450 g cabbage finely into thin ribbons while the dal cooks.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a kadhai on medium; add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop, then add 1 tsp urad dal and 2 dried red chillies torn in half and fry until golden.
Add 12 curry leaves and 2 chopped green chillies, let them crackle for 15 seconds, then add the shredded cabbage with 1 tsp salt and toss well.
Cover and cook the cabbage on low for 6-8 minutes until it wilts and softens, then fold in the cooked moong dal and stir on medium for 3 minutes so the dal warms through and any moisture dries off.
Switch off the flame and fold in 4 tbsp grated fresh coconut, tossing to coat everything evenly.
tips: Cook the moong dal only until just soft and grainy; overcooked mushy dal makes the poriyal pasty instead of textured.
Drain the dal well before adding it in so the poriyal stays dry rather than turning into a thick mash.
A squeeze of lime at the end brightens the mild dal-and-cabbage flavour beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with rasam rice and a crisp appalam; the added dal makes this hearty enough to pair with just curd rice on its own.

variations.name: Andhra Cabbage Fry (Cabbage Vepudu)
variations.description: Andhra style dials up the heat and skips the coconut, frying the cabbage drier with garlic, cumin and a spike of red chilli powder until it browns at the edges. This cabbage vepudu is bolder and punchier, meant to be a fiery dry accompaniment to plain rice and ghee.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A sturdier oil for the hotter, drier fry of an Andhra vepudu

steps: Shred 500 g cabbage finely and crush 6 garlic cloves roughly so they stay chunky in the tempering.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium; add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and let them splutter for 30 seconds.
Add 1 tsp urad dal, the crushed garlic and 2 dried red chillies torn in half, and fry for 1 minute until the garlic turns golden and fragrant, then add 12 curry leaves for 10 seconds.
Add the cabbage with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, toss well, then cover and cook on low for 6 minutes until it wilts.
Uncover, add 1 tsp red chilli powder, raise the heat to medium-high and stir-fry for 6-7 minutes, spreading the cabbage across the pan, until it dries out and the edges catch a light brown char.
Taste, adjust salt, and switch off once the cabbage is dry and roasted rather than steamy.
tips: The high-heat uncovered fry at the end is what gives Andhra vepudu its signature roasted, dry character.
Keep stirring in the final stage so the cabbage browns evenly rather than scorching in patches.
Fry the garlic to a proper gold - it is the backbone of the flavour and should never go in raw at the end.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice, a spoon of ghee and pappu or a tangy pulusu; it also makes a fiery dry side to curd rice.

variations.name: Cabbage and Carrot Poriyal
variations.description: Adding grated carrot to the cabbage brings colour, natural sweetness and a little more body to the poriyal. The two vegetables cook down together under a coconut oil tempering and a coconut finish, making a cheerful, mildly sweet stir-fry that children take to easily.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil complements the natural sweetness of carrot and cabbage in this everyday poriyal

steps: Shred 350 g cabbage finely and grate 2 medium carrots so both are in thin, quick-cooking pieces.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a kadhai on medium; add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop, then add 1 tsp urad dal and 1 tsp chana dal and fry until golden.
Add 12 curry leaves, 2 chopped green chillies and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them crackle for 15 seconds.
Add the cabbage and carrot with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, toss well, then cover and cook on low for 6-8 minutes until both soften while keeping a slight bite.
Uncover and stir on medium for 2 minutes to dry off the moisture released by the vegetables.
Switch off the flame and fold in 5 tbsp grated fresh coconut, tossing until evenly coated.
tips: Grate the carrot rather than chopping it so it cooks in the same time as the shredded cabbage.
The carrot adds its own sweetness, so keep the green chilli to balance rather than adding sugar.
Do not overcook or the carrot goes limp; both vegetables should stay bright and just-tender.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sambar rice or curd rice; its bright colour makes it a cheerful addition to a South Indian lunch plate or lunchbox.

variations.name: Classic Corn Capsicum Sabzi
variations.description: This Classic Corn Capsicum Sabzi is a quick, colourful dry stir-fry of sweet corn and crunchy capsicum tossed in a simple onion-tomato masala. The corn stays juicy and the capsicum keeps its bite, making it a bright, fuss-free everyday side.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil that keeps the stir-fry light and lets the vegetables shine

steps: Boil the 1.5 cups sweet corn kernels in salted water for 6 minutes until just tender, then drain and keep aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai over medium-high heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle for 15 seconds.
Add the finely chopped onion and saute for 4 minutes until soft, then stir in 1 tsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the chopped tomato with 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp salt and cook for 4 minutes until the tomato softens.
Tip in the diced 2 capsicums and stir-fry on high heat for 3 minutes so they stay crisp and bright.
Add the boiled corn and toss for 3 minutes until everything is well coated and dry.
Sprinkle 0.25 tsp garam masala, stir once and serve hot as a colourful side.
tips: Cook the capsicum on high heat for a short time to keep its crunch and vivid colour.
Boil the corn ahead so the sabzi comes together in minutes on a busy day.
A squeeze of lemon at the end lifts the sweetness of the corn beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve rolled inside a hot chapati as a quick wrap, or alongside dal and rice for a light lunch.

variations.name: Restaurant-style Corn Capsicum
variations.description: A creamy restaurant-style semi-dry version where corn and capsicum are bound in a lightly buttery tomato masala with a spoon of cream and crushed kasuri methi. It is richer and more indulgent than the everyday sabzi, perfect for a small celebration.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: gives the masala a buttery restaurant-style richness and blooms the cumin

steps: Boil the 1.5 cups corn kernels in salted water for 6 minutes until tender and drain.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle for 15 seconds.
Add the finely chopped onion and saute for 5 minutes until golden, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Pour in 0.5 cup tomato puree with 1 tsp chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp salt and cook for 5 minutes until the ghee separates.
Add the diced 2 capsicums and stir-fry on high for 2 minutes, then add the boiled corn and cook 2 more minutes.
Lower the heat and stir in 3 tbsp cream and 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi, simmering for 2 minutes so the masala turns glossy without splitting.
Finish with 0.5 tsp garam masala, stir gently and serve warm.
tips: Add the cream only on low heat and keep stirring so it does not curdle in the tangy masala.
Roast the kasuri methi on a dry pan before crushing to release its full aroma.
Keep the capsicum slightly crunchy so it contrasts the soft creamy masala.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or laccha paratha and a bowl of boondi raita for a mini feast.

variations.name: Indo-Chinese Corn Capsicum
variations.description: A fusion street-style stir-fry where corn and capsicum are tossed high in a garlicky soy and chilli sauce for a sticky, savoury-sweet glaze. Quick and punchy with a hint of pepper, it borrows the wok energy of Indian-Chinese carts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: lends a nutty wok aroma that defines the Indo-Chinese stir-fry

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: balances the salty soy and chilli with a clean natural sweetness

steps: Boil the 1.5 cups corn kernels in salted water for 5 minutes until just tender and drain well.
Mix 1 tsp cornflour with 3 tbsp water and set the slurry aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a wok on high heat, add the finely chopped garlic, slit green chillies and the white parts of the spring onion and stir-fry for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the diced 2 capsicums and stir-fry on high for 2 minutes so they blister slightly but stay crunchy.
Toss in the boiled corn, then add 1 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tbsp chilli sauce, 0.5 tsp black pepper, 1 tsp Anveshan Honey and 0.5 tsp salt and stir for 1 minute.
Pour in the cornflour slurry and toss for 1 minute until the sauce thickens into a glossy glaze that coats the vegetables.
Garnish with the chopped spring onion greens and serve immediately while hot and crisp.
tips: Keep the flame high throughout so the vegetables char lightly instead of stewing.
Adjust the honey and chilli sauce to balance sweet and heat to your taste.
Have all ingredients prepped before you start, as this stir-fry cooks in minutes.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a starter on its own, or over hakka noodles or fried rice for a fusion meal.

variations.name: Masala Corn Capsicum with Besan
variations.description: A dhaba-style dry sabzi where a sprinkle of roasted besan coats the corn and capsicum in a spiced, slightly crumbly masala that clings to every kernel. The gram flour soaks up the oil and spices, giving a satisfying, savoury dryness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: pungent wood-pressed oil that gives the dhaba-style masala its earthy kick

steps: Boil the 1.5 cups corn kernels in salted water for 6 minutes until tender and drain well.
Dry-roast the 2 tbsp besan in a pan on low heat for 3 minutes until it smells nutty and turns a shade darker, then set aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just smokes, lower the heat and add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp ajwain and let them crackle for 15 seconds.
Add the finely chopped onion and saute for 4 minutes until soft, then add 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp salt.
Add the diced 2 capsicums and stir-fry on high for 3 minutes, then tip in the boiled corn and toss for 2 minutes.
Sprinkle the roasted besan over the vegetables and toss continuously for 3 minutes so it coats everything in a dry, spiced crumble.
Finish with 0.5 tsp amchur, stir once and serve the dry masala sabzi hot.
tips: Roast the besan properly until nutty, as raw gram flour tastes bitter and pasty.
Heat mustard oil to smoking point first to mellow its sharpness before tempering.
Toss constantly after adding besan so it clings evenly and does not clump.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot ajwain parathas and a spoon of plain yogurt for a rustic dhaba-style lunch.

variations.name: Classic Dahi Aloo
variations.description: This Classic Dahi Aloo simmers tender baby potatoes in a smooth, tangy yogurt gravy scented with cumin and coriander. The whisked curd turns silky and mildly sour against the soft potatoes, making a light, homely curry that comes together fast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the whole spices and enriches the tangy yogurt gravy

steps: Boil the 500 g baby potatoes until tender, peel them and lightly prick each with a fork so they soak up the gravy.
Whisk the 1 cup yogurt with 1 tbsp besan, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder until smooth and lump-free.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle for 20 seconds.
Add the finely chopped onion and saute for 5 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Lower the heat, pour in the whisked yogurt mixture and stir continuously for 4 minutes so it warms gently without splitting.
Add the boiled potatoes with 1 tsp salt and half a cup of water, cover and simmer on low for 8 minutes until the gravy thickens.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala, stir once and serve hot garnished with coriander.
tips: Whisk the besan into the yogurt to stop the curd from splitting when it heats.
Always add yogurt on low heat and keep stirring until it comes to a gentle simmer.
Prick the boiled potatoes so they absorb the tangy gravy right to the centre.
