variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot pooris or jeera rice and a side of sliced onions and lemon.

variations.name: Rajasthani Dahi Aloo
variations.description: A spicy Rajasthani rendition where baby potatoes swim in a fiery yogurt gravy tempered with whole red chillies, cloves and a generous dose of coriander. Bold and tangy, it is built for the desert palate and pairs beautifully with bajra roti.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: pungent wood-pressed oil that gives the fiery gravy its earthy Rajasthani base

steps: Boil the 500 g baby potatoes until tender, peel and prick each one with a fork.
Whisk the 1.25 cups yogurt with 1.5 tbsp besan, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder until smooth.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just smokes, lower the heat and add 1 tsp cumin seeds, 3 whole red chillies and 3 cloves and let them crackle for 20 seconds.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and saute for 1 minute until the raw smell fades.
Lower the heat, pour in the whisked yogurt mixture and stir constantly for 5 minutes so it heats without curdling and the besan cooks through.
Add the boiled potatoes with 1 tsp salt and a cup of water, cover and simmer on low for 8 minutes until the gravy turns rich and fiery.
Simmer uncovered for 2 more minutes to thicken and serve hot.
tips: Cooking the besan-yogurt mixture for a few minutes removes any raw gram-flour taste.
Heat the mustard oil to smoking first to soften its sharpness before tempering.
Keep stirring the yogurt on low heat until it simmers so it never splits.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra roti or steamed rice and a side of raw onion and green chilli.

variations.name: No-Onion-No-Garlic Dahi Aloo
variations.description: A satvik dahi aloo that skips onion and garlic, drawing warmth from cumin, asafoetida and ginger in the tempering. The tangy yogurt gravy stays light and clean, making it perfect for fasting days and Jain kitchens while keeping the comfort intact.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the cumin and hing that build flavour without onion or garlic

steps: Boil the 500 g baby potatoes until tender, peel and prick each with a fork.
Whisk the 1 cup yogurt with 1 tbsp besan, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder until smooth and lump-free.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them sizzle for 15 seconds.
Add the grated ginger and slit green chillies and saute for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Lower the heat, pour in the whisked yogurt mixture and stir continuously for 4 minutes so it heats gently without splitting.
Add the boiled potatoes with 1 tsp salt and half a cup of water, cover and simmer on low for 7 minutes until the gravy thickens.
Rest for 5 minutes off heat so the satvik flavours settle, then serve hot.
tips: Asafoetida gives a savoury depth that stands in for the missing onion and garlic.
Whisk besan into the yogurt so the gravy stays smooth and does not split on heating.
Keep the heat low while cooking the curd and stir until it reaches a gentle simmer.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice or soft satvik rotis and a cucumber salad.

variations.name: Kashmiri Dum Dahi Aloo
variations.description: A festive Kashmiri-style dahi aloo where fried baby potatoes are slow-cooked on dum in a fennel-and-ginger scented yogurt gravy tinged red with Kashmiri chilli. Aromatic with cardamom and dried mint, it is a gently spiced, elegant curry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the potatoes and carries the fennel and ginger aroma of a Kashmiri gravy

steps: Boil the 500 g baby potatoes until just tender, peel and prick them all over with a fork.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan and fry the potatoes for 5 minutes until golden all over, then remove and set aside.
Whisk the 1.25 cups yogurt with 1.5 tsp fennel powder, 1 tsp dry ginger powder and 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder until smooth.
In the same ghee add 1 tsp cumin seeds, 3 cardamom and 3 cloves and let them crackle for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Lower the heat, pour in the whisked yogurt mixture and stir constantly for 5 minutes so it heats gently and turns a warm red without splitting.
Return the fried potatoes with 1 tsp salt and half a cup of water, cover and cook on very low dum heat for 12 minutes so they absorb the gravy.
Crush 0.5 tsp dried mint over the top, stir once and serve hot.
tips: Frying the potatoes before the dum gives them a firm skin that holds the gravy.
Use Kashmiri chilli for the signature red colour without overwhelming heat.
Cook on the lowest heat during dum so the yogurt gravy stays smooth and glossy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed basmati rice or a soft naan for an elegant Kashmiri-style meal.

variations.name: Classic Dahi Puri
variations.description: This Classic Dahi Puri fills crisp hollow puris with spiced potato, tops them with cool sweetened yogurt and a swirl of tamarind and green chutneys, then finishes with sev and pomegranate. Each puri is a single-bite balance of crunch, creamy curd, sweet, sour and spice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: deep-frying the puris in wood-pressed oil makes them puff crisp and hollow

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens both the yogurt and tamarind chutney with a natural mellow depth

steps: Knead 1 cup semolina with 2 tbsp flour and 6 tbsp water into a stiff dough, rest 20 minutes, roll thin, cut small rounds, and deep-fry in Anveshan Groundnut Oil at medium heat until each puffs into a crisp hollow puri.
Whisk the 2.5 cups yogurt smooth with 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.5 tsp salt, then chill it well.
Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and a splash of water for 5 minutes into a thick sweet-sour chutney.
Mash the 3 boiled potatoes with the 0.5 cup boiled moong sprouts, 0.5 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp chaat masala for the filling.
Crack a hole in the top of each puri and spoon in the potato-sprout filling, then arrange them on a platter.
Top each filled puri with a spoon of chilled yogurt, drizzle with tamarind and green chutney, dust with 1 tsp roasted cumin powder and chaat masala, and finish with sev, pomegranate and coriander.
tips: Whisk the yogurt until pourable and chill it so it flows smoothly over each puri.
Fill and top the puris only just before serving so they stay crisp under the yogurt.
Balance the yogurt with a little jaggery and salt so it is neither too sour nor too sweet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve six puris per plate, finished with an extra drizzle of both chutneys and a scatter of pomegranate.

variations.name: Sprouts Dahi Puri
variations.description: A protein-packed version that fills the puris generously with boiled mixed sprouts and uses a lightly set low-fat yogurt. It keeps the cooling, tangy character of dahi puri while making it a more nourishing, wholesome snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: light wood-pressed oil fries crisp hollow puris without heaviness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: gives natural sweetness to the yogurt and tamarind chutney in the lighter build

steps: Knead 1 cup semolina with 2 tbsp flour and 6 tbsp water into a stiff dough, rest 20 minutes, roll thin, cut rounds, and deep-fry in Anveshan Sunflower Oil at medium heat until puffed and crisp.
Steam the 1.5 cups mixed sprouts with a pinch of salt for 6 to 8 minutes until just tender, then cool.
Whisk the 2.5 cups yogurt smooth with 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.5 tsp salt and chill.
Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder for 5 minutes into a sweet-sour chutney and cool it.
Crack a hole in each puri and fill with the cooked sprouts mixed with finely diced cucumber and 0.5 tsp chaat masala.
Top each with chilled yogurt, drizzle tamarind and green chutney, dust with 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, and finish with a little sev, pomegranate and coriander.
tips: Steam the sprouts just until tender so they keep their crunch and their nutrition.
Go light on the sev here so the fresh sprouts and yogurt remain the focus.
Use thick set yogurt so the higher moisture of the sprouts does not make the puris collapse.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a filling, protein-rich snack topped with extra cucumber and pomegranate for freshness.

variations.name: Ragda Dahi Puri
variations.description: A hearty Mumbai stall version that stuffs the puris with warm white-pea ragda before the cool yogurt and chutneys go on. The interplay of hot spiced ragda and chilled curd makes this the most filling, satisfying dahi puri of all.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil fries sturdy puris that hold the warm ragda filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: balances the tamarind chutney and sweetened yogurt over the savoury ragda

steps: Knead 1 cup semolina with 2 tbsp flour and 6 tbsp water into a stiff dough, rest 20 minutes, roll thin, cut rounds, and deep-fry in Anveshan Groundnut Oil at medium heat until crisp and hollow.

Pressure-cook 1 cup soaked white peas with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 2.5 cups water for 6 whistles, then temper with 1 tsp cumin seeds bloomed in a little of the oil and simmer 8 minutes into a thick ragda.
Whisk the 2 cups yogurt smooth with 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.5 tsp salt and chill.
Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder for 5 minutes into a sweet-sour chutney.
Crack a hole in each puri and spoon in a little warm ragda until half full.
Top each ragda-filled puri with chilled yogurt, drizzle both chutneys, dust with 1 tsp chaat masala, and finish with sev and coriander to serve at once.
tips: Keep the ragda thick so it stays inside the puri without breaking the crisp shell.
Assemble one plate at a time, as the warm ragda softens the puris faster than dry fillings.
The contrast of hot ragda and cold yogurt is the whole point, so serve the moment they are topped.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a plate with a spoon, since these brim over with ragda and yogurt and are best eaten right away.

variations.name: Avocado Dahi Puri
variations.description: A contemporary fusion that swaps some of the potato for a spiced smashed avocado, lending the puris a buttery richness against the tangy yogurt. Bright with lime and coriander, it is a modern cafe reinvention of the beloved chaat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: light wood-pressed oil for frying crisp puris to hold the avocado filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the yogurt and tamarind chutney against the rich avocado

steps: Knead 1 cup semolina with 2 tbsp flour and 6 tbsp water into a stiff dough, rest 20 minutes, roll thin, cut rounds, and deep-fry in Anveshan Sunflower Oil at medium heat until crisp and hollow.
Mash the 2 avocados with the 1 boiled potato, 1 tbsp lime juice, 0.5 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp chaat masala into a chunky, spiced filling.
Whisk the 2 cups yogurt smooth with 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and a pinch of salt and chill.
Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder for 5 minutes into a sweet-sour chutney and cool it.
Crack a hole in each puri and spoon in the smashed avocado filling.
Top with chilled yogurt, drizzle both chutneys, dust with the remaining chaat masala, and finish with sev and coriander to serve immediately.
tips: Add lime to the avocado at once so the filling stays green and does not brown.
Keep the avocado chunky rather than fully pureed for a pleasing texture against the crisp puri.
Assemble just before serving, as ripe avocado and yogurt both soften the puris quickly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as an elegant chaat-style appetiser at a party, garnished with extra coriander and a lime wedge.

variations.name: Classic Dahi Vada
variations.description: Dahi Vada is a cooling favourite of soft urad dal dumplings soaked until pillowy, then drowned in sweetened, whisked yogurt. Topped with roasted cumin, chilli and chutneys, it is a beloved festival and summer snack across North India.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: deep-fries the vadas light before they soak, keeping them airy not greasy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the whisked yogurt naturally in place of refined sugar

steps: Soak 1.5 cups urad dal for 4 hours, drain well, and grind to a smooth, fluffy batter using minimal water, then whip in air and add 0.5 tsp salt.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to about 180C and fry small spoonfuls of batter in batches for 4 minutes until golden and cooked through.
Slide the fried vadas straight into a bowl of warm water and soak for 20 minutes until they turn very soft and swollen.
Whisk 3 cups curd smooth with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.5 tsp salt until it is creamy and pourable.
Gently press each soaked vada between your palms to squeeze out excess water, then arrange them in a serving dish.
Pour the sweetened yogurt over to cover, drizzle 4 tbsp tamarind and 3 tbsp green chutney, and dust with 1 tsp roasted cumin and 0.5 tsp chilli powder before chilling and serving.
tips: Soak the fried vadas in warm, not cold, water so they soften right through to the centre.
Squeeze the vadas gently but fully, or trapped water will dilute the yogurt on the plate.
Chill the assembled dahi vada for at least an hour so the flavours meld and it eats cool and refreshing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Finish with a sprinkle of pomegranate and fine sev, and serve cold as a festive starter or chaat.

variations.name: South Indian Thayir Vadai
variations.description: The southern cousin of dahi vada, thayir vadai bathes soft urad vadas in lightly salted curd finished with a fragrant mustard and curry leaf tempering. It is savoury rather than sweet, cool and gently spiced.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for deep-frying the vadas to a light golden before soaking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: carries the mustard-curry leaf tempering with an authentic southern aroma

steps: Soak 1.5 cups urad dal for 4 hours, drain, and grind to a fluffy batter with little water, then whip and add 0.5 tsp salt.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C and fry small holed vadas in batches for 4 minutes until golden and firm.
Soak the fried vadas in warm water for 20 minutes until soft, then squeeze gently and set aside.
Whisk 3 cups curd with 0.75 tsp salt, 1 inch grated ginger and 2 chopped green chillies until smooth and creamy.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 12 curry leaves for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Place the squeezed vadas in a dish, pour over the seasoned curd, top with the hot tempering and 2 tbsp coriander, and chill before serving.
tips: Pour the sizzling tempering over just before serving so the aroma stays bright.
Keep the curd lightly salted and savoury; this southern version skips the sweet chutneys.
Use slightly sour curd for the most authentic tang, whisking it very smooth first.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled as part of a South Indian meal or festive sadya, with a little extra tempering spooned on top.

variations.name: Baked Appe Dahi Vada
variations.description: A lighter dahi vada where the dumplings are cooked in a paniyaram pan with a little ghee instead of deep-frying. They still turn soft and spongy after soaking, making a healthier version of the festive favourite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the appe moulds so the dumplings brown gently without deep-frying

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the yogurt naturally for the classic dahi vada balance

steps: Soak 1.5 cups urad dal for 4 hours, drain, and grind to a light fluffy batter with minimal water, then whip in air and add 0.5 tsp salt.
Heat an appe pan on medium and brush each mould with Anveshan Ghee.
Spoon batter into each cavity, cover for 2 minutes, then flip with a skewer and cook until golden and cooked through, about 4 minutes total.
Drop the cooked dumplings into warm water and soak for 15 minutes until soft, then squeeze gently.
Whisk 3 cups curd smooth with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.5 tsp salt until creamy.
Arrange the squeezed dumplings in a dish, pour over the sweet yogurt, drizzle 4 tbsp tamarind chutney, dust with 1 tsp roasted cumin and 0.5 tsp chilli, and chill before serving.
tips: Whip plenty of air into the batter, as the appe-pan version relies on that for a soft crumb.
Cover the moulds in the first stage so the centres set before flipping.
These soak faster than deep-fried vadas, so check after 15 minutes to avoid them falling apart.
variations.servingSuggestion: Top with pomegranate seeds and coriander for a lighter festive chaat that skips the frying.

variations.name: Moong Dal Dahi Vada
variations.description: A more digestible version made with skinned moong dal, which fries into especially soft, delicate dumplings. Lighter on the stomach than the urad dal classic, it is lovely for those who find the traditional version heavy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: deep-fries the delicate moong vadas to a pale gold without heaviness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: gives the yogurt its gentle natural sweetness

steps: Soak 1.5 cups yellow moong dal for 3 hours, drain, and grind to a smooth thick batter with 1 inch ginger and 2 green chillies using minimal water.
Whip the batter well and season with 0.5 tsp salt so it is light and airy.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 175C and fry small spoonfuls in batches for 3 to 4 minutes until pale golden and cooked.
Soak the fried vadas in warm water for 15 minutes until very soft, then squeeze them gently.
Whisk 3 cups curd with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.5 tsp salt until smooth and creamy.
Arrange the vadas in a dish, cover with the sweet yogurt, drizzle 3 tbsp green chutney, dust with 1 tsp roasted cumin, and chill before serving.
tips: Moong dal vadas are more delicate, so fry at a slightly lower heat and handle them gently.
Do not over-soak, as moong vadas soften faster than urad ones and can break apart.
A pinch of asafoetida in the batter aids digestion and adds a subtle savoury depth.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled with a scatter of boondi and coriander for a light, easy-to-digest chaat.

variations.name: Classic Mathanga Erissery
variations.description: The definitive Onam-sadya erissery from central Kerala, where golden pumpkin and creamy red cowpeas are mashed together and bound in a ground coconut-cumin paste. The soul of the dish is the finishing tempering of roasted coconut crisped in coconut oil until nutty and brown.

ingredients.name: Yellow pumpkin
ingredients.note: peeled and cubed

ingredients.name: Red cowpeas
ingredients.note: van payar, soaked overnight

ingredients.name: Grated fresh coconut
ingredients.note: for the ground paste

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed, essential for the browned-coconut tempering that defines erissery

ingredients.name: Shallots
ingredients.note: sliced

steps: Pressure-cook 1/2 cup soaked red cowpeas with 1.5 cups water and a pinch of salt for about 4 whistles until soft but still holding shape, then set aside without draining.

In a pot, add the cubed pumpkin with 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 slit green chillies, 1 tsp salt and 3/4 cup water; cover and cook on medium heat for 10-12 minutes until the pumpkin is fork-tender.
Meanwhile grind 3/4 cup grated coconut with 1/2 tsp cumin seeds and a splash of water into a slightly coarse paste.
Add the cooked cowpeas along with their liquid to the softened pumpkin, then lightly mash a portion with the back of the ladle so the dish turns thick and part-creamy.
Stir in the ground coconut-cumin paste and simmer on low heat for 5-6 minutes until the raw coconut smell fades and the mixture thickens to a scoopable consistency.

For the tempering, heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan, splutter 1/2 tsp mustard seeds, add 2 dry red chillies, 4 sliced shallots and 1/4 cup grated coconut, and fry for 3-4 minutes until the coconut turns deep golden-brown.
Pour this fragrant tempering with the curry leaves over the erissery, fold gently, and rest covered for 5 minutes so the roasted aroma soaks in before serving.
tips: Brown the tempering coconut slowly and patiently; this deep roast is what separates erissery from an ordinary pumpkin curry.
Mash only part of the pumpkin and cowpeas so the dish keeps a pleasant mix of smooth and whole textures.
Use starchy old pumpkin rather than watery young ones for a naturally thick, sweet result.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as part of an Onam sadya on a banana leaf with rice, or pair with plain steamed rice and a spoon of pickle for an everyday lunch.

variations.name: Vella Erissery
variations.description: The paler, gentler erissery of Palakkad Brahmin kitchens, made without red chilli powder so the sweetness of ash gourd and yam shines through a milky coconut-cumin paste. It is mild and soothing, relying on green chillies and pepper for a soft warmth rather than fiery heat.

ingredients.name: Ash gourd
ingredients.note: peeled and cubed

ingredients.name: Elephant yam
ingredients.note: peeled and cubed

ingredients.name: Red cowpeas
ingredients.note: soaked overnight

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: keeps the tempering pale and fragrant without darkening the white gravy

steps: Pressure-cook 1/2 cup soaked cowpeas with a pinch of salt and 1.5 cups water for 4 whistles until tender, and keep aside with the cooking liquid.
Cook the cubed ash gourd and yam with 1/4 tsp turmeric, 3 slit green chillies, 1 tsp salt and 1/2 cup water on medium heat for 10 minutes until soft.
Grind 3/4 cup grated coconut with 3/4 tsp cumin seeds and 1/2 tsp black pepper to a smooth, milky paste with a little water.
Add the cooked cowpeas with their liquid to the vegetables and mash lightly so the pot thickens while keeping some whole pieces.
Pour in the ground coconut paste and simmer very gently on low heat for 5 minutes, stirring so it stays creamy white and never comes to a rolling boil.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan, splutter 1/2 tsp mustard seeds, add 3 tbsp grated coconut and curry leaves and fry only until pale gold, then pour over the erissery and fold through gently.
tips: Stop the tempering coconut at a light gold, not brown, to keep this version true to its pale, delicate character.
Add the ground paste off high heat and simmer softly so the coconut milk-like base does not split.
A little extra crushed pepper at the end gives gentle warmth without turning the dish red.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot steamed rice and a drizzle of raw coconut oil, alongside a sharp mango pickle to cut the mildness.

variations.name: Chena Erissery
variations.description: A yam-forward erissery beloved in Thrissur homes, where meaty elephant yam replaces pumpkin for an earthier, more substantial dish. The generous browned-coconut tempering clings to the starchy yam cubes, making it hearty enough to anchor a simple rice meal.

ingredients.name: Elephant yam
ingredients.note: peeled and cubed

ingredients.name: Red cowpeas
ingredients.note: soaked overnight

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: for grinding into the paste

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: crisps the tempering coconut to a nutty brown that coats the yam

ingredients.name: Shallots
ingredients.note: sliced

steps: Pressure-cook 1/2 cup soaked cowpeas with 1.5 cups water and a pinch of salt for about 4 whistles until soft, and reserve with the liquid.
Boil the cubed yam with 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp salt and 3/4 cup water on medium heat for 12-14 minutes until a knife slips through easily.
Grind 3/4 cup grated coconut with 1/2 tsp cumin seeds and 3 garlic cloves into a coarse paste using a little water.
Add the cooked cowpeas with their liquid to the yam and mash roughly so the starchy yam thickens the pot naturally.
Stir in the ground coconut-garlic paste and simmer on low heat for 6 minutes until thick and the raw smell disappears.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan, splutter 1/2 tsp mustard seeds, add 2 dry red chillies, 5 sliced shallots and 1/3 cup grated coconut, and fry for 4 minutes until deep golden-brown.
Pour the tempering with the curry leaves over the erissery, fold through, and let it stand covered for 5 minutes so the yam absorbs the roasted flavour.
tips: Rub your hands with a little oil before cutting raw yam to avoid the mild itch some varieties cause.
The garlic in the ground paste is a Thrissur touch that deepens the yam's earthiness; skip it for a temple-style version.
Yam absorbs liquid as it rests, so keep the erissery slightly looser than you want it to end up.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rice and a tart puliyinji on the side, or pair with rice and rasam for a soothing everyday South Indian meal.

variations.name: Sweet-Balanced Pumpkin Erissery
variations.description: A home-style pumpkin erissery that leans into the natural sweetness of the gourd with a whisper of jaggery, balanced by extra pepper and roasted coconut. The gentle sweet-savoury tension makes it a favourite with children and a comforting scoop against plain rice.

ingredients.name: Yellow pumpkin
ingredients.note: peeled and cubed

ingredients.name: Red cowpeas
ingredients.note: soaked overnight

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a small spoon that rounds the pumpkin's sweetness without any refined sugar

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: for the signature browned-coconut tempering

steps: Pressure-cook 1/2 cup soaked cowpeas with 1.5 cups water and a pinch of salt for 4 whistles until tender, then keep aside with the cooking water.
Cook the cubed pumpkin with 1/2 tsp turmeric, 2 slit green chillies, 1 tsp salt and 1/2 cup water on medium heat for 10 minutes until soft and collapsing at the edges.
Grind 3/4 cup grated coconut with 1/2 tsp cumin seeds and 3/4 tsp black pepper to a slightly coarse paste.
Add the cooked cowpeas with their liquid and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder to the pumpkin, mash lightly, and simmer for 3 minutes so the jaggery dissolves evenly.
Stir in the ground coconut paste and cook on low heat for 5 minutes until thickened and the raw coconut smell has gone.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan, splutter 1/2 tsp mustard seeds, add 2 dry red chillies and 1/4 cup grated coconut, fry until deep brown, then pour with the curry leaves over the erissery and fold in gently.
tips: Use only a small spoon of jaggery so it balances rather than sweetens; the dish should still read as savoury.
Extra pepper in the ground paste keeps the sweetness in check and adds a grown-up warmth.
If the pumpkin is already very sweet, halve the jaggery and taste before the tempering goes on.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a sharp lime pickle, or alongside a peppery rasam so the sweet and tangy dishes play off each other.

variations.name: Classic Idiyappam
variations.description: Kerala's featherlight rice string hoppers, pressed into lacy nests and steamed until soft and glistening. Roasted rice flour is scalded with boiling water into a warm dough, extruded through a hand press and cooked in minutes over steam. Traditionally cradled in a bowl of cardamom-scented sweet coconut milk for a gentle breakfast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Brushed over the idli plates and the press so the delicate strands lift off cleanly without tearing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Melted into warm coconut milk it gives the traditional caramel-toned sweet accompaniment its earthy depth

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A teaspoon drizzled over the hot hoppers rounds out the coconut with a nutty richness

steps: Lightly brush the holes of your idli or idiyappam plates with a little Anveshan Coconut Oil and keep the steamer ready with 2 inches of water heating on medium flame.

Bring 1.75 cups water to a rolling boil with 0.75 tsp salt and 1 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, then pour it in a steady stream over 2 cups roasted rice flour while stirring with a spoon until it forms a shaggy mass.
Once cool enough to touch, knead the mixture for 2-3 minutes into a smooth, soft, non-sticky dough; if it cracks, sprinkle in a spoon of hot water at a time until pliable.
Fill an idiyappam press with the warm dough and squeeze it in tight little spirals onto each greased plate, then sprinkle a pinch of the grated coconut over every nest.
Steam the plates over medium heat for 6-8 minutes until the strands turn from chalky white to glossy and set, then let them rest 2 minutes before lifting off gently.

Warm 1 cup thin coconut milk on low heat without boiling, stir in 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.25 tsp cardamom until dissolved, and serve alongside the hoppers finished with a drizzle of Anveshan Ghee.
tips: Work the dough while it is still warm; a cooled dough turns stiff and the strands snap as they emerge from the press.
If you only have raw rice flour, dry-roast it on low heat for 4-5 minutes until just warm and no longer raw-smelling before scalding.
Do not oversteam; past 8 minutes the hoppers dry out and clump instead of staying separate and springy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve nested in a shallow bowl with the sweet coconut milk poured around the base, or pair savoury with a Kerala vegetable ishtu (stew) and pappadam on the side.

variations.name: Ragi Idiyappam
variations.description: A wholesome finger-millet version that swaps part of the rice flour for nutty, iron-rich ragi, turning the hoppers a soft mocha brown. The millet lends an earthy, slightly grainy bite that stands up beautifully to spicy curries. A favourite in health-conscious Karnataka and Kerala homes for a filling, low-glycaemic breakfast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Greases the press and plates so the denser millet strands release without breaking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A final drizzle keeps the fibre-rich strands moist and adds a mellow aroma

steps: Dry-roast 1 cup ragi flour on low heat for 3-4 minutes, stirring constantly until it smells toasty, then mix it with 1 cup roasted rice flour and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds in a wide bowl.
Grease the idiyappam plates and press with a little Anveshan Coconut Oil and set the steamer to heat on medium flame.
Boil 1.75 cups water with 0.75 tsp salt and 1 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, pour it over the flour mixture in stages, and stir into a rough dough with a spoon.
When cool enough to handle, knead 3 minutes into a smooth soft dough, adding a splash of hot water if it feels dry or crumbly at the edges.
Press the dough in spirals onto the greased plates, scatter grated coconut over each nest, and steam over medium heat for 8-10 minutes until the millet strands look set and matte.
Rest 2 minutes, lift the hoppers off carefully, and finish with a drizzle of Anveshan Ghee before serving warm.
tips: Ragi dough is stiffer than plain rice dough, so keep a bowl of hot water handy and re-soften the dough between batches.
Steam these a couple of minutes longer than white idiyappam, as the millet takes slightly more time to cook through.
The cumin is optional but cuts the earthiness of ragi and pairs especially well with coconut chutney.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best with a fiery Kerala kadala (black chickpea) curry or a coconut-heavy vegetable kurma that soaks into the porous strands.

variations.name: Sweet Coconut-Jaggery Idiyappam
variations.description: A dessert-leaning treatment where freshly steamed hoppers are tossed while hot with molten jaggery, toasted coconut and cardamom until every strand glistens. The warm ghee coats the rice noodles so they stay soft and separate rather than clumping. Think of it as a South Indian answer to sweetened vermicelli, eaten as an after-school treat or festive breakfast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Greases the plates so the strands steam cleanly before their sweet toss

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Melted into a thick syrup it clings to the hot strands, giving them their glossy caramel coat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Toasts the coconut and keeps the sweetened hoppers soft and glistening

steps: Grease the idiyappam plates with a little Anveshan Coconut Oil, boil 1.75 cups water with 0.25 tsp salt, and scald 2 cups roasted rice flour into a soft dough as for classic hoppers.
Press the dough into nests and steam over medium heat for 6-8 minutes until glossy and set, then loosen the strands gently with a fork so they do not stick together.
Melt 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide pan on medium heat and fry 10 halved cashews until pale gold, about 1 minute, then scoop them out and set aside.
In the same pan add 0.75 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water and stir on low heat for 3-4 minutes until it melts into a thick, glossy syrup that coats the spoon.
Add 0.5 cups grated coconut and 0.5 tsp cardamom to the syrup and cook 2 minutes until fragrant and slightly sticky.
Fold the steamed hoppers gently into the jaggery-coconut mixture with the remaining 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, toss for a minute until every strand is coated, and scatter the fried cashews over the top.
tips: Toss the hoppers while they are still warm; cold strands turn brittle and break instead of soaking up the syrup.
Strain the melted jaggery if your block is unrefined and gritty, so the finished dish stays smooth.
Do not let the syrup harden past the sticky stage or it will set into candy and clump the strands.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm in small bowls as a festive sweet, with a spoon of thick coconut cream on the side for those who like it richer.

variations.name: Masala Idiyappam
variations.description: A savoury upma-style makeover where day-old or freshly steamed hoppers are broken up and stir-fried with a crackling South Indian tempering. Mustard seeds, curry leaves, onion and carrot fold through the strands for a quick one-plate meal. This is the clever way Kerala and Tamil kitchens turn leftover idiyappam into a spicy lunchbox favourite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: The traditional Kerala fat for tempering, it carries the mustard and curry-leaf aroma right through the strands

steps: If starting fresh, steam idiyappam and loosen it into strands; if using leftovers, crumble 4 cups of it gently with your fingers so it does not mat together.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a wide kadhai on medium flame and crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds for 30 seconds until they pop, then add 1 tsp urad dal and fry until golden.
Toss in 12 curry leaves and 2 slit green chillies, let them sizzle for 15 seconds, then add 1 finely sliced onion and cook 3-4 minutes until soft and translucent.
Stir in 1 grated carrot and 0.25 tsp turmeric and saute for 2-3 minutes until the carrot softens and the mix smells sweet.
Lower the heat, add the loosened strands with 0.75 tsp salt, and toss gently for 3-4 minutes until everything is evenly coated and heated through.
Turn off the flame, squeeze in 1 tbsp lemon juice, mix once, and serve warm straight from the pan.
tips: Use a light hand while tossing so the fragile strands stay long instead of breaking into mush.
A cup of steamed peas or a handful of roasted peanuts stirred in at the end makes this a more substantial meal.
Day-old refrigerated idiyappam actually stir-fries better than fresh, as the drier strands stay separate.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pack it into a lunchbox with a wedge of lemon and a spoon of coconut chutney, or serve at home with plain yogurt to cool the chilli.

variations.name: Classic Steamed Idli
variations.description: The definitive South Indian idli: pillowy, snow-white steamed cakes made from a naturally fermented batter of parboiled rice and urad dal. Light, spongy and gently sour, they are the gold standard of Indian breakfasts, meant to be dunked in sambar and chutney while still warm.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: A light smear of gingelly oil on the idli plates lets the steamed cakes lift off cleanly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A brush of bilona ghee over the hot idlis adds aroma and a soft sheen before serving

steps: Rinse and soak 2 cups idli rice in one bowl, and 1/2 cup urad dal with 1/2 tsp fenugreek seeds in another, both for 5 to 6 hours; soak 2 tbsp poha in the last 30 minutes.

Grind the urad dal and fenugreek first with a little cold water to a light, fluffy, airy batter, then grind the rice and soaked poha to a slightly grainy paste using only about 1.5 cups water in total.
Combine both batters in a large vessel, add 1.25 tsp salt, and mix thoroughly with your hand for 2 minutes to incorporate air; the batter should be thick but pourable.
Cover and ferment in a warm spot for 8 to 12 hours until the batter doubles in volume and turns bubbly and pleasantly sour.
Grease the idli plates with a little Anveshan Sesame Oil, pour the batter into each mould without stirring it down too much, and steam in a covered idli pot for 10 to 12 minutes.
Check with a toothpick, which should come out clean; rest the idlis for 2 minutes, then unmould, brush lightly with Anveshan Ghee, and serve hot.
tips: Do not add salt before grinding in cold climates — mix it in after grinding and adjust once the batter has fermented.
In cool weather, keep the batter inside a switched-off oven with the light on to help it ferment overnight.
Never over-mix fermented batter before steaming; folding gently keeps the trapped air that makes idlis fluffy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with sambar, coconut chutney and a spoon of gingelly-oil idli podi for the complete Tamil breakfast plate.

variations.name: Kanchipuram Idli
variations.description: The famous temple idli of Kanchipuram, steamed with crushed pepper, cumin, ginger and curry leaves folded right into the batter, and enriched with ghee. Traditionally set in cloth-lined moulds or dried leaf cups, it is denser, spicier and more aromatic than a plain idli, almost a meal on its own.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee both tempers the spices and enriches the batter, giving Kanchipuram idli its temple-prasadam richness

steps: Soak 1.5 cups idli rice and 3/4 cup urad dal separately for 5 hours, then grind them together to a slightly coarse, thick batter using about 1.25 cups water; add 1.25 tsp salt and 1/4 tsp asafoetida.
Cover and ferment the batter in a warm place for 8 to 10 hours until risen and bubbly; the coarser grind gives Kanchipuram idli its characteristic denser bite.

Coarsely crush 1 tbsp peppercorns and 1 tsp cumin seeds; heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan and fry 12 cashews until golden, then add the crushed pepper-cumin, 1 inch minced ginger, 15 torn curry leaves and 1/4 tsp dry ginger powder for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Fold this ghee tempering into the fermented batter gently so it is evenly spiced without deflating the air.

Grease small steel tumblers or idli moulds with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, pour in the batter to two-thirds height, and steam in a covered pot for 15 to 18 minutes as these thicker idlis take longer.
Test with a skewer, which should come out clean; rest 5 minutes, then unmould and cut into thick wedges to serve.
tips: Grind this batter a touch coarser than for plain idli — the slight graininess is authentic to the temple version.
Steam in tall tumblers or cloth-lined moulds for the traditional cylindrical shape, then slice into rounds.
The pepper and ginger make these idlis keep well for lunchboxes without needing much accompaniment.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm wedges with coconut chutney and a small bowl of milagai podi, exactly as offered as prasadam at Kanchipuram's temples.

variations.name: Thatte Idli
variations.description: The wide, flat plate idli of Karnataka's Bidadi belt, steamed in broad shallow moulds so it turns out big, soft and disc-like. The slightly thinner batter and generous surface make it exceptionally light and porous, perfect for soaking up a bowl of vibrant hotel-style saagu or chutney.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil greases the wide thatte plates and gives the idli's base a subtle Karnataka fragrance

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A brush of ghee over the finished thatte idli keeps the broad surface soft and glossy

steps: Soak 2 cups idli rice with 2 tbsp sabudana in one bowl and 1/2 cup urad dal with 1/2 tsp fenugreek seeds in another for 5 hours; soak 1/4 cup poha in the last 30 minutes for extra softness.
Grind the urad dal to a fluffy batter first, then grind the rice, sabudana and poha to a smooth paste, using about 1.75 cups water so the final batter is a shade thinner than plain idli batter.
Combine both batters with 1.25 tsp salt, mix well, cover, and ferment in a warm place for 8 to 12 hours until frothy and doubled.
Grease the broad, flat thatte plates generously with Anveshan Coconut Oil so the wide idlis release cleanly.
Pour a ladle of batter onto each plate and spread it slightly with the back of the ladle into a thin, even disc, then stack and steam in a covered steamer for 12 to 14 minutes.
Let the plates cool for 3 minutes, slide the soft disc-shaped idlis off, brush with Anveshan Ghee, and serve immediately.
tips: The poha and sago are key to the melt-in-mouth softness that thatte idli is prized for, so do not skip them.
Keep the batter slightly looser than for regular idli so it spreads into the classic wide, thin shape.
Cool the plates for a few minutes before unmoulding, as these large idlis tear if lifted too hot.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the wide soft idlis with hotel-style vegetable saagu, coconut chutney and a dab of butter, Bidadi highway style.

variations.name: Classic Jeera Aloo
variations.description: This Classic Jeera Aloo is a simple dry sabzi of boiled potato cubes tossed in a fragrant cumin tempering with turmeric and a hint of amchur. The cumin perfumes every piece while the potato edges turn lightly golden, making a quick, comforting side.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the cumin to a nutty aroma that defines this dish

steps: Boil the 4 potatoes until just tender, cool, peel and cut into bite-sized cubes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over medium heat, add 1.5 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle and turn nutty for about 20 seconds.
Add the slit green chillies and saute for 20 seconds, then lower the heat and add 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp chilli powder and 1 tsp coriander powder.
Immediately add the potato cubes with 0.75 tsp salt and toss well so every piece is coated in the golden spiced ghee.
Stir-fry on medium-high heat for 6 minutes, turning gently, until the potato edges turn lightly golden and crisp.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp amchur and toss for a minute to add a tangy lift.
Garnish with 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander and serve hot.
tips: Boil the potatoes just until tender so they hold their shape and do not turn mushy.
Add the ground spices off high heat so they do not burn in the hot ghee.
Let the potatoes sit undisturbed for a minute between tosses to crisp the edges.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot pooris or dal-rice, or as a light side with plain yogurt and papad.

variations.name: Vrat-style Jeera Aloo
variations.description: A fasting-friendly jeera aloo made without turmeric, onion or garlic, seasoned only with rock salt and roasted cumin for a clean, satvik flavour. Cooked in ghee with a squeeze of lemon, it is a staple for Navratri and Ekadashi vrat plates.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the pure fat allowed on fasting days that blooms the cumin beautifully

steps: Boil the 4 potatoes until tender, cool, peel and cut into bite-sized cubes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over medium heat, add 1.5 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle for 20 seconds until nutty.
Add the grated ginger and slit green chillies and saute for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the potato cubes with 0.75 tsp rock salt and 0.5 tsp black pepper and toss gently to coat.
Stir-fry on medium-high heat for 6 minutes, turning occasionally, until the potatoes are lightly golden at the edges.
Turn off the heat and drizzle 1 tbsp lemon juice over the potatoes, tossing once.
Garnish with 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander and serve hot on your vrat thali.
tips: Use only rock salt and skip turmeric to keep the dish strictly fasting-compliant.
Add the lemon juice off the heat so its fresh tang is not cooked away.
Black pepper replaces red chilli powder for a milder fasting-friendly heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with kuttu or singhare ki puri and a cooling cucumber-peanut raita for vrat.

variations.name: Dhaba-style Masala Jeera Aloo
variations.description: A bolder dhaba rendition where the cumin tempering is layered with onions, ginger-garlic and a punchy spice mix cooked in mustard oil. The potatoes are shallow-tossed until crisp-edged and coated in a robust, roadside-style dry masala.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: pungent wood-pressed oil that gives the potatoes their bold dhaba flavour

steps: Boil the 4 potatoes until just tender, cool, peel and cut into bite-sized cubes.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just smokes, lower the heat and add 1.5 tsp cumin seeds, letting them crackle for 20 seconds.
Add the finely chopped onion and slit green chillies and fry for 5 minutes until the onion turns golden.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute, then add 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt.
Add the potato cubes and toss well to coat in the masala, then stir-fry on medium-high for 6 minutes until the edges crisp.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala and 0.5 tsp amchur and toss for a minute.
Serve hot garnished with fresh coriander for a robust dhaba-style side.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to smoking point first to mellow its raw pungency.
Let the potatoes rest between tosses so they develop crisp, golden edges.
A little extra amchur or a squeeze of lemon sharpens the dhaba-style tang.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot ajwain parathas or stuffed kulchas and a raw onion-lemon salad.

variations.name: South-Indian Style Jeera Aloo
variations.description: A South-Indian twist where the cumin potatoes get a fragrant tempering of mustard seeds, curry leaves and urad dal in coconut oil. A touch of grated coconut finishes the dish, giving the familiar jeera aloo a fresh coastal aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed coconut oil that lends the tempering its authentic southern aroma

steps: Boil the 4 potatoes until tender, cool, peel and cut into bite-sized cubes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadai over medium heat, add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and let them splutter for 15 seconds.
Add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1 tsp urad dal and fry for 20 seconds until the dal turns golden.
Add the curry leaves and slit green chillies and let them crackle for 15 seconds, then add 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp chilli powder.
Add the potato cubes with 0.75 tsp salt and toss well to coat in the fragrant tempering.
Stir-fry on medium heat for 6 minutes until the potatoes are lightly golden and well seasoned.
Sprinkle 2 tbsp grated coconut, toss for a minute and serve hot.
tips: Fry the urad dal just until golden for a nutty crunch without bitterness.
Use fresh grated coconut for the best aroma, adding it right at the end.
Curry leaves must be dry when added so they crackle and release their scent.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and rasam, or as a dry side with curd rice and pickle.

variations.name: Classic Kerala Kadala Curry
variations.description: The iconic Kerala breakfast curry of black chickpeas (kadala) in a dark, roasted coconut gravy. Whole spices and grated coconut are toasted to a deep brown before grinding, giving the curry its signature almost-black colour and earthy, nutty depth. It is the soulmate of soft puttu and appam.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil is the defining fat of Kerala cooking — it roasts the coconut and finishes the tempering

steps: Soak 1 cup black chickpeas overnight in plenty of water, then pressure-cook with 1/2 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 5 to 6 whistles until soft but not mushy; reserve the cooking liquid.

In a dry pan on medium-low heat, roast 1 cup grated coconut with 1.5 tbsp coriander seeds, 4 dried red chillies and 1/2 tsp fennel seeds for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring constantly until the coconut turns deep golden-brown and smells nutty.
Cool the roasted mixture and grind it with a little water to a smooth, dark paste.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan on medium heat, sauté 1 finely chopped onion with 1 inch minced ginger and 5 minced garlic cloves until golden, about 5 minutes, then add 1/2 tsp turmeric and cook 30 seconds.

Add the ground coconut paste and cook for 3 minutes, then tip in the cooked chickpeas with enough reserved liquid to make a medium gravy, 1/2 tsp garam masala and the remaining salt; simmer for 12 to 15 minutes until dark and thickened.
In a small pan heat the last 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 15 curry leaves, and pour this sizzling tempering over the curry before serving.
tips: Roast the coconut slowly and patiently to a true dark brown — this is what gives Kerala kadala curry its colour and depth, so do not rush it.
Do not discard the chickpea cooking water; it carries flavour and gives the gravy a natural body.
The curry thickens as it sits, so keep it slightly loose if you plan to serve it later with puttu.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve steaming hot with puttu, appam or plain steamed rice, and a sliced banana on the side in true Kerala breakfast style.

variations.name: Varutharacha Kadala Curry
variations.description: A deeper, richer Kottayam-style version where the roasted coconut masala (varutharacha) is taken darker and enriched with extra whole spices like cinnamon and cloves. The result is a thick, intensely aromatic gravy with a mahogany colour, closer to a festive Sunday special than an everyday curry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil deepens the roasted-coconut masala and gives the final tempering its Kerala fragrance

steps: Soak 1 cup black chickpeas overnight, then pressure-cook with 1/2 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 whistles until tender; reserve the cooking liquid.

Dry-roast 1.25 cups grated coconut on medium-low heat with 2 tbsp coriander seeds, 5 dried red chillies, 1 inch cinnamon, 4 cloves and 1 tsp fennel seeds for 10 to 12 minutes until the coconut is a deep chocolate-brown.
Cool and grind the roasted mixture with a little warm water to a very smooth, dark paste.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan on medium heat and sauté 6 chopped shallots with 1 inch minced ginger until deep golden, then add 1/2 tsp turmeric and the ground paste and fry for 4 minutes until the oil begins to separate.
Add the cooked chickpeas with enough reserved liquid for a thick gravy and the remaining salt, and simmer on low heat for 15 to 18 minutes so the flavours meld and the gravy darkens further.
Heat the final 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds with the remaining 4 sliced shallots and 20 curry leaves until crisp, and pour this over the curry.
tips: Take the coconut a shade darker than the classic version, but stop the moment it smells nutty rather than burnt.
Shallots instead of onion give a sweeter, more traditional Kottayam base and a smoother gravy.
This richer curry tastes even better the next day, so it is worth making a double batch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best with soft appams or Kerala red rice, and a spoon of extra curry-leaf tempering on top for a festive breakfast spread.

variations.name: Coconut-Milk Kadala Curry
variations.description: A milder, creamier take that skips the roasted coconut masala and instead finishes the black chickpeas in fresh coconut milk. Pale, mellow and lightly spiced, it is the gentle version served to children and elders, letting the sweetness of the chickpeas and coconut come through.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil starts the base and its tempering ties the mild curry to its Kerala roots

steps: Soak 1 cup black chickpeas overnight and pressure-cook with 1/2 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 whistles until soft; reserve the cooking liquid.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan on medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 15 curry leaves, then add 1 finely chopped onion, 1 inch minced ginger and 2 slit green chillies and sauté until the onion is soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add 1 chopped tomato and cook until it turns pulpy, then stir in 1.5 tbsp coriander powder and 1/2 tsp turmeric on low heat for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the cooked chickpeas with 1 cup of the reserved liquid and the remaining salt, and simmer for 10 minutes so the chickpeas absorb the masala.

Lower the heat to a bare simmer and pour in 1 cup thick coconut milk with 1/2 tsp garam masala, stirring gently and warming through for 3 to 4 minutes without letting it boil so the coconut milk does not split.
Switch off and rest the curry covered for 5 minutes so the coconut milk settles into a smooth, mild gravy.
tips: Add the coconut milk only on the lowest heat and never let it boil, or it will curdle and turn grainy.
For a thicker curry, mash a spoonful of the cooked chickpeas before adding the coconut milk.
This gentler version is perfect for kids; reduce the green chillies to one if serving very young children.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft idiyappam, appam or ghee rice, letting the creamy gravy soak into the strands.

variations.name: Punjabi-Style Kala Chana Masala
variations.description: A North Indian reinterpretation where the same black chickpeas are cooked in a robust onion-tomato masala finished in ghee, with dried mango and garam masala instead of coconut. It is dry-ish, tangy and hearty, the kind of kala chana served at breakfast with bhatura or with a wedge of lemon and sliced onion.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee gives the North Indian masala a rich, rounded finish that oil cannot match

steps: Soak 1 cup black chickpeas overnight and pressure-cook with 1/2 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 whistles until soft; reserve the cooking liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 15 seconds, then add 2 finely chopped onions and fry until deep golden, about 7 minutes.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 2 slit green chillies for 1 minute, then add 2 pureed tomatoes and cook until the ghee separates at the edges, around 6 minutes.
Lower the heat and add 1.5 tbsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp amchur, roasting for 30 seconds until the masala smells cooked.
Add the cooked chickpeas with 1.5 cups reserved liquid and the remaining salt, and simmer for 12 to 15 minutes, mashing a few chickpeas against the pan to thicken the gravy.
Sprinkle in 1 tsp garam masala and 3 tbsp chopped coriander, simmer 2 minutes more, and serve.
tips: For a restaurant-style dark colour, fry the onions until genuinely brown before adding the tomatoes.
Mashing a handful of chickpeas is the trick to a thick clinging gravy without any flour.
Add the amchur towards the end so its tang stays bright rather than cooking away.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with bhatura or kulcha, or with steamed rice, topped with sliced onion, green chilli and a squeeze of lemon.

variations.name: Classic Kara Kuzhambu
variations.description: A fiery Tamil Nadu tamarind gravy whose name literally means spicy kuzhambu. Unlike the vathal version it is built around fresh vegetables and a bold chilli-coriander base, simmered in gingelly oil until thick, dark and clinging. It is the everyday heat that a South Indian rice plate is built around.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil gives kara kuzhambu its authentic body and helps it keep well

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A touch of jaggery softens the aggressive tamarind-and-chilli edge without making it sweet

steps: Soak 30 g tamarind in 2 cups warm water for 10 minutes and strain to a smooth extract; quarter 3 small brinjals and cut 1 drumstick into 2-inch batons, keeping the brinjal in water so it does not brown.

Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadai on medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1/2 tsp fenugreek seeds for 20 seconds, then add 15 curry leaves, 10 peeled shallots and 8 crushed garlic cloves and sauté until golden, about 3 minutes.
Add the drumstick and brinjal and stir-fry for 4 minutes on medium heat until the brinjal skins begin to blister and the vegetables are lightly seared.
Lower the flame, sprinkle in 2 tbsp sambar powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1/4 tsp turmeric, and roast for 20 seconds until fragrant, then pour in the tamarind extract with 1 tsp salt.
Simmer uncovered on medium-low heat for 15 to 18 minutes until the vegetables are tender and pools of sesame oil surface on a darkened gravy.
Stir 1 tsp rice flour into 2 tbsp water and add it with 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, cooking 2 more minutes until the kuzhambu turns thick and glossy.
tips: Sear the brinjal and drumstick well before adding tamarind; boiling raw vegetables in the sour base leaves them bland.
Kara kuzhambu should be noticeably thicker than sambar — reduce it patiently rather than adding rice flour twice.
It keeps for 2 to 3 days refrigerated and only deepens in flavour, so it is ideal for making ahead.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rice and a spoon of ghee, balanced by a cooling vegetable poriyal and plain curd on the side.

variations.name: Poondu (Garlic) Kara Kuzhambu
variations.description: A rustic Kongunadu favourite loaded with whole garlic cloves that turn soft and sweet in the tamarind gravy. Traditionally eaten for its warming, digestive qualities, this garlic-forward kuzhambu is thick, punchy and aromatic, with the gentle heat of freshly pounded pepper.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: A generous pour of gingelly oil confits the garlic and gives this kuzhambu its rich mouthfeel

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Balances the sharp tamarind and complements the sweetness of the softened garlic

steps: Coarsely pound 1 tbsp black peppercorns with 1 tsp cumin seeds in a mortar to a gritty powder; soak 30 g tamarind in 2 cups warm water and strain to a smooth extract.
Heat 5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadai on medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1/2 tsp fenugreek seeds, then add 15 curry leaves and 8 peeled shallots.
Add all 25 peeled garlic cloves whole and fry on low heat for 4 to 5 minutes until they turn golden and their raw pungency mellows into a sweet aroma.
Stir in 1.5 tbsp sambar powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric and the pounded pepper-cumin mix on low heat for 20 seconds, then pour in the tamarind extract with 1 tsp salt.
Simmer uncovered on medium-low heat for 16 to 18 minutes until the garlic is soft enough to crush against the pan and sesame oil floats on a thickened gravy.
Finish with 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer 2 minutes more, and switch off once the kuzhambu clings thickly to the spoon.
tips: Fry the garlic slowly on low heat; browning it too fast makes the cloves bitter instead of sweet.
Freshly pounded pepper gives a warmer, rounder heat than bottled pepper powder, so take the extra minute.
This garlic kuzhambu is traditionally eaten to ease colds — a small bowl with rice and ghee is deeply comforting.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve mixed into hot rice with a drizzle of sesame oil and a side of fried vadagam or sun-dried mor milagai for crunch.

variations.name: Chettinad Kara Kuzhambu
variations.description: The Chettinad kitchen's answer to a spicy gravy, thickened with a freshly ground paste of roasted coconut, fennel and red chillies. Layered with mushrooms or mixed vegetables, it carries the region's trademark aromatic heat and a thick, luscious body that coats every grain of rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil carries the roasted Chettinad spice paste and gives the gravy its glossy richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Rounds the pepper and tamarind heat into the balanced Chettinad profile

steps: Dry-roast 1 tbsp coriander seeds, 1 tsp fennel seeds and 5 dried red chillies for 2 minutes, add 1/3 cup grated coconut and toast until pale gold, cool, and grind to a smooth paste with a little water.
Soak 25 g tamarind in 1.5 cups warm water and strain to a smooth extract; quarter 200 g mushrooms, and finely chop 1 onion and 1 tomato.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadai on medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, add 15 curry leaves and the chopped onion, and sauté until golden, about 4 minutes.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then add the tomato and 1/4 tsp turmeric and cook until the tomato breaks down and the oil separates.
Add the quartered mushrooms and sauté 3 minutes until they release and reabsorb their moisture, then pour in the tamarind extract with 1 tsp salt and simmer 8 minutes.
Stir in the ground coconut-spice paste and 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer gently for 6 minutes until thick and aromatic, and switch off before it boils hard so the coconut stays smooth.
tips: Grind the coconut masala fresh for the true Chettinad aroma; roast the spices only until fragrant, never dark.
Sauté the mushrooms until their water evaporates so they do not thin down the gravy later.
For a vegetable version, swap the mushrooms for 2 cups of chopped mixed vegetables like brinjal, drumstick and pumpkin.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rice, a wedge of lime and a crisp urulai roast, or mop it up with soft idiyappam for a Chettinad-style dinner.

variations.name: Ennai Kathirikai Kara Kuzhambu
variations.description: A festive stuffed-brinjal kuzhambu where small aubergines are slit, packed with a roasted peanut-sesame-spice masala, and simmered whole in a spicy tamarind gravy. Ennai means oil, and the dish is defined by the glossy gingelly oil that pools around the tender, flavour-soaked brinjals.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: This dish is named for its oil — gingelly oil both fries the brinjals and enriches the tamarind gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Balances the tamarind and marries with the sweet roasted peanuts in the stuffing

steps: Dry-roast 3 tbsp peanuts, 1 tbsp sesame seeds, 1 tbsp coriander seeds and 4 dried red chillies until fragrant, add 2 tbsp grated coconut for the last minute, cool, and grind to a coarse-thick masala with a pinch of salt.
Slit 8 small brinjals into a cross from the base, keeping the stem intact, and stuff each generously with the ground masala; reserve any leftover masala.
Soak 25 g tamarind in 1.5 cups warm water and strain to a smooth extract.

Heat 5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a wide pan on medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, add 15 curry leaves and 10 peeled shallots, then place the stuffed brinjals in and fry gently for 5 minutes, turning until the skins blister on all sides.
Pour in the tamarind extract, the reserved masala, 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, cover, and simmer on low heat for 15 minutes until the brinjals are fork-tender.
Uncover, stir in 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, and simmer 3 more minutes until the gravy thickens and sesame oil glistens around the soft brinjals.
tips: Keep the brinjal stems on so the stuffed halves hold together while frying and simmering.
Grind the masala thick, not watery, so it stays packed inside the brinjals instead of leaking out.
Simmer covered and resist stirring too much — gentle cooking keeps the delicate stuffed brinjals whole.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the stuffed brinjals and gravy over hot rice, or alongside soft chapatis, with a simple carrot salad to cut the richness.

variations.name: Classic Masala Vada
variations.description: Masala Vada, also called paruppu vadai, is a crisp South Indian fritter of coarsely ground chana dal spiked with chilli, fennel and curry leaves. The rough, half-ground texture gives it a wonderful crunch that shatters into a savoury, lentil-rich centre.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: deep-fries the vadas to an even crunch while staying light and clean-tasting

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups chana dal in 2 cups water for 2 hours, then drain thoroughly and set aside a fistful of whole soaked dal.
Grind the rest coarsely with 3 dried red chillies, 1 tsp fennel seeds, 1 inch ginger and 1 tsp salt, using no water, to a rough, thick paste.
Mix in the reserved whole dal, finely chopped onion, 12 torn curry leaves and 3 tbsp coriander for crunch and flavour.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai to about 180C, until a pinch of batter sizzles up steadily.
Take small portions, flatten each into a thick patty on your palm, and gently slide into the hot oil in batches.
Fry for 4 to 5 minutes, turning until deep golden and crisp on both sides, then drain on paper and serve hot.
tips: Grind the dal coarse and without water, as a smooth or wet batter makes soft vadas that soak up oil.
Reserving a handful of whole soaked dal to fold in gives the signature crunchy bite.
Add the salt and onion just before frying so the batter does not turn watery and hard to shape.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with coconut chutney and filter coffee, a classic South Indian evening tiffin.

variations.name: Keerai Masala Vada
variations.description: A Tamil favourite that folds finely chopped spinach or amaranth greens into the chana dal batter. The keerai keeps the vadas moist inside while the coarse dal crust stays crunchy, adding colour and iron to the humble fritter.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: deep-fries the greens-studded vadas to a crisp golden shell

steps: Soak 1.5 cups chana dal in 2 cups water for 2 hours, then drain well and reserve a small handful of whole dal.
Grind the rest coarsely with 3 dried red chillies, 1 tsp fennel seeds, 1 inch ginger and 1 tsp salt, without adding water.
Wash and finely chop 1.5 cups spinach and pat it dry, then mix it into the batter with the reserved dal, chopped onion and 12 torn curry leaves.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to about 180C so a bit of batter rises quickly to the top.
Shape small thick patties and slide them into the oil in batches, taking care as the greens can spit.
Fry for 4 to 5 minutes until deep golden and crisp, then drain on paper and serve warm.
tips: Dry the chopped spinach well before mixing, as wet greens cause the oil to splutter and soften the crust.
Add the greens just before frying so they do not wilt and release water into the batter.
Keep the patties a little thinner so the moist, greens-filled centre cooks through fully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a tangy tomato thokku or coconut chutney for a nourishing tea-time snack.

variations.name: Mixed Dal Protein Vada
variations.description: A heartier vada that blends chana dal with toor and moong dal for a deeper flavour and extra protein. The three-lentil mix fries into an especially crunchy, satisfying fritter that stays crisp for hours.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: deep-fries the mixed-dal vadas evenly for a long-lasting crunch

steps: Soak 1 cup chana dal, 0.5 cup toor dal and 0.25 cup moong dal together in 2.5 cups water for 2 hours, then drain very well.
Reserve a small handful of the mixed dal and grind the rest coarsely with 4 dried red chillies, 1 tsp fennel, 4 garlic cloves and 1 tsp salt without water.
Fold in the reserved whole dal, finely chopped onion and 12 torn curry leaves for texture.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to about 180C until a bit of batter sizzles up at once.
Flatten small portions into thick patties and lower them gently into the oil in batches.
Fry for 5 minutes, turning until deep golden and very crisp, then drain and serve hot.
tips: The toor dal adds crunch while moong keeps the centre from turning too dense, so keep the ratio balanced.
Drain the mixed dal thoroughly, as toor holds more water and can slacken the batter.
These stay crisp for hours, making them ideal for packing into a travel or picnic box.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with mint chutney and sliced onion, or crumble over a salad for a protein-rich crunch.

variations.name: Air-Fried Masala Vada
variations.description: A guilt-free version that air-fries the coarse chana dal patties with just a brush of ghee. It delivers the crunchy crust and savoury lentil bite of the classic with a fraction of the oil.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: brushed over the patties so they crisp and brown in the air fryer

steps: Soak 1.5 cups chana dal in 2 cups water for 2 hours, drain well, and reserve a small handful of whole dal.
Grind the rest coarsely with 3 dried red chillies, 1 tsp fennel, 1 inch ginger and 1 tsp salt without water, then mix in the whole dal, chopped onion, 12 curry leaves and 3 tbsp coriander.
Preheat the air fryer to 180C for 3 minutes so it is hot when the vadas go in.
Shape the batter into thick patties, brush both sides generously with Anveshan Ghee, and arrange them in a single layer in the basket.
Air-fry at 180C for 12 minutes, flip and brush with more ghee, then cook another 8 minutes until golden and crisp.
Rest for a minute so the crust firms, then serve hot with chutney.
tips: Brush ghee on both sides and again after flipping, as this is what browns and crisps the crust.
Do not overcrowd the basket; leave space so hot air circulates and every vada crisps evenly.
Make the patties slightly thinner than the fried version so they cook through in the air fryer.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney or a bowl of hot sambar for a lighter evening snack.

variations.name: Classic Medu Vada
variations.description: Medu Vada is the beloved South Indian breakfast doughnut of fluffy fried urad dal, crisp and golden outside and soft as a cloud within. The airy batter, whipped light and shaped with a hole, is the mark of a well-made vada.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a clean wood-pressed oil for deep-frying that keeps the vadas light, not greasy

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups urad dal for 3 to 4 hours, then drain very thoroughly so the batter stays stiff.
Grind the dal to a smooth, fluffy paste using only tiny splashes of water, up to 0.25 cup total, until it is light enough to float a pinch in water.
Whip the batter by hand for 2 minutes to trap air, then fold in 2 chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 1 tsp crushed peppercorns, 1 tsp cumin, 10 torn curry leaves and 1 tsp salt.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai to about 180C, until a drop of batter rises steadily to the surface.
Wet your palm, take a lemon-sized ball of batter, flatten it and poke a hole in the centre, then gently slide it into the hot oil.
Fry 4 to 5 vadas at a time for about 4 minutes, turning until deep golden and crisp all over, then drain on paper and serve hot.
tips: Drain the soaked dal well and grind with minimal water; a watery batter will not hold shape or stay fluffy.
Test doneness by dropping a pinch of batter in water; if it floats, the batter has enough air to fry light.
Keep a bowl of water to wet your hand between shaping vadas so the batter does not stick.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot with coconut chutney and sambar, or dunk into sambar for a classic vada dip.

variations.name: Onion Pepper Medu Vada
variations.description: This crunchier take studs the vada batter with finely chopped onion and cracked pepper for extra bite and a savoury edge. The onion crisps as it fries, giving a delightful texture against the soft interior.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: deep-fries the onion-studded vadas to an even crunchy gold

steps: Soak 1.5 cups urad dal for 3 to 4 hours, drain well, and grind to a smooth fluffy batter using only up to 0.25 cup water.
Whip the batter for a couple of minutes, then fold in 2 tbsp rice flour for extra crunch along with 1 tsp salt.
Mix in the finely chopped onion, 1.5 tsp cracked peppercorns, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger and 12 torn curry leaves just before frying.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to about 180C so a bit of batter sizzles up at once.
Wet your hand, shape a portion into a patty with a central hole, and slide it carefully into the oil.
Fry in batches for 4 to 5 minutes, turning to a deep even gold, then lift onto paper and serve crisp and hot.
tips: Add the onion only just before frying, as salted onion releases water and slackens the batter.
The spoon of rice flour keeps the crust extra crunchy even after the vadas cool a little.
Fry at a steady medium-high; too low and the onion vadas drink oil and turn soggy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a spicy tomato-onion chutney and hot filter coffee for an evening tiffin treat.

variations.name: Appe-Pan Medu Vada
variations.description: A lighter, guilt-free version cooked in a paniyaram (appe) pan with just a little ghee instead of deep-frying. The vadas turn out round, golden and soft, with a fraction of the oil of the classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: spooned into each mould so the vadas brown and lift out cleanly without deep-frying

steps: Soak 1.5 cups urad dal for 3 to 4 hours, drain well, and grind to a light fluffy batter with up to 0.3 cup water, keeping it slightly softer than deep-fry batter.
Whip in air by hand, then fold in 2 chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 1 tsp crushed pepper, 1 tsp cumin, 10 torn curry leaves and 1 tsp salt.
Heat an appe pan on medium and spoon a few drops of Anveshan Ghee into each mould.
Pour a spoon of batter into each mould, filling about three-quarters, and cover for 2 minutes so the tops set and rise.
Add a little more Anveshan Ghee around the edges, then flip each vada with a skewer and cook the other side for 2 minutes until golden.
Turn once more if needed for even browning, then lift out and serve warm and soft.
tips: Keep this batter a touch looser than deep-fry batter so it settles neatly into the moulds.
Cover in the first stage so the tops cook through before you flip and they do not stay raw inside.
A drop of ghee in each cavity before pouring stops sticking and gives a lovely golden crust.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and a small bowl of sambar for a lighter breakfast that skips the deep-frying.

variations.name: Sambar Vada (Vada Sambar)
variations.description: A comforting Tamil-style plate where hot medu vadas are dunked into a bowl of tangy vegetable sambar until they soak up the spiced broth. The soft, flavour-drenched vada is a tiffin-house favourite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for deep-frying the vadas crisp before they soak in the sambar

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: tempers the sambar with an authentic South Indian aroma

steps: Pressure-cook 0.75 cup toor dal with 2 cups water until completely soft, then mash it smooth and keep aside.
Simmer 1.5 cups mixed vegetables with tamarind extract, 2 tbsp sambar powder, 1 tsp salt and 1.5 cups water for 10 minutes until tender, then stir in the mashed dal and loosen with water.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 10 curry leaves, and pour this tempering over the sambar; keep it hot.
Soak 1.5 cups urad dal for 3 hours, drain, and grind to a fluffy batter with minimal water, then whip in 0.5 tsp salt.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C, shape holed vadas with a wet hand, and fry in batches for 4 minutes until crisp and golden.
Dip each hot vada briefly in warm water, squeeze gently, then place in a bowl and ladle the hot sambar over so it soaks through before serving.
tips: A quick dip in warm water before adding sambar helps the vada drink up the broth without turning oily.
Serve within a few minutes of soaking so the vada stays soft but not disintegrated.
Make the sambar slightly thin, as the vadas will absorb liquid and thicken the bowl as they sit.
variations.servingSuggestion: Top with chopped coriander and a spoon of coconut chutney on the side for the full tiffin-centre plate.

variations.name: Classic Neer Dosa
variations.description: Neer Dosa is a soft, lacy rice-and-coconut crepe from the Tulu Nadu coast of Karnataka, where 'neer' means water for its pourably thin batter. It needs no fermentation and no urad dal, cooking up delicate and paper-thin with tiny holes across the surface.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: greases the tawa lightly and gives the dosa its coastal Mangalorean aroma

steps: Rinse and soak 2 cups raw dosa rice in plenty of water for at least 4 hours, then drain it well before grinding.
Grind the soaked rice with 0.5 cup grated coconut, 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and about 1.5 cups water to a very smooth, lump-free batter.
Transfer to a bowl, add 1 tsp salt and thin with the remaining 2 cups water until the batter is as runny as thin milk and coats the back of a spoon only faintly.
Heat a flat tawa over medium-high heat, rub it with a few drops of Anveshan Coconut Oil, and pour a ladle of batter from the outer edge inward so it fills any gaps with a lacy surface.
Cover with a lid and cook for about 2 minutes on medium heat until the top is set, the edges lift and tiny holes appear all over; do not flip.
Fold the soft dosa into a quarter, slide onto a plate, and repeat, stirring the batter each time as the rice tends to settle.
tips: The batter must be watery, not thick, or the dosa will turn dense instead of lacy; always stir before each ladle.
Do not spread the batter with the ladle like a regular dosa; pour and let it find its own level for the classic net texture.
Cook covered and never flip, as neer dosa is steamed-cooked on one side only to stay pillowy soft.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with coconut chutney, a spicy chicken-style veg curry or a drizzle of jaggery syrup and fresh coconut.

variations.name: Mangalorean Coconut Neer Dosa
variations.description: This richer Mangalorean version doubles the fresh coconut so the dosa turns extra soft, faintly sweet and fragrant. It is the way coastal Karnataka homes serve it alongside a fiery coconut curry for weekend breakfasts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
