ingredients.note: brushed on the tawa and stirred into batter for a deep coastal coconut fragrance

steps: Soak 2 cups raw dosa rice for 4 hours, then drain and add it to the grinder with 1 cup grated coconut and 0.25 cup cooked rice for extra softness.
Grind with roughly 1.5 cups water to a silky, thick paste, then pour into a bowl and stir in 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil.
Add 1 tsp salt and loosen the batter with the remaining 2 cups water until it flows freely like thin buttermilk.
Heat a tawa over medium-high, smear it with Anveshan Coconut Oil using a halved onion or cloth, and pour the batter from the rim inward in a swirling motion.
Cover and cook for 2 to 3 minutes until the surface looks dry and glossy with holes and the edges curl away from the pan.
Fold into a triangle without flipping, keep warm under a cloth, and continue with the rest of the batter.
tips: The spoon of cooked rice keeps these dosas supple for hours, ideal for packing into a lunchbox.
Wiping the hot tawa with a halved onion before the first dosa stops sticking better than oil alone.
If the batter thickens on standing, add a splash of water, as coconut-heavy batter tends to firm up.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a coconut-based veg kurma or chana gassi, and finish with sweetened coconut milk for a true coastal spread.

variations.name: Masala Neer Dosa
variations.description: A satisfying stuffed take where soft neer dosas are folded around a lightly spiced coconut-potato filling. It turns the delicate crepe into a complete, portable meal that children and adults both love.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: used for both the tempering of the filling and greasing the tawa

steps: Soak 2 cups raw dosa rice for 4 hours, drain, and grind with 0.5 cup grated coconut and 1.5 cups water to a smooth batter, then loosen with 2 cups water and 1 tsp salt until pourably thin.
Boil 3 potatoes until fork-tender, peel and mash them coarsely while still warm so they mix easily with the tempering.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 10 curry leaves and 2 chopped green chillies and fry for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the chopped onion and saute for 3 minutes until soft, stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.25 tsp salt, then fold in the mashed potato and cook 2 minutes into a dry masala.
Grease a hot tawa with Anveshan Coconut Oil, pour the thin batter from the edge inward, cover and cook 2 minutes until set with a lacy top.
Place a spoon of the warm potato masala along one side, roll or fold the dosa over it, and serve hot with chutney.
tips: Keep the filling dry and not watery, or it will make the soft dosa tear when folded.
Cool the dosa slightly before filling, as a piping-hot crepe is fragile and hard to roll.
Make the masala a little extra and serve any leftovers as a side; it doubles as a quick potato palya.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the rolls with red coconut-chilli chutney and a small bowl of sambar for dunking.

variations.name: Ragi Neer Dosa
variations.description: A wholesome millet twist that blends finger millet with rice for an earthy, iron-rich version of the coastal classic. The ragi lends a warm brown colour and nutty depth while keeping the signature soft, lacy texture.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: brushed over each hot dosa to balance the earthy ragi with a rich aroma

steps: Soak 1.5 cups raw dosa rice for 4 hours, drain, and grind with 0.5 cup grated coconut, 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 1.5 cups water to a smooth batter.
Transfer to a bowl, whisk in 0.5 cup ragi flour a little at a time so no lumps form, then add 1 tsp salt.
Thin the mixture with the remaining 2 cups water until it is runny enough to pour in a thin stream.
Heat a tawa on medium-high, grease lightly, and pour the batter from the outer edge inward, letting it settle into a lacy round on its own.
Cover and cook for about 2 minutes until the top sets, tiny holes form and the edges loosen from the pan.
Brush the hot dosa lightly with Anveshan Ghee, fold into a quarter, and repeat, stirring the batter well before each pour.
tips: Whisk the ragi flour in thoroughly, as it settles fast and can leave a raw streak if poorly mixed.
Ragi batter cooks a touch slower, so give each dosa an extra 20 to 30 seconds under the lid.
A brush of ghee not only adds flavour but keeps the millet dosa from drying out as it cools.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a jaggery-coconut mix or a tangy tomato chutney for a nourishing, high-fibre breakfast.

variations.name: Classic Palak Corn
variations.description: This Classic Palak Corn nestles sweet, juicy corn kernels in a silky bright-green spinach gravy finished with a touch of cream. The natural sugar of the corn plays against the mild earthiness of blanched palak for a curry that is comforting yet vibrant.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the cumin and carries the fresh flavour of the palak puree

steps: Boil the 1.5 cups sweet corn kernels in salted water for 6 minutes until just tender, then drain and set aside.
Blanch the 5 cups spinach in boiling water for 2 minutes, drop into cold water to lock the colour, then blend with the 2 green chillies into a smooth bright puree.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle for about 20 seconds until aromatic.
Add the finely chopped onion and saute for 5 minutes until soft and golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until the raw smell fades.
Add the chopped tomato with 1 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 4 minutes until the tomato collapses and the ghee begins to separate.
Tip in the boiled corn, stir for 2 minutes, then pour in the spinach puree with half a cup of water and simmer on low for 5 minutes.
Swirl in 2 tbsp cream and 0.5 tsp garam masala off high heat, warm through for 1 minute and serve hot.
tips: Shock the spinach in ice water right after blanching so the gravy stays a vivid green instead of turning olive.
Add the cream only on low heat and stir gently so it blends smoothly without splitting.
For extra sweetness use fresh milky corn in season, or blanch frozen kernels for 3 minutes.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulkas or jeera rice and a wedge of lemon on the side for a light home-style meal.

variations.name: Punjabi Palak Corn
variations.description: A hearty Punjabi take where the corn simmers in a robust spinach base built on slow-browned onions, ginger and a generous knob of butter. It leans thick and rustic, closer to a saag, and is meant to be scooped up with makki or tandoori roti.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the onion masala to a deep Punjabi brown and enriches the thick saag

steps: Pressure-cook or boil the 6 cups spinach with the 2 green chillies for 5 minutes, cool slightly and coarsely blend so a little texture remains in the saag.
Boil the 1.5 cups corn kernels in salted water for 6 minutes until tender, then drain and keep aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them sizzle for 20 seconds.
Add the finely chopped onions and fry patiently for 8 to 10 minutes until deep golden, then add the crushed ginger and garlic and cook 1 minute.
Stir in the chopped tomatoes with 1 tsp chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and bhuno for 6 minutes until the ghee pools at the edges.
Add the boiled corn and the spinach puree, lower the heat and simmer uncovered for 8 minutes so the saag thickens and mellows.
Crush 1 tsp kasuri methi over the top, stir once and finish with a small extra spoon of ghee before serving.
tips: Coarsely blend rather than fully pureeing the spinach to get the rustic saag texture Punjabi kitchens prefer.
A pinch of sugar or the corn's own sweetness balances the slight bitterness of the greens.
Let the saag rest for ten minutes off heat so the flavours deepen before you serve.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best with makki di roti or a thick tandoori roti, topped with a dab of white butter and sliced onions.

variations.name: Creamy Malai Palak Corn
variations.description: A restaurant-style rendition made luxuriously smooth with a cashew paste and malai, giving the green gravy a pale, glossy sheen. The corn stays plump and sweet against the mild, buttery spinach for a party-worthy curry that even fussy eaters love.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: adds a smooth richness that ties the cashew and malai gravy together

steps: Soak the 12 cashews in warm water for 10 minutes, then blend to a smooth thick paste with a little of the soaking water.
Blanch the 5 cups spinach for 2 minutes, refresh in cold water and blend with the 2 green chillies to a fine puree.
Boil the 1.5 cups corn kernels in salted water for 6 minutes until tender and drain.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat, add 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, then the finely chopped onion and saute for 5 minutes until soft but not browned to keep the gravy pale.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute, then stir in the cashew paste and 1 tsp coriander powder and cook gently for 3 minutes.
Pour in the spinach puree with the boiled corn and 1 tsp salt, add half a cup of water and simmer on low for 5 minutes.
Lower the heat fully, swirl in 4 tbsp cream and 0.5 tsp garam masala, warm for 2 minutes without boiling and serve glossy and hot.
tips: Keep the onion pale and avoid browning so the malai gravy holds its soft green colour.
Reserve a spoon of cream to swirl on top just before serving for a restaurant-style finish.
Blend the cashews very smooth so there is no graininess in the final curry.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or laccha paratha and a saffron pulao for a festive vegetarian spread.

variations.name: No-Onion-No-Garlic Palak Corn
variations.description: A satvik palak corn that skips onion and garlic and leans on asafoetida, ginger and ripe tomato for its savoury depth. Light and clean-tasting, it suits fasting days and Jain kitchens while keeping the sweet corn and fresh spinach front and centre.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the cumin and hing that build flavour in place of onion and garlic

steps: Blanch the 5 cups spinach for 2 minutes, refresh in cold water and blend with the 2 green chillies and 8 cashews into a smooth green puree.
Boil the 1.5 cups corn kernels in salted water for 6 minutes until tender and drain.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them sizzle for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add the grated ginger and the finely chopped tomatoes with 1 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 5 minutes until the tomato turns pulpy.
Stir in the boiled corn and cook for 2 minutes so it takes on the tempered flavour.
Pour in the spinach-cashew puree with half a cup of water and simmer on low for 6 minutes until the gravy is creamy and thickened.
Finish with 0.5 tsp garam masala, rest for 5 minutes off heat and serve so the satvik flavours settle.
tips: Use fully ripe red tomatoes for natural sweetness and body since there is no onion base here.
The cashews lend the creaminess that a browned onion base would otherwise provide.
A pinch of dry ginger powder can be added for extra warmth on a fasting day.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice or soft satvik rotis and a cooling cucumber raita for an everyday meal.

variations.name: Classic Pani Puri
variations.description: This Classic Pani Puri is India's most loved street snack of hollow crisp semolina puris filled with spiced potato-chickpea stuffing and a shot of cool, tangy mint-coriander water. Each puri bursts in the mouth with a rush of sour, spicy, sweet and minty flavours in a single crunchy bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: deep-frying in wood-pressed groundnut oil puffs the puris crisp and hollow

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: balances the tangy pani with a natural sweetness in place of refined sugar

steps: Knead 1 cup semolina with 2 tbsp fine flour and about 6 tbsp water into a stiff, smooth dough, cover and rest for 20 minutes.
Roll the dough thin, cut small rounds, and deep-fry them in hot Anveshan Groundnut Oil at medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes, pressing gently until each puffs into a crisp hollow puri.
Blend 1 cup mint, 0.5 cup coriander, 3 green chillies and 1 inch ginger into a smooth paste with a little water.
Stir the paste into 4 cups chilled water with 3 tbsp tamarind pulp, 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1.5 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp black salt and 1 tsp salt, then chill the pani for 30 minutes.
Mash the 2 boiled potatoes with the 0.5 cup boiled chickpeas, 1 tsp chaat masala and a pinch of salt to make the filling.
Crack a small hole in each puri, spoon in the potato-chickpea filling, dip fully into the spiced pani, and eat immediately before it softens.
tips: Fry the puris at steady medium heat and press them under the oil so they puff evenly and stay crisp for days.
Chill the pani thoroughly and add a few boondi or mint leaves floating on top for an authentic touch.
Store the fried puris airtight and fill only at the moment of serving so they never turn soggy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the puris, filling and chilled pani separately so each person can assemble and pop them one crunchy bite at a time.

variations.name: Meetha Khajur-Imli Pani Puri
variations.description: A sweeter version built around a dark date-tamarind meetha pani alongside the spicy one, giving eaters the classic double-water experience. The khajur-imli water is thick, jammy and mellow, a soothing contrast to the fiery teekha pani.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: a light wood-pressed oil that fries the puris crisp without a heavy aftertaste

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: gives the date-tamarind pani its deep caramel sweetness

steps: Knead 1 cup semolina with 2 tbsp flour and 6 tbsp water into a firm dough, rest 20 minutes, roll thin, cut rounds and deep-fry in Anveshan Sunflower Oil at medium heat until puffed and crisp.
Soak the 8 dates and 4 tbsp tamarind in warm water for 15 minutes until soft.
Blend the soaked dates and tamarind with 4 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder into a smooth thick paste and pass it through a sieve.
Loosen the paste with 3 cups chilled water and stir in 1.5 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp dry ginger powder, 1 tsp black salt, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, then chill the meetha pani.
Mash the 2 boiled potatoes with 0.5 cup boiled moong sprouts and 1 tsp chaat masala for a lighter filling.
Crack each puri, add the filling, and dip generously into the sweet date-tamarind pani before eating at once.
tips: Sieve the date-tamarind paste well so the meetha pani pours cleanly without stringy fibres.
Keep the meetha pani slightly thicker than the spicy pani so it clings inside the puri.
A pinch of dry ginger powder deepens the warmth and keeps the sweet water from feeling flat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Offer both the sweet and a spicy pani side by side so guests can dip each puri in their favourite or alternate between the two.

variations.name: Banarasi Hing-Jeera Pani Puri
variations.description: The Banarasi style favours a pungent, digestive pani sharp with asafoetida, roasted cumin and black pepper rather than heavy mint. Locals call it the hing-jeera jal, and it is prized for its bracing, appetite-whetting kick over sweetness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: traditional wood-pressed groundnut oil fries the puris to a sturdy Banarasi crisp

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: just a touch balances the sharp hing-jeera water without making it sweet

steps: Knead 1 cup semolina with 2 tbsp flour and 6 tbsp water into a stiff dough, rest 20 minutes, then roll thin, cut rounds and deep-fry in Anveshan Groundnut Oil at medium heat until they puff crisp and hollow.
Blend 0.5 cup mint, 0.5 cup coriander and 3 green chillies into a fine paste with a little water.

Whisk the paste into 4 cups chilled water with 3 tbsp tamarind pulp, 0.5 tsp asafoetida, 2 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp black pepper, 1.5 tsp black salt, 1 tsp salt and 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder.
Rest the pani in the fridge for 30 minutes so the asafoetida and spices infuse into a sharp, digestive water.
Mash the 3 boiled potatoes with a pinch of black salt and roasted cumin to make a simple spiced filling.
Poke a hole in each puri, spoon in the potato filling, dip deep into the pungent hing-jeera pani and eat before it softens.
tips: Bloom the asafoetida by dissolving it in a little warm water first so it disperses evenly through the pani.
Keep sweetness minimal here, as the Banarasi character comes from the sharp, spicy, digestive profile.
Let the pani rest at least half an hour so the hing and cumin mellow into a rounded pungency.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve this bracing pani in small kulhads alongside the filled puris for a true Banaras-ghat experience.

variations.name: Ragda Pani Puri
variations.description: A Mumbai stall favourite where the puris are filled with warm spiced white-pea ragda instead of dry potato, then topped with both sweet and spicy waters. The hot, creamy ragda against the cold tangy pani makes for an indulgent, meal-like chaat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: light wood-pressed oil for frying puris that hold up to warm ragda filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the meetha pani that tops the savoury ragda-filled puris

steps: Knead 1 cup semolina with 2 tbsp flour and 6 tbsp water into a firm dough, rest 20 minutes, roll thin, cut rounds and deep-fry in Anveshan Sunflower Oil at medium heat until puffed and crisp.
Pressure-cook 1 cup soaked white peas with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 2.5 cups water for 6 whistles, then mash lightly into a warm, thick ragda.

Blend 1 cup mint, 0.5 cup coriander and 3 green chillies, then stir into 3 cups chilled water with 3 tbsp tamarind, 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1.5 tsp roasted cumin, 1 tsp black salt and 0.5 tsp salt.
Chill the sweet-spicy pani for 30 minutes while keeping the ragda warm on a low flame.
Crack a hole in each puri and spoon in a little warm ragda until half full.
Top each ragda-filled puri with a splash of chilled pani, a pinch of chaat masala and a sprinkle of nylon sev, and eat right away while hot and cold mingle.
tips: Keep the ragda pourable but not runny so it fills the puri without collapsing the crisp shell.
Fill with ragda and top with pani only at the last second, as this version softens fastest.
A sprinkle of sev and finely chopped onion on top adds crunch against the creamy ragda.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a plate rather than by hand, since these ragda-filled puris are best eaten with a spoon as they brim over.

variations.name: Classic Papdi Chaat
variations.description: This Classic Papdi Chaat layers crisp fried flour papdis with soft boiled potato and chickpeas, cool whisked yogurt, and tangy tamarind and green chutneys. Finished with sev, roasted cumin and coriander, it is the quintessential North Indian chaat of crunch, creaminess and sweet-sour spice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: deep-frying the papdi in wood-pressed oil gives crisp, sturdy, non-greasy discs

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the tamarind chutney and yogurt with a natural depth

steps: Knead 1.5 cups refined flour with 0.5 tsp salt, 0.5 tsp ajwain and 2 tbsp of the oil into a stiff dough with about 6 tbsp water, then rest 20 minutes.
Roll the dough thin, prick well with a fork, cut 24 rounds, and deep-fry in Anveshan Groundnut Oil at medium heat for 3 minutes each until flat, crisp and pale golden.
Whisk the 2.5 cups yogurt smooth with 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.5 tsp salt and chill it.
Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder for 5 minutes into a thick sweet-sour chutney.
Arrange the papdis on a platter, top each with a little mashed boiled potato and a few boiled chickpeas.

Spoon the chilled yogurt over generously, drizzle tamarind and green chutney, dust with 1.5 tsp roasted cumin, 0.5 tsp red chilli and 0.5 tsp black salt, and finish with sev and coriander to serve at once.
tips: Prick the papdi dough well before frying so the discs stay flat and turn shatteringly crisp.
Assemble just before serving so the papdis keep their crunch under the yogurt.
Fry the papdis a day ahead and store airtight, since they keep crisp for over a week.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a wide platter so each papdi holds its toppings, with extra chutney and sev on the side.

variations.name: Palak Patta Chaat
variations.description: This Lucknawi favourite swaps papdi for whole spinach leaves fried in a crisp gram-flour batter, then loaded with yogurt and chutneys. The crackling battered leaves stay crisp under the toppings, offering a greener, more delicate crunch than plain papdi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: deep-frying the battered spinach in wood-pressed oil gives a shatter-crisp coating

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the tamarind chutney and yogurt to balance the crisp greens

steps: Whisk 1 cup besan with 0.5 tsp salt, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and enough water to make a smooth, coating batter.
Dip each of the 20 spinach leaves in the batter and deep-fry in Anveshan Groundnut Oil at medium-high heat for 2 to 3 minutes until crisp and golden, then drain.
Whisk the 2.5 cups yogurt smooth with 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.5 tsp salt and chill.
Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder for 5 minutes into a thick sweet-sour chutney.
Arrange the crisp spinach fritters on a platter and spoon the chilled yogurt over them.
Drizzle with tamarind and green chutney, dust with 1.5 tsp roasted cumin and 0.5 tsp black salt, and finish with sev, pomegranate and coriander to serve immediately.
tips: Keep the besan batter thin enough to just cling so the leaves fry crisp and lacy, not thick and doughy.
Fry the leaves in small batches at steady heat so they crisp evenly without absorbing oil.
Top and serve within a couple of minutes, as the battered leaves soften once the yogurt goes on.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as an elegant starter, arranged in a single layer and showered with pomegranate for a jewelled finish.

variations.name: Sattu Papdi Chaat
variations.description: A nourishing Bihari-inspired twist where the papdis are made with protein-rich roasted gram flour and the potato is swapped for a spiced sattu-chickpea layer. It delivers all the crunch and tang of classic papdi chaat with a wholesome, high-protein base.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: roasted gram sattu makes protein-rich papdis and a nutty spiced base layer

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: deep-frying the sattu papdis in wood-pressed oil keeps them crisp and light

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the tamarind chutney and yogurt over the earthy sattu

steps: Knead 0.5 cup Anveshan Sattu with 0.75 cup refined flour, 0.5 tsp salt and about 6 tbsp water into a stiff dough and rest 15 minutes.
Roll the dough thin, prick well, cut 24 rounds, and deep-fry in Anveshan Groundnut Oil at medium heat for 3 minutes each until crisp and golden.
Mix the remaining 0.5 cup Anveshan Sattu with the boiled chickpeas, 0.5 tsp black salt and a little water into a thick, spoonable spiced layer.
Whisk the 2.5 cups yogurt smooth with 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.5 tsp salt and chill, then simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder into a chutney.
Arrange the sattu papdis on a platter and top each with a spoon of the sattu-chickpea layer.
Spoon over the chilled yogurt, drizzle tamarind and green chutney, dust with 1.5 tsp roasted cumin, and finish with sev and coriander to serve at once.
tips: Blend the sattu with a little flour so the papdis roll out smoothly and fry crisp rather than crumbly.
Loosen the sattu layer with just enough water to spread, as sattu thickens quickly on standing.
The nutty sattu pairs beautifully with tangy yogurt, so keep the chutneys balanced and not too sweet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a high-protein snack or light meal, finished with extra roasted cumin and fresh coriander.

variations.name: Fruit Papdi Chaat
variations.description: A refreshing summer version that tops the crisp papdis with diced seasonal fruit like pomegranate, banana and guava alongside the yogurt and chutneys. Sweet, tangy and cooling, it is a lighter, fruitier spin on the traditional chaat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil fries crisp papdis to hold the juicy fruit toppings

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the tamarind chutney and yogurt to complement the fresh fruit

steps: Knead 1.5 cups refined flour with 0.5 tsp salt and 6 tbsp water into a stiff dough, roll thin, prick, cut 24 rounds, and deep-fry in Anveshan Groundnut Oil at medium heat until flat and crisp.
Whisk the 2 cups yogurt smooth with 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.25 tsp salt and chill.
Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder for 5 minutes into a sweet-sour chutney and cool it.
Dice the banana and guava and toss with the pomegranate, 1 tsp chaat masala and 0.5 tsp black salt.
Arrange the crisp papdis on a platter and top each with the spiced fruit mix.
Spoon the chilled yogurt over, drizzle tamarind and green chutney, dust with the remaining chaat masala and 1 tsp roasted cumin, and finish with sev and coriander to serve at once.
tips: Toss the banana in the chutney or lime at once so it does not brown before serving.
Choose firm, slightly tart fruit so it holds shape and cuts through the sweet chutney.
Assemble at the last minute so the papdis stay crisp under the juicy fruit and yogurt.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a light, refreshing summer chaat, topped with extra pomegranate and a dusting of chaat masala.

variations.name: Classic Pesarattu
variations.description: Pesarattu is an Andhra breakfast dosa made from whole green gram rather than rice and urad dal, so it needs no fermentation. It cooks up green-flecked and lightly crisp, high in protein and traditionally spread with a paste of ginger, green chilli and cumin.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: drizzled at the edges to crisp the dosa the way Andhra tiffin centres do

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups whole green moong with 0.25 cup raw rice for 5 to 6 hours until the grains swell and soften.
Drain and grind with 3 green chillies, 1 inch ginger, 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 tsp salt and about 1 cup water to a slightly coarse, thick batter.
The batter should be thick yet spreadable like regular dosa batter; adjust with a little water and use it straight away with no fermentation.
Heat a tawa on medium, pour a ladle in the centre and spread outward in a spiral into a medium-thick round.
Scatter finely chopped onion over the top, press lightly, and drizzle Anveshan Groundnut Oil around the edges.
Cook for 2 to 3 minutes until the base is golden and crisp, flip for 1 minute, then fold and serve hot.
tips: A handful of rice in the grind helps the pesarattu crisp up rather than staying rubbery.
Grind the batter slightly coarse for the authentic texture; a paste-smooth batter turns gummy.
Spread the batter a touch thicker than a plain dosa, as green gram cooks best with a little body.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the classic way with ginger chutney (allam pachadi) and a bowl of upma tucked inside as MLA pesarattu.

variations.name: MLA Pesarattu with Upma
variations.description: The iconic MLA pesarattu of Andhra tiffin houses folds a soft rava upma into the crisp green-gram dosa. The pairing of nutty upma and lentil crepe makes it a hearty, restaurant-style breakfast in one fold.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the rava for the upma and crisps the dosa edges with rich flavour

steps: Soak 1.5 cups whole green moong with 0.25 cup rice for 5 hours, drain, and grind with 3 green chillies, 1 inch ginger, 1 tsp salt and 1 cup water to a thick, slightly coarse batter.
For the upma, heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, add 10 curry leaves and chopped onion and saute 3 minutes, then roast 1 cup rava for 2 minutes until fragrant.
Pour in 2.5 cups hot water with 0.5 tsp salt, stir continuously off high heat, cover, and cook 3 minutes until the upma is soft and fluffy, then keep warm.
Heat a tawa on medium, spread a ladle of the green-gram batter into a medium-thick round, and drizzle Anveshan Ghee around the edges.
Cook for 3 minutes until the base is crisp and golden, then place a generous line of warm upma across one half.
Fold the pesarattu over the upma into a half-moon, press gently, and serve immediately with chutney.
tips: Keep the upma soft and not dry so the folded pesarattu stays moist inside.
Make the dosa slightly larger than usual to comfortably wrap around the upma filling.
Roast the rava well before adding water, as under-roasted rava makes a sticky, lumpy upma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with allam pachadi (ginger chutney) and coconut chutney, the classic duo for MLA pesarattu.

variations.name: Oats Pesarattu
variations.description: A fibre-boosted twist that blends rolled oats into the green-gram batter for a lighter, heart-friendly dosa. It keeps the protein of moong while adding the soluble fibre of oats, staying crisp at the edges and soft within.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a light wood-pressed oil to crisp the edges without heaviness

steps: Soak 1.5 cups whole green moong for 5 hours, then drain and add to the grinder with 0.5 cup rolled oats.
Grind with 3 green chillies, 1 inch ginger, 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 tsp salt and about 1.25 cups water to a thick, spreadable batter and use it fresh.
Mix 3 tbsp chopped coriander into the batter for freshness and check the consistency is like a dosa batter.
Heat a tawa on medium, pour a ladle in the centre and spread outward into a thin-to-medium round.
Sprinkle finely chopped onion over the top and drizzle Anveshan Groundnut Oil around the rim.
Cook 2 to 3 minutes until crisp and golden underneath, flip for 1 minute, then fold and serve warm.
tips: Powder the oats slightly in the grinder first if you prefer a smoother, more even batter.
Oats thicken the batter as it stands, so keep a little extra water handy to loosen it.
Spread these a touch thinner for maximum crispness, as the oats can otherwise feel dense.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a light coriander-mint chutney and a bowl of curd for a wholesome, low-guilt breakfast.

variations.name: Cheese Corn Pesarattu
variations.description: A playful, kid-friendly version that tops the crisp green-gram dosa with sweet corn and melting cheese. It sneaks protein-rich moong into a fussy eater's plate while still tasting like a treat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: crisps the base and helps the cheese melt into a golden top

steps: Soak 1.5 cups whole green moong with 0.25 cup raw rice for 5 hours, drain, and grind with 2 green chillies, 1 inch ginger, 1 tsp salt and 1 cup water to a thick batter.
Steam or boil 0.75 cup sweet corn kernels for 3 minutes until just tender, then keep ready.
Heat a tawa on medium, pour a ladle of batter and spread into a medium-thick round.
Scatter a spoon of chopped onion, a handful of sweet corn and 0.75 cup grated cheese over the top, then drizzle Anveshan Ghee around the edges.
Cover for 2 minutes so the cheese melts, then uncover and cook until the base turns crisp and golden.
Fold the dosa in half over the melted cheese and corn, cut across, and serve hot to eager kids.
tips: Cover the dosa briefly so the cheese melts before the base over-browns.
Use a mild cheese that melts smoothly rather than a sharp one children may reject.
Keep the batter slightly thick so it holds the weight of the corn and cheese topping.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a mild tomato chutney or ketchup on the side for a fun, protein-packed after-school snack.

variations.name: Classic Plain Dosa
variations.description: The everyday South Indian crepe: a naturally fermented rice-and-urad batter spread thin on a hot tava and cooked until lacy and golden at the edges. Crisp on the outside and soft where it meets the pan, a good plain dosa is all about the ferment and the sizzle of gingelly oil on cast iron.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: A drizzle of gingelly oil around each dosa is what crisps the edges and seasons the tava

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A smear of ghee on the last dosa gives an aromatic, golden finish

steps: Soak 2 cups dosa rice in one bowl, and 1/2 cup urad dal with 1 tbsp chana dal and 1/2 tsp fenugreek seeds in another, for 5 to 6 hours; soak 2 tbsp poha for the last 30 minutes.
Grind the dal and fenugreek to a smooth, fluffy batter, then grind the rice and poha to a fine paste, using about 2 cups water so the combined batter is smooth and just pourable.
Mix both batters with 1.25 tsp salt, cover, and ferment in a warm place for 8 to 12 hours until risen and bubbly.

Stir the fermented batter and thin it with a little water to an easily spreadable, pourable consistency; heat a cast-iron tava on medium-high until a sprinkle of water skitters and evaporates at once.
Pour a ladleful of batter in the centre and spread it in a quick outward spiral into a thin circle, then drizzle 1/2 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil around the edges.

Cook for about 2 minutes until the base is golden-brown and crisp and the surface looks dry, then fold and remove; wipe the tava, brush the last dosa with Anveshan Ghee, and serve each dosa hot off the pan.
tips: Rub a halved onion over the hot tava before the first dosa to season it and stop sticking.
If the tava is too hot the batter clumps; sprinkle a little water and wipe it before the next dosa to reset the temperature.
Slightly thinner batter gives crisper dosas, so adjust with water one ladle at a time.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve straight off the tava with coconut chutney, sambar and a spoon of gingelly-oil idli podi.

variations.name: Masala Dosa
variations.description: The restaurant classic: a golden crisp dosa wrapped around a soft potato masala tempered with mustard, curry leaves and turmeric-tinted onions. The contrast of the shatteringly crisp crepe and the mellow spiced potato inside makes it the most loved dosa on any South Indian menu.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil crisps the dosa and tempers the potato masala the South Indian way

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A brush of ghee on the dosa gives the classic hotel-style golden, aromatic crust

steps: Boil 4 potatoes until soft, peel and roughly mash them; heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pan and splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds with 1 tbsp chana dal until golden.
Add 2 sliced onions, 2 slit green chillies, 1 inch minced ginger and 15 curry leaves and saute for 4 minutes until the onions soften, then stir in 1/2 tsp turmeric.
Add the mashed potato with 1/4 cup water and 1.25 tsp salt, mix to a soft, lump-free masala, cook 3 minutes, fold in 3 tbsp coriander, and keep warm.
Heat a cast-iron tava on medium-high, pour a ladle of dosa batter and spread it thin, then drizzle 1/2 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil around the edge and cook until the base is deep golden and crisp.
Brush the crisp dosa with a little Anveshan Ghee, place a portion of potato masala along the centre, and fold the dosa over it into a roll or half-moon.
Slide it onto a plate and serve at once, repeating for the remaining dosas while the masala stays warm.
tips: Keep the potato masala soft and slightly moist so it spreads easily and does not tear the crisp dosa.
Let the dosa cook undisturbed until the edges lift on their own; flipping too early makes it soggy instead of crisp.
A well-seasoned cast-iron tava gives the crispest masala dosa, so avoid a cold or freshly washed pan.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney, tomato chutney and a bowl of hot sambar, exactly like a Bengaluru darshini plate.

variations.name: Ghee Roast Dosa
variations.description: A luxurious, extra-crisp dosa roasted entirely in ghee until it turns a deep reddish-gold and shatters at the touch. Often smeared with a fiery red chilli-garlic paste before rolling into a tall cone, the ghee roast is the indulgent showpiece of any tiffin menu.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: This dosa is roasted generously in ghee, which is what gives it the deep golden crunch and aroma

steps: Soak 5 dried red chillies and 5 g tamarind in 1/4 cup hot water for 10 minutes, then grind with 6 garlic cloves, 1/2 tsp cumin seeds and 1/2 tsp salt to a thick, smooth red paste.
Stir the fermented batter and thin it slightly to a spreadable consistency; heat a cast-iron tava on medium heat until evenly hot.
Pour a ladle of batter and spread it thin, then generously drizzle about 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee around and over the dosa.
Roast on medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes without flipping, spreading a little more ghee, until the base turns a deep reddish-gold and crisps all over.
Smear 1 to 2 tsp of the red chilli-garlic paste over the crisp surface and sprinkle a little idli podi across it.
Fold or roll the dosa tightly into a cone or triangle while still crisp, and serve immediately before it softens.
tips: Roast on medium, not high heat; ghee roast needs time to crisp evenly into that signature reddish colour.
Do not flip a ghee roast dosa — it is cooked on one side only so the top stays soft and the base shatters.
Keep the chilli-garlic paste thick so it clings to the dosa instead of making it soggy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the crisp cone with coconut chutney and sambar, and an extra bowl of the red chutney for dipping.

variations.name: Podi Dosa
variations.description: A quick, addictive dosa lavished with spicy gingelly-oil podi that soaks into the crisp crepe. The gunpowder-and-oil smear turns a plain dosa into a bold, fiery snack, folded into a triangle and eaten hot with nothing more than a bit of chutney.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil is mixed with the podi to make the classic spicy smear and to crisp the dosa

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A little ghee added to the podi smear rounds the heat and adds aroma

steps: In a small bowl mix 5 tbsp idli podi with 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee to a thick, spreadable paste; finely chop 1 onion.
Stir the fermented batter and thin it to a spreadable consistency; heat a cast-iron tava on medium-high until hot.
Pour a ladle of batter, spread it thin into a circle, and drizzle 1/2 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil around the edges.
Once the base begins to crisp, spread 1 to 2 tsp of the podi-oil paste evenly over the top and scatter a little chopped onion and a few torn curry leaves.
Cook for 2 to 3 minutes until the underside is deep golden and crisp and the podi has soaked in and turned fragrant.
Fold the dosa into a triangle, press lightly, and serve hot; repeat for the remaining dosas.
tips: Adjust the podi paste heat by mixing in a little more oil if your gunpowder is very spicy.
Press the onions gently into the batter so they stick and lightly char instead of falling off.
Use a fresh, aromatic idli podi; stale gunpowder makes a dull-tasting podi dosa.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a cooling coconut chutney and a glass of buttermilk to balance the fiery podi.

variations.name: Classic Temple Puliyodarai
variations.description: The revered Tamil Nadu temple prasadam, where rice is bathed in a slow-cooked tamarind pulikachal thick with sesame, roasted gram and a fragrant homemade puli podi. Unlike everyday tamarind rice, temple puliyodarai is darker, oilier and matured, so the flavours deepen for hours. Served on a banana leaf, it is the taste of countless Perumal koils across the south.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Temple puliyodarai is generously oiled with gingelly so it keeps for a full day without souring

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A traditional pinch of jaggery mellows the pulikachal's fierce sourness

ingredients.name: Fenugreek seeds
ingredients.note: Roasted and ground into the puli podi, never used raw

steps: Cook 1.5 cups rice with 3 cups water until the grains are firm and separate, spread on a wide plate to cool, and drizzle over 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and 1/4 tsp turmeric.
For the puli podi, dry-roast 1/2 tsp fenugreek, 2 tbsp sesame seeds and 3 red chillies on low heat until the fenugreek is reddish and aromatic, cool and grind to a fine fragrant powder.
Soak the large tamarind ball in 1.5 cups hot water for 15 minutes and squeeze out a thick, dark extract.
Heat 5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a heavy kadhai, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then fry 2 tbsp chana dal, 1 tbsp urad dal and 1/4 cup peanuts until deep golden, about 3 minutes.
Add 3 remaining red chillies, 15 curry leaves and 1/2 tsp asafoetida, fry 20 seconds, then pour in the tamarind extract with 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1.5 tsp salt.

Simmer this pulikachal on low-medium heat for 15 minutes, stirring often, until it turns almost black, thick and the sesame oil floats clearly on top, then mix in the ground puli podi and cook 2 minutes more.
Fold the cooled rice into the kadhai a little at a time until every grain glistens dark and even; cover and rest at least 30 minutes so the temple flavours mature before serving.
tips: The pulikachal is ready only when oil separates and floats; under-cooked, it tastes raw and will not keep like true temple prasadam.
Puliyodarai genuinely tastes better after a few hours, so make it well ahead and never refrigerate before the flavours have matured.
Store leftover pulikachal under a layer of sesame oil in a glass jar; a spoonful revives plain rice on any busy day.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a banana leaf with a papad, a spoon of thick curd and fried mor milagai (curd chillies) for the complete temple-prasadam experience.

variations.name: Iyengar Puli Sadam
variations.description: The Iyengar household version passed down through generations, milder in chilli but layered with dry coconut, coriander seed and extra roasted gram for a rounder, nuttier profile. No onion or garlic touches this pot, keeping it strictly satvik. It is the puliyodarai that mothers pack for long train journeys because it survives the heat and only improves with time.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: The satvik Iyengar kitchen relies on pure gingelly oil for both cooking and keeping quality

ingredients.name: Fenugreek seeds
ingredients.note: Roasted with the podi spices to avoid any raw bitterness

steps: Cook 1.5 cups rice with 3 cups water to firm, separate grains, spread out to cool and toss with 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and 1/4 tsp turmeric.

For the Iyengar podi, dry-roast 2 tbsp chana dal, 1 tbsp coriander seeds, 1/2 tsp fenugreek, 1 tbsp sesame seeds, 3 red chillies and 3 tbsp dry coconut on low heat until golden and fragrant, cool and grind to a coarse powder.
Soak the large tamarind ball in 1.5 cups hot water and squeeze out a thick extract.
Heat 5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then fry 1 tbsp chana dal, 1 tbsp urad dal and 1/4 cup peanuts until golden brown, about 3 minutes.
Add 2 remaining red chillies, 15 curry leaves and 1/2 tsp asafoetida, fry 20 seconds, then pour in the tamarind extract with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp salt.
Simmer the pulikachal 12 minutes until thick and oil-glossed, stir in the coconut-gram podi and cook another 2 minutes to a fragrant, spoon-coating paste.
Mix the cooled rice into the paste gently and thoroughly, then rest covered for at least 30 minutes so the satvik flavours settle before serving.
tips: Dry coconut and roasted gram give this version its nutty roundness; use fresh coconut only if you plan to eat it the same day, as it shortens shelf life.
Iyengar puli sadam is deliberately gentle on heat, so the dish keeps well and suits children and elders alike.
For travel, pack it slightly extra-oily and it will stay perfect and unrefrigerated for up to a day.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with vathal (sun-dried fryums), a small mound of curd rice and a piece of appalam for a classic Iyengar meal.

variations.name: Kalyana Puliyodarai
variations.description: The lavish wedding-feast rendition served on Tamil Nadu's banquet leaves, richer with cashews alongside peanuts and an extra-thick pulikachal for a bold, festive punch. Caterers make it in vast urulis so the flavours have hours to deepen before the muhurtham lunch. Glossy, generously nutty and unforgettably tangy, it is the puliyodarai that guests remember long after the wedding.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Caterers use gingelly oil lavishly for the signature banquet gloss and aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A festive spoon of ghee to fry the cashews for wedding-style richness

ingredients.name: Fenugreek seeds
ingredients.note: Roasted into the podi so it never tastes raw

steps: Cook 1.5 cups rice with 3 cups water to firm, separate grains, spread out to cool and coat with 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and 1/4 tsp turmeric.
For the festive podi, dry-roast 1/2 tsp fenugreek, 2 tbsp sesame seeds and 4 red chillies on low heat until deeply aromatic, cool and grind fine.
Soak the large tamarind ball in 1.75 cups hot water and extract a thick, dark pulp.

Fry 3 tbsp cashews in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until golden and set aside, then in the same kadhai heat 5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and fry 2 tbsp chana dal, 1 tbsp urad dal and 1/4 cup peanuts until golden.
Add 3 remaining red chillies, 18 curry leaves and 1/2 tsp asafoetida, fry 20 seconds, then pour in the tamarind extract with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1.75 tsp salt.
Simmer the pulikachal 15 minutes until very thick, glossy and oil-separated, stir in the ground podi and the fried cashews, and cook 2 minutes more.
Fold the cooled rice through the rich paste until every grain is coated deep and glossy, then rest covered at least 45 minutes so it matures to banquet standard.
tips: Wedding puliyodarai is made bolder and slightly saltier than home versions because it is eaten in small quantities alongside many other dishes.
Frying the cashews in ghee before the main tempering keeps them crunchy right through the resting period.
The longer this sits, the better it tastes, so caterers always make it the night before the function.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a banana leaf as part of a South Indian wedding spread, next to vada, payasam and a spoon of thick curd.

variations.name: Instant Puliyodarai from Podi
variations.description: A pantry-clever shortcut that builds the whole dish around a fast homemade puliyodarai podi and ready tamarind, delivering temple flavour on a weeknight timeline. The concentrated podi carries the sesame, gram and chilli notes that would otherwise take a long simmer to develop. Ideal when the craving strikes but there is no time for a slow pulikachal.

ingredients.name: Cooked rice
ingredients.note: Cooled with separate grains

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Carries the gingelly aroma essential to any puliyodarai, even a quick one

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Balances the fast tamarind base without a long reduction

ingredients.name: Chana dal
ingredients.note: Two tbsp roasted into the podi, one tbsp fried in the tempering

ingredients.name: Fenugreek seeds
ingredients.note: Roasted into the podi, never raw

steps: Dry-roast 2 tbsp chana dal, 2 tbsp sesame seeds, 3 red chillies and 1/4 tsp fenugreek on low heat until golden and fragrant, cool and grind to a coarse puliyodarai podi.
Spread 4 cups cooled rice on a plate and fluff with 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil so the grains stay separate.
Soak the small tamarind ball in 3/4 cup hot water for 10 minutes and squeeze out a thick extract.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then fry the remaining 1 tbsp chana dal and 1/4 cup peanuts until golden, about 3 minutes.
Add 2 remaining red chillies, 12 curry leaves and 1/2 tsp asafoetida, fry 20 seconds, then pour in the tamarind extract with 1/2 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1.25 tsp salt.
Simmer 6 minutes until the mixture thickens and the oil just begins to separate, then stir in the ground podi and cook 1 minute more.
Add the fluffed rice, fold gently until evenly coated, and rest 15 minutes to let the quick pulikachal soak in before serving.
tips: Roast a large jar of the podi in advance; with it on hand, this dish comes together in the time it takes to warm the tempering.
Because the podi carries most of the flavour, keep the tamarind base a little thinner so the rice does not turn dry.
A short rest of even fifteen minutes noticeably improves the taste, so make it before you start the rest of the meal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a quick vendakkai fry or plain curd, and scatter extra fried peanuts on top for crunch.

variations.name: Classic Kerala Puttu
variations.description: The iconic Kerala breakfast of steamed rice-flour and coconut layered into a soft, crumbly cylinder in a puttu maker. Moistened rice flour is packed loosely between beds of grated coconut and steamed until it holds its shape yet melts on the tongue. Eaten with sweet ripe banana and a river of ghee, or paired with spicy kadala curry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Drizzled over each hot cylinder as it slides out, it is the traditional finish that makes puttu irresistible

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Sprinkled with the banana it is the classic sweet way Malayalis eat their morning puttu

steps: Spread 2 cups puttu podi in a wide bowl, add 0.75 tsp salt, and sprinkle 0.75 cups water over it a little at a time while raking with your fingers until the flour holds its shape when pressed but crumbles when rubbed.
Rest the moistened flour for 10 minutes, then pass it through your fingers or a coarse sieve to break up any lumps into an even, fluffy crumb.
Fill the perforated base of the puttu maker with 2 tbsp grated coconut, then loosely spoon in a layer of the flour, another spoon of coconut, and continue alternating without pressing down.
Set the cylinder over a pot of boiling water or the puttu kudam and steam on medium-high heat for 6-8 minutes until steam rises freely from the top and the mixture looks set.
Push the cooked puttu out gently with the stick onto a plate, keeping the cylinder intact, and drizzle each piece generously with warm Anveshan Ghee.
Serve with sliced ripe banana sprinkled with Anveshan Jaggery Powder alongside, mashing a little into each mouthful of puttu.
tips: The moisture test is everything: squeeze a fistful, and if it clumps into a solid ball you have added too much water, so mix in a little dry flour.
Do not pack the layers tightly, or the puttu turns dense; loose filling is what gives it the signature soft crumble.
Warm the ghee slightly before drizzling so it soaks in rather than sitting on the surface.
variations.servingSuggestion: For a savoury plate, serve with black chickpea kadala curry and pappadam instead of banana, letting the gravy moisten each forkful.

variations.name: Ragi Puttu
variations.description: A nourishing finger-millet puttu that trades white rice for iron-rich ragi, giving the steamed cylinder a deep chocolate hue and an earthy, wholesome flavour. Popular across Karnataka and Kerala as a diabetic-friendly, high-fibre breakfast. The nutty millet is beautifully offset by sweet coconut and a drizzle of ghee.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Drizzled over the dark millet cylinders to keep the fibre-rich crumb soft and add richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Tossed through the coconut layers, its caramel notes balance the earthiness of ragi

steps: Dry-roast 2 cups ragi flour on low heat for 3-4 minutes until it smells toasty, then cool it slightly and mix in 0.75 tsp salt and 0.25 tsp cardamom.
Sprinkle 0.75 cups water gradually over the flour, raking with your fingers, until it reaches the crumbly stage that holds shape when pressed but breaks apart when rubbed.
Rest 10 minutes, then rub the mixture through your fingers to loosen it into a fine, even crumb with no wet lumps.
Toss 1 cup grated coconut with 4 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, then layer the puttu maker with coconut and ragi crumb alternately, keeping every layer loose and airy.
Steam over boiling water on medium-high heat for 8-10 minutes until steam pours freely from the top and the cylinder feels firm to a gentle touch.
Ease the puttu out with the stick and finish each cylinder with a drizzle of warm Anveshan Ghee before serving hot.
tips: Roasting the ragi first removes any raw, bitter edge and makes the finished puttu far more fragrant.
Ragi absorbs water faster than rice flour, so add the water slowly and stop the moment the crumb clumps.
Steam two minutes longer than rice puttu, as the dense millet needs a little extra time to cook through.
variations.servingSuggestion: Delicious with a bowl of thin coconut milk poured over, or served savoury-style with a tangy green-gram curry.

variations.name: Sweet Coconut-Jaggery Puttu
variations.description: A dessert puttu from Kerala's temple kitchens where the steamed crumb is lavished with a warm mixture of melted jaggery, toasted coconut and cashews. The rice cylinders soak up the caramel and turn into a soft, fudgy sweet often made during festivals like Onam. Cardamom and ghee lift it into celebratory territory.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Melted into a syrup and folded through, it turns the plain steamed crumb into a soft fudgy sweet

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Fries the cashews and binds the sweet mixture with a glossy, nutty richness

steps: Moisten 2 cups puttu podi with 0.25 tsp salt and 0.75 cups water to the crumbly stage, rest 10 minutes, and rub it into a fine, even crumb.
Layer the puttu maker with grated coconut and the flour crumb, then steam over boiling water on medium-high heat for 6-8 minutes until set, and crumble the cylinder loosely into a bowl.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide pan on medium flame and fry 12 halved cashews and 2 tbsp raisins for about a minute until the cashews are gold and the raisins plump, then set them aside.
In the same pan melt 0.75 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 3 tbsp water on low heat for 3-4 minutes until it becomes a thick, glossy syrup.
Stir the remaining coconut and 0.5 tsp cardamom into the syrup and cook 2 minutes until sticky and fragrant.
Fold the crumbled puttu and the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee into the jaggery mixture, toss gently for 2 minutes until evenly coated, and scatter the fried cashews and raisins on top.
tips: Keep the syrup at the soft, pourable stage; if it hardens it will clump the crumb into stiff lumps.
Steam the plain puttu first and sweeten it afterwards, so the jaggery does not scorch inside the steamer.
A pinch of dry ginger powder alongside the cardamom gives it a warming, festive edge.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as an Onam or Vishu treat, with a small bowl of extra thick coconut milk for spooning over.

variations.name: Coconut-Shell Puttu with Kadala Curry Style
variations.description: A rustic, savoury take that leans fully into puttu as a hearty main, seasoning the rice crumb itself with cumin and shallots before steaming. The pale cylinders are then tossed briefly in a coconut-oil tempering so each bite carries a whisper of curry-leaf aroma. Built to be torn into a bowl of spicy black chickpea kadala curry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: The tempering fat that lends the finished cylinders their unmistakable Malabar aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon that softens the savoury crumb and helps it soak up curry

steps: Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and lightly toast 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 4 finely chopped shallots for 2 minutes until soft, then cool completely.
Mix the cooled shallot-cumin into 2 cups puttu podi with 1 tsp salt, then sprinkle in 0.75 cups water gradually and rake to the crumbly stage that clumps when pressed.
Rest 10 minutes, rub the flour into a fine crumb, then layer it loosely with grated coconut in the puttu maker.
Steam over boiling water on medium-high heat for 7-9 minutes until steam rises freely and the cylinder is firm, then push it out and crumble it coarsely.
Heat the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan, crackle 0.5 tsp mustard seeds for 30 seconds until they pop, and add 10 curry leaves for a further 10 seconds.
Tip the crumbled puttu into the tempering with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, toss gently for 2 minutes until fragrant and warmed through, and serve immediately.
tips: Cook the shallots and cumin fully before adding to the flour; raw shallot moisture would make the crumb soggy.
Keep the tempering toss brief so the strands do not turn oily or break down into paste.
For a heartier plate, fold a handful of steamed peas into the tempering along with the puttu.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle a generous bowl of black chickpea kadala curry alongside and let diners crumble the seasoned puttu straight into the gravy.

variations.name: Classic Ragda Pattice
variations.description: This Classic Ragda Pattice is Mumbai's beloved street chaat of crisp golden potato patties drowned in a spiced dried-white-pea curry called ragda. Topped with tangy tamarind and fresh green chutneys, chopped onion, crunchy sev and coriander, it hits sweet, sour, spicy and savoury in every spoonful.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: shallow-frying the pattice in nutty bilona ghee gives a crisp golden crust

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the tamarind chutney with a deep mineral note instead of refined sugar

steps: Soak 1.5 cups dried white peas in plenty of water overnight, then pressure-cook them with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 5 to 6 whistles until completely soft and mushy.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, add 1 tsp red chilli powder off the heat, then stir in the cooked peas and simmer for 8 minutes, lightly mashing until the ragda is thick and creamy.
Boil and peel the 4 potatoes, mash them while warm with 2 tbsp cornflour and 0.5 tsp salt, and shape into 8 smooth flat patties about 1 cm thick.
Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on a griddle over medium heat and shallow-fry the patties for 3 to 4 minutes per side until deeply golden and crisp.
Simmer the 3 tbsp tamarind pulp with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and a splash of water for 5 minutes until it thickens into a glossy pouring chutney.
Place 2 hot pattice on each plate, ladle over a generous cup of steaming ragda, drizzle with tamarind and green chutney, and finish with chopped onion, 1 tsp chaat masala, nylon sev and coriander.
tips: Mash the potatoes while still warm and bind with cornflour so the pattice hold together without cracking during frying.
Keep the ragda loose and pourable, adding hot water if it thickens too much on standing, as it firms up as it cools.
Assemble each plate only just before serving so the pattice stay crisp under the warm ragda.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot in a shallow bowl with an extra wedge of lime and a sprinkle of finely chopped raw onion on the side.

variations.name: Gujarati Ragda Petis
variations.description: The Gujarati Ragda Petis leans sweeter and tangier, with a lightly sweetened ragda and an extra pour of date-tamarind chutney typical of Kathiawadi chaat stalls. Garnished with pomegranate and roasted peanuts, it balances the region's signature sweet-savoury contrast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil gives the petis a light crisp shell true to Gujarati stalls

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: lends the ragda and chutney the gentle sweetness Gujarati chaat is known for

steps: Soak 1.5 cups white peas overnight and pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 whistles until soft, then lightly mash to a thick ragda.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, add the peas with 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and simmer for 8 minutes so the ragda turns subtly sweet and glossy.
Boil, peel and mash the 4 potatoes with 0.5 tsp salt, shape into 8 flat petis, and shallow-fry in the remaining 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil for 3 minutes per side until golden.
Soak the 6 dates and 3 tbsp tamarind in warm water, blend with the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, and simmer 5 minutes into a thick sweet-sour chutney.
Set 2 petis on each plate and spoon over a ladle of the warm sweetened ragda until they are half submerged.
Finish with a generous drizzle of the date-tamarind chutney and green chutney, then scatter pomegranate, roasted peanuts, 1 tsp chaat masala, sev and coriander.
tips: Blend the dates thoroughly for a silky chutney, straining if needed so no fibrous bits remain.
Balance the sweetness with a pinch of black salt in the ragda so it does not turn cloying.
Toast the peanuts fresh and add them at the very end to keep their crunch against the soft ragda.
variations.servingSuggestion: Present in a wide bowl with a lime wedge and extra pomegranate on top for a jewel-like Kathiawadi finish.

variations.name: Corn and Cheese Stuffed Ragda Pattice
variations.description: A modern cafe-style twist where each pattice hides a molten filling of spiced sweet corn and cheese that oozes when broken over the ragda. The creamy stuffing plays against the tangy pea curry and sharp chutneys for an indulgent, crowd-pleasing chaat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: griddling the stuffed pattice in ghee crisps the shell while the cheese melts inside

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: rounds the tamarind chutney with a caramel depth that suits the rich filling

steps: Pressure-cook 1.5 cups soaked white peas with 1 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 whistles, then temper with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1 tsp red chilli powder and simmer 8 minutes into a thick ragda.
Boil, peel and mash the 5 potatoes with 2 tbsp cornflour and 0.5 tsp salt to a firm, pliable dough.
Mix the 0.75 cup sweet corn with 0.75 cup grated mozzarella, a pinch of salt and 0.5 tsp chaat masala for the filling.
Flatten a portion of potato in your palm, place a spoon of the corn-cheese mix in the centre, seal and shape into 8 stuffed patties.
Griddle the pattice in the remaining 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat for 4 minutes per side until crisp, golden and the cheese softens within.
Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder for 5 minutes, then plate 2 pattice, ladle over hot ragda, drizzle both chutneys, and top with 1 tsp chaat masala, sev and coriander.
tips: Seal the stuffed edges well and chill the pattice for 15 minutes so the cheese does not leak while frying.
Use a firm potato dough with enough cornflour, as a wet mix will burst open on the griddle.
Break the pattice open at the table so guests see the molten corn-cheese centre spill into the ragda.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve one stuffed pattice cut in half to reveal the melting centre, with a side of extra green chutney for dipping.

variations.name: Jain Ragda Pattice
variations.description: A Jain-friendly version made entirely without onion, garlic or potato, using raw banana for the pattice and a ginger-scented ragda. It keeps all the tangy, spicy, sweet chaat character while respecting a strict Jain kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a neutral wood-pressed oil crisps the raw-banana pattice without any onion-garlic tempering

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the tamarind chutney naturally for the Jain assembly

steps: Pressure-cook 1.5 cups soaked white peas with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 whistles until soft, then mash lightly to a thick ragda.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and add grated ginger and 2 chopped green chillies for 30 seconds, then add the peas with 1 tsp red chilli powder and simmer 8 minutes.
Boil the 5 raw bananas in their skins until tender, peel and mash them with 2 tbsp cornflour and 0.5 tsp salt into a firm dough, then shape into 8 flat patties.
Shallow-fry the raw-banana patties in the remaining 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil for 3 to 4 minutes per side until golden and crisp.
Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and a little water for 5 minutes into a glossy sweet-sour chutney.
Plate 2 patties, ladle over the ginger-spiced ragda, drizzle with the tamarind chutney, and finish with 1 tsp chaat masala, nylon sev and plenty of coriander.
tips: Boil the raw bananas whole in the skin so they do not turn watery and the pattice stay firm.
Skip onion and garlic entirely and lean on ginger, green chilli and chaat masala to build flavour.
Rub a little oil on your palms when shaping the sticky raw-banana dough so it does not cling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with an onion-free green chutney and a wedge of lime for guests keeping a Jain diet.

variations.name: Classic Rava Idli
variations.description: The beloved instant idli made from roasted semolina and curd, needing no fermentation or overnight soaking. A quick tempering of mustard, cashews and curry leaves runs through the fluffy cakes, and a pinch of fruit salt gives them their signature soft, airy crumb in minutes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee roasts the rava for a nutty aroma and gives these instant idlis their soft richness

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium heat and fry 12 cashews until golden, remove them, then in the same ghee splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tbsp chana dal until the dal turns golden.

Add 2 minced green chillies, 1 inch minced ginger and 12 curry leaves, sauté 20 seconds, then tip in 1.5 cups rava and roast on low heat for 4 to 5 minutes until it smells nutty and turns a shade darker; cool slightly.

In a bowl whisk 1 cup curd with 1/2 cup water and 1 tsp salt, then stir in the roasted rava, the fried cashews and 2 tbsp chopped coriander to a thick, lump-free batter; rest 10 minutes so the rava swells.
Loosen the rested batter with a little water if needed to a thick dropping consistency, then just before steaming sprinkle in 1 tsp fruit salt and fold gently as the batter turns frothy.
Grease the idli plates with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, spoon in the aerated batter without stirring it down, and press a cashew into the centre of each.
Steam in a covered idli pot for 10 to 12 minutes until a toothpick comes out clean, rest 2 minutes, and unmould the soft idlis.
tips: Add the fruit salt only at the very last moment before steaming; if it fizzes and sits, the idlis will turn dense.
Roast the rava until fragrant so the idlis are not raw-tasting or sticky.
Slightly sour curd works best here as it mimics the tang of a fermented idli batter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a coconut chutney and a small bowl of sambar, or a spicy tomato chutney for a quick weekday breakfast.

variations.name: Vegetable Rava Idli
variations.description: A colourful, nourishing version studded with grated carrot, peas and beans folded into the semolina batter. The vegetables add sweetness, crunch and colour, turning a plain instant idli into a wholesome one-dish breakfast that children happily eat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee roasts the rava and carries the vegetable tempering through the fluffy idlis

steps: Grate 1 carrot, finely chop 6 French beans and keep 1/4 cup peas ready; heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium heat and splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds with 1 tbsp urad dal until golden.
Add 2 minced green chillies and 12 curry leaves, then stir in the carrot, beans and peas and saute for 3 minutes until they soften slightly but stay bright.
Add 1.5 cups rava to the same pan and roast on low heat for 4 minutes until fragrant, then cool the mixture slightly.
Whisk 1 cup curd with 1/2 cup water and 1 tsp salt, fold in the roasted rava-vegetable mixture and 2 tbsp coriander to a thick batter, and rest 10 minutes for the rava to swell.
Adjust with a splash of water to a thick dropping consistency, then sprinkle in 1 tsp fruit salt just before steaming and fold gently until frothy.
Grease the idli plates with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, spoon in the batter, and steam covered for 11 to 13 minutes until a toothpick comes out clean.
tips: Grate the carrot finely so it cooks through in the short steaming time and does not stay crunchy.
Do not overcook the vegetables in the tempering; they should stay vibrant to speckle the pale idlis.
This batter cannot wait once eno is added, so have your steamer hot and ready before folding it in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with mint-coriander chutney and sambar; these veg-packed idlis also travel well in a lunchbox with a smear of chutney.

variations.name: Oats Rava Idli
variations.description: A lighter, high-fibre twist that blends powdered oats with the semolina, keeping the instant idli soft while adding wholegrain goodness. Tangy curd and a classic tempering keep it comforting and familiar, but each cake carries the slow-release energy of oats for a healthier breakfast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee roasts the oats and rava together and keeps the fibre-rich idlis tender

steps: Dry-roast 1 cup rolled oats on medium-low heat for 3 minutes until they smell toasty, cool, and grind to a coarse powder.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tbsp urad dal, then add 2 minced green chillies, 1 inch minced ginger and 12 curry leaves; add 3/4 cup rava and roast for 3 minutes until fragrant.
In a bowl combine the powdered oats, the roasted rava tempering, 1 finely grated small carrot and 1 tsp salt, then whisk in 1 cup curd with about 1/2 cup water to a thick batter and rest 10 minutes.
Loosen the batter with a little water to a thick dropping consistency if it has stiffened as the oats absorb liquid.
Sprinkle in 1 tsp fruit salt just before steaming and fold gently until the batter looks light and frothy.
Grease the plates with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, spoon in the batter, and steam covered for 11 to 13 minutes until a toothpick comes out clean.
tips: Roasting and powdering the oats keeps the idlis from turning gummy and helps them rise evenly.
Oats drink up more liquid than rava, so keep extra curd or water handy to adjust the batter before steaming.
Use thick curd with a good tang to balance the mild sweetness of the oats.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a roasted-tomato chutney or coconut chutney for a filling, fibre-rich breakfast that keeps you full till lunch.

variations.name: Masala Rava Idli Fry
variations.description: A clever way to revive leftover rava idlis by tossing them in a spicy tempering with onions, curry leaves and podi until the edges crisp up. Part snack, part breakfast, this tangy stir-fry turns yesterday's idlis into an irresistible plate that disappears fast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil crisps the idli cubes and carries the podi flavour beautifully

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of ghee gives the fried idli cubes a glossy, aromatic coat

steps: Cut 8 leftover rava idlis into bite-sized cubes and keep them ready; slice 1 onion thinly.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a wide pan on medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tbsp urad dal until golden, then add 15 curry leaves.
Add the sliced onion and saute for 3 minutes until soft and translucent, then stir in 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1/2 tsp red chilli powder for 15 seconds.
Add the idli cubes and 1/2 tsp salt, and toss gently on medium-high heat for 4 to 5 minutes until the edges turn golden and crisp.
Sprinkle 2 tbsp idli podi over the idlis and toss for another 2 minutes so every cube is coated in the spicy powder.
Drizzle 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, fold in 2 tbsp coriander, and serve immediately while crisp.
tips: Use idlis that are at least a few hours old; fresh warm idlis crumble when tossed.
Toss gently with a flat spatula so the cubes crisp without breaking into a mash.
Adjust the podi to taste; it already carries salt and chilli, so add extra salt sparingly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot as a breakfast or tea-time snack with a bowl of curd or a squeeze of lemon to cut the spice.

variations.name: Classic Rava Upma
variations.description: The plain, no-frills semolina upma that anchors South Indian breakfast tables, soft and fluffy with just onion, green chilli and a mustard-curry leaf tempering. Roasting the rava well is the whole secret to its grainy-yet-tender bite. Ready in twenty minutes, it is the humble comfort food you can make with your eyes half shut on a busy morning.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Folded in at the end for the classic glossy, aromatic finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed oil gives a clean tempering base without overpowering the rava

steps: Dry-roast 1.5 cups semolina in a heavy kadhai over medium-low heat, stirring constantly for 5 minutes until it smells nutty and turns just a shade darker, then transfer to a plate.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then fry 1 tbsp urad dal, 1 tbsp chana dal and 10 cashews until golden, about 2 minutes.
Add 12 curry leaves, 2 slit green chillies, grated 1 inch ginger and 1 chopped onion, sauteing until the onion turns soft and translucent, about 3 minutes.
Pour in 3.5 cups water with 1.25 tsp salt and bring to a rolling boil over high heat.
Lower the flame and add the roasted rava in a thin, steady stream with one hand while stirring vigorously with the other so no lumps form.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 3-4 minutes until all the water is absorbed and the upma looks fluffy and holds together softly.
Fold in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, switch off the heat and rest covered for 2 minutes so the grains plump before serving.
tips: Roast the rava until it just changes colour and smells toasty; under-roasted rava turns the upma gummy.
The 1 to 2.3 rava-to-water ratio gives a soft upma, but reduce the water slightly for a firmer, grainier bite.
A pinch of sugar with the salt is a traditional touch that quietly lifts the flavour without making it sweet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot with coconut chutney and a wedge of lime, or with sugar and ripe banana in the old-fashioned way alongside filter coffee.

variations.name: Ghee Roast Rava Upma
variations.description: An indulgent version where the semolina is roasted entirely in ghee until deeply golden, giving the upma a rich, almost halwa-like aroma and a luxurious mouthfeel. The generous ghee makes every grain glisten and stay separate. This is the upma reserved for lazy weekend breakfasts when comfort matters more than restraint.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Used to roast the rava fully and again at the finish for a rich, nutty depth

steps: Melt 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai and roast 1.5 cups semolina over medium-low heat for 6-7 minutes, stirring constantly, until it turns richly golden and smells like toasted nuts, then set aside.
In the same kadhai, heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1/2 tsp lightly crushed peppercorns, then fry 1 tbsp urad dal and 15 cashews until golden.
Add 12 curry leaves, 2 slit green chillies, grated 1 inch ginger and 1 chopped onion, sauteing until the onion softens, about 3 minutes.
Pour in 3.5 cups water with 1.25 tsp salt and bring to a strong boil.
Reduce the heat and rain in the ghee-roasted rava in a slow stream, stirring hard to keep the mixture perfectly smooth.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 4 minutes until the water is absorbed and the upma is fluffy and glistening.
Fold in the final 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, rest covered 2 minutes, and serve while the ghee aroma is at its peak.
tips: Roasting rava in ghee rather than dry keeps the grains beautifully separate, but watch the heat so the ghee does not brown too far.
The crushed peppercorns add a gentle warmth that cuts the richness; leave them coarse so you catch them in occasional bites.
This upma sets firmer as it cools because of the ghee, so serve it fresh and hot for the best texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a tangy tomato chutney or plain curd, and a strong filter coffee to balance the richness.

variations.name: Coconut Rava Upma
variations.description: A Tamil Nadu home-style upma finished with a generous handful of fresh grated coconut that lends sweetness, moisture and fragrance. The coconut is stirred in at the end so it stays fresh and juicy rather than cooked away. Light, aromatic and subtly sweet, it is the way many Tamil grandmothers still make their morning upma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil echoes the fresh coconut and gives an unmistakable Tamil aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon that softens the upma and marries with the coconut

steps: Dry-roast 1.5 cups semolina over medium-low heat for 5 minutes until nutty and pale, then set aside on a plate.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, and fry 1 tbsp urad dal and 1 tbsp chana dal until golden.
Add 15 curry leaves, 3 slit green chillies, grated 1 inch ginger and 1 small chopped onion, sauteing until the onion turns soft, about 3 minutes.
Pour in 3.25 cups water with 1.25 tsp salt and bring to a brisk boil.
Lower the heat and stream in the roasted rava while stirring continuously to keep it lump-free.
Cover and cook on low for 3-4 minutes until the water is fully absorbed and the upma is soft and fluffy.
Switch off the heat, fold in 1/2 cup fresh grated coconut and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, rest covered 2 minutes, and serve warm.
tips: Add the coconut only after the heat is off; cooking it dulls both its colour and its fresh sweetness.
Use slightly less water than usual because the coconut adds its own moisture to the finished upma.
Frozen coconut works if thawed and brought to room temperature, but fresh gives the truest Tamil flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jaggery-sweetened coconut on the side, or with a tangy tomato thokku and hot filter coffee.

variations.name: Onion Chilli Rava Upma
