variations.description: A punchy Andhra-leaning upma loaded with sliced onions and extra green chillies, fried until the onions turn sweet and golden, giving the dish a savoury depth and gentle heat. There are no other vegetables to distract from the caramelised onion flavour. Simple, sharp and deeply satisfying, it is proof that onion and chilli alone can carry a whole breakfast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed oil fries the onions to a sweet gold and keeps the upma light

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon that mellows the chilli heat with a soft richness

steps: Dry-roast 1.5 cups semolina over medium-low heat for 5 minutes until fragrant and pale, then reserve on a plate.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1/2 tsp cumin seeds, then fry 1 tbsp urad dal and 3 tbsp peanuts until golden and crisp.
Add 15 curry leaves, 4 slit green chillies and grated 1 inch ginger, followed by 2 thinly sliced onions, and saute a full 6-7 minutes until the onions turn soft, sweet and lightly golden.
Pour in 3.5 cups water with 1.25 tsp salt and bring to a rolling boil.
Lower the heat and add the roasted rava in a thin stream, stirring briskly to prevent lumps.
Cover and cook on low for 4 minutes until the water is absorbed and the upma is fluffy and flecked with golden onion.
Fold in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, rest covered 2 minutes, and serve hot.
tips: Take your time browning the onions; their sweetness is the backbone of this minimalist upma.
Adjust the green chillies to taste, but the Andhra spirit of this dish leans deliberately toward the fiery side.
Toasted peanuts instead of cashews add a rustic crunch that suits the onion-forward flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling coconut chutney or plain curd, and a wedge of lime to brighten the caramelised onion.

variations.name: Classic Tiffin Sambar
variations.description: The everyday South Indian sambar built on soft toor dal, tangy tamarind and a homemade roasted spice powder, studded with drumstick, pumpkin and shallots. A final tempering of mustard and dry chillies crisped in gingelly oil gives it the aroma that greets you at any tiffin house.

ingredients.name: Toor dal
ingredients.note: pressure-cooked soft and mashed

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked in warm water for pulp

ingredients.name: Drumstick
ingredients.note: cut into 2 inch pieces

ingredients.name: Yellow pumpkin
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Shallots
ingredients.note: peeled whole

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the classic pinch of sweetness that balances the tamarind sourness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed gingelly oil, the authentic fat for a Tamil tempering

steps: Pressure-cook 3/4 cup toor dal with 2 cups water and 1/2 tsp turmeric for 4-5 whistles until completely soft, then whisk smooth and set aside.
Boil the drumstick, cubed pumpkin, 10 whole shallots and chopped tomato with 1.5 cups water and 1 tsp salt on medium heat for 10 minutes until the vegetables turn just tender.

Squeeze out the tamarind pulp into 1/2 cup water, add it to the vegetables along with 2 tbsp sambar powder and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, and simmer for 6-7 minutes until the raw tamarind smell fades.
Stir in the mashed dal with another 1/2 cup water and the remaining 1/4 tsp salt, then simmer gently for 5 minutes until the sambar reaches a pourable, slightly thick consistency.

In a small pan heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1/4 tsp fenugreek seeds, then add 2 dry red chillies, 1/4 tsp asafoetida and 2 sprigs curry leaves and fry for 30 seconds until aromatic.
Pour the sizzling tempering over the sambar, cover immediately to trap the aroma, and rest for 3 minutes before serving hot.
tips: Cook the dal until it is truly soft and lump-free; a grainy dal makes a thin, watery sambar.
Add the tamarind before the dal so its sourness cooks out into the vegetables rather than tasting raw.
Whole shallots simmered until sweet are the heart of tiffin sambar, so resist swapping them for chopped onion.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle generously over hot idlis and dosas, or serve with steamed rice topped with a spoon of ghee and a crisp appalam.

variations.name: Udupi Arachuvitta Sambar
variations.description: The temple-town classic where the spice powder is freshly roasted and ground with coconut for each pot, giving a thicker, fragrant gravy quite unlike the everyday version. Ground coconut lends body and a subtle sweetness that carries the sambar deep into festival territory.

ingredients.name: Toor dal
ingredients.note: cooked soft

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked for pulp

ingredients.name: Ash gourd
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Carrot
ingredients.note: diced

ingredients.name: Chana dal
ingredients.note: for the roast-and-grind masala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the coastal Karnataka fat that suits the coconut-rich masala

steps: In a dry pan on low heat, roast 1.5 tbsp coriander seeds, 1 tbsp chana dal, 5 dry red chillies and 1/4 tsp fenugreek seeds for 3-4 minutes until deep golden and fragrant.
Add 1/3 cup grated coconut to the same pan and roast for another 2 minutes until it turns light brown, then grind everything with a little water into a smooth masala paste.
Boil the cubed ash gourd and diced carrot with 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 1.5 cups water on medium heat for 10 minutes until tender.
Squeeze the tamarind pulp into the vegetables, add the ground coconut masala and simmer on medium heat for 6-7 minutes until the gravy thickens and smells roasted.
Whisk in 3/4 cup cooked toor dal with 1/2 cup water and the remaining salt, then simmer gently for 5 minutes until well combined and glossy.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds with 1/4 tsp asafoetida and 2 sprigs curry leaves for 30 seconds, and pour this tempering over the sambar before serving.
tips: Roast the masala ingredients on a low flame so the spices toast evenly without any bitter burnt notes.
Grind the coconut masala fresh just before cooking; a stored paste loses the aroma that defines this style.
This sambar thickens noticeably on standing, so keep it a touch thin if serving after a delay.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft idlis and a spoon of coconut chutney, or over rice with a fried papad for a satisfying temple-style meal.

variations.name: Drumstick Sambar
variations.description: A drumstick-forward sambar where the pods take centre stage, their pulp scooped straight into the tangy dal. Loaded with extra tamarind and a bold sambar masala, it is the thin, sour, deeply savoury style favoured for pouring over rice with a fried papad.

ingredients.name: Toor dal
ingredients.note: cooked soft and mashed

ingredients.name: Drumstick
ingredients.note: cut into 3 inch pieces

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked for a strong pulp

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: sliced

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: tempers the extra tamarind so the sambar tastes rounded, not sharp

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: gingelly oil for the classic Tamil tadka aroma

steps: Boil the drumstick pieces, sliced onion and chopped tomato with 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 1.5 cups water on medium heat for 10-12 minutes until the drumsticks are tender and easy to scoop.
Squeeze the tamarind pulp into 3/4 cup water and add it to the pot with 2.5 tbsp sambar powder and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, then simmer for 7 minutes until the sourness mellows.
Whisk in 3/4 cup mashed toor dal with another 3/4 cup water and the remaining salt, and simmer on low heat for 5 minutes to a thin, pourable sambar.
Taste and adjust, keeping the balance clearly tangy and savoury with just a hint of sweetness in the background.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a small pan, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1/2 tsp cumin seeds, then add 2 dry red chillies, 1/4 tsp asafoetida and 2 sprigs curry leaves and fry for 30 seconds.
Pour the crackling tempering over the sambar, cover to lock in the aroma, and let it stand for 3 minutes before serving.
tips: Choose plump, fresh drumsticks whose flesh scoops out easily; woody pods leave little to enjoy.
Keep this sambar deliberately thin so it soaks fully into rice rather than sitting on top.
Eat the drumstick by drawing the soft inner pulp through your teeth and discarding the fibrous shell.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pour over a mound of hot rice with a dab of ghee and a crunchy fried papad, or serve with medu vada for a classic combination.

variations.name: Hotel-style Vegetable Sambar
variations.description: The thick, mildly sweet, richly aromatic sambar served in South Indian tiffin restaurants, loaded with mixed vegetables and finished with a ghee tempering. A small ground coconut-fried gram paste gives it the creamy body and gentle sheen that sets restaurant sambar apart from the home pot.

ingredients.name: Toor dal
ingredients.note: cooked very soft

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked for pulp

ingredients.name: Carrot
ingredients.note: diced

ingredients.name: Potato
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Green beans
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Shallots
ingredients.note: whole

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Grated fresh coconut
ingredients.note: for the smoothening paste

ingredients.name: Roasted gram
ingredients.note: pottukadalai, for body

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the gentle sweetness that gives hotel sambar its rounded taste

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the aromatic tempering fat that makes this taste of a tiffin restaurant

steps: Boil the diced carrot, cubed potato, chopped beans, 8 whole shallots and chopped tomato with 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 1.5 cups water on medium heat for 12 minutes until soft.
Grind 3 tbsp grated coconut with 1 tbsp roasted gram and a splash of water into a smooth paste for body.
Add the squeezed tamarind pulp, 2 tbsp sambar powder and 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder to the vegetables and simmer for 6 minutes until the raw smells cook off.
Whisk in 3/4 cup cooked toor dal and the ground coconut paste with 3/4 cup water, then simmer on low heat for 6-7 minutes until thick, creamy and glossy.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, add 2 dry red chillies and 2 sprigs curry leaves and fry for 30 seconds until the ghee smells nutty.
Pour the ghee tempering over the sambar, stir once, and cover for 3 minutes so the restaurant-style aroma settles before serving.
tips: The coconut and roasted gram paste is the restaurant secret for a thick, smooth body without a floury taste.
Keep this sambar noticeably thicker than home style so it clings to idli and dosa.
A ghee tempering rather than oil is what gives hotel sambar its signature richness, so do not substitute it here.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a stack of soft idlis, ghee-roast dosa or medu vada, with coconut chutney alongside for the full tiffin experience.

variations.name: Classic Set Dosa
variations.description: Set Dosa is a soft, thick, spongy dosa from Karnataka, served in a stack or 'set' of two or three. Poha and a little sugar in the fermented batter give it a cloud-like, holey top that soaks up chutney and sagu beautifully.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: drizzled around each dosa for a soft base and buttery Karnataka-style finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a touch in the batter feeds fermentation and rounds the flavour without refined sugar

steps: Soak 2 cups idli rice with 0.5 tsp fenugreek seeds in one bowl and 0.5 cup urad dal in another for 5 hours, and soak 0.5 cup poha for the last 20 minutes.
Grind the urad dal with a little water to a light, fluffy paste, then grind the rice, fenugreek and soaked poha together to a slightly coarse batter.
Mix both batters with 1 tsp salt and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, cover, and ferment in a warm place for 8 to 10 hours until doubled and bubbly.
Stir the risen batter gently and adjust with a little water until it is thick but still spoonably pourable, like a soft cake batter.
Heat a tawa on medium, pour a ladle of batter into a thick round without spreading, drizzle Anveshan Ghee around the edge, and cover for 2 minutes until the top is full of holes and set.
Do not flip if the top has cooked through, or flip for 20 seconds for a light base, then serve two or three stacked as a warm set.
tips: Poha is the secret to the spongy, holey top, so do not skip it or the dosa turns flat.
Keep the batter thick and pour without spreading; a spread batter gives a thin dosa, not a set dosa.
Ferment in a warm oven with just the light on if your kitchen is cold, to get a reliable rise.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a stack with vegetable sagu, coconut chutney and a spoon of extra ghee melting on top.

variations.name: Davanagere Benne Set Dosa
variations.description: Inspired by the famous benne (butter) dosas of Davanagere, this version is loaded with generous ghee for an irresistibly soft, faintly crisp-edged set. A small amount of sugar and a longer ferment give it the signature melt-in-mouth character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the heart of a benne dosa, poured liberally for softness and golden lacy edges

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: aids fermentation and gives the dosa its subtle Davanagere sweetness

steps: Soak 2 cups idli rice, 0.5 cup urad dal and 2 tbsp sabudana together in water for 5 hours, and soak 0.5 cup poha in the final 20 minutes.
Grind everything together to a smooth, thick batter using minimal water so it stays airy and holds its body.
Add 1 tsp salt and 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, mix well, and ferment covered for 10 to 12 hours until well risen with a spongy surface.
Give the batter a gentle stir and check that it is thick and dropping consistency, adding only a little water if needed.
Pour a thick ladleful onto a medium-hot tawa without spreading, generously spoon Anveshan Ghee around and over the top, and cover for 2 to 3 minutes.
Cook until the base is pale gold and the top is soft and full of holes, then fold and serve two together while dripping with ghee.
tips: The sago adds an extra soft, slightly gooey crumb that defines the Davanagere style.
Be generous with the ghee; the whole point of a benne set dosa is its rich, buttery softness.
Keep the flame at medium so the base browns gently while the thick top steams through fully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with potato palya, spicy red garlic chutney and a bowl of sagu for the true Davanagere experience.

variations.name: Rava Set Dosa
variations.description: A quick, no-ferment set dosa made with semolina and curd for busy mornings. The batter rests for just twenty minutes yet still delivers soft, spongy dosas with a lightly tangy taste.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: drizzled around each dosa so the instant batter still cooks up soft and rich

steps: Whisk 1 cup fine semolina, 0.5 cup rice flour and 0.75 cup curd in a bowl, then add water gradually to make a thick, lump-free pouring batter.
Stir in 1 tsp salt, 2 finely chopped green chillies and 2 tbsp coriander, cover, and rest for 20 minutes so the rava swells.
Just before cooking, mix in 0.25 tsp baking soda and loosen with a splash of water if the batter has thickened too much.
Heat a tawa on medium, pour a thick ladle without spreading, and drizzle Anveshan Ghee generously around the edges.
Cover and cook for about 2 minutes until the top is set and dotted with holes and the base is golden.
Flip for 30 seconds for a firmer base if you like, then serve two stacked and hot.
tips: Add the baking soda only just before cooking, as its lift fades quickly once mixed in.
Rest the batter the full 20 minutes so the semolina hydrates and the dosa does not taste grainy.
Keep the batter thick like the fermented version; too thin and you lose the spongy set texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Great with quick mint-coconut chutney and a mug of filter coffee when you have no time to ferment.

variations.name: Veggie Uttapam Set Dosa
variations.description: This wholesome take presses a colourful layer of chopped vegetables onto the spongy set dosa as it cooks, turning it into an uttapam-style stack. It is a fibre-rich one-plate breakfast that needs little more than chutney on the side.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: drizzled around the edges for a nutty aroma that suits the loaded vegetable top

steps: Soak 2 cups idli rice and 0.5 cup urad dal separately for 5 hours, with 0.5 cup poha added to the rice for the last 20 minutes, then grind each to a batter.
Combine the batters with 1 tsp salt, ferment covered for 8 to 10 hours until risen and bubbly, then stir gently to a thick pouring consistency.
Finely chop the onion, tomato, capsicum, carrot, 2 green chillies and 3 tbsp coriander and keep them mixed in a bowl.
Heat a tawa on medium, pour a thick ladle of batter into a round, and immediately scatter a handful of the chopped vegetables over the top, pressing lightly.
Drizzle Anveshan Sesame Oil around the edges, cover, and cook for 3 minutes until the base is golden and the vegetables soften into the spongy top.
Flip briefly for 30 seconds to sear the vegetable side, then serve the stack hot with chutney.
tips: Chop the vegetables small and even so they cook through in the time the dosa needs.
Press the vegetables gently into the wet batter so they anchor and do not fall off on flipping.
Keep the flame at medium; too high and the base burns before the veg-laden top can set.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and a light rasam on the side for a complete, satisfying breakfast.

variations.name: Classic Sev Puri
variations.description: This Classic Sev Puri is a Mumbai chaat of flat crisp papdis topped with spiced mashed potato, diced onion, tangy tamarind and spicy green chutneys, then buried under a mound of fine nylon sev. Each bite delivers crunch, creaminess, sweet-sour chutney and a fresh burst of coriander all at once.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: deep-frying the papdi in wood-pressed oil gives flat, crisp, non-greasy bases

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the tamarind chutney with a natural caramel note

steps: Knead 1.5 cups refined flour with 0.5 tsp salt and about 6 tbsp water into a stiff dough, roll thin, prick with a fork, cut 24 rounds, and deep-fry in Anveshan Groundnut Oil at medium heat for 3 minutes until flat and crisp.
Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind pulp with 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and a little water for 5 minutes into a thick sweet-sour chutney and cool it.
Mash the 3 boiled potatoes with 0.5 tsp salt, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp chaat masala into a smooth topping.
Arrange the crisp papdis on a platter and spread a spoon of the spiced potato on each one.
Drizzle every papdi with tamarind chutney and green chutney, then scatter finely chopped onion and 1 tsp chaat masala over the top.
Cover the whole platter thickly with nylon sev, garnish with coriander, and serve immediately before the papdis soften.
tips: Prick the papdi dough well before frying so they stay flat and crisp instead of puffing up.
Assemble and serve within minutes, as the chutneys quickly soften the papdi bases.
Keep the potato topping at room temperature so it spreads easily and does not wet the papdi.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the assembled platter at once with extra sev and lime wedges so guests can add more to taste.

variations.name: Sev Batata Puri
variations.description: The classic Gujarati sev batata puri leans heavily on soft spiced potato cubes and a double hit of sweet and green chutney, making it juicier and tangier than the standard sev puri. Batata means potato, and here it is the generous, comforting star of every bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: light wood-pressed oil fries crisp papdi bases that hold the juicy potato

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: gives the Gujarati-sweet tamarind chutney its signature mellow sweetness

steps: Knead 1.5 cups refined flour with 0.5 tsp salt and 6 tbsp water into a firm dough, roll thin, prick, cut 24 rounds, and deep-fry in Anveshan Sunflower Oil at medium heat until flat and crisp.
Blend the soaked 5 dates and 3 tbsp tamarind with 4 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and simmer 5 minutes into a thick, sweet date-tamarind chutney.
Cut the 4 boiled potatoes into small cubes and toss them with 0.5 tsp salt and 1 tsp chaat masala.
Top each crisp papdi with a spoonful of the seasoned potato cubes and a little chopped onion.
Drizzle generously with the sweet date-tamarind chutney and green chutney so each papdi is well coated.
Bury the platter under nylon sev, scatter pomegranate, remaining chaat masala and coriander, and serve at once.
tips: Dice the potatoes small and even so every papdi gets a tidy, bite-sized potato topping.
Lean sweeter with the chutney here, as the Gujarati style is meant to taste noticeably sweet-tangy.
Add a few pomegranate seeds for juicy pops that cut through the soft potato.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a wide plate garnished with pomegranate and coriander, alongside masala chai.

variations.name: Dahi Sev Puri
variations.description: A cooling version where each papdi is crowned with chilled whisked yogurt before the chutneys and sev, softening the heat and adding a creamy tang. It is the ideal choice for a hot day, marrying crunch, spice and soothing curd.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil fries sturdy papdi that stay crisp under the yogurt

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens both the tamarind chutney and the whisked yogurt topping

steps: Knead 1.5 cups refined flour with 0.5 tsp salt and 6 tbsp water, roll thin, prick, cut 24 rounds, and deep-fry in Anveshan Groundnut Oil at medium heat until flat and crisp.
Whisk the 2 cups yogurt smooth with 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and a pinch of salt, then chill it well.
Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder for 5 minutes into a sweet-sour chutney and cool.
Mash the 3 boiled potatoes with 0.5 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and spread a little on each crisp papdi.
Spoon a dollop of the sweetened chilled yogurt over each papdi, then drizzle with tamarind and green chutney.
Dust with 1 tsp roasted cumin powder and 1 tsp chaat masala, cover with nylon sev and coriander, and serve immediately.
tips: Whisk and chill the yogurt so it pours smoothly and stays cool against the crisp papdi.
Add the yogurt and sev at the very end so the papdi does not go soft before serving.
A pinch of black salt in the yogurt deepens its tang and balances the sweetness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled on a hot afternoon, finished with a final dusting of roasted cumin and red chilli powder.

variations.name: Cheese Sev Puri
variations.description: A modern party twist that finishes the loaded papdis with a flurry of grated cheese over the sev for a creamy, savoury edge. This cafe-style fusion keeps the tangy chutney base but adds a rich, kid-friendly cheesy top layer.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: light wood-pressed oil fries crisp papdi that stand up to the cheesy topping

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: keeps the tamarind chutney naturally sweet to balance the savoury cheese

steps: Knead 1.5 cups refined flour with 0.5 tsp salt and 6 tbsp water, roll thin, prick, cut 24 rounds, and deep-fry in Anveshan Sunflower Oil at medium heat until flat and crisp.
Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder for 5 minutes into a thick sweet-sour chutney and cool it.
Mash the 3 boiled potatoes with 0.5 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp chaat masala and spread a spoon on each crisp papdi.
Drizzle every papdi with tamarind and green chutney and scatter finely chopped onion over the top.
Sprinkle 1 tsp chaat masala, cover the platter with nylon sev, and then grate the 0.75 cup cheese thickly over everything.
Garnish with coriander and serve immediately while the papdi is crisp and the cheese sits fresh on top.
tips: Grate the cheese fresh over the assembled platter so it stays in soft, distinct strands.
Use a firm processed or cheddar cheese that grates cleanly rather than a soft crumbly one.
Serve at once, as the cheese and sev both soften quickly once the chutneys are added.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a fun party starter with extra grated cheese and a squeeze of lime for guests to customise.

variations.name: Classic Sweet Pongal
variations.description: Sweet Pongal, or chakkara pongal, is a festive South Indian pudding of rice and moong dal cooked soft, then sweetened with melted jaggery and enriched with ghee-fried cashews and raisins. Fragrant with cardamom, it is the traditional offering for the Pongal harvest festival.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the natural sweetener that gives this pongal its deep caramel colour and flavour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the cashews and raisins and gives the pudding its glossy, rich finish

steps: Dry-roast 0.5 cup moong dal for 2 minutes until fragrant, then rinse it with 1 cup rice together.
Pressure-cook the rice and dal with 4 cups water and 0.5 cup milk for 5 whistles until very soft and mushy, then mash to a smooth mass.
Melt 1.25 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 0.5 cup water in a separate pan over low heat, then strain out any grit and simmer to a thick syrup.
Pour the strained jaggery syrup into the mashed rice-dal and cook on low heat for 5 minutes, stirring, until it thickens and comes together.
Heat 5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan, fry 12 cashews to golden, add 2 tbsp raisins until they plump, then pour it all in.
Stir in 0.5 tsp cardamom powder, mix until glossy, and serve the sweet pongal warm.
tips: Never add raw jaggery straight to milk-cooked rice; melt and strain it first so the dish does not curdle or taste gritty.
Keep the pongal slightly loose, as it thickens a lot once it cools.
Add most of the ghee towards the end for the richest aroma and a beautiful sheen.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a festival prasadam or dessert, with an extra drizzle of ghee and a few whole cashews on top.

variations.name: Coconut Jaggery Sweet Pongal
variations.description: A coastal twist that folds fresh coconut and coconut milk into the jaggery pongal for a fragrant, tropical richness. Coconut oil-fried nuts add a distinctive aroma that sets it apart from the ghee-only classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted and strained to sweeten the coconut-rich pudding naturally

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: fries the nuts and lends a fragrant coastal aroma to the pongal

steps: Dry-roast 0.5 cup moong dal for 2 minutes, then rinse with 1 cup rice and pressure-cook with 3.5 cups water for 5 whistles until soft, then mash.
Melt 1.25 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 0.5 cup water, strain, and simmer to a thick syrup.
Stir the syrup into the mashed rice-dal on low heat for 4 minutes, then fold in 0.5 cup grated coconut.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, fry 12 cashews golden and 2 tbsp raisins until plump, and pour it in with 0.5 tsp cardamom.
Add 1 cup coconut milk off high heat, stirring gently so it does not split, and warm through for 2 minutes.
Cook to a soft, creamy consistency and serve the coconut sweet pongal warm.
tips: Add the coconut milk on low heat at the end so it stays smooth and does not curdle.
Frying the cashews in coconut oil deepens the tropical aroma that defines this version.
Fresh grated coconut gives the best texture, but desiccated coconut works if soaked briefly in warm milk.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm topped with toasted coconut flakes, a lovely dessert after a South Indian feast.

variations.name: Millet Sweet Pongal
variations.description: A nourishing take that replaces rice with foxtail millet, keeping the jaggery, ghee and cardamom that define sweet pongal. The millet lends a subtle nuttiness and extra fibre while staying soft and pudding-like.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted and strained to sweeten the millet pongal with rich caramel notes

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the nuts and keeps the millet pongal moist and glossy

steps: Dry-roast 0.5 cup moong dal for 2 minutes, then rinse 1 cup foxtail millet well with it to remove any dust.
Pressure-cook the millet and dal with 4.5 cups water for 5 whistles until very soft, then mash to a porridge.
Melt 1.25 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 0.5 cup water, strain out grit, and simmer to a thick syrup.
Stir the syrup into the mashed millet-dal on low heat for 5 minutes until it thickens and combines.
Heat 5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, fry 12 cashews golden and 2 tbsp raisins until plump, then pour it in with 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp dry ginger powder.
Loosen with a splash of hot water if needed, as millet sets thicker than rice, and serve warm.
tips: Rinse the foxtail millet thoroughly and cook it a touch softer than rice for the best pudding texture.
A pinch of dry ginger powder aids digestion and adds a warm note that suits the millet beautifully.
Keep this version slightly looser at the end, as millet firms up more than rice on cooling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a wholesome festival sweet, garnished with extra ghee-fried cashews.

variations.name: Classic Tamarind Rice
variations.description: The South Indian lunchbox staple where cooked rice is coated in a tangy, spicy tamarind paste crackling with mustard, chana dal and roasted peanuts. The sourness of tamarind, the nuttiness of the tempering and a whisper of jaggery come together in perfect balance. It keeps for hours without a fridge, which is exactly why it fills every travel tiffin down south.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: The authentic gingelly oil that gives tamarind rice its distinctive nutty aroma and glossy coat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Rounds off the tamarind's sharp sourness without making the rice sweet

steps: Cook 1.5 cups rice with 3 cups water until each grain is separate and firm, spread it on a wide plate to cool, and drizzle over 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil so the grains do not clump.
Soak the lemon-sized tamarind ball in 1 cup hot water for 15 minutes, then squeeze and strain to extract a thick, dark pulp.
Dry-roast 1 tbsp sesame seeds until they pop, cool, and grind coarsely to add a nutty depth later.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadhai, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 1.5 tbsp chana dal, 1 tbsp urad dal and 1/4 cup peanuts, frying until the dals turn golden and the peanuts crisp, about 3 minutes.
Toss in 3 broken red chillies, 12 curry leaves and 1/4 tsp asafoetida, fry 20 seconds, then pour in the tamarind extract with 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp salt.
Simmer this pulikachal paste on medium heat for 8 minutes until it thickens, darkens and the oil begins to separate at the edges, a sign the raw tamarind has cooked out.
Add the cooled rice and the ground sesame, mixing gently with a light hand until every grain is evenly coated; rest 10 minutes for the flavours to soak in before serving.
tips: Always cool the rice before mixing; hot rice breaks into mush when tossed with the thick tamarind paste.
The pulikachal paste keeps refrigerated for two weeks, so make a double batch and stir a spoonful into plain rice any day.
Use gingelly (sesame) oil rather than a neutral oil; it is the single ingredient that makes this taste authentically South Indian.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature with crisp fried papad, a fistful of extra roasted peanuts on top and a cooling bowl of plain curd.

variations.name: Andhra Pulihora
variations.description: Andhra Pradesh's festival tamarind rice, fierier and more aromatic than its neighbours, with a signature ground powder of roasted fenugreek, sesame and red chilli stirred through at the end. Made for temple offerings and Ugadi feasts, it carries a bracing sourness tamed by generous tempering. The methi-sesame podi is what sets the Andhra version unmistakably apart.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Andhra pulihora uses a heavy hand of gingelly oil for its glossy sheen and long shelf life

ingredients.name: Fenugreek seeds
ingredients.note: Dry-roasted and ground into the podi, never added raw

steps: Cook 1.5 cups rice to firm, separate grains with 3 cups water, spread out to cool and rub in 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and 1/4 tsp turmeric so the rice turns pale yellow and non-sticky.
For the Andhra podi, dry-roast 1/2 tsp fenugreek, 2 tbsp sesame seeds and 3 red chillies separately on low heat until the fenugreek is reddish-brown and fragrant, cool and grind to a coarse powder.
Soak the large tamarind ball in 1.25 cups hot water for 15 minutes and squeeze out a thick extract.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then fry 2 tbsp chana dal, 1 tbsp urad dal and 1/3 cup peanuts until golden, about 3 minutes.
Add 3 remaining red chillies, 3 slit green chillies, 15 curry leaves and 1/2 tsp asafoetida, fry 30 seconds, then pour in the tamarind extract with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp salt.
Cook the tamarind mixture down on medium heat for 10 minutes until it turns glossy and thick and the oil rises to the surface, then stir in the roasted podi and simmer 2 more minutes.
Tip the cooled rice into the pan and fold gently until uniformly coated a deep golden-brown; leave to rest at least 15 minutes so the sour-spicy flavours penetrate every grain.
tips: The fenugreek-sesame podi is the heart of Andhra pulihora, so grind it fresh and add it only after the tamarind has cooked to keep its aroma bright.
Andhra style is meant to taste boldly sour and spicy, but if it overwhelms, a small pinch of jaggery pulls it back into balance.
Rest the finished rice for at least fifteen minutes, ideally an hour, as pulihora genuinely improves as it sits.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at Ugadi with fried vadiyalu, a slice of cucumber and a dollop of thick yogurt to counter the heat.

variations.name: Peanut-Sesame Puliyogare
variations.description: The Karnataka darshini classic, distinguished by a fragrant homemade puliyogare gojju built on roasted peanuts, sesame, dry coconut and a hint of jaggery for the state's beloved sweet-sour balance. It is thicker, richer and mellower than the Andhra version, coating the rice in a dark, glistening paste. A spoon of this gojju transforms plain rice into a feast in minutes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Essential for the gojju's body and its ability to keep the rice fresh for a full day

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Karnataka puliyogare leans gently sweet-sour, and jaggery gives that rounded finish

steps: Cook 1.5 cups rice to firm, separate grains, spread to cool and coat with 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil.

For the puliyogare powder, dry-roast 2 tbsp chana dal, 1 tbsp coriander seeds, 4 red chillies, 2 tbsp sesame seeds and 3 tbsp dry coconut separately until golden and fragrant, cool and grind to a coarse podi.
Soak the large tamarind ball in 1.5 cups hot water for 15 minutes and extract a thick pulp.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, fry 1/3 cup peanuts until crisp, then add 2 remaining red chillies, 15 curry leaves and 1/2 tsp asafoetida for 20 seconds.
Pour in the tamarind extract with 1/2 tsp turmeric, 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1.5 tsp salt, and simmer 12 minutes until it reduces to a thick, dark, oil-glossed gojju.
Stir the ground podi into the gojju and cook 2 minutes more so it soaks up the tamarind and turns into a fragrant paste that pulls away from the pan.
Fold half the gojju through the cooled rice until richly coated, adding more to taste; rest 15 minutes and reserve the extra gojju in a jar for later use.
tips: The gojju is concentrated, so start with half and build up; you can always add more but cannot take it out.
Stored in a clean glass jar topped with a film of sesame oil, this gojju lasts a month in the fridge and only deepens in flavour.
Dry coconut, not fresh, is used here because it grinds into the powder without adding moisture that would spoil the shelf life.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Bengaluru way with a crisp potato chip, a spoon of plain curd and a wedge of raw mango on the side.

variations.name: Quick Instant Tamarind Rice
variations.description: A weeknight rescue that turns leftover rice into a satisfying meal in under twenty minutes using ready tamarind concentrate and a fast tempering. It sacrifices none of the tangy, nutty character of the slow-cooked original, relying on a punchy tempering and a quick sesame finish. Perfect for busy mornings when the lunchbox has to be packed in a hurry.

ingredients.name: Cooked rice
ingredients.note: Day-old or freshly cooled rice with separate grains

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Delivers the classic gingelly aroma even in this speeded-up version

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Balances the concentrated tamarind quickly without needing to simmer long

steps: Spread 4 cups cooked rice on a wide plate and fluff to separate the grains, drizzling over 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil to prevent clumping.
Dry-roast 1 tbsp sesame seeds until they crackle, then set aside for a finishing sprinkle.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadhai, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, and fry 1.5 tbsp chana dal with 1/4 cup peanuts until golden and crunchy, about 3 minutes.
Add 3 broken red chillies, 2 slit green chillies, 12 curry leaves and 1/4 tsp asafoetida, frying 20 seconds until aromatic.
Whisk 2 tbsp tamarind concentrate with 1/4 cup water, 1/2 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp salt, pour into the pan and simmer 3 minutes until thick and glossy.
Switch off the heat, add the fluffed rice and toss gently until evenly coated a pale golden-brown.
Sprinkle the roasted sesame over the top, mix once more and rest 5 minutes before packing or serving.
tips: Tamarind concentrates vary in strength, so start with a little, taste, and add more rather than over-souring the rice.
Cold leftover rice actually works better than fresh here because the drier grains absorb the tempering without turning sticky.
Fry a bigger batch of the peanut-dal tempering and store it airtight to cut the cook time to under ten minutes next time.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pack into a tiffin with a handful of extra fried peanuts and a small tub of thick curd, or serve with plain potato fry alongside.

variations.name: Classic Tomato Rasam
variations.description: The bright, tangy everyday rasam of Tamil homes, where ripe tomatoes and tamarind are simmered with fresh rasam powder and crowned with a ghee tempering of mustard and cumin. It is thin, aromatic and restorative, meant to be sipped or poured over rice on a tired evening.

ingredients.name: Ripe tomatoes
ingredients.note: roughly chopped

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked in warm water for pulp

ingredients.name: Toor dal
ingredients.note: cooked soft and mashed, for body

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a small pinch that softens the tamarind and tomato tang

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: crushed

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the tempering fat that carries the rasam's classic aroma

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Squeeze the tomatoes by hand into a pot along with the tamarind pulp extracted in 1 cup water, 3 crushed garlic cloves, 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt.
Add 1.5 tbsp rasam powder and 1/2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, then bring to a gentle simmer on medium heat for 8-10 minutes until the raw tamarind smell disappears and the tomatoes collapse.
Stir in 2 tbsp mashed toor dal loosened with 3/4 cup water, then lower the heat so the rasam froths at the edges but never boils hard, which would make it dull and flat.
Simmer gently for 4-5 minutes until the rasam turns cloudy and aromatic, then switch off the heat before it reduces too much.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan, splutter 1/2 tsp mustard seeds and 1/2 tsp cumin seeds, then add 2 dry red chillies, 1/4 tsp asafoetida and 2 sprigs curry leaves and fry for 30 seconds.
Pour the sizzling tempering over the rasam, cover for 2 minutes to trap the aroma, then finish with 3 tbsp chopped fresh coriander before serving.
tips: Never let rasam reach a rolling boil once the dal goes in; a bare froth keeps its aroma fresh and lively.
Squeezing the tomatoes by hand releases more flavour than chopping and gives the rasam a fuller body.
Make a double batch of rasam powder and store it airtight so a pot of rasam is only minutes away.
variations.servingSuggestion: Sip it warm from a tumbler as a starter, or pour over steamed rice with a spoon of ghee and a crisp appalam on the side.

variations.name: Andhra Tomato Charu
variations.description: The fiery Andhra take on tomato rasam, where extra green chillies and a bold hit of crushed pepper make a charu that clears the sinuses. Thinner and spicier than the Tamil version, it is poured lavishly over rice with a spoon of ghee to take the edge off the heat.

ingredients.name: Ripe tomatoes
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked for pulp

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

ingredients.name: Black peppercorns
ingredients.note: coarsely crushed

ingredients.name: Toor dal
ingredients.note: cooked and mashed

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: cools and rounds the sharp heat of the charu

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: crushed

steps: Simmer the chopped tomatoes with the tamarind pulp extracted in 1.5 cups water, 3 slit green chillies, 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt on medium heat for 8 minutes.
Add 1.5 tsp coarsely crushed peppercorns and 1 tsp cumin seeds and cook for 3 more minutes until the tomatoes soften completely and the charu smells sharp and peppery.
Stir in 3 tbsp mashed toor dal loosened with 1 cup water to keep the charu deliberately thin, then simmer gently on low heat for 4 minutes without boiling.
Taste and keep the balance clearly hot and tangy, adding a splash of water if it has reduced too much.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan, splutter 1/2 tsp mustard seeds, add 4 crushed garlic cloves and fry until golden, then add 2 dry red chillies, 1/4 tsp asafoetida and 2 sprigs curry leaves.
Pour the tempering over the charu, cover for 2 minutes, and finish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander before serving very hot.
tips: Keep the charu thin and pourable; Andhra style is meant to flood the rice rather than sit thick.
Crush the pepper coarsely just before cooking so its heat stays bright and fragrant.
A generous spoon of ghee over the rice is not optional here, as it balances the pronounced heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pour over hot rice with a big spoon of ghee and a fried papad, or serve with a mild potato fry to offset the spice.

variations.name: No-Dal Instant Tomato Rasam
variations.description: A fuss-free rasam for busy days that skips the dal entirely, leaning on ripe tomatoes and a quick pounded pepper-cumin masala for body. Ready in under twenty minutes, it captures all the tang and aroma of the classic with none of the pressure-cooking.

ingredients.name: Ripe tomatoes
ingredients.note: pureed

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked for a mild pulp

ingredients.name: Cumin seeds
ingredients.note: for the pounded masala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: balances the tomato tang in this quick rasam

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the finishing tempering that makes even a shortcut rasam smell homemade

steps: Pound 1 tsp peppercorns, 1 tsp cumin seeds and 3 garlic cloves in a mortar into a coarse, fragrant masala.

Pour the pureed tomatoes into a pot with the tamarind pulp extracted in 1.5 cups water, 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder, the pounded masala, 1/2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp salt.
Bring to a gentle simmer on medium heat for 8-10 minutes until the raw tomato and tamarind smells disappear and the rasam turns fragrant.
Lower the heat and let it froth at the edges for 3 minutes without boiling hard, adding a splash of water if it thickens too much.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan, splutter 1/2 tsp mustard seeds, then add 2 dry red chillies, 1/4 tsp asafoetida and 2 sprigs curry leaves and fry for 30 seconds until aromatic.
Pour the tempering over the rasam, cover for 2 minutes, and scatter 3 tbsp chopped coriander on top before serving.
tips: Pureeing the tomatoes gives this dal-free rasam enough body to feel complete on its own.
The pounded fresh masala does the work of rasam powder here, so make it just before cooking.
If you like it a shade thicker, mash in a boiled potato-sized spoon of leftover cooked rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot rice for a five-minute comfort meal, or sip warm as a light soup when you want something quick and soothing.

variations.name: Classic Sundakkai Vatha Kuzhambu
variations.description: The definitive Tamil Brahmin tamarind gravy, built on sun-dried turkey berries (sundakkai vathal) fried dark in gingelly oil. It is deliberately thick, glossy and bitter-tangy-sweet all at once, a preserving-season dish meant to keep for days and coat hot rice with a spoonful of ghee.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil is non-negotiable here — it fries the vathal and is what makes the kuzhambu keep for days

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A spoon of jaggery rounds the tamarind sourness into the classic tangy-sweet balance

steps: Soak 30 g tamarind in 2 cups warm water for 10 minutes, then squeeze and strain to get a smooth, seed-free extract; keep it aside.

Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a heavy kadai on medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1/2 tsp fenugreek seeds for about 20 seconds, then add 3 broken dried red chillies, 15 curry leaves, 1/4 tsp asafoetida and 10 crushed garlic cloves and fry until the garlic turns pale gold.
Tip in 3 tbsp sundakkai vathal and fry on low heat for 2 to 3 minutes until they turn a deep coffee-brown and smell toasty, taking care not to blacken them into bitterness.
Lower the flame, stir in 2 tbsp sambar powder and 1/4 tsp turmeric for 15 seconds until fragrant, then immediately pour in the tamarind extract and 1 tsp salt so the powder does not scorch.
Simmer uncovered on medium-low heat for 15 to 18 minutes, until the raw tamarind smell disappears and pools of sesame oil rise to the surface, showing the kuzhambu is ready.
Stir 1 tsp rice flour into 2 tbsp cold water and pour it in with 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder; cook 2 more minutes until the gravy thickens to a glossy, coating consistency, then switch off.
tips: Vatha kuzhambu actually tastes better the next day once the vathal softens and the flavours mellow, so make it ahead and refrigerate.
If it turns too sour, do not add water — stir in an extra 1 tsp jaggery and a splash more sesame oil to rebalance it.
Keep the flame low while frying the vathal; scorched turkey berries turn the whole pot bitter and cannot be rescued.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot steamed rice with a teaspoon of ghee, crisp appalam and a simple stir-fried potato curry on the side for a classic Tamil lunch.

variations.name: Vengaya Vatha Kuzhambu
variations.description: A homely Kongunadu version that swaps dried vathal for whole shallots (chinna vengayam) simmered until meltingly soft in the tamarind gravy. The small onions turn sweet and jammy, giving the sour base a mellow, comforting body that everyone at the table fights over.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil sautés the shallots slowly and gives this onion kuzhambu its signature glossy finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Balances the tamarind and echoes the natural sweetness of the caramelised shallots

steps: Soak 25 g tamarind in 2 cups warm water for 10 minutes and strain out a smooth pulp; peel 20 small shallots and keep them whole, and chop 1 tomato finely.

Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadai on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds with 1/2 tsp fenugreek seeds for 20 seconds, then add 15 curry leaves, 8 crushed garlic cloves and 1/4 tsp asafoetida.

Add the 20 whole shallots and sauté on medium-low heat for 6 to 7 minutes until they turn glossy and their edges caramelise to golden-brown, then stir in the chopped tomato and cook until it collapses.
Lower the heat, add 2 tbsp sambar powder and 1/4 tsp turmeric and roast for 20 seconds until aromatic, then pour in the tamarind extract along with 1 tsp salt.
Simmer uncovered for 18 to 20 minutes on medium-low heat until the shallots are meltingly soft and sesame oil floats on top of a thickened gravy.
Whisk 1 tsp rice flour into 2 tbsp water, stir it in with 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, and cook 2 minutes more until the kuzhambu is thick and coats a spoon.
tips: Choose firm, small sambar onions and keep them whole — chopped onions dissolve and rob the dish of its signature sweet bites.
Sauté the shallots patiently; rushing this step leaves them raw-tasting inside the sour gravy.
A pinch of extra jaggery at the end deepens the caramel note if your tamarind is very sharp.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with hot rice and sesame-oil-drizzled sutta appalam, or spoon it over curd rice for a tangy contrast at the end of a meal.

variations.name: Chettinad Vatha Kuzhambu
variations.description: The bold Chettinad rendition, where a freshly dry-roasted and ground masala of peppercorns, coriander and fennel replaces plain sambar powder. Manathakkali vathal adds gentle bitterness and the pepper-heavy paste gives this kuzhambu the deep, aromatic fire the region is famous for.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Chettinad cooking is generous with gingelly oil — it carries the roasted-spice aroma and preserves the gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Tempers the sharp pepper and tamarind into a rounded Chettinad balance

steps: Dry-roast 2 tbsp coriander seeds, 1 tbsp black peppercorns, 1 tsp fennel seeds, 1 tbsp toor dal and 4 dried red chillies on low heat for 3 minutes until deeply fragrant, cool, and grind to a fine powder.
Soak 30 g tamarind in 2 cups warm water for 10 minutes and strain to a smooth extract.
Heat 5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadai on medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1/2 tsp fenugreek seeds, then fry 12 crushed garlic cloves and 15 curry leaves until golden.
Add 3 tbsp manathakkali vathal and fry on low heat for 2 minutes until they puff and darken, releasing their nutty-bitter aroma.
Pour in the tamarind extract, add the freshly ground Chettinad masala, 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, and bring to a rolling simmer.
Cook uncovered on medium-low heat for 15 to 18 minutes until thick and oil separates at the edges, then stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and simmer 2 more minutes before switching off.
tips: Grind the spice mix fresh for each batch; a pre-ground store powder will never give the peppery Chettinad punch this version needs.
The toor dal in the masala thickens the gravy naturally, so you can skip rice flour altogether here.
Let the kuzhambu rest 30 minutes off the heat before serving so the roasted spices bloom fully into the tamarind.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice, a dollop of ghee and a crisp keerai vadai or fried papad to stand up to the bold pepper heat.

variations.name: Arachuvitta Vatha Kuzhambu
variations.description: A richer temple-style version thickened with a freshly ground paste of roasted coconut, chana dal and red chillies (arachuvitta means freshly ground). The coconut masala gives the tamarind gravy a velvety, almost creamy body without any dairy, and a mellow, layered heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil roasts the coconut masala and lends the finished gravy its authentic sheen

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Balances the tamarind against the sweet roasted coconut paste

steps: Heat 1 tsp of the Anveshan Sesame Oil and roast 1 tbsp chana dal, 1 tbsp coriander seeds and 4 dried red chillies until golden, then add 1/3 cup grated coconut and toast 1 minute until it just turns pale gold; cool and grind with a little water to a smooth paste.
Soak 25 g tamarind in 1.5 cups warm water for 10 minutes and strain to a smooth extract.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadai on medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1/2 tsp fenugreek seeds, then add 15 curry leaves and 1/4 tsp asafoetida.
Add 2 tbsp sundakkai vathal and fry on low heat for about 2 minutes until they darken and smell toasty.
Pour in the tamarind extract with 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, and simmer for 8 minutes until the raw sourness fades.

Stir in the ground coconut paste and 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer gently for 6 to 8 minutes until the gravy thickens to a creamy, oil-flecked consistency, and switch off before it boils hard so the coconut does not turn grainy.
tips: Add the coconut paste on a gentle simmer, never a rapid boil, or it can split and turn the gravy grainy.
This version is best eaten the same day; the fresh coconut does not keep as long as a plain vatha kuzhambu.
Rinse the grinder with 2 tbsp water and add it to the pot so none of the precious masala is wasted.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle over hot rice topped with a spoon of ghee and serve with a dry beans poriyal and roasted appalam for a hearty South Indian thali.

variations.name: Classic Kerala Vegetable Stew
variations.description: The gentle Nadan ishtu of central Kerala, where carrots, beans and potatoes poach in two grades of coconut milk perfumed with cinnamon, cloves and curry leaves. There is no chilli powder here, only slit green chillies and whole spices, so the finish is creamy, mild and faintly sweet.

ingredients.name: Potato
ingredients.note: peeled and cubed

ingredients.name: Carrot
ingredients.note: cut into batons

ingredients.name: Green beans
ingredients.note: cut into 2 cm pieces

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed, it gives this stew its unmistakable Kerala aroma

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: thinly sliced

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: julienned

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit lengthwise

ingredients.name: Thin coconut milk
ingredients.note: second-press, for simmering the vegetables

ingredients.name: Thick coconut milk
ingredients.note: first-press, added off the boil

steps: Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a wide pan on medium heat, then drop in 1 inch cinnamon, 4 cloves and 3 lightly cracked cardamom pods and let them sizzle for about 40 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 thinly sliced onion, the ginger juliennes, 3 slit green chillies and 1 sprig of curry leaves; saute gently for 4-5 minutes until the onion turns soft and translucent without browning.
Tip in the cubed potato, carrot batons, beans and 1/4 cup peas along with 1 tsp salt, stir to coat, then pour in 1.5 cups thin coconut milk.
Cover and simmer on low heat for 12-15 minutes, stirring once or twice, until the potatoes are fork-tender and the vegetables have soaked up the spiced liquid.
Lower the flame to its minimum, pour in 1 cup thick coconut milk and warm through for just 2 minutes without letting it boil, so the milk stays silky and does not split.
Switch off the heat, scatter the remaining curry leaves over the top and drizzle a teaspoon of raw Anveshan Coconut Oil across the surface; rest covered for 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Never let the stew boil once the thick coconut milk goes in; a bare simmer keeps it from curdling into grainy specks.
Cut all the vegetables to a similar size so they finish cooking together and none turn mushy while others stay raw.
The stew thickens as it rests; loosen a reheated batch with a splash of warm thin coconut milk rather than water.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot with lacy appams or soft idiyappam, or ladle it over ghee rice for a comforting weekday dinner.

variations.name: Sadya-style Vegetable Stew
variations.description: The festive banquet version served on a banana leaf during Onam, made richer with a hand-ground paste of raw coconut, shallots and fennel that thickens the gravy naturally. A tempering of crackled mustard and roasted shallots crowns it, giving far more depth than the everyday stew.

ingredients.name: Potato
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Carrot
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Ash gourd
ingredients.note: peeled and cubed

ingredients.name: Green beans
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the sadya fat that carries the roasted-shallot tempering

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Whole black pepper
ingredients.note: coarsely crushed

steps: Grind 3/4 cup grated coconut with 1/2 tsp fennel seeds, 4 shallots and 1/4 cup water to a smooth white paste and set it aside for the gravy base.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan on medium heat, add the remaining 4 sliced shallots, chopped ginger, 3 slit green chillies and 1 sprig curry leaves and saute for 3 minutes until softened.
Add the cubed potato, carrot, ash gourd and beans with 1 tsp salt and 1 cup water, cover and simmer on low heat for 12 minutes until the vegetables are almost tender.
Stir in the ground coconut paste and 1/2 tsp coarsely crushed pepper, then cook uncovered for 5 minutes so the gravy thickens and loses its raw coconut smell.
Lower the heat and pour in 1 cup thick coconut milk, warming it through for 2 minutes without boiling until the stew turns glossy and pale ivory.

In a small ladle heat the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, splutter 1/2 tsp mustard seeds with the second sprig of curry leaves for 30 seconds, and pour this sizzling tempering over the stew before serving.
tips: Grind the coconut paste as fine as possible; any coarse bits leave the gravy gritty rather than velvety.
Ash gourd releases water as it cooks, so keep the added water modest or the stew turns thin.
Prepare the vegetables and coconut paste the night before a sadya so only the final simmer and tempering remain on the day.
variations.servingSuggestion: Spoon it beside steamed red matta rice on a banana leaf with olan and thoran, or pair with plain appams for a festive breakfast.

variations.name: Pepper Vegetable Stew
variations.description: A warming monsoon rendition from the Malabar highlands where freshly crushed black pepper, not green chilli, drives the heat. The coconut milk stays generous so the pepper glows through the creaminess rather than searing, making it a favourite when the rains set in.

ingredients.name: Potato
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Carrot
ingredients.note: diced

ingredients.name: Cauliflower
ingredients.note: small florets

ingredients.name: Green beans
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the base fat that rounds off the sharp pepper heat

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: sliced

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: julienned

ingredients.name: Black peppercorns
ingredients.note: coarsely crushed

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan on medium heat, add 1 inch cinnamon and 3 cloves and let them crackle for 30 seconds until aromatic.
Add 1 sliced onion, 1.5 inch ginger juliennes, 2 slit green chillies and 1 sprig curry leaves and saute for 4-5 minutes until the onion is soft and just turning gold.
Stir in 1.5 tsp coarsely crushed black peppercorns and roast for 40 seconds until the kitchen fills with a warm peppery smell, taking care not to let them burn.
Add the potato, carrot, cauliflower and beans with 1 tsp salt and 1.5 cups thin coconut milk, cover and simmer on low heat for 14-15 minutes until the vegetables turn tender.
Reduce the flame to its lowest, pour in 1 cup thick coconut milk and heat through for 2 minutes without boiling, so the pepper mellows into the creamy base.
Finish with the second sprig of curry leaves and a fresh pinch of crushed pepper on top, then rest the stew covered for 4 minutes before ladling out.
tips: Crush the peppercorns just before cooking; pre-ground pepper loses the fruity aroma that makes this version special.
Add half the pepper during cooking and the rest at the end for both depth and a fresh top note.
If the heat feels strong, an extra splash of thick coconut milk tames it instantly without dulling the flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle it over steaming appams on a rainy evening, or serve with plain steamed rice and a side of pappadam for crunch.

variations.name: Kadala Curry-style Chickpea Stew
variations.description: A heartier, protein-packed twist that folds soft-cooked white chickpeas into the classic coconut-milk stew alongside the vegetables. The chickpeas soak up the whole-spice-scented gravy, turning a gentle side dish into a one-pot meal that still stays true to its Kerala roots.

ingredients.name: White chickpeas
ingredients.note: soaked overnight and pressure-cooked soft

ingredients.name: Potato
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Carrot
ingredients.note: diced

ingredients.name: Green beans
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed, it binds the chickpeas and vegetables in one aroma

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: sliced

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: julienned

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

steps: Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan on medium heat, add 1 inch cinnamon, 3 cloves and 1/2 tsp fennel seeds and let them sizzle for 40 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 sliced onion, ginger juliennes, 3 slit green chillies and 1 sprig curry leaves and saute for 5 minutes until the onion softens and smells sweet.
Tip in the cubed potato, carrot and beans with 1 tsp salt, stir for a minute, then pour in 1.5 cups thin coconut milk and simmer covered on low heat for 10 minutes.
Add the pressure-cooked chickpeas and cook uncovered for another 8 minutes until the vegetables are tender and the chickpeas have absorbed the spiced gravy.
Lower the flame to its minimum and pour in 1 cup thick coconut milk, warming it through for 2 minutes without boiling so it stays creamy and smooth.
Switch off the heat, drizzle a teaspoon of raw Anveshan Coconut Oil and scatter the second sprig of curry leaves over the top; rest covered for 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Cook the chickpeas until they crush easily between two fingers; firm chickpeas stay chalky against the creamy gravy.
Add the chickpeas only after the vegetables have started softening so they do not turn the stew starchy too early.
A pinch of crushed fennel stirred in at the end lifts the whole pot with a sweet, aniseedy warmth.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft appams or Malabar parotta for a filling brunch, or pair with steamed rice and lime pickle for a wholesome lunch.

variations.name: Classic Vegetable Upma
variations.description: A wholesome South Indian breakfast of roasted semolina cooked fluffy with carrots, beans, peas and a fragrant mustard-curry leaf tempering. The rava is dry-roasted first so the finished upma stays soft yet grainy, never sticky. Quick, filling and endlessly comforting, it is the dish that starts millions of mornings across the peninsula.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Finishes the upma with a soft sheen and nutty aroma that oil alone cannot give

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed oil for a clean tempering that lets the vegetables shine

steps: Dry-roast 1.5 cups semolina in a kadhai over medium-low heat, stirring constantly for 4-5 minutes until it smells nutty and turns a shade paler, then tip onto a plate to stop the cooking.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then fry 1 tbsp urad dal, 1 tbsp chana dal and 10 cashews until golden, about 2 minutes.
Add 12 curry leaves, 2 slit green chillies, grated 1 inch ginger and 1 chopped medium onion, sauteing until the onion softens and turns translucent, about 3 minutes.
Stir in 1 diced carrot, 8 chopped beans and 1/3 cup peas with 1/4 tsp salt, cover and cook 4 minutes until the vegetables are just tender but still bright.
Pour in 3.5 cups water with 1 tsp salt and bring to a rolling boil, letting the vegetables bubble in it for 2 minutes.
Lower the heat and add the roasted semolina in a slow stream with one hand while stirring briskly with the other to prevent any lumps forming.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 3-4 minutes until the water is fully absorbed and the upma looks fluffy, then fold in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and rest covered 2 minutes before serving.
tips: The golden ratio is roughly 1 part rava to 2.3 parts water for a soft upma; less water gives a drier, grainier result if you prefer.
Adding the rava in a thin stream while stirring vigorously is the single trick that guarantees a lump-free texture.
A teaspoon of sugar added with the salt is a common South Indian touch that rounds out the flavour beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with coconut chutney and a wedge of lime, or the classic pairing of upma with sweetened banana and a cup of filter coffee.

variations.name: Karnataka Khara Bath
variations.description: Bengaluru's iconic spiced upma, deepened with vangi bath or khara bath powder, tomato and a hint of tamarind for the darshini-hotel signature. It is bolder, redder and more masaledar than plain vegetable upma, often served as one half of the famous chow-chow bath duo. Every spoonful hums with the fragrance of freshly ground South Indian spices.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Khara bath is famously ghee-rich, both in the cooking and drizzled at the finish

ingredients.name: Khara bath powder
ingredients.note: The vangi-bath style masala that defines this dish

steps: Dry-roast 1.5 cups coarse bansi rava over medium heat for 5 minutes until fragrant and lightly coloured, then set aside on a plate.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, and fry 1 tbsp urad dal, 1 tbsp chana dal and 12 cashews until golden.
Add 12 curry leaves, 3 slit green chillies and 1 large chopped onion, sauteing until the onion is soft, about 3 minutes, then stir in 1 chopped tomato and cook until it collapses.
Mix in 1 diced carrot and 1/3 cup peas with 2 tsp khara bath powder and 1/2 tsp tamarind paste, stir-frying 2 minutes so the masala coats the vegetables and loses its raw smell.
Pour in 3.5 cups water with 1.25 tsp salt, bring to a vigorous boil and simmer 3 minutes until the vegetables are tender.
Lower the heat and rain in the roasted rava while stirring constantly, breaking up any lumps as they form.
Cover and cook on low for 4 minutes until thick and fluffy, then fold in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and rest 2 minutes before serving.
tips: Coarse bansi rava holds the spices and stays grainy, which is why khara bath uses it rather than fine semolina.
If you lack khara bath powder, a mix of 1 tsp sambar powder with 1/2 tsp garam masala makes a fair stand-in.
The tamarind should be barely detectable, just enough to lift the masala without turning the dish sour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as chow-chow bath, pairing a scoop of this khara bath with sweet kesari bath, coconut chutney and hot filter coffee.

variations.name: Tomato Vegetable Upma
variations.description: A tangy, colourful twist where ripe tomatoes are cooked down into the base, tinting the upma a warm orange and lending a gentle sourness that brightens the whole dish. The extra moisture from the tomatoes keeps it especially soft and moist. A favourite with children who find plain upma dull, it needs little more than a squeeze of lime to sing.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed oil carries the tomato tang cleanly without a greasy aftertaste

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon that rounds the tomato's acidity with mellow richness

steps: Dry-roast 1.5 cups semolina over medium-low heat for 4-5 minutes until nutty and pale, then reserve on a plate.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, fry 1 tbsp urad dal until golden, then add 12 curry leaves and 2 slit green chillies.
Add 1 chopped onion and 1 tsp ginger-garlic paste, sauteing 3 minutes until the raw smell goes, then stir in 1 small diced carrot and 1/4 cup peas and cook 3 minutes.
Add 3 chopped tomatoes with 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder and 1/4 tsp salt, cooking covered for 5 minutes until the tomatoes break down into a thick, pulpy mash.
Pour in 3 cups water with 1 tsp salt and bring to a boil, letting it bubble for 2 minutes so the flavours meld.
Reduce the heat to low and add the roasted rava in a steady stream, stirring hard to keep it smooth and lump-free.
Cover and cook 4 minutes until the water is absorbed and the upma turns fluffy and orange, then fold in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and rest 2 minutes.
tips: Ripe, juicy tomatoes matter here; pale winter tomatoes give neither the colour nor the tang the dish depends on.
Because tomatoes add liquid, hold back a couple of tablespoons of water and add only if the upma looks too dry.
A pinch of sugar tames any excess tomato sourness and deepens the overall colour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain coconut chutney or a dollop of thick curd, garnished with fresh coriander and a squeeze of lime.

variations.name: Masala Sambar Upma
variations.description: A hearty one-pot where upma meets the flavours of sambar, cooked with a spoon of sambar powder, a handful of soaked toor dal and extra vegetables for a meal-in-itself breakfast. The dal adds body and protein while the sambar powder lends that unmistakable tiffin-centre aroma. Robust and satisfying, it needs no accompaniment beyond a spoon of ghee.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rounds out the sambar spices and gives the upma a glossy, aromatic finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil deepens the sambar-style flavour the way it does in tiffin sambar

ingredients.name: Toor dal
ingredients.note: Soaked 20 minutes so it cooks soft along with the upma

steps: Soak 3 tbsp toor dal in warm water for 20 minutes, then drain; separately dry-roast 1.5 cups semolina over medium-low heat for 5 minutes until fragrant and set aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, fry 1 tbsp urad dal until golden, then add 1/4 tsp asafoetida and 12 curry leaves.
Add 1 chopped onion and saute 3 minutes until soft, then stir in 1 diced carrot, 6 chopped beans and 1/4 cup peas along with the drained toor dal.
Sprinkle in 1.5 tsp sambar powder and stir-fry 2 minutes so the masala coats the vegetables and dal and smells toasty.
Pour in 3.75 cups water with 1.25 tsp salt, bring to a boil and simmer 6 minutes until the toor dal is nearly soft and the vegetables are tender.
Lower the heat and add the roasted rava in a slow stream, stirring continuously to keep it smooth.
Cover and cook on low for 4-5 minutes until the water is absorbed and the dal is fully cooked, then fold in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and rest 2 minutes before serving.
tips: Soaking the toor dal first is essential; unsoaked dal stays hard while the upma finishes cooking around it.
Use slightly more water than plain upma because the dal absorbs its share as it softens.
This eats like a full meal, so it is a smart make-ahead breakfast that reheats well with a splash of hot water.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on its own with a spoon of extra ghee and a papad, or with a simple tomato-onion raita on the side.

variations.name: Classic Ven Pongal
variations.description: Ven Pongal is a comforting South Indian breakfast of rice and moong dal cooked soft and creamy, then tempered with black pepper, cumin, ginger and cashews in ghee. It is soothing, mildly spiced and a temple-prasadam favourite across Tamil Nadu.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the pepper and cumin and gives pongal its rich, glossy finish

steps: Dry-roast 0.5 cup moong dal in a pan for 2 minutes until it smells nutty, then rinse it with 1 cup rice together.
Pressure-cook the rice and dal with 4.5 cups water and 1.25 tsp salt for 5 whistles until very soft and mushy, then mash lightly.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan over medium heat and fry 12 cashews until golden, then remove and set aside.
In the same ghee, add 1.5 tsp crushed peppercorns and 1 tsp cumin and let them crackle for 30 seconds, then add 1 inch grated ginger, 12 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida.
Pour this hot tempering along with the fried cashews into the cooked rice-dal and mix well over low heat.
Loosen with a little hot water if needed to a soft, creamy consistency, then serve steaming hot.
tips: Roasting the moong dal before cooking deepens the flavour and stops the pongal tasting flat.
Keep the pongal soft and slightly loose, as it thickens quickly on standing.
Crush the peppercorns coarsely rather than powdering them for pleasant bursts of warmth.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with coconut chutney, sambar and a spoon of extra ghee melting on top, the temple-style way.

variations.name: Millet Ven Pongal
variations.description: A wholesome twist that swaps rice for little millet or barnyard millet, keeping the classic pepper-cumin tempering. It is lighter and lower on the glycemic index while staying just as creamy and comforting.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: tempers the spices and keeps the millet pongal moist and rich

steps: Dry-roast 0.5 cup moong dal for 2 minutes until fragrant, then rinse it well with 1 cup little millet.
Pressure-cook the millet and dal with 5 cups water and 1.25 tsp salt for 5 whistles until soft and porridge-like, then mash gently.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan and fry 12 cashews to golden, then lift them out.
Into the same ghee add 1.5 tsp crushed pepper and 1 tsp cumin, let them splutter, then add 1 inch grated ginger, 12 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida.
Stir the hot tempering and fried cashews into the cooked millet-dal over low heat until evenly combined.
Adjust with hot water to a creamy consistency, as millet firms up faster than rice, and serve hot.
tips: Millet absorbs more water than rice, so keep the pongal looser than usual at the mixing stage.
Rinse the millet well before cooking to remove any bitterness and improve the texture.
Serve millet pongal soon after making, as it sets thick quickly once off the heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tiffin sambar and coconut chutney for a light, diabetic-friendly breakfast.

variations.name: Rava Ven Pongal
variations.description: A speedy version made with roasted semolina instead of rice, ready in minutes without a pressure cooker. The rava cooks into a soft, savoury pongal with the same aromatic pepper-cumin-ghee tempering.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the rava and carries the pepper-cumin tempering for a rich finish

steps: Pressure-cook 0.5 cup moong dal with 1.5 cups water for 3 whistles until soft, then mash and keep aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan and roast 1 cup coarse rava over medium heat for 3 minutes until fragrant but not browned.
In a separate small pan heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, fry 12 cashews golden and remove, then splutter 1.5 tsp crushed pepper and 1 tsp cumin with 1 inch ginger, 12 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida.
Pour 2.5 cups hot water and 1.25 tsp salt into the roasted rava, stirring continuously off high heat to avoid lumps.
Add the mashed dal and the tempering with cashews, and cook 3 minutes until thick and soft.
Loosen with a little hot water for a creamy finish, then serve hot right away.
tips: Add the hot water to the rava gradually while stirring to keep the pongal lump-free.
Roast the rava just until aromatic; browning it makes the pongal grainy rather than soft.
Serve immediately, as rava pongal thickens and sets faster than the rice version.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with coconut chutney and a bowl of sambar for a fuss-free weekday breakfast.

variations.name: Vegetable Ven Pongal
variations.description: A nourishing one-pot version studded with carrots, beans and green peas for colour, fibre and a complete meal. The vegetables cook right along with the rice and dal, soaking up the peppery ghee tempering.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: tempers the spices and enriches the vegetable-laden pongal

steps: Dry-roast 0.5 cup moong dal for 2 minutes, then rinse with 1 cup rice, and finely chop the carrot, 8 beans and keep 0.5 cup peas ready.
Pressure-cook the rice, dal and vegetables together with 4.5 cups water and 1.25 tsp salt for 5 whistles until soft, then mash lightly.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan and fry 12 cashews golden, then remove them.
In the same ghee splutter 1.5 tsp crushed pepper and 1 tsp cumin, then add 1 inch grated ginger and 12 curry leaves and fry 20 seconds.
Stir the tempering and cashews into the cooked pongal over low heat until everything is well combined.
Adjust with hot water to a creamy consistency and serve the vegetable pongal hot.
tips: Chop the vegetables small so they cook fully soft along with the rice and dal.
This version is a meal on its own, so keep it a little looser to eat like a savoury porridge.
Add a handful of extra peas for colour and natural sweetness that balances the pepper.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a light coconut chutney or plain curd, ideal as a wholesome lunchbox or dinner bowl.

variations.name: Classic Vermicelli Upma
variations.description: A light, quick South Indian breakfast of roasted vermicelli tossed with vegetables and a mustard-curry leaf tempering, softer and more delicate than rava upma. Roasting the semiya first keeps the strands separate and springy rather than clumped. Ready in twenty minutes, it is a lunchbox and evening-snack favourite across Indian homes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasts the vermicelli to a golden hue and finishes the dish with a soft aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed oil for a clean tempering that keeps the semiya light
