steps: Roast 2 cups vermicelli in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium-low heat, stirring constantly for 3-4 minutes until evenly golden, then set aside; skip this if using pre-roasted semiya.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then fry 1 tbsp urad dal, 1 tbsp chana dal and 10 cashews until golden.
Add 12 curry leaves, 2 slit green chillies, grated 1 inch ginger and 1 chopped onion, sauteing until the onion softens, about 3 minutes.
Stir in 1 diced carrot and 1/3 cup peas with a pinch of salt, cover and cook 3 minutes until just tender.
Pour in 3 cups water with 1 tsp salt and bring to a boil, then add the roasted vermicelli and stir once to submerge it evenly.
Cover and cook on low heat for 4-5 minutes until the water is absorbed and the strands are soft but still separate, stirring once midway.
Fold in the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, switch off the heat and rest covered 2 minutes before fluffing gently and serving.
tips: Vermicelli needs less water than rava, roughly 1.5 parts water to 1 part semiya, or it turns mushy.
Stir as little as possible once the water goes in, so the delicate strands do not break or clump.
A squeeze of lime just before serving lifts the whole dish and keeps the strands bright.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with coconut chutney or a simple tomato ketchup for children, and a wedge of lime on the side.

variations.name: Tomato Vermicelli Upma
variations.description: A tangy, vibrant semiya upma where tomatoes and a touch of chilli powder cook into a light masala base that coats every strand in a warm orange hue. The tomato keeps the vermicelli moist and adds a gentle sourness that makes it especially moreish. A colourful, kid-friendly breakfast that needs nothing more than a spoon of curd.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed oil carries the tomato masala cleanly and roasts the semiya well

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon that softens the tomato tang with a mellow richness

steps: Roast 2 cups vermicelli in 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium-low heat until golden, about 4 minutes, then set aside.
Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, fry 1 tbsp urad dal until golden, then add 12 curry leaves and 2 slit green chillies.
Add 1 chopped onion and 1 tsp ginger-garlic paste, sauteing 3 minutes until the raw smell fades.
Stir in 3 chopped tomatoes with 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder and 1/4 tsp salt, cover and cook 5 minutes until the tomatoes collapse into a thick pulp.
Pour in 2.75 cups water with 3/4 tsp salt and bring to a boil, then add the roasted vermicelli and stir once to coat.
Cover and cook on low for 4-5 minutes until the water is absorbed and the strands are tender and orange.
Fold in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, rest covered 2 minutes, and serve garnished with fresh coriander.
tips: Ripe, juicy tomatoes give the best colour and tang; underripe ones leave the dish pale and flat.
Because tomatoes release liquid, keep the added water slightly low and top up only if needed.
A small pinch of sugar balances any sharp sourness and deepens the tomato colour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling boondi raita or plain curd, and a squeeze of lime for extra brightness.

variations.name: Lemon Vermicelli Upma
variations.description: A zesty, turmeric-tinted semiya upma finished with fresh lemon juice, roasted peanuts and a crackling tempering, inspired by South India's beloved lemon rice. The vermicelli stays separate and springy, each strand coated in a bright, tangy yellow. Light and refreshing, it makes a wonderful summer breakfast or a quick, cooling tiffin.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil gives the lemony upma its authentic South Indian aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon that rounds the tang and roasts the vermicelli evenly

steps: Roast 2 cups vermicelli in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium-low heat until golden, about 4 minutes, then set aside.
Bring 3 cups water to a boil with 1/2 tsp salt, add the roasted vermicelli and cook 4-5 minutes until just tender, then drain and spread on a plate to cool and stay separate.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then fry 1 tbsp urad dal, 1 tbsp chana dal and 1/4 cup peanuts until golden and crisp.
Add 15 curry leaves, 3 slit green chillies, grated 1 inch ginger and 1/4 tsp asafoetida, frying 20 seconds until aromatic.
Sprinkle in 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1/2 tsp salt, stir for 10 seconds off high heat so the turmeric does not burn.
Add the cooked vermicelli and toss gently until every strand is coated an even yellow.
Switch off the heat, squeeze in the juice of 1 large lemon, fold through gently and rest 2 minutes before serving.
tips: Cooking and draining the vermicelli separately, rather than absorbing the water, keeps the strands firm enough to toss without breaking.
Always add the lemon juice off the heat; boiling it turns the flavour bitter.
Let the cooked vermicelli cool a little before tossing so it does not clump under the tangy tempering.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature with fried papad and a spoon of thick curd, or pack it as a refreshing summer lunchbox.

variations.name: Masala Vegetable Semiya
variations.description: A robust, spice-forward semiya upma cooked with mixed vegetables, garam masala and a hint of tomato for an almost pulao-like richness. This is the hearty version that eats like a full meal, popular for evening tiffin and packed lunches. The extra spices and vegetables turn humble vermicelli into something genuinely special.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasts the vermicelli and lends the masala version a rich, pulao-like aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed oil for sauteing the vegetables and blooming the whole spices

steps: Roast 2 cups vermicelli in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium-low heat until golden, about 4 minutes, then set aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, add 1 bay leaf, 1 inch cinnamon and 3 cloves, and let them sizzle for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 chopped onion, 10 curry leaves and 1 tsp ginger-garlic paste, sauteing 3 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 chopped tomato and cook until it softens.
Add 1 diced carrot, 6 chopped beans and 1/3 cup peas with 3/4 tsp garam masala, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder and 1/4 tsp salt, stir-frying 3 minutes until the masala coats everything.
Pour in 3 cups water with 3/4 tsp salt and bring to a boil, then add the roasted vermicelli and stir once to distribute.
Cover and cook on low for 5 minutes until the water is absorbed and the vegetables are tender.
Fold in the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, rest covered 2 minutes, and serve garnished with coriander.
tips: Bloom the whole spices in hot oil first so they perfume the whole dish rather than sitting raw in it.
Cut the vegetables small and even so they cook through in the short time the vermicelli needs.
This version reheats beautifully with a splash of hot water, making it an ideal make-ahead lunchbox.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling onion-cucumber raita and a wedge of lime, treating it like a light vegetable pulao.

variations.name: Classic Beans Thoran
variations.description: The definitive Kerala thoran: finely chopped french beans steamed until just tender, then bound with a coarsely pounded paste of fresh coconut, cumin, garlic and green chilli that perfumes every piece. Tempered in coconut oil with mustard and curry leaves, it is the fragrant, faintly sweet dry side that anchors a Kerala sadya.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: The soul of a Kerala thoran - its sweet aroma carries the fresh coconut and curry leaf tempering

steps: String and chop 400 g french beans as finely as you can into 0.5 cm pieces, since the fine cut lets the coconut cling and the beans steam quickly.
In a mixer or with a stone, pulse 6 tbsp grated coconut with 0.5 tsp cumin, 3 garlic cloves, 2 green chillies and 4 shallots into a coarse, dry crumble without any water.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a kadhai on medium; add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop for about 30 seconds, then add 1 tsp urad dal and 2 dried red chillies and fry until golden.
Toss in 12 curry leaves and let them crackle for 10 seconds, then add the chopped beans with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt and stir well.
Sprinkle in 3 tbsp water, cover and steam on low heat for 8-10 minutes, stirring once, until the beans are crisp-tender and bright green.
Uncover, add the coarse coconut paste and fold it through, cooking on low for 3-4 minutes until the raw smell of coconut and garlic disappears and the thoran turns dry and fragrant.
tips: Pulse the coconut paste dry and coarse - a watery grind turns the thoran pasty instead of light and crumbly.
Chop the beans very fine so they steam through in the same time the coconut takes to lose its raw edge.
A well-made thoran should be completely dry; if any water pools, stir uncovered on medium for a minute longer.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a dry side on a Kerala meal with sambar, rice and a spoon of ghee, or alongside kaalan and pappadam on a sadya plate.

variations.name: Beans Mezhukkupuratti
variations.description: The coconut-free cousin of the thoran, mezhukkupuratti is a glossy, slow-sauteed stir-fry where beans are cooked down with sliced shallots and dried red chilli until they shrink and turn a little chewy at the edges. Without coconut, the pure taste of the beans and the wood-pressed coconut oil comes through, with a gentle heat from chilli and pepper.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Mezhukku means to coat in oil, so a fragrant wood-pressed coconut oil is the whole point of the dish

steps: Chop 400 g french beans into slightly larger 1 cm pieces so they hold their shape through the longer saute without turning to mush.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a kadhai on medium; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and let them splutter, then add 3 dried red chillies torn in half.
Add 8 sliced shallots and 4 sliced garlic cloves and fry for 3-4 minutes until the shallots soften and turn pale gold, then toss in 12 curry leaves.
Add the beans with 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, stir to coat, then sprinkle in 4 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 10 minutes until nearly tender.
Uncover, raise the heat to medium and stir-fry uncovered for 6-7 minutes, letting the beans dry out, shrink and catch a few browned edges.
Sprinkle 0.25 tsp black pepper powder over the beans, toss for a final minute so they glisten in the oil, and switch off.
tips: Cut the beans a little larger than for a thoran; the long saute would break down finely chopped pieces.
Do not rush the final uncovered fry - the browned, chewy edges are what define a good mezhukkupuratti.
Sliced shallots melt into a sweet base; regular onion works but tastes flatter and wetter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with rice and a soupy moru curry or sambar, where its dry, chilli-flecked bite balances the tangy gravy.

variations.name: Beans and Cherupayar Thoran
variations.description: A heartier thoran that folds cooked whole green moong (cherupayar) into the beans, giving the dish a nutty bite and a boost of protein. The soft, earthy lentils and crisp beans share a coconut-cumin coat, making this a homely, filling one-pot side popular in central Kerala kitchens.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Ties the earthy moong and crisp beans together under the classic Kerala coconut-oil tempering

steps: Soak 0.5 cup whole green moong for 30 minutes, then pressure-cook with a pinch of salt and 1.5 cups water for 2 whistles until soft but still holding shape, and drain any excess water.
Chop 300 g french beans finely into 0.5 cm pieces while the moong cooks.
Coarsely crush 5 tbsp grated coconut with 0.5 tsp cumin, 2 green chillies and 5 shallots into a dry crumble without water.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a kadhai on medium; add 1 tsp mustard seeds, let them pop, then add 12 curry leaves and let them crackle for 10 seconds.
Add the beans with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, sprinkle in 3 tbsp water, cover and steam on low for 8 minutes until crisp-tender.
Fold in the cooked moong and the coconut crumble and cook uncovered on low for 3-4 minutes, stirring gently, until dry and fragrant and the coconut has lost its raw smell.
tips: Cook the moong just until soft; overcooked lentils turn mushy and muddy the texture of the thoran.
Drain the moong well so no cooking water carries into the pan and leaves the thoran wet.
Fold gently at the end so the tender moong stays whole rather than breaking into a paste.
variations.servingSuggestion: Filling enough to serve with just rice and a spoon of tangy buttermilk, or as a protein-rich side on a simple weekday sadya.

variations.name: Varutharacha Beans Thoran
variations.description: In this Malabar-leaning take the coconut is roasted to a deep golden brown with fennel, shallots and coriander seeds before it meets the beans, lending a toasty, almost nutty depth that a fresh coconut thoran never has. The darker paste coats the beans in a warm, fragrant crumble that tastes richer and more festive.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Grounds the toasted-coconut masala in the authentic sweetness of a Malabar kitchen

steps: Chop 400 g french beans finely into 0.5 cm pieces and set aside.

In a dry pan on low heat, roast 6 tbsp grated coconut with 0.5 tsp fennel, 1 tsp coriander seeds, 2 dried red chillies and 4 sliced shallots, stirring constantly for 6-8 minutes until the coconut turns deep golden brown and smells toasty.
Cool the roasted mix and pulse it in a mixer to a coarse, dry paste without water.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a kadhai on medium; add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 dried red chilli, let them splutter, then add the remaining 2 sliced shallots and 12 curry leaves and fry for 2 minutes.
Add the beans with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, sprinkle in 3 tbsp water, cover and steam on low for 8-10 minutes until crisp-tender.
Uncover, fold in the roasted coconut paste and cook on low for 3 minutes, tossing until the dark, fragrant crumble coats every piece and the pan is dry.
tips: Roast the coconut low and slow to a even brown; scorched coconut turns bitter and ruins the paste.
Keep the roasted paste coarse and dry so the thoran stays crumbly rather than clumping together.
Make a double batch of the roasted coconut masala and refrigerate it to speed up the next thoran or avial.
variations.servingSuggestion: Rich enough to headline a festive Onam sadya beside olan and pachadi, or serve with Malabar-style rice and a dollop of curd.

variations.name: Classic Kutchi Dabeli
variations.description: This Classic Kutchi Dabeli is the beloved street snack of Kutch, a soft pav split and packed with a sweet-spicy mashed potato filling scented with special dabeli masala. The bun is crisped in ghee and the potato is studded with pomegranate, roasted peanuts, sev and two chutneys for a burst of sweet, tangy and crunchy in every bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: toasting the split pav in bilona ghee gives the dabeli its signature buttery, crisp edge

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the tamarind-date chutney with a deep caramel note without refined sugar

steps: Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind pulp with 6 pitted dates and 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 1 cup water for 8 minutes, then blend to a smooth glossy sweet-tangy chutney and cool.
Mash the 4 boiled potatoes while still warm with 2 tbsp dabeli masala and 0.5 tsp salt until smooth and evenly spiced.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan, spread the mashed potato flat and cook over medium heat for 3 minutes, then spread 4 tbsp of the sweet chutney over the surface.
Press pomegranate seeds, 0.5 cup masala peanuts, chopped onion and coriander over the warm potato layer so they stud the filling.
Slit the 8 pav without cutting through, spread garlic chutney inside one face and sweet chutney on the other, and stuff generously with the potato mixture, dredging the exposed filling in nylon sev.
Melt the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on a griddle and toast the stuffed dabeli on both cut sides over medium heat for 2 minutes each until golden and crisp, then serve hot.
tips: Keep the mashed potato slightly moist and smooth, as a lumpy filling will not hold the chutneys well.
Roll the exposed filling edges in extra sev just before serving so it stays crunchy.
Make the sweet date-tamarind chutney a day ahead; it thickens and deepens in flavour overnight.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve immediately on a plate with an extra mound of sev, pomegranate and a wedge of lime alongside a cup of masala chai.

variations.name: Cheese Dabeli
variations.description: A gooey modern twist where a slice of melting cheese is layered into the hot potato-stuffed pav so it turns molten as the bun toasts. The richness of the cheese balances the sweet-spicy dabeli masala, making it a favourite with kids and college crowds at street stalls.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: griddling the cheese dabeli in ghee helps the cheese melt evenly into the crisp pav

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: keeps the date chutney glossy and mellow against the salty cheese

steps: Blend 2 tbsp tamarind, 5 dates and 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder simmered in 0.75 cup water for 8 minutes into a thick sweet-sour chutney and cool.
Mash the 4 warm boiled potatoes with 2 tbsp dabeli masala and 0.5 tsp salt until smooth, then warm the mixture in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee for 3 minutes.
Slit the 8 pav, spread garlic chutney on one inner face and sweet chutney on the other, and pack in a thick layer of the spiced potato.
Lay half a slice of cheese over the potato inside each pav, scatter masala peanuts and coriander on top and press the bun closed.
Roll the exposed filling in nylon sev so the edges are thickly coated.

Melt the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on a hot griddle and toast each dabeli for 2 to 3 minutes per side over medium-low heat until the cheese turns molten and the pav is deep golden, then serve at once.
tips: Toast on medium-low heat so the cheese melts fully before the bun over-browns.
Use a firm melting cheese; overly soft cheese will ooze out before the pav crisps.
Serve straight off the griddle, as the cheese sets quickly once it cools.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a side of extra garlic chutney and a chilled glass of masala buttermilk to cut the richness.

variations.name: Jain Dabeli
variations.description: A no-onion, no-garlic Jain rendition that swaps potato for boiled raw banana and green peas, seasoned entirely with dabeli masala, ginger and a hint of asafoetida. It keeps every sweet-spicy-crunchy note of the original while respecting Jain dietary rules.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooming the asafoetida and toasting the pav in ghee builds flavour without onion or garlic

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the date chutney that carries this garlic-free dabeli

steps: Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 6 dates and 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 1 cup water for 8 minutes and blend to a smooth chutney, then cool.
Boil the 3 raw bananas whole for 15 minutes until soft, peel and mash them with the 0.5 cup boiled green peas while warm.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, bloom 0.25 tsp asafoetida and grated ginger for 30 seconds, then add the mashed banana, 2 tbsp dabeli masala and 0.5 tsp salt and cook for 4 minutes.
Press pomegranate, masala peanuts and coriander into the warm filling and spread 3 tbsp sweet chutney over the top.
Slit the 8 pav, spread the remaining sweet chutney inside, stuff with the banana filling and dredge the exposed edges in nylon sev.
Toast the stuffed dabeli in the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on a griddle for 2 minutes per side over medium heat until golden and crisp, then serve warm.
tips: Boil the raw bananas in their skins so the flesh stays firm and mashes smoothly.
A pinch of extra asafoetida deepens the savoury base that would normally come from onion and garlic.
Skip the store garlic chutney and lean on the ginger and dabeli masala for the punch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a banana leaf with extra pomegranate and a lime wedge, ideal for Jain festival platters.

variations.name: Schezwan Dabeli
variations.description: An Indo-Chinese street fusion that spikes the potato filling with fiery schezwan sauce and folds in crunchy shredded cabbage and spring onion. The garlicky heat of the schezwan replaces the sweet chutney's dominance, giving a bold, tangy-hot dabeli that has become a food-truck hit.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed sesame oil lends a nutty depth that suits the Indo-Chinese schezwan filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a touch balances the sharp heat of the schezwan sauce

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, saute the minced garlic and shredded cabbage and capsicum over high heat for 3 minutes until just wilted but crunchy.
Add the mashed boiled potatoes, 3 tbsp schezwan sauce, 1 tsp soy sauce, 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.75 tsp salt and stir-fry for 4 minutes into a spicy filling.
Fold in the chopped spring onion and roasted peanuts and cook 1 minute more, then take off the heat.
Slit the 8 pav, smear extra schezwan sauce inside and pack them generously with the hot filling.
Dredge the exposed filling in nylon sev and coriander so the edges are thickly coated.
Toast the dabeli on a griddle in the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil for 2 minutes per side over medium heat until crisp and golden, then serve immediately.
tips: Stir-fry the cabbage and capsicum on high heat so they stay crunchy, not soggy.
Adjust the schezwan quantity to your heat tolerance, as sauces vary widely in fire.
Add the peanuts last so they keep their crunch inside the soft filling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with extra schezwan mayo for dipping and a side of crisp fried noodles for full Indo-Chinese effect.

variations.name: Classic Steamed Dudhi Muthia
variations.description: The everyday Gujarati farsan of grated bottle gourd bound with coarse wheat flour and besan, gently spiced and steamed into soft, fist-shaped logs. Sliced and finished with a sputtering sesame-seed tempering, it is the light, wholesome tea-time snack that fills every Kathiawadi tiffin.

ingredients.name: Bottle gourd (dudhi)
ingredients.note: peeled and grated, water squeezed out and reserved

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: coarse heritage wheat flour gives the muthia its signature nutty bite

ingredients.name: Besan
ingredients.note: gram flour for binding

ingredients.name: Semolina
ingredients.note: for a light, fluffy crumb

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the gentle Gujarati sweetness that rounds out the batter

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil, 1 tbsp in the dough and 2 tbsp for the crackling tempering

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander
ingredients.note: chopped, for garnish

steps: Squeeze the 2 cups grated bottle gourd firmly over a bowl and reserve the extracted water, keeping the drained gourd aside for the dough.

In a large bowl combine the drained dudhi with 1 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 cup besan, 2 tbsp semolina, 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 tbsp lemon juice, 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and 1 tsp salt.
Bring the mixture together into a soft, non-sticky dough, adding the reserved gourd water a spoon at a time only if it feels dry, and grease your palms lightly.
Shape the dough into 3 smooth cylindrical logs about 5 cm thick and place them on a greased steamer plate with space between each.
Steam the logs on medium heat for 18-20 minutes until a knife inserted into the centre comes out clean and the surface springs back, then cool for 10 minutes and slice into 1.5 cm rounds.

Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a wide pan, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds with 1 tbsp sesame seeds, 1/4 tsp asafoetida and 1 sprig curry leaves for 30 seconds until aromatic, then toss the muthia slices gently for 3-4 minutes until the edges turn golden.
Switch off, scatter 3 tbsp chopped coriander over the top and serve warm.
tips: Do not over-squeeze the dudhi to bone dry; a little of its moisture keeps the muthia soft rather than dense.
Steam only until a tester comes clean, as over-steaming makes the logs gummy and hard to slice neatly.
Toss the slices gently in the tempering so they crisp at the edges without breaking apart.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with green coriander chutney and a cup of masala chai, or pack into a tiffin as a light, protein-rich snack.

variations.name: Pan-Fried Sekela Muthia
variations.description: A crisper take where the steamed dudhi logs are sliced and shallow-fried in ghee until deeply golden and crackly at the edges, the way many Surti homes finish leftover muthia. The extra colour and crunch turn a soft snack into an irresistible, almost cutlet-like treat.

ingredients.name: Bottle gourd (dudhi)
ingredients.note: grated and squeezed

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: heritage wheat flour that fries to a sturdy, crisp edge

ingredients.name: Rice flour
ingredients.note: for extra crispness when fried

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee for shallow-frying gives a nutty crust the steamed version never has

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Squeeze the 2 cups grated bottle gourd well and combine it with 1 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 cup besan, 2 tbsp rice flour, 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder, 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp sugar, 1 tbsp lemon juice, 1 tbsp sesame seeds and 1 tsp salt.
Knead into a firm dough using the gourd's own moisture, then roll into 2 thick logs and steam on medium heat for 18 minutes until set and cooked through.
Cool the logs completely for 15 minutes so they firm up, then slice into 1 cm thick rounds that will hold together while frying.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a flat pan on medium heat until it shimmers, then lay the slices in a single layer without crowding.
Shallow-fry for 3-4 minutes per side until each round is deep golden and crisp at the rim, pressing lightly with a spatula for even colour.
Drain on the pan edge, scatter 3 tbsp chopped coriander over the hot muthia and serve at once while crackly.
tips: Chill the steamed logs before slicing so the rounds stay intact in the hot ghee.
Fry on steady medium heat; too high burns the sesame while the inside stays cold.
A spoon of rice flour in the dough is the trick for that shatter-crisp fried edge.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile onto a platter with tamarind-date chutney and a wedge of lemon as a party starter, or serve alongside evening chai.

variations.name: Methi Dudhi Muthia
variations.description: A greener, more aromatic muthia where a generous handful of fresh fenugreek leaves joins the bottle gourd, lending the mildly bitter, herby fragrance prized in Gujarati kitchens. Jowar flour in the mix makes it earthier and gluten-lighter than the wheat-only classic.

ingredients.name: Bottle gourd (dudhi)
ingredients.note: grated and squeezed

ingredients.name: Fresh fenugreek leaves (methi)
ingredients.note: finely chopped and washed

ingredients.name: Jowar flour
ingredients.note: sorghum flour for an earthy crumb

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: balances the pleasant bitterness of the fresh methi

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil for the dough and the sesame tempering

steps: Sprinkle a little salt over the 1 cup chopped methi, rest for 5 minutes and squeeze out the bitter liquid, then combine it with the squeezed 1.5 cups dudhi.

Add 3/4 cup jowar flour, 1/2 cup besan, 1/4 cup wheat flour, 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and 1 tsp salt to the vegetables.
Knead into a soft dough that just holds together; jowar needs a little of the reserved gourd water to bind smoothly.
Shape into 3 logs, place on a greased steamer plate and steam on medium heat for 18-20 minutes until firm and a tester comes out clean.
Cool for 10 minutes, slice into rounds, then heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tbsp sesame seeds and 1/4 tsp asafoetida for 30 seconds.
Toss the muthia slices in the tempering for 3-4 minutes until lightly crisped and coated, then serve warm.
tips: Salt and squeeze the methi first to tame its bitterness before it goes into the dough.
Jowar flour has no gluten, so handle the dough gently and bind with just enough moisture to shape logs.
This muthia dries out faster than the wheat version, so steam and temper it close to serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sweet chundo or garlic chutney and buttermilk for a rustic Kathiawadi snack plate.

variations.name: Baked Mixed-Millet Muthia
variations.description: A lighter, oven-baked muthia for the health-conscious, built on a blend of bajra and jowar with oats for fibre and no deep-frying at all. Baking gives an even golden crust while keeping the inside moist, a modern spin on the steamed Gujarati original.

ingredients.name: Bottle gourd (dudhi)
ingredients.note: grated and squeezed

ingredients.name: Bajra flour
ingredients.note: pearl millet flour

ingredients.name: Rolled oats
ingredients.note: powdered coarsely

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil brushed on for a golden bake and a light sesame tempering

ingredients.name: Fruit salt (eno)
ingredients.note: for a lighter crumb

steps: Preheat the oven to 190C and line a tray with parchment. Squeeze the 1.5 cups grated dudhi and place it in a bowl.

Mix in 1/2 cup bajra flour, 1/2 cup jowar flour, 1/3 cup powdered oats, 1/3 cup besan, 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1/2 tsp crushed pepper, 1 tbsp lemon juice, 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and 1 tsp salt.
Just before shaping, fold in 1/2 tsp fruit salt and bring the mixture into a soft dough, then form into 3 logs and place on the tray.
Brush the logs with a little Anveshan Groundnut Oil, scatter 1 tbsp sesame seeds on top, and bake for 25-28 minutes until firm and golden, turning once halfway.
Cool the baked logs for 10 minutes and slice into 1.5 cm rounds that hold their shape.
Warm the remaining oil in a pan, crisp the slices for 2-3 minutes until the sesame edges toast, and serve warm.
tips: Add the fruit salt at the very end and shape quickly so the aeration is not lost before baking.
Millet doughs bake drier than wheat, so do not skip brushing the logs with oil for a moist crust.
Powder the oats coarsely rather than fine so the muthia keeps a pleasant, hearty texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with mint-yogurt dip as a guilt-free evening snack, or crumble over a salad bowl for added crunch and fibre.

variations.name: Classic Rajasthani Gatte Ki Sabzi
variations.description: The definitive Marwari dish of steamed besan dumplings simmered in a tangy, spiced yogurt gravy. Gram-flour logs are boiled until firm, sliced into coins and dropped into a whisked-curd curry loosened with the gatta cooking water, giving a light, sour, everyday sabzi built for a land where fresh vegetables were scarce.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee tempers the gravy and glosses the gatte the way every Marwari kitchen finishes this dish

steps: In a bowl mix 1 cup besan with 0.5 tsp ajwain, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp of the ghee and a pinch of hing, then add water little by little to knead a stiff, smooth dough, about 5 minutes.

Roll the dough into 3 finger-thick ropes, drop them into a wide pan of boiling salted water and simmer for 10 to 12 minutes until they float and feel firm; lift them out, reserve the cooking water, and cut the ropes into 1 cm coins once cool.
Whisk 1 cup yogurt smooth with the remaining turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tbsp coriander powder so it does not split when heated.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and the remaining hing for 20 seconds, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 1 minute until raw smell goes.

Lower the heat to minimum, pour in the spiced yogurt and stir continuously for 4 to 5 minutes until it comes to a gentle simmer and thickens slightly without curdling, then add 2 cups of the reserved gatta water and the remaining salt.
Slide in the gatta coins, simmer uncovered on low for 8 to 10 minutes until the gravy coats a spoon, finish with 0.5 tsp garam masala and 3 tbsp chopped coriander, and rest 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Always keep the heat low while the yogurt cooks and stir without stopping until it simmers, or the curd will split into grains.
Boil the gatte only until they float and feel springy; overcooking makes them hard and rubbery.
The gravy thickens as the gatte keep soaking, so leave it slightly thinner than you want and loosen with reserved water before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulka, bajra roti or steamed rice, with a spoon of extra ghee melted on top and a side of sliced onion.

variations.name: Shahi Gatte in Cashew Gravy
variations.description: A royal, festive reinterpretation from the Rajasthani thakur kitchens where the besan gatte rest in a creamy cashew-and-onion gravy instead of tart curd. The masala is mild, nutty and faintly sweet, the gatte kneaded richer with ghee so they stay soft, making this the version reserved for weddings and guests.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Generous ghee keeps the gatte tender and gives the shahi gravy its wedding-feast richness

steps: Knead 1 cup besan with 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, adding water slowly to a firm smooth dough, then roll into ropes and boil in salted water for 12 minutes until they float; reserve the water and slice into coins.
Soak 15 cashews in warm water for 10 minutes, then grind with 2 boiled onions and 1 tomato to a smooth pale paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the cashew-onion paste and cook on medium-low for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring often, until the ghee separates and the paste no longer smells raw.
Stir in the remaining turmeric, 1 tbsp coriander powder and 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder for 30 seconds, then add 2 cups reserved gatta water and the remaining salt and bring to a simmer.

Lower the heat, add the gatta coins and simmer for 8 minutes, then stir in 3 tbsp cream off the boil, 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi and 0.5 tsp garam masala, and warm through for 2 minutes before serving.
tips: Boil the onions before grinding for a pale, sweet gravy without any sharp raw-onion bite.
Add the cream on low heat so the shahi gravy stays glossy and does not break.
Knead a little extra ghee into the dough for softer gatte that suit this rich, mild curry.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan, missi roti or jeera rice, garnished with a swirl of cream and slivered cashews for a festive spread.

variations.name: Govind Gatte (Stuffed Fried Gatte)
variations.description: The grand Jaipur banquet gatta: thick besan logs stuffed with a spiced dry-fruit and coconut filling, deep-fried until golden, then simmered in a robust onion-tomato gravy. Sliced open, each piece reveals a jewelled centre, making Govind gatte the showpiece of a Rajasthani feast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee binds the rich stuffing and finishes the gravy with a nutty Rajasthani aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A clean wood-pressed oil for deep-frying keeps the gatte crisp without a heavy aftertaste

steps: Knead 1.5 cups besan with 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and enough water into a firm, pliable dough and rest it covered for 10 minutes.
Chop 10 cashews and 1 tbsp raisins fine and mix with 2 tbsp desiccated coconut, 0.25 tsp garam masala and a pinch of salt to make the sweet-spiced stuffing.

Divide the dough into 6 balls, flatten each, place a spoon of stuffing in the centre, seal into a smooth thick log, and steam or boil the logs for 10 minutes until firm; cool and cut into 2 cm thick pieces.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to 170C and fry the gatta pieces in batches for 3 to 4 minutes until golden and crisp, then drain on paper.

In a kadai heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, add 2 chopped onions and fry until golden, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 2 pureed tomatoes and cook until the ghee separates, about 8 minutes.

Add the remaining turmeric, 1.5 tbsp coriander powder, 1 tsp chilli powder and 2 cups water with the remaining salt, simmer 5 minutes, slide in the fried gatte and simmer 6 to 8 minutes until they drink up the gravy; finish with 0.5 tsp garam masala.
tips: Seal the stuffing carefully with no cracks, or the filling will leak out while boiling and frying.
Fry the gatte just until golden; too dark and they turn hard inside the gravy.
Add the fried gatte to the gravy only 10 minutes before serving so they stay slightly firm and do not disintegrate.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve this festive gatta with saffron pulao or laccha paratha, slicing each piece to reveal the stuffing on the plate.

variations.name: Achari Pyaaz Gatte
variations.description: A punchy Shekhawati twist where the gatte swim in a tangy pickle-spiced gravy built on browned onions and a fresh five-seed achari tempering. Fennel, nigella, mustard and fenugreek give it the unmistakable perfume of Rajasthani pickle, sharp and warming rather than creamy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Pungent wood-pressed mustard oil is the soul of any achari masala and carries the pickle spices

steps: Knead 1 cup besan with 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp salt and 1 tbsp of the mustard oil, adding water slowly into a firm dough, roll into ropes and boil in salted water for 12 minutes until they float; reserve the water and cut into coins.
Coarsely crush together 1 tsp fennel, 0.5 tsp nigella, 0.5 tsp mustard, 0.25 tsp methi and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds to make the achari spice mix.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai to smoking point, then lower the heat and add the crushed achari spices, letting them splutter for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add 2 finely chopped onions and fry on medium for 6 to 7 minutes until deep golden, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute.

Turn the heat low, whisk 0.5 cup yogurt with the remaining turmeric, 1 tsp chilli powder and 1 tbsp coriander powder, pour it in and stir constantly for 4 minutes until it simmers without splitting, then add 2 cups reserved gatta water and the remaining salt.
Add the gatta coins and simmer uncovered on low for 10 minutes until the tangy gravy clings to them, then rest 5 minutes so the pickle spices bloom before serving.
tips: Heat the mustard oil until it just smokes and then lower the flame before adding spices to tame its raw sharpness.
Crush the achari seeds coarsely, not to a powder, so you get bursts of fennel and nigella in every bite.
Whisk the yogurt well and add it on the lowest heat with constant stirring to keep the achari gravy smooth.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain paratha or bajra roti and a side of raw onion rings, with a spoon of mango pickle to echo the achari notes.

variations.name: Classic Kala Chana Curry
variations.description: A hearty North Indian everyday curry of black chickpeas simmered soft and finished in a dry-ish onion-tomato masala. The nutty chana holds its bite while a spoon of ghee and a hit of amchur give it the tangy, homely flavour that pairs with roti or rice. This is the version cooked on fasting days and lazy Sundays alike.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee blooms the whole spices and rounds out the tangy masala with a nutty richness

steps: Soak 1 cup black chickpeas overnight in plenty of water, then pressure-cook with 1/2 tsp salt, 1 bay leaf and 3 cups water for 6 whistles until soft but still holding shape; reserve the cooking liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 15 seconds until fragrant, then add 2 finely chopped onions and fry until deep golden, about 7 minutes.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute until the raw smell goes, then add 2 pureed tomatoes and cook until the ghee separates at the edges, around 6 minutes.
Lower the heat and add 1.5 tbsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp amchur, roasting for 30 seconds until the masala smells cooked and glossy.
Add the cooked chickpeas with 1.5 cups reserved liquid and the remaining salt, and simmer for 12 to 15 minutes, mashing a spoonful of chana against the pan so the gravy clings.
Sprinkle in 1 tsp garam masala and 3 tbsp chopped coriander, simmer 2 minutes more, and serve warm.
tips: Mashing a handful of the cooked chana is the trick to a thick, coating gravy without any flour or cream.
Add the amchur near the end so its tang stays bright instead of cooking away.
Soaking overnight is essential; a quick soak leaves the chana chewy no matter how long you cook it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with phulka roti or jeera rice, topped with sliced onion, a green chilli and a squeeze of lemon on the side.

variations.name: Sindhi Kala Chana with Potato
variations.description: A tangy Sindhi-style tokri where black chickpeas and soft potato cubes share a tamarind-spiked gravy. The souring comes from tamarind rather than tomato, and a generous hit of cumin and dried mint makes it distinctly Sindhi. It is traditionally eaten with warm phulka or as part of a Sunday dal-pakwan spread.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil gives the tamarind gravy a clean, mildly nutty backbone typical of Sindhi cooking

steps: Soak 1 cup black chickpeas overnight, then pressure-cook with 1/2 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 whistles until tender; reserve the cooking liquid.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pot on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 15 seconds, then add 2 finely chopped onions and 2 slit green chillies and fry until golden-brown, about 7 minutes.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute, then stir in 1.5 tbsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1/2 tsp turmeric with a splash of water so the spices do not burn.
Add 2 potatoes cut into 2 cm cubes and toss in the masala for 2 minutes, then pour in the cooked chana with 2 cups reserved liquid and the remaining salt.
Cover and simmer for 15 minutes until the potato is fork-tender, then stir in 2 tbsp tamarind pulp and 1 tsp dried mint powder and simmer 5 minutes more so the gravy turns tangy and slightly thick.
Lightly mash a few potato pieces into the gravy to bind it, and rest covered for 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Cut the potatoes evenly so they cook through at the same time as the gravy thickens.
Adjust tamarind to taste at the end; Sindhi kala chana should be pleasantly sour but not sharp.
A pinch of dried mint stirred in just before serving lifts the whole pot with freshness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with warm phulka or crisp fried pakwan, and a bowl of sweetened boondi raita to balance the tang.

variations.name: South Indian Kala Chana Sundal
variations.description: A dry, temple-style stir-fry where boiled black chickpeas are tossed with a mustard-and-curry-leaf tempering and fresh coconut. Bright, light and completely gravy-free, this sundal is made as prasadam during Navratri and eaten warm by the handful. Coconut oil and a whisper of asafoetida make it unmistakably South Indian.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil carries the mustard tempering and gives the sundal its temple-kitchen aroma

steps: Soak 1 cup black chickpeas overnight, then pressure-cook with 1 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 whistles until soft but firm, and drain thoroughly so the sundal stays dry.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a wide pan on medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them splutter, then add 1 tsp urad dal and 2 broken dried red chillies and fry until the dal turns golden.
Add 1/4 tsp asafoetida, 15 curry leaves, 2 slit green chillies and 1 inch finely minced ginger, and saute for 30 seconds until aromatic.
Tip in the drained chickpeas and toss on medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes so they take on the tempering and any surface moisture evaporates.
Turn off the heat, add 1/2 cup fresh grated coconut and fold through gently for 1 minute using the residual warmth so the coconut stays fresh and fragrant.
Check salt and serve warm as a snack or prasadam.
tips: Drain the boiled chana really well; any clinging water makes the sundal soggy instead of light and separate.
Add the coconut off the heat so it stays sweet and does not brown.
A squeeze of lemon just before eating brightens the dish if you like it tangy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm in a leaf cup as a festive Navratri snack, or alongside rasam rice for a light South Indian meal.

variations.name: Bengali-Style Kala Chana with Coconut
variations.description: A lightly sweet Bengali cholar-style preparation where black chickpeas simmer in a mustard-oil gravy studded with fried coconut chips and warmed by whole garam masala. A touch of jaggery balances the heat of ginger and cumin, giving the classic sweet-savoury Bengal flavour. It is a festive dish served at pujas and family lunches.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Pungent wood-pressed mustard oil frames the sweet-savoury Bengali gravy and fries the coconut chips

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A spoon of jaggery gives the signature gentle sweetness that balances the ginger and chilli

steps: Soak 1 cup black chickpeas overnight, then pressure-cook with 1/2 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 whistles until soft; reserve the cooking liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai to smoking point and lower the heat, then fry 1/4 cup coconut chips until golden and set them aside.
In the same oil crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, 2 bay leaves, 1 inch cinnamon and 3 cardamom pods for 30 seconds, then add 1 tbsp ginger paste and fry for 1 minute.
Add 1 tsp cumin powder, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 3/4 tsp red chilli powder with a splash of water and cook for 1 minute until the oil floats to the top.
Add the cooked chana with 1.5 cups reserved liquid, the remaining salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, and simmer for 12 minutes until the gravy thickens slightly.
Stir in the fried coconut chips and 1/2 tsp garam masala, simmer 2 minutes more, and serve warm.
tips: Always heat mustard oil to smoking and then cool slightly before cooking, to mellow its raw pungency.
Keep the sweetness subtle; the jaggery should only balance the spice, not turn the dish into a dessert.
Add the fried coconut chips near the end so they stay a little crunchy in the gravy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with luchi or steamed rice as part of a Bengali festive thali, alongside a wedge of lemon.

variations.name: Classic Khandvi
variations.description: The definitive Gujarati khandvi: a smooth gram-flour and sour-buttermilk batter cooked to a spreadable paste, thinly smeared on the back of steel plates, then rolled into delicate golden spirals. A crackling mustard-and-sesame tempering with curry leaves and fresh coconut crowns each melt-in-the-mouth roll.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Toasty wood-pressed gingelly oil carries the mustard tempering and keeps the rolls glossy, not greasy

steps: Whisk 1 cup besan with 1.5 cups sour buttermilk and 1 cup water in a bowl until completely lump-free, then stir in 1 tsp ginger-green chilli paste, 0.25 tsp Anveshan Turmeric powder and 1 tsp salt to make a thin, pourable batter.

Pour the batter into a heavy non-stick pan and cook on medium-low heat, stirring constantly with a flat spatula for 10-12 minutes, until it thickens into a smooth glossy paste that leaves the sides of the pan and coats the spatula heavily.

Working fast while the paste is hot, spread a thin even layer over the back of 3-4 greased steel plates or a clean countertop, smoothing it with an offset spatula, and let it set for 4-5 minutes until firm to the touch.
Cut the set sheets into 2-inch-wide strips, gently roll each strip into a tight spiral, and arrange the khandvi rolls seam-side down on a serving plate.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a small pan on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp sesame seeds for 30 seconds, then add 10 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and fry for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Pour the sizzling tempering evenly over the rolls, then scatter 3 tbsp fresh grated coconut and 3 tbsp chopped coriander on top before serving.
tips: Test the paste before spreading: smear a little on a plate and try to roll it after a minute — if it cracks it needs more cooking, if it slumps cook 2 minutes longer.
Grease the plates very lightly with oil so the sheet peels cleanly without tearing when you cut the strips.
Spread the paste the moment it is done; it stiffens as it cools and becomes impossible to smear thinly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature as a tea-time snack or farsan with a bowl of coriander-mint chutney and hot masala chai poured on the side.

variations.name: Nylon Khandvi
variations.description: The prized ultra-thin 'nylon' khandvi that halwais of Surat are famous for: a wetter batter and longer cooking yield sheets so fine they turn almost translucent, rolling into feather-light spirals that dissolve on the tongue. A restrained ghee tempering keeps the focus on that gossamer texture.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A light bilona-ghee tempering suits the delicate nylon rolls better than a heavier oil

steps: Sift 1 cup besan into a bowl to remove every lump, then whisk in 0.75 cup yogurt, 2 cups water, 1 tsp lemon juice, 0.5 tsp green chilli paste, 0.25 tsp Anveshan Turmeric powder and 1 tsp salt until the batter is silky and very thin.
Strain the batter once through a fine sieve into a heavy pan to guarantee a nylon-smooth finish, discarding any grainy bits left behind.
Cook on medium-low heat, stirring without pause for 14-16 minutes; the extra water means it takes longer to thicken, so wait until it is a glossy paste that firmly ribbons off the spatula.
Immediately spread the hot paste in the thinnest possible film over the backs of greased steel plates, working quickly across as many plates as you have, and let them set for 3-4 minutes.
Cut into 1.5-inch strips and roll each into a slim, tight spiral; because the sheet is so fine, roll gently so it does not tear.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium heat, splutter 0.75 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, add 8 curry leaves for 15 seconds, then spoon over the rolls and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: The wetter batter is the whole secret to nylon khandvi — resist adding extra besan even if it looks too runny at first.
Spread on the underside of plates rather than the countertop; the smoother steel surface gives a finer, more even sheet.
Skip the coconut garnish here so nothing weighs down the delicate translucent rolls.
variations.servingSuggestion: Plate the pale rolls in a single layer and serve slightly chilled with sweet-and-spicy date-tamarind chutney for a striking festive farsan.

variations.name: Green Chutney Khandvi
variations.description: A vibrant party twist where each khandvi sheet is spread with a bright coriander-mint-coconut chutney before rolling, so every spiral hides a ribbon of fresh green heat. The herby filling and a garlicky tempering make these rolls far punchier than the classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Clean wood-pressed groundnut oil fries the garlic tempering without masking the fresh herb filling

steps: Grind 1 cup coriander, 0.5 cup mint, 0.25 cup grated coconut, 3 garlic cloves and 2 green chillies with a splash of water into a thick, spreadable green chutney and set aside.

Whisk 1 cup besan with 1.5 cups sour buttermilk, 1 cup water, 1 tsp salt and 0.25 tsp Anveshan Turmeric powder until smooth, then cook in a heavy pan on medium-low heat, stirring constantly for 10-12 minutes, until it becomes a thick spreadable paste.
Spread the hot paste thinly over the backs of greased steel plates and let it set for 4-5 minutes until firm.
Smear a thin even layer of the green chutney over each set sheet, then cut into 2-inch strips and roll each strip snugly so the chutney forms a spiral inside.
Arrange the rolls seam-side down; heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds for 30 seconds, add 10 curry leaves for 15 seconds until they turn crisp, and pour over the rolls.
Rest the tempered rolls for 5 minutes so the chutney flavour seeps into the besan, then serve.
tips: Keep the chutney thick, not watery; a runny filling soaks into the sheet and makes rolling messy.
Spread only a thin chutney layer — too much and the rolls unravel as you slice them.
Make the chutney a day ahead and refrigerate; its flavour deepens and it spreads more easily when cold.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these green-swirled rolls as a colourful starter with a wedge of lime and a small bowl of sweetened yogurt for dipping.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Suralichi Vadi Khandvi
variations.description: Maharashtra's cousin of khandvi, suralichi vadi, folds fresh coconut, coriander and a whisper of jaggery right into the rolls, then finishes them with a peanut-studded tempering. The result is warmer and faintly sweet-savoury, a festive farsan distinct from the tangy Gujarati original.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A spoon of pure jaggery powder gives suralichi vadi its gentle Maharashtrian sweet-savoury balance

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the traditional Maharashtrian tempering fat and echoes the crushed-peanut garnish

steps: Whisk 1 cup besan with 1 cup yogurt and 1.25 cups water until smooth, then mix in 1 tsp ginger paste, 1 tsp green chilli paste, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp salt to make a thin batter.
Cook the batter in a heavy pan on medium-low heat, stirring constantly for 11-13 minutes, until it thickens to a glossy paste that pulls cleanly from the sides of the pan.
Spread the hot paste thinly over greased steel plates, immediately scatter half the grated coconut and half the coriander over the surface, and let it set for 4-5 minutes.
Cut the herb-flecked sheets into 2.5-inch strips and roll each into a firm spiral so the coconut and coriander spiral inside the vadi.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 1 tsp sesame seeds for 30 seconds, then stir in 3 tbsp crushed roasted peanuts and fry for 30 seconds until golden.
Pour the peanut tempering over the rolls and finish with the remaining coconut and coriander scattered on top.
tips: Press the coconut and coriander lightly into the hot sheet so they stick and do not fall off when you roll.
The jaggery should only whisper in the background; a single teaspoon is enough to round out the tang, not sweeten the vadi.
Crush the peanuts coarsely with a rolling pin so their crunch stands out against the soft rolls.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve suralichi vadi at Diwali or Ganpati as farsan alongside a cup of masala chai, with extra crushed peanuts on the side for those who love the crunch.

variations.name: Classic Navratan Korma
variations.description: Navratan Korma is a regal nine-jewel curry of mixed vegetables, paneer, fruits and nuts simmered in a mildly sweet, cashew-cream gravy. This classic balances crunchy nuts, soft vegetables and juicy fruit in a pale, silky sauce that tastes indulgent yet gentle on the palate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: carries the mild whole spices and lends the korma its signature velvety richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: adds the gentle sweetness that defines a korma without any refined sugar

steps: Boil the 2 cups mixed vegetables and 0.5 cup peas in salted water for 6 minutes until just tender, then drain and set aside to keep their colour.
Soak the 15 cashews in warm water for 10 minutes, then blend with the boiled onions into a smooth pale paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat, add 3 lightly crushed cardamoms and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, and saute for 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in the cashew-onion paste with 1 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 6 to 7 minutes until the ghee separates and the paste turns creamy.
Add a cup of water, the boiled vegetables and 0.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, then simmer gently for 5 minutes so the flavours meld.
Lower the heat, stir in 3 tbsp cream, the 100 g cubed paneer and 0.25 cup pineapple, warm through for 2 minutes, and garnish with 2 tbsp pomegranate seeds before serving.
tips: Blanch the vegetables only until just tender so they hold their shape and colour in the pale gravy.
Add the cream on low heat and stir gently to keep the delicate white gravy from splitting.
Scatter the fruit and pomegranate just before serving so they stay fresh and juicy rather than stewed.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan, laccha paratha or a saffron pulao, topped with a few fried cashews and raisins for a festive touch.

variations.name: Shahi Mughlai Navratan Korma
variations.description: A royal Mughlai rendition enriched with a saffron-scented cashew and melon-seed gravy, finished with khoya for a lush, banquet-worthy texture. Deeper and more aromatic than the everyday korma, it carries the perfume of saffron and warm whole spices fit for a wedding feast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: essential for a Mughlai korma, it fries the whole spices and enriches the shahi gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk it gives the korma its royal golden hue and aroma

steps: Soak the 0.25 tsp Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside so it releases its colour and aroma.
Blanch the 2 cups mixed vegetables for 5 minutes until just tender, then drain, and blend the 15 cashews, 2 tbsp melon seeds and boiled onions into a fine paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan over medium heat, add the cinnamon, 4 cardamoms and 3 cloves, and let them sizzle for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute, then stir in the cashew-melon paste and saute for 7 minutes until the ghee separates and it turns ivory-smooth.
Whisk the 3 tbsp curd smooth, lower the heat and stir it in with 1 tsp salt and 0.25 tsp white pepper, then add a cup of water and the blanched vegetables.
Simmer for 6 minutes, then fold in the grated khoya, the 120 g paneer cubes and the saffron milk, warm through for 3 minutes and serve gleaming and golden.
tips: Grate the khoya so it melts smoothly into the gravy instead of forming lumps.
Always add whisked curd off the boil and stir constantly to prevent the shahi gravy from curdling.
A drop more saffron milk brushed on top just before serving deepens both colour and fragrance.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with sheermal, roghni naan or a delicate zafrani pulao, garnished with slivered almonds and a swirl of cream.

variations.name: South-Indian Vegetable Kurma
variations.description: A coconut-based kurma from the South, where the nine vegetables simmer in a ground paste of fresh coconut, roasted poppy seeds and fennel tempered with curry leaves. Lighter and more aromatic than the creamy North Indian korma, it carries a fragrant coconut sweetness and a gentle green-chilli heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the authentic South-Indian fat that carries the curry leaf and fennel tempering

steps: Grind the 0.5 cup coconut, 2 tbsp roasted gram, 1 tbsp poppy seeds, 1 tsp fennel and 3 green chillies with a little water into a smooth paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan over medium heat, add the cinnamon and 12 curry leaves, and let them crackle for 20 seconds.
Add the finely chopped onion and saute for 4 minutes until soft, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute until the raw smell fades.
Add the chopped tomato with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 4 minutes until the tomato collapses into the base.
Tip in the 2.5 cups mixed vegetables with 1.5 cups water, cover and simmer for 12 minutes until the vegetables are fork-tender.
Stir in the ground coconut paste, simmer on low for 5 minutes until the kurma thickens to a spoonable gravy, and serve hot.
tips: Add the coconut paste only in the last few minutes and keep the heat low so the gravy stays fragrant and does not turn grainy.
Use a mix of soft-cooking vegetables like potato and carrot so the kurma has body and creaminess.
A squeeze of lemon at the end brightens the coconut richness beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft parotta, appam, idiyappam or plain steamed rice for a comforting South Indian meal.

variations.name: Restaurant-style White Navratan Korma
variations.description: The pristine white korma served at Indian restaurants, built on a no-tomato cashew, curd and cream base that stays snow-pale and luxuriously smooth. Its mild, milky sweetness studded with fruit and nuts makes it the crowd-pleasing centrepiece of any buffet spread.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: keeps the gravy pale while adding a clean richness the white korma is known for

steps: Boil the 2 onions, 20 cashews and 2 green chillies in a cup of water for 8 minutes, then cool and blend to a completely smooth white paste.
Blanch the 2 cups mixed vegetables for 5 minutes until just tender and drain, keeping them pale rather than browned.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat, add 1 bay leaf and 3 cardamoms, and warm for 30 seconds without letting them darken.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and saute for 1 minute, then pour in the white cashew-onion paste and cook gently for 6 minutes without browning it.
Whisk the 0.25 cup curd smooth, lower the heat and stir it in with 1 tsp salt, 0.5 tsp white pepper and a cup of water, then add the blanched vegetables.
Simmer for 5 minutes, fold in the 100 g paneer, 4 tbsp cream and 3 tbsp fried nuts and raisins, warm through for 2 minutes and serve pristine white.
tips: Keep the flame low throughout so nothing browns, which is the secret to a truly white restaurant korma.
Use thick, sour-free curd and whisk it well before adding to avoid any curdling or grainy texture.
Fry the nuts and raisins in a little ghee separately and add at the end for the classic garnish and crunch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with pillowy butter naan or a mild peas pulao, finished with a drizzle of cream and a sprinkle of chopped pistachios.

variations.name: Classic Instant Oats Dosa
variations.description: A no-ferment, no-grind breakfast crepe where powdered oats are whisked with a little rice flour and curd into a thin batter you pour straight onto the tava. It cooks up soft in the middle with delicately crisp edges, giving you a wholesome, fibre-rich dosa in the time it takes the pan to heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed gingelly oil gives the instant oats dosa a South Indian aroma and browns the edges beautifully

steps: Dry-grind 1 cup rolled oats to a fine powder in a mixer, then whisk it with 1/4 cup rice flour, 1/3 cup curd and about 2.5 cups water into a thin, lump-free batter and rest it for 10 minutes so the oats absorb the liquid.

Stir in 1 tsp cumin seeds, 2 finely chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 1 small finely chopped onion, 3 tbsp chopped coriander and 1 tsp salt; the batter should pour in a thin stream, so loosen with water if it has thickened.
Heat a flat tava on medium-high until a water drop dances and vanishes in 2 seconds, then rub it with a few drops of Anveshan Sesame Oil using a folded cloth.
Stir the batter and pour a ladleful from the outer edge inward in a spiral without spreading it, letting it settle into a thin round with small holes across the middle.
Drizzle 1/2 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil around the rim and cook undisturbed for about 2 minutes on medium-high until the base is golden and the top looks dry and set.
Fold the dosa over and lift it off; repeat with the rest, stirring the batter each time as the ground oats settle to the bottom quickly.
tips: Grind the oats fine — coarse oats leave gritty specks and stop the dosa from spreading into a smooth round.
Rest the batter the full 10 minutes; freshly mixed oats batter is watery and firms up nicely as the flour hydrates.
If dosas come out pale, raise the heat and give each one an extra 30 seconds before folding.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and a bowl of drumstick sambar, or a tangy tomato chutney for a lighter morning plate.

variations.name: Crispy Oats Rava Dosa
variations.description: The lacy, restaurant-style avatar where powdered oats join fine semolina and rice flour in a watery batter you pour rather than spread. Cashews, pepper and curry leaves crackle through a net-thin crepe that fries to a shattering golden crisp, proving oats can be as indulgent as they are wholesome.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: light wood-pressed sunflower oil fries the lacy oats-rava dosa to a clean golden crisp without weighing it down

steps: Coarsely powder 1/2 cup rolled oats, then whisk it with 1/2 cup fine semolina, 1/2 cup rice flour, 1 tsp salt and about 3.5 cups water into a very thin, milk-like batter and rest it for 15 minutes so the rava swells.

Stir in 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 tsp crushed black pepper, 2 finely chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 12 torn curry leaves and 10 slivered cashews; the batter must stay runny, so thin with water if the rava has thickened it.
Heat a tava on medium-high until very hot and grease it with a few drops of Anveshan Sunflower Oil, since a hot pan is what makes the lace form.
Stir the batter well and pour it from a height in a thin stream, filling gaps from the outer edge toward the centre, and never spread it with the ladle.
Drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Sunflower Oil over and around the dosa and cook undisturbed for 2 to 3 minutes on medium-high until the underside turns crisp and evenly golden-brown.
When the edges lift on their own, fold the dosa without flipping and slide it out crackling; stir the batter thoroughly before each dosa as it settles fast.
tips: This batter should be thinner than you think — if it mounds when poured, add more water or the net will not form.
Wait until the edges lift by themselves before folding; touching it early tears the delicate lace.
Wipe the tava with a halved onion between dosas to stop the rava from sticking and to keep each one evenly browned.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot with coconut chutney and a fiery tomato-garlic chutney so the crispness is caught at its peak.

variations.name: Vegetable Oats Uttapam
variations.description: A thick, soft oats uttapam pressed with a confetti of carrot, capsicum, onion and tomato that toasts into the surface. Fermented lightly with curd and cooked slow in ghee, it is a spongy, veg-packed griddle cake that eats like a savoury pancake and hides a full serving of vegetables.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee cooks the thick uttapam slow and golden while keeping the crumb soft and moist

steps: Powder 1 cup rolled oats coarsely and mix with 1/2 cup semolina, 1/2 cup curd, 1 tsp salt and about 1 cup water into a thick, spoonable batter — much thicker than a dosa batter — and rest it for 15 minutes to swell.
Finely chop 1 carrot, 1 capsicum, 1 onion, 1 tomato, 2 green chillies and 3 tbsp coriander, keeping the pieces small so they cook through, and set them together in a bowl.
Check the rested batter; it should drop thickly from the spoon and mound slightly, so stir in a little water only if it has gone stiff.
Heat a tava on medium, grease with a few drops of Anveshan Ghee, then pour a ladle of batter and spread it gently into a thick 6 inch round without thinning it out.
Scatter a generous handful of the chopped vegetables over the top, press them in lightly with the back of the ladle, and drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee around the edges.
Cook covered on medium for about 3 minutes until the base is golden and set, then flip and cook the vegetable side for 2 minutes until the onions char slightly and the uttapam is cooked through.
tips: Keep the batter thick so the vegetables sit on the surface rather than sinking; a thin batter gives a floppy uttapam that will not hold the toppings.
Cook covered on medium heat so the thick centre steams through without the base burning.
Chop the vegetables small and uniform — large chunks stay raw and make the uttapam hard to flip.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling mint-coriander chutney and a bowl of curd, or a smear of red chilli-garlic chutney over the vegetable side.

variations.name: Ragi-Oats Millet Dosa
variations.description: A doubly wholesome crepe that folds earthy finger-millet flour into the oats batter for a darker, nuttier dosa with extra fibre and iron. A quick tempering of mustard, curry leaves and grated coconut stirred through the batter gives every bite a coastal, savoury depth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil ties the millet-oats batter together with a fragrant, coastal South Indian finish

steps: Powder 3/4 cup rolled oats fine, then whisk with 1/2 cup ragi flour, 1/4 cup rice flour, 1/3 cup curd, 1 tsp salt and about 2.5 cups water into a thin, pourable batter and rest for 10 minutes.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan on medium, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds for 20 seconds, then toss in 12 curry leaves and 2 chopped green chillies and fry for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Pour this hot tempering along with 3 tbsp grated coconut into the batter and stir well; check the flow and loosen with a splash of water so it pours thin.
Heat a tava on medium-high until a water drop sizzles off in 2 seconds, then grease it with a few drops of Anveshan Coconut Oil.
Stir the batter and pour a ladleful from the rim inward in a spiral without spreading, drizzling 1/2 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil around the edges.
Cook undisturbed for about 2 minutes on medium-high until the base is deep golden-brown and the top is set, then fold and serve; stir the batter before each dosa as the millet settles.
tips: Ragi and oats both settle fast, so stir the batter thoroughly before every ladle to keep the dosas an even colour.
Add the coconut tempering only just before cooking; sitting too long makes the batter sour and the coconut release water.
For a crisper dosa, spread the poured batter slightly thinner and cook 30 seconds longer on medium-high heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with fresh coconut chutney and a spoon of jaggery-sweetened ginger chutney for a nutty, wholesome tiffin plate.

variations.name: Classic Ragi Dosa
variations.description: An instant Karnataka-style crepe where finger-millet flour is whisked with a little rice flour and curd into a pourable batter that needs no fermenting or grinding. The dosa comes off the tava thin and lacy at the edges with a soft, faintly earthy centre, and it goes from craving to plate in under twenty minutes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed gingelly oil gives instant ragi dosa its authentic South Indian aroma and crisps the lacy edges

steps: In a large bowl whisk 1 cup ragi flour, 1/4 cup rice flour and 1/4 cup curd with about 2.5 cups water until you have a thin, lump-free batter roughly the consistency of buttermilk. Rest it for 10 minutes so the flour hydrates.

Stir in 1 tsp cumin seeds, 2 finely chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 1 small finely chopped onion, 3 tbsp chopped coriander and 1 tsp salt, then check the flow — it should coat a spoon and pour in a thin stream, so loosen with a splash of water if it has thickened.
Heat a flat tava on medium-high until a drop of water skitters and evaporates in 2 seconds, then rub the surface with a few drops of Anveshan Sesame Oil using a halved onion or cloth.
Pour a ladleful of batter from the outer rim inward in a spiral — do not spread it with the ladle, as this thin batter sets into a natural lace with tiny holes across the middle.
Drizzle 1/2 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil around the edges and cook undisturbed for about 2 minutes on medium-high, until the underside is reddish-brown and the top looks dry and set.
Fold the dosa in half or roll it up and serve straight off the tava; repeat with the remaining batter, stirring it well before each pour since ragi settles quickly to the bottom.
tips: Ragi settles fast, so give the batter a brisk stir before every single ladle or your later dosas will turn out pale and watery.
If the first dosa sticks, your tava is not hot enough — wait for the water-drop test before pouring the next one.
Keep the batter thin and pourable; a thick batter gives a dense pancake rather than a crisp, holey dosa.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and a small bowl of hot sambar, or a spoon of spicy tomato-garlic chutney for a lighter breakfast plate.

variations.name: Fermented Ragi Dosa
variations.description: The old-school village method from rural Karnataka where whole ragi is soaked and ground with urad dal and fenugreek, then left overnight to ferment. The wait rewards you with a naturally sour, feather-light dosa that browns to a beautiful mahogany and carries a depth that no instant batter can match.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil lends the fermented dosa a coastal Karnataka fragrance and a glossy, crisp finish

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup whole ragi and 1/2 cup idli rice together in one bowl, and 1/3 cup urad dal with 1/2 tsp fenugreek seeds in another, both for 5 to 6 hours; soak 2 tbsp poha in a splash of water for the last 20 minutes.

Grind the urad dal and fenugreek first with a little water into a smooth, fluffy batter that ribbons off the spatula, then grind the ragi, rice and soaked poha together into a slightly grainy paste using about 1.5 cups water in total.

Combine both batters in a large vessel with 1 tsp salt, mixing well with your hand for a minute to encourage fermentation, then cover and leave in a warm spot for 8 to 10 hours until the batter rises and smells pleasantly sour.
Stir the risen batter gently and adjust with a little water so it pours thickly but still spreads; heat a tava on medium and grease it with a few drops of Anveshan Coconut Oil.

Pour a ladle of batter at the centre and spread it outward in a spiral into a 7 inch round, then drizzle 1/2 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil around the rim and cook for about 2 minutes until the base is deep golden-brown and lacy.
Cover for 30 seconds to steam-set the top, then lift and fold; the dosa should be soft in the middle with crisp edges. Repeat, keeping the heat at medium so the ragi browns evenly without burning.
tips: In cold weather, ferment the batter inside a switched-off oven with the light on, or the ragi batter can take up to 14 hours to rise.
Do not skip the poha — it makes fermented ragi dosa noticeably softer and helps it crisp at the edges.
Refrigerate leftover batter for up to 3 days; bring it to room temperature and add a pinch of salt before making the next batch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with coconut-mint chutney and a Mangalorean-style vegetable sagu, finishing with a small pat of butter melting into the hot dosa.

variations.name: Crispy Ragi Rava Dosa
variations.description: A shatteringly crisp, net-like dosa where ragi flour meets fine semolina and rice flour in a watery batter you pour, never spread. Studded with cashews, curry leaves and pepper, it fries up golden-brown and paper-thin, giving the wholesome finger millet a genuinely indulgent, restaurant-style crunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: light wood-pressed sunflower oil fries the lacy rava dosa to a clean, golden crispness without heaviness

steps: Whisk 1/2 cup ragi flour, 1/2 cup fine semolina and 1/2 cup rice flour with 1 tsp salt and about 3.5 cups water into a very thin, watery batter — the texture of thin milk — and rest it for 15 minutes so the rava swells.

Stir in 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 tsp crushed black pepper, 2 finely chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 12 torn curry leaves and 10 cashews broken into slivers; the batter must stay runny, so add water if the rava has thickened it.
Heat a tava on medium-high until quite hot, then lightly grease with a few drops of Anveshan Sunflower Oil — a hot pan is essential for the lacy holes to form.

Stir the batter well and pour it from a height in a thin stream, working from the outer edge toward the centre to fill gaps; do not spread with the ladle, letting the batter settle into a natural net.
Drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Sunflower Oil over and around the dosa and cook undisturbed on medium-high for 2 to 3 minutes until the underside is crisp and evenly golden-brown.
Once the edges lift on their own, fold the dosa in half without flipping and slide it out crisp; stir the batter thoroughly before each dosa as the flours settle quickly.
tips: The batter for a rava dosa must be far thinner than a normal dosa batter — if it holds its shape when poured, it is too thick for the lace to form.
Let each dosa cook fully until the edges lift by themselves; flipping or lifting too soon tears the delicate net.
Keep the heat on the higher side throughout; a lukewarm tava gives a soggy, pale dosa instead of a crackling one.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve immediately with coconut chutney and a tangy tomato-onion chutney so the crispness is enjoyed before it softens.

variations.name: Masala Ragi Dosa
variations.description: A hearty tiffin-centre favourite: the instant ragi crepe wrapped around a golden turmeric potato masala loaded with onions and curry leaves. The nutty millet and the soft, gently spiced filling make a filling, wholesome dosa that eats like a full meal rather than a snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee roasts the masala dosa golden and enriches the earthy ragi with a nutty richness

steps: Boil 4 potatoes until fork-tender, peel and crush them coarsely; whisk 1 cup ragi flour and 1/4 cup rice flour with 1 tsp salt and about 2.5 cups water into a thin pourable batter and rest it for 10 minutes.
