Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal for 30 seconds until the dal turns golden, then add 12 curry leaves and 3 slit green chillies and let them crackle.
Add 2 thinly sliced onions and saute for 4 minutes until soft and translucent, then stir in 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1/2 tsp salt and cook another minute until the raw turmeric smell lifts.
Fold in the crushed potatoes with a splash of water, mashing lightly, and cook for 3 minutes until the masala is moist and holds together; finish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander and keep warm.

Heat a tava on medium-high, grease with a few drops of Anveshan Ghee, then pour a ladle of the ragi batter in a spiral and drizzle 1/2 tsp ghee around the edges; cook for about 2 minutes until the base is browned and set.

Place a generous spoon of the potato masala along the centre, fold the dosa over it and press gently, then slide onto a plate; repeat, stirring the batter before each pour so the ragi stays evenly suspended.
tips: Keep the potato masala on the moist side — a dry filling makes the folded dosa crack and crumble.
Make the masala ahead and reheat it with a splash of water; the dosas then come together in minutes.
For extra hold, let the poured dosa cook a full 30 seconds longer before adding the filling so the base is sturdy enough to fold.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve open-faced with the masala peeking out, alongside coconut chutney and a ladle of sambar poured over the folded end.

variations.name: Classic Samosa Chaat
variations.description: This Classic Samosa Chaat crushes a hot potato samosa under a ladle of spiced chana chole, then drowns it in sweet tamarind chutney, green chutney and whisked yogurt. It is a North Indian roadside institution, at once crisp, soft, tangy, sweet and cooling, finished with sev and a snow of chaat masala.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: tempering the chole in bilona ghee gives the chaat a rich, rounded base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the tamarind chutney with a mellow caramel note instead of refined sugar

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup soaked kabuli chana with 0.5 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 whistles until soft, then drain, reserving a little cooking liquid.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, saute the chopped onion and tomato for 5 minutes, add 1.5 tbsp chole masala and 0.5 tsp salt, then stir in the cooked chana with a splash of the liquid and simmer 8 minutes into a thick chole.
Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 0.75 cup water for 6 minutes into a glossy sweet-sour chutney and cool.
Whisk the 1 cup yogurt smooth with a pinch of salt until pourable.
Place a hot samosa on each plate and crush it open with a spoon, then ladle over a generous scoop of the warm chole.
Drizzle with whisked yogurt, tamarind chutney and green chutney, dust with 1 tsp chaat masala, shower with nylon sev and coriander, and serve at once.
tips: Use freshly fried, hot samosas so the pastry stays crisp under the chole.
Keep the chole slightly loose so it soaks into the crushed samosa without drying out.
Chill the whisked yogurt so it contrasts the warm chole and spicy chutneys.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a wide plate topped with extra sev, a sprinkle of pomegranate and a lime wedge on the side.

variations.name: Dahi Samosa Chaat
variations.description: A cooling yogurt-forward version that skips the heavy chole and instead smothers the crushed samosa in generous whisked dahi, both chutneys and a dusting of roasted cumin. Light, tangy and refreshing, it is the go-to summer avatar of samosa chaat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoon of warm ghee brushed over the crushed samosa lifts the aroma of the dahi chaat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: balances the sourness of the yogurt in the sweet tamarind chutney

steps: Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 0.75 cup water for 6 minutes into a smooth sweet chutney and cool completely.
Whisk the 2 cups yogurt with 0.5 tsp salt and a splash of water until smooth and pourable, then chill.
Warm the 4 samosas, brush the tops lightly with 1 tbsp melted Anveshan Ghee, and crush each open on a plate.
Scatter diced boiled potato over the crushed samosa for extra softness and body.
Ladle over the chilled whisked yogurt so it pools around the samosa, then drizzle with tamarind and green chutney.
Dust with 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 0.25 tsp salt, top with pomegranate, nylon sev and coriander, and serve immediately.
tips: Chill the yogurt well so the chaat is refreshingly cool against the warm samosa.
Add a pinch of black salt to the yogurt for an extra tangy street-style flavour.
Assemble just before serving so the samosa does not turn fully soggy under the dahi.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a cooling summer chaat with extra pomegranate and a scattering of fresh mint leaves.

variations.name: Amritsari Chole Samosa Chaat
variations.description: A hearty Punjabi take built on dark, robust Amritsari chole cooked with tea-blackened gravy and whole spices, ladled thickly over the samosa with barely any yogurt. It is filling and boldly spiced, the kind eaten as a full meal at Amritsar dhabas.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the dark Amritsari chole is finished in bilona ghee for a rich dhaba aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a small amount rounds the tangy tamarind in the robust chole

steps: Pressure-cook 1.25 cups soaked kabuli chana with the 2 tea bags, 1 tsp salt and 4 cups water for 8 whistles until very soft and dark, then discard the tea bags.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, saute 2 chopped onions and 1.5 tbsp ginger garlic paste over medium heat for 8 minutes until deep brown.
Add the pureed tomatoes and 2 tbsp chana masala and cook for 6 minutes until the ghee separates at the edges.
Tip in the cooked chana with its liquid, 2 tbsp tamarind pulp, 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.5 tsp salt, and simmer 12 minutes into a thick dark gravy, lightly mashing some chana to thicken.
Place a samosa on each plate, crush it open and ladle over a generous scoop of the hot Amritsari chole.
Top with slivered ginger, slit green chillies and plenty of coriander, and serve piping hot as a substantial chaat.
tips: The tea bags deepen the chole to the classic near-black Amritsari colour without artificial dye.
Mash a spoonful of the cooked chana into the gravy to thicken it naturally.
Skip the yogurt and sev here so the bold, spicy chole stays the hero.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve dhaba-style with slivered raw onion, a green chilli and a lemon wedge, hearty enough to be a meal.

variations.name: Ragda Samosa Chaat
variations.description: The Mumbai avatar tops the crushed samosa with a soupy white-pea ragda instead of chana, the peas cooked to a soft, savoury stew and ladled hot over the pastry. Lighter and more soothing than chole, it is the samosa chaat you find at Mumbai's evening stalls.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: tempering the ragda in wood-pressed groundnut oil suits the Mumbai street style

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the tamarind chutney that laces the soft white-pea ragda

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup soaked white peas with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 whistles until very soft, then lightly mash to a soupy consistency.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, saute the chopped onion for 4 minutes, add 1 tbsp goda masala and 0.5 tsp salt, then add the mashed peas with a cup of water and simmer 8 minutes into a loose ragda.
Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 0.75 cup water for 6 minutes into a sweet-sour chutney and cool.
Crush a hot samosa open on each plate and ladle over a generous scoop of the warm soupy ragda.
Drizzle with the tamarind chutney and green chutney and dust with 1 tsp chaat masala.
Scatter chopped raw onion, nylon sev and coriander over the top and serve immediately while hot.
tips: Keep the ragda loose and soupy so it soaks generously into the crushed samosa.
Soak the white peas overnight so they cook down to a creamy, soft stew.
A pinch of goda masala at the end lifts the ragda with its dark Maharashtrian aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a deep bowl with extra raw onion and a lemon wedge, Mumbai stall style.

variations.name: Classic Kerala Appam
variations.description: The lacy Kerala hopper with a soft, spongy centre and crisp, feather-thin edges, ground from raw rice and fermented with a little cooked rice and coconut. Made in a curved appam kadai, it swells into a bowl shape that cradles stew or sweet coconut milk, tasting faintly of toddy-style fermentation.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: a light smear of cold-pressed coconut oil crisps the lacy appam edges and adds authentic Kerala fragrance

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups raw rice for 4 to 5 hours, then drain and grind it with 1/2 cup cooked rice and 3/4 cup grated coconut, adding about 1 cup water, into a smooth, slightly flowing batter.
Dissolve 1/2 tsp active dry yeast and 2 tsp sugar in 1/4 cup warm water and rest for 10 minutes until it froths, then whisk this into the ground batter.
Cover the batter and leave it in a warm place for 8 to 10 hours until it doubles, turns bubbly and smells lightly sweet-sour from fermentation.
Stir in 1 tsp salt and check the consistency; the batter should be thin enough to swirl and coat the pan, so loosen with a little water if needed.

Heat an appam kadai on medium, rub it with a few drops of Anveshan Coconut Oil, pour in a ladle of batter, then immediately lift and rotate the pan so the batter coats the sides in a thin lace while a thicker pool settles at the centre.
Cover and cook on medium for about 2 minutes without flipping, until the edges are golden and crisp and the spongy centre is just set, then lift out the bowl-shaped appam gently.
tips: Swirl the pan the instant the batter hits it — waiting even a few seconds means the batter sets before it can coat the sides into lace.
The centre should stay soft and spongy while only the edges crisp; do not flip an appam or you lose its signature shape.
If the batter over-ferments and smells too sour, a pinch of sugar and a spoon of fresh coconut milk revives the flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a mildly spiced Kerala vegetable stew in coconut milk, or simply with sweetened thick coconut milk for breakfast.

variations.name: Sweet Vellayappam
variations.description: The festive sweet hopper studded with sugar, cumin and crushed cardamom, cooked flat like a small round cake rather than a bowl. Naturally sweet and speckled, vellayappam is offered at church feasts and made for children, with a soft, cake-like crumb and lightly crisp base.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: unrefined jaggery gives vellayappam a warm caramel sweetness far richer than plain sugar

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil crisps the base of these little sweet cakes and complements the jaggery

steps: Soak 1.5 cups raw rice for 5 hours, drain, and grind with 1/3 cup cooked rice and 1 cup grated coconut using about 3/4 cup water into a smooth, thick batter.
Proof 1/2 tsp yeast in 1/4 cup warm water with a spoon of the jaggery for 10 minutes until frothy, then mix it into the batter and ferment covered for 7 to 8 hours until risen and bubbly.

Dissolve the remaining Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 2 tbsp warm water, strain out grit, and stir this syrup into the fermented batter along with 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1/2 tsp cardamom powder and 1/4 tsp salt.
Let the sweetened batter rest for 20 minutes so the flavours meld, keeping it thick and dropping — vellayappam is cooked flat, not swirled.
Heat a flat appam pan or small kadai on medium, grease with a few drops of Anveshan Coconut Oil, and pour a small ladle of batter into a thick 4 inch round without spreading.
Cover and cook on medium-low for about 3 minutes until the base is golden and crisp, then flip and cook the other side for 2 minutes until the little cake is cooked through and lightly browned.
tips: Keep the batter thick like a pancake batter; vellayappam is meant to be a small round cake, not a lacy hopper.
Cook on medium-low so the jaggery in the batter browns gently without burning before the centre sets.
Toast the cumin seeds lightly in a dry pan before adding for a warmer, rounder aroma in the sweet batter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm on their own as a teatime sweet, or alongside a cup of strong Kerala filter coffee for a festive treat.

variations.name: Instant Rava Appam
variations.description: A quick weeknight hopper that skips soaking, grinding and overnight fermenting altogether — semolina and curd stand in, leavened in minutes with a pinch of soda for the same lacy edge. It gives you soft-centred, crisp-rimmed appams whenever a craving strikes, no planning required.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil lends the instant appam a true Kerala aroma the quick method would otherwise miss

steps: Grind 1/2 cup grated coconut with 1/2 cup water into a smooth paste, then whisk it with 1 cup fine semolina, 1/2 cup rice flour, 1/2 cup curd, 1 tsp sugar and 3/4 tsp salt into a thick batter.
Add about 3/4 cup more water to loosen the batter to a swirling, coating consistency, and rest it for 15 minutes so the rava absorbs the liquid and softens.
Just before cooking, stir 1/4 tsp baking soda into the batter; it will froth up lightly, which mimics the airy lace of a fermented appam.
Heat an appam kadai on medium, wipe it with a few drops of Anveshan Coconut Oil, and pour a ladle of the frothy batter into the centre.
Immediately lift and rotate the pan so the batter coats the sides thinly while a thicker pool rests at the middle, forming the classic bowl shape.
Cover and cook on medium for about 2 minutes until the edges are crisp and golden and the centre is soft and set, then lift the appam out without flipping.
tips: Add the soda only at the last moment before cooking; its lift fades fast, so use the batter within 15 minutes.
Rest the batter long enough for the rava to swell, or the appams will taste raw and grainy in the centre.
Grinding the coconut into the batter, rather than leaving it grated, gives a smoother lace and even browning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a quick coconut-milk vegetable korma or a simple potato stew for a fuss-free appam dinner.

variations.name: Classic Cabbage Thoran
variations.description: A Kerala everyday favourite: finely shredded cabbage wilted just enough to stay crunchy, tossed with a coarse coconut-cumin-garlic crumble and a coconut-oil tempering of mustard and curry leaves. It is light, sweet and quick, the kind of dry side that turns a plate of rice and sambar into a proper meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Its sweet fragrance is what makes a Kerala cabbage thoran taste unmistakably nadan

steps: Shred 500 g cabbage as finely as possible into thin ribbons so it wilts quickly and takes on the coconut evenly.
Coarsely crush 6 tbsp grated coconut with 0.5 tsp cumin, 3 garlic cloves, 2 green chillies and 4 shallots into a dry crumble without adding water.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a kadhai on medium; add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop, then add 1 tsp urad dal and 2 dried red chillies and fry until golden.
Toss in 12 curry leaves and let them crackle for 10 seconds, then add the shredded cabbage with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt.
Stir well, cover and cook on low heat for 6-7 minutes, stirring once, until the cabbage wilts but keeps a slight crunch and no water pools.
Uncover, add the coconut crumble and toss on low for 2-3 minutes until the raw coconut smell fades and the thoran is dry and fragrant.
tips: Cabbage releases water as it cooks, so do not add any extra; cover and let its own steam soften it.
Stop while the cabbage still has a little bite - overcooked thoran turns soft, grey and watery.
Add the coconut only at the end so it stays sweet and fluffy against the warm cabbage.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a dry side with sambar rice, rasam rice or curd rice, or tuck it into a Kerala meal beside erissery and pappadam.

variations.name: Cabbage, Carrot and Peas Thoran
variations.description: A colourful sadya-style thoran where shredded cabbage shares the pan with sweet carrot and green peas, each vegetable adding its own bite and sweetness under a single coconut crumble. Brighter and more festive than the plain version, it is a favourite when a meal needs a splash of colour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Binds the three vegetables under one sweet, curry-leaf-scented tempering

steps: Shred 350 g cabbage finely, grate 1 large carrot and keep 0.5 cup green peas ready; if using dried peas, boil them soft first.
Coarsely crush 5 tbsp grated coconut with 0.5 tsp cumin and 2 green chillies into a dry crumble without water.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a kadhai on medium; add 1 tsp mustard seeds, let them pop, then add 1 tsp urad dal and fry until golden, and toss in 12 curry leaves.
Add the peas first with 0.25 tsp turmeric and cook covered on low for 3 minutes, then add the cabbage and carrot with 1 tsp salt and stir well.
Cover and cook on low for 6-7 minutes, stirring once, until the vegetables wilt but stay bright and just crunchy.
Uncover, fold in the coconut crumble and toss on low for 2 minutes until dry and fragrant, then switch off.
tips: Add the harder peas and carrot before the quick-wilting cabbage so everything finishes at the same time.
Grate the carrot rather than dicing it so it cooks in the same few minutes as the cabbage.
Keep the flame low throughout to protect the bright colours; high heat dulls the carrot and peas.
variations.servingSuggestion: A colourful side for a festive thali or lunchbox; it pairs equally well with chapati and dal or with rice and rasam.

variations.name: Cabbage Foogath
variations.description: The Goan-Konkani foogath treats cabbage differently, sauteing it first with sliced onion and green chilli before a light dusting of coconut, so the flavour is savoury and oniony rather than sweet-coconutty. A splash of lime at the end lends the bright, faintly tangy edge that sets a foogath apart from a Kerala thoran.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coastal Konkani kitchens saute their foogath in coconut oil for a mellow, sweet base

steps: Shred 500 g cabbage finely and slice 1 large onion thin so both cook down at the same pace.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a kadhai on medium; add 1 tsp mustard seeds, let them pop, then add 1 tsp urad dal and fry until golden.
Add the sliced onion, 3 slit green chillies, 1 inch chopped ginger and 10 curry leaves and saute for 3-4 minutes until the onion turns soft and translucent.
Add the cabbage with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, stir well, cover and cook on low for 7-8 minutes, stirring once, until the cabbage wilts and softens.
Uncover, raise the heat to medium and stir for 2 minutes to dry off any moisture, then scatter in 3 tbsp grated coconut and toss for a minute.
Switch off the flame, squeeze in 1 tbsp lime juice and toss well so the tang lifts the whole dish.
tips: Saute the onion properly before the cabbage; its sweetness is the backbone of a foogath.
Add the lime only after the heat is off so it stays bright and does not turn bitter.
Use far less coconut than a thoran - here it is a light finish, not the main flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with Goan-style rice and a bowl of dalitoy, or as a tangy side with chapati and a coconut-based fish-free curry.

variations.name: Cabbage and Moong Dal Thoran (Parippu Thoran)
variations.description: This wholesome thoran cooks skinned moong dal soft and folds it through the shredded cabbage, so each bite carries a creamy, nutty lentil alongside the crunch. The dal makes it more filling and protein-rich, a favourite when the thoran needs to stand in as a light meal on its own.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Carries the coconut and curry leaf tempering that lifts the soft, earthy moong dal

steps: Dry-roast 0.33 cup moong dal in a pan on low for 2-3 minutes until it smells nutty, then boil it in 1 cup water for about 8 minutes until just soft but still holding shape, and drain.
Shred 400 g cabbage finely while the dal cooks.
Coarsely crush 5 tbsp grated coconut with 0.5 tsp cumin and 2 green chillies into a dry crumble without water.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a kadhai on medium; add 1 tsp mustard seeds, let them pop, then add 2 dried red chillies and 12 curry leaves and let them crackle.
Add the cabbage with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, cover and cook on low for 6 minutes until wilted, then fold in the cooked moong dal.
Add the coconut crumble and toss on low for 2-3 minutes until dry and fragrant, taking care to keep the dal grains intact.
tips: Roasting the dal before boiling gives it a nutty aroma and helps it hold shape instead of turning to mush.
Cook the dal only until just tender; a firm grain keeps the thoran from becoming pasty.
Drain the dal thoroughly so no cooking liquid makes the cabbage watery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Substantial enough to serve with just rice and a spoon of ghee, or as a nourishing side with rasam and pappadam.

variations.name: Classic Dahi Bhalla
variations.description: This Classic Dahi Bhalla features feather-soft urad dal vadas soaked until spongy, then blanketed in sweetened whisked yogurt and crowned with tamarind and green chutney. A Delhi and Punjab festive favourite, it is cooling, sweet-tangy and melt-in-the-mouth, finished with roasted cumin, chilli and a flurry of sev.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: deep-frying the bhallas in wood-pressed sunflower oil keeps them light and clean-tasting

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens both the whisked yogurt and the tamarind chutney with natural caramel depth

steps: Soak 1 cup urad dal for 4 hours, then grind to a fluffy, thick batter with minimal water, adding grated ginger, chopped green chilli and 0.5 tsp salt, and whip it well until light.
Heat the Anveshan Sunflower Oil to medium and slide in spoonfuls of batter, frying the bhallas for 4 to 5 minutes until golden and cooked through.
Soak the fried bhallas in warm salted water for 20 minutes until soft and spongy, then gently squeeze out the water between your palms.
Whisk the 3 cups yogurt smooth with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.25 tsp salt until sweet and pourable, then chill.
Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 0.5 cup water for 6 minutes into a sweet-sour chutney and cool.

Arrange the squeezed bhallas on a platter, pour over the sweet yogurt, drizzle with tamarind and green chutney, dust with 1.5 tsp roasted cumin and 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, top with sev and coriander, and serve chilled.
tips: Whip the batter until a small drop floats in water, the sign of aerated bhallas that turn spongy.
Soak the fried bhallas in warm, not hot, water so they soften without breaking apart.
Squeeze the bhallas gently so they stay intact yet drink up the sweet yogurt.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled in a shallow bowl with extra chutneys, a dusting of cumin and a few pomegranate seeds for colour.

variations.name: South Indian Thayir Vadai
variations.description: The Tamil thayir vadai bathes soft medu-vada style urad fritters in lightly salted, unsweetened yogurt and finishes them with a hot mustard-curry-leaf tempering rather than sweet chutneys. It is savoury, cooling and fragrant, a temple-town classic distinct from the sweet North Indian bhalla.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: frying the vadai in wood-pressed coconut oil lends the authentic South Indian aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: the mustard and curry-leaf tempering is bloomed in nutty wood-pressed sesame oil

steps: Grind 1 cup soaked urad dal to a fluffy batter with minimal water, mix in chopped green chilli, grated ginger and 0.5 tsp salt, and whip until light.
Heat the Anveshan Coconut Oil to medium, shape the batter into small doughnut vadais and fry for 4 to 5 minutes until golden and crisp.
Soak the fried vadais in warm water for 15 minutes, then gently squeeze out the water.
Whisk the 3 cups yogurt smooth with 0.5 tsp salt, keeping it savoury and unsweetened, then submerge the squeezed vadais in it and chill for 20 minutes.
Heat 2 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds, dried red chillies, curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Pour the hot tempering over the yogurt-soaked vadais, scatter grated carrot and coriander on top, and serve chilled.
tips: Keep the yogurt savoury and lightly salted, as thayir vadai is never sweetened like dahi bhalla.
Soak the vadais long enough that they absorb the yogurt and turn pillowy soft.
Pour the tempering while it is still sizzling so its aroma infuses the yogurt.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled as a South Indian tiffin side or starter, garnished with extra curry-leaf tempering and grated carrot.

variations.name: Moong Dal Dahi Bhalla
variations.description: A lighter, quicker version using yellow moong dal instead of urad, which grinds into an easy batter and fries into delicate, softer bhallas. Gentler on digestion and faster to make, it still soaks up sweet yogurt and chutneys beautifully for an everyday chaat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: the soft moong bhallas fry light and clean in wood-pressed sunflower oil

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the yogurt and tamarind chutney over the delicate moong bhallas

steps: Soak 1 cup moong dal for 3 hours, then grind to a thick smooth batter with minimal water, mix in grated ginger, chopped green chilli and 0.5 tsp salt, and whisk until fluffy.
Heat the Anveshan Sunflower Oil to medium and fry small spoonfuls of batter for 3 to 4 minutes until pale golden and cooked through.
Soak the fried moong bhallas in warm salted water for 12 minutes until soft, then gently press out the water.
Whisk the 3 cups yogurt smooth with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 0.5 tsp black salt and 0.25 tsp salt, then chill.
Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 0.5 cup water for 6 minutes into a sweet chutney and cool.
Lay the bhallas on a plate, cover with the sweet yogurt, drizzle tamarind and green chutney, dust with 1.5 tsp roasted cumin, top with sev and coriander, and serve chilled.
tips: Moong bhallas are delicate, so soak them for less time than urad ones to avoid crumbling.
Grind the moong batter thick, as too much water gives flat, oily fritters.
Add the black salt to the yogurt for a lightly tangy, digestive edge.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a light everyday chaat with an extra spoon of chutney and a sprinkle of pomegranate.

variations.name: Palak Dahi Bhalla
variations.description: A vibrant green twist that folds finely chopped spinach into the urad batter, giving nutrient-rich bhallas with a subtle earthy flavour and pretty flecks of green. Topped with the usual sweet yogurt and chutneys, it sneaks greens into a festive favourite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the spinach bhallas crisp beautifully in wood-pressed groundnut oil

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the yogurt and chutney draped over the green bhallas

steps: Grind 1 cup soaked urad dal to a fluffy batter with minimal water, then fold in 1 cup finely chopped spinach, grated ginger, chopped green chilli and 0.5 tsp salt and whip until light.
Heat the Anveshan Groundnut Oil to medium and fry spoonfuls of the green batter for 4 to 5 minutes until golden and cooked through.
Soak the fried bhallas in warm salted water for 18 minutes until spongy, then squeeze out the water gently.
Whisk the 3 cups yogurt with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.25 tsp salt until smooth and sweet, then chill.
Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 0.5 cup water for 6 minutes into a chutney and cool.
Arrange the green bhallas on a platter, pour over the sweet yogurt, drizzle both chutneys, dust with 1.5 tsp roasted cumin, and top with sev and pomegranate before serving chilled.
tips: Chop the spinach very fine and squeeze out its moisture so the batter stays thick.
Do not add extra water once the spinach goes in, as it releases liquid while frying.
The pomegranate garnish contrasts prettily against the green-flecked bhallas.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled as a colourful festive chaat, garnished with extra pomegranate and a light dusting of cumin.

variations.name: Classic Fermented Handvo
variations.description: The definitive Gujarati handvo: a coarsely ground, overnight-fermented batter of rice and mixed lentils folded with grated bottle gourd, then cooked slowly until a deep golden crust forms over a soft, tangy interior. A lavish sesame-and-mustard tempering pressed into the top is what makes every slice crackle.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil in the tempering and around the edges builds handvo's signature crackling golden crust

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup rice with 0.5 cup chana dal, 0.25 cup toor dal and 0.25 cup urad dal together for 4-5 hours, then grind coarsely with a little water into a thick idli-like batter.
Stir in 0.75 cup whisked yogurt, cover, and leave the batter to ferment in a warm spot for 8 hours or overnight until it smells pleasantly sour and rises slightly.

Squeeze 1.5 cups grated bottle gourd and fold it into the batter with 1.5 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp salt; just before cooking, sprinkle 1 tsp eno and mix until the batter turns airy.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a heavy non-stick pan on medium heat, crackle 1.5 tsp mustard seeds, 2 tbsp sesame seeds and 0.5 tsp asafoetida with 12 curry leaves for 40 seconds, then pour half the tempering over the batter and reserve the rest.
Pour the batter into the same pan in an even layer, drizzle the reserved tempering on top, cover, and cook on low heat for 18-20 minutes until the base forms a dark golden crust.

Carefully flip the handvo, add another 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil around the edges, and cook the second side uncovered for 10-12 minutes until both crusts are crisp; cool slightly and cut into squares.
tips: Grind the batter coarse, not silky — a little grit gives handvo its characteristic hearty texture.
Cook strictly on low heat; rushing on high burns the crust before the inside sets.
If short on time, a well-fermented batter can rest overnight in the fridge and be brought to room temperature before adding eno.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the crisp golden squares warm with green chutney and sweet tamarind chutney, or a simple bowl of masala chai.

variations.name: Instant Semolina Handvo
variations.description: A same-day handvo that skips soaking, grinding and fermenting entirely: semolina and gram flour are whisked with yogurt, rested briefly, and lifted with fruit salt. It bakes up just as golden-crusted and savoury, ready in under an hour for a weeknight craving.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Neutral wood-pressed groundnut oil crisps the instant handvo base evenly and keeps it light

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups semolina and 0.5 cup besan with 1 cup yogurt and 0.5 cup water into a thick lump-free batter, then rest it for 15-20 minutes so the rava swells and softens.
Stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt, adjusting with a splash of water to a thick pouring consistency.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a small pan, crackle 1.5 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tsp cumin seeds, 2 tbsp sesame seeds and 12 curry leaves for 40 seconds until the sesame is golden.
Stir half the tempering into the batter, then sprinkle in 1.5 tsp eno and fold gently until the batter turns visibly frothy and airy.
Immediately pour the batter into a heavy non-stick pan greased with 1 tbsp oil, drizzle the remaining tempering on top, cover, and cook on low heat for 15-16 minutes until the base is deep golden.
Flip the handvo, add 1 tbsp oil around the edges, and cook uncovered for another 8-10 minutes until crisp on both sides; cut into squares and serve.
tips: Add the eno only at the last moment and cook straight away, or the batter loses its lift and bakes dense.
Rest the batter long enough for the semolina to absorb the yogurt, otherwise the handvo tastes grainy.
For a browner crust, sprinkle a few extra sesame seeds into the greased pan before pouring the batter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm wedges with coriander-mint chutney and a hot cup of adrak chai for a quick evening snack.

variations.name: Mixed Vegetable Handvo
variations.description: A colourful, vegetable-packed handvo where grated carrot, green peas, sweet corn and capsicum are folded through a gram-flour-rich batter, turning the humble cake into a near-complete meal. Every bite is dotted with soft vegetables against the crisp sesame crust.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil crisps the vegetable-laden batter into a sturdy golden crust that holds the mix-ins

steps: Whisk 1 cup semolina and 0.75 cup besan with 1 cup yogurt into a thick batter and rest for 15 minutes to let the rava swell.

Fold in 0.5 cup grated carrot, 0.5 cup green peas, 0.5 cup sweet corn and 0.5 cup chopped capsicum along with 1.5 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a small pan, crackle 1.5 tsp mustard seeds and 2 tbsp sesame seeds with 10 curry leaves for 40 seconds, then stir half into the batter.
Sprinkle 1.5 tsp eno over the batter and fold gently until frothy, then pour into a heavy non-stick pan greased with 1 tbsp oil and drizzle the remaining tempering on top.
Cover and cook on low heat for 16-18 minutes until the base sets into a firm golden crust and the vegetables soften into the batter.
Flip carefully, add 1 tbsp oil around the edges, and cook uncovered for 10-12 minutes until both sides are crisp; rest 5 minutes, then cut into thick squares.
tips: Chop the vegetables small and uniform so they cook through in the same time as the batter.
Do not add extra water; the vegetables release moisture as they cook and can loosen the batter.
Frozen peas and corn work well straight from the freezer — just thaw and pat them dry first.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve this hearty handvo warm with a bowl of cool yogurt and green chutney as a wholesome lunchbox meal.

variations.name: Baked Oats and Ragi Handvo
variations.description: A nourishing, oven-baked handvo built on ground oats and finger-millet flour instead of rice, delivering a fibre-rich, protein-forward cake with the same tangy yogurt lift. Baking gives an all-over even crust with far less oil, ideal for a lighter, wholesome bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: A modest drizzle of wood-pressed gingelly oil is all the baked handvo needs for a crisp top and nutty aroma

steps: Grind 1 cup rolled oats to a coarse flour, then whisk with 0.5 cup ragi flour, 0.5 cup besan and 1 cup yogurt into a thick batter and rest for 15 minutes.

Fold in 0.75 cup squeezed grated bottle gourd, 1.5 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt, loosening with a little water to a thick spoonable batter.
Preheat the oven to 200C and grease a baking tin with a little of the sesame oil.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a small pan, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds and 2 tbsp sesame seeds with 10 curry leaves for 40 seconds, then stir half into the batter.
Sprinkle 1.5 tsp eno over the batter, fold until airy, pour into the tin, and drizzle the remaining tempering plus the last 1 tbsp oil over the top.
Bake for 30-35 minutes until the top is firm and golden and a skewer comes out clean; cool for 10 minutes before cutting into squares.
tips: Grind the oats fresh and coarse; store-bought oat flour can turn the handvo gummy.
Ragi browns quickly, so tent the tin with foil for the last 10 minutes if the top darkens too fast.
This baked version keeps well for two days and makes an excellent high-fibre breakfast reheated lightly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the wholesome squares warm with a spoon of thick yogurt and coriander chutney, or pack cold into a healthy tiffin.

variations.name: Classic Punjabi Chana Masala
variations.description: The definitive Punjabi chole where white chickpeas simmer in a deep, dark onion-tomato masala spiced with homemade chole masala. A muslin bundle of tea leaves gives the gravy its restaurant-dark colour, while amchur and anardana bring the trademark tang. This is the chole that partners bhatura at every North Indian Sunday brunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee gives the chole its rich, glossy finish and rounds the sharp spices

steps: Soak 1 cup white chickpeas overnight, then pressure-cook with 1/2 tsp salt, 3 cups water and 1 tbsp black tea tied in a muslin cloth for 6 whistles until soft; discard the tea bundle and reserve the liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add 3 finely chopped onions and fry until genuinely brown, about 9 minutes, for a dark gravy.
Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 2 slit green chillies for 1 minute, then add 3 pureed tomatoes and cook until the ghee separates, around 7 minutes.
Lower the heat and add 2 tbsp chole masala, 1 tbsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp amchur, roasting for 1 minute until dark and fragrant.
Add the cooked chickpeas with 2 cups reserved liquid and the remaining salt, and simmer for 15 minutes, mashing a spoonful of chana to thicken the gravy naturally.
Garnish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander and rest for 5 minutes so the chole deepens in flavour before serving.
tips: The tea bundle is the classic trick for a dark, dhaba-style colour without any artificial help.
Fry the onions until truly brown, not just golden, for the authentic depth of Punjabi chole.
Chole always taste better after resting, so make them an hour ahead if you can.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot with fluffy bhatura or kulcha, sliced onion rings, green chilli and a wedge of lemon.

variations.name: Amritsari Pindi Chana
variations.description: A rustic Amritsari-style dry chana that skips onion and tomato entirely, taking its dark colour from tea and its tang from pomegranate seeds and dried mango. The chickpeas are coated in a nearly gravy-less spiced mixture finished with a smoky mustard-oil tempering. Earthy, tangy and intensely spiced, it is a Punjabi street classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Smoking-hot mustard oil gives pindi chana its characteristic pungent, street-style finish

steps: Soak 1 cup white chickpeas overnight, then pressure-cook with 1/2 tsp salt, 3 cups water and 1 tbsp black tea in a muslin bundle for 7 whistles until very soft; drain, saving a little liquid, and discard the bundle.

While still warm, toss the drained chickpeas with 1.5 tbsp anardana powder, 1 tsp amchur, 1.5 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1/2 tsp black salt, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1/2 tsp black pepper and the remaining salt until well coated.
Add 2 to 3 tablespoons of the reserved liquid and mash lightly so the spices form a clinging, almost dry coating on the chana.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a small pan to smoking, then lower the heat and add 1 inch julienned ginger and 3 slit green chillies and fry for 30 seconds until sizzling.
Pour this hot tempering over the spiced chickpeas along with 1 tsp garam masala and fold everything through gently.
Cover and rest for 10 minutes so the flavours soak in, then serve warm garnished with extra ginger juliennes.
tips: Cook the chickpeas until very soft here; pindi chana should be tender enough to take on the dry masala.
Anardana is essential to the authentic tang, but amchur alone works if you cannot find it.
Keep it nearly dry; unlike Punjabi chole, pindi chana should coat the chickpeas, not swim in gravy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bhatura or aloo kulcha, topped with ginger juliennes, sliced onion and a squeeze of lemon.

variations.name: Restaurant-Style Creamy Chana Masala
variations.description: A rich, mild restaurant take where the chickpeas rest in a smooth cashew-and-tomato gravy finished with cream and a touch of kasuri methi. Less tangy and far more luxurious than the street version, it appeals to those who like their chole silky and gentle. Ghee and a butter finish give it a hotel-buffet sheen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee builds the luxurious base and gives the creamy gravy its restaurant-style richness

steps: Soak 1 cup white chickpeas overnight and pressure-cook with 1/2 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 whistles until soft; reserve the cooking liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add 2 chopped onions and saute until soft and pale golden, about 6 minutes, keeping them light in colour.
Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then 3 chopped tomatoes and 12 cashews, and cook covered for 8 minutes until pulpy; cool and blend to a very smooth puree.
Return the puree to the pan on low heat, add 1 tbsp coriander powder, 3/4 tsp red chilli powder and 1/2 tsp turmeric, and cook for 4 minutes until the ghee floats on top.
Add the cooked chickpeas with 1.5 cups reserved liquid and the remaining salt, and simmer gently for 12 minutes until the gravy is thick and velvety.
Lower the heat, stir in 3 tbsp cream, 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi and 1 tsp garam masala, warm through for 2 minutes without boiling, and serve.
tips: Keep the onions pale, not brown, so the gravy stays the light golden colour of a restaurant chana.
Blend the tomato-cashew base really smooth for that signature silky texture.
Add the cream on low heat and do not boil after, or the gravy can split and lose its sheen.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or jeera rice, swirled with an extra spoon of cream and a scatter of coriander.

variations.name: Chatpata Chana Chaat Masala
variations.description: A zingy, light dry-toss where boiled chickpeas meet crunchy onion, tomato and cucumber in a tangy chaat dressing. No gravy, no long cooking, just bright chaat masala, lemon and a wood-pressed oil temper for warmth. It works as a protein-rich snack, a summery lunch or a party starter.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A light groundnut-oil temper carries the cumin and gives the cold chaat a warm, nutty base

steps: Soak 1 cup white chickpeas overnight, then pressure-cook with 1/2 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 whistles until soft but still firm, and drain completely.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a small pan on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds until fragrant, then pour this warm temper over the drained chickpeas and let them cool a little.
Finely chop 1 onion, 1 tomato, 1 small cucumber and 2 green chillies and add them to the chickpeas.
Sprinkle over 1.5 tsp chaat masala, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining salt, and toss well.
Squeeze in 2 tbsp lemon juice and fold in 3 tbsp chopped coriander, tasting and adjusting the tang and salt.
Rest for 5 minutes so the flavours mingle, then serve at room temperature or lightly chilled.
tips: Drain the chickpeas thoroughly and cool them before mixing so the chaat stays crisp, not watery.
Add the salt and lemon just before serving if you want the vegetables to stay crunchy.
A handful of pomegranate seeds or crushed papdi turns this into a party-worthy chaat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a light snack or starter, topped with pomegranate seeds and a few crushed papdi for crunch.

variations.name: Classic Kesari Bath
variations.description: Karnataka's beloved saffron semolina sweet, roasted in ghee until fragrant and cooked with just enough water and sugar to turn glossy and spoonable. Real saffron gives it a warm amber glow and floral perfume, while ghee-fried cashews and raisins run through every soft, melting mouthful.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: generous bilona ghee is what gives authentic kesari bath its glossy, non-sticky texture and rich aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: a few strands of pure Kashmiri saffron steeped in warm milk give kesari bath its signature colour and floral scent

steps: Steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside so the colour and aroma bloom while you cook.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai on medium and fry 12 cashews and 2 tbsp raisins until the nuts turn golden and the raisins plump, about 1 minute, then scoop them out and reserve.
In the same ghee, roast 1 cup semolina on medium-low for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring constantly, until it smells nutty and turns a shade darker without browning.

Bring 2.5 cups water to a rolling boil in a separate pan, then pour it into the roasted rava in a slow, steady stream while stirring hard to prevent lumps, and cook covered on low for 3 minutes until the water is absorbed and the rava is soft.

Add 1 cup sugar and the saffron milk and stir vigorously on low heat; the mixture will loosen as the sugar melts, so keep stirring for 3 to 4 minutes until it thickens back into a glossy, cohesive mass.

Drizzle in the remaining 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee a little at a time, stirring until it is absorbed and the kesari bath glistens and leaves the sides of the pan, then fold in 1/2 tsp cardamom powder and the fried cashews and raisins.
tips: Pour boiling water, never cold, into the roasted rava — cold water makes the semolina clump into stubborn lumps.
Add the sugar only after the rava is fully cooked; sugar added early stops the semolina from softening properly.
If it stiffens on standing, stir in a spoon of hot milk or ghee to bring back the glossy, scoopable texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm in a mound, pressed into a katori and unmoulded for a temple-style presentation, alongside a crisp khara bath for the classic 'chow chow bath' pairing.

variations.name: Jaggery Kesari Bath
variations.description: A wholesome, unrefined take that swaps white sugar for mineral-rich jaggery, deepening the sweet into a caramel-toffee register that pairs beautifully with saffron and ghee. The colour turns a darker gold and the flavour gains a rustic, earthy roundness that feels like a village festival kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee balances the deep molasses notes of jaggery and keeps the kesari glossy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: unrefined jaggery powder dissolves cleanly and lends a caramel depth that white sugar cannot

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: pure saffron strands keep the floral colour glowing even against the darker jaggery

steps: Soak 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk to release its colour, and melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 1/4 cup water in a small pan on low heat into a smooth syrup, then strain out any grit.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium and fry 10 slivered almonds and 2 tbsp dry coconut slivers until golden and fragrant, about 1 minute, then set them aside.
Roast 1 cup semolina in the same ghee on medium-low for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring, until it smells nutty and turns lightly golden.
Pour in 2 cups boiling water in a thin stream while stirring hard to avoid lumps, cover, and cook on low for 3 minutes until the rava swells soft and absorbs the water.

Lower the heat, pour in the strained jaggery syrup and the saffron milk, and stir constantly for 4 minutes as the mixture loosens and then thickens back to a glossy mass — keeping the heat low so the jaggery does not scorch.
Add the remaining 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee gradually, stirring until absorbed, then fold in 1/2 tsp cardamom powder, 1/4 tsp dry ginger powder and the fried almonds and coconut.
tips: Always melt and strain the jaggery first — unstrained jaggery carries sand and fibre that ruin the smooth texture.
Keep the flame low once the jaggery goes in, as jaggery burns and turns bitter far faster than white sugar.
The pinch of dry ginger powder is a traditional trick that keeps this richer, jaggery version easy to digest.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm topped with extra toasted coconut slivers, ideal as a festive naivedyam offering or a wholesome winter dessert.

variations.name: Pineapple Kesari Bath
variations.description: The Udupi hotel classic where sweet-tart pineapple is simmered into the semolina, its juice perfuming every grain and cutting through the ghee. Bright saffron and a scatter of pineapple pieces make this the celebratory, fruit-forward version served at South Indian weddings and Sunday breakfasts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee carries the pineapple's fragrance through the rava and gives a glossy, non-sticky set

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: saffron deepens the golden hue and adds a floral note that flatters the tangy pineapple

steps: Steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk, and finely chop 1 cup ripe pineapple, keeping a few small pieces aside for garnish.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium and fry 12 cashews until golden, about 1 minute, then remove them and reserve.
In the same ghee, saute the chopped pineapple for 3 minutes on medium until it softens and releases its juice, then roast 1 cup semolina into the pan for 4 minutes on medium-low until nutty.
Pour in 2 cups boiling water in a slow stream while stirring hard to avoid lumps, cover, and cook on low for 3 minutes until the rava is soft and the water absorbed.
Add 1 cup sugar, the saffron milk and a pinch of yellow colour, stirring on low for 3 to 4 minutes as the mixture loosens with the melting sugar and then thickens into a glossy mass.
Stir in the remaining 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee a little at a time until absorbed, then fold in 1/2 tsp cardamom powder, the fried cashews and the reserved pineapple pieces.
tips: Use ripe, sweet pineapple; sour, unripe fruit can make the semolina taste raw and overly tangy.
Cook the pineapple down before adding rava so its extra moisture does not leave the kesari watery.
Reduce the sugar slightly if the pineapple is very sweet, tasting once the fruit is folded in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm garnished with fresh pineapple bits and a few saffron strands, a bright finish to a South Indian festive meal.

variations.name: Rava-Kesari Sheera Wedges
variations.description: A firmer, denser kesari cooked with a touch less water and extra ghee, then set in a greased tray and cut into diamond wedges like a mithai. Loaded with saffron, cardamom and a heavier hand of nuts, these sliceable pieces are made to be packed into festive boxes and eaten with the fingers.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the extra bilona ghee sets these wedges firm and gives clean, glossy edges when sliced

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: saffron colours the set kesari a rich even gold that looks striking in cut diamonds

steps: Steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk, and grease a small tray or plate with a little ghee so the set kesari will release cleanly.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai on medium and fry 15 cashews and 10 slivered pistachios until golden, about 1 minute, then reserve, keeping a few nuts for the top.
Roast 1 cup fine semolina in the same ghee on medium-low for 5 minutes, stirring steadily, until deeply nutty and evenly warmed.
Pour in 2 cups boiling water in a thin stream while stirring hard against lumps, cover, and cook on low for 3 minutes until the rava is fully soft.

Add 1 cup sugar and the saffron milk, stir on low for 4 minutes until the sugar melts and the mixture thickens, then drizzle in the remaining 5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee gradually, stirring until the mass turns dense, glossy and pulls cleanly from the pan.

Fold in 3/4 tsp cardamom powder, 1/4 tsp nutmeg powder and the fried nuts, then press the hot mixture firmly into the greased tray, smooth the top, scatter the reserved nuts, and cool for 20 minutes before slicing into diamonds.
tips: Use slightly less water and more ghee than a spoonable kesari so the mixture sets firm enough to hold a clean cut.
Press the hot mixture down hard while it is still warm; a loosely packed tray crumbles instead of slicing neatly.
Let it cool and firm for a full 20 minutes before cutting, or the wedges will lose their sharp edges.
variations.servingSuggestion: Arrange the diamond wedges on a festive platter dusted with slivered pistachios, perfect for a Diwali sweet box or after-meal treat.

variations.name: Classic Poricha Kootu
variations.description: The everyday Tamil kootu: mixed vegetables simmered soft with moong dal and bound in a freshly ground paste of coconut, cumin and pepper, then finished with a fragrant ghee tempering of urad dal and red chilli. Poricha kootu skips tamarind entirely, so it tastes mild, creamy and comforting, the gentle middle of a South Indian meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A ghee tempering gives poricha kootu its rounded, homely richness

steps: Pressure-cook 0.5 cup moong dal with 1.5 cups water and 0.25 tsp turmeric for 3 whistles until soft, then mash lightly and keep aside.
Boil 2 cups chopped mixed vegetables with 1 tsp salt and just enough water to cover on medium for 8-10 minutes until fork-tender but not falling apart.
Grind 0.33 cup grated coconut with 1 tsp cumin, 0.5 tsp peppercorns and 2 green chillies into a smooth paste with a little water.
Add the cooked dal and the ground coconut paste to the vegetables and simmer on low for 5-6 minutes, stirring, until the kootu thickens to a soft, spoonable consistency.

In a small pan heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal and fry until the dal is golden, then add 2 dried red chillies, 10 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida.
Pour the sizzling tempering over the kootu, stir once and simmer for a final minute so the aromas soak in.
tips: Grind the coconut paste smooth rather than coarse so the kootu turns creamy, not grainy.
Keep the vegetables just tender; boiling them to mush loses their distinct bite in the finished dish.
Poricha kootu has no tamarind by design, so resist adding any souring agent - its charm is the mildness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rice and a spoon of ghee alongside a sharper rasam, or as a soothing side to spicy curries and pickle.

variations.name: Chow Chow Kootu
variations.description: A silky, single-vegetable kootu where chayote (chow chow) is simmered with chana dal until melt-soft and finished with a coconut-cumin paste. The chana dal keeps a little bite against the tender squash, and a coconut-oil tempering with mustard gives it a coastal fragrance distinct from the ghee-tempered classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: A coconut-oil tempering keeps this chayote kootu light and coastal in flavour

steps: Soak 0.5 cup chana dal for 20 minutes, then pressure-cook with 1.5 cups water and 0.25 tsp turmeric for 3-4 whistles until soft but still holding shape.
Peel and cube 3 cups chayote and boil with 1 tsp salt and water to cover on medium for 8 minutes until tender and translucent.
Grind 0.33 cup grated coconut with 1 tsp cumin and 3 green chillies into a smooth paste with a splash of water.
Add the cooked chana dal and the coconut paste to the chayote, stir in 1 tsp rice flour slaked in 2 tbsp water, and simmer on low for 6 minutes until glossy and lightly thickened.
In a small pan heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil on medium; add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal, fry until golden, then add 2 dried red chillies and 10 curry leaves.
Tip the tempering into the kootu, stir through and simmer for a final minute before switching off.
tips: The teaspoon of rice flour gives the kootu a light body without making it heavy or gluey.
Cook the chana dal until soft but intact so it contrasts nicely with the melting chayote.
Chayote can be watery, so use only enough boiling water to cover and drain excess before adding the paste.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with steamed rice and a tangy vatha kuzhambu, or serve with chapati as a mild, wholesome side.

variations.name: Keerai Kootu (Spinach Kootu)
variations.description: A nourishing green kootu where finely chopped spinach wilts into soft-cooked moong dal, brightened by a coconut-cumin-garlic paste. The iron-rich greens and creamy dal come together into a soft, earthy dish, finished with a garlicky ghee tempering that gives it a home-kitchen warmth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A garlic-ghee tempering rounds out the earthy spinach and dal beautifully

steps: Pressure-cook 0.5 cup moong dal with 1.5 cups water and 0.25 tsp turmeric for 3 whistles until soft, then mash lightly.
Add 4 cups finely chopped spinach and 1 tsp salt to the dal and simmer on medium for 5 minutes until the greens wilt down completely.
Grind 0.25 cup grated coconut with 1 tsp cumin, 2 garlic cloves and 2 green chillies into a coarse paste with a little water.
Stir the coconut paste into the spinach-dal and simmer on low for 4-5 minutes until thick and well combined.

In a small pan heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, let them pop, then add the remaining 2 garlic cloves crushed, 2 dried red chillies and 10 curry leaves and fry until the garlic is golden.
Pour the garlicky tempering over the kootu, stir and simmer for a final minute so the aroma infuses.
tips: Wilt the spinach only briefly; overcooking dulls its bright green and washes out the flavour.
Two hits of garlic - one in the paste and one in the tempering - give this kootu its signature depth.
Palak, amaranth or a mix of local greens all work; adjust the cooking time to how tender they are.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rice and ghee and a crisp appalam, or as an iron-rich side to a coconut-heavy meal.

variations.name: Palakkad Molagootal
variations.description: The Palakkad Iyer molagootal is a coconut-forward kootu ground with red chillies and a spoon of roasted urad dal, giving it a deeper, faintly smoky base than the pepper-cumin classic. Made with pumpkin and beans, it is finished with the region's hallmark coconut-oil tempering of mustard and extra urad dal for crunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: The defining Palakkad finish, its aroma is inseparable from a proper molagootal

steps: Pressure-cook 0.5 cup toor dal with 1.5 cups water and 0.25 tsp turmeric for 4 whistles until very soft, and mash smooth.
Boil 2.5 cups cubed pumpkin and beans with 1 tsp salt and water to cover on medium for 8-10 minutes until tender.
Dry-roast 1 tsp urad dal and 3 dried red chillies in a pan until golden, then grind with 0.5 cup grated coconut and 1 tsp cumin into a smooth paste with water.
Add the mashed dal and the ground coconut paste to the vegetables and simmer on low for 6-7 minutes until the molagootal is thick and creamy.
In a small pan heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil on medium; add 1 tsp mustard seeds and the remaining 1 tsp urad dal, fry until golden, then add 10 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida.
Pour the crackling tempering over the molagootal, stir once and simmer for a final minute before serving.
tips: Roasting the urad dal and red chillies before grinding is the step that gives molagootal its signature depth.
Use toor dal here rather than moong for the fuller body this Palakkad dish is known for.
Grind the coconut very smooth so the molagootal is velvety rather than grainy.
variations.servingSuggestion: A Palakkad staple served with rice, a spoon of ghee and a dry curry like beans usili, with pappadam on the side.

variations.name: Classic Mixed Sprouts Curry
variations.description: A wholesome everyday curry of mixed sprouted beans simmered in a homely onion-tomato masala. The sprouts stay tender-crisp and nutty, soaking up a lightly spiced gravy that makes a protein-packed weekday meal. It is the kind of nourishing dish home cooks turn to for a healthy dinner without fuss.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil keeps the everyday curry light while carrying the tempering flavours

steps: Pressure-cook 2 cups mixed sprouts with 1/2 tsp salt and 1 cup water for 1 whistle only, so they stay tender but not mushy; set aside with the liquid.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 15 seconds, then add 2 finely chopped onions and fry until golden, about 6 minutes.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 2 slit green chillies for 1 minute, then add 2 pureed tomatoes and cook until the oil separates, around 5 minutes.
Lower the heat and add 1.5 tbsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1/2 tsp turmeric, roasting for 30 seconds with a splash of water so they do not burn.
Add the cooked sprouts with their liquid and the remaining salt, and simmer for 8 to 10 minutes until the gravy thickens and coats the sprouts.
Finish with 1 tsp garam masala and 3 tbsp chopped coriander, simmer 2 minutes, and serve warm.
tips: Cook the sprouts only briefly; over-boiling makes them mushy and dulls their fresh, nutty bite.
For a thicker gravy, blend a small ladle of the cooked sprouts and stir it back in.
Homemade mixed sprouts of moong, moth and chana give the best texture and flavour balance.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with phulka roti or steamed rice, and a squeeze of lemon to brighten the sprouts.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Sprouts Usal
variations.description: A fragrant Maharashtrian usal where mixed sprouts are simmered with roasted goda masala and coconut for a dark, aromatic gravy. Sweet, spicy and earthy all at once, it is finished with a curry-leaf tempering and a hint of jaggery. Traditionally eaten with bread pav or bhakri, it is comfort food across Maharashtra.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the traditional Maharashtrian fat and carries the goda masala tempering

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A touch of jaggery gives the usal its signature sweet-spicy Maharashtrian balance

steps: Pressure-cook 2 cups mixed sprouts with 1/2 tsp salt and 1 cup water for 1 whistle so they stay firm; keep aside with the liquid.
Dry-roast 1/3 cup grated coconut in a pan until golden, then grind it with 1 chopped onion to a coarse paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pot on medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp cumin seeds, add 12 curry leaves, then saute 1 chopped onion until golden, about 5 minutes.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then the coconut-onion paste, 1.5 tbsp goda masala, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1/2 tsp turmeric, and fry for 4 minutes until the oil separates.
Add the cooked sprouts with their liquid, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and the remaining salt, and simmer for 10 minutes until the dark gravy thickens.
Rest covered for 5 minutes so the goda masala deepens, then serve warm.
tips: Roasting the coconut before grinding gives the usal its dark colour and nutty depth.
Goda masala is the soul of this dish; do not substitute regular garam masala if you want it authentic.
Keep the gravy slightly loose as it thickens on standing, especially if serving with pav.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with soft pav or jowar bhakri, topped with chopped onion, coriander and a squeeze of lemon.

variations.name: Kerala Coconut Sprouts Curry
variations.description: A creamy South Indian version where mixed sprouts simmer in a fresh coconut-milk gravy scented with fennel and curry leaves. Mild, mellow and pale, it lets the sweetness of the sprouts and coconut shine without heavy spicing. Coconut oil tempering ties it firmly to the Kerala kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil gives the mild curry its unmistakable Kerala fragrance

steps: Pressure-cook 2 cups mixed sprouts with 1/2 tsp salt and 1 cup water for 1 whistle so they stay tender-crisp; keep aside with the liquid.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan on medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1/2 tsp fennel seeds, add 15 curry leaves, then saute 1 chopped onion, 1 inch minced ginger and 2 slit green chillies until soft, about 5 minutes.
Add 1 chopped tomato and cook until pulpy, then stir in 1.5 tbsp coriander powder and 1/2 tsp turmeric on low heat for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the cooked sprouts with their liquid and the remaining salt, and simmer for 8 minutes so they absorb the masala.
Lower the heat to a bare simmer and pour in 1 cup thick coconut milk, warming through for 3 to 4 minutes without boiling so it does not split.
Switch off and rest the curry covered for 5 minutes so the coconut milk settles into a smooth, mild gravy.
tips: Add the coconut milk only on the lowest heat and never boil it, or the gravy will curdle.
Fennel seeds are the quiet signature here; do not skip them for the true Kerala aroma.
For a thicker curry, mash a spoonful of sprouts before adding the coconut milk.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with appam, idiyappam or ghee rice, letting the creamy coconut gravy soak in.

variations.name: Gujarati Sweet-and-Sour Sprouts
variations.description: A light Gujarati-style shaak where mixed sprouts are simmered in a thin, gently sweet-and-sour gravy thickened with a little besan. Jaggery, ginger and green chilli give the classic Gujarati balance, while a mustard-cumin tempering keeps it bright. It is an everyday dish meant for soft rotli and rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the classic Gujarati cooking fat and carries the light tempering

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery brings the gentle sweetness that defines Gujarati sweet-and-sour shaak

steps: Pressure-cook 2 cups mixed sprouts with 1/2 tsp salt and 1.5 cups water for 1 whistle so they stay tender; keep aside with the liquid.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan on medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add 1/4 tsp asafoetida and 10 curry leaves.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and 1 chopped tomato, and cook for 3 minutes until the tomato softens.
Whisk 1 tbsp besan into 1/2 cup water until lump-free, then pour it in with 1/2 tsp turmeric and stir constantly for 2 minutes so the besan cooks and thickens the gravy.
Add the cooked sprouts with their liquid, 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and the remaining salt, and simmer for 8 minutes until the gravy is smooth and lightly thick.
Turn off the heat, stir in 1 tbsp lemon juice, and rest for 3 minutes before serving.
tips: Whisk the besan into cold water off the heat to avoid lumps in the gravy.
Balance sweet, sour and salt at the end; Gujarati shaak should taste harmoniously rounded.
Keep the gravy thin and pourable, as it thickens further on standing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft rotli or steamed rice and a spoon of plain yogurt on the side.

variations.name: Classic Matki Usal
variations.description: The everyday Maharashtrian matki usal where sprouted moth beans simmer in a light onion-and-goda-masala gravy. Nutty, mildly spiced and quick to make, it is a staple that turns a humble legume into a nourishing meal. A curry-leaf tempering and fresh coconut on top make it fragrant and homely.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the traditional Maharashtrian fat that carries the mustard-and-curry-leaf tempering

steps: Pressure-cook 2 cups sprouted moth beans with 1/2 tsp salt and 1 cup water for 1 whistle so they stay tender but intact; keep aside with the liquid.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pot on medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add 12 curry leaves and 2 finely chopped onions and fry until golden, about 6 minutes.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then add 1 chopped tomato and cook until soft, around 3 minutes.
Lower the heat and add 1 tbsp goda masala, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1/2 tsp turmeric with a splash of water, roasting for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the cooked matki with its liquid and the remaining salt, and simmer for 8 to 10 minutes until the light gravy coats the beans.
Fold in 3 tbsp fresh grated coconut, simmer 1 minute, and serve warm.
tips: Cook the matki only until just tender; overcooking turns the delicate sprouts to mush.
Goda masala gives the authentic Maharashtrian flavour; garam masala is a poorer substitute.
Add the coconut near the end so it stays fresh and fragrant.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with bhakri, chapati or steamed rice, topped with chopped coriander and extra coconut.

variations.name: Puneri Misal-Style Matki
variations.description: A fiery Puneri misal-style matki with a deep red kolhapuri-spiced tarri gravy poured over sprouted moth beans. Bold, oily and blazing hot, it is built to be topped with farsan, onion and lemon at breakfast. The separate spicy tarri is what turns everyday usal into an addictive misal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A generous pour of groundnut oil gives the fiery tarri its glossy red slick on top

steps: Pressure-cook 2 cups sprouted moth beans with 1/2 tsp salt and 1.5 cups water for 2 whistles until soft, and lightly mash a few to thicken; keep aside.
Dry-roast 1/2 cup grated coconut with 2 chopped onions until deep brown, then grind with 8 garlic cloves and 1 inch ginger to a dark paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pot on medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, add the ground paste and fry for 5 minutes until the oil starts to leave the sides.

Add 2 tbsp kolhapuri kanda-lasun masala, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1/2 tsp turmeric, cook 1 minute, then pour in 3 cups hot water and the remaining salt to make a thin, fiery tarri; simmer 10 minutes until a red oil layer floats on top.
In serving bowls, spoon the cooked matki as a base and ladle the hot tarri generously over it.
Top with 1 chopped raw onion, 1 cup farsan and a drizzle of the last 1 tbsp oil, and serve immediately with lemon.
tips: The floating red oil layer is the mark of a proper tarri, so do not skimp on the oil while frying the masala.
Assemble misal just before eating so the farsan stays crunchy on top.
Keep extra hot tarri on the side for those who want it spicier, misal-house style.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot with pav, topped with farsan, raw onion, coriander and a big squeeze of lemon.

variations.name: Rajasthani Dry Moth Beans
variations.description: A dry, robust Rajasthani preparation where moth beans are cooked without sprouting into a spicy, nearly gravy-less dish finished in mustard oil. Amchur and coriander give it a desert-kitchen tang, and it stays dry enough to pack for travel. This is the humble bean that also gives Bikaneri bhujia its name.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Pungent mustard oil gives the dry Rajasthani beans their characteristic sharp, earthy edge

steps: Soak 1 cup whole moth beans for 4 hours, then pressure-cook with 1/2 tsp salt and 2 cups water for 3 whistles until just soft; drain well so the dish can stay dry.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai to smoking, lower the heat, then crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1/4 tsp asafoetida for 15 seconds.
Add 1 finely chopped onion and fry until golden-brown, about 6 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute.
Lower the heat and add 1.5 tbsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp amchur with a splash of water, roasting for 1 minute until glossy.
Add the drained moth beans and the remaining salt, and toss on medium heat for 6 to 8 minutes until the masala coats the beans and everything looks dry.
Sprinkle in 1 tsp garam masala and 3 tbsp chopped coriander, toss once more, and serve.
tips: Drain the boiled beans thoroughly so the dish stays dry and the masala clings.
Heat mustard oil to smoking first, then cool slightly, to soften its raw pungency.
This dry preparation keeps well for a day and travels beautifully in a tiffin.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra roti and a dollop of ghee, or stuff into a paratha for a hearty travel meal.

variations.name: Gujarati Matki Nu Shaak
variations.description: A gently sweet-and-sour Gujarati shaak where sprouted moth beans simmer in a thin tomato gravy lightly thickened with besan. Jaggery, ginger and green chilli create the rounded Gujarati flavour, and a hing-cumin tempering keeps it fragrant. It is a soft, comforting everyday dish for rotli and rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the classic Gujarati fat that carries the delicate hing-cumin tempering

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery gives the shaak its characteristic gentle Gujarati sweetness

steps: Pressure-cook 2 cups sprouted moth beans with 1/2 tsp salt and 1.5 cups water for 1 whistle so they stay tender; keep aside with the liquid.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan on medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add 1/4 tsp asafoetida and 10 curry leaves.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and 2 chopped tomatoes, and cook for 4 minutes until the tomato turns pulpy.
Whisk 1 tbsp besan into 1/2 cup water until smooth, pour it in with 1/2 tsp turmeric, and stir constantly for 2 minutes so the besan cooks and thickens the gravy.
Add the cooked matki with its liquid, 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and the remaining salt, and simmer for 8 minutes until lightly thick.
Rest covered for 3 minutes so the flavours balance, then serve warm.
tips: Whisk the besan into cold water off the heat so the gravy stays smooth and lump-free.
Taste and balance the sweet, sour and salt at the end for the classic Gujarati harmony.
Keep the gravy pourable as it thickens further on standing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft rotli, steamed rice and a spoon of plain yogurt for a light Gujarati meal.

variations.name: Classic Doodhi Muthia
variations.description: The quintessential steamed Gujarati muthia: grated bottle gourd bound with gram flour, wheat and a little semolina, shaped into logs by the fist, and steamed until spongy. Sliced and finished in a mustard-sesame tempering with curry leaves, it is the healthiest, most beloved of all farsan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Wheat Flour
ingredients.note: Nutty khapli atta gives the muthia a wholesome bite and steams into a softer, more digestible dumpling than refined flour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A teaspoon of jaggery gives the batter the subtle sweet edge typical of Gujarati muthia

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil ties the sesame tempering together and keeps the muthia moist

steps: Squeeze 2 cups grated bottle gourd lightly to remove excess water but keep it slightly moist, then combine in a bowl with 1 cup besan, 0.5 cup Anveshan Khapli Wheat Flour and 0.25 cup semolina.

Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1.5 tsp salt and 1 tbsp of the sesame oil, then knead into a soft non-sticky dough, using the gourd's own moisture and only a splash of water if needed.
Grease your palms and shape the dough into 2-3 smooth cylindrical logs about 5 inches long, pressing firmly so they hold together while steaming.

Steam the logs in a greased steamer on medium heat for 18-20 minutes, until a skewer inserted into the centre comes out clean and the surface springs back to the touch; cool for 10 minutes, then slice into 0.75-inch rounds.
Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a wide pan on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds and 2 tbsp sesame seeds for 40 seconds, then add 12 curry leaves until they turn crisp.
Add the muthia slices and toss gently for 4-5 minutes until they are lightly golden and heated through, then garnish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander before serving.
tips: Do not over-squeeze the bottle gourd; a little moisture keeps the muthia soft, while a bone-dry mix turns dense and hard.
Adjust flour last — add the besan and atta gradually until the dough just holds a shape, since gourds vary in water content.
Steamed muthia freezes well; slice and pan-toss straight from frozen whenever you want a quick farsan.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the golden rounds warm with green coriander chutney and a cup of masala chai as an evening snack.

variations.name: Methi Muthia
variations.description: A punchier winter muthia built on fresh fenugreek leaves instead of bottle gourd, so every bite carries methi's pleasant bitterness against warm spices. Steamed then tempered, these firmer, greener dumplings are a Gujarati cold-season staple.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Wheat Flour
ingredients.note: Khapli atta adds structure to the methi dough so the dumplings hold shape while staying tender

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery counters methi's bitterness and rounds out the spicing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil in the dough and tempering keeps the firm methi muthia rich but clean

steps: Wash and finely chop 2 cups methi leaves, sprinkle with a little salt, rest for 10 minutes, then squeeze out the released water to reduce the bitterness.

Combine the squeezed methi with 1.25 cups besan, 0.5 cup Anveshan Khapli Wheat Flour, 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic-green chilli paste, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tbsp dhana-jeera, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1.5 tsp salt and 1 tbsp groundnut oil.
Knead into a stiff dough using only a little water, since methi releases moisture as it sits, then shape into 3 firm logs with greased palms.
Steam the logs on medium heat for 18-20 minutes until firm and a skewer comes out clean; cool and slice into 0.75-inch rounds.
Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, 1.5 tbsp sesame seeds and 0.5 tsp asafoetida for 40 seconds until fragrant.
Toss the methi muthia slices in the tempering for 4-5 minutes until golden and crisp at the edges, then serve hot.
tips: Salting and squeezing the methi is the key step; skip it and the muthia turns unpleasantly bitter.
Keep the methi dough stiffer than a doodhi muthia dough, as there is no watery gourd to bind it.
A pinch of baking soda in the dough gives an even fluffier steam if you like a lighter texture.
