variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these winter muthia hot with a bowl of sweet mango chhundo or garlic chutney alongside chai.

variations.name: Crispy Fried Muthia
variations.description: The indulgent fried avatar where the doodhi-besan dough is rolled into small dumplings and deep-fried straight, no steaming, until they turn crunchy-golden outside and stay soft within. A festive, crowd-pleasing snack quite unlike the everyday steamed version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: High-smoke-point wood-pressed groundnut oil fries the dumplings to an even crunch without any greasy aftertaste

steps: Squeeze most of the water from 1.5 cups grated bottle gourd, then mix with 1 cup besan, 0.5 cup semolina, 2 tbsp rice flour, 2 tbsp sesame seeds and 3 tbsp chopped coriander in a bowl.
Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp carom seeds and 1.5 tsp salt, then knead into a firm dough that holds a shape; rest for 10 minutes.
Roll the dough into small oval dumplings about the size of a walnut, pressing firmly so they do not break apart in the oil.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai to a medium 170C, testing with a pinch of dough that should rise steadily with tiny bubbles.
Fry the muthia in batches for 5-6 minutes, turning often, until deep golden and crisp all over; do not crowd the pan or they cook unevenly.
Drain on a rack and serve hot; the carom seeds and rice flour keep them crunchy and easy to digest.
tips: Keep the dough firm — a wet mix absorbs oil and turns the dumplings soggy instead of crisp.
Fry at a steady medium heat; too hot and they brown before the centre cooks, too cool and they drink oil.
Add the semolina and let the dough rest so the rava swells, giving a crunchier bite.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the hot fried dumplings with tangy green chutney and sweet tamarind chutney as a festive teatime treat.

variations.name: Mixed Millet Muthia
variations.description: A wholesome winter muthia that swaps refined flour for hearty pearl millet and sorghum flours with grated bottle gourd and spinach, for a fibre-rich, gluten-conscious dumpling. Earthy and rustic, it is the kind of nourishing farsan Gujarati grandmothers make in the cold months.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil binds the millet dough and carries the tempering for these hearty dumplings

steps: Squeeze the excess water from 1.5 cups grated bottle gourd, then combine with 1 cup chopped spinach, 0.75 cup bajra flour, 0.5 cup jowar flour and 0.5 cup besan in a bowl.

Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp salt and 1 tbsp groundnut oil, then knead into a soft dough, letting the gourd and spinach moisture bind the gluten-free flours.
Grease your palms and shape the dough into 3 short thick logs, pressing firmly since millet flours are more crumbly than wheat.
Steam the logs on medium heat for 20-22 minutes until set and a skewer comes out clean; cool for 10 minutes and slice into thick 1-inch rounds.
Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 1.5 tbsp sesame seeds for 40 seconds, then add 10 curry leaves.
Toss the millet muthia slices in the tempering for 4-5 minutes until warmed and lightly crusted, handling gently as they are more fragile, then serve.
tips: Millet doughs crack easily; keep them slightly wetter than wheat doughs and pack the logs tightly.
Steam a little longer than a wheat muthia, as bajra and jowar take extra time to cook through.
Slice thicker rounds for this version so the crumblier millet dumplings hold together during tempering.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these rustic dumplings warm with a dollop of white butter and garlic chutney for a nourishing winter snack.

variations.name: Classic Ash Gourd Olan
variations.description: The gentlest dish on the sadya, olan simmers cubes of ash gourd and red cowpeas in coconut milk with just slit green chillies and curry leaves, finished with a raw drizzle of coconut oil. There is no tempering and almost no spice, so the dish tastes clean, milky and soothing, a quiet counterpoint to the sharper curries on a Kerala feast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Drizzled raw at the end, its aroma is the single defining flourish of an olan

steps: Soak 0.5 cup red cowpeas overnight, then pressure-cook with 2 cups water for 4-5 whistles until soft but still whole, and drain.
Peel 400 g ash gourd, remove the seeds and cut into thin 3 cm squares no more than 0.5 cm thick so they cook through gently.
Put the ash gourd in a pot with 3 slit green chillies, 1 tsp salt and just enough water to half-cover, and simmer uncovered on medium for 8-10 minutes until translucent and tender.
Add the cooked cowpeas and 1.5 cups thin coconut milk and simmer gently on low for 5 minutes, never letting it reach a rolling boil so the milk does not split.
Lower the heat, stir in 0.5 cup thick coconut milk and 12 curry leaves and warm through for 2 minutes without boiling, then switch off.
Drizzle 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil over the top and cover for 5 minutes so its aroma infuses before serving.
tips: Add the thick coconut milk only on low heat and never boil it, or the olan will curdle and turn grainy.
Cut the ash gourd thin and even so it turns tender and translucent without falling apart.
The raw coconut oil finish is essential; adding it during cooking loses the fresh aroma entirely.
variations.servingSuggestion: An essential part of the Onam and Vishu sadya, served with rice; its mildness balances spicier sides like sambar and pickle.

variations.name: Mathanga Olan (Pumpkin Olan)
variations.description: Swapping ash gourd for golden pumpkin gives this olan a natural sweetness and a sunny colour, while a few julienned strips of ginger lend a gentle warmth the classic version leaves out. The pumpkin softens into silky pieces that soak up the coconut milk, making this a slightly richer, sweeter take.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: The raw drizzle that finishes every olan, especially fragrant against sweet pumpkin

steps: Soak 0.5 cup red cowpeas overnight, then pressure-cook with 2 cups water for 4-5 whistles until soft but whole, and drain.
Peel 400 g pumpkin and cut into 3 cm cubes about 1 cm thick, keeping them slightly chunky as pumpkin softens fast.
Simmer the pumpkin in a pot with 3 slit green chillies, 1 inch julienned ginger, 1 tsp salt and a little water to half-cover on medium for 7-8 minutes until just fork-tender.
Add the cooked cowpeas and 1.5 cups thin coconut milk and simmer gently on low for 5 minutes without letting it boil hard.
Reduce the heat to the lowest setting, stir in 0.5 cup thick coconut milk and 12 curry leaves, and warm for 2 minutes without boiling.
Switch off and drizzle 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil over the surface, then cover for 5 minutes to let the aroma settle in.
tips: Watch the pumpkin closely; it turns tender much faster than ash gourd and can collapse into mush.
The ginger should whisper, not shout - a single inch is enough to warm the sweetness of the pumpkin.
Keep the pot below a boil once the coconut milk goes in to protect its smooth, un-split texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a sadya plate with rice where its sweetness plays against tangy pulissery and spicy sambar.

variations.name: Cucumber Olan (Vellarikka Olan)
variations.description: This lighter olan uses tender field cucumber and creamy white peas in place of ash gourd and cowpeas, giving a fresher, crisper bite that stays firm in the coconut milk. It is a summer-leaning version, cooling and delicate, often made when the local vellarikka is in season.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Finishes the olan raw, its aroma echoing the fresh coconut milk

steps: Soak 0.5 cup white peas overnight, then pressure-cook with 2 cups water for 5-6 whistles until soft but holding shape, and drain.
Peel and deseed 400 g field cucumber and cut into 3 cm cubes about 1 cm thick.
Simmer the cucumber in a pot with 4 slit green chillies, 1 tsp salt and a little water to half-cover on medium for 6-7 minutes until just tender but still crisp at the centre.
Add the cooked white peas and 1.5 cups thin coconut milk and simmer very gently on low for 4-5 minutes without boiling.
Lower the heat fully, stir in 0.5 cup thick coconut milk and 12 curry leaves, and warm for 2 minutes off the boil.
Switch off and drizzle 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil over the top, covering for 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Choose a tender, pale field cucumber rather than a hard salad cucumber, which stays crunchy and raw-tasting.
Cook the cucumber just to tender so it keeps a fresh, cooling bite rather than going limp.
White peas need a longer soak and cook than cowpeas, so start them well ahead.
variations.servingSuggestion: A refreshing side for a summer meal with rice and a tart mango pachadi, or alongside a simple thoran and pappadam.

variations.name: Sadya Olan with Drumstick
variations.description: A grander, feast-day olan that brings ash gourd and pumpkin together and adds meaty drumstick pieces, so the coconut milk carries three textures at once. The drumstick lends a subtle vegetal depth and the two gourds balance mild and sweet, making this the fullest version served at large sadyas.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: The raw finishing drizzle that unifies the three vegetables under one coconut aroma

steps: Soak 0.5 cup red cowpeas overnight, then pressure-cook with 2 cups water for 4-5 whistles until soft but whole, and drain.
Cut 250 g ash gourd and 200 g pumpkin into thin 3 cm squares, and scrape 1 drumstick before cutting into 3 inch batons.
Simmer the drumstick first in a pot with a little water and 1.25 tsp salt on medium for 5 minutes, then add both gourds and 4 slit green chillies and cook 8-10 minutes until all are tender.
Add the cooked cowpeas and 2 cups thin coconut milk and simmer gently on low for 5 minutes, keeping it below a boil.
Reduce the heat fully, stir in 0.5 cup thick coconut milk and 15 curry leaves, and warm for 2-3 minutes without boiling.
Switch off and drizzle 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil across the surface, then cover for 5 minutes to let the flavours marry.
tips: Start the drumstick before the gourds since it takes the longest to turn tender.
Encourage guests to squeeze the soft drumstick flesh into the coconut milk as they eat for extra flavour.
Scale up gently for a crowd, but keep the coconut milk off the boil no matter the batch size.
variations.servingSuggestion: A centrepiece olan for a full sadya, served with rice and ghee amid avial, kaalan and a tangy pachadi.

variations.name: Classic Patra
variations.description: The beloved Gujarati farsan of colocasia leaves layered with a sweet-sour-spicy gram-flour paste, rolled tight, steamed until firm, then sliced and tempered with mustard and sesame. Tamarind and jaggery in the paste give it the signature khatta-meetha balance that defines authentic patra.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Pure jaggery powder gives the paste its authentic mellow sweetness to balance the tangy tamarind

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil in the tempering echoes the sesame seeds and gives patra its nutty finish

steps: Wash 8 colocasia leaves, pat dry, trim the hard stalks, and run a rolling pin firmly over the thick central veins to flatten them so the leaves roll without cracking.

Mix 1.5 cups besan with 2 tbsp tamarind pulp, 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1.5 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tbsp dhana-jeera powder and 1.5 tsp salt, adding water little by little to a thick spreadable paste.

Lay a leaf vein-side up, smear a thin even layer of paste over it, place a second leaf on top, coat again, and repeat to stack 3-4 leaves; fold in the sides and roll tightly into a firm log, making 2-3 logs.

Steam the logs in a greased steamer on medium heat for 20-22 minutes, until a knife inserted into the centre comes out clean and the surface is no longer sticky; cool completely, then slice into 1-inch rounds.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a wide pan on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds, 2 tbsp sesame seeds and 0.5 tsp asafoetida for 40 seconds until the sesame turns golden and fragrant.
Lay the patra slices in the tempering and pan-fry gently for 3-4 minutes per side until the edges crisp and turn deep gold, then scatter 3 tbsp grated coconut over the top before serving.
tips: Flattening the leaf veins with a rolling pin is essential — it stops the leaves cracking and neutralises the itch-causing sap when combined with the tamarind.
Cool the steamed logs fully before slicing; hot patra crumbles and will not hold neat rounds.
Taste the paste before rolling and adjust tamarind or jaggery — it should be assertively sweet-sour since steaming mellows it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the coconut-topped rounds warm as a tea-time farsan with green chutney and a cup of ginger chai.

variations.name: Crispy Fried Patra
variations.description: Steamed patra logs taken one delicious step further: sliced thin and shallow-fried in wood-pressed oil until the edges shatter like crisps while the centre stays soft. A dusting of sesame and a squeeze of lime turn this into an addictive fried snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery in the paste caramelises lightly on frying, deepening the sweet-sour crunch

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Neutral wood-pressed groundnut oil crisps the slices to a clean golden shatter without heaviness

steps: Prepare 8 colocasia leaves by trimming stalks and rolling a pin over the veins to flatten them, then set aside.

Mix 1.5 cups besan with 2 tbsp rice flour, 2 tbsp tamarind pulp, 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1.5 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp salt into a thick paste; the rice flour is the secret to extra crispness.
Smear the paste over stacked leaves, roll into tight logs, and steam on medium heat for 20 minutes until firm and cooked through; cool fully and slice into thin 0.5-inch rounds.
Heat 0.5 cup Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a wide pan on medium-high heat until shimmering, then slide in the slices in a single layer without crowding.
Shallow-fry for 3-4 minutes per side, pressing lightly with a spatula, until both faces are deep golden and the edges are visibly crisp; drain on a rack.
While hot, sprinkle over 2 tbsp toasted sesame seeds and squeeze the juice of 1 lime across the slices before serving immediately.
tips: Slice the logs thinner than for classic patra; thin rounds crisp all the way through when fried.
Keep the oil at a steady medium-high — too cool and the slices soak up oil, too hot and the jaggery burns before they crisp.
Fry just before serving; patra crisps lose their crunch within an hour of standing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile the crisp rounds in a bowl as a monsoon snack with hot masala chai, or serve as a crunchy starter with sweet tamarind chutney for dipping.

variations.name: Patra Nu Shaak
variations.description: A homely Gujarati sabzi that turns leftover or fresh patra rounds into a comforting main, simmered in a light tomato-yogurt gravy spiced with dhana-jeera. The steamed rolls soak up the tangy sauce and soften into a warm, spoonable curry unlike the dry snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil forms a clean base for the tempering and gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A teaspoon of jaggery rounds the tomato-yogurt gravy into the classic Gujarati sweet-tangy note

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida for 30 seconds, then add 10 curry leaves.
Add 1 finely chopped onion and sauté for 4-5 minutes until soft and translucent, then pour in the puree of 2 tomatoes and cook for 5-6 minutes until the oil separates at the edges.
Lower the heat and whisk in 0.5 cup yogurt slowly so it does not split, then add 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp dhana-jeera, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp salt.
Pour in 1 cup water, bring to a gentle simmer, and cook the gravy for 4-5 minutes until it thickens slightly and the raw spice smell disappears.
Gently slide in 16 steamed patra rounds, spoon the gravy over them, and simmer on low for 6-7 minutes so they absorb the sauce without breaking apart.
Turn off the heat, garnish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander, and rest for 5 minutes before serving so the flavours meld.
tips: Add the patra rounds only at the end and simmer gently; vigorous boiling makes them disintegrate into the gravy.
Whisk the yogurt smooth and add it off high heat to keep the gravy from curdling.
This is the perfect way to use up patra from the previous day — day-old rounds hold their shape even better in the sauce.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle over steamed rice or serve with soft phulka and a side of plain yogurt for a satisfying Gujarati lunch.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Aluchi Vadi
variations.description: Maharashtra's alu wadi, where the colocasia rolls are spiced with warm goda masala and studded with crushed peanuts instead of the Gujarati tamarind-jaggery balance. Steamed then tempered with sesame and curry leaves, the vadis are earthier and more savoury, a Konkani festive favourite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery balances the goda masala the way Maharashtrian kitchens intend, without turning the vadi sweet

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the traditional Konkani tempering fat and reinforces the crushed-peanut flavour

steps: Trim and flatten the veins of 8 colocasia leaves with a rolling pin so they roll without tearing.

Combine 1.5 cups besan with 1.5 tbsp goda masala, 0.33 cup ground roasted peanuts, 1 tbsp tamarind pulp, 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic-green chilli paste, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp salt, adding water to a thick spreadable paste.
Spread the paste over stacked leaves, roll into firm logs, and steam on medium heat for 20-22 minutes until a knife comes out clean; cool and slice into 1-inch vadis.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a wide pan on medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 2 tbsp sesame seeds for 40 seconds, then add 10 curry leaves until crisp.
Lay the vadis into the tempering and shallow-fry for 3-4 minutes per side until golden and lightly crisped at the edges.
Finish with 3 tbsp fresh grated coconut scattered over the hot vadis before serving.
tips: Goda masala is the defining flavour here — do not swap it for garam masala, which would taste completely different.
Grind the peanuts coarsely so their nutty crunch survives the steaming and frying.
Steam a day ahead and shallow-fry fresh; the vadis firm up overnight and slice more cleanly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a Konkani festive snack with a bowl of coconut chutney, or alongside varan-bhaat for a traditional Maharashtrian thali.

variations.name: Classic Milagu Rasam
variations.description: The definitive peppery rasam of Tamil Nadu, built on a fresh pound of black pepper and cumin loosened with tamarind and a little cooked toor dal water. It is thin, aromatic and warming, the pepper hitting the back of the throat while the tamarind keeps it bright, finished with a ghee tempering that carries the whole dish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The ghee tempering carries the freshly pounded pepper aroma into every spoon

steps: Pressure-cook 3 tbsp toor dal with 1 cup water for 3 whistles until soft, mash, and reserve the thin dal water. Soak 1 lemon-sized ball of tamarind in 1.5 cups warm water and extract the juice.
Coarsely pound 1.5 tsp peppercorns and 1 tsp cumin with 3 garlic cloves in a mortar into a fragrant, gritty mix, not a fine powder.

Pour the tamarind extract into a pot, add 1 chopped tomato, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 0.25 tsp asafoetida, and simmer on medium for 6-7 minutes until the raw tamarind smell goes and the tomato collapses.

Stir in the pounded pepper-cumin-garlic and the reserved dal water, top up to a thin consistency, and bring to a gentle frothing just below a boil - never a rolling boil - for 2-3 minutes until the surface foams.
In a small pan heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 1 dried red chilli, let them splutter, then add 10 curry leaves.
Pour the tempering into the rasam, switch off, and stir in 2 tbsp chopped coriander leaves so the aroma stays fresh.
tips: Never let rasam boil hard; the froth stage just below a boil is where the aroma peaks and the flavour stays bright.
Pound the pepper fresh and coarse rather than using packaged powder, which tastes flat and dusty.
Add the dal water only to loosen; too much dal makes the rasam cloudy and heavy instead of thin and clear.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle over hot rice with a spoon of ghee, or sip it warm from a tumbler to clear a blocked nose on a rainy day.

variations.name: Poondu Milagu Rasam
variations.description: A garlic-lover's pepper rasam where a whole head of crushed garlic is fried into the tempering and simmered into the tamarind base, its sweetness taming the sharp pepper into a mellow, deeply savoury broth. Believed to aid digestion and immunity, this thick-with-garlic rasam is the one South Indian homes make when someone is under the weather.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Frying the garlic in ghee coaxes out its sweetness and mellows the pepper's bite

steps: Soak 1 lemon-sized ball of tamarind in 2 cups warm water and extract a thin juice. Lightly crush 15 garlic cloves so they are broken but chunky.
Coarsely pound 1.5 tsp peppercorns with 1 tsp cumin in a mortar into a gritty mix.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot on medium; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 2 dried red chillies, let them splutter, then add the crushed garlic and fry for 2-3 minutes until it turns golden and sweet-smelling.

Add 12 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida, then pour in the tamarind water with 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp rasam powder and 1 tsp salt, and simmer on medium for 8 minutes until the garlic softens fully.
Stir in the pounded pepper-cumin and simmer on low just to the frothing point below a boil for 2-3 minutes, so the pepper releases its aroma without turning bitter.
Switch off and stir in 2 tbsp chopped coriander leaves before serving.
tips: Fry the garlic slowly to golden; rushed, raw-tasting garlic makes the rasam harsh instead of mellow.
Keep the garlic cloves whole or roughly crushed so diners can bite into their soft sweetness.
This rasam thickens as it stands from the garlic, so loosen with a little hot water when reheating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best over plain rice with a dab of ghee and a fried appalam, or served as a restorative soup when fighting a cold.

variations.name: Jeera Milagu Rasam (No-Tamarind)
variations.description: A clear, medicinal pepper rasam made without tamarind or dal, so it stays thin as a broth and gentle on the stomach. Pepper, cumin, dry ginger and garlic steep in water with a little tomato for colour, making a soothing sip traditionally given for colds, fevers and a heavy meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon of ghee softens the sharp pepper-ginger broth into a soothing sip

steps: Coarsely pound 2 tsp peppercorns, 1.5 tsp cumin and 1 tsp coriander seeds together with 4 garlic cloves into a gritty mix.

Bring 3 cups water to a simmer in a pot with 1 small chopped tomato, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp dry ginger powder, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 0.75 tsp salt, and cook on medium for 6-7 minutes until the tomato softens.
Stir in the pounded pepper-cumin-coriander and simmer on low for 4-5 minutes, letting the broth turn fragrant without boiling hard.
Bring it just to the frothing point below a boil and switch off the heat so the aroma stays sharp and fresh.
In a small pan heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, let them pop, then add 10 curry leaves.
Pour the tempering into the rasam and cover for 2 minutes so the flavours settle before sipping.
tips: Skip the tamarind and dal entirely; this rasam is meant to be clear, thin and easy on the stomach.
The dry ginger is the medicinal heart of this version, so do not leave it out.
Drink it hot in a tumbler rather than over rice to get the full soothing, warming effect.
variations.servingSuggestion: Sip warm from a cup as a comforting soup on a cold or rainy day, or serve as a light broth before a heavy meal.

variations.name: Tomato Pepper Rasam
variations.description: The bright, tangy pepper rasam served in South Indian restaurants, where ripe tomatoes are cooked down into a thicker, redder base and lifted with a generous hit of crushed pepper. It is fuller-bodied and more tomato-forward than the classic, its glossy colour and rounded tang making it an instant crowd-pleaser.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A ghee tempering rounds the tangy tomato base and blooms the pepper aroma

steps: Pressure-cook 2 tbsp toor dal with 0.75 cup water for 3 whistles until soft and mash smooth. Chop 4 ripe tomatoes and mash two of them well by hand.
Coarsely pound 1 tsp peppercorns and 1 tsp cumin with 4 garlic cloves in a mortar.

Simmer the tomatoes in a pot with 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp rasam powder, 1 tsp salt, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 2 cups water on medium for 8 minutes until the tomatoes break down and the mixture turns pulpy and red.
Stir in the mashed dal and the pounded pepper-cumin-garlic, add a little more water for a pourable consistency, and simmer on low to the frothing point below a boil for 3 minutes.
In a small pan heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 1 dried red chilli, let them splutter, then add 12 curry leaves.
Pour the tempering over the rasam, switch off, and stir in 3 tbsp chopped coriander leaves for a fresh, restaurant-style finish.
tips: Use fully ripe, red tomatoes for the sweet-tart balance that defines this version; sour, hard ones taste flat.
Mashing some of the tomato by hand gives the rasam its characteristic thick, glossy body.
Adjust water at the end to taste - keep it pourable, not thick like a dal, for the right restaurant texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a starter soup in small bowls, or ladle generously over rice with a crisp vadam alongside.

variations.name: Classic Ragi Mudde
variations.description: The staple smooth ball of southern Karnataka, made by cooking finger-millet flour into boiling water until it forms a stiff, lump-free dough, then rolling it into a soft, glossy sphere. Eaten without chewing — swallowed in small dipped morsels — it is nourishing farmer's food, high in calcium and built to sustain a long day.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoon of bilona ghee smoothed over the hot mudde keeps it glossy and stops a skin from forming

steps: Bring 3.5 cups water to a rolling boil in a heavy pot with 3/4 tsp salt and 1/2 cup cooked rice, mashing the rice lightly into the water so it helps bind the dough.
Sprinkle in 1/2 cup of the ragi flour and stir it into the boiling water, letting it cook for 2 minutes to form a loose slurry that thickens the base.
Lower the heat, add the remaining 1.5 cups ragi flour in a mound at the centre, poke a few holes through it with a wooden spoon handle, cover, and let it steam undisturbed for 4 minutes.

Uncover and, using a sturdy wooden mudde kolu or spoon, mix vigorously in firm strokes, pressing any lumps against the side of the pot, for about 5 minutes until the mass is smooth, stiff and pulls together.
Cook the smoothed dough on low for another 2 minutes, folding it over on itself, until it stops sticking to the pot and looks glossy and cohesive.
Wet your palms or a bowl, transfer a portion of the hot dough, and roll it into a smooth round ball, then rub the surface with a little Anveshan Ghee to keep it soft; repeat for the rest.
tips: The dough must be cooked stiff and completely lump-free — undercooked mudde tastes raw and sticks to the throat.
Roll the balls while the dough is still very hot, using wet hands, or it hardens and cracks as it cools.
The cooked rice is a traditional binder that makes the mudde smoother and easier to shape; do not skip it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a runny bassaru or a spicy soppina saaru, swallowing small ghee-rubbed morsels dipped in the hot gravy the traditional way.

variations.name: Mixed-Millet Mudde
variations.description: A heartier field-worker's mudde where finger millet is bolstered with pearl millet and sorghum flours for a deeper, toastier flavour and even more sustained energy. The blend gives a slightly denser, nuttier ball beloved in the drier belts of north Karnataka where these coarse millets thrive.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee rubbed over the coarse millet ball keeps its denser surface soft and glossy

steps: Whisk together 1.25 cups ragi flour, 1/2 cup pearl millet flour and 1/2 cup sorghum flour in a bowl and keep aside; the coarser millets need a little more water than plain ragi.
Bring 4 cups water to a rolling boil with 3/4 tsp salt and 1/2 cup mashed cooked rice, then stir in 1/2 cup of the mixed flour and let it cook for 2 minutes into a thick slurry.
Lower the heat, mound the remaining flour blend at the centre, make a few holes through it with a spoon handle, cover, and steam for 5 minutes so the coarse grains soften.
Uncover and mix hard with a wooden mudde stick for 6 minutes, crushing every lump against the pot wall until the dough turns smooth, stiff and homogeneous.
Cook the mass on low for a further 3 minutes, folding it repeatedly, until it leaves the sides of the pot clean and no dry flour remains.
With wet hands, roll the hot dough into smooth firm balls and rub each with a little Anveshan Ghee to keep the denser surface supple.
tips: Coarse bajra and jowar flours need extra cooking and mixing time; rush this and the mudde turns gritty.
Add a touch more boiling water if the mixed dough feels too stiff to mix, since these millets absorb more than ragi alone.
Sieve the millet flours together first to break up any lumps before they hit the water.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a robust avarekalu bassaru or a spicy ennegayi curry, the earthy millets standing up well to a strong gravy.

variations.name: Tempered Ragi Sankati
variations.description: The Rayalaseema cousin of mudde, where finger-millet dough is loosened with rice and finished with a fragrant tempering of mustard, curry leaves and green chilli stirred right in. Softer and lightly seasoned rather than plain, this sankati is scooped up with buttermilk or a fiery chutney across the Andhra-Karnataka border.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil carries the Rayalaseema tempering that flavours this softer sankati

steps: Rinse 3/4 cup rice and boil it with 4.5 cups water and 1 tsp salt on medium heat for about 12 minutes until the grains are very soft and the water is milky, keeping the pot loose and watery.

Meanwhile heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a small pan on medium, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tsp urad dal and 1/2 tsp cumin for 30 seconds until the dal is golden, then add 12 curry leaves and 3 chopped green chillies and fry 30 seconds until fragrant.
Lower the heat under the soft rice, sprinkle in 1.5 cups ragi flour a little at a time while stirring, and let it steam covered for 3 minutes over the rice.
Mix hard with a wooden spoon for 5 minutes, breaking every lump against the side of the pot, until the dough is smooth, soft and slightly looser than a classic stiff mudde.
Pour the hot tempering over the dough and fold it through so the mustard, chilli and curry leaves streak evenly across the sankati.
Cook on low for 2 more minutes, then with wet hands shape the warm dough into soft rounds, leaving them a touch softer than firm mudde since sankati is meant to be tender.
tips: Sankati is deliberately softer than Karnataka mudde, so keep the rice base wetter and do not over-stiffen the dough.
Fold the tempering in at the very end so the curry leaves and chilli stay bright and aromatic.
If the dough tightens too much as it cools, sprinkle in a spoon of hot water and mix again to loosen it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with spiced buttermilk (majjiga) or a fiery gongura-onion chutney, mashing small pieces of the soft sankati into each.

variations.name: Ragi Halbai Sweet Mudde
variations.description: A sweet festive spin from coastal Karnataka where ragi is cooked with jaggery and coconut milk into a soft, halbai-like fudge that sets into a spoonable sweet ball. Cardamom and ghee-fried coconut turn the humble millet into a dark, glistening dessert served at temple feasts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: unrefined jaggery gives this sweet ragi mudde its dark caramel depth and mineral richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee fries the coconut and keeps the sweet millet fudge glossy and non-sticky

steps: Melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 1/4 cup water in a heavy pan on low heat, then strain out grit and return the clear syrup to the pan.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan and fry 10 cashews and 1/4 cup grated coconut until golden, about 1 minute, then set aside.
Add 2 cups thin coconut milk and a pinch of salt to the jaggery syrup and warm it on low; do not let it boil hard or the coconut milk may split.
Whisk 1 cup ragi flour into 1/2 cup of cold water first to make a lump-free paste, then pour this into the warm jaggery-coconut milk while stirring constantly.
Cook on low, stirring without pause, for about 10 minutes until the mixture thickens into a glossy, fudge-like mass that pulls away from the sides of the pan.
Stir in the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 1/2 tsp cardamom powder and the fried coconut and cashews, then let it cool slightly and roll into soft sweet balls or press into a greased plate to set.
tips: Mix the ragi flour into cold liquid first — adding it straight to hot syrup guarantees stubborn lumps.
Keep the coconut milk on a gentle simmer and never a rolling boil so it stays smooth and does not curdle.
For a firmer sweet, cook 2 minutes longer until the mass leaves the pan cleanly, then set and cut into squares.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a festive dessert, dusted with a little extra cardamom, or chilled and sliced like a soft millet barfi.

variations.name: Classic Raj Kachori
variations.description: This Classic Raj Kachori is the king of chaats, a large hollow crisp puri cracked open and heaped with spiced potato, boiled moong, whisked yogurt and a cascade of chutneys. Every spoon delivers crunch, creamy yogurt, sweet-tangy tamarind and a shower of sev and pomegranate, all from one grand edible bowl.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: a little nutty khapli atta in the dough makes a sturdier, more digestible kachori shell

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: deep-frying the hollow kachoris in wood-pressed sunflower oil keeps them crisp and light

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the tamarind chutney flooding the kachori without refined sugar

steps: Mix 1 cup semolina with 0.25 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta and 0.5 tsp salt, add about 6 tbsp water and knead into a stiff, smooth dough, then rest covered for 20 minutes.
Roll the dough into 4 large thick puris and deep-fry them one at a time in medium-hot Anveshan Sunflower Oil for 4 to 5 minutes, spooning oil over so they puff into big hollow crisp shells.
Whisk the 2 cups yogurt smooth with a pinch of salt, and simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 0.75 cup water for 6 minutes into a sweet chutney.
Crack a coin-sized hole in the top of each cooled kachori and fill with diced boiled potato, boiled moong, 1.5 tsp chaat masala and 1 tsp roasted cumin.
Pour in generous whisked yogurt, then drizzle tamarind chutney and green chutney until the kachori overflows.
Top each with a heap of nylon sev, pomegranate and coriander and serve immediately before the shell softens.
tips: Fry the puris on medium heat and baste with oil so they balloon into hollow crisp shells.
Keep the dough stiff, as a soft dough will not puff into the signature hollow ball.
Assemble each kachori just before eating so the crisp shell holds its crunch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve one grand kachori per person on a wide plate, garnished with extra pomegranate and a final drizzle of both chutneys.

variations.name: Ragda Raj Kachori
variations.description: A heartier version where the hollow kachori is filled with hot, soupy white-pea ragda before the yogurt and chutneys go on, turning the chaat into a warming, substantial treat. The soft spiced peas soak into the shell for a comforting contrast of hot filling and cool yogurt.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli atta strengthens the shell so it holds the hot ragda without collapsing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: frying the kachori shells in wood-pressed sunflower oil gives an even, light crisp

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the tamarind chutney that laces the ragda-filled kachori

steps: Knead 1 cup semolina with 0.25 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 tsp salt and about 6 tbsp water into a stiff dough and rest 20 minutes, then roll and deep-fry 4 large hollow puris in medium-hot Anveshan Sunflower Oil for 5 minutes each.
Pressure-cook 1 cup soaked white peas with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 whistles until soft, then lightly mash to a soupy ragda.
Simmer the mashed peas with 1 tbsp goda masala, chopped onion and 0.5 tsp salt for 8 minutes until thick and spiced.
Whisk the 1.5 cups yogurt smooth, and simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 0.75 cup water for 6 minutes into a chutney.
Crack open the top of each kachori and spoon in the hot ragda, then pour over whisked yogurt and drizzle both chutneys.
Dust with 1.5 tsp chaat masala, top with nylon sev and coriander, and serve at once while the ragda is hot.
tips: Keep the ragda thick enough to hold in the shell yet loose enough to spoon easily.
Fill with the hot ragda only at the last moment so the kachori stays crisp.
Balance the hot ragda with well-chilled yogurt for the classic hot-cold contrast.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a filling one-bowl chaat with extra ragda on the side for topping up.

variations.name: Sprouts Raj Kachori
variations.description: A protein-packed, lighter rendition loaded with boiled mixed sprouts, diced cucumber and tomato in place of heavy potato, with a lightly sweetened yogurt. It keeps the drama of the giant crisp shell while making the filling fresh, crunchy and nutritious.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: nutty khapli atta adds fibre and structure to the healthier kachori shell

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil fries the shells crisp for the wholesome sprouts version

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: lightly sweetens the yogurt and tamarind chutney over the fresh sprout filling

steps: Knead 1 cup semolina with 0.25 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 tsp salt and about 6 tbsp water into a stiff dough, rest 20 minutes, then roll and deep-fry 4 large hollow puris in medium-hot Anveshan Groundnut Oil for 5 minutes each.
Steam the 1.5 cups mixed sprouts with a pinch of salt for 6 minutes until just tender but still crunchy, then cool.
Whisk the 2 cups yogurt smooth with 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and a pinch of salt, and simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 0.75 cup water for 6 minutes into a chutney.
Crack open each kachori and fill with the cooked sprouts, diced cucumber and tomato, then sprinkle 1.5 tsp chaat masala and 1 tsp roasted cumin.
Pour in the lightly sweet yogurt and drizzle tamarind and green chutney over the filling.
Top generously with pomegranate and coriander and serve immediately as a fresh, protein-rich chaat.
tips: Cook the sprouts only until just tender so they retain their crunch and nutrients.
Skip the sev to keep this version light, letting the sprouts and veg carry the texture.
Add the cucumber and tomato at the end so they stay crisp and juicy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a wholesome party starter, each kachori piled high with sprouts and pomegranate.

variations.name: Dahi Papdi Raj Kachori
variations.description: An extra-indulgent dahi-heavy avatar where crushed crisp papdi is layered into the kachori along with a double dose of thick sweetened yogurt, so every bite is creamy and rich. Bits of papdi add a second crunch beneath the sev-topped shell for a decadent chaat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli atta gives the shell a sturdy, nutty bite to hold the heavy dahi

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: frying the shells in wood-pressed sunflower oil keeps them crisp under the yogurt

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the thick yogurt and tamarind chutney that define this dahi-rich chaat

steps: Knead 1 cup semolina with 0.25 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 tsp salt and about 6 tbsp water into a stiff dough, rest 20 minutes, then roll and deep-fry 4 large hollow puris in medium-hot Anveshan Sunflower Oil for 5 minutes each.
Whisk the 3 cups yogurt very smooth with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and a pinch of salt until thick and pourable, then chill.
Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 0.5 cup water for 6 minutes into a chutney and cool.
Crack open each kachori and layer in crushed papdi, diced boiled potato, 1.5 tsp chaat masala and 1 tsp roasted cumin.
Flood each shell with the thick sweet yogurt, then drizzle tamarind and green chutney so it marbles the top.
Finish with a heap of nylon sev, pomegranate and a little more crushed papdi, and serve immediately.
tips: Layer the crushed papdi inside just before serving so it keeps a distinct crunch under the dahi.
Use thick, well-set yogurt so the chaat stays creamy rather than watery.
A double drizzle of chutney over the pale yogurt makes for a striking marbled finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a rich, festive chaat with an extra bowl of chilled sweet yogurt for those who want more.

variations.name: Classic Punjabi Samosa
variations.description: This Classic Punjabi Samosa wraps a flaky, blistered maida pastry around a chunky spiced potato-and-pea filling perfumed with cumin, coriander and amchur. Deep-fried low and slow so the crust turns pale, crisp and bubbled, it is the definitive tea-time snack served hot with tangy chutneys.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: using nutty khapli atta for the pastry gives a wholesome, sturdy yet flaky samosa crust

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: deep-frying low and slow in wood-pressed sunflower oil gives the pale, blistered classic crust

steps: Rub 4 tbsp of the sunflower oil and 0.5 tsp carom seeds into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, then knead with about 0.5 cup water into a stiff, smooth dough and rest covered for 30 minutes.
Heat 2 tbsp oil and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, add grated ginger and chopped green chilli, then add the coarsely mashed boiled potatoes and 0.5 cup cooked green peas.
Stir in 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp amchur, 0.5 tsp garam masala and 0.75 tsp salt and cook for 4 minutes, then mix in coriander and cool the filling completely.
Divide the dough, roll each ball into an oval and cut in half, form a cone from each half, fill with the potato mixture and seal the edges with a little water.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Sunflower Oil to low-medium and slide in the samosas, frying gently for 10 to 12 minutes while the oil slowly rises in heat until pale golden and blistered.
Drain on a rack and serve the crisp samosas hot with tamarind and green chutney.
tips: Fry on low heat first so the crust turns blistered and crisp rather than smooth and soft.
Keep the dough stiff and rest it well, as a soft dough gives limp, oily samosas.
Cool the filling fully before shaping so the sealed cones do not tear or open while frying.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot with mint-coriander chutney, sweet tamarind chutney and a cup of masala chai.

variations.name: Onion Samosa
variations.description: The slim, crackly Hyderabadi onion samosa folds a raw spiced onion filling into a thin patti wrapper, frying up shatteringly crisp and small enough to eat in a few bites. Sharp with onion, chilli and curry leaf, it is the iconic Irani-cafe and roadside snack of the Deccan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the thin onion samosas fry shatteringly crisp in wood-pressed groundnut oil

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: a flour-and-water paste from khapli atta seals the patti edges cleanly

steps: Thinly slice 3 onions, mix with 0.75 tsp salt and rest 10 minutes, then squeeze out the released water so the filling stays dry.
Toss the squeezed onion with chopped green chilli, torn curry leaves, 1 tsp chaat masala, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder and coriander.
Make a thick sealing paste by whisking 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta with 3 tbsp water until smooth and lump-free.
Fold each samosa patti into a cone, spoon in the onion filling, then fold into a tight triangle and seal the flap with the flour paste.
Heat the Anveshan Groundnut Oil to medium and fry the samosas in batches for 4 to 5 minutes, turning, until deep golden and crackling crisp.
Drain well and serve the hot onion samosas at once with green chutney.
tips: Squeeze the salted onions well, as excess moisture makes the thin samosas soggy and hard to seal.
Fry on steady medium heat so the thin patti crisps evenly without browning too fast.
Seal every edge firmly with the flour paste so the loose filling does not spill into the oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot and crisp with green chutney and cutting chai, Irani-cafe style.

variations.name: Baked Samosa
variations.description: A lighter oven-baked samosa that skips deep-frying yet still delivers a crisp, golden crust brushed with ghee. The same spiced potato-pea filling stays true to the original, making this a guilt-free way to enjoy the classic snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli atta bakes into a firm, wholesome crust that crisps without frying

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: brushing bilona ghee over the pastry helps the baked samosas turn golden and crisp

steps: Rub 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, then knead with about 0.5 cup water into a stiff dough and rest covered for 30 minutes.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, add grated ginger and green chilli, then the mashed potatoes and peas.
Stir in 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp amchur, 0.5 tsp garam masala and 0.75 tsp salt, cook 4 minutes, fold in coriander and cool fully.
Shape the dough into cones, fill with the potato mixture, seal the edges with water and place on a lined tray.
Brush the samosas all over with the remaining melted Anveshan Ghee and bake in an oven preheated to 200 C for 25 to 30 minutes, turning once, until golden and crisp.
Cool for 5 minutes so the crust firms up, then serve warm with chutneys.
tips: Brush ghee generously so the baked crust browns and crisps like a fried one.
Roll the pastry a touch thinner than for frying so it bakes through evenly.
Turn the samosas halfway through baking for an all-round golden colour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a lighter snack with mint chutney and a squeeze of lemon.

variations.name: Paneer Corn Samosa
variations.description: A rich party-style samosa stuffed with crumbled paneer, sweet corn and capsicum in a creamy, mildly spiced filling instead of potato. The soft cheesy centre against the flaky crust makes it a crowd-pleasing cocktail snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli atta makes a sturdy flaky shell for the rich paneer-corn filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: deep-frying in wood-pressed sunflower oil crisps the shell around the creamy filling

steps: Rub 4 tbsp of the sunflower oil into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, knead with about 0.5 cup water into a stiff dough and rest 30 minutes.
Heat 2 tbsp oil, crackle 0.75 tsp cumin seeds, add grated ginger, green chilli and chopped onion and saute 3 minutes.
Add the boiled sweet corn and chopped capsicum, cook 3 minutes, then fold in crumbled paneer, 0.5 tsp garam masala, 0.5 tsp black pepper and 0.5 tsp salt and cook 2 minutes before cooling.
Shape the dough into cones, fill with the paneer-corn mixture, seal the edges with water and press firmly.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Sunflower Oil to medium and fry the samosas for 6 to 7 minutes, turning, until golden and crisp.
Drain on a rack and serve the hot paneer corn samosas with green chutney or ketchup.
tips: Do not overfill, as the soft paneer filling can burst a thin cone while frying.
Cook the filling until fairly dry so the paneer holds together inside the crust.
Fry on steady medium heat so the rich filling heats through as the shell crisps.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a party starter with mint mayo dip and a scatter of chaat masala on top.

variations.name: Classic Batata Nu Shaak
variations.description: The everyday Gujarati potato curry: cubed potatoes simmered in a light onion-tomato masala lifted with the gentle sweetness of jaggery and warmth of dhana-jeera. Semi-dry and comforting, it is the dish that turns up in countless Gujarati lunchboxes and thalis.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Clean wood-pressed groundnut oil keeps this everyday shaak light while coating the potatoes evenly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A spoon of jaggery gives the shaak its signature gentle Gujarati sweetness against the spices

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 finely chopped onion and 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and sauté for 4 minutes until the onion turns soft and pale gold.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp dhana-jeera and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 4-5 minutes until the tomatoes soften and the oil begins to separate.
Add 4 cubed potatoes and toss to coat in the masala, then pour in 1.25 cups water, cover, and simmer on medium-low for 12-14 minutes until the potatoes are fork-tender.
Stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, lightly mash a few potato cubes to thicken the gravy, and cook uncovered for 2-3 minutes until it clings to the potatoes.
Garnish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander and serve warm.
tips: Cut the potatoes into even cubes so they cook through at the same rate.
Mashing a few pieces gives the semi-dry shaak its clingy, homely texture without any flour.
A squeeze of lemon at the end brightens the sweet-savoury balance if the tomatoes were mild.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulka or puri and a spoon of mango pickle for a classic Gujarati lunch.

variations.name: Rasawala Batata Nu Shaak
variations.description: The soupy, no-onion version made for puris: soft potato chunks float in a thin, golden gram-flour-thickened gravy fragrant with ginger and asafoetida. Light and slurpable, this is the classic wedding-breakfast pairing served in a katori beside hot puffed puris.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil tempers the spices for a clean, light rasa gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery rounds the thin gravy into the sweet-tangy rasa that puris are meant to soak up

steps: Whisk 2 tbsp besan into 2 cups water with 0.5 tsp turmeric until smooth and lump-free, and keep this thickening slurry ready.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pot on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 0.5 tsp asafoetida with 10 curry leaves for 30 seconds.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and fry for 30 seconds, then pour in the besan slurry, stirring constantly so it does not form lumps as it heats.
Add 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp dhana-jeera and 1 tsp salt, bring to a gentle boil, and simmer for 6-7 minutes until the raw besan smell disappears and the gravy thickens slightly.
Add 4 boiled and cubed potatoes and 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, then simmer for 6-7 minutes so the potatoes soak up the thin rasa; add more water if it thickens too much.
Finish with 1 tbsp lemon juice and 3 tbsp chopped coriander, keeping the gravy pourable and light.
tips: Keep the gravy thin and pourable; it should be sippable from a katori, not thick like a sabzi.
Add the besan slurry to hot oil while stirring nonstop to guarantee a lump-free rasa.
Boil the potatoes just before adding so they stay soft and drink up the gravy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot in a small bowl beside a stack of fluffy puris, the classic Gujarati festive breakfast pairing.

variations.name: Sukha Sekela Batata
variations.description: A dry, roasted potato preparation where boiled cubes are tossed with a toasty sesame-coconut-peanut masala until the edges crisp and every piece is coated in nutty, spicy crumbs. No gravy at all, just deeply flavoured potatoes that make an addictive dry side.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Toasty gingelly oil doubles down on the sesame masala and helps the potatoes crisp at the edges

steps: Dry-roast 2 tbsp sesame seeds and 3 tbsp grated dry coconut in a pan on low heat for 2-3 minutes until golden and fragrant, then coarsely crush together with 3 tbsp roasted peanuts.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a wide pan on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds with 10 curry leaves for 30 seconds.
Add 4 boiled and cubed potatoes and spread them out, letting them sear undisturbed for 3-4 minutes so the base crisps before you toss.
Sprinkle in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp dhana-jeera and 1 tsp salt, and toss for 2 minutes so the spices coat every cube.
Add the crushed sesame-coconut-peanut mixture and toss for another 3-4 minutes until the potatoes are dry, crusty and evenly coated.
Finish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander and serve immediately while the edges are still crisp.
tips: Let the potatoes sit undisturbed in the pan between tosses so they develop a proper crust.
Use slightly firm boiled potatoes; overcooked ones break apart when tossed.
The dry masala can be made in bulk and stored to speed up this dish on busy days.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a dry side with dal-rice and rotli, or stuff into a hot roti roll with a smear of green chutney.

variations.name: Green Masala Batata Nu Shaak
variations.description: A fresh, herb-forward take where potatoes simmer in a vibrant paste of coriander, mint, coconut and green chilli, giving a bright green curry that tastes of the garden. Cooler and fresher than the tomato version, it is a favourite when winter herbs are at their best.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil carries the fresh green paste without dulling its bright colour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A touch of jaggery softens the green chilli heat and rounds the herb paste

steps: Grind 1 cup coriander, 0.25 cup mint, 0.33 cup grated coconut, 3 green chillies and 1 inch ginger with a splash of water into a smooth bright green paste.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida for 30 seconds, then add 1 chopped onion and fry for 3-4 minutes until soft.
Add the green paste and saute for 3-4 minutes on medium-low, stirring often, until the raw herb smell mellows and the oil beads at the edges; keep the heat moderate so the paste stays green.
Add 4 cubed potatoes with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, toss to coat, then pour in 1.25 cups water and simmer covered for 12-14 minutes until the potatoes are tender.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and simmer uncovered for 2-3 minutes until the gravy thickens and clings to the potatoes.
Finish with 1 tbsp lemon juice off the heat to keep the paste vivid and fresh-tasting.
tips: Cook the green paste on moderate heat only; high heat dulls its bright colour to a drab olive.
Add the lemon at the very end, as cooking acid too long flattens the fresh herb flavour.
Blanch the coriander and mint for 10 seconds before grinding to lock in an even greener paste.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve this fragrant green curry with jeera rice or soft rotli and a side of plain yogurt to cool the chilli heat.

variations.name: Classic Moong Dal Kachori
variations.description: This Classic Moong Dal Kachori seals a dry, fragrant filling of roasted yellow moong dal, fennel and warm spices inside a flaky khasta crust fried low until it blisters. A North Indian tea-time and travel staple, it stays crisp for days and bursts with spiced, nutty flavour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli atta gives the khasta shell a nutty depth while keeping it flaky

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: slow-frying in wood-pressed groundnut oil produces the pale, bubbled khasta crust

steps: Soak 0.75 cup moong dal for 2 hours, then drain and coarsely grind it without water into a rough paste.
Rub 4 tbsp of the groundnut oil into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt until crumbly, then knead with about 0.5 cup water into a soft dough and rest 30 minutes.
Heat 3 tbsp oil, crackle 0.25 tsp asafoetida, 1.5 tsp fennel, 1 tsp cumin and 1 tsp crushed coriander seeds, add grated ginger, then the ground dal.
Roast the dal over medium-low heat for 8 minutes with 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp amchur, 0.5 tsp garam masala and 0.75 tsp salt until dry, crumbly and fragrant, then cool.
Fill thick dough discs with the dal mixture, seal and flatten gently into kachoris.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil to low and fry the kachoris slowly for 12 to 15 minutes until puffed, blistered and pale golden, then drain and serve.
tips: Roast the dal filling until completely dry so the kachoris stay crisp and keep for days.
Fry on very low heat so the crust turns flaky and khasta rather than hard.
Grind the soaked dal coarse, not smooth, for the right crumbly filling texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sweet tamarind chutney and spicy green chutney, or alongside aloo sabzi for breakfast.

variations.name: Banarasi Urad Dal Kachori
variations.description: The Banaras-style kachori uses a black urad dal filling ground with ginger and green chilli, giving a moister, more robust centre than moong. Fried until deep golden and served with hing-spiked aloo curry, it is the soul of a Kashi morning.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli atta gives a robust flaky crust to match the hearty urad filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: pungent wood-pressed mustard oil lends the authentic Banarasi aroma

steps: Soak 0.75 cup urad dal for 3 hours, drain well, then grind coarsely with ginger and green chilli using no water.
Rub 4 tbsp of the mustard oil, heated and cooled, into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, then knead with about 0.5 cup water into a soft dough and rest 30 minutes.
Heat 3 tbsp mustard oil, crackle 0.5 tsp asafoetida, 1.5 tsp fennel and 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add the ground urad paste.
Roast the urad over medium heat for 10 minutes with 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp garam masala and 0.75 tsp salt until dry and aromatic, then cool.
Fill and seal thick dough discs with the urad mixture and flatten into kachoris.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Mustard Oil to low-medium and fry the kachoris for 12 to 15 minutes until deep golden and crisp, then serve.
tips: Roast the urad filling longer than moong, as it holds more moisture and must dry fully.
The generous asafoetida is key to the classic Banarasi aroma and easier digestion.
Heat and cool the mustard oil before adding to the dough to soften its pungency.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve Banaras style with a runny hing-tempered aloo curry and a wedge of lemon.

variations.name: Baked Dal Kachori
variations.description: A lighter baked kachori that skips deep-frying while keeping a flaky, ghee-glazed khasta shell and the classic dry moong filling. It is a make-ahead, less-oily option for those who want the crunch without the fry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli atta bakes into a firm, flaky shell without frying

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee shortens the dough and glazes the baked kachoris golden and crisp

steps: Soak 0.75 cup moong dal for 2 hours, drain and grind coarsely without water.
Rub 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt until crumbly, then knead with about 0.5 cup water into a soft dough and rest 30 minutes.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 0.25 tsp asafoetida, 1.5 tsp fennel and 1 tsp cumin, add grated ginger and the ground dal, and roast 8 minutes with 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp amchur, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp garam masala and 0.75 tsp salt until dry, then cool.
Fill and seal thick dough discs with the dal mixture, flatten into kachoris and place on a lined tray.
Brush the tops with the remaining melted Anveshan Ghee and bake in an oven preheated to 190 C for 28 to 32 minutes, turning once, until golden and flaky.
Rest 5 minutes so the crust firms up, then serve warm with chutney.
tips: Prick each kachori once so steam escapes and the shell bakes crisp, not puffy and hollow.
Brush ghee generously for a golden colour that mimics the fried version.
These keep well in an airtight box and re-crisp in a hot oven for a few minutes.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a lighter snack with tamarind chutney and a hot cup of chai.

variations.name: Chana Dal Khasta Kachori Chaat
variations.description: A chaat-ready version filled with a spiced roasted chana dal mixture, then broken open and loaded with yogurt, chutneys and sev in the style of Lucknow's matar kachori chaat. The nutty chana dal filling holds up beautifully under the tangy toppings.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli atta gives a sturdy khasta shell that holds up under chaat toppings

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: frying in wood-pressed sunflower oil keeps the chaat kachoris light and crisp

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the tamarind chutney poured over the kachori chaat

steps: Soak 0.75 cup chana dal for 3 hours, boil until just tender but not mushy, drain well and coarsely mash.
Rub 4 tbsp of the sunflower oil into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, knead with about 0.5 cup water into a soft dough and rest 30 minutes.
Heat 3 tbsp oil, crackle 1.5 tsp fennel and 1 tsp cumin seeds, add the mashed chana dal and roast 8 minutes with 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp amchur and 0.75 tsp salt until dry, then cool.
Fill and seal thick dough discs with the chana dal mixture, flatten into kachoris, and fry in low-medium Anveshan Sunflower Oil for 12 to 14 minutes until crisp and golden.
Whisk the 1.5 cups yogurt smooth, and simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 0.75 cup water for 6 minutes into a chutney.
Crack open each kachori, spoon over yogurt, tamarind and green chutney, dust with 1 tsp chaat masala and finish with nylon sev before serving at once.
tips: Boil the chana dal only until just tender so the filling stays dry and roasts well.
Assemble the chaat just before eating so the kachori shell keeps its crunch.
Fry the kachoris a little sturdier here so they hold up under the wet toppings.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a loaded kachori chaat topped with pomegranate and extra sev, Lucknow style.

variations.name: Classic Green Peas Masala
variations.description: A simple, satisfying curry of sweet green peas simmered in a spiced onion-tomato masala. The natural sweetness of the peas plays against a tangy, mildly hot gravy that comes together in half an hour. It is a quick weeknight favourite that pairs with roti, poori or plain rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee blooms the cumin and gives the everyday masala a rich, homely aroma

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 15 seconds until fragrant.
Add 2 finely chopped onions and 2 slit green chillies and fry until golden, about 6 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute.
Add 2 pureed tomatoes and cook until the ghee separates at the edges, around 5 minutes.
Lower the heat and add 1.5 tbsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1/2 tsp turmeric, roasting for 30 seconds with a splash of water so they do not scorch.
Add 2 cups green peas with 1 cup water and 1 tsp salt, cover and simmer for 10 to 12 minutes until the peas are tender and the gravy thickens.
Stir in 1 tsp garam masala and 3 tbsp chopped coriander, simmer 2 minutes, and serve warm.
tips: If using frozen peas, add them a little later as they cook faster than fresh ones.
Mash a spoonful of cooked peas into the gravy to thicken it without cream.
A pinch of sugar or a few extra sweet peas balances the tang of the tomatoes.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with phulka, poori or jeera rice, with a wedge of lemon on the side.

variations.name: Restaurant-Style Matar Makhani
variations.description: A rich, creamy restaurant take where green peas nestle in a smooth cashew-tomato makhani gravy. Buttery, mildly sweet and finished with cream and kasuri methi, it turns humble peas into an indulgent main. This is the version that looks and tastes like it came from a hotel buffet.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee builds the makhani base and gives the creamy gravy its glossy restaurant richness

steps: Boil 4 chopped tomatoes, 1 chopped onion and 15 cashews with 1 cup water for 10 minutes until soft, then cool and blend to a very smooth puree and strain for a silky gravy.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium heat, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 1 minute until the raw smell goes.
Pour in the strained puree, add 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tbsp coriander powder and 1/2 tsp sugar, and cook on medium-low for 8 minutes until the ghee floats and the gravy darkens.
Add 2 cups green peas with 1/2 cup water and 1 tsp salt, cover and simmer for 8 to 10 minutes until the peas are tender and the gravy is thick.
Lower the heat and stir in 4 tbsp cream, 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi and 3/4 tsp garam masala, warming through for 2 minutes without boiling.
Swirl in an extra spoon of cream on top and serve hot.
tips: Straining the tomato-cashew puree is the secret to a truly velvety makhani gravy.
A little sugar balances the tomato acidity and gives the makhani its rounded, mild taste.
Add the cream on low heat only, so the gravy stays smooth and does not split.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or laccha paratha, finished with a swirl of cream and crushed kasuri methi.

variations.name: Kerala Green Peas Curry
variations.description: A fragrant Kerala-style curry where green peas simmer in a coconut-milk gravy scented with fennel, curry leaves and whole spices. Mild, creamy and pale gold, it is a popular vegetarian side for appam and Malabar parotta. Coconut oil tempering gives it an unmistakable South Indian character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil gives the curry its authentic Kerala aroma and finishes the tempering

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan on medium heat, add 1/2 tsp fennel seeds, 1 inch cinnamon and 3 cloves and let them sizzle for 20 seconds.
Add 15 curry leaves, 1 sliced onion, 1 inch minced ginger and 2 slit green chillies, and saute until the onion is soft and golden, about 6 minutes.
Add 1 chopped tomato and cook until pulpy, then stir in 1.5 tbsp coriander powder and 1/2 tsp turmeric on low heat for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 2 cups green peas with 1 cup water and 1 tsp salt, cover and simmer for 10 minutes until the peas are tender.
Lower the heat to a bare simmer and pour in 1 cup thick coconut milk, warming through for 3 to 4 minutes without letting it boil so it does not split.
Switch off and rest covered for 5 minutes so the coconut milk settles into a smooth, mild curry.
tips: Add the coconut milk only on the lowest heat and never boil it, or the gravy will curdle.
Fennel and whole spices give this curry its Kerala fragrance, so bloom them well at the start.
For a thicker curry, mash a few peas before adding the coconut milk.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with appam, Malabar parotta or ghee rice, letting the creamy gravy soak into every bite.

variations.name: Hara Masala Green Peas
variations.description: A vibrant green curry where peas are simmered in a fresh coriander-mint-and-green-chilli paste instead of the usual red masala. Herby, bright and lightly tangy, it is a refreshing change that tastes of the garden. A yogurt finish keeps the gravy mellow and the colour a beautiful emerald.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee mellows the sharp green paste and gives the herby curry a rounded richness

steps: Blend 1 cup coriander, 1/2 cup mint, 3 green chillies and 10 cashews with a little water to a smooth green paste and set aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add 1 finely chopped onion and fry until soft and pale golden, about 5 minutes.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then pour in the green paste and 1 tbsp coriander powder and cook for 4 minutes until the raw smell disappears.
Add 2 cups green peas with 3/4 cup water and 1 tsp salt, cover and simmer for 10 minutes until the peas are tender.
Lower the heat and stir in 1/4 cup whisked yogurt slowly so it does not split, warming through for 2 minutes.
Finish with 1/2 tsp garam masala, simmer 1 minute, and serve the emerald curry warm.
tips: Blanch the coriander and mint briefly before blending to lock in a brighter green colour.
Whisk the yogurt smooth and add it off high heat so the gravy stays creamy, not curdled.
Do not overcook after adding the herbs, or the fresh green flavour and colour will fade.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tandoori roti or saffron pulao, garnished with a swirl of yogurt and mint leaves.

variations.name: Classic Khaman Dhokla
variations.description: This Classic Khaman Dhokla is the soft, spongy Gujarati steamed cake of gram flour, leavened with Eno so it rises fluffy and honeycombed. A tangy-sweet tempering of mustard, curry leaves and green chilli soaks in, and a shower of coconut and coriander finishes this beloved teatime snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: the mustard and curry-leaf tempering is bloomed in nutty wood-pressed sesame oil

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: dissolved in the tempering water, it gives the khaman its signature sweet-tangy soak

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups besan with 2 tbsp semolina, 0.25 cup yogurt, grated ginger, 1 crushed green chilli, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp salt and about 0.75 cup water into a smooth, thick pourable batter and rest 10 minutes.
Grease a tray and bring water to a boil in a steamer, then stir 1 tsp Eno into the batter with a splash of water until it froths and doubles.
Immediately pour the aerated batter into the tray and steam over medium heat for 15 minutes until a skewer comes out clean and the khaman is spongy.
Cool the khaman for 5 minutes until it firms up, then cut it into neat 2-inch squares in the tray.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds, curry leaves and slit green chillies, then carefully add 0.5 cup water with 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.25 tsp salt and simmer 2 minutes.
Pour the sweet tempering evenly over the khaman so it soaks in, garnish with grated coconut and coriander, and serve soft and moist.
tips: Add the Eno only at the last second and steam immediately, or the trapped air escapes and the khaman turns dense.
Keep the batter thick but pourable, as a thin batter gives a flat, rubbery cake.
Pour the warm sweet tempering over slightly cooled khaman so it drinks it up without going soggy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve soft squares with green chutney and a hot cup of masala chai, garnished with extra coconut.

variations.name: Nylon Khaman
variations.description: The ultra-soft, jiggly Surti nylon khaman is prized for its melt-in-the-mouth sponge and bright yellow crumb, made with a citric-acid lift and a touch more oil in the batter. It is the softest khaman of all, dripping with a generous sweet tempering.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: extra wood-pressed sesame oil in the batter and tempering gives nylon khaman its silky softness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a heavier sweet soak is what makes Surti nylon khaman so moist

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups besan with 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, 0.5 tsp citric acid dissolved in water, grated ginger, 1 crushed green chilli, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp salt and about 0.9 cup water into a smooth, slightly thin batter and rest 10 minutes.
Grease a tray and get the steamer boiling, then whisk 1.25 tsp Eno with a splash of water into the batter until it froths high.
Pour the frothy batter into the tray at once and steam over medium-high heat for 15 minutes until very spongy and a skewer comes clean.
Cool the very soft khaman for a few minutes until set, then cut it gently into squares.

Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp crushed black pepper, curry leaves and slit green chillies, then add 0.6 cup water with 4 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.25 tsp salt and simmer 2 minutes.
Drench the khaman with the generous sweet tempering, garnish with coconut, toasted sesame seeds and coriander, and serve extra soft and moist.
tips: The citric acid plus a little extra oil is the trick to the signature jiggly nylon texture.
Use a slightly thinner batter than classic khaman for the softest, spongiest crumb.
Be generous with the sweet water tempering, as nylon khaman is meant to be very moist.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the soft squares dripping with tempering, topped with plenty of coconut, alongside fried green chillies.

variations.name: Sandwich Khaman
variations.description: A layered party khaman where two sheets of soft steamed cake sandwich a spread of green chutney and a sprinkle of sev, then get cut into neat squares. The chutney middle adds a fresh, spicy contrast to the sweet sponge for an eye-catching snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: the tempering that moistens both khaman layers is bloomed in wood-pressed sesame oil

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: gives the sweet-tangy soak that balances the spicy chutney filling

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups besan with 2 tbsp semolina, 0.25 cup yogurt, 1 crushed green chilli, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp salt and about 0.75 cup water into a smooth thick batter and rest 10 minutes.
Add 1 tsp Eno with a splash of water, whisk until frothy, then steam in two greased trays over medium heat for 15 minutes each until spongy.
Cool the two khaman sheets, then spread 6 tbsp green chutney evenly over one sheet and scatter half the sev on top.
Invert the second sheet over the first to sandwich them, pressing very gently, and cut into neat squares.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds, curry leaves and slit green chillies, add 0.5 cup water with 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.25 tsp salt and simmer 2 minutes.
Spoon the sweet tempering over the sandwiched squares, garnish with the rest of the sev and coriander, and serve.
tips: Steam the two sheets a little thinner than usual so the finished sandwich is not too tall.
Cool the sheets fully before layering so they do not tear when stacked.
Spread the chutney right to the edges so every square has a chutney middle.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the two-tone squares on a platter as an attractive party snack, each topped with a dot of extra chutney.

variations.name: Masala Sev Khaman
variations.description: The Vadodara-style masala khaman crumbles the soft cake and tosses it with a spiced sugar-water soak, then piles on pomegranate, crunchy sev, green chilli and raw onion. Eaten with a spoon, it is a sweet-savoury-crunchy heap rather than neat squares, sold hot at Gujarati morning stalls.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: the aromatic mustard tempering is bloomed in wood-pressed sesame oil for the masala khaman

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the sweet soak that coats the crumbled khaman relies on natural jaggery sweetness

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups besan with 2 tbsp semolina, grated ginger, 1 crushed green chilli, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp salt and about 0.75 cup water into a thick smooth batter and rest 10 minutes.
Add 1 tsp Eno with a splash of water, whisk until frothy, and steam in a greased tray over medium heat for 15 minutes until spongy, then cool and crumble coarsely by hand.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds, curry leaves and 3 slit green chillies, then add 0.75 cup water with 4 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.25 tsp salt and simmer 2 minutes.
Pour the warm sweet tempering over the crumbled khaman and toss gently so every crumb is moist and glossy.
Fold in chopped raw onion and half the pomegranate.
Pile the masala khaman into bowls, shower generously with nylon sev, the rest of the pomegranate and coriander, and serve warm with a spoon.
tips: Crumble the khaman while slightly warm so it drinks up the sweet tempering evenly.
Add the sev only at serving so it stays crunchy against the moist crumble.
Balance the sweet soak with plenty of green chilli and onion for the true Vadodara flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm in bowls topped with a mountain of sev and pomegranate, eaten with a spoon like a chaat.

variations.name: Classic Lemon Rasam
variations.description: A tamarind-free rasam that draws its tang from fresh lemon squeezed in at the very end, so the sourness stays bright and floral rather than dark and deep. Cooked toor dal gives it a light body while green chilli and ginger add a clean heat, making this a refreshing, sunny-tasting rasam quite unlike the usual tamarind kind.
