ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A ghee tempering warms the fresh, citrusy rasam without dulling the lemon

steps: Pressure-cook 0.33 cup toor dal with 1.5 cups water for 3 whistles until very soft, then mash and thin with another cup of water.
Coarsely pound 1 tsp cumin and 0.5 tsp peppercorns in a mortar and keep aside.

Bring the thinned dal to a simmer in a pot with 1 small chopped tomato, 2 slit green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 0.25 tsp asafoetida on medium for 6-7 minutes until the tomato softens.
Add the pounded cumin-pepper and simmer on low just to the frothing point below a boil for 2 minutes, then switch off the heat completely.
Only once the rasam has stopped boiling, stir in 3 tbsp lemon juice so the citrus stays fresh and does not turn bitter.
In a small pan heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, let them pop, add 10 curry leaves, then pour over the rasam and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Add the lemon juice only after switching off the flame; boiling lemon turns the rasam bitter.
Keep the dal thin so the lemon flavour shines rather than being weighed down by a heavy base.
Taste and adjust lemon at the end since acidity varies fruit to fruit.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot rice with a spoon of ghee and a fried papad, or sip as a light, digestive after a rich meal.

variations.name: Lemon Coriander Rasam
variations.description: This aromatic version grinds a fistful of fresh coriander with cumin and green chilli into a green paste that stirs through the lemony broth, layering a herby, garden-fresh fragrance over the citrus. The result is a vivid, pale-green rasam that tastes lively and cooling, wonderful in warm weather.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The ghee tempering blooms the coriander paste and softens the lemon tang

steps: Pressure-cook 0.25 cup moong dal with 1 cup water for 3 whistles until soft, mash, and thin with 1.5 cups water.
Grind 1 cup fresh coriander with stems together with 1 tsp cumin, 3 green chillies and 1 inch ginger into a smooth green paste with a splash of water.
Bring the thinned dal to a simmer in a pot with 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 0.25 tsp asafoetida on medium for 4 minutes.
Stir in the coriander paste and simmer on low for 3-4 minutes just to the frothing point below a boil, keeping the vivid green colour, then switch off.
Once off the heat, stir in 3 tbsp lemon juice so the citrus stays bright against the herby base.
In a small pan heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 10 curry leaves, let them crackle, and pour the tempering over the rasam.
tips: Do not overcook after adding the coriander paste, or the fresh green colour turns dull and khaki.
Use the coriander stems too - they carry as much aroma as the leaves and grind smoothly.
Both lemon and coriander fade with reheating, so make this rasam close to serving time.
variations.servingSuggestion: Lovely as a warm sipping soup in a cup, or over rice with a simple potato roast on the side.

variations.name: Ginger Mint Lemon Rasam
variations.description: A soothing, spa-like rasam where plenty of fresh ginger and a handful of mint join the lemon, creating a warming yet cooling broth that settles a heavy stomach. There is no dal at all, so it stays crystal thin and clear, the ginger heat and mint coolness playing off the citrus in every sip.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A little ghee gives body to the dal-free broth and mellows the ginger heat

steps: Coarsely pound 1 tsp cumin and 0.5 tsp peppercorns in a mortar and lightly crush 0.5 cup mint leaves to release their oils.

Bring 3.5 cups water to a simmer in a pot with 2 inch grated ginger, 2 slit green chillies, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 0.75 tsp salt, and cook on medium for 5 minutes until the ginger flavour infuses.
Add the pounded cumin-pepper and the crushed mint and simmer on low for 3 minutes to the frothing point below a boil, then switch off.
Once the pot is off the heat, stir in 3 tbsp lemon juice so the citrus and mint stay fresh and lively.
In a small pan heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, let them pop, then add 10 curry leaves.
Pour the tempering over the rasam and cover for 2 minutes so the mint and ginger aromas settle before serving.
tips: Add the mint late and off strong heat so it stays fragrant rather than turning dark and stewed.
This dal-free rasam is meant to be thin and clear - resist thickening it, as its lightness is the point.
Extra ginger makes it more warming; dial it up when serving as a cold-weather comfort drink.
variations.servingSuggestion: Sip warm as a digestive after a festive meal, or serve in small cups as a fragrant soup before dinner.

variations.name: Paruppu Lemon Rasam with Jaggery
variations.description: A rounded, homely lemon rasam thickened with plenty of soft toor dal and balanced by a small spoon of jaggery, so the citrus tang is met with a gentle sweetness and a fuller body. This is the comforting, meal-anchoring version, less of a thin soup and more of a satisfying dal-rasam to mix generously into rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee ties the dal, lemon and jaggery into one rounded, comforting rasam

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A whisper of unrefined jaggery balances the sharp lemon without making the rasam sweet

steps: Pressure-cook 0.5 cup toor dal with 1.5 cups water for 4 whistles until very soft, mash well, and thin with 1 cup water for a fuller-bodied rasam.
Bring the dal to a simmer in a pot with 2 slit green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 0.25 tsp asafoetida on medium for 5 minutes.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp coarsely pounded cumin, and simmer on low for 3 minutes to the frothing point below a boil, then switch off.
Once off the heat, stir in 2.5 tbsp lemon juice so the tang stays bright against the sweet dal base.
In a small pan heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 1 dried red chilli, let them splutter, then add 10 curry leaves.
Pour the tempering over the rasam and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander leaves.
tips: The jaggery should only round the sourness, not sweeten the rasam - a single teaspoon is plenty.
Keep this version a touch thicker than a sipping rasam so it clings to rice properly.
Add lemon after the heat is off and taste, since the jaggery and dal both blunt the perceived sourness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Made to be mixed into a mound of hot rice with ghee and a crisp vegetable poriyal on the side.

variations.name: Classic Misal Pav
variations.description: The soul-warming Maharashtrian breakfast of sprouted moth beans (matki) in a spiced gravy, crowned with a fiery, oily red kat, crunchy farsan, raw onion and lemon. Every spoon is a play of textures — soft usal, crisp mixture and pillowy pav dunked to soak up the tarri.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil is the authentic Maharashtrian fat and floats atop the fiery red kat as it should

steps: Pressure cook 2 cups sprouted matki with 2 cups water, 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1/2 tsp salt for 2 whistles until just soft but still holding shape, then set aside without draining.
For the kat masala, dry-roast 1/2 cup grated dry coconut and 1 sliced onion on medium until deep brown and fragrant, cool, and grind with a splash of water into a smooth dark paste.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pot on medium, saute 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 1 chopped onion for 4 minutes, add 2 chopped tomatoes and cook 5 minutes until pulpy, then stir in the ground coconut-onion paste.

Add 1.5 tbsp goda masala, 1 tbsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, cook 3 minutes until the oil separates, then add the cooked matki with 3 cups water and simmer for 12 minutes into a thin, flavourful usal.

For the fiery tarri, heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil until hot, take it off the heat, stir in the remaining 1 tbsp Kashmiri chilli powder to bloom, and ladle this red oil over the top of the usal.
Ladle the hot usal into bowls, top each with a fistful of farsan, chopped raw onion, coriander and a squeeze of lemon, and serve with soft pav for dunking into the tarri.
tips: Add the farsan only at the moment of serving, since it turns soggy within minutes of hitting the hot gravy.
The floating red tarri is what defines misal; bloom the chilli in off-the-heat hot oil so it colours without burning bitter.
Keep the usal thin and brothy — misal should be a soupy curry you can dunk pav into, not a thick sabzi.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with extra tarri on the side for the brave, more farsan, raw onion, lemon wedges and buttered pav to soak up every drop.

variations.name: Kolhapuri Misal
variations.description: The legendary blistering misal of Kolhapur, built on the region's incendiary lasun-kanda masala and a slick of fiery red kat that floats a finger deep. This is the version that makes eyes water and noses run — served with extra tarri, curd on standby, and a badge of honour for finishing it.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil carries the ferocious Kolhapuri kat and floats blazing red over the top

steps: Soak 1/2 cup dried white peas overnight, then pressure cook them with 1.5 cups sprouted matki, 3 cups water, 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1/2 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft, and keep the cooking liquid.

Dry-roast 3/4 cup grated dry coconut with 2 sliced onions on medium until dark brown and aromatic, then grind with 12 garlic cloves, 1 inch ginger and a splash of water into a smooth, dark, pungent paste.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pot, saute 2 chopped onions for 5 minutes until golden, add the ground masala paste and fry for 5 minutes until the oil oozes out at the edges.

Add 2.5 tbsp Kolhapuri masala, 1 tbsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, cook 2 minutes, then tip in the cooked beans with their liquid plus 2 cups water and simmer 15 minutes into a thin, fierce usal.

Make the tarri by heating the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil until smoking, taking it off the flame, and stirring in the last 1 tbsp Kashmiri chilli powder; pour this blazing red oil over the simmering usal.
Ladle into bowls, heap on farsan, raw onion and coriander, and serve with soft pav and extra tarri for those who dare.
tips: Adding white peas alongside the matki is the Kolhapuri way, giving the usal more body and a heartier bite.
Roast the coconut and onion until genuinely dark — this deep browning is what gives Kolhapuri misal its signature colour and smoke.
Keep curd or buttermilk ready; this misal is authentically brutal in heat and needs a cooling counterpoint.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a mountain of farsan, raw onion, lemon and buttered pav, plus a bowl of curd on the side to survive the heat.

variations.name: Puneri Misal
variations.description: The gentler, subtly sweet misal of Pune, milder in heat and often topped with poha and a sprinkle of sev alongside the farsan. Goda masala and a touch of jaggery round out the gravy, making this the balanced, breakfast-friendly cousin that lets the sprouts and spices shine rather than the fire.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil gives the Puneri usal its authentic base without overpowering the milder spicing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a spoon of unrefined jaggery gives Puneri misal its signature gentle sweet-savoury balance

steps: Pressure cook 2 cups sprouted matki with 2 cups water, a pinch of turmeric and 1/2 tsp salt for 2 whistles until soft, keeping the liquid.
Dry-roast 1/2 cup grated dry coconut with 1 sliced onion until light golden and nutty, then grind to a smooth paste with a little water.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pot, saute 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 1 chopped onion for 4 minutes, add 2 chopped tomatoes, cook 5 minutes, then stir in the coconut paste.

Add 2 tbsp goda masala, 1 tbsp red chilli powder, 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp salt, cook 3 minutes until fragrant, then add the cooked matki with its liquid plus 2 cups water and simmer 12 minutes into a medium-thick usal.
Warm 1 cup cooked poha and keep it ready as the Puneri-style base layer for each serving.
Spoon a bed of poha into each bowl, ladle the mild usal over it, top with farsan, chopped onion, coriander and a little sev, and serve with soft pav.
tips: The layer of poha at the base is the Puneri signature; it soaks up the gravy and softens the overall heat.
Keep the chilli gentle here and let the goda masala and jaggery define the flavour instead of raw fire.
Warm the poha just before serving so it stays soft and does not clump at the bottom of the bowl.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve topped with fine sev, raw onion and coriander over the poha base, with lemon wedges and soft pav for a balanced breakfast plate.

variations.name: Mixed Sprouts Misal
variations.description: A wholesome, protein-packed spin that swaps the single matki for a medley of sprouted moong, chana and moth beans, giving varied textures and a nutty depth to the usal. Cooked in ghee with a moderate spicing, it is the nourishing, everyday version made for a filling and healthy meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee gives this nourishing mixed-sprout usal a rounded richness and a gentler finish than oil

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil blooms the chilli for the tarri drizzled over the top

steps: Pressure cook 2.5 cups mixed sprouted beans with 3 cups water, a pinch of turmeric and 1/2 tsp salt for 3 whistles until all the beans are soft, keeping the cooking liquid.
Dry-roast 1/2 cup grated dry coconut with 1 sliced onion until golden and fragrant, then grind to a smooth paste with a little water.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot on medium, splutter 1 tsp cumin seeds, add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 1 chopped onion, and saute 4 minutes until golden.
Add 2 chopped tomatoes and cook 5 minutes until soft, stir in the coconut paste, 1.5 tbsp goda masala, 1 tbsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook 3 minutes until the ghee separates.

Add the cooked mixed sprouts with their liquid plus 2 cups water and simmer for 12 minutes into a hearty usal, then bloom the remaining 1/2 tbsp chilli powder in 2 tbsp hot Anveshan Groundnut Oil off the heat and drizzle it over.
Ladle the usal into bowls, top each with farsan, chopped raw onion and coriander, and serve with soft pav and lemon wedges.
tips: Cook the mixed sprouts just until tender; chana takes longer than moong, so sprout them a day ahead or soak the chana longer.
Using ghee for the usal and oil only for the tarri gives a richer, gentler misal that suits a family meal.
This version keeps well and even tastes better the next day, as the mixed beans soak up the masala overnight.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a wholesome one-bowl meal topped with farsan, onion and coriander, with pav and a wedge of lemon for a protein-rich lunch.

variations.name: Classic Ash Gourd Mor Kuzhambu
variations.description: The definitive Tamil yogurt curry: whisked sour curd loosened with water and thickened by a ground paste of coconut, soaked chana dal, cumin and green chilli, gently warmed with cubes of ash gourd until it just coats the spoon. Kept below a boil so the curd never splits, it is finished with a coconut-oil tempering of mustard, fenugreek and curry leaves.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: The coconut-oil tempering is the coastal soul of a proper mor kuzhambu

steps: Soak 1.5 tbsp chana dal in water for 30 minutes, then grind it with 0.33 cup grated coconut, 1 tsp cumin, 3 green chillies and 1 inch ginger into a smooth paste with a little water.
Boil 2 cups cubed ash gourd with 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and water to half-cover on medium for 7-8 minutes until tender and translucent.
Whisk 2 cups sour curd smooth with 1 cup water so it is lump-free and pourable.
Add the ground paste to the cooked ash gourd and simmer on low for 5 minutes until the raw dal smell disappears and it thickens slightly.
Lower the heat to the minimum, pour in the whisked curd and warm gently for 2-3 minutes, stirring constantly and never letting it boil, so the curd stays smooth and does not split.

In a small pan heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.25 tsp fenugreek seeds and 2 dried red chillies, let them splutter, add 10 curry leaves, and pour over the kuzhambu.
tips: Add the curd only on the lowest heat and never boil it, or the kuzhambu will curdle into grainy strands.
Slightly sour curd gives the best flavour; if yours is fresh, let it sit out a few hours first.
Grind the chana dal paste smooth so it thickens the curry without leaving a gritty texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle over hot rice with a dry poriyal and appalam, its cooling tang balancing a spicy side beautifully.

variations.name: Vendakkai Mor Kuzhambu
variations.description: Here okra is sauteed until its stickiness cooks off and its edges crisp before it slips into the yogurt gravy, so the pods stay firm and soak up the tang without turning slimy. The fried okra gives this mor kuzhambu a heartier, more textured bite than the melting ash-gourd version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Used both to fry the okra and to temper, tying the dish together in one fat

steps: Wipe 250 g okra dry, trim and cut into 2 cm pieces, then saute in 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil on medium for 6-7 minutes until the stickiness cooks off and the edges brown; set aside.
Soak 1.5 tbsp toor dal for 30 minutes and grind with 0.33 cup grated coconut, 1 tsp cumin, 1 tsp coriander seeds and 3 green chillies into a smooth paste with a little water.
Whisk 2 cups sour curd with 1 cup water until smooth and lump-free.
Simmer the ground paste with 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 0.75 cup water on medium for 5 minutes until the raw smell goes, then fold in the fried okra.
Reduce the heat to the minimum, pour in the whisked curd and warm gently for 2-3 minutes, stirring constantly and never boiling, so the gravy stays smooth.

In a small pan heat the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.25 tsp fenugreek and 2 dried red chillies, let them splutter, add 10 curry leaves, and pour over the kuzhambu.
tips: Dry the okra completely and fry it before adding, so it stays firm and never turns slimy in the curd.
Add the fried okra late so it holds its shape and a little crispness in the finished gravy.
Keep the flame at its lowest once the curd goes in, stirring the whole time to prevent splitting.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best over plain rice with a spoon of ghee; the firm okra makes it satisfying enough to need only a papad alongside.

variations.name: Kerala Pulissery
variations.description: The Kerala cousin of mor kuzhambu, pulissery is thinner and turmeric-bright, made with sweet pumpkin simmered in a coconut-cumin paste and finished with plenty of curd and a curry-leaf-heavy tempering. The pumpkin's sweetness against the sour curd gives it a gentle, sunny character distinct from the Tamil style.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil and a heavy curry-leaf tempering give pulissery its Kerala signature

steps: Boil 2 cups cubed pumpkin with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and water to half-cover on medium for 8 minutes until soft enough to mash lightly at the edges.
Grind 0.5 cup grated coconut with 1 tsp cumin and 2 green chillies into a smooth paste with a little water.
Add the coconut paste to the cooked pumpkin and simmer on low for 4-5 minutes until the raw smell goes and the gravy turns golden and thick.
Whisk 2 cups sour curd smooth, lower the heat to the minimum, and stir it in gently for 2-3 minutes without ever boiling so the pulissery stays creamy.
In a small pan heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil; add 0.75 tsp mustard seeds, 0.25 tsp fenugreek and 3 dried red chillies, let them splutter until the mustard pops.
Add 15 curry leaves to the tempering, let them crackle for 10 seconds, and pour the whole sizzling mix over the pulissery.
tips: Pulissery is thinner than Tamil mor kuzhambu, so keep it pourable rather than thick.
A generous hand with curry leaves in the tempering is what gives pulissery its Kerala aroma.
Ripe pumpkin brings natural sweetness; a pinch of jaggery can stand in if yours is bland.
variations.servingSuggestion: A staple on the Kerala sadya, served with rice, a thoran and pappadam, its sweet-sour warmth rounding out the plate.

variations.name: Chow Chow Mor Kuzhambu
variations.description: A gentle, everyday mor kuzhambu made with soft cubes of chayote and a coconut paste ground with toor dal and a little raw rice for extra body, so the curry clings nicely to rice. The mild chayote lets the tangy curd and cumin take centre stage in this light, homely version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: The coconut-oil tempering lends its mellow aroma to the mild chayote gravy

steps: Soak 1 tbsp toor dal and 1 tsp raw rice together for 30 minutes, then grind with 0.33 cup grated coconut, 1 tsp cumin and 3 green chillies into a smooth paste with a little water.
Peel and cube 2 cups chayote and boil with 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and water to half-cover on medium for 7 minutes until tender and translucent.
Whisk 2 cups sour curd with 0.75 cup water until smooth and pourable.
Add the ground paste to the cooked chayote and simmer on low for 5 minutes until the raw dal-rice smell goes and the gravy thickens lightly.
Reduce the heat to the minimum, pour in the whisked curd and warm for 2-3 minutes, stirring constantly and never boiling, so it stays smooth.

In a small pan heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.25 tsp fenugreek and 2 dried red chillies, let them splutter, add 10 curry leaves, and pour over the kuzhambu.
tips: The teaspoon of raw rice in the paste gives the curry a gentle body that clings to rice.
Cook the chayote just to translucent; it turns watery and loses its bite if boiled too long.
If the gravy thickens too much on standing, loosen it with a splash of water on low heat, not high.
variations.servingSuggestion: A comforting everyday curry over rice with a dry curry like potato roast and a crisp appalam.

variations.name: Classic Mysore Rasam
variations.description: The signature rasam of old Mysore, thickened and perfumed with a freshly ground paste of coconut roasted with coriander, chana dal and red chillies. Richer and more full-bodied than a plain rasam, it balances tamarind tang, tomato and a touch of jaggery against the toasty coconut spice, all rounded off with a fragrant ghee tempering.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee both roasts the spice paste and tempers the rasam, deepening its toasty aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A Mysore touch of unrefined jaggery balances the tamarind and coconut spice

steps: Pressure-cook 0.33 cup toor dal with 1 cup water for 3 whistles until soft and mash. Soak 1 lemon-sized ball of tamarind in 1.5 cups warm water and extract the juice.

In 0.5 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee, roast 1.5 tsp coriander seeds, 1 tsp chana dal and 3 dried red chillies on low until golden, then add 3 tbsp grated coconut and roast 2 minutes more until it turns light brown and toasty.
Cool and grind the roasted mixture into a smooth paste with a little water.
Pour the tamarind extract into a pot with 1 chopped tomato, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and simmer on medium for 7 minutes until the raw smell goes.
Stir in the mashed dal, the ground coconut-spice paste and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, add water to a pourable consistency, and simmer on low to the frothing point below a boil for 3 minutes.
In a small pan heat the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 10 curry leaves, let them crackle, pour over the rasam and finish with 2 tbsp coriander leaves.
tips: Roast the coconut only to light brown; scorched coconut turns the whole rasam bitter.
Grind the spice paste smooth so the rasam is velvety rather than gritty.
The jaggery is a balancer, not a sweetener - one teaspoon rounds the tang without making it sweet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot rice with a spoon of ghee and a crisp appalam; its richness pairs well with a light poriyal.

variations.name: Iyengar Mysore Rasam
variations.description: The Iyengar kitchen's version leans fragrant and festive, grinding fresh coconut with coriander, a clove and a cardamom alongside the red chillies for a subtly perfumed, temple-style rasam. It is slightly sweeter and more aromatic than the everyday version, the warm spices lifting it into something special for feast days.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries the warm clove-cardamom aroma that marks the Iyengar style

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A slightly generous jaggery gives this temple-style rasam its gentle sweetness

steps: Pressure-cook 0.33 cup toor dal with 1 cup water for 3 whistles and mash. Soak 1 small ball of tamarind in 1.5 cups warm water and extract the juice.
In 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, roast 1.5 tsp coriander seeds, 2 dried red chillies, 1 clove and 1 cardamom pod on low until fragrant, then add 4 tbsp grated coconut and roast until pale gold.
Grind the roasted spices and coconut into a smooth, fragrant paste with a little water.
Simmer the tamarind extract in a pot with 1 chopped tomato, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 0.25 tsp asafoetida on medium for 7 minutes.
Add the mashed dal, the ground paste and 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, thin with water, and simmer on low to the frothing point below a boil for 3 minutes so the warm spices bloom.
In a small pan heat the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 10 curry leaves, and pour the sizzling tempering over the rasam.
tips: Use just one clove and one cardamom; more will overpower the delicate coconut base.
This version skips the coriander-leaf garnish so the ground warm spices stay the star.
A little extra coconut keeps the Iyengar rasam thicker and more luxurious than the everyday one.
variations.servingSuggestion: A festive rasam for a wedding-style meal, served over rice with ghee alongside kootu and vadai.

variations.name: Pepper Mysore Rasam
variations.description: A bolder, hotter Mysore rasam that folds freshly pounded black pepper and cumin into the roasted coconut paste and drops the jaggery, so the toasty coconut meets a real kick of heat. This is the version for pepper-lovers and cold days, robust and warming with a deep, spicy finish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee blooms the pepper and roasted coconut into a warming, robust rasam

steps: Pressure-cook 0.33 cup toor dal with 1 cup water for 3 whistles and mash. Soak 1 lemon-sized ball of tamarind in 1.5 cups warm water and extract the juice.
In 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, roast 1.5 tsp peppercorns, 1 tsp cumin, 1 tsp coriander seeds and 2 dried red chillies on low until fragrant, then add 3 tbsp grated coconut and roast to light brown.
Grind the roasted mixture with 3 crushed garlic cloves into a smooth, spicy paste with a little water.
Simmer the tamarind extract in a pot with 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 0.25 tsp asafoetida on medium for 6 minutes.
Add the mashed dal and the pepper-coconut paste, thin with water to a pourable rasam, and simmer on low to the frothing point below a boil for 3 minutes so the pepper heat mellows into the broth.
In a small pan heat the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 10 curry leaves, pour over the rasam and finish with 2 tbsp coriander leaves.
tips: Roast the pepper only briefly with the coconut; over-roasting makes the heat harsh rather than warm.
Skip the jaggery here so the spicy, savoury character stays front and centre.
Add the garlic to the paste rather than the tempering so it melts into the body of the rasam.
variations.servingSuggestion: A warming rasam for cold or rainy days, best over rice with ghee or sipped hot from a tumbler.

variations.name: Lemon Mysore Rasam
variations.description: A lighter reinvention that keeps the signature roasted coconut paste but drops the tamarind, drawing its tang instead from fresh lemon stirred in at the end. The citrus keeps the toasty coconut rasam bright and clean rather than dark, making a fresher, more delicate Mysore rasam for a summer table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee roasts the coconut paste and tempers the rasam, framing the fresh lemon

steps: Pressure-cook 0.33 cup toor dal with 1.5 cups water for 3 whistles until soft, mash, and thin with 1 cup water.

In 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, roast 1.5 tsp coriander seeds, 1 tsp chana dal and 2 dried red chillies on low until golden, add 3 tbsp grated coconut and roast to light brown, then grind smooth with water.
Bring the thinned dal to a simmer in a pot with 1 small chopped tomato, 1 slit green chilli, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 0.25 tsp asafoetida on medium for 6 minutes.
Stir in the roasted coconut paste and simmer on low to the frothing point below a boil for 3 minutes, then switch off the heat.
Only after the rasam stops boiling, stir in 2.5 tbsp lemon juice so the tang stays fresh against the toasty coconut.
In a small pan heat the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 10 curry leaves, and pour the tempering over the rasam.
tips: Add the lemon strictly off the heat; boiling it over the coconut paste turns the rasam bitter.
Without tamarind this rasam is paler and fresher, so use ripe tomato for a little colour and depth.
Balance the lemon at the very end to taste, since the roasted coconut softens the perceived sourness.
variations.servingSuggestion: A bright, summery rasam over rice with ghee, or served as a light soup before a coconut-rich main.

variations.name: Classic Mumbai Pav Bhaji
variations.description: The definitive Mumbai street version: a mash of potato, cauliflower, peas and capsicum simmered with tomatoes and pav bhaji masala until deep red and buttery smooth. Cooked and finished in ghee and served with soft pav toasted till golden, it is the smoky, tangy plate that defines the city's chowpatty nights.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee both cooks the bhaji and toasts the pav, giving the signature rich, buttery street-cart flavour

steps: Pressure cook 3 diced potatoes, 1 cup cauliflower florets and 1/2 cup green peas with 1 cup water and 1/2 tsp salt for 3 whistles until very soft, then mash them coarsely and keep aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide pan on medium, add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 2 finely chopped onions, and saute for 5 minutes until soft and pale golden.

Add 1 finely chopped capsicum and cook 3 minutes, then add 4 finely chopped tomatoes with 1 tsp salt and cook for 8 minutes, mashing, until the tomatoes break down into a thick pulp and the ghee separates at the edges.

Stir in 1.5 tbsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 2.5 tbsp pav bhaji masala and cook for 1 minute on low, then add the mashed vegetables with 1 cup hot water and mash everything together with a potato masher.

Simmer the bhaji on medium-low for 10 minutes, mashing and stirring often and adding hot water to keep it saucy, until it turns deep red, glossy and smooth, then finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and half the coriander.

Slit 8 pav horizontally, smear the hot tava with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and a pinch of pav bhaji masala, and toast the pav cut-side down for 1 minute until golden and crisp, then serve with the bhaji, raw onion, coriander and lemon wedges.
tips: Mash the bhaji longer than feels necessary — a truly smooth, lump-free texture is what separates cart-style pav bhaji from a plain vegetable mash.
Kashmiri chilli powder gives the bright red colour without harsh heat; adjust the pav bhaji masala for spice instead.
Keep a kettle of hot water handy and loosen the bhaji as it thickens, since it keeps drinking up liquid as it simmers.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile the bhaji with a knob of butter, a mound of finely chopped raw onion, extra coriander and a lemon wedge, with the toasted pav alongside for scooping.

variations.name: Jain Pav Bhaji
variations.description: The no-onion, no-garlic version served across Gujarat and Mumbai's Jain community, where raw banana and extra tomato build the body that onions usually give. A ginger-and-green-chilli base keeps it lively, proving pav bhaji loses none of its buttery, tangy soul without the alliums.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee gives the Jain bhaji its buttery richness in place of the depth onions would add

steps: Pressure cook 3 diced potatoes, 1 peeled and chopped raw banana, 1 cup cauliflower florets and 1/2 cup peas with 1 cup water and 1/2 tsp salt for 3 whistles until very soft, then mash coarsely.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide pan on medium, add 2 inch grated ginger and 3 finely chopped green chillies, and saute for 1 minute until the raw smell lifts.
Add 1 finely chopped capsicum and cook 3 minutes, then add 6 finely chopped tomatoes with 1 tsp salt and cook for 10 minutes, mashing, until they collapse into a thick, glossy pulp.
Stir in 1.5 tbsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 2.5 tbsp pav bhaji masala, cook 1 minute on low, then add the mashed vegetables with 1 cup hot water.
Mash and simmer the bhaji on medium-low for 12 minutes, adding hot water as needed, until it turns thick, deep red and smooth, then finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and half the coriander.
Toast 8 slit pav on a tava smeared with the last 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and a pinch of masala until golden and crisp, and serve with the bhaji and lemon wedges.
tips: Raw banana is the Jain secret for body and creaminess; cook it fully soft or it lends a starchy, raw edge.
Use extra tomatoes to make up for the missing onion sweetness, and cook them down thoroughly for depth.
A little grated ginger stirred in at the end lifts the whole bhaji since there is no garlic to carry the aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with buttery toasted pav, a squeeze of lemon and chopped coriander, skipping the raw onion to keep it strictly Jain.

variations.name: Kolhapuri Tawa Pav Bhaji
variations.description: A fiery Maharashtrian tawa-style bhaji built on the searing kanda-lasun and Kolhapuri masala of the region, cooked hard on a flat griddle so it catches a smoky char. Punchier and darker than the Mumbai plate, it is for those who like their pav bhaji with real heat and a griddled edge.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil is the authentic Maharashtrian cooking fat that stands up to the fierce Kolhapuri masala on a hot tava

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of bilona ghee rounds off the fiery bhaji and toasts the pav golden

steps: Pressure cook 3 diced potatoes, 1 cup cauliflower and 1/2 cup peas with 1 cup water and 1/2 tsp salt for 3 whistles until soft, then mash coarsely.

Pound 10 garlic cloves and 4 dry red chillies into a coarse paste; heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on a wide tava on medium-high and fry this paste for 1 minute until it smells pungent and toasted.
Add 3 finely chopped onions and cook hard for 6 minutes until deep golden, then add 4 chopped tomatoes and 1 tsp salt and mash them down over high heat for 8 minutes until thick and darkened.
Stir in 2 tbsp Kolhapuri masala and 1.5 tbsp pav bhaji masala, cook 1 minute, then add the mashed vegetables with 1 cup hot water and mash it all together on the tava.

Cook the bhaji on medium-high for 10 minutes, spreading it thin across the hot tava and scraping it up repeatedly so it catches a smoky char, adding hot water to keep it moving, then finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee.
Toast 8 slit pav on the same tava with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and a pinch of Kolhapuri masala until crisp and red-edged, and serve with the fiery bhaji and coriander.
tips: Cook the bhaji hard on a wide tava and let it stick and char slightly before scraping — that smoky tawa edge is the whole point.
Kolhapuri masala is intensely hot, so start with less and build up; the fresh garlic-chilli paste already adds serious fire.
Freshly pounded garlic and dry chilli beat any paste from a jar for this pungent, rustic Maharashtrian flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve blazing hot with extra raw onion, a wedge of lemon and a dab of ghee, keeping cold buttermilk on hand to temper the heat.

variations.name: Classic Jodhpuri Pyaaz Kachori
variations.description: This Classic Jodhpuri Pyaaz Kachori encases a spiced brown-onion filling in a shatteringly flaky khasta crust fried low and slow until it puffs and bubbles. A Rajasthani breakfast legend, it is crisp outside, soft-spiced inside, and traditionally drenched in sweet-and-hot chutneys.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli atta gives the khasta crust a nutty flavour while staying flaky

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: slow-frying in wood-pressed groundnut oil gives the classic pale, blistered khasta shell

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the tamarind chutney served over the Jodhpuri kachori

steps: Rub 4 tbsp of the groundnut oil into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt until it clumps when pressed, then knead with about 0.5 cup water into a soft dough and rest 30 minutes.
Heat 3 tbsp oil and crackle 1 tsp fennel, 1 tsp crushed coriander and 0.75 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add 3 finely chopped onions and saute 8 minutes until golden brown.
Add 3 tbsp besan, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp garam masala and 0.75 tsp salt and cook 4 minutes until the besan is roasted and the filling is dry, then cool.
Roll small dough balls into thick discs, place a spoon of onion filling in each, gather and seal, then gently flatten into filled kachoris.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil to low and slide in the kachoris, frying very slowly for 12 to 15 minutes while the oil warms so they puff, blister and turn pale golden.
Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 0.75 cup water for 6 minutes into a chutney, and serve the crisp kachoris hot with it and coriander.
tips: Fry on very low heat, as high heat browns the crust before it turns flaky and khasta.
Roast the besan well in the filling so it binds the onions and loses its raw smell.
Rub enough oil into the flour that it holds shape when pressed, the secret to a flaky shell.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot for breakfast with sweet tamarind and spicy green chutney, Jodhpur style.

variations.name: Baked Pyaaz Kachori
variations.description: An oven-baked take that keeps the flaky khasta character with far less oil, the crust brushed with ghee for colour and crunch. The same fragrant brown-onion filling makes it a lighter way to enjoy the Rajasthani classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli atta bakes into a firm, flaky khasta shell without deep-frying

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee both shortens the dough and glazes the kachoris golden in the oven

steps: Rub 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt until crumbly, then knead with about 0.5 cup water into a soft dough and rest 30 minutes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp fennel, 1 tsp crushed coriander seeds and 0.5 tsp nigella seeds, then add 3 chopped onions and cook 8 minutes until golden.
Stir in 3 tbsp besan, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp garam masala, 0.75 tsp amchur and 0.75 tsp salt and roast 4 minutes until dry, then cool.
Fill and seal thick dough discs with the onion mixture, flatten gently into kachoris and arrange on a lined tray.
Brush the tops with the remaining melted Anveshan Ghee and bake in an oven preheated to 190 C for 28 to 32 minutes, turning once, until golden and flaky.
Rest 5 minutes so the crust firms, then serve warm with coriander and chutney.
tips: Bake at a moderate temperature so the crust flakes and dries rather than hardening.
Poke a tiny hole in the top of each kachori so steam escapes and the shell stays crisp.
Rest the baked kachoris briefly, as the khasta crust firms up as it cools.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a lighter tea-time snack with mint chutney and masala chai.

variations.name: Marwari Spicy Pyaaz Kachori
variations.description: A fiery Marwari version that amps up the heat with extra red chilli, crushed peppercorns and a hit of dry mango, giving a boldly spiced onion filling. It is the intensely flavoured kachori that seasoned Rajasthani palates reach for.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli atta stands up to the bold spicing with a nutty, flaky crust

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: pungent wood-pressed mustard oil deepens the fiery Marwari flavour

steps: Heat 4 tbsp of the mustard oil to smoking, cool slightly, then rub into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt and knead with about 0.5 cup water into a soft dough, resting 30 minutes.
Heat 3 tbsp mustard oil, crackle 1 tsp fennel, 1 tsp crushed coriander seeds and 1 tsp crushed peppercorns, then add 3 chopped onions and chopped green chilli and cook 8 minutes until golden.
Add 3 tbsp besan, 2 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp dry mango powder, 0.75 tsp garam masala and 0.75 tsp salt and roast 4 minutes until dry and fiery, then cool.
Fill and seal thick dough discs with the spicy onion mixture and flatten gently into kachoris.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Mustard Oil to low and fry the kachoris slowly for 12 to 15 minutes until puffed, blistered and golden.
Drain and serve the fiery kachoris hot with coriander and a cooling yogurt dip.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to smoking and cool it before use to mellow its raw pungency.
Adjust the chilli to taste, as authentic Marwari kachoris are meant to be seriously hot.
Serve a cooling raita alongside to balance the intense spice of this version.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a bowl of chilled boondi raita to temper the fire.

variations.name: Mini Cocktail Pyaaz Kachori
variations.description: Bite-sized cocktail kachoris made for parties, each a two-bite crisp shell of the fragrant onion filling, perfect for passing around on trays. Smaller and quicker to fry evenly, they are dressed up chaat-style with yogurt, chutney and sev.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli atta gives these mini kachoris a wholesome flaky bite

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the small kachoris crisp evenly in wood-pressed groundnut oil

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the tamarind chutney drizzled over the chaat-style minis

steps: Rub 4 tbsp of the groundnut oil into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, then knead with about 0.5 cup water into a soft dough and rest 30 minutes.

Heat 2 tbsp oil, crackle 1 tsp fennel and 0.75 tsp cumin seeds, add 2 chopped onions and cook 6 minutes until golden, then stir in 2 tbsp besan, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp salt and roast 3 minutes before cooling.
Pinch off small dough balls, fill each with a little onion mixture, seal and flatten into mini kachoris.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil to low-medium and fry the minis in batches for 8 to 10 minutes until puffed and golden.
Whisk the 1 cup yogurt smooth, and simmer 2 tbsp tamarind with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 0.5 cup water for 6 minutes into a chutney.
Arrange the mini kachoris on a platter, crack the tops, spoon over yogurt and tamarind chutney, and finish with nylon sev and coriander before serving.
tips: Keep the kachoris small and uniform so they fry through evenly in the same time.
Top with yogurt and chutney only just before serving so the minis stay crisp.
Fry a batch ahead and re-crisp briefly in a hot oven right before the party.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as passed canapes on a platter, each mini kachori dressed with a dot of chutney and a pinch of sev.

variations.name: Classic Ringan No Olo
variations.description: The rustic Gujarati smoked brinjal mash, where a fat purple aubergine is fire-roasted until collapsing, then mashed raw with crushed garlic, green chilli, coriander and a bold pour of wood-pressed groundnut oil. Barely cooked and boldly smoky, olo is all about the roasted flavour of the brinjal itself.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A generous pour of raw wood-pressed groundnut oil is the traditional dressing that makes olo rich and glossy

steps: Rub 1 large brinjal with a few drops of oil, prick it all over with a fork, and roast directly over a medium flame for 12-15 minutes, turning every 3 minutes, until the skin is charred black and the flesh is completely soft.
Rest the brinjal covered for 5 minutes, then peel off the charred skin, discard the stem, and mash the smoky flesh coarsely with a fork.
Crush 6 garlic cloves with 3 green chillies and a pinch of salt in a mortar into a rough paste, keeping some texture.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan on medium heat, crackle 0.5 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, add 1 finely chopped onion and the garlic-chilli paste, and fry for 3-4 minutes until the onion just softens.

Add 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, fry for 20 seconds, then fold in the mashed brinjal and 1 tsp salt and cook for just 3-4 minutes so it warms through without losing its smoky freshness.
Turn off the heat and stir in 4 tbsp chopped coriander and 1 tbsp lemon juice, keeping the olo rustic and coarse rather than smooth.
tips: Char the brinjal well over an open flame; the smokiness is the whole point of olo and cannot be faked in a pan.
Keep the mash coarse with visible strands, not a smooth puree, for authentic texture.
Choose a light, glossy brinjal that feels hollow when tapped, as it has fewer seeds and roasts sweeter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature with hot bajra rotla and a dollop of white butter, the classic Gujarati winter pairing.

variations.name: Surti Lilo Lasan No Olo
variations.description: Surat's beloved winter version, fragrant with fresh green garlic (lilo lasan) that lends a mellow, grassy pungency you only get in the cold months. Spring onions and extra coriander make this olo greener, softer and far more aromatic than the everyday one.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil carries the delicate green-garlic aroma that defines this Surti winter olo

steps: Roast 1 large brinjal over a medium flame for 12-15 minutes, turning every 3 minutes, until charred and fully collapsed; cool, peel and mash coarsely.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan on medium heat and crackle 0.5 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds.
Add 0.5 cup chopped green garlic and 3 finely chopped green chillies and saute for 2-3 minutes until the green garlic wilts and smells sweet, taking care not to brown it.
Stir in 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp red chilli powder for 20 seconds, then fold in the mashed brinjal and 1 tsp salt and warm through for 3-4 minutes.
Add 0.5 cup chopped spring onions with their greens and cook for just 1 minute so they keep their fresh crunch.
Take off the heat and finish with 4 tbsp chopped coriander and 1 tbsp lemon juice.
tips: Fresh green garlic is seasonal; if unavailable, use the white parts of spring onion plus a little regular garlic as a stand-in.
Do not brown the green garlic; it should stay pale and sweet, not toasted and sharp.
Add the spring onion greens at the very end so they wilt only slightly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot jowar or bajra rotla and jaggery on the side, the way Surti households eat it through winter.

variations.name: Kathiyawadi Ringan No Olo
variations.description: A robust Saurashtra version that dresses the smoked brinjal with a toasty tempering of sesame, crushed peanuts and plenty of garlic, cooked a little longer for a deeper, spicier mash. Earthier and heartier than the raw classic, it stands up to thick millet rotlas.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Nutty gingelly oil reinforces the sesame-peanut tempering typical of Kathiyawadi cooking

steps: Roast 1 large brinjal over a medium flame for 12-15 minutes, turning often, until the skin is fully charred and the flesh collapses; peel and mash coarsely.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadai on medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 1.5 tbsp sesame seeds for 30 seconds until the sesame turns golden.
Add 8 lightly crushed garlic cloves and fry for 1 minute until fragrant and pale gold, then add 1 chopped onion and saute for 4 minutes until soft.
Stir in 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp dhana-jeera, fry for 30 seconds, then fold in the mashed brinjal and 1 tsp salt.
Add 3 tbsp crushed roasted peanuts and cook on medium-low for 6-7 minutes, stirring often, until the olo thickens, darkens and takes on a nutty depth.
Finish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander stirred through in the last minute.
tips: Toast the sesame seeds until just golden for the fullest nutty aroma, but pull them off before they brown and turn bitter.
Crush the peanuts coarsely so they add crunch rather than disappearing into the mash.
This heartier olo keeps well and tastes even better the next day once the flavours meld.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thick bajra rotla, sliced raw onion and a green chilli fried in oil for the full Kathiyawadi experience.

variations.name: Ringan Bateta No Olo
variations.description: A more filling version where a boiled potato is mashed into the smoked brinjal, mellowing the smokiness and turning the olo into a substantial, spoonable dish. The potato softens the sharp edges and stretches the beloved mash into a proper meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil binds the potato and brinjal into a rich, glossy mash

steps: Roast 1 large brinjal over a medium flame for 12-15 minutes until charred and soft, then peel and mash together with 2 boiled mashed potatoes into a coarse mixture.
Crush 6 garlic cloves with 3 green chillies into a rough paste in a mortar.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan on medium heat, crackle 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida for 20 seconds, then add 1 chopped onion and the garlic-chilli paste and fry for 4 minutes until soft.
Add 1 chopped tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder and cook for 3-4 minutes until the tomato breaks down.
Fold in the brinjal-potato mash and 1 tsp salt and cook on medium-low for 5-6 minutes, stirring, until everything comes together into a thick, cohesive mash.
Finish with 4 tbsp chopped coriander stirred through, and serve warm.
tips: Mash the potato while still warm so it blends smoothly into the brinjal without lumps.
Keep the potato-to-brinjal ratio modest so the smoky flavour still leads.
A squeeze of lemon at the end lifts the richer, potato-heavy mash.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve this hearty mash with hot phulka or as a filling stuffed into a toasted pav with extra coriander.

variations.name: Classic Sev Tameta Nu Shaak
variations.description: A quintessential Gujarati everyday curry of ripe tomatoes simmered into a sweet-tangy-spicy gravy, crowned with crunchy gram-flour sev that half-melts into the sauce. Quick, comforting and endlessly popular, it balances jaggery's sweetness against tomato's tang in the classic Gujarati way.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Clean wood-pressed groundnut oil lets the fresh tomato flavour lead without any heaviness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery is the soul of this shaak, balancing the tomatoes into the signature khatta-meetha gravy

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 finely chopped onion and 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and sauté for 3-4 minutes until the onion softens and turns translucent.

Tip in 5 finely chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp dhana-jeera and 1 tsp salt, cover, and cook for 8-10 minutes until the tomatoes collapse into a pulpy gravy and the oil separates.
Stir in 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 cup water, then simmer uncovered for 5-6 minutes until the gravy thickens to a light saucy consistency and tastes balanced sweet-and-tangy.
Taste and adjust salt or jaggery, then turn off the heat and let the shaak rest for 2 minutes so it stops bubbling.
Just before serving, scatter 1 cup nylon sev and 3 tbsp chopped coriander generously over the top so the sev stays crisp on the surface and softens where it meets the gravy.
tips: Add the sev only at the table; stirred in early it turns to mush and loses its signature crunch.
Use ripe red tomatoes for natural sweetness; sour ones will need a touch more jaggery to balance.
For a thicker gravy, mash a few tomato pieces against the side of the pan as they cook.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with soft phulka or bhakri, keeping a bowl of extra sev on the table to sprinkle over each helping.

variations.name: Kathiyawadi Sev Tameta
variations.description: The fiery Saurashtra rendition, where a rough garlic-red chilli paste and a smoky Kathiyawadi spice hit make the tomato gravy bold and pungent rather than sweet. Rustic and robust, it trades the classic jaggery for garlicky heat and finishes with a shower of thick sev.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Kathiyawadi cooking leans on generous wood-pressed groundnut oil to carry the garlic-chilli punch

steps: Pound 8 garlic cloves with 4 dried red chillies and a pinch of salt into a coarse paste using a mortar and pestle, keeping some texture rather than a smooth blend.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add 1 chopped onion and fry for 4-5 minutes until golden.
Add the pounded garlic-chilli paste and fry for 1-2 minutes until the raw garlic smell disappears and the oil turns red.
Add 5 chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 2 tsp dhana-jeera, 1 tsp Kathiyawadi masala and 1 tsp salt, cover, and cook for 8-10 minutes until pulpy and glossy.
Pour in 0.75 cup water and simmer uncovered for 5 minutes until the gravy thickens and darkens; this version stays savoury and hot, not sweet.
Top with 1 cup thick sev and 3 tbsp chopped coriander at the moment of serving so the sturdy sev keeps its bite.
tips: Pounding the garlic and chillies coarsely, rather than blending, gives the authentic rustic Kathiyawadi texture.
Use thick jada sev here; it stands up to the bold gravy far better than fine nylon sev.
If you cannot find ready Kathiyawadi masala, a mix of extra dhana-jeera and a pinch of clove powder comes close.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot with thick bajra rotla smeared with white butter and a raw onion wedge on the side.

variations.name: Jain Sev Tameta Nu Shaak
variations.description: A Jain-friendly version made without onion or garlic, relying on ripe tomatoes, ginger, green chilli and a spoon of gram flour to build body and depth. Asafoetida stands in for the missing aromatics, and jaggery keeps the beloved sweet-tangy balance intact.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Nutty wood-pressed gingelly oil adds a savoury base that compensates for the absent onion and garlic

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery keeps the classic Gujarati sweet-tangy note alive even without onion and garlic

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadai on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 0.5 tsp asafoetida for 30 seconds, letting the generous hing stand in for the aromatics.
Add 2 slit green chillies and 1 tbsp grated ginger and fry for 30 seconds, then sprinkle in 1.5 tbsp besan and roast for 1 minute until it smells nutty and toasted.
Pour in the puree of 4 tomatoes along with 2 finely chopped tomatoes and cook on medium heat for 8-10 minutes until the raw tomato smell fades and the gravy thickens.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp dhana-jeera, 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp salt with 0.75 cup water, and simmer for 5 minutes until glossy and balanced.
Taste and adjust the sweet-sour balance, then switch off the heat and rest the shaak for 2 minutes.
Shower 1 cup nylon sev and 3 tbsp chopped coriander over the top just before serving.
tips: Roasting the besan well is essential; undercooked gram flour leaves a raw, pasty taste in the gravy.
The extra asafoetida is what gives the no-onion-garlic version its savoury depth, so do not reduce it.
Add the sev at the table to keep it crisp, as with every sev tameta.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with warm Jain-style plain parathas or steamed rice and a wedge of lemon on the side.

variations.name: Classic Mumbai Vada Pav
variations.description: Mumbai's original burger: a spiced potato ball dipped in besan batter and deep-fried golden, tucked into a soft pav slathered with dry garlic chutney and green chutney. The crackle of the crisp vada against pillowy bread, a fried green chilli on the side, is street food perfection.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil is the classic Maharashtrian frying medium and gives the vada a clean, crisp shell

steps: Boil 4 potatoes until soft, peel and mash them smooth; heat 2 tbsp of the Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan on medium, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 12 curry leaves, 3 chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger and 6 crushed garlic cloves and fry 1 minute.
Stir in 1/2 tsp turmeric, then add the mashed potato with 1 tsp salt and mix well for 2 minutes; cool the mixture and shape it into 8 tight lemon-sized balls.
For the dry garlic chutney, dry-roast 3 tbsp grated coconut and the remaining 6 garlic cloves, then pound with 2 tsp red chilli powder and 1/2 tsp salt into a coarse red powder.
Whisk 1 cup besan with 1/2 tsp salt, a pinch of turmeric and enough water (about 3/4 cup) into a smooth, coating batter the thickness of cream.

Heat the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai to 180C until a drop of batter rises quickly, dip each potato ball fully in the batter, and slide it into the oil; fry 3 to 4 at a time for about 4 minutes, turning, until golden and crisp all over.
Slit 8 pav without cutting through, spread the inside with green chutney and a sprinkle of the dry garlic chutney, press a hot vada inside each, and serve with a fried green chilli.
tips: Make sure the oil is properly hot at 180C before frying, or the besan coating drinks up oil and turns soft instead of crisp.
Shape the potato balls tightly with slightly damp hands so they do not crack open in the hot oil.
A pinch of baking soda whisked into the besan batter gives a lighter, crispier shell if you like it extra crunchy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with an extra spoon of dry garlic chutney, tangy green chutney and a salted fried green chilli on the side, cutting-chai alongside.

variations.name: Schezwan Vada Pav
variations.description: The Indo-Chinese street mash-up sweeping Mumbai stalls, where the classic vada meets a fiery, garlicky schezwan sauce smeared thick inside the pav. Spring onion and a hint of soy in the potato filling give it an unmistakable street-Chinese kick while keeping the beloved crunch intact.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: neutral wood-pressed sunflower oil fries these vadas crisp without competing with the bold schezwan flavours

steps: Boil and mash 4 potatoes; heat 2 tbsp of the Anveshan Sunflower Oil on medium, saute 8 finely chopped garlic cloves and 3 chopped green chillies for 1 minute, then add the white parts of 4 spring onions and cook 2 minutes.
Add 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp soy sauce, 1/2 tsp black pepper and 1 tbsp schezwan sauce, then fold in the mashed potato with 1 tsp salt and the chopped spring onion greens; mix for 2 minutes and cool.
Shape the spiced potato into 8 firm balls with lightly oiled hands, keeping them compact so they hold in the fryer.
Whisk 1 cup besan with 1/4 tsp salt and about 3/4 cup water into a smooth coating batter the thickness of cream.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Sunflower Oil to 180C, dip each ball fully in the batter and fry 3 to 4 at a time for about 4 minutes, turning, until deep golden and crisp.
Slit 8 pav, spread the inside generously with the remaining schezwan sauce, press a hot vada into each and top with a little extra sauce and spring onion greens.
tips: Bottled schezwan sauces vary in heat and salt, so taste and adjust the salt in the potato mix accordingly.
Keep the potato compact and not too wet; excess sauce in the filling makes the vada hard to shape and fry.
For extra street-style flavour, toast the schezwan-smeared pav briefly on a hot tava before assembling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with extra schezwan sauce for dipping and a scatter of spring onion greens, ideal with a cold cola on a rainy Mumbai evening.

variations.name: Cheese Butter Vada Pav
variations.description: The gooey modern favourite where a molten cheese slice is folded into the potato core so it oozes when you bite in, all cradled in a butter-toasted pav. Milder and richer than the street classic, it is the crowd-pleasing version that has taken over college canteens and food trucks.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil fries a crisp shell sturdy enough to hold the molten cheese centre

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee toasts the pav to a rich golden crust that pairs with the melting cheese

steps: Boil and mash 4 potatoes; heat 2 tbsp of the Anveshan Groundnut Oil, saute 6 crushed garlic cloves, 3 chopped green chillies and 1 inch grated ginger for 1 minute, add 1/2 tsp turmeric, then fold in the potato with 1 tsp salt and 3 tbsp coriander and cool.
Divide the potato into 8 portions, flatten each, place a mozzarella cube in the centre, and seal the potato around it into a tight ball so the cheese is fully enclosed.
Whisk 1 cup besan with 1/4 tsp salt and about 3/4 cup water into a smooth, thick coating batter that will seal in the cheese.

Heat the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C, dip each stuffed ball fully in the thick batter and fry 3 to 4 at a time for about 4 minutes until deep golden and crisp, keeping the coating intact so no cheese escapes.
Slit 8 pav, spread the insides with grated processed cheese, and toast them cut-side down on a tava with 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until the cheese softens and the bread is golden.
Press a hot cheese vada into each toasted pav and serve at once while the mozzarella centre is still molten and stretchy.
tips: Seal the potato fully around the cheese cube with no cracks, or the cheese leaks out and spatters in the hot oil.
Use a thicker besan batter than usual to form a sturdy shell that keeps the molten centre inside.
Serve immediately; the cheese pull is best in the first few minutes before it cools and firms up.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with tangy green chutney and ketchup for the cheese lovers, breaking one open to show the stretchy mozzarella centre.

variations.name: Baked Sattu Vada Pav
variations.description: A guilt-free reboot where the potato vada is bound with protein-rich roasted gram sattu and baked instead of deep-fried, keeping the spice and crunch while cutting the oil right down. A brush of ghee gives a golden crust, so you get the vada pav craving satisfied with a lighter, wholesome bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: roasted gram sattu binds and coats the baked vada, adding protein and a nutty crust in place of besan batter

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a brush of bilona ghee gives the baked vadas a golden, crisp finish without deep-frying

steps: Preheat the oven to 200C and boil and mash 4 potatoes; heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 12 curry leaves, 3 chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger and 6 crushed garlic cloves and fry 1 minute.
Add 1/2 tsp turmeric and fold in the mashed potato with 1 tsp salt and 3 tbsp coriander; mix well, then work in 1/4 cup Anveshan Sattu to bind the mixture into a firm, shapeable dough and cool it.
Shape the mixture into 8 slightly flattened patties so they bake evenly, and press each lightly into the remaining 1/4 cup Anveshan Sattu to coat the outside for a crust.
Arrange the patties on a lined tray, brush the tops generously with 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, and bake at 200C for 15 minutes.
Flip the vadas, brush the other side with the remaining ghee, and bake another 10 minutes until both sides are golden and crisp-edged.
For the dry chutney, pound 4 roasted garlic cloves with 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1/2 tsp salt; slit 8 pav, sprinkle the chutney inside, press a baked vada in each and serve warm.
tips: Sattu binds the potato firmly enough to bake without a batter; add it a spoon at a time until the mix holds a shape.
Flatten the vadas into patties rather than balls so the centre cooks through in the oven.
Brush the ghee generously and bake at a high heat to get the closest thing to a fried crust without the oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with fresh green chutney and a side salad, a lighter take that still hits the vada pav spot for a weekday lunch.

variations.name: Classic Veg Jalfrezi
variations.description: A vibrant stir-fried medley of crunchy vegetables tossed in a tangy, lightly spiced tomato sauce. Peppers, carrots and beans stay crisp-tender and glossy, with a sweet-sour edge from tomato and a splash of vinegar. Quick and colourful, it is the Anglo-Indian favourite that bridges a stir-fry and a curry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil takes high heat well, keeping the vegetables glossy and crisp in the stir-fry

steps: Cut 2 capsicums, 1 carrot, 10 beans and 2 onions into thin, even batons so they cook fast and stay crunchy.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a wok on high heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add the onions and stir-fry for 2 minutes until they soften but keep some bite.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 30 seconds, then the carrot and beans and stir-fry on high for 3 minutes.
Add the capsicum with 3/4 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tbsp coriander powder and 1/2 tsp turmeric, tossing for 2 minutes so the spices coat everything.
Add 2 tomatoes cut into thin wedges and 1 tsp salt, and stir-fry for 3 minutes until the tomato just softens but does not turn mushy.
Splash in 1 tsp vinegar and 1/2 tsp garam masala, toss for 1 minute on high heat, and serve immediately while glossy and crisp.
tips: Cut everything into even batons and cook on high heat so the vegetables stay crisp, not soggy.
Add the tomato last so it softens but keeps its shape rather than turning into gravy.
The vinegar splash at the end is what gives jalfrezi its signature tang, so do not skip it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with tandoori roti, laccha paratha or as a colourful side with dal and rice.

variations.name: Restaurant Gravy Veg Jalfrezi
variations.description: A semi-gravy restaurant version where the stir-fried vegetables are simmered in a tangy tomato-onion sauce with a touch of tomato ketchup for gloss and sweetness. Saucier than the dry classic, it clings richly to the vegetables and mops up beautifully with naan. This is the jalfrezi you find on restaurant menus.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil holds up to the high-heat searing that gives the gravy its restaurant depth

steps: Cut 2 capsicums, 1 carrot, 8 beans, 6 baby corns and 2 onions into thin batons; keep the onion pieces slightly separated into layers.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a wok on high heat and sear all the vegetables for 4 minutes until lightly charred at the edges but still crisp, then remove and set aside.
In the same wok add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute, then pour in 3/4 cup tomato puree and cook for 5 minutes until it thickens and the oil separates.
Add 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tbsp coriander powder and 1 tsp cumin powder with a splash of water, and cook for 2 minutes until the masala smells done.
Stir in 2 tbsp tomato ketchup and 1/2 cup water to make a glossy semi-gravy, then return the seared vegetables with 1 tsp salt and simmer for 4 minutes.
Finish with 1/2 tsp garam masala, toss to coat the vegetables in the clinging sauce, and serve hot.
tips: Searing the vegetables first on high heat gives that smoky restaurant-style charred edge.
A spoon of ketchup adds the glossy sweet-tang that defines the restaurant gravy version.
Keep the gravy semi-thick so it coats the vegetables rather than drowning them.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or veg fried rice, garnished with coriander and thin ginger juliennes.

variations.name: Paneer Jalfrezi
variations.description: A protein-rich twist where golden pan-fried paneer joins the crunchy peppers and onions in the tangy jalfrezi toss. The soft paneer soaks up the sweet-sour sauce while the vegetables stay crisp, making a more substantial main. Ghee gives the paneer a lovely browned edge and richness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee browns the paneer to a golden edge and enriches the tangy stir-fry

steps: Cut 250 g paneer, 2 capsicums and 2 onions into thick matchsticks; keep the paneer pieces slightly larger so they hold together.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium-high heat and fry the paneer batons for 2 minutes until golden on the edges, then remove and set aside.
Add the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then stir-fry the onions on high heat for 2 minutes until they soften but keep bite.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 30 seconds, then the capsicum with 3/4 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tbsp coriander powder and 1/2 tsp turmeric, tossing for 3 minutes.
Add 2 tomatoes cut into wedges and 1 tsp salt, stir-fry for 3 minutes, then return the paneer and toss gently for 2 minutes so it soaks up the masala.
Crush in 1 tsp kasuri methi, splash 1 tsp vinegar, toss for 1 minute, and serve hot.
tips: Fry the paneer only until lightly golden and add it back at the end so it stays soft, not rubbery.
Soak store-bought paneer in warm water for 10 minutes before frying for a softer bite.
Toss gently once the paneer is back in so the pieces do not crumble.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with laccha paratha or garlic naan, topped with a squeeze of lemon and coriander.

variations.name: Sweet-and-Sour Chinese-Style Veg Jalfrezi
variations.description: An Indo-Chinese fusion take where the crunchy jalfrezi vegetables are tossed in a glossy sweet-and-sour sauce with soy, vinegar and a hint of jaggery. Wok-charred and sticky, it sits between a jalfrezi and a chilli stir-fry. High-heat cooking keeps every pepper snappy and bright.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed sesame oil gives the Indo-Chinese toss its nutty, aromatic wok finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery gives the sweet-and-sour sauce a rounded natural sweetness instead of refined sugar

steps: Cut 2 capsicums, 2 onions, 1 carrot and 8 beans into thin diagonal batons, and finely chop 6 garlic cloves and 1 inch ginger.
Whisk 1 tbsp cornflour into 1/2 cup water with 1.5 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tbsp rice vinegar, 2 tbsp ketchup and 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder to make the sweet-and-sour sauce.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a wok on high heat, add the chopped garlic and ginger and stir-fry for 30 seconds until aromatic.
Add the carrot and beans and stir-fry on high for 2 minutes, then add the onions and capsicum and toss for 3 minutes until charred at the edges but still crunchy.
Pour in the sweet-and-sour sauce with 3/4 tsp salt and stir constantly for 2 minutes until the sauce thickens and glazes the vegetables.
Toss on high heat for 1 more minute so everything turns glossy and sticky, then serve immediately.
tips: Keep the heat high and work fast so the vegetables char lightly yet stay snappy.
Have the sauce mixed and ready before you start, as the stir-fry moves quickly.
Adjust the jaggery and vinegar at the end to get the sweet-sour balance you like.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot over veg hakka noodles or fried rice, garnished with spring onion greens.

variations.name: Classic Veg Kolhapuri
variations.description: A fiery mixed-vegetable curry from Kolhapur built on a dark, roasted coconut-and-spice masala. Assorted vegetables simmer in a bold, deep-red gravy that is famously spicy and intensely aromatic. Freshly ground kolhapuri masala with sesame, coconut and dry chillies gives it a signature heat and depth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the classic Maharashtrian fat that fries the roasted masala without masking its heat

steps: Dry-roast 1/2 cup grated coconut, 1 tbsp sesame seeds, 1 tbsp coriander seeds and 5 dried red chillies on medium-low heat until deep brown and fragrant, about 6 minutes.
Cool the roasted mixture and grind it with 1 chopped onion and a little water to a smooth dark paste.
Parboil 3 cups mixed vegetables in salted water for 5 minutes until just tender, then drain.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan on medium heat, saute 1 chopped onion until golden, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 2 pureed tomatoes and cook until the oil separates, about 6 minutes.
Add the ground kolhapuri paste, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder and fry for 5 minutes until the oil floats and the masala turns dark.
Add the parboiled vegetables with 1.5 cups water and the remaining salt, simmer for 10 minutes, then finish with 1 tsp garam masala and 3 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Roast the coconut and spices patiently to a deep brown for the authentic dark, spicy gravy.
Parboil the vegetables only until just tender so they hold their shape in the curry.
Kolhapuri is meant to be fiery, but you can reduce the dried chillies for a gentler heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with jowar bhakri, chapati or steamed rice, with sliced onion and lemon on the side.

variations.name: Restaurant-Style Veg Kolhapuri Gravy
variations.description: A smoother, richer restaurant version where the fiery kolhapuri masala is mellowed into a glossy cashew-thickened gravy. The vegetables sit in a semi-thick, deeply spiced sauce with a subtle creaminess that tames the heat. It is the version served in dhabas and family restaurants across Maharashtra.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil fries the roasted masala paste and gives the gravy a clean, restaurant-style base

steps: Soak 12 cashews and 1 tbsp poppy seeds in warm water for 15 minutes, then grind with 1/3 cup grated coconut to a smooth white paste.
Boil 2 chopped onions for 5 minutes, cool and grind to a smooth onion paste; parboil 3 cups mixed vegetables until just tender and drain.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan on medium heat, add the onion paste and 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 6 minutes until pale and thick.
Add 3 pureed tomatoes, 2 tbsp kolhapuri masala, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1/2 tsp turmeric, and cook for 6 minutes until the oil separates.
Stir in the cashew-coconut paste and cook for 3 minutes, then add the parboiled vegetables with 1.5 cups water and the remaining salt and simmer for 10 minutes.
Lower the heat, swirl in 2 tbsp cream, warm through for 2 minutes without boiling, and serve.
tips: The cashew-poppy paste smooths and thickens the gravy while gently taming the kolhapuri heat.
Grinding boiled onion into a paste gives the smooth, glossy restaurant texture.
Add the cream at the very end on low heat so the gravy stays silky.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan, tandoori roti or ghee rice, garnished with a swirl of cream and coriander.

variations.name: Dry Kolhapuri Sukka
variations.description: A dry, roasted sukka-style kolhapuri where the vegetables are coated in a thick, almost gravy-less spiced coconut masala. Toasty, intensely flavoured and only lightly moist, it makes a punchy side rather than a curry. The dry format lets the roasted kolhapuri spices cling to every piece of vegetable.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil toasts the coconut masala and helps it cling as a dry coating on the vegetables

steps: Dry-roast 3/4 cup grated coconut with 5 dried red chillies, 1 tbsp coriander seeds and 1 tsp cumin seeds until deep golden-brown, about 6 minutes.
Cool and coarsely grind the roasted mixture with 8 garlic cloves, keeping it dry and grainy rather than a smooth paste.
Parboil 3 cups mixed vegetables in salted water for 5 minutes until just tender, then drain thoroughly.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a wide pan on medium heat and fry 2 finely chopped onions until deep golden, about 7 minutes.
Add 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder, then the parboiled vegetables and the coarse coconut masala, and toss on medium-high heat for 6 to 8 minutes until dry and well coated.
Sprinkle in 1 tsp garam masala, the remaining salt and 3 tbsp chopped coriander, toss once more, and serve.
tips: Grind the roasted coconut coarse and dry so it coats the vegetables rather than turning saucy.
Drain the parboiled vegetables well; extra water stops the masala from clinging.
Toss on high heat at the end for a lightly toasted, dry finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a spicy dry side with dal-rice and phulka, or as a starter with lemon and sliced onion.

variations.name: Malvani Veg Kolhapuri
variations.description: A coastal Malvani-inflected version where the kolhapuri masala meets coconut milk and the distinctive Malvani spice blend for a rounder, coastal heat. The gravy is redder and slightly tangy with kokum, balancing the fire with a whisper of the sea. It bridges the ghati heat of Kolhapur with the coconut coast of Malvan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil ties the fiery masala to the Malvani coast and deepens the coconut flavour

steps: Parboil 3 cups mixed vegetables in salted water for 5 minutes until just tender, then drain and set aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan on medium heat, add 12 curry leaves and 2 finely chopped onions and fry until deep golden, about 7 minutes.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then 2 pureed tomatoes and cook until pulpy, around 5 minutes.
Stir in 2 tbsp Malvani masala, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder, and fry for 3 minutes until the oil separates and the gravy turns red.
