Add the parboiled vegetables, 3 kokum pieces, 1 cup water and the remaining salt, and simmer for 8 minutes so the vegetables soak up the spice.
Lower the heat, pour in 1 cup thin coconut milk, warm through for 3 minutes without boiling, and finish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Kokum gives a gentle coastal tang; soak the pieces in a little warm water first if they are very dry.
Add the coconut milk on low heat only, so the gravy stays smooth and does not split.
Malvani masala is fierier than kolhapuri masala, so adjust the extra chilli powder to taste.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with rice bhakri, neer dosa or steamed rice, garnished with coriander and a coconut-oil drizzle.

variations.name: Classic Veg Makhanwala
variations.description: A rich Punjabi restaurant classic where mixed vegetables bathe in a velvety buttery tomato gravy. The smooth makhani base is mildly sweet, glossy and fragrant with kasuri methi, coating tender vegetables in creamy comfort. It is the vegetarian cousin of butter chicken, beloved at wedding buffets.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee builds the makhani base and gives the buttery gravy its glossy, festive richness

steps: Boil 5 chopped tomatoes, 1 chopped onion and 15 cashews with 1 cup water for 10 minutes until soft, then cool, blend smooth and strain for a silky gravy.
Parboil 3 cups mixed vegetables in salted water for 5 minutes until just tender, then drain and set aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium heat, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in the strained tomato-cashew puree, add 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tbsp coriander powder and 1/2 tsp sugar, and cook for 8 minutes until the ghee floats and the gravy thickens.
Add the parboiled vegetables with 1/2 cup water and 1 tsp salt, cover and simmer for 8 minutes so they soak up the buttery gravy.
Lower the heat, stir in 4 tbsp cream, 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi and 3/4 tsp garam masala, warm through for 2 minutes without boiling, and serve.
tips: Straining the tomato-cashew puree is the key to the signature smooth, glossy makhani texture.
A little sugar balances the tomato acidity and gives makhanwala its gentle sweetness.
Add the cream on low heat only, and never boil after, so the gravy stays silky.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or jeera rice, finished with a swirl of cream and a scatter of kasuri methi.

variations.name: Dhaba-Style Veg Makhanwala
variations.description: A rustic dhaba version cooked in a handi with a chunkier onion-tomato masala and a smoky charcoal finish. Less silky and more robust than the restaurant version, it carries a bold, homely spicing and a hint of dhungar smoke. It is the hearty makhanwala served hot off the highway tandoor.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee gives the handi gravy its rich dhaba aroma and glossy finish

steps: Parboil 3 cups mixed vegetables in salted water for 5 minutes until just tender, then drain and set aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a handi on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add 3 finely chopped onions and fry until deep golden-brown, about 8 minutes.
Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then 4 finely chopped tomatoes and cook covered until pulpy and the ghee separates, around 8 minutes.
Lower the heat and add 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tbsp coriander powder and 1/2 tsp turmeric, roasting for 1 minute until the masala looks glossy.
Add the parboiled vegetables with 1 cup water and the remaining salt, cover and simmer for 10 minutes, then stir in 2 tbsp cream and 1 tsp garam masala.

For the dhaba smokiness, place a small bowl in the handi with a lit charcoal piece, drizzle a little ghee over it, cover for 2 minutes to trap the smoke, then remove and finish with 1 tsp kasuri methi and 3 tbsp coriander.
tips: The charcoal dhungar step is optional but gives the true smoky dhaba aroma, so try it if you can.
Brown the onions well and keep the tomato masala chunky for the rustic dhaba texture.
Use less cream than the restaurant version to keep it robust rather than plush.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tandoori roti or laccha paratha, topped with coriander, ginger juliennes and a ghee drizzle.

variations.name: White Makhani Veg Makhanwala
variations.description: A regal white-gravy variation where the vegetables rest in a pale, creamy cashew-and-melon-seed sauce with no tomato at all. Delicately spiced with cardamom and white pepper, it is mild, elegant and mildly sweet, in the Mughlai shahi tradition. Saffron threads lend fragrance and a faint golden glow.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries the delicate white gravy and gives it a shahi, buttery smoothness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: A few saffron threads add fragrance and a faint golden glow to the pale shahi gravy

steps: Soak 18 cashews and 1 tbsp melon seeds in warm water for 15 minutes, then grind to a very smooth white paste; soak 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk.
Boil 2 chopped onions with 2 slit green chillies for 5 minutes, cool and grind to a smooth pale paste; parboil 3 cups mixed vegetables until just tender and drain.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on low-medium heat, add 3 lightly crushed cardamom pods and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, and fry gently for 1 minute without browning.
Add the onion paste and cook on low heat for 5 minutes, keeping it pale, then stir in the cashew-melon paste and cook 3 minutes without letting it colour.
Whisk 1/3 cup yogurt smooth and add it slowly off the heat, then return to low heat with 3/4 cup water, 1/2 tsp white pepper and 1 tsp salt and simmer for 5 minutes.
Add the parboiled vegetables and simmer 6 minutes, then stir in 3 tbsp cream and the saffron milk, warm through for 2 minutes without boiling, and serve.
tips: Keep the heat low throughout and do not brown the onion or cashew paste, so the gravy stays white.
Add the yogurt off the heat and whisk it in slowly so it does not split in the delicate gravy.
White pepper instead of red chilli keeps both the heat gentle and the colour pale.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with saffron pulao or sheermal, garnished with slivered almonds and a few saffron strands.

variations.name: Jain Veg Makhanwala (No Onion-Garlic)
variations.description: A satvik Jain version of the buttery classic made entirely without onion, garlic or root vegetables. The creamy tomato-cashew gravy leans on ginger-free spicing, magaz and cream for body, with above-ground vegetables like cauliflower and capsicum. It proves makhanwala can be just as rich within Jain rules.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee gives the onion-free Jain gravy its buttery body and richness

steps: Boil 5 chopped tomatoes with 16 cashews and 1 tbsp melon seeds and 1 cup water for 10 minutes until soft, then cool, blend smooth and strain for a silky gravy.
Parboil 3 cups of above-ground vegetables and paneer cubes in salted water for 4 minutes until just tender, then drain.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 15 seconds until fragrant.
Pour in the strained tomato-cashew puree, add 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tbsp coriander powder and 1/2 tsp sugar, and cook for 8 minutes until the ghee floats and the gravy thickens.
Add the parboiled vegetables and paneer with 1/2 cup water and 1 tsp salt, and simmer for 6 minutes so they take on the gravy.
Lower the heat, stir in 4 tbsp cream, 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi and 3/4 tsp garam masala, warm through for 2 minutes without boiling, and serve.
tips: The cashew and magaz paste replaces the body that onion usually gives, so grind it really smooth.
Use only above-ground vegetables to keep the dish strictly Jain; skip potato and carrot.
A little sugar rounds out the tomato tang in the absence of onion sweetness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with phulka or plain jeera rice, finished with a swirl of cream and crushed kasuri methi.

variations.name: Classic Surti Undhiyu
variations.description: The grand Surti winter casserole that anchors every Gujarati Uttarayan feast: surti papdi, purple yam, sweet potato, raw banana and stuffed baby brinjals slow-cooked with fried methi muthia in a fragrant green masala of coconut, coriander and fresh green garlic. Rich, sweet-savoury and deeply aromatic, it is Gujarat's most celebrated one-pot dish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil both fries the muthia and slow-cooks the vegetables, the traditional undhiyu fat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery gives the masala its signature Surti sweet-savoury balance against the earthy winter vegetables

steps: Make the muthia by kneading 0.75 cup besan with 0.75 cup chopped methi leaves, 0.5 tsp ajwain, a pinch of turmeric, 0.5 tsp salt and a little oil into a firm dough, then shape into small dumplings and deep-fry in Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium heat for 4-5 minutes until golden; drain and set aside.

Grind or mix a green masala from 0.75 cup grated coconut, 1 cup coriander, 0.5 cup green garlic, 2 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, 2 tbsp sesame seeds, 2 tbsp dhana-jeera, 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp salt into a thick coarse paste.
Slit 6 small brinjals and 8 baby potatoes and stuff them generously with a spoonful of the green masala, reserving the rest.

Heat 5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a heavy-bottomed pot, add the 300 g destringed papdi and toss with 2 tbsp of the masala, then layer in the 250 g cubed yam, sweet potato, raw banana, stuffed potatoes and stuffed brinjals.

Spread the remaining green masala over the layers, sprinkle 0.5 cup water around the sides, cover tightly, and cook on low heat for 35-40 minutes, gently turning once midway, until all the vegetables are fork-tender.
Fold in the fried muthia in the last 8-10 minutes so they soak up the juices without turning soggy, then rest the undhiyu covered for 10 minutes and garnish with extra coriander before serving.
tips: Layer the vegetables by cooking time, hardest at the bottom nearest the heat, so everything finishes together without overcooking the softer pieces.
Cook strictly on low heat and resist stirring too often; undhiyu is meant to steam gently in its own masala, not fry.
Fry the muthia a shade darker than you think, as they soften considerably once added to the pot.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the festive undhiyu hot with puris and a bowl of shrikhand, the classic Gujarati Uttarayan spread.

variations.name: Kathiyawadi Undhiyu
variations.description: The bolder Saurashtra rendition that drops the muthia and sweetness in favour of a fiery garlic-and-red-chilli masala thickened with roasted peanuts and sesame. Smoky, pungent and far spicier than the Surti classic, it lets the winter vegetables carry a robust, rustic heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Nutty gingelly oil deepens the sesame-peanut masala that defines this robust Kathiyawadi undhiyu

steps: Dry-roast 3 tbsp sesame seeds and 0.5 cup grated dry coconut on low heat for 2-3 minutes, then grind with 12 garlic cloves, 5 dried red chillies and 0.5 cup roasted peanuts into a coarse, fiery masala.
Mix this masala with 2 tbsp dhana-jeera, 2 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp salt, then slit 6 brinjals and 10 baby potatoes and stuff them with a generous spoon of the paste.
Heat 0.4 cup Anveshan Sesame Oil in a heavy pot on medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 1 chopped onion and fry for 4 minutes until golden.
Add the 250 g destringed papdi and 250 g cubed yam, toss with 2 tbsp of the remaining masala, and cook for 5 minutes, then nestle in the stuffed potatoes and brinjals.

Spread any leftover masala over the top, add 0.5 cup water, cover tightly, and cook on low heat for 30-35 minutes, turning gently once, until the vegetables are tender and coated in a thick, oily red masala.
Rest for 10 minutes, then garnish with 0.5 cup chopped coriander and serve; this version stays savoury-hot with no added sweetness.
tips: Grind the peanut-sesame masala coarse, not smooth, for the rugged Kathiyawadi texture.
The stuffing is where all the heat lives, so pack the brinjals and potatoes generously.
This undhiyu keeps well and tastes even fierier the next day once the masala settles into the vegetables.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thick bajra rotla and white butter, plus sliced onion and a green chilli on the side.

variations.name: Instant Pressure-Cooker Undhiyu
variations.description: A weeknight shortcut that captures undhiyu's spirit in a fraction of the time by pressure-cooking the vegetables with a quick green masala, no muthia-frying or long slow layering. It trades a little depth for speed while keeping the coconut-coriander soul intact.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil tempers the masala and gives the quick undhiyu a clean, rich body

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A spoon of jaggery restores the sweet-savoury balance the long slow cooking would normally build

steps: Mix a quick masala from 0.5 cup grated coconut, 0.75 cup coriander, 2 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, 1.5 tbsp dhana-jeera, 0.75 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 2 tsp salt into a thick paste.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pressure cooker on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp ajwain and 0.25 tsp asafoetida for 30 seconds.
Add the 250 g destringed papdi, 3 cubed potatoes, 1 cubed sweet potato, 4 quartered brinjals and 0.75 cup green peas, then fold in the green masala until every piece is coated.
Pour in 0.5 cup water, close the lid, and pressure-cook on medium heat for 2 whistles, then turn off and let the pressure release naturally.
Open the cooker, gently fold the vegetables so the masala that settled at the bottom coats everything, and simmer uncovered for 3-4 minutes to thicken if watery.
Rest for 5 minutes and serve; the natural release keeps the softer vegetables intact rather than mushy.
tips: Cut the harder vegetables slightly smaller than the softer ones so everything cooks evenly in two whistles.
Let the pressure drop naturally; force-releasing it breaks down the delicate papdi and brinjal.
Add a handful of leftover fried muthia at the end if you have them, for a nod to the classic.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve this quick undhiyu with hot phulka or steamed rice for an easy weeknight Gujarati meal.

variations.name: Umbadiyu Green Herb Undhiyu
variations.description: The rustic South-Gujarat umbadiyu, a barely-spiced smoked cousin of undhiyu where whole vegetables are cooked with an abundance of fresh green garlic, ajwain and coconut and no onion, tomato or heavy masala. Earthy, herby and clean, it lets the winter produce and green garlic shine on their own.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A generous slick of wood-pressed groundnut oil is all the fat this minimal, herb-led umbadiyu needs

steps: Mix a fresh green masala by hand from 1 cup chopped green garlic, 0.75 cup grated coconut, 1 cup coriander, 4 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp ajwain, 0.75 tsp turmeric, 1 tbsp dhana-jeera and 2 tsp salt, keeping it coarse and chunky.
Slit 6 whole brinjals and stuff them with a spoon of the green masala, reserving the rest.
Pour 5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil into a heavy pot and layer in the 250 g destringed papdi, then the 200 g cubed yam, sweet potato and raw banana slices, scattering masala between each layer.
Set the stuffed brinjals on top, spread the remaining green masala over everything, and sprinkle 0.5 cup water around the edges.
Cover tightly and cook on very low heat for 35-40 minutes without stirring, letting the vegetables steam in the herby oil until fork-tender and infused with green garlic.
Gently fold once at the end to coat everything in the pan juices, rest for 10 minutes, and serve without any added sweetness.
tips: Green garlic is essential and seasonal; this dish is built around its mellow, grassy pungency, so use it generously.
Keep the heat very low and do not stir mid-cook, so the layered vegetables steam gently rather than fry.
The whole point is minimalism, so resist adding onion, tomato or garam masala, which would turn it into ordinary undhiyu.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve this earthy umbadiyu with hot bajra rotla and a wedge of lemon, the way South-Gujarat villages eat it in winter.

variations.name: Classic Dry Gobi Manchurian
variations.description: This Classic Gobi Manchurian is the beloved Indo-Chinese starter of crisp-fried cauliflower florets tossed in a punchy soy-garlic-chilli sauce. Served semi-dry, each floret stays crunchy on the outside while soaking up the glossy, tangy-spicy coating.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: its high smoke point fries the florets crisp without turning greasy

steps: Cut 1 medium cauliflower into bite-sized florets and blanch them in salted hot water for 3 minutes, then drain thoroughly and pat dry.
Whisk 4 tbsp cornflour, 3 tbsp all-purpose flour, 0.5 tsp salt and enough water to make a thick coating batter, then dip the florets to coat evenly.
Heat 1 cup Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180 C and deep-fry the florets in batches for 4 to 5 minutes until golden and crisp, then drain on paper.
In a wok, keep 2 tbsp of the frying oil and stir-fry the finely chopped garlic, ginger and 3 green chillies on high heat for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the cubed onion and capsicum and toss on high for 2 minutes, then pour in 2 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tbsp green chilli sauce, 2 tbsp ketchup and 0.5 tsp salt and cook for 1 minute until glossy.
Add the fried cauliflower, toss on high heat for 1 to 2 minutes to coat every floret, garnish with 4 tbsp spring onion and serve immediately.
tips: Blanch the cauliflower before frying so the insides cook through while the coating turns crisp.
Toss and serve within minutes, as the florets soften quickly once they meet the sauce.
For extra crunch, double-fry the florets for a minute just before tossing them in the sauce.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot as a starter with extra spring onion greens, or alongside hakka noodles as a main.

variations.name: Gravy Gobi Manchurian
variations.description: The restaurant-style saucy version where fried cauliflower simmers in a thick, glossy brown Manchurian gravy. Built to be spooned over rice or noodles, it trades the dry starter's crunch for a slurp-worthy, deeply savoury sauce.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: a light wood-pressed oil that keeps the deep-fried florets clean-tasting

steps: Blanch 1 medium cauliflower cut into florets for 3 minutes, drain, then coat in a batter of 3 tbsp cornflour, 3 tbsp all-purpose flour, 0.5 tsp salt and water.
Deep-fry the florets in 1 cup Anveshan Sunflower Oil at 180 C for 4 to 5 minutes until golden and crisp, then set aside.
In 2 tbsp of the oil, stir-fry the minced garlic, ginger and chopped onion on high heat for 2 minutes until aromatic.
Pour in 2 cups vegetable stock, 2 tbsp soy sauce, 1.5 tbsp red chilli sauce, 1 tsp vinegar, 0.5 tsp black pepper and 0.5 tsp salt and bring to a boil.
Mix the remaining 2 tbsp cornflour with 4 tbsp cold water and stir it into the gravy, cooking for 2 to 3 minutes until it turns thick and glossy.
Add the fried cauliflower, simmer for 2 minutes so the florets absorb the sauce, garnish with 4 tbsp spring onion and serve hot.
tips: Always slurry the cornflour in cold water before adding, or it will clump in the hot gravy.
Add the florets just before serving if you want them to keep a little crunch inside the sauce.
A pinch of sugar rounds off the tang of the vinegar and chilli sauce beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle generously over steamed rice or hakka noodles and finish with a scatter of spring onion greens.

variations.name: Schezwan Gobi Manchurian
variations.description: A fiery avatar where the fried cauliflower is tossed in a bold, garlicky Schezwan sauce loaded with dry red chillies. Spicier and more pungent than the classic, it carries a lingering heat that makes it a favourite for chilli lovers.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: withstands high heat to fry the florets and bloom the fiery chilli paste

steps: Blanch 1 medium cauliflower cut into florets for 3 minutes, drain, then coat in a thick batter of 4 tbsp cornflour, 2 tbsp rice flour, 0.5 tsp salt and water.
Deep-fry the florets in 1 cup Anveshan Groundnut Oil at 180 C for 5 minutes until extra crisp, then drain well.
In 2 tbsp of the oil, fry 5 broken dry red chillies and minced garlic on high heat for 30 seconds until they release a sharp aroma.
Add the grated ginger and chopped onion and stir-fry for 2 minutes, then stir in 4 tbsp Schezwan sauce, 1 tbsp soy sauce, 0.5 tsp sugar and 0.5 tsp salt and cook for 1 minute.
Add the fried cauliflower and toss on high heat for 2 minutes so every floret is coated in the deep-red fiery sauce.
Garnish with 4 tbsp spring onion, give a final toss off the heat, and serve at once while crunchy.
tips: The rice flour in the batter keeps the florets crunchier for longer under the spicy sauce.
Adjust the Schezwan sauce gradually, as brands vary widely in heat and salt.
Fry the dry chillies only until aromatic; burnt chillies turn the sauce bitter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a bold starter with a cooling cucumber-onion salad, or over schezwan fried rice.

variations.name: Baked Gobi Manchurian
variations.description: A lighter oven-baked take where the battered cauliflower is roasted crisp instead of deep-fried, then folded into a quick stir-fried Manchurian sauce. It delivers the familiar tang and crunch with a fraction of the oil, ideal for a healthier weeknight treat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: a light brush and finishing drizzle add a nutty Indo-Chinese aroma

steps: Preheat the oven to 220 C and blanch 1 medium cauliflower cut into florets for 3 minutes, then drain and pat dry.
Whisk 4 tbsp cornflour, 3 tbsp chickpea flour, 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, 0.5 tsp salt and water into a thick batter and coat the florets.
Arrange the florets on a lined tray, bake for 20 to 22 minutes turning once, until crisp and golden at the edges.
Meanwhile heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a wok and stir-fry the minced garlic, ginger and 2 green chillies on high for 30 seconds.
Add the chopped onion, toss for 2 minutes, then add 2 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tbsp green chilli sauce, 2 tbsp ketchup and 0.5 tsp salt and cook for 1 minute until glossy.
Fold in the baked cauliflower, toss for 1 minute, garnish with 4 tbsp spring onion and serve immediately.
tips: Space the florets apart on the tray so they roast crisp instead of steaming together.
Chickpea flour in the batter helps it cling and crisp better in the dry oven heat.
Toss the baked florets in the sauce only at the last moment to keep their crunch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a lighter party starter with a lime wedge, or over a bowl of clear vegetable soup.

variations.name: Classic Gobi Matar
variations.description: This Classic Gobi Matar is a homely North-Indian dry sabzi of cauliflower florets and green peas cooked with onion, tomato and everyday spices until just tender. The florets stay separate and lightly caramelised, making it a perfect no-fuss lunchbox and roti companion.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: its pungent warmth is the traditional fat for this dry Punjabi sabzi

steps: Cut 1 medium cauliflower into bite-sized florets, wash them, and drain well so they roast rather than steam in the pan.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a wide kadai to smoking point, then lower the heat to medium and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 20 seconds.
Add the finely chopped large onion and saute on medium heat for 4 to 5 minutes until soft and golden at the edges.

Stir in 1 tbsp ginger garlic paste and cook for 1 minute, then add the chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 4 minutes until the tomatoes break down and oil separates.
Add the cauliflower florets and 1 cup green peas, toss to coat in the masala, cover and cook on low heat for 12 to 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the gobi is fork-tender with a light char.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala, fold gently, garnish with 3 tbsp fresh coriander and serve hot.
tips: Keep the lid on but stir every few minutes so the florets cook through without turning mushy or sticking.
If using frozen peas, add them in the last 6 minutes so they stay bright green and do not overcook.
A squeeze of lemon at the end lifts the whole sabzi and balances the mustard oil's pungency.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulka rotis and a bowl of boondi raita, or tuck it into a paratha roll for lunch.

variations.name: Bengali Gobi Matar with Panch Phoron
variations.description: A Bengali-style phulkopir torkari where cauliflower and peas are tempered with the five-spice panch phoron and finished with a subtle sweetness. Slow-cooked in mustard oil, it turns deeply aromatic with a gentle, homely warmth quite different from the North-Indian version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: essential for authentic Bengali torkari, lending its signature sharp aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a touch of unrefined sweetness balances the spices the Bengali way

steps: Cut 1 medium cauliflower into florets and dice 1 potato, then lightly fry both in 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil on medium heat for 5 minutes until golden-edged, and set aside.
In the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil, add 1 bay leaf and 1 tsp panch phoron and let the seeds splutter for about 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 tbsp ginger paste and 2 slit green chillies and saute for 1 minute, then stir in the chopped tomato, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp cumin powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 3 minutes until pulpy.
Return the fried cauliflower and potato, add 1 cup green peas, and mix gently to coat everything in the masala.
Pour in half a cup of hot water, cover, and simmer on low heat for 12 to 15 minutes until the vegetables are tender and the gravy is nearly dry.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, cook uncovered for 2 minutes, and serve warm.
tips: Do not grind the panch phoron; the whole seeds are meant to stay intact for bursts of flavour.
Frying the potato and cauliflower first keeps them from breaking during the simmer.
This torkari tastes even better after resting for an hour as the panch phoron aroma deepens.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with steamed rice and a drizzle of ghee, or with luchi for a classic Bengali breakfast.

variations.name: Restaurant-Style Gobi Matar Masala
variations.description: A richer semi-dry version where cauliflower and peas simmer in a smooth onion-tomato-cashew masala finished with cream and kasuri methi. It is more indulgent than the everyday sabzi, with a glossy coating built for special-occasion thalis.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee gives the masala a rich restaurant-style body and aroma

steps: Boil the chopped onions, tomatoes and 12 cashews in 1 cup water for 8 minutes, cool, and blend to a smooth puree.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan, add 1 tbsp ginger garlic paste and saute on medium heat for 1 minute until raw smell fades.
Pour in the blended puree along with 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook on medium heat for 8 to 10 minutes until the ghee separates at the edges.
Add the cauliflower florets and 1 cup green peas, mix well, add half a cup of water, cover and simmer on low heat for 12 minutes until the gobi is tender.
Crush 1 tsp kasuri methi between your palms and add it with 0.5 tsp garam masala, then stir in 3 tbsp fresh cream and cook for 2 minutes on low heat.
Simmer for a final minute until the masala clings glossily to the florets, then serve hot.
tips: Blend the masala completely smooth and strain it if you want the silkiest restaurant finish.
Add the cream on low heat only, so it enriches the gravy without splitting.
Par-boiling the cauliflower for 3 minutes before adding speeds up cooking for last-minute guests.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or jeera rice and a wedge of onion, garnished with a swirl of cream.

variations.name: South-Indian Gobi Matar Poriyal
variations.description: A Tamil-style poriyal where cauliflower and peas are stir-fried with a mustard-curry-leaf tempering and finished with fresh grated coconut. Light, dry and gently spiced, it swaps the North-Indian masala for the clean, nutty flavours of a South-Indian meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed coconut oil gives the poriyal its authentic South-Indian fragrance

steps: Cut 1 medium cauliflower into small florets and steam them with 1 cup green peas and 0.25 tsp turmeric for 6 minutes until just tender but firm.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan and crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 1 tsp urad dal and fry until golden, about 30 seconds.
Add 2 broken dry red chillies, 12 curry leaves, 2 slit green chillies and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them splutter for 20 seconds.
Add the steamed cauliflower and peas along with 1 tsp salt and toss gently on medium heat for 4 to 5 minutes until any moisture dries off.
Sprinkle 4 tbsp grated coconut over the vegetables and stir-fry for 2 minutes until the coconut is warm and fragrant but still fresh.
Turn off the heat and serve the poriyal warm as a dry side dish.
tips: Steam the cauliflower only until just tender so it holds its shape during the stir-fry.
Use fresh grated coconut for the best flavour, adding it right at the end so it stays moist.
Roasting the urad dal to a golden colour is key for the nutty crunch that defines a good poriyal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a side with sambar rice, rasam rice or curd rice for a complete South-Indian meal.

variations.name: Classic Hyderabadi Dum Veg Biryani
variations.description: The definitive Nizami biryani where marinated vegetables and half-cooked basmati are layered raw and finished on slow dum, so the rice steams in the fragrant spice-and-mint vapours. Fried onions, saffron milk and mint perfume every grain while the vegetables cook gently in their own yogurt marinade. Sealed and cooked undisturbed, it emerges with separate, glossy grains and a deep, layered aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Fries the birista and is drizzled between layers so each spoonful of rice carries a nutty richness

ingredients.name: Whole spices (bay leaf, cardamom, cloves, cinnamon)
Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Steeped in warm milk and drizzled over the top layer for the signature golden streaks and floral aroma

steps: Marinate 3 cups mixed vegetables with 1 cup thick yogurt, 2 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 2 tsp biryani masala, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, half the mint and coriander and 1 tsp salt, and rest 20 minutes.
Thinly slice 3 onions and fry in 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium heat for 10-12 minutes until deep golden and crisp, then drain the birista on paper, reserving the ghee.
Soak 2 cups basmati 20 minutes, then boil in plenty of salted water with the whole spices for 6-7 minutes until 70 percent cooked with a firm core, and drain.

In a heavy pot spread the marinated vegetables, layer over the drained rice, scatter half the birista, remaining mint and coriander, and drizzle 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee plus the Anveshan Saffron steeped in 3 tbsp warm milk.
Cover with a tight lid or seal with dough, cook on high for 3 minutes until you hear a sizzle, then reduce to the lowest flame over a tava and dum for 25 minutes.
Rest 10 minutes off the heat, then open and gently fold from the bottom with a flat spoon so the vegetables and golden rice mix without breaking the grains.
tips: Undercook the rice to exactly 70 percent; it finishes cooking on dum and will turn mushy if boiled fully first.
A cast-iron tava under the pot diffuses the heat and prevents the bottom layer from scorching during the long dum.
Fry the onions till genuinely deep-golden and crisp, as pale birista turns soggy and robs the biryani of its signature sweetness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling mirchi ka salan or a simple onion-tomato raita and a wedge of lemon to cut the richness.

variations.name: Kachi-Style Raw Layer Veg Biryani
variations.description: A purist take on the Hyderabadi kachi method where firm vegetables and soaked raw rice cook together entirely on dum, with no pre-boiling of the rice. Everything depends on precise liquid and a flour-sealed lid that traps every drop of steam. The result is intensely aromatic rice that has absorbed the vegetable-yogurt juices directly.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Fries the birista and enriches the raw rice layer so it cooks up glossy despite the no-boil method

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Bloomed in warm milk and poured over the raw rice so the colour seeps down as the dum steams

steps: Fry 3 thinly sliced onions in 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium heat for 10-12 minutes until crisp and golden, then drain and reserve.
Marinate 3 cups baby potatoes and carrots with 1.25 cups yogurt, 2 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 1 tbsp green chilli paste, 1.5 tsp garam masala, half the mint and 1.5 tsp salt for 20 minutes.
Rinse and soak 2 cups basmati for 30 minutes, then drain; spread the marinated vegetables in a heavy pot and pile the raw soaked rice evenly on top.
Pour 2.5 cups hot water gently down the side, scatter the birista and remaining mint, drizzle 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and the Anveshan Saffron steeped in 0.25 cups warm milk.
Seal the lid with a rope of whole-wheat dough, cook on high 5 minutes until steam builds, then dum on the lowest flame over a tava for 30 minutes.
Rest 10 minutes, crack the seal, and fluff gently from the edges so the fully-cooked grains lift away from the tender vegetables.
tips: Measure the water precisely at 1.25 times the rice volume, since there is no boiling stage to correct a wet pot.
Use quick-cooking vegetables like baby potatoes and carrots; dense ones may stay firm in the same time the rice needs.
Do not lift the lid during dum, as losing the trapped steam leaves the raw rice unevenly cooked.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a tangy tomato-peanut chutney and thin sliced onions soaked in lemon for a true kachi-biryani spread.

variations.name: Restaurant-Style Paneer Veg Biryani
variations.description: The rich, mildly spiced biryani you find at Hyderabadi restaurants, built on a fried-paneer and cashew base with a creamier, redder gravy layered under the rice. Kasuri methi and a touch of cream round the edges for a crowd-pleasing plate. It is showier and milder than the home dum, made to be scooped straight from a sizzling handi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Fries the paneer and onions to a golden base, giving the restaurant gravy its glossy richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: A neutral wood-pressed oil for shallow-frying the paneer without masking its milky flavour

steps: Shallow-fry 250 g paneer cubes in 2 tbsp Anveshan Sunflower Oil on medium heat for 2-3 minutes until light gold, then lift out and soak in warm salted water to keep them soft.
Soak a handful of cashews, grind to a smooth paste, and boil 2 cups basmati in salted water for 6 minutes until 70 percent done, then drain.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, fry 3 sliced onions on medium heat for 8 minutes until golden, add 2 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until the raw smell fades.
Stir in 1 cup tomato puree, the cashew paste, 2 tsp biryani masala and 1.5 tsp salt, and simmer 8 minutes until the gravy thickens and releases ghee at the edges.
Fold in the fried paneer, crushed 1 tbsp kasuri methi and 3 tbsp cream off high heat, then layer the drained rice over the gravy and scatter coriander.
Cover and dum on the lowest flame for 15 minutes, then rest 8 minutes and fold gently so the creamy paneer gravy coats the rice.
tips: Soak the fried paneer in warm water so the cubes stay pillowy instead of turning rubbery in the finished biryani.
Add the cream only after lowering the heat, or the acidic tomato gravy can cause it to split.
For a smoky dhaba touch, rest a burning charcoal in a small bowl inside the pot for two minutes before the final dum.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a hot handi with a boondi raita and a side of pickled onions, garnished with a swirl of cream and fried cashews.

variations.name: Tehari One-Pot Veg Biryani
variations.description: A homely, economical tehari where rice and vegetables cook together in one pot with the spices, skipping the separate boil-and-layer ritual. Popular in everyday Hyderabadi and Awadhi kitchens, it leans on whole spices and green chilli heat rather than heavy marination. Quick, forgiving and deeply comforting, it is the weeknight cousin of the grand dum biryani.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Blooms the whole spices at the start so the one-pot rice carries a warm, layered aroma

ingredients.name: Whole spices (cinnamon, cloves, cardamom, shahi jeera)

steps: Rinse and soak 2 cups basmati for 20 minutes and drain; heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot and crackle the whole spices for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 2 sliced onions and fry on medium heat for 6-7 minutes until golden, then stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 3 slit green chillies for 1 minute.
Mix in 2 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1.5 tsp salt, and cook 4 minutes until the tomatoes collapse into a thick masala.
Add 3 cups mixed vegetables and saute 3 minutes, then fold in the drained rice and half the mint and coriander and toast gently for 2 minutes.
Pour in 3.25 cups hot water, bring to a rolling boil, taste for salt, then cover and cook on the lowest flame for 15 minutes until the water is absorbed.
Rest 10 minutes off the heat, then fluff with a fork, scattering the remaining mint and coriander over the top.
tips: Keep the water at roughly 1.6 times the soaked rice so the one-pot grains stay separate and never gluey.
Toast the drained rice in the masala for a couple of minutes before adding water; it helps the grains hold their shape.
Let the pot rest undisturbed after cooking so the steam finishes the grains and they lift cleanly with a fork.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve straight from the pot with a bowl of cucumber-onion raita and crisp papad for a fuss-free weeknight meal.

variations.name: Classic Surti Lilva Kachori
variations.description: The winter treasure of Surat: fresh tuvar lilva coarsely crushed and cooked with coconut, sesame and a sweet-sour spice hit, then sealed in a khapli atta shell and fried until it blisters. The filling stays green and nubbly rather than pasty, and each bite swings from savoury to a gentle jaggery sweetness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: emmer wheat gives the kachori shell a nutty crunch and lets it fry crisp without the maida a shop version leans on

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil fries the kachoris clean and flake-crisp, and its faint nuttiness suits the coconut filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: unrefined jaggery gives the Surti sweet-sour balance its warm molasses note instead of flat white sugar

steps: Rub 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil into 1.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt until the flour clumps when pressed, then add roughly 0.5 cup water little by little and knead a firm, tight dough; cover and rest it for 20 minutes.
Pulse 2 cups fresh tuvar lilva in short bursts to a coarse crush with visible half-peas, never a smooth paste, so the filling keeps its signature nubbly bite.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add 1.5 tbsp green chilli-ginger paste and fry for 1 minute until the raw smell lifts.

Add the crushed lilva with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt and saute on medium-low for 6-7 minutes until the peas lose their raw grassiness, then stir in 0.5 cup grated coconut, 2 tbsp sesame seeds and 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook 3 more minutes until dry and glossy; finish off the heat with 1 tbsp lemon juice and 3 tbsp coriander, then cool completely.

Divide the rested dough into 10 balls, roll each into a 3 inch cup, spoon in about 1.5 tbsp cooled filling, gather the edges over the top, pinch shut and flatten gently into a thick round without exposing the filling.

Heat the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil to a moderate 150C and slip in 3-4 kachoris at a time, frying on low-medium for 7-8 minutes and turning often until they are pale gold, blistered and crisp right through; drain on a rack, not paper, so they stay shatteringly crisp.
tips: Fry on a moderate, patient heat — rushing on high leaves the shell raw and doughy inside while browning outside too fast.
Use lilva while the peas are still bright and tender; older, starchy lilva turns the filling gluey and dull.
Cool the filling fully before stuffing, as warm filling steams the dough and makes the kachoris burst in the oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with sweet date-tamarind chutney and a fiery green coriander chutney, and a cup of masala chai on a cold Surat evening.

variations.name: Kathiyawadi Lilva Kachori (Green Garlic & Peanut)
variations.description: The bolder Saurashtra cousin: the lilva filling is fired up with pounded green garlic, crushed roasted peanuts and a rough red-chilli heat, with the sweetness dialled right back. Rolled into smaller, sharper kachoris, it eats hot and pungent, the way roadside stalls around Rajkot serve it in winter.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: the sturdy emmer shell holds up to this drier, spicier filling and crisps without cracking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Saurashtra fries almost everything in groundnut oil, and the wood-pressed version keeps that regional flavour honest

steps: Knead a firm dough from 1.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 tsp ajwain seeds, 0.5 tsp salt and 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil rubbed in, adding about 0.5 cup water; wrap and rest for 20 minutes while you build the filling.
Coarsely crush 2 cups fresh tuvar lilva to a rough, grainy texture, keeping plenty of broken half-peas for bite.
Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, add 0.25 tsp hing and 4 tbsp chopped green garlic and fry for 90 seconds until the garlic smells sweet and toasty.

Tip in the crushed lilva with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander-cumin powder and 1 tsp salt and roast on medium-low for 7-8 minutes until dry and fragrant, then fold through 0.5 cup crushed roasted peanuts and 1 tbsp lemon juice and cool the mixture fully.
Shape 12 small dough cups, fill each with about 1 tbsp of the spicy lilva, seal the edges tightly and press into compact 2 inch rounds so no filling peeks out.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 150C and fry the kachoris in small batches on low-medium for 6-7 minutes, turning frequently, until deep gold and hard-crisp; lift onto a rack to drain.
tips: Green garlic in peak winter is the authentic hit; out of season use 2 tbsp regular garlic plus 2 tbsp chopped garlic chives.
Crush the peanuts by hand so they stay in gritty pieces — a mixer turns them to paste and kills the crunch.
Keep these kachoris small and thick-walled; the drier, hotter filling needs a sturdier shell than the sweet Surti version.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with garlic-heavy lasan chutney and a glass of chaas, or tuck two into a pav for a rough-and-ready Kathiyawadi snack.

variations.name: Baked Lilva Kachori (Multigrain, Poha-Bound)
variations.description: A lighter oven take for those who love the filling but not the frying: the lilva is bound with a little roasted poha for body, packed into a multigrain shell brushed with olive oil, and baked until the crust turns biscuity and golden. Fewer calories, none of the sog, and it keeps beautifully in a lunchbox.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Multigrain Atta
ingredients.note: the multigrain blend bakes into a firm, biscuity crust that browns nicely without deep frying

ingredients.name: Anveshan Olive Oil
ingredients.note: olive oil goes into the dough and brushes the tops so the baked shell colours richly with almost no fat pooling

steps: Knead 1.5 cups Anveshan Multigrain Atta with 2 tbsp Anveshan Olive Oil, 0.5 tsp salt and about 0.5 cup water into a firm but pliable dough, then rest it covered for 20 minutes.
Dry-roast 3 tbsp thick poha on low heat for 2-3 minutes until crisp, then crush lightly — it will drink up any moisture and keep the baked filling from turning wet.
Coarsely crush 2 cups fresh tuvar lilva, then heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Olive Oil in a pan on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1 tsp crushed fennel for 30 seconds.

Add 1 inch grated ginger and 3 chopped green chillies for 1 minute, then the crushed lilva with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp amchur and 1 tsp salt; saute 6-7 minutes until dry, stir in the roasted poha and 3 tbsp coriander, and cool completely.

Roll the dough into 10 cups, fill each with about 1.5 tbsp of the lilva mixture, seal well and shape into neat rounds, then arrange on a lined tray and brush all over with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Olive Oil.
Bake in an oven preheated to 190C for 22-25 minutes, turning once halfway, until the shells are firm, golden and biscuity to the tap; cool 5 minutes on the tray so they crisp up before serving.
tips: Roasted poha is the secret to a dry baked filling — skip it and the moisture from the lilva will steam the crust soft.
Do not roll the shells too thin; a slightly thicker wall keeps the baked kachori from cracking as it colours.
These reheat well at 160C for 5 minutes, making them ideal for prepping a day ahead for tiffins.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling mint-yogurt dip and a wedge of lemon, or pack alongside a fresh cucumber salad for a wholesome tiffin.

variations.name: Lilva Kachori Chaat (Ragda-Topped)
variations.description: A street-cart reinvention where the crisp lilva kachori is crushed open and drowned in warm white-pea ragda, then loaded with yogurt, chutneys, onion and sev. It turns a winter snack into a full plate — hot, cold, sweet, sour and crunchy all colliding in one spoon.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoon of bilona ghee tempers the ragda and gives the chaat base a rich, rounded aroma the street version lacks

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery sweetens the tamarind chutney with a mellow, mineral depth instead of one-note sugar

steps: Soak 1 cup dried white peas overnight, then pressure cook with 3 cups water and 0.5 tsp salt for 5-6 whistles until completely soft and mashable.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium heat, add 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and the drained peas, mash a third of them against the pan, add a ladle of the cooking water and simmer 5 minutes into a thick, pourable ragda seasoned with 0.5 tsp salt.
Make a quick sweet chutney by simmering 3 tbsp tamarind pulp with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 0.5 tsp roasted cumin and a splash of water for 4-5 minutes until it coats a spoon, then cool.
Whisk 1 cup yogurt smooth with a pinch of salt and keep the coriander-mint chutney and chopped onion ready in separate bowls.

For each plate, crush 2 lilva kachoris open into a bowl, ladle over a generous spoon of hot ragda, then drizzle 2 tbsp whisked yogurt, 1 tbsp tamarind-jaggery chutney and 1 tbsp green chutney across the top.

Scatter chopped onion, a dusting of the remaining roasted cumin and red chilli, a fistful of nylon sev and fresh coriander over each portion and serve at once while the ragda is still warm and the sev crisp.
tips: Assemble each plate only when you are ready to eat; the sev and kachori turn soggy within minutes of the ragda hitting them.
Keep the ragda loose and pourable — if it thickens on standing, loosen it with a little hot water before serving.
Slightly stale, extra-crisp kachoris actually work better here, as they hold their crunch a moment longer under the toppings.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in wide bowls as a winter chaat-party centrepiece, with extra sev, chutneys and lemon wedges on the side for everyone to pile on.

variations.name: Classic Gujarati Methi Thepla
variations.description: The definitive Gujarati travel bread, a soft-yet-sturdy flatbread rolled thin from a wheat dough marbled with fresh fenugreek leaves, curd and dhana-jeera. Kneading in a little oil and yogurt keeps the theplas pliable for days, which is why every Gujarati train journey packs a stack of them. Roasted golden on the tava, they carry a gentle bitterness from the methi balanced by warm spice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The nutty ancient-wheat flour gives the thepla a soft crumb and keeps it pliable for days of travel

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A spoonful is worked into the dough for suppleness and the rest roasts each thepla to a golden, freckled finish

steps: In a wide bowl combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.25 cups besan, 1 cup finely chopped fenugreek leaves, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tbsp coriander-cumin powder, 1 tbsp sesame seeds, 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and 1 tsp salt, tossing so the methi is coated in flour.
Add 0.25 cups curd and 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, then drizzle in the 0.25 cups water a little at a time and knead 5 minutes into a smooth, medium-firm dough; rest it covered for 15 minutes.
Divide the dough into 12 balls, dust one with flour, and roll it out on a board into a thin 6-inch round, keeping the thickness even so it roasts evenly.
Lay the thepla on a medium-hot tava and cook for about 40 seconds until pale bubbles rise, then flip it over.
Smear 0.5 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on the surface, flip again, and press the edges with a spatula until golden-brown spots appear, about 1 minute per side.
Stack the cooked theplas under a cloth and repeat with the rest, rolling and roasting each one fresh.
tips: Chop the methi finely and add a pinch of salt to it 5 minutes before mixing; the leaves wilt and release moisture, so you need very little extra water.
Keep the dough slightly firmer than roti dough, which lets you roll the theplas paper-thin without them tearing.
Cooled theplas keep 3-4 days in an airtight box; a smear of oil while roasting is what gives them that shelf life.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a mound of sweet-sour chundo (mango chhundo), a dab of thick curd and a wedge of lemon pickle, Gujarati-thali style.

variations.name: Bajra Methi Thepla
variations.description: A rustic Kathiyawad winter version that swaps half the wheat for pearl-millet flour, giving a heavier, warming thepla richly flavoured with ajwain and crushed garlic. The bajra makes it denser and more filling than the classic, ideal against cold-weather appetites. It is patted a touch thicker to keep the low-gluten dough from cracking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Kneaded in for elasticity that the gluten-free bajra lacks, and drizzled on the tava to crisp the base

steps: Mix 1 cup bajra flour, 1 cup whole wheat flour, 0.75 cups chopped fenugreek, 1 tbsp garlic paste, 1 tsp carom seeds, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tbsp sesame seeds and 1 tsp salt in a bowl.
Work in 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, then add about 0.75 cups hot water a little at a time and knead 4-5 minutes into a firm but pliable dough while it is still warm.
Divide into 10 balls and roll each on a floured board into a 5-inch round about 3 mm thick, slightly thicker than a wheat thepla so the millet does not crack.
Slide onto a medium-hot tava, cook 45 seconds until the underside sets, then flip.
Drizzle 0.5 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil around the edge, flip once more, and roast each side 1-2 minutes, pressing gently until brown flecks form.
Wrap the finished theplas in a cloth to keep them soft and continue with the remaining dough.
tips: Knead bajra dough with hot water and work fast; the warmth gelatinises the starch and holds the crumbly millet together.
If the dough cracks at the edges while rolling, pinch and smooth them shut with a wet finger before it splits further.
These are heartier and best eaten warm, though they still pack well for a day's outing with a little extra oil in the dough.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a fiery garlic-chilli lasun chutney and a bowl of buttermilk (chaas) to cut the density of the millet.

variations.name: Dudhi Thepla
variations.description: A moist, mellow thepla from Surat kitchens where grated bottle gourd replaces most of the fenugreek, lending sweetness and a tender bite that stays soft long after cooking. The gourd's own water binds the dough so barely any is added, and a whisper of methi keeps it recognisably a thepla. A gentler take that children and elders both favour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Its warm nuttiness rounds out the mild gourd and roasts the theplas to a soft, golden finish

steps: Grate 1 cup bottle gourd, add 0.5 tsp of the salt, and set it aside 5 minutes so it weeps its moisture, but do not squeeze it dry.

In a bowl combine 2 cups whole wheat flour, the gourd with its liquid, 0.25 cups chopped fenugreek, 2 tbsp besan, 1 tbsp chilli-ginger paste, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp coriander powder, 1 tbsp sesame seeds, 3 tbsp coriander leaves and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt.
Add 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and knead into a soft dough using the gourd's water alone; add a splash more only if it feels dry, then rest 15 minutes.
Roll each of 12 balls into a thin 6-inch round on a floured board, dusting as needed since this dough is softer than usual.
Cook on a medium-hot tava for 40 seconds a side, smearing 0.5 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil on each face and pressing until golden spots appear.
Stack under a cloth and repeat, rolling each thepla just before it goes on the pan.
tips: Do not squeeze the grated gourd; its water is what binds this dough, so you may need no added liquid at all.
If the batter-soft dough sticks while rolling, chill it for 10 minutes to firm it up before shaping.
The gourd keeps these the softest of all theplas, staying tender in a lunchbox for a full day.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a spoon of jaggery-sweetened tomato sambharo or plain sweet mango pickle to lift the gentle, moist thepla.

variations.name: Sattu Protein Methi Thepla
variations.description: A modern high-protein reinvention that folds roasted-gram sattu and flax into the classic methi dough for a nuttier, more sustaining flatbread favoured by fitness-minded kitchens. The sattu deepens the savoury flavour and adds a subtle earthiness alongside the fenugreek. It stays satisfying for hours, making it a smart breakfast or gym-bag bread.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Roasted-gram flour packs the thepla with plant protein and a toasty, nutty depth the classic version lacks

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasts the protein-dense thepla to a fragrant golden finish and carries the fenugreek aroma

steps: Combine 1.5 cups whole wheat flour, 0.5 cups Anveshan Sattu, 0.75 cups chopped fenugreek, 2 tbsp flax powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tbsp ginger-chilli paste and 1 tsp salt in a bowl.

Add 0.3 cups curd and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then work in the 0.25 cups water gradually to make a firm, smooth dough; sattu drinks liquid, so add a little more water only if needed, then rest 15 minutes.
Divide into 11 balls and roll each into a thin 6-inch round, dusting lightly with flour so the sattu dough does not stick.
Place on a medium-hot tava, cook 40 seconds until bubbles form, and flip.
Brush 0.5 tsp Anveshan Ghee over the surface, flip again, and press until both faces are golden-brown, about 1 minute a side.
Keep the roasted theplas warm under a cloth and continue with the remaining dough.
tips: Sattu absorbs more water as it rests, so if the dough tightens up before rolling, wet your hands and re-knead briefly.
Toast the flax powder in a dry pan for a minute to bring out its nuttiness and stop it turning gummy.
Because of the sattu and flax these theplas keep you full for hours, making them a good pre-workout or lunchbox bread.
variations.servingSuggestion: Roll one around a smear of hung-curd dip with grated cucumber for a high-protein wrap, or serve alongside a bowl of masala chaas.

variations.name: Classic Palak Pakora
variations.description: Palak Pakora is the monsoon-favourite fritter of chopped spinach bound in a spiced gram-flour batter and fried till lacy and crisp. A little rice flour in the batter keeps the edges shatteringly crunchy while the spinach stays tender and green inside.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: deep-fries the pakoras light and crisp without a greasy aftertaste

steps: Wash 3 cups spinach well, chop it fine, and pat it dry so the batter does not turn watery later.

In a bowl combine 1.5 cups besan, 2 tbsp rice flour, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp ajwain and 1 tsp salt, then add the spinach, thinly sliced onion, 2 chopped green chillies and grated ginger.
Sprinkle in 0.5 cup water a little at a time and mix to a thick, just-coating batter that clings to the spinach without dripping.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai to about 180C, until a drop of batter sizzles and rises in a couple of seconds.
Drop in small, uneven cluster-shaped portions and fry in batches for 4 to 5 minutes, turning once, until deep golden and crisp.
Lift out with a slotted spoon, drain on paper, and serve piping hot for the best crunch.
tips: Keep the batter thick and add water drop by drop, as a runny batter gives soft, oil-heavy pakoras.
Fry on medium-high heat; too cool and they soak oil, too hot and they brown before cooking through.
Re-crisp any leftovers in a hot pan or air fryer for two minutes rather than a microwave, which turns them soggy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with green mint chutney and a cup of masala chai on a rainy evening.

variations.name: Palak Patta Chaat
variations.description: A Prayagraj street sensation where whole spinach leaves are dipped in a thin batter, fried to a crisp wafer, then loaded with yogurt, chutneys and sev. Each bite layers the crunch of the leaf with cool curd and sweet-tangy tamarind for a proper chaat experience.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: fries the coated leaves into thin, crackly wafers

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the tamarind chutney with a deep, mellow warmth

steps: Whisk 1 cup besan, 3 tbsp rice flour, 0.5 tsp of the salt and 0.5 cup water into a smooth, thin batter that coats a leaf lightly.
Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind pulp with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 0.5 tsp roasted cumin and a pinch of salt for 4 minutes to a pourable sweet-tangy chutney, then cool.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to about 180C, dip each spinach leaf in batter, and fry 8 to 10 leaves in batches for 2 to 3 minutes until crisp and pale gold.
Drain the fried leaves on paper and arrange them on a plate just before serving so they stay crackly.
Spoon over the whisked yogurt, drizzle generously with the tamarind chutney, and dust with the remaining roasted cumin and 1 tsp chaat masala.
Scatter 0.5 cup sev and 3 tbsp chopped coriander on top and serve at once while the leaves are still crisp.
tips: Use firm, large spinach leaves and keep the batter thin so it fries into a light, crisp shell rather than a thick fritter.
Assemble each plate only at the moment of serving, as the yogurt and chutney soften the leaves quickly.
Chill the whisked yogurt beforehand so the hot-cold contrast comes through in every bite.
variations.servingSuggestion: Plate individually as a starter at a chaat party, finishing each with a little pomegranate for jewel-like colour.

variations.name: Crispy South-Style Palak Pakoda
variations.description: This Andhra-inspired pakoda leans on rice and corn flour, curry leaves and sesame for a firm, biscuit-like crunch that holds for hours. Ginger-garlic and asafoetida give it the savoury, moreish depth of a Chennai tiffin-centre snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: its high smoke point fries the pakoda extra crisp and stable

steps: Combine 1 cup besan, 0.5 cup rice flour and 2 tbsp corn flour with 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 1 tsp salt in a wide bowl.
Add 3 cups chopped spinach, 15 torn curry leaves, 1 tbsp sesame seeds, 3 slit green chillies and 1 tsp ginger-garlic paste, and rub everything together so the spinach starts releasing moisture.
Sprinkle in just 0.5 cup water and mix to a very stiff, crumbly dough rather than a loose batter, which is what gives the firm crunch.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Sunflower Oil to about 175C, until a shred of batter sizzles gently and floats up.
Pinch off small irregular clusters, drop them into the oil in batches, and fry for 5 to 6 minutes, turning, until dark golden and hard-crisp.
Drain on paper and cool for a minute so they firm up into a snackable, long-lasting crunch.
tips: Keep the mix stiff and barely moist; the water from the spinach is often enough to bind it.
The corn and rice flour combination is the secret to a crunch that survives being stored in a tin.
Fry at a slightly lower heat and longer so the thick clusters dry out fully and stay crisp.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and filter coffee, or pack into an airtight jar as a tea-time namkeen.

variations.name: Baked Khapli Palak Pakora
variations.description: A lighter, oven-baked take that swaps some besan for nutty khapli atta and a brush of ghee instead of a deep-fry. The pakoras emerge craggy and golden with a wholesome, slightly rustic bite that is easy on the stomach.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: adds a nutty, high-fibre body that browns beautifully in the oven

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: brushed over the pakoras so they crisp and turn golden while baking

steps: Preheat the oven to 200C and line a tray with parchment brushed lightly with a little of the Anveshan Ghee.
In a bowl mix 1 cup besan, 0.5 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp ajwain and 1 tsp salt.
Add 3 cups chopped spinach, sliced onion, 2 chopped green chillies and grated ginger, then bring together with 0.33 cup water into a thick, scoopable batter.
Spoon craggy mounds onto the tray, leaving space between them, and brush the tops generously with Anveshan Ghee.
Bake for 15 minutes, flip each pakora and brush again with ghee, then bake another 12 to 15 minutes until golden and crisp at the edges.
Rest for 2 minutes so the crust firms, then serve warm.
tips: Keep the mounds small and craggy, as rough edges crisp far better in the oven than smooth balls.
Brushing ghee both times is essential for browning; skip it and the pakoras stay pale and dry.
The khapli atta makes these filling, so serve a couple fewer per person than the fried version.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of thick hung-curd dip and a squeeze of lemon for a guilt-free tea-time plate.

variations.name: Classic Panchmel Dal
variations.description: The soul of a Rajasthani thali: five lentils in equal measure simmered soft, then finished with a fierce ghee tadka of cumin, garlic and red chilli. Also called panchratna dal, it is earthy and full-bodied, built to be poured over baati or ladled beside steamed rice.

ingredients.name: Toor dal
ingredients.note: rinsed until the water runs clear

ingredients.name: Moong dal
ingredients.note: yellow split

ingredients.name: Urad dal
ingredients.note: split, with skin

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee gives the tadka the nutty depth that defines a Rajasthani dal

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Dry red chillies
ingredients.note: broken

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Combine the five dals in a bowl, rinse three or four times until the water runs clear, then soak for 20 minutes while you prepare the other ingredients.

Drain and add the dals to a pressure cooker with 3 cups water, 1/2 tsp turmeric powder and 1 tsp of the salt; cook on medium heat for 5-6 whistles until every lentil is completely soft, then let the pressure release naturally.
Open the cooker and whisk the dal lightly so the mix looks creamy but still has body; add 1/2 cup hot water if it has thickened too much and keep it on a low simmer.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small tadka pan on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add 1/4 tsp asafoetida, 6 chopped garlic cloves and 3 broken dry red chillies and fry until the garlic turns pale gold, about 1 minute.

Lower the heat, stir in 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder for 10 seconds so they bloom without burning, then add 1 chopped tomato and the remaining 1/2 tsp salt and cook for 3-4 minutes until the tomato collapses and the ghee separates.
Pour the sizzling tadka into the simmering dal, stir well, and let it bubble together for 4-5 minutes so the flavours marry.
Sprinkle 1/2 tsp garam masala and 2 tbsp chopped coriander over the top, give a final stir, and serve piping hot.
tips: Keeping the five dals in equal quarter-cup measures is what gives panchmel its balanced body; skew it toward chana dal and the dal turns heavy and grainy.
If the dal thickens on standing, loosen it only with hot water so the tadka aroma is not diluted by a cold pour.
A second small spoon of raw Anveshan Ghee stirred in just before serving lifts the whole dish, the way it is done in Rajasthani homes.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle generously over hot dal-baati or beside jeera rice, with a side of garlic chutney and sliced onion to cut the richness.

variations.name: Marwari No-Onion No-Garlic Panchmel Dal
variations.description: The traditional Marwari temple-style version cooked without onion or garlic, relying instead on ginger, green chilli and a generous hand of asafoetida bloomed in ghee. Dried mango and a touch of jaggery give it the sweet-tangy roundness that distinguishes Shekhawati kitchens.

ingredients.name: Urad dal
ingredients.note: split, with skin

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the only fat in this pure-veg dal, so its bilona flavour has to carry the whole tempering

ingredients.name: Asafoetida
ingredients.note: a generous pinch stands in for the missing garlic

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: grated

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a small sweetness that rounds the tang, the Marwari way, without refined sugar

steps: Rinse the five dals together well, then pressure-cook them with 3 cups water, 1/2 tsp turmeric powder and 1 tsp salt for 5-6 whistles on medium heat until butter-soft; let the pressure drop on its own.
Whisk the cooked dal until creamy, loosen with about 1/2 cup hot water to a pourable consistency, and keep it on a gentle simmer.
Warm 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a tadka pan on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds with 3 cloves for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Reduce the heat and add 1/2 tsp asafoetida, the grated ginger and 2 slit green chillies; fry for about 1 minute until the ginger loses its raw smell and the kitchen fills with hing.
Stir in 1 tsp Kashmiri red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder off the direct flame for 10 seconds, then pour this tempering straight into the simmering dal.
Add 1 tsp amchur, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and the remaining 1/2 tsp salt, then simmer the dal for 6-7 minutes until it thickens slightly and the sweet-sour balance settles.
Finish with 2 tbsp chopped fresh coriander and serve hot, ideally with a plain rice or bajra roti.
tips: Because there is no onion or garlic, use a genuinely generous half-teaspoon of asafoetida bloomed properly in ghee; that is what carries the savoury base.
Add the amchur and jaggery together and taste as you go, aiming for a gentle sweet-sour lilt rather than a pronounced sweetness.
This dal sits well for a fasting-friendly thali and reheats without losing its balance if you add only hot water.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra roti and a spoon of white butter, or over plain steamed rice with a side of kachri chutney for a Marwari lunch.

variations.name: Dhaba-Style Tadka Panchmel Dal
variations.description: The highway-dhaba treatment where the five-lentil base is simmered smoky and given a double tadka: one folded in and a second smoking one poured tableside over crushed kasuri methi. Mustard oil in the first tempering gives it the pungent, robust edge that dal-lovers chase at truck stops.

ingredients.name: Urad dal
ingredients.note: split, with skin

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: kachi ghani oil gives the base tadka the pungent bite dhabas are known for

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: reserved for the smoking finishing tadka poured tableside

ingredients.name: Kasuri methi
ingredients.note: crushed between the palms

steps: Rinse the five dals and pressure-cook them with 3.5 cups water, 1/2 tsp turmeric powder and 1 tsp salt for 6 whistles on medium heat until fully broken down; mash lightly and keep warm.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just smokes, lower the heat, then add 2 chopped onions and fry for 7-8 minutes until deep golden brown.

Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for a minute, then add 2 chopped tomatoes with 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and the remaining 1/2 tsp salt; bhuno for 5-6 minutes until the masala turns thick and glossy.
Pour the cooked dal into this masala with about 1 cup hot water, stir well, and let it simmer on low heat for 8-10 minutes so it takes on a smoky, restaurant-like body.
Just before serving, heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan until it shimmers, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 3 dry red chillies for 30 seconds until the chillies darken.
Take the dal off the heat, scatter 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi and 1/2 tsp garam masala over the surface, then pour the smoking ghee tadka on top so it sizzles dramatically.
Fold the tadka through only halfway so streaks of ghee and chilli stay visible, and serve at once while it still crackles.
tips: Frying the onions to a genuine deep brown in mustard oil is what builds the dhaba colour and depth; pale onions give a flat dal.
Pour the finishing ghee tadka literally at the table so the aroma hits before the first bite, the way dhabas serve it.
For extra smokiness, place a live coal in a small bowl set on the dal, drip a few drops of ghee on it, and cover for two minutes before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter-brushed tandoori roti or laccha paratha, a raw onion-lemon salad, and a green chilli on the side.

variations.name: One-Pot Coconut Panchmel Dal
variations.description: A Southern reimagining of the Rajasthani classic where the five lentils meet a curry-leaf and coconut tempering in sesame oil, brightened with tamarind. It trades the heavy ghee richness for a lighter, tangy, aromatic bowl that eats beautifully with rice.

ingredients.name: Urad dal
ingredients.note: split

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked in 1/4 cup warm water and strained

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed gingelly oil is the authentic fat for a South Indian tempering

ingredients.name: Shallots
ingredients.note: thinly sliced

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: crushed

steps: Rinse the five dals and pressure-cook with 3 cups water, 1/2 tsp turmeric powder and 1 tsp salt for 5 whistles until soft; whisk lightly and keep on a low simmer.
Stir the strained tamarind water and 1.5 tsp sambar powder into the simmering dal and let it bubble for 5 minutes so the sourness cooks in and the raw edge softens.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a small pan on medium heat and pop 1 tsp mustard seeds for 30 seconds until they finish spluttering.

Add 2 sprigs curry leaves and 2 dry red chillies, let them crisp for 15 seconds, then add 8 sliced shallots and 4 crushed garlic cloves and fry for 4-5 minutes until the shallots turn golden and sweet.
Tip in 1/3 cup grated coconut and toast for 1-2 minutes until it smells nutty and turns pale gold at the edges.
Pour this tempering into the dal along with the remaining 1/2 tsp salt, simmer everything together for 4 minutes, then finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and serve hot.
Adjust the consistency with a splash of hot water if it thickens, keeping it loose enough to coat rice.
tips: Add the tamarind only after the dal is fully cooked; souring agents added early keep lentils from softening properly.
Toasting the coconut in the tempering rather than adding it raw gives the dal a deeper, rounder aroma.
Use fresh shallots rather than large onions here; their sweetness is central to the Southern character of this bowl.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot steamed rice with a spoon of extra sesame oil and a crisp appalam, or alongside idli for a hearty South Indian breakfast.

variations.name: Classic Aloo Bonda
variations.description: Aloo Bonda is a South Indian tiffin favourite, a ball of mustard-and-curry-leaf tempered potato mash cloaked in besan batter and fried to a golden sphere. The soft, lemony potato centre and crisp shell make it the perfect partner to coconut chutney and coffee.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: fries the bondas with a subtle South Indian aroma and does the tempering

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal until the dal turns golden, then add 12 curry leaves, 3 chopped green chillies, grated 1 inch ginger, 0.25 tsp hing and 0.25 tsp turmeric.
Add 4 mashed potatoes, 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 3 tbsp coriander, mix well, cook 2 minutes, then cool and roll into 12 balls.
Whisk 1.5 cups besan with 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.25 tsp salt and 0.75 cup water into a smooth, thick batter.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadai to about 180C, until a drop of batter rises at once.
Dip each potato ball fully in batter and lower gently into the oil, frying 4 to 5 at a time.
Fry for 4 to 5 minutes, turning, until golden and crisp all over, then drain and serve hot.
tips: Use dry, well-mashed potato with no lumps so the balls hold together smoothly in the batter.
Add a pinch of rice flour to the batter for an extra-crisp shell that stays firm longer.
Fry at a steady 180C so the shell sets fast and the bonda does not drink up oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with coconut chutney and a tumbler of filter coffee for a classic evening tiffin.

variations.name: Kerala Coconut-Shallot Bonda
variations.description: A Malabar-style bonda where the potato is studded with fresh grated coconut and sweet shallots for a fragrant, slightly sweet centre. Fried in coconut oil, it carries the unmistakable aroma of a Kerala tea shop.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the defining Kerala aroma for both the tempering and the fry

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 15 curry leaves, 8 sliced shallots, 3 chopped green chillies and grated 1 inch ginger, and saute until the shallots soften.
Add 0.5 cup grated coconut and 0.25 tsp turmeric, fry 1 minute, then mix in 4 mashed potatoes and 1 tsp salt and cook 2 minutes.
Cool the filling and shape it into 12 balls, pressing firmly so the coconut binds in.
Whisk 1.5 cups besan with 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.25 tsp salt and 0.75 cup water into a thick coating batter.
Heat the rest of the Anveshan Coconut Oil to about 180C, dip each ball in batter, and fry in batches for 5 minutes until golden.
Drain on paper and serve hot while the coconut aroma is at its peak.
tips: Slice the shallots thin and cook them till just soft so they sweeten the filling without turning watery.
Use fresh, not desiccated, coconut for the juicy, fragrant centre typical of Kerala bondas.
Squeeze out any moisture from the mashed potato so the coconut-rich filling stays firm enough to shape.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a spicy red coconut chutney and strong Malabar chai on a rainy afternoon.

variations.name: Schezwan Masala Bonda
variations.description: An Indo-Chinese street twist where the potato filling is fired up with schezwan sauce, capsicum and spring onion for a tangy, garlicky kick. The familiar bonda shell hides a bold, saucy centre that appeals to a younger crowd.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: neutral oil that lets the schezwan flavour lead and fries the bonda crisp

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sunflower Oil, saute 5 minced garlic cloves for 30 seconds, then add 0.5 cup capsicum and the white parts of the spring onion and stir-fry 2 minutes on high.
Add 2 tbsp schezwan sauce, 1 tsp soy sauce and 0.5 tsp black pepper, then mix in 4 mashed potatoes and 1 tsp salt and cook 2 minutes until thick.
Fold in the spring onion greens, cool the filling, and roll into 12 firm balls.
Whisk 1.5 cups besan with 2 tbsp corn flour, 0.25 tsp salt and 0.75 cup water into a thick, crisp-frying batter.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Sunflower Oil to about 180C, dip each ball in batter, and fry in batches for 4 to 5 minutes until golden.
Drain and serve hot while the saucy centre is still warm and punchy.
tips: Cook the filling until quite dry, as schezwan sauce adds moisture that can loosen the balls.
The corn flour in the batter gives a crackly Indo-Chinese style crust that suits this filling.
Adjust the schezwan sauce to taste, since brands vary widely in heat and saltiness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with extra schezwan sauce and a cold soft drink as a fun Indo-Chinese starter.

variations.name: Baked Aloo Bonda
variations.description: A guilt-free oven version where the batter-coated potato balls are baked with a brush of ghee to a golden, crackly finish. It keeps the comforting spiced potato centre while cutting the oil to a minimum.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: used for the tempering and brushed over the bondas so they crisp in the oven

steps: Preheat the oven to 200C and line a tray with parchment brushed with a little Anveshan Ghee.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, add 12 curry leaves, 3 minced green chillies, grated 1 inch ginger and 0.25 tsp turmeric, then mix in 4 mashed potatoes, 1 tsp salt and 3 tbsp coriander and cook 2 minutes.
Cool the filling and roll into 12 balls.
Whisk 1 cup besan with 2 tbsp semolina, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.25 tsp salt and 0.5 cup water into a thick coating batter, then dip each ball.
