Arrange on the tray, brush the tops generously with Anveshan Ghee, and bake for 15 minutes.
Turn each bonda, brush again with ghee, and bake another 12 to 15 minutes until golden and crisp, then serve warm.
tips: The spoon of semolina in the batter helps the baked shell crisp up despite the lack of deep oil.
Do not crowd the tray; leaving space lets the hot air crisp every side of the bonda.
Brush ghee both times, as this is what gives the baked bondas their golden colour and crunch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney or a bowl of hot sambar for a lighter tiffin.

variations.name: Classic Aloo Poha
variations.description: This Classic Aloo Poha is the light, fluffy Maharashtrian breakfast of flattened rice tossed with soft potato cubes, onions and a mustard-curry leaf tempering. Each flake stays separate and pale gold, brightened with lemon, a whisper of sweetness and crunchy fried peanuts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil gives the tempering its classic nutty Maharashtrian aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a pinch balances the lemon and salt the way Maharashtrian homes finish poha

steps: Rinse the 2 cups thick poha gently in a colander under running water for a few seconds, then leave to drain and soften for 10 minutes until the flakes fluff up but do not turn mushy.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a wide kadhai over medium heat and fry the 0.5 cup peanuts for 2 minutes until crunchy and golden, then scoop them out and set aside.
Into the same oil crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add the 12 curry leaves and 3 slit green chillies and let them splutter for about 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add the 2 diced potatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, cover and cook over medium-low heat for 7 to 8 minutes, stirring once, until the cubes are tender and lightly golden.
Stir in the sliced 1 onion and 1 tsp salt and saute for 3 minutes until the onion softens and turns translucent.
Fold in the drained poha and fried peanuts, sprinkle over 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, cover for 2 minutes to warm through, then switch off and finish with 2 tbsp lemon juice and the coriander.
tips: Use thick poha and rinse it only briefly, as thin poha or over-soaking turns the dish into a paste.
Let the rinsed poha rest until it fluffs and crushes softly between your fingers before adding it.
Add the lemon juice off the heat so it stays bright rather than turning bitter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot topped with fine sev, a lemon wedge and a scatter of pomegranate seeds, with a cup of masala chai.

variations.name: Indori Poha
variations.description: Indore's famous morning poha is steamed soft and fluffy, dusted with tangy jeeravan masala and mounted with crunchy sev, fennel, raw onion and jewel-like pomegranate. It is sweeter, spicier and more aromatic than the everyday version, with a signature fennel-fragrant finish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee lends the buttery richness that defines authentic Indori poha

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the pronounced sweetness is a hallmark of Indore-style poha

steps: Rinse the 2 cups thick poha in a colander, sprinkle lightly with water, mix in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp salt, and rest for 12 minutes until plump.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp fennel seeds and 1 tsp mustard seeds for 20 seconds until aromatic.
Add the 2 diced potatoes and 2 slit green chillies, cover and cook over medium-low heat for 8 minutes until the potatoes are soft and lightly browned.
Tip in the rested poha and fold gently, then steam covered on the lowest heat for 3 minutes until the flakes turn glossy and fluffy.
Switch off, squeeze in 2 tbsp lemon juice and mix through the coriander.
Pile into bowls and top generously with 2 tsp jeeravan masala, 1 cup nylon sev, the finely chopped onion and 0.5 cup pomegranate seeds just before serving.
tips: Steam rather than stir-fry the poha so it stays feather-light in true Indori style.
Add the sev only at the table so it stays crackling crisp against the soft poha.
If you cannot find jeeravan masala, a blend of roasted cumin, dry mango and fennel powder comes close.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with piping hot jalebi on the side and a glass of ginger chai for the full Indore breakfast experience.

variations.name: Nagpuri Tarri Poha
variations.description: Nagpur's beloved tarri poha crowns soft flattened rice with a fiery, garlicky black-chana curry called tarri, plus crunchy farsan and raw onion. Spicy, savoury and satisfying, it eats more like a hearty street meal than a light breakfast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil carries the robust garlic-heavy tarri masala beautifully

steps: Soak the 1 cup black chickpeas overnight, then pressure-cook with a pinch of salt for 5 whistles until completely soft, reserving the cooking water.
For the tarri, heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and fry 1 chopped onion with the 8 crushed garlic cloves over medium heat for 5 minutes until deep golden.
Add 2 tbsp kanda lasun masala and the cooked chickpeas with 1 cup of their water, and simmer over medium-low heat for 8 minutes into a spicy, oily red gravy.
Rinse the 2 cups poha, mix in 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, and rest for 10 minutes until fluffy.
In a separate pan heat the remaining 2 tbsp oil, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds and the 10 curry leaves, then fold in the poha and warm through for 3 minutes covered.
Mound the poha into bowls, ladle the hot tarri over the centre, and finish with the second raw chopped onion, 1 cup farsan, 2 tbsp lemon juice and coriander.
tips: Make the tarri a little loose and oily, as it is meant to soak into and moisten the poha.
Keep the tarri and poha separate until serving so the flakes do not go soggy in advance.
Adjust the kanda lasun masala to taste, as Nagpuri tarri is traditionally quite fiery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with extra tarri on the side, a wedge of lemon and thick slices of soft bread to mop up the gravy.

variations.name: South Indian Aval Upma
variations.description: This South Indian take treats poha as aval, tempered with urad and chana dal, ginger and curry leaves in coconut oil, and finished with a shower of fresh grated coconut. It is savoury, dal-crunchy and coconut-fragrant, with no sweetness or lemon-forward tang.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil gives this aval upma its authentic South Indian fragrance

steps: Rinse the 2 cups thick poha in a colander, sprinkle with a little water and 0.25 tsp turmeric, and rest for 10 minutes until softened and fluffy.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadhai over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds, then fry 1 tbsp urad dal and 1 tbsp chana dal for a minute until golden.
Add the 15 curry leaves, 3 slit green chillies and 1 inch grated ginger and let them sizzle for 20 seconds until aromatic.
Stir in the diced potato, cover and cook over medium-low heat for 6 minutes, then add the sliced onion and 1 tsp salt and saute for 3 minutes until soft.
Fold in the rested poha gently and steam covered on low heat for 3 minutes until warmed through and glossy.
Switch off the heat, mix through the 0.5 cup grated coconut and coriander, and serve warm.
tips: Toast the urad and chana dal until just golden so they add a nutty crunch without turning bitter.
Use fresh grated coconut off the heat to keep its sweetness and moisture in the upma.
Skip the lemon here, as the coconut and dal give this version its rounded South Indian flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with coconut chutney and a small tumbler of filter coffee for a South Indian tiffin breakfast.

variations.name: Classic Amritsari Aloo Kulcha
variations.description: The iconic street kulcha of Amritsar: a fermented flour shell stuffed with spiced mashed potato, rolled thin, dotted with kalonji and coriander, and roasted until shatteringly crisp and blistered. It is finished with a reckless amount of ghee and traditionally served smashed open. Crunchy outside, soft and tangy within, it is a meal in itself.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Blended in for a little wholesome body without losing the classic crisp maida shell

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: Helps the dough ferment and softens the crumb of the crisp kulcha

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Lavishly brushed on the crust for the trademark Amritsari crunch and gloss

steps: Mix 1.5 cups maida, 1/2 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 tsp baking powder, 1/4 tsp baking soda, 1 tsp Anveshan Khandsari and 1/2 tsp salt, then knead with 1/4 cup yogurt and about 1/2 cup water into a soft, smooth dough; cover and rest in a warm place for 2 hours to ferment lightly.
Grate 3 boiled potatoes and mix with 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp amchur powder, 1/2 tsp salt and 2 tbsp coriander into a dry, well-seasoned filling.
Divide the rested dough into 6 balls; flatten each into a disc, place 2-3 tbsp of the potato filling in the centre, gather the edges over it, and pinch closed.
Dust with dry flour and roll each stuffed ball into an oval about 7 inches long, then press a sprinkle of kalonji and chopped coriander onto the top and roll once more so they stick.
Heat a tava on high, wet the plain underside with water, and slap the kulcha down water-side to the pan; cook 1 minute until the surface bubbles and sets.
Invert the tava directly over the flame and char the top for 40-50 seconds until blistered dark in patches, then lift off with tongs.
Brush each hot kulcha generously with melted Anveshan Ghee, press lightly to crisp, and serve smashed open in the Amritsari style.
tips: Keep the potato filling dry; any moisture makes the kulcha soggy and impossible to roll thin.
The two-hour rest is what gives the authentic slightly-sour, airy crumb, so do not rush it.
Roll a touch thinner than a paratha and char hard; Amritsari kulcha is meant to be crisp, not soft.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the traditional way with spicy pindi chole, a dab of white butter, sliced onions and a tangy tamarind chutney.

variations.name: Paneer Kulcha
variations.description: A richer take that trades potato for crumbled paneer seasoned with ginger, chilli and kasuri methi, giving a soft, protein-packed centre inside the crisp Amritsari shell. The paneer stays fluffy and mildly tangy while the crust crackles. It is the kulcha for those who want their bread to carry a bit of heft.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Lends a subtle nuttiness and a sturdier crust for the softer paneer filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: Encourages a gentle ferment for the classic airy kulcha texture

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Brushed thickly on the crust for the signature crisp, glossy finish

steps: Knead 1.5 cups maida, 1/2 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 tsp baking powder, 1 tsp Anveshan Khandsari and 1/2 tsp salt with 1/4 cup yogurt and about 1/2 cup water into a soft dough; cover and rest 2 hours to ferment.

Mash 1.5 cups crumbled paneer with 1 inch grated ginger, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi, 1/2 tsp garam masala, 1/2 tsp salt and 3 tbsp coriander into a soft but non-wet filling.
Divide the dough into 6 balls, flatten each into a cup, spoon in 3 tbsp of the paneer filling, seal the edges together, and pinch shut.
Roll each ball into a 7-inch oval, dusting lightly, and press coriander onto the top with one final gentle roll so the filling stays sealed.
On a hot tava, wet the underside, stick the kulcha down, and cook 1 minute until the surface bubbles across.
Flip the tava over the flame and blister the top for 40 seconds until charred in spots, or cover and brown the second side directly on the tava.
Brush each hot kulcha generously with melted Anveshan Ghee and serve while the shell is crisp and the paneer warm.
tips: Squeeze any whey from the paneer before mixing so the filling stays dry and the kulcha crisps properly.
Do not overwork the paneer or it turns rubbery; mash just until it holds together with the spices.
Fresh homemade paneer gives the softest, most fragrant filling, far better than firm store blocks.
variations.servingSuggestion: Delicious with amritsari chole or a simple tomato-onion salad and a bowl of mint raita.

variations.name: Onion Kulcha
variations.description: A sharp, savoury kulcha stuffed with finely chopped onion, green chilli and anardana that turns sweet and jammy as it roasts. The dhaba favourite is famous for its juicy, slightly caramelised onion centre against the crackling maida crust. Simple, punchy and endlessly moreish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Adds body to the crust so it holds the juicy onion filling without going limp

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: Aids fermentation and rounds off the sharp raw onion

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Brushed on to crisp the crust and carry the roasted-onion aroma

steps: Knead 1.5 cups maida, 1/2 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/4 tsp baking soda, 1 tsp Anveshan Khandsari and 1/2 tsp salt with 1/4 cup yogurt and about 1/2 cup water into a soft dough; cover and ferment 2 hours.
Finely chop 2 onions, sprinkle with 1/4 tsp salt, wait 5 minutes, and squeeze out the released water firmly so the filling will not turn soggy.
Mix the squeezed onion with 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp anardana powder, 1/2 tsp chilli flakes and 3 tbsp coriander into a bright, tangy filling.
Divide the dough into 6 balls, flatten each, fill with 3 tbsp of the onion mix, gather and seal the edges, then roll into 7-inch ovals pressing kalonji onto the top.

On a hot tava, wet the base and stick the kulcha down; cook 1 minute until it bubbles, then invert the tava over the flame to blister the top for 40-50 seconds until charred and the onions inside smell sweet.
Lift off with tongs and brush each hot kulcha generously with melted Anveshan Ghee.
Press lightly to crisp and serve immediately, torn open to reveal the juicy onion centre.
tips: Squeezing the salted onion is essential; skip it and the water will steam the crust into a chewy mess.
Anardana gives a fruity tang without adding moisture, which lemon juice would; seek it out for this filling.
Char the kulcha well so the onion softens and sweetens rather than staying raw and sharp.
variations.servingSuggestion: A natural match for dal makhani or chole, with extra white butter and a raw onion-lemon salad on the side.

variations.name: Gobi Kulcha
variations.description: A hearty winter kulcha stuffed with spiced grated cauliflower that cooks to a fragrant, slightly sweet softness inside the crisp shell. Ginger, ajwain and green chilli keep it lively while the cauliflower lends its distinctive earthy aroma. A robust, filling take that stands proudly beside the potato original.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Strengthens the crust to hold the moist cauliflower filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: Supports the light fermentation for a tender kulcha crumb

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Brushed thickly for the crisp, golden Amritsari-style finish

steps: Knead 1.5 cups maida, 1/2 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 tsp baking powder, 1 tsp Anveshan Khandsari and 1/2 tsp salt with 1/4 cup yogurt and about 1/2 cup water into a soft dough; cover and rest 2 hours.
Grate 2 cups cauliflower, sprinkle with 1/2 tsp salt, rest 10 minutes, then squeeze out as much water as you can with your hands or a cloth so the filling is nearly dry.
Lightly crush 1/2 tsp ajwain between your fingers and mix it into the cauliflower with 1 inch grated ginger, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp coriander powder and 3 tbsp coriander leaves.
Divide the dough into 6 balls, flatten each, fill with 3 tbsp of the cauliflower mix, seal the edges tightly, and roll into 7-inch ovals dusting lightly.

On a hot tava, wet the underside and stick the kulcha down; cook 1 minute until bubbled, then flip over the flame to char the top for 40-50 seconds until spotted and the cauliflower inside turns fragrant.
Cover and cook the second side on the tava for another minute so the cauliflower steams through fully.
Brush each hot kulcha generously with melted Anveshan Ghee and serve crisp, smashed open to release the aroma.
tips: Squeezing the grated cauliflower dry is the difference between a crisp kulcha and a torn, soggy one.
Crush the ajwain rather than leaving it whole, so it perfumes the filling without hard raw seeds.
Cook these a touch longer than potato kulcha to ensure the cauliflower loses its raw bite.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a bowl of chole or dal, plenty of white butter and a sharp mango pickle on the side.

variations.name: Classic Hyderabadi Bagara Rice
variations.description: A simple, deeply aromatic Hyderabadi rice tempered with whole spices, curry leaves and green chillies, meant to be the mild counterpart to a fiery salan or curry. The rice is cooked with a fragrant tarka rather than heavy masala, so it stays pale and lightly spiced. Every grain carries the warmth of cardamom, cloves and cumin without any gravy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Blooms the whole-spice tarka so the plain rice picks up a warm, fragrant depth

ingredients.name: Whole spices (bay leaf, cardamom, cloves, cinnamon, shahi jeera)

steps: Rinse and soak 2 cups basmati for 20 minutes and drain; heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot on medium flame.
Fry 0.25 cups cashews for 1 minute until golden and lift them out, then crackle the whole spices in the same ghee for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 sliced onion and 3 slit green chillies, fry 6 minutes until the onion turns soft and pale gold, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 12 curry leaves for 1 minute.
Add the drained rice and 1.25 tsp salt, toast gently for 2 minutes until the grains are coated in the fragrant ghee.
Pour in 3.25 cups hot water, bring to a rolling boil, then cover and cook on the lowest flame for 12 minutes until the water is absorbed.
Rest 10 minutes off the heat, then fold in the fried cashews and 0.25 cups coriander and fluff so the pale, aromatic grains stay separate.
tips: Keep the onion pale gold rather than brown; bagara rice should stay light in colour to contrast a rich salan.
Measure the water at about 1.6 times the soaked rice so the grains cook fluffy and never sticky.
Toast the rice briefly in the tarka before adding water so each grain stays firm and separate.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with the classic mirchi ka salan or a tangy bagara baingan, letting the mild rice soak up the spicy gravy.

variations.name: Bagara Khana with Peanut-Sesame Salan Base
variations.description: A richer wedding-style bagara khana where a roasted peanut, sesame and coconut paste is stirred into the tarka before the rice cooks, giving a nutty, faintly tangy body. This is the version served at Hyderabadi feasts, one shade more indulgent than the everyday tempered rice. The ground paste clings to the grains and makes the rice satisfying enough to eat with just yogurt.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Blooms the tarka and fries the nut paste so the rice takes on a rich, roasted depth

ingredients.name: Whole spices (bay leaf, cloves, cardamom, cumin)

steps: Dry-roast 0.33 cups peanuts, 2 tbsp sesame and 3 tbsp coconut until golden, cool, then grind to a coarse paste with a splash of water and 1 tsp tamarind pulp.
Soak 2 cups basmati 20 minutes and drain; heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and crackle the whole spices for 30 seconds.
Add 1 sliced onion and 3 slit green chillies, fry 6 minutes until soft and pale gold, then add 12 curry leaves for 30 seconds.
Stir in the ground peanut-sesame paste and fry 3 minutes on medium heat until it darkens and the ghee separates at the edges.
Add the drained rice and 1.25 tsp salt, toast 2 minutes, then pour in 3.25 cups hot water and bring to a rolling boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest flame for 12 minutes, rest 10 minutes, and fluff so the nutty masala coats every grain.
tips: Grind the nut paste coarse, not smooth, so it clings to the rice with a pleasant texture rather than turning gluey.
Roast the peanuts and sesame just to golden; over-roasting makes the paste bitter and darkens the rice too much.
Add the tamarind while grinding so its tang is evenly distributed instead of streaking the finished rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a simple cucumber raita and fried papad; the nutty rice is rich enough to need little else.

variations.name: Coconut-Milk Bagara Rice
variations.description: A coastal-leaning version where the rice cooks partly in coconut milk, giving the tempered grains a silky, mildly sweet body that pairs beautifully with spicy curries. The coconut mellows the green-chilli heat while curry leaves keep it firmly southern. It is a softer, more luxurious bagara rice for feast-day thalis.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: The coastal cooking fat that blooms the tarka and echoes the coconut milk for a rounded southern flavour

steps: Rinse and soak 2 cups basmati for 20 minutes and drain; heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a heavy pot on medium flame.
Splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, add the whole spices for 30 seconds, then add 14 curry leaves and 3 slit green chillies.
Add 1 sliced onion and 1 inch julienned ginger, and fry 6 minutes until the onion is soft and pale.
Add the drained rice and 1.25 tsp salt, toast 2 minutes, then pour in 1.25 cups coconut milk and 2 cups hot water and bring to a gentle boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest flame for 12 minutes, watching that the coconut milk does not catch on the base.
Rest 10 minutes off the heat, then fluff gently so the silky grains stay separate and glossy.
tips: Use a heavy-bottomed pot and keep the flame low, since coconut milk scorches far more readily than plain water.
Balance the coconut milk with an equal measure of water so the rice cooks through without turning heavy.
Add the coconut milk cold rather than hot so it blends smoothly and does not split against the tarka.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a fiery Andhra-style tomato pachadi or a coconut-based vegetable stew for a coastal thali.

variations.name: Mixed Millet Bagara Rice
variations.description: A wholesome reinvention using foxtail or barnyard millet in place of rice, tempered with the same fragrant bagara tarka for an earthy, high-fibre plate. The millet keeps a nutty bite and soaks up the spiced ghee beautifully. It is the health-forward version that still eats like a proper Hyderabadi feast rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Blooms the whole-spice tarka so the earthy millet takes on a warm, fragrant richness

ingredients.name: Whole spices (bay leaf, cloves, cardamom, cumin)

steps: Rinse 1.5 cups foxtail millet well and soak 15 minutes, then drain; heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot on medium flame.
Fry 1 tbsp chana dal until golden, add the whole spices for 30 seconds, then add 1 sliced onion and 3 slit green chillies and fry 6 minutes until soft.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 12 curry leaves for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the drained millet and 1.25 tsp salt, toast 2 minutes, then pour in 3 cups hot water and bring to a boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest flame for 14 minutes until the millet is tender and the water is absorbed.
Rest 10 minutes off the heat, fold in 0.25 cups roasted peanuts and 0.25 cups coriander, and fluff with a fork.
tips: Rinse the millet thoroughly and soak briefly so it cooks evenly and loses any faint bitterness.
Use about two parts water to one part millet, as it absorbs a little more liquid than basmati rice.
Let the cooked millet rest fully before fluffing, since disturbing it hot makes the grains clump.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a spicy peanut chutney or a bowl of thin rasam for a light yet filling millet meal.

variations.name: Classic Rajasthani Bajra Roti
variations.description: The winter staple of Rajasthan and Haryana, a thick, rustic pearl-millet round patted by hand and roasted till it puffs with earthy warmth. Gluten-free bajra needs hot water and a steady palm, giving a dense, nutty roti that is meant to be eaten hot with a river of ghee. Nothing fancy, just the deeply satisfying bread of the desert winter.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Poured generously over the hot roti in the Rajasthani way, soaking into the porous millet crumb

steps: Bring 1.25 cups water to a boil with 0.75 tsp salt, then pour it over 2 cups bajra flour mixed with 0.5 tsp carom seeds and stir into a rough dough.
As soon as it is cool enough to handle, knead the warm dough 5 minutes with your palm heel until it turns smooth and holds together without cracking.
Take a large ball, flatten it between your palms, and pat it out on a sheet of parchment with wet fingers into a thick 5-inch round.
Lift it carefully onto a medium-hot tava and cook the base for about 2 minutes until brown spots form.
Flip, cook the second side 1-2 minutes, then lift with tongs and hold over a direct flame until the roti swells; the thick bajra puffs only in patches.
Slide onto a plate, pour 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the hot surface, and repeat with the remaining dough.
tips: Bajra has no gluten, so knead while the dough is warm; the hot water is the only thing binding it.
Pat between your palms if patting on a board feels hard; keep your hands wet so the crumbly dough does not split.
Serve immediately, as bajra roti turns hard and dry within minutes of cooling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot and ghee-drenched with lehsun ki chutney and a bowl of gatte ki sabzi, or crumble it into hot milk with jaggery for a rustic dessert.

variations.name: Bajra Methi Dhebra
variations.description: The Gujarati-Kathiyawadi cousin of bajra roti, a softer spiced round loaded with fresh fenugreek, curd and sesame that keeps for a day of travel. Curd and oil in the dough make it pliable in a way the plain roti never is, and the methi lends a gentle bitterness. Rolled thin and roasted, it eats more like a savoury flatbread than a rustic roti.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A spoonful balances the fenugreek's bitterness with a clean caramel sweetness, the classic Kathiyawadi touch

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Worked into the dough for the suppleness bajra lacks and used to shallow-roast each dhebra golden

steps: In a bowl combine 1.5 cups bajra flour, 0.5 cups whole wheat flour, 0.75 cups chopped fenugreek, 1 tbsp sesame seeds, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.75 tsp salt.
Add 0.25 cups curd and 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, then knead into a firm dough, adding a splash of water only if the methi and curd do not moisten it enough; rest 15 minutes.
Roll each of 10 balls on a floured board into a 5-inch round, dusting well since the bajra-heavy dough is prone to sticking and cracking.
Place on a medium-hot tava and cook 45 seconds until the base sets, then flip.
Drizzle 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil around the edge, flip once more, and roast each side 1-2 minutes, pressing until golden-brown flecks appear.
Stack the dhebras and cool them uncovered so they stay firm for packing.
tips: The bit of wheat flour and curd is what makes dhebra rollable and soft; pure bajra alone will crack.
A teaspoon of jaggery balances the methi's bitterness and is the classic Kathiyawadi touch, so do not skip it.
Cool completely before stacking; these keep 2 days at room temperature and travel beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of chilled masala chaas and a spoon of sweet mango chhundo, the traditional dhebra pairing.

variations.name: Lehsun Bajra Roti
variations.description: A boldly flavoured Rajasthani take where a fiery paste of garlic, red chilli and cumin is worked straight into the millet dough, turning the plain roti into a meal on its own. The raw garlic mellows and sweetens as the roti roasts, perfuming the whole kitchen. Rustic, pungent and warming, it is desert winter comfort at its most direct.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Its sharp pungency stands up to the garlic and roasts the base of the roti with a distinctive bite

steps: Pound 8 garlic cloves with 3 dry red chillies and 1 tsp cumin seeds into a coarse paste in a mortar.
Mix the paste into 2 cups bajra flour with 3 tbsp chopped coriander and 0.75 tsp salt in a bowl.
Pour in about 1.25 cups boiling water, stir, and once bearable, knead the warm dough 4-5 minutes until smooth and crack-free.
Pat a ball into a thick 5-inch round on parchment with wet fingers, mending any cracks at the rim as you go.
Cook on a medium-hot tava 2 minutes a side, drizzling 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil around the edge, until deeply spotted and fragrant.
Finish over a direct flame for a few seconds to puff, then serve at once, repeating with the rest of the dough.
tips: Keep the garlic-chilli paste coarse; little bursts of garlic through the roti are the whole point of this version.
Heat the mustard oil to smoking once and cool it before using if you prefer a milder, mellower pungency.
This roti is filling enough to eat with just curd, though it firms up fast, so cook and serve one at a time.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a bowl of thick curd or plain buttermilk and a raw onion, letting the garlic roti carry the meal.

variations.name: Bajra-Jowar Double Millet Roti
variations.description: A balanced two-millet roti that softens dense bajra with an equal measure of sorghum, giving a lighter, more pliable round than pure pearl millet allows. The blend is gentler on the stomach and easier to pat out, making it a practical everyday version. It carries the nuttiness of both grains without the heaviness of either alone.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Smeared over the warm double-millet roti to enrich the two earthy grains

steps: Combine 1 cup bajra flour, 1 cup jowar flour and 0.5 tsp carom seeds in a bowl.
Boil 1.25 cups water with 0.75 tsp salt, pour it over the flour, stir into a mass, and knead the warm dough 5 minutes until smooth.
Pat a ball on parchment with wet fingers into a 6-inch round; the jowar makes this easier to shape thin than a pure bajra roti.
Cook on a medium-hot tava 1-2 minutes until the base spots brown, wetting the top surface halfway to help it puff.
Flip, set the second side, then puff over a direct flame until it balloons in patches.
Smear 0.75 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the hot roti and repeat with the remaining dough.
tips: Equal jowar makes this dough more forgiving, so it is the easiest millet roti for a beginner to pat thin.
Keep the water genuinely boiling when you add it; both millets need heat to bind without gluten.
These stay pliable a little longer than pure bajra roti but are still best eaten fresh and hot.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a Rajasthani ker-sangri sabzi or a simple dal, spooning extra ghee over the roti before each bite.

variations.name: Classic Batata Vada
variations.description: Batata Vada is Maharashtra's beloved potato fritter, a ball of mashed potato tempered with mustard seeds, curry leaves and ginger-garlic, jacketed in a spiced gram-flour batter and fried golden. The soft, tangy potato centre against the crisp besan shell is the heart of the humble vada pav.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: fries the vadas to an even golden crust and is also used for the tempering

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 12 curry leaves, a paste of 3 green chillies, 1 inch ginger and 5 garlic cloves, and 0.25 tsp turmeric, and fry for 1 minute.
Add 4 boiled, mashed potatoes, 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 3 tbsp coriander, mix well, and cook 2 minutes until the mixture comes together; cool and roll into 10 to 12 balls.
Whisk 1.5 cups besan with 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.25 tsp salt and 0.75 cup water into a smooth, thick coating batter that ribbons off the spoon.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai to about 180C, until a drop of batter puffs up quickly.
Dip each potato ball fully in the batter and lower it gently into the oil, frying 4 to 5 at a time.
Fry for 4 to 5 minutes, turning, until the shell is even gold and crisp, then drain on paper and serve hot.
tips: Boil the potatoes a day ahead and cool fully; dry, non-watery potato holds its shape in the oil.
Keep the batter thick enough to fully cloak the ball, or the potato peeks out and browns unevenly.
A pinch of baking soda in the batter gives a slightly puffier, crisper jacket if you like it airy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Tuck into a soft pav with dry garlic chutney and fried green chillies for the classic vada pav.

variations.name: Kolhapuri Masala Batata Vada
variations.description: A fiery western-Maharashtra version where the potato filling is layered with earthy goda masala, roasted peanuts and sesame for a nutty, aromatic heat. The extra spice and crushed peanut give the centre a coarser, more robust bite than the mild classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: carries the goda masala tempering and fries the vadas crisp

steps: Dry-roast 1 tbsp sesame and 3 tbsp peanuts separately until fragrant, then coarsely crush them together.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin, add crushed 6 garlic cloves, 1.5 tsp goda masala, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.25 tsp turmeric, and fry 30 seconds until aromatic.
Add 4 mashed potatoes, the crushed peanut-sesame, 1 tsp salt and 3 tbsp coriander, mix well, cool, and shape into 10 to 12 balls.
Whisk 1.5 cups besan with 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.25 tsp salt and 0.75 cup water to a smooth thick batter.
Heat the rest of the Anveshan Groundnut Oil to about 180C, dip each ball in batter, and slide into the oil in batches.
Fry for 5 minutes, turning, until deep golden and crisp, then drain and serve hot with the nutty aroma still rising.
tips: Roast and crush the peanuts coarse, not fine, so you get little bursts of crunch in the soft filling.
Goda masala can be sharp, so start with the stated amount and adjust once you taste the filling.
This spicier filling pairs beautifully with a plain pav and no chutney, letting the masala shine.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a fiery lasooni (garlic) chutney and thick slices of raw onion, Kolhapur style.

variations.name: Cheese-Burst Batata Vada
variations.description: A modern crowd-pleaser where a nugget of mozzarella is hidden inside the classic potato ball so it melts into a molten pull when you bite in. Chilli flakes and coriander in the potato balance the richness of the gooey cheese core.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: its neutral taste keeps the cheesy vada clean and the shell crisp

steps: Mash 4 boiled potatoes with 1 tsp salt, 1 tsp chilli flakes, 2 chopped green chillies, grated 1 inch ginger, 0.5 tsp black pepper and 3 tbsp coriander into a firm, non-sticky mixture.
Take a portion in your palm, press a mozzarella cube into the centre, and seal the potato fully around it into a smooth ball; repeat to make about 12.
Whisk 1.5 cups besan with 2 tbsp corn flour, 0.25 tsp salt and 0.75 cup water into a thick, gap-free coating batter.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Sunflower Oil to about 180C, until a drop of batter rises briskly.
Dip each stuffed ball fully in batter and fry 3 to 4 at a time for 4 to 5 minutes, turning, until golden and sealed.
Drain briefly and serve within a few minutes while the cheese centre is still hot and stretchy.
tips: Seal the potato completely around the cheese with no cracks, or the mozzarella will leak into the oil.
The corn flour in the batter helps it seal tight and stay crisp against the melting cheese.
Serve immediately; the molten pull is best in the first few minutes and firms up as it cools.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a spicy schezwan or tangy tomato dip so the heat cuts through the melting cheese.

variations.name: Appe-Pan Batata Vada
variations.description: A near-fried texture with a fraction of the oil, made by cooking batter-dipped potato balls in the little cups of an appe (paniyaram) pan with just ghee. You get a crisp, golden dome and soft centre without a kadai of oil.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: spooned into each mould so the vadas brown and crisp without deep-frying

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, add 12 curry leaves, minced 3 green chillies and 1 inch ginger, and 0.25 tsp turmeric, then fry for 1 minute.
Mix in 4 mashed potatoes, 1 tsp salt and 3 tbsp coriander, cook 2 minutes, cool, and roll into small 20 to 24 balls.
Whisk 1 cup besan with 2 tbsp semolina, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.25 tsp salt and 0.5 cup water into a thick batter, then coat each ball.
Heat an appe pan on medium, spoon 0.5 tsp Anveshan Ghee into each mould, and place a coated ball in each cup.
Cook covered for 4 to 5 minutes, turn each ball with a skewer, add a few drops more ghee, and cook another 4 minutes until golden all over.
Lift out when the domes are crisp and evenly browned, and serve hot straight from the pan.
tips: Make the balls smaller than for deep-frying so they cook through inside the shallow moulds.
The spoon of semolina in the batter gives a crisper crust to make up for the lack of deep oil.
Turn the balls only once a golden crust has set, or they may stick and tear in the mould.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a lighter tea-time snack with coconut chutney or a quick coriander-mint dip.

variations.name: Classic Rajasthani Gatte Ki Sabzi
variations.description: Spiced gram-flour logs are steamed, sliced into coins and simmered in a tangy yogurt gravy in the true Marwari style. The gatte stay soft and porous, soaking up a curry that is at once sour, warming and deeply savoury, making it the definitive no-vegetable Rajasthani main.

ingredients.name: Besan
ingredients.note: for the gatte dough

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: moyan for tender gatte and the fat for the gravy tempering

ingredients.name: Baking soda
ingredients.note: keeps the gatte soft and porous

ingredients.name: Yogurt
ingredients.note: whisked smooth, slightly sour

steps: Mix 1 cup besan with 1/2 tsp carom seeds, 1/4 tsp baking soda, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder, 1/4 tsp salt and 1 tbsp melted Anveshan Ghee, then add water little by little to make a firm, smooth dough.
Divide the dough and roll into 3 thin cylinders about 1 cm thick; slide them into a pot of boiling water and cook on medium heat for 10-12 minutes until they float and feel firm.
Lift the logs out, cool for 5 minutes, and slice into 1 cm coins; reserve the cooking water for the gravy.

Whisk 1 cup yogurt with 1/2 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder until completely smooth; heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1/4 tsp asafoetida and 2 dry red chillies for 30 seconds.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry 1 minute, then lower the heat and pour in the spiced yogurt, stirring constantly for 3 minutes so it warms without splitting.
Add 1.5 cups of the reserved gatta water and 1 tsp salt, simmer 6-7 minutes until the gravy thickens and the raw smell goes, then slide in the gatta coins and simmer 5 minutes.
Stir in 1/2 tsp garam masala, finish with 2 tbsp coriander, and serve hot.
tips: Do not over-knead or overboil the gatte; too much handling makes them dense and rubbery instead of soft and spongy.
Add the yogurt on the lowest heat and keep stirring in one direction until it comes to a simmer, the surest way to stop it curdling.
Slice the gatte only after they cool slightly; hot logs crumble under the knife.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice or phulka and a spoon of ghee; leftover gatta water makes a lovely base to loosen the curry the next day.

variations.name: Govind Gatte
variations.description: A royal, festive gatta where each log is stuffed with a rich paste of cashews, raisins and spices before steaming, then bathed in a creamy onion-cashew gravy. Sliced open, the gatte reveal a jewelled centre, making this the celebratory cousin of the everyday version.

ingredients.name: Besan
ingredients.note: for the gatte dough

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: moyan and gravy fat for a rich, shahi finish

ingredients.name: Cashews
ingredients.note: half for the stuffing, half soaked for the gravy

ingredients.name: Raisins
ingredients.note: chopped, for the stuffing

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: boiled and pureed

steps: Knead 1 cup besan with 1/2 tsp carom seeds, 1/4 tsp salt and 1 tbsp melted Anveshan Ghee, adding water to a firm dough; make a stuffing by mashing 1.5 tbsp chopped cashews, 1 tbsp raisins, 1/2 tsp fennel powder and a pinch of salt.

Take small portions of dough, flatten each, place a little stuffing in the centre, seal and roll into short thick logs; steam them in a steamer for 12 minutes until firm, then cool and slice into thick coins.
Soak the remaining 1.5 tbsp cashews in warm water for 10 minutes and grind to a smooth paste; keep the boiled onion puree ready.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the onion puree, and bhuno on medium heat for 6-7 minutes until it turns pale gold and the ghee separates.
Lower the heat and stir in 1/2 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp Kashmiri red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, then add the cashew paste and cook 2 minutes.
Pour in 1.5 cups hot water, simmer 5 minutes, then reduce the heat and swirl in 3 tbsp cream so it does not split; gently add the stuffed gatta coins.
Simmer 5 minutes, stir in 1/2 tsp garam masala, and finish with 2 tbsp coriander.
tips: Steam rather than boil the stuffed gatte so the filling stays sealed inside instead of leaching into the water.
Add the cream on low heat and do not boil hard afterwards, or the shahi gravy will turn grainy.
Slice the stuffed logs thick, around 2 cm, so each coin shows off its jewelled centre.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jeera rice, butter naan or a saffron pulao for a festive Rajasthani spread.

variations.name: Methi Gatte Ki Sabzi
variations.description: Fresh fenugreek leaves are kneaded straight into the gatta dough, lacing the logs with a gentle bitterness that plays against a tangy tomato-yogurt gravy. It is greener and earthier than the classic, a winter favourite when methi is at its best.

ingredients.name: Besan
ingredients.note: for the gatte dough

ingredients.name: Fresh fenugreek leaves
ingredients.note: chopped fine, kneaded into the dough

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil for tender gatte and a clean, earthy gravy

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: pureed

ingredients.name: Yogurt
ingredients.note: whisked smooth

ingredients.name: Kasuri methi
ingredients.note: crushed, to deepen the methi note

steps: Knead 1 cup besan with 1/2 cup chopped fresh fenugreek leaves, 1/2 tsp carom seeds, 1/4 tsp baking soda, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder, 1/4 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, adding water to a firm dough.
Roll into 3 thin logs, boil in water on medium heat for 10-12 minutes until they float, then cool and slice into coins; save 1.5 cups of the cooking water.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, add 1 chopped onion and fry 5 minutes until golden.

Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then add the puree of 2 tomatoes with 1/2 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and bhuno 5 minutes until thick.
Lower the heat and whisk in 1/2 cup yogurt gradually, stirring constantly for 2 minutes so it blends smoothly, then add the reserved gatta water and simmer 5 minutes.
Slide in the methi gatta coins, simmer 5 minutes so they absorb the gravy, and crush 1 tsp kasuri methi over the top.
Check the salt, simmer 1 more minute, and serve hot.
tips: Squeeze the chopped methi with a pinch of salt and drain it before kneading, or the extra moisture makes the dough sticky and the gatte dense.
Fresh methi in season gives the cleanest flavour; out of season, use 1/4 cup and lean on the kasuri methi finish.
The gravy thickens as it cools, so keep it slightly thin if you plan to reheat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot bajra or wheat rotis and a wedge of lemon; it also pairs beautifully with plain khichdi.

variations.name: Sukhe Masala Gatte
variations.description: A dry, party-style preparation where boiled gatta coins are shallow-fried until crisp-edged, then tossed with sauteed onions and a coarse dry masala. With no gravy, the gatte turn golden and chewy with a savoury coating, perfect as a starter or a dry side.

ingredients.name: Besan
ingredients.note: for the gatte dough

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: a light wood-pressed oil for shallow-frying the gatte crisp

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: cut into thin slices

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: julienned

steps: Knead 1 cup besan with 1/2 tsp carom seeds, 1/4 tsp baking soda, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder, 1/2 tsp salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Sunflower Oil, adding water to a firm dough; roll into 3 thin logs.
Boil the logs in water on medium heat for 10-12 minutes until firm, cool, and slice into 1 cm coins.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sunflower Oil in a pan and shallow-fry the gatta coins in batches for 3-4 minutes, turning, until golden and crisp at the edges; drain on a plate.

In the same pan add the remaining 1 tbsp oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add 2 sliced onions, 2 slit green chillies and the ginger juliennes and saute 5-6 minutes until the onions are soft and browning.
Lower the heat and add 1/2 tsp turmeric powder, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder with a splash of water, cooking 1 minute into a coarse masala.
Return the fried gatte, toss on medium-high heat for 2-3 minutes so the masala coats and crisps onto them.
Sprinkle 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp amchur and the remaining salt, toss, and finish with 2 tbsp coriander.
tips: Fry the gatte just until crisp-edged; over-frying dries out the centre and they turn hard.
Keep the masala dry with only a spoon of water so the coins stay crunchy rather than turning soft.
Serve immediately with cocktail sticks for a starter; the crisp edges soften if left too long.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a dry starter with mint chutney and onion rings, or as a side with dal-rice for a Rajasthani meal.

variations.name: Classic Bhatura
variations.description: The big, golden, dramatically puffed bread that partners chole across North India: a soft maida-and-semolina dough leavened with yogurt and a whisper of soda, rested until relaxed, then deep-fried so it balloons instantly. The outside is lightly crisp, the inside soft and chewy. Fried in wood-pressed oil, it is greaseless and clean-tasting.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: Balances the yogurt tang and helps the dough ferment for a good puff

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed oil fries clean and light so the bhatura is not greasy

steps: In a bowl mix 2 cups maida, 1/4 cup fine semolina, 1/2 tsp baking powder, 1/4 tsp baking soda, 1 tsp Anveshan Khandsari and 1 tsp salt.
Add 1/2 cup yogurt and knead, adding up to 1/4 cup warm water gradually, into a soft, smooth dough; rub 1 tsp Anveshan Sunflower Oil over it, cover, and rest in a warm place for 2 to 3 hours.
Knead the rested dough once more for a minute, then divide into 8 balls and keep them covered so they do not dry out.
Roll each ball into an oval or round about 5-6 inches across and 3 mm thick, using a little oil rather than dry flour so the surface stays smooth for frying.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Sunflower Oil in a kadhai to about 180C, hot enough that a pinch of dough rises at once with steady bubbles.
Slide in one bhatura and immediately press it gently under the oil with a slotted spoon; it will balloon in seconds, so flip it after 20-30 seconds and fry the other side until pale gold.
Lift out onto a rack or paper, drain briefly, and serve piping hot while it is still puffed and soft.
tips: The rest is what makes bhatura puff; an under-rested dough fries flat and dense.
Roll with oil, not dry flour, because loose flour burns in the oil and turns it bitter and dark.
Keep the oil hot and press the bhatura down as it hits the surface to force the signature balloon.
variations.servingSuggestion: The classic pairing is spicy pindi chole with sliced onion, green chilli and a wedge of lemon.

variations.name: Instant No-Yeast Bhatura
variations.description: A quick weekday bhatura for when the craving strikes but there is no time to rest a fermented dough. Thick yogurt plus baking soda and powder deliver the lift in just twenty minutes, giving a bread that puffs well and stays soft. Semolina keeps a pleasant chew without the long wait.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A quick sweet note that helps browning and balances the sour curd

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil has a high smoke point ideal for clean deep-frying

steps: Whisk 3/4 cup thick yogurt with 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder until smooth and the jaggery dissolves.
Mix 2 cups maida, 3 tbsp fine semolina, 1/2 tsp baking soda, 1 tsp baking powder and 1 tsp salt, then add the sweetened yogurt and knead into a soft dough, using a splash of water only if needed.
Cover with a damp cloth and rest just 20-25 minutes, long enough for the semolina to hydrate and the leaveners to activate.
Divide into 8 balls and roll each into a 5-inch round about 3 mm thick, smoothing with a little oil rather than dry flour.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai to 180C, testing with a dough pinch that should surface quickly with lively bubbles.
Fry one bhatura at a time, pressing it under the oil so it puffs within seconds, then flipping after 25 seconds and frying until both sides are golden.
Drain on a rack and serve hot straight away, as no-rest bhaturas soften fastest as they cool.
tips: Use genuinely thick, sour yogurt; thin curd makes a sticky dough that will not puff.
Do not let the shaped dough sit long before frying or the chemical leaveners fizzle out.
If a bhatura refuses to puff, your oil is too cool; wait for it to come back up to temperature between batches.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with quick amritsari chole and a plate of pickled onions and green chillies.

variations.name: Whole Wheat Bhatura
variations.description: A wholesome bhatura that swaps most of the maida for nutty khapli wheat, giving an earthier flavour and a little more fibre while still puffing beautifully. It fries a shade darker and tastes heartier, a version that sits easier without sacrificing the fun of a ballooning bread. Best eaten hot with a robust chole.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Gives the bhatura a nutty, wholesome flavour and gentle bite

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: Helps the wholemeal dough brown and balances the yogurt

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: Light wood-pressed oil that keeps the heavier wheat bhatura from tasting greasy

steps: Combine 1.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 cup maida, 1/4 tsp baking soda, 1 tsp baking powder, 1 tsp Anveshan Khandsari and 1 tsp salt in a bowl.
Add 1/2 cup yogurt and knead with up to 1/4 cup warm water into a soft dough, a touch softer than roti dough; rub with oil, cover, and rest 1.5 to 2 hours.
Knead briefly again, then divide into 8 balls and keep covered under a damp cloth.
Roll each ball into a 5-6 inch round about 3-4 mm thick, since wholemeal dough is best rolled slightly thicker to puff well, using oil to smooth the surface.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Sunflower Oil to about 185C, hot enough for a dough pinch to rise briskly.
Slide in a bhatura, press it under the oil so it balloons, then flip after 25-30 seconds and fry until an even golden-brown, a little darker than a maida bhatura.
Drain well and serve hot, as the wheat crumb firms faster than a maida one.
tips: Keep some maida in the blend for stretch; an all-wheat dough tends to puff less and crack.
Give the dough its full rest so the khapli bran softens and the bread stays tender.
Roll wholemeal bhaturas slightly thicker than white ones to help them balloon reliably.
variations.servingSuggestion: Wonderful with a hearty kabuli chana masala, sliced radish and a dollop of thick curd.

variations.name: Paneer Stuffed Bhatura
variations.description: A festive, indulgent bhatura hiding a spiced paneer filling that puffs into a soft pocket around the stuffing. Popular in Delhi and Punjab dhabas, it turns the humble fried bread into a substantial treat with a creamy, chilli-flecked centre. One of these with chole is a full plate on its own.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: Ferments the dough and balances the yogurt for a good puff

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: High smoke-point wood-pressed oil for a clean, non-greasy deep fry

steps: Mix 2 cups maida, 1/4 cup semolina, 1/2 tsp baking powder, 1 tsp Anveshan Khandsari and 1 tsp salt, add 1/2 cup yogurt, and knead with up to 1/4 cup warm water into a soft dough; oil, cover, and rest 2 hours.
Mash 1 cup crumbled paneer with 2 chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1/4 tsp salt and 3 tbsp coriander into a dry, well-seasoned filling.
Divide the rested dough into 8 balls; flatten each into a small cup, place 1.5 tbsp of paneer filling inside, gather the edges over it, and pinch firmly shut.
Roll each stuffed ball gently into a 5-inch round about 4 mm thick, using oil and light pressure so the filling stays sealed and does not tear through.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C, checking that a dough pinch surfaces quickly with steady bubbling.
Fry one at a time, pressing gently so it puffs around the filling, flipping after 30 seconds and frying until golden on both sides.
Drain on a rack and serve hot, cut open to reveal the spiced paneer centre.
tips: Keep the paneer filling dry and finely mashed so it does not pierce the dough while rolling.
Seal the seam thoroughly and roll gently; a leaking bhatura will spit and fry unevenly.
Roll these a little thicker than plain bhatura so the pocket has room to puff around the filling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with tangy chole, a side of pickled carrots and a cooling boondi raita for a hearty meal.

variations.name: Classic Aloo Bread Pakora
variations.description: This Classic Bread Pakora sandwiches a spiced mashed-potato filling between bread slices, dips them in a seasoned besan batter and deep-fries them to a crackling golden crust. Crisp outside and soft-stuffed within, it is the ultimate rainy-day North Indian teatime snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil fries the pakoras crisp without any greasy aftertaste

steps: Boil and mash the 3 potatoes, then mix in the chopped 2 green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp red chilli, 0.75 tsp amchur, coriander and 0.5 tsp salt into a smooth filling.
Whisk the 1.5 cups besan with 2 tbsp rice flour, 0.5 tsp red chilli, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp salt and about 1 cup water into a smooth, thick coating batter.
Spread the potato filling generously over 4 bread slices and top with the remaining slices, pressing gently, then cut each into two triangles.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai over medium heat to 180 C, until a drop of batter rises steadily to the surface.
Dip each stuffed triangle fully into the batter to coat, then slide into the hot oil and fry for 4 to 5 minutes, turning, until deep golden and crisp.
Drain on a rack and serve hot while the crust is crackling.
tips: Keep the batter thick enough to cling, as thin batter slides off and leaves the bread exposed.
Fry on steady medium heat so the coating cooks through before it browns too fast.
Add the rice flour to the batter for an extra-crisp, longer-lasting crunch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with green mint chutney, sweet tamarind chutney and a cup of adrak chai.

variations.name: Punjabi Plain Bread Pakora
variations.description: The unstuffed Punjabi dhaba style simply dips plain bread triangles into an ajwain-spiked besan batter and fries them crisp, no potato filling in sight. Faster and lighter, these golden fritters are all about the crackly, carom-scented besan crust.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: light wood-pressed sunflower oil gives a clean, crisp fry for these plain pakoras

steps: Whisk the 2 cups besan with 3 tbsp rice flour, 1 tsp ajwain, 1 tsp red chilli, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.25 tsp baking soda and 1 tsp salt.
Add about 1.25 cups water gradually and whisk to a smooth, ribbon-like batter, then beat for a minute to make it airy, and mix in the coriander.
Cut each of the 8 bread slices into two triangles, trimming the crusts if you prefer.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Sunflower Oil in a kadhai over medium heat to 180 C, testing with a drop of batter that should sizzle and rise.
Dip each bread triangle into the batter to coat evenly, then fry in batches for 3 to 4 minutes, turning, until puffed, golden and crisp.
Drain on a rack and serve immediately while hot and crunchy.
tips: Beat the batter well to trap air, which makes the plain pakoras puff up and stay light.
Do not soak the bread in batter, just coat and fry quickly so it does not turn soggy.
A pinch of baking soda keeps the crust crisp and airy rather than dense.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with tangy imli chutney and sliced onions, dhaba-style, alongside strong milky chai.

variations.name: Paneer Bread Pakora
variations.description: A rich twist that layers a slice of paneer with a smear of green chutney and spiced onion-capsicum between the bread before battering and frying. The molten, tangy paneer centre makes these fritters heartier and more indulgent than the potato classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil crisps the coating around the soft paneer centre

steps: Cut the 250 g paneer into thick slabs and toss with 1 tsp chaat masala and 0.75 tsp red chilli, then finely chop the capsicum and onion.
Whisk the 1.5 cups besan with 2 tbsp rice flour, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and about 1 cup water into a smooth, thick batter.
Spread green chutney over 4 bread slices, layer with a paneer slab and a scatter of chopped onion and capsicum, then close with the remaining slices and halve into triangles.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai over medium heat to 180 C, checked with a rising drop of batter.
Coat each stuffed triangle thickly in batter and fry for 4 to 5 minutes, turning, until deep golden and crisp all over.
Drain well and serve hot so the paneer stays soft inside.
tips: Use fresh, soft paneer so the centre stays tender and does not turn rubbery when fried.
Seal the edges by pressing the batter-coated bread so the filling does not slip out.
Smear the chutney right up to the edges for a burst of flavour in every bite.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with extra green chutney and a sprinkle of chaat masala, cut open to show the paneer layer.

variations.name: Baked Veg Bread Pakora
variations.description: A lighter oven-baked take stuffed with a colourful potato, peas and corn filling and brushed with olive oil instead of deep-frying. It delivers the spiced, crisp-edged comfort of bread pakora with a fraction of the oil, ideal for a guilt-free snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Olive Oil
ingredients.note: brushing with olive oil bakes the pakoras crisp with far less fat

steps: Boil and mash the 2 potatoes and mix with the boiled 0.5 cup peas and 0.5 cup sweet corn, then add 2 chopped green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.75 tsp amchur, coriander and 0.5 tsp salt.
Whisk the 1 cup besan with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp salt and about 0.75 cup water into a thick batter, and preheat the oven to 200 C.
Spread the veg filling over 4 bread slices, cover with the remaining slices, press and cut each into two triangles.
Dip each triangle lightly into the batter to coat and place on a lined baking tray, then brush both sides generously with Anveshan Olive Oil.
Bake at 200 C for 22 to 25 minutes, flipping halfway and brushing again, until the coating is set, golden and crisp at the edges.
Rest for 2 minutes and serve warm.
tips: Keep the batter coating thin for baking so it crisps rather than staying doughy.
Brush oil on both sides and again after flipping for even browning without frying.
Switch on the top grill for the last 2 minutes if you want a deeper golden crust.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a yogurt-mint dip and a fresh cucumber salad for a lighter teatime plate.

variations.name: Classic Butter Naan
variations.description: The soft, glossy butter naan every North Indian restaurant leans on: a yeast-risen dough kept extra tender with milk and yogurt, then drowned in melted butter and ghee the moment it leaves the heat. The crumb is cloud-soft, the top freckled with char, and the whole thing glistens invitingly. It is built to soak up gravy without falling apart.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Adds wholesome body so the soft naan can hold a heavy butter finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: Wakes up the yeast and lightly sweetens the tender crumb

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Blended with butter for a richer, more aromatic gloss than butter alone

steps: Froth 1 tsp active dry yeast and 1 tsp Anveshan Khandsari in 1/2 cup warm milk for 10 minutes until it foams up thickly.

Whisk 1.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 cup maida, 1/2 tsp baking powder and 1 tsp salt together, add the yeast milk and 3 tbsp yogurt, and knead 6-7 minutes into a soft, supple dough; cover and prove for 1 hour until doubled.
Punch down, divide into 6 balls, rest 10 minutes, then roll each into a 7-inch oval about 4 mm thick and press a pinch of nigella seeds onto the top.
On a smoking-hot tava, wet the underside of the naan and slap it down water-side to the pan; cook 1 minute until large bubbles form across the surface.
Invert the tava over the open flame and char the top for 30-40 seconds until blistered and spotted brown, then remove with tongs.
While each naan is still blazing hot, brush it lavishly with a mix of melted white butter and Anveshan Ghee so it soaks in and glistens.
Stack in a warm cloth-lined basket and serve at once, brushing on a little extra butter just before it goes to the table.
tips: Melt the butter and ghee together and keep the mix warm; cold butter sits on top instead of soaking into the crumb.
Keep the dough on the softer side; a stiff dough gives a bready naan that fights the butter rather than absorbing it.
Do not skip the yogurt, as its acidity is what keeps the naan tender for hours after cooking.
variations.servingSuggestion: The natural partner to paneer butter masala or dal makhani, with a side of pickled onions and a lemon wedge.

variations.name: Restaurant-Style Malai Butter Naan
variations.description: The plush, ultra-white naan from the tandoor counters of big-city restaurants, enriched with fresh cream and a touch of kasuri methi for that signature aroma. Made largely with maida and cream, it turns out feather-light with a melt-in-mouth crumb, then gets a double butter brush. This is the indulgent, celebration-night version of butter naan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: Feeds the yeast and gives the pale crust a delicate sweetness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Layered with butter for the deep, aromatic finish restaurants are known for

steps: Activate 1 tsp yeast with 1.5 tsp Anveshan Khandsari in 1/2 cup warm milk, waiting 10 minutes for a foamy head to form.

Combine 2 cups maida, 1/2 tsp baking powder and 1 tsp salt, then add the yeast milk and 3 tbsp fresh cream and knead 7-8 minutes into a very soft, elastic dough; oil, cover, and prove 1 to 1.5 hours until doubled and airy.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi between your palms and knead it lightly into the risen dough, then divide into 6 balls and rest 10 minutes.
Roll each ball into a plump 7-inch oval, keeping it a touch thicker than usual so it stays pillowy, and sprinkle the top with nigella seeds.
On a very hot tava, moisten the base of the naan and press it down, cook 1 minute until it puffs and bubbles, then flip the tava over the flame to char the top for 30 seconds.
Brush the searing naan first with melted white butter, then with a light coat of melted Anveshan Ghee, letting each layer soak in.
Serve straight away, glossy and steaming, with an extra butter dab melting on top for the full restaurant effect.
tips: Fresh cream is what makes this naan white and cottony; do not substitute more yogurt or it will turn tangy and dense.
Crush the kasuri methi fine so it perfumes the dough evenly rather than leaving grassy specks.
Roll these slightly thick and do not over-char; the appeal here is softness, not a rustic blistered crust.
variations.servingSuggestion: Made for shahi paneer, murgh-style soya curry or navratan korma, with a saffron lassi to finish the feast.

variations.name: Whole Wheat Butter Naan
variations.description: A guilt-lighter butter naan that skips maida entirely for nutty khapli wheat, leavened the quick way with yogurt and baking soda. It carries the same generous butter finish but with an earthier crumb and a gentle tang from the curd. Proof that a wholesome naan need not feel like a compromise.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: The sole flour here, giving a fibre-rich, nutty naan with no refined maida

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A mineral sweetness that pairs naturally with the earthy wheat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rounds out the butter finish and keeps the wholemeal crumb soft

steps: Whisk 1/2 cup thick yogurt with 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder until dissolved, and lightly crush 1/2 tsp ajwain seeds between your fingers to release their aroma.
Mix 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/4 tsp baking soda, 1 tsp baking powder, 1 tsp salt and the crushed ajwain, then work in the sweetened yogurt and up to 1/4 cup warm milk to form a soft dough.
Knead 5 minutes until smooth, cover with a damp cloth, and rest 25 minutes so the leaveners and gluten do their work.
Divide into 6 balls and roll each into a 7-inch oval about 4-5 mm thick, since wholemeal naan is best a little sturdier than a maida one.
Heat a tava until smoking, wet the base of a naan, stick it down, and cook 1 minute until bubbles appear; flip over the flame or cover to brown the second side, about 40 seconds.
Brush each hot naan generously with a warm blend of melted white butter and Anveshan Ghee so the crumb drinks it in.
Keep the naans wrapped in cloth as you cook the batch, then serve warm before the wholemeal crumb tightens.
tips: Wholemeal naan dries faster than maida naan, so butter it the instant it comes off the heat and keep it covered.
If the dough feels stiff, add milk a spoon at a time; khapli atta absorbs more liquid than white flour.
A five-second reheat over a low flame with a fresh dab of ghee brings leftovers right back to soft.
variations.servingSuggestion: Lovely with a rustic dal tadka, bhindi masala or a simple aloo-matar, alongside a bowl of cucumber raita.

variations.name: Cheese Butter Naan
variations.description: A crowd-pleasing stuffed twist where the buttery naan hides a molten core of grated cheese spiked with chilli flakes and coriander. Pull it apart and the cheese stretches in long ropes, while the outside stays soft and butter-glazed. This is the naan that turns dinner into a treat for kids and grown-ups alike.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its strength keeps the molten cheese sealed inside without the base tearing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: Activates the yeast for a soft dough that encases the filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Brushed on the crust so the cheesy naan finishes glossy and fragrant

steps: Foam 1 tsp yeast with 1 tsp Anveshan Khandsari in 1/2 cup warm milk for 10 minutes until frothy.
Knead 1.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 cup maida and 1 tsp salt with the yeast milk and 3 tbsp yogurt into a soft dough, then cover and prove 1 hour until doubled.
Toss 1 cup grated mozzarella and 1/2 cup grated processed cheese with 1 tsp chilli flakes and 3 tbsp chopped coriander to make the filling.
Punch down the dough and divide into 6 balls; flatten each into a 4-inch disc, place 2-3 tbsp of the cheese mix in the centre, gather the edges over it, pinch tightly shut, and flatten gently.
Dust lightly and roll each stuffed ball into a 6-inch oval with soft, even strokes so the cheese stays sealed inside and does not burst through.
On a hot tava, wet the base of the naan, stick it down, and cook 1 minute; flip over the flame or cover to brown the top for 40 seconds, until the cheese inside melts and the crust spots brown.
Brush each hot naan with a warm mix of white butter and melted Anveshan Ghee, cut into halves so the cheese pulls, and serve immediately while molten.
tips: Seal the seam thoroughly and roll gently; a weak seal lets the cheese leak out and scorch on the tava.
A blend of mozzarella for stretch and processed cheese for flavour gives the best pull and taste.
Serve within a couple of minutes, as the cheese firms up quickly once the naan cools.
variations.servingSuggestion: A hit with a tangy tomato-based paneer tikka masala or simply a bowl of spicy makhani gravy for dipping.

variations.name: Classic Chilli Potato
variations.description: This Classic Chilli Potato is a street-style Indo-Chinese snack of crisp-fried potato fingers tossed in a glossy soy-chilli-garlic sauce. Crunchy outside, fluffy inside and coated in a sweet-spicy-tangy glaze, it is the ultimate moreish nibble with an ice-cold drink.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: its high smoke point fries the potato fingers golden and crisp

steps: Peel and cut 4 large potatoes into thick fingers, soak them in water for 10 minutes to remove starch, then drain and pat completely dry.
Toss the potato fingers with 4 tbsp cornflour, 2 tbsp rice flour and 0.5 tsp salt until each piece is evenly dusted.
Heat 1 cup Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180 C and deep-fry the potatoes in batches for 5 to 6 minutes until golden and crisp, then drain on paper.
In 2 tbsp of the same oil, stir-fry the minced garlic, ginger and 3 green chillies on high heat for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the cubed onion and toss for 1 minute, then pour in 2 tbsp soy sauce, 1.5 tbsp red chilli sauce, 2 tbsp ketchup, 1 tsp vinegar and 0.5 tsp salt and cook for 1 minute until glossy.
Add the fried potatoes, toss on high heat for 1 to 2 minutes to coat, garnish with 3 tbsp spring onion and serve immediately.
tips: Soaking the cut potatoes removes surface starch, which is the secret to a shatteringly crisp fry.
Serve straight away, as the coating softens the potatoes within minutes of tossing.
For extra crispness, fry once at 160 C to cook through, then again at 190 C just before saucing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot as a starter with toothpicks and a side of extra chilli sauce for dipping.

variations.name: Honey Chilli Potato
variations.description: The wildly popular sweet-and-spicy version where crisp potato fingers are glazed in a sticky honey-chilli-garlic sauce and finished with toasted sesame. The honey lends a glossy caramel edge that balances the heat, making it irresistibly sticky and addictive.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: a light wood-pressed oil that keeps the fried fingers clean and crisp

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: raw honey glazes the potatoes with a glossy caramel sweetness that tames the chilli

steps: Cut 4 large potatoes into thin fingers, soak for 10 minutes, drain and dry, then coat in 5 tbsp cornflour with 0.5 tsp salt.
Deep-fry the fingers in 1 cup Anveshan Sunflower Oil at 180 C for 5 to 6 minutes until deeply golden and crisp, then drain.
In 2 tbsp of the oil, stir-fry the finely minced garlic and 1.5 tsp red chilli flakes on medium-high heat for 40 seconds until aromatic.
Add 2 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tbsp red chilli sauce, 1 tsp vinegar and 0.5 tsp salt, then stir in 3 tbsp Anveshan Honey and simmer for 1 minute until the sauce turns glossy and sticky.
Add the fried potatoes and toss on high heat for 1 to 2 minutes so the honey glaze coats every finger.
Sprinkle 1 tbsp toasted sesame seeds and 3 tbsp spring onion, toss once, and serve immediately.
tips: Add the honey off very high heat and simmer briefly, so it glazes without turning bitter.
A thin, even cut on the potatoes gives the maximum crisp surface for the sticky glaze.
Toss quickly and serve at once, as the honey sauce softens the crunch fast.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a party starter garnished with extra sesame, or as a sweet-spicy side to fried rice.

variations.name: Schezwan Chilli Potato
variations.description: A fiery Sichuan-inspired version where crisp potato fingers are tossed in a bold, garlicky Schezwan sauce loaded with dry red chillies. Hotter and more pungent than the classic, it has a numbing, lip-tingling heat that keeps you reaching for more.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: handles high heat to fry the fingers and bloom the fiery Schezwan paste

steps: Cut 4 large potatoes into fingers, soak for 10 minutes, drain and dry, then dust with 4 tbsp cornflour, 2 tbsp rice flour and 0.5 tsp salt.
Deep-fry in 1 cup Anveshan Groundnut Oil at 180 C for 5 to 6 minutes until crisp and golden, then drain on paper.
In 2 tbsp of the oil, fry 5 broken dry red chillies and minced garlic on high heat for 30 seconds until sharply aromatic.
Add the chopped onion and toss for 1 minute, then stir in 4 tbsp Schezwan sauce, 1 tbsp soy sauce, 0.5 tsp sugar and 0.5 tsp salt and cook for 1 minute.
Add the fried potatoes and toss on high heat for 2 minutes until every finger is coated in the deep-red fiery sauce.
Garnish with 3 tbsp spring onion, toss once off the heat, and serve at once while crunchy.
tips: The rice flour keeps the potatoes crisp for longer under the heavy Schezwan coating.
Taste before adding all the salt, since Schezwan sauce is already quite salty.
A splash of vinegar at the end brightens the deep chilli-garlic flavours.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a fiery starter with a cooling raita dip, or alongside schezwan noodles.

variations.name: Air-Fried Chilli Potato
variations.description: A lighter take where the potato fingers are air-fried to a crisp and tossed in a quick low-oil soy-chilli sauce. It captures the crunch and tang of the deep-fried classic with a fraction of the fat, perfect for a guilt-free snack craving.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: a light toss coating plus finishing drizzle lends a nutty aroma with little oil

steps: Cut 4 large potatoes into fingers, soak for 10 minutes, drain and dry, then toss with 3 tbsp cornflour, 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and 0.5 tsp salt.
Air-fry the coated fingers at 200 C for 15 to 18 minutes, shaking the basket twice, until golden and crisp.
Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a wok and stir-fry the minced garlic and 2 green chillies on high for 30 seconds.
Add the cubed onion and capsicum and toss for 2 minutes, then add 2 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tbsp red chilli sauce, 1.5 tbsp ketchup and 0.5 tsp salt and cook for 1 minute.
Add the air-fried potatoes and toss on high heat for 1 minute so they take on the glossy sauce.
Garnish with 3 tbsp spring onion, toss once, and serve immediately while hot.
tips: Preheat the air fryer and avoid crowding the basket so the fingers crisp evenly.
A light coat of oil before air-frying is what gives the potatoes their golden crunch.
Serve straight from the toss, as air-fried potatoes lose their crisp even faster than fried ones.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a lighter snack with a squeeze of lime and a bowl of clear soup on the side.

variations.name: Classic Rajasthani Dal Baati
variations.description: The iconic Rajasthani plate: dense, cracked wheat baatis baked until golden, split open and drowned in warm ghee, served with a hearty panchmel dal. The baatis carry a coarse, crumbly bite from semolina in the dough and are unapologetically rich, meant for festive and everyday feasting alike.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: nutty heritage wheat gives the baati its authentic coarse, crumbly bite

ingredients.name: Semolina
ingredients.note: fine rava, for extra crunch

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: part goes into the dough as moyan, the rest for dunking the split baatis

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Mix 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/4 cup semolina, 1/2 tsp carom seeds, 1/4 tsp baking soda and 1 tsp salt, then rub in 4 tbsp melted Anveshan Ghee until the flour holds shape when pressed in your fist.
Add water a little at a time, about 1/2 cup, to make a stiff, tight dough; cover and rest it for 20 minutes, then divide into 8 balls and press a small dimple into the centre of each.
Bake the baatis in an oven preheated to 200C for 35-40 minutes, turning once halfway, until deep golden and cracked; a tap should sound hollow.
Meanwhile rinse the toor, chana and moong dals and pressure-cook with 3 cups water, 1/2 tsp turmeric powder and 1 tsp salt for 5-6 whistles until soft, then whisk creamy.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, add 6 chopped garlic cloves and fry until golden, then add 1 chopped tomato with 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder and cook 4 minutes until the ghee separates.
Pour this tadka into the dal, add 1/2 tsp garam masala, simmer 5 minutes, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
Break the hot baatis in half, dunk them in the remaining warm Anveshan Ghee until soaked, and serve two per person drowned in the hot dal.
tips: The dough must be stiff, almost hard; a soft dough gives dense baatis that will not crack open or bake through.
Bake low and slow rather than hot and fast so the centre cooks before the crust over-browns.
Crush the hot baatis and mix them right into the dal with extra ghee for the classic churma-free 'dal-choorma' bite.
variations.servingSuggestion: Plate with a bowl of dal, a spoon of garlic chutney, sliced raw onion and a wedge of lime; a scoop of churma alongside makes it a full Rajasthani thali.

variations.name: Bafla Baati
