variations.description: The Malwa and Indori cousin of baati: the wheat balls are first boiled in salted water until they float, then baked or fried, giving a softer, smoother interior than the classic cracked baati. Boiling in water is the signature step that sets bafla apart and lets it drink in even more ghee.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: heritage wheat holds together through the boil-then-bake bafla method

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: moyan in the dough plus a deep bath for the boiled baflas

ingredients.name: Yogurt
ingredients.note: whisked, for a softer crumb

ingredients.name: Salt
ingredients.note: half for the dough, half for the boiling water

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 2 tbsp semolina, 1/2 tsp carom seeds, 1/4 tsp baking soda and 3/4 tsp salt, rub in 3 tbsp melted Anveshan Ghee and 3 tbsp whisked yogurt, then knead with a little water into a firm but pliable dough and rest 20 minutes.
Shape the dough into 8 smooth balls and drop them into a wide pot of boiling water salted with 3/4 tsp salt; boil on medium heat for 10-12 minutes until they rise and bob at the surface.
Lift the boiled baflas out with a slotted spoon, drain well, then bake in a 200C oven for 25 minutes, turning once, until golden and lightly crusted.
For the dal, rinse 1/2 cup toor dal and pressure-cook with 2.5 cups water, 1/2 tsp turmeric powder and 3/4 tsp salt for 4-5 whistles until soft, then whisk.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds with 2 dry red chillies, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry 1 minute, then add 1 chopped tomato, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder and cook 4 minutes until thick.
Stir the tempering into the dal, simmer 5 minutes, and scatter 2 tbsp coriander on top.
Break the baked baflas, dip them generously in warm Anveshan Ghee, and serve swimming in the hot dal.
tips: The bafla is ready to lift from the boil the moment it floats; leaving it longer makes it waterlogged and heavy.
The yogurt and the boiling step together are what give bafla its trademark soft, melting centre versus the crunchier classic baati.
Bake the boiled baflas the same day; refrigerated boiled dough turns gummy when baked later.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve Indori-style with dal poured over, a bowl of sweet churma on the side, and a dollop of extra ghee melting on top.

variations.name: Masala Stuffed Baati
variations.description: A festive upgrade where each baati hides a spiced peas-and-paneer filling that steams inside as the shell bakes. Split one open and the savoury centre spills into the ghee-soaked crumb, turning a rustic staple into a plate that needs little more than dal beside it.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: sturdy heritage-wheat shell that holds a stuffing without splitting

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: moyan for the dough and a warm bath for the split baatis

ingredients.name: Green peas
ingredients.note: boiled and coarsely mashed

ingredients.name: Paneer
ingredients.note: crumbled

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: grated

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/4 cup semolina, 1/2 tsp carom seeds, 3/4 tsp salt and 3 tbsp melted Anveshan Ghee, adding water to a stiff dough; rest 20 minutes.

Make the filling by mixing the mashed peas and crumbled paneer with grated ginger, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1/2 tsp amchur, a pinch of salt and 2 tbsp coriander until it holds together.

Divide the dough into 8 balls, flatten each into a disc, place a spoon of filling in the centre, seal into a smooth ball and dimple the top; bake at 200C for 35-40 minutes, turning once, until golden and firm.
For the dal, pressure-cook 1/2 cup masoor dal with 2.5 cups water, 1/2 tsp turmeric powder and 3/4 tsp salt for 4 whistles until soft, then whisk.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, add 1 chopped onion and fry to golden, then add 1 chopped tomato and 1 tsp red chilli powder and cook 4 minutes to a thick masala.
Fold the tempering into the dal, simmer 5 minutes, and top with 1 tbsp coriander.
Split the stuffed baatis, dip the halves in warm Anveshan Ghee so the crumb drinks it in, and serve with the hot dal.
tips: Seal the stuffing edges thoroughly and keep the shell an even thickness, or the baati cracks and the filling leaks during baking.
Squeeze any moisture from the boiled peas before mashing; a wet filling steams the shell soggy from inside.
These reheat well in a hot oven for 8 minutes; avoid the microwave, which turns the crust leathery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve one stuffed baati per person with dal, mint chutney and a kachumber salad, letting the filling be the star so the dal can be lighter.

variations.name: Air-Fryer Dal Baati
variations.description: A lighter, modern take that gets the cracked, golden baati crust from an air fryer instead of an open flame or heavy oven, using far less ghee in the dough. Paired with a quick single-lentil dal, it keeps the rustic spirit intact for a weeknight without the fireside effort.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: high-fibre heritage wheat crisps beautifully in dry air-fryer heat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a lighter hand of moyan plus a modest dip, keeping the dish leaner

ingredients.name: Moong dal
ingredients.note: yellow split, quick-cooking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: a light wood-pressed oil to brush the baatis before air-frying

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: grated

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Mix 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 3 tbsp semolina, 1/2 tsp carom seeds, 1/4 tsp baking soda and 3/4 tsp salt, rub in 3 tbsp melted Anveshan Ghee, then knead with water into a stiff dough and rest 15 minutes.
Shape into 8 balls, dimple each, and brush lightly all over with 1 tbsp Anveshan Sunflower Oil.
Air-fry at 180C for 22-25 minutes, shaking or turning the basket twice, until the baatis are deep golden and crackled with a hollow tap.
While they cook, pressure-cook 1/2 cup moong dal with 2.5 cups water, 1/2 tsp turmeric powder and 3/4 tsp salt for 3-4 whistles until soft, then whisk smooth.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds with 1/4 tsp asafoetida, add the grated ginger and 2 slit green chillies for 1 minute, then add 1 chopped tomato and 3/4 tsp red chilli powder and cook 3 minutes until soft.
Stir the tadka into the dal, simmer 4 minutes, and finish with 2 tbsp coriander.
Split the air-fried baatis, brush or lightly dip them in warm Anveshan Ghee, and serve hot with the dal.
tips: Air fryers run hot at the edges, so turn the baatis twice for an even crust and to stop one side scorching.
Keep the dough as stiff as the classic version; air-frying will not rescue a soft, underworked dough.
Because there is less ghee in the dough, do not skip the final warm-ghee brush; it is what makes the crumb taste indulgent.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with the moong dal, a spoon of tangy tomato chutney and cucumber sticks for a lighter, everyday version of the classic feast.

variations.name: Classic Gujarati Dal Dhokli
variations.description: The ultimate Gujarati one-pot comfort meal: diamond-cut spiced wheat strips simmered right in a sweet-sour toor dal until they turn silky and drink up the flavour. Peanuts, a ghee tadka and a whisper of jaggery make it the kind of soft, soupy bowl that tastes like a grandmother's kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: emmer wheat rolls into supple dhokli strips that stay tender in the dal instead of turning gummy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the finishing bilona-ghee tadka is what perfumes the whole pot and gives Gujarati dal dhokli its signature aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: unrefined jaggery gives the sweet-sour balance a rounded, molasses depth central to this dish

steps: Knead 1 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp turmeric, a pinch of salt, 1 tsp oil and about 6 tbsp water into a firm, tight dough, then rest it covered for 15 minutes; roll thin and cut into 1 inch diamonds.

Pressure cook 0.75 cup toor dal with 3 cups water and 3 tbsp raw peanuts for 4-5 whistles until the dal is completely soft, then whisk it smooth and thin it to a flowing consistency with 2 more cups hot water.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a large pot on medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard and 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, add 10 curry leaves and 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and fry for 1 minute.
Pour in the whisked dal with 2 tbsp tamarind pulp, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1.25 tsp salt, and bring to a rolling boil for 4-5 minutes so the flavours marry.

Drop the dhokli diamonds in one at a time into the boiling dal, stirring gently so they do not stick, then simmer uncovered on medium-low for 15-18 minutes until the strips are cooked through and the dal turns silky.
Rest the pot off the heat for 5 minutes so the dhokli plumps and absorbs flavour, then stir through 3 tbsp chopped coriander and serve steaming, ladling extra dal over each bowl.
tips: Add the dhokli to actively boiling dal, not a gentle simmer, or the strips clump together and turn doughy.
Keep the dal deliberately thin; the dhokli drinks up liquid as it sits, and a thick pot turns stodgy within minutes.
A squeeze of lemon at the table lifts the sweet-sour balance if the dal has mellowed on standing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot in deep bowls with an extra drizzle of ghee, a side of chopped raw onion and a wedge of lemon, eaten with a spoon like a hearty stew.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Varan Phal (Chakolya)
variations.description: Maharashtra's earthy cousin of dal dhokli, where goda-masala-spiced toor varan carries the wheat phal and there is no sweet-sour tamarind at all. Kokum lends a gentle tartness and goda masala brings its smoky coconut warmth, making this a darker, spicier, more savoury bowl than the Gujarati one.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: the wholegrain emmer phal soaks up the smoky varan without going mushy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee blooms the goda masala tempering and rounds out the earthy varan

steps: Make a firm dough from 1 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, a pinch of salt, 1 tsp oil and about 6 tbsp water, rest it 15 minutes, then roll thin and cut into 1 inch squares (phal).
Pressure cook 0.75 cup toor dal with 3 cups water for 4-5 whistles until very soft, then whisk smooth and loosen with 2 cups hot water to a thin varan.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot on medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard and 0.5 tsp cumin, add 0.25 tsp hing and 8 curry leaves, then stir in 1.5 tbsp goda masala and 2 tbsp dry coconut and fry just 20 seconds off high heat so the masala does not scorch.
Pour in the whisked dal with the remaining 1 tsp red chilli powder, 4 kokum petals and 1.25 tsp salt and boil hard for 5 minutes so the kokum releases its tang and colour.
Slide the wheat squares into the boiling varan a few at a time, stirring gently, and simmer on medium-low for 15-18 minutes until the phal is tender and the varan thickens slightly around them.
Take the pot off the heat, rest 5 minutes, discard the spent kokum, and finish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander before serving hot.
tips: Add goda masala off high heat and only briefly — it turns bitter the instant it burns in hot ghee.
Kokum, not tamarind or jaggery, is the correct souring agent here; it gives varan phal its clean, un-sweet tartness.
If you cannot find goda masala, blend 1 tsp garam masala with 0.5 tsp roasted sesame powder, though it will miss the stone-flower smokiness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle into bowls with a spoon of ghee and serve with a side of tel-lavlela raw onion and papad, the way it is eaten in Pune and Nashik homes.

variations.name: Rajasthani-Malwa Dal Dhokli (Spicy)
variations.description: The fiery border-belt version from the Rajasthan-Malwa region, where the dhokli rides in a garlicky mixed-lentil dal fired with a red-hot Kashmiri-chilli tadka and no sweetness at all. Ajwain in the dough and a garlic-chilli chhaunk poured over at the end make this the boldest, most robust bowl of the lot.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: sturdy emmer dhokli stands up to the assertive garlic-chilli dal without falling apart

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rajasthani cooking is unstinting with ghee, and it carries the fierce garlic-chilli tadka poured over the top

steps: Knead 1 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp ajwain seeds, 0.5 tsp turmeric, a pinch of salt, 1 tsp oil and about 6 tbsp water into a firm dough, rest 15 minutes, then roll thin and cut into 1 inch diamonds.
Pressure cook 0.5 cup toor dal and 0.25 cup chana dal together with 3 cups water for 5 whistles until fully soft, whisk lightly to keep some texture, and loosen with 2 cups hot water.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin, add half the crushed garlic and 1 chopped tomato, fry 3-4 minutes until pulpy, then add 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt.

Pour in the mixed dal, bring to a hard boil for 5 minutes, then drop in the dhokli diamonds a few at a time and simmer on medium-low for 15-18 minutes until the strips are cooked through and the dal is robust and thick.

In a small pan heat the remaining 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, fry the rest of the crushed garlic with 3 broken dried red chillies until deep golden, then take off the heat and stir in the remaining 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder.
Pour this sizzling garlic-chilli tadka over the pot, stir once, and finish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander before serving fiery and hot.
tips: Mixing chana dal into the toor gives this version a heartier, coarser body than the all-toor Gujarati bowl.
Add the Kashmiri chilli powder to the off-heat tadka so it blooms red without burning and turning acrid.
There is deliberately no jaggery here; if you crave a hint of balance, a squeeze of lemon suits it better than sugar.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice or plain phulka and a spoon of extra garlic tadka on top, plus sliced raw onion and green chilli on the side.

variations.name: Jain No-Onion-No-Garlic Dal Dhokli
variations.description: A satvik, everyday version cooked entirely without onion, garlic, ginger or tomato, leaning instead on hing, green chilli and a moringa boost for depth. It stays true to the sweet-sour Gujarati soul while being gentle on the stomach — the kind of light, wholesome bowl made on fasting-adjacent days.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: emmer wheat keeps the dhokli soft and nutritious in this lighter satvik pot

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee carries the hing-cumin tadka that stands in for the missing onion-garlic base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Moringa Powder
ingredients.note: a spoon of moringa adds a savoury green depth and a quiet nutrition boost where garlic and onion would normally build flavour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery keeps the classic Gujarati sweet-sour note intact without any pungent aromatics

steps: Knead 1 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp turmeric, a pinch of salt, 1 tsp oil and about 6 tbsp water into a firm dough, rest it 15 minutes, then roll thin and cut into 1 inch diamonds.
Pressure cook 0.75 cup toor dal with 3 cups water for 4-5 whistles until very soft, whisk smooth, stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Moringa Powder while warm, and thin with 2 cups hot water.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, add a generous 0.5 tsp hing, 10 curry leaves and 3 slit green chillies, and let them sizzle for 40 seconds until fragrant.

Pour in the moringa-enriched dal with 2 tbsp tamarind pulp, 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt, and boil hard for 5 minutes to bring the sweet-sour balance together.
Add the dhokli diamonds a few at a time into the boiling dal, stir gently to stop sticking, and simmer on medium-low for 15-18 minutes until the strips turn silky and cooked through.
Rest the pot off the heat for 5 minutes so the dhokli plumps, then stir in 3 tbsp chopped coriander and serve hot in deep bowls.
tips: Stir the moringa powder into warm, not boiling, dal so its delicate nutrients and grassy note are preserved.
Use a full half-teaspoon of hing here — with no onion or garlic, it is doing the heavy lifting on aroma.
This version thickens faster without the fat of a heavy tadka, so keep extra hot water handy to loosen it before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve simply with a bowl of plain curd and a spoon of sweet mango chhundo, keeping the whole meal satvik and light.

variations.name: Classic Vegetable Dalia Khichdi
variations.description: This Classic Dalia Khichdi is a wholesome one-pot of roasted broken wheat and yellow moong dal simmered soft with carrots, peas and beans in a cumin-ghee tempering. Comforting and lightly spiced, it is the nourishing porridge Indian homes reach for when they want something gentle yet filling.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasting the dalia in bilona ghee deepens its nutty aroma and keeps the grains separate

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pressure cooker over medium heat and dry-roast the 1 cup broken wheat and 0.5 cup moong dal together for 3 minutes until they smell nutty and turn a shade darker, then set aside.
In the same cooker heat the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida for 15 seconds, then add 1 inch grated ginger and 2 chopped green chillies.
Add the chopped carrot, 0.5 cup peas, 8 chopped beans and 1 tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric and saute for 3 minutes until the tomato softens.
Return the roasted dalia and dal, pour in 4 cups water and 1.25 tsp salt, and stir well to combine.
Close the lid and pressure-cook over medium heat for 4 whistles, then lower the flame and cook 3 more minutes so the grains turn soft and porridge-like.
Let the pressure release naturally, open, stir in a splash of hot water if too thick, and serve steaming hot.
tips: Roasting the dalia and dal first keeps the khichdi from turning gluey and adds a toasty depth.
Adjust the water for your preferred texture, using more for a softer, spoonable porridge.
Rest the khichdi for 5 minutes before serving, as it thickens naturally as it cools.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a bowl of cool boondi raita, mango pickle and an extra drizzle of ghee on top.

variations.name: Masala Dalia Khichdi
variations.description: This restaurant-style version cooks the broken wheat in a rich onion-tomato-ginger-garlic masala with garam masala and a hit of red chilli, finishing with fried cashews. Bolder and more gravy-like than the plain khichdi, it turns humble dalia into a satisfying spiced main.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee gives the masala base a glossy restaurant-style richness

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pressure cooker over medium heat and fry the 12 cashews until golden, then remove and reserve them for garnish.
In the same ghee drop in 1 bay leaf, add the 2 finely chopped onions and saute for 5 minutes until golden brown.

Stir in 1 tbsp ginger garlic paste and cook for a minute, then add the 2 pureed tomatoes with 1 tsp red chilli, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp garam masala and cook for 5 minutes until the ghee separates.
Add the diced capsicum and the 1 cup broken wheat with 0.25 cup moong dal and roast in the masala for 3 minutes until well coated.
Pour in 3.5 cups water and 1.25 tsp salt, stir, close the lid and pressure-cook over medium heat for 4 whistles.
Allow the pressure to release naturally, open and stir, then serve hot topped with the fried cashews.
tips: Brown the onions well before adding tomatoes, as this builds the deep restaurant-style base.
Roast the dalia in the masala so each grain stays distinct in the finished dish.
Loosen with a little hot water when reheating, as the masala khichdi firms up on standing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a dollop of butter, sliced onions and a lemon wedge, alongside papad for crunch.

variations.name: Dalia Ven Pongal
variations.description: A South Indian spin that cooks broken wheat with moong dal into a creamy pongal, tempered with crushed black pepper, cumin, ginger and cashews in ghee with curry leaves. Peppery and soothing rather than tomato-spiced, it is a comforting tiffin bowl.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a generous pour of ghee is essential to the silky richness of pongal

steps: Dry-roast the 0.5 cup moong dal in a pressure cooker over medium heat for 3 minutes until fragrant, then add the 1 cup broken wheat, 4.5 cups water and 1.25 tsp salt.
Pressure-cook over medium heat for 5 whistles, then let the pressure settle and mash the mixture lightly into a soft, creamy pongal.
Coarsely crush the 1.5 tsp peppercorns and 1 tsp cumin together for the tempering.

Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan over medium heat and fry the 15 cashews until golden, then add the crushed pepper-cumin, 0.25 tsp asafoetida, 1 inch chopped ginger, 1 slit green chilli and 15 curry leaves and sizzle for 30 seconds.
Pour the sizzling ghee tempering over the pongal and fold it through thoroughly.
Loosen with a splash of hot water if needed and serve piping hot while creamy.
tips: Coarsely crush the pepper and cumin rather than powdering them for bursts of warm spice.
Keep the pongal loose, as it thickens quickly and stiffens once it cools.
Do not skimp on the ghee tempering, as it carries the signature aroma of this dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with coconut chutney and a bowl of tangy sambar for a classic South Indian tiffin plate.

variations.name: Palak Dalia Khichdi
variations.description: This green, iron-rich version simmers broken wheat with moong dal and a vivid spinach puree brightened by garlic and cumin. Wholesome and mildly spiced, it is a sneaky way to fold greens into a comforting bowl for children and grown-ups alike.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee mellows the spinach and enriches this green khichdi

steps: Blanch the 4 cups spinach in hot water for 2 minutes, refresh under cold water, then blend to a smooth green puree and set aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pressure cooker over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and the 5 sliced garlic cloves until golden and fragrant.
Add the chopped onion, 2 green chillies and 1 inch grated ginger and saute for 3 minutes, then stir in the chopped tomato and 0.5 tsp turmeric and cook until soft.
Add the 1 cup broken wheat and 0.5 cup moong dal and roast for 2 minutes, then pour in the spinach puree, 4 cups water and 1.25 tsp salt.
Close the lid and pressure-cook over medium heat for 4 whistles until the grains are soft and the khichdi is a deep green.
Let the pressure release naturally, stir well, adjust the consistency with hot water and serve hot.
tips: Blanch and shock the spinach so the khichdi keeps its bright green colour rather than dulling.
Add the spinach puree only with the grains so it does not lose its fresh flavour to long frying.
A squeeze of lemon at the end lifts the greens and balances the earthiness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a spoon of white butter and crisp roasted papad, plus a wedge of lemon on the side.

variations.name: Classic Garlic Naan
variations.description: The beloved garlic naan of every North Indian menu: a soft, yeast-risen bread pressed with a fragrant mince of raw garlic and coriander that toasts to golden bits over the flame. A ghee brush at the end carries the garlic aroma into every bite. Chewy, blistered and unabashedly garlicky, it is the bread people order two of.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Gives the naan a wholesome chew that stands up to a heavy garlic topping

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: Feeds the yeast and softens the sharpness of the raw garlic

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Melded with crushed garlic for the finishing brush that defines this naan

steps: Dissolve 1 tsp Anveshan Khandsari and 1 tsp yeast in 1/2 cup warm milk and rest 10 minutes until it foams up thickly.

Combine 1.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 cup maida, 1/2 tsp baking powder and 1 tsp salt, add the yeast milk and 3 tbsp yogurt, and knead 6-7 minutes into a soft dough; cover and prove 1 hour until doubled.
Finely chop 8 garlic cloves and 1/4 cup coriander together into a coarse, fragrant mince.

Punch down the dough, divide into 6 balls, rest 10 minutes, and roll each into a 7-inch oval; scatter the garlic-coriander mince and a pinch of nigella over the top and roll once more so it presses in.

On a smoking-hot tava, wet the plain underside and stick the naan down garlic-side up; cook 1 minute until it bubbles, then invert the tava over the flame to char the garlic for 30-40 seconds until it smells toasty and turns golden.
Meanwhile warm 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with a crushed garlic clove for one minute to infuse it.
Brush each hot naan with the garlic ghee, stack in a cloth, and serve straight away while the garlic is fragrant and just short of caramelised.
tips: Chop the garlic rather than pasting it, so it toasts into sweet golden flecks instead of scorching.
Char the garlic side directly over the flame for the best flavour, watching closely so it browns but never blackens.
The garlic-infused ghee can be made ahead and kept warm; it is what carries the aroma right through the naan.
variations.servingSuggestion: Perfect with dal makhani, kadhai paneer or a robust mushroom masala, with sliced onions and green chutney alongside.

variations.name: Restaurant Butter Garlic Naan
variations.description: The extravagant version from the tandoor line, where soft maida-rich naan is buried under roasted garlic, chilli flakes and a river of garlic butter. Cream in the dough keeps it pillowy while the garlic goes deep and mellow-sweet from roasting first. This is garlic naan turned all the way up.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: A small addition for chew without losing the pale, soft restaurant texture

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: Activates the yeast and balances the mellow roasted garlic

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Combined with butter and roasted garlic for a lavish finishing glaze

steps: Foam 1 tsp yeast with 1.5 tsp Anveshan Khandsari in 1/2 cup warm milk for 10 minutes until frothy and risen.
Knead 1.5 cups maida, 1/2 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta and 1 tsp salt with the yeast milk and 2 tbsp cream into a very soft dough, then cover and prove 1 to 1.5 hours until doubled.
Gently roast 8 of the garlic cloves in 1 tbsp of the white butter over low heat for 3-4 minutes until soft and golden, then chop them along with 4 raw cloves so you have both mellow and sharp garlic.
Punch down the dough, divide into 6 balls, and roll each into a plump 7-inch oval; press on a spoon of the mixed garlic, a pinch of chilli flakes and some coriander, rolling once to embed.
On a very hot tava, wet the base and stick the naan down, cook 1 minute until bubbled, then flip over the flame to char the garlic top for 30 seconds.
Warm the remaining white butter with 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and the leftover roasted garlic to make a loose garlic butter.
Brush each hot naan heavily with the garlic butter and shower with extra coriander before serving piping hot.
tips: Roasting most of the garlic first tames the raw bite and gives a sweet, deep flavour that plain minced garlic cannot.
Keep a few cloves raw for a fresh top note; the contrast between roasted and raw garlic is what makes this version pop.
Do not over-brown the naan itself; here the softness is the point and the garlic butter provides the richness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with shahi paneer, paneer lababdar or a creamy soya chaap curry, with a saffron lassi to cool the palate.

variations.name: Cheese Garlic Naan
variations.description: A stuffed indulgence that marries the two most-ordered naans into one: a garlic-crowned bread with a molten cheese heart. The garlic toasts on top while mozzarella melts within, so every torn piece delivers stretch, aroma and butter all at once. It is the ultimate order for a table that cannot decide.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Strong enough to seal the cheese inside while the garlic toasts on top

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: Activates the yeast for a soft dough that wraps the filling neatly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Infused with garlic and brushed on so the cheesy naan finishes glossy

steps: Foam 1 tsp yeast with 1 tsp Anveshan Khandsari in 1/2 cup warm milk for 10 minutes, then knead into 1.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 cup maida, 1 tsp salt and 3 tbsp yogurt to make a soft dough; prove 1 hour until doubled.
Finely chop 8 garlic cloves and 3 tbsp coriander, keeping a spoon of the garlic aside for the finishing ghee.
Punch down the dough and divide into 6 balls; flatten each into a disc, pile 3 tbsp grated mozzarella in the centre, gather and pinch the edges shut, and press flat.
Roll each stuffed ball gently into a 6-inch oval, then press chopped garlic, coriander and a pinch of chilli flakes onto the top and roll once lightly to fix them.
On a hot tava, wet the base of the naan and stick it down, cook 1 minute, then flip over the flame or cover to brown the garlic top for 40 seconds, by which time the cheese inside melts.
Warm 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with the reserved garlic for a minute until fragrant.
Brush each hot naan with the garlic ghee, cut in half so the cheese pulls into strands, and serve immediately.
tips: Grate the cheese cold and pack it in tightly, then seal the seam well so it melts inside rather than leaking out.
Roll slowly and evenly; rushing splits the dough and the cheese escapes onto the tava.
Serve within two minutes while the cheese still stretches, as it sets quickly once cooled.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pairs beautifully with a spicy paneer tikka masala or simply a bowl of makhani gravy for dunking.

variations.name: Multigrain Roasted Garlic Naan
variations.description: A wholesome, aromatic garlic naan built on hearty multigrain atta and finished in wood-pressed olive oil rather than butter. Slow-roasted garlic gives it a mellow, savoury depth while sesame adds crunch, making it lighter yet just as satisfying. This is the garlic naan for a health-minded table that still wants flavour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Multigrain Atta
ingredients.note: Wheat, millet and pulses give a nutty, fibre-rich naan that suits roasted garlic

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: Feeds the yeast and echoes the sweetness of the slow-roasted garlic

ingredients.name: Anveshan Olive Oil
ingredients.note: Roasts the garlic and brushes the naan for a lighter, heart-friendly finish

steps: Stir 1 tbsp Anveshan Honey and 1 tsp yeast into 1/2 cup warm water and rest 10 minutes until foamy.

Mix 2 cups Anveshan Multigrain Atta, 1/2 tsp baking powder and 1 tsp salt, add the yeast water and 1/4 cup yogurt, and knead 7-8 minutes into a soft dough; cover and prove 1 to 1.5 hours until well risen.
Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Olive Oil over low heat, add 10 sliced garlic cloves, and roast gently for 4-5 minutes until soft and pale gold, then lift out the garlic and reserve the oil.
Punch down the dough, divide into 6 balls, roll each into a 6-7 inch oval, and press on the roasted garlic, 3 tbsp coriander and 1 tbsp sesame seeds, rolling once to embed them.
On a hot tava, wet the base and stick the naan down, cook 1 minute until bubbled, then flip over the flame to toast the garlic and sesame for 30-40 seconds until fragrant.
Brush each hot naan with the reserved garlic-infused Anveshan Olive Oil for a light, savoury sheen.
Stack in a cloth and serve warm, before the wholemeal crumb tightens.
tips: Roast the garlic slowly and low; rushing it over high heat turns the slices bitter instead of sweet.
Multigrain dough needs a longer, warmer proof than white-flour naan, so give it the full rise.
Toast the sesame side last over the flame for maximum nuttiness without scorching the seeds.
variations.servingSuggestion: Great with a protein-rich rajma or dal tadka, alongside a crunchy kachumber salad and mint raita.

variations.name: Classic Gujarati Kadhi
variations.description: The delicate, drinkable kadhi of Gujarat: thin and pourable, walking the sweet-sour tightrope with jaggery and sour yogurt, and perfumed by a ghee tadka of cloves, cinnamon and curry leaves. Unlike the thick northern kadhis it carries no pakoras, meant instead to be sipped alongside khichdi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee carries the whole-spice tadka that defines Gujarati kadhi's fragrance

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: unrefined jaggery gives the sweet side of the sweet-sour balance a mellow depth white sugar cannot

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups sour yogurt with 3 tbsp besan and 3.5 cups water until completely smooth and thin, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and 1 tsp salt.
Pour the mixture into a pot and bring it to a boil over medium heat, stirring constantly in one direction so the yogurt does not split as it heats.
Once it boils, lower the flame and simmer gently for 10-12 minutes, stirring often, until the raw besan smell goes and the kadhi is silky but still thin and pourable.
Stir in 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and simmer 2 minutes until it dissolves, tasting to confirm a gentle sweet-sour balance rather than a sharp or sugary one.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan on medium heat, crackle 0.5 tsp mustard and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, then add 3 cloves, 1 inch cinnamon, 2 dried red chillies, 10 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp hing and fry 30 seconds until fragrant.
Pour the sizzling tadka over the kadhi, cover for 2 minutes to trap the aroma, then finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and serve hot.
tips: Keep this kadhi deliberately thin and pourable; a thick Gujarati kadhi is considered a mistake, not a virtue.
Stir in one direction until the first boil to keep the yogurt from curdling into grainy strands.
Balance is everything — taste and adjust jaggery and salt so neither the sweet nor the sour dominates.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside soft moong dal khichdi with a spoon of ghee, or sip it warm as a soup between courses of a Gujarati thali.

variations.name: Gujarati Kadhi with Methi Muthia
variations.description: A heartier festive version where soft steamed fenugreek muthia dumplings are simmered in the sweet-sour kadhi until they turn plump and spongy. The khapli-atta muthia soak up the tangy broth, turning a light side dish into a satisfying one-pot meal for a Sunday lunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: emmer wheat makes the methi muthia light and spongy so they soak up the kadhi without turning dense

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the ghee tadka perfumes the kadhi and a little in the muthia keeps them tender

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery keeps the signature Gujarati sweet-sour balance in the broth around the dumplings

steps: Make the muthia dough by mixing 0.5 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1 tbsp besan, 0.75 cup chopped methi, 1 tbsp sesame seeds, 0.5 tsp ajwain, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and a little water into a firm dough; roll into small cylinders.
Steam the muthia cylinders in a greased steamer for 12-15 minutes until a skewer comes out clean, then cool slightly and cut into 1 inch pieces.

Whisk 1.5 cups sour yogurt with the remaining 2 tbsp besan and 3 cups water until smooth, stir in 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and 0.75 tsp salt, and bring to a boil in a pot, stirring constantly so it does not split.

Simmer the kadhi on low for 10 minutes until the besan cooks out, then stir in 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and slip in the steamed muthia pieces to simmer 6-7 minutes so they plump and soak up the broth.
Heat the remaining ghee in a small pan, crackle 0.5 tsp mustard and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, add 10 curry leaves, and fry 20 seconds until fragrant.
Pour the tadka over the kadhi, cover 2 minutes, and serve hot with the tender muthia bobbing in the sweet-sour broth.
tips: Do not oversteam the muthia or they turn rubbery; they are done the moment a skewer comes out clean.
Add the muthia only near the end of the simmer, as long cooking makes them break apart into the kadhi.
Leftover steamed muthia can be pan-tossed with a mustard tadka the next day for a quick snack.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a light one-pot meal with plain steamed rice or on its own in bowls, garnished with extra coriander.

variations.name: Kathiyawadi Spicy Kadhi (Garlic-Forward)
variations.description: The bolder Saurashtra kadhi that trades most of the sweetness for a fierce garlic-and-red-chilli tadka. Thinner and sharper, with only a whisper of jaggery and no whole garam spices, it is built to cut through the region's oil-rich food and is poured generously over bajra rotla.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee carries the fierce garlic-and-red-chilli tadka that defines the Kathiyawadi style

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: just a whisper of jaggery here, only to round the edges rather than sweeten the kadhi

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups sour yogurt with 3 tbsp besan and 3.5 cups water until smooth and thin, then add 3 slit green chillies and 1 tsp salt.
Bring the mixture to a boil in a pot over medium heat, stirring constantly in one direction to keep the yogurt from curdling.
Lower the heat and simmer for 10-12 minutes, stirring often, until the besan is cooked out and the kadhi is thin and clean-tasting.
Stir in just 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder for colour and a gentle rounding, keeping this kadhi firmly on the spicy side.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan on medium heat, crackle 0.5 tsp mustard and 0.75 tsp cumin seeds, then add 8 crushed garlic cloves, 3 dried red chillies, 12 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp hing and fry until the garlic is deep golden.
Pour this pungent garlic tadka over the kadhi, cover 2 minutes, and finish with 2 tbsp coriander before serving fiery and hot.
tips: Fry the garlic to a deep gold, not pale, for the toasty pungency that separates Kathiyawadi kadhi from the sweet central-Gujarat one.
Keep the jaggery to barely a teaspoon; this version should read as spicy-tangy, not sweet.
A very sour yogurt works best here, as the sharpness stands up to the heavy garlic tadka.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pour generously over hot bajra rotla with a knob of white butter, or serve with rice and a fried green chilli on the side.

variations.name: Bhinda ni Kadhi (Fried Okra Kadhi)
variations.description: A South Gujarat speciality where crisp-fried okra is floated in the sweet-sour kadhi just before serving, so the pieces stay crunchy at the edges and slippery within. The okra's gentle body and the kadhi's tang make an unusual, textural pairing beloved around Surat and Navsari.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil shallow-fries the okra crisp and non-slimy, the way South Gujarat kitchens prefer

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the ghee tadka rounds out the kadhi and ties the fried okra into the sweet-sour broth

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery keeps the classic sweet-sour Gujarati balance around the okra

steps: Slice 200 g okra into 1 inch pieces and shallow-fry them in 0.5 cup Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium-high heat for 6-7 minutes until crisp and browned at the edges, then drain and set aside.
Whisk 1.5 cups sour yogurt with 3 tbsp besan, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 3.5 cups water until smooth and thin, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and 1 tsp salt.
Bring the kadhi to a boil in a pot over medium heat, stirring constantly in one direction so the yogurt stays smooth, then simmer on low for 10 minutes until the besan cooks out.
Stir in 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and simmer 2 minutes to set the sweet-sour balance.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan, crackle 0.5 tsp mustard and 0.5 tsp cumin, add 10 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp hing, and pour this tadka into the kadhi.
Add the fried okra to the pot just 2 minutes before serving so the pieces stay crisp at the edges while soaking up a little of the tangy broth.
tips: Fry the okra until genuinely crisp and add it at the very end, or it turns slimy and dulls the whole kadhi.
Do not wash the okra after slicing; pat it dry beforehand so it browns instead of steaming in the pan.
Serve immediately after adding the okra, as it softens quickly once submerged in the warm broth.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over steamed rice or with soft rotli, letting each diner spoon extra crisp okra on top just before eating.

variations.name: Classic Veg Hakka Noodles
variations.description: This Classic Veg Hakka Noodles is the beloved Indo-Chinese stir-fry of springy noodles tossed on high heat with julienned vegetables and a light soy-based seasoning. Non-sticky, smoky and studded with crunchy veg, it is the ultimate quick one-wok meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: its nutty aroma is the hallmark of authentic Indo-Chinese wok noodles

steps: Boil 300 g hakka noodles in plenty of salted water with a few drops of oil for 4 to 5 minutes until just done, then drain, rinse under cold water and toss with 1 tsp oil to keep them separate.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a wide wok until shimmering, add the minced garlic and ginger, and stir-fry on high heat for 30 seconds.
Add the julienned carrot, capsicum and 1 cup shredded cabbage and stir-fry on high for 2 to 3 minutes so they stay crunchy with a slight char.
Pour in 2 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tbsp green chilli sauce, 1 tsp vinegar, 0.5 tsp black pepper and 0.5 tsp salt and toss for 30 seconds.
Add the boiled noodles and toss vigorously on high heat for 2 to 3 minutes, lifting and folding so they coat evenly without breaking.
Stir in 4 tbsp chopped spring onion, give a final toss, and serve immediately while hot.
tips: Rinse the boiled noodles in cold water at once to stop cooking and prevent stickiness.
Cook everything on the highest flame to get the smoky wok flavour known as wok hei.
Cut all vegetables into thin, even matchsticks so they cook fast and mix uniformly with the noodles.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot on its own or paired with chilli paneer or gobi manchurian for a full Indo-Chinese spread.

variations.name: Schezwan Hakka Noodles
variations.description: A fiery version tossed in bold homemade-style Schezwan sauce with dry red chillies and extra garlic. Deep red, spicy and pungent, it turns the everyday stir-fry into a chilli lover's plate with a lingering, garlicky heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: handles the high wok heat needed to fry the fiery Schezwan paste

steps: Boil 300 g hakka noodles in salted water for 4 to 5 minutes until just cooked, drain, rinse cold and toss with a little oil.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a wok, add 4 broken dry red chillies and the minced garlic, and fry on high for 40 seconds until aromatic.
Add the julienned carrot, capsicum and 0.5 cup finely sliced french beans and stir-fry on high heat for 3 minutes to keep them crunchy.
Stir in 3 tbsp Schezwan sauce, 1 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tsp vinegar and 0.5 tsp salt and toss for 1 minute until the vegetables are coated in the red paste.
Add the boiled noodles and toss vigorously on high heat for 3 minutes so every strand turns fiery red and glossy.
Fold in 4 tbsp spring onion, toss once more, and serve at once while steaming.
tips: Adjust the Schezwan sauce gradually, tasting as you go, since brands vary in heat.
A generous amount of garlic is what gives Schezwan noodles their signature punch.
Fry the dry chillies only until fragrant so they do not turn the noodles bitter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a fried egg or veg manchurian on the side for a hearty spicy meal.

variations.name: Garlic Paneer Hakka Noodles
variations.description: A heartier, protein-rich version studded with pan-tossed garlic paneer cubes alongside the vegetables. The soft paneer and extra garlic make it more substantial than the classic, turning a side into a satisfying one-bowl meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: a nutty base for tossing the noodles and searing the paneer

steps: Boil 300 g hakka noodles in salted water for 4 to 5 minutes, drain, rinse cold and toss with a little oil to keep separate.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a wok and sear the 200 g paneer cubes with a third of the minced garlic on high heat for 2 minutes until golden, then set aside.
In the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, fry the rest of the minced garlic on high for 30 seconds, then add the julienned carrot, capsicum and 1 cup cabbage and stir-fry for 3 minutes.
Pour in 2 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tbsp red chilli sauce, 0.5 tsp black pepper and 0.5 tsp salt and toss for 30 seconds.
Add the boiled noodles and seared paneer and toss vigorously on high heat for 3 minutes so everything mixes evenly.
Fold in 4 tbsp spring onion, toss once, and serve immediately while hot.
tips: Sear the paneer separately first so it stays golden and does not crumble into the noodles.
Soak firm paneer in warm water for 10 minutes beforehand to keep it soft after searing.
Load in extra garlic for the boldest flavour, as it is the star of this version.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a filling standalone meal with a wedge of lime and a drizzle of chilli oil.

variations.name: Chilli Garlic Hakka Noodles
variations.description: A punchy version built on a bloomed chilli-garlic paste with red chilli flakes and a hit of vinegar, milder than Schezwan but bolder than the classic. Slick, garlicky and tangy, it hits the sweet spot for those who want heat without a heavy sauce.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: high smoke point for blooming the chilli-garlic paste on searing heat

steps: Boil 300 g hakka noodles in salted water for 4 to 5 minutes, drain, rinse cold and toss with a little oil.
Crush the 12 garlic cloves coarsely, then heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and fry the garlic with 1.5 tsp red chilli flakes on medium-high heat for 40 seconds until fragrant and just golden.
Add the sliced onion, julienned carrot and capsicum and stir-fry on high heat for 3 minutes so they keep their crunch.
Pour in 2 tbsp soy sauce, 1.5 tsp vinegar, 0.5 tsp sugar and 0.5 tsp salt and toss for 30 seconds until glossy.
Add the boiled noodles and toss vigorously on high heat for 3 minutes so the chilli-garlic coats every strand.
Fold in 4 tbsp spring onion, toss once, and serve immediately.
tips: Coarsely crush rather than mince the garlic so it stays juicy and infuses the oil deeply.
The pinch of sugar rounds off the vinegar and chilli into a balanced tang.
Bloom the chilli flakes just until fragrant to avoid a scorched, bitter edge.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve topped with crispy fried garlic and extra chilli flakes for those who love more heat.

variations.name: Classic Indori Poha with Jeeravan
variations.description: The famous street breakfast of Indore, a fluffy fennel-scented poha steamed soft and dusted generously with the city's signature jeeravan masala for a sweet, tangy, faintly musky hit. It is finished with raw onion, crisp sev, pomegranate and a squeeze of lemon in true Indori style. Lighter and steamier than Maharashtrian poha, it is unmistakable for its jeeravan sprinkle.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A wood-pressed oil that blooms the fennel-mustard tempering with the nutty base note of Indori poha

steps: Rinse 2 cups thick poha gently in a colander until just soft and leave to drain, then fluff with a fork so the flakes separate.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard and 1 tsp fennel seeds, then add 2 chopped green chillies and 12 curry leaves for 30 seconds.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp sugar and 0.75 tsp salt, then fold in the drained poha until evenly pale yellow.
Sprinkle 2 tablespoons of water over the poha, cover, and steam on the lowest heat for 3-4 minutes until the flakes turn soft and fluffy.
Turn off the heat and dust 1 tsp jeeravan masala through the poha, tossing so the tangy spice coats the flakes.
Top each serving with chopped onion, 0.5 cups sev, 0.25 cups pomegranate, a squeeze of lemon and the remaining jeeravan dusted over the top.
tips: The jeeravan masala is the soul of this dish, so dust a little into the poha and more on top for the true Indori taste.
Steam the poha with a sprinkle of water under a lid; this extra fluffing step is what makes Indori poha so light.
Add fennel to the tempering, as its gentle sweetness is a defining note that sets Indori poha apart.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot heaped with extra sev, a wedge of lemon and a side of hot jalebi, the classic Indori breakfast pairing.

variations.name: Indori Poha with Ratlami Sev and Usal
variations.description: A hearty market-style plate where the jeeravan poha is topped with a ladle of spicy white-pea usal and a shower of coarse Ratlami sev, turning breakfast into a full meal. The gravy soaks into the flakes while the sev stays crunchy on top. This is how many Indore stalls serve it to a hungrier crowd.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Blooms the poha tempering and the separate usal masala with a robust nutty base

steps: Rinse 2 cups thick poha gently in a colander until just soft, drain and fluff; then make the usal by heating 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and frying half the chopped onion 3 minutes.
Add 1 cup cooked white peas, 1.5 tsp goda masala, 0.5 tsp salt and half a cup of water, and simmer 8 minutes into a thick spiced gravy.
For the poha, heat the remaining 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard and 1 tsp fennel seeds, then add 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp sugar and 0.5 tsp salt.
Fold in the drained poha, sprinkle 2 tablespoons water, cover and steam 3-4 minutes until fluffy, then dust 1 tsp jeeravan through it.
Plate the jeeravan poha and ladle the hot white-pea usal generously over one side.
Shower 0.5 cups Ratlami sev, the remaining raw onion, a squeeze of lemon and the rest of the jeeravan over the top and serve at once.
tips: Keep the usal slightly thick so it sits on the poha without making the whole plate soupy.
Add the Ratlami sev only at serving, since its coarse strands go soggy quickly once they meet the warm gravy.
Soak the white peas overnight and cook them soft, as firm peas make the usal heavy and dull.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve immediately with extra lemon and chopped coriander, best eaten while the sev still crackles over the usal.

variations.name: Indori Poha with Tempered Pomegranate and Grapes
variations.description: A fresher, fruitier Indori plate that leans into the city's love of pomegranate by finishing the jeeravan poha with both pomegranate and halved green grapes for pops of sweet-tart juice. The steamed poha stays light while the fruit and jeeravan play off each other. It is a brighter, more summery take on the street classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Blooms the fennel-mustard tempering with a nutty base that grounds the fruity topping

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: A drizzle stirred in for a natural sweet edge that plays against the tangy jeeravan and tart fruit

steps: Rinse 2 cups thick poha gently in a colander until just soft, drain and fluff with a fork so the flakes separate.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard and 1 tsp fennel seeds, then add 2 chopped green chillies and 12 curry leaves for 30 seconds.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt, then fold in the drained poha until evenly pale yellow.
Sprinkle 2 tablespoons water, cover, and steam on the lowest heat for 3-4 minutes until the flakes turn soft and fluffy.
Turn off the heat, drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Honey and dust 1 tsp jeeravan through the poha, tossing gently.
Top with 0.5 cups pomegranate, 0.5 cups halved green grapes, a squeeze of lemon and the remaining jeeravan, then serve fresh.
tips: Halve the grapes so their juice mingles into the poha instead of rolling off the plate whole.
Add the honey off the heat so it stays fragrant and simply glosses the warm flakes.
Keep the fruit topping generous and add it last so it stays crisp and jewel-bright against the pale poha.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a light summer breakfast with a glass of chilled buttermilk, letting the fruit keep it refreshing.

variations.name: Ghee-Roasted Indori Poha with Cashews
variations.description: A richer festive-morning version where the poha is finished in nutty ghee and folded with ghee-roasted cashews, giving a fuller aroma beneath the signature jeeravan dusting. The ghee rounds the tangy masala and makes the flakes glossy and fragrant. It is the indulgent home-kitchen upgrade to the everyday street poha.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasts the cashews and glosses the poha, rounding the tangy jeeravan with a nutty richness

steps: Rinse 2 cups thick poha gently in a colander until just soft, drain and fluff with a fork.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, roast 0.33 cups cashews for 2 minutes until golden, and lift them out.
In the same ghee splutter 1 tsp mustard and 1 tsp fennel seeds, then add 2 chopped green chillies and 12 curry leaves for 30 seconds.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp sugar and 0.75 tsp salt, fold in the drained poha, sprinkle 2 tablespoons water, cover and steam 3-4 minutes until fluffy.
Turn off the heat, fold in the roasted cashews and dust 1 tsp jeeravan through the poha.
Top with chopped onion, 0.5 cups sev, a squeeze of lemon and the remaining jeeravan, then serve warm.
tips: Roast the cashews slowly in the ghee so they turn evenly golden without scorching and stay crunchy.
Finishing in ghee makes the flakes glossy, so use a light hand with the water while steaming to avoid stickiness.
Add the roasted cashews at the end so they keep their bite against the soft, fragrant poha.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with masala chai and a side of hot jalebi for a rich, festive Indori-style breakfast.

variations.name: Classic Maharashtrian Jowar Bhakri
variations.description: The daily bread of rural Maharashtra, a soft-centred sorghum flatbread patted out by hand from a warm-water dough and puffed over an open flame. Gluten-free jowar demands hot water and a firm palm, and the reward is a nutty, wheat-free round that pairs with everything from thecha to pithla. Traditionally cooked half on the tava and finished directly on the coals until it balloons.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Smeared over the hot bhakri the moment it comes off the flame, melting into the porous crumb

steps: Bring 1.25 cups water to a rolling boil with 0.75 tsp salt, then pour it over 2 cups jowar flour mixed with 0.5 tsp carom seeds and 1 tbsp sesame seeds in a bowl, stirring until it clumps together.
Once cool enough to touch, knead the warm dough for 4-5 minutes, pressing with your palm heel until it turns smooth and free of cracks.
Take a large ball, place it on a lightly floured surface or a sheet of parchment, and pat it outward with flat wet fingers into a 6-inch round of even thickness.
Lift it onto a medium-hot tava, and after 30 seconds smear a little water over the top surface with your palm.
Cook until the underside shows brown spots, about 1-2 minutes, then flip; once the second side sets, lift the bhakri with tongs and hold it over a direct flame until it puffs into a dome.
Slide it onto a plate, smear 0.75 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the hot surface, and repeat with the remaining dough.
tips: Knead the dough while it is still warm; hot water gelatinises the jowar starch, which is the only thing binding this gluten-free flour.
Wetting the top surface before cooking creates the steam that makes the bhakri puff over the flame.
Pat, do not roll; a rolling pin tears jowar dough, while wet fingers give the even round it needs to balloon.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot with green-chilli thecha, a knob of white butter and a raw onion, or with pithla for the classic zunka-bhakri plate.

variations.name: Garlic-Peanut Jowar Bhakri
variations.description: A Khandeshi-style bhakri where crushed garlic, roasted peanuts and red chilli are kneaded straight into the sorghum dough, so every bite carries the punch of a thecha built right in. The peanuts add richness and a coarse crunch to the soft millet round. Robust and boldly flavoured, it can hold its own with just a bowl of curd.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Echoes the peanut theme and roasts the base of the studded bhakri to a crisp finish

steps: Crush 6 garlic cloves with 3 tbsp roasted peanuts and 1 tsp red chilli powder to a coarse paste in a mortar, keeping some peanut texture.
Mix this into 2 cups jowar flour with 1 tsp cumin seeds, 3 tbsp chopped coriander and 0.75 tsp salt in a bowl.
Pour in about 1.25 cups boiling water, stir, and once bearable, knead the warm dough 4-5 minutes until smooth and crack-free.
Pat a ball into a 6-inch round on parchment with wet fingers, keeping it slightly thick so the peanut bits do not tear through.
Cook on a medium-hot tava 1-2 minutes a side, drizzling 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil around the edge, then puff it briefly over a direct flame.
Repeat with the remaining dough, stacking the bhakris under a cloth to keep them warm.
tips: Leave the peanuts coarse rather than powdered; the little nuggets are what give this bhakri its signature crunch.
This studded dough tears more easily, so pat it a touch thicker and mend any cracks with a wet fingertip.
Dry-roast and cool the peanuts before crushing so they stay crisp inside the bread instead of turning soft.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain chilled curd or buttermilk alone; the garlic and peanut built into the bhakri need no separate accompaniment.

variations.name: Masala Onion Jowar Bhakri (Dhebra-Style)
variations.description: A soft, seasoned bhakri in the spirit of a Gujarati dhebra, worked with finely chopped onion, sesame and warm spices so it eats almost like a savoury pancake. The onion moisture keeps the crumb tender and the sesame lends a toasty finish. This is the version made when the bhakri is meant to be a snack in its own right.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Kneaded in and drizzled on the tava, it amplifies the toasted-sesame flavour and softens the millet

steps: In a bowl mix 2 cups jowar flour, 1 finely chopped onion, 1 tbsp sesame seeds, 0.5 tsp carom seeds, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp coriander-cumin powder, 2 minced green chillies and 0.75 tsp salt.
Add 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, then pour in about 1 cup hot water gradually; the onion releases liquid, so knead into a soft dough adding water cautiously.
Rest the warm dough 10 minutes, then pat a ball on parchment into a 5-inch round a little thicker than a plain bhakri.
Transfer to a medium-hot tava and cook 1-2 minutes until the base is speckled, drizzling 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil around the rim.
Flip, drizzle a little more oil, and roast the second side 1-2 minutes, pressing gently until golden; skip the open flame as the onion makes it too soft to puff cleanly.
Repeat with the rest of the dough and serve the masala bhakris warm.
tips: Chop the onion very fine so it distributes evenly and does not create weak spots that tear the dough.
Cook these fully on the tava rather than over a flame; the moist onion dough is better shallow-roasted than puffed.
Add the salt just before kneading so the onion does not weep too much and turn the dough unworkable.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a teatime snack with a cup of masala chai and a dollop of garlic pickle, or with a mango chhundo for sweetness.

variations.name: Jowar-Bajra Mixed Millet Bhakri
variations.description: A darker, denser winter bhakri that blends pearl millet into the sorghum for extra warmth and a deeper, earthy flavour prized in Marathwada households. The bajra adds body and a faint sweetness while making the round more filling. Best eaten hot off the tava, when the two millets are at their most fragrant.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A generous smear over the hot mixed-millet bhakri tempers the earthy bajra and adds richness

steps: Combine 1.25 cups jowar flour, 0.75 cups bajra flour, 0.5 tsp carom seeds and 0.75 tsp salt in a bowl.
Pour over about 1.25 cups boiling water, stir into a shaggy mass, and knead the warm dough 5 minutes until smooth; the bajra makes it stiffer, so wet your palm as you work.
Pat a ball on parchment with wet fingers into a 6-inch round, keeping it a shade thicker than a plain jowar bhakri to stop the denser dough cracking.
Cook on a medium-hot tava, wetting the top surface after 30 seconds, until the base is spotted brown, about 2 minutes.
Flip, set the second side, then lift with tongs and hold over a direct flame until it puffs; the mixed millet puffs more shyly than pure jowar.
Smear 0.75 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the hot bhakri and repeat with the remaining dough.
tips: The extra bajra makes a stiffer dough, so keep a bowl of warm water beside you to wet your hands while patting.
Eat these fresh; mixed-millet bhakri firms up faster than the all-jowar kind as it cools.
A pinch of carom seed is not optional here, as it eases the digestion of the heavier bajra.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a fiery baingan bharta or a bowl of amti dal, letting the ghee-smeared bhakri soak up the gravy.

variations.name: Classic Afghan Kabuli Pulao
variations.description: The celebrated Afghan pulao where long-grain rice is steamed over a sweet caramel base and crowned with a glossy tangle of julienned carrots and raisins fried in ghee. Chickpeas fold through the rice for body while the caramelised sugar gives the grains their signature amber sheen. Fragrant with cardamom and cumin, it is a festive centrepiece meant to be piled high on a platter.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Caramelises the onions for the amber base and fries the carrot-raisin garnish to a glossy finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Melted into a dark caramel that tints the rice amber and gives the pulao its signature gentle sweetness

ingredients.name: Whole spices (cardamom, cloves, cinnamon, cumin seeds)

steps: Rinse and soak 2 cups basmati for 30 minutes and drain; cut 2 carrots into fine matchsticks.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan, fry the carrot sticks 3 minutes, add 0.33 cups raisins and the slivered nuts until the raisins plump, then set the garnish aside.
In a heavy pot melt 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium heat until it turns to a dark amber caramel, about 2 minutes.
Add 2 sliced onions and the whole spices, fry 8 minutes until deep golden, then stir in 1 tsp coriander powder, 1 cup chickpeas and 1.5 tsp salt.
Add the drained rice, toast 2 minutes, pour in 2.5 cups hot water, bring to a boil, then cover on the lowest flame for 12 minutes.
Rest 10 minutes, fluff the amber rice with a fork, and pile the fried carrot, raisin and nut garnish generously over the top.
tips: Watch the jaggery caramel closely; take it off the moment it turns amber, as a burnt caramel makes the whole pot bitter.
Julienne the carrots as fine as possible so they curl into glossy ribbons rather than staying stiff sticks.
Soak the rice a full 30 minutes so the grains lengthen and stay separate in the classic long-grain pile.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve heaped on a platter with an Afghan-style green chilli-coriander chutney and a bowl of plain yogurt.

variations.name: Kabuli Pulao with Paneer Koftas
variations.description: A vegetarian reinvention that stands in for the traditional lamb with soft pan-fried paneer-and-potato koftas nestled through the sweet carrot rice. The koftas soak up the cardamom-scented steam and add a rich, protein-forward bite. It turns the festive pulao into a complete meal without losing the amber caramel character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Caramelises the onion base and fries the carrot garnish for the pulao's amber glow

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A neutral wood-pressed oil for shallow-frying the paneer koftas to a golden, non-greasy crust

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Caramelised to tint the rice amber and lend the traditional gentle sweetness

steps: Mash 1 cup grated paneer with 1 boiled potato, 2 tbsp cornflour and 0.5 tsp salt, roll into 12 small koftas, and shallow-fry in 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil for 3 minutes until golden all over.
Soak 2 cups basmati 30 minutes and drain; fry 2 carrots cut into matchsticks in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with 0.33 cups raisins until glossy, and reserve the garnish.
Melt 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until it forms a dark amber caramel, about 2 minutes on medium heat.
Add 2 sliced onions and the whole spices, fry 8 minutes until golden, then add the drained rice, 1 tsp salt and toast 2 minutes.
Pour in 2.5 cups hot water, bring to a boil, gently tuck the fried koftas into the rice, then cover on the lowest flame for 12 minutes.
Rest 10 minutes, fluff carefully around the koftas, and crown with the fried carrot-raisin garnish.
tips: Bind the koftas with cornflour and chill them 10 minutes before frying so they hold shape in the hot oil.
Add the koftas after the water so they steam gently on top and stay soft rather than breaking into the rice.
Fry the koftas until firm-golden, since a fragile crust falls apart when folded through the fluffy pulao.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a tangy tomato-coriander chutney and a cucumber raita to balance the rich paneer koftas.

variations.name: Brown Chana Kabuli Pulao
variations.description: An earthier, more rustic version swapping pale kabuli chana for nutty brown chana and finishing with a smoky cumin tempering. The dark chickpeas hold a firmer bite and lend the rice a deeper, grounded flavour against the sweet carrots. It is the wholesome, fibre-rich take that eats like a full meal on its own.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Caramelises the onions and blooms the cumin tempering for a smoky, grounded aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Caramelised for the amber tint and to balance the earthy brown chana with a touch of sweetness

steps: Soak 2 cups basmati 30 minutes and drain; fry 2 carrots cut into matchsticks with 0.25 cups raisins in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until glossy and reserve.
Melt 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee to a dark amber caramel, about 2 minutes on medium heat.
Crackle 1.5 tsp cumin seeds and the whole spices for 30 seconds, add 2 sliced onions, and fry 8 minutes until deep golden.
Stir in 1 cup cooked brown chana, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp crushed black pepper and 1.5 tsp salt, and saute 2 minutes.
Add the drained rice, toast 2 minutes, pour in 2.5 cups hot water, bring to a boil, then cover on the lowest flame for 12 minutes.
Rest 10 minutes, fluff the amber rice with a fork, and top with the fried carrot-raisin garnish.
tips: Cook the brown chana until soft but still holding shape, as it stays firmer than kabuli chana and should not turn mushy.
Bloom extra cumin in the ghee for a smokier profile that stands up to the robust brown chickpeas.
Reserve a little chana cooking liquor to replace some of the water for a deeper, more savoury rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a smoky roasted-tomato chutney and a spoon of thick curd for a hearty wholegrain plate.

variations.name: Restaurant-Style Zafrani Kabuli Pulao
variations.description: A dressed-up banquet version where saffron milk and a layer of birista lift the sweet carrot rice, and the caramel is deepened with a splash of rose water. Richer and more perfumed than the home version, it is finished under dum for restaurant-grade fluffiness. This is the pulao plated at Afghan restaurants, glossy and generously garnished.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Fries the birista, caramelises the base and glazes the garnish for a restaurant-grade richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Steeped in warm milk and drizzled over the rice for a golden bloom and floral banquet aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Caramelised for the classic amber tint and gentle sweetness of a Kabuli pulao

steps: Soak 2 cups basmati 30 minutes and drain; steep the Anveshan Saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk and fry 3 sliced onions in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee for 12 minutes until crisp golden birista.
In 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee fry 2 carrots cut into matchsticks with 0.33 cups raisins until glossy, then reserve this garnish.
Melt 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee to a dark amber caramel, add the whole spices, 1 cup chickpeas and 1.5 tsp salt, and saute 2 minutes.
Add the drained rice, toast 2 minutes, pour in 2.5 cups hot water, bring to a boil, then scatter half the birista and the saffron milk over the top.
Cover and dum on the lowest flame over a tava for 15 minutes, then sprinkle 0.5 tsp rose water and rest 10 minutes.
Fluff gently, then crown with the fried carrot-raisin garnish and the remaining crisp birista.
tips: Finishing the pulao on a low dum over a tava gives the restaurant-style separate, glossy grains.
Fry the birista until genuinely crisp and deep-golden so it stays crunchy as a garnish rather than going limp.
Sprinkle the rose water only at the end and sparingly, as too much turns the delicate perfume soapy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a large platter with a green chutney, sliced onions and a bowl of chilled yogurt for a banquet spread.

variations.name: Classic Kadhi Pakora
variations.description: The comforting North Indian staple: a tangy besan-yogurt curry simmered slow until velvety, then studded with crisp onion pakoras that drink up the sauce. A ghee tadka of cumin, fenugreek and dried red chillies crackled over the top gives every spoonful its warm, homely aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the finishing bilona-ghee tadka of cumin and red chilli is what gives classic kadhi its signature homely aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: light wood-pressed sunflower oil fries the onion pakoras crisp and clean without weighing them down

steps: Whisk 0.5 cup besan into 1.5 cups sour yogurt with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 3 cups water until absolutely lump-free, then keep this kadhi mixture aside.
For the pakoras, mix the remaining 0.25 cup besan with 2 sliced onions, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp salt and a splash of water into a thick, clinging batter.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Sunflower Oil to 170C and drop in small spoonfuls of the onion batter, frying in batches for 3-4 minutes until deep golden and crisp, then drain on a rack.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot on medium heat, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry 1 minute, then pour in the kadhi mixture and bring to a boil, stirring constantly so it does not curdle.

Lower the heat and simmer the kadhi uncovered for 25-30 minutes, stirring every few minutes, until it thickens to a coating consistency and the raw besan smell disappears; season with the remaining 1 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp red chilli powder.

Slip the fried pakoras into the kadhi and simmer 5 more minutes, then in a small pan heat the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin, 0.5 tsp fenugreek seeds, 3 dried red chillies, 10 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp hing, and pour this sizzling tadka over the pot before serving.
tips: Keep stirring the kadhi constantly until it reaches a boil the first time; this is the only way to stop the yogurt from splitting.
Add the pakoras only a few minutes before serving if you like them firm, or earlier if you prefer them soft and sauce-soaked.
A pleasantly sour yogurt is essential; if yours is fresh, leave the mixture out for an hour to sharpen before cooking.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve ladled over steamed rice with a spoon of ghee, a papad and a sharp mango pickle on the side.

variations.name: Palak Pakora Kadhi (Mustard-Oil Tempered)
variations.description: A greener, sharper kadhi built on spinach pakoras and a pungent mustard-oil tempering with garlic and kalonji. The spinach fritters stay soft in the tangy curry while the mustard-oil chhaunk gives it an earthy, eastern-India edge quite unlike the ghee-tempered classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: kachi ghani mustard oil fries the spinach pakoras and tempers the kadhi with an earthy pungency the classic lacks

steps: Whisk 0.5 cup besan into 1.5 cups sour yogurt with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 3 cups water until smooth and lump-free, then set the kadhi mixture aside.
Mix the remaining 0.25 cup besan with 1.5 cups chopped spinach, 0.5 tsp ajwain, 2 chopped green chillies, 0.5 tsp salt and a little water into a thick pakora batter.

Heat 2 cups Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, cool it 30 seconds, then fry small spoonfuls of the spinach batter for 3-4 minutes until crisp and dark green at the edges; drain on a rack, leaving 2 tbsp oil in the pan.
In that reserved mustard oil, fry half the crushed garlic for 1 minute, pour in the kadhi mixture and bring to a boil while stirring constantly to keep it from splitting.
Simmer the kadhi uncovered on low for 25-30 minutes until thick and glossy, seasoning with 1 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, then slide in the spinach pakoras and cook 5 minutes more.

Heat 2 tbsp fresh Anveshan Mustard Oil in a small pan, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp kalonji, add the remaining crushed garlic and 1 chopped green chilli until golden, pour this over the kadhi and finish with 3 tbsp coriander.
tips: Squeeze excess water from the chopped spinach before mixing the batter, or the pakoras turn limp instead of crisp.
Heat mustard oil to smoking point once before frying to tame its raw sharpness, both for the pakoras and the tadka.
This kadhi tastes even better reheated, once the spinach pakoras have fully soaked up the tangy curry.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice or hot phulkas and a side of raw onion rings soaked in lemon.

variations.name: Methi-Corn Pakora Kadhi (Coriander-Seed Tadka)
variations.description: A fragrant twist pairing bittersweet fresh fenugreek with sweet corn in the pakoras, set in a lightly jaggery-balanced kadhi tempered with crushed coriander seeds in groundnut oil. The corn bursts sweet against the methi's edge, making this the most aromatic and gently sweet of the kadhis.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil fries the methi-corn pakoras nutty-crisp and carries the coriander-seed tadka beautifully

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a spoon of jaggery balances the methi's bitterness and the yogurt's sourness with a mellow warmth

steps: Whisk 0.5 cup besan into 1.5 cups sour yogurt with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 3 cups water until silky and lump-free, and keep the kadhi mixture ready.
Combine the remaining 0.25 cup besan with 1 cup chopped methi leaves, 0.5 cup sweet corn, 1 chopped green chilli, 0.5 tsp salt and a splash of water into a thick pakora batter.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 170C and fry small clusters of the methi-corn batter for 3-4 minutes until golden and crisp, then drain on a rack and set 2 tbsp oil aside.
In the reserved oil, saute 1 inch grated ginger and 2 chopped green chillies for 1 minute, pour in the kadhi mixture and bring to a boil, stirring nonstop to keep the yogurt smooth.
Simmer uncovered on low for 25-30 minutes until thick, then stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1.5 tsp salt, taste for the sweet-sour balance, and drop in the pakoras to cook 5 minutes.
Heat 2 tbsp fresh Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a small pan, crackle 1 tsp cumin, 1 tbsp crushed coriander seeds and 12 curry leaves for 40 seconds, and pour this fragrant tadka over the finished kadhi.
tips: Rub the chopped methi with a little salt and squeeze after 10 minutes to remove excess bitterness before making the batter.
Crush the coriander seeds only coarsely so they pop and release aroma in the hot oil rather than dissolving.
Keep the jaggery subtle — it should round the sourness, not turn the kadhi into a sweet Gujarati-style curry.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jeera rice or soft rotis and a cooling cucumber raita to offset the aromatic, gently sweet curry.

variations.name: Baked Sattu Pakora Light Kadhi
variations.description: A lighter, protein-rich reinvention where the pakoras are bound with roasted sattu and baked instead of deep-fried, then dropped into a leaner kadhi finished with a pepper-cumin tadka. It keeps the tang and comfort intact while cutting the oil dramatically — a guilt-free everyday bowl.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: roasted gram sattu binds the baked pakoras with plant protein and a nutty depth so they hold shape without frying

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: just a light brush of wood-pressed sunflower oil crisps the baked pakoras and carries the tadka

steps: Whisk 0.5 cup besan into 1.5 cups low-fat yogurt with 0.75 tsp turmeric and 3 cups water until smooth, and set this kadhi mixture aside.

For the baked pakoras, mix 0.5 cup Anveshan Sattu with 1 finely chopped onion, 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp salt and just enough water to make a thick, scoopable mixture.
Shape the mixture into small balls, place on a lined tray, brush with 1 tbsp Anveshan Sunflower Oil, and bake at 200C for 15-18 minutes, turning once, until firm and golden.

Bring the kadhi mixture to a boil in a pot over medium heat, stirring constantly, then lower the flame and simmer uncovered for 25-30 minutes until thickened, seasoning with 1 tsp salt and 0.25 tsp red chilli powder.
Slide the baked sattu pakoras into the kadhi and simmer for 5 minutes so they soften slightly and soak up the tang.

Heat the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Sunflower Oil in a small pan, crackle 1 tsp cumin, 0.5 tsp fenugreek seeds, 0.5 tsp crushed black pepper and 10 curry leaves for 30 seconds, and pour this light tadka over the kadhi before serving.
tips: Keep the sattu mixture stiff enough to hold a ball; too much water and the baked pakoras spread and flatten.
