Add the baked pakoras just before serving if you want them firm, as they soften faster than fried ones in the curry.
Using low-fat yogurt and baking makes this a genuinely lighter kadhi, ideal for those watching their oil intake.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with brown rice or millet roti and a side of steamed greens for a wholesome, high-protein meal.

variations.name: Classic Kashmiri Fruit-and-Nut Pulao
variations.description: A gently sweet, festive rice from the valley where fragrant basmati is simmered with whole warm spices, then crowned with fried nuts, pomegranate and slivers of apple and pineapple. Saffron and a pinch of sugar give it a delicate golden sweetness that plays against the crunch of cashews and almonds. It is a celebratory pulao meant to be the centrepiece of a vegetarian spread.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Blooms the whole spices and fries the nuts, lending the sweet pulao its rich festive aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Steeped in warm milk to tint the rice a pale gold and add the valley's signature floral note

ingredients.name: Whole spices (cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, bay leaf)
Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: An unrefined sugar that lends a soft caramel sweetness to balance the warm spices without turning cloying

steps: Rinse and soak 1.5 cups basmati for 20 minutes and drain; steep the Anveshan Saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk and set aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot on medium flame and fry 0.25 cups cashews and 0.25 cups almonds for 2 minutes until golden, then lift them out.
In the same ghee crackle the whole spices for 30 seconds until fragrant, then add the drained rice and toast gently for 2 minutes.
Pour in 2.5 cups hot water, the saffron milk, 1 tsp Anveshan Khandsari and 1 tsp salt, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on the lowest flame for 12 minutes.
Rest 10 minutes off the heat, then fluff the rice with a fork so each grain stays separate and lightly golden.
Fold in the fried nuts, 0.5 cups pomegranate, 0.5 diced apple and 0.5 cups pineapple just before serving so the fruit stays fresh and crunchy.
tips: Add the fresh fruit only at the end; folding it in while the rice is hot makes it soggy and dulls its colour.
Keep the sweetness gentle with just a teaspoon of khandsari, as this pulao should whisper sweet rather than taste like dessert.
Toast the drained rice in ghee before adding water so the grains stay firm and separate under the fruit.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside a cooling dahi ki chutney or a mild paneer korma, letting the sweet rice offset a savoury gravy.

variations.name: Honey-Glazed Dry Fruit Kashmiri Pulao
variations.description: A richer, dessert-leaning version where the nuts and dried fruit are glazed in honey before crowning the saffron rice, giving a glossy, sticky-sweet finish. Dates, figs and raisins deepen the caramel notes while the honey lacquer makes every nut glisten. This is the pulao for weddings and Eid tables, more indulgent than the everyday fruit version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Fries the whole spices and dried fruit, carrying the honey glaze deep into the pulao

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: Glazes the warm nuts and dried fruit into a glossy, sticky crown over the saffron rice

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Bloomed in warm milk for the golden hue and floral aroma that defines a valley pulao

steps: Soak 1.5 cups basmati 20 minutes and drain; steep the Anveshan Saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk and chop the figs and dates into slivers.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle the whole spices for 30 seconds, add the drained rice and toast 2 minutes until the grains look glossy.
Pour in 2.5 cups hot water, the saffron milk and 1 tsp salt, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on the lowest flame for 12 minutes and rest 10 minutes.
In a small pan warm the remaining ghee, fry 0.25 cups pistachios, 0.25 cups walnuts, the fig-date slivers and 0.25 cups raisins for 2 minutes until the raisins puff.
Turn off the heat, drizzle 2 tbsp Anveshan Honey over the warm nuts and swirl for 30 seconds until they are evenly glazed and glossy.
Fluff the rested rice with a fork and spoon the honey-glazed dry fruit over the top just before serving so the glaze stays shiny.
tips: Add the honey only after taking the pan off the heat, as boiling honey turns bitter and loses its floral aroma.
Soak the figs and dates in warm water for ten minutes if they are very dry, so they turn plump rather than chewy.
Make the glazed dry fruit ahead and warm it briefly at serving time to revive the glossy lacquer.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a festive centrepiece with a bowl of spiced yogurt and a mild vegetable stew to balance the sweetness.

variations.name: Coconut-Milk Kashmiri Pulao
variations.description: A creamy southern-influenced twist where the rice simmers in coconut milk instead of water, giving a mellow, faintly sweet body that carries the saffron beautifully. The coconut richness softens the warm spices while fresh fruit and nuts keep it in the Kashmiri spirit. It is a fusion pulao, silkier and more rounded than the classic water-cooked version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Blooms the spices and echoes the coconut milk for a rounded, tropical depth in the pulao

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Steeped in warm milk to gild the coconut rice and keep the valley's floral signature

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A whisper of unrefined sweetness that marries the coconut and saffron without any refined sugar

steps: Soak 1.5 cups basmati 20 minutes and drain; steep the Anveshan Saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk and dice the apple.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pot on medium flame, fry 0.25 cups cashews for 2 minutes until golden, and lift them out.
Crackle the whole spices in the same oil for 30 seconds, add the drained rice and toast gently for 2 minutes.
Pour in 1.25 cups coconut milk, 1.25 cups hot water, the saffron milk, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp salt, and bring to a gentle boil.
Cover and cook on the lowest flame for 12 minutes, taking care the coconut milk does not catch, then rest 10 minutes off the heat.
Fluff with a fork and fold in the fried cashews, diced apple and 0.5 cups black grapes just before serving.
tips: Use a heavy-bottomed pot and the lowest flame, since coconut milk scorches far more easily than plain water.
Balance the coconut milk with an equal measure of water so the rice cooks through without turning heavy.
Stir the jaggery powder in fully before covering the pot so it dissolves evenly through the coconut rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a tangy raw-mango pachadi or a light vegetable stew to cut through the coconut creaminess.

variations.name: Zafrani Brown Rice Kashmiri Pulao
variations.description: A wholesome reworking using nutty brown basmati that stands up to the saffron and warm spices with a chewier bite and earthier aroma. The longer cook lets the grains soak up the zafrani milk deeply, while apricots and pumpkin seeds bring modern crunch. It is the health-conscious take on the festive valley pulao, hearty enough to eat on its own.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Toasts the nutty brown grains and blooms the spices so the wholegrain pulao stays fragrant

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Steeped in warm milk to gild the brown rice and keep the festive zafrani character

ingredients.name: Whole spices (cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, bay leaf)
Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: A light drizzle stirred in at the end for a mellow sweetness that suits the earthy brown rice

steps: Soak 1.5 cups brown basmati for at least 30 minutes and drain; steep the Anveshan Saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk and slice the apricots.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, toast 0.25 cups almond slivers and 0.25 cups pumpkin seeds for 2 minutes until fragrant, and set them aside.
Crackle the whole spices in the ghee for 30 seconds, add the drained brown rice and toast for 3 minutes until nutty.
Pour in 3 cups hot water, the saffron milk and 1 tsp salt, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on the lowest flame for 25-28 minutes until tender.
Rest 10 minutes off the heat, drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Honey over the warm rice, and fluff gently with a fork.
Fold in the toasted nuts and seeds, the sliced apricots and 0.5 cups pomegranate just before serving.
tips: Brown rice needs nearly double the cooking time of white basmati, so soak it well and be patient with the simmer.
Add roughly two parts water to one part brown rice, since the bran layer absorbs more liquid than polished grains.
Toast the seeds separately and add them last so they keep their crunch against the chewy wholegrain rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a bowl of hung-curd raita and a squeeze of orange for a wholesome, protein-rich plate.

variations.name: Classic Punjabi Lobia Masala
variations.description: Creamy black-eyed peas simmered in a slow-cooked onion-tomato masala until the gravy turns thick and clings to each bean. A hearty, protein-packed Punjabi everyday curry, it is warmly spiced with a mellow ghee finish that makes it taste like it cooked all afternoon.

ingredients.name: Black-eyed peas
ingredients.note: soaked 4 hours or overnight

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee builds the base masala and finishes the curry with a rounded aroma

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: pureed

ingredients.name: Kasuri methi
ingredients.note: crushed

steps: Drain the soaked black-eyed peas and pressure-cook with 2.5 cups water, 1/4 tsp turmeric powder and 1/2 tsp salt for 3-4 whistles until soft but still whole; keep with the cooking liquid.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1 bay leaf for 30 seconds, then add 2 chopped onions and fry 7-8 minutes until deep golden.

Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then pour in the puree of 3 tomatoes with 1/4 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp cumin powder and 3/4 tsp salt.
Bhuno the masala on medium heat for 7-8 minutes, until it darkens, thickens and the ghee separates at the edges.
Tip in the cooked lobia along with their liquid, mash a spoonful of beans against the pan to thicken the gravy, and simmer on low heat for 12-15 minutes so the flavours meld.
Crush 1 tsp kasuri methi over the curry and stir in 1/2 tsp garam masala, adding a little hot water if the gravy gets too thick.
Simmer 2 more minutes, finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander, and serve hot.
tips: Soak the peas well; unsoaked lobia cook unevenly and some stay chalky in the centre.
Mashing a spoonful of the cooked beans is the trick to a naturally creamy gravy without any cream.
The curry thickens on standing, so loosen with hot water when reheating rather than overcooking it fresh.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice or hot rotis, a spoon of ghee and a sliced onion-lemon salad on the side.

variations.name: South Indian Coconut Lobia Curry
variations.description: A Kerala-inspired stew where black-eyed peas simmer in a fragrant ground coconut masala finished with curry leaves crackled in coconut oil. Fennel and roasted coconut give it a sweet, aromatic depth entirely different from the tomato-based northern curry.

ingredients.name: Black-eyed peas
ingredients.note: soaked 4 hours

ingredients.name: Grated fresh coconut
ingredients.note: for the ground masala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil gives this stew its unmistakable Kerala aroma

ingredients.name: Shallots
ingredients.note: half for the paste, half sliced

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked and strained

steps: Pressure-cook the soaked black-eyed peas with 2 cups water, 1/2 tsp turmeric powder and 1/2 tsp salt for 3-4 whistles until tender; keep aside with the liquid.
Dry-roast 3/4 cup grated coconut with 1 tsp fennel seeds and 3 dry red chillies in a pan on low heat for 3-4 minutes until golden and fragrant, then cool.
Grind the roasted coconut mixture with 4 shallots, 4 garlic cloves and 1.5 tsp coriander powder into a smooth paste using a little water.

Add the coconut paste to the cooked peas along with the strained tamarind, 1/2 tsp salt and 1 cup water; simmer on medium heat for 10-12 minutes until the gravy thickens and the raw coconut smell disappears.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds for 30 seconds, then add 2 sprigs curry leaves and the remaining sliced shallots and fry until golden.
Pour this crackling tempering over the simmering curry and fold it through gently.
Simmer 2 more minutes so the aromas settle, then serve hot.
tips: Roast the coconut only until pale gold; burnt coconut turns the whole gravy bitter and dark.
Add tamarind after the peas are fully cooked so the acid does not keep them firm.
A final drizzle of raw coconut oil over the served curry deepens that coastal aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with red matta rice, appam or steamed rice, with a crisp pappadam on the side.

variations.name: Rajasthani Gud-Amchur Lobia
variations.description: A sweet-and-sour desert take where black-eyed peas cook in a curd-free spiced gravy balanced with jaggery and amchur. Bloomed in mustard oil with a fistful of garlic, it is tangy, gently sweet and robust, meant to be soaked up with bajra roti.

ingredients.name: Black-eyed peas
ingredients.note: soaked 4 hours

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: kachi ghani oil gives this sweet-sour gravy its pungent Rajasthani base

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: crushed

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the sweet counterpoint to the amchur tang, in place of refined sugar

steps: Pressure-cook the soaked black-eyed peas with 2.5 cups water, 1/4 tsp turmeric powder and 1/2 tsp salt for 3-4 whistles until tender; reserve with the liquid.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just smokes, lower the heat, and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1/4 tsp asafoetida for 20 seconds.

Add 8 crushed garlic cloves and 1 chopped onion and fry 5-6 minutes until golden, then add 2 chopped tomatoes with 1/4 tsp turmeric powder, 1.5 tsp Kashmiri red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1/2 tsp salt.
Bhuno for 5 minutes until the masala thickens and the oil separates, then add the cooked peas with their liquid and 1/2 cup hot water.
Simmer on medium heat for 8-10 minutes, mashing a few beans to thicken the gravy.
Stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp amchur, and simmer 3-4 minutes until the sweet-sour balance settles and the gravy glazes the beans.
Finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and serve hot.
tips: Taste as you balance the jaggery and amchur; aim for a curry that is tangy first with just a rounding sweetness behind it.
Let the mustard oil reach its smoke point once so it loses its raw sharpness before the garlic goes in.
This curry deepens overnight, so it makes an excellent make-ahead dish for a Rajasthani thali.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra or makki roti and a spoon of white butter, or with plain rice and papad.

variations.name: Sundal-Style Dry Lobia
variations.description: A dry, temple-style stir-fry where cooked black-eyed peas are tossed with a coconut, mustard and curry-leaf tempering until every bean is coated and glossy. Light, protein-rich and gravy-free, it doubles as a wholesome snack or a quick side with rice and rasam.

ingredients.name: Black-eyed peas
ingredients.note: soaked 4 hours

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed gingelly oil is the classic fat for a South Indian sundal

ingredients.name: Urad dal
ingredients.note: for a nutty crackle in the tempering

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: finely chopped

steps: Pressure-cook the soaked black-eyed peas with 2 cups water, 1/4 tsp turmeric powder and 1/2 tsp salt for just 2-3 whistles so they stay firm and whole, then drain thoroughly.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadai on medium heat, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal for 30 seconds until the dal turns golden.
Add 2 dry red chillies, 2 sprigs curry leaves and 1/4 tsp asafoetida, and let them crisp for 15 seconds.
Add 2 chopped green chillies and the chopped ginger, saute for 1 minute until fragrant, then tip in the drained peas.
Toss the peas on medium heat for 4-5 minutes so they dry out slightly and take on the tempering, adding the remaining 1/4 tsp salt.
Add 1/2 cup grated coconut and toss for 2 minutes just until the coconut warms and smells sweet.
Take off the heat, squeeze in 1 tsp lemon juice, toss once, and serve warm.
tips: Cook the peas only until just tender for a sundal; mushy beans clump instead of staying separate and glossy.
Drain the peas very well before tempering so the dish stays dry and the coconut does not go pasty.
Add the coconut at the very end and off strong heat to keep it fresh and sweet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a protein-rich evening snack, a festive naivedyam, or a dry side alongside sambar rice and rasam.

variations.name: Classic Punjabi Makki Ki Roti
variations.description: The golden winter bread of Punjab, a thick cornmeal round patted between the palms and roasted till it turns crisp-edged and sunshine-yellow. Maize flour has no gluten, so hot water and patient palm-work bind the dough that is famously tricky to shape. Served drowning in white butter, it is one half of the immortal makki di roti te sarson da saag.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasts the delicate corn roti to golden crispness and is smeared on top the moment it leaves the tava

steps: Bring 1.25 cups water to a boil with 0.75 tsp salt, then pour it gradually over 2 cups maize flour mixed with 0.5 tsp carom seeds, stirring with a spoon.
Once cool enough to handle, knead the warm dough 5 minutes until it is smooth, soft and free of cracks, adding a little hot water if it feels dry.
Take a ball, place it between two sheets of greased parchment, and press with your palm or a flat lid into a 5-inch round about 4 mm thick.
Peel off the top sheet, invert the roti onto your hand, then slide it onto a medium-hot tava and peel away the second sheet.
Cook 1-2 minutes until the base is set with golden spots, flip, drizzle 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee around the edge, and roast the second side until crisp and freckled.
Smear 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the hot roti and repeat with the remaining dough, keeping the cooked ones warm.
tips: Knead the dough warm and keep it covered; cornmeal dough dries and crumbles the moment it cools.
Press between greased parchment rather than rolling, which is the surest way to shape this fragile gluten-free dough without tearing.
Add a spoon of hot water and re-knead if the dough starts cracking at the edges as you work through the batch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with sarson da saag topped with white butter, a jaggery cube and thick lassi for the definitive Punjabi winter plate.

variations.name: Mooli-Stuffed Makki Ki Roti
variations.description: A heartier Punjabi variation where spiced grated radish is folded into the cornmeal dough, its juices keeping the notoriously dry roti moist and tender. The mooli adds a peppery sharpness and makes the roti a fuller meal on cold mornings. A clever farmhouse trick that turns the fragile corn bread into something forgiving and flavourful.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasts the radish-studded roti golden and keeps the moist crumb from sticking to the tava

steps: Grate 1 cup radish, mix in 0.5 tsp of the salt, rest 10 minutes, then squeeze out and reserve the water for the dough.
Combine 2 cups maize flour with the squeezed radish, 2 minced green chillies, 3 tbsp coriander, 0.5 tsp ajwain, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 0.25 tsp salt.
Add the reserved radish water plus enough of the 0.75 cups hot water to knead a soft, warm dough, then rest it covered 10 minutes.
Press a ball between two greased parchment sheets into a 5-inch round, taking care the radish shreds do not tear the surface.
Slide onto a medium-hot tava, cook 1-2 minutes until spotted, flip, drizzle 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee around the edge, and roast until golden on both sides.
Smear a little Anveshan Ghee on top and repeat with the rest of the dough, serving the rotis warm.
tips: Save the water squeezed from the radish; it is seasoned and helps bind the dough with less plain water.
The radish moisture makes this the easiest makki roti to shape, so it is a good place for beginners to start.
Press a little thicker than plain makki roti so the radish shreds stay sealed and do not poke through.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of thick curd and a knob of white butter; the cooling curd offsets the peppery radish.

variations.name: Makki-Besan Missi Roti
variations.description: A sturdier, more pliable version that binds the cornmeal with gram flour and a little wheat, so the roti can be rolled rather than pressed and holds together far better. The besan adds protein and a savoury depth that stands up to bold sabzis. This is the practical everyday makki roti for cooks who find the pure corn version too fragile.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Its pungent bite suits the besan and roasts the blended roti to a deep golden crust

steps: Mix 1.25 cups maize flour, 0.5 cups besan and 0.25 cups whole wheat flour with 1 finely chopped onion, 1 inch grated ginger, 0.5 tsp ajwain, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.75 tsp salt.
Work in 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil, then add about 0.75 cups warm water gradually and knead a soft, pliable dough; the wheat and besan let it hold together, so rest it 15 minutes.
Dust a ball with flour and roll it out on a board into a 6-inch round about 4 mm thick, which this blended dough allows without cracking.
Place on a medium-hot tava and cook 1 minute until the base sets, then flip.
Drizzle 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil around the edge, flip once more, and roast each side 1-2 minutes until deeply golden and cooked through.
Repeat with the remaining dough, stacking the rotis under a cloth to stay soft.
tips: The besan and wheat give this dough enough structure to roll with a pin, unlike pure makki roti which must be pressed.
Cook besan-based rotis a touch longer on medium heat so the gram flour loses its raw smell.
Chop the onion very fine so it does not create tears when you roll the roti thin.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of dal makhani or a spiced yogurt kadhi, letting the sturdy roti scoop up the gravy.

variations.name: Palak Makki Ki Roti
variations.description: A vivid green cornmeal roti enriched with pureed spinach and garlic that softens the dough and turns it a beautiful jade. The spinach not only moistens the crumb but slips extra iron into the winter staple, a favourite way to feed children their greens. Roasted in ghee, it is nourishing, mild and quietly striking on the plate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasts the spinach roti to a soft golden finish and carries the garlic aroma through the crumb

steps: Blanch a bunch of spinach briefly and blend to a smooth 0.75 cups puree with 4 garlic cloves and 1 green chilli.
Combine 2 cups maize flour with 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 0.75 tsp salt, then mix in the warm spinach puree.
Add the 0.5 cups hot water a little at a time and knead a soft, warm dough; the puree does much of the moistening, so add water cautiously and rest 10 minutes.
Press a ball between two greased parchment sheets into a 5-inch round about 4 mm thick.
Slide onto a medium-hot tava, cook 1-2 minutes until set, flip, drizzle 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee around the edge, and roast until golden on both sides.
Smear a little Anveshan Ghee over the hot roti and repeat with the remaining dough.
tips: Blend the spinach warm and smooth; stray leaf pieces create weak spots that tear the fragile corn dough.
The spinach puree makes the dough softer than plain makki roti, so keep extra dry flour on hand for dusting.
Use the roti dough within the hour, as the spinach can turn it slack and sticky if left too long.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of plain curd whisked with roasted cumin, or a corn-and-methi sabzi, letting the green roti take centre stage.

variations.name: Classic Malai Chaap
variations.description: Soy chaap pieces pan-seared golden and folded into a mild, luxurious white gravy of cashews, cream and fried onions perfumed with cardamom. Rich, silky and gently spiced, it is the restaurant-favourite vegetarian showstopper that mops up beautifully with butter naan.

ingredients.name: Soy chaap
ingredients.note: sticks, cut into 1-inch pieces

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee sears the chaap and enriches the white gravy

ingredients.name: Cashews
ingredients.note: soaked in warm water 15 minutes

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: thinly sliced

ingredients.name: Yogurt
ingredients.note: whisked smooth

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

ingredients.name: Kasuri methi
ingredients.note: crushed

steps: Squeeze the soy chaap dry, cut into 1-inch pieces, and sear in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium-high heat for 4-5 minutes until golden on all sides; lift out and set aside.
In the same pan add the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 3 green cardamoms, then add 2 sliced onions and fry 6-7 minutes until soft and pale gold, taking care not to brown them.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute, then cool the mixture slightly and grind it with the soaked cashews into a smooth white paste using a little water.
Return the paste to the pan on low heat, whisk in 1/4 cup yogurt gradually so it does not split, and cook 3-4 minutes until the raw smell goes and the gravy thickens.
Add 1 cup hot water, 2 slit green chillies, 1/2 tsp white pepper powder and 1 tsp salt, and simmer gently for 5 minutes to a silky, pale gravy.
Slide in the seared chaap, simmer 5 minutes so the pieces absorb the gravy, then lower the heat and swirl in 1/4 cup cream.
Crush 1 tsp kasuri methi and 1/4 tsp garam masala over the top, warm through for 1 minute without boiling, and serve.
tips: Keep the onions from browning; a truly white malai gravy depends on pale, softened onions rather than caramelised ones.
Squeeze the chaap well before searing so it browns rather than steams and stays springy inside.
Add the cream off the boil at the very end so the gravy stays glossy and does not separate.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan, laccha paratha or saffron pulao, garnished with a swirl of cream and slivered almonds.

variations.name: Tandoori Afghani Chaap
variations.description: Chaap marinated in a hung-curd, cashew and white-pepper paste, then charred over a flame before a quick toss in a mild buttery glaze. Smoky, creamy and mild, this Afghani-style version leans on the grill rather than a heavy gravy, with a signature coal-smoke finish.

ingredients.name: Soy chaap
ingredients.note: sticks, halved lengthwise

ingredients.name: Hung curd
ingredients.note: thick, for the marinade

ingredients.name: Cashew paste
ingredients.note: from cashews soaked and ground

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: for basting the chaap on the grill and the final buttery glaze

ingredients.name: Cornflour
ingredients.note: to bind the marinade

ingredients.name: Charcoal
ingredients.note: for the dhungar smoke

steps: Whisk 1/2 cup hung curd with 3 tbsp cashew paste, 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 1 tsp green chilli paste, 3/4 tsp white pepper powder, 1/4 tsp cardamom powder, 1 tbsp cornflour and 3/4 tsp salt into a thick pale marinade.
Coat the halved chaap sticks fully in the marinade and rest for 20 minutes so the flavours soak in.
Thread or lay the chaap on a grill rack and char over a medium flame for 8-10 minutes, turning and basting with 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, until edges blister and the coating sets to pale gold.
Place the grilled chaap in a bowl, set a small heatproof cup in the centre, and heat 1 piece of charcoal until glowing red.
Put the hot coal in the cup, drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee over it, cover the bowl immediately, and let the smoke infuse for 3-4 minutes.
Uncover, transfer the chaap to a warm pan, drizzle 2 tbsp cream and warm gently for 1 minute so it glazes without drying out.
Sprinkle 1/2 tsp chaat masala, toss once, and serve smoky and hot.
tips: Use genuinely thick hung curd; thin curd slides off the chaap and will not char into a coating.
The dhungar coal-smoke step is what gives the Afghani signature, so do not skip it if you want that tandoor aroma.
Grill just until the edges blister; over-charring makes the chaap chewy and dry.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a starter with mint chutney, onion rings and lemon wedges, or tuck into a rumali roti roll.

variations.name: Dhaba Masala Chaap
variations.description: A robust, tangy roadside-style curry where seared chaap simmers in a spicy onion-tomato gravy sharpened with kasuri methi and a splash of mustard-oil pungency. Bolder and redder than the creamy malai, it is built for tearing into with a hot tandoori roti.

ingredients.name: Soy chaap
ingredients.note: cut into 1-inch pieces

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: kachi ghani oil gives the gravy its pungent dhaba edge

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: pureed

ingredients.name: Kasuri methi
ingredients.note: crushed

steps: Squeeze the chaap dry, cut into 1-inch pieces, and sear in 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil (heated to smoking then cooled slightly) over medium-high heat for 4-5 minutes until browned; remove and set aside.
Add the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add 2 chopped onions and fry 7-8 minutes until deep golden brown.

Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then pour in the puree of 3 tomatoes with 1/2 tsp turmeric powder, 1.5 tsp Kashmiri red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp cumin powder and 1 tsp salt.
Bhuno on medium heat for 7-8 minutes until the masala turns brick-red, thickens and the oil separates at the edges.
Add 1.5 cups hot water, bring to a simmer, then slide in the seared chaap and cook on low heat for 10 minutes so the pieces soak up the gravy.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi and sprinkle 1/2 tsp garam masala over the curry, simmer 2 minutes, and adjust with hot water if it thickens too much.
Finish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander and serve hot.
tips: Fry the onions to a genuine deep brown for the dhaba colour and body; pale onions leave the gravy thin and flat.
Sear the chaap first so it holds its shape and does not turn spongy in the gravy.
For extra smokiness, finish with a quick coal-smoke infusion before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter-brushed tandoori roti or laccha paratha, sliced onions and a green chilli on the side.

variations.name: Kadhai Dry Chaap
variations.description: A semi-dry kadhai preparation where chaap is tossed with chunky peppers and onions in a coarse, freshly pounded coriander-chilli masala. Gravy-free and intensely spiced, it clings to the chaap in a glossy coat, making a fantastic dry starter or a bold side.

ingredients.name: Soy chaap
ingredients.note: cut into 1-inch pieces

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil for high-heat searing and tossing the kadhai masala

ingredients.name: Coriander seeds
ingredients.note: coarsely pounded

ingredients.name: Dry red chillies
ingredients.note: coarsely pounded with the coriander

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: cut into thick squares

ingredients.name: Capsicum
ingredients.note: cut into thick squares

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Kasuri methi
ingredients.note: crushed

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: julienned for garnish

steps: Dry-roast 1 tbsp coriander seeds with 3 dry red chillies on low heat for 2 minutes until fragrant, then pound coarsely in a mortar to make the kadhai masala.
Squeeze the chaap dry, cut into 1-inch pieces, and sear in 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium-high heat for 4-5 minutes until golden; remove and set aside.
In the same pan add the remaining 1 tbsp oil, tip in the onion and capsicum squares, and stir-fry on high heat for 2-3 minutes until they char at the edges but stay crunchy; scoop out and reserve.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste to the pan, fry 1 minute, then add 2 chopped tomatoes with 1/2 tsp turmeric powder, 3/4 tsp red chilli powder, the pounded kadhai masala and 3/4 tsp salt.
Cook on medium heat for 5-6 minutes until the tomatoes break down into a thick, coarse masala with the oil peeking through.
Return the seared chaap and the charred peppers and onions, tossing on high heat for 3-4 minutes so the masala coats everything and stays dry.
Crush 1 tsp kasuri methi over the top, garnish with ginger juliennes and 2 tbsp coriander, and serve hot.
tips: Pound the coriander and chillies coarsely rather than grinding fine; the uneven texture is what makes a kadhai masala.
Keep the peppers and onions crunchy by charring them fast on high heat and adding them back only at the end.
Keep the masala thick and dry so it clings to the chaap; add no water at all.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a dry starter or a side with rotis and dal, with lemon wedges and onion rings alongside.

variations.name: Classic Rajasthani Mangodi Ki Sabzi
variations.description: Sun-dried moong dal dumplings, or mangodi, fried golden and then simmered in a tangy yogurt-tomato gravy until they soften and drink up the masala. A pantry staple of Rajasthani homes, it turns humble dried nuggets into a soulful, protein-rich curry with a satisfying chew.

ingredients.name: Mangodi
ingredients.note: dried moong dal dumplings

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: for frying the mangodi golden and building the tempering

ingredients.name: Yogurt
ingredients.note: whisked smooth

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: pureed

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat and fry 1 cup mangodi for 3-4 minutes, stirring constantly, until they turn deep golden and smell roasted, then lift out and set aside.
In the same kadai add the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1/4 tsp asafoetida for 30 seconds, then add 1 chopped onion and fry 5 minutes until golden.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then add the puree of 2 tomatoes with 1/2 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt.
Bhuno the masala for 5-6 minutes until it thickens and the ghee separates, then lower the heat and stir in 1/2 cup whisked yogurt a spoon at a time so it blends without curdling.
Add the fried mangodi with 2 cups hot water, cover, and simmer on low heat for 15-18 minutes until the dumplings swell soft and the gravy thickens around them.
Uncover, check that the mangodi are tender all the way through, and add a splash of hot water if the gravy has reduced too far.
Stir in 1/2 tsp garam masala, finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander, and serve hot.
tips: Fry the mangodi patiently to a real golden brown; underfried dumplings stay hard in the centre no matter how long they simmer.
Add the yogurt off high heat and stir it in gradually, or the gravy will split into grainy curds.
Mangodi keep absorbing liquid as they sit, so serve soon after cooking or loosen with hot water before reheating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulka or steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, with sliced onion and green chilli on the side.

variations.name: Aloo Mangodi
variations.description: The everyday household version where cubed potatoes join the mangodi in a light onion-tomato gravy, stretching the dumplings into a filling family curry. The potatoes turn creamy and the mangodi stay chewy, making a comforting one-pot sabzi that needs nothing more than roti.

ingredients.name: Mangodi
ingredients.note: dried moong dal dumplings

ingredients.name: Potatoes
ingredients.note: cut into 2 cm cubes

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil fries the mangodi crisp and stands up to a long bhuno

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: grated

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: finely chopped

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pressure cooker on medium heat and fry 3/4 cup mangodi for 3 minutes until golden, then remove and keep aside.
In the same oil crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1/4 tsp asafoetida, add 2 chopped onions and 2 slit green chillies, and fry 6 minutes until golden.

Add the grated ginger for 30 seconds, then add 2 chopped tomatoes with 1/2 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt; cook 5 minutes until the masala is thick and glossy.
Add the potato cubes and toss to coat, then return the fried mangodi and pour in 2.5 cups hot water.
Close the cooker and cook on medium heat for 3 whistles, then let the pressure release naturally so the mangodi and potatoes finish softening in the steam.
Open the cooker, stir in 1/2 tsp amchur, and simmer uncovered for 3-4 minutes to thicken the gravy to a spoonable consistency.
Finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and serve hot.
tips: Cut the potatoes a touch larger than the mangodi so both finish cooking at the same time in the cooker.
If you prefer a thicker gravy, mash one or two potato cubes against the side of the cooker and stir them back in.
Soak the mangodi in warm water for 10 minutes before frying if yours are very hard; it speeds up their softening.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rotis and a bowl of plain yogurt, or ladle over rice for a comforting single-plate meal.

variations.name: Marwari Lehsuni Mangodi
variations.description: A robust garlic-forward version from Marwar cooked in pungent mustard oil with a curd-free, fiery red gravy. Crushed garlic and Kashmiri chilli give it a deep colour and a warming heat, while a hint of kachri tang keeps the rich dumplings lively.

ingredients.name: Mangodi
ingredients.note: dried moong dal dumplings

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: kachi ghani oil gives this garlicky gravy its sharp Marwari character

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: crushed to a coarse paste

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: grated

ingredients.name: Kashmiri red chilli powder
ingredients.note: for a deep red colour

ingredients.name: Kachri powder
ingredients.note: for desert tang

ingredients.name: Besan
ingredients.note: to give the gravy body

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just smokes, then lower the heat and fry 1 cup mangodi for 3-4 minutes until deep golden; remove and set aside.

In the same oil crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1/4 tsp fenugreek seeds for 20 seconds, then add 1/2 tsp asafoetida and the crushed garlic and grated ginger, frying 2 minutes until the garlic is golden and fragrant.
Lower the heat and add 1 tbsp besan, toasting it with the garlic for 1 minute, then stir in 2 tsp Kashmiri red chilli powder, 1/2 tsp turmeric powder and 2 tsp coriander powder for 10 seconds.
Pour in 2.5 cups hot water while whisking so the besan does not clump, add 1 tsp salt and 1 tsp kachri powder, and bring to a simmer.
Add the fried mangodi, cover, and cook on low heat for 15-18 minutes until the dumplings swell tender and the gravy turns a glossy brick-red.
Uncover and simmer 3 more minutes to thicken, adjusting with hot water if needed.
Finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and serve hot with plenty of the garlicky red gravy.
tips: Crush the garlic coarsely rather than making a fine paste; the little nubs give bursts of flavour that define this version.
Let the mustard oil hit its smoke point once so its raw pungency mellows before the garlic goes in.
The besan both thickens the gravy and rounds off the sharp mustard oil, so do not skip toasting it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra roti and a raw onion, or with jeera rice and a spoon of white butter to temper the heat.

variations.name: Sukhi Mangodi Masala
variations.description: A dry, stir-fried version where the fried mangodi are tossed with onions, peppers and a coarse spice mix until every dumpling wears a toasty masala coat. With no gravy, the mangodi stay chewy and intensely flavoured, making it a great tiffin-box sabzi or a crunchy side.

ingredients.name: Mangodi
ingredients.note: dried moong dal dumplings

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee fries the mangodi and carries the dry masala coat

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: cut into thin wedges

ingredients.name: Capsicum
ingredients.note: diced

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

steps: Soak 1 cup mangodi in warm water for 15 minutes, then drain well so they will cook through without a gravy.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat and fry the drained mangodi for 3-4 minutes until golden, then push them to one side.
Add the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add 2 onion wedges and 2 slit green chillies and saute 3 minutes until the onions soften at the edges.
Stir in 2 tsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then add 1/2 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder with 3 tbsp water to make a quick masala paste.
Toss the mangodi through the masala with the diced capsicum, sprinkle 1/2 cup hot water, cover, and cook on low heat for 8-10 minutes until the mangodi are tender and the pan is dry.
Uncover, raise the heat, and stir-fry 2 minutes so the masala clings and toasts onto the dumplings.
Sprinkle 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp amchur and 1 tsp salt, toss well, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Soaking the mangodi before frying is key in a dry sabzi; without a gravy to soften them, unsoaked dumplings stay hard.
Keep the capsicum slightly crunchy by adding it midway rather than at the start, for a fresher bite against the chewy mangodi.
A final squeeze of lemon in place of some amchur brightens the dry masala nicely.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pack it into a tiffin with rotis, or serve as a dry side alongside dal-rice and a bowl of curd.

variations.name: Classic Masala Oats
variations.description: This Classic Masala Oats cooks rolled oats into a savoury, porridge-like bowl with onion, tomato, peas and carrot in a fragrant cumin-ghee base. Lightly spiced and ready in minutes, it is the wholesome, comforting way to turn plain oats into a satisfying Indian meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee gives this savoury oats bowl a rounded, home-style richness

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 15 seconds until fragrant.
Add the chopped onion, 1 inch grated ginger and 2 green chillies and saute for 3 minutes until the onion turns soft and translucent.
Stir in the chopped tomato, grated carrot and 0.5 cup peas with 0.5 tsp turmeric and cook for 4 minutes until the tomato breaks down.
Add the 1.5 cups rolled oats and toast for a minute, then pour in 3 cups water with 1 tsp salt and stir well.
Simmer over medium-low heat for 5 minutes, stirring, until the oats swell and the mixture turns thick and porridge-like.
Sprinkle in 0.5 tsp garam masala and the coriander, mix through and serve hot.
tips: Add the oats near the end so they cook just until soft and do not turn into a paste.
Adjust the water for your preferred texture, using more for a soupier, spoonable bowl.
A squeeze of lemon at the finish lifts the spices and brightens the whole dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot in bowls with a drizzle of ghee, a lemon wedge and a few roasted peanuts scattered over.

variations.name: Tomato Masala Oats
variations.description: A quick, tangy bowl built on a tomato-rich base spiked with pav bhaji masala and garlic, finished with a knob of butter. Saucier and more robustly spiced than the classic, this comfort-food style oats eats almost like a spiced tomato soup with body.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil forms a clean base for the tangy tomato masala

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan over medium heat and saute the 5 crushed garlic cloves and chopped onion for 3 minutes until golden.
Add the diced capsicum and the 3 pureed tomatoes and cook for 5 minutes until the puree thickens and the oil begins to separate.
Stir in 1.5 tsp pav bhaji masala, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt and fry for a minute until deeply aromatic.
Add the 1.5 cups rolled oats and 3 cups water, stir well, and simmer over medium-low heat for 5 minutes until thick and saucy.
Mash lightly with the back of the ladle for a smoother, pav-bhaji-like texture.
Finish with 1 tbsp butter and the coriander, stir until glossy and serve hot.
tips: Cook the tomato puree until the oil separates so the base tastes rich, not raw.
Mash the oats a little for that signature smooth, saucy pav-bhaji-style consistency.
Keep it slightly loose, as this style thickens quickly once off the heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with buttered toast or a soft pav for dipping, topped with chopped raw onion and lemon.

variations.name: Oats Upma
variations.description: This South Indian style dry-roasts the oats and cooks them upma-style with a mustard, urad and chana dal tempering, curry leaves and vegetables in coconut oil. Fluffy and separate rather than porridge-like, it is finished with fresh coconut and a squeeze of lemon.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil gives this oats upma its South Indian fragrance

steps: Dry-roast the 1.5 cups rolled oats in a pan over medium heat for 3 minutes until fragrant, then set aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in the same pan and crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds, then fry 1 tbsp urad dal and 1 tbsp chana dal until golden.
Add the 15 curry leaves, 2 green chillies and 1 inch chopped ginger and sizzle for 20 seconds, then add the chopped onion and grated carrot and saute for 3 minutes.
Pour in 2.5 cups water with 1 tsp salt and bring to a boil.
Lower the heat, stir in the roasted oats gradually so no lumps form, and cook covered for 4 minutes until the water is absorbed and the oats are fluffy.
Switch off, fold in 0.25 cup grated coconut and 1 tbsp lemon juice, and serve warm.
tips: Dry-roast the oats first so the upma stays fluffy and the grains hold their shape.
Add the oats to boiling water gradually while stirring to keep the upma lump-free.
Rest it covered for a couple of minutes so the oats finish steaming and separate nicely.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with coconut chutney and a small cup of sambar for a South Indian breakfast plate.

variations.name: Palak Sprouts Masala Oats
variations.description: A nutrient-dense green bowl that simmers oats with spinach and boiled moong sprouts, seasoned with garlic and crushed black pepper. Earthy, fibre-rich and protein-packed, it is a fitness-friendly savoury oats that stays light yet deeply satisfying.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee softens the spinach and rounds out this wholesome green bowl

steps: Blanch the 3 cups spinach in hot water for 2 minutes, refresh in cold water and chop finely or lightly puree.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and the 5 sliced garlic cloves until golden and fragrant.
Add the chopped onion and 1 green chilli and saute for 3 minutes, then stir in the 1 cup moong sprouts and cook for 3 minutes until just tender.
Add the chopped spinach and 0.75 tsp black pepper powder, then tip in the 1.5 cups rolled oats and toast for a minute.
Pour in 3 cups water with 1 tsp salt and simmer over medium-low heat for 5 minutes until the oats swell and the bowl turns thick and green.
Finish with 1 tbsp lemon juice, stir through and serve hot.
tips: Blanch and refresh the spinach so the oats stay a vivid green rather than turning dull.
Cook the sprouts just until crisp-tender so they keep their bite and nutrients.
Season generously with black pepper, which pairs beautifully with the earthy greens.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot topped with roasted flax seeds and a swirl of curd for a protein-rich fitness bowl.

variations.name: Classic Jodhpuri Mirchi Vada
variations.description: Mirchi Vada is Jodhpur's famous monsoon snack of large mild bhavnagri chillies stuffed with a tangy spiced potato mash, dipped in besan batter and fried till puffed and golden. The gentle heat of the chilli against the amchur-laced potato and crisp jacket makes it irresistible with a fresh pav.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: deep-fries the stuffed chillies to a light, even golden crust

steps: Slit each of the 8 bhavnagri chillies lengthwise on one side, scoop out the seeds, and set them aside.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 0.5 tsp cumin, crush and add 1 tsp fennel, then add 3 mashed potatoes, 1 tsp amchur, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 3 tbsp coriander and cook 2 minutes.
Cool the filling and pack it firmly into each slit chilli, pressing the slit closed around it.
Whisk 1.5 cups besan with 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.25 tsp salt and 0.75 cup water into a thick, smooth coating batter.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil to about 175C, dip each stuffed chilli fully in batter, and lower it in gently.
Fry 3 to 4 at a time for 4 to 5 minutes, turning, until the jacket is puffed and golden, then drain and serve hot.
tips: Use fat, pale bhavnagri chillies which are mild; taste one first, as an occasional batch can be sharp.
Pack the potato in tight and pinch the slit shut so the filling does not spill out while frying.
Fry at a moderate 175C so the chilli softens and the thick jacket cooks without over-browning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot in a split pav with tamarind and mint chutneys, Jodhpur breakfast style.

variations.name: Rajasthani Peanut-Sesame Mirchi Vada
variations.description: A drier Marwari filling built on coarsely crushed roasted peanuts, sesame and fennel instead of potato, giving a nutty, khatta-meetha crunch inside the chilli. The stuffing clings without mashing, so each bite has texture against the crisp besan shell.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: fries the nut-stuffed chillies crisp and toasts the sesame in the tempering

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: rounds the filling with a sweet-sour Marwari balance against the amchur

steps: Slit and deseed the 8 chillies, keeping them whole and intact for stuffing.
Dry-roast 2 tbsp sesame until they pop, then coarsely crush them with 0.5 cup roasted peanuts and 1.5 tsp fennel.

Mix the crushed nuts with 1.5 tsp amchur, 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt into a coarse, moist stuffing, then pack it firmly into each chilli.
Whisk 1.5 cups besan with 0.75 cup water and a pinch of salt into a thick coating batter.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to about 175C, dip each stuffed chilli in batter, and fry in batches for 4 to 5 minutes until golden.
Drain on paper and serve warm so the nutty stuffing stays crunchy.
tips: Crush the peanuts coarse so the filling has bite; a fine powder turns pasty and dull.
The jaggery and amchur should balance to a khatta-meetha note, so taste and adjust before stuffing.
This dry filling keeps well, so you can stuff the chillies a few hours ahead and fry to order.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a standalone tea-time snack with a wedge of lemon; it needs no chutney thanks to the tangy filling.

variations.name: Cheese-Corn Mirchi Vada
variations.description: A fusion take that fills mild chillies with a creamy blend of grated cheese, sweet corn and herbs that turns molten inside the fried shell. The gooey, mildly sweet centre makes it a hit with children and party crowds alike.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: its clean, neutral taste keeps the cheesy filling the star

steps: Slit and deseed the 8 chillies carefully, keeping them whole.
Mash 0.5 cup boiled corn lightly, then mix with 1 cup grated cheese, 0.5 tsp black pepper, 1 tsp chilli flakes, 0.5 tsp oregano and 2 tbsp coriander into a thick, bindable filling.
Stuff each chilli firmly with the cheese-corn mixture and press the slit closed so nothing leaks.
Whisk 1.5 cups besan with 3 tbsp corn flour, 1 tsp salt and 0.75 cup water into a thick, sealing batter.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Sunflower Oil to about 170C, dip each stuffed chilli in batter, and fry 3 at a time for 3 to 4 minutes until golden.
Drain and serve within a few minutes while the cheese is still soft and stretchy inside.
tips: Chill the stuffed chillies for 10 minutes before frying so the cheese sets and is less likely to ooze.
Fry at a slightly lower heat so the shell colours gently without the cheese bursting out.
Serve immediately, as the cheese firms up quickly and loses its molten pull once cold.
variations.servingSuggestion: Plate with a tangy schezwan mayo dip as a party starter that disappears fast.

variations.name: Baked Khapli Mirchi Vada
variations.description: A lighter oven version where the potato-stuffed chillies wear a batter enriched with nutty khapli atta and are baked with a brush of ghee instead of deep-fried. The crust turns craggy and golden while keeping the snack far lighter on oil.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: adds a nutty, fibre-rich body to the batter that crisps well in the oven

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: brushed over the vadas so they brown and crisp while baking

steps: Preheat the oven to 200C and line a tray with parchment brushed with a little Anveshan Ghee.

Slit and deseed the 8 chillies, then mix 3 mashed potatoes with 1 tsp crushed fennel, 1 tsp amchur, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 3 tbsp coriander and stuff each chilli firmly.
Whisk 1 cup besan with 0.33 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.25 tsp salt and 0.5 cup water into a thick coating batter.
Dip each stuffed chilli fully in batter, place on the tray, and brush the tops generously with Anveshan Ghee.
Bake for 15 minutes, turn each vada and brush again with ghee, then bake another 12 to 15 minutes until golden and crisp at the edges.
Rest for 2 minutes and serve warm.
tips: Coat the chillies in a thicker batter than for frying, as the oven needs more body to crisp up.
Brush ghee both before and after turning; this is what browns the baked crust properly.
Space the vadas well apart on the tray so hot air circulates and the batter dries rather than steams.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling mint-curd dip and sliced onion for a lighter afternoon snack.

variations.name: Classic Punjabi Missi Roti
variations.description: A rustic North Indian flatbread of wheat and gram flour spiked with onion, ajwain and green chilli, roasted till nutty and golden. The besan gives it a savoury depth and a slightly crumbly bite that ordinary roti lacks, while the spices make it flavourful enough to eat almost on its own. A dhaba and home favourite finished with a generous smear of ghee.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Worked into the dough for softness and smeared over each roti for a nutty, golden finish

steps: In a bowl combine 1.5 cups whole wheat flour, 1 cup besan, 1 finely chopped onion, 2 minced green chillies, 0.5 tsp ajwain, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 3 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp salt.
Add 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then pour in the 0.75 cups water gradually and knead a soft, smooth dough; rest it covered for 15 minutes.
Divide into 8 balls, dust one with flour, and roll it out on a board into a 6-inch round about 4 mm thick.
Place on a medium-hot tava and cook 45 seconds until pale bubbles appear, then flip.
Smear 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the surface, flip again, and press the edges until golden-brown spots form, about 1 minute a side.
Stack the cooked rotis under a cloth and repeat with the remaining dough.
tips: Roll missi roti a little thicker than a plain chapati; the besan makes it crumbly and thin ones crack.
Cook on medium heat so the gram flour toasts through and loses its raw taste without scorching.
Chop the onion very fine, or it will tear the dough and leak moisture while rolling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a dollop of white butter, a wedge of onion and a bowl of dal, or with a tangy aam ka achaar.

variations.name: Rajasthani Bajra Missi Roti
variations.description: A desert version that folds pearl-millet flour into the besan-wheat base and dials up the whole spices, giving a heavier, boldly aromatic roti built for cold Rajasthani nights. Crushed coriander and fennel seed run through the crumb alongside a warmth of red chilli. Robust and earthy, it is meant to be eaten hot with plenty of ghee.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The desert fat of choice, worked in and poured over each hot roti to enrich the earthy millet blend

steps: Combine 1 cup besan, 0.75 cups bajra flour, 0.5 cups whole wheat flour, 1 tsp crushed coriander seeds, 1 tsp fennel seeds, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 1 tsp salt.
Rub in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until the flour is crumbly, then add about 0.75 cups warm water and knead a firm dough; rest it 15 minutes.
Roll each of 8 balls on a well-floured board into a 5-inch round, keeping it slightly thick since the bajra makes the dough prone to cracking.
Cook on a medium-hot tava 1 minute until the base sets, then flip.
Drizzle 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee around the edge, flip once more, and roast each side 1-2 minutes until deeply spotted and fragrant.
Serve the rotis hot, repeating with the remaining dough.
tips: Rubbing ghee into the flour first (moyan) keeps this millet-heavy roti tender rather than hard.
Crush the coriander and fennel coarsely just before mixing so their aroma is at its brightest.
Keep the rounds a little thick and mend edge cracks with a wet finger, as bajra has no gluten to hold it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with ker sangri or gatte ki sabzi and a bowl of chaas, in the true Marwari thali fashion.

variations.name: Tandoori Missi Roti
variations.description: The dhaba-tandoor version, a thicker missi roti slapped onto the hot clay wall (or a heavy tava-and-grill setup at home) so it blisters and chars while staying pillowy within. Yogurt in the dough gives a faint tang and extra softness that suits the fierce heat. Brushed with ghee and studded with kalonji, it eats like a savoury naan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Brushed over the blistered roti as it comes off the heat, melting into the charred tops

steps: Mix 1.5 cups whole wheat flour, 1 cup besan, 1 tsp nigella seeds, 0.5 tsp ajwain, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.25 tsp baking soda and 1 tsp salt in a bowl.
Add 0.3 cups curd, then work in about 0.4 cups warm water to knead a soft dough; cover and rest it 30 minutes so it relaxes for the high heat.
Roll each of 7 balls into a thick 6-inch oval, pressing a few kalonji seeds onto the surface, and dampen one side lightly with water.
Slap the wet side onto a very hot heavy tava so it sticks, cook 1 minute until bubbles rise, then invert the tava over the flame to char the top like a tandoor.
When brown-black blisters form, lift the roti off, or flip and press on the tava until both sides are spotted and cooked through.
Brush the hot roti generously with Anveshan Ghee and repeat with the remaining dough.
tips: Resting the dough a full 30 minutes with curd and soda is what gives the tandoori roti its soft, blistered chew.
Wetting one face makes the roti cling to the inverted tava so you can char the top over the flame at home.
Keep the flame high and work fast; a slow roast dries out this thicker roti instead of blistering it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with dal makhani or paneer butter masala and a raw onion-lachcha, tandoori-dhaba style.

variations.name: Sattu Missi Roti
variations.description: A Bihari-inspired twist that swaps the gram flour for roasted-gram sattu, giving a deeper toasted flavour and a protein boost while keeping the savoury missi character. The sattu lends a coarse, nutty texture and a smokiness that plain besan cannot. Studded with mustard-oil-fried onion and green chilli, it is filling enough to be a meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Roasted-gram flour gives this missi roti a smoky depth and a protein lift the classic besan version lacks

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Its sharp Bihari pungency fries the onion for the dough and roasts each roti to a golden edge

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a small pan and fry 1 finely chopped onion with 1 inch grated ginger until soft and pale golden, about 4 minutes, then cool.
In a bowl combine 1.5 cups whole wheat flour, 0.75 cups Anveshan Sattu, the cooled onion, 2 minced green chillies, 0.5 tsp ajwain, 0.5 tsp kalonji and 1 tsp salt.
Add about 0.75 cups warm water gradually and knead a soft dough; sattu drinks water, so add a little extra if it tightens, then rest 15 minutes.
Roll each of 8 balls on a floured board into a 6-inch round about 4 mm thick.
Cook on a medium-hot tava 45 seconds, flip, drizzle 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil around the edge, and roast each side 1-2 minutes until golden and spotted.
Stack under a cloth and repeat with the remaining dough.
tips: Frying the onion first, rather than adding it raw, stops the sattu dough turning wet and keeps the roti from tearing.
Sattu absorbs water as it rests, so knead the dough a touch softer than you think you need.
Toast the roti fully on medium heat so the sattu's raw-gram edge cooks off and its nuttiness comes forward.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a smear of white butter, chokha (mashed spiced potato or brinjal) and a green-chilli pickle, Bihari style.

variations.name: Classic Naan
variations.description: The definitive Punjabi tandoor bread reimagined for a home stove: a yeast-leavened, yogurt-softened dough that puffs into pillowy ovals with charred blisters and a chewy pull. A blend of khapli wheat and a little maida keeps it stretchy yet wholesome, while a final ghee brush gives that unmistakable dhaba sheen. Served hot off the tava, it stays soft for hours.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Stone-ground emmer gives the naan body and a nutty depth that plain maida naan lacks

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: Unrefined cane sugar feeds the yeast and lends a faint caramel note to the crust

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Brushed on hot naan for the glossy, aromatic finish of a tandoor bread

steps: Dissolve 1 tsp Anveshan Khandsari and 1 tsp active dry yeast in 1/2 cup warm milk (just blood-warm, never hot) and leave undisturbed for 8-10 minutes until it turns frothy and smells yeasty.
In a wide bowl whisk together 1.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 cup maida, 1/2 tsp baking powder and 1 tsp salt, then make a well and pour in the frothy yeast mixture along with 3 tbsp yogurt.

Bring the dough together, adding up to 3 tbsp water a little at a time, and knead on the counter for 6-7 minutes into a soft, slightly tacky dough; smear the ball with 1/2 tsp Anveshan Ghee, cover, and let it rise in a warm spot for about 1 hour until doubled.

Punch down the risen dough, divide into 6 equal balls, and rest them covered for 10 minutes; roll each into a 7-inch teardrop about 4 mm thick, pressing a pinch of nigella seeds and chopped coriander into the top.

Heat a heavy iron tava on high until smoking, brush the plain underside of a rolled naan lightly with water, and slap it water-side down so it sticks; cook for about 1 minute until large bubbles form.
Invert the tava directly over the flame so the top blisters and chars in spots, 30-40 seconds, then lift the naan off with tongs; repeat for the rest.
Brush each hot naan generously with melted Anveshan Ghee, stack in a cloth-lined basket, and serve immediately while soft and steaming.
tips: The dough should feel softer than roti dough; if it firms up while resting, wet your palms rather than adding dry flour when shaping.
No open flame? Cook the naan covered on the hot tava for the second side; the trapped steam puffs it almost as well as a tandoor.
Sticking the water-side to the tava is the trick that lets you flip it over the flame without it falling off.
variations.servingSuggestion: Tear alongside a rich dal makhani or paneer butter masala, with sliced onions and a wedge of lemon on the side.

variations.name: No-Yeast Yogurt Naan
variations.description: For cooks who want naan tonight without waiting on a rise, this version leans on thick yogurt plus baking soda and baking powder for its lift. The tang of curd and a hint of jaggery balance beautifully, and the crumb comes out soft and faintly sour, closer to a Delhi-restaurant naan than a bakery one. Ready in under an hour, start to plate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Holds the soft yogurt dough together without the stretch that only yeast can give

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A touch of mineral sweetness that offsets the sourness of the curd

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Finishes the naan with a rich, buttery gloss straight off the tava

steps: Sift 1.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta and 1/2 cup maida with 1/4 tsp baking soda, 1 tsp baking powder and 1 tsp salt into a large bowl so the leaveners distribute evenly.
Whisk 1/2 cup thick yogurt with 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder until the jaggery dissolves, then add it to the flour along with up to 1/4 cup warm milk, mixing to a shaggy mass.
Knead the dough on a lightly greased surface for 4-5 minutes until soft and smooth, cover with a damp cloth, and rest for 20-25 minutes so the baking powder activates and the gluten relaxes.
Divide into 6 balls and roll each into a 7-inch oval about 4 mm thick, scattering nigella and sesame seeds on top and pressing them in gently with the rolling pin.
Heat a cast-iron tava on high until a drop of water skitters, brush the underside of one naan with water, and press it water-side down onto the tava; cook 45-60 seconds until the surface bubbles.
Flip the tava over the direct flame to blister the top for about 30 seconds, or cover and cook the second side on the tava itself until golden-brown patches appear.
Slather each hot naan with melted Anveshan Ghee and serve at once, as no-yeast naan is at its softest in the first few minutes.
tips: Use yogurt that is genuinely thick and sour; watery curd makes the dough sticky and the naan flat.
Do not let the shaped dough sit too long before cooking, or the chemical leaveners lose their fizz and the naan turns dense.
A reheat over a low flame for ten seconds per side revives leftovers far better than a microwave.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with chana masala or a tangy kadhai paneer, and a bowl of sliced cucumber-onion salad dressed with lemon.

variations.name: Multigrain Naan
variations.description: A wholesome upgrade that swaps the usual white flour for hearty multigrain atta, sweetened with honey instead of sugar and studded with sesame. It bakes up a shade denser and earthier than classic naan, with a satisfying chew and a toasty aroma. This is the naan for anyone who wants the indulgence with more fibre and grain character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Multigrain Atta
ingredients.note: A blend of wheat, millet and pulses that gives the naan its nutty, fibre-rich bite

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: Feeds the yeast and lends a floral sweetness that suits the grainy dough

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Brushed on to soften the naturally firmer multigrain crumb

steps: Stir 1 tbsp Anveshan Honey and 1 tsp active dry yeast into 1/2 cup warm water and set aside for 10 minutes until a thick, bubbly foam forms on top.
Combine 2 cups Anveshan Multigrain Atta, 1/2 tsp baking powder and 1 tsp salt in a bowl, pour in the yeast water and 1/4 cup yogurt, and mix into a rough dough.

Knead for 7-8 minutes, adding up to 3 tbsp milk as needed, until the dough is soft and only slightly sticky; multigrain flour drinks more liquid than maida, so keep it supple. Coat with 1/2 tsp Anveshan Ghee, cover, and prove for 1 to 1.5 hours until well risen.
Deflate the dough, divide into 6 balls, rest 10 minutes, then roll each into an oval about 6-7 inches long, pressing white sesame seeds firmly into the surface.
On a smoking-hot tava, moisten the underside of a naan with a wet hand, stick it on water-side down, and cook 1 minute until it domes and bubbles.
Char the top by inverting the tava over the flame for 30-40 seconds until the sesame toasts and dark spots appear, then remove with tongs.
Brush each naan with melted Anveshan Ghee and keep wrapped in a cloth so the firmer crumb stays soft until served.
tips: Multigrain dough needs a longer, warmer rise than maida naan because the bran slows the yeast; be patient with the proof.
If the rolled naan resists and springs back, let it rest another five minutes so the gluten relaxes before the final roll.
Toast the sesame side last over the flame for the deepest nutty flavour without burning the seeds.
variations.servingSuggestion: Excellent with a protein-forward dal tadka or paneer bhurji, rounded out with a mint-yogurt raita.

variations.name: Chilli Coriander Naan
variations.description: A punchy restaurant favourite where the plain canvas is loaded with green chilli, garlic and a thick carpet of fresh coriander before it hits the tava. The herbs char slightly and perfume the whole kitchen, while ajwain and chilli flakes give a warm, sinus-clearing kick. It is the naan you order when you want the bread to have as much personality as the curry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its sturdy crumb carries the heavy herb topping without tearing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: Activates the yeast and balances the heat of the chillies

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Carries the garlic aroma when brushed over the finished naan

steps: Proof 1 tsp active dry yeast with 1 tsp Anveshan Khandsari in 1/2 cup warm milk for about 10 minutes until frothy and risen.
Mix 1.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, 1/2 cup maida and 1 tsp salt, add the yeast milk and 3 tbsp yogurt, and knead 6-7 minutes into a soft dough; oil the bowl, cover, and prove 1 hour until doubled.
Meanwhile finely chop 3 green chillies, 5 garlic cloves and 1/2 cup coriander, and toss them together with 1/2 tsp ajwain and 1 tsp chilli flakes into a fragrant topping mix.

Punch down the dough, divide into 6 balls, and roll each into a 7-inch oval; press a generous spoon of the chilli-garlic-coriander mix onto the top and give it one more light roll so it embeds into the surface.

On a smoking-hot tava, wet the plain underside and stick the naan down topping-side up; cook 1 minute until bubbles rise, then invert the tava over the flame to char the herbs for 30 seconds until they smell toasty and singed.
Lift the naan off with tongs and brush the hot herbed surface with melted Anveshan Ghee so the garlic aroma blooms.
Stack the naans in a cloth and serve immediately, while the chillies and garlic are at their most fragrant.
tips: Chop the garlic rather than mincing it to a paste, so it chars into sweet golden bits instead of burning bitter.
Press the topping in firmly at the rolling stage; loose herbs will fall off when you flip the naan over the flame.
For extra restaurant flair, mix a crushed garlic clove into the finishing ghee before brushing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best mopped through a creamy dal makhani or kadhai mushroom, with a cooling boondi raita to tame the heat.

variations.name: Classic Vegetable Oats Chilla
variations.description: This Classic Oats Chilla blends powdered oats with besan into a savoury batter loaded with onion, tomato and grated carrot, cooked into thin golden pancakes. Wholesome and protein-rich, it is a quick, guilt-free breakfast that crisps at the edges and stays soft within.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a light brush of wood-pressed oil crisps the chilla edges without heaviness

steps: Grind the 1.5 cups rolled oats to a coarse flour in a mixer and tip it into a bowl with the 0.5 cup besan.
Add 1 tsp cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, then whisk in 1.25 cups water to a smooth, spreadable batter and rest it for 10 minutes.
Stir in the finely chopped onion, tomato, grated carrot, 2 green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger and the coriander until evenly mixed.
Heat a non-stick tawa over medium heat, brush with a little Anveshan Groundnut Oil, and pour a ladle of batter, spreading it into a thin round.
Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges and cook for 3 minutes until the base is golden and set, then flip and cook the other side for 2 minutes.
Repeat with the remaining batter, brushing the tawa each time, and serve the chillas hot off the pan.
tips: Rest the batter so the ground oats absorb water and the chillas hold together when flipped.
Keep the batter pourable but not runny, adjusting with a splash of water if it thickens on standing.
Spread the batter thin and cook on steady medium heat for lacy, crisp-edged chillas.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with green coriander-mint chutney and a bowl of thick curd on the side.

variations.name: Moong Dal Oats Chilla
variations.description: This high-protein version grinds soaked yellow moong dal with oats into a light, fluffy batter tempered with cumin and ginger. Softer and more savoury-nutty than the besan style, it is a filling, easily digestible breakfast that keeps you full for hours.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: cooking the chillas in ghee gives the moong dal a rich, wholesome finish

steps: Soak the 1 cup moong dal for 3 hours, drain, and grind with the 1 cup rolled oats, 2 green chillies and 1 inch ginger to a smooth batter using 0.5 cup water.
Transfer to a bowl and season with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 1 tsp salt, whisking to a light, aerated batter.
Dry-roast 1 tsp cumin seeds in a small pan until fragrant, crush lightly, and stir them into the batter along with the chopped onion and coriander.
Heat a tawa over medium heat, smear with a little Anveshan Ghee, and spread a ladle of batter into a medium round.
Cook for 3 minutes until the base is golden and lifts easily, then flip, add a few drops of ghee and cook 2 minutes more until cooked through.
Make the remaining chillas the same way and serve hot and soft off the tawa.
tips: Soak the dal well so it grinds silky smooth for tender, hole-free chillas.
Whisk the ground batter to incorporate air, which makes the chillas light and soft.
Bloom or roast the cumin first rather than adding raw seeds so the flavour is fully released.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot rolled around a spoon of spiced paneer bhurji, with tomato chutney alongside.

variations.name: Sattu Oats Chilla
variations.description: A Bihari-inspired protein powerhouse that combines oats with roasted sattu, sharpened with mustard oil, ajwain, kalonji and pungent onion. Earthy, savoury and boldly spiced, this chilla carries the rustic character of Bihar's beloved sattu.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: roasted sattu adds an earthy, high-protein backbone unique to this chilla

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: pungent wood-pressed mustard oil gives the chilla its authentic Bihari sharpness

steps: Grind the 1 cup rolled oats to a coarse flour and combine in a bowl with the 0.75 cup Anveshan Sattu.
Add 0.5 tsp ajwain, 0.5 tsp kalonji, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, then whisk in 1.5 cups water to a smooth, lump-free batter and rest 10 minutes.
Stir in the finely chopped onion, 2 green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger and the coriander.
Heat a tawa over medium heat and rub it with a little Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just begins to smoke, which mellows its raw pungency.
Pour a ladle of batter, spread into a round, drizzle mustard oil around the edges and cook for 3 minutes until the base is crisp and golden.
Flip and cook the second side for 2 minutes until firm, then repeat with the rest and serve hot.
tips: Heat the mustard oil until it just smokes before cooking to tame its raw sharpness.
Sattu thickens the batter as it rests, so loosen with a little water before each chilla.
A squeeze of lemon in the batter brightens the earthy sattu beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with pickle-spiked onion salad and a dollop of chokha or plain curd on the side.

variations.name: Instant Curd-Rava Oats Chilla
variations.description: A no-grind instant version that whisks oats with semolina and curd into a quick batter dotted with colourful diced vegetables. Ready in minutes with no soaking, it delivers soft, tangy chillas with a pleasant rava bite, perfect for busy mornings.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: light wood-pressed sunflower oil keeps these instant chillas crisp and neutral

steps: Grind the 1 cup rolled oats to a coarse powder and whisk in a bowl with the 0.5 cup semolina and 1 cup curd.
Add 1 tsp cumin powder, 1 tsp salt and 0.5 cup water and whisk to a thick pancake batter, then rest for 8 minutes so the rava swells.
Fold in the finely diced capsicum, grated carrot, 2 chopped green chillies and the coriander.
Heat a tawa over medium heat, brush with Anveshan Sunflower Oil, and spread a ladle of batter into a thick round.
Cook for 3 minutes until golden underneath, drizzle a little oil, flip and cook the other side for 2 minutes.
Continue with the remaining batter, loosening with a splash of water if needed, and serve hot.
tips: Rest the batter briefly so the semolina absorbs moisture and the chillas do not taste grainy.
Use slightly sour curd for a pleasant tang that balances the vegetables.
Keep these a touch thicker than other chillas so the soft rava crumb shines through.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with coconut chutney or a quick tomato-garlic dip for a fast, filling snack.

variations.name: Classic Paneer Pakora
variations.description: This Classic Paneer Pakora dips thick fingers of fresh paneer in a spiced besan batter and fries them into crisp golden fritters with a soft, melting centre. Ajwain-scented and dusted with chaat masala, it is the quintessential monsoon snack served hot with chutney.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil fries the pakoras crisp with a clean, light finish

steps: Cut the 300 g paneer into thick fingers about 1 cm wide and pat them dry.
