Whisk the 1.25 cups besan with 2 tbsp rice flour, 0.5 tsp ajwain, 1 tsp red chilli, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.25 tsp baking soda and 1 tsp salt.
Add about 0.75 cup water gradually and whisk to a smooth, thick batter that coats the back of a spoon.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai over medium heat to 180 C, testing with a drop of batter that should rise and sizzle.
Dip each paneer finger into the batter to coat fully, then slide into the hot oil and fry in batches for 3 to 4 minutes, turning, until golden and crisp.
Drain on a rack, dust with 1 tsp chaat masala and serve hot.
tips: Pat the paneer dry so the batter clings evenly and does not slip off in the oil.
Keep the batter thick enough to coat, as runny batter leaves patches uncovered.
Fry at a steady medium heat so the coating crisps before the paneer overcooks.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with green mint-coriander chutney and a lemon wedge, alongside a cup of ginger chai.

variations.name: Amritsari Paneer Pakora
variations.description: The Amritsari style loads the batter with kasuri methi, corn flour and extra rice flour for a shatteringly crisp, thick coating, then double-fries for maximum crunch. Robustly spiced with garam masala, these fritters are the crunchy Punjabi dhaba classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: neutral wood-pressed sunflower oil gives a clean base for the double-fried crunch

steps: Cut the 300 g paneer into thick square slabs and pat them dry.
Whisk the 1.25 cups besan with 4 tbsp rice flour, 2 tbsp corn flour, the crushed 1 tbsp kasuri methi, 0.75 tsp garam masala, 1.25 tsp red chilli, 0.5 tsp ajwain and 1 tsp salt.
Add about 0.75 cup water and whisk to a thick, clingy batter that heavily coats the paneer.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Sunflower Oil in a kadhai over medium heat to 170 C and fry the coated slabs for 3 minutes until pale golden, then remove and rest them.
Raise the oil to 190 C and fry the pakoras a second time for 2 minutes until deeply golden and shatteringly crisp.
Drain on a rack and serve hot with the crunch intact.
tips: Double-frying is the secret to the extra-crisp Amritsari crust, so do not skip the second fry.
Crush the kasuri methi between your palms before adding it to release its full aroma.
The corn and rice flour make the coating crisp, so keep the batter thick and generous.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with pudina chutney and a sprinkle of chaat masala, with sliced onions and lemon on the side.

variations.name: Stuffed Paneer Pakora
variations.description: This indulgent version sandwiches a layer of tangy mint-coriander chutney between two paneer slices before battering and frying, so each bite bursts with fresh green chutney against the crisp shell. It is a flavour-packed upgrade on the plain fritter.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil keeps the shell crisp around the chutney-filled centre

steps: Cut the 300 g paneer into thin slices and pair them up by size to make sandwiches.
Spread a thick layer of mint coriander chutney over one slice of each pair, sprinkle with a little chaat masala, and press the second slice on top.
Whisk the 1.25 cups besan with 2 tbsp rice flour, 0.5 tsp ajwain, 1 tsp red chilli, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and about 0.75 cup water into a smooth, thick batter.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai over medium heat to 180 C, tested with a rising drop of batter.
Carefully dip each paneer sandwich into the batter to seal all edges, then fry for 3 to 4 minutes, turning gently, until golden and crisp.
Drain on a rack, dust with the remaining chaat masala and serve hot.
tips: Seal the edges well with batter so the chutney does not leak out into the hot oil.
Use a thick, not watery, chutney so the filling stays put between the paneer slices.
Handle the sandwiches gently when frying so they do not come apart in the oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot, halved to reveal the green chutney layer, with sweet tamarind chutney for dipping.

variations.name: Tandoori Air-Fried Paneer Pakora
variations.description: A lighter, smoky version where paneer cubes are marinated in spiced hung curd with tandoori masala and air-fried until charred at the edges, skipping the deep-fry entirely. Tangy, spiced and low in oil, it eats like a healthy paneer tikka snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: a spoon of mustard oil in the marinade gives an authentic smoky tandoori pungency

steps: Cut the 300 g paneer into 2 cm cubes and pat them dry.
Dry-roast the 3 tbsp besan in a pan over low heat for 2 minutes until it smells nutty, which removes the raw taste from the marinade.

Whisk the 0.75 cup hung curd with the roasted besan, 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil, 1.5 tsp tandoori masala, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli, 1 tbsp ginger garlic paste, the crushed 1 tsp kasuri methi, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 0.75 tsp salt.
Fold the paneer cubes into the marinade until evenly coated and rest for 20 minutes in the fridge.
Preheat the air fryer to 200 C, arrange the cubes in a single layer, and air-fry for 12 minutes, turning once, until charred and crisp at the edges.
Dust with 1 tsp chaat masala and serve hot.
tips: Roast the besan before adding it so the marinade does not taste raw and floury.
Use thick hung curd so the marinade clings and chars rather than sliding off.
Do not overcrowd the air-fryer basket so the cubes crisp instead of steaming.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot on skewers with mint chutney, onion rings and a squeeze of lemon as a light starter.

variations.name: Classic Rajasthani Papad Ki Sabzi
variations.description: A desert-kitchen lifesaver born of scarcity: crisp papads simmered briefly in a tangy yogurt-and-besan gravy until they turn silky and slurpable. Ready in minutes with no fresh vegetables, it is the quintessential Marwari standby, tart, warmly spiced and endlessly comforting.

ingredients.name: Bikaneri papad
ingredients.note: moong or urad, broken into pieces

ingredients.name: Yogurt
ingredients.note: whisked smooth, slightly sour

ingredients.name: Besan
ingredients.note: to thicken and stop the curd splitting

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee carries the tempering and gives the gravy its Marwari richness

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: grated

ingredients.name: Salt
ingredients.note: papad is already salty, so go light

steps: Whisk 1 cup yogurt with 2 tbsp besan, 1/2 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1.5 cups water until completely lump-free; keep this mixture ready beside the stove.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1/2 tsp mustard seeds for 30 seconds until they splutter.
Add 1/4 tsp asafoetida, 2 dry red chillies and the grated ginger, and fry for about 30 seconds until fragrant.
Lower the heat to minimum and pour in the yogurt-besan mixture, stirring continuously in one direction for 2-3 minutes so the curd warms gradually and does not split.
Raise the heat to medium and simmer the gravy for 6-8 minutes, stirring often, until it thickens slightly and loses the raw besan smell.
Break 3 papads into rough 2-inch pieces, slide them into the simmering gravy, and cook for just 2-3 minutes until they soften but still hold their shape.
Stir in 1/2 tsp salt and 1/2 tsp garam masala, switch off the heat, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander before serving right away.
tips: Never boil the curd on high heat before it is stabilised with besan and stirred; a rushed pour is the classic reason the gravy curdles.
Add the papad at the very end and serve immediately; sitting too long turns the pieces mushy and pasty.
Slightly sour, day-old yogurt gives the most authentic tang; if yours is fresh, add a squeeze of lemon at the finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with bajra roti or steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, a classic quick meal when the vegetable basket is empty.

variations.name: Marwari Ras-Wali Papad Ki Sabzi
variations.description: The fiery no-yogurt version from interior Marwar, where papad is cooked in a thin, tomato-free red gravy built purely from besan, ghee and desert spices. Kachri and amchur supply the tang instead of curd, giving a leaner, sharper ras that soaks beautifully into roti.

ingredients.name: Bikaneri papad
ingredients.note: broken into pieces

ingredients.name: Besan
ingredients.note: the sole body of this yogurt-free gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: kachi ghani oil gives this desert gravy its pungent Marwari backbone

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: crushed

ingredients.name: Kashmiri red chilli powder
ingredients.note: mostly for a deep red ras

ingredients.name: Kachri powder
ingredients.note: wild desert melon, for sourness

steps: Dry-roast 3 tbsp besan in a kadai on low heat for 2-3 minutes until it smells nutty and turns a shade darker, then tip it out and reserve.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in the same kadai until it just smokes, lower the heat, and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1/4 tsp fenugreek seeds for 20 seconds.
Add 1/2 tsp asafoetida and 5 crushed garlic cloves and fry for 1 minute until the garlic is golden and aromatic.
Lower the heat and stir in 1.5 tsp Kashmiri red chilli powder, 1/2 tsp turmeric powder and 2 tsp coriander powder for 10 seconds, then add the roasted besan and toast together for 1 minute.

Pour in 2 cups hot water in a steady stream while whisking so no lumps form, add 1 tsp kachri powder, 1/2 tsp amchur and 1/2 tsp salt, and simmer for 8-10 minutes until the ras thickens to a light pouring gravy.
Break 3 papads into pieces, slip them into the ras, and cook for 2-3 minutes until just softened but not disintegrated.
Finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and serve at once while the gravy is thin and glossy.
tips: Roasting the besan first is essential in a curd-free ras; raw besan leaves a pasty, beany taste with nothing to mask it.
If you cannot find kachri, double the amchur or add a squeeze of lemon off the heat for the same desert tang.
Keep this gravy on the thinner side; ras-wali sabzi is meant to be soaked up, not scooped.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot bajra or makki roti and a raw onion, letting the thin red ras soak into the bread.

variations.name: Hari Chutney Papad Ki Sabzi
variations.description: A fresh, herby reinvention where papad simmers in a bright coriander-mint gravy loosened with a little yogurt. The green paste and a hit of ginger make it vivid and zingy, a lighter counterpoint to the usual red and tangy versions, and it comes together just as fast.

ingredients.name: Bikaneri papad
ingredients.note: broken into pieces

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: packed, for the green paste

ingredients.name: Mint leaves
ingredients.note: packed

ingredients.name: Yogurt
ingredients.note: whisked, to loosen the paste

ingredients.name: Besan
ingredients.note: to stabilise the yogurt

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a clean wood-pressed oil that lets the fresh herbs shine through

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

steps: Blend 1 cup coriander, 1/2 cup mint, 3 green chillies and 1.5 inch ginger with 3 tbsp water into a smooth green paste; separately whisk 1/2 cup yogurt with 1 tbsp besan until lump-free.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add 1/4 tsp asafoetida.
Add 1 finely chopped onion and saute for 4-5 minutes until soft and pale gold.

Lower the heat and pour in the yogurt-besan mixture, stirring constantly for 2 minutes so it warms without splitting, then add the green paste, 1/4 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder and 1/2 tsp salt.
Add 1 cup water, raise to medium heat, and simmer the green gravy for 6-7 minutes until it thickens lightly and the raw herb smell mellows into a fragrant one.
Break 3 papads into pieces and slide them in, cooking for just 2 minutes until softened.
Switch off the heat and serve immediately while the gravy is still a vivid green.
tips: Add the green paste after the yogurt has stabilised and keep the simmer gentle; hard boiling dulls the fresh green colour.
Do not over-blend the herbs into a warm paste; a quick blitz with cold water keeps the colour bright.
A squeeze of lime just before serving lifts the mint and keeps the gravy tasting fresh.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulkas or jeera rice, with a wedge of lime and thin onion rings for a fresh, herby lunch.

variations.name: Sukha Bhuna Papad Churi
variations.description: A dry, snacky version where roasted papad is crushed and tossed with a quick onion-tomato masala until every shard is coated and just-softened, with no gravy at all. It eats like a warm papad chaat-sabzi, crunchy at the edges and spiced through, ready in ten minutes flat.

ingredients.name: Bikaneri papad
ingredients.note: dry-roasted and hand-crushed into shards

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee coats the crushed papad and toasts the masala

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Roast 4 papads directly over a low flame or in a dry pan until crisp and blistered, then crush them by hand into rough 1-inch shards and set aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1/2 tsp mustard seeds for 30 seconds, then add 1/4 tsp asafoetida.
Add 1 chopped onion and 2 chopped green chillies and saute for 3-4 minutes until the onion softens and turns light gold.
Add 1 chopped tomato with 1/4 tsp turmeric powder, 3/4 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp coriander powder, and cook for 3-4 minutes until the tomato collapses into a thick, dry masala.
Lower the heat, tip in the crushed papad, and toss quickly for 1-2 minutes so every shard is coated but still has a little crunch.
Sprinkle 1/2 tsp roasted cumin powder and 1/2 tsp chaat masala over the top and toss once more off the heat.
Finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and 1 tsp lemon juice, and serve straight away before it loses its bite.
tips: Keep the toss to under two minutes; the whole point of this version is that the papad stays part-crisp rather than melting into a gravy.
Add no water at all; any moisture beyond the tomato turns the shards soggy and defeats the dish.
Serve the moment it is done, as the papad softens quickly once it sits on the plate.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a warm side or quick snack with roti and dal, or pile it onto plain khichdi for a crunchy contrast.

variations.name: Classic Kanda Poha
variations.description: The everyday Maharashtrian breakfast of flattened rice rinsed just until soft, then tossed with a mustard-and-curry-leaf tempering, softened onion and turmeric until fluffy and pale gold. Peanuts add crunch while lemon and coriander lift every mouthful. Light, quick and endlessly comforting, it is the breakfast that starts countless Indian mornings.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A wood-pressed oil that blooms the mustard tempering and fries the peanuts with a nutty depth

steps: Put 2 cups thick poha in a colander and rinse gently under running water until just soft, then leave to drain; the flakes should crush between fingers but not turn mushy.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan on medium flame and fry 0.33 cups raw peanuts for 2-3 minutes until golden, then lift them out.
In the same oil splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, add 2 chopped green chillies and 12 curry leaves for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 sliced onion and saute 4 minutes until soft and translucent, then stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp sugar and 0.75 tsp salt.
Fluff the drained poha with a fork, fold it in gently along with the fried peanuts, and toss on low heat for 2 minutes until evenly yellow and steaming.
Turn off the heat, squeeze in 1 tbsp lemon juice, scatter 3 tbsp coriander, and serve warm.
tips: Use thick poha and rinse it in a colander, never soak it in a bowl, or the flakes turn to a sticky paste.
If the poha feels dry after resting, sprinkle a tablespoon of water and cover for a minute to steam it soft.
Balance the sugar and lemon so the poha lands sweet-tangy, the hallmark of a well-made kanda poha.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot masala chai, a wedge of lemon and a sprinkle of crisp sev over the top.

variations.name: Batata Poha with Potato
variations.description: A heartier version where soft-cooked cubes of potato are folded through the flattened rice, making a more filling breakfast without the onion. Popular in many Gujarati and Maharashtrian homes on no-onion days, it leans on potato, peanuts and a bright lemon finish. The potato soaks up the turmeric tempering and turns every bite substantial.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Fries the potato cubes crisp-edged and blooms the mustard tempering with a nutty aroma

steps: Rinse 2 cups thick poha gently in a colander until just soft and leave to drain while you cook the potatoes.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, fry 0.33 cups peanuts until golden and remove, then add 2 potatoes cut into small cubes and fry 6 minutes until tender and golden at the edges.
Push the potato aside, splutter 1 tsp mustard and 0.5 tsp cumin in the oil, then add 2 chopped green chillies and 12 curry leaves for 30 seconds.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp sugar and 0.75 tsp salt, coating the potato cubes evenly.
Fold in the drained poha and fried peanuts, and toss gently on low heat for 2-3 minutes until everything is hot and evenly yellow.
Turn off the heat, squeeze in 1 tbsp lemon juice, scatter 3 tbsp coriander, and serve warm.
tips: Cut the potato into small even cubes so they cook through in the same time it takes to crisp the edges.
Fry the potato fully before adding the poha, since the delicate flakes cannot withstand the longer cooking.
Skip the onion entirely here for a true batata poha, letting the potato carry the body of the dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cup of ginger chai and a dusting of nylon sev for crunch and a little heat.

variations.name: Dadpe Poha (No-Cook Raw Poha)
variations.description: A Konkan speciality where thin poha is not cooked at all but marinated with raw onion, fresh coconut, coriander and a sizzling tempering poured over the top, then covered to steam in its own warmth. It stays fresh, crunchy-soft and vividly herby, unlike the stovetop version. Traditionally made for evening snacks and monsoon afternoons, it comes together in minutes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: The authentic Konkan fat for the tempering, poured hot over the raw poha to release its aroma

steps: In a wide bowl gently mix 2 cups thin poha with 1 finely chopped onion, 0.5 cups grated coconut, 1 tsp sugar, 0.75 tsp salt and 0.25 cups coriander, crushing lightly with your fingers.
Sprinkle 1.5 tbsp lemon juice and 2 tablespoons of water over the mixture and toss so the flakes just moisten and soften.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan until shimmering, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 3 slit green chillies, 12 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida.
Pour the sizzling tempering evenly over the poha and fold it through so the aromas coat every flake.
Cover the bowl and let it stand for 10 minutes so the thin poha steams soft in its own moisture.
Fluff once more and serve at room temperature, adjusting lemon and salt to taste.
tips: Use thin poha for dadpe, as thick flakes stay hard without cooking and will not soften from moisture alone.
Moisten sparingly with lemon and a splash of water; too much liquid makes the raw poha soggy and flat.
Rest it covered for a full ten minutes so the flavours meld and the flakes turn tender before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve fresh at room temperature with a hot cup of tea; it is best eaten within an hour of tossing.

variations.name: Dahi Poha (Curd Poha)
variations.description: A cooling no-cook South Indian style where soaked poha is folded into whisked curd with a fresh mustard-curry-leaf tempering, much like a soft rice salad. Refreshing and gentle on the stomach, it is a favourite summer breakfast and prasad dish. The tang of curd against the crackle of the tempering makes it light yet satisfying.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Blooms the mustard and urad tempering that is poured over the cool curd poha for a fragrant crackle

steps: Rinse 2 cups thick poha gently in a colander until just soft and leave to drain for 5 minutes.
Whisk 1.5 cups fresh curd smooth with 0.75 tsp salt and 1 inch grated ginger, then fold in the softened poha until evenly coated.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal until the dal turns golden.
Add 2 chopped green chillies and 12 curry leaves, fry 20 seconds until the leaves crisp and turn fragrant.
Pour the hot tempering over the curd poha and fold it through gently so the crackle is distributed.
Chill 15 minutes, then top with 0.25 cups pomegranate and 3 tbsp coriander before serving cool.
tips: Use fresh, mildly sour curd; an overly tangy curd overwhelms the delicate poha and turns the dish sharp.
Loosen with a splash of milk or water if the mixture thickens on standing, as poha keeps absorbing curd.
Pour the tempering while it is still sizzling so the mustard and curry leaves perfume the cool curd instantly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled as a light summer breakfast or as prasad, topped with pomegranate and a little grated carrot.

variations.name: Classic Punjabi Kadhi
variations.description: The thick, deep-golden kadhi of Punjabi homes, cooked far longer than its southern cousins until it turns rich and clinging, then loaded with big onion pakoras. A generous mustard-oil fry for the fritters and a ghee tadka of whole red chillies and fenugreek give it its unmistakable robust character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Punjab fries its pakoras in pungent kachi ghani mustard oil, which gives the fritters their bold, earthy backbone

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the final ghee tadka of whole red chillies and fenugreek is the signature flourish of a Punjabi kadhi

steps: Whisk 0.75 cup besan into 2 cups sour yogurt with 1 tsp turmeric and 4 cups water until completely smooth, then set this kadhi base aside to season while you fry.

Mix the remaining 0.25 cup besan with 2 sliced onions, 0.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 0.5 tsp salt and a splash of water into a thick batter, then fry generous spoonfuls in 2 cups Anveshan Mustard Oil heated to 175C for 4-5 minutes until deep golden; drain and reserve 2 tbsp oil.
In the reserved mustard oil, fry 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, pour in the kadhi base and bring to a boil while stirring constantly so the yogurt does not curdle.

Lower the heat and simmer the kadhi uncovered for 35-40 minutes, stirring often, until it turns thick, glossy and deep gold — Punjabi kadhi is cooked much longer than other styles for this body; season with 1.25 tsp salt and 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder.
Drop the onion pakoras into the thick kadhi and simmer 8-10 minutes so they swell and soak up the tangy sauce without disintegrating.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan, crackle 1 tsp cumin, 0.75 tsp fenugreek seeds, 4 whole dried red chillies and 0.25 tsp hing until the chillies darken, then pour this sizzling tadka over the kadhi and cover for 2 minutes before serving.
tips: The long, slow simmer is what makes a kadhi Punjabi; do not rush it, or the curry stays thin and the besan tastes raw.
Fry the pakoras a little larger than usual so they hold their shape through the extended simmer in the sauce.
Whole dried red chillies in the tadka should be allowed to blacken slightly for that toasty aroma, but not burn to ash.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve ladled thickly over steamed rice with a spoon of ghee, a wedge of onion and a crisp roasted papad on the side.

variations.name: Amritsari Pakora Kadhi (Aloo-Pyaaz, Dhungar Smoked)
variations.description: The Amritsar special: a tangier, kasuri-methi-scented kadhi with hearty potato-onion pakoras and a whisper of charcoal smoke. Ajwain in the batter and a coriander-seed ghee tadka set it apart, while the dhungar finish lends the whole pot a gentle tandoori depth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil fries the sturdy aloo-pyaaz pakoras crisp and holds them through the simmer

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the coriander-seed ghee tadka and the charcoal-smoke drizzle build the Amritsari kadhi's layered aroma

steps: Whisk 0.75 cup besan into 2 cups sour yogurt with 1 tsp turmeric and 4 cups water until smooth, then set the kadhi base aside.

Mix the remaining 0.25 cup besan with 1 grated potato, 1 chopped onion, 0.5 tsp ajwain, 0.5 tsp salt and a splash of water into a thick batter, and fry spoonfuls in 2 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil at 175C for 4-5 minutes until golden; drain and keep 2 tbsp oil.
In the reserved oil, saute 1.5 inch grated ginger for 1 minute, pour in the kadhi base and bring to a boil, stirring nonstop so it stays smooth.
Simmer uncovered on low for 35-40 minutes until thick and glossy, crushing in 1 tbsp kasuri methi in the last 10 minutes and seasoning with 1.25 tsp salt and 1.5 tsp red chilli powder.
Add the aloo-pyaaz pakoras and simmer 8-10 minutes, then heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan, crackle 1 tsp cumin and 1 tbsp crushed coriander seeds, and pour this tadka over the kadhi.

For the dhungar finish, set a small bowl on the kadhi, place a glowing charcoal piece in it, drizzle a few drops of ghee over the coal, cover the pot for 2 minutes to catch the smoke, then remove and serve.
tips: Squeeze the grated potato dry before mixing, or the pakora batter turns watery and the fritters soak up too much oil.
Crush the kasuri methi between your palms as it goes in to release its full aroma into the kadhi.
The charcoal dhungar is optional but gives the authentic Amritsari smokiness; use only food-grade charcoal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jeera rice or tandoori roti and a side of sliced radish and green chilli, Amritsar-dhaba style.

variations.name: Dhaba-style Lahori Garlic Kadhi (Lauki Pakora)
variations.description: A rustic highway-dhaba version fired up with a heavy garlic tempering and light bottle-gourd pakoras that stay soft and juicy in the curry. Crushed coriander and a double dose of garlic — some in the kadhi, more in the sizzling tadka — make it the most robust, garlicky kadhi of the set.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the pungent mustard oil suits the garlic-forward dhaba profile and fries the lauki pakoras light and crisp

steps: Whisk 0.75 cup besan into 2 cups sour yogurt with 1 tsp turmeric and 4 cups water until lump-free and set the kadhi base aside.

Squeeze 1.5 cups grated bottle gourd dry, mix with the remaining 0.25 cup besan, 2 chopped green chillies, 0.5 tsp salt and a little water, then fry spoonfuls in 2 cups Anveshan Mustard Oil heated to 175C and cooled 30 seconds, cooking 3-4 minutes until pale gold; drain and keep 3 tbsp oil.
In the reserved oil, fry half the crushed garlic and 1 chopped green chilli for 1 minute, pour in the kadhi base and bring to a boil while stirring constantly.
Simmer uncovered on low for 35-40 minutes until thick and deep gold, seasoning with 1.25 tsp salt, 1 tbsp crushed coriander seeds and 1 tsp red chilli powder as it cooks.
Slide the lauki pakoras into the kadhi and simmer 6-8 minutes so they turn soft and juicy in the sauce.

Heat 3 tbsp fresh Anveshan Mustard Oil in a small pan, fry the remaining crushed garlic with 4 dried red chillies and 1 tsp cumin until deep golden, stir in the remaining 0.5 tsp red chilli powder off the heat, pour over the kadhi and finish with 3 tbsp coriander.
tips: Lauki pakoras are lighter than potato ones and can turn mushy, so add them near the end of the simmer.
Fry the garlic to a deep gold, not pale, for the toasty punch that defines this dhaba kadhi.
Squeeze the grated lauki really well; its high water content will otherwise thin both the batter and the fritters.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot steamed rice and a raw onion-and-green-chilli salad, dhaba-thali style, with the garlic tadka still crackling.

variations.name: Jain Punjabi Kadhi (No Onion, No Garlic)
variations.description: A satvik Punjabi kadhi made without onion, garlic or root vegetables, using raw-banana pakoras and a hing-ginger base for depth. It keeps the thick, tangy, ghee-tempered soul of the original while staying entirely Jain-friendly — proof the dish never needed the aromatics to shine.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: with no onion or garlic, the bilona-ghee tadka of cumin, fenugreek and hing does all the aromatic work

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: neutral wood-pressed sunflower oil fries the raw-banana pakoras crisp without any pungent aromatics

steps: Whisk 0.75 cup besan into 2 cups sour yogurt with 1 tsp turmeric and 4 cups water until smooth, and set the kadhi base aside.

Mix the remaining 0.25 cup besan with 1.5 cups grated raw banana, 0.5 tsp ajwain, 2 chopped green chillies, 0.5 tsp salt and a splash of water, then fry spoonfuls in 2 cups Anveshan Sunflower Oil at 175C for 3-4 minutes until crisp and golden, and drain the pakoras on a rack.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot on medium heat, add a generous 0.5 tsp hing and 2 inch grated ginger and fry 40 seconds, then pour in the kadhi base and bring to a boil, stirring constantly.
Simmer uncovered on low for 35-40 minutes until thick and glossy, seasoning with 1.25 tsp salt and 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, until the besan is fully cooked and the raw smell is gone.
Add the raw-banana pakoras and simmer 8-10 minutes so they swell and absorb the tangy curry.

Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan, crackle 1 tsp cumin, 0.75 tsp fenugreek seeds and 2 chopped green chillies with a final pinch of hing, and pour this fragrant tadka over the kadhi before serving.
tips: Use a full half-teaspoon of hing here — without onion and garlic, it carries the savoury depth of the whole dish.
Rub the grated raw banana with a little lemon to stop it browning before you fry the pakoras.
This kadhi keeps satvik discipline while tasting rich, so it is perfect for fasting-adjacent family meals.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice or phulka and a spoon of ghee, keeping the meal satvik with a side of cucumber and mint.

variations.name: Classic Puri
variations.description: The everyday puffed bread of Indian breakfasts and festivals: a stiff whole-wheat dough rolled into small discs and deep-fried so they balloon into golden globes. Made with nutty khapli atta and fried in wood-pressed oil, these puris are light, crisp at the edges and soft within. They puff on contact and deflate into tender folds as they cool.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Stone-ground emmer gives puris a nutty flavour and a sturdy crumb that puffs reliably

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rubbed into the dough as moyan for crisp, tender puris

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil fries hot and clean so the puris stay light

steps: Mix 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 3/4 tsp salt, rub in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until the flour looks crumbly, then knead with about 3/4 cup water into a stiff, firm dough that is tighter than roti dough.
Cover the dough and rest it for 10-15 minutes so it relaxes, then knead once more until smooth.
Divide into 16 small balls and roll each into a 4-inch disc about 2 mm thick, using a smear of oil rather than dry flour so the surface stays clean for frying.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai to about 190C, hot enough that a dough scrap shoots up immediately.
Slide in one puri and press it gently under the oil with the back of a slotted spoon in quick circles; it will puff into a ball within seconds.
Flip the puri, fry the second side for 10-15 seconds until pale golden, then lift it out and drain upright against the side of the kadhai.
Serve the puris hot and puffed, straight from the pan for the best texture.
tips: Keep the dough firm; a soft dough absorbs oil and the puris turn greasy instead of puffing.
Roll evenly with no thick centre, as an uneven puri puffs only partway.
Fry hot and fast; low oil makes the puri drink oil and stay flat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with aloo sabzi, a bowl of sooji halwa and a spoon of mango pickle for a classic festive breakfast.

variations.name: Masala Puri
variations.description: A spiced everyday puri kneaded with ajwain, crushed fennel and chilli so each bite carries warmth and fragrance even before you dip it. The seeds bloom in the hot oil as it fries, perfuming the whole kitchen. Robust and aromatic, these puris are good enough to eat with just a squeeze of lemon.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its nutty depth stands up to the bold spice mix worked into the dough

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: Light wood-pressed oil for frying, with a spoon rubbed into the dough as moyan

steps: Combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 3/4 tsp salt, 3/4 tsp ajwain, 1 tsp crushed fennel, 3/4 tsp red chilli powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi in a bowl.
Rub in 1 tbsp Anveshan Sunflower Oil until crumbly, then knead with about 3/4 cup water into a stiff, firm dough; cover and rest 15 minutes.
Knead the dough smooth again and divide into 16 small balls.
Roll each ball into a 4-inch disc about 2 mm thick, smoothing with a little oil instead of dry flour.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Sunflower Oil to about 190C, testing that a dough scrap rises at once with brisk bubbles.
Slide in a puri and press it under the oil in gentle circles until it puffs into a ball, about 15 seconds, then flip and fry the second side until golden and the spices smell fragrant.
Drain upright and serve the masala puris hot, when the ajwain and fennel aroma is at its peak.
tips: Crush the fennel and ajwain lightly so their oils release into the dough and the puri fries fragrant.
Do not overload the chilli; the goal is warmth and aroma, not raw heat that overpowers the accompaniment.
These keep their crunch longer than plain puris, making them a good travel and tiffin option.
variations.servingSuggestion: Delicious with a simple potato-tomato curry, or on their own with tea and a sharp lime pickle.

variations.name: Palak Puri
variations.description: A vibrant green puri kneaded with fresh spinach puree, giving it a jewel colour, a subtle earthiness and a nutrition boost the kids never notice. The spinach keeps the crumb soft while the puris puff just as proudly as plain ones. A festive-looking bread that turns an everyday sabzi into something special.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Balances the moist spinach puree so the dough stays firm enough to puff

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rubbed into the dough as moyan to keep the green puris crisp and tender

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed oil for a clean, light deep fry that shows off the colour

steps: Blanch 2 cups spinach in boiling water for 1 minute, refresh in cold water to hold the colour, then blend with 2 green chillies and 1/2 inch ginger into a smooth, thick puree without adding water.

Mix 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 3/4 tsp salt and 1/2 tsp roasted cumin powder, rub in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then knead with the spinach puree into a stiff dough, adding a spoon of water only if it is too dry.
Cover and rest the dough 15 minutes, then knead once more until smooth and evenly green.
Divide into 16 balls and roll each into a 4-inch disc about 2 mm thick, using a smear of oil to keep the surface clean.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to about 190C, hot enough that a dough scrap surfaces instantly.
Fry one puri at a time, pressing it under the oil in circles until it balloons, then flipping to cook the second side for 10-15 seconds until set and just golden at the edges.
Drain upright and serve the green puris hot and puffed.
tips: Blanch and shock the spinach to lock in the bright colour; over-boiling turns the puris a dull khaki.
Keep the puree thick and water-free so the dough stays firm enough to puff.
Do not fry too dark, or the green fades; pull the puris out as soon as the edges turn light gold.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with aloo dum or a chana curry, and a bowl of thick sweetened yogurt on the side.

variations.name: Sooji Crisp Puri
variations.description: A crunchier, longer-lasting puri built on a base of fine semolina blended with wheat, the kind packed for train journeys and picnics because it stays crisp for hours. The sooji gives a delicate crackle and a pale, even puff. These are the puris that hold their shape long after plain ones have gone soft.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Binds the semolina and adds a nutty backbone so the crisp puris do not crack apart

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A generous moyan is what gives these puris their long-lasting crunch

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: Light wood-pressed oil that keeps the crisp puris from tasting heavy

steps: Mix 1 cup fine semolina, 1 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta, 3/4 tsp salt and 1/2 tsp black pepper powder in a bowl.
Rub in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee thoroughly until the mix holds shape when pressed in your fist, then knead with about 1/2 cup warm water into a stiff, firm dough.
Cover and rest the dough for 20 minutes so the semolina hydrates fully, which prevents the puris from cracking while frying.
Knead once more, divide into 16 small balls, and roll each into a 3.5-inch disc about 2 mm thick, smoothing with a touch of oil.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Sunflower Oil to a moderate 175C, slightly cooler than for wheat puris so the sooji cooks through and crisps rather than browning too fast.
Fry each puri, pressing gently until it puffs, then turning and cooking both sides slowly until pale gold and crisp, about 40 seconds total.
Drain thoroughly and cool completely; these puris crisp up further as they sit and keep for two to three days.
tips: Rest the dough long enough for the semolina to soften, or the puris crack and splinter in the oil.
Fry at a moderate temperature so the interior dries out and the puri turns properly crisp rather than staying chewy.
Cool fully before storing in an airtight tin, where they stay crunchy for two to three days.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ideal travel food with a dry aloo sabzi and mango pickle, or served with masala chai as a teatime snack.

variations.name: Classic Ragi Malt Porridge
variations.description: This Classic Ragi Malt cooks a smooth finger-millet slurry into creamy milk, sweetened with jaggery and scented with cardamom. Iron-rich, mildly nutty and gently sweet, it is the nourishing South Indian malt served warm for breakfast or as a soothing evening drink-thick porridge.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery sweetens the malt naturally and complements ragi's earthy notes

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoon of ghee smooths the porridge and adds a rich finish

steps: Whisk the 0.5 cup ragi flour into 1.5 cups cold water until completely smooth with no lumps.
Pour the slurry into a heavy pan and cook over medium-low heat, stirring constantly, for 5 minutes until it thickens and turns glossy and darker.
Add the 2.5 cups milk gradually while stirring and simmer gently for 5 minutes until creamy and smooth.
Stir in 0.5 tsp cardamom powder, the chopped almonds and 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and cook for 2 more minutes.
Switch off the heat and let the porridge cool for 3 minutes so it is warm but not boiling.
Mix in 0.5 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder until fully dissolved and serve warm.
tips: Whisk the ragi into cold water before heating so the porridge stays silky and lump-free.
Add the jaggery only off the heat once slightly cooled, so the milk does not split.
Stir constantly while the slurry cooks, as ragi thickens fast and can catch at the base.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm in a tall glass or bowl, topped with a few slivered almonds and a pinch of cardamom.

variations.name: Ragi Ambli Buttermilk Porridge
variations.description: A traditional Karnataka summer cooler where cooked ragi is thinned with tangy buttermilk and finished with a mustard-curry leaf tempering. Savoury, cooling and probiotic-rich, this ambli is sipped cold to beat the heat rather than eaten as a sweet.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: coconut oil carries the South Indian tempering that flavours this savoury ambli

steps: Whisk the 0.5 cup ragi flour into 2 cups cold water until smooth, then cook over medium-low heat for 6 minutes, stirring, until thick and glossy.
Spread the cooked ragi in a bowl and let it cool completely to room temperature.
Whisk the cooled ragi with the 2 cups buttermilk and 1 tsp salt until smooth and pourable.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add the 12 curry leaves, 2 slit green chillies and 1 inch chopped ginger and sizzle for 20 seconds.
Pour the sizzling tempering over the ragi buttermilk and stir in the finely chopped onion and coriander.
Chill for 30 minutes and serve cold as a savoury cooler.
tips: Cool the cooked ragi fully before adding buttermilk so the curd does not split from the heat.
Keep the ambli pourable and drinkable, thinning with extra buttermilk or water as needed.
Serve well chilled, as this dish is meant to cool the body in hot weather.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve cold in tumblers with a side of raw onion, green chilli and a spoon of pickle in true Karnataka style.

variations.name: Ragi Banana Porridge
variations.description: A naturally sweet, wholesome porridge where cooked ragi is blended creamy with ripe banana and milk, then finished with honey and cardamom. Smooth, mild and energising, it is a gentle bowl loved by children and anyone wanting an easy, sustaining breakfast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a touch of ghee makes this porridge extra smooth and easy to digest

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: honey stirred in off the heat sweetens the porridge gently over the banana

steps: Whisk the 0.5 cup ragi flour into 1.5 cups cold water until smooth, then cook over medium-low heat for 5 minutes, stirring, until thick and glossy.
Add the 2.5 cups milk gradually and simmer for 5 minutes until the porridge is creamy.
Mash the 2 ripe bananas to a smooth pulp and stir into the porridge with 0.5 tsp cardamom powder.
Add the chopped cashews and 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and cook for 1 minute, then take off the heat.
Let the porridge cool for 4 minutes so it is warm rather than hot.
Stir in 3 tbsp Anveshan Honey until blended and serve warm.
tips: Use very ripe, spotted bananas for maximum natural sweetness and a smooth texture.
Add the honey only after cooling slightly, so its flavour and goodness are preserved.
Blend the porridge for a few seconds if you want an ultra-smooth, spoonable consistency.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm topped with banana slices and a few crushed cashews for a comforting breakfast bowl.

variations.name: Ragi Almond Saffron Porridge
variations.description: An indulgent version enriched with a spoon of dry-fruit paak, saffron-infused milk and ground almonds for a luxurious, kesar-scented bowl. Thick, aromatic and studded with pistachios, this ragi porridge feels like a nourishing dessert.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Dry Fruit Paak
ingredients.note: dry-fruit paak adds instant nutty richness and gentle sweetness to the malt

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: saffron steeped in warm milk gives the porridge its golden hue and aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee lends a silky, rich mouthfeel to this festive porridge

steps: Soak the pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside to bloom, and soak the 15 almonds, then grind them to a fine paste.
Whisk the 0.5 cup ragi flour into 1 cup cold water until smooth, then cook over medium-low heat for 5 minutes, stirring, until thick and glossy.
Add the 3 cups milk gradually and simmer for 5 minutes, then stir in the almond paste and cook for 3 minutes until creamy.
Mix in the saffron milk, 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and simmer for 2 minutes.
Take the pan off the heat and let the porridge cool for 3 minutes.
Stir in 3 tbsp Anveshan Dry Fruit Paak until blended and serve warm topped with chopped pistachios.
tips: Bloom the saffron in warm milk first to release its full colour and fragrance.
Grind the soaked almonds smooth for a rich body without any grittiness.
The dry-fruit paak adds sweetness, so taste before adding any extra sweetener.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm in small bowls garnished with saffron strands and slivered pistachios as a nourishing treat.

variations.name: Classic Rumali Roti
variations.description: The gossamer handkerchief bread of Mughlai kitchens, stretched paper-thin and cooked draped over an inverted kadai until it is so light it can be folded like cloth. A soft, well-rested dough of refined and wheat flour is the secret to its stretch. Served folded into quarters, it is the elegant scoop for rich North Indian curries and kebabs.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Kneaded in and used to grease the dough as it rests, giving the elasticity needed to stretch it tissue-thin

steps: Combine 1.5 cups maida, 0.5 cups whole wheat flour, 0.25 tsp baking soda and 0.75 tsp salt, then add 0.25 cups milk and 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil.
Add the 0.5 cups warm water gradually and knead 8-10 minutes into a very soft, elastic dough, then rub it with the remaining oil and rest it covered for 1 hour.
Divide into 6 balls, roll one out as thin as possible on a large floured surface, then lift and gently stretch it over the backs of your hands until nearly translucent.
Invert a heavy kadai over the flame and heat it well, then drape the stretched roti over the domed base.
Cook 30-40 seconds until pale spots appear on the underside, then flip it over the dome and cook the other side 20 seconds; do not let it crisp.
Fold the hot roti into a triangle like a handkerchief and repeat with the remaining dough, keeping them covered so they stay soft.
tips: Rest the dough a full hour; the long relaxation is what lets the gluten stretch tissue-thin without tearing.
Keep the heat high and the cooking brief, as rumali roti must stay soft and foldable, never crisp.
Stretch over the backs of your hands after rolling to get it thinner than a pin ever could.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve folded alongside a rich butter chicken-style paneer makhani or seekh-style veg kebabs with mint chutney.

variations.name: Whole Wheat Khapli Rumali Roti
variations.description: A wholesome reinvention that drops the refined flour entirely for nutty Anveshan khapli atta, proving the handkerchief roti can be made healthier without losing its drape. Curd in the dough compensates for the extra bran, keeping it supple enough to stretch thin. The result is earthier and more filling, with the same signature fold.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Ancient-wheat flour replaces the maida entirely, lending a nutty flavour while its fine gluten still stretches thin

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Kneaded in for suppleness and rubbed over the resting dough so the whole-wheat version still stretches without cracking

steps: Mix 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.25 tsp baking soda and 0.75 tsp salt, then add 0.25 cups curd and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee.
Pour in about 0.6 cups warm water and knead 8-10 minutes into a very soft, smooth dough; whole wheat needs a touch more water than maida.
Rub the dough with the remaining ghee, cover, and rest it a full hour so the gluten relaxes enough to stretch.
Roll a ball out thin on a floured surface, then drape it over the backs of your hands and ease it wider until nearly see-through.
Heat an inverted heavy kadai over the flame, lay the roti on the dome, and cook 30-40 seconds a side until soft spots form, keeping it pliable.
Fold into a handkerchief triangle and repeat, stacking the rotis under a cloth to keep them from drying.
tips: Curd is essential here; it tenderises the bran-heavy dough so it can stretch like a maida rumali.
Whole wheat tears more easily, so stretch slowly over your knuckles and stop the moment you see light through it.
Rest is non-negotiable, and a warm spot speeds the gluten relaxation for a stretchier dough.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a robust dal makhani or a kadai vegetable, where the nutty roti holds up to bold gravies.

variations.name: Multigrain Rumali Roti
variations.description: A fibre-rich take that blends Anveshan multigrain atta with a little refined flour for structure, giving a speckled handkerchief roti with a deeper, grainy aroma. The mix of grains adds nutrition and a subtle sweetness while still stretching respectably thin. A modern everyday version for households that want the drama of rumali with more wholesomeness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Multigrain Atta
ingredients.note: A blend of grains gives the roti a speckled look and grainy aroma while keeping enough gluten to stretch

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: A light, neutral oil kneaded in and used to coat the resting dough for a clean stretch

steps: Combine 1.5 cups Anveshan Multigrain Atta, 0.5 cups maida, 0.25 tsp baking soda and 0.75 tsp salt, then add 0.25 cups milk and 1 tbsp Anveshan Sunflower Oil.
Add the 0.5 cups warm water gradually and knead 8-10 minutes into a soft, elastic dough.
Coat the dough with the remaining sunflower oil, cover, and rest it for 1 hour.
Roll a ball thin on a floured board, then stretch it over the backs of your hands until it is wide and nearly translucent.
Drape over an inverted hot kadai and cook 30-40 seconds a side until pale spots appear, keeping it soft and foldable.
Fold into a handkerchief and continue with the remaining dough, covering the stack as you go.
tips: The small measure of maida is what gives the multigrain dough enough gluten to stretch; do not omit it.
Grainy doughs dry faster, so keep the balls covered and work one at a time.
If the roti resists stretching, let it rest another 15 minutes rather than forcing it, which causes tears.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a light vegetable korma or a chana masala, letting the grainy roti soak up the sauce.

variations.name: Pudina Rumali Roti
variations.description: A fragrant restaurant-style rumali flecked with dried mint and crushed garlic worked right into the dough, so each translucent fold carries a cooling herbal aroma. The mint plays beautifully against smoky tandoori curries and makes the roti special enough to notice on its own. A subtle but memorable upgrade on the plain handkerchief bread.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Kneaded in and rubbed over the dough for stretch, carrying the mint and garlic evenly through the roti

steps: Combine 1.5 cups maida, 0.5 cups whole wheat flour, 1 tbsp dried mint powder, 1 tsp garlic paste, 0.25 tsp baking soda and 0.75 tsp salt in a bowl.
Add 0.25 cups milk and 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, then work in the 0.5 cups warm water and knead 8-10 minutes into a soft, springy dough.
Rub the dough with the remaining oil, cover, and rest it for 1 hour so it will stretch thin.
Roll a ball out thin, then drape and stretch it over the backs of your hands until nearly translucent, keeping the mint flecks visible.
Cook over an inverted hot kadai 30-40 seconds a side until soft spots appear, keeping it pliable rather than crisp.
Fold the fragrant roti into a handkerchief and repeat with the rest of the dough.
tips: Use dried mint powder rather than fresh leaves, which release water and make the dough hard to stretch.
A light hand with garlic is best, as too much will scorch and turn bitter on the hot dome.
Rest the dough well; the herbs do not affect the stretch, but under-rested gluten will still tear.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a smoky baingan bharta or a paneer tikka masala, where the mint roti refreshes each rich bite.

variations.name: Classic Maharashtrian Sabudana Khichdi
variations.description: The definitive fasting dish of soaked tapioca pearls tossed with crushed roasted peanuts, potato and green chilli until each pearl turns glossy, separate and translucent. Cumin, curry leaves and a squeeze of lemon keep it light while the peanuts add crunch and body. Made without onion or garlic, it is the classic vrat breakfast of Maharashtra.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The fasting-friendly fat that blooms the cumin and keeps the tapioca pearls glossy and non-sticky

steps: Rinse 1 cup sabudana until the water runs clear, then soak in just enough water to cover for 5 hours or overnight until each pearl swells and crushes easily.
Drain the soaked sabudana well, coarsely crush 0.5 cups roasted peanuts, and toss the pearls with the peanut powder and 0.75 tsp rock salt so they stay separate.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium flame, crackle 1 tsp cumin for 30 seconds, then add 2 chopped green chillies and 10 curry leaves for 30 seconds.
Add 1 diced boiled potato and saute 2 minutes until lightly golden at the edges.
Tip in the peanut-coated sabudana and stir gently on low heat for 4-5 minutes until the pearls turn translucent and glossy, never sticky.
Turn off the heat, squeeze in 1 tbsp lemon juice, fold through 3 tbsp coriander, and serve hot.
tips: Soak the sabudana with water just level to the pearls; too much water makes them mushy and they clump into a lump.
Coating the drained pearls in crushed peanut powder before frying is the key trick that keeps them separate.
Cook only until translucent and stop; overcooking on high heat turns the pearls gummy and sticky.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a bowl of cool, lightly sweetened peanut curd and an extra wedge of lemon on the side.

variations.name: Nashik Faral Sabudana Khichdi
variations.description: The road-stall faral style from Nashik, richer with ghee and a heavier hand of crushed peanuts and sugar for a sweet-savoury balance beloved across Maharashtra. A little grated coconut and extra lemon brighten every bite. It is the indulgent, restaurant-plate version of the humble fasting khichdi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A generous glossing of ghee gives the faral-style khichdi its rich sheen and street-stall aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: An unrefined sweetener stirred in for the signature sweet-savoury Nashik balance without white sugar

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup sabudana in just enough water to cover for 5 hours until the pearls swell and crush easily, then drain thoroughly.
Coarsely crush 0.75 cups roasted peanuts and toss the drained pearls with the peanut powder, 0.75 tsp rock salt and 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium flame, crackle 1 tsp cumin for 30 seconds, then add 3 chopped green chillies for 30 seconds.
Add 1 diced boiled potato and saute 2 minutes until golden, then tip in the peanut-coated sabudana.
Stir gently on low heat for 5 minutes until the pearls turn translucent and glossy, taking care they do not clump.
Turn off the heat, fold in 3 tbsp grated coconut, 1.5 tbsp lemon juice and 3 tbsp coriander, and serve hot.
tips: Balance the jaggery with plenty of lemon so the khichdi lands sweet-tangy rather than merely sweet.
Use more ghee than the everyday version; the extra fat is what gives faral-stall khichdi its glossy richness.
Add the fresh coconut off the heat so it stays moist and does not dry out against the hot pearls.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a spoon of thick sweetened curd and a small heap of extra crushed peanuts scattered on top.

variations.name: Sabudana Khichdi with Roasted Makhana
variations.description: A fasting-friendly upgrade where ghee-roasted fox nuts are folded through the tapioca pearls for airy, popcorn-like crunch alongside the peanuts. The makhana keeps the khichdi light yet more filling and adds a pleasant contrast to the soft pearls. It is a modern vrat plate that eats like a wholesome snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasts the makhana to a crisp crunch and glosses the pearls for a fasting-friendly finish

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup sabudana in just enough water to cover for 5 hours until the pearls crush easily, then drain thoroughly.
Roast 1 cup makhana in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on low heat for 4-5 minutes until crisp, season with a little rock salt and 0.25 tsp black pepper, and set aside.
Crush 0.33 cups roasted peanuts and toss the drained pearls with the peanut powder and 0.75 tsp rock salt so they stay separate.
Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin for 30 seconds, add 2 chopped green chillies and 10 curry leaves, then saute 1 diced boiled potato for 2 minutes.
Tip in the peanut-coated sabudana and stir gently on low heat for 4-5 minutes until the pearls turn translucent and glossy.
Turn off the heat, fold in the roasted makhana, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 3 tbsp coriander, and serve at once so the fox nuts stay crunchy.
tips: Roast the makhana until it snaps crisp, testing one; under-roasted fox nuts go chewy once folded in.
Add the makhana only at the very end so it keeps its crunch against the soft, glossy pearls.
Break larger fox nuts in half before roasting so they distribute evenly through the khichdi.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve immediately with cool cucumber-mint curd; eat promptly while the makhana is still audibly crisp.

variations.name: Sabudana Khichdi Tikki
variations.description: A crisp-edged reinvention where the classic khichdi is shaped into patties and shallow-fried in ghee until golden and lacy outside while staying soft within. Perfect for using up leftover khichdi or serving it as a fasting snack. The griddled crust adds a whole new texture to the familiar peanut-and-potato mix.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Shallow-fries the tikkis to a lacy golden crust while keeping the inside soft

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup sabudana in just enough water to cover for 5 hours until the pearls crush easily, then drain thoroughly.
Coarsely crush 0.5 cups roasted peanuts and mash 2 boiled potatoes, then combine with the drained pearls, 2 minced green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger and 0.75 tsp rock salt.
Toast 1 tsp cumin in a dry pan for 30 seconds, crush lightly, and mix it in with 2 tbsp rajgira flour, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 3 tbsp coriander to bind the dough.
Shape the mixture into 8 flat patties about half an inch thick, pressing firmly so they hold together.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on a tava on medium flame and shallow-fry the tikkis in batches for 3 minutes a side until golden and lacy-crisp.
Drain on paper and serve hot, crisp side up, while the crust is still crackling.
tips: Bind with rajgira or kuttu flour rather than water so the tikkis stay fasting-friendly and do not fall apart.
Toast the cumin and crush it rather than adding raw seeds, so the spice is evenly through the soft mixture.
Chill the shaped patties for 10 minutes before frying and they will hold their edge in the hot ghee.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a green coriander-peanut chutney or sweetened curd for dipping the crisp tikkis.

variations.name: Classic Sabudana Thalipeeth
variations.description: Sabudana Thalipeeth is a Maharashtrian fasting griddle cake of soaked tapioca pearls bound with mashed potato and crushed peanuts, patted flat and roasted in ghee till crisp and golden. Made with rock salt and no grains, it is the ideal upvas snack, soft within and crackly at the edges.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts each thalipeeth to a crisp golden base with a nutty upvas-friendly richness

steps: Rinse 1 cup sabudana until the water runs clear, then soak in just enough water to cover for 5 hours until each pearl is soft and squishes between your fingers; drain any excess.

Coarsely crush 0.5 cup roasted peanuts and mix with the sabudana, 3 mashed potatoes, 1 tsp cumin seeds, 3 minced green chillies, grated 1 inch ginger, 1 tsp rock salt, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 3 tbsp coriander into a firm dough.
Divide into 6 portions and pat each into a thick round directly on a greased sheet or wet palm, making a small hole in the centre.
Heat a tawa on medium, add 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee, and slide on a thalipeeth, drizzling a little ghee into the central hole.
Cook covered for 3 to 4 minutes until the base is golden and crisp, then flip and cook another 3 minutes with more ghee.
Serve hot off the tawa while the edges are still crackling, cooking the rest the same way.
tips: Soak the sabudana in minimal water; too much makes the pearls mushy and the thalipeeth sticky.
Pat the cakes on a greased sheet rather than rolling, as the dough is too delicate for a pin.
Cook covered on medium heat so the inside sets before the base over-browns.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with cooling peanut-curd (dahi) and a wedge of lemon for a satisfying vrat meal.

variations.name: Crispy Rajgira Sabudana Thalipeeth
variations.description: An extra-crisp upvas version bound with a little rajgira (amaranth) flour and sesame that lets the cake brown into a shattering crust. The amaranth also makes it more filling and adds a gentle nutty note to the tapioca base.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: gives a light, crisp roasted base and suits the sesame-studded crust

steps: Soak 1 cup rinsed sabudana in just enough water to cover for 5 hours until soft, then drain well.

Crush 0.5 cup roasted peanuts coarsely and mix with the sabudana, 2 mashed potatoes, 0.33 cup rajgira flour, 2 tbsp sesame seeds, 1 tsp cumin, 3 minced green chillies, 1 tsp rock salt and 3 tbsp coriander into a firm dough.
Divide into 6 and pat each into a thin round on a greased sheet, pressing a few extra sesame seeds onto the top for crunch.
Heat a tawa on medium, add 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, and place a thalipeeth on it.
Cook for 3 to 4 minutes until the sesame-flecked base is deep golden and crisp, then flip with more oil and cook 3 minutes more.
Serve immediately while shatteringly crisp, cooking the remaining cakes the same way.
tips: The rajgira flour tightens the dough, so use fewer potatoes here to keep it from turning dense.
Pat these thinner than the classic for maximum crunch, since the amaranth crisps beautifully.
Press sesame onto the surface just before roasting so it toasts and clings rather than falling off.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of chilled sweetened curd for a filling, energising fasting breakfast.

variations.name: Paneer-Stuffed Sabudana Thalipeeth
variations.description: A richer fasting treat where the tapioca cake is folded around a spiced paneer core that stays soft and creamy inside the crisp shell. The mild paneer with green chilli and pepper turns a simple thalipeeth into a hearty one-dish upvas meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the stuffed cakes crisp while keeping the paneer centre soft

steps: Soak 1 cup rinsed sabudana in just enough water for 5 hours until soft, then drain thoroughly.
For the filling, mix 1 cup grated paneer with 1 minced green chilli, 0.5 tsp black pepper, a pinch of rock salt and 1 tbsp coriander, and set aside.
For the dough, crush 0.33 cup roasted peanuts and combine with the sabudana, 3 mashed potatoes, 1 tsp cumin, 2 minced green chillies, grated 1 inch ginger, 1 tsp rock salt and 2 tbsp coriander.
Flatten a portion of dough on a greased sheet, place a spoon of paneer filling in the centre, seal the dough over it, and gently pat into a stuffed round.
Heat a tawa on medium, add 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee, and cook each thalipeeth covered for 4 minutes until the base is golden.
Flip carefully, add more ghee, cook 3 minutes until crisp, and serve hot with the soft paneer inside.
tips: Keep the paneer filling fairly dry and seal the dough well so it does not burst on the tawa.
Pat the stuffed cakes a little thicker so there is room for the filling without tearing the surface.
Fresh, soft paneer works best; if it is firm, mash it well so the centre stays creamy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a spoon of green coriander chutney and sliced cucumber for a complete fasting plate.

variations.name: Masala Sabudana Thalipeeth
variations.description: A non-fasting everyday version that adds onion, chaat masala and red chilli for a punchier, tangier griddle cake to enjoy any day. The onion adds sweetness and juiciness while chaat masala lifts the whole thing to a street-snack flavour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: roasts the masala cakes crisp and lets the chaat spices shine

steps: Soak 1 cup rinsed sabudana in just enough water for 5 hours until soft, then drain well.

Crush 0.5 cup roasted peanuts coarsely and mix with the sabudana, 3 mashed potatoes, finely chopped onion, 1 tsp cumin, 1 tsp chaat masala, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 minced green chillies, 1 tsp salt and 3 tbsp coriander.
Divide into 6 portions and pat each into a thick round on a greased sheet with a hole in the centre.
Heat a tawa on medium, add 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, and slide on a thalipeeth, drizzling oil into the hole.
Cook covered 3 to 4 minutes until golden and crisp, then flip with more oil and cook 3 minutes more.
Serve hot, cooking the rest the same way, dusting a little extra chaat masala on top.
tips: Squeeze the moisture out of the chopped onion so it does not slacken the sabudana dough.
Add the onion just before cooking so it stays fresh and juicy rather than weeping into the mix.
A final dusting of chaat masala after cooking gives a bright, tangy street-food finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sweet tamarind chutney and a cup of masala chai as a hearty everyday snack.

variations.name: Classic Punjabi Sarson Ka Saag
variations.description: The winter heart of Punjab: mustard greens slow-simmered with spinach and bathua, hand-mashed with a wooden ghotni, thickened with makki flour and finished with a garlic-ginger ghee tadka. It is coarse, mineral and deeply green, meant to be scooped with makki di roti under a knob of melting ghee.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the final garlic-ginger tadka in bilona ghee is the soul of Punjabi saag and the ghee melted on top at the table is non-negotiable

steps: Wash and roughly chop 500 g mustard greens, 150 g spinach and 100 g bathua, then boil them in a pot with 1.5 cups water, half the ginger, 3 green chillies and 1 tsp salt for 30-35 minutes on medium heat until utterly collapsed and soft.
Add 3 tbsp maize flour to the boiled greens and mash everything vigorously with a wooden ghotni or masher for 6-8 minutes until the saag is coarse-textured and cohesive, never a smooth puree.
Return the mashed saag to low heat and let it blip gently for 15 minutes, stirring often so it does not catch, until it thickens and the raw mustard edge mellows into a rounded, earthy flavour.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan on medium heat, add 10 finely chopped garlic cloves and fry until pale gold, then add 1 finely chopped onion, the remaining grated ginger and 1 slit green chilli and cook 4-5 minutes until golden.
Stir in 1 tsp red chilli powder off the heat, then pour this sizzling tadka into the simmering saag, holding back a spoonful for the top, and stir it through with the remaining 0.5 tsp salt.
Simmer the tempered saag another 5 minutes so the flavours fuse, then serve with the reserved garlicky ghee spooned over and an extra pat of ghee melting on top.
tips: Bathua is the traditional third green and cuts the sharpness of mustard; if unavailable, increase the spinach slightly to keep the balance.
Mash by hand rather than blending — the coarse, rustic texture from a ghotni is what separates real saag from a green soup.
Saag always tastes better the next day, so make it ahead and reheat gently with a splash of water and a fresh spoon of ghee.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with makki di roti, a large knob of ghee, thick jaggery on the side and a glass of buttermilk for the full Punjab winter plate.

variations.name: Restaurant-style Makhani Sarson Ka Saag
variations.description: The plush dhaba-restaurant rendition, smoothed with a tomato-onion masala base and enriched with white butter and a swirl of cream. Softer, richer and a shade less bitter than the rustic original, it is the version served in silver katoris with a smoky dhungar finish and buttered naan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee builds the rich tomato-onion masala that gives this version its restaurant smoothness

steps: Boil 500 g chopped mustard greens and 200 g spinach with 3 slit green chillies, 1 cup water and 1 tsp salt for 30 minutes until soft, then mash with 2 tbsp maize flour to a coarse but slightly smoother texture than the rustic saag and set aside.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat, add 2 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry 1 minute, then add 2 pureed onions and cook 8-9 minutes until the moisture evaporates and the puree turns golden.
Add 2 pureed tomatoes with 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 0.5 tsp salt and bhuno for 6-7 minutes until the masala thickens and the ghee separates at the edges.
Fold the mashed greens into the masala, add 0.5 cup water, and simmer on low for 12-15 minutes, stirring often, so the saag takes on the rich tomato-onion base.
Beat in 2 tbsp white butter and 2 tbsp cream off high heat along with 0.5 tsp garam masala, keeping the last 1 tbsp cream for the top.

For the dhungar finish, place a small bowl in the pan, put a glowing charcoal piece in it, drizzle the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the coal, cover for 2 minutes to trap the smoke, then remove, swirl in the reserved cream and serve.
tips: Pureeing the onions and tomatoes rather than chopping them gives this version its characteristic smooth, restaurant-style body.
The optional charcoal dhungar step adds a subtle tandoori smokiness; skip it safely if you do not have food-grade charcoal.
Add the cream and butter off high heat so the dairy melts in silkily instead of splitting.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a katori topped with a cream swirl and a cube of white butter, alongside butter naan or lachha paratha and a side of pickled onions.

variations.name: Pahari Himachali Sarson Saag (Mixed Greens)
variations.description: A hill-country take from Himachal where mustard shares the pot with radish greens and fenugreek, soured lightly with dahi and tempered in pungent mustard oil rather than ghee. Rougher and more herbal than the plains version, it carries the cold-weather bite of the mountains.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: kachi ghani mustard oil is the authentic hill-kitchen fat here and its pungency matches the wild mountain greens

steps: Boil 400 g mustard greens, 150 g radish greens and 100 g methi leaves with 1.5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric, half the ginger and 1 tsp salt for 30 minutes until fully soft and drooping.
Add 2 tbsp maize flour and mash the greens coarsely with a masher for 6-7 minutes, then simmer on low for 12 minutes until thick, stirring so the base does not scorch.
Take the pot off direct high heat, then whisk in 3 tbsp dahi gradually so it blends without splitting and gives the saag a gentle tang.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pan until it just smokes, lower the flame for 30 seconds to mellow it, then add 3 broken dried red chillies, 12 crushed garlic cloves and the remaining chopped ginger and fry until deep golden.
Add 1 chopped onion to the tadka and cook 4-5 minutes until browned at the edges, then pour the sizzling temper into the saag with the remaining 0.5 tsp salt.
Simmer the tempered saag for 6-7 minutes so the mustard oil and dahi settle into the greens, then serve hot straight from the pot.
tips: Always heat mustard oil to smoking point once and cool it slightly before frying, or the tadka tastes raw and harsh.
Whisk the dahi in off high heat and in a slow stream so it enriches the saag without curdling.
Radish greens can turn bitter if overgrown; pick young, tender leaves for the cleanest hill flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thick bajra or makki roti, a dollop of white butter and a side of mooli slices, the way it is eaten in Himachali winter kitchens.

variations.name: Sarson Aur Palak Saag with Sattu Makki Roti Crumble
variations.description: A modern, protein-forward spin that stirs roasted sattu into the finished saag for extra body and nutrition, then tops each bowl with a crunchy sattu-makki roti crumble. It keeps the mustard-greens soul intact while making the dish heartier and more filling in a single bowl.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee tempers the saag and toasts the roti crumble to a nutty crunch

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: roasted gram sattu stirred in adds plant protein and a savoury nuttiness that thickens the saag without makki flour alone

steps: Boil 450 g mustard greens and 250 g spinach with 1.5 cups water, 3 slit green chillies, half the ginger and 1 tsp salt for 30 minutes until completely soft.

Mash the greens coarsely with a masher, then stir 1 tbsp Anveshan Sattu dissolved in a little water into the pot and simmer 12 minutes until thick, adding the sattu slurry gradually so it does not lump.

For the crumble, mix 3 tbsp maize flour with 2 tbsp Anveshan Sattu, a pinch of salt and enough water to make a stiff dough, roll a small thick roti and dry-roast it, then toast it in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until crisp and crush into coarse crumbs.

Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium heat, fry 10 chopped garlic cloves until golden, add 1 chopped onion, the remaining grated ginger and 1 slit green chilli and cook 4-5 minutes until browned.
Stir in 1 tsp red chilli powder off the heat, pour the tadka into the saag with the remaining 0.5 tsp salt, and simmer together for 6-7 minutes.
Ladle the saag into bowls and top each with a generous scatter of the crunchy sattu-makki crumble just before serving so it stays crisp.
tips: Dissolve the sattu in cold water before adding it to hot saag; dropping dry sattu straight in makes it clump instantly.
Add the crumble only at the table — it softens quickly once it sits in the warm saag.
The sattu makes this saag more filling, so a slightly thinner consistency keeps it from feeling heavy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a one-bowl meal topped with the roti crumble and a spoon of ghee, with a wedge of lemon and sliced radish alongside.

variations.name: Classic Schezwan Fried Rice
variations.description: This Classic Schezwan Fried Rice is a fiery Indo-Chinese stir-fry where fluffy rice is tossed with crunchy vegetables and a bold, garlicky Schezwan sauce. Deep red, spicy and smoky, it delivers a lip-tingling heat balanced by the sweetness of the vegetables.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: handles the searing heat needed to bloom the Schezwan paste

steps: Cool 4 cups of cooked rice on a wide plate so the grains stay firm and separate.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a wok until shimmering, add the minced garlic and stir-fry on high heat for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the finely diced carrot, capsicum, 0.5 cup french beans and 0.5 cup cabbage and stir-fry on high for 3 minutes so they keep their crunch.
Stir in 3.5 tbsp Schezwan sauce, 1 tbsp soy sauce and 0.5 tsp salt and toss for 1 minute until the vegetables are evenly coated in red.
Add the cooled rice and toss vigorously on high heat for 3 minutes, lifting and folding so every grain turns fiery and glossy.
Fold in 4 tbsp chopped spring onion, give a final toss, and serve immediately while steaming hot.
tips: Use day-old chilled rice for the driest, most separate grains that soak up the sauce without clumping.
Add the Schezwan sauce gradually and taste, as brands differ widely in heat and salt.
Keep the flame on the highest setting throughout for the signature smoky wok flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with veg manchurian gravy or a bowl of hot-and-sour soup for a complete meal.

variations.name: Paneer Schezwan Fried Rice
variations.description: A protein-rich take where golden seared paneer cubes join the fiery rice, adding softness against the heat. More filling than the classic, the mild paneer soaks up the Schezwan sauce and turns this into a satisfying one-bowl meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: a nutty base for searing the paneer and finishing the fiery rice

steps: Cool 4 cups of cooked rice and cut 200 g paneer into small cubes.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a wok and sear the paneer cubes on high heat for 2 minutes until golden-edged, then set aside.
In the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, stir-fry the minced garlic on high for 30 seconds, then add the cubed onion, capsicum and 0.5 cup green peas and stir-fry for 3 minutes.
Stir in 3 tbsp Schezwan sauce, 1 tbsp soy sauce and 0.5 tsp salt and toss for 1 minute until coated in red.
Add the cooled rice and toss vigorously on high heat for 3 minutes so every grain is fiery, then fold in the seared paneer.
Garnish with 4 tbsp spring onion, toss once, and serve immediately while the paneer is still soft.
tips: Sear the paneer separately and add it last so the cubes stay whole and golden.
Soak firm paneer in warm water for 10 minutes before searing to keep it tender.
The mild paneer helps temper the Schezwan heat, so you can be generous with the sauce.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a hearty standalone meal with a cooling cucumber raita on the side.

variations.name: Mushroom Baby Corn Schezwan Rice
variations.description: An earthy, restaurant-style version loaded with meaty mushrooms and sweet baby corn that give the fiery rice a satisfying chew. The umami of the mushrooms deepens the Schezwan flavour, making this the most substantial and savoury of the takes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: sears the mushrooms hot and fast so they brown instead of stewing

steps: Cool 4 cups of cooked rice, slice 1.5 cups mushrooms, and halve 1 cup baby corn lengthwise.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a wok until very hot and sear the mushrooms on high heat for 3 minutes until browned and their water has evaporated.
Add the minced garlic and ginger and fry for 30 seconds, then add the baby corn and diced capsicum and stir-fry on high for 3 minutes.
Stir in 3.5 tbsp Schezwan sauce, 1 tbsp soy sauce, 0.5 tsp black pepper and 0.5 tsp salt and toss for 1 minute until glossy.
Add the cooled rice and toss vigorously on high heat for 3 minutes so the fiery sauce coats every grain.
