Sprinkle 1/2 tsp amchur and 1/2 tsp garam masala, toss well for 1 minute, and take off the heat.
Finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and serve hot.
tips: Cut the potatoes slightly smaller than the cauliflower so both finish cooking at the same time.
Resist stirring too often while the vegetables cook; frequent stirring breaks the florets and turns the sabzi mushy.
If the vegetables catch before softening, sprinkle a tablespoon of hot water down the side rather than stirring hard.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulkas or ajwain paratha, a bowl of curd and a lemon wedge for a simple homestyle lunch.

variations.name: Punjabi Dhaba Aloo Gobi Matar
variations.description: A robust dhaba-style version where the cauliflower is first seared in ghee, then the vegetables are folded through a bhuna onion-tomato masala with kasuri methi. Richer and more aromatic than the plain dry sabzi, it carries the smoky depth of a highway kitchen.

ingredients.name: Potatoes
ingredients.note: cut into wedges

ingredients.name: Cauliflower
ingredients.note: large florets

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee sears the gobi and gives the masala its dhaba aroma

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Kasuri methi
ingredients.note: crushed between the palms

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: julienned for garnish

steps: Melt 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide pan on medium-high heat and sear the cauliflower florets in a single layer for 5-6 minutes, turning once, until blistered brown; lift out and set aside.
In the same pan add the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add 2 chopped onions and fry 7-8 minutes until deep golden.

Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then add 2 chopped tomatoes with 1/2 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp Kashmiri red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and bhuno 5-6 minutes until the ghee separates.
Add the potato wedges, coat well, splash in 1/4 cup hot water, cover and cook on low heat for 10 minutes until the potatoes are halfway tender.
Return the seared cauliflower, add 3/4 cup green peas, fold gently, cover and cook for 10 minutes until all the vegetables are tender.
Uncover, raise the heat, and toss for 2 minutes to dry the masala so it clings to the vegetables.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi and sprinkle 1/2 tsp garam masala over the top, toss, and garnish with ginger juliennes before serving.
tips: Searing the gobi separately before it meets the masala is the dhaba secret that adds a smoky, browned edge.
Crush the kasuri methi only at the moment of adding so its perfume stays alive.
A final teaspoon of warm ghee spooned over the sabzi just before serving lifts the whole dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tandoori roti or laccha paratha, a mound of vinegared onions and a glass of lassi.

variations.name: Bengali Panch Phoron Aloo Gobi Matar
variations.description: A no-onion, no-garlic Bengali chorchori where the vegetables are tempered with the five-spice panch phoron in pungent mustard oil and finished with a ginger-tomato masala. A whisper of jaggery balances the heat, giving it a sweet-savoury warmth unlike the northern versions.

ingredients.name: Potatoes
ingredients.note: cut into thick fingers

ingredients.name: Cauliflower
ingredients.note: medium florets

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: kachi ghani pungency is the backbone of a Bengali chorchori

ingredients.name: Panch phoron
ingredients.note: the Bengali five-spice mix

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the traditional Bengali touch of sweetness, without refined sugar

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just smokes, then lower the heat and fry the cauliflower florets for 4-5 minutes until pale gold; lift out and set aside.
In the same oil temper 1 tsp panch phoron and 2 dry red chillies for 30 seconds until the seeds crackle and smell toasty.
Add 1 tbsp ginger paste and 2 slit green chillies for 1 minute, then add 2 chopped tomatoes with 1/2 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp cumin powder, 3/4 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt.
Cook the masala for 4-5 minutes until it thickens, then add the potato fingers, toss to coat, and cook covered on low heat for 8 minutes.
Return the fried cauliflower, add 3/4 cup green peas and 1/4 cup hot water, cover, and cook 10 minutes until all the vegetables are tender.
Uncover, stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, and toss on medium heat for 2-3 minutes until the sabzi is dry and glazed.
Finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and serve hot.
tips: Let the mustard oil reach its smoke point once before frying so its raw bitterness mellows.
Do not crush the panch phoron; the whole seeds tempered in hot oil are what give the dish its Bengali character.
Balance the jaggery to a gentle sweetness that rounds the mustard-oil pungency rather than dominating it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a dollop of ghee, or with soft luchis for a Sunday Bengali meal.

variations.name: Restaurant-Style Aloo Gobi Matar Masala
variations.description: A rich, semi-gravy restaurant take where the vegetables sit in a silky cashew-tomato masala finished with cream and butter. Glossier and more indulgent than the dry home version, it is the kind of aloo gobi matar you would scoop up with naan at a dinner table.

ingredients.name: Potatoes
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Cauliflower
ingredients.note: medium florets

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee for a restaurant-rich base and finish

ingredients.name: Cashews
ingredients.note: soaked and ground to a paste

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: pureed

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: pureed

ingredients.name: Kasuri methi
ingredients.note: crushed

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan and lightly fry the potato cubes and cauliflower florets for 5-6 minutes until golden at the edges; remove and set aside.
In the same pan add the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, add the onion puree and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, and bhuno on medium heat for 7-8 minutes until pale gold and the raw smell goes.
Add the tomato puree with 1/2 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp Kashmiri red chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook 6-7 minutes until the masala thickens and the ghee separates.
Stir in the cashew paste and cook 2 minutes, then add 1.25 cups hot water and bring to a gentle simmer to form a silky gravy.
Add the fried potatoes and cauliflower with 3/4 cup green peas, cover, and simmer on low heat for 12-14 minutes until the vegetables are tender and the gravy coats them.
Lower the heat and swirl in 3 tbsp cream, then crush 1 tsp kasuri methi and sprinkle 1/2 tsp garam masala over the top.
Warm through for 2 minutes without boiling hard, and serve with a swirl of cream on top.
tips: Grind the soaked cashews really smooth so the gravy turns silky rather than grainy.
Add the cream on low heat at the end and avoid a hard boil so it does not split.
Keep this one semi-gravy rather than dry; a little extra hot water gives the glossy restaurant finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan, garlic naan or jeera rice, garnished with cream and coriander for a dinner-party spread.

variations.name: Classic Luchi
variations.description: The soft, pale, pillowy fried bread of Bengal, made from fine white flour and fried at a gentle heat so it puffs milky-white rather than golden. Unlike a puri it stays tender and undyed, its surface smooth and matte. Fried in wood-pressed oil with a touch of ghee, luchi is the centrepiece of Bengali breakfasts and pujo feasts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rubbed into the flour as moyan, the ghee gives luchi its signature soft, short crumb

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: A pinch of unrefined sugar for the faint sweetness typical of Bengali luchi dough

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: Light wood-pressed oil that fries the luchi clean without colouring it dark

steps: Mix 2 cups maida with 1/2 tsp salt and 1/2 tsp Anveshan Khandsari, then rub in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until the flour resembles damp breadcrumbs.
Knead with about 0.6 cup warm water into a smooth, medium-firm dough that is softer than puri dough but not sticky; cover and rest 20-30 minutes.
Divide the dough into 16 small balls and keep them covered under a damp cloth so they do not form a skin.
Smear a little oil on the rolling surface and roll each ball into a 4-inch round about 2 mm thick, keeping the thickness even and avoiding dry flour so the luchi stays white.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Sunflower Oil in a kadhai to a moderate 165-170C, cooler than for puris, so the luchi puffs pale rather than browning.
Slide in one luchi and press it gently under the oil with a slotted spoon; it will balloon in a few seconds, so flip it, fry the second side for 10 seconds without letting it colour, and lift out.
Drain briefly and serve the luchis hot, soft and milky-white, straight from the kadhai.
tips: Fry at a lower temperature than puris; the whole charm of luchi is that it stays pale, not golden.
Never use dry flour for rolling, as loose flour burns and speckles the white surface with brown spots.
A generous ghee moyan keeps the luchi soft for hours, which is why it packs so well for outings.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the Bengali way with cholar dal, aloor dom or a simple begun bhaja, and rosogolla to finish.

variations.name: Radhaballavi
variations.description: The celebrated stuffed luchi of Bengal, its white shell hiding a spiced filling of ground urad dal fragrant with fennel, ginger and hing. Each bite gives way from soft crust to savoury, faintly sweet dal within. A Sunday-breakfast and festival favourite that turns the humble luchi into something festive.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Used as moyan in the dough and to cook the dal filling for a rich aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: Light wood-pressed oil for a clean fry that keeps the shell pale

steps: Soak 1/2 cup urad dal for 3 hours, drain, and grind to a thick coarse paste with 1 inch ginger and 2 green chillies, using minimal water.

Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, splutter 1/4 tsp hing and 1 tsp lightly crushed fennel for 20 seconds, then add the dal paste with 1/4 tsp salt and cook 4-5 minutes over low heat, stirring, until dry and crumbly; cool completely.
Mix 2 cups maida with 1/2 tsp salt, rub in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, and knead with about 0.6 cup warm water into a smooth, medium-firm dough; rest 20 minutes.
Divide the dough into 14 balls; flatten each into a small cup, place 1 tbsp of the cooled dal filling inside, gather the edges over it, and pinch shut, then flatten gently.
Roll each stuffed ball carefully into a 4-inch round about 3 mm thick with light strokes, using oil not flour, so the filling stays sealed inside.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Sunflower Oil to a moderate 170C and fry each radhaballavi, pressing until it puffs, then turning to fry both sides until just set and barely coloured, about 30 seconds.
Drain and serve the radhaballavi hot, cut open to show the fragrant dal centre.
tips: Cook the dal filling until it is dry and crumbly; a moist filling tears the dough and stops it puffing.
Grind the dal coarse and season it gently, as Bengali radhaballavi is mild and lightly sweet, not fiery.
Seal the seam well and roll with an even hand so the filling does not push through the delicate shell.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with cholar dal or a mildly spiced aloor dom, the classic Bengali stuffed-luchi breakfast pairing.

variations.name: Koraishutir Luchi
variations.description: A winter delicacy from Bengali homes, this luchi is stuffed with a sweet-savoury paste of fresh green peas spiced with ginger and green chilli. The bright pea filling stays moist and faintly sweet against the soft white shell, a seasonal treat made when the year's first peas arrive. Delicate, festive and unmistakably Bengali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Moyan for the dough and the fat used to cook the sweet pea filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: Light wood-pressed oil for a clean fry that keeps the shell pale and soft

steps: Blanch 1.5 cups fresh green peas for 2 minutes, drain, and coarsely grind with 1 inch ginger and 2 green chillies into a thick paste without adding water.

Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, splutter 1/2 tsp cumin and 1/4 tsp hing for 15 seconds, then add the pea paste with 1/4 tsp salt and saute 4-5 minutes over medium heat until it thickens into a dry, moldable filling; cool fully.
Mix 2 cups maida with 1/2 tsp salt, rub in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, and knead with about 0.6 cup warm water into a smooth, medium-firm dough; rest 20 minutes.
Divide into 14 balls; flatten each into a cup, spoon in 1 tbsp of the cooled pea filling, gather and pinch the edges shut, then press flat.
Roll each stuffed ball gently into a 4-inch round about 3 mm thick using oil, keeping the pressure light so the filling stays enclosed.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Sunflower Oil to a moderate 170C and fry each luchi, pressing until it puffs, then flipping to cook both sides until just set and pale, about 30 seconds.
Drain and serve the koraishutir luchi hot, when the sweet pea aroma is freshest.
tips: Dry the pea filling well on the heat; wet filling leaks and prevents the luchi from puffing.
Use tender fresh peas for the natural sweetness; older or frozen peas need a pinch of sugar to match.
Roll gently and seal firmly, as the moist pea paste is more prone to bursting than a dal filling.
variations.servingSuggestion: A winter favourite with aloor dom or a light dhonepata-flecked potato curry and a sweet tomato chutney.

variations.name: Atta Luchi
variations.description: The everyday wholemeal luchi of thrifty Bengali kitchens, made with nutty khapli wheat instead of white flour for an earthier, more filling bread. It fries a shade darker and tastes heartier than the pale classic, closer to a soft puri but with luchi's tender ghee-rich crumb. A wholesome daily version without the festival richness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Nutty wholemeal flour that gives the atta luchi its earthy flavour and body

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A generous moyan keeps the wholemeal luchi soft despite the heavier flour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: Light wood-pressed oil so the wholemeal luchi fries clean, not greasy

steps: Mix 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/2 tsp salt and 1/2 tsp nigella seeds, then rub in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until the flour turns crumbly.
Knead with about 3/4 cup warm water into a smooth, medium-firm dough, a little softer than puri dough; cover and rest 20 minutes.
Divide the dough into 16 small balls and keep them covered under a damp cloth.
Smear the surface with oil and roll each ball into a 4-inch round about 2-3 mm thick, using no dry flour so the surface stays smooth.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Sunflower Oil to about 175C, slightly hotter than for white luchi since the wholemeal dough needs a touch more heat to puff.
Fry each luchi, pressing gently under the oil until it balloons, then turning to fry the second side for 10-15 seconds until light golden.
Drain and serve the atta luchis hot; they are heartier than the white version and stay soft for a long while.
tips: Keep a generous ghee moyan, because wholemeal flour without enough fat gives a tough, dry luchi.
Fry a little hotter than white luchi so the denser dough puffs fully rather than staying flat.
These pack even better than white luchi for travel, holding their softness for hours.
variations.servingSuggestion: Everyday-perfect with a simple aloo-phulkopir dalna or begun bhaja, and a spoon of tomato-date chutney.

variations.name: Classic Sindhi Kadhi
variations.description: The Sunday ritual of Sindhi kitchens and, unlike other kadhis, made with no yogurt at all: besan is roasted golden in oil, then simmered with tamarind and a medley of vegetables into a tangy, brothy curry. Drumstick, okra and potato bob in a sauce that is sour, savoury and faintly sweet, traditionally poured over rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil roasts the besan to a deep nutty gold, the flavour foundation of the whole kadhi

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a spoon of jaggery rounds the tamarind's sourness into the signature Sindhi sweet-sour-tangy balance

steps: Shallow-fry 8 whole okra in 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil for 4-5 minutes until seared and no longer sticky, then set aside to keep them from making the kadhi slimy.

Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a heavy pot on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin and 0.5 tsp fenugreek seeds, add 12 curry leaves and 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, then tip in 0.5 cup besan and roast on low for 5-6 minutes, stirring, until it is deep golden and smells nutty.
Add 1 chopped tomato and cook 2 minutes, then pour in 4 cups hot water in a slow stream while whisking hard so the roasted besan does not form lumps.

Stir in 3 tbsp tamarind pulp, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp salt, bring to a boil, then add the drumstick fingers, cubed potato and cluster beans and simmer on medium-low for 18-20 minutes until the vegetables are tender.
Add the seared okra and 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and simmer 6-7 minutes more until the okra is cooked but still holds its shape and the kadhi thickens to a light, pourable curry.
Taste and adjust the tamarind and jaggery so the kadhi is boldly sour with a gentle sweet backnote, then rest 5 minutes off the heat before serving.
tips: Roast the besan patiently to a real golden brown; underroasted besan leaves the kadhi pasty and raw-tasting.
Sear the okra separately and add it late so it never turns slimy in the tangy broth.
Add the hot water in a thin stream while whisking to guarantee a lump-free curry every time.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the classic way over plain steamed rice with a side of aloo tuk (twice-fried potatoes) and sweet boondi, the traditional Sindhi kadhi-chawal spread.

variations.name: Bhee ji Kadhi (Lotus Stem Sindhi Kadhi)
variations.description: A prized Sindhi variation built around bhee — lotus stem — sliced into rounds that stay pleasantly crunchy in the tangy besan broth. Carom seeds in the tempering aid its digestion, and the earthy, fibrous lotus stem gives this kadhi a texture no vegetable version can match.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: neutral wood-pressed sunflower oil roasts the besan cleanly and lets the earthy lotus stem lead the flavour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery balances the tamarind into the classic Sindhi sweet-sour profile around the lotus stem

steps: Scrub 300 g lotus stem well, slice into thin rounds, and pressure cook with 1 cup water and 0.5 tsp salt for 3-4 whistles until just tender but still crunchy, since raw bhee stays fibrous otherwise.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sunflower Oil in a heavy pot on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin and 0.5 tsp ajwain seeds, add 12 curry leaves, 1.5 inch grated ginger and 3 slit green chillies, then stir in 0.5 cup besan and roast on low for 5-6 minutes to a nutty gold.
Add 1 chopped tomato, cook 2 minutes, then whisk in 4 cups hot water gradually so the besan stays smooth and lump-free.
Stir in 3 tbsp tamarind pulp, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, bring to a boil and simmer 10 minutes so the kadhi thickens lightly.
Add the cooked lotus stem rounds and 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and simmer 12-15 minutes so the bhee absorbs the tang while keeping its bite.
Adjust tamarind and jaggery to taste and rest the kadhi 5 minutes off the heat so the flavours settle before serving.
tips: Always pre-cook lotus stem before adding it to the kadhi; it stays woody if simmered raw in the broth alone.
Slice the bhee thin and evenly so every round softens to the same crunchy-tender point.
Carom seeds are traditional with lotus stem here — they cut its heaviness and make it easier to digest.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over steamed rice with a side of fried papad and mango pickle, letting the crunchy lotus stem be the star of the plate.

variations.name: Winter Sindhi Kadhi (Cauliflower & Carrot)
variations.description: The cold-season Sindhi kadhi that swaps in cauliflower, carrot and fresh green peas, with whole coriander and fennel toasted into the tempering for a warming aromatic lift. Sweeter from the winter vegetables and rounder in spice, it is the version made when the markets fill with fresh produce.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: groundnut oil roasts the besan and blooms the toasted whole spices for this warming winter kadhi

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery deepens the sweet-sour balance against the tamarind and the naturally sweet winter vegetables

steps: Toast 1 tbsp coriander seeds and 1 tsp fennel seeds on a dry pan for 90 seconds until fragrant, then crush them coarsely in a mortar.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a heavy pot on medium heat, crackle 0.75 tsp cumin, add 12 curry leaves, the crushed coriander-fennel and 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, then stir in 0.5 cup besan and roast on low for 5-6 minutes to a nutty gold.
Whisk in 4 cups hot water in a slow stream so the besan stays lump-free, then add 2.5 tbsp tamarind pulp, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.25 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp salt and bring to a boil.
Add the cauliflower florets and carrot cubes and simmer on medium-low for 12-14 minutes until they are just tender.
Stir in 0.5 cup green peas and 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and simmer 5-6 minutes more until the peas are soft and the kadhi thickens to a light curry.
Taste and balance the tamarind and jaggery, then rest 5 minutes off the heat so the toasted-spice aroma blooms before serving.
tips: Toast and coarsely crush the whole spices rather than using powders; the bursts of coriander and fennel define this winter version.
Do not overcook the cauliflower, or it disintegrates and clouds the broth; pull it the moment it turns fork-tender.
Fresh green peas taste sweeter than frozen here and are worth seeking out in season.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot steamed rice with a spoon of ghee and a side of crisp fried potatoes, ideal for a winter Sunday lunch.

variations.name: Palak-Arbi Sindhi Kadhi (Moringa Boost)
variations.description: A nourishing everyday take that stirs spinach and pan-crisped colocasia into the tangy kadhi and slips in a spoon of moringa for an extra green lift. Lighter on oil and heavier on greens, it turns the traditional Sunday indulgence into a wholesome weekday bowl.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: a lighter pour of wood-pressed sunflower oil keeps this greens-forward kadhi lean while still roasting the besan well

ingredients.name: Anveshan Moringa Powder
ingredients.note: a spoon of moringa deepens the green flavour and adds iron and nutrition to the everyday kadhi

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery balances the tamarind sourness into the Sindhi sweet-sour signature

steps: Pan-crisp the 6 boiled and halved colocasia pieces in 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Sunflower Oil for 4-5 minutes until golden at the cut faces, then set aside so they stay firm in the kadhi.

Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Sunflower Oil in a heavy pot on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin and 0.5 tsp fenugreek seeds, add 12 curry leaves and 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, then stir in 0.5 cup besan and roast on low for 5-6 minutes to a nutty gold.
Whisk in 4 cups hot water gradually to keep the besan smooth, then add 2.5 tbsp tamarind pulp, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.25 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp salt and bring to a boil.
Add 2 cups chopped spinach and the crisped colocasia and simmer on medium-low for 10-12 minutes until the spinach melts into the broth and the arbi is tender.
Dissolve 1 tsp Anveshan Moringa Powder in a little water and stir it in along with 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, then simmer 3-4 minutes more, keeping the heat gentle to protect the moringa.
Taste and adjust the tamarind and jaggery, then rest 5 minutes off the heat before serving this hearty green kadhi.
tips: Boil and crisp the colocasia before adding it, as raw arbi is fibrous and can irritate the throat if undercooked.
Stir the moringa into gently simmering, not boiling, kadhi to preserve its nutrients and fresh green note.
Squeeze a little lemon at the table if you want extra brightness against the earthy greens.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over brown rice or with a millet roti for a wholesome, greens-rich weekday meal, garnished with fresh coriander.

variations.name: Classic Marwari Ker Sangri
variations.description: The iconic dry sabzi of the Thar desert, made from sun-dried ker berries and sangri beans that are soaked, boiled and then slow-tempered in ghee with whole spices, dried red chillies and amchur. Studded with plump raisins for sweet relief, it is tangy, spicy and built to keep for days without refrigeration.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Marwari cooking is generous with ghee here, and bilona ghee blooms the whole spices and coats the sabzi so it keeps for days

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a whisper of jaggery rounds the sharp amchur sourness the way desert cooks balance this dry sabzi

steps: Soak 1 cup dried sangri and 0.5 cup dried ker separately in plenty of water overnight, then boil them together with 0.5 tsp salt and a pinch of turmeric for 12-15 minutes until softened; drain well and pat dry.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin and 0.5 tsp ajwain seeds, then add 4 broken dried red chillies and 0.25 tsp hing and fry for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Lower the heat, add 1 tbsp coriander powder, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp turmeric with a splash of water so the spices do not burn, and cook 30 seconds until they bloom into a paste.
Add the boiled ker and sangri with 0.75 tsp salt and toss on medium heat for 6-8 minutes, stirring often, until every piece is coated and lightly crisped at the edges.
Stir in 3 tbsp raisins, 1.5 tsp amchur and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook 3-4 minutes more until the raisins plump and the sabzi turns glossy and dry.
Rest off the heat for 5 minutes so the tangy-sweet flavours settle into the beans and berries before serving.
tips: Soaking overnight and boiling is essential; ker and sangri are intensely astringent and salty when under-prepared.
Keep the sabzi dry and well-coated in ghee — this is what lets authentic ker sangri travel for days without spoiling.
If the ker berries taste too sharp, add an extra teaspoon of raisins or jaggery to soften the tang.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature with bajra roti and a dollop of ghee, or pack it for travel alongside plain parathas the way Marwari families do.

variations.name: Dahi-wali Ker Sangri
variations.description: A softer, gravied Marwari version where the boiled ker and sangri are simmered in a whisked-yogurt masala into a semi-dry, tangy sabzi. The dahi mellows the astringency and gives a creamy coating, making this the more forgiving, home-style face of the desert classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: pungent kachi ghani mustard oil is the traditional fat for the dahi-based Marwari sabzi and stands up to the sour yogurt

steps: Soak 1 cup sangri and 0.5 cup ker separately overnight, then boil together with 0.5 tsp salt for 12-15 minutes until tender; drain and set aside.
Whisk 0.75 cup yogurt smooth with 1 tbsp besan, 1 tbsp coriander powder, 1.25 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp turmeric into a lump-free masala paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just smokes, cool it 30 seconds, then crackle 1 tsp cumin and 1 tsp fennel seeds with 3 broken dried red chillies and 0.25 tsp hing.
Lower the heat and pour in the whisked yogurt masala, stirring continuously for 4-5 minutes so it does not split, until it thickens and the raw besan smell disappears.
Add the boiled ker and sangri with 0.75 tsp salt and 0.5 cup water and simmer on medium-low for 8-10 minutes until the sabzi turns semi-dry and the beans soak up the tangy gravy.
Cook off any excess moisture in the last 2 minutes so the yogurt masala clings to each piece, then rest 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Always add the yogurt masala off high heat and keep stirring, or it curdles into grainy strands.
The dahi tames the astringency of ker beautifully, so this version needs no amchur or jaggery for balance.
Keep a little gravy in this one; unlike the dry classic, it is meant to be slightly saucy for scooping with roti.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with soft phulkas or missi roti and a side of sliced onion and green chilli.

variations.name: Panchkuta (Five-Ingredient Rajasthani Ker Sangri)
variations.description: The festive Marwari panchkuta, where ker and sangri join kumatiya seeds and dried gunda berries in the classic five-wild-ingredient medley of the desert. Cooked in mustard oil with a tangy amchur finish and a touch of jaggery, it is the ceremonial version served at weddings and made to last for weeks.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: mustard oil is the authentic panchkuta fat, its pungency preserving the sabzi for the weeks it is meant to last

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery balances the amchur and the astringent wild berries in this ceremonial medley

steps: Soak 0.75 cup sangri, 0.5 cup ker, 3 tbsp kumatiya seeds and 3 tbsp dried gunda separately overnight, then boil them all together with 0.5 tsp salt and a pinch of turmeric for 15-18 minutes until softened; drain thoroughly.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just smokes, cool it 30 seconds, then crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds with 5 broken dried red chillies and a generous 0.5 tsp hing.
Lower the heat, add 1 tbsp coriander powder, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp turmeric with a splash of water, and cook 30 seconds until the spices bloom.
Add the boiled five-ingredient medley with 1 tsp salt and toss on medium heat for 8-10 minutes, stirring often, until everything is well coated and the surfaces catch a little colour.
Sprinkle in 2 tsp amchur and 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook 3-4 minutes more until the sabzi is dry, glossy and boldly tangy.
Rest the panchkuta off the heat for 10 minutes so the wild berries absorb the masala fully before serving.
tips: Kumatiya seeds are the sharpest of the five, so give them a slightly longer soak and boil to mellow their bitterness.
Panchkuta is cooked deliberately dry with plenty of mustard oil, which is what lets it keep for two to three weeks.
Gunda berries can be sticky; boil them until they release their seeds and turn tender before adding to the pan.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at festive Marwari meals with bajra or makki roti, ghee and a bowl of kadhi, or carry it on journeys as it keeps for weeks.

variations.name: Achari Ker Sangri with Cashew (Party-style)
variations.description: A richer, celebratory rendition finished with a panch phoran pickle-spice tempering, fried cashews and raisins, and a kasuri methi lift. The pickling spices and nutty crunch dress the humble desert sabzi up for a dinner-party table while keeping its trademark tangy backbone.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee fries the cashews golden and carries the pickle-spice tempering for this party-style version

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery balances the achari tang and the amchur into a rounded sweet-sour finish

steps: Soak 1 cup sangri and 0.5 cup ker separately overnight, then boil together with 0.5 tsp salt for 12-15 minutes until tender and drain well.

Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat and fry 3 tbsp cashews until golden, then lift them out and in the same ghee crackle 1 tbsp panch phoran with 3 dried red chillies and 0.25 tsp hing for 30 seconds.
Lower the heat, add 1 tbsp coriander powder, 1.25 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp turmeric with a splash of water, and cook 30 seconds until the pickling spices bloom aromatic.
Add the boiled ker and sangri with 0.75 tsp salt and toss on medium heat for 6-8 minutes until well coated and lightly crisped.
Stir in 2 tbsp raisins, 1.5 tsp amchur, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi and cook 3 minutes until glossy and dry.
Fold the fried cashews back in, rest 5 minutes off the heat, and serve the sabzi crowned with the nutty crunch.
tips: Fry the cashews first and add them back at the very end so they stay crisp against the soft beans.
Panch phoran is the achari signature here; toast it just until it splutters, as over-frying turns the fenugreek in it bitter.
Crush the kasuri methi between your palms as it goes in to release its full aroma into the rich sabzi.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a special-occasion side with lachha paratha or missi roti, garnished with extra fried cashews and a wedge of lemon.

variations.name: Classic Aloo Posto
variations.description: The quintessential Bengali comfort dish: diced potatoes cooked in a generous poppy-seed paste until the posto clings to every piece in a soft, nutty coating. Slit green chillies and a nigella tempering in mustard oil give it its clean, homely bite, and a raw drizzle of mustard oil at the end keeps it unmistakably Bengali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed kachi ghani oil, half cooked and half drizzled raw, is what makes posto taste of Bengal

steps: Soak 5 tbsp poppy seeds in warm water for 20 minutes, then grind them with 2 green chillies and a splash of water into a thick, smooth, creamy paste with no visible grains.
Peel and dice 4 medium potatoes into 1/2 inch cubes. Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai until it just smokes, then lower the heat and let it cool for 20 seconds to mellow.
Crackle 1/2 tsp nigella seeds and 2 slit green chillies in the oil for 20 seconds, then add the potato cubes and 1/2 tsp turmeric and fry on medium heat for 5 minutes until the edges turn pale gold.
Pour in 1 cup water with 1 tsp salt, cover, and simmer on medium-low for 8 to 10 minutes until the potatoes are just tender and most of the water has gone.
Stir in the poppy paste and cook uncovered on low heat for 5 minutes, folding gently, until the posto turns thick and coats the potatoes and the oil beads at the edges.
Switch off the heat, drizzle the remaining 1 tbsp raw Anveshan Mustard Oil over the top, cover, and rest for 3 minutes so the pungency perfumes the dish before serving.
tips: Grind the poppy seeds with as little water as possible into a genuinely smooth paste; grainy posto never develops its signature creamy cling.
The final raw drizzle of mustard oil is essential and non-negotiable, since cooking would strip the pungent aroma that defines aloo posto.
Keep the flame low once the paste is in; poppy scorches quickly and a browned paste turns the pale dish bitter and grey.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steaming rice and a spoon of ghee, or alongside a bowl of thin masoor dal for the archetypal Bengali summer lunch.

variations.name: Aloo Peyaj Posto
variations.description: The East Bengal household take stirs sliced onions into the posto, browning them first so the dish gains a sweet, savoury depth the classic does not have. Dried red chilli replaces the nigella temper, giving a warmer heat, and the result is a heartier, faintly caramel posto meant to be mashed into rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: browning onions in pungent wood-pressed oil builds the sweet-savoury base of this Bangal version

steps: Soak 4 tbsp poppy seeds in warm water for 20 minutes and grind them with 2 green chillies to a smooth, thick paste. Peel and cube 3 potatoes and thinly slice 2 onions.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the flame, and crackle 2 dried red chillies for 15 seconds until they darken and smell toasty.
Add the sliced onions and fry on medium heat for 6 to 7 minutes, stirring often, until they turn soft and golden brown at the edges, building the sweet base of the dish.
Add the potato cubes, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 slit green chilli, and fry for 4 minutes, then pour in 3/4 cup water with 1 tsp salt, cover, and simmer for 8 minutes until the potatoes are tender.
Stir in the poppy paste and cook uncovered on low for 5 minutes, folding until the posto thickens, darkens slightly from the onions and clings to every piece.
Drop in the last slit green chilli, cover, and rest 3 minutes off the heat so the onion-sweetened posto settles before serving.
tips: Take the onions to a proper golden brown, not just translucent; their caramel is the whole point of the peyaj version.
Slightly less poppy is needed here since the onions add their own body to the coating.
If the posto tastes flat, a extra slit green chilli mashed in at the end sharpens the onion sweetness beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best with plain rice and a wedge of lime, or tucked into a folded roti as a quick, satisfying lunch wrap.

variations.name: Aloo Jhinge Posto
variations.description: A summer favourite pairing potato with jhinge (ridge gourd), whose watery flesh melts into the poppy paste and keeps the dish light and juicy. A little fresh coconut ground into the posto rounds it out, making this the most tender and delicate of the posto family.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: its sharpness lifts the mild ridge gourd and keeps this juicy posto from tasting flat

steps: Peel 2 ridge gourds and cut into batons, dice 2 potatoes small, and grind 4 tbsp soaked poppy seeds with 3 tbsp fresh grated coconut and 2 green chillies into a smooth paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it smokes, lower the heat, and crackle 1/2 tsp nigella seeds with 1 slit green chilli for 20 seconds.
Add the potato cubes and 1/4 tsp turmeric and fry on medium for 4 minutes, then add the ridge gourd batons and cook 3 minutes until they begin to release their water.
Cover and cook on medium-low for 6 to 8 minutes with 1 tsp salt, letting the ridge gourd's own moisture steam everything soft; add a splash of water only if the pan runs dry.
Stir in the coconut-poppy paste and simmer uncovered on low for 5 minutes until the posto thickens into a juicy, pale coating around the vegetables.
Finish with the last 1 tbsp raw Anveshan Mustard Oil drizzled over, rest 3 minutes covered, and serve while still moist.
tips: Ridge gourd throws off a lot of water, so hold back on added liquid or the posto will turn soupy instead of clinging.
Add the ridge gourd after the potatoes have a head start, since it cooks far faster and would otherwise collapse.
The coconut is what balances the ridge gourd's mildness, so grind it fresh rather than reaching for desiccated.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over gobindobhog rice as a light monsoon lunch, with a side of crisp fried bori for contrast.

variations.name: Kancha Posto Bata
variations.description: The purist's posto, where boiled potatoes are dressed in a completely raw, uncooked poppy-and-green-chilli paste whipped with mustard oil, never touching the flame. This kancha (raw) style is startlingly fresh and pungent, closer to a Bengali chutney-coated potato than a cooked curry, and is prized in summer for its cooling simplicity.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: used entirely raw here, whisked cold into the paste so its full pungency stays intact

steps: Boil 4 potatoes whole with their skins until just tender, about 15 minutes, then cool, peel, and break them into rough bite-size chunks by hand rather than cutting.
Soak 5 tbsp poppy seeds in warm water for 20 minutes, then grind them with 4 green chillies, 1 tsp salt and only 2 tbsp water into a very thick, smooth, luminous white paste.
Scrape the paste into a bowl and beat in 2.5 tbsp raw Anveshan Mustard Oil a little at a time with a spoon, whisking until the paste turns glossy and pale and smells sharply of mustard.
Fold the warm potato chunks through the raw paste gently so each piece is thickly coated but stays intact, then mix in 3 tbsp chopped coriander.
Slit the last green chilli and press it into the top, drizzle over the remaining 1/2 tbsp raw mustard oil, and let it sit 10 minutes for the flavours to bloom.
Serve at room temperature, never reheated, so the raw posto keeps its fresh, pungent character.
tips: Do not cook this posto at all after mixing; heat is what would flatten the whole point of the raw kancha style.
Beat the mustard oil in gradually like a dressing so it emulsifies into the paste rather than pooling separately.
Break the potatoes by hand for craggy edges that grab far more paste than clean knife cuts would.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a cooling side with a mound of plain rice and a bowl of chilled masoor dal on a hot summer afternoon.

variations.name: Classic Bihari Anarsa
variations.description: Anarsa is a festive fried sweet from Bihar and Maharashtra made from fermented ground rice and jaggery, coated in sesame seeds. The batter rests for days to develop its signature honeycomb interior and crisp lacy edges that puff up in hot ghee.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the traditional sweetener that ferments with the rice to give anarsa its flavour and colour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: worked into the dough and used to shallow-fry the anarsa to a lacy crisp

steps: Soak 1 cup raw rice in water for 3 days, changing the water daily, then drain and spread it on a cloth to dry in the shade for 2 hours.
Grind the semi-dry rice to a fine flour and mix it with 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.5 tsp cardamom into a stiff dough, adding 2 tbsp milk if needed.
Rub 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee into the dough, cover it, and let it rest and ferment for 6 to 8 hours at room temperature until slightly aromatic.
Pinch small balls, press each onto a sesame-sprinkled sheet, and pat into a flat disc so one side is coated in 0.33 cup white sesame seeds.
Heat oil with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee to a medium-low temperature and slide in the anarsa sesame-side up, without disturbing, letting it puff and rise.
Fry gently for 3 to 4 minutes, spooning hot oil over the top, until the edges turn golden and lacy, then drain on a rack.
tips: Do not flip the anarsa repeatedly; let it set and puff undisturbed or it will disintegrate in the oil.
The dough must rest long enough to ferment slightly, which is what creates the airy honeycomb texture.
Fry one test piece first; if it spreads, knead in a little rice flour to firm the dough.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the crisp sesame-studded anarsa during Diwali or Lakshmi Puja, stacked on a brass plate.

variations.name: Poppy Seed Anarsa
variations.description: The Maharashtrian anarse rolls the discs in khus khus poppy seeds instead of sesame, giving a nuttier crunch and paler crust. This version leans a touch softer inside and is a staple of the Diwali faral platter.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: ferments with the rice flour to build the anarsa's deep sweetness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: enriches the dough and fries the discs to a delicate crisp

steps: Soak 1 cup raw rice for 3 days, refreshing the water daily, then drain and dry in the shade for 2 hours.
Grind to a fine flour and combine with 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.5 tsp cardamom into a firm dough, loosening with 2 tbsp milk only if needed.
Work in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then cover and ferment the dough for 8 hours until faintly sour and pliable.
Shape small balls and press each into 0.33 cup white poppy seeds so one face is fully coated, patting into a thin disc.
Heat oil with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee to medium-low and lower the anarsa in poppy-side up, letting it puff without stirring.
Fry for 3 to 4 minutes, basting with hot oil, until pale gold and crisp at the edges, then lift onto a rack to drain.
tips: Poppy seeds brown faster than sesame, so keep the oil a shade cooler to avoid a scorched crust.
Rest the dough overnight for the best puff, as under-fermented dough fries flat and dense.
Handle the discs gently; poppy-coated anarse are more delicate than the sesame version.
variations.servingSuggestion: Include these on the Diwali faral thali alongside chakli and shankarpali for a classic Maharashtrian spread.

variations.name: Instant Rice Flour Anarsa
variations.description: A same-day anarsa that skips the multi-day rice soak by using ready rice flour lightly fermented with yogurt. It captures the sesame crust and jaggery sweetness for cooks who cannot plan days ahead.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted into a syrup to sweeten and bind the instant dough

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: softens the dough and shallow-fries the anarsa golden

steps: Melt 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water into a thick syrup over low heat and strain out any grit.
Mix the warm syrup into 1.5 cups rice flour with 3 tbsp yogurt, 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 0.5 tsp cardamom to form a soft dough.
Cover and rest the dough in a warm spot for 2 to 3 hours so the yogurt lends a gentle tang and lift.
Pinch balls and press each into 0.33 cup sesame seeds, patting into thin discs on a greased sheet.
Heat oil with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee to medium-low and slide the anarsa in sesame-side up without disturbing.
Fry for 3 minutes, basting with hot oil, until the edges crisp and turn golden, then drain on a rack.
tips: The yogurt shortcut will not puff as dramatically as fermented rice, but gives a pleasant crisp all the same.
Keep the dough soft; a stiff instant dough fries hard rather than lacy.
Fry a test disc and adjust with a spoon of rice flour if the dough spreads too much.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these same-day anarsa fresh and warm, a quick fix when festival prep runs short on time.

variations.name: Coconut Anarsa
variations.description: A coastal variation that folds desiccated coconut into the fermented rice dough for a fragrant, chewy centre. Fried in coconut oil and rolled in sesame, it carries a distinct tropical aroma over the classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the fermented rice and coconut dough with caramel depth

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: fries the anarsa and reinforces the tropical coconut aroma

steps: Soak 1 cup raw rice for 3 days with daily water changes, then drain and shade-dry for 2 hours before grinding to a fine flour.
Mix the flour with 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 0.5 cup desiccated coconut and 0.5 tsp cardamom into a firm dough, adding 2 tbsp milk as needed.
Work in 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, cover, and ferment the dough for 8 hours until aromatic.
Shape balls and press each into 0.33 cup sesame seeds, patting into thin discs on a greased surface.
Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil with a little frying oil to medium-low and lower the anarsa in sesame-side up.
Fry undisturbed for 3 to 4 minutes, basting with hot oil, until golden and crisp-edged, then drain well.
tips: Toast the desiccated coconut lightly before adding for a deeper aroma and to remove excess moisture.
Coconut in the dough makes it richer, so keep the frying temperature gentle to avoid quick browning.
Let the fried anarsa cool fully so the coconut centre firms to a pleasant chew.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the coconut anarsa with filter coffee for a coastal-style festive snack.

variations.name: Classic Hyderabadi Bagara Baingan
variations.description: The iconic Hyderabadi curry of baby brinjals bathed in a luxurious gravy of roasted peanuts, sesame, coconut and tamarind. The nut paste is cooked down until the oil glistens, then the fried brinjals soak up the tangy, nutty sauce, making the classic accompaniment to Hyderabadi bagara khana and biryani.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: the traditional til oil that fries the brinjals and carries the nutty Hyderabadi gravy

steps: Dry-roast 4 tbsp peanuts, 2 tbsp sesame seeds and 3 tbsp coconut separately on low until golden, then grind with 1 chopped onion and a little water to a smooth paste.
Slit the 10 brinjals into a cross keeping the stems on, and shallow-fry in 5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil for 5 minutes until the skins blister; lift out and set aside.
In the same oil add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 12 curry leaves, let them splutter for 15 seconds, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry 1 minute.
Add the ground peanut-sesame-coconut paste with 1.5 tsp chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt and cook on medium for 7 minutes until the oil surfaces at the edges.
Stir in 1.5 tsp tamarind paste and 2 cups hot water, bring to a gentle simmer, then slide in the fried brinjals and spoon the gravy over them.
Cover and simmer on low for 15 minutes until the brinjals are meltingly soft and the gravy thickens and turns glossy, then rest 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Roast the peanuts, sesame and coconut separately so each browns evenly without any turning bitter.
Keep the heat low once the brinjals are in the gravy so they cook through without breaking apart.
The gravy thickens as it rests, so keep it a touch thinner and adjust with hot water before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bagara khana, plain steamed rice or as the classic side to a Hyderabadi vegetable biryani.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Bagara Baingan
variations.description: A fiery, coconut-free Andhra rendition where the gravy is built on dry-roasted peanuts, coriander and cumin seeds with a bold hit of red chilli. Sharper and hotter than the Hyderabadi original, it leans on freshly ground whole spices and tamarind for a rustic, intensely savoury heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the wood-pressed oil that fries the brinjals and cooks this fiery Andhra gravy

steps: Dry-roast 5 tbsp peanuts, 1.5 tbsp coriander seeds, 1 tsp cumin seeds and 5 dried red chillies on low for 3 minutes until fragrant, then grind to a coarse paste with 1 chopped onion and 6 garlic cloves.
Slit the 10 brinjals into a cross keeping the stems on, and shallow-fry in 5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil for 5 minutes until blistered; lift out and set aside.
In the same oil add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 15 curry leaves, let them crackle for 15 seconds.
Add the ground spicy peanut paste with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt and cook on medium for 7 minutes, stirring, until it darkens and the oil surfaces.
Stir in 2 tsp tamarind paste and 2 cups hot water, bring to a simmer, then slide in the fried brinjals.
Cover and simmer on low for 15 minutes until the brinjals are soft and the gravy is thick, dark and fiery, then rest 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Adjust the number of dried red chillies to your heat tolerance, as this Andhra version is meant to be hot.
Grind the roasted spices coarse rather than silky for a rustic, textured gravy.
More tamarind balances the chilli heat, so taste and add a little extra if it feels too sharp.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain rice and a spoon of ghee, or with ragi mudde to temper the fiery gravy.

variations.name: Shahi Cashew-Poppy Bagara Baingan
variations.description: A regal, mild reinterpretation from the nizami kitchens where the brinjals rest in a pale, creamy gravy of cashews, poppy seeds and cream instead of peanuts and tamarind. Fragrant with cardamom and finished with saffron, this white bagara baingan is the elegant banquet version for special occasions.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the rich fat that fries the brinjals and gives the shahi white gravy its nizami depth

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk to give the shahi gravy its golden fragrance and colour

steps: Soak 15 cashews and 1.5 tbsp poppy seeds in warm water for 15 minutes, then grind with 2 boiled onions and 3 green chillies to a smooth pale paste; steep a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk.
Slit the 10 brinjals into a cross keeping the stems on, and shallow-fry in 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee for 5 minutes until softened; lift out and set aside.
In the same ghee crackle 4 cardamom and the 1 inch cinnamon for 20 seconds, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the cashew-poppy-onion paste and cook on medium-low for 8 minutes, stirring often, until it no longer smells raw and the ghee separates, keeping it pale.
Add 0.5 tsp white pepper, 1.25 tsp salt and 1.5 cups hot water, bring to a gentle simmer, then slide in the fried brinjals.
Cover and simmer on low for 12 minutes, then stir in 3 tbsp cream and the saffron milk off the boil, warm through for 2 minutes and serve.
tips: Boil the onions before grinding to keep the gravy pale and free of any sharp raw-onion bite.
Add the cream and saffron milk off the heat so the shahi gravy stays smooth and does not split.
Keep the spicing gentle and aromatic, as this version is about elegance rather than heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with saffron pulao, sheermal or rumali roti for a festive nizami spread, garnished with slivered cashews.

variations.name: Til-Gud Dry Bagara Baingan
variations.description: A semi-dry, sweet-savoury take where the brinjals are coated in a thick roasted sesame and peanut masala loosened with just a little tamarind and jaggery, leaving almost no gravy. The nutty coating clings to each glossy brinjal, making it a rich dry side rather than a pool of curry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: the nutty oil that cooks the brinjals and deepens the roasted til coating

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: brings the sweet-savoury til-gud balance to this semi-dry coating

steps: Dry-roast 4 tbsp sesame seeds on low until golden and popping, then grind with 2 tbsp roasted peanuts and 5 garlic cloves to a coarse thick paste.
Slit the 10 brinjals into a cross keeping the stems on and shallow-fry in 4 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil for 6 minutes until softened; lift out and set aside.
In the same oil add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 12 curry leaves, let them splutter for 15 seconds.
Add the ground sesame-peanut paste with 1.5 tsp chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt and roast on medium for 4 minutes until thick and fragrant.
Stir in 1 tsp tamarind paste, 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and just 0.5 cup hot water, then return the fried brinjals and toss to coat.
Cover and cook on low for 12 minutes, turning gently, until the brinjals are soft and wrapped in a thick sticky coating with almost no gravy left, then serve.
tips: Roast the sesame just until it turns golden and starts popping, as over-roasting makes it bitter.
Keep the water minimal so the masala stays as a thick clinging coating rather than a gravy.
Balance the jaggery and tamarind at the end so the coating finishes sweet, sour and nutty together.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a rich dry side with jowar bhakri or plain rice and a bowl of curd to cool the palate.

variations.name: Classic Balushahi
variations.description: Balushahi is a North Indian glazed sweet, cousin to the doughnut, made from a ghee-rich flour dough that is fried slowly on low heat until flaky, then dipped in sugar syrup. The trademark crack on top and crisp-yet-crumbly interior come from resting the dough and frying it gently.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: rubbed into the flour as moyan to create the flaky, crumbly layers

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: cooked to a one-thread syrup that glazes the fried balushahi

steps: Rub 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee into 2 cups maida with 0.25 tsp baking soda until the mixture resembles breadcrumbs and holds shape when pressed.
Add 0.25 cup yogurt and just enough water to bring it into a soft dough; do not knead, gather it gently and rest it covered for 20 minutes.
Divide the dough into 12 balls, shaping each smooth and pressing a small dimple in the centre with your thumb.
Heat Anveshan Ghee or oil for frying to a low temperature and slide in the balushahi; fry very slowly for 12 to 15 minutes, turning, until pale golden and flaky throughout.
Meanwhile boil 1.5 cups Anveshan Khandsari with 0.75 cup water and 0.5 tsp cardamom to a sticky one-thread syrup.
Drain the fried balushahi, soak them in the warm syrup for 5 minutes until glazed, then lift out, garnish with 2 tbsp slivered pistachios, and dry on a rack.
tips: Fry on the lowest heat possible; high heat browns the outside while leaving the centre raw and doughy.
The syrup should be warm, not hot, when you dip, so the glaze crystallises into a delicate white coat.
Rest the dough and avoid kneading, as overworking develops gluten and makes the balushahi hard.
variations.servingSuggestion: Let the glaze set for an hour, then serve these flaky glazed sweets at festivals alongside a cup of chai.

variations.name: Khoya Balushahi
variations.description: A richer halwai-style balushahi where khoya is worked into the dough for an extra-soft, melt-in-mouth crumb. This wedding-favourite version is denser and more indulgent than the everyday one, holding the syrup glaze beautifully.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the moyan that combines with khoya for an especially tender, flaky crumb

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: boiled to a one-thread glaze for the rich khoya sweets

steps: Rub 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee and 0.5 cup grated khoya into 2 cups maida with 0.25 tsp baking soda until crumbly and evenly combined.
Bind gently with 3 tbsp yogurt and a splash of water into a soft dough, then rest it covered for 25 minutes without kneading.
Shape into 12 balls, each with a thumb dimple, keeping the surface smooth to prevent cracking while frying.
Fry in low-heat ghee or oil for 14 minutes, turning gently, until pale gold and cooked to the centre.
Boil 1.5 cups Anveshan Khandsari with 0.75 cup water and a pinch of saffron to a one-thread syrup.
Soak the fried balushahi in the warm saffron syrup for 6 minutes, then rest on a rack so the glaze sets into a soft crust.
tips: Ensure the khoya is fresh and soft; dry khoya makes the dough stiff and hard to shape.
Because khoya dough browns faster, keep the heat even lower and be patient with the fry.
These stay soft for days in an airtight box, actually improving a day after the syrup soaks in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the saffron-glazed balushahi at weddings, topped with a few strands of saffron for a regal look.

variations.name: Whole Wheat Jaggery Balushahi
variations.description: A wholesome reinvention using nutty khapli atta instead of maida and a jaggery glaze in place of white sugar. It trades pale delicacy for a deeper, earthier balushahi that still fries up flaky and satisfying.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: ancient wheat flour that gives the balushahi a nutty depth and wholesome bite

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the moyan rubbed into the atta for flakiness despite the heavier flour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: cooked to a one-thread syrup for an earthy caramel glaze

steps: Rub 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.25 tsp baking soda until it clumps when pressed.
Bind with 0.25 cup yogurt and a little water into a soft dough, mixing in 0.5 tsp crushed fennel, then rest it 20 minutes.
Shape into 12 dimpled balls, keeping them slightly smaller since wheat dough is denser than maida.
Fry on low heat in ghee or oil for 15 minutes, turning often, until deep golden and cooked through to the middle.
Melt 1.25 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 0.75 cup water, strain, and cook to a sticky one-thread syrup.
Dip the fried balushahi in the warm jaggery syrup for 6 minutes, garnish with 2 tbsp chopped almonds, and dry on a rack.
tips: Khapli atta absorbs more moisture, so add water slowly to avoid a stiff, cracking dough.
Crushed fennel cuts the richness of the jaggery and adds a lovely aromatic note.
Jaggery glaze stays slightly sticky rather than crystallising white, which is normal for this version.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these earthy balushahi warm in winter with a glass of jaggery-sweetened milk.

variations.name: Classic Basundi
variations.description: The Gujarati and Maharashtrian reduced-milk sweet, thinner and more pourable than rabri, simmered with a few strands of saffron until it turns a pale cream. Studded with charoli and slivered nuts and scented with cardamom and nutmeg, it is the festive dessert of Diwali and family feasts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: khandsari keeps the basundi pale cream and lightly sweet, letting the saffron and nutmeg shine

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: pure saffron steeped in warm milk gives basundi its soft golden tint and aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a little bilona ghee toasts the charoli and almond garnish for the finished basundi

steps: Steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk, and pour 6 cups full-fat milk into a wide heavy kadhai.
Bring the milk to a boil, then simmer on medium-low for about 35 minutes, stirring frequently and scraping the sides so the malai keeps blending back into the milk.
Continue until the milk reduces to a little more than half its volume and turns a thick but still pourable, pale cream basundi.
Stir in 1/3 cup Anveshan Khandsari and the saffron milk and simmer for 5 minutes until dissolved and lightly thickened.
Toast 2 tbsp charoli, 12 slivered almonds and 10 pistachios in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee for 1 minute, then stir most of them in with 1/2 tsp cardamom powder and 1/8 tsp nutmeg powder.
Garnish with the reserved nuts, chill the basundi for 3 hours, and serve cold.
tips: Unlike rabri, keep basundi stirred so the malai blends back in, giving a smooth pourable texture rather than ribbons.
Stop reducing while the basundi still coats a spoon thinly, as it thickens noticeably once chilled.
The pinch of nutmeg is the Gujarati signature that distinguishes basundi from a plain reduced milk.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled in small bowls or glasses topped with charoli and slivered nuts, traditionally paired with hot pooris at a festive Gujarati meal.

variations.name: Sitaphal Basundi
variations.description: A seasonal Maharashtrian favourite where sweet, fragrant custard apple pulp is folded into cooled basundi for a heavenly perfume and creamy texture. Made only in the short sitaphal season, it is a treasured winter dessert quite unlike the plain saffron version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: less khandsari is used since the ripe custard apple lends plenty of natural sweetness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee toasts the pistachio garnish for the fruity basundi

steps: Pour 6 cups full-fat milk into a wide kadhai, bring to a boil, then simmer on medium-low for about 35 minutes, stirring, until it reduces to a thick, pourable basundi.
Stir in 1/4 cup Anveshan Khandsari, 1/2 tsp cardamom powder and 1/8 tsp nutmeg powder and simmer for 4 minutes until dissolved.
Take the pan off the heat and cool the basundi completely to room temperature, then chill it until cold.
Meanwhile deseed ripe custard apples to get 1 cup smooth pulp, discarding every hard black seed.
Gently fold the custard apple pulp into the cold basundi, mixing only until combined so the fruit stays fragrant and fresh.
Toast 12 pistachios and 10 slivered almonds in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee for 1 minute, fold half in, and garnish with the rest before serving.
tips: Fold the custard apple into fully cold basundi only, as adding it to warm milk can turn the pulp bitter and split the milk.
Remove every seed carefully, since even one crushed custard apple seed makes the dessert taste bitter.
Serve this the same day, as custard apple loses its delicate aroma if stored too long.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve well chilled in glasses topped with pistachios, a prized seasonal treat during the short winter custard apple season.

variations.name: Angoor Basundi
variations.description: A celebratory version where tiny soft chhena dumplings, like miniature rasgullas, are simmered and suspended in the saffron basundi. The little spongy 'angoor' balls soak up the sweet milk, giving a delightful two-textured dessert for weddings and special occasions.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: khandsari sweetens both the sugar syrup for the chhena balls and the basundi itself

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: pure saffron colours the basundi gold, making the white chhena balls stand out like little grapes

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee toasts the pistachio garnish for the finished angoor basundi

steps: Boil 3 cups milk for chhena, add 2 tbsp lemon juice off the heat to curdle it, then strain the chhena through muslin, rinse and squeeze, and knead it smooth for 5 minutes before rolling into 20 tiny marble-sized balls.

Make a light syrup by boiling 3 cups water with 1/4 cup Anveshan Khandsari, drop in the chhena balls, cover, and simmer for 12 minutes until they swell and turn spongy, then cool and gently squeeze out the syrup.
Separately, simmer 5 cups full-fat milk in a wide kadhai for about 30 minutes, stirring, until it reduces to a thick pourable basundi, and steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk.
Stir the remaining 1/4 cup Anveshan Khandsari, the saffron milk and 1/2 tsp cardamom powder into the basundi and simmer for 4 minutes.
Slip the drained chhena balls gently into the warm basundi and simmer for 3 minutes so they soak up the sweet milk.
Cool and chill for 3 hours, then serve topped with 12 pistachios toasted in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee.
tips: Knead the chhena until smooth and non-grainy, or the little balls will crack while simmering.
Keep the chhena balls small, as they double in size in the syrup and should stay grape-like in the basundi.
Squeeze the balls free of syrup before adding them to the basundi so they drink up the flavoured milk instead.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled with several chhena balls in each bowl and a scatter of pistachios, a showstopper dessert for a wedding feast.

variations.name: Gur Basundi
variations.description: A wholesome unrefined take where the reduced milk is sweetened with jaggery, deepening the basundi to a warm honey-brown with an earthy caramel note. Finished with roasted dry fruits and a hint of dry ginger, it is a nourishing winter version of the Gujarati classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery deepens the basundi to a honey-brown and lends an earthy caramel sweetness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee roasts the cashew and almond garnish for the jaggery basundi

steps: Pour 6 cups full-fat milk into a wide kadhai, bring to a boil, then simmer on medium-low for about 35 minutes, stirring, until it reduces to a thick pourable basundi.
Melt 1/2 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 3 tbsp water in a separate pan, then strain out any grit to leave a clean syrup.
Cool the reduced milk for a couple of minutes and set the flame to its lowest, then stir the jaggery syrup in slowly so the milk does not curdle.
Simmer gently for 3 minutes with 1/2 tsp cardamom powder and 1/4 tsp dry ginger powder until the basundi turns an even honey-brown.
Roast 10 cashews, 10 slivered almonds and 2 tbsp charoli in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee for 1 minute until golden, then fold most of them in.
Garnish with the reserved nuts, chill for 3 hours, and serve cold.
tips: Cool the reduced milk slightly before adding jaggery and keep the heat low, or the basundi will split.
Strain the melted jaggery well so no grit dulls the smooth texture of the basundi.
The pinch of dry ginger warms this richer jaggery version and keeps it easy on the stomach.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled topped with roasted cashews and charoli, a wholesome winter dessert with an earthy sweetness.

variations.name: Classic Beetroot Sabzi
variations.description: A simple North Indian dry sabzi of grated beetroot cooked with cumin, onion and everyday spices until sweet and tender. The earthy, jewel-red beetroot mellows into a mildly spiced side that is as pretty on the plate as it is wholesome.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the cumin and rounds off the earthy sweetness of the beetroot

steps: Peel and coarsely grate 500 g beetroot and finely chop the onion, 1 inch ginger and 2 green chillies.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them splutter for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add the chopped onion, ginger and green chillies and saute for 4 minutes until the onion softens and turns light golden.
Add 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp coriander powder and 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, stir for 30 seconds, then add the grated beetroot and 1 tsp salt.
Toss well, cover and cook on low for 10 minutes, stirring twice, until the beetroot is tender and has darkened to a deep red.
Uncover, add 0.5 tsp amchur, stir on medium for 2 minutes to dry off any moisture, garnish with 2 tbsp coriander and serve hot.
tips: Grate the beetroot rather than chopping so it cooks quickly and evenly in its own moisture.
The amchur at the end balances the natural sweetness of the beetroot with a gentle tang.
Cook covered on low so the beetroot softens without needing added water and keeps its colour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with phulka and dal, or stuff it into a wrap with a dollop of curd for a vibrant lunch.

variations.name: Beetroot Poriyal with Coconut
variations.description: A Tamil-style beetroot poriyal tempered with mustard, urad dal and curry leaves in coconut oil, then showered with fresh grated coconut. The coconut tames the earthiness and adds a sweet, nutty finish to the bright red shreds.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: carries the mustard and curry-leaf tadka and complements the sweet beetroot

steps: Peel and grate 500 g beetroot finely and chop 2 green chillies.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a kadhai over medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop, then add 1 tsp urad dal and 2 broken dried red chillies and fry until the dal turns golden.
Add 12 curry leaves, the chopped green chillies and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them crackle for 15 seconds.
Add the grated beetroot with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, toss well, then cover and cook on low for 8 minutes until tender, sprinkling a tablespoon of water only if it sticks.
Uncover and stir on medium for 2 minutes so any moisture dries off and the poriyal stays dry.
Switch off the flame and fold in 5 tbsp grated fresh coconut, tossing until the beetroot is evenly coated and glistening.
tips: Add the coconut off the heat so it stays sweet and does not brown against the hot pan.
Beetroot cooks fast when finely grated, so check at eight minutes to avoid overcooking.
Wear gloves or oil your hands while grating to avoid staining them deep pink.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sambar rice or curd rice; its bright colour brightens up any South Indian thali.

variations.name: Beetroot Peanut Sabzi (Maharashtrian)
variations.description: A Maharashtrian beetroot bhaji finished with a coarse roasted-peanut powder and a hint of jaggery for a sweet-savoury balance. The crushed peanuts add crunch and body while the jaggery draws out the beetroot's natural sweetness beautifully.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the classic Maharashtrian cooking oil that pairs naturally with the roasted-peanut finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a spoonful of unrefined jaggery deepens the beetroot's earthy sweetness the Maharashtrian way

steps: Peel and grate 500 g beetroot, and coarsely crush 0.33 cup roasted peanuts into a gritty powder.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a kadhai over medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin and let them splutter, then add 10 curry leaves and 2 slit green chillies.
Add the grated beetroot with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, toss well, then cover and cook on low for 9 minutes until tender.
Stir in 0.5 tsp goda masala and half the crushed peanut powder, and cook uncovered for 2 minutes so the flavours meld.
Add 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and stir for 1 minute until it melts and glazes the beetroot.
Finish with 1 tsp lemon juice and the remaining peanut powder, toss once, and serve warm with the peanuts still crunchy.
tips: Keep half the peanut powder for the finish so it stays crunchy rather than softening in the sabzi.
The jaggery and lemon together give the sweet-sour balance typical of Maharashtrian bhaji, so add both.
Goda masala gives an authentic aroma, but a pinch of garam masala works if you cannot find it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri or soft chapatis and a bowl of varan-bhaat for a Maharashtrian meal.

variations.name: Beetroot Thoran (Kerala-style)
variations.description: A Kerala thoran where finely chopped beetroot is steam-cooked and tossed with a coarse coconut-cumin-garlic paste crushed in a mortar. Fragrant with curry leaves and just a little heat, it stays drier and chunkier than a poriyal with the coconut ground in rather than sprinkled on.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the defining Kerala fat that ties the crushed coconut paste to the beetroot

steps: Peel and finely chop 500 g beetroot into tiny cubes rather than grating it, so it stays chunky in the thoran.
In a mortar, coarsely crush 0.5 cup grated coconut with 3 garlic cloves, 0.75 tsp cumin and 4 shallots so it stays textured, not smooth.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a kadhai over medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop, then add 2 broken dried red chillies and 12 curry leaves.
Add the chopped beetroot with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, toss, then cover and cook on low for 9 minutes, sprinkling 2 tbsp water so it steam-cooks tender.
Add the crushed coconut mixture, toss well, and cook uncovered on medium for 4 minutes so the coconut lightly roasts and any moisture dries off.
Taste, adjust salt, and serve the thoran warm and dry with the coconut fragrant and just-toasted.
tips: Crush the coconut coarsely so the thoran keeps its characteristic texture rather than turning pasty.
Chop the beetroot small and even so it cooks through quickly with just a splash of water.
A final minute of dry roasting brings out the coconut aroma that sets a thoran apart from a poriyal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as part of a Kerala sadya with rice, sambar and pulissery, or simply with rice and rasam.

variations.name: Classic Bharwa Baingan
variations.description: The everyday North Indian stuffed baby brinjal, slit into a cross and packed with a roasted besan, coriander and amchur masala. The little eggplants are slow-cooked in wood-pressed oil until collapsing-soft, their skins wrinkled and the tangy stuffing melting into a dry, spice-crusted sabzi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil that slow-cooks the stuffed brinjals to a soft, glossy finish

steps: Wash the 10 baby brinjals, keep the stems on, and make two deep cross-slits from the base without cutting through, then keep them in salted water.

Dry-roast the 4 tbsp besan on low for 4 minutes until nutty, then mix with 2 tsp coriander powder, 1.5 tsp fennel powder, 1.5 tsp amchur, 1 tsp chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 1 tbsp of the oil into a crumbly stuffing.
Pat the brinjals dry and press the roasted spice-besan stuffing firmly into each slit.
Heat the remaining 4 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a wide pan on medium, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them sizzle for 15 seconds.
Arrange the stuffed brinjals in a single layer, cover and cook on low for 18 minutes, turning gently every 5 minutes, until the skins wrinkle and a knife slides through easily.
Scatter any leftover stuffing over the top, cook uncovered for 3 minutes and serve hot.
tips: Do not slit the brinjals all the way through so the stuffing stays packed inside while cooking.
Roast the besan properly so the stuffing tastes nutty rather than raw and pasty.
Cook covered on the lowest heat and turn gently to soften the brinjals without spilling the filling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot bajra roti or phulka and a bowl of plain curd for a rustic everyday meal.

variations.name: Hyderabadi Peanut-Sesame Bharwa Baingan
variations.description: The Deccan classic where small brinjals are stuffed and then simmered in a luxurious peanut, sesame and coconut gravy sharpened with tamarind. Rich, nutty and tangy, this gravied bharwa baingan is a world apart from the dry North Indian sabzi and is a Hyderabadi feast staple.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: the nutty Deccan oil that fries the brinjals and carries the peanut-sesame gravy

steps: Dry-roast 4 tbsp peanuts, 2 tbsp sesame seeds and 3 tbsp coconut separately on low until golden, then grind them with 1 chopped onion to a smooth thick paste with a little water.
Slit the 10 brinjals into a cross keeping the stems on, and shallow-fry them in 4 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil for 5 minutes until the skins blister; lift out and set aside.
In the same oil add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 12 curry leaves, let them splutter for 15 seconds, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry 1 minute.
Add the ground peanut-sesame-coconut paste with 1.5 tsp chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt and cook on medium for 6 minutes until the oil surfaces.
Stir in 1.5 tsp tamarind paste and 1.5 cups hot water, bring to a gentle simmer, then slide in the fried brinjals and press them into the gravy.
Cover and simmer on low for 15 minutes until the brinjals are meltingly soft and the gravy is thick and glossy, then rest 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Roast the peanuts, sesame and coconut separately as each browns at a different speed and burnt nuts turn bitter.
Keep the heat low once the brinjals go in so they cook through without breaking apart.
Balance the tamarind and chilli at the end; the gravy should taste nutty, tangy and spicy all at once.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice, bagara khana or soft rumali roti to soak up the rich peanut gravy.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Bharli Vangi
variations.description: The Marathi stuffed brinjal cooked in an aromatic goda-masala and dry-coconut gravy with a signature dark, sweet-spicy depth. Freshly roasted coconut and peanuts meet the warm notes of goda masala and a touch of jaggery, giving a curry unlike any northern or Deccan version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
