ingredients.note: the wood-pressed oil that roasts the masala base for this Maharashtrian curry

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the touch of sweetness that balances the dark goda masala in Marathi style

steps: Dry-roast 4 tbsp dry coconut on low until deep golden, then grind with 3 tbsp roasted peanuts and 1 chopped onion to a coarse paste.
Mix half of this paste with 1 tsp goda masala, 0.75 tsp chilli powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt to make the stuffing, then pack it into the cross-slit brinjals.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai, add 1 tsp mustard seeds, let them pop, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry 1 minute.
Add the remaining coconut-peanut paste with the remaining 1 tsp goda masala, 0.75 tsp chilli powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric and remaining salt and roast on medium for 6 minutes until dark and fragrant.
Stir in 1 tsp tamarind paste, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1.5 cups hot water, bring to a simmer, then lower in the stuffed brinjals.
Cover and simmer on low for 16 minutes until the brinjals are tender and the gravy is dark and thick, then rest 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Roast the dry coconut until it is properly dark for the authentic deep colour of bharli vangi.
Goda masala is the heart of this dish, so use a fresh fragrant batch rather than plain garam masala.
Balance jaggery and tamarind so the gravy finishes sweet, sour and spicy in the Marathi way.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri or steamed rice topped with a spoon of the dark gravy and a wedge of lime.

variations.name: Gujarati Ringan no Bharwa
variations.description: The Gujarati stuffed brinjal with a distinctive sweet-and-sour besan stuffing brightened by jaggery, lemon and a generous handful of coriander. Cooked gently in wood-pressed oil, the little eggplants turn soft and glossy with a filling that hums with the classic Gujarati balance of sweet, sour and mild heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday Gujarati wood-pressed oil that cooks the brinjals soft and glossy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the sweetness that defines the Gujarati sweet-and-sour stuffing

steps: Dry-roast the 4 tbsp besan on low for 4 minutes until nutty and pale gold.

Mix the roasted besan with the 0.5 cup chopped coriander, 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 tbsp lemon juice, 2 tsp dhana-jeera powder, 1 tbsp green chilli-ginger paste, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp chilli powder, 1 tsp salt and 1 tbsp oil into a moist sweet-sour stuffing.
Pack the stuffing firmly into the cross-slit of each of the 10 brinjals.
Heat the remaining 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a wide pan, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them splutter for 15 seconds.
Arrange the stuffed brinjals in a single layer, cover and cook on low for 18 minutes, turning gently every 5 minutes, until soft and glossy.
Scatter the remaining stuffing over the top, cook uncovered for 3 minutes and finish with extra fresh coriander before serving.
tips: Keep the stuffing moist with the lemon and coriander so it packs easily and stays juicy while cooking.
Balance the jaggery and lemon to hit the classic Gujarati sweet-sour note without either overpowering.
Cook low and slow so the brinjals steam soft in their own moisture without extra water.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulka or bajra rotla and a spoon of ghee, alongside plain khichdi for a Gujarati thali.

variations.name: Classic Bharwa Bhindi
variations.description: The definitive North Indian stuffed okra, where whole bhindi are slit and packed with a roasted besan-and-spice masala sharpened by amchur and fennel. Slow-pan-fried until tender, the pods stay crisp on the outside while the tangy stuffing melts inside, making a beloved dry sabzi for lunchboxes and everyday meals.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil that slow-fries the stuffed pods to a tender, non-slimy finish

steps: Wash the 300 g okra, wipe completely dry, trim the tops and make a lengthwise slit in each without cutting through.

Dry-roast the 4 tbsp besan in a pan on low for 4 minutes until nutty and pale gold, then mix with 2 tsp coriander powder, 1.5 tsp fennel powder, 1.5 tsp amchur, 1 tsp chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 1 tbsp of the oil to make a crumbly stuffing.
Pack the roasted spice-besan stuffing firmly into the slit of each okra pod.
Heat the remaining 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a wide pan on medium, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them sizzle for 15 seconds.
Lay the stuffed okra in a single layer, cover and cook on low for 14 minutes, turning gently every 4 minutes, until the pods are tender and blistered on all sides.
Uncover, sprinkle any leftover stuffing over the top and cook 3 minutes on medium until crisp, then serve hot.
tips: Wipe the okra bone-dry before slitting, as any moisture makes the sabzi slimy while cooking.
Roast the besan well so the stuffing tastes nutty instead of raw and pasty.
Cook covered on low and turn gently so the pods soften without the stuffing spilling out.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulka or ajwain paratha and a bowl of boondi raita for a satisfying dry meal.

variations.name: Achari Bharwa Bhindi
variations.description: A tangy pickle-spiced stuffed okra where the filling is built on a freshly crushed five-seed achari masala bloomed in pungent mustard oil. Nigella, fennel and mustard give the pods the sharp, sour perfume of a Punjabi pickle, quite different from the mild classic version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the pungent oil that is the soul of any achari masala and cooks the stuffed pods

steps: Wash and wipe the 300 g okra completely dry, trim the tops and slit each lengthwise without cutting through.
Dry-roast 1.5 tsp fennel, 0.75 tsp nigella, 1 tsp mustard, 0.25 tsp fenugreek and 1 tsp cumin on low for 2 minutes, then coarsely crush them into an achari spice mix.
Mix the crushed achari spices with 1.5 tsp amchur, 1 tsp chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 1 tbsp of the mustard oil into a moist crumbly stuffing.
Pack the achari stuffing firmly into the slit of each okra pod.
Heat the remaining 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, lower the heat, lay in the stuffed okra in a single layer, cover and cook on low for 14 minutes, turning gently every 4 minutes.
Uncover, scatter any leftover achari masala over the pods and cook 3 minutes on medium until the spices bloom and the pods crisp, then serve hot.
tips: Crush the achari seeds coarsely, not to a fine powder, so you get bursts of fennel and nigella in each bite.
Smoke the mustard oil first and then lower the heat before cooking to soften its raw sharpness.
A squeeze of lemon at the end lifts the tangy achari notes even higher.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain paratha and raw onion rings, with a spoon of mango pickle alongside to echo the flavours.

variations.name: South Indian Peanut-Coconut Bharwa Bhindi
variations.description: A nutty southern take where the okra is stuffed with a roasted peanut, sesame and coconut masala and finished with a mustard-curry leaf tempering in sesame oil. The filling is toasty and mildly tangy with tamarind, giving the pods a completely different, richer character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: the nutty southern oil that carries the peanut-sesame stuffing and tempering

steps: Wash and wipe the 300 g okra dry, trim the tops and slit each lengthwise without cutting through.
Dry-roast 2 tbsp sesame seeds and 3 tbsp desiccated coconut on low for 3 minutes until golden, then grind coarsely with the 4 tbsp roasted peanuts.
Mix the ground peanut-sesame-coconut with 1 tsp tamarind paste, 1 tsp chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 1 tbsp of the sesame oil into a thick stuffing.
Pack the nutty stuffing firmly into the slit of each okra pod.
Heat the remaining 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a wide pan, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop, then add 12 curry leaves for 10 seconds.
Lay in the stuffed okra, cover and cook on low for 14 minutes, turning gently every 4 minutes, then uncover and cook 3 minutes until the pods are tender and the stuffing is toasty; serve hot.
tips: Roast the sesame and coconut only until pale gold, as burnt sesame turns the stuffing bitter.
Grind the peanuts coarse rather than into a paste so the stuffing stays crumbly and packs easily.
The tamarind keeps the filling moist, so add a little more if the mixture feels too dry to pack.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or with curd rice for a comforting South Indian plate.

variations.name: Dahi Bharwa Bhindi Curry
variations.description: A creamy departure where the classic stuffed okra pods are simmered briefly in a mild spiced yogurt gravy instead of being served dry. The tangy curd sauce softens the pods and turns the dish into a light gravy sabzi, perfect for scooping up with roti.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the stuffed pods and tempers the yogurt gravy to a smooth finish

steps: Wipe the 300 g okra dry, trim and slit each pod, then dry-roast 3 tbsp besan for 3 minutes and mix with 1 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp amchur, 0.5 tsp salt and a little ghee to stuff the pods.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan and shallow-fry the stuffed okra on medium for 6 minutes until blistered, then lift them out and set aside.
In the same ghee add 1 tsp cumin seeds, then the chopped onion and fry for 4 minutes until soft, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Add 0.5 tsp turmeric, the remaining 1 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp chilli powder and remaining salt with a splash of water and cook 2 minutes into a masala.
Lower the heat to minimum, pour in 1 cup whisked yogurt and stir constantly for 4 minutes until it simmers gently without splitting, then add 0.5 cup water.
Slide in the fried stuffed okra, simmer on low for 6 minutes until the gravy coats the pods, finish with 0.5 tsp garam masala and serve hot.
tips: Whisk the yogurt smooth and add it on the lowest heat with constant stirring so the gravy does not curdle.
Fry the stuffed pods first so they hold their shape and do not turn slimy in the gravy.
Keep the simmer short, as the okra should soak up flavour without falling apart.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulka or jeera rice, spooning the tangy yogurt gravy generously over each pod.

variations.name: Classic Aloo Bharwa Shimla Mirch
variations.description: The classic dhaba-style stuffed capsicum filled with a spiced mashed-potato masala sharpened by amchur and fennel. Whole peppers are packed tight, then slow-pan-cooked until the skins blister and soften while the tangy potato filling sets, making a hearty dry sabzi for any meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil that cooks the stuffed peppers to a blistered, tender finish

steps: Slice the tops off the 4 capsicums and hollow out the seeds and membranes to make cups.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan, add 1 tsp cumin seeds, let them crackle, then add the 3 mashed boiled potatoes with 2 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp fennel powder, 1.5 tsp amchur, 1 tsp chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp garam masala and 1 tsp salt and cook 4 minutes into a dry filling.
Cool the filling slightly and pack it firmly into each hollowed capsicum.
Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a wide pan on medium and place the stuffed capsicums on their sides.
Cover and cook on low for 14 minutes, rolling them every 4 minutes, until the skins blister and soften all around.
Uncover and cook 3 minutes to lightly char the peppers, then serve hot cut in halves.
tips: Cook the potato filling before stuffing so the raw spice edge is gone and the masala tastes rounded.
Choose squat, even capsicums that sit steadily in the pan and cook evenly on all sides.
Roll the peppers gently every few minutes so every side blisters without the filling falling out.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulka or jeera rice and a bowl of dal for a comforting home-style plate.

variations.name: Paneer Bharwa Shimla Mirch
variations.description: A richer restaurant-style stuffed capsicum filled with crumbled paneer, sauteed onion and a hint of kasuri methi. The soft cheesy filling stays moist and mildly spiced, turning the humble pepper into an indulgent starter or party side that needs no potato at all.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: sautes the paneer filling and gives the stuffed peppers a rich finish

steps: Slice the tops off the 4 capsicums and scoop out the seeds to make clean cups.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan, add 1 tsp cumin seeds, then the chopped onion and fry 3 minutes until soft, add 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and cook 1 minute.

Add the 250 g crumbled paneer with 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.75 tsp chilli powder, 0.5 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi, 3 tbsp coriander and 0.75 tsp salt and stir gently for 2 minutes, then cool the filling.
Pack the paneer filling firmly into each hollowed capsicum.
Heat the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide pan on medium and lay the stuffed peppers on their sides.
Cover and cook on low for 12 minutes, rolling every 4 minutes, until the skins soften and lightly char, then serve hot.
tips: Do not overcook the paneer filling before stuffing or it will turn rubbery inside the pepper.
Grate a little of the paneer for a smoother filling that packs tightly and holds together.
A pinch of chaat masala over the finished peppers gives a lovely tangy restaurant-style lift.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a starter with mint chutney, or with butter naan and dal makhani for a richer meal.

variations.name: Besan Masala Bharwa Shimla Mirch
variations.description: A Rajasthani-leaning version stuffed with a roasted gram-flour masala instead of potato, giving a nutty, dry, spice-forward filling that clings to the pepper walls. The toasted besan soaks up the oil and spices into a crumbly, intensely savoury bharwa that keeps beautifully for lunchboxes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the pungent oil that roasts the besan filling and cooks the peppers

steps: Slice the tops off the 4 capsicums and remove the seeds to make cups.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pan until it just smokes, lower the heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida, then add the 0.75 cup besan and roast on low for 6 minutes until deep golden and nutty.
Stir in 2 tsp coriander powder, 1.5 tsp fennel powder, 1.5 tsp amchur, 1 tsp chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt and roast 1 more minute, then cool the crumbly filling.
Pack the roasted besan masala firmly into each hollowed capsicum.
Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a wide pan on medium and place the stuffed peppers on their sides.
Cover and cook on low for 14 minutes, rolling every 4 minutes, until the skins blister and the besan sets, then serve hot.
tips: Roast the besan slowly and evenly until it smells nutty, as under-roasted besan tastes raw and pasty.
Let the filling cool before stuffing so it stays crumbly and packs in without turning gummy.
This dry besan sabzi travels well and tastes just as good at room temperature in a lunchbox.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain paratha or bajra roti and a spoon of yogurt to offset the rich besan filling.

variations.name: Corn-Cheese Bharwa Shimla Mirch
variations.description: A modern crowd-pleasing version stuffed with sweet corn, mashed potato and melting cheese, finished with a dusting of chaat masala. Baked-style in a covered pan, the peppers turn soft and smoky while the cheesy corn filling oozes, making it an instant favourite with children and at parties.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: sautes the corn filling and cooks the peppers with a rich buttery aroma

steps: Slice the tops off the 4 capsicums and hollow out the seeds to make cups.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan, add 0.75 tsp cumin seeds, then the chopped onion and green chillies and saute for 3 minutes until soft.
Add the 1 cup boiled corn and 2 mashed potatoes with 0.5 tsp black pepper, 0.75 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp of the chaat masala, cook 3 minutes, then cool and fold in 0.5 cup grated cheese.
Pack the corn-cheese filling firmly into each hollowed capsicum.

Heat the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide pan on medium, place the peppers on their sides, cover and cook on low for 14 minutes, rolling every 4 minutes, until soft and the cheese melts inside.
Dust the tops with the remaining 0.5 tsp chaat masala and serve hot.
tips: Fold the cheese into the cooled filling so it stays intact until it melts inside the cooking pepper.
Coarsely crush half the corn for a filling that binds better and packs without spilling.
A short blast under a grill at the end gives a lovely smoky char and bubbling cheese top.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot as a party starter with tomato ketchup and green chutney, or tucked into soft dinner rolls.

variations.name: Classic Cabbage Matar Sabzi
variations.description: A homely North Indian dry sabzi of finely shredded cabbage and green peas cooked with cumin, turmeric and a touch of ginger. Quick and light, the cabbage stays just-tender and sweet while the peas add little bursts of colour and freshness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the cumin and turmeric so the sabzi carries a warm, nutty aroma

steps: Shred 500 g cabbage finely into thin ribbons and finely chop the onion, tomato, 1 inch ginger and 2 green chillies.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them splutter for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add the chopped onion, ginger and green chillies and saute for 4 minutes until the onion turns soft and translucent.
Add the tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 3 minutes until the tomato softens into the masala.
Add the shredded cabbage and 0.75 cup green peas, toss well to coat, then cover and cook on low for 8 minutes, stirring once, until the cabbage wilts but keeps a slight bite.
Uncover, raise the heat and stir for 2 minutes to dry off any moisture, sprinkle 0.25 tsp garam masala and 2 tbsp coriander, and serve hot.
tips: Never add water to cabbage sabzi, as the cabbage steams perfectly in its own moisture under a lid.
Cook covered on low first, then uncover to dry off, so the sabzi is soft yet not watery.
Use fresh green peas in season for the sweetest flavour, or thaw frozen ones before adding.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulkas and a bowl of dal, or roll it into a paratha wrap for a quick lunch.

variations.name: South-Indian Cabbage Peas Poriyal
variations.description: The Tamil-style dry cabbage and peas tempered with mustard seeds, urad dal and curry leaves in coconut oil, then finished with fresh grated coconut. Lighter and subtly sweet, it keeps the cabbage just-cooked and lets the coconut and curry leaf aroma lead.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the authentic South Indian fat that carries the mustard and curry-leaf tempering

steps: Shred 500 g cabbage finely and keep 0.5 cup green peas ready, boiling frozen peas for 2 minutes if needed.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a kadhai over medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop, then add 1 tsp urad dal, 1 tsp chana dal and 2 broken dried red chillies and fry until the dals turn golden.
Add 12 curry leaves, 2 chopped green chillies and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them crackle for 15 seconds until aromatic.
Add the shredded cabbage and peas with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, toss well, then cover and cook on low for 7 minutes until the cabbage wilts but keeps a slight bite.
Uncover, raise the heat and stir for 2 minutes to dry off the moisture so the poriyal is not watery.
Switch off the flame and fold in 5 tbsp grated fresh coconut, tossing until it coats the cabbage while still sweet and raw.
tips: Add the coconut off the heat so it stays fresh and sweet rather than browning against the hot pan.
Fry the dals to a proper gold in the tempering for the signature nutty crunch of a poriyal.
Keep the cabbage slightly crunchy; a limp, overcooked poriyal loses its fresh character.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sambar rice and a papad, or as a light dry side with rasam and steamed rice.

variations.name: Cabbage Peas Besan Sabzi (Sindhi-style)
variations.description: A Sindhi-inspired version where roasted besan is sprinkled over the cabbage and peas so it coats each shred in a savoury, nutty crumb. The gram flour thickens the sabzi slightly and gives it a distinctive toasted flavour quite unlike the plain stir-fry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a sturdy oil that roasts the besan coating to a deep, nutty gold

steps: Shred 500 g cabbage finely and keep 0.75 cup green peas ready.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a kadhai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin and 0.25 tsp ajwain and let them splutter for 20 seconds.
Add the chopped onion and 1 tsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 4 minutes until the onion is soft, then add 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder.
Add the cabbage and peas with 1 tsp salt, toss well, cover and cook on low for 8 minutes until the cabbage wilts and softens.
Sprinkle 3 tbsp besan evenly over the vegetables, then stir-fry uncovered on medium for 5 minutes so the raw flour roasts and coats every shred without lumping.
Finish with 0.5 tsp amchur, stir through for 1 minute, and serve hot with the toasted besan clinging to the cabbage.
tips: Sprinkle the besan a little at a time and keep stirring so it toasts evenly instead of forming raw lumps.
Make sure the besan loses its raw smell and turns golden, which takes a good four to five minutes.
The amchur at the end lifts the nutty besan with a welcome tang, so do not skip it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft rotis or bajra roti and a spoon of yogurt to offset the toasty besan.

variations.name: Cabbage Peas Kootu (Coconut-Dal Style)
variations.description: A saucier Kerala-style kootu where the cabbage and peas simmer with soft moong dal and a ground coconut-cumin paste into a semi-gravy. Creamy, mild and comforting, it turns the humble cabbage into a nourishing lentil dish rather than a dry stir-fry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: carries the mustard and curry-leaf tempering that finishes a Kerala kootu

steps: Pressure-cook 0.33 cup moong dal with 1.25 cups water and 0.25 tsp turmeric for about 8 minutes until soft, then lightly mash.
Grind 0.5 cup fresh coconut, 1 tsp cumin and 2 green chillies with a splash of water into a coarse paste.
Add 400 g shredded cabbage, 0.5 cup peas, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt to the mashed dal with half a cup of water, and simmer on medium for 8 minutes until the cabbage turns tender.
Stir in the ground coconut paste and simmer gently on low for 5 minutes so the raw coconut cooks through into a creamy semi-gravy.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a small pan over medium heat, add 0.75 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop, then add 2 broken dried red chillies and 12 curry leaves.
Pour this crackling tempering over the kootu, stir once, and serve warm as a comforting semi-gravy dish.
tips: Cook the moong dal until just soft so the kootu is creamy without turning into a paste.
Add the coconut paste on low heat so the kootu stays smooth and does not split.
Keep the consistency loose and spoonable, as a kootu should never be as dry as a poriyal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or alongside sambar and rasam in a full South Indian meal.

variations.name: Classic Carrot Beans Poriyal
variations.description: The everyday Tamil poriyal of finely chopped carrot and green beans steam-cooked and tempered with mustard, urad dal and curry leaves, finished with fresh coconut. Bright, lightly spiced and just-tender, it is the quintessential dry vegetable side of a South Indian meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the authentic base that carries the mustard and curry-leaf tempering of a poriyal

steps: Finely chop 3 carrots and 200 g green beans into small even pieces so they cook at the same rate.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a kadhai over medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop, then add 1 tsp urad dal, 1 tsp chana dal and 2 broken dried red chillies and fry until the dals turn golden.
Add 12 curry leaves, 2 chopped green chillies and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them crackle for 15 seconds.
Add the chopped carrot and beans with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, toss well, then cover and cook on low for 8 minutes, sprinkling 2 tbsp water so they steam tender while keeping a slight bite.
Uncover and stir on medium for 2 minutes so any moisture dries off and the poriyal stays dry.
Switch off the flame and fold in 5 tbsp grated fresh coconut, tossing until the vegetables are evenly coated and glistening.
tips: Chop the carrot and beans to the same small size so neither is undercooked nor mushy.
Use only a splash of water and cook covered, letting the vegetables steam in their own moisture.
Add the coconut off the heat so it stays fresh and sweet rather than drying out against the pan.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sambar rice and appalam, or as a light dry side to rasam and steamed rice.

variations.name: Carrot Beans Paruppu Usili
variations.description: A Tamil Brahmin classic where soaked chana and toor dal are ground, steamed and crumbled into fluffy lentil granules, then tossed with the carrot and beans. Protein-rich and beautifully textured, the usili turns a simple stir-fry into a substantial, savoury dish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: helps crumble and roast the steamed lentil granules to a light, dry crumb

steps: Soak 0.5 cup chana dal and 0.25 cup toor dal for 2 hours, then grind with 4 dried red chillies, 0.5 tsp asafoetida and 0.5 tsp salt into a coarse thick paste without water.
Spread the paste in a greased plate and steam for 12 minutes until firm, then cool and crumble it into fine granules with your fingers.
Finely chop 2 carrots and 250 g beans and steam or cook them with a splash of water and 0.25 tsp turmeric for 6 minutes until just tender.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a kadhai over medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal and let them splutter, then add 12 curry leaves.
Add the crumbled lentil granules and stir-fry on medium for 6 minutes until they turn dry, golden and fluffy.
Add the cooked carrot and beans with 0.5 tsp salt, toss together for 3 minutes so the vegetables coat the usili crumbs, and serve warm.
tips: Grind the dal coarse and thick without water so the steamed cake crumbles into light granules.
Roast the crumbled lentils patiently until dry and golden, as soggy usili loses its charm.
Steam the vegetables separately so they stay bright and do not overcook while the usili roasts.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with mor kuzhambu or rasam and rice; the lentil usili makes this hearty enough for a main.

variations.name: North-Indian Carrot Beans Masala Sabzi
variations.description: A North Indian dry sabzi where carrot and beans are cooked with onion, tomato and warm ground spices instead of a coconut tempering. Earthier and more robustly spiced, it swaps mustard seeds and curry leaves for cumin, coriander and amchur.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the cumin and rounds out the warm North Indian masala over the vegetables

steps: Finely chop 3 carrots and 200 g green beans into small even pieces and finely chop the onion and tomato.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them splutter for 20 seconds.
Add the chopped onion and 1 tsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 4 minutes until the onion turns light golden.
Add the tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 3 minutes until the tomato softens.
Add the carrot and beans, toss well, then cover and cook on low for 9 minutes, stirring once, until tender with a slight bite.
Uncover, add 0.5 tsp amchur and 0.25 tsp garam masala, stir on medium for 2 minutes to dry off, and serve hot.
tips: Cook the vegetables covered on low so they soften in their own steam without added water.
Amchur and garam masala at the end keep their aroma bright, so add them near the finish.
Cut the carrot and beans small and even so they cook through in the same time.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rotis and dal, or pack it into a tiffin with rice for an easy lunch.

variations.name: Carrot Beans Coconut Stir-fry with Cashews
variations.description: A festive Kerala-style thoran-adjacent stir-fry where the carrot and beans meet a fragrant crushed coconut-cumin paste and a garnish of ghee-roasted cashews. Richer and slightly sweet, the cashews add a celebratory crunch to the everyday vegetables.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: carries the tempering and binds the crushed coconut paste to the vegetables

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: used to roast the cashews to a fragrant gold for the festive garnish

steps: Finely chop 3 carrots and 200 g beans, and coarsely crush 0.5 cup coconut with 0.75 tsp cumin and 5 shallots in a mortar.
Roast 12 cashews in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over low heat for 2 minutes until golden, then remove and set aside.
In the same pan heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil over medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop, then add 12 curry leaves.
Add the carrot and beans with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, toss, then cover and cook on low for 8 minutes with a splash of water until just tender.
Add the crushed coconut mixture and stir-fry uncovered on medium for 3 minutes so the coconut lightly toasts and any moisture dries off.
Scatter the ghee-roasted cashews over the top, toss once, and serve warm as a festive vegetable side.
tips: Roast the cashews separately in ghee so they stay crunchy and do not soften in the stir-fry.
Crush the coconut coarse for texture, and toast it briefly at the end for a nutty aroma.
Shallots ground into the coconut paste give a sweetness that plain onions cannot match.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as part of a sadya spread with rice and sambar, or alongside curd rice for a comforting meal.

variations.name: Classic Bengali Cham Cham
variations.description: A beloved Bengali sweet of oblong chhena logs poached in light syrup until spongy, then rolled in fine coconut or khoya. Softer and denser than a rasgulla and shaped like little cylinders, they carry a gentle sweetness and a pretty pale-golden tint from a lightly caramelised syrup.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: makes the pale one-string syrup that poaches the logs and lends a faint caramel colour

steps: Boil 1.5 litres milk, remove from the heat and add 3 tbsp diluted lemon juice, stirring until the chhena separates, then strain, rinse and hang for 30 minutes.
Knead the chhena with 1 tsp semolina and 1 tsp maida for 8 minutes until very smooth, then shape into 10 oblong logs about 5 cm long.
Boil 1.5 cups Anveshan Khandsari Sugar with 4 cups water and the crushed 3 cardamoms to a thin syrup at a rolling boil.
Slide in the logs, cover and boil hard for 15 minutes, adding a splash of hot water twice so the syrup stays thin as they swell.
Let the logs cool in the syrup for 30 minutes so they firm up and hold their oblong shape.
Stir 1 tsp rose water into the syrup, lift out each cham cham and let the surface dry slightly.
Roll every log in desiccated coconut to coat and chill before serving.
tips: Add a little maida to the chhena so the logs hold their oblong shape without breaking.
Keep the syrup thin and at a hard boil so the cham cham cooks spongy, not hard.
Let them firm up in the syrup before rolling, or the soft logs will lose their shape.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled, coconut-rolled, on a platter for festivals and Bengali sweet-plate celebrations.

variations.name: Malai Cham Cham
variations.description: A richer stuffed cham cham, slit lengthwise and filled with a sweet khoya-and-cream malai before being coated in coconut and topped with a cherry. The creamy filling turns each oblong into a decadent two-bite indulgence, a fixture on wedding sweet trays.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: sweetens the poaching syrup gently so the rich malai filling stands out

steps: Curdle 1.5 litres boiled milk with 3 tbsp diluted lemon juice, strain, rinse and hang the chhena for 30 minutes.
Knead the chhena with 1 tsp semolina and 1 tsp maida for 8 minutes until smooth, then shape into 10 oblong logs.
Boil 1.5 cups Anveshan Khandsari Sugar with 4 cups water, poach the logs on a hard boil covered for 15 minutes, then cool them in the syrup for 30 minutes.
For the filling, cook the 0.5 cup khoya with 3 tbsp fresh cream and 0.5 tsp cardamom powder on low heat for 4 minutes into a soft spreadable malai, then cool.
Gently squeeze the excess syrup from each log and slit it lengthwise without cutting all the way through.
Pipe or spoon the cooled malai into each slit, then roll the sides in desiccated coconut.
Top each stuffed cham cham with half a glace cherry and chill before serving.
tips: Cool the malai fully before filling so it holds its shape inside the soft log.
Squeeze out the syrup gently before slitting so there is room for the creamy filling.
Chill the finished sweets so the malai sets and the cham cham slices cleanly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled on a decorative tray, cherry-topped, as the centrepiece of a festive mithai selection.

variations.name: Kesar Cham Cham
variations.description: A saffron-kissed cham cham where both the chhena and the syrup are tinted gold, giving the oblong sweets a warm hue and a floral perfume. Rolled in crushed pistachios instead of coconut, they look and taste festive, richer and more aromatic than the plain white version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: carries the saffron colour cleanly into the syrup without dulling it

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in milk to tint the chhena and syrup gold and lend a floral aroma

steps: Curdle 1.5 litres boiled milk with 3 tbsp diluted lemon juice, strain, rinse and hang the chhena for 30 minutes.
Soak the pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk, then knead half of it into the chhena along with 1 tsp semolina, 1 tsp maida and 0.5 tsp cardamom powder for 8 minutes until smooth.
Shape the golden chhena into 10 oblong logs of even size.
Boil 1.5 cups Anveshan Khandsari Sugar with 4 cups water and the remaining saffron milk into a thin syrup at a rolling boil.
Slide in the logs, cover and boil hard for 15 minutes, then cool them in the saffron syrup for 30 minutes.
Gently lift out each cham cham and let the surface dry for a few minutes.
Roll every log in the crushed pistachios and chill before serving.
tips: Reserve half the saffron milk for the syrup so the colour runs right through the sweet.
Keep the boil vigorous so the saffron logs stay spongy and light.
Roll in pistachios only once the surface is dry so the nuts stick in a neat coat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled and pistachio-crusted, arranged with a few saffron strands scattered over the platter.

variations.name: Nolen Gur Cham Cham
variations.description: A winter Bengali take that poaches the chhena logs in a date-palm jaggery syrup, giving them a caramel-brown coat and a smoky molasses depth. The unrefined sweetness pairs naturally with a khoya coating, making these seasonal cham chams richer and more rustic than the classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: replaces refined sugar to give the logs their caramel colour and smoky winter depth

steps: Curdle 1.5 litres boiled milk with 3 tbsp diluted lemon juice, strain, rinse and hang the chhena for 30 minutes.
Knead the chhena with 1 tsp semolina and 1 tsp maida for 8 minutes until smooth, then shape into 10 oblong logs.
Dissolve 1.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 4 cups water with the bay leaf, bring to a boil and strain out any grit before returning to a hard boil.
Slide in the logs, cover and boil vigorously for 15 minutes, adding a little hot water so the syrup stays thin as they swell.
Let the cham chams cool in the caramel syrup for 30 minutes to soak up the colour and aroma.
Grate the 5 tbsp khoya and mix with 0.5 tsp cardamom powder to make a soft crumbly coating.
Lift out each log, let it dry slightly and roll it in the cardamom khoya before chilling.
tips: Strain the jaggery syrup before poaching so no sediment sticks to the logs.
Use aromatic date-palm jaggery if you can find it for the truest winter flavour.
Coat in khoya rather than coconut here, as it suits the deep caramel notes better.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled in khoya coating with a small drizzle of warm jaggery syrup for a rustic winter treat.

variations.name: Classic Chana Saag
variations.description: Chana saag marries soft-cooked white chickpeas with a silky puree of spinach, finished with a ghee tempering of cumin and garlic. This everyday North Indian dish is wholesome and iron-rich, with the nutty chickpeas holding their shape against the smooth, gently spiced greens.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the cumin and garlic tempering that perfumes the whole pan of greens

steps: Soak 1 cup kabuli chana overnight, then pressure-cook with 3 cups water and 0.5 tsp salt for about 15 minutes until the chickpeas are soft enough to crush between two fingers.
Blanch 400 g spinach in boiling water for 2 minutes, drain into cold water to keep it green, then blend with 2 green chillies into a coarse puree.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them splutter for 20 seconds, then add the chopped garlic and ginger and fry for 1 minute until golden.

Add the finely chopped onion and saute for 5 minutes until light brown, then add the chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp salt and cook for 6 minutes until the ghee separates.
Tip in the cooked chickpeas with half a cup of their cooking water and simmer for 5 minutes so they soak up the masala.
Stir in the spinach puree, lower the heat and simmer gently for 6 minutes, then finish with 0.5 tsp garam masala and serve hot.
tips: Blanch and shock the spinach in cold water so the saag keeps its bright green colour instead of turning olive.
Reserve the chickpea cooking water and use it to loosen the saag, as it adds body and flavour.
A pinch of asafoetida in the tempering makes the chickpeas easier to digest.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulkas or jeera rice and a wedge of lemon, with sliced onions and a dollop of ghee on top.

variations.name: Punjabi Chana Saag with Makki Roti
variations.description: A rustic Punjabi take where the greens are slow-cooked with a little makki flour for body and finished with a smoking-hot mustard-oil tempering of whole red chillies and garlic. Hearty and robust, it echoes the beloved sarson-da-saag tradition while the chickpeas add heft and protein.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: its sharp pungency is the soul of a Punjabi saag tempering over greens and chana

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoonful stirred in at the end gives the saag its signature glossy richness

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup soaked kabuli chana with 3 cups water and 0.5 tsp salt for 15 minutes until soft, then set aside with the cooking liquid.

Boil 300 g spinach and 200 g mustard greens with the green chillies and 1 inch ginger in a cup of water for 15 minutes until fully tender, then coarsely mash with a wooden churner rather than blending smooth.
Whisk 2 tbsp makki atta into half a cup of water, stir it into the mashed greens and simmer on low for 10 minutes until thickened and glossy.
Add the cooked chickpeas with a cup of their liquid and 0.75 tsp salt, and simmer the saag together for 8 minutes so the flavours marry.

Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil in a small pan until it just smokes, lower the heat, add the sliced garlic, remaining ginger julienne and 3 broken dried red chillies, and fry until deep golden.
Add the chopped onion to the tempering and fry for 3 minutes until soft, pour this sizzling tadka over the saag, stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and serve steaming.
tips: Heat the mustard oil until it just smokes and then cool it slightly before tempering to mellow its raw pungency.
Mash the greens by hand for the rustic, textured feel of an authentic Punjabi saag rather than a smooth puree.
The makki flour both thickens and lends a subtle sweetness, so add it slowly to avoid lumps.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with makki di roti, a knob of white butter and thick jaggery on the side for the classic winter Punjabi meal.

variations.name: Dhaba-style Chana Saag Masala
variations.description: The highway-dhaba version turns up the spice with a bhuna onion-tomato masala, kasuri methi and a chunkier, drier finish that clings to the chickpeas. Smoky and bold, it trades the smooth pureed greens for roughly chopped spinach cooked down into a thick, glossy masala.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: stands up to the high-heat bhuna that gives dhaba masala its roasted depth

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup soaked kabuli chana with 3 cups water and 0.5 tsp salt for 15 minutes until soft, and roughly chop 350 g spinach without pureeing it.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a heavy kadhai over medium-high heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1 bay leaf and let them crackle for 20 seconds.
Add the finely chopped onions and fry hard for 7 minutes until deep golden brown, then add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute until the raw smell goes.
Add the pureed tomatoes with 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp salt, and bhuna on medium-high for 8 minutes until the oil separates at the edges.
Add the chopped spinach and cook uncovered on high for 5 minutes until it wilts and its water evaporates, then add the chickpeas with half a cup of their liquid.
Simmer for 6 minutes until thick and glossy, crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the top, sprinkle 0.75 tsp garam masala and serve hot.
tips: Fry the onions until genuinely brown, as this bhuna stage is what gives the dish its deep dhaba flavour.
Keep the spinach roughly chopped and cook it fast on high so it stays textured rather than dissolving.
Toast the kasuri methi in your palm before crumbling it in to release its full aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tandoori roti or laccha paratha, a sliced onion-and-lemon salad and a cooling boondi raita.

variations.name: Coconut Chana Saag (South-style)
variations.description: A South Indian reinterpretation where the chickpeas and greens simmer in a fragrant coconut-and-curry-leaf base tempered in coconut oil. Lighter and subtly sweet from fresh coconut, it swaps the North Indian garam masala for the crackle of mustard seeds and the warmth of freshly ground pepper.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: carries the mustard and curry-leaf tempering that defines a South Indian greens curry

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup soaked kabuli chana with 3 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 15 minutes until soft, keeping the cooking liquid.
Grind 0.5 cup fresh coconut with 0.75 tsp cumin, 0.75 tsp black pepper and a splash of water into a smooth paste.
Chop 350 g spinach finely and cook it with the chickpeas and their liquid on medium for 6 minutes until wilted and just tender.
Stir the ground coconut paste into the chana-saag with 0.75 tsp salt and simmer gently on low for 6 minutes so the raw coconut cooks through without splitting.

Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a small pan over medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop, then add 2 broken dried red chillies, 8 halved shallots and 15 curry leaves and fry until the shallots turn golden.
Pour this fragrant tempering over the curry, stir once and simmer for 2 minutes before serving warm.
tips: Add the coconut paste on low heat and keep stirring so the gravy stays smooth and does not turn grainy.
Fry the shallots in the tempering until golden for a sweet depth that balances the greens.
Freshly crushed pepper rather than chilli powder gives this version its clean South Indian heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed red rice, appam or plain dosa, with a spoon of extra coconut oil drizzled on top.

variations.name: Classic Cholar Dal
variations.description: A festive Bengali chana dal, cooked soft and kept just this side of sweet with jaggery, then studded with ghee-fried coconut chips and finished with a whole garam masala tempering. Raisins add pops of sweetness and the ginger keeps it grounded, making it the classic partner to hot, puffed luchis at Sunday breakfasts and pujas.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee both fries the coconut chips golden and carries the whole-spice tempering that defines cholar dal

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: unrefined jaggery gives the gentle, rounded sweetness this dal is loved for, without the flat edge of white sugar

steps: Rinse 1 cup chana dal and pressure cook it with 2.5 cups water, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 4 whistles on medium heat, until the grains are soft but still hold their shape rather than dissolving.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan and fry the 1/3 cup diced fresh coconut on medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes until the chips turn golden and smell toasty, then lift them out and reserve.

In the same pan warm the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, add 2 bay leaves, 2 dried red chillies, 1 inch cinnamon, 3 cardamoms, 3 cloves and 1 tsp cumin seeds, and let them crackle for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger paste and fry for 30 seconds, then pour the whole tempering into the cooked dal along with the fried coconut chips and 2 tbsp raisins.
Add 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and simmer the dal on low heat for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring, until it thickens to a pourable-but-clinging consistency and the coconut plumps up.
Taste and adjust salt against the sweetness, then rest the dal covered for 5 minutes so the whole spices infuse before serving.
tips: Cook the chana dal just until it holds shape; a mushy, broken dal loses the distinct-grain texture that cholar dal is prized for.
Fry the coconut chips only to pale gold, as they darken further in the hot dal and can turn bitter if overcooked.
Balance is everything here, so add jaggery a little at a time and stop while the dal is only faintly sweet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with freshly fried luchis or radhaballavi for the definitive Bengali festive breakfast.

variations.name: Bhoger Cholar Dal
variations.description: The strictly no-onion, no-garlic cholar dal offered as bhog during Durga Puja and cooked entirely in ghee for a purer, more aromatic pot. Cashews join the raisins and coconut, and the dal is finished with a hand-crushed roasted garam masala that gives the temple version its heady, unmistakable fragrance.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a bhog dish is generous with ghee, which fries the cashews and blooms the roasted garam masala at the finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the pronounced jaggery sweetness marks this out as an offering dal, richer than an everyday one

steps: Pressure cook 1 cup rinsed chana dal with 2.5 cups water, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 4 whistles on medium heat until soft yet whole, then keep it warm.
Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and fry 3 tbsp cashews and the 1/3 cup diced coconut together on medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes until both turn golden, then remove them and reserve.

Add the remaining 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee to the pan, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, 2 bay leaves and 2 dried red chillies for 30 seconds, then fry 1 tbsp ginger paste for another 30 seconds until the raw smell lifts.
Tip this tempering into the cooked dal along with the fried cashews and coconut and 2 tbsp raisins, and stir well over low heat.
Add 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and simmer for 6 to 8 minutes until the dal thickens and glosses, then sprinkle over 1 tsp roasted garam masala powder and fold it through off the heat.
Cover and let the bhoger dal rest for 5 minutes so the roasted spices bloom into the ghee before it is served.
tips: For a true bhog flavour, dry-roast the garam masala whole and crush it fresh; pre-ground powder loses the aroma that defines this version.
Keep the pot free of onion and garlic to stay faithful to the offering; the ghee and whole spices supply all the depth needed.
This dal thickens as it cools, so pull it off the heat while still a touch looser than you want it on the plate.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle over a puja thali beside khichuri, labra and a piece of fried pumpkin for the classic bhog spread.

variations.name: Gurer Cholar Dal
variations.description: A winter special sweetened with nolen gur, the fragrant date-palm jaggery that appears only in the cold months, giving the dal a smoky-caramel depth that ordinary jaggery cannot match. Warming cinnamon and a pinch of fennel play up the seasonal aroma, making this the cosiest of cholar dals.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee carries the smoky sweetness of nolen gur and keeps the winter dal glossy and rich

steps: Pressure cook 1 cup rinsed chana dal with 2.5 cups water, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 4 whistles on medium heat until tender but not broken, and keep it warm.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and fry the 1/4 cup diced coconut for 2 minutes until golden, then set the chips aside.
Add the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee to the pan and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1/2 tsp fennel seeds, 1 inch cinnamon, 1 bay leaf and 2 dried red chillies for 30 seconds until deeply fragrant.
Fry 1 tbsp ginger paste for 30 seconds, then stir the tempering and the fried coconut into the cooked dal and simmer on low for 4 minutes.
Lower the heat further and melt in 3 tbsp nolen gur, stirring constantly for 3 to 4 minutes so the date-palm jaggery dissolves without seizing and the dal turns a warm, deep amber.
Rest the dal covered for 5 minutes so the smoky gur aroma settles through it before serving.
tips: Add nolen gur only on the lowest heat and never let the dal boil hard afterwards, or the delicate palm-jaggery aroma cooks off.
If nolen gur is unavailable out of season, patali gur shaved fine is the closest substitute for that smoky note.
The fennel is subtle but essential; it echoes the winter warmth of the gur without making the dal taste of aniseed.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm on a winter morning with crisp koraishutir kochuri (green pea puris) and a slice of nolen gur sandesh to follow.

variations.name: Narkel Cholar Dal
variations.description: A coconut-forward rendition finished with a splash of coconut milk for a plush, almost curry-like body, alongside the usual fried coconut chips. Milder and creamier than the classic, it leans into the Bengali love of narkel and pairs the sweetness of jaggery with the mellow fat of coconut.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: just enough bilona ghee to fry the coconut and temper the spices before the coconut milk takes over

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: its gentle sweetness marries the coconut milk into a rounded, creamy finish

steps: Pressure cook 1 cup rinsed chana dal with 2.5 cups water, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 4 whistles on medium heat until soft yet whole, then keep it warm.
Fry the 1/3 cup diced coconut in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes until golden, and set the chips aside.
Warm the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1 bay leaf for 20 seconds, add 2 slit green chillies and 1 tbsp ginger paste and fry for 30 seconds.
Stir this tempering and the fried coconut into the dal, add 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, and simmer on low for 5 minutes until it thickens.
Lower the heat to its gentlest and pour in 1/2 cup coconut milk, stirring for 2 to 3 minutes without letting it boil so the dal turns creamy and pale.
Rest the dal covered for 5 minutes so the coconut flavour deepens, and serve while still glossy and loose.
tips: Add coconut milk only off a hard boil; a rolling simmer will split it and leave the creamy dal looking grainy.
Use the thicker top of a can of coconut milk for body, saving the thin liquid to loosen the dal if it over-thickens.
Green chillies rather than dried red suit this milder version, keeping the heat fresh against the sweet coconut.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain luchi or steamed rice, topped with a few extra fried coconut chips for crunch.

variations.name: Classic Dhokar Dalna
variations.description: A beloved Bengali vegetarian centrepiece where spiced chana dal is cooked into a firm cake, cut into diamonds, fried crisp, and then simmered in a light potato-and-tomato gravy scented with ginger and garam masala. The dhoka soaks up the gravy at the edges while staying dense inside, giving the dish its signature two-textured pleasure.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil fries the dhoka to a firm golden crust and gives the gravy its Bengali pungency

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of bilona ghee lifts the dalna with warmth just before serving

steps: Soak 1 cup chana dal for 4 hours, drain, and grind it with 2 green chillies, 1 tbsp ginger paste and only a splash of water into a thick, coarse-smooth batter that holds its shape.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai on medium, crackle 1/2 tsp cumin seeds and 1/4 tsp hing for 20 seconds, then add the dal batter with 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1/2 tsp salt and stir-cook for 6 to 7 minutes until it thickens into a stiff mass that leaves the pan.
Spread the hot mixture 1/2 inch thick on a greased plate, smooth the top, cool for 15 minutes until set, then cut it into diamond-shaped pieces.
Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and shallow-fry the dhoka diamonds in batches on medium heat for about 2 minutes a side until golden and crusted, then lift them onto a plate.

In the same oil crackle 1/2 tsp cumin seeds and 1 bay leaf, add 2 cubed potatoes and fry 3 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger paste, 2 pureed tomatoes, 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp cumin powder and 3/4 tsp salt and cook 4 minutes until the oil separates.

Pour in 2 cups hot water, simmer 8 to 10 minutes until the potatoes are tender and the gravy thickens, then slide in the fried dhoka, cook 2 minutes, and finish with 1/2 tsp garam masala and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee off the heat.
tips: Add the fried dhoka to the gravy only in the last couple of minutes; simmered too long, the cakes drink up the gravy and crumble.
Grind the dal thick with minimal water, or the batter never sets firm enough to cut and fry into clean diamonds.
Fry the dhoka a shade darker than looks necessary, since the crust softens once it meets the gravy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice or soft luchis, the gravy spooned generously and a couple of dhoka pieces per plate.

variations.name: Niramish Bhoger Dhokar Dalna
variations.description: The temple-offering version made without onion or garlic, where the gravy leans on hing, ginger and roasted cumin-coriander for depth, and everything is cooked in ghee for a purer aroma. It is a staple of Bengali puja bhog, gentler and more fragrant than the everyday dalna.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a bhog dalna is cooked in ghee throughout, giving the onion-free gravy its rich, offering-day fragrance

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: reserved for frying the dhoka firm and golden before the ghee gravy takes over

steps: Soak 1 cup chana dal for 4 hours, drain, and grind with 1 tbsp ginger paste and a splash of water to a thick batter. Cook it in 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil with 1/2 tsp cumin seeds, 1/4 tsp hing, 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1/2 tsp salt for 6 to 7 minutes until stiff.
Spread the paste 1/2 inch thick on a greased plate, cool 15 minutes until firm, and cut into diamonds.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and shallow-fry the dhoka on medium for 2 minutes a side until golden and crusted, then set aside.
In a clean pan warm 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1/2 tsp cumin seeds, 2 bay leaves, 2 dried red chillies and 1/4 tsp hing for 30 seconds, then add 2 cubed potatoes and fry 3 minutes.

Stir in 1 tbsp ginger paste, 1/2 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp roasted cumin-coriander powder, 1/2 tsp sugar and 3/4 tsp salt with a splash of water, and cook 3 minutes into a thick masala until the ghee glistens at the edges.
Add 2 cups hot water, simmer 8 to 10 minutes until the potatoes soften and the gravy bodies up, slide in the fried dhoka for the last 2 minutes, and rest covered before serving.
tips: Roast whole cumin and coriander and grind them fresh for the gravy; the toasty powder replaces the depth that onion would otherwise give.
The pinch of sugar is a Bengali balancing trick, not a sweetener, so keep it subtle against the savoury ghee gravy.
Keep the ginger generous, since in a no-onion-garlic bhog it carries most of the aromatic weight.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as part of a puja thali with khichuri, begun bhaja and a piece of fried potol.

variations.name: Narkel Dhokar Dalna
variations.description: A richer take where fresh coconut and chopped cashews are folded into the dal batter, so each fried diamond hides pockets of sweet coconut and crunch. The gravy is rounded with a little more ginger and a hint of garam masala, making this a wedding-feast version of the humble dalna.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: fries the coconut-studded dhoka firm and gives the festive gravy its sharp Bengali base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: swirled in at the end to gild this richer, wedding-style dalna

steps: Soak 1 cup chana dal for 4 hours, drain, and grind with 2 green chillies and 1 tbsp ginger paste to a thick batter. Cook it in 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil with 1/2 tsp cumin, 1/4 tsp hing, 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1/2 tsp salt for 5 minutes, then fold in 1/3 cup grated coconut and 3 tbsp chopped cashews and cook 2 minutes more until stiff.
Spread the mixture 1/2 inch thick on a greased plate, cool 15 minutes to set, and cut into diamond pieces.
Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and shallow-fry the coconut dhoka on medium for 2 minutes a side until golden, then reserve.

In the same oil crackle 1/2 tsp cumin seeds, add 2 cubed potatoes and fry 3 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger paste, 1 pureed tomato, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 3/4 tsp salt and cook 4 minutes until the oil separates.
Add 2 cups hot water and simmer 8 to 10 minutes until the potatoes are tender and the gravy thickens, then slide in the fried dhoka for 2 minutes.
Finish with 3/4 tsp garam masala and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee stirred in off the heat, and rest covered for 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Chop the cashews small so the dhoka still sets firm; large pieces create weak spots that break when you cut the diamonds.
Fold the coconut in only after the batter has stiffened, or the extra moisture keeps the cake from holding together.
This richer dhoka is delicate, so turn the pieces gently in the gravy with a flat spoon rather than stirring.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at a festive meal with pulao or luchi, the coconut dhoka making it hearty enough to anchor the plate.

variations.name: Classic Gawar Phali Sabzi
variations.description: This Classic Gawar Phali is a simple dry sabzi of cluster beans cooked with a cumin-hing tempering until tender and just spiced. Naturally slightly bitter, the beans mellow into a wholesome everyday side that pairs with any North Indian meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil that gently mellows the beans and blooms the tempering

steps: String the 400 g cluster beans and cut into 2 cm pieces, then boil with a pinch of salt for 6 minutes to reduce the bitterness and drain.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai, add 1 tsp cumin and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them sizzle for 15 seconds.
Add the grated ginger and slit green chillies and saute for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt on low heat for 20 seconds.
Add the parboiled beans and toss well to coat them evenly in the spices.
Cover and cook on low for 10 minutes, stirring once, until the beans are soft and take on the masala.
Uncover, add 1 tsp amchur, fry 2 minutes to dry any moisture and serve hot.
tips: Parboiling the beans first tames their natural bitterness and shortens the cooking time.
Choose young, tender pods that snap crisply for the sweetest, least fibrous sabzi.
A pinch of hing aids digestion and adds savoury depth to these earthy beans.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot chapatis and a bowl of curd for a light, everyday meal.

variations.name: Gujarati Gawar Phali Nu Shaak
variations.description: A Gujarati shaak where cluster beans are cooked with roasted peanuts and a touch of jaggery for the classic sweet-savoury balance. A besan sprinkle thickens the masala into a soft coat, making this a beloved everyday western Indian side.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday Gujarati oil that pairs naturally with the peanut and jaggery notes

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: adds the gentle sweetness that defines a Gujarati shaak

steps: String and cut the 400 g cluster beans into 2 cm pieces and coarsely crush the 3 tbsp roasted peanuts.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai, add 1 tsp mustard and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and let them splutter for 15 seconds.
Add 0.25 tsp asafoetida and the slit green chillies, then add 2 tbsp besan and roast on low for 2 minutes until nutty.
Add the beans with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp dhana jeera and 1 tsp salt and toss to coat.
Add the crushed peanuts and a quarter cup of water, cover and cook on low for 12 minutes until tender.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook 2 minutes so the sweet-savoury balance develops.
Uncover, dry off any excess moisture over 2 minutes and serve warm with coriander.
tips: Roast the besan properly so it thickens the shaak without tasting raw or pasty.
Crushed peanuts add the nutty body typical of a Gujarati bean shaak.
Keep the jaggery subtle so it rounds the flavour rather than making it sweet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft rotli and a bowl of dal-bhaat for a homely Gujarati thali.

variations.name: Rajasthani Gawar Dahi Sabzi
variations.description: A Marwari-style sabzi where cluster beans simmer in a spiced curd gravy that turns creamy and tangy. Cooked in mustard oil with a besan-thickened yogurt base, it is a rich, comforting take suited to Rajasthan's love of dahi-based dishes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the pungent Rajasthani oil that stands up to the tangy curd gravy

steps: String and cut the 400 g cluster beans into 2 cm pieces and boil with a pinch of salt for 8 minutes until tender, then drain.
Whisk the 0.75 cup curd with 1.5 tbsp besan, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder until completely smooth.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it smokes, lower the heat and add 1 tsp cumin, 0.25 tsp fenugreek seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida to sizzle 15 seconds.
Lower the flame fully and pour in the whisked curd mixture, stirring continuously for 4 minutes so it does not split.
Simmer the gravy on low for 5 minutes, stirring often, until it thickens and the raw besan smell fades.
Add the boiled beans and 1 tsp salt and simmer on low for 6 minutes so they soak up the tangy gravy.
Adjust the seasoning, cook 1 minute more and serve hot with a coriander garnish.
tips: Whisk the besan into the curd before it hits the pan so the gravy stays lump-free.
Keep stirring on low heat while the curd cooks so it thickens smoothly without curdling.
The methi dana adds a mild bitterness that is characteristic of Marwari dahi sabzis.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra roti or steamed rice and a spoon of ghee for a Rajasthani meal.

variations.name: South-Indian Gawar Coconut Poriyal
variations.description: A southern poriyal where cluster beans are steamed and tossed with a mustard-curry-leaf tempering and grated coconut. Simple and mildly spiced in coconut oil, it keeps the beans crisp-tender and lets their fresh green flavour come through.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: gives the poriyal its southern aroma and carries the mustard tempering

steps: String and finely chop the 400 g cluster beans, then steam with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 8 minutes until tender.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop for 15 seconds.
Add 1 tsp urad dal and 2 broken dry red chillies and fry for 40 seconds until the dal turns golden.
Add the 10 curry leaves and let them crisp for 10 seconds until fragrant.
Add the steamed beans with 0.75 tsp sambar powder and toss on medium heat for 3 minutes.
Fold in the 0.5 cup grated coconut and stir-fry for 2 minutes until warmed through and just dry.
Check the salt, cook 1 more minute and serve warm.
tips: Chop the beans finely so they steam quickly and mix evenly with the coconut.
Fry the urad dal until golden for the crunchy contrast typical of a poriyal.
Steam rather than boil so the beans keep their bright colour and gentle bite.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with curd rice or sambar rice and a crunchy papad for a light southern meal.

variations.name: Classic Plain Ghevar
variations.description: Ghevar is a Rajasthani festival disc with a lacy honeycomb texture, made by drizzling a cold ghee-and-flour batter into hot ghee inside a tall ring mould. Crisp, porous and golden, the plain version is soaked in cardamom syrup and traditionally made for Teej and Raksha Bandhan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: cooked to a one-string syrup that soaks the porous disc without making it soggy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: both rubbed cold into the batter for the honeycomb and used to deep-fry the disc

steps: Rub 0.5 cup solidified Anveshan Ghee with a few ice cubes until pale and creamy, then whisk in 2 cups maida and 0.5 cup milk.
Gradually beat in 3 cups ice-cold water to make a thin, smooth, milk-like batter, keeping it chilled throughout.
Dissolve 1.5 cups Anveshan Khandsari in 0.75 cup water with 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.5 tsp lemon juice, and simmer 7 minutes to a one-string syrup kept warm.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Ghee in a tall narrow pot until smoking hot, then pour a thin stream of batter into the centre so it spreads and sizzles into a lacy web.
Keep adding batter through the central hole in 4 to 5 pours, letting each set, until a thick honeycomb disc builds up, then fry 4 to 5 minutes until golden and crisp.
Lift the ghevar out with a skewer through the hole, drain, drizzle warm syrup over it, top with 2 tbsp pistachios, and serve.
tips: The batter must be ice-cold and thin while the ghee is smoking hot; this temperature clash is what forms the honeycomb.
Pour the batter in a slow thin stream from a height into the centre, waiting for the fizzing to subside between pours.
Drizzle only a little syrup so the ghevar stays crisp; a full soak turns it limp.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature as a Teej centrepiece, cut into wedges with a light dusting of powdered cardamom.

variations.name: Malai Ghevar
variations.description: The showstopper Jaipur wedding ghevar, where a crisp plain disc is crowned with a thick layer of chilled saffron rabri and a shower of nuts. The contrast of the crunchy honeycomb base soaking up cool, creamy malai is what makes this the most prized version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: makes both the disc-soaking syrup and sweetens the thick rabri topping

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped into the rabri to colour and perfume the creamy topping

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: rubbed cold into the batter and used to deep-fry the honeycomb disc

steps: Rub 0.5 cup cold Anveshan Ghee with ice until creamy, whisk in 2 cups maida and 0.5 cup milk, then beat in 3 cups ice-cold water to a thin batter.
Warm 1.5 cups rabri with a pinch of Anveshan Saffron and 0.5 tsp cardamom, sweeten with 0.5 cup of the Anveshan Khandsari, then chill it thoroughly.
Dissolve the remaining 1 cup Anveshan Khandsari in 0.75 cup water and simmer to a one-string syrup kept warm.
Heat the rest of the Anveshan Ghee until smoking and build a honeycomb disc with 4 to 5 slow central pours of the cold batter, frying 5 minutes to crisp golden.
Drain the disc, drizzle it lightly with warm syrup, and let it cool to room temperature so it stays crisp.
Spread the chilled saffron rabri thickly over the top, scatter 3 tbsp slivered nuts, and serve at once.
tips: Cool the fried disc completely before topping, or the warm ghevar will melt the rabri into a puddle.
Keep the rabri very thick and cold so it sits proud on the disc instead of soaking straight through.
Assemble just before serving to keep the honeycomb base crunchy under the creamy layer.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled as a wedding-season showpiece, cut into wedges so each shows the crisp base and creamy crown.

variations.name: Mawa Ghevar
variations.description: A richer ghevar where khoya is beaten into the batter, giving the honeycomb disc a denser, moister crumb and a milky depth. The fried disc is soaked more generously in syrup and layered with reduced mawa, making it the most indulgent of the family.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: cooked to a slightly thicker syrup to soak the dense mawa honeycomb

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: rubbed cold into the batter and used to fry the rich mawa disc

steps: Rub 0.5 cup cold Anveshan Ghee with ice until creamy, then whisk in 2 cups maida, 0.75 cup grated khoya and 0.75 cup milk.
Beat in 2.5 cups ice-cold water gradually to a smooth thin batter that still carries the mawa richness, keeping it chilled.
Dissolve 1.75 cups Anveshan Khandsari in 0.75 cup water with 0.5 tsp cardamom and simmer 8 minutes to a thick one-string syrup kept warm.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Ghee until smoking and build the honeycomb disc with 5 slow central pours, frying 5 to 6 minutes until golden and set.
Lift the disc out and soak it generously with the warm syrup so the mawa-rich crumb drinks it in.
Scatter 3 tbsp slivered almonds over the moist disc and serve warm.
tips: Grate the khoya fine and blend it fully into the batter so it does not clog the pouring stream.
Mawa ghevar is meant to be moist, so soak it more than the plain version for the right texture.
Fry a touch longer than plain ghevar, as the khoya makes the disc denser and slower to crisp.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm or at room temperature as a rich festive sweet, garnished with edible silver leaf for occasions.

variations.name: Khapli Honey-Soaked Ghevar
variations.description: A mindful reimagining that swaps refined flour for nutty khapli wheat and finishes the crisp disc with a light honey-cardamom drizzle instead of a heavy sugar soak. It keeps the lacy honeycomb magic while leaning wholegrain and naturally sweetened.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: gives the honeycomb disc a nutty wholegrain flavour and golden colour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: warmed with cardamom and drizzled over the disc as a natural finishing syrup

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: rubbed cold into the batter and used to fry the wholewheat honeycomb disc

steps: Rub 0.5 cup cold Anveshan Ghee with ice until creamy, then whisk in 1.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta and 0.5 cup cornflour with 0.5 cup milk.
Beat in 3 cups ice-cold water to a thin, smooth batter and keep it well chilled while the ghee heats.
Gently warm 0.75 cup Anveshan Honey with 0.5 tsp cardamom until just pourable, taking care not to boil it, and set aside.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Ghee until smoking and build the honeycomb disc with 4 to 5 slow central pours, frying 5 minutes until crisp and golden.
Drain the disc well, then drizzle the warm cardamom honey evenly over its lacy surface.
Scatter 3 tbsp pistachios and 1 tbsp dried rose petals over the top and serve at room temperature.
tips: Never boil the honey; warm it just enough to pour so its delicate flavour and goodness stay intact.
The cornflour keeps the wholewheat disc light and crisp, so do not skip it.
Drizzle the honey rather than soaking, as khapli discs absorb fast and can go soft quickly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature as a wholesome festive sweet, lovely with a cup of kesar or cardamom tea.

variations.name: Classic Khoya Gujiya
variations.description: Gujiya is the quintessential Holi sweet, a crescent pastry with a crimped edge stuffed with a rich khoya, coconut and nut filling, deep-fried till golden and dipped in light sugar syrup. The flaky ghee-shortened shell shatters to reveal a fragrant, cardamom-scented centre.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: makes a nutty, sturdy pastry shell that fries crisp and holds the rich filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: half powdered into the filling and half cooked to a syrup for the final dip

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: 4 tbsp rubbed into the dough as shortening and the rest used to deep-fry the gujiyas

steps: Rub 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta until crumbly, then knead with about 0.5 cup water into a stiff, firm dough and rest it covered for 30 minutes.
Roast 1 cup crumbled khoya in a dry pan on low for 5 minutes until light golden, then cool slightly.
Mix the khoya with 0.5 cup desiccated coconut, 0.5 cup chopped nuts, 3 tbsp raisins, 0.5 cup powdered Anveshan Khandsari and 0.75 tsp cardamom into a firm filling.
Roll the dough into small 4-inch discs, place a spoon of filling on one half, moisten the edge, fold into a crescent and crimp tightly sealed.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Ghee on low-medium and fry the gujiyas in batches for 5 to 6 minutes, turning, until pale golden and crisp.
Cook the remaining 0.75 cup Anveshan Khandsari with 0.25 cup water to a one-string syrup, dip each gujiya for 20 seconds, and cool on a rack.
tips: Fry gujiyas on low heat so the shell cooks through and turns crisp without browning too fast.
Seal the crimped edge firmly, as any gap lets the filling leak and spoil the frying ghee.
Cool the khoya filling before stuffing so it stays firm and does not make the pastry soggy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature as a Holi treat, arranged on a platter and dusted with a little slivered pistachio.

variations.name: Dry Coconut Gujiya
variations.description: The Maharashtrian karanji, a dry gujiya with no syrup dip, filled with a fragrant mixture of roasted coconut, poppy seeds and jaggery. The shell is made extra flaky by layering it with a ghee-and-cornflour paste, giving a shatteringly crisp bite that keeps for days.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: forms the layered, flaky karanji shell that stays crisp for days

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the roasted coconut filling with a deep, earthy caramel note

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: rubbed into the dough, blended into the layering paste, and used to fry the karanji

steps: Rub 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, knead with about 0.5 cup water into a stiff dough, and rest it covered for 30 minutes.
Dry-roast 1.5 cups grated dry coconut and 2 tbsp poppy seeds on low until golden and fragrant, then cool and mix with 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 0.75 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp nutmeg.
Whisk 2 tbsp melted Anveshan Ghee with 2 tbsp cornflour into a smooth spreadable paste for layering.
Roll two thin discs, spread the ghee-cornflour paste on one, stack the second on top, and re-roll to create flaky layers before cutting into 4-inch rounds.
Fill each round with the coconut mixture, fold into a crescent, and crimp or twist the edge into the traditional karanji pattern.
Fry in the remaining Anveshan Ghee on low for 6 to 7 minutes until pale gold and blistered, then cool completely before storing.
tips: The ghee-cornflour paste between layers is the secret to a karanji that flakes into crisp sheets.
Cool the coconut filling fully; adding jaggery to warm coconut makes it melt and go sticky.
Fry on very low heat, as these dry gujiyas need slow cooking to crisp through without darkening.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature as a Diwali or Holi snack that keeps for a week in an airtight tin.

variations.name: Chandrakala
variations.description: Chandrakala is the syrup-drenched cousin of gujiya, shaped as a full round pocket rather than a crescent and soaked deeply in saffron sugar syrup until glistening. The khoya and dry-fruit filling turns soft and juicy inside the syrup-laden shell for a truly rich mithai.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: half in the filling and half boiled to a deep syrup that fully soaks the round pockets

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped into the soaking syrup to tint and perfume the chandrakala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: shortens the dough and deep-fries the pockets to a golden crisp before soaking

steps: Rub 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee into 2 cups maida, knead with about 0.5 cup water into a firm dough, and rest it 30 minutes.
Roast 1 cup khoya golden, cool, then mix with 0.5 cup chopped nuts, 2 tbsp chironji, 0.5 cup powdered Anveshan Khandsari and 0.75 tsp cardamom.
Roll two small discs, place filling in the centre of one, cover with the second, and press and crimp the edges into a sealed round pocket.
Prick each pocket lightly with a fork and fry in the remaining Anveshan Ghee on low for 6 minutes until crisp and golden.
Boil the remaining 1.5 cups Anveshan Khandsari with 0.75 cup water and a pinch of Anveshan Saffron to a two-string syrup.
Soak the fried pockets in the warm syrup for 3 to 4 minutes until they turn glossy and juicy, then lift out and serve.
tips: Prick the pockets before frying so steam escapes and they do not burst in the ghee.
Use a slightly thicker two-string syrup here so the round pockets soak up plenty without going limp.
Fry until firm and deep golden, as a well-fried shell holds the syrup soak without falling apart.
