variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm or chilled as a rich festive sweet, garnished with slivered pistachios and a few saffron strands.

variations.name: Baked Dry-Fruit Gujiya
variations.description: A lighter baked gujiya that skips deep-frying entirely, brushed with ghee and oven-crisped to a golden shell. The no-cook filling leans on roasted dry fruits, dates and sattu for a wholesome, protein-rich centre with no added sugar.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: makes a nutty wholegrain shell that bakes crisp with just a brush of ghee

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: roasted gram flour that adds nutty protein and body to the dry-fruit filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a small amount to bind and lightly sweeten the naturally sweet date filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: rubbed into the dough and brushed over the gujiyas so they bake golden and crisp

steps: Rub 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, knead with about 0.4 cup milk into a firm dough, and rest it 20 minutes.
Dry-roast 0.5 cup Anveshan Sattu and 0.75 cup chopped nuts on low for 3 minutes until fragrant, then cool.
Mix the roasted sattu and nuts with 0.75 cup chopped dates, 0.25 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.75 tsp cardamom into a firm, mouldable filling.
Roll the dough into 4-inch discs, fill each, fold into a crescent, and crimp the edge tightly sealed.
Arrange the gujiyas on a lined tray, brush all over with the remaining 2 tbsp melted Anveshan Ghee, and bake at 180 degrees Celsius for 22 to 25 minutes.
Turn once halfway and bake until evenly golden and crisp, then cool on a rack before serving.
tips: Brush ghee generously before and midway through baking so the shell browns and crisps without frying.
The date and sattu filling needs no sugar syrup, making these a lighter everyday festive option.
Seal the edges very well and roll the shell thin, as baked gujiyas will not self-seal in hot fat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a wholesome festive snack, wonderful with masala chai and needing no sugary dip.

variations.name: Classic Khoya Gulab Jamun
variations.description: The definitive festive sweet of soft khoya dumplings fried to a deep chestnut brown and soaked until they drink up a fragrant cardamom syrup. Made the traditional way with fresh khoya, they turn meltingly soft in the centre yet hold a delicate skin, weeping syrup at the first bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the traditional frying medium that gives the jamun an even golden crust and rich aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: unrefined cane sugar that makes a clean, mild syrup for soaking the jamuns

steps: Dissolve 2 cups Anveshan Khandsari Sugar in 2 cups water with the crushed 4 cardamoms and a pinch of saffron, and simmer for 8 minutes to a slightly sticky one-thread syrup, then keep warm.
Grate the 1 cup khoya finely and mix with 3 tbsp maida and 0.25 tsp baking soda, adding milk a spoon at a time to bring it into a soft, smooth, crack-free dough.
Roll the dough into 16 smooth balls without any surface cracks, keeping them covered so they do not dry out.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Ghee to a low-medium temperature of about 130 C, testing with a small piece of dough that should rise slowly without browning at once.
Fry the balls in batches on low heat for 6 to 7 minutes, gently rolling them so they colour to an even deep brown all over.
Lift the jamuns straight into the warm syrup and let them soak for at least 2 hours so they double in size and turn spongy.
Stir 1 tsp rose water into the syrup just before serving and offer the jamuns warm.
tips: Fry on low heat so the centres cook through before the surface darkens.
Keep the syrup warm but never boiling when adding jamuns, so they absorb it without breaking.
Smooth crack-free balls are essential, as cracks make the jamuns split open while frying.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a scoop of vanilla ice cream or a drizzle of extra saffron syrup for a festive dessert.

variations.name: Instant Milk Powder Gulab Jamun
variations.description: A foolproof, quick take that builds the dough from milk powder instead of khoya, coming together in minutes yet frying up just as soft and syrup-soaked. Perfect for a last-minute craving, it gives reliably tender jamuns without the hunt for fresh mawa.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the delicate milk-powder dough gently to a soft golden shell

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: makes a light natural syrup that the instant jamuns soak up quickly

steps: Boil 1.75 cups Anveshan Khandsari Sugar with 1.75 cups water and the crushed 4 cardamoms for 6 minutes to a sticky syrup, add 0.5 tsp lemon juice to stop it crystallising and keep it warm.
In a bowl mix 1 cup milk powder, 4 tbsp maida and 0.25 tsp baking soda, then rub in 1 tbsp melted ghee until crumbly.
Add warm milk a spoon at a time, mixing gently, to form a soft sticky dough, then rest it covered for 10 minutes so the milk powder hydrates.
Grease your palms with a little ghee and roll the dough into 16 smooth crack-free balls.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Ghee to a low temperature and fry the balls in small batches for 5 to 6 minutes, keeping them moving until evenly deep golden.
Drop the hot jamuns into the warm syrup and leave them to soak for at least 1 hour until plump and spongy.
Serve warm, spooning a little extra syrup over each just before eating.
tips: Rest the dough so the milk powder absorbs the milk, otherwise the jamuns can crack when fried.
Do not over-knead, as too much handling makes the instant dough dense and hard.
The lemon juice keeps the syrup smooth and prevents it turning grainy on cooling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm alongside a cup of masala chai, or chill and top with chopped pistachios.

variations.name: Kala Jamun
variations.description: A darker, festive cousin of the gulab jamun with a deep near-black caramelised crust and a firmer, denser bite, made by blending khoya with chhena. Fried longer and rolled in sugar after a shorter soak, it stays chewy outside while the paneer keeps the inside moist.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the jamuns long and slow to develop the signature dark caramel crust

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: used both for the soaking syrup and for the final sugar coating

steps: Simmer 1.5 cups Anveshan Khandsari Sugar with 1.5 cups water and 0.5 tsp cardamom powder for 7 minutes to a one-thread syrup and keep warm, reserving 0.5 cup dry sugar for coating.
Mash the 1 cup khoya and 0.5 cup chhena together until completely smooth, then work in 3 tbsp maida and 0.25 tsp baking soda with a little milk to a firm dough.
Shape the dough into 14 slightly oval balls, tucking a few chopped pistachios into the centre of each.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Ghee to medium-low and fry the balls for 8 to 9 minutes, turning constantly until they darken to a deep, almost blackish brown.
Rest the fried jamuns for 5 minutes, then soak them in the warm syrup for just 30 minutes so they stay firm rather than fully soft.
Lift them out, let the surface dry slightly, then roll each in the reserved dry khandsari sugar for a crackly coat.
Garnish with the remaining pistachios and serve at room temperature.
tips: Adding chhena keeps the dense kala jamun moist despite the long, dark frying.
Fry darker and longer than a regular jamun, but keep the heat low so the inside still cooks.
A shorter soak keeps kala jamun chewy, unlike the fully spongy gulab jamun.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve cut in half to show the moist centre, alongside a scoop of rabri or thickened milk.

variations.name: Bread Gulab Jamun
variations.description: A clever shortcut that turns everyday bread into soft syrup-soaked jamuns in under half an hour, with no khoya or resting needed. The bread crumb fries into a tender dumpling that soaks up cardamom syrup beautifully, a favourite quick fix for sudden guests.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the soft bread balls quickly to a golden, crack-free finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: makes the light cardamom syrup that the bread jamuns absorb

steps: Boil 1.5 cups Anveshan Khandsari Sugar with 1.5 cups water and the crushed 4 cardamoms for 6 minutes into a light syrup and keep it warm.
Trim the crusts off the 8 bread slices and grind them to fine crumbs, then mix in 2 tbsp milk powder.
Add the 0.5 cup milk a little at a time and knead into a smooth soft dough that just holds together without sticking.
Roll the dough into 16 small smooth balls, pressing out any cracks with lightly greased palms.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Ghee to medium-low and fry the balls for 4 to 5 minutes, rolling gently until evenly golden brown.
Immediately slip the hot balls into the warm syrup and let them soak for 30 minutes until soft and plump.
Stir 1 tsp rose water into the syrup, garnish with chopped almonds and serve warm.
tips: Add milk gradually, since too much makes the bread dough sticky and hard to shape.
Fry these quickly and serve soon, as bread jamuns turn soft faster than khoya ones.
Use day-old bread for firmer crumbs that bind into a neater dough.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm right after soaking, topped with slivered almonds and a few strands of saffron.

variations.name: Classic Imarti
variations.description: Imarti, also called jangiri, is a North Indian festival sweet piped from a ground urad-dal batter into an ornate flower shape, deep-fried crisp and steeped in fragrant sugar syrup. Unlike jalebi, its dense dal batter gives a chewy, meaty bite that holds syrup beautifully in every loop.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped into the syrup to give imarti its classic warm orange tint and aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: cooked to a one-string syrup that soaks the crisp dal loops without collapsing them

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the traditional frying fat that crisps the loops and enriches their flavour

steps: Soak 1 cup urad dal in water for 4 hours, drain, and grind it with minimal water into a thick, fluffy, spoonable batter.
Beat 2 tbsp rice flour and a pinch of orange colour into the batter for 3 to 4 minutes until it is airy and holds a soft peak.
Dissolve 1.5 cups Anveshan Khandsari in 1 cup water with a pinch of Anveshan Saffron, 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.5 tsp lemon juice, and simmer 7 minutes to a one-string syrup kept warm.
Fill the batter into a piping cloth with a small hole and pipe concentric flower loops directly into 2 cups hot Anveshan Ghee heated on medium.
Fry each imarti 1 to 2 minutes per side until crisp and golden, keeping the ghee at a steady medium heat.
Soak the fried loops in the warm syrup for 1 minute so they absorb it fully, lift out, and serve warm.
tips: Whip the batter well so it traps air; a beaten batter fries into light, crisp imarti rather than dense ones.
Pipe a small test loop first to check the batter flows in a steady ribbon without breaking.
Keep the syrup at one-string consistency; if it hardens on cooling, warm it with a splash of water before dipping.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a Diwali or wedding sweet, classically paired with a bowl of thick, chilled rabri.

variations.name: Jodhpuri Jaggery Imarti
variations.description: A rustic Marwari take where the crisp urad-dal loops are steeped in a spiced jaggery syrup instead of white sugar, giving a darker colour and earthy caramel depth. A whisper of dry ginger and fennel in the syrup makes it warming and festive.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted and strained into a spiced caramel syrup that soaks the crisp dal loops

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a wood-pressed oil that fries the loops crisp with a clean, nutty character

steps: Soak 1 cup urad dal for 4 hours, drain, and grind to a thick fluffy batter using as little water as possible.
Whip in 2 tbsp rice flour and 0.25 tsp baking soda for 4 minutes until the batter is light and holds its shape.
Melt 1.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 1 cup water, strain out grit, add 0.5 tsp fennel, 0.25 tsp dry ginger and 0.5 tsp cardamom, and simmer 6 minutes to a one-string syrup kept warm.
Pipe flower-shaped loops from a piping cloth into 2 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil heated to a steady medium.
Fry 1 to 2 minutes per side until the loops are deep golden and crisp, then drain off the excess oil.
Dip the hot imarti in the warm jaggery syrup for 1 minute, lift out, and serve warm and glossy.
tips: Strain the melted jaggery twice, as any grit will lodge in the crevices of the loops and taste sandy.
The spiced jaggery syrup is thinner than sugar syrup, so soak the loops a touch longer to load them up.
Grind the dal cold and thick; a watery batter will not pipe clean flower shapes.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm at a winter festival meal, wonderful with a glass of hot spiced milk or badam doodh.

variations.name: Kesar Pista Imarti
variations.description: A regal Lucknawi rendition drenched in a saffron-heavy syrup enriched with rose water and finished with a generous shower of green pistachios. The batter is smooth and airy, and the loops turn a luminous saffron gold that reads as pure celebration.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: used generously so the syrup glows deep gold and perfumes every loop

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: boiled to a one-string syrup that carries the saffron and rose into the loops

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the loops to a rich golden crispness fit for this royal sweet

steps: Soak 1 cup urad dal for 4 hours, drain, and grind with 2 tbsp milk into a very smooth, thick, fluffy batter.
Whip 2 tbsp cornflour into the batter for 4 minutes until it is airy and forms soft peaks.
Dissolve 1.5 cups Anveshan Khandsari in 1 cup water, add 0.5 tsp Anveshan Saffron and 0.5 tsp cardamom, and simmer 7 minutes to a one-string syrup, then stir in 1 tsp rose water off the heat.
Pipe delicate flower loops into 2 cups Anveshan Ghee heated on medium and fry 1 to 2 minutes per side until golden and crisp.
Soak the loops in the warm saffron syrup for 1 minute until they turn a rich gold and drink it in.
Lift out, shower with 3 tbsp slivered pistachios, and serve these fragrant imarti warm.
tips: Grinding the dal with a little milk instead of water gives an extra-smooth, luxurious batter.
Add rose water only after the syrup comes off the heat, as boiling drives off its delicate scent.
Bloom the saffron in a spoon of warm syrup for five minutes first to draw out maximum colour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm at a wedding or Eid table, garnished with a few saffron strands and edible rose petals.

variations.name: Baked Air-Fryer Imarti
variations.description: A lighter reimagining that pipes the same airy urad-dal loops but crisps them in an air fryer with just a brush of ghee, cutting the deep-frying oil dramatically. The loops turn golden and firm, then soak up a light saffron syrup for all the festive flavour with less richness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped into the light syrup for colour and fragrance without heaviness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: cooked to a slightly thinner syrup that soaks the air-crisped loops gently

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: brushed lightly over the loops so they crisp and brown in the air fryer

steps: Soak 1 cup urad dal for 4 hours, drain, and grind to a thick, fluffy batter using minimal water.
Beat in 2 tbsp rice flour and 0.25 tsp baking soda for 4 minutes until the batter is light and pipeable.
Dissolve 1.25 cups Anveshan Khandsari in 1 cup water with a pinch of Anveshan Saffron, 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.5 tsp lemon juice, and simmer 6 minutes to a soft one-string syrup kept warm.
Pipe flower loops onto a greased perforated air-fryer tray and brush each generously with some of the 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee.
Air-fry at 180 degrees Celsius for 10 to 12 minutes, brushing with more ghee and turning once, until the loops are golden and firm.
Soak the hot loops in the warm syrup for 1 to 2 minutes so the drier baked batter absorbs it, then serve warm.
tips: Brush ghee on both sides during air-frying, as the loops need surface fat to brown and crisp without oil.
Air-fried loops are drier than deep-fried ones, so keep the syrup a little thinner and soak them longer.
Pipe the loops slightly thicker than usual so they hold together on the tray without a bath of hot oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a lighter festive dessert, lovely with a scoop of chilled yogurt shrikhand on the side.

variations.name: Classic Jalebi
variations.description: Jalebi is North India's most beloved festival sweet, a lacy spiral of fermented flour batter deep-fried till glass-crisp and soaked in warm saffron sugar syrup. The overnight fermentation gives it a faint tang and the signature airy, crackling crunch that shatters when you bite in.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped into the syrup for the deep amber glow and aroma of authentic jalebi

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: cooked to a one-string syrup that soaks the crisp spirals without turning them soggy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the traditional frying medium that fries the spirals crisp and gives them a rich flavour

steps: Whisk 1 cup maida, 2 tbsp besan and 1 tbsp cornflour with 3 tbsp curd and about 0.5 cup water into a smooth, thick, lump-free batter of pouring ribbon consistency.
Cover and ferment the batter in a warm spot for 10 to 12 hours until it smells faintly sour and shows tiny bubbles on the surface.
Dissolve 1.5 cups Anveshan Khandsari in 0.75 cup water, add a pinch of Anveshan Saffron and 0.5 tsp cardamom, and simmer 6 to 7 minutes to a sticky one-string syrup, then keep it warm.
Stir 0.5 tsp lemon juice into the batter and fill it into a squeeze bottle or a piping cloth with a small nozzle.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Ghee in a wide flat pan on medium and pipe tight overlapping spirals directly into the hot ghee, frying 1 to 2 minutes per side until golden and crisp.
Lift the jalebis, drain for a few seconds, then dunk them in the warm syrup for 30 seconds so they drink it in, and serve hot and glistening.
tips: Keep the batter thick enough to hold its shape as it hits the ghee; a runny batter will not form clean spirals.
The syrup must be warm, not hot, when you dip; too hot and the jalebis go limp, too cold and they will not absorb.
Fry only until deep golden, as under-fried jalebis stay chewy instead of crackling crisp.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot on their own or the classic way beside a bowl of warm rabri or a cool glass of milk.

variations.name: Instant Crispy Jalebi
variations.description: A same-day jalebi that skips the overnight ferment entirely, using fruit salt to aerate the batter so you get crackling spirals within the hour. A generous hit of cornflour is the trick to keeping them crisp for hours after frying.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: boiled to a sticky one-string syrup that instantly soaks the freshly fried spirals

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: a clean wood-pressed oil for deep-frying that keeps the instant jalebis light and crisp

steps: Whisk 1 cup maida and 3 tbsp cornflour with 2 tbsp curd and about 0.5 cup water into a smooth, thick, flowing batter with no lumps.
Dissolve 1.5 cups Anveshan Khandsari in 0.75 cup water with 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.5 tsp lemon juice, and simmer 6 minutes to a one-string syrup, then keep warm.
Just before frying, sprinkle 1 tsp eno and a pinch of yellow colour over the batter and fold gently for 20 seconds until it looks light and slightly frothy.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Sunflower Oil in a flat pan on medium and pipe quick spirals from a squeeze bottle straight into the hot oil.
Fry each batch 1 to 2 minutes per side until deep golden and crisp, pressing them under the oil so they colour evenly.
Dip the hot spirals in the warm syrup for 20 to 30 seconds, lift out, and serve immediately while they still crackle.
tips: Add the eno only at the last moment and fry straight away, as the fizz that lifts the batter fades quickly.
Extra cornflour is what keeps these instant jalebis crisp for longer, so do not reduce it.
If the batter thickens while resting, loosen it with a teaspoon of water rather than more flour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile them warm on a platter dusted with slivered pistachios, perfect for a last-minute festive spread.

variations.name: Mawa Jalebi
variations.description: The famous fat, juicy jalebi of Indore and Jabalpur, made from a rich khoya batter rather than fermented flour. These plump spirals stay soft and molten inside, oozing syrup with every bite, and are traditionally sold by weight rather than the piece.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: infused into the syrup to perfume the rich mawa spirals and tint them gold

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: simmered to a one-string syrup thick enough to cling to the plump mawa jalebis

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: used to deep-fry the mawa spirals to a rich golden softness

steps: Grate 1 cup khoya and mash it smooth with 4 tbsp maida, 0.25 tsp baking powder and enough of the 0.25 cup milk to make a soft, thick, pipeable batter.
Dissolve 1.5 cups Anveshan Khandsari in 0.75 cup water with a pinch of Anveshan Saffron and 0.5 tsp cardamom, and simmer 7 minutes to a one-string syrup kept warm.
Rest the batter for 10 minutes, then spoon it into a piping bag fitted with a plain round nozzle.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Ghee on low to medium and pipe thick two-turn spirals into the ghee, frying gently 2 to 3 minutes per side until golden but still soft inside.
Drain the spirals briefly, then soak them in the warm syrup for 1 to 2 full minutes so the porous mawa drinks it deep.
Lift out, sprinkle with 2 tbsp chopped pistachios, and serve these juicy jalebis warm.
tips: Fry mawa jalebis on lower heat than flour ones, as the khoya browns fast and can burn before cooking through.
Soak them a little longer than regular jalebi so the dense batter absorbs enough syrup to stay moist.
Fresh soft khoya makes the smoothest batter; if yours is dry, crumble and knead it with a splash more milk.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a rich Malwa-region dessert, wonderful with a scoop of vanilla or kesar ice cream.

variations.name: Khapli Wheat Jaggery Jalebi
variations.description: A rustic, wholesome jalebi built on nutty khapli wheat batter and soaked in mineral-rich jaggery syrup instead of white sugar. It trades some of the shatter-crisp lightness for a deeper, caramel-toned sweetness and a satisfying wholegrain bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: gives the batter a nutty wholegrain body and a rustic golden colour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted and strained into a caramel syrup that soaks the wholewheat spirals

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a wood-pressed oil that fries the wheat spirals crisp with a clean, nutty note

steps: Whisk 1 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta and 3 tbsp besan with 3 tbsp curd and about 0.6 cup water into a smooth, thick pouring batter, then rest it 30 minutes.
Melt 1.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 0.75 cup water, strain out any grit, add 0.5 tsp crushed fennel and 0.5 tsp cardamom, and simmer 6 minutes to a sticky one-string syrup kept warm.
Just before frying, beat 0.25 tsp baking soda into the batter until it looks light and slightly aerated.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a flat pan on medium and pipe compact spirals from a squeeze bottle into the hot oil.
Fry 1 to 2 minutes per side until the wholewheat spirals turn deep golden brown and firm at the edges.
Soak the hot jalebis in the warm jaggery syrup for 30 to 40 seconds, drain, and serve warm.
tips: Rest the khapli batter so the wholegrain hydrates fully, giving crisper spirals and fewer breakages.
Always strain melted jaggery before syrup-making, as it carries fine grit that would make the sweet gritty.
These wheat jalebis soften faster than maida ones, so fry and dip in small fresh batches.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a feel-good festive treat, delicious alongside a cup of masala chai on a winter morning.

variations.name: Classic Marwari Kachri Ki Sabzi
variations.description: This Classic Kachri Ki Sabzi is a rustic Rajasthani dry sabzi made from the tangy wild desert cucumber, cooked with a robust mustard-oil tempering. Naturally sour and firm, the kachri crisps at the edges and soaks up bold Marwari spices for a true taste of the desert.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the pungent desert-kitchen oil that stands up to the tangy kachri and bold spices

steps: Wash and slice the 400 g kachri into thin rounds, discarding any very hard seeds from the centre.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just smokes, lower the heat and add 1 tsp cumin and 0.25 tsp asafoetida to sizzle 15 seconds.
Add the grated ginger and slit green chillies and saute for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.25 tsp chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp fennel powder and 1 tsp salt on low for 20 seconds.
Add the sliced kachri and toss well to coat in the spices.
Cover and cook on low for 10 minutes, stirring once, until the kachri softens and releases its tangy juices.
Uncover and stir-fry on medium for 3 minutes until the edges crisp and the sabzi is dry, then serve hot.
tips: Kachri is naturally sour, so it needs no amchur or lemon at all.
Slice the rounds thin so the firm wild cucumber cooks through evenly.
Fennel powder is the classic Marwari touch that rounds the sharp tang of kachri.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra roti and a dollop of white butter for a rustic Rajasthani meal.

variations.name: Kachri Besan Sabzi
variations.description: A richer take where kachri is bound in a roasted gram-flour masala that thickens into a savoury coat on each slice. The nutty besan mellows the wild cucumber's sourness and makes a heartier dry sabzi for the thali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: roasted gram flour that coats the kachri and mellows its wild sourness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil that roasts the sattu smoothly without turning it bitter

steps: Wash and slice the 400 g kachri into thin rounds.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai, add 1 tsp cumin and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them sizzle 15 seconds.
Add 3 tbsp Anveshan Sattu and roast on low heat for 2 minutes until it smells nutty and darkens a shade.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt so the spices coat the roasted sattu.
Add the sliced kachri and toss well so the sattu masala clings to every piece.
Sprinkle two tablespoons of water, cover and cook on low for 10 minutes until the kachri is soft.
Uncover, add 0.5 tsp garam masala, dry off any moisture over 2 minutes and serve hot.
tips: Roast the sattu in the oil first so it loses any raw, pasty taste.
Keep the heat low after adding sattu as it can scorch quickly.
The besan-like sattu tempers the sourness, so no souring agent is needed.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulkas and a bowl of plain curd for a filling meal.

variations.name: Kachri Aloo Ki Sabzi
variations.description: A homely combination where tangy kachri is cooked with soft potato cubes so the mild starch balances the wild cucumber's sourness. The potato soaks up the spiced juices making a filling, everyday dry sabzi popular across Rajasthani homes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the pungent oil that ties the tangy kachri and soft potato together

steps: Wash and slice the 300 g kachri thin, and cube the 3 potatoes into small pieces.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it smokes, lower the heat and add 1 tsp cumin seeds to crackle for 15 seconds.
Add the finely chopped onion and saute for 4 minutes, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt for 20 seconds.
Add the potato cubes and kachri slices and toss to coat in the masala.
Sprinkle a quarter cup of water, cover and cook on low for 14 minutes, stirring gently, until the potato is fork-tender.
Uncover, add 0.5 tsp garam masala, dry off the moisture over 2 minutes and serve hot.
tips: Cut the potato small so it cooks in the same time as the firm kachri.
The potato naturally softens the sourness, so no extra souring agent is needed.
Cook covered on low so both vegetables steam soft without extra water.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot chapatis and a side of sliced onion and green chilli.

variations.name: Kachri Dahi Ki Sabzi
variations.description: A cooling curd-based rendition where kachri simmers in a lightly spiced yogurt gravy that softens its wild tang into a creamy tartness. The mild, soupy sabzi is a soothing counterpoint to Rajasthan's fiery dry preparations.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the desert oil that lends body and pungency to the tangy curd gravy

steps: Wash and slice the 350 g kachri into thin rounds and boil with a pinch of salt for 6 minutes, then drain.
Whisk the 0.75 cup curd with 1.5 tbsp besan, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder until completely smooth.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it smokes, lower the heat and add 1 tsp cumin, 0.25 tsp fenugreek seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida for 15 seconds.
Lower the flame fully and pour in the whisked curd, stirring continuously for 4 minutes so it does not split.
Simmer the gravy on low for 5 minutes until it thickens and the raw besan smell disappears.
Add the boiled kachri and 1 tsp salt and simmer on low for 6 minutes so it soaks up the tangy gravy.
Adjust the seasoning, cook 1 minute more and serve hot with coriander.
tips: Whisk the besan into the curd off the heat so the gravy stays free of lumps.
Keep stirring on low while the curd cooks so it thickens smoothly without curdling.
Boiling the kachri first softens its firm flesh before it goes into the gravy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice or bajra roti and a spoon of ghee to round it off.

variations.name: Classic Punjabi Kadhi Chawal
variations.description: A soul-warming bowl of tangy yogurt-and-besan curry simmered low until thick and silky, studded with soft golden pakoras, spooned over steamed rice. The slow cooking mellows the sourness of the yogurt into a rounded, comforting depth that defines a Punjabi Sunday lunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: carries the final tempering and rounds the tang of the kadhi with a nutty finish

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups sour yogurt with 0.5 cup besan, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp salt and 4 cups water into a smooth lump-free mixture.

For the pakoras, mix the remaining 0.25 cup besan with the chopped onion, a pinch of salt and a little water into a thick batter, then deep-fry small fritters in Anveshan Ghee until golden and set aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a deep pot, add 1 tsp cumin, 0.5 tsp methi seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them crackle for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Pour in the yogurt-besan mixture, bring it to a boil while stirring constantly so it does not split, then lower the heat.
Simmer uncovered on low for 30 minutes, stirring every few minutes, until the kadhi thickens and turns silky and glossy.
Slip the fried pakoras into the simmering kadhi and cook a further 8 minutes so they soak up the gravy and turn soft.
Finish with a tempering of 1 tbsp hot ghee bloomed with 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder poured over the top, and serve with steamed basmati rice.
tips: Keep stirring until the first boil, as this is when the yogurt is most likely to curdle.
Use slightly sour yogurt, since fresh sweet curd makes a flat-tasting kadhi.
Add the pakoras only near the end so they stay soft yet still hold their shape.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle generously over hot rice with the chilli tempering on top and a side of mango pickle.

variations.name: Gujarati Sweet Kadhi Chawal
variations.description: A thinner, drinkable Gujarati kadhi balanced between sweet and sour, without any pakoras, tempered with curry leaves, ginger and green chilli. Jaggery lends a gentle sweetness that offsets the yogurt tang, making it light enough to sip alongside rice or on its own.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the curry-leaf tempering that perfumes this delicate sweet-sour kadhi

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the natural sweetener that gives Gujarati kadhi its gentle sweet balance

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups yogurt with 3 tbsp besan and 4 cups water until completely smooth and free of lumps.
Boil 1.5 cups basmati rice in salted water for 10 minutes until tender, drain and keep warm.
Pour the yogurt mixture into a pot with the grated 1 inch ginger, slit green chillies, 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp salt, and bring to a boil while stirring constantly.
Lower the heat and simmer uncovered for 12 minutes, stirring often, until the kadhi is smooth and lightly thickened but still pourable.
In a small pan heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin, the 2 cloves, 1 inch cinnamon and 12 curry leaves and let them splutter for 20 seconds.
Pour this sizzling tempering into the kadhi, stir once and simmer another 2 minutes to marry the flavours.
Serve the thin sweet-sour kadhi hot over the steamed rice.
tips: Keep this kadhi thin and pourable, quite unlike the thick Punjabi version.
Adjust the jaggery and yogurt so the kadhi tastes gently sweet with a soft tang.
Do not let it boil hard for long, or the delicate yogurt base can turn grainy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or sip warm from a bowl like a soup.

variations.name: Sindhi Kadhi Chawal
variations.description: A tangy, vegetable-laden Sindhi kadhi that is uniquely made without yogurt, thickened instead by roasting besan in oil and soured with tamarind. Drumsticks, cluster beans and okra simmer in the tomato-tinged gravy, making it a hearty one-pot curry poured over rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil that roasts the besan to a deep nutty base for the yogurt-free kadhi

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pot, add 1 tsp cumin, 0.5 tsp methi seeds and 10 curry leaves and let them crackle for 20 seconds.
Add 0.5 cup besan and roast on low heat for 5 minutes, stirring constantly, until it turns golden and smells nutty.
Add the chopped tomatoes, 1 tsp chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp salt, then slowly pour in 4 cups water while whisking so no lumps form.
Bring to a boil, add the drumstick batons and cluster beans, and simmer for 12 minutes until they begin to soften.
Meanwhile shallow-fry the okra in a little oil for 4 minutes to stop it turning slimy, then add it to the kadhi.
Stir in 2 tbsp tamarind pulp and simmer another 8 minutes until the gravy is thick and the vegetables are fully tender.
Cook 1.5 cups basmati rice separately until fluffy and serve the hot Sindhi kadhi ladled over it.
tips: Roast the besan patiently, as this nutty base replaces yogurt as the soul of a Sindhi kadhi.
Fry the okra separately first so it does not make the kadhi sticky.
Balance the tamarind at the end so the sourness is bright but not overpowering.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over rice with a side of crisp aloo tuk or fried potato wedges for the authentic Sindhi combination.

variations.name: No-Onion-No-Garlic Kadhi Chawal
variations.description: A pure satvik kadhi that skips onion, garlic and pakoras entirely, relying on asafoetida and ginger for savoury depth. Light and smooth, it is the everyday fasting-friendly bowl of many households, gentle on the stomach and ready in under half an hour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the hing and cumin tempering that gives this onion-free kadhi its savoury warmth

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups yogurt with 4 tbsp besan, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp chilli powder, 1 tsp salt and 4 cups water until perfectly smooth.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot, add 1 tsp cumin, 0.25 tsp methi seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them sizzle for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add the grated 1 inch ginger and slit green chillies and saute for 30 seconds until the raw aroma lifts.
Pour in the yogurt-besan mixture and bring to a boil while stirring continuously so it stays smooth and does not split.
Lower the heat and simmer uncovered for 18 minutes, stirring often, until the kadhi thickens to a silky pourable gravy.
Cook 1.5 cups basmati rice separately until fluffy while the kadhi simmers.
Rest the kadhi 5 minutes off the heat and serve hot over the steamed rice.
tips: The asafoetida provides the savoury base that onion and garlic would otherwise give.
Stir constantly until the first boil to keep the yogurt from curdling.
Thin with a little hot water if the kadhi thickens too much as it sits.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain rice, a spoon of ghee and roasted papad for a light, satvik meal.

variations.name: Classic Kalakand
variations.description: Kalakand is a soft, grainy milk fudge from Alwar in Rajasthan, made by curdling milk just enough to give it a crumbly, moist texture before setting it with sugar and cardamom. Unlike smooth barfi, its charm lies in the slightly granular bite and milky richness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined sugar that sweetens the grainy milk solids without masking their flavour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the setting tray and adds a gentle richness to the fudge

steps: Bring 1 litre of the full-fat milk to a boil in a heavy pan, then lower the heat and add 2 tbsp lemon juice a little at a time, stirring, until the milk just curdles into soft grains.
Cook the curdled milk for 2 minutes only, so the paneer grains stay soft and moist rather than firm.
In a separate wide pan, boil the remaining 0.5 litre milk over medium heat, stirring often, until it reduces by half to a thick, creamy base, about 12 minutes.
Add the soft curdled grains to the reduced milk and cook on low heat, stirring, for 8 minutes until the mixture thickens and comes together.
Stir in 0.5 cup Anveshan Khandsari and cook for another 6 minutes until the mixture pulls away from the pan yet stays moist and grainy.
Mix in 0.5 tsp cardamom powder, spread into a ghee-greased tray, top with 2 tbsp slivered pistachios, and set for 2 hours before cutting into squares.
tips: Do not over-cook the curdled grains, as firm paneer gives a rubbery kalakand instead of a soft, grainy one.
Keep the finished mixture slightly moist when you spread it, since it firms up considerably as it cools.
A pinch of alum can be used instead of lemon for a milder curdle, but rinse the grains well if you do.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the grainy squares at room temperature during festivals, garnished with an extra sprinkle of pistachios.

variations.name: Instant Paneer Kalakand
variations.description: A ten-minute cheat's kalakand that skips the long milk reduction by combining crumbled fresh paneer with condensed milk. It delivers the signature grainy texture almost instantly, making it the go-to when guests arrive unannounced.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: keeps the quick fudge from sticking and adds a rich finish

steps: Crumble 2 cups fresh paneer finely by hand or in a processor so the texture stays grainy, not paste-like.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a non-stick pan over low heat and add the crumbled paneer, stirring for 2 minutes.
Pour in 1 cup condensed milk and 0.5 cup milk powder, then stir continuously on low heat for 6 to 7 minutes until the mixture thickens and leaves the sides.
Mix in 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and switch off the heat once the mass is thick but still moist.
Spread the mixture into a ghee-greased tray, pressing it into an even layer with a spatula.
Scatter 2 tbsp chopped almonds on top, press gently, and refrigerate for 1 hour before cutting into squares.
tips: Use soft, fresh paneer rather than firm store blocks, as dry paneer gives a stiff, dense result.
Stop cooking while the mixture is still slightly loose, since condensed milk sets hard once cool.
For extra grain, reserve a handful of paneer and fold it in right at the end without cooking.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled, cut into small bites, as a fuss-free party sweet alongside fresh fruit.

variations.name: Kesar Malai Kalakand
variations.description: A richer wedding-style kalakand layered with saffron and reduced cream for a melt-in-the-mouth softness. Bloomed Anveshan Saffron tints it gold and lends a luxurious aroma that lifts it well above the everyday version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: keeps the pale base bright so the saffron colour stands out

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm milk to perfume and colour the creamy fudge

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the tray and enriches the malai layer

steps: Soak 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside to bloom for 10 minutes.
Boil 1 litre milk, then curdle it gently with 2 tbsp lemon juice into soft grains and cook for just 2 minutes before draining lightly.
Reduce the remaining 0.5 litre milk with 0.5 cup fresh cream over medium heat, stirring, for 12 minutes until thick and creamy.
Add the soft grains and 0.5 cup Anveshan Khandsari to the reduced cream and cook on low heat for 8 minutes, then stir in the saffron milk.
Continue cooking for 4 more minutes until thick yet moist, then spread the golden mixture into a ghee-greased tray.
Garnish with 2 tbsp chopped pistachios and rose petals, press gently, and set for 2 hours before slicing.
tips: Adding cream to the reduction gives this kalakand its signature malai softness, so do not skip it.
Bloom the saffron fully before adding, as this releases both its colour and fragrance evenly.
Chill briefly before cutting, but bring back to room temperature to serve for the softest bite.
variations.servingSuggestion: Present the saffron squares on a silver thali at weddings, each topped with a pistachio and a rose petal.

variations.name: Chocolate Kalakand
variations.description: A playful fusion that swirls cocoa through half the grainy milk fudge for a marbled chocolate-and-milk effect. The classic curdled-milk texture stays intact while cocoa adds a modern, kid-friendly twist.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: balances the slight bitterness of cocoa with a clean sweetness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the tray and helps the cocoa blend into the fudge smoothly

steps: Boil 1 litre milk and curdle it gently with 2 tbsp lemon juice into soft grains, cooking for just 2 minutes to keep them moist.
Reduce the remaining 0.5 litre milk over medium heat for 12 minutes until thick, then add the grains and 0.6 cup Anveshan Khandsari.
Cook the mixture on low heat for 8 minutes until it thickens and pulls away from the pan.
Divide the mixture in two; leave one half plain with 0.25 tsp cardamom, and stir 2 tbsp cocoa powder with 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee into the other half over low heat for 2 minutes.
Spoon dollops of the plain and chocolate mixtures alternately into a greased tray, then drag a skewer through to create a marbled pattern.
Scatter 2 tbsp chopped hazelnuts over the top, press lightly, and set for 2 hours before cutting into squares.
tips: Marble the two mixtures while both are still warm so they merge at the edges but keep their distinct colours.
Sift the cocoa to avoid dry lumps, and taste for sweetness since cocoa adds a mild bitter edge.
Toast the hazelnuts lightly before chopping to deepen their flavour against the cocoa.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the marbled squares as a novelty dessert at children's celebrations or a modern festive spread.

variations.name: Classic Kathal Ki Sabzi
variations.description: This Classic Kathal Ki Sabzi turns meaty cubes of raw jackfruit into a dry, deeply spiced North Indian sabzi with a satisfying chew that many call the vegetarian mutton. The kathal is first shallow-fried to seal it, then bhunoed in an onion-tomato masala until every piece is coated in fragrant spice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the pungent oil that seals the jackfruit and gives this sabzi its earthy North Indian character

steps: Oil your hands and knife, then cut the 500 g raw jackfruit into 4 cm cubes discarding the hard core, and rinse well.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just smokes, then shallow-fry the jackfruit cubes in batches for 5 minutes each until light golden, and set them aside.
In the same oil lower the heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1 bay leaf and let them crackle for 20 seconds until aromatic.
Add the finely chopped onions and fry for 6 minutes until golden, then stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until the raw smell fades.
Add the chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and bhuno for 6 minutes until the oil separates.
Return the fried jackfruit, toss to coat, add half a cup of hot water, cover and cook on low for 12 minutes until the cubes are fork-tender.
Uncover, sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala, dry off any moisture over 2 minutes and serve hot with fresh coriander.
tips: Oil your hands and blade before cutting kathal, as its sticky sap clings stubbornly to skin.
Shallow-frying the cubes first stops them from turning mushy during the final cooking.
If short on time, pressure-cook the fried cubes for one whistle instead of the covered simmer.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulkas or jeera rice and a wedge of lemon to lift the earthy spice.

variations.name: Achari Kathal
variations.description: A tangy pickle-spiced take where raw jackfruit soaks up a fennel, nigella and mustard tempering that mirrors the flavour of Indian achaar. A finish of whisked curd off the heat gives it a mellow, lip-smacking sourness quite unlike the everyday dry sabzi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the classic base for achari flavours that carries the pickling spices beautifully

steps: Oil your hands, cube the 500 g jackfruit into 4 cm pieces and rinse, then whisk the 0.5 cup curd smooth with 0.5 tsp turmeric and keep aside.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it smokes, shallow-fry the jackfruit for 6 minutes until golden and lift out.
Lower the heat and make the achari tadka by adding 1 tsp fennel, 0.5 tsp nigella, 0.5 tsp mustard, 0.25 tsp fenugreek and 2 broken dry red chillies, frying for 30 seconds until they splutter.
Add the finely chopped onion and saute for 4 minutes until soft and pale gold.
Stir in 1 tsp chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, return the jackfruit, and toss for 2 minutes to coat in the pickling spices.
Lower the flame fully, pour in the whisked curd and stir continuously for 3 minutes so it does not split, then add half a cup of water.
Cover and simmer for 10 minutes until tender, finish with 1 tsp amchur, and serve warm.
tips: Always whisk the curd and add it on low heat while stirring so it blends without curdling.
Lightly crush the fennel and nigella between your palms to release more of their pickle aroma.
A spoon of ready achaar masala can be added for an even sharper pickle-shop flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with plain paratha and a cooling boondi raita to balance the tangy heat.

variations.name: Restaurant-Style Kathal Masala
variations.description: A rich dhaba-restaurant gravy where jackfruit simmers in a silky cashew-tomato base finished with cream and kasuri methi. The luscious masala clings to the meaty cubes making it a showpiece curry for special vegetarian spreads.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: gives the restaurant gravy its glossy richness and rounds off the spices

steps: Oil your hands, cube the 500 g jackfruit, and boil it with a pinch of salt for 10 minutes until just tender, then drain.
Soak the 12 cashews in warm water for 10 minutes, then blend with the chopped onions and tomatoes into a smooth paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over medium heat, add 3 cardamom pods and let them puff for 20 seconds.
Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry 1 minute, then pour in the onion-tomato-cashew paste and cook for 10 minutes, stirring, until the ghee separates.
Add 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and cook 2 minutes until the masala turns glossy and deep red.
Add the boiled jackfruit with one cup of hot water, cover and simmer on low for 12 minutes so the cubes soak up the gravy.
Lower the heat, stir in 3 tbsp cream, crushed 1 tsp kasuri methi and 0.5 tsp garam masala, simmer 2 minutes and serve.
tips: Boiling the jackfruit before it meets the gravy keeps the cooking time short and even.
Soaked cashews blend into a lump-free paste that gives the gravy its restaurant sheen.
Add the cream on low heat so the rich gravy stays smooth and does not split.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or laccha paratha and a side of sliced onion salad for a festive meal.

variations.name: South-Indian Coconut Kathal
variations.description: A coastal Kerala-style rendition where jackfruit is simmered in a freshly ground coconut masala and finished with a curry-leaf and mustard tempering in coconut oil. Mild, aromatic and slightly sweet, it is a world away from the fiery North Indian versions.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the defining Kerala fat that carries the curry-leaf tadka and rounds the coconut masala

steps: Oil your hands, cube the 500 g jackfruit and boil it with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 12 minutes until tender, then drain.
Grind the 0.75 cup grated coconut with the slit green chillies, 0.5 tsp cumin and a splash of water into a coarse paste.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan, add the sliced shallots and saute for 3 minutes until soft and golden.
Add the boiled jackfruit and the ground coconut paste, mix well, and simmer for 8 minutes on low so the flavours mingle.
In a separate small pan heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop for 15 seconds.
Add 2 broken dry red chillies and 12 curry leaves to the tempering and fry for 20 seconds until crisp and fragrant.
Pour the sizzling tempering over the jackfruit, fold gently, and serve warm.
tips: Grind the coconut coarsely rather than to a fine paste for the right rustic texture.
Use small pearl shallots for the authentic sweet depth of a Kerala thoran-style dish.
Add the coconut paste only after the jackfruit is soft so it does not turn grainy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed matta rice and a bowl of thin rasam or plain curd for a coastal thali.

variations.name: Classic Lauki Kofta
variations.description: Grated bottle gourd is bound with besan into soft dumplings, fried golden and simmered in a spiced onion-tomato gravy. This comforting North Indian curry is light yet satisfying, the melt-in-mouth koftas soaking up a tangy, mildly spiced sauce.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: cooks the gravy base and lends the koftas a rich, buttery finish as they simmer

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for deep-frying the koftas to an even golden crust without any greasiness

steps: Peel and grate 500 g bottle gourd, squeeze out and reserve its water, then mix the pulp with 0.5 cup besan, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp salt and a pinch of red chilli into a firm dough that just holds shape.
Heat 1 cup Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil to 170C, shape the mixture into 12 small balls, and deep-fry them in batches for 4 to 5 minutes until evenly golden, then drain on paper.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them splutter for 20 seconds, then add the finely chopped onions and fry for 6 minutes until golden.

Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute, then add the pureed tomatoes with 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 8 minutes until the ghee separates.
Pour in the reserved lauki water plus enough water to make 2 cups of gravy, bring to a boil, then lower the heat and simmer for 5 minutes.
Slip in the fried koftas just 3 minutes before serving so they stay soft, sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala and 3 tbsp chopped coriander and serve hot.
tips: Squeeze the grated lauki really well and add besan gradually, as too much water makes the koftas fall apart in the oil.
Fry one test kofta first, and if it disintegrates add a spoon more besan to firm up the mixture.
Add the koftas to the gravy only just before serving so they hold their shape and do not turn mushy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jeera rice or tawa rotis, garnished with a swirl of cream and extra coriander.

variations.name: Shahi Malai Lauki Kofta
variations.description: A rich restaurant-style version where the koftas are stuffed with a nut-and-raisin filling and bathed in a creamy cashew-and-white-gravy. Mildly sweet and luxuriously smooth, this pale, saffron-kissed curry turns humble bottle gourd into banquet food.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: enriches the delicate cashew gravy and keeps it pale and glossy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: a neutral oil for frying so the shahi koftas stay light in colour and flavour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk it gives the shahi gravy its golden hue and royal aroma

steps: Grate 500 g bottle gourd, squeeze it dry, and mix the pulp with 0.5 cup besan and 0.5 tsp salt into a firm dough.

Chop 8 cashews and 2 tbsp raisins for the filling, then shape the dough around a spoon of this mixture to make 10 stuffed balls and deep-fry them in 1 cup Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sunflower Oil at 170C for 5 minutes until pale gold.
Boil the 2 onions and remaining 12 cashews in a cup of water for 8 minutes, cool and blend to a completely smooth white paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat, add 3 lightly crushed cardamoms, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the cashew-onion paste with 1 tsp salt and 0.25 tsp white pepper and cook gently on low for 7 minutes without browning, then add 1.5 cups water and simmer for 5 minutes.
Lower the heat, stir in 4 tbsp cream and the saffron milk, slip in the fried koftas 3 minutes before serving, and finish gleaming golden and creamy.
tips: Keep the flame low while cooking the cashew paste so the gravy stays pale rather than browning.
Steep the saffron in warm milk for ten minutes so it releases both colour and fragrance fully.
Assemble the koftas into the gravy at the table if you can, so they keep their soft, stuffed centre.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan, sheermal or a mild zafrani pulao, garnished with slivered pistachios and a saffron strand.

variations.name: Baked Lauki Kofta Curry
variations.description: A lighter everyday version where the koftas are baked or air-fried instead of deep-fried and simmered in a lean tomato-yogurt gravy. Just as tender inside but far less oily, it lets the fresh bottle gourd flavour shine through a bright, tangy sauce.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a small amount tempers the gravy and brushes the koftas before baking for a golden crust

steps: Grate 500 g bottle gourd, squeeze it dry, and mix the pulp with 0.5 cup besan, 2 tbsp oats flour, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt into a firm dough.
Shape into 12 balls, brush lightly with a little Anveshan Ghee, and bake at 200C for 20 minutes, turning once, until golden and firm on the outside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them splutter, then add the chopped onion and fry for 5 minutes until soft.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the pureed tomatoes with 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 8 minutes until thick and glossy.
Whisk 0.5 cup curd smooth, lower the heat and stir it in slowly so it does not split, then add 1.5 cups water and simmer the gravy for 6 minutes.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the top, add the baked koftas 3 minutes before serving so they stay tender, and serve warm.
tips: Adding oats flour helps the baked koftas bind firmly without deep-frying and keeps them from cracking.
Always add the whisked curd off the boil and stir continuously to keep the gravy from curdling.
If baking, brush the koftas with a little ghee halfway through so they colour evenly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with phulka or brown rice and a kachumber salad for a lighter, wholesome meal.

variations.name: Bengali Lau Kofta (Mustard-style)
variations.description: A Bengali interpretation where the lau koftas swim in a light mustard-and-poppy-seed gravy fragrant with nigella and green chilli, cooked in pungent mustard oil. Sharper and more aromatic than the North Indian curry, it carries the unmistakable kick of freshly ground mustard.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the defining Bengali fat for both frying the koftas and building the pungent mustard gravy

steps: Grate 500 g bottle gourd, squeeze it dry, and mix with 0.5 cup besan, 2 tbsp rice flour, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt into a firm dough, then shape into 12 balls.
Heat 0.5 cup Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until it just smokes, then fry the koftas in batches on medium for 5 minutes until golden and crisp, and remove, leaving about 3 tbsp oil in the pan.
Soak 2 tbsp mustard seeds and 1 tbsp poppy seeds in warm water for 15 minutes, then grind with 2 green chillies into a smooth paste.
Reheat the oil, add 0.5 tsp nigella seeds and 2 slit green chillies and let them crackle for 15 seconds, then add the chopped tomato and cook for 3 minutes until soft.
Stir in the mustard-poppy paste with 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp sugar, cook for 2 minutes, then add 2 cups water and simmer the gravy for 6 minutes.
Slip in the fried koftas, simmer gently for 4 minutes so they drink up the mustard gravy, and serve hot with the oil floating on top.
tips: Soak the mustard seeds before grinding and add a pinch of salt to the paste to keep it from turning bitter.
A little sugar is traditional in Bengali gravies and balances the sharpness of the mustard beautifully.
Fry the koftas until properly crisp so they hold together in the thin mustard gravy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice, letting the pungent mustard gravy soak into each spoonful.

variations.name: Classic Malpua
variations.description: Malpua is an ancient Indian sweet pancake made from a lightly fermented flour and milk batter, fried in ghee until the edges turn lacy and crisp while the centre stays soft, then soaked in cardamom sugar syrup. Fennel and a hint of black pepper give it its signature warm aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: cooked to a one-string syrup that soaks the fried pancakes to juicy softness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: shallow-fries the malpuas so the edges crisp into a lacy golden frill

steps: Whisk 1 cup maida and 2 tbsp semolina with 1.25 cups milk into a smooth, thin, lump-free batter of pouring consistency.
Stir in 1 tsp crushed fennel and 0.25 tsp black pepper, cover, and rest the batter for 1 hour so the semolina swells.
Dissolve 1.25 cups Anveshan Khandsari in 0.5 cup water with 0.5 tsp cardamom and simmer 6 minutes to a sticky one-string syrup, then keep it warm.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan on medium and pour in a ladle of batter, letting it spread into a 4-inch disc with lacy edges.
Fry 1 to 2 minutes per side, spooning hot ghee over the top, until both sides are golden and the frilled edges are crisp.
Dip each hot malpua in the warm syrup for 30 seconds, lift out, garnish with 2 tbsp pistachios, and serve warm.
tips: Keep the batter thin and pourable; a thick batter gives dense malpuas without the signature crisp lace edge.
Fry on steady medium heat, as high heat browns the outside before the centre sets.
Resting the batter is essential so the semolina hydrates and the pancakes hold together in the ghee.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a generous drizzle of chilled rabri spooned over the top, the classic malpua-rabri pairing.

variations.name: Bengali Rabri Malpua
variations.description: The Bengali sweet-shop malpua is made almost entirely from reduced milk and khoya, giving thick, small, intensely rich pancakes with a custardy centre. Fried in ghee and drowned in syrup, they are traditionally crowned with saffron rabri during festivals like Poila Boishakh.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: infused into both the syrup and the rabri topping for colour and fragrance

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: boiled to a one-string syrup that soaks the rich milk pancakes deeply

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the dense milk pancakes to a golden, custardy softness

steps: Grate 0.75 cup khoya and whisk it smooth with 3 tbsp maida and 1 cup milk into a thick, slightly grainy pancake batter.
Stir in 0.5 tsp crushed fennel and rest the batter for 20 minutes until it thickens slightly.
Dissolve 1.25 cups Anveshan Khandsari in 0.5 cup water with a pinch of Anveshan Saffron and 0.5 tsp cardamom, and simmer 6 minutes to a one-string syrup kept warm.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium-low and drop small ladles of batter to form thick 3-inch discs.
Fry gently 2 minutes per side, basting with ghee, until deep golden and set but still soft in the middle.
Soak the malpuas in warm syrup for 1 minute, plate them, and spoon 1 cup saffron rabri generously over the top before serving.
tips: These khoya-rich pancakes are thicker and denser, so fry them smaller and slower than flour malpuas.
Do not thin the batter too much; a thick batter is what gives the signature custardy Bengali centre.
Serve soon after topping with rabri, as the pancakes are at their best warm under cool, creamy rabri.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a festive Bengali dessert, chilled slightly and layered with extra rabri and a scatter of chopped nuts.

variations.name: Kela Malpua
variations.description: A homely Bihari and eastern UP malpua where mashed ripe banana sweetens and binds a wholewheat batter, so it needs far less syrup. The banana caramelises at the edges into a fragrant, toffee-like frill, making these a beloved teej and festival treat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: gives the banana pancakes a nutty wholegrain body and rustic character

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the batter itself so these malpuas need only a light syrup dip

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the banana batter so the edges caramelise into a crisp toffee frill

steps: Mash 2 ripe bananas smooth and whisk them with 1 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.75 cup milk into a thick, pourable batter.
Stir in 1 tsp crushed fennel, 0.5 tsp cardamom and 3 tbsp grated coconut, then rest the batter for 20 minutes.
Loosen the batter with up to 0.25 cup water if needed to a thick dropping consistency that spreads slowly.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium and pour small ladles into 3-inch discs, spooning ghee around the edges.
Fry 2 minutes per side until deep golden and the banana edges caramelise into a crisp, fragrant frill.
Drain the malpuas on a rack and serve warm, needing no syrup thanks to the sweet banana-jaggery batter.
tips: Use very ripe, spotted bananas, as they mash smoother and lend the deepest natural sweetness and aroma.
Because the batter is already sweet, a quick dip in light syrup or none at all keeps these from being cloying.
Fry on medium so the sugars in the banana caramelise slowly instead of burning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a rustic festival sweet, dusted with a little more coconut or a drizzle of honey.

variations.name: Coconut Rava Malpua
variations.description: A coastal malpua built on semolina and fresh coconut fried in fragrant coconut oil, giving a coarser, chewier texture with a tropical aroma. Popular along the Konkan coast, these are soaked in a light cardamom syrup that lets the coconut shine.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: cooked to a light one-string syrup that soaks the coconut pancakes

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: fries the pancakes and layers in the fragrant coastal coconut aroma

steps: Whisk 1 cup semolina and 0.75 cup grated coconut with 1 cup coconut milk into a thick batter, then rest it 30 minutes so the rava swells.
Dissolve 1 cup Anveshan Khandsari in 0.5 cup water with 0.5 tsp cardamom and simmer 5 minutes to a light one-string syrup kept warm.
Stir 0.5 tsp crushed fennel and 2 tbsp chopped cashews into the rested batter and loosen with a splash of water if too stiff.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan on medium and pour small ladles into 3-inch discs.
Fry 2 minutes per side, adding oil as needed, until golden and crisp-edged with a chewy coconut centre.
Dip the warm malpuas briefly in the syrup for 20 to 30 seconds and serve warm.
tips: Rest the semolina batter fully so the grains soften, otherwise the pancakes turn gritty.
Fresh coconut gives the best chew and aroma, but desiccated coconut soaked in warm coconut milk also works.
Keep the syrup light and the dip brief, as the coconut flavour is delicate and easily masked by heavy syrup.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a coastal festival sweet, topped with toasted coconut flakes and extra fried cashews.

variations.name: Classic Amrakhand
variations.description: The summer star of Maharashtra and Gujarat, where thick hung curd is whisked smooth with sweet Alphonso mango puree into a sunny, creamy amrakhand. Tangy yogurt and fragrant mango balance perfectly, making it the dessert of choice through the short mango season.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: finely ground khandsari sweetens the amrakhand gently, letting the ripe mango flavour lead

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a little bilona ghee toasts the almond garnish that crowns the chilled amrakhand

steps: Hang 4 cups full-fat yogurt in muslin in the fridge for 6 to 8 hours until it drains into about 2 cups of thick hung curd.
Grind 1/2 cup Anveshan Khandsari to a fine powder, then whisk it into the hung curd gradually until completely smooth.
Fold in 1 cup Alphonso mango puree and 1/2 tsp cardamom powder, whisking gently until the amrakhand is an even sunny yellow and lump-free.
Taste and adjust the sweetness, keeping in mind the mango already brings plenty of its own.
Toast 12 slivered almonds in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee for 1 minute until fragrant, then fold half in.
Chill the amrakhand for at least 2 hours, then serve topped with fresh mango cubes and the reserved toasted almonds.
tips: Use ripe, non-fibrous mangoes like Alphonso or Kesar so the amrakhand stays smooth and intensely fruity.
Whisk the mango in gently, as over-beating can make the shrikhand loose and thin.
If your mangoes are very sweet, cut back the khandsari and let the fruit carry the sweetness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve well chilled in katoris topped with fresh mango cubes, alongside hot pooris for a classic summer festive meal.

variations.name: Kesar Pista Mango Shrikhand
variations.description: A regal version where saffron and a heavy hand of ground pistachios join the mango, giving a deeper gold colour and a nutty, aromatic richness. Speckled green and gold, this is the celebration amrakhand made for special guests and festive spreads.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: khandsari keeps the shrikhand pale so the saffron gold and pistachio green show clearly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: pure saffron steeped in warm milk deepens the colour and adds a floral note to the mango cream

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee toasts the pistachio slivers that garnish the saffron shrikhand

steps: Hang 4 cups full-fat yogurt in muslin in the fridge for 6 to 8 hours until it drains into about 2 cups of thick hung curd, and steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk.
Grind 15 pistachios to a slightly coarse powder, and grind 1/2 cup Anveshan Khandsari fine.
Whisk the powdered khandsari into the hung curd until smooth, then fold in 1 cup Alphonso mango puree.
Whisk in the saffron milk, the ground pistachios and 1/2 tsp cardamom powder until the shrikhand turns a rich gold flecked with green.
Toast the remaining 5 pistachio slivers in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee for 1 minute, then reserve them for garnish.
Chill for 2 hours and serve topped with the toasted pistachios and a few saffron strands.
tips: Grind the pistachios only slightly coarse so they lend texture and colour without turning the shrikhand pasty.
Steep the saffron in warm milk for at least 10 minutes to draw out its full colour before whisking it in.
Blanch and peel the pistachios for the brightest green flecks in the finished shrikhand.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled in glasses layered with a spoon of mango puree, garnished with pistachios and saffron, a jewelled dessert for a festive dinner.

variations.name: Vegan Mango Shrikhand
variations.description: A dairy-free amrakhand built on thick strained coconut yogurt blended with cashew cream and mango, sweetened with jaggery. Rich, tangy and tropical, it delivers all the creaminess of the classic without any dairy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery pairs naturally with the coconut and mango for a warm, dairy-free sweetness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed coconut oil toasts the pistachio garnish and reinforces the tropical aroma

steps: Hang 3 cups thick coconut yogurt in muslin in the fridge for 4 to 5 hours to drain off excess liquid and concentrate it.
Soak 1/2 cup cashews in hot water for 20 minutes, then blend them with a splash of water into a smooth, thick cream.
Melt 1/3 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water, strain out grit, and cool the syrup.
Whisk the strained coconut yogurt with the cashew cream, jaggery syrup and 1/2 tsp cardamom powder until silky and smooth.
Fold in 1 cup Alphonso mango puree until the shrikhand is an even golden and creamy, then chill for 2 hours.
Toast 12 pistachio slivers in 1 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil for 1 minute and serve the shrikhand topped with them and fresh mango cubes.
tips: Drain the coconut yogurt well, as thin yogurt makes a runny shrikhand that will not hold its creamy body.
Blend the soaked cashews until completely smooth so the shrikhand has no grainy texture.
Use full-fat coconut yogurt for the richest result, and chill thoroughly before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled in glasses topped with mango cubes and toasted pistachios, a luscious dairy-free dessert for vegan guests.

variations.name: Mango Shrikhand Parfait
variations.description: A modern plated take where classic mango shrikhand is layered in glasses with crushed nutty biscuit and fresh mango for a chic parfait. The contrast of creamy amrakhand, crunchy crumb and juicy fruit turns the traditional sweet into an elegant dinner-party dessert.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: khandsari sweetens the shrikhand layer gently so the mango stays the star of the parfait

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee binds the crushed biscuit crumb into a buttery, crunchy parfait base

steps: Hang 4 cups full-fat yogurt in muslin in the fridge for 6 to 8 hours until it drains into about 2 cups of thick hung curd.
Grind 1/2 cup Anveshan Khandsari fine, whisk it into the hung curd until smooth, then fold in 1 cup mango puree and 1/2 tsp cardamom powder to make the shrikhand.
Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and mix it into 1 cup crushed digestive biscuits until the crumb clumps together like wet sand.
Press a spoonful of the buttery crumb into the base of four serving glasses to form the bottom layer.
Spoon over a layer of mango shrikhand, then a layer of fresh mango cubes, and repeat the crumb, shrikhand and mango layers once more.
Chill the parfaits for 2 hours and top with 12 chopped pistachios and a few mango cubes just before serving.
tips: Assemble the parfaits shortly before serving so the biscuit crumb keeps some of its crunch against the creamy shrikhand.
Use chilled, firm mango cubes so the layers stay distinct and do not bleed into the cream.
For a no-biscuit version, use a ghee-toasted mix of crushed nuts and oats as the crunchy layer.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the layered parfaits in clear glasses so the mango, cream and crumb show through, an elegant close to a summer dinner party.

variations.name: Classic Methi Malai Mushroom
variations.description: This Classic Methi Malai Mushroom simmers button mushrooms in a creamy cashew gravy laced with fresh fenugreek leaves. The gentle bitterness of methi cuts through the rich malai base, creating the restaurant-favourite balance of sweet, creamy and mildly herby.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: gives the malai gravy its rich base and rounds off the methi's bitterness

steps: Boil the 2 chopped onions with the 12 cashews and 2 green cardamoms for 6 minutes, cool and blend to a smooth white paste.
Wash and quarter the 300 g mushrooms, and chop the 1 cup fenugreek leaves finely after rinsing them well.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle for 15 seconds.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the slit green chillies and fry for 1 minute, then pour in the onion-cashew paste and cook 6 minutes until it thickens and the ghee separates.
Add the quartered mushrooms with 1 tsp salt and cook for 5 minutes until they release and reabsorb their water.
Stir in the chopped methi and cook 4 minutes until it wilts and its bitterness softens into the gravy.
Lower the heat, add 4 tbsp cream and 0.5 tsp garam masala, simmer 3 minutes until creamy and serve hot.
tips: Blanch the methi in hot water for a minute and squeeze it if you prefer a milder bitterness.
Boil the onions before blending so the gravy stays pale and does not brown.
Add the cream on low heat so the malai gravy stays smooth and never splits.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or jeera rice and a side of kachumber salad.

variations.name: Restaurant-Style Methi Malai Mushroom
variations.description: A luxurious restaurant rendition with a double-rich base of cashew and khoya, finished with cream and a hint of white pepper for an ivory, velvety gravy. The mushrooms and methi float in a decadent sauce meant for special occasions.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: builds the rich restaurant base and gives the ivory gravy its sheen

steps: Boil the 2 chopped onions with 15 cashews and 3 cardamoms for 7 minutes, cool and blend into a silky paste.
Wash and slice the 300 g mushrooms, and finely chop the 1 cup methi leaves after rinsing.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and saute for 1 minute without letting it brown.
Pour in the onion-cashew paste and cook on low for 7 minutes, stirring constantly, until thick and the ghee separates at the edges.
Crumble in the 3 tbsp khoya and stir for 2 minutes until it melts smoothly into the gravy.
Add the sliced mushrooms with 1 tsp salt and cook 5 minutes, then add the chopped methi and cook 4 minutes until wilted.
Lower the heat, stir in 5 tbsp cream, 0.25 tsp white pepper and 0.5 tsp sugar, simmer 3 minutes and serve.
tips: Grating the khoya before adding helps it melt evenly without forming lumps.
White pepper keeps the gravy pale while adding a gentle heat, unlike black pepper.
Cook the onion paste on low so it stays ivory rather than colouring the rich gravy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with laccha paratha or saffron pulao and a chilled glass of sweet lassi.

variations.name: Kasuri Methi Malai Mushroom
variations.description: A quick everyday version that swaps fresh fenugreek for aromatic kasuri methi, making it possible any time of year. The dried leaves lend a concentrated, toasty aroma to a lighter cashew-cream gravy for a fuss-free weeknight dinner.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: toasts the kasuri methi to release its aroma and enriches the quick gravy

steps: Soak the 10 cashews in the 0.5 cup warm milk for 10 minutes, then blend with the chopped onion into a smooth paste.
Wash and quarter the 300 g mushrooms and keep aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle for 15 seconds.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the slit green chillies and fry 1 minute, then add the onion-cashew-milk paste and cook 5 minutes until it thickens.
Add the quartered mushrooms with 1 tsp salt and cook 5 minutes until they soften and release their liquid.
Crush the 2 tbsp kasuri methi between your palms and stir it in, cooking 2 minutes to release its toasty aroma.
Lower the heat, add 3 tbsp cream and 0.5 tsp garam masala, simmer 2 minutes and serve hot.
tips: Always crush kasuri methi between the palms before adding to release its full fragrance.
Soaking cashews in warm milk gives a quicker, silkier paste than water.
This version keeps well, as dried methi holds its flavour better than fresh in leftovers.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tawa roti or steamed basmati rice for an easy weeknight dinner.

variations.name: Dhaba-Style Methi Mushroom Masala
variations.description: A rustic dhaba take with a bolder onion-tomato masala where the malai plays a supporting role to a spicier, saucier gravy. Cooked in mustard oil with a smoky bhuna base, it delivers robust, roadside flavour rather than delicate creaminess.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: gives the dhaba gravy its smoky, robust base and pungent depth

steps: Wash and quarter the 300 g mushrooms and finely chop the 1 cup methi leaves after rinsing.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it smokes, lower the heat and add 1 tsp cumin seeds to crackle 15 seconds.
Add the finely chopped onions and fry for 6 minutes until deep golden, then add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Add the pureed tomatoes with 1.25 tsp chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and bhuno for 6 minutes until the oil separates.
Add the quartered mushrooms and cook 5 minutes until they soften and release their liquid into the masala.
Stir in the chopped methi and cook 4 minutes until it wilts and blends into the saucy gravy.
