Lower the heat, swirl in 2 tbsp cream and 0.5 tsp garam masala, simmer 2 minutes and serve hot.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to smoking point first so its raw pungency mellows.
Keep the gravy saucier than the malai versions for an authentic dhaba texture.
Add just a little cream at the end so it enriches without hiding the bold spices.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thick tandoori roti or missi roti and a raw onion salad with lemon.

variations.name: Classic Milk Barfi
variations.description: Milk barfi, or doodh peda's fudgy cousin, is a soft North Indian sweet made by slow-roasting khoya until it turns creamy, then setting it with sugar and cardamom into firm diamonds. This classic keeps the colour pale and the flavour milky, finished with a scatter of pistachio slivers.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined cane sugar that keeps the barfi pale while lending a clean sweetness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the setting tray and keeps the roasting khoya from catching

steps: Grease a small tray with a little Anveshan Ghee and line it with parchment so the set barfi lifts out cleanly.
Warm 2 cups grated khoya in a heavy non-stick pan over low heat with 2 tbsp milk, stirring for about 5 minutes until it softens to a smooth, creamy mass.
Add 0.75 cup Anveshan Khandsari and keep stirring on low heat; the mixture will loosen and turn liquid, about 4 minutes, then begin to thicken again.
Cook, stirring constantly, for 8 to 10 minutes until the khoya pulls away from the sides of the pan and leaves a light film of fat, a sign it is ready to set.
Turn off the heat, mix in 0.5 tsp cardamom powder, and pour the mixture into the greased tray, pressing it into an even half-inch layer.
Scatter 2 tbsp slivered pistachios over the top, press gently, and cool for 2 hours until firm before cutting into diamonds.
tips: Do not over-roast the khoya after adding sugar, or the barfi turns hard and chewy instead of soft and sliceable.
If your khoya is dry and crumbly, add an extra tablespoon of milk while softening it for a smoother set.
Cut the barfi only after it has cooled completely, as warm barfi tears rather than giving clean edges.
variations.servingSuggestion: Arrange the diamonds in a mithai box lined with edible silver leaf for festivals, or serve alongside evening chai.

variations.name: Kesar Milk Barfi
variations.description: A saffron-scented festive version where strands of Anveshan Saffron bloom in warm milk to stain the barfi a warm gold. Rose water and crushed almonds make it richer and more aromatic than the plain milk classic, perfect for Diwali gifting.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: keeps the base pale so the saffron colour shows through beautifully

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm milk to colour and perfume the entire barfi

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the tray and adds a rich sheen to the festive fudge

steps: Soak 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk for 10 minutes until the milk turns a deep golden orange.
Grease a tray with Anveshan Ghee and keep it ready near the stove for quick setting.
Melt 2 cups grated khoya in a heavy pan over low heat, stirring for about 5 minutes until creamy, then pour in the saffron milk and stir it through.
Add 0.75 cup Anveshan Khandsari and cook on low heat, stirring, for 10 minutes until the mixture thickens and leaves the sides of the pan.
Fold in 2 tbsp of the chopped almonds and 0.5 tsp rose water off the heat, then spread the fudge into the greased tray in an even layer.
Sprinkle the remaining 1 tbsp almonds over the top, press lightly, and let it set for 2 hours before slicing into squares.
tips: Bloom the saffron in warm, not boiling, milk so its colour and aroma release fully without turning bitter.
Add the rose water only after switching off the heat, as its fragrance evaporates quickly over a flame.
For a marbled look, swirl a spoon of plain khoya through the saffron mixture just before it sets.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in gold-foil cases as a festival gift, topped with a single saffron strand on each piece.

variations.name: Instant Milk Powder Barfi
variations.description: A shortcut barfi made without khoya, using full-fat milk powder cooked with cream and ghee into a soft fudge in under fifteen minutes. It is the reliable version for last-minute gifting when there is no time to reduce milk or source mawa.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: cooks the milk powder to a fudgy texture and prevents any raw powdery taste

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: dissolves into the hot milk mixture for a clean, natural sweetness

steps: Warm 0.25 cup milk with 0.5 cup fresh cream and 0.5 cup Anveshan Khandsari in a non-stick pan over low heat until the sugar dissolves, about 2 minutes.
Lower the heat, add 1.5 cups full-fat milk powder gradually, and whisk quickly so no lumps form.
Stir in 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and cook the mixture on low heat for 5 to 6 minutes, stirring constantly, until it thickens into a soft dough that leaves the pan.
Mix in 0.5 tsp cardamom powder, then spread the mixture into a ghee-greased tray in a half-inch layer.
Press 2 tbsp chopped cashews evenly over the surface while the barfi is still warm.
Cool for 1 hour until set, then cut into neat squares and serve.
tips: Keep the heat low throughout, as milk powder scorches easily and turns the barfi bitter.
If the mixture stays too soft, cook it a minute longer; if it turns grainy, add a splash of warm milk to smooth it.
This barfi sets faster in the refrigerator but tastes best served at room temperature.
variations.servingSuggestion: Dust the squares with a little extra cardamom and serve as a quick after-dinner sweet with masala chai.

variations.name: Chocolate Milk Barfi
variations.description: A two-tone fusion barfi with a plain milk layer set beneath a cocoa-rich chocolate layer, giving children and grown-ups the best of pedas and fudge. The khoya base stays traditional while cocoa and walnuts modernise the top.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: sweetens both layers with a mellow, unrefined taste

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the tray and helps the cocoa blend smoothly into the top layer

steps: Soften 2 cups grated khoya with 3 tbsp milk in a heavy pan over low heat for 5 minutes, then stir in 0.75 cup Anveshan Khandsari and cook for 8 minutes until thick.
Divide the cooked khoya into two equal portions and keep one warm in the pan.
Press the plain portion into a ghee-greased tray as the bottom layer, smoothing it flat with a spatula.
Return the second portion to low heat, mix in 3 tbsp cocoa powder, 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 0.5 tsp vanilla, and stir for 2 minutes until glossy and smooth.
Spread the chocolate layer over the plain base and level it carefully with the back of a spoon.
Scatter 3 tbsp chopped walnuts over the top, press gently, and set for 2 hours before cutting into two-tone squares.
tips: Spread the bottom layer while it is warm and slightly tacky so the chocolate layer bonds and does not separate when cut.
Sift the cocoa powder before adding it to avoid dry specks in the finished barfi.
Warm the knife under hot water and wipe it between cuts for clean, professional-looking edges.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the striped squares chilled on a dessert platter, ideal for children's parties and festive dessert tables.

variations.name: Kesar Mishti Doi
variations.description: A festive version set with caramelised khandsari sugar and infused with saffron, giving it a golden tint and a floral aroma alongside the caramel sweetness. Garnished with nuts, it is a more dressed-up sweet yogurt suited to celebrations and special-occasion thalis.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: part is caramelised to a deep amber to colour and flavour the doi

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk to tint the doi gold and lend a delicate floral aroma

steps: Simmer 1 litre full-fat milk on medium heat for 18 minutes, stirring often, until it reduces to about two-thirds.
In a separate small pan caramelise 0.25 cup Anveshan Khandsari Sugar on low heat for 4 minutes until it melts to a deep amber, then carefully stir it into the hot milk until dissolved.
Add the remaining 0.5 cup Anveshan Khandsari Sugar and stir off the boil until fully dissolved.
Soak the pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 1 tbsp warm milk and stir it in, then cool the milk until just lukewarm.
Whisk the 4 tbsp yogurt smooth and gently mix it into the lukewarm milk with 0.25 tsp cardamom powder, then strain into serving bowls.
Cover and set in a warm draught-free place for 6 to 8 hours until firm.
Chill for 4 hours, garnish with chopped pistachios and serve cold.
tips: Watch the caramel closely and pull it off the heat at deep amber, as it burns and turns bitter quickly.
Add the caramel to hot milk carefully, standing back, as it will splutter.
Set the doi somewhere warm and still so the culture works evenly and it does not turn watery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled in individual bowls, saffron-flecked and pistachio-topped, for a festive dessert course.

variations.name: Baked Mishti Doi
variations.description: A fuss-free modern take that skips fermentation entirely, blending yogurt with condensed and evaporated milk and baking it in a water bath until just set. The result is a silky, cheesecake-like sweet yogurt with a reliable caramel richness, ready the same afternoon without waiting overnight.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted into a caramel that deepens the colour and lends a smoky sweetness to the baked doi

steps: Preheat the oven to 180 C and warm 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 1 tbsp water in a pan on low heat for 2 minutes until it melts into a smooth caramel.
In a bowl whisk together 1 cup condensed milk, 1 cup evaporated milk and 1 cup thick yogurt until completely smooth.
Whisk in the melted jaggery caramel and 0.25 tsp cardamom powder until evenly coloured.
Pour the mixture into a ceramic dish and cover the top loosely with foil.
Place the dish in a larger tray and pour hot water halfway up its sides to make a water bath.
Bake for 30 minutes until the edges are set but the centre still has a gentle wobble.
Cool to room temperature, then chill for 4 hours, garnish with chopped almonds and serve cold.
tips: The water bath is essential to keep the doi silky and stop the edges from cracking.
Take it out while the centre still wobbles, as it firms up fully once chilled.
Use thick set yogurt rather than runny curd so the baked doi holds together well.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled and scooped into bowls, almond-topped, as a quick same-day take on the Bengali classic.

variations.name: Bhapa Doi
variations.description: A steamed cousin of mishti doi enriched with condensed milk and khoya, giving a dense, sliceable set with a delicate saffron perfume. Steaming rather than fermenting makes it foolproof and quick, producing a rich sweet yogurt pudding studded with nuts that slices cleanly like a cake.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk to perfume and lightly colour the steamed doi

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: adds a caramel note and natural sweetness to the steamed pudding

steps: Soak the pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside to bloom for 5 minutes.
In a bowl whisk 1 cup thick yogurt, 0.75 cup condensed milk and the grated 0.25 cup khoya until smooth and lump-free.
Whisk in 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, the saffron milk and 0.25 tsp cardamom powder until evenly combined.
Pour the mixture into a greased steel tin and cover the top tightly with foil so no steam-water drips in.
Set the tin in a steamer or a large pot with an inch of simmering water and a trivet, cover and steam on medium heat for 22 minutes.
Check that a skewer inserted in the centre comes out clean and the pudding is just set, then turn off the heat.
Cool to room temperature, chill for 4 hours, garnish with pistachios and slice to serve.
tips: Cover the tin tightly so condensing steam does not drip in and make the doi watery.
Do not over-steam, as the pudding firms further on chilling and can turn rubbery if overcooked.
Whisk the khoya in well so there are no grainy lumps in the smooth set.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled and sliced into neat wedges, pistachio-topped, like a Bengali steamed yogurt cake.

variations.name: Classic Mixed Veg Curry
variations.description: A home-style North Indian mixed vegetable curry where potato, cauliflower, carrot, beans and peas simmer in a spiced onion-tomato gravy. Comforting and versatile, it pulls together whatever is in the crisper into one warmly spiced, everyday pot.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the whole spices and gives the everyday gravy a homely richness

steps: Chop the potato, carrot, cauliflower and beans into bite-sized pieces and keep 0.5 cup peas ready.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them splutter for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add the finely chopped onions and fry for 6 minutes until golden, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute.
Add the pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt, and cook for 8 minutes until the ghee separates.
Add all the chopped vegetables and peas, toss to coat, then pour in 2 cups water, cover and simmer on medium for 12 minutes until the vegetables are fork-tender.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala, simmer uncovered for 2 minutes to thicken the gravy slightly, and serve hot.
tips: Add the vegetables in order of cooking time, starting with potato and carrot, so nothing turns mushy.
Puree the tomatoes for a smooth gravy, or leave them chopped for a more rustic, home-style texture.
A spoon of the ghee stirred in at the end adds a lovely finishing aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with rotis, jeera rice or pooris, with a wedge of lemon and sliced onions alongside.

variations.name: Restaurant-style Veg Kadai Curry
variations.description: A bold kadai-style curry where the mixed vegetables are tossed with capsicum in a freshly pounded coriander-and-red-chilli kadai masala and a semi-dry tomato gravy. Smoky, aromatic and clinging to the vegetables, it delivers the punchy flavour of a restaurant kadai.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: stands up to the high-heat kadai tossing that gives this curry its roasted edge

steps: Dry-roast 1.5 tbsp coriander seeds and 4 dried red chillies for 2 minutes until fragrant, then coarsely pound them into a gritty kadai masala.
Parboil the chopped potato, cauliflower, carrot and 0.5 cup peas in salted water for 6 minutes until just tender, then drain.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a kadhai over medium-high heat, add the diced onions and stir-fry for 5 minutes until they take on colour at the edges.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the diced capsicum, toss for 2 minutes, then add the chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.25 tsp salt and half the pounded kadai masala.
Cook on high for 6 minutes until the tomatoes break down and the oil separates into a thick, glossy base.
Add the parboiled vegetables and the remaining kadai masala, toss on high for 4 minutes so the masala clings, crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the top, and serve semi-dry.
tips: Pound the kadai masala fresh and coarse; the gritty texture is what defines a true kadai dish.
Add the capsicum early enough to soften but keep the high heat so it stays vibrant and slightly crunchy.
Parboiling the hard vegetables first keeps the final toss quick so everything stays bright and roasted.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan, laccha paratha or tandoori roti, garnished with ginger juliennes and onion rings.

variations.name: Coconut Milk Mixed Veg Stew
variations.description: A gentle Kerala-style stew where the mixed vegetables simmer in coconut milk scented with whole spices, ginger and curry leaves in coconut oil. Pale, mildly spiced and soothing, it lets the sweetness of the vegetables and coconut lead with barely any chilli heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: carries the whole spices and curry leaves for an authentic Kerala stew

steps: Chop the potato, carrot and beans into batons and keep 0.5 cup peas ready, and separate the thick and thin coconut milk if using fresh.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil in a pan over medium heat, add the cinnamon, 3 cloves and 0.5 tsp peppercorns and let them sizzle for 30 seconds.
Add the sliced onion, 1.5 inch ginger juliennes, 3 slit green chillies and 15 curry leaves and saute for 4 minutes until the onion softens without browning.
Add the chopped vegetables with 1 tsp salt and a cup of water, cover and simmer on medium for 12 minutes until they are fork-tender.
Lower the heat and pour in 1.5 cups coconut milk, then warm through gently for 4 minutes without letting it boil so it does not split.
Switch off the flame, drizzle a teaspoon of raw coconut oil over the top for aroma, and serve the stew warm.
tips: Add the coconut milk on low heat and never let it boil, or it will curdle and turn grainy.
Keep the spicing gentle and let the whole spices and ginger flavour the stew rather than chilli powder.
A final drizzle of raw coconut oil is traditional and lifts the whole dish with its aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with appam, idiyappam or soft plain rice for a classic Kerala breakfast or light dinner.

variations.name: Punjabi Mixed Veg with Makhani Gravy
variations.description: A rich Punjabi rendition where the mixed vegetables bask in a buttery tomato-cashew makhani gravy finished with cream and kasuri methi. Velvety, mildly sweet and indulgent, it dresses everyday vegetables in the plush sauce usually reserved for paneer.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: gives the makhani gravy its glossy, buttery richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a touch of unrefined sweetness balances the tang of the tomato makhani gravy

steps: Boil 5 tomatoes, 1 onion and 15 cashews in a cup of water for 10 minutes, cool, and blend into a completely smooth puree, then strain for silkiness.
Parboil the chopped potato, cauliflower, carrot and 0.5 cup peas in salted water for 6 minutes until just tender, then drain.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and saute for 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in the strained tomato-cashew puree with 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt, and simmer on low for 12 minutes, stirring, until it thickens and the ghee floats on top.
Add the parboiled vegetables with a cup of water and 0.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, and simmer gently for 6 minutes so they absorb the gravy.
Lower the heat, stir in 4 tbsp cream, crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi over the top, warm through for 2 minutes, and serve rich and glossy.
tips: Strain the tomato-cashew puree for the signature silky smoothness of a makhani gravy.
Simmer the gravy patiently on low until the ghee separates, which is when the flavour deepens.
Add the cream off the boil and stir gently so the gravy stays smooth and does not split.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or laccha paratha, finished with a swirl of cream and a few crushed kasuri methi leaves.

variations.name: Classic Mochar Ghonto
variations.description: The beloved Bengali dry curry of finely chopped banana blossom cooked down with potato, coconut and Bengal-gram until soft and mildly sweet. The mocha is boiled first to tame its astringency, then slow-cooked in a ginger-cumin masala and finished with roasted coconut and ghee for a comforting festive relish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the earthy Bengali oil that blooms the whole spices for this dry ghonto

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: stirred in at the end with garam masala for the classic ghonto aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the gentle sweetness that defines a Bengali mochar ghonto

steps: Soak 3 tbsp chana dal for 30 minutes, then boil the 3 cups chopped mocha with the dal, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt in water for 12 minutes until soft; drain well and lightly mash.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just smokes, lower the heat and add 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 bay leaf and 2 dried red chillies, letting them crackle for 20 seconds.
Add 1 tbsp ginger paste and fry 1 minute, then add the potato cubes with the remaining 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp cumin powder and the remaining salt and saute for 3 minutes.
Add the boiled mocha-dal mixture, mix well, cover and cook on low for 12 minutes, stirring often, until the potato is soft and the mixture is dry and fluffy.
Sprinkle in the 0.5 cup grated coconut and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook uncovered for 4 minutes, stirring, until everything looks glossy and well roasted.
Finish with 0.5 tsp Bengali garam masala and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, stir through and rest 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Rub a little oil on your palms before chopping the mocha to stop the sticky sap from staining your hands.
Boil the banana blossom well first, as this removes its natural bitterness and astringency.
Keep cooking until the mixture is completely dry and crumbly, which is the hallmark of a good ghonto.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a dry side with steaming rice and a drizzle of ghee, or alongside luchi for a Sunday lunch.

variations.name: Narkel-Chholar Mochar Ghonto
variations.description: A festive richer ghonto where the banana blossom is bound with cooked chholar dal, plump raisins and coconut cubes for a sweet-savoury bite. Fried coconut slivers and cashews stud the dry mixture, making this the celebratory version served at pujas and weddings.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the coconut and cashews and gives this festive ghonto its rich aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: lifts the sweet-savoury balance of this celebratory dal-studded ghonto

steps: Soak 0.5 cup chholar dal for 30 minutes, then boil until just soft but still holding shape, about 15 minutes, and drain.
Boil the 3 cups chopped mocha with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 12 minutes until soft, drain well and mash lightly.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai, fry the 3 tbsp coconut cubes and 10 cashews for 2 minutes until golden, lift them out, then add 1.5 tbsp raisins to the ghee for 15 seconds until they plump and remove.
In the same ghee crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, 3 cardamom and the 1 inch cinnamon for 20 seconds, add 1 tbsp ginger paste and fry 1 minute.
Add the boiled mocha and dal with the remaining 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp cumin powder and remaining salt, cover and cook on low for 12 minutes until dry and well blended.
Stir in 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder with the fried coconut, cashews and raisins, cook uncovered 3 minutes and serve warm.
tips: Boil the chholar dal only until it holds its shape so it does not turn mushy when mixed in.
Fry the coconut cubes and cashews first and add them last so they stay crunchy in the finished ghonto.
This version keeps well for a day and the flavours deepen, making it ideal to cook ahead for a feast.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot luchi or radhaballavi, or as a sweet-savoury side on a puja thali with pulao.

variations.name: Niramish Mochar Ghonto
variations.description: The pure satvik ghonto made without onion or garlic, seasoned only with grated ginger, whole cumin and a hint of asafoetida. Lighter and cleaner than the festive version, it lets the delicate nutty flavour of the banana blossom shine, and is the everyday temple-style relish of Bengali homes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the satvik fat that tempers the cumin and hing for this no-onion-garlic ghonto

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the gentle rounding sweetness this clean satvik ghonto needs

steps: Boil the 3 cups chopped mocha with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 12 minutes until soft, drain thoroughly and mash lightly.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium, add 1 tsp cumin seeds, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 1 bay leaf and let them splutter for 20 seconds.

Add the 1.5 tbsp grated ginger and slit green chillies, fry for 1 minute, then add the potato cubes with the remaining 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder and remaining salt and saute 3 minutes.
Add the boiled mocha, mix well, cover and cook on low for 12 minutes, stirring often, until the potato is tender and the mixture turns dry.
Stir in the 0.5 cup grated coconut and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and roast uncovered for 4 minutes until fragrant and crumbly.
Rest 5 minutes off the heat so the flavours settle, then serve warm.
tips: Squeeze out excess water from the boiled mocha before frying so the ghonto turns properly dry.
Grated ginger and green chilli give all the warmth this satvik version needs without any onion or garlic.
Add the coconut towards the end so it stays fresh and lightly roasted rather than soggy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain rice and a spoon of ghee, or with cholar dal and luchi for a festival meal.

variations.name: Mocha Ghonto in Coconut Milk
variations.description: A softer, creamier take where the banana blossom simmers gently in coconut milk instead of turning fully dry, leaving it moist and mildly sweet. Tempered with mustard and curry leaves in coconut oil, it borrows a coastal accent while keeping the Bengali soul of the dish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the coastal fat that tempers the mustard and curry leaves for this creamy version

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: balances the coconut milk with a soft sweetness in this coastal-style ghonto

steps: Boil the 3 cups chopped mocha with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt for 12 minutes until soft, then drain well.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadai on medium, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop, then add 12 curry leaves and the slit green chillies for 15 seconds.
Add the 1 tbsp grated ginger and potato cubes and saute for 3 minutes, then stir in the remaining 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp cumin powder and remaining salt.
Add the boiled mocha with 0.5 cup water, cover and cook on low for 10 minutes until the potato is tender.
Lower the heat to minimum, pour in 1 cup thin coconut milk and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and simmer gently for 4 minutes without boiling so the coconut milk does not split.
Rest 5 minutes off the heat to let the creamy gravy thicken slightly, then serve warm.
tips: Add the coconut milk on the lowest heat and never let it boil hard, or it will curdle and turn grainy.
Keep this version a little moist rather than dry, as the coconut milk is the point of difference.
A final tempering of curry leaves in a spoon of hot coconut oil poured over the top lifts the aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice or appam, letting the mild coconut gravy soak into each mouthful.

variations.name: Classic Ukadiche Modak
variations.description: Ukadiche modak are the steamed rice-flour dumplings offered to Lord Ganesha in Maharashtra, filled with a fragrant coconut and jaggery mixture. The translucent pleated shell encases a warm, cardamom-scented filling that oozes ghee at the first bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melts with coconut into the classic sweet filling for the dumplings

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: cooks the filling and is drizzled over the steamed modak to finish

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and cook 1 cup grated coconut with 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder over low heat for 6 to 7 minutes until the moisture dries and the mixture holds together, then mix in 0.5 tsp cardamom and 1 tsp poppy seeds and cool.
Bring 1 cup water to a rolling boil with a pinch of salt and 1 tsp ghee, then lower the heat and stir in 1 cup rice flour all at once until it forms a shaggy mass.
Cover and steam-cook the flour off the heat for 3 minutes, then knead the warm dough with greased hands until smooth and pliable.
Pinch a lemon-sized ball, flatten it into a shallow cup in your palm, and pinch 8 to 9 pleats around the rim.
Place a spoon of the coconut-jaggery filling inside, gather the pleats to a peak, and seal the top; repeat for all the dough.
Steam the shaped modak in a greased steamer for 10 to 12 minutes until the shells turn glossy and translucent, then drizzle with warm Anveshan Ghee and serve.
tips: Keep the rice dough covered with a damp cloth while shaping, as it dries and cracks quickly.
Do not overcook the filling; it should be moist and just holding, since it dries further on cooling.
Grease your palms and the steamer with ghee so the delicate shells do not tear or stick.
variations.servingSuggestion: Offer the hot modak as naivedya during Ganesh Chaturthi, served with an extra pool of warm ghee.

variations.name: Fried Maharashtrian Modak
variations.description: The talniche modak is a deep-fried wheat-shell version with a longer shelf life than the steamed kind, prized for its crisp golden crust. The same coconut-jaggery heart stays inside a flaky fried casing that travels well as prasad.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: forms a sturdy, nutty shell that crisps up golden when fried

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the coconut filling with a deep caramel note

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: rubbed into the dough as moyan for a flaky fried crust

steps: Cook 1 cup grated coconut with 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder over low heat for 7 minutes until dry, then mix in 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp nutmeg and cool.
Rub 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee into 1.25 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, then bind with about 0.5 cup water into a firm, smooth dough and rest it 20 minutes.
Roll small portions of dough into thin discs, place a spoon of filling in the centre, and pinch the edges into a pleated modak peak.
Seal each modak well so no filling escapes during frying, keeping the shaped ones covered.
Heat oil for frying to a medium-low temperature and fry the modak in batches for 5 to 6 minutes, turning, until crisp and deep golden.
Drain on a rack and cool completely so the shells crisp up before serving or storing.
tips: Fry on medium-low heat so the thick shell cooks through without the outside darkening too fast.
Seal the pleats firmly and check for gaps, as leaking jaggery will burn in the oil.
These keep for several days in an airtight tin, unlike the steamed version which is best eaten fresh.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pack the crisp fried modak as travel-friendly prasad or an offering for guests during festivals.

variations.name: Chocolate Modak
variations.description: A contemporary no-cook fusion modak made by shaping a mixture of melted chocolate, khoya and nuts in a modak mould. Loved by children, it keeps the iconic Ganesha shape while swapping the coconut heart for a rich chocolate-nut centre.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the mould and gives the chocolate mixture a glossy set

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: adds a touch of sweetness to balance the dark chocolate

steps: Melt 1 cup chopped dark chocolate gently over a double boiler with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until smooth and glossy.
In a pan over low heat, cook 0.75 cup grated khoya with 2 tbsp milk and 2 tbsp Anveshan Khandsari for 3 minutes until soft, then cool slightly.
Mix the melted chocolate, softened khoya, 1 tbsp cocoa powder and 3 tbsp chopped nuts into a thick, mouldable mixture.
Chill the mixture for 10 minutes until firm enough to shape but still pliable.
Grease a modak mould with ghee, press portions of the mixture in to take the pleated shape, and unmould gently.
Set the shaped chocolate modak in the refrigerator for 20 minutes until firm before serving.
tips: Do not overheat the chocolate, as it seizes; melt it slowly over gentle heat for a smooth set.
If the mixture is too soft to mould, chill it longer rather than adding more khoya.
Dust the finished modak with a little cocoa or edible glitter for a festive presentation.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these chocolate modak chilled as a modern Ganesh Chaturthi treat that delights children.

variations.name: Dry Fruit Mawa Modak
variations.description: An instant mawa modak bound with a paste of dates and mixed dry fruits, needing no steaming or frying. The naturally sweet date base and roasted nuts make it a wholesome, refined-sugar-conscious offering shaped in the traditional mould.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the nuts and binds the mawa into a pliable dough for moulding

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: lightly sweetens the mawa to complement the dates

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and roast 0.5 cup chopped mixed nuts for 2 minutes until fragrant, then set aside.
In the same pan add 0.5 cup chopped dates with a splash of water and mash over low heat for 3 minutes into a soft paste.
Add 1 cup grated khoya and 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, cooking on low heat for 5 minutes until the mixture thickens into a dough.
Mix in the roasted nuts, 0.5 tsp cardamom, 1 tsp roasted poppy seeds and the remaining 1 tbsp ghee, then let it cool until mouldable.
Grease a modak mould with ghee, press the warm mixture in firmly to shape the pleats, and release gently.
Repeat with the rest of the mixture and let the modak firm up at room temperature for 30 minutes before serving.
tips: Cook the khoya just until it leaves the pan; overcooking makes the modak hard and difficult to mould.
Warm the mixture slightly if it stiffens while shaping, as it moulds best when barely warm.
Choose soft, moist dates so the paste binds well without extra sugar.
variations.servingSuggestion: Offer these wholesome mawa modak as a nourishing prasad, ideal for guests who prefer less sugar.

variations.name: Classic Ghee Mysore Pak
variations.description: Mysore Pak is a legendary Karnataka sweet born in the royal kitchens of Mysore, made by cooking gram flour in a flood of hot ghee and sugar syrup until it sets into a rich, porous fudge. The classic version is dense yet melting, with a deep roasted-gram aroma and a crumbly bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: boiled to a one-string syrup that binds the roasted gram flour into fudge

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: poured in hot and generously to fry the besan and create the signature porous set

steps: Sieve 1 cup besan and keep 1.5 cups Anveshan Ghee hot in a separate pan so it is ready to add in a steady stream.
Dissolve 1.5 cups Anveshan Khandsari in 0.5 cup water and boil for 5 minutes until it reaches a sticky one-string consistency.
Lower the heat, whisk the sieved besan into the syrup in a thin stream so no lumps form, stirring constantly.
Begin adding the hot Anveshan Ghee a ladle at a time, stirring vigorously, letting each addition absorb before the next, over 10 to 12 minutes.
Cook until the mixture turns frothy, porous and starts leaving the sides of the pan while the ghee just begins to separate, then stir in 0.5 tsp cardamom.
Pour into a greased tray, scatter 2 tbsp slivered pistachios over the top, and while still warm cut into squares, letting them set for 15 minutes before lifting out.
tips: Keep the ghee hot throughout; adding cold ghee stops the frothing that gives Mysore Pak its porous texture.
Cut the sweet while it is still warm, as it turns too hard and crumbly to slice once fully cooled.
Stir without stopping once the besan goes in, or it will clump and cook unevenly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature as a festival mithai, especially for Diwali and weddings, with a cup of filter coffee.

variations.name: Soft Melt-in-Mouth Mysore Pak
variations.description: The soft Krishna-sweets style Mysore Pak, drowned in even more ghee so it turns feather-light and porous, dissolving instantly on the tongue. A splash of milk in the syrup keeps the crumb tender and moist rather than the firm, toffee-like classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: cooked to a soft one-string syrup for the tender, melting soft set

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: used lavishly so the sweet turns airy, porous and melts on the tongue

steps: Sieve 1 cup besan twice and mix it with 4 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee into a smooth, lump-free slurry so it blends instantly into the syrup.
Boil 1.5 cups Anveshan Khandsari with 0.5 cup water and 2 tbsp milk for 4 minutes to a soft one-string syrup, skimming off any froth.
Keep the remaining Anveshan Ghee hot, then pour the besan slurry into the syrup on low heat, stirring fast to a smooth mass.
Add the hot ghee in small ladles while stirring, letting each be absorbed, until the mixture turns pale, frothy and full of tiny bubbles, about 12 minutes.
Stop the moment it looks airy and foamy but is still soft and flowing, then stir in 0.5 tsp cardamom.
Pour into a greased tray, mark into squares while warm, and let it set 20 minutes into a soft, porous slab.
tips: Making a besan-ghee slurry first is the trick to a lump-free, ultra-smooth soft Mysore Pak.
Stop cooking while the mixture is still soft and pourable; overcooking turns the soft version hard.
Use the fullest amount of ghee for the airiest, most melting texture; the excess drains off as it sets.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve fresh and slightly warm when it is at its most melting, ideal as a rich festive gift box sweet.

variations.name: Jaggery Mysore Pak
variations.description: A rustic, wholesome Mysore Pak sweetened entirely with jaggery instead of white sugar, giving a darker colour and a warm, molasses-rich depth. A pinch of dry ginger cuts the richness and makes it especially comforting in the cooler months.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted and strained into a syrup that gives the fudge a deep caramel colour and flavour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: poured in hot to fry the besan and set the jaggery fudge with a porous crumb

steps: Sieve 1 cup besan and keep 1.5 cups Anveshan Ghee hot and ready in a separate pan.
Melt 1.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 0.5 cup water, strain out grit, and boil 5 minutes to a sticky one-string syrup.
Lower the heat and whisk the besan into the jaggery syrup in a thin steady stream, stirring hard to keep it smooth.
Add the hot Anveshan Ghee a ladle at a time over 10 minutes, stirring constantly, until the mixture froths and thickens.
Cook until it turns porous and pulls from the pan sides as the ghee begins to separate, then mix in 0.25 tsp dry ginger and 0.5 tsp cardamom.
Pour into a greased tray, cut into squares while warm, and let it firm up for 15 minutes.
tips: Strain the melted jaggery well, as its natural grit would make the fudge sandy.
Jaggery syrup catches and burns faster than sugar, so keep the flame low once the besan goes in.
The dry ginger balances the deep sweetness of jaggery and aids digestion of this rich sweet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature as a winter festival sweet, delicious alongside a warm glass of masala milk.

variations.name: Chocolate Mysore Pak
variations.description: A modern fusion Mysore Pak marbled with cocoa, giving the classic gram-flour fudge a rich chocolate depth that appeals to younger palates. A scatter of roasted almonds on top adds crunch, turning a traditional mithai into a festive dessert-bar hybrid.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: boiled to a one-string syrup that binds the cocoa-gram fudge together

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the besan and cocoa and sets the fudge with a glossy, porous crumb

steps: Sieve 1 cup besan with 3 tbsp cocoa powder together and keep 1.75 cups Anveshan Ghee hot and ready.
Boil 1.5 cups Anveshan Khandsari with 0.5 cup water for 5 minutes to a sticky one-string syrup.
Lower the heat and whisk the besan-cocoa mix into the syrup in a thin stream, stirring fast to keep it smooth.
Add the hot Anveshan Ghee a ladle at a time over 10 to 12 minutes, stirring, until the mixture froths and thickens to a glossy mass.
Cook until it turns porous and leaves the pan sides as the ghee starts to separate, then stir in 0.5 tsp cardamom.
Pour into a greased tray, press 3 tbsp chopped almonds over the top, cut into squares while warm, and set 15 minutes.
tips: Sift the cocoa with the besan so it disperses evenly with no bitter dry pockets.
Cocoa can taste bitter if scorched, so keep the flame low and stir constantly once it goes in.
Press the almonds on while the slab is warm so they stick firmly as it sets.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature as a crowd-pleasing fusion mithai, cut into small squares for a festive dessert platter.

variations.name: Classic Petha Ki Sabzi
variations.description: This Classic Petha Ki Sabzi simmers soft cubes of ash gourd in a light onion-tomato masala until they turn translucent and melt-in-the-mouth. A gentle everyday North Indian curry, it lets the cooling, mildly sweet character of the ash gourd shine through the spices.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil that keeps the light gourd curry clean and blooms the spices well

steps: Peel and deseed the 500 g ash gourd and cut it into 3 cm cubes.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle for 15 seconds.
Add the finely chopped onion and saute for 4 minutes until soft, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Add the chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and cook 5 minutes until pulpy.
Add the ash gourd cubes and toss to coat in the masala for 2 minutes.
Cover and cook on low for 12 minutes, stirring gently, until the gourd turns soft and translucent and releases its own water.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala, stir once and serve hot garnished with coriander.
tips: Ash gourd releases plenty of water, so add little or none extra while cooking.
Do not overcook or the cubes will collapse; stop as soon as they turn translucent.
Choose a mature ash gourd with a firm white flesh for cubes that hold their shape.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulkas or steamed rice and a bowl of moong dal for a light meal.

variations.name: Rajasthani Besan Petha Sabzi
variations.description: A Marwari-style sabzi where ash gourd is cooked with roasted gram flour that thickens the masala into a clingy, savoury coat. The besan adds a nutty body and holds the spices to each cube, making a rich dry sabzi typical of Rajasthani thalis.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: roasted gram flour that thickens the masala and gives the Marwari sabzi its nutty body

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the pungent Rajasthani cooking fat that stands up to the robust dry spices

steps: Peel, deseed and cube the 500 g ash gourd into 3 cm pieces.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just smokes, then lower the heat and add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida to sizzle for 15 seconds.
Add 3 tbsp Anveshan Sattu and roast it in the oil on low heat for 2 minutes until it smells nutty and turns a shade darker.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.25 tsp chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and cook 20 seconds so the spices coat the sattu.
Add the ash gourd cubes and toss well so the roasted sattu masala clings to every piece.
Sprinkle two tablespoons of water, cover and cook on low for 12 minutes until the gourd is soft and the masala is dry and clingy.
Finish with 1 tsp amchur, toss once and serve hot with fresh coriander.
tips: Roast the sattu in the oil before adding the vegetable so it loses any raw, pasty taste.
Keep the heat low after adding sattu as it can catch and burn quickly.
Add only a splash of water since the gourd and sattu together need very little moisture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra roti and a dollop of white butter for an authentic Rajasthani plate.

variations.name: South-Indian Ash Gourd Kootu
variations.description: A comforting Tamil kootu where ash gourd is simmered with soft moong dal and a freshly ground coconut-cumin paste. Creamy, mild and lightly spiced with a coconut-oil tempering, it is a wholesome southern side that pairs beautifully with rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: gives the kootu its authentic southern aroma and carries the mustard tempering

steps: Pressure-cook the 0.5 cup moong dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.5 cups water for 3 whistles until soft, then mash lightly.
Peel, deseed and cube the 400 g ash gourd and simmer it in 1 cup water with 1 tsp salt for 8 minutes until tender.
Grind the 0.5 cup grated coconut with 1 tsp cumin and 2 green chillies into a smooth paste with a little water.
Add the cooked dal and the coconut paste to the softened gourd and simmer together on low for 6 minutes, stirring, so it does not stick.
In a small pan heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop for 15 seconds.
Add 1 broken dry red chilli and 10 curry leaves to the tempering and fry for 15 seconds until crisp.
Pour the sizzling tempering over the kootu, stir once and serve warm.
tips: Add the coconut paste on low heat so the kootu stays smooth and does not turn grainy.
Keep the kootu slightly loose as it thickens further on standing.
Cook the dal until fully soft so it blends creamily into the ash gourd.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, alongside a crisp appalam.

variations.name: Gujarati Khatti-Mithi Petha Sabzi
variations.description: A Gujarati sweet-and-sour rendition where ash gourd simmers in a jaggery-tamarind masala for a signature khatti-mithi balance. Lightly spiced and glossy, it delivers the tang-sweet flavour that defines a classic Gujarati vegetable.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the everyday Gujarati cooking oil that keeps this khatti-mithi sabzi light

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: brings the natural sweetness that balances the tamarind in a Gujarati sabzi

steps: Peel, deseed and cube the 500 g ash gourd into bite-sized pieces.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin and let them splutter for 15 seconds.
Add 0.25 tsp asafoetida and the slit green chillies and fry for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add the ash gourd with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp dhana jeera and 1 tsp salt, and toss to coat for 2 minutes.
Cover and cook on low for 10 minutes until the gourd turns soft and translucent in its own moisture.
Stir in 1 tbsp tamarind pulp and 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and simmer 3 minutes until the masala turns glossy and sweet-sour.
Adjust the salt, cook 1 minute more and serve warm with a coriander garnish.
tips: Balance the tamarind and jaggery to taste so neither the sour nor the sweet overpowers.
Add the tamarind and jaggery only after the gourd is soft so the flavours stay bright.
Dhana jeera powder is key to the mild, rounded spicing of a Gujarati sabzi.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft rotli and a bowl of plain moong dal or khichdi for a homely Gujarati thali.

variations.name: Classic Kesar Phirni
variations.description: The North Indian festive pudding made from coarsely ground soaked rice cooked in milk until thick and spoonable, set in earthen bowls that absorb excess moisture and lend a subtle clay aroma. Perfumed with saffron and cardamom, phirni is denser and grainier than kheer and always served well chilled.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: khandsari sweetens the phirni cleanly while keeping its pale, milky colour intact

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: a pinch of pure saffron steeped in warm milk gives phirni its gentle gold tint and signature perfume

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a little bilona ghee to fry the pistachio garnish adds aroma and a glossy finish to the set phirni

steps: Rinse 1/3 cup basmati rice, soak it in water for 30 minutes, then drain and grind it with 1/4 cup water into a slightly coarse, rava-like paste, not a smooth batter.
Steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside to bloom.
Bring 4 cups full-fat milk to a boil in a heavy pan, then lower the heat and add the ground rice paste in a thin stream while whisking continuously to prevent lumps.
Cook on low heat for 15 to 18 minutes, stirring constantly and scraping the base, until the rice is fully cooked and the phirni thickens to a soft dropping consistency.
Stir in 1/2 cup Anveshan Khandsari and the saffron milk and cook for 4 more minutes until dissolved, then add 1/2 tsp cardamom powder off the heat.
Fry 12 pistachios and 10 slivered almonds in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee for 1 minute, stir half in, pour the phirni into earthen bowls, chill for 3 hours, and garnish with the rest.
tips: Grind the rice coarse like fine semolina, as a fully smooth paste makes the phirni pasty instead of pleasantly grainy.
Whisk the rice paste into hot milk in a thin stream while stirring, or it will seize into stubborn lumps.
Setting the phirni in unglazed earthen bowls draws out extra moisture and gives the authentic clay-scented finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve thoroughly chilled in earthen kulhads topped with saffron strands and slivered pistachios, a classic Eid and festival dessert.

variations.name: Badam Phirni
variations.description: A luxurious version where ground almonds join the rice paste, giving the phirni a nutty depth and a thicker, fudgier set. Pale gold and intensely aromatic, this is the sweet-shop phirni made for grand occasions and gifting.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: khandsari keeps the almond phirni softly sweet without overpowering the delicate nut flavour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee fries the flaked almond garnish for a toasty aroma over the creamy set phirni

steps: Rinse 1/4 cup basmati rice and soak for 30 minutes, and separately soak 20 almonds in hot water for 20 minutes, then peel them.
Grind the drained rice with 1/4 cup water into a coarse paste, and grind the peeled almonds into a fine paste with a little milk.
Bring 4 cups full-fat milk to a boil, lower the heat, and whisk in the rice paste in a thin stream, cooking for 12 minutes on low until it thickens.
Stir in the ground almond paste and cook for another 6 minutes, stirring constantly, until the phirni turns thick, fudgy and pale gold.
Add 1/2 cup Anveshan Khandsari and cook for 4 minutes until dissolved, then finish with 1/2 tsp cardamom powder and 1/2 tsp rose water off the heat.
Toast the remaining 10 flaked almonds and 2 tbsp charoli in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee for 1 minute, pour the phirni into bowls, chill for 3 hours, and top with the toasted nuts.
tips: Peel and grind the almonds smooth so the phirni stays silky rather than gritty.
This version sets firmer than plain phirni thanks to the almonds, so serve it slightly less reduced.
A restrained splash of rose water lifts the almond aroma; too much makes it taste like perfume.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled in shallow bowls scattered with toasted almond flakes and charoli, a rich dessert for Diwali or a dinner party.

variations.name: Gulab Phirni
variations.description: A romantic pink-hued phirni scented with rose and finished with crushed dried rose petals and a spoon of gulkand. Delicate and floral, it is the summer version served at Mughlai feasts and celebrations of the monsoon.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: khandsari keeps the phirni pale so the rose petals and pink tint show through clearly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee fries the pistachio and petal garnish for a fragrant, glossy topping

steps: Rinse 1/3 cup basmati rice, soak for 30 minutes, then drain and grind with 1/4 cup water into a coarse paste.
Bring 4 cups full-fat milk to a boil, lower the heat, and whisk in the rice paste in a thin stream, cooking on low for 16 minutes until thickened and creamy.
Stir in 1/2 cup Anveshan Khandsari and cook for 4 minutes until it dissolves and the phirni is smooth.
Turn off the heat, mash 2 tbsp gulkand smooth and stir it in along with 1 tsp rose water and 1/2 tsp cardamom powder, which tints the phirni a soft pink.
Crush half the dried rose petals and fold them in, then pour the phirni into serving bowls and chill for 3 hours.
Fry 12 pistachios in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee for 1 minute, scatter them with the remaining rose petals over the set phirni just before serving.
tips: Stir the gulkand and rose water in only after the heat is off, so the delicate floral aroma is not cooked away.
Use edible, pesticide-free dried rose petals, and crush them lightly to release fragrance without bitterness.
For a deeper pink, mash the gulkand thoroughly rather than adding artificial colour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled topped with fresh rose petals and pistachio slivers, an elegant floral dessert for a summer celebration.

variations.name: Aam Phirni
variations.description: A summer mango phirni where sweet Alphonso puree is folded into the cooled rice pudding for a fruity, sunny finish. The mango keeps it bright and fresh, making it the seasonal favourite when the fruit is at its ripest.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: less khandsari is used here since the ripe mango brings its own natural sweetness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee fries the almond garnish that finishes the fruity phirni

steps: Rinse 1/3 cup basmati rice, soak for 30 minutes, then drain and grind with 1/4 cup water into a coarse paste.
Bring 3.5 cups full-fat milk to a boil, lower the heat, whisk in the rice paste in a thin stream, and cook on low for 16 minutes until thick and creamy.
Stir in 1/3 cup Anveshan Khandsari and 1/2 tsp cardamom powder, cook for 3 minutes until dissolved, then take the pan off the heat and cool the phirni to room temperature.
Once cooled, gently fold in 1 cup Alphonso mango puree, mixing well so the mango does not curdle the still-warm milk.
Fold in half the fresh mango cubes, pour the phirni into serving bowls, and chill for 3 hours until set and cold.
Fry 10 slivered almonds in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee for 1 minute and scatter them with the remaining mango cubes over the phirni before serving.
tips: Cool the rice pudding fully before adding mango puree, as folding fruit into hot milk can split it.
Use ripe, non-fibrous mangoes like Alphonso or Kesar so the phirni stays smooth and intensely fruity.
Reduce the sweetener further if your mangoes are very sweet, tasting once the puree is folded in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled topped with fresh mango cubes and slivered almonds, a bright seasonal dessert at the peak of summer.

variations.name: Classic Phulkopir Dalna
variations.description: The definitive Bengali winter curry of golden-fried cauliflower florets and potato cubes simmered in a light ginger-tomato gravy scented with whole garam masala. The cauliflower is shallow-fried first so it holds its shape and turns nutty, then finished with a spoon of ghee for that unmistakable home-kitchen aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the pungent Bengali oil that fries the florets golden and gives the dalna its earthy base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: stirred in at the end for the characteristic finishing aroma of a Bengali dalna

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the small pinch of sweetness that balances the spices in the classic Bengali style

steps: Cut the cauliflower into medium florets and the 2 potatoes into thick wedges, then rub them with 0.25 tsp of the turmeric and a little salt.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just smokes, lower the heat and shallow-fry the florets and potato for about 6 minutes until golden-edged, then lift them out and set aside.
In the same oil add 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 bay leaf, the 1 inch cinnamon and 3 cardamom pods and let them crackle for 20 seconds until fragrant.

Add 1 tbsp ginger paste and fry for 1 minute, then add the chopped tomato with the remaining 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp cumin powder, 0.75 tsp chilli powder and 1 tsp salt and cook for 4 minutes until the oil separates.

Return the fried cauliflower and potato, toss to coat, pour in 1.5 cups hot water, cover and simmer on low for 12 minutes until the vegetables are fork-tender and the gravy has reduced to a light coating.
Stir in 0.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 0.5 tsp garam masala and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, simmer 1 minute and rest covered for 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Fry the cauliflower only until the edges catch colour, as this keeps the florets intact through the simmer.
Keep the gravy light and clinging rather than soupy, which is how a Bengali dalna is meant to be.
Add the ghee and garam masala right at the end off the boil so their aroma stays fresh on the plate.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with steamed gobindobhog rice or luchi, with a wedge of lime and a fried green chilli on the side.

variations.name: Niramish Phulkopir Dalna
variations.description: The satvik temple-style dalna cooked without onion or garlic, where the spice comes from a fragrant panch phoron tempering and a whisper of asafoetida. Ground roasted cumin and grated ginger carry the flavour, making this the version served on festival and no-onion-garlic days across Bengal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the satvik fat that fries the florets and carries the panch phoron in this no-onion-garlic dalna

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a small pinch to round off the tang the traditional niramish way

steps: Cut the cauliflower into florets and the 2 potatoes into cubes and toss them with 0.25 tsp turmeric and a little salt.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium, shallow-fry the florets and potato for 6 minutes until lightly golden, then lift them out and keep aside.
In the same ghee add 1 tsp panch phoron and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them splutter for 20 seconds until the fenugreek turns fragrant.

Add 1.5 tbsp ginger paste and the slit green chillies, fry for 1 minute, then stir in the remaining 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt with a splash of water and cook 2 minutes into a thick masala.
Return the fried vegetables, coat well, add 1.5 cups hot water, cover and simmer on low for 12 minutes until soft and the gravy thickens to a light coating.
Finish with 0.5 tsp Bengali garam masala and 0.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, stir gently and rest 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Do not let the panch phoron burn; the moment the fenugreek darkens it turns bitter, so keep the heat moderate.
Grated fresh ginger instead of paste gives an even cleaner satvik flavour if you have time.
A splash of water while frying the spices stops them catching and keeps the masala smooth.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice and a dollop of ghee, or with soft koraishutir kochuri for a festival lunch.

variations.name: Koraishutir Narkel Phulkopi
variations.description: A richer winter dalna loaded with sweet green peas and a fresh coconut paste that turns the gravy creamy and faintly sweet. The ground coconut and poppy seeds give it a Bengali festive character quite different from the everyday thin dalna, with peas bursting soft against the golden cauliflower.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: fries the florets and blooms the spices for this festive coconut-rich dalna

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: deepens the natural sweetness of peas and coconut in this festive version

steps: Soak 1 tbsp poppy seeds in warm water for 10 minutes, then grind with the 0.5 cup grated coconut and 2 green chillies to a smooth paste.
Cut the cauliflower into florets, rub with 0.25 tsp turmeric and salt, and shallow-fry in 4 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil for 6 minutes until golden; lift out and reserve.
In the same oil add 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 bay leaf and the remaining slit green chilli and let them crackle for 20 seconds.

Add 1 tbsp ginger paste and fry 1 minute, then add the coconut-poppy paste with the remaining 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp cumin powder and 1 tsp salt and cook 4 minutes until the raw smell goes and oil edges appear.
Add the 1 cup green peas and the fried cauliflower, toss well, pour in 1 cup hot water, cover and simmer on low for 10 minutes until the peas are soft and the gravy turns creamy.
Stir in 0.75 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer 1 minute and rest 5 minutes so the coconut gravy settles before serving.
tips: Grind the coconut and poppy really smooth for a silky gravy without any grainy texture.
Add the coconut paste on medium heat and stir often so it does not catch and turn bitter.
Fresh winter peas taste sweetest here, but frozen peas work well if added straight from the freezer.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulka, radhaballavi or plain rice, garnished with a few whole fried cashews for a festive touch.

variations.name: Kosha Phulkopi
variations.description: A dry, deeply browned Bengali roast where the cauliflower is slow-cooked in a thick onion-tomato masala until every floret is caramelised and coated in glossy spice. There is almost no gravy, just a sticky bhuna masala clinging to the vegetables, making it a robust dhaba-style side rather than the usual light curry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: browns the onions and roasts the florets to a sticky kosha finish

steps: Cut the cauliflower into florets and the potato into small cubes, rub with 0.25 tsp turmeric and salt, and shallow-fry in 4 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil for 7 minutes until well browned; lift out and set aside.
In the same oil add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 2 whole dried red chillies and let them darken for 15 seconds.
Add the finely chopped onions and fry patiently for 8 minutes until deep brown, then stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until the raw smell fades.

Add the chopped tomatoes with the remaining 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and bhuno for 6 minutes until the oil separates and the masala goes glossy.
Return the fried cauliflower and potato, toss to coat, add just 0.5 cup hot water, cover and cook on low for 12 minutes, stirring twice, until tender.
Uncover and roast on medium for 4 minutes to dry the masala into a sticky coating, finish with 0.75 tsp garam masala and serve hot.
tips: Brown the onions slowly and fully, as the dark colour and depth of a kosha comes from that patience.
Keep the water minimal so the masala stays thick and clings to each floret rather than turning into gravy.
Roast uncovered at the end for a few minutes to get the signature glossy, sticky kosha texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a dry side with dal-rice, or pile it into a paratha roll with sliced onion and green chutney.

variations.name: Classic Maharashtrian Puran Poli
variations.description: The festival sweet of every Maharashtrian home during Holi and Ganesh Chaturthi: chana dal slow-cooked with jaggery into a fragrant puran, then sealed inside a saffron-tinted khapli dough and griddled until translucent and freckled. Cardamom and nutmeg keep the filling perfumed rather than cloying, and a puran poli done right is soft enough to fold without cracking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: emmer wheat rolls into a stretchy, forgiving cover that thins over the soft puran without splitting

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee soaks the resting dough supple and later crisps each poli to a golden lace

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: unrefined jaggery melts into the dal for the deep caramel note that white sugar can never give a puran

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: a few strands bloomed in warm milk tint the puran a festive amber and lift its aroma

steps: Rinse 1 cup chana dal well and pressure cook it with 2.5 cups water for 4 whistles on medium heat, until a grain collapses at the lightest press. Drain the dal thoroughly in a colander, saving the cooking liquid for a katachi amti on the side.

Knead 1.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1/4 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 1/2 cup water into a very soft, slightly sticky dough, then smear it with another 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and rest it covered for 30 minutes so it turns silky.

Tip the drained dal into a heavy pan with 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook on low heat for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring constantly, until the jaggery melts and the mixture thickens enough to hold a clean line when you drag a spoon through it.

Take the pan off the heat and mix in 1/2 tsp cardamom powder, 1/4 tsp nutmeg powder and the milk-soaked Anveshan Saffron, then mash everything hot through a masher or puran yantra until the puran is smooth and lump-free; cool it fully before shaping.

Divide the dough and the puran into 8 balls each, keeping the puran balls slightly larger. Flatten a dough ball into a 4 inch cup, seat a puran ball inside, gather the edges over the top and pinch shut, then roll out very gently on a floured surface to a 7 inch round.

Roast each poli on a medium-hot tava for about 1 minute a side until pale brown blisters appear, then brush both faces with the remaining Anveshan Ghee and cook 30 seconds more per side until translucent, golden and softly puffed.
tips: Grind or mash the puran while it is still warm; once cold it stiffens and turns grainy, leaving the filling impossible to spread evenly.
If the puran feels loose and refuses to hold shape, dry it on low heat for 3 more minutes rather than adding flour, which would deaden its flavour.
Roll from the centre outward in short, light strokes so the puran distributes without bursting through the thin khapli cover.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with an extra spoon of melted Anveshan Ghee poured over the top and a small bowl of thin katachi amti made from the reserved dal water alongside.

variations.name: Karnataka Coconut Holige
variations.description: Known as holige or obbattu across Karnataka, this southern cousin folds fresh grated coconut into the chana-jaggery filling and wraps it in a paper-thin, turmeric-gold cover rolled out on a greased banana leaf. It is markedly more delicate than the Maharashtrian poli, almost see-through, with the coconut lending a moist, chewy sweetness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: kneaded loose and rested in oil, khapli stretches thin enough for the near-transparent holige cover

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil soaks the dough overnight-soft, the way holige makers keep it stretchy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: brushed on the hot griddle so each holige toasts fragrant and pliable

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the milder measure lets the fresh coconut come through rather than pure sweetness

steps: Pressure cook 1 cup rinsed chana dal with 2.5 cups water for 4 whistles on medium heat until butter-soft, then drain it completely so the filling will not turn watery once the coconut goes in.

Knead 1.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1/4 tsp salt and about 1/2 cup water into a slack, sticky dough, then pour 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over it and rest it covered for at least 1 hour, letting the oil relax the gluten.

Cook the drained dal with 3/4 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder in a pan on low heat for 6 to 7 minutes until thick, then stir in 3/4 cup fresh grated coconut and cook 3 minutes more until the mixture pulls cleanly from the sides.
Switch off the heat, mix in 1/2 tsp cardamom powder and mash the warm filling smooth, then cool it and roll into 8 balls a touch bigger than the dough portions.

Grease a banana leaf or oiled sheet with a little groundnut oil, place a small dough ball on it, top with a filling ball and press outward with oiled fingertips into a very thin 8 inch round, coaxing rather than rolling so it does not tear.

Slide the holige onto a medium tava, peel away the leaf, and cook about 45 seconds a side, brushing with Anveshan Ghee, until faint gold spots bloom and the cover turns translucent over the coconut filling.
tips: Use fresh, moist coconut, not desiccated; dry coconut drinks up the jaggery syrup and leaves the filling stiff and crumbly.
Pressing on a greased banana leaf is far easier than rolling for beginners, since the leaf lets you spread the fragile cover paper-thin without sticking.
Eat holige the day it is made; the fresh coconut filling does not keep well beyond a day even when refrigerated.
variations.servingSuggestion: In Karnataka it is served drizzled with warm ghee and a thin stream of sweetened coconut milk, or alongside a cup of spiced saaru for a sweet-savoury contrast.

variations.name: Gujarati Toor Puran Poli
variations.description: Gujarat's vedmi-style puran poli swaps chana dal for toor dal, giving a softer, faintly earthier puran that is generous with ghee and nutmeg. It leans richer and less grainy than the Maharashtrian version, and is traditionally eaten swimming in warm ghee with a glass of milk at festival lunches.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: the wholegrain cover balances the very sweet toor puran with a nutty, wheaty backbone

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Gujarati vedmi is unapologetically ghee-rich, in the dough, the puran and poured over at the table

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted into soft toor dal it sets into a glossy, spoonable puran

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in a spoon of warm milk to gild the puran and scent the whole poli

steps: Rinse 1 cup toor dal and pressure cook it with 2.5 cups water for 4 to 5 whistles on medium heat until completely mushy, then drain off all the excess liquid so the puran can thicken properly.

Knead 1.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1/4 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 1/2 cup water into a soft, pliable dough, coat it with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and rest it covered for 30 minutes.

Mash the drained toor dal smooth, then cook it with 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on low heat for 10 minutes, stirring, until it thickens into a glossy paste that pulls away from the pan.
Off the heat, beat in 1/2 tsp nutmeg powder, 1/2 tsp cardamom powder and the saffron-infused milk, then cool the puran until it is firm enough to shape into 8 balls.
Roll each rested dough ball into a small disc, seat a puran ball in the centre, seal the edges over the top and roll out gently to a 7 inch round, dusting lightly with atta to stop any sticking.
Cook on a medium tava for about a minute a side until golden freckles form, brushing generously with the remaining Anveshan Ghee, until the poli is soft, shiny and cooked through.
tips: Toor dal holds more water than chana, so drain it aggressively and dry the puran a couple of extra minutes or the filling will ooze while rolling.
A softer puran suits toor dal, so aim for a spoonable, fudge-like set rather than the firm ball of a Maharashtrian filling.
Make the puran a day ahead and refrigerate; it firms beautifully overnight and rolls far more cleanly the next morning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve Gujarati-style, torn into a bowl and drowned in warm ghee and cold milk, or paired with spicy aloo nu shaak for the classic sweet-and-savoury festival plate.

variations.name: Dry Fruit & Poppy Puran Poli
variations.description: A celebration-day upgrade where the chana-jaggery puran is studded with toasted poppy seeds and a handful of chopped almonds, cashews and pistachios for crunch, then rounded with rose. It is the richest of the polis, meant for weddings and Diwali, with pockets of nutty texture in every folded bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: the sturdier emmer cover carries the heavier dry-fruit puran without tearing at the seams

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: used to toast the nuts and gild the polis, tying the richer filling together

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: kept slightly restrained so the nuts and rose read clearly against the caramel

steps: Pressure cook 1 cup rinsed chana dal with 2.5 cups water for 4 whistles on medium heat until very soft, then drain it thoroughly and set it aside to steam-dry for a few minutes.

Knead 1.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1/4 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 1/2 cup water into a soft dough, oil the surface with a little more ghee and rest it covered for 30 minutes.
Dry-toast 2 tbsp white poppy seeds on low heat for 2 minutes until they smell nutty, then warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and fry the 1/3 cup chopped mixed nuts for 2 minutes until golden and fragrant.

Cook the drained dal with 3/4 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder on low heat for 7 to 8 minutes until thick, then fold in the toasted poppy seeds, fried nuts, 1/2 tsp cardamom powder and 1/2 tsp rose water; mash coarsely so some nut texture survives, and cool fully.

Divide dough and filling into 8 portions each, cup a dough disc around a filling ball, pinch the top closed and roll out carefully to a 7 inch round, keeping the pressure even so the nuts do not pierce the cover.
Griddle each poli on a medium tava for about a minute a side, brushing with the remaining Anveshan Ghee, until deep gold with toasted freckles and a faint scent of rose.
tips: Chop the nuts fine and even; large shards act like blades and will puncture the thin poli as you roll it.
Toast poppy seeds just until fragrant and never let them brown, since scorched poppy turns the whole filling bitter.
This richer poli keeps for two days in an airtight box and reheats well with a dab of ghee on a warm tava.
variations.servingSuggestion: Plate it for a festive spread with a scoop of vanilla-free saffron kheer or a cardamom shrikhand, letting the two sweets play off each other.

variations.name: Classic Malai Rabri
variations.description: The North Indian sweet-shop rabri, made by slowly reducing full-fat milk while repeatedly collecting the thick malai skin at the sides of the pan. Sweetened lightly and scented with saffron and cardamom, it is a luscious tangle of milky ribbons served chilled with jalebi or on its own.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: khandsari sweetens the reduced milk without dulling its creamy ivory colour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: pure saffron steeped in warm milk gives rabri its gentle gold streaks and floral aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a little bilona ghee fries the pistachio garnish that finishes the chilled rabri

steps: Steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk, and pour 6 cups full-fat milk into a wide, heavy-bottomed kadhai.
Bring the milk to a boil, then lower the heat to a steady simmer and cook, stirring occasionally, for about 45 minutes as the milk reduces.
As a thick malai skin forms on the surface and sides, keep gently pushing it to the edge of the pan with a spatula and letting it dry into ribbons.
When the milk has reduced to roughly a third of its volume and is thick and creamy, scrape all the collected malai back in and stir gently.
Add 1/3 cup Anveshan Khandsari, the saffron milk and 1/2 tsp cardamom powder, and simmer for 5 minutes until dissolved and the rabri is thick and glossy.
Fry 12 pistachios and 10 slivered almonds in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee for 1 minute, stir half in, chill the rabri for 3 hours, and garnish with the rest.
tips: Use the widest pan you have, as a large surface area forms more malai and reduces the milk faster.
Do not stir constantly; letting the skin form and collecting it at the sides is what gives rabri its signature ribbons.
Add the sweetener only near the end, since sugar added early slows the reduction and can catch at the base.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve well chilled in shallow bowls topped with saffron and pistachios, or spooned alongside hot crisp jalebis for the classic pairing.

variations.name: Instant Paneer Rabri
variations.description: A clever shortcut rabri that mimics the reduced-milk texture using crumbled fresh paneer and a little milk powder, ready in a fraction of the time. The paneer breaks into soft granules just like collected malai, giving a rich, grainy rabri for last-minute cravings.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: khandsari sweetens the quick rabri cleanly while keeping its pale, milky colour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee toasts the almond garnish for aroma over the speedy rabri

steps: Bring 3 cups full-fat milk to a boil in a heavy pan, then lower the heat to a gentle simmer.
Whisk 1/4 cup milk powder with a few spoons of the warm milk into a smooth paste, then stir it back into the pan and cook for 3 minutes to thicken the base.
Crumble 1 cup fresh paneer finely and add it to the simmering milk, stirring, so it breaks into soft granules resembling collected malai.
Cook on low for 8 minutes, stirring often, until the mixture thickens to a grainy, spoonable rabri.
Stir in 1/3 cup Anveshan Khandsari and 1/2 tsp cardamom powder and simmer for 3 minutes until dissolved and glossy.
Toast 12 slivered almonds in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee for 1 minute, fold half in, chill for 1 hour, and top with the rest and 1 tbsp rose petals.
tips: Crumble the paneer as finely as possible so it mimics the delicate granules of slow-cooked malai.
Use soft, fresh paneer rather than firm block paneer, which stays rubbery and will not blend smoothly.
This quick rabri thickens as it chills, so take it off the heat while still slightly loose.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled in small glasses topped with rose petals and almonds, an instant dessert when guests arrive unannounced.

variations.name: Gur ki Rabri
variations.description: A rustic winter rabri sweetened with jaggery instead of sugar, turning the reduced milk a warm toffee brown with an earthy, caramel depth. A pinch of dry ginger keeps it warming, making it the village-style rabri of the cold months.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery turns the reduced milk a caramel brown and lends the earthy sweetness that defines gur ki rabri

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee fries the walnut and cashew garnish for a toasty winter finish

steps: Pour 6 cups full-fat milk into a wide heavy kadhai, bring to a boil, then simmer on low for about 45 minutes, collecting the malai skin at the sides as the milk reduces.
