When the milk has thickened to a third of its volume, scrape the collected malai back in and stir gently to make a creamy rabri.
Melt 1/2 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 3 tbsp water in a separate pan, then strain out any grit to leave a smooth syrup.
Turn the flame to its lowest, cool the rabri for a couple of minutes, then stir the jaggery syrup in slowly so the reduced milk does not curdle.
Simmer gently for 3 minutes with 1/2 tsp cardamom powder and 1/4 tsp dry ginger powder until the rabri turns an even toffee brown.
Fry 8 chopped walnuts and 10 cashews in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee for 1 minute, fold half in, chill, and garnish with the rest.
tips: Cool the reduced milk slightly and keep the heat low before adding jaggery, or the acidity will split the rabri.
Melt and strain the jaggery first so no grit clouds the smooth, creamy texture.
Chopped walnuts suit this earthy jaggery version better than the usual pistachios of the classic.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve slightly warm on a winter evening topped with toasted walnuts, or chilled with a drizzle of extra jaggery syrup.

variations.name: Rose Malai Rabri
variations.description: A delicate pink rabri perfumed with rose and gulkand, finished with dried petals for a floral, celebratory feel. The reduced milk carries the rose beautifully, making this the version served at weddings and Valentine's-style dinners.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: khandsari keeps the rabri pale so the rose tint and petals stand out

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee fries the pistachio garnish over the rose-scented rabri

steps: Pour 6 cups full-fat milk into a wide heavy kadhai, bring to a boil, then simmer on low for about 40 minutes, pushing the malai skin to the sides as the milk reduces.
When the milk is reduced to a third and creamy, scrape the collected malai back in and stir gently to a thick rabri.
Stir in 1/3 cup Anveshan Khandsari and 1/2 tsp cardamom powder and simmer for 4 minutes until dissolved.
Turn off the heat, mash 2 tbsp gulkand until smooth and stir it in with 1 tsp rose water, which tints the rabri a soft pink and perfumes it.
Crush half the dried rose petals and fold them in, then chill the rabri for 3 hours.
Fry 12 pistachios in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee for 1 minute and scatter them with the remaining rose petals over the chilled rabri before serving.
tips: Add the gulkand and rose water only off the heat, so the floral aroma is not lost to cooking.
Mash the gulkand thoroughly for an even pink colour without needing artificial food dye.
Use food-grade dried rose petals and crush them lightly to add fragrance without bitterness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled in glass bowls topped with rose petals and pistachios, an elegant floral dessert for a romantic dinner.

variations.name: Classic Punjabi Rajma Chawal
variations.description: The definitive North Indian comfort meal of red kidney beans simmered soft in a thick onion-tomato masala, ladled over fluffy steamed rice. The beans are cooked until some break down and naturally thicken the gravy to a creamy, spoon-coating richness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the masala to a deep brown and gives the gravy its signature homely richness

steps: Soak 1 cup rajma overnight in plenty of water, then pressure-cook with 3 cups fresh water and 0.75 tsp salt for 6 to 7 whistles until the beans mash easily between two fingers.
Rinse 1.5 cups basmati rice, then boil in salted water for 10 minutes until just tender, drain and keep the fluffy grains aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle for 15 seconds until fragrant.
Add the finely chopped onions and fry for 8 minutes until deep golden, then stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until the raw smell fades.
Add the pureed tomatoes with 1.5 tsp chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt, and bhuno for 8 minutes until the ghee separates at the edges.
Tip in the cooked rajma along with its cooking liquid, mash a few beans against the side of the pan, and simmer uncovered for 15 minutes until the gravy turns thick and creamy.
Sprinkle 0.75 tsp garam masala, stir once and serve the hot rajma over the steamed rice.
tips: Mashing a ladleful of beans into the gravy thickens it naturally without any cream or flour.
Always soak the rajma overnight so it cooks fully soft and stays easy to digest.
A splash of the bean stock loosens the gravy if it thickens too much on standing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a wedge of lemon, sliced onion rings and a spoon of tangy mango pickle on the side.

variations.name: Amritsari Dhaba Rajma
variations.description: A rustic highway-dhaba rendition where the beans simmer low and slow in a mustard-oil masala finished with a smoky tempering and crushed kasuri methi. The gravy is darker, punchier and clings thickly, meant to be scooped up over a mound of rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the pungent dhaba fat that gives the gravy its dark, earthy backbone

steps: Soak 1 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 3 cups water, the 2 bay leaves, 1 black cardamom and 0.75 tsp salt for 7 whistles until very soft.
Boil 1.5 cups basmati rice in salted water for 10 minutes until tender, drain and keep warm.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a heavy kadai until it just smokes, then lower the heat and fry the 2 finely chopped large onions for 10 minutes until deep brown.
Add a paste of the 2 inch ginger and 8 garlic cloves and fry for 2 minutes, then add the pureed tomatoes with 2 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp salt.
Bhuno this masala patiently for 10 minutes until it darkens and the oil pools at the sides of the pan.
Add the cooked rajma with its liquid, mash a handful of beans, and simmer uncovered on low for 18 minutes so the gravy reduces and turns glossy.
Crush 1.5 tsp kasuri methi between your palms over the pot, stir through and serve the smoky rajma over the rice.
tips: Let the mustard oil reach smoking point once to mellow its sharpness before frying the onions.
The black cardamom cooked with the beans is what lends the dhaba its faint smoky aroma.
Cook the gravy longer and thicker than usual, as dhaba rajma is meant to be almost semi-dry.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile over rice with a dollop of white butter melting on top and a raw onion-and-green-chilli salad.

variations.name: Kashmiri Rajma with Rice
variations.description: The prized dark-red rajma of the Jammu belt, cooked without heavy onion in a fennel and dry-ginger spiced gravy that tastes bright and aromatic rather than heavy. Small dense beans and Kashmiri chilli give it a glowing red colour and a distinctive perfumed warmth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the authentic Kashmiri cooking fat that carries the fennel and dry ginger aromas

steps: Soak 1 cup rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 3 cups water and 0.75 tsp salt for 7 whistles until the beans are meltingly soft.
Boil 1.5 cups basmati rice in salted water for 10 minutes until just done, then drain and keep aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking point, reduce the heat and add 0.25 tsp asafoetida, the 3 cloves, 3 cardamoms and 1 inch cinnamon and let them sizzle for 20 seconds.
Add the pureed tomatoes with 2 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 2 tsp fennel powder, 1 tsp dry ginger powder and 0.75 tsp salt, and cook for 8 minutes until the masala thickens and darkens.
Pour in the cooked rajma with its stock, mash a few spoonfuls of beans, and simmer uncovered for 15 minutes until the gravy turns a deep glossy red.
Adjust the consistency with a little hot water so it stays pourable, then simmer 2 more minutes.
Rest the rajma covered for 5 minutes to let the fennel aroma bloom, then serve over the steamed rice.
tips: Fennel and dry ginger, not onion and garlic, define the true Kashmiri flavour, so do not add them.
Kashmiri chilli powder gives the deep red colour without much heat, so use it generously.
The gravy tastes even better the next day once the perfumed spices settle into the beans.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain rice and a bowl of Kashmiri-style seasoned yogurt or a simple radish salad.

variations.name: One-Pot Rajma Pulao
variations.description: A clever weeknight take that turns the classic thali into a single fragrant pot, cooking soaked beans and basmati together with whole spices so every grain is flavoured. It carries all the warmth of rajma chawal but comes together with far less fuss and washing up.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: coats the rice grains and toasts the whole spices for a rich pulao aroma

steps: Soak 0.75 cup rajma overnight and 1.5 cups basmati rice for 30 minutes, then drain both separately.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pressure cooker over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin, the bay leaf, 1 inch cinnamon, 4 cloves and 3 cardamoms and let them crackle for 20 seconds.
Add the thinly sliced large onion and fry for 6 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Add the chopped tomato with 1 tsp chilli powder and 1 tsp salt and cook 3 minutes until softened, then add the drained rajma and toss to coat.
Pour in 2.5 cups hot water, close the cooker and pressure-cook for 5 whistles until the beans are nearly soft.
Open once the pressure drops, add the drained rice, 0.5 tsp salt and top up with just enough hot water to sit 1 cm above the rice, then cook for 2 whistles.
Rest 10 minutes, sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala, fluff gently with a fork and serve.
tips: Cook the beans almost fully before adding rice, since rice needs far less time than rajma.
Keep the water level exactly one finger above the rice for perfectly separate grains.
Let the pulao rest undisturbed after cooking so the grains firm up and do not turn mushy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve straight from the pot with a cooling boondi raita and papad for an easy one-dish dinner.

variations.name: Classic Bengali Rasgulla
variations.description: The iconic spongy Bengali sweet of fresh chhena balls simmered in a light sugar syrup until they swell to airy, juicy spheres. Made from milk curdled just right and kneaded smooth, each rasgulla releases a burst of delicate syrup when pressed, with barely any sweetness masking the milky freshness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: unrefined cane sugar that keeps the soaking syrup clean and light so the chhena flavour shines

steps: Bring 1.5 litres full-fat milk to a boil, turn off the heat and stir in 3 tbsp lemon juice mixed with a little water until the milk fully splits into curds and clear whey.
Pour the curds into a muslin cloth, rinse under cold water to remove the lemon tang, gather and hang for 30 minutes so the chhena is moist but not dripping.
Knead the chhena with 1 tsp fine semolina on a plate for 8 minutes with the heel of your palm until it turns smooth, soft and slightly greasy.
Roll into 12 small crack-free balls, remembering they will double in size while cooking.
Dissolve 1.5 cups Anveshan Khandsari Sugar in 4 cups water with the crushed 3 cardamoms and bring to a rolling boil in a wide deep pot.
Gently slide in the chhena balls, cover and boil vigorously for 15 minutes, adding a splash of hot water twice to keep the syrup thin as the balls swell.
Turn off the heat, stir in 1 tsp rose water, and let the rasgullas cool in the syrup before chilling and serving cold.
tips: Knead the chhena long enough that it feels smooth and leaves a little grease on your palm, which is the secret to spongy rasgullas.
Keep the syrup at a hard boil and thin, since a thick or gentle syrup makes the balls hard.
Do not overcrowd the pot, as the balls need room to expand freely.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve well chilled in small bowls with a little of the syrup and a sprinkle of chopped pistachios.

variations.name: Nolen Gur Rasgulla
variations.description: A prized winter Bengali speciality where the light sugar syrup is replaced by fragrant date-palm jaggery, tinting the spongy chhena balls a warm caramel brown. The jaggery lends a smoky, molasses-like depth that makes these seasonal rasgullas taste richer and more aromatic than the classic white ones.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: stands in for the traditional nolen gur to give the syrup its caramel colour and smoky depth

steps: Boil 1.5 litres milk, switch off the heat and add 3 tbsp diluted lemon juice, stirring until it curdles cleanly into chhena and whey.
Strain through muslin, rinse with cold water, and hang for 30 minutes until the chhena is soft but no longer wet.
Knead the chhena with 1 tsp semolina for 8 minutes until smooth and pliable, then shape into 12 small crack-free balls.
Dissolve 1.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 4 cups water, add the bay leaf and crushed 3 cardamoms, bring to a boil and strain out any grit before returning it to a rolling boil.
Slide in the chhena balls, cover and boil hard for 15 minutes, topping up with a little hot water so the syrup stays thin as the balls double.
Switch off the heat and let the rasgullas rest in the warm jaggery syrup for 20 minutes to soak up the colour and aroma.
Chill thoroughly and serve cold, bathed in the caramel syrup.
tips: Strain the jaggery syrup before boiling the balls so no sediment clings to the chhena.
Use good aromatic jaggery, as its smoky notes are the whole point of this winter version.
Boil the balls just as vigorously as for white rasgulla so they stay light and spongy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled in earthen bowls, the way seasonal nolen gur sweets are traditionally offered in Bengal.

variations.name: Kesar Rajbhog
variations.description: The grand, festive big brother of the rasgulla, where larger saffron-tinted chhena balls are stuffed with a rich filling of dry fruits, khoya and cardamom before poaching in syrup. Cutting one open reveals a jewelled centre, making rajbhog a celebratory showpiece sweet for weddings and pujas.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: makes the mild saffron syrup that lets the rich filling stay the star

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: tints both the chhena and the syrup a festive gold and lends a floral aroma

steps: Curdle 1.5 litres boiled milk with 3 tbsp diluted lemon juice, strain through muslin, rinse and hang the chhena for 30 minutes until moist but firm.
Soak the pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 1 tbsp warm milk, then knead half of it into the chhena along with 1 tsp semolina for 8 minutes until smooth and golden.
For the filling, mix the 3 tbsp khoya with the chopped cashews, pistachios, 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and a little of the saffron milk into a soft stuffing.
Divide the chhena into 8 portions, flatten each, place a spoon of filling in the centre and seal into a large smooth crack-free ball.
Boil 1.5 cups Anveshan Khandsari Sugar with 4 cups water and the remaining saffron milk into a thin syrup at a rolling boil.
Slide in the stuffed balls, cover and boil hard for 18 minutes, adding hot water as needed so the large rajbhogs cook through and swell.
Cool them in the syrup, then chill and serve halved to show the dry-fruit centre.
tips: Seal the filling well so no cracks form, or the rajbhog can burst open while boiling.
Make the balls larger than rasgullas but boil a few minutes longer so the centres set.
Reserve some saffron milk for the syrup to carry the colour right through the sweet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled and halved, garnished with saffron strands and slivered pistachios for a wedding-worthy platter.

variations.name: Coconut Chhena Rasgulla
variations.description: A South-meets-East twist where desiccated coconut is worked into the chhena and the poached balls are rolled in more coconut, giving a gentle chew and tropical fragrance. The coconut adds texture and a subtle sweetness that sets these apart from the plain milky classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: sweetens the light syrup without overpowering the delicate coconut aroma

steps: Boil 1.5 litres milk, take it off the heat and add 3 tbsp diluted lemon juice, stirring gently until the chhena separates from the whey.
Strain, rinse under cold water and hang the chhena for 30 minutes until soft but not wet.
Knead the chhena with 1 tsp semolina, 2 tbsp desiccated coconut and 0.5 tsp cardamom powder for 8 minutes until smooth and cohesive.
Roll into 12 small crack-free balls, keeping in mind they will expand as they cook.
Boil 1.5 cups Anveshan Khandsari Sugar with 4 cups water to a thin rolling-boil syrup in a wide pot.
Add the coconut chhena balls, cover and boil hard for 15 minutes, splashing in hot water to keep the syrup light as they swell.
Cool the balls in the syrup, then roll each in the remaining 3 tbsp desiccated coconut and chill before serving.
tips: Use fine desiccated coconut so the chhena still kneads smooth and does not crack.
Boil the balls hard as always, as the coconut can otherwise make them a touch dense.
Roll in fresh coconut only just before serving so the coating stays dry and pretty.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled, rolled in coconut, with a small bowl of the syrup for spooning over.

variations.name: Classic Rasmalai
variations.description: Soft flattened chhena discs first poached in syrup, then gently squeezed and steeped in a thickened saffron-and-cardamom milk until they turn plump and creamy. The chilled discs soak up the rich rabri so each spoonful is pillowy chhena bathed in fragrant, nutty milk.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: sweetens both the poaching syrup and the rabri without clouding the milky flavour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk to colour and perfume the rabri a delicate gold

steps: Boil 1 litre of the milk, take it off the heat and add 3 tbsp diluted lemon juice, stirring until it curdles into chhena, then strain, rinse and hang for 30 minutes.
Knead the chhena with 1 tsp semolina for 8 minutes until smooth, shape into 12 balls and flatten each into a disc about 1 cm thick.
Boil 1 cup Anveshan Khandsari Sugar with 4 cups water and the crushed 3 cardamoms, slide in the discs, cover and boil hard for 12 minutes until they swell and float.
Meanwhile simmer the remaining 1 litre milk on medium heat for 25 minutes, stirring often, until it reduces to a thick creamy rabri.
Steep the pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp of the hot rabri, then stir it back in along with the remaining 0.75 cup khandsari sugar and 2 crushed cardamoms, and simmer 3 more minutes off the boil.
Gently press each poached disc between your palms to squeeze out the syrup, then slip it into the warm rabri.
Simmer the discs in the rabri for 5 minutes on low, then chill for at least 3 hours and serve cold garnished with pistachios and almonds.
tips: Flatten the discs evenly so they cook through and soak up the rabri uniformly.
Squeeze out the poaching syrup gently before adding the discs to the milk, so they drink up the rabri instead.
Reduce the milk slowly on medium heat to build a naturally thick rabri without scorching.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve well chilled in shallow bowls with plenty of saffron milk and a scatter of slivered nuts.

variations.name: Angoori Rasmalai
variations.description: A dainty version where the chhena is rolled into tiny grape-sized balls instead of discs, giving little bursts of softness in every spoon of saffron milk. Their small size means they soak the rabri faster and are wonderful served in a glass as a spoonable dessert for a crowd.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: keeps the syrup and rabri mildly sweet so the tiny chhena balls stay delicate

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: gives the rabri its signature golden hue and floral aroma

steps: Curdle 1 litre boiled milk with 3 tbsp diluted lemon juice, strain, rinse under cold water and hang the chhena for 30 minutes.
Knead the chhena with 1 tsp semolina for 8 minutes until smooth, then roll into about 24 tiny grape-sized balls.
Boil 1 cup Anveshan Khandsari Sugar with 4 cups water, drop in the little balls, cover and boil hard for 10 minutes until they double and float.
Reduce the remaining 1 litre milk on medium heat for 22 minutes, stirring often, until thick and creamy.
Soak the pinch of Anveshan Saffron in a little warm milk and stir it into the rabri with the remaining 0.75 cup khandsari sugar and 0.5 tsp cardamom powder, simmering 3 minutes off the boil.
Squeeze each tiny ball lightly to remove the syrup and drop them into the warm saffron rabri.
Stir in 1 tsp rose water, chill for 3 hours and serve cold in glasses topped with pistachios.
tips: Roll the balls small and uniform so they cook evenly and look neat in the glass.
The little balls soak faster than discs, so a couple of hours of chilling is enough.
Add rose water only after the milk cools so its fragrance is not lost to the heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in tall glasses like a rabri dessert, spooned up with the soft angoori balls throughout.

variations.name: Instant Bread Rasmalai
variations.description: A quick cheat that skips chhena-making by soaking soft bread rounds in a saffron rabri, ready in a fraction of the time yet strikingly similar to the real thing. The bread drinks up the sweet milk to become tender and creamy, perfect for a last-minute dessert.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: sweetens the quick rabri gently so the bread soaks up a mild, milky syrup

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: colours and perfumes the instant rabri just like the classic version

steps: Simmer 1 litre full-fat milk on medium heat for 15 minutes, whisking in 0.5 cup milk powder until it thickens into a quick rabri.
Soak the pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 1 tbsp warm milk, then stir it into the rabri with 0.75 cup Anveshan Khandsari Sugar and 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and simmer 3 minutes off the boil.
Cut the 8 bread slices into rounds using a cutter or the rim of a glass, discarding the trimmings.
Warm the rabri to just below a simmer and turn off the heat so it does not scald the bread.
Dip each bread round briefly into the warm rabri for a few seconds so it softens but does not fall apart, then lay it in a serving dish.
Pour the remaining warm rabri over all the rounds so they are half submerged, and let them soak for 20 minutes.
Chill for 2 hours and serve cold, garnished generously with pistachios and almonds.
tips: Dip the bread only briefly, as over-soaking makes it disintegrate into the milk.
Use fresh soft bread and cut neat rounds so the dessert looks like true rasmalai.
Keep the rabri slightly thick so it clings to the bread rather than making it soggy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled with extra saffron rabri poured over and a dusting of crushed nuts on top.

variations.name: Mango Rasmalai
variations.description: A summery twist where ripe mango pulp is folded into the rabri, turning the saffron milk into a fragrant golden mango cream that cloaks the soft chhena discs. The fruity sweetness plays beautifully against the milky chhena, making it a seasonal favourite when mangoes are at their peak.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: lightly sweetens the poaching syrup while the mango carries most of the sweetness in the rabri

steps: Curdle 1 litre boiled milk with 3 tbsp diluted lemon juice, strain, rinse and hang the chhena for 30 minutes.
Knead the chhena with 1 tsp semolina for 8 minutes, shape into 12 balls and flatten into discs.
Boil 1 cup Anveshan Khandsari Sugar with 4 cups water, poach the discs covered on a hard boil for 12 minutes until they swell, then set aside.
Reduce the remaining 1 litre milk on medium heat for 22 minutes with a pinch of saffron until thick, then cool it until just warm.
Whisk 1 cup mango pulp with the remaining 0.25 cup khandsari sugar and 0.5 tsp cardamom powder into the cooled rabri, keeping it off the heat so it does not split.
Gently squeeze the poached discs and immerse them in the mango rabri.
Chill for at least 3 hours and serve cold, garnished with chopped pistachios.
tips: Add the mango pulp only after the milk has cooled, as boiling can curdle the fruit acids.
Use a sweet non-fibrous mango like Alphonso for a smooth, richly flavoured rabri.
Reduce the sugar in the rabri to account for the natural sweetness of the mango.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled topped with a few fresh mango cubes and pistachios for a vibrant summer dessert.

variations.name: Classic Rice Kheer
variations.description: The definitive North Indian chawal ki kheer, where a small handful of basmati simmers slowly in full-fat milk until the grains burst and the milk turns thick, ivory and creamy. Perfumed with cardamom and studded with ghee-fried nuts, it is the sweet that ends every festive thali and family celebration.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined khandsari keeps the kheer a pale ivory while adding a gentle mineral sweetness that white sugar lacks

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoon of bilona ghee to fry the nuts adds a nutty aroma and glossy richness to the finished kheer

steps: Rinse 1/4 cup basmati rice until the water runs clear, then soak it in fresh water for 15 minutes and drain, which helps the grains cook soft and split creamily.
Bring 5 cups full-fat milk to a gentle boil in a heavy-bottomed pan on medium heat, stirring often and scraping the sides so the milk does not catch or scorch.

Add the drained rice and simmer on low heat for 30 to 35 minutes, stirring every few minutes, until the grains are completely soft and the milk has reduced and thickened to a creamy pouring consistency.
Meanwhile heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan and fry 10 cashews, 10 slivered almonds and 2 tbsp raisins until the nuts are golden and the raisins plump, about 1 minute, then set aside.
Stir in 1/2 cup Anveshan Khandsari and cook on low for 4 to 5 minutes until it fully dissolves and the kheer thickens again, tasting to check the sweetness.
Turn off the heat, fold in 1/2 tsp cardamom powder and most of the fried nuts and raisins, and garnish with the rest before serving.
tips: Add the khandsari only after the rice is fully cooked, as sweeteners added early toughen the grains and stop them softening.
Keep the kheer a touch looser than you want it, because it thickens noticeably as it cools and sets.
For an extra-creamy body, mash a few spoons of the cooked rice against the side of the pan before sweetening.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm in winter or chilled in summer, garnished with a few saffron strands and slivered pistachios, alongside hot pooris for a classic festive pairing.

variations.name: Bengali Gurer Payesh
variations.description: The Bengali festival payesh made with fragrant short-grain gobindobhog rice and sweetened entirely with date-palm jaggery for a smoky caramel depth. Cooked low and slow with a bay leaf, it turns a warm toffee brown and is the sweet made for birthdays and Poush Sankranti.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery gives payesh its signature smoky-caramel flavour and warm brown colour that define the Bengali version

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the rice is tossed in bilona ghee first, a Bengali trick that keeps each grain separate and fragrant

steps: Rinse 1/4 cup gobindobhog rice gently and drain, then toss it with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 3 lightly crushed cardamom pods, letting it rest for 10 minutes to absorb the aroma.
Bring 5 cups full-fat milk to a boil in a heavy pan with 1 bay leaf, then simmer on medium-low for 10 minutes, stirring, until it thickens slightly.
Add the ghee-coated rice and cook on low heat for 30 minutes, stirring often, until the grains are soft and the milk reduces to a thick, creamy payesh.
Melt 3/4 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water in a separate pan on low heat, then strain out any grit to leave a clean syrup.
Turn the flame to its lowest, remove the bay leaf, and stir the strained jaggery syrup into the payesh in a thin stream while stirring constantly so the milk does not split.
Simmer for 3 to 4 minutes until glossy, fold in 10 cashews and 2 tbsp raisins, and serve warm or chilled.
tips: Always add jaggery off the boil and with the heat at its lowest, or the acidity in the jaggery will curdle the reduced milk.
Tossing the rice in ghee before cooking keeps the delicate gobindobhog grains intact instead of turning mushy.
Nolen gur (liquid date jaggery) can replace the powder in winter for an even more aromatic, authentic payesh.
variations.servingSuggestion: Traditionally served cold in a clay bowl at the end of a Bengali feast, or offered as bhog during Lakshmi Puja.

variations.name: Kesar Badam Rice Kheer
variations.description: A richer sweet-shop style kheer thickened with ground almond paste and glowing with real saffron. The almonds give it a luxurious body and a pale gold colour, making it the indulgent version you find at wedding buffets and mithai counters.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: khandsari sweetens without masking the delicate saffron and almond flavours of this refined kheer

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: a generous pinch of pure saffron steeped in warm milk gives this kheer its gold colour and floral perfume

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee fries the pistachio garnish and lends the finished kheer a rich sheen

steps: Soak 15 almonds in hot water for 15 minutes, then peel and grind them with a little milk into a smooth paste, and steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk.
Rinse and soak 1/4 cup basmati rice for 15 minutes, drain, then simmer it in 5 cups full-fat milk on low heat for 30 minutes, stirring, until the grains are soft and the milk thickens.
Stir in the ground almond paste and cook for another 5 minutes on low, which thickens the kheer and gives it a velvety body.
Add 1/2 cup Anveshan Khandsari and the saffron milk, stirring for 4 minutes until the sweetener dissolves and the kheer turns a pale gold.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and lightly fry the remaining 5 slivered almonds and 12 pistachios until golden, about 1 minute, then stir most of them in.
Finish with 1/2 tsp cardamom powder and 1/2 tsp rose water off the heat, then garnish with the reserved nuts and a few saffron strands.
tips: Grind the almonds fine and smooth so the kheer stays silky rather than grainy on the tongue.
Steep the saffron in warm, not boiling, milk to draw out maximum colour without dulling the aroma.
Add rose water only at the very end and sparingly, as too much turns the delicate kheer perfumey.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve well chilled in small kulhads topped with saffron strands and slivered pistachios, a fitting close to a rich Mughlai meal.

variations.name: Coconut Milk Rice Kheer
variations.description: A dairy-free rice kheer simmered entirely in creamy coconut milk and sweetened with jaggery for a mellow tropical flavour. Cashews and raisins fried in coconut oil deepen the coastal aroma, making it a wholesome pudding that anyone can enjoy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery pairs naturally with coconut milk, lending a caramel warmth that suits this dairy-free kheer

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed coconut oil fries the nuts and reinforces the fragrant coastal character of this kheer

steps: Rinse 1/4 cup basmati rice and soak for 15 minutes, then drain and simmer it in 2 cups thin coconut milk on low heat for 20 minutes, stirring often, until the grains turn soft.
Add 3 cups thick coconut milk and cook gently on low for another 10 minutes, stirring so it does not stick, until the kheer thickens to a creamy consistency.
Melt 1/2 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water in a small pan, strain out any grit, and keep the syrup ready.
Lower the flame completely and stir the strained jaggery syrup into the kheer slowly, keeping the heat gentle so the coconut milk stays smooth and does not split.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and fry 12 cashews golden, 2 tbsp raisins until plump and 3 tbsp grated coconut until lightly toasted, about 2 minutes.
Fold the fried nuts, raisins and coconut into the kheer with 1/2 tsp cardamom powder and warm through for a minute before serving.
tips: Cook the rice in thin coconut milk first and add the thick milk later, so the rich cream does not scorch during the long simmer.
Keep the heat low once the jaggery goes in, because coconut milk splits more easily than dairy when overheated.
If the kheer tightens on cooling, loosen it with a splash of warm coconut milk rather than water.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled topped with toasted coconut flakes and a few fried cashews, a refreshing dairy-free dessert after a South Indian meal.

variations.name: Classic Sabudana Kheer
variations.description: A silky pudding of soaked tapioca pearls simmered in full-fat milk until they turn glassy and plump, sweetened lightly and scented with cardamom. The pearls suspend like little pearls of jelly in the creamy milk, making this the comforting kheer of everyday celebrations.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: khandsari dissolves cleanly and keeps this milk kheer pale and delicately sweet

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee fries the cashews and raisins that garnish the kheer with a rich aroma

steps: Rinse 1/2 cup sabudana thoroughly and soak it in 1/2 cup water for 20 minutes until the pearls swell and turn soft but still hold their shape.
Bring 4 cups full-fat milk to a gentle boil in a heavy pan on medium heat, stirring so it does not catch at the bottom.
Add the soaked, drained sabudana and simmer on low heat for 12 to 15 minutes, stirring often, until the pearls turn translucent and the milk thickens slightly.
Stir in 1/2 cup Anveshan Khandsari and cook for 4 minutes on low until it dissolves and the kheer thickens back to a creamy pouring consistency.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan and fry 10 cashews to golden and 2 tbsp raisins until they plump, about 1 minute.
Fold the fried nuts and raisins into the kheer with 1/2 tsp cardamom powder and serve warm or chilled.
tips: Do not over-soak the sabudana or it disintegrates; the pearls should be soft enough to press but still whole.
Stir frequently once the sabudana is in the milk, as tapioca sinks and sticks to the base very quickly.
The kheer thickens a lot on cooling, so keep it loose and thin it with warm milk before serving if needed.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled in small bowls topped with slivered almonds and a pinch of cardamom, a soothing dessert on a hot day.

variations.name: Vrat Sabudana Kheer
variations.description: The fasting-day version made for Navratri and Ekadashi, sweetened with mineral-rich jaggery instead of sugar and enriched with ghee-fried makhana. Warm, filling and free of grains, it keeps you satisfied through a day of vrat while feeling like a treat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery is the traditional vrat-friendly sweetener and adds a caramel depth to the fasting kheer

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee roasts the makhana until crisp and lends the fasting kheer its rich, satisfying finish

steps: Rinse and soak 1/2 cup sabudana in 1/2 cup water for 20 minutes until softened, then drain.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan and roast 3/4 cup makhana on low heat for 4 to 5 minutes until crisp, then crush half of them coarsely and keep the rest whole.
Bring 4 cups full-fat milk to a boil in a heavy pan, add the soaked sabudana, and simmer on low for 12 minutes, stirring, until the pearls turn translucent.
Stir in the crushed makhana and slivered almonds and cook for another 3 minutes so they soften into the creamy kheer.
Melt 1/2 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 1/2 cup water, strain out grit, lower the flame, and stir the syrup into the kheer slowly so the milk does not curdle.
Finish with 1/2 tsp cardamom powder, 1/4 tsp dry ginger powder and the whole roasted makhana on top, then serve warm.
tips: Roast the makhana until they crunch when bitten, so they hold a little bite even after simmering in the milk.
Always melt and strain the jaggery and add it off the boil, or the reduced milk will split.
The pinch of dry ginger powder warms the kheer and makes it easier to digest during a fast.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm during Navratri or Ekadashi with a scatter of whole roasted makhana, a wholesome vrat dessert that doubles as a light meal.

variations.name: Coconut Sabudana Kheer
variations.description: A dairy-free coastal version where the tapioca pearls swim in fragrant coconut milk sweetened with jaggery. Cashews toasted in coconut oil and a scatter of fresh coconut give it a tropical richness quite different from the milk-based classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery melds beautifully with coconut milk for a mellow, caramel-toned dairy-free kheer

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed coconut oil toasts the cashews and deepens the coastal aroma of this kheer

steps: Rinse and soak 1/2 cup sabudana in 1/2 cup water for 20 minutes until soft, then drain.
Bring 2 cups thin coconut milk to a gentle simmer, add the soaked sabudana, and cook on low for 12 minutes, stirring, until the pearls turn glassy.
Pour in 2 cups thick coconut milk and warm through on low heat for 4 minutes, stirring gently so the cream stays smooth.
Melt 1/2 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 1/2 cup water, strain, then lower the flame and stir the syrup in slowly to keep the coconut milk from splitting.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and toast 12 cashews golden and 1/4 cup grated coconut until fragrant, about 2 minutes.
Fold the toasted cashews and coconut into the kheer with 1/2 tsp cardamom powder and serve warm or chilled.
tips: Add the thick coconut milk only near the end and keep the flame low, as it curdles quickly at high heat.
Toasting the fresh coconut before folding it in gives a nutty depth that raw coconut cannot match.
If the kheer gets too thick as it cools, loosen it with a little extra coconut milk, never water.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled with toasted coconut flakes on top, a light dairy-free finish to a festive meal.

variations.name: Kesar Sabudana Kheer
variations.description: An indulgent saffron-laced version thickened with a spoon of milk powder and glowing gold, made for weddings and grand occasions. A heavier hand of pistachios and almonds and a whisper of nutmeg turn the humble sabudana kheer into a jewelled dessert.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: khandsari keeps this saffron kheer softly sweet without clouding its golden colour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: pure saffron steeped in warm milk gives the kheer its royal gold hue and floral fragrance

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee fries the pistachios and almonds for a glossy, aromatic garnish

steps: Rinse and soak 1/2 cup sabudana in water for 20 minutes until soft, drain, and steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk.
Bring 4 cups full-fat milk to a boil, add the soaked sabudana, and simmer on low for 12 minutes, stirring, until the pearls turn translucent.
Whisk 3 tbsp milk powder with a few spoons of the warm kheer into a smooth paste, then stir it back in and cook for 3 minutes to thicken the body.
Add 1/2 cup Anveshan Khandsari and the saffron milk, stirring for 4 minutes until the sweetener dissolves and the kheer glows gold.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and fry 12 pistachios and 10 slivered almonds until golden, about 1 minute, then stir most of them in.
Finish with 1/2 tsp cardamom powder and 1/8 tsp nutmeg powder, garnish with the reserved nuts and a few saffron strands, and serve chilled.
tips: Dissolve the milk powder in a little warm kheer first to avoid lumps when it goes into the pan.
Steep the saffron in warm milk for at least 10 minutes so it releases its full colour and scent.
Chill this kheer well before serving, as the saffron and nutmeg flavours deepen and marry as it sits.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve well chilled in kulhads topped with saffron strands and slivered pistachios, an opulent close to a wedding feast.

variations.name: Classic Makha Sandesh
variations.description: The elegant Bengali chhena fudge made by gently cooking fresh chhena with sugar until it just comes together, then shaping it into soft, melt-in-the-mouth morsels. Unlike syrupy sweets it is dry and delicate, prized for the pure, milky taste of well-made chhena and only lightly perfumed with cardamom.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: finely powdered so it melts smoothly into the chhena for a clean, delicate sweetness

steps: Boil 1.5 litres full-fat milk, take it off the heat and stir in 3 tbsp diluted lemon juice until it curdles into soft chhena and clear whey.
Strain through muslin, rinse under cold water to remove the tang, and hang for 20 minutes so the chhena stays moist but not wet.
Knead the chhena on a plate with the heel of your palm for 6 minutes until completely smooth and free of grain.
Mix in 0.5 cup finely powdered Anveshan Khandsari Sugar and cook the chhena in a non-stick pan on the lowest heat for 6 minutes, stirring constantly, until it thickens into a soft pliable mass.
Do not overcook, as the mixture should still be soft and glossy when you take it off the heat, then mix in 0.5 tsp cardamom powder.
Cool slightly, then shape into 14 small rounds or press into a greased mould while still warm.
Press a few chopped pistachios and a strand of saffron onto each and cool fully before serving.
tips: Cook the chhena on very low heat and stop while it is still soft, or the sandesh turns hard and grainy.
Knead the chhena thoroughly first, since any graininess will carry into the finished sweet.
Powder the sugar finely so it dissolves evenly without leaving a crunch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature on a decorative plate as a light finish to a Bengali meal.

variations.name: Nolen Gur Sandesh
variations.description: The celebrated winter sandesh sweetened with fragrant date-palm jaggery instead of sugar, which turns it a soft caramel brown with a deep, smoky molasses flavour. Considered the finest form of the sweet in Bengal, it captures the essence of the cold-season gur harvest in every tender bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: stands in for nolen gur to give the sandesh its caramel colour and smoky winter depth

steps: Curdle 1.5 litres boiled milk with 3 tbsp diluted lemon juice, strain through muslin, rinse and hang for 20 minutes.
Knead the chhena for 6 minutes on a plate until smooth and free of any grain.
Warm 0.5 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 1 tbsp water in a non-stick pan on low heat for 2 minutes until it melts into a smooth syrup.
Add the kneaded chhena to the melted jaggery and cook on the lowest heat for 6 minutes, stirring constantly, until it comes together into a soft glossy mass.
Take it off the heat while still soft, mix in 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and let it cool for a few minutes until it can be handled.
Shape into 14 small discs or press into moulds while warm.
Press a few chopped cashews on top of each and cool completely before serving.
tips: Melt the jaggery separately and strain it if gritty so the sandesh stays smooth.
Stop cooking while the mixture is still soft, as jaggery firms up more on cooling.
Choose good aromatic date-palm jaggery for the true winter sandesh character.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature, ideally the same day, to enjoy the fresh smoky jaggery aroma at its best.

variations.name: Kesar Pista Sandesh
variations.description: A festive dressed-up sandesh enriched with khoya and saffron-soaked milk, giving it a golden hue and a nutty richness studded with pistachios. Pressed into pretty carved moulds, it is the sort of celebratory sweet offered during pujas and gifted in decorative boxes during the festive season.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: gives a clean sweetness that lets the saffron and pistachio flavours come forward

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk to tint the sandesh gold and add a floral festive aroma

steps: Curdle 1.5 litres boiled milk with 3 tbsp diluted lemon juice, strain, rinse and hang the chhena for 20 minutes.
Soak the pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 1 tbsp warm milk and set aside to bloom.
Knead the chhena with the grated 3 tbsp khoya for 6 minutes until smooth and rich.
Mix in 0.5 cup finely powdered Anveshan Khandsari Sugar and cook in a non-stick pan on the lowest heat for 6 minutes, stirring constantly, until it forms a soft mass.
Stir in the saffron milk, 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and half the chopped pistachios, and cook 1 more minute before taking it off the heat.
While still warm, press the mixture into greased carved moulds or shape into 14 neat rounds.
Garnish each with the remaining pistachios and a few saffron strands and cool before unmoulding.
tips: Adding khoya makes this sandesh richer and helps it hold intricate mould patterns.
Bloom the saffron in warm milk first so its colour and aroma spread evenly.
Grease the moulds lightly so the delicate sandesh releases cleanly without cracking.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled in decorative moulded shapes as festive gifting sweets alongside other mithai.

variations.name: Aam Sandesh
variations.description: A summery sandesh where ripe mango pulp is cooked into the chhena, tinting it sunny yellow and lending a fruity fragrance that balances the milky base. Made only when mangoes are in season, it is a bright, cheerful twist on the classic that disappears quickly off the plate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: lightly sweetens the chhena so the natural mango sweetness leads

steps: Curdle 1.5 litres boiled milk with 3 tbsp diluted lemon juice, strain, rinse and hang the chhena for 20 minutes.
Knead the chhena for 6 minutes until completely smooth.
Simmer 0.5 cup mango pulp in a non-stick pan on low heat for 4 minutes until slightly thickened to remove the raw taste.
Add the kneaded chhena and 0.33 cup powdered Anveshan Khandsari Sugar to the mango and cook on the lowest heat for 7 minutes, stirring constantly, until it thickens into a soft mass.
Mix in 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and take it off the heat while still soft and glossy.
Cool slightly, then shape into 14 small rounds or press into moulds.
Garnish each with chopped almonds and chill briefly before serving.
tips: Thicken the mango pulp first so the sandesh is not too wet to set.
Use a sweet non-fibrous mango so the fudge stays smooth and richly flavoured.
Reduce the sugar to suit how sweet your mangoes are, tasting as you cook.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled, almond-topped, as a refreshing seasonal dessert at the end of a summer lunch.

variations.name: Classic Sem Ki Phali Sabzi
variations.description: This Classic Sem Ki Phali is a dry winter sabzi of tender broad beans stir-cooked in a simple cumin and ginger masala. The flat green pods keep a slight bite while soaking up the spices, making a homely North Indian side that celebrates the seasonal bean.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the traditional winter oil that suits the earthy broad beans and blooms the spices

steps: String the 400 g broad beans and slice them diagonally into 2 cm pieces.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just smokes, lower the heat and add 1 tsp cumin and 0.25 tsp asafoetida to sizzle 15 seconds.
Add the finely chopped onion and grated ginger and saute for 4 minutes until the onion softens.
Add the chopped tomato with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and cook 4 minutes until pulpy.
Add the sliced beans and toss well to coat in the masala for 2 minutes.
Sprinkle three tablespoons of water, cover and cook on low for 12 minutes, stirring once, until the beans are tender but still bright.
Finish with 0.75 tsp amchur, toss and serve hot with fresh coriander.
tips: String the beans well by snapping the tip and pulling along the seam to remove the fibre.
Cook covered with just a little water so the beans steam soft without losing colour.
Slice thin diagonal pieces so the firm pods cook through evenly and quickly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulkas and a bowl of dal for a comforting winter lunch.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Sem Phali with Coconut
variations.description: A Maharashtrian usal-style rendition where broad beans are tossed with earthy goda masala and finished with fresh coconut. The warm, slightly sweet spice blend and a peanut crunch give this version a distinctly western-ghats flavour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the classic Maharashtrian cooking oil that pairs with the peanut and coconut notes

steps: String the 400 g broad beans and cut into 2 cm pieces, and coarsely crush the 3 tbsp roasted peanuts.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai, add 1 tsp mustard and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and let them splutter for 15 seconds.
Add 8 curry leaves and the slit green chillies and fry for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add the sliced beans with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt and toss for 2 minutes to coat.
Add the crushed peanuts and three tablespoons of water, cover and cook on low for 10 minutes until the beans turn tender.
Sprinkle 1.5 tsp goda masala and stir for 2 minutes so the warm spice coats everything.
Fold in the 0.33 cup grated coconut, cook 1 minute and serve warm.
tips: Goda masala is the heart of this dish; its jaggery-coconut warmth cannot be swapped for garam masala.
Crushed peanuts add both body and a nutty crunch typical of Maharashtrian bean sabzis.
Add the coconut at the very end so it stays moist and fragrant rather than dry.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri and a bowl of varan dal for an authentic Maharashtrian plate.

variations.name: Punjabi Sem Aloo Masala
variations.description: A hearty Punjabi take where broad beans are cooked with potato in a bhuna onion-tomato masala enriched with ghee and kasuri methi. The soft potato and firm beans in a robust gravy make it a filling, dhaba-style everyday sabzi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: browns the Punjabi masala richly and rounds off the robust spices

steps: String and slice the 350 g broad beans, and cube the 2 potatoes into small pieces.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them sizzle for 20 seconds.
Add the finely chopped onions and fry for 7 minutes until deep golden, then add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Add the pureed tomatoes with 1.5 tsp chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and bhuno for 6 minutes until the ghee separates.
Add the potato and beans, toss to coat, then add half a cup of hot water, cover and cook on low for 15 minutes until both are tender.
Uncover and cook 2 minutes on higher heat to thicken the masala into a clinging coat.
Crush 1 tsp kasuri methi over the top, add 0.5 tsp garam masala, stir and serve hot.
tips: Cut the potato slightly smaller than the beans so both finish cooking at the same time.
Brown the onions well as the depth of a Punjabi masala rests on that caramelisation.
Crushing kasuri methi between the palms before adding releases its full aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tandoori roti or laccha paratha and a side of onion-lemon salad.

variations.name: South-Indian Sem Phali Poriyal
variations.description: A light Tamil-style poriyal where finely chopped broad beans are steam-cooked and tossed with a mustard-urad tempering and fresh coconut in coconut oil. Barely spiced and naturally sweet, it is a clean, everyday side for a rice meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: lends the poriyal its southern aroma and carries the mustard-urad tempering

steps: String and finely chop the 400 g broad beans, then steam them with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 8 minutes until just tender.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop for 15 seconds.
Add 1 tsp urad dal and 1 tsp chana dal and fry for 40 seconds until they turn golden.
Add 2 broken dry red chillies and 10 curry leaves and fry for 15 seconds until crisp and fragrant.
Add the steamed beans and toss on medium heat for 3 minutes so they take on the tempering.
Add the 0.5 cup grated coconut and stir-fry for 2 minutes until the coconut is warmed through and just dry.
Check the salt, cook 1 minute more and serve warm as a poriyal.
tips: Chop the beans finely so they steam quickly and mix evenly with the coconut.
Fry both dals to a golden colour for the signature nutty crunch of a poriyal.
Add the coconut at the end so it stays fresh and lightly moist, not toasted dry.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sambar rice or curd rice and a crisp papad for a wholesome southern meal.

variations.name: Classic Seviyan Kheer
variations.description: The beloved vermicelli milk pudding where fine seviyan is roasted golden in ghee, then simmered in milk until soft and sweetened with cardamom-scented syrup. Quick to make yet festive, it appears on tables at Eid, Rakhi and every happy occasion across North India.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee roasts the vermicelli to a nutty gold, the step that gives this kheer its aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: khandsari sweetens the kheer cleanly and keeps its pale, milky colour

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan and fry 10 cashews, 10 slivered almonds and 2 tbsp raisins until the nuts are golden and the raisins plump, then scoop them out and reserve.
In the same ghee, roast 1 cup fine vermicelli on medium-low heat for 3 to 4 minutes, stirring constantly, until it turns an even golden brown and smells nutty.
Pour in 4 cups full-fat milk carefully, bring to a boil, then simmer on low for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring, until the vermicelli is soft and the milk thickens slightly.
Stir in 1/2 cup Anveshan Khandsari and cook for 4 minutes on low until it dissolves and the kheer reaches a creamy consistency.
Fold in 1/2 tsp cardamom powder and most of the fried nuts and raisins, keeping some for the top.
Turn off the heat and let it rest for a few minutes so the flavours settle, then garnish and serve warm or chilled.
tips: Roast the vermicelli slowly and evenly to a deep gold, as under-roasted seviyan turns gluey in the milk.
Add the khandsari only after the vermicelli is soft, since sweeteners added early slow down the cooking.
The kheer thickens quickly on standing because vermicelli keeps absorbing milk, so loosen with warm milk before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm or chilled in bowls topped with extra fried nuts, a festive sweet especially loved as sheer khurma's simpler cousin at Eid.

variations.name: Sheer Khurma
variations.description: The royal Hyderabadi Eid pudding where roasted vermicelli simmers in milk enriched with chopped dates and a lavish medley of dry fruits. Thicker and more indulgent than everyday seviyan kheer, it is the dish that breaks the Ramzan fast in grand style.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: generous bilona ghee roasts the vermicelli and fries the dry fruits for the richness sheer khurma demands

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: less khandsari is needed since the dates lend their own deep sweetness to this rich pudding

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: a pinch of pure saffron steeped in warm milk gives sheer khurma its regal colour and perfume

steps: Steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk, and heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan.
Fry 15 slivered almonds, 12 pistachios, 10 cashews and 2 tbsp chironji until golden, about 2 minutes, then remove and reserve, and lightly saute 10 chopped dates in the same ghee for 1 minute.
Add 3/4 cup vermicelli to the pan and roast on medium-low for 3 minutes until golden and nutty.
Pour in 5 cups full-fat milk, bring to a boil, then simmer on low for 15 minutes, stirring often, until the vermicelli is very soft and the milk reduces to a rich, thick pudding.
Stir in 1/3 cup Anveshan Khandsari and the saffron milk and cook for 4 minutes until dissolved and glossy.
Fold in 1/2 tsp cardamom powder and most of the fried dry fruits, garnish with the rest, and serve warm.
tips: Simmer the milk longer than for plain seviyan kheer, as sheer khurma is meant to be thick and luxuriously rich.
Soft, sticky dates like Kimia melt into the milk and thicken it naturally, so chop them small.
Make it a day ahead if you like, as the flavours of saffron, dates and dry fruits deepen beautifully overnight.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm at dawn to break the Eid fast, or chilled later in the day, topped with saffron strands and slivered pistachios.

variations.name: Meethi Seviyan (Dry)
variations.description: The dry, non-milk version where roasted vermicelli is steamed soft with jaggery water until every strand glistens separately. Studded with coconut and ghee-fried nuts, this festive dry seviyan is eaten by the forkful rather than the spoon, quite unlike the creamy kheer.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee keeps the strands glossy and separate and fries the nuts for this dry sweet

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery gives the dry seviyan its caramel colour and earthy sweetness without any milk

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide pan and fry 12 cashews, 2 tbsp raisins and 1/3 cup grated coconut until golden, then set aside, leaving the ghee in the pan.
If using un-roasted vermicelli, toast 1.5 cups in the same ghee for 3 minutes until golden; otherwise warm the roasted vermicelli through for a minute.
Melt 3/4 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 1.5 cups water on low heat, then strain out any grit to leave a clean jaggery water.
Pour the strained jaggery water over the vermicelli, add 1/2 tsp fennel seeds, cover, and steam on low heat for 6 to 8 minutes until the water is fully absorbed and the strands turn soft.
Uncover and fluff gently with a fork, letting any remaining moisture evaporate so the strands stay separate and glossy.
Fold in 1/2 tsp cardamom powder and most of the fried nuts and coconut, garnish with the rest, and serve warm.
tips: Use just enough jaggery water to cook the vermicelli through, so it steams soft without turning into a mush.
Fluff with a fork rather than a spoon to keep the delicate strands whole and separate.
Strain the melted jaggery well, as any grit will spoil the clean look and texture of the dry seviyan.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a dry festive sweet at breakfast or after a meal, garnished with toasted coconut and a few whole cashews.

variations.name: Coconut Seviyan Kheer
variations.description: A dairy-free take where roasted vermicelli simmers in fragrant coconut milk sweetened with jaggery. Cashews toasted in coconut oil and a hint of nutmeg give it a coastal warmth that stands apart from the milk-based original.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed coconut oil roasts the vermicelli and toasts the nuts, deepening the coastal aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery marries with coconut milk for a mellow caramel sweetness in this dairy-free kheer

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan and fry 12 cashews golden and 2 tbsp raisins until plump, about 1 minute, then reserve.
In the same oil, roast 1 cup vermicelli on medium-low for 3 minutes until golden and nutty.
Pour in 2 cups thin coconut milk, bring to a gentle simmer, and cook on low for 8 minutes, stirring, until the vermicelli softens.
Add 2 cups thick coconut milk and warm through on low heat for 3 minutes, stirring gently so it does not split.
Melt 1/2 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 1/4 cup water, strain, then lower the flame and stir the syrup in slowly to keep the coconut milk smooth.
Fold in 1/2 tsp cardamom powder, 1/8 tsp nutmeg powder and the fried cashews and raisins, then serve warm or chilled.
tips: Add the thick coconut milk and the jaggery syrup on low heat, as coconut milk curdles far more easily than dairy.
Roast the vermicelli well so it holds its shape in the coconut milk instead of going soft too fast.
A tiny pinch of nutmeg lends warmth that beautifully offsets the sweetness of the coconut and jaggery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled topped with toasted coconut and cashews, a light dairy-free dessert for a festive spread.

variations.name: Classic Sugar-Glazed Shakkarpara
variations.description: Shakkarpara, also called shankarpali, are crisp diamond-shaped fried bites coated in a crackly sugar glaze. A festive Diwali staple across North and West India, they stay crunchy for weeks and are the perfect sweet nibble with tea.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: rubbed into the flour as moyan for a crisp, short bite

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: cooked to a one-thread syrup for the classic crackly sugar coating

steps: Rub 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee into 2 cups maida with a pinch of salt until the mixture holds shape when pressed.
Add water little by little to form a firm, stiff dough, then cover and rest it for 15 minutes.
Roll the dough into a thick sheet and cut it into small diamonds with a knife or cutter.
Heat oil for frying to a medium-low temperature and fry the diamonds in batches for 5 to 6 minutes, stirring, until pale golden and crisp, then drain.
Boil 0.75 cup Anveshan Khandsari with 0.5 cup water and 0.5 tsp cardamom to a sticky one-thread syrup.
Toss the fried diamonds in the warm syrup off the heat, stirring until each is coated and the sugar crystallises into a white frost, then spread to cool.
tips: Fry on medium-low heat so the diamonds cook crisp all the way through without browning too quickly.
Take the syrup exactly to one thread; undercooked syrup stays wet, overcooked syrup turns hard and clumpy.
Keep tossing until the glaze dries to a frost, then cool completely before storing airtight.
variations.servingSuggestion: Store in a jar and serve the frosted diamonds as an anytime Diwali snack with masala chai.

variations.name: Namak Para (Savoury)
variations.description: The salty sibling of shakkarpara, namak para are crisp flaky diamonds seasoned with ajwain and cumin instead of sugar. Layered with ghee for extra flakiness, they are the savoury half of every festive snack tin.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: rubbed in generously as moyan for extra flaky, crisp layers

steps: Crush 1 tsp ajwain and 1 tsp cumin lightly, then rub them with 5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 1 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp pepper into 2 cups maida until crumbly.
Add water gradually to make a firm, tight dough and rest it covered for 15 minutes.
Roll the dough into a thick sheet and cut it into small even diamonds.
Heat oil for frying to a medium-low temperature and fry the diamonds in batches for 6 to 7 minutes, stirring occasionally, until golden and crisp.
Drain the namak para on a rack and let them cool so they crisp up fully.
Taste one and dust with a little extra salt if needed before storing airtight.
tips: Crush the ajwain and cumin so their oils release; whole seeds give a weaker flavour in the fry.
The more ghee you rub in, the flakier the para, but too much makes the dough hard to roll.
Fry low and slow for an even crunch, as high heat leaves the centres soft.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the savoury diamonds alongside sweet shakkarpara so guests get both flavours from the festive tin.

variations.name: Whole Wheat Jaggery Shakkarpara
variations.description: A wholesome version made with nutty khapli atta and glazed in jaggery instead of white sugar, giving deeper flavour and a rustic amber coat. It is a more nourishing take on the festive diamond that does not compromise on crunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: ancient wheat flour that gives a nutty, wholesome crunch to the diamonds

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the moyan that keeps the wheat diamonds short and crisp

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: cooked to a one-thread syrup for a rustic amber glaze

steps: Rub 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp crushed fennel until the mixture clumps when pressed.
Bring together a firm dough with water added slowly, then rest it for 15 minutes.
Roll into a thick sheet and cut into small diamonds, keeping them slightly thicker as wheat crisps denser.
Fry the diamonds in medium-low oil for 6 to 7 minutes, stirring, until deep golden and crunchy, then drain.
Melt 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 0.5 cup water, strain, and cook to a one-thread syrup with 0.5 tsp cardamom.
Toss the fried diamonds in the warm jaggery syrup off the heat until evenly coated and just tacky, then spread to cool and set.
tips: Jaggery glaze stays glossy rather than frosting white, which is the natural look of this version.
Khapli atta needs a touch more water, so add it gradually to reach a firm, non-cracking dough.
Spread the coated diamonds in a single layer to cool so they do not clump together.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these amber-glazed diamonds as a wholesome festive nibble with a warm cup of masala milk.

variations.name: Baked Masala Shakkarpara
variations.description: A lighter oven-baked shakkarpara seasoned with a sweet-savoury masala rub, offering the crunch without deep frying. Brushed with ghee and baked till crisp, it is a guilt-lighter snack that still satisfies the festive craving.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: rubbed into the dough and brushed on top to crisp the diamonds in the oven

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: powdered into the dough for a subtle sweetness in the baked bites

steps: Mix 1.5 cups maida with 0.5 cup fine semolina, 3 tbsp powdered Anveshan Khandsari, 0.5 tsp cumin powder and 0.5 tsp black salt in a bowl.
Rub in 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until crumbly, then bind with 3 tbsp yogurt and a little water into a firm dough and rest it 15 minutes.
Roll the dough into a thick sheet and cut into small diamonds, arranging them on a lined baking tray.
Brush the tops with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee for colour and crunch.
Bake in a preheated oven at 180 C for 20 to 25 minutes, turning once halfway, until evenly golden and crisp.
Cool the baked diamonds completely on the tray, where they crisp up further, before storing airtight.
tips: Adding semolina gives the baked diamonds the crunch that frying would otherwise provide.
Watch the last few minutes closely, as baked shakkarpara go from golden to over-brown fast.
Let them cool fully before tasting, since they firm and crisp as they come to room temperature.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the baked masala diamonds as a lighter tea-time snack for health-conscious festive guests.

variations.name: Classic Kesar Elaichi Shrikhand
variations.description: The silky Gujarati and Maharashtrian dessert made by straining thick yogurt overnight into hung curd, then whisking it smooth with powdered sugar, saffron and cardamom. Cool, tangy-sweet and luxuriously creamy, it is the classic accompaniment to hot pooris at a festive meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: khandsari ground fine dissolves smoothly into the hung curd and keeps the shrikhand pale and clean-tasting

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: pure saffron steeped in warm milk gives shrikhand its golden colour and unmistakable perfume

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a little bilona ghee toasts the pistachio and almond garnish that crowns the chilled shrikhand

steps: Spoon 4 cups full-fat yogurt into a muslin cloth, tie it up, and hang it over a bowl in the fridge for 6 to 8 hours until all the whey drains and you are left with about 2 cups of thick hung curd.
Steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk for 10 minutes so it releases its colour and aroma.
Grind 3/4 cup Anveshan Khandsari to a fine powder, then whisk it into the hung curd a little at a time until completely smooth and no grains remain.
Whisk in the saffron milk and 1/2 tsp cardamom powder until the shrikhand turns an even pale gold and is silky and lump-free.
Toast 12 pistachios and 10 slivered almonds in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee for 1 minute until fragrant, then fold half into the shrikhand.
Chill the shrikhand for at least 2 hours, then serve topped with the reserved toasted nuts and a few saffron strands.
tips: Use thick, fresh yogurt that is not sour, as the whey-draining concentrates any tang along with the creaminess.
Grind the khandsari to a powder before adding it, since coarse crystals leave the shrikhand gritty.
Whisk gently rather than beating hard, and pass it through a sieve once if you want an ultra-smooth, glossy finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve well chilled in katoris with hot pooris for the traditional puran-poli-style feast, or on its own as a light dessert.

variations.name: Dry Fruit Matho Shrikhand
variations.description: A rich Gujarati matho loaded with a generous medley of chopped nuts and charoli folded right through the creamy hung curd, not just sprinkled on top. Every spoon carries crunch alongside the saffron-cardamom cream, making it the indulgent version for grand occasions.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: finely ground khandsari sweetens the matho without masking the flavour of the many nuts

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee toasts the generous medley of nuts and charoli that runs through this rich shrikhand

steps: Hang 4 cups full-fat yogurt in muslin in the fridge for 6 to 8 hours until it drains into about 2 cups of thick hung curd.
Grind 3/4 cup Anveshan Khandsari to a fine powder, then whisk it into the hung curd gradually until fully dissolved and smooth.
Heat 2 tsp Anveshan Ghee and toast 15 chopped cashews, 15 slivered almonds, 15 pistachios and 3 tbsp charoli for 2 minutes until golden and fragrant, then cool them.
Fold most of the toasted nuts into the shrikhand along with 1/2 tsp cardamom powder and 1/8 tsp nutmeg powder, keeping some for the top.
Whisk once more so the nuts distribute evenly and the shrikhand stays creamy around them.
Chill for 2 hours and serve topped with the reserved toasted nuts and charoli.
tips: Toast the nuts before folding them in, as raw nuts turn soft and lose their crunch once mixed into the curd.
Chop the cashews and almonds small so the shrikhand stays spoonable and the crunch is in every bite.
Add the nuts just before serving if making ahead, so they keep their crispness in the creamy base.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled in bowls with an extra shower of charoli and pistachios, a decadent dessert for Diwali or a wedding thali.

variations.name: Gur Shrikhand
variations.description: A wholesome unrefined version sweetened with jaggery instead of sugar, tinting the hung curd a soft caramel beige with a mellow molasses depth. Warming spices and toasted walnuts make it an earthy, nourishing spin on the festive classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: finely powdered jaggery lends the shrikhand a caramel colour and earthy sweetness in place of white sugar

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee toasts the walnut and cashew garnish for the jaggery shrikhand

steps: Hang 4 cups full-fat yogurt in muslin in the fridge for 6 to 8 hours until you have about 2 cups of thick hung curd.
Grind 2/3 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder to a fine powder, sieving out any grit, so it can be whisked in smoothly.
Whisk the powdered jaggery into the hung curd a little at a time until fully dissolved and the shrikhand turns an even caramel beige.
Whisk in 1/2 tsp cardamom powder, 1/8 tsp cinnamon powder and 1/8 tsp dry ginger powder until the spices blend evenly.
Toast 8 chopped walnuts and 10 cashews in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee for 1 minute, then fold half into the shrikhand.
Chill for 2 hours and serve topped with the remaining toasted walnuts and cashews.
tips: Sieve the powdered jaggery first, as unstrained jaggery leaves grit that will not dissolve in the cold curd.
Whisk the jaggery in gradually; adding it all at once can make the shrikhand watery as it draws out moisture.
Toasted walnuts suit this earthy jaggery version far better than the usual pistachio garnish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled with toasted walnuts on top, a wholesome winter dessert or a naturally sweetened alternative for the health-conscious.

variations.name: Piyush
variations.description: The Maharashtrian and Gujarati summer drink made by thinning saffron shrikhand with chilled buttermilk into a thick, sippable nectar. Spiced with cardamom and nutmeg and served ice-cold, this pourable cousin of shrikhand cools you through the hottest afternoons.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: finely ground khandsari dissolves into the drink smoothly and keeps piyush pale and refreshing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: pure saffron steeped in warm milk gives piyush its golden colour and festive aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee toasts the pistachio slivers floated on top of the chilled drink

steps: Hang 3 cups full-fat yogurt in muslin in the fridge for 5 to 6 hours until it drains into about 1.5 cups of thick hung curd, and steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk.
Grind 2/3 cup Anveshan Khandsari fine and whisk it into the hung curd until smooth and fully dissolved.
Whisk in the saffron milk, 1/2 tsp cardamom powder and 1/8 tsp nutmeg powder until evenly coloured and fragrant.
Gradually whisk in 1.5 cups chilled buttermilk until the mixture loosens into a thick but pourable, lassi-like drink.
Taste and adjust, adding a splash more buttermilk if you prefer it thinner, then chill the piyush for 1 hour.
Toast 12 pistachio slivers in 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee for 1 minute, pour the piyush into glasses, and float the pistachios and a few saffron strands on top.
tips: Add the buttermilk gradually and whisk well, so the piyush stays smooth and does not turn lumpy.
Keep both the hung curd and the buttermilk well chilled, as piyush is meant to be served ice-cold.
Adjust the thickness to taste; some like it thick enough to spoon, others prefer it easily sippable.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in tall glasses over a few ice cubes, garnished with pistachios and saffron, as a cooling festive drink or a light dessert in one.

variations.name: Classic Bengali Shukto
variations.description: The dish that traditionally opens a Bengali lunch, shukto is a gently bitter medley where bitter gourd, drumstick, raw banana and potato simmer in a milk-loosened gravy thickened with a mustard-and-poppy paste. Fried bori and a radhuni-scented tempering give it its unmistakable savour, and the bitterness is meant to whet, not overwhelm, the appetite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed kachi ghani oil fries the bitter gourd and bori with the pungency Bengali cooks insist on

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of bilona ghee rounds the bitterness and perfumes the pot

steps: Cut the bitter gourd, drumstick, raw banana, potato, brinjal and radish into even finger-length batons. Soak 1 tbsp poppy seeds and 1 tbsp mustard seeds in warm water for 15 minutes, then grind them to a smooth paste with a little water.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai until it just smokes, lower the heat, and fry the 8 bori for about 1 minute until deep gold; lift them out, then fry the bitter gourd batons for 2 minutes until their edges crisp and set them aside.

In the same oil add 1 bay leaf and 1/2 tsp radhuni seeds and let them crackle for 20 seconds, then add the potato, raw banana, drumstick and radish and saute on medium heat for 4 minutes until the vegetables glisten and their surfaces turn pale.

Pour in 1.5 cups hot water with 1 tsp salt and 1 tbsp ginger paste, cover and simmer on medium-low for 8 to 10 minutes until the vegetables are just tender, then slip in the fried bitter gourd and brinjal and cook 3 minutes more.

Lower the heat and stir in the poppy-mustard paste, cooking gently for 2 minutes so the raw edge cooks off, then pour in 1/2 cup milk off the boil and simmer on the lowest heat for 3 minutes so it thickens without splitting.
Return the fried bori to warm through, finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee stirred in off the heat, and rest the shukto covered for 5 minutes so the flavours settle before serving.
tips: Add milk only after lowering the flame; a rolling boil will curdle it and cloud the delicate gravy.
Fry the bitter gourd separately and add it late so it stays crisp-edged and its bitterness perfumes rather than floods the dish.
Drop the fried bori in only at the end, or they soften into mush and lose their signature spongy bite.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve first in a Bengali meal, ladled over a mound of hot steamed rice, before any dal or fish course follows.

variations.name: Niramish Ghee Shukto
variations.description: A no-onion, no-garlic, milk-free rendition made for puja days, where the vegetables are simmered in water and finished purely in ghee and a fragrant poppy paste. Without milk it stays lighter and cleaner, letting the bitterness of the karela and the sweetness of pumpkin sing against a paanch phoron tempering.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: with no milk in the pot, bilona ghee becomes the whole richness of this austere puja-day shukto

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a whisper of unrefined sweetness offsets the karela the traditional Bengali way

steps: Cut the pumpkin, raw papaya, potato and ridge gourd into thick batons and the bitter gourd into thin rings. Soak 2 tbsp poppy seeds in warm water for 15 minutes and grind to a silky white paste.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium and fry the bitter gourd rings for 2 minutes until lightly browned and crisp at the rim, then remove them so they do not turn the whole dish bitter.

Add another 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee to the pan, crackle 1 tsp paanch phoron with 1 bay leaf and 1 dried red chilli for 20 seconds, then toss in the potato, pumpkin, papaya and ridge gourd and saute on medium heat for 4 minutes.
Pour in 1.5 cups hot water with 1 tsp salt and 1 tbsp ginger paste, cover, and simmer on medium-low for 10 minutes until the vegetables are fork-tender and the pumpkin begins to melt into the broth.
Stir in the poppy paste and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, return the fried bitter gourd, and cook uncovered on low for 4 minutes until the gravy turns creamy and coats the vegetables.
Finish with the last 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee swirled in off the heat and let it stand covered for 5 minutes so the paanch phoron aroma deepens before serving.
