tips: A ripe chunk of pumpkin naturally thickens and sweetens this milk-free version, so choose a mature, deep-orange piece.
Grind the poppy seeds with just a splash of water into a thick paste; too much water makes the gravy thin and grey.
Since there is no milk, this shukto keeps a day in the fridge and actually tastes rounder reheated gently the next day.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ideal as the opening course of a vegetarian puja thali, served over rice with a wedge of lime and a pinch of salt on the side.

variations.name: Dhakai Coconut Shukto
variations.description: The East Bengal kitchens of Dhaka make a richer shukto, grinding coconut into the mustard-poppy paste and finishing with more milk for a plush, ivory gravy. It is sweeter and creamier than the Kolkata version, with the coconut softening the bitterness into something almost velvety.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the pungent wood-pressed oil balances the sweetness the coconut and milk bring to this Dhaka style

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: stirred in at the end to lacquer the creamy coconut gravy

steps: Cut the drumstick, sweet potato, potato and broad beans into batons and the bitter gourd into slim slices. Soak 1 tbsp poppy seeds and 1 tbsp mustard seeds for 15 minutes, then grind them with 1/3 cup fresh grated coconut into a smooth, thick paste.
Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking point, lower the flame, and fry the bitter gourd slices for 2 minutes until browned at the edges; scoop them out and reserve.
Temper 1 tsp paanch phoron and 1 bay leaf in the same oil for 20 seconds, then add the potato, sweet potato, drumstick and broad beans and saute on medium for 4 minutes until glossy.
Add 1.5 cups hot water, 1 tsp salt and 1 tbsp ginger paste, cover, and cook on medium-low for 10 minutes until the vegetables soften and the sweet potato starts to yield.

Lower the heat, stir in the coconut-poppy-mustard paste and the reserved bitter gourd, and simmer for 3 minutes, then pour in 3/4 cup milk off the boil and cook the gentlest 4 minutes until the gravy turns thick and ivory.
Swirl in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee off the heat and let the shukto rest covered for 5 minutes so the coconut sweetness melds through before serving.
tips: Keep the heat low once coconut paste and milk are in; both scorch and split easily and the gravy should stay pale, not browned.
Sweet potato is the East Bengal signature here and does double duty, sweetening and thickening the gravy as it breaks down.
Grind the coconut fresh rather than using desiccated, which turns the smooth Dhakai gravy gritty.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve this creamier shukto over fragrant gobindobhog rice, letting the coconut gravy soak into the short grains.

variations.name: Sojne Winter Shukto
variations.description: A cold-season shukto built around plentiful drumsticks and their leaves, with methi lending its own clean bitterness alongside the karela. Lighter on paste and heavier on greens, it is the version Bengali households cook when winter vegetables crowd the market, brothy and warming rather than rich.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: its sharpness stands up to the double bitterness of drumstick and fenugreek greens

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: finishes the brothy winter pot with a mellow, nutty warmth

steps: Cut the drumsticks into 3 inch logs, dice the carrot and potato into batons, and slice the bitter gourd thin. Soak 1 tbsp poppy seeds for 15 minutes and grind to a smooth paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the flame, and fry the bitter gourd slices for 2 minutes until crisp-edged; lift out and reserve.
Crackle 1/2 tsp radhuni seeds, 2 dried red chillies and 1 bay leaf in the same oil for 20 seconds, then add the potato, carrot, drumstick and 1/2 cup green peas and saute on medium for 4 minutes.

Stir in 1 cup chopped fresh fenugreek leaves and cook 2 minutes until wilted, then add 1.5 cups hot water, 1 tsp salt and 1 tbsp ginger paste, cover, and simmer on medium-low for 10 minutes until the drumsticks are tender.
Add the poppy paste and the fried bitter gourd and cook uncovered on low for 4 minutes, letting the broth reduce slightly and turn silky.
Finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee off the heat and rest the shukto for 5 minutes so the fenugreek and drumstick flavours settle before it goes to the table.
tips: Use fenugreek leaves sparingly and pick out the coarse stems; too much makes the pot aggressively bitter rather than pleasantly so.
Scrape and suck the drumstick pods at the table Bengali-style; their soft pulp is the reward of this winter version.
This brothier shukto is best eaten fresh and hot, as the greens dull in colour if it sits too long.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle over hot rice as a light winter-lunch opener, with a squeeze of lime and a side of plain fried bori.

variations.name: Classic Sohan Papdi
variations.description: Sohan papdi is a cube-shaped North Indian sweet famous for its flaky, thread-like layers that melt on the tongue. It is made by whisking a roasted gram-flour and ghee roux into a hot sugar syrup at the exact thread stage, then pulling it into gossamer strands.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the flours and forms the fat that gives the papdi its signature flaky threads

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: cooked to a two-thread syrup that sets the whisked flour into crisp layers

steps: Sieve 1 cup besan with 0.25 cup maida, then roast the mixture in 0.75 cup Anveshan Ghee over low heat, stirring constantly, for 12 to 15 minutes until it turns fragrant and light golden.
Meanwhile, boil 1.5 cups Anveshan Khandsari with 0.75 cup water and 1 tbsp milk over medium heat; skim off the froth and cook to a two-thread consistency, about 8 minutes.
Pour the hot syrup in a steady stream into the roasted flour roux off the heat, whisking vigorously as it combines.
Keep whisking and lifting the mixture with a fork as it cools slightly; long silky threads will begin to form within 2 to 3 minutes.
Quickly transfer the fluffy mixture into a ghee-greased tray, press it into a one-inch layer, and sprinkle 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and 3 tbsp slivered nuts over the top.
Press the nuts in gently and let the slab cool for 2 hours until firm, then cut into squares that reveal flaky layers.
tips: The two-thread syrup stage is critical; test by pulling a cooled drop between two fingers to see two threads before mixing.
Whisk the moment the syrup meets the flour, as the threads form only while the mixture is warm and pliable.
Store in an airtight tin, since sohan papdi turns soft and loses its flakiness in humid air.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the flaky cubes with afternoon chai, or box them with dried rose petals as a Diwali gift.

variations.name: Besan Ladoo-Style Sohan Papdi
variations.description: A rustic all-besan version that skips the maida entirely for a deeper roasted-gram flavour reminiscent of besan ladoo. The higher gram-flour ratio gives a slightly denser, more nutty flake that traditionalists prefer.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: slow-roasts the pure gram flour for a deep nutty aroma and flaky layers

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: gives this rustic version a warm caramel colour and earthy sweetness

steps: Roast 1.5 cups besan in 0.75 cup Anveshan Ghee over low heat, stirring without pause, for 15 minutes until it darkens to a rich golden brown and smells deeply nutty.
In a separate pan, melt 1.25 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 0.5 cup water, strain out any grit, and cook to a soft two-thread syrup over medium heat.
Pour the strained jaggery syrup into the roasted besan off the heat and whisk hard until it lightens and threads begin to appear.
Fold in 2 tbsp melon seeds as you whisk so they distribute through the forming flakes.
Press the mixture into a greased tray in an even layer and scatter 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and 2 tbsp slivered almonds on top.
Cool the slab for 2 hours until set, then cut into rustic squares with visible caramel-toned layers.
tips: Strain the jaggery syrup carefully, as unrefined jaggery carries grit that would spoil the smooth flake.
Jaggery syrup reaches the thread stage faster than white sugar, so watch it closely to avoid overcooking.
The all-besan flake is denser, so press it a little more firmly for clean-cutting squares.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these earthy cubes warmed slightly in winter, pairing beautifully with a glass of hot masala milk.

variations.name: Dry Fruit Sohan Papdi
variations.description: A premium celebration version loaded with a generous mix of chopped nuts folded right into the flaky layers, not just sprinkled on top. Every bite carries crunch against the melting threads, making it a lavish festive gift.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the flours and binds the abundant nuts into flaky layers

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: forms the two-thread syrup that sets the rich, nutty flake

steps: Roast 1 cup besan with 0.25 cup maida in 0.75 cup Anveshan Ghee over low heat for 13 minutes until golden and aromatic.
Boil 1.5 cups Anveshan Khandsari with 0.75 cup water to a two-thread syrup, then add 1 tbsp saffron-milk for colour and fragrance.
Whisk the hot syrup into the roasted flour off the heat until the mixture turns fluffy and threads begin to form.
Fold in 0.5 cup of the chopped mixed nuts and 0.5 tsp cardamom powder while whisking, keeping the flakes airy.
Press the nut-laden mixture into a greased tray and cover the top with the remaining 0.25 cup chopped nuts, pressing gently.
Let the slab firm up for 2 hours, then cut into generous squares packed with dry fruit through every layer.
tips: Chop the nuts small and even so they fold into the threads without breaking the delicate layers.
Add the saffron-milk to the syrup, not the flour, so the colour spreads evenly through the sweet.
Because the nuts add weight, cool this version fully before cutting to keep the squares from crumbling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Box these lavish cubes with a dusting of edible silver leaf for premium festival and wedding hampers.

variations.name: Chocolate Sohan Papdi
variations.description: A modern fusion where cocoa is folded into the flaky roux for a chocolate-scented sohan papdi that still shatters into delicate threads. It bridges nostalgic mithai and contemporary chocolate for younger palates.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the flours and carries the cocoa evenly through the flaky layers

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: sets the cocoa-laced flake with a clean sweetness that balances the cocoa

steps: Roast 1 cup besan with 0.25 cup maida in 0.75 cup Anveshan Ghee over low heat for 12 minutes until golden, then stir in 2 tbsp sifted cocoa powder and roast 1 minute more.
Boil 1.5 cups Anveshan Khandsari with 0.75 cup water to a two-thread syrup over medium heat, about 8 minutes.
Pour the syrup into the cocoa roux off the heat and whisk hard, adding 0.5 tsp vanilla, until threads begin to form.
Continue lifting and whisking the warm mixture until it turns fluffy and light chocolate-brown.
Press into a greased tray in a one-inch layer and scatter 3 tbsp chopped walnuts over the top.
Cool for 2 hours until firm, then cut into squares that flake apart into cocoa-scented threads.
tips: Add the cocoa near the end of roasting so it warms through without turning bitter.
Keep the syrup exactly at two threads; cocoa can mask visual cues, so rely on the finger test.
Pair with walnuts rather than pistachios, as their bitterness complements the chocolate note.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the cocoa cubes as a fusion dessert with vanilla ice cream or after a modern Indian meal.

variations.name: Classic Sooji Halwa
variations.description: Sooji halwa, or rava sheera, is the quickest Indian pudding, made by roasting semolina in ghee until golden and nutty, then swelling it with hot sweetened water. Soft, glossy and cardamom-scented, it is the go-to prasad and comfort dessert across India.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the semolina to a golden nuttiness and gives the halwa its glossy richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: dissolves into the hot water to sweeten the halwa naturally

steps: Heat 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan and fry 3 tbsp cashews and raisins until golden and plump, then set them aside.
Add 1 cup semolina to the same ghee and roast over low heat, stirring constantly, for 8 to 10 minutes until it turns golden and smells nutty.
Meanwhile boil 2.5 cups water with 0.75 cup Anveshan Khandsari until the sugar dissolves fully.
Pour the hot sweetened water very carefully into the roasted semolina, standing back as it splutters, and stir hard to prevent lumps.
Cook on low heat for 3 to 4 minutes, stirring, until the semolina absorbs the liquid and thickens into a glossy mass that leaves the pan.
Mix in 0.5 tsp cardamom and the fried nuts, then serve the halwa warm.
tips: Roast the semolina patiently until golden; under-roasted rava tastes raw and gives a pasty halwa.
Always use hot water, not cold, and add it away from your face to avoid dangerous splutters.
For a richer halwa, replace part of the water with hot milk for a creamier finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as prasad or dessert, garnished with extra fried cashews and a light dusting of cardamom.

variations.name: Mohanbhog Jaggery Halwa
variations.description: The Bengali mohanbhog swaps white sugar for jaggery and finishes with a hint of nutmeg and bay leaf, giving a darker, more aromatic halwa. Cooked entirely in milk, it is a temple offering richer and deeper than the everyday sheera.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the semolina and lends the mohanbhog its temple-style richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted and strained to give the halwa a deep caramel colour and flavour

steps: Heat 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee, briefly crackle 1 bay leaf, fry 3 tbsp cashews and raisins to golden, and set the nuts aside.
Roast 1 cup semolina in the ghee over low heat for 9 minutes until golden and fragrant.
Separately warm 2.5 cups milk, and in another pan melt 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water and strain out any grit.
Pour the hot milk into the roasted semolina, stirring hard to avoid lumps, and cook for 3 minutes until it thickens.
Lower the heat and stir in the strained jaggery syrup off the boil so the milk does not curdle, cooking gently for 2 minutes.
Add 0.25 tsp nutmeg and the fried nuts, mix until glossy, and serve the mohanbhog warm.
tips: Add the jaggery only after lowering the heat, as pouring it into boiling milk can split the halwa.
The bay leaf and nutmeg are what give mohanbhog its distinctive Bengali aroma, so do not skip them.
Strain the jaggery syrup well to keep the halwa smooth and free of grit.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the jaggery halwa warm as bhog during Bengali pujas, with a spoon of ghee on top.

variations.name: Kesar Badam Sooji Halwa
variations.description: A luxurious wedding-style halwa enriched with saffron, ground almonds and full-fat milk for a saffron-gold, nutty pudding. Richer and more fragrant than the plain version, it is the halwa served at celebrations and shraddh feasts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: generously roasts the semolina for the rich, glossy celebration halwa

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: sweetens the milk base while keeping the saffron colour bright

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm milk to colour and perfume the rich halwa

steps: Soak 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp of warm milk taken from the 2.5 cups and set aside to bloom.
Heat 0.6 cup Anveshan Ghee, fry 3 tbsp sliced almonds and pistachios to golden, and reserve.
Roast 1 cup semolina with 0.25 cup almond powder in the ghee over low heat for 9 minutes until golden and nutty.
Warm the remaining milk with 0.75 cup Anveshan Khandsari until dissolved, then pour it into the semolina, stirring hard to avoid lumps.
Add the bloomed saffron milk and cook on low heat for 4 minutes until the halwa thickens and turns a rich gold.
Fold in the reserved nuts, mix until glossy, and serve the saffron halwa warm.
tips: Adding almond powder with the semolina deepens the nuttiness and makes the halwa extra rich.
Bloom the saffron in warm milk first so its colour spreads evenly through the pudding.
Keep the halwa slightly loose, as the almond powder and milk thicken it further on cooling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve this saffron badam halwa at weddings and festivals, garnished with a few saffron strands and slivered nuts.

variations.name: Wheat Flour Atta Halwa
variations.description: Kada prasad or atte ka halwa uses roasted whole-wheat flour instead of semolina, giving a denser, deeply nutty pudding served in gurudwaras. Cooked slow in ghee and jaggery, it is wholesome, grounding and intensely aromatic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: ancient whole-wheat flour roasted low and slow for a deeply nutty halwa

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the atta to a rich brown and gives the prasad its signature richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted into the water to sweeten the halwa with earthy caramel notes

steps: Heat 0.6 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai over low heat and add 1 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta.
Roast the atta patiently, stirring without pause, for 12 to 15 minutes until it turns rich reddish-brown and smells deeply nutty.
Meanwhile melt 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 2.5 cups water over low heat and strain out any grit.
Pour the hot jaggery water into the roasted atta very carefully, standing back from the fierce splutter, and stir hard to break lumps.
Cook on low heat for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring constantly, until the halwa thickens, turns glossy and releases ghee at the edges.
Mix in 0.5 tsp cardamom and 2 tbsp chopped almonds, then serve the kada prasad warm.
tips: The long, slow roast of the atta is essential; rushing it leaves a raw taste and pale colour.
Add the hot liquid gradually and away from your face, as atta halwa splutters more violently than sooji.
This halwa drinks up ghee, so do not reduce it if you want the authentic glossy gurudwara texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the wheat halwa warm as kada prasad, traditionally offered in cupped hands, garnished with almonds.

variations.name: Classic Suran Ki Sabzi
variations.description: This Classic Suran Ki Sabzi cooks elephant-foot yam into a dry, spiced side with crisp golden edges and a soft floury centre. A staple of North Indian and Bihari kitchens, especially during festivals, it balances the yam's earthiness with a bright amchur tang.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the pungent oil that crisps the yam edges and cuts its natural earthiness

steps: Peel and cube the 500 g yam, then boil it with a pinch of turmeric and salt for 8 minutes until just tender, and drain well.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it smokes, lower the heat and add 1 tsp cumin seeds to crackle for 15 seconds.
Add the grated ginger and slit green chillies and saute for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt on low heat for 20 seconds so the spices bloom without burning.
Add the boiled yam cubes and toss to coat, then spread them out and let them fry undisturbed for 4 minutes to crisp the base.
Turn the cubes and fry another 6 minutes, stirring occasionally, until golden and slightly crusted at the edges.
Sprinkle 1 tsp amchur and 0.5 tsp garam masala, toss once and serve hot with coriander.
tips: Rub a little oil on your hands before peeling yam, as it can cause a mild itch on bare skin.
Par-boil the yam first so the final fry only needs to crisp and flavour the cubes.
Let the cubes sit undisturbed while frying to develop a proper golden crust.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with dal-rice and a spoon of ghee, or tuck it into a roti roll for a hearty lunch.

variations.name: Bengali Ol Bhaja Style Suran
variations.description: A Bengali ol-style preparation where yam batons are tempered with panch phoron and a hint of mustard paste for a nutty, slightly sharp finish. The five-spice tempering gives it an unmistakable eastern Indian aroma quite distinct from the amchur-led North Indian version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: essential to Bengali cooking and the natural partner to the mustard paste here

steps: Peel and cut the 500 g yam into thick batons, then boil with 0.5 tsp turmeric and salt for 7 minutes until just soft, and drain.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it smokes to mellow its sharpness, then lower the heat.
Add 1 tsp panch phoron, 1 bay leaf and 2 broken dry red chillies and let them splutter for 20 seconds until aromatic.
Add the yam batons and 1 tsp salt and fry on medium heat for 6 minutes, turning, until the edges catch a golden colour.
Whisk the 1 tbsp mustard paste with a little water, add it with the slit green chillies, and toss for 2 minutes so it coats every piece.
Cover and cook on low for 6 minutes until the yam is soft and the pungent mustard has mellowed.
Uncover, add 0.25 tsp sugar to balance, fry 2 minutes to dry off and serve.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to smoking point first so its raw pungency softens before cooking.
Soak the mustard seeds before grinding to a paste to avoid any bitter aftertaste.
A pinch of sugar is traditional in Bengali cooking and rounds out the sharp mustard.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a drizzle of raw mustard oil, alongside a wedge of lemon.

variations.name: Chatpata Tawa Suran Fry
variations.description: A street-style tawa fry where thin yam slices are shallow-crisped and tossed in a tangy chaat masala and roasted spice mix. Crisp at the edges and soft within, this snacky version bursts with sour-spicy flavour perfect for tea-time.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil that shallow-crisps the yam slices to a light golden crunch

steps: Peel the 500 g yam and slice it into 1 cm thick discs, then boil with 0.5 tsp turmeric for 6 minutes until just tender and pat dry.
Toss the dried slices with 2 tbsp rice flour, 1 tsp chilli powder and 0.75 tsp salt so they are lightly coated.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on a flat tawa over medium heat until shimmering.
Lay the coated slices in a single layer and shallow-fry for 4 minutes per side until crisp and golden brown.
Drain the crisped slices on a plate and while still hot dust with 1 tsp chaat masala, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder and 0.5 tsp black salt.
Squeeze over 1 tbsp lemon juice and toss gently so every slice is coated in the tangy spice mix.
Serve immediately while crisp, garnished with fresh coriander and thin onion rings.
tips: The rice flour coating is the secret to slices that stay crisp rather than turning soggy.
Add the chaat masala and lemon only after frying so the tang stays fresh and sharp.
Keep the slices in one layer and give them space so they crisp instead of steaming.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a tea-time snack with green chutney and a hot cup of masala chai.

variations.name: South-Indian Suran Curry Leaf Fry
variations.description: A South Indian poriyal-inspired stir-fry where yam cubes are tossed with a curry-leaf and urad dal tempering and finished with fresh coconut. Light, nutty and mildly spiced in coconut oil, it makes a wholesome everyday side for rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: carries the curry-leaf tempering and lends the poriyal its authentic southern aroma

steps: Peel and finely dice the 500 g yam, then boil with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 7 minutes until tender and drain.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop for 15 seconds.
Add 1 tsp urad dal and 2 broken dry red chillies and fry for 30 seconds until the dal turns golden.
Toss in the 12 curry leaves and let them crisp for 10 seconds until fragrant.
Add the boiled yam with 1 tsp sambar powder and toss on medium heat for 6 minutes until the cubes take on the spice.
Add the 0.5 cup grated coconut and stir-fry for 3 minutes until the coconut is lightly toasted and dry.
Check the salt, cook 1 more minute and serve warm as a poriyal.
tips: Dice the yam small so it cooks through quickly and soaks up the tempering evenly.
Add the coconut towards the end so it stays fresh and just lightly toasted.
Fry the urad dal until golden for that signature nutty crunch in the tempering.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sambar rice or curd rice and a crisp papad for a comforting South Indian meal.

variations.name: Classic Tindora Fry
variations.description: This Classic Tindora Fry crisps thin slices of ivy gourd in a simple cumin-turmeric tempering until the edges turn golden and lightly chewy. A quick, low-fuss North Indian stir-fry, it turns the humble tindora into a moreish everyday side.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil that crisps the ivy gourd slices to a golden edge

steps: Wash and thinly slice the 400 g ivy gourd lengthwise into quarters.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them sizzle for 15 seconds.
Add the slit green chillies and the sliced tindora and toss well to coat in the oil.
Spread the slices out and let them fry undisturbed for 5 minutes to start crisping.
Add 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, toss, and stir-fry uncovered for 10 minutes until golden and tender.
Increase the heat for the last 2 minutes to crisp the edges, stirring often so they do not burn.
Sprinkle 0.75 tsp amchur, toss once and serve hot.
tips: Slice the tindora thin and even so every piece crisps at the same rate.
Cook uncovered so the moisture escapes and the slices fry rather than steam.
Discard any hard, red-centred pieces as those are overripe and turn mushy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with dal-rice or roll it into a hot roti with a smear of curd for lunch.

variations.name: Andhra Tindora Peanut Fry
variations.description: A fiery Andhra-style dondakaya fry where ivy gourd is tossed with a roasted peanut-sesame podi and plenty of red chilli. The coarse nutty powder clings to the crisp slices for a spicy, aromatic side that defines Telugu home cooking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: the nutty southern oil that deepens the peanut-sesame podi flavour

steps: Dry-roast the 3 tbsp peanuts, 1 tbsp sesame seeds and 3 dry red chillies for 3 minutes, cool and grind to a coarse podi with the garlic.
Wash and quarter the 400 g ivy gourd into thin lengths.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadai, add 1 tsp mustard and 1 tsp urad dal and let them splutter for 20 seconds until golden.
Add the 10 curry leaves and the sliced tindora with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, and toss to coat.
Stir-fry uncovered on medium heat for 12 minutes until the slices turn golden and crisp at the edges.
Add the ground peanut-sesame podi and toss for 3 minutes so the coarse powder coats every slice.
Cook 1 minute more until fragrant and dry, then serve hot.
tips: Grind the podi coarse, not fine, so it gives a nutty crunch rather than a paste.
Add the podi only after the tindora is crisp so it toasts without going soggy.
Adjust the dry red chillies to your heat tolerance as Andhra fries run fiery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or with plain curd rice.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Tondli Coconut Bhaji
variations.description: A Maharashtrian tondli bhaji where ivy gourd is stir-cooked with goda masala and finished with fresh coconut and coriander. The warm sweet-spice blend and coconut give it a gentle, homely flavour distinct from the fiery southern fries.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the classic Maharashtrian cooking oil that suits the coconut and goda masala

steps: Wash and slice the 400 g ivy gourd into thin rounds.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai, add 1 tsp mustard, 0.5 tsp cumin and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them splutter 15 seconds.
Add 8 curry leaves and the slit green chillies and fry for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add the sliced tindora with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt and toss to coat.
Cover and cook on low for 10 minutes, stirring once, until the rounds turn soft.
Uncover, add 1.5 tsp goda masala and stir-fry on medium for 3 minutes until the moisture dries off.
Fold in the 0.33 cup grated coconut, cook 1 minute and serve warm with coriander.
tips: Slicing into thin rounds helps the ivy gourd cook evenly under cover.
Goda masala gives the signature warm-sweet Maharashtrian note that garam masala cannot.
Add the coconut last so it stays fresh and moist rather than dry and toasted.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri or soft chapatis and a bowl of varan dal.

variations.name: Punjabi Masala Tindora
variations.description: A robust Punjabi version where ivy gourd is cooked in a bhuna onion-tomato masala until saucy and richly spiced. Cooked in ghee with kasuri methi, it turns the light stir-fry into a heartier, dhaba-style semi-dry sabzi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: browns the onion-tomato masala richly and rounds off the Punjabi spices

steps: Wash and slice the 400 g ivy gourd into thin lengths.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them sizzle for 20 seconds.
Add the finely chopped onions and fry for 7 minutes until golden, then add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Add the pureed tomatoes with 1.25 tsp chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and bhuno for 6 minutes until the ghee separates.
Add the sliced tindora and toss to coat, then cover and cook on low for 12 minutes, stirring once, until tender.
Uncover and cook 3 minutes on higher heat so the masala thickens and clings to the slices.
Crush 1 tsp kasuri methi over the top, add 0.5 tsp garam masala, stir and serve hot.
tips: Brown the onions patiently as the depth of a Punjabi masala rests on that step.
Cook the tindora covered first so it softens before the masala is reduced.
Crush the kasuri methi between the palms just before adding to release its aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tandoori roti or laccha paratha and a side of onion salad.

variations.name: Classic Turai Ki Sabzi
variations.description: A light, homely dry sabzi of ridge gourd cooked in its own moisture with a simple cumin, onion and tomato masala. The turai softens and turns almost silky, needing no added water, making a quick everyday North Indian side that is gentle on the stomach and quietly comforting.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil that keeps this light sabzi clean and blooms the cumin

steps: Peel the ridges off the 500 g turai, cube it into bite-sized pieces and keep aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle for 15 seconds.
Add the chopped onion and saute for 3 minutes until soft, then add 1 tbsp grated ginger and the slit green chillies and cook 1 minute.
Add the chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp chilli powder and 1 tsp salt and cook 3 minutes until pulpy.
Add the turai cubes, toss well, cover and cook on low for 12 minutes, stirring twice, until it releases its water and turns soft and silky.
Uncover and cook 2 minutes on medium to dry any excess moisture, then serve hot with fresh coriander.
tips: Ridge gourd releases plenty of water on its own, so resist adding any extra while it cooks.
Peel only the tough ridges and keep some green skin for a little texture and colour.
If the sabzi turns watery, uncover and cook it down on medium rather than draining the flavourful liquid.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulka and a bowl of moong dal for a light, everyday home meal.

variations.name: Turai Chana Dal
variations.description: A heartier version where ridge gourd is cooked with soaked Bengal gram so the soft dal adds body and a nutty bite against the silky turai. Tempered simply with cumin and hing, it becomes a wholesome one-pot sabzi-dal that turns a plain gourd into a filling meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: tempers the cumin and hing and rounds off this wholesome dal-sabzi

steps: Soak 0.5 cup chana dal for 30 minutes, then pressure-cook with 0.25 tsp turmeric, a little salt and 1 cup water for 3 whistles until just soft but not mushy.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them sizzle for 15 seconds.

Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the slit green chillies, fry 1 minute, then add the chopped tomatoes with the remaining 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.75 tsp chilli powder and 1 tsp salt and cook 4 minutes until pulpy.
Add the 500 g cubed turai, toss well, cover and cook on low for 10 minutes until it softens and releases its water.
Add the cooked chana dal with its liquid, mix gently and simmer uncovered for 6 minutes until the flavours meld and the mixture thickens.
Finish with 0.5 tsp garam masala, stir once and serve hot garnished with coriander.
tips: Cook the chana dal until just tender so it holds its shape and does not dissolve into the turai.
Do not add extra water, as the ridge gourd and dal liquid give plenty of moisture on their own.
This version thickens on standing, so loosen with a splash of hot water if reheating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rice or roti, with a spoon of ghee melted on top for a satisfying one-dish meal.

variations.name: South Indian Turai Kootu
variations.description: A Tamil-style ridge gourd kootu where the gourd simmers with moong dal and a freshly ground coconut, cumin and green chilli paste, finished with a mustard and curry leaf tempering. Mild, creamy and lightly spiced, it is comfort food from the southern kitchen served over rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the coastal oil that tempers the mustard and curry leaves for this southern kootu

steps: Pressure-cook 0.5 cup moong dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.5 cups water for 3 whistles until soft, then mash lightly.
Boil the 500 g cubed turai with 0.5 cup water and 1 tsp salt in a pot for 6 minutes until just tender.
Grind the 0.5 cup grated coconut with 1 tsp cumin seeds and 3 green chillies to a smooth paste with a little water.
Add the cooked dal and the coconut paste to the boiled turai and simmer on low for 6 minutes until it thickens into a creamy kootu, stirring gently.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan, add 1 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tsp urad dal, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 12 curry leaves and let them splutter until the dal turns golden.
Pour the sizzling tempering over the kootu, stir once and serve hot.
tips: Do not overcook the turai before adding the dal, or it will disintegrate into the kootu.
Grind the coconut paste smooth for a creamy texture and add it on low heat so it does not curdle.
The kootu thickens as it cools, so keep it slightly loose and adjust with hot water before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot steamed rice with a spoon of ghee, or as a side with sambar rice and papad.

variations.name: Turai Pyaaz Masala
variations.description: A more robust dhaba-style ridge gourd cooked down in a bhuna onion-tomato masala with garlic and kasuri methi until it turns rich and semi-dry. The gourd almost melts into the deeply spiced masala, giving a fuller-flavoured sabzi that stands up to thick rotis.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: browns the onions and deepens the bhuna masala for this dhaba-style sabzi

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just smokes, lower the heat and add 1 tsp cumin seeds to crackle for 15 seconds.
Add the 2 finely chopped onions and 6 chopped garlic cloves and fry for 6 minutes until deep golden, then add 1 tbsp grated ginger and cook 1 minute.
Add the pureed tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt and bhuno for 5 minutes until the oil separates.
Add the 500 g cubed turai, toss to coat in the masala, cover and cook on low for 12 minutes until it softens and releases its water.
Uncover and cook 3 minutes on medium to reduce the moisture into a thick, clinging semi-dry masala.
Crush 1 tsp kasuri methi over the top, add 0.5 tsp garam masala, stir and serve hot.
tips: Brown the onions and garlic well for the deep bhuna base that makes this version taste rich.
Cook the masala uncovered at the end to reduce the gourd water into a thick clinging sauce.
Mash a few pieces of the cooked turai into the masala to naturally thicken the semi-dry sabzi.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thick tandoori roti or missi roti and a side of sliced onion and lemon.

variations.name: Classic Veg Handi
variations.description: A slow-simmered mixed vegetable curry cooked in a heavy handi so the flavours deepen and concentrate under a tight lid. Studded with paneer and finished with a smoky whole-spice masala, it is earthier and more layered than a quick everyday sabzi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the traditional handi fat that carries the whole spices through the slow simmer

steps: Chop 2.5 cups mixed vegetables into bite-sized pieces and lightly saute them with the 100 g paneer cubes in a spoon of ghee until the edges catch colour, then set aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy handi over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin, 1 bay leaf and 1 black cardamom, and let them crackle for 30 seconds.
Add the finely chopped onions and fry for 7 minutes until deep golden, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the pureed tomatoes with 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt, and cook for 8 minutes until the ghee separates.
Whisk 0.25 cup curd smooth, lower the heat and stir it in slowly so it does not split, then add the sauteed vegetables, peas and 1.5 cups water.
Cover the handi tightly and simmer on low for 15 minutes until the vegetables are tender and the gravy thickens, then fold in the paneer, sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala, and serve hot.
tips: Sear the vegetables first so they hold their shape and gain a light smokiness during the slow simmer.
Cook in a heavy-bottomed handi with a tight lid so the steam and flavours stay locked in.
Add the whisked curd off the boil and stir constantly to keep the gravy smooth.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve straight from the handi with tandoori roti, naan or jeera rice, garnished with ginger juliennes.

variations.name: Dum Veg Handi (Sealed-lid Style)
variations.description: A dum-style handi where the half-cooked vegetables finish over the gentlest heat under a dough-sealed lid, trapping every aromatic vapour of saffron and whole spices. The result is meltingly tender vegetables perfumed right through, in the style of a Awadhi dum curry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: essential for a dum handi, it carries the aromatics through the sealed slow cook

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk it perfumes the sealed handi with a royal aroma and golden tint

steps: Soak 0.25 tsp Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk, and boil the 2 onions with 12 cashews for 8 minutes, then blend into a smooth pale paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a handi over medium heat, add 4 cardamoms, cinnamon and 3 cloves, and let them sizzle for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the cashew-onion paste and cook gently for 6 minutes without browning, then add 1 tsp coriander powder, 0.25 tsp white pepper and 1.25 tsp salt.
Whisk 0.5 cup curd smooth, lower the heat and stir it in slowly, then add the 2.5 cups vegetables with a cup of water and bring to a gentle simmer.
Pour the saffron milk over the top, cover the handi with a lid, and seal the rim with a rope of whole wheat dough to trap the steam.
Cook on the lowest heat for 20 minutes, switch off and let it rest sealed for 5 minutes, then break the seal at the table and serve the fragrant dum handi.
tips: Seal the lid with dough so no aroma escapes; this trapped steam is what makes a true dum dish.
Keep the flame at its lowest during dum, placing a tawa under the handi if needed to diffuse the heat.
Break the seal only at serving so guests get the full burst of saffron and spice aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sheermal, roghni naan or a delicate zafrani pulao for a regal spread.

variations.name: Kolhapuri Veg Handi
variations.description: A fiery Maharashtrian handi built on a freshly roasted and ground Kolhapuri masala of dry coconut, sesame and red chillies. Dark, spicy and intensely aromatic, it is the boldest of the mixed vegetable curries and unmistakably fiery.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the robust oil that fries the dark Kolhapuri masala without burning

steps: Dry-roast 0.33 cup dry coconut, 1 tbsp sesame seeds, 5 dried red chillies and 1 tbsp coriander seeds separately until each is fragrant and browned, then grind with a little water into a dark, coarse Kolhapuri masala.
Parboil the 2.5 cups mixed vegetables and 0.5 cup peas in salted water for 6 minutes until just tender, then drain.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a handi over medium heat, add the finely chopped onions and fry for 7 minutes until deep brown.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt, and cook for 6 minutes until the tomatoes break down.
Stir in the ground Kolhapuri masala and fry on medium for 4 minutes until the oil separates and the masala turns fragrant and dark.
Add the parboiled vegetables with 1.5 cups water, cover and simmer on low for 10 minutes until the gravy thickens and coats the vegetables, then serve fiery hot.
tips: Roast the coconut, sesame and chillies until properly dark, as this is what gives Kolhapuri masala its colour and depth.
Fry the ground masala well until the oil separates so the raw spice edge cooks off.
Adjust the number of red chillies to your heat tolerance, as an authentic Kolhapuri is meant to be fiery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri, plain rice or bread rolls, with sliced onion and lemon to cool the heat.

variations.name: Handi Veg Hyderabadi (Coconut-Peanut Style)
variations.description: A Hyderabadi handi where the vegetables simmer in a tangy peanut-coconut-tamarind gravy tempered with curry leaves. Nutty, tangy and richly textured, it draws on the same ground-nut base that flavours a Hyderabadi mirchi ka salan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: the traditional Hyderabadi til oil that deepens the nutty peanut-coconut gravy

steps: Dry-roast 0.33 cup peanuts, 3 tbsp dry coconut and 1 tbsp sesame seeds until golden, then grind with a splash of water into a smooth nutty paste, and soak 1 tbsp tamarind in warm water for its pulp.
Parboil the 2.5 cups mixed vegetables in salted water for 6 minutes until just tender, then drain.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil in a handi over medium heat, add 0.75 tsp mustard and 0.75 tsp cumin and let them splutter, then add 12 curry leaves.
Add the finely chopped onions and fry for 6 minutes until golden, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute.
Stir in the ground peanut-coconut paste with 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt, and fry on medium for 5 minutes until the oil floats.
Add the parboiled vegetables, the tamarind pulp and 1.5 cups water, cover and simmer on low for 10 minutes until the gravy thickens into a nutty, tangy curry, then serve hot.
tips: Grind the roasted peanuts and coconut smooth for a rich body, straining if you prefer a silkier gravy.
Balance the tamarind with a little more or less to get the signature sweet-sour-nutty flavour.
Simmer gently once the vegetables are in so the thick gravy does not catch at the bottom of the handi.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bagara rice, plain rice or roti, with a wedge of lemon to lift the nutty gravy.

variations.name: Classic Begun Bhaja
variations.description: The simplest, most iconic Bengali side: thick rounds of brinjal rubbed with turmeric, salt and a little chilli, then shallow-fried in mustard oil until the edges caramelise and the centre turns silky and custard-soft. Nothing more is needed, and its smoky, oil-slicked simplicity is exactly why it opens so many Bengali meals.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed kachi ghani oil is the soul of begun bhaja, lending the smoky pungency that makes the plain slices sing

steps: Slice 1 large round brinjal into 1/2 inch thick discs and rub both faces of each with a mix of 3/4 tsp turmeric, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder, 1/4 tsp sugar and 3/4 tsp salt, then let them sit for 10 minutes to draw out moisture.
Heat 5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a flat pan until it just reaches smoking point, then lower the heat and let it settle for 20 seconds so the raw pungency mellows.
Lay the brinjal slices in a single layer and shallow-fry on medium heat for 4 to 5 minutes without moving them, until the underside is deep golden and caramelised.
Flip each slice carefully and fry the second side for another 4 minutes, pressing lightly with a spatula so the centre cooks through to a soft, creamy texture.
Once both sides are burnished and the flesh yields easily to a fork, lift the slices onto paper to drain the excess oil.
Serve hot and fresh, as begun bhaja loses its crisp edge and turns limp if it sits too long.
tips: Salt the slices and wait ten minutes before frying; the drawn-out moisture lets them crisp instead of steaming in the pan.
Keep the heat at medium and resist flipping too early, since a single long sear is what gives the caramelised crust.
Choose a firm, glossy brinjal with few seeds; older seedy ones turn bitter and mushy when fried.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as the first bite of a Bengali lunch, with hot rice and a spoon of dal, or alongside khichuri on a rainy afternoon.

variations.name: Crispy Besan Begun Bhaja
variations.description: A crunchier cousin where the brinjal slices are dipped in a spiced besan batter before frying, so they emerge with a shatteringly crisp golden jacket around the melting flesh. This pakora-style begun bhaja is the one that disappears fastest off the table, halfway between a fritter and a fry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the deeper pool of pungent oil fries the besan jacket to an even, blistered crisp

steps: Cut 2 long brinjals into 1/3 inch thick diagonal slices and toss them lightly with 1/4 tsp of the turmeric and a pinch of the salt while you make the batter.

Whisk 3/4 cup besan and 2 tbsp rice flour with 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 3/4 tsp red chilli powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1/4 tsp hing and 3/4 tsp salt, then add about 1/2 cup water in a stream to make a smooth batter that coats the back of a spoon.
Heat 6 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai to smoking, then lower to medium so a drop of batter sizzles up steadily without browning instantly.
Dip each brinjal slice into the batter to coat evenly, let the excess drip off, and slide it into the hot oil, frying a few at a time for about 3 minutes until the underside is crisp and golden.
Turn and fry the other side for 2 to 3 minutes until the whole jacket is deep gold and crackly, then lift onto paper to drain.
Serve immediately while the besan crust is still shatteringly crisp, before the steam from the brinjal softens it.
tips: The spoon of rice flour is the secret to a crust that stays crisp rather than going soft within minutes.
Keep the batter thick enough to cling; a runny batter slides off and leaves bald patches on the slices.
Do not crowd the pan, since too many slices at once drop the oil temperature and the coating turns oily instead of crisp.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a monsoon snack with kasundi mustard and a cup of tea, or as a crunchy side to plain khichuri.

variations.name: Posto-Crusted Begun Bhaja
variations.description: A textural twist where the brinjal slices are pressed into a poppy-seed and semolina crust before frying, giving a nutty, sandy crunch that shatters over the soft interior. The poppy toasts as it fries, filling the kitchen with a warm, sesame-like aroma unique to this version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: its sharpness offsets the nutty poppy crust and fries it to an even, speckled gold

steps: Slice 1 large brinjal into 1/2 inch rounds and rub them with 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder and 3/4 tsp salt, then rest for 10 minutes.
On a plate, mix 3 tbsp poppy seeds with 3 tbsp fine semolina to make the coating. In a separate bowl, stir 2 tbsp rice flour with about 3 tbsp water into a thin, sticky slurry.
Dip each seasoned brinjal slice into the rice-flour slurry, then press both faces firmly into the poppy-semolina mix so the crust adheres in an even layer.
Heat 5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, lower to medium, and lay in the coated slices, frying for about 4 minutes until the underside is golden and the poppy smells toasted.
Flip gently and fry the second side for 3 to 4 minutes until crisp and speckled, pressing lightly so the centre softens through.
Drain on paper and serve at once, while the poppy crust is still crunchy and fragrant.
tips: The rice-flour slurry is the glue; without it the poppy and semolina slide off in the hot oil.
Fry on steady medium heat, since too high a flame scorches the poppy seeds before the brinjal cooks through.
Press the crust on firmly and let the slices rest a minute before frying so the coating sets and does not shed.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a bowl of aloo posto for a poppy-themed Bengali lunch, or on its own with a squeeze of lime.

variations.name: Jaggery-Chilli Begun Bhaja
variations.description: A sweet-and-hot rendition where the fried brinjal is tossed in a quick jaggery, tamarind and chilli glaze that clings in a glossy, sticky coat. It plays the smoky brinjal against tangy-sweet notes for a side that eats almost like a chutney-glazed relish, popular in East Bengal homes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: fries the brinjal and forms the base of the sticky sweet-hot glaze

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: unrefined jaggery melts into a glossy caramel glaze that clings to the smoky slices

steps: Slice 1 large brinjal into 1/2 inch rounds, rub with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1/2 tsp of the salt, and rest 10 minutes.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the heat, and shallow-fry the brinjal for 4 minutes a side until deep golden and soft, then lift onto a plate.
In the same pan, with 1 tbsp oil left, crackle 1/2 tsp nigella seeds and 2 dried red chillies for 20 seconds until fragrant.

Lower the heat and add 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 tbsp tamarind paste, 1 tsp red chilli powder, the remaining 1/4 tsp salt and 2 tbsp water, stirring for 2 minutes until it melts into a glossy, syrupy glaze.
Return the fried brinjal to the pan and turn the slices gently in the glaze for 1 to 2 minutes until each is coated and sticky.
Take off the heat and serve warm, letting the glaze set slightly into a shiny coat over the smoky slices.
tips: Keep the glaze on low heat and watch it closely; jaggery can go from syrupy to burnt in under a minute.
Balance the glaze to taste, adding a touch more tamarind if it skews too sweet or more jaggery if too sharp.
Toss the brinjal in the glaze only briefly, since long stirring breaks the soft fried slices apart.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a sweet-spicy side with plain rice and dal, or as a relish-like accompaniment to a simple khichuri.

variations.name: Classic Dum Ki Arbi
variations.description: Boiled and shallow-fried colocasia is slow-cooked on dum in a tangy yogurt-and-spice masala until each piece drinks up the flavour. Creamy inside with a lightly crisped surface, this North Indian favourite balances the earthiness of arbi with a gentle tang.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: shallow-fries the arbi and carries the dum masala into every crevice

steps: Boil 500 g arbi for about 12 minutes until just tender, then peel, halve the larger pieces, and pat completely dry.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat and shallow-fry the arbi for 6 minutes until golden and lightly crisp, then remove and set aside.
In the same ghee add 1 tsp cumin and the finely chopped onions and fry for 6 minutes until golden, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute.
Lower the heat, add 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp fennel powder, then whisk 0.75 cup curd smooth and stir it in slowly so it does not split.
Return the fried arbi with 1.25 tsp salt and half a cup of water, stir gently, then cover with a tight lid and cook on the lowest heat on dum for 12 minutes so the arbi soaks up the masala.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp garam masala and 3 tbsp coriander, give one gentle stir, and serve hot.
tips: Boil the arbi only until just tender and dry it well, or it will turn slimy and stick to the pan.
Add the whisked curd on low heat and stir constantly to keep the masala from curdling.
Cook on the lowest heat under a tight lid so the arbi absorbs the flavour without breaking apart.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulkas or jeera rice, with a bowl of dal and a wedge of lemon on the side.

variations.name: Banarasi Dum Arbi (Fried and Stuffed)
variations.description: A Banarasi-style dum arbi where the fried colocasia is flattened, filled with a tangy spiced masala, and finished on dum in a light gravy. The stuffing of amchur, fennel and roasted spices makes every bite sharp, aromatic and festive.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the pungent oil that gives Banarasi arbi its characteristic sharp, earthy edge

steps: Boil 500 g arbi until just tender, peel, and gently press each piece flat between your palms without breaking it.

Dry-roast 1.5 tsp fennel and 1 tbsp coriander seeds until fragrant, coarsely crush them, then mix with 2 tbsp besan, 1 tsp amchur, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt into a dry stuffing.
Press a little of the spice-besan mixture onto each flattened arbi piece so it clings to the surface.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Mustard Oil until it just smokes, lower the heat, add 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 0.5 tsp nigella seeds, and let them crackle for 15 seconds.
Lay the stuffed arbi in the pan and shallow-fry on medium for 8 minutes, turning gently, until the besan crust turns deep golden and crisp.
Sprinkle half a cup of water and 0.75 tsp salt, cover and cook on dum on the lowest heat for 8 minutes, garnish with 3 tbsp coriander, and serve hot.
tips: Press the boiled arbi gently so it flattens without splitting, giving more surface for the crust.
Heat the mustard oil until it just smokes and cool it slightly before frying to mellow the sharpness.
Roast and crush the whole spices fresh for the vivid, tangy Banarasi flavour that powders cannot match.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a dry, tangy side with dal-rice or pooris, with sliced onions and a green chutney.

variations.name: Hyderabadi Dum Ki Arbi
variations.description: A Hyderabadi dum where the arbi bathes in a rich sesame-peanut-coconut gravy tangy with tamarind and cooked slow under a lid. Nutty, tangy and lush, it mirrors the beloved salan style with colocasia standing in for the usual chillies.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: the traditional til oil that deepens the nutty salan-style gravy

steps: Boil 500 g arbi until just tender, peel, and shallow-fry in a little sesame oil for 5 minutes until golden, then set aside, and soak 1 tbsp tamarind in warm water for its pulp.
Dry-roast 0.33 cup peanuts, 1.5 tbsp sesame seeds and 3 tbsp dry coconut until golden, then grind with a splash of water into a smooth nutty paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Sesame Oil in a kadhai over medium heat, add 0.75 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop, then add 12 curry leaves.
Add the finely chopped onions and fry for 6 minutes until golden, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Stir in the ground peanut-sesame paste with 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt, and fry for 5 minutes until the oil separates.
Add the fried arbi, tamarind pulp and 1.5 cups water, cover and cook on dum on low for 12 minutes until the gravy thickens and clings to the arbi, then serve hot.
tips: Grind the roasted nuts and coconut smooth for a rich gravy, adding water little by little.
Balance the tamarind carefully so the gravy is pleasantly sour rather than sharp.
Fry the arbi first so it holds its shape and does not disintegrate in the thick gravy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bagara rice, plain rice or roti, garnished with a few extra curry leaves fried in oil.

variations.name: Arbi Ajwaini Fry (Dry Dum)
variations.description: A dry, crisp version where the arbi is dum-cooked briefly with ajwain, garlic and a bold dry-spice coating until every piece is roasted and golden. Almost like a spiced roast, it is the crunchiest, most snackable take on colocasia.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: gives the arbi its even golden roast without soaking in too much oil

steps: Boil 500 g arbi until just tender, peel, halve the larger pieces, and pat them thoroughly dry.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil in a wide pan over medium heat, add 0.75 tsp ajwain, 0.75 tsp cumin and the roughly crushed garlic, and fry for 1 minute until the garlic turns golden.
Add the arbi and toss to coat, then spread it in a single layer and let it fry undisturbed for 5 minutes so the underside crisps.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp salt, toss well, then cover and cook on low dum for 6 minutes so the spices cling.
Uncover, raise the heat and stir-fry for 5 minutes, turning occasionally, until every piece is deep golden and crisp at the edges.
Switch off, dust with 0.75 tsp amchur and 0.5 tsp chaat masala, toss once, and serve hot and crunchy.
tips: Dry the boiled arbi completely before frying, as any moisture makes it slimy instead of crisp.
Spread the arbi in a single layer and resist stirring too soon so it develops a proper golden crust.
Add the amchur and chaat masala off the heat so they stay tangy and bright.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a dry side or tea-time snack with dal-rice, or with mint chutney as a spiced starter.

variations.name: Classic Kaju Katli
variations.description: Kaju Katli is India's most gifted mithai, wafer-thin diamonds of smooth cashew fudge made from just cashew powder and sugar syrup cooked to the perfect setting point. Silky, barely sweet and crowned with edible silver leaf, it melts cleanly on the tongue with a pure cashew flavour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: cooked to a one-string syrup that binds the cashew powder into a smooth, sliceable fudge

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the surface and hands so the soft cashew dough can be rolled thin without sticking

steps: Grind 1 cup cashews to a fine, dry powder in short pulses so the nuts stay cool and do not release oil, then sieve it.
Boil 0.5 cup Anveshan Khandsari with 0.25 cup water for 4 to 5 minutes until it reaches a sticky one-string consistency.
Lower the heat, tip in the cashew powder and 0.25 tsp cardamom, and stir constantly for 4 to 5 minutes until it forms a soft, non-sticky dough.
Turn the warm dough onto a greased surface, smear 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee on your palms, and knead it smooth while still warm.
Roll the dough between two sheets of parchment to an even 3-millimetre thickness and press 2 sheets of silver leaf onto the top.
Cool for 10 minutes, then cut into diamonds with a sharp knife and lift them out once fully set.
tips: Pulse the cashews in short bursts; over-grinding warms them and releases oil that makes the fudge greasy.
Stop cooking the moment the mass leaves the pan as a dough, as overcooking makes the katli hard and dry.
Knead while warm for a crack-free sheet; a cooled dough tears when you try to roll it thin.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature as a festival gift sweet, arranged as glinting silver diamonds in a mithai box.

variations.name: Kesar Kaju Katli
variations.description: A festive golden version where saffron steeped in warm milk perfumes and tints the cashew fudge a delicate amber. Slightly softer than the classic thanks to the milk, it carries a floral saffron aroma that makes it a prized Diwali gift.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: cooked to a one-string syrup that sets the saffron cashew dough

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk to colour and perfume the fudge a delicate gold

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the surface so the softer saffron dough rolls out smoothly

steps: Warm 1 tbsp milk and steep a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in it for 10 minutes until the milk turns deep gold.
Grind 1 cup cashews to a fine dry powder in short pulses and sieve to remove any coarse bits.
Boil 0.5 cup Anveshan Khandsari with 0.25 cup water to a one-string syrup, then stir in the saffron milk.
Lower the heat, add the cashew powder and 0.25 tsp cardamom, and stir 4 to 5 minutes to a soft golden dough.
Grease your palms with 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee, knead the warm dough smooth, and roll it to 3 millimetres between parchment sheets.
Press 2 tbsp slivered pistachios over the top, cool 10 minutes, and cut into diamonds once set.
tips: Bloom the saffron fully in warm milk first to draw out maximum colour and fragrance.
The added milk makes this dough softer, so give it a couple of extra minutes on low heat to set right.
Keep the flame low after adding the powder, as milk-enriched fudge scorches faster.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a luxurious Diwali gift sweet, the golden diamonds studded with green pistachio for contrast.

variations.name: Chocolate Kaju Katli
variations.description: A two-tone fusion katli where a layer of cocoa-laced cashew fudge is pressed onto a plain layer, giving a striking brown-and-cream diamond. The gentle bitterness of cocoa balances the sweetness and makes this a hit with children at festival time.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: cooked to a one-string syrup that binds both the plain and cocoa cashew layers

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the surface and helps the cocoa layer stay pliable for rolling

steps: Grind 1 cup cashews to a fine dry powder in short pulses and sieve it well.
Boil 0.5 cup Anveshan Khandsari with 0.25 cup water to a one-string syrup, then add the cashew powder and 0.25 tsp cardamom and stir to a soft dough.
Divide the warm dough in two, knead 1.5 tbsp cocoa powder into one half with a little of the Anveshan Ghee until evenly brown.
Roll the plain half to a 3-millimetre sheet between parchment, then roll the cocoa half to the same size.
Lay the cocoa sheet over the plain sheet, press gently so they bond, and scatter 2 tbsp chopped pistachios on top.
Cool for 10 minutes, then cut into two-tone diamonds and lift them out once set.
tips: Work quickly while both doughs are warm, as they bond cleanly only before they cool and firm up.
Sieve the cocoa into the dough to avoid bitter dry specks in the chocolate layer.
Roll both sheets to the same thickness so the finished diamonds have even, neat layers.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature as a modern festive treat, the layered diamonds looking elegant on a dessert platter.

variations.name: Kaju Pista Rolls
variations.description: An elegant variation where the cashew dough is wrapped around a vivid green pistachio-rose filling and sliced into pinwheel rounds. The rose-scented pistachio core against the pale cashew wrap makes a jewel-like sweet for special occasions.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: cooked to a one-string syrup to bind both the cashew wrap and the pistachio filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the parchment so the rolls can be shaped tightly without tearing

steps: Grind 1 cup cashews and 0.5 cup pistachios separately into fine dry powders, keeping the vivid green pistachio powder aside.
Boil 0.75 cup Anveshan Khandsari with 0.3 cup water to a one-string syrup, then split it between two pans.
Cook the cashew powder in one portion of syrup with 0.25 tsp cardamom to a soft pale dough, and the pistachio powder in the other with 1 tsp rose water and 1 tbsp milk to a green dough.
Roll the cashew dough into a thin rectangle on greased parchment, then roll the pistachio dough to a slightly smaller rectangle.
Lay the pistachio sheet over the cashew sheet, roll them up tightly into a log using the parchment, and smooth the seam.
Chill the log for 15 minutes, then slice into 1-centimetre pinwheel rounds and serve.
tips: Keep both doughs warm and pliable while rolling, as cooled dough cracks instead of curling into a log.
Roll the log firmly with no air gaps so the pinwheel spiral stays neat when sliced.
Chill briefly before slicing for clean rounds, and use a sharp knife wiped between cuts.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled as an eye-catching festive sweet, the green-and-cream pinwheels arranged on a decorative tray.

variations.name: Classic Parwal Ki Sabzi
variations.description: A simple North Indian dry sabzi of pointed gourd cooked in a cumin, onion and tomato masala until tender and lightly browned. The parwal is halved and sauteed so it stays firm with a gentle bite, making a quick, everyday side that pairs with any dal and roti.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil that sautes the parwal to a light golden edge

steps: Lightly scrape the skin of the 400 g parwal, halve each lengthwise and keep aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle for 15 seconds.
Add the chopped onion and saute for 3 minutes until soft, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until the raw smell fades.
Add the chopped tomatoes with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.75 tsp chilli powder and 1 tsp salt and cook 4 minutes until pulpy.
Add the halved parwal, toss to coat, cover and cook on low for 12 minutes, stirring twice, until tender with a light golden edge.
Sprinkle 0.75 tsp amchur, cook uncovered 2 minutes and serve hot with fresh coriander.
tips: Only lightly scrape the parwal skin, as most of it is tender and adds flavour and colour.
Cook covered on low so the gourd steams tender without needing added water.
Add the amchur at the end for a fresh tang that lifts the mild flavour of the gourd.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulka and a bowl of arhar dal for a light everyday meal.

variations.name: Bengali Aloo Potol
variations.description: The Bengali aloo potol where pointed gourd and potato are fried golden, then simmered in a light ginger-tomato gravy scented with panch phoron and finished with ghee. The parwal turns silky and the gravy stays thin and fragrant, a comforting everyday curry from the eastern kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the Bengali oil that fries the potol golden and blooms the panch phoron

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: stirred in at the end for the classic aloo potol finishing aroma

steps: Lightly scrape and score the 400 g whole parwal, rub with 0.25 tsp turmeric and salt, and cut the 2 potatoes into wedges.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai, fry the parwal and potato for 6 minutes until golden all over, then lift out and set aside.
In the same oil add 1 tsp panch phoron and let it splutter for 20 seconds until the fenugreek turns fragrant.

Add 1 tbsp ginger paste and the slit green chillies, fry 1 minute, then add the chopped tomato with the remaining 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp cumin powder, 0.5 tsp chilli powder and 1 tsp salt and cook 4 minutes until pulpy.
Return the fried parwal and potato, add 1.5 cups hot water, cover and simmer on low for 12 minutes until both are tender and the gravy is light.
Stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, simmer 1 minute and rest 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Do not let the panch phoron burn, as darkened fenugreek turns the gravy bitter.
Fry the potol and potato well first so they hold their shape and soak up the light gravy.
Keep the gravy thin and fragrant, which is how a Bengali aloo potol is meant to be.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice or luchi and a wedge of lime for a comforting Bengali lunch.

variations.name: Bharwa Parwal
variations.description: A festive stuffed pointed gourd where each parwal is hollowed and packed with a roasted besan, coconut and spice masala, then slow-cooked until tender. Sliced open, the gourd reveals a nutty, tangy filling, turning the humble vegetable into a rich celebratory side.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil that slow-cooks the stuffed parwal to a tender finish

steps: Lightly scrape the 12 parwal, slit each lengthwise on one side without cutting through and gently scoop out the seeds.

Dry-roast the 4 tbsp besan and 2 tbsp desiccated coconut on low for 4 minutes until nutty, then mix with 2 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp fennel powder, 1.5 tsp amchur, 1 tsp chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 1 tbsp oil into a crumbly stuffing.
Pack the roasted spice-besan-coconut stuffing firmly into each hollowed parwal.
Heat the remaining 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a wide pan, add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle for 15 seconds.
Arrange the stuffed parwal in a single layer, cover and cook on low for 15 minutes, turning gently every 4 minutes, until tender and golden on all sides.
Scatter any leftover stuffing over the top, cook uncovered 3 minutes and serve hot.
tips: Scoop out only the mature hard seeds and keep the tender flesh so the parwal holds together.
Roast the besan and coconut well so the stuffing tastes nutty rather than raw.
Cook covered on low and turn gently so the gourds soften without the stuffing spilling out.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulka or puri and a bowl of curd for a rustic festive spread.

variations.name: Dahi Parwal
variations.description: A cooling North Indian curry where fried pointed gourd simmers in a mildly spiced yogurt gravy tempered with whole spices. The tangy curd sauce turns silky against the soft parwal, making a light gravy dish that is especially welcome in the summer months.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the parwal and tempers the yogurt gravy to a smooth finish

steps: Lightly scrape and halve the 400 g parwal, then shallow-fry in 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee for 5 minutes until golden; lift out and set aside.
In the same ghee add 1 tsp cumin seeds, 2 cardamom and 1 bay leaf and let them crackle for 20 seconds.
Add the chopped onion and fry 4 minutes until soft, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
Add 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.75 tsp chilli powder and 1 tsp salt with a splash of water and cook 2 minutes into a masala.
Lower the heat to minimum, pour in 1 cup whisked yogurt and stir constantly for 4 minutes until it simmers gently without splitting, then add 0.5 cup water.
Slide in the fried parwal, simmer on low for 8 minutes until soft and the gravy coats them, finish with 0.5 tsp garam masala and serve hot.
tips: Whisk the yogurt smooth and add it on the lowest heat with constant stirring so it does not curdle.
Fry the parwal first so it holds its shape and soaks up the tangy yogurt gravy.
A pinch of sugar or a little cream can be added to mellow the tang if the yogurt is very sour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jeera rice or soft phulka, spooning the silky yogurt gravy generously over each piece.

variations.name: Classic Badam Barfi
variations.description: Badam Barfi is a rich almond fudge made by cooking blanched almond powder with sugar syrup until it sets into soft, sliceable squares. Fragrant with cardamom and finished with silver leaf, it has a fine, slightly grainy almond texture that is prized as a festival and gifting sweet.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: cooked to a one-string syrup that binds the almond powder into a soft, sliceable barfi

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: cooked into the fudge for richness and to keep it from sticking as it sets

steps: Blanch 1.5 cups almonds in hot water for 5 minutes, slip off the skins, and dry them well before grinding to a fine powder.
Boil 0.75 cup Anveshan Khandsari with 0.3 cup water for 4 to 5 minutes to a sticky one-string syrup.
Lower the heat, stir in the almond powder and 0.5 tsp cardamom, and cook 5 to 6 minutes until it thickens into a soft mass.
Add 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and keep stirring until the mixture pulls together and leaves the sides of the pan.
Turn it onto a greased tray, flatten to an even 1-centimetre slab, and press 2 sheets of silver leaf over the top.
Cool for 15 minutes, then cut into neat squares and lift them out once set.
tips: Dry the blanched almonds thoroughly before grinding, as damp nuts turn into a paste instead of powder.
Stop cooking when the mass leaves the pan; overcooking gives a dry, crumbly barfi that will not slice cleanly.
Grind the almonds with a spoon of the sugar to keep them from turning oily during grinding.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature as a festival gift sweet, the silver-topped squares arranged in a decorative mithai box.

variations.name: Kesar Badam Barfi
variations.description: A richer, softer almond barfi enriched with saffron milk that turns it a warm gold and lends a heady floral aroma. The extra milk gives a creamier, melt-in-the-mouth crumb studded with slivered pistachios, making it a regal Diwali offering.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: cooked to a one-string syrup that sets the saffron-milk almond fudge

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm milk to tint and perfume the barfi a rich gold

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: enriches the softer fudge and helps it release cleanly from the tray

steps: Warm 0.25 cup milk and steep a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in it for 10 minutes until deep gold.
Blanch and skin 1.5 cups almonds, dry them, and grind to a fine powder.
Boil 0.75 cup Anveshan Khandsari with 0.2 cup water to a one-string syrup, then stir in the saffron milk and simmer 2 minutes.
Lower the heat, add the almond powder and 0.5 tsp cardamom, and cook 6 to 7 minutes to a soft, glossy mass.
Stir in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until the mixture thickens and pulls away from the pan, then spread it in a greased tray.
Scatter 3 tbsp slivered pistachios over the top, cool 15 minutes, and cut into squares once set.
tips: The added saffron milk makes a softer barfi, so cook a couple of minutes longer to reach a sliceable set.
Bloom the saffron fully first for the deepest colour and aroma throughout the fudge.
Keep the heat low after adding milk and almond powder, as this richer mix scorches easily.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a luxurious festive sweet, the golden pistachio-topped squares perfect for a Diwali gifting hamper.

variations.name: Chocolate Almond Barfi
variations.description: A fusion barfi where cocoa is folded into the almond fudge for a rich, brownie-like depth, topped with crunchy chopped walnuts. The gentle bitterness of cocoa tempers the sweetness, giving a grown-up chocolate-almond sweet that still sets like a classic barfi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: cooked to a one-string syrup that binds the cocoa-almond fudge

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: carries the cocoa smoothly through the fudge and gives it a glossy set

steps: Blanch, skin and dry 1.5 cups almonds, then grind them to a fine powder and sift 2.5 tbsp cocoa alongside.
Boil 0.75 cup Anveshan Khandsari with 0.3 cup water to a one-string syrup.
Lower the heat, whisk in the almond powder, sifted cocoa and 0.5 tsp cardamom, and cook 5 minutes to a thick mass.
Stir in 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and keep cooking until the glossy dough leaves the sides of the pan.
Spread it into a greased tray, press 3 tbsp chopped walnuts over the surface, and level it to a 1-centimetre slab.
Cool for 15 minutes, then cut into squares and lift them out once firmly set.
tips: Sift the cocoa with the almond powder so it blends in evenly with no bitter dry pockets.
Keep the flame low once cocoa goes in, as it scorches and turns bitter over high heat.
Press the walnuts on while the slab is warm so they anchor firmly as the barfi sets.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature as a modern festive treat, cut into small squares for a dessert or gifting platter.

variations.name: Anjeer Badam Barfi
variations.description: A wholesome fig-and-almond barfi sweetened almost entirely by dried figs, with only a touch of jaggery to bind. Chewy, dense and naturally sweet, it is a nourishing sugar-light sweet often served during fasts and to growing children.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a small amount to bind the fig paste and deepen its natural sweetness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the almonds and keeps the sticky fig mixture from catching the pan

steps: Soak 1.5 cups dried figs in warm water for 15 minutes, drain, and grind to a coarse sticky paste with 2 tbsp water.
Dry-roast 1 cup almonds in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee for 4 minutes until fragrant, cool, and chop them coarsely.
Cook the fig paste with 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder in a pan on low for 6 to 7 minutes until it thickens and pulls together.
Stir in the chopped almonds, remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp dry ginger, and cook 3 more minutes.
Transfer the sticky mass onto a greased sheet and roll or press it into a 1.5-centimetre slab.
Chill for 20 minutes to firm it up, then cut into squares or bars and serve.
tips: Choose soft, moist figs; hard dried figs need longer soaking to grind into a smooth paste.
This barfi is naturally sticky, so chilling before cutting is essential for clean pieces.
Leave the almonds coarse for a pleasant chew against the dense, chewy fig base.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled as an energy-rich sweet for fasting days or lunchboxes, cut into small bars for easy snacking.

variations.name: Classic Labra
