variations.description: A soft, sweetish Bengali medley in which a whole market's worth of winter vegetables are cooked down together until they meld into a mellow, spoonable mash, tempered with paanch phoron and finished with ghee. The pumpkin and sweet potato dissolve to bind everything, while radish and beans keep some bite, making it the ultimate use-it-all comfort dish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the pungent wood-pressed oil is the traditional cooking fat that gives labra its earthy backbone

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of bilona ghee rounds the medley and lends its signature puja-day aroma

steps: Cut the pumpkin, potato, sweet potato, radish, flat beans and brinjal into roughly even 1 inch pieces, keeping the harder radish and potato slightly smaller so everything cooks evenly.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadhai to smoking, lower the heat, and crackle 1 tsp paanch phoron, 2 bay leaves and 2 dried red chillies for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add all the cut vegetables with 3/4 tsp turmeric, 1 tbsp ginger paste and 1.25 tsp salt, and saute on medium heat for 5 minutes until they are well coated and glistening.
Cover and cook on low heat for 18 to 20 minutes, stirring occasionally, letting the vegetables release their own water and turn completely soft; add only a small splash of water if the pan dries out.
Uncover, mash the softer pumpkin and sweet potato lightly against the pan so they bind the medley, then stir in 1/2 tsp sugar and cook 3 minutes more until thick and jammy.
Finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee stirred through off the heat and rest covered for 5 minutes so the paanch phoron aroma settles before serving.
tips: Let the vegetables cook in their own moisture rather than adding water; labra should be soft and dense, not soupy.
Cut a mix of soft and firm vegetables so some melt to bind the dish while others hold their shape for texture.
Add the sugar only near the end; it balances the earthiness of mustard oil without making the dish overtly sweet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as part of a bhog thali with khichuri and begun bhaja, or simply over hot rice with a wedge of lime.

variations.name: Bhoger Labra
variations.description: The Durga Puja offering version, cooked without onion or garlic and enriched with fried bori and a hand-ground roasted bhaja masala of cumin and dried chilli sprinkled over at the end. Cauliflower and raw papaya join the medley, and generous ghee makes this the festive, temple-kitchen labra served beside khichuri to hundreds.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a bhog labra is cooked richly in ghee, giving the onion-free medley its offering-day fragrance

steps: Make a bhaja masala by dry-roasting 1 tsp cumin seeds with 2 dried red chillies on low heat for 2 minutes until fragrant, then grinding them to a coarse powder and setting it aside.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and fry the 10 bori on medium for 1 minute until golden, then lift them out to keep them crisp.

In the same pan warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp paanch phoron, 2 bay leaves and 1 dried red chilli for 30 seconds, then add the pumpkin, cauliflower, raw papaya and potato with 3/4 tsp turmeric, 1 tbsp ginger paste and 1.25 tsp salt.
Saute for 5 minutes, then cover and cook on low for 18 to 20 minutes until everything is soft, stirring now and then and adding only a splash of water if needed.
Mash the pumpkin lightly to bind the medley, stir in 1/2 tsp sugar and the fried bori, and cook 2 minutes so the bori just softens at the edges.
Sprinkle over the roasted bhaja masala, fold it through off the heat, and rest covered for 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Add the fried bori near the end so they stay spongy inside rather than dissolving into the vegetables.
The freshly ground bhaja masala is the soul of a bhog labra, so roast and grind it fresh rather than using packaged powder.
Keep it strictly onion and garlic free to stay true to the offering; ginger and roasted spice carry all the flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a puja thali alongside bhog khichuri, cholar dal and a piece of fried pumpkin.

variations.name: Palong Shaak Labra
variations.description: A greens-forward labra where spinach and red amaranth are wilted into the root vegetables, giving a darker, more mineral-rich medley with a fresher edge. The greens cut the sweetness of the pumpkin, making this a lighter, more everyday version than the festive labras.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: its sharpness balances the earthy greens and keeps this lighter labra lively

steps: Roughly chop 2 cups spinach and 1 cup red amaranth leaves, and cut the pumpkin, potato and ridge gourd into 1 inch pieces.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the heat, and crackle 1 tsp paanch phoron and 2 dried red chillies for 20 seconds, then add 4 sliced garlic cloves and fry 30 seconds until pale gold.
Add the pumpkin, potato and ridge gourd with 1/2 tsp turmeric, 2 slit green chillies and 1 tsp salt, and saute on medium for 4 minutes.
Cover and cook on low for 10 minutes until the roots begin to soften, then pile in the chopped spinach and amaranth and stir until they wilt down, about 3 minutes.
Uncover and cook on medium for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring, until the greens and vegetables collapse together and any water thrown off by the greens evaporates.
Mash lightly to bind, check the salt, and serve warm while the greens are still a fresh deep green.
tips: Cook the greens uncovered at the end so their water boils off; trapped moisture makes this labra watery.
Add the amaranth for colour and the spinach for volume; together they keep the medley from tasting flat.
A little garlic suits this everyday version and deepens the greens, though you can leave it out for a purer labra.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot rice with a drizzle of raw mustard oil and a fried papad for a simple, wholesome lunch.

variations.name: Mishti Kumro Chhola Labra
variations.description: A heartier, sweeter labra built around plenty of pumpkin and soaked white chickpeas, with grated coconut and a jaggery finish for the classic Bengali sweet-savoury balance. The chickpeas give it body and protein, turning a vegetable side into something substantial enough to anchor a meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: its pungency grounds the sweet pumpkin and coconut so the dish stays savoury

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: finishes the medley with warmth and ties the coconut and jaggery together

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: unrefined jaggery gives the gentle sweetness that defines this Bengali sweet-savoury labra

steps: Pressure cook 3/4 cup soaked white chickpeas with 1.5 cups water and 1/2 tsp salt for 4 whistles until tender, and drain. Cut 2 cups pumpkin and 1 potato into 1 inch pieces.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the heat, and crackle 1 tsp paanch phoron, 1 bay leaf and 2 dried red chillies for 30 seconds.
Add the pumpkin and potato with 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 tbsp ginger paste and 1/2 tsp salt, and saute on medium for 4 minutes until glossy.
Cover and cook on low for 12 to 15 minutes until the pumpkin turns soft and jammy, then stir in the cooked chickpeas and 1/4 cup grated coconut and cook 4 minutes more.
Mash some of the pumpkin against the pan to bind the medley, then stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook 2 minutes until it melts through and glosses the dish.
Finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee off the heat and rest covered for 5 minutes so the sweet-savoury flavours settle before serving.
tips: Use a ripe, deep-orange pumpkin so it melts into a natural sauce that coats the chickpeas.
Cook the chickpeas soft but not falling apart, so they keep some bite against the soft pumpkin.
Add jaggery last and taste as you go; the coconut is already sweet, so the dish needs only a gentle lift.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot luchi or rice as a filling main-course labra, with a sharp lime pickle to cut the sweetness.

variations.name: Classic Mixed Chorchori
variations.description: A dry Bengali stir-fry where an assortment of vegetables is cooked in their own moisture and bound with a pungent mustard-and-poppy paste, so each piece keeps its shape and identity rather than melting together. Unlike the soft labra, chorchori stays dry and textured, its edges lightly caramelised and its flavour sharp with mustard oil and green chilli.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil both cooks the vegetables and sharpens the mustard paste that defines a chorchori

steps: Cut the potato, brinjal, pumpkin, radish and flat beans into thin batons of roughly equal size so they cook at the same rate. Soak 1 tbsp mustard seeds and 1 tbsp poppy seeds for 15 minutes, then grind with 2 green chillies to a smooth paste.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the heat, and crackle 1 tsp paanch phoron and 2 dried red chillies for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add all the vegetable batons with 3/4 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, and saute on medium-high for 5 minutes so the edges begin to sear and colour.
Cover and cook on low for 12 to 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, letting the vegetables soften in their own steam with no added water; the radish and pumpkin will release enough moisture.
Uncover, stir in the mustard-poppy paste and 1 slit green chilli, and cook on medium for 5 minutes, tossing, until the paste coats the vegetables and the mixture turns dry and glossy.
Cook a final 2 minutes undisturbed so the bottom catches lightly, then serve while the vegetables still hold their shape.
tips: Cook the vegetables in their own moisture; adding water turns a chorchori into a curry and loses its dry, seared character.
Cut everything into similar thin batons so nothing turns to mush before the rest is done.
Grind the mustard with a green chilli and a pinch of salt to keep the paste from turning bitter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice and a spoon of dal, or as one of several small dishes in a Bengali thali.

variations.name: Aloo Potol Chorchori
variations.description: A summer favourite pairing potato with potol (pointed gourd), lightly browned and finished with a smooth mustard paste and nigella temper. The potol stays juicy inside its blistered skin while the potatoes turn golden, making this one of the most-loved everyday chorchoris of Bengal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: browns the potol and potato and carries the sharp mustard paste through the dish

steps: Lightly scrape the skin of 6 potol and halve them lengthwise, and cut 2 potatoes into thick batons. Soak 1.5 tbsp mustard seeds for 15 minutes and grind with 2 green chillies and a pinch of salt to a smooth paste.

Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the heat, and fry the potol and potato with 1/4 tsp turmeric on medium for 6 to 7 minutes until both are golden and blistered, then push them to one side.
In the clear space crackle 1/2 tsp nigella seeds and 2 slit green chillies for 20 seconds until they sputter and smell nutty.
Stir everything together with the remaining 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, cover, and cook on low for 8 minutes until the potol is tender right through.
Add the mustard paste with a bare 2 tbsp water, and cook uncovered on medium for 4 minutes, tossing, until the paste dries onto the vegetables and the oil glistens.
Rest for 3 minutes off the heat so the mustard mellows slightly before serving.
tips: Fry the potol until properly blistered; this searing is what keeps them juicy inside while the paste coats the outside.
Use only a splash of water with the mustard paste, or the chorchori loses its characteristic dryness.
Grind the mustard fresh and use it the same day, as the paste turns sharp and bitter if it sits.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rice and a thin dal, or with dry rotis for a light, quick weekday lunch.

variations.name: Khosha Chorchori
variations.description: The ultimate Bengali thrift dish, made entirely from vegetable peels and stalks, potato skins, pumpkin rind, ridge gourd peel and pea pods, that would otherwise be thrown away. Cooked down with mustard paste and nigella, it turns kitchen scraps into a deeply savoury, faintly bitter delicacy that regulars actively crave.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: its bold pungency gives the humble peels the depth they need to shine as a dish in their own right

steps: Chop 1 cup potato peels, 1 cup pumpkin peel, 1 cup ridge gourd peel and 1/2 cup tender pea pods into small, even pieces and rinse them well. Soak 1 tbsp mustard seeds for 15 minutes and grind with 2 green chillies to a smooth paste.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the heat, and crackle 1/2 tsp nigella seeds and 2 dried red chillies for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add all the chopped peels and pods with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 3/4 tsp salt, and saute on medium for 5 minutes until they wilt and begin to colour.
Cover and cook on low for 10 to 12 minutes, stirring now and then, until the peels turn completely soft and any moisture cooks off.
Stir in the mustard paste and 1 slit green chilli and cook uncovered on medium for 4 minutes, tossing, until the mixture is dry, dark and glossy.
Let it catch lightly on the base for a final minute, then serve while warm.
tips: Use only fresh, tender peels the same day you peel the vegetables; wilted or thick woody skins turn stringy.
Chop the peels small and even so they cook down uniformly into a cohesive dish.
A dry, well-cooked finish is essential here, since the peels taste raw and grassy if the moisture is not driven off.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a savoury first course with plain rice, in the Bengali way of starting a meal with something bitter or sharp.

variations.name: Sojne Data Chorchori
variations.description: A spring chorchori built around drumsticks, whose soft pulp you scrape at the table, cooked with potato and brinjal and a touch of jaggery for the sweet-savoury Bengali balance. Fried bori add crunch, and a mustard paste finish ties the whole rustic, seasonal dish together.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: fries the bori and cooks the drumsticks with the pungency this spring chorchori needs

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a whisper of unrefined jaggery gives the sweet-savoury lilt Bengalis love against the mustard

steps: Cut 3 drumsticks into 3 inch logs, and dice 2 potatoes and 1 brinjal into batons. Soak 1 tbsp mustard seeds for 15 minutes and grind with 2 green chillies to a smooth paste.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the heat, and fry the 10 bori for 1 minute until golden, then lift them out to stay crisp.
In the same oil crackle 1 tsp paanch phoron for 20 seconds, then add the drumstick, potato and brinjal with 3/4 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt and saute on medium for 5 minutes.
Cover and cook on low for 12 to 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the drumsticks are tender and the potatoes cooked through in their own steam.
Stir in the mustard paste, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 slit green chilli, and cook uncovered on medium for 4 minutes until the paste dries onto the vegetables.
Fold the fried bori back in for the last minute so they keep some crunch, then serve warm.
tips: Add the bori right at the end so they stay crisp rather than turning soggy in the moisture.
The pinch of jaggery is a balancing note against the sharp mustard, not a sweetener, so keep it restrained.
Leave the drumsticks in generous logs so there is enough soft pulp to scrape and enjoy at the table.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rice and a bowl of thin dal, encouraging everyone to scrape the drumstick pods with their fingers.

variations.name: Classic Aate Ka Halwa
variations.description: Aate ka halwa is the everyday North Indian pudding of whole-wheat flour slow-roasted in ghee until reddish-brown, then swelled with hot sweetened water into a glossy, deeply nutty mass. Fragrant with cardamom and studded with fried nuts, it is comfort food and prasad in equal measure.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: ancient whole-wheat flour that roasts to a deep nutty brown for a hearty halwa

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the atta to a glossy richness and gives the halwa its signature aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: dissolved into the hot water to sweeten the halwa with a clean, mild sweetness

steps: Heat 0.6 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai and fry 3 tbsp cashews and raisins over medium heat until golden and plump, about 2 minutes, then lift them out.
Add 1 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta to the ghee and roast over low heat, stirring without pause, for 12 to 15 minutes until it turns reddish-brown and smells deeply nutty.
While the atta roasts, boil 2.5 cups water with 0.75 cup Anveshan Khandsari until the sugar fully dissolves, then keep it hot.
Pour the hot sweetened water into the roasted atta very carefully, standing back from the fierce splutter, and stir hard to break every lump.
Cook on low heat for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring constantly, until the halwa thickens into a glossy mass that releases ghee at the edges.
Fold in 0.5 tsp cardamom and the fried nuts, then serve the halwa warm.
tips: The long, slow roast is everything; a pale, under-roasted atta leaves a raw, pasty taste in the finished halwa.
Always add the liquid hot and away from your face, as atta halwa splutters more violently than sooji.
If the halwa stiffens on standing, loosen it with a splash of hot milk and a knob of ghee before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm in bowls as a winter dessert or prasad, garnished with extra fried cashews and a drizzle of ghee.

variations.name: Gurudwara Kada Prasad
variations.description: Kada prasad is the sacred halwa of Sikh gurudwaras, made in equal measures of atta, ghee and jaggery water so it turns dense, dark and intensely aromatic. Cooked slow and blessed before serving, it is grounding, unctuous and traditionally offered in cupped hands.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: roasted low and slow to give the prasad its dense, temple-style body

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: used in equal measure to the atta for the rich, glistening kada prasad texture

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted into the water to sweeten the prasad with earthy caramel depth

steps: Melt 0.9 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 3 cups water over low heat, stir until dissolved, then strain out any grit and keep the syrup hot.
Heat 1 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy iron kadhai and add 1 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta once the ghee is hot.
Roast the atta over low heat, stirring continuously, for 12 to 15 minutes until it turns rich reddish-brown and smells strongly nutty.
Pour the hot jaggery water into the roasted atta in a slow stream, standing well back from the splutter, and stir hard to keep it lump-free.
Cook on low heat for 5 to 6 minutes, stirring without stopping, until the prasad thickens and ghee pools at the sides of the pan.
Stir in 0.5 tsp cardamom and serve the kada prasad warm, straight from the kadhai.
tips: Traditional kada prasad uses equal parts atta, ghee and sweetener, so resist the urge to cut the ghee.
Melting and straining the jaggery keeps the prasad smooth and free of the fine grit whole jaggery can carry.
Keep the flame low throughout; a high flame scorches the atta and turns the prasad bitter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a spiritual offering, ladled into cupped hands or small bowls, without any garnish in the traditional style.

variations.name: Kesar Badam Atta Halwa
variations.description: A celebration-grade atta halwa enriched with full-fat milk, ground almonds and bloomed saffron for a creamy, saffron-gold pudding. Softer and more fragrant than the water version, it is the halwa reserved for weddings and festive feasts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: roasted in ghee to a golden brown for a rich, milk-swelled festive halwa

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the atta and almond powder together for a luxurious, glossy finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: sweetens the warm milk while keeping the saffron colour bright and clear

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm milk to colour and perfume the rich halwa

steps: Soak 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp of warm milk taken from the 2.5 cups and set aside to bloom.
Heat 0.6 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan, fry 3 tbsp sliced almonds and pistachios to golden, about 2 minutes, and reserve.
Add 1 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.25 cup almond powder to the ghee and roast over low heat for 12 minutes until golden and nutty.
Warm the remaining milk with 0.75 cup Anveshan Khandsari until dissolved, then pour it into the roasted atta, stirring hard to avoid lumps.
Add the bloomed saffron milk and cook on low heat for 4 to 5 minutes until the halwa thickens and turns a rich gold.
Fold in the reserved nuts, mix until glossy, and serve the kesar badam halwa warm.
tips: Adding almond powder along with the atta deepens the nuttiness and gives the halwa a plush, rich body.
Bloom the saffron in warm milk first so its colour and aroma spread evenly through the pudding.
Keep the halwa slightly loose, as milk and almond powder thicken it further as it cools.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve this saffron atta halwa at weddings and festivals, garnished with slivered pistachios and a few saffron strands.

variations.name: Gond Panjiri Atta Halwa
variations.description: A warming winter halwa in which puffed edible gum and melon seeds are folded into jaggery-sweetened atta halwa, a tonic traditionally given to new mothers and eaten on cold mornings. The crackle of fried gond and the earthy jaggery make it heartier and more restorative than the plain version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: roasted deep and slow as the wholesome base for this winter tonic halwa

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the edible gum to a puff and roasts the atta for a rich, warming halwa

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted into milk to sweeten the halwa with warming, mineral-rich caramel notes

steps: Heat 0.7 cup Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai and fry 3 tbsp edible gum in batches over low heat until each piece puffs and turns white, then crush the puffs coarsely and set aside.
In the same ghee lightly roast 2 tbsp melon seeds and 3 tbsp chopped almonds until fragrant, about 1 minute, and reserve them.
Add 1 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta to the ghee and roast over low heat, stirring constantly, for 12 to 14 minutes until reddish-brown and nutty.
Warm 2 cups milk with 0.8 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder just until the jaggery melts, keeping it off a hard boil so it does not curdle, then strain.
Pour the warm jaggery milk into the roasted atta off the high flame, stirring hard, and cook on low heat for 4 to 5 minutes until thick and glossy.
Fold in the crushed gond, melon seeds, almonds and 0.5 tsp cardamom, then serve the panjiri halwa warm.
tips: Fry the gond on low heat and wait for each piece to puff fully; unpuffed gum stays hard and chewy in the halwa.
Add the jaggery milk off the boil, as pouring jaggery into fiercely boiling milk can split it.
This halwa keeps well for a week in the fridge and reheats beautifully with a spoon of ghee.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm on winter mornings as an energising tonic, topped with extra puffed gond and chopped almonds.

variations.name: Classic Aloo Halwa
variations.description: Aloo halwa is a surprising, silky pudding made from boiled and mashed potato cooked slow in ghee and milk until it turns glossy and fudgy. Naturally soft and neutral, the potato drinks up cardamom and nuts to become a rich, comforting sweet often made for fasting days.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: cooks the mashed potato until glossy and smooths away any starchy raw taste

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: sweetens the potato halwa cleanly to a soft, fudgy set

steps: Boil 3 to 4 medium potatoes until very soft, peel them warm, and mash to a completely smooth, lump-free 2 cups.
Heat 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan and fry 3 tbsp cashews and raisins to golden, about 2 minutes, then lift them out.
Add the mashed potato to the ghee and cook over low heat, stirring and pressing, for 8 to 10 minutes until it turns glossy and loses its raw starchy smell.
Pour in 1 cup milk and cook 5 minutes, stirring, until the potato absorbs it and thickens again.
Stir in 0.6 cup Anveshan Khandsari and cook 5 to 6 minutes until the sugar melts and the halwa pulls together into a soft, glossy mass.
Fold in 0.5 tsp cardamom and the fried nuts, then serve the aloo halwa warm.
tips: Mash the potatoes while warm and completely smooth, as cold potato turns gluey and leaves lumps in the halwa.
Cook the potato well in ghee before sweetening so no raw starch taste remains.
Keep the flame low after adding sugar, as the halwa thickens fast and can catch at the base.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm in bowls as a fasting-day or festive dessert, garnished with fried cashews and a pinch of cardamom.

variations.name: Kesar Khoya Aloo Halwa
variations.description: A festive, decadent version enriched with khoya and bloomed saffron, turning the humble potato into a saffron-gold, mithai-rich halwa. Denser and more aromatic than the classic, it is dressed with pistachios for the celebration table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: cooks the potato and carries the khoya for a rich, mithai-like halwa

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: sweetens the khoya-rich halwa while keeping the saffron colour bright

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm milk to give the halwa its saffron-gold colour and aroma

steps: Soak 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 0.5 cup warm milk and set aside to bloom.
Boil, peel and mash the potatoes to a smooth 2 cups while still warm.
Heat 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee and cook the mashed potato over low heat for 8 to 10 minutes until glossy and no longer raw-smelling.
Add the saffron milk and cook 4 minutes until absorbed, then stir in 0.75 cup grated khoya and cook 4 minutes until it melts in.
Stir in 0.6 cup Anveshan Khandsari and cook 5 to 6 minutes until the sugar melts and the halwa turns thick, glossy and rich gold.
Fold in 0.5 tsp cardamom and half the pistachios, then serve warm garnished with the rest.
tips: Cook the potato thoroughly in ghee before adding khoya so the halwa never tastes starchy.
Bloom the saffron in warm milk first for an even colour rather than orange streaks.
For a firmer, sliceable sweet, press the finished halwa into a greased tray and cut into squares once cool.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a festive mithai, topped with slivered pistachios and a whisper of edible silver leaf.

variations.name: Jaggery Coconut Aloo Halwa
variations.description: A rustic, dairy-light version that sweetens the mashed potato with jaggery and folds in toasted coconut for a chewy, caramel-toned halwa. Earthier and less milky than the classic, it leans on gud and coconut for its warmth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: cooks the potato and toasts the coconut for a nutty, caramel-scented halwa

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted in off the heat to sweeten the halwa with earthy caramel depth

steps: Boil, peel and mash the potatoes smooth to 2 cups while warm.
Heat 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai, fry 3 tbsp cashews to golden, then toast 0.5 cup grated coconut for 1 minute until fragrant and set both aside.
Add the mashed potato to the ghee and cook over low heat for 8 to 10 minutes until glossy and free of any raw smell.
Melt 0.6 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 0.5 cup water over low heat, strain out grit, then stir it into the potato off the boil.
Cook 5 to 6 minutes, stirring, until the halwa absorbs the syrup and thickens into a chewy, glossy mass.
Fold in the toasted coconut, cashews and 0.5 tsp cardamom, then serve the halwa warm.
tips: Add the jaggery syrup off the boil so it blends in smoothly without seizing the potato.
Toast the coconut only until fragrant; over-browning turns it bitter and muddies the halwa.
This halwa can be shaped into ladoos once cool enough to handle.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with an extra scatter of toasted coconut, or shape into ladoos for a rustic festive treat.

variations.name: Vrat Aloo Halwa with Makhana
variations.description: A fasting-day version that folds ghee-roasted makhana into the potato halwa for a light crunch, using ingredients allowed during Navratri vrat. The puffed lotus seeds and singhara-free simplicity make it a wholesome, energy-giving upvaas sweet.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the makhana crisp and cooks the potato for a light fasting halwa

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: sweetens the vrat halwa gently and is permitted on most fasting days

steps: Heat 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai and roast 1 cup makhana over low heat for 4 to 5 minutes until crisp, then crush half coarsely and keep the rest whole.
Boil, peel and mash the potatoes smooth to 2 cups while warm.
Add the mashed potato to the ghee and cook over low heat for 8 to 10 minutes until glossy and no longer raw.
Pour in 1 cup milk and cook 5 minutes, stirring, until absorbed and the potato thickens.
Stir in 0.5 cup Anveshan Khandsari and cook 5 minutes until the sugar melts and the halwa turns glossy and thick.
Fold in the crushed makhana, 3 tbsp chopped almonds and 0.5 tsp cardamom, then serve warm topped with the whole makhana.
tips: Roast the makhana until it snaps crisp, as under-roasted fox nuts turn chewy once folded into the halwa.
Add the crushed makhana at the very end so it keeps a little crunch against the soft potato.
Swap milk for water and khandsari for jaggery if your fast forbids dairy and refined sugar.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a Navratri upvaas dessert, topped with whole roasted makhana and chopped almonds.

variations.name: Classic Amritsari Chole
variations.description: The dark, tangy chole of Amritsar, where chickpeas are boiled with tea and whole spices, then folded into a deeply bhuna onion-tomato masala sharp with anardana and amchur. The gravy clings glossy and near-black to each chana, tangy and full-bodied, the definitive partner to a puffy Amritsari kulcha.

ingredients.name: White chickpeas (kabuli chana)
ingredients.note: soaked overnight

ingredients.name: Black tea
ingredients.note: tied in a muslin bundle

ingredients.name: Black cardamom
ingredients.note: added to the cooking water

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee gives the dark gravy its glossy richness and rounds the sharp spices

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: pureed

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup soaked chickpeas with 1/2 tsp salt, 3 cups water, 1 tbsp tea in a muslin bundle and 1 black cardamom for 6-7 whistles until soft; discard the bundle and cardamom and reserve the dark liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add the chopped onions and fry for 9-10 minutes until genuinely deep brown for a dark gravy.
Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 2 slit green chillies for a minute, then pour in the tomato puree and cook for 7-8 minutes until the ghee separates.
Lower the heat and add 2 tbsp chole masala, 1 tbsp anardana powder, 1 tsp amchur and 1 tsp red chilli powder, roasting for a minute until dark and fragrant.
Tip in the cooked chickpeas with 2 cups of the reserved liquid and the remaining 3/4 tsp salt, then simmer for 15-18 minutes, mashing a spoonful of chana to thicken the gravy naturally.
Cook until the gravy turns glossy and clings to the chana rather than running thin.
Garnish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander and rest 5 minutes before serving so the flavour deepens.
tips: Frying the onions to a true deep brown, not just golden, is the single biggest factor in the authentic dark colour.
Anardana is what gives Amritsari chole its signature tang; add it with the dry spices so it toasts and blooms.
Chole always taste better after resting, so make them an hour ahead if you can and reheat with a splash of hot water.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot with Amritsari kulcha or bhatura, sliced onion rings, a green chilli and a wedge of lemon.

variations.name: Chole Bhature Halwai-Style
variations.description: The plush, slightly sweet-edged chole that halwai shops pair with pillowy bhature, built on a base of boiled potato and a whole-spice bouquet garni for body. Softer and more rounded than the sharp Amritsari version, it is thick, mildly spiced and made to be scooped up with fried bread.

ingredients.name: White chickpeas (kabuli chana)
ingredients.note: soaked overnight

ingredients.name: Potato
ingredients.note: boiled and mashed, for body

ingredients.name: Black tea
ingredients.note: tied in a muslin bundle

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee gives the halwai-style chole their soft, glossy richness

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: pureed

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a whisper of jaggery gives the halwai-style gravy its gently rounded edge without refined sugar

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup soaked chickpeas with 1/2 tsp salt, 3 cups water and 1 tbsp tea in a muslin bundle for 6-7 whistles until very soft; discard the bundle and reserve the liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat, add 1 bay leaf, 1 inch cinnamon and 3 cloves for 30 seconds, then add the chopped onions and fry for 7-8 minutes until golden brown.
Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for a minute, then the tomato puree with 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, and cook for 7 minutes until the ghee separates and the masala turns a warm red.
Stir in 1.5 tbsp chole masala for a minute, then add the cooked chickpeas with 2 cups reserved liquid and the mashed boiled potato to thicken the base.
Simmer on low heat for 15 minutes, mashing gently, until the gravy turns thick, soft and clingy.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and the remaining 3/4 tsp salt, and cook another 3 minutes so the flavours round out.
Rest 5 minutes and serve hot, the chole thick enough to sit on a bhatura.
tips: The mashed potato is the halwai trick for a thick, velvety gravy without cream, so do not skip it.
Keep the spicing gentler than Amritsari chole; this version leans soft and rounded rather than sharply tangy.
Make the chole thicker than you think, as they loosen slightly once ladled beside hot bhature.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with freshly fried bhature, a side of pickled carrots and onions, and a wedge of lemon.

variations.name: Palak Chole
variations.description: A wholesome green take where the chickpeas simmer in a spinach-laced gravy, giving the dish a fresh, slightly mineral edge and a lovely emerald colour. Lighter and less tangy than street chole, it folds a vegetable into the protein for a balanced, everyday meal.

ingredients.name: White chickpeas (kabuli chana)
ingredients.note: soaked overnight

ingredients.name: Spinach (palak)
ingredients.note: blanched and pureed

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee keeps the spinach gravy silky and rounds its mineral edge

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Kasuri methi (dried fenugreek)
ingredients.note: crushed

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup soaked chickpeas with 1/2 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 whistles until soft, and reserve the liquid.
Blanch 300 g spinach in boiling water for 2 minutes, refresh in cold water to keep the colour bright, then blend to a smooth puree.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add the chopped onion and chopped green chillies and fry for 5 minutes until golden.
Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for a minute, then the chopped tomatoes with 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1/2 tsp turmeric, and cook for 5-6 minutes until pulpy and the ghee separates.
Add the cooked chickpeas with 1 cup reserved liquid and the remaining 3/4 tsp salt, and simmer for 8 minutes so they absorb the masala.
Lower the heat and stir in the spinach puree, cooking gently for 5 minutes so it stays green and does not lose its freshness to high heat.
Finish with 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi and 1/2 tsp garam masala, and serve warm.
tips: Blanch and shock the spinach so the gravy keeps its bright green colour rather than turning dull olive.
Add the spinach puree towards the end and keep the heat low, as long boiling dulls both the colour and taste.
A spoon of fresh cream or curd can be swirled in for a richer palak chole if you like.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jeera rice or tandoori roti, topped with a swirl of ghee and a few ginger juliennes.

variations.name: Restaurant-Style Creamy Chole
variations.description: A rich, mild hotel-buffet version where the chickpeas rest in a smooth cashew-and-tomato gravy finished with cream and kasuri methi. Far gentler and more luxurious than the sharp street chole, it is silky, lightly spiced and made to please every palate at the table.

ingredients.name: White chickpeas (kabuli chana)
ingredients.note: soaked overnight

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee builds the luxurious base and gives the creamy gravy its restaurant sheen

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup soaked chickpeas with 1/2 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 whistles until soft, and reserve the cooking liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add the chopped onions and saute for 6 minutes until soft and pale golden, keeping them light.
Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for a minute, then the chopped tomatoes and 12 cashews, and cook covered for 8 minutes until pulpy; cool and blend to a very smooth puree.
Return the puree to low heat, add 1 tbsp coriander powder, 3/4 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1/2 tsp turmeric, and cook for 4 minutes until the ghee floats on top.
Add the cooked chickpeas with 1.5 cups reserved liquid and the remaining 3/4 tsp salt, and simmer gently for 12 minutes until the gravy is thick and velvety.
Lower the heat, stir in 3 tbsp cream, 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi and 1 tsp garam masala, and warm through for 2 minutes without boiling.
Serve with an extra swirl of cream on top.
tips: Keep the onions pale, not brown, so the gravy stays the light golden colour of a restaurant chana.
Blend the tomato-cashew base really smooth for that signature silky texture.
Add the cream on low heat and do not boil after, or the gravy can split and lose its sheen.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or jeera rice, swirled with extra cream and a scatter of coriander.

variations.name: Classic Badam Halwa
variations.description: Badam halwa is a luxurious almond pudding made by grinding soaked almonds to a smooth paste and cooking it slow in ghee and milk until it turns glossy and pulls off the pan. Rich, nutty and cardamom-scented, it is a festival and wedding sweet that tastes of pure almond.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: cooked into the almond paste in stages so the halwa turns glossy and non-sticky

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: sweetens the almond paste to a soft, spoonable halwa without overpowering the nuts

steps: Soak 1.5 cups almonds in hot water for 20 minutes, slip off the skins, and grind them with 1 cup milk to a smooth, fine paste.
Heat 2 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee in a heavy nonstick pan and pour in the almond paste, stirring over low heat for 8 to 10 minutes until it thickens and loses its raw smell.
Add 0.6 cup Anveshan Khandsari and keep stirring; the mixture will loosen as the sugar melts, then start to thicken again over 5 minutes.
Drizzle in the remaining ghee a spoon at a time, stirring after each addition, until the halwa turns glossy and absorbs the fat.
Cook a further 4 to 5 minutes until the halwa comes together into a soft mass that leaves the sides of the pan.
Stir in 0.5 tsp cardamom, garnish with sliced almonds, and serve the badam halwa warm.
tips: Grind the almonds slightly coarse rather than to a butter, so the halwa keeps a pleasant grainy bite.
Add the ghee gradually; dumping it in at once makes the halwa greasy and stops it binding.
Cook on low heat throughout, as almond paste scorches quickly and turns the halwa bitter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm in small bowls as a festive dessert, garnished with sliced almonds and a light dusting of cardamom.

variations.name: Kesar Malai Badam Halwa
variations.description: A regal wedding halwa where saffron and fresh cream turn the almond paste into a deep saffron-gold, melt-in-the-mouth pudding. Creamier and more fragrant than the classic, it is the badam halwa served on silver at grand celebrations.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: cooked into the almond paste in stages for a rich, glossy saffron halwa

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: sweetens the halwa while keeping the saffron colour clear and radiant

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm milk to give the halwa its saffron-gold colour and heady aroma

steps: Soak 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp of warm milk taken from the 1 cup and set aside to bloom.
Soak 1.5 cups almonds in hot water for 20 minutes, peel, and grind with the remaining milk to a smooth paste.
Heat 2 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee, add the almond paste, and stir over low heat for 8 minutes until thick and no longer raw.
Stir in 0.6 cup Anveshan Khandsari and the bloomed saffron milk, cooking 5 minutes as the mixture loosens and then thickens to a rich gold.
Add the remaining ghee spoon by spoon, then fold in 0.25 cup fresh cream off the boil and cook gently for 3 to 4 minutes until glossy.
Garnish with sliced pistachios and serve the kesar malai badam halwa warm.
tips: Fold the cream in off the heat and warm gently so it enriches the halwa without curdling.
Bloom the saffron first so its colour disperses evenly instead of streaking the halwa.
This halwa firms as it cools, so keep it a touch looser than you want the final texture to be.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm at weddings and festivals, spread in a shallow dish and topped with pistachios and a few saffron strands.

variations.name: Jaggery Badam Halwa
variations.description: A dairy-free, wholesome take that sweetens the almond paste with jaggery and cooks it in water for a darker, caramel-toned halwa with a whisper of nutmeg. Earthier and less rich than the milk version, it suits those avoiding refined sugar and dairy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: cooked into the almond paste in stages for a glossy, jaggery-sweetened halwa

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted and strained to sweeten the halwa with deep, earthy caramel notes

steps: Soak 1.5 cups almonds in hot water for 20 minutes, slip off the skins, and grind with 0.5 cup water to a smooth paste.
Melt 0.6 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder in the remaining 0.5 cup water over low heat, then strain out any grit and keep aside.
Heat 2 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan, fry 2 tbsp cashews to golden, and reserve them.
Add the almond paste to the ghee and stir over low heat for 8 to 10 minutes until thick and no longer raw-smelling.
Pour in the strained jaggery syrup off the boil and cook 6 to 7 minutes, adding the rest of the ghee gradually, until the halwa turns glossy and leaves the pan.
Stir in 0.25 tsp nutmeg, 0.5 tsp cardamom and the fried cashews, then serve the jaggery badam halwa warm.
tips: Add the jaggery syrup off the boil, as very hot jaggery can make the almond paste seize and turn grainy.
Strain the melted jaggery well to keep the halwa smooth and free of sediment.
Nutmeg and jaggery are natural partners here, but use nutmeg sparingly as it turns bitter in excess.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a wholesome dessert or festive prasad, garnished with fried cashews and a pinch of nutmeg.

variations.name: Khoya Badam Halwa
variations.description: The sweet-shop version folds crumbled khoya into the almond paste for a denser, fudgier halwa that can be set and sliced like burfi. Richer and grainier than the pudding style, it is the badam halwa sold by weight at festive mithai counters.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: binds the almond and khoya into a dense, sliceable sweet-shop halwa

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: sweetens the khoya-rich halwa to a firm, mithai-like set

steps: Soak 1.5 cups almonds in hot water for 20 minutes, peel, and grind with 0.5 cup warm milk to a smooth paste.
Heat 2 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan, add the almond paste, and stir over low heat for 8 minutes until thick and no longer raw.
Crumble in 0.75 cup grated khoya and cook 4 to 5 minutes, stirring, until it melts into the almond paste.
Add 0.5 cup Anveshan Khandsari and the remaining ghee, stirring for 5 to 6 minutes until the sugar melts and the halwa pulls together into a dense mass.
Stir in 0.5 tsp cardamom, then spread the halwa in a greased tray and smooth the top to an even slab.
Press 2 sheets of silver leaf over the surface, cool for 15 minutes, and cut into squares or serve warm by the spoon.
tips: Roast the khoya briefly before adding sugar if it smells milky-raw, for a deeper halwai flavour.
For clean burfi-style slices, let the slab cool fully before cutting; warm halwa tears rather than cuts.
Fresh, soft khoya melts smoothly, while dry khoya leaves grains, so grate it fine and add a splash of milk if stiff.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature as a rich gifting mithai, the silver-topped squares arranged in a decorative box.

variations.name: Classic Besan Halwa
variations.description: Besan halwa is a deeply aromatic pudding of gram flour roasted slow in ghee until it turns golden and releases its toasty, nutty scent, then sweetened with hot syrup. Grainy, rich and cardamom-scented, it is a quick North Indian comfort sweet and prasad.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the besan low and slow until golden and gives the halwa its glossy richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: dissolved into hot water to sweeten the roasted besan cleanly

steps: Heat 0.6 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai over low heat and stir in 1 cup besan.
Roast the besan patiently, stirring without pause, for 12 to 15 minutes until it turns golden, loosens in the ghee and smells toasty and nutty.
While it roasts, boil 2 cups water with 0.6 cup Anveshan Khandsari until the sugar dissolves, then keep it hot.
Pour the hot syrup into the roasted besan very carefully, standing back from the splutter, and stir hard to break every lump.
Cook on low heat for 3 to 4 minutes, stirring constantly, until the halwa thickens into a glossy mass that leaves the pan.
Mix in 0.5 tsp cardamom and 3 tbsp chopped almonds, then serve the besan halwa warm.
tips: Besan can catch and clump early in roasting, so keep the flame low and the spatula moving throughout.
The halwa is ready when the besan smells nutty and the ghee separates; a raw, pale mix tastes bitter and floury.
Add the syrup hot and away from your face, as besan halwa splutters fiercely when the liquid hits.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm in bowls as a winter dessert or prasad, garnished with chopped almonds and a pinch of cardamom.

variations.name: Gujarati Mohanthal
variations.description: Mohanthal is the Gujarati festive version, made with coarse besan bound by khoya and set into fudgy, grainy squares rather than a soft halwa. Saffron and a milk-ghee moistening give it the characteristic sandy texture and rich, temple-sweet flavour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: moistens the besan into grains and roasts it to a golden, sandy mohanthal texture

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: cooked to a one-string syrup that sets the mohanthal into firm, fudgy squares

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk to give the mohanthal its golden hue and festive aroma

steps: Rub 1.5 cups coarse besan with 3 tbsp melted ghee and 3 tbsp warm milk into which 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron has been steeped, then rest 15 minutes and pass through a coarse sieve to form grains.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai and roast the besan grains over low heat for 12 to 14 minutes until golden and sandy-smelling.
Stir in 0.5 cup grated khoya and roast a further 3 minutes until it blends in and the mixture smells rich, then take off the heat.
In a separate pan boil 0.75 cup Anveshan Khandsari with 0.3 cup water to a sticky one-string syrup, about 4 to 5 minutes.
Pour the syrup into the warm besan, add 0.5 tsp cardamom, and stir quickly until it thickens and just holds together.
Spread into a greased tray, press sliced pistachios and almonds over the top, cool 30 minutes, and cut into diamonds.
tips: The ghee-and-milk rub before roasting is what creates mohanthal's signature grainy, sandy texture, so do not skip it.
Judge the one-string syrup carefully; too thin and the mohanthal will not set, too thick and it turns hard and dry.
Cut while just warm and firm, not cold and brittle, for clean-edged diamonds.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the set diamonds at room temperature during Diwali and weddings, arranged in a mithai box lined with nuts.

variations.name: Jaggery Gond Besan Halwa
variations.description: A warming winter tonic version where fried edible gum is folded into jaggery-sweetened besan halwa, traditionally eaten for strength in the cold months. The crackle of puffed gond and the earthy jaggery make it heartier and more restorative than the everyday halwa.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the edible gum to a puff and roasts the besan for a rich winter halwa

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted into water and strained to sweeten the halwa with warming caramel notes

steps: Heat 0.7 cup Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai and fry 3 tbsp edible gum in batches over low heat until each piece puffs up and turns white, then crush the puffs coarsely and set aside.
Add 1 cup besan to the same ghee and roast over low heat, stirring constantly, for 12 to 14 minutes until golden and nutty.
Meanwhile melt 0.7 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 1.75 cups water over low heat and strain out any grit.
Pour the hot jaggery water into the roasted besan off the boil, stirring hard to break lumps, and cook 3 to 4 minutes until thick and glossy.
Fold in the crushed gond, 3 tbsp chopped almonds, 0.25 tsp dry ginger powder and 0.5 tsp cardamom.
Stir over low heat for 1 more minute so the flavours meld, then serve the winter halwa warm.
tips: Fry the gond gently and wait for each piece to puff fully, or it stays hard and stony in the halwa.
Dry ginger adds warmth and aids digestion, which is why it belongs in this cold-weather tonic.
This halwa keeps for a week refrigerated and can be rolled into ladoos once cool.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm on winter mornings as an energising sweet, topped with extra puffed gond and chopped almonds.

variations.name: Besan Coconut Milk Halwa
variations.description: A South Indian style besan halwa simmered with coconut milk instead of water, giving a softer, more tropical pudding with a gentle coconut sweetness. Finished with toasted coconut and cashews, it is silkier and more fragrant than the plain roasted version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the besan and toasts the coconut for a fragrant South Indian halwa

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: dissolved into the coconut milk to sweeten the halwa without hiding the coconut

steps: Heat 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai, fry 3 tbsp cashews to golden, then toast 0.25 cup grated coconut for 1 minute until fragrant and set both aside.
Add 1 cup besan to the ghee and roast over low heat, stirring constantly, for 12 minutes until golden and nutty.
Warm 1.75 cups coconut milk with 0.6 cup Anveshan Khandsari until the sugar dissolves, keeping it just below a boil.
Pour the warm sweet coconut milk into the roasted besan off the high flame, stirring hard to keep it lump-free.
Cook on low heat for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring, until the halwa thickens into a soft, glossy mass and the coconut milk is absorbed.
Fold in the toasted coconut, cashews and 0.5 tsp cardamom, then serve the halwa warm.
tips: Add the coconut milk warm, not boiling, and keep the heat low so it does not split into the halwa.
This halwa stays softer than the water version, so cook just until it leaves the pan for a spoonable texture.
Use thick, first-press coconut milk for the richest flavour, thinning it slightly with water if too heavy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm after a South Indian meal, garnished with toasted coconut and cashews for a tropical finish.

variations.name: Classic Rajasthani Churma Ladoo
variations.description: The traditional Rajasthani churma ladoo, where firm wheat dough dumplings are deep-fried, cooled, ground coarse and then bound with ghee and jaggery. The double process of frying and grinding gives a uniquely coarse, sandy crumb unlike any other ladoo. Fragrant with cardamom and clove, it is the sweet that crowns a Marwari dal-baati feast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: coarse-milled khapli fries into the crumbly muthia churma needs

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: used to bind the ground churma and for deep-frying the dumplings

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the classic Rajasthani sweetener, giving churma its dark caramel note

steps: Mix 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with the semolina and 3 tbsp warm Anveshan Bilona Ghee, then knead with just enough water to make a very stiff, tight dough and rest it for 15 minutes.
Shape the dough into small thick discs (muthia) and deep-fry them in ghee on low heat for 10-12 minutes until deeply golden and cooked through to the centre.
Cool the fried muthia completely, break them up, and grind to a coarse sandy powder in batches, sieving out any large bits and re-grinding them.
Warm 3 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee and toast the chopped almonds for 2 minutes, then mix them into the ground churma.
While the churma is still warm, add 1.25 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder, the remaining melted ghee, 1 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp clove powder, mixing until it clumps when pressed.
Press into 12 firm round ladoos while warm, working the mixture hard so they hold, and rest for 30 minutes to set.
tips: Fry the muthia on low heat so they cook through; high heat browns the outside while leaving the centre raw and doughy.
Grind the churma coarse, not fine, as the sandy texture is the signature of a proper churma ladoo.
If the ladoos won't bind, warm the mixture and add a spoon more melted ghee rather than extra jaggery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these alongside dal and baati with a puddle of extra ghee, the classic Rajasthani thali finish.

variations.name: Baked Baati Churma Ladoo
variations.description: This version crushes traditional oven-baked baati instead of deep-fried muthia, giving a smokier, less oily churma with a rustic bite. Baking the dough balls until they crack and turn nutty is the old kitchen method before frying became common. The result is lighter on the stomach yet deeply flavoured.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: bakes into firm baati that crush to a smoky churma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: worked into the dough as moyan and drizzled over the baked baati

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: binds the crushed baati into ladoos with a mellow sweetness

steps: Combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with the semolina and 4 tbsp warm Anveshan Bilona Ghee, then knead with the milk into a stiff dough and rest for 15 minutes.
Shape into 8 tight balls, press a dimple in each, and bake at 180C for 30-35 minutes, turning once, until they crack open and turn deep golden.
Cool the baati fully, break them apart, and grind to a coarse churma, discarding no crumbs.
Warm 4 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee, toast the chopped pistachios for 1 minute, and mix them into the ground churma.
While warm, add 1.25 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder, the remaining melted ghee, 1 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp nutmeg, mixing until the churma holds together.
Press into 12 firm ladoos while warm and let them rest for 30 minutes before serving.
tips: Bake the baati until they visibly crack; that is the sign the inside is cooked through and will grind cleanly.
A drizzle of warm ghee over the hot baati before grinding deepens the flavour and helps binding.
This baked churma is lighter than the fried kind but keeps for fewer days, so eat within a week.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a small bowl of extra melted ghee for drizzling, echoing the traditional dal-baati-churma spread.

variations.name: Besan Churma Ladoo
variations.description: A smoother, quicker churma ladoo that builds the crumb from thick fried besan pearls rather than wheat dumplings, giving a finer texture and a nuttier flavour. The gram-flour base means no kneading or long frying of dough, just a batter dropped and fried. It sits somewhere between churma and besan ladoo.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: binds the ground besan churma and lends its mithai aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: gives the besan churma a rustic caramel depth

steps: Rub 2.5 cups besan with 3 tbsp warm Anveshan Bilona Ghee and the milk to form a stiff, crumbly dough, then press it through a slotted spoon into hot ghee.
Deep-fry the besan pearls on low-medium heat for 4-5 minutes until golden and cooked through, then drain well.
Cool the fried besan completely and grind to a coarse churma, re-grinding any larger clusters.
Warm 3 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee and toast the chopped cashews and melon seeds for 2 minutes, then fold them into the churma.
While warm, mix in 1.25 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder, the remaining melted ghee and 1 tsp cardamom until the mixture binds when pressed.
Shape into 12 firm ladoos while warm and rest them for 40 minutes so the besan sets fully.
tips: Fry the besan pearls on gentle heat so the insides cook; rushing leaves a raw gram taste in the churma.
Grind while fully cool, as warm besan turns pasty in the grinder instead of powdery.
Keep the flame low; besan burns quickly and even slight scorching turns the churma bitter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Offer these finer-textured ladoos at teatime or as a Diwali box filler alongside dry mithai.

variations.name: Dry-Fruit Churma Ladoo
variations.description: A wedding-grade churma ladoo loaded with ground almonds, cashews and pistachios so nearly half the ball is nuts, making it richer and more festive than the everyday kind. The dry fruit is both mixed in and dusted on for a luxurious finish. This is the churma ladoo made for special occasions and gifting.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: fried into muthia that grind to the churma base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: binds the nut-heavy churma and fries the muthia

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: less is needed here since the dry fruits add richness

steps: Knead 1.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 3 tbsp warm Anveshan Bilona Ghee and a little water into a stiff dough, shape into thick discs, and deep-fry on low heat for 10-12 minutes until golden through.
Cool the muthia fully and grind to a coarse churma.
Coarsely grind half the almonds, cashews and pistachios and chop the rest, keeping a spoon of chopped nuts aside for garnish.
Warm the remaining Anveshan Bilona Ghee, crush the saffron into it, and stir in both the ground and chopped nuts for 1 minute until fragrant.
Mix the nutty ghee into the churma with 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp cardamom while warm, pressing until it binds.
Shape into 12 firm ladoos, roll their tops in the reserved chopped nuts, and rest for 30 minutes to set.
tips: Grind only half the nuts and chop the rest, so you get both a rich base and a satisfying crunch.
Because of the high nut content, less jaggery is needed; taste as you go so it doesn't turn cloying.
These keep well for two weeks and make an impressive homemade gift when boxed with a nut garnish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Present these nut-crusted ladoos in a decorated mithai box for weddings and festivals, each topped with a sliver of pistachio.

variations.name: Classic White Coconut Chutney
variations.description: The snow-white coconut chutney that comes with every plate of idli and dosa across South India. Fresh coconut is ground with roasted chana dal and green chilli into a smooth, mild paste, then crowned with a coconut-oil tempering of mustard seeds and curry leaves. Simple, cooling and endlessly comforting.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: The authentic tempering fat that carries the mustard and curry-leaf aroma into a coconut chutney

steps: Grind 1 cup grated coconut, 3 tbsp roasted chana dal, 2 green chillies, 0.5 inch ginger and 0.75 tsp salt with 0.5 cups water to a smooth, thick chutney.
Transfer to a bowl and adjust with a little more water until it reaches a soft dropping consistency.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan on medium flame until it shimmers.
Add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them splutter for 20 seconds, then add 1 tsp urad dal and 1 broken red chilli and fry until the dal is golden.
Drop in 10 curry leaves, let them crackle for 5 seconds, and pour the hot tempering over the chutney.
Fold the tempering in lightly just before serving so it stays aromatic.
tips: Roasted chana dal is what keeps the chutney thick and prevents it from turning watery.
Grind with cold water so the coconut does not heat up and taste flat.
It thickens as it sits, so keep a little water aside to loosen it before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot idlis, crisp dosas or medu vada, with a bowl of sambar alongside.

variations.name: Red Coconut Chutney
variations.description: A fiery Tamil kara chutney where coconut meets a paste of dry red chillies, garlic and tamarind for a rust-red, punchy dip. Sesame oil in the tempering deepens its earthy heat, a world apart from the mild white version. This is the bolder chutney served with ghee-roast dosa and pongal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil deepens the earthy heat of the red chillies in true Tamil style

steps: Heat 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pan and saute 5 red chillies, 4 garlic cloves and 4 shallots for 3 minutes until softened and fragrant.
Cool the mixture, then grind it with 1 cup grated coconut, 1.5 tsp tamarind and 0.75 tsp salt and 0.5 cups water to a smooth rust-red chutney.
Transfer to a bowl and loosen with a splash of water if it is too stiff.
Heat the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a small pan until it shimmers.
Add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop for 20 seconds, then toss in 10 curry leaves and let them crackle.
Pour the tempering over the chutney and stir it through just before serving.
tips: Sauteing the chillies and garlic before grinding rounds off the raw heat into a deeper flavour.
Use Kashmiri red chillies if you want the colour without overwhelming heat.
Shallots melt into the chutney better than large onions and give a sweeter background.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with ghee-roast dosa, ven pongal or upma, where its heat cuts through the richness.

variations.name: Coconut-Coriander Green Chutney
variations.description: A herby green coconut chutney popular in Karnataka and Kerala, where coconut is ground with a generous handful of coriander and mint for a fresh, fragrant twist. Milder than the red version and greener than the classic white, it brings a cooling herb note to the plate. A groundnut-oil tempering keeps it light and aromatic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A light wood-pressed oil that keeps the herb-forward chutney fresh without weighing it down

steps: Grind 1 cup grated coconut, 0.5 cups coriander, 0.25 cups mint, 3 green chillies, 2 tbsp roasted chana dal, 1 tsp lemon juice and 0.75 tsp salt with 0.5 cups water to a smooth green chutney.
Transfer to a bowl and thin with a little water to a soft, spoonable consistency.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a small pan on medium flame until it shimmers.
Add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them splutter for 20 seconds until they stop popping.
Toss in 10 curry leaves, let them crisp for 5 seconds, and pour the tempering over the chutney.
Stir gently and serve, ideally within an hour while the herbs are bright.
tips: Add the mint sparingly; too much overpowers the coconut and turns the chutney bitter.
A squeeze of lemon keeps the green colour vivid and lifts the coconut.
Serve fresh, as the herbs darken faster than in a plain coconut chutney.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with rava dosa, uttapam or as a fresh dip for hot onion bhajji.

variations.name: Peanut-Coconut Chutney
variations.description: An Andhra-style chutney where roasted peanuts join the coconut for a thicker, richer, nuttier dip. Garlic and tamarind give it depth, and the peanuts add a satisfying heft that plain coconut chutney lacks. A sesame-oil tempering ties the flavours together for a chutney that eats almost like a meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil in the tempering echoes the roasted peanuts and rounds out the chutney

steps: Grind 0.5 cups roasted peanuts, 0.75 cups grated coconut, 3 green chillies, 3 garlic cloves, 1 tsp tamarind and 0.75 tsp salt with 0.6 cups water to a thick, creamy chutney.
Transfer to a bowl and loosen with a little water, keeping it thicker than a plain coconut chutney.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a small pan on medium flame until it shimmers.
Add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin and let them splutter for 20 seconds.
Toss in 10 curry leaves, let them crackle, and pour the sizzling tempering over the chutney.
Stir it through and rest 5 minutes so the garlic mellows into the nuts before serving.
tips: Grind the peanuts first with a little water so they break down smoothly before adding the coconut.
Keep the chutney thick; the peanuts are meant to give it a rich, dip-like body.
Roast raw peanuts fresh and rub off the skins for the cleanest, sweetest flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with pesarattu, upma or dosa, or as a hearty spread beside steamed rice and ghee.

variations.name: Classic Coriander Chutney
variations.description: The everyday green chutney of North Indian kitchens, ground fresh from coriander with green chilli, ginger and a squeeze of lemon. A spoon of sattu gives it just enough body to cling to a samosa or pakora without any oil. Bright, zingy and ready in five minutes, it is the workhorse dip of the tea-time table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Roasted-gram sattu replaces the usual chana dal, thickening the chutney and rounding its raw edge

steps: Rinse and roughly chop 2 cups coriander, leaving the tender stems on, and add them to a blender jar.
Add 2 green chillies, 1 inch ginger, 2 garlic cloves, 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder and 0.75 tsp salt.
Spoon in 2 tbsp Anveshan Sattu, which thickens the chutney and softens the sharpness of the raw greens.
Pour in 1 tbsp lemon juice and 3 tbsp cold water, then grind to a smooth, thick paste, scraping the sides once.
Add another tablespoon of cold water only if needed to keep the blades turning, taking care not to thin it too much.
Taste and adjust salt and lemon, then transfer to a bowl and serve fresh.
tips: Use ice-cold water while grinding to keep the chutney a vivid green instead of dull khaki.
The sattu lets you skip oil while still giving the chutney enough body to coat a fritter.
Grind in short pulses; over-blending heats the leaves and turns the colour brown.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a dip with hot samosas and pakoras, or thin it with a little water to drizzle over chaat.

variations.name: South Indian Coriander-Coconut Chutney
variations.description: A Tamil-style kothamalli chutney where coriander is ground with fresh coconut and roasted chana dal, then finished with a coconut-oil tempering. The coconut mellows the herb into something creamy and mild, and a little tamarind keeps it lively. It is the classic green partner to idli and dosa.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: The South Indian tempering fat that fries the mustard and dal and lifts the coconut's sweetness

steps: Grind 1.5 cups coriander, 0.5 cups grated coconut, 2 tbsp roasted chana dal, 3 green chillies, 1 tsp tamarind and 0.75 tsp salt with 0.5 cups water to a smooth chutney.
Pour the chutney into a serving bowl and loosen with a splash more water if it is too thick to pour.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan on medium flame until it shimmers.
Add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them splutter for 20 seconds, then add 1 tsp urad dal and fry until golden.
Drop in 10 curry leaves, let them crackle for 5 seconds, and pour the hot tempering over the chutney.
Fold the tempering through just before serving so the aroma stays bright.
tips: Roasted chana dal both thickens the chutney and gives it a gentle nutty flavour, so do not skip it.
Add tamarind a little at a time; too much overpowers the delicate coconut and coriander.
This chutney thickens as it sits, so keep a little warm water aside to loosen it before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside crisp dosas and a bowl of sambar, or with steamed idlis for a classic Tamil breakfast.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Coriander-Peanut Chutney
variations.description: A robust, rustic chutney from Maharashtra that grinds coriander with roasted peanuts and plenty of garlic for a thick, nutty spread. Groundnut oil in the tempering echoes the peanuts and gives it a warm depth. Coarser and more filling than a plain green chutney, it doubles as a sandwich spread.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A wood-pressed groundnut oil whose flavour mirrors the roasted peanuts in the chutney

steps: Dry-grind 0.5 cups roasted peanuts to a coarse powder, then add 1.5 cups coriander, 5 garlic cloves, 2 green chillies, 1 tbsp lemon juice, 0.5 tsp sugar and 0.75 tsp salt.
Add about 0.25 cups water and grind to a thick, coarse chutney with visible flecks of peanut.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a small pan on medium flame until it shimmers.
Crackle 0.5 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds until fragrant, then turn off the heat.
Pour the hot cumin oil over the ground chutney and stir it through for a glossy finish.
Rest 5 minutes so the garlic mellows into the peanuts before serving.
tips: Keep the grind coarse; the crunch of roasted peanut is the whole character of this chutney.
A pinch of sugar softens the sharp raw garlic without making the chutney sweet.
Thicken with an extra spoon of peanut powder if you want to use it as a sandwich spread.
variations.servingSuggestion: Slather on bread for a Mumbai-style green sandwich, or serve as a nutty dip with thalipeeth and hot tea.

variations.name: Creamy Coriander-Curd Chutney
variations.description: The cool, pale-green chutney served with tandoori platters at Indian restaurants, where hung curd smooths the coriander into a rich dip. Black salt and roasted cumin give it a chaat-like tang, and a touch of honey rounds the edges. Thicker and creamier than a watery green chutney, it clings beautifully to grilled starters.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: A teaspoon of raw honey balances the tang of the curd without the flat sweetness of sugar

steps: Grind 1.5 cups coriander with 2 green chillies, 0.5 inch ginger and 1 tsp lemon juice to a smooth thick paste, using no more than a spoon of water.
Whisk 0.75 cups hung curd in a bowl until it is completely smooth and lump-free.
Fold the ground coriander paste into the curd until the mixture turns an even pale green.
Stir in 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp black salt and 0.5 tsp regular salt.
Drizzle in 1 tsp Anveshan Honey and mix well, then taste and adjust the salt and tang.
Chill for 15 minutes before serving so it thickens and the flavours settle.
tips: Use thick hung curd, not runny yogurt, or the chutney will not hold its creamy body.
Add the coriander paste to the curd rather than blending them together, which keeps the curd from splitting.
Make it a couple of hours ahead and refrigerate; the flavour deepens as it rests.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled as a dip for paneer tikka, seekh kebabs and hara-bhara kebab, or spread inside a kathi roll.

variations.name: Classic Dry Fruit Chikki
variations.description: Classic Dry Fruit Chikki is a luxurious brittle packed with almonds, cashews and pistachios bound in hard-crack jaggery. Loaded with whole and slivered nuts, it snaps into rich, satisfying shards that are equal parts sweet and nourishing.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: cooked to hard-crack, it binds the whole nuts into a firm snappable brittle

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the slab and lightly toasts the nuts for extra aroma

steps: Coarsely chop 0.5 cup almonds, 0.5 cup cashews and 0.25 cup pistachios and dry-roast them for 3 minutes until warm and fragrant.
Grease a marble slab and rolling pin with a little of the 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee.
Melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 1 tbsp water and the remaining ghee over low heat for about 6 minutes.
Cook to hard-crack stage, testing that a drop snaps in cold water, then stir in all the nuts, 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and a pinch of salt.
Pour onto the greased slab and roll out about half a centimetre thick before it sets.
Score into squares while warm, cool fully, then break into rich nutty shards.
tips: Warm the nuts before adding so they do not cool and seize the jaggery too fast.
Keep the layer even so every shard has a good mix of all three nuts.
Cool completely before breaking or the chikki will bend instead of snapping.
variations.servingSuggestion: Arrange the shards on a festive platter or wrap individually as premium gifting.

variations.name: Mixed Seed Chikki
variations.description: A modern energy-bar style chikki that swaps some nuts for pumpkin, sunflower and flax seeds boosted with moringa for a nutrient-dense snack. Lighter and crunchier than the nut-heavy classic, it is a favourite pre-workout and lunchbox bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: binds the seeds into firm bars at hard-crack stage

ingredients.name: Anveshan Moringa Powder
ingredients.note: stirred in off the heat to fortify the bars with iron and greens without a raw taste

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: greases the tray and keeps the seed bars from sticking

steps: Dry-roast 0.33 cup pumpkin seeds, 0.33 cup sunflower seeds and 0.25 cup flax seeds until they crackle, then add 0.25 cup chopped almonds and warm through.
Grease a tray and rolling pin with the 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil.
Melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 1 tbsp water over low heat and cook to hard-crack stage, about 6 minutes.
Take the pan off the heat and quickly stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Moringa Powder, 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and a pinch of salt.
Fold in the warm seeds and nuts, then press the mixture into the greased tray and roll it flat and firm.
Score into slim bars while warm and snap them apart once completely cooled.
tips: Add the moringa off the heat so its nutrients and colour are not scorched.
Press the seed mix firmly or the bars will crumble when broken.
These bars keep for two weeks airtight and travel well without melting.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pack a bar into a gym bag or lunchbox as a wholesome energy snack.

variations.name: Chocolate Dry Fruit Chikki
variations.description: An indulgent dessert-style chikki where the nutty jaggery brittle is half-dipped in dark chocolate and scattered with sea salt. The bittersweet chocolate against the caramel-jaggery nuts makes it a grown-up treat that feels like a premium confection.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: forms the caramel base that contrasts with the dark chocolate coat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the slab and gives the brittle a smooth glossy set

steps: Coarsely chop and warm 0.5 cup almonds, 0.33 cup cashews and 0.33 cup walnuts in a dry pan for 3 minutes.
Grease a slab with the 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 1 tbsp water to hard-crack stage over low heat.
Stir in the warm nuts and 0.5 tsp cardamom powder, pour onto the slab and roll thin, then score into bars and cool fully.
Melt the 150 g dark chocolate gently over barely simmering water until smooth and glossy.
Dip one half of each cooled chikki bar into the melted chocolate and lay on lined paper.
Scatter a few sea salt flakes over the wet chocolate and chill for 15 minutes until the coating sets.
tips: Let the chikki cool completely before dipping or the chocolate will slide off.
Temper the chocolate gently so the coating stays firm at room temperature.
A light scatter of sea salt lifts both the chocolate and the jaggery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Plate the chocolate-dipped shards as a petit-four with after-dinner coffee.

variations.name: Honey Nut Crunch Chikki
variations.description: A softer, chewier chikki bound with honey and a touch of jaggery instead of a hard-set caramel, studded with dates and raisins for natural stickiness. The honey keeps it pliable and gives a floral sweetness closer to a granola cluster than a glassy brittle.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: keeps the crunch pliable and adds a floral note the jaggery alone cannot

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a small amount firms the honey enough to hold the clusters together

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the tray and helps toast the nuts

steps: Dry-roast 0.5 cup almonds and 0.33 cup cashews for 3 minutes, then coarsely chop with 0.33 cup dates.
Grease a tray with the 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and keep it ready.
Warm 0.5 cup Anveshan Honey with 0.33 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder over low heat, stirring, for about 5 minutes until it thickens and reaches a soft ball stage.
