Take off the heat and quickly fold in the nuts, chopped dates, 0.25 cup raisins, 0.5 tsp cinnamon powder and a pinch of salt.
Spread the sticky mixture onto the greased tray and press it firm and even with a greased spatula.
Cool for 20 minutes until set but chewy, then cut into squares with a greased knife.
tips: Do not boil the honey hard or it turns bitter; a gentle thicken is enough.
The dates and raisins add natural stickiness that helps the clusters hold.
Store in the fridge in warm weather as the honey keeps these softer than a brittle.
variations.servingSuggestion: Cut into rough clusters and serve over yogurt or on its own as a chewy trail snack.

variations.name: Classic Dry Fruit Milkshake
variations.description: A thick, indulgent milkshake blended from soaked almonds, cashews and pistachios with chilled milk, the kind served at Indian juice centres in frosted steel glasses. Naturally sweet, nutty and creamy, it is a wholesome energy-booster crowned with slivered nuts and a hint of cardamom.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: raw honey blended in cold sweetens the shake naturally and complements the roasted nuttiness without refined sugar

steps: Soak 15 almonds, 12 cashews, 10 pistachios and 4 pitted dates in warm water for 20 minutes, then peel the almonds for a smoother, whiter shake.
Drain the nuts and dates and blend them with 1 cup of the chilled milk into a very fine, smooth paste, scraping down the sides so no grit remains.
Add the remaining 2 cups chilled milk and 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and blend on high for 1 minute until thick and frothy.
Blend in 4 tbsp Anveshan Honey briefly, just enough to combine without warming the mixture.
Drop in 1 cup ice cubes and pulse for a few seconds until the shake is icy cold and lightly aerated.
Pour into chilled glasses and top with a few chopped pistachios and slivered almonds before serving.
tips: Soaking and peeling the nuts is what gives a silky, grit-free shake — skipping it leaves a grainy texture.
Dates add natural caramel sweetness and body, letting you use less honey overall.
Blend the nut paste with a little milk first, then dilute; this extracts maximum creaminess from the nuts.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in frosted glasses garnished with a dusting of cardamom and chopped nuts, as a filling breakfast shake or an afternoon energy drink.

variations.name: Kesar Badam Thandai Shake
variations.description: A festive, thandai-inspired dry fruit shake perfumed with saffron, fennel and rose, layering the cooling spice mix of Holi over a rich almond-milk base. Fragrant and pale gold, it drinks like a celebration and is a favourite for summer gatherings.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: pure Kashmiri saffron steeped in warm milk gives the shake its golden colour and floral thandai character

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: khandsari dissolves cleanly into the spiced milk keeping the pale golden hue of the thandai intact

steps: Steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside so the colour and aroma bloom.
Soak 20 almonds, 1 tbsp fennel seeds, 6 white peppercorns and 1 tsp poppy seeds together in warm water for 20 minutes, then peel the almonds.
Drain and blend the soaked nuts and spices with 1 cup chilled milk into a very fine, aromatic paste, then strain it through muslin for a silky shake.
Return the strained milk to the blender with the remaining 2 cups chilled milk, the saffron milk, 5 tbsp Anveshan Khandsari Sugar and 0.5 tsp cardamom powder, and blend until smooth and frothy.
Blend in 1 tsp rose water briefly, then add 1 cup ice cubes and pulse until icy cold.
Pour into glasses, garnish with a few saffron strands and slivered almonds, and serve well chilled.
tips: Strain the spiced nut paste through muslin for the classic silky thandai texture free of poppy-seed grit.
Steep the saffron in warm milk first — dropping dry strands into the cold shake wastes their colour and scent.
Prepare the thandai concentrate a day ahead and blend with milk and ice just before serving for the freshest aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in tall glasses with a saffron-almond garnish and dried rose petals, a festive cooler for Holi or summer parties.

variations.name: Roasted Nut Ghee Shake
variations.description: A deeper, toastier milkshake where the dry fruits are roasted in ghee before blending, coaxing out a caramelised, praline-like flavour. Richer and more aromatic than the soaked classic, it is an indulgent winter treat that tastes almost like drinking a nut halwa.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee gently roasts the nuts to a praline-like aroma that defines this richer winter shake

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: unrefined jaggery deepens the toasted-nut flavour with a caramel note that white sugar cannot match

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium-low and roast 12 almonds, 12 cashews and 8 walnuts for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring, until golden and fragrant.
Set aside a few roasted nuts for garnish and let the rest cool for 10 minutes so they blend smoothly.
Blend the cooled roasted nuts with 1 cup chilled milk into a fine, nutty paste.
Add the remaining 2 cups chilled milk, 4 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 0.5 tsp cinnamon powder and a scant 0.125 tsp nutmeg powder, and blend on high until thick and smooth.
Add 0.5 cup ice cubes and pulse briefly to chill without over-diluting the rich shake.
Pour into glasses, crush the reserved roasted nuts over the top, and serve cold.
tips: Roast the nuts on low heat and watch closely — ghee-roasted nuts turn from golden to burnt very quickly.
Cool the roasted nuts fully before blending, or the warmth can make the milk taste cooked and thin.
Dissolve the jaggery in a splash of warm milk first if it does not blend smooth, then chill before combining.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve slightly less icy and more rich, topped with crushed roasted nuts and a pinch of cinnamon, as an indulgent winter dessert-drink.

variations.name: Dry Fruit Date Vegan Shake
variations.description: A dairy-free dry fruit shake built on homemade almond milk and blended with dates and figs for natural sweetness. Light yet satisfying, it is smooth, subtly sweet and completely plant-based, ideal for those avoiding dairy without giving up a creamy nutty shake.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: just a little raw honey rounds out the natural fruit sweetness if the dates and figs need a lift

steps: Soak 25 almonds overnight or in warm water for 30 minutes, then peel them for a whiter, smoother milk.
Blend the peeled almonds with 3 cups water until very fine, then strain through a nut-milk bag or muslin to yield smooth almond milk.
Soak 6 dates, 4 dried figs and 10 cashews in warm water for 15 minutes until soft, then drain.
Blend the soaked dates, figs and cashews with 1 cup of the almond milk into a smooth, caramel-coloured paste.
Add the remaining almond milk, 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and 0.25 tsp cinnamon powder and blend until thick and frothy, adding 2 tbsp Anveshan Honey only if extra sweetness is wanted.
Blend in 1 cup ice cubes until icy cold, pour into glasses, and serve chilled.
tips: Strain the almond milk well for a smooth shake, and save the leftover almond pulp to add to breakfast porridge.
Very soft, sticky dates and figs give the most natural sweetness, often making added honey unnecessary.
For a nut-milk shortcut, use store-bought unsweetened almond milk and start from the date-fig blending step.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled in glasses dusted with cinnamon, a wholesome dairy-free breakfast or a light plant-based dessert drink.

variations.name: Classic Til Gajak
variations.description: Classic Til Gajak is the flaky, layered winter brittle of Morena and Agra, made by repeatedly folding and beating roasted sesame into a pulled jaggery syrup. Its signature is a dry, crumbly, almost laminated texture that shatters into fine flakes, quite different from a glassy chikki.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: pulled to hard-crack and folded repeatedly to give gajak its flaky layers

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the slab and helps laminate the sesame into thin brittle sheets

steps: Dry-roast 1.5 cups sesame seeds over low heat until golden and popping, then coarsely pound half of them in a mortar.
Grease a marble slab generously with some of the 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee.
Melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water and remaining ghee over low heat and cook to hard-crack stage, about 8 minutes.
Mix in the whole and pounded sesame with 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and 0.25 tsp dry ginger powder, then tip onto the slab.
While warm, roll it out, fold it over on itself and roll again, repeating several times so thin sesame layers build up.
Roll the folded slab thin a final time, cut into rectangles and cool until dry and crumbly.
tips: The repeated fold-and-roll is what creates gajak's flaky layers, so keep the mixture workable.
Work on a warm slab in winter; if it sets too fast the layers will not form.
Pounding half the sesame gives the characteristic fine, dry crumble.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the flaky rectangles with hot milk or masala chai on a cold winter evening.

variations.name: Gud Peanut Gajak
variations.description: A rustic Bundelkhand-style gajak that folds coarsely crushed roasted peanuts into the sesame layers for a chunkier, nuttier winter slab. Denser and more filling than the fine til gajak, it is sold in thick blocks at village winter fairs.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: binds the peanuts and sesame into a firm block at hard-crack stage

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: greases the slab and reinforces the roasted-peanut character

steps: Roast 1 cup sesame seeds until golden, then crush 1 cup roasted peanuts coarsely, leaving some halves.
Grease a slab and rolling pin with the 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil.
Melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water over low heat and cook to hard-crack stage, about 8 minutes.
Fold in the sesame, crushed peanuts, 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and 0.25 tsp salt until evenly combined.
Tip onto the greased slab, fold once or twice and roll into a thick even block while warm.
Cut into sturdy squares and cool completely until firm and crunchy.
tips: Keep the peanuts coarse so the block stays chunky rather than powdery.
Roll this one thicker than fine gajak to suit its heartier texture.
A little salt keeps the peanut richness from feeling cloying.
variations.servingSuggestion: Break off thick pieces to eat as a warming, high-energy winter snack.

variations.name: Khoya Gajak
variations.description: A rich Mathura-style gajak enriched with khoya and slivered almonds, giving the sesame brittle a soft, milky, fudge-like centre. Less shatter, more melt, this festive version bridges the gap between a dry gajak and a barfi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a softer set balances the milky khoya for a fudge-like gajak

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the khoya to a golden aroma and greases the setting tray

steps: Dry-roast 1 cup sesame seeds until golden and coarsely pound them, then set aside.
Roast 0.5 cup khoya in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over low heat for 5 minutes until light golden and fragrant.
Add 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tbsp water to the khoya and cook, stirring, for 6 minutes until it forms a soft mass that leaves the pan.
Fold in the pounded sesame, 0.25 cup slivered almonds, 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and the saffron strands.
Spread the mixture into a tray greased with the remaining ghee and press it even and firm.
Cool for 20 minutes until set but soft, then cut into diamonds.
tips: Roast the khoya well or the gajak may taste raw and turn sour quickly.
This softer gajak keeps best in the fridge and is not meant to shatter like the classic.
Warm the almonds slightly so they slice cleanly into the soft mass.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the soft diamonds slightly warmed as a rich festival mithai with a garnish of saffron.

variations.name: Roll Gajak
variations.description: The showpiece rolled gajak where a thin sesame sheet is wrapped tightly around a soft khandsari-ghee filling, then sliced into pinwheels. Each round reveals a spiral of crisp shell and creamy centre, a specialty of old Delhi winter sweet shops.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: pale khandsari keeps the outer sesame sheet light-coloured for a pretty spiral

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: whipped into the soft filling to give the roll its creamy melting centre

steps: Roast 1 cup sesame seeds until golden and coarsely pound them, keeping them warm.
Melt 1 cup Anveshan Khandsari with 2 tbsp water over low heat to hard-crack stage, then mix in the pounded sesame.
Roll this sesame mixture between greased sheets into a very thin rectangular sheet while still warm.
For the filling, whip 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with 0.33 cup milk powder, 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and a pinch of salt into a soft spreadable paste.
Spread the filling over the warm sesame sheet, scatter 2 tbsp chopped pistachios, then roll it up tightly from one long edge.
Brush with the remaining ghee, cool until firm, then slice into pinwheel rounds with a sharp greased knife.
tips: Roll the sesame sheet while genuinely warm and pliable or it will crack when rolled.
Chill the roll briefly before slicing so the pinwheels cut cleanly.
Keep the filling soft, not runny, so it stays put inside the spiral.
variations.servingSuggestion: Fan the pinwheel slices on a platter to show off the spiral for a festive display.

variations.name: Classic Gond Ke Ladoo
variations.description: The quintessential North Indian winter ladoo built on edible gum fried in ghee until it puffs into crisp white nuggets, folded through roasted whole-wheat flour and jaggery. The gond gives a signature light crunch inside a dense, warming ball believed to strengthen joints and bones. It is the sweet every household stocks from December through the cold months.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: roast this until nutty to give the ladoo its dense wholegrain body

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: the gum must fry in plenty of this to puff up properly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melts just enough to bind the crunchy gum and flour

steps: Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat and fry the gond in small batches for about 1 minute each, until every piece swells into a puffed white ball; drain and crush coarsely once cool.
In the same ghee, toast the almonds, cashews and melon seeds for 2 minutes until fragrant, then remove and chop the nuts.
Add the remaining ghee and roast 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta on low heat for 22-25 minutes, stirring constantly, until deep golden and strongly nutty.
Let the roasted flour cool for 8-10 minutes until just warm so the jaggery binds without turning to syrup.
Mix in 1.25 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder, the crushed gum, chopped nuts, melon seeds and 1 tsp cardamom powder until the mixture clumps when pressed.
Roll into 14 firm round ladoos while warm and rest them for an hour to set before storing in an airtight tin.
tips: Fry the gum on medium heat only; too hot and it browns and turns bitter, too cool and it stays hard inside.
If the mix crumbles while rolling, warm it briefly and add a spoon of melted ghee to bring it together.
These keep for up to a month and are traditionally eaten one a day through winter for warmth.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a glass of hot milk at breakfast, or offer on a festive thali during Sankranti and family winter gatherings.

variations.name: Maharashtrian Dink Ladoo
variations.description: The Maharashtrian dink ladoo leans on dry coconut, poppy seeds and khaskhas alongside the fried gum, giving a coarser, more textured ball than the North Indian style. Traditionally made after childbirth, it is packed with edible gum and dry fruit for strength. The toasted copra and poppy seeds give it a distinctly western-Indian aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: fry the dink and coconut in this until crisp and fragrant

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted into a soft binding paste to hold the coarse mixture

steps: Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat and fry the dink in batches for about 1 minute each until it puffs into white balls; cool and crush coarsely.
Dry-roast the poppy seeds in the kadhai for 1 minute until they pop, then toast the grated copra for 3 minutes until pale gold and set both aside.
Add the remaining ghee and roast the 0.75 cup wheat flour on low heat for 12-15 minutes until golden and nutty, then toast the almonds for 2 minutes and chop them.
Melt 1.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water in a separate pan over low heat until it forms a thick syrup, about 4 minutes.
Off the heat, combine the roasted flour, crushed dink, copra, poppy seeds, almonds, chopped dates and 0.5 tsp nutmeg, then pour in the jaggery syrup and mix quickly.
While warm enough to handle, press into 14 firm ladoos and let them cool completely before storing.
tips: Work fast once the jaggery syrup is in, as it stiffens as it cools and the ladoos become hard to shape.
Toast the copra only until pale gold; browning it makes the ladoo taste burnt.
These are traditionally given to nursing mothers, so keep the dink and dry-fruit quantities generous.
variations.servingSuggestion: Offer these coarse, coconut-rich ladoos with a cup of masala chai, or pack them as a nourishing gift during Diwali and postpartum visits.

variations.name: Flourless Gond Dry-Fruit Ladoo
variations.description: A grain-free take that drops the atta entirely and binds fried gum with a thick paste of dates and mixed nuts, making a chewy, protein-dense ball with no added flour. It suits anyone avoiding wheat while still craving the winter crunch of gond. The natural date sweetness means very little extra jaggery is needed.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: just enough to puff the gum and toast the nuts

ingredients.name: Anveshan Dry Fruit Paak
ingredients.note: adds a ready mix of caramelised nuts that deepens the flavour and helps bind

steps: Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat and fry the gond in batches for about 1 minute each until puffed and white; cool and crush coarsely.
In the remaining ghee, toast the almonds, cashews and pistachios for 3 minutes until lightly golden, then chop them roughly.
Chop the pitted dates finely and mash them in a warm pan over low heat for 3-4 minutes until they turn into a soft sticky paste.
Stir the Anveshan Dry Fruit Paak into the warm date paste until evenly blended and glossy.
Off the heat, mix the chopped nuts, crushed gum and 1 tsp cardamom into the date mixture until everything holds together in a thick, tacky mass.
Grease your palms with a little ghee and press the warm mixture into 12 firm ladoos, then chill for 20 minutes to set.
tips: Use soft, moist dates; dry ones won't bind and you will be forced to add sticky syrup.
If the mixture is too wet to roll, refrigerate it for 15 minutes and it will firm up enough to shape.
These are naturally sweet, so taste before adding anything more; the date and paak usually suffice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these fudgy, no-flour ladoos as a post-workout energy bite or an after-dinner sweet with a demitasse of kahwa.

variations.name: Gond Panjiri Ladoo with Sonth
variations.description: A warming panjiri-style gond ladoo spiced heavily with dry ginger, fennel and edible gum, closer to the strengthening mixture served to new mothers but rolled into balls. The sonth and fennel give it a medicinal warmth the plain version lacks, and coarsely crushed makhana adds an airy crunch. It is the most spice-forward ladoo of the set.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: the wholegrain base holds the warming spices and gum together

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: fry the gum and makhana in this before roasting the flour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: binds the spiced panjiri mix into firm rounds

steps: Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat and fry the gond in batches for about 1 minute each until puffed white; cool and crush coarsely.
In the same ghee, fry the makhana for 4-5 minutes until crisp and snappable, then crush them coarsely; toast the almonds for 2 minutes and chop.
Add the remaining ghee and roast 1.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta on low heat for 22-25 minutes until deep golden and nutty.
Stir the crushed fennel seeds and 1.5 tsp dry ginger powder into the hot flour and cook for a further minute until aromatic.
Cool the mixture for 8-10 minutes until warm, then mix in 1.25 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder, the crushed gum, makhana, almonds and 1 tsp cardamom until it binds when pressed.
Shape into 14 firm ladoos while warm and rest for an hour so the makhana crunch settles.
tips: Fry the makhana until fully crisp before crushing, or they turn chewy and soften the ladoo.
The sonth makes these quite warming, so a smaller ladoo is plenty on milder days.
Store away from moisture; the crushed makhana loses its crunch if the tin isn't airtight.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve one with hot ginger-cardamom milk on the coldest mornings, or share during Lohri as a warming festive treat.

variations.name: Classic Andhra Gongura Pachadi
variations.description: The iconic Andhra chutney built on gongura (sorrel) leaves, whose intense natural sourness needs no tamarind. The leaves are sauteed until they collapse, ground with roasted spices and red chillies, then crowned with a garlic-heavy tempering. Deeply tangy and fiery, it is the pride of Telugu kitchens and the ultimate companion to hot rice and ghee.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil is the authentic fat for gongura pachadi, sauteing the leaves and carrying the garlic tempering that defines it

steps: Dry-roast 1 tbsp coriander seeds, 1 tsp cumin, 0.25 tsp fenugreek and 6 dried red chillies in a pan on medium flame for 2 minutes until fragrant, then set aside to cool.
In the same pan heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and saute 4 cups washed gongura leaves for 6-8 minutes until they wilt fully and the moisture cooks off.
Cool both mixtures, then grind them together with 1.25 tsp salt to a coarse chutney without any water, as the leaves release their own moisture.
For the tempering, heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then fry 8 crushed garlic cloves until golden.
Add 1 sprig curry leaves, let them crackle, and pour the whole garlicky tempering over the ground pachadi.
Mix well and rest 15 minutes so the flavours meld into the classic sharp, savoury gongura chutney.
tips: Pick only tender gongura leaves off the stems; the stalks are fibrous and stay bitter even after cooking.
Cook the leaves until all their water evaporates, or the pachadi will be watery and spoil faster.
The generous garlic tempering is essential to gongura pachadi, so do not reduce it; it tames the sourness beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steaming rice topped with a spoon of ghee and thinly sliced raw onion on the side.

variations.name: Gongura Peanut Pachadi
variations.description: A nuttier, milder Rayalaseema-style pachadi where roasted peanuts are ground into the sorrel base, softening its sharp tang with a creamy, earthy body. The peanuts give it heft and a subtle sweetness that makes it approachable for those new to gongura. It clings richly to rice and doubles as a spread.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil echoes the peanuts and gives this pachadi a rounded, robust base

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan and fry 5 dried red chillies and 1 tsp cumin for 1 minute, then remove.
In the same oil saute 4 cups gongura leaves for 6-8 minutes until wilted and dry, and let them cool.
Grind the leaves with the fried chillies, 0.5 cups roasted peanuts, 3 garlic cloves and 1.25 tsp salt to a thick, coarse chutney, adding no water.
Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal until golden, then add 2 sliced garlic cloves and fry until light brown.
Toss in 1 sprig curry leaves and pour the sizzling tempering over the pachadi.
Stir thoroughly and let it stand 10 minutes so the peanuts and sorrel settle into a creamy, tangy chutney.
tips: Grind the peanuts along with the leaves rather than sprinkling them on top so they thicken the whole chutney evenly.
For extra crunch, reserve a spoon of crushed peanuts and stir them in at the end.
This milder version keeps well for a week refrigerated and travels well for journeys with curd rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Spread on hot phulka or mix into curd rice for a nutty, tangy lunch that packs beautifully.

variations.name: Gongura Onion Pachadi
variations.description: A homestyle version where sweet sauteed onions are folded into the sorrel base, balancing gongura's sharp acidity with mellow, jammy depth. The onions turn the chutney softer and rounder, making it a family favourite that even children enjoy. Its deep maroon colour and savoury-sweet edge set it apart from the fiery classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Sautes the onions to a sweet softness and doubles as the aromatic base for the leaves

steps: Dry-roast 1 tsp coriander seeds, 1 tsp cumin and 5 dried red chillies for 2 minutes, then set aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and saute 2 sliced large onions for 8 minutes until soft, sweet and golden at the edges, then scoop out half for later.
To the pan add 4 cups gongura leaves and cook 6-7 minutes until fully wilted and dry.
Cool and grind the wilted leaves, the sauteed onion left in the pan, the roasted spices and 1.25 tsp salt to a coarse chutney.
Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, fry 4 sliced garlic cloves and the reserved onions until browned, and add 1 sprig curry leaves.
Fold this tempering with its caramelised onions into the pachadi and rest 10 minutes before serving.
tips: Reserving half the onions for the tempering gives two textures, jammy inside and crisp-brown on top.
Choose ripe red onions for their natural sweetness, which best counters the sorrel's tang.
If it tastes too sour on the day, an extra spoon of sauteed onion mellows it further.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside jowar roti or ragi mudde with a dollop of curd to complete a rustic Telugu thali.

variations.name: Instant Raw Gongura Thokku
variations.description: A quick, bright pachadi where the sorrel leaves are only briefly blanched then ground raw with green chillies for a fresher, sharper flavour than the slow-cooked classic. Green chillies replace red for a grassier heat, and a light tempering finishes it in minutes. Perfect when gongura is in season and you want its tang at its most vivid.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: A raw drizzle plus the tempering keeps this quick thokku moist and preserves its bright colour

steps: Blanch 4 cups gongura leaves in boiling water for 1 minute, drain well, and squeeze out the excess water.
Grind the blanched leaves with 6 green chillies, 1 tsp cumin, 1 inch ginger and 1.25 tsp salt to a coarse, vivid green chutney without water.
Transfer to a bowl and drizzle 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil over the top.
Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal, then fry 3 sliced garlic cloves until pale gold.
Add 1 sprig curry leaves, let it crackle, and pour the tempering over the chutney.
Stir once and serve fresh while the colour is bright and the flavour sharp.
tips: A quick 1-minute blanch tames just enough of the raw bite while keeping the fresh green colour intact.
Squeeze the blanched leaves firmly, as any trapped water makes the thokku loose and dilutes the tang.
Green chillies give a brighter heat than red here, so adjust the count to your spice tolerance.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rice and a spoon of ghee, or use as a zingy green spread inside dosa rolls.

variations.name: Classic Jaljeera
variations.description: North India's most refreshing summer cooler, built on a bright green mint-and-coriander paste sharpened with lemon, roasted cumin and black salt. It is tangy, mildly spicy and deeply digestive, the kind of glass handed out at wedding welcome counters and roadside thela stalls alike.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: raw wildflower honey rounds off the tang without the flat sweetness of white sugar and dissolves smoothly in cold water

steps: Rinse 1 cup mint leaves and 0.5 cup coriander leaves well, then blend them with 1 inch ginger, 1 green chilli and a splash of water into a smooth, vivid green paste, about 1 minute.
Tip the paste into a large jug and whisk in 1.5 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp black salt, 1 tsp dry mango powder and 0.5 tsp black pepper powder until evenly combined.
Add 3 tbsp lemon juice and 2 tbsp Anveshan Honey and stir vigorously for about 30 seconds until the honey fully dissolves and the mix smells sharp and fragrant.
Pour in 4 cups chilled water in a steady stream, whisking constantly so the herb paste disperses evenly rather than sinking to the bottom.
Taste and adjust, adding a little more lemon for tang or honey for balance, then strain through a coarse sieve if you prefer a clearer drink or leave it rustic with the herb flecks.
Drop 1 cup ice cubes into the jug, stir once, and pour into tall glasses to serve ice-cold.
tips: Dry-roast whole cumin until it darkens and smells smoky before grinding — pre-ground cumin tastes flat and loses the signature jaljeera aroma.
Make the green paste up to a day ahead and refrigerate it; whisk into water only when serving so the colour stays bright and does not oxidise.
For a fizzy version, replace half the chilled water with cold soda added just before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in tall glasses rimmed with black salt and garnished with a mint sprig and a thin lemon wheel, alongside fried snacks like samosas or pakoras.

variations.name: Banarasi Imli Jaljeera
variations.description: The dark, tamarind-forward jaljeera famous in the lanes of Varanasi, where sweet-sour imli pulp replaces lemon and a handful of soaked boondi bobs in every glass. Jaggery deepens it into a molasses-tinged, almost chaat-like drink you scoop up with a spoon as much as sip.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: unrefined jaggery melts into the tamarind pulp giving this Banarasi version its dark, toffee-edged sweetness

steps: Soak 3 tbsp tamarind in 1 cup hot water for 15 minutes, then squeeze and strain out a thick, smooth pulp, discarding the seeds and fibre.
Warm the tamarind pulp gently and stir in 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder on low heat for about 2 minutes until the jaggery fully melts, then cool it completely.
Whisk 2 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp black salt, 1 tsp chaat masala, 1 tsp dry mint powder, 0.5 tsp ginger powder and 0.5 tsp black pepper powder into the cooled tamarind-jaggery base.
Pour in 4 cups chilled water gradually, stirring until the spiced pulp dissolves into a uniform dark, tangy liquid.
Soak 0.5 cup boondi in plain water for 2 minutes until just softened, then drain and divide it between the serving glasses.
Add 1 cup ice cubes to the jug, stir, and pour the jaljeera over the boondi so it floats — serve at once before the boondi turns soggy.
tips: Melt the jaggery into the tamarind while warm and strain again — this catches any grit and gives a silky base.
Add the soaked boondi only at the moment of serving; sitting too long it swells and turns mushy.
Keep the tamarind base refrigerated for up to three days and dilute a fresh glass whenever you like.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in kulhads or glass tumblers with extra boondi floating on top and a pinch of chaat masala dusted over, as a tangy palate-cleanser between chaat courses.

variations.name: Aam Jaljeera
variations.description: A summer-only variation that swaps citrus for the pulp of boiled raw mangoes, giving a thick, fruity tang closer to aam panna but carrying the classic cumin-and-black-salt jaljeera backbone. Cooling, restorative and famously good against heat-stroke, it is the drink of choice through the fiercest weeks of May.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: unrefined khandsari balances the sourness of raw mango cleanly while keeping the drink pale and natural-tasting

steps: Pressure-cook 2 whole raw mangoes with 1 cup water for 2 whistles, or boil them for 12 minutes until the flesh is completely soft, then cool and peel.
Squeeze and scoop out all the pulp into a blender, discarding skin and stone, and blend with 0.5 cup mint leaves and 4 tbsp Anveshan Khandsari Sugar into a smooth green-gold puree.
Transfer the puree to a jug and whisk in 2 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1.25 tsp black salt, 0.5 tsp black pepper powder and 0.5 tsp fennel powder until well blended.
Add 4 cups chilled water little by little, whisking so the thick pulp loosens into a pourable, cloudy drink.
Taste for the sweet-sour balance and adjust with a little more khandsari or black salt as the mango's tartness varies.
Stir in 1 cup ice cubes and serve immediately in chilled glasses.
tips: Choose firm, very sour green mangoes — sweet or ripe ones give a flat drink that lacks the cooling tang.
The mango pulp base freezes well in an ice tray; blend a cube into water for an instant single glass.
A tiny pinch of roasted fennel powder soothes the stomach and lifts the aroma of the raw mango.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve thick and slushy over crushed ice with a mint sprig, as a mid-afternoon heat-beater or a welcome drink at summer gatherings.

variations.name: Instant Jaljeera Masala Cooler
variations.description: A pantry-friendly jaljeera built from a homemade dry masala powder rather than fresh herbs, so a glass comes together in under a minute whenever the craving strikes. Powdered dry mint, amchur and a blend of roasted spices deliver the full tangy-digestive punch straight from the jar.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: a spoon of raw honey per jug softens the sharp dry-spice edge and gives body without clouding the drink

steps: Dry-roast the coriander seed powder and cumin powder together in a pan on low heat for 1 minute until fragrant, then cool completely so the mix stays free-flowing.

In a bowl, combine 2 tbsp dry mint powder, the roasted cumin and coriander, 2 tsp dry mango powder, 1.5 tsp black salt, 0.5 tsp dry ginger powder, 1 pinch asafoetida and 0.5 tsp black pepper powder into an even jaljeera masala.
Spoon 4 to 5 tsp of this masala into a large jug and whisk in 2 tbsp lemon juice and 2 tbsp Anveshan Honey until it forms a smooth slurry.
Pour in 4 cups chilled water gradually, whisking hard so the powder blends without settling into lumps at the base.
Let it rest for 3 to 4 minutes so the dry mint rehydrates and the flavours bloom, then whisk once more.
Add 1 cup ice cubes and serve, keeping the leftover dry masala in an airtight jar for the next round.
tips: Store the dry masala in a sealed jar away from moisture and it stays potent for two to three months.
Let the mixed drink rest a few minutes before serving so the dry mint fully hydrates and stops tasting powdery.
Scale a single glass with 1 heaped tsp masala to 1 cup water when you do not want to make a whole jug.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in small glasses as a quick pre-meal digestive, or carry the dry masala jar while travelling to mix an instant cooler anywhere.

variations.name: Classic Kokum Sharbat
variations.description: A ruby-pink coastal cooler made from dried kokum, whose deep tartness and natural cooling quality make it the Konkan answer to summer heat. Steeped into a concentrate and sweetened just enough, it is sharp, fruity and faintly astringent, finished with roasted cumin and a whisper of black salt.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: unrefined khandsari dissolves into a clear syrup that lets the ruby kokum colour and tartness shine through

steps: Rinse 20 dried kokum petals and soak them in 1.5 cups warm water for 30 minutes until they plump and the water turns deep pink.
Simmer the soaked kokum with its water on low heat for 8 to 10 minutes, pressing the petals with a spoon to release all their colour and tartness.
Add 0.75 cup Anveshan Khandsari Sugar and stir for 3 to 4 minutes until it dissolves fully and the mixture thickens into a glossy, syrupy concentrate.
Strain the concentrate through a fine sieve, pressing the pulp firmly, then cool it to room temperature and whisk in 1 tsp roasted cumin powder and 0.75 tsp black salt.
To serve, pour 3 to 4 tbsp of the concentrate into each glass and top up with chilled water, stirring to a rich rose-pink.
Drop in a few mint leaves and 1 cup ice cubes across the glasses, and serve chilled.
tips: Press the kokum petals hard while simmering — most of the colour and tartness lives in the flesh, not the soaking water.
The strained concentrate keeps refrigerated for two weeks, so make a batch and dilute glasses on demand.
Adjust the concentrate-to-water ratio to taste; kokum's sharpness varies a lot with how dry the petals are.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve tall and icy with a mint sprig, a natural digestive after a heavy coastal thali or a rich, spicy lunch.

variations.name: Masala Kokum Sharbat
variations.description: A punchier version that layers roasted spices and a hit of ginger over the tart kokum base, closer to a savoury-sweet panha than a plain squash. Jaggery lends earthy depth and the spice edge makes it doubly effective as a digestive after oily food.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: unrefined jaggery gives this spiced version a molasses depth that stands up to the ginger and roasted spices

steps: Soak 22 dried kokum petals in 1.5 cups warm water for 30 minutes, then simmer on low with 1 inch grated ginger for 10 minutes, mashing to extract full colour and tang.
Stir in 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook for another 4 minutes on low until it melts into a dark, syrupy concentrate, keeping the flame gentle so the jaggery does not scorch.
Strain the concentrate through a fine sieve, pressing out every drop, then cool it and discard the spent pulp and ginger.
Whisk 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp black pepper powder, 0.75 tsp black salt and 0.25 tsp cardamom powder into the cooled concentrate until evenly spiced.
Pour 3 to 4 tbsp of concentrate into each glass and top with chilled water, stirring to a deep rose colour.
Add 1 cup ice cubes and serve, with an extra pinch of roasted cumin dusted over the top.
tips: Grate the ginger fine so it releases its heat into the simmering base rather than sitting in fibrous strands.
Strain the jaggery concentrate twice for a silky drink free of any grit or fibre.
This spiced concentrate is stronger than the classic — start with less per glass and build up to taste.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve slightly stronger and colder as an after-meal digestive, especially following fried snacks or a spicy Malvani spread.

variations.name: Kokum Ginger Fizz
variations.description: A modern party twist where the tart kokum concentrate meets chilled soda and fresh lime for a sparkling, mocktail-style refresher. Honey keeps it light and floral, and the fizz turns the humble sharbat into a celebratory welcome drink.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: raw honey keeps this fizzy version light and floral, dissolving into the concentrate without clouding the sparkle

steps: Soak 18 dried kokum petals in 1.25 cups warm water for 25 minutes, then simmer on low for 8 minutes with 0.5 inch crushed ginger to draw out a ruby concentrate.
Take the pan off the heat, let it cool for 5 minutes, then stir in 5 tbsp Anveshan Honey off the heat so its aroma and nutrients are preserved.
Strain the concentrate, press out the pulp, and whisk in 2 tbsp fresh lime juice and 0.5 tsp black salt once fully cooled.
Muddle a couple of basil leaves in the base of each serving glass to release their fragrance, then divide the ice cubes among the glasses.
Pour 3 to 4 tbsp of kokum concentrate over the ice in each glass, filling it about a third of the way.
Top up with chilled soda water, stir once gently to keep the fizz, garnish with a basil leaf, and serve straight away.
tips: Add the honey only after the concentrate cools off the boil, so its delicate flavour and goodness stay intact.
Pour the soda last and stir minimally — over-stirring flattens the bubbles that make this drink special.
Keep the kokum concentrate chilled and top with soda per glass so nothing goes flat waiting.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in stemmed glasses with a basil sprig and a thin lime wheel as a non-alcoholic welcome drink at summer parties.

variations.name: Kokum Amrakhand Cooler
variations.description: A dessert-leaning blend where tart kokum concentrate is whipped with thick chilled yogurt into a coral-pink, lassi-like cooler. Creamy and tangy at once, cooled with cardamom, it eats almost like a drinkable shrikhand and doubles as a light summer sweet.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: khandsari whips smoothly into the yogurt without graininess, balancing the sharp kokum in this creamy cooler

steps: Soak 16 dried kokum petals in 1 cup warm water for 25 minutes, then simmer on low for 8 minutes and strain to a thick, tart concentrate; cool it fully.
Whisk 1.5 cups thick chilled yogurt with 0.5 cup Anveshan Khandsari Sugar until completely smooth and the sugar has dissolved, about 2 minutes.
Blend the sweetened yogurt with the cooled kokum concentrate, 1 cup chilled milk, 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and 0.25 tsp black salt on medium speed until frothy and uniformly coral-pink.
Taste and adjust — add a touch more khandsari if the yogurt is very sour, or more concentrate for a sharper tang.
Divide 1 cup ice cubes among four glasses and pour the blended cooler over.
Scatter 2 tbsp chopped pistachios on top and serve immediately while it is thick and cold.
tips: Use thick, well-set yogurt and keep it cold so the drink stays creamy rather than thin and watery.
Blend the yogurt only briefly once cold — over-blending warms it and can make it taste sour.
For a thicker, spoonable shrikhand-style version, hang the yogurt for an hour and skip the added milk.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in short tumblers topped with pistachio slivers and a dusting of cardamom, as a light dessert-drink after a Konkani meal.

variations.name: Classic Lauki Halwa
variations.description: Lauki halwa, also called dudhi halwa, is a slow-cooked pudding of grated bottle gourd simmered in milk until it reduces to a soft, fudgy mass. Cooked in ghee and gently sweetened, it is a light, milky festive sweet flecked with cardamom and fried nuts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: sautes the grated lauki to remove its raw smell and enriches the milky halwa

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: sweetens the reduced lauki and milk without masking its delicate flavour

steps: Peel and grate enough bottle gourd to yield 4 cups, then gently squeeze out excess water and reserve the pulp.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan and fry 3 tbsp cashews and raisins until golden, about 2 minutes, then lift them out.
Add the grated lauki to the ghee and saute over medium heat for 6 to 7 minutes until it softens and loses its raw smell.
Pour in 3 cups full-fat milk and simmer on medium-low heat for 20 to 25 minutes, stirring often, until the milk reduces and the lauki turns soft and pulpy.
Stir in 0.5 cup Anveshan Khandsari and cook a further 6 to 8 minutes until the sugar melts and the halwa thickens to a fudgy mass.
Mix in 0.5 tsp cardamom and the fried nuts, then serve the lauki halwa warm.
tips: Squeeze the grated lauki lightly, not bone-dry, so the halwa stays moist while the milk still reduces well.
Add the sugar only after the lauki is fully soft, as it releases water and slows the cooking if added early.
Stir often during the milk reduction to prevent the halwa catching and scorching at the base.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm or chilled in bowls, garnished with slivered nuts and a pinch of cardamom, alongside a festive meal.

variations.name: Halwai Khoya Lauki Halwa
variations.description: The sweet-shop version enriches the lauki with crumbled khoya so it sets thicker, richer and grainier, closer to a mithai than a pudding. Saffron and extra ghee give it the deep, milky decadence of a professional halwai's tray.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: sautes the lauki and carries the khoya for a rich, sweet-shop finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: sweetens the khoya-enriched halwa to a firm, mithai-like set

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm milk to lend the halwa its golden halwai colour and aroma

steps: Soak 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 0.5 cup warm milk and set aside to bloom while you prepare the lauki.
Peel and grate the bottle gourd to yield 4 cups, then squeeze out the excess water and reserve.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai and saute the grated lauki over medium heat for 8 to 10 minutes until soft and dry-looking.
Add the saffron milk and cook for 5 minutes until absorbed, then stir in 1 cup grated khoya and cook 4 to 5 minutes until it melts into the lauki.
Add 0.6 cup Anveshan Khandsari and cook, stirring, for 6 to 7 minutes until the sugar melts and the halwa pulls together into a thick, glossy mass.
Finish with 0.5 tsp cardamom, fold through half the pistachios, and serve garnished with the rest.
tips: Cook the lauki until it looks dry before adding khoya, or the halwa turns loose and watery.
Crumble the khoya finely so it melts evenly without leaving grainy lumps in the halwa.
For a firmer, sliceable halwa, press it into a greased tray and cut into squares once cool.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a rich festive mithai, topped with pistachios and a whisper of edible silver leaf.

variations.name: Jaggery Coconut Lauki Halwa
variations.description: A rustic, dairy-light take that sweetens the lauki with jaggery and folds in fresh coconut for a chewy, caramel-toned halwa. Earthier and less milky than the classic, it leans on the natural sweetness of gourd and gud.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: sautes the lauki and coconut for a nutty, caramel-scented rustic halwa

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted in off the heat to sweeten the halwa with deep, earthy caramel

steps: Peel and grate the bottle gourd to yield 4 cups, then squeeze out most of the water and reserve the pulp.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai, fry 3 tbsp cashews to golden, then lightly toast 0.5 cup grated coconut for 1 minute and set both aside.
Saute the grated lauki in the same ghee over medium heat for 8 minutes until soft and its raw smell is gone.
Pour in 1 cup milk and simmer for 12 to 15 minutes, stirring, until the milk is absorbed and the lauki is pulpy.
Lower the heat and stir in 0.6 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder off the boil so the milk does not split, cooking 4 to 5 minutes until it thickens.
Fold in the toasted coconut, cashews and 0.5 tsp cardamom, then serve the halwa warm.
tips: Add the jaggery only after taking the pan off a hard boil, as it can curdle the small amount of milk.
Toast the coconut just until fragrant; browning it too much makes the halwa taste bitter.
Fresh coconut gives the best chew, but desiccated coconut soaked in warm milk works at a pinch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with an extra scatter of toasted coconut, or chilled as a rustic dessert after a South Indian meal.

variations.name: Kesar Malai Lauki Halwa
variations.description: A regal, creamy lauki halwa finished with fresh cream and saffron for a pale-gold, melt-in-the-mouth pudding. Silkier and more luxurious than the everyday version, it is dressed with rose and slivered almonds for the festive table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: sautes the lauki and enriches the cream-finished halwa for a silky body

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: sweetens the malai halwa while keeping the saffron colour bright and clean

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm milk to give the halwa its pale-gold hue and floral aroma

steps: Soak 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp of warm milk taken from the 3 cups and set aside to bloom.
Peel and grate the bottle gourd to yield 4 cups, squeeze out excess water, and reserve the pulp.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and saute the grated lauki over medium heat for 7 minutes until soft and fragrant.
Add the remaining milk and simmer on medium-low heat for 20 to 25 minutes, stirring, until it reduces and the lauki is pulpy.
Stir in 0.6 cup Anveshan Khandsari and the bloomed saffron milk, cooking 5 minutes until thick, then lower the heat and fold in 0.5 cup fresh cream off the boil.
Warm through for 2 minutes without boiling, add 0.5 tsp cardamom, and serve garnished with slivered almonds.
tips: Add the cream off the boil and warm gently so it enriches the halwa without splitting.
Reduce the milk well before adding cream, or the halwa stays thin and soupy.
A drop of rose water stirred in at the end lifts this halwa into a truly regal dessert.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled in small glasses as a dinner-party dessert, topped with saffron strands, almond slivers and dried rose petals.

variations.name: Sweet and Sour Lemon Pickle
variations.description: A North Indian nimbu ka meetha achar where cured lemon pieces are cooked into a glossy jaggery syrup spiked with warm garam spices, turning sharp and sweet at once. The dark, sticky pickle is gentle enough for children and a favourite with stuffed parathas. Its balance of sweet, sour and spice makes it disappear fast from the jar.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Melted into a dark syrup, it gives this pickle its signature sweet-sour balance and glossy coat

steps: Cut 10 dry lemons into 8 pieces each, toss with 3 tbsp salt, and keep covered in a dry bowl for 4-5 days, shaking daily until the rinds soften.
Once soft, transfer the lemons and their released juice to a heavy pan and add 2 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder.
Cook on medium flame for 12-15 minutes, stirring, until the jaggery melts and thickens into a syrup that coats the lemon pieces.
Lower the heat and stir in 2 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tbsp fennel powder, 1 tsp black pepper, 2 tsp chilli powder and 1 tsp black salt.
Simmer another 3 minutes until the syrup turns thick and dark, then switch off.
Cool completely and store in a dry jar; the flavour deepens further over the first week.
tips: Curing the lemons in salt for a few days first removes bitterness before the sweet cooking, so do not rush it.
Cook the syrup only until it coats the pieces; if boiled too long the jaggery sets rock-hard on cooling.
A pinch of extra black salt lifts the whole thing if it tastes flat once cooled.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with hot aloo or gobi parathas, or serve as a sweet accent beside a spicy thali.

variations.name: South Indian Tempered Lemon Pickle
variations.description: A tangy, oil-rich lemon pickle in the Tamil-Andhra style, finished with a mustard-fenugreek tempering and a generous pour of gingelly oil that carries the spices deep into the rinds. Ready in a day rather than weeks, it is sharp, savoury and fiery. The hot tempering is what sets it apart from the slow-cured northern jar.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil is the South Indian pickling fat, blooming the tempering and preserving the tangy rinds

steps: Cut 10 dry lemons into small pieces, mix with 4 tbsp salt and 1 tsp turmeric, and keep in a dry jar for 3-4 days, shaking daily until the skins soften.
Stir 3 tbsp chilli powder and 1 tsp fenugreek powder into the softened lemons.
Heat 0.75 cups Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pan until it shimmers, then lower the flame to medium.
Splutter 1 tbsp mustard seeds, add 0.5 tsp asafoetida and 2 sprigs curry leaves, and let them crackle for 30 seconds.
Switch off, let the tempering cool for a minute, then pour it over the spiced lemon pieces and mix thoroughly.
Pack into a dry jar with the oil covering the top and rest a day before serving; it keeps for months refrigerated.
tips: The salt-cure step is still needed to soften the rinds; the tempering only adds flavour, not curing.
Keep a layer of gingelly oil floating on top to seal the pickle and extend its life.
Warm, not smoking, oil for the tempering keeps the curry leaves crisp and the asafoetida from burning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with curd rice or lemon rice, and drizzle the spiced oil over hot steamed rice for extra punch.

variations.name: Instant Grated Lemon Ginger Pickle
variations.description: A bright, fresh same-day pickle where lemon is combined with plenty of ginger and green chilli for a zingy, digestive relish rather than a matured achar. Lightly cooked to soften the rind quickly, it keeps its fresh yellow colour and clean sourness. This is the pickle to make when you want tang tonight, not next month.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: Stirred in off the heat, it rounds the sharp lemon and ginger with a mellow floral sweetness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: A light saute in gingelly oil softens the rind fast and gives the fresh pickle body

steps: Cut 4 lemons into small pieces and juliennne 3 inches of ginger and 6 green chillies.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pan on medium flame and add the ginger and chillies, sauteing 2 minutes until fragrant.
Add the lemon pieces, 2 tbsp salt and the juice of the remaining 2 lemons, then cover and cook 6-8 minutes until the rinds soften.
Stir in 1 tsp roasted cumin powder and 0.5 tsp black pepper and cook 1 more minute.
Switch off the flame, cool for 5 minutes, then stir in 2 tbsp Anveshan Honey so it does not lose its raw goodness.
Cool completely and store in a dry jar; it is ready at once and keeps 2 weeks refrigerated.
tips: Adding the honey off the heat keeps its flavour and benefits intact, so never boil it in.
The extra ginger makes this a gentle digestive, ideal after a heavy meal.
Keep it refrigerated as it has less salt than a cured pickle and is meant to be eaten fresh.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve a spoon alongside dal-rice or with a warm paratha, or nibble a piece before a meal to spark the appetite.

variations.name: Classic Aam ki Launji
variations.description: A North Indian summer favourite where firm raw mango is simmered with jaggery and whole spices into a glossy sweet-sour-spicy relish. Fennel, nigella and cumin bloom in hot oil before the mango goes in, giving the launji its signature aroma. It keeps for weeks and turns a simple dal-roti meal into something special.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A neutral wood-pressed oil that blooms the whole spices without masking the mango's tang

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Melts into a deep caramel syrup that balances the sour mango far better than refined sugar

steps: Peel 2 raw mangoes and cut the flesh into thin 1-inch strips, discarding the stones and reserving any juice.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a heavy pan on medium flame and crackle 1 tsp fennel, 0.5 tsp nigella and 0.5 tsp cumin for about 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the mango strips with 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 0.75 tsp salt, and saute for 3-4 minutes until the edges soften.
Pour in 0.75 cups water, cover, and simmer on low for 8-10 minutes until the mango turns translucent and tender.
Stir in 0.75 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook uncovered for 6-8 minutes, stirring often, until the syrup thickens and coats the mango with a glossy sheen.
Turn off the heat, let it cool completely so it thickens further, and transfer to a clean dry jar.
tips: Choose a sour, firm mango like a raw totapuri; a stringy or half-ripe one turns mushy and loses its bite.
The launji thickens noticeably as it cools, so pull it off the heat while the syrup still looks slightly runny.
Stored in a sterilised jar in the fridge it keeps for up to three weeks; always use a dry spoon.
variations.servingSuggestion: Spoon alongside plain parathas and a bowl of curd, or serve as a sweet-tart counterpoint to a spicy rajma-chawal plate.

variations.name: Bengali Aam Chutney
variations.description: A thin, syrupy Bengali aamer chatni served near the end of a festive meal to cleanse the palate. Mustard oil and the five-spice panch phoron give it a sharp, aromatic base, while raisins and jaggery lend fruity sweetness. Traditionally eaten with papad after the main course rather than as a side.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: The pungent Bengali cooking fat that gives this chatni its unmistakable sharp aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Dissolves into a light amber syrup that keeps the chatni fruity rather than cloying

steps: Peel 2 raw mangoes and cut them into thin wedges, keeping the pieces roughly even so they cook at the same rate.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pan until it just smokes, lower the flame, and temper 1 tsp panch phoron and 1 broken red chilli for 20 seconds until they splutter.
Add the mango wedges with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt, and stir-fry for 2-3 minutes until they glisten.
Pour in 1.25 cups water, cover, and simmer on low for 8-10 minutes until the mango is soft but still holding shape.
Add 0.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 2 tbsp raisins, and simmer uncovered for 5-6 minutes until the chatni is loose and syrupy.
Sprinkle 0.5 tsp roasted panch phoron powder, stir once, and cool; it should stay pourable, not jam-like.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to smoking point first, then cool it slightly before tempering, to mellow its raw pungency.
This chatni is meant to be thin and drinkable; if it sets too thick on cooling, loosen it with a spoon of warm water.
Dry-roasting and grinding a little extra panch phoron to finish gives the classic Bengali fragrance.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled in a small bowl at the close of a rice meal, scooped up with crisp fried papad in true Bengali fashion.

variations.name: South Indian Mango Pachadi
variations.description: A Tamil-style grated raw mango pachadi finished with fresh coconut and a crackling coconut-oil tempering. Quick to make and bright with mustard seeds and curry leaves, it balances sour mango against a whisper of jaggery. Unlike the slow North Indian launji, this one comes together in minutes and is eaten fresh.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: The classic Tamil tempering fat that carries the mustard and curry-leaf aroma into the pachadi

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Just a spoonful to round off the sourness without turning the pachadi sweet

steps: Peel and finely grate 1 large raw mango, then grind it briefly with 0.5 cups grated coconut and 2 green chillies to a coarse, textured paste.
Transfer the paste to a bowl, mix in 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.5 tsp salt, and taste to balance the sour and sweet.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan on medium flame until it shimmers.
Add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop for 20 seconds, then add 1 tsp urad dal and 2 broken red chillies and fry until the dal turns golden.
Toss in 10 curry leaves, let them crisp for 5 seconds, and pour the sizzling tempering over the mango-coconut mixture.
Stir everything together and rest 5 minutes so the flavours meld before serving.
tips: Grind the mango coarsely, not to a smooth puree; a little texture is what defines a good pachadi.
Use a sharply sour mango so the single spoon of jaggery is enough to balance it.
Eat within a day for the freshest taste, as the raw grated mango does not keep like a cooked chutney.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a tangy side with curd rice or lemon rice, where its coconut sweetness cuts through the richness.

variations.name: Gujarati Chundo
variations.description: The famous Gujarati chundo, a sweet grated-mango preserve traditionally set in the summer sun until the syrup runs thick and glassy. Sweetened with jaggery and spiced with roasted cumin and chilli, it balances sugar, sour and heat in every spoon. This stove-top method captures the same shine without waiting on the weather.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Draws water from the grated mango and cooks down into the thick, glossy syrup that defines chundo

steps: Peel and coarsely grate 3 raw mangoes to yield about 2 cups of shreds, discarding the stones.
In a bowl mix the grated mango with 1.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt, and let it stand for 30 minutes until the jaggery starts to dissolve into a syrup.
Tip the mixture into a heavy pan and cook on low-medium, stirring often, for 12-15 minutes as the syrup rises and reduces.
Test the thickness by dropping a little syrup on a plate; it is ready when it holds a soft one-string consistency and the shreds turn translucent.
Stir in 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 0.25 tsp cardamom powder, cook 1 more minute, and switch off.
Cool completely, then bottle in a clean dry jar where it thickens to a spoonable, jam-like preserve.
tips: Do not overcook past the one-string stage or the chundo will crystallise and harden once cold.
Add the roasted cumin and chilli only at the end so their aroma stays bright in the finished preserve.
For the traditional sun-set version, cover the jar with muslin and leave it in strong sunlight for 4-5 days, stirring daily.
variations.servingSuggestion: Spread thickly inside a hot thepla or serve beside khichdi and kadhi for the classic sweet note of a Gujarati thali.

variations.name: Classic Punjabi Aam ka Achar
variations.description: The quintessential North Indian raw-mango pickle where firm sour mango pieces are cured in salt, coated in coarsely ground fennel, mustard and fenugreek, and matured under a blanket of mustard oil. Sun-ripened over days, it turns dark, glossy and intensely tangy. A jar of this on the shelf is the mark of a well-run Punjabi kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Heated to smoking and cooled, this wood-pressed mustard oil is the pungent preserving medium that submerges and matures the pickle

steps: Wash and wipe 1 kg raw mangoes completely dry, then cut into 1-inch pieces with the tender inner shell, discarding the hard seed.
Toss the pieces with 3 tbsp salt and 1 tbsp turmeric, spread in a clean dry bowl, cover with a cloth, and leave 6-8 hours until they release water.
Dry-roast 4 tbsp fennel, 3 tbsp mustard seeds and 2 tbsp fenugreek on low flame for 2 minutes, cool, and grind coarse.
Drain the mango pieces, pat them dry, and mix with the ground spices, 1 tbsp nigella, remaining 1 tbsp turmeric, 3 tbsp chilli powder and 3 tbsp salt until every piece is coated.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Mustard Oil until it smokes, switch off, and cool completely, then pour enough over the mango to submerge it and pack into a sterile dry jar.
Cover the mouth with muslin and sun the jar for 5-7 days, stirring daily with a dry spoon, until the pieces soften and darken.
tips: Every utensil, jar and spoon must be bone dry, as a single drop of water invites mould and spoils the whole batch.
Heating the mustard oil to smoking point removes its raw pungency and is essential for a long shelf life.
Keep the pickle always submerged under oil; top up with more cooled mustard oil if the level drops.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve a piece alongside dal-chawal, curd rice or stuffed parathas, with the spiced oil drizzled over plain rice.

variations.name: Andhra Avakaya
variations.description: The legendary Andhra mango pickle, ferociously hot and coarse, built on a high ratio of ground mustard and red chilli powder that forms a thick spice paste around each mango piece. Unlike northern pickles it is not sun-cured but matured in a crock under gingelly and mustard oil. A spoon with hot rice and ghee is a Telugu institution.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil is the classic avakaya medium, binding the fiery spice paste and preserving the mango

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: A splash added on top lends the sharp pungency that distinguishes a true avakaya

steps: Wipe 1 kg mangoes fully dry and chop into large 1.5-inch chunks keeping a bit of the inner shell so pieces hold together.
Dry-roast 2 tbsp fenugreek on low flame for 1 minute, cool, and grind to a fine powder.
In a large dry bowl combine 1 cup mustard powder, 1 cup chilli powder, 0.75 cup salt, 1 tbsp turmeric and the fenugreek powder.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Sesame Oil until it smokes, cool fully, then mix half of it into the spices to a thick paste.
Fold the mango chunks and 20 garlic cloves through the paste until coated, pack into a dry ceramic jar, and pour the remaining sesame oil plus 0.5 cup cooled Anveshan Mustard Oil on top to seal.
Cover and rest in a cool dark spot for 8-10 days, stirring with a dry spoon every 2 days until the mango softens and the oil floats clear on top.
tips: Use the special hard, extra-sour avakaya mango variety if you can find it, as regular mangoes turn mushy in this strong brine.
The pickle looks alarmingly dry at first, but the mango releases juice over days and loosens the paste, so resist adding water.
Always keep a clean layer of oil floating on top to lock out air and preserve the batch for a year.
variations.servingSuggestion: Mash a piece into steaming rice with a generous spoon of ghee, the classic first meal of an Andhra summer.

variations.name: Gujarati Chunda
variations.description: A sweet-and-spicy grated mango preserve from Gujarat where shredded raw mango is cooked down with jaggery into a glistening, syrupy pickle flecked with roasted cumin and chilli. It has none of the oil or heat of a savoury achar, instead balancing sharp mango against caramel sweetness. Traditionally set in the sun until the syrup reaches a thick, one-string consistency.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Replaces refined sugar to cook the grated mango into a mineral-rich, deep amber syrup

steps: Peel and coarsely grate 1 kg raw mangoes, then toss with 2 tsp salt and 1 tsp turmeric and set aside 1 hour to draw out juice.
Transfer the grated mango with its juices to a heavy pan, add 3 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder, and cook on medium flame stirring often.
Simmer 20-25 minutes as the jaggery melts and the mixture thickens into a glossy syrup that coats the mango strands.
Test for doneness by lifting a spoon; the syrup should fall in a thick single thread rather than a runny drizzle.
Switch off and stir in 2 tsp roasted cumin powder, 2 tsp chilli powder and 0.5 tsp cardamom powder while still warm.
Cool completely and store in a dry sterile jar, where it keeps for months without any oil.
tips: Cook only to a one-string consistency; over-boiling turns the chunda hard and grainy once it cools.
Roast and grind the cumin fresh, as its smoky note is what balances the deep jaggery sweetness.
If you prefer the sun-set method, mix everything raw and leave the covered bowl in strong sun for 8-10 days, stirring daily.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a sweet foil to spicy theplas, khakhra, or a plain aloo paratha, or spread on hot buttered toast.

variations.name: Instant Cooked Mango Pickle
variations.description: A quick tempered pickle ready to eat the same day, where mango pieces are simmered briefly in a hot spice tempering rather than cured over weeks. The gentle cooking softens the mango and blooms the spices instantly, giving a fresh tangy pickle without the wait. Ideal when a craving strikes and there is no matured jar in the house.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A spoonful rounds the tang with a gentle sweetness and gives the instant pickle a glossy finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Heated till smoking then cooled slightly, it tempers the spices and lightly cooks the mango

steps: Wash, dry and cut 3 raw mangoes into small 0.5-inch pieces with the tender shell.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pan until it just smokes, then lower the flame to medium.
Splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp fenugreek for 30 seconds, add 0.25 tsp asafoetida, and let it foam.
Add the mango pieces with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp chilli powder, 1 tsp fennel powder and 2 tsp salt, and stir well to coat.
Cover and cook on low flame for 8-10 minutes until the mango just softens but still holds shape, then stir in 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder until it dissolves.
Cool completely and store in a dry jar; it is ready to eat at once and keeps 2-3 weeks refrigerated.
tips: Cut the pieces small so they soften quickly in the short cooking time.
Cook only until the mango turns tender-crisp; overcooking makes it mushy and loses the fresh bite.
Let it sit a few hours before serving so the spices penetrate, though it can be eaten straight away.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve fresh with hot khichdi, curd rice or a simple dal-roti meal for an instant burst of tang.

variations.name: Classic Masala Chaas
variations.description: The everyday spiced buttermilk of North Indian homes, thinner and lighter than lassi: curd whisked down with plenty of water, seasoned with roasted cumin and black salt, and finished with a fragrant Anveshan Ghee tadka of jeera and hing. It is the drink that closes a heavy meal and settles the stomach in one glass.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A jeera-hing tadka in bilona ghee gives dhaba-style chaas its digestive, aromatic finish

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups curd with 2.5 cups chilled water until it is thin, smooth and lightly frothy, the classic pourable chaas consistency.
Stir in 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp black salt and 0.25 tsp black pepper until dissolved evenly.
Heat 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan on medium heat and crackle 0.5 tsp cumin seeds for about 15 seconds until fragrant.
Switch off the heat and add 0.25 tsp hing to the ghee, letting it fizz for 5 seconds without burning.
Cool the tadka slightly, then stir it into the chaas along with 6 torn mint leaves and 1 tbsp chopped coriander.
Chill for 10 minutes and serve in 4 glasses, stirring once before pouring.
tips: Chaas should be thin enough to gulp, not sip; if it coats the glass like lassi, whisk in more water.
Add the hing off the heat, as it scorches in seconds and turns the whole tadka bitter.
Sour curd actually works better here than for lassi, since the extra water tames the tang.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at the end of a rich dal-rice or rajma-chawal meal, or keep a jug in the fridge through summer to sip through the afternoon.

variations.name: South Indian Neer More
variations.description: The Tamil-Kerala spiced buttermilk drunk to beat the coastal heat: watery, gentle curd tempered in Anveshan Coconut Oil with mustard, curry leaves and hing, sharpened by ginger and green chilli. Lighter than North Indian chaas and never blended thick, it is sipped through the day and offered at temples as a cooling prasadam.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil is the native cooking fat of the South and gives neer more its coastal aroma

steps: Whisk 1 cup curd with 3 cups chilled water and 0.5 tsp salt until very thin and watery, the way neer more is always kept.
Add 1 tsp grated ginger and 1 chopped green chilli to the buttermilk and set it in the fridge.
Heat 1 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan on medium and splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds for about 15 seconds.
Add 0.5 tsp urad dal and fry until it turns light gold, then drop in 12 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp hing and let them crackle for 10 seconds.
Cool the tempering for a minute and stir it into the chilled buttermilk so the curd does not warm up.
Finish with 1 tbsp chopped coriander and serve in 4 glasses without any ice, lightly chilled.
tips: Neer more is meant to be almost water-thin; resist adding more curd or it starts drinking like North Indian chaas.
Fresh curry leaves fried in coconut oil are the whole soul of the drink, so do not skip or substitute them.
A grating of fresh coconut stirred in at the end is a lovely Kerala addition if you have it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a between-meals cooler or pour a small tumbler alongside a South Indian rice thali; it also revives you instantly after time in the sun.

variations.name: Gujarati Vaghareli Chaas
variations.description: The sweet-savoury tempered buttermilk of a Gujarati thali, where a mustard-cumin vaghar in Anveshan Groundnut Oil meets a small pinch of Anveshan Jaggery Powder to hit the region's signature balance. Warmly spiced with green chilli and ginger paste, it is served in a katori and drunk between mouthfuls of rice and shaak.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Peanut oil is the everyday Gujarati cooking fat and carries the vaghar without overpowering the curd

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A tiny amount of jaggery gives the sweet-savoury balance that defines Gujarati chaas

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups curd with 2.5 cups chilled water, 0.5 tsp salt and 1 tsp ginger-green chilli paste until smooth and pourable.
Dissolve 0.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder into the buttermilk by whisking well, then chill it.
Heat 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a small pan on medium and pop 0.5 tsp mustard seeds fully, about 20 seconds.
Add 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, 8 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp hing and let them crackle for 10 seconds until aromatic.
Cool the vaghar briefly, then stir it through the chilled buttermilk in a steady stream.
Garnish with 1 tbsp chopped coriander and serve in small katoris or glasses alongside the meal.
tips: The jaggery should be barely detectable; you want a rounded, mellow chaas, not a sweet one.
Gujarati chaas is traditionally served at room temperature or only lightly chilled, never icy, so the vaghar stays fragrant.
Grind a fresh ginger-chilli paste for the day rather than using a jarred one; the difference in freshness is obvious.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle into katoris as part of a full Gujarati thali with dal, kadhi, shaak and rotli; it also makes a soothing plain drink with khichdi on a light-supper night.

variations.name: Jaljeera Masala Chaas
variations.description: A punchy street-style chaas that borrows the tongue-tingling spice blend of jaljeera, with amchur, dry mint and roasted cumin, then rounds the sourness with a touch of Anveshan Honey. Tangy, minty and deeply refreshing, it is the drink that revives you at a north Indian bazaar in peak summer.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: Raw honey balances the sharp amchur and lemon so the chaas tastes tangy, not sour

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups curd with 2.5 cups chilled water until thin and smooth, then set aside.
In a small bowl mix 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp amchur, 0.75 tsp black salt, 0.5 tsp dry mint powder and 0.5 tsp chaat masala into your jaljeera blend.
Whisk this spice blend into the buttermilk along with 0.5 tsp grated ginger until no dry pockets remain.
Stir in 2 tsp Anveshan Honey and 1 tsp lemon juice, tasting so the drink lands tangy and balanced rather than harshly sour.
Tear in 8 mint leaves and chill the chaas for 15 minutes so the spices bloom into the curd.
Stir well and serve in 4 glasses over ice, with an extra pinch of chaat masala on top.
tips: Bloom the dry spices into the buttermilk and give it 15 minutes; freshly mixed, the amchur tastes raw and chalky.
Adjust honey and lemon together, a little at a time, until the sweet-sour balance feels right on your tongue.
Keep a jar of the dry jaljeera blend ready so you can shake up a glass in seconds on a hot day.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled with chaat, kachori or any fried street snack; a salted rim and a lemon wheel on the glass turn it into a mocktail for guests.

variations.name: Classic Pudina Chutney
variations.description: A refreshing raw pudina chutney where fresh mint is ground with a little coriander, green chilli and ginger, then sharpened with lemon and roasted cumin. A spoon of sattu gives it body so it holds on a fritter without any oil. Cooling, tangy and vivid green, it is the classic sidekick to tikkas and chaat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Roasted-gram sattu thickens the raw chutney and tames the sharpness of the mint

steps: Pick 1.5 cups mint leaves off their stems, which can taste bitter, and add them to a blender with 0.5 cups coriander.
Add 2 green chillies, 0.5 inch ginger, 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp black salt and 0.5 tsp regular salt.
Spoon in 2 tbsp Anveshan Sattu to thicken the chutney and mellow the raw mint.
Pour in 1 tbsp lemon juice and 3 tbsp cold water, then grind to a smooth, thick paste.
Scrape down the sides and pulse again, adding a little more cold water only if the blades stall.
Taste for salt and sourness, then transfer to a bowl and serve fresh.
tips: Use only the leaves; mint stems carry a bitter note that dulls the fresh flavour.
Grind with chilled water and in short bursts to lock in the bright green colour.
A little black salt gives the chutney its signature chaat-shop tang, so do not swap it out entirely.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with paneer tikka and kebabs, or thin it slightly to spoon over aloo tikki and dahi chaat.

variations.name: Mint-Yogurt Cooling Chutney
variations.description: A creamy mint-and-yogurt chutney that behaves like a thin raita, cooling the palate against rich tandoori food. Whisked hung curd carries the mint, while black salt and roasted cumin add a savoury tang and honey softens the edge. Pale mint-green and lightly sweet, it is the dip that tames the heat of a grill.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: A spoon of raw honey balances the tang of the curd and the heat of the mint

steps: Grind 1 cup mint leaves with 1 green chilli and 1 tsp lemon juice to a smooth paste using barely a spoon of water.
Whisk 1 cup hung curd in a bowl until it is silky and free of lumps.
Stir the mint paste into the curd until the mixture turns an even pale green.
Season with 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp black salt and 0.5 tsp regular salt.
Drizzle in 1 tsp Anveshan Honey, mix well, and taste to balance the tang and sweetness.
Refrigerate for 15 minutes so it thickens slightly and the flavours settle before serving.
tips: Use thick, well-drained hung curd so the chutney stays creamy rather than watery.
Blend the mint separately and fold it in, which stops the yogurt from turning grainy.
If it thickens too much in the fridge, loosen with a spoon of chilled milk, not water, to keep it rich.
