variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled beside biryani and grilled kebabs, or as a cooling dip for crisp onion pakoras.

variations.name: Mint-Onion Chutney
variations.description: The dark, punchy mint-onion chutney set out in little steel bowls at Punjabi dhabas. Raw onion and a hit of tamarind give it a sweet-sour bite, while mustard oil lends the sharp, roadside pungency. Thicker and gutsier than a delicate green chutney, it is made to be scooped up by the fistful with tandoori roti.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: A spoon of raw wood-pressed mustard oil gives this chutney its sharp, unmistakable dhaba pungency

steps: Roughly chop 1 onion and add it to a blender with 1 cup mint leaves and 2 green chillies.
Add 1 tsp tamarind, 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 0.75 tsp salt.
Pour in 2 tbsp water and grind to a thick, coarse chutney, keeping a little texture from the onion.
Transfer to a bowl and stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil, which sharpens the whole chutney with its pungency.
Taste and adjust the salt and tamarind so the sweet-sour balance is pronounced.
Rest for 10 minutes so the raw onion softens into the mint before serving.
tips: Squeeze the ground chutney lightly if the onion releases too much water and thins it out.
Use the mustard oil raw and unheated; that biting edge is what makes it taste like a dhaba.
It tastes best a couple of hours after making, once the onion loses its raw sharpness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot tandoori rotis and dal makhani, or alongside a plate of amritsari kulcha.

variations.name: Mint-Coconut Chutney
variations.description: A South Indian take that grinds mint with fresh coconut and roasted chana dal into a smooth, mild chutney finished with a coconut-oil tempering. The coconut rounds out the mint's sharpness into something gentle and creamy, and curry leaves give it a fragrant snap. It is a cooling green partner for dosa and idli.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: The classic tempering fat that fries the mustard and dal and complements the fresh coconut

steps: Grind 1 cup mint, 0.5 cups grated coconut, 2 tbsp roasted chana dal, 2 green chillies, 0.5 inch ginger and 0.75 tsp salt with 0.5 cups water to a smooth chutney.
Transfer to a bowl and loosen with a splash of water if it is too thick to spoon.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan on medium flame until it shimmers.
Add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop for 20 seconds, then add 1 tsp urad dal and fry until golden.
Toss in 10 curry leaves, let them crackle for 5 seconds, and pour the sizzling tempering over the chutney.
Stir it through gently just before serving so the tempering aroma stays fresh.
tips: Blanch the mint in hot water for 10 seconds before grinding to keep the chutney a bright green.
Roasted chana dal thickens the chutney and adds a nutty note, so measure it generously.
Serve within a few hours, as mint darkens faster than coriander once ground.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with crisp masala dosa and hot sambar, or with steamed idlis for a fragrant breakfast plate.

variations.name: Classic Motichoor Ladoo
variations.description: The celebrated wedding sweet of tiny gram-flour pearls, fried through a fine perforated ladle so the boondi come out as small as poppy seeds, then soaked in one-string sugar syrup and pressed while warm. The pearls stay soft and just cling together, melting on the tongue. Getting the boondi tiny and evenly round is the whole art of motichoor.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: cooked to a one-string syrup that keeps the pearls soft and glossy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: greases your palms and enriches the finished ladoo

steps: Whisk 2 cups fine besan with about 1 cup water into a smooth, lump-free pouring batter of thin dropping consistency and rest it for 10 minutes.
Dissolve 2 cups Anveshan Khandsari Sugar in the remaining water and cook to a one-string syrup, about 8 minutes, then keep it warm with 1 tsp cardamom and a pinch of camphor stirred in.
Heat the oil to medium, hold a fine-holed perforated ladle over it, and pour batter through so tiny pearls drop and fry for about 1 minute until just set but not crisp.
Drain the boondi and drop them straight into the warm syrup, pressing gently so every pearl soaks; repeat until all the batter is fried.
Let the soaked boondi sit for 10 minutes until they swell and the syrup is mostly absorbed, then mix in the melon seeds and 1 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee.
Grease your palms with the remaining ghee and press portions firmly into 14 soft ladoos while still warm, resting them for 30 minutes to hold shape.
tips: Keep the batter thin enough to fall as tiny drops; a thick batter gives long tails instead of round pearls.
Fry the boondi only until set, not crisp, or they won't soak the syrup and the ladoo will be hard.
If the ladoos won't hold, the syrup was too thin; warm the mix and simmer briefly to thicken, then re-shape.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at weddings and pujas on a garnished platter, each ladoo crowned with a sliver of pistachio or edible silver leaf.

variations.name: Kesar Motichoor Ladoo
variations.description: A saffron-perfumed motichoor where the pearls take on a warm orange glow and floral aroma from generous kesar bloomed into the syrup. This is the version seen at grand weddings, richer and more fragrant than the plain one. A tint of saffron in the batter itself deepens the colour of every pearl.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: the syrup base that carries the saffron into every pearl

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm milk for colour, and a few strands crushed into the batter

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: enriches the pearls and greases your palms for shaping

steps: Soak 1 tsp Anveshan Saffron in the warm milk for 10 minutes, then crush half the strands into a smooth besan batter made with about 1 cup water.
Cook 2 cups Anveshan Khandsari Sugar with the remaining water to a one-string syrup, about 8 minutes, and stir in the saffron milk, 1 tsp cardamom and keep warm.
Heat the oil to medium and pour the saffron batter through a fine perforated ladle so tiny pearls drop and fry for about 1 minute until just set.
Drain each batch of boondi into the warm saffron syrup, pressing gently so the colour and aroma soak in.
After all the batter is fried, rest the soaked boondi for 10 minutes to swell, then mix in the slivered pistachios and 1 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee.
Grease your palms with the remaining ghee and press into 14 soft ladoos while warm, resting 30 minutes to set.
tips: Bloom the saffron in warm milk first; adding it dry wastes most of its colour and scent.
A touch of saffron in the batter as well as the syrup gives a far more even glow than syrup alone.
Do not over-fry the pearls, or the saffron syrup can't penetrate and the ladoo turns dense.
variations.servingSuggestion: Present these golden-orange ladoos on a festive thali garnished with pistachio and a whisper of silver leaf for weddings.

variations.name: Jaggery Motichoor Ladoo
variations.description: A rustic, less-refined take that soaks the tiny boondi in jaggery syrup instead of white sugar, giving deep amber pearls with a earthy caramel note. It is a wholesome twist that trades the pale prettiness of classic motichoor for richer flavour. The jaggery syrup needs careful straining to stay clear.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted and strained into a one-string syrup that colours the pearls amber

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: enriches the ladoo and stops the jaggery pearls sticking to your palms

steps: Whisk 2 cups fine besan with about 1 cup water into a smooth, thin dropping batter and rest for 10 minutes.
Melt 2 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with the remaining water, strain out any grit, then cook to a one-string syrup and stir in 1 tsp cardamom and 0.5 tsp dry ginger.
Heat the groundnut oil to medium and pour the batter through a fine perforated ladle so tiny pearls fall and fry for about 1 minute until just set.
Drain each batch and slip the pearls into the warm jaggery syrup, pressing so they soak evenly.
Rest the soaked boondi for 10 minutes to absorb the syrup, then mix in the chopped cashews and 1 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee.
Grease your palms with the remaining ghee and press into 14 soft ladoos while warm, letting them set for 30 minutes.
tips: Always strain the melted jaggery; unstrained grit makes the syrup cloudy and the pearls gritty.
The dry ginger cuts the heaviness of jaggery and keeps these winter-friendly.
Jaggery syrup thickens faster than sugar, so keep it warm and loose while you finish frying.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these amber ladoos during Sankranti and winter festivals with a glass of warm milk.

variations.name: Mawa Motichoor Ladoo
variations.description: An extra-rich motichoor folded with crumbled khoya so the pearls bind into a softer, creamier ladoo that melts even faster than the classic. The mawa adds a milk-fudge richness prized in Benares-style motichoor. These are the most indulgent and the most perishable of the four.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: cooked to a one-string syrup to soak the pearls before the mawa is folded in

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: cooks the mawa lightly and greases your palms

steps: Whisk 2 cups fine besan with about 1 cup water into a smooth thin batter and rest for 10 minutes.
Cook 2 cups Anveshan Khandsari Sugar with the remaining water to a one-string syrup, about 8 minutes, then stir in 1 tsp cardamom and keep warm.
Heat the oil to medium and pour the batter through a fine perforated ladle so tiny pearls drop and fry for about 1 minute until just set, then soak each batch in the warm syrup.
Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee in a pan and cook the grated khoya on low heat for 3-4 minutes until soft and just golden.
Fold the warm mawa and slivered almonds into the syrup-soaked boondi until evenly combined and the mixture turns creamy.
Grease your palms with the remaining ghee and press into 14 soft ladoos while warm, then chill for 20 minutes to firm up.
tips: Cook the mawa only until soft; over-browning makes it grainy and the ladoos dry.
Because of the khoya, refrigerate these and eat within 2-3 days.
Fold the mawa in while everything is warm so it melts evenly instead of leaving lumps.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these creamy ladoos chilled at Diwali, garnished with slivered almonds and a light dusting of cardamom.

variations.name: Classic Murmura Ladoo
variations.description: These Classic Murmura Ladoos are airy puffed-rice balls bound in a soft-crack jaggery syrup scented with cardamom, a beloved winter and festival sweet across Maharashtra and North India. Light as a whisper yet satisfyingly crunchy, they come together in minutes with almost no equipment.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melts into a glossy soft-crack syrup that binds the light murmura without any refined sugar

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoon in the syrup keeps the ladoos from turning sticky and adds a nutty aroma

steps: Dry-roast the 4 cups puffed rice in a wide kadai over low heat for 3 to 4 minutes until crisp, then tip into a large bowl and keep warm.
In the same kadai warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then add 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 3 tbsp water and melt over low heat, stirring, for about 5 minutes.
Cook the syrup until it reaches soft-crack stage, when a drop dropped in cold water forms a firm ball, about 3 more minutes, then switch off the heat.
Quickly stir in 0.5 tsp cardamom powder, 0.25 tsp dry ginger powder, a pinch of salt and 3 tbsp roasted peanuts.
Pour the hot syrup over the warm puffed rice and fold fast with a greased spatula until every grain is coated.
While still warm enough to handle, grease your palms with ghee and press firmly into 12 lemon-sized ladoos, then cool completely so they set crisp.
tips: Test the syrup carefully in cold water; too soft and the ladoos slump, too hard and they turn into a brittle you cannot roll.
Shape the ladoos while the mixture is warm but bearable, pressing firmly so they hold without falling apart.
Store in an airtight jar for up to two weeks; a moisture-free jar keeps the murmura from going chewy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile into a brass bowl for Diwali or Makar Sankranti and serve alongside warm masala chai.

variations.name: Coconut Murmura Ladoo
variations.description: This coastal-style ladoo folds toasted desiccated coconut and coconut oil through the puffed rice for a fragrant, faintly tropical sweetness. The coconut crisps in the syrup and gives every bite a delicate flaky richness quite unlike the plain classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: pairs beautifully with coconut, giving a caramel-toffee note as it reaches soft-crack

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: doubles the coconut aroma and keeps the syrup from crystallising

steps: Dry-roast the 4 cups puffed rice over low heat for 3 minutes until crisp and set aside in a large bowl.
Toast 0.5 cup desiccated coconut in the dry kadai for 2 minutes until pale golden and fragrant, then add to the puffed rice.
Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in the kadai, fry 3 tbsp cashews and 2 tbsp raisins until the cashews turn golden, then lift them into the bowl.
Add 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 3 tbsp water to the same oil and melt over low heat for 6 to 7 minutes until it reaches soft-crack stage.
Turn off the heat, stir in 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and a pinch of salt, then pour the syrup over the coconut and puffed-rice mixture.
Fold quickly with a greased spatula and press into 12 firm ladoos with greased palms, then cool completely until crunchy.
tips: Toast the coconut only until pale gold; over-browning turns it bitter and speckles the ladoos.
Coconut oil sets harder than ghee, so work fast once the syrup is poured.
Keep the roasted coconut and nuts warm so the syrup does not seize on contact.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with filter coffee or pack into a festive box lined with butter paper for gifting.

variations.name: Chocolate Murmura Ladoo
variations.description: A quick no-cook twist that binds puffed rice with melted dark chocolate and honey instead of jaggery syrup, so children can help roll them. Fudgy, crackly and lunchbox-friendly, these need no candy-thermometer precision and set firm in the fridge.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: binds the mixture and adds a floral sweetness without any cooked sugar syrup

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: melted into the chocolate for a glossy, snappy set

steps: Crisp the 3 cups puffed rice in a dry pan for 3 minutes, then cool and place in a large bowl with 3 tbsp chopped almonds.
Melt the 150 g dark chocolate with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a bowl set over barely simmering water, stirring until smooth and glossy.
Take the bowl off the heat and whisk in 3 tbsp Anveshan Honey, 2 tbsp cocoa powder, 0.5 tsp vanilla extract and a pinch of salt.
Pour the warm chocolate over the puffed rice and fold until every grain is evenly coated and the mixture holds together.
With lightly greased palms, roll into 14 small ladoos and press each in 2 tbsp desiccated coconut to coat.
Chill the ladoos on a lined tray for 20 minutes until firm, then store in the fridge.
tips: Let the chocolate cool slightly before adding honey so it does not seize into a grainy lump.
Roll the ladoos small; the chocolate is rich and a little goes a long way.
These keep best refrigerated and soften if left out in a warm kitchen for long.
variations.servingSuggestion: Tuck two into a school lunchbox or serve chilled as an after-dinner treat with cold milk.

variations.name: Classic South Indian Onion Tomato Chutney
variations.description: A tangy, mildly sweet chutney from Tamil kitchens where onions and ripe tomatoes are sauteed soft, ground smooth, and finished with a crackling mustard-curry-leaf tempering. It sits somewhere between a chutney and a thick sauce, glossy and spoonable. This is the everyday partner to idli and dosa that no South Indian breakfast table is complete without.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: The traditional gingelly oil for South Indian chutneys, it sautes the base and later carries the tempering with a warm, nutty depth

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pan on medium flame and fry 4 dried red chillies and 4 garlic cloves for 1 minute until the chillies darken and smell toasty.
Add 3 sliced onions and a pinch of salt, and saute for 6-7 minutes until soft and translucent with lightly browned edges.
Tip in 4 chopped tomatoes and 1 tsp tamarind, cover, and cook 8 minutes until the tomatoes collapse into a jammy pulp and the raw smell disappears.
Cool the mixture completely, add 1 tsp salt, and grind to a smooth chutney in a mixer with a splash of water only if needed.
For the tempering, heat the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal for 30 seconds until the dal is golden, then throw in 1 sprig curry leaves.
Pour the sizzling tempering over the ground chutney and stir it through just before serving.
tips: Cool the sauteed onion-tomato fully before grinding, as hot ingredients turn a smooth chutney watery and dull its colour.
For a milder chutney, deseed the red chillies; for a fierier one, add a couple of extra alongside the garlic.
It keeps 3-4 days refrigerated in a clean jar; add the tempering fresh each time for the best aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Spoon generously alongside crisp dosa, soft idli or medu vada, with a bowl of hot sambar on the side.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Kara Chutney
variations.description: A fiery, no-holds-barred Andhra take where extra red chillies and a bolder hit of tamarind give the onion-tomato base a deep red, lip-tingling heat. Ground slightly coarse, it clings thickly to whatever it touches. This is the chutney that wakes up a plate of plain rice or a bland tiffin in seconds.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil gives this Andhra chutney its characteristic robust body and a clean, high-heat fry

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai on medium flame and fry 1 tbsp chana dal, 1 tsp cumin and 8 dried red chillies for about 2 minutes until the dal is golden and the chillies swell.
Add 3 chopped onions and saute 6 minutes until deeply softened and edged with brown.
Stir in 3 chopped tomatoes and 1 tbsp tamarind, then cook uncovered 8 minutes until thick, oil-flecked and pulpy.
Let it cool, add 1.25 tsp salt, and grind to a slightly coarse, brick-red chutney without adding water.
Heat the last 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 sprig curry leaves for 30 seconds, and fold this tempering into the chutney.
Rest the chutney 10 minutes before serving so the heat and tang settle into a rounded, robust flavour.
tips: Toasting the chana dal and chillies first is what gives Andhra chutneys their signature nutty, roasted backbone, so do not skip that step.
Grind it coarse rather than silky; the slight texture is authentic and holds up better against plain rice.
A teaspoon of jaggery balances the fire if it turns out too sharp for your table.
variations.servingSuggestion: Mix a spoonful into hot steamed rice with a drizzle of extra oil and ghee, or serve it as a punchy side to pesarattu.

variations.name: Hotel-Style Smooth Kara Chutney
variations.description: The silky, orange-red chutney served in Chennai tiffin hotels, thickened and rounded with a handful of roasted chana dal and a knob of ghee for gloss. Grinding the dal in gives it body without any coconut, so it stays smooth and pours like a sauce. Its restaurant polish comes from a long, patient saute and a final buttery sheen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Stirred in at the finish it gives the hotel-style chutney its glossy sheen and mellow richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Used to saute the base low and slow so the onions turn sweet without browning harshly

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pan on medium-low flame, add 5 dried red chillies and 1 inch chopped ginger, and fry 1 minute until aromatic.
Add 4 thinly sliced onions and cook slowly for 10 minutes, stirring often, until they turn soft, sweet and pale gold.
Add 3 chopped tomatoes and 1 tsp tamarind and cook 8 minutes until fully broken down and thick.
Cool, then grind with 3 tbsp roasted chana dal and 1 tsp salt to a completely smooth, pourable chutney, adding a little warm water for the right consistency.
In a small pan heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 sprig curry leaves, and pour over the chutney.
Swirl in the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee off the heat for a final glossy, restaurant-style finish.
tips: Roasted chana dal is the hotel secret for body; it thickens the chutney smoothly without any coconut or cashew.
Keep the flame low while cooking the onions so they caramelise sweetly instead of scorching, which is what gives the mellow depth.
Thin any leftovers with a spoon of warm water before serving, as the dal makes it set thick in the fridge.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve pooled beside ghee roast dosa or set idli, letting its smooth sauce-like texture soak into every bite.

variations.name: No-Cook Onion Tomato Coconut Chutney
variations.description: A quick raw-ground chutney for busy mornings, blending fresh onion and tomato with coconut and green chilli straight in the mixer, then finishing with a hot tempering that lightly cooks the mix. It is fresher and brighter than the sauteed versions, with a crunch of raw onion still coming through. Ready in ten minutes when the tava is already hot.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Its clean tropical aroma lifts the raw coconut and makes the hot tempering fragrant

steps: Grind 1 roughly chopped onion, 2 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 cups grated coconut, 3 green chillies, 2 tbsp roasted peanuts, 0.5 tsp tamarind and 1 tsp salt to a coarse chutney with a splash of water.
Scrape the raw chutney into a serving bowl and taste to adjust salt and chilli.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan on medium flame until it shimmers.
Splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal for 30 seconds until the dal turns golden, then add 1 sprig curry leaves and let them crackle.
Pour the hot tempering directly over the raw chutney, where it will sizzle and lightly cook the surface.
Stir once and serve immediately while the tempering aroma is at its peak.
tips: Use a firm, mildly sweet onion so the raw bite stays pleasant rather than pungent.
The peanuts add body and a faint sweetness that stands in for a longer cooked base, so keep them in.
This is best eaten fresh; the raw onion turns sharp if stored more than a few hours.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with hot uttapam or ghee-roasted rava dosa, where the fresh, crunchy chutney contrasts the soft bread.

variations.name: Classic Pindi Chana
variations.description: The rustic Rawalpindi-style chickpeas that skip onion and tomato entirely, taking their dark colour from tea and their tang from pomegranate and dried-mango powders. The chana is coated in a nearly dry, intensely spiced mixture and finished with a smoking mustard-oil temper. Earthy, tangy and boldly spiced, it is a Punjabi street legend.

ingredients.name: White chickpeas (kabuli chana)
ingredients.note: soaked overnight

ingredients.name: Black tea
ingredients.note: tied in a muslin bundle

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: smoking-hot mustard oil gives pindi chana its characteristic pungent, street-style finish

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: julienned

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup soaked chickpeas with 1/2 tsp salt, 3 cups water and 1 tbsp black tea in a muslin bundle for 7 whistles until very soft; discard the bundle and reserve a little liquid.

While the chana is still warm, toss it with 1.5 tbsp anardana powder, 1 tsp amchur, 1.5 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1/2 tsp black salt, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1/2 tsp black pepper and the remaining 3/4 tsp salt until well coated.
Add 2-3 tablespoons of the reserved liquid and mash a few chickpeas lightly so the spices form a clinging, nearly dry coating.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a small pan to smoking, then lower the heat and add half the ginger juliennes and all the slit green chillies and fry for 30 seconds until sizzling.
Pour this hot tempering over the spiced chickpeas along with 1 tsp garam masala and fold everything through gently.
Cover and rest for 10 minutes so the flavours soak in and the coating clings tightly to each chana.
Serve warm, garnished with the remaining raw ginger juliennes.
tips: Cook the chickpeas until genuinely soft; pindi chana needs to be tender enough to take on the dry masala.
Anardana is essential to the authentic tang, but a little extra amchur works if you cannot find it.
Keep it nearly dry, coating the chickpeas rather than swimming them in gravy, which is what sets pindi apart from Punjabi chole.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bhatura or aloo kulcha, topped with ginger juliennes, sliced onion and a squeeze of lemon.

variations.name: Peshawari Chana with Whole Spices
variations.description: A frontier-style dark chana where whole garam masala is dry-roasted and freshly ground into the dish, giving it a deep, aromatic warmth over the usual tang. The chickpeas take on a near-black colour from tea and roasted spices, making it richer and more perfumed than the classic Rawalpindi version.

ingredients.name: White chickpeas (kabuli chana)
ingredients.note: soaked overnight

ingredients.name: Black tea
ingredients.note: tied in a muslin bundle

ingredients.name: Dried amla pieces
ingredients.note: added to the cooking water for a darker colour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee carries the freshly ground whole spices and gives the chana its Peshawari richness

ingredients.name: Cinnamon
ingredients.note: for the roasted masala

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: julienned

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup soaked chickpeas with 1/2 tsp salt, 3 cups water, 2 dried amla pieces and 1 tbsp tea in a muslin bundle for 7 whistles until soft and dark; discard the bundle and amla, saving the liquid.

Dry-roast the cinnamon, cloves, both cardamoms, 1 tbsp coriander seeds, 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1 tbsp anardana in a pan on low heat for 3-4 minutes until fragrant, then cool and grind to a coarse powder.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat and fry half the ginger juliennes and the slit green chillies for a minute until sizzling.
Add the drained chickpeas and the freshly ground roasted masala, and toss on medium heat for 3-4 minutes so the spices coat and darken the chana.
Pour in 1/2 cup of the reserved cooking liquid and the remaining 3/4 tsp salt, then simmer for 8-10 minutes, mashing a few chickpeas so a thick, spice-heavy coating forms.
Cook until the liquid has almost dried up and the ghee glistens through the masala.
Rest for 5 minutes and serve warm, topped with the reserved raw ginger juliennes.
tips: Grinding the whole spices fresh, just before cooking, is what gives this version its distinctive Peshawari aroma.
The amla in the cooking water deepens the colour naturally and adds a faint sourness that suits the dish.
Toss the chana in the dry masala before adding any liquid so the spices toast onto the surface rather than just boiling in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with warm naan or tandoori roti and a kachumber of onion, tomato and mint.

variations.name: Chana Aloo Pindi
variations.description: A heartier one-dish version where cubes of potato are simmered and crisped along with the chickpeas, soaking up the same tangy pindi masala. The soft, spice-coated aloo makes the dish more filling and family-friendly while keeping the signature dry, chatpata character.

ingredients.name: White chickpeas (kabuli chana)
ingredients.note: soaked overnight

ingredients.name: Potato
ingredients.note: peeled and cubed

ingredients.name: Black tea
ingredients.note: tied in a muslin bundle

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil crisps the potato and carries the dry masala

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: julienned

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup soaked chickpeas with 1/2 tsp salt, 3 cups water and 1 tbsp tea in a muslin bundle for 7 whistles until soft; discard the bundle and drain, reserving a little liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, crackle 1/2 tsp ajwain, then add the cubed potato and fry for 8-10 minutes until golden and cooked through.
Add the drained chickpeas and toss with the potato for 2-3 minutes so both take on a light crisp.
Lower the heat and sprinkle in 1.5 tsp amchur, 1.5 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp chaat masala, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and the remaining 3/4 tsp salt, tossing to coat.
Add 3-4 tablespoons of the reserved liquid and mash a few chickpeas so the masala clings, then cook for 5 minutes until nearly dry.
Fold in half the ginger juliennes and cook another 2 minutes so the flavours meld.
Finish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander and the remaining ginger, and serve warm.
tips: Fry the potato cubes properly golden before adding spices so they hold shape and do not turn mushy.
The chaat masala and amchur together give this version its extra chatpata punch, so adjust to your tang preference.
Keep the dish on the drier side; a little crispness on the aloo and chana is what makes it moreish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with poori or kulcha, or pack it into a paratha roll with sliced onion and mint chutney.

variations.name: Hariyali Green Pindi Chana
variations.description: A fresh green twist where the dry chickpeas are tossed through a vibrant coriander-mint-green chilli paste instead of the usual dark spice mix. Bright, herby and lightly tangy, it trades the smoky brown look of classic pindi for a fragrant green coat, finished with a ghee-cumin temper.

ingredients.name: White chickpeas (kabuli chana)
ingredients.note: soaked overnight

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: packed, for the paste

ingredients.name: Fresh mint leaves
ingredients.note: packed, for the paste

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: for the paste

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee blooms the cumin and rounds the sharp green herbs

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: half in the paste, half julienned

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: for the paste

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup soaked chickpeas with 1/2 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6-7 whistles until soft, then drain, keeping a little liquid.
Grind 1 cup coriander, 1/2 cup mint, 4 green chillies, half the ginger and 5 garlic cloves with a splash of water into a coarse green paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Lower the heat and add the green paste, frying for 4-5 minutes until it darkens slightly and the raw smell of the herbs cooks off.
Add the drained chickpeas, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp amchur and the remaining 3/4 tsp salt, and toss to coat every chana in the green masala.
Add 3-4 tablespoons of the reserved liquid, mash a few chickpeas and cook for 6-8 minutes until nearly dry and glossy.
Finish with 1 tbsp lemon juice and the reserved ginger juliennes, and serve warm.
tips: Fry the green paste well until its raw edge disappears, or the dish will taste grassy rather than fragrant.
Keep the chickpeas whole and the masala clinging so it stays a dry, herby toss rather than a gravy.
Add the lemon right at the end so its brightness lifts the herbs instead of being cooked away.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with mint paratha or as a stuffing for kulcha, with a side of pickled onions and yogurt.

variations.name: Classic Atta Pinni
variations.description: The definitive Punjabi winter pinni made by slow-roasting whole-wheat flour in ghee until deeply nutty, then binding it with melted jaggery and a generous scatter of gum, nuts and seeds. Each ball is dense, grainy and warming, meant to be eaten with a glass of hot milk on cold mornings. The long, patient roast is what separates a great pinni from a raw, pasty one.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: the stone-ground khapli gives pinni its coarse, nutty bite

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: roast the flour low and slow in this so it turns golden without scorching

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melts into a soft binding paste that keeps the pinni chewy, not brittle

steps: Warm 3 tbsp of the Anveshan Bilona Ghee in a heavy kadhai over medium heat and fry the edible gum in batches for about 1 minute each, until each piece puffs into a light white ball; drain and crush coarsely once cool.
In the same ghee, lightly toast the almonds, cashews and melon seeds for 2 minutes until fragrant, then remove and chop the nuts roughly.
Add the remaining ghee to the kadhai, tip in 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, and roast on low heat for 25-30 minutes, stirring constantly, until it turns a deep golden brown and smells strongly nutty.
Turn off the heat and let the roasted flour cool for 8-10 minutes until just warm to the touch, so the jaggery won't melt into a syrup and harden.
Mix in 1.25 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder, the puffed gum, chopped nuts, melon seeds, 1 tsp cardamom powder and 0.25 tsp nutmeg, stirring until the jaggery softens and the mixture clumps when pressed.
While still warm, take small handfuls and press firmly between your palms into tight round pinnis, about 12 in all; set aside for an hour to firm up before storing.
tips: If the mixture feels too dry to bind, drizzle in 1-2 tbsp of warm melted ghee rather than adding more jaggery, which would make it sticky.
Fry the gond until it puffs fully but stays white; browned gum turns bitter and ruins the whole batch.
Stored in an airtight steel tin, these keep beautifully for up to three weeks and actually deepen in flavour after a day.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve one warm pinni alongside a tumbler of hot saffron milk as a winter breakfast, or offer them on a brass thali during Lohri and Sankranti gatherings.

variations.name: Maa Di Pinni (Urad Dal)
variations.description: A richer, more festive pinni built on ground urad dal instead of wheat, the version Punjabi grandmothers make for new mothers and freezing winters. Soaking, grinding and slow-frying the dal gives a deeply savoury-sweet ball with a fudgy, almost halwa-like centre. It is heavier and more nourishing than the plain atta kind.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: the ground dal drinks up ghee as it fries, which is what makes maa di pinni so rich

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: balances the earthy urad with a mellow caramel sweetness

steps: Soak 2 cups split urad dal in water for 4 hours, drain well, and grind to a coarse thick paste without adding extra water; spread it out and rub in the 2 tbsp milk to create a crumbly texture.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat and fry the edible gum until it puffs white, about 1 minute, then crush it coarsely once cool.

Pour the remaining Anveshan Bilona Ghee into the kadhai and fry the ground dal on low-medium heat for 30-35 minutes, stirring without pause, until it breaks into golden granules and releases a rich roasted aroma.
Toast the pistachios and almonds for 2 minutes in the ghee, then chop them and add the dried date powder off the heat.
Let the fried dal cool for 10 minutes until warm, then fold in 1.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder, the crushed gum, chopped nuts and 1 tsp cardamom until it clumps softly.
Shape into 12 firm rounds while warm, pressing hard so they hold, and rest them for an hour before storing in a tin.
tips: Grind the dal coarse, not silky, otherwise the pinni turns pasty instead of granular.
Roast the dal until you can no longer smell any raw beany note, or the finished pinni will taste flat.
These are especially given to nursing mothers in Punjab; keep the gond generous as it is traditionally valued for post-partum strength.
variations.servingSuggestion: Plate these darker, denser pinnis with a few whole soaked almonds on the side and a cup of masala doodh for an indulgent winter nightcap.

variations.name: Besan Pinni
variations.description: A quicker weekday pinni that swaps wheat for gram flour, giving a smoother, mithai-shop texture close to besan ladoo but pressed into rustic pinni rounds. The besan is bhunoed until it turns reddish-gold and grainy, then bound with jaggery for a warm, caramel finish. It comes together in half the time of the dal version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: essential for the classic mithai aroma as the besan roasts

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: gives besan pinni a deeper, more rustic note than white sugar would

steps: Melt 2 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee in a kadhai on medium heat and fry the gond until it swells into white puffs, roughly 1 minute, then set aside and crush.

Add the rest of the Anveshan Bilona Ghee, tip in 2.5 cups coarse besan, and roast on low heat for 20-22 minutes, stirring continuously, until it darkens to a reddish-gold and smells like fresh mithai.
Stir in the fennel seeds and toast for another minute so they crackle lightly and perfume the flour.
Take the kadhai off the heat and let the besan cool for 8 minutes until only warm, so the jaggery blends smoothly instead of melting.
Fold in 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder, the crushed gum, chopped walnuts, raisins and 1 tsp cardamom powder until the mixture holds together when squeezed.
Press into 10 firm rounds while warm and let them set for 45 minutes before storing.
tips: Use coarse besan rather than fine, as it gives the grainy bite a pinni should have.
Keep the flame low throughout; besan scorches fast and turns bitter over medium-high heat.
If the rounds crack while shaping, warm the mix for 30 seconds to loosen the ghee and they will bind again.
variations.servingSuggestion: Dust the finished pinnis with a little slivered pistachio and serve at teatime with adrak chai during the cold months.

variations.name: Panjiri Pinni with Makhana
variations.description: A panjiri-inspired pinni loaded with roasted fox nuts, coriander seed and edible gum, closer to the strengthening mixture new mothers eat but pressed into portable balls. The makhana adds a light crunch against the dense roasted flour, and warming spices like dry ginger make it the most medicinal-tasting of the four. It is the pinni to reach for on the coldest, achiest winter days.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: the wholegrain base carries the warming panjiri spices well

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: fry the makhana and gum in this until crisp before roasting the flour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: binds the crunchy panjiri mix into rounds without a sugar syrup

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat and fry the makhana for 4-5 minutes until they turn crisp and snap easily; remove and crush coarsely.
In the same ghee fry the gond until it puffs white, about 1 minute, and lightly toast the almonds and grated copra for 2 minutes, then set all aside and crush the nuts and gum.
Add the remaining Anveshan Bilona Ghee and roast 1.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta on low heat for 22-25 minutes until deep golden and nutty.
Stir the crushed coriander seeds and 1 tsp dry ginger powder into the hot flour and cook for a further minute until aromatic.
Cool the mixture for 8-10 minutes until warm, then mix in 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder, the crushed makhana, gum, copra, almonds and 1 tsp cardamom until it binds when pressed.
Shape into 12 firm rounds while warm and let them rest for an hour so the makhana crunch settles into the ball.
tips: Fry the makhana until fully crisp before crushing, or they stay chewy and the pinni won't hold its light texture.
Crush the makhana coarse so you still get little crunchy pockets in each bite.
This spiced, makhana-heavy version is traditionally eaten for warmth and stamina, so don't skip the sonth and coriander.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these with a warm glass of turmeric milk after a day out in the cold, or pack them as an energising trekking snack.

variations.name: Classic Ragi Malt
variations.description: A South Indian nourishing drink of finger-millet flour cooked into a smooth, porridge-like malt and lightly sweetened, traditionally given for strength and cooling. Cooked slowly so the ragi loses its raw edge, it turns silky and comforting, sipped warm at breakfast or chilled through summer afternoons.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: unrefined jaggery sweetens the malt with iron and minerals that complement calcium-rich ragi for a wholesome drink

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoon of bilona ghee stirred in at the end rounds off the earthy ragi and makes the malt glossy and easy to digest

steps: Whisk 0.5 cup ragi flour into 1.5 cups room-temperature water until absolutely smooth with no lumps, which is the key to a silky malt.
Pour the slurry into a heavy pan and cook on medium-low, stirring constantly, for 6 to 7 minutes until it thickens, turns glossy and loses its raw, chalky smell.
Add 2 cups milk in a steady stream while stirring, along with a pinch of salt, and simmer gently for another 4 minutes until it comes to a smooth, pourable consistency.
Melt 5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water in a separate pan into a syrup, strain it, and stir it into the malt off high heat so the milk does not curdle.
Stir in 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee, mixing until the malt is glossy and fragrant.
Ladle into glasses or bowls, top with 2 tbsp chopped almonds, and serve warm or chilled as you prefer.
tips: Always mix the ragi flour into cold or room-temperature water first — adding it to hot liquid guarantees lumps.
Add the jaggery syrup only after lowering the heat, since jaggery poured into boiling milk can split it.
Cook the ragi slurry until it turns glossy and smells nutty; under-cooked ragi leaves a raw, bitter aftertaste.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm in the morning for a filling start, or pour over ice on hot days topped with slivered almonds as a cooling energy drink.

variations.name: Sprouted Ragi Malt
variations.description: The traditional strengthening tonic made from sprouted, sun-dried and roasted ragi, whose malting turns the millet sweeter, more digestible and richer in nutrients. Nutty and deeply satisfying, it is the classic weaning and post-workout drink of Karnataka households, sweetened lightly with honey.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: raw honey sweetens the malted ragi gently and is stirred in warm, never boiled, to keep its enzymes intact

steps: Whisk 0.5 cup sprouted ragi flour into 2 cups cold water until perfectly smooth, breaking up any lumps against the side of the bowl.
Cook the slurry on medium-low, stirring without stopping, for 6 minutes until it thickens to a glossy porridge and smells sweetly malted.
Pour in 1.5 cups milk with a pinch of salt and simmer gently for 3 to 4 minutes to a smooth, drinkable consistency.
Take the pan off the heat and let it cool for 5 minutes until warm but no longer steaming hot.
Stir in 4 tbsp Anveshan Honey, 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and 0.25 tsp dry ginger powder, mixing until the honey fully dissolves.
Fold in 2 tbsp finely chopped dates for extra sweetness and texture, and serve warm.
tips: Sprouted ragi flour cooks faster and tastes naturally sweeter, so you need far less added sweetener than plain ragi.
Cool the malt to warm before adding honey — boiling honey destroys its enzymes and can make it bitter.
Make sprouted ragi flour in bulk by sprouting, drying and roasting the grain, then storing the powder airtight for months.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a wholesome breakfast drink or a post-exercise recovery malt, with a few extra chopped dates stirred through.

variations.name: Ragi Banana Smoothie Malt
variations.description: A chilled, blender-made take where cooked ragi is whipped with ripe banana and cold milk into a thick, creamy smoothie. Naturally sweet from the fruit and lightly spiced, it is a no-fuss breakfast-in-a-glass that children happily drink and athletes love for slow-release energy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: raw honey blended in cold complements the banana's natural sweetness without overpowering the earthy ragi

steps: Whisk 0.33 cup ragi flour into 1 cup cold water and cook on medium-low, stirring constantly, for 6 minutes until thickened and glossy, then cool it completely.
Spread the cooked ragi in a shallow dish and refrigerate for 15 minutes so it chills fully before blending.
Add the cooled ragi, 2 ripe bananas, 2 cups chilled milk, 0.5 tsp cinnamon powder and 2 tbsp roasted peanut powder to a blender.
Blend on high for about 1 minute until thick, smooth and frothy, then blend in 1 cup ice cubes for a few seconds to chill and lighten it.
Add 3 tbsp Anveshan Honey and pulse briefly just to combine without heating the mix.
Pour into tall glasses and serve immediately while thick and cold.
tips: Cook and chill the ragi ahead so the smoothie blends up icy cold rather than lukewarm.
Very ripe, spotty bananas give the most natural sweetness and let you cut back on honey.
For a vegan version, swap the milk for chilled almond or oat milk and the drink stays just as creamy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in tall glasses dusted with cinnamon and a sprinkle of peanut powder, ideal as a grab-and-go breakfast or a filling mid-morning snack.

variations.name: Savoury Ragi Ambali
variations.description: The rustic Karnataka-Andhra ambali, a fermented, buttermilk-based ragi drink that is savoury rather than sweet and famed as a cooling, gut-friendly summer staple for farm workers. Tangy with curd, tempered lightly and seasoned with green chilli and curry leaves, it is a probiotic meal in a glass.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil carries the tempering aromatics cleanly into this savoury ragi drink

steps: Whisk 0.5 cup ragi flour into 2 cups cold water until smooth, then cook on medium-low, stirring constantly, for 7 minutes until it thickens into a glossy porridge and loses its raw smell.
Cool the cooked ragi completely to room temperature, then leave it covered for 4 to 6 hours (or overnight) to ferment slightly and turn pleasantly sour.
Whisk 2 cups buttermilk with 0.75 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp grated ginger into the fermented ragi until it becomes a smooth, pourable drink.
Heat 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a small pan on medium and crackle 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds until they pop, about 30 seconds.
Add 1 slit green chilli and 8 curry leaves to the oil and fry for 15 seconds until fragrant, then pour this tempering over the ragi buttermilk.
Stir in 2 tbsp chopped coriander, mix well, and serve at room temperature or lightly chilled.
tips: Ferment the cooked ragi overnight in warm weather for the classic tangy ambali flavour and probiotic benefit.
Keep the drink thin and pourable — ambali is meant to be sipped, so add extra buttermilk or water if it thickens on standing.
Bloom the mustard and cumin fully in hot oil; raw seeds stirred in would taste harsh in this uncooked drink.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in steel tumblers at room temperature alongside a raw onion and green chilli, the traditional cooling midday drink during peak summer.

variations.name: Classic Rava Coconut Ladoo
variations.description: The everyday South and West Indian rava ladoo, made by roasting semolina in ghee with fresh coconut and binding it with a little warm milk so the balls stay soft. The result is fragrant with cardamom, studded with fried cashews and raisins, and just moist enough to hold without a sugar syrup. It is the festival ladoo children learn to roll first.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: roast the rava in this until it smells nutty but stays pale

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: powder this unrefined sugar fine so it dissolves into the warm rava

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee in a kadhai over medium heat and fry the cashews until golden and the raisins until plump, about 2 minutes, then set aside.
Add the remaining ghee and roast 2 cups fine rava on low-medium heat for 8-10 minutes, stirring constantly, until it feels light and smells nutty but stays pale.
Add the grated coconut and roast together for another 3-4 minutes until the coconut loses its raw moisture.
Turn off the heat and let the mixture cool for 5 minutes, then grind 1.25 cups Anveshan Khandsari Sugar to a fine powder and mix it in along with 1 tsp cardamom, the fried cashews and raisins.
Sprinkle in the warm milk a spoon at a time, mixing after each addition, until the crumbly rava just holds together when pressed.
Roll into 12 tight ladoos while still warm and let them firm up for 30 minutes before serving.
tips: Add the milk sparingly; too much and the ladoos turn sticky and won't keep beyond a day.
Roasting the coconut with the rava is what lets these keep for 3-4 days at room temperature.
If the mix won't bind, warm it slightly and add a teaspoon more melted ghee rather than more milk.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve fresh and soft on a festival thali, or offer as prasad after a home puja alongside sliced fruit.

variations.name: Rava Besan Ladoo
variations.description: A richer hybrid that folds roasted gram flour into the semolina, giving a denser, more mithai-like ladoo with the graininess of rava and the depth of besan. The two flours are roasted separately so each develops its own aroma before being combined. It is a favourite when you want something more substantial than plain rava ladoo.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: the besan needs generous ghee to roast without clumping

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: powdered fine, it sweetens the blend with a mellow molasses note

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee in a kadhai and roast 1.5 cups rava on low-medium heat for 8-10 minutes until light and nutty, then transfer to a bowl.
Add the remaining ghee to the same pan and roast 1 cup coarse besan on low heat for 12-15 minutes, stirring constantly, until it turns reddish-gold and smells like mithai.
Combine the roasted rava and besan, then toast the chopped almonds and pistachios in any leftover ghee for 2 minutes and stir them in.
Let the combined flours cool for 6-8 minutes until just warm so the sugar doesn't melt.
Grind 1.25 cups Anveshan Khandsari Sugar to a fine powder and mix it in with 1 tsp cardamom, then drizzle in the warm milk until the mixture binds when pressed.
Shape into 12 firm ladoos while warm and rest them for 40 minutes so the besan sets.
tips: Roast the two flours separately; besan takes far longer than rava and would leave the semolina raw if combined too early.
Keep the flame low for the besan, which scorches and turns bitter over higher heat.
A pinch more warm milk fixes a crumbly mix, but add it drop by drop to avoid stickiness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Garnish each with a single split pistachio and serve at Diwali alongside other dry mithai on a decorated platter.

variations.name: Rava Ladoo with Jaggery Syrup
variations.description: A rustic Maharashtrian-leaning version bound with a thick jaggery syrup instead of powdered sugar, giving deeper caramel colour and a firmer, longer-keeping ladoo. Cooking the semolina into the syrup at soft-ball stage gives a chewy set with no milk at all, so it travels and stores far better. The dry coconut adds a toothsome texture.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: roast the rava in this and use a little more to grease your palms

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted to a soft-ball syrup, it sets the ladoo firm without any milk

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee in a kadhai and fry the cashews until golden, about 2 minutes, then set aside.
Add the remaining ghee and roast 2 cups rava on low-medium heat for 8-10 minutes until light, then toast the grated copra with it for 3 more minutes.
In a separate pan, melt 1.25 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 4 tbsp water over low heat and cook to a thick soft-ball syrup, about 5-6 minutes, testing that a drop holds shape in cold water.
Pour the hot jaggery syrup into the roasted rava, add the fried cashews, 0.5 tsp dry ginger and 1 tsp cardamom, and mix quickly before it stiffens.
Let the mixture cool for just 3-4 minutes until it is warm enough to handle but still pliable.
Grease your palms with ghee and press into 12 firm ladoos, working fast, then leave them to set for 30 minutes.
tips: Get the syrup to soft-ball stage; under-cooked syrup leaves the ladoos loose and over-cooked syrup makes them rock hard.
Shape quickly, as the jaggery mixture firms rapidly as it cools; re-warm briefly if it hardens before you finish.
These keep for over a week thanks to the syrup and no milk, making them ideal for gifting and travel.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these deep-amber ladoos during Sankranti with sesame chikki, or pack them for long journeys as they resist spoiling.

variations.name: Saffron Rava Mawa Ladoo
variations.description: A festive, dairy-rich upgrade that folds crumbled khoya and saffron into the roasted rava for a soft, melt-in-the-mouth ladoo closer to milk mithai. The saffron lends warmth and colour while the mawa keeps each ball moist and luxurious. This is the version to make for Diwali when you want something clearly indulgent.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: roast the rava in this before the mawa is folded in

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: powdered fine so it melts smoothly into the mawa

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: bloom the strands in warm milk to draw out colour and aroma

steps: Soak a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in the 3 tbsp warm milk and set aside to bloom for 10 minutes.
Heat the Anveshan Bilona Ghee in a kadhai and roast 1.5 cups rava on low-medium heat for 8-10 minutes until light and nutty.
Add the crumbled khoya and cook together on low heat for 4-5 minutes, stirring, until the mawa melts and coats the rava evenly.
Turn off the heat and let the mixture cool for 6 minutes until warm, then grind 1 cup Anveshan Khandsari Sugar fine and mix it in with 1 tsp cardamom.
Stir in the saffron milk and chopped pistachios until the mixture is moist and just binds when pressed.
Roll into 12 soft ladoos while warm, press a pistachio sliver on top of each, and chill for 20 minutes to set.
tips: Use fresh khoya and cook it only until melted; over-roasting makes the ladoos dry and grainy.
Because of the mawa, these are best refrigerated and eaten within 3-4 days.
Bloom the saffron in warm milk rather than adding it dry, or you lose most of its colour and scent.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these golden, saffron-flecked ladoos chilled on a silver plate for Diwali, garnished with edible silver leaf if you like.

variations.name: Classic Punjabi Rongi
variations.description: The everyday Punjabi black-eyed pea curry, rongi, where softened cowpeas simmer in a bhuna onion-tomato masala rounded with ghee. Wholesome, protein-rich and gently spiced, it is the kind of homely dal-sabzi hybrid that turns a plate of rice and roti into a full meal.

ingredients.name: Black-eyed peas (lobia)
ingredients.note: soaked 4 hours

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee gives the masala a rich, homely finish

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: pureed

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup soaked lobia with 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1/2 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 4-5 whistles until soft but still holding shape, then set aside with its liquid.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add the chopped onions and fry for 6-7 minutes until golden brown.
Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 2 slit green chillies and cook for a minute until the raw smell goes, then pour in the tomato puree.
Cook the tomato masala for 6-7 minutes until it thickens and the ghee separates at the edges, then stir in 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder and roast for 30 seconds.
Tip in the cooked lobia along with its cooking liquid and the remaining 3/4 tsp salt, and simmer on low heat for 12-15 minutes so the peas soak up the masala.
Mash a spoonful of the lobia against the side of the pan to thicken the gravy naturally, then sprinkle 1/2 tsp garam masala.
Finish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander and serve hot.
tips: Do not overcook the lobia in the cooker; it should stay whole so the curry has bite rather than turning mushy.
Mashing just a few peas thickens the gravy without any flour or cream.
A squeeze of lemon at the end lifts the whole curry and balances the earthiness of the beans.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice or hot phulka, a wedge of lemon and a side of sliced onion and green chilli.

variations.name: Rajasthani Sweet-Tangy Rongi
variations.description: A Marwari take on cowpeas cooked without onion or tomato, leaning on a yogurt-and-besan base soured with amchur and gently sweetened with jaggery. Asafoetida bloomed in ghee carries the savoury depth, giving a light, tangy-sweet curry quite unlike the Punjabi bhuna version.

ingredients.name: Black-eyed peas (lobia)
ingredients.note: soaked 4 hours

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the only fat in this no-onion curry, so its flavour carries the tempering

ingredients.name: Yogurt
ingredients.note: whisked smooth

ingredients.name: Besan (gram flour)
ingredients.note: to stop the yogurt splitting

ingredients.name: Asafoetida
ingredients.note: a generous pinch stands in for garlic

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: grated

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a gentle sweetness that rounds the tang the Marwari way, without refined sugar

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup soaked lobia with 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1/2 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 4-5 whistles until tender, and keep aside with the liquid.
Whisk 1/2 cup yogurt with 1 tbsp besan and 1/2 cup water until completely smooth so it will not curdle when cooked.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then lower the flame and add 1/2 tsp asafoetida, the grated ginger and 2 slit green chillies and fry for a minute until fragrant.
Turn the heat to low and pour in the yogurt-besan mixture, stirring continuously for 3-4 minutes as it warms so it thickens smoothly without splitting.
Add 1.5 tsp coriander powder and the cooked lobia with its liquid, then simmer on low heat for 12-15 minutes until the curry thickens and the flour taste cooks out.
Stir in 1 tsp amchur, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and the remaining 3/4 tsp salt, and simmer another 4-5 minutes until the sweet-sour balance settles.
Serve warm, the curry loose enough to pour over rice.
tips: Always slacken the yogurt with besan and add it off high heat, stirring constantly, so the gravy stays silky and never curdles.
Balance amchur and jaggery to taste, aiming for a gentle sweet-sour lilt rather than an obvious sweetness.
This curry is naturally onion-and-garlic free, making it perfect for a fasting-friendly or satvik thali.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over plain steamed rice or with bajra roti and a spoon of white butter for a Marwari-style lunch.

variations.name: Dry Masala Rongi Sundal
variations.description: A Southern dry-toss where boiled cowpeas meet a coconut, curry-leaf and mustard-seed tempering in fragrant coconut oil. Light, nutty and gently spiced rather than gravied, this sundal-style rongi works as a warm salad, a snack or a protein-rich side with rice.

ingredients.name: Black-eyed peas (lobia)
ingredients.note: soaked 4 hours

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed coconut oil is the authentic fat for a South Indian sundal tempering

ingredients.name: Urad dal
ingredients.note: for the tempering

ingredients.name: Dry red chillies
ingredients.note: broken

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup soaked lobia with 1/2 tsp salt and 2.5 cups water for 3-4 whistles until just tender but still firm, then drain thoroughly so the sundal stays dry.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadai on medium heat and pop 1 tsp mustard seeds until they finish spluttering, about 30 seconds.
Add 1 tsp urad dal, 2 broken dry red chillies, 2 sprigs curry leaves and 1/4 tsp asafoetida and fry for 20 seconds until the dal turns golden and the leaves crisp.
Stir in the chopped ginger and green chillies and saute for a minute until fragrant, then tip in the drained lobia and the remaining 1/4 tsp salt.
Toss on medium heat for 3-4 minutes so the peas dry out slightly and absorb the tempering.
Add 1/2 cup grated coconut and toss for another 2 minutes until it smells nutty and coats the peas.
Turn off the heat, squeeze in 1 tbsp lemon juice, and serve warm.
tips: Keep the lobia firm and drain it well; a wet or overcooked pea turns the sundal soggy instead of dry and nutty.
Fresh grated coconut is far better here than desiccated, which can taste dry and dull the dish.
Add the lemon only after switching off the heat so its brightness is not cooked away.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a warm snack with chai, or alongside rasam rice and a papad for a light South Indian meal.

variations.name: Dhaba-Style Rongi Masala
variations.description: The bold roadside version where cowpeas simmer in a smoky mustard-oil masala loaded with browned onions, ginger and a finishing kasuri methi tadka. Thicker, spicier and darker than the home-style rongi, it is the kind of hearty bean curry ladled out at Punjab highway stops.

ingredients.name: Black-eyed peas (lobia)
ingredients.note: soaked 4 hours

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: kachi ghani mustard oil gives the masala its pungent, robust dhaba edge

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Kasuri methi (dried fenugreek)
ingredients.note: crushed

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup soaked lobia with 1/2 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 4-5 whistles until soft, and keep with the cooking liquid.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just smokes, lower the heat, add 1 bay leaf and 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add the chopped onions and fry for 8-9 minutes until deep golden brown.

Add 2 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for a minute, then the chopped tomatoes with 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, and bhuno for 6-7 minutes until the masala turns thick and glossy.
Add the cooked lobia with its liquid and the remaining 3/4 tsp salt, then simmer on low heat for 15 minutes, mashing a few peas so the gravy turns rich and clingy.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi between your palms and stir it in along with 1 tsp garam masala, simmering another 3 minutes.
Adjust the consistency with a splash of hot water if needed, keeping it thick enough to coat a roti.
Finish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander and serve hot.
tips: Browning the onions properly in smoking mustard oil is what builds the dark, smoky dhaba character.
Crush the kasuri methi between your palms before adding so its aroma releases fully into the gravy.
This rongi thickens as it rests, so loosen leftovers with hot water and a pinch of garam masala when reheating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tandoori roti or laccha paratha, a raw onion-lemon salad and a green chilli on the side.

variations.name: Classic Salted Lassi
variations.description: The North Indian namkeen lassi that cools you down on a punishing summer afternoon: thick hand-whisked curd loosened just enough to sip, seasoned with black salt and roasted cumin and lifted by a hot Anveshan Ghee tempering of jeera. Where sweet lassi is a dessert, this savoury one is a digestive, meant to be drunk with lunch rather than after it.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A jeera tempering in bilona ghee is what turns plain salted curd into a proper chaunk-wali lassi

steps: Whisk 2 cups thick curd with 1 cup chilled water in a deep bowl for about a minute until it is completely smooth, lump-free and lightly frothy on top.
Beat in 0.5 tsp black salt, 0.25 tsp regular salt, 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder and 0.25 tsp black pepper until every seasoning dissolves evenly.
Heat 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee in a small tadka pan on medium heat and crackle 0.5 tsp cumin seeds for about 20 seconds until they darken a shade and smell toasty.
Pour the sizzling ghee-cumin tempering straight into the lassi and stir once so a nutty aroma streaks right through the drink.
Tear 8 mint leaves, drop them in with 6 ice cubes and stir well to chill everything down.
Pour into 4 glasses and serve at once while it is cold, foamy and freshly tempered.
tips: Use curd that is set firm and not sour; over-fermented curd makes the lassi taste sharp no matter how much you season it.
Let the ghee tadka cool for a few seconds before it hits the curd if your kitchen is warm, so the drink stays cold and does not turn watery.
Whisk by hand rather than blending; a blender aerates it into a milkshake, while hand-whisking keeps the traditional thick, drinkable body.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside a heavy stuffed-paratha or biryani lunch where its salt and cumin cut through the richness; a small bowl of it also settles the stomach after a spicy meal.

variations.name: Rajasthani Chaunk Salted Lassi
variations.description: A desert-country namkeen lassi finished with a full Rajasthani chaunk of mustard, hing and curry leaves crackled in Anveshan Ghee, poured smoking over cold seasoned curd. The tempering gives it the savoury, almost kadhi-like depth that plain salted lassi never has, making it as much a light meal as a drink.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The chaunk relies on ghee to carry mustard and curry-leaf aroma into the cold curd

steps: Whisk 2 cups thick curd with 1 cup chilled water until smooth, then mix in 0.5 tsp black salt and 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder and keep it in the fridge.
Heat 1.5 tsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan over medium heat until it melts and shimmers with a nutty smell.
Add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop completely for about 20 seconds, then add 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 0.25 tsp hing.
Drop in 10 curry leaves, 1 slit green chilli and 0.5 tsp grated ginger and fry for 15-20 seconds until the leaves turn crisp and glossy.
Let the chaunk cool for a minute, then stir it into the chilled lassi in a slow stream so the hot fat does not split the curd.
Scatter over 1 tbsp chopped coriander and serve in 4 tall glasses over a little ice.
tips: Cooling the tempering for a minute is important; curd added to very hot ghee can curdle into grainy flecks.
For an authentic touch, rub the empty glasses with a little kala namak before pouring so the first sip is extra savoury.
Make the seasoned curd base a few hours ahead, but add the fresh chaunk only just before serving so it stays aromatic.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with hot bajra roti and a dab of white butter, or serve it as the cooling counterpoint to a fiery Rajasthani laal maas thali for the non-vegetarian table alongside.

variations.name: Pudina Green Salted Lassi
variations.description: A vivid green namkeen lassi blended with a fistful of mint and coriander, sharp ginger and green chilli, then rounded with a whisper of Anveshan Honey so the salt and sour sit in perfect balance. It drinks like a savoury smoothie, herb-forward and refreshing, and pairs beautifully with fried snacks.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: A single spoon of raw honey rounds off the tang without turning this savoury lassi sweet

steps: In a blender combine 0.5 cup mint, 0.25 cup coriander, 1 green chilli and 0.5 inch ginger with a splash of water and blend to a fine green paste.
Add 2 cups thick curd and 1 cup chilled water and blend for about 30 seconds until pale green, smooth and frothy.
Add 0.75 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp black salt, 0.5 tsp chaat masala and 1 tsp lemon juice and pulse briefly to mix.
Blend in 1 tsp Anveshan Honey just enough to round off the salt and sourness so the herbs shine through.
Taste and adjust the salt, then chill the lassi for about 15 minutes for the flavours to settle and deepen in colour.
Pour into 4 glasses, float a few whole mint leaves on top and serve cold.
tips: Blend the herbs first with a little water; crammed straight into thick curd they stay in coarse specks instead of colouring the drink.
If it tastes flat, the fix is almost always a pinch more black salt rather than more chilli.
This one separates faster than plain lassi because of the herb fibre, so give it a quick stir if it sits.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve icy cold with hot pakoras, samosas or a plate of aloo tikki; the mint cuts the oil far better than ketchup or sweet chutney.

variations.name: Bihari Sattu Namkeen Lassi
variations.description: A protein-loaded Bihari take where nutty Anveshan Sattu is whisked into thinned curd and finished, as the old kitchens do, with just a few drops of raw Anveshan Mustard Oil for pungency. Thicker and more filling than ordinary lassi, it doubles as a summer breakfast that keeps farmhands going through the heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Roasted Bengal-gram sattu makes this lassi filling and gut-friendly, the classic Bihari cooler

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: A few raw drops of kachi ghani mustard oil give the sharp pungency Bihari sattu drinks are known for

steps: In a bowl, whisk 3 tbsp Anveshan Sattu with a little of the water, adding it slowly, until you have a smooth lump-free paste.
Whisk in 1.5 cups thick curd and the remaining chilled water until the mixture is thin and pourable like buttermilk.
Stir in 0.5 tsp black salt, 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder and 0.25 tsp black pepper until fully dissolved.
Add 1 finely chopped green chilli, 2 tbsp finely chopped onion and 1 tbsp coriander leaves and mix through.
Finish with 0.5 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil stirred in for the unmistakable pungent Bihari edge, then chill for 10 minutes.
Serve in 4 glasses and stir each one just before drinking, as sattu naturally settles to the bottom.
tips: Always dissolve the sattu in a little liquid first; tipped straight into the full curd it clumps and never smooths out.
Keep the mustard oil to a few drops unless you grew up on it; it is meant to be a sharp background note, not the main flavour.
For a milder version skip the onion and mustard oil and add extra mint; it becomes gentle enough for children.
variations.servingSuggestion: Drink it as a mid-morning cooler on an empty stomach, or serve with litti-chokha where its cool, salty body balances the smoky roasted sattu balls on the plate.

variations.name: Classic Sarson da Saag
variations.description: The quintessential Punjabi winter dish: mustard greens simmered soft with a little spinach, thickened with cornmeal and finished with a fragrant ghee-and-garlic tadka. Slow cooking mellows the pepperiness of the sarson into something silky and earthy, best mopped up with makki di roti and a knob of white butter.

ingredients.name: Mustard greens (sarson)
ingredients.note: roughly chopped, tough stalks removed

ingredients.name: Spinach (palak)
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Bathua leaves
ingredients.note: optional, adds body

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: half grated, half julienned

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee gives the tadka the nutty richness that defines an authentic saag

steps: Wash the sarson, palak and bathua thoroughly in several changes of water, then add them to a pressure cooker with the slit green chillies, grated ginger, 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 1 cup water, and cook for 5-6 whistles on medium heat until completely soft.
Open the cooker once the pressure settles, then blend the greens coarsely with a hand blender so the saag stays slightly textured rather than a smooth puree.

Whisk 3 tbsp makki atta with 1/2 cup water until lump-free and stir it into the greens, then simmer uncovered on low heat for 20-25 minutes, stirring often, until the raw cornmeal smell disappears and the saag thickens.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan on medium heat, add the chopped garlic and julienned ginger and fry until pale gold, about 1 minute, then add the chopped onion and cook for 4-5 minutes until soft and golden.
Stir in 1 tsp red chilli powder off the direct flame for 10 seconds so it blooms without scorching, then pour this sizzling tadka into the simmering saag.
Add the remaining 1/4 tsp salt, simmer everything together for 5 minutes so the tadka soaks in, and mash a few times with a wooden masher for the classic homely texture.
Serve piping hot with an extra teaspoon of raw Anveshan Ghee melting on top.
tips: The longer you simmer sarson saag on low heat, the sweeter and silkier it becomes; an hour is not too long in Punjabi kitchens.
If the saag tastes sharp, a pinch more cornmeal and ten extra minutes of cooking rounds off the mustard bite.
Saag deepens overnight, so make it a day ahead and reheat gently with a fresh spoon of ghee before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot makki di roti, a dollop of white butter, jaggery on the side and a glass of chaas for the classic Punjabi winter meal.

variations.name: Dhaba-Style Mustard-Oil Saag
variations.description: The robust highway-dhaba version where the greens carry a heavier onion-tomato masala and a pungent mustard-oil tadka layered over a smoking ghee finish. It is spicier, darker and more assertive than the homestyle saag, built to stand up to thick makki rotis and cold winter nights.

ingredients.name: Mustard greens (sarson)
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Spinach (palak)
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: kachi ghani mustard oil gives the dhaba saag its signature pungent, robust edge

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: reserved for the smoking finishing tadka poured over the top

ingredients.name: Dry red chillies
ingredients.note: broken

steps: Pressure-cook the sarson and palak with the chopped green chillies, 1 tsp salt and 1 cup water for 5-6 whistles until soft, then blend coarsely and stir in the makki atta slaked in 1/2 cup water.
Simmer the greens on low heat for 20 minutes, stirring so the cornmeal cooks through and the saag thickens to a rustic body.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just smokes, lower the heat, then add the chopped onions and fry for 7-8 minutes until deep golden brown.

Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for a minute, then the chopped tomatoes with 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 1/4 tsp salt, and bhuno for 5-6 minutes until the masala turns thick and the oil separates.
Fold the cooked saag into this masala with a splash of hot water, and simmer together for 8-10 minutes so it takes on a smoky, robust depth.

In a small pan heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until shimmering, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 3 broken dry red chillies for 30 seconds until the chillies darken, then pour this smoking tadka over the saag and stir in 1/2 tsp garam masala.
Serve at once while the tadka still crackles on the surface.
tips: Frying the onions to a genuine deep brown in mustard oil is what gives this saag its dhaba colour and body.
Heat the mustard oil to smoking first, then lower the flame, so its raw pungency mellows into a rounder heat.
For extra smokiness, rest a live coal in a bowl on the saag, drip ghee over it and cover for two minutes before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with thick ghee-brushed makki di roti, sliced radish, green chilli and a raw onion salad for a proper truck-stop feast.

variations.name: Mixed Winter Greens Saag
variations.description: A lighter, greener saag that balances sharp sarson with methi, bathua and radish leaves for a layered, slightly bitter-sweet flavour beloved in the Punjab-Himachal foothills. There is no onion-tomato masala here; the greens shine through a simple garlic-ginger ghee tadka, making it fresher and less heavy than the classic.

ingredients.name: Mustard greens (sarson)
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Fresh fenugreek leaves (methi)
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Bathua leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Radish leaves
ingredients.note: chopped, from fresh mooli tops

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee lets the fresh greens stay the hero without a heavy masala

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: julienned

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

steps: Wash all four greens carefully in several changes of water to rid them of grit, then pressure-cook them with the slit green chillies, 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 3/4 cup water for 4-5 whistles until tender.
Once the pressure releases, blend the greens only very coarsely so this saag keeps a fresh, chunky character.
Slake 2 tbsp makki atta in 1/3 cup water and stir it into the greens, then simmer on low heat for 15-18 minutes until the cornmeal cooks in and the raw smell is gone.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium heat, add the chopped garlic and julienned ginger and fry gently for 1-2 minutes until fragrant and pale gold.
Stir 1 tsp coriander powder into the tadka for 10 seconds, then tip the whole thing into the simmering greens with the remaining 1/4 tsp salt.
Simmer together for 5 minutes, tasting to check the methi bitterness has softened into the background, and mash lightly for a rustic finish.
