Serve warm with a fresh drizzle of ghee, keeping the saag looser and greener than the classic version.
tips: Balance the greens so no single one dominates; too much methi turns the saag bitter, too much radish leaf turns it sharp.
This lighter saag does not keep as long as the classic, so cook only what you will eat within a day.
A pinch of jaggery at the end tames any lingering bitterness from the methi and radish leaves.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft bajra or makki roti and a bowl of thick curd, letting the fresh greens shine alongside a simple pickle.

variations.name: Makki di Roti
variations.description: The golden cornmeal flatbread that partners sarson saag: nutty maize flour bound with a touch of khapli atta so it rolls without cracking, patted into rustic discs and cooked on a hot tawa until speckled. Brushed generously with ghee, it is crisp at the edges and soft within, the definitive winter roti of Punjab.

ingredients.name: Maize flour (makki atta)
ingredients.note: fine yellow cornmeal

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: a little khapli binds the gluten-free cornmeal so the roti rolls without cracking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: for brushing each roti hot off the tawa, the way it is served with saag

ingredients.name: Grated radish (mooli)
ingredients.note: optional, adds moisture and flavour

ingredients.name: Green chilli
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Warm water
ingredients.note: approximately, added gradually

steps: In a wide bowl mix 2 cups makki atta with 1/4 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta, 3/4 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp ajwain, the grated radish, chopped green chilli and coriander.
Add warm water a little at a time, working it in with your knuckles, until you have a soft, pliable dough; makki atta drinks water slowly, so knead for a good 4-5 minutes until smooth and non-sticky.
Divide the dough into 8 balls and keep them covered with a damp cloth so they do not dry out and crack.
Place one ball between two sheets of greased plastic or a moist cloth and press gently with your palm into a 6-inch disc about 5 mm thick, patching any cracked edges with wet fingers.
Heat a tawa on medium heat and cook the roti for about 1.5 minutes until the underside sets and turns speckled, then flip and cook the other side for a minute.
Brush both sides generously with Anveshan Ghee and press lightly with a cloth so it puffs slightly and crisps at the edges, cooking another 30 seconds per side until golden.
Serve straight off the tawa while hot, repeating with the remaining dough.
tips: Keep the dough covered at all times and warm the water you knead with; cold makki dough cracks the moment you try to roll it.
If patting by hand feels tricky, roll between two greased plastic sheets and simply peel the top layer off before transferring to the tawa.
Grated radish or even warm boiled potato worked into the dough makes the roti far more forgiving and less prone to breaking.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with sarson da saag, a mound of white butter and a dab of jaggery, or with a simple dal and pickle for a rustic winter lunch.

variations.name: Classic Sol Kadhi
variations.description: The pale-pink Konkani cooler-cum-digestive where tart kokum concentrate meets fresh, silky coconut milk. Soothing after a fiery coastal meal, it is at once cooling, faintly sweet and gently sour, finished with a raw tempering of garlic, green chilli and coriander.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil echoes the coconut milk and carries the raw garlic-cumin tempering authentically

steps: Soak 10 dried kokum petals in 0.5 cup warm water for 20 minutes until softened and the water turns deep pink, then set aside with the soaking liquid.
Blend 1.5 cups grated coconut with 1.5 cups warm water, then strain through a muslin cloth, pressing hard, to extract thick, silky coconut milk.
Combine the coconut milk with the kokum petals and their pink soaking water in a bowl, add 0.75 tsp salt, and let it rest for 10 minutes so the colour bleeds into the milk.
Gently press and remove the kokum petals, adjusting the colour and tang by adding a little more soaking water for a deeper pink and sharper sourness.

Heat 1 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan on medium and crackle 0.5 tsp cumin seeds, then add 3 crushed garlic cloves, 1 slit green chilli and 6 curry leaves and fry for 20 seconds until aromatic.
Pour the tempering over the sol kadhi, stir in 2 tbsp chopped coriander, and serve at room temperature or lightly chilled.
tips: Never boil sol kadhi — heat splits the coconut milk and dulls the fresh pink colour, so keep everything gently warm at most.
Control the pink and the sourness with the kokum soaking water rather than adding the petals directly, which can over-sour the drink.
Squeeze the coconut through muslin for the thickest milk; a second thinner extraction can loosen it if it turns too rich.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled in a bowl or glass alongside steamed rice as a digestive to close a Malvani fish-thali-style meal, or sip it on its own after spicy food.

variations.name: Malvani Spiced Sol Kadhi
variations.description: A bolder Malvani rendition where the coconut milk is ground with green chilli, ginger and garlic before the kokum goes in, giving a spicier, more full-bodied kadhi. Thicker and punchier than the classic, it is often eaten as a soupy accompaniment to rice rather than sipped plain.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil deepens the coconut base and blooms the mustard-curry leaf tempering for this spicier Malvani style

steps: Soak 12 dried kokum petals in 0.5 cup warm water for 20 minutes until soft and deeply coloured.
Blend 2 cups grated coconut with 2 green chillies, 1 inch ginger, 2 garlic cloves and 1.5 cups warm water into a smooth, aromatic paste.
Strain the blended mixture through muslin, pressing firmly, to yield a thick spiced coconut milk, and repeat with a little extra water for a second lighter extract.
Combine the coconut milk with the soaked kokum and its pink water, add 0.75 tsp salt, and rest for 10 minutes; then press out and remove the petals to fix the tang.
Heat 1 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan, crackle 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, add 2 crushed garlic cloves and 8 curry leaves and fry for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Pour the tempering over the kadhi, stir through 2 tbsp chopped coriander, and serve barely chilled.
tips: Grind the aromatics into the coconut before straining so the heat infuses the milk evenly rather than sitting as bits.
This version is thicker and spicier — thin it with a little coconut water if you want to sip it rather than pour it over rice.
Keep it off the heat entirely after adding coconut milk to prevent splitting and preserve the pink hue.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle over hot steamed rice as a light, tangy curry, or serve in bowls with papad as a soupy starter to a Malvani spread.

variations.name: Instant Sol Kadhi with Agal
variations.description: A weeknight shortcut using ready kokum agal (thick kokum extract) and canned or store coconut milk, so a chilled glass is ready in ten minutes flat. It keeps all the cooling, digestive character of the classic without the coconut-grinding, ideal when you want sol kadhi in a hurry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: a teaspoon of cold-pressed coconut oil lifts the ready-made base and fries the garlic tempering to restore fresh aroma

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups thick coconut milk with 1.5 cups water in a bowl until smooth and uniformly creamy.
Stir in 4 tbsp kokum agal a little at a time, tasting as you go, until the drink turns pale pink and pleasantly sour.
Add 0.5 tsp salt and mix well, then adjust with more agal for tang or water to thin as needed.
Heat 1 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan on medium and crackle 0.5 tsp cumin seeds until fragrant, about 20 seconds.
Add 2 crushed garlic cloves, 1 slit green chilli and 6 curry leaves to the oil and fry for 15 seconds until the garlic just turns aromatic.
Pour the hot tempering over the kadhi, stir in 2 tbsp chopped coriander, chill for 10 minutes, and serve.
tips: Add the concentrated kokum agal gradually — it is far stronger than soaked petals and easily over-sours the drink.
If using canned coconut milk, whisk it well first as it separates in the tin.
Keep the base chilled and add the tempering just before serving so the garlic aroma stays fresh.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled in glasses as a fast after-meal digestive, perfect for weeknights when you crave sol kadhi without the prep.

variations.name: Ginger-Jaggery Sol Kadhi
variations.description: A gentler, sweet-leaning version where a touch of jaggery and extra ginger soften the sourness into a mellow, warming digestive that even children enjoy. The coconut turns creamier and the ginger adds a soothing heat, making it as much a comfort drink as a palate cleanser.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a little unrefined jaggery mellows the kokum's sharp tang into a soothing sweet-sour balance for this gentler version

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil blooms the cumin tempering and reinforces the creamy coconut base

steps: Soak 9 dried kokum petals in 0.5 cup warm water for 20 minutes until soft and pink.
Blend 1.5 cups grated coconut with 1 inch ginger and 1.5 cups warm water, then strain through muslin, pressing well, into a smooth gingery coconut milk.
Dissolve 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder in the kokum soaking water and strain out any grit, then stir this sweet-sour liquid into the coconut milk with 0.5 tsp salt.
Add the soaked kokum petals, rest for 10 minutes, then press and remove them once the colour and balance are right.
Heat 1 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan, crackle 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 0.5 inch julienned ginger, then add 6 curry leaves and fry for 20 seconds.
Pour the tempering over the kadhi, stir in 2 tbsp chopped coriander, and serve lightly chilled.
tips: Dissolve the jaggery in the warm kokum water rather than the cold coconut milk so it melts smoothly and strains clean.
Keep the sweetness subtle — a hint of jaggery should round the tang, not turn the drink into a dessert.
Extra fresh ginger both in the milk and the tempering makes this the most warming, digestive-friendly version.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve gently chilled as a soothing after-dinner digestive, especially good following a rich or oily meal when a mellow sweetness is welcome.

variations.name: Classic Sweet Boondi
variations.description: Classic Sweet Boondi is made of tiny golden gram-flour pearls fried through a perforated ladle and soaked in a fragrant one-string sugar syrup laced with cardamom. Soft yet with a gentle bite, it is a temple-prasad staple and the base of every good boondi ladoo.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined khandsari makes a clean one-string syrup with a soft caramel edge

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil fries the pearls to an even gold without any raw smell

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups besan with enough water and a pinch of baking soda into a smooth lump-free batter of thick pouring consistency and a pinch of yellow colour.
Dissolve 1.25 cups Anveshan Khandsari in 1 cup water and simmer with 0.5 tsp lemon juice until it reaches one-string consistency, about 8 minutes, then keep warm.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to medium and hold a perforated boondi ladle over the pan, pouring batter across it so droplets fall in.
Fry each batch for about 1 minute until the pearls are just set and pale gold, not crisp, then lift out and drain briefly.
Slide the hot boondi straight into the warm syrup, stir in 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and 1 tbsp melon seeds and let them soak for 10 minutes.
Fold gently so the pearls absorb the syrup evenly and serve warm or at room temperature.
tips: Keep the batter at a thick pouring consistency; too thin and the pearls grow tails instead of round beads.
Wipe the underside of the ladle between batches so the droplets fall cleanly.
Do not over-fry; boondi should stay soft to drink in the syrup properly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as prasad in small leaf bowls, or press warm into boondi ladoos for a festival platter.

variations.name: Kesar Boondi
variations.description: This royal Rajasthani take steeps the syrup with saffron strands and finishes the boondi with slivered pistachios for a golden, aromatic sweet fit for weddings. The saffron perfumes every pearl and lends a warm amber colour without any artificial dye.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: carries the saffron cleanly and sets into a delicate one-string syrup

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: frying in bilona ghee gives these wedding-grade boondi a rich mithai-shop aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm milk to colour and perfume the entire syrup

steps: Soak 0.25 tsp Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk for 10 minutes until it releases a deep golden hue.
Whisk 1.5 cups besan with water and a pinch of baking soda into a smooth thick pouring batter and rest it for 10 minutes.
Dissolve 1.25 cups Anveshan Khandsari in 1 cup water, add the saffron milk and 0.5 tsp lemon juice, and simmer to one-string consistency, then keep warm.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Ghee to medium and drop the batter through a boondi ladle in batches, frying each for a minute until soft and just set.
Transfer the fried pearls straight into the saffron syrup, stir in 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and soak for 10 minutes.
Fold through 3 tbsp slivered pistachios and serve warm so the saffron aroma is at its fullest.
tips: Bloom saffron in warm, not hot, milk to draw out colour without dulling the fragrance.
Frying in ghee gives a superior aroma but keep the heat medium so the pearls do not brown.
Reserve a few pistachio slivers to scatter on top just before serving for a jewelled look.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in silver katoris at a wedding feast, garnished with a few extra saffron strands.

variations.name: Coconut Boondi
variations.description: A South Indian temple-style boondi where toasted coconut and a coconut-oil fry give the pearls a nutty, faintly savoury depth against the sweet syrup. Curry leaves and a whisper of edible camphor make it unmistakably prasadam from a Tamil kovil kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: temple-style boondi uses jaggery for a darker, earthier prasadam sweetness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: frying in coconut oil gives the authentic kovil aroma and flavour

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups besan with water and a pinch of baking soda into a smooth thick pouring batter.
Melt 1.25 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 1 cup water, strain out grit, and simmer to one-string consistency, then keep warm.
Toast 0.5 cup grated coconut in a dry pan until golden and fragrant, then set aside.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Coconut Oil to medium, fry 2 tbsp cashews until golden, then drop batter through a boondi ladle in batches for a minute each until just set.
Slide the hot pearls into the jaggery syrup with the toasted coconut, fried cashews, 0.5 tsp cardamom powder, 0.25 tsp dry ginger powder and a pinch of edible camphor.
Fold gently and let the boondi soak for 10 minutes so the coconut and camphor perfume every bite.
tips: Strain the jaggery syrup through muslin to remove any sand before boiling to one string.
Use edible camphor with a very light hand; a pinch is enough to scent the whole batch.
Toast the coconut just before mixing so it stays fragrant and does not go rubbery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Offer warm as prasadam on a banana leaf, topped with a few extra fried cashews.

variations.name: Boondi Ladoo
variations.description: The festive format that presses sweet boondi into round ladoos bound with extra syrup, edible gum and nuts so they hold their shape. Slightly firmer and denser than loose boondi, these are the golden ladoos handed out at every Ganesh and wedding celebration.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: a slightly thicker two-string syrup is needed so the ladoos bind and hold

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoonful is also worked into the warm boondi so the ladoos roll smoothly

steps: Make a smooth thick pouring batter from 2 cups besan, water and a pinch of baking soda.
Simmer 1.5 cups Anveshan Khandsari with 1.25 cups water and 0.5 tsp lemon juice to a firm two-string consistency, then keep warm.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Ghee to medium, fry 1 tbsp edible gum until it puffs and lift it out, then fry 3 tbsp cashews and 2 tbsp raisins and set aside.
Drop the batter through a boondi ladle in batches, frying each for a minute until just set, and add the pearls directly to the warm syrup.
Stir in the crushed fried gum, cashews, raisins, 1 tbsp melon seeds and 0.75 tsp cardamom powder, then let the mixture rest 10 minutes until sticky.
While still warm, grease your palms with ghee and press firmly into 12 round ladoos, then cool until they set firm.
tips: A two-string syrup is essential; a one-string syrup leaves the ladoos too loose to hold.
Roll while the boondi is warm and tacky; once cold it will not bind into balls.
Fried edible gum adds crunch and helps the ladoos keep their shape for days.
variations.servingSuggestion: Stack the golden ladoos in a decorated box for festival gifting or temple offering.

variations.name: Classic Til Chikki
variations.description: Classic Til Chikki is a thin, glassy brittle of roasted white sesame set in hard-crack jaggery, snapped into shards for Makar Sankranti. It carries a nutty toastiness and a clean caramel crackle, and is prized as a warming, iron-rich winter sweet.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: cooked to hard-crack it sets the sesame into a clear, snappable brittle

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the surface and stops the jaggery from sticking as it sets

steps: Dry-roast 1 cup white sesame seeds over low heat for 3 to 4 minutes until they pop and turn pale golden, then set aside.
Grease a steel plate or marble slab and a rolling pin with a little of the 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee.
Melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 1 tbsp water and the remaining ghee over low heat, stirring, for about 6 minutes.
Cook to hard-crack stage, when a drop in cold water snaps cleanly, then quickly stir in the sesame, 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and a pinch of salt.
Pour the mixture onto the greased slab and roll it out thin and even before it starts to set.
Score into diamonds while warm, then cool completely and snap along the lines into crisp shards.
tips: The jaggery must reach hard-crack or the chikki will stay chewy instead of snapping.
Work fast once the sesame goes in; the mixture stiffens within a minute.
Roll between two sheets of greased butter paper if you do not have a marble slab.
variations.servingSuggestion: Stack the shards in a jar for Sankranti and serve with hot ginger chai.

variations.name: Peanut Til Chikki
variations.description: This heartier version balances the fine sesame with coarsely crushed roasted peanuts, giving the brittle a chunkier crunch and a groundnut richness. The two textures together make it more filling and a popular roadside winter snack across Maharashtra.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: binds the sesame and peanuts into a firm hard-crack brittle

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: greases the slab and echoes the peanut flavour of the chikki

steps: Roast 0.5 cup sesame seeds until golden, then coarsely crush 0.75 cup roasted peanuts, keeping some halves for crunch.
Grease a slab and rolling pin with the 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil.
Melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 1 tbsp water over low heat and cook to hard-crack stage, about 7 minutes.
Turn off the heat and quickly fold in the sesame, crushed peanuts, 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and 0.25 tsp salt.
Tip onto the greased slab and roll out about half a centimetre thick while still hot.
Score into squares while warm and break apart once fully cooled and crisp.
tips: Crush the peanuts coarsely so you still get satisfying nutty chunks in each shard.
A little salt sharpens the peanut flavour against the sweet jaggery.
Store airtight; peanuts turn soft if the chikki is left exposed to air.
variations.servingSuggestion: Break into rough pieces and serve as an energy-rich trekking or tea-time snack.

variations.name: Coconut Til Chikki
variations.description: A coastal spin that layers thin ribbons of toasted dry coconut with the sesame, giving the brittle a flaky, fragrant sweetness. The coconut lightens the chikki and adds a delicate golden colour and tropical aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sets the coconut and sesame into a light, flaky brittle

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: greases the slab and deepens the coconut fragrance

steps: Dry-roast 0.5 cup sesame seeds until golden, then lightly toast 0.5 cup thin dry-coconut slices in the same pan until pale gold.
Grease a slab and rolling pin with the 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil.
Melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 1 tbsp water over low heat and cook to hard-crack stage, about 6 minutes.
Remove from the heat and quickly stir in the sesame, toasted coconut, 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and a pinch of salt.
Pour onto the greased slab and roll out thin and even before the mixture sets.
Cut into diamonds while warm and snap into crisp flaky shards once cooled.
tips: Toast the coconut only until pale gold or it will taste burnt and bitter.
Thin coconut slices give a prettier flaky brittle than desiccated coconut.
Keep the shards airtight so the coconut stays crisp and does not turn chewy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a festive platter alongside classic til shards for a two-tone chikki spread.

variations.name: Til Gud Rolls
variations.description: A softer, chewier take that keeps the jaggery at soft-crack stage and shapes the warm sesame mixture into bite-sized logs instead of a hard slab. Gentler on the teeth and enriched with dry ginger, these are made for elders and small children at Sankranti.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: cooked only to soft-crack so the rolls stay pliable and chewy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: keeps the mixture soft enough to roll and adds a mellow richness

steps: Dry-roast 1 cup sesame seeds until golden and fragrant, then set aside; lightly toast 2 tbsp poppy seeds as well.
Warm 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, add 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tbsp water, and melt over low heat for about 5 minutes.
Cook only to soft-crack stage, when a drop in cold water forms a firm but pliable ball, then switch off the heat.
Stir in the roasted sesame, 0.5 tsp dry ginger powder, 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and a pinch of salt until evenly combined.
While warm, take small portions and roll them between greased palms into short logs, then roll each log in the toasted poppy seeds.
Cool the rolls on a greased tray until firm but still chewy, about 15 minutes.
tips: Stopping at soft-crack is what keeps these chewy; take them further and they turn brittle.
Grease your palms well as the warm mixture is very sticky to shape.
The poppy-seed coating adds a pretty finish and a gentle nutty crunch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Offer the soft rolls to elders and children who find hard chikki difficult to bite.

variations.name: Classic Spiced Amla Pickle
variations.description: A wholesome winter pickle where vitamin-C-rich Indian gooseberries are steamed until tender, separated into segments, and cured in a warming fennel-mustard masala under mustard oil. The amla loses its raw astringency and turns tangy, soft and deeply flavourful. A spoon a day of this tart pickle is a time-honoured way to build immunity through the cold months.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Smoked and cooled, it submerges the gooseberry segments and matures the pickle with its pungent warmth

steps: Steam 500 g washed amla for 10-12 minutes until a knife slides in easily, then cool and separate each into its natural segments, discarding the seeds.
Dry-roast 3 tbsp fennel, 2 tbsp mustard seeds and 1 tbsp fenugreek for 2 minutes, cool, and grind to a coarse powder.
Toss the amla segments with the ground spices, 1 tsp nigella, 1 tbsp turmeric, 2 tbsp chilli powder and 3 tbsp salt.
Heat 1 cup Anveshan Mustard Oil until it smokes, cool completely, then mix most of it through the amla and pack into a dry jar.
Pour the remaining oil on top so the segments are submerged, cover, and keep in the sun for 4-5 days.
Shake the jar daily until the amla darkens, softens and soaks up the tangy masala.
tips: Steaming rather than boiling keeps the amla from turning watery and preserves more of its nutrients.
Let the steamed amla cool fully before mixing, as heat plus oil can cause the pickle to spoil.
Keep the segments under oil at all times and use a dry spoon so the jar lasts all winter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve a segment with dal-rice or parathas, or eat one on an empty stomach as a traditional immunity booster.

variations.name: Sweet Amla Jaggery Pickle
variations.description: A gentle sweet-and-sour amla pickle where the steamed gooseberries are simmered in a spiced jaggery syrup until glossy and tender, mellowing their sharpness into something almost dessert-like. Warm notes of cardamom and roasted cumin round out the tang. Easier on the palate than the fiery oil pickle and loved by children.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Cooked into a spiced syrup, it turns the tart gooseberries into a mellow sweet-sour preserve

steps: Steam 500 g amla for 10-12 minutes until soft, cool, and break into segments, discarding the seeds.
In a heavy pan combine 2 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with a splash of water and melt it on medium flame into a syrup.
Add the amla segments and simmer 12-15 minutes, stirring, until they turn glossy and soak up the syrup.
Cook until the syrup thickens enough to coat a spoon in a thick single thread.
Switch off and stir in 1 tbsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp black pepper, 0.5 tsp cardamom, 1 tsp dry ginger, 1 tsp chilli powder and 1 tsp black salt.
Cool completely and store in a dry jar; it needs no oil and keeps for months.
tips: Stop cooking at a one-thread syrup; boiled further the jaggery hardens and the amla turns chewy.
The dry ginger and black pepper make this both tasty and gently warming for winter digestion.
If the amla is very sour, an extra handful of jaggery balances it without making it cloying.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a sweet relish with parathas or curd rice, or spoon over warm porridge for a tangy lift.

variations.name: South Indian Amla Thokku
variations.description: A cooked Tamil-style gooseberry thokku where grated amla is simmered down in gingelly oil with a mustard tempering and tamarind into a thick, spoonable relish. Fully cooked rather than sun-cured, it has a mellow jammy texture and a savoury tang. A little stirred into hot rice with ghee makes a nourishing, everyday meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil slow-cooks the grated amla and preserves the finished thokku

steps: Steam 500 g amla for 8-10 minutes until just soft, cool, discard the seeds, and grate or mash the flesh coarse.
Soak 1 tbsp tamarind in a little warm water and extract a thick pulp.
Heat 0.5 cups Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadhai on medium flame, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, add 0.5 tsp asafoetida and 2 sprigs curry leaves.
Add the mashed amla, tamarind pulp, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 tbsp chilli powder and 2.5 tbsp salt, and cook stirring for 12-15 minutes.
Stir in 0.5 tsp fenugreek powder and cook until the oil separates and the thokku turns thick and dark.
Cool completely and store in a dry jar; the flavours deepen over a couple of days.
tips: Cook until the oil clearly separates so the moisture has reduced enough for the thokku to keep well.
Use pre-roasted fenugreek powder stirred in near the end so it does not turn bitter.
Grating the amla gives a smoother thokku, while a coarse mash keeps a bit of texture, so choose to taste.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve a spoon mixed into hot rice with ghee, or as a tangy side to curd rice and dosa.

variations.name: Instant Grated Amla Pickle
variations.description: A quick, fresh amla pickle where grated raw gooseberry is tossed with roasted ground spices and a hot tempering, ready in hours without steaming or curing. It keeps the amla's bright, sharp tang and maximum vitamin C. The pickle to make when you want the gooseberry's goodness with none of the wait.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Smoked and slightly cooled, it tempers the spices and coats the fresh grated gooseberry

steps: Wash and dry 300 g amla, then grate the flesh coarsely off the seeds and discard the seeds.
Dry-roast 1 tbsp cumin and 0.5 tsp carom seeds for 1 minute until fragrant, cool, and grind coarse.
Toss the grated amla with the ground spices, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tbsp chilli powder, 1 tsp black salt and 1.5 tbsp salt.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it smokes, lower the flame, add 0.25 tsp asafoetida, and let it foam.
Pour the hot tempering over the grated amla mixture and stir well to coat.
Rest 3-4 hours at room temperature before serving; it keeps a week refrigerated.
tips: Grating raw amla keeps its vitamin C intact, unlike steaming, so this is the most nourishing quick option.
Smoking the mustard oil removes its raw sharpness before it goes over the fresh gooseberry.
Make small batches, as the raw grated amla is best eaten fresh within a few days.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve fresh with dal-rice, khichdi or parathas, or eat a spoonful before meals as a tangy tonic.

variations.name: Classic Kesar Badam Milk
variations.description: The warm, restorative almond milk of Indian winters and wedding feasts: full-fat milk simmered down and thickened with a paste of blanched almonds, perfumed with Anveshan Saffron and cardamom and sweetened with Anveshan Khandsari. Rich but never cloying, it is the nightcap grandmothers pressed on children to build strength.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: Unrefined khandsari dissolves cleanly and lets the almond and saffron flavours stay in front

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Saffron gives badam milk its golden colour and the fragrance that makes it feel festive

steps: Soak 25 almonds in hot water for 15 minutes, then slip off the skins and grind them to a fine smooth paste with a little milk.
Warm 0.25 cup of the milk and steep 15 Anveshan Saffron strands in it for 10 minutes until richly coloured.
Bring the remaining milk to a boil in a heavy pan, then lower to a gentle simmer and cook for 8-10 minutes, stirring, until slightly reduced.
Whisk in the almond paste and simmer for another 5 minutes on low, stirring constantly so it does not stick, until the milk thickens and turns creamy.
Add the saffron milk, 5 tbsp Anveshan Khandsari, 5 crushed cardamom pods and 0.125 tsp nutmeg and stir until the sweetener dissolves.
Serve hot in 4 cups topped with slivered pistachios, or chill it thoroughly for an equally loved cold version.
tips: Grind the almonds really fine; a coarse paste leaves a grainy milk instead of a velvety one.
Keep the heat low once the paste goes in, as thick almond milk scorches on the base very easily.
For a deeper colour without more saffron, add a single strand of saffron directly to each serving cup.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a bedtime drink in winter, or pour chilled over ice at a summer gathering with a dusting of crushed pistachio and a saffron strand floated on top.

variations.name: Instant Badam Milk Masala
variations.description: A make-ahead dry badam milk powder, ground from roasted almonds, cashews and warming spices, so a spoon stirred into hot milk gives you instant kesar badam doodh on a busy morning. Sweetened right into the blend with Anveshan Khandsari and coloured with Anveshan Saffron, it keeps for weeks in a jar.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: Ground into the mix, khandsari sweetens each cup evenly without a separate sugar step

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Crushed into the powder, saffron colours and scents the milk the moment it is stirred in

steps: Dry-roast 30 almonds and 10 cashews in a pan on low heat for 4-5 minutes until they smell toasty, then cool completely.
Grind the cooled nuts with 8 cardamom pods, 6 peppercorns, 15 Anveshan Saffron strands, 0.25 tsp dry ginger and 0.25 tsp nutmeg to a slightly coarse powder.
Pulse in 6 tbsp Anveshan Khandsari in short bursts so the mix stays a dry powder and does not turn oily.
Store the badam milk masala in an airtight jar; it keeps well for up to three weeks.
To serve, bring 4 cups milk to a boil, lower the heat and whisk in 6-8 tbsp of the masala, simmering for 3-4 minutes until thickened and golden.
Pour hot into 4 cups and finish each with a pinch of the dry masala sprinkled on top.
tips: Cool the nuts fully before grinding; warm nuts release oil and clump the powder into a paste.
Grind in short pulses and stop the moment it looks powdery, as over-grinding turns it into almond butter.
Keep the jar in the fridge in summer so the roasted nut oils do not go rancid.
variations.servingSuggestion: Keep the jar handy for quick winter mornings, or stir the masala into warm milk for kids before bed; it also makes a lovely edible gift in a labelled jar.

variations.name: Vegan Almond Doodh
variations.description: A dairy-free badam milk made from scratch, blending soaked almonds with water into a fresh almond milk, then simmering it with dates and Anveshan Jaggery Powder for an unrefined sweetness. Pure almond and saffron with no dairy at all, it is lighter than the classic yet still warming and nourishing.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery keeps this plant-based milk unrefined and adds a soft caramel note to the almond

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: A saffron infusion gives the dairy-free doodh its golden colour and gentle aroma

steps: Soak 1 cup almonds in water overnight or in hot water for 1 hour, then drain and peel off the skins.
Blend the peeled almonds with 4 cups fresh water and 4 deseeded dates for 2 minutes until completely smooth.
Strain the mixture through a nut-milk bag or muslin, pressing to extract every drop of almond milk.
Warm 2 tbsp of the milk and steep 12 Anveshan Saffron strands for 8 minutes, then pour into the strained milk.
Simmer the almond milk gently for 6-8 minutes with 5 crushed cardamom pods and 0.25 tsp cinnamon, then whisk in 4 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder off high heat until dissolved.
Serve warm or chilled in 4 glasses, garnished with 1 tbsp slivered almonds.
tips: Save the strained almond pulp; dried out, it works as almond flour for baking or in energy balls.
Add the jaggery off high heat and stir gently, as boiling hard after it goes in can curdle the plant milk.
Blend and strain twice if you want an ultra-smooth, barista-style almond milk.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve to vegan or lactose-intolerant guests warm before bed, or chill and use it as a wholesome base for smoothies and overnight oats the next morning.

variations.name: Dry-Fruit Paak Badam Milk
variations.description: A rich winter tonic version where a spoon of Anveshan Dry Fruit Paak melts into hot almond-thickened milk finished with a little Anveshan Ghee, turning the everyday drink into an energy-dense nightcap. Warming, nutty and deeply satisfying, it is the kind of drink that fortifies you against a cold-country chill.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Dry Fruit Paak
ingredients.note: The dry-fruit paak melts in to sweeten and enrich the milk with concentrated nuts and warming spices

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon of bilona ghee gives the tonic its warming winter richness and glossy finish

steps: Soak 20 almonds in hot water for 15 minutes, peel, and grind to a fine paste with a little milk along with 6 walnut halves.
Heat 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan on medium and lightly toast 4 crushed cardamom pods for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Pour in 4 cups milk, bring to a boil, then lower to a simmer and cook for 6-8 minutes until slightly reduced.
Whisk in the almond-walnut paste with 0.25 tsp dry ginger and 0.125 tsp nutmeg and simmer for 4-5 minutes on low, stirring so it does not catch.
Take the pan off the heat, stir in 3 tbsp Anveshan Dry Fruit Paak and whisk until it melts fully into the milk.
Serve piping hot in 4 cups, ideal for a cold winter night.
tips: Melt the dry-fruit paak off the heat so its delicate aromatics are not boiled away.
This drink is deliberately rich; keep portions small and skip any extra sugar as the paak already sweetens it.
For a thinner tonic, hold back the walnuts and use 5 tbsp of milk more.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a fortifying nightcap through winter, or give a warm cupful to anyone recovering from a cold or fever alongside a light meal.

variations.name: Classic Boondi Ladoo
variations.description: The temple-favourite ladoo of plump gram-flour pearls, fried through a wide-holed ladle so each boondi stays distinct and slightly chewy, then bound in one-string sugar syrup. Unlike the melt-in-mouth motichoor, these pearls hold their shape and give a pleasant bite. Bright with cardamom and dotted with fried cashews, it is the classic prasad ladoo.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: cooked to a one-string syrup that coats and binds the distinct pearls

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the cashews and greases your palms for shaping

steps: Whisk 2 cups besan with about 1 cup water into a smooth batter of thick dropping consistency and rest for 10 minutes.
Cook 2 cups Anveshan Khandsari Sugar with the remaining water to a one-string syrup, about 8 minutes, then stir in 1 tsp cardamom and keep warm.
Fry the chopped cashews and raisins in 1 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee until golden and plump, then set aside.
Heat the oil to medium and pour the batter through a wide-holed perforated ladle so round pearls drop; fry each batch for about 2 minutes until just cooked but still soft.
Stir the drained boondi into the warm syrup with the fried nuts and melon seeds, and let them soak for 10 minutes until the syrup clings.
Grease your palms with the remaining ghee and press portions firmly into 14 ladoos while warm, resting 30 minutes to hold shape.
tips: Use a wide-holed ladle for boondi so the pearls stay plump and distinct, unlike the tiny motichoor drops.
Keep the batter at thick dropping consistency; too thin and the pearls flatten instead of staying round.
If the ladoos crumble, the syrup was under-cooked; thicken it briefly and re-press the warm mix.
variations.servingSuggestion: Offer as temple prasad or festival sweet on a banana leaf, each ladoo topped with a whole fried cashew.

variations.name: Kesari Boondi Ladoo
variations.description: A saffron-and-cardamom boondi ladoo where the pearls glow deep orange, a South Indian marriage-hall staple. Blooming saffron in the syrup gives both colour and a floral fragrance that lifts the humble gram flour. Fried curry-leaf-free but heavy on cashew, it is festive and aromatic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: the syrup base carrying saffron colour and scent into the pearls

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm milk to tint the syrup a rich orange

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the cashews and greases your palms

steps: Soak 1 tsp Anveshan Saffron in the warm milk for 10 minutes to draw out its colour.
Whisk 2 cups besan with about 1 cup water into a smooth thick dropping batter and rest for 10 minutes.
Cook 2 cups Anveshan Khandsari Sugar with the remaining water to a one-string syrup, stir in the saffron milk and 1.5 tsp cardamom, and keep warm.
Fry the chopped cashews in 1 tbsp Anveshan Bilona Ghee until golden, then set aside.

Heat the oil to medium, pour the batter through a wide-holed ladle so round pearls drop, and fry each batch about 2 minutes until just cooked; stir into the saffron syrup with the cashews and soak 10 minutes.
Grease your palms with the remaining ghee and press into 14 firm ladoos while warm, resting 30 minutes to set.
tips: Bloom the saffron in warm milk rather than adding it dry, or the colour stays weak.
Extra cardamom balances the saffron beautifully here, so don't cut it back.
Soak the pearls only until the syrup clings; over-soaking makes boondi ladoo soggy rather than firm.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these vivid orange ladoos at South Indian weddings and Navratri, garnished with a whole golden cashew.

variations.name: Coconut Boondi Ladoo
variations.description: A coastal twist that rolls syrup-soaked boondi with toasted dry coconut for extra chew and a tropical aroma, then finishes each ball in a coconut coating. The coconut cuts the sweetness and adds texture the plain version lacks. It is popular through Karnataka and Konkan festival kitchens.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: syrup that binds the pearls before the coconut is folded in

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil for deep-frying
ingredients.note: frying the boondi in this deepens the coconut theme of the ladoo

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: toasts the coconut and greases your palms

steps: Whisk 2 cups besan with about 1 cup water into a smooth thick dropping batter and rest for 10 minutes.
Cook 2 cups Anveshan Khandsari Sugar with the remaining water to a one-string syrup, stir in 1 tsp cardamom, and keep warm.
Toast the grated copra and chopped cashews in the Anveshan Bilona Ghee for 3 minutes until pale gold, reserving 3 tbsp coconut for coating.
Heat the Anveshan Coconut Oil to medium, pour the batter through a wide-holed ladle so round pearls drop, and fry each batch about 2 minutes until just cooked.
Stir the drained boondi, toasted coconut and cashews into the warm syrup and soak for 10 minutes until it clings.
Grease your palms, press into 14 firm ladoos while warm, and roll each in the reserved toasted coconut before setting for 30 minutes.
tips: Toast the copra only to pale gold; browning it makes the ladoo taste burnt.
Frying in coconut oil ties the whole flavour together, but keep the heat steady so it doesn't smoke.
Rolling the finished ladoos in coconut hides any cracks and adds an attractive snowy finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these coconut-coated ladoos at Konkan and Karnataka festivals, or offer as prasad after a coastal temple visit.

variations.name: Jaggery Boondi Ladoo
variations.description: A wholesome winter boondi ladoo where the plump pearls are bound in jaggery syrup instead of sugar, giving an earthy amber sweet with a firmer bite. The jaggery and a hint of dry ginger make it warming and less cloying. It keeps longer than the sugar version, ideal for gifting through the cold season.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted and strained to a one-string syrup that binds the pearls amber

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil for deep-frying
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil fries the boondi clean without any refined-oil aftertaste

ingredients.name: Anveshan Bilona Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the nuts and greases your palms

steps: Whisk 2 cups besan with about 1 cup water into a smooth thick dropping batter and rest for 10 minutes.
Melt 2 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with the remaining water, strain out grit, then cook to a one-string syrup and stir in 1 tsp cardamom and 0.5 tsp dry ginger.
Fry the chopped almonds in the Anveshan Bilona Ghee until golden, about 2 minutes, and set aside.
Heat the Anveshan Groundnut Oil to medium, pour the batter through a wide-holed ladle so round pearls drop, and fry each batch about 2 minutes until just cooked.
Stir the drained boondi and fried almonds into the warm jaggery syrup and soak for 10 minutes until it clings.
Grease your palms with ghee and press into 14 firm ladoos while warm, resting 30 minutes to hold shape.
tips: Strain the melted jaggery to remove grit, or the pearls turn gritty and the syrup stays cloudy.
Jaggery syrup sets faster than sugar, so keep it warm and work quickly while shaping.
The dry ginger keeps these winter-appropriate and helps them digest despite the richness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these amber ladoos through winter and Sankranti with warm milk, or box them as a wholesome festive gift.

variations.name: Classic Chana Dal Halwa
variations.description: Chana dal halwa is a rich, labour-of-love pudding of soaked split gram ground to a paste and roasted long and slow in ghee until deeply golden and fragrant, then simmered with sweetened milk. Grainy, aromatic and intensely rich, it is a Rajasthani wedding and winter classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the dal paste long and slow until golden, giving the halwa its rich body

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: dissolved into the milk to sweeten the roasted dal cleanly

steps: Soak 1 cup chana dal for 4 hours, drain well, and grind to a slightly coarse, thick paste using very little water.
Heat 0.75 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai and add the dal paste, stirring constantly over low-medium heat.
Roast the paste patiently for 25 to 30 minutes, breaking up lumps, until it turns golden-brown, grainy and releases ghee with a deeply nutty aroma.
Warm 2.5 cups milk with 0.75 cup Anveshan Khandsari until dissolved, then pour it into the roasted dal in stages, stirring hard to avoid lumps.
Cook on low heat for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring, until the halwa drinks up the milk and thickens into a glossy mass that leaves the pan.
Fry 3 tbsp cashews and almonds in a little ghee, fold them in with 0.5 tsp cardamom, and serve the halwa warm.
tips: The long roast of the dal paste is the whole secret; rushing it leaves a raw, pasty halwa, so keep stirring.
Grind the dal with minimal water so the paste roasts rather than steams in the ghee.
If lumps form when the milk goes in, mash them against the pan or blitz briefly for a smooth finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm in bowls as a Rajasthani winter or wedding dessert, generously garnished with fried nuts.

variations.name: Kesar Mawa Chana Dal Halwa
variations.description: The banquet version enriches the roasted dal with khoya and bloomed saffron for a denser, saffron-gold halwa dripping with ghee. Richer and more aromatic than the classic, it is the halwa served on silver at Rajasthani feasts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the dal and carries the khoya for a rich, banquet-style halwa

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: sweetens the mawa-rich halwa while keeping the saffron colour radiant

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm milk to give the halwa its saffron-gold colour and aroma

steps: Soak 1 cup chana dal for 4 hours, drain, and grind to a thick, slightly coarse paste with minimal water; soak 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk.
Heat 0.75 cup Anveshan Ghee and roast the dal paste over low-medium heat for 25 to 30 minutes until golden, grainy and ghee-releasing.
Warm 2 cups milk with 0.75 cup Anveshan Khandsari and the bloomed saffron milk, then pour into the dal in stages, stirring hard to keep it smooth.
Cook 6 to 7 minutes until the milk is absorbed, then stir in 0.75 cup grated khoya and cook a further 4 minutes until it melts in.
Continue cooking on low heat for 3 to 4 minutes until the halwa turns thick, glossy and a rich saffron gold.
Fold in 0.5 tsp cardamom and half the pistachios, then serve warm garnished with the rest.
tips: Add the khoya only after the dal has absorbed the milk, so the halwa binds richly rather than turning loose.
Bloom the saffron in warm milk first so its colour spreads evenly through the pudding.
This halwa reheats beautifully with a splash of milk and a spoon of ghee to loosen it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm at feasts and weddings, spread in a shallow dish and topped with pistachios and saffron strands.

variations.name: Jaggery Chana Dal Halwa
variations.description: A rustic, dairy-light version that sweetens the roasted dal with jaggery and coconut water instead of milk, giving a darker, earthier halwa. Deeper and less rich than the classic, it echoes the flavours of a South Indian chana dal payasam turned thick.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the dal paste to a deep gold for a rustic, jaggery-sweetened halwa

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted and strained to sweeten the halwa with dark, earthy caramel notes

steps: Soak 1 cup chana dal for 4 hours, drain, and grind to a thick paste with minimal water.
Heat 0.6 cup Anveshan Ghee, fry 3 tbsp cashews and lightly toast 0.25 cup grated coconut, then set both aside.
Add the dal paste to the ghee and roast over low-medium heat for 25 to 30 minutes until golden, grainy and nutty.
Melt 0.8 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 2.5 cups water over low heat and strain out any grit.
Pour the warm jaggery water into the roasted dal off the boil, stirring hard, and cook 8 to 10 minutes until thick and glossy.
Fold in the toasted coconut, cashews and 0.5 tsp cardamom, then serve the halwa warm.
tips: Use water rather than milk here so the jaggery cannot curdle the halwa.
Strain the melted jaggery well to keep the halwa smooth and grit-free.
The coconut adds a South Indian note, but toast it lightly so it does not turn bitter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a rustic festive sweet, garnished with fried cashews and a little extra toasted coconut.

variations.name: Chana Dal Coconut Halwa
variations.description: A South Indian style halwa where the roasted dal is finished with thick coconut milk instead of dairy, giving a silky, tropical pudding fragrant with cardamom. Softer and more delicate than the Rajasthani classic, it eats almost like a set payasam.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the dal paste and fries the nuts for a fragrant coconut halwa

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: dissolved into the coconut milk to sweeten the halwa without hiding the coconut

steps: Soak 1 cup chana dal for 4 hours, drain, and grind to a thick paste with minimal water.
Heat 0.6 cup Anveshan Ghee, fry 3 tbsp cashews and raisins to golden, and set them aside.
Add the dal paste to the ghee and roast over low-medium heat for 25 to 30 minutes until golden, grainy and deeply nutty.
Warm 2 cups coconut milk with 0.7 cup Anveshan Khandsari until the sugar dissolves, keeping it just below a boil.
Pour the warm sweet coconut milk into the roasted dal off the high flame, stirring hard, and cook 6 to 8 minutes until it thickens to a silky, glossy halwa.
Fold in 0.5 tsp cardamom, 0.25 tsp nutmeg and the fried nuts, then serve warm.
tips: Add the coconut milk warm and keep the flame low so it thickens smoothly without splitting.
This halwa stays softer than the milk version, so cook just until it holds its shape on a spoon.
A pinch of nutmeg lifts the coconut beautifully, but keep it light so it does not turn bitter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm or lightly chilled after a South Indian meal, garnished with fried cashews and raisins.

variations.name: Classic Dhaba Dal Fry
variations.description: The comforting mixed-lentil dal fry of North Indian dhabas, where toor and masoor are simmered soft, then bhuna-ed into a golden onion-tomato masala and finished with a sizzling ghee-cumin tadka. Thick, hearty and gently smoky, it is the everyday dal that makes rice and roti feel like a feast.

ingredients.name: Toor dal (arhar)
ingredients.note: rinsed well

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee gives the tadka the nutty depth that defines a good dal fry

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Rinse the toor and masoor dals together, then pressure-cook with 3 cups water, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 4-5 whistles until soft; whisk lightly so it looks creamy but still has body.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add the chopped onions and fry for 6-7 minutes until golden brown.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 2 slit green chillies for a minute, then the chopped tomatoes with 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder.
Bhuno the masala for 5-6 minutes until the tomatoes collapse and the ghee separates at the edges.
Pour in the cooked dal with about 1 cup hot water and the remaining 1/4 tsp salt, and simmer on low heat for 8-10 minutes so the dal takes on the masala and thickens.
Stir in 1/2 tsp garam masala, then mash a little against the side for a homely texture.
Finish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander and serve hot with a last drizzle of ghee.
tips: Whisk the cooked dal before adding it to the masala so the fry turns creamy rather than watery.
Fry the onions to a proper golden brown for the characteristic dhaba colour and depth.
Loosen the dal only with hot water if it thickens on standing, so the tadka aroma stays undiluted.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jeera rice or tandoori roti, a raw onion salad and a wedge of lemon.

variations.name: Punjabi Butter Dal Fry
variations.description: A richer, creamier dal fry finished with butter, a splash of cream and a fragrant kasuri methi tadka. Milder and more velvety than the standard dhaba version, this is the plush dal that turns up at Punjabi weddings and Sunday lunches, luxurious enough to eat with plain rice.

ingredients.name: Toor dal (arhar)
ingredients.note: rinsed well

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee builds the base while butter finishes it, for a plush Punjabi richness

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: pureed

ingredients.name: Kasuri methi (dried fenugreek)
ingredients.note: crushed

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup toor dal with 3 cups water, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 5 whistles until very soft, then whisk until smooth and creamy.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add the chopped onions and saute for 6 minutes until soft and light golden.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for a minute, then the tomato puree with 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, and cook for 6-7 minutes until thick and glossy.
Pour in the whisked dal with 1 cup hot water and the remaining 1/4 tsp salt, and simmer on low heat for 8 minutes until velvety.
Stir in 2 tbsp butter and 2 tbsp cream on low heat, letting the butter melt into the dal without boiling.
Crush 1 tbsp kasuri methi between your palms and add it with 1/2 tsp garam masala, simmering 2 more minutes.
Serve hot with a final knob of butter melting on top.
tips: Use only toor dal here for the smoothest, creamiest butter dal; mixed dals give a coarser texture.
Add the butter and cream off the boil so they stay silky and do not split.
Crushed kasuri methi is what gives Punjabi butter dal its signature aroma, so do not leave it out.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice or butter naan, garnished with a swirl of cream and a few coriander leaves.

variations.name: Mustard-Oil Dhaba Dal Fry
variations.description: The pungent highway version where the dal base is layered with a mustard-oil onion masala and finished with a smoking double tadka of ghee, garlic and dry red chilli poured tableside. Bold, robust and smoky, it is dal fry at its most assertive, made to stand up to thick rotis and cold nights.

ingredients.name: Toor dal (arhar)
ingredients.note: rinsed well

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: kachi ghani mustard oil gives the base masala its pungent, robust dhaba bite

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: reserved for the smoking finishing tadka poured over the dal at the table

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: sliced, for the finishing tadka

ingredients.name: Dry red chillies
ingredients.note: broken

ingredients.name: Kasuri methi (dried fenugreek)
ingredients.note: crushed

steps: Rinse the three dals together and pressure-cook with 3.5 cups water, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 5-6 whistles until soft; mash lightly and keep warm.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just smokes, lower the heat, then add the chopped onions and fry for 7-8 minutes until deep golden brown.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for a minute, then the chopped tomatoes with 1 tsp red chilli powder and the remaining 1/4 tsp salt, and bhuno for 5-6 minutes until the masala turns thick.
Pour the cooked dal into the masala with 1 cup hot water and simmer on low heat for 8-10 minutes so it takes on a smoky, restaurant-like body.

Just before serving, heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan until shimmering, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, 6 sliced garlic cloves and 3 broken dry red chillies for 30-40 seconds until the garlic is golden and the chillies darken.
Scatter 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi over the dal, then pour the smoking ghee tadka on top so it sizzles dramatically.
Fold the tadka through only halfway so streaks of garlic and chilli stay visible, and serve at once.
tips: Brown the onions properly in smoking mustard oil for the deep colour and pungent edge that dhaba dal is known for.
Pour the finishing ghee tadka right at the table so the garlic aroma hits before the first bite.
For extra smokiness, rest a live coal in a bowl on the dal, drip ghee on it and cover for two minutes before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter-brushed tandoori roti or laccha paratha and a sharp onion-lemon salad.

variations.name: Palak Dal Fry
variations.description: A wholesome green dal fry where moong and toor simmer with spinach for a lighter, mineral-rich bowl that still carries a proper ghee tadka. The spinach melts into the dal, giving it a fresh colour and a nourishing edge, making it a favourite way to sneak greens onto the plate.

ingredients.name: Moong dal (yellow)
ingredients.note: rinsed

ingredients.name: Toor dal (arhar)
ingredients.note: rinsed

ingredients.name: Spinach (palak)
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee blooms the garlic tadka that lifts the mild spinach dal

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

steps: Rinse the moong and toor dals and pressure-cook with 3 cups water, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 4 whistles until soft, then whisk lightly.
Add the finely chopped spinach to the hot dal and simmer on low heat for 6-7 minutes until it wilts and melts into the dal.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add 6 chopped garlic cloves and 2 slit green chillies and fry until the garlic turns pale gold, about a minute.
Add the chopped onion and cook for 4 minutes until golden, then add the chopped tomato and 3/4 tsp red chilli powder and cook for 3-4 minutes until soft.
Pour this tadka into the spinach dal along with the remaining 1/4 tsp salt, and simmer together for 5 minutes so the flavours marry.
Adjust the consistency with a splash of hot water, keeping it pourable.
Finish with 1 tbsp lemon juice and serve hot.
tips: Add the chopped spinach to the cooked dal rather than pressure-cooking it in, so it keeps a fresher colour and taste.
A generous hand of garlic in the ghee tadka is what makes this simple green dal sing.
Finish with lemon off the heat to brighten the spinach and balance the earthiness of the dals.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a dollop of ghee, or with phulka and a side of pickle for a light, nourishing meal.

variations.name: Classic South Indian Filter Coffee
variations.description: The iconic Tamil-Brahmin degree coffee, brewed as a thick dark decoction dripped through a traditional steel filter and mixed with hot frothy milk. Pulled between tumbler and davara until aerated and foamy, it is aromatic, strong and perfectly balanced, the ritual morning cup of South India.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: unrefined jaggery sweetens the decoction with a caramel note that complements the roasted coffee and chicory

steps: Add 6 tbsp filter coffee powder to the upper cup of a South Indian steel filter and press it down lightly with the plunger to form an even bed.
Pour 1.5 cups just-off-the-boil hot water over the grounds, cover with the lid, and let it drip slowly for 12 to 15 minutes into the lower cup to yield a thick, dark decoction.
Heat 3 cups full-fat milk in a pan until it comes to a rolling boil, keeping it hot and frothy.
For each serving, pour about 3 tbsp of the strong decoction into a tumbler, add 5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.25 tsp cardamom powder divided across the cups, and top up with the hot milk.
Pull the coffee by pouring it back and forth between the tumbler and davara from a height several times until it froths and mixes evenly.
Serve immediately in the traditional tumbler and davara while piping hot and foamy.
tips: Use water just off the boil, not fully boiling, over the grounds — too-hot water scorches the coffee and turns the decoction bitter.
Let the decoction drip undisturbed; pressing or rushing it makes a weak, cloudy brew.
Pull the coffee from a good height between two vessels to build the signature frothy top and cool it to drinking temperature.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot in a steel tumbler and davara set with a side of the same, alongside crisp dosa or idli for the classic South Indian breakfast.

variations.name: Bella Coffee (Jaggery Filter Coffee)
variations.description: A rustic Karnataka-style filter coffee sweetened entirely with jaggery decoction and scented with dry ginger and cardamom, once the everyday village cup. Earthy, warming and deeply aromatic, it swaps refined sugar for melted jaggery that lends a gentle molasses richness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted jaggery decoction is the heart of bella coffee, giving an earthy molasses sweetness in place of sugar

steps: Add 6 tbsp filter coffee powder to a steel filter, level it, and pour 1.5 cups hot water over; cover and let it drip for 12 to 15 minutes into a strong decoction.
Meanwhile, melt 6 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 0.25 cup water in a small pan on low heat into a smooth syrup, then strain out any grit.
Boil 2.5 cups full-fat milk in a pan, then lower the heat and stir in 0.25 tsp dry ginger powder and 0.25 tsp cardamom powder.
Add the strained jaggery syrup to the spiced milk off the boil, stirring gently so the milk does not curdle from the jaggery.
Pour about 3 tbsp decoction into each cup and top with the warm jaggery-spiced milk, adjusting strength to taste.
Pull the coffee between two tumblers a few times to froth and blend it, then serve hot.
tips: Always melt and strain the jaggery separately and add it off the heat, since jaggery dropped into boiling milk splits it.
A pinch of dry ginger not only adds warmth but also helps keep the jaggery-milk from curdling.
Keep the decoction strong here, as the earthy jaggery can otherwise overwhelm a weak brew.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot in steel tumblers on cold mornings, a rustic sugar-free coffee that pairs well with wholegrain breakfast bakes.

variations.name: Filter Coffee Cold Brew
variations.description: A modern iced version where the filter coffee decoction is chilled and poured over ice with cold sweetened milk for a smooth, mellow cooler. Less acidic and gently sweet, it keeps the unmistakable chicory-coffee character of filter coffee in a refreshing summer format.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: raw honey dissolves smoothly into cold milk and sweetens the iced coffee without the graininess of sugar

steps: Brew a strong decoction by adding 7 tbsp filter coffee powder to a steel filter and dripping 1.5 cups hot water through for 15 minutes.
Cool the decoction completely, then refrigerate it for at least 30 minutes until well chilled.
Whisk 2.5 cups chilled milk with 5 tbsp Anveshan Honey and 0.25 tsp cardamom powder until the honey fully dissolves.
Fill four tall glasses with 2 cups ice cubes divided between them.
Pour about 3 tbsp of the chilled decoction into each glass, then top up with the sweetened cold milk and stir gently.
Dust a little cocoa powder over the top of each glass and serve immediately with a straw.
tips: Chill the decoction thoroughly before mixing so the ice does not melt fast and dilute the coffee.
Brew the decoction a touch stronger than usual, since serving it over ice naturally softens the intensity.
For a frothy cold coffee, blend the chilled decoction, milk, honey and a couple of ice cubes for 30 seconds before pouring.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve tall over plenty of ice with a dusting of cocoa, a refreshing summer twist on filter coffee for warm afternoons.

variations.name: Ghee Bulletproof Filter Coffee
variations.description: A rich, frothy filter coffee blended with a spoon of ghee for a creamy, energising cup in the bulletproof style, adapted to Indian tastes. Velvety and satisfying, the ghee gives lasting energy and a smooth mouthfeel that turns the morning brew into a light meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoon of bilona ghee blended in makes the coffee creamy and frothy while giving slow-release, satisfying energy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: unrefined jaggery balances the richness of the ghee with a gentle caramel sweetness

steps: Add 6 tbsp filter coffee powder to a steel filter and pour 1.5 cups hot water through, letting it drip for 12 to 15 minutes into a strong decoction.
Boil 2.5 cups full-fat milk in a pan and keep it hot.
Add the hot decoction, hot milk, 2 tsp Anveshan Ghee, 4 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.25 tsp cinnamon powder to a blender.
Blend on high for 20 to 30 seconds until the coffee is creamy, emulsified and topped with a thick froth.
Taste and adjust the jaggery for sweetness, then blend again briefly if needed.
Pour into cups and serve immediately while hot and foamy.
tips: Blend the ghee in while everything is hot so it emulsifies fully rather than floating as an oily film.
Start with just 2 tsp ghee across four cups and increase gradually as you get used to the richness.
A pinch of cinnamon or cardamom cuts through the ghee and keeps the cup from feeling heavy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot and frothy as an energising breakfast-in-a-cup, ideal on busy mornings when you want coffee to keep you full.

variations.name: Classic Maharashtrian Dry Garlic Chutney
variations.description: The fiery red lasun khobra chutney of Maharashtra, a dry powder of garlic pounded with dry coconut, roasted peanuts and red chilli. Coarse, spicy and intensely garlicky, it clings to a vada pav or a fistful of bhakri. A little groundnut oil crisps the garlic and binds the crumbly, rust-red mixture.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Crisps the garlic and toasts the coconut, binding the dry chutney with a nutty warmth

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan and fry 15 garlic cloves on low for 3-4 minutes until pale golden, then set aside.
In the same pan dry-roast 0.5 cups grated dry coconut for 2-3 minutes until it turns light brown and fragrant.
Add 0.5 tsp cumin seeds to the pan for the last 30 seconds, then cool everything completely.
Grind the fried garlic, roasted coconut, cumin and 0.25 cups roasted peanuts in short pulses to a coarse crumble.
Add 2 tbsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt and pulse briefly to combine without releasing the oils.
Rub the chutney between your fingers to check it is dry and crumbly, then store in an airtight jar.
tips: Pulse in short bursts; over-grinding warms the coconut and peanuts and turns the chutney pasty.
Fry the garlic just until golden, as browning it too far makes the chutney bitter.
Kept dry in an airtight jar it stays fresh for up to a month at room temperature.
variations.servingSuggestion: Sprinkle inside a vada pav with the fried chilli, or serve alongside jowar bhakri and pithla.

variations.name: Rajasthani Wet Garlic-Chilli Chutney
variations.description: A blazing red wet chutney from Rajasthan, ground from soaked dry red chillies and a generous fistful of garlic into a fiery paste. Cumin and lemon sharpen it, and a splash of mustard oil gives the desert pungency. Bold and unapologetically hot, it is meant in small dabs beside dal-baati and bajra roti.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil fries the garlic paste and gives this Rajasthani chutney its sharp desert bite

steps: Soak 12 Kashmiri or Mathania red chillies in hot water for 15 minutes until softened, then drain.
Grind the soaked chillies with 20 garlic cloves, 1 tbsp lemon juice, 1 tsp salt and 0.25 cups water to a smooth red paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pan until it just smokes, then lower the flame to mellow its rawness.
Add 1 tsp cumin seeds and let them crackle for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Tip in the chilli-garlic paste and fry on low for 4-5 minutes, stirring constantly, until the raw smell goes and the oil separates.
Cool completely and store in a clean dry jar, where the oil layer helps it keep.
tips: Use Kashmiri chillies for a deep red colour with manageable heat, or add hotter chillies to taste.
Frying the paste until the oil separates cooks out the raw garlic and helps the chutney last longer.
A thin film of mustard oil on top acts as a natural seal, keeping it fresh for two weeks.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve a small dab with dal-baati, bajra roti and a bowl of chaas to cool the heat.

variations.name: South Indian Garlic-Coconut Chutney
variations.description: A South Indian poondu chutney where garlic is ground with fresh coconut and tamarind into a smooth, tangy dip finished with a sesame-oil tempering. The coconut softens the garlic's punch into something rounded and mellow, with dry red chilli for warmth. It is a garlicky, wholesome partner for idli, dosa and rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil sautes the garlic and blooms the tempering, rounding its pungency in South Indian style

steps: Heat 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pan and saute 10 garlic cloves and 4 red chillies for 2-3 minutes until the garlic is golden.
Cool the mixture and grind it with 0.75 cups grated coconut, 1 tsp tamarind and 0.75 tsp salt and 0.5 cups water to a smooth chutney.
Transfer to a bowl and loosen with a little water to a soft, spoonable consistency.
Heat the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a small pan until it shimmers.
Add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal and fry for 20 seconds until the dal turns golden.
Toss in 10 curry leaves, let them crackle, and pour the tempering over the chutney before serving.
tips: Sauteing the garlic before grinding tames its raw sharpness into a mellow, sweet depth.
Add tamarind gradually; just enough gives a pleasant tang without souring the coconut.
This chutney is best fresh but keeps for a day in the fridge; stir before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with idli, dosa and pongal, or mix a spoon into hot rice with a drizzle of sesame oil.

variations.name: Garlic-Tomato Chutney
variations.description: A robust chutney where roasted garlic and tomatoes are cooked down into a thick, tangy-sweet dip with a lingering garlicky heat. The tomatoes mellow the garlic and give it a saucy body, while a coconut-oil tempering keeps it aromatic. Heartier than a dry garlic powder, it is a versatile spread for parathas and toast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Sautes the garlic and tomatoes and carries the mustard tempering into this saucy chutney

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan and saute 12 garlic cloves and 4 red chillies for 2-3 minutes until the garlic turns golden.
Add 3 chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp tamarind and 0.75 tsp salt, and cook for 8-10 minutes until the tomatoes collapse into a thick pulp.
Cool the mixture and grind it to a smooth, thick chutney without adding water.
Heat the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan until it shimmers.
Add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin and let them splutter for 20 seconds.
Toss in 10 curry leaves, let them crackle, pour the tempering over the chutney, and stir it through.
tips: Cook the tomatoes down until thick and jammy so the chutney keeps well and does not weep water.
Leave the garlic slightly chunky if you like a more pronounced bite in the finished chutney.
A pinch of jaggery balances the tang nicely if your tomatoes are very sour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Spread on hot buttered toast or a paratha, or serve as a punchy side with curd rice.

variations.name: Classic Rajasthani Hari Mirch ka Achar
variations.description: The beloved Rajasthani green chilli pickle where thick, mild chillies are slit and tossed in a coarse fennel-mustard-fenugreek masala loosened with lemon juice and mustard oil. It is tangy and warming rather than blistering, since the fat chillies used are gently hot. A jar matures in days and enlivens any simple dal-roti meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Smoked and cooled, it binds the coarse masala and preserves the chillies with its pungent bite

steps: Wash and wipe 250 g thick green chillies completely dry, remove the stems, and slit each lengthwise or cut into 1-inch pieces.
Dry-roast 3 tbsp fennel, 2 tbsp mustard seeds and 1 tbsp fenugreek on low flame for 2 minutes, cool, and grind to a coarse powder.
Mix the ground spices with 1 tsp turmeric, 1 tbsp amchur and 2 tbsp salt, then rub this masala into the chilli pieces.
Heat 0.5 cups Anveshan Mustard Oil until it smokes, cool slightly, add 0.5 tsp asafoetida, and pour the warm oil over the chillies.
Stir in 4 tbsp lemon juice, mix everything so the chillies are well coated, and pack into a dry sterile jar.
Keep the jar in the sun for 3-4 days, shaking daily, until the chillies soften slightly and soak up the tangy masala.
tips: Choose the fat, light-green Bhavnagri chillies which are mild; slim dark chillies make the pickle punishingly hot.
Grind the fennel and mustard coarse, not fine, for the authentic crunchy texture of this pickle.
Lemon juice both preserves and tenderises the chillies, so it is not optional here.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra roti and a dollop of ghee, or alongside a bowl of plain moong dal and rice.

variations.name: Stuffed Bharwa Green Chilli Pickle
variations.description: A festive North Indian pickle where whole mild chillies are slit and stuffed with a coarse toasted spice filling before being packed in mustard oil. Each chilli becomes a little parcel of fennel, mustard and amchur that bursts with flavour when bitten. More laborious than a tossed pickle but far more impressive on the table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Some is bound into the stuffing and the rest submerges the stuffed chillies to preserve them

steps: Wash and dry 300 g large mild chillies, slit each lengthwise on one side without cutting through, and gently scrape out the seeds.
Dry-roast 4 tbsp fennel, 2 tbsp coriander seeds, 3 tbsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp fenugreek for 2-3 minutes, cool, and grind to a coarse masala.
Mix the ground spices with 2 tbsp amchur, 1 tsp turmeric, 2.5 tbsp salt and 3 tbsp of the mustard oil to a crumbly, moist stuffing.
Pack the stuffing firmly into each slit chilli using a small spoon or your fingers.
Arrange the stuffed chillies snugly in a dry jar, then heat the remaining Anveshan Mustard Oil until it smokes, cool it, and pour it over to cover.
Sun the jar for 4-5 days, turning the chillies gently each day until they soften and absorb the oil and masala.
tips: Bind the stuffing with a little mustard oil so it holds together and does not fall out of the chillies.
Handle the chillies gently while stuffing so they do not tear; a wide slit makes filling far easier.
Keep the chillies fully submerged in oil in the jar to prevent any spoilage during maturing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve a whole stuffed chilli with parathas or a festive rice pulao, slicing it open to reveal the spiced centre.

variations.name: South Indian Green Chilli Thokku
variations.description: A cooked Tamil-style green chilli relish where ground chillies are simmered down in gingelly oil with tamarind and jaggery into a thick, spoonable thokku. Unlike the raw northern pickles it is fully cooked, giving a mellow, jammy heat with a sweet-sour edge. A little goes a long way beside curd rice or dosa.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Balances the heat and tamarind with a gentle sweetness and gives the thokku its glossy sheen

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil cooks the chilli paste down slowly and preserves the finished thokku

steps: Grind 200 g green chillies with 2 tbsp tamarind and a little water to a coarse paste.
Heat 0.5 cups Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadhai on medium flame, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, add 0.5 tsp asafoetida and 2 sprigs curry leaves.
Pour in the chilli-tamarind paste along with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 2 tbsp salt, and cook stirring for 10 minutes as it bubbles and thickens.
Add 0.5 tsp fenugreek powder and 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, and continue cooking 8-10 minutes.
Cook until the oil separates and floats to the sides and the thokku turns thick, dark and glossy.
Cool completely and store in a dry jar; the flavour deepens over 2-3 days.
tips: Cook until the oil clearly separates, which is the sign the thokku is done and will keep well.
Use gently roasted fenugreek powder rather than raw seeds, as unroasted fenugreek turns the thokku bitter.
Blend the chillies coarse rather than smooth for a more textured, authentic thokku.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve a small spoon with curd rice, idli or dosa, where its jammy heat balances the plain base.

variations.name: Instant Lemon Green Chilli Pickle
variations.description: A quick, fresh no-cook pickle where slit chillies are simply tossed with roasted ground spices and lots of lemon juice, ready to eat within hours. The acid softens the chillies fast and keeps the pickle bright and lively. Perfect for a small batch when the big matured jar runs dry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
