ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: rounds out the natural sweetness of the jackfruit preserve without overpowering it

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: loosens the sticky jackfruit preserve and fries the cashews to a fragrant gold

steps: Soak 0.5 cup rice ada in hot water for 20 minutes, boil 5 minutes until soft, and drain well.
Warm 1 cup jackfruit preserve with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over low heat, stirring, until it loosens into a smooth paste, about 4 minutes.
Melt 0.5 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 0.25 cup water, strain, and stir it into the loosened jackfruit.
Add the drained ada and cook on low heat for 8 minutes until glossy, then pour in 2 cups thin coconut milk and simmer 6 minutes until thickened.
Lower the heat, stir in 1 cup thick coconut milk and warm for 2 minutes without boiling.
In the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, fry 2 tbsp cashews until golden, then fold in with 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp dry ginger and serve warm.
tips: Loosen the jackfruit preserve in ghee first, or it stays in stubborn lumps that never fully dissolve.
Taste before adding all the jaggery, as the sweetness of jackfruit preserve varies a lot by batch.
This pradhaman is best made when jackfruit preserve is fresh; a good store-bought chakka varatti works well too.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a seasonal monsoon dessert, its fruity amber colour garnished with a few ghee-fried cashews.

variations.name: Classic Adhirasam
variations.description: A revered Tamil Diwali sweet of soaked, ground rice kneaded with molten jaggery into a fudgy dough, rested, patted into discs and deep-fried until deep mahogany and chewy-soft. Getting the jaggery to the right one-string consistency is the whole art of adhirasam. Fragrant with cardamom and dry ginger, it keeps for days and only mellows in flavour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Cooked to a one-string syrup, it gives adhirasam its dark colour and chew

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed oil for deep-frying the discs to an even mahogany

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Worked into the dough for softness and a richer flavour

steps: Soak 2 cups raw rice for 2 hours, drain and spread on a cloth to dry for 30 minutes until just barely damp, then grind to a fine flour and sift.
Melt 1.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 1/2 cup water, strain out grit, and boil to a one-string consistency, tested when a drop between finger and thumb forms a single thread.
Lower the heat and stir the rice flour into the hot syrup a little at a time with 1 tsp cardamom, 1/2 tsp dry ginger, 1 tbsp sesame seeds and a pinch of salt to a soft dough.
Work in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, cover the dough and rest it overnight or at least 6 hours so it firms and matures.
Grease your palms and a sheet of banana leaf or plastic, then pat a lemon-sized ball into a thin disc about 3 inches wide.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to medium; slide in one disc, and once it puffs, gently press it down with a slotted spoon and fry until deep mahogany, about 1 minute per side.
Lift out and immediately press between two flat ladles to squeeze out excess oil, then cool completely before storing.
tips: The one-string jaggery consistency is critical; too little and the dough will not bind, too much and the adhirasam turns hard.
Resting the dough overnight is not optional; it is what gives adhirasam its signature soft, chewy texture.
Fry on medium heat only, as high heat browns the outside before the inside cooks and the sweet stays raw.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a Diwali or Karthigai sweet, stacked and pressed, alongside savoury murukku on the festival platter.

variations.name: Ellu Adhirasam
variations.description: A nutty version where the discs are pressed generously with white sesame before frying, so the outside turns crisp and speckled while the centre stays fudgy. The toasted sesame adds a fragrant crunch that sets it apart from the plain sweet. It is a Chettinad favourite, richer and more aromatic than the everyday adhirasam.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Boiled to a one-string syrup to bind the sesame-studded dough

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil for frying doubles the sesame aroma of this version

steps: Soak 2 cups raw rice for 2 hours, drain, dry on a cloth for 30 minutes until just damp, then grind to a fine flour and sift.
Lightly dry-roast 2 tbsp of the sesame seeds until they pop and reserve the rest raw for coating.
Melt 1.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 1/2 cup water, strain, and boil to a one-string consistency.
Stir the rice flour into the hot syrup with the roasted sesame, 1 tsp cardamom, 1/2 tsp dry ginger and a pinch of salt to a soft dough, then cover and rest overnight.
Grease your palms, pat a lemon-sized ball into a 3-inch disc, and press both sides firmly into the reserved raw sesame so they stick.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Sesame Oil to medium, slide in a disc, press it gently once it puffs, and fry until deep golden-brown and the sesame is toasted, about 1 minute per side.
Drain and press between two ladles to remove excess oil, then cool completely before storing.
tips: Press the raw sesame on firmly just before frying so it toasts in the oil rather than falling off.
Frying in gingelly oil rather than a neutral oil intensifies the sesame character of this version.
As with all adhirasam, rest the dough overnight for the right chewy-soft centre.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on the Diwali platter where its speckled, toasted crust stands out beside plain adhirasam and murukku.

variations.name: Coconut Kajjaya
variations.description: The Karnataka cousin of adhirasam, enriched with fresh grated coconut worked into the rice-jaggery dough for a moister, more tropical crumb. The coconut keeps the discs soft and adds a delicate sweetness. Made for Deepavali and Naraka Chaturdashi, kajjaya is a little lighter and more fragrant than its Tamil counterpart.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Cooked to a one-string syrup to bind the coconut-rich dough

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil for frying reinforces the coconut flavour of kajjaya

steps: Soak 2 cups raw rice for 2 hours, drain, dry on a cloth for 30 minutes until just damp, then grind to a fine flour and sift.
Melt 1.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 1/2 cup water, strain, and boil to a one-string consistency.
Stir the rice flour into the hot syrup with 1/2 cup grated coconut, 1 tsp cardamom, 1 tbsp poppy seeds and a pinch of salt to a soft dough.
Cover and rest the dough for at least 6 hours or overnight so it firms and the coconut moisture settles in.
Grease your palms and pat a lemon-sized ball into a 3-inch disc on a greased sheet.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Coconut Oil to medium, slide in a disc, press it gently once it puffs, and fry until golden-brown, about 1 minute per side.
Drain and press between two ladles to remove excess oil, then cool completely before storing.
tips: Because the coconut adds moisture, keep the syrup a touch thicker than for plain adhirasam so the dough still binds.
Kajjaya does not keep as long as plain adhirasam owing to the fresh coconut, so eat within three days.
Fry on steady medium heat so the coconut inside cooks without the outside burning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a Deepavali sweet the Karnataka way, warm with a cup of filter coffee.

variations.name: Instant Rice Flour Adhirasam
variations.description: A shortcut version using ready store-bought rice flour lightly roasted to mimic the traditional ground rice, cutting out the long soaking and drying. It delivers the same fudgy, jaggery-rich sweet in a fraction of the time. A boon for last-minute festival cooking when there is no time to grind rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Boiled to a one-string syrup to bind the roasted rice flour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed oil for deep-frying the discs evenly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Worked into the dough to keep this quick version soft

steps: Dry-roast 2 cups rice flour on low heat for 4-5 minutes until warm and faintly fragrant but not coloured, then cool and sift.
Melt 1.25 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 1/2 cup water, strain out grit, and boil to a one-string consistency.
Stir the roasted rice flour into the hot syrup with 1 tsp cardamom, 1/2 tsp dry ginger, 1 tbsp sesame seeds and a pinch of salt to a soft dough.
Work in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, cover and rest the dough for at least 3 hours so it firms up.
Grease your palms and pat a lemon-sized ball into a thin 3-inch disc on a greased sheet.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to medium, slide in a disc, press it gently once it puffs, and fry until deep mahogany, about 1 minute per side.
Drain and press between two ladles to squeeze out oil, then cool completely before storing.
tips: Roast the store rice flour gently to drive off its raw smell; this small step makes it taste closer to traditional.
Even in the instant version, rest the dough a few hours or the adhirasam will crack while frying.
If the dough feels dry, mix in a spoon of warm jaggery syrup rather than water to keep it binding.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a quick festival sweet when time is short, pressed and cooled beside other Diwali snacks.

variations.name: Classic Alsande Tonak
variations.description: A fiery Goan Saraswat curry of cowpeas (alsande) simmered soft and bathed in a dark roasted masala of coconut, red chilli and warm spices sharpened with tamarind. Robust, spicy and deeply aromatic, tonak is the classic accompaniment to pao at Goan breakfast stalls and family tables alike.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil is the Goan Saraswat fat that carries the roasted tonak masala

steps: Soak 1 cup cowpeas overnight, then pressure-cook with 3 cups water and 0.25 tsp turmeric for 5-6 whistles until soft but still holding shape.
Dry-roast the coriander, cumin, peppercorns, cloves, cinnamon and dried red chillies until fragrant, then roast 0.75 cup grated coconut with one sliced onion until deep golden-brown.
Grind the roasted spices, coconut-onion and 1.5 tsp tamarind into a smooth, dark masala with a little water.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil on medium; saute the remaining sliced onion for 6 minutes until golden, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for a minute.
Stir in the ground masala and cook for 6-7 minutes until the oil separates and the paste darkens and smells roasted.
Add the cooked cowpeas with their liquid and 1 tsp salt, simmer on low for 10-12 minutes until the gravy thickens and the flavours meld, adding hot water to reach a pourable consistency.
tips: Roasting one onion along with the coconut deepens the masala's colour and gives tonak its signature dark body.
Cook the cowpeas until just soft; overcooked beans turn to mush and cloud the gravy.
Tonak is meant to be spicy - Kashmiri chillies give colour, so add a hotter chilli if you want more heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Classically mopped up with soft Goan pao at breakfast, or served with steamed rice for a hearty meal.

variations.name: Black-Eyed Peas & Potato Tonak
variations.description: A homelier, more filling tonak where soft potato chunks join the black-eyed peas, thickening the gravy and mellowing its heat a little. The potato soaks up the roasted masala and turns this into a satisfying one-pot curry for a family lunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil roots the roasted tonak masala in authentic Goan flavour

steps: Soak 0.75 cup black-eyed peas for 4 hours, then pressure-cook with 2.5 cups water and 0.25 tsp turmeric for 4-5 whistles until soft.
Dry-roast the coriander, fennel, cloves, cinnamon and dried red chillies until fragrant, then roast 0.75 cup grated coconut to deep golden-brown; grind with 1 tsp tamarind into a smooth masala.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil on medium; saute the sliced onions for 6-7 minutes until golden, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for a minute.
Stir in the ground masala and cook for 5-6 minutes until the oil separates, then add 2 cups cubed potato and toss to coat.
Add the cooked peas with their liquid, 1 tsp salt and 1 cup hot water, cover and simmer on low for 12 minutes until the potato is tender.
Uncover and simmer for 3 minutes to thicken the gravy so it clings to the potato and peas.
tips: The potato naturally thickens the gravy, so keep a little extra hot water on hand to loosen it if needed.
Fennel softens the heat and adds a gentle sweetness that suits this milder, family-friendly version.
Add the potato raw into the masala so it takes on colour and flavour as it cooks.
variations.servingSuggestion: A comforting one-pot curry with pao or chapatis, filling enough to need only a slice of onion and lime alongside.

variations.name: Mixed Sprouts Tonak
variations.description: A nutritious twist where a mix of sprouted moth beans and moong replaces plain cowpeas, their nutty sweetness and extra protein lifting the fiery masala. Lighter and quicker than the overnight-soaked classic, it is a wholesome way to enjoy tonak on a busy day.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil carries the roasted masala over the delicate sprouts

steps: Steam 2 cups mixed sprouts with a pinch of salt for 6-7 minutes until just tender but still holding a bite; set aside.
Dry-roast the coriander, cumin, cloves, cinnamon and dried red chillies until fragrant, then roast 0.75 cup grated coconut to deep golden-brown; grind with 1 tsp tamarind into a smooth masala.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil on medium; saute the sliced onions for 6 minutes until golden, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 0.25 tsp turmeric and fry for a minute.
Stir in the ground masala and cook for 5-6 minutes until the oil separates and the paste darkens.
Add the steamed sprouts and 1 tsp salt, toss to coat, then pour in 1.5 cups hot water.
Simmer on low for 8-10 minutes until the sprouts are cooked through and the gravy thickens around them.
tips: Steam the sprouts only until just tender so they keep their nutty texture in the finished curry.
Because sprouts cook fast, they need less simmering than dried cowpeas - watch that they do not go mushy.
A mix of moth and moong gives the best balance of sweetness and body; add matki for extra bite.
variations.servingSuggestion: A protein-rich curry with pao or phulkas, or spooned over rice with a squeeze of lime.

variations.name: Kulith (Horse Gram) Tonak
variations.description: A rustic Ghati-Konkan version made with earthy horse gram (kulith), long prized as a warming, protein-dense winter food. Its distinctive nutty, slightly bitter depth stands up boldly to the roasted masala, making this the most robust and traditional of the tonak family.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil balances the earthy horse gram with a mellow coastal note

steps: Soak 1 cup horse gram overnight, then pressure-cook with 4 cups water and 0.25 tsp turmeric for 7-8 whistles until soft, as it takes longer than other beans.
Dry-roast the coriander, cumin, peppercorns, cloves, cinnamon and dried red chillies until fragrant, then roast 0.75 cup grated coconut with 6 garlic cloves until deep brown.
Grind the roasted spices, coconut-garlic and 1.5 tsp tamarind into a smooth, dark masala with a little water.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil on medium; saute the sliced onions for 7 minutes until deep golden.
Stir in the ground masala and cook for 6-7 minutes until the oil separates and the masala smells deeply roasted.
Add the cooked horse gram with its liquid and 1 tsp salt, simmer on low for 12-15 minutes until the gravy thickens and takes on the earthy kulith depth, loosening with hot water as needed.
tips: Horse gram is hard and needs a long soak and extra whistles, so do not rush the cooking.
Roasting garlic into the masala rounds out horse gram's characteristic bitterness.
Save the cooking liquid - it is nutritious and gives the gravy its authentic earthy base.
variations.servingSuggestion: A warming winter curry served with hot rice and ghee, or with bhakri for a rustic Konkan meal.

variations.name: Classic Aluchi Patal Bhaji
variations.description: The thin, tangy colocasia-leaf curry of Maharashtra, where shredded alu leaves are simmered soft and thickened with besan, then balanced with tamarind and jaggery and studded with peanuts and chana dal. Sweet, sour and earthy, patal means thin, and this brothy curry is meant to be poured over rice.

ingredients.name: Colocasia leaves
ingredients.note: alu leaves, stems removed and finely shredded

ingredients.name: Chana dal
ingredients.note: soaked 30 minutes

ingredients.name: Raw peanuts
ingredients.note: soaked

ingredients.name: Besan
ingredients.note: to thicken

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil is the everyday Maharashtrian fat for this curry

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked and pulped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: unrefined jaggery is essential to balance the sourness of the alu leaves and tamarind

steps: Remove the thick stems from the 15 colocasia leaves, shred them finely, and pressure-cook the shreds with the soaked 1/4 cup chana dal, 1/4 cup peanuts, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 2 cups water for 3-4 whistles until everything is very soft.
Open the cooker, add the 1.5 tbsp tamarind pulp and 1.5 tbsp jaggery powder, and simmer for 5 minutes so the sourness of the raw leaves cooks off completely.
Whisk 3 tbsp besan into 1/2 cup water until smooth, pour it into the simmering curry while stirring, and cook for 6-7 minutes until it thickens to a thin, pourable body.
Stir in 1.5 tsp goda masala, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt, and simmer another 4 minutes so the spices meld.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a small pan on medium heat and splutter 1/2 tsp mustard seeds and 1/2 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add 1/4 tsp asafoetida.
Pour the sizzling tempering into the curry, stir well, and let it bubble together for 2 minutes.
Check the sweet-sour balance, loosen with hot water if needed to keep it thin, and serve hot.
tips: Colocasia leaves can be throat-itching if undercooked, so always add tamarind and cook the leaves thoroughly soft; the acid neutralises the irritant.
Keep the curry genuinely thin, as the name patal suggests; it thickens on standing, so loosen with hot water before serving.
Balance is everything here; taste and adjust the tamarind and jaggery until the sour and sweet sit evenly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle over hot steamed rice with a spoon of ghee, or serve as a thin curry alongside bhakri and a dry sabzi.

variations.name: Konkani Aluchi Bhaji with Coconut
variations.description: The coastal Konkan version enriched with a ground fresh-coconut and roasted-coriander paste and soured with kokum instead of tamarind. Cooked in fragrant coconut oil, it is thicker, rounder and more aromatic than the inland patal bhaji.

ingredients.name: Colocasia leaves
ingredients.note: alu leaves, finely shredded

ingredients.name: Chana dal
ingredients.note: soaked

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil gives the bhaji its distinct Konkan coastal aroma

ingredients.name: Kokum
ingredients.note: petals

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: rounds off the kokum sourness the Konkan way, without refined sugar

steps: Pressure-cook the finely shredded 15 colocasia leaves with the soaked 1/4 cup chana dal, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 2 cups water for 3-4 whistles until butter-soft.
Meanwhile, dry-roast 1 tbsp coriander seeds until fragrant and grind them with 1/2 cup fresh coconut and a little water into a smooth paste.
Open the cooker, add 4 kokum petals and 1 tbsp jaggery powder, and simmer for 5 minutes to cook out the leaves' rawness.
Stir in the coconut paste with 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt, and simmer for 8-10 minutes until the bhaji thickens and turns aromatic.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan on medium heat and splutter 1/2 tsp mustard seeds and 1/2 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add 10 curry leaves.
Pour the tempering into the bhaji and stir it through, simmering for another 2 minutes.
Taste for the sweet-sour balance and serve warm.
tips: Kokum lends a fruitier, gentler sourness than tamarind and is the authentic Konkan souring agent here; add it early so it cooks in.
Grinding the coconut with roasted coriander seeds is what gives this bhaji its rounded, aromatic base.
This version is thicker than the classic patal, so keep it spoonable rather than pouring-thin.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a spoon of coconut oil drizzled on top, or with soft rice bhakri for a coastal meal.

variations.name: Vidarbha Spicy Aluchi Bhaji
variations.description: A fierier Vidarbha rendition darkened with kala masala and extra garlic, thickened here with a little rice flour for a heartier body. It trades the gentle sweet-sour lilt for a robust, garlicky heat that stands up to a thick bhakri.

ingredients.name: Colocasia leaves
ingredients.note: alu leaves, finely shredded

ingredients.name: Chana dal
ingredients.note: soaked

ingredients.name: Rice flour
ingredients.note: to thicken

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the base fat that carries the fiery garlic tempering of the Vidarbha style

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: crushed

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked and pulped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a modest amount to keep the tang in check against the strong masala

steps: Pressure-cook the shredded 15 colocasia leaves with the soaked 1/4 cup chana dal, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 2 cups water for 3-4 whistles until fully soft.
Add 1.5 tbsp tamarind pulp and 1 tbsp jaggery powder and simmer for 5 minutes to remove the leaves' rawness.
Whisk 3 tbsp rice flour into 1/2 cup water and stir it into the curry, cooking for 6-7 minutes until it thickens to a hearty body.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a small pan on medium heat, crackle 1/2 tsp cumin seeds, then add 10 crushed garlic cloves and fry for 1 minute until golden and fragrant.
Add 1/4 tsp asafoetida, 2 tsp kala masala and 1.5 tsp red chilli powder off the heat for 10 seconds so they bloom without burning.
Pour this fiery tempering into the curry with 1.25 tsp salt and simmer everything for 5 minutes so the flavours marry.
Adjust salt and heat, and serve hot with the garlicky oil floating on top.
tips: The generous garlic and kala masala define this version, so bloom them properly in hot oil for full aroma.
Rice flour gives a smoother, heartier thickness than besan; whisk it into water first to avoid lumps.
Keep the jaggery low here so the dish stays savoury and hot rather than sweet-sour like the classic.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thick jowar bhakri and a raw onion, or over rice with a dollop of ghee to temper the heat.

variations.name: Aluchya Panachi Sukhi Bhaji
variations.description: A dry stir-fry of colocasia leaves rather than a thin curry, where the shredded leaves are steamed then tossed with garlic, peanuts and coconut until they turn a deep, savoury tangle. With no gravy at all, it makes a textured dry sabzi that eats well with chapati.

ingredients.name: Colocasia leaves
ingredients.note: alu leaves, finely shredded

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the higher amount helps stir-fry the leaves dry and stop them turning slimy

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: crushed

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked and pulped

steps: Steam the shredded 15 colocasia leaves with 1 tbsp tamarind pulp for 12-15 minutes until completely soft and no longer itchy, then set aside.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat and splutter 1/2 tsp mustard seeds and 1/2 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add 1/4 tsp asafoetida.
Add 8 crushed garlic cloves and fry for 1 minute until golden, then add the steamed leaves with 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt.
Stir-fry on medium heat for 6-8 minutes, pressing the leaves against the pan, until they lose all moisture and start to catch and darken.
Add 1 tsp goda masala and 1/4 cup roasted peanut powder and toss for another 2-3 minutes so it turns dry and clumpy.
Fold in 1/4 cup grated coconut and stir for a minute until fragrant.
Taste for salt and tang, and serve the dry bhaji warm.
tips: Steam the leaves with tamarind first; this both softens them and kills any throat-itch before the stir-fry.
Keep stir-frying until the leaves are genuinely dry, since any leftover moisture makes colocasia slimy.
The peanut powder soaks up moisture and adds body, so add it generously to keep the bhaji dry and clumpy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a dry sabzi with hot chapati or bhakri and a bowl of plain dal-rice on the side.

variations.name: Classic Maharashtrian Amti
variations.description: The everyday Maharashtrian toor dal, thin and tangy, built on the sweet-hot goda masala and balanced with tamarind and jaggery. Fragrant with a mustard-cumin tempering and a little coconut, it is the pourable dal that completes a Marathi varan-bhaat plate.

ingredients.name: Toor dal
ingredients.note: rinsed well

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee tempering is what gives a home-style amti its rounded aroma

ingredients.name: Goda masala
ingredients.note: the sweet dark Maharashtrian blend

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked and pulped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: unrefined jaggery gives amti its signature sweet-sour balance against the tamarind

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Rinse 1 cup toor dal and pressure-cook it with 3 cups water and 1/2 tsp turmeric for 4-5 whistles until completely soft, then whisk it smooth.
Loosen the dal with about 1.5 cups hot water to a thin, pourable consistency and bring it to a gentle simmer.
Add 1 tbsp tamarind pulp, 1.5 tbsp jaggery powder, 2 tsp goda masala, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt, and simmer for 8-10 minutes so the flavours meld.
Stir in 3 tbsp grated coconut and simmer another 2 minutes for body and aroma.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan on medium heat and splutter 1/2 tsp mustard seeds and 1/2 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add 1/4 tsp asafoetida and 10 curry leaves.
Pour the sizzling tempering into the amti, stir well, and let it bubble together for 2 minutes.
Finish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander and serve hot and thin.
tips: Goda masala is the heart of amti and cannot be swapped for garam masala; its sweet, dark profile is what makes the dal distinctly Maharashtrian.
Keep the amti thin and pourable, as it is meant to be mixed into rice; it thickens on standing.
Taste and adjust the tamarind and jaggery together to land on a gentle sweet-sour balance rather than a sharp one.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle over hot steamed rice with a spoon of ghee, or serve as a thin dal alongside bhakri and a dry bhaji.

variations.name: Kolhapuri Tikhat Amti
variations.description: The fiery Kolhapuri amti, thinner and hotter, coloured deep red with roasted-coconut kut and the region's lasun masala. Where the classic leans sweet-sour, this one leans blazing and garlicky, meant for those who love their dal with a real kick.

ingredients.name: Toor dal
ingredients.note: rinsed well

ingredients.name: Grated dry coconut
ingredients.note: khobra, roasted dark

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: carries the fierce Kolhapuri garlic-coconut masala

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: crushed

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Red chilli powder
ingredients.note: fiery variety

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked and pulped

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup toor dal with 3 cups water and 1/2 tsp turmeric for 4-5 whistles until soft, then whisk smooth and keep on a low simmer.
Dry-roast 1/3 cup dry coconut on a tava until deep brown, then grind it to a coarse paste with a splash of water.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a small pan on medium heat and splutter 1/2 tsp mustard seeds and 1/2 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add 8 crushed garlic cloves and 1 chopped onion and fry for 4-5 minutes until brown.
Add the roasted coconut paste with 2 tsp Kolhapuri masala and 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, and cook for 2-3 minutes until the oil turns red.
Tip this masala into the simmering dal along with 1 tbsp tamarind pulp and 1.25 tsp salt, and add 1.5 cups hot water to keep it thin.
Simmer the amti for 10 minutes so it turns fiery red and the flavours deepen.
Finish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander and serve piping hot.
tips: Roast the dry coconut until genuinely dark for the smoky depth and red colour of a Kolhapuri kut.
Keep it thinner than the classic amti; this dal is meant to be a hot, brothy pour over rice.
Skip the jaggery here, since Kolhapuri amti is savoury and hot rather than sweet-sour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over plain rice with a spoon of raw groundnut oil and a papad, with buttermilk on the side to cool the heat.

variations.name: No-Onion No-Garlic Upvas Amti
variations.description: A pure, satvik amti made without onion or garlic, relying on ginger, green chilli and a generous pinch of asafoetida bloomed in ghee. Gently sweet-sour with goda masala and jaggery, it is the version cooked for festivals and no-onion-garlic days.

ingredients.name: Toor dal
ingredients.note: rinsed well

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the only fat in this pure-veg amti, so its bilona flavour carries the whole tempering

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: grated

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked and pulped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: balances the tamarind gently in this festival-style dal

ingredients.name: Asafoetida
ingredients.note: a generous pinch stands in for the missing garlic

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup toor dal with 3 cups water and 1/2 tsp turmeric for 4-5 whistles until butter-soft, then whisk smooth and loosen with 1.5 cups hot water.
Bring the dal to a gentle simmer and add 1 tbsp tamarind pulp, 1.5 tbsp jaggery powder, 2 tsp goda masala and 1.25 tsp salt.
Simmer for 8-10 minutes so the sweet-sour flavours settle into the dal.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan on medium heat and splutter 1/2 tsp mustard seeds and 1/2 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds.
Add a generous 1/2 tsp asafoetida, the grated ginger, 3 slit green chillies and 10 curry leaves, and fry for about a minute until the ginger loses its raw smell and the hing blooms.
Pour the tempering into the amti, stir well, and simmer everything together for 3-4 minutes.
Finish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander and serve hot.
tips: With no onion or garlic, use a genuinely generous half-teaspoon of asafoetida bloomed properly in ghee to carry the savoury base.
Ginger and green chilli provide the warmth here, so add them fresh and do not brown them, just soften.
This amti suits a festive or fasting thali and reheats well if loosened only with hot water.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rice and a spoon of ghee, or alongside sabudana khichdi and a wedge of lime for a satvik meal.

variations.name: Classic Arisi Upma
variations.description: A rustic Kongunadu breakfast where coarsely ground raw rice and a little toor dal are steamed with a pepper-cumin tempering into a soft, savoury porridge. Arisi upma is old-fashioned comfort food, heavier and more filling than semiya upma. The crushed pepper and cumin give it its characteristic warmth and digestive quality.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Finishes the upma with richness and keeps the ground rice from drying out

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil gives the tempering an earthy Kongunadu depth

steps: Dry-roast 1 cup raw rice with 2 tbsp toor dal on low heat for 3 minutes until warm and fragrant, cool slightly, then pulse in a mixer to a coarse rava-like texture.
Coarsely crush 1.5 tsp peppercorns and 1.5 tsp cumin together in a mortar to a rough powder.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, fry 1 tbsp urad dal until golden, then add the crushed pepper-cumin, 12 curry leaves and 1/4 tsp asafoetida for 20 seconds.
Pour in 3 cups water with 1 tsp salt and bring to a rolling boil.
Lower the heat and add the coarse rice-dal mixture in a slow stream, stirring constantly to prevent lumps.
Cover and cook on very low heat for 12-15 minutes, stirring every few minutes, until the rice is fully soft and the mixture pulls together.
Fold in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 3 tbsp grated coconut, rest covered 3 minutes and serve hot.
tips: Grind the rice coarse like semolina, not fine, or the upma turns gluey.
Arisi upma needs generous ghee to taste right; it dries out quickly otherwise.
Keep the heat low while cooking and stir often, as the ground rice catches at the base easily.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot with coconut chutney, a spicy idli podi mixed with sesame oil, or a simple jaggery on the side.

variations.name: Kara Arisi Upma
variations.description: A fiery version cooked with sauteed onions, a paste of red chillies and a heavier tempering for those who like their arisi upma with real heat and bite. The onions add sweetness and body while the chilli brings a warming burn. This is the hearty, savoury version that eats like a full meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil carries the spicy onion base and coats the ground rice

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon that rounds off the heat and keeps the upma moist

steps: Dry-roast 1 cup raw rice with 2 tbsp toor dal until fragrant, cool and pulse to a coarse rava texture.
Grind 4 red chillies and 5 garlic cloves to a coarse paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, fry 1 tbsp urad dal and 1 tbsp chana dal until golden, then add 15 curry leaves and 1/4 tsp asafoetida.
Add 2 chopped onions and the chilli-garlic paste, sauteing for 4 minutes until the onions turn soft and the raw garlic smell fades.
Pour in 3 cups water with 1 tsp salt and bring to a rolling boil, then lower the heat and add the coarse rice in a slow stream, stirring hard to avoid lumps.
Cover and cook on very low heat for 12-15 minutes, stirring often, until the rice is soft and the mixture holds together.
Fold in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, rest covered 3 minutes and serve hot.
tips: Fry the onions well before adding water so they sweeten and balance the chilli heat.
Add the chilli-garlic paste to taste; four chillies makes a genuinely spicy upma.
Stir the rice in slowly and constantly at first, which is the only way to keep it lump-free.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a cooling coconut chutney and thick curd to temper the heat, or with a boiled egg for non-vegetarians.

variations.name: Coconut Milk Arisi Upma
variations.description: A richer, softer version cooked in thin coconut milk instead of water, giving the ground rice a creamy sweetness and silkier finish. The coconut milk turns this humble breakfast almost festive. It is a Chettinad-style indulgence, mild and fragrant, that melts in the mouth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Enriches the coconut milk base and finishes the upma with a nutty aroma

steps: Dry-roast 1 cup raw rice with 2 tbsp toor dal until fragrant, cool and pulse to a coarse rava texture.
Coarsely crush 1.5 tsp peppercorns with 1 tsp cumin in a mortar.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, fry 1 tbsp urad dal and 12 cashews until golden, then add the crushed pepper-cumin, 2 slit green chillies, 12 curry leaves and 1/4 tsp asafoetida.
Pour in 3 cups thin coconut milk with 1 tsp salt and bring gently to a boil, stirring so it does not catch or split.
Lower the heat and add the coarse rice in a slow stream, stirring constantly to prevent lumps.
Cover and cook on very low heat for 12-15 minutes, stirring often, until the rice is soft and creamy.
Fold in the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, rest covered 3 minutes and serve warm.
tips: Use thin (second-press) coconut milk for cooking so it does not split; a spoon of thick milk can be swirled in at the end.
Keep the heat low once the coconut milk goes in, as it scorches faster than water.
This version is richer, so serve it with something tangy like a tomato chutney to balance.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a sharp tomato thokku or lime pickle, letting the tang cut through the creamy coconut richness.

variations.name: Millet Arisi Upma
variations.description: A wholesome modern twist that swaps part of the rice for foxtail millet, giving the upma extra fibre and a lovely nutty bite while keeping its traditional pepper-cumin soul. The millet makes it lighter on the stomach and more nourishing. It is a health-conscious take that loses none of the comforting character of the original.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Keeps the fibrous millet moist and adds a nourishing richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed oil for a light, clean tempering

steps: Dry-roast 3/4 cup foxtail millet, 1/4 cup raw rice and 2 tbsp moong dal on low heat until fragrant, cool and pulse to a coarse rava texture.
Coarsely crush 1 tsp peppercorns with 1.5 tsp cumin in a mortar.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, add the crushed pepper-cumin, grated 1 inch ginger, 12 curry leaves and 1/4 tsp asafoetida for 20 seconds.
Pour in 3.25 cups water with 1 tsp salt and bring to a rolling boil.
Lower the heat and add the coarse millet-rice mixture in a slow stream, stirring constantly to avoid lumps.
Cover and cook on very low heat for 13-15 minutes, stirring often, until the millet is fully soft; it needs slightly more water than plain rice.
Fold in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 3 tbsp grated coconut, rest covered 3 minutes and serve hot.
tips: Millet absorbs more water than rice, so keep a little hot water handy to loosen if it stiffens.
Roast the millet well to bring out its nutty aroma and stop it turning gummy.
Ghee is important here to keep the fibrous millet upma soft and appetising.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with coconut chutney and a spicy sesame-oil idli podi, or a small bowl of thin sambar.

variations.name: Classic Maharashtrian Batata Bhaji
variations.description: The soft, turmeric-yellow potato bhaji that fills every Maharashtrian vada pav and travels in every train tiffin: boiled potatoes broken into chunks and tossed in a mustard-cumin tempering with green chilli, curry leaves and a bright hit of lemon. Simple, comforting and just faintly tangy, it is the everyday potato dish of the Deccan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the everyday Maharashtrian cooking fat for a phodni-based bhaji

steps: Boil 5 potatoes until soft, peel, and break them roughly by hand into bite-sized chunks rather than dicing neatly.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on medium; add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them splutter, then 0.5 tsp cumin, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 12 curry leaves.
Add the chopped onion and slit green chillies and saute for 3-4 minutes until the onion turns soft and translucent.
Sprinkle in 0.5 tsp turmeric, stir for 20 seconds until the raw smell goes, then add the potato chunks and 1 tsp salt.
Add 0.25 cup water, mix gently and cook covered on low for 4-5 minutes so the potatoes soak up the flavours and turn moist.
Switch off, fold in 1 tbsp lemon juice and 3 tbsp chopped coriander, and toss lightly to keep the chunks intact.
tips: Break the boiled potatoes by hand rather than dicing them, so they stay soft and soak up the tempering.
A splash of water and a covered rest makes the bhaji moist and fluffy rather than dry and stiff.
Add the lemon off the heat so its brightness stays fresh and does not cook away.
variations.servingSuggestion: Stuff into a pav for the classic batata vada, or serve with pooris or as a side with dal-rice and pickle.

variations.name: Kanda Batata Bhaji
variations.description: A sweeter, onion-forward variation where thinly sliced onions are cooked down until soft and golden alongside the potatoes, melting into a moist, savoury-sweet bhaji. The generous onion makes this version richer and more substantial than the plain classic, popular as a poori-side and sabudana companion.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil carries the sweet, softened onions and the mustard tempering

steps: Boil 4 potatoes until soft, peel, and break into chunks; keep aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on medium; add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them splutter, then 0.5 tsp cumin, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 12 curry leaves.
Add 3 thinly sliced onions, the slit green chillies and 1 tsp grated ginger and saute for 6-7 minutes until the onions soften and turn pale golden.
Sprinkle in 0.5 tsp turmeric, stir for 20 seconds, then add the potato chunks and 1 tsp salt.
Add 0.25 cup water, cover and cook on low for 4-5 minutes so the onions melt into the potatoes and everything turns moist.
Switch off and fold through 3 tbsp chopped coriander before serving.
tips: Cook the onions patiently until soft and sweet; rushing leaves them sharp against the mild potato.
Slice the onions thin so they melt into the bhaji rather than staying in distinct pieces.
Skip the lemon here, since the sweetness of the cooked onions is meant to lead the flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Excellent with pooris or phulkas, and the traditional side to sabudana khichdi on fasting-adjacent meals.

variations.name: Batata Matar Bhaji with Goda Masala
variations.description: A festive Puneri version where sweet green peas join the potatoes and a spoon of fragrant goda masala lends its dark, faintly sweet warmth of clove, cinnamon and sesame. Richer and more aromatic than the everyday bhaji, this is the potato dish that graces a Maharashtrian festive thali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Groundnut oil is the traditional base for a goda-masala Maharashtrian bhaji

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A touch of jaggery is classic with goda masala, rounding its dark warmth

steps: Boil 4 potatoes until soft, peel and break into chunks; keep aside with 1 cup green peas.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil on medium; add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop, then 0.5 tsp cumin, 0.25 tsp asafoetida and 12 curry leaves.
Add the chopped onion and slit green chillies and saute for 3-4 minutes until soft, then add 1 cup green peas and cook for 3 minutes.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp goda masala and fry for 30 seconds until fragrant and the raw spice smell lifts.
Add the potato chunks and 1 tsp salt with 0.33 cup water, cover and cook on low for 5 minutes until the peas are tender and the potatoes take on the masala.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, mix gently, and finish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Bloom the goda masala briefly in the tempering so its dark, sweet aroma opens up fully.
Goda masala is the soul of this version, quite different from garam masala - do not swap it.
The jaggery is not meant to sweeten but to round the goda masala; keep it to a small spoon.
variations.servingSuggestion: A festive-thali potato served with chapatis or pooris, alongside varan-bhaat and a wedge of lime.

variations.name: Classic Goan Beans Foogath
variations.description: A quick, dry Goan stir-fry where finely chopped French beans are steamed tender in their own moisture and tossed with fresh grated coconut, green chilli and a mustard-urad tempering. Light, faintly sweet and coconut-fragrant, foogath is the everyday vegetable that rounds out a coastal fish-curry-rice plate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil is the authentic Goan fat that carries the grated-coconut finish

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil on medium; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal and fry until the dal is golden and the seeds pop.
Add 2 dried red chillies and 10 curry leaves, then the chopped onion and slit green chillies, and saute for 3-4 minutes until the onion softens and turns translucent.
Stir in 400 g finely chopped French beans with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt and toss to coat in the tempering.
Sprinkle in 3 tbsp water, cover and steam on low for 8-10 minutes, stirring once, until the beans are just tender but still bright green.
Uncover, raise the heat and toss for 2 minutes to drive off any moisture so the foogath turns dry.
Fold in 0.5 cup grated coconut, toss for a final minute until warmed through, and switch off.
tips: Chop the beans small and even so they cook quickly and stay bright rather than khaki.
Add the coconut only at the end so it stays fresh and moist rather than drying out.
Steam with the minimum water and finish uncovered so the foogath is dry, never soggy.
variations.servingSuggestion: A classic side to Goan fish curry and rice, or served with dal-rice and a wedge of lime for an everyday meal.

variations.name: Cabbage-Carrot Foogath
variations.description: A cheerful, colourful foogath of shredded cabbage and grated carrot cooked quickly so they keep a slight crunch, then tossed with coconut and a splash of lime. The natural sweetness of cabbage and carrot makes this a milder, more festive version than the beans classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil keeps this quick cabbage foogath light and coastal

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil on medium; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal and fry until the dal is golden.
Add 10 curry leaves and the chopped onion with slit green chillies and saute for 3 minutes until the onion softens.
Add 3 cups shredded cabbage and 1 cup grated carrot with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt and toss well on medium-high.
Cover and cook for 5-6 minutes, stirring once, until the cabbage wilts but still keeps a slight crunch.
Uncover and toss on high for 2 minutes to dry off any moisture and keep the vegetables vibrant.
Turn off the heat, fold in 0.5 cup grated coconut and 1 tsp lime juice, and toss to combine.
tips: Cook cabbage on higher heat and briefly so it stays sweet and crisp rather than turning limp and sulphurous.
The lime at the end lifts the natural sweetness; add it off the heat so it stays fresh.
Grate the carrot rather than dicing it so it cooks in the same short time as the cabbage.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot chapatis and dal, or as a bright side on a rice plate with sambar and papad.

variations.name: Sprouted Moong Beans Foogath
variations.description: A protein-packed foogath where sprouted whole moong is steamed just soft and tossed with French beans, coconut and a garlic-forward tempering for extra bite. The sprouts add a nutty chew and make this the most nourishing, meal-worthy version of the dish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil binds the sprouts, beans and coconut in true Goan style

steps: Steam 1.5 cups sprouted whole moong with a pinch of salt for 6-7 minutes until just tender but still holding a nutty bite; set aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil on medium; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and let them pop, then add 4 crushed garlic cloves and fry until golden.
Add 10 curry leaves, the chopped onion and slit green chillies and saute for 3 minutes until the onion softens.
Stir in 200 g chopped French beans with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, sprinkle 3 tbsp water, cover and steam on low for 7-8 minutes until the beans are tender.
Fold in the steamed sprouts, raise the heat and toss for 2-3 minutes until dry and heated through.
Add 0.5 cup grated coconut, toss for a final minute, and switch off.
tips: Steam the sprouts separately and only until just tender so they keep their signature crunch.
Crushed garlic in the tempering gives this heartier version a savoury depth the classic skips.
Do not add water to the sprouts as they cook; steaming keeps them intact and prevents mushiness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Substantial enough to serve with just phulkas and curd, or as a wholesome side on a rice-and-dal thali.

variations.name: Mangalorean Beans Sukka Foogath
variations.description: A South Canara take where the beans are tossed in a freshly ground masala of roasted coconut, red chilli, coriander and tamarind, giving it a deeper, spicier, faintly tangy coat than the plain coconut version. This sukka-style foogath is drier and more robustly seasoned, closer to a dry curry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil both roasts the masala and finishes this Mangalorean sukka

steps: Dry-roast 1 tbsp coriander seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin and 4 dried red chillies until fragrant, then grind with 0.5 cup grated coconut, 3 garlic cloves and 1 tsp tamarind into a coarse, thick masala with a little water.
Boil 400 g chopped French beans with 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and water to barely cover for 8-9 minutes until just tender, then drain well.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil on medium; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 10 curry leaves and let them splutter.
Add the chopped onion and saute for 3-4 minutes until soft and lightly golden.
Stir in the ground masala and cook on medium for 4 minutes until it darkens, thickens and the raw smell disappears.
Fold in the cooked beans, toss on medium-high for 3-4 minutes until dry and evenly coated, and switch off.
tips: Byadgi chillies give a deep red colour with mild heat; adjust the number to your spice tolerance.
Drain the boiled beans thoroughly so the ground masala clings rather than sliding off in water.
Grind the masala coarse, not smooth, for the authentic textured coat of a Mangalorean sukka.
variations.servingSuggestion: Excellent with neer dosa or plain rice and a thin dal, its spicy-tangy coat carrying the meal.

variations.name: Classic Maharashtrian Bhakarwadi
variations.description: The iconic Pune tea-time snack: a firm besan-and-maida sheet spread with a fragrant dry-coconut, sesame and spice masala, rolled tight, sliced into pinwheels and fried slow. Each bite unspools into crisp spirals with a sweet-hot-tangy filling.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: 2 tbsp warmed into the dough as moyan and the rest for a slow, even deep fry

steps: Dry-roast the grated copra, sesame, coriander and fennel seeds separately over low heat until fragrant, cool, then coarsely grind with red chili powder, amchur, powdered sugar and a pinch of salt into a textured filling.

Mix besan and maida with turmeric and salt, rub in 2 tbsp warm Anveshan Groundnut Oil until crumbly, then add water little by little to knead a stiff, smooth dough; rest 20 minutes under a damp cloth.
Divide into 3 balls and roll each into a thin 20 cm circle, brush lightly with a water-flour paste, and scatter a third of the filling evenly, pressing it in so it grips.
Roll each circle into a tight log, seal the edge with more paste, and slice into 2 cm thick pinwheels; press the cut ends gently so they don't unravel.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil to a low-medium 150°C and fry the pinwheels for 8-10 minutes, turning often, until deep gold and crisp all through.
Drain on a rack, cool fully so they harden, and store airtight for up to 3 weeks.
tips: Fry on low heat with patience; a hot fry browns the outside while the layered centre stays doughy and chewy.
Roll the dough as thin as you can without tearing, thick sheets give heavy, bready bhakarwadi instead of delicate spirals.
If pinwheels open up in the oil, your seal was dry, use a slightly wetter flour paste and press the seam firmly next time.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these classic spirals alongside cutting chai, or set out in a bowl as a moreish starter before a Maharashtrian thali.

variations.name: Gujarati Khatta-Meetha Bhakarwadi
variations.description: The famous Gujarati sweet-and-sour bhakarwadi, where the filling leans on jaggery and tamarind for a pronounced khatta-meetha tang against gentle heat. Slightly larger and softer-spiced than the Pune version, it is the pinwheel that Ahmedabad farsan shops are known for.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the sweet backbone of the khatta-meetha filling, richer and more mineral than white sugar

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: 2 tbsp as moyan in the dough and the rest for a clean, light deep fry

steps: Roast the desiccated coconut, poppy seeds and fennel over low heat until aromatic, cool, then grind coarsely with coriander powder, Kashmiri chili, garam masala and a little salt.
Mix in the Anveshan Jaggery Powder and tamarind pulp to bind the masala into a sticky, tangy-sweet filling; it should clump when pressed.
Knead besan and maida with salt and 2 tbsp warm Anveshan Sunflower Oil into a stiff dough with just enough water, then rest it 20 minutes.
Roll into thin circles, brush with flour paste, spread the khatta-meetha filling, roll into tight logs and cut into 2.5 cm pinwheels, sealing the ends.
Fry in the remaining Anveshan Sunflower Oil at a low-medium 150°C for about 9 minutes, turning, until evenly deep gold; the jaggery can catch, so keep the heat gentle.
Drain and cool completely on a rack before storing airtight; the tang deepens after a day.
tips: Because jaggery browns fast, hold the oil a shade cooler than for classic bhakarwadi and fry a touch longer.
Use thick, seedless tamarind pulp; watery pulp makes the filling loose and it leaks while frying.
Balance is everything, taste the filling and adjust jaggery and tamarind until it is equal parts sweet and sour before rolling.
variations.servingSuggestion: A staple of the Gujarati farsan platter, serve with fafda and a cup of masala chai, or pack as a travel snack that keeps for weeks.

variations.name: Baked Khapli Bhakarwadi
variations.description: A lighter, wholesome bhakarwadi with the sheet made from nutty Khapli wheat atta and baked instead of deep-fried, so you get the same crisp spirals with a fraction of the oil. The filling stays true to the classic coconut-sesame masala.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: ancient-grain wheat flour rolls into a sturdy, fibre-rich sheet that crisps beautifully in the oven

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: 2 tbsp as moyan for shortness and 1 tbsp melted to brush the pinwheels before baking

steps: Roast the copra, sesame and fennel over low heat until fragrant, cool and grind coarsely with red chili powder, amchur, coriander powder and a pinch of salt.
Mix Anveshan Khapli Atta and besan with turmeric and salt, rub in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then knead a firm but pliable dough with warm water; rest 15 minutes.
Roll into thin circles, brush with a little water, spread the filling, roll into tight logs and slice into 2 cm pinwheels, pressing the ends to seal.
Arrange the pinwheels cut-side up on a lined tray, brush the tops with the remaining melted Anveshan Ghee.
Bake in an oven preheated to 180°C for 25-30 minutes, turning once halfway, until crisp and golden-brown on both sides.
Cool completely on the tray so they firm up fully, then store airtight; they crisp further as they cool.
tips: Khapli dough is less stretchy than maida, so roll slowly and patch any cracks rather than forcing it thin in one go.
Brushing with ghee is what gives baked bhakarwadi its golden colour and richness, do not skip it.
If they feel soft straight from the oven, give them 5 extra minutes at 150°C; they should snap once cooled.
variations.servingSuggestion: A smart everyday snack for lunchboxes and travel, serve with a green coriander-mint chutney for dipping.

variations.name: Lehsuni Spicy Dry Bhakarwadi
variations.description: A fiery, savoury-only bhakarwadi with no sweetness at all: the filling is packed with dried garlic, roasted peanuts and dry red chili for a punchy Kolhapuri-style heat. These dark, garlicky pinwheels are for those who like their farsan bold.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: 2 tbsp as moyan and the rest for deep-frying these spirals slow and crisp

steps: Dry-roast the sesame seeds and crushed peanuts for a minute, then mix with dry garlic powder, Kolhapuri masala, red chili flakes, cumin powder and salt into a coarse, fiery filling.
Knead besan and maida with turmeric, salt and 2 tbsp warm Anveshan Groundnut Oil into a stiff dough with just enough water, and rest it 20 minutes.
Roll the dough into thin circles, brush with flour-water paste, and press the garlic filling evenly across each.
Roll into tight logs, seal the seam, and cut into 2 cm pinwheels, pinching the ends so the spirals stay put.
Fry in the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil at a low-medium 150°C for 8-10 minutes, turning, until deep golden and crisp right through.
Drain on a rack and cool completely before storing airtight; the garlic flavour intensifies overnight.
tips: Use dry, coarse garlic powder rather than fresh garlic, moisture from fresh cloves makes the filling leak and spit in the oil.
Crush the peanuts, don't powder them; small nubs give a welcome crunch inside the crisp spiral.
Dial the chili flakes up or down freely, this version is meant to carry real heat but should never turn bitter, so don't over-roast the masala.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these bold garlicky spirals as a spicy accompaniment to beer or with a cooling glass of chaas to temper the heat.

variations.name: Classic Bharli Vangi
variations.description: Small purple brinjals slit into a cross and stuffed with a roasted peanut, coconut and sesame masala, then simmered gently in their own thick, nutty gravy. This is the Maharashtrian home-style version, sweet-savoury and deeply aromatic, the star of any festive thali.

ingredients.name: Small brinjals
ingredients.note: tender, with stalks on

ingredients.name: Grated dry coconut
ingredients.note: khobra, lightly roasted

ingredients.name: White sesame seeds
ingredients.note: roasted

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil marries perfectly with the peanut masala of this dish

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Goda masala
ingredients.note: the sweet Maharashtrian spice blend

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the touch of unrefined jaggery gives the gravy its signature sweet-savoury Maharashtrian balance

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked and pulped

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Slit each of the 8 brinjals into a cross from the base, keeping the stalk end intact, and drop them into salted water so they do not brown.

Coarsely grind the 1/2 cup roasted peanuts, 1/3 cup roasted coconut and 2 tbsp roasted sesame together, then mix with 2 tsp goda masala, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp jaggery powder and 3/4 tsp salt into a dry stuffing.
Pat the brinjals dry and pack the masala firmly into each slit, keeping aside any leftover stuffing for the gravy.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, add 2 chopped onions and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, and fry for 6-7 minutes until golden.
Add the reserved stuffing and cook for 2 minutes, then nestle the stuffed brinjals in a single layer, pour in 1.5 cups hot water and the tamarind pulp with the remaining 1/2 tsp salt.
Cover and simmer on low heat for 18-20 minutes, turning the brinjals gently once, until they are fork-tender and the gravy thickens with oil floating on top.
Sprinkle 3 tbsp chopped coriander over the top and rest for 5 minutes before serving so the flavours settle.
tips: Choose small, glossy, heavy brinjals with tight skin; loose seedy ones turn bitter and mushy in the gravy.
Stuff them just before cooking and keep them submerged in salted water until then so the cut faces do not oxidise and darken.
The peanut masala thickens the gravy as it cooks, so keep the water on the generous side and let it reduce naturally.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri or soft chapati and a side of plain varan-bhaat, letting the nutty gravy soak into the rice.

variations.name: Kolhapuri Bharli Vangi
variations.description: The fiery Kolhapuri stuffed brinjal, where the peanut masala is darkened with kala masala and a fistful of fresh coconut ground into a thin, spicy tarri that pools red around the eggplants. It is hotter, leaner and more pungent than the sweet home version.

ingredients.name: Small brinjals
ingredients.note: tender, with stalks on

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the generous pour of wood-pressed oil carries the fierce Kolhapuri masala

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: 1 sliced and roasted, 1 finely chopped

ingredients.name: Kala masala
ingredients.note: dark Maharashtrian blend

ingredients.name: Kolhapuri red chilli powder
ingredients.note: Sankeshwari or Lavangi for heat

ingredients.name: Dry coconut
ingredients.note: roasted dark for the masala

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked and pulped

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Dry-roast 1 sliced onion, 1/2 cup fresh coconut and 2 tbsp dry coconut on a hot tava until deep brown and fragrant, then grind with 1/4 cup peanuts and a little water into a dark, coarse masala paste.
Reserve half the paste and mix the other half with 2 tsp kala masala, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 3/4 tsp salt into a thick stuffing.
Slit the 8 brinjals crosswise keeping the stalk intact and pack the stuffing firmly into each.
Heat 5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, add 1 chopped onion and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 5 minutes until brown.
Add the reserved ground masala and the remaining 1 tsp chilli powder and cook for 3-4 minutes until the oil separates and the paste smells roasted.
Slide in the stuffed brinjals, add the tamarind pulp, 2 cups hot water and the remaining 1/2 tsp salt, cover and simmer on low for 18-20 minutes until tender and the tarri turns fiery red.
Garnish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander and serve with the spicy gravy spooned over.
tips: Roasting the coconut and onion until genuinely dark is what gives Kolhapuri gravy its colour and smokiness; pale masala tastes flat.
Keep this gravy thinner than the classic so the tarri can be sopped up with bhakri.
Skim the red oil that rises and spoon it over the brinjals just before serving for the authentic Kolhapuri look.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri and raw sliced onion, or with hot rice and a bowl of solkadhi to soothe the chilli heat.

variations.name: Khandeshi Bharit-Style Bharli Vangi
variations.description: A Khandesh-inspired take that leans on toasted white sesame and a smoky note, with the brinjals first charred lightly before stuffing so the skins carry a whisper of roast. The sesame-heavy masala gives a distinctive earthy, slightly bitter depth unique to north Maharashtra.

ingredients.name: Small brinjals
ingredients.note: tender, with stalks on

ingredients.name: White sesame seeds
ingredients.note: roasted golden

ingredients.name: Roasted chana dal
ingredients.note: daliya

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the classic Khandeshi cooking fat for its clean, nutty aroma

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: crushed

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a small hit of unrefined jaggery softens the earthy bitterness of the sesame masala

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked and pulped

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Grind 1/3 cup roasted sesame with 3 tbsp roasted chana dal to a coarse powder, then mix with 2 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander-cumin powder, 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp jaggery powder, 4 crushed garlic cloves and 3/4 tsp salt into a thick stuffing.
Slit the 8 brinjals into a cross keeping the stalk on, and char them lightly on all sides over a medium flame or hot tava for 2-3 minutes just to catch a little colour.
Pack the sesame stuffing firmly into each charred brinjal, reserving the extra.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, add the remaining 4 crushed garlic cloves and 2 chopped onions and fry for 6-7 minutes until golden.
Add the leftover stuffing, cook for 2 minutes, then lay in the brinjals, add the tamarind pulp, 1.5 cups hot water and the remaining 1/2 tsp salt.
Cover and simmer on low for 18-20 minutes, turning once, until the brinjals are soft and the sesame gravy thickens.
Scatter 3 tbsp chopped coriander over the top and serve hot.
tips: Roast the sesame only until pale gold; take it too dark and the masala turns unpleasantly bitter.
The light char before stuffing is what sets this apart, lending a subtle smokiness to every bite, so do not skip it.
Grind the sesame coarse, not to a paste, so the gravy keeps a pleasant grainy texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve Khandesh-style with jowar bhakri and a raw onion, or alongside a plain khichdi with a spoon of ghee.

variations.name: Malvani Coconut Bharli Vangi
variations.description: The coastal Konkan version bathed in a fresh coconut and Malvani-masala gravy, fragrant with kokum and a hint of coriander seed. Lighter and more aromatic than the inland versions, it carries the sea-facing warmth of the Sindhudurg coast.

ingredients.name: Small brinjals
ingredients.note: tender, with stalks on

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil is the defining fat of Malvani coastal cooking

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: 1 sliced, 1 chopped

ingredients.name: Kokum
ingredients.note: petals

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Dry-roast 1 sliced onion, 1/2 cup fresh coconut and 1 tbsp coriander seeds on a tava until golden and fragrant, then grind to a smooth paste with a little water.
Mix the remaining 1/4 cup fresh coconut with 2 tsp Malvani masala, 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1/2 tsp of the chilli powder and 1/2 tsp salt to make the stuffing.
Slit the 8 brinjals crosswise keeping the stalks on and pack them with the coconut stuffing.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, add 1 chopped onion and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 5-6 minutes until soft and light gold.
Add the ground coconut paste and the remaining 1 tsp chilli powder, cook for 3-4 minutes until the oil separates, then slide in the stuffed brinjals.
Pour in 2 cups hot water, add 3 kokum petals and the remaining 3/4 tsp salt, cover and simmer on low for 18-20 minutes until the brinjals are tender and the gravy is aromatic.
Finish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander and serve hot with the coconut gravy.
tips: Add the kokum rather than tamarind here; its fruity sourness is what makes the gravy taste distinctly Konkani.
Grind the roasted coconut paste smooth for a velvety gravy, and do not let it boil too hard once added so the coconut does not turn grainy.
Cold-pressed coconut oil has a strong aroma, so a little goes a long way; the dish should smell of the coast, not be greasy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and solkadhi, or with soft rice bhakri (tandlachi bhakri) for a complete Malvani meal.

variations.name: Classic Bisi Bele Bath
variations.description: Karnataka's legendary one-pot of rice and toor dal cooked with mixed vegetables, tamarind and a fragrant house-ground bisi bele bath powder rich in dals, coconut and marathi moggu. Thick, unctuous and best served piping hot with a river of ghee, its name literally means hot lentil rice. A comforting, nourishing meal that rewards a freshly ground masala.

ingredients.name: Rice
ingredients.note: Sona masuri, cooked soft

ingredients.name: Toor dal
ingredients.note: Pressure-cooked until completely soft

ingredients.name: Mixed vegetables
ingredients.note: Carrot, beans, potato, peas and capsicum in chunks

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The traditional finishing and tempering fat that makes bisi bele bath luxuriant

ingredients.name: Chana dal
ingredients.note: For the masala, roasted golden

steps: Dry-roast 2 tbsp chana dal, 2 tbsp coriander seeds, 6 dry red chillies, 2 marathi moggu, 1 inch cinnamon and 4 cloves over low heat for 4 minutes, add 1/4 cup dry coconut for the last minute, cool and grind to a fine bisi bele bath powder.
Pressure-cook 3/4 cup toor dal with 1/2 tsp turmeric until mushy, and separately cook 1 cup rice soft; keep both ready.
Boil 2 cups mixed vegetables in salted water until just tender, then add 2 tbsp tamarind pulp and simmer for 3 minutes to take off the raw edge.
Stir the ground masala and the cooked toor dal into the vegetables, add 2 tsp salt and about 2 cups water, and simmer for 8-10 minutes until it smells rich and rounded.
Fold in the cooked rice and 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, stirring over low heat for 5 minutes to a thick, flowing, porridge-like consistency, loosening with hot water as needed.

Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, fry 12 cashews golden with 1/2 tsp asafoetida and 15 curry leaves, and pour this sizzling tempering over the bath before serving.
tips: Bisi bele bath thickens dramatically as it cools, so keep it looser than you think on the stove and thin with hot water when reheating.
Grind the masala fresh for the fullest aroma; the marathi moggu and roasted coconut fade quickly once powdered.
Cook the dal and rice softer than usual, as the dish is meant to be creamy and cohesive rather than grainy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve blazing hot in deep bowls with an extra spoon of ghee, crisp boondi or khara sev on top, and a cooling raita alongside.

variations.name: MTR Restaurant-Style Bisi Bele Bath
variations.description: The plush, ghee-laden version made famous by Bengaluru's iconic tiffin rooms, smoother and richer than the home style with a silkier consistency and a heavier hand of cashews and copra. A hint of extra spice powder and a longer simmer give it that unmistakable restaurant depth. Served with a mountain of khara boondi that softens luxuriously into each spoonful.

ingredients.name: Rice
ingredients.note: Cooked very soft for a smooth texture

ingredients.name: Toor dal
ingredients.note: Cooked until it collapses

ingredients.name: Mixed vegetables
ingredients.note: Carrot, beans and peas cut fine

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The lavish ghee is what gives the restaurant version its glossy, indulgent finish

steps: Roast 2 tbsp chana dal, 1 tbsp urad dal, 2 tbsp coriander seeds, 7 dry red chillies and 2 marathi moggu over low heat for 4 minutes, add 1/3 cup copra for the final minute, cool and grind to a very fine powder.
Pressure-cook 1 cup toor dal with 1/2 tsp turmeric until completely broken down, and cook 1 cup rice soft; mash both lightly for a smoother base.
Boil 1.5 cups fine-cut vegetables until soft, add 2 tbsp tamarind pulp and 1 tbsp jaggery and simmer for 4 minutes.
Stir in the ground masala, the mashed dal, 2 tsp salt and about 2.5 cups water and simmer for 12 minutes, stirring often, until thick and glossy.
Fold in the rice with 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and cook on low for 6-7 minutes to a smooth, flowing consistency, adding hot water so it stays pourable.
Heat the remaining 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, fry 20 cashews to deep gold with 1/2 tsp asafoetida and 18 curry leaves, and pour this over the bath just before serving.
tips: Lightly mashing the cooked dal and rice is the trick to the silky, restaurant-smooth texture.
A little jaggery is the secret restaurant touch that balances the tamarind and rounds the whole dish.
Serve immediately with khara boondi so it soaks in slightly, the way the classic tiffin rooms do.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in the tiffin-room style with a generous heap of khara boondi, potato chips and a cooling onion raita.

variations.name: Millet Bisi Bele Bath
variations.description: A wholesome makeover using little millet in place of white rice, keeping the full-bodied masala and vegetables while adding fibre and a nutty bite. The millet drinks up the spiced dal beautifully and stays creamy with the right water ratio. A lighter yet deeply satisfying bowl for those who want the flavour without the polished rice.

ingredients.name: Little millet
ingredients.note: Rinsed well and soaked 20 minutes, cooked soft

ingredients.name: Toor dal
ingredients.note: Pressure-cooked until mushy

ingredients.name: Mixed vegetables
ingredients.note: Carrot, beans, pumpkin and peas

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Keeps the nutty millet creamy and adds the traditional richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A little wood-pressed oil in the tempering keeps the dish lighter

steps: Roast 2 tbsp chana dal, 2 tbsp coriander seeds, 5 dry red chillies, 1 inch cinnamon and 3 cloves over low heat for 4 minutes, add 1/4 cup dry coconut for the final minute, cool and grind to a fine powder.
Cook the soaked little millet in 2.5 cups water until soft and fluffy, and separately pressure-cook 3/4 cup toor dal with 1/2 tsp turmeric until mushy.
Boil 2 cups mixed vegetables until tender, add 2 tbsp tamarind pulp and simmer for 3 minutes to soften the tang.
Stir in the ground masala, the cooked toor dal and 2 tsp salt with about 2 cups water, and simmer for 8-10 minutes until it thickens and smells rich.
Fold in the cooked millet with 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and cook gently for 5 minutes to a creamy, flowing consistency, adding hot water as the millet drinks it up.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, fry 3 tbsp peanuts crunchy with 1/2 tsp asafoetida and 15 curry leaves, and pour over the bath before serving.
tips: Millet absorbs more liquid than rice and firms up fast, so keep the bath noticeably loose and serve hot.
Soaking the millet before cooking makes it fluffier and easier to digest in this rich dish.
Revive leftovers with plenty of hot water and a fresh spoon of ghee, since millet sets much firmer than rice on cooling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve steaming hot with roasted peanuts and khara boondi on top and a bowl of thin buttermilk on the side.

variations.name: Quick Cooker Bisi Bele Bath
variations.description: A single-pressure-cooker weeknight version where rice, dal and vegetables cook together with a ready bisi bele bath powder, cutting the effort without losing the soul of the dish. Everything softens into one comforting, spiced pot in a fraction of the time. Ideal when you crave the classic on a busy evening with minimal washing up.

ingredients.name: Rice
ingredients.note: Rinsed

ingredients.name: Toor dal
ingredients.note: Rinsed, cooks with the rice

ingredients.name: Mixed vegetables
ingredients.note: Carrot, beans, potato and peas in chunks

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Stirred in and used for the tempering to give the quick version real depth

ingredients.name: Bisi bele bath powder
ingredients.note: A good ready blend replaces the freshly ground masala

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pressure cooker over medium heat, add 1 sliced onion and saute for 3 minutes until soft, then add 1 chopped tomato and cook for 2 minutes until pulpy.
Stir in 4 tbsp bisi bele bath powder and 1/2 tsp turmeric for 20 seconds, then add 2 cups mixed vegetables and toss to coat.
Add the rinsed 1 cup rice and 3/4 cup toor dal, 2 tbsp tamarind pulp, 2 tsp salt and 5 cups hot water, and stir well to combine.
Close the cooker and cook for 4 whistles, then switch off and let the pressure release naturally so everything turns soft and cohesive.
Open, stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and mash lightly to a thick, flowing consistency, loosening with hot water if needed.
Heat the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, fry 12 cashews golden with 1/2 tsp asafoetida and 15 curry leaves, and pour this tempering over the top before serving.
tips: Use the full five cups of water, as rice and dal cooking together need extra liquid for the right creamy texture.
Ready powders differ in salt and heat, so taste after opening the cooker and adjust before the final tempering.
Let the pressure fall on its own; opening early leaves the dal grainy instead of soft and blended.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with khara boondi, thin potato chips and a bowl of curd, with lemon wedges for those who like it tangier.

variations.name: Classic Maharashtrian Chakli
variations.description: The definitive Diwali chakli: a tight, deep-fried spiral of rice flour and roasted gram flour spiced with sesame, cumin and ajwain. A splash of hot oil worked into the flour (mohan) gives it that signature shatter-crisp bite that stays crunchy for weeks.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: 2 tbsp heated as mohan into the flour for shortness, the rest for deep-frying

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: neutral, high-smoke-point oil for a clean deep fry that keeps the chakli pale-gold

steps: In a wide bowl whisk together the rice flour, besan and roasted urad dal flour with salt, red chili powder, turmeric, cumin seeds, ajwain, sesame seeds and hing until the spices are evenly streaked through, about 1 minute.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil until it just shimmers, then pour it hot over the flour and rub it in with your fingertips for 2 minutes until the mix holds shape when pressed in a fist.
Add the hot water a little at a time, kneading into a firm, smooth, non-sticky dough; it should be stiffer than chapati dough so the spirals hold their edge. Cover and rest 10 minutes.
Fill a chakli press fitted with the star disc, and pipe tight 6 cm spirals onto a greased sheet or parchment, sealing the loose end by pressing gently so they don't unravel in the oil.
Heat the Anveshan Groundnut Oil to a medium 170°C, then slide in 3-4 chaklis at a time and fry, turning once, for about 5 minutes until the bubbling slows and they turn pale gold and rigid.
Lift onto a rack or paper, cool completely so they crisp fully, then store in an airtight tin for up to 3 weeks.
tips: If the first chakli cracks or bursts, the dough is too dry, knead in a teaspoon of warm water; if it drinks up oil and softens, the oil is too cool, so raise the heat before the next batch.
Keep the unused dough covered with a damp cloth at all times, as rice-flour dough dries and turns crumbly within minutes.
