Frying on a steady medium heat is the whole secret; too hot browns the outside while the core stays raw and chewy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile into a steel dabba as part of a Diwali faral platter alongside chivda and shankarpali, with hot masala chai to cut the richness.

variations.name: Roasted Multigrain Bhajani Chakli
variations.description: A rustic, nutty chakli built on a home-roasted multigrain flour blend instead of plain rice flour, the way old Maharashtrian households prepared bhajani in bulk. Coriander and fennel replace the usual chili-forward profile for a mellow, aromatic crunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Multigrain Atta
ingredients.note: dry-roasted till fragrant to form the wholesome bhajani base for a nuttier, higher-fibre chakli

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: warm bilona ghee kneaded in as mohan for a short, melt-in-mouth crumb

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: light wood-pressed oil for deep-frying that lets the roasted-grain aroma come through

steps: Dry-roast the Anveshan Multigrain Atta, roasted rice and coriander and fennel seeds separately over low heat until each smells toasty, about 4-5 minutes, then cool and grind everything to a fine flour with the roasted chana dal.
Sieve the ground bhajani into a bowl and mix in salt, turmeric, black sesame seeds and green chili paste until uniform.
Melt and warm the Anveshan Ghee, pour it into the flour and rub through for 2 minutes so a fistful clumps together, the sign of enough mohan.
Pour in hot water gradually and knead to a firm, pliable dough that is stiff enough to hold ridges; cover and let it rest 10 minutes so the flours hydrate.
Load the press with the star disc and pipe compact spirals onto greased paper, tucking each tail under to seal it.

Heat the Anveshan Sunflower Oil to 165-170°C and fry the chaklis in small batches for 5-6 minutes until the sizzle quietens and they are deep gold and firm, then drain on a rack and cool fully before storing.
tips: Grinding the roasted grains as fine as store rava-free flour is key; coarse bhajani makes chaklis that split while frying.
Roast the grains a day ahead and grind fresh, the flour stays aromatic and the dough behaves better.
For an even richer crumb, replace the water with warm buttermilk, which also lends a faint tang.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these earthy chaklis with a bowl of sweet mango chunda or a cup of jaggery-sweetened kadak chai for a wholesome tea-time snack.

variations.name: Instant Poha Butter Chakli
variations.description: A shortcut chakli for cooks without a bhajani stock: thick poha is ground with rice flour and bound with butter and curd for an extra-flaky, melt-on-the-tongue spiral. It fries faster and lighter than the classic while still snapping cleanly.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed coconut oil gives a delicate crispness and subtle sweetness to these lighter chaklis

steps: Grind the thick poha to a fine powder in a dry grinder, then whisk it with the rice flour, salt, cumin seeds, white pepper, red chili powder and hing.
Rub the softened butter into the flour with your fingertips for 2 minutes until it resembles moist breadcrumbs, then work in the fresh curd.
Add warm water little by little and knead to a soft yet firm dough that presses easily but is not sticky; rest it covered for 8 minutes.
Fill the chakli press and pipe small, snug spirals onto greased paper, sealing each end with a light press so they hold together.
Heat the Anveshan Coconut Oil to a moderate 165°C and gently lower in 3-4 chaklis, frying for about 4 minutes until pale gold and the bubbling has almost stopped.
Drain on a rack, cool completely so they firm up, and store airtight; eat within two weeks as the curd makes them a touch less shelf-stable.
tips: Curd plus butter makes the dough softer than rice-only versions, so pipe onto paper first and slide the paper near the oil to release cleanly.
If chaklis brown too quickly and stay soft inside, your oil is above 175°C, let it cool a minute between batches.
A pinch of powdered sugar in the dough balances the coconut oil and rounds out the flavour beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: These light, buttery spirals pair perfectly with filter coffee and make a quick after-school snack served with a squeeze of lime and chaat masala.

variations.name: Palak Lehsuni Masala Chakli
variations.description: A vivid green, garlicky twist that folds spinach puree and roasted garlic into the dough for a savory, restaurant-style chakli. Punchy with garam masala and dried mint, it is the boldest spiral on the platter and needs no chutney alongside.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: 2 tbsp as mohan and the rest for a clean deep fry that keeps the green colour bright

steps: Blanch a handful of spinach for 1 minute, shock in cold water and blend to a smooth 0.5 cup puree; this both colours and part-hydrates the dough.
Mix rice flour and besan with salt, garam masala, dried mint, crushed kasuri methi, red chili powder and ajwain in a bowl.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil until shimmering and rub it into the flour for 2 minutes, then add the garlic paste and spinach puree.
Knead into a firm, green, non-sticky dough, adding only a spoon or two of water if needed since the puree carries most of the moisture; rest covered 10 minutes.
Press the dough through the star disc into tight spirals on greased paper, sealing the ends so they don't open up while frying.

Heat the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 170°C and fry in batches for about 5 minutes until the bubbles subside and the chaklis are crisp and deep olive-green, then cool fully on a rack before storing airtight.
tips: Squeeze the blanched spinach well before blending; excess water makes a slack dough that soaks up oil.
Fry these slightly hotter than pale chaklis so the moisture from the puree cooks off and they stay crunchy for days.
Swap the garlic for extra ginger and green chili if you want a milder, more fragrant version for kids.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a cocktail-hour nibble with a cooling mint-yogurt dip, where the garlicky spinach spirals stand in for fried papad.

variations.name: Classic Lemon Chitranna
variations.description: Karnataka's sunny lemon rice, where cooled rice is tossed with a bright turmeric-yellow tempering of mustard, dals, peanuts and curry leaves, then finished with a generous squeeze of fresh lemon off the heat. The dals fried till crunchy give little bursts of nuttiness in every mouthful. Quick, tangy and endlessly comforting, it is the go-to breakfast and lunchbox rice across the state.

ingredients.name: Cooked rice
ingredients.note: Cooled with grains separated, ideally day-old

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil gives the tempering its authentic South-Indian aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing drop of ghee rounds off the tang and adds gloss

ingredients.name: Lemon juice
ingredients.note: Always added off the heat so it stays bright, not bitter

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a wide pan over medium heat and splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 1 tbsp chana dal, 1 tbsp urad dal and 1/4 cup peanuts and fry until the dals are golden and the peanuts crunchy, about 2 minutes.
Add 3 slit green chillies, 2 broken dry red chillies, 1/2 tsp asafoetida and 15 curry leaves and let them crackle for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Lower the heat, sprinkle in 1/2 tsp turmeric and stir for 5 seconds so it blooms without burning and turns the oil a rich yellow.
Add 3 cups cooled rice and 1.25 tsp salt and fold gently with a flat spatula until every grain is evenly coated a bright yellow, warming through for 2-3 minutes.
Switch off the heat, drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and squeeze in 3 tbsp lemon juice, then fold once so the tang stays fresh and lively.
Finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and serve warm or at room temperature.
tips: Always add the lemon juice after turning off the heat; boiling it makes the chitranna taste bitter.
Use cooled, separated rice so the tempering coats each grain instead of clumping into a sticky mass.
Adjust lemon at the end to taste, as its sourness varies and you want a clear, bright tang.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a spoon of thick curd, fried papad and a handful of extra fried peanuts, or pack it warm into a lunchbox.

variations.name: Mavinakayi Chitranna
variations.description: The spring version that swaps lemon for grated raw mango, giving a deeper, fruitier sourness that clings to the rice rather than just brightening it. The mango is sauteed briefly in the tempering so its tang mellows into the grains. Made across Karnataka when green mangoes are in season, it is tangier and more textured than the lemon original.

ingredients.name: Cooked rice
ingredients.note: Cooled and separated

ingredients.name: Grated raw mango
ingredients.note: Firm, sour green mango, peeled and grated

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil complements the fresh mango with a coastal fragrance

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan over medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then fry 1 tbsp chana dal, 1 tbsp urad dal and 1/4 cup peanuts until golden and crunchy.
Add 4 slit green chillies, grated 1 inch ginger, 1/2 tsp asafoetida and 15 curry leaves and saute for 30 seconds until aromatic.
Stir in 1 cup grated raw mango and 1/2 tsp turmeric and cook over medium heat for 4-5 minutes until the mango softens and its raw sharpness mellows.
Add 1/3 cup fresh grated coconut and 1.25 tsp salt and cook for 2 minutes until the mixture smells fragrant and just holds together.
Take the pan off the heat, add 3 cups cooled rice and fold gently until the grains are evenly coated and pale yellow.
Rest for 10 minutes so the mango tang soaks into the rice, then finish with 2 tbsp coriander before serving.
tips: The sourness depends entirely on the mango, so taste a shred first and adjust the quantity to your fruit.
Do not overcook the mango into a mush; it should keep a little bite so the chitranna stays textured.
Fresh coconut is key here as it softens the mango's sharpness, so avoid the desiccated kind in this version.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature with a cooling curd pachadi and crisp fried sandige for a proper Karnataka summer plate.

variations.name: Vegetable Masala Chitranna
variations.description: A heartier, meal-in-itself chitranna loaded with carrot, beans and green peas and lifted with a light dusting of vangi bath powder for extra warmth. The vegetables give colour and crunch while lemon keeps the signature tang. This is the version packed for long train journeys and school tiffins when a plain lemon rice needs more heft.

ingredients.name: Cooked rice
ingredients.note: Cooled and separated

ingredients.name: Carrot
ingredients.note: Finely diced

ingredients.name: Green beans
ingredients.note: Finely chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Carries the tempering and lightly fries the vegetables

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon lends richness to this fuller, vegetable-laden version

ingredients.name: Vangi bath powder
ingredients.note: A small pinch for extra warmth without overpowering the lemon

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan over medium heat, fry 10 cashews until golden and set aside, then in the same oil splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tbsp chana dal and 1 tbsp urad dal until the dals redden.
Add 2 slit green chillies and 12 curry leaves, then tip in the diced carrot, chopped beans and 1/3 cup peas and saute for 5-6 minutes until just tender but still crunchy.
Sprinkle in 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp vangi bath powder and stir for 20 seconds so the spices coat the vegetables.
Add 3 cups cooled rice and 1.25 tsp salt and fold gently until the grains and vegetables are evenly mixed and warmed through, about 3 minutes.
Switch off the heat, drizzle 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and squeeze in 2.5 tbsp lemon juice, folding once so the tang stays fresh.
Scatter the fried cashews and 2 tbsp coriander over the top and serve warm.
tips: Keep the vegetables diced small and evenly so they cook quickly and mix through the rice neatly.
Use the vangi bath powder with a light hand; it is meant to support, not overshadow, the lemon tang.
This fuller chitranna holds up well for hours, making it ideal for lunchboxes and picnics.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of spiced curd and a fried papad, or on its own as a complete one-dish lunch with extra lemon wedges.

variations.name: Coconut Chitranna
variations.description: The coastal Mangalorean version leans on a fragrant paste of fresh coconut, green chilli and ginger ground into the rice, giving a creamy, mildly sweet base before the lemon lifts it. Coconut oil in the tempering ties it firmly to the Tulu coast. Softer and mellower than the sharp classic, it is a soothing everyday rice.

ingredients.name: Cooked rice
ingredients.note: Cooled and separated

ingredients.name: Fresh grated coconut
ingredients.note: Ground into a light paste with chilli and ginger

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil is the backbone flavour of this coastal version

steps: Grind 1/2 cup fresh coconut with 3 green chillies and 1 inch ginger and a splash of water into a coarse, moist paste and set aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan over medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then fry 1 tbsp urad dal and 1 tbsp chana dal until golden, adding 2 broken dry red chillies at the end.
Add 1/2 tsp asafoetida and 15 curry leaves, then stir in the ground coconut paste and 1/2 tsp turmeric and saute over medium heat for 3-4 minutes until the raw coconut smell disappears.
Season with 1.25 tsp salt, then add 3 cups cooled rice and fold gently until the creamy coconut base coats every grain, warming through for 2-3 minutes.
Switch off the heat and squeeze in 2 tbsp lemon juice, folding once so the tang brightens the mellow coconut base.
Finish with 2 tbsp coriander and serve warm or at room temperature.
tips: Saute the coconut paste until its raw smell fades or the finished rice will taste chalky rather than creamy.
Keep the coconut paste coarse rather than smooth so it gives a pleasant texture against the soft rice.
This version dries out on standing, so refresh it with a teaspoon of coconut oil rather than water when reheating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a tangy tomato gojju or a simple cucumber koshimbir, and a piece of fried happala on the side.

variations.name: Classic Fried Thin-Poha Chivda
variations.description: The quintessential Diwali chivda: gossamer-thin nylon poha fried to a cloud-light crunch and tossed with peanuts, cashews, fried curry leaves and slivered dry coconut. Turmeric, chili and a whisper of powdered sugar give it the classic sweet-salty-spicy balance.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for deep-frying the poha crisp and light; strain and reuse for everyday cooking

steps: Heat the Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180°C and, working in small batches, fry the thin poha in a mesh ladle for just 5-8 seconds until it turns opaque white and puffs, then drain over the pot; do not let it brown.
In the same oil fry the peanuts until the skins crackle, then the cashews to pale gold, then the sliced copra briefly, lifting each out separately onto paper.
Fry the slit green chilies and curry leaves for a few seconds until they stop spluttering and go crisp, then drain.
Leave about 1 tbsp oil in a wide pan on low heat, add turmeric and red chili powder off the flame so they don't burn, and stir for 5 seconds.
Tip in the fried poha, peanuts, cashews, daliya, copra, chilies and curry leaves, sprinkle the salt and powdered sugar, and toss gently for a minute until everything is evenly coated.
Cool completely on a wide tray before packing into an airtight tin so it stays crunchy for up to a month.
tips: Test one flake first, if it puffs instantly the oil is ready; if it sinks and browns, cool the oil slightly to avoid a bitter batch.
Add the spice powders off the heat, a hot pan scorches turmeric in seconds and turns the chivda bitter.
For extra crunch that lasts, make sure the poha is bone dry, spread it in the sun for an hour before frying if it feels limp.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve heaped in a bowl for Diwali guests with cups of adrak chai, or pack into small pouches as edible festival favours.

variations.name: Roasted Thick-Poha Diet Chivda
variations.description: A guilt-free, no-deep-fry chivda where thick poha is dry-roasted to a nutty crunch and tossed in a light tempered oil. Loaded with roasted (not fried) peanuts and seeds, it is the everyday tin cousin of the festive fried version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: just enough light wood-pressed oil to carry the tempering, no deep-frying

steps: Dry-roast the thick poha in a heavy pan over medium-low heat, stirring constantly for 6-8 minutes until it turns crisp and a flake snaps cleanly, then tip onto a plate.
Roast the pumpkin seeds in the same pan for a minute until they pop, and set aside with the already-roasted peanuts and daliya.
Heat the Anveshan Sunflower Oil, crackle the mustard seeds, then add hing, curry leaves and chopped green chilies and fry for 30 seconds until the leaves go crisp.
Lower the heat, stir in turmeric for 5 seconds off the flame so it doesn't scorch, then return the pan to low heat.
Add the roasted poha, peanuts, daliya and pumpkin seeds, sprinkle salt and powdered jaggery, and toss for 2 minutes so the light tempering coats every flake.
Cool fully on a tray, then store airtight; because it uses barely any oil it keeps well for 2-3 weeks.
tips: Roast the poha low and slow, high heat browns the edges before the centre crisps and leaves a raw, papery bite.
A microwave shortcut works too, spread the poha and cook on high for 3-4 minutes in bursts, stirring between each.
Keep the jaggery to a whisper; it is there to round the salt, not to sweeten, and too much makes the chivda clump.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ideal as a light evening munch with green tea, or scattered over a bowl of curd with cucumber for an instant savoury snack.

variations.name: Makai Cornflakes Chivda
variations.description: A modern, extra-crunchy chivda built on golden corn flakes instead of poha, quickly fried till they balloon and stay shatteringly crisp. Sweet-salty with raisins and cashews, it is the kid-favourite bowl that disappears fastest at any party.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: light, neutral wood-pressed oil for a quick puffing fry that keeps flakes pale gold

steps: Heat the Anveshan Sunflower Oil to 180°C, then fry the corn flakes in a mesh ladle for just 5 seconds per batch until they swell and lighten, and drain immediately so they don't colour.
In the same oil fry the cashews and almond slivers to pale gold, then the raisins for a few seconds until they plump, lifting each onto paper.
Fry the slit chilies and curry leaves until crisp, about 15 seconds, then drain.
Transfer the fried flakes and nuts to a wide bowl while still warm.
Sprinkle over the salt, black salt, chaat masala and powdered sugar, add the raisins, chilies and curry leaves, and toss gently for a minute so the seasoning clings.
Cool completely before storing airtight; eat within two weeks as corn flakes soften faster than poha.
tips: Buy plain, unfrosted corn flakes; sweetened breakfast flakes burn and turn syrupy in hot oil.
Season while warm so the powders stick, but only pack once fully cool or trapped steam will make the flakes chewy.
For a savoury-only version skip the sugar and raisins and double the chaat masala and black salt.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a big sharing bowl for movie night or cricket matches with tall glasses of nimbu paani.

variations.name: Sweet-Spicy Gud Poha Chivda
variations.description: A sticky, addictive Maharashtrian-style chivda where fried poha is bound in a quick jaggery glaze so each flake carries a sweet-hot-tangy shell. Studded with roasted peanuts and dry coconut, it sits somewhere between a snack and a mithai.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for frying the poha light and crisp before the jaggery glaze goes on

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted into a quick glaze for a mineral-rich sweet-spicy coating instead of refined sugar

steps: Fry the thin poha in the Anveshan Groundnut Oil at 180°C for 5-8 seconds per batch until puffed and white, then drain well; fry the sliced copra and sesame seeds briefly and set aside with the roasted peanuts.
Fry the curry leaves for a few seconds until crisp, then reserve.
In a wide pan on low heat melt the Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 1 tbsp water, stirring for 2-3 minutes until it bubbles and forms a loose syrup that coats a spoon.
Take the pan off the heat, quickly stir in the red chili powder, amchur, fennel powder and salt into the syrup so they bloom without burning.
Working fast, fold in the fried poha, peanuts, copra, sesame and curry leaves, tossing for a minute until every flake wears a thin sweet-spicy glaze.
Spread on a greased tray, break up any clumps as it cools, and store airtight once completely cold and crisp.
tips: Stop the jaggery at the soft-syrup stage; boil it too long and it hardens into candy that sets the chivda into a solid block.
Toss while the glaze is warm and pliable, then separate the flakes as they cool so they stay loose and snackable.
A pinch of dry ginger powder in the glaze adds a warming edge and helps balance the sweetness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Offer this sweet-and-spicy chivda as a festive naivedya-style treat with milky tea, or crumble it over vanilla ice cream for a fun fusion dessert.

variations.name: Classic Curd Semiya
variations.description: A cooling South Indian version of curd rice made with soft-cooked vermicelli folded into whisked yogurt and a mustard-curry leaf tempering. Thayir semiya is lighter than thayir sadam and beloved as a summer lunchbox and temple offering. Creamy, gently tangy and studded with cashews, it soothes on the hottest days.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasts the vermicelli to golden and adds a mellow richness to the curd

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed oil for a clean tempering that keeps the dish light

steps: Roast 1.5 cups vermicelli in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium-low heat, stirring for 3 minutes until evenly golden.
Bring 4 cups water to a boil with 1/2 tsp salt, add the roasted vermicelli and cook 4 minutes until soft, then drain and rinse briefly under cool water to stop the cooking.
Whisk 2 cups thick curd with 1/4 cup milk and 1/2 tsp salt until smooth and pourable.
Fold the cooled, drained vermicelli into the whisked curd along with grated 1 inch ginger.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, fry 1 tsp urad dal and 10 cashews until golden, then add 2 slit green chillies, 12 curry leaves and 1/4 tsp asafoetida for 20 seconds.
Pour the hot tempering over the curd semiya and mix gently to distribute.
Rest 10 minutes for the vermicelli to soak up the curd, adding a splash of milk if it thickens too much before serving.
tips: Cook the vermicelli until fully soft; unlike upma it should be tender, not springy, for curd semiya.
Use slightly sour, thick curd for the best flavour, and loosen with milk rather than water to keep it creamy.
If making ahead, keep the curd a little loose as the vermicelli keeps absorbing it and thickens over time.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled with a spoon of mango or lime pickle on the side and a few pomegranate pearls on top.

variations.name: Fruity Curd Semiya
variations.description: A festive, garnish-rich version topped with pomegranate pearls, grated carrot and green grapes, the way it is served at Tamil weddings and temple counters. The bursts of sweet fruit against the tangy curd make it a crowd-pleaser, especially for children. It looks as good as it tastes, jewelled with colour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasts the vermicelli and lends a festive richness to the sweet-tangy base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed oil for a light, clean tempering over the fruity curd

steps: Roast 1.5 cups vermicelli in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium-low heat until golden, about 3 minutes.
Boil the vermicelli in 4 cups salted water for 4 minutes until soft, then drain and cool under running water.
Whisk 2 cups thick curd smooth with 1/2 tsp salt and fold in the cooled vermicelli and 1 small grated carrot.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, fry 1 tsp urad dal and 8 cashews until golden, then add 1 slit green chilli, 10 curry leaves and 1/4 tsp asafoetida for 20 seconds.
Stir the tempering through the curd semiya and rest 5 minutes to soften.
Just before serving, fold in half the pomegranate pearls and halved grapes so they stay whole and juicy.
Top with the remaining pomegranate and grapes and serve chilled for the prettiest effect.
tips: Add the fruit only at the end; folded in too early it bleeds colour and turns the curd watery.
Grapes and pomegranate are traditional, but chopped mango or apple work beautifully in season.
Keep the tempering mild with just one chilli so the sweet fruit and tangy curd stay the stars.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve well chilled in a wide bowl showered with extra pomegranate, ideal for a summer party or festive lunch.

variations.name: Ginger-Chilli Curd Semiya
variations.description: A punchier, restaurant-tiffin style with a bold ginger, green chilli and coriander flavour whisked right into the curd, plus a heavier tempering. The extra ginger gives it warmth and a clean, sharp finish that grown-ups love. It is the version that holds its own as a light main rather than a mild side.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasts the vermicelli evenly and softens the sharp ginger-chilli edge

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil gives the spicy tempering an earthy South Indian depth

steps: Roast 1.5 cups vermicelli in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium-low heat until golden, about 3 minutes.
Boil the vermicelli in 4 cups salted water for 4 minutes until soft, drain and rinse under cool water.
Grind 2 inch ginger, 3 green chillies and 3 tbsp coriander leaves to a coarse paste and whisk it into 2 cups thick curd with 1 tsp salt.
Fold the cooled vermicelli into the spiced curd until well coated.

Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, fry 1 tsp urad dal and 1 tsp chana dal until golden, then add 1 broken red chilli, 12 curry leaves and 1/4 tsp asafoetida for 20 seconds.
Pour the tempering over the curd semiya and mix through thoroughly.
Rest 10 minutes so the ginger-chilli flavour mellows and the vermicelli softens before serving.
tips: Grinding the ginger and chilli into the curd spreads the heat evenly rather than leaving hot pockets.
Add a spoon of chopped coriander at the end too for a fresh, herby lift.
Because this version is boldly flavoured, keep the curd on the thicker side so it clings to the strands.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve cool with a fried mor milagai and a wedge of lime, hearty enough to eat as a light one-bowl meal.

variations.name: Creamy Cashew Curd Semiya
variations.description: An indulgent version enriched with a smooth ground cashew paste and a splash of fresh cream, giving the curd a luxurious, restaurant-style body. It is milder and richer than the everyday version, the kind served at celebrations. The cashew base makes it silky enough to feel special without any heaviness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasts the vermicelli and enriches the creamy cashew base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed oil for a neutral, clean tempering over the rich curd

steps: Roast 1.5 cups vermicelli in 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium-low heat until golden, about 3 minutes.
Boil the vermicelli in 4 cups salted water for 4 minutes until soft, drain and cool under running water.
Soak half the cashews in warm water for 10 minutes and grind to a smooth paste with a little water, keeping the rest whole for the tempering.
Whisk 2 cups thick curd with the cashew paste, 3 tbsp fresh cream and 1 tsp salt until silky, then fold in the cooled vermicelli.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, fry 1 tsp urad dal and the reserved whole cashews until golden, then add 2 slit green chillies, 12 curry leaves and 1/4 tsp asafoetida for 20 seconds.
Pour the tempering over the creamy curd semiya and fold through gently.
Chill for 15 minutes so it sets to a luscious, spoonable consistency before serving.
tips: Grind the soaked cashews really smooth so the curd stays silky rather than grainy.
The cream is optional but lifts this into celebration territory; a spoon of milk works for a lighter version.
Keep it barely spiced so the delicate cashew richness comes through.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled as a refined side at a festive meal, garnished with a few fried cashews and a sprinkle of pomegranate.

variations.name: Classic Kerala Ela Ada
variations.description: Ela Ada is Kerala's beloved rainy-season snack of soft steamed rice dough parcels wrapped in fragrant banana leaf. A thin sheet of moist rice flour is spread on the leaf, filled with a warm coconut-jaggery mixture, folded and steamed until the leaf perfumes the dough. Unwrapped hot, it is soft, sweet and faintly smoky.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Melted with the coconut into a sticky sweet filling that is the heart of every ada

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Smeared on the banana leaf and the dough so the ada peels off cleanly and glistens

steps: Bring 2 cups water with 0.5 tsp salt to a rolling boil, lower the heat, and stir in 2 cups roasted rice flour all at once, mixing fast until it clumps into a shaggy dough with no dry pockets.
Cover and rest 10 minutes, then knead the warm dough with lightly greased hands into a smooth, pliable ball that does not crack.
For the filling, cook 1.5 cups grated coconut with 0.75 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder on low heat for 5 to 6 minutes until sticky, then stir in 0.5 tsp cardamom and cool.
Wilt the banana leaf pieces over a low flame for a few seconds until supple, wipe with a little Anveshan Ghee, and pat a lemon-sized ball of dough into a thin oval on each leaf.
Spoon 2 tbsp of the coconut-jaggery filling onto one half, fold the leaf over to seal the ada into a half-moon, and press the edges lightly.
Steam the parcels on medium-high heat for 10 to 12 minutes until the dough turns glossy and pulls away from the leaf, then serve warm in the wrapper.
tips: Add the rice flour to boiling water off a lower flame and stir without pause, or the dough turns lumpy and hard to spread.
Grease your palms with ghee while patting the dough so it spreads thin without sticking or tearing.
Do not overload the filling; a thin, even smear seals better and cooks through evenly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a cup of strong Kerala chai, letting each person unwrap their own leaf-scented parcel at the table.

variations.name: Chakka Ada (Ripe Jackfruit)
variations.description: This monsoon favourite swaps the plain coconut filling for lusciously ripe jackfruit cooked down into a fragrant halwa-like jam. The natural fruit sugars caramelise against the jaggery, giving the steamed parcel a heady tropical aroma. It is the way Kerala homes use up a glut of ripe chakka in season.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Cooks the jackfruit down into a sticky preserve that oozes sweetly inside the ada

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Fries the jackfruit jam so it thickens without catching and adds a Malabar aroma

steps: Deseed and chop 2 cups ripe jackfruit bulbs, then blend to a coarse pulp with a splash of water.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a heavy pan, add the jackfruit pulp with 0.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder, and cook on medium-low for 12 to 15 minutes, stirring, until it thickens into a glossy jam.
Fold 0.75 cups grated coconut and 0.25 tsp dry ginger powder into the jam, cook 2 more minutes until it leaves the sides of the pan, and cool completely.
Boil 2 cups water with 0.5 tsp salt, stir in 2 cups roasted rice flour off the heat until it forms a dough, cover 10 minutes, then knead smooth with greased hands.
Soften the banana leaves over a flame, pat a ball of dough into a thin oval on each, spoon the jackfruit filling onto one half, and fold into a sealed half-moon.
Steam on medium-high heat for 12 minutes until the dough turns translucent and firm, then serve warm still folded in the leaf.
tips: Cook the jackfruit jam until it is thick and no longer runny, or the moist filling will make the dough split while steaming.
Choose very ripe, soft jackfruit for the deepest flavour and to cut down on added jaggery.
The jam keeps refrigerated for a week, so make a batch ahead and steam fresh ada on demand.
variations.servingSuggestion: Wonderful with a small bowl of thick coconut milk for spooning over each opened parcel.

variations.name: Ethakka Ada (Banana-Coconut)
variations.description: A softer, mellower ada filled with mashed Kerala nendran banana folded through toasted coconut and jaggery. The ripe banana keeps the filling creamy and the whole parcel almost custardy once steamed. It is a gentle, child-friendly version made in homes when bananas are plentiful.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Balances the creamy banana filling with mineral-rich caramel sweetness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Toasts the coconut and enriches the banana mash for a fudgy centre

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan and fry 10 chopped cashews for a minute until golden, then add 1 cup grated coconut and toast on medium for 3 minutes until lightly coloured.
Mash 2 ripe nendran bananas smooth, add them to the pan with 0.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.5 tsp cardamom, and cook 5 minutes until thick and jammy, then cool.
Boil 2 cups water with 0.5 tsp salt, stir in 2 cups roasted rice flour off the heat to a dough, rest covered 10 minutes, and knead smooth with greased hands.
Wilt the banana leaves over a flame, spread a thin oval of dough on each, and spoon the banana-coconut filling over one half.
Fold each leaf into a sealed half-moon, pressing the edges so the soft filling stays inside.
Steam on medium-high heat for 10 to 12 minutes until the dough is glossy and set, then serve warm in the leaf.
tips: Use fully ripe, sweet bananas so the filling stays creamy and needs less jaggery.
Cook the mash until it holds together on the spoon, as a runny filling seeps out and tears the ada.
A pinch of nutmeg with the cardamom deepens the banana flavour beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as an evening tea-time treat with a sprinkle of extra toasted coconut on the side.

variations.name: Khapli Wheat Ellada (Sesame-Jaggery)
variations.description: A nourishing wholegrain twist that builds the dough from nutty khapli wheat instead of rice and fills it with a toasted sesame-jaggery mixture. The ancient-grain wrapper is chewier and more filling, while the sesame gives a deep, nutty crunch against the sweet centre. A wholesome reinvention of the leaf-steamed classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Ancient emmer wheat that makes a chewier, fibre-rich wrapper in place of white rice flour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Melted with toasted sesame into a nutty praline-like filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Greases the leaf and dough so the wholewheat ada does not stick while steaming

steps: Dry-roast 0.75 cups white sesame seeds on medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes until they pop and turn golden, then cool and pulse coarsely.
Melt 0.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water on low heat, stir in the crushed sesame, 0.5 cups grated coconut and 0.5 tsp cardamom, cook 2 minutes until sticky, and cool.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt and about 1 cup water into a soft, smooth dough, adding water little by little, and rest it 15 minutes.
Soften the banana leaves over a flame, rub with a little Anveshan Ghee, and roll or pat a ball of dough into a thin round on each leaf.
Place 2 tbsp of the sesame-jaggery filling on one half, fold the leaf over into a half-moon, and press the edges to seal.
Steam on medium-high heat for 12 to 14 minutes until the wholewheat dough is cooked through and firm, then serve warm.
tips: Khapli dough needs a few minutes of rest so the bran hydrates and rolls out without cracking.
Roast the sesame just until fragrant; overtoasted seeds turn bitter and spoil the filling.
Roll this dough a touch thicker than rice ada, as wholewheat needs slightly longer to steam through.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a drizzle of warm honey over the opened parcel for an extra-wholesome finish.

variations.name: Classic Ellu Sadam
variations.description: A fragrant Tamil sesame rice where cooked rice is tossed with a freshly ground podi of roasted white sesame, urad dal and red chilli. Nutty, mildly spicy and long-keeping, it is a favourite temple prasadam and travel lunch across Tamil Nadu. The gingelly tempering and toasted sesame give it a deep, warm aroma that fills the kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil deepens the toasted sesame flavour that defines ellu sadam

steps: Cook 1.5 cups rice with 3 cups water until each grain is separate and firm, spread on a plate to cool and drizzle over 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil so it does not clump.
Dry-roast 1/2 cup white sesame seeds on low heat, stirring constantly for 3 minutes until they turn light golden and pop, then set aside to cool.
In the same pan dry-roast 2 tbsp urad dal and 4 red chillies until the dal is golden and fragrant, about 2 minutes.
Grind the roasted sesame, urad dal, red chillies, 1/2 tsp asafoetida and 1 tsp salt to a coarse, slightly oily podi.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, add 15 curry leaves and 1/4 tsp turmeric off high heat so it does not burn.
Add the cooled rice and the ground sesame podi with the remaining 1/4 tsp salt, and fold gently until every grain is evenly coated.
Rest for 10 minutes so the nutty podi soaks into the rice before serving warm or at room temperature.
tips: Roast the sesame on low heat and stop the moment they turn golden; over-roasted seeds taste bitter.
Grind the podi coarse, not to a paste, so the sesame oils bind the rice without turning it pasty.
The podi keeps airtight for two weeks, so grind extra and stir a few spoons into plain rice any day.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a crisp potato roast or fried appalam and a bowl of thick curd to balance the nuttiness.

variations.name: Karuppu Ellu Sadam
variations.description: A rustic, iron-rich version made with roasted black sesame and a touch of jaggery, giving the rice a striking grey hue and a deeper, almost bittersweet nuttiness. Black sesame is treasured in Tamil cooking for its warmth in winter and its health benefits. The jaggery rounds the intensity of the black seeds into something surprisingly moreish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil reinforces the earthy depth of the roasted black sesame

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Mellows the slight bitterness of black sesame into a rounded sweet-nutty finish

steps: Cook 1.5 cups rice with 3 cups water to firm, separate grains, spread out to cool and rub with 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil.
Dry-roast 1/2 cup black sesame on low heat for 3 minutes until they crackle and smell nutty, then cool; they are ready when a seed crushes easily between two fingers.
Dry-roast 1.5 tbsp urad dal, 3 red chillies and 1 tsp peppercorns until the dal is golden, about 2 minutes.
Grind the black sesame, roasted dal, chillies, peppercorns, 1/2 tsp asafoetida, 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp salt to a coarse grey podi.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, and add 12 curry leaves for 15 seconds.
Tip in the cooled rice and the black sesame podi with the remaining 1/4 tsp salt, folding gently until the rice turns an even greyish hue.
Rest 10 minutes so the earthy podi settles into the grains before serving.
tips: Black sesame burns faster than white, so keep the heat low and stir without stopping.
The jaggery is what balances black sesame's edge, so do not skip it even though the dish is savoury.
This version is especially warming in winter and pairs beautifully with a simple mor kuzhambu.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a dollop of curd and a spicy vathal to cut through the deep, nutty richness.

variations.name: Coconut Ellu Sadam
variations.description: A softer, aromatic take where roasted coconut is ground into the sesame podi, lending sweetness and a fuller body to the rice. The coconut tempers the sesame's intensity and makes this version especially popular with children. Finished with a generous cashew tempering, it eats almost like a mild festive rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil layers a fragrant coconut note over the sesame podi

steps: Cook 1.5 cups rice with 3 cups water to firm, separate grains and spread out to cool, drizzling with 1 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil.
Dry-roast 1/3 cup white sesame until golden and popping, then remove; in the same pan roast 1/2 cup grated coconut on low until it turns light golden and dry, about 3 minutes.
Dry-roast 1.5 tbsp urad dal, 1 tbsp chana dal and 3 red chillies until the dals are golden.
Grind the roasted sesame, coconut, dals, chillies, 1/2 tsp asafoetida and 1 tsp salt to a coarse, fragrant podi.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, fry 12 cashews until golden, then add 15 curry leaves for 15 seconds.
Add the cooled rice and the coconut-sesame podi with the remaining 1/4 tsp salt, folding gently until evenly coated.
Rest 10 minutes so the coconut aroma infuses the rice before serving warm.
tips: Roast the grated coconut until dry, or the moisture will make the podi clumpy and shorten its shelf life.
Fresh coconut gives the best aroma, but roast it thoroughly so the rice stays loose and separate.
Because of the coconut, this version is best eaten the same day rather than stored for a trip.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a tangy tomato thokku or a spoon of lime pickle to offset the mild sweetness.

variations.name: Kara Ellu Podi Sadam
variations.description: A fiery version built on a spicier podi loaded with extra red chillies, roasted chana dal and a hint of garlic, for those who like their sesame rice with real heat. The garlic and dal give it a savoury depth while the chillies bring a slow, building burn. This is the version that turns a plain lunchbox into something you remember.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil carries the fiery podi and gives the rice its glossy coat

steps: Cook 1.5 cups rice with 3 cups water to firm, separate grains and spread out to cool with 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil.
Dry-roast 1/3 cup white sesame until golden and popping, then remove and cool.
Dry-roast 1 tbsp urad dal and 7 red chillies until the dal is golden and the chillies turn crisp, about 2 minutes.
Grind the roasted sesame, urad dal, red chillies, 2 tbsp roasted chana dal, 4 garlic cloves, 1/2 tsp asafoetida and 1 tsp salt to a coarse, fiery podi.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, fry 1/4 cup peanuts until crisp, then add 15 curry leaves for 15 seconds.
Add the cooled rice and the spicy podi with the remaining 1/4 tsp salt, folding gently until every grain is coated a deep golden.
Rest 10 minutes so the heat mellows slightly and the flavours meld before serving.
tips: Add the garlic raw to the grinder; it cooks into the podi and the tempering carries no raw taste.
Adjust the chillies to your heat tolerance; seven makes a genuinely spicy rice.
The crunchy fried peanuts are essential here, giving bite against the fine, hot podi.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pack into a lunchbox with plenty of thick curd and a mild vegetable stir-fry to tame the heat.

variations.name: Classic Ennegayi
variations.description: Ennegayi is the iconic North Karnataka stuffed brinjal, where small purple baingans are slit and packed with a roasted peanut, sesame and coconut masala, then slow-cooked in oil until glossy. The stuffing turns rich and nutty while the brinjal softens into every crevice, making it the definitive partner for jolada rotti.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil that slow-cooks the stuffed brinjals and carries the nutty masala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: balances the tamarind tang with a rounded caramel sweetness typical of the region

steps: Dry-roast 0.33 cup peanuts on low heat for 5 minutes until spotted, then roast 3 tbsp sesame seeds and 0.25 cup desiccated coconut separately for 2 minutes each until golden and fragrant.

Grind the roasted peanuts, sesame, both coconuts, 1 tbsp tamarind, 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1.5 tsp chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp cumin and 1 tsp salt to a thick coarse paste using a little water.
Wash 10 small brinjals, keep the stems on and make a deep cross-slit from the base without cutting through, then soak them briefly in salted water.
Pat the brinjals dry and press the ground masala firmly into each slit, reserving the leftover paste.
Heat 5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a wide kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and a sprig of curry leaves and let them splutter for 20 seconds.
Arrange the stuffed brinjals in a single layer, cover and cook on low for 12 minutes, turning gently every 4 minutes so all sides brown.
Stir the reserved masala into half a cup of water, pour it around the brinjals, cover and simmer 8 minutes until the oil glistens on top and the brinjals are fork-tender.
tips: Roast each nut and seed separately as they brown at different speeds and burnt sesame turns the masala bitter.
Do not slit the brinjals all the way through so the stuffing stays sealed inside during cooking.
The gravy thickens as it rests, so add a splash of hot water if reheating the next day.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with warm jolada rotti (sorghum flatbread) or steamed rice topped with a spoon of the glossy masala oil.

variations.name: Shenga Ennegayi (Peanut-Forward Dry)
variations.description: A drier Dharwad-belt version built almost entirely on freshly roasted peanuts, with barely any coconut so the groundnut flavour dominates. The masala clings tightly to the brinjal skins and there is no gravy, giving a robust, oil-slicked sabzi meant to be eaten with bhakri.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: doubles down on the peanut theme and shallow-fries the brinjals to a dry finish

steps: Dry-roast 0.66 cup peanuts on low heat for 6 minutes until deeply spotted, cool and rub off the skins for a cleaner masala.
In the same pan dry-roast 2 tsp coriander seeds, 1 tsp cumin and 5 Byadgi chillies for 2 minutes until aromatic.
Grind the roasted peanuts, spices, 8 garlic cloves, 1 tsp amchur, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt to a thick dry paste with just 2 tablespoons of water.
Slit 10 brinjals in a cross from the base, keeping the stems intact, and pack the dry peanut masala firmly into each.
Heat 5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and a sprig of curry leaves and let them crackle for 15 seconds.
Lay the stuffed brinjals in a single layer, cover and cook on low for 15 minutes, turning every 4 minutes so the masala crust browns without burning.
Uncover, raise the heat for 3 minutes to dry any moisture and finish with the last of the masala scattered over the top.
tips: Rubbing the skins off the roasted peanuts gives a smoother, less bitter stuffing.
Keep the water minimal while grinding so the masala stays a thick dry paste that crusts nicely.
Byadgi chillies give a deep red colour with gentle heat, so adjust the count for a milder finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with jowar bhakri and a raw onion wedge, or tuck the dry brinjals into a roti roll for a rustic lunch.

variations.name: Malnad Coconut Ennegayi
variations.description: From the coastal Malnad region, this ennegayi swaps the peanut base for a wet fresh-coconut masala perfumed with roasted gram and curry leaves. The stuffing is softer and creamier, and the brinjals finish in a light coconut gravy rather than the drier ghat-side style.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the coastal fat that reinforces the fresh coconut masala and its aroma

steps: Grind 0.75 cup fresh grated coconut, 3 tbsp roasted gram, 3 green chillies, 1 inch ginger, 0.5 tbsp tamarind, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 2 tbsp coriander leaves and 1 tsp salt to a thick wet paste with a little water.
Slit 10 brinjals in a cross from the base, keeping the stems on, and soak them in salted water for 5 minutes.
Pat the brinjals dry and stuff each generously with the fresh coconut masala, saving the rest.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tsp urad dal and 2 sprigs of curry leaves and let them splutter for 20 seconds.
Place the stuffed brinjals in a single layer, cover and cook on low for 10 minutes, turning gently twice.
Loosen the reserved masala with three-quarters of a cup of water, pour it in, cover and simmer 10 minutes until the brinjals are soft and the coconut gravy thickens.
Finish with the remaining chopped coriander and rest 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Use fresh grated coconut rather than dry copra for the soft, sweet Malnad character.
Add the tamarind sparingly here as the gravy is meant to be mild and coconut-led.
Roasted gram thickens the masala naturally, so avoid over-watering the final gravy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot steamed rice with a drizzle of coconut oil, or alongside neer dosa for a coastal spread.

variations.name: Sesame-Til Ennegayi
variations.description: A dark, intense take where roasted white sesame forms the heart of the stuffing, lending a bittersweet toastiness and a near-black masala. Finished in wood-pressed sesame oil, it is the most aromatic ennegayi, with the til flavour running through every bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed til oil that echoes and deepens the roasted sesame stuffing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: rounds off the toasty sesame bitterness with a mellow sweetness

steps: Dry-roast 0.5 cup sesame seeds on low heat for 3 minutes until they turn golden and start to pop, then set aside to cool.
In the same pan roast 3 tbsp copra, 4 Byadgi chillies and 2 tsp coriander seeds for 2 minutes until fragrant.
Grind the roasted sesame, copra, chillies, coriander seeds, 6 garlic cloves, 1 tbsp tamarind, 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 1 tsp salt to a thick coarse paste with a little water.
Slit 10 brinjals in a cross from the base, keeping the stems intact, and pack the sesame masala into each.
Heat 5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadai over medium heat, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and a sprig of curry leaves and let them splutter for 15 seconds.
Arrange the stuffed brinjals in a single layer, cover and cook on low for 12 minutes, turning every 4 minutes to brown all sides.
Stir the leftover masala into half a cup of water, pour around the brinjals, cover and simmer 8 minutes until glossy and tender.
tips: Pull the sesame off the heat the moment it pops, as over-roasted til turns sharply bitter.
A little jaggery is essential here to counter the natural bitterness of heavily roasted sesame.
Grind the masala coarse rather than smooth so the stuffing has a pleasant grainy bite.
variations.servingSuggestion: Delicious with sajje rotti (pearl millet flatbread) or mixed into hot rice as a quick sesame-brinjal rice.

variations.name: Classic Gujarati Fafda
variations.description: The smooth, crisp gram-flour strip that Gujarat wakes up to on Sundays and Dussehra. A besan dough softened with papad khar and oil is smeared into long thin ribbons on a board and deep-fried till pale gold, giving a crackly outside and a tender, ajwain-scented chew.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: 3 tbsp warmed into the dough as moyan and the rest for deep-frying the ribbons crisp

steps: Dissolve the papad khar in 2 tbsp warm water and rub it into the besan along with crushed ajwain, black pepper, turmeric and salt.
Work in 3 tbsp warm Anveshan Groundnut Oil, then add the remaining water little by little and knead a smooth, firm, pliable dough; rest 15 minutes.
Grease a wooden board or the back of a steel plate; take a small ball and, using the heel of your palm, smear it into a long, thin 12 cm ribbon in one confident stroke.
Slide a flat knife or scraper under the ribbon to lift it cleanly without tearing.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil to a medium 170°C and gently lay in the ribbons, frying for 2-3 minutes, turning once, until pale gold and crisp at the edges but still slightly tender.
Drain on a rack and serve warm the same day, or cool fully and store airtight for up to a week.
tips: Coarse besan makes better fafda than fine flour; it gives the strips their characteristic slightly grainy, crisp texture.
The smearing stroke takes practice, keep the board well greased and press firmly and evenly in a single motion for uniform ribbons.
Do not over-fry, fafda should stay pale with just a tender-crisp bite, not deep brown and hard.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the classic Gujarati way with fried green chilies, sweet-sour papaya sambharo and a bowl of kadhi for a festive breakfast.

variations.name: Tikha Masala Fafda
variations.description: A fiery Kathiawadi-style fafda where the besan dough is charged with red chili, garlic and cumin for a bold, spicy strip that needs no chutney. Darker and punchier than the mild classic, it is made for those who like their farsan with real heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: 3 tbsp as moyan and the rest for deep-frying; its nutty depth suits the bold spicing

steps: Dissolve the papad khar in 2 tbsp warm water, then rub it into the besan with red chili powder, cumin powder, turmeric and salt.
Mix in the garlic paste and 3 tbsp warm Anveshan Sesame Oil, then add the remaining water gradually and knead a firm, smooth dough; rest 15 minutes.
Grease a board and, with the heel of your palm, smear small balls into long thin 12 cm ribbons in one firm stroke.
Lift each ribbon with a flat scraper so it stays intact.
Fry in the remaining Anveshan Sesame Oil at a medium 170°C for 2-3 minutes, turning once, until crisp-edged and a spiced reddish-gold; keep the heat steady so the garlic doesn't burn.
Drain on a rack and serve warm, or cool and store airtight for up to five days.
tips: Use a smooth garlic paste with no chunks, as bits of raw garlic scorch and turn bitter in the hot oil.
Because chili and garlic can darken fast, fry these a touch cooler and shorter than the plain classic.
Taste-balance the dough before frying; it should read boldly spicy but still let the besan flavour through.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these spicy strips with cooling chaas and a wedge of raw onion, or crumble over a fafda-chaat with curd and tamarind.

variations.name: Methi Fafda Gathiya
variations.description: A herby cross between fafda and soft gathiya, kneaded with dried fenugreek and coriander and pressed a touch thicker for a more tender, melt-in-mouth strip. The methi lends a gentle bitterness that balances the nutty gram flour beautifully.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: 3 tbsp as moyan and the rest for a clean deep fry that keeps the strips light

steps: Crush the kasuri methi into the besan, then add coarsely crushed coriander seeds, sesame seeds, white pepper and salt.
Dissolve the papad khar in 2 tbsp warm water and rub it in with 3 tbsp warm Anveshan Sunflower Oil.
Add the remaining water gradually and knead a soft-yet-firm, smooth dough; rest 15 minutes so the methi hydrates.
Grease a board and smear small balls into slightly thicker 12 cm ribbons than classic fafda for a more tender gathiya-like bite.
Fry in the remaining Anveshan Sunflower Oil at a medium 165°C for 2-3 minutes, turning once, until pale gold and just crisp at the edges.
Drain on a rack and serve warm, or cool completely and store airtight for up to five days.
tips: Pressing these a little thicker gives the signature soft, melt-in-mouth gathiya texture rather than a crisp cracker.
Toast the kasuri methi for a few seconds before crushing to bring out its aroma without adding moisture.
A slightly softer dough works here; if it feels stiff, wet your palm before smearing each ribbon.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair these soft methi strips with sweet chutney and fried chilies, or tuck into a soft pav with green chutney for a quick bite.

variations.name: Jeera Ajwain Papdi Fafda
variations.description: A thinner, extra-crackly fafda pressed almost paper-thin and fried a shade crisper, seasoned simply with roasted cumin and ajwain for a clean, aromatic snap. This is the papdi-style fafda made to be stored and eaten straight from the tin.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: 3 tbsp as moyan and the rest for a clean deep fry; its light sweetness rounds the cumin

steps: Dissolve the papad khar in 2 tbsp warm water and rub it into the besan with roasted cumin powder, crushed ajwain, hing, turmeric and salt.
Work in 3 tbsp warm Anveshan Coconut Oil, then add the remaining water gradually and knead a firm, smooth dough; rest 15 minutes.
Grease a board well and smear small balls into extra-thin, long 14 cm ribbons using a firm single stroke of your palm.
Lift each ribbon carefully with a flat scraper, keeping it whole.
Fry in the remaining Anveshan Coconut Oil at a medium 170°C for about 3 minutes, turning once, until fully crisp and pale gold all through.
Drain well on a rack and cool completely so they turn shatter-crisp, then store airtight for up to ten days.
tips: Smearing thinner and frying a minute longer than classic fafda is what makes this version snap crisp for storage.
Use roasted cumin powder rather than raw seeds so the flavour is deep and there are no hard seeds in the thin strip.
Drain thoroughly and cool fully before packing; any warmth trapped in the tin will soften the crackly strips.
variations.servingSuggestion: Keep a tin of these crisp strips for tea time, served with a quick coriander-mint chutney or a sweet date-tamarind dip.

variations.name: Classic Gujarati Farsi Puri
variations.description: The crackly, flaky Gujarati farsan puri that shatters at first bite. A stiff maida-and-rava dough enriched with ghee moyan and studded with crushed black pepper and ajwain is rolled thick, pricked, and fried low and slow so the layers stay pale and crisp for weeks.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: warmed and rubbed in as generous moyan, this is what gives farsi puri its flaky shortness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: light, neutral wood-pressed oil for a slow deep fry that keeps the puris pale gold

steps: Combine maida, rava, salt, coarsely crushed peppercorns and ajwain in a bowl and mix well.
Rub in the warm Anveshan Ghee thoroughly for 2-3 minutes until the flour holds a firm shape when pressed in your fist, the test for enough moyan.
Add cold water a little at a time and knead a very stiff, tight dough, stiffer than for chapati; cover and rest 20 minutes.
Divide and roll into slightly thick sheets, prick all over with a fork to stop them puffing, and cut into rounds or diamonds.
Heat the Anveshan Sunflower Oil to a low 140-150°C and slide in a batch; fry gently for 6-7 minutes, turning, until crisp and very pale gold, never brown.
Drain on a rack, cool completely so they turn glassy-crisp, and store airtight for up to a month.
tips: The dough must be genuinely stiff; a soft dough gives puris that bubble up and soften instead of staying flat and flaky.
Low and slow is the rule, high heat colours them too fast and leaves a doughy centre that goes chewy on cooling.
Prick every puri well, unpricked ones balloon like phulka and lose the signature crackly texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as part of a Diwali farsan box with chevdo and mathiya, or crumble over undhiyu; keeps beautifully for weeks in a tin.

variations.name: Methi Kasuri Farsi Puri
variations.description: A herb-forward farsi puri laced with crushed kasuri methi and green chili for a savoury, slightly bitter fragrance that lifts the plain classic. The dried fenugreek perfumes each flaky layer and pairs beautifully with an evening cup of tea.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: warmed and worked in as moyan; its nutty depth complements the methi

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: clean, neutral oil for a slow deep fry so the herb flavour stays forward

steps: Crush the kasuri methi between your palms into the maida, then add cumin seeds, turmeric and salt and mix.
Rub the warm Anveshan Sesame Oil into the flour for 2-3 minutes until a squeezed fistful holds together firmly.
Work in the green chili paste, then add cold water gradually and knead a tight, stiff dough; cover and rest 20 minutes.
Roll into slightly thick sheets, prick densely with a fork, and cut into rounds so they fry flat.
Fry in the Anveshan Groundnut Oil at a low 145°C for 6-7 minutes, turning, until crisp and light gold with green flecks of methi showing.
Cool fully on a rack before storing airtight; the methi aroma deepens after a day in the tin.
tips: Toast the kasuri methi for 10 seconds in a dry pan first to wake up its aroma before crushing it in.
Keep the green chili paste smooth and small in quantity so it flavours without wetting the stiff dough.
If the flecks brown too dark, your oil crept above 160°C, pull the heat back for the next batch.
variations.servingSuggestion: These herby puris shine with a bowl of thick sweet shrikhand or a dollop of tangy tomato chutney at tea time.

variations.name: Khapli Wholewheat Farsi Puri
variations.description: A nuttier, more wholesome take that swaps refined maida for ancient-grain Khapli wheat atta, giving a golden, earthy puri with real bite. It carries more fibre and a deeper flavour while keeping the trademark flaky crunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: stone-ground ancient wheat gives a nutty, high-fibre puri that still crisps up well

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: extra moyan here since wholewheat needs more fat to turn flaky rather than hard

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for a slow, even deep fry that brings the atta to a warm gold

steps: Mix the Anveshan Khapli Atta with salt, crushed pepper, ajwain and sesame seeds in a bowl.
Rub in the warm Anveshan Ghee for 3 minutes until the flour clumps firmly when pressed; wholewheat drinks more fat, so be generous.
Add warm water gradually and knead a stiff yet workable dough, then cover and rest 20 minutes so the bran softens.
Roll into medium-thick sheets, prick thoroughly with a fork, and cut into rounds or squares.
Fry in the Anveshan Groundnut Oil at a low 145-150°C for 7-8 minutes, turning, until crisp and golden-brown right through.
Drain on a rack and cool completely; store airtight, where they stay crunchy for up to three weeks.
tips: Rest the dough a little longer than a maida version so the wheat bran hydrates and the puris don't crack at the edges.
Roll these a touch thinner than the classic since wholewheat fries denser and can feel heavy if left thick.
Use warm water, not cold, for khapli dough; it makes the stiff dough far easier to roll without splitting.
variations.servingSuggestion: A wholesome tea-time cracker, serve topped with a smear of white butter and a sprinkle of chaat masala.

variations.name: Multigrain Teekhi Masala Farsi Puri
variations.description: A bold, spicy multigrain farsi puri where a red-chili and coriander masala is kneaded right into a wholesome multigrain dough. Crunchy, warming and deeply savoury, it eats more like a spiced cracker than a plain puri.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Multigrain Atta
ingredients.note: a blend of grains and pulses for a hearty, fibre-rich spiced cracker base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: warmed as moyan; its subtle sweetness offsets the chili heat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: light oil for a slow deep fry that keeps the spices from scorching

steps: Mix the Anveshan Multigrain Atta with red chili powder, coriander powder, cumin seeds, turmeric, hing and salt until the spices are evenly distributed.
Rub in the warm Anveshan Coconut Oil for 3 minutes until the seasoned flour holds together in a pressed lump.
Add warm water little by little and knead a firm, stiff dough, then cover and rest 20 minutes.
Roll into medium-thick sheets, prick well with a fork, and cut into small squares or rounds for easy snacking.
Fry in the Anveshan Sunflower Oil at a low 145°C for 7 minutes, turning, until crisp and a deep spiced red-gold; keep the heat gentle so the chili doesn't blacken.
Cool completely on a rack, then store airtight; these spicy crackers stay crunchy for weeks.
tips: Add the chili and coriander to the dry flour, not the oil, so the spices distribute evenly and don't burn during frying.
Because multigrain dough is denser, roll thin and fry a minute or two longer than white-flour puris.
For a smoky twist, swap half the red chili for Kashmiri chili plus a pinch of degi mirch for colour without extra heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these spicy multigrain crackers with a bowl of thick hung-curd dip or alongside soup as a wholesome crouton substitute.

variations.name: Classic Menthya Gojju
variations.description: Gojju is the Karnataka sweet-sour-spicy gravy built on tamarind and jaggery, and this classic fenugreek (menthya) version balances the bitterness of roasted methi with a roasted coconut-sesame masala. Thick, glossy and intensely flavoured, it keeps for days and is spooned in small amounts alongside rice and ghee.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the sweet half of the sweet-sour balance that defines a true gojju

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed til oil that tempers the gojju and echoes the roasted sesame masala

steps: Soak 2 tbsp tamarind in 1.5 cups warm water for 10 minutes and extract a thick pulp.
Dry-roast 1 tsp fenugreek seeds, 5 Byadgi chillies, 1 tbsp coriander seeds, 2 tbsp sesame and 3 tbsp copra separately on low heat until each is fragrant, taking care the methi only just darkens.
Grind the roasted ingredients to a smooth paste with a little water.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadai, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 2 sprigs curry leaves and let them splutter for 15 seconds.
Pour in the tamarind extract with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt and simmer for 5 minutes to cook off the raw sourness.
Stir in the ground masala and 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and simmer on low for 10 minutes, stirring often, until thick and glossy and the oil floats on top.
Cool completely so the gojju thickens further before serving.
tips: Roast the fenugreek only until it just darkens, as over-roasting makes the gojju bitter.
The gojju thickens a lot as it cools, so pull it off the heat while still slightly loose.
Stored in a clean jar it keeps for a week and the flavour deepens over the first two days.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve a small spoonful with hot rice and a drizzle of ghee, or as a tangy relish beside curd rice.

variations.name: Pineapple Gojju
variations.description: A vibrant Udupi-style gojju where juicy pineapple chunks simmer in the tamarind-jaggery base, their natural sweetness playing against the tang and heat. Fresh ground coconut rounds it into a luscious fruit curry that is a highlight of festive banana-leaf meals.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: deepens the pineapple's sweetness and balances the tamarind tang

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: coastal fat for the tempering that suits the fruity Udupi profile

steps: Chop 2 cups pineapple into small chunks and simmer with 1 cup water, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 8 minutes until soft.
Dry-roast 4 Byadgi chillies, 1 tbsp coriander seeds and 1 tbsp sesame for 2 minutes, then grind with 0.5 cup coconut to a smooth paste.
Extract a thin pulp from 1 tbsp tamarind soaked in half a cup of warm water.
Stir the ground paste and tamarind pulp into the softened pineapple and simmer for 6 minutes.
Add 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook another 4 minutes until the gravy is thick and coats the fruit.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 2 sprigs curry leaves and splutter for 15 seconds.
Pour the tempering over the gojju, stir once and serve warm.
tips: Use a ripe but firm pineapple so the chunks hold their shape in the gravy.
Taste and adjust jaggery to the tartness of your pineapple for the right sweet-sour balance.
A little extra ground coconut makes the gravy richer for a festive spread.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a sweet-sour highlight on a South Indian thali, alongside rice, rasam and a dry palya.

variations.name: Bendekayi Gojju (Okra)
variations.description: A savoury vegetable gojju where fried okra rounds are simmered in the tangy tamarind-jaggery gravy until they drink up the flavours. Less sweet than the fruit versions and thicker in body, it is a everyday Karnataka side that eats almost like a semi-dry curry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: just enough sweetness to round the tang without making the vegetable gojju dessert-like

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil to shallow-fry the okra crisp before it simmers in the gravy

steps: Wipe 250 g okra dry, slice into 2 cm rounds and shallow-fry in 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat for 8 minutes until crisp and non-sticky, then set aside.
Dry-roast 4 Byadgi chillies, 1 tbsp coriander seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin and 3 tbsp copra for 2 minutes, then grind to a smooth paste with a little water.
Extract a thick pulp from 1.5 tbsp tamarind soaked in 1 cup warm water.
In the same pan, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 2 sprigs curry leaves to the residual oil and splutter for 15 seconds.
Pour in the tamarind pulp with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt and simmer 5 minutes, then stir in the ground masala and cook 5 minutes more.
Add the fried okra and 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and simmer gently for 6 minutes until the gravy thickens and clings to the okra.
Rest for a few minutes so the okra absorbs the gojju before serving.
tips: Fry the okra until fully crisp so it stays intact and does not turn slimy in the gravy.
Keep the jaggery restrained here since this is a savoury vegetable gojju, not a sweet one.
Add the okra towards the end so it holds a little texture in the finished dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or alongside jolada rotti and curd.

variations.name: Capsicum Menasinakayi Gojju
variations.description: A quick gojju featuring charred capsicum simmered in a peanut-thickened tamarind-jaggery gravy, giving a smoky-sweet edge and a creamy body. The roasted peanuts set it apart from the coconut-based versions, making it richer and slightly nutty.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: balances the tamarind and softens the smoky heat of the roasted capsicum

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil that ties into the peanut-thickened gravy

steps: Dry-roast 0.33 cup peanuts for 5 minutes, then roast 3 Byadgi chillies, 1 tbsp sesame and 1 tbsp coriander seeds for 2 minutes, and grind everything to a paste with a little water.
Cut 3 capsicums into chunks and char them in a dry pan or over an open flame for 5 minutes until blistered and smoky.
Extract a thick pulp from 1.5 tbsp tamarind soaked in 1 cup warm water.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 2 sprigs curry leaves and splutter for 15 seconds.
Add the tamarind pulp with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, simmer 5 minutes, then stir in the peanut masala and cook 4 minutes.
Add the charred capsicum and 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and simmer 6 minutes until the gravy thickens to a creamy coat.
Serve warm, letting it rest briefly so the smoky flavour settles in.
tips: Char the capsicum well for a smoky depth that lifts this gojju above a plain one.
Roasted peanuts thicken the gravy naturally, so add water gradually to control the body.
A slightly coarse peanut grind gives a pleasant texture to the finished gojju.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain rice and pappadam, or as a bold side to curd rice for contrast.

variations.name: Classic Mixed Vegetable Kara Kozhambu
variations.description: Kara Kozhambu is a fiery, tangy Tamil tamarind gravy thickened with a freshly ground roasted coconut-and-spice masala. This classic version simmers soft brinjal, drumstick and pumpkin in the spicy tamarind base until they soak up the bold flavours, making a robust gravy that stands up to plain rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed til oil that is essential to a good kara kozhambu and mellows the tamarind

steps: Soak 2 tbsp tamarind in 2 cups warm water for 10 minutes and extract a thick pulp.
Dry-roast 1.5 tbsp coriander seeds, 5 red chillies and 1 tbsp chana dal until golden, then grind with 0.33 cup coconut to a smooth paste.
Chop 1 brinjal, cut 1 drumstick into fingers and dice 150 g pumpkin into chunks.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadai, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 0.25 tsp fenugreek and let them splutter for 15 seconds, then add 2 sprigs curry leaves.
Add the vegetables and saute for 3 minutes, then pour in the tamarind extract with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tbsp sambar powder and 1 tsp salt and simmer 10 minutes until the vegetables soften.
Stir in the ground coconut masala and simmer another 8 minutes until the gravy thickens and the oil floats on top.
Rest for a few minutes so the flavours settle before serving.
tips: Roasting the coconut masala until deep golden gives the gravy its rich body and colour.
Simmer until the sesame oil surfaces, which signals the raw tamarind has cooked off.
The kozhambu thickens on standing, so keep it a little loose while cooking.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot steamed rice and a spoon of sesame oil, with a dry poriyal and appalam on the side.

variations.name: Vengaya (Shallot) Kara Kozhambu
variations.description: A homely favourite where whole small shallots are sauteed until sweet and simmered in the spicy tamarind gravy, their mellow sweetness balancing the heat. This onion-forward version is thinner and deeply savoury, a everyday Tamil kozhambu that tastes even better the next day.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed til oil to slow-fry the shallots sweet and balance the tang

steps: Peel 20 shallots and keep them whole, and soak 2 tbsp tamarind in 2 cups warm water to extract a thick pulp.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadai, add 1 tsp mustard seeds, 0.25 tsp fenugreek and 0.5 tsp cumin and let them splutter for 15 seconds.
Add the whole shallots, 6 garlic cloves and 2 sprigs curry leaves and saute on medium for 6 minutes until the shallots turn golden and sweet.
Add the chopped tomato and cook 3 minutes until it breaks down.
Pour in the tamarind extract with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tbsp sambar powder and 1 tsp salt and simmer 12 minutes until the shallots are soft and the gravy reduces.
Continue cooking until the oil separates and floats on top, about 3 more minutes.
Switch off and let it rest so the shallots soak up the gravy.
tips: Fry the shallots patiently until golden, as their caramel sweetness is the heart of this kozhambu.
Keep the shallots whole so they turn meltingly soft in the gravy.
This kozhambu deepens in flavour overnight, so it is worth making ahead.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best with plain rice and a dollop of ghee, paired with a simple potato roast and papad.

variations.name: Poondu (Garlic) Kara Kozhambu
variations.description: A pungent, medicinal-tasting kozhambu packed with whole garlic cloves that turn soft and sweet in the tamarind gravy, traditionally eaten to aid digestion. Thick and intensely spicy with roasted pepper and cumin, it is a Chettinad-style comfort gravy for cold or rainy days.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed til oil that fries the garlic and rounds the sharp tamarind heat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a small touch to soften the pungent garlic-and-tamarind gravy

steps: Peel 25 garlic cloves and keep them whole, and extract a thick pulp from 2 tbsp tamarind soaked in 2 cups warm water.
Dry-roast 1.5 tbsp coriander seeds, 1 tsp peppercorns, 1 tsp cumin and 5 red chillies until fragrant, then grind to a smooth powder with a little water.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 0.25 tsp fenugreek and splutter for 15 seconds, then add 2 sprigs curry leaves.
Add the whole garlic cloves and fry on medium for 4 minutes until lightly golden and aromatic.
Pour in the tamarind extract with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt and simmer 10 minutes until the garlic softens.
Stir in the ground spice paste and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and simmer 8 minutes until thick and the oil separates.
Rest before serving so the garlic mellows into the gravy.
tips: Fry the garlic gently so it turns sweet and does not burn or taste harsh.
A teaspoon of jaggery takes the edge off the strong garlic and tamarind.
This keeps for two to three days and the garlic flavour deepens beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rice and sesame oil, ideal as a warming, digestive gravy on rainy days.

variations.name: Sundakkai Vatha Kara Kozhambu
variations.description: A pantry-friendly no-vegetable version built on sun-dried turkey berries (sundakkai vathal) fried crisp and simmered in the tamarind gravy. It is thicker, tangier and long-keeping, the kind of everyday kozhambu made when fresh vegetables run low, with the vathal adding a pleasant bitter crunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed til oil to fry the vathal crisp and enrich the long-keeping gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: balances the strong tang of the concentrated tamarind gravy

steps: Extract a thick pulp from 2.5 tbsp tamarind soaked in 2 cups warm water.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadai, add 3 tbsp sundakkai vathal and fry for 1 minute until crisp and darkened, then remove and set aside.
