In the same oil, add 1 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp fenugreek and 1 tsp toor dal and splutter for 15 seconds, then add 2 sprigs curry leaves and 0.5 tsp hing.
Pour in the tamarind extract with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tbsp sambar powder and 1 tsp salt and simmer 12 minutes until it reduces and darkens.
Return the fried vathal and add 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, then simmer 5 minutes more.
Mix 1 tsp rice flour with a little water and stir it in, cooking 3 minutes until the gravy thickens and the oil separates.
Cool slightly before serving as it thickens further.
tips: Fry the vathal only briefly, as it burns and turns very bitter in seconds.
The rice flour slurry gives body without diluting the concentrated tamarind flavour.
This vathal kozhambu keeps for nearly a week and travels well for journeys.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice, sesame oil and a simple appalam or a dry potato poriyal.

variations.name: Classic Katachi Amti
variations.description: The thrifty genius of the Maharashtrian puran poli kitchen: the spiced, tangy-sweet broth spun from the leftover water in which chana dal was boiled for the puran. Goda masala, jaggery and tamarind turn that humble stock into a thin, aromatic amti that is sipped like soup or ladled over hot rice. It is light on the belly yet layered with dark roasted-spice depth.

ingredients.name: Chana dal cooking water (kat)
ingredients.note: The starchy liquid drained after boiling chana dal for puran poli

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Its clean molasses sweetness balances the goda masala without the burnt edge of dark gur

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The tadka fat that carries the goda masala and blooms the hing into the amti

ingredients.name: Goda masala
ingredients.note: The dark Maharashtrian blend of stone flower, sesame and dry coconut that defines this amti

steps: Dry-roast 3 tbsp grated dry coconut in a small pan over low heat for 3-4 minutes until it turns fragrant and pale gold, then set aside; this deepens the amti's nutty backbone.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a saucepan over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds until they pop, about 30 seconds, then add 1 tsp cumin, 1/4 tsp asafoetida, 2 broken dry red chillies and 10 curry leaves and let them sizzle for 15 seconds.
Lower the flame and stir in 2 tbsp goda masala, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder for just 10 seconds so the spices bloom in the ghee without scorching.
Pour in 3 cups chana dal kat along with 3 tbsp reserved cooked dal and the roasted coconut, add 1 tbsp tamarind pulp and 1.5 tsp salt, and bring to a gentle boil.
Add 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, then simmer uncovered on low heat for 8-10 minutes until the amti smells rounded and the raw tamarind edge softens; it should stay thin and pourable, not thick.
Taste and adjust the sweet-sour-salt balance, finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander, and switch off before it reduces too far.
tips: The kat naturally thickens as it sits, so loosen the amti with a splash of hot water before reheating and re-check the salt.
If you have no leftover puran poli water, simmer 1/4 cup chana dal in 4 cups water until very soft and use that liquid as the kat.
Keep the amti deliberately thin; a watery, sippable consistency is the whole point of katachi amti and distinguishes it from a regular dal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot in small bowls alongside warm puran poli and a spoon of ghee, letting diners sip the amti between rich, sweet bites of the poli.

variations.name: Kolhapuri Katachi Amti
variations.description: Kolhapur cannot resist heat, and its katachi amti swaps the gentle goda masala for fiery kanda-lasun masala loaded with garlic, onion and Lavangi chillies. The jaggery is dialled back to a whisper so the amti stays sharp, dark and blazing rather than sweet. This is the version that clears the sinuses and demands a mound of plain rice to tame it.

ingredients.name: Chana dal cooking water (kat)
ingredients.note: The strained boiling water from chana dal cooked for puran

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the traditional Kolhapuri tadka fat and stands up to the fierce spice load

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Just a whisper to round the burn, never enough to make this amti sweet

ingredients.name: Kanda-lasun masala
ingredients.note: The pungent Kolhapuri onion-garlic chilli blend that replaces goda masala here

steps: Crush 6 garlic cloves coarsely with a pinch of salt so their oils release, keeping them chunky rather than a smooth paste for that rustic Kolhapuri texture.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a saucepan over medium heat until it shimmers, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 1 tsp cumin, the crushed garlic, 1/4 tsp asafoetida and 10 curry leaves and fry until the garlic turns pale gold, about a minute.
Reduce the heat and stir in 2 tbsp kanda-lasun masala, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp red chilli powder for 10 seconds, standing back from the sharp fumes as they bloom.
Pour in 3 cups chana dal kat with 2 tbsp reserved dal, drop in 4 kokum petals for the sour note, add 1.5 tsp salt and bring to a rolling boil.
Simmer uncovered on low heat for 10-12 minutes so the garlic melts into the broth and the masala loses its raw edge, then stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder just to soften the heat.
Fish out the spent kokum if you prefer, scatter 2 tbsp coriander over the top, and serve while the amti is aggressively hot.
tips: Kanda-lasun masala already carries plenty of salt and chilli, so add the red chilli powder gradually and taste as you go.
Kokum keeps the amti a clean garnet colour where tamarind would muddy it; soak the petals in a little warm water first if they are very dry.
For an even smokier Kolhapuri edge, char the crushed garlic a shade darker before the liquid goes in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with plain steamed rice, a dollop of thick curd and fried papad, and keep a wedge of raw onion on the side in true Kolhapuri fashion.

variations.name: Konkani Coconut Katachi Amti
variations.description: Down the Konkan coast the amti turns silky and mellow, thickened with a fresh coconut and roasted spice paste rather than dry goda masala. Kokum lends a fruity sourness in place of tamarind, and coconut oil in the tempering perfumes the whole pot. The result is gentler, creamier and faintly sweet, a coastal cousin of the fiery ghat versions.

ingredients.name: Chana dal cooking water (kat)
ingredients.note: Strained water from boiled chana dal, the base of every katachi amti

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil ties the tempering to the coastal coconut paste with true Konkan fragrance

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A soft sweetness that the Konkan palate expects against the kokum sourness

steps: Warm a small pan and dry-roast 1 tbsp coriander seeds with 3 dry red chillies for 2 minutes until fragrant, then grind them with 1/2 cup fresh grated coconut and a splash of water into a smooth, thick paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil over medium heat, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1/2 tsp cumin, then add 1/4 tsp asafoetida and 12 curry leaves and let them crackle for 15 seconds.
Add the ground coconut-spice paste and 1/2 tsp turmeric and saute for 2-3 minutes until the raw coconut smell fades and the oil just begins to separate at the edges.
Pour in 3 cups chana dal kat with 3 tbsp reserved dal, drop in 5 kokum petals, season with 1.5 tsp salt and bring to a gentle boil while stirring to dissolve the paste.
Stir in 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and simmer on low heat for 8 minutes until the amti thickens slightly to a light, creamy pour and the flavours marry.
Finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and serve warm, taking care not to boil hard once the coconut is in so it stays smooth.
tips: Grind the coconut paste as fine as your mixer allows; any grittiness will settle at the bottom of the amti.
Add the coconut paste before the liquid so it toasts a little, which prevents the finished amti from tasting raw and chalky.
This version thickens more than the classic on standing, so thin it with warm water rather than reheating it hard, which can split the coconut.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle over soft steamed rice with a side of fried modak or serve as a warming bowl with coconut rice and a crisp sandge papad.

variations.name: Quick Everyday Katachi Amti
variations.description: A weekday shortcut for when there is no puran poli to yield leftover kat: you build the same broth directly from a small batch of freshly boiled chana dal and its cooking water. Lighter on spice and quicker to assemble, it keeps the signature sweet-tangy-savoury profile intact for an everyday bowl. Perfect over rice on a busy night with almost no planning.

ingredients.name: Chana dal
ingredients.note: Boiled fresh and its cooking water used as the kat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A modest ghee tadka gives this fuss-free version its comforting richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Dissolves quickly into the hot broth to lift the everyday amti

steps: Rinse 1/3 cup chana dal and pressure-cook it with 4 cups water for 4 whistles until very soft, then lightly mash a few spoonfuls into the water and keep the rest of the dal and its liquid together as your kat.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1/2 tsp cumin, then add 1/4 tsp asafoetida and 8 curry leaves and fry for 15 seconds until aromatic.
Lower the heat and stir in 1 tbsp goda masala, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 3/4 tsp red chilli powder for about 10 seconds so they bloom without burning.
Pour the cooked dal and its water straight into the pan, add 2 tsp tamarind pulp and 1.25 tsp salt, and bring to a boil, loosening with a little extra water if it looks too thick.
Add 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and simmer on low for 6-7 minutes until the amti tastes balanced and smells of roasted goda masala.
Garnish with 2 tbsp coriander and serve hot; it should stay light and brothy enough to sip.
tips: Reserve most of the dal solids for a separate dish if you want a truly thin amti, using mainly the starchy water here.
A pinch more tamarind or jaggery at the end lets you tune the balance to your taste without recooking.
This keeps well for a day in the fridge and actually deepens in flavour, so it is worth making a slightly larger batch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Spoon generously over hot rice with a teaspoon of ghee, or serve as a light soup with roasted papad on the side for a quick supper.

variations.name: Classic Palak Keerai Masiyal
variations.description: A soft, soupy Tamil mash of spinach cooked down and lightly pureed with green chilli and a little cooked moong dal for body, kept plain and clean so the greens shine. It is finished with a ghee tempering of mustard, urad dal, red chilli and asafoetida that gives the humble mash its comforting fragrance.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A ghee tempering with hing is the traditional finish that makes keerai masiyal aromatic

steps: Pressure-cook 0.25 cup moong dal with 0.75 cup water and 0.25 tsp turmeric for 3 whistles until soft, then mash and keep aside.
Boil 5 cups chopped spinach with 3 green chillies, 0.5 tsp cumin, 1 tsp salt and 0.5 cup water on medium for 6-7 minutes until fully wilted and soft.
Cool slightly and pulse the spinach to a coarse mash with a hand blender or by hand, keeping a little texture rather than a smooth puree.
Stir in the mashed moong dal and simmer on low for 4 minutes until the masiyal is thick, glossy and spoonable.
In a small pan heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal, fry until golden, then add 2 dried red chillies and 0.25 tsp asafoetida.
Pour the sizzling ghee tempering over the masiyal, stir once and rest covered for a minute so the aroma settles in.
tips: Keep the mash coarse rather than a fine puree - a little texture is what makes it a masiyal.
The moong dal is only for body, so use a light hand or the greens will be overwhelmed.
Add salt after the greens wilt, since spinach releases water and the volume shrinks a lot.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot rice with a spoon of ghee and a fried appalam, or alongside a spicy kuzhambu as a cooling counterpoint.

variations.name: Arai Keerai Masiyal with Garlic
variations.description: A rustic version using tender arai keerai (amaranth greens) mashed with cooked toor dal and finished with a bold garlic tempering in coconut oil. The double hit of garlic - crushed into the greens and crisped in the tempering - gives this masiyal an earthy, pungent depth beloved in village kitchens.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: A garlic-heavy coconut-oil tempering suits the earthy amaranth greens

steps: Pressure-cook 0.25 cup toor dal with 0.75 cup water and 0.25 tsp turmeric for 4 whistles until very soft, then mash smooth.
Boil 5 cups amaranth greens with 4 crushed garlic cloves, 2 green chillies, 0.5 tsp cumin, 1 tsp salt and 0.5 cup water on medium for 7 minutes until soft.
Cool a little and mash the greens coarsely by hand or with a wooden masher, leaving some texture intact.
Fold in the mashed toor dal and simmer on low for 4 minutes until the masiyal is thick and comes together.

In a small pan heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, let them pop, then add the remaining 4 garlic cloves sliced, 2 dried red chillies and 10 curry leaves and fry until the garlic is golden.
Pour the garlicky tempering over the masiyal, stir through and simmer for a final minute so the aroma infuses.
tips: Amaranth wilts down dramatically, so start with a generous heap of greens for a good yield.
Crush the garlic for the greens but slice it for the tempering so you get both mellow and sharp notes.
A wooden hand masher gives a better rustic texture here than a blender, which can over-smooth it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Wonderful over rice with a drizzle of coconut oil and a side of fried vathal, or scooped up with hot rotis.

variations.name: Murungai Keerai Masiyal
variations.description: A nourishing mash of iron-rich drumstick leaves (murungai keerai) cooked with moong dal and a touch of coconut ground in for smoothness. Milder and more mineral than spinach, these leaves make a wholesome masiyal that Tamil homes turn to as a gentle everyday tonic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A ghee tempering balances the slightly bitter, mineral drumstick leaves

steps: Pressure-cook 0.33 cup moong dal with 1 cup water and 0.25 tsp turmeric for 3 whistles until soft, then mash lightly.
Pick 4 cups drumstick leaves off their stems, rinse well, and boil with 2 green chillies, 0.5 tsp cumin, 1 tsp salt and 0.5 cup water on medium for 6 minutes until tender.
Grind 2 tbsp grated coconut with the remaining 0.25 tsp cumin into a coarse paste, then mash it into the cooked greens for a smooth body.
Add the mashed moong dal and simmer on low for 4-5 minutes until the masiyal thickens and the flavours meld.
In a small pan heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal, fry until golden, then add 2 dried red chillies and 0.25 tsp asafoetida.
Pour the ghee tempering over the masiyal, stir once and rest covered for a minute before serving.
tips: Strip only the leaves off the drumstick stalks, as the stems stay fibrous even after cooking.
The spoon of coconut ground in softens the mineral edge these leaves naturally carry.
Do not overcook the leaves or they darken and turn faintly bitter; a short boil keeps them sweet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Traditionally eaten with rice and ghee as a health-giving meal, with a spicy pickle or vathal for contrast.

variations.name: Molakootal Masiyal (Kerala-style)
variations.description: The Kerala cousin of the mash, where mixed greens are cooked down and blended with a coconut, cumin and red-chilli paste for a richer, coconut-forward body. Finished with the region's signature coconut-oil tempering of mustard and urad dal, it is thicker and more fragrant than the plain Tamil masiyal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: The coconut-oil tempering is the defining Kerala signature of this mash

steps: Pressure-cook 0.33 cup moong dal with 1 cup water and 0.25 tsp turmeric for 3 whistles until soft, then mash.
Boil 5 cups mixed greens with 1 tsp salt and 0.5 cup water on medium for 6 minutes until fully wilted, and drain any excess liquid.
Grind 0.33 cup grated coconut with 1 tsp cumin and 2 dried red chillies into a smooth paste with a little water.
Combine the wilted greens, mashed dal and coconut paste and simmer on low for 5 minutes until thick and creamy.

In a small pan heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil on medium; add 0.75 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal, fry until golden, then add the remaining 1 dried red chilli, 12 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida.
Tip the crackling tempering over the masiyal, stir once and simmer for a final minute before serving.
tips: Drain the boiled greens well before adding the coconut paste, or the mash will stay watery.
Grind the coconut smooth so this version turns velvety, distinguishing it from the coarse Tamil mash.
A blend of spinach and amaranth gives the best balance of colour, sweetness and body.
variations.servingSuggestion: A staple on the Kerala meal, spooned over rice with a spoon of coconut oil and a crisp pappadam on the side.

variations.name: Classic Jeera Khakhra
variations.description: The everyday Gujarati breakfast cracker: a thin wholewheat flatbread rolled paper-thin and dry-roasted on a tawa while pressed with a cloth until it turns crisp, blistered and shatter-light. Cumin and a hint of turmeric keep it fragrant and clean.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: nutty ancient-grain wheat that rolls thin and roasts to a clean, crisp khakhra

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: 1 tbsp kneaded in for softness and 1 tbsp to smear on the hot khakhras as they roast

steps: Mix the Anveshan Khapli Atta with cumin seeds, turmeric, red chili powder and salt, then rub in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee.
Add water a little at a time and knead a firm, smooth, non-sticky dough, then cover and rest 15 minutes so it rolls easily.
Divide into small lemon-sized balls and roll each out as thin as possible into a 15 cm circle, dusting with flour to prevent sticking.
Place a rolled circle on a medium-hot tawa, cook 20 seconds, flip, then press all over with a folded cloth or wooden press, rotating, so it crisps evenly without burning.
Smear a few drops of the remaining Anveshan Ghee on each side as it crisps, and cook 2-3 minutes total until pale golden, blistered and rigid.
Cool flat on a rack so they stay crisp, then stack and store airtight for up to two weeks.
tips: Roll as thin as you possibly can; thick khakhras stay chewy in the middle no matter how long you press them.
Keep the tawa on medium, not high, so the khakhra dries and crisps rather than scorching before it is cooked through.
Press with the cloth continuously and rotate; any spot you miss will stay soft and go soggy on cooling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve for breakfast with a mug of masala chai, topped with white butter or a little pickle, or crumble over curd.

variations.name: Methi Khakhra
variations.description: A fragrant fenugreek khakhra where fresh or dried methi is worked into the wholewheat dough, giving a gently bitter, herby crisp that Gujarati households love with morning tea. Sesame adds a nutty crunch to every blistered bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: 1 tbsp in the dough and 1 tbsp to brush while roasting; its nuttiness suits the methi

steps: Crush the kasuri methi into the wheat flour and besan, then add sesame seeds, turmeric, green chili paste and salt.
Rub in 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, then add water gradually and knead a firm, smooth dough; rest it 15 minutes.
Roll small balls into very thin 15 cm circles, dusting lightly with flour so they don't stick.
Roast on a medium-hot tawa, flipping after 20 seconds, then press firmly with a folded cloth all over while rotating so the herb-flecked circle crisps evenly.
Brush a few drops of the remaining Anveshan Sesame Oil on each side and continue pressing for 2-3 minutes until crisp, blistered and light gold.
Cool flat on a rack, then store airtight; the methi aroma deepens over a day.
tips: The spoon of besan gives methi khakhra a savoury depth and helps it crisp a touch faster.
If using fresh methi leaves instead of dried, chop finely and knead a stiffer dough, as they release water.
Press hardest around the edges, which tend to stay soft and chewy on a herb-loaded khakhra.
variations.servingSuggestion: A wholesome diabetic-friendly snack, serve these methi khakhras with a spoon of sweet chunda or plain thick curd.

variations.name: Masala Multigrain Khakhra
variations.description: A hearty, spice-loaded khakhra built on a multigrain flour blend for extra fibre and a robust, chatpata masala kneaded through. Nuttier and more filling than plain wheat, it eats like a wholesome crisp cracker on its own.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Multigrain Atta
ingredients.note: a grain-and-pulse blend that roasts into a hearty, high-fibre masala khakhra

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: 1 tbsp in the dough and 1 tbsp to smear on the roasting khakhras

steps: Mix the Anveshan Multigrain Atta with red chili powder, coriander powder, ajwain, cumin seeds, hing and salt.
Rub in 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, then add water gradually and knead a firm, non-sticky dough; rest 15 minutes.
Divide into balls and roll each very thin into a 15 cm circle, dusting with a little flour.
Roast on a medium tawa, flip after 20 seconds, then press with a folded cloth all over while turning so the spiced circle crisps without scorching.
Smear a few drops of the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil on each side and press for 2-3 minutes until crisp, blistered and deep gold.
Cool flat on a rack, then stack and store airtight for up to two weeks.
tips: Multigrain dough is a little less stretchy, so rest it well and roll patiently to get it thin enough to crisp.
Add the spices to the dry flour so they distribute evenly and don't burn on the tawa.
Roast on medium heat; multigrain khakhras scorch faster than plain wheat because of the added pulses.
variations.servingSuggestion: A filling, wholesome snack on its own, serve with a bowl of masala chaas or a garlic-tomato dip.

variations.name: Sattu Protein Khakhra
variations.description: A protein-boosted khakhra where roasted-gram sattu is blended into the wheat dough for a nutty, filling crisp that keeps you fuller for longer. Lightly spiced with ajwain and black pepper, it is a smart, wholesome snack for the health-conscious.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: roasted-gram flour that adds plant protein and a nutty depth to the khakhra

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: 1 tbsp in the dough for softness and 1 tbsp to smear while roasting

steps: Mix the wheat flour and Anveshan Sattu with ajwain, crushed black pepper, nigella seeds, turmeric and salt.
Rub in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then add water gradually and knead a firm, smooth dough; sattu drinks water, so add a little extra if it feels dry, and rest 15 minutes.
Roll small balls into thin 15 cm circles, dusting with flour to keep them from sticking.
Roast on a medium tawa, flip after 20 seconds, then press firmly with a folded cloth all over while rotating so the circle crisps evenly.
Smear a few drops of the remaining Anveshan Ghee on each side and press for 2-3 minutes until crisp, blistered and golden.
Cool flat on a rack, then store airtight; these keep crisp and wholesome for up to ten days.
tips: Sattu makes the dough thirstier than plain atta, so keep a little extra water handy while kneading.
Do not exceed one part sattu to three parts wheat, or the khakhra turns crumbly and hard to roll thin.
Roast on steady medium heat, as sattu can catch and taste bitter if the tawa runs too hot.
variations.servingSuggestion: A high-protein tea-time or pre-workout snack, serve with hung curd seasoned with roasted cumin and black salt.

variations.name: Classic Moong Dal Kosambari
variations.description: Kosambari is a fresh South Indian lentil salad made with soaked raw moong dal tossed with cucumber, coconut and a bright lemon dressing. Crowned with a quick mustard-and-curry-leaf tempering, it is a protein-rich, no-cook side served at festivals and everyday meals alike, prized for its crunch and cooling freshness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: for a light tempering that suits the raw coconut-and-lentil freshness

steps: Rinse 0.5 cup moong dal and soak it in plenty of water for 1 hour, then drain thoroughly until no water remains.
Finely chop 1 cucumber and 2 green chillies and add them to the drained dal with 0.25 cup grated coconut.
Squeeze in the juice of 1 lemon, add 0.5 tsp salt and 3 tbsp chopped coriander and toss gently to combine.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan, add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp urad dal and let them splutter for 15 seconds.
Add a sprig of curry leaves and 0.25 tsp hing to the tempering and switch off after 5 seconds.
Pour the tempering over the salad and fold it through just before serving.
Serve immediately while the dal is crisp and the cucumber fresh.
tips: Drain the soaked dal really well so the salad does not turn watery.
Add the lemon and salt only just before serving to keep everything crunchy.
One hour of soaking is enough; over-soaked dal turns soft and loses its bite.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled as a starter or as a cooling side on a festive banana-leaf meal.

variations.name: Channa Dal Carrot Kosambari
variations.description: This Rama Navami favourite uses soaked chana dal for a firmer, nuttier bite, brightened with plenty of grated carrot for colour and natural sweetness. It is heartier than the moong version and the carrot gives it a festive orange glow on the plate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: carries the tempering over the sweet carrot-and-lentil base

steps: Rinse 0.5 cup chana dal and soak it for 2 hours as it is firmer than moong, then drain it completely.
Grate 2 carrots and mix them with the drained chana dal, 0.25 cup coconut and 2 finely chopped green chillies.
Add the finely grated 0.5 inch ginger, the juice of 1 lemon, 0.5 tsp salt and 3 tbsp chopped coriander and toss well.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan, add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 1 dry red chilli and splutter for 15 seconds.
Add a sprig of curry leaves, let it crackle for 5 seconds and turn off the heat.
Pour the tempering over the salad and mix gently.
Rest for 5 minutes so the flavours meld, then serve.
tips: Chana dal needs a full 2 hours of soaking to become tender enough to eat raw.
Bite a soaked grain to check it is soft but still holds shape before using.
The grated ginger adds a warm note that balances the sweetness of the carrot.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a colourful festive side with panakam and neer mor during Rama Navami.

variations.name: Raw Mango Moong Kosambari
variations.description: A seasonal summer version where grated raw mango replaces lemon, lending a sharp, fruity tang and tiny bursts of sourness throughout. The mango keeps the moong dal salad lively and needs no citrus, making it a beloved warm-weather kosambari.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil for a nutty tempering that complements the sour mango

steps: Rinse 0.5 cup moong dal and soak for 1 hour, then drain completely.
Mix the drained dal with 0.5 cup grated raw mango, 0.33 cup coconut and 2 finely chopped green chillies.
Add 0.5 tsp salt and 3 tbsp chopped coriander and toss gently, tasting as the mango provides all the sourness.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, add 2 tbsp peanuts and fry for 2 minutes until they crackle and colour.
Add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp urad dal, splutter for 15 seconds, then add a sprig of curry leaves.
Pour the peanut tempering over the salad and fold it through.
Serve right away while the mango is crisp and tangy.
tips: Pick a firm, very sour raw mango for the best tang, and skip the lemon entirely.
Adjust salt after adding the mango, as sourness affects how salty it tastes.
The fried peanuts add a lovely crunch that pairs well with the sour mango.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a refreshing summer side with curd rice or a light lemon rice.

variations.name: Sprouted Moong Kosambari
variations.description: A wholesome, gut-friendly twist using sprouted whole green moong for extra nutrition and a satisfying crunch. Tomato and pomegranate add juicy freshness, turning the humble kosambari into an almost chaat-like protein bowl that works as a light meal on its own.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: light tempering fat that keeps the sprouted salad wholesome

steps: If the sprouts are very raw, steam 1.5 cups sprouted moong for 4 minutes to soften slightly, then cool.
Finely chop 1 tomato and mix it with the sprouts, 0.25 cup pomegranate seeds, 0.25 cup coconut and 2 chopped green chillies.
Add the juice of 1 lemon, 0.5 tsp salt, 0.5 tsp chaat masala and 3 tbsp coriander and toss gently.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and let them splutter for 15 seconds.
Add a sprig of curry leaves, crackle for 5 seconds and switch off.
Pour the tempering over the salad and fold it in.
Serve fresh as a light protein-packed bowl.
tips: A quick 4-minute steam makes raw sprouts easier to digest while keeping the crunch.
Add the tomato and pomegranate just before serving so the salad stays fresh, not soggy.
A pinch of chaat masala turns this into a satisfying chaat-style snack.
variations.servingSuggestion: Enjoy on its own as a light evening snack or as a nourishing side to a bowl of rasam rice.

variations.name: Classic Kotimbir Vadi
variations.description: The beloved Maharashtrian coriander fritter: a spiced besan and coriander batter steamed into a firm cake, cut into squares and shallow-fried till the edges crisp. Fragrant with fresh kothimbir and sesame, it is the tea-time snack every Marathi household makes.

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: tightly packed, finely chopped

ingredients.name: Besan
ingredients.note: sifted

ingredients.name: Rice flour
ingredients.note: for crispness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a little in the batter and the rest for shallow-frying the vadis crisp

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: crushed

steps: In a bowl mix 2 cups chopped coriander, 1 cup besan, 2 tbsp rice flour, 1.5 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, 5 crushed garlic cloves, 1 tbsp sesame seeds, 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander-cumin powder, 1/2 tsp sugar and 1 tsp salt.
Add 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and just enough water, about 1/3 cup, to bring it to a thick, spoonable batter, then stir in 1/4 tsp baking soda.
Grease a steel plate or thali, pour in the batter and spread it 2 cm thick, then steam in a covered steamer or pressure cooker without the weight for 15-18 minutes.
Test with a knife; it should come out clean and the cake should feel firm and spring back, then cool it completely for 15 minutes.
Cut the set cake into 1.5-inch squares or diamonds with a greased knife.
Heat the remaining 4 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan on medium heat and shallow-fry the vadis in batches for 2-3 minutes per side until golden and crisp at the edges.
Drain on a plate, sprinkle the remaining 1/2 tbsp sesame seeds over the top, and serve hot.
tips: Cool the steamed cake fully before cutting; warm cake crumbles and the vadis fall apart in the pan.
Keep the batter thick, like a soft dough-batter, so the vadis hold their shape and fry crisp rather than greasy.
Steam a day ahead and refrigerate the cake, then fry fresh just before serving for the crispest edges.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with green chutney or a garlic-red chilli chutney and a cup of adrak chai as an evening snack.

variations.name: Air-Fried Kotimbir Vadi
variations.description: A lighter take where the steamed coriander cubes are brushed with oil and air-fried until crackling and golden with almost no frying fat. It keeps all the herby, garlicky flavour of the classic while making it a guilt-free snack you can eat by the handful.

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Besan
ingredients.note: sifted

ingredients.name: Semolina
ingredients.note: fine rava, for extra crunch

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: just enough to bind the batter and brush the cubes before air-frying

steps: Mix 2 cups chopped coriander, 1 cup besan, 2 tbsp semolina, 1.5 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, 1 tbsp sesame seeds, 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1/2 tsp amchur and 1 tsp salt in a bowl.
Add 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and about 1/3 cup water to make a thick batter, then fold in 1/4 tsp baking soda.
Grease a plate, spread the batter 2 cm thick and steam for 15-18 minutes until a knife comes out clean, then cool completely.
Cut the firm cake into 1.5-inch cubes and brush all sides lightly with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil.
Preheat the air fryer to 190C, arrange the cubes in a single layer with space between them, and air-fry for 10-12 minutes.
Turn the cubes halfway and air-fry until deep golden and crisp on all sides.
Sprinkle the remaining 1/2 tbsp sesame seeds over the hot vadis and serve immediately.
tips: Adding semolina to the batter gives the air-fried cubes a crunch that makes up for the lack of deep-frying.
Do not crowd the air-fryer basket; the cubes need space around them to crisp evenly rather than steam.
A light second brush of oil at the halfway turn helps the surface colour to a proper golden crunch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a tangy green chutney or sweet-sour tamarind chutney, or toss the crisp cubes into a bhel for extra bite.

variations.name: Peanut-Sesame Kotimbir Vadi
variations.description: A richer, nuttier version studded with coarsely crushed roasted peanuts and a heavy hand of sesame, giving each fried square a crackly, textured bite. The peanut adds body and a subtle sweetness that plays against the fresh coriander.

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Besan
ingredients.note: sifted

ingredients.name: Roasted peanuts
ingredients.note: coarsely crushed

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for the batter and for shallow-frying the peanut-studded vadis

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a spoon of unrefined jaggery balances the nutty peanut and the coriander's slight bitterness

steps: Combine 2 cups chopped coriander, 3/4 cup besan, 1/3 cup crushed peanuts, 3 tbsp rice flour, 1.5 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, 2 tbsp sesame seeds, 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp jaggery powder and 1 tsp salt in a bowl.
Add 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and roughly 1/3 cup water to form a thick batter, then mix in 1/4 tsp baking soda.
Grease a plate, spread the batter 2 cm thick, and steam for 16-18 minutes until firm and a knife comes out clean; cool fully.
Cut the set cake into squares and press a few extra sesame seeds onto the cut faces.
Heat the remaining 4 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan on medium heat and shallow-fry the squares for 2-3 minutes a side until deeply golden and crackly.
The crushed peanuts should crisp at the edges and smell toasty as they fry.
Drain and serve hot with the remaining 1 tbsp sesame scattered over.
tips: Crush the peanuts coarse, not fine, so you get little pockets of crunch through the soft cake.
The extra rice flour keeps these firmer, which matters because the peanuts can otherwise make the cut squares crumbly.
Fry on steady medium heat; too hot and the sesame burns before the inside warms through.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a dry garlic-peanut chutney or plain green chutney, alongside hot chai on a rainy evening.

variations.name: Steamed Kotimbir Muthia
variations.description: A no-fry, tempered version where the coriander-besan dough is shaped into logs, steamed and sliced, then tossed in a mustard-sesame tadka rather than fried. Soft, light and fresh, it is the healthy face of kothimbir vadi that keeps well for lunchboxes.

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Besan
ingredients.note: sifted

ingredients.name: Whole wheat flour
ingredients.note: to bind the dough

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: used entirely in the light finishing tadka that flavours the steamed logs

ingredients.name: Grated fresh coconut
ingredients.note: for garnish

steps: Mix 2 cups chopped coriander, 1 cup besan, 3 tbsp wheat flour, 1.5 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt with a little water into a soft, non-sticky dough.
Grease your palms with a little oil and roll the dough into 2 thick logs about 1.5 inches across.
Steam the logs in a greased steamer for 15-18 minutes until firm and a skewer comes out clean, then cool for 10 minutes and slice into 1 cm rounds.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan on medium heat and splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1.5 tbsp sesame seeds for 40 seconds until they pop and turn golden.
Add 1/4 tsp asafoetida and 12 curry leaves, let them crackle for 15 seconds, then add the sliced muthia rounds.
Toss gently on medium heat for 3-4 minutes until the slices are coated in the tadka and lightly crisp at the cut faces.
Garnish with 2 tbsp grated coconut and serve warm.
tips: Keep the dough soft but not sticky; if it is too wet the logs will not slice cleanly after steaming.
Toss the slices gently in the tadka so they hold together, since there is no frying to firm them up.
These stay soft and travel well, making them an ideal no-fry tiffin snack that needs no chutney.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a light snack or a side, with a cup of chai or a bowl of plain yogurt on the side.

variations.name: Classic Sweet Kozhukattai (Modakam)
variations.description: The auspicious Tamil steamed dumpling offered to Lord Ganesha, with a delicate rice-flour shell hugging a warm coconut-jaggery centre called poornam. The pleated pouch is steamed until the outer skin turns glossy and translucent over the sweet, cardamom-scented filling. Soft, festive and gone in two bites.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Melted with coconut into the classic poornam that fills every festive modakam

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rubbed into the hot dough for a supple, non-cracking shell and glossy finish

steps: For the poornam, cook 1 cup grated coconut with 0.75 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder on medium-low heat for 6 to 7 minutes until sticky and able to hold a ball, then mix in 0.5 tsp cardamom and cool.
Boil 1.25 cups water with 0.25 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp of the ghee, lower the heat, and stir in 1 cup rice flour all at once until it gathers into a soft dough.
Cover 10 minutes, then knead the warm dough with the remaining Anveshan Ghee until smooth, crack-free and pliable.
Pinch off a lime-sized ball, press it into a small cup shape in your greased palm, spoon in 1 tsp poornam, and pleat the edges up to a sealed peak.
Arrange the shaped kozhukattai on a greased steamer plate, leaving space between them so they do not stick.
Steam on medium-high heat for 8 to 10 minutes until the shells turn shiny and translucent, then rest 2 minutes before lifting off.
tips: Keep the dough covered with a damp cloth while shaping, as it dries and cracks quickly in the air.
If the shell splits while pleating, the dough is too dry; wet your fingers and knead in a few drops of warm water.
Steam just until glossy; over-steaming makes the shells slump and turn gummy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Offer as naivedyam during Vinayaka Chaturthi, then serve warm with a small bowl of extra grated coconut.

variations.name: Ellu Kozhukattai (Sesame-Jaggery)
variations.description: A rustic Chettinad-style dumpling filled with toasted black sesame ground into jaggery for a smoky, nutty poornam. The dark, aromatic filling is prized for its warming quality and is a temple favourite in the sesame-growing south. Each bite crunches faintly before melting into sweetness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Ground with roasted sesame into a dark, praline-like filling unique to this dumpling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: A few drops greasing the palm and dough, echoing the sesame theme of the filling

steps: Dry-roast 0.75 cups black sesame seeds on low heat for 3 to 4 minutes until they crackle and smell nutty, then cool.
Grind the sesame with 0.5 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 2 tbsp grated copra and 0.5 tsp cardamom to a coarse, moist mix that clumps when pressed.
Boil 1.25 cups water with 0.25 tsp salt, stir in 1 cup rice flour off the heat to a soft dough, cover 10 minutes, then knead smooth with a little Anveshan Sesame Oil on your palms.
Press a ball of dough into a small cup in your greased palm, place 1 tsp of the sesame filling inside, and pleat closed into a peaked pouch.
Set the dumplings on a greased steamer plate with gaps between them.
Steam on medium-high heat for 8 to 10 minutes until the shells are glossy and translucent, then cool slightly before serving.
tips: Grind the sesame filling only coarsely, as over-grinding releases oil and turns it into a paste that is hard to fill.
Roast the sesame gently; scorched seeds make the filling bitter.
Press the filling firm before enclosing so the loose sesame does not spill during pleating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm alongside classic coconut modakam so guests can compare the light and dark fillings.

variations.name: Uppu Kozhukattai (Savoury Steamed)
variations.description: The salty, tempered cousin of the sweet modakam, where seasoned rice dough is rolled into small ovals or pinched pidi shapes and steamed with no filling. A mustard-and-urad tempering with green chilli and curry leaf runs right through the dough, making it a wholesome, savoury tiffin. Popular as an easy weekday breakfast across Tamil homes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Carries the mustard-urad tempering that seasons the savoury dough through and through

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tbsp urad dal until the dal turns golden, then add 2 chopped green chillies, 12 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida.
Pour in 2 cups water with 1 tsp salt and 0.5 cups grated coconut, bring to a boil, then lower the heat.
Stir in 1.5 cups rice flour all at once, mixing quickly until it forms a soft, lump-free dough, then cover and rest 10 minutes.
Knead the warm dough smooth with greased hands and roll small portions into oval dumplings or press with your fingers into ridged pidi shapes.
Arrange the shapes on a greased steamer plate with a little space between each.
Steam on medium-high heat for 8 to 10 minutes until firm and no longer sticky to the touch, then serve warm.
tips: Get the salt right in the boiling water, as you cannot adjust seasoning once the dough is formed.
Grease your palms while shaping so the sticky dough rolls into clean ovals.
Leftovers can be pan-tossed in a little coconut oil the next day for a crisp-edged snack.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with coconut chutney or a spoon of molaga podi mixed with sesame oil for dipping.

variations.name: Paruppu Kozhukattai (Chana Dal)
variations.description: A protein-rich savoury dumpling stuffed with coarsely steamed chana dal seasoned with green chilli, ginger and coconut. The nutty lentil filling makes this the heartiest of the kozhukattai family, often made for Karthigai Deepam alongside the sweet ones. A tempering of mustard and curry leaf perfumes the crumbly poornam.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Tempers the lentil filling with mustard and curry leaf for a fragrant savoury poornam

steps: Soak 0.75 cups chana dal for 30 minutes, drain, and steam or coarsely pulse it so the grains stay separate and just cooked, not mushy.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, then add 2 minced green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger, 10 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida.
Fold in the crushed chana dal, 0.5 cups grated coconut and 0.5 tsp salt, cook 2 minutes until dry and crumbly, and cool.
Boil 1.25 cups water with 0.25 tsp salt, stir in 1 cup rice flour off the heat to a soft dough, cover 10 minutes, and knead smooth with greased hands.
Shape a ball of dough into a cup, fill with 1 tsp of the lentil poornam, and pleat closed into a sealed dumpling.
Steam on medium-high heat for 8 to 10 minutes until the shells turn glossy and set, then serve warm.
tips: Do not overcook the chana dal; it should hold its shape so the filling stays dry and does not turn pasty.
Cool the filling fully before stuffing, or the steam trapped inside can crack the shells.
A squeeze of lemon into the filling brightens the earthy lentil flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a savoury festival tiffin with mor (spiced buttermilk) to cut the richness.

variations.name: Classic Kuzhi Paniyaram
variations.description: Golden, crisp-shelled savoury dumplings made from fermented idli-dosa batter cooked in a special dimpled paniyaram pan. The outside turns crunchy while the inside stays soft and fluffy, a brilliant way to use up leftover batter. A tempering of mustard, urad dal and onion stirred through gives each ball its savoury bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil crisps the paniyaram shells to a deep golden and adds aroma

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a small pan, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, fry 1 tsp urad dal and 1 tsp chana dal until golden, then add 10 curry leaves and 1/4 tsp asafoetida.
Add 1 chopped onion, 2 chopped green chillies and grated 1 inch ginger, sauteing 3 minutes until the onion softens.
Stir in 1 small grated carrot and cook 2 minutes, then cool the mixture completely.
Fold the cooled tempering, 2 tbsp chopped coriander and 1/2 tsp salt into 2 cups of thick fermented idli-dosa batter.
Heat the paniyaram pan and add a few drops of Anveshan Sesame Oil into each dimple, then pour batter to fill each about three-quarters full.
Cook covered on medium heat for 3-4 minutes until the underside is golden and crisp, then flip each ball with a skewer.
Cook the other side 2-3 minutes until evenly golden all over, and serve hot straight from the pan.
tips: Use batter that is thick and well-fermented; thin or fresh batter makes soggy paniyarams.
If the batter is a day old and slightly sour, add a pinch of baking soda for a fluffier result.
Wait for the shell to crisp before flipping, or the ball will tear and stick to the pan.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with coconut chutney and a spicy tomato chutney, or a bowl of sambar for dipping.

variations.name: Podi Kuzhi Paniyaram
variations.description: A punchy version where a spoon of spicy idli podi is stirred into the batter and the cooked balls are tossed in more podi with sesame oil, gunpowder-style. The result is fiery, nutty and deeply savoury, a favourite with those who find plain paniyaram too mild. Each crisp ball carries the unmistakable lentil-and-chilli depth of the podi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil both crisps the shells and binds the finishing podi coat

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, fry 1 tsp urad dal and 1 broken red chilli until golden, then add 10 curry leaves and 1/4 tsp asafoetida.
Add 1 finely chopped small onion and saute 2 minutes until soft, then cool completely.
Fold the cooled tempering, 2 tbsp idli podi and 1/4 tsp salt into 2 cups thick fermented batter and mix well.
Heat the paniyaram pan, add a few drops of Anveshan Sesame Oil to each dimple, and fill each three-quarters with the podi batter.
Cook covered on medium heat for 3-4 minutes until the base is crisp and golden, then flip each ball with a skewer.
Cook the second side 2-3 minutes until golden all over, then tip the hot paniyarams into a bowl.
Drizzle the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and 1 tbsp idli podi over the bowl and toss so every ball is coated in the fiery powder.
tips: Use a good homemade or store idli podi; its lentil-chilli balance defines this dish.
Toss the paniyarams in podi while piping hot so the powder clings to the oily shell.
Reduce the podi in the batter if serving to children, keeping the coating separate on the side.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot as a spicy snack with plain curd or a coconut chutney to cool the palate.

variations.name: Rava Kuzhi Paniyaram
variations.description: A quick, no-ferment version made with semolina and curd whisked into an instant batter, ready in minutes when you have no idli batter on hand. The rava gives the balls a pleasant crumbly-crisp texture. Loaded with onion, carrot and coriander, it is an easy after-school snack that comes together fast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed oil crisps the rava shells cleanly without heaviness

steps: Dry-roast 1.5 cups semolina on medium heat for 3 minutes until warm and fragrant but not browned, then cool.
Whisk the roasted rava with 1 cup thick curd, 3/4 tsp salt and about 1/3 cup water to a thick, dropping batter and rest 15 minutes to soften.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, add 10 curry leaves and 2 chopped green chillies, then 1 chopped onion and grated 1 inch ginger, sauteing 2 minutes until soft.
Fold the tempering, 1 small grated carrot and 2 tbsp chopped coriander into the rested batter, loosening with a splash of water if it has thickened.
Heat the paniyaram pan, add a few drops of Anveshan Groundnut Oil to each dimple, and fill each three-quarters with batter.
Cook covered on medium heat for 3-4 minutes until the base is golden and set, then flip each ball with a skewer.
Cook the second side 2-3 minutes until crisp and golden, and serve hot immediately.
tips: Rest the batter so the rava absorbs the curd and swells; a stiff batter gives dense balls.
Add a pinch of baking soda just before cooking for extra-fluffy instant paniyarams.
Roast the rava well so the paniyarams hold their shape and do not turn pasty.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with coconut chutney or a tangy tomato-onion chutney as a quick evening snack.

variations.name: Vegetable Kuzhi Paniyaram
variations.description: A wholesome version packed with finely chopped cabbage, carrot, capsicum and coriander folded into the fermented batter, turning a snack into a near-complete meal. The vegetables add colour, crunch and nutrition, making these a great way to feed greens to fussy eaters. Each crisp ball reveals a soft, veg-flecked centre.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil gives the veg-packed shells a crisp, golden crust

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, fry 1 tsp urad dal until golden, then add 10 curry leaves, 2 chopped green chillies and grated 1 inch ginger.
Add 1 chopped small onion and saute 2 minutes, then stir in 1/2 cup finely chopped cabbage, 1 grated carrot and 1/2 chopped capsicum and cook 3 minutes until just softened.
Cool the vegetable mixture completely so it does not thin the batter.
Fold the cooled vegetables, 3 tbsp chopped coriander and 1/2 tsp salt into 2 cups thick fermented batter.
Heat the paniyaram pan, add a few drops of Anveshan Sesame Oil to each dimple, and fill each three-quarters with the vegetable batter.
Cook covered on medium heat for 3-4 minutes until the base is crisp and golden, then flip each ball with a skewer.
Cook the other side 2-3 minutes until golden all over and serve hot.
tips: Chop the vegetables very fine so they cook through and the balls hold together.
Cook and cool the vegetables before adding, as raw grated veg releases water and slackens the batter.
Keep the batter thick; the vegetables add moisture, so avoid loosening it further.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with mint-coriander chutney and a bowl of piping sambar for a filling tiffin.

variations.name: Classic Ash Gourd Majjige Huli
variations.description: Majjige Huli is a soothing Karnataka yogurt curry where a ground coconut-cumin-green chilli paste is stirred into whisked buttermilk and gently warmed with soft ash gourd. It is mild, tangy and comforting, tempered with mustard and curry leaves, and is the everyday cooling counterpoint to a spicy South Indian meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the coastal fat for the tempering that lifts the mild coconut curry

steps: Peel and cube 300 g ash gourd, add half a cup of water and 0.5 tsp salt and simmer covered for 8 minutes until translucent and just tender.
Soak 1 tbsp rice in warm water for 10 minutes, then grind it with 0.5 cup coconut, 3 green chillies and 1 tsp cumin to a smooth paste.
Whisk 2 cups curd until lump-free, then stir in the ground coconut paste and 0.5 tsp salt.
Pour the buttermilk mixture over the cooked ash gourd and warm on the lowest heat, stirring constantly, for 3 minutes until it just begins to steam but never boils.
Turn off the heat the moment tiny bubbles appear at the edges so the curd does not split.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan, add 1 tsp mustard seeds, 2 dry red chillies, 2 sprigs curry leaves and 0.25 tsp hing and let them splutter for 15 seconds.
Pour the tempering over the majjige huli, stir once gently and serve warm.
tips: Use slightly sour curd for the best tang and never let the curry boil or it will curdle.
The tablespoon of ground rice thickens the curry and helps stop the buttermilk from separating.
Add salt only after mixing in the curd, as salting curd early makes it release water.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve ladled over hot steamed rice with a papad, or as a light cooling side to a spicy palya.

variations.name: Cucumber Majjige Huli
variations.description: A raw-vegetable version using crisp Mangalore cucumber (southekayi) that stays slightly crunchy in the cool buttermilk. Lighter and fresher than the ash gourd version, it needs almost no cooking and is a favourite in Udupi homes during the hot months.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: keeps the tempering true to the light coastal profile of this fresh curry

steps: Peel and finely chop 2 cucumbers, sprinkle 0.5 tsp salt over them and let them sit 5 minutes, then squeeze out excess water lightly.
Grind 0.5 cup coconut, 2 green chillies, 1 tsp cumin and 0.5 inch ginger to a smooth paste with a little water.
Whisk 2 cups curd smooth and stir in the ground paste and 0.5 tsp salt.
Fold the chopped cucumber into the seasoned buttermilk and warm it very gently for just 2 minutes on the lowest heat so it stays crunchy and does not curdle.
Switch off the heat as soon as it feels warm to the touch, well before any boil.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, add 1 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp urad dal and 2 sprigs curry leaves and let them splutter for 15 seconds.
Pour the sizzling tempering over the curry, stir gently and serve at room temperature.
tips: Squeeze the salted cucumber lightly so the curry does not turn watery on standing.
Keep the heating to a bare minimum so the cucumber retains its refreshing crunch.
This tastes best slightly chilled, making it ideal for summer lunches.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best spooned over cooked rice or sipped alongside a spicy vegetable rice like bisi bele bath.

variations.name: Bendekayi Majjige Huli (Okra)
variations.description: Here crisp fried okra rounds are the star, adding a savoury bite and a subtle body to the buttermilk curry. The okra is pan-fried first to remove its stickiness, then folded into the coconut buttermilk, giving a heartier majjige huli than the usual watery vegetables.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil to shallow-fry the okra crisp and non-slimy before it meets the curd

steps: Wipe 250 g okra dry and slice into 1 cm rounds, then shallow-fry them in 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat for 8 minutes until crisp and no longer sticky, and set aside.
Grind 0.5 cup coconut, 3 green chillies, 1 tsp cumin and 2 tbsp roasted gram to a smooth paste with a little water.
Whisk 2 cups curd until smooth and stir in the ground paste and 1 tsp salt.
Warm the seasoned buttermilk on the lowest heat for 3 minutes, stirring constantly, until it just steams, then switch off before it boils.
Fold in most of the fried okra, reserving a handful for garnish, and let it soak for a minute in the warm curry.
Heat the same pan with the residual oil, add 1 tsp mustard seeds, 2 dry red chillies, 2 sprigs curry leaves and 0.25 tsp hing and splutter for 15 seconds.
Pour the tempering over the curry, top with the reserved crisp okra and serve warm.
tips: Fry the okra until fully crisp so it stays firm and does not turn slimy in the curd.
Add the fried okra just before serving so it keeps some of its texture.
Roasted gram in the paste gives extra thickness that suits this heartier version.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a dry palya, or with soft rice mudde for a filling Karnataka meal.

variations.name: Mangalore Sonne Majjige Huli (Dumpling)
variations.description: A festive Mangalorean version where soft steamed lentil dumplings called sonne are simmered in the coconut buttermilk instead of vegetables. The little spiced dumplings soak up the tangy curry and turn pillowy, making this a special-occasion majjige huli quite unlike the everyday one.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: greases the steamer and flavours the tempering in true Mangalorean style

steps: Soak 0.5 cup toor dal for 2 hours, drain and coarsely grind with 2 green chillies, 0.5 tsp cumin, 0.5 inch ginger and 0.5 tsp salt without water.
Shape the dal mixture into small marble-sized dumplings, grease the steamer plate with a little Anveshan Coconut Oil and steam them for 12 minutes until firm.
Grind 0.66 cup coconut, 2 green chillies, 1 tsp cumin and 0.5 inch ginger to a smooth paste with a little water.
Whisk 2 cups curd smooth, stir in the coconut paste and 0.5 tsp salt, and warm gently for 3 minutes on the lowest heat without boiling.
Slide the steamed dumplings into the warm buttermilk curry and let them soak for 4 minutes off the heat so they plump up.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, add 1 tsp mustard seeds, 2 dry red chillies and 2 sprigs curry leaves and splutter for 15 seconds.
Pour the tempering over the curry, stir very gently to keep the dumplings whole and serve warm.
tips: Grind the soaked dal without water so the dumplings hold together while steaming.
Add the dumplings only after the curd is off the heat so the curry stays smooth.
Steam the dumplings a little ahead of time so they firm up before going into the curry.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a centrepiece with plain rice and a coconut chutney for a traditional coastal feast.

variations.name: Classic Masale Bhat
variations.description: The one-pot pride of Maharashtrian wedding feasts: fragrant rice cooked with tender ivy gourd, a lavish spoon of goda masala and a shower of fresh coconut. The tondli lends a gentle crunch while the dark masala perfumes every grain with clove, cinnamon and stone-flower. Traditionally cooked slow so the rice stays separate and glossy with ghee.

ingredients.name: Rice
ingredients.note: Ambemohar or any short-grain rice, soaked 20 minutes and drained

ingredients.name: Tondli (ivy gourd)
ingredients.note: Slit lengthwise into quarters so it cooks through

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The traditional fat for masale bhat that keeps the grains glossy and separate

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A customary pinch of sweetness that rounds the sharp goda masala

ingredients.name: Goda masala
ingredients.note: The soul of the dish; the roasted Maharashtrian blend that colours and scents the rice

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot over medium heat and fry 10 cashews until golden, then lift them out and set aside for the garnish.

In the same ghee crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp cumin, add 1/4 tsp asafoetida and 10 curry leaves, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and cook for 30 seconds until the raw smell lifts.
Add the slit tondli and saute over medium heat for 4-5 minutes until it loses its rawness and the cut edges turn glossy.
Stir in 2 tbsp goda masala, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder for 20 seconds, then fold in the drained rice and toast for 2 minutes so every grain is coated in the dark masala.
Pour in 3 cups hot water, add 1.5 tsp salt and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, stir once, cover and cook on low heat for 12-15 minutes until the water is absorbed and the rice is tender but separate.
Rest off the heat for 5 minutes, then fluff gently and fold in 1/3 cup fresh coconut, the fried cashews and 3 tbsp coriander before serving.
tips: Toasting the rice in the masala before adding water is what keeps the grains separate rather than sticky, so do not skip it.
If tondli is out of season, use tender brinjal or a mix of green peas and cauliflower cut small.
Warm goda masala loses its aroma fast once ground, so buy or make it in small batches for the freshest bhat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot topped with extra ghee and coconut, with a bowl of cooling plain curd or a mathachi kadhi alongside to offset the spice.

variations.name: Peshwai Wedding Masale Bhat
variations.description: The opulent banquet version served at Pune weddings, richer and studded with green peas, cauliflower and a generous scatter of fried cashews and raisins. Whole spices and saffron lift it into festive territory, and the rice is cooked looser and more perfumed than the everyday pot. A celebratory bhat meant to anchor a full Maharashtrian thali.

ingredients.name: Basmati rice
ingredients.note: Soaked 20 minutes for long, festive grains

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A lavish hand with ghee is expected in the wedding version for its festive richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Steeped in warm milk to give the celebratory bhat its golden bloom and aroma

steps: Soak 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside to bloom while you prepare the rest.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide pot over medium heat, fry 15 cashews and 2 tbsp raisins until the nuts are golden and the raisins plump, then scoop them out for garnishing.
Into the same ghee drop 1 inch cinnamon, 4 cloves, 3 cardamom pods and 1 bay leaf, let them fragrance the fat for 20 seconds, then add 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and stir for 30 seconds.

Add 1 cup cauliflower florets and saute for 3 minutes, then stir in 2 tbsp goda masala and 1/2 tsp turmeric for 15 seconds, followed by the drained rice and 1/2 cup peas, tossing gently for 2 minutes.
Pour in 3 cups hot water and 1.5 tsp salt, stir once, cover and cook on low heat for 13-15 minutes until the grains are just tender and stand apart.
Drizzle the saffron milk over the top, rest covered for 5 minutes, then fold through gently and finish with the fried cashews, raisins and 3 tbsp coriander.
tips: Fold the peas in with the rice rather than earlier so they stay bright green and do not turn drab.
For a true banquet look, reserve half the saffron milk to drizzle over the plated bhat just before it reaches the table.
Keep the whole spices intact and large so guests can push them aside easily as they eat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Present as the centrepiece of a thali with tomat saar, a sweet shrikhand and crisp kurdai papad for a full Peshwai spread.

variations.name: Vidarbha Spicy Masale Bhat
variations.description: From the fiery kitchens of eastern Maharashtra comes a darker, hotter masale bhat built on peppery Saoji-style spicing and a punch of dry coconut and poppy paste. The heat is upfront and the colour deep mahogany, with brinjal and drumstick giving it heft. This is the robust, no-frills bhat that stands up to Vidarbha's love of chilli.

ingredients.name: Rice
ingredients.note: Soaked 20 minutes and drained

ingredients.name: Brinjal
ingredients.note: Cubed and held in salted water to stop browning

ingredients.name: Drumstick
ingredients.note: Cut into 2-inch batons

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the everyday Vidarbha cooking fat and carries the fierce masala well

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of ghee softens the sharp heat and adds gloss

ingredients.name: Dry coconut
ingredients.note: Roasted dark for the signature nutty depth

steps: Dry-roast 1/4 cup dry coconut, 1 tbsp poppy seeds and 1 tsp black peppercorns in a pan over low heat for 3-4 minutes until deeply fragrant, then grind to a coarse paste with a little water.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a heavy pot over medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp cumin, add 1/4 tsp asafoetida, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste until it smells cooked, about a minute.
Add the cubed brinjal and drumstick batons and saute for 5 minutes until the brinjal edges soften, then stir in the ground coconut-poppy paste and cook for 2 minutes.
Add 1.5 tbsp goda masala, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, fry for 20 seconds, then tip in the drained rice and toast for 2 minutes until glossy and dark.
Pour in 3 cups hot water with 1.5 tsp salt, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on low heat for 13-15 minutes until the water is gone and the rice is tender.
Rest 5 minutes off the heat, drizzle 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the top, fluff gently and scatter 3 tbsp coriander before serving.
tips: Roast the coconut-poppy mix a shade darker than looks comfortable; that toasted depth is what defines the Vidarbha style.
Soaking the cut brinjal in salted water keeps it from turning black and mushy in the finished bhat.
Add the chilli powder to taste if serving children, since the peppercorn paste already brings a slow, building heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling boondi raita, thin buttermilk and a wedge of lemon to temper the deliberate heat of this eastern-Maharashtra bhat.

variations.name: Millet Masale Bhat
variations.description: A wholesome reinvention that swaps white rice for nutty foxtail millet, keeping every bit of the goda masala fragrance while adding fibre and a pleasant bite. The millet drinks up the spices beautifully and stays fluffy when cooked with the right water ratio. A lighter, everyday-nutritious take that still tastes unmistakably like masale bhat.

ingredients.name: Foxtail millet
ingredients.note: Rinsed well and soaked 20 minutes so it cooks evenly

ingredients.name: Mixed vegetables
ingredients.note: Carrot, beans and green peas diced small

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Keeps the nutty millet grains from clumping and adds gentle richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A little wood-pressed oil in the tempering keeps the dish light and heart-friendly

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pot over medium heat and roast 3 tbsp peanuts until they crackle and turn golden, then set them aside for the finish.
Add 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee to the pot, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp cumin, then add 1/4 tsp asafoetida, 10 curry leaves and 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and cook for 30 seconds.
Stir in the diced mixed vegetables and saute for 4 minutes until they brighten, then add 2 tbsp goda masala and 1/2 tsp turmeric and fry for 20 seconds.
Drain the soaked foxtail millet, add it to the pot and toast for 2 minutes so the grains coat with the masala and stay separate after cooking.
Pour in 3.5 cups hot water with 1.5 tsp salt, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on low heat for 15-16 minutes until the millet is fluffy and all the water is absorbed.
Rest 5 minutes, drizzle the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then fluff and fold in the roasted peanuts, 1/4 cup coconut and 3 tbsp coriander.
tips: Millet needs a touch more water than rice, so keep to the higher ratio and let it rest covered for a fluffier grain.
Toasting the millet after soaking, not before, keeps it from turning gummy while still preventing clumps.
This bhat is best eaten fresh; millet firms up on cooling, so sprinkle warm water and steam briefly to revive leftovers.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a bowl of thin spiced buttermilk and a green cucumber koshimbir for a light, gut-friendly Maharashtrian meal.

variations.name: Classic Punjabi Mathri
variations.description: The definitive North Indian tea-time cracker: a stiff maida dough shortened with plenty of ghee, spiked with ajwain and crushed black pepper, then rolled thick, pricked and fried slow to a pale, flaky disc. Crisp enough to keep for weeks in a tin.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: warmed and rubbed in as moyan; the higher the ghee, the flakier and shorter the mathri

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: light oil for a slow deep fry that keeps the mathri pale and even

steps: Mix the maida with salt, ajwain and coarsely crushed peppercorns in a wide bowl.
Rub in the warm Anveshan Ghee for 3 minutes until the flour clumps firmly when squeezed, confirming enough moyan for flakiness.
Add cold water little by little and knead a very stiff, tight dough; cover and rest 20 minutes.
Pinch off small balls, flatten into thick 6 cm discs, and prick each all over with a fork so they don't puff.
Heat the Anveshan Sunflower Oil to a low 140-150°C and fry the mathris in batches for 8-10 minutes, turning, until crisp and very pale gold.
Drain on a rack, cool fully so they harden and turn glassy, then store airtight for up to a month.
tips: A firm dough is essential; soft dough gives mathris that bubble and go soft instead of staying dense and flaky.
Fry on genuinely low heat, if they brown fast the middle stays raw and turns chewy once cool.
For extra shortness, chill the kneaded dough for 15 minutes before rolling; the ghee sets and flakes better.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sweet mango pickle and a hot cup of masala chai, or as a base for quick canapes topped with chutney.

variations.name: Methi Mathri
variations.description: A fragrant Rajasthani-style mathri kneaded with dried fenugreek and a little kasoori-methi warmth. The gentle bitterness of methi against the flaky, peppery cracker makes it the most-loved variety in Marwari pickle jars.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: 5 tbsp warmed as moyan and the rest for a slow deep fry

steps: Crush the kasuri methi into the maida and rava, then add crushed coriander seeds, red chili powder, turmeric and salt and mix.
Rub in 5 tbsp warm Anveshan Groundnut Oil for 3 minutes until the seasoned flour holds shape when pressed.
Add cold water gradually and knead a stiff, firm dough, then cover and rest 20 minutes.
Shape into thick discs, slightly smaller than the classic, and prick each well with a fork.
Fry in the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil at a low 145°C for 8-9 minutes, turning, until crisp and flecked golden with methi.
Cool completely on a rack before storing airtight; the methi aroma matures over a day or two.
tips: Adding a little rava to the maida gives methi mathri an extra-crunchy, sandy bite that holds up in pickle oil.
Do not skimp on resting; rested dough rolls smoother and the mathris fry more evenly.
Toast the kasuri methi briefly before crushing to intensify its aroma without adding any moisture.
variations.servingSuggestion: The classic partner to spicy Rajasthani ker-sangri or aam ka achar, served with masala chai on a winter afternoon.

variations.name: Suji Crispy Mathri
variations.description: A lighter, sandier mathri built largely on fine semolina, which fries up glass-crisp and stays crunchier longer than an all-maida disc. Sesame and cumin give it a toasty, nutty finish that eats almost like a savoury biscuit.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: nutty wood-pressed oil as moyan that pairs with the sesame seeds

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: for a clean, slow deep fry that keeps the semolina crackers pale

steps: Mix the fine semolina and maida with sesame seeds, cumin seeds, crushed pepper and salt.
Rub in the warm Anveshan Sesame Oil for 3 minutes until the mixture clumps firmly in your fist.
Add warm milk a little at a time and knead a stiff dough, then rest it a full 20 minutes so the semolina swells and softens.
Roll or press into thick discs and prick each thoroughly with a fork to keep them flat.
Fry in the Anveshan Sunflower Oil at a low 140°C for 9-10 minutes, turning, until crisp and pale gold; semolina needs a patient, gentle fry.
Cool completely on a rack so they crisp fully, then store airtight for up to three weeks.
tips: Resting is non-negotiable for suji mathri, unrested semolina stays gritty and the discs can crack while frying.
Kneading with warm milk gives a richer, more biscuit-like crumb than water; do not let it make the dough soft.
Fry a shade lower and longer than maida mathri, as semolina colours unevenly if rushed.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these crunchy semolina discs with a cup of adrak chai, or dust with a little powdered sugar for a sweet-savoury nibble.

variations.name: Wholewheat Khapli Masala Mathri
variations.description: A wholesome, deeply spiced mathri made with nutty Khapli wheat atta and a robust cumin-chili masala kneaded through. Higher in fibre and earthier in flavour, it is the everyday health-conscious cracker that still snaps crisp.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: ancient-grain wheat flour for a nutty, high-fibre masala mathri that still crisps well

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: generous moyan since wholewheat needs more fat to turn flaky rather than tough

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for a slow deep fry that brings the atta to a warm golden brown

steps: Mix the Anveshan Khapli Atta with cumin seeds, red chili powder, ajwain, coriander powder, hing and salt.
Rub in the warm Anveshan Ghee for 3 minutes until the spiced flour holds firmly when pressed in a fist.
Add warm water gradually and knead a stiff yet pliable dough, then cover and rest 20 minutes so the bran hydrates.
Shape into thick discs and prick each generously with a fork to keep them from ballooning.
Fry in the Anveshan Groundnut Oil at a low 145-150°C for 9-10 minutes, turning, until crisp and golden-brown right through.
Cool completely on a rack, then store airtight; these hearty crackers keep crunchy for two to three weeks.
tips: Roll wholewheat mathri a little thinner than maida versions so the denser dough cooks crisp all the way through.
Warm water makes stiff khapli dough much easier to shape without cracking at the edges.
If the discs feel hard rather than flaky, increase the ghee by a spoon next time, wholewheat needs more fat than maida.
variations.servingSuggestion: A hearty accompaniment to a bowl of dahi or a wholesome office-snack, serve with a spoon of garlic pickle on the side.

variations.name: Classic Matki Usal
variations.description: Sprouted moth beans simmered with onion, tomato and goda masala into a light, brothy everyday curry that is a Maharashtrian protein staple. Gently spiced and finished with coconut and coriander, it is wholesome comfort food eaten with bhakri or pav.

ingredients.name: Sprouted moth beans
ingredients.note: matki, sprouted 1-2 days

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil is the traditional fat for a Maharashtrian usal

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat and splutter 1/2 tsp mustard seeds and 1/2 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add 1/4 tsp asafoetida.
Add 2 chopped onions and fry for 5-6 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for a minute until the raw smell lifts.
Add 1 chopped tomato and cook for 3 minutes until soft, then lower the heat and add 1.5 tsp goda masala, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1/2 tsp turmeric, roasting for 30 seconds.
Tip in the 2 cups sprouted matki with 1.25 tsp salt and stir to coat every sprout in the masala.
Pour in 2 cups hot water, bring to a boil, then cover and simmer on low heat for 12-15 minutes until the sprouts are soft but not mushy and the broth is aromatic.
Stir in 3 tbsp grated coconut and simmer for another 2 minutes so it melds into the curry.
Finish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander and serve hot as a light, brothy usal.
tips: Sprout the matki just to short tails; over-long sprouts turn the usal bitter and take longer to cook soft.
Keep the usal on the brothy side, as the sprouts drink up liquid on standing and it thickens quickly.
A squeeze of lime at the table brightens the whole bowl and balances the earthy goda masala.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot pav or bhakri, or ladle over steamed rice with a wedge of lime and a sprinkle of raw onion.

variations.name: Kolhapuri Matki Usal
variations.description: The fiery Kolhapuri usal swimming in a thin, red rassa built on roasted coconut and lasun masala, the same base that crowns a plate of misal. It is spicier and thinner than the home version, made to be topped with farsan and eaten with pav.

ingredients.name: Sprouted moth beans
ingredients.note: matki

ingredients.name: Grated dry coconut
ingredients.note: khobra

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: carries the fierce Kolhapuri kat masala that defines this usal

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: 1 sliced and roasted, 1 chopped

ingredients.name: Red chilli powder
ingredients.note: fiery variety

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked and pulped

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Dry-roast 1 sliced onion and 1/2 cup dry coconut on a tava until deep golden brown, then grind to a coarse paste with a splash of water.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, crackle 1/2 tsp cumin seeds, add 1 chopped onion and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for 5 minutes until brown.
Add the roasted coconut paste with 2 tsp Kolhapuri masala, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1/2 tsp turmeric, and cook for 3-4 minutes until the oil floats red on top.
Add the 2 cups sprouted matki and 1.25 tsp salt, stir to coat, then pour in 3 cups hot water and the tamarind pulp.
Bring to a boil and simmer on low for 15 minutes until the sprouts are soft and the rassa turns thin and fiery red.
