Skim a little of the red oil that rises for garnish, and check the seasoning.
Ladle into bowls, drizzle the reserved red oil on top, and finish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander.
tips: Roast the dry coconut and onion until genuinely dark for the deep colour and smoky depth of a real Kolhapuri kat.
Keep the rassa thin and pourable; this usal is meant to be a spicy broth, not a thick curry.
It gets even better the next day as the sprouts soak up the masala, so make extra if you can.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve misal-style topped with farsan, chopped onion and lime, with soft pav to mop up the fiery red rassa.

variations.name: Sukhi Matki Usal
variations.description: A dry, stir-fried version with no gravy at all, where the sprouts are tossed in a light mustard-and-curry-leaf tempering with plenty of coconut and lime. Quick and clean-tasting, it works as a high-protein snack or a dry sabzi in a lunchbox.

ingredients.name: Sprouted moth beans
ingredients.note: matki

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: keeps the dry usal light and lets the tempering shine

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: crushed

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat and splutter 1/2 tsp mustard seeds and 1/2 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add 1/4 tsp asafoetida and 12 curry leaves.
Add 5 crushed garlic cloves and 3 chopped green chillies and fry for 40 seconds until fragrant.
Add the 2 cups sprouted matki, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, and toss well to coat.
Sprinkle in just 1/4 cup water, cover and steam on low heat for 8-10 minutes until the sprouts are tender but still hold their shape.
Uncover and stir-fry on medium heat for 2-3 minutes to drive off any moisture so the usal turns dry.
Switch off the heat, add 1/4 cup grated coconut and 1 tbsp lime juice, and toss through.
Finish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander and serve warm.
tips: Add only a small amount of water and let it steam, then dry it off; this keeps the sprouts firm and the usal from turning to mush.
Squeeze the lime in off the heat so its fresh sourness is not cooked away.
This dry usal packs well for tiffin and is great cold, tossed with a little extra coconut before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a light snack with hot chai, or as a dry side with dal-rice and a spoon of ghee.

variations.name: Goan-Style Coconut Matki Usal
variations.description: A creamy, coastal reimagining where the sprouts simmer in fresh coconut milk with a green paste of coriander, chilli and ginger, finished in fragrant coconut oil. Mild, aromatic and slightly sweet, it is a gentler counterpoint to the fiery Kolhapuri bowl.

ingredients.name: Sprouted moth beans
ingredients.note: matki

ingredients.name: Coconut milk
ingredients.note: thick, second-press

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil deepens the coastal coconut character of this usal

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: for the green paste, plus extra to garnish

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

steps: Grind 1/2 cup coriander leaves, 3 green chillies and 1 inch ginger with a splash of water into a bright green paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, crackle 1/2 tsp cumin seeds and 10 curry leaves for 20 seconds, then add 1 chopped onion and fry for 4-5 minutes until soft.
Add the green paste and 1/2 tsp turmeric and saute for 2 minutes until the raw smell disappears and the oil glistens.
Add the 2 cups sprouted matki and 1 tsp salt, stir to coat, then pour in 1.5 cups hot water and simmer covered on low for 12 minutes until the sprouts turn tender.
Lower the heat, pour in 1 cup coconut milk, and warm through gently for 3-4 minutes without letting it come to a hard boil so it does not split.
Switch off the heat and stir in 1 tsp lime juice.
Garnish with extra chopped coriander and serve warm and creamy.
tips: Add the coconut milk on low heat and never let it boil hard, or it will separate into grainy curds.
The green paste should stay vibrant, so cook it just until the raw edge is gone rather than browning it.
For a richer bowl, use thick first-press coconut milk and reduce the water accordingly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice or appams, or with a soft ghee-brushed chapati to soak up the creamy coconut gravy.

variations.name: Classic Milagu Kuzhambu
variations.description: A dark, peppery Tamil tamarind gravy built on a freshly ground paste of black peppercorns, toor dal and cumin, tempered richly in gingelly oil. Warming and medicinal, it is the dish Tamil homes turn to when someone has a cold or a heavy stomach. Thick enough to coat rice and keep for days, it needs only hot rice and a spoon of ghee to shine.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil gives milagu kuzhambu its authentic body and long fridge life

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A pinch softens the sharp tamarind and pepper without sweetening the gravy

steps: Soak the lemon-sized tamarind ball in 1.5 cups hot water for 15 minutes, then squeeze and strain to a thick, dark extract.

Dry-roast 2 tbsp black peppercorns, 1 tbsp toor dal, 1 tsp cumin, 1 tbsp coriander seeds and 2 red chillies on low heat until the dal is golden and fragrant, about 3 minutes, then cool and grind to a fine powder.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadhai, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 15 curry leaves and 1/2 tsp asafoetida and let them crackle for 20 seconds.
Pour in the tamarind extract with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt, and bring to a rolling boil for 4 minutes to cook off the raw sourness.
Stir in the ground pepper powder and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, mixing well so no lumps remain.
Simmer uncovered on medium-low heat for 10 minutes until the gravy thickens, darkens and the sesame oil floats to the surface.
Switch off and rest 10 minutes; the kuzhambu will thicken further and taste even better once the flavours settle.
tips: The dish keeps for four to five days refrigerated and deepens in flavour, so it is worth making a large batch.
If the pepper heat feels too strong, stir in an extra half teaspoon of jaggery rather than adding water.
Let the oil visibly separate before switching off; that is the sign the tamarind has fully cooked and the gravy will not taste raw.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot rice with a generous spoon of Anveshan Ghee, a papad and a simple potato roast on the side.

variations.name: Poondu Milagu Kuzhambu
variations.description: A robust garlic-forward version where whole peeled garlic cloves are fried until nutty and simmered into the peppery tamarind gravy. The garlic turns soft and sweet, mellowing the pepper and adding the earthy punch Chettinad kitchens love. It is prized as a tonic after childbirth and on cold, rainy days.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: A heavy hand of gingelly oil fries the garlic and enriches this tonic gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Balances the pepper heat and lets the sweet fried garlic come through

steps: Soak the lemon-sized tamarind ball in 1.5 cups hot water for 15 minutes and strain out a thick extract.
Dry-roast 1.5 tbsp peppercorns, 1 tbsp toor dal, 1 tsp cumin and 3 red chillies on low heat until aromatic, about 3 minutes, then cool and grind to a coarse powder.
Heat 5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, add 20 peeled garlic cloves whole and fry on medium heat until golden and blistered, about 4 minutes, then lift out half the cloves and reserve.
To the same oil add 1 tsp mustard seeds, 1/4 tsp fenugreek, 15 curry leaves and 1/2 tsp asafoetida, letting them splutter for 20 seconds.
Pour in the tamarind extract with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt, add the fried garlic back and boil hard for 5 minutes.
Stir in the ground pepper powder and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, then simmer on low for 10 minutes until thick and the oil separates.
Drop in the reserved garlic cloves, switch off, scatter over 2 tbsp chopped coriander leaves and rest 10 minutes so the garlic softens into the gravy.
tips: Fry the garlic gently so it turns sweet and golden rather than bitter and burnt.
The fenugreek is optional but adds a subtle bitterness that classic Chettinad cooks prize; skip it if you prefer.
This gravy tastes best the next day once the garlic has fully melted into it, so make it ahead.
variations.servingSuggestion: Spoon over hot rice with a drizzle of raw gingelly oil and a crunchy appalam, or mix into curd rice for a peppery kick.

variations.name: Milagu Jeeraga Kuzhambu
variations.description: A lighter, thinner take that doubles the cumin against the pepper for a more digestive, rasam-adjacent gravy without any dal or coriander. It is the classic sick-day kuzhambu, gentle on the stomach yet bracing with pepper and cumin. Poured thin over rice, it clears a blocked nose in minutes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil carries the pepper-cumin aroma and soothes the throat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Just enough to round the sour-hot edge of this medicinal gravy

steps: Soak the small tamarind ball in 2 cups hot water for 12 minutes and strain to a thin extract.
Coarsely crush 1 tbsp peppercorns, 2 tbsp cumin seeds and 6 garlic cloves together in a mortar to a rough, fragrant paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, add 1 broken red chilli, 12 curry leaves and 1/2 tsp asafoetida for 20 seconds.
Add the crushed pepper-cumin-garlic paste and saute for 1 minute on low until the raw garlic smell fades and it turns aromatic.
Pour in the tamarind extract with 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, and bring to a boil for 4 minutes.
Stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and simmer on low for 8 minutes until slightly thickened but still pourable.
Switch off while it is still thin and soupy, and rest 5 minutes before serving over rice.
tips: Keep this one thinner than a regular kuzhambu; it is meant to be spooned generously over plain rice.
Crushing rather than powdering the spices leaves little bursts of pepper and cumin that make it taste fresh.
A spoonful taken warm on its own works as a soothing peppery broth for a cold.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pour hot over rice mashed with a little ghee, alongside a crisp fried papad and steamed sweet potato.

variations.name: Vengaya Milagu Kuzhambu
variations.description: A sweeter, richer variation where sambar onions are fried whole until caramelised and simmered into the peppery tamarind base. The little shallots turn jammy and soft, balancing the pepper with a deep, sweet onion flavour. This is the festive, meal-worthy version served at Tamil weekend lunches.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Gingelly oil caramelises the shallots and thickens this rich onion gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Amplifies the natural sweetness of the fried sambar onions

steps: Soak the lemon-sized tamarind ball in 1.5 cups hot water for 15 minutes and strain to a thick extract.
Dry-roast 1.5 tbsp peppercorns, 1.5 tbsp coriander seeds, 1 tbsp toor dal, 3 red chillies and 2 tbsp grated coconut until golden, then cool and grind to a smooth paste with a little water.
Heat 5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and fry 20 peeled sambar onions whole on medium heat for 5 minutes until golden and blistered all over.
Push the onions aside, add 1 tsp mustard seeds, 15 curry leaves and 1/2 tsp asafoetida to the oil and let them splutter for 20 seconds.
Pour in the tamarind extract with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt, and boil with the onions for 5 minutes until the shallots turn tender.
Stir in the ground coconut-pepper paste and 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, then simmer on low for 12 minutes until thick and glossy with oil floating on top.
Scatter over 2 tbsp chopped coriander leaves, then rest 10 minutes so the shallots soak up the gravy and turn meltingly soft before serving.
tips: Keep the sambar onions whole so they stay juicy and turn jammy rather than dissolving into the gravy.
The ground coconut thickens this version, so stir often in the last few minutes to stop it catching at the base.
Peeling twenty small onions is tedious, so soak them in warm water for ten minutes first and the skins slip off easily.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rice and a spoon of ghee, a vegetable poriyal and thick curd to offset the richness.

variations.name: Classic South Indian Mixture
variations.description: The beloved namkeen medley of thin sev, fried gram, peanuts, cashews and crisp curry leaves tossed with chilli and asafoetida. Every South Indian Diwali tin holds a batch of this addictive savoury mix. Salty, spicy and endlessly crunchy, it is built from many little fried components.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Clean wood-pressed oil for frying every component of the mix crisp and light

steps: Make a sev dough by mixing 1.5 cups besan, 0.5 cups rice flour, 0.5 tsp chilli powder, a pinch of asafoetida and 0.5 tsp salt with about 0.5 cups water, then rest it.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C and press the dough through a fine sev disc into the oil, frying in batches for 2 minutes until pale gold, then drain.
In the same oil, fry 0.5 cups peanuts, 0.25 cups cashews and 0.5 cups roasted gram separately for a minute or two each until crisp, and fry 20 curry leaves for 15 seconds until they crackle.
Toss 0.5 cups thin poha into the hot oil for 10 seconds until it puffs, then lift out at once so it does not brown.
Crush the cooled sev lightly and combine it in a large bowl with all the fried nuts, gram, poha and curry leaves.
Sprinkle over the remaining 1 tsp chilli powder, 0.5 tsp asafoetida and 1 tsp salt, toss thoroughly while warm, and cool completely before storing.
tips: Fry each component separately, as they cook at different speeds and burning one spoils the whole batch.
Season the mix while it is still warm so the spices cling evenly to every piece.
Cool fully before storing in an airtight tin, or trapped steam turns the mixture soft.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in bowls through the Diwali week, or sprinkle over a plate of chopped onion and tomato for instant chaat.

variations.name: Kerala Coconut Mixture
variations.description: The Malabar take on mixture, fried in coconut oil and shot through with thin slivers of fried coconut and extra curry leaf. The coconut turns golden and chewy-crisp, giving the mix a distinctive sweet-savoury aroma. It is the tea-shop mixture of Kerala and coastal Karnataka.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: The signature Malabar frying fat that gives this mixture its unmistakable coconut aroma

steps: Mix 1.5 cups besan, 0.5 cups rice flour, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp chilli powder and 0.5 tsp salt with about 0.5 cups water into a sev dough and rest it.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Coconut Oil to 180C and press the dough through a sev disc, frying in batches for 2 minutes until crisp, then drain.
Fry 0.5 cups thin copra slivers for about a minute until golden, keeping a close watch as coconut browns fast, then lift out.
Fry 0.5 cups peanuts and 0.5 cups roasted gram until crisp, and crackle 30 curry leaves for 15 seconds each in the same oil.
Combine the sev, fried coconut, peanuts, gram and curry leaves in a large bowl.
Dust with the remaining 0.5 tsp chilli powder, 1 tsp pepper powder and 1 tsp salt, toss well while warm, and cool completely.
tips: Slice the copra thin and even so it fries to a crisp gold without any raw white centres.
Pull the coconut out the second it colours, as it turns from golden to burnt in moments.
The extra curry leaf is essential here; it defines the Kerala flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a coastal tea-shop snack with strong sulaimani or black tea.

variations.name: Spicy Madras Mixture
variations.description: A fiery Chennai-style mixture layered with crunchy boondi, extra chilli and a garlic-laced masala for serious heat. Boondi pearls add a distinct pop against the sev and nuts. This is the punchy version sold by weight at bustling Madras sweet shops.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Deep-fries both the sev and the boondi to a robust, spicy crunch

steps: Divide the besan: make a thick pourable boondi batter from 1 cup besan with water, and a firmer sev dough from the other 1 cup besan with 0.5 cups rice flour, 1 tsp chilli powder and 0.5 tsp salt.
Heat 3.5 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C, drop the boondi batter through a perforated ladle in batches, and fry the pearls for a minute until crisp, then drain.
Press the sev dough through a disc into the same oil and fry until pale gold, then fry 0.5 cups peanuts and 0.5 cups fried gram until crunchy.
Crackle 20 curry leaves and 6 sliced garlic cloves in the oil for 20 seconds until the garlic is golden and fragrant, then lift out.
Combine the boondi, sev, peanuts, gram, curry leaves and fried garlic in a big bowl.
Sprinkle over the remaining 1.5 tsp chilli powder, 1 tsp chaat masala, 0.5 tsp asafoetida and 1 tsp salt, toss well while warm, and cool fully.
tips: Keep the boondi batter smooth and lump-free so the pearls fry round rather than tailed.
Fry the garlic only until pale gold, as burnt garlic turns the whole mix bitter.
Add the chaat masala only after cooling slightly so its aroma is not lost to the heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a bold party namkeen with cold drinks, or bump up any bhel with a handful.

variations.name: Roasted Poha Mixture (Light)
variations.description: A lighter mixture built mostly on dry-roasted thin poha and roasted nuts rather than deep-fried sev, tempered with a little ghee and spices. It keeps the crunch and flavour of the classic with far less oil. A pantry-friendly, everyday version you can throw together in minutes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Toasts the poha and nuts and carries the tempering for a lightly roasted mix

steps: Dry-roast 3 cups thin poha in a wide pan on low heat for 4 to 5 minutes until crisp and crackly, then set aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, roast 0.75 cups peanuts and 0.25 cups cashews for 3 minutes until golden, then add 0.5 cups roasted gram for a minute.
Splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds in the same ghee, add 20 curry leaves and 0.5 tsp asafoetida, and let them crackle for 20 seconds.
Lower the heat, stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp chilli powder so they bloom without burning.
Tip the roasted poha back in with 1 tsp salt and toss everything on low heat for 2 minutes until evenly coated.
Cool completely so the poha crisps up, then store in an airtight tin.
tips: Roast the poha until it shatters when pressed, which is the key to a lasting crunch without frying.
Add the spice powders off high heat so they do not scorch in the ghee.
Toss in a spoon of raisins or dried coconut for a sweet-savoury lunchbox version.
variations.servingSuggestion: A guilt-light tea-time snack that travels well in lunchboxes and keeps for a week.

variations.name: Classic White Pumpkin More Kuzhambu
variations.description: The definitive Tamil buttermilk curry: sour curd whisked thin and thickened with a ground paste of coconut, soaked toor dal, cumin and green chilli, gently warmed with cubes of white pumpkin until it just coats the spoon. Held below a boil so the curd never splits, it is finished with a coconut-oil tempering of mustard, fenugreek and curry leaves.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: The coconut-oil tempering is the coastal heart of a proper more kuzhambu

steps: Soak 1.5 tbsp toor dal in water for 30 minutes, then grind with 0.33 cup grated coconut, 1 tsp cumin, 3 green chillies and 1 inch ginger into a smooth paste with a little water.
Boil 2 cups cubed white pumpkin with 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and water to half-cover on medium for 7-8 minutes until tender and translucent.
Whisk 2 cups sour curd smooth with 1 cup water so it is lump-free and pourable.
Add the ground paste to the cooked pumpkin and simmer on low for 5 minutes until the raw dal smell disappears and it thickens slightly.
Lower the heat to the minimum, pour in the whisked curd and warm gently for 2-3 minutes, stirring constantly and never boiling, so the curd stays smooth.

In a small pan heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.25 tsp fenugreek and 2 dried red chillies, let them splutter, add 10 curry leaves, and pour over the kuzhambu.
tips: Add the curd only on the lowest heat and never boil it, or the kuzhambu will curdle into grainy strands.
Slightly sour curd gives the best flavour; if yours is fresh, let it sit out a few hours first.
Grind the toor dal paste smooth so it thickens the curry without leaving a gritty texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle over hot rice with a dry poriyal and appalam, its cooling tang balancing a spicy side beautifully.

variations.name: Seppankizhangu More Kuzhambu
variations.description: A heartier version where colocasia (arbi) is boiled, peeled and shallow-fried until golden before it slips into the buttermilk gravy, lending a soft, almost creamy centre with crisped edges. The fried taro makes this more kuzhambu substantial enough to anchor a simple rice meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Used to shallow-fry the colocasia and to temper, unifying the dish in one fat

steps: Boil 300 g colocasia until just fork-tender, cool, peel and halve, then shallow-fry in 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil on medium for 6-7 minutes until golden and crisp-edged; set aside.
Soak 1.5 tbsp chana dal for 30 minutes and grind with 0.33 cup grated coconut, 1 tsp cumin, 1 tsp coriander seeds and 3 green chillies into a smooth paste.
Whisk 2 cups sour curd with 1 cup water until smooth and lump-free.
Simmer the ground paste with 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 0.75 cup water on medium for 5 minutes until the raw smell goes, then fold in the fried colocasia.
Reduce the heat to the minimum, pour in the whisked curd and warm for 2-3 minutes, stirring constantly and never boiling, so the gravy stays smooth.

In a small pan heat the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.25 tsp fenugreek and 2 dried red chillies, splutter, add 10 curry leaves, and pour over the kuzhambu.
tips: Boil the colocasia just until tender before peeling; overcooking makes it slippery and hard to fry crisp.
Fold the fried taro in late so it keeps its golden edges in the finished buttermilk gravy.
Keep the flame at its lowest once the curd goes in, stirring throughout to prevent splitting.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best over plain rice with a spoon of ghee; the crisp taro makes it filling enough to need only a papad alongside.

variations.name: Vendakkai More Kuzhambu
variations.description: Here okra is sauteed until its stickiness cooks off and its edges brown before it joins the buttermilk gravy, so the pods stay firm and soak up the tang without turning slimy. Ground with a little roasted gram, this version has a nuttier, more textured character than the melting-vegetable classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Frying the okra and tempering in coconut oil ties this kuzhambu together

steps: Wipe 250 g okra dry, trim and cut into 2 cm pieces, then saute in 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil on medium for 6-7 minutes until the stickiness cooks off and the edges brown; set aside.
Grind 0.33 cup grated coconut with 2 tbsp roasted gram, 1 tsp cumin and 3 green chillies into a smooth paste with a little water.
Whisk 2 cups sour curd with 1 cup water until smooth and lump-free.
Simmer the ground paste with 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 0.75 cup water on medium for 5 minutes until the raw smell goes, then fold in the fried okra.
Reduce the heat to the minimum, pour in the whisked curd and warm for 2-3 minutes, stirring constantly and never boiling, so the gravy stays smooth.

In a small pan heat the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.25 tsp fenugreek and 2 dried red chillies, splutter, add 10 curry leaves, and pour over the kuzhambu.
tips: Dry the okra fully and fry it before adding, so it stays firm and never turns slimy in the curd.
Roasted gram thickens the paste while adding a gentle nuttiness that suits the firm okra.
Add the fried okra late so it holds its shape and a hint of crispness in the finished gravy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over rice with a dry potato roast; the firm okra makes it satisfying with just a crisp appalam.

variations.name: Mangai More Kuzhambu
variations.description: A summer version from the Tamil kitchen where tart raw mango is simmered soft and its tang layers over the sour curd for a bright, mouth-puckering finish. A pinch of jaggery rounds the sharpness, making this the most vivid and refreshing of the more kuzhambu family.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil tempers the sharpness of raw mango with a mellow coastal note

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A whisper of jaggery softens the raw-mango tartness without making it sweet

steps: Boil 1 cup cubed raw mango with 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp salt and 0.5 cup water on medium for 6-7 minutes until the flesh turns pulpy and soft.
Grind 0.33 cup grated coconut with 1 tsp cumin and 3 green chillies into a smooth paste with a little water.
Stir the coconut paste and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder into the cooked mango and simmer on low for 4 minutes until the raw smell goes and the tartness mellows.
Whisk 1.5 cups sour curd with 0.5 cup water until smooth, lower the heat to the minimum, and stir it in for 2-3 minutes without ever boiling so it stays creamy.
In a small pan heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 0.25 tsp fenugreek and 2 dried red chillies, let them splutter.
Add 10 curry leaves to the tempering, let them crackle for 10 seconds, and pour the sizzling mix over the kuzhambu.
tips: Use a firm, very sour mango; a ripe or mildly tart one will make the curry flat.
Taste before adding curd and adjust the jaggery so the mango stays bright but not aggressive.
Because the mango already brings acidity, use slightly less curd than a regular more kuzhambu.
variations.servingSuggestion: A cooling summer favourite over rice, best with a dry beans poriyal and papad to offset its lively tang.

variations.name: Classic Rice-Urad Murukku
variations.description: The iconic spiral snack pressed from a rice and roasted urad dal dough through a star mould into hot oil. Crunchy, savoury and faintly nutty, it is a Diwali essential across Tamil homes. The tight coils fry to a golden lace that snaps cleanly with each bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rubbed warm into the flour as the shortening for a melt-in-mouth crunch

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Neutral wood-pressed oil for deep-frying that keeps the spirals crisp and light

steps: Sieve 2 cups rice flour with 0.5 cups urad dal flour, then mix in 1 tbsp sesame, 1 tsp cumin, 0.5 tsp asafoetida and 1 tsp salt.
Rub in 2 tbsp softened Anveshan Ghee until the mix resembles crumbs, then add about 0.75 cups water gradually to a smooth, soft, non-sticky dough.
Fill a murukku press fitted with a three-hole star disc and keep the dough covered so it does not dry out.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to about 180C until a bit of dough rises steadily to the surface.
Press the dough directly over the oil in tight concentric spirals, sealing the loose end against the coil.
Fry 2 to 3 murukku at a time for 3 to 4 minutes, turning once, until the bubbling stops and they are pale gold, then drain on paper.
tips: Keep the dough soft and pliable; a stiff dough breaks and clogs the press.
Wait until the loud sizzling quietens before lifting them out, which signals the moisture is gone and they are crisp.
Roast the urad flour lightly beforehand for the classic nutty flavour and even frying.
variations.servingSuggestion: Store in an airtight tin and serve through the Diwali week with hot coffee or as a lunchbox crunch.

variations.name: Thenkuzhal Butter Murukku
variations.description: The softer, whiter Thenkuzhal murukku built on rice flour and skinned urad, enriched with butter and a hint of roasted moong for a melt-in-mouth texture. Pressed through a single-hole disc, it fries into smooth ropes rather than sharp stars. Delicate and buttery, it dissolves almost instantly.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Deep-fries the delicate ropes to a pale, even crisp with a subtle aroma

steps: Mix 2 cups rice flour, 0.5 cups urad dal flour and 2 tbsp moong dal flour with 1 tsp cumin, 0.5 tsp asafoetida and 1 tsp salt.
Rub in 3 tbsp soft butter thoroughly until the flour feels moist and crumbly, which is what gives Thenkuzhal its melting texture.
Add about 0.75 cups water little by little to make a smooth, soft dough and fill a press fitted with a single-hole disc.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Coconut Oil to about 175C, a touch cooler than usual so the delicate ropes stay pale.
Press loose coils straight over the oil and fry 2 to 3 at a time for 3 minutes, turning once, until the sizzling calms.
Lift out while still very light in colour and drain on paper, as they should stay whitish, not golden.
tips: Use enough butter for the signature melt; too little and the murukku turns hard instead of tender.
Fry at a slightly lower temperature so they cook through without browning.
Sieve the flours together twice for the smooth, knot-free ropes typical of Thenkuzhal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these delicate white murukku to elders and children who prefer a softer, less spicy crunch.

variations.name: Garlic Kai Murukku
variations.description: A pungent, hand-twisted murukku laced with pounded garlic and red chilli for a fiery kick. Shaped by hand into looped coils rather than pressed, it carries a rustic, chunky bite. The garlic fries crisp and perfumes the whole batch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Warmed shortening that keeps the hand-shaped coils crisp and rich

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Deep-fries the garlicky loops to a deep, crackling gold

steps: Pound 10 garlic cloves to a paste and mix with 1.5 tsp chilli powder, then bloom 1 tsp ajwain by warming it briefly in a dry pan and crushing lightly.
Combine 2 cups rice flour, 0.5 cups roasted gram flour, 0.5 tsp asafoetida and 1 tsp salt with the garlic paste and crushed ajwain.
Rub in 2 tbsp warm Anveshan Ghee, then add about 0.75 cups water gradually to a firm but pliable dough.
Take small portions, roll into thin ropes on a greased surface, and loop each into a coiled murukku by hand.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C and fry the coils 3 to 4 at a time for 4 minutes, turning, until deep gold and the bubbling stops.
Drain on paper and cool fully so the garlic crunch sets firm.
tips: Bloom the ajwain first so it is fragrant rather than raw and sharp in the dough.
Roll the ropes evenly thin, as thick loops stay chewy in the middle.
Fry these a shade darker for the garlic to caramelise and mellow.
variations.servingSuggestion: Great with an evening drink or crumbled over curd rice for a spicy, garlicky crunch.

variations.name: Multigrain Ragi Murukku
variations.description: A nourishing murukku built on multigrain flour and ragi that trades some of the refined rice flour for wholegrains and fibre. The spirals fry a rustic brown with a heartier, nuttier crunch. A modern, wholesome spin for the health-conscious festive table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Multigrain Atta
ingredients.note: A blend of wholegrains that adds fibre and a nutty depth to the spirals

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Shortening that keeps the wholegrain dough from frying dense and hard

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Deep-fries the multigrain spirals to a crisp, even finish

steps: Mix 1 cup Anveshan Multigrain Atta, 0.75 cups rice flour, 0.5 cups ragi flour and 0.25 cups urad dal flour with 1 tbsp sesame, 1 tsp cumin, 0.5 tsp asafoetida and 1 tsp salt.
Rub in 2 tbsp softened Anveshan Ghee until crumbly, then add about 0.8 cups water gradually to a soft, smooth dough, using a touch more water than for plain rice murukku.
Fill a murukku press with a star disc and keep the dough covered while you work.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C until a scrap of dough rises promptly.
Press tight spirals over the oil and fry 2 to 3 at a time for 4 minutes, turning once, until the sizzling settles.
Because the dough is dark, judge doneness by the quietened bubbling and drain on paper.
tips: Wholegrain flours drink more water, so keep the dough soft or the spirals will crack in the press.
Go by sound not colour, as the multigrain and ragi mask browning.
Add a little extra ghee if the dough feels tight, which keeps the fried murukku from turning hard.
variations.servingSuggestion: A wholesome anytime snack that pairs well with chai and sits lighter than the classic.

variations.name: Classic Goan Mushroom Xacuti
variations.description: The definitive Goan xacuti, where button mushrooms simmer in a dark, complex masala of roasted coconut and a dozen whole spices ground with tamarind. Nutty, faintly sweet from the browned coconut and layered with clove, star anise and poppy seed, it is one of the most aromatic curries of the Konkan coast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil is the traditional Goan fat that carries the roasted-coconut xacuti masala

steps: Dry-roast the coriander, cumin, poppy seeds, peppercorns, cloves, cinnamon, star anise and dried red chillies on low until fragrant, then roast 0.75 cup grated coconut separately until golden-brown.
Grind the roasted spices and coconut with 1 tsp tamarind and a little water into a smooth, dark masala paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil on medium; add the sliced onions and saute for 6-7 minutes until deep golden.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 0.25 tsp turmeric and fry for a minute until the raw smell goes.
Stir in the ground xacuti masala and cook on medium for 5 minutes until the oil separates at the edges and the paste darkens.
Add 400 g halved mushrooms, 1 tsp salt and 1.5 cups hot water, then simmer on low for 12-14 minutes until the mushrooms are cooked and the gravy thickens to a glossy coat.
tips: Roast the coconut slowly to a deep brown - this browning is what gives xacuti its signature dark colour and nutty depth.
Mushrooms release water as they cook, so add the water in stages and adjust to the gravy you want.
Grind the masala truly smooth so the many spices meld into one seamless, rich base.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with Goan pao, sannas or steamed rice, letting the bread soak up the deeply spiced gravy.

variations.name: Mushroom & Green Peas Xacuti
variations.description: A homelier version that folds sweet green peas in with the mushrooms, their pops of sweetness playing against the dark, spicy masala. The peas also lend body, turning this into a fuller, more festive one-pot curry for a family meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil grounds the xacuti masala in authentic Goan flavour

steps: Dry-roast the coriander, fennel, poppy seeds, cloves, cinnamon and dried red chillies until fragrant, then roast 0.75 cup grated coconut separately to a deep golden brown.
Grind the roasted spices and coconut with 1 tsp tamarind and a little water into a smooth masala paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil on medium; saute the sliced onions for 6-7 minutes until deep golden, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 0.25 tsp turmeric and fry for a minute.
Stir in the ground masala and cook for 5 minutes until the oil separates and the paste darkens.
Add 1 cup green peas and 1.25 cups hot water, cover and simmer for 6 minutes until the peas are almost done.
Add 300 g halved mushrooms and 1 tsp salt and simmer uncovered for 8-10 minutes until both vegetables are cooked and the gravy is glossy.
tips: The fennel in this version brings a gentle sweetness that pairs naturally with the peas.
Add fresh peas earlier than mushrooms since they take longer; frozen peas can go in with the mushrooms.
If the gravy tightens too much, loosen with hot water rather than cold to keep the masala smooth.
variations.servingSuggestion: Lovely with jeera rice or soft chapatis, the sweet peas making it especially child-friendly.

variations.name: Creamy Coconut-Milk Mushroom Xacuti
variations.description: A silkier restaurant-style rendition where the roasted masala is loosened with thick coconut milk instead of water, giving a richer, mellower gravy that still carries the deep xacuti spicing. The coconut milk rounds the heat and lends a luxurious sheen ideal for a special dinner.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil deepens the roasted masala before the coconut milk goes in

steps: Dry-roast the coriander, cumin, peppercorns, cloves, cinnamon and dried red chillies until fragrant, then roast 0.5 cup grated coconut to golden brown.
Grind the roasted spices and coconut into a smooth paste with a little water, keeping it thick.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil on medium; saute the sliced onions for 6-7 minutes until golden, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 0.25 tsp turmeric and fry for a minute.
Add the ground masala and cook for 5 minutes until the oil separates and the paste darkens, then pour in 1 cup hot water.
Add 400 g halved mushrooms and 1 tsp salt and simmer on medium for 10 minutes until the mushrooms are cooked through.
Lower the heat, stir in 1 cup thick coconut milk and warm gently for 2-3 minutes without boiling so the milk does not split, then switch off.
tips: Add the coconut milk only at the end on low heat so it enriches the gravy without curdling.
Use slightly fewer chillies here since the coconut milk mellows and rounds the spice.
For a thicker finish, simmer the mushrooms a little longer before the coconut milk goes in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Rich enough for a celebration, served with appam, neer dosa or ghee rice to soak up the creamy gravy.

variations.name: Dry Mushroom Xacuti Sukka
variations.description: A drier, roast-forward version where the xacuti masala is cooked down until it clings to the mushrooms as a thick, almost caramelised coat rather than a gravy. Intensely spiced and nutty, this sukka style is served as a starter or a robust dry side rather than a curry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: A little extra coconut oil helps the dry masala caramelise onto the mushrooms

steps: Dry-roast the coriander, cumin, cloves, cinnamon and dried red chillies until fragrant, then roast 0.5 cup of the grated coconut to deep brown, reserving 0.25 cup fresh.
Grind the roasted spices, roasted coconut, 6 garlic cloves and 1 tsp tamarind into a thick, coarse masala with minimal water.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil on medium; add 10 curry leaves and the finely chopped onions and saute for 6-7 minutes until browned.
Add 0.25 tsp turmeric and the ground masala and cook for 5-6 minutes until it turns dark and the oil separates.

Add 400 g quartered mushrooms and 1 tsp salt, toss to coat, and cook uncovered on medium-high for 8-10 minutes, stirring, until the mushrooms release and then reabsorb their moisture and the masala clings dry.
Fold in the reserved 0.25 cup fresh coconut, toss for a final minute, and switch off.
tips: Cook uncovered on higher heat so the mushroom water evaporates and the masala coats rather than pools.
The final handful of fresh coconut lifts the dry, roasted masala with a fresh contrast.
Byadgi chillies keep this vividly red while letting you use six for depth without excess heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a dry starter with lime wedges, or as a bold side to dal-rice or neer dosa.

variations.name: Classic Namak Para
variations.description: The homely North Indian nibble of crisp fried diamonds: a stiff maida dough with ajwain and ghee, rolled, cut into little strips and fried low to a pale, shatter-crisp finish. Mildly salty and endlessly snackable, it is a staple of every festival tin.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: warmed and rubbed in as moyan for a short, crumbly bite

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: neutral light oil for a slow, even deep fry that keeps the strips pale

steps: Mix the maida with salt, ajwain and cumin seeds in a bowl.
Rub in the warm Anveshan Ghee for 2-3 minutes until the flour clumps together when pressed in your fist.
Add cold water gradually and knead a stiff, tight dough; cover and rest 15 minutes.
Roll the dough into a slightly thick sheet, then cut into 3 cm diamonds or thin strips with a knife or cutter.
Heat the Anveshan Sunflower Oil to a low 150°C and fry the strips in batches for 6-7 minutes, stirring, until crisp and pale gold.
Drain on a rack, cool completely so they turn crunchy, and store airtight for up to a month.
tips: Keep the dough firm; a soft dough absorbs oil and gives greasy, soft namak para instead of light crisp ones.
Fry low and stir often so every strip colours evenly without any browning.
Cut the strips a uniform thickness so they all crisp at the same rate in a single batch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a bowl with evening chai, or toss warm with a little chaat masala for an instant chatpata twist.

variations.name: Palak Namak Para
variations.description: A vivid green namak para where spinach puree is kneaded into the dough for colour, a mild earthiness and a sneaky dose of greens. The strips fry up crisp with pretty olive tones, making them a hit with children who dodge their vegetables.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: 4 tbsp as moyan and the rest for a slow deep fry that keeps the green bright

steps: Blanch a handful of spinach for a minute, refresh in cold water and blend to a smooth 0.5 cup puree.
Mix maida and rava with salt and cumin seeds, then rub in 4 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil until the flour holds shape when squeezed.
Add the green chili paste, ginger paste and spinach puree and knead a stiff dough, adding only a spoon of water if needed since the puree hydrates it.
Rest 15 minutes, then roll into a slightly thick sheet and cut into small diamonds or strips.
Fry in the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil at a low-medium 155°C for 6-7 minutes, stirring, until crisp and olive-green; frying a touch hotter drives off the puree's moisture.
Drain on a rack and cool completely before storing airtight; they stay crisp for two to three weeks.
tips: Squeeze the blanched spinach well before blending, an over-wet puree slackens the dough and the strips soak up oil.
Adding rava keeps these greens-loaded strips extra crunchy despite the moisture from the puree.
For a milder version for toddlers, drop the green chili and add a pinch of amchur for a gentle tang instead.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pack these green strips into lunchboxes or serve as a colourful party bowl with a mint-yogurt dip.

variations.name: Baked Multigrain Namak Para
variations.description: A wholesome, oven-baked namak para made with fibre-rich multigrain flour and just a brush of oil, so you get crisp savoury strips with none of the deep-frying. Seasoned with ajwain and sesame, they make a genuinely healthy tin snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Multigrain Atta
ingredients.note: a grain-and-pulse blend that bakes into hearty, high-fibre crisp strips

ingredients.name: Anveshan Olive Oil
ingredients.note: 3 tbsp as moyan in the dough and 2 tbsp to brush the strips before baking

steps: Mix the Anveshan Multigrain Atta with salt, ajwain, sesame seeds, crushed pepper and dried oregano.
Rub in 3 tbsp Anveshan Olive Oil for 2 minutes until the flour holds together when pressed.
Add warm water gradually and knead a firm but pliable dough, then rest it 15 minutes.
Roll into a thin sheet, brush with the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Olive Oil, and cut into small diamonds; spread on a lined baking tray in a single layer.
Bake in an oven preheated to 180°C for 22-25 minutes, tossing once halfway, until crisp and golden-brown.
Cool completely on the tray so they harden fully, then store airtight; they crisp further as they cool.
tips: Roll the dough genuinely thin, baked strips will not crisp in the centre if they are cut too thick.
Toss the strips once during baking so both sides colour evenly without any staying pale.
If any strips feel soft after cooling, return them to a 150°C oven for 5 minutes to drive off the last moisture.
variations.servingSuggestion: A smart low-oil munch for the tea tray or work desk, serve with a tangy tomato-garlic dip or hummus.

variations.name: Masala Chatpata Namak Para
variations.description: A punchy, chatpata version tossed in a red-chili and chaat-masala coating so every diamond delivers a tangy, spicy hit. Bolder and darker than the plain classic, these are the strips that vanish first from the party bowl.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: 4 tbsp as moyan and the rest for a slow deep fry; its subtle sweetness offsets the spice

steps: Mix maida and besan with salt, cumin seeds and 0.75 tsp of the red chili powder, keeping the rest aside for the coating.
Rub in 4 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil for 2-3 minutes until the flour holds shape when pressed.
Add cold water gradually and knead a stiff dough, rest 15 minutes, then roll and cut into small diamonds.
Fry the diamonds in the remaining Anveshan Coconut Oil at a low 150°C for 6-7 minutes, stirring, until crisp and light gold.
While still warm, toss the strips in a bowl with the reserved red chili powder, chaat masala, amchur and black salt so the spices cling.
Cool completely before storing airtight; the chatpata coating stays vivid for weeks.
tips: Toss the spice mix on while the strips are warm so it sticks, but pack only once fully cool to avoid steaming them soft.
The little besan in the dough gives a savoury depth and a slightly sturdier strip that carries the coating well.
Adjust the chaat masala and amchur to taste after the first toss; you want equal tang and heat, not just chili.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these chatpata diamonds as a bar snack with cold drinks, or scatter over bhel and sev puri for extra crunch.

variations.name: Classic Neyyappam
variations.description: Neyyappam takes its name from ney, ghee, in which these jaggery-sweetened rice fritters are shallow-fried until dark and lacy-edged. Softer and richer than their coconut-oil cousins, they are the beloved temple prasadam of Kerala, fragrant with cardamom and ghee.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted into a syrup that sweetens the batter and gives the fritters their dark colour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the namesake frying fat that gives neyyappam their soft richness and aroma

steps: Melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 0.5 cup water over low heat, strain out grit and cool the syrup to lukewarm.
Mash 1 ripe banana smooth, whisk it into the syrup, then stir in 1.5 cups rice flour to a thick, lump-free batter.
Fry 3 tbsp coconut bits in 1 tsp of the ghee until golden, then fold them in with 1 tbsp sesame seeds, 0.5 tsp cardamom, 0.25 tsp dry ginger and a pinch of baking soda; rest 30 minutes.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Ghee in an appakara or deep pan over medium heat until a drop of batter rises at once.
Drop rounded spoonfuls of batter into the ghee and fry for 3 to 4 minutes, turning, until deep reddish-brown with crisp, lacy edges.
Lift out with a slotted spoon, drain briefly and serve the neyyappam warm.
tips: Frying in ghee rather than oil is what gives neyyappam their signature softness and fragrance, so do not substitute.
Rest the batter 30 minutes so the rice flour hydrates fully and the centres cook soft.
Keep the ghee at steady medium heat; too hot chars the outside before the middle sets.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as temple prasadam or a festive teatime sweet, piled up while the edges are still crisp.

variations.name: Khapli Wheat Neyyappam
variations.description: A nuttier, wholegrain neyyappam made with ancient khapli wheat flour, giving fritters with a heartier bite and deeper flavour. Fennel and grated coconut lend a warm, aniseed fragrance that pairs beautifully with the ghee.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: ancient wheat flour that gives the fritters a nutty, wholesome body

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted into a syrup to sweeten and darken the wholegrain batter

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the namesake frying fat that crisps the wholegrain fritters and adds richness

steps: Melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 0.5 cup water over low heat, strain, and cool to lukewarm.
Mash 1 ripe banana and whisk it into the syrup, then stir in 1.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta to a thick, smooth batter.
Fold in 0.25 cup grated coconut, 1 tsp lightly crushed fennel seeds, 0.5 tsp cardamom and a pinch of baking soda; rest the batter 40 minutes.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Ghee in a deep pan over medium heat until a drop of batter rises at once.
Drop rounded spoonfuls into the ghee and fry for 4 to 5 minutes, turning, until deep brown and cooked through, as wheat batter needs a little longer.
Drain briefly and serve the khapli neyyappam warm.
tips: Wholegrain khapli batter absorbs more liquid, so rest it longer and loosen with a splash of water if it stiffens.
Crush the fennel lightly first so it perfumes the batter without leaving hard seeds in the fritters.
Fry a shade lower and longer than rice neyyappam so the denser wheat centres cook through fully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a wholesome festive snack, their nutty crust needing no garnish at all.

variations.name: Aripodi Coconut Neyyappam
variations.description: The old-school version made from freshly soaked and ground raw rice rather than flour, giving exceptionally soft, tender fritters with a fine crumb. Generous grated coconut and a whisper of cumin make these the neyyappam served at traditional Kerala temple feasts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted into a syrup that sweetens the ground-rice batter and deepens its colour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the namesake frying fat that gives these fritters their soft, rich crumb

steps: Soak 1.5 cups raw rice for 3 hours, then drain and grind with 0.5 cup water to a smooth, thick batter.
Melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water, strain, cool, and whisk it into the ground-rice batter.
Fry 3 tbsp coconut bits in 1 tsp of the ghee until golden, then fold them in with 0.5 cup grated coconut, 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp cumin; rest 1 hour.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Ghee in a deep pan over medium heat until a drop of batter rises at once.
Drop rounded spoonfuls into the ghee and fry for 3 to 4 minutes, turning, until deep brown and puffed with soft centres.
Drain briefly and serve the aripodi neyyappam warm.
tips: Grinding soaked raw rice gives a far softer, more tender fritter than packaged rice flour, so it is worth the extra step.
Keep the ground batter thick like idli batter; if too thin the fritters flatten and soak up ghee.
A one-hour rest lets the batter mellow and the jaggery meld through for the sweetest, most even flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as an authentic temple-style prasadam, best enjoyed fresh while the crumb is soft and moist.

variations.name: Chakka Neyyappam
variations.description: A monsoon-season neyyappam enriched with thick jackfruit preserve, giving a fudgy, honeyed sweetness and a rich amber colour. The jackfruit keeps the fritters especially moist while the ghee frying lends its unmistakable temple fragrance.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: rounds out the jackfruit preserve's sweetness and deepens the fritters' colour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the namesake frying fat that crisps the fritters and adds a fragrant richness

steps: Warm 0.75 cup jackfruit preserve with 1 tsp of the ghee over low heat until it loosens into a smooth paste, about 4 minutes.
Melt 0.5 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water, strain, and stir it into the loosened jackfruit with 0.25 cup water.
Whisk in 1 cup rice flour to a thick batter, then fold in 0.25 cup grated coconut, 0.5 tsp cardamom, 0.25 tsp dry ginger and a pinch of baking soda; rest 30 minutes.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Ghee in a deep pan over medium heat until a drop of batter rises at once.
Drop rounded spoonfuls into the ghee and fry for 3 to 4 minutes, turning, until deep amber-brown and puffed.
Drain briefly and serve the chakka neyyappam warm.
tips: Loosen the sticky jackfruit preserve in ghee first, or it never blends smoothly into the batter.
Taste for sweetness before adding all the jaggery, as jackfruit preserve is already quite sweet.
These fritters stay moist for a day thanks to the jackfruit, making them good for a make-ahead festive box.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm during the jackfruit season as a rich, fudgy festive treat with hot chai or filter coffee.

variations.name: Classic Nippattu
variations.description: Karnataka's crisp fried rice cracker, richer than its Tamil cousin thanks to crushed peanuts, roasted gram and dry coconut worked right into the dough. The nutty flecks fry up crunchy against the flat, golden disc. A Bangalore bakery and festival staple eaten with hot coffee.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Hot shortening rubbed into the flour for a short, crisp cracker that melts on the bite

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed oil for deep-frying the discs to an even, non-greasy crunch

steps: Coarsely crush 0.5 cups roasted peanuts and 0.25 cups roasted gram, and grate 3 tbsp dry coconut, keeping some texture.
Mix 2 cups rice flour with the crushed nuts, coconut, 1.5 tsp chilli powder, 0.5 tsp asafoetida, 12 torn curry leaves and 1 tsp salt.
Rub in 3 tbsp hot Anveshan Ghee until the mix clumps when pressed, then add about 0.66 cups water gradually to a stiff, non-sticky dough and rest 15 minutes.
Take small balls and pat each into a thin flat disc on a greased sheet or palm, pricking with a fork so they stay flat.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C until a scrap of dough rises steadily.
Slide in 3 to 4 discs at a time and fry for 3 to 4 minutes, turning, until the bubbling stops and they are golden, then drain on paper.
tips: Crush the peanuts coarsely so you get little crunchy bits rather than a paste in the dough.
Keep the dough firm; a soft dough tears while patting and soaks up oil.
Prick each disc well so it fries flat and crisp rather than puffing up.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with filter coffee for an authentic Bangalore evening snack, or alongside a spread of Diwali sweets.

variations.name: Masala Onion Nippattu
variations.description: A savoury, oniony nippattu where finely chopped onion, ginger and green chilli are kneaded into the dough for a soft-centred, deeply flavoured cracker. The onion caramelises as it fries, giving a moist, bhajji-like richness inside a crisp shell. A tea-stall favourite across northern Karnataka.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Shortening that keeps the onion-rich dough crisp despite its extra moisture

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Deep-fries the masala discs to a crisp golden edge

steps: Mix 2 cups rice flour and 0.5 cups besan with 1 tsp cumin, 0.5 tsp asafoetida and 1 tsp salt.
Add 1 finely chopped onion, 3 minced green chillies, 1 inch grated ginger and 3 tbsp chopped coriander, then rub in 3 tbsp hot Anveshan Ghee.
Bring the dough together with only about 0.33 cups water, since the onion releases moisture, aiming for a firm dough, and use it within 20 minutes.
Pat small balls into thin discs on a greased sheet and prick each with a fork.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C and fry the discs 3 to 4 at a time for 4 minutes, turning, until golden and the sizzling settles.
Drain on paper and cool a little so the crisp edges firm up around the soft centre.
tips: Add the onion just before frying, as salted onion keeps leaching water and slackens the dough.
Use very little added water because the vegetables provide plenty of moisture.
Fry at a steady medium-high so the oniony centre cooks through without the outside burning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best eaten fresh and warm with a cup of chai on a rainy evening.

variations.name: Methi Nippattu
variations.description: A fragrant nippattu folded with fresh fenugreek leaves and a touch of sesame for a slightly bitter, herby edge that balances the richness. The methi flecks the golden discs green and lends a wholesome, distinctive aroma. A seasonal favourite when fresh fenugreek is in the markets.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Shortening that mellows the bitterness of methi and crisps the discs

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Deep-fries the herby crackers to a speckled golden crisp

steps: Wash and finely chop 0.75 cups fresh methi leaves, sprinkle with a little salt, rest 10 minutes, and squeeze out the bitter juice.
Crush 0.33 cups roasted gram coarsely and mix into 2 cups rice flour with 2 tbsp sesame, 1.5 tsp chilli powder, 0.5 tsp ajwain, 0.5 tsp asafoetida and 1 tsp salt.
Add the squeezed methi and rub in 3 tbsp hot Anveshan Ghee, then bring together with about 0.5 cups water into a firm dough.
Pat small balls into thin discs on a greased sheet and prick each all over with a fork.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C and fry the discs in batches for 4 minutes, turning, until the bubbling calms and they are golden and speckled.
Drain on paper and cool fully before storing.
tips: Squeeze the salted methi well to remove excess bitterness and moisture before adding it.
Use fresh methi rather than dried for the brightest colour and aroma.
Rub the ghee in thoroughly so the herby dough still fries short and crisp.
variations.servingSuggestion: A wholesome, herby cracker to serve with coconut chutney or a spiced yogurt dip.

variations.name: Ragi Multigrain Nippattu
variations.description: A nourishing nippattu that swaps part of the rice flour for finger millet and multigrain atta, deepening the colour and adding fibre. The wholegrains give a heartier, nuttier crunch while the peanuts keep the classic character. A modern, health-forward take on the Karnataka cracker.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Multigrain Atta
ingredients.note: A wholegrain blend that adds fibre and a rustic bite to the crackers

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Shortening that stops the wholegrain dough frying dense and keeps it crisp

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Deep-fries the millet crackers to a crisp, even finish

steps: Coarsely crush 0.5 cups roasted peanuts and mix 1 cup ragi flour, 0.5 cups Anveshan Multigrain Atta and 0.75 cups rice flour with the peanuts, 2 tbsp sesame, 1.5 tsp chilli powder, 0.5 tsp asafoetida, 12 torn curry leaves and 1 tsp salt.
Rub in 3 tbsp hot Anveshan Ghee until crumbly, then add about 0.6 cups water gradually to a firm dough and rest 15 minutes.
Pat small balls into thin discs on a greased sheet and prick each with a fork.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C until a scrap of dough rises promptly.
Fry the discs 3 to 4 at a time for 4 minutes, turning once, and judge doneness by the quietened bubbling since the dark dough hides browning.
Drain on paper and cool completely so the wholegrain crackers turn fully crisp.
tips: The dark ragi masks colour, so go by the calming sizzle to know when they are done.
Wholegrain flours absorb more water, so add it slowly and keep the dough just firm.
Do not skip the rice flour, as it provides the crispness the millets lack on their own.
variations.servingSuggestion: A wholesome, higher-fibre cracker to enjoy with masala chai or a bowl of curd.

variations.name: Classic Palada Payasam
variations.description: Palada payasam is the milky Onam classic where wafer-thin rice ada is simmered slowly in reducing milk until the whole pudding turns a soft rosy pink. Sweetened gently and scented with cardamom, it is the patient, spoon-coating payasam that crowns the Sadya.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: sweetens the milk cleanly and helps it caramelise to the signature pink

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: coats the ada and fries the cashews for a fragrant, glossy payasam

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm milk to deepen the rosy colour and add fragrance

steps: Soak 0.75 cup rice ada in hot water for 15 minutes, then drain and toss it in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee.
Bring 5 cups full-fat milk to a boil in a heavy pan, add the ada and simmer on low heat for 35 to 40 minutes, stirring often, until the milk reduces and turns pale pink.
Stir in 0.7 cup Anveshan Khandsari and the pinch of bloomed Anveshan Saffron and cook another 6 to 8 minutes until the payasam thickens and deepens in colour.
In the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, fry 2 tbsp cashews over medium heat until golden, about 2 minutes.
Fold in the fried cashews and 0.5 tsp cardamom and simmer for a final minute.
Turn off the heat and serve the palada payasam warm, or chill it for a thicker, more set pudding.
tips: The slow reduction over low heat is what turns palada payasam its trademark rosy pink, so never rush it.
Stir often and scrape the sides, as milk this rich catches and scorches easily in a thin pan.
Add the sugar only after the ada has softened and the milk has reduced, or it slows the cooking.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm or chilled as the finale of an Onam Sadya, garnished with a few extra ghee-fried cashews.

variations.name: Instant Palada Payasam
variations.description: A shortcut palada that skips the long reduction by leaning on sweetened condensed milk, giving the same creamy, rosy pudding in a fraction of the time. It is the version busy home cooks turn to when a Sadya has to come together fast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: coats the ada and fries the nuts for a rich finish in this quick version

steps: Soak 0.75 cup rice ada in hot water for 15 minutes, then drain and pressure cook with 1 cup of the milk for 2 whistles until soft.
Transfer to a heavy pan, add the remaining 2 cups milk and simmer on low heat for 8 minutes until slightly reduced.
Stir in 0.75 cup sweetened condensed milk and cook for 6 to 8 minutes until the payasam thickens and turns pale cream-pink.
In 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, fry 2 tbsp cashews and 1 tbsp raisins until golden, about 2 minutes.
Fold in the fried nuts and 0.5 tsp cardamom and simmer for a final minute.
Turn off the heat and serve the instant palada payasam warm or chilled.
tips: Condensed milk is already sweet, so taste before adding any extra sweetener to avoid a cloying payasam.
Pressure cooking the ada first is what makes this version quick, so do not skip that step.
Simmer gently once the condensed milk goes in, as it can catch and scorch quickly on a high flame.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm or chilled as a fuss-free Sadya dessert, topped with fried cashews and raisins.

variations.name: Saffron Badam Palada Payasam
variations.description: A wedding-grade palada enriched with ground almonds and a generous bloom of saffron, giving a thick, golden, luxuriously nutty pudding. The almond powder plushes the milk while slivered almonds add a delicate crunch to the soft ada.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm milk to colour and perfume this rich festive payasam

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: sweetens the almond-thickened milk while keeping the saffron gold bright

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: coats the ada and fries the slivered almonds for a luxurious finish

steps: Soak 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk taken from the 4.5 cups and set aside to bloom.
Soak 0.75 cup rice ada in hot water for 15 minutes, then drain and toss in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee.
Bring the remaining milk to a boil, add the ada and simmer on low heat for 30 minutes, stirring often, until reduced and pale pink.
Whisk in 0.25 cup almond powder and cook for 4 minutes until the payasam thickens and turns plush, then stir in 0.7 cup Anveshan Khandsari and the saffron milk.
In the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, fry 3 tbsp slivered almonds until pale gold, about 1 minute.
Fold in the fried almonds and 0.5 tsp cardamom, simmer 2 minutes, then serve the saffron badam palada warm.
tips: Whisk the almond powder in slowly to keep the payasam smooth and free of lumps.
Bloom the saffron in warm milk first so its colour and aroma spread evenly through the pudding.
The almond powder thickens the payasam a lot as it cools, so keep it noticeably loose when hot.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve this saffron-almond palada at weddings and festivals, garnished with slivered pistachios and saffron strands.

variations.name: Jaggery Ada Payasam
variations.description: The jaggery-and-coconut-milk cousin of palada, where the same soft rice ada is simmered in coconut milk and molten jaggery rather than dairy for a dark, glossy, dairy-free pudding. Coconut-oil-fried coconut bits give it a fragrant Kerala finish quite unlike the milky version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted into a dark syrup that coats the ada for a glossy, caramel-rich payasam

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: fries the coconut and cashews for the signature Kerala aroma

steps: Soak 0.75 cup rice ada in hot water for 20 minutes, boil for 5 minutes until soft, and drain well.
Melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 0.25 cup water over low heat, strain out grit and simmer to a thick syrup, about 5 minutes.
Add the drained ada to the syrup and cook on low heat for 8 minutes, stirring, until it turns glossy and dark.
Pour in 2 cups thin coconut milk and simmer for 6 minutes until the payasam thickens to a pouring consistency.
Lower the heat, stir in 1 cup thick coconut milk and warm for 2 minutes without letting it boil so it does not split.
In 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, fry 3 tbsp coconut bits and 2 tbsp cashews until golden, then fold in with 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp dry ginger and serve warm.
tips: Keep the thick coconut milk off the boil, as it splits far more readily than the thin milk.
This dairy-free version is a lifesaver when you want palada flavours without milk, and it keeps longer too.
The payasam thickens as it cools, so loosen it with a splash of thin coconut milk when reheating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a dairy-free Sadya dessert on a banana leaf, topped with coconut-oil-fried coconut bits.

variations.name: Classic Paruppu Payasam
variations.description: Paruppu payasam is the Tamil jaggery pudding of roasted moong dal cooked soft, sweetened with molten jaggery and enriched with coconut milk. Nutty, golden and finished with coconut-oil-fried coconut and cashews, it is the payasam served on festival days and at Sadya feasts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted into a syrup to sweeten the dal payasam with earthy caramel depth

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the dal and fries the coconut for a deeply nutty payasam

steps: Dry roast 0.75 cup moong dal in a pan over low heat for 3 to 4 minutes until golden and nutty, then rinse.
Pressure cook the roasted dal with 2.5 cups water for 4 whistles until very soft, then mash lightly.
Melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 0.25 cup water over low heat, strain out grit and simmer to a thick syrup, about 4 minutes.
Add the mashed dal to the jaggery syrup and simmer on low heat for 6 minutes until well combined and glossy.
Lower the heat, pour in 1 cup thick coconut milk and warm for 2 minutes without letting it boil so it does not split.
In 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, fry 3 tbsp coconut bits and 2 tbsp cashews until golden, then fold them in with 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp dry ginger and serve warm.
tips: Roasting the moong dal before cooking is the key step that gives this payasam its signature nutty aroma.
Add coconut milk only at the end and off a rolling boil, or it will curdle into grainy specks.
The payasam thickens as it cools, so keep it loose and reheat gently with a splash of coconut milk.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm on a banana leaf at a Sadya, or in bowls topped with extra fried coconut bits and cashews.

variations.name: Kadalai Paruppu Payasam
variations.description: Made with Bengal gram instead of moong, this payasam is heartier and more robustly nutty, the dal holding a little bite even when cooked soft. A grating of nutmeg and coconut-oil-fried garnish make it a temple-festival favourite in the Tamil-Kerala border kitchens.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted into a dark syrup that suits the robust chana dal payasam

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: fries the coconut and cashews and lends the payasam its Kerala fragrance

steps: Dry roast 0.75 cup Bengal gram over low heat for 4 minutes until golden and fragrant, then rinse.
Pressure cook the dal with 3 cups water for 6 whistles until soft but still holding a little shape, then lightly mash half of it.
Melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 0.25 cup water, strain, and simmer to a thick syrup, about 5 minutes.
Add the cooked chana dal to the syrup and simmer on low heat for 6 to 8 minutes until glossy and well combined.
Lower the heat and stir in 1 cup thick coconut milk, warming for 2 minutes without boiling so it stays smooth.
In 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, fry 3 tbsp coconut bits and 2 tbsp cashews until golden, then fold them in with 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp grated nutmeg and serve warm.
tips: Leave some of the chana dal whole for texture, as fully mashing it loses the pleasant bite this payasam is loved for.
Chana dal takes longer to soften than moong, so give it the full pressure-cooking time before adding jaggery.
A little grated nutmeg lifts the earthy chana dal beautifully; add it right at the end so its aroma stays fresh.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a festival dessert, ladled into bowls and finished with a scatter of coconut-oil-fried coconut.

variations.name: Paasi Paruppu Rice Payasam
variations.description: A softer, milk-based payasam combining moong dal with a little rice so the two cook down into a smooth, porridge-like sweet. Cooked in milk and gently sweetened, it is a comforting everyday version that children love.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted and stirred into the cooked dal-rice for a mellow caramel sweetness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the dal and fries the nuts for a fragrant, comforting payasam

steps: Dry roast 0.5 cup moong dal in a little ghee over low heat for 3 minutes until golden, then rinse it with 0.25 cup raw rice.
Pressure cook the dal and rice with 2 cups water for 5 whistles until very soft, then mash to a smooth porridge.
Add 2 cups full-fat milk and simmer on low heat for 6 to 8 minutes until the mixture is creamy and slightly thickened.
Melt 0.8 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water, strain, then take the payasam off the heat and stir the syrup in so the milk does not curdle.
In 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, fry 2 tbsp cashews and 1 tbsp raisins until golden, about 2 minutes.
Fold in the fried nuts and 0.5 tsp cardamom, then serve the paasi paruppu payasam warm.
tips: Adding rice with the dal makes the payasam naturally creamy and thick without any coconut milk.
Stir in the jaggery only after taking the pan off the heat, as jaggery meeting hot milk on the flame will split it.
Loosen with warm milk before serving, as the rice and dal thicken the payasam considerably as it stands.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a gentle everyday sweet or after-school treat, garnished with a few golden fried cashews.

variations.name: Palm Jaggery Paruppu Payasam
variations.description: A fully plant-based payasam sweetened with dark palm jaggery and layered with both thin and thick coconut milk for a rich, glossy finish. Cooked entirely in coconut oil, it has a smoky-sweet depth that sets it apart from the everyday version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: roasts the dal and fries the coconut for a deeply aromatic vegan payasam

steps: Roast 0.75 cup moong dal in 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil over low heat for 3 minutes until golden, then rinse.
Cook the dal with 2 cups thin coconut milk on low heat for 15 to 18 minutes, stirring often, until very soft and mashable.
Melt 1 cup palm jaggery with 0.25 cup water, strain out grit, and simmer to a thick dark syrup, about 5 minutes.
Stir the syrup into the cooked dal and simmer on low heat for 5 minutes until glossy and well combined.
Lower the heat, pour in 1 cup thick coconut milk and warm for 2 minutes without boiling so it stays smooth.
In the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, fry 3 tbsp coconut bits and 2 tbsp cashews until golden, then fold in with 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp dry ginger and serve warm.
tips: Cooking the dal in thin coconut milk instead of water builds a richer base for this dairy-free payasam.
Palm jaggery carries more grit than regular jaggery, so always melt and strain it before adding.
Keep both additions of coconut milk off the boil to protect their creamy texture from splitting.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a vegan festive dessert, topped generously with coconut-oil-fried coconut bits and cashews.

variations.name: Classic French Beans Paruppu Usili
variations.description: Paruppu Usili is a beloved Tamil Brahmin dish where soaked toor and chana dal are spiced, steamed and crumbled, then tossed with finely chopped French beans until the whole thing turns into a savoury, protein-rich crumble. Dry and fragrant with a lentil bite in every mouthful, it is a staple of festive sappadu.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed til oil that fries the lentil crumble to a dry, aromatic finish

steps: Soak 0.5 cup toor dal and 0.25 cup chana dal together for 1 hour, then drain very well.
Grind the drained dals with 4 red chillies, 0.5 tsp hing and 0.75 tsp salt to a coarse thick paste without water.
Spread the paste in a greased plate and steam for 12 minutes until firm and cooked through, then cool and crumble it fine with your fingers.
Meanwhile finely chop 300 g French beans and steam or cook them with a little water and 0.25 tsp salt for 6 minutes until just tender, then drain.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadai, add 1 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tsp urad dal, 2 sprigs curry leaves and 0.5 tsp turmeric and splutter for 15 seconds.
Add the crumbled lentil mixture and roast on medium heat for 6 minutes, stirring, until dry and golden.
Fold in the cooked beans and toss for 3 minutes until evenly combined and fragrant.
tips: Grind the dal coarse and without water so the steamed cake crumbles rather than turning pasty.
Roast the crumbled dal well until dry, as any moisture makes the usili clumpy.
Steam the beans only until just tender so they keep a slight bite against the crumble.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rice, a spoon of ghee and mor kuzhambu or rasam for a classic Tamil meal.

variations.name: Kothavarangai (Cluster Beans) Usili
variations.description: A rustic version made with cluster beans, whose slight bitterness is prized in Tamil kitchens and pairs beautifully with the spiced lentil crumble. Chana dal dominates the mix here for a firmer, coarser texture that clings to the sturdy beans.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil that roasts the coarse chana dal crumble to a nutty dryness

steps: Soak 0.5 cup chana dal and 0.25 cup toor dal for 1 hour and drain thoroughly.
Grind the dals with 5 red chillies, 0.5 tsp peppercorns, 0.5 tsp hing and 0.75 tsp salt to a coarse paste without water.
Steam the paste in a greased plate for 12 minutes, cool and crumble it coarsely.
String and finely chop 300 g cluster beans and cook them with a little water and 0.25 tsp salt for 8 minutes until tender, as cluster beans take longer, then drain.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, add 1 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tsp urad dal, 2 sprigs curry leaves and 0.5 tsp turmeric and splutter for 15 seconds.
Add the crumbled dal and roast for 7 minutes until dry, coarse and golden.
Toss in the cooked cluster beans and stir-fry 3 minutes until well combined.
tips: Cluster beans need longer cooking than French beans, so boil them until fully tender first.
The extra chana dal and pepper give this version its firmer texture and gentle heat.
A whiff of hing balances the natural mild bitterness of the cluster beans.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pairs wonderfully with vatha kuzhambu and rice, or as a dry side to sambar sadam.

variations.name: Vazhaipoo (Banana Flower) Usili
variations.description: A special-occasion usili using cleaned banana flower florets, which bring an earthy, fibrous texture and a subtle astringency that the lentil crumble mellows. Cleaning the vazhaipoo takes patience, but the result is a nutritious, deeply traditional dish rarely found outside home kitchens.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed til oil that fries the crumble and suits the earthy banana flower

steps: Clean the banana flower by removing the stiff style and calyx from each floret, chop finely and drop into 1 cup buttermilk to stop discolouring.
Soak 0.5 cup toor dal and 0.25 cup chana dal for 1 hour and drain well.
Grind the dals with 4 red chillies, 0.5 tsp hing and 0.75 tsp salt to a coarse paste, steam it for 12 minutes, cool and crumble.
Drain the chopped banana flower, squeeze it dry and cook with a little water and 0.25 tsp salt for 8 minutes until tender.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, add 1 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tsp urad dal, 2 sprigs curry leaves and 0.5 tsp turmeric and splutter for 15 seconds.
Add the crumbled dal and roast for 6 minutes until dry and golden.
Fold in the cooked banana flower and stir-fry 4 minutes until well mixed and fragrant.
tips: Rub a little oil on your hands before cleaning the banana flower to prevent staining.
Soaking the chopped florets in buttermilk keeps them from darkening and softens astringency.
Squeeze the banana flower well before cooking so the usili stays dry.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a nutritious festive side with rice, ghee and a bowl of more kuzhambu.

variations.name: Cabbage Paruppu Usili
variations.description: A quick weekday usili using finely shredded cabbage, which needs no pre-cooking and turns sweet and tender as it steams in the crumble. Faster and lighter than the classic, it is a clever way to get children to eat their lentils and greens together.
