ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil that roasts the crumble and lightly steams the cabbage

steps: Soak 0.5 cup toor dal and 0.25 cup chana dal for 1 hour and drain thoroughly.
Grind the dals with 4 red chillies, 1 green chilli, 0.5 tsp hing and 0.75 tsp salt to a coarse paste without water.
Steam the paste for 12 minutes, cool and crumble it fine.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai, add 1 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tsp urad dal, 2 sprigs curry leaves and 0.5 tsp turmeric and splutter for 15 seconds.
Add 3 cups finely shredded cabbage and 0.25 tsp salt, cover and cook on medium for 5 minutes until it wilts and softens.
Add the crumbled dal and roast uncovered for 6 minutes, stirring, until dry and golden.
Toss everything together for 2 minutes until the cabbage and crumble are evenly mixed.
tips: Shred the cabbage fine so it cooks quickly and blends into the crumble.
Cabbage releases moisture, so roast the mix uncovered at the end to keep it dry.
This no-boil version comes together fast, making it perfect for busy weekdays.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with rice and rasam or as a dry side alongside curd rice for a comforting meal.

variations.name: Classic Paal Payasam
variations.description: Paal payasam is the temple-style rice pudding of South India, made by simmering a handful of rice in whole milk until it reduces to a rosy, spoon-coating cream. Sweetened simply and scented with cardamom, it is the offering ladled out at Ambalappuzha and countless home celebrations.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined sugar that sweetens the payasam cleanly without dulling the milk's rosy colour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the cashews and adds a faint nutty richness to the pudding

steps: Rinse 0.3 cup raw rice and bring 5 cups full-fat milk to a boil in a heavy-bottomed pan over medium heat.
Add the rice and simmer on low heat for 35 to 40 minutes, stirring often and scraping the sides, until the milk reduces by nearly half and turns creamy and faintly pink.
Stir in 0.6 cup Anveshan Khandsari and cook for another 4 to 5 minutes until dissolved and the payasam thickens slightly.
In 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, fry 2 tbsp cashews and 1 tbsp raisins over medium heat until golden and plump, about 2 minutes.
Fold the fried nuts and 0.5 tsp cardamom into the payasam and simmer for a final minute.
Turn off the heat and serve the paal payasam warm, or chill it for a thicker set.
tips: Use a heavy pan and low heat throughout; a thin pan scorches the milk and gives the payasam a burnt edge.
The slow reduction is what turns the milk rosy and creamy, so resist rushing it on a high flame.
Add the sugar only after the rice is fully cooked, as sugar added early keeps the grains from softening.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm or chilled in small tumblers as a temple-style dessert, garnished with a few extra fried cashews.

variations.name: Nei Payasam
variations.description: The Kerala jaggery payasam, where reddish rice is cooked and drowned in molten jaggery and coconut milk rather than dairy, giving a dark, glossy, deeply caramelised pudding. Finished with coconut-oil-fried coconut bits, it is the unctuous sweet served on a leaf at Sadya feasts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted into a dark syrup that gives nei payasam its glossy caramel body

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: fries the coconut and cashews and lends the payasam its unmistakable Kerala aroma

steps: Rinse 0.75 cup rosematta rice and pressure cook with 2.5 cups water for 5 whistles until soft and slightly mushy.
Melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 0.25 cup water over low heat, strain out grit and simmer to a thick syrup, about 5 minutes.
Add the cooked rice to the jaggery syrup and simmer on low heat for 8 to 10 minutes, mashing lightly, until dark and glossy.
Lower the heat, pour in 1 cup thick coconut milk and warm gently for 2 minutes without letting it boil so it does not split.
In 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, fry 3 tbsp coconut bits and 2 tbsp cashews until golden, about 3 minutes.
Stir in the fried coconut and cashews, 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp dry ginger, then serve the nei payasam warm.
tips: Add the coconut milk off the boil and never let it bubble hard, or it will curdle into grainy specks.
Rosematta rice gives the most authentic earthy flavour, but any short-grain rice cooked soft will work.
The payasam thickens as it cools, so keep it a little loose and reheat gently with a splash of coconut milk.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm on a banana leaf at the end of a Sadya, or in bowls topped with extra coconut-oil-fried coconut bits.

variations.name: Aval Payasam
variations.description: A quick payasam built on poha, where the flattened rice melts into warm milk to give a soft, comforting pudding in under twenty minutes. Barely any cooking is needed, making it the go-to sweet for sudden guests and small pujas.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted separately and added off heat to sweeten the milky aval payasam without curdling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the poha and fries the nuts for a fragrant, nutty payasam

steps: In 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, fry 2 tbsp cashews, 1 tbsp raisins and 2 tbsp coconut bits over medium heat until golden, then lift them out.
In the same ghee, roast 0.75 cup thick poha for 2 minutes until fragrant and lightly crisp.
Pour in 4 cups full-fat milk, bring to a gentle simmer and cook on low heat for 8 to 10 minutes until the poha softens and the milk thickens.
Separately melt 0.6 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water, strain, and set the syrup aside.
Take the payasam off the heat, let it cool for a minute, then stir in the jaggery syrup so the milk does not curdle.
Fold in the fried nuts, coconut and 0.5 tsp cardamom, then serve the aval payasam warm.
tips: Always add jaggery to the milk off the heat and slightly cooled, as hot milk meeting jaggery on the flame will split.
Roasting the poha in ghee first keeps it from turning to complete mush in the milk.
If the payasam thickens too much on standing, loosen it with a little warm milk before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a fuss-free festival dessert, garnished with fried coconut bits and a few golden cashews.

variations.name: Javvarisi Payasam
variations.description: A translucent, pearly payasam made with tapioca sago that swells into soft jelly-like beads in sweetened milk. Light yet festive, its bouncy pearls and cardamom fragrance make it a favourite for Navratri and small home celebrations.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: sweetens the payasam cleanly while keeping the sago pearls clear and glossy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the cashews and gives the payasam a delicate nutty finish

steps: Soak 0.4 cup sago pearls in 1.5 cups water for 20 minutes, then simmer over medium heat for 6 to 8 minutes until they turn fully translucent.
In a separate heavy pan, bring 4 cups full-fat milk to a boil and simmer on low heat for 8 minutes until slightly reduced.
Add the cooked translucent sago to the milk and simmer together for 5 minutes until the pudding thickens and the pearls float.
Stir in 0.6 cup Anveshan Khandsari with a pinch of saffron and cook for 3 minutes until dissolved and the milk turns pale gold.
In 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, fry 2 tbsp cashews and 1 tbsp raisins until golden, about 2 minutes.
Fold in the fried nuts and 0.5 tsp cardamom, then serve the javvarisi payasam warm or chilled.
tips: Cook the sago until every pearl is fully clear before adding it to the milk, as any white centre stays chalky.
Sago keeps swelling as it sits, so keep the payasam loose and thin it with warm milk before serving.
Rinse the cooked sago briefly under warm water if it feels sticky to keep the payasam from turning gluey.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm on cool evenings or well chilled in summer, garnished with saffron strands and slivered nuts.

variations.name: Classic Pithla
variations.description: The soul-food gram-flour curry of the Maharashtrian farmhouse, thin and pourable, thick with garlic and green chilli and finished with a snap of mustard and curry leaf. Made in minutes from pantry staples, it is the everyday companion to jowar bhakri and hot rice.

ingredients.name: Besan
ingredients.note: sifted

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil is the traditional Maharashtrian fat and gives the tempering its aroma

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: crushed to a coarse paste

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Whisk 3/4 cup besan into 2.5 cups water with 1/2 tsp turmeric powder and 1 tsp salt until completely smooth and free of lumps, and keep it beside the stove.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat and splutter 1/2 tsp mustard seeds and 1/2 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add 1/4 tsp asafoetida and 10 curry leaves.
Add 8 crushed garlic cloves and 4 chopped green chillies and fry for 40 seconds until fragrant, then add 1 chopped onion and cook for 4-5 minutes until soft.
Give the besan slurry a final stir and pour it into the pan in a steady stream while whisking hard so it stays smooth.
Bring it to a gentle boil, then lower the heat and simmer for 7-8 minutes, stirring often, until the raw besan smell goes and it thickens to a pourable, gravy-like consistency.
Adjust with a splash of hot water if it gets too thick, keeping it loose enough to run off a spoon.
Stir in 3 tbsp chopped coriander, drizzle a little raw groundnut oil over the top, and serve piping hot.
tips: Whisk the besan into cold water before it touches the heat; adding dry flour to a hot pan is what causes stubborn lumps.
Pithla thickens a lot as it cools, so pull it off the heat while it still looks slightly thin.
For the classic garlicky punch, do not skimp on the garlic, and crush it coarsely rather than mincing so you get little bursts of it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle over hot steamed rice with a spoon of ghee and a fried papad, or scoop it up with jowar bhakri and a slice of raw onion for the definitive zunka-bhakri plate.

variations.name: Jhunka Pithla with Kanda
variations.description: A thicker, onion-forward version that sits halfway between pithla and zunka, generous with browned onion and tomato so it eats almost like a soft porridge. This is the heartier bowl families make when the pithla is the main event rather than a quick side.

ingredients.name: Besan
ingredients.note: sifted

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the extra oil helps caramelise the onions that thicken this heartier pithla

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Whisk 1 cup besan into 2 cups water with 1/2 tsp turmeric powder and 1 tsp salt until smooth and set aside.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, crackle 1/2 tsp cumin seeds, then add 3 chopped onions and fry for 7-8 minutes until golden brown.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 3 chopped green chillies for a minute, then add 1 chopped tomato and cook for 3-4 minutes until it collapses.
Add 1 tsp red chilli powder, stir for 20 seconds, then pour in the besan slurry in a stream while whisking constantly.
Bring to a boil and simmer on low heat for 8-9 minutes, stirring often, until it thickens into a soft, spoonable mass with the oil beginning to surface.
Loosen with a little hot water only if it turns stiff, keeping it thicker than a classic pithla.
Finish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander and serve hot with a dab of butter melting on top.
tips: Browning the onions well gives this version its natural sweetness and body, so do not rush that step.
Keep it thick and porridge-like on purpose; this pithla is meant to be scooped, not poured.
A pinch of jaggery stirred in at the end balances the tomato's acidity if your tomatoes are very sour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft bajra bhakri and a raw onion salad, or spoon it over jeera rice with a side of fried green chillies.

variations.name: Takatla Pithla
variations.description: The tangy buttermilk pithla of Marathwada, where sour taak replaces plain water to give a silky, gently sour curry that is easy on the stomach. Lighter and quicker than the classic, it is a summer favourite eaten with rice or bhakri when the heat kills the appetite.

ingredients.name: Besan
ingredients.note: sifted

ingredients.name: Buttermilk
ingredients.note: thin and sour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee tempering balances the sourness of the buttermilk beautifully

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: crushed

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Whisk 1/2 cup besan into 2.5 cups thin sour buttermilk with 1/2 tsp turmeric powder and 1 tsp salt until perfectly smooth, and keep it ready.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat and splutter 1/2 tsp mustard seeds and 1/2 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add 1/4 tsp asafoetida and 10 curry leaves.
Add 6 crushed garlic cloves and 3 slit green chillies and fry for 40 seconds until the garlic just turns pale.
Lower the heat right down and pour in the besan-buttermilk mixture, stirring continuously so the buttermilk does not split.
Cook on low heat for 8-9 minutes, stirring frequently, until it thickens to a smooth, pourable curry and the raw besan taste is gone.
Taste for salt and sourness, then switch off the heat while it is still silky and slightly thin.
Garnish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and serve warm.
tips: Keep the flame low from the moment the buttermilk goes in; a fierce boil will curdle it into grainy specks.
Use genuinely sour buttermilk for the authentic Marathwada tang, and never add extra water, as the taak provides all the liquid.
This pithla is best eaten fresh; it thickens into a paste on standing, so reheat gently with a splash of buttermilk.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot steamed rice with a spoon of ghee and roasted papad, ideal as a light, cooling summer lunch.

variations.name: Kolhapuri Tikhat Pithla
variations.description: The fiery Kolhapuri rendition stained red with the region's signature lasun-tikhat garlic-chilli masala and a scattering of fresh coconut. Bolder and spicier than any other pithla, it is built for people who want their gram-flour curry to bite back.

ingredients.name: Besan
ingredients.note: sifted

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: carries the fiery Kolhapuri garlic-chilli tempering that defines this pithla

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: crushed

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Red chilli powder
ingredients.note: preferably fiery Lavangi or Sankeshwari

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Whisk 3/4 cup besan into 2.5 cups water with 1/2 tsp turmeric powder and 1 tsp salt until smooth and lump-free, and set it aside.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat and splutter 1/2 tsp mustard seeds and 1/2 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds.
Add 10 crushed garlic cloves and fry for 1 minute until aromatic, then add 1 chopped onion and cook for 4-5 minutes until soft and golden.
Lower the heat and add 1.5 tsp Kolhapuri kanda-lasun masala and 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, roasting for 30 seconds until the oil floods red, being careful not to burn them.
Pour in the besan slurry in a stream while whisking hard, bring to a boil, then simmer on low for 8-9 minutes until it thickens and the spices meld.
Stir in 3 tbsp grated coconut and cook for another minute, loosening with a little hot water if needed.
Finish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander and serve blazing hot.
tips: Kolhapuri chillies are genuinely hot, so start with less and build up; the masala and chilli powder together carry serious heat.
Add the fresh coconut near the end so it keeps a little bite and sweet aroma rather than dissolving completely.
A teaspoon of the frying oil skimmed off the top and drizzled over each serving is the authentic fiery Kolhapuri flourish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jowar bhakri, a wedge of raw onion and a slice of lime to cut the heat, with plenty of buttermilk on the side.

variations.name: Classic Mixed-Vegetable Poricha Kuzhambu
variations.description: A mild Tamil Brahmin stew where mixed vegetables and soft moong dal are bound in a freshly ground coconut, cumin and pepper paste, deliberately left tamarind-free so it tastes gentle and creamy. A ghee tempering of urad dal, mustard and red chilli finishes it with a homely, rounded warmth that soothes a spicy meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The urad-dal ghee tempering gives poricha kuzhambu its soft, nutty finish

steps: Pressure-cook 0.5 cup moong dal with 1.5 cups water and 0.25 tsp turmeric for 3 whistles until soft, then mash lightly and set aside.
Boil 2 cups chopped mixed vegetables with 1 tsp salt and just enough water to cover on medium for 8-10 minutes until fork-tender but still holding shape.
Grind 0.33 cup grated coconut with 1 tsp cumin, 0.5 tsp peppercorns and 2 green chillies into a smooth paste with a splash of water.
Add the mashed dal and the coconut paste to the vegetables and simmer on low for 5-6 minutes, stirring, until it thickens to a soft, spoonable stew.

In a small pan heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal, fry until the dal is golden, then add 2 dried red chillies, 10 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida.
Pour the sizzling ghee tempering over the kuzhambu, stir once and simmer for a final minute so the aromas soak in.
tips: Grind the coconut paste truly smooth so the stew turns creamy rather than grainy.
Poricha kuzhambu has no tamarind by design, so resist any souring agent - the mildness is the point.
Keep the vegetables just tender; boiling them to mush loses their distinct bite in the finished dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot rice with a spoon of ghee and a sharp rasam or vatha kuzhambu alongside to play off its gentle creaminess.

variations.name: Keerai Poricha Kuzhambu
variations.description: A greener, more rustic take where finely chopped spinach wilts into soft toor dal and a garlic-spiked coconut paste, giving the stew an earthy, iron-rich body. The coconut-oil tempering with extra garlic sets it apart from the ghee-finished mixed-vegetable classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: A garlic and coconut-oil tempering lifts the earthy greens with coastal warmth

steps: Pressure-cook 0.5 cup toor dal with 1.5 cups water and 0.25 tsp turmeric for 4 whistles until very soft, then mash smooth.
Add 4 cups finely chopped spinach and 1 tsp salt to the dal and simmer on medium for 5 minutes until the greens wilt down completely.
Grind 0.33 cup grated coconut with 1 tsp cumin, 2 garlic cloves and 2 green chillies into a coarse paste with a little water.
Stir the coconut paste into the spinach-dal, add 1 tsp rice flour slaked in 2 tbsp water, and simmer on low for 5 minutes until thickened and glossy.

In a small pan heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, let them pop, then add the remaining 3 garlic cloves crushed, 2 dried red chillies and 10 curry leaves and fry until the garlic is golden.
Pour the garlicky tempering over the kuzhambu, stir through and simmer for a final minute so the aroma infuses.
tips: Wilt the spinach only briefly; overcooking dulls its bright green and washes out the flavour.
The teaspoon of rice flour gives the stew a light body that clings to rice without turning gluey.
Amaranth, mixed local greens or a spinach-methi blend all work; adjust the wilting time to how tender they are.
variations.servingSuggestion: Spoon over rice with a dab of ghee and a crisp appalam for an iron-rich, comforting plate.

variations.name: Chow Chow Poricha Kuzhambu
variations.description: A silky single-vegetable version where cubes of chayote simmer with chana dal until melt-soft, thickened by a coconut paste ground with roasted red chilli for a faintly smoky edge. The chana dal holds a gentle bite against the tender squash, making it heartier than the moong-dal classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A ghee tempering rounds out the mild chayote with a warm, nutty aroma

steps: Soak 0.5 cup chana dal for 20 minutes, then pressure-cook with 1.5 cups water and 0.25 tsp turmeric for 3-4 whistles until soft but still intact.
Peel and cube 3 cups chayote and boil with 1 tsp salt and water to cover on medium for 8 minutes until tender and translucent.
Dry-roast 2 dried red chillies until fragrant, then grind with 0.33 cup grated coconut and 1 tsp cumin into a smooth paste with a splash of water.
Add the cooked chana dal and the coconut paste to the chayote and simmer on low for 6 minutes until glossy and lightly thickened.

In a small pan heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal, fry until golden, then add the remaining 1 dried red chilli, 10 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida.
Tip the tempering into the kuzhambu, stir through and simmer for a final minute before switching off.
tips: Cook the chana dal until soft but whole so it contrasts nicely with the melting chayote.
Roasting the red chillies before grinding gives this version its gentle, smoky undertone.
Chayote is watery, so use only enough boiling water to cover and drain any excess before adding the paste.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pairs beautifully with steamed rice and a tangy vatha kuzhambu, or with chapati as a wholesome, mild side.

variations.name: Manathakkali Poricha Kuzhambu
variations.description: A traditional country version built around fresh manathakkali (black nightshade) greens and a masoor-moong dal blend, prized in Tamil homes as a cooling, digestive stew. A coconut-oil tempering with plenty of curry leaves gives it a bright, herbal lift distinct from the richer classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: A curry-leaf-heavy coconut-oil tempering suits the herbal manathakkali greens

steps: Pressure-cook 0.33 cup moong dal and 0.25 cup masoor dal together with 1.75 cups water and 0.25 tsp turmeric for 3 whistles until soft, then mash lightly.
Add 3 cups cleaned manathakkali greens and 1 tsp salt to the dal and simmer on medium for 6 minutes until the greens are fully tender.
Grind 0.33 cup grated coconut with 1 tsp cumin, 0.5 tsp peppercorns and 2 green chillies into a smooth paste with a little water.
Stir the coconut paste into the dal and greens and simmer on low for 5 minutes until the stew is thick and well combined.
In a small pan heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil; add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, let them splutter, then add 2 dried red chillies and 15 curry leaves and fry until crisp.
Pour the fragrant tempering over the kuzhambu, stir once and rest it covered for a minute before serving.
tips: Clean the manathakkali greens well and pluck only the tender leaves and shoots for the softest texture.
The moong-masoor blend cooks faster and lighter than toor dal, keeping this stew easy on the stomach.
If fresh nightshade greens are hard to find, tender amaranth or ponnanganni keerai make a fine substitute.
variations.servingSuggestion: Traditionally eaten over rice with ghee and dried sundakkai vathal fried crisp on the side for contrast.

variations.name: Classic Carrot Poriyal
variations.description: Carrot Poriyal is the quintessential Tamil dry stir-fry where finely chopped carrots are cooked just until tender and finished with fresh grated coconut. A simple mustard, urad dal and curry leaf tempering keeps it light and fragrant, letting the natural sweetness of the carrots shine as an everyday side.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the classic South Indian fat that keeps the poriyal light and aromatic

steps: Peel and finely chop 4 carrots into small even pieces so they cook quickly and uniformly.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a kadai, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and let them splutter for 10 seconds.
Add 1 tsp urad dal, 1 tsp chana dal and 2 dry red chillies and fry until the dals turn golden, about 30 seconds.
Add the slit green chilli, 2 sprigs curry leaves and 0.25 tsp hing and let them crackle briefly.
Add the chopped carrots with 0.75 tsp salt, sprinkle 2 tablespoons of water, cover and cook on low for 8 minutes until just tender.
Uncover and stir-fry for 2 minutes to dry any moisture while keeping the carrots slightly crisp.
Switch off, mix in 0.33 cup grated coconut and toss well before serving.
tips: Chop the carrots small and even so they cook through without turning mushy.
Add the coconut only after switching off the heat to keep it fresh and moist.
A splash of water and a lid steam the carrots gently without any browning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a bright dry side with sambar rice or curd rice, or alongside rasam and appalam.

variations.name: Carrot Beans Poriyal
variations.description: A colourful two-vegetable poriyal combining sweet carrot with crunchy French beans for contrast in both colour and texture. Popular in Tamil marriage feasts, it is finished with coconut and a hint of green chilli, making a wholesome mixed side that brightens any thali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: keeps the mixed-veg poriyal fragrant and true to its Tamil roots

steps: Finely chop 2 carrots and 150 g French beans into small even pieces, keeping the beans slightly finer as they take longer to cook.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal and fry until the dal is golden.
Add 2 slit green chillies, the grated 0.5 inch ginger, 2 sprigs curry leaves and 0.25 tsp hing and crackle for 15 seconds.
Add the beans first with 0.75 tsp salt and a splash of water, cover and cook 5 minutes as they need a head start.
Add the carrots, cover and cook a further 6 minutes until both vegetables are just tender.
Uncover and stir-fry 2 minutes to dry the moisture.
Turn off the heat and toss through 0.33 cup grated coconut before serving.
tips: Give the beans a head start since they take longer to soften than the carrots.
Keep the vegetables slightly crunchy so the poriyal has texture, not mush.
Fresh ginger adds a subtle warmth that lifts the mixed vegetables.
variations.servingSuggestion: A festive dry side for a banana-leaf sappadu with sambar, rasam, rice and payasam.

variations.name: Carrot Paruppu Poriyal (Lentil)
variations.description: A protein-boosted poriyal where cooked moong dal is tossed with the carrots, giving a heartier, slightly creamy stir-fry. The soft dal clings to the sweet carrot and the dish needs no coconut, making it a nourishing everyday side that doubles as a light meal with rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil that gives the dal-carrot stir-fry a light nutty base

steps: Dry-roast 0.33 cup moong dal for 2 minutes until aromatic, then pressure-cook or simmer it with 1 cup water and 0.25 tsp turmeric until soft but not mushy, and drain any excess.
Peel and finely chop 4 carrots into small pieces.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, add 1 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tsp urad dal and 2 dry red chillies and fry until golden.
Add the slit green chilli, 2 sprigs curry leaves and 0.25 tsp hing and crackle for 15 seconds.
Add the chopped carrots with 0.75 tsp salt and a splash of water, cover and cook 8 minutes until tender.
Fold in the cooked moong dal and stir-fry gently for 3 minutes until it coats the carrots and any moisture dries.
Serve warm as a comforting, coconut-free poriyal.
tips: Roast the moong dal before cooking for a nuttier flavour and firmer, separate grains.
Cook the dal just until soft so it holds shape and does not turn to a paste.
This version keeps well and packs neatly into a lunchbox with rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rice and a spoon of ghee, or alongside vatha kuzhambu for a filling plate.

variations.name: Carrot Pepper Poriyal (Milagu)
variations.description: A coconut-free, no-onion peppery stir-fry where freshly crushed black pepper and cumin coat the carrots for a warming, aromatic finish. Light and mildly spicy, this Chettinad-leaning milagu poriyal is a comforting side often made during rains or for an upset stomach.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed til oil that suits the warming pepper-cumin seasoning

steps: Coarsely crush 1 tsp peppercorns with 1 tsp cumin seeds in a mortar to release their aroma.
Peel and finely chop 4 carrots into small even pieces.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadai, add 1 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tsp urad dal and 1 dry red chilli and fry until golden.
Add 2 sprigs curry leaves and 0.25 tsp hing and let them crackle for 10 seconds.
Add the chopped carrots with 0.75 tsp salt and a splash of water, cover and cook on low for 8 minutes until tender.
Uncover, sprinkle in the crushed pepper-cumin mix and stir-fry 3 minutes until the carrots are dry and well coated.
Serve warm as a fragrant, coconut-free peppery side.
tips: Crush the pepper and cumin fresh just before adding for the strongest aroma.
Add the pepper towards the end so its warmth stays bright and does not turn dull.
This soothing, coconut-free poriyal is gentle enough for light meals.
variations.servingSuggestion: Comforting with plain rice and rasam, or as a warming side during the monsoon season.

variations.name: Classic Pulikachal (Tamarind Rice Paste)
variations.description: Pulikachal is the concentrated tamarind rice paste from Tamil Nadu that transforms plain rice into instant puliyodarai. A robust roasted-spice powder is simmered with thick tamarind extract, sesame oil and jaggery until it turns into a glossy dark relish that keeps for weeks and coats every grain with tangy, spicy depth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed til oil is the soul of pulikachal and preserves the paste for weeks

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: rounds the sharp tamarind sourness without making the paste sweet

steps: Soak 1 cup tamarind in 2 cups hot water for 15 minutes and extract a very thick pulp.
Dry-roast 2 tbsp coriander seeds, 1 tsp fenugreek, 2 tbsp chana dal and 4 red chillies until golden, then roast 2 tbsp sesame separately and grind everything to a coarse powder.
Heat 0.5 cup Anveshan Sesame Oil in a heavy kadai, add 1 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tbsp urad dal, 0.33 cup peanuts and the remaining 4 red chillies and fry until the peanuts colour.
Add 3 sprigs curry leaves, 0.5 tsp hing and 0.5 tsp turmeric and let them sizzle for 15 seconds.
Pour in the thick tamarind extract with 1.5 tsp salt and simmer on low for 12 minutes until it darkens and thickens.
Stir in the ground spice powder and 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook another 8 minutes until the oil separates and the paste is glossy and thick.
Cool completely before storing in a clean dry jar.
tips: Extract the tamarind as thick as possible so you do not need to over-reduce the paste.
Cook until the sesame oil clearly separates, which is the sign the paste will keep well.
Use a dry spoon each time; stored well it lasts three to four weeks in the fridge.
variations.servingSuggestion: Mix 2 tablespoons into a bowl of cooled cooked rice with a little extra sesame oil for instant puliyodarai.

variations.name: Iyengar Temple Pulikachal
variations.description: The prasadam-style pulikachal served in Iyengar temples, distinguished by its generous roasted-gram and copra powder and a warm hint of dry ginger. It is milder in chilli but deeply aromatic, giving the puliyodarai its signature temple fragrance and slightly thicker, clinging texture.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: the traditional temple fat that carries the prasadam aroma and preserves the paste

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a restrained touch of sweetness typical of the temple version

steps: Soak 1 cup tamarind in 2 cups hot water and extract a thick pulp.
Dry-roast 2 tbsp coriander seeds, 5 red chillies and 1 tsp peppercorns until fragrant, then grind with 3 tbsp roasted gram, 3 tbsp copra and 1 tsp dry ginger powder to a slightly coarse powder.
Heat 0.5 cup Anveshan Sesame Oil, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and 0.25 cup peanuts and fry until the peanuts are golden.
Add 3 sprigs curry leaves, 0.5 tsp hing and 0.5 tsp turmeric and let them crackle for 15 seconds.
Pour in the tamarind extract with 1.5 tsp salt and simmer on low for 12 minutes until reduced and dark.
Stir in the ground gram-copra powder and 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook 8 minutes until thick and the oil separates.
Cool fully before bottling.
tips: The roasted gram and copra powder gives the temple version its characteristic thick, clinging body.
Keep the chilli gentle and let the pepper and dry ginger provide the warmth.
Rest the finished paste overnight for the flavours to bloom into true prasadam taste.
variations.servingSuggestion: Fold into warm rice with cashews and extra curry leaves for an authentic temple-style puliyodarai.

variations.name: Ellu Pulikachal (Sesame-Heavy)
variations.description: A nutty variation loaded with roasted white sesame ground into the base, giving the tamarind paste a rich, almost creamy body and a pronounced til aroma. The extra sesame makes it less sharp and more mellow, ideal for those who find plain pulikachal too tangy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: doubles the sesame theme and keeps the nutty paste well preserved

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: balances the tang so the roasted sesame flavour can come forward

steps: Soak 1 cup tamarind in 2 cups hot water and extract a thick pulp.
Dry-roast 0.5 cup sesame on low heat for 3 minutes until it pops, then roast 3 Byadgi chillies and 3 tbsp copra separately, and grind everything to a coarse-creamy powder.
Heat 0.5 cup Anveshan Sesame Oil, add 1 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tbsp urad dal, 3 tbsp cashews and the remaining 3 Byadgi chillies and fry until the cashews are golden, about 40 seconds.
Add 3 sprigs curry leaves, 0.5 tsp hing and 0.5 tsp turmeric and let them sizzle briefly.
Pour in the tamarind extract with 1.5 tsp salt and simmer 10 minutes until it darkens.
Stir in the sesame powder and 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook 8 minutes until thick, glossy and the oil surfaces.
Cool the paste completely so it firms up, then store it in a clean dry jar for up to three weeks.
tips: Take the sesame off the heat as soon as it pops, since burnt til turns the whole paste bitter.
Grinding half the sesame smooth and half coarse gives the best creamy-yet-textured body.
This mellower version is a good introduction to pulikachal for tangy-averse eaters.
variations.servingSuggestion: Mix into rice and top with fried cashews and a spoon of sesame oil for a rich ellu sadam.

variations.name: Puli Inji Pulikachal (Ginger)
variations.description: A ginger-forward take inspired by Kerala's puli inji, where a generous amount of fresh ginger goes into the tamarind base for a warming, digestive kick. Brighter and more pungent than the standard paste, it doubles beautifully as a sweet-sour-spicy ginger relish on its own.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed til oil that fries the ginger and preserves the relish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a fuller sweetness to balance the strong ginger and tamarind

steps: Soak 0.75 cup tamarind in 1.5 cups hot water and extract a thick pulp.
Peel and finely mince 4 inches of ginger, keeping it fairly fine so it melts into the paste.
Dry-roast 1 tbsp coriander seeds, 0.5 tsp fenugreek and 3 red chillies, and grind to a coarse powder.
Heat 0.5 cup Anveshan Sesame Oil, add 1 tsp mustard seeds and the remaining 3 red chillies, then add the minced ginger and fry for 4 minutes until fragrant and softened.
Add 3 sprigs curry leaves, 0.5 tsp hing and 0.5 tsp turmeric, then pour in the tamarind extract with 1.5 tsp salt and simmer 10 minutes.
Stir in the ground powder and 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook 8 minutes until thick, dark and the oil separates.
Cool completely before storing.
tips: Fry the ginger patiently so its raw pungency mellows into a warm, rounded flavour.
This version leans sweeter to tame the ginger, so add jaggery to taste as you go.
It works both mixed into rice and served as a tangy ginger pickle beside a meal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a puli inji relish on a sadya, or stir into rice for a warming ginger puliyodarai.

variations.name: Classic Puliyogare
variations.description: Karnataka's iconic tamarind rice, built on a slow-cooked pulikachal, a dark, glossy tamarind concentrate simmered with jaggery, sesame and a roasted spice powder until thick. Folded through cooled rice with plenty of curry leaves and roasted peanuts, it delivers the signature sweet-sour-spicy punch that keeps for days. A travel food, a temple prasadam and a lunchbox hero all at once.

ingredients.name: Cooked rice
ingredients.note: Cooled day-old rice, grains rubbed loose

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: Soaked in hot water for a thick extract

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil is the soul of pulikachal, carrying the tamarind and spice

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Balances the sharp tamarind into the signature sweet-sour pulikachal

ingredients.name: Sesame seeds
ingredients.note: Roasted and ground into the finishing powder

steps: Dry-roast 1 tbsp coriander seeds, 1 tbsp chana dal, 3 dry red chillies and 2 tbsp sesame seeds over low heat until golden and fragrant, cool, and grind to a coarse puliyogare powder.
Soak the tamarind in 1 cup hot water for 15 minutes and squeeze out a thick, dark extract, discarding the fibres.

Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a heavy pan over medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tbsp urad dal, add 2 remaining red chillies, 1/4 cup peanuts, 1/2 tsp asafoetida and 15 curry leaves and fry until the peanuts turn crunchy.
Pour in the tamarind extract with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp salt, bring to a boil, then simmer on low for 10-12 minutes until it darkens and thickens to a jammy pulikachal that coats the spoon.
Stir in 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and the ground puliyogare powder and cook for 3 more minutes until the oil glistens on the surface.
Take 4-5 tbsp of this pulikachal and fold it through 3 cups cooled rice a little at a time until evenly coated, then let it rest 15 minutes so the flavour soaks in before serving.
tips: Make a big jar of pulikachal in advance; it keeps for two to three weeks refrigerated and just needs folding into fresh rice.
Always mix into cooled, not hot, rice so the grains stay separate and do not turn sticky and clumpy.
Let the mixed rice sit for at least fifteen minutes before serving; puliyogare tastes markedly better once rested.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature with fried papad, a bowl of thick curd and a handful of extra fried peanuts and boondi on the side.

variations.name: Iyengar Temple Puliyogare
variations.description: The prasadam version handed out at Iyengar temples is darker, more aromatic and generous with a dry gojju powder rich in roasted copra and sesame. Extra hing and a restrained sweetness make it fragrant rather than tangy-sweet, and it is always glossed with plenty of gingelly oil. This is the puliyogare that perfumes an entire temple courtyard.

ingredients.name: Cooked rice
ingredients.note: Sona masuri, cooked firm and spread to cool

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: Soaked for a thick prasadam-strength extract

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Temple puliyogare is unapologetically rich in gingelly oil for its glossy finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A gentle sweetness, kept restrained in the temple style

ingredients.name: Copra (dry coconut)
ingredients.note: Roasted dark for the signature gojju powder

steps: Roast 1/4 cup copra, 3 tbsp sesame seeds, 1.5 tbsp coriander seeds, 4 dry red chillies and 1/2 tsp fenugreek separately over low heat until each is deeply fragrant, cool, and grind to a fine gojju powder.
Soak the tamarind in 1 cup hot water and extract a thick, dark juice, straining out all the fibre.

Heat 5 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadhai over medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tbsp chana dal, add 2 remaining red chillies, 3/4 tsp asafoetida and 20 curry leaves and let them crackle for 30 seconds.
Pour in the tamarind extract with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp salt, bring to a boil and simmer on low for 12 minutes until it reduces to a thick, oil-slicked concentrate.
Add 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and the ground gojju powder, stirring for 3-4 minutes until the mixture is glossy and pulls together.
Fold generous spoonfuls of this concentrate into 3 cups cooled rice, mixing gently until each grain is a warm mahogany, then rest covered for 20 minutes.
tips: The dry gojju powder is what distinguishes temple puliyogare, so roast each spice separately for even, controlled colour.
A slightly higher dose of asafoetida gives the authentic prasadam fragrance, so do not be shy with it.
Sprinkle a little extra gojju powder over the plated rice for a stronger aroma when serving guests.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a banana leaf at room temperature with a small mound of curd rice and a fried vadam for a true temple-meal feel.

variations.name: Raw Mango Puliyogare
variations.description: A summer variation where grated green mango replaces the cooked tamarind, giving a brighter, fresher sourness and a lighter colour. There is no long simmered pulikachal here; the mango is tempered quickly with spices and tossed straight through the rice. Zingy, quick and seasonal, it is the puliyogare to make when raw mangoes flood the market.

ingredients.name: Cooked rice
ingredients.note: Cooled and separated

ingredients.name: Grated raw mango
ingredients.note: Sour green mango, peeled and grated fine

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil suits the fresh, summery profile of the mango version

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon lends the traditional gingelly depth without heaviness

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan over medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tbsp chana dal and 1 tbsp urad dal until the dals redden, then add 1/4 cup peanuts and fry until crunchy.
Add 2 broken dry red chillies, 3 slit green chillies, 1/2 tsp asafoetida and 15 curry leaves and let them sizzle for 20 seconds.
Stir in 1 cup grated raw mango and 1/2 tsp turmeric and cook over medium heat for 4-5 minutes until the mango softens and loses its raw pungency but stays tangy.
Add 1/3 cup fresh grated coconut and 1.25 tsp salt and cook for 2 more minutes until the mixture is fragrant and just holds together.
Take the pan off the heat, add 3 cups cooled rice and fold gently until the grains are evenly flecked with the mango tempering.
Drizzle 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil over the top, toss once more, and let it rest 10 minutes for the flavours to meld before serving.
tips: Taste your mango first; a very sour one needs less, while a mild one may want an extra squeeze of lemon at the end.
Cook the mango just until it softens, since overcooking dulls the fresh tang that makes this version special.
This is best eaten the same day, as the grated mango loosens water overnight and softens the rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature with crunchy fried sandige and a cooling cucumber-curd pachadi to balance the tang.

variations.name: Andhra-Style Pulihora
variations.description: The neighbouring Andhra take turns up the heat and the tang, with a fiery menthi (fenugreek) podi and extra dry red chillies giving it a bolder, spicier backbone than its Karnataka cousin. Chana and urad dal fried till nutty add crunch, and the rice glows deep golden with turmeric. Robust, hot and unmistakably Telugu.

ingredients.name: Cooked rice
ingredients.note: Cooled, with a spoon of oil rubbed in to separate grains

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: Soaked for a strong, tangy extract

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the everyday Andhra frying fat for a robust pulihora

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Just enough to round the fierce tamarind-chilli edge, not to sweeten

ingredients.name: Fenugreek seeds
ingredients.note: Roasted and ground into the signature menthi podi

steps: Roast 1 tsp fenugreek seeds, 2 tbsp sesame seeds and 4 dry red chillies separately over low heat until fragrant, cool, and grind to a fine menthi podi.
Soak the tamarind in 1 cup hot water and squeeze out a strong, thick extract, discarding the pulp fibres.

Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a heavy pan over medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 1.5 tbsp chana dal, 1.5 tbsp urad dal and 1/4 cup peanuts and fry until everything is deep golden and crunchy.
Add the remaining 4 dry red chillies, 3/4 tsp asafoetida and 18 curry leaves, then pour in the tamarind extract with 3/4 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp salt.
Simmer on low for 10-12 minutes until the mixture thickens and the oil floats to the surface, then stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and the menthi podi and cook for 3 more minutes.
Fold the hot pulihora paste through 3 cups cooled rice a few spoons at a time until evenly coated and deep gold, then rest 15 minutes so the heat and tang settle in.
tips: The menthi podi should be used sparingly and tasted as you go, since too much fenugreek turns the rice bitter.
Andhra pulihora is meant to be assertively sour and hot, so hold back on jaggery if you want it truly authentic.
It keeps beautifully for two days at room temperature, making it a classic travel and festival food.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with fried green chillies, crisp appadam and a bowl of plain curd to cool the palate between fiery bites.

variations.name: Classic Ragi Rotti
variations.description: The everyday South Karnataka breakfast where finger-millet flour is mixed with chopped onion, green chilli, coconut and cumin, then patted directly onto a hot tava with wet fingers. There is no rolling; the dough is spread thin by hand and cooked with holes for steam. Earthy, nutty and studded with crunch, it is a nourishing gluten-free start to the day.

ingredients.name: Ragi flour
ingredients.note: Fine finger-millet flour, the base of the rotti

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: Very finely chopped so the rotti pats out evenly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil for drizzling around the rotti gives the authentic Malnad aroma

ingredients.name: Hot water
ingredients.note: Added a little at a time to make a soft, spreadable dough

steps: In a wide bowl combine 2 cups ragi flour, 1 finely chopped onion, 1/4 cup grated coconut, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp cumin, 10 chopped curry leaves, 3 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp salt, rubbing the onion in so it releases a little moisture.
Pour in about 1 cup hot water in stages, mixing with a spoon then your hand, to form a soft, moist dough that just holds together without being runny.

Wet your palm, take a lemon-sized ball, and pat it directly onto a cold or lightly greased tava into a thin 6-inch round, dipping your fingers in water as you spread and poking three or four holes for steam.
Place the tava on medium heat, drizzle 1/2 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil into the holes and around the edge, cover and cook for about 2 minutes until the base sets and browns.
Flip carefully and cook the second side uncovered for 1-2 minutes until brown spots appear and the rotti smells toasty and nutty.
Slide off, wipe the tava, and repeat with the remaining dough, patting each rotti fresh so it does not dry out.
tips: Patting onto a cold tava and then heating it makes the first flip far easier for beginners.
Keep your fingers wet throughout; ragi dough is sticky and water is what lets you spread it thin without tearing.
Mix only as much dough as you will cook immediately, since the onion makes it weep and go soggy on standing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot off the tava with coconut chutney, a dab of butter and a cup of filter coffee for a classic Karnataka breakfast.

variations.name: Soft Kneaded Ragi Roti
variations.description: A gentler, rollable version for those who find patting tricky: ragi flour is scalded with boiling water and kneaded with a little khapli atta into a smooth, pliable dough that rolls out like a chapati. There is no onion or coconut here, just a plain, soft, foldable flatbread that pairs with any curry. Ideal for lunchboxes and for easing millet into everyday rotis.

ingredients.name: Ragi flour
ingredients.note: Scalded with boiling water to make it pliable

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: A little emmer wheat gives the millet enough gluten to roll into soft, foldable rotis

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Brushed on the hot rotis to keep them soft and pliable

ingredients.name: Boiling water
ingredients.note: Poured over the ragi flour to cook and bind it

steps: Put 1.5 cups ragi flour, 1 tbsp sesame seeds and 3/4 tsp salt in a bowl, pour over about 1.25 cups boiling water and stir quickly with a spoon until it forms a shaggy, steaming mass.
When cool enough to handle, add 1/2 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta and knead firmly for 4-5 minutes into a smooth, non-sticky dough, using a few drops of warm water if it feels dry.
Cover and rest the dough for 10 minutes, then divide into 8 equal balls and keep them under a damp cloth.
Dust with a little khapli atta and roll each ball into a 6-inch round with gentle, even pressure, turning it often so it does not stick.
Cook on a medium-hot tava for about a minute until the base shows small bubbles, flip, press the edges with a cloth, and cook the second side until brown spots form.
Brush each hot roti with a little Anveshan Ghee, stack in a cloth-lined box, and serve warm and folded.
tips: Scalding the ragi with boiling water is what makes it rollable, so do not skip this step or use cold water.
Roll gently and keep the roti a touch thicker than a wheat chapati, as ragi dough tears more easily.
Wrapping the cooked rotis in a cloth traps steam and keeps them soft for hours in a tiffin.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a simple dal, avial or any dry sabzi, or with a smear of ghee and jaggery for a quick sweet roll.

variations.name: Mixed Vegetable Ragi Rotti
variations.description: A colourful, nutrient-dense patted rotti packed with grated carrot, chopped dill and capsicum alongside the millet, turning breakfast into a near-complete meal. The vegetables keep it moist and add sweetness against the earthy ragi. A favourite way to sneak greens and colour onto a child's plate.

ingredients.name: Ragi flour
ingredients.note: The millet base of the rotti

ingredients.name: Chopped dill leaves
ingredients.note: Sabsige soppu, for a fragrant herby lift

ingredients.name: Capsicum
ingredients.note: Finely chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil for cooking gives these veg-loaded rottis a crisp, golden base

ingredients.name: Hot water
ingredients.note: The vegetables release water, so add less

steps: Combine 2 cups ragi flour, 1/2 cup grated carrot, 1/4 cup chopped dill, 1/3 cup chopped capsicum, 1 tbsp grated ginger, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp cumin and 1 tsp salt in a wide bowl and mix well.
Add about 3/4 cup hot water gradually, mixing into a soft, moist dough; because the vegetables weep, add water carefully so it does not turn loose.
Wet your palm, take a lemon-sized portion and pat it onto a lightly greased tava into a thin 6-inch round, dipping fingers in water and making a few holes for steam.
Set on medium heat, drizzle 1/2 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil into the holes and edges, cover, and cook for 2-3 minutes until the base is set and crisp.
Flip and cook the second side uncovered for about 2 minutes until golden-brown spots appear and the vegetables look cooked.
Remove, wipe the tava clean, and pat out the next rotti fresh, repeating until the dough is used up.
tips: Squeeze the grated carrot lightly if it is very juicy, so the dough does not become too wet to pat.
Dill can be swapped for chopped methi or spring onion greens depending on what is fresh.
Cook these a shade longer than plain ragi rotti so the capsicum and carrot lose their raw crunch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a bowl of thick curd, a green chutney and a wedge of lime for a wholesome one-plate breakfast.

variations.name: Crispy Sesame Ragi Rotti
variations.description: A thin, shatteringly crisp version leaning towards a Davanagere-style snack, where rice flour and toasted sesame join the ragi and ajwain, red chilli and butter give it a spiced richness. Patted extra thin and cooked slow, it crackles at the edges like a savoury cracker. Best eaten straight off the tava with a smear of white butter.

ingredients.name: Ragi flour
ingredients.note: The millet base

ingredients.name: Rice flour
ingredients.note: Adds crispness and helps the rotti spread thin

ingredients.name: Sesame seeds
ingredients.note: Toasted for a nutty crunch

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Used to shallow-roast the thin rottis to a crisp, buttery finish

steps: Toast 2 tbsp sesame seeds in a dry pan over low heat for a minute until they pop and smell nutty, then tip into a bowl.
Add 1.5 cups ragi flour, 1/2 cup rice flour, 1 tsp ajwain, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tbsp coriander, 1 tsp salt and the softened 2 tbsp white butter, rubbing the butter through the flour.
Pour in about 1 cup hot water in stages and mix into a soft, smooth dough that spreads easily when patted.
Wet your fingers and pat a lemon-sized ball onto a lightly greased tava into a very thin 7-inch round, making several holes so it crisps rather than steams.
Cook on low to medium heat, drizzling 1/2 tsp Anveshan Ghee around and into the holes, for 3-4 minutes until the base turns deep and crisp before flipping.
Flip and cook the second side with another 1/2 tsp ghee until it is browned and crackly at the edges, then serve at once.
tips: Cook these slower and thinner than a regular ragi rotti; low heat and patience are what make them shatter-crisp.
The rice flour is essential for the crackle, so do not replace it with more ragi.
These stay crisp for a few hours, making them a good tea-time snack rather than a soft breakfast.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a knob of white butter melting on top and a spicy tomato-garlic chutney, alongside hot tea.

variations.name: Classic Ribbon Pakoda (Ola Pakoda)
variations.description: Flat, ribbon-like ropes of gram-and-rice dough pressed into hot oil and fried until they crackle, also called Ola Pakoda for their palm-leaf shape. Seasoned with chilli and asafoetida, they are a Diwali staple that stays crisp for weeks. Long, wavy and shatteringly crunchy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Hot shortening rubbed into the flour for a light, crisp ribbon that never turns hard

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Clean wood-pressed oil for deep-frying the ribbons to a golden snap

steps: Mix 1.5 cups besan and 1 cup rice flour with 1.5 tsp chilli powder, 0.5 tsp asafoetida, 0.5 tsp ajwain and 1 tsp salt in a wide bowl.
Rub in 2 tbsp hot Anveshan Ghee until the mix clumps when pressed, then add about 0.66 cups water gradually to a smooth, soft, non-sticky dough.
Fill a press fitted with the flat ribbon disc and keep the dough covered so it stays pliable.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to about 180C until a scrap of dough rises steadily.
Press long, overlapping ribbons across the surface of the oil, working in a zigzag so they do not clump together.
Fry for 3 to 4 minutes, turning once, until the bubbling quietens and the ribbons are golden and crisp, then drain on paper.
tips: Keep the besan-to-rice ratio at about three to two, as too much besan makes the ribbons soft and too much rice makes them brittle.
Lift the ribbons out the moment the loud sizzle subsides for maximum crunch.
Break the cooled ribbons into shorter lengths for easy storage in a tin.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a Diwali munchie alongside sweet boondi ladoo, or crumble over rasam rice for crunch.

variations.name: Sesame Ribbon Pakoda
variations.description: A nuttier ribbon pakoda generously worked with white sesame and a whisper of roasted cumin. The sesame toasts as the ribbons fry, adding tiny crunchy specks and a warm aroma. It is the fragrant version that fills the kitchen with the smell of festival cooking.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Shortening that deepens the toasty sesame note running through the ribbons

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Neutral frying oil that lets the sesame aroma shine while crisping the ribbons

steps: Mix 1.5 cups besan and 1 cup rice flour with 3 tbsp sesame seeds, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp chilli powder, 0.5 tsp asafoetida and 1 tsp salt.
Rub in 2 tbsp warm Anveshan Sesame Oil until the flour holds together, then add about 0.66 cups water to a soft, pliable dough.
Load a press with the ribbon disc and keep the dough covered under a damp cloth.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C until a bit of dough floats up briskly.
Press wavy ribbons over the oil in a criss-cross so they stay separate, and fry for 3 to 4 minutes, turning once.
Lift out when the sizzling calms and the sesame smells toasted, then drain on paper.
tips: Do not over-add sesame or the ribbons weaken and break; three tablespoons is the sweet spot.
Use roasted cumin powder rather than raw seeds so the flavour is even through the dough.
Store only when fully cool, as warm ribbons trap steam and soften the sesame crunch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a cup of adrak chai; the sesame ribbons are especially good on a cold evening.

variations.name: Garlic-Chilli Ribbon Pakoda
variations.description: A fiery ribbon pakoda charged with pounded garlic and extra red chilli for a bold, savoury punch. The garlic crisps within the ribbons and gives an addictive, chaat-shop heat. This is the version that vanishes fastest at any festive spread.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Shortening that carries the garlic-chilli heat and keeps the ribbons crisp

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Deep-fries the spicy ribbons to a deep golden crunch

steps: Pound 8 garlic cloves to a smooth paste and combine with 2 tsp chilli powder and 0.5 tsp pepper powder.
Mix 1.5 cups besan and 1 cup rice flour with 0.5 tsp asafoetida and 1 tsp salt, then stir in the garlic-chilli paste.
Rub in 2 tbsp hot Anveshan Ghee, then add about 0.66 cups water gradually to a soft, smooth dough.
Fill the press with the ribbon disc and heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C.
Press long ribbons over the oil in a zigzag and fry for 3 to 4 minutes, turning once, until deep gold and the bubbling subsides.
Drain on paper and cool fully so the garlic heat sets into a firm crunch.
tips: Grind the garlic to a fine paste so it distributes evenly and does not scorch in patches.
Add a pinch of sugar to round off the sharp garlic and chilli.
Fry these a touch darker than plain ribbons for the fullest garlic flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a spicy cocktail snack with chilled buttermilk or a cool raita on the side.

variations.name: Sattu Ribbon Pakoda
variations.description: A protein-rich ribbon pakoda that swaps ordinary gram flour for roasted-gram sattu, giving a deeper roasted flavour and a lighter, more digestible crunch. The pre-roasted sattu needs less oil and fries especially crisp. A wholesome reinvention of the festive favourite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Roasted gram flour that replaces raw besan for a nuttier, more digestible ribbon

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Warm shortening that binds the sattu dough into pliable, crisp-frying ribbons

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Deep-fries the sattu ribbons to a crisp, even gold

steps: Mix 1.5 cups Anveshan Sattu with 1 cup rice flour, 1.5 tsp chilli powder, 0.5 tsp ajwain, 0.5 tsp asafoetida, 1 tbsp sesame and 1 tsp salt.
Rub in 2 tbsp hot Anveshan Ghee until crumbly, then add about 0.7 cups water gradually to a soft dough, as sattu absorbs a little more moisture than besan.
Fill a press with the ribbon disc and keep the dough covered while you heat the oil.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C until a scrap of dough rises promptly.
Press wavy ribbons across the oil in a criss-cross and fry for 3 minutes, turning once, until the sizzle quietens.
Because sattu is already roasted these crisp quickly, so drain them the moment they turn golden.
tips: Sattu is pre-roasted, so these fry faster than besan ribbons; watch them closely to avoid over-browning.
Add water slowly, as sattu can go from crumbly to sticky in a splash.
The roasted sattu gives a savoury depth, so you can ease back on the chilli if you like it milder.
variations.servingSuggestion: A lighter, higher-protein festive snack that pairs well with masala chai or a fruit chaat.

variations.name: Classic Sakkarai Pongal
variations.description: Sakkarai pongal is the Tamil harvest sweet of rice and moong dal cooked soft, then folded into molten jaggery and finished with a generous ladle of ghee. Fragrant with cardamom, edible camphor and ghee-fried cashews, it is the first thing offered on Pongal morning and at every temple.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted into a syrup to sweeten the pongal with deep, mineral-rich caramel

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: poured in through cooking to give the pongal its glossy sheen and temple aroma

steps: Dry roast 0.25 cup yellow moong dal in a pan over low heat for about 2 minutes until it smells nutty, then rinse it with 1 cup raw rice.
Pressure cook the rice and dal with 4 cups water and 0.5 cup milk for 5 whistles until very soft and mushy, then mash lightly.
Melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 0.5 cup water over low heat, stir until dissolved, strain out grit and simmer to a sticky syrup, about 4 minutes.
Add the mashed rice-dal to the jaggery syrup and cook on low heat for 5 minutes, pouring in 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee a little at a time until glossy.
In the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, fry 2 tbsp cashews and 1 tbsp raisins until golden and plump, about 2 minutes.
Fold in the fried nuts, 0.5 tsp cardamom, 0.25 tsp dry ginger and a pinch of edible camphor, then serve the pongal warm.
tips: Cook the rice and dal until genuinely mushy; a grainy pongal never turns creamy no matter how much ghee you add.
Always add jaggery as a strained syrup after the rice is cooked, since jaggery hardens raw grains if added too early.
Edible camphor is potent, so a single pinch is enough to lend that unmistakable temple fragrance.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as prasadam or festive breakfast, drizzled with extra ghee and topped with a few whole fried cashews.

variations.name: Kovil Sakkarai Pongal
variations.description: The temple-kitchen version cooked for deities, richer with coconut slivers, freshly grated nutmeg and a heavier hand of ghee. Slow-simmered in a bronze uruli, it turns dense, dark and intensely aromatic, the pongal that fills a whole sanctum with its scent.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: used generously for the dark, dense temple pongal offered to deities

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: poured lavishly so the pongal glistens and pools ghee in true kovil style

steps: Rinse 1 cup raw rice with 0.3 cup moong dal and pressure cook with 4 cups water for 6 whistles until collapsing and soft.
Melt 1.25 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 0.5 cup water over low heat, strain the syrup clean and reduce it until thick and glossy, about 5 minutes.
Tip the mashed rice-dal into the syrup and simmer on low heat for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring as it darkens and thickens.
In 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee fry 3 tbsp cashews and 3 tbsp fresh coconut slivers until both turn golden, about 3 minutes.
Pour in the remaining 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee gradually while stirring until the pongal turns deep amber and releases ghee at the edges.
Fold in the fried cashews and coconut, 0.5 tsp cardamom, 0.25 tsp grated nutmeg and a pinch of edible camphor, then serve hot.
tips: A wide heavy uruli or kadhai lets the pongal reduce and darken evenly, which is what gives the temple version its depth.
Toast the coconut slivers until just golden; over-browning turns them bitter against the sweet jaggery.
Do not stint on the ghee here, as the glossy pooling richness is the whole character of kovil pongal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a banana leaf as temple prasadam, mounded high and finished with an extra spoon of warm ghee poured over the top.

variations.name: Thinai Sakkarai Pongal
variations.description: A wholesome, gluten-light twist made with foxtail millet in place of rice, giving a lighter, nuttier pongal that still turns creamy against the jaggery. Popular with those cutting back on white rice, it keeps every bit of the festive flavour with more fibre and a delicate grassy sweetness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the millet pongal with earthy caramel that suits its nutty grain

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: keeps the light millet creamy and glossy rather than dry

steps: Rinse 1 cup foxtail millet several times, then dry roast 0.25 cup moong dal over low heat for 2 minutes until fragrant.
Pressure cook the millet and dal with 4 cups water and 0.5 cup milk for 4 whistles until soft and porridge-like, then mash gently.
Melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 0.5 cup water, strain out grit and simmer to a light syrup, about 4 minutes.
Stir the cooked millet-dal into the syrup and cook on low heat for 4 to 5 minutes, adding 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee gradually until creamy.
Fry 2 tbsp cashews and 2 tbsp coconut slivers in the last 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until golden, about 2 minutes.
Fold in the fried nuts and coconut, 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp dry ginger, then serve the millet pongal warm.
tips: Rinse foxtail millet well and cook it a touch softer than rice, as millet firms up quickly once it cools.
A splash of hot milk revives the pongal beautifully if it stiffens on standing.
Foxtail millet drinks up liquid, so keep a little extra hot water handy to loosen the pongal to the texture you like.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve this lighter pongal warm for a festive breakfast, alongside a small cup of coffee, topped with toasted coconut slivers.

variations.name: Akkaravadisal
variations.description: Akkaravadisal is the decadent Srirangam temple cousin of pongal, cooked almost entirely in milk until silky, then loaded with saffron, nutmeg and a river of ghee. Softer, richer and more pudding-like than everyday pongal, it is the offering reserved for the grandest festival days.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted into the milk-cooked rice for a mellow, caramel-rich sweetness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: added in a lavish stream for the signature silky, ghee-laden akkaravadisal

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm milk to perfume and gild this festive temple pudding

steps: Soak 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk taken from the 4 cups and set aside to bloom.
Rinse 1 cup raw rice with 0.25 cup moong dal and pressure cook with the remaining milk for 5 whistles until very soft and creamy.
Melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 0.25 cup water, strain, and simmer to a thick syrup, about 4 minutes.
Mash the milk-cooked rice, stir it into the jaggery syrup and cook on low heat for 6 to 8 minutes, adding 6 tbsp Anveshan Ghee gradually until silky.
Fry 3 tbsp cashews in the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until golden, about 2 minutes, then stir them in with the bloomed saffron milk.
Finish with 0.5 tsp cardamom, 0.25 tsp grated nutmeg and a pinch of edible camphor, then serve the akkaravadisal warm and glossy.
tips: Cooking the rice fully in milk rather than water is what gives akkaravadisal its luxurious, pudding-soft body.
Keep the flame low once the milk and jaggery meet so the pudding stays smooth and does not catch.
It should be pourably soft when hot, as it thickens considerably as it cools; loosen with warm milk if needed.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm in small bowls as a grand festive dessert, with a final drizzle of ghee and a few saffron strands on top.

variations.name: Classic Semiya Payasam
variations.description: Semiya payasam is the everyday South Indian kheer of ghee-roasted vermicelli simmered in sweetened milk until soft and silky. Perfumed with cardamom and saffron and studded with fried cashews and raisins, it is the fastest festive sweet in the Tamil kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: sweetens the milk cleanly so the roasted vermicelli flavour stays forward

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the vermicelli golden and fries the nuts for a fragrant payasam

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm milk to gild and perfume the payasam

steps: Soak 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk taken from the 4 cups and set aside.
In 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, fry 2 tbsp cashews and 1 tbsp raisins over medium heat until golden and plump, then lift them out.
In the same ghee, roast 0.75 cup vermicelli, stirring constantly, for 2 to 3 minutes until evenly golden.
Pour in the remaining milk, bring to a gentle boil and simmer on low heat for 8 to 10 minutes until the vermicelli is soft and the milk thickens.
Stir in 0.6 cup Anveshan Khandsari and the bloomed saffron milk and cook for 3 minutes until dissolved.
Fold in the fried nuts and 0.5 tsp cardamom, then serve the semiya payasam warm or chilled.
tips: Roast the vermicelli to an even gold before adding milk, as this stops it turning to mush and adds a nutty depth.
Vermicelli keeps drinking up milk, so keep the payasam loose and thin it with warm milk before serving.
Add the sugar only after the vermicelli has softened, or the strands stay firm at the centre.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a quick festive dessert or chilled in tumblers on a hot day, topped with extra fried cashews.

variations.name: Coconut Milk Semiya Payasam
variations.description: A dairy-free take where roasted vermicelli is simmered in coconut milk and sweetened with jaggery for a caramel-rich, tropical payasam. Fried coconut bits and coconut oil give it an unmistakable Kerala fragrance while keeping it entirely plant-based.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted separately and stirred in off heat to sweeten the coconut payasam without splitting

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: roasts the vermicelli and fries the coconut for a fragrant, tropical payasam

steps: In 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, fry 3 tbsp coconut bits and 2 tbsp cashews over medium heat until golden, about 3 minutes, then lift them out.
In the same oil, roast 0.75 cup vermicelli for 2 to 3 minutes until golden and fragrant.
Add 2 cups water, bring to a boil and simmer on low heat for 6 to 8 minutes until the vermicelli is soft.
Separately melt 0.7 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water, strain, and set the syrup aside.
Lower the heat, pour in 1.5 cups thick coconut milk and the strained jaggery syrup, and warm for 2 minutes without letting it boil so it does not curdle.
Stir in the fried coconut and cashews, 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp dry ginger, then serve warm.
tips: Add the coconut milk and jaggery only at the end and never let them boil, or the coconut milk will split.
Cook the vermicelli in water first so you use less coconut milk and keep the payasam from turning heavy.
A pinch of dry ginger cuts the richness of the coconut milk and aids digestion after a heavy meal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a vegan festive sweet, garnished with extra coconut-oil-fried coconut bits and cashews.

variations.name: Semiya Sabudana Payasam
variations.description: A textural payasam that pairs soft vermicelli with translucent sago pearls, giving every spoon both silky strands and gentle chew. The pearls thicken the milk naturally, making this a slightly more substantial and festive version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: sweetens the milk while keeping the sago pearls clear and glossy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the vermicelli and fries the nuts for a rich, aromatic payasam

steps: Soak 0.25 cup sago pearls in 1 cup water for 20 minutes, then simmer for 6 minutes until fully translucent and set aside.
In 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, fry 2 tbsp cashews and 1 tbsp raisins until golden, about 2 minutes, then lift them out.
In the same ghee, roast 0.5 cup vermicelli for 2 minutes until golden, then pour in 4 cups full-fat milk.
Simmer on low heat for 8 minutes until the vermicelli softens, then add the cooked sago and cook another 4 minutes until the pudding thickens.
Stir in 0.6 cup Anveshan Khandsari and cook for 3 minutes until dissolved and creamy.
Fold in the fried nuts and 0.5 tsp cardamom, then serve the payasam warm.
tips: Cook the sago separately until fully clear before adding, so it does not turn the milk cloudy or stay chalky.
Both vermicelli and sago keep swelling, so make this payasam looser than you think and adjust with warm milk.
Stir gently after adding sago, as vigorous stirring can make the pearls break and go gluey.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a heartier festive dessert, garnished with slivered nuts and a light dusting of cardamom.

variations.name: Badam Kesar Semiya Payasam
variations.description: A celebration-grade payasam enriched with ground almonds and bloomed saffron, giving a thick, golden, nutty pudding fit for weddings. The almond powder plushes up the milk while slivered almonds add a delicate crunch to every spoon.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm milk to colour and perfume this rich festive payasam

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: sweetens the almond-thickened milk without dulling the saffron gold

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the vermicelli and fries the slivered almonds for a luxurious finish

steps: Soak 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk taken from the 4 cups and set aside to bloom.
In 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, fry 3 tbsp slivered almonds over medium heat until pale gold, about 1 minute, then lift them out.
In the same ghee, roast 0.75 cup vermicelli for 2 to 3 minutes until golden, then pour in the remaining milk.
Simmer on low heat for 8 minutes until soft, then whisk in 0.25 cup almond powder and cook 3 minutes until the payasam thickens.
Stir in 0.6 cup Anveshan Khandsari and the bloomed saffron milk and cook for 3 minutes until dissolved and golden.
Fold in the fried slivered almonds and 0.5 tsp cardamom, then serve the badam semiya payasam warm.
tips: Whisk the almond powder in slowly to avoid lumps and give the payasam a smooth, plush body.
Bloom the saffron in warm milk first so both its colour and aroma spread evenly through the pudding.
This payasam thickens a lot as it cools thanks to the almond powder, so keep it noticeably loose while hot.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve this saffron-almond payasam at weddings and festivals, garnished with slivered pistachios and saffron strands.

variations.name: Classic Semiya Upma
variations.description: The everyday South Indian breakfast of roasted vermicelli steamed with a simple mustard and curry leaf tempering until the strands turn soft yet separate. Plain, quick and comforting, it is what most Tamil homes make on a busy morning. Roasting the semiya first is the secret to keeping it fluffy rather than sticky.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasts the vermicelli golden and finishes the upma with a gentle aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed oil for a clean tempering that keeps the strands light

steps: Roast 2 cups vermicelli in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium-low heat, stirring for 3-4 minutes until evenly golden, then set aside; skip if using pre-roasted semiya.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, fry 1 tbsp urad dal and 10 cashews until golden.
Add 12 curry leaves, 2 slit green chillies and grated 1 inch ginger, then 1 chopped onion, sauteing 3 minutes until the onion softens.
Pour in 3 cups water with 1 tsp salt and bring to a rolling boil.
Add the roasted vermicelli and stir once to submerge it evenly in the water.
Cover and cook on low for 4-5 minutes until the water is absorbed and the strands are soft but still separate, stirring once midway.
Fold in the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, switch off and rest covered 2 minutes before fluffing and serving.
tips: Use about 1.5 parts water to 1 part semiya; too much water turns it into a paste.
Roasting the vermicelli to a proper golden is the single step that keeps it fluffy and non-sticky.
A squeeze of lime just before serving lifts the whole dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with coconut chutney, a spoon of sugar for those who like it sweet, and a wedge of lime.

variations.name: Vegetable Semiya Upma
variations.description: A wholesome version loaded with carrot, beans and peas, turning the humble semiya into a colourful, near-complete meal. The vegetables add sweetness, bite and colour while keeping the dish light. It is the go-to for packing a nutritious tiffin that children will actually finish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Roasts the vermicelli and enriches the vegetable-studded upma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed oil for sauteing the vegetables cleanly

steps: Roast 2 cups vermicelli in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium-low heat until evenly golden, about 4 minutes, then set aside.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, fry 1 tbsp urad dal and 1 tbsp chana dal until golden, then add 12 curry leaves and 2 slit green chillies.
Add 1 chopped onion and grated 1 inch ginger, sauteing 2 minutes, then stir in 1 diced carrot, 8 chopped beans and 1/3 cup peas with a pinch of salt.
Cover and cook the vegetables for 4 minutes until just tender but still bright.
Pour in 3 cups water with 1 tsp salt and bring to a rolling boil, then add the roasted vermicelli and stir once.
