Cover and cook on low for 5 minutes until the water is absorbed and the strands are soft.
Fold in the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, rest covered 2 minutes and serve garnished with coriander.
tips: Dice the vegetables small and even so they cook through in the short steaming time.
Do not overcook the vegetables in step three; they finish cooking with the vermicelli.
This version reheats well with a splash of hot water, making it an ideal make-ahead lunchbox.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a coconut chutney or a cooling boondi raita and a wedge of lime.

variations.name: Tomato Semiya Upma
variations.description: A tangy, vibrant version where tomatoes cook into a light masala that coats every strand in a warm orange hue. The tomato keeps the semiya moist and adds a gentle sourness that makes it especially moreish. A colourful, forgiving breakfast that needs nothing more than a spoon of curd.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed oil carries the tomato masala and roasts the semiya well

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon that softens the tomato tang with mellow richness

steps: Roast 2 cups vermicelli in 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium-low heat until golden, about 4 minutes, then set aside.
Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, fry 1 tbsp urad dal until golden, then add 12 curry leaves and 2 slit green chillies.
Add 1 chopped onion and 1 tsp ginger-garlic paste, sauteing 3 minutes until the raw smell fades.
Stir in 3 chopped tomatoes with 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder and 1/4 tsp salt, cover and cook 5 minutes until the tomatoes collapse into a thick pulp.
Pour in 2.75 cups water with 3/4 tsp salt and bring to a boil, then add the roasted vermicelli and stir once to coat.
Cover and cook on low for 4-5 minutes until the water is absorbed and the strands are tender and orange.
Fold in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, rest covered 2 minutes and serve garnished with coriander.
tips: Ripe, juicy tomatoes give the best colour and tang; underripe ones leave it pale and flat.
Because tomatoes release liquid, keep the water slightly low and top up only if needed.
A small pinch of sugar balances any sharp sourness and deepens the tomato colour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling onion raita or plain curd and a squeeze of lime for extra brightness.

variations.name: Coconut Semiya Upma
variations.description: A Kerala-leaning version finished with fresh grated coconut and a coconut-oil tempering, giving the semiya a fragrant sweetness and glossy sheen. The coconut mellows the dish and pairs beautifully with the mustard and curry leaves. It is a lighter, aromatic alternative that feels distinctly coastal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil gives this upma its fragrant coastal aroma

steps: Roast 2 cups vermicelli in 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil over medium-low heat until golden, about 4 minutes, then set aside.
Heat the remaining 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, fry 1 tbsp urad dal, 10 cashews and 1 broken red chilli until golden.
Add 15 curry leaves, 3 slit green chillies and grated 1 inch ginger, then 1 chopped onion, sauteing 3 minutes until soft.
Pour in 3 cups water with 1 tsp salt and bring to a rolling boil.
Add the roasted vermicelli, stir once, then cover and cook on low for 4-5 minutes until the water is absorbed.
Fold in 1/2 cup fresh grated coconut off the heat so it stays fragrant and does not toughen.
Rest covered 2 minutes, then fluff gently and serve warm.
tips: Add the fresh coconut at the very end; cooking it long dries it out and dulls the aroma.
Coconut oil solidifies when cool, so serve this upma warm for the best texture.
A little grated coconut fried lightly for garnish adds a lovely toasted note on top.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a fresh coriander-coconut chutney and a banana on the side for a coastal breakfast.

variations.name: Classic Kadalai Sundal (Chickpea)
variations.description: The quintessential South Indian tempered legume snack, made with white chickpeas tossed in a mustard-and-urad tadka fragrant with curry leaf and fresh coconut. Offered during Navratri and handed out at temples, it is light, protein-packed and lightly spiced. A squeeze of lemon keeps every bite bright.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: The authentic South Indian tempering fat that lifts the mustard-curry leaf aroma

steps: Soak 1.5 cups white chickpeas overnight, then pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp salt for 3 to 4 whistles until soft but still holding shape, and drain well.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan on medium, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal until the dal is golden.
Add 2 broken red chillies, 1 slit green chilli, 12 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and let them crackle for 20 seconds.
Tip in the drained chickpeas with the remaining 0.25 tsp salt and toss on medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes until dry and coated.
Turn off the heat, fold in 0.5 cups grated coconut, and stir for a minute so it warms through without browning.
Finish with 1 tbsp lemon juice, toss once, and serve warm or at room temperature.
tips: Cook the chickpeas just until tender; overcooked ones turn mushy and the sundal loses its bite.
Add the coconut off the heat so it stays fresh and does not dry out.
Drain the chickpeas thoroughly so the tempering coats them instead of steaming them.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a Navratri golu offering in little leaf cups, or as a light evening snack with filter coffee.

variations.name: Verkadalai Sundal (Peanut)
variations.description: A Marina-beach style sundal made with boiled peanuts instead of legumes, tossed with raw mango and a punchy tempering. The soft, buttery peanuts against tangy green mango and coconut make this the most moreish street version. It is scooped hot into paper cones along the Chennai shoreline.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A wood-pressed oil that doubles down on the nutty peanut flavour of this beach snack

steps: Boil 1.5 cups raw peanuts with 0.5 tsp salt and enough water for 15 to 18 minutes until soft but not falling apart, then drain.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 2 broken red chillies, 10 curry leaves, 1 inch grated ginger and 0.25 tsp asafoetida.
Add the drained peanuts with the remaining 0.25 tsp salt and toss on medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes.
Turn off the heat and fold in 0.5 cups finely chopped raw mango for a sharp, tangy hit.
Stir in 0.5 cups grated coconut and toss for a minute so everything warms evenly.
Taste, adjust salt, and serve hot in the classic beach-cone style.
tips: Use skin-on peanuts if you like a slight bite; the reddish skins hold together better when boiled.
Add the raw mango right at the end so it stays crunchy and fresh-tasting.
If mango is out of season, a squeeze of lime gives a similar tang.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in paper cones for a beach-side feel, with an extra wedge of lime on the side.

variations.name: Pattani Sundal (White Peas Masala)
variations.description: A masala-forward sundal built on dried white peas and finished with a freshly ground coconut-chilli paste for extra body and heat. Chopped onion and tomato give it a chaat-like richness that sets it apart from the dry temple version. It is the heartier, spicier sundal sold at festival stalls.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Sautes the onion masala base that gives this sundal its chaat-like richness

steps: Soak 1.5 cups dried white peas overnight, then pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp salt for 4 to 5 whistles until soft, and drain.
Grind 0.5 cups grated coconut with 2 green chillies and 0.5 tsp fennel seeds to a coarse paste with a splash of water.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 10 curry leaves, then saute 1 chopped onion until soft.
Add 1 chopped tomato and 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and cook 3 minutes until the tomato breaks down.
Stir in the coconut paste and cook 2 minutes, then add the cooked peas with the remaining 0.25 tsp salt and toss 3 to 4 minutes until well coated.
Check the seasoning and serve hot while the masala clings to every pea.
tips: Soak the white peas fully overnight, as under-soaked peas stay hard even after pressure-cooking.
Grind the coconut paste coarse, not smooth, so the sundal keeps some texture.
For a tangier finish, add a pinch of amchur along with the chilli powder.
variations.servingSuggestion: Top with chopped onion, coriander and a dusting of chaat masala to serve it street-stall style.

variations.name: Vella Sundal (Sweet Jaggery)
variations.description: A sweet Navratri neivedyam where cooked chickpeas are bound in a molten jaggery syrup with coconut and cardamom. Unlike the savoury versions, this is a gently sweet, sticky offering finished with ghee-fried cashews. It is made on specific days of the golu festival as a change from the salted sundals.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Melted into a syrup that coats the chickpeas for this sweet festival sundal

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Fries the cashews and glosses the sticky jaggery coating

steps: Soak 1.5 cups chickpeas overnight and pressure-cook with 0.25 tsp salt for 3 to 4 whistles until tender, then drain well.
Melt 0.75 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 3 tbsp water on low heat for 3 to 4 minutes until it forms a thick, one-string syrup.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan and fry 10 halved cashews until golden, then lift them out and set aside.
Pour the jaggery syrup into the ghee, add the cooked chickpeas, and toss on low heat for 3 minutes until the syrup coats them stickily.
Fold in 0.5 cups grated coconut, 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp dry ginger powder and stir for a minute until fragrant.
Scatter the fried cashews over the top and serve warm.
tips: Cook the syrup only to a soft one-string stage; harder syrup will make the sundal clumpy and stiff.
Toss on low heat once the syrup goes in, as high heat crystallises the jaggery.
A pinch of dry ginger cuts the sweetness and makes it easier on the stomach.
variations.servingSuggestion: Offer warm as festival prasad, garnished with a little extra fresh coconut on top.

variations.name: Classic Sweet Paniyaram
variations.description: Soft, melt-in-the-mouth jaggery dumplings made from a rice-and-lentil batter sweetened with molten jaggery and studded with coconut, cooked golden in a dimpled paniyaram pan. A beloved Tamil festival and Karthigai treat, crisp outside and pillowy within. The cardamom and coconut give each ball a warm, homely fragrance.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Dissolves into a rich molten syrup that sweetens and colours the batter

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Cooks the paniyarams to a golden crust and adds a festive richness

steps: Soak 1 cup raw rice with 2 tbsp urad dal for 4 hours, then grind to a smooth, thick batter using a little water and rest 1 hour.
Melt 3/4 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 1/4 cup water on low heat, then strain out any grit and cool slightly.
Mash 1 small banana and whisk it with the jaggery syrup into the batter along with 1/2 tsp cardamom powder, 1/3 cup grated coconut and a pinch of salt to a thick, dropping consistency.
Rest the sweet batter 15 minutes so it thickens; it should coat the back of a spoon.
Heat the paniyaram pan, add 1/2 tsp Anveshan Ghee into each dimple, and fill each three-quarters with the sweet batter.
Cook covered on medium-low heat for 4 minutes until the base is deep golden, then flip each ball gently with a skewer.
Cook the other side 3 minutes until golden all over and cooked through, and serve warm.
tips: Keep the heat medium-low; jaggery browns fast and the insides need time to cook through.
The batter should be thick like idli batter, or the paniyarams will not hold their round shape.
Mashed banana keeps these soft for hours, making them ideal for a festival platter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a Karthigai Deepam or evening treat, dusted with a little extra coconut.

variations.name: Nendran Banana Paniyaram
variations.description: A Kerala-Tamil border favourite built on ripe nendran bananas and wheat flour rather than a ground rice batter, giving a dense, fudgy, caramel-sweet ball. The banana does most of the sweetening, helped by a little jaggery. Quick to whisk together, it needs no soaking or grinding.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Whole Wheat Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Khapli atta binds the mashed banana into a nutty, wholesome ball

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Deepens the caramel sweetness of the ripe bananas

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil fries the shells to a fragrant golden crust

steps: Mash 3 ripe nendran bananas to a smooth pulp with a fork or masher.
Whisk in 1/3 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder until it dissolves into the warm banana pulp.

Fold in 1 cup Anveshan Whole Wheat Khapli Atta, 2 tbsp rice flour, 1/4 cup grated coconut, 1/2 tsp cardamom, a pinch of salt and a pinch of baking soda to a thick, dropping batter, adding a splash of water only if needed.
Rest the batter 10 minutes so the atta hydrates and the flavours meld.
Heat the paniyaram pan, add 1/2 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil to each dimple, and fill each three-quarters with batter.
Cook covered on medium-low heat for 4 minutes until the base is deep golden, then flip each ball with a skewer.
Cook the other side 3 minutes until cooked through and golden, and serve warm.
tips: Use very ripe, spotty bananas for the deepest natural sweetness and best texture.
The rice flour gives a slight crispness to the shell; skip it for an even softer ball.
Do not overmix once the atta goes in, or the paniyarams turn tough and chewy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a teatime sweet with filter coffee, or pack a few into a lunchbox as a wholesome treat.

variations.name: Coconut-Cardamom Paniyaram
variations.description: A rich, aromatic version where fresh coconut milk replaces water in the batter and generous grated coconut studs each ball, giving a moist, fragrant crumb. It is the celebratory paniyaram, softer and more perfumed than the everyday one. The coconut milk lends a subtle sweetness that plays beautifully against the jaggery.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Melts into the coconut-milk batter for a rounded, mellow sweetness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil doubles the coconut aroma while crisping the shells

steps: Soak 1 cup raw rice with 2 tbsp urad dal for 4 hours, then grind to a smooth, thick batter and rest 1 hour.
Melt 3/4 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 1/4 cup water on low heat, strain and cool slightly.
Whisk the jaggery syrup and 1/2 cup thick coconut milk into the batter with 3/4 tsp cardamom, 1/4 tsp dry ginger powder, 1/2 cup grated coconut and a pinch of salt to a thick, dropping batter.
Rest the batter 15 minutes so it thickens to a spoon-coating consistency.
Heat the paniyaram pan, add 1/2 tsp Anveshan Coconut Oil to each dimple, and fill each three-quarters with batter.
Cook covered on medium-low heat for 4 minutes until the base is deep golden, then flip each ball with a skewer.
Cook the other side 3 minutes until golden and cooked through, and serve warm.
tips: Add the coconut milk off the heat and cook gently so it does not split in the batter.
The pinch of dry ginger powder is a traditional touch that keeps the rich coconut from feeling heavy.
These are at their fragrant best warm and fresh, so cook them just before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm at a festive spread alongside a bowl of thin payasam for a coconut-rich sweet course.

variations.name: Instant Wheat Paniyaram
variations.description: A quick, no-grind version made with whole wheat flour, jaggery and mashed banana whisked into an instant batter, perfect when a sweet craving strikes without any soaking ahead. Wholesome and lightly spiced, these come together in under half an hour. The wheat gives them a satisfying, nutty density.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Whole Wheat Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Nutty khapli wheat forms a wholesome instant batter with no fermentation

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Dissolves quickly into the batter for an even, mellow sweetness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Cooks the wheat paniyarams golden and keeps them soft

steps: Dissolve 1/2 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 1/2 cup warm water, then strain out any grit.
Mash 1 medium banana smooth and whisk it into the jaggery water.
Fold in 1 cup Anveshan Whole Wheat Khapli Atta, 3 tbsp rice flour, 1/4 cup grated coconut, 1/2 tsp cardamom and a pinch of salt to a smooth, thick, lump-free batter.
Rest the batter 10 minutes, then stir in a pinch of baking soda just before cooking for a fluffier ball.
Heat the paniyaram pan, add 1/2 tsp Anveshan Ghee to each dimple, and fill each three-quarters with batter.
Cook covered on medium-low heat for 4 minutes until the base is deep golden, then flip each ball with a skewer.
Cook the other side 3 minutes until cooked through and golden, and serve warm.
tips: Whisk out all lumps before resting, as wheat flour clumps more than rice batter.
Add the baking soda only at the last minute so its lift is not wasted before cooking.
Keep the batter pourable but thick; too thin and the paniyarams will not round up in the pan.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a quick teatime sweet with masala chai or filter coffee.

variations.name: Classic Thattai
variations.description: A crisp, coin-flat Tamil cracker of rice flour studded with soaked chana dal, sesame and curry leaf, deep-fried to a shattering crunch. Made in bulk for Krishna Jayanthi and Diwali, its dimpled surface fries up bubbly and light. Each bite crackles with dal and pops with sesame.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Clean wood-pressed oil for deep-frying that keeps the crackers light and non-greasy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Rubbed hot into the flour as the shortening that makes the thattai crisp, not hard

steps: Soak 3 tbsp chana dal for 30 minutes and drain, then mix 2 cups rice flour, 0.25 cups roasted gram flour, 2 tbsp urad dal flour, 1 tsp chilli powder, 0.5 tsp asafoetida and 1 tsp salt in a bowl.
Add the soaked dal, 1 tbsp sesame seeds and 12 torn curry leaves, then pour in 2 tbsp hot Anveshan Coconut Oil and rub it through so the flour holds shape when pressed.
Add about 0.75 cups water a little at a time to make a stiff, non-sticky dough, then rest it covered for 15 minutes.
Pinch small balls, place each between greased sheets, and press or pat into thin flat discs, pricking each with a fork so they do not puff.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to about 180C until a pinch of dough rises steadily.
Slide in 3 to 4 thattai at a time and fry for 3 to 4 minutes, turning, until the bubbling stops and they are pale gold and crisp, then drain on paper.
tips: Keep the dough stiff; a wet dough absorbs oil and the thattai turn soft instead of crisp.
Prick each disc well so it stays flat and crackly rather than ballooning up.
Fry on steady medium heat, as too-hot oil browns the outside before the centre crisps.
variations.servingSuggestion: Store in an airtight tin and serve as a Diwali snack with a cup of masala chai.

variations.name: Garlic-Pepper Thattai
variations.description: A bold, garlicky thattai where crushed garlic and freshly cracked pepper replace the milder chilli of the classic. The garlic crisps as it fries, lending a savoury, almost chaat-like punch. This is the version snack lovers reach for first at the Diwali table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Deep-fries the garlicky discs to an even, shattering crisp

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Hot shortening rubbed into the dough for the signature flaky crunch

steps: Crush 8 garlic cloves, 1.5 tsp peppercorns and 3 red chillies together into a coarse, pungent paste.
Mix 2 cups rice flour, 0.25 cups roasted gram flour, 0.5 tsp asafoetida and 1 tsp salt, then add the garlic-pepper paste, 1 tbsp sesame and 15 torn curry leaves.
Rub in 2 tbsp hot Anveshan Coconut Oil, then add about 0.75 cups water gradually to form a stiff dough and rest it 15 minutes.
Pat small balls into thin discs between greased sheets and prick each all over with a fork.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C and fry the discs in small batches for 3 to 4 minutes until the sizzling calms and they turn golden.
Drain on paper and cool fully before storing so they stay crackling crisp.
tips: Crush the garlic coarsely rather than to a wet paste, or the extra moisture softens the dough.
Fry these a shade darker than the classic for the garlic to release its full aroma.
Add a pinch of sugar to the dough to balance the sharp garlic and pepper.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile into a bowl for game-night munching alongside a cooling mint-yogurt dip.

variations.name: Peanut-Coconut Thattai
variations.description: A richer, crunchier thattai loaded with crushed roasted peanuts and dry coconut for a nutty, almost brittle bite. The added fat from the peanuts makes these especially short and flaky. It is the indulgent festival version that never lasts past the first evening.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Deep-frying in coconut oil complements the copra and peanut for a fragrant crunch

steps: Coarsely crush 0.33 cups roasted peanuts and grate 3 tbsp dry coconut, keeping some texture in both.
Mix 2 cups rice flour, 3 tbsp roasted gram flour, 1 tsp chilli powder, 1 tsp cumin, 0.5 tsp asafoetida and 1 tsp salt, then add the peanuts, copra and 12 torn curry leaves.
Rub in 2 tbsp of hot Anveshan Coconut Oil taken from the frying pan, then add about 0.75 cups water to form a firm dough and rest 15 minutes.
Press balls into thin discs between greased sheets and prick each thoroughly with a fork.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Coconut Oil to 180C and fry the thattai in batches for 4 minutes until the bubbles subside and they are golden.
Drain on paper and cool completely to let the peanut crunch set.
tips: Crush the peanuts, do not powder them, so you get little pockets of crunch in each cracker.
Since peanuts add fat, use a touch less shortening or the dough turns too short to roll.
Cool fully before storing, as trapped warmth makes the copra go soft.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a tea-time nibble with a sweet like Mysore pak for a festive spread.

variations.name: Ragi Thattai
variations.description: A wholesome finger-millet thattai that tints the crackers a rustic brown and adds an earthy, nutty depth. Ragi brings fibre and calcium to the festive snack while keeping the signature crunch intact. A guilt-lighter cracker for those who want their Diwali treats a little healthier.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed frying oil that keeps the millet crackers crisp without heaviness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Hot shortening worked into the ragi dough so it fries flaky rather than dense

steps: Soak 3 tbsp chana dal for 30 minutes and drain, then grind 3 green chillies and 1 inch ginger to a coarse paste.
Mix 1.25 cups ragi flour, 0.75 cups rice flour, 0.5 tsp asafoetida and 1 tsp salt, then add the chilli-ginger paste, soaked dal, 1 tbsp sesame and 12 torn curry leaves.
Rub in 2 tbsp hot Anveshan Coconut Oil, add about 0.66 cups water gradually to a stiff dough, and rest 15 minutes.
Pat small balls into thin discs between greased sheets and prick each all over with a fork.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C and fry in batches for 4 minutes until the sizzling settles and the edges firm up.
Drain on paper; because ragi is dark, judge doneness by the calmed bubbling rather than colour.
tips: Ragi hides browning, so go by the sound; when the oil stops bubbling hard, the thattai is done.
Do not skip the rice flour, as it lends the crispness that ragi alone cannot give.
Keep the dough slightly stiffer than the classic, since ragi tends to hold more moisture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Offer as a healthier festive cracker with a bowl of spiced buttermilk to sip alongside.

variations.name: Classic Unniyappam
variations.description: Unniyappam are the little round Kerala sweet fritters of rice flour, mashed banana and jaggery, fried in coconut oil until dark, crisp-edged and soft within. Studded with fried coconut bits and sesame, they are the temple offering and teatime treat of central Kerala.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted into a syrup that sweetens the batter and gives the fritters their dark colour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the traditional frying fat that gives unniyappam their signature Kerala aroma

steps: Melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 0.5 cup water over low heat, strain out grit and cool the syrup to lukewarm.
Mash 2 ripe bananas smooth and whisk them into the jaggery syrup, then stir in 1.5 cups rice flour to a thick, lump-free batter.

Fry 3 tbsp coconut bits in 1 tsp of the coconut oil until golden, then fold them in with 1 tbsp sesame seeds, 0.5 tsp cardamom, 0.25 tsp dry ginger and a pinch of baking soda; rest the batter 30 minutes.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Coconut Oil in an appakara or deep pan over medium heat until a drop of batter sizzles and rises at once.
Drop rounded spoonfuls of batter into the oil and fry for 3 to 4 minutes, turning, until deep reddish-brown and puffed with crisp edges.
Lift out with a slotted spoon, drain on paper and serve the unniyappam warm.
tips: Rest the batter for at least 30 minutes so the rice flour hydrates and the fritters turn soft inside.
Keep the oil at a steady medium heat; too hot burns the outside before the centre cooks through.
The batter should be thick enough to hold a mound on the spoon, so adjust with a little rice flour or water.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a temple offering or with evening chai, piled in a bowl while still crisp at the edges.

variations.name: Khapli Wheat Unniyappam
variations.description: A wholesome twist made with ancient khapli wheat flour instead of rice, giving nuttier, more robust fritters with a satisfying bite. Fennel and grated coconut lend a fragrant, faintly aniseed warmth that sets these apart from the everyday version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: ancient wheat flour that gives the fritters a nutty, wholesome body

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted into a syrup to sweeten and darken the wholegrain batter

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the traditional frying fat that crisps the fritters and adds a Kerala aroma

steps: Melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 0.5 cup water over low heat, strain, and cool the syrup to lukewarm.
Mash 2 ripe bananas and whisk them into the syrup, then stir in 1.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta to a thick, smooth batter.
Fold in 0.25 cup grated coconut, 1 tsp lightly crushed fennel seeds, 0.5 tsp cardamom and a pinch of baking soda, then rest the batter 40 minutes.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Coconut Oil in a deep pan over medium heat until a drop of batter rises at once.
Drop rounded spoonfuls into the oil and fry for 4 to 5 minutes, turning, until deep brown and cooked through, as wheat batter needs a touch longer than rice.
Drain on paper and serve the khapli unniyappam warm.
tips: Khapli batter drinks up more liquid than rice flour, so let it rest longer and loosen with a splash of water if stiff.
Crush the fennel lightly before adding to release its aroma without leaving hard whole seeds in the fritters.
Fry these a shade longer and at slightly lower heat, as wholegrain fritters cook through more slowly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a wholesome teatime snack, dusted with nothing more than their own crisp, nutty crust.

variations.name: Chakka Unniyappam
variations.description: A seasonal favourite where ripe jackfruit is blended into the batter for a honeyed, floral sweetness and a golden crumb. Cashew bits and a hint of cumin give these fritters a festive, almost perfumed character during the jackfruit months.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: rounds out the jackfruit's natural sweetness and deepens the fritters' colour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the traditional frying fat that crisps the fritters and adds Kerala fragrance

steps: Blend 1 cup deseeded ripe jackfruit to a smooth pulp with 0.25 cup water.
Melt 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water, strain, and stir it into the jackfruit pulp.
Whisk in 1.25 cups rice flour to a thick batter, then fold in 0.25 cup grated coconut, 2 tbsp cashew bits, 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp cumin; rest 30 minutes.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Coconut Oil in a deep pan over medium heat until a drop of batter rises at once.
Drop rounded spoonfuls into the oil and fry for 3 to 4 minutes, turning, until deep golden-brown and puffed.
Drain on paper and serve the chakka unniyappam warm.
tips: Use very ripe, fragrant jackfruit for the fullest flavour, and cut back the jaggery if the fruit is especially sweet.
Blend the jackfruit smooth so no fibrous strands catch in the batter and tear the fritters.
A pinch of cumin against the sweet jackfruit is a traditional touch that keeps the fritters from tasting flat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm during the jackfruit season as a fragrant festive snack, best eaten fresh while crisp.

variations.name: Instant Rava Unniyappam
variations.description: A no-soak, no-wait version built on semolina and yogurt that comes together in minutes when a craving strikes. The yogurt lends a gentle tang and keeps the fritters soft, while a little baking soda gives an instant, airy puff.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted into a syrup to sweeten the quick semolina batter and colour the fritters

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the traditional frying fat that crisps the fritters and adds a Kerala aroma

steps: Melt 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water, strain, and cool to lukewarm.
Mash 2 ripe bananas and whisk them into the syrup with 0.25 cup yogurt, then stir in 1.5 cups fine semolina to a thick batter.
Fold in 3 tbsp coconut bits, 1 tbsp sesame seeds, 0.5 tsp cardamom and a pinch of baking soda, and rest the batter for just 15 minutes so the semolina swells.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Coconut Oil in a deep pan over medium heat until a drop of batter rises at once.
Drop rounded spoonfuls into the oil and fry for 3 to 4 minutes, turning, until golden-brown and puffed.
Drain on paper and serve the instant unniyappam warm.
tips: Only a short 15-minute rest is needed here, as the semolina and yogurt swell quickly into a fry-ready batter.
Add the baking soda just before frying so its lift is not lost while the batter stands.
If the batter thickens too much on standing, loosen it with a spoon of yogurt rather than water.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a last-minute sweet snack for surprise guests, alongside cups of hot masala chai.

variations.name: Classic Vaingya Chi Bhaji
variations.description: A homely Maharashtrian brinjal sabzi of cubed eggplant tossed with onion, a nutty peanut-coconut masala and a whisper of jaggery and goda masala. Quick and everyday, it is the kind of soft, savoury-sweet bhaji that turns up beside dal and rice on a weeknight.

ingredients.name: Brinjal
ingredients.note: cut into 1-inch cubes

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil pairs naturally with the peanut masala

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the small hit of unrefined jaggery gives the bhaji its gentle Maharashtrian sweet-savoury lift

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Cut 500 g brinjal into 1-inch cubes and drop them into salted water so they do not brown while you prepare the tempering.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat and splutter 1/2 tsp mustard seeds and 1/2 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add 1/4 tsp asafoetida.
Add 2 chopped onions and fry for 4-5 minutes until soft and pale gold.
Drain the brinjal well, add it to the pan with 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, and toss to coat.
Sprinkle in 2 tbsp water, cover and cook on low heat for 10-12 minutes, stirring once or twice, until the brinjal is completely soft.
Add 1.5 tsp goda masala, 3 tbsp roasted peanut powder, 3 tbsp grated coconut and 1 tsp jaggery powder, and stir gently for 2-3 minutes so the masala coats every piece.
Fold in 3 tbsp chopped coriander and serve warm.
tips: Keep the brinjal cubes chunky; small pieces disintegrate into a mush before they cook through.
Add the peanut powder and coconut only near the end so they stay fragrant and do not turn pasty.
If the brinjal sticks, sprinkle a little more water rather than extra oil, and always cook covered so it steams tender.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulka or bhakri and a bowl of varan-bhaat, with a slice of lime and papad on the side.

variations.name: Vangyache Bharit
variations.description: The smoky Khandesh classic where a large brinjal is fire-roasted until the skin chars, then peeled and mashed with raw onion, green chilli and coriander. Barely cooked and intensely smoky, it is a rustic, textured bharit worlds apart from a stir-fried bhaji.

ingredients.name: Large brinjal
ingredients.note: big round bharta variety, about 500 g

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: raw wood-pressed oil stirred into a Khandeshi bharit is traditional and adds nutty aroma

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped raw

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: crushed

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Rub the whole brinjal with a little oil, pierce it in a few places, and roast it directly over a medium gas flame, turning often, for 10-12 minutes until the skin is fully charred and the flesh collapses.
Cool the brinjal, peel off all the blackened skin, and mash the smoky flesh coarsely with a fork, leaving some texture.
Mix the mashed brinjal with 1 finely chopped raw onion, 4 chopped green chillies and 1 tsp salt while it is still warm.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a small pan on medium heat and splutter 1/2 tsp mustard seeds and 1/2 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add 1/4 tsp asafoetida and 6 crushed garlic cloves and fry for 40 seconds.
Add 1/4 tsp turmeric to the tempering, switch off the heat, and pour the whole sizzling tadka over the mashed brinjal.
Fold everything together well so the raw onion softens slightly in the hot oil and the smoky flesh takes on the garlic aroma.
Stir in 1/4 cup chopped coriander and serve at room temperature.
tips: Roast the brinjal over an open flame, not in a pan, for the authentic smoky bharit flavour; the charred skin is where all the aroma comes from.
Keep the mash coarse and the onion raw so the bharit stays textured and fresh rather than turning into a smooth paste.
Choose a large, light brinjal that feels hollow; heavy seedy ones make the bharit bitter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve Khandeshi-style with hot jowar or bajra bhakri and a raw onion, or scoop it up with pieces of soft chapati.

variations.name: Batata-Vangi Rassa Bhaji
variations.description: A comforting potato-and-brinjal curry in a light onion-tomato gravy, the everyday combination Maharashtrian homes make when they want a saucy bhaji to eat with chapati. The potato thickens the rassa while the brinjal melts into it, mildly spiced and family-friendly.

ingredients.name: Brinjal
ingredients.note: cut into chunks

ingredients.name: Potato
ingredients.note: peeled and cubed

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the base fat for the everyday Maharashtrian rassa

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, crackle 1/2 tsp cumin seeds, then add 2 chopped onions and fry for 5-6 minutes until golden.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for a minute, then add 2 chopped tomatoes and cook for 4 minutes until soft and pulpy.
Lower the heat and add 1.5 tsp kala masala, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1/2 tsp turmeric, roasting for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the 2 cubed potatoes and 300 g brinjal chunks with 1.25 tsp salt and toss to coat in the masala.
Pour in 2 cups hot water, bring to a boil, then cover and simmer on low for 15-18 minutes until the potato is tender and the brinjal has melted into a light gravy.
Mash a few potato pieces against the side of the pan to thicken the rassa naturally, and simmer 2 more minutes.
Finish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander and serve hot.
tips: Add the potato and brinjal together so they finish cooking at the same time; the potato holds shape while the brinjal collapses to thicken the gravy.
Mashing a few potato cubes into the rassa gives body without any flour or cream.
Kala masala can be swapped for goda masala plus a pinch of extra chilli if that is what you have.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulka or chapati, or with steamed rice topped with a spoon of ghee.

variations.name: Dahi Vaingya Chi Bhaji
variations.description: A gentler, creamy version where soft-cooked brinjal is finished in a lightly spiced whisked yogurt sauce, mellowing the eggplant into something almost silky. Mild and cooling, it is a nice change from the nutty and smoky styles, especially in warmer months.

ingredients.name: Brinjal
ingredients.note: cut into chunks

ingredients.name: Yogurt
ingredients.note: thick, whisked smooth

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee gives the yogurt sauce a rich, rounded finish

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: grated

ingredients.name: Besan
ingredients.note: whisked into the yogurt to stop it splitting

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Whisk 3/4 cup yogurt with 1 tsp besan until smooth so it will not split when heated, and keep it ready.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat, crackle 1/2 tsp cumin seeds, then add 1 chopped onion, 3 slit green chillies and 1 inch grated ginger and fry for 4-5 minutes until soft.
Add the 500 g brinjal chunks with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, sprinkle in 3 tbsp water, cover and cook on low for 10-12 minutes until the brinjal is very soft.
Lower the heat right down, stir in 1.5 tsp coriander powder, then pour in the whisked yogurt while stirring continuously so it blends smoothly.
Cook gently for 4-5 minutes on low heat, stirring often, until the sauce thickens slightly and coats the brinjal without boiling hard.
Taste for salt and switch off the heat while the sauce is still creamy.
Garnish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and serve warm.
tips: Whisking a spoon of besan into the yogurt and keeping the heat low is the key to a smooth sauce that does not curdle.
Cook the brinjal fully soft before the yogurt goes in, since the sauce should only be warmed through, not boiled.
A pinch of sugar or jaggery can be added if your yogurt is very sour, to keep the sauce mellow.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft jeera rice or plain chapati, letting the cool yogurt sauce balance a spicier dal alongside.

variations.name: Classic Vangi Bath
variations.description: Karnataka's beloved brinjal rice, where tender purple eggplant is simmered in a freshly ground vangi bath masala of roasted chana dal, coriander, dry coconut and red chillies. The masala clings to every grain, giving a warm, tangy-nutty flavour with a whisper of tamarind. Best made with day-old rice so the grains stay separate and drink up the spice.

ingredients.name: Cooked rice
ingredients.note: Preferably cooled day-old rice for separate grains

ingredients.name: Brinjal
ingredients.note: Small purple brinjals cut into wedges, kept in salted water

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Finishing the bath in ghee gives the masala-coated rice its glossy sheen

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil is the authentic base fat for sauteing the brinjal

ingredients.name: Chana dal
ingredients.note: For the fresh masala, roasted till golden

steps: Dry-roast 2 tbsp chana dal, 1.5 tbsp coriander seeds, 5 dry red chillies, 1 inch cinnamon and 3 cloves over low heat for 3-4 minutes until the dal is golden and aromatic, add 3 tbsp dry coconut for the last minute, then cool and grind to a slightly coarse powder.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a wide pan over medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal until the dal reddens, then add 12 curry leaves.
Add the drained brinjal wedges and 1/2 tsp turmeric and saute for 6-7 minutes until the brinjal is soft and lightly browned at the edges.
Stir in 1 tbsp tamarind pulp, the freshly ground masala and 1.5 tsp salt, adding a splash of water to make a thick coating paste, and cook for 3 minutes until it smells roasted and the oil surfaces.
Fold in 3 cups cooked rice gently so the grains stay whole, coating them evenly with the masala, and warm through for 3-4 minutes.
Drizzle 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the top, fold once more, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander before serving.
tips: Grinding the masala fresh for each batch makes a dramatic difference; the roasted-coconut aroma fades within days once ground.
Fold the rice with a light hand using a flat spatula so the grains coat evenly without breaking into mush.
Salting and soaking the cut brinjal draws out bitterness and helps it brown instead of steaming in the pan.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a bowl of plain curd, a crisp papad and a wedge of lemon; a spoon of extra ghee on top is very welcome.

variations.name: Iyengar Vangi Bath
variations.description: The temple-town Iyengar rendition leans tangier and more perfumed, using a MTR-style masala heavy on marathi moggu, star anise and copra, brightened with a bolder hit of tamarind. It is milder in chilli but deeper in aroma, the kind ladled from big vessels at Mylapore weddings. The rice stays soft and glistens with sesame oil.

ingredients.name: Cooked rice
ingredients.note: Sona masuri cooked slightly firm and cooled

ingredients.name: Brinjal
ingredients.note: Long green or purple brinjal in wedges

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed gingelly oil is the defining fat of Iyengar rice dishes

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The customary sweet note that balances the generous tamarind in temple-style bath

ingredients.name: Marathi moggu
ingredients.note: Kapok buds that give Iyengar masala its distinctive musky note

steps: Dry-roast 2 tbsp chana dal, 2 tbsp coriander seeds, 4 dry red chillies, 2 marathi moggu and 1 star anise over low heat for 4 minutes, add 1/4 cup copra for the final minute, then cool and grind to a fine powder.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadhai over medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp bengal gram, then add 1/2 tsp asafoetida and 15 curry leaves.
Add the brinjal wedges and 1/2 tsp turmeric and cook for 7 minutes until meltingly soft, letting the sesame oil coat them well.
Pour in 2 tbsp tamarind pulp loosened with 1/4 cup water, add 1.5 tsp salt and 1.5 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, and simmer for 3 minutes until the raw tang mellows.
Stir in the ground masala and cook for 2 minutes to a thick, glistening paste, then fold in 3 cups cooked rice gently until every grain is coated a warm brown.
Cover and let it rest on the lowest heat for 4 minutes so the flavours settle into the soft rice before serving.
tips: Marathi moggu and star anise are what set the Iyengar masala apart, so seek them out rather than substituting garam masala.
Let the finished bath rest covered for ten minutes off the heat; Iyengar cooks insist it tastes far better after this pause.
Use gingelly oil generously here, as its nutty pungency is a defining flavour, not just a cooking medium.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature the traditional way, with a spoon of thick curd, fried appalam and a piece of vadu mango pickle.

variations.name: Peanut-Coconut Vangi Bath
variations.description: A richer North Karnataka home style where roasted peanuts and fresh coconut go into both the masala and the garnish, giving a creamy, nutty body quite unlike the drier classic. The brinjal is cooked until it almost melts into the rice, and a coconut-milk finish keeps it luscious. Comforting, mild and satisfying for a family lunch.

ingredients.name: Cooked rice
ingredients.note: Cooled and separated

ingredients.name: Brinjal
ingredients.note: Cubed, held in salted water

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Cold-pressed coconut oil deepens the coconut theme running through this version

ingredients.name: Roasted peanuts
ingredients.note: Half ground into the masala, half kept whole for garnish

steps: Dry-roast 1 tbsp chana dal, 1.5 tbsp coriander seeds and 4 dry red chillies for 3 minutes, cool, then grind with half the roasted peanuts and 1/3 cup fresh coconut into a coarse, fragrant paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan over medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal, then add 12 curry leaves.
Add the cubed brinjal and 1/2 tsp turmeric and saute for 7-8 minutes until very soft and beginning to collapse.
Stir in the ground peanut-coconut masala, 1 tbsp tamarind pulp and 1.5 tsp salt with a splash of water, and cook for 3 minutes until thick and glossy.
Lower the heat, pour in 1/4 cup coconut milk off the boil so it does not split, and stir to a creamy coating gravy.
Fold in 3 cups cooked rice gently, warm through for 3 minutes, and finish with the reserved whole peanuts and 2 tbsp coriander.
tips: Add the coconut milk only after lowering the heat, and never boil it hard, or it will curdle and turn grainy.
Grinding the peanuts into the masala rather than only garnishing gives the whole dish its signature creamy body.
If the bath feels dry on standing, revive it with a spoonful more warm coconut milk rather than water.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a sharp raw-onion and green-chilli kachumber and extra roasted peanuts scattered on top for crunch.

variations.name: One-Pot Instant Vangi Bath
variations.description: A weeknight rescue that cooks raw rice and brinjal together in a single pot using a quick ready-ground vangi bath powder, so there is no leftover rice required and no separate masala roasting. The grains soak up the spice as they steam, giving a fuss-free bath in under half an hour. Ideal for lunchboxes and busy mornings.

ingredients.name: Rice
ingredients.note: Rinsed and soaked 15 minutes

ingredients.name: Brinjal
ingredients.note: Cubed just before cooking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Gives the quick one-pot bath the richness the slow version gets from fresh masala

ingredients.name: Vangi bath powder
ingredients.note: A good ready-ground blend stands in for freshly roasted masala

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pressure cooker over medium heat and fry 10 cashews until golden, then remove and reserve for garnish.
In the same ghee splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal, add 12 curry leaves and 1 sliced onion, and saute for 3 minutes until the onion softens.
Add 1 chopped tomato and cook for 2 minutes until pulpy, then stir in 3 tbsp vangi bath powder and 1/2 tsp turmeric for 20 seconds.
Add the cubed brinjal and 1 tbsp tamarind pulp, saute for 3 minutes, then tip in the drained rice and toss gently for 2 minutes to coat.
Pour in 3 cups hot water with 1.5 tsp salt, stir once, close the cooker and cook for 2 whistles, then switch off and let the pressure release naturally.
Open, fluff gently with a fork, and finish with the fried cashews and 2 tbsp coriander before serving.
tips: Natural pressure release keeps the grains intact; forcing it out early makes the rice mushy.
Ready vangi bath powders vary in salt and heat, so add salt cautiously and taste after opening the cooker.
A final spoon of ghee stirred through the hot rice mimics the richness of the slow-cooked classic beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pack into a lunchbox with a small tub of curd and mango pickle, or serve fresh with fried papad and sliced onion.

variations.name: Classic Mixed Veg Xacuti
variations.description: A vegetarian rendering of Goa's iconic xacuti, where a medley of potato, carrot, beans and cauliflower simmers in a dark roasted-coconut masala layered with clove, star anise and poppy seed. The browned coconut gives the gravy its signature nutty sweetness and deep colour, one of the Konkan coast's most beloved festive curries.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil is the authentic Goan fat that carries the roasted xacuti masala

steps: Dry-roast the coriander, cumin, poppy seeds, peppercorns, cloves, cinnamon, star anise and dried red chillies on low until fragrant, then roast 0.75 cup grated coconut separately until deep golden-brown.
Grind the roasted spices and coconut with 1 tsp tamarind and a little water into a smooth, dark masala.
Boil 4 cups mixed vegetables with 1 tsp salt and water to cover for 8-10 minutes until just fork-tender, then drain and reserve the water.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil on medium; saute the sliced onions for 6-7 minutes until deep golden, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 0.25 tsp turmeric and fry for a minute.
Stir in the ground xacuti masala and cook for 5 minutes until the oil separates and the paste darkens.
Add the boiled vegetables and 1.5 cups of the reserved water and simmer on low for 8 minutes until the gravy thickens and coats the vegetables in a glossy sheen.
tips: Roast the coconut to a deep brown - that browning is the source of xacuti's dark colour and nutty depth.
Cut all the vegetables to a similar size so they cook evenly and finish together.
Boil the vegetables only until just tender; they finish cooking in the gravy and should not turn mushy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with Goan pao, sannas or steamed rice to soak up the deeply spiced gravy.

variations.name: Cauliflower-Potato Xacuti
variations.description: A robust two-vegetable version where hearty cauliflower florets and potato cubes are pan-fried before simmering, so they hold their shape and soak up the roasted masala. Fewer vegetables and a thicker gravy make this the most substantial, dinner-anchoring take on veg xacuti.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil both fries the vegetables and carries the roasted masala

steps: Dry-roast the coriander, fennel, cloves, cinnamon and dried red chillies until fragrant, then roast 0.75 cup grated coconut to deep golden-brown; grind together with 1 tsp tamarind into a smooth masala.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil and pan-fry the cauliflower and potato with a pinch of salt on medium for 6-7 minutes until browned at the edges; set aside.
In the same pan heat the remaining 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil and saute the sliced onions for 6-7 minutes until deep golden.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 0.25 tsp turmeric, fry for a minute, then stir in the ground masala and cook for 5 minutes until the oil separates.
Add the fried cauliflower and potato with 1 tsp salt and 1.5 cups hot water, cover and simmer on low for 10 minutes until the potato is tender.
Uncover and simmer for 2-3 minutes more to thicken the gravy so it clings to the vegetables.
tips: Pan-frying the cauliflower and potato first keeps them intact and deepens their flavour in the gravy.
Keep this gravy thicker than the mixed-veg version so it coats the sturdier vegetables.
Fennel in the masala lends a sweet warmth that suits the earthy potato particularly well.
variations.servingSuggestion: Hearty with chapatis or poee, or spooned over steamed rice for a filling weekday dinner.

variations.name: Raw Jackfruit Xacuti
variations.description: A prized version using meaty chunks of raw jackfruit (kathal), whose dense, fibrous texture soaks up the roasted masala like nothing else and gives the curry an almost hearty, satisfying chew. This is a monsoon-season Goan favourite, rich and deeply spiced.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil suits the dense jackfruit and the dark roasted masala

steps: Oil your hands and knife, cut 4 cups raw jackfruit into chunks, and boil with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 12-15 minutes until just tender, then drain.
Dry-roast the coriander, cumin, poppy seeds, cloves, cinnamon, nutmeg and dried red chillies until fragrant, then roast 0.75 cup grated coconut to deep brown.
Grind the roasted spices and coconut with 1.5 tsp tamarind into a smooth, dark masala with a little water.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil on medium; saute the sliced onions for 7 minutes until deep golden, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and fry for a minute.
Stir in the ground masala and cook for 5-6 minutes until the oil separates and it darkens, then add the boiled jackfruit and toss to coat.
Pour in 1.5 cups hot water and simmer on low for 12 minutes until the jackfruit is fully tender and the gravy is thick and glossy.
tips: Oil your hands and blade before cutting jackfruit, as its sap is sticky and hard to wash off.
Par-boil the jackfruit first so it turns fully tender, since it will not soften much further in the gravy.
A little extra tamarind here balances the dense, mildly sweet jackfruit beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: A monsoon special served with pao or rice, its meaty texture making it hearty enough to star at the table.

variations.name: Soya Chunk Veg Xacuti
variations.description: A high-protein weeknight version where springy soya chunks and green peas take the place of mixed vegetables, soaking up the roasted masala like little sponges. Quick to put together and satisfyingly meaty, it makes the xacuti a filling main on its own.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Coconut oil ties the soya chunks to the traditional roasted xacuti masala

steps: Boil 1.5 cups soya chunks in salted water for 5 minutes, drain, rinse under cold water and squeeze out the excess so they stay springy.
Dry-roast the coriander, cumin, peppercorns, cloves, cinnamon and dried red chillies until fragrant, then roast 0.75 cup grated coconut to deep brown; grind with 1 tsp tamarind into a smooth masala.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Wood-Pressed Coconut Oil on medium; saute the chopped onions for 6 minutes until golden, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 0.25 tsp turmeric and fry for a minute.
Stir in the ground masala and cook for 5 minutes until the oil separates and it darkens.
Add 0.75 cup green peas and 1.5 cups hot water and simmer for 5 minutes, then add the squeezed soya chunks and 1 tsp salt.
Simmer on low for 8-10 minutes until the soya plumps up with gravy and the masala thickens around it.
tips: Squeeze the boiled soya chunks well so they absorb the masala instead of staying watery.
Add the soya after the gravy is built so it soaks up flavour rather than turning rubbery.
Keep the gravy slightly thin at first, as the soya will drink up a fair amount as it simmers.
variations.servingSuggestion: A protein-rich main with rotis or steamed rice, needing only a simple salad alongside.

variations.name: Classic Zunka
variations.description: The dry, crumbly cousin of pithla and the everyday partner to jowar bhakri across rural Maharashtra. Besan is roasted into a hot garlic-and-onion tempering with just enough sprinkled water to set into soft, separate flakes rather than a paste. It is quick, rustic and deeply savoury.

ingredients.name: Besan
ingredients.note: sifted to remove lumps

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil is the everyday cooking fat of a Maharashtrian kitchen and carries the tempering

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: crushed

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Dry-roast 1 cup besan in a kadai on low heat for 3-4 minutes, stirring constantly, just until it smells nutty and turns a shade darker, then tip it onto a plate and set aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in the same kadai on medium heat and splutter 1/2 tsp mustard seeds and 1/2 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add 1/4 tsp asafoetida and 10 curry leaves.
Add 6 crushed garlic cloves and 3 chopped green chillies and fry for 40 seconds until the raw garlic smell lifts, then add 2 chopped onions and cook for 5-6 minutes until soft and pale gold.
Sprinkle in 1/2 tsp turmeric powder and 1 tsp salt, stir for 20 seconds, then pour in 1.25 cups hot water and bring it to a rolling boil.
Lower the heat and rain in the roasted besan in a thin stream with one hand while stirring hard with the other so no lumps form, until it comes together into a thick mass, about 2 minutes.
Cover and steam on the lowest heat for 5-6 minutes, then uncover and break the mixture with the back of the spoon into loose, crumbly flakes rather than a smooth paste.
Fold in 3 tbsp chopped coriander, drizzle a little extra groundnut oil over the top, and serve hot and crumbly.
tips: The whole trick to zunka is the water ratio: too much and it turns into pithla, so add the besan to just-boiling water and stop the moment it clumps.
Roasting the besan first removes its raw beany taste and helps the flakes stay separate instead of gummy.
Leftover zunka reheats beautifully the next morning; crisp it in a little groundnut oil and stuff it into a bhakri roll for lunch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve mounded beside a hot jowar or bajra bhakri with a raw onion wedge, a green chilli and a dollop of white butter to press into each bite.

variations.name: Varhadi Kanda Zunka
variations.description: The fiery Vidarbha take from the Varhad belt, loaded with browned onion and a spoon of dark kala masala that stains it a deep brick red. Toasted sesame and peanut powder give it body and a smoky heat that the region is famous for. This is a bolder, spicier plate than the everyday version.

ingredients.name: Besan
ingredients.note: sifted

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: the extra spoon of wood-pressed oil is what fries the onions deep enough for a Varhadi zunka

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: White sesame seeds
ingredients.note: dry-roasted and coarsely ground

ingredients.name: Kala masala
ingredients.note: Maharashtrian goda-style dark spice blend

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Roast 1 cup besan on low heat for 4 minutes until nutty and set it aside, then dry-roast 2 tbsp sesame seeds separately until they pop and grind them coarse with the 2 tbsp peanut powder.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai on medium heat, crackle 1/2 tsp cumin seeds, then add 3 chopped onions and fry for 8-9 minutes until deep brown at the edges.

Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for a minute, then lower the heat and add 1.5 tsp kala masala, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1/2 tsp turmeric powder and roast for 30 seconds until the oil turns red.
Add the sesame-peanut powder and 1 tsp salt, stir for a minute, then pour in 1.25 cups hot water and bring to a strong boil.
Sprinkle the roasted besan in slowly while stirring vigorously to keep it lump-free, cooking until it gathers into a thick, spiced mass, about 2 minutes.
Cover and steam on the lowest heat for 6 minutes, then break it up into coarse, spicy crumbs with the spoon.
Finish with 3 tbsp chopped coriander and a last drizzle of groundnut oil, and serve while steaming hot.
tips: Frying the onions to a true deep brown is non-negotiable here; it is the base colour and sweetness that balances the fierce kala masala.
If kala masala is hard to find, use 1 tsp goda masala with an extra 1/2 tsp chilli powder and a pinch of clove powder.
The sesame-peanut powder must be coarse, not fine, so it lends texture; grind it in short pulses and stop while it is still gritty.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile it beside a thick jowar bhakri with sliced raw onion and a wedge of lime, Varhadi-style, and a glass of buttermilk to cool the heat.

variations.name: Set Zunka Vadi
variations.description: The party format where zunka is cooked a touch wetter, spread flat on a greased plate, set firm, then cut into diamonds and topped with a sizzling sesame tempering. It turns the humble crumble into a tea-time snack that holds its shape and travels well in a tiffin.

ingredients.name: Besan
ingredients.note: sifted

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: used both in the batter and the finishing tempering that crowns the vadis

ingredients.name: Sour yogurt
ingredients.note: whisked smooth

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Grated fresh coconut
ingredients.note: for garnish

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups besan with 1/4 cup sour yogurt, 1 tbsp green chilli-ginger paste, 1/2 tsp turmeric powder, 1 tsp salt and 2 cups water into a smooth lump-free batter.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a heavy kadai on medium heat, pour in the batter, and cook while stirring continuously for 8-10 minutes until it thickens into a glossy mass that pulls away from the sides.
Grease a large plate or thali with a little oil, spread the hot mixture 1 cm thick with a flat spatula, smooth the top, and let it set and cool for 15 minutes.
Cut the set slab into diamonds or squares with a greased knife and gently lift them apart onto a serving plate.

For the tempering, heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a small pan on medium heat and splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tbsp sesame seeds for 40 seconds, then add 1/4 tsp asafoetida and 12 curry leaves.
Spoon the sizzling tempering evenly over the cut vadis so every piece catches some sesame and curry leaf.
Scatter 3 tbsp chopped coriander and 2 tbsp grated coconut over the top and serve warm or at room temperature.
tips: Stir the batter without stopping while it cooks; the moment you leave it, the base scorches and the vadis taste bitter.
Spread the slab while it is piping hot because it sets fast, and always grease the plate first so the pieces release cleanly.
These keep well for a day; pan-crisp leftover vadis in a little groundnut oil to revive them for the next round of tea.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the diamonds on a platter with green chutney and a hot cup of masala chai as an evening snack, or pack them into a lunchbox with a squeeze of lime.

variations.name: Takatla Zunka
variations.description: A softer, tangy village version where the besan is slaked in sour buttermilk before it hits the pan, giving gently moist, melt-in-mouth flakes with a pleasant sourness. Finished in ghee with green garlic when in season, it is the comforting winter face of zunka.

ingredients.name: Besan
ingredients.note: sifted

ingredients.name: Buttermilk
ingredients.note: thin and slightly sour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee rounds off the sourness of the buttermilk and gives the flakes a rich finish

ingredients.name: Green garlic
ingredients.note: chopped, or 5 regular garlic cloves crushed

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Whisk 1 cup besan into 1.5 cups thin sour buttermilk with 1/2 tsp turmeric powder and 1 tsp salt until completely smooth, and let it rest for 10 minutes.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat and splutter 1/2 tsp mustard seeds and 1/2 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds, then add 1/4 tsp asafoetida.
Add 1/2 cup chopped green garlic and 3 slit green chillies and fry for 1-2 minutes until the green garlic wilts and smells sweet.
Lower the heat and pour in the besan-buttermilk mixture, stirring constantly so it does not split, and cook for 5-6 minutes until it thickens and the raw smell disappears.
Keep stirring as it draws together, then let it cook a further 3-4 minutes on low until it forms soft, moist clumps that leave the sides of the pan.
Gently break the mass into tender flakes, taste for salt, and switch off the heat.
Fold in 2 tbsp chopped coriander and serve warm with an extra drizzle of ghee on top.
tips: Keep the heat low once the buttermilk goes in so it does not curdle; a steady gentle simmer gives the softest flakes.
Slightly sour, day-old buttermilk works best here; if yours is fresh, add a squeeze of lime at the end for the signature tang.
Green garlic is seasonal, so out of winter use crushed regular garlic plus a little chopped spring onion green for the same aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve this soft zunka with hot bajra bhakri and a spoon of fresh white butter, or alongside plain rice and a bowl of thin dal for a light meal.

variations.name: Classic Jolada Rotti
variations.description: The daily bread of North Karnataka, a plain, unleavened sorghum flatbread patted thin by hand from jowar flour scalded with hot water. Cooked on a tava and then puffed over an open flame, it turns soft-centred with a faint sweet-earthy jowar flavour. Traditionally eaten with fiery ennegayi and a dab of white butter, it is the sturdy staple of the Deccan plateau.

ingredients.name: Jowar flour
ingredients.note: Fine sorghum flour, plus extra for dusting

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: A spoon of emmer wheat binds the gluten-free jowar so beginners can pat it without cracking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Smeared on the hot rotti to keep it soft and add the traditional aroma

ingredients.name: Boiling water
ingredients.note: Scalds the flour so it binds into a pliable dough

ingredients.name: Rice flour
ingredients.note: For dusting while patting

steps: Mix 2 cups jowar flour, 2 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta and 1/2 tsp salt in a bowl, then pour in about 1.25 cups boiling water and stir quickly with a spoon into a shaggy, steaming mass.
As soon as it is cool enough to touch, knead firmly for 5-6 minutes into a smooth, warm, non-sticky dough, sprinkling a little hot water if it cracks.
Divide into 6 balls, keep them covered, and dust your board generously with rice flour to stop sticking.
Take one ball and pat it out with your palm and fingers into a thin 7-inch round, rotating and dusting as you go, or roll gently using rice flour if patting feels hard.
Cook on a medium-hot tava for about a minute until the underside dries and pale spots form, flip, and cook the second side for another minute.
Lift with tongs and hold the rotti over a direct low flame for a few seconds until it puffs, then smear with a little Anveshan Ghee and keep wrapped in a cloth.
tips: The dough must be kneaded while still warm; once cold, jowar stiffens and cracks at the edges when patted.
Dust with rice flour rather than more jowar, as it keeps the surface smooth and helps the rotti puff.
Stack the cooked rottis in a cloth-lined casserole so the trapped steam keeps them soft and foldable.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the North Karnataka way with badanekayi ennegayi, a heap of raw onion, groundnut chutney podi and a dab of white butter.

variations.name: Soft Curd Jolada Roti
variations.description: A softer, foldable everyday version enriched with a little curd and oil in the dough, which keeps the jowar supple for hours and makes it easier to roll than pat. Ajwain adds a gentle warmth and helps digestion. This is the pliable jolada roti packed into farmers' lunch bundles that stays soft well past midday.

ingredients.name: Jowar flour
ingredients.note: Sorghum flour, the base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Multigrain Atta
ingredients.note: A little multigrain flour adds binding and keeps the roti soft and rollable

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A spoon worked into the dough keeps these rotis supple for hours

ingredients.name: Curd
ingredients.note: Softens the dough and lends a faint tang

ingredients.name: Rice flour
ingredients.note: For dusting

steps: Combine 2 cups jowar flour, 1/4 cup Anveshan Multigrain Atta, 1 tsp ajwain and 3/4 tsp salt in a bowl and mix well.
Add 1/4 cup curd and 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, then pour in about 3/4 cup warm water in stages and knead for 5 minutes into a soft, smooth dough.
Rub the remaining 1 tbsp oil over the dough, cover, and rest for 15 minutes so the jowar hydrates fully and rolls without cracking.
Divide into 6 balls, dust with rice flour, and roll each into a 7-inch round with light, even pressure, turning frequently.
Cook on a medium-hot tava for about a minute until bubbles rise, flip, press gently with a cloth so it puffs, and cook the second side to pale brown spots.
Stack the finished rotis wrapped in a cloth and serve soft and folded.
tips: The curd and oil are what keep these soft, so do not skip them if you want a foldable, lunchbox-friendly roti.
Rest the dough well; jowar with curd rolls far more easily after fifteen minutes of hydration.
If the dough feels sticky from the curd, dust with a little extra rice flour rather than adding more jowar.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a moist brinjal palya or a dal and a spoon of curd, ideal rolled up for a portable meal.

variations.name: Sajje-Jolada Mixed Millet Rotti
variations.description: A rustic pearl-millet and sorghum combination from the drier belts of North Karnataka, where bajra flour joins the jowar and toasted sesame runs through the dough for warmth and richness. Denser and more warming than the plain rotti, it suits cold-weather meals. The two millets together give a deeper, more complex earthiness.

ingredients.name: Jowar flour
ingredients.note: Sorghum, the main millet

ingredients.name: Bajra flour
ingredients.note: Pearl millet for warmth and a deeper flavour

ingredients.name: Sesame seeds
ingredients.note: Toasted, worked through the dough

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Smeared on the hot rotti to offset the dense bajra and keep it soft

ingredients.name: Carom (ajwain) seeds
ingredients.note: Aids digestion of the heavier bajra

ingredients.name: Rice flour
ingredients.note: For dusting

steps: Toast 2 tbsp sesame seeds in a dry pan over low heat for a minute until fragrant, then mix them with 1.5 cups jowar flour, 3/4 cup bajra flour, 1 tsp ajwain and 3/4 tsp salt.
Pour in about 1.25 cups boiling water and stir quickly into a shaggy mass, then knead while warm for 6 minutes into a smooth, firm dough.
Cover and rest for 10 minutes, then divide into 6 balls and keep them under a cloth so they do not dry.
Dust the board with rice flour and pat or gently roll each ball into a thick 6-inch round, as this heavier dough tears if spread too thin.
Cook on a medium tava for about 90 seconds per side until firm brown spots appear, then puff briefly over a low direct flame.
Smear each hot rotti with a little Anveshan Ghee and stack wrapped in a cloth to keep them from stiffening.
tips: Keep these rottis a touch thicker than plain jolada rotti, since the bajra makes the dough more fragile.
Bajra rottis firm up faster than jowar, so eat them hot or wrap them well straight off the tava.
The toasted sesame is worth the extra minute; it lifts the earthy millet with a nutty warmth.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a garlicky groundnut chutney, jaggery and a spoon of ghee, the classic winter pairing across the North Karnataka countryside.

variations.name: Methi Masala Jolada Rotti
variations.description: A savoury, spiced variation where chopped fenugreek greens, onion and green chilli are worked straight into the jowar dough, turning the plain flatbread into a flavour-packed one-dish meal. The methi keeps it moist and slightly bitter-sweet against the earthy sorghum. Hearty enough to eat with just curd, it is a clever way to use up a bunch of fresh greens.

ingredients.name: Jowar flour
ingredients.note: Sorghum base

ingredients.name: Fresh methi leaves
ingredients.note: Fenugreek greens, chopped fine

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: Very finely chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil for cooking gives the spiced rotti a crisp golden base

ingredients.name: Hot water
ingredients.note: The greens release moisture, so add less

ingredients.name: Rice flour
ingredients.note: For dusting

steps: In a bowl combine 2 cups jowar flour, 1 cup chopped methi leaves, 1 finely chopped small onion, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp cumin, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder and 3/4 tsp salt, rubbing so the methi and onion release moisture.
Add 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, then pour in about 3/4 cup hot water gradually and knead into a soft, moist dough, keeping it firm enough to pat.
Rest the dough covered for 10 minutes, divide into 6 balls, and dust the board with rice flour.
Pat or gently roll each ball into a 6-inch round, keeping it slightly thick so the greens do not cause tears.
Cook on a medium tava, drizzling 1/2 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil around the edges, for about 2 minutes per side until golden-brown and cooked through.
Serve hot off the tava, or stack wrapped in a cloth to keep soft.
tips: Squeeze the chopped methi with a little salt for five minutes and drain it, so the dough does not turn watery.
A pinch of jaggery in the dough balances the natural bitterness of the fenugreek greens nicely.
These spiced rottis are filling enough to eat with just a bowl of curd or a simple pickle.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with thick curd, a spoon of ghee and mango pickle, or with a bowl of yogurt kadhi for a satisfying meal.

variations.name: Classic Bikaneri Aloo Bhujia
variations.description: The iconic Bikaner namkeen: fine, crisp noodles of gram flour and mashed potato spiced with clove and black pepper. The potato gives it a lighter, almost powdery crunch that dissolves on the tongue, quite unlike plain besan sev. This is the golden bhujia that Rajasthan built an entire snack industry on.

ingredients.name: Boiled potato
ingredients.note: Boiled, cooled and grated fine so it blends smoothly into the dough

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: For deep-frying to that pale Bikaneri gold without heaviness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The moyan that gives the potato bhujia its melting, powdery crunch

ingredients.name: Clove powder
ingredients.note: The subtle warm note that marks true Bikaneri bhujia

steps: Grate 1 cup cooled boiled potato and mix into 1.5 cups besan with 1 tsp salt, 1/4 tsp clove powder, 1/2 tsp black pepper, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1/4 tsp asafoetida.
Rub 2 tbsp warm melted Anveshan Ghee into the mix, then add water a spoon at a time, up to about 3 tbsp, kneading to a stiff, smooth dough that just presses through a die.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to a moderate 180 C, testing with a thread of dough that rises steadily.
Fill a bhujia press with the fine die and press the dough into the oil in slow circles, keeping the fine strands loose and even across the surface.
Fry 45-60 seconds, stirring gently, until the loud sizzle fades and the bhujia is uniformly pale gold and crisp.
Lift onto kitchen paper, break into loose clusters, and cool completely so the potato crunch sets.
tips: The potato must be fully cooled and free of lumps; warm potato makes a sticky dough that clogs the press.
Keep the dough on the stiff side, as too much water gives soft, oily bhujia that will not stay crisp.
Cooled and stored airtight, this bhujia keeps its crunch for two to three weeks.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a teatime namkeen, scatter over chaat and dahi puri, or sprinkle onto poha and upma for a crisp finish.

variations.name: Tikha Aloo Bhujia
variations.description: A fiery Marwari version that trades the gentle clove note for a bold hit of red chilli, amchur and black salt, so every strand crackles with heat and tang. Slightly coarser than the Bikaneri classic, it is built for those who eat namkeen with chai and want it to fight back. The dried mango powder gives a sour edge that keeps you reaching for more.

ingredients.name: Boiled potato
ingredients.note: Grated fine and fully cooled for a smooth, spicy dough

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: For deep-frying the spicy strands to a crisp reddish gold

ingredients.name: Amchur powder
ingredients.note: Dried mango powder for the signature tangy kick

steps: Grate 1 cup cooled boiled potato into 1.5 cups besan and add 2 tsp hot red chilli powder, 1 tsp amchur, 1/2 tsp black salt, 1 tsp roasted cumin, 1/2 tsp ginger powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric and 3/4 tsp salt.
Drizzle in 2 tbsp of hot Anveshan Groundnut Oil taken from the frying pan, rub it through, then knead with up to 3 tbsp water to a stiff, smooth dough.
Heat the remaining oil to a moderate 180 C and check with a thread of dough that surfaces with a lively sizzle.
Press the dough through a medium bhujia die into the oil in wide sweeps so the spicy strands land loosely and cook evenly.
Fry 45-60 seconds until crisp and deep gold, keeping the heat steady so the chilli does not blacken.
Drain on paper, cool fully, and toss with a final pinch of amchur if you want an extra sour hit.
tips: Using hot oil as the moyan instead of ghee gives this version a crunchier, more rustic bite.
Add the amchur to taste at the end too; a light dusting on the cooled bhujia sharpens the tang.
Wear the chilli lightly on your hands by oiling them before kneading the spicy dough.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with cutting chai and sliced onion, or use to spike up bhel and jhaal muri where you want real heat.

variations.name: Falahari Aloo Bhujia
variations.description: A fasting-friendly bhujia that swaps gram flour for kuttu (buckwheat) flour and leans entirely on potato, so it is suitable for Navratri and Ekadashi vrat. Seasoned only with rock salt and black pepper, it fries into a crisp, nutty tangle without any grain or lentil. A clever way to keep the crunch alive on fasting days.

ingredients.name: Boiled potato
ingredients.note: Mashed very smooth; it binds the gluten-free kuttu flour into a pressable dough

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: For deep-frying; permitted in most vrat kitchens and keeps the strands light

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee moyan adds fasting-friendly richness and a tender crunch
