steps: Mash 1.5 cups boiled potato completely smooth and combine with 1 cup kuttu flour, 1 tsp rock salt, 1 tsp black pepper, 1 tsp roasted cumin, 1 tsp green chilli paste and 1 tsp lemon juice.
Rub in 2 tbsp warm melted Anveshan Ghee and bring the mix together into a firm, smooth dough, adding at most 1 tbsp water since the potato holds plenty of moisture.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to a moderate 175 C, a touch lower than for besan bhujia because kuttu browns faster.
Press the dough through a fine or medium die into the oil in slow circles, working in small batches so the delicate strands do not clump.
Fry 40-50 seconds until the sizzle quietens and the bhujia is crisp and light brown, then lift promptly before it darkens.
Drain on paper and cool fully; the buckwheat crunch firms up as it cools.
tips: Kuttu dough has no gluten, so keep it firm and press gently; if it crumbles, mash in a little more potato.
Fry at a slightly lower heat than besan bhujia, as buckwheat scorches quickly and turns bitter.
Season and serve the same day, as buckwheat snacks lose their crispness faster than gram-flour ones.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve during vrat with sweet potato chaat or a bowl of curd, and a wedge of lemon for those keeping a fast.

variations.name: Methi Masala Aloo Bhujia
variations.description: A herby, spice-loaded take that folds crushed kasuri methi and a warm garam-masala blend into the potato-besan dough for a fuller, more aromatic snack. The dried fenugreek adds a savoury bitterness that plays beautifully against the sweet potato base. It reads like a cross between bhujia and a spiced sev, meant for serious namkeen lovers.

ingredients.name: Boiled potato
ingredients.note: Grated fine and cooled for a smooth dough

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: For deep-frying the herbed strands to a fragrant crisp

ingredients.name: Kasuri methi
ingredients.note: Crushed between the palms to release its aroma into the dough

steps: Crush 2 tbsp kasuri methi between your palms and mix into 1.5 cups besan with 1 cup grated potato, 1 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp coriander powder, 1/2 tsp fennel powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1/4 tsp asafoetida and 1 tsp salt.
Add 2 tbsp hot oil from the pan, rub it in, then knead with up to 3 tbsp water to a stiff, pliable dough.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to a moderate 180 C and confirm with a dough thread that rises steadily.
Press the dough through a medium bhujia die into the oil in loose circular passes so the herb-flecked strands stay separate.
Fry 45-60 seconds until crisp and golden and the kasuri methi smells toasted, then lift and drain on paper.
Cool fully before storing so the masala crunch sets firm.
tips: Crush the kasuri methi finely, since long stalks catch in the press and clog the die.
Toast the garam masala nose-close first if it smells flat, to wake up the aroma before it goes in the dough.
A pinch of amchur at the end brightens the earthy fenugreek if you like a little tang.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a rich cocktail-hour namkeen with drinks, or crush over a masala chaat where its herby depth adds another layer.

variations.name: Classic Bengali Aloo Chop
variations.description: Aloo Chop is Kolkata's iconic tele-bhaja, a spiced mashed-potato patty jacketed in besan batter and fried until the shell shatters into a soft, warm centre. Roasted bhaja masala and a hint of ginger give the filling its distinctive Bengali fragrance, best eaten straight from the karai.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil is the authentic Bengali frying fat and lends the chop a clean, pungent crispness

steps: Heat 2 tbsp of the Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pan on medium, saute the chopped onion, 1 inch grated ginger and 3 chopped green chillies for 3 minutes until soft.
Add 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp roasted cumin-coriander powder, stir 30 seconds, then fold in the mashed potato with 1 tsp salt and cook 2 minutes.
Cool the filling, then shape it into 8 flat oval patties pressed firm so they hold in the oil.
Whisk 1 cup besan, 2 tbsp rice flour and 0.25 tsp salt with 0.5 cup water into a smooth, thick coating batter.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Mustard Oil until it smokes, cool to about 180C, dip each patty fully in batter, and fry three at a time for 3 to 4 minutes, turning, until deep golden and crisp.
Drain on paper and serve piping hot with kasundi or muri.
tips: Cool the potato filling completely before shaping, or warm patties crack and absorb oil.
Keep the besan batter thick so it forms an unbroken shell around the soft filling.
The rice flour in the batter is the trick to a crust that stays crisp for longer.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with kasundi mustard, a fried green chilli and muri, or tuck into a soft pau for a Kolkata-style chop roll.

variations.name: Bread-Crumbed Paneer-Cored Aloo Chop
variations.description: Modelled on the Kolkata cutlet counter, this version wraps the spiced potato around a spiced paneer heart, then dips it in a light slurry and rolls it in golden breadcrumbs for a shatter-crisp coat. The creamy paneer centre against the crunchy crumb makes it a heartier, more festive chop.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: its high smoke point crisps the breadcrumb shell to an even golden without burning

steps: Heat 2 tbsp of the Anveshan Sunflower Oil, saute the onion and 2 chopped green chillies for 2 minutes, add 1 tsp ginger-garlic paste and cook another minute.
Add 1 tsp garam masala, fold in the mashed potato with 1 tsp salt and 3 tbsp coriander, cook 2 minutes, and cool completely.
Season the grated paneer with a pinch of salt, then divide the potato into 8, flatten each, place a spoon of paneer in the centre, and seal the potato around it into a smooth oval.
Whisk 4 tbsp cornflour, 0.25 tsp salt and 5 tbsp water into a thin slurry, dip each chop, then roll firmly in 1 cup breadcrumbs to coat.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Sunflower Oil to about 180C and fry the chops three at a time for 3 to 4 minutes, turning, until evenly golden and crisp.
Drain on paper and serve hot so the crumb stays crunchy and the paneer centre soft.
tips: Press the potato firmly around the paneer with no gaps so it does not split open while frying.
Chill the crumbed chops for 15 minutes before frying to set the coating and keep it from flaking.
Use dry, coarse breadcrumbs for a sturdier, crunchier shell than fine ones.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with kasundi, tomato sauce and onion rings dusted with lime, cutting each open to show the paneer heart.

variations.name: Peanut-Raisin Sweet-Savoury Aloo Chop
variations.description: This East-Bengali style chop tucks a sweet-savoury filling of roasted peanuts, raisins and jaggery-tinged spice into the potato, echoing the shingara tradition. The gentle sweetness against the pungent mustard-oil crust makes it a nostalgic, festive treat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: its pungent bite balances the sweet filling and fries a crisp golden shell

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: adds the gentle molasses sweetness that defines this shingara-style filling

steps: Heat 2 tbsp of the Anveshan Mustard Oil, crackle 0.5 tsp panch phoron, add 1 inch grated ginger, then fold in the mashed potato.
Stir in 0.33 cup crushed peanuts, 2 tbsp raisins, 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 0.5 tsp roasted fennel and 1 tsp salt, and cook 2 minutes until the jaggery melts through; cool completely.
Shape the sweet-savoury filling into 8 firm ovals with lightly oiled hands.
Whisk 1 cup besan, 2 tbsp rice flour and a pinch of salt with 0.5 cup water into a thick, smooth batter.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Mustard Oil until it smokes, cool to about 180C, dip each oval fully in batter, and fry three at a time for 3 to 4 minutes until deep golden.
Drain on paper and serve warm so the sweet filling stays soft against the crisp shell.
tips: Melt the jaggery fully into the warm potato so there are no gritty pockets in the filling.
Toast the peanuts well for crunch and a deeper flavour that stands up to the sweetness.
Keep the sweetness gentle, as the chop should read savoury-first with a sweet surprise.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a sharp kasundi to offset the sweetness, ideal as a puja-pandal style evening snack.

variations.name: Baked Khapli Aloo Chop
variations.description: A lighter oven-baked chop crusted in nutty khapli atta and semolina rather than deep-fried batter, brushed with ghee for a golden shell. It keeps the spiced Bengali filling intact while dropping the oil for an everyday-friendly version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: forms a nutty, high-fibre crust that browns crisp in the oven without frying

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: brushed over the chops so they crisp and turn golden while baking

steps: Preheat the oven to 200C and line a tray with parchment brushed lightly with a little Anveshan Ghee.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan, saute the onion, ginger and 2 chopped green chillies for 2 minutes, add 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp roasted cumin, then fold in the potato with 1 tsp salt and 3 tbsp coriander; cool.
Whisk 0.5 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta and 0.25 tsp salt with 4 tbsp water into a thin coating slurry.
Shape the filling into 8 ovals, dip each in the khapli slurry, then roll in 0.33 cup semolina for a crunchy crust.
Arrange on the tray, brush the tops with Anveshan Ghee, bake 15 minutes, flip and brush again, then bake another 12 to 15 minutes until golden and crisp.
Rest for 2 minutes so the crust firms, then serve warm.
tips: The semolina coating is what gives the baked chop its crunch, so roll it on generously.
Brush ghee on both bakes for browning; without it the crust stays pale and dry.
Bake at a high heat and do not overcrowd the tray so the chops crisp rather than steam.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with green chutney and a fresh salad for a lighter tea-time or lunchbox chop.

variations.name: Classic South Indian Aloo Kurma
variations.description: A comforting South Indian potato curry where soft potato cubes simmer in a fragrant ground paste of coconut, roasted gram and fennel, tempered with curry leaves. Mild, creamy and lightly spiced, this coconut kurma is the everyday partner to poori, chapati and set dosa across Tamil and Kannada kitchens.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed coconut oil is the authentic South Indian fat that carries the curry leaf and fennel tempering

steps: Boil the 4 cubed potatoes in salted water for 8 minutes until just fork-tender, then drain and set aside.
Grind the 0.5 cup coconut, 2 tbsp roasted gram, 1 tsp fennel and 3 green chillies with a little water into a smooth paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan over medium heat, add the cinnamon and 12 curry leaves, and let them crackle for 20 seconds.
Add the finely chopped onion and saute for 4 minutes until soft and translucent, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the chopped tomato with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, cook for 4 minutes until the tomato collapses, then add the boiled potatoes and 1.5 cups water.
Stir in the ground coconut paste, simmer on low for 8 minutes until the gravy thickens to a creamy spoonable kurma, and serve hot.
tips: Boil the potatoes only until just tender so they hold their shape in the gravy rather than dissolving.
Add the coconut paste towards the end and simmer gently so the gravy stays fragrant and does not turn grainy.
A squeeze of lemon at the end brightens the mild coconut richness beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with soft poori, chapati, set dosa or plain steamed rice for a classic South Indian breakfast or lunch.

variations.name: Hotel-style White Aloo Kurma
variations.description: The pale, creamy kurma served with parotta at Tamil Nadu hotels, built on a no-tomato cashew and coconut paste that stays snowy white and richly smooth. Green chillies bring gentle heat while curd lends a subtle tang, making this the crowd-pleasing kurma of Sunday tiffin outings.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: coconut oil keeps the white kurma authentically South Indian while staying pale and clean-tasting

steps: Grind the 12 cashews, 0.33 cup coconut, 1 tbsp poppy seeds and 4 green chillies with a little water into a completely smooth white paste.
Boil the 4 cubed potatoes for 8 minutes until just tender and drain, keeping them pale rather than browned.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan over medium heat, add 1 bay leaf and 2 cardamoms, and warm for 30 seconds without letting them darken.
Add the finely chopped onion and saute gently for 5 minutes without browning, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute.
Pour in the white cashew-coconut paste with 1 tsp salt and 1.5 cups water, add the boiled potatoes, and simmer on low for 6 minutes.
Whisk the 3 tbsp curd smooth, lower the heat and stir it in, warm through for 2 minutes without boiling, and serve the pristine white kurma hot.
tips: Keep the flame low throughout so nothing browns, which is the secret to a truly white hotel kurma.
Whisk the curd well and add off the boil to keep it from splitting the delicate white gravy.
Soak the cashews and poppy seeds for ten minutes before grinding for the smoothest, creamiest paste.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with flaky Kerala parotta, idiyappam or ghee roast dosa, garnished with a sprig of coriander and a fried cashew.

variations.name: Chettinad Pepper Aloo Kurma
variations.description: A bold, peppery kurma from the Chettinad country, where potatoes simmer in a dark roasted masala of black pepper, fennel and star anise ground with coconut. Deeply aromatic and fiery, this version trades the mild creaminess of the classic for a robust, spice-forward punch that stands up to any bread.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: nutty wood-pressed sesame oil is the traditional Chettinad cooking fat that deepens the roasted masala

steps: Dry-roast 1.5 tsp peppercorns, 1 tsp fennel, 1 star anise and 3 dry red chillies for 2 minutes until fragrant, then grind with the 0.33 cup coconut into a coarse dark paste.
Boil the 4 cubed potatoes for 8 minutes until just tender and drain.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pan over medium heat and add 15 curry leaves, letting them crackle for 20 seconds.
Add the finely chopped onion and saute for 5 minutes until deep golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute.
Add the chopped tomatoes with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, cook for 5 minutes until pulpy, then stir in the roasted pepper-coconut paste and cook for 2 minutes.
Add the boiled potatoes and 1.5 cups water, simmer on low for 8 minutes until the kurma thickens and turns a deep reddish-brown, and serve hot.
tips: Roast the whole spices until just fragrant, not burnt, to keep the masala aromatic rather than bitter.
Adjust the pepper to taste; Chettinad kurma is meant to be assertively peppery rather than chilli-hot.
Let it rest for ten minutes before serving so the roasted spices deepen and meld into the gravy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with parotta, ghee rice or dosa, alongside a cooling raita to balance the bold Chettinad heat.

variations.name: Kaima Mint-Coriander Aloo Kurma
variations.description: A vibrant green kurma where baby potatoes bathe in a fresh paste of mint, coriander and green chilli brightened with coconut. Herbaceous and fragrant with a mild heat, this verdant version is a refreshing change from coconut-brown kurmas and looks stunning ladled beside a pilaf.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: coconut oil lets the fresh mint and coriander flavours stay clean and bright in the green kurma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of ghee rounds off the herby green gravy with a gentle richness

steps: Boil the 16 baby potatoes until just tender, about 10 minutes, then peel and lightly prick each so they soak up the gravy.
Grind the 0.5 cup mint, 0.75 cup coriander, 0.25 cup coconut, 3 green chillies and 8 cashews with a little water into a smooth green paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan over medium heat, add 0.5 tsp fennel, and let it sizzle for 20 seconds.
Add the finely chopped onion and saute for 4 minutes until soft, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute until the raw smell fades.
Pour in the green paste with 1 tsp salt and cook on medium for 4 minutes until the raw herb smell mellows and the oil surfaces, then add the boiled potatoes and 1 cup water.
Simmer on low for 6 minutes until the gravy thickens, finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee stirred through, and serve the green kurma hot.
tips: Cook the green paste just until the raw smell fades to keep the gravy a fresh green rather than dull khaki.
Prick the boiled baby potatoes so they drink up the herby gravy from the inside.
A pinch of sugar preserves the bright green colour and balances the chilli heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jeera pulao, ghee rice or soft phulka, garnished with a swirl of cream and fresh coriander for a striking green plate.

variations.name: Classic Assamese Aloo Pitika
variations.description: Aloo Pitika is the humble heart of every Assamese thali, boiled potatoes mashed with raw mustard oil, chopped onion, green chilli and coriander. No cooking, no fuss, just the sharp bite of mustard oil against soft potato that makes it the perfect companion to rice and dal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: raw wood-pressed mustard oil is the defining pungent note stirred into the mash uncooked

steps: Boil 4 potatoes until very soft, peel them while still warm, and mash them smooth in a wide bowl.
Add the finely chopped onion, 3 chopped green chillies, 0.5 inch grated ginger and 4 tbsp coriander to the warm mash.
Pour in 2 tbsp raw Anveshan Mustard Oil and 1 tsp salt over the mixture.
Mix everything together thoroughly with your hand or a spoon until the mustard oil coats the mash evenly.
Taste and adjust salt and chilli, then shape into a smooth mound or small rounds.
Serve at room temperature so the raw mustard oil stays sharp and fragrant.
tips: Use raw, unheated mustard oil for the authentic pungent kick that defines aloo pitika.
Mash the potatoes while warm, as they take on the flavours far better than cold ones.
Rinse the chopped onion briefly if you want to soften its raw sharpness in the mix.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside hot rice, a bowl of dal and a wedge of lime as the comforting centre of an Assamese thali.

variations.name: Roasted Tomato-Garlic Pitika
variations.description: A smoky cousin where fire-roasted tomatoes and charred garlic are pounded into the potato mash, giving a tangy, deeply aromatic pitika. The blistered skins lend a subtle smokiness that turns the simple mash into something crave-worthy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: stirred in raw to sharpen the smoky roasted tomato and garlic

steps: Char 2 tomatoes and 6 garlic cloves directly over an open flame until the skins blister and blacken, then peel and roughly mash them.
Boil, peel and mash 4 potatoes while warm in a wide bowl.
Crush 2 roasted dried red chillies and add them with the roasted tomato-garlic pulp to the potato.
Add the chopped onion, 2 green chillies, 4 tbsp coriander, 1 tsp salt and 2 tbsp raw Anveshan Mustard Oil.
Mix thoroughly until the smoky pulp and mustard oil are evenly worked through the mash.
Shape into a mound and serve at room temperature so the smoky aroma comes through.
tips: Roast the tomatoes until the skin is fully charred, as that blister is where the smoky flavour lives.
Peel the roasted garlic and mash it well so no sharp raw pieces remain.
Add the mustard oil last and raw to keep its pungency lively against the smoke.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a khar or dal, the smoky mash cutting through a simple meal beautifully.

variations.name: Ghee-Tempered Kharoli Pitika
variations.description: A richer take where a fragrant ghee tempering of panch phoron and curry leaves is poured sizzling over the mash, warming the pitika and rounding the raw mustard bite. The hot tarka melts into the potato for a mellow, aromatic version served warm.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee carries a sizzling tempering that mellows and warms the mash

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: a small raw drizzle keeps the signature Assamese pungency alive

steps: Boil, peel and mash 4 potatoes while warm, then mix in the chopped onion, 0.5 inch grated ginger, 3 tbsp coriander, 1 tsp salt and 1 tbsp raw Anveshan Mustard Oil.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan on medium until it shimmers.
Add 0.5 tsp panch phoron and let it crackle for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Toss in 2 broken dried red chillies and 10 curry leaves and fry for 15 seconds until the leaves crisp.
Pour the sizzling ghee tempering over the mashed potato and fold it through quickly.
Shape into a warm mound and serve at once while the tempering aroma is fresh.
tips: Pour the tempering while it is still sizzling so its aroma blooms into the mash.
Keep the panch phoron from browning too far, as burnt spices turn the tarka bitter.
A small drizzle of raw mustard oil at the end preserves the Assamese pungency under the warm ghee.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with rice and a dal, or scoop into soft rotis for a quick, aromatic wrap.

variations.name: Sesame-Peanut Pitika
variations.description: A textured version enriched with toasted sesame and crushed roasted peanuts pounded into the mash, adding nuttiness and a gentle crunch. Sesame oil deepens the flavour, giving a pitika with more body that eats almost like a dip.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed sesame oil deepens the toasty, nutty character of this pitika

steps: Toast 2 tbsp sesame seeds in a dry pan until golden and popping, then set aside; crush 3 tbsp roasted peanuts coarsely.
Boil, peel and mash 4 potatoes while warm in a wide bowl.
Add the chopped onion, 3 green chillies, the toasted sesame, crushed peanuts and 3 tbsp coriander.
Pour in 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 1 tsp salt.
Mix thoroughly until the nutty bits and sesame oil are evenly folded through the mash.
Shape into a mound or quenelles and serve at room temperature.
tips: Toast the sesame seeds just until golden, as they burn and turn bitter very quickly.
Crush the peanuts coarsely so they add crunch rather than disappearing into the mash.
The lemon lifts the nutty richness, so add it to taste at the end.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with rice and dal, or as a nutty dip with warm parathas and crisp cucumber sticks.

variations.name: Classic Aloo Tikki Chaat
variations.description: Crisp golden potato tikkis are shallow-fried in ghee, then broken open and smothered in cool whisked yogurt, sweet tamarind and spicy green chutneys. The soft spiced potato centre against the crunchy crust and tangy toppings makes this the quintessential North Indian street chaat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: shallow-frying the tikkis in bilona ghee builds a deeply golden, aromatic crust

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the tamarind chutney with a rich natural depth

steps: Boil and mash the 6 potatoes while still warm, then mix in 3 tbsp cornflour, 2 chopped green chillies, 0.75 tsp salt and 1 tsp chaat masala until it forms a firm dough.
Shape into 8 flat round tikkis about 1.5 cm thick, pressing them so they hold together without cracking.
Heat 5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on a tawa over medium heat and shallow-fry the tikkis for 5 to 6 minutes a side until deeply golden and crisp.
Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and a splash of water for 5 minutes into a thick sweet-sour chutney, and whisk the 2 cups yogurt smooth with 0.25 tsp salt.
Place two hot tikkis on each plate and press the centres lightly to open them up.
Spoon over the whisked yogurt, then drizzle with the tamarind chutney and 4 tbsp green chutney.
Dust with 0.5 tsp chaat masala, 1 tsp roasted cumin, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp black salt, top with sev and coriander, and serve at once.
tips: Mash the potatoes while warm and add cornflour so the tikkis bind firmly and do not fall apart in the pan.
Fry on steady medium heat and resist flipping too early so a proper crust forms.
Assemble just before serving so the crust stays crisp under the yogurt and chutneys.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot straight off the tawa with the chutneys drizzled last so the tikki keeps its crunch.

variations.name: Ram Ladoo Style Tikki Chaat
variations.description: This UP halwai style stuffs each tikki with a spiced green pea and paneer filling before frying, so cracking one open reveals a savoury heart. Served over a bed of chutneys and yogurt with pomegranate, it is heartier and more festive than the plain mashed-potato tikki.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: frying the stuffed tikkis in ghee gives a rich crust that seals the filling inside

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: balances the tamarind chutney over the savoury stuffed tikki

steps: Boil and mash the 6 potatoes warm, then mix in 3 tbsp cornflour, 0.5 tsp salt and 1 tsp chaat masala to a firm dough.
Coarsely mash 1 cup boiled green peas and mix with the crumbled 0.5 cup paneer, 1 inch grated ginger, 0.75 tsp garam masala and 0.25 tsp salt for the filling.
Flatten a portion of potato dough on your palm, place a spoon of the pea-paneer filling in the centre, seal, and press into a stuffed tikki.
Heat 5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on a tawa over medium heat and fry the stuffed tikkis 5 to 6 minutes a side until golden and crisp.
Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder for 5 minutes into a thick chutney, and whisk the 1.5 cups yogurt smooth.
Set two tikkis on each plate, spoon over yogurt, then drizzle tamarind chutney and 4 tbsp green chutney.
Dust with 0.5 tsp chaat masala, scatter pomegranate and coriander, and serve hot so the filling is still soft.
tips: Seal the filling fully inside the potato so it does not leak into the ghee while frying.
Dry the mashed peas well so the filling stays firm and the tikki holds its shape.
Serve immediately after cutting open so the warm pea-paneer centre contrasts the cool yogurt.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve split open so the green filling shows, finished with extra pomegranate for colour and crunch.

variations.name: Ragda Tikki Chaat
variations.description: The Indori and Mumbai favourite drowns crisp tikkis in a hot, spiced white-pea ragda gravy before the chutneys and onion go on. The warm, soupy peas soaking into the crunchy potato patty make this the most comforting and filling version of tikki chaat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: frying the tikkis in ghee gives a crust sturdy enough to stand up to the hot ragda

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the tamarind chutney that balances the spicy pea gravy

steps: Soak 1 cup white peas overnight, then pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 5 to 6 whistles until completely soft.
Mash a ladle of the cooked peas into the pot and simmer 10 minutes with 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp roasted cumin into a thick pourable ragda.
Boil and mash the 6 potatoes warm, mix with 3 tbsp cornflour and 0.5 tsp salt, and shape into 8 tikkis.
Heat 5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on a tawa over medium heat and fry the tikkis 5 to 6 minutes a side until crisp and golden.
Simmer 2 tbsp tamarind with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder for 4 minutes into a sweet-sour chutney.
Place two hot tikkis on each plate and ladle the steaming ragda generously over them.
Drizzle with tamarind and 3 tbsp green chutney, sprinkle 1.5 tsp chaat masala, finely chopped onion, sev and coriander, and serve hot.
tips: Cook the white peas until fully collapsing so the ragda is thick and creamy rather than watery.
Keep the ragda hot and ladle it over the tikkis at the last second so the contrast of hot gravy and crisp crust holds.
Fry the tikkis a touch firmer than usual so they do not disintegrate under the wet ragda.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a deep plate so the ragda pools around the tikkis, with extra onion and lime on the side.

variations.name: Air-Fried Sattu Tikki Chaat
variations.description: A lighter, protein-boosted take that binds the potato with roasted gram sattu and air-fries the tikkis to a crunch with barely any oil. The nutty sattu adds body and keeps the tikkis firm, making this a wholesome everyday chaat with all the street flavour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: roasted gram sattu binds the tikkis firmly and adds plant protein and a nutty flavour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a light brush of wood-pressed oil crisps the tikkis in the air fryer with minimal fat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: sweetens the tamarind chutney naturally for the lighter chaat

steps: Boil and mash the 5 potatoes warm, then knead in 0.5 cup Anveshan Sattu, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp chaat masala and 0.75 tsp salt into a firm, non-sticky dough.
Shape into 8 flat tikkis and brush both sides lightly with the 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil.
Air-fry at 190 C for 18 to 20 minutes, flipping once halfway, until the tikkis are golden and crisp on both faces.
Simmer 2 tbsp tamarind with 2 tbsp Anveshan Honey for 4 minutes into a sweet-sour chutney and cool it, then whisk the 2 cups yogurt smooth with 0.25 tsp salt.
Set two hot tikkis on each plate and spoon over the whisked yogurt.
Drizzle with the tamarind chutney and 4 tbsp green chutney, dust with 0.5 tsp chaat masala, 1 tsp roasted cumin and 0.5 tsp black salt, and finish with coriander before serving.
tips: Sattu absorbs moisture, so add it gradually until the dough is firm but not dry and crumbly.
Preheat the air fryer so the tikkis crisp quickly and do not dry out.
Stir the honey into the chutney off the heat so its flavour stays bright.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a filling high-protein snack with extra green chutney and a wedge of lime alongside.

variations.name: Classic Bengali Aloor Dom
variations.description: The beloved Bengali baby-potato curry where whole boiled potatoes are simmered in a glossy mustard-oil gravy of onion, tomato, ginger and Bengali garam masala. The potatoes are lightly pricked and fried so they drink up the spices, giving a dish that is at once homely and festive. A pinch of sweetness and a slick of pungent mustard oil are what make it unmistakably Bengali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil gives Bengali aloor dom its signature pungent warmth; heat it to smoking first to mellow the sharpness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A touch of jaggery instead of white sugar balances the tomato and mustard oil the way Bengali cooks intend

steps: Boil 500 g baby potatoes until just tender, peel them, and prick each one lightly with a fork so they soak up the gravy.

Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just begins to smoke, lower the heat to medium, and fry the potatoes with 1/2 tsp turmeric and a pinch of salt for 5 to 6 minutes until golden and blistered, then lift them out.

In the same oil crackle 1 bay leaf, add 2 finely chopped onions and fry on medium heat until deep golden, about 7 minutes, then stir in 1.5 tbsp ginger paste and 1 tbsp garlic paste and cook for 1 minute until the raw smell goes.

Add 2 pureed tomatoes and cook until the oil separates at the edges, around 6 minutes, then lower the heat and add 1.5 tsp cumin powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, frying for 40 seconds until the masala smells roasted.

Return the fried potatoes, add 1.5 cups hot water, 1/2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and the remaining salt, cover and simmer on low heat for 12 to 15 minutes until the gravy thickens and clings to the potatoes.
Finish with 3/4 tsp Bengali garam masala, rest covered for 5 minutes, and serve.
tips: Pricking the boiled potatoes before frying is the small step that lets them absorb the masala instead of staying bland inside.
If the gravy turns too tangy from the tomatoes, an extra pinch of jaggery powder rounds it out beautifully.
Make it a few hours ahead; aloor dom deepens in flavour as it sits and reheats wonderfully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with luchi, radhaballavi or plain steamed rice, with a wedge of lemon and a green chilli on the side.

variations.name: Niramish Bhoger Aloor Dom
variations.description: The temple-offering (bhog) version cooked entirely without onion or garlic, the way it is made during Durga Puja and served on a banana leaf. Ginger, asafoetida and whole cumin carry all the aroma, while ghee and Bengali garam masala give a pure, sattvic richness. It is lighter and sweeter than the everyday curry, meant to be eaten with khichuri.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee finishes the sattvic bhog gravy with the fragrance that defines Bengali temple cooking

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: A little wood-pressed mustard oil for frying keeps the dish rooted in Bengali flavour even without onion or garlic

steps: Boil 500 g baby potatoes until just tender, peel, and prick lightly so they absorb the gravy well.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until smoking, reduce to medium, and shallow-fry the potatoes with 1/2 tsp turmeric for 5 minutes until golden, then set aside.
In the same oil temper 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 dried red chilli, 1 bay leaf and 1/4 tsp asafoetida for 20 seconds until fragrant, then add 2 tbsp ginger paste and fry on low heat for 1 minute.
Add 1 grated large tomato and cook for 4 minutes until pulpy, then stir in 1.5 tsp cumin powder, 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and cook 40 seconds until the masala releases oil.
Return the potatoes with 1.5 cups hot water, 3/4 tsp sugar and the salt, cover and simmer on low heat for 12 minutes until the gravy is thick and glossy.
Swirl in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 3/4 tsp Bengali garam masala, rest covered for 5 minutes, and serve.
tips: Ginger paste does the heavy lifting here, so use it generously and fry it well to build depth without onion or garlic.
Finishing with ghee off the heat keeps its aroma intact, which is the soul of a bhog dish.
This niramish version is naturally sweeter; adjust the sugar to taste but do not skip it entirely.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a banana leaf alongside bhoger khichuri and a sweet tomato chutney for a festive Puja spread.

variations.name: Doi Aloor Dom
variations.description: A creamy, mildly spiced version where whisked yogurt and a cashew paste replace tomatoes, giving a pale, velvety gravy with a gentle tang. There is no fiery heat here, only the fragrance of whole spices and the smoothness of curd, making it a banquet-style dish for guests. The potatoes stay whole and glossy in the rich white gravy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries the whole spices and keeps the yogurt gravy rich without a mustard-oil sharpness

steps: Boil 500 g baby potatoes until just tender, peel, and prick them; soak 12 cashews in warm water for 10 minutes and grind to a smooth paste.
Whisk 3/4 cup thick yogurt with 1 tsp cumin powder, 1/2 tsp turmeric and the cashew paste until completely lump-free and keep aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat and fry the potatoes with a pinch of salt for 5 minutes until pale gold, then remove them.
In the same ghee temper 1 bay leaf, 1 inch cinnamon, 4 cardamom pods and 4 cloves for 20 seconds, then add 1.5 tbsp ginger paste and 3 slit green chillies and fry for 1 minute.

Lower the heat to the minimum and pour in the whisked yogurt mixture, stirring continuously for 3 to 4 minutes so it warms without splitting, then return the potatoes with 1 cup hot water, 1 tsp sugar and the salt.
Cover and simmer gently for 10 to 12 minutes until the gravy is creamy, finish with 1/2 tsp Bengali garam masala, and serve.
tips: Always add the yogurt on the lowest heat and keep stirring; boiling it hard will make the gravy curdle and turn grainy.
The cashew paste is what gives body and a subtle sweetness, so do not skip it in this version.
Keep the green chillies whole and slit for aroma without overwhelming the delicate white gravy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with fragrant basanti pulao or soft parathas at a special-occasion Bengali lunch.

variations.name: Kosha Aloor Dom
variations.description: A darker, drier, deeply spiced version in the kosha (slow-bhuna) style, where the potatoes are cooked down with fried onions and a dry-roasted spice blend until the masala clings thickly with barely any gravy. The long slow cooking gives an almost caramelised depth and a rich mahogany colour. This is the version that disappears fast at a Sunday feast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Generous wood-pressed mustard oil is essential for a proper kosha, letting the masala fry down slowly to a deep colour

steps: Dry-roast 1.5 tbsp coriander seeds, 1 tbsp cumin seeds and 3 dried red chillies on low heat for 2 minutes until fragrant, cool, and grind to a coarse powder.
Boil 500 g baby potatoes until just tender, peel, and prick them all over with a fork.
Heat 5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until smoking, lower to medium, and fry the potatoes with 1/2 tsp turmeric until deep golden all over, about 7 minutes, then remove.
In the same oil temper 1 inch cinnamon and 3 cardamom pods, then add 3 thinly sliced onions and fry patiently on medium-low heat for 12 to 14 minutes until dark brown and jammy.
Add 2 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 2 minutes, then stir in the freshly ground spice powder and 2 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder with a splash of water, frying until the oil separates.

Return the potatoes, add only 1/2 cup hot water and the salt, cover and slow-cook on low heat for 15 minutes, stirring now and then, until the masala is thick, dark and clinging with almost no gravy; finish with 1 tsp Bengali garam masala.
tips: The secret to kosha is patience: fry the onions truly dark and cook the potatoes on low heat so the masala reduces and coats rather than pools.
Freshly ground roasted coriander and cumin give a far deeper flavour than pre-ground powders here.
Keep the water minimal; this is meant to be a semi-dry, intensely spiced dish, not a runny curry.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot luchi or paratha, or as a rich side with plain rice and dal at a leisurely weekend meal.

variations.name: Classic Amitar Khar (Raw Papaya)
variations.description: Khar is the soul of an Assamese meal, an alkaline dish traditionally cooked with khar water filtered through sun-dried banana-peel ash. This classic amitar khar simmers raw papaya in that alkaline broth with just green chilli and mustard oil, giving a clean, mildly bitter, deeply comforting curry eaten at the start of a meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil is the traditional Assamese cooking fat that carries the khar's earthy character

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just smokes, then lower to medium and temper 0.25 tsp fenugreek seeds and 1 bay leaf for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 inch grated ginger and 3 slit green chillies, stir for 30 seconds, then add the raw papaya cubes and saute for 3 minutes.
Pour in 0.5 cup khar water and 1.5 cups water, add 1 tsp salt, and bring to a gentle boil.
Cover and simmer on medium-low for 15 to 18 minutes until the papaya is very soft and the liquid reduces to a light, slippery gravy.
Mash a few papaya cubes against the side of the pan to lightly thicken the broth.
Simmer uncovered for 2 more minutes until it turns glossy, then serve hot over rice.
tips: If you cannot source traditional khar, dissolve a pinch of food-grade baking soda in half a cup of water as a substitute.
Never add turmeric to a classic khar, as it clouds the clean, pale look the dish is known for.
Cook the papaya until it almost melts, since khar is meant to be soft and soupy rather than firm.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve first in the meal over hot steamed rice with a wedge of lemon, the way Assamese thalis traditionally open.

variations.name: Matimah Diya Khar (Black Gram)
variations.description: A heartier khar from central Assam where fried black-gram dal fritters or roasted whole urad are simmered in the alkaline broth with ash gourd, giving a nutty, protein-rich bite. The crackle of the fried dal against the soft alkaline gravy makes it a festive, filling version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: fries the urad dal to a nutty crisp and tempers the alkaline broth

steps: Dry-roast 0.33 cup split black gram in a pan until deep golden and aromatic, then set aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it smokes, lower the heat, and fry 1 bay leaf, 4 crushed garlic cloves and 1 inch grated ginger for 1 minute.
Add the roasted black gram and ash gourd cubes with 3 slit green chillies and saute 3 minutes.
Pour in 0.5 cup khar water and 2 cups water, add 1 tsp salt, and bring to a boil.
Cover and simmer on medium-low for 18 to 20 minutes until the gourd is soft and the dal has plumped and turned tender.
Uncover, simmer 3 more minutes until the broth thickens slightly, and serve hot.
tips: Roast the black gram well so it stays nutty and does not turn mushy in the long simmer.
Ash gourd cooks fast, so cut it a little larger than the dal to keep some texture.
Substitute a pinch of baking soda in water if traditional khar is unavailable.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over rice as a wholesome main, paired with a simple aloo pitika and a squeeze of lime.

variations.name: Lai Xaak Khar (Mustard Greens)
variations.description: A winter khar built on lai xaak, Assam's tender mustard greens, wilted into the alkaline broth for a slightly bitter, iron-rich dish. The greens turn silky and the khar mellows their sharpness into a soothing, nourishing bowl.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: its pungency complements the mustard greens and rounds the alkaline broth

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it smokes, lower the heat, and crackle 2 dried red chillies and 5 crushed garlic cloves for 1 minute until golden.
Add the cubed potato and 3 slit green chillies and saute for 3 minutes.
Add the chopped mustard greens in batches, stirring until they wilt down, about 4 minutes.
Pour in 0.5 cup khar water and 1 cup water, add 1 tsp salt, and bring to a simmer.
Cover and cook on medium-low for 10 to 12 minutes until the greens are silky and the potato is soft.
Uncover and cook off most of the liquid, stirring, until it turns into a moist, glossy saag; serve hot.
tips: Wash the greens thoroughly and chop the thick stems finer so they cook as fast as the leaves.
The khar tames the bitterness of lai xaak, so add it early rather than at the end.
Use a pinch of baking soda in water if you do not have traditional khar to hand.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot rice and a dollop of ghee, a warming winter side that pairs well with a tangy tomato chutney.

variations.name: Kol Khar (Banana with Coconut)
variations.description: A softer, rounder khar made with raw banana and finished with a spoon of coconut, giving a creamy body quite unlike the lean classic. The banana thickens the alkaline broth naturally while coconut oil lends a gentle sweetness that families in lower Assam favour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed coconut oil deepens the coconut note and gives this khar its rounded, creamy character

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil on medium, temper 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and 1 bay leaf for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 inch grated ginger and 3 slit green chillies, stir 30 seconds, then add the raw banana cubes and saute 3 minutes.
Pour in 0.5 cup khar water and 1.5 cups water, add 1 tsp salt, and bring to a gentle boil.
Cover and simmer on medium-low for 15 minutes until the banana is very soft and starting to break down.
Stir in 0.33 cup grated coconut and mash a few banana pieces to thicken the broth to a creamy consistency.
Simmer 3 more minutes until glossy and serve hot over rice.
tips: Rub your hands and knife with a little oil before peeling raw banana to avoid staining and stickiness.
Add the coconut towards the end so it stays fragrant and does not turn grainy.
A pinch of baking soda dissolved in water stands in for traditional khar when needed.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over rice as a comforting opener, with a side of fried potato and a spoon of curd to balance.

variations.name: Classic Hyderabadi Bagara Baingan
variations.description: The iconic Hyderabadi brinjal curry where small aubergines simmer in a luscious ground gravy of roasted peanuts, sesame, coconut and tamarind. Nutty, tangy and glossy with a deep brown sheen, it is the wedding-feast partner to bagara khana and biryani across the Deccan.

ingredients.name: Small brinjals
ingredients.note: slit into quarters keeping the stalk

ingredients.name: Roasted peanuts
ingredients.note: for the nutty ground gravy

ingredients.name: Sesame seeds
ingredients.note: roasted

ingredients.name: Dry coconut
ingredients.note: grated and roasted

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked for pulp

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: sliced and browned

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed gingelly oil, the authentic Deccan fat for frying the brinjals and gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: balances the tamarind sourness to the classic sweet-sour-nutty finish

steps: Dry-roast 3 tbsp peanuts, 2 tbsp sesame seeds and 2 tbsp dry coconut separately on low heat until golden, cool, then grind with the browned onions into a smooth thick paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pan over medium heat and fry the 8 slit brinjals for 5 minutes until the skins blister and soften, then remove and set aside.
In the same oil splutter 1/2 tsp cumin seeds and 1 sprig curry leaves, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and saute for 1 minute until fragrant.
Stir in the ground peanut-sesame paste with 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp coriander powder, and cook for 6 minutes until the oil floats and the paste darkens.
Add the squeezed tamarind pulp, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1.25 tsp salt and 1.5 cups water, and simmer for 5 minutes until the gravy turns thick and glossy.
Slide the fried brinjals back in, cover and simmer on low for 8 minutes until they soak up the gravy and turn meltingly soft, then serve.
tips: Fry the brinjals first so they hold their shape and do not disintegrate into the gravy later.
Roast each nut and seed separately, as they brown at different rates and a burnt one turns the whole gravy bitter.
The gravy should coat the brinjals thickly; add hot water a little at a time to reach that clinging consistency.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside bagara khana, Hyderabadi biryani or plain jeera rice, with a bowl of dahi ki chutney.

variations.name: Shahi Cashew Bagara Baingan
variations.description: The richer nizami banquet version where cashews and poppy seeds join the peanut-sesame grind and a spoon of khoya rounds the gravy, giving a plusher, more luxurious brinjal curry. Deeper and creamier than the everyday version, it is reserved for grand dawats.

ingredients.name: Small brinjals
ingredients.note: slit into quarters

ingredients.name: Cashew nuts
ingredients.note: soaked, for a plush grind

ingredients.name: Poppy seeds
ingredients.note: soaked, for creaminess

ingredients.name: Khoya (mawa)
ingredients.note: grated, to enrich the gravy

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked for a gentle tang

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: browned

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the banquet fat that fries the brinjals and enriches the shahi gravy

steps: Soak 12 cashews and 1 tbsp poppy seeds for 15 minutes, then grind with 2 tbsp roasted peanuts and the browned onions into a smooth, pale-brown paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat, gently fry the 8 slit brinjals for 5 minutes until softened, and set aside.
In the same ghee sizzle the 3 cardamoms and 1 inch cinnamon for 30 seconds, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute.
Add the cashew-peanut paste with 1 tsp red chilli powder and cook gently for 6 minutes on medium-low, stirring so it does not brown too dark.
Stir in the squeezed tamarind, grated khoya, 1.25 tsp salt and 1.5 cups water, and simmer for 5 minutes until the gravy turns rich and velvety.
Return the brinjals, sprinkle 1/2 tsp garam masala, cover and simmer on low for 8 minutes until they are tender and coated, then serve.
tips: Grate the khoya finely so it melts smoothly into the gravy without lumps.
This version leans creamy and mild, so keep the tamarind light to let the richness lead.
A drizzle of warm ghee on top just before serving deepens the banquet aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sheermal, roomali roti or a delicate zafrani pulao for a nizami spread.

variations.name: Tawa Bagara Baingan Fry
variations.description: A drier, roasted take where the brinjals are pan-seared and tossed in a thick clinging peanut-sesame masala rather than a pouring gravy, giving a semi-dry side with charred, caramelised edges. Punchier and more textural than the saucy classic, it doubles as a starter or a rice accompaniment.

ingredients.name: Small brinjals
ingredients.note: halved lengthwise

ingredients.name: Roasted peanuts
ingredients.note: coarsely crushed for texture

ingredients.name: Sesame seeds
ingredients.note: roasted

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil that sears the brinjals with a nutty char

ingredients.name: Amchur powder
ingredients.note: for a dry tang instead of tamarind

steps: Dry-roast 4 tbsp peanuts and 2 tbsp sesame seeds until golden, cool, then pulse to a coarse crushed mix, keeping some crunch.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on a wide tawa over medium-high heat and sear the 10 halved brinjals cut-side down for 5-6 minutes until charred and tender, then push to one side.
In the same tawa splutter 1/2 tsp cumin seeds and 2 sprigs curry leaves, add the chopped onion and fry for 5 minutes until deep golden.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, and cook for 2 minutes until the raw smell fades.
Add the coarse peanut-sesame mix, 1 tsp amchur powder and 1 tsp salt, then toss the seared brinjals through with a sprinkle of water so the masala clings.
Cook uncovered on medium heat for 5 minutes, tossing gently, until the brinjals are glazed and semi-dry, then serve hot.
tips: Keep the crushed peanuts coarse rather than a paste, as the crunch is the point of this dry version.
Sear the brinjals undisturbed to build char before tossing them in the masala.
Amchur gives a clean dry tang here; use it instead of tamarind to keep the dish from going saucy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a starter with toothpicks, or as a dry side with dal and rice or chapati.

variations.name: Andhra Gutti Vankaya Kura
variations.description: The Andhra stuffed-brinjal cousin, where each aubergine is filled with a dry roasted-peanut, sesame and red-chilli masala before being simmered in a light tamarind gravy. Spicier and more rustic than the Hyderabadi version, the stuffing packs the flavour right inside each brinjal.

ingredients.name: Small brinjals
ingredients.note: slit into a cross keeping the base intact

ingredients.name: Roasted peanuts
ingredients.note: ground for the stuffing

ingredients.name: Sesame seeds
ingredients.note: roasted, for the stuffing

ingredients.name: Dry coconut
ingredients.note: roasted

ingredients.name: Red chilli powder
ingredients.note: Andhra-style heat

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked for a light gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: the pungent gingelly oil that suits the fiery Andhra stuffing

steps: Grind 4 tbsp roasted peanuts, 2 tbsp roasted sesame, 2 tbsp roasted coconut, 2 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander powder and 1/2 tsp salt into a coarse dry stuffing.
Slit each brinjal into a cross from the base upward without separating the pieces, and pack the peanut stuffing firmly into each pocket, reserving the leftover mix.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pan over medium heat, splutter 1/2 tsp mustard and 1/2 tsp cumin seeds with 2 sprigs curry leaves.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the stuffed brinjals, cover and cook on low for 8 minutes, turning gently so all sides soften without breaking.
Add the squeezed tamarind pulp, the reserved stuffing, 1/2 tsp turmeric, 3/4 tsp salt and 1 cup water, and simmer for 8 minutes until a light clinging gravy forms.
Cook covered until the brinjals are fork-soft and the oil surfaces, about 4 more minutes, then serve hot.
tips: Leave the base of each brinjal intact so the stuffing stays packed inside during cooking.
Turn the brinjals gently and infrequently so they cook through without falling apart.
This is meant to be fiery; reduce the chilli powder to 1 tsp for a milder pocketful.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or with jowar roti for a rustic Andhra meal.

variations.name: Classic Basket Chaat
variations.description: This Lucknawi tokri chaat serves a crisp edible basket woven from fried potato threads and loaded with spiced ragda, sweet curd and three chutneys. The shattering potato shell against the soft filling and cool yogurt is what makes this the showpiece of North Indian chaat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: deep-frying the grated-potato baskets in wood-pressed oil gives a clean crackling shell

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the tamarind chutney with a deep caramel note

steps: Soak 1 cup white peas overnight, then pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp salt and a cup of water for 4 whistles until soft, and mash lightly into a thick ragda.
Peel and coarsely grate the 4 potatoes, rinse in cold water to remove starch, squeeze completely dry and toss with 3 tbsp cornflour and 0.5 tsp salt.

Press a handful of the grated potato between two small metal sieves or ladles to shape a basket, then lower into 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil heated to 180 C and fry for 4 to 5 minutes until golden and rigid, releasing 4 baskets in total.
Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind pulp with 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and a splash of water for 5 minutes into a glossy sweet-sour chutney, then cool.
Whisk the 1.5 cups yogurt smooth with a pinch of black salt and chill, and stir the warm ragda with 1 tsp chaat masala and 0.5 tsp red chilli powder.
Set each crisp basket on a plate, spoon in the warm ragda, then top with whisked yogurt, tamarind and green chutney.
Dust with the remaining chaat masala, 1.5 tsp roasted cumin, red chilli powder and black salt, then finish with sev, pomegranate and coriander and serve at once.
tips: Squeeze the grated potato bone-dry before shaping or the baskets will spit and refuse to crisp.
Fry the baskets a few hours ahead and re-crisp in a hot oven, assembling only at serving time so they stay shattering.
Keep the ragda thick, as a runny filling will collapse the delicate potato shell.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve one loaded basket per person on a wide plate with extra chutney on the side to spoon over as it is eaten.

variations.name: Ragda Basket Chaat
variations.description: The Bombay avatar fills the crisp basket with a hot, garlicky white-pea ragda simmered with onion-tomato masala and finishes it with crunchy fried potato threads instead of sev. It is heartier and more savoury than the Lucknawi version, eating almost like a chaat in a bowl.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil crisps the baskets and gives the ragda tadka a nutty base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: rounds the tangy ragda and tamarind with gentle sweetness

steps: Soak 1.5 cups white peas overnight and pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt for 5 whistles until completely soft.
Heat 3 tbsp of the Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan, saute 2 chopped onions until golden, add 1.5 tbsp ginger garlic paste and 2 chopped tomatoes, and cook down for 8 minutes into a thick masala.
Stir in 1.5 tsp goda masala, 1 tsp red chilli powder and the cooked peas with their water, mash a quarter of them and simmer 10 minutes into a pourable ragda seasoned with the remaining salt.
Peel and grate the 4 potatoes, rinse and squeeze dry, then toss with 3 tbsp cornflour and shape into baskets between two sieves.
Deep-fry the baskets in the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil at 180 C for 4 to 5 minutes until rigid and golden, and fry a small handful of loose potato threads separately for garnish.
Simmer 2 tbsp tamarind with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder for 4 minutes into a tangy-sweet chutney.
Fill each hot basket with ladlefuls of the spiced ragda, drizzle with tamarind chutney, dust with 1.5 tsp chaat masala and pile on the crisp potato threads and coriander before serving.
tips: Keep a little cooking liquid so the ragda stays saucy and soaks into the basket without dissolving it.
Fry the garnish threads to a deep gold, as they replace sev for the crunch in this style.
Add a pinch of extra goda masala at the end to keep the Maharashtrian aroma forward.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot with a wedge of lime and thinly sliced raw onion tossed in chaat masala on the side.

variations.name: Palak Patta Basket Chaat
variations.description: Here crisp fried spinach leaves replace the potato weave to form a lacy green basket that shatters at a touch. Piled with chana, beaten curd, pomegranate and chutneys, it is the delicate, restaurant-style chaat that has become a modern menu favourite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: crisps the batter-dipped spinach leaves into shattering baskets without greasiness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: sweetens the beaten curd drizzle for a mellow finish over the greens

steps: Whisk 0.75 cup besan with 2 tbsp rice flour, 0.5 tsp salt, 0.25 tsp red chilli powder and enough cold water to make a thin coating batter.
Wash and pat the 24 spinach leaves fully dry, then dip each leaf in the batter and drape three or four leaves inside a small ladle to form a basket.
Lower the ladle into 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil heated to 175 C and fry each basket for 2 to 3 minutes until the leaves are crisp and translucent, making four baskets.
Whisk the 1.5 cups yogurt smooth with 2 tbsp Anveshan Honey and the remaining salt and chill, and warm the 1 cup boiled chickpeas with a pinch of chaat masala.
Set each crisp spinach basket on a plate and spoon in the warm chickpeas as the base layer.
Drizzle over the sweetened curd, tamarind chutney and green chutney, then dust with 1.5 tsp chaat masala, 1 tsp roasted cumin and the remaining chilli powder.
Scatter pomegranate, sev and a torn coriander leaf over the top and serve immediately before the leaves soften.
tips: Dry the spinach leaves thoroughly and use a thin batter so the baskets stay lacy rather than doughy.
Fry on slightly lower heat than potato baskets so the leaves crisp without scorching.
Assemble one basket at a time and eat straight away, as fried spinach wilts within minutes of the curd touching it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Plate as an elegant starter, one green basket per guest, finished with a single mint sprig and a dusting of pomegranate.

variations.name: Baked Basket Chaat
variations.description: A lighter reworking that shapes the potato baskets over an inverted muffin tin and bakes them crisp with a brush of ghee instead of deep-frying. Filled with sprouts, curd and chutneys, it keeps the drama of the tokri chaat with far less oil.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: brushing the potato baskets with ghee helps them bake to a golden crisp shell

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the tamarind chutney for the lighter baked chaat

steps: Preheat the oven to 200 C and lightly grease the backs of an inverted muffin tin with a little of the Anveshan Ghee.
Peel and grate the 4 potatoes, rinse and squeeze completely dry, then mix with 3 tbsp cornflour and 0.5 tsp salt.

Drape the grated potato over four inverted muffin cups to form basket shapes, brush generously with the remaining Anveshan Ghee, and bake for 25 to 30 minutes until golden and firm, then cool before lifting off.
Steam the 1 cup moong sprouts for 4 minutes until just tender and toss with a pinch of black salt and 0.5 tsp chaat masala.
Whisk the 1.5 cups yogurt smooth with the remaining salt and chill, and simmer 2 tbsp tamarind with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder for 4 minutes into a sweet-sour chutney.
Set each baked basket on a plate and fill with the warm spiced sprouts.
Spoon over the chilled curd, tamarind and green chutney, dust with the remaining chaat masala, 1 tsp roasted cumin and black salt, and finish with pomegranate, peanuts and coriander before serving.
tips: Squeeze the potato as dry as possible so the baked baskets hold their shape and crisp evenly.
Let the baskets cool fully on the tin before lifting so they set rigid and do not tear.
Fill and top just before serving, since baked baskets soften faster than fried ones once the curd is added.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a wholesome tea-time chaat with a glass of chilled buttermilk alongside.

variations.name: Classic Bedai
variations.description: This Agra-Mathura bedai is a puffed wheat puri stuffed with a spiced urad-dal paste and fried until it balloons golden and crisp. Eaten hot with a tangy potato sabzi, it is the definitive Braj breakfast, hearty, aromatic and utterly satisfying.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: the sturdy heritage wheat puffs into a crisp bedai shell that holds its shape

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: worked into the dough as moyan for a crisp, short-textured puri

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: frying in pungent mustard oil gives the authentic Braj bedai its earthy aroma

steps: Rub 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, then knead with about ¾ cup water into a firm, smooth dough and rest it covered for 30 minutes.
Soak the 0.75 cup urad dal for 3 hours, drain and grind to a thick coarse paste without adding water.
Crush the 1.5 tsp fennel roughly and mix it with the ground dal along with the grated 1 inch ginger, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp garam masala and the remaining salt.
Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin and 0.5 tsp asafoetida, stir in the dal mixture and cook 6 to 7 minutes until dry and crumbly, then cool completely.
Divide the dough into 12 balls, flatten each, place a spoon of the dal filling inside, seal well and roll gently into a 4 inch disc without tearing.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking then reduce to 170 C, and slip in one bedai at a time, pressing lightly with a slotted spoon so it puffs.
Fry each for about 3 minutes, turning once, until puffed, golden and crisp, then drain and serve hot.
tips: Cook the urad filling until fully dry, as damp dal will make the bedai tear or refuse to puff.
Roll gently and evenly so the filling stays sealed and the puri balloons in the oil.
Baste the puri with hot oil while frying to encourage a full, even puff.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a runny, tangy aloo ki sabzi and a spoon of pickle for a classic Agra breakfast.

variations.name: Moong Dal Bedai
variations.description: This lighter bedai swaps the heavy urad for a spiced yellow-moong filling that fries softer and digests easier. The moong lends a gentle sweetness and a paler puff, making it a favourite for those who find the classic urad version too rich.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: gives a wholesome puri that puffs light around the soft moong filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: moyan of ghee keeps the shell crisp and short

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: neutral wood-pressed oil fries the lighter bedai clean and golden

steps: Rub 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, knead with about ¾ cup water to a firm dough and rest covered for 30 minutes.
Soak the 0.75 cup moong dal for 2 hours, drain and grind to a coarse thick paste with the 2 green chillies and no added water.
Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin, 1.5 tsp crushed fennel and 0.5 tsp asafoetida over medium heat.
Add the moong paste with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp amchur and the remaining salt, and stir-fry 7 minutes until dry and light, then cool.
Divide the dough into 12 balls, stuff each with the moong filling, seal and roll gently into 4 inch discs.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 170 C and fry the bedai one at a time, basting with hot oil until they puff.
Turn once and fry each for about 3 minutes to a pale gold crisp, then drain and serve warm.
tips: Grind the moong just coarse enough to bind, since too fine a paste turns pasty when fried.
Moong fillings dry faster than urad, so watch the pan to avoid over-roasting.
Keep the oil at a steady medium so these lighter puris puff without browning too fast.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a light jeera-tempered aloo sabzi and a bowl of sweet boondi raita.

variations.name: Rajasthani Pyaaz Bedai
variations.description: The Rajasthani take folds sharp onion, garlic and extra red chilli into the urad filling for a fierier, more pungent bedai. Robust and boldly spiced, it is built to stand up to a spicy kachori sabzi on a Marwari breakfast thali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: the robust wheat suits the assertive onion-garlic filling and fries crisp

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: rubbed into the flour for a short, crisp Marwari-style puri

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: pungent mustard oil matches the fiery onion-garlic bedai and fries it deep golden

steps: Rub 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, knead with about ¾ cup water to a firm dough and rest covered for 30 minutes.
Soak the 0.75 cup urad dal for 3 hours, drain and grind to a thick coarse paste without water.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking then lower the heat, and crackle 1 tsp cumin, 1.5 tsp crushed fennel and 0.5 tsp asafoetida.

Add the finely chopped onion and crushed garlic and fry 4 minutes, then stir in the dal paste, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and the remaining salt and cook 7 minutes until dry, then cool.
Divide the dough into 12 balls, stuff with the pungent filling, seal and roll gently into 4 inch discs.
Reheat the remaining Anveshan Mustard Oil to 170 C and fry the bedai one at a time, basting until each puffs and turns deep golden.
Fry about 3 minutes per piece until crisp, then drain on a rack and serve piping hot.
tips: Fry the onion and garlic until their moisture leaves fully so the filling stays dry and the puri puffs.
Adjust the chilli to taste, but this bedai is meant to be noticeably spicier than the classic.
Heat the mustard oil to smoking first so its sharpness mellows into a pleasant earthiness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a Marwari thali with a spicy kachori aloo sabzi and a dollop of garlic chutney.

variations.name: Classic Bengali Beguni
variations.description: Beguni is Kolkata's beloved evening snack of thin brinjal slices cloaked in a spiced gram-flour batter and fried in mustard oil until lacy and crisp. Nigella and a whisper of poppy seed in the batter give it the unmistakable pungent-sweet Bengali character served with muri and puffed-rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil gives beguni its authentic Bengali pungency and a clean, crisp shell

steps: Slice 1 large brinjal lengthwise into thin, even pieces about half a centimetre thick, rub with 0.25 tsp of the salt and 0.25 tsp turmeric, and set aside for 10 minutes.

Whisk 1 cup besan, 3 tbsp rice flour, 0.5 tsp nigella seeds, 1 tsp poppy seeds, the remaining 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp sugar and remaining salt with 0.5 cup water into a smooth, thick coating batter.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just smokes, then lower the flame to medium so it settles to about 180C.
Dip each brinjal slice fully into the batter so it is evenly coated and slide it gently into the hot oil.
Fry three or four slices at a time for 3 to 4 minutes, turning once, until deep golden and crisp at the edges.
Lift out with a slotted spoon, drain on paper, and serve piping hot while the coating is still crackly.
tips: Always heat mustard oil until it smokes, then cool it slightly before frying so the raw pungency mellows.
Keep the brinjal slices thin and uniform so they cook through in the time the batter takes to crisp.
Add water to the batter a little at a time, as a runny batter slides off and gives soft, oily beguni.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with steamed rice and dal as a starter, or with muri and a cup of cha on a rainy Kolkata evening.

variations.name: Kasundi Mustard Beguni
variations.description: This bold take folds Bengal's sharp fermented mustard kasundi and a fresh mustard paste right into the batter, so every crisp slice carries a nose-tingling heat. It is the version that pairs beautifully with a khichuri lunch and turns a simple fritter into a pungent showstopper.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: doubles down on the mustard theme and fries the coating to a sharp, crisp finish

steps: Cut 1 large brinjal into round slices about half a centimetre thick and rub with 0.25 tsp salt and 0.25 tsp of the turmeric.
Whisk 1 cup besan and 2 tbsp cornflour with 2 tbsp kasundi, 1 tbsp yellow mustard paste, the green chilli paste, remaining turmeric, remaining salt and 0.4 cup water into a smooth, pungent batter.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Mustard Oil until it smokes, then bring it down to a steady medium heat around 180C.
Coat each brinjal round thickly in the mustard batter so none of the flesh shows through.
Fry in batches for 3 to 4 minutes, turning once, until the coating is golden and blistered.
Drain on paper and serve immediately so the sharp mustard aroma is at its liveliest.
tips: Whisk the raw mustard paste and kasundi into the batter only just before frying, as sitting too long makes it bitter.
The cornflour keeps this batter extra crisp despite the wet kasundi, so do not skip it.
Balance the heat with a pinch of sugar in the batter if your kasundi is very sharp.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve alongside a bowl of hot bhaja moong dal khichuri, letting the mustard fritters cut through the comforting lentils.

variations.name: Crispy Rice-Flour Beguni
variations.description: A tea-stall favourite built for maximum crunch, using a rice-and-semolina batter that stays shatteringly crisp for hours even after it cools. A dusting of chaat masala at the end lifts it into a moreish, snack-jar-worthy fritter.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: its high smoke point fries the rice-flour coating extra crisp and stable

steps: Slice 1 brinjal into thin rounds and pat them dry so the crisp coating adheres well.

Combine 0.75 cup rice flour, 0.5 cup besan, 3 tbsp semolina, 0.5 tsp crushed ajwain, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, then whisk in 0.6 cup water into a smooth, pourable batter.
Let the batter rest for 10 minutes so the semolina swells and the coating fries up firmer.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Sunflower Oil to about 175C, until a drop of batter sizzles and rises quickly.
Dip each brinjal slice in the batter and fry in batches for 4 to 5 minutes, turning, until pale gold and very crisp.
Drain on paper, dust immediately with 1 tsp chaat masala, and cool for a minute so they firm into a snappy crunch.
tips: Resting the semolina batter is the secret to a crunch that survives being packed into a tin.
Fry a little longer at a slightly lower heat so the thicker rice-flour shell dries out fully.
Dust the chaat masala while the fritters are still hot so it clings evenly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile into a bowl with a squeeze of lemon and green chutney as a tea-time namkeen, or pack into a jar for lunchboxes.

variations.name: Baked Khapli Beguni
variations.description: A lighter oven-baked reboot that trades the deep-fry for a nutty khapli-atta crust and a brush of ghee, giving craggy, golden brinjal slices that are easy on the stomach. It keeps the spiced Bengali soul of beguni while cutting the oil right down.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: adds a nutty, high-fibre crust that browns beautifully in the oven

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: brushed over the slices so they crisp and turn golden while baking

steps: Preheat the oven to 200C and line a tray with parchment brushed lightly with a little Anveshan Ghee.
Slice 1 brinjal into thick rounds, rub with 0.25 tsp salt and 0.25 tsp of the turmeric, and rest for 10 minutes.

Whisk 0.75 cup besan, 0.5 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 tsp nigella, 1 tsp red chilli powder, remaining turmeric, 0.5 tsp roasted cumin and remaining salt with 0.4 cup water into a thick, clinging batter.
Coat each brinjal round in the batter, lay them on the tray, and brush the tops generously with Anveshan Ghee.
Bake for 15 minutes, flip each slice and brush again with ghee, then bake another 12 to 15 minutes until golden and crisp at the edges.
Rest for 2 minutes so the khapli crust firms, then serve warm.
tips: Brushing ghee both times is essential for browning; skip it and the slices stay pale and dry.
Keep the batter thick so it forms a proper crust rather than sliding off in the oven.
Salting and resting the brinjal draws out moisture so the baked slices do not turn watery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a bowl of thick hung-curd dip and a kasundi drizzle for a guilt-free tea-time plate.

variations.name: Classic Bhoger Khichuri
variations.description: The rainy-day and festival khichuri of Bengal, made with roasted moong dal and gobindobhog rice cooked to a soft, porridge-like comfort. Roasting the dal first is the step that gives this khichuri its nutty aroma and sets it apart from a plain khichdi. A finish of ghee and Bengali garam masala turns it into the classic bhog offering.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee is stirred in at the end to give bhoger khichuri its unmistakable temple-kitchen fragrance

steps: Dry-roast 1 cup moong dal in a kadai on medium-low heat for 3 to 4 minutes until it turns golden and smells nutty, then rinse it with 1 cup rinsed gobindobhog rice and drain.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pressure cooker on medium heat and fry 1 cubed potato and 1 cup cauliflower florets until lightly golden, then set them aside.
In the same cooker heat 1 more tbsp ghee, temper 1 tsp cumin seeds, 2 bay leaves and 2 dried red chillies for 20 seconds, then add 1.5 tbsp ginger paste and fry for 1 minute.
Add the drained rice and dal with 3/4 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp cumin powder and fry for 2 minutes, then pour in 5 cups hot water, the fried vegetables, 1/2 cup green peas, 1.5 tsp salt and 1 tsp sugar.
Close the lid and pressure-cook for 2 whistles, then let the pressure release naturally so the grains stay soft and blended.
Open, stir in the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 3/4 tsp Bengali garam masala, and loosen with a little hot water if needed to a soft, flowing consistency.
tips: Roasting the moong dal is non-negotiable for authentic flavour; take it to a golden colour but stop before it darkens.
Bhoger khichuri should be soft and slightly runny, not dry, so keep a kettle of hot water handy to adjust.
Fry the potato and cauliflower separately so they hold their shape and add texture against the soft grains.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot with begun bhaja, labra and a wedge of lime, exactly as it is offered during Durga Puja.

variations.name: Bhuna Moong Khichuri with Panch Phoron
variations.description: A more rustic, everyday khichuri tempered with Bengal's five-spice panch phoron instead of cumin, giving little bursts of fenugreek and fennel through the soft grains. It skips the heavier vegetables and leans on mustard oil for a homely, weekday character. Slightly drier and earthier than the festival version, it is the khichuri of a stormy afternoon.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil gives this everyday khichuri its earthy Bengali pungency

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A spoon of bilona ghee stirred in at the end lifts the humble khichuri with aroma

steps: Dry-roast 1 cup moong dal on medium-low heat for 3 minutes until golden and aromatic, rinse with 1 cup rice, and drain well.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pressure cooker until smoking, lower to medium, and temper 1.5 tsp panch phoron, 3 dried red chillies and 1 bay leaf for 20 seconds until they crackle.
Add 1.5 inch julienned ginger and 3 slit green chillies and fry for 40 seconds, then add 1 chopped tomato and cook for 3 minutes until soft.
Tip in the drained rice and dal with 3/4 tsp turmeric and fry for 2 minutes to coat, then add 4.5 cups hot water and 1.5 tsp salt and stir well.
Close the lid and cook for 2 whistles, then let the pressure fall naturally so the grains soften fully.
Open, fold in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, and adjust to a soft but slightly textured consistency, not as runny as the bhog version.
tips: Panch phoron must be tempered whole in hot oil so each seed blooms; adding it later leaves it raw and bitter.
This khichuri is meant to be a touch drier, so use a little less water if you prefer distinct grains.
Julienned ginger rather than paste gives pleasant little bites of warmth throughout.
variations.servingSuggestion: Best enjoyed with aloo bhaja, a fried egg or papad and a spoon of mango pickle on a rainy day.

variations.name: Niramish Sabji Khichuri
variations.description: A wholesome, vegetable-loaded khichuri where the grains almost play second fiddle to a medley of seasonal vegetables like carrot, beans, potato and cauliflower. It is heartier and more colourful than the classic, cooked without onion or garlic in the niramish style. This is the one-pot meal that needs nothing more than a squeeze of lime.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee both fries the vegetables and finishes the khichuri, keeping the niramish dish rich and fragrant

steps: Dry-roast 3/4 cup moong dal until golden, rinse with 1 cup gobindobhog rice, and drain.
