Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot on medium heat and fry 1 cubed potato, 1 sliced carrot, 10 chopped beans and 1 cup cauliflower until the edges brown, about 6 minutes, then remove.
In the same ghee temper 1 tsp cumin seeds, 2 bay leaves, 1 inch cinnamon and 3 cardamom pods for 20 seconds, then add 1.5 tbsp ginger paste and fry for 1 minute.
Add the rice and dal with 3/4 tsp turmeric and fry for 2 minutes, then pour in 5 cups hot water, the fried vegetables, 1/2 cup peas and 1.5 tsp salt.
Cover and simmer on low heat for 22 to 25 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the grains are soft and the vegetables tender, adding hot water if it thickens too much.
Finish with the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 3/4 tsp Bengali garam masala and rest covered for 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Cut the vegetables to a similar size so they cook evenly alongside the grains.
Frying the vegetables first keeps them from turning to mush during the long simmer.
This stovetop method gives a creamier texture than the pressure cooker, but stir often so it does not catch at the bottom.
variations.servingSuggestion: A complete meal on its own; serve with a dollop of ghee, papad and tomato chutney.

variations.name: Sona Moong Bhaja Khichuri
variations.description: A lighter, drier khichuri where both the roasted moong dal and the rice are fried well in ghee before cooking, so the finished grains stay separate and fluffy rather than soft and blended. Minimal water and a bright tempering give it a pulao-like elegance. This is the khichuri for those who dislike the porridge texture and want each grain to stand.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Generous ghee for frying the grains gives this drier khichuri its rich, pulao-like separateness

steps: Dry-roast 1 cup moong dal until golden, rinse with 1 cup gobindobhog rice, and drain thoroughly so the grains are dry.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot on medium heat and fry 15 cashews and 2 tbsp raisins until pale gold, then scoop them out.
In the same ghee temper 1 tsp cumin seeds, 2 bay leaves, 4 cardamom pods, 4 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon for 20 seconds, add 1 tbsp ginger paste and 3 slit green chillies and fry for 1 minute.
Add the drained rice and dal with 1/2 tsp turmeric and fry on medium heat for 4 to 5 minutes until the grains turn glossy and smell toasted.
Pour in 3.5 cups hot water, 1.5 tsp salt and 1 tsp sugar, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on the lowest heat for 12 to 14 minutes until the water is absorbed and the grains are just tender.
Fluff gently, fold in the fried cashews and raisins, and rest covered for 5 minutes so each grain stays separate.
tips: Use less water than a soft khichuri and resist stirring once it is covered, so the grains stay fluffy and distinct.
Frying the drained grains well in ghee is what prevents them from clumping into porridge.
The cashews and raisins give a festive, mildly sweet character; add them at the end to keep them crunchy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve like a pulao with a dry aloor dom or a rich cholar dal for a celebratory Bengali lunch.

variations.name: Classic Mixed Vegetable Besara
variations.description: Besara is the pungent Odia curry defined by a freshly ground paste of mustard seeds and garlic that coats a medley of vegetables. Sharp, earthy and thickened only by the mustard itself, it is finished with a panch phutana tempering in mustard oil that gives it its unmistakable bite.

ingredients.name: Potato
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Brinjal
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Pumpkin
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Raw Banana
ingredients.note: cut into chunks

ingredients.name: Mustard Seeds
ingredients.note: for the ground paste

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: for the paste

ingredients.name: Green Chilli
ingredients.note: for the paste

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil that doubles the pungency of the mustard paste

steps: Soak 2 tbsp mustard seeds for 10 minutes, then grind with 5 garlic cloves and 2 green chillies to a smooth paste, adding a little water.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the heat, and saute the cubed potato, brinjal, pumpkin and raw banana with 0.5 tsp turmeric for 4 minutes.
Add 1 cup water and 1 tsp salt, cover, and cook on medium heat for 10 minutes until the vegetables are nearly tender.
Stir in the ground mustard paste and simmer gently for 5-6 minutes until the raw pungency mellows and the gravy thickens around the vegetables.
In a small pan heat the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil, splutter 1 tsp panch phutana with 2 dry red chillies and 1 sprig curry leaves.
Pour the tempering over the besara, stir once, and serve hot.
tips: Grind the mustard with green chilli and a pinch of salt to keep the paste from turning bitter.
Do not boil the curry hard after adding the mustard paste, as overheating makes mustard taste acrid.
Soaking the mustard seeds before grinding gives a smoother paste and a rounder, less harsh flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with steamed rice and a drizzle of raw mustard oil, alongside a simple dal for a rustic Odia meal.

variations.name: Aloo Baigana Besara
variations.description: A homely besara focused on just potato and brinjal, the two vegetables simmered until melting in the sharp mustard gravy. Simpler than the mixed version, it lets the creamy brinjal soak up the pungent paste for a deeply satisfying everyday curry.

ingredients.name: Potato
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Brinjal
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Mustard Seeds
ingredients.note: for the paste

ingredients.name: Cumin Seeds
ingredients.note: half for the paste

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: for the paste

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil for frying and to deepen the pungent gravy

steps: Soak 1.5 tbsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp cumin for 10 minutes, then grind with 4 garlic cloves to a smooth paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, reduce the heat, and fry the cubed potato and brinjal with 0.5 tsp turmeric for 5 minutes until lightly golden.
Add the chopped tomato and 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and cook 2 minutes until the tomato softens.
Pour in 1 cup water and 1 tsp salt, cover, and simmer on medium heat for 10 minutes until the vegetables are soft.
Stir in the mustard paste and the remaining 0.5 tsp cumin, then simmer gently for 5 minutes until the gravy clings to the vegetables.
Finish with a tempering of the last 1 tbsp mustard oil crackled with 2 dry red chillies poured over the top, then serve hot.
tips: Fry the brinjal well at the start so it turns creamy and does not stay spongy in the gravy.
A mix of mustard and cumin in the paste softens the sharpness while keeping the besara character.
Keep the gravy thick and clinging rather than watery so it coats the soft vegetables.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with rice or parathas, with a raw onion and lime on the side to cut the pungency.

variations.name: Sajana Chuin Besara
variations.description: A drumstick besara where tender pods and potato simmer in the mustard gravy, their fragrance mingling with the sharp paste. A spoon of ground poppy seeds smooths the gravy into a slightly creamy, coating consistency that clings to the drumsticks.

ingredients.name: Drumstick
ingredients.note: cut into 3 inch pieces

ingredients.name: Potato
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Mustard Seeds
ingredients.note: for the paste

ingredients.name: Poppy Seeds
ingredients.note: for a creamy paste

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: for the paste

ingredients.name: Green Chilli
ingredients.note: for the paste

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil that carries the drumstick fragrance and mustard bite

steps: Soak 2 tbsp mustard seeds and 1 tbsp poppy seeds for 10 minutes, then grind with 4 garlic cloves and 2 green chillies to a smooth, slightly creamy paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the heat, and fry the drumstick pieces and cubed potato with 0.5 tsp turmeric for 4 minutes.
Add 1.25 cups water and 1 tsp salt, cover, and cook on medium heat for 12 minutes until the drumsticks turn tender.
Stir in the mustard-poppy paste and simmer gently for 5-6 minutes until the gravy thickens to a creamy coating.
Heat the last 1 tbsp mustard oil, splutter 1 tsp panch phutana with 2 dry red chillies, and pour it over the curry.
Rest the besara for 3 minutes, then serve hot so the drumstick flavour settles into the gravy.
tips: The spoon of poppy seeds rounds out the mustard sharpness and gives the gravy a gentle creaminess.
Cook the drumsticks until the pulp is soft enough to draw out easily at the table.
Simmer, never boil hard, after the paste goes in so the mustard stays fragrant and not bitter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with steamed rice, drawing the soft pulp from the drumsticks and mopping up the creamy gravy.

variations.name: Machha-style Besara Kakharu
variations.description: A robust pumpkin besara built in the style of the classic fish curry, minus the fish, where a methi-and-mustard tempering gives a bittersweet edge. The soft pumpkin melts into a thick, golden mustard gravy that is bold and rustic.

ingredients.name: Pumpkin
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Mustard Seeds
ingredients.note: for the paste

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: for the paste

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: for the paste

ingredients.name: Fenugreek Seeds
ingredients.note: for the tempering

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil for the authentic fish-curry-style pungency

steps: Soak 2 tbsp mustard seeds for 10 minutes, then grind with 5 garlic cloves and 1 inch ginger to a smooth paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the heat, and splutter 0.5 tsp fenugreek seeds with 2 dry red chillies until the methi darkens.
Add the chopped tomato, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder and cook 3 minutes until the tomato breaks down.
Add the cubed pumpkin with 1 tsp salt and 1 cup water, cover, and cook on medium heat for 10 minutes until soft.
Stir in the mustard paste and simmer gently for 5 minutes, mashing a little pumpkin so the gravy turns thick and golden.
Rest the besara kakharu for a few minutes, then serve hot with the fenugreek aroma running through it.
tips: Toast the fenugreek only until golden; if it blackens it turns the whole gravy bitter.
Mash some of the soft pumpkin into the gravy for a naturally thick, clinging consistency.
This bold style stands up to extra chilli, so adjust the heat to taste without losing the mustard character.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with plain rice and a wedge of lime, a rustic pairing that mirrors the classic fish-curry meal.

variations.name: Classic Bhuni Khichdi
variations.description: A deeply flavoured khichdi where the rice and dal are dry-roasted and then bhuno-ed in a spiced onion-tomato masala before water is added, giving toasty, separate grains rather than a soft mush. The roasting builds a nutty, almost biryani-like aroma that plain khichdi never has. It is a satisfying one-pot meal that eats like a light pulao.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee is used to bhuno the grains and masala, giving the khichdi its rich toasted depth

steps: Dry-roast 3/4 cup moong dal on medium-low heat for 3 minutes until golden and nutty, rinse with 1 cup rice, and drain well.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pressure cooker on medium heat and temper 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 bay leaf, 3 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon for 20 seconds until aromatic.
Add 1 finely chopped large onion and fry until golden, about 5 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until the raw smell disappears.

Add 1 chopped large tomato and cook until pulpy, then lower the heat and add 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp coriander powder, frying for 40 seconds until the masala releases ghee.
Tip in the drained rice and dal and bhuno on medium heat for 4 to 5 minutes until the grains are well coated and smell toasted, then add 3.5 cups hot water and 1.5 tsp salt.
Close the lid, cook for 3 whistles, let the pressure release naturally, then fluff gently, sprinkle 1/2 tsp garam masala, and serve.
tips: The bhuno step of frying the grains in the masala is what gives this khichdi its distinct toasty aroma, so do not shorten it.
Use slightly less water than a soft khichdi so the grains stay separate and pulao-like.
Let the pressure fall on its own; opening early can leave the grains unevenly cooked.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with plain yogurt, a dollop of ghee, roasted papad and a spoon of pickle.

variations.name: Masala Vegetable Bhuni Khichdi
variations.description: A hearty, colourful bhuni khichdi loaded with carrots, beans, peas and cauliflower that are sauteed into the roasted masala before the grains go in. The vegetables add sweetness and body, turning it into a complete, wholesome meal. It is spicier and more substantial than the classic, ideal when the khichdi is the whole dinner.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed groundnut oil sautes the vegetables cleanly and lets the spices shine in this loaded khichdi

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of ghee rounds off the spiced vegetable khichdi with aroma

steps: Dry-roast 3/4 cup toor dal for 3 minutes until fragrant, rinse with 1 cup rice, and drain.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pressure cooker on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add 1 chopped onion and fry until golden, about 5 minutes.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute, then add 1 chopped tomato and cook until soft, and stir in 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1.25 tsp red chilli powder and cook 30 seconds.
Add 1 sliced carrot, 10 chopped beans, 1 cup cauliflower and 1/2 cup peas and saute for 4 minutes, then add the drained rice and dal and bhuno for 3 minutes.
Pour in 4 cups hot water and 1.5 tsp salt, close the lid, and cook for 3 whistles, letting the pressure release naturally.
Open, fold in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 3/4 tsp garam masala, and rest for 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Toor dal holds its shape better than moong here and stands up to the vegetables.
Cut all the vegetables to a similar size so they cook evenly with the grains.
Add a splash of hot water when reheating, as this khichdi firms up considerably as it cools.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling boondi raita, roasted papad and a lime pickle for a filling weeknight meal.

variations.name: Sattu Bhuni Khichdi
variations.description: A nourishing protein-boosted take where roasted Bengal-gram sattu is stirred into the bhuno-ed grains, deepening the nuttiness and adding earthy body. Popular as a strengthening meal, it carries a rustic Bihar-Bengal border character. The sattu thickens the khichdi slightly and makes it especially filling and wholesome.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee bhunos the grains and carries the roasted sattu flavour through the khichdi

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Roasted Bengal-gram sattu adds plant protein and a deep nutty body found in no ordinary khichdi

steps: Dry-roast 1/2 cup moong dal for 3 minutes until golden, rinse with 1 cup rice, and drain.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pressure cooker on medium heat and temper 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1/2 tsp ajwain for 20 seconds until they crackle.
Add 1 chopped onion, 1 inch minced ginger and 3 slit green chillies and fry for 4 minutes until the onion softens, then add 1/2 tsp turmeric and 3/4 tsp red chilli powder and cook 30 seconds.
Add the drained rice and dal and bhuno for 3 minutes, then pour in 3.5 cups hot water and 1.5 tsp salt and close the lid for 3 whistles.
In a bowl, whisk 3 tbsp Anveshan Sattu with 1/2 cup water to a smooth lump-free slurry so it does not form clumps in the khichdi.
Once the pressure releases, open the cooker, stir in the sattu slurry on low heat for 2 to 3 minutes until thickened, finish with 1/2 tsp garam masala and 3 tbsp coriander, and serve.
tips: Always mix the sattu into water first to a smooth slurry, as adding it dry to the hot khichdi will make it lumpy.
Add the sattu at the end and cook only briefly so it thickens without turning pasty.
This is an excellent high-protein meal for growing children and post-workout dinners.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot topped with extra ghee, sliced onion, green chilli and a squeeze of lemon.

variations.name: Dhaba-Style Masala Bhuni Khichdi
variations.description: A robust, smoky roadside version fried in mustard oil with a bold whole-spice tadka and a generous hit of dry masalas, finished with a fresh onion-tomato tarka poured on top. It is spicier, oilier and more aromatic than home-style khichdi, with the unmistakable punch of a highway dhaba. The double tempering gives it real character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Pungent wood-pressed mustard oil gives this khichdi its bold, smoky dhaba character

steps: Dry-roast 1/2 cup moong dal and 1/4 cup toor dal together for 3 minutes until golden, rinse with 1 cup rice, and drain.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pressure cooker until smoking, lower to medium, and temper 1 tsp cumin seeds, 2 dried red chillies and 1 bay leaf for 20 seconds.
Add 1 chopped onion and fry until golden, add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute, then add 1 chopped tomato and cook until pulpy.

Stir in 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1 tsp coriander powder, then add the drained grains and bhuno for 4 minutes; pour in 3.75 cups hot water and 1.5 tsp salt and cook for 3 whistles.
For the finishing tarka, heat the remaining 1 tbsp mustard oil in a small pan, fry 1 chopped onion until brown, add 1 chopped tomato and 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi, and cook to a thick masala.
Once the pressure releases, pour the sizzling tarka over the khichdi, sprinkle 3/4 tsp garam masala, fold through gently, and serve smoking hot.
tips: The second tarka poured on top is what gives this its dhaba punch, so do not skip it for a milder finish.
Heat the mustard oil to smoking point before use to mellow its sharpness into a pleasant pungency.
Keep it slightly looser than home khichdi, as the dhaba style is meant to be moist and rich.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a mound of sliced onions, green chilli, white butter and a garlic pickle for the full dhaba experience.

variations.name: Classic Chakuli Pitha
variations.description: Chakuli pitha is the everyday Odia rice-and-lentil pancake, poured from a lightly fermented batter of raw rice and urad dal onto a hot tawa into soft, spongy rounds. Thicker than a dosa and pillowy in the middle, it is the classic breakfast partner for ghuguni and coconut chutney.

ingredients.name: Raw Rice
ingredients.note: soaked 4 hours

ingredients.name: Urad Dal
ingredients.note: soaked with the rice

ingredients.name: Fenugreek Seeds
ingredients.note: soaked for a better ferment

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: smears the tawa so each chakuli lifts off soft with lacy edges

ingredients.name: Water
ingredients.note: for grinding and thinning

steps: Grind 2 cups soaked rice with 0.5 cup urad dal and 0.5 tsp fenugreek seeds, adding water little by little, to a smooth pourable batter.
Add 1 tsp salt, cover and ferment the batter in a warm spot for 6-8 hours until it rises and smells pleasantly sour.
Stir the batter and loosen it with a splash of water to a thick pouring consistency that coats a spoon.
Heat a tawa on medium, smear it with a little Anveshan Ghee, and pour a ladle of batter, spreading it gently into a thick round.
Cover and cook for about 2 minutes until the top is set with tiny holes and the base is golden, drizzling a little more ghee at the edges.
Flip and cook the other side for a minute until spotted brown, then serve the chakuli pitha hot off the tawa.
tips: Keep the batter thicker than dosa batter so the pancakes stay soft and spongy rather than crisp.
Cover the pan while cooking the first side to trap steam and cook the middle through evenly.
In cold weather ferment the batter inside a switched-off oven with the light on for reliable rise.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with ghuguni, a dry potato curry or coconut chutney for a classic Odia breakfast.

variations.name: Masala Onion Chakuli
variations.description: A savoury loaded chakuli where the poured batter is scattered with onion, green chilli and fresh coriander that half-sink into the pancake as it cooks. The crunchy topping and mustard tempering make it a heartier, spicier cousin of the plain version.

ingredients.name: Raw Rice
ingredients.note: soaked and ground

ingredients.name: Urad Dal
ingredients.note: soaked with the rice

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Green Chilli
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Coriander Leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: for the tempering and to crisp the loaded edges

steps: Grind 2 cups soaked rice with 0.5 cup urad dal to a smooth batter, add 1 tsp salt, and ferment 6-8 hours until risen.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 0.5 tsp mustard seeds with 1 sprig curry leaves, and stir this tempering into the batter.
Heat a tawa on medium, smear with a little oil, and pour a ladle of batter into a thick round.
Immediately scatter chopped onion, 2 chopped green chillies and coriander over the top and press them lightly so they stick.
Cover and cook for 2-3 minutes, drizzling oil at the edges, until the base is golden and the onions soften.
Flip and cook the topped side for a minute until the onions char slightly, then serve hot.
tips: Chop the onions fine so they cook through in the time the pancake takes and do not stay raw.
Press the toppings in gently right after pouring, before the surface sets, so they anchor into the batter.
Cook these a touch longer on the topping side to get the sweet, caramelised onion flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with coconut chutney and a bowl of ghuguni, or roll one up as a quick savoury snack.

variations.name: Crispy Sada Chakuli
variations.description: A thinner, crisper chakuli made with a higher proportion of urad dal and a splash of rice flour for lacy, golden edges. Spread wide and thin like a dosa, it shatters at the rim while staying soft in the centre, best eaten straight off the pan.

ingredients.name: Raw Rice
ingredients.note: soaked and ground

ingredients.name: Urad Dal
ingredients.note: extra for crispness

ingredients.name: Rice Flour
ingredients.note: for lacy crisp edges

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed gingelly oil that crisps the thin edges to gold

steps: Grind 2 cups soaked rice with 0.75 cup urad dal to a smooth batter, add 1 tsp salt, and ferment 6-8 hours until risen.
Whisk in 3 tbsp rice flour, 0.5 tsp cumin seeds and enough water to make a thin, easily pourable batter.
Heat a tawa on medium-high, smear with Anveshan Sesame Oil, and pour a ladle of batter spreading it outward into a thin round.
Drizzle oil around the rim and cook without covering for 2-3 minutes until the edges lift and turn crisp and golden.
Flip briefly for 30 seconds to set the other side, keeping the centre soft.
Fold and serve the crispy sada chakuli immediately while the edges are still shatteringly crisp.
tips: Keep this batter distinctly thinner than the classic so it spreads and crisps like a dosa.
Cook on higher heat and without a lid so moisture escapes and the edges go lacy.
Serve at once, as thin chakuli loses its crispness quickly once stacked.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve crisp and hot with a fiery tomato-garlic chutney or coconut chutney and filter coffee.

variations.name: Ragi Chakuli
variations.description: A nourishing millet chakuli where finger millet replaces part of the rice, lending an earthy, nutty flavour and a deeper colour. Soft and wholesome, it is a fibre-rich morning pancake that keeps you full while carrying all the comfort of the original.

ingredients.name: Raw Rice
ingredients.note: soaked and ground

ingredients.name: Urad Dal
ingredients.note: soaked with the rice

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the tawa and enriches the earthy millet pancakes

steps: Grind 1 cup soaked rice with 0.5 cup urad dal and 0.5 tsp fenugreek seeds to a smooth batter.
Whisk in 1 cup ragi flour and 1 tsp grated ginger with enough water to a thick pouring consistency, add 1 tsp salt, and ferment 6-8 hours.
Stir the risen batter well; ragi settles, so mix it back to an even thick batter before cooking.
Heat a tawa on medium, smear with Anveshan Ghee, and pour a ladle into a thick round, spreading it gently.
Cover and cook for about 2 minutes until the surface sets and the base browns, drizzling ghee at the edges.
Flip and cook the other side for a minute until firm, then serve the ragi chakuli warm.
tips: Ragi flour sinks to the bottom, so stir the batter each time before ladling for even pancakes.
Keep the flame at medium, as ragi browns fast and can taste bitter if the pan is too hot.
A little grated ginger cuts the earthiness of the millet and warms the whole pancake.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with coconut chutney or a spoon of jaggery and ghee for a wholesome breakfast.

variations.name: Classic Chana Chaat
variations.description: Boiled white chickpeas are tossed with onion, tomato, lime and tangy chaat masala for a protein-packed, refreshing street snack. The firm nutty chickpeas soak up the sour-spicy dressing while staying satisfying and hearty in every spoonful.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoon of ghee warmed through the chickpeas rounds the tang and adds richness

steps: Soak 1.5 cups chickpeas overnight, then pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 5 to 6 whistles until soft but holding shape, and drain.
Warm the drained chickpeas with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee for a minute so they glisten and take on the aroma.
Tip the chickpeas into a bowl and add finely chopped 1 onion, 1 tomato and 2 green chillies.
Sprinkle over 1.5 tsp chaat masala, 1 tsp roasted cumin, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 0.5 tsp black salt.
Squeeze in 2 tbsp lime juice and toss until the chickpeas are evenly coated in the tangy spice.
Fold through the coriander and serve warm or at room temperature.
tips: Cook the chickpeas until tender but still firm so they do not turn mushy in the chaat.
Add the tomato just before serving so the chaat does not go watery.
Toss with lime and spices while the chickpeas are warm so they absorb more flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in bowls with an extra lime wedge and a sprinkle of chaat masala, with crisp papdi on the side.

variations.name: Pindi Chana Chaat
variations.description: This Rawalpindi-style chaat cooks the chickpeas dark and robust with tea-water, dried pomegranate seeds and a deep chana masala before they are tossed with onion and ginger juliennes. Earthy, tangy and boldly spiced, it eats almost like a dry pindi chole in chaat form.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the chickpeas are tossed in ghee with the dry masala for a rich pindi finish

steps: Soak 1.5 cups chickpeas overnight, then pressure-cook with 2 tea bags, 0.75 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 whistles until soft and dark, then discard the tea bags and drain.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat and add 2 tsp chana masala, 1.5 tsp anardana powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, sizzling for 30 seconds.
Add the drained chickpeas and toss over medium heat for 4 minutes so they darken and soak up the dry masala.
Take off the heat and stir in 0.25 tsp salt and 1 tbsp lime juice.
Tip into a bowl and add finely chopped 1 onion, 2 green chillies and 1.5 inch ginger juliennes.
Fold through the coriander and serve warm while the masala is fragrant and clinging to the chickpeas.
tips: The tea bags deepen the chickpeas to the classic dark pindi colour, so do not skip them.
Anardana brings the signature tang, so add it while the masala toasts for the fullest flavour.
Cut the ginger into fine juliennes rather than mincing so it gives fresh bursts of heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm topped with extra ginger juliennes and green chilli, with lime wedges and sliced onion alongside.

variations.name: Dahi Chana Chaat
variations.description: A cooling version where the boiled chickpeas are folded into thick sweetened yogurt with tamarind and green chutneys, sev and pomegranate. The creamy tang of the curd softens the spice and makes this a refreshing, dahi-bhalla-like bowl built on protein-rich chana.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the whisked curd and the tamarind drizzle with a warm natural depth

steps: Soak 1.5 cups chickpeas overnight, pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 5 to 6 whistles until soft, and drain and cool.
Whisk the 2.5 cups yogurt smooth with 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 0.25 tsp salt and a pinch of black salt.
Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder for 4 minutes into a sweet-sour chutney and cool it.
Fold most of the cooled chickpeas into the sweetened curd and spoon into bowls.
Drizzle the tamarind chutney and 3 tbsp green chutney over the top.
Dust with 1.5 tsp chaat masala, 1 tsp roasted cumin and the remaining black salt, then top with the reserved chickpeas, pomegranate, sev and coriander and serve chilled.
tips: Cool the chickpeas fully before folding them into the curd so the yogurt stays thick.
Whisk the jaggery into the curd off any heat so it dissolves smoothly.
Add the sev at the last moment so it stays crunchy against the creamy chana.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled in bowls with extra pomegranate and a final swirl of both chutneys on top.

variations.name: Kala Chana Sundal Chaat
variations.description: A South Indian temple-prasadam style using nutty brown kala chana tempered with mustard seeds, curry leaves and fresh coconut instead of the usual chaat masala. Warm, dry and lightly spiced, it is a wholesome, sattvic take that swaps the North Indian tang for a fragrant coconut finish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: tempering in wood-pressed coconut oil gives the sundal its authentic South Indian aroma

steps: Soak 1.5 cups kala chana overnight, then pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 to 7 whistles until tender, and drain.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp urad dal until the dal turns golden.
Add 12 curry leaves, 2 broken dried chillies, 1 chopped green chilli, 0.5 inch grated ginger and 0.25 tsp asafoetida and fry for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Tip in the drained kala chana and toss over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes so they take on the tempering.
Stir in the 0.5 cup fresh grated coconut and 0.25 tsp salt and cook for another 2 minutes until dry and aromatic.
Scatter coriander over and serve warm as a wholesome sundal-style chaat.
tips: Cook the kala chana fully soft, as brown chana takes longer than white chickpeas.
Add the coconut at the end and cook briefly so it stays moist and fragrant, not toasted dry.
Keep it low on chilli for the traditional sattvic temple flavour, adding more only if you like heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm in leaf bowls or cups as a festive prasadam-style snack, with lime wedges on the side.

variations.name: Classic Chana Ghugni
variations.description: This Bengali chana ghugni simmers dark chickpeas in a fragrant onion-ginger masala with a hint of coconut and a whisper of sugar. Rich, subtly sweet and finished with roasted cumin, it is the beloved breakfast and evening snack served with luchi across Bengal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: pungent wood-pressed mustard oil forms the authentic Bengali base of the ghugni

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of ghee lends the classic rich aroma

steps: Soak 1.5 cups chickpeas overnight, then pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 to 7 whistles until soft but intact.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the flame, and fry the 3 tbsp diced coconut until lightly golden, then set aside.
In the same oil crackle 1 tsp cumin and 1 bay leaf, add the 2 chopped onions and fry 8 minutes until deep golden.
Add the grated ginger and chopped tomato and cook 4 minutes, then stir in 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder with a splash of water until the oil separates.
Add the cooked chickpeas with their liquid and 0.5 tsp sugar, mash a few to thicken, and simmer 15 minutes until stew-like and seasoned with the remaining salt.
Stir in the fried coconut and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and cook two more minutes.
Finish with 1 tsp roasted cumin powder and coriander and serve hot.
tips: Soak the chickpeas overnight and cook them fully soft so they absorb the masala.
Frying the coconut before adding gives a nutty depth typical of Bengali ghugni.
A pinch of sugar is traditional here and balances the mustard oil and spice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with luchi or radhaballavi, topped with fried coconut and chopped coriander.

variations.name: Kolkata Cholar Ghugni
variations.description: The Kolkata cart version pairs the chickpea ghugni with crisp fried aloo cubes, raw onion, green chilli and a tangy tamarind drizzle for a loaded street snack. Sharper and more textured than the home curry, it is scooped up with crushed papdi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: fries the aloo cubes and builds the pungent street-ghugni masala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the tamarind drizzle for the signature sweet-sour street finish

steps: Soak 1.5 cups chickpeas overnight and pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 whistles until soft.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the heat and fry the cubed 2 potatoes for 6 minutes until golden and crisp, then lift out.
In the same oil crackle 1 tsp cumin, add one chopped onion and the grated ginger and fry 6 minutes until golden.
Add the cooked chickpeas with their liquid and the remaining salt, mash a few and simmer 12 minutes into a loose stew, then fold the fried potatoes back in.
Soak 2 tbsp tamarind in warm water, strain, and mix with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder into a sweet-sour drizzle.
Ladle the hot ghugni into bowls and top with the remaining raw chopped onion and slit green chillies.
Drizzle over the tamarind water, dust with 1.5 tsp roasted cumin and 1.5 tsp chaat masala, crush papdi over the top and finish with coriander before serving.
tips: Fry the potato cubes separately and add them late so they keep a crisp edge in the stew.
Add the papdi only just before eating so it stays crunchy under the ghugni.
Keep the tamarind drizzle sharp and sweet to lift the whole bowl street-style.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a bowl with extra crushed papdi and a lemon wedge, the way Kolkata evening carts plate it.

variations.name: Dhaba Chana Ghugni
variations.description: A robust Punjabi-dhaba take that cooks the chickpeas in a deep onion-tomato gravy with dried pomegranate and a smoky garam-masala finish. Thicker and spicier than the Bengali version, it eats like a hearty chana masala meant for kulcha.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee gives the dhaba gravy its rich, glossy body and aroma

steps: Soak 1.5 cups chickpeas overnight and pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 to 7 whistles until soft.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin, then add the 3 finely chopped onions and fry 10 minutes until deep brown.
Add 1.5 tbsp ginger garlic paste and fry a minute, then the 3 pureed tomatoes with 1 tsp red chilli powder and 2 tsp coriander powder and cook 8 minutes until the ghee separates.
Stir in 1.5 tsp anardana powder and the cooked chickpeas with a cup of their liquid, mashing a handful to thicken the gravy.
Simmer for 12 minutes until the gravy is thick and clinging, seasoning with the remaining salt.
Finish with 0.75 tsp garam masala and 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi and cook two more minutes.
Garnish with coriander and serve hot.
tips: Brown the onions deeply, as their colour is what gives the dhaba gravy its dark richness.
Anardana adds the tangy depth of a true chana masala, so do not skip it.
Mash a portion of the chickpeas to thicken the gravy naturally without any flour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot butter kulcha or bhatura and a plate of sliced onion, lemon and green chilli.

variations.name: Sukha Chana Ghugni
variations.description: This dry, stir-fried ghugni tosses the boiled chickpeas in a quick tempered masala with coconut and curry leaves until every pea is coated and glossy. Light and snackable rather than saucy, it is a South-leaning sundal-style version perfect for tea time.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed coconut oil gives the dry ghugni its fragrant southern character

steps: Soak 1.5 cups chickpeas overnight and pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 6 whistles until soft, then drain well.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tsp urad dal, the 2 dried red chillies and 0.25 tsp asafoetida over medium heat.
Add the 12 curry leaves, grated ginger and slit green chillies and fry for a minute until fragrant.
Tip in the drained chickpeas with the remaining salt and toss for 5 to 6 minutes over medium heat until dry and glossy.
Add the 0.5 cup fresh grated coconut and stir-fry two more minutes until it just warms through and coats the chickpeas.
Turn off the heat and squeeze over 1 tbsp lemon juice.
Fold in coriander and serve warm as a light snack.
tips: Drain the chickpeas well so the stir-fry stays dry rather than turning mushy.
Add the coconut near the end so it stays fresh and does not brown or dry out.
Finish with lemon off the heat to keep the citrus bright against the coconut.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm in small bowls as a protein-rich tea-time snack with a cup of filter coffee.

variations.name: Classic Chana Kurma
variations.description: A soft-cooked white chickpea curry simmered in a fragrant ground paste of fresh coconut, roasted gram and fennel, the way South Indian tiffin houses serve it beside parotta. The gravy is mild, coconut-sweet and lightly spiced, letting the nutty chana shine without any heavy cream.

ingredients.name: White chickpeas
ingredients.note: soaked overnight and pressure-cooked soft

ingredients.name: Fresh coconut
ingredients.note: grated, for the ground paste

ingredients.name: Roasted gram
ingredients.note: pottukadalai, for body

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the coastal fat that carries the curry-leaf tempering and suits the coconut paste

steps: Soak 1 cup white chickpeas overnight, then pressure-cook with 3 cups water and 1/2 tsp salt for 5-6 whistles until they crush easily between two fingers, reserving the cooking liquid.
Grind 1/2 cup grated coconut, 2 tbsp roasted gram, 1 tsp fennel seeds and 3 green chillies with a little water into a smooth pouring paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan over medium heat, drop in the 1 inch cinnamon and 1 sprig curry leaves, and let them crackle for 20 seconds until aromatic.
Add the chopped onion and saute for 4 minutes until soft and pale gold, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute until the raw smell lifts.
Add the chopped tomato with 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp coriander powder and 3/4 tsp salt, and cook for 4 minutes until the tomato collapses and the oil beads at the edges.
Tip in the cooked chickpeas with 1.5 cups of their liquid, simmer for 6 minutes, then stir in the ground coconut paste and cook on low for 5 minutes until the kurma thickens to a spoonable gravy.
tips: Reserve the chickpea cooking water and use it instead of plain water so the kurma tastes deeper and glossier.
Add the coconut paste only at the end on low heat, or the gravy can turn grainy and lose its fragrance.
A pinch more roasted gram in the grind thickens the gravy naturally if it looks too thin.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with flaky Malabar parotta or soft aappam, with a wedge of lime and sliced onion on the side.

variations.name: Kerala Kadala Kurma
variations.description: The Malabar temple-breakfast curry where grated coconut is dry-roasted to a deep mahogany before grinding, giving the chickpea kurma a dark, smoky, intensely aromatic gravy. Warm garam whole spices and coconut oil make it richer and earthier than the pale tiffin-house version.

ingredients.name: White chickpeas
ingredients.note: soaked and pressure-cooked soft

ingredients.name: Fresh coconut
ingredients.note: grated, to be dry-roasted dark

ingredients.name: Shallots
ingredients.note: half for the roast, half sliced

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the defining Malabar fat that binds the roasted-coconut masala

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: julienned

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup soaked chickpeas with 3 cups water, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1/2 tsp salt for 5-6 whistles until soft, and keep the liquid.

In a dry pan on low heat, roast 3/4 cup grated coconut with 4 shallots, 1 tbsp coriander seeds, 4 dry red chillies, 1 tsp fennel and the cloves for 6-7 minutes, stirring, until the coconut turns deep brown and smells toasted.
Cool the roasted mixture and grind it with a little water into a dark, slightly coarse paste that smells nutty and smoky.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan over medium heat, splutter the 1 inch cinnamon and 2 sprigs curry leaves, then add the remaining sliced shallots and julienned ginger and fry for 4 minutes until golden.
Add the cooked chickpeas with 1.5 cups of their liquid and 3/4 tsp salt, then stir in the dark roasted paste and simmer on medium-low for 8 minutes until the gravy turns thick and glossy.
Finish with 1/2 tsp garam masala, cook for 1 more minute, and rest covered for 3 minutes so the smoky aroma settles before serving.
tips: Roast the coconut patiently on low heat to a chocolate brown; rushing it on high heat scorches it bitter.
Grind the masala slightly coarse rather than silky for the rustic Malabar texture.
This kurma deepens overnight, so it tastes even better reheated the next morning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with puttu, appam or plain steamed red rice for an authentic Kerala breakfast plate.

variations.name: Restaurant White Chana Kurma
variations.description: The pale, creamy chickpea kurma of North Indian restaurant buffets, built on a no-tomato cashew and poppy-seed paste enriched with curd and finished with ghee. Its milky, mildly sweet body and smooth ivory colour make it the gentle crowd-pleaser of the spread.

ingredients.name: White chickpeas
ingredients.note: pressure-cooked soft

ingredients.name: Cashew nuts
ingredients.note: soaked for the white paste

ingredients.name: Poppy seeds
ingredients.note: soaked, for creaminess

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: boiled for the pale paste

ingredients.name: Curd
ingredients.note: thick and whisked smooth

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: keeps the gravy pale while lending the clean richness a white kurma is known for

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: rounds the mild kurma with a whisper of sweetness instead of refined sugar

steps: Boil the 2 onions, 15 cashews, 1 tbsp poppy seeds and 2 green chillies in a cup of water for 8 minutes, then cool and blend into a completely smooth white paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat, warm the 1 bay leaf and 3 cardamoms for 30 seconds without letting them darken, then add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and saute for 1 minute.
Pour in the white cashew-onion paste and cook gently for 6 minutes on low heat, stirring constantly so it stays pale and does not brown.
Whisk 1/4 cup curd smooth, lower the heat fully and stir it in with 1 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp white pepper and 1/2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder to keep it from splitting.
Add the cooked chickpeas with 1 cup water, cover and simmer on low for 8 minutes until the gravy turns thick, silky and ivory-pale.
Adjust to a creamy pouring consistency, warm through for 2 more minutes, and serve garnished with a swirl of cream.
tips: Keep the flame low from start to finish; any browning ruins the signature white colour.
Use thick, sour-free curd and add it off the boil to prevent curdling in the delicate gravy.
Soaked poppy seeds grind smoother and give a creamier body than adding them dry.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan, laccha paratha or a mild jeera pulao, topped with fried cashews and raisins.

variations.name: Andhra Senaga Kurma
variations.description: A fiery Andhra take where the chickpeas simmer in a bold ground masala of red chillies, roasted peanuts and sesame, tempered in gingelly oil for a pungent, spice-forward gravy. Far punchier than the coconut kurmas, it delivers the deep red heat and nutty tang that define Rayalaseema cooking.

ingredients.name: White chickpeas
ingredients.note: pressure-cooked soft

ingredients.name: Roasted peanuts
ingredients.note: for the nutty ground masala

ingredients.name: Sesame seeds
ingredients.note: roasted

ingredients.name: Dry red chillies
ingredients.note: byadgi for colour

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: sliced

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed gingelly oil, the authentic pungent fat for an Andhra gravy

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup soaked chickpeas with 3 cups water and 1/2 tsp salt for 5-6 whistles until soft, and keep the liquid.
Grind 3 tbsp roasted peanuts, 1 tbsp roasted sesame seeds and 5 dry red chillies with 1 chopped tomato and a little water into a thick, deep-red masala paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pan over medium heat, splutter 1/2 tsp mustard and 1/2 tsp cumin seeds with 1 sprig curry leaves for 20 seconds.
Add the sliced onions and fry for 5 minutes until browned, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the remaining chopped tomato and cook for 3 minutes until pulpy.
Pour in the ground peanut-chilli masala with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, and fry for 6 minutes until the oil separates and the raw chilli smell fades.
Add the chickpeas with 1.5 cups of their liquid and 3/4 tsp salt, simmer for 8 minutes until the gravy thickens to a rich, fiery red, and serve hot.
tips: Use byadgi chillies for a glowing red colour without punishing heat, or blend in guntur if you want it truly fiery.
Frying the ground masala until the oil separates is essential to cook off the raw peanut taste.
A splash of tamarind water at the end lifts the nutty richness with a gentle tang.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice and a dollop of ghee, or with ragi mudde and raw onion for a rustic Rayalaseema meal.

variations.name: Classic Chanar Dalna
variations.description: A festive Bengali curry of soft home-made chhana (paneer) dumplings simmered in a light, spiced potato gravy fragrant with ginger and Bengali garam masala. The chhana balls are gently fried until golden before joining the curry, staying soft and porous to soak up the flavours. It is a niramish delicacy served on special vegetarian days and pujas.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil fries the chhana balls and builds the classic Bengali gravy base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of bilona ghee gives the dalna its festive fragrance

steps: Knead 1.5 cups fresh chhana with 2 tbsp plain flour and a pinch of salt for 4 to 5 minutes until smooth, then roll into 12 small balls.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until smoking, lower to medium-low, and fry the chhana balls gently until golden all over, about 4 minutes, then lift them out carefully.
In the same oil fry 2 cubed potatoes with 1/2 tsp turmeric until golden, then set aside; temper 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1 bay leaf for 20 seconds.

Add 1.5 tbsp ginger paste and 1 grated tomato and cook for 4 minutes, then add 1 tsp cumin powder, 1 tsp coriander powder and 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and fry for 40 seconds until the oil separates.
Add the fried potatoes with 2 cups hot water, 1/2 tsp sugar and the salt, and simmer for 8 minutes until the potatoes are tender and the gravy thickens slightly.
Slide in the chhana balls, simmer gently for 5 minutes so they absorb the gravy, finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 3/4 tsp Bengali garam masala, and serve.
tips: Knead the chhana really well until it is smooth and the balls do not crack, or they will break in the gravy.
Fry the chhana balls on low heat so they cook through without hardening on the outside.
Add the balls only in the last few minutes so they stay soft and do not disintegrate.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with luchi, basanti pulao or steamed rice at a festive vegetarian lunch.

variations.name: Doi Chanar Dalna
variations.description: A richer, creamier version where the chhana dumplings simmer in a smooth yogurt-and-cashew gravy instead of the tomato-based classic, giving a pale, luscious curry with a gentle tang. It skips the potato and leans on whole spices and curd for depth. This is the more indulgent, banquet-style chanar dalna.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries the whole spices and keeps the yogurt gravy rich and smooth

steps: Knead 1.5 cups chhana with 2 tbsp plain flour and a pinch of salt until smooth, shape into 12 balls, and soak 12 cashews in warm water for 10 minutes, then grind to a paste.
Whisk 3/4 cup yogurt with 1 tsp cumin powder and the cashew paste until smooth and lump-free, and keep aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium-low heat and fry the chhana balls until pale gold, about 4 minutes, then remove them gently.
In the same ghee temper 1 bay leaf, 1 inch cinnamon, 4 cardamom pods and 4 cloves for 20 seconds, then add 1.5 tbsp ginger paste and 3 slit green chillies and fry for 1 minute.
Lower the heat to minimum and pour in the whisked yogurt mixture, stirring continuously for 3 minutes so it does not split, then add 1 cup hot water, 1 tsp sugar and the salt.
Slide in the chhana balls and simmer very gently for 6 minutes, finish with 1/2 tsp Bengali garam masala, and serve.
tips: Add the yogurt only on the lowest heat and keep stirring, or the gravy will curdle.
The cashew paste gives the gravy body and a subtle sweetness that balances the tang of the curd.
Slit the green chillies rather than chopping them for aroma without making the mild gravy too hot.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with fragrant basanti pulao or soft parathas for a rich celebratory meal.

variations.name: Peas and Chhana Ball Curry (Motorshutir Chanar Dalna)
variations.description: A winter-favourite variation where sweet green peas join the chhana dumplings in a light, gingery gravy, bringing bursts of colour and natural sweetness. The peas and potato-free lighter base make it fresher and more seasonal than the classic. It is the version that appears on Bengali tables in the cool months when fresh peas are plentiful.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Mustard oil fries the chhana balls and gives the peas gravy its Bengali pungency

steps: Knead 1.5 cups chhana with 2 tbsp plain flour and a pinch of salt until smooth and shape into 12 balls.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until smoking, lower to medium-low, and fry the chhana balls until golden, about 4 minutes, then remove.
In the same oil temper 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1 dried red chilli for 20 seconds, then add 2 tbsp ginger paste and fry for 1 minute.
Add 1 grated tomato and cook for 3 minutes, then add 1 tsp cumin powder, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and fry for 40 seconds; stir in 1 cup green peas and saute for 2 minutes.
Pour in 1.75 cups hot water with 3/4 tsp sugar and the salt and simmer for 6 minutes until the peas are tender and the gravy lightly thickens.
Add the chhana balls, simmer gently for 5 minutes, finish with 3/4 tsp Bengali garam masala, and serve.
tips: Fresh winter peas give the best sweetness; if using frozen, add them a couple of minutes later so they do not overcook.
Keep this gravy light and slightly sweet to let the peas shine.
Handle the chhana balls gently in the gravy so they stay whole among the peas.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot luchi or steamed rice on a cool winter afternoon.

variations.name: Rich Kaju Chanar Kalia
variations.description: A luxurious wedding-feast style kalia where the chhana dumplings bathe in a deep, glossy, cashew-enriched red gravy heavy with whole garam masala and a touch of ghee-fried onion. Richer, sweeter and more festive than the everyday dalna, it has the celebratory colour and sheen of a Bengali biye-bari dish. This is chanar dalna dressed for a banquet.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee gives the celebratory kalia its rich sheen and carries the whole spices

steps: Knead 1.5 cups chhana with 2 tbsp plain flour and a pinch of salt until smooth, shape into 12 balls, and soak 15 cashews in warm water, then grind to a smooth paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium-low heat and fry the chhana balls until golden, about 4 minutes, then remove.
In the same ghee temper 1 inch cinnamon, 4 cardamom pods and 4 cloves, add 2 finely chopped onions, and fry until deep golden, about 8 minutes.
Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute, then add 2 pureed tomatoes and cook until the ghee separates, and stir in 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1 tsp coriander powder.
Add the cashew paste and fry for 2 minutes, then pour in 1.75 cups hot water with 1 tsp sugar and the salt and simmer for 6 minutes to a glossy, thick gravy.
Slide in the chhana balls, simmer gently for 5 minutes, finish with 3/4 tsp Bengali garam masala, and serve.
tips: Fry the onions to a genuine deep golden for the rich colour and sweetness a kalia needs.
The cashew paste both thickens and enriches; grind it very smooth for a glossy finish.
This gravy should be thicker and more luxurious than the classic dalna, so keep the water measured.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at a celebration with basanti pulao, luchi or ghee rice and a sweet chutney to follow.

variations.name: Classic Nimapara Chhena Jhili
variations.description: The pride of Nimapara in Odisha, these soft chhena dumplings are deep-fried to a rich brown and steeped in light cardamom sugar syrup until they turn juicy and spongy. Unlike gulab jamun they are made purely from fresh chhena, giving a delicate milky flavour and a melting, syrup-laden bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the dumplings are traditionally fried in pure bilona ghee, which gives them their deep brown colour and rich aroma

steps: Boil 2 cups sugar with 2 cups water and 0.5 tsp cardamom for 6 minutes to a thin, sticky syrup, then keep it warm on the lowest heat.
Knead the 1.5 cups fresh chhena with 2 tbsp semolina, 1 tbsp maida and 0.125 tsp baking soda for 7 to 8 minutes until completely smooth and soft.
Roll the dough into 16 small crack-free balls, then gently elongate each into a small oval, the classic jhili shape.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Ghee to a low 140C and fry the ovals in batches for 7 to 8 minutes, turning gently, until deep golden-brown all over.
Add 0.5 tsp lemon juice to the warm syrup to keep it from crystallising, then slide the hot fried jhili straight into the syrup.
Simmer them in the syrup on very low heat for 4 minutes, then rest for at least 2 hours so they soak up the syrup and double in size before serving.
tips: Fry on low heat so the dumplings cook through to the centre without the outside browning too soon.
Knead the chhena until truly smooth, as any grain or crack causes the jhili to break apart while frying.
Drop the hot fried dumplings into warm, not boiling, syrup so they absorb it evenly and turn spongy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the syrup-soaked ovals warm or at room temperature, two to a bowl with a little syrup, as a festive Odia dessert.

variations.name: Saffron Rose Chhena Jhili
variations.description: A fragrant celebration version where the soaking syrup is infused with saffron and rose, turning the dumplings a blush gold and lending a floral perfume to every juicy bite. A scatter of slivered pistachios makes these look like jewels, perfect for weddings and grand festivals.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: saffron infuses the syrup with a golden colour and floral aroma that seeps into the spongy dumplings

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: light wood-pressed sunflower oil fries the dumplings to an even gold, letting the saffron colour shine through

steps: Boil 2 cups sugar with 2 cups water for 6 minutes to a sticky syrup, then stir in 0.25 tsp Anveshan Saffron and 0.5 tsp cardamom and keep it warm.
Knead the 1.5 cups chhena with 2 tbsp semolina and 0.125 tsp baking soda for 8 minutes until smooth and soft.
Shape the dough into 16 small smooth ovals, keeping your palms lightly greased to avoid cracks.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Sunflower Oil to a low 140C and fry the ovals for 7 to 8 minutes until an even golden brown, then drain briefly.
Slide the hot dumplings into the warm saffron syrup and simmer on the lowest heat for 4 minutes, then stir in 1.5 tsp rose water off the heat.
Rest the jhili for 2 hours to soak, then garnish with slivered pistachios and a few saffron strands before serving in the golden syrup.
tips: Add the rose water only after switching off the heat so its delicate aroma stays intact.
Bloom the saffron directly in the hot syrup so its colour and scent infuse deep into the dumplings.
Keep the frying oil at a steady low temperature for an even gold that shows off the saffron tint.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled in a shallow bowl with the saffron syrup, topped with pistachios and edible rose petals for an opulent festive dessert.

variations.name: Jaggery Syrup Chhena Jhili
variations.description: A wholesome, unrefined version where the dumplings soak in a spiced jaggery syrup instead of white sugar, taking on a warm amber colour and a deep caramel sweetness. A pinch of dry ginger and fennel in the syrup gives it a gently spiced, digestive warmth that suits cooler months.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery syrup gives the dumplings a warm amber hue and deep caramel sweetness free of refined sugar

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee frying gives a rich brown crust that pairs beautifully with the earthy jaggery syrup

steps: Melt 2 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 cups water, bring to a boil, and strain the syrup to remove grit, then return it with 0.5 tsp crushed fennel, 0.25 tsp dry ginger and 0.5 tsp cardamom and keep warm.
Knead the 1.5 cups chhena with 2 tbsp semolina, 1 tbsp maida and 0.125 tsp baking soda for 8 minutes until soft and smooth.
Roll the dough into 16 smooth ovals without cracks, keeping your palms lightly greased.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Ghee to a low 140C and fry the ovals for 7 to 8 minutes, turning gently, until deep reddish-brown, then drain.
Lower the hot dumplings into the warm jaggery syrup and simmer on the lowest heat for 4 minutes without letting it boil hard.
Rest the jhili for 2 to 3 hours so they drink up the spiced jaggery syrup and turn plump before serving.
tips: Always strain the jaggery syrup, as unfiltered jaggery carries sediment that clouds the sweet.
Keep the syrup thin, since jaggery thickens faster than sugar and can turn the coating chewy.
The fennel and dry ginger are traditional digestives that balance the richness of this fried sweet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm in the amber jaggery syrup on a winter evening, dusted with a little grated dry coconut for a rustic finish.

variations.name: Rabri-Stuffed Chhena Jhili
variations.description: An indulgent twist where each chhena oval hides a core of thickened rabri and chopped nuts before frying and soaking in syrup. Biting through the spongy syrup-soaked shell into the creamy rabri centre gives a double hit of richness that turns a simple sweet into a showstopper.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee frying gives a sturdy golden shell strong enough to hold the rabri filling without leaking

steps: Boil 2 cups sugar with 2 cups water and 0.25 tsp cardamom for 6 minutes to a sticky syrup and keep warm on low heat.
Mash the 0.33 cup khoya with 3 tbsp chopped nuts and 0.25 tsp cardamom, and roll into 14 tiny pellets for the filling.
Knead the 1.5 cups chhena with 2 tbsp semolina, 1 tbsp cornflour and 0.125 tsp baking soda for 8 minutes until smooth, then divide into 14 portions.
Flatten each portion, place a khoya pellet in the centre, seal it completely, and shape into a crack-free oval so the filling stays sealed.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Ghee to a low 140C and fry the stuffed ovals for 8 minutes, turning gently, until deep golden and firm, then drain.
Slide the hot dumplings into the warm syrup, simmer 4 minutes on low, and rest 2 hours so the shell soaks up syrup around the creamy rabri core.
tips: Seal the filling with no cracks or the rabri will leak and the dumpling will burst while frying.
The cornflour strengthens the shell so it holds the filling and stays intact in the syrup.
Chill the khoya pellets before stuffing so they hold shape and are easier to seal inside the chhena.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve slightly warm and cut one open at the table to show the molten rabri centre, garnished with slivered almonds over the syrup.

variations.name: Classic Chhena Poda
variations.description: Odisha's iconic 'burnt cheese' cake, made by baking fresh chhena with sugar and semolina until the surface caramelises to a deep mahogany crust. The inside stays moist and spongy with a smoky-sweet flavour and the perfume of cardamom, a temple sweet said to be Lord Jagannath's favourite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee greases the tin and enriches the batter, helping the crust caramelise to a glossy mahogany

steps: Knead the 2 cups fresh chhena with your palm on a plate for 6 to 7 minutes until it turns completely smooth and grainless with a soft, dough-like texture.

Mix in 0.75 cup sugar and rest for 10 minutes until the sugar melts, then work in 3 tbsp semolina, 0.5 tsp cardamom powder, 0.25 tsp baking soda, the 10 chopped cashews and 2 tbsp raisins into a smooth batter.
Melt 2 tbsp sugar in a heavy baking tin over low heat until it turns golden-brown caramel, then swirl to coat the base and grease the sides generously with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee.
Pour the chhena batter over the set caramel, level the top, and drizzle the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee across the surface.
Bake in an oven preheated to 180C for 45 to 50 minutes until the top turns deep brown and a skewer inserted in the centre comes out clean.
Let the chhena poda cool completely for at least 30 minutes so it sets firm, then invert onto a plate to reveal the caramelised top and slice into wedges.
tips: Use fresh, moist chhena and knead it thoroughly; grainy or dry chhena gives a crumbly rather than spongy poda.
Do not rush the cooling, as the poda firms up and slices cleanly only once fully cool.
For an authentic smoky note, bake a little longer until the top is genuinely dark, stopping just before it turns bitter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature in thick caramel-topped wedges, ideal as a festive dessert or an afternoon treat with masala chai.

variations.name: Jaggery Chhena Poda
variations.description: A rustic, unrefined version sweetened entirely with jaggery, which deepens the caramel notes into a smoky toffee register and turns the crumb a warm brown. The mineral richness of jaggery pairs naturally with the smoky baked chhena, making this the wholesome, old-world take once cooked over wood embers.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: unrefined jaggery lends the poda a smoky toffee depth and natural caramel colour no white sugar can match

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee balances the molasses notes of jaggery and keeps the crumb moist

steps: Knead the 2 cups fresh chhena on a plate for 7 minutes until smooth and free of grains, working out any lumps with the heel of your hand.
Melt 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 3 tbsp water in a pan over low heat into a smooth syrup, then strain out any grit and cool it slightly.
Mix the cooled jaggery syrup into the chhena along with 3 tbsp semolina, 0.25 tsp baking soda, 0.5 tsp cardamom, 0.25 tsp nutmeg, 10 slivered almonds and 3 tbsp grated coconut into a smooth batter.
Grease a heavy baking tin well with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, line the base with a banana leaf or parchment if you have it, and pour in the batter, levelling the top.
Drizzle the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the surface and bake in an oven preheated to 175C for 45 to 50 minutes until the top is deep brown and set.
Cool the poda fully for 30 minutes so the jaggery crumb firms up, then unmould and cut into thick wedges.
tips: Always melt and strain the jaggery first to remove sand and fibre that would leave the poda gritty.
Bake at a slightly lower temperature than the sugar version, as jaggery browns and can scorch faster.
The banana leaf lining adds a subtle traditional aroma and helps the poda release cleanly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm or cool with a dusting of toasted coconut, a wholesome festive sweet that pairs well with a cup of ginger tea.

variations.name: Saffron Pistachio Chhena Poda
variations.description: A festive, dressed-up rendition perfumed with saffron and studded with slivered pistachios and a splash of rose, giving the humble baked chhena a regal, mithai-shop finish. The saffron threads turn the crumb a delicate gold while a saffron-cream swirl on top makes each wedge look and taste celebratory.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: saffron steeped in warm milk tints the crumb gold and lends a floral aroma that lifts the baked chhena

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee carries the saffron and keeps this richer poda moist and glossy

steps: Steep 0.25 tsp Anveshan Saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk and set aside so it releases its colour and aroma.
Knead the 2 cups fresh chhena for 7 minutes until silky smooth, then beat in 0.33 cup condensed milk, 0.33 cup sugar, 3 tbsp semolina, 0.25 tsp baking soda, 0.5 tsp cardamom and 1 tsp rose water.
Fold in most of the saffron milk and half the slivered pistachios, reserving a little saffron milk and pistachios for the top, into a smooth pourable batter.
Grease a baking tin generously with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, pour in the batter, level it, and drizzle the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the surface.
Swirl the reserved saffron milk on top, scatter the remaining pistachios, and bake in an oven preheated to 180C for 45 to 50 minutes until the top is golden-brown and set.
Cool the poda for 30 minutes to firm up, then unmould and slice into wedges showing the saffron-flecked crumb.
tips: The condensed milk makes this poda extra moist, so reduce the sugar accordingly to keep it from being cloying.
Reserve some saffron milk to swirl on top for a bakery-style marbled finish.
Toast the pistachios lightly before slivering to deepen their colour and crunch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled slices garnished with extra saffron strands and pistachio slivers, an elegant finish to a festive dinner or a gift-worthy mithai-box sweet.

variations.name: Stovetop Pan Chhena Poda
variations.description: A clever no-oven method that recreates the smoky caramelised poda entirely on a covered heavy pan set over a salt bed, perfect for kitchens without a baking oven. Slow-cooking on the stove gives an even deeper burnt-caramel base and a moist centre, keeping the rustic charm of the original wood-fired sweet.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined khandsari sugar melts into a clean caramel and sweetens the poda without any chemical bleaching

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee coats the pan so the poda releases cleanly and crisps to a caramel base

steps: Knead the 2 cups fresh chhena for 7 minutes until smooth, then mix in 0.75 cup Anveshan Khandsari and rest for 10 minutes until it melts into the chhena.
Work in 3 tbsp semolina, 1 tbsp wheat flour, 0.25 tsp baking soda, 0.5 tsp cardamom, 10 chopped cashews and 2 tbsp raisins into a smooth, thick batter.
Spread 1.5 cups rock salt in a large heavy pot to make a heat-diffusing bed, place a trivet on it, cover and preheat on low for 10 minutes.
Grease a smaller heavy tin generously with 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, pour in the batter, level it, and drizzle the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on top.
Set the tin on the trivet over the hot salt bed, cover the pot tightly, and cook on low heat for 45 to 50 minutes until the top is browned and a skewer comes out clean.
Turn off the heat and let the poda cool in the covered pot for 20 minutes, then unmould and slice into caramel-based wedges.
tips: The salt bed acts like an oven floor, diffusing heat evenly so the poda does not scorch at the base.
Keep the flame low and steady throughout; high heat burns the bottom before the centre sets.
A spoon of wheat flour alongside the semolina gives extra structure for a firm stovetop set.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the wedges warm with the caramelised base facing up, alongside a scoop of plain vanilla ice cream for a contrast of hot and cold.

variations.name: Classic Corn Chaat
variations.description: Sweet steamed corn kernels are tossed warm with onion, tomato, lime and tangy chaat masala for a quick, bright street snack. The juicy pop of the corn against the sharp spice and fresh coriander makes this the easiest, most refreshing chaat to put together.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoon of ghee tossed through the warm corn adds a glossy richness and aroma

steps: Steam or boil the 2 cups sweet corn kernels for 6 to 7 minutes until just tender, then drain well.
Toss the warm corn with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee so each kernel glistens and takes on the aroma.
Finely chop 1 onion, 1 tomato and 2 green chillies and add them to the corn.
Sprinkle over 1.5 tsp chaat masala, 1 tsp roasted cumin, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp black salt and 0.5 tsp salt.
Squeeze in 2 tbsp lime juice and toss everything together until the corn is evenly coated in the tangy spice.
Fold through the coriander and serve warm while the corn is still juicy and fragrant.
tips: Do not overcook the corn, as a short steam keeps the kernels sweet and snappy.
Toss with lime and spices while the corn is warm so it soaks up the flavour better.
Add the tomato just before serving so it does not make the chaat watery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm in small cups or cones with an extra lime wedge and a pinch of chaat masala on top.

variations.name: Masala Butter Corn Chaat
variations.description: The multiplex-style version tosses the corn in ghee with a spicy dry masala and finishes it with a squeeze of lime and grated cheese that melts into the warm kernels. Rich, buttery and mildly spiced, it is the indulgent cup of corn everyone reaches for at the cinema.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the corn is tossed in ghee for the buttery multiplex richness without processed butter

steps: Steam the 2 cups sweet corn for 6 minutes until tender and drain thoroughly.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat and toss the corn with finely chopped 0.5 capsicum for 2 minutes until glossy and hot.
Sprinkle in 0.75 tsp black pepper, 1 tsp oregano, 0.75 tsp red chilli flakes, 1 tsp chaat masala and 0.5 tsp salt and toss for another minute.
Take the pan off the heat and squeeze in 1 tbsp lime juice, stirring to coat the kernels.
Tip the hot corn into cups and immediately grate 0.5 cup cheese over the top so it softens into the warmth.
Scatter coriander over and serve at once while buttery and molten.
tips: Grate the cheese over the corn while it is piping hot so it turns soft and clingy.
Keep the spice dry and finish with lime off the heat so the flavours stay punchy.
Use a firm cheese that melts gently so it coats rather than turning oily.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in paper cups with a fork, dusted with extra chilli flakes and oregano like cinema corn.

variations.name: Charred Corn Chaat
variations.description: Inspired by roadside bhutta, the kernels are dry-roasted until smoky and blistered, then rubbed with the classic lime, salt and red chilli mix. The charred edges add a deep smokiness that sets this apart from the soft steamed version, with a squeeze of lime cutting through.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a little wood-pressed oil helps the kernels blister and char without sticking to the pan

steps: Steam the 2 cups sweet corn for 4 minutes until just tender and pat the kernels completely dry.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a heavy pan over high heat and add the corn in a single layer.
Let the kernels sit and blister for 3 to 4 minutes, tossing occasionally, until charred brown-black in patches and smoky.
Tip the smoky corn into a bowl with 3 tbsp chopped spring onion, 0.33 cup roasted peanuts and 2 chopped green chillies.
Sprinkle over 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp chaat masala, 1 tsp roasted cumin, 0.5 tsp black salt and 0.5 tsp salt, then squeeze in 2 tbsp lime juice.
Toss well, fold through the coriander, and serve warm so the smoky aroma comes through.
tips: Dry the kernels fully before they hit the pan so they char rather than steam.
Use a hot heavy pan and resist stirring too often so the corn blisters properly.
Rub in the lime and chilli while warm, bhutta style, so the flavours cling to the charred kernels.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a lime wedge dipped in chilli-salt on the side for rubbing over, like roadside bhutta.

variations.name: Dahi Corn Chaat
variations.description: A cooling twist that folds the sweet corn into thick whisked yogurt with pomegranate, sev and both chutneys for a creamy, tangy chaat bowl. The soft curd and juicy corn together make a refreshing, mild version perfect for a hot afternoon.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: sweetens the whisked curd gently to balance the tang and spice

steps: Steam the 2 cups sweet corn for 6 minutes until tender, drain well, and let it cool to warm.
Whisk the 2 cups yogurt smooth with 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Honey, 0.5 tsp salt and a pinch of black salt until creamy and pourable.
Fold most of the cooled corn into the sweetened curd, keeping a little back for the top.
Spoon the corn-curd into bowls and drizzle over the tamarind and green chutneys.
Dust with 1.5 tsp chaat masala, 1 tsp roasted cumin and the remaining black salt.
Top with the reserved corn, pomegranate, sev and coriander, and serve chilled.
tips: Cool the corn before folding it into the curd so the yogurt does not turn thin and warm.
Whisk the honey into the curd off any heat so its flavour stays fresh.
Add the sev only at serving so it stays crisp against the creamy curd.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled in bowls as a cooling summer chaat, finished with extra pomegranate for colour.

variations.name: Classic Dahi Wada Punjabi
variations.description: This Punjabi Dahi Wada soaks pillowy fried urad dal vadas in thick, lightly sweetened whisked yogurt, then crowns them with tangy tamarind chutney and warm roasted spices. The vadas drink up the curd until spoon-soft, giving a cooling, sweet-sour-savoury mouthful in every bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: deep-frying the vadas in wood-pressed groundnut oil keeps them light and free of any heavy aftertaste

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the whisked yogurt and the tamarind chutney with a rounded caramel note

steps: Soak 1 cup urad dal in water for 4 hours, drain, and grind to a thick fluffy batter with only a splash of water, then whisk it hard by hand for 3 minutes until light enough to float a drop in water.
Fold 1 inch grated ginger, 2 chopped green chillies and 0.5 tsp salt into the batter, and heat 2 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 170 C over medium heat.
Slide in spoonfuls of batter and fry the vadas for 4 to 5 minutes, turning, until pale gold and puffed, then drain and drop them straight into a bowl of warm salted water to soak for 15 minutes.
Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind pulp with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and a splash of water for 5 minutes into a thick sweet-sour chutney and cool it.
Whisk the 3 cups yogurt smooth with 0.5 tsp salt and a pinch of black salt until pourable and creamy.
Gently squeeze each soaked vada between your palms to press out the water, then arrange them in a serving dish and pour the whisked yogurt over to cover.
Drizzle with the tamarind chutney and dust generously with 1.5 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 0.75 tsp black salt, then scatter coriander and serve chilled.
tips: Whisk the ground batter until a small drop floats in water, as this aeration is what makes the vadas soft and spongy.
Soak the fried vadas in warm rather than cold water so they turn tender without going soggy.
Assemble and chill for 30 minutes before serving so the vadas fully absorb the yogurt.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve cold in shallow bowls with an extra drizzle of tamarind chutney and a final pinch of roasted cumin over each portion.

variations.name: Delhi Dahi Bhalla
variations.description: The Chandni Chowk dahi bhalla is softer and more loaded, finished with both a green mint chutney and a dark date-tamarind chutney, jewelled with pomegranate and crunchy boondi. It leans sweeter and more festive than the plain Punjabi version, the way old Delhi sweet shops pile it high.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: frying the bhallas in light wood-pressed sunflower oil keeps them pale and delicate for the soft Delhi style

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: deepens the date-tamarind chutney to the dark sweet-sour tone of old Delhi carts

steps: Soak 1 cup urad dal for 4 hours, grind to a fluffy batter with minimal water, and beat it well until airy and light.
Season the batter with 0.5 tsp salt, heat 2 cups Anveshan Sunflower Oil to 170 C, and fry spoonfuls for 4 minutes until just pale gold and soft, avoiding a hard crust.
Drain the bhallas and soak them in warm water for 20 minutes until very tender, then squeeze gently between the palms.
Blend 6 soaked dates with 3 tbsp tamarind and 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer 5 minutes into a thick dark chutney, and cool it.
