Whisk the 3 cups yogurt with 0.5 tsp salt until smooth and pourable, and chill.
Layer the squeezed bhallas in a dish, cover with the chilled yogurt, then spoon over the date-tamarind chutney and 4 tbsp green chutney in generous swirls.
Finish with a dusting of 1.5 tsp roasted cumin and 0.75 tsp black salt, then shower over boondi, pomegranate and coriander and serve at once.
tips: Fry only until pale so the bhallas stay soft enough to melt in the mouth after soaking.
Add the boondi just before serving so it keeps a little crunch against the soft bhallas.
Balance both chutneys generously, as the Delhi style is meant to taste sweet-forward and layered.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a wide platter topped with extra pomegranate and a lattice of both chutneys for a festive spread.

variations.name: South Indian Thayir Vada
variations.description: This Tamil thayir vada bathes medu-style urad vadas in salted, unsweetened curd finished with a sizzling tempering of mustard seeds, curry leaves and dried chilli. Fresh grated coconut and a hint of green chilli make it savoury and aromatic rather than sweet, a cooling South Indian counterpoint to the Punjabi original.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: frying the vadas in wood-pressed sesame oil lends the earthy South Indian aroma this dish is known for

steps: Soak 1 cup urad dal for 4 hours, grind to a thick fluffy batter with very little water, and whip it by hand until light and airy.
Mix in 1 inch grated ginger, 1 chopped green chilli and 0.5 tsp salt, then heat 2 cups Anveshan Sesame Oil to 175 C.
Wet your fingers, shape small doughnut rounds, and fry them for 4 to 5 minutes until golden and cooked through, then soak in warm water for 15 minutes.
Whisk the 3 cups yogurt with 0.5 tsp salt and the grated coconut until smooth, then squeeze the vadas and settle them into the curd.

Heat 2 tsp of the frying oil in a small pan and crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds, then add 2 broken dried chillies, the remaining slit green chilli, 12 curry leaves and 0.25 tsp asafoetida until the leaves turn crisp.
Pour the hot tempering over the curd-soaked vadas so it sizzles, scatter coriander, and rest for 20 minutes before serving cool.
tips: Grate the coconut fresh and stir it into the curd for the authentic South Indian sweetness without any sugar.
Pour the tempering while it is still sizzling so the aroma of curry leaves and mustard infuses the curd.
Rest the assembled dish so the vadas absorb the tempered yogurt and turn meltingly soft.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve lightly chilled as a side to a South Indian meal or on its own with extra curry-leaf tempering spooned over.

variations.name: Moong Dal Dahi Wada
variations.description: A lighter, easier-to-digest take that blends split moong dal into the usual urad batter for softer, quicker-soaking vadas. The curd is sweetened gently with honey and the whole dish stays delicate, making it a friendlier version for those who find classic urad vadas heavy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil fries the lighter moong vadas crisp without weighing them down

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: sweetens the whisked curd naturally so the delicate vadas are not overpowered

steps: Soak 0.5 cup urad dal and 0.5 cup moong dal together for 3 hours, drain, and grind to a fluffy batter with a bare splash of water.
Beat the batter well until light, then fold in 1 inch grated ginger, 2 chopped green chillies and 0.5 tsp salt.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 170 C and fry small spoonfuls for 3 to 4 minutes until golden, then soak the vadas in warm water for 10 minutes.
Whisk the 3 cups yogurt smooth with 2 tbsp Anveshan Honey and 0.5 tsp salt until pourable and lightly sweet.
Squeeze each moong vada gently and arrange them in a serving dish, then pour the honeyed curd over to cover them fully.
Dust with 1.5 tsp roasted cumin, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 0.75 tsp black salt, scatter coriander, and chill for 20 minutes before serving.
tips: The moong-urad mix ferments and fries faster, so watch the oil so the lighter vadas do not brown too quickly.
Stir the honey into the curd only once it is off any heat so its flavour and goodness stay intact.
These vadas soak faster than pure urad ones, so a 10 minute water soak is enough before squeezing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled as a light summer snack with a drizzle of extra honey-sweetened curd and a sprinkle of roasted cumin.

variations.name: Classic Hyderabadi Bottle-Gourd Dalcha
variations.description: The classic Hyderabadi dalcha of soft chana dal simmered with chunks of bottle gourd in a tangy tamarind broth, finished with a fragrant garlic and curry-leaf tempering. Mildly sour and comforting, it is the traditional partner to bagara khana at Deccan weddings, kept vegetarian here.

ingredients.name: Chana dal
ingredients.note: soaked 30 minutes and pressure-cooked soft

ingredients.name: Bottle gourd
ingredients.note: peeled and cubed

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked for pulp

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed gingelly oil for the authentic Deccan tempering

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: sliced, for the tempering

steps: Pressure-cook 3/4 cup soaked chana dal with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 2.5 cups water for 5-6 whistles until soft but still holding shape, then lightly mash half of it.
In a pot heat 1 tbsp of the Anveshan Sesame Oil, saute the chopped onion for 4 minutes, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the chopped tomato, and cook for 3 minutes until pulpy.
Add the cubed bottle gourd with 1 tsp red chilli powder and 3/4 tsp salt, and cook for 6 minutes until it begins to soften.
Stir in the cooked chana dal, the squeezed tamarind pulp and 1.5 cups water, and simmer on medium heat for 12 minutes until the gourd is tender and the broth turns tangy.
Adjust to a medium-thick, pourable consistency and check the salt and sourness.

Heat the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard and 1/2 tsp cumin seeds, add 5 sliced garlic cloves, 2 dry red chillies and 2 sprigs curry leaves, fry until golden, and pour over the dalcha.
tips: Cook the chana dal so it stays just intact; mashing only half keeps the dalcha both creamy and textured.
Bottle gourd releases water as it cooks, so add the extra water gradually to control the consistency.
Balance the tamarind carefully; dalcha should be gently tangy, not aggressively sour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bagara khana or plain steamed rice, with a squeeze of lime and fried papad alongside.

variations.name: Toor Dal Kaddu Dalcha
variations.description: A softer, faster version made with toor dal and sweet yellow pumpkin instead of chana dal and gourd, giving a smoother, mellower dalcha with a natural sweetness against the tamarind. Lighter on the stomach and quicker to cook, it is the gentle everyday take.

ingredients.name: Toor dal
ingredients.note: pressure-cooked soft

ingredients.name: Yellow pumpkin
ingredients.note: peeled and cubed

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked for a light tang

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the mellow fat that suits the sweet pumpkin and soft toor dal

steps: Pressure-cook 3/4 cup toor dal with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 2.5 cups water for 4 whistles until soft, then whisk smooth.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot over medium heat, splutter 1 tsp cumin seeds with 2 sprigs curry leaves, add the chopped onion and 3 slit green chillies and fry for 4 minutes.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 3/4 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp coriander powder, and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the 2 cups cubed pumpkin with 3/4 tsp salt and 1 cup water, cover and cook for 8 minutes until it turns soft and starts to break at the edges.
Pour in the whisked toor dal and the squeezed tamarind pulp with the remaining salt, and simmer on medium heat for 8 minutes until creamy and gently tangy.
Mash a little of the pumpkin into the broth for body, cook for 2 more minutes, and serve warm.
tips: Yellow pumpkin cooks fast and sweet, so add only a little tamarind to keep the balance gentle.
Whisk the toor dal smooth for a creamier dalcha than the chunkier chana-dal version.
Mashing some pumpkin into the broth thickens it naturally without any flour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over steamed rice with a spoon of ghee, or with soft phulka for a light meal.

variations.name: Mixed-Veg Coconut Dalcha
variations.description: A coastal-style dalcha loaded with mixed vegetables and finished with a ground fresh-coconut paste, giving a thicker, aromatic curry with less pronounced sourness. Heartier and more coconut-scented than the classic, it eats almost like a substantial stew.

ingredients.name: Chana dal
ingredients.note: pressure-cooked soft

ingredients.name: Mixed vegetables (carrot, beans, bottle gourd, drumstick)
ingredients.note: cut into chunks

ingredients.name: Fresh coconut
ingredients.note: ground into a paste

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked for a mild tang

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the coastal fat that ties the coconut-paste gravy together

steps: Pressure-cook 1/2 cup chana dal with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 2 cups water for 5 whistles until soft but intact, and grind 1/3 cup coconut with 2 green chillies into a smooth paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pot over medium heat, splutter 1/2 tsp mustard and 1/2 tsp cumin seeds with 2 sprigs curry leaves.
Add the chopped onion and fry for 4 minutes, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 3/4 tsp red chilli powder and cook for 1 minute.
Add the 2 cups mixed vegetables with 3/4 tsp salt and 1.5 cups water, cover and simmer for 12 minutes until the drumstick and gourd are tender.
Stir in the cooked chana dal and the squeezed tamarind pulp, simmer for 5 minutes, then add the ground coconut paste and cook on low for 4 minutes.
Simmer until the dalcha thickens to a rich stew-like gravy and the coconut smells fragrant, then serve hot.
tips: Add the coconut paste last and keep the heat low so the gravy stays fragrant and does not turn grainy.
A mix of vegetables that hold their shape, like carrot and drumstick, gives this dalcha its hearty character.
Keep the tamarind light, as the coconut is meant to lead over the sourness here.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with ghee rice, appam or plain steamed rice for a coconut-rich coastal meal.

variations.name: Masoor Dalcha with Spinach
variations.description: A quicker weeknight dalcha built on split masoor dal that cooks in minutes, brightened with spinach and a tangy tomato-tamarind base. Softer and faster than the chana-dal original, the red lentils break down into a smooth, comforting body threaded with green.

ingredients.name: Masoor dal
ingredients.note: split red lentils, quick-cooking

ingredients.name: Spinach
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked for a light tang

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil that keeps the quick dalcha light and clean

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: crushed

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

steps: Pressure-cook 3/4 cup masoor dal with the chopped tomatoes, 2 slit green chillies, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 3 cups water for 3-4 whistles until soft and broken down, then whisk smooth.
Add the 2 cups chopped spinach to the hot dal and simmer on medium heat for 5 minutes until wilted and deep green.
Stir in the squeezed tamarind pulp with 1/2 tsp red chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt, and simmer for 5 minutes to a medium consistency.
Loosen with hot water as needed so the dalcha stays soft and pourable, and keep it warm.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a small pan, splutter 1 tsp cumin seeds, add 6 crushed garlic cloves and 2 dry red chillies, and fry for 40 seconds until golden.
Pour the sizzling tempering over the dalcha, cover for 2 minutes, and serve hot.
tips: Masoor dal cooks much faster than chana, so watch it and stop before it turns to mush.
Add the spinach after the dal is cooked to keep it bright rather than khaki.
This lighter dalcha thickens as it stands, so keep it a touch loose off the heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice or hot rotis, with a spoon of ghee and a slice of lemon.

variations.name: Classic Toor Dal Dalma
variations.description: Dalma is the soul-food of Odisha, a wholesome one-pot dish where toor dal is cooked soft with chunks of vegetables and finished with a roasted-cumin tempering and grated coconut. Cooked without onion or garlic, its comfort comes from the earthy dal, sweet pumpkin and the fragrant panch phutana tadka.

ingredients.name: Toor Dal
ingredients.note: pressure-cooked soft

ingredients.name: Raw Banana
ingredients.note: cut into chunks

ingredients.name: Yellow Pumpkin
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Brinjal
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Colocasia (Arbi)
ingredients.note: peeled and halved

ingredients.name: Cumin Seeds
ingredients.note: for the roasted powder

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: carries the cumin tempering that gives dalma its signature aroma

ingredients.name: Panch Phutana
ingredients.note: Odia five-seed mix

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup toor dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 3 cups water for 3 whistles until soft, then whisk lightly.
Add the raw banana, cubed pumpkin, brinjal and halved colocasia to the dal with 1 tsp salt and simmer on medium heat for 12-15 minutes until the vegetables are tender.
Meanwhile dry-roast 1 tsp cumin seeds with 1 dry red chilli until dark and fragrant, then grind to a coarse powder.
Stir the roasted cumin powder and 3 tbsp grated coconut into the simmering dalma and cook another 3 minutes so the flavours meld.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan, splutter 1 tsp panch phutana with 1 bay leaf and the remaining dry red chilli until aromatic.
Pour the sizzling tempering over the dalma, stir once, and rest it covered for 5 minutes before serving hot.
tips: Dry-roasting and grinding the cumin fresh is the heart of dalma, so do not swap it for plain cumin powder.
Keep the vegetables in bold chunks so they hold their shape and do not dissolve into the dal.
Add the coconut towards the end so it keeps its fresh sweetness rather than cooking away.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot over steamed rice with a wedge of lime and a fried papad, or with soft rotis for a wholesome meal.

variations.name: Jagannath Temple Dalma
variations.description: The sattvic dalma offered as mahaprasad at the Jagannath temple in Puri, cooked in earthen pots with pure ghee and absolutely no onion or garlic. Enriched with soaked chana dal alongside the toor and a generous hand of ginger, it is milder, richer and deeply aromatic.

ingredients.name: Toor Dal
ingredients.note: cooked soft

ingredients.name: Chana Dal
ingredients.note: soaked, for a nutty bite

ingredients.name: Yellow Pumpkin
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Papaya (Raw)
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Colocasia (Arbi)
ingredients.note: peeled and halved

ingredients.name: Cumin Seeds
ingredients.note: for roasting

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the pure fat that makes this temple dalma rich and fragrant

steps: Pressure-cook 0.75 cup toor dal with 0.25 cup soaked chana dal, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 3 cups water for 4 whistles until both are soft.
Add the cubed pumpkin, raw papaya and halved colocasia with 1 tbsp grated ginger and 1 tsp salt, then simmer on medium heat for 12-15 minutes until tender.
Dry-roast 1 tsp cumin seeds with 1 dry red chilli until fragrant and grind to a coarse powder.
Stir the roasted powder and 4 tbsp grated coconut into the dalma and simmer another 4 minutes on low heat.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, splutter 1 tsp panch phutana with 1 bay leaf and the remaining chilli until they crackle and darken.
Pour the ghee tempering over the temple dalma, cover, and let it rest 5 minutes so the aroma settles before serving.
tips: The extra ghee and the ban on onion and garlic are what make this taste of the Puri kitchen, so keep it sattvic.
Soak the chana dal well so it cooks as soft as the toor and does not stay firm.
A cast-iron or clay pot lends a faint earthiness that mimics the temple's traditional vessels.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as bhog over plain rice with a spoon of ghee, ideally alongside saga bhaja and a sweet kheer.

variations.name: Moong Dal Dalma
variations.description: A lighter, quicker dalma built on roasted yellow moong dal, which cooks faster and tastes gentler than toor. With crunchy raw peanuts and a bright mustard-oil tempering, it is the everyday weekday version that sits easy on the stomach.

ingredients.name: Yellow Moong Dal
ingredients.note: dry-roasted, then cooked

ingredients.name: Bottle Gourd (Lauki)
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Potato
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Cumin Seeds
ingredients.note: for roasting

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil for a pungent, bright Odia tempering

steps: Dry-roast 1 cup yellow moong dal for 3 minutes until golden and nutty, then pressure-cook it with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 3 tbsp raw peanuts and 3 cups water for 2 whistles.
Add the cubed lauki, potato and chopped tomato with 1 tsp salt, then simmer on medium heat for 10 minutes until the vegetables soften.
Dry-roast 1 tsp cumin seeds with 1 dry red chilli and grind to a coarse powder.
Stir the roasted cumin powder into the dalma and simmer for 3 minutes to a light, pourable consistency.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the heat, and splutter 1 tsp panch phutana with the remaining chilli and 1 sprig curry leaves.
Pour the pungent tempering over the moong dalma, stir once, and serve hot.
tips: Roasting the moong dal before cooking gives this lighter dalma a lovely nutty depth.
Heat the mustard oil until it just smokes, then cool it slightly, to mellow its raw sharpness.
Use quick-cooking vegetables like lauki and potato so the whole dish comes together in half an hour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with steamed rice and a squeeze of lime, or with plain rotis for a light dinner.

variations.name: Dry Roasted Dalma (Sukhila Dalma)
variations.description: A thick, near-dry dalma where the dal and vegetables are cooked down until they cling together, then finished with extra roasted coconut and a heavy cumin-chilli tadka. Robust and intensely flavoured, it is served almost like a mash rather than a pourable dal.

ingredients.name: Toor Dal
ingredients.note: cooked soft, kept thick

ingredients.name: Yam (Suran)
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Broad Beans (Sem)
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Brinjal
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Grated Coconut
ingredients.note: roasted

ingredients.name: Cumin Seeds
ingredients.note: for the roasted powder

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: for the bold tempering and to gloss the thick dalma

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup toor dal with 0.5 tsp turmeric and just 2 cups water for 3 whistles so it stays thick, then mash lightly.
Add the cubed yam, chopped broad beans and brinjal with 1 tsp salt, and simmer uncovered on medium heat for 15 minutes until the mix thickens and the water evaporates.
Dry-roast 1.5 tsp cumin seeds with 2 dry red chillies until dark, then grind to a coarse powder.
Roast 6 tbsp grated coconut in a dry pan until golden and stir it with the cumin powder into the thick dalma.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, splutter 1 tsp panch phutana with 1 bay leaf and the remaining chilli until fragrant.
Fold the tempering through the dry dalma and cook 2 more minutes until it clings together, then serve hot.
tips: Use less water and simmer uncovered so the dalma reduces to a thick, scoopable mash.
Roasting the coconut until golden gives this dry version a deep, toasty backbone.
Firm vegetables like yam and broad beans hold up best in this reduced, robust style.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a thick side with rice and dali, or scoop it up with hot rotis and a raw onion salad.

variations.name: Classic White & Green Sandwich Dhokla
variations.description: A striking two-tone steamed cake: a pale, tangy gram-flour layer topped with a herby green coriander-mint layer, joined by a smear of chutney in the middle. Each square delivers soft, spongy dhokla with a fresh green finish and the classic sweet-sour Gujarati temper poured over. It is as much a showpiece as a snack.

ingredients.name: Fine semolina
ingredients.note: A little rava gives the sponge extra body and a cleaner cut

ingredients.name: Coriander-mint paste
ingredients.note: Blended fresh for the vivid green top layer

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A spoon in each batter and the rest for the mustard-seed tempering

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Melted into the tempering water for the signature sweet-sour Gujarati finish

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups besan, 2 tbsp semolina, 1/2 cup curd, 1 tbsp green chilli-ginger paste, 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt, 1 tsp oil, 1 tbsp lemon juice and about 1 cup water into a smooth, thick pouring batter; rest 15 minutes, then split into two equal bowls.
Stir 1/3 cup coriander-mint paste into one bowl to make the green batter, leaving the other pale, and grease a steamer tin while you bring the steamer water to a rolling boil.
Add 1/2 tsp Eno to the white batter, fold gently as it froths, pour into the tin and steam over high heat for 8-10 minutes until a skewer comes out clean.
Spread a thin layer of extra coriander chutney over the set white base, then add 1/2 tsp Eno to the green batter, pour it on top and steam a further 10-12 minutes until springy.
Cool 10 minutes, run a knife around the edge and cut into squares, keeping the two coloured layers intact.

For the temper, heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds and 10 curry leaves, add 1/2 cup water and 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer 2 minutes and spoon evenly over the cut dhokla so it soaks in.
tips: Add Eno only just before steaming each layer and do not overmix, or the trapped air escapes and the sponge turns dense.
Steam the white layer until fully set before adding the green batter, otherwise the two layers marble instead of staying distinct.
The jaggery tempering water should be poured while warm so it seeps through and keeps the dhokla moist for hours.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the two-tone squares garnished with grated coconut and coriander, alongside extra green chutney and a sweet-tamarind chutney for dipping.

variations.name: Instant Rava Sandwich Dhokla
variations.description: A no-fermentation weeknight version built on semolina and curd, so the batter goes from bowl to steamer in minutes. The white rava layer stays wonderfully moist and slightly grainy, crowned with a quick green pea-coriander layer for colour. Perfect when you want sandwich dhokla without planning ahead.

ingredients.name: Green peas paste
ingredients.note: Boiled peas blended with coriander for the green top layer

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: A little in the batter and the rest for a nutty mustard tempering

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: Unrefined sugar dissolved in the tempering for a mellow sweetness

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups fine semolina with 3/4 cup curd, 1 tbsp green chilli-ginger paste, 1 tsp salt, 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, 1 tbsp lemon juice and enough water to make a thick, smooth batter; rest 10 minutes so the rava swells, then divide into two bowls.
Stir 1/3 cup green peas paste into one bowl for the green layer and set the steamer water boiling; grease a tin.
Add 1/2 tsp Eno to the plain rava batter, fold as it foams, pour into the tin and steam on high for 8-10 minutes until set.
Add 1/2 tsp Eno to the green batter, pour over the set white layer and steam a further 10 minutes until a skewer comes out clean.
Cool 10 minutes and cut into neat squares, keeping the pale and green layers visible.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tsp sesame seeds and 10 curry leaves, add 1/2 cup water with 1 tbsp Anveshan Khandsari, boil 2 minutes and pour over the dhokla.
tips: Rest the rava batter at least ten minutes so the semolina absorbs moisture, or the dhokla can turn dry.
Because there is no fermentation, steam immediately after adding Eno for the lightest sponge.
If the batter thickens too much while resting, loosen it with a splash of water before adding Eno.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a fresh coconut chutney and a cup of masala chai for a quick evening snack.

variations.name: Moong Dal Sandwich Dhokla
variations.description: A protein-rich take where a soaked-and-ground yellow moong batter forms the pale base, layered with a spinach-moong green top. Lighter and more digestible than besan dhokla, with a delicate, custardy crumb that melts on the tongue. This is the version health-conscious Gujarati homes turn to.

ingredients.name: Yellow moong dal
ingredients.note: Soaked 4 hours and ground to a smooth batter

ingredients.name: Spinach puree
ingredients.note: Blanched and blended for the green layer

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A little in the batter and the rest for tempering the soft dhokla

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Dissolved in the tempering water for the classic sweet-sour balance

steps: Grind 1.5 cups soaked yellow moong dal with 1/3 cup curd and a little water to a smooth, thick pouring batter, then whisk in 1 tbsp green chilli-ginger paste, 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt, 1 tsp oil and 1 tbsp lemon juice; divide into two bowls.
Stir 1/3 cup spinach puree into one bowl for the green layer and bring the steamer to a rolling boil; grease a tin.
Add 1/2 tsp Eno to the plain moong batter, fold until frothy, pour into the tin and steam on high for 10 minutes until set.
Add 1/2 tsp Eno to the spinach batter, pour over the base and steam another 10-12 minutes until a skewer comes out clean.
Cool 10 minutes, then cut into squares with the two layers clearly banded.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds and 10 curry leaves, add 1/2 cup water and 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer 2 minutes and spoon over the dhokla.
tips: Grind the moong batter smooth but not watery; too thin and the delicate sponge will not hold two layers.
Moong dhokla sets softer than besan, so cool it fully before cutting to get clean squares.
A pinch of asafoetida in the batter keeps this protein-rich version easy on the stomach.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the pale-and-green squares with mint chutney and a light salad for a nourishing tiffin or brunch.

variations.name: Sattu & Palak Sandwich Dhokla
variations.description: A nutty, high-protein reinvention where roasted-gram sattu enriches the pale layer and a spinach layer crowns it, making a filling that eats heartier than any besan dhokla. The sattu lends a toasty depth and a slightly denser, satisfying crumb. A modern, wholesome twist that still steams up soft and pours over sweet-sour.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Roasted gram flour that adds nutty protein and body to the white layer

ingredients.name: Spinach puree
ingredients.note: For the vivid green top layer

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: In the batter and the tempering, its toasty note pairs with the roasted sattu

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: For the sweet-sour tempering that keeps the dense sponge moist

steps: Whisk 1 cup Anveshan Sattu and 1/2 cup besan with 1/2 cup curd, 1 tbsp green chilli-ginger paste, 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt, 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, 1 tbsp lemon juice and about 1.25 cups water into a smooth, thick batter, since sattu drinks more water; rest 15 minutes and divide in two.
Stir 1/3 cup spinach puree into one bowl for the green layer and set the steamer water boiling; grease a tin.
Add 1/2 tsp Eno to the sattu batter, fold until it froths, pour into the tin and steam on high for 10-12 minutes until set.
Add 1/2 tsp Eno to the spinach batter, pour over the base and steam a further 12 minutes until a skewer comes out clean.
Cool 10 minutes and cut into squares, keeping the toasty base and green top clearly layered.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 10 curry leaves, add 1/2 cup water with 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, boil 2 minutes and pour over the dhokla.
tips: Sattu absorbs more liquid than besan, so keep the batter pourable and a touch thinner than it first looks.
This sponge is denser, so steam a couple of minutes longer than a plain besan dhokla to cook it through.
Generously soaking it with the warm jaggery temper offsets the natural dryness of sattu.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a protein-packed breakfast with mint-coriander chutney and a glass of buttermilk to round out the meal.

variations.name: Classic Dhonepata Bora
variations.description: Crisp, lacy Bengali coriander fritters where a fistful of fresh dhonepata is bound with a light besan batter and fried in mustard oil until golden and shatteringly crisp at the edges. The coriander stays vividly green and fragrant inside, and green chilli gives a gentle kick. These are the monsoon-afternoon nibbles served with rice and dal or with evening tea.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil for frying gives these bora their authentic pungent Bengali flavour and golden crunch

steps: Wash and finely chop 2 cups fresh coriander with 3 green chillies and place in a bowl.
Add 3/4 cup besan, 3 tbsp rice flour, 1/2 tsp nigella seeds, 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder, a pinch of baking soda and 3/4 tsp salt to the coriander.
Sprinkle in about 5 to 6 tbsp water little by little and mix to a thick, clinging batter that just coats the coriander, not a runny one.
Heat 1 cup Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it just smokes, then lower to medium so the bora cook through without burning.
Drop in small flattened spoonfuls of the batter and fry in batches for 3 to 4 minutes, turning once, until deep golden and crisp at the edges.
Drain the bora on paper and serve hot while they are at their crispest.
tips: Keep the batter thick and barely wet so the fritters stay lacy and crisp rather than doughy.
The rice flour is the trick to an extra-crunchy edge, so do not leave it out.
Fry on medium heat; too hot and they brown before cooking, too low and they drink up oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot as a starter to a rice-and-dal meal, or with muri and tea on a rainy evening.

variations.name: Posto Dhonepata Bora
variations.description: A richer, nuttier version where ground poppy seeds and fresh coconut are blended with the coriander, giving fritters that are soft and moist within and crisp without. The posto lends a subtle creaminess and the coconut a gentle sweetness quite different from the plain besan bora. These are a small delicacy, denser and more indulgent.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Mustard oil fries these posto bora to a golden crisp while keeping their Bengali character

steps: Soak 3 tbsp poppy seeds in warm water for 15 minutes, then grind with 1/4 cup grated coconut, 3 green chillies and 1 inch ginger to a coarse, thick paste using minimal water.
Finely chop 1.5 cups fresh coriander and mix it into the poppy-coconut paste.
Add 1/3 cup besan, 2 tbsp rice flour, 1/2 tsp cumin powder and 3/4 tsp salt and combine into a thick, scoopable batter, adding only a splash of water if needed.
Heat 1 cup Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it smokes, then lower to medium heat.
Shape the batter into small flattened rounds and fry in batches for 3 to 4 minutes, turning once, until golden and set.
Drain on paper and serve warm so the crisp exterior and soft posto centre are at their best.
tips: Grind the poppy and coconut coarse rather than smooth for a pleasant texture in the fritter.
Use minimal water when grinding and mixing, as posto releases moisture and can loosen the batter.
These are denser than besan bora, so keep them small and thin so the centre cooks through.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a rich starter with the first course of rice, or on their own with a squeeze of lime.

variations.name: Dhonepata o Cholar Dal Bora
variations.description: A crunchier, protein-rich version built on a coarsely ground soaked chana dal batter studded with fresh coriander, giving fritters with a satisfying grainy bite like a Bengali dal vada. The lentil base makes them heartier and more filling than flour-bound bora. Golden and craggy, they hold their crunch long after frying.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Mustard oil gives the lentil bora their crisp golden shell and unmistakable Bengali aroma

steps: Soak 1 cup chana dal in water for 3 to 4 hours, then drain well and grind to a coarse, thick paste with 3 green chillies and 1 inch ginger, using no water.
Mix in 1.5 cups finely chopped coriander, 1 finely chopped small onion, 1/2 tsp fennel seeds, 1/4 tsp turmeric and 3/4 tsp salt to a thick, mouldable batter.
Heat 1 cup Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until it smokes, then lower to medium heat.
Shape the batter into small flattened patties and slide them into the oil, frying in batches for 4 to 5 minutes, turning once, until deep golden and crunchy.
Drain on paper towels to remove excess oil.
Serve hot and crisp, as the lentil bora soften if left too long.
tips: Grind the soaked dal without water for a batter that holds together and fries crisp.
Leave the dal a little coarse for the signature grainy crunch of a lentil bora.
Fry on steady medium heat so the thick patties cook through to the centre without burning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coriander-mint chutney or with rice and dal as a crunchy side.

variations.name: Pan-Fried Sattu Dhonepata Bora
variations.description: A lighter, healthier take where roasted sattu replaces most of the besan and the coriander fritters are shallow-fried in an appe pan with just a little ghee, using far less oil than deep-frying. The sattu adds nutty protein and keeps them soft inside with a golden crust. It is the guilt-free, everyday version for a wholesome snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Roasted Bengal-gram sattu adds nutty protein and lets these bora crisp up with very little oil

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A little ghee to shallow-fry gives a golden crust while keeping the bora light

steps: Finely chop 1.5 cups fresh coriander with 3 green chillies and grate in 1 inch ginger.
Add 3/4 cup Anveshan Sattu, 1/4 cup besan, 1/2 tsp ajwain, 1/4 tsp turmeric, a pinch of baking soda and 3/4 tsp salt, and mix with about 1/2 cup water to a thick, dropping batter.
Heat an appe pan on medium heat and brush each mould with a little Anveshan Ghee.
Spoon the batter into the moulds and cook covered for 3 to 4 minutes until the underside is golden and set.
Drizzle a few drops of ghee over each, flip carefully, and cook the other side for 3 minutes until golden and cooked through.
Serve warm straight from the pan for the best texture.
tips: Whisk the sattu in well so there are no dry lumps, as it thickens the batter quickly.
Keep the heat medium and cover the pan so the thick bora cook through to the centre.
For a fully deep-fried finish you can also fry these, but the appe pan keeps them light and low-oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a wholesome tea-time snack with green chutney or a bowl of yogurt.

variations.name: Classic Enchor Er Dalna
variations.description: The prized Bengali raw-jackfruit curry, known as gaach-patha or tree-mutton for its meaty texture, simmered in a spiced potato gravy with ginger and Bengali garam masala. The jackfruit chunks are boiled and fried until golden, taking on a satisfying, chewy bite. It is a beloved niramish dish that mimics a rich meat curry without any meat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil fries the jackfruit and gives this niramish curry its robust Bengali base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of bilona ghee lifts the dalna with festive aroma

steps: Oil your hands, cut 500 g raw jackfruit into 2-inch chunks, and boil them with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 12 to 15 minutes until fork-tender, then drain.

Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until smoking, lower to medium, and fry the jackfruit chunks until golden and lightly crisped, about 5 minutes, then remove; fry 2 cubed potatoes until golden and set aside.
In the same oil temper 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 bay leaf and 1 inch cinnamon for 20 seconds, then add 2 tbsp ginger paste and 1 grated tomato and cook for 4 minutes.
Add 1 tsp cumin powder, 1 tsp coriander powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and fry for 40 seconds until the oil separates.
Return the jackfruit and potatoes with 2.5 cups hot water, 1/2 tsp sugar and the remaining salt, cover, and simmer for 15 minutes until the potatoes are soft and the gravy thickens.
Finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 3/4 tsp Bengali garam masala, rest for 5 minutes, and serve.
tips: Oil your hands and knife before cutting raw jackfruit, as its sticky sap is otherwise very hard to wash off.
Boil the jackfruit until properly tender before frying, since it will not soften much further in the gravy.
This curry tastes even better the next day once the jackfruit has soaked up the masala.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with luchi, paratha or steamed rice, treating it as the meaty centrepiece of a vegetarian meal.

variations.name: Kancha Kathaler Kosha (Dry Roasted Jackfruit)
variations.description: A rich, semi-dry kosha version where boiled jackfruit is slow-cooked with browned onions and a bold whole-spice masala until the gravy reduces to a thick, dark coating. There are no potatoes here, only intensely spiced jackfruit that eats remarkably like a dry mutton kosha. It is the indulgent, feast-day preparation.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Generous mustard oil lets the onions and masala fry down to a deep, clinging kosha

steps: Cut 500 g raw jackfruit into chunks with oiled hands and boil with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 12 to 15 minutes until tender, then drain.
Heat 5 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until smoking, lower to medium, and fry the jackfruit until deep golden, about 6 minutes, then set aside.
In the same oil temper 1 bay leaf, 1 inch cinnamon, 4 cardamom pods and 4 cloves, then add 3 thinly sliced onions and fry patiently for 12 minutes until dark brown.

Add 2 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook 2 minutes, then lower the heat and whisk in 1/4 cup yogurt with 2 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 1/4 tsp turmeric, stirring so it does not split.
Return the jackfruit, add 1/2 tsp sugar, the remaining salt and just 3/4 cup hot water, cover, and slow-cook on low heat for 15 minutes, stirring now and then until the masala clings darkly.
Uncover and cook off any excess liquid, finish with 1 tsp Bengali garam masala, and serve semi-dry.
tips: Brown the onions truly dark for the deep colour and richness that define a kosha.
Whisk the yogurt in on low heat and keep stirring so it thickens the masala without curdling.
Keep the water minimal and cook it down; this dish should coat the jackfruit, not swim in gravy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot luchi, paratha or ghee rice as a rich, meat-like centrepiece.

variations.name: Enchor Er Dalna with Coconut and Poppy
variations.description: A milder, nutty version where a ground coconut-and-poppy-seed paste replaces the tomato, giving a pale, subtly sweet gravy that clings to the jackfruit. Popular in East-Bengal homes, it is gentler and more aromatic than the fiery classic. The coconut lends body and a soft, comforting sweetness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Mustard oil fries the jackfruit and blooms the whole spices for an East-Bengal style gravy

steps: Cut 500 g raw jackfruit into chunks with oiled hands and boil with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 12 to 15 minutes until tender, then drain.
Soak 1.5 tbsp poppy seeds in warm water for 15 minutes and grind with 1/2 cup grated coconut and 2 green chillies to a smooth paste.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until smoking, lower to medium, and fry the jackfruit and 1 cubed potato until golden, about 6 minutes, then remove.
In the same oil temper 1 tsp panch phoron and 1 bay leaf for 20 seconds, add 1.5 tbsp ginger paste and 1 slit green chilli, and fry for 1 minute.

Add the coconut-poppy paste with 1 tsp cumin powder and 1/4 tsp turmeric and fry for 3 minutes until fragrant and the oil edges out, then return the jackfruit and potato with 2 cups hot water, 3/4 tsp sugar and the salt.
Cover and simmer for 15 minutes until the potato is soft and the gravy is creamy, finish with 1/2 tsp Bengali garam masala, and serve.
tips: Grind the coconut and poppy very smooth for a silky gravy that coats the jackfruit well.
Panch phoron gives this version its East-Bengal fragrance, so bloom it fully in the hot oil.
Keep the heat gentle after adding the paste so the coconut does not catch and turn grainy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain steamed rice and a wedge of lime for a mellow, homely lunch.

variations.name: Doi Enchor
variations.description: A creamy, tangy take where the fried jackfruit simmers in a whisked-yogurt gravy scented with whole garam masala and ghee, giving a pale, luscious curry without any tomato. The curd tenderises the jackfruit and lends a gentle sourness that offsets its richness. It is an elegant, guest-worthy preparation.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee carries the whole spices and keeps the yogurt gravy rich and glossy

steps: Cut 500 g raw jackfruit into chunks with oiled hands and boil with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 12 to 15 minutes until tender, then drain.
Soak 12 cashews in warm water and grind to a paste, then whisk it into 3/4 cup yogurt with 1 tsp cumin powder until smooth and lump-free.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat and fry the jackfruit until pale gold, about 5 minutes, then remove.
In the same ghee temper 1 bay leaf, 1 inch cinnamon, 4 cardamom pods and 4 cloves for 20 seconds, then add 1.5 tbsp ginger paste and 3 slit green chillies and fry for 1 minute.
Lower the heat to minimum and pour in the whisked yogurt, stirring for 3 minutes so it does not split, then return the jackfruit with 1.25 cups hot water, 3/4 tsp sugar and the salt.
Cover and simmer gently for 12 minutes until the gravy is creamy, finish with 1/2 tsp Bengali garam masala, and serve.
tips: Whisk the cashew paste into the yogurt before cooking; this stabilises it and helps prevent curdling.
Keep the heat low the moment the yogurt goes in and stir continuously.
The gentle sourness of curd suits jackfruit beautifully, so do not mask it with extra spice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with basanti pulao or ghee rice for an elegant vegetarian dinner.

variations.name: Classic Fruit Chaat
variations.description: A bright medley of seasonal fruits tossed with lime, black salt and roasted cumin for the perfect sweet-tangy-savoury balance. The chaat masala lifts the natural sweetness of the fruit into something far more exciting than a plain fruit bowl.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: a drizzle of honey rounds the tartness and glosses the fruit naturally in place of sugar

steps: Chop the apple, banana and papaya into bite-sized cubes and add them to a bowl with 0.75 cup grapes and 0.5 cup pomegranate.
Squeeze 2 tbsp lime juice over the fruit at once so the apple and banana do not brown.
Drizzle 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Honey over the fruit and toss gently to coat.
Sprinkle in 1.5 tsp chaat masala, 1 tsp roasted cumin, 0.5 tsp black salt and 0.25 tsp black pepper.
Fold everything together lightly so the fruit stays whole and gets evenly seasoned.
Scatter chopped mint over the top and serve chilled straight away.
tips: Add the lime as soon as the fruit is cut so the apple and banana keep their fresh colour.
Toss just before serving so the fruit stays firm and does not release too much juice.
Adjust the black salt and chaat masala to taste, as different fruits vary in sweetness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled in bowls with an extra pinch of chaat masala and a few pomegranate seeds on top.

variations.name: Delhi Anaar Fruit Chaat
variations.description: The Old Delhi winter chaat leans heavily on pomegranate, guava and boiled sweet potato, dressed with a sharp ginger-spiked masala and plenty of lime. It is warmer, earthier and more savoury than a simple fruit bowl, the way carts near Jama Masjid serve it in the cold months.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a little jaggery in the dressing gives the earthy Delhi masala its warm sweet edge

steps: Boil the 2 sweet potatoes until just tender, cool, peel and cut into cubes.
Chop the guava and banana into cubes and combine with the sweet potato and 1 cup pomegranate in a bowl.
Stir 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder into 3 tbsp lime juice with 1 inch grated ginger until dissolved into a tangy dressing.
Pour the dressing over the fruit and toss to coat everything evenly.
Sprinkle in 2 tsp chaat masala, 1.5 tsp roasted cumin, 0.75 tsp black salt and 0.5 tsp red chilli powder.
Fold gently, scatter coriander over the top, and serve at room temperature the way the Delhi carts do.
tips: Cook the sweet potato just until tender so it holds its shape in the chaat.
Grate the ginger fine so its heat spreads through the dressing without stringy bits.
This chaat tastes best fresh and lightly warm, so serve soon after tossing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a bowl with an extra squeeze of lime and a final dusting of roasted cumin, winter-cart style.

variations.name: Creamy Fruit Cream Chaat
variations.description: A dessert-leaning version that folds the chopped fruit into thick whipped yogurt sweetened with honey, laced with cardamom and a light dusting of chaat masala for a savoury whisper. Cool and creamy, it sits somewhere between fruit chaat and a fruit cream dessert.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: sweetens the hung curd naturally into a light cream for the fruit

steps: Whisk the 1.5 cups hung curd with 3 tbsp Anveshan Honey and 0.5 tsp cardamom powder until thick, smooth and creamy.
Chop the apple and banana into small cubes and toss them with 1 tbsp lime juice to stop browning.
Fold the apple, banana, 0.75 cup grapes and 0.5 cup pomegranate into the sweetened curd cream.
Add a light 0.5 tsp dusting of chaat masala and stir once for a gentle savoury note.
Chill the fruit cream for at least 30 minutes so it sets and the flavours meld.
Top with chopped mixed nuts and mint just before serving cold.
tips: Use thick hung curd so the cream stays firm and does not turn runny around the fruit.
Keep the chaat masala light here so it lifts the sweetness without overpowering the cream.
Add the nuts only at serving so they stay crunchy against the soft cream.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve well chilled in dessert bowls topped with extra pomegranate and slivered nuts.

variations.name: Tropical Chilli-Lime Fruit Chaat
variations.description: A vibrant tropical spin with mango, pineapple and kiwi in a fiery chilli-lime dressing that plays sweet fruit against a real kick of heat. The bold sour-spicy hit makes this the most lively, summery version, closer to a Mexican-style spiced fruit cup.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: balances the fiery lime dressing and glosses the tropical fruit naturally

steps: Cut the mango, pineapple and peeled kiwi into bite-sized chunks and combine with 0.5 cup pomegranate in a bowl.
Whisk 3 tbsp lime juice with 2 tbsp Anveshan Honey and 1 tsp red chilli powder into a bright, fiery dressing.
Pour the chilli-lime dressing over the fruit and toss so every piece is glossed and coated.
Sprinkle over 1.5 tsp chaat masala and 0.5 tsp black salt and fold gently.
Rest the chaat for 5 minutes so the fruit soaks up the sweet-hot dressing.
Scatter coriander and mint over the top and serve well chilled.
tips: Use ripe but firm fruit so the chunks hold up in the tangy dressing.
Adjust the chilli powder to your heat tolerance, as this version is meant to bite.
Chill the fruit beforehand so the finished chaat is bracingly cold and refreshing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in cups with a lime wedge and a light extra dusting of chilli powder for a spicy summer cooler.

variations.name: Classic Sugar Gaja
variations.description: Odisha's beloved tea-time sweet of crisp fried dough strips glazed in a thin sugar syrup that sets into a delicate white frosting. Lightly flaky and shatteringly crisp, each ghee-fried strip carries a hint of cardamom under its sugary shell, a market-stall favourite that keeps for days.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee rubbed into the flour as moyan gives the gaja its signature flaky, melt-in-mouth crispness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil deep-fries the strips clean and crisp without any greasy aftertaste

steps: Rub 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee into 2 cups maida with 2 tbsp semolina and 0.25 tsp salt until the mixture holds shape when pressed in your fist.
Add water little by little, about 0.5 cup, to knead a stiff, firm dough, then cover and rest it for 20 minutes.
Roll the dough into thick rounds, cut into strips about 6 cm long and 1 cm wide, and prick each lightly with a fork so they do not puff.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to a moderate 150C and fry the strips in batches for 6 to 7 minutes, turning, until pale golden and crisp all through, then drain.
Boil 1.5 cups sugar with 0.75 cup water and 0.5 tsp cardamom to a one-string consistency, about 6 minutes, then switch off.
Toss the fried strips in the warm syrup until well coated, lift them out onto a tray, and let the syrup dry into a white crust before storing.
tips: Fry on moderate, not high, heat so the strips cook through and stay crisp rather than browning too fast.
The syrup must reach a firm one-string stage or the sugar coating will stay sticky instead of setting white.
Store fully cooled and dried in an airtight jar, where gaja stays crisp for up to two weeks.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the frosted strips alongside masala chai or pack them into a festive snack box for Diwali and Raja parba.

variations.name: Jaggery Til Gaja
variations.description: A rustic winter version coated in jaggery syrup and rolled in toasted sesame, giving the crisp strips a caramel-brown glaze and a nutty crunch. The mineral warmth of jaggery and the aroma of til make this the wholesome makar sankranti gaja enjoyed across Odia villages in the cold months.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee moyan keeps the strips flaky and stops the jaggery glaze from turning them hard

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil fries the strips evenly for a clean, crisp base under the jaggery coat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery gives a deep caramel glaze and earthy sweetness that pairs perfectly with toasted sesame

steps: Rub 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee into 1.5 cups maida mixed with 0.5 cup wheat flour and 0.25 tsp salt until crumbly, then knead a stiff dough with about 0.4 cup water and rest 20 minutes.
Toast 4 tbsp sesame seeds in a dry pan for 2 minutes until golden and fragrant, then set aside.
Roll the dough thick, cut into 6 cm strips, prick with a fork, and deep-fry in 2 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil at 150C for 6 to 7 minutes until crisp and pale gold, then drain.
Melt 1.25 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 0.5 cup water and cook to a thick one-string syrup, about 7 minutes, then stir in 0.5 tsp cardamom and switch off.
Toss the fried strips in the warm jaggery syrup until evenly coated, then immediately sprinkle over the toasted sesame so it sticks.
Spread the coated strips on a greased tray in a single layer and let the jaggery glaze firm up before serving or storing.
tips: Cook the jaggery syrup only to a firm one-string stage; undercooked, the glaze stays tacky and will not set.
Add the sesame while the glaze is still warm and sticky so it adheres in an even crust.
A little wheat flour in the dough gives a sturdier strip that stands up to the heavier jaggery coat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these til-crusted strips warm during Sankranti festivities or pack them as an energy-rich winter travel snack.

variations.name: Khapli Wheat Gaja
variations.description: A nourishing whole-grain rendition made entirely with khapli atta instead of refined maida, giving the strips a nutty, wheaty bite and a rustic golden colour. Lighter on the gut and richer in fibre, these honey-glazed strips prove a traditional fried sweet can also be a mindful indulgence.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: ancient khapli wheat replaces maida for a nutty, fibre-rich strip that stays satisfyingly crisp

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: extra ghee moyan is needed as whole wheat needs more fat to fry up flaky and light

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: light wood-pressed sunflower oil fries the wheat strips crisp without overpowering their nutty flavour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: raw honey glaze adds floral sweetness and pairs naturally with the wholesome khapli wheat

steps: Rub 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp crushed fennel and 0.25 tsp salt until the flour clumps when pressed.
Knead a firm, tight dough with about 0.6 cup water, cover, and rest for 20 minutes so the wheat hydrates fully.
Roll out thick, cut into 6 cm strips, prick each with a fork, and fry in 2 cups Anveshan Sunflower Oil at 150C for 7 to 8 minutes until deep golden and crisp through, then drain.
Boil 0.5 cup sugar with 0.33 cup water to a one-string syrup, take off the heat, and stir in 0.5 cup Anveshan Honey and 0.5 tsp cardamom once slightly cooled to protect the honey.
Toss the crisp strips in the warm honey-sugar glaze until coated on all sides.
Spread them on a tray to let the glaze set into a light sheen before serving or storing airtight.
tips: Whole wheat needs more ghee moyan and a touch longer frying than maida to turn out crisp rather than hard.
Stir the honey in only after the syrup has cooled a little, as high heat destroys honey's aroma and benefits.
Roll the strips slightly thinner than the maida version so the denser wheat dough still fries crisp all through.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these nutty golden strips with a cup of turmeric latte or masala chai as a guilt-free festive treat.

variations.name: Layered Flaky Coconut Gaja
variations.description: An elaborate khaja-inspired version where the dough is layered with a ghee-rice-flour paste, rolled, and cut so each strip fries up into visible flaky sheets. Filled with a sweet coconut dusting and soaked in cardamom syrup, this festive gaja shatters into delicate leaves at every bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee whisked with rice flour makes the sata paste that creates the signature flaky layers

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil fries the layered strips slowly so every leaf crisps and separates

steps: Knead 2 cups maida with 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 0.25 tsp salt and about 0.5 cup water into a firm smooth dough, and rest it for 20 minutes.
Whisk the remaining 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee with 3 tbsp rice flour into a smooth spreadable sata paste.
Roll the dough into a large thin sheet, brush it all over with the sata paste, scatter 4 tbsp desiccated coconut, then roll it up tightly into a log and cut into 2 cm thick pinwheels.
Gently flatten each pinwheel into an oval strip keeping the spiral visible, and fry in 2 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil at a low 140C for 8 to 9 minutes until the layers open up and crisp to pale gold.
Boil 1.5 cups sugar with 0.75 cup water and 0.5 tsp cardamom to a one-string syrup, about 6 minutes.
Dip the fried layered strips in the warm syrup for a few seconds, lift out, and rest on a rack so the glaze sets while keeping the flaky layers crisp.
tips: Fry the layered strips on low heat so the sheets separate and crisp fully without browning outside.
Roll the dough log tightly and evenly so the spiral layers hold their shape when fried.
Dip in syrup only briefly; a long soak collapses the delicate flaky leaves into a soggy mass.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the flaky spirals on a festive platter dusted with extra coconut, a showpiece sweet for weddings and Odia festivals.

variations.name: Classic Papdi Gathiya
variations.description: The soft, melt-in-the-mouth Gujarati farsan that begins every Ahmedabad morning with fafda-jalebi. Unlike crisp sev, papdi gathiya is pressed into thick, flat ribbons that stay pillowy inside thanks to a warm ghee moyan and a whisper of baking soda. Ajwain and coarse pepper give it its unmistakable savoury, faintly bitter edge.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: For deep-frying; its high smoke point keeps the ribbons pale and soft rather than browning them

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The warm ghee moyan is what makes gathiya crumble softly instead of snapping like sev

ingredients.name: Ajwain seeds
ingredients.note: Coarsely crushed so its thymol aroma runs through every ribbon

steps: In a wide bowl whisk 2 cups besan with 1.5 tsp salt, 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1/4 tsp asafoetida, 1 tsp crushed ajwain, 1 tsp coarse black pepper and 1/2 tsp baking soda until evenly speckled.

Warm 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until just melted and rub it thoroughly into the flour with your fingertips for 2 minutes; a pinch squeezed in your palm should hold its shape, which tells you the moyan is right.
Add about 1/2 cup warm water a little at a time and knead 4-5 minutes into a smooth, semi-soft dough that is stickier than roti dough; rest it covered for 10 minutes.

Fit a gathiya press or a wide flat-slotted plate, load a portion of dough, and heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to a moderate 170 C, testing with a pinch of dough that should rise lazily without browning.
Press the dough directly over the oil in long flat ribbons, moving your hand in a slow arc so they do not clump, and fry each batch 2-3 minutes without letting them colour past pale gold.
Lift out the moment the sizzling quietens and the ribbons feel set but still soft, drain on a rack, and let them firm up for 10 minutes before eating.
tips: Keep the oil at a steady moderate heat; too hot and the gathiya browns and hardens, too cool and it drinks oil and turns greasy.
If the dough tears while pressing rather than flowing, sprinkle in a teaspoon of warm water and knead again to loosen it.
Stored airtight, classic gathiya stays soft for four to five days and revives with a two-minute warm in a low oven.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve heaped with fried green chillies, a mound of raw papaya sambharo and hot jalebis for the definitive Gujarati breakfast plate.

variations.name: Mari Gathiya
variations.description: The bold Saurashtra cousin, packed with freshly pounded black pepper and toasted coriander seed for a warming, peppery bite that lingers. Kathiyawadi kitchens skip the ghee moyan and rely on hot oil worked into the flour, giving a slightly crisper, more rustic ribbon. This is the gathiya chai-shops sell by weight for monsoon evenings.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Both for the hot-oil moyan and the deep-fry; its clean nutty note suits the pepper-forward flavour

ingredients.name: Freshly pounded black pepper
ingredients.note: Pounded coarse in a mortar so you get bursts of heat rather than an even dusting

ingredients.name: Toasted coriander seeds
ingredients.note: Dry-roasted then coarsely crushed to add a citrusy backbone to the pepper

steps: Dry-roast 1 tsp coriander seeds until fragrant, cool and crush coarse, then mix into 2 cups besan along with 1.5 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp asafoetida, 2 tsp pounded black pepper, 1/2 tsp white pepper and 1/2 tsp baking soda.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil until smoking, pour it carefully over the flour and stir with a spoon, then rub in once cool enough to handle so the mix turns crumbly and holds together when pressed.
Knead in roughly 1/2 cup warm water to a smooth, slightly sticky dough and rest it covered for 10 minutes while you heat the remaining oil to a moderate 170 C.
Load the gathiya press and squeeze flat ribbons straight into the oil in slow sweeping motions, keeping the batch loose so the peppery strands do not fuse together.
Fry 2-3 minutes until the bubbling slows and the ribbons are set but only lightly golden, turning once for even cooking.
Drain on a wire rack and rest 10 minutes; the pepper heat deepens as they cool and settle.
tips: Pound the pepper fresh just before mixing; pre-ground pepper loses the volatile oils that make this gathiya sing.
The hot-oil moyan can spit, so pour it away from you and stir with a long spoon before touching the dough.
For extra crunch typical of Saurashtra, fry a shade longer to a deeper gold and cool completely before storing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with kadak masala chai and a small bowl of chundo, the sweet-spicy mango pickle that offsets the pepper beautifully.

variations.name: Methi Gathiya
variations.description: A fragrant winter variation studded with fresh fenugreek leaves and a hint of green chilli, giving the soft ribbons a gentle bitterness and herby aroma. The moisture from the methi keeps the inside especially tender, while a touch of ghee moyan balances the leaf's sharpness. It is the farsan Gujarati homes make when methi floods the markets.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: For deep-frying at a steady moderate heat so the herby ribbons stay soft

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rounds off the slight bitterness of fresh fenugreek in the moyan

ingredients.name: Fresh fenugreek leaves
ingredients.note: Finely chopped and squeezed dry so they do not make the dough wet

steps: Wash, finely chop and firmly squeeze 1/2 cup fresh fenugreek leaves, then mix into 2 cups besan with 1.5 tsp salt, 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1/2 tsp crushed ajwain, 1 tbsp sesame seeds, 1 tsp green chilli paste and 1/2 tsp baking soda.
Rub 2 tbsp warm melted Anveshan Ghee through the flour for 2 minutes until crumbly, then add only about 1/3 cup warm water, since the methi releases moisture, and knead to a smooth semi-soft dough.
Rest the dough covered for 10 minutes and heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to a moderate 170 C, checking with a pinch that floats up gently.
Press the dough through a gathiya press into the oil in long flat ribbons, sweeping your hand so the herb-flecked strands stay separate.
Fry each batch 2-3 minutes until set and pale gold, keeping the heat moderate so the fenugreek does not scorch, then lift onto a rack.
Let the ribbons rest 10 minutes to firm up; the methi aroma blooms fully as they cool.
tips: Squeeze the chopped methi hard in a muslin cloth; excess leaf moisture makes the dough slack and the gathiya oily.
A pinch of jaggery in the dough can tame the bitterness further if your fenugreek is very sharp.
These are best eaten the same day, as the fresh methi shortens their shelf life to a couple of days.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a green coriander-mint chutney and masala chai, or crumble over a bowl of curd for a quick herby snack.

variations.name: Vaghareli Gathiya
variations.description: The clever Gujarati way to revive a day-old batch: soft gathiya is tossed through a bright mustard-and-curry-leaf tempering with onions, turmeric and green chilli until it half-softens into a warm, tangy snack. Sugar and lemon lift it into the classic Gujarati sweet-sour register. Served hot, it eats almost like a light poha.

ingredients.name: Prepared soft gathiya
ingredients.note: Best made from slightly stale gathiya, which soaks up the tempering without turning mushy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Its toasty depth carries the vaghar and coats the gathiya with gloss

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The signature Gujarati sweet note that balances the lemon and chilli

steps: Break 3 cups prepared soft gathiya into rough 2-inch pieces and keep ready in a bowl.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a kadhai over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1/2 tsp cumin for about 20 seconds until they pop.
Add 12 curry leaves and 2 slit green chillies, let them sizzle 10 seconds, then add 1 thinly sliced medium onion and saute 3-4 minutes until translucent and soft.
Sprinkle in 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1/4 tsp salt, lower the heat, and add 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder with a splash of water so it melts into a glossy sauce.
Fold in the broken gathiya and toss gently for a minute so the pieces soften slightly and take on the yellow tempering without breaking to crumbs.
Switch off, stir through 1 tbsp lemon juice and 2 tbsp chopped coriander, and serve immediately while warm and just-tender.
tips: Do not overcook once the gathiya goes in; a minute is enough or it turns pasty rather than pleasantly soft.
Freshly fried gathiya is too crisp to absorb the vaghar well, so this dish is the perfect use for a leftover batch.
Add a handful of pomegranate seeds or fine sev at the table for crunch and colour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a warm evening farsan with hot chai, topped with extra coriander and a few pomegranate arils for contrast.

variations.name: Classic Ghanta Tarkari
variations.description: Ghanta tarkari is Odisha's grand festival curry, a generous jumble of many vegetables cooked with soaked black chana and finished with roasted coconut and a panch phutana tempering. Made for Kumar Purnima and other feasts, it is thick, mildly sweet and fragrant, meant to use up the season's produce in one glorious pot.

ingredients.name: Black Chana
ingredients.note: soaked overnight and boiled

ingredients.name: Pumpkin
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Raw Banana
ingredients.note: chunked

ingredients.name: Sweet Potato
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Yam (Suran)
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Broad Beans (Sem)
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Grated Coconut
ingredients.note: roasted for the paste

ingredients.name: Cumin Seeds
ingredients.note: for the roasted paste

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: for the paste

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: for the panch phutana tempering that crowns this festive curry

steps: Boil the soaked black chana with 2 cups water until just tender, about 15 minutes, and keep the cooking water.
Add the pumpkin, raw banana, sweet potato, yam and broad beans to the chana with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, then simmer on medium heat for 15 minutes until all the vegetables are soft.
Roast 4 tbsp grated coconut in a dry pan until golden and grind it with 1 tsp roasted cumin and 1 inch ginger into a coarse paste.
Stir the coconut paste into the pot and simmer 5 minutes so the gravy thickens and turns fragrant, mashing a few pieces for body.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, splutter 1 tsp panch phutana with 1 bay leaf and 2 dry red chillies until aromatic.
Pour the tempering over the ghanta tarkari, stir once, and rest it covered for 5 minutes before serving hot.
tips: Use a wide variety of seasonal vegetables in small amounts, as the medley is the whole point of ghanta.
Roast the coconut until deep golden for the nutty depth that separates ghanta from an everyday mixed curry.
Soak and boil the black chana well ahead so it is tender before the vegetables go in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a festive centrepiece with rice, khechudi or puri, garnished with a little extra roasted coconut.

variations.name: Temple Ghanta Tarkari
variations.description: The sattvic Kumar Purnima version cooked without onion or garlic, offered first to the deities before the family eats. Ginger, roasted cumin and pure ghee do all the work, giving a pristine, aromatic curry that tastes of ritual and celebration.

ingredients.name: Black Chana
ingredients.note: soaked and boiled

ingredients.name: Potato
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Pumpkin
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Colocasia (Arbi)
ingredients.note: halved

ingredients.name: Papaya (Raw)
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Grated Coconut
ingredients.note: for the paste

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: for the paste

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the pure fat that makes this offering rich and aromatic

steps: Boil the soaked black chana until tender, then add the potato, pumpkin, colocasia, raw papaya and green peas with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 3 slit green chillies and 1 tsp salt.
Simmer with 2 cups water on medium heat for 15 minutes until every vegetable is soft.
Grind 5 tbsp grated coconut with 1 tsp cumin and 1.5 inch ginger into a smooth paste.
Stir the paste into the pot and cook 5 minutes so the gravy thickens and smells of coconut and ginger.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, splutter 1 tsp panch phutana with 1 bay leaf until it crackles.
Pour the ghee tempering over the temple ghanta, cover, and rest 5 minutes so it settles before offering and serving.
tips: Keep it strictly free of onion and garlic to stay true to the sattvic festival tradition.
Extra ginger takes the place of garlic here, so use a generous piece for warmth and aroma.
Cook the vegetables until quite soft, as a slightly mashed, thick ghanta is the desired festive texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Offer first as bhog, then serve with ghee rice or puri and a sweet like kheer for a complete Kumar Purnima meal.

variations.name: Mixed Sprouts Ghanta
variations.description: A wholesome everyday take that swaps the single black chana for a handful of mixed sprouted beans, boosting protein and giving a lively, nutty texture. Lighter and quicker than the festival pot, it keeps the roasted coconut and five-seed tempering intact.

ingredients.name: Mixed Bean Sprouts
ingredients.note: moong, moth and chana

ingredients.name: Potato
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Carrot
ingredients.note: diced

ingredients.name: French Beans
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Pumpkin
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Grated Coconut
ingredients.note: roasted for the paste

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil for a lighter everyday tempering

steps: Boil 1 cup mixed bean sprouts with 1.5 cups water for 8 minutes until just tender but still holding shape.
Add the cubed potato, diced carrot, chopped french beans and pumpkin with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, then simmer 10 minutes until soft.
Roast 3 tbsp grated coconut until golden and grind with 1 tsp cumin and 1 inch ginger into a coarse paste.
Stir the paste into the vegetables and cook 4 minutes so the gravy thickens lightly around the sprouts.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp panch phutana with 2 dry red chillies until fragrant.
Pour the tempering over the sprouts ghanta, stir once, and serve warm.
tips: Do not overcook the sprouts, or they turn mushy; a slight bite keeps this version lively.
Any mix of sprouted beans works, so use whatever you have to boost the protein.
Keep the gravy lighter than the festival version for an easy, wholesome weekday meal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with rice or rotis as a protein-packed everyday main, with a squeeze of lime on top.

variations.name: Dry Ghanta Bhaja
variations.description: A near-dry, stir-fried avatar where the mixed vegetables and boiled chana are tossed in a heavy roasted-coconut and mustard-oil coating until they caramelise at the edges. Robust and toasty, it is served as a hearty side rather than a gravy dish.

ingredients.name: Black Chana
ingredients.note: soaked and boiled

ingredients.name: Potato
ingredients.note: cubed small

ingredients.name: Yam (Suran)
ingredients.note: cubed small

ingredients.name: Cauliflower
ingredients.note: small florets

ingredients.name: Green Beans
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Grated Coconut
ingredients.note: roasted

ingredients.name: Cumin Powder
ingredients.note: roasted

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: crushed

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil for the toasty, robust stir-fry

steps: Parboil the cubed potato, yam, cauliflower florets and chopped beans with a little salt for 6 minutes, then drain well.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the heat, and splutter 1 tsp panch phutana with 3 dry red chillies.
Add 5 crushed garlic cloves and the boiled black chana and fry for 2 minutes until the garlic is golden.
Add the drained vegetables with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt and stir-fry on medium-high heat for 8 minutes until they brown at the edges.
Sprinkle in 5 tbsp roasted grated coconut and 1 tsp roasted cumin powder and toss for 3 minutes until everything is dry and toasty.
Serve the dry ghanta bhaja hot as a robust, caramelised side.
tips: Parboil and drain the vegetables thoroughly so they fry and brown rather than steam in the pan.
Keep the heat high while tossing so the edges caramelise for that signature toasty flavour.
Add the roasted coconut only near the end so it coats the vegetables without burning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot as a dry side with dal and rice, or pack it into a lunchbox with rotis.

variations.name: Classic Ghugni
variations.description: This eastern-Indian ghugni simmers dried white peas in a light onion-ginger masala until soft and stew-like, finished with roasted cumin and lemon. Warming, mildly spiced and comforting, it is the everyday breakfast and tea-time curry of Bengal, Bihar and Odisha.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: pungent wood-pressed mustard oil gives the ghugni its authentic eastern base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoon of ghee stirred in at the end rounds the curry with richness

steps: Soak 1.5 cups white peas overnight, then pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 4 to 5 whistles until soft but still holding shape.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the flame, and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1 bay leaf until fragrant.
Add the 2 finely chopped onions and saute over medium heat for 7 minutes until golden, then add the grated ginger and chopped tomato and cook 4 minutes to a soft masala.
Stir in 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder with a splash of water and fry for a minute until the oil separates.
Tip in the cooked peas with their liquid, mash a few against the pan to thicken, and simmer for 12 to 15 minutes until stew-like and seasoned with the remaining salt.
Finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder and 1 tbsp lemon juice, stirring gently.
Garnish with fresh coriander and serve hot.
tips: Soak the peas fully overnight so they cook evenly to a soft, creamy stew.
Mash a spoonful of the cooked peas into the gravy to thicken it naturally without flour.
Add the roasted cumin and lemon right at the end so their aroma stays bright.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot in a bowl topped with chopped raw onion, green chilli and a wedge of lemon, with puri or bread on the side.

variations.name: Ghugni Chaat
variations.description: The Kolkata street version turns ghugni into a tangy chaat, ladled hot and showered with raw onion, tamarind water, bhujia and a heavy dusting of roasted spices. Sold from kerosene stoves on every corner, it is punchier and more sour than the homely curry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil gives the street ghugni its sharp, savoury base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the tamarind water for the signature sweet-sour chaat drizzle

steps: Soak 1.5 cups white peas overnight and pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 5 whistles until soft.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin, then add one chopped onion and the grated ginger and fry 6 minutes until golden.
Add the cooked peas with their water and the remaining salt and simmer 10 minutes, mashing a few peas so it thickens into a loose stew.
Soak 2 tbsp tamarind in warm water, strain, and mix the pulp with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder into a sweet-sour tamarind water.
Ladle the hot ghugni into bowls and top each with the remaining raw chopped onion and slit green chillies.
Drizzle over the tamarind water, then dust generously with 1.5 tsp roasted cumin powder and 1.5 tsp chaat masala.
Finish with a squeeze of lemon, a handful of bhujia sev and plenty of coriander, and serve at once.
tips: Keep the ghugni a little loose, as the chaat is meant to be spoonable and saucy under the toppings.
Add the bhujia only just before eating so it stays crisp against the wet ghugni.
Balance the tamarind water to taste, keeping it distinctly sweet-sour for the street effect.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in paper bowls with extra bhujia and a lemon wedge, the way Kolkata carts hand it over.

variations.name: Darbhanga Aloo Ghugni
variations.description: The Bihari style thickens the white-pea ghugni with soft potato cubes and a robust garlic-heavy masala for a heartier, drier curry. Spiced with garam masala and finished with mustard oil, it is filling enough to eat with roti as a full meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: generous mustard oil carries the bold garlic masala of the Bihari ghugni

steps: Soak 1.5 cups white peas overnight and pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp salt and 2.5 cups water for 4 whistles until soft.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin, then add the cubed 2 potatoes and fry 5 minutes until their edges turn golden.
Push the potatoes aside, add the 2 chopped onions with the crushed garlic and grated ginger and fry 7 minutes until deep golden.
Add the 2 chopped tomatoes, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder and cook 5 minutes into a thick masala.
Tip in the cooked peas with just enough of their liquid to keep it semi-dry, and simmer 12 minutes until the potatoes are tender and the gravy clings.
Season with the remaining salt and 0.75 tsp garam masala and cook two more minutes.
Garnish with coriander and serve hot with roti.
tips: Fry the potato cubes first so they hold their shape and do not disintegrate into the gravy.
