Use plenty of garlic, as the pungent garlic-mustard base is what marks the Bihari style.
Keep the curry semi-dry so it scoops up neatly with roti rather than running like a soup.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulka roti or paratha and a side of raw onion and green chilli.

variations.name: Odia Nariyal Ghugni
variations.description: The Odia rendition rounds the white-pea curry with ground coconut and a warming panchphoran temper for a subtly sweet, aromatic gravy. Milder and nuttier than the Bengali or Bihari versions, it is a beloved festival and breakfast ghugni of coastal Odisha.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed coconut oil deepens the coastal Odia flavour of the curry

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of ghee enriches the mild coconut gravy

steps: Soak 1.5 cups white peas overnight and pressure-cook with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp salt and 3 cups water for 4 to 5 whistles until soft.
Grind the 0.5 cup fresh coconut with the grated ginger and a little water into a smooth paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, add 1 tsp panchphoran and 1 bay leaf and let them splutter over medium heat.
Add the 2 chopped onions and fry 7 minutes until golden, then add the chopped tomato and cook 3 minutes to soften.
Stir in the coconut-ginger paste with 1.5 tsp coriander powder and fry for 4 minutes until the raw smell goes and the oil edges out.
Add the cooked peas with their liquid and the remaining salt and simmer 12 minutes into a mildly sweet, thick gravy.
Finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 0.5 tsp garam masala, garnish with coriander and serve hot.
tips: Grind the coconut smooth so the gravy turns silky rather than grainy.
Toast the panchphoran gently, as scorched fenugreek in it will turn the curry bitter.
Balance the natural sweetness of coconut with the tomato so the gravy stays rounded, not cloying.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft luchi or steamed rice, garnished with extra grated coconut on top.

variations.name: Classic Kachori Chaat
variations.description: Crisp fried moong dal kachoris are crushed open and heaped with cool yogurt, sweet-sour tamarind chutney, spicy green chutney and a shower of sev. The flaky spiced-lentil shell soaks up just enough of the toppings to soften at the edges while staying crunchy inside.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: stone-milled khapli atta makes a flaky, wholesome kachori shell in place of refined maida

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: deep-frying in wood-pressed groundnut oil crisps the kachoris evenly and keeps them light

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the tamarind chutney with a deep natural note

steps: Rub 3 tbsp of the groundnut oil into 1.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, then knead with about 0.5 cup water into a firm dough and rest 20 minutes.
Coarsely grind 0.5 cup soaked moong dal and saute it in 1 tbsp oil over medium heat with 1 tsp fennel powder, 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and 0.25 tsp salt for 4 minutes until dry and fragrant.
Stuff spoonfuls of the cooled dal filling into small dough discs, seal, and gently flatten each into a 3 inch kachori.
Deep-fry in 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil at 150 C over low-medium heat for 8 to 10 minutes, turning, until puffed, pale gold and crisp, then drain.
Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder for 5 minutes into a thick chutney, and whisk the 2 cups yogurt smooth with 0.25 tsp salt.
Crush two kachoris onto each plate, breaking the shells open, and spoon over the whisked yogurt.
Drizzle with tamarind and 4 tbsp green chutney, dust with 1.5 tsp chaat masala, 1 tsp roasted cumin and 0.25 tsp red chilli powder, top with sev and coriander, and serve at once.
tips: Fry the kachoris low and slow so the shells cook through flaky and crisp rather than browning raw.
Cool the dal filling completely before stuffing so the kachoris seal without splitting.
Crush and top the kachoris only when serving so they keep their crunch under the yogurt.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a plate with an extra spoon of both chutneys and a lime wedge so each mouthful stays lively.

variations.name: Banarasi Matar Kachori Chaat
variations.description: The Varanasi winter classic uses a spiced fresh green pea filling instead of dal, and the crushed kachoris are topped with a warm potato-tomato subzi rather than yogurt. Bright, tangy and served hot, it is the beloved kachori-sabzi eaten at Banaras street stalls at dawn.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli atta gives the pea kachori a nutty, flaky shell true to a wholesome Banarasi kitchen

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: frying and cooking in pungent wood-pressed mustard oil gives the authentic eastern UP flavour

steps: Rub 3 tbsp mustard oil into 1.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, knead with about 0.5 cup water into a firm dough, and rest 20 minutes.
Coarsely mash 1.5 cups green peas and saute in 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil over medium heat with 1 inch grated ginger, 2 chopped chillies and 0.25 tsp salt for 5 minutes until dry, then cool.
Stuff the pea filling into dough discs, seal and flatten into 3 inch kachoris, then deep-fry in the remaining Anveshan Mustard Oil at 150 C for 8 to 10 minutes until crisp and pale gold.

For the subzi, heat 2 tbsp mustard oil to smoking, cool slightly, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, add the mashed boiled potatoes, chopped tomatoes, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp coriander powder and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder.
Add 2 cups water and simmer the subzi for 12 minutes with 0.75 tsp salt and 0.5 tsp garam masala until thick and tangy.
Crush two kachoris into each bowl, ladle the hot potato-tomato subzi over them, scatter coriander, and serve steaming.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to smoking and cool it slightly before use to mellow its raw pungency.
Keep the pea filling on the drier side so the kachoris seal and fry without bursting.
Serve the moment the subzi is ladled over so the shells soak just a little while staying crisp.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot in a bowl with a wedge of lime and a slit green chilli on the side, Banaras breakfast style.

variations.name: Dahi Kachori Chaat
variations.description: A cooling, yogurt-heavy version where whole crisp kachoris are set on a bed of thick sweetened curd and drowned in tamarind chutney, pomegranate and sev. The emphasis shifts to the creamy tang of the curd against the flaky shell, making it a softer, more indulgent chaat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli atta gives a sturdy flaky shell that holds up under the generous curd

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil fries the kachoris light so they do not turn greasy under the yogurt

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens both the whisked curd and the tamarind chutney

steps: Rub 3 tbsp oil into 1.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, knead with about 0.5 cup water into a firm dough, and rest 20 minutes.
Grind 0.5 cup soaked moong dal coarsely and saute in 1 tbsp oil with 1 tsp fennel powder and 0.25 tsp salt for 4 minutes until dry, then cool.
Stuff the filling into dough discs, seal, flatten into small kachoris, and deep-fry in 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil at 150 C for 8 to 10 minutes until crisp, then cool.
Whisk the 3 cups yogurt smooth with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.25 tsp salt, and simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder into a chutney.
Spread a thick layer of the sweetened curd on each plate and set two whole kachoris on top, cracking their tops open.
Pour more curd into and over the kachoris, drizzle with tamarind chutney, and dust with 1.5 tsp roasted cumin and 0.75 tsp black salt.
Shower with pomegranate, sev and coriander, and serve chilled while the shells are still crisp.
tips: Chill the sweetened curd so it stays thick and drapes the kachoris rather than running off the plate.
Keep the kachoris whole here and let only their cracked tops soak so you get both crunch and softness.
Add sev and pomegranate at the very end so they stay crisp and jewel-bright.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve cold as an indulgent chaat, finished with an extra swirl of curd and a scatter of pomegranate.

variations.name: Baked Kachori Chaat
variations.description: A lighter everyday version where the dal-stuffed kachoris are brushed with oil and baked crisp rather than deep-fried, then crushed under quick chutneys and yogurt. It keeps the flaky, spiced character with a fraction of the oil, ideal for a wholesome tea-time chaat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli atta bakes into a firm, nutty flaky shell without needing deep frying

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: rubbing and brushing with wood-pressed sunflower oil crisps the baked kachoris golden with little fat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: sweetens the tamarind chutney naturally for the lighter baked chaat

steps: Rub 3 tbsp Anveshan Sunflower Oil into 1.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt, knead with about 0.5 cup water into a firm dough, and rest 20 minutes.
Coarsely grind 0.5 cup soaked moong dal and saute in 1 tbsp sunflower oil with 1 tsp fennel powder and 0.25 tsp salt for 4 minutes until dry, then cool.
Stuff the filling into dough discs, seal and flatten into small kachoris, then brush all over with the remaining Anveshan Sunflower Oil.
Bake at 190 C for 25 to 28 minutes, turning once, until the kachoris are firm, golden and crisp, then cool.
Simmer 2 tbsp tamarind with 2 tbsp Anveshan Honey for 4 minutes into a chutney, and whisk the 2 cups yogurt smooth with 0.25 tsp salt.
Crush two baked kachoris onto each plate, spoon over the yogurt, and drizzle with tamarind and 4 tbsp green chutney.
Dust with 1.5 tsp chaat masala and 1 tsp roasted cumin, top with sev and coriander, and serve straight away.
tips: Bake until deep golden and firm so the shells stay crisp when the toppings go on.
Cool the baked kachoris fully, as they crisp up further as they sit.
Baked shells soften faster than fried, so crush and dress them only at serving time.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a lighter tea-time chaat with the chutneys on the side so guests dress their own.

variations.name: Classic Temple Kadamba Sadam
variations.description: A hearty South Indian one-pot rice cooked with toor dal, seasonal vegetables and tamarind, seasoned with a homemade roasted kadamba spice powder. Served as temple prasadam in Tamil Nadu, it is tangy, mildly spiced and comforting, with a ghee tempering that perfumes every grain.

ingredients.name: Raw rice
ingredients.note: sona masoori, washed

ingredients.name: Toor dal
ingredients.note: cooked soft with the rice

ingredients.name: Mixed vegetables (carrot, beans, pumpkin, brinjal)
ingredients.note: diced

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked for pulp

ingredients.name: Coriander seeds
ingredients.note: for the kadamba powder

ingredients.name: Chana dal
ingredients.note: for the roast-and-grind powder

ingredients.name: Grated coconut
ingredients.note: roasted, for the powder

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the temple-style finishing fat that perfumes the mixed rice

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rice with 1/3 cup toor dal, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 3.5 cups water for 4 whistles until soft and mushy, then mash lightly and set aside.
Dry-roast 1.5 tbsp coriander seeds, 1 tbsp chana dal, 4 dry red chillies and 2 tbsp coconut on low heat for 3-4 minutes until golden, cool and grind to a coarse kadamba powder.
Boil the 2 cups diced vegetables with 1 cup water and 1/2 tsp salt for 8 minutes until tender.
Squeeze the tamarind into 1/2 cup water and add it to the vegetables with the ground kadamba powder and 3/4 tsp salt, then simmer for 5 minutes until the raw tamarind smell fades.
Fold the mashed rice-dal into the vegetables, adding a little hot water to loosen it to a soft, scoopable consistency, and simmer for 3 minutes so the flavours marry.
In a small pan heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds with 1/4 tsp asafoetida and 2 sprigs curry leaves, and pour this sizzling tempering over the rice before serving.
tips: Cook the rice and dal a touch mushier than usual so the finished kadamba sadam stays soft and cohesive.
Grind the spice powder fresh for each batch; it is the soul of the dish and fades quickly once stored.
Keep the rice a little loose as it firms up considerably on standing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a crisp appalam, potato roast and a spoon of thick curd on the side.

variations.name: Karnataka Huli Kadamba Sadam
variations.description: The Karnataka rendition closer to a spiced sambar-rice, where the rice and dal simmer with vegetables in a coconut-rich sambar masala and a dash of jaggery. Thicker and warmer-spiced than the Tamil temple version, it carries the sweet-sour balance beloved in Bangalore homes.

ingredients.name: Raw rice
ingredients.note: washed

ingredients.name: Toor dal
ingredients.note: cooked soft

ingredients.name: Mixed vegetables (beans, carrot, capsicum, potato)
ingredients.note: diced

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked for pulp

ingredients.name: Sambar powder
ingredients.note: Karnataka style

ingredients.name: Grated coconut
ingredients.note: ground into the masala

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the signature Karnataka sweetness that balances the tamarind

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the coastal Karnataka fat for the tempering

ingredients.name: Cashew nuts
ingredients.note: for the tempering

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rice and 1/2 cup toor dal together with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 4 cups water for 4-5 whistles until very soft, then mash lightly.
Grind 1/4 cup grated coconut with 2 tbsp sambar powder and a little water into a smooth masala paste.
Boil the 2 cups diced vegetables in 1.5 cups water with 1/2 tsp salt for 8 minutes until tender.
Add the squeezed tamarind pulp, the coconut-sambar paste, 2 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 3/4 tsp salt, and simmer for 6 minutes until thick and glossy.
Stir in the mashed rice-dal with a cup of hot water and simmer for 4 minutes to a thick, sambar-rice consistency, mixing well.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil, fry 10 cashews until golden, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds with 1/4 tsp asafoetida and 2 sprigs curry leaves, and pour over the rice.
tips: The jaggery is what defines the Karnataka sweet-sour profile, so add it before tasting for salt and tang.
Keep this version thicker and softer than Tamil kadamba, closer to a comforting sambar-rice.
Fry the cashews first in the coconut oil, then temper the seeds in the same fat for a richer garnish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a fried papad, boondi raita and a wedge of lime for a Bangalore-style comfort meal.

variations.name: Coconut-Milk Kadamba Sadam
variations.description: A fragrant, milder mixed rice where the grains and vegetables cook in coconut milk with whole garam spices rather than tamarind, giving a gently sweet, aromatic pilaf-like dish. Free of any sourness, it is the festive, soothing take that pairs beautifully with a tangy pickle.

ingredients.name: Raw rice
ingredients.note: washed and drained

ingredients.name: Moong dal
ingredients.note: lightly roasted

ingredients.name: Mixed vegetables (carrot, beans, peas, potato)
ingredients.note: diced small

ingredients.name: Thin coconut milk
ingredients.note: for cooking the rice

ingredients.name: Thick coconut milk
ingredients.note: added at the end

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: julienned

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the whole spices and gives the fragrant rice its festive richness

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot over medium heat and fry 10 cashews until golden, then remove and set aside for garnish.
In the same ghee, sizzle the 1 inch cinnamon, 3 cloves, 3 cardamoms and 1 bay leaf for 30 seconds, then add the slit green chillies and julienned ginger and fry for 1 minute.
Add the 1.5 cups diced vegetables and the roasted 1/4 cup moong dal and saute for 2 minutes to coat them in the spiced ghee.
Add the washed 1 cup rice with 2 cups thin coconut milk and 1.25 tsp salt, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on low for 12-14 minutes until the rice is fluffy and the liquid is absorbed.
Pour in 1/2 cup thick coconut milk off the direct heat, fold gently so the grains stay separate, and warm through for 2 minutes without boiling hard.
Rest covered for 5 minutes, then fluff, scatter the fried cashews on top and serve fragrant and warm.
tips: Add the thick coconut milk only at the end and off high heat so it does not split.
Use lightly roasted moong dal rather than toor here, as it stays intact and nutty in the fragrant rice.
A tangy lime or mango pickle is the perfect foil for this sweet, sour-free version.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a sharp mango pickle, papad and a cooling cucumber raita for a festive plate.

variations.name: Iyengar Ghee Kadamba Sadam
variations.description: The Iyengar wedding-kitchen mixed rice, generous with ghee and a distinctive spice grind of roasted lentils, peppercorns and dry ginger, studded with drumstick and avarakkai. Richer and more peppery than the everyday version, it is the ceremonial rice ladled onto banana leaves at festivals.

ingredients.name: Raw rice
ingredients.note: washed

ingredients.name: Toor dal
ingredients.note: cooked soft

ingredients.name: Vegetables (drumstick, avarakkai, chow-chow, carrot)
ingredients.note: cut into fingers

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked for pulp

ingredients.name: Coriander seeds
ingredients.note: for the peppery powder

ingredients.name: Black peppercorns
ingredients.note: for the distinctive heat

ingredients.name: Urad dal
ingredients.note: for the roast-and-grind powder

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: used generously as befits an Iyengar festive rice, both in the grind and the tempering

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup rice and 1/2 cup toor dal with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 4 cups water for 4-5 whistles until soft, then mash lightly.
In 1 tsp ghee, roast 1 tbsp coriander seeds, 1 tsp peppercorns, 1 tbsp urad dal, 3 dry red chillies and 1/4 tsp asafoetida on low heat for 3 minutes until golden, then grind to a coarse powder.
Boil the 2 cups cut vegetables in 1.5 cups water with 1/2 tsp salt for 10 minutes until the drumstick is tender.
Squeeze in the tamarind pulp, add the freshly ground peppery powder and 3/4 tsp salt, and simmer for 6 minutes until aromatic and slightly thick.
Fold the mashed rice-dal into the vegetables with 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and a cup of hot water, mixing until soft and glistening, and simmer for 3 minutes.
Heat the remaining ghee, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds with 1/4 tsp asafoetida and 2 sprigs curry leaves, and pour this over the rice before serving on a banana leaf.
tips: The peppercorns give this version its signature warmth, so grind them coarse for little bursts of heat.
Be generous with ghee here, as its richness is what marks the festive Iyengar style.
Drumstick and flat beans are traditional; scoop the soft drumstick pulp as you eat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a banana leaf with vadai, thick curd and a spicy appalam for a festival lunch.

variations.name: Classic Kanika
variations.description: Kanika is Odisha's fragrant sweet ghee rice, gently sweetened with jaggery and perfumed with whole spices, cardamom and ghee-fried cashews and raisins. Milder than a dessert yet richer than a pulao, it is the mildly sweet rice offered as Jagannath bhog and served at every celebratory Odia meal.

ingredients.name: Basmati Rice
ingredients.note: soaked 20 minutes and drained

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the fat that toasts the rice and spices for kanika's signature aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: the gentle sweetener that colours the rice a warm amber and rounds its flavour

steps: Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan and fry 12 cashews to golden and 2 tbsp raisins until they plump, then scoop them out and set aside.
In the same ghee splutter 4 cardamom pods, 3 cloves, 1 inch cinnamon and 1 bay leaf until fragrant, about 30 seconds.
Add the drained basmati rice and toast it gently for 2-3 minutes until each grain is coated and glossy.
Pour in 2.5 cups water with 0.25 tsp salt, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on low heat for 12 minutes until the rice is just done and the water absorbed.
Melt 0.5 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water into a syrup, then fold it gently through the hot rice so the grains turn amber without breaking.
Cover and rest 5 minutes on the lowest heat, scatter the fried cashews and raisins over the top, and serve the kanika warm.
tips: Fold the jaggery syrup in gently at the end so the rice takes on colour and sweetness without turning sticky.
Toasting the drained rice in ghee before adding water keeps the grains separate and fluffy.
Add the jaggery only after the rice is cooked, since jaggery added early can stop the rice from softening.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a festive rice alongside dalma and a tangy vegetable curry, or on its own as a light sweet.

variations.name: Saffron Kanika
variations.description: A regal version scented and tinted with saffron steeped in warm milk, giving the sweet rice a golden hue and a floral depth. Extra dry fruits and a hint of nutmeg make this the celebratory kanika reserved for weddings and grand feasts.

ingredients.name: Basmati Rice
ingredients.note: soaked and drained

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: toasts the rice and fries the nuts for a rich, aromatic base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm milk to lend a golden hue and floral aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the rice while letting the saffron colour shine through

ingredients.name: Warm Milk
ingredients.note: to soak the saffron

ingredients.name: Almonds
ingredients.note: slivered

steps: Soak a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk and set aside to bloom into a golden liquid.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and fry 10 cashews, 10 slivered almonds and 2 tbsp raisins until golden, then remove and reserve.
In the same ghee splutter 4 cardamom pods and 3 cloves, add the drained rice, and toast for 2-3 minutes until glossy.
Pour in 2.5 cups water with 0.25 tsp salt, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on low heat for 12 minutes until the rice is tender.
Melt 0.5 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water, fold it through the rice with the saffron milk and a pinch of nutmeg until evenly golden.
Rest covered for 5 minutes, top with the fried nuts and raisins, and serve the saffron kanika warm.
tips: Bloom the saffron in warm milk for at least 10 minutes to draw out its full colour and aroma.
Add the saffron milk with the jaggery so the golden colour spreads evenly through the rice.
Use only a pinch of nutmeg, as its warmth should whisper behind the saffron, not dominate.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm at a celebration alongside rich curries, garnished with a few extra saffron strands and slivered almonds.

variations.name: Coconut Milk Kanika
variations.description: A coastal twist where the rice is simmered in coconut milk instead of water, lending a creamy richness and tropical fragrance. Coconut oil-fried cashews and a scatter of toasted coconut deepen the flavour of this softer, more luscious kanika.

ingredients.name: Basmati Rice
ingredients.note: soaked and drained

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: fries the nuts and lends a fragrant coastal aroma to the rice

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the coconut-rich rice with a warm caramel note

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and fry 12 cashews to golden and 2 tbsp raisins until plump, then remove and set aside.
In the same oil splutter 4 cardamom pods, 2 cloves and 1 bay leaf, add the drained rice, and toast for 2-3 minutes.
Pour in 1.5 cups water with 0.25 tsp salt, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on low heat for 10 minutes until nearly done.
Add 1 cup coconut milk off high heat, stirring gently so it does not split, and cook covered another 4 minutes until the rice is soft and creamy.
Melt 0.5 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water and fold it through the rice until evenly amber.
Rest 5 minutes, scatter the fried cashews, raisins and 3 tbsp toasted coconut flakes on top, and serve the coconut kanika warm.
tips: Add the coconut milk towards the end and keep the heat low so it stays smooth and does not curdle.
Use thick coconut milk for the creamiest result, thinning with a splash of water if it seems too rich.
Toast the coconut flakes separately until just golden for a fragrant, crunchy finish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm topped with extra toasted coconut, lovely after a coastal-style vegetable curry.

variations.name: Temple Abhada Kanika
variations.description: The revered kanika cooked as mahaprasad in the Jagannath temple kitchen, made with fragrant short-grain gobindobhog rice, pure ghee and a whisper of edible camphor. Cooked without any onion or garlic, it is barely sweet, deeply aromatic and steeped in devotion.

ingredients.name: Gobindobhog Rice
ingredients.note: short-grain aromatic rice, soaked and drained

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the pure fat central to this temple-style offering

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: lightly sweetens the sacred rice without overpowering the aroma

steps: Heat 5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and gently fry 12 cashews to golden and 2 tbsp raisins until plump, then remove and reserve.
In the ghee splutter 5 cardamom pods, 3 cloves, 1 inch cinnamon and 2 bay leaves until aromatic.
Add the drained gobindobhog rice and toast it very gently for 2 minutes, taking care not to break the delicate grains.
Pour in 2.5 cups water with 0.25 tsp salt, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on low heat for 10-12 minutes until soft and fragrant.
Melt 0.4 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water and fold it through the rice with a tiny pinch of edible camphor.
Rest covered for 5 minutes, top with the fried cashews and raisins, and serve the abhada kanika warm as bhog.
tips: Gobindobhog rice is delicate, so toast and stir it gently to keep the short grains intact.
Use only a whisper of edible camphor, as its temple aroma is powerful and easily overdone.
Keep this kanika only lightly sweet, in keeping with the restrained, sattvic temple style.
variations.servingSuggestion: Offer as bhog, then serve warm on a banana leaf with dalma and saga bhaja for an authentic mahaprasad thali.

variations.name: Classic Nylon Khaman
variations.description: The bright yellow, ultra-soft steamed cake that Gujaratis eat for breakfast, tea and everything between. A quick gram-flour batter raised with Eno steams into a jiggly, porous sponge, then a warm sugar-water tempering soaks it sweet, sour and spongy. Nylon khaman is prized for being so light it almost dissolves.

ingredients.name: Fine semolina
ingredients.note: A touch of rava gives the sponge a cleaner cut

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A little in the batter and the rest for the mustard-chilli tempering

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: Unrefined sugar dissolved in the tempering water for the classic sweet-sour soak

ingredients.name: Citric acid
ingredients.note: Gives the batter its signature tang and helps it rise white and porous

steps: Whisk 2 cups besan, 1 tbsp semolina, 1 tbsp green chilli-ginger paste, 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp citric acid, 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and about 1.25 cups water into a smooth, lump-free batter of thick pouring consistency; rest 10 minutes.
Bring the steamer water to a rolling boil and grease a wide tin so the khaman comes out easily.
Sprinkle 1.5 tsp Eno over the batter and fold gently in one direction for a few seconds as it froths and nearly doubles; do not overmix.
Pour immediately into the tin, level the top, and steam on high heat for 15 minutes until the sponge is set and a skewer comes out clean.
Cool 10 minutes, cut into squares, and heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil to crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds, 4 slit green chillies and 10 curry leaves.
Add 1 cup water and 3 tbsp Anveshan Khandsari to the temper, boil 2-3 minutes until the sugar dissolves, and pour it all over the khaman so it soaks up and turns spongy.
tips: The batter must be lump-free and freshly beaten; resting too long before Eno makes a flat, dense khaman.
Pour the sugar-water tempering while warm and let the khaman sit 15 minutes so it drinks every drop and stays moist.
If your khaman feels rubbery, you overmixed after adding Eno; fold just until combined next time.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the fluffy squares showered with fresh coriander and grated coconut, alongside fried green chillies and green chutney.

variations.name: Amiri Khaman
variations.description: The much-loved Surti street snack, also called sev khamani, where soft khaman is crumbled and tossed through a garlicky mustard tempering, then buried under sev, pomegranate and coconut. Sweet, tangy, garlicky and crunchy all at once, it turns a plain steamed cake into a festival of textures. Vendors sell it by the plateful for breakfast in Surat.

ingredients.name: Prepared khaman
ingredients.note: Coarsely crumbled by hand; day-old khaman crumbles best

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Carries the garlic tempering and gives the crumble a glossy, toasty coat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The sweet note that defines the sweet-garlicky Surti flavour

ingredients.name: Garlic cloves
ingredients.note: Crushed coarse for the signature garlicky tadka

steps: Crumble 4 cups prepared khaman coarsely by hand into a bowl so it stays fluffy with a few small lumps.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tbsp sesame seeds, then add 6 crushed garlic cloves, 3 slit green chillies and 10 curry leaves and fry until the garlic is pale gold and fragrant, about a minute.
Stir 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder into the hot tempering with 2 tbsp water so it melts into a glossy sauce.
Pour the tempering over the crumbled khaman and fold gently until every crumb is coated, then squeeze in 1 tbsp lemon juice.
Transfer to a serving plate and top generously with 1 cup nylon sev, 1/4 cup pomegranate seeds, 3 tbsp grated coconut and 3 tbsp coriander.
Serve at once while the sev is crisp and the khaman still warm from the tempering.
tips: Use day-old or slightly firm khaman; very fresh, wet khaman turns pasty when tossed with the tempering.
Add the sev only at the moment of serving so it stays crunchy against the soft crumble.
Balance to taste at the end; a little more jaggery or lemon adjusts the sweet-sour to your liking.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve Surti-style in a bowl with an extra wedge of lemon and hot masala chai for a classic Gujarati breakfast.

variations.name: Traditional Chana Dal Khaman
variations.description: The old-school khaman made the slow way, from soaked and ground chana dal fermented overnight rather than instant besan and Eno. The natural fermentation gives a deeper, tangy flavour and an airy, honeycombed crumb no shortcut can match. This is how grandmothers made khaman before fruit salt existed.

ingredients.name: Chana dal
ingredients.note: Soaked 5 hours and ground to a smooth, thick batter

ingredients.name: Curd
ingredients.note: Kick-starts the overnight fermentation

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: In the batter and the tempering for a clean finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: For the mild sweet-sour tempering water

ingredients.name: Eno fruit salt
ingredients.note: Just a little extra lift on top of the natural fermentation

steps: Grind 1.5 cups soaked chana dal with 1/2 cup curd and a little water to a smooth, thick batter, cover and ferment in a warm spot for 8 hours or overnight until it turns bubbly and rises.
Stir the fermented batter down and mix in 1 tbsp green chilli-ginger paste, 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt; the consistency should be thick but pourable.
Bring the steamer to a rolling boil, grease a tin, and fold 1/2 tsp Eno into the batter for an extra lift just before steaming.
Pour into the tin, level the top and steam on high 18-20 minutes until the honeycombed sponge is set and a skewer comes out clean.
Cool 10 minutes and cut into squares, then heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil to splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tsp sesame seeds and 10 curry leaves.
Add 1/2 cup water with 2 tbsp Anveshan Khandsari, boil 2 minutes and pour the temper over the khaman so it soaks in.
tips: Ferment in a warm place; in cold weather keep the batter in an off oven with the light on to help it rise.
Grind the dal smooth but keep the batter thick, since a watery batter ferments poorly and steams dense.
The natural sourness means you need far less citric acid or lemon than an instant khaman.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the airy, tangy squares with fresh coriander chutney and a cup of chai, the way it was eaten before instant mixes.

variations.name: Coriander Garlic Green Khaman
variations.description: A fragrant green khaman where a fresh coriander, mint and garlic paste is beaten right into the batter, tinting it herby green and layering in a savoury punch. Softer on the sweetness and heavier on the herbs, it eats almost like a spiced dhokla. A vivid, aromatic twist on the yellow classic.

ingredients.name: Coriander-mint-garlic paste
ingredients.note: Fresh-blended coriander, mint and garlic for colour and savoury depth

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: In the batter and the tempering

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A restrained sweet note to balance the herbs and garlic in the temper

steps: Whisk 2 cups besan with 1/3 cup coriander-mint-garlic paste, 1/3 cup curd, 1 tbsp green chilli-ginger paste, 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp lemon juice, 1 tsp oil and about 1 cup water into a smooth green batter of thick pouring consistency; rest 10 minutes.
Bring the steamer to a rolling boil and grease a tin.
Sprinkle 1.5 tsp Eno over the batter, fold gently until it froths and pales a shade, and pour at once into the tin.
Level the top and steam on high 15 minutes until the green sponge springs back and a skewer comes out clean.
Cool 10 minutes and cut into squares, then heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil to crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tsp sesame seeds and 10 curry leaves.
Add 1/2 cup water with 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, boil 2 minutes and spoon over the green khaman so it soaks in.
tips: Blend the herb paste smooth and add it fresh, as sitting too long dulls both colour and aroma.
Keep the sugar light here so the herby, garlicky character stays in front.
A squeeze of extra lemon over the cut squares brightens the green flavour at serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the herby green squares with a garlic-coconut chutney and buttermilk for a savoury afternoon snack.

variations.name: Classic Khasta Kachori
variations.description: This Marwari khasta kachori encases a dry, intensely spiced moong-dal filling in an ultra-flaky shell fried low and slow until it shatters. The crisp, layered crust and the fragrant fennel-and-hing lentil masala make it the definitive halwai-style tea-time kachori.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: the heritage wheat gives the khasta shell body while staying wonderfully flaky

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a heavy moyan of ghee is what creates the crumbling, short-textured khasta layers

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: very slow frying in wood-pressed oil sets the flaky shell without darkening it

steps: Rub 6 tbsp Anveshan Ghee into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.75 tsp salt until the mixture holds shape when pressed, then bind with cold water into a firm dough and rest covered for 30 minutes.
Soak the 0.75 cup moong dal for 2 hours, drain well and grind to a coarse, dry rava-like texture without adding water.
Crush the 2 tsp fennel and 1.5 tsp coriander seeds coarsely, then heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and crackle them with 1 tsp cumin and 0.5 tsp asafoetida over medium heat.

Add the ground dal and 2 tbsp besan and roast for 6 to 7 minutes until dry and fragrant, then stir in 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.75 tsp garam masala, 1.5 tsp amchur and the remaining salt and cool completely.
Divide the dough into 12 balls, cup each into a shallow bowl, place a spoon of the dry filling inside and pleat the edges shut, then press very gently into thick discs.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil to a low 150 C and slide in the kachoris, frying undisturbed for 3 minutes until they float and blister.
Continue frying on low for 12 to 14 minutes total, turning occasionally, until pale golden, crisp and shattering, then drain on a rack.
tips: Grind the dal dry and coarse so the filling roasts crisp rather than turning into a paste.
Fry strictly on low heat for the true khasta layers, as high heat browns the shell before it flakes.
Do not press hard while shaping or the shell will not develop its hollow, blistered crust.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature with sweet tamarind chutney, or crush and top with curd and chutneys for kachori chaat.

variations.name: Pyaaz Kachori
variations.description: Jodhpur's famous pyaaz kachori stuffs a sweet-savoury caramelised onion masala bound with besan into a large flaky shell. Richer and more robust than the dal version, it is the iconic breakfast kachori of Rajasthan, drenched in tangy chutney.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: makes a sturdy flaky shell strong enough for the moist onion filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the moyan of ghee gives the large Jodhpuri kachori its crumbling crust

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: some fries the onions and the rest deep-fries the kachoris slow and crisp

steps: Rub 5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.75 tsp salt, bind to a firm dough with cold water and rest covered for 25 minutes.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and crackle 1 tsp cumin, 1.5 tsp fennel and 0.5 tsp nigella seeds, then add the 4 finely chopped onions.
Saute the onions over medium heat for 10 minutes until soft and lightly golden, then stir in 4 tbsp besan and roast for 4 minutes until nutty.
Season with 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp amchur and the remaining salt, cook 3 more minutes and cool the filling fully.
Divide the dough into 10 balls, flatten each into a cup, fill generously with the onion masala, seal and shape into large thick discs.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil to a low 150 C and fry the kachoris undisturbed until they float, then turn.
Fry slowly for 14 to 16 minutes total until deep golden, puffed and crisp, then drain on a rack and serve.
tips: Cook the onions until their moisture fully evaporates, or the large kachoris will turn soggy inside.
Roast the besan well so it binds the filling and adds the characteristic nutty aroma.
Fry these bigger kachoris extra slow so the thick shell crisps all the way through.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve Jodhpur-style broken open and topped with sweet and green chutneys, with a side of hot jalebi.

variations.name: Raj Kachori
variations.description: The grand raj kachori fries one giant hollow shell that is cracked open and loaded with ragda, curd, sprouts, chutneys and sev. It is less a kachori and more a whole chaat in a bowl, the king of the Delhi chaat counter.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: blended into the shell dough for a wholesome yet crisp hollow puri

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: hot then low frying puffs the shells hollow and crisp for stuffing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the tamarind chutney that drenches the loaded shell

steps: Knead 1 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 cup semolina, 0.5 tsp salt and warm water into a stiff dough, then rest it covered for 30 minutes so the semolina swells.

Roll the dough into 4 large thick discs, prick lightly, and fry each in Anveshan Groundnut Oil that starts hot at 180 C then drops to 150 C, spooning oil over until they balloon into hollow crisp shells.
Boil the 0.75 cup soaked white peas soft and mash into a loose ragda seasoned with 1 tsp chaat masala and 0.25 tsp salt.
Whisk the 1.5 cups yogurt smooth with the remaining salt and chill, and simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder for 5 minutes into a sweet-sour chutney.
Crack a small hole in the top of each crisp shell and fill first with warm ragda and steamed moong sprouts.
Pour over the chilled curd until the shell is drenched, then drizzle tamarind and green chutney generously.
Dust with the remaining chaat masala, 1.5 tsp roasted cumin and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, and crown with sev and pomegranate before serving at once.
tips: Add semolina to the dough and rest it well so the shells puff hollow enough to hold the fillings.
Start frying hot to puff the shell, then lower the heat to crisp it without burning.
Assemble each raj kachori only when ready to eat so the shell stays crisp under the curd.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve one loaded shell per person as a meal-sized chaat, with extra chutneys passed at the table.

variations.name: Classic Hyderabadi Khatti Dal
variations.description: The everyday Hyderabadi tangy dal of soft toor lentils soured generously with tamarind and tomato, balanced by green chilli and a garlicky curry-leaf tempering. Thin, pourable and pleasantly sour, it is the humble backbone of a Deccan home meal over rice.

ingredients.name: Toor dal
ingredients.note: pressure-cooked soft and mashed

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked for a tangy pulp

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed gingelly oil for the authentic Deccan tadka

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: crushed, for the tempering

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup toor dal with the 2 chopped tomatoes, 3 slit green chillies, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 3 cups water for 4-5 whistles until very soft, then whisk smooth.
Squeeze the tamarind into 1/2 cup water and stir the pulp into the dal with 3/4 tsp red chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt.
Simmer the dal on medium heat for 8 minutes until the raw tamarind smell cooks off and it reaches a thin, pourable consistency, adding hot water if needed.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a small pan over medium heat, splutter 1 tsp mustard and 1/2 tsp cumin seeds until they pop.
Add 6 crushed garlic cloves, 2 dry red chillies, 1/4 tsp asafoetida and 2 sprigs curry leaves, and fry for 40 seconds until the garlic turns golden.
Pour the sizzling tempering over the dal, cover immediately to trap the aroma, and rest for 3 minutes before serving.
tips: Cook the tomatoes along with the dal so they melt in and thicken the sourness naturally.
Keep the dal deliberately thin and pourable, as khatti dal is meant to soak into rice.
Add the tamarind to taste; it should be clearly tangy but not sharp enough to sting.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot steamed rice with a spoon of ghee, mango pickle and a papad on the side.

variations.name: Palak Khatti Dal
variations.description: A greener, heartier version where a generous bunch of spinach wilts into the tangy toor dal, softening the sourness and adding an earthy body. More wholesome than the plain dal, it turns the everyday khatti dal into a one-pot dal-saag over rice.

ingredients.name: Toor dal
ingredients.note: pressure-cooked soft

ingredients.name: Spinach
ingredients.note: chopped, packed

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked, a gentler tang

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the rich tempering fat that rounds the spinach and tamarind

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: sliced

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup toor dal with the chopped onion, tomato, 2 slit green chillies, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 3 cups water for 4-5 whistles until soft, then whisk smooth.
Add the 3 cups chopped spinach to the hot dal and simmer on medium heat for 6 minutes until it wilts and turns deep green.
Squeeze in the tamarind pulp with 1/2 tsp red chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt, and simmer for 5 minutes until the flavours meld into a thick dal.
Loosen with hot water to a medium-thick consistency and keep the dal simmering gently.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan, splutter 1 tsp cumin seeds, add 5 sliced garlic cloves and 2 dry red chillies, and fry for 40 seconds until golden.
Pour the ghee tempering over the dal, cover for 3 minutes to lock in the aroma, and serve warm.
tips: Add the spinach only after the dal is cooked so it keeps its bright green colour.
The spinach mellows the tang, so use a little less tamarind than the classic dal.
A ghee tempering rather than oil complements the earthy spinach beautifully here.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice or hot phulka, with a wedge of lemon to brighten each bite.

variations.name: Dhaba Lehsuni Khatti Dal
variations.description: A robust, garlic-heavy rendition with a double tempering and a smoky dhungar finish, giving the tangy dal a bold roadside-dhaba character. Far punchier than the home version, it leans on fried garlic and a charcoal smoke for a deeply savoury, aromatic bowl.

ingredients.name: Toor dal
ingredients.note: pressure-cooked soft

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked for pulp

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: half crushed, half sliced for a double garlic hit

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the pungent dhaba fat, heated to smoking for the bold tempering

ingredients.name: Coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped, to finish

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup toor dal with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 3 cups water for 4-5 whistles until soft, then whisk smooth.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, lower the heat, add the chopped onion and 6 crushed garlic cloves, and fry for 5 minutes until deep golden.
Add the 2 chopped tomatoes with 1 tsp red chilli powder and cook for 4 minutes until pulpy, then stir in the cooked dal, the squeezed tamarind pulp and 1.25 tsp salt.
Simmer on medium heat for 8 minutes until the dal is thick and the raw tamarind smell fades, adding hot water to loosen it.
In a small pan heat the remaining 1 tbsp mustard oil, fry the 6 sliced garlic cloves with 1 tsp cumin and 3 dry red chillies until crisp and golden, and pour over the dal.
Sprinkle 1/2 tsp garam masala and 3 tbsp coriander, and for a dhaba smoke place a hot charcoal in a small bowl over the dal, drizzle with oil, cover for 2 minutes, then serve.
tips: Two rounds of garlic, crushed in the base and sliced-crisp on top, give this its unmistakable dhaba punch.
The optional charcoal dhungar adds real smokiness; keep the lid tight for two full minutes.
Heat the mustard oil to smoking first to soften its sharpness before frying.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tandoori roti, laccha onion and a green chilli for a hearty dhaba-style plate.

variations.name: Methi Khatti Dal
variations.description: A version fragrant with fresh fenugreek leaves, whose gentle bitterness plays against the tamarind sourness for a more complex, aromatic dal. The methi keeps it light yet distinctive, a winter favourite in Deccan kitchens when fresh fenugreek is in season.

ingredients.name: Toor dal
ingredients.note: pressure-cooked soft

ingredients.name: Fresh fenugreek leaves
ingredients.note: chopped and washed

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked for a milder tang

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil that carries the tempering without masking the methi

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: sliced

steps: Pressure-cook 1 cup toor dal with the chopped tomato, 3 slit green chillies, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 3 cups water for 4-5 whistles until soft, then whisk smooth.
Add the 1.5 cups chopped fenugreek leaves to the hot dal and simmer on medium heat for 6 minutes until they soften and their bitterness mellows.
Stir in the squeezed tamarind pulp with 1/2 tsp red chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt, and simmer for 5 minutes to a medium consistency.
Adjust with hot water so the dal stays pourable, and keep it warm on low heat.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a small pan, splutter 1/2 tsp mustard and 1/2 tsp cumin seeds, add 5 sliced garlic cloves and 1 sprig curry leaves and fry for 40 seconds until golden.
Pour the tempering over the dal, cover for 3 minutes to settle the aroma, and serve hot.
tips: Wash the fenugreek well and use only the leaves, as the stems can turn the dal bitter.
A small pinch of jaggery can offset the methi bitterness if your leaves are very sharp.
Add the methi after cooking the dal so it stays fresh and green rather than stewed dull.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed rice or jowar roti, with a dollop of white butter melting on top.

variations.name: Classic Odia Khechudi
variations.description: Odisha's comforting one-pot of rice and roasted moong dal simmered soft with turmeric, ginger and a whisper of whole spice, finished with a generous spoon of ghee. Unlike a plain khichdi this Odia version leans golden and aromatic, the roasted dal lending a nutty depth that makes it a everyday soul-food.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee both tempers the whole spices and is stirred through at the end for the signature Odia richness

steps: Dry-roast the 0.75 cup moong dal in a pan over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes until it turns golden and smells nutty, then rinse it with the 1 cup rice until the water runs clear.

Pressure-cook the rice and dal with 4 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric, half the grated ginger and 1 tsp salt for 3 whistles, then let the pressure release naturally so the grains turn soft and porridge-like.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin, 1 bay leaf, 2 dry red chillies and 2 lightly crushed cardamoms, and let them sizzle for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the remaining grated ginger to the tempering and fry for 20 seconds until the raw smell fades and it turns aromatic.
Pour the hot ghee tempering into the cooked khechudi, stir in the remaining 0.25 tsp salt, and mix well so every grain glistens with ghee.
Simmer the mixed khechudi on low for 2 minutes, adding a splash of hot water if it thickens too much, and serve piping hot while it is still loose and creamy.
tips: Roasting the moong dal before cooking is the Odia signature that gives the khechudi its nutty aroma, so do not skip it.
Keep the texture loose and pourable, as it firms up considerably on standing; loosen with hot water before serving.
Stir the ghee tempering in at the very end rather than cooking it in, so the aroma stays bright and fresh.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a side of fried papad, a dollop of ghee on top and a tangy tomato-date khatta or plain curd for a complete Odia comfort meal.

variations.name: Jagannath Temple Mahaprasad Khechudi
variations.description: The sacred khechudi cooked in earthen pots as bhoga at the Jagannath temple in Puri, laden with seasonal vegetables, panch phoron and pure ghee. Studded with cauliflower, potato and grated coconut, it is richer and more festive than daily khichdi, carrying the fragrant restraint of temple cooking that uses no onion or garlic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: temple bhoga is cooked purely in ghee, which fries the vegetables and perfumes the whole pot

steps: Dry-roast the 0.75 cup moong dal over medium heat for 4 minutes until golden and fragrant, then rinse it with the 1 cup rice and drain well.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pot over medium heat, add 1 tsp panch phoron, 2 bay leaves and 3 dry red chillies, and let them crackle for 30 seconds until aromatic.
Add the cubed potato and 1 cup cauliflower florets, and saute for 4 minutes until their edges turn light golden, then stir in the grated ginger, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp cumin-coriander powder.

Add the rinsed rice and dal with 4.5 cups water, 3 tbsp grated coconut and 1.5 tsp salt, and bring to a rolling boil, then cover and simmer on low for 18 to 20 minutes until the grains and vegetables are soft.
Stir the khechudi gently so it stays creamy, mashing a few potato pieces into the mix to thicken it naturally.
Drizzle the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the top, cover for 2 minutes to let the aroma settle, and serve hot as a sacred, satisfying meal.
tips: Temple bhoga uses no onion or garlic, so let the panch phoron, ginger and ghee carry all the flavour.
Cut the vegetables into even, slightly larger pieces so they cook through without turning to mush before the grains soften.
A pinch of sugar balances the vegetables beautifully and is traditional in Odia temple khechudi.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a banana leaf with dalma, saga bhaja and tomato khajuri chutney, the way it is offered as mahaprasad at Puri.

variations.name: Peanut Winter Khechudi
variations.description: A hearty winter version enriched with roasted peanuts and warming whole garam masala, cooked in nutty groundnut oil for a rustic village character. The peanuts add crunch and protein while black pepper and cloves give a gentle heat that makes this the khechudi Odia families crave on cold evenings.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil echoes the roasted peanuts and gives the khechudi its earthy winter aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a final spoon of bilona ghee rounds off the peppery peanut khechudi with richness

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pressure cooker over medium heat and fry the 0.33 cup peanuts for 2 minutes until they turn crisp and golden, then scoop out half for garnish.
Into the same oil add 8 peppercorns, 3 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon, and let them sizzle for 30 seconds until fragrant, then add the grated ginger and 2 slit green chillies and fry for 30 seconds.
Dry-roast the 0.5 cup moong dal separately for 3 minutes until golden, then rinse with the 1 cup rice and add both to the cooker along with the remaining peanuts.
Pour in 4 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1.25 tsp salt, stir well, and pressure-cook for 3 whistles, then let the pressure fall naturally so the grains and peanuts soften.
Open the cooker, stir the khechudi to a creamy consistency, and loosen with a little hot water if it has thickened too much.
Swirl in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, scatter the reserved fried peanuts on top, and serve hot with the pepper warmth coming through.
tips: Fry the peanuts first and reserve some for garnish so the khechudi has both softened and crunchy peanuts.
Crush the peppercorns lightly before adding if you want a bolder, more warming winter heat.
Soak the moong dal for ten minutes if you prefer an even softer, quicker-cooking khechudi.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve steaming hot with a wedge of lemon, roasted papad and a fiery green chilli-garlic chutney to match the peppery peanuts.

variations.name: Millet Khechudi with Greens
variations.description: A modern, fibre-rich take that swaps part of the rice for pearl millet and folds in spinach for a nutrient-dense one-pot meal. Earthy bajra and tender greens make it heartier and more grounding than the classic, while a mustard-oil tempering lends the pungent bite Odia kitchens love.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil gives this wholesome khechudi its characteristic Odia pungency and depth

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a finishing spoon of ghee mellows the sharp mustard oil and enriches the millet

steps: Soak the 0.5 cup pearl millet in water for 15 minutes, then dry-roast the 0.5 cup moong dal for 3 minutes until golden and rinse it with the 0.5 cup rice.

Pressure-cook the drained millet, rice and dal with 5 cups water, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 5 whistles, giving the tougher millet time to turn fully soft, then release the pressure naturally.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pan until it shimmers and just begins to smoke, then lower the heat and add 1 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp cumin and 2 dry red chillies.
When the seeds splutter, add the sliced garlic and fry for 40 seconds until light golden, then stir in the 1.5 cups chopped spinach and saute for 2 minutes until it wilts.
Tip the wilted spinach tempering into the cooked khechudi, add the remaining 0.25 tsp salt, and stir to combine into a thick, green-flecked porridge.
Simmer for 2 minutes, finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee stirred through, and serve hot while creamy and loose.
tips: Heat mustard oil until it shimmers to mellow its raw sharpness before adding the seeds.
Pearl millet needs longer cooking than rice, so soak it well and give the cooker a couple of extra whistles.
Add the spinach only in the tempering at the end so it keeps its bright colour and does not turn muddy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a side of curd, roasted papad and a lemon wedge, making a balanced, high-fibre meal on its own.

variations.name: Classic Litti Chokha
variations.description: Bihar's iconic litti chokha pairs coal-roasted wheat balls stuffed with spiced sattu against a smoky mash of fire-charred brinjal, potato and tomato. The nutty roasted-gram filling and the ghee-drenched crust with the rustic chokha make it a soulful, wholesome one-plate meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: the heritage wheat makes a firm litti shell that roasts crisp over coals

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: roasted-gram sattu is the nutty, protein-rich heart of the litti stuffing

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the roasted littis are dunked in warm ghee for the signature rich finish

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp of the Anveshan Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and about ¾ cup water into a firm dough and rest it covered for 30 minutes.

Mix 1 cup Anveshan Sattu with half the crushed garlic, half the grated ginger, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp ajwain, 1.5 tbsp pickle masala, 2 tbsp mustard oil, 0.5 tsp salt and a splash of water into a crumbly moist filling.
Divide the dough into 10 balls, flatten each, spoon in the sattu filling, seal the edges and shape back into smooth balls.
Roast the littis over glowing charcoal or in a 220 C oven for 25 to 30 minutes, turning, until the shells are cracked, browned and cooked through.
Meanwhile char the brinjal, 3 potatoes and 3 tomatoes directly over a flame until blackened and soft, then peel and mash them together.
Mix the mash with the remaining garlic, ginger and green chillies, a drizzle of mustard oil, the remaining salt and plenty of coriander to make the chokha.
Dunk the hot roasted littis in the remaining warm Anveshan Ghee and serve at once with the smoky chokha alongside.
tips: Keep the sattu filling just moist enough to hold, as a dry mix will spill out while shaping.
Char the vegetables over an open flame for the authentic smoky chokha rather than boiling them.
Seal the littis well and roast slowly so the thick shell cooks through without burning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the ghee-soaked littis broken open over the chokha with a raw onion and a green chilli on the side.

variations.name: Appe Pan Litti Chokha
variations.description: This home-friendly version cooks small sattu littis in a greased appe pan on the stovetop, giving evenly browned crisp balls without coals or an oven. Paired with a quick tomato-garlic chokha, it brings the Bihari classic to any kitchen in half the time.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: forms small tender litti balls that brown neatly in the appe pan

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: the nutty roasted-gram filling that defines the litti

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the appe moulds and glazes the cooked littis for richness

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and about ¾ cup water into a firm dough and rest 20 minutes.

Combine 1 cup Anveshan Sattu with half the crushed garlic, the grated ginger, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp ajwain, 2 tbsp mustard oil, 1 tbsp lemon juice, 0.5 tsp salt and a little water into a moist crumbly filling.
Divide the dough into 16 small balls, fill each with sattu, seal and roll smooth so they fit the appe moulds.
Grease the appe pan wells with a little Anveshan Ghee, set the littis in, cover and cook on low for 12 to 15 minutes, turning every few minutes until browned all over.
For the chokha, char the 4 tomatoes over a flame until blistered, then peel and mash with the chopped onion, remaining garlic and green chilli.
Season the chokha with a drizzle of mustard oil, the remaining salt and coriander, and mix well.
Brush the hot littis with the remaining warm Anveshan Ghee and serve straight from the pan with the tomato chokha.
tips: Make the littis small so they cook through evenly in the appe pan without staying doughy inside.
Keep the flame low and turn often so the shells brown gradually rather than scorching.
A little lemon in the sattu keeps the filling moist and adds the tang of the classic version.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the pan-cooked littis with tomato chokha and a bowl of thin dal poured over for a comforting supper.

variations.name: Aloo Litti Chokha
variations.description: A softer variation that stuffs the wheat balls with a spiced mashed-potato filling instead of sattu, giving a mellower, comforting litti. Served with a charred brinjal-tomato chokha, it suits those who prefer a gentler, non-gram stuffing.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: makes a firm shell that roasts crisp around the soft potato filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: dunking the roasted littis in ghee gives the rich, glossy finish

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and about ¾ cup water into a firm dough and rest 30 minutes.

Boil 3 of the potatoes, mash them and mix with the chopped onion, half the crushed garlic, half the ginger, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp cumin dry-roasted and crushed, 1 tsp amchur, 1 tbsp mustard oil and 0.5 tsp salt.
Divide the dough into 10 balls, fill each with the potato masala, seal and shape into smooth balls.
Roast the littis over charcoal or in a 220 C oven for 25 to 30 minutes, turning, until the shells crack and brown.
Char the brinjal, remaining 2 potatoes and 3 tomatoes over a flame until soft, then peel and mash for the chokha.
Mix the mash with the remaining garlic, ginger and green chilli, 2 tbsp mustard oil, the remaining salt and coriander.
Dip the hot littis in the warm remaining Anveshan Ghee and serve with the smoky chokha.
tips: Cool the mashed-potato filling before stuffing so it firms up and seals easily inside the dough.
Roast the raw cumin first and crush it, never adding whole seeds to the uncooked potato mix.
Roast the littis a little longer than sattu ones, as the moist potato heart needs more time.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the potato-stuffed littis over the chokha with a wedge of lemon and sliced radish.

variations.name: Baked Litti with Dhaniya Chokha
variations.description: An oven-baked litti brushed with ghee and served with a fresh green coriander-and-green-chilli chokha for a brighter, herbier plate. The baking gives an even crust without a grill, while the vibrant raw chokha lightens the traditionally rich dish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: bakes into a firm, evenly browned litti shell

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: the roasted-gram filling that carries the litti's nutty character

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: brushed on before baking and drizzled after for a rich crust

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and about ¾ cup water into a firm dough, rest 30 minutes, then preheat the oven to 220 C.

Mix 1 cup Anveshan Sattu with half the crushed garlic, the grated ginger, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp ajwain, 2 tbsp mustard oil, 1 tbsp lemon juice, 0.5 tsp salt and a little water into a moist filling.
Divide the dough into 10 balls, stuff with the sattu mix, seal and shape smooth, then set on a lined tray and brush with Anveshan Ghee.
Bake for 25 to 30 minutes, turning once, until the shells are cracked, golden and cooked through.
For the green chokha, coarsely pound the coriander, remaining garlic, 3 green chillies and roasted peanuts into a chunky relish.
Season the chokha with 1 tbsp mustard oil, the remaining lemon juice and salt and mix well.
Drizzle the hot baked littis with the remaining warm Anveshan Ghee and serve with the fresh green chokha.
tips: Turn the littis midway through baking so both sides brown and the shell cooks evenly.
Keep the green chokha raw and coarse for a bright, herby contrast to the rich littis.
Add the peanuts to the chokha for a light crunch that stands in for the usual charred vegetables.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the baked littis with the vibrant green chokha and a small bowl of plain dal on the side.

variations.name: Classic Odia Banana Malpua
variations.description: Odisha's home-style malpua, where mashed ripe banana enriches the flour batter into fluffy, lace-edged pancakes fried in ghee and dipped in cardamom syrup. The banana lends natural sweetness and a soft, custardy centre with crisp frilly edges, a temple and festival favourite across Odia households.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: shallow-frying in bilona ghee gives the malpua its lacy crisp edges and unmistakable aroma

steps: Boil 1 cup sugar with 0.5 cup water and 0.25 tsp cardamom to a one-string syrup, about 6 minutes, then keep it warm.
Mash the 2 ripe bananas smooth, then whisk in 0.75 cup maida, 3 tbsp semolina, 0.5 cup milk, 1 tsp lightly crushed fennel and 6 crushed peppercorns into a smooth, pourable batter.
Rest the batter for 15 minutes so the semolina swells and the fennel infuses, then adjust with a little milk if too thick.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a shallow pan on medium heat and pour in a ladle of batter, letting it spread into a small round with lacy edges.
Fry for about 2 minutes each side until deep golden and crisp at the rim, adding more ghee for each malpua, and drain briefly.
Dip each hot malpua in the warm syrup for 30 seconds, lift out, and serve while the edges are still crisp and the centre soft.
tips: Use well-ripened, spotty bananas for the best natural sweetness and a soft custardy centre.
Rest the batter so the semolina hydrates, which gives the malpua its characteristic frilly lace edges.
Dip in warm syrup only briefly so the edges stay crisp rather than turning soggy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the syrup-glistened malpuas warm, two to a plate, topped with slivered almonds as a festive dessert or Holi treat.

variations.name: Jaggery Banana Malpua
variations.description: A wholesome unrefined version where the batter and the syrup both draw sweetness from jaggery, deepening the banana malpua into a rich caramel-brown treat. The molasses warmth of jaggery marries with ripe banana and fennel for a rustic, old-fashioned pancake that needs no white sugar at all.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery both sweetens the batter and makes the dipping syrup, lending a caramel depth to the banana malpua

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee frying balances the earthy jaggery and crisps the malpua edges

steps: Melt 0.66 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 0.5 cup water into a syrup, strain out grit, add 0.25 tsp cardamom, and keep it warm.
Mash the 2 bananas and whisk in 0.75 cup wheat flour, 3 tbsp semolina, 0.5 cup milk, the remaining 0.33 cup jaggery powder, 1 tsp crushed fennel and 0.25 tsp dry ginger into a smooth batter.
Rest the batter 15 minutes until the semolina swells, loosening with a splash of milk if it thickens.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a shallow pan on medium heat, pour a ladle of batter, and let it spread into a lacy round.
Fry each side for about 2 minutes until deep brown and crisp-edged, adding fresh ghee per malpua, then drain.
Dip the hot malpuas in the warm jaggery syrup for half a minute and serve, the caramel notes shining through.
tips: Strain the jaggery well for both batter and syrup so no grit spoils the smooth pancakes.
Fry on steady medium heat, as jaggery in the batter browns faster and can scorch on high heat.
The dry ginger cuts the richness and keeps this jaggery-heavy version easy to digest.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm drizzled with extra jaggery syrup and a scatter of toasted sesame for a rustic winter dessert.

variations.name: Rabri Malpua
variations.description: The banquet version where crisp banana malpuas are crowned with thick saffron rabri and a shower of nuts, turning a humble pancake into a regal dessert. The cold creamy rabri against the warm syrup-soaked malpua creates the beloved hot-and-cold contrast served at grand Odia weddings.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee crisps the malpua edges to hold up under the weight of the rich rabri

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: saffron colours and perfumes the rabri that crowns each malpua

steps: Reduce the 750 ml milk in a heavy pan for 25 minutes until thick, then stir in 0.5 cup of the sugar, 0.25 tsp Anveshan Saffron and 0.25 tsp cardamom to make the rabri and chill it.
Boil the remaining 0.5 cup sugar with 0.5 cup water and 0.25 tsp cardamom to a one-string syrup and keep warm.
Mash the 1 banana and whisk with 0.75 cup maida and 2 tbsp semolina, adding a little water to make a smooth pourable batter, then rest 15 minutes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a shallow pan on medium heat and fry ladlefuls of batter into small rounds for 2 minutes each side until golden and lacy, adding ghee as needed.
Dip each hot malpua briefly in the warm syrup, then arrange them on a plate.
Spoon the chilled saffron rabri generously over the warm malpuas and finish with 3 tbsp chopped nuts just before serving.
tips: Keep the malpuas slightly crisp-edged so they do not collapse under the weight of the rabri.
Make the rabri ahead and chill it well; the temperature contrast with the warm malpua is the whole charm.
Assemble at the last minute so the malpua stays crisp beneath the creamy topping.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve immediately with the cold rabri melting over the warm pancake, garnished with pistachio slivers and a few saffron strands.

variations.name: Coconut Khapli Malpua
variations.description: A nourishing whole-grain take made with khapli atta and fresh coconut folded into the banana batter, giving the malpua a nutty, textured bite and a tropical fragrance. Sweetened lightly with honey syrup, it is a fibre-rich, mindful version that keeps the festive spirit without refined flour or sugar.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: nutty ancient khapli wheat replaces maida for a wholesome, fibre-rich malpua with a heartier bite

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed coconut oil frying echoes the fresh coconut and gives a light tropical aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: raw honey syrup lightly sweetens the malpua with a floral note in place of refined sugar

steps: Warm 0.5 cup Anveshan Honey with 0.25 cup water and 0.25 tsp cardamom on the lowest heat just until pourable, taking care not to boil the honey, then set aside.
Mash the 2 bananas and whisk in 0.75 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.33 cup grated coconut, 0.5 cup milk, 1 tsp crushed fennel and 0.25 tsp cardamom into a thick, spoonable batter.
Rest the batter 15 minutes so the wheat hydrates, then loosen with a splash of milk if needed to a droppable consistency.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a shallow pan on medium heat and drop in small rounds of batter, flattening slightly.
Fry each side for 2 to 3 minutes until golden brown and cooked through, adding oil as needed since whole wheat drinks up more.
Drizzle the warm honey syrup over the hot malpuas rather than dipping, so the honey stays fresh, and serve at once.
tips: Drizzle rather than soak in honey syrup, and keep the honey warm not hot, to preserve its aroma and benefits.
Whole wheat batter is thicker, so fry the malpuas a little smaller and slower to cook them through.
Fresh coconut adds moisture, so hold back a little milk until you see the batter consistency.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a sprinkle of toasted coconut and a few chopped walnuts, a wholesome dessert that pairs well with masala chai.

variations.name: Classic Bengali Masoor Dal
variations.description: The everyday Bengali red-lentil dal, thin and comforting, finished with a fragrant tempering of nigella seeds and green chillies in mustard oil. Masoor dal cooks quickly to a soft, mildly sweet dal that is the backbone of a Bengali lunch. The phoron of kalonji is what gives it its distinctive homely aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil in the tempering gives Bengali masoor dal its authentic pungent finish

steps: Rinse 1 cup masoor dal well and pressure-cook with 3 cups water, 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 inch grated ginger and 1/2 tsp salt for 2 whistles until completely soft.
Open the cooker, add 1 chopped tomato and the remaining salt, and simmer on low heat for 5 minutes, whisking lightly to a smooth, flowing dal.
In a small pan heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, then lower the heat to medium.
Temper 1/2 tsp nigella seeds, 2 dried red chillies and 2 slit green chillies in the oil for 20 seconds until they crackle and turn fragrant.
Pour the sizzling tempering over the simmering dal and stir it in, then cover immediately to trap the aroma for 2 minutes.
Garnish with 2 tbsp chopped coriander and serve hot.
tips: Masoor dal cooks fast, so two whistles are plenty; overcooking makes it gluey.
Add the tomato after cooking the dal so it keeps a fresh, gentle tang.
Keep this dal thin and pourable, the way it is meant to be eaten over rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over steamed rice with a wedge of lime, some aloo bhaja and a green chilli on the side.

variations.name: Tomato-Garlic Masoor Dal
variations.description: A robust version where a generous garlic-and-tomato tempering in ghee is poured over the red-lentil dal, giving it a punchy, savoury depth quite unlike the delicate classic. The garlic is fried to golden and mingles with cumin for a warming, hearty bowl. This is the comforting dal for a cold-weather dinner.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee fries the garlic to a nutty gold and enriches this hearty tempered dal

steps: Rinse 1 cup masoor dal and pressure-cook with 3 cups water, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1/2 tsp salt for 2 whistles until soft, then whisk to a smooth consistency.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan on medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 2 dried red chillies for 15 seconds.
Add 8 thinly sliced garlic cloves and fry until golden and fragrant, about 1 minute, taking care not to burn them.
Add 1 finely chopped small onion and fry until soft, then add 2 chopped tomatoes and cook for 4 minutes until pulpy, and stir in 3/4 tsp red chilli powder.
Pour the cooked dal into the tempering with the remaining salt and simmer together on low heat for 5 minutes so the flavours meld.
Garnish with 2 tbsp coriander and serve hot.
tips: Fry the garlic just to golden; a burnt clove will turn the whole dal bitter.
Simmering the cooked dal into the tempering, rather than pouring tempering on top, gives a deeper garlicky flavour here.
A splash of hot water loosens the dal if it thickens on standing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Delicious with jeera rice or hot rotis and a simple cucumber salad.

variations.name: Masoor Dal with Coconut and Panch Phoron
variations.description: A sweeter, aromatic East-Bengal style masoor dal brightened with slivers of fresh coconut and tempered with the five-spice panch phoron. The coconut adds gentle richness and bite while panch phoron lends a complex, layered fragrance. It is a festive, slightly special-occasion dal, a touch sweet in the traditional Bengali way.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Mustard oil blooms the panch phoron and keeps this dal rooted in East-Bengal flavour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A little jaggery instead of sugar gives the traditional gentle sweetness Bengali dals are known for

steps: Rinse 1 cup masoor dal and pressure-cook with 3 cups water, 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 inch grated ginger and 1/2 tsp salt for 2 whistles until soft, then whisk smooth.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pan until smoking, lower to medium, and fry 1/4 cup coconut slivers until pale golden, then scoop them out.
In the same oil temper 1 tsp panch phoron, 2 dried red chillies and 1 bay leaf for 20 seconds until the seeds crackle.
Pour in the cooked dal with the remaining salt, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 2 slit green chillies, and simmer on low heat for 5 minutes.
Stir most of the fried coconut into the dal, reserving a little for garnish, and simmer 2 minutes more.
Top with the reserved coconut slivers and serve hot.
tips: Fry the coconut slivers only to pale gold so they stay crunchy in the finished dal.
Panch phoron must bloom in hot oil to release its layered aroma; do not add it to the dal raw.
The jaggery is meant to be subtle, just balancing the spice, so keep it to a teaspoon.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with steamed rice, a fried begun bhaja and a slice of lime for an East-Bengal style lunch.

variations.name: Masoor Dal Fry with Spinach
variations.description: A wholesome, restaurant-style dal fry where the red lentils are enriched with chopped spinach and a well-fried onion-tomato masala, giving a thicker, greener, more substantial bowl. The spinach melts into the dal, adding colour, iron and body. This heartier version needs little on the side to make a meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee gives the dal fry its rich, restaurant-style finish and carries the masala

steps: Rinse 1 cup masoor dal and pressure-cook with 2.5 cups water, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1/2 tsp salt for 2 whistles until soft.
