Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add 5 minced garlic cloves and fry until golden, about 40 seconds.
Add 1 chopped onion and 2 slit green chillies and fry until the onion is soft, then add 1 chopped large tomato and cook until pulpy.
Stir in 1/2 tsp turmeric, 3/4 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp coriander powder and cook 40 seconds, then add 2 cups chopped spinach and saute for 3 minutes until wilted.
Pour in the cooked dal with the remaining salt and 1/2 cup hot water and simmer on low heat for 6 to 7 minutes so the spinach melts into the dal.
Sprinkle 1/2 tsp garam masala, stir through, and serve hot.
tips: Chop the spinach finely so it dissolves into the dal rather than sitting in clumps.
This dal is meant to be thicker than the classic; add water sparingly.
A squeeze of lime at the end brightens the spinach and balances the richness of the ghee.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with jeera rice or tawa rotis and a side of sliced onions and pickle.

variations.name: Classic Matar Kachori
variations.description: This North Indian winter kachori packs a spiced coarse-crushed green-pea filling into a crisp, flaky shell fried to golden puffed rounds. The sweet burst of fresh peas against the ginger, fennel and hing masala makes it a beloved cold-weather snack with sweet chutney.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: the nutty heritage wheat makes a sturdy yet flaky kachori shell that holds the moist filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: rubbed into the flour as moyan, it gives the shell its signature khasta crumble

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: slow deep-frying in wood-pressed oil keeps the shells crisp and light

steps: Rub 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.75 tsp salt until it clumps when pressed, then add water a little at a time to make a firm, smooth dough and rest it covered for 20 minutes.
Coarsely crush the 2 cups green peas with the ginger and 3 green chillies into a chunky paste, not a smooth puree.
Heat 2 tbsp of the Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan and crackle 1 tsp cumin and 1.5 tsp fennel seeds with 0.25 tsp asafoetida over medium heat until fragrant.

Add the crushed pea mixture, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.75 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp amchur and the remaining salt, and cook for 8 to 10 minutes until the moisture dries off and the masala leaves the pan.
Cool the filling completely, then divide the dough into 12 balls, flatten each, spoon in the filling and pleat the edges to seal into a stuffed pouch.
Gently flatten each stuffed ball into a thick disc with your palm, taking care not to expose the filling.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil to a medium 160 C and fry the kachoris in batches for 7 to 8 minutes, turning, until puffed, pale golden and crisp, then drain and serve.
tips: Dry the pea filling well, as any moisture will make the kachoris burst or turn soggy while frying.
Fry on medium-low heat so the shells cook through and stay crisp rather than browning too fast outside.
Rest the fried kachoris on a rack, not paper, so steam escapes and they hold their crunch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with sweet tamarind chutney and a sharp green coriander-mint chutney for dipping.

variations.name: Koraishutir Kochuri
variations.description: The Bengali koraishutir kochuri wraps a smooth, delicately spiced green-pea paste scented with roasted cumin and ginger inside a soft maida shell fried to a pale puff. Milder and subtly sweet, it is a winter breakfast classic eaten with cholar dal or aloor dom.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: stands in for maida to make a soft yet wholesome kochuri shell

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: worked into the dough for the tender, faintly rich Bengali shell

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: neutral wood-pressed oil for frying so the delicate pea flavour stays forward

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and about ¾ cup water into a soft, pliable dough and rest it covered for 20 minutes.
Blanch the 2 cups green peas for 3 minutes, drain, and grind with the 1 inch ginger and 2 green chillies into a smooth thick paste.
Warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Sunflower Oil in a pan, add 0.5 tsp nigella seeds, then the pea paste, 1.5 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp sugar and the remaining salt.
Stir-fry the paste over medium-low heat for 8 to 10 minutes until it thickens into a dry, mouldable filling and cool it fully.
Divide the dough into 12 balls, flatten each, place a spoon of filling in the centre and gather the edges to seal, then roll gently into a small disc.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Sunflower Oil to a moderate 165 C and slide in the kochuris one at a time, spooning oil over the top so they puff into balls.
Fry each for about 3 minutes until pale gold and puffed, keeping them light rather than deeply browned, then drain and serve warm.
tips: Grind the peas smooth for the authentic kochuri texture, unlike the coarse North Indian filling.
Keep the frying oil moderate and baste the tops so the kochuris balloon without browning too much.
A teaspoon of sugar in the filling is traditional and balances the ginger and chilli.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the puffed kochuris with cholar dal or a lightly spiced aloor dom for a classic Bengali winter breakfast.

variations.name: Hing Matar Kachori
variations.description: The Banarasi style leans heavily on asafoetida and whole coriander for a boldly aromatic, mildly pungent pea filling inside an extra-flaky shell. It is the fragrant, spice-forward kachori sold at Kashi tea stalls, meant to be eaten with a fiery aloo sabzi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: the robust wheat gives a rugged flaky shell that suits the strong hing filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a generous moyan of ghee makes the Banarasi kachori especially khasta and short

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: frying in pungent mustard oil lends the sharp, earthy note typical of Kashi kachoris

steps: Rub 5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee into 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.75 tsp salt, then bind with cold water into a stiff dough and rest covered for 20 minutes.
Coarsely crush the 2 cups green peas with the 1.5 inch ginger, and crack the 2 tsp coriander seeds and 1 tsp fennel roughly in a mortar.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking point then lower the flame, and crackle 0.5 tsp asafoetida with the crushed coriander and fennel until deeply fragrant.
Add the crushed peas, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp amchur and the remaining salt, and cook over medium heat for 10 minutes until dry and aromatic, then cool.
Divide the dough into 12 portions, cup each into a bowl shape, fill with the spiced peas and seal, then press gently into thick discs.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Mustard Oil to 160 C, letting it lose its raw smell first, and fry the kachoris in batches for 8 minutes until crisp and golden.
Turn them once or twice so they puff evenly, then drain on a rack and serve hot with the spice aroma still rising.
tips: Always heat mustard oil to smoking and cool slightly before frying to mellow its raw pungency.
Crush the coriander and fennel coarsely so you get little bursts of aroma in every bite.
Use the full amount of hing, as the assertive asafoetida is the defining note of this Banarasi kachori.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve Kashi-style with a thin, tangy potato sabzi and a cup of kulhad chai.

variations.name: Classic Hyderabadi Mirchi Ka Salan
variations.description: The classic biryani companion of long bhavnagri chillies bathed in a tangy, nutty gravy of roasted peanuts, sesame, coconut and tamarind. Mild-heat chillies mellow into the sweet-sour-nutty sauce, making this the definitive Hyderabadi salan ladled beside dum biryani.

ingredients.name: Bhavnagri green chillies
ingredients.note: the mild long variety, slit lengthwise

ingredients.name: Roasted peanuts
ingredients.note: for the nutty base

ingredients.name: Sesame seeds
ingredients.note: roasted

ingredients.name: Dry coconut
ingredients.note: roasted

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: soaked for pulp

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: browned

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed gingelly oil, the authentic Deccan fat for salan

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: balances the tamarind into the classic salan sweet-sour finish

steps: Dry-roast 3 tbsp peanuts, 2 tbsp sesame and 2 tbsp coconut separately until golden, cool, then grind with the browned onion into a smooth thick paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pan over medium heat and shallow-fry the 10 slit chillies for 3 minutes until blistered, then remove and set aside.
In the same oil splutter 1/2 tsp cumin seeds, 1/4 tsp nigella seeds and 1 sprig curry leaves, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and saute for 1 minute.
Add the ground peanut-sesame paste with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder, and cook for 6 minutes until the oil separates and the paste turns nutty brown.
Stir in the squeezed tamarind pulp, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1.25 tsp salt and 1.5 cups water, and simmer for 6 minutes until thick and glossy.
Return the fried chillies, cover and simmer on low for 8 minutes until they soften and soak up the gravy, then rest before serving.
tips: Use mild bhavnagri or banana chillies; slitting them and removing some seeds keeps the heat gentle.
Roast the peanuts, sesame and coconut separately since each toasts at its own pace.
The salan tastes better after resting an hour, letting the chillies drink in the tangy gravy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as the classic side to Hyderabadi dum biryani, with a bowl of dahi ki chutney and sliced onions.

variations.name: Tamatar Mirchi Ka Salan
variations.description: A tangier, tomato-forward salan where a ripe tomato base joins a lighter peanut grind, giving a brighter red gravy with less nutty heaviness. Fresher and more piquant than the classic, it suits those who want the chillies in a livelier, everyday sauce.

ingredients.name: Bhavnagri green chillies
ingredients.note: slit lengthwise

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: pureed for the tangy base

ingredients.name: Roasted peanuts
ingredients.note: a lighter nutty note

ingredients.name: Sesame seeds
ingredients.note: roasted

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil that keeps the tomato gravy clean and bright

ingredients.name: Kasuri methi
ingredients.note: crushed, to finish

steps: Grind 2 tbsp roasted peanuts and 1 tbsp roasted sesame into a coarse powder and set aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan over medium heat and fry the 10 slit chillies for 3 minutes until blistered, then remove.
In the same oil splutter 1/2 tsp cumin seeds and 1 sprig curry leaves, add the chopped onion and fry for 4 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste.
Pour in the tomato puree with 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, and cook for 6 minutes until the puree thickens and the oil surfaces.
Stir in the peanut-sesame powder, 1 tsp salt and 1.25 cups water, and simmer for 5 minutes until the gravy turns a glossy tangy red.
Return the chillies, crush in 1/2 tsp kasuri methi, cover and simmer on low for 6 minutes until softened, then serve.
tips: Use ripe red tomatoes for a naturally tangy gravy that needs no tamarind.
Keep the peanut quantity modest so the tomato brightness stays in front.
A pinch of sugar can round any sharp tomatoes if they turn too acidic.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain pulao, jeera rice or soft phulka for an everyday meal, not just biryani.

variations.name: Cashew-Coconut Mirchi Salan
variations.description: A plusher, milder salan where cashews and fresh coconut milk replace much of the peanut grind, giving a pale, creamy, banquet-style gravy around the chillies. Silkier and gentler than the rustic classic, it is the refined version for a formal biryani spread.

ingredients.name: Bhavnagri green chillies
ingredients.note: slit lengthwise

ingredients.name: Cashew nuts
ingredients.note: soaked, for a creamy grind

ingredients.name: Thick coconut milk
ingredients.note: added off the heat

ingredients.name: Poppy seeds
ingredients.note: soaked, for body

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: boiled for a pale paste

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: keeps the salan pale and lends a clean banquet-style richness

ingredients.name: Lemon juice
ingredients.note: for a gentle tang instead of tamarind

steps: Soak 15 cashews and 1 tbsp poppy seeds for 15 minutes, then grind with the boiled onion into a smooth white paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat and gently fry the 10 slit chillies for 3 minutes until softened but still pale, then remove.
In the same ghee sizzle 1/2 tsp cumin seeds and 3 cardamoms for 30 seconds, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute without browning.
Add the cashew paste with 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1/2 tsp white pepper, and cook gently for 5 minutes on low heat, keeping it pale.
Pour in 1 cup water and 1 tsp salt, return the chillies, and simmer on low for 6 minutes until they soften into the creamy gravy.
Lower the heat fully, stir in 1/2 cup thick coconut milk and 2 tsp lemon juice, warm through for 2 minutes without boiling, and serve.
tips: Add the coconut milk off high heat and do not let it boil, or it may split in the pale gravy.
Lemon juice gives a fresh, gentle tang here that suits the creamy base better than tamarind.
Keep the flame low throughout so the salan stays ivory rather than browning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a delicate vegetable dum biryani or saffron pulao for a refined banquet plate.

variations.name: Achari Mirchi Salan
variations.description: A punchy pickle-spiced version tempered with the five achari seeds and finished with mustard tang, where the chillies swim in a bold, sour, spice-crackling gravy. Sharper and more assertive than the classic, it borrows the aggressive aromatics of North Indian pickle for a lively kick.

ingredients.name: Bhavnagri green chillies
ingredients.note: slit lengthwise

ingredients.name: Roasted peanuts
ingredients.note: for the ground base

ingredients.name: Sesame seeds
ingredients.note: roasted

ingredients.name: Curd
ingredients.note: whisked, for a pickle-style tang

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: browned

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: heated to smoking, the pungent fat that defines an achari gravy

ingredients.name: Fennel seeds
ingredients.note: part of the achari mix

steps: Grind 3 tbsp roasted peanuts and 1 tbsp roasted sesame with the browned onion into a thick paste and set aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, lower the heat, and fry the 10 slit chillies for 3 minutes until blistered, then remove.
In the same oil crackle 1 tsp fennel, 1/2 tsp nigella, 1/4 tsp fenugreek, 1/2 tsp mustard and 1/2 tsp cumin seeds for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and the peanut paste with 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp red chilli powder, and cook for 6 minutes until the oil separates.
Lower the heat and whisk in 1/4 cup curd slowly so it does not split, then add 1 tsp salt and 1.25 cups water and simmer for 5 minutes.
Return the chillies, cover and simmer on low for 6 minutes until they soften into the tangy, pickle-scented gravy, then serve.
tips: Heat the mustard oil until it smokes first to tame its raw pungency, then lower the heat before frying.
Add the curd off the boil and stir constantly so the achari gravy stays smooth.
The five-seed achari tempering is the heart of this take, so measure the seeds rather than eyeballing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain paratha, khichdi or jeera rice for a sharp, pickle-spiced accompaniment.

variations.name: Classic Veg Mughlai Paratha
variations.description: Mughlai Paratha is Kolkata's grand stuffed flatbread, a thinly stretched dough parcel packed with a spiced vegetable filling, folded into a square and shallow-fried until crisp and flaky. This vegetarian version swaps the traditional keema for a fragrant potato-pea mash, keeping the signature golden, layered crunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: nutty khapli atta makes a supple dough that stretches thin and fries crisp in place of maida

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee shallow-fries the parcels to a rich, flaky golden crust

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 0.75 cup water into a soft, smooth, non-sticky dough, then rest it covered for 20 minutes.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, add the onion, ginger and green chillies and fry 3 minutes, then add 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp garam masala.
Fold in the mashed potato and peas with the remaining salt and 4 tbsp coriander, cook 3 minutes into a firm dry filling, and cool.
Divide the dough into 4, roll each into a very thin large square, place a quarter of the filling in the centre, and fold the four sides over into a sealed parcel.
Heat a flat tava with 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on medium, place a parcel seam-side down, and shallow-fry 3 to 4 minutes per side, adding ghee at the edges, until deep golden and crisp.
Fry the remaining parcels the same way and serve hot, cut in halves.
tips: Roll the dough as thin as you can without tearing so the fried paratha stays light and flaky rather than doughy.
Keep the filling dry and cooled so the parcel does not turn soggy or burst open while frying.
Fry on steady medium heat and baste with ghee so the layers crisp evenly to golden.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a simple aloo-dum, kasundi and a sliced onion-cucumber salad for a classic Kolkata meal.

variations.name: Paneer Mughlai Paratha
variations.description: A rich, protein-packed take where the parcel is filled with crumbled paneer spiced with kasuri methi and pepper, giving a soft, savoury centre. It is the indulgent version that turns a Sunday brunch into a treat, fried crisp in wood-pressed oil.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: makes a pliable dough that stretches thin around the rich paneer filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil fries the parcels to a light, crisp golden shell

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp of the Anveshan Groundnut Oil and about 0.75 cup water into a soft, smooth dough, and rest it 20 minutes.

Mix the crumbled paneer with the onion, 1 inch grated ginger, 3 green chillies, 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi, 0.75 tsp black pepper, 1 tsp chaat masala, the remaining salt and 4 tbsp coriander into a dry, spiced filling.
Divide the dough into 4 and roll each into a very thin large square on a lightly oiled surface.
Place a quarter of the paneer filling in the centre of each and fold the sides over into a neat sealed square parcel.
Heat a tava with 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium, fry each parcel seam-side down for 3 to 4 minutes per side, adding oil at the edges, until golden and crisp.
Serve hot, cut into halves, so the soft paneer centre shows.
tips: Use firm, well-drained paneer and keep the filling dry, as wet paneer makes the parcel tear.
Crush the kasuri methi between your palms before adding to release its aroma into the filling.
Do not overstuff, or the thin dough splits and the paneer leaks while frying.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with mint-yogurt raita and a squeeze of lemon, ideal as a filling weekend brunch.

variations.name: Sattu-Stuffed Mughlai Paratha
variations.description: This lean, rustic crossover borrows Bihar's spiced roasted-gram sattu filling and folds it into the Bengali mughlai parcel, giving a punchy, tangy, high-protein centre. Sharp with mustard oil, garlic and pickle masala, it is a robust everyday version that needs no side dish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Multigrain Atta
ingredients.note: hearty multigrain atta makes a sturdy dough that carries the robust sattu filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: roasted gram sattu is the spiced high-protein heart of this parcel

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: pungent mustard oil binds the sattu filling and fries the parcels with a sharp bite

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Multigrain Atta with 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and about 0.75 cup water into a firm, smooth dough, and rest 20 minutes.

In a bowl mix 1 cup Anveshan Sattu with the chopped garlic, 3 green chillies, 1 inch ginger, 0.5 tsp ajwain, 2 tsp pickle masala, 1 tbsp lemon juice, 4 tbsp coriander, the remaining salt and 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil into a moist, crumbly filling.
Divide the dough into 4 and roll each into a thin large square.
Spread a quarter of the sattu filling over the centre and fold the four sides into a sealed square parcel.
Heat a tava with 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil on medium, fry each parcel 3 to 4 minutes per side, drizzling oil at the edges, until crisp and golden-brown.
Serve hot, cut in halves, straight off the tava.
tips: Moisten the sattu filling just enough with mustard oil and lemon so it holds but does not go pasty.
Seal the edges firmly, as the loose sattu can spill if the parcel is not closed well.
Let the mustard oil heat and smoke lightly before frying so its raw sharpness mellows.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with mango pickle, raw onion rings and a dollop of curd for a rustic, filling meal on its own.

variations.name: Baked Whole-Wheat Mughlai Parcel
variations.description: A lighter oven-baked parcel using a soft whole-grain dough and a mixed-veg filling, brushed with ghee for a golden, flaky finish without the shallow-fry. It keeps the stuffed-square charm of the mughlai paratha while being gentle enough for an everyday dinner.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Multigrain Atta
ingredients.note: wholesome multigrain atta bakes into a soft, flaky parcel

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: brushed over the parcels so they crisp and turn golden in the oven

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Multigrain Atta with 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and about 0.8 cup water into a soft dough, and rest 20 minutes; preheat the oven to 200C.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, add the onion and 1.5 tsp ginger-green chilli paste, fry 2 minutes, then add the cabbage, carrot and corn and cook 5 minutes until dry.
Season with 1 tsp roasted cumin, 0.5 tsp black pepper, the remaining salt and 4 tbsp coriander, cook 2 minutes, and cool.
Divide the dough into 4, roll each into a thin square, place a quarter of the filling in the centre, and fold into a sealed parcel.
Arrange the parcels on a lined tray, brush the tops with Anveshan Ghee, and bake for 15 minutes.
Flip, brush again with ghee, and bake another 10 to 12 minutes until golden and crisp; serve warm, cut in halves.
tips: Squeeze any excess water from the grated cabbage and carrot so the baked parcel stays crisp.
Brush ghee generously on both bakes so the whole-wheat dough browns instead of drying out.
Roll the dough thin and seal well so the parcel bakes flaky rather than bready.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a bowl of tomato-coconut chutney or curd, a wholesome weeknight dinner parcel.

variations.name: Classic Bengali Peyaji
variations.description: Peyaji is Bengal's answer to the onion pakora, thinly sliced onions bound in a minimal spiced besan coating and fried in mustard oil until crisp and sweet. Nigella seeds and green chilli give it a fragrant bite, and unlike the North Indian version the onion, not the batter, is the hero.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil gives peyaji its authentic Bengali sharpness and a crisp finish

steps: Thinly slice 3 onions, add 1 tsp salt, and rest for 10 minutes so they soften and release their own moisture.
Add 0.75 cup besan, 2 tbsp rice flour, 0.5 tsp nigella seeds, 3 chopped green chillies, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, and toss so the flour just coats the onions.
Sprinkle in only 3 tbsp water and mix into a thick, barely-wet mass that clings without dripping.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Mustard Oil until it just smokes, then lower to medium so it settles to about 180C.
Drop in small, loose clusters of the onion mixture and fry in batches for 4 to 5 minutes, turning, until deep golden and crisp.
Drain on paper and serve hot, when the onions are at their sweetest and the edges are shattering-crisp.
tips: Let the salted onions release their water and add very little extra, or the peyaji turn soft and oily.
Keep the clusters loose and uneven, as ragged edges crisp far better than tight, packed balls.
Heat the mustard oil to smoking then cool it slightly so its raw sharpness mellows before frying.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with steamed rice and dal to start a meal, or with muri and cha as a rainy-evening snack.

variations.name: Coconut Curry-Leaf Peyaji
variations.description: This aromatic take borrows fresh coconut, curry leaves and a touch of fennel from the south, giving the onion fritter a sweet, fragrant lift. The coconut caramelises at the edges for a nutty crunch that sets it apart from the plain Bengali original.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed coconut oil deepens the coastal aroma and fries the fritters crisp

steps: Slice 3 onions thin, mix with 1 tsp salt, and rest 10 minutes until they soften and weep.
Add 0.75 cup besan, 0.33 cup grated coconut, 15 chopped curry leaves, 0.5 tsp fennel seeds, 1 inch grated ginger, 2 chopped green chillies and 0.25 tsp turmeric, and toss to coat.
Sprinkle over 3 tbsp water and bring together into a thick, clinging mixture that holds a loose clump.
Heat 2.5 cups Anveshan Coconut Oil to about 175C, until a shred of mixture sizzles and floats up.
Drop small clusters into the oil and fry in batches for 4 to 5 minutes, turning, until golden with browned coconut flecks.
Drain on paper and serve hot so the toasted coconut stays crunchy.
tips: Use freshly grated coconut rather than desiccated, which can burn and turn bitter in the oil.
Chop the curry leaves so their flavour spreads through every bite instead of just the surface.
Fry on steady medium heat so the coconut toasts golden without scorching.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and filter coffee, or alongside a bowl of rasam rice for a fragrant south-meets-east plate.

variations.name: Sattu Protein Peyaji
variations.description: A wholesome upgrade where roasted-gram sattu replaces part of the besan, boosting protein and lending a deep, roasted nuttiness to the fritter. Ajwain and a hint of amchur keep it light and digestible while the sattu crisps up beautifully.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: roasted gram sattu adds protein and a nutty, savoury crunch in place of some besan

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil fries the sattu coating light and clean

steps: Slice 3 onions thin, toss with 1 tsp salt, and leave for 10 minutes to soften.
Add 0.5 cup Anveshan Sattu, 0.33 cup besan, 0.5 tsp ajwain, 0.5 tsp amchur, 2 chopped green chillies, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 3 tbsp coriander, and mix to coat.
Sprinkle in about 4 tbsp water, since sattu drinks up more moisture, and bring to a thick, holdable mixture.
Heat 2.5 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to about 180C, until a drop of the mix rises briskly.
Drop small clusters and fry in batches for 4 to 5 minutes, turning, until dark golden and crisp.
Drain on paper and serve hot; the sattu keeps them satisfying and filling.
tips: Sattu absorbs water fast, so add it gradually and stop while the mix is still thick and clumpy.
The amchur brightens the roasted sattu, so do not leave it out.
These are more filling than plain peyaji, so serve a couple fewer per person.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with mint-coriander chutney and a glass of chaas for a protein-packed monsoon snack.

variations.name: Baked Air-Fryer Peyaji
variations.description: A near oil-free version for the health-conscious, where the spiced onion clusters are tossed with a spoon of ghee and crisped in an air fryer or hot oven. They come out craggy and golden with a wholesome bite and none of the deep-fry heaviness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: a spoon of nutty khapli atta helps the clusters hold and brown in dry heat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: tossed through the mix so the air-fried fritters crisp and turn golden

steps: Slice 3 onions thin, mix with 1 tsp salt, and rest for 10 minutes so they release moisture and need no added water.

Add 0.66 cup besan, 3 tbsp Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 tsp nigella, 2 chopped green chillies, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, and toss into a thick, clinging mix using only the onion's own water.
Drizzle in 2 tbsp melted Anveshan Ghee and mix so every cluster is lightly coated for browning.
Preheat the air fryer or oven to 200C and arrange loose clusters on a lined tray or basket, spaced apart.
Air-fry or bake for 12 minutes, turn each cluster, then cook another 8 to 10 minutes until golden and crisp-edged.
Rest for 2 minutes so they firm up, then serve warm.
tips: Rely on the salted onion's own moisture; adding water makes the clusters steam rather than crisp.
Space the clusters well apart so hot air circulates and browns them evenly.
Toss in the ghee thoroughly, as any dry patches will stay pale and floury.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a tamarind-date chutney and a side salad for a lighter tea-time plate.

variations.name: Classic Arisa Pitha
variations.description: Arisa pitha is a cherished Odia festival cake made from a soft dough of ground raw rice and thick jaggery syrup, patted into discs and deep-fried until mahogany-dark and glossy. Crisp at the edges and chewy within, its sesame-studded top and deep caramel flavour make it a Sankranti staple.

ingredients.name: Raw Rice
ingredients.note: soaked, dried and ground to a fine flour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: boiled into a thick syrup that both sweetens and binds the rice dough

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil for deep-frying the discs to a clean, even crispness

steps: Boil 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 0.5 cup water on medium heat until it reaches a thick one-string consistency, about 6-7 minutes.
Lower the heat, stir in 2 cups fine rice flour a little at a time with 0.5 tsp cardamom and a pinch of salt until it forms a soft, warm dough.
Cover and rest the dough for 20 minutes, then knead it smooth with lightly oiled hands so it holds together without cracking.
Pinch off lemon-sized balls, flatten each into a 3 inch disc on an oiled sheet, and press white sesame seeds firmly onto the top.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to medium and slide in the discs one at a time, frying on low-medium for 3-4 minutes until deep reddish-brown.
Drain the arisa pitha on a rack and cool completely so it firms up to the classic chewy-crisp bite before serving.
tips: Get the jaggery syrup to a firm one-string stage; too thin and the dough spreads, too thick and it turns hard.
Fry on a gentle flame so the discs cook through to the centre before the outside darkens.
Rest the fried pithas for a few hours, as they crisp and set beautifully as they cool.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a Makar Sankranti sweet with other pithas, or store in a tin and offer with afternoon tea for days.

variations.name: Kakara Pitha
variations.description: Kakara pitha is a crescent-shaped Odia fritter with a semolina-and-wheat shell wrapped around a warm coconut-jaggery stuffing. Deep-fried to a golden crackle, it hides a fragrant, moist centre spiced with cardamom and black pepper, a temple offering turned teatime treat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: ancient-grain wheat flour that gives the shell a sturdy, wholesome bite

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melts with coconut into the warm, sticky filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: neutral wood-pressed oil for frying the crescents evenly golden

steps: Roast 1 cup grated coconut for 3 minutes, add 0.5 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp black pepper, and cook to a sticky filling, then cool.
Bring 1 cup water with a pinch of salt to a boil, lower the heat and stir in 1 cup semolina, cooking 2 minutes until it thickens into a soft mass.
Turn off the heat, work in 0.5 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta while warm, and knead to a smooth, pliable dough, resting it 10 minutes.
Divide the dough into balls, flatten each into a small disc, place a spoon of coconut filling in the centre and fold into a sealed half-moon.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Sunflower Oil to medium and fry the crescents 3-4 minutes, turning once, until golden and crisp all over.
Drain the kakara pitha on paper and serve warm so the coconut centre stays soft and fragrant.
tips: Seal the edges firmly, pressing out any air, so the filling does not burst into the hot oil.
Knead the dough while it is still warm; a cold semolina dough cracks and is hard to shape.
Fry on medium heat so the thick shell cooks through without the outside browning too fast.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a festival snack with a cup of ginger tea, or offer as bhog at a Lakshmi Puja.

variations.name: Manda Pitha
variations.description: Manda pitha is a soft steamed dumpling of rice flour dough encasing a coconut, jaggery and poppy-seed filling. Gently steamed rather than fried, it is the lightest of the pithas, with a delicate translucent skin and a warm, fragrant centre offered during Manabasa Gurubar.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the coconut-poppy filling with a soft caramel note

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the palms and steamer so the delicate dumplings do not stick

steps: Dry-roast 1 tbsp poppy seeds for a minute, add 1 cup grated coconut and roast 2 minutes, then stir in 0.5 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.5 tsp cardamom and cook to a sticky filling.
Pour 1.5 cups boiling water with a pinch of salt over 2 cups rice flour and mix quickly with a spoon until it comes together as a shaggy dough.
Grease your palms with a little Anveshan Ghee and knead the warm dough smooth and pliable, keeping it covered so it does not dry.
Take a small ball, cup it into a hollow bowl, fill with a spoon of coconut mixture and pinch the top closed into a smooth dumpling.
Arrange the dumplings on a greased steamer plate without touching and steam on medium heat for 12-15 minutes until the skin turns glossy.
Rest the manda pitha for 5 minutes so the skin firms slightly, then serve warm.
tips: Knead the dough with hot water and while warm for a smooth skin that does not crack during steaming.
Do not oversteam, or the dumplings turn gummy; they are done when the surface looks translucent and set.
Keep the dough covered with a damp cloth at all times, as rice flour dries out and cracks very quickly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a light, steamed festival sweet, drizzled with a little extra ghee if you like.

variations.name: Poda Pitha
variations.description: Poda pitha, literally burnt cake, is a slow-baked Odia delicacy of fermented rice and urad batter studded with coconut, jaggery and cashews. Baked low and long until the crust chars and caramelises, it has a smoky rim and a dense, moist, pudding-like crumb famously loved by Lord Jagannath.

ingredients.name: Raw Rice
ingredients.note: soaked and ground with the dal

ingredients.name: Urad Dal
ingredients.note: soaked for the batter

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the batter and caramelises into the signature dark crust

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: coats the tin and enriches the crumb for a moist, aromatic cake

ingredients.name: Cashew Nuts
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Grind 1.5 cups soaked rice with 0.5 cup soaked urad dal to a thick batter, add 0.5 tsp salt and ferment covered for 6-8 hours until risen and airy.
Stir 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder into the fermented batter until dissolved, then fold in 1 cup grated coconut, 3 tbsp chopped cashews, 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp black pepper.
Grease a deep tin generously with 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and pour in the batter, which should sit about two inches deep.
Bake in an oven preheated to 160C for 55-60 minutes, or cook covered on a heavy tawa on low heat, until a skewer comes out clean.
Brush the top with the remaining Anveshan Ghee in the last 10 minutes so the crust turns deep, glossy brown.
Cool the poda pitha completely in the tin, then unmould and slice into thick wedges to reveal the moist crumb.
tips: A good long fermentation gives the cake its lift and its faint pleasant tang, so do not rush this step.
Bake low and slow; a high flame chars the crust before the dense centre has cooked through.
The black pepper is traditional and cuts the sweetness, so do not leave it out despite it being a sweet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve thick wedges at room temperature as a festival cake, keeping well for two to three days in a tin.

variations.name: Classic Assamese Poita Bhat
variations.description: Poita Bhat is Assam's cooling breakfast of rice soaked overnight in water until it gently ferments, then eaten with raw mustard oil, onion and green chilli. Loved by farmers before a day in the fields, it is light, probiotic and endlessly comforting on a hot morning.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: raw wood-pressed mustard oil is stirred in fresh for the signature pungent lift

steps: Cook 3 cups short-grain rice until just soft, spread it out and cool it completely to room temperature.
Transfer the cooled rice to a clay pot or bowl, pour over 3 cups water to cover, and leave it at room temperature overnight for 8 to 10 hours to ferment gently.
In the morning the rice will smell mildly sour and taste tangy; drain off the excess water, keeping the grains moist.
Add the chopped onion, 3 green chillies, 3 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp salt to the soaked rice.
Drizzle over 2 tbsp raw Anveshan Mustard Oil and mix gently so the grains stay whole.
Serve at room temperature, ideally in the clay pot it soaked in.
tips: Use day-old or freshly cooked and fully cooled rice; warm rice turns mushy and over-sours overnight.
A clay or earthen pot keeps the rice cool and gives the best gentle fermentation.
Keep the raw mustard oil generous, as it is the flavour that defines poita bhat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with aloo pitika, a fried dried chilli, pickle and a wedge of lemon for the traditional Assamese breakfast spread.

variations.name: Doi Poita Bhat (Curd Style)
variations.description: A festive Bohag Bihu version where the fermented rice is loosened with cool curd and a touch of jaggery, then topped with banana for a sweet-savoury bowl. Creamy and gently sour, it is the celebratory way Assamese families eat poita during the spring festival.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: deep molasses sweetness that balances the sour fermented rice, the traditional Bihu pairing

steps: Cook 3 cups short-grain rice until soft, cool it fully, cover with 3 cups water, and leave to ferment overnight for 8 to 10 hours.
In the morning drain off the soaking water from the mildly soured rice, keeping the grains moist.
Whisk 1 cup yogurt with 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.25 tsp cardamom until the jaggery dissolves.
Fold the sweetened curd into the fermented rice with a pinch of salt until creamy and loose.
Top with 2 sliced bananas and 3 tbsp grated coconut.
Serve chilled or at room temperature as a cooling festive bowl.
tips: Dissolve the jaggery fully in the curd first so there are no gritty bits in the bowl.
Use thick, fresh curd; sour curd on top of the fermented rice can make it too tangy.
Add the banana just before serving so it does not brown or turn mushy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a light Bihu breakfast or a cooling summer dessert-style bowl, with extra jaggery on the side for sweet tooths.

variations.name: Tempered Bhaja Poita Bhat
variations.description: A warm, savoury version finished with a sizzling mustard-oil tempering of garlic, dried chilli and panch phoron poured over the fermented rice. The hot tarka wakes up the cool grains and adds a smoky, garlicky depth that makes it a fuller meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: heated to smoking for a garlicky tempering poured sizzling over the rice

steps: Cook 3 cups short-grain rice, cool it fully, cover with 3 cups water, and ferment overnight for 8 to 10 hours.
In the morning drain the soured rice, then mix in the chopped onion, 3 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp salt.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a small pan until it just smokes, then lower the heat.
Add 0.5 tsp panch phoron, 6 sliced garlic cloves, 3 broken dried red chillies and 10 curry leaves, and fry 40 seconds until the garlic is golden and aromatic.
Pour the sizzling tempering over the fermented rice and fold it through quickly.
Serve warm while the tarka aroma is at its liveliest.
tips: Fry the garlic just to golden, as burnt garlic makes the whole tempering bitter.
Pour the tarka while sizzling hot so it warms the cool rice and blooms the spices.
Drain the rice well before tempering so the tarka clings rather than pooling watery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a fried papad and a spoon of tangy pickle for a heartier midday meal.

variations.name: Xaak Aru Til Poita Bhat (Greens and Sesame)
variations.description: A nourishing version studded with blanched greens and toasted sesame, dressed in nutty sesame oil for extra minerals and body. The soft greens and crunchy sesame turn the plain fermented rice into a wholesome one-bowl breakfast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed sesame oil dresses the rice with a deep, nutty warmth

steps: Cook 3 cups short-grain rice, cool it fully, cover with 3 cups water, and ferment overnight for 8 to 10 hours.
Blanch 1.5 cups greens in boiling water for 1 minute, drain, squeeze dry and chop finely.
Toast 2 tbsp sesame seeds in a dry pan until golden and popping.
Drain the fermented rice and add the chopped greens, toasted sesame, 3 green chillies, 0.5 inch grated ginger and 1 tsp salt.
Drizzle over 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and 1 tbsp lemon juice and mix gently.
Serve at room temperature as a wholesome, mineral-rich bowl.
tips: Squeeze the blanched greens dry so they do not water down the rice.
Toast the sesame just to golden for a nutty crunch, since it burns quickly.
The lemon keeps the greens bright and lifts the nutty sesame oil.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a side of curd and roasted papad for a filling, nutritious start to the day.

variations.name: Classic Raj Kachori Chaat
variations.description: Raj Kachori is the king of chaats, a large hollow crisp shell cracked open and packed with boiled potato, chickpeas, sprouts, whisked yogurt and a riot of chutneys. Every spoonful shatters into crunch and then floods with cool curd, sweet-sour tamarind and warm spice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: a little stone-milled khapli atta in the dough makes the puffed shells sturdier and nuttier than plain refined flour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: deep-frying in wood-pressed groundnut oil puffs the shells to an even golden crisp

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the tamarind chutney with a deep natural sweetness

steps: Knead 1 cup semolina with 0.25 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 tsp salt and about 6 tbsp water into a stiff, smooth dough and rest it under a damp cloth for 20 minutes.

Divide into 4 balls, roll each into a 5 inch disc, and deep-fry one at a time in 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil at 160 C, spooning oil over the top until each puffs into a large hollow ball and turns golden and crisp, about 5 minutes.
Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind pulp with 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and a splash of water for 6 minutes into a thick sweet-sour chutney and cool it.
Whisk the 2.5 cups yogurt smooth with 0.5 tsp salt and a pinch of black salt until pourable, and mash the boiled 2 potatoes coarsely.
Crack a coin-sized hole in the top of each cooled shell and fill with mashed potato, boiled chickpeas and a spoon of whisked yogurt.
Pour more yogurt to fill the shell, then drizzle generously with tamarind chutney and 4 tbsp green chutney.
Dust with 1.5 tsp roasted cumin, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp black salt, then top with sev and coriander and serve immediately.
tips: Keep the frying oil at a steady moderate heat so the discs puff hollow instead of browning before they inflate.
Fill and top the shells only just before serving so they stay crisp under the yogurt.
If a shell does not puff, use it crushed as a base layer so nothing is wasted.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve each loaded shell on its own plate so guests can crack in with a spoon and get every layer at once.

variations.name: Marwari Raj Kachori
variations.description: The Rajasthani halwai style stuffs the giant shell with moong dal, crunchy boondi and pomegranate alongside the usual fillings, leaning richer and sweeter with a heavier hand of curd and dry-fruit garnish. It is the celebratory thali version served at Marwari weddings and festivals.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: stone-milled khapli atta strengthens the dough so the large festive shells hold their shape

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil fries the shells clean and golden for the halwai finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: gives the tamarind chutney the deep sweet body typical of Marwari chaat

steps: Knead 1 cup semolina with 0.25 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 tsp salt and about 6 tbsp water into a firm dough, then rest it 20 minutes under a damp cloth.
Boil 0.5 cup moong dal until just soft but holding shape, drain well, and lightly season with 0.25 tsp salt.
Roll the dough into four 5 inch discs and deep-fry in 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil at 160 C, basting with oil, until each balloons into a crisp hollow shell, about 5 minutes each.
Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder for 6 minutes into a thick chutney, and whisk 3 cups yogurt smooth with 0.5 tsp salt.
Crack open each shell and layer in the boiled moong dal, a spoon of whisked yogurt, boondi and pomegranate.
Flood with more yogurt, then swirl over the tamarind chutney and 4 tbsp green chutney.
Finish with 1.5 tsp roasted cumin, 1 tsp black salt, toasted cashews, more boondi, pomegranate and coriander, and serve at once.
tips: Cook the moong dal just to al dente so it stays as distinct grains inside the shell rather than turning to paste.
Toast the cashews in a dry pan first so their crunch and aroma stand out in the rich filling.
Add the boondi in two stages, inside and on top, so there is crunch through every layer.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as the showpiece of a festive chaat platter, dressed with extra pomegranate and a shower of boondi.

variations.name: Baked Raj Kachori
variations.description: A lighter reinvention where the shells are brushed with wood-pressed oil and baked until crisp instead of deep-fried, then filled with the usual chaat medley. It trades a little of the airy puff for a wholesome crunch and far less oil, without losing the fun of cracking into a loaded shell.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: extra khapli atta gives the baked shells a firm wholemeal crunch that holds up without frying

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: brushing the shells with wood-pressed sunflower oil crisps them golden in the oven with minimal fat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the tamarind chutney naturally for the lighter chaat

steps: Knead 1 cup semolina with 0.5 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Sunflower Oil and about 7 tbsp water into a firm dough, then rest it 20 minutes.
Roll into four 5 inch discs, drape each over an inverted oiled steel bowl or a muffin-tin cup to form a dome, and prick lightly with a fork.
Brush all over with the remaining Anveshan Sunflower Oil and bake at 190 C for 22 to 25 minutes until firm, golden and crisp, then cool on the mould.
Simmer 3 tbsp tamarind with 3 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder for 6 minutes into a thick chutney, and whisk 2.5 cups yogurt smooth with 0.5 tsp salt.
Ease each crisp dome off its mould, fill with mashed boiled potato, boiled moong, finely chopped onion and cucumber and a spoon of yogurt, then pour over more yogurt.
Drizzle with tamarind chutney and 4 tbsp green chutney, dust with 1.5 tsp roasted cumin and 1 tsp black salt, top with sev, pomegranate and coriander, and serve straight away.
tips: Bake the shells over a mould so they hold a deep bowl shape ready to be loaded.
Cool the baked shells fully before filling, as they crisp further as they sit.
Baked shells soften faster once wet, so assemble each one only at the moment of serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a lighter party chaat with bowls of chutney and sev on the side so guests build their own.

variations.name: Hariyali Raj Kachori
variations.description: This sharp, herb-forward version skews away from the sweet-heavy classic, loading the shell with a bright mint-coriander green chutney, crunchy raw onion, cucumber and a squeeze of lime for a fresher, tangier bite. The curd is kept thin and lightly salted so the green heat and citrus lead.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: khapli atta gives the shells body to carry the crunchy fresh fillings

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil puffs and crisps the shells cleanly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: a spoon of honey rounds the sharp green chutney without making the chaat sweet

steps: Knead 1 cup semolina with 0.25 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta, 0.5 tsp salt and about 6 tbsp water into a stiff dough and rest it 20 minutes.
Roll into four 5 inch discs and deep-fry in 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil at 160 C, basting with oil until each puffs hollow and crisp, about 5 minutes each, then cool.
Stir 1 tbsp Anveshan Honey into the 6 tbsp green chutney to round its sharpness, and whisk the 2 cups yogurt thin with 0.5 tsp salt.
Finely chop 1 onion and 1 cucumber and toss with 2 tbsp lime juice and 0.25 tsp black salt for a crunchy fresh relish.
Crack open each shell and fill with boiled chickpeas, the onion-cucumber relish and a spoon of the thin curd.
Spoon over the honeyed green chutney generously, dust with 1.5 tsp roasted cumin and 0.75 tsp black salt, shower with coriander, and serve immediately while sharp and crisp.
tips: Keep the curd thin and lightly salted here so the green chutney and lime stay in the lead.
Salt the onion and cucumber only just before filling so they stay crunchy and do not weep.
Loosen the green chutney with a little water if needed so it drizzles rather than sits in clumps.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with extra lime wedges and a small bowl of the green chutney for those who want it fiercer.

variations.name: Classic Kendrapada Rasabali
variations.description: The famous temple sweet of Kendrapada, where soft chhena patties are deep-fried to a reddish gold and soaked in thick, cardamom-scented reduced milk. The flat discs drink up the rabri until they turn pillowy and molten, delivering a melt-in-the-mouth richness offered daily to Lord Baladevjew.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the chhena patties are traditionally fried in pure bilona ghee, which gives them their reddish colour and rich aroma

steps: Bring the 1 litre milk to a boil in a heavy pan and simmer on medium-low for 25 minutes, stirring often, until it reduces by half to a thick rabri, then stir in 0.5 cup sugar and 0.25 tsp cardamom and switch off.
Knead the 1.5 cups fresh chhena with 2 tbsp semolina, 1 tbsp maida and 0.125 tsp baking soda for 6 minutes until smooth and pliable.
Divide the dough into 10 balls, flatten each into a small disc about 5 cm wide, and press a slight dimple in the centre so it cooks evenly.
Heat 1 cup Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai to a gentle medium heat and fry the discs in batches for 5 to 6 minutes, turning, until they are deep reddish-gold on both sides, then drain.
Slip the fried patties gently into the warm rabri along with the remaining 0.25 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp black pepper, and simmer on very low for 5 minutes so they absorb the milk.
Rest the rasabali for at least 2 hours so the patties soak up the rabri and turn soft, then garnish with 10 sliced cashews and serve.
tips: Fry the patties on medium heat only; too hot and they brown outside while staying raw within.
The pinch of black pepper is the authentic Kendrapada touch that cuts the richness of the rabri.
Rasabali tastes best after a few hours of soaking, so make it ahead and let the patties drink up the milk.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve slightly warm or chilled in a shallow bowl with plenty of rabri spooned over, garnished with cashews and a few strands of saffron.

variations.name: Saffron Kesar Rasabali
variations.description: A luxurious version where the rabri is infused with saffron and a hint of rose, turning the soaking milk a glowing gold and lending a floral perfume to the soft chhena patties. Slivered almonds and pistachios crown each disc, making this the wedding-feast rasabali that looks as opulent as it tastes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: saffron steeped in warm milk turns the rabri golden and gives the rasabali its regal floral aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee fries the patties to an even gold and enriches the saffron rabri

steps: Steep 0.25 tsp Anveshan Saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk taken from the litre, and reduce the remaining milk in a heavy pan for 25 minutes until thick and creamy.
Stir 0.66 cup sugar, the saffron milk, 0.5 tsp cardamom and 1 tsp rose water into the reduced rabri and simmer for 2 minutes, then switch off.
Knead the 1.5 cups chhena with 2 tbsp semolina and 0.125 tsp baking soda for 6 minutes until smooth, then shape into 10 flat discs with a centre dimple.
Heat 1 cup Anveshan Ghee to gentle medium heat and fry the discs for 5 to 6 minutes, turning, until evenly golden, then drain on a rack.
Lower the fried patties into the warm saffron rabri and simmer on very low for 5 minutes so they begin absorbing the fragrant milk.
Chill the rasabali for 2 hours, then garnish generously with slivered almonds and pistachios before serving in the glowing golden rabri.
tips: Bloom the saffron in warm milk rather than water so it dissolves fully into the rabri for an even colour.
Keep a few strands of saffron aside to scatter on top for a striking finish.
Add the rose water off the heat so its delicate aroma is not cooked away.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled in small glass bowls so the golden rabri shows through, topped with a shower of nuts and rose petals for a festive dessert.

variations.name: Jaggery Rabri Rasabali
variations.description: A wholesome countryside take where the reduced milk is sweetened with jaggery instead of sugar, giving the rabri a warm caramel-brown hue and a deep, earthy sweetness. The molasses notes of jaggery pair beautifully with the ghee-fried chhena, making this a rustic, mineral-rich version of the temple classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery gives the rabri a caramel depth and earthy sweetness that plain sugar cannot, without splitting the milk when added off heat

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee fries the patties reddish-gold and complements the molasses notes of the jaggery rabri

steps: Reduce the 1 litre milk in a heavy pan over medium-low heat for 25 minutes, stirring often, until thick, then take it off the heat and let it cool to warm.

Melt 0.66 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 3 tbsp water into a syrup, strain out grit, and stir it into the warm rabri off the heat with 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp dry ginger so the milk does not curdle.
Knead the 1.5 cups chhena with 2 tbsp semolina, 1 tbsp maida and 0.125 tsp baking soda for 6 minutes until smooth, then form 10 dimpled discs.
Heat 1 cup Anveshan Ghee to gentle medium heat and fry the discs for 5 to 6 minutes until reddish-gold, then drain well.
Slide the fried patties into the warm jaggery rabri and warm gently on the lowest heat for 4 minutes without boiling so the milk stays smooth.
Rest the rasabali for 2 hours to soak, then garnish with chopped walnuts and serve in the caramel-toned rabri.
tips: Add the jaggery syrup only after the milk is off the boil, or the acidity in jaggery will split the rabri.
The pinch of dry ginger keeps this richer jaggery version easy to digest and adds a subtle warmth.
Strain the jaggery syrup well so no grit clouds the smooth rabri.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm on a cold evening with the caramel rabri pooled around the patties, finished with toasted walnuts for a rustic winter dessert.

variations.name: Baked Nut-Stuffed Rasabali
variations.description: A modern lighter twist where the chhena discs are stuffed with a khoya and nut filling, gently baked instead of deep-fried, then bathed in a slim, quick rabri. Baking keeps the patties tender with far less fat, while the hidden nutty core turns each bite into a small surprise.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a light brushing of bilona ghee before baking keeps the patties moist and golden without deep-frying

steps: Reduce the 750 ml milk with 0.33 cup sugar and 0.25 tsp cardamom in a heavy pan for 18 minutes to a pourable rabri, then stir in 3 tbsp condensed milk and switch off.
Mash the 0.25 cup khoya with 3 tbsp chopped nuts and a pinch of cardamom to make a stuffing, and shape it into 8 small pellets.

Knead the 1.5 cups chhena with 2 tbsp semolina, 1 tbsp cornflour and 0.125 tsp baking soda for 6 minutes until smooth, divide into 8 balls, flatten each, place a khoya pellet inside and seal into a stuffed disc.
Brush the discs all over with 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, arrange on a lined tray, and bake in an oven preheated to 190C for 18 to 20 minutes until golden and set.
Slip the warm baked patties into the rabri and let them soak on the lowest heat for 4 minutes so the milk seeps into the tender chhena.
Chill the stuffed rasabali for 1 hour, spoon over extra rabri, and garnish with a few chopped nuts before serving.
tips: Seal the stuffed discs carefully with no cracks so the khoya filling does not leak out while baking.
The cornflour helps bind the baked patties, giving them structure without deep-frying.
Bake just until golden; overbaking dries out the chhena and it will not soak up the rabri well.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled, cut a patty open at the table to reveal the nutty core, with extra rabri and a sprinkle of rose petals for a lighter festive finish.

variations.name: Classic Instant Rava Dhokla
variations.description: The quickest dhokla of all: a semolina-and-curd batter that needs no fermentation and steams into a soft, moist sponge in minutes. The rava gives it a gentle grainy bite the classic besan version lacks, finished with the essential mustard-curry-leaf temper. This is the go-to when unexpected guests arrive and chai is already on.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A spoon in the batter and the rest for the mustard tempering

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Melted into the tempering water for the classic sweet-sour finish

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups fine semolina with 3/4 cup curd, 1 tbsp green chilli-ginger paste, 3/4 tsp salt, 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and 1 tbsp lemon juice, adding a little water to a thick, smooth pouring batter, and rest 10 minutes so the rava swells.
Bring the steamer water to a rolling boil and grease a dhokla tin generously.
Sprinkle 1 tsp Eno over the batter, fold gently as it froths and expands, then pour immediately into the greased tin and level the top.
Steam on high heat for 12-14 minutes until the sponge springs back and a skewer inserted in the centre comes out clean.
Cool 10 minutes, run a knife around the edge and cut into squares or diamonds.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tsp sesame seeds and 10 curry leaves, add 1/2 cup water with 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, boil 2 minutes and pour evenly over the dhokla so it drinks the syrup.
tips: Rest the batter at least ten minutes so the rava absorbs moisture; skip this and the dhokla turns dry and dense.
Steam the moment Eno is folded in, because the trapped air starts escaping within a minute.
If the sponge looks dry, spoon a little extra warm tempering water over it and let it soak in.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with green coriander chutney and a sweet date-tamarind chutney, garnished with fresh coriander and grated coconut.

variations.name: Mixed Vegetable Rava Dhokla
variations.description: A colourful, wholesome upgrade with grated carrot, green peas and capsicum folded through the semolina batter, turning each square into a confetti of vegetables. The veg adds sweetness, crunch and nutrition, making it a favourite for children's tiffins. Softer and more substantial than the plain version.

ingredients.name: Green peas
ingredients.note: Lightly boiled so they stay bright and tender in the sponge

ingredients.name: Capsicum
ingredients.note: Finely chopped for colour and a mild crunch

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: In the batter and the tempering to keep the veg-loaded sponge moist

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: For the sweet-sour tempering water

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups fine semolina with 3/4 cup curd, 1 tbsp green chilli-ginger paste, 3/4 tsp salt, 1 tsp oil and 1 tbsp lemon juice into a thick batter and rest 10 minutes.
Fold in 1/3 cup grated carrot, 1/4 cup boiled green peas, 1/4 cup chopped capsicum and 2 tbsp coriander, loosening with a little water if the batter has thickened.
Set the steamer boiling, grease a tin, then sprinkle 1 tsp Eno over the batter and fold gently until frothy.
Pour into the tin, level the surface so the vegetables spread evenly, and steam on high 13-15 minutes until a skewer comes out clean.
Cool 10 minutes and cut into squares dotted with the coloured vegetables.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds and 10 curry leaves, add 1/2 cup water with 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer 2 minutes and pour over the dhokla.
tips: Pat the grated vegetables dry before folding them in, or their moisture will slacken the batter.
Boil the peas only briefly so they keep their colour and do not sink to the bottom of the sponge.
Chop the vegetables small and even so every square gets a fair share and cuts cleanly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a colourful lunchbox snack with mint chutney, or plate for guests topped with pomegranate seeds and coriander.

variations.name: Palak Rava Dhokla
variations.description: A vivid green rava dhokla enriched with fresh spinach puree and a hint of garlic, giving an earthy depth and a beautiful colour. The spinach keeps the sponge extra moist while adding iron and goodness. A garlicky sesame tempering finishes it with a savoury, almost South-Indian edge.

ingredients.name: Spinach puree
ingredients.note: Blanched and blended smooth for colour and moisture

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: In the batter and the garlicky tempering for a toasty, savoury finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: Balances the earthy spinach in the tempering water

ingredients.name: Garlic cloves
ingredients.note: Slivered for the tempering

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups fine semolina with 1/2 cup curd, 1/2 cup spinach puree, 1 tbsp green chilli-ginger paste, 3/4 tsp salt, 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and 2 tsp lemon juice into a thick green batter and rest 10 minutes.
Set the steamer boiling and grease a tin while the batter swells.
Sprinkle 1 tsp Eno over the batter, fold gently until pale and frothy, then pour into the tin and level the top.
Steam on high 13-15 minutes until the green sponge springs back and a skewer comes out clean, then cool 10 minutes and cut into squares.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, add 4 slivered garlic cloves and fry to pale gold, then crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tsp sesame seeds and 10 curry leaves.
Pour in 1/3 cup water with 1 tbsp Anveshan Khandsari, boil 2 minutes and spoon the garlicky temper over the dhokla so it soaks in.
tips: Blanch the spinach only briefly and cool it before blending, so the batter keeps its bright green.
Do not skip resting; the rava needs time to soften even with the spinach moisture.
Fry the garlic just to gold, since burnt garlic will turn the delicate temper bitter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the green squares with a cooling boondi raita and a garlic chutney for a savoury, iron-rich snack.

variations.name: Masala Tadka Rava Dhokla
variations.description: A punchier rava dhokla spiked with roasted cumin, crushed pepper and chaat masala in the batter, then drenched in a generous chilli-and-sesame tempering. Where the classic is mellow, this one carries real spice and a tangy finish. Built for those who like their dhokla with attitude.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: In the batter and for the spicy tempering

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Balances the extra chilli in the sweet-sour temper

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups fine semolina with 3/4 cup curd, 1 tbsp green chilli-ginger paste, 1 tsp roasted cumin, 1/2 tsp crushed pepper, 1 tsp chaat masala, 3/4 tsp salt, 1 tsp oil and 1 tbsp lemon juice into a thick batter and rest 10 minutes.
Set the steamer boiling and grease a tin, then sprinkle 1 tsp Eno over the batter and fold gently until frothy.
Pour into the tin, level the top and steam on high 12-14 minutes until a skewer comes out clean.
Cool 10 minutes and cut into squares.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp sesame seeds, then add 4 slit green chillies and 12 curry leaves and fry 20 seconds.
Pour in 1/2 cup water with 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, boil 2 minutes and drench the dhokla, laying the fried chillies on top.
tips: Toast the cumin fresh for the masala; stale cumin powder mutes the whole batter.
Load the tempering with extra green chillies if you want it fiery, then remove them before serving to control the heat.
A final dusting of chaat masala over the cut squares sharpens the tang just before serving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these spicy squares with a cooling cucumber raita and extra green chutney to temper the heat.

variations.name: Classic Bangalore Vegetable Saagu
variations.description: The pale, fragrant Karnataka mixed-vegetable gravy built on a freshly ground paste of coconut, roasted gram and fennel, the everyday companion to set dosa and poori in Bangalore darshinis. Soft-cooked carrot, beans and potato float in a mildly spiced, coconut-scented sauce that is comforting rather than fiery.

ingredients.name: Mixed vegetables (carrot, beans, potato, peas)
ingredients.note: diced small and even

ingredients.name: Fresh coconut
ingredients.note: grated, for the ground paste

ingredients.name: Roasted gram
ingredients.note: pottukadalai, for body

ingredients.name: Coriander leaves
ingredients.note: a handful for the fresh green paste

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed neutral oil that keeps the saagu light and lets the coconut lead

steps: Grind 1/2 cup grated coconut, 2 tbsp roasted gram, 1 tsp fennel seeds, 3 green chillies and 1/4 cup coriander leaves with a little water into a smooth pale-green paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sunflower Oil in a pan over medium heat, splutter 1/2 tsp mustard and 1/2 tsp cumin seeds with 1 sprig curry leaves for 20 seconds.
Add the chopped onion and saute for 3 minutes until translucent, taking care not to brown it so the saagu stays pale.
Tip in the 3 cups diced vegetables with 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 1.5 cups water, cover and simmer for 12 minutes until fork-tender.
Stir in the ground coconut paste with another 1/2 cup water and simmer on low for 5 minutes until the gravy thickens to a light, spoonable consistency.
Taste and adjust salt, then rest covered for 2 minutes so the fennel and coconut aromas settle before serving.
tips: Dice the vegetables small and uniform so they all cook tender at the same time.
Keep the onion pale and the flame gentle after adding the coconut paste to preserve the delicate colour.
Add a splash of hot water if the saagu thickens on standing, as it firms up as the coconut sets.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with spongy set dosa, poori or rava idli, the classic Karnataka tiffin trio.

variations.name: Kurma-style Cashew Saagu
variations.description: The richer darshini-hotel saagu where soaked cashews join the coconut grind for a plush, ivory gravy with a faint sweetness. A pinch of garam whole spices and a ghee tempering make it fuller and more festive than the everyday version, ideal when the saagu is the centrepiece.

ingredients.name: Mixed vegetables (carrot, beans, potato, cauliflower)
ingredients.note: diced small

ingredients.name: Fresh coconut
ingredients.note: grated

ingredients.name: Cashew nuts
ingredients.note: soaked, for a creamy grind

ingredients.name: Poppy seeds
ingredients.note: soaked, for body

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the aromatic fat that gives this hotel-style saagu its plush finish

steps: Soak 12 cashews and 1 tbsp poppy seeds for 15 minutes, then grind with 1/3 cup coconut and 3 green chillies into a smooth, creamy white paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat, sizzle the 1 inch cinnamon and 2 cardamoms for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the chopped onion and cook for 3 minutes until soft, then stir in 1 tsp ginger-garlic paste and the chopped tomato and cook for 3 minutes until pulpy.
Add the 3 cups diced vegetables with 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 1.5 cups water, cover and simmer for 12 minutes until tender.
Lower the heat and stir in the cashew-coconut paste with 1/2 cup water, simmering gently for 5 minutes until the gravy turns thick, creamy and pale ivory.
Warm through for 2 more minutes without boiling hard so the cashew gravy stays smooth, then serve.
tips: Soaked cashews and poppy seeds blend into a silkier paste than dry ones and enrich the gravy noticeably.
Keep the heat low once the paste goes in so the creamy gravy does not catch or split.
A few extra soaked cashews thicken the saagu without any flour if you like it plusher.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft set dosa, akki roti or a buttery poori for a slightly indulgent Karnataka breakfast.

variations.name: Mangalore Roasted-Coconut Saagu
variations.description: A coastal twist where coconut and spices are dry-roasted golden before grinding, giving the vegetable saagu a deeper amber colour and a toasty, aromatic body. Tempered in coconut oil with curry leaves, it trades the pale mildness of the city version for a warm, roasted coastal character.

ingredients.name: Mixed vegetables (carrot, beans, potato, chayote)
ingredients.note: diced

ingredients.name: Fresh coconut
ingredients.note: grated, to be roasted golden

ingredients.name: Chana dal
ingredients.note: for the roast-and-grind masala

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: sliced

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the coastal fat that deepens the roasted-coconut aroma of this saagu

ingredients.name: Tamarind
ingredients.note: for a faint coastal tang

steps: In a dry pan on low heat, roast 1 tbsp coriander seeds, 1 tbsp chana dal, 3 dry red chillies and 1 tsp fennel for 3 minutes, then add 1/2 cup coconut and roast 3 more minutes until golden and fragrant.
Cool the roasted mixture and grind it with a little tamarind and water into a smooth amber paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan over medium heat, splutter 1/2 tsp mustard seeds and 2 sprigs curry leaves for 20 seconds.
Add the sliced onion and fry for 4 minutes until light golden, then add the 3 cups diced vegetables with 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 1.5 cups water.
Cover and simmer for 12 minutes until the vegetables are tender, then stir in the roasted coconut paste with 1/2 cup water.
Simmer on low for 6 minutes until the saagu turns thick and amber with a toasty aroma, and serve warm.
tips: Roast the coconut only to a light gold, not brown, so the saagu stays warm-toned rather than dark and bitter.
The tiny bit of tamarind is what balances the roasted sweetness, so do not skip it.
Chayote and potato hold their shape well and suit this heartier coastal gravy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with neer dosa, red-rice sannas or plain rice for a coastal Karnataka spread.

variations.name: Tomato Rava Saagu
variations.description: A brighter, tomato-forward saagu thickened lightly with roasted semolina instead of a heavy coconut grind, giving a tangy, quick-cooking gravy popular with rava idli and dosa. Fresh coriander and green chilli keep it lively, while the tomato base makes it lighter and more piquant than the coconut classics.

ingredients.name: Mixed vegetables (potato, peas, carrot)
ingredients.note: diced small

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: chopped, for a tangy base

ingredients.name: Roasted semolina
ingredients.note: rava, for a light thickening

ingredients.name: Fresh coconut
ingredients.note: a small amount, ground with the chillies

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil that stands up to the tangy tomato base without turning heavy

ingredients.name: Coriander leaves
ingredients.note: chopped, to finish

steps: Grind 2 tbsp coconut with 3 green chillies and a splash of water into a coarse paste and set aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan over medium heat, splutter 1/2 tsp mustard and 1/2 tsp cumin seeds with 1 sprig curry leaves.
Add the chopped onion and saute for 3 minutes, then add the 3 chopped tomatoes with 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt and cook for 5 minutes until soft and pulpy.
Add the 2.5 cups diced vegetables with 1.5 cups water, cover and simmer for 10 minutes until tender and the tomato has melted into the gravy.
Sprinkle in 1 tbsp roasted semolina while stirring briskly to avoid lumps, then add the coconut-chilli paste and simmer for 4 minutes until lightly thickened.
Stir in 3 tbsp chopped coriander, cook for 1 minute, and serve the tangy saagu hot.
tips: Roast the semolina beforehand and add it in a thin stream while stirring so it thickens smoothly without clumping.
Use ripe, tangy tomatoes; this saagu leans on their acidity rather than tamarind for brightness.
Keep it slightly loose as the semolina continues to absorb liquid as it stands.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with rava idli, masala dosa or plain steamed rice for a quick, tangy tiffin.

variations.name: Classic Mixed Vegetable Santula
variations.description: Santula is Odisha's gentle, everyday stew of boiled vegetables lightly seasoned with garlic, green chilli and a cumin tempering. Barely spiced so the natural sweetness of the vegetables shines, it is home cooking at its most comforting, light on the stomach yet deeply satisfying with rice.

ingredients.name: Potato
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Brinjal
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Raw Papaya
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Pumpkin
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Green Chilli
ingredients.note: slit

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: crushed

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil for the classic pungent Odia tempering

ingredients.name: Coriander Leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Boil the cubed potato, brinjal, raw papaya and pumpkin with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 3 slit green chillies, 1 tsp salt and 2 cups water on medium heat for 12-15 minutes until just tender.
Lightly mash a few pieces against the side of the pan to thicken the broth while leaving most chunks whole.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, then lower the heat to mellow it.
Splutter 1 tsp cumin seeds and 2 dry red chillies in the oil, add 4 crushed garlic cloves, and fry until the garlic turns pale gold.
Pour this tempering into the boiled vegetables, stir gently, and simmer everything together for 3-4 minutes.
Finish with chopped coriander and serve the santula warm, keeping it soupy rather than dry.
tips: Do not over-spice; santula is meant to taste clean and gentle, letting each vegetable come through.
Crush rather than chop the garlic so it perfumes the oil without leaving raw bites.
Mash a couple of potato pieces into the broth to give the light stew a little natural body.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or alongside dal and a fried papad for a simple meal.

variations.name: Dahi Santula
variations.description: A creamy variant where whisked curd is stirred into the boiled vegetables off the heat, giving the light stew a gentle tang and silky body. Milder than the mustard-oil classic, it is soothing comfort food often made for those recovering from illness.

ingredients.name: Bottle Gourd (Lauki)
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Potato
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Carrot
ingredients.note: diced

ingredients.name: Whisked Curd
ingredients.note: at room temperature

ingredients.name: Green Chilli
ingredients.note: slit

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: carries the mild cumin tempering that suits the curd-based stew

ingredients.name: Coriander Leaves
ingredients.note: chopped

steps: Boil the cubed lauki, potato and diced carrot with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 slit green chillies, 1 tsp salt and 1.5 cups water on medium heat for 12 minutes until soft.
Lower the flame and let the mixture cool slightly so the curd will not split when added.
Whisk 0.75 cup curd smooth, stir it gently into the warm vegetables, and warm through on low heat without boiling.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan and splutter 1 tsp cumin seeds with 1 sprig curry leaves until aromatic.
Pour the ghee tempering over the dahi santula and fold it in gently.
Finish with chopped coriander and serve the santula warm and creamy.
tips: Always add the curd off high heat and stir constantly so it stays smooth and does not curdle.
Use fresh, not very sour, curd for a mellow tang that suits this soothing stew.
Keep the vegetables soft and the stew loose, as the curd thickens it as it stands.
