variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with soft steamed rice, ideal as a light and soothing meal on a tired day.

variations.name: Sajana Chuin Santula
variations.description: A spring-season santula built around tender drumsticks, whose fragrant pods perfume the whole stew, rounded out with potato and a handful of moong dal for body. The soft drumstick pulp and mildly thickened broth make it a seasonal favourite eaten by drawing the pods through your teeth.

ingredients.name: Drumstick
ingredients.note: cut into 3 inch pieces

ingredients.name: Potato
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Yellow Moong Dal
ingredients.note: for light body

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Green Chilli
ingredients.note: slit

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: crushed

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil for a clean tempering that lets the drumstick shine

steps: Rinse 3 tbsp moong dal and boil it with the drumstick pieces, cubed potato, chopped tomato, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 2.5 cups water on medium heat for 15 minutes.
Add the slit green chillies and simmer until the drumsticks are tender and the dal has dissolved into a light broth.
Lightly mash the potato into the broth to give the santula a gentle body.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, splutter 1 tsp cumin seeds and 2 dry red chillies, then add 3 crushed garlic cloves and fry to pale gold.
Pour the tempering into the stew and simmer everything together for 4 minutes.
Serve the sajana chuin santula warm, eating the drumsticks by drawing the soft pulp from the pods.
tips: Choose plump, fresh drumsticks whose pulp scoops out easily rather than woody, fibrous ones.
The spoon of moong dal is enough to lightly thicken the broth without turning it into a dal.
Add the drumsticks early so they cook fully and release their fragrance into the stew.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with steamed rice, letting everyone suck the tender pulp from the drumstick pods at the table.

variations.name: Saga Santula
variations.description: A greens-forward santula where a bunch of spinach or amaranth leaves wilts into the boiled vegetables, turning the stew earthy and iron-rich. A garlic-heavy mustard tempering lifts the greens, making it a nourishing everyday dish from the Odia kitchen.

ingredients.name: Spinach (Palak)
ingredients.note: roughly chopped

ingredients.name: Potato
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Pumpkin
ingredients.note: cubed

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: sliced

ingredients.name: Green Chilli
ingredients.note: slit

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: crushed

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil whose pungency lifts the earthy greens

steps: Boil the cubed potato and pumpkin with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 2 slit green chillies, 1 tsp salt and 1.5 cups water on medium heat for 10 minutes until nearly soft.
Add 3 cups chopped spinach and cook 4-5 minutes until the leaves wilt and collapse into the stew.
Lightly mash some potato to bind the greens and vegetables into a cohesive stew.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the heat, and splutter 1 tsp cumin seeds with 2 dry red chillies.
Add the sliced onion and 6 crushed garlic cloves to the oil and fry until golden and fragrant.
Pour the tempering over the greens, simmer 3 minutes, and serve the saga santula warm.
tips: Add the greens only after the harder vegetables are nearly done so they keep their colour and freshness.
This version welcomes plenty of garlic, which stands up well to the earthy spinach.
Use amaranth or any local seasonal greens in place of spinach for an equally authentic result.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with rice and a dollop of ghee, or as an iron-rich side with dal and roti.

variations.name: Classic Sattu Litti
variations.description: The definitive Bihari sattu litti is a firm wheat ball packed with tangy roasted-gram flour, kalonji, pickle masala and mustard oil, roasted over coals until the shell cracks and blisters. Drenched in warm ghee, its nutty, pungent filling is deeply satisfying.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: the heritage wheat forms a firm litti shell that roasts to a cracked crust

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: roasted-gram sattu is the tangy, protein-rich core of the litti

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: warm ghee is drizzled over and into the roasted littis for the classic rich finish

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and about ¾ cup water into a firm, non-sticky dough and rest it covered for 25 minutes.

In a bowl mix 1.25 cups Anveshan Sattu with the crushed garlic, grated ginger, chopped green chillies, 1 tsp nigella seeds, 1 tsp ajwain, 2 tbsp pickle masala, 3 tbsp mustard oil, 2 tbsp lemon juice, coriander and the remaining salt.
Sprinkle in a little water so the sattu filling just clumps together while staying crumbly.
Divide the dough into 10 balls, flatten each into a cup, pack in the sattu filling, seal the edges and roll back into smooth balls.
Roast the littis over glowing charcoal or in a 220 C oven for 25 to 30 minutes, turning every few minutes, until the shells are cracked, browned and cooked through.
Tap off any ash and, while still hot, dip each litti in the remaining warm Anveshan Ghee so it soaks into the cracks.
Rest the littis for two minutes so the ghee absorbs, then serve hot.
tips: Moisten the sattu filling only lightly, as a wet stuffing steams the shell and stops it cracking.
Turn the littis often over the coals so they roast evenly without one side charring.
Dunk them in ghee the moment they come off the heat so it seeps deep into the filling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with baingan bharta or a bowl of thin arhar dal and sliced onion with green chilli.

variations.name: Pyaaz Sattu Litti
variations.description: This herbier litti folds finely chopped onion, mint and coriander into the sattu for a fresher, juicier filling with extra crunch. The aromatics keep the stuffing moist and lively, making it a popular market-stall version across Patna.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: forms the firm litti shell around the moist onion-herb filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: the roasted-gram base that soaks up the onion and herb juices

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: drizzled over the roasted littis for the traditional rich finish

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and about ¾ cup water into a firm dough and rest covered for 25 minutes.
Finely chop the large onion, mint and coriander and mix with 1.25 cups Anveshan Sattu, the crushed garlic, chopped green chillies and 1 tsp ajwain.
Add 3 tbsp mustard oil, 2 tbsp lemon juice and the remaining salt, tossing lightly so the herbs and onion stay distinct and the mix is just moist.
Divide the dough into 10 balls, cup each, pack in the onion-herb sattu, seal and roll into smooth balls.
Roast over charcoal or in a 220 C oven for 25 to 30 minutes, turning, until the shells crack and brown.
Dip the hot littis in the remaining warm Anveshan Ghee so it seeps into the fragrant filling.
Rest for two minutes and serve warm while the onion and herbs are still juicy inside.
tips: Squeeze a little water from the chopped onion so the filling stays moist but not wet.
Fill and roast promptly, as the salted onion will keep releasing juice if the mix sits too long.
Fresh mint added just before stuffing keeps its lift, so do not chop it far ahead.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling boondi raita and a spoon of lemon pickle to echo the tangy filling.

variations.name: Baati-style Sattu Litti
variations.description: Baked low and slow like a Rajasthani baati, this litti develops a thick, hard, deeply golden crust that crumbles when cracked open. Sturdier and longer-keeping than the coal-roasted version, it is made to be soaked generously in ghee and dal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: bakes into the thick, hard, crumbly baati-style crust

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: the roasted-gram filling that stays firm inside the baked shell

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: some binds the dough and the rest generously soaks the baked baatis

steps: Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.25 cup semolina, 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, 0.5 tsp salt and just enough water into a stiff, tight dough, then rest 25 minutes and preheat the oven to 200 C.

Mix 1.25 cups Anveshan Sattu with the crushed garlic, grated ginger, green chillies, 1 tsp ajwain, 2 tbsp pickle masala, 3 tbsp mustard oil, 2 tbsp lemon juice and the remaining salt into a crumbly filling.
Divide the stiff dough into 10 balls, pack each with the sattu, seal tightly and shape into dense rounds.
Arrange the baatis on a tray and bake for 35 to 40 minutes, turning twice, until the crust is thick, hard and deep golden all over.
Let the baatis cool for a minute, then crack each open slightly so the centre can soak up fat.
Pour the remaining warm Anveshan Ghee generously over the cracked baatis so it soaks right through.
Serve hot while the crust is crumbly and saturated with ghee.
tips: Add semolina and keep the dough stiff so the shell bakes hard and crumbly like a true baati.
Bake slow and turn the baatis so the thick crust cooks through without burning.
Crack them open before adding ghee so the fat reaches the dense centre.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve baati-style crushed into a bowl of panchmel dal with an extra spoon of ghee on top.

variations.name: Classic Nylon Sev
variations.description: The fine, feather-light gram-flour noodles that top every plate of chaat and bhel across India. Called nylon sev for its almost translucent thinness, it shatters into a crisp, savoury tangle the moment it hits your tongue. A slack, well-oiled batter pressed through a fine die is the whole secret to that delicate crunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: For deep-frying; keeps the fine strands pale and glassy without any heavy aftertaste

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Rubbed into the flour as moyan so the sev fries up shatter-crisp rather than hard

steps: Sift 2 cups besan into a bowl with 1 tsp salt, 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1/2 tsp red chilli powder, 1/4 tsp asafoetida and a scant 1/8 tsp baking soda so there are no lumps.
Rub 2 tbsp warm melted Anveshan Ghee into the flour for 2 minutes, then whisk in about 2/3 cup warm water to a smooth, lump-free batter the thickness of soft dough that just holds a shape.
Heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to a moderately high 180 C, testing with a drop of batter that should rise quickly with a steady sizzle.
Fill a sev press fitted with the finest die, hold it over the oil and press in slow circles so the thin strands fall in an even, lacy layer across the surface.
Fry just 30-45 seconds until the loud sizzling settles to a whisper and the sev turns pale gold; do not let it brown or it tastes bitter.
Lift with a slotted spoon onto kitchen paper, break gently into clusters, and cool fully so it crisps to a shatter.
tips: The batter must be soft enough to press easily; if your arm strains, beat in a tablespoon more warm water.
Fry in thin single layers rather than crowding the oil, which drops the temperature and makes soggy sev.
Cooled completely and stored airtight, nylon sev stays crisp for up to three weeks.
variations.servingSuggestion: Scatter generously over sev puri, bhel or a bowl of dahi to add instant crunch, or serve plain alongside evening chai.

variations.name: Ratlami Sev
variations.description: The famously aromatic sev from Ratlam in Malwa, thicker than nylon sev and heady with clove, black pepper and a hit of raw carom. Chickpea-based with a fragrant spice bloom worked right into the dough, it eats almost like a spiced namkeen on its own. One handful and the warm clove note tells you exactly where it comes from.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: For deep-frying the sturdier Malwa-style strands to an even crisp

ingredients.name: Cloves
ingredients.note: Dry-roasted and ground; the defining aroma of authentic Ratlami sev

ingredients.name: Black peppercorns
ingredients.note: Roasted with the cloves and ground coarse

steps: Dry-roast 6 cloves and 1 tsp peppercorns for a minute until fragrant, cool and grind coarse, then mix into 2 cups besan with 1 tsp ajwain, 1/2 tsp ginger powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1/2 tsp asafoetida and 1 tsp salt.
Heat 3 tbsp oil until smoking, pour over the spiced flour and stir, then rub in once bearable so the mix turns crumbly and clumps when pressed.
Knead in about 1/2 cup warm water to a firm-ish, smooth dough, cover and rest 10 minutes while heating 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to a moderate 175 C.
Load a sev press with a medium die and press the dough into the oil in wide circular sweeps so the thicker strands land loosely.
Fry 1-2 minutes, turning once, until the sizzle quietens and the sev is an even reddish-gold and crisp through.
Drain on a rack and cool fully; the clove aroma intensifies as it rests.
tips: Grind the cloves and pepper fresh each time; their volatile oils fade fast once powdered.
A medium die, not the finest one, gives Ratlami sev its characteristic sturdy bite.
Fry a shade deeper than nylon sev so the thicker strands crisp all the way to the centre.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a standalone teatime namkeen with a wedge of lemon, or crush over poha the Malwa way for a spiced crunch.

variations.name: Lasaniya Sev
variations.description: A punchy garlic sev beloved in Kathiawad, where a fiery paste of raw garlic and red chilli is beaten into the dough so every strand carries a pungent, spicy kick. Slightly thicker than nylon sev, it doubles as a fierce chaat topping and a snack in its own right. The aroma alone clears a room.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: For deep-frying; its neutral body lets the garlic and chilli dominate

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Worked into the dough as moyan; its toasty note deepens the garlic flavour

ingredients.name: Garlic cloves
ingredients.note: Crushed to a fine paste for maximum pungency in every strand

steps: Crush 12 garlic cloves to a smooth paste and mix into 2 cups besan along with 2 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1/2 tsp black pepper, 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1/8 tsp baking soda and 1 tsp salt.
Rub 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil into the flour for 2 minutes until it looks like damp crumbs, then knead in about 1/2 cup warm water to a smooth, slightly soft dough.
Rest the dough covered for 10 minutes and heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to a moderate 180 C.
Press the dough through a medium sev die directly into the oil in loose, sweeping circles so the strands stay separate.
Fry 45-60 seconds, turning once, until the strands are crisp and the garlic smells toasted rather than raw; keep the heat steady so they do not scorch.
Drain on paper and cool fully before breaking into clusters.
tips: Fry the garlic dough promptly; raw garlic paste can make the dough weep if it sits too long.
Use Kashmiri chilli for deep red colour with manageable heat, or half hot chilli if you want it fierce.
Because of the garlic, store this sev separately so its aroma does not travel to milder snacks.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pile onto sev tameta nu shaak or crush over a plate of dahi vada for a garlicky punch, or nibble straight with drinks.

variations.name: Palak Sev
variations.description: A vivid green sev made by kneading fresh spinach puree into the gram-flour dough, giving both colour and a mild earthy sweetness. Lighter on spice so the palak flavour shines, it is a favourite party namkeen and a striking chaat garnish. The spinach also lends a touch of moisture that fries into an extra-crisp strand.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: For deep-frying the green strands to a crisp without dulling their colour

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: The moyan that keeps spinach sev tender-crisp instead of brittle

ingredients.name: Fresh spinach puree
ingredients.note: Blanched and blended smooth, then cooled, for even green colour

steps: Blanch a handful of spinach for 30 seconds, refresh in cold water and blend to a smooth 1/2 cup puree, then cool it completely.
Mix 2 cups besan with 1 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp cumin powder, 1/2 tsp chaat masala, 1 tsp green chilli paste, 1/4 tsp asafoetida and 1/8 tsp baking soda.
Rub in 2 tbsp warm melted Anveshan Ghee, then knead with the cooled spinach puree, adding a spoon of water only if needed, to a smooth soft dough; the puree usually supplies enough moisture.
Rest the dough 10 minutes and heat 3 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to a moderate 180 C.
Press the dough through a fine sev die into the oil in even circular sweeps so the green strands fall in a lacy layer.
Fry 30-45 seconds until the sizzle drops and the sev is crisp but still bright green; over-frying will brown and dull it, so lift promptly and drain.
tips: Cool the spinach puree fully before kneading, or the warmth can activate the soda too early and slacken the dough.
Keep the oil at a steady moderate heat; too hot and the green turns khaki within seconds.
Blot the puree if very watery so you do not have to add extra besan and lose the colour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Use as a colourful topping for chaats and canapes, or serve in a bowl mixed with roasted peanuts and a squeeze of lemon.

variations.name: Classic Sprout Chaat
variations.description: Crunchy mixed sprouts are lightly steamed and tossed raw-fresh with onion, tomato, lime and chaat masala for a light, protein-rich snack. The nutty bite of the sprouts against the tangy dressing makes this the healthiest, quickest chaat to throw together.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a light toss in wood-pressed oil glosses the steamed sprouts and carries the spices

steps: Steam the 2 cups mixed sprouts for 6 to 7 minutes until just tender-crisp, then cool them under cold water and drain.
Toss the sprouts with 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil so they glisten and separate.
Add finely chopped 1 onion, 1 tomato, 1 cucumber and 2 green chillies to the sprouts.
Sprinkle over 1.5 tsp chaat masala, 1 tsp roasted cumin, 0.5 tsp black salt and 0.5 tsp salt.
Squeeze in 2 tbsp lime juice and toss everything until evenly coated in the tangy dressing.
Fold through the coriander and serve fresh at room temperature.
tips: Steam the sprouts only briefly so they stay crunchy rather than turning soft.
Cool them quickly under cold water to lock in the crunch and bright colour.
Add the tomato and lime just before serving so the chaat stays fresh and not watery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve fresh in bowls with an extra squeeze of lime and a pinch of chaat masala on top.

variations.name: Tadka Sprout Chaat
variations.description: Here the sprouts are cooked into a warm, spiced dry stir-fry with a cumin-mustard tempering, turmeric and ginger before a final squeeze of lime. Warm and savoury rather than salad-fresh, it eats like a quick sprout usal and is a heartier version for cooler days.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil carries the cumin-mustard tempering for a warm dry stir-fry

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan over medium heat and crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.5 tsp mustard seeds until they splutter.
Add finely chopped 1 onion and 1 inch grated ginger and saute for 3 minutes until the onion softens and turns pale gold.
Stir in 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp coriander powder and 0.5 tsp red chilli powder and fry for 30 seconds.
Add the 2 cups mixed sprouts with 0.75 tsp salt and a splash of water, cover, and cook for 6 to 7 minutes until tender but still nutty.
Uncover and toss on high heat for a minute so any water evaporates and the sprouts turn dry and glossy.
Take off the heat, sprinkle 1 tsp chaat masala and 1.5 tbsp lime juice, fold through the coriander, and serve warm.
tips: Bloom the whole cumin and mustard in hot oil first so the tempering flavours the whole dish.
Cook the sprouts covered with just a splash of water so they steam soft without going mushy.
Finish with lime off the heat so its brightness is not cooked away.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a light meal or snack with pav or rotli, topped with extra coriander and lime.

variations.name: Dahi Sprout Chaat
variations.description: A cooling bowl where steamed sprouts are dressed in thick whisked yogurt with tamarind and green chutneys, sev and pomegranate. The creamy curd tempers the raw crunch and the chutneys bring the sweet-sour street flavour, making a wholesome dahi-chaat that is still light.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: sweetens the whisked curd gently to balance the tang and spice

steps: Steam the 2 cups mixed sprouts for 6 minutes until just tender, cool under cold water, and drain well.
Whisk the 2 cups yogurt smooth with 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Honey, 0.5 tsp salt and a pinch of black salt until creamy.
Fold most of the cooled sprouts into the sweetened curd and spoon into bowls.
Drizzle over the tamarind and green chutneys in generous swirls.
Dust with 1.5 tsp chaat masala, 1 tsp roasted cumin and the remaining black salt.
Top with the reserved sprouts, pomegranate, sev and coriander, and serve chilled.
tips: Cool the steamed sprouts fully before folding them in so the curd stays thick.
Whisk the honey into the curd off any heat so its flavour stays fresh.
Add the sev only at serving so it keeps its crunch against the creamy sprouts.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled in bowls with extra pomegranate and a final drizzle of both chutneys on top.

variations.name: Sprout Bhel Chaat
variations.description: A Mumbai bhel twist that tosses the steamed sprouts with puffed rice, crushed papdi, chopped raw mango and both chutneys for a crackling, tangy jhaal-muri-like mix. The puffed rice and papdi bring crunch while the sprouts add protein, all dressed to order just before eating.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the tamarind chutney that binds the bhel with a deep natural note

steps: Steam the 1.5 cups mixed sprouts for 6 minutes until just tender, cool and drain thoroughly.
Simmer 2 tbsp tamarind with 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and a splash of water for 4 minutes into a thick sweet-sour chutney and cool it.
In a large dry bowl, combine the 2 cups puffed rice, the steamed sprouts, finely chopped 1 onion and 0.5 cup chopped raw mango.
Add the tamarind chutney, 3 tbsp green chutney, 1.5 tsp chaat masala and 0.5 tsp salt and toss quickly to coat.
Crush the 12 papdi coarsely and fold them in along with most of the sev.
Top with the remaining sev and coriander and serve immediately before the puffed rice softens.
tips: Dry the sprouts well so the puffed rice does not turn soggy when tossed.
Mix and dress the bhel only at the moment of serving so it stays crackling crisp.
The raw mango brings the tang, so add a little more if it is not sour enough.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at once in cones or bowls with extra sev and a wedge of lime for squeezing over.

variations.name: Classic Bengali Shukto
variations.description: The quintessential Bengali medley of mixed vegetables and bitter gourd in a pale, mildly bitter-sweet gravy thickened with a mustard-and-poppy-seed paste and a splash of milk. Traditionally served at the start of a meal to awaken the palate, it balances the bitterness of uchhe against sweet sweet-potato and creamy milk. The finishing spice is radhuni, the aroma that makes a shukto authentic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Wood-pressed mustard oil fries the vegetables and carries the mustard-poppy paste in this delicate medley

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A finishing spoon of bilona ghee rounds off the gentle bitterness of a classic shukto

steps: Cut the bitter gourd, raw banana, brinjal, sweet potato, radish and drumstick into finger-length batons; soak 1 tbsp mustard seeds and 1 tbsp poppy seeds in warm water for 15 minutes and grind to a smooth paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai on medium heat and fry 8 bori until golden and crisp, then remove; in the same oil lightly fry the bitter gourd batons for 3 minutes and set aside.
In the remaining oil temper 1 tsp panch phoron until it crackles, add 1 tbsp ginger paste, and fry for 40 seconds.
Add all the remaining vegetables with 1 tsp salt and 1.5 cups hot water, cover, and simmer on medium-low heat for 10 to 12 minutes until just tender.
Stir in the mustard-poppy paste and 1/2 cup milk on low heat, add back the fried bitter gourd, and simmer gently for 5 minutes without boiling hard so the milk does not split.
Crush the fried bori and scatter over the top, finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 1/2 tsp radhuni bloomed in a little hot ghee, and serve.
tips: Fry the bitter gourd separately and add it back at the end so its bitterness stays gentle and does not spread through the dish.
Keep the milk on low heat and never let it boil vigorously, or the shukto will curdle.
Radhuni is the signature finishing spice; if unavailable use a pinch of celery seed, but it truly makes the dish.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm at the very beginning of the meal with the first helping of steamed rice, before the dal and other dishes.

variations.name: Dudh Shukto
variations.description: A richer, creamier, less bitter version where a generous amount of milk and a smooth poppy-and-cashew paste dominate, giving a pale, almost sweet gravy with only a whisper of bitterness. There is no mustard paste here, so the flavour is mellow and comforting. This is the refined banquet shukto served to guests.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee replaces most of the mustard oil here for a gentler, milk-rich shukto suited to guests

steps: Soak 1.5 tbsp poppy seeds and 10 cashews in warm water for 15 minutes and grind to a very smooth, creamy paste.

Cut the bitter gourd, drumstick, raw banana, sweet potato and potato into batons; heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on medium heat and lightly fry the bitter gourd for 3 minutes, then set it aside.
In the same ghee temper 1 bay leaf and 1/2 tsp radhuni for 20 seconds, add 1 tbsp ginger paste, and fry for 40 seconds.
Add the remaining vegetables with 1 tsp salt and 1 cup hot water, cover, and simmer on medium-low heat for 12 minutes until tender.
Lower the heat and stir in the poppy-cashew paste and 1 cup milk with 1/2 tsp sugar, add back the fried bitter gourd, and warm gently for 5 minutes without boiling so the milk stays smooth.
Rest covered for 3 minutes to let the creamy gravy settle, then serve.
tips: Grinding the poppy and cashew to a truly smooth paste is what gives this its velvety body.
Use less bitter gourd than the classic so the milky sweetness comes through.
Warm the milk gently and keep the heat low throughout to avoid any curdling in this delicate gravy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as an elegant first course with hot rice, ahead of the richer dishes of a festive Bengali thali.

variations.name: Neem Begun Shukto
variations.description: A lighter, brothier springtime shukto where the bitterness comes from tender neem leaves fried crisp with brinjal, rather than bitter gourd. It uses fewer vegetables and no milk, giving a thin, clean, medicinal-tasting broth prized for its cleansing qualities. Traditionally eaten in the Bengali new-year season, it is bracing and simple.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Pungent mustard oil is needed to fry the neem leaves crisp and carry this bracing broth

steps: Cut the brinjal, raw banana, potato and radish into small batons and keep them ready.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until smoking, lower to medium, and fry 1/2 cup neem leaves for 1 minute until crisp and deep green, then lift them out.
In the same oil fry the brinjal batons for 3 minutes until lightly softened, then temper 1 tsp panch phoron and 1 dried red chilli for 20 seconds.
Add 1 tbsp ginger paste and fry for 40 seconds, then add the remaining vegetables, 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt with 2 cups hot water.
Cover and simmer on medium-low heat for 12 to 14 minutes until the vegetables are just tender and the broth is fragrant.
Crumble the fried neem leaves back over the top, simmer for 1 minute, and serve as a thin, clean broth.
tips: Fry the neem leaves only briefly until crisp; over-frying turns them harshly bitter.
This shukto is meant to be thin and broth-like, so do not thicken it with any paste.
Adding the crisp neem at the end keeps its bitterness bright rather than muddy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Sip alongside the first mouthfuls of plain rice at the start of a spring or new-year meal.

variations.name: Dry Bhaja Shukto
variations.description: An unusual near-dry version where the mixed vegetables and bitter gourd are stir-fried and coated in a thick mustard-poppy masala with almost no gravy, so it eats more like a dry sabzi with a bitter-sweet edge. Crisp fried bori are folded through for crunch. It is a modern, everyday adaptation for those who find the milky gravy too rich.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: A little extra mustard oil is needed to fry the vegetables to a dry, glossy coating

steps: Soak 1 tbsp mustard seeds and 1 tbsp poppy seeds in warm water for 15 minutes and grind to a thick, smooth paste; cut the vegetables into small even pieces.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a kadai until smoking, lower to medium, and fry 10 bori until golden and crisp, then remove.
Fry the bitter gourd pieces for 3 minutes until lightly crisp and set aside, then temper 1/2 tsp radhuni in the same oil for 15 seconds.
Add 1 tbsp ginger paste and all the remaining vegetables with 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, and stir-fry on medium heat for 8 minutes, sprinkling a little water only if they stick.
Add the thick mustard-poppy paste and cook for 4 to 5 minutes, tossing until it coats the vegetables and there is barely any liquid left.
Fold the fried bitter gourd and crushed bori through the dry mixture and serve warm.
tips: Keep the mustard-poppy paste thick so the finished dish stays dry and clinging, not saucy.
Do not over-grind the mustard or soak it too briefly, as under-processed mustard turns the dish sharply bitter.
Add the crisp bori at the very end so they keep their crunch against the soft vegetables.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a dry side with rice and a thin dal, offering the bitter-sweet note without a heavy gravy.

variations.name: Classic Til Pitha
variations.description: Til pitha is the beloved Magh Bihu sweet of Assam, a paper-thin crepe of glutinous bora rice flour cooked on a hot griddle and wrapped around a warm filling of roasted black sesame and jaggery. It has crisp folded edges, a soft chewy middle and a nutty, molasses-sweet centre that defines the harvest festival.

ingredients.name: Glutinous Rice Flour (Bora Saul)
ingredients.note: sticky rice flour, lightly dampened

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melts into the roasted sesame to make the classic molasses-sweet filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: brushes the finished rolls for a glossy, fragrant sheen

steps: Dry-roast 1 cup black sesame seeds in a pan on low heat for 3-4 minutes until they crackle and smell nutty, then cool and coarsely crush them.
Warm 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder in the same pan on low heat until just melted, mix in the crushed sesame and 0.25 tsp cardamom powder, and cook 2 minutes to a sticky filling.
Rub 3 tbsp water and a pinch of salt into 2 cups glutinous rice flour so it feels like damp sand that clumps when pressed, then pass it through a coarse sieve.
Heat a flat griddle on medium and sprinkle a thin, even layer of the damp flour in a rectangle; within a minute it melts and fuses into a soft translucent crepe.
Spread a line of the warm sesame-jaggery filling along one edge, then quickly roll the crepe over it into a tight log while it is still pliable.
Press the seam to seal, brush the roll with Anveshan Ghee, crisp it for 30 seconds on each side, and serve the til pitha warm.
tips: Keep the flour just damp, never wet; a wet mix will not melt into a crepe but form a paste instead.
Work fast once the crepe sets, as it cracks if you try to roll it after it cools and stiffens.
Make the filling a day ahead and warm it slightly before use so it spreads without tearing the delicate crepe.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a cup of red tea during Magh Bihu, or alongside a bowl of curd and extra jaggery for a festive breakfast.

variations.name: Narikol Til Pitha
variations.description: A coastal-Assam favourite where freshly grated coconut is roasted with jaggery and sesame into a moist, fudgy filling for the rice crepe. The coconut keeps the centre soft for days and adds a mellow sweetness that balances the toasty sesame.

ingredients.name: Glutinous Rice Flour (Bora Saul)
ingredients.note: lightly dampened for the crepe

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: binds the coconut and sesame into a fudgy narikol filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: greases the griddle and deepens the coconut aroma of the crepe

steps: Dry-roast 0.5 cup white sesame seeds on low heat for 3 minutes until pale gold, then set them aside.
In the same pan roast 1 cup grated coconut for 3-4 minutes until it smells sweet, add 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and cook until melted and sticky, then fold in the sesame and 0.5 tsp cardamom.
Rub 3 tbsp water and a pinch of salt into 2 cups glutinous rice flour until it clumps like damp sand, then sieve it coarsely.
Grease a flat griddle with a little Anveshan Coconut Oil, sprinkle a thin rectangle of the damp flour on medium heat, and let it melt into a soft crepe in about a minute.
Lay a generous line of the warm coconut filling along one edge and roll the crepe snugly around it while still warm.
Seal the seam, roast the roll for 30 seconds a side, and serve the narikol til pitha warm or at room temperature.
tips: Use fresh coconut for a moist filling; desiccated coconut turns the centre dry and crumbly.
Cook the coconut-jaggery mix until it leaves the sides of the pan so the filling does not leak while rolling.
These stay soft longer than the plain version thanks to the coconut, making them ideal to pack and gift.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a festive sweet with a glass of warm milk, or slice into rounds to plate alongside other Bihu treats.

variations.name: Khoya Til Pitha
variations.description: An indulgent take that enriches the sesame filling with milky khoya, turning the humble Bihu crepe into a mithai-like treat. The khoya melts into the jaggery and sesame for a rich, fudgy centre with a gentle cardamom perfume.

ingredients.name: Glutinous Rice Flour (Bora Saul)
ingredients.note: lightly dampened for the crepe

ingredients.name: Khoya (Mawa)
ingredients.note: grated

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: sweetens the khoya-sesame filling without overpowering the milk

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: cooks the khoya and gives the rolls a rich mithai-like finish

steps: Dry-roast 0.75 cup black sesame seeds on low heat for 3 minutes until they pop, then crush them coarsely.
Melt 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and cook 0.5 cup grated khoya on low heat for 3-4 minutes until it turns light golden and grainy, stirring so it does not catch.
Add 0.5 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder to the khoya, stir until it melts, then fold in the sesame, 0.5 tsp cardamom and 2 tbsp chopped almonds and cool to a soft filling.
Rub 3 tbsp water and a pinch of salt into 2 cups glutinous rice flour until it clumps, then sieve it coarsely.
On a medium griddle sprinkle a thin rectangle of the damp flour, let it fuse into a crepe in a minute, and lay a line of the khoya filling along one edge.
Roll the crepe tight, brush with the remaining Anveshan Ghee, crisp both sides briefly, and serve the khoya til pitha warm.
tips: Cook the khoya gently so it does not brown too much, which would make the filling taste burnt.
Let the khoya filling cool to just warm before rolling, as a piping-hot filling will tear the crepe.
For extra richness stir a spoon of chopped pistachios into the filling before folding.
variations.servingSuggestion: Plate warm and dust with a little extra cardamom, serving these as a dessert after a festive Assamese thali.

variations.name: Peanut-Sesame Til Pitha
variations.description: A crunchy modern twist that folds roasted peanuts into the sesame filling and finishes each roll with a thread of honey. The peanuts add a robust crunch and the honey glaze gives a glossy, floral sweetness distinct from the usual jaggery centre.

ingredients.name: Glutinous Rice Flour (Bora Saul)
ingredients.note: lightly dampened for the crepe

ingredients.name: Roasted Peanuts
ingredients.note: skinned and crushed

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: binds the peanut-sesame crunch into a sticky filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: drizzled over the finished rolls for a glossy floral glaze

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: lightly greases the griddle and echoes the peanut flavour

steps: Dry-roast 0.5 cup white sesame seeds for 3 minutes until pale gold, then coarsely crush them with 0.5 cup roasted skinned peanuts.
Warm 0.5 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder in a pan on low heat until melted, stir in the peanut-sesame crush and 0.25 tsp cinnamon powder, and cook 2 minutes to a sticky, crunchy filling.
Rub 3 tbsp water and a pinch of salt into 2 cups glutinous rice flour until it clumps like damp sand, then sieve coarsely.
Lightly grease a medium griddle with Anveshan Groundnut Oil, sprinkle a thin rectangle of the damp flour, and let it melt into a crepe within a minute.
Spoon a line of the peanut filling along one edge and roll the crepe firmly around it while still warm and flexible.
Crisp the roll for 30 seconds a side, drizzle 2 tbsp Anveshan Honey over the warm pithas, and serve at once.
tips: Crush the peanuts coarsely rather than to a powder so the filling keeps a satisfying crunch.
Add the honey only after the pithas are off the heat, since heating honey dulls its floral aroma.
Store any extra filling in an airtight jar; it doubles as a crunchy topping for curd or toast.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with an extra drizzle of honey and a sprinkle of crushed peanuts, delicious with masala chai.

variations.name: Classic Hyderabadi Tomato Kut
variations.description: A thick, tangy Hyderabadi tomato curry where ripe tomatoes are cooked down and lightly thickened with roasted gram flour, then finished with a fragrant garlic and curry-leaf tempering. Sweet-sour and comforting, this old Deccan home dish is traditionally spooned over rice with a boiled egg, kept purely vegetarian here.

ingredients.name: Ripe tomatoes
ingredients.note: roughly chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: roasted gram flour that thickens the kut smoothly with a nutty note

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: finely chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed gingelly oil for the authentic Deccan tempering

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: sliced, for the tempering

steps: Boil the 6 chopped tomatoes with 1 cup water for 8 minutes until completely soft, cool, then blend to a smooth puree and strain out the skins.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pan over medium heat, splutter 1/2 tsp cumin seeds, add the chopped onion and 3 slit green chillies, and fry for 4 minutes until soft.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste with 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp coriander powder, and cook for 2 minutes until fragrant.
Pour in the tomato puree with 1.25 tsp salt, bring to a simmer, and cook on medium-low for 10 minutes until it thickens and darkens.
Whisk 2 tbsp Anveshan Sattu into 1/2 cup water until lump-free, stir it into the simmering tomato and cook for 6 minutes until the kut turns thick and velvety.
In a small pan heat a little oil, fry 6 sliced garlic cloves until golden with 2 dry red chillies and 2 sprigs curry leaves, and pour this tempering over the kut before serving.
tips: Strain the tomato puree for a silky kut, or leave it rustic if you prefer some texture.
Whisk the sattu into cold water before adding so it never forms lumps in the hot curry.
The kut should be thick enough to coat a spoon; simmer longer if it stays watery.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle over hot steamed rice with a spoon of ghee, or scoop with soft phulka for a comforting meal.

variations.name: Peanut Tomato Kut
variations.description: A richer version thickened with a ground roasted-peanut paste instead of gram flour, giving the tomato curry a creamy, nutty body and a fuller mouthfeel. The peanuts round the tang of the tomatoes into a satisfying, protein-rich gravy.

ingredients.name: Ripe tomatoes
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Roasted peanuts
ingredients.note: ground into a smooth paste

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil that echoes and deepens the peanut base

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: rounds the tomato tang against the nutty peanut base

steps: Blend the 6 chopped tomatoes to a smooth puree and grind 1/3 cup roasted peanuts with a little water into a thick paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan over medium heat, splutter 1/2 tsp mustard and 1/2 tsp cumin seeds with 2 sprigs curry leaves.
Add the chopped onion and 2 slit green chillies and fry for 4 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute.
Add 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp coriander powder, then pour in the tomato puree with 1.25 tsp salt and cook for 8 minutes until thick.
Stir in the peanut paste with 3/4 cup water and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, and simmer on low for 8 minutes until the kut turns creamy and the oil floats.
Adjust to a thick, spoonable consistency, cook for 2 more minutes, and serve hot.
tips: Grind the peanuts really smooth so the kut is creamy rather than gritty.
The peanut paste thickens fast, so keep a little hot water handy to loosen it.
A squeeze of lime at the end lifts the nutty richness if the tomatoes are not tangy enough.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over jeera rice or with millet roti, topped with a few crushed roasted peanuts.

variations.name: Andhra Tomato Pappu Kut
variations.description: An Andhra-leaning version where a little soft-cooked toor dal is folded into the tomato base for a heartier, protein-rich kut with a mellower tang. Between a curry and a thin dal, it is the everyday version that turns a bowl of rice into a full meal.

ingredients.name: Ripe tomatoes
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Toor dal
ingredients.note: pressure-cooked soft and mashed

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: the gingelly oil that gives the Andhra tempering its aroma

ingredients.name: Green chillies
ingredients.note: slit

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: crushed

steps: Pressure-cook 1/2 cup toor dal with 1.5 cups water and 1/2 tsp turmeric for 4 whistles until soft, then whisk smooth.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pan over medium heat, splutter 1/2 tsp mustard and 1/2 tsp cumin seeds with 2 dry red chillies, 1/4 tsp asafoetida and 2 sprigs curry leaves.
Add the chopped onion, 3 slit green chillies and 5 crushed garlic cloves, and fry for 4 minutes until golden.
Add the 5 chopped tomatoes with 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt, cover and cook for 10 minutes until they collapse into a pulpy mash.
Stir in the mashed toor dal with 1 cup water and simmer on medium-low for 8 minutes until the kut thickens and the flavours meld.
Mash the tomatoes lightly against the pan for a smoother body, simmer for 2 more minutes, and serve hot.
tips: Cook the dal until truly soft so it melts seamlessly into the tomato base.
Crushed raw garlic in the tempering gives this version its rustic Andhra punch.
Keep it slightly thinner than the classic kut so it mixes well into rice.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot rice with a spoon of ghee and a fried papad, or with ragi mudde.

variations.name: Coconut Tomato Kut
variations.description: A coastal-Deccan twist finished with fresh coconut milk that softens the tomato tang into a mellow, faintly sweet gravy with a silky sheen. Gentler and more aromatic than the sharp classic, it carries a coconut-oil and curry-leaf tempering for a southern coastal character.

ingredients.name: Ripe tomatoes
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Thick coconut milk
ingredients.note: added off the heat

ingredients.name: Grated coconut
ingredients.note: ground with the chillies

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: chopped

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: the coastal fat that ties the coconut gravy together

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: julienned

steps: Grind 3 tbsp grated coconut with 3 green chillies and a splash of water into a smooth paste and set aside.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan over medium heat, splutter 1/2 tsp mustard and 1/2 tsp cumin seeds with 2 sprigs curry leaves.
Add the chopped onion and julienned ginger and fry for 4 minutes until soft and pale gold.
Add the 5 chopped tomatoes with 1/2 tsp turmeric, 3/4 tsp red chilli powder and 1 tsp salt, cover and cook for 10 minutes until they break down.
Stir in the coconut paste with 3/4 cup water and simmer on medium-low for 6 minutes until the gravy thickens and turns fragrant.
Lower the heat fully, pour in 1/2 cup thick coconut milk, warm through for 2 minutes without boiling, and serve.
tips: Add the coconut milk off the boil and never let it bubble hard, or it will split.
The ground coconut paste plus coconut milk gives a double coconut depth; do not skip either.
A curry-leaf-heavy tempering suits this coastal version, so use two generous sprigs.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with appam, neer dosa or plain rice for a mellow coastal-style meal.

variations.name: Classic Tiranga Dhokla
variations.description: A patriotic three-layered steamed cake in saffron, white and green, made to celebrate Independence and Republic Day across Gujarat. A saffron-tinted carrot layer, a plain gram-flour middle and a coriander-green top steam together into one soft, spongy block. Cut into squares, it is as much a centrepiece as a snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: Steeped in warm water to naturally tint the top saffron layer a true kesari orange

ingredients.name: Carrot puree
ingredients.note: Deepens the saffron layer to a warm orange

ingredients.name: Coriander-mint paste
ingredients.note: For the vivid green base layer

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A little in the batter and the rest for the mustard tempering

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Melted into the tempering water for the classic sweet-sour finish

steps: Steep a pinch of Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm water for 10 minutes. Whisk 2 cups besan, 3/4 cup curd, 1 tbsp green chilli-ginger paste, 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1.25 tsp salt, 1 tsp oil, 1 tbsp lemon juice and about 1.25 cups water into a smooth, thick batter and divide into three bowls.

Colour the bowls: stir the saffron water and 1/4 cup carrot puree into the first for orange, leave the second plain white, and mix 1/3 cup coriander-mint paste into the third for green; set the steamer boiling and grease a tin.
Add 1/2 tsp Eno to the green batter, fold until frothy, pour into the tin and steam on high 8-10 minutes until just set, as this becomes the bottom layer.
Add 1/2 tsp Eno to the white batter, pour gently over the green layer and steam a further 8-10 minutes until set.
Add 1/2 tsp Eno to the orange batter, pour on top and steam a final 10 minutes until a skewer comes out clean; cool 15 minutes before cutting into neat squares so all three bands show.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds and 12 curry leaves, add 1/2 cup water with 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer 2 minutes and spoon evenly over the tricolour dhokla.
tips: Steam each layer until just set before pouring the next, or the colours bleed and the tricolour effect is lost.
Pour each new layer gently over the back of a spoon so it settles without denting the layer below.
Make it a day ahead if needed; the jaggery tempering keeps all three layers moist and the colours sharp.
variations.servingSuggestion: Present the sliced tricolour squares on a white platter with green chutney and sweet chutney, ideal for a festive Independence Day spread.

variations.name: Instant Rava Tricolour Dhokla
variations.description: A quick semolina-and-curd tricolour that skips fermentation entirely, coming together in under an hour. The saffron carrot, plain and spinach layers steam moist and slightly grainy, holding their colours crisply. Ideal when you want the festive look without the overnight wait.

ingredients.name: Carrot puree
ingredients.note: For the natural orange layer

ingredients.name: Spinach puree
ingredients.note: For the green layer

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: In the batter and the tempering for a nutty depth

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: Unrefined sugar for a gentle sweetness in the temper

steps: Whisk 2 cups fine semolina with 1 cup curd, 1 tbsp green chilli-ginger paste, 1.25 tsp salt, 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, 1 tbsp lemon juice and enough water to make a thick, smooth batter; rest 10 minutes so the rava swells, then divide into three bowls.
Stir 1/3 cup carrot puree into the first bowl for orange, leave the second plain, and mix 1/3 cup spinach puree into the third for green; set the steamer boiling and grease a tin.
Add 1/2 tsp Eno to the green batter, fold quickly and pour into the tin, steaming on high 8-10 minutes until set.
Add 1/2 tsp Eno to the plain batter, pour over the green layer and steam a further 8-10 minutes until firm.
Add 1/2 tsp Eno to the carrot batter, pour on top and steam 10 minutes until a skewer comes out clean; cool 15 minutes and cut into squares.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tsp sesame seeds and 12 curry leaves, add 1/2 cup water with 1 tbsp Anveshan Khandsari, boil 2 minutes and pour over the dhokla.
tips: Rest the rava batter properly so it thickens; runny layers merge and lose the tricolour effect.
Add Eno to one bowl at a time right before steaming that layer, never all at once.
Wipe the steamer lid dry between layers so condensation does not drip and pit the surface.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the bright squares with coconut chutney and a spicy garlic chutney for a fuss-free festive platter.

variations.name: Moong Dal Tricolour Dhokla
variations.description: A protein-forward tricolour ground from soaked yellow moong, giving an especially soft, custardy crumb across all three bands. Beetroot tints the top layer a rosy orange, plain moong forms the middle, and spinach greens the base. Lighter and more nourishing than the besan original, it is a favourite for kids' tiffins.

ingredients.name: Yellow moong dal
ingredients.note: Soaked 4 hours and ground smooth for a soft sponge

ingredients.name: Beetroot puree
ingredients.note: Lends the top layer a natural warm orange-pink

ingredients.name: Spinach puree
ingredients.note: For the green base layer

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: In the batter and for tempering the delicate dhokla

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: For the sweet-sour tempering water

steps: Grind 2 cups soaked yellow moong dal with 1/2 cup curd and a little water to a smooth, thick batter, then whisk in 1 tbsp green chilli-ginger paste, 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1.25 tsp salt, 1 tsp oil and 1 tbsp lemon juice; divide into three bowls.
Mix 1/4 cup beetroot puree into the first bowl for orange, leave the second plain, and stir 1/3 cup spinach puree into the third for green; set the steamer boiling and grease a tin.
Add 1/2 tsp Eno to the green batter, fold until frothy, pour into the tin and steam on high 9-10 minutes until set.
Add 1/2 tsp Eno to the plain batter, pour over the green and steam a further 9-10 minutes until firm.
Add 1/2 tsp Eno to the beetroot batter, pour on top and steam 10-12 minutes until a skewer comes out clean; cool 15 minutes and cut into squares.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds and 12 curry leaves, add 1/2 cup water with 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, simmer 2 minutes and spoon over the dhokla.
tips: Moong batter sets softer than besan, so steam each layer a minute longer to firm it before the next goes on.
Add beetroot puree sparingly; too much turns the top magenta rather than a warm saffron-orange.
Cool the block completely before cutting or the tender layers tear.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pack into lunchboxes with a small pot of mint chutney, or serve warm with buttermilk for a light, protein-rich snack.

variations.name: Multigrain Tricolour Dhokla
variations.description: A wholesome instant tricolour built on multigrain flour and curd, giving a nuttier, fibre-rich sponge with a rustic golden crumb. Carrot, plain and spinach layers keep the festive look while the multigrain base makes it more filling. A modern healthy spin that steams up surprisingly soft.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Multigrain Atta
ingredients.note: A blend of grains and pulses that makes a fibre-rich, nutty dhokla sponge

ingredients.name: Besan (gram flour)
ingredients.note: Helps the multigrain batter bind and rise softly

ingredients.name: Carrot puree
ingredients.note: For the orange layer

ingredients.name: Spinach puree
ingredients.note: For the green layer

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: In the batter and tempering, its toasty note suits the grainy sponge

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: For the sweet-sour tempering that keeps the fibre-rich sponge moist

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups Anveshan Multigrain Atta and 1/2 cup besan with 1 cup curd, 1 tbsp green chilli-ginger paste, 1.25 tsp salt, 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, 1 tbsp lemon juice and about 1.25 cups water into a smooth, thick batter; rest 15 minutes, then divide into three bowls.
Stir 1/3 cup carrot puree into the first for orange, leave the second plain, and mix 1/3 cup spinach puree into the third for green; set the steamer boiling and grease a tin.
Add 1/2 tsp Eno to the green batter, fold until frothy, pour into the tin and steam on high 9-10 minutes until set.
Add 1/2 tsp Eno to the plain batter, pour over the green layer and steam a further 9-10 minutes until firm.
Add 1/2 tsp Eno to the carrot batter, pour on top and steam 10-12 minutes until a skewer comes out clean; cool 15 minutes and cut into squares.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 12 curry leaves, add 1/2 cup water with 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, boil 2 minutes and pour over the dhokla.
tips: Multigrain flour drinks more water, so keep the batter pourable and rest it so the grains hydrate fully.
The small amount of besan is important for lift; leave it out and the sponge turns dense.
Steam a couple of minutes longer than a besan dhokla, as the grainy batter needs more time to set.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve this hearty tricolour with a tangy tomato chutney and a fresh salad for a wholesome breakfast or brunch.

variations.name: Classic Bengali Beetroot Veg Chop
variations.description: Veg Chop is the winter jewel of Kolkata's tele-bhaja shops, a ruby-red mash of beetroot, carrot and potato spiked with bhaja masala, coated in besan and fried crisp. The natural sweetness of beetroot against the pungent mustard-oil shell is what makes this chop unforgettable.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: authentic Bengali frying fat whose pungency balances the sweet beetroot filling

steps: Heat 2 tbsp of the Anveshan Mustard Oil on medium, saute 1 inch grated ginger and 2 chopped green chillies for 1 minute.
Add the grated beetroot and carrot and cook 6 to 7 minutes until the moisture dries off, then fold in the mashed potato, 3 tbsp crushed peanuts, 1.5 tsp bhaja masala and 1 tsp salt.
Cook 3 more minutes into a firm, dry mash, then cool completely and shape into 8 flat ovals.
Whisk 1 cup besan, 2 tbsp rice flour and 0.25 tsp salt with 0.5 cup water into a smooth, thick batter.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Mustard Oil until it smokes, cool to about 180C, dip each oval fully, and fry three at a time for 3 to 4 minutes until deep golden and crisp.
Drain on paper and serve piping hot with kasundi.
tips: Dry the beetroot mixture well on the stove or the filling stays wet and the chops fall apart in oil.
Chill the shaped ovals for 15 minutes before frying so they hold their shape better.
A spoon of crushed peanut in the filling adds body and a lovely bite to the soft mash.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with kasundi mustard and a fried green chilli, or with muri as a classic Kolkata winter-evening snack.

variations.name: Bread-Crumbed Bhetki-Style Veg Cutlet
variations.description: A club-kitchen style cutlet where the beetroot-veg mash is shaped into a diamond, dipped in slurry and rolled in golden breadcrumbs for a shatter-crisp coat. Worcestershire-free and vegetarian, it channels the old Anglo-Bengali cutlet served with kasundi and salad.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: its high smoke point crisps the crumb coat evenly golden

steps: Heat 2 tbsp of the Anveshan Sunflower Oil, saute the onion for 2 minutes, add 1 tsp ginger-garlic paste and cook a minute.
Add the grated beetroot and cook 6 minutes until dry, then fold in the mashed potato, 0.5 cup peas, 1 tsp garam masala, 0.5 tsp black pepper, 1 tsp salt and 3 tbsp coriander; cook 2 minutes and cool.
Shape the mash into 8 flat diamond cutlets pressed firm.
Whisk 4 tbsp cornflour, 0.25 tsp salt and 5 tbsp water into a thin slurry, dip each cutlet, then coat thickly in 1.25 cups breadcrumbs.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Sunflower Oil to about 180C and shallow-fry the cutlets in batches for 3 to 4 minutes per side until deep golden and crisp.
Drain on paper and serve hot with kasundi and salad.
tips: Double-crumb the cutlets by dipping and coating twice for an extra-sturdy, restaurant-crisp shell.
Chill the crumbed cutlets before frying so the coating sets and does not slip off.
Keep the mash on the drier side so the diamonds hold their sharp edges.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with kasundi, tomato sauce and a lime-dressed onion-cucumber salad, plated as a sit-down starter.

variations.name: Sattu Mixed-Veg Chop
variations.description: A protein-boosted chop where roasted-gram sattu binds a colourful mix of beans, carrot and cabbage instead of a heavy potato base, giving a firmer, nuttier bite. Lighter than the classic yet just as satisfying, it fries up crisp with a wholesome centre.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: roasted gram sattu binds the vegetables and adds protein and a nutty crust in place of potato

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil fries the chops light and clean

steps: Heat 2 tbsp of the Anveshan Groundnut Oil, add 1.5 tsp ginger-green chilli paste, then the chopped beans, cabbage, carrot and grated beetroot, and stir-fry 7 to 8 minutes until dry and just tender.
Stir in 1 tsp roasted cumin, 0.5 tsp amchur, 1 tsp salt and 3 tbsp coriander, then take off the heat and work in 0.5 cup Anveshan Sattu to bind into a firm, shapeable mixture.
Add up to 3 tbsp water only if needed, then cool and shape into 8 firm ovals or discs.
Roll each chop lightly in a spoonful of dry sattu to give a nutty outer crust.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil to about 180C and fry the chops in batches for 4 to 5 minutes, turning, until golden and crisp.
Drain on paper and serve hot with a squeeze of lime.
tips: Cook the vegetables until properly dry so the sattu can bind them into a firm chop.
Add sattu off the heat and only enough to hold the mix, as too much makes it dense.
These are more filling than potato chops, so serve fewer per person.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with mint-coriander chutney and a glass of chaas for a protein-rich, wholesome snack.

variations.name: Baked Khapli Beetroot Chop
variations.description: An oven-baked take that crusts the sweet beetroot-veg mash in nutty khapli atta and semolina, brushed with ghee for a golden shell without deep-frying. It keeps the jewel-red colour and Bengali spicing while making the chop an everyday-light treat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: forms a nutty, high-fibre crust that browns crisp in the oven

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: brushed over the chops so they crisp and turn golden while baking

steps: Preheat the oven to 200C and line a tray with parchment brushed lightly with Anveshan Ghee.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, saute 1 inch grated ginger and 2 chopped green chillies for 1 minute, add the grated beetroot and carrot, and cook 7 minutes until dry.
Fold in the mashed potato, 1.5 tsp bhaja masala and 1 tsp salt, cook 2 minutes into a firm dry mash, and cool.
Whisk 0.5 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta and 0.25 tsp salt with 4 tbsp water into a thin slurry, shape the mash into 8 ovals, dip in the slurry, then roll in 0.33 cup semolina.
Arrange on the tray, brush with Anveshan Ghee, bake 15 minutes, flip and brush again, then bake another 12 to 15 minutes until golden and crisp.
Rest 2 minutes so the crust firms, then serve warm.
tips: Cook the beetroot mash quite dry so the baked chops keep their shape and crust well.
The semolina crust needs generous ghee on both bakes to brown properly.
Space the chops apart on the tray so hot air crisps them instead of steaming.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with kasundi and a beet-and-orange salad for a colourful, lighter winter plate.

variations.name: Classic South Indian Vegetable Kurma
variations.description: A fragrant medley of mixed vegetables simmered in a freshly ground coconut, roasted-gram and fennel paste, tempered with curry leaves in coconut oil. Mildly spiced and creamy, this everyday kurma from Tamil kitchens is the classic companion to parotta, chapati and idiyappam.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed coconut oil carries the curry leaf and fennel tempering that defines a South Indian kurma

steps: Boil the 3 cups mixed vegetables in salted water for 6 minutes until just tender, then drain and keep their colour.
Grind the 0.5 cup coconut, 2 tbsp roasted gram, 1 tsp fennel and 3 green chillies with a little water into a smooth paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan over medium heat, add the cinnamon and 12 curry leaves, and let them crackle for 20 seconds.
Add the finely chopped onion and saute for 4 minutes until soft, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the chopped tomato with 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, cook for 4 minutes until it collapses, then add the boiled vegetables and 1.5 cups water.
Stir in the ground coconut paste and simmer on low for 7 minutes until the kurma thickens to a creamy, spoonable gravy, and serve hot.
tips: Blanch the vegetables only until just tender so they hold their shape in the gravy.
Add the coconut paste towards the end and keep the heat low so the gravy stays fragrant and smooth.
A pinch of sugar and a squeeze of lemon at the end balance and brighten the coconut richness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with Kerala parotta, chapati, idiyappam or ghee rice for a satisfying South Indian meal.

variations.name: Malabar Coconut-Milk Vegetable Kurma
variations.description: The silky Kerala version where vegetables simmer in fresh coconut milk perfumed with whole garam masala and a cashew paste, finished with a coconut oil and shallot tempering. Rich, glossy and gently sweet from the coconut milk, this is the celebratory kurma of Malabar breakfast tables.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: coconut oil fries the shallots and whole spices that flavour this Malabar coconut-milk kurma

steps: Soak the 12 cashews in warm water for 10 minutes, then grind to a smooth paste, and boil the 3 cups mixed vegetables for 6 minutes until just tender.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan over medium heat, add 1 tsp fennel, 3 cloves, 1 inch cinnamon and 12 curry leaves, and let them sizzle for 30 seconds.
Add the sliced shallots and 3 slit green chillies and saute for 4 minutes until the shallots turn soft and golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute.
Add 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt, the boiled vegetables, the cashew paste and 1 cup water, and simmer on medium for 6 minutes until slightly thickened.
Lower the heat right down and pour in 1 cup thick coconut milk, stirring gently and warming through for 2 minutes without letting it boil so it does not split.
Switch off, rest for 2 minutes so the flavours settle, and serve the glossy coconut-milk kurma hot.
tips: Add the thick coconut milk on the lowest heat and never boil it, or the gravy will curdle and turn oily.
Fried shallots give a sweeter, deeper base than regular onions and are worth seeking out.
The cashew paste thickens the gravy so it clings to the vegetables without overpowering the coconut milk.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with appam, idiyappam, malabar parotta or ghee rice, garnished with a swirl of coconut milk and fried curry leaves.

variations.name: Bangalore Hotel Vegetable Saagu
variations.description: The Karnataka saagu served with rava idli and set dosa, thickened with a fragrant paste of roasted coconut, poppy seeds, cinnamon and coriander seeds. Lighter and more aromatic than a creamy korma, its distinctive spice-forward coconut paste and a hint of tang define Bangalore's darshini breakfast counters.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: light wood-pressed sunflower oil keeps the saagu clean-tasting so the roasted spice paste shines

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoon of bilona ghee in the tempering adds the aroma typical of hotel-style saagu

steps: Dry-roast 1 tbsp coriander seeds, 1 tbsp poppy seeds and 1 tbsp roasted gram for 2 minutes until fragrant, then grind with the 0.33 cup coconut and 3 green chillies into a smooth paste.
Boil the 3 cups mixed vegetables with 0.25 tsp turmeric for 7 minutes until soft, keeping the cooking water.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sunflower Oil in a pan over medium heat, add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 12 curry leaves, and let them splutter for 20 seconds.
Add the finely chopped onion and saute for 4 minutes until soft and light golden.
Add the boiled vegetables with their water, 1 tsp salt and the ground spice paste, then simmer on medium for 8 minutes until the saagu thickens to a pourable, aromatic gravy.
Finish with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee stirred through for aroma and serve the saagu hot.
tips: Roasting the coriander and poppy seeds before grinding is what gives saagu its distinctive fragrance.
Keep the saagu slightly thinner than a korma, as it is meant to be a pourable accompaniment to soft breakfasts.
A small piece of tamarind or a squeeze of lemon adds the gentle tang typical of Bangalore hotel saagu.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve pourable and hot alongside rava idli, set dosa, poori or khara bath for an authentic Karnataka breakfast.

variations.name: Andhra Spicy Tomato Vegetable Kurma
variations.description: A fiery Andhra-style kurma built on a tangy tomato and red-chilli base rather than a pale coconut one, with a little coconut ground in just for body. Bold with red chilli heat and the tartness of tomato and tamarind, this robust version is made for mopping up with hot rotis and rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil stands up to the bold red chilli and gives this Andhra kurma its earthy body

steps: Boil the 3 cups mixed vegetables for 6 minutes until just tender and drain, and grind the 3 tomatoes with 3 tbsp coconut into a puree.
Heat 2.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin and 12 curry leaves, and let them crackle for 20 seconds.
Add the finely chopped onion and saute for 5 minutes until deep golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute.
Add the tomato-coconut puree with 1.5 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, and cook on medium for 6 minutes until the oil separates.
Stir in 1 tsp tamarind paste and the boiled vegetables with 1 cup water, and simmer on low for 8 minutes until the spicy gravy thickens and coats the vegetables.
Rest for 5 minutes so the flavours deepen, and serve the fiery kurma hot.
tips: Cook the tomato base until the oil clearly separates so the raw tartness mellows into a rich gravy.
Balance the tamarind and chilli to taste; the kurma should be tangy and hot in equal measure.
A small jaggery piece can be added to round off the sharpness if the tomatoes are very sour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with chapati, pulka, jeera rice or dosa, with a bowl of curd on the side to temper the Andhra heat.

variations.name: Classic Khatta Dhokla
variations.description: The traditional white, tangy dhokla of Gujarat, steamed from a naturally fermented rice-and-chana-dal batter with no Eno in sight. The overnight ferment gives it a pleasant sourness and a soft, close crumb quite different from spongy yellow khaman. A simple mustard-and-chilli temper is all it needs.

ingredients.name: Parboiled rice
ingredients.note: Soaked 5 hours with the dal for a smooth grind

ingredients.name: Chana dal
ingredients.note: Soaked with the rice; gives the batter its body and gentle nuttiness

ingredients.name: Sour buttermilk
ingredients.note: Drives the fermentation and lends the signature khatta tang

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A little in the batter and the rest for the mustard-sesame tempering

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A pinch in the temper rounds off the natural sourness the Gujarati way

steps: Grind 1.5 cups soaked parboiled rice and 1/2 cup soaked chana dal with 1 cup sour buttermilk to a smooth, thick batter, then cover and ferment in a warm place for 8-10 hours until it turns bubbly and smells pleasantly sour.
Stir the risen batter down gently and mix in 1 tbsp green chilli-ginger paste, 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil to a thick pouring consistency.
Bring the steamer water to a rolling boil, grease a tin, pour in the batter and level the top.
Steam on high heat for 18-20 minutes until the white sponge is set and a skewer inserted in the centre comes out clean.
Cool 10 minutes and cut into squares.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tsp sesame seeds, 3 slit green chillies and 10 curry leaves, stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder until it melts, and pour the temper evenly over the dhokla.
tips: The sourness deepens with fermentation time, so ferment longer in winter and less in humid summer heat.
Do not beat the batter hard after fermenting; gentle mixing keeps the trapped air and a lighter crumb.
Grease the tin well, as khatta dhokla is stickier than besan versions and can cling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the white squares warm with fresh green chutney and a bowl of chaas, or alongside a spicy garlic chutney for contrast.

variations.name: Idada
variations.description: The soft, savoury white dhokla of Kathiawad, made with rice and urad dal instead of chana dal and studded with coarsely crushed black pepper and cumin. Idada ferments into an especially light, cloud-like sponge with no sweetness at all, meant to be eaten hot off the steamer. Peppery, tangy and utterly comforting.

ingredients.name: Parboiled rice
ingredients.note: Soaked separately from the urad for a fluffier grind

ingredients.name: Urad dal (split)
ingredients.note: Soaked and ground; gives idada its light, airy crumb

ingredients.name: Sour curd
ingredients.note: For fermentation and a mild tang

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: In the batter and the tempering, its toasty note suits the peppery idada

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Just a pinch in the temper to balance the sour ferment

steps: Grind 1.5 cups soaked parboiled rice and 1/2 cup soaked urad dal with 3/4 cup sour curd to a smooth, thick batter, then ferment covered in a warm spot for 8-10 hours until light and bubbly.
Fold in 1 tbsp green chilli-ginger paste, 1 tsp coarsely crushed black pepper, 1/2 tsp cumin seeds, 1 tsp salt and 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil without deflating the batter.
Bring the steamer to a rolling boil, grease a tin, pour in the batter and dot the surface with a little extra crushed pepper.
Steam on high for 15-18 minutes until the pale, airy sponge springs back and a skewer comes out clean.
Cool 10 minutes and cut into soft squares.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1/2 tsp cumin with 10 curry leaves, stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder to melt, and pour over the idada.
tips: Urad dal batter is more delicate than chana dal, so handle it gently and steam it a touch less to keep it cloud-soft.
Crack the pepper coarsely so you get little bursts of heat through the mild, tangy sponge.
Idada is best eaten hot; as it cools the urad crumb firms up, so serve straight from the steamer.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot with green coriander chutney and a drizzle of extra sesame-tempered oil, Kathiawadi style.

variations.name: Moong Khatta Dhokla
variations.description: A lighter, easy-to-digest khatta dhokla built on rice and green moong dal, giving a paler, more delicate sponge with a mellow tang. The moong ferments gently and steams into a tender crumb that sits easy on the stomach. A wholesome everyday choice for a light breakfast.

ingredients.name: Parboiled rice
ingredients.note: Soaked with the moong for grinding

ingredients.name: Green moong dal (split)
ingredients.note: Soaked and ground; makes an especially light, digestible dhokla

ingredients.name: Sour buttermilk
ingredients.note: For the gentle khatta ferment

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: In the batter and for the light tempering

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A pinch in the temper to soften the sourness

steps: Grind 1.5 cups soaked parboiled rice and 1/2 cup soaked green moong dal with 1 cup sour buttermilk to a smooth batter, then ferment covered in a warm place for 8 hours until bubbly and lightly soured.
Gently mix in 1 tbsp green chilli-ginger paste, 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1/4 tsp asafoetida, 1 tsp salt and 1 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil to a thick pouring batter.
Bring the steamer to a rolling boil, grease a tin, pour in the batter and level the top.
Steam on high for 16-18 minutes until the tender pale-green sponge is set and a skewer comes out clean.
Cool 10 minutes and cut into squares.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1/2 tsp cumin with 10 curry leaves, stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder to melt, and pour over the dhokla.
tips: Moong batter ferments faster than chana dal, so check it earlier in warm weather to avoid over-souring.
A pinch of asafoetida in the batter keeps this light dhokla especially easy on digestion.
Steam gently and do not overcook, as the moong crumb dries out quicker than a chana dal one.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the delicate squares with a mild coconut-coriander chutney and warm chaas for a light, comforting meal.

variations.name: Millet Khatta Dhokla
variations.description: A modern, gluten-free khatta dhokla where foxtail millet replaces most of the rice, giving a nuttier flavour and a boost of fibre and minerals. It ferments and steams just like the classic, into a soft, tangy square with a rustic golden crumb. A wholesome reinvention for health-conscious kitchens.

ingredients.name: Foxtail millet
ingredients.note: Soaked 5 hours; lends a nutty flavour and fibre in place of white rice

ingredients.name: Chana dal
ingredients.note: Soaked with the millet for body and protein

ingredients.name: Sour buttermilk
ingredients.note: For the khatta ferment

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: In the batter and the tempering; its toastiness complements the millet

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A pinch in the temper to balance the tang

steps: Grind 1.5 cups soaked foxtail millet and 1/2 cup soaked chana dal with 1 cup sour buttermilk to a smooth, thick batter, then ferment covered in a warm place for 8-10 hours until bubbly and sour.
Stir in 1 tbsp green chilli-ginger paste, 1/4 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil to a thick pouring consistency without deflating the batter.
Bring the steamer to a rolling boil, grease a tin, pour in the batter and level the top.
Steam on high for 18-20 minutes until the golden sponge is set and a skewer comes out clean.
Cool 10 minutes and cut into squares.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tsp sesame seeds, 3 slit green chillies and 10 curry leaves, stir in 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder to melt, and pour over the dhokla.
tips: Millet drinks more water than rice, so keep the batter a touch looser and check it while grinding.
Ferment fully for a light crumb, as under-fermented millet batter steams dense and heavy.
Serve fresh; millet dhokla firms up faster than rice dhokla, so a quick re-steam revives leftovers.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the nutty squares with a fresh mint chutney and a side of sprout salad for a fibre-rich, wholesome breakfast.

variations.name: Classic Achari Paneer Tikka
variations.description: Achari Paneer Tikka is the tangy, pickle-spiced cousin of the classic tikka, where paneer is marinated in a hung-curd base loaded with roasted achari spices like fennel, mustard and nigella. The result is char-grilled cubes carrying the sharp, mouth-watering flavour of an Indian mango pickle.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: brushes the tikka on the grill for a golden, aromatic char

steps: Dry-roast 1 tbsp fennel, 1 tsp mustard seeds, 0.5 tsp nigella and 0.25 tsp fenugreek on low heat for 2 minutes until fragrant, then coarsely grind them into an achari masala.
Roast 1 tbsp besan separately in the same pan for 1 minute until nutty, which stops the marinade from turning watery on the grill.
Whisk 0.75 cup hung curd with the ground achari masala, roasted besan, 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt into a thick coating marinade.
