steps: Wipe 400 g mushrooms clean and lightly score the caps so the creamy marinade clings better.
Whisk 4 tbsp cream, 3 tbsp grated cheese, 0.25 cup hung curd and 2 tbsp cashew paste into a smooth, thick base.
Stir in 1 tsp green chilli paste, 0.5 tsp white pepper, 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 1 tbsp cornflour, 0.25 tsp cardamom powder and 0.75 tsp salt to keep the marinade pale and fragrant.
Coat the mushrooms thickly and chill for 25 minutes so the malai sets firmly around each cap.
Skewer and grill on a tawa brushed with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee for 8 minutes on medium heat, turning gently until the coat turns golden.
Brush with the remaining ghee, grill 2 minutes more until the crust caramelises, and serve warm.
tips: Keep the heat medium, not high, so the creamy coat browns slowly instead of burning.
The cornflour binds the cream and cheese so the malai does not drip off while grilling.
A tiny pinch of saffron soaked in warm cream deepens the colour and aroma of the malai coat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a warm plate with a coriander-yogurt dip and a light dusting of cardamom for a festive starter.

variations.name: Peri-Peri Mushroom Tikka
variations.description: A fiery Indo-Portuguese twist where mushrooms are tossed in a smoky peri-peri marinade of roasted red chilli, garlic and paprika, then grilled to a tangy, lip-tingling char. The bright red spice rub and a finishing squeeze of lemon make it a modern grill-house favourite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: carries the peri-peri paste and crisps the mushroom edges on the grill

steps: Soak 5 Kashmiri dry red chillies in warm water for 10 minutes, then blend with 8 garlic cloves, 1.5 tsp paprika, 2 tbsp lemon juice, 1 tsp vinegar and 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil into a smooth peri-peri paste.
Wipe 400 g mushrooms clean and toss them with the peri-peri paste, 1 tsp oregano, 0.5 tsp black pepper and 0.75 tsp salt until well coated.
Add the mixed bell pepper chunks to the same bowl and marinate everything for 20 minutes.
Skewer the mushrooms and peppers and grill on a hot tawa or grill pan for 8 minutes, turning until charred and blistered.
Drizzle the remaining 1 tbsp oil over the skewers and grill 2 minutes more so the edges crisp and catch colour.
Finish with an extra squeeze of lemon and serve hot while the peri-peri tang is sharp.
tips: Kashmiri chillies give the bright red colour with moderate heat; add a hotter chilli only if you want real fire.
Do not skip the vinegar, as its acidity is what makes a peri-peri marinade taste authentically tangy.
Grill fast on high heat so the mushrooms char before the garlic in the paste turns bitter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a garlic-mayo dip and toasted bread, or stuff into a wrap with lettuce for a spicy roll.

variations.name: Stuffed Tandoori Mushroom Caps
variations.description: Here larger mushroom caps are hollowed and stuffed with a spiced paneer-and-herb filling, then grilled cap-side down so the stuffing turns golden. It transforms the humble tikka into an elegant, two-bite appetiser with a molten, savoury centre.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: sautes the filling and brushes the caps for a golden tandoori finish

steps: Gently twist the stems out of 16 large mushrooms to create hollow caps, then finely chop the stems for the filling.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 0.5 tsp cumin for 20 seconds, add the chopped onion and 1 tsp ginger-garlic paste and saute for 3 minutes until soft.
Add the chopped stems and cook 2 minutes until dry, then take off the heat and mix in 150 g grated paneer, 0.75 tsp chilli powder, 0.5 tsp garam masala, 3 tbsp coriander and 0.75 tsp salt.
Spoon the filling into each cap, press firmly, and top with a little grated cheese.
Brush a grill pan and the cap edges with the remaining Anveshan Ghee and grill filling-side up on medium heat for 10 minutes until the caps soften and the cheese melts golden.
Dust with 0.5 tsp chaat masala and serve warm as bite-sized starters.
tips: Cook the filling until quite dry so it does not make the caps watery while grilling.
Choose deep, sturdy caps that hold the stuffing without collapsing on the heat.
Cover the pan loosely for the last few minutes to melt the cheese without burning the caps.
variations.servingSuggestion: Arrange on a platter with toothpicks and a drizzle of mint chutney for an elegant cocktail-party bite.

variations.name: Classic Nargisi Kofta
variations.description: A vegetarian tribute to the royal nargisi kofta, where a spiced paneer shell wraps a whole baby potato so each halved kofta reveals an egg-like eye. The golden dumplings simmer in a robust onion-tomato gravy, turning a banquet showpiece into a wholesome vegetarian curry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: builds the deep onion-tomato masala and gives the gravy its glossy richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: deep-fries the koftas to a firm golden shell that holds the potato core intact

steps: Boil and peel the 10 baby potatoes, then mash the 2 boiled potatoes with the 150 g grated paneer, 3 tbsp cornflour and 0.5 tsp salt into a firm, pliable dough.
Flatten a portion of dough on your palm, place a baby potato in the centre, seal it fully into a smooth egg shape, and repeat for all the koftas.
Deep-fry the koftas in the hot Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat for 4 minutes until evenly golden and firm, then drain on paper.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat, add the finely chopped onions and saute for 7 minutes until deep golden brown.

Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute, then add the pureed tomatoes with 1 tsp chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt, and cook for 8 minutes until the ghee separates.
Add 1.5 cups water and simmer for 5 minutes, sprinkle in 0.5 tsp garam masala, then halve the koftas and lay them cut-side up in the gravy just before serving.
tips: Seal the shell around the potato completely with no cracks, or the kofta will split open in the hot oil.
Halve the koftas only at serving time so the pretty egg-like cross-section stays intact.
Fry a test kofta first; if it breaks, work in another spoon of cornflour to firm the dough.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tandoori roti or jeera rice, the halved koftas arranged cut-side up so guests see the egg-like centre.

variations.name: Hyderabadi Nargisi Kofta
variations.description: A Deccani rendition where a boiled-chana core sits inside a beetroot-tinted potato shell, simmering in a tangy sesame-peanut gravy sharpened with tamarind. The nutty, slightly sour sauce and the surprise centre make this a bold departure from the creamy northern styles.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: its toasty depth defines the Hyderabadi til-based gravy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: fries the koftas to a sturdy crust that survives the tangy gravy

steps: Mash the 4 boiled potatoes with 3 tbsp cornflour and 0.5 tsp salt, then wrap a spoonful of the boiled chana inside each portion and shape into 8 smooth ovals.
Deep-fry the koftas in the hot Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat for 4 minutes until golden and firm, then set aside on paper.
Dry-roast the 3 tbsp peanuts, 2 tbsp sesame seeds and 2 tbsp dry coconut in a pan until fragrant, cool, and grind with a little water into a coarse paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pan over medium heat, add 10 curry leaves and the chopped onions, and saute for 6 minutes until browned.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and cook for 1 minute, then stir in the peanut-sesame paste with 1 tsp chilli powder and 0.75 tsp salt and cook for 5 minutes until the oil surfaces.
Pour in 1.5 cups water and 1 tbsp tamarind pulp, simmer for 6 minutes until the gravy turns glossy and tangy, then halve the koftas and add them just before serving.
tips: Roast the peanuts, sesame and coconut only until aromatic; scorching them turns the gravy bitter.
Adjust the tamarind at the end so the sourness balances the nutty richness to your taste.
Keep the koftas out of the gravy until serving so the tangy sauce does not soften them prematurely.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with bagara khana or plain rice, with a wedge of lime and sliced onion on the side for a Deccani touch.

variations.name: Makhani Nargisi Kofta
variations.description: The koftas here bathe in a velvety tomato-butter makhani gravy, their potato-paneer shells hiding a molten cheese-and-nut core. Silky, mildly sweet and blushing red, this version turns the nargisi kofta into a crowd-pleasing celebration dish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: gives the makhani gravy its luxurious buttery body and sheen

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: a clean neutral oil that fries the stuffed koftas to a golden shell

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: balances the tomato tang with a gentle natural sweetness typical of makhani gravy

steps: Mash the 4 boiled potatoes with 3 tbsp cornflour and 0.5 tsp salt, wrap a cube of cheese and a little grated paneer inside each portion, and shape into 8 smooth eggs.
Deep-fry the koftas in the hot Anveshan Sunflower Oil over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes until golden, then drain and rest them.
Boil the 5 tomatoes and 12 cashews in a cup of water for 8 minutes, cool, blend smooth, and strain the puree for a silky texture.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, and saute for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Pour in the strained tomato-cashew puree with 0.75 tsp salt and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, and simmer for 12 minutes, stirring, until it thickens and the ghee floats on top.
Crush 1 tsp kasuri methi over the gravy, stir in 4 tbsp cream off the heat, and slide the halved koftas in cut-side up right before serving.
tips: Strain the tomato-cashew puree for the signature glossy, lump-free makhani texture.
Wrap the cheese core well so it melts inside rather than leaking out during frying.
A knob of extra ghee stirred in at the end gives the classic restaurant-style shine.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or laccha paratha, finishing with a cream swirl and a pinch of crushed kasuri methi.

variations.name: Kashmiri Yakhni Nargisi Kofta
variations.description: Inspired by Kashmiri yakhni, these koftas rest in a pale curd gravy scented with fennel and dry ginger and coloured with a touch of Kashmiri chilli. No onion or tomato clouds the sauce, letting the aromatic yogurt base and the halved koftas shine in delicate harmony.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the authentic pungent fat of Kashmiri kitchens that underpins a true yakhni

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: fries the koftas cleanly so the pale yakhni gravy stays uncoloured

steps: Mash the 4 boiled potatoes with the 100 g grated paneer, 3 tbsp cornflour and 0.5 tsp salt, wrap a walnut piece inside each, and shape into 8 smooth ovals.
Deep-fry the koftas in the hot Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes until pale gold, then drain and reserve.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pan to smoking, lower the heat, add the cinnamon and 3 cardamoms, and let them crackle for 20 seconds.
Whisk the 1 cup curd smooth with 1.5 tsp fennel powder, 1 tsp dry ginger, 0.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli and 0.75 tsp salt, then pour into the pan on the lowest heat, stirring continuously.
Keep stirring the yakhni for 6 minutes as it warms and thickens without boiling over, then add 0.5 cup water to loosen it to a pourable gravy.
Simmer gently for another 4 minutes until fragrant, then halve the koftas and slip them in just before serving so they stay tender.
tips: Whisk the curd smooth and add it on the lowest heat, stirring nonstop, so the yakhni never splits.
Heat mustard oil until it smokes first, then cool it slightly to mellow its raw sharpness.
Keep the gravy pale by avoiding onion or tomato, letting the fennel and ginger aroma lead.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with steamed Kashmiri rice or a simple pulao, garnished with a light dusting of fennel powder.

variations.name: Classic Punjabi Pakora Kadhi
variations.description: The iconic thick, tangy Punjabi kadhi swimming with soft onion pakoras that soak up the golden, well-simmered besan-yogurt gravy. Cooked low for nearly an hour so the sourness deepens, then crowned with a fiery red-chilli ghee tarka. This is Sunday-lunch royalty over plain rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee makes the final red-chilli tarka that defines Punjabi kadhi

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil for deep-frying crisp, non-greasy pakoras

steps: Whisk 2 cups sour yogurt with ½ cup besan, turmeric, red chilli powder and salt into 5 cups water until perfectly smooth and thin.
For the pakoras, mix the remaining ½ cup besan with sliced onion, chopped green chilli, a pinch of salt and just enough water to make a thick, scoopable batter.
Heat the Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C and deep-fry spoonfuls of batter in batches until golden and crisp, about 3 minutes each, then drain.
In a large pot heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle cumin and fenugreek seeds with the ginger-garlic paste for 30 seconds, then pour in the yogurt batter.
Bring to a boil while stirring so the yogurt does not split, then simmer uncovered on low heat for 30 minutes, stirring occasionally, until thick and deep yellow.
Slide the pakoras in, simmer 8 minutes so they turn plump and soft, then finish with a tarka of the remaining ghee sizzled with red chilli powder poured over the top.
tips: Drop the pakoras in only 10 minutes before serving so they stay just soft, not disintegrated.
A long, patient simmer is the secret; under-cooked kadhi tastes raw and floury.
If the kadhi thickens too much, loosen with hot water, never cold, to keep it smooth.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot over steamed rice with a dollop of ghee, sliced onion and a mango pickle on the side.

variations.name: Amritsari Palak Pakora Kadhi
variations.description: An Amritsari twist where the fritters are made with chopped spinach folded into the besan batter, adding colour, iron and a slight bitterness that cuts the tang. The gravy stays classic and thick but the greens make it heartier. A one-pot meal beloved in Punjab's winter kitchens.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: kachi ghani mustard oil deep-fries the spinach pakoras with a robust Amritsari edge

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee for the finishing garlic-chilli tarka

steps: Whisk 2 cups sour yogurt with ½ cup besan, turmeric, red chilli powder and salt into 5 cups water until smooth.
Mix the remaining ½ cup besan with finely chopped spinach, ajwain and a pinch of salt, adding a splash of water to make a thick batter.
Heat the Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking then lower slightly and deep-fry spinach pakoras in batches for 3 minutes until crisp and deep green-gold, then drain.
In a large pot temper cumin and fenugreek seeds in 1 tbsp of the frying oil, pour in the yogurt batter and bring to a boil while stirring to prevent splitting.
Simmer uncovered on low for 30 minutes until thick and glossy, then drop in the spinach pakoras and cook 8 minutes more.
Finish with a tarka of Anveshan Ghee sizzled with sliced garlic and red chilli powder poured sizzling over the kadhi.
tips: Squeeze the chopped spinach lightly so the pakora batter stays thick and fries crisp.
Bloom the mustard oil to smoking before frying to remove its raw pungency.
The garlic tarka is what makes this Amritsari, so brown the garlic until nutty, not burnt.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tandoori roti or jeera rice and a side of sliced radish and green chillies.

variations.name: Restaurant-Style Paneer Pakora Kadhi
variations.description: A richer party version where cubes of paneer are batter-fried into pakoras and folded into a smoother, cream-finished kadhi. The paneer stays juicy inside its crisp coat and turns the humble kadhi into a special-occasion dish. Milder and more luxurious than the rustic classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: light wood-pressed sunflower oil fries the paneer pakoras crisp and clean

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee for the mild cumin-and-kasuri-methi tarka

steps: Whisk 2 cups yogurt with ½ cup besan, turmeric, red chilli powder and salt into 5 cups water until silky and smooth.
Make a thick coating batter from the remaining ½ cup besan, a pinch of salt and water, dip the paneer cubes and deep-fry in Anveshan Sunflower Oil at 180C for 2 minutes until pale gold.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot, temper cumin and ginger-garlic paste for 30 seconds, then pour in the yogurt batter and bring to a boil while stirring.
Simmer uncovered on low for 22 minutes until smooth and medium-thick, then stir in the fresh cream off the boil for a velvety finish.
Add the paneer pakoras and simmer gently for 5 minutes so they soften slightly without going soggy.
Crush the kasuri methi over the top and finish with a tarka of the remaining ghee and a pinch of red chilli powder.
tips: Soak the fried paneer pakoras in warm water for a minute before adding if you prefer them extra soft.
Add cream only after lowering the heat so it blends without splitting.
Keep the kadhi slightly thinner than usual as the paneer will soak up gravy on standing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or saffron pulao and a cucumber-mint raita for a festive spread.

variations.name: Air-Fried Light Pakora Kadhi
variations.description: A lighter everyday version where the onion-besan pakoras are air-fried to a crisp instead of deep-fried, and the gravy is built on low-fat yogurt tempered in minimal ghee. All the tang and comfort of the classic with a fraction of the oil. Perfect for weeknights when you crave kadhi without the heaviness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: just a little bilona ghee for the tempering keeps this version light yet flavourful

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a light brush of wood-pressed groundnut oil crisps the air-fried pakoras

steps: Whisk 2 cups yogurt with ½ cup besan, turmeric, red chilli powder and salt into 5 cups water until smooth.
Mix the remaining ½ cup besan with sliced onion, chopped coriander, grated ginger, a pinch of salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil into a thick batter.
Shape small fritters, place in a preheated 200C air-fryer and cook for 12 minutes, turning once, until golden and crisp.
Heat the Anveshan Ghee in a pot, crackle cumin and fenugreek seeds for 30 seconds, then pour in the yogurt batter and bring to a boil while stirring constantly.
Simmer uncovered on low heat for 28 minutes until thickened and the raw besan smell is gone.
Add the air-fried pakoras just 5 minutes before serving so they keep a little bite.
tips: Brushing the pakora batter with oil helps them crisp in the air-fryer despite less fat.
Add the air-fried pakoras at the very end since they soften faster than deep-fried ones.
A squeeze of lemon at the finish brightens the leaner gravy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over brown rice or with a millet roti and a fresh kachumber salad for a wholesome meal.

variations.name: Classic Palak Kadhi
variations.description: A vibrant green kadhi where fresh spinach is pureed into the tangy besan-yogurt gravy, giving it colour, body and a gentle earthiness. Lighter and more nutritious than a plain kadhi, it is finished with a fragrant cumin-and-garlic ghee tempering. A lovely way to sneak greens into a comforting bowl of curry and rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee carries the cumin-garlic tempering over the green kadhi

steps: Blanch the spinach in boiling water for 2 minutes, refresh in cold water, then blend with the green chilli and ginger into a smooth puree.
Whisk the sour yogurt with besan, turmeric, red chilli powder and salt into 3 cups water until lump-free.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot, crackle cumin and fenugreek seeds for 30 seconds, then pour in the yogurt batter and bring to a boil while stirring so it does not split.
Simmer uncovered on low heat for 15 minutes until the raw besan smell is gone and the kadhi thickens.
Stir in the spinach puree and simmer 6 more minutes on low, keeping the heat gentle so the green colour stays bright.
Finish with a tempering of the remaining ghee sizzled with sliced garlic until golden, poured over the kadhi.
tips: Blanch and shock the spinach to lock in the vivid green colour.
Add the puree in the last few minutes and avoid hard boiling so the green does not dull.
A squeeze of lemon at the end brightens both the colour and the tang.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over steamed rice with a spoon of ghee and a crisp papad, or with soft phulkas.

variations.name: Palak Pakora Kadhi
variations.description: A heartier version of the green kadhi loaded with crisp spinach-besan pakoras that soak up the tangy gravy until soft. The double dose of spinach, in both puree and fritters, makes it a satisfying one-pot meal. Rustic, filling and full of iron.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil deep-fries the spinach pakoras light and crisp

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee for the finishing cumin-garlic tarka

steps: Blend 2 cups of the spinach with green chilli into a puree, and finely chop the remaining 2 cups for the pakoras.
Mix the chopped spinach with ½ cup besan, ajwain, a pinch of salt and a splash of water into a thick batter, then deep-fry spoonfuls in Anveshan Groundnut Oil at 180C for 3 minutes until crisp.
Whisk the sour yogurt with the remaining ½ cup besan, turmeric, red chilli powder and salt into 3.5 cups water until smooth.
Temper cumin in 1 tbsp of the frying oil, pour in the yogurt batter and bring to a boil while stirring so it stays smooth.
Simmer uncovered on low for 18 minutes, then stir in the spinach puree and cook 5 more minutes on gentle heat.
Add the pakoras 6 minutes before serving and finish with a tarka of Anveshan Ghee, cumin and sliced garlic.
tips: Add the pakoras near the end so they stay soft-centred rather than falling apart.
Chop the spinach for the fritters finely so they hold together while frying.
Reserve a few pakoras to add crisp just at serving for a mix of textures.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over jeera rice or with tandoori roti and a raw onion salad for a filling winter lunch.

variations.name: South-Indian Palak Majjige Kadhi
variations.description: A Karnataka-style majjige huli where spinach simmers in a coconut-cumin buttermilk gravy, lightly thickened and tempered in coconut oil with mustard and curry leaves. Cooling, mildly spiced and coconut-scented, it is quite distinct from the north Indian besan kadhi. Comfort food for a hot day with rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: cold-pressed coconut oil gives the tempering its authentic coastal aroma

steps: Grind the fresh coconut, cumin, green chilli and soaked rice with a little water into a very smooth paste.
Chop the spinach and cook it with ½ cup water and turmeric for 5 minutes until wilted and soft.
Stir the coconut paste into the spinach and simmer 5 minutes until the gravy thickens lightly.
Lower the heat, whisk the buttermilk smooth and pour it in with the salt, warming gently without letting it boil so it does not split.
Heat the Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan and splutter mustard seeds, dried red chillies and curry leaves for 30 seconds.
Pour the coconut-oil tempering over the kadhi and serve warm, not boiling hot.
tips: Never boil the buttermilk after adding, as it will curdle; keep it just warm.
The spoon of soaked rice in the paste naturally thickens the gravy without besan.
Use slightly sour buttermilk for the best majjige huli flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm over hot rice with a spoon of coconut oil and a crunchy sandige or papad on the side.

variations.name: Sindhi Palak Sai Bhaji Kadhi
variations.description: Inspired by Sindhi sai bhaji, this thick green curry mashes spinach with chana dal and a medley of vegetables into a besan-thickened, yogurt-soured gravy. Wholesome and almost stew-like, it is a meal in itself rather than a thin kadhi. Earthy, tangy and deeply comforting.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: kachi ghani mustard oil gives the Sindhi sai bhaji its robust, pungent base

steps: Soak the chana dal for 30 minutes, then pressure-cook with the chopped spinach, dill, tomato, turmeric and 1.5 cups water for 4 whistles until soft.
Whisk the yogurt with besan and ½ cup water until smooth to keep the gravy tangy and thick.
Heat the Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, lower the heat and crackle cumin with crushed garlic until golden, about 1 minute.
Mash the cooked dal-spinach mixture coarsely, add it to the tempering with red chilli powder and salt, and simmer 5 minutes.
Lower the heat and stir in the yogurt-besan mix, cooking gently for 10 minutes until thick and glossy without splitting.
Adjust salt and consistency with a splash of hot water, then simmer 2 more minutes and serve.
tips: Mash rather than blend the mixture for the authentic rustic sai bhaji texture.
Add the yogurt on low heat and stir steadily so the thick gravy does not curdle.
Dill is traditional and adds a lovely aroma, but you can swap in a little fenugreek.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve thick with steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or with Sindhi koki flatbread for a complete meal.

variations.name: Classic Paneer Kofta
variations.description: Soft dumplings of grated paneer, lightly bound and fried golden, then simmered in a everyday onion-tomato gravy. Homely yet special, the koftas stay pillowy inside and drink up the tangy, spiced sauce for a comforting weeknight main.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: builds the onion-tomato masala and gives the gravy a glossy, rich finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: fries the delicate paneer koftas to a firm golden shell

steps: Grate the 250 g paneer with the 1 boiled potato, add 2 tbsp cornflour and 0.5 tsp salt, and knead into a smooth, crack-free dough.
Roll into 10 balls and deep-fry in the hot Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat for 3 minutes until golden, then drain on paper.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat, add the finely chopped onions, and saute for 6 minutes until golden brown.

Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then stir in the pureed tomatoes with 1 tsp chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt, and cook for 8 minutes until the ghee separates.
Pour in 1.5 cups water, simmer for 5 minutes until the gravy thickens, and sprinkle in 0.5 tsp garam masala.
Slip the koftas into the gravy just 2 minutes before serving so they warm through yet stay whole.
tips: Knead the paneer well until the dough is smooth so the koftas do not crack while frying.
The boiled potato binds the koftas without cornflour heaviness; keep it to one for softness.
Add the koftas at the last minute, as long simmering makes soft paneer koftas fall apart.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulka or jeera rice and a side of sliced onions and lemon.

variations.name: Palak Paneer Kofta
variations.description: Golden paneer koftas bathe in a vibrant spinach gravy, marrying the classic palak paneer with the drama of dumplings. The earthy, garlicky greens balance the creamy koftas, giving you a nutritious dish that looks as good as it tastes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: tempers the garlic and finishes the spinach gravy with a silky richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: fries the paneer koftas golden so they contrast the green gravy

steps: Grate 200 g of the paneer, add 2 tbsp cornflour and 0.5 tsp salt, knead smooth, and roll into 10 balls; cut the rest into cubes for garnish.
Deep-fry the koftas in the hot Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat for 3 minutes until golden, then drain.
Blanch the 4 cups spinach in boiling water for 2 minutes, plunge into cold water to keep its colour, then blend with 2 green chillies into a smooth puree.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin, the chopped garlic and onion, and saute for 4 minutes until soft and golden.
Add the chopped tomato and cook for 3 minutes, then pour in the spinach puree with 0.5 tsp salt and simmer on low for 5 minutes so it stays bright green.
Stir in 0.5 tsp garam masala and 2 tbsp cream off the heat, then place the koftas on top just before serving so they do not sink and soften.
tips: Blanch and shock the spinach in cold water to lock in the vivid green colour.
Cook the spinach puree only briefly on low heat, since overcooking dulls its colour and flavour.
Add the koftas right before serving, spooning gravy over them, so they stay golden and firm.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with garlic naan or tandoori roti, finished with a swirl of cream and a few pan-fried paneer cubes.

variations.name: Achari Paneer Kofta
variations.description: Paneer koftas swim in a tangy pickle-spiced gravy built on the five-seed panch phoran and mustard oil. Sharp, aromatic and lip-smacking, this achari version borrows the soul of North Indian pickles to give the humble kofta a bold, zesty personality.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the pungent oil that gives achari gravies their characteristic pickle-like sharpness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: a neutral oil to deep-fry the paneer koftas cleanly

steps: Grate the 250 g paneer with 2 tbsp cornflour and 0.5 tsp salt, knead smooth, and roll into 10 balls.
Deep-fry the koftas in the hot Anveshan Sunflower Oil over medium heat for 3 minutes until golden, then drain on paper.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil until it smokes, lower the heat, and crackle 1 tsp fennel, 0.5 tsp mustard, 0.5 tsp kalonji, 0.25 tsp methi and 0.5 tsp cumin for 30 seconds.
Add the finely chopped onions and saute for 6 minutes until golden, then stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute.
Whisk the 0.5 cup curd with 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.75 tsp salt, lower the heat, and stir it in slowly so it does not split, cooking for 4 minutes until the oil surfaces.
Pour in 1.5 cups water, simmer for 6 minutes until the tangy gravy thickens, then add the koftas 2 minutes before serving.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to smoking first, then cool slightly, to tame its raw pungency.
Add the whisked curd on low heat and keep stirring so the achari gravy stays smooth.
Lightly crush the whole seeds before tempering to release more of their pickle aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with warm laccha paratha or steamed rice, with a spoon of mango pickle alongside for a true achari meal.

variations.name: Paneer Kofta Korma
variations.description: A festive rendition where paneer koftas rest in a fragrant cashew-and-poppy korma perfumed with whole spices and rose. Mild, nutty and luxuriously smooth, this korma-style gravy dresses the koftas up for special occasions and holiday tables.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the whole spices and enriches the smooth korma base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: fries the paneer koftas to a delicate golden crust

steps: Grate the 250 g paneer with 2 tbsp cornflour and 0.5 tsp salt, knead smooth, roll into 10 balls, and deep-fry in the hot Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat for 3 minutes until golden.
Boil the 2 onions, 15 cashews and 1 tbsp poppy seeds in a cup of water for 8 minutes, cool, and blend to a smooth pale paste.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over low heat, add the cinnamon, 3 cardamoms and 3 cloves, and let them sizzle for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then stir in the cashew-poppy paste with 0.5 tsp salt and cook for 6 minutes without browning.
Whisk the 3 tbsp curd smooth, lower the heat, and stir it in with 1 cup water, simmering for 5 minutes until the korma turns creamy.
Add 0.5 tsp rose water off the heat and gently place the koftas in the korma just before serving so they stay soft.
tips: Keep the flame low while cooking the paste so the korma stays pale and does not brown.
Soak the cashews and poppy seeds well for the smoothest possible korma texture.
Add rose water sparingly at the end, as too much can overwhelm the delicate korma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sheermal or a fragrant pulao, garnished with slivered almonds and dried rose petals.

variations.name: Classic Qubani Ka Meetha
variations.description: The signature Hyderabadi wedding dessert of dried apricots slow-stewed into a glossy, jammy compote, sweet-tart and deeply fragrant. Traditionally the apricots are simmered with their own kernels for an almond-like note and served with a pool of chilled cream or custard, a beloved close to a nawabi feast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoon of ghee gives the stewed apricots their glossy sheen and rounds the sweetness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: steeped in warm water to lift the apricot compote with a floral aroma and deeper amber tone

steps: Rinse 250 g dried apricots and soak them in 3 cups water for at least 4 hours or overnight until plump and soft.
Crack the apricots open, remove the stones, and set the flesh aside; crack 10 of the stones to retrieve the soft inner kernels and blanch them to slip off the skins.
Simmer the soaked apricots with their soaking water and 0.75 cup sugar on medium-low for 20 to 25 minutes, mashing lightly, until they collapse into a thick, glossy jam-like compote.
Steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm water and stir it in with 0.25 tsp cardamom, 1 tsp lemon juice and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, cooking 3 more minutes until glossy.
Fold in most of the peeled kernels, keeping a few for garnish, and let the meetha cool to room temperature so it thickens further.
Chill the compote and serve topped with 0.5 cup lightly whipped fresh cream and the reserved kernels.
tips: Soak the apricots long enough that they turn truly plump, or they will stay chewy and refuse to break down.
The apricot kernels taste like almonds and are traditional, but you can substitute blanched almonds if unavailable.
A squeeze of lemon keeps the compote from turning cloyingly sweet and brightens the apricot flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled in a glass bowl with a layer of cream or vanilla custard and a scatter of kernels, the classic finish to a Hyderabadi biryani spread.

variations.name: Qubani Ka Meetha with Custard
variations.description: A dinner-party favourite that pairs the tangy stewed apricot compote with a silky homemade vanilla custard poured over the top. The cool, creamy custard against the warm-toned, sweet-sour apricots is the pairing most Hyderabadi restaurants serve today.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: gives the apricot compote its glossy finish before the custard goes on top

steps: Soak 250 g dried apricots in 3 cups water for 4 hours until plump, then destone them and reserve the flesh.

Simmer the apricots with their soaking water and 0.75 cup sugar on medium-low for 22 minutes, mashing, until they form a thick glossy compote, then stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 0.25 tsp cardamom and cool.
For the custard, whisk 2 tbsp custard powder into 4 tbsp cold milk taken from the 500 ml until smooth and lump-free.
Heat the remaining milk with 3 tbsp sugar to a gentle boil, pour in the custard paste in a stream while whisking, and cook 3 to 4 minutes on low until it thickens to a pouring custard.
Cool the custard, stirring occasionally to stop a skin forming, then chill both the compote and custard separately.
Spoon the apricot compote into bowls, pour the chilled custard over, and finish with 2 tbsp chopped pistachios.
tips: Whisk the custard powder into cold milk first; adding it to hot milk causes stubborn lumps.
Keep the custard slightly loose as it thickens further once chilled.
Assemble just before serving so the custard stays distinct and does not sink into the compote.
variations.servingSuggestion: Layer the compote and custard in tall glasses for an elegant parfait, topped with pistachios and a mint sprig.

variations.name: Honey Fresh Apricot Meetha
variations.description: A summer version made with fresh ripe apricots instead of dried, gently poached and sweetened with honey for a lighter, brighter compote. The fruit keeps more of its natural tang and needs far less cooking, making it a fresher, less jammy take on the classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: sweetens the poached fresh apricots naturally while keeping their bright tang

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a touch of ghee glosses the fresh compote and softens its edges

steps: Halve and destone 600 g fresh ripe apricots, keeping a few halves whole for texture.
Simmer the apricots with 0.75 cup water and 1 inch cinnamon stick on medium for 10 minutes until the fruit softens and releases its juice.
Mash lightly to a chunky compote, then stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and 0.25 tsp cardamom and cook 3 more minutes.
Take off the heat, cool for 5 minutes, then stir in 5 tbsp Anveshan Honey and 0.5 tsp vanilla so the honey stays fragrant and raw.
Discard the cinnamon stick and chill the compote for at least an hour.
Serve topped with a spoon of Greek yogurt and 3 tbsp slivered almonds.
tips: Choose ripe but firm apricots so the compote stays chunky rather than turning to complete mush.
Add the honey off the heat to preserve its aroma and enzymes.
A dollop of chilled yogurt balances the sweetness beautifully in this fresher version.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled over Greek yogurt or a scoop of vanilla ice cream for a light summer dessert.

variations.name: Apricot Meetha Phirni Cups
variations.description: A plated twist that spoons the classic apricot compote over a set saffron rice phirni in individual cups, marrying two royal Hyderabadi sweets in one dish. The soft, cardamom-scented rice pudding base makes the sweet-tart apricot layer sing.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: glosses the apricot compote that tops the set phirni

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: colours and perfumes the rice phirni base under the apricot layer

steps: Soak 200 g dried apricots in 2.5 cups water for 4 hours, then destone and simmer them with 0.5 cup sugar on medium-low for 20 minutes into a thick compote, finishing with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, and cool.
Soak 3 tbsp basmati rice for 20 minutes, drain, and grind to a coarse paste with a little of the milk.
Bring 600 ml full-fat milk to a boil, whisk in the rice paste, and simmer on low for 15 minutes, stirring constantly, until it thickens to a smooth phirni.
Steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and stir it in with 0.33 cup sugar and 0.5 tsp cardamom, cooking 3 minutes more until creamy.
Divide the warm phirni among 4 cups and chill for 2 hours until set.
Spoon the cooled apricot compote over each set phirni cup and finish with 2 tbsp chopped pistachios.
tips: Grind the rice to a coarse, not fine, paste for the traditional grainy phirni texture.
Stir the phirni constantly on low heat so the ground rice does not sink and scorch.
Set the phirni fully before adding the apricot layer so the two stay as distinct bands.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in clay matka cups for an authentic touch, chilled, with a saffron strand crowning each apricot layer.

variations.name: Classic Rajasthani Kadhi
variations.description: The authentic Marwari kadhi is thin, sharply tangy and pakora-free, its smoothness coming from a well-whisked besan-yogurt base cooked down and doubly tempered with garlic, hing and red chillies. Quick to make and fiercely flavourful, it is the everyday curry of Rajasthani thalis. Meant to be ladled generously over steaming rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee makes the classic double tempering that defines Marwari kadhi

steps: Whisk the sour yogurt, besan, turmeric, red chilli powder, coriander powder and salt into 4 cups water until perfectly smooth.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pot, crackle cumin, mustard and fenugreek seeds with the cloves and hing for 30 seconds.
Pour in the yogurt batter and bring to a boil while stirring continuously so it stays silky and does not split.
Lower the heat and simmer uncovered for 20 minutes, keeping the kadhi thin and letting the sourness deepen.
In a small pan heat the remaining Anveshan Ghee and fry the dried red chillies until they darken, about 40 seconds.
Pour this second tempering over the finished kadhi and cover for 2 minutes to trap the aroma before serving.
tips: The double tempering, one at the start and one at the end, is the heart of Rajasthani kadhi.
Keep it thin and pourable, quite unlike the thick Punjabi style.
Very sour yogurt gives the best flavour; if yours is mild, add a little dried mango powder.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve ladled over plain rice with a side of gatte ki sabzi and crisp papad for a Marwari thali.

variations.name: Marwari Gatta Kadhi
variations.description: A festive Rajasthani kadhi studded with soft steamed besan dumplings called gatte that simmer in the tangy gravy until they turn spongy and flavour-soaked. The gatte make it a filling one-pot meal beloved at Marwari weddings. Robust, spiced and hearty compared to the plain classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee binds the gatta dough and enriches the tempering

steps: Knead 1 cup besan with ajwain, a pinch of turmeric, ½ tsp salt, 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and just enough water into a stiff dough, then roll into finger-thick logs.
Boil the logs in water for 8 minutes until they float and feel firm, then cool and slice into ½-inch gatte, reserving the cooking water.
Whisk the sour yogurt with the remaining ¼ cup besan, turmeric, red chilli powder, coriander powder and salt into the reserved water to make 4 cups of smooth batter.
Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle cumin, hing and crushed garlic for 30 seconds, then pour in the yogurt batter and bring to a boil while stirring.
Simmer uncovered on low for 18 minutes, then slide in the gatte and cook 8 more minutes until they plump and absorb the tang.
Finish with a tempering of the remaining ghee sizzled with dried red chillies poured over the kadhi.
tips: Do not overcook the gatta logs while boiling or they turn hard; they should be just firm.
Save the gatta boiling water, as it carries besan flavour perfect for the gravy.
Add the sliced gatte late so they stay spongy rather than dissolving.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot rice or with bajra roti and a spoon of ghee, alongside sliced onions and green chilli.

variations.name: Rajasthani Sattu Kadhi
variations.description: A nourishing modern twist where part of the besan is replaced with roasted sattu, deepening the nutty flavour and boosting protein while keeping the kadhi thin and tangy. The sattu gives a rustic, earthy body and a beautiful toasted aroma. A wholesome everyday version rooted in Rajasthani simplicity.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: roasted sattu replaces part of the besan for a nuttier, protein-rich kadhi

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil carries the earthy garlic-cumin tempering

steps: Whisk the sour yogurt with the Anveshan Sattu, besan, turmeric, red chilli powder and salt into 4 cups water until smooth, breaking up any sattu lumps.
Heat the Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pot, crackle cumin and fenugreek seeds with hing, crushed garlic and slit green chilli for 30 seconds until golden.
Pour in the yogurt-sattu batter and bring to a boil while stirring constantly so it does not split.
Lower the heat and simmer uncovered for 20 minutes until the kadhi thickens slightly and the sattu smells toasty.
Taste and adjust the sourness and salt, loosening with a little hot water if it has thickened too much.
Rest off heat for 3 minutes so the sattu settles into a smooth body before serving.
tips: Sattu can thicken faster than besan, so keep extra hot water handy to adjust consistency.
Whisk well to break sattu lumps before heating, as they are harder to smooth out once hot.
The garlic tempering pairs beautifully with sattu's earthy note, so do not skip it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over rice or with a millet roti and a raw onion salad for a filling, protein-packed meal.

variations.name: Rajasthani Mangodi Kadhi
variations.description: A rustic desert-kitchen version enriched with mangodi, the sun-dried moong dal nuggets, fried until crisp and simmered in the tangy kadhi until they soften into savoury morsels. The mangodi lend a chewy protein bite and a distinctive nutty flavour. A pantry-driven classic from Rajasthan's arid regions.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: kachi ghani mustard oil fries the mangodi and gives the kadhi a pungent desert kick

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and fry the mangodi over medium heat, stirring, for 3 minutes until deep golden and aromatic, then set aside.
Whisk the sour yogurt, besan, turmeric, red chilli powder, coriander powder and salt into 4 cups water until smooth.
In the same pot heat the remaining mustard oil, crackle cumin and mustard seeds with hing and grated ginger for 30 seconds.
Pour in the yogurt batter and bring to a boil while stirring so the kadhi stays smooth and does not split.
Add the fried mangodi and simmer uncovered on low heat for 20 minutes until they soften and swell in the tangy gravy.
Taste for salt and sourness, loosen with hot water if needed, and serve hot.
tips: Fry the mangodi just until golden; over-browning makes them bitter.
Give the mangodi a full 20-minute simmer so they turn tender all the way through.
Soak the fried mangodi in hot water for 5 minutes first if you want them extra soft and quick-cooking.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve over hot rice or with phulka and a side of ker sangri for a true Marwari spread.

variations.name: Classic Rajgira Chikki
variations.description: Rajgira Chikki is a crunchy North Indian brittle of popped amaranth seeds bound in molten jaggery, a favourite fasting-day energy snack. The tiny popped grains give it an airy, feather-light crunch quite unlike a dense peanut chikki.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted to the hard-crack stage, it is the only sweetener and binder for this brittle

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the pan and syrup so the chikki sets glossy and lifts off cleanly

steps: Heat a heavy dry pan on medium and pop 1 cup rajgira a tablespoon at a time, swirling for about 10 seconds each until the seeds puff white, then set the popped amaranth aside.
Grease a steel plate and a rolling pin with a little of the 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and keep them ready before you start the syrup.
Melt 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water in the pan on low heat, then simmer for about 4 minutes to the hard-crack stage, when a drop hardens instantly in cold water.
Stir in the remaining Anveshan Ghee, 0.25 tsp cardamom powder and 0.25 tsp dry ginger powder, then quickly fold in the popped rajgira until every grain is coated.
Tip the hot mixture onto the greased plate and roll it out about 0.5 cm thick with the greased pin, working fast before it hardens.
Score into squares while still warm, let it cool for 10 minutes until firm and crisp, then snap along the lines and store airtight.
tips: Test the syrup obsessively; a drop must set brittle in cold water, or the chikki will stay chewy instead of snapping crisp.
Pop the rajgira in small batches on a properly hot pan, as too much at once steams rather than pops.
Work quickly once the syrup and grains are mixed, since jaggery sets fast and cracks if you roll it cold.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a mid-morning energy bite with a glass of milk, or pack broken pieces as a fasting-day travel snack.

variations.name: Rajgira Peanut Chikki
variations.description: This heartier version anchors the light popped amaranth with roasted peanuts and a whisper of sesame, giving a satisfying nutty crunch. The peanuts add protein and richness that make it a more filling snack bar.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: cooked to hard-crack stage to bind the nuts and popped amaranth into a firm slab

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: greases the setting plate and adds a glossy richness to the peanut brittle

steps: Pop 0.5 cup rajgira a spoonful at a time on a hot dry pan until puffed, then dry-roast 2 tbsp sesame seeds until they pop, and crush the 0.75 cup roasted peanuts coarsely.
Grease a steel plate and rolling pin with part of the 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and keep them within reach.
Melt 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water on low heat and simmer about 4 minutes to the hard-crack stage, testing a drop in cold water.
Off the heat, stir in the remaining Anveshan Ghee and 0.25 tsp cardamom, then fold in the popped rajgira, crushed peanuts and toasted sesame all at once.
Pour onto the greased plate and roll to a 0.5 cm slab quickly before the jaggery firms up.
Mark into bars while warm, cool 10 minutes until hard, then break along the lines and store airtight.
tips: Crush the peanuts only coarsely; too fine a powder makes the chikki dense and hard to bite through.
Keep the peanut-to-amaranth balance so the brittle still shatters lightly rather than turning into a solid nut bar.
If the slab cracks unevenly, warm the plate briefly over low heat to soften and re-press it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pack as a protein-rich lunchbox treat or serve alongside masala chai for an afternoon pick-me-up.

variations.name: Rajgira Dry Fruit Ladoo
variations.description: The same popped amaranth is shaped into soft round ladoos bound with honey and chopped dry fruits instead of a hard brittle. Dates and nuts make these a no-cook, chewy energy ball perfect for fasting or as a wholesome snack for children.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: binds the popped amaranth and dates into soft ladoos without cooking a syrup

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: warms the date paste and coats your palms so the ladoos roll smooth

steps: Pop 1 cup rajgira in small batches on a hot dry pan until fully puffed, then set aside to cool.
Chop 10 dates finely and warm them with 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on low heat for 3 minutes, mashing to a sticky paste.
Dry-roast 10 almonds and 10 cashews until fragrant, cool, and chop them coarsely.
In a bowl, combine the popped rajgira, date paste, chopped nuts, 0.25 tsp cardamom and 2 tbsp Anveshan Honey, mixing until it just holds together.
Grease your palms lightly and press the warm mixture into 12 firm walnut-sized ladoos.
Let the ladoos rest for 10 minutes to firm up, then store airtight for up to a week.
tips: Shape the ladoos while the mixture is still warm from the ghee, as it stiffens and crumbles once fully cold.
If the mix will not hold, add another teaspoon of honey rather than more ghee to keep it from turning oily.
Use soft, moist dates; dry ones will not bind and the ladoos will fall apart.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve two ladoos as a pre-workout snack or offer them as a nourishing homemade sweet during festivals.

variations.name: Coconut Sesame Rajgira Chikki
variations.description: A fragrant twist that layers dry coconut and plenty of toasted sesame with the popped amaranth for a chikki that smells of a coastal sweet shop. The coconut turns golden in the jaggery, lending caramelised aroma and extra crunch.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted to hard-crack stage to hold the coconut, sesame and amaranth in a crisp slab

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: greases the plate and deepens the coconut aroma of this chikki

steps: Pop 0.5 cup rajgira in batches on a hot dry pan, then dry-roast 0.33 cup sesame until it crackles and lightly toast 0.5 cup coconut slices until pale gold.
Grease a plate and rolling pin with the 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and keep them ready.
Melt 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water on low heat and cook about 4 minutes to the hard-crack stage, checking a drop in cold water.
Take off the heat, stir in 0.25 tsp cardamom, then fold in the popped rajgira, toasted sesame and coconut slices swiftly.
Spread onto the greased plate and roll to a thin even slab before the syrup stiffens.
Score into diamonds while warm, cool for 10 minutes until crisp, then break apart and store airtight.
tips: Toast the coconut only to pale gold before adding, as it browns further in the hot jaggery and can turn bitter.
The extra sesame makes this chikki thinner and more brittle, so roll it as soon as the grains are folded in.
Store with a piece of dry coconut in the jar to keep the chikki from softening in humid weather.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve small diamonds as a festive mithai-tray addition or crumble over a bowl of yogurt for crunch.

variations.name: Classic Rajma Galouti
variations.description: A vegetarian homage to the legendary Lucknawi galouti, where soft-cooked kidney beans are mashed to a paste, spiced with fragrant galouti masala and seared into kababs that dissolve on the tongue. Rich, aromatic and impossibly tender, they bring royal Awadhi refinement to a humble bean.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the soul of galouti, it fries the onions and sears the kababs to a melting crust

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: roasted gram sattu binds the soft bean paste so the kababs hold without going dense

steps: Soak the 1.5 cups rajma overnight, then pressure-cook with 3 cups water for 5 to 6 whistles until completely soft, and drain thoroughly.
Grind the cardamom, cloves and cinnamon into a fine galouti masala, and thinly slice and fry the 2 onions in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until deep golden.

Mash the drained rajma to a smooth paste, then mix with the fried onions, 3 tbsp Anveshan Sattu, 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, the galouti masala, 0.25 tsp mace, 0.25 tsp nutmeg, 0.75 tsp chilli powder and 1 tsp salt.
Chill the mixture for 30 minutes so it firms up, then shape into 10 small flat patties with lightly greased palms.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on a flat griddle over medium heat and sear the kababs for 2 to 3 minutes per side until a golden crust forms.
Turn them gently only once, drain briefly on paper, and serve piping hot while they are meltingly soft inside.
tips: Cook and drain the rajma until dry, as any excess moisture makes the galouti impossible to shape.
Chill the mixture well before shaping so the delicate patties do not fall apart on the griddle.
Grind your own galouti masala fresh for the authentic Awadhi aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with ultra-thin warqi paratha or rumali roti, a squeeze of lime and finely sliced onion.

variations.name: Awadhi Smoked Rajma Galouti
variations.description: The kababs get the royal dhungar treatment, infused with the aroma of ghee-doused charcoal and finished with kewra for an unmistakable Awadhi banquet fragrance. A smoky, perfumed upgrade that recreates the theatre of a Lucknawi dawat at home.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: poured over hot charcoal for the smoke and used to sear the kababs

steps: Soak the 1.5 cups rajma overnight, pressure-cook with 3 cups water for 6 whistles until very soft, and drain well.

Fry the thinly sliced 2 onions in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until deep golden, then mash the rajma smooth and mix with the onions, 3 tbsp roasted gram flour, 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 2 tbsp cashew paste, 1 tsp garam masala, 0.25 tsp mace, 0.75 tsp chilli powder and 1 tsp salt.
Heat a piece of charcoal until red-hot, place it in a small bowl set in the centre of the mixture, drizzle 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over it, cover, and let it smoke for 5 minutes.
Remove the charcoal, stir in 0.5 tsp kewra water, and chill the smoked mixture for 30 minutes.
Shape into 10 flat patties and sear on a griddle in 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes per side until golden.
Turn once gently, drain on paper, and serve hot to enjoy the lingering smoky aroma.
tips: Keep the charcoal in a small bowl, never touching the mixture directly, for a clean smoke.
Cover tightly during the dhungar so the smoke stays trapped and flavours the kababs deeply.
Add kewra water only after smoking, off the heat, so its fragrance is not lost.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sheermal and a mint chutney, garnished with onion rings and a wedge of lime.

variations.name: Beetroot Rajma Galouti
variations.description: A jewel-toned version where roasted beetroot deepens both the colour and the earthy sweetness of the melting rajma kababs. The ruby patties look spectacular on a platter and carry a gentle, wholesome sweetness beneath the warm galouti spices.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the onions and sears the ruby kababs to a caramelised crust

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: soaks up the beetroot moisture and binds the soft kabab mixture

steps: Soak the 1.5 cups rajma overnight, pressure-cook with 3 cups water for 6 whistles until soft, and drain well.
Grate the 1 cup beetroot and dry-roast it in a pan on medium heat for 5 minutes to remove moisture, then cool.
Grind the cardamom and cloves fine, fry the sliced 2 onions in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until golden, and mash the rajma smooth.

Mix the rajma, roasted beetroot, fried onions, 4 tbsp Anveshan Sattu, 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, the ground spices, 0.5 tsp roasted cumin, 0.5 tsp black pepper, 0.5 tsp chilli powder and 1 tsp salt into a firm ruby mixture.
Chill for 30 minutes, then shape into 10 flat patties with greased palms.
Sear on a griddle in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes per side until a crust forms, then serve hot.
tips: Dry-roast the beetroot thoroughly so it does not release water and soften the patties.
Add more sattu if needed, since beetroot varies in moisture between batches.
The colour deepens as the kababs sear, so do not mistake the crust for burning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with laccha paratha and a hung-curd dip, scattered with fresh coriander and pomegranate seeds.

variations.name: Hara Rajma Galouti
variations.description: A fresh, green-hued take where mint, coriander and spinach are blended into the melting rajma kababs for a herby lift against the warm spices. Bright and fragrant, these patties feel lighter on the palate while keeping the signature galouti softness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: sears the herby kababs to a golden crust while keeping the inside soft

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: balances the moisture from the greens and binds the kababs firmly

steps: Soak the 1.5 cups rajma overnight, pressure-cook with 3 cups water for 6 whistles until soft, and drain thoroughly.
Blanch the 1 cup spinach for 1 minute, squeeze it dry, and grind with the mint, coriander and 3 green chillies into a thick green paste.
Mash the rajma smooth, then mix with the green paste, 4 tbsp Anveshan Sattu, 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, ground cardamom, 0.5 tsp roasted cumin, 0.5 tsp chaat masala and 1 tsp salt.
Chill the green mixture for 30 minutes so it firms up enough to shape.
Form into 10 flat patties with greased palms and sear on a griddle in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes per side.
Add the remaining ghee as needed, turn once gently, and serve hot with the herby aroma still fresh.
tips: Squeeze the blanched spinach very dry so the greens flavour the kababs without loosening them.
Grind the herbs with minimal water for a concentrated, vivid green paste.
Serve soon after searing, as the fresh herb aroma fades if the kababs sit too long.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with warm phulka or mini pav and a tangy tamarind chutney for contrast.

variations.name: Classic Rajma Tikki
variations.description: Rajma Tikki turns leftover or freshly boiled kidney beans into a hearty, protein-rich patty spiced like a North Indian rajma masala. Mashed beans, a little boiled potato and roasted sattu bind into a firm cake that shallow-fries to a crisp, savoury crust.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: shallow-frying in bilona ghee crisps the tikki and deepens the rajma-masala aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: roasted sattu binds the mashed beans and adds nutty, protein-rich body

steps: Drain the 2 cups boiled rajma well and mash it coarsely, leaving a few whole beans for texture.
Boil, peel and mash the 2 potatoes and combine them with the mashed rajma in a large bowl.
Dry-roast 3 tbsp Anveshan Sattu for a minute and mix it in to bind the beans and soak up moisture.

Add the finely chopped onion, 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp amchur, 3 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp salt, then knead firm and shape into 10 patties.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on a griddle over medium heat and shallow-fry the tikkis for 3 to 4 minutes per side until a crisp brown crust forms.
Top up with the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee between batches and drain the tikkis on paper before serving hot.
tips: Drain the rajma thoroughly and mash it fairly dry, as wet beans make tikkis that break apart.
Keep a few beans whole for a pleasant bite against the smooth mashed base.
If the mix feels loose, chill it for 15 minutes before shaping so the tikkis hold their form.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with mint chutney and pickled onions, or sandwich in a pav for a rajma burger.

variations.name: Rajma Galouti-Style Tikki
variations.description: Inspired by the melt-in-the-mouth Awadhi galouti, this tikki is bound with fried-onion paste and a whisper of aromatic spices for an ultra-soft, delicate patty. Roasted chana flour and a slow ghee-sear give it a silky interior that barely holds together, in the best way.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a generous ghee sear gives the galouti its rich, melting Awadhi character

steps: Drain and mash the 2 cups boiled rajma to a completely smooth paste with no whole beans remaining.
Blend the 0.5 cup fried onion with 2 tbsp cashew paste and 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste into a smooth wet paste.

Mix the onion-cashew paste into the mashed rajma with 4 tbsp roasted chana flour, 0.5 tsp garam masala, 0.25 tsp cardamom powder, 0.5 tsp white pepper, 0.5 tsp rose water and 1 tsp salt into a soft, delicate dough.
Rest the mixture in the fridge for 20 minutes so it firms just enough to shape into 10 thin, small patties.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on a flat pan over low-medium heat and gently slide in the tikkis, cooking undisturbed for 3 minutes so the base sets before turning.
Turn carefully, add more Anveshan Ghee around the edges, and cook another 3 minutes until golden and just set, keeping them soft inside.
tips: Keep these tikkis small and thin so the delicate galouti texture cooks through without falling apart.
Cook on gentle heat and let each side set fully before turning, as rushing will break the soft patty.
The fried-onion paste is what gives the melting texture, so do not substitute it with raw onion.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on warm ulte tawe ka paratha with a swipe of green chutney and thin onion laccha.

variations.name: Rajma Cheese Stuffed Tikki
variations.description: A loaded, indulgent tikki where the spiced rajma patty conceals a gooey cheese and jalapeno centre. The tangy beans and stretchy melted cheese make this a hit with kids and a fun twist on the humble bean cutlet.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil shallow-fries the stuffed tikki to a light, crisp shell

steps: Drain and mash the 2 cups boiled rajma with the 2 boiled and peeled potatoes into a firm base.
Mix in 0.5 cup bread crumbs, the finely chopped onion, 1 tsp chaat masala and 1 tsp salt and knead into a shapeable dough.
Combine 0.75 cup grated cheddar with 3 tbsp chopped jalapeno, 1 tsp oregano and 1 tsp chilli flakes for the molten filling.
Flatten a portion of the rajma dough, place a spoon of the cheese filling in the centre, seal well and shape into 8 stuffed patties.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on a griddle over medium heat and cook the tikkis for 4 minutes per side until crisp and golden.
Fry the rest in the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil and serve at once so the cheese stays stretchy inside.
tips: Chill the stuffed tikkis for 15 minutes before frying so the cheese does not burst out on the pan.
Add enough bread crumbs to the dough to keep the shell firm around the soft filling.
Pat the jalapenos dry before mixing so extra brine does not loosen the filling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a chunky salsa or chipotle mayo and a cold drink for a fun anytime snack.

variations.name: Baked Rajma Oats Tikki
variations.description: A lighter oven-baked version where rolled oats replace potato and add a wholesome chew to the spiced kidney beans. Brushed with wood-pressed oil and baked till golden, these tikkis are high in fibre and easy on the conscience.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: brushed over the tikkis so they crisp and brown evenly in the oven

steps: Preheat the oven to 200C and line a tray with parchment brushed lightly with a little Anveshan Sunflower Oil.
Dry-roast 1 cup rolled oats for 2 minutes, then coarsely grind half of them and keep the rest whole for chew.
Drain and mash the 2 cups boiled rajma, then mix in the oats, 0.5 cup grated carrot and 0.5 cup chopped spring onion.
Add grated ginger, 1 tsp cumin powder, 1 tsp coriander powder, 1 tsp chilli flakes, 3 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp salt, knead firm and shape into 10 patties.
Arrange the tikkis on the tray, brush the tops well with Anveshan Sunflower Oil, and bake for 15 minutes.
Flip, brush again with oil, and bake another 12 to 15 minutes until golden and crisp, then rest 2 minutes before serving.
tips: Let the mixed dough rest for 10 minutes so the oats absorb moisture and bind the tikkis firmly.
Grind only half the oats so you keep a pleasant, hearty texture in the baked patty.
Brush oil on both bakes to get an even golden colour without deep-frying.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a yogurt-dill dip and a crisp salad for a wholesome, light lunch.

variations.name: Classic Banana Rava Sheera
variations.description: This is the beloved kela sheera, a semolina halwa in which ripe mashed banana is folded into ghee-roasted rava for a naturally fruity, deeply fragrant sweet. The banana melts into the rava, keeping it moist and lending a mellow honeyed sweetness that needs only a little added sugar.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the rava golden and carries the banana's honeyed aroma through the sheera

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: adds just enough clean sweetness to lift the natural sugars of the banana

steps: Heat 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai and fry 3 tbsp cashews and raisins over medium heat until golden, then lift them out.
Add 1 cup fine semolina to the ghee and roast over low heat, stirring constantly, for 8 minutes until golden and nutty.
Stir in 2 mashed ripe bananas and cook for 2 minutes until the fruit softens further and smells fragrant.
Heat 1.5 cups milk with 0.5 cup water and 0.5 cup Anveshan Khandsari until dissolved, then pour it slowly into the rava, stirring hard to avoid lumps.
Cover and cook on low heat for 4 to 5 minutes until the rava swells and absorbs the liquid into a soft, moist mass.
Fold in 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and the fried nuts, fluff with a fork and serve the banana sheera warm.
tips: Use fully ripe, spotty bananas for the sweetest, most fragrant sheera; firm bananas stay bland and starchy.
Add the banana to the roasted rava before the liquid so it cooks in and does not turn stringy.
Because banana adds moisture, keep the milk on the lower side or the sheera turns sticky.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as an everyday or festive sweet, garnished with fried cashews and a sprinkle of cardamom.

variations.name: Udupi Banana Sajjige
variations.description: The Udupi temple version of banana sheera, called sajjige, brightened with fresh coconut and a pinch of saffron so the rava turns fragrant and golden. Softer and more aromatic than the North Indian style, it is a classic tiffin and prasad sweet of coastal Karnataka.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the rava and fries the cashews for this fragrant coastal sajjige

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm water to give the sajjige its golden temple hue

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: sweetens the sajjige cleanly, letting the coconut and banana shine

steps: Bloom 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 3 tbsp warm water from the 2 cups and set aside.
Heat 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai, fry 3 tbsp cashews to golden, then lift out and roast 1 cup fine semolina in the same ghee for 8 minutes.
Stir in 2 mashed bananas and 0.25 cup grated coconut and cook for 2 minutes until fragrant.
Pour in the remaining water and the saffron water carefully, stirring hard, then cover and cook on low heat for 4 minutes until the rava swells.
Add 0.6 cup Anveshan Khandsari and cook for 3 minutes until the sugar melts and the sajjige turns glossy.
Fold in 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and the fried cashews, then serve the sajjige warm.
tips: Fresh grated coconut is key to the coastal flavour; desiccated coconut tastes drier and less fragrant.
Add the sugar after the rava is cooked so the grains soften fully before the syrup goes in.
Sajjige is traditionally soft and moist, so keep it loose rather than cooking it stiff.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as an Udupi tiffin sweet or temple prasad, garnished with fried cashews and a little grated coconut.

variations.name: Jaggery Banana Sheera
variations.description: A wholesome, refined-sugar-free banana sheera sweetened only with jaggery, giving a caramel-dark halwa where the earthy jaggery marries the honeyed banana. Chopped walnuts and a hint of cinnamon make it a hearty, nourishing sweet.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the rava golden for this earthy jaggery-and-banana sheera

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted into water to sweeten the sheera with a deep caramel note

steps: Melt 0.6 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 2 cups water over low heat, strain out any grit and keep the syrup hot.
Heat 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai, toast 3 tbsp chopped walnuts for 1 minute, then set aside.
Add 1 cup fine semolina to the ghee and roast over low heat for 8 minutes until golden, then stir in 2 mashed bananas and cook for 2 minutes.
Pour the hot jaggery water slowly into the rava off the high flame, stirring hard so it stays lump-free and does not scorch.
Cover and cook on low heat for 4 to 5 minutes until the rava swells and drinks up the syrup into a soft mass.
Fold in 0.25 tsp cinnamon, 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and the toasted walnuts, then serve warm.
tips: Add the jaggery water off the boil, as pouring it onto fiercely hot rava can make it seize and clump.
The banana and jaggery both brown the sheera, so a dark colour here is flavour, not scorching.
A little cinnamon plays beautifully with banana; leave it out for a plainer, more traditional taste.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a wholesome winter sweet, topped with toasted walnuts and a light dusting of cinnamon.

variations.name: Kesar Dry Fruit Banana Sheera
variations.description: A festive, indulgent banana sheera made rich with reduced milk, ground dry-fruit paste and bloomed saffron for a plush, golden halwa flecked with slivered nuts. It is the celebration-grade version, softer and more perfumed than the everyday kela sheera.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the rava golden for this plush, festive banana sheera

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm milk to colour and perfume the rich banana sheera

ingredients.name: Anveshan Dry Fruit Paak
ingredients.note: stirred in for a nutty richness that deepens the festive sheera

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: sweetens the sheera while keeping the saffron colour bright

steps: Bloom 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk from the 2 cups and set aside.
Heat 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai and roast 1 cup fine semolina over low heat for 8 minutes until golden and nutty.
Stir in 2 mashed bananas and 3 tbsp Anveshan Dry Fruit Paak and cook for 2 minutes until fragrant.
Heat the remaining milk with 0.5 cup Anveshan Khandsari until dissolved, then pour it slowly into the rava, stirring hard to avoid lumps.
Add the bloomed saffron milk and cook on low heat for 5 minutes until the rava swells and the sheera turns a rich gold.
Fold in 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and half the slivered nuts, then serve warm topped with the rest.
tips: Stir the dry-fruit paste in with the banana so it disperses evenly rather than clumping.
Keep the sheera loose and moist, as milk and dry fruit thicken it further as it cools.
Bloom the saffron in warm milk first so its colour and fragrance spread through the whole halwa.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm at festivals and celebrations, crowned with slivered pistachios, almonds and a few saffron strands.

variations.name: Classic Ghee-Roasted Makhana
variations.description: Roasted Makhana is the crunchy, guilt-free snack of foxnuts slow-roasted in ghee until impossibly crisp, then seasoned simply with rock salt and pepper. Light, high in protein and fasting-friendly, it is the healthy answer to a bowl of chips.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the foxnuts evenly to a deep, lasting crunch and carries the seasoning

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadai on low heat until it melts and coats the base.
Add 4 cups makhana and stir continuously on low heat for about 10 minutes so they roast evenly without browning too fast.
Keep roasting until a foxnut snaps crisply when pressed and feels light, a sign they are fully done.
Sprinkle in 0.75 tsp sendha namak, 0.5 tsp black pepper and 0.5 tsp roasted cumin powder, tossing so the seasoning coats every piece.
Roast for 2 more minutes so the spices toast and cling, then turn off the heat.
Cool completely in the pan so they crisp up further, then store airtight.
tips: Roast low and slow; high heat browns the outside while the centre stays chewy.
Cool them fully before storing, as they crisp further as they cool and go soft if sealed warm.
Test one by snapping it; a clean crisp break means the whole batch is ready.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a tea-time snack or pack into small jars as a fasting-friendly, protein-rich nibble for travel.

variations.name: Peri-Peri Makhana
variations.description: A fiery, moreish version tossed in a tangy peri-peri style spice blend with chilli, garlic and a hint of dried mango powder. These addictive crunchy foxnuts rival any packet of flavoured chips but stay wholesome and roasted, not fried.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the foxnuts crisp and helps the peri-peri spices stick evenly

steps: Mix 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp garlic powder, 0.5 tsp amchur, 1 tsp paprika, 0.75 tsp salt and 0.25 tsp sugar in a small bowl to make the peri-peri blend.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on low and add 4 cups makhana.
Roast the foxnuts on low heat for about 10 minutes, stirring constantly, until they snap crisp.
Lower the heat, sprinkle the peri-peri blend over the hot makhana, and toss for 2 minutes so the spices toast and cling.
Check that every piece is evenly coated and fragrant, then turn off the heat.
Cool fully in the pan so they turn extra crisp, then store airtight to keep the crunch.
tips: Mix the spice blend beforehand so you can toss it in quickly while the makhana are hot and receptive.
The tiny bit of sugar rounds out the heat and tang, balancing the peri-peri flavour.
Add the spices on low heat so the chilli powder toasts without scorching and turning bitter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a party bowl snack with drinks, or pack as a spicy, crunchy alternative to namkeen.

variations.name: Jaggery Caramel Makhana
variations.description: A sweet treat where crisp roasted foxnuts are tossed in a quick jaggery caramel until each one wears a shiny, brittle coat. Fragrant with cardamom, these caramel foxnuts are like a healthier, lighter version of caramel popcorn.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted to a caramel that coats each foxnut in a shiny, brittle shell

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the foxnuts and keeps the jaggery caramel smooth and glossy

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai and roast 4 cups makhana on low for 10 minutes until crisp, then tip them onto a plate.
In the same pan, melt 0.5 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 2 tbsp water and the remaining 1 tbsp ghee on low heat.
Simmer the syrup for about 3 minutes to the soft-crack stage, when a drop dropped in cold water forms a firm thread.
Stir in 0.5 tsp cardamom and 3 tbsp chopped almonds, then quickly add the roasted makhana and toss fast to coat every piece.
Spread the coated foxnuts on a greased plate in a single layer so they do not clump together.
Cool completely until the caramel sets brittle, then break apart any clusters and store airtight.
tips: Cook the jaggery only to the soft-crack stage; too little and the coating stays sticky, too much and it turns bitter.
Work fast once the makhana hit the caramel, as jaggery sets quickly and the pieces will clump.
Spread them out immediately on a greased plate so each foxnut stays separate and crisp.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a festive sweet snack or a lighter alternative to caramel popcorn at movie night.

variations.name: Chaat Masala Makhana
variations.description: A zingy street-style version tossed with tangy chaat masala, turmeric and roasted cumin for a bright yellow, lip-smacking snack. The tangy-savoury coating makes these foxnuts disappear fast from the bowl at any gathering.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the foxnuts crisp and helps the tangy masala adhere

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadai on low and stir in 0.25 tsp turmeric so it colours the ghee.
Add 4 cups makhana and roast on low heat for about 10 minutes, stirring constantly, until they turn pale gold and crisp.
Test that a foxnut snaps cleanly, then lower the heat to its minimum.
Sprinkle 1.5 tsp chaat masala, 0.5 tsp roasted cumin, 0.5 tsp black salt and 0.5 tsp red chilli powder over the hot makhana.
Toss well for 2 minutes so the tangy spices toast lightly and coat every piece evenly.
Turn off the heat, cool fully in the pan for maximum crunch, then store airtight.
tips: Bloom the turmeric in ghee first for an even golden colour without a raw earthy taste.
