Chaat masala already carries salt, so taste before adding more black salt.
Add all the powdered spices off high heat so the chaat masala keeps its tang and does not turn dull.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a bowl with a squeeze of lemon and a sprinkle of fresh coriander for a tangy tea-time treat.

variations.name: Classic Sabudana Tikki
variations.description: Sabudana Tikki is the beloved vrat-friendly patty of soaked tapioca pearls, mashed potato and crushed roasted peanuts, seasoned simply with green chilli and rock salt. Fried in ghee, the outside turns lacy and crisp while the inside stays soft and pleasantly chewy, perfect for fasting days.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: frying in bilona ghee crisps the tikki and keeps it vrat-appropriate

steps: Rinse 1 cup sabudana until the water runs clear, then soak it in just enough water to cover for 5 hours or overnight until each pearl swells and mashes easily between two fingers.
Boil, peel and mash the 3 potatoes smooth, then drain any water from the soaked sabudana thoroughly.

Combine the sabudana and mashed potato with 0.5 cup crushed roasted peanuts, grated ginger, 2 finely chopped green chillies, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tbsp lemon juice, 3 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp rock salt.
Knead gently into a soft dough and shape into 10 round patties, moistening your palms with a little water to stop sticking.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on a griddle over medium heat and shallow-fry the tikkis for 3 to 4 minutes per side until crisp and pale golden.
Fry the remaining tikkis in the rest of the Anveshan Ghee and drain briefly on paper before serving hot.
tips: Get the soak right by using minimal water, so the pearls are soft and separate rather than mushy or hard in the centre.
Crushed roasted peanuts are essential for both flavour and binding, so do not skip them.
Fry on steady medium heat, as too high a flame browns the outside before the sabudana turns translucent.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with cooling vrat-style peanut curd chutney and a wedge of lemon.

variations.name: Sabudana Corn Tikki
variations.description: A juicy, mildly sweet variation that folds crushed sweet corn and finely chopped capsicum into the tapioca base for pops of colour and crunch. Black pepper keeps it lively and the corn adds a natural sweetness that makes these especially popular with children.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee gives these corn tikkis a crisp shell and rich aroma

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup sabudana in just enough water to cover for 5 hours until the pearls turn soft and translucent, then drain well.
Crush the 1 cup sweet corn coarsely so it releases its juice yet keeps some whole kernels for bite.
Boil and mash the 2 potatoes, then mix them with the drained sabudana, crushed corn and 0.5 cup chopped capsicum.
Fold in 0.33 cup crushed roasted peanuts, 2 chopped green chillies, 0.5 tsp black pepper, 3 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp rock salt, and knead into a soft dough before shaping into 10 patties.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on a griddle over medium heat and shallow-fry the tikkis for 4 minutes per side until golden and set.
Cook the rest in the remaining Anveshan Ghee and drain on paper before serving warm.
tips: Crush the corn only lightly, keeping some kernels intact so you get little bursts of sweetness in each bite.
Pat the capsicum dry so the extra moisture does not make the dough sticky and hard to shape.
If the mixture feels wet from the corn, add a spoon more crushed peanuts to firm it up.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a sweet-tangy tomato chutney and hot masala chai for a satisfying tea-time snack.

variations.name: Sabudana Sweet Potato Tikki
variations.description: This fasting-special swaps regular potato for naturally sweet shakarkandi and finishes with fresh coconut and raisins for a subtly sweet, festive tikki. Fried in wood-pressed groundnut oil, it carries a warm, mellow flavour ideal for Navratri thalis.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil fries these festive tikkis light and crisp

steps: Soak 1 cup sabudana in just enough water to cover for 5 hours until soft and translucent, then drain thoroughly.
Mash the 2 cups boiled sweet potato until smooth and combine it with the drained sabudana in a bowl.
Mix in 0.5 cup crushed roasted peanuts, 0.33 cup grated coconut, 2 tbsp raisins, grated ginger, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder and 1 tsp rock salt.
Knead gently into a soft, slightly sweet dough and shape into 10 patties with moistened palms.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on a griddle over medium heat and fry the tikkis for 3 to 4 minutes per side until golden and crisp.
Cook the remaining tikkis in the rest of the Anveshan Groundnut Oil and drain on paper before serving warm.
tips: Choose a firm, less watery sweet potato variety so the tikkis stay shapeable and do not turn mushy.
Toast the grated coconut for a minute if you want a deeper nutty aroma in the mix.
Balance the natural sweetness with an extra green chilli if you prefer a savoury edge.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a Navratri thali with sweetened curd and a sprinkle of pomegranate for a festive touch.

variations.name: Sabudana Paneer Tikki
variations.description: A richer, protein-boosted take where soft crumbled paneer melts into the tapioca base for a creamy, filling patty. Cashews and a hint of black pepper give it an indulgent flavour that turns the humble fasting tikki into a hearty starter.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee crisps these rich paneer tikkis and lifts their aroma

steps: Soak 1 cup sabudana in just enough water to cover for 5 hours until soft and translucent, then drain well.
Boil and mash the 2 potatoes, then mix them with the drained sabudana and 1 cup crumbled paneer into a rich base.
Lightly toast 0.33 cup chopped cashews in a dry pan for a minute and fold them in with 2 tbsp raisins.
Add 2 chopped green chillies, 0.5 tsp black pepper, 3 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp rock salt, knead into a soft dough and shape into 10 patties.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on a griddle over medium heat and fry the tikkis for 3 to 4 minutes per side until golden and crisp.
Cook the rest in the remaining Anveshan Ghee and drain on paper, serving hot so the paneer stays soft.
tips: Use fresh, soft paneer and crumble it fine so it blends smoothly into the tapioca base.
Toast the cashews first for a nuttier depth against the mild paneer.
Keep the dough soft but shapeable; if it loosens, chill it for 10 minutes before frying.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a chilled mint-curd dip and lemon wedges as a filling festive starter.

variations.name: Classic Maharashtrian Sabudana Vada
variations.description: Sabudana vada is the crown of the Maharashtrian fasting kitchen, a crisp golden fritter of soaked tapioca pearls bound with mashed potato and crushed roasted peanuts, spiked with green chilli and cumin. Fried till shatteringly crisp outside and soft within, it is the ultimate upvas snack with cool curd.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil for deep-frying the vadas to a clean, crisp golden shell

steps: Rinse 1 cup sabudana until the water runs clear, then soak in just enough water to cover for 5 hours until each pearl is soft and squishes easily.
Drain the sabudana well and mix with 2 mashed potatoes, 0.75 cup crushed roasted peanuts, 2 minced green chillies, 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1 tsp grated ginger.
Add 3 tbsp chopped coriander, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 1 tsp rock salt and knead into a soft dough, then shape into 12 flat patties.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai to 170C, testing with a pinch of dough that should rise steadily with bubbles.
Slide in the vadas a few at a time and fry over medium heat for 4 to 5 minutes, turning once, until deep golden and crisp all over.
Drain the vadas on paper and serve hot with cool peanut-curd dip.
tips: Soak the sabudana in minimal water; a soggy soak makes the batter watery and the vadas absorb oil and burst.
Fry on steady medium heat, as too-hot oil browns the outside before the inside cooks through.
Crushed roasted peanuts, not powder, give that essential nutty crunch inside the vada.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a bowl of lightly salted curd or a green coriander chutney for a satisfying fasting snack.

variations.name: Appe-Pan Sabudana Vada
variations.description: A lighter, low-oil rendition shaped in a paniyaram appe pan so each vada crisps in just a few drops of ghee instead of a deep fry. The little balls turn golden and crunchy outside while staying pillowy within, a guilt-free take on the fasting favourite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: spooned into the appe moulds to crisp the vadas golden with very little fat

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup sabudana in just enough water for 5 hours until the pearls are soft and squish easily, then drain well.
Mix the sabudana with 2 mashed potatoes, 0.5 cup crushed roasted peanuts, 2 minced green chillies and 1 tsp roasted cumin powder.
Stir in 12 chopped curry leaves, 3 tbsp chopped coriander and 1 tsp rock salt, then knead to a soft dough and roll into small balls.
Heat an appe pan on medium, spoon a little of the 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee into each mould and set a ball into each hollow.
Cover and cook for 4 to 5 minutes, then turn each ball with a skewer and cook 4 minutes more until golden and crisp all around.
Lift out the vadas and serve hot with curd, using the remaining ghee to cook the next batch.
tips: Use roasted cumin powder rather than raw seeds here, since the gentle appe heat will not bloom whole seeds.
Keep the balls small so the centre cooks through before the shell over-browns in the mould.
A well-seasoned or non-stick appe pan releases the vadas cleanly with barely any ghee.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot straight from the pan with a coconut-coriander chutney or lightly salted curd for a lighter fasting bite.

variations.name: Sweet Potato Sabudana Vada
variations.description: A subtly sweet, nourishing twist that swaps starchy potato for mashed roasted sweet potato, giving the vada a mellow caramel edge and a beautiful orange crumb. A little cinnamon and coriander balance the sweetness, making these vadas a wholesome upvas snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil for a clean, crisp deep-fry that lets the sweet potato colour show

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup sabudana in just enough water for 5 hours until soft, then drain thoroughly.
Mix the sabudana with 2 mashed roasted sweet potatoes, 0.5 cup crushed roasted peanuts and 2 minced green chillies.
Add 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.25 tsp cinnamon powder, 3 tbsp chopped coriander, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 1 tsp rock salt and knead to a soft dough, then shape 12 patties.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai to 170C until a pinch of dough rises steadily with bubbles.
Fry the vadas in batches over medium heat for 4 to 5 minutes, turning once, until crisp and deep orange-gold.
Drain on paper and serve the sweet potato vadas hot with a tangy curd dip.
tips: Roast the sweet potatoes rather than boiling them, so the flesh stays dry and the batter does not turn watery.
Since sweet potato is soft, add it a little at a time until the dough just holds, to avoid a mushy mix.
The lemon and green chilli are important here to cut the natural sweetness of the tuber.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with salted curd or a date-tamarind chutney, whose tang plays off the sweet orange crumb.

variations.name: Kuttu Coated Crispy Sabudana Vada
variations.description: For those who love maximum crunch, these vadas are rolled in buckwheat flour before frying, forming an extra-shattering, craggy crust that stays crisp far longer. Ajwain-scented and studded with peanuts, they are the crispiest upvas vada on the fasting table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed oil that fries the kuttu-crusted vadas to a shatteringly crisp gold

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup sabudana in just enough water for 5 hours until soft, then drain well.
Warm 1 tbsp of the Anveshan Groundnut Oil and crackle 0.5 tsp ajwain in it for 20 seconds, then mix this tempered oil into the drained sabudana.
Add 2 mashed potatoes, 0.5 cup crushed peanuts, 2 minced green chillies, 1 tsp grated ginger and 1 tsp rock salt and knead to a firm dough, then shape 12 patties.
Spread 0.3 cup buckwheat flour on a plate and press each patty into it so both sides are lightly coated.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 175C and fry the coated vadas in batches for 4 to 5 minutes, turning once, until craggy and deep gold.
Drain on paper and serve the extra-crispy vadas hot right away.
tips: Bloom the ajwain in hot oil first, as raw carom seeds are harsh and never soften in the batter.
The kuttu coating should be a thin dusting, not a thick cake, or it turns doughy in the oil.
Fry and serve immediately; the buckwheat crust is at its crispest in the first few minutes.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot with cool salted curd, letting the craggy kuttu crust stay crisp against the creamy dip.

variations.name: Classic Samak Khichdi
variations.description: Samak Khichdi is the comforting one-pot fasting meal of barnyard millet simmered soft with potato and crunchy peanuts in a cumin-ghee base. Wholesome and gentle on the stomach, it is the go-to Navratri dish that satisfies without breaking the fast.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the cumin and enriches the khichdi to a comforting, glossy finish

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup samak for 10 minutes, then drain; peel and dice 2 potatoes into small cubes.
Dry-roast 0.25 cup peanuts, cool, and coarsely crush half of them for body while keeping half whole.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pressure cooker, splutter 1 tsp cumin, then add 2 slit green chillies and 1 inch grated ginger for 20 seconds.
Add the diced potato and the peanuts, saute for 2 minutes, then stir in the drained samak with 1.25 tsp sendha namak.
Pour in 3 cups water, close the cooker, and cook for 2 whistles, then let the pressure release naturally.
Open, mash lightly for a soft khichdi texture, fold in 2 tbsp coriander, and serve hot with a spoon of ghee on top.
tips: Keep the water on the higher side, as khichdi should be soft and porridge-like, not dry like pulao.
The mix of crushed and whole peanuts gives both body and a satisfying crunch.
Finish with a drizzle of raw ghee off the heat for the most fragrant, comforting bowl.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot with a bowl of chilled sweetened curd and a wedge of lemon during vrat.

variations.name: Samak Sabudana Khichdi
variations.description: This double-fasting-grain version folds soaked sabudana pearls into the millet khichdi, giving a delightful chewy-soft contrast against the fluffy samak. The tapioca turns glossy and translucent, making the dish more festive and filling.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: keeps the sabudana pearls separate and glossy as they turn translucent

steps: Soak 0.5 cup sabudana in just enough water to cover for 4 hours until the pearls are plump and squash easily, then drain fully.
Rinse and soak 0.75 cup samak separately for 10 minutes and drain; dice 1 potato small and coarsely crush 0.33 cup roasted peanuts.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, splutter 1 tsp cumin, add 2 chopped green chillies and the diced potato, and saute for 3 minutes until the potato softens.
Add the drained samak with 1.75 cups water and 1 tsp sendha namak, cover, and simmer for 10 minutes until the millet is nearly cooked.
Fold in the drained sabudana and crushed peanuts, then cook uncovered for 4 minutes, stirring gently, until the pearls turn translucent.
Turn off the heat, squeeze in 1 tbsp lemon juice, mix, and serve hot without over-stirring.
tips: Soak the sabudana until a pearl mashes with no hard white centre, or it stays raw and gritty.
Add the sabudana only at the end and stir gently, as overcooking makes the pearls clump into a sticky mass.
Cook the samak and sabudana in separate stages so each keeps its own texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a dollop of curd and a sprinkle of extra crushed peanuts for a festive fasting brunch.

variations.name: Samak Vegetable Khichdi
variations.description: A wholesome vrat khichdi loaded with soft chunks of bottle gourd, carrot and pumpkin for extra nourishment and colour. The vegetables melt into the millet, making a light yet complete fasting meal that eats like comfort food.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the cumin and gives the vegetable khichdi its comforting richness

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup samak for 10 minutes and drain; peel and dice 1 cup lauki, 1 carrot and 1 cup pumpkin into small pieces.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pressure cooker, splutter 1 tsp cumin, then add 2 slit green chillies and 1 inch grated ginger.
Add all the diced vegetables and saute for 4 minutes until they soften slightly at the edges.
Stir in the drained samak, 1.25 tsp sendha namak and 0.5 tsp black pepper, then pour in 3.5 cups water.
Close the cooker and cook for 2 whistles, then let the pressure fall naturally.
Open, mash lightly to a soft khichdi, adjust with hot water if thick, and serve hot with a spoon of ghee.
tips: Dice all the vegetables to a similar small size so they cook evenly with the quick millet.
Lauki and pumpkin release water, so add the liquid a little conservatively and adjust at the end.
A generous grind of black pepper aids digestion and suits the mild vegetables well.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a cooling boondi-free cucumber raita made with rock salt for a nourishing vrat dinner.

variations.name: Samak Peanut Masala Khichdi
variations.description: A punchier Maharashtrian-style vrat khichdi built on a fragrant roasted-peanut and cumin masala with plenty of green chilli heat. The ground peanut coats the millet in a nutty richness that makes this the most flavourful version of all.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: carries the roasted-peanut masala and enriches the spiced khichdi

steps: Coarsely grind 0.5 cup roasted peanuts with 3 green chillies and 1 inch ginger to a rough, textured paste.
Rinse and soak 1 cup samak for 10 minutes and drain; dice 1 potato small.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, splutter 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add the peanut-chilli paste and saute for 2 minutes until it smells toasty.
Add the diced potato and 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, stir for 2 minutes, then tip in the drained samak with 1.25 tsp sendha namak.
Pour in 3 cups water, bring to a boil, then cover and simmer on low for about 14 minutes until soft and the water is absorbed.
Rest 5 minutes, squeeze in 1 tbsp lemon juice, fluff gently, and serve hot.
tips: Grind the peanut masala coarse, not smooth, so it lends both flavour and a bit of crunch.
Saute the peanut paste well before adding water, as raw peanut paste tastes flat.
Balance the heat of three chillies with the lemon at the end for a bright, rounded flavour.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot topped with a swirl of curd and a few whole roasted peanuts for a robust, satisfying fast-day plate.

variations.name: Classic Samak Rice
variations.description: Samak Rice is the fluffy fasting staple of barnyard millet cooked light and separate like steamed rice, seasoned only with cumin and rock salt. Though called rice, samak is a tiny gluten-free millet that swells soft and makes the perfect vrat base for any curry.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the cumin and coats the millet so the grains stay separate and glossy

steps: Rinse 1 cup samak millet in two changes of water and soak it for 10 minutes, then drain well.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium and splutter 1 tsp cumin seeds until fragrant, about 20 seconds.
Add 1 slit green chilli, stir for a few seconds, then tip in the drained samak and toast it for 1 minute so the grains coat with ghee.
Pour in 2 cups water and 1 tsp sendha namak, stir once, and bring to a boil.
Cover, lower the heat to a gentle simmer, and cook undisturbed for about 12 minutes until the water is absorbed and the millet is soft and fluffy.
Rest covered for 5 minutes, fluff gently with a fork, garnish with 2 tbsp coriander, and serve hot.
tips: Use a 1:2 millet-to-water ratio and do not stir while it cooks, so the grains stay separate rather than mushy.
Rest it covered off the heat before fluffing, which lets the samak finish steaming without breaking.
Toast the drained millet in ghee for a minute for a nuttier flavour and better separation.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot as a vrat rice with vrat ke aloo, peanut curry, or simply a bowl of sweetened curd.

variations.name: Samak Vrat Pulao
variations.description: A one-pot fasting pulao where the barnyard millet is cooked with potato, peanuts and mild whole spices for a fuller meal. Everything simmers together so each grain carries the aroma of ghee-toasted spice and crunchy peanut.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: toasts the spices and peanuts to build the pulao's aroma

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup samak for 10 minutes, then drain; peel and dice 1 potato into small cubes.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and fry 3 tbsp raw peanuts until golden, then scoop half out for garnish.
In the same ghee, splutter 1 tsp cumin, 2 cloves and 1 inch cinnamon, then add 2 slit green chillies and the diced potato and saute for 3 minutes.
Stir in the drained samak and toast for 1 minute, then add 2 cups water and 1 tsp sendha namak and bring to a boil.
Cover and simmer on low for about 14 minutes until the millet and potato are tender and the water is absorbed.
Rest 5 minutes, fluff gently, top with the reserved peanuts and 2 tbsp coriander, and serve hot.
tips: Dice the potato small so it cooks through in the same time as the quick-cooking millet.
Reserve some fried peanuts for the top so they stay crunchy against the soft pulao.
Fish out the whole cloves and cinnamon before serving if serving to children.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve this hearty pulao with a bowl of cucumber-peanut raita made with rock salt for a complete vrat meal.

variations.name: Samak Lemon Rice
variations.description: A zesty South-Indian-style vrat rice where cooled barnyard millet is tossed in a bright lemon and peanut tempering. Tangy, nutty and fresh, it is a fasting twist on chitranna that stays light and never heavy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: a fasting-friendly oil that carries the peanut and chilli tempering

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup samak for 10 minutes, drain, and cook with 2 cups water and a pinch of rock salt until fluffy, then spread it out to cool completely.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and fry 3 tbsp raw peanuts until golden and crisp.
Add 1 tsp cumin, 2 slit green chillies, 10 curry leaves and 1 inch julienned ginger, and let them crackle for 30 seconds.
Lower the heat and add the cooled millet along with the remaining sendha namak, tossing gently so the grains do not break.
Turn off the heat, drizzle in 3 tbsp lemon juice, and fold through so every grain glistens tangy.
Serve warm or at room temperature, garnished with a few extra curry leaves.
tips: Cool the cooked millet fully before tempering so it stays separate and does not turn pasty.
Add the lemon juice off the heat, as cooking it turns the flavour bitter.
Julienned ginger and curry leaves are what give this its authentic chitranna aroma, so do not skip them.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature with a spoon of fasting-friendly potato chips or plain curd on the side.

variations.name: Samak Coconut Curd Rice
variations.description: A cooling summer-fast dish where soft-cooked barnyard millet is mashed slightly and folded with fresh curd and grated coconut. A gentle coconut-oil tempering of cumin and chilli lifts this soothing, probiotic-rich vrat bowl.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: carries the fasting tempering and adds a mellow coastal aroma to the curd rice

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup samak for 10 minutes, drain, and cook with 2.5 cups water until very soft, then lightly mash and cool to room temperature.
Fold 1 cup fresh curd, 0.25 cup grated coconut and 1 tsp sendha namak into the cooled millet until creamy.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan on medium.
Splutter 1 tsp cumin, add 1 slit green chilli, 8 curry leaves and 0.5 inch grated ginger, and let them sizzle for 20 seconds.
Pour the hot tempering over the curd-millet mixture and fold it through gently.
Chill for 15 minutes if you like it cool, then serve garnished with a little more coconut.
tips: Cook the millet softer than usual and mash lightly, as curd rice should be creamy, not grainy.
Let the millet cool fully before adding curd, or the heat will make the yogurt sour and thin.
Loosen with a splash of milk or extra curd if it thickens after chilling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled with a fasting-friendly mango or lemon pickle for a soothing hot-weather vrat lunch.

variations.name: Classic Maharashtrian Sheera
variations.description: Sheera is the Maharashtrian semolina sweet offered as satyanarayan prasad, made by roasting fine rava in ghee until golden and swelling it with hot sweet milk into a soft, fluffy halwa. Perfumed with cardamom and dotted with fried cashews and raisins, it is quick, fragrant and deeply comforting.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the rava to a golden, fragrant grain and fries the nuts for the sheera

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: dissolved into the hot milk to sweeten the sheera with a clean sweetness

steps: Heat 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai and fry 3 tbsp cashews and raisins over medium heat until golden and plump, then lift them out.
Add 1 cup fine semolina to the ghee and roast over low heat, stirring constantly, for 8 to 10 minutes until it turns golden and smells nutty.
Meanwhile heat 1.5 cups milk with 1 cup water and 0.75 cup Anveshan Khandsari until the sugar dissolves, then keep it hot.
Pour the hot sweet milk slowly into the roasted rava, standing back from the splutter, and stir hard to keep it lump-free.
Cover and cook on low heat for 4 to 5 minutes until the rava swells, absorbs the liquid and turns fluffy.
Fold in 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and the fried nuts, fluff with a fork and serve the sheera warm.
tips: Roast the rava patiently to a golden hue; under-roasted rava turns pasty and sticky instead of fluffy.
Keep the milk hot when you add it, as cold liquid on hot rava forms stubborn lumps.
The classic prasad ratio is roughly 1 rava to half ghee to three-quarters sugar, so resist cutting the ghee too far.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as satyanarayan prasad or an everyday sweet, garnished with extra fried cashews and a few raisins.

variations.name: Ananas Sheera
variations.description: A Konkani-style pineapple sheera where sweet-tart pineapple is simmered into the rava for a fragrant, tangy twist on the classic. A few saffron strands turn it golden and the fruit keeps it moist and refreshing.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the rava golden and carries the pineapple's fragrance through the sheera

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: balances the tartness of the pineapple with a clean sweetness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm milk to give the pineapple sheera a golden glow

steps: Bloom 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk from the 1 cup and set aside.
Heat 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai, fry 3 tbsp cashews until golden, then lift out, and roast 1 cup fine semolina in the same ghee for 8 minutes until golden.
In a separate pan cook 1 cup finely chopped pineapple over medium heat for 5 minutes until soft and pulpy.
Heat 1 cup milk with 1 cup water and 0.6 cup Anveshan Khandsari until dissolved, then pour it slowly into the roasted rava, stirring hard to avoid lumps.
Stir in the cooked pineapple and the bloomed saffron milk and cook on low heat for 5 minutes until the rava swells and turns fluffy.
Fold in the fried cashews, fluff with a fork and serve the ananas sheera warm.
tips: Cook the pineapple down separately first, as its acidity can otherwise stop the rava from softening properly.
Use ripe, sweet pineapple; sharp under-ripe fruit leaves the sheera sour even after cooking.
A pinch of edible yellow colour is traditional at temples, but saffron gives a natural glow instead.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a festive fruit sheera, garnished with fried cashews and a few reserved pineapple bits.

variations.name: Kesari Bath
variations.description: The Karnataka temple-and-tiffin classic, a vivid saffron-gold rava sweet that is softer and more ghee-laden than its Maharashtrian cousin, with a signature perfume of cardamom and clove. Fried cashews and raisins in every spoon make it the beloved half of the khara-bath-kesari-bath duo.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the rava and is folded in generously for the silky kesari bath finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: bloomed in warm water to give kesari bath its signature saffron gold

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: sweetens the rava while keeping the saffron colour bright and clear

steps: Bloom 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 3 tbsp warm water taken from the 2.5 cups and set aside.
Heat 0.6 cup Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai, fry 3 tbsp cashews and raisins until golden, then lift out, keeping 2 tbsp ghee in the pan.
Add 1 cup fine semolina and roast over low heat for 8 minutes until golden, then pour in the remaining water and the saffron water carefully, stirring hard.
Cover and cook on low heat for 4 minutes until the rava absorbs the water and swells to a soft mass.
Stir in 0.75 cup Anveshan Khandsari and the reserved ghee and cook for 4 minutes until the sugar melts and the kesari turns glossy.
Fold in 0.5 tsp cardamom powder, 1 pinch clove powder and the fried nuts, then serve the kesari bath warm.
tips: Add the water in one confident pour and stir hard, as kesari bath lumps faster than milk-based sheera.
Add the sugar only after the rava is cooked, so the grains soften fully before the syrup goes in.
Kesari bath sets firm as it cools; press leftovers into a tray and cut into squares for a snack.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a breakfast sweet alongside khara bath, or set firm and slice into squares for tiffin.

variations.name: Jaggery Rava Sheera
variations.description: A rustic, wholesome sheera sweetened with jaggery instead of sugar and finished with toasted coconut, giving a warm, caramel-brown halwa with an earthy depth. It is the kind of everyday sweet made for a light, mineral-rich prasad.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: roasts the rava to a golden grain for this earthy jaggery sheera

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: melted into water to sweeten the sheera with a warm caramel depth

steps: Melt 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder in 2.5 cups water over low heat, strain out any grit, and keep the syrup hot.
Heat 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai, toast 3 tbsp chopped almonds and 0.25 cup grated coconut until golden, then set aside.
Add 1 cup fine semolina to the ghee and roast over low heat for 8 to 10 minutes until golden and nutty.
Pour the hot jaggery water slowly into the roasted rava off the high flame, stirring hard so it stays lump-free and does not scorch.
Cover and cook on low heat for 4 to 5 minutes until the rava swells and absorbs the syrup into a soft mass.
Fold in 0.5 tsp cardamom powder, 0.25 tsp dry ginger powder, the toasted coconut and almonds, then serve warm.
tips: Always melt and strain the jaggery first, since raw jaggery grit gives the sheera a rough texture.
Add the jaggery water off the boil to keep the rava from clumping and the jaggery from burning.
Jaggery sheera browns more than sugar versions; that deeper colour is the flavour, not a burn.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a wholesome prasad or winter sweet, topped with toasted coconut and chopped almonds.

variations.name: Classic Soya Chaap Tikka
variations.description: Soya Chaap Tikka takes protein-rich soy chaap sticks, simmers them soft, then marinates and char-grills them in a tandoori spiced curd. The chaap turns springy and meaty with smoky, blistered edges, making it the vegetarian answer to a classic seekh grill.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: brushes the chaap on the grill for a golden, smoky char

steps: Boil 6 soya chaap sticks in salted water for 6 minutes to soften and remove any raw soy smell, then drain, cool and cut into thick 1-inch pieces.

Roast 1 tbsp besan on a dry pan for 1 minute until nutty, then whisk it into 0.5 cup hung curd with 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1 tsp tandoori masala, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 1 tsp salt.
Crush in 1 tsp kasuri methi and 0.5 tsp garam masala, then coat the chaap pieces thickly and marinate for 30 minutes.
Thread the chaap onto skewers and grill on a hot tawa brushed with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee for 8 minutes, turning until charred on all sides.
Brush with the remaining ghee and grill 2 minutes more until the edges blister and turn deep golden.
Dust with 0.5 tsp chaat masala and serve hot with onion rings.
tips: Always boil the chaap first; grilling it raw leaves a rubbery texture and beany taste.
Squeeze the boiled chaap gently to remove excess water so the marinade clings instead of sliding off.
Roasted besan in the marinade gives a crisp coat and stops the curd from turning watery on heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a starter with mint chutney and sliced onions, or slide off the skewer into a laccha paratha roll.

variations.name: Malai Soya Chaap Tikka
variations.description: A rich, mild grill where the chaap is coated in a creamy cheese-and-cashew marinade spiced only with white pepper and cardamom. It stays pale and juicy with a lightly caramelised malai crust, offering a delicate contrast to fiery tandoori versions.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: grills the malai-coated chaap to a rich golden crust

steps: Boil 6 soya chaap sticks in salted water for 6 minutes, drain, cool and cut into thick pieces, pressing out excess water.
Whisk 4 tbsp cream, 3 tbsp grated cheese, 2 tbsp cashew paste and 0.25 cup hung curd into a smooth, thick malai base.
Stir in 1 tsp green chilli paste, 0.5 tsp white pepper, 0.25 tsp cardamom powder, 1 tbsp cornflour and 0.75 tsp salt to keep the marinade pale and aromatic.
Coat the chaap pieces thickly and chill for 30 minutes so the creamy layer sets firmly.
Skewer and grill on a tawa brushed with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee for 8 minutes on medium heat, turning gently until golden.
Brush with the remaining ghee and grill 2 minutes more until the malai crust caramelises lightly, then serve warm.
tips: Grill on medium heat so the creamy coat browns gently rather than scorching.
The cornflour binds the cream and cheese so the coating stays put on the skewer.
A few strands of saffron soaked in warm cream lend a golden hue and a subtle fragrance.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coriander-mint dip and warm rumali roti, garnished with a pinch of cardamom.

variations.name: Achari Soya Chaap Tikka
variations.description: A tangy pickle-spiced grill where the chaap soaks up a mustard-oil marinade fragrant with fennel, nigella and roasted mustard. The sharp achari notes and pungent oil give the soy sticks a bold, mouth-watering kick unlike the usual tandoori style.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: its pungency forms the base of the achari marinade and grilling char

steps: Boil 6 soya chaap sticks in salted water for 6 minutes, drain, cool and cut into thick pieces, squeezing out extra water.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking point and cool it fully so its raw pungency mellows.
Dry-roast 1 tbsp fennel, 1 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp nigella for 2 minutes and grind coarse into an achari masala.

Whisk 0.5 cup yogurt with 2 tbsp of the cooled mustard oil, the ground masala, 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 1.5 tsp chilli powder, 1 tsp amchur, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, then coat the chaap and rest 30 minutes.
Skewer and grill on a smoking tawa for 8 minutes, turning until deeply charred, then drizzle the last 1 tbsp mustard oil over and sear 2 minutes more.
Serve hot with a squeeze of lemon while the achari tang is sharp.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to smoking point before cooling, or the marinade will taste raw and bitter.
Grind the achari spices coarse so you get little bursts of pickle flavour in every bite.
A tablespoon of grated raw mango folded into the marinade heightens the achari tang beautifully.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a bed of sliced onions with pickled chillies and a lemon wedge for a punchy starter.

variations.name: Afghani Soya Chaap Tikka
variations.description: A luxurious white grill inspired by Afghani kababs, where the chaap is marinated in a creamy cashew, curd and pepper mixture with no red chilli or turmeric. The pale, nutty coat grills to a soft golden blush, giving a mild, buttery-rich tikka.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: grills the Afghani white coat to a delicate golden blush

steps: Boil 6 soya chaap sticks in salted water for 6 minutes, drain, cool and cut into thick pieces, pressing out the moisture.
Blend 3 tbsp cashew paste, 0.5 cup hung curd, 2 tbsp cream and 1 tbsp melon seed paste into a silky white marinade.
Season with 0.75 tsp white pepper, 0.25 tsp cardamom, 0.25 tsp mace, 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 0.75 tsp salt, keeping the mix free of any colouring spice.
Coat the chaap generously and chill for 40 minutes so the nutty marinade sets thick around each piece.
Skewer and grill on a tawa brushed with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee for 9 minutes on medium-low heat, turning until barely blushed golden without darkening.
Brush with the remaining ghee, warm through for 2 minutes, and serve at once while soft and creamy.
tips: Keep the heat gentle and avoid charring; an Afghani tikka should stay pale ivory, not brown.
Melon seed and cashew pastes give body and a subtle sweetness that defines the Afghani style.
Blend the marinade truly smooth so the white coat looks glossy and elegant on the plate.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a mild garlic-yogurt dip and a sprinkle of rose petals for a refined banquet-style starter.

variations.name: Classic Soya Seekh Kabab
variations.description: Soya Seekh Kabab is a hearty vegetarian answer to the meaty seekh, where rehydrated soya granules are ground with warm spices and griddled into juicy, charred fingers. Boiled potato and roasted sattu bind the mixture so it stays firm on the skewer while the outside crisps beautifully.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: griddling the seekh in nutty bilona ghee builds the charred, aromatic crust

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: roasted sattu binds the kabab and adds a protein-rich earthy body in place of gram flour

steps: Soak 1.5 cups soya granules in 4 cups boiling water for 10 minutes until plump, then drain and squeeze out every drop of water so the kababs do not turn soggy.
Boil the 2 potatoes until fork-tender, peel and mash them smooth while warm to act as the binder for the soya.
Pulse the squeezed soya with the finely chopped onion, 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 2 green chillies in a processor to a coarse, mince-like grain.

Tip the mixture into a bowl with the mashed potato, 3 tbsp Anveshan Sattu, 1 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp chaat masala, 3 tbsp coriander and 1 tsp salt, then knead into a firm, non-sticky dough.
Grease your palms and press portions around greased flat skewers into 12 cm seekh fingers, or shape into thick logs if you are not using skewers.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on a flat griddle over medium heat and cook the kababs, turning every couple of minutes, for 8 to 10 minutes until evenly browned with charred edges and firm to the touch.
tips: Squeeze the soaked soya really dry, as trapped water is the main reason seekh kababs fall apart on the griddle.
Roast the sattu-bound mixture a few minutes ahead and chill it for 15 minutes so it holds its shape better while shaping.
If the dough feels loose, add another spoon of sattu rather than more potato, which can turn the kababs gummy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Slide the hot kababs off the skewers onto a bed of sliced onion rings, squeeze over lemon and serve with mint chutney.

variations.name: Charcoal-Smoked Tandoori Soya Seekh
variations.description: This tandoori-style seekh is marinated in hung curd and kasuri methi, then finished with a dramatic dhungar smoking that lends it a genuine coal-fired aroma. Wood-pressed mustard oil in the marinade gives the pungent, restaurant-grade edge you expect from a tandoor.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil in the marinade gives the seekh its sharp, tandoor-style pungency

steps: Soak 1.5 cups soya granules in boiling water for 10 minutes, drain and squeeze bone-dry, then pulse to a coarse mince in a processor.
Roast 3 tbsp besan in a dry pan for 2 minutes until fragrant so it loses its raw smell before it goes into the kabab.

Mix the soya mince with 0.5 cup hung curd, the roasted besan, finely chopped onion, 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi, 1.5 tsp tandoori masala, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 3 tbsp coriander, 1 tsp salt and 1 tbsp of the Anveshan Mustard Oil into a firm marinated dough.
Shape the mixture around greased skewers into seekh fingers and rest them in the fridge for 15 minutes so they set.
Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, cool slightly, then griddle or grill the seekh over medium-high heat for 8 to 10 minutes, turning and basting, until charred and firm.

Place the cooked seekh in a deep bowl, set a heated piece of charcoal in a small steel cup among them, drizzle a few drops of mustard oil onto the coal, cover for 4 minutes to capture the smoke, then uncover and serve.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to smoking point and cool it before using so its raw sharpness mellows into a rounded pungency.
Keep the dhungar bowl tightly covered for the full 4 minutes to let the smoky aroma seep deep into the kababs.
Use thick hung curd, not runny yogurt, or the marinade will loosen the mince and make skewering difficult.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve straight from the smoking bowl with a side of pickled onions and a green chutney sharpened with extra mint.

variations.name: Hariyali Soya Seekh
variations.description: A vibrant green seekh where the soya is blitzed with spinach, mint and coriander for a herb-forward, fresh-tasting kabab. Soaked poha keeps the fingers moist and tender while wood-pressed groundnut oil crisps the surface without weighing them down.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: light wood-pressed groundnut oil crisps the herb-packed seekh without masking its freshness

steps: Soak 1.5 cups soya granules in boiling water for 10 minutes, then drain and squeeze out all the water thoroughly.
Rinse 0.33 cup poha and soak it for 5 minutes until soft, then squeeze lightly so it stays moist but not wet.
Blanch the 1.5 cups spinach for 30 seconds, refresh in cold water, and blend it with the mint, coriander, 3 green chillies and 1 inch ginger into a thick green paste.
Pulse the squeezed soya coarse, then knead it with the green paste, soaked poha, 3 tbsp roasted chana dal powder, 1 tsp amchur, 1 tsp cumin powder and 1 tsp salt into a firm, bright-green dough.
Shape the mixture into slim seekh logs around greased skewers, pressing firmly so they hold together.
Brush the seekh with a little Anveshan Groundnut Oil and griddle over medium heat for 8 to 10 minutes, turning and basting with the rest of the oil, until the edges char and the kababs feel set.
tips: Blanch the spinach only briefly and cool it fast so the seekh keeps its vivid green rather than turning drab olive.
Squeeze the soaked poha gently so it adds moisture without loosening the dough into a paste.
Taste and add extra amchur if you want a sharper tang to lift the herby flavours.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a platter scattered with fresh mint leaves and thin lemon wedges alongside a cool cucumber raita.

variations.name: Peshawari Cheese Soya Seekh
variations.description: A rich, indulgent seekh studded with molten cheese and bound with cashew paste for a creamy, restaurant-style bite. Sweet capsicum and white pepper give it a Peshawari mildness, while ghee on the griddle turns the outside golden and glossy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee on the griddle gives these cheesy seekh a glossy golden crust and a rich aroma

steps: Soak 1.5 cups soya granules in boiling water for 10 minutes, drain and squeeze completely dry, then pulse to a fine mince.
Combine the soya mince with 3 tbsp cashew paste, the finely chopped onion, 0.5 cup capsicum and 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste in a large bowl.
Add 0.75 cup grated cheese, 3 tbsp cornflour, 1 tsp garam masala, 0.5 tsp white pepper, 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi and 1 tsp salt, and knead into a firm, cohesive dough.
Shape the mixture around greased skewers into plump seekh fingers, sealing the cheese well inside, and chill for 15 minutes so they firm up.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on a griddle over medium heat and lay on the seekh, cooking for 8 to 10 minutes and turning gently so the cheese melts inside as the outside turns golden.
Rest the seekh for a minute off the heat so the cheese sets slightly and does not spill when you slide them off the skewers.
tips: Chill the shaped seekh well so the cheese stays contained and the kababs do not slump on the hot griddle.
Use a firm processed cheese rather than soft mozzarella, which can leak out too quickly during cooking.
Add the cheese cold and work fast so it does not soften and make the dough sticky before shaping.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these rich seekh with a squeeze of lemon and a sweetish onion-tomato salad to cut through the creaminess.

variations.name: Classic Stuffed Tandoori Aloo
variations.description: Tandoori Aloo takes baby potatoes, hollows them out and fills them with a spiced paneer-nut stuffing before grilling in a tandoori curd marinade. The crisp, smoky potato shell gives way to a rich, savoury centre, making it a hearty vegetarian starter.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: sautes the stuffing and brushes the potatoes for a golden tandoori grill

steps: Boil 12 baby potatoes until just fork-tender, about 12 minutes, then cool, halve them and scoop out the centres to make little cups.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, saute 0.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, add the scooped potato flesh, 100 g grated paneer, 2 tbsp cashews, 0.5 tsp garam masala, 3 tbsp coriander and 0.5 tsp salt, and cook 3 minutes into a dry filling.
Press the filling firmly into the potato cups and sandwich the halves back together.
Whisk 0.5 cup hung curd with 0.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1 tsp tandoori masala and 0.5 tsp salt, and coat the stuffed potatoes all over.
Skewer or place on a tawa brushed with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and grill for 10 minutes, turning and brushing with the last ghee until charred and crisp.
Dust with 0.5 tsp chaat masala and serve hot straight off the grill.
tips: Boil the potatoes only until just tender so they hold their shape when scooped and grilled.
Keep the stuffing dry and pack it tight so it does not spill out on the heat.
Choose evenly sized baby potatoes so they grill and char at the same rate.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a starter with mint chutney and onion rings, or plate over a green salad for a light meal.

variations.name: Punjabi Tandoori Aloo Tikka
variations.description: A rustic dhaba-style grill using whole baby potatoes marinated in a pungent mustard-oil and yogurt masala, skewered and charred without any stuffing. The pierced potatoes drink up the fiery marinade for a bold, no-fuss Punjabi starter.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: gives the marinade its sharp Punjabi pungency and grills the potatoes deep golden

steps: Boil 16 baby potatoes until just tender, about 12 minutes, then peel and prick each one all over with a fork so the marinade seeps in.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking point, cool it, then roast 1.5 tbsp besan on a dry pan for a minute until nutty.

Whisk 0.5 cup yogurt with 2 tbsp of the cooled mustard oil, the roasted besan, 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 2 tsp chilli powder, 0.5 tsp ajwain, 1 tsp kasuri methi, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 1 tsp salt.
Coat the pricked potatoes thickly and marinate for 30 minutes so they absorb the pungent masala.
Skewer the potatoes and grill on a smoking tawa for 12 minutes, turning until charred and crusted all over.
Drizzle the last 1 tbsp mustard oil over and sear 2 minutes more for a glossy, blistered finish before serving hot.
tips: Prick the potatoes deeply so the marinade penetrates past the skin into the flesh.
Heat the mustard oil to smoking point first to tame its rawness before mixing into the marinade.
Roasted besan thickens the coat and gives a lovely crust when the potatoes hit the heat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve dhaba-style on a steel plate with raw onion rings, green chutney and a lemon wedge.

variations.name: Malai Tandoori Aloo
variations.description: A creamy, mild take where boiled baby potatoes are coated in a cheese-cashew malai marinade and grilled to a soft golden crust. The rich, pale coating and gentle spicing make it a family-friendly starter free of fiery heat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: grills the malai-coated potatoes to a rich golden crust

steps: Boil 16 baby potatoes until just tender, about 12 minutes, then peel and lightly score each so the creamy coat grips.
Whisk 4 tbsp cream, 3 tbsp grated cheese, 2 tbsp cashew paste and 0.25 cup hung curd into a smooth, thick malai base.
Stir in 1 tsp green chilli paste, 0.5 tsp white pepper, 1 tbsp cornflour, 0.25 tsp cardamom and 0.75 tsp salt to keep the marinade pale and fragrant.
Coat the potatoes thickly and chill for 25 minutes so the malai layer firms up around each one.
Skewer and grill on a tawa brushed with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee for 10 minutes on medium heat, turning gently until golden.
Brush with the remaining ghee and grill 2 minutes more until the crust caramelises, then serve warm.
tips: Keep the grill on medium so the creamy coat browns slowly without scorching.
Cornflour binds the cream and cheese so the coating clings to the smooth potatoes.
Score the potatoes lightly so the malai has grooves to hold onto during grilling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coriander-yogurt dip and a light dusting of cardamom for a mild, crowd-pleasing starter.

variations.name: Air-Fried Peri-Peri Tandoori Aloo
variations.description: A lighter, contemporary version where marinated baby potatoes are crisped in an air fryer and tossed in a smoky peri-peri spice mix. It delivers a crunchy, tangy potato bite with minimal oil, perfect for a guilt-free snack.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: tossed with the potatoes so they crisp golden in the air fryer

steps: Boil 16 baby potatoes until just tender, about 12 minutes, then drain fully and let them steam-dry for 5 minutes.
Toss the warm potatoes with 2 tbsp cornflour, 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil and 0.25 tsp of the salt until lightly coated for extra crispness.
Preheat the air fryer to 200C for 4 minutes, add the potatoes in a single layer, and air-fry for 15 minutes, shaking halfway, until crisp and golden.
Meanwhile mix 1.5 tsp paprika, 1 tsp garlic powder, 1 tsp chilli flakes, 1 tsp oregano, 0.5 tsp black pepper and the remaining 0.5 tsp salt into a peri-peri dust.
Tip the hot crisp potatoes into a bowl, sprinkle over the peri-peri mix and 1 tbsp lemon juice, and toss until evenly coated.
Serve immediately while hot and crunchy for the best texture and tang.
tips: Steam-dry the boiled potatoes fully before coating, as surface moisture stops them crisping.
The cornflour toss is the trick to a shatteringly crisp air-fried skin without deep-frying.
Add the peri-peri dust only after air-frying so the spices stay bright and do not burn.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve in a paper cone with a garlic-mayo dip as a movie-night or party snack.

variations.name: Classic Tandoori Gobi
variations.description: Tandoori Gobi takes cauliflower florets, blanches them, then coats them in a spiced tandoori curd marinade and grills them until charred and smoky. The florets stay crisp-tender inside with blistered, spiced edges, making a striking vegetarian grill.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: brushes the florets on the grill for a golden, smoky char

steps: Blanch 500 g cauliflower florets in salted hot water for 3 minutes, then drain and pat them thoroughly dry so they take a char rather than steam.
Roast 2 tbsp besan on a dry pan for 2 minutes until nutty, which gives body to the coat and removes any raw-flour taste.

Whisk the roasted besan into 0.5 cup hung curd with 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1 tsp tandoori masala, 0.5 tsp ajwain, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 1 tsp salt.
Coat the dry florets thickly in this marinade and rest for 20 minutes so they soak up the spice.
Thread onto skewers and grill on a hot tawa brushed with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee for 10 minutes, turning and brushing with the last ghee until charred and crisp.
Dust with 0.5 tsp chaat masala and serve hot straight off the skewer.
tips: Pat the blanched florets completely dry, as any water dilutes the marinade and prevents charring.
Roasted besan is key to a coat that crisps rather than sliding off the smooth florets.
Grill on high heat quickly so the gobi chars while staying crisp-tender inside.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a starter with mint chutney and onion rings, or over a salad with a lemon wedge.

variations.name: Amritsari Achari Tandoori Gobi
variations.description: A punchy Amritsari-style grill where the cauliflower is marinated in a pungent mustard-oil pickle masala studded with fennel, nigella and roasted mustard. The sharp achari notes and bright colour make this a bold, tangy twist on the tandoori classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: forms the pungent achari base and grills the florets deep golden

steps: Blanch 500 g cauliflower florets in salted hot water for 3 minutes, drain and pat completely dry.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking point and cool it fully so the pungency softens.
Dry-roast 1 tbsp fennel, 1 tsp mustard seeds and 0.5 tsp nigella for 2 minutes and grind coarse into an achari masala.

Whisk 0.5 cup yogurt with 2 tbsp of the cooled mustard oil, the ground masala, 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 2 tsp chilli powder, 1 tsp amchur, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, then coat the florets and rest 25 minutes.
Skewer and grill on a smoking tawa for 10 minutes, turning until deeply charred, then drizzle the last 1 tbsp mustard oil over and sear 2 minutes more.
Serve hot with a squeeze of lemon while the achari tang is at its sharpest.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to smoking point before use so the marinade tastes nutty, not raw.
Grind the achari spices coarse for little bursts of pickle flavour on each floret.
Blanch just until crisp-tender so the florets hold together on the skewer.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on sliced onions with pickled green chillies and a lemon wedge for a fiery starter.

variations.name: Gobi 65 Grill
variations.description: A South-Indian inspired grill blending the tandoori idea with the flavours of Gobi 65, using a curry-leaf, ginger and red-chilli marinade finished with a curry-leaf tempering. The florets carry a tangy, curry-leaf-scented heat quite distinct from the North-Indian tandoori.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: brushes the florets and tempers the curry leaves for an authentic South-Indian aroma

steps: Blanch 500 g cauliflower florets in salted hot water for 3 minutes, drain and pat dry thoroughly.
Whisk 0.33 cup yogurt with 2 tbsp rice flour, 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 2 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp green chilli paste, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 1 tsp salt into a thick, bright coat.
Fold the dry florets into the marinade and rest for 20 minutes so the rice flour crust sets.
Skewer and grill on a tawa brushed with 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil for 10 minutes, turning until charred and crisp at the edges.
In a small pan heat the remaining 1 tbsp coconut oil, crackle 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and 20 curry leaves for 30 seconds until they splutter and crisp.
Pour the sizzling curry-leaf tempering over the grilled gobi and toss, then serve hot.
tips: Rice flour in the marinade gives the signature crunchy crust of a 65-style dish.
Fry the curry leaves just until crisp so they shatter fragrantly over the florets.
Add a pinch of extra chilli if you want the fiery kick that defines a classic 65.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with coconut chutney and lemon wedges, or alongside curd rice as a spicy accompaniment.

variations.name: Whole Roasted Tandoori Gobi
variations.description: A dramatic centrepiece where a whole cauliflower is steamed, slathered in a rich tandoori-cashew marinade and roasted until deeply charred outside and tender within. Carved at the table, it turns the humble gobi into a showstopping feast dish.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: brushed over the whole cauliflower for a glossy, deep-charred roast

steps: Trim 1 large cauliflower to a flat base and steam it whole for 12 minutes until a knife slides in with slight resistance, then cool.

Whisk 0.75 cup hung curd with 3 tbsp cashew paste, 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 2 tsp chilli powder, 0.75 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi, 1 tsp coriander powder and 1.25 tsp salt into a thick marinade.
Slather the marinade all over the cauliflower, working it into the crevices, and rest for 30 minutes.
Preheat the oven to 220C, set the cauliflower on a lined tray, brush generously with 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, and roast for 30 minutes.
Brush with the remaining 1 tbsp ghee and roast another 8 to 10 minutes until deeply charred and tender to the core.
Dust with 0.5 tsp chaat masala, rest 5 minutes, then carve into wedges at the table and serve.
tips: Steam the cauliflower until just tender first, or the outside chars long before the centre cooks.
Cashew paste keeps the marinade thick so it clings to the whole head without dripping.
Rest the roast a few minutes before carving so the wedges hold together cleanly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Present whole on a platter with lemon wedges and mint chutney, carving wedges over saffron pulao.

variations.name: Classic Til Ki Chutney
variations.description: A rustic Hyderabadi chutney of dry-roasted sesame seeds ground with tamarind, garlic and red chillies into a nutty, tangy paste. Traditionally served with khichdi or plain rice, its toasty sesame aroma and gentle heat make it a beloved everyday accompaniment across old-city kitchens.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: doubles down on the toasty til flavour and carries the tempering that finishes the chutney

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a small hit of natural sweetness rounds off the tamarind's sourness and the chilli heat

steps: Dry-roast 0.75 cup white sesame seeds in a heavy pan on medium-low for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring constantly, until they turn pale gold and start to pop and smell nutty, then tip them onto a plate to cool.
In the same pan add 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and roast 4 dry red chillies, 5 garlic cloves and 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 1 minute until the garlic softens and the chillies darken slightly.
Grind the cooled sesame, the roasted chilli-garlic mix, 1 tbsp tamarind, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.75 tsp salt with 0.25 cup water into a slightly coarse, spoonable paste.
Heat the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a small pan on medium, add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds and let them crackle for about 20 seconds, then toss in 1 sprig curry leaves until they turn crisp.
Pour the sizzling tempering over the ground chutney and stir it through so the mustard and curry-leaf aroma infuses the paste.
Taste and adjust salt or tamarind, then rest the chutney for 10 minutes to let the flavours settle before serving.
tips: Roast the sesame on low heat only until pale gold; over-browned seeds turn the chutney bitter and dull the nutty flavour.
Keep the paste slightly coarse rather than silky for the traditional grainy texture that clings to rice.
Stored in a clean jar in the fridge it keeps for up to a week, so it is worth grinding a double batch.
variations.servingSuggestion: Spoon over hot rice with a pool of ghee, or serve alongside pesarattu and dosa as a change from coconut chutney.

variations.name: Peanut Til Ki Chutney
variations.description: A heartier Telangana-style version that grinds roasted peanuts alongside the sesame for extra body and a creamy, savoury depth. Sauteed onion and a heavier hand of red chilli give it a warm, robust flavour that stands up to jowar roti and mudda pappu rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil echoes the roasted peanut base and fries the onion for the chutney

steps: Dry-roast 0.5 cup white sesame seeds on medium-low for 4 minutes until golden and popping, then set aside; if your peanuts are raw, roast 0.5 cup separately until the skins loosen.
Heat 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan on medium and saute 1 thinly sliced small onion with 5 dry red chillies and 4 garlic cloves for 4 to 5 minutes until the onion turns soft and golden.
Grind the roasted sesame, roasted peanuts, the sauteed onion mixture, 1 tbsp tamarind, 1 tsp cumin seeds and 0.75 tsp salt with 0.33 cup water into a thick, textured paste.
Heat the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a small pan, crackle 0.5 tsp mustard seeds for about 20 seconds, then add 1 sprig curry leaves until crisp.
Pour this tempering over the ground chutney and mix well so the aroma runs right through it.
Loosen with a splash of water if too thick, check the salt, and serve at room temperature.
tips: Rub the skins off the roasted peanuts before grinding for a smoother, less bitter chutney.
Frying the onion until properly golden is what gives this version its savoury, almost gravy-like richness.
It thickens as the peanuts absorb moisture, so keep it a touch loose when you grind.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a substantial side with jowar roti or dosa, or thin it slightly to use as a dip for millet crackers.

variations.name: Coconut Til Chutney
variations.description: A fresher, milder coastal take that balances the toasted sesame with grated coconut, green chillies and ginger for a bright, aromatic chutney. A South Indian chana-dal and urad-dal tempering gives it a nutty crunch that pairs beautifully with idli and dosa.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: carries the coastal tempering and deepens the fresh coconut fragrance of this chutney

steps: Dry-roast 0.5 cup white sesame seeds on medium-low for 4 minutes until golden and fragrant, then cool them on a plate.
Grind the roasted sesame with 0.75 cup grated coconut, 3 green chillies, 1 inch ginger and 0.75 tsp salt, adding 0.5 cup water gradually, into a smooth, pourable chutney.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a small pan on medium and add 1 tbsp chana dal and 1 tsp urad dal, frying until they turn golden, about 1 minute.
Add 0.5 tsp mustard seeds, 1 broken dry red chilli and 1 sprig curry leaves and let them crackle and crisp for about 20 seconds.
Pour the hot tempering over the ground chutney and fold it through gently.
Adjust salt and consistency, then serve fresh while the coconut is at its most fragrant.
tips: Use fresh, soft coconut rather than desiccated for the juiciest, most fragrant chutney.
This coconut version is best eaten the same day, as fresh coconut sours quickly even in the fridge.
For a milder chutney deseed the green chillies before grinding.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a cooling counterpoint to spicy sambar with idli, dosa or medu vada.

variations.name: Dry Til Podi
variations.description: A dry, shelf-stable sesame podi ground from roasted til, garlic and red chilli into a coarse, sprinkleable powder rather than a wet paste. Mixed with a spoon of sesame oil at the table, it becomes an instant chutney and a fragrant travel-friendly staple in Hyderabadi tiffin boxes.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: stirred into a spoon of the dry podi at the table to turn the powder into a fragrant chutney

steps: Dry-roast 1 cup white sesame seeds on medium-low for 5 minutes, stirring constantly, until evenly golden and popping, then tip onto a wide plate to cool completely.
In the same pan dry-roast 6 dry red chillies, 1 tbsp coriander seeds and 1 tsp cumin seeds for about 1 minute until aromatic, then cool them with the sesame.
Add 6 garlic cloves and 1 tsp dried tamarind and pulse everything together in a dry grinder with 1 tsp salt.
Grind in short bursts to a coarse, sandy powder, stopping before the sesame releases its oil and clumps into a paste.
Cool the podi fully, then store it in a dry airtight jar where it keeps for several weeks.
To serve, mix 2 tablespoons of the podi with 1 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil into a quick paste, adding a few more drops of oil as needed.
tips: Grind in short pulses; continuous grinding heats the sesame and turns the podi oily and pasty instead of dry.
Make sure everything is bone-dry before grinding so the podi stays free-flowing and stores well.
Increase or reduce the red chillies to set the heat level exactly to your taste.
variations.servingSuggestion: Sprinkle over hot rice with ghee, dust onto plain dosa, or carry the jar for instant chutney while travelling.

variations.name: Classic Veg Galouti Kabab
variations.description: Veg Galouti is the vegetarian tribute to Lucknow's melt-in-the-mouth galouti kabab, built from a soft mash of raw banana, peas and roasted chana with fragrant aromatic spices. Pan-seared in ghee, each kabab dissolves on the tongue with a rich, buttery Awadhi spicing.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: sears the delicate kababs to a golden crust and carries the Awadhi aromas

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: roasted gram flour that binds the soft mash without making it heavy

steps: Mash the 2 boiled raw bananas and 0.5 cup boiled peas together into a smooth, lump-free paste while still warm.

Mix in 3 tbsp Anveshan Sattu, 3 tbsp crushed fried onion, 2 tbsp cashew paste, 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 0.75 tsp garam masala, 0.25 tsp cardamom, 0.25 tsp mace, 0.5 tsp kewra water and 0.75 tsp salt into a soft, pliable dough.
Chill the mixture for 20 minutes so it firms enough to shape into small, flat, coin-like patties.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on a flat tawa on medium heat until it shimmers.
Slide in the kababs and pan-sear for 3 minutes each side, adding the remaining ghee as needed, until golden and crisp-edged but still soft within.
Lift gently with a flat spatula and serve hot, as galouti kababs are fragile by nature.
tips: Keep the mash smooth and the kababs thin, as galouti should melt rather than hold a firm bite.
The roasted sattu binds better than raw flour and keeps the kabab light instead of doughy.
Chill the mixture well before frying so the soft patties do not break apart on the tawa.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on warm ulte-tawe ka paratha with thin onion rings and a drizzle of green chutney.

variations.name: Rajma Galouti Kabab
variations.description: A heartier galouti built on a base of soft-cooked red kidney beans mashed with paneer, giving a protein-rich melt with earthy depth. The rajma lends a creamy body while the classic Awadhi spicing keeps it delicate and aromatic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: pan-sears the soft kababs golden and enriches the aromatic mix

steps: Drain 1 cup soft-boiled rajma well and mash it with 100 g grated paneer into a smooth, thick paste.

Mix in 3 tbsp roasted chana powder, 3 tbsp crushed fried onion, 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 0.75 tsp garam masala, 0.5 tsp roasted cumin, 2 chopped green chillies, 3 tbsp coriander and 0.75 tsp salt into a pliable dough.
Rest the mixture for 15 minutes, then shape into small, flat round patties.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on a flat tawa on medium heat until it shimmers.
Pan-sear the kababs for 3 minutes each side, adding the remaining ghee as needed, until deep golden and crisp-edged.
Lift carefully and serve warm while the centres are soft and creamy.
tips: Cook the rajma very soft so it mashes smoothly without leaving grainy skins.
Roasted chana powder both binds and adds a nutty depth that suits the earthy rajma.
Grate the paneer fine so it blends invisibly into the mash for a seamless melt.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a tangy onion-tomato salad and pudina chutney inside a soft roomali roll.

variations.name: Beetroot Galouti Kabab
variations.description: A jewel-toned galouti where roasted beetroot lends a natural ruby colour and gentle sweetness to the melt-in-mouth kabab. Bound with khoya and warm spices, it is as striking to look at as it is soft on the palate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: sears the ruby kababs to a caramelised edge and enriches the mix

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: roasted gram flour that soaks up beetroot moisture and binds the soft mash

steps: Squeeze the 1.5 cups grated roasted beetroot in a cloth to remove excess juice so the mixture is not watery.
In a pan dry-cook the beetroot with 0.5 cup crumbled khoya for 4 minutes on low heat until thick and dry, then cool.

Mix in 3 tbsp Anveshan Sattu, 2 tbsp cashew paste, 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 0.75 tsp garam masala, 0.5 tsp roasted fennel powder, 0.5 tsp black pepper, 0.5 tsp rose water and 0.75 tsp salt into a firm, shapeable dough.
Chill for 20 minutes, then shape into small, flat ruby-red patties.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on a flat tawa on medium heat and slide in the kababs.
Sear for 3 minutes each side, adding the remaining ghee as needed, until the edges caramelise and crisp, then serve warm.
tips: Squeeze and dry-cook the beetroot well; excess moisture is the main reason these kababs fall apart.
The khoya adds richness and helps the sweet beetroot hold together during searing.
Do not over-brown, as the ruby colour is the whole appeal of this kabab.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a white platter for colour contrast, with a mint-yogurt dip and thin cucumber slices.

variations.name: Kathal Galouti Kabab
variations.description: This robust galouti uses tender raw jackfruit, whose fibrous, meaty texture mashes into a remarkably kabab-like melt. Slow-spiced with Awadhi aromatics and a hint of smoke, it is a deeply savoury, restaurant-style vegetarian galouti.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: sears the kababs golden and carries the smoky Awadhi spicing

steps: Boil 2 cups raw jackfruit until very soft, about 15 minutes, drain well and mash it into a fibrous, smooth paste.

Mix in 3 tbsp roasted chana powder, 4 tbsp crushed fried onion, 2 tbsp cashew paste, 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 0.75 tsp garam masala, 0.5 tsp mace-cardamom powder, 0.5 tsp black pepper and 0.75 tsp salt into a firm dough.
Place the bowl of mixture beside a small cup holding a red-hot charcoal piece, drizzle a little Anveshan Ghee over the coal, cover for 3 minutes to smoke, then remove the coal.
Chill the smoked mixture for 15 minutes and shape into small flat patties.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on a tawa on medium heat and sear the kababs for 3 minutes each side, adding ghee as needed, until golden and crisp.
Lift gently and serve hot with the smoky aroma still lingering.
tips: Boil the jackfruit until it mashes easily; undercooked kathal stays stringy and hard to bind.
The charcoal smoking step gives the meaty, dhaba-like depth that sets this galouti apart.
Squeeze out any water from the boiled jackfruit so the kababs hold firm while searing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sirke wale pyaaz and a warm sheermal, finishing with a squeeze of lemon.

variations.name: Classic Mixed Veg Kofta Curry
variations.description: A wholesome curry where dumplings of grated carrot, beans and potato fry golden and simmer in a spiced onion-tomato gravy. A brilliant way to sneak vegetables into a hearty main, the koftas stay tender while soaking up the tangy, warming sauce.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: builds the onion-tomato base and lends the gravy a homely richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: fries the vegetable koftas to a crisp golden shell

steps: Grate the 2 cups mixed vegetables, squeeze out excess water, then mix with 0.5 cup besan, chopped green chillies and 0.5 tsp salt into a thick, holdable dough.
Shape into 12 small balls and deep-fry in the hot Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes until golden and crisp, then drain.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat, add the finely chopped onions, and saute for 6 minutes until golden brown.

Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then stir in the pureed tomatoes with 1 tsp chilli powder, 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt, and cook for 8 minutes until the ghee separates.
Pour in 1.5 cups water, simmer for 5 minutes until the gravy thickens, and sprinkle in 0.5 tsp garam masala.
Add the koftas to the gravy just 2 minutes before serving so they stay whole and do not turn mushy.
tips: Squeeze the grated vegetables dry so the koftas hold together and do not soak up oil.
If the dough feels loose, add another spoon of besan so the koftas keep their shape.
Combine koftas and gravy at the last moment to keep the dumplings from falling apart.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with tandoori roti or steamed rice and a cooling cucumber raita.

variations.name: Lauki Kofta Curry
variations.description: A light, home-style curry of bottle gourd koftas simmered in a tangy yogurt-tomato gravy. Gentle on the stomach and low in oil, the lauki keeps the koftas moist and soft while the mildly spiced sauce makes it a soothing everyday meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: tempers the cumin and gives the light gravy a comforting aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: fries the soft lauki koftas to a firm golden crust

steps: Grate the 3 cups lauki, squeeze out its water thoroughly, then mix with 0.5 cup besan, 0.25 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt into a thick batter.
Shape into 12 small koftas and deep-fry in the hot Anveshan Sunflower Oil over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes until golden, then drain.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin, let it splutter, then add the chopped onion and saute for 4 minutes until soft.
Add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then the pureed tomatoes with 1.5 tsp coriander powder, 0.25 tsp turmeric, 0.75 tsp chilli powder and 0.75 tsp salt, and cook for 6 minutes until thick.
Whisk the 0.5 cup curd smooth, lower the heat, and stir it in slowly so it does not split, then add 1.5 cups water and simmer for 5 minutes.
Slip the koftas into the light gravy 2 minutes before serving so they soak up flavour yet stay soft.
tips: Squeeze the lauki very well; its high water content otherwise makes the koftas break in oil.
Add the whisked curd off the boil and stir constantly to keep the gravy from curdling.
This curry is best eaten fresh, as the delicate lauki koftas soften if left sitting too long.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft phulka or plain steamed rice for a light, wholesome lunch.

variations.name: Malai Veg Kofta
variations.description: A rich restaurant-style curry where mixed vegetable koftas float in a creamy cashew-tomato gravy finished with fresh cream. Indulgent and mildly sweet, this crowd-pleasing version turns a simple veg kofta into a party centrepiece.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: gives the malai gravy its rich, velvety mouthfeel

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: fries the vegetable koftas golden and crisp

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: balances the tomato tang with a mellow natural sweetness

steps: Grate and squeeze the 2 cups mixed vegetables, mix with 50 g grated paneer, 0.5 cup besan and 0.5 tsp salt, and shape into 12 koftas.
Deep-fry the koftas in the hot Anveshan Groundnut Oil over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes until golden, then drain.
Boil the 4 tomatoes, 1 onion and 15 cashews in a cup of water for 8 minutes, cool, blend, and strain into a smooth puree.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan over medium heat, add 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, and saute for 30 seconds.
Pour in the strained puree with 0.75 tsp salt and 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, and simmer for 10 minutes, stirring, until thick and glossy.
Crush 1 tsp kasuri methi in, stir 4 tbsp cream off the heat, and add the koftas just before serving so they stay intact.
tips: Strain the cashew-tomato puree for the smooth, restaurant-style malai texture.
Add cream off the heat so the rich gravy does not split or turn oily.
Toss the koftas in a little gravy first so they flavour up without going soggy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter naan or a mild pulao, drizzled with cream and a sprinkle of chopped coriander.

variations.name: Punjabi Dhaba Veg Kofta
variations.description: A robust dhaba-style curry with rustic vegetable koftas in a thick, deeply browned onion-tomato masala loaded with garam spices. Bolder and spicier than the home version, it carries the smoky, garlicky punch you expect from a roadside Punjabi dhaba.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the dhaba fat that fries the masala to a deep, smoky brown

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: gives the koftas the pungent edge typical of Punjabi dhaba frying

steps: Grate and squeeze the 2 cups mixed vegetables, mix with 0.5 cup besan, chopped green chillies and 0.5 tsp salt, and shape into 12 koftas.
Deep-fry the koftas in the hot Anveshan Mustard Oil over medium heat for 4 minutes until deep golden, then drain and set aside.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan over medium heat, add 1 tsp cumin, then the finely chopped onions, and fry for 8 minutes until deep brown.

Add 1.5 tbsp ginger-garlic paste for 1 minute, then the pureed tomatoes with 1.5 tsp chilli powder, 2 tsp coriander powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt, and cook for 10 minutes until the ghee pools at the edges.
Pour in 2 cups water, simmer for 6 minutes until the gravy turns thick and glossy, and stir in 1 tsp garam masala.
Add the koftas to the gravy just before serving and finish with a spoon of ghee for the classic dhaba sheen.
