tips: Brown the onions patiently to a deep colour for the authentic dark, robust dhaba gravy.
Heat the mustard oil to smoking before frying so the koftas lose the raw pungency.
Add the koftas last so they hold shape in the thick, heavily spiced masala.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with butter-smeared tandoori roti or lachha paratha, topped with raw onion rings and coriander.

variations.name: Classic Vrat Ke Aloo
variations.description: Vrat Ke Aloo is the quintessential fasting potato curry of boiled potatoes simmered in a light tomato base with cumin, rock salt and green chilli. Quick and comforting, it is the dish that partners kuttu puri and samak rice on every Navratri thali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the cumin and gives the fasting curry its rich, rounded base

steps: Peel 4 boiled potatoes and roughly crush them by hand into uneven chunks, which helps thicken the gravy.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan and splutter 1 tsp cumin seeds until fragrant, about 20 seconds.
Add 2 slit green chillies and 1 inch grated ginger, saute 30 seconds, then add 2 pureed tomatoes and cook for 5 minutes until the ghee separates.
Stir in 1 tsp roasted cumin powder and 1.25 tsp sendha namak, then add the crushed potatoes and mix to coat.
Pour in 2 cups water, bring to a boil, then simmer for 8 minutes until the gravy thickens slightly and turns flavourful.
Lightly mash a few potato pieces against the pan for body, garnish with 3 tbsp coriander, and serve hot.
tips: Hand-crush rather than dice the potatoes, so their rough edges dissolve and naturally thicken the curry.
Use only roasted cumin powder and rock salt to keep it strictly fasting-friendly.
Simmer a few minutes longer for a thicker gravy that clings beautifully to kuttu puri.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with kuttu ki puri or samak rice, with a wedge of lemon to squeeze over.

variations.name: Dahi Wale Vrat Aloo
variations.description: A creamy Banarasi-style fasting curry where boiled potatoes simmer in a whisked-yogurt gravy tempered with cumin and green chilli. The tangy, silky sauce clings to the potatoes and is milder and richer than the tomato version.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the whole spices for the tempering that flavours the yogurt gravy

steps: Peel and dice 4 boiled potatoes into chunks; whisk 1 cup curd smooth with 1.5 cups water and 1 tsp roasted cumin powder.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan and splutter 1 tsp cumin seeds, then add 2 slit green chillies and 1 inch grated ginger for 30 seconds.
Lower the heat completely, pour in the whisked yogurt slowly, and stir continuously so it does not split.
Once it comes to a gentle simmer, add the potato chunks, 1.25 tsp sendha namak and 0.5 tsp black pepper.
Simmer uncovered on low for 8 minutes, stirring now and then, until the gravy thickens and coats the potatoes.
Garnish with 3 tbsp coriander and serve hot, being careful to keep the heat gentle throughout.
tips: Add the yogurt only on low heat and keep stirring, as high heat will curdle it instantly.
Whisk the curd with the water beforehand for the smoothest, lump-free gravy.
A pinch of black pepper is essential here, as it balances the tang of the yogurt.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with samak rice or kuttu puri, finishing with a light dusting of roasted cumin over the bowl.

variations.name: Jeera Vrat Ke Sukhe Aloo
variations.description: A dry, stir-fried fasting potato where cubes are tossed in plenty of cumin and green chilli until the edges crisp and gold. With no gravy at all, it is perfect for packing in a tiffin or eating with puri on the go.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: fries the potatoes so their edges crisp golden with a nutty cumin aroma

steps: Peel 5 boiled potatoes and cut them into even 2 cm cubes so they crisp uniformly.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a wide pan on medium-high and splutter 1.5 tsp cumin seeds until deep and fragrant.
Add 2 chopped green chillies and 1 inch julienned ginger, stir for 30 seconds, then tip in the potato cubes.
Spread the cubes in a single layer and let them fry undisturbed for 3 minutes, then toss and fry another 4 minutes until the edges turn golden and crisp.
Sprinkle 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 0.5 tsp black pepper and 1 tsp sendha namak, tossing to coat evenly.
Turn off the heat, squeeze in 1 tbsp lemon juice, scatter 3 tbsp coriander, and serve hot.
tips: Let the potatoes sit undisturbed between tosses so they develop a crisp golden crust instead of turning mushy.
Use a wide pan and a single layer, as crowding steams the potatoes rather than frying them.
Add the salt and powders near the end so they cling to the crisp surface without burning.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pack into a fasting tiffin with kuttu puri, or serve as a dry side with a bowl of sweetened curd.

variations.name: Khatti Meethi Vrat Aloo
variations.description: A Gujarati-leaning fasting potato balanced between tangy and sweet, with lemon for sourness and a touch of jaggery for roundness. The glossy sweet-sour sauce and warm cumin make this a lively change from the usual savoury vrat aloo.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: blooms the cumin base for this tangy-sweet fasting curry

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: rounds the tang with a natural caramel sweetness

steps: Peel 4 boiled potatoes and cut into medium chunks.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and splutter 1 tsp cumin, then add 2 slit green chillies and 1 inch grated ginger for 30 seconds.
Add the potato chunks and toss for 2 minutes, then pour in 1.5 cups water with 1 tsp sendha namak and 0.5 tsp black pepper.
Simmer for 6 minutes until the potatoes soak up flavour and the gravy reduces a little.
Stir in 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder until it dissolves, then turn off the heat and add 2 tbsp lemon juice.
Taste and adjust the sweet-sour balance, garnish with 3 tbsp coriander, and serve warm.
tips: Add the jaggery first and the lemon last, tasting as you go to strike your preferred sweet-sour balance.
Keep the gravy glossy and light rather than thick, so it stays refreshing.
Dissolve the jaggery fully off a rolling boil so the sauce turns smooth and shiny.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain samak rice, where the tangy-sweet sauce brightens the mild millet beautifully.

variations.name: Classic Dahi Baingan
variations.description: Tender fried brinjal rounds bathed in a lightly spiced, gently soured yogurt gravy that clings to every slice. The creamy dahi mellows the smoky fried eggplant while a cumin-and-curry-leaf tempering lifts it. A quick, homely curry that turns a humble vegetable into something special.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee fries the brinjal and carries the cumin tempering

steps: Slice the brinjal into ½-inch rounds, rub with a pinch of salt and turmeric, and shallow-fry in 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over medium heat for 3 minutes per side until golden and soft, then set aside.
Whisk the yogurt with the besan, remaining turmeric, red chilli powder and salt until smooth, adding the besan to stop it splitting.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Ghee in a pan and crackle cumin, curry leaves, slit green chilli and grated ginger for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Lower the heat, pour in the whisked yogurt and stir continuously as it warms so it does not curdle, cooking 4 minutes until it thickens slightly.
Gently slide in the fried brinjal rounds and simmer on low for 5 minutes so they soak up the tangy gravy.
Fold in chopped coriander and serve warm.
tips: Whisking a spoon of besan into the yogurt keeps the gravy from splitting on the heat.
Salt the brinjal slices for 10 minutes and pat dry to draw out bitterness before frying.
Keep the heat low once the yogurt goes in; a hard boil will curdle it.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulkas or steamed rice and a simple dal for a comforting everyday meal.

variations.name: Odia Dahi Baigana
variations.description: The temple-style Odia dahi baigana where fried brinjal is folded into a cooling, mustard-tempered yogurt seasoned with a signature pancha phutana spice mix. Served at room temperature, it is tangy, subtly sweet and beloved as a mahaprasad side. The panch phoron sets it apart from north Indian versions.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: kachi ghani mustard oil fries the brinjal and gives the authentic Odia pungency

steps: Cut the brinjal into cubes, toss with turmeric and a little salt, and fry in 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil over medium heat for 6 minutes until soft and browned, then cool.
Whisk the yogurt smooth with roasted cumin powder, sugar, salt and finely chopped green chilli until creamy.
Gently fold the cooled fried brinjal into the seasoned yogurt so the pieces stay whole.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Mustard Oil in a small pan and splutter the panch phoron, dried red chillies and curry leaves for 30 seconds until aromatic.
Pour the sizzling tempering over the yogurt-brinjal mixture and fold it through gently.
Rest for 10 minutes at room temperature so the flavours settle before serving.
tips: Cool the fried brinjal before mixing so the yogurt stays cool and does not split.
Panch phoron is essential to the Odia character, so do not substitute plain cumin.
This dish is best served at room temperature rather than piping hot.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature as a side with steamed rice, dalma and a wedge of lemon in true Odia thali style.

variations.name: Hyderabadi Dahi Baingan Curry
variations.description: A rich Hyderabadi-style gravy where small brinjals simmer in a nutty peanut-sesame yogurt masala, tangy and mildly spiced with a tamarind edge. The thick, glossy curry coats the eggplants in layers of flavour, quite unlike a simple dahi coating. A festive dish that eats beautifully with biryani or roti.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed sesame oil deepens the nutty Hyderabadi masala base

steps: Dry-roast the peanuts, sesame seeds and desiccated coconut separately until golden, then grind with a little water into a smooth paste.
Slit the small brinjals into quarters keeping the stem intact, and shallow-fry in 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil for 4 minutes until lightly browned, then set aside.
Heat the remaining sesame oil, fry the finely chopped onion until golden, add ginger-garlic paste and cook 1 minute until the raw smell goes.
Add the ground peanut-sesame paste with turmeric, red chilli powder, coriander powder and salt, and cook 4 minutes until the oil separates.
Lower the heat, whisk in the yogurt and 1 cup water stirring steadily so it does not split, then add tamarind pulp and bring to a gentle simmer.
Slide in the fried brinjals, cover and simmer on low for 12 minutes until they are tender and the gravy turns thick and glossy.
tips: Grind the roasted nuts and seeds finely for a smooth, restaurant-style gravy.
Add the yogurt on low heat and keep stirring to prevent it curdling into the nutty base.
Keep the brinjal stems on so the pieces hold together during the simmer.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with Hyderabadi bagara rice, plain biryani or soft roti and a side of raita.

variations.name: Roasted Baingan Bharta Dahi Curry
variations.description: A smoky twist where whole brinjal is fire-roasted and mashed bharta-style, then simmered into a tangy yogurt gravy for a rustic, deeply flavoured curry. The charred eggplant lends a distinctive smokiness that the cool dahi balances. Thick, earthy and very different from the sliced-and-fried classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil carries the onion-garlic base for the smoky curry

steps: Roast the whole brinjals directly over a flame or under a grill, turning, for about 10 minutes until the skin chars and blisters and the flesh collapses.
Cool, peel off the charred skin, and mash the smoky flesh coarsely with a fork.
Whisk the yogurt with the besan, turmeric, red chilli powder and salt until smooth so it stays stable on heat.
Heat the Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle cumin, add chopped onion, crushed garlic and slit green chilli, and fry over medium heat for 5 minutes until golden.
Lower the heat, pour in the whisked yogurt and stir steadily for 3 minutes as it warms so it does not split, then stir in the mashed brinjal.
Simmer on low for 6 minutes until thick and well blended, fold in coriander, and serve warm.
tips: Roast the brinjal until fully collapsed for the deepest smoky flavour.
Whisk besan into the yogurt so the tangy gravy does not curdle when heated.
A drop of mustard oil stirred in at the end amplifies the rustic smokiness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot bajra or wheat rotis, a raw onion salad and a spoon of white butter.

variations.name: Classic Gujarati Lapsi
variations.description: A homely festive sweet of broken wheat roasted in ghee until nutty, then cooked soft and sweetened with jaggery and cardamom. Made on auspicious days across Gujarat and Rajasthan, its fudgy, grainy texture and deep caramel warmth come entirely from patient roasting and good ghee.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Bilona ghee roasts the broken wheat to a nutty aroma and gives lapsi its glossy finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery sweetens the lapsi with a warm caramel depth that pairs with roasted wheat

steps: Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan on medium and roast 1 cup coarse broken wheat, stirring constantly, for 8 to 10 minutes until it turns deep golden and smells nutty.
Carefully pour in 3 cups hot water, standing back as it will splutter, then lower the heat and simmer covered for 12 to 15 minutes until the grains swell soft and most water is absorbed.
Meanwhile melt 0.75 cup jaggery powder with 0.25 cup water in a small pan on low, stirring, until it dissolves into a syrup, then strain out any grit.
Pour the jaggery syrup into the cooked wheat and stir on low for 5 minutes until it is fully absorbed and the lapsi turns glossy and thick.
In a small pan fry 10 almonds, 10 cashews and 2 tbsp raisins in the remaining 1 tbsp ghee until golden and the raisins plump up.
Stir the fried nuts, 0.5 tsp cardamom and 0.125 tsp nutmeg into the lapsi, cook 2 minutes more, and serve warm.
tips: Roast the wheat slowly and thoroughly, as this deep toasting is what gives lapsi its signature nutty flavour.
Always add the jaggery after the wheat is cooked soft; adding it early toughens the grains.
Adjust water at the end for texture, keeping it a touch loose since lapsi thickens as it sits.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a festive prasad or after a meal, with an extra drizzle of ghee on top.

variations.name: Doodhwali Lapsi with Khandsari
variations.description: A creamy kheer-like lapsi where roasted broken wheat is simmered in milk and sweetened with mild khandsari and saffron. Softer and richer than the water-based version, it eats like a warm wheat pudding, popular for pujas and gentle winter desserts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee roasts the wheat before it simmers gently in milk for a creamy pudding

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari Sugar
ingredients.note: Mild unrefined khandsari sweetens the milky lapsi without masking the saffron

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: A pinch of saffron gives the milk lapsi its aroma and pale-gold colour

steps: Warm 2 tbsp milk, soak 0.25 tsp saffron in it and set aside to bloom.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan on medium and roast 0.75 cup broken wheat for 8 minutes until golden and fragrant.
Add 1 cup water and simmer on low for 8 minutes until the wheat softens and drinks up the water.
Pour in 4 cups milk, bring to a gentle simmer and cook on low for 15 minutes, stirring often, until the wheat is very soft and the milk thickens.
Lower the heat and stir in 0.5 cup khandsari and the saffron milk, cooking gently for 4 minutes until the sweetener dissolves without letting it boil hard.
Fold in 0.5 tsp cardamom, 12 slivered pistachios and 10 chopped almonds, simmer 2 minutes, and serve warm or chilled.
tips: Cook the wheat in a little water first so the milk is not overworked and stays from catching at the base.
Add the khandsari towards the end and keep the heat low so the milk does not split.
It thickens considerably on cooling, so loosen with a splash of warm milk if serving later.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as a comforting pudding or chilled in summer, topped with extra saffron strands.

variations.name: Dry-Fruit Loaded Rajasthani Lapsi
variations.description: A festive Rajasthani lapsi turned rich and celebratory with a heavy hand of ghee-fried dry fruits, desiccated coconut and melon seeds folded through the jaggery-sweetened wheat. Made for weddings and big festivals, it is the most indulgent, nut-studded version of the sweet.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A generous measure of ghee fries the many dry fruits and enriches this festive lapsi

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery brings the deep sweetness that carries the abundant nuts and coconut

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a small pan and fry 15 chopped almonds, 15 cashews, 12 pistachios, 3 tbsp raisins, 3 tbsp desiccated coconut and 2 tbsp melon seeds separately until golden, then set aside.
In a heavy pan heat 3 tbsp ghee on medium and roast 1 cup broken wheat for 9 to 10 minutes until deep golden and nutty.
Add 3 cups hot water carefully, lower the heat and simmer covered for 12 to 15 minutes until the grains swell soft.
Melt 0.75 cup jaggery powder with 0.25 cup water into a strained syrup, then stir it into the cooked wheat and cook on low for 5 minutes until glossy and thick.
Fold in three-quarters of the fried dry fruits, 0.5 tsp cardamom and a final 1 tbsp ghee, and cook 2 minutes so the flavours meld.
Scatter the reserved dry fruits and coconut over the top and serve warm.
tips: Fry each dry fruit just to golden and keep some aside for garnish so the top looks festive.
Toast the melon seeds gently until they puff; they burn quickly on high heat.
Keep the lapsi slightly loose as the wheat and nuts keep absorbing moisture on standing.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm at weddings and festivals in a silver bowl, finished with a sheet of edible silver leaf if you like.

variations.name: Coconut Jaggery Lapsi with Coconut Oil
variations.description: A coastal-leaning lapsi where fresh coconut and a hint of wood-pressed coconut oil round out the roasted wheat, sweetened with jaggery for a tropical, fragrant twist. The coconut gives it a mellow sweetness and lightness distinct from the ghee-heavy classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Ghee roasts the wheat and balances the coconut with a nutty richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: A spoon of wood-pressed coconut oil deepens the tropical coconut aroma of this lapsi

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Jaggery sweetens the coconut lapsi with a warm, molasses depth

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan on medium and roast 1 cup broken wheat for 9 minutes until golden and nutty.
Add 3 cups hot water carefully, lower the heat and simmer covered for 12 to 15 minutes until the grains turn soft.
Stir in 0.5 cup grated fresh coconut and cook for 3 minutes so it releases its aroma into the wheat.
Melt 0.75 cup jaggery powder with 0.25 cup water into a strained syrup, pour it into the wheat and cook on low for 5 minutes until glossy and thick.
In a small pan warm 1 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil and fry 12 cashews and 2 tbsp raisins until golden.
Fold the fried nuts, 0.5 tsp cardamom and the coconut oil into the lapsi, cook 2 minutes, and serve warm.
tips: Add the fresh coconut before the jaggery so it cooks into the wheat rather than sitting on top.
Use only a spoon of coconut oil for aroma; too much overpowers the jaggery.
Fresh coconut can turn the lapsi sticky, so keep the water on the generous side.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a scatter of fresh coconut, alongside a cup of filter coffee.

variations.name: Classic Malai Paneer Tikka
variations.description: Malai Paneer Tikka is the mild, creamy cousin of the fiery red tikka, with paneer cubes bathed in a rich marinade of hung curd, cream, cashew and cheese. Grilled till the edges catch colour, it stays lush and melt-in-the-mouth with a delicate white-pepper and cardamom warmth.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: basting the tikka with ghee on the grill gives a glossy, aromatic finish

steps: Whisk 0.75 cup hung curd with 0.25 cup fresh cream, 3 tbsp cashew paste, 0.25 cup grated cheese, 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 1 tsp green chilli paste, 0.5 tsp white pepper, 0.25 tsp cardamom powder, 2 tbsp cornflour and 1 tsp salt into a thick creamy marinade.
Fold in the 400 g paneer cubes along with 2 cm chunks of capsicum and onion, coating everything evenly, and marinate for at least 1 hour in the fridge.
Thread the paneer, capsicum and onion alternately onto skewers, packing them snugly without squashing the paneer.
Preheat a grill or oven to 220C, or heat a heavy tawa, and cook the skewers for 12 to 15 minutes, turning, until the marinade sets and the edges turn pale gold.
Baste the tikka with Anveshan Ghee once or twice during grilling so it stays moist and picks up a glossy sheen.
Rest the skewers for 2 minutes, then slide off the tikka and finish with a squeeze of lemon.
tips: Use thick hung curd and add cornflour so the creamy marinade clings to the paneer instead of sliding off.
Do not over-grill, as malai tikka is meant to stay soft and creamy rather than dry and charred.
Soak wooden skewers in water for 20 minutes so they do not scorch under the grill.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a sizzler plate with onion rings, mint chutney and a dusting of chaat masala.

variations.name: Kesar Malai Paneer Tikka
variations.description: A regal, saffron-kissed version where strands of saffron steeped in warm milk tint the malai marinade a pale gold and lend a floral aroma. Nutmeg and cream make it especially rich, turning the tikka into a wedding-feast showpiece.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: saffron steeped in warm milk tints and perfumes the malai marinade

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: basting with ghee lifts the saffron aroma and glosses the tikka

steps: Steep 0.25 tsp Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk for 10 minutes until the milk turns deep gold.

Whisk 0.75 cup hung curd with 0.33 cup cream, 3 tbsp cashew paste, 1 tbsp ginger paste, 0.5 tsp white pepper, 0.25 tsp nutmeg powder, 2 tbsp cornflour, 1 tsp salt and the saffron milk into a smooth golden marinade.
Coat the 400 g paneer cubes and chunks of capsicum and onion in the marinade and rest for 1 hour in the fridge.
Thread the paneer and vegetables onto soaked skewers, alternating for colour.
Grill or bake at 220C for 12 to 15 minutes, turning, until the marinade sets to a pale saffron gold, basting with Anveshan Ghee midway.
Rest 2 minutes and slide off the tikka, garnishing with a few extra saffron strands.
tips: Steep the saffron in warm, not boiling, milk to draw out its colour and aroma without dulling it.
Keep the marinade pale by avoiding chilli powder, letting the saffron colour shine through.
Add a pinch more nutmeg only at the end, as too much can turn the delicate flavour bitter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a bed of saffron-tinged onion salad with warm sheermal or naan for a festive spread.

variations.name: Achari Malai Paneer Tikka
variations.description: A tangy, pickle-spiced twist where a mustard-oil achari tempering of five pickling spices is folded into the creamy marinade. The result is a paneer tikka with a bold, sour-savoury North Indian pickle character balanced by the mellow malai base.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: hot mustard oil blooms the pickling spices to build the achari character

steps: Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking point, cool it for a minute, then splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tsp fennel seeds, 0.25 tsp fenugreek seeds and 0.5 tsp nigella seeds for 30 seconds until fragrant, and cool this achari tempering fully.
Whisk 0.75 cup hung curd with 0.25 cup cream, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 1 tsp salt and the cooled achari oil with its spices into a tangy marinade.
Coat the 400 g paneer cubes and chunks of capsicum and onion, then marinate for at least 1 hour.
Thread the paneer and vegetables onto soaked skewers, alternating pieces.
Grill or bake at 220C for 12 to 15 minutes, turning, until the edges catch colour and the marinade sets with a pickle-like aroma.
Rest 2 minutes, slide off the tikka and finish with a squeeze of lemon and a scatter of sliced onion.
tips: Always bloom the pickling seeds in hot oil first, as raw seeds would taste harsh in the marinade.
Cool the tempered oil completely before mixing it into the curd so the yogurt does not split.
Let the tikka marinate a full hour so the achari flavours penetrate the paneer.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a fennel-spiked onion salad and a wedge of lemon to echo the pickle notes.

variations.name: Charcoal-Smoked Mawa Malai Tikka
variations.description: A restaurant-grade tandoori take enriched with grated mawa for an extra-lush marinade and finished with a coal dhungar for genuine smokiness. Kasuri methi and chaat masala give it that unmistakable tandoor-house aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee basting and a few drops on the coal deepen the smoky tandoori aroma

steps: Whisk 0.75 cup hung curd with 0.33 cup grated mawa, 0.25 cup grated cheese, 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi, 0.5 tsp white pepper, 1 tsp chaat masala, 2 tbsp cornflour and 1 tsp salt into a rich, thick marinade.
Coat the 400 g paneer cubes and chunks of capsicum and onion and marinate for 1 hour in the fridge.
Thread onto soaked skewers and grill or bake at 220C for 12 to 15 minutes, turning and basting with Anveshan Ghee, until the marinade sets and the edges char.
Transfer the grilled tikka to a deep bowl and nestle a small steel cup among the pieces.
Place a red-hot piece of charcoal in the cup, drizzle a little Anveshan Ghee over it to release smoke, and cover the bowl tightly for 4 minutes.
Uncover, give the tikka a gentle toss to spread the smoky aroma, and serve at once.
tips: Grate the mawa fine and whisk it in well so it dissolves into a silky, lump-free marinade.
Keep the dhungar bowl covered for the full 4 minutes to trap the maximum smoky flavour.
Char the edges slightly on the grill before smoking for a true tandoor-house taste.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve straight from the smoky bowl with mint chutney, onion rings and a lemon wedge.

variations.name: Classic Veg Seekh Kabab
variations.description: Boiled mixed vegetables and paneer are mashed with roasted gram and warm spices, moulded onto skewers and griddled until charred and fragrant. These smoky, well-spiced seekhs deliver all the satisfaction of the tandoor from an ordinary stovetop pan.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bastes the seekhs on the griddle for a golden char and rich aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: roasted gram sattu absorbs moisture and binds the seekh so it grips the skewer

steps: Boil the 2 cups mixed vegetables until soft, drain very well, and mash with the 2 boiled potatoes and 0.5 cup grated paneer into a dry, smooth mixture.

Dry-roast the 4 tbsp Anveshan Sattu on low heat for 2 minutes, cool, and mix into the mash with 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, chopped chillies, 1 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp chilli powder, 0.5 tsp chaat masala, coriander and 1 tsp salt.
Chill the mixture for 20 minutes, then take a portion and press it firmly around a greased skewer into a 4-inch log, repeating for all the seekhs.
Heat a flat griddle over medium heat and brush with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then lay the skewers down and cook for 3 to 4 minutes, rotating for even browning.
Baste the seekhs with the remaining Anveshan Ghee as they cook, turning until charred and crisp on all sides, about 8 minutes total.
Slide the kababs off the skewers, dust with a little chaat masala, and serve immediately while hot.
tips: Drain and mash the vegetables until dry, as any moisture makes the seekhs slip off the skewer.
Grease the skewer and your palms so the mixture presses on smoothly and releases cleanly.
Chill the mixture before shaping so the seekhs firm up and hold their log shape on the griddle.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with mint chutney, onion rings and a lemon wedge, wrapped in a warm roomali roti if you like.

variations.name: Paneer Seekh Kabab
variations.description: A protein-rich version built mostly on grated paneer, giving the seekhs a soft, milky bite laced with cardamom and white pepper. Milder and creamier than the vegetable version, these pale golden kababs are a favourite with children and adults alike.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bastes the paneer seekhs for a delicate golden crust

steps: Grate the 300 g paneer with the 1 boiled potato and knead until completely smooth and free of lumps.
Mix in 3 tbsp cornflour, 2 tbsp cashew paste, finely chopped chilli and ginger, 0.25 tsp cardamom powder, 0.5 tsp white pepper, 0.5 tsp garam masala, coriander and 0.75 tsp salt into a firm dough.
Chill for 20 minutes, then press portions firmly around greased skewers into smooth 4-inch logs.
Heat a griddle over medium heat, brush with 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, and lay the skewers down to cook for 3 minutes.
Baste with the remaining Anveshan Ghee and rotate the seekhs for 6 to 7 minutes until evenly pale golden all around.
Ease the kababs off the skewers and serve hot, sprinkled with a little chaat masala.
tips: Knead the paneer thoroughly so the seekhs are smooth and do not crack while cooking.
The cornflour and cashew paste keep these soft seekhs bound; do not skip either.
Cook on gentle heat, as paneer browns fast and can turn rubbery over high flame.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a creamy mint-yogurt dip and thinly sliced onions dressed in lemon and chaat masala.

variations.name: Corn and Cheese Seekh Kabab
variations.description: Sweet corn kernels and grated cheese make these seekhs juicy, gooey and irresistibly moreish, with a hint of green chilli for balance. A modern, crowd-pleasing twist that oozes cheese from a lightly charred, crisp exterior.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: brushed over the seekhs so they crisp and char on the griddle

steps: Coarsely crush the 1.5 cups sweet corn, leaving some whole kernels for texture, and mash with the 2 boiled potatoes.
Mix in the 0.75 cup grated cheese, 0.5 cup bread crumbs, finely chopped capsicum, chilli and ginger, 0.5 tsp black pepper, 0.5 tsp chaat masala, coriander and 0.75 tsp salt into a firm mixture.
Chill for 20 minutes, then press portions firmly around greased skewers into 4-inch logs, sealing the cheese inside.
Heat a griddle over medium heat and brush it with 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, then lay the skewers to cook for 3 minutes.
Brush the seekhs with the remaining oil and rotate them for 7 to 8 minutes until golden and lightly charred all over.
Slide the kababs off the skewers and serve at once while the cheese is still molten inside.
tips: Use extra bread crumbs if the mixture feels wet, so the cheesy seekhs hold on the skewer.
Cook just until charred and serve immediately, as the cheese firms up as it cools.
Crush only part of the corn so you keep pockets of juicy whole kernels.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a smoky chipotle-style tomato dip or a tangy schezwan chutney for a fusion snack platter.

variations.name: Tandoori Smoked Veg Seekh Kabab
variations.description: The seekhs are rubbed with tandoori masala and given a charcoal dhungar for that unmistakable smoky, restaurant tandoor flavour. Deeply spiced and aromatic, they capture the char and perfume of a clay oven right on your griddle.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: the pungent oil that gives tandoori kababs their characteristic sharpness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: poured over the hot charcoal to smoke the seekhs

steps: Boil the 2 cups mixed vegetables until soft, drain very well, and mash with the 2 boiled potatoes into a dry mixture.

Dry-roast the 4 tbsp roasted gram flour further for a minute, then mix into the mash with 3 tbsp hung curd, 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 1.5 tsp tandoori masala, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli, crushed kasuri methi and 1 tsp salt.
Place a red-hot piece of charcoal in a small bowl in the centre of the mixture, drizzle 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over it, cover, and smoke for 5 minutes.
Remove the charcoal, chill the smoked mixture for 20 minutes, then press portions firmly around greased skewers into 4-inch logs.
Heat a griddle over medium heat, brush with 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil, and cook the skewers for 3 minutes before basting with more oil.
Rotate and baste the seekhs for 7 to 8 minutes until charred and crisp, then slide off and serve smoking hot.
tips: Smoke the mixture with the lid tightly closed so the seekhs absorb the full charcoal aroma.
Heat the mustard oil until it smokes and cool it before brushing to soften its raw pungency.
Keep the vegetable mash dry so the tandoori seekhs char rather than steam on the griddle.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a mint-coriander chutney, pickled onions and lemon, or tuck into a roomali roll for a smoky wrap.

variations.name: Classic Hariyali Paneer Tikka
variations.description: Hariyali Paneer Tikka coats paneer cubes in a vivid green marinade of fresh mint and coriander sharpened with green chilli and hung curd. Grilled till the herby crust catches colour, it is fresh, tangy and fragrant, with roasted sattu thickening the marinade so it clings to every cube.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: basting with ghee glosses the herby crust and keeps the paneer moist

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: roasted sattu thickens the green marinade so it clings without dripping, replacing gram flour

steps: Blend 1 cup mint, 1 cup coriander and 3 green chillies with a splash of water into a thick, smooth green paste.
Whisk the green paste with 0.5 cup hung curd, 2 tbsp Anveshan Sattu, 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 1 tsp chaat masala, 2 tbsp cornflour and 1 tsp salt into a clinging marinade.
Fold in the 400 g paneer cubes and 2 cm chunks of capsicum and onion, coating well, and marinate for at least 1 hour in the fridge.
Thread the paneer and vegetables alternately onto soaked skewers, packing them close but not crushed.
Grill or bake at 220C for 12 to 15 minutes, turning, until the green crust sets and the edges catch a light char, basting with Anveshan Ghee midway.
Rest the skewers for 2 minutes, slide off the tikka and finish with a squeeze of lemon.
tips: Blend the herbs with minimal water and thicken with sattu so the marinade coats rather than runs off.
Roast the sattu smell out beforehand if you like, so the marinade tastes clean and fresh.
Do not marinate longer than a few hours, as the herbs can darken and turn the coating dull.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a bed of shredded cabbage and onion with extra mint chutney and a lemon wedge.

variations.name: Tandoori Charcoal Hariyali Tikka
variations.description: A restaurant-style green tikka bound with roasted besan and mustard oil for a robust, pungent depth, then finished with a coal dhungar for real tandoor smokiness. Kasuri methi rounds out the herb marinade into something bold and aromatic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed mustard oil gives the green marinade a sharp, tandoor-style pungency

steps: Roast 3 tbsp besan in a dry pan for 2 minutes until nutty, then blend 0.75 cup mint, 0.75 cup coriander and 3 green chillies into a thick paste.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil to smoking, cool slightly, and whisk it into the green paste with 0.5 cup hung curd, the roasted besan, 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 1 tbsp crushed kasuri methi and 1 tsp salt.
Coat the 400 g paneer cubes and chunks of capsicum and onion in the marinade and rest for 1 hour.
Thread onto soaked skewers and grill or bake at 220C for 12 to 15 minutes, turning, until the crust sets and the edges char.
Place the tikka in a deep bowl with a small steel cup in the centre, set a hot piece of charcoal in it, drizzle a little mustard oil over the coal and cover tightly for 4 minutes.
Uncover, toss gently to spread the smoke, and serve immediately.
tips: Heat the mustard oil to smoking and cool it before use so its raw pungency softens into flavour.
Roast the besan well so it thickens the marinade without leaving a raw, pasty taste.
Cover the dhungar bowl tightly for the full 4 minutes to lock in the smoky aroma.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve from the smoky bowl with sirka onions and a green chutney for a dhaba-style plate.

variations.name: Palak Hariyali Paneer Tikka
variations.description: A lush, creamy green tikka where blanched spinach deepens the colour and cashew paste and cream make the marinade rich and velvety. Milder than the classic, it is a smooth, restaurant-style version that stays soft and indulgent off the grill.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: basting with ghee keeps the creamy spinach tikka glossy and soft

steps: Blanch 1.5 cups spinach for 30 seconds and refresh in cold water, then blend it with 0.5 cup coriander and 2 green chillies into a smooth green puree.
Whisk the puree with 0.5 cup hung curd, 0.25 cup cream, 2 tbsp cashew paste, 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 2 tbsp cornflour and 1 tsp salt into a rich, velvety marinade.
Coat the 400 g paneer cubes and chunks of capsicum and onion and rest for 1 hour in the fridge.
Thread the paneer and vegetables onto soaked skewers, alternating for colour.
Grill or bake at 220C for 12 to 15 minutes, turning gently and basting with Anveshan Ghee, until the marinade sets to a deep green.
Rest 2 minutes, slide off the tikka and finish with a light squeeze of lemon.
tips: Blanch the spinach briefly and cool it fast so the marinade stays a vivid green rather than dull.
Cashew paste and cream keep this tikka soft, so avoid over-grilling which would dry it out.
Add the cream off the heat into the cooled puree so the marinade does not split.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with garlic naan and a cooling boondi raita for a rich, satisfying meal.

variations.name: Coconut-Mint Hariyali Tikka
variations.description: A South Indian riff where fresh coconut, curry leaves and mint form the green paste, giving the paneer a sweet, aromatic coastal flavour. Grilled in wood-pressed coconut oil, it carries the unmistakable fragrance of a Kerala kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed coconut oil grills the tikka with a warm, coastal aroma

steps: Warm 1 tsp of the Anveshan Coconut Oil and toss 15 curry leaves in it for 20 seconds until crisp and fragrant.
Blend the curry leaves with 0.75 cup mint, 0.75 cup coriander, 0.5 cup grated coconut, 3 green chillies, 1 inch ginger and 2 tbsp roasted chana dal into a thick green paste.
Mix the paste with 1 tbsp lemon juice, 2 tbsp cornflour, 1 tsp salt and 1 tbsp of the coconut oil into a clinging marinade, then coat the 400 g paneer, capsicum and onion and rest for 1 hour.
Thread the paneer and vegetables onto soaked skewers, alternating pieces.
Grill or bake at 220C for 12 to 15 minutes, turning and basting with the remaining Anveshan Coconut Oil, until the coating sets and the edges brown.
Rest 2 minutes, slide off the tikka and scatter with a few extra crisp curry leaves.
tips: Crisp the curry leaves in coconut oil first so their aroma infuses the whole marinade.
Roasted chana dal thickens the paste and binds it, so grind it in well for a smooth coating.
Use fresh, not desiccated, coconut so the marinade stays moist and sweet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a coconut chutney and steamed lemon rice for a full South Indian spread.

variations.name: Classic Kathiyawadi Bajra Rotla
variations.description: The signature bread of the Kathiyawad region of Saurashtra, a thick, sturdy pearl-millet round patted large and roasted slowly till its craggy surface chars in spots. Kathiyawadi cooks pat it broader and thicker than a Gujarati rotlo, giving a robust bread built to soak up fiery chutneys and pools of ghee. Earthy, dense and deeply satisfying, it is the anchor of a rustic Saurashtrian thali.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Poured lavishly over the hot rotla in the Kathiyawadi way, drenching the thick charred crumb

steps: Bring 1.25 cups water to a rolling boil with 0.5 tsp salt, pour it over 2 cups bajra flour mixed with 0.5 tsp carom seeds, and stir into a shaggy mass.
As soon as it is bearable to touch, knead the warm dough for 5 to 6 minutes with your palm heel until it is smooth, dense and crack-free.
Wet your palms well and pat a large ball back and forth into a broad, thick 7-inch round, pressing 1 tbsp sesame seeds onto the surface and mending cracks at the rim as you go.
Slide it carefully onto a medium-hot tava and cook the base 3 minutes until firm with brown patches, then flip.
Cook the second side 2 minutes, then hold the rotla over a low direct flame, turning, until it chars in spots and puffs in patches.
Transfer to a plate, pour 1.25 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the hot surface so it soaks in, and repeat with the remaining dough.
tips: Kathiyawadi rotla is patted thicker and broader than a regular rotlo, so knead the dough a touch stiffer to hold the size.
Keep your palms wet throughout; the gluten-free millet dough cracks the instant your hands dry out.
Serve straight off the flame, as the thick rotla hardens quickly and is meant to be eaten hot and ghee-soaked.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with fiery lehsun ni chutney, a bowl of chaas and jaggery, and a Kathiyawadi ringan no olo for the full Saurashtrian spread.

variations.name: Nagli-Bajra Rotla
variations.description: A darker, mineral-rich rotla that blends pearl millet with nagli, the finger millet beloved across the millet belt of western India. Ragi deepens the colour to a rustic brown and adds a faint cocoa earthiness while making the round a touch more binding than pure bajra. It is the wholesome everyday rotla eaten by farming families for its slow-burning, sustaining energy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Rubbed over the hot tava so the dark, dense rotla lifts cleanly and browns evenly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Smeared over the dark hot rotla to enrich the earthy finger-millet crumb

steps: Combine 1.25 cups bajra flour and 0.75 cups nagli flour in a wide bowl.
Boil 1.33 cups water with 0.5 tsp salt, pour it over the flours, stir into a mass, and once bearable knead the warm dough 5 minutes until smooth and dense.
Wet your palms and pat a large ball into a thick 6-inch round; the ragi makes the dough slightly more cohesive and easier to handle.
Rub the medium-hot tava with a little Anveshan Groundnut Oil, lay on the rotla, and cook 3 minutes until the darker base sets with brown flecks, then flip and cook the second side 2 minutes.
Blister the rotla over a low direct flame, turning, until it puffs in patches and the surface chars lightly.
Smear 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the hot rotla and repeat with the remaining dough.
tips: Ragi darkens as it cooks, so judge doneness by the brown flecks and firm feel rather than by deep colour.
The water must be fully boiling to bind two gluten-free millets, and add the last splash slowly as ragi drinks it up.
This rotla keeps you full for hours, so serve it for a working lunch with a substantial sabzi.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pair with a bowl of spiced kadhi or a garlicky lasaniya bataka, letting the earthy rotla balance the tang and heat.

variations.name: Jeera-Marcha Masala Rotla
variations.description: A savoury Kathiyawadi rotla with cumin, coarse green chilli and fresh coriander kneaded right into the millet, turning the plain bread into a spiced meal on its own. The green chilli brings a clean farmhouse heat while cumin and turmeric warm the earthy crumb through and through. Roasted in groundnut oil and finished with ghee, it needs little more than curd to satisfy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Used both to roast the spiced rotla and to finish it, mellowing the chilli heat with its richness

steps: Pound 3 green chillies with 1 tsp cumin seeds into a coarse paste in a mortar.
Mix the paste into 2 cups bajra flour with 3 tbsp chopped coriander, 0.5 tsp turmeric and 0.5 tsp salt in a wide bowl.
Pour in about 1.25 cups boiling water, stir into a mass, and once bearable knead the warm dough 5 minutes until smooth and crack-free.
Wet your palms and pat a large ball into a thick 6-inch round, mending any rim cracks as you shape it.
Cook on a medium-hot tava 2 to 3 minutes a side, smearing 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee around the edge, until the spiced surface is golden and fragrant.
Blister over a low flame until it puffs in patches, smear another 0.5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the top, and repeat with the rest.
tips: Never scatter whole cumin into the raw dough alone; pounding it with the chillies releases its oils so the flavour spreads evenly.
Adjust the green chilli to your heat tolerance, as three medium chillies give a genuine Kathiyawadi kick.
The coriander adds moisture, so hold back a spoon of water and add it only if the dough stays crumbly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a bowl of thick sweetened curd and sliced raw onion, which tame the chilli and complete the meal.

variations.name: Besan-Bajra Rotla
variations.description: A heartier, protein-rich rotla where gram flour is folded into the pearl millet, lending a savoury roasted-chana aroma and a slightly firmer, less crumbly bite. The besan tightens the gluten-free dough so it patts out more easily and holds a sturdier round, while mustard oil gives a pungent Kathiyawadi edge. It is the rotla farmers favour on days that call for extra staying power.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: One spoon worked into the dough and the rest to roast the rotla, its sharpness cutting the rich besan

steps: In a bowl combine 1.5 cups bajra flour, 0.5 cups gram flour, 0.5 tsp ajwain seeds, 0.75 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tbsp chopped coriander leaves and 0.5 tsp salt.
Boil 1.2 cups water, pour it over the flours with 1 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil, stir into a mass, and once bearable knead 5 minutes into a smooth, firm dough.
Wet your palms and pat a large ball into a thick 6-inch round; the besan makes this dough noticeably sturdier to shape than pure bajra.
Cook on a medium-hot tava 2 to 3 minutes until the base sets, then flip and drizzle 0.75 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil around the edge.
Flip once more and roast each side until the besan surface turns deep golden and smells nutty and toasted.
Blister briefly over a low flame until it puffs in patches, then serve hot and repeat with the remaining dough.
tips: Toast the besan lightly in a dry pan before mixing if you want an even deeper roasted-gram aroma in the rotla.
Besan absorbs less water than millet, so add the last of the water gradually to avoid a sticky dough.
Heat the mustard oil once to smoking and cool it before kneading if you prefer a milder, rounder pungency.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a green chilli-garlic chutney and a bowl of plain buttermilk, the mustard-and-chana notes standing up to bold sides.

variations.name: Classic Methi Bajra Thepla
variations.description: The traveller's flatbread of Gujarat, a soft spiced pearl-millet round bound with curd and fresh fenugreek that stays supple for two full days of a journey. Bajra brings its dense, nutty earthiness while a measure of wheat and a spoon of curd give the thepla just enough stretch to roll thin. Rolled paper-thin and roasted in oil, it is the definitive tiffin bread of a Gujarati kitchen.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Two spoons worked into the dough for the suppleness bajra lacks, the rest used to roast each thepla golden

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Brushed over the finished stack to keep the theplas soft and glossy for packing

steps: In a wide bowl mix 1.5 cups bajra flour, 0.5 cups whole wheat flour, 1 cup finely chopped fenugreek, 1 tbsp sesame seeds, 1 tsp ginger-garlic paste, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 0.5 tsp carom seeds and 0.75 tsp salt.

Add 0.25 cups curd and 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, then knead into a firm but pliable dough, adding water only a tablespoon at a time since the methi and curd release moisture; rest it covered for 15 minutes.
Divide into 12 balls and roll each on a lightly floured board into a thin 6-inch round, dusting often as the bajra-heavy dough tends to stick.
Lay a thepla on a medium-hot tava and cook for about 45 seconds until tiny bubbles rise and the base sets, then flip.
Drizzle 0.5 tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil around the edge, flip again, and press with a spatula for 1 minute a side until golden-brown flecks appear all over.
Stack the theplas, brush the top of the pile with Anveshan Ghee, and cool them uncovered so they stay soft yet firm enough to pack.
tips: The wheat flour and curd are what let a gluten-free bajra dough roll thin without cracking, so do not leave them out.
If fresh methi is bitter, sprinkle the chopped leaves with a little salt, rest 10 minutes and squeeze out the dark juice before adding.
Cooled theplas keep 2 days at room temperature and travel beautifully; reheat briefly on a tava to revive their softness.
variations.servingSuggestion: Pack with a jar of sweet mango chhundo and thick set curd, or serve warm at home with a wedge of lime pickle and masala chaas.

variations.name: Doodhi Bajra Thepla
variations.description: A moist, mellow thepla where grated bottle gourd melts into the pearl-millet dough, its watery flesh binding the crumbly flour so no extra liquid is needed. The doodhi keeps these rounds tender and light against the density of the bajra, and a whisper of jaggery rounds off the mustard oil's bite. It is the gentler, everyday thepla for a summer lunchbox.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A single spoon lifts the mild doodhi and balances the mustard oil's sharpness the Gujarati way

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Two spoons kneaded in and the rest used to roast the theplas, its pungency waking up the gentle gourd

steps: Squeeze the 1 cup grated bottle gourd lightly to remove only the excess drip, keeping most of its moisture to bind the dough.

In a bowl combine 1.5 cups bajra flour, 0.5 cups whole wheat flour, the gourd, 3 tbsp chopped coriander, 1 tsp green chilli-ginger paste, 1 tsp cumin powder, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tbsp sesame seeds, 1 tsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.75 tsp salt.
Add 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil and knead into a soft dough using the gourd's own water; add a splash more only if it stays crumbly, then rest 15 minutes.
Roll each of 12 balls into a thin 6-inch round on a floured board, dusting generously as this moist dough is stickier than most.
Cook on a medium-hot tava for about 40 seconds until the base firms, then flip and drizzle 0.5 tsp Anveshan Mustard Oil around the rim.
Flip once more and roast each side for a minute, pressing gently until deep golden spots form, then stack and cool uncovered.
tips: Do not wring the doodhi dry; its water is what binds a gluten-free dough, so squeeze out only the loose drip.
Heat the mustard oil to smoking once and cool it before kneading if you prefer its pungency milder for children.
These stay soft for a full day; if the mixed dough turns watery on standing, work in a little extra bajra flour before rolling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a cooling bowl of boondi raita or a spoon of garlic-tomato chutney, letting the tender thepla soak it up.

variations.name: Palak Lehsun Bajra Thepla
variations.description: A vivid green thepla built on a smooth spinach puree and pounded fresh garlic, giving the earthy pearl millet a savoury, almost restaurant-style depth. The spinach keeps the rounds moist and supple while roasted cumin and coriander perfume every bite. Nutty from sesame oil and pungent with garlic, it eats as much like a snack as a lunchbox bread.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Its toasty nuttiness matches the pounded garlic and roasts each green thepla to a fragrant finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Brushed over the hot stack to enrich the spinach dough and keep the rounds glossy

steps: Pound 5 garlic cloves with 2 green chillies into a coarse paste in a mortar.
In a bowl mix 1.5 cups bajra flour, 0.5 cups whole wheat flour, the garlic-chilli paste, 1 tsp roasted cumin powder, 1 tsp coriander powder, 1 tbsp sesame seeds and 0.75 tsp salt.
Add 0.75 cups spinach puree and 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, then knead into a firm green dough, adding water only if needed; rest 15 minutes.
Roll each of 12 balls into a thin 6-inch round on a floured board, dusting well so the moist dough does not tear.
Cook on a medium-hot tava about 45 seconds until the base sets, flip, and drizzle 0.5 tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil around the edge.
Flip again and press for a minute a side until golden flecks show through the green, then stack, brush the top with Anveshan Ghee and cool uncovered.
tips: Blanch the spinach for 30 seconds before pureeing to lock in the bright green and cut any raw grassiness.
Keep the garlic paste coarse so little bursts of it come through the roasted thepla rather than disappearing.
If the puree makes the dough slack, dust in a spoon of bajra flour rather than wheat to keep the millet flavour forward.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve rolled around a smear of fresh coriander-mint chutney with a glass of buttermilk, or plate alongside plain curd for a quick tiffin.

variations.name: Meethi Gud Bajra Thepla
variations.description: The festive sweet cousin of the everyday thepla, where jaggery and fennel turn pearl millet into a soft, faintly caramel flatbread eaten as a treat or a fasting food. Milk and ghee make the dough rich and tender, while cardamom and saunf lend a warm perfume. Griddled slowly so the jaggery does not scorch, these keep for days and are meant to be torn and eaten on their own.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Dissolved in warm milk to sweeten and colour the dough, giving these theplas their gentle caramel note

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Two spoons kneaded in for a rich short crumb and the rest used to roast each sweet round slowly

steps: Warm 0.33 cups milk and stir in 5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder until it fully dissolves, then let it cool to lukewarm.
In a bowl mix 1.5 cups bajra flour, 0.5 cups whole wheat flour, 1 tsp lightly crushed fennel seeds, 0.25 tsp cardamom powder, 1 tbsp sesame seeds and 0.25 tsp salt.
Pour in the jaggery milk and 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then knead into a soft dough, adding a splash of warm milk if it feels dry; rest 15 minutes.
Roll each of 12 balls into a slightly thick 5-inch round on a floured board, handling gently as the sweet dough is delicate.
Cook on a low-to-medium tava for about a minute a side, keeping the heat gentle so the jaggery browns slowly rather than burning.
Smear 0.5 tsp Anveshan Ghee on each side and roast until deep golden and fragrant, then cool the theplas flat before stacking.
tips: Keep the flame low throughout; jaggery scorches fast and a high tava will leave bitter black patches.
Crush the fennel coarsely rather than leaving it whole so its sweetness spreads evenly through each bite.
These sweet theplas keep 3 to 4 days in a tin and make an excellent fasting or travel snack eaten just as they are.
variations.servingSuggestion: Enjoy warm with a cup of masala chai or a bowl of cold plain milk, or serve as a mithai-style treat after a light meal.

variations.name: Classic Gujarati Bharela Marcha
variations.description: Mild, plump Bhavnagri chillies slit and packed with a roasted stuffing of gram flour, peanuts, sesame and coconut, sweetened just so with jaggery in true Gujarati style. Cooked covered until the chillies soften and the filling turns fragrant, they are a beloved thali and travel snack. Every bite is nutty, tangy and gently sweet against the fresh chilli.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Roasts the besan filling and later shallow-cooks the stuffed chillies to a soft finish

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The signature Gujarati sweet note that balances the tang and heat

steps: Dry-roast ¾ cup besan in a pan on low heat for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring constantly, until it turns a shade darker and smells nutty, then tip it into a bowl to cool.

Dry-roast 2 tbsp sesame seeds until they pop, and mix them with the besan, ⅓ cup ground peanuts, 3 tbsp coconut, 2 tsp coriander-cumin powder, ½ tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 2 tbsp lemon juice, coriander and 1 tsp salt into a crumbly stuffing.
Slit the 12 Bhavnagri chillies lengthwise without cutting through, remove the seeds for a milder result, and pack each firmly with the stuffing.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a wide pan on medium, lay the stuffed chillies in a single layer, and cook for 3 minutes until the undersides blister.
Sprinkle over any leftover stuffing, cover the pan, and cook on low for 10 to 12 minutes, turning the chillies gently every few minutes so they soften evenly without burning.
Uncover, raise the heat for a minute to crisp the filling, and serve the chillies glossy and tender.
tips: Roast the besan patiently on low heat; raw gram flour tastes pasty and ruins the nutty character of the filling.
Bhavnagri chillies are usually mild, but taste one first; if they run hot, soak the slit chillies in salted water for 10 minutes before stuffing.
These keep well for a day and taste even better cold, making them a classic addition to a travel tiffin with theplas.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a thali side with dal-rice and rotli, or tuck a couple into a thepla roll with a smear of curd for a punchy lunchbox.

variations.name: Achari Bharela Marcha
variations.description: A tangy pickle-spiced version where the chillies are stuffed with a coarse masala of mustard, fennel and nigella bloomed in mustard oil, echoing the flavours of a north-Indian aam ka achar. Sharp, sour and pungent, it forgoes sweetness entirely. These stuffed chillies double as an instant pickle-like relish alongside dal and rice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Mustard Oil
ingredients.note: Smoked lightly first, it gives the achari stuffing its authentic pickle pungency

steps: Dry-roast 2 tbsp mustard seeds, 2 tbsp fennel seeds and 1 tsp fenugreek seeds separately on low heat until fragrant, cool, and grind coarsely so the spices stay gritty, not powdery.

Mix the ground spices with 1 tsp kalonji, 1 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1.5 tsp amchur, ½ tsp hing and 1 tsp salt, then bind the masala with 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil into a moist, clumping stuffing.
Slit the 12 chillies lengthwise, scoop out the seeds, and pack each tightly with the achari masala.
Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Mustard Oil in a pan on medium until it just smokes, then lower the heat and lay in the stuffed chillies.
Cover and cook on low for 10 to 12 minutes, turning gently, until the chillies wrinkle and soften and the masala smells like fresh pickle.
Uncover and cook 2 more minutes to dry off any excess oil, then serve warm or at room temperature.
tips: Heat the mustard oil until it just smokes before cooking to strip its raw bite; this is essential for a true achari taste.
Grind the spices coarse, not fine, so the stuffing has the rustic crunch of a real pickle masala.
These improve overnight as the amchur and spices meld, so refrigerate and enjoy over three or four days as a pickle.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a zingy relish beside plain khichdi, dal-chawal or curd rice, where the sour-pungent chillies cut through the mildness.

variations.name: Aloo Bharela Marcha
variations.description: A more filling take where the chillies are stuffed with spiced mashed potato and finished in a light tomato-onion masala so they turn into a proper sabzi. The soft potato tempers the chilli while a tangy gravy binds the dish. It is the version that turns a handful of chillies into a satisfying main.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Cooks the stuffed chillies and the tomato masala to a glossy sabzi

steps: Mash 3 boiled potatoes with 1 tsp amchur, ½ tsp garam masala, ¼ tsp turmeric, half the coriander and ½ tsp salt into a smooth, well-seasoned stuffing.
Slit the 10 chillies, deseed them, and pack each firmly with the potato mixture.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan on medium, lay in the stuffed chillies, and cook for 5 minutes turning gently until blistered; lift them out and set aside.
In the same pan add 2 tbsp more Anveshan Groundnut Oil, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds, add the chopped onion, and saute for 4 minutes until golden.
Stir in 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, cook 1 minute, then add the tomato puree, 2 tsp coriander powder, ¼ tsp turmeric and remaining salt, and simmer for 6 minutes until the oil separates.
Return the chillies to the masala, spoon it over them, cover, and simmer on low for 6 minutes until the chillies are soft; garnish with coriander and serve.
tips: Keep the mashed potato on the drier side so the stuffing does not ooze out while the chillies cook.
Blister the stuffed chillies before adding them to the gravy so they hold their shape and gain a roasted note.
Simmer the finished dish on low; boiling hard splits the chillies and spills the filling into the masala.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve this as a semi-dry sabzi with hot phulkas or jeera rice and a squeeze of lemon for a comforting everyday meal.

variations.name: Sattu Bharela Marcha
variations.description: A nourishing twist where roasted-gram sattu forms the stuffing, seasoned with pickle spices and green chilli-ginger for a protein-packed filling that needs no besan-roasting. Cooked in sesame oil, the chillies stay light yet hearty. It borrows the beloved sattu-stuffing idea and folds it into a Gujarati chilli.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Pre-roasted gram flour makes a ready, protein-rich stuffing with no cooking needed

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Half binds the sattu filling, half cooks the chillies to a nutty finish

steps: In a bowl mix ¾ cup Anveshan Sattu with 2 tsp ginger-green chilli paste, ½ tsp ajwain, ½ tsp kalonji, 1.5 tsp amchur, 1 tsp red chilli powder, coriander and 1 tsp salt.
Drizzle in 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and 2 tbsp water and rub the mixture until it just clumps into a moist, packable stuffing.
Slit the 12 chillies lengthwise, deseed them, and pack each firmly with the sattu filling.
Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a pan on medium, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds for 20 seconds, then lay in the stuffed chillies.
Cover and cook on low for 10 to 12 minutes, turning the chillies gently every few minutes, until they wrinkle and soften and the sattu smells toasty.
Uncover, cook 2 minutes to firm the filling, and serve warm.
tips: Moisten the sattu just enough to clump; too much water makes it dense, too little and it crumbles out of the chilli.
Sattu is already roasted, so keep the heat gentle to avoid drying the filling into a hard lump.
This high-protein version travels superbly and stays tasty at room temperature for a full day.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain paratha and a bowl of chaas for a filling, protein-forward lunch, or pack them for a wholesome picnic box.

variations.name: Classic Doodh Pak
variations.description: The festive Gujarati rice-and-milk pudding, thicker and richer than everyday kheer, made by simmering full-fat milk down slowly with a handful of rice until creamy and reduced. Saffron, cardamom and charoli give it its temple-festival fragrance, and it is traditionally eaten warm poured over hot puris.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined khandsari sweetens the doodh pak cleanly and lets the saffron and milk shine

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: a few strands of pure saffron give doodh pak its golden hue and signature festive aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a spoon of bilona ghee to fry the nuts adds richness and a fragrant finish

steps: Rinse 3 tbsp basmati rice, soak for 20 minutes, then drain and coarsely crush so the grains break slightly, which helps thicken the pudding.
Bring 1.25 litres full-fat milk to a boil in a heavy-bottomed pan, then lower to a gentle simmer and add the crushed rice, stirring often to prevent sticking.
Steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp of the warm milk, and separately heat 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee to fry 2 tbsp almonds, 1 tbsp pistachios and 1 tbsp chironji until golden, about 1 minute.
Simmer the milk and rice on low for 30 to 35 minutes, scraping the sides frequently, until the mixture reduces by about a third and turns thick and creamy.
Stir in 0.5 cup Anveshan Khandsari and the saffron milk, then simmer for 5 more minutes until the sugar dissolves and the pudding coats a spoon.
Turn off the heat, fold in 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and the fried nuts, and rest for 5 minutes before serving warm.
tips: Use a heavy-bottomed pan and stir often, as milk this rich scorches on the base within seconds if neglected.
Crushing the soaked rice slightly releases starch that thickens the doodh pak without needing extra rice.
It thickens considerably as it cools, so take it off the heat while still a touch pourable.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm in bowls poured over hot puris, the classic Gujarati festival pairing, garnished with saffron strands.

variations.name: Gud Doodh Pak
variations.description: A rustic, unrefined doodh pak sweetened with jaggery stirred in gently off the heat so the milk stays silky and never curdles. The jaggery lends a warm caramel note and honey-brown tint, making this the wholesome, village-style version for Sankranti and winter feasts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery stirred in off the heat gives a caramel warmth without splitting the milk

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: a little bilona ghee fries the nuts for a rich, fragrant garnish

steps: Rinse and soak 3 tbsp basmati rice for 20 minutes, then drain and crush coarsely.
Boil 1.25 litres full-fat milk in a heavy pan, lower to a simmer, add the crushed rice, and cook on low for 30 to 35 minutes, stirring often, until thick and creamy.
Meanwhile heat 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and fry 2 tbsp cashews, 1 tbsp walnuts and 1 tbsp dry coconut slivers until golden, about 1 minute, then reserve.
Turn off the heat completely and let the thickened milk cool for 4 to 5 minutes so it is warm but no longer boiling.
Stir in 0.6 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder gradually until fully dissolved, adding it only to the cooled milk so it does not curdle.
Fold in 0.25 tsp dry ginger powder, 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and the fried nuts and coconut, then serve warm.
tips: Always take the milk off the heat and let it cool before adding jaggery, or the acidity will split the milk.
The pinch of dry ginger both aids digestion and stops the jaggery-milk from feeling heavy.
If a few grains of jaggery grit remain, strain the jaggery melted with a spoon of water before adding.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm at winter festivals with soft puris or on its own in earthen bowls for a rustic touch.

variations.name: Makhana Badam Doodh Pak
variations.description: A protein-rich, grain-free doodh pak that swaps rice for ghee-roasted fox nuts and ground almonds, thickening the milk into a nutty, luxurious pudding. Light yet indulgent, it is a fasting-friendly and wholesome take that feels every bit as festive as the classic.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee roasts the makhana crisp so they stay slightly chewy in the milk rather than turning mushy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: khandsari sweetens the nutty pudding gently and cleanly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: saffron adds a golden festive glow and floral aroma to the makhana pudding

steps: Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan and roast 1 cup fox nuts on low for 4 to 5 minutes until crisp, then coarsely crush half of them and keep the rest whole.
Bring 1.25 litres full-fat milk to a boil in a heavy pan, add 3 tbsp ground almonds, and simmer on low for 15 minutes, stirring, until it starts to thicken.
Steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp of the warm milk, then add all the roasted fox nuts to the simmering milk.
Continue simmering on low for 15 to 18 minutes, stirring often, until the makhana soften and swell and the milk reduces to a creamy pudding.
Stir in 0.5 cup Anveshan Khandsari and the saffron milk and cook for 4 minutes until the sugar dissolves and the pudding thickens.
Turn off the heat, fold in 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and 2 tbsp slivered pistachios, and rest for 5 minutes before serving warm or chilled.
tips: Crush half the makhana so they melt into the milk to thicken it while the rest stay pleasantly chewy.
Roast the fox nuts until they are properly crisp, or they can turn rubbery in the milk.
Ground almonds do the thickening work here, so add them early to give the pudding body.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve this grain-free pudding warm or chilled in small bowls, ideal for fasting days and topped with extra pistachio.

variations.name: Shahi Kesar-Pista Doodh Pak
variations.description: An extravagant restaurant-style doodh pak enriched with khoya and a generous scatter of pistachios and almonds, cooked thicker and denser for a truly royal dessert. Rose water and a double dose of saffron lift it into a fragrant, celebration-worthy pudding.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: khandsari balances the rich khoya without an overly sugary edge

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: a double pinch of saffron gives this royal version a deep amber colour and intense aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee fries the generous nuts for a rich, aromatic finish

steps: Rinse, soak and coarsely crush 3 tbsp basmati rice, and steep 2 pinches Anveshan Saffron in 3 tbsp warm milk.
Boil 1.25 litres full-fat milk in a heavy pan, add the crushed rice, and simmer on low for 30 minutes, stirring often, until thick and reduced.
Heat 1 tsp Anveshan Ghee and fry 3 tbsp pistachios and 3 tbsp almonds until golden, about 1 minute, then reserve half for garnish.
Stir 0.33 cup grated khoya into the simmering milk and cook for 5 minutes until it melts in and the pudding turns dense and creamy.
Add 0.5 cup Anveshan Khandsari and the saffron milk, simmer for 5 minutes, then turn off the heat and stir in 0.5 tsp rose water, 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and half the fried nuts.
Rest for 5 minutes, then serve garnished with the reserved pistachios and almonds and a few saffron strands.
tips: Add the rose water only after the heat is off, as boiling drives off its delicate fragrance.
Grate the khoya finely so it dissolves smoothly without leaving lumps in the pudding.
For an even richer set, chill it for a few hours until it thickens to a spoonable, almost basundi-like texture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve chilled in ornate bowls at weddings and celebrations, showered with slivered pistachios and rose petals.

variations.name: Classic Fada Ni Lapsi
variations.description: The auspicious Gujarati broken-wheat pudding served at weddings and housewarmings, where coarse fada is slow-roasted in ghee until deeply nutty, then swelled soft in water and sweetened with mineral-rich jaggery. Each grain stays separate and glossy, laced with cardamom and ghee-fried nuts.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee roasts the fada to a deep nutty aroma and keeps every grain separate and glossy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: unrefined jaggery gives lapsi its traditional caramel depth and earthy sweetness

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai on medium and fry 12 cashews, 10 slivered almonds and 2 tbsp raisins until the nuts turn golden and the raisins plump, about 1 minute, then scoop them out and reserve.
Add the remaining 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee to the same pan and roast 1 cup broken wheat on medium-low for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring constantly, until it smells toasty and turns a rich reddish-brown.
Pour in 3 cups hot water carefully as it will splutter, stir well, cover, and simmer on low for 12 to 15 minutes until the fada is fully soft and the water is almost absorbed.

Lower the heat and stir in 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder; it will loosen the mixture as it melts, so keep stirring for 3 to 4 minutes until the jaggery dissolves and the lapsi thickens back to a glossy, spoonable mass.
Fold in 0.5 tsp cardamom powder, 0.25 tsp nutmeg powder and most of the fried nuts, keeping a few for the top.
Cover and rest off the heat for 5 minutes so the grains drink up the last of the moisture, then garnish with the reserved nuts before serving warm.
tips: Roast the fada patiently on low heat until it is genuinely dark and fragrant — under-roasted grains taste raw and clump together.
Always add the jaggery after the wheat is fully cooked; added early it toughens the grains and stops them softening.
If the lapsi stiffens on standing, loosen it with a splash of hot water or milk and a small spoon of ghee.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm mounded in a bowl with an extra drizzle of ghee, traditionally alongside a savoury dal and rice as the sweet opening to a Gujarati feast.

variations.name: Doodhwali Kesar Lapsi
variations.description: A richer, celebratory lapsi cooked in full-fat milk instead of water so the broken wheat turns creamy and pudding-like, delicately sweetened with khandsari and perfumed with real saffron. Pistachios and chironji give it a shahi character fit for festival thalis.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee toasts the fine fada so it stays separate even as the milk turns it creamy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined khandsari sweetens gently without masking the saffron and milk

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: a few strands of pure saffron steeped in warm milk give the lapsi a golden glow and floral aroma

steps: Steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk taken from the measured milk and set it aside to bloom.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan on medium and lightly fry 2 tbsp slivered pistachios and 1 tbsp chironji for 40 seconds, then remove and reserve.
In the same ghee roast 0.75 cup fine broken wheat on medium-low for 6 to 7 minutes, stirring, until it smells nutty and turns light golden.

Pour in 1 cup water, cover, and cook on low for 8 minutes until absorbed, then add 3.5 cups warm milk and simmer uncovered on low for 12 to 15 minutes, stirring often, until the fada is soft and the mixture is creamy.
Lower the heat and stir in 0.5 cup Anveshan Khandsari and the saffron milk, cooking gently for 4 minutes until the sugar melts and the lapsi thickens to a loose pudding.
Fold in 0.5 tsp cardamom powder, the remaining 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and most of the fried nuts, then garnish and serve warm.
tips: Use fine-grade fada here so it cooks tender in the milk without turning grainy.
Keep the heat low once the milk goes in and stir often, as milk lapsi scorches on the base quickly.
It thickens noticeably as it cools, so pull it off the heat while still a touch loose.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm or chilled in small bowls topped with saffron strands and slivered pistachios, an elegant close to a festive lunch.

variations.name: Khajur Dry-Fruit Lapsi
variations.description: A wholesome, iron-rich lapsi sweetened almost entirely with soft dates and a whisper of jaggery, packed with walnuts, dry ginger and edible gum for a nourishing winter sweet. It is denser and darker than the classic, with a fudgy, energy-giving richness once served to new mothers.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: extra ghee fries the edible gum and carries the deep date sweetness through every grain

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: a small amount of jaggery rounds out the natural sweetness of the dates

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium and fry 2 tbsp edible gum in batches until each puffs up and turns crisp, about 30 seconds, then drain, lightly crush, and fry 3 tbsp walnuts for 40 seconds and reserve.
Add the remaining 4 tbsp Anveshan Ghee and roast 1 cup coarse broken wheat on medium-low for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring, until deeply nutty and reddish-brown.
Pour in 3 cups hot water carefully, add the chopped 1 cup dates, cover, and simmer on low for 12 to 15 minutes until the fada is soft and the dates have melted into the grains.
Stir in 0.25 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder on low heat for 3 minutes until it dissolves and the mixture turns glossy and thick.
Fold in 0.5 tsp dry ginger powder, 0.5 tsp cardamom powder, the crushed fried gum and the walnuts.
Cover and rest off the heat for 5 minutes so the flavours meld, then serve warm and fudgy.
tips: Fry the edible gum until it fully puffs and stays crunchy — undercooked gond turns chewy and hard in the finished lapsi.
Taste before adding all the jaggery, as very sweet dates may need even less.
This keeps and firms up beautifully, making excellent nourishing winter laddoo-like scoops the next day.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm in winter with a glass of hot milk, or roll the cooled mixture into balls for a wholesome energy snack.

variations.name: Nariyal-Gud Festive Lapsi
variations.description: A fragrant coastal-Gujarati take where fresh grated coconut and toasted fennel are cooked into the jaggery lapsi, giving it a sweet aromatic lift and a moist, tender crumb. Melon seeds and poppy seeds add gentle crunch, making this the version reserved for Sankranti and satyanarayan pujas.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee blooms the fennel and toasts the coconut so their aroma perfumes the whole pudding

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery marries with fresh coconut for a rustic, festive sweetness

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a kadhai on medium and toast 1 tbsp poppy seeds and 2 tbsp melon seeds for 40 seconds until they crackle, then remove and reserve.
Add the remaining 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, crackle 1 tsp fennel seeds for 20 seconds, then stir in 0.5 cup fresh grated coconut and toast for 2 minutes until it smells sweet and turns pale gold.
Add 1 cup coarse broken wheat and roast on medium-low for 8 minutes, stirring, until the grains are nutty and reddish-brown.
Pour in 3 cups hot water carefully, cover, and simmer on low for 12 to 15 minutes until the fada is soft and the water is nearly gone.
