Lower the heat and stir in 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder for 3 to 4 minutes until melted and glossy, then fold in 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and the toasted seeds.
Rest covered off the heat for 5 minutes so the coconut aroma settles in, then serve warm.
tips: Toast the fresh coconut only until pale gold; browning it too far turns the lapsi bitter.
Bloom the fennel seeds in hot ghee first rather than adding them raw, so their aroma spreads evenly.
Use fresh, moist coconut rather than desiccated for the softest, most fragrant result.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm as puja prasad garnished with a few extra toasted melon seeds and a drizzle of ghee.

variations.name: Classic Gol Papdi
variations.description: The thin, sesame-topped cousin of sukhdi, where roasted wheat flour and jaggery are spread whisper-thin and cut into neat diamonds that crackle and melt at once. A splash of warm milk stirred in at the end keeps these squares softer and more delicate than a chunky sukhdi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee roasts the flour to a nutty gold and gives the thin papdi its melting bite

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery is the traditional sweetener that sets the papdi and gives its warm caramel colour

steps: Grease a flat tray or thali generously with ghee and sprinkle 1 tbsp of the sesame seeds across the base so they set into the underside.
Melt 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai on low heat, add 1 cup whole wheat flour, and roast, stirring constantly, for 8 to 10 minutes until golden-brown and biscuity.
Take the pan off the heat, let it cool for 1 minute, then stir in 2 tbsp warm milk which will bubble up and make the flour fluffy.
Quickly add 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.5 tsp cardamom powder, stirring fast until the jaggery melts into a smooth glossy paste.
Immediately pour onto the greased tray and spread as thin as possible, about 0.5 cm, with the back of a greased spoon, then scatter the remaining 1 tbsp sesame over the top and press lightly.
Score into small diamonds while hot and let cool for 12 to 15 minutes until firm before separating the pieces.
tips: The splash of warm milk is the secret to gol papdi's softer, lighter texture compared with dense sukhdi.
Spread the mixture the moment it is ready, as jaggery stiffens within a minute of coming off the heat.
Keep the layer genuinely thin so the diamonds stay delicate and snap cleanly.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these thin diamonds with afternoon chai, or pack them for journeys since they keep well for over a week.

variations.name: Besan Gol Papdi
variations.description: A grainier, more aromatic papdi where a portion of the wheat is replaced with roasted gram flour, lending a mohanthal-like fudginess and a deeper toasted fragrance. The besan gives these squares a beautiful golden hue and a slightly richer, more festive character.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee roasts the besan-wheat blend into a fragrant, fudgy base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery pairs with roasted gram flour for a mohanthal-like sweetness

steps: Rub 1 tbsp of the ghee and 1 tbsp milk into 0.5 cup besan to make a crumbly mixture, which gives the papdi its characteristic grainy texture, and let it rest for 5 minutes.

Melt the remaining ghee to make about 0.5 cup in a heavy pan on low, add the moistened besan crumbs and 0.5 cup whole wheat flour, and roast together for 10 to 12 minutes, stirring, until deeply golden and richly fragrant.
Take off the heat and cool for a minute so the mixture stops sizzling.
Stir in 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.5 tsp cardamom powder swiftly until the jaggery melts and the mixture is glossy.
Spread onto a greased tray to about 0.75 cm thick with a greased spoon and press 2 tbsp slivered pistachios over the surface.
Score into diamonds while warm and leave to set for 15 minutes before separating.
tips: Moistening the besan with ghee and milk first creates the prized grainy, melt-in-mouth crumb.
Roast the besan thoroughly until it loses all raw smell, or the papdi will taste chalky.
Do not spread this version too thin, as the besan makes it more fragile than plain wheat papdi.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these golden diamonds on a festive platter garnished with extra pistachio, a richer treat for Diwali gatherings.

variations.name: Nariyal Gol Papdi
variations.description: A coconut-laden papdi where toasted desiccated coconut is folded through the jaggery-wheat base and pressed onto the top, giving a fragrant, chewy-crisp finish. The coconut adds moisture and a tropical sweetness that makes these squares especially popular with children.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee toasts the coconut and flour together into a fragrant golden base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery and coconut are a classic Gujarati sweet pairing, warm and rustic

steps: Dry-toast 0.33 cup desiccated coconut in a pan on low for 2 minutes until pale gold and fragrant, then set aside, reserving 2 tbsp for topping.
Grease a tray and sprinkle the reserved 2 tbsp coconut over the base.
Melt 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan on low, add 1 cup whole wheat flour, and roast for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring, until golden and nutty.
Take off the heat, cool briefly, then stir in 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 0.5 tsp cardamom powder, 0.5 tsp crushed fennel and the remaining toasted coconut until smooth and glossy.
Spread the mixture onto the coconut-lined tray to about 0.75 cm thick with a greased spoon and press the surface smooth.
Score into diamonds while warm and cool for 15 minutes before lifting out the pieces.
tips: Toast the coconut gently and separately so it stays fragrant without scorching in the hot flour.
The crushed fennel adds a subtle aniseed lift that suits the coconut — do not skip it.
Use fine desiccated coconut for smooth diamonds, or coarse for a chewier, more textured papdi.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these coconut diamonds as a tea-time snack or a lunchbox treat, dusted with a little extra toasted coconut.

variations.name: Kaju-Badam Rich Gol Papdi
variations.description: A luxurious festive papdi crowded with finely chopped cashews and almonds worked right into the batter and layered thickly on top, turning the humble square into a mithai-box centrepiece. Saffron warms the jaggery base to a deeper amber and a floral aroma.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: extra ghee keeps this nut-heavy papdi soft and helps carry the saffron aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery sets the rich papdi with a warm, festive sweetness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: a few strands of pure saffron steeped in milk deepen the colour and add a festive floral note

steps: Steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside to bloom.
Grease a tray and scatter half of the chopped cashews and almonds across the base.
Melt 0.55 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan on low, add 1 cup whole wheat flour, and roast for 9 to 10 minutes, stirring, until golden and nutty.
Take off the heat, stir in the saffron milk so it froths, then quickly add 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.5 tsp cardamom powder, mixing until smooth and glossy.
Fold in half the remaining nuts, spread the mixture onto the tray to about 0.75 cm thick, and press the rest of the chopped nuts firmly over the top.
Score into diamonds while warm and cool for 18 to 20 minutes until set before separating.
tips: Chop the nuts fine so the thin papdi still cuts cleanly without cracking around the pieces.
Add the saffron milk off the heat so its delicate aroma is not scorched by the hot ghee.
This richer papdi benefits from a slightly thicker spread to hold all the nuts together.
variations.servingSuggestion: Present these saffron-nut diamonds in a mithai box as a Diwali gift, or serve with a bowl of warm badam milk.

variations.name: Classic Surti Locho
variations.description: Surat's happy accident, born when a batch of khaman refused to set and someone served the soft, half-cooked mixture anyway. This locho is a spoonable steamed savoury of chana dal and besan, mashed warm and loaded with oil, butter, sev, chopped onion and a shake of pungent masala. It is eaten steaming hot from a plate, never cut into pieces.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Poured warm over each serving, it gives the mashed locho its glossy richness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: A knob melted on top is the traditional finish that makes locho indulgent

steps: Soak 1 cup chana dal in plenty of water for 4 hours, drain, and grind with about ¾ cup fresh water into a slightly coarse, thick batter, then stir in ½ cup besan.
Add 2 tsp ginger-green chilli paste, ½ tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt with another ½ cup water to loosen it to a thick pourable batter, cover, and let it rest 30 minutes to ferment lightly.

Fold 1 tsp Eno through the batter for 5 seconds until frothy, pour into a greased steel plate, and steam over rolling water for 18 to 20 minutes; the centre should stay deliberately soft and slightly wobbly, not firm.
While hot, mash the steamed mixture roughly with the back of a spoon right in the plate so it turns into a soft, lump-free pudding.
Warm 4 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and pour it over the mashed locho, then dot 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee on top so it melts into the warmth.
Finish each serving with a shower of sev, chopped onion, 2 tsp sanchal masala and coriander, and serve immediately with a spoon while piping hot.
tips: Locho is meant to be under-set and soft, so resist steaming it firm; pull it off the heat while the middle still jiggles.
A slightly coarse dal grind gives locho its characteristic grainy body; a silky-smooth batter turns out too pasty.
Serve it the instant it is mashed and topped, as locho loses its charm once it cools and stiffens.
variations.servingSuggestion: Ladle onto a plate with extra sev, a wedge of lemon and green chutney, and eat with a spoon alongside masala chai the way Surat's evening stalls serve it.

variations.name: Surti Cheese Locho
variations.description: The cheese-loaded version that took over Surat's street corners, where the hot mashed locho is buried under a snowdrift of grated cheese that melts on contact. Butter and sev pile on top, making it gooey, rich and unapologetically indulgent. It is the crowd-pleaser that turned a humble accident into a food-truck star.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Melted over the hot locho to carry the cheese into every mouthful

steps: Soak 1 cup chana dal for 4 hours, drain, and grind with ¾ cup water to a slightly coarse thick batter, then mix in ½ cup besan.
Stir in 2 tsp green chilli paste, ½ tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and enough water to reach a thick pourable batter, then rest for 30 minutes.
Fold in 1 tsp Eno until frothy, pour into a greased plate, and steam 18 minutes over high heat so the locho stays soft and just-set in the middle.
Mash the hot locho coarsely in the plate, then pour over 3 tbsp melted Anveshan Ghee and fold it through so the mixture turns silky.
While the locho is still steaming hot, blanket the surface with 1 cup grated cheese and let the heat melt it for a minute into a gooey layer.
Top with fine sev, chopped onion, 2 tsp chaat masala, ½ tsp black pepper and coriander, and serve at once before the cheese firms.
tips: Grate the cheese fresh and add it while the locho is scalding hot; pre-warmed or foil-covered locho will not melt it the same way.
Use a mild processed or mozzarella-style cheese so it goes stringy rather than sharp and salty.
Chaat masala and black pepper cut the richness of the cheese; do not skip them or the plate turns cloying.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve on a wide plate with buttered pav on the side to scoop up the cheesy locho, plus green chutney and lemon for those who want it sharper.

variations.name: Vatana Green Peas Locho
variations.description: A winter Surti treat where a paste of fresh green peas is beaten into the batter, turning the locho pale green and giving it a sweet, spring-like flavour. Crushed peas and mint on top keep it seasonal and fresh. It is lighter than the classic and shows off the market's best winter matar.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Warmed and poured over to gloss the pea-flecked locho

steps: Soak 1 cup chana dal for 4 hours, drain, and grind with ¾ cup water to a coarse thick batter; separately, crush ¾ cup of the green peas to a rough paste, keeping ¼ cup whole for garnish.
Mix the dal batter with the pea paste and ¼ cup besan, then beat in 2 tsp ginger-green chilli paste, 1 tsp sugar, 1 tsp salt and 1 tbsp lemon juice until smooth and thick.
Rest the batter for 30 minutes, then fold in 1 tsp Eno until frothy and pour into a greased plate.
Steam over rolling water for 18 to 20 minutes, keeping the centre soft and green, then mash the hot locho coarsely in the plate.
Warm 4 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil and pour it over the mashed locho, folding it through for a glossy finish.
Scatter the reserved crushed peas, sev, 2 tsp sanchal masala and chopped mint over the top and serve steaming hot.
tips: Use tender fresh winter peas; older or frozen peas taste starchy and mute the sweet green flavour this version relies on.
Crush the peas rather than pureeing them smooth so you keep little bursts of texture through the soft locho.
Add the mint only at the finish, since its aroma fades quickly once it hits the hot mixture.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve garnished with extra peas and a lemon wedge alongside a coriander-mint chutney, a fresh winter counterpoint to heavier fried snacks.

variations.name: Sattu Multigrain Locho
variations.description: A nourishing reinvention that swaps part of the besan for protein-rich sattu and a spoon of multigrain atta, giving the locho a nuttier body and extra fibre without losing its trademark softness. A cumin-and-curry-leaf tempering keeps it savoury and light. It is the everyday-healthy version for those who want the comfort with more goodness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Roasted gram flour adds nutty protein and a rustic body the besan version lacks

ingredients.name: Anveshan Multigrain Atta
ingredients.note: A spoon binds the batter and lends fibre without weighing down the softness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Used for a light cumin tempering poured over each serving

steps: Soak ¾ cup chana dal for 4 hours, drain, and grind with ¾ cup water to a coarse thick batter, then whisk in ½ cup Anveshan Sattu and 2 tbsp Anveshan Multigrain Atta.
Beat in 2 tsp ginger-green chilli paste, ½ tsp turmeric, 1 tsp salt and enough of the remaining water to make a thick pourable batter, then rest it for 30 minutes.
Fold 1 tsp Eno through until frothy, pour into a greased plate, and steam over high heat for 18 to 20 minutes so the centre stays soft.
Mash the hot locho coarsely in the plate until it is smooth and spoonable.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 10 curry leaves for 20 seconds, and pour this tempering over the mashed locho.
Top with sev, chopped onion and coriander and serve hot as a wholesome anytime bowl.
tips: Sattu drinks up water quickly, so keep a little extra warm water on hand to loosen the batter to a pourable thickness before steaming.
Do not add more than a couple of spoons of multigrain atta or the locho turns dense; it is there only to bind and enrich.
This heartier version keeps you full longer, making it a good pre-workout or school-morning bowl.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a side of thin buttermilk and a spoon of green chutney for a filling, protein-forward breakfast that still tastes like classic locho.

variations.name: Classic Magas Ladoo
variations.description: The beloved Gujarati gram-flour sweet, where thick besan is roasted patiently in plenty of ghee until it turns fudge-fragrant, cooled slightly, and bound with powdered sugar into soft, round ladoos. Unlike syrup-set mohanthal, magas uses no sugar syrup at all, giving a light, sandy, melt-on-the-tongue crumb.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: generous bilona ghee roasts the besan to a nutty aroma and lets the ladoos bind without any syrup

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari, finely powdered
ingredients.note: finely powdered khandsari folds cold into the roasted besan for magas's signature sandy sweetness

steps: Rub 2 tbsp of the ghee and 2 tbsp milk into 2 cups coarse besan until it forms damp crumbs, rest for 10 minutes, then sieve to break lumps and create even granules.
Melt the remaining ghee to make 0.75 cup total in a heavy kadhai on low heat and add the besan granules, roasting and stirring for 15 to 18 minutes until deep golden and richly fragrant.
Take the pan off the heat and let the roasted besan cool for 8 to 10 minutes until just warm to the touch, as adding sugar to hot besan melts it and ruins the texture.
Fold in 1 cup finely powdered Anveshan Khandsari and 0.75 tsp cardamom powder, mixing until the crumbs hold together when pressed.
Add half of the slivered almonds and pistachios, then roll the mixture into walnut-sized ladoos while pressing firmly so they bind.
Press a few reserved nut slivers onto each ladoo and let them set for 20 minutes to firm up before serving.
tips: Cool the roasted besan until only just warm before adding the sugar, or the ladoos turn dense and hard.
If the mixture is too dry to bind, drizzle in a spoon of warm melted ghee until it holds together.
Powder the khandsari very fine so the ladoos stay smooth and sandy rather than gritty.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these soft ladoos at festivals and pujas, arranged on a silver thali garnished with slivered pistachios.

variations.name: Coconut Magas Barfi
variations.description: A fragrant set-and-slice magas where toasted desiccated coconut is folded through the roasted besan and pressed into a tray to cut into barfi diamonds. The coconut adds chew and a tropical sweetness, giving a firmer, sliceable sweet rather than the soft classic ladoo.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee toasts the besan and coconut together into a fragrant base that slices cleanly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari, powdered
ingredients.note: powdered khandsari sweetens the barfi gently without a sugary edge

steps: Dry-toast 0.5 cup desiccated coconut in a pan on low for 2 minutes until pale gold, then set aside, reserving 2 tbsp for topping.
Rub 2 tbsp ghee and 2 tbsp milk into 2 cups coarse besan to make damp crumbs, rest 10 minutes, and sieve into granules.

Melt the remaining ghee to make 0.75 cup total in a heavy pan on low and roast the besan granules for 15 minutes, stirring, until deep golden and nutty, then stir in the toasted coconut and roast 2 more minutes.
Cool for 6 to 8 minutes until just warm, then fold in 1 cup powdered Anveshan Khandsari, 0.75 tsp cardamom powder and 0.25 tsp nutmeg powder until evenly combined.
Press the mixture firmly into a greased tray about 1.5 cm thick and smooth the top with a greased spoon.
Scatter the reserved 2 tbsp coconut over the surface, press lightly, and cool for 25 minutes before cutting into diamonds.
tips: Press the warm mixture down hard in the tray so the barfi holds a clean cut and does not crumble.
Toast the coconut only to pale gold; over-browning makes the barfi taste bitter.
Let it cool completely before slicing so the diamonds keep their sharp edges.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these coconut diamonds in a festive box, dusted with a little extra toasted coconut for garnish.

variations.name: Jaggery Magas Ladoo
variations.description: A wholesome, unrefined magas bound with powdered jaggery instead of sugar, deepening the ladoos to a warm amber with a caramel-molasses richness. Sesame and a touch of dry ginger make these a nourishing winter sweet that keeps for weeks.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: extra ghee keeps the jaggery-bound ladoos soft and helps them roll smoothly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: powdered jaggery gives these ladoos a warm caramel colour and earthy sweetness

steps: Dry-roast 3 tbsp sesame seeds in a pan for 2 minutes until they pop and turn golden, then set aside.
Melt 0.8 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai on low, add 2 cups coarse besan directly, and roast for 16 to 18 minutes, stirring constantly, until deep golden and heavily fragrant.
Take off the heat and cool for 10 minutes until just warm, as jaggery must never meet very hot besan or it melts and hardens.
Fold in 1 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 0.5 tsp dry ginger powder, 0.75 tsp cardamom powder, the toasted sesame and 3 tbsp chopped cashews until the mixture holds together.
Press and roll the warm mixture into firm walnut-sized ladoos, working while it is still pliable.
Set the ladoos aside for 20 to 25 minutes to firm up before storing or serving.
tips: Powdered jaggery can be lumpy, so sieve or crumble it fine before folding in for smooth ladoos.
Roll the ladoos while the mixture is warm and pliable; once cool, jaggery sets and it will not bind.
The dry ginger is a traditional digestive touch that suits this heavier winter version.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these amber ladoos with warm milk on cold mornings as a strengthening seasonal sweet.

variations.name: Dry-Fruit Kesar Magas
variations.description: A luxurious festive magas enriched with khoya and crowded with chopped cashews, almonds and saffron, giving a moist, indulgent ladoo that borders on royal. The khoya adds a milky richness and the saffron a floral perfume, elevating the humble besan sweet for special occasions.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee roasts the besan and marries the khoya and nuts into a rich, moist crumb

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari, powdered
ingredients.note: powdered khandsari sweetens the rich ladoos cleanly without overpowering the saffron

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: pure saffron steeped in milk lends a festive golden colour and floral aroma

steps: Steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk and set aside to bloom.
Melt 0.75 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai on low, add 2 cups coarse besan, and roast for 14 to 16 minutes, stirring, until deep golden and nutty.
Stir in 0.5 cup grated khoya and roast for 3 more minutes until it melts in and smells rich, then take off the heat.
Cool for 8 minutes until just warm, then fold in the saffron milk, 1 cup powdered Anveshan Khandsari, 0.75 tsp cardamom powder and half the chopped cashews and almonds.
Once the mixture holds together, roll into walnut-sized ladoos, pressing firmly so the khoya binds them.
Press the remaining chopped nuts onto each ladoo and let them set for 25 minutes before serving.
tips: Use fresh khoya and fold it in off very high heat so it enriches without making the mixture greasy.
Add the saffron milk while the besan is warm, not hot, so the colour and aroma stay vivid.
These richer ladoos are best eaten within four to five days as the khoya shortens their shelf life.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these saffron-flecked ladoos as a premium festival offering, garnished with a single saffron strand on each.

variations.name: Classic Kesar Mohanthal
variations.description: The regal Gujarati gram-flour fudge, where coarse besan is bound with ghee and milk into fragrant crumbs, roasted slow, then set with a single-thread sugar syrup and khoya into firm, grainy squares. Saffron and cardamom perfume every bite, with a texture that is at once fudgy and delicately sandy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: generous bilona ghee roasts the besan crumbs and gives mohanthal its signature rich, melting grain

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: unrefined khandsari makes a clean single-thread syrup without the harshness of white sugar

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: pure saffron steeped in warm milk gives mohanthal its golden hue and floral aroma

steps: Rub 3 tbsp of the ghee and 3 tbsp milk into 2 cups coarse besan until the mixture resembles damp breadcrumbs, then rest for 10 minutes and pass through a coarse sieve to form even granules.
Steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 1 tbsp warm milk and set aside.

Melt the remaining ghee to make 0.75 cup total in a heavy kadhai on low, add the besan granules, and roast for 15 to 18 minutes, stirring constantly, until deep golden and intensely nutty, then stir in 0.5 cup grated khoya and roast 3 more minutes and turn off the heat.
Meanwhile boil 1.25 cups Anveshan Khandsari with 0.75 cup water on medium until it reaches a one-thread consistency, about 6 to 7 minutes, testing by stretching a drop between finger and thumb.

Pour the hot syrup into the roasted besan in a steady stream while stirring hard, add the saffron milk and 0.75 tsp cardamom powder, and stir for 2 to 3 minutes until it thickens and starts leaving the sides of the pan.
Spread the mixture into a greased tray about 1.5 cm thick, scatter 3 tbsp slivered almonds and pistachios and press them in, then cool for 30 minutes before cutting into squares.
tips: The one-thread syrup stage is critical: too thin and the mohanthal will not set, too thick and it turns hard and sugary.
Rubbing ghee and milk into the besan and sieving it is what creates the prized grainy, non-pasty texture.
Let it cool completely and set for at least half an hour before cutting, or the squares will not hold their shape.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature from a mithai box garnished with saffron strands, a classic Gujarati festival and wedding sweet.

variations.name: Jaggery Mohanthal
variations.description: An earthier, unrefined mohanthal set with a jaggery syrup instead of sugar, giving the fudge a deep molasses-brown colour and a rustic caramel richness. A hint of dry ginger keeps the heavier jaggery version easy on the stomach, making it a wholesome festive choice.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee balances the deep molasses notes of jaggery and keeps the besan crumbs melting

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery gives this mohanthal its dark caramel colour and earthy, unrefined sweetness

steps: Rub 3 tbsp ghee and 3 tbsp milk into 2 cups coarse besan to make damp crumbs, rest 10 minutes, and sieve into even granules.
Melt the remaining ghee to make 0.75 cup total in a heavy kadhai on low and roast the besan granules for 15 to 18 minutes, stirring, until deep golden and nutty, then turn off the heat.
In a separate pan melt 1.25 cups Anveshan Jaggery Powder with 0.5 cup water on low, simmer for 4 to 5 minutes until it forms a thick syrup, then strain out any grit.

Pour the strained jaggery syrup into the roasted besan while stirring hard on low heat, add 0.25 tsp dry ginger, 0.75 tsp cardamom and 0.25 tsp nutmeg, and stir for 3 to 4 minutes until thick and pulling from the pan.
Fold in half of 3 tbsp chopped walnuts and almonds, then spread into a greased tray about 1.5 cm thick.
Press the remaining nuts over the top and cool for 30 to 40 minutes before cutting into squares.
tips: Always strain the melted jaggery, as raw jaggery carries sand and fibre that spoil the smooth set.
Keep the heat low once the jaggery goes in, since it scorches and turns bitter faster than sugar syrup.
Jaggery mohanthal stays a little softer than the sugar version, so give it extra cooling time to firm up.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these dark, rustic squares warm in winter with a cup of masala chai for a wholesome festive treat.

variations.name: Quick Milk-Powder Mohanthal
variations.description: A clever shortcut mohanthal that skips khoya and long syrup work, using milk powder for richness and a quick sugar-milk cook that sets reliably in under half an hour. It delivers the same grainy, cardamom-scented fudge for a last-minute festival craving.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee roasts the besan and milk powder into a rich, fudgy crumb without needing khoya

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari, powdered
ingredients.note: powdered khandsari dissolves quickly into the milk for a fast, foolproof set

steps: Rub 3 tbsp ghee and 3 tbsp of the milk into 2 cups coarse besan to form damp crumbs, rest 5 minutes, and sieve into granules.
Melt the remaining ghee to make 0.75 cup total in a heavy pan on low and roast the besan granules for 12 to 14 minutes, stirring, until golden and nutty.
Stir in 0.5 cup milk powder and roast for 2 more minutes until fragrant, then turn the heat to very low.
Add the remaining milk to make about 0.5 cup along with 1 cup powdered Anveshan Khandsari, stirring quickly for 3 to 4 minutes as the sugar melts and the mixture thickens into a glossy mass.
Fold in 0.75 tsp cardamom powder, then spread into a greased tray about 1.5 cm thick.
Press 3 tbsp slivered almonds over the top and cool for 25 minutes before cutting into squares.
tips: Keep the heat very low after adding milk and sugar, as milk powder catches and browns quickly.
Powder the khandsari finely so it melts smoothly and does not leave a grainy sugar crunch.
If the mixture feels too soft, cook a minute longer until it clearly leaves the sides of the pan.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these quick squares fresh with tea, an easy homemade mithai for unexpected guests.

variations.name: Rajasthani Grainy Mohanthal
variations.description: The Rajasthani rendition, coarser and more granular than the Gujarati original, built on thick besan crumbs cooked in extra ghee and set softer so it can almost be spooned. Poppy seeds and a heavier hand of nuts give it a nubbly, indulgent texture beloved at Marwari celebrations.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: the extra ghee gives the Rajasthani version its softer, spoonable, richly grainy set

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: khandsari syrup binds the coarse crumbs while keeping the fudge tender

steps: Rub 4 tbsp ghee and 4 tbsp milk into 2 cups thick besan to make coarse damp crumbs, rest 10 minutes, and break up any large lumps by hand for a deliberately grainy texture.
Melt the remaining ghee to make 0.9 cup total in a heavy kadhai on low and roast the besan crumbs for 16 to 18 minutes, stirring, until deep golden brown and heavily fragrant.
Boil 1.25 cups Anveshan Khandsari with 0.75 cup water on medium for 6 minutes to a soft one-thread syrup.
Pour the syrup into the roasted besan while stirring on low, add 0.75 tsp cardamom powder, and cook for just 2 minutes so it stays soft and grainy rather than fully firm.
Fold in half of 0.33 cup chopped mixed nuts, then spread into a greased tray about 2 cm thick.
Toast 1 tbsp poppy seeds in a dry pan for 30 seconds and scatter over the top with the remaining nuts, then cool for 30 minutes before cutting into thick squares.
tips: Use thick laddoo-grade besan and keep the crumbs coarse for the authentic Rajasthani granular bite.
Cook the syrup-besan mixture only briefly so this version stays soft and almost spoonable.
The extra ghee may pool at the edges as it cools; simply spoon it back over the top before it sets.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these thick, nubbly squares warm at a Marwari feast, topped with poppy seeds and a scatter of nuts.

variations.name: Classic Surti Ponk Vada
variations.description: A fleeting winter delicacy from Surat, made only in the short weeks when ponk, the milky-tender green jowar, floods the markets. The soft grains are bound with a little gram flour and spice, then fried into crisp-outside, juicy-inside fritters. Each vada pops with the sweet, grassy bite of fresh ponk you cannot get any other time of year.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Its high smoke point fries the vadas crisp while keeping the ponk juicy inside

steps: Coarsely crush 1.5 cups of the ponk in a mortar so half the grains break and half stay whole, keeping the mixture chunky rather than a smooth paste, and leave ½ cup grains fully whole for bite.

Combine the crushed and whole ponk with ½ cup besan, 2 tsp ginger-green chilli paste, 2 tbsp green garlic, 3 tbsp coriander, ½ tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tbsp sesame seeds, ¼ tsp baking soda and 1 tsp salt.
Mix into a thick, just-holding dough without any water; the ponk's own moisture should bind it, so add a spoon of besan if it feels wet.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadai to 170C, until a pinch of batter dropped in rises steadily with small bubbles.
Shape the mixture into small walnut-sized rounds and slide 5 or 6 at a time into the oil, frying for 3 to 4 minutes on medium heat until deep golden and crisp all over.
Drain the vadas on paper and fry the next batch, keeping the oil at a steady medium so the insides cook through before the crust darkens.
tips: Crush only part of the ponk; leaving some grains whole gives the vadas their signature juicy pop against the crisp shell.
Do not add water, as ponk releases enough moisture on its own and a wet mix makes the vadas soak up oil.
Ponk has a very short season, so freeze extra grains flat in a bag to make these fritters through the year.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve piping hot with green garlic chutney and a sprinkle of sev, exactly as Surat's winter stalls plate their ponk, with hot chai alongside.

variations.name: Appe-Pan Ponk Vada
variations.description: A lighter, ghee-basted take that trades the deep-fry for an appe pan, giving round, golden ponk dumplings with a fraction of the oil. The batter is loosened slightly and studded with the whole tender grains so each ball still bursts with ponk. It is the guilt-free way to enjoy the winter treat by the plateful.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Brushed into each appe mould, it crisps the dumplings golden with a nutty aroma

steps: Coarsely crush 1.5 cups ponk, leaving ½ cup whole, and mix with ½ cup besan, 3 tbsp semolina, 3 tbsp curd, 2 tsp ginger-green chilli paste, 3 tbsp coriander, ½ tsp turmeric, chopped curry leaves and 1 tsp salt.
Let the batter rest 15 minutes so the semolina swells, then fold in ½ tsp Eno until it turns light and airy.
Heat an appe pan on medium and brush each mould with a little Anveshan Ghee until it shimmers.
Spoon the batter into the moulds to fill them three-quarters, cover, and cook for 4 minutes until the undersides are golden and set.
Flip each dumpling with a skewer, drizzle a few drops of Anveshan Ghee around them, and cook another 3 to 4 minutes until evenly browned and crisp.
Repeat with the remaining batter, keeping the heat at medium so the centres cook through without the shells scorching.
tips: Add the Eno only just before cooking; if it sits, the fizz dies and the dumplings turn dense.
Keep the pan on steady medium heat, as high heat browns the outside before the ponk inside is cooked.
A well-seasoned or non-stick appe pan lets you use minimal ghee while still getting a crisp golden shell.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the hot dumplings with coconut-coriander chutney and a bowl of sweet-sour date chutney for dipping, a lighter snack for tea-time guests.

variations.name: Corn-Cheese Ponk Vada
variations.description: A modern Surti street-food mashup where sweet corn kernels and a molten cheese centre join the ponk, giving a sweet-savoury fritter that oozes when you bite in. The corn echoes the ponk's own sweetness while the cheese adds indulgence. It is the version that lures kids to the winter ponk stall.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Fries the corn-ponk shell crisp while the cheese core stays molten

steps: Crush 1.5 cups ponk and ¾ cup sweet corn coarsely together, then mix with ⅓ cup besan, 2 tbsp cornflour, 1 tbsp green chilli paste, ½ tsp black pepper, 3 tbsp coriander, 1 tsp chaat masala and 1 tsp salt into a thick, mouldable dough.
Take a lemon-sized portion, flatten it on your palm, place a mozzarella cube in the centre, and seal the dough over it into a smooth stuffed ball; make about 16.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 175C, hot enough that a dough scrap sizzles up at once.
Slide 4 or 5 stuffed balls into the oil and fry on medium-high for 3 to 4 minutes, turning, until they are deep golden and crisp on all sides.
Lift them out the moment the shell is set and crisp so the cheese inside stays molten rather than leaking.
Drain briefly and serve immediately while the centres are still stretchy and hot.
tips: Seal the cheese completely with no cracks, or it will burst and leak into the oil during frying.
Keep the oil at a steady 175C; too cool and the shell absorbs oil before crisping, too hot and it browns before the cheese melts.
Serve within minutes, as the cheese firms up quickly once the vadas cool.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with spicy schezwan-style chutney and a dusting of extra chaat masala, a fusion snack that pairs well with a glass of cold masala cola.

variations.name: Green Garlic Ponk Vada
variations.description: This version leans fully into Surat's winter pantry, folding a generous mash of green garlic, spinach and coriander into the ponk so the fritters turn deeply green and aromatic. A hint of roasted sattu binds them and adds a nutty backbone. Pungent, herby and rustic, it is the ponk vada that regulars ask for by name.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Roasted gram flour binds the wet greens and lends a toasty, nutty depth

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A clean-tasting fry that lets the green garlic aroma shine

steps: Dry-roast 1 tsp cumin seeds in a pan for 40 seconds until fragrant, cool, and crush coarsely.
Coarsely crush 1.5 cups ponk, leaving ½ cup whole, and combine with the crushed cumin, ⅓ cup green garlic, ½ cup spinach, ¼ cup coriander, 3 minced green chillies, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 1 tsp salt.
Work in ⅓ cup Anveshan Sattu a little at a time until the mixture holds together into a firm, moist green dough without any added water.
Heat 2 cups Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 170C, until a dough scrap rises with a gentle sizzle.
Shape the dough into small flattened patties and fry 4 or 5 at a time on medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes per batch until crisp and dark green-brown.
Drain on paper and serve the herby vadas hot, frying the remaining patties in the same steady oil.
tips: Squeeze the chopped spinach dry before mixing so the extra water does not soften the dough and force in more sattu.
Green garlic mellows as it fries, so use the full amount for a fritter that stays fragrant rather than bland.
Add the sattu gradually; too much makes the vadas heavy and dry, so stop as soon as the dough just binds.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a sharp lemon-garlic chutney and thin onion rings, a rustic winter snack that eats beautifully with a bowl of hot dal or chai.

variations.name: Classic Gujarati Bajra no Rotlo
variations.description: The everyday winter bread of rural Gujarat, a thick, hand-patted pearl-millet round with a rustic craggy surface and a dense, nutty crumb. Built on bajra flour and boiling water with just a hint of carom, it is patted between wet palms and roasted till it blisters, then finished with a generous smear of ghee. This is the honest, filling rotlo eaten with olo, chutney and buttermilk across Gujarati farmhouses.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Rubbed over the hot tava so the thick rotlo releases cleanly and the base browns evenly

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Smeared thickly over the hot rotlo so it soaks into the porous millet crumb, the traditional Gujarati finish

steps: Bring 1.25 cups water to a rolling boil with 0.5 tsp salt, then pour it over 2 cups bajra flour mixed with 0.5 tsp carom seeds and stir into a rough shaggy mass.
As soon as it is cool enough to handle, knead the warm dough for 5 minutes with the heel of your palm until it is smooth and holds together without cracking.
Take a large ball, wet your palms, and pat it back and forth between your hands into a thick 6-inch round, or press it out on wet parchment.
Rub the medium-hot tava with a little Anveshan Groundnut Oil, lift the rotlo on, and cook the base for about 2 to 3 minutes until brown spots appear underneath.
Flip, cook the second side 2 minutes, then set the rotlo directly over a low flame until it swells and blisters in patches, turning once.
Slide onto a plate, smear 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the hot craggy surface, and repeat with the remaining dough.
tips: Bajra has no gluten, so knead while the dough is still warm; the boiling water is the only thing binding it together.
Keep your palms wet the whole time you pat; the crumbly dough splits the moment your hands go dry.
Serve a rotlo the minute it comes off the flame, as pearl millet turns hard and dry within a few minutes of cooling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot and ghee-soaked with ringan no olo (smoked aubergine mash), a mound of jaggery, and a tall glass of chaas.

variations.name: Makai-Bajra no Rotlo
variations.description: A softer, sweeter rotlo that marries pearl millet with an equal measure of maize flour, giving a golden round that is easier to pat and gentler on the palate. The makai lends a mild sweetness and a lighter crumb than pure bajra allows, making this the rotlo of choice when the plain one feels too heavy. It is a farmhouse variation born of whatever grain the season offered.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Smeared generously over the finished golden round to enrich the mild, sweet maize crumb

steps: Combine 1 cup bajra flour, 1 cup maize flour and 1 tbsp sesame seeds in a wide bowl.
Boil 1.33 cups water with 0.5 tsp salt, pour it over the flours, stir into a mass, and once bearable knead the warm dough for 5 minutes until smooth and pliable.
Wet your palms and pat a large ball into a thick 6-inch round, pressing a few extra sesame seeds onto the surface; the maize makes this noticeably easier to shape than pure bajra.
Cook on a medium-hot tava for 2 minutes until the base turns golden with brown flecks, then flip.
Cook the second side 2 minutes, then puff it over a low flame until it blisters in patches and the sesame toasts fragrant.
Smear 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee over the hot rotlo and repeat with the remaining dough.
tips: Both millet and maize are gluten-free, so the water must be genuinely boiling to bind the dough without cracks.
Maize flour thickens as it hydrates, so add the last splash of water gradually until the dough just holds.
This blend stays pliable a little longer than plain bajra rotlo but is still best eaten hot off the tava.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with sarson-style green garlic chutney and a bowl of thick curd, or pair with a Kathiyawadi sev tameta nu shaak.

variations.name: Gud-Ghee Rotla no Choodo
variations.description: A beloved way to finish a rotlo, where the hot pearl-millet bread is crumbled by hand and worked with jaggery and warm ghee into a rich, sweet mash eaten as a meal in itself. Nothing is wasted and everything is comforting: the earthy millet, the caramel jaggery and the fragrant ghee melt into a rustic dessert-cum-supper. Elders across Gujarat swear by this as the most nourishing end to a winter day.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Melted into the crumbled hot rotlo where it softens into a caramel binder for the choodo

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: Warmed and folded generously through the crumble, the fat that carries the jaggery into every crumb

steps: Boil 1.25 cups water with 0.25 tsp salt, pour over 2 cups bajra flour, stir into a mass and knead the warm dough 5 minutes until smooth.
Pat each ball into a thick 6-inch round with wet palms and roast on a medium-hot tava 2 to 3 minutes a side, then blister over a low flame.
While the rotlos are still hot, tear them into a large bowl and crumble them coarsely with your fingers into rough millet pieces.
Warm 5 tbsp Anveshan Ghee until just melted and pour it over the hot crumbs, tossing so every piece is coated and glistening.
Add 6 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 0.25 tsp cardamom powder and mix well, pressing lightly so the jaggery melts and binds the choodo.
Serve warm in mounds while the ghee is still soft and the jaggery has just melted through.
tips: Crumble the rotlos while piping hot; the residual heat is what melts the jaggery and ghee into a cohesive mash.
Use freshly patted rotlos rather than day-old ones, as stale millet turns the choodo gritty instead of soft.
Adjust jaggery to taste and add a handful of crushed roasted peanuts for a nuttier, more filling version.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm in a bowl with a glass of cold milk poured alongside, or top with a spoon of extra ghee for the traditional indulgence.

variations.name: Til-Lasan Rotlo
variations.description: A savoury, boldly flavoured rotlo studded with toasted sesame and a coarse garlic-chilli pounding worked straight into the millet dough. The raw garlic mellows and sweetens as the thick round roasts, while sesame gives a nutty crunch to the craggy crust. Roasted in fragrant sesame oil, this is the rotlo that needs little more than a bowl of curd to become a full meal.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Its toasty depth doubles down on the sesame seeds and roasts the thick rotlo to a fragrant crust

steps: Pound 6 garlic cloves with 2 dry red chillies and 0.5 tsp cumin seeds into a coarse paste in a mortar.
Mix the paste into 2 cups bajra flour along with 2 tbsp sesame seeds and 0.5 tsp salt in a wide bowl.
Pour in about 1.25 cups boiling water, stir into a mass, and once bearable knead the warm dough 5 minutes until smooth and crack-free.
Wet your palms and pat a large ball into a thick 6-inch round, mending any cracks at the rim as you shape it.
Cook on a medium-hot tava 2 to 3 minutes a side, drizzling 0.75 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil around the edge, until deeply spotted and fragrant.
Blister over a low flame for a few seconds until it puffs in patches, then serve at once and repeat with the rest.
tips: Keep the garlic-chilli paste coarse so pockets of roasted garlic burst through the rotlo rather than vanishing into the dough.
Toast the sesame seeds lightly before adding them for a deeper nutty aroma in every bite.
This rotlo is filling enough to eat with just curd, but it firms up fast, so cook and serve one round at a time.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a bowl of chilled buttermilk and a raw onion, letting the garlic-sesame crust carry the meal.

variations.name: Classic Surti Sev Khamani
variations.description: A Surti breakfast icon where day-old khaman is coarsely crumbled, freshened with a sizzling sesame-oil tempering, and heaped with crunchy sev, pomegranate and coriander. The contrast of soft spiced crumbs against crisp sev is the whole point, and a hint of jaggery keeps the Gujarati sweet-savoury balance intact. It is scooped up warm at Surat's morning stalls with a wedge of lime.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: Its toasty depth carries the tempering that flavours the crumbled khaman

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: The unrefined sweetness balances the tang without the flat edge of white sugar

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups besan with 1 cup water, 2 tsp ginger-green chilli paste, ½ tsp turmeric, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 1 tsp salt into a smooth lump-free batter of thick pouring consistency, then rest it for 10 minutes.

Just before steaming, sprinkle 1 tsp Eno over the batter and fold gently for 5 seconds until it turns frothy and doubles; pour into a greased tray and steam over rolling water for 15 minutes until a skewer comes out clean.
Cool the khaman for 10 minutes, then crumble it coarsely with your fingers into rough pea-sized pieces so the texture stays fluffy rather than pasty.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a small pan on medium heat, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp sesame seeds for 20 seconds, add ¼ tsp hing, then pour this hot tempering evenly over the crumbled khaman and toss.
Dissolve 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Khandsari in the remaining 1 tbsp lemon juice with a splash of warm water and drizzle it over the crumbs, tossing until every piece is glossy and lightly sweet-tart.
Just before serving, fold in half the sev and coriander, then top with the rest of the sev, pomegranate seeds and coriander so the garnish stays crunchy.
tips: Day-old khaman crumbles into cleaner grains than fresh warm khaman, which tends to smear; steam it a night ahead for the best texture.
Add the sev only at the last minute, as it turns soggy within ten minutes of touching the moist crumbs.
If your khaman turns out dense, it was over-folded after adding Eno; fold just until frothy and steam immediately.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm in a bowl with an extra fistful of sev on top and green chutney and hot masala chai on the side for an authentic Surti nashto.

variations.name: Nylon Soft Sev Khamani
variations.description: The melt-in-the-mouth halwai version, where the crumbled khaman is loosened with warm milk and extra tempering until it turns almost creamy, then blanketed in fine nylon sev and a dusting of powdered khandsari. Softer and richer than the street style, it barely needs chewing. This is the plateful sold under glass at Surat's mithai counters.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: A generous pour keeps the crumbs silky and soft in this halwai-style plate

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari
ingredients.note: Half sweetens the crumbs, half is powdered fine for the signature dusting

steps: Beat 1.5 cups besan with 1 cup water, 1 tbsp green chilli paste, ½ tsp turmeric, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 1 tsp salt into a smooth batter and let it stand for 10 minutes.
Fold 1 tsp Eno through the batter for 5 seconds until aerated, pour into a greased tin and steam over high heat for 15 minutes; test with a skewer for a clean, springy khaman.
Cool for 10 minutes, then crumble very finely and drizzle 4 tbsp warm milk over the crumbs, tossing so they plump up and soften evenly.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 10 curry leaves for 20 seconds, then pour the sizzling oil over the crumbs and mix until they turn glossy and loose.
Sprinkle 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Khandsari over the warm crumbs and fold until it melts in; grind the remaining 1.5 tbsp khandsari to a fine powder for finishing.
Pile the soft khamani into a dish, cover the whole surface thickly with fine nylon sev, and finish with the powdered khandsari dusted over the top just before serving.
tips: The warm-milk soak is what makes this version melt-soft; add it while the crumbs are still warm so they drink it in.
Use the finest nylon sev you can find, as the thin strands soften pleasantly against the creamy crumbs instead of staying stiff.
This style is meant to be eaten within the hour; refrigeration firms the milk-softened crumbs and dulls them.
variations.servingSuggestion: Present in a shallow bowl with the sev mounded high and a few pomegranate jewels for colour; pair with fafda and jalebi for a classic Gujarati sweet-shop breakfast.

variations.name: Green Coriander Sev Khamani
variations.description: A bright, herb-forward take where a fresh coriander, mint and green-garlic chutney is folded through the crumbs, tinting the whole dish green and lifting it with raw pungency. Grated coconut adds sweetness and a coastal note that suits Surat's love of green garlic in winter. Sharper and fresher than the classic, it eats like a chaat.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Neutral enough to let the green-garlic chutney flavour lead

steps: Blend 1 cup coriander, ¼ cup mint, 3 tbsp green garlic, 3 green chillies, 3 tbsp grated coconut, 1 tbsp lemon juice and a pinch of salt with a splash of water into a thick, vivid green chutney and set aside.
Whisk 1.5 cups besan with 1 cup water, ½ tsp turmeric, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 1 tsp salt into a smooth batter and rest for 10 minutes.
Fold in 1 tsp Eno until frothy, pour into a greased tray, and steam over high heat for 15 minutes until the khaman is set and springy; cool for 10 minutes.
Crumble the cooled khaman coarsely, then fold in three-quarters of the green chutney until every crumb is streaked green and fragrant.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium, pop 1 tsp mustard seeds for 20 seconds, and pour the hot tempering over the crumbs, tossing to coat.
Spread the green khamani on a plate, dot with the reserved chutney, scatter the sev over the top, and serve at once while the sev is crisp.
tips: Green garlic is seasonal; out of season, use 1 tbsp regular garlic plus extra coriander stalks to keep the pungent backbone.
Blend the chutney with minimal water so it stays thick and does not turn the crumbs wet and heavy.
Fold the chutney in only when you are ready to serve, as the acid slowly dulls the bright green over a couple of hours.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve as a chaat-style plate with an extra squeeze of lemon, a sprinkle of sev and thin onion rings, alongside sweet tamarind chutney for guests who want contrast.

variations.name: Kathiyawadi Lasaniya Sev Khamani
variations.description: The fiery Saurashtra cousin, where a pounded garlic and red-chilli paste is bloomed in the tempering so the crumbs turn rust-red and boldly pungent. There is no sweetness to soften it here, just heat, garlic and the crunch of thick sev. It is the version that pairs with a glass of chaas to put out the fire.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: The Kathiyawadi choice; it fries the garlic-chilli paste to a deep aroma

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups besan with 1 cup water, ½ tsp turmeric, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 1 tsp salt into a smooth batter and rest for 10 minutes.
Fold 1 tsp Eno through the batter until frothy, pour into a greased tray and steam over high heat for 15 minutes; cool 10 minutes, then crumble coarsely.
Pound 8 garlic cloves with a pinch of salt into a rough paste, then stir in 2 tsp Kashmiri red chilli powder and 1 tbsp water to make a loose red masala.

Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 12 curry leaves for 20 seconds, then add the garlic-chilli paste and fry for 45 seconds until the raw garlic smell turns nutty and the oil runs red.
Pour the sizzling red tempering over the crumbled khaman and toss thoroughly until every grain is stained rust-red and coated in the garlicky oil.
Fold in half the sev and coriander, then top with the remaining thick sev and coriander and serve while punchy and warm.
tips: Pound the garlic rather than mincing it; the coarse crush releases more pungent oils that define the Kathiyawadi character.
Fry the chilli paste only until the oil separates and reddens; take it further and the chilli scorches bitter.
Skip the sugar entirely here, as this style is meant to be sharp and savoury unlike the sweeter Surti original.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thick sev, sliced raw onion and green chillies, and a tall glass of salted buttermilk to balance the garlic-chilli heat.

variations.name: Classic Kesar Shrikhand with Puri
variations.description: The quintessential Gujarati-Maharashtrian festive plate: thick, silky hung yogurt whipped smooth with saffron, cardamom and khandsari, served with hot, puffed whole-wheat puris. The tang of the strained curd against the crisp, ghee-fried puris is a match made for wedding thalis and Diwali lunches.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari, powdered
ingredients.note: finely powdered khandsari dissolves smoothly into the hung curd for a clean, floral sweetness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: saffron steeped in warm milk gives shrikhand its glowing colour and signature aroma

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil fries the puris crisp and puffed with a clean, neutral taste

steps: Spoon 4 cups yogurt into a muslin cloth, tie it up, and hang over a bowl for 4 to 5 hours in the fridge until all the whey drains and a thick chakka remains.

Steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk, then whisk the hung curd with 0.75 cup powdered Anveshan Khandsari, the saffron milk and 0.5 tsp cardamom powder until completely smooth and creamy, and chill.
For the puris, knead 2 cups whole wheat flour, 2 tbsp semolina, 0.5 tsp salt and 1 tbsp of the oil with about 0.75 cup water into a stiff, smooth dough, then rest it covered for 15 minutes.
Divide the dough into small balls and roll each into a 10 cm disc, keeping them slightly thick so they puff.

Heat the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a kadhai to 180C, then slide in one puri at a time, pressing gently with a slotted spoon until it balloons, and fry for about 40 seconds per side until pale golden and crisp.
Drain the puris on paper, fold 2 tbsp slivered pistachios into the chilled shrikhand, and serve the cold shrikhand alongside the hot puris.
tips: Hang the curd long enough that it is genuinely thick, or the shrikhand will be runny and refuse to hold peaks.
Fry the puris in oil that is hot enough to puff them instantly; cool oil makes them soak fat and stay flat.
Whisk the shrikhand only until smooth — over-beating can thin it out.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the chilled saffron shrikhand in a bowl beside a stack of hot puris, garnished with pistachio and a few saffron strands, as the centrepiece of a festive thali.

variations.name: Aamrakhand with Puri
variations.description: The summer favourite where ripe alphonso mango pulp is folded into hung curd for a sunny, fruit-forward shrikhand, served with crisp puris. Sweet-tart and fragrant, aamrakhand needs little added sugar and turns the classic plate into a seasonal celebration.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari, powdered
ingredients.note: only a little khandsari is needed since the ripe mango brings most of the sweetness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: light wood-pressed sunflower oil fries the puris golden and crisp without heaviness

steps: Hang 4 cups yogurt in muslin for 4 to 5 hours in the fridge until it becomes a thick chakka.
Whisk the hung curd smooth with 1 cup ripe mango pulp, 0.33 cup powdered Anveshan Khandsari and 0.5 tsp cardamom powder until creamy and evenly coloured, then chill.
Knead 2 cups whole wheat flour, 0.25 tsp ajwain, 0.5 tsp salt and 1 tbsp of the oil with about 0.75 cup water into a stiff dough, and rest 15 minutes.
Roll the dough into small 10 cm discs, keeping them slightly thick so they balloon.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Sunflower Oil to 180C and fry the puris one at a time, pressing gently until each puffs, for about 40 seconds a side until golden.
Drain the puris, top the chilled aamrakhand with 2 tbsp slivered almonds, and serve the cold shrikhand with the hot puris.
tips: Use thick, ripe, low-fibre mango pulp; watery or stringy mango will loosen the shrikhand.
Taste before adding all the khandsari, as very sweet alphonso may need even less.
The ajwain in the puri dough gently balances the richness and aids digestion.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the golden aamrakhand chilled beside hot puris on a summer lunch thali, scattered with almonds and a mint leaf.

variations.name: Matho Dry-Fruit Shrikhand with Puri
variations.description: The richer Kathiyawadi matho, a nut-and-spice-laden shrikhand studded with charoli, chopped nuts, nutmeg and a whisper of black pepper for warmth. Denser and more textured than plain shrikhand, it is the indulgent version served at grand Gujarati feasts with hot puris.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khandsari, powdered
ingredients.note: khandsari sweetens the rich matho cleanly against the warm spices

ingredients.name: Anveshan Saffron
ingredients.note: saffron adds colour and floral depth to the spiced dry-fruit shrikhand

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed groundnut oil gives the puris a crisp, clean puff for the rich matho

steps: Hang 4 cups yogurt in muslin for 5 hours until very thick, and steep 1 pinch Anveshan Saffron in 2 tbsp warm milk.

Whisk the hung curd smooth with 0.75 cup powdered Anveshan Khandsari, the saffron milk, 0.25 tsp nutmeg, 0.25 tsp black pepper and 0.5 tsp cardamom, then fold in 2 tbsp charoli and half of 3 tbsp chopped nuts and chill.
Knead 1 cup maida and 1 cup whole wheat flour with 0.5 tsp salt and 1 tbsp oil and about 0.7 cup water into a stiff dough, then rest 15 minutes.
Roll into small 10 cm discs, keeping them a touch thick to puff well.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 180C and fry each puri, pressing gently until it balloons, for about 40 seconds a side until crisp and golden.
Drain the puris, top the chilled matho with the remaining chopped nuts, and serve cold alongside the hot puris.
tips: The whisper of black pepper is traditional in matho — keep it subtle so it warms rather than bites.
Fold the charoli and nuts in just before serving so they keep their crunch.
A blend of maida and wheat flour gives these puris an extra crisp, festive puff.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve this spiced dry-fruit shrikhand chilled with hot puris at a grand feast, garnished generously with charoli and chopped nuts.

variations.name: Honey-Fig Shrikhand with Khapli Puri
variations.description: A wholesome, refined-sugar-free take where hung curd is sweetened with honey and studded with chopped dried figs, served with nutty ancient-grain khapli puris. Naturally sweet and fibre-rich, it is a lighter, guilt-free rendition of the festive plate.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Honey
ingredients.note: raw honey folded into the cold curd sweetens it naturally with a floral note

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: ancient emmer-wheat flour makes nutty, wholesome puris that suit the honey shrikhand

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sunflower Oil
ingredients.note: light wood-pressed sunflower oil fries the khapli puris crisp without weighing them down

steps: Hang 4 cups yogurt in muslin for 4 to 5 hours until thick, then soak 5 chopped dried figs in 2 tbsp warm water for 10 minutes to soften.
Whisk the hung curd smooth, then gently fold in 5 tbsp Anveshan Honey, 0.5 tsp cardamom powder, the softened figs and half of 2 tbsp chopped walnuts, keeping the honey off any heat, and chill.
Knead 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with 0.5 tsp salt and 1 tbsp of the oil and about 0.85 cup water into a stiff but pliable dough, and rest 15 minutes.
Roll into small 10 cm discs, keeping them slightly thick as khapli dough puffs a little less than refined flour.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Sunflower Oil to 180C and fry each puri, pressing gently to help it balloon, for about 45 seconds a side until crisp and golden.
Drain the puris, top the chilled honey-fig shrikhand with the remaining walnuts, and serve cold with the hot khapli puris.
tips: Add the honey only to the cold curd and never heat it, so its raw floral character and nutrients stay intact.
Khapli dough needs a touch more water and a slightly thicker roll to puff well when fried.
Soaking the figs first keeps them soft and juicy rather than chewy in the shrikhand.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve this naturally sweetened shrikhand chilled with warm khapli puris for a wholesome festive or fasting-friendly treat.

variations.name: Classic Sukhdi
variations.description: The soulful Gujarati comfort sweet made from just three things done right: whole wheat flour roasted low and slow in ghee until it smells like toasted biscuits, then bound with molten jaggery and set into soft, melt-in-the-mouth squares. No fuss, no syrup, just deep nutty warmth in every bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: generous bilona ghee is the heart of sukhdi, roasting the flour to a nutty aroma and giving the squares their melting softness

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: unrefined jaggery sets the sukhdi and lends its signature caramel warmth

steps: Grease a small steel plate or tray with a little ghee and scatter half of 2 tbsp slivered almonds across the base so they stud the underside of the sukhdi.

Melt 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy kadhai on low heat, then add 1 cup whole wheat flour and roast, stirring constantly, for 8 to 10 minutes until it turns golden-brown and gives off a strong toasted, biscuity aroma.
Turn off the heat and let the mixture cool for 1 minute so it stops bubbling, then quickly stir in 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder until it melts completely into a smooth, glossy paste.
Work fast as the jaggery sets rapidly, stirring in 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and mixing until fully combined.
Pour the hot mixture into the greased tray, spread it evenly to about 1 cm thick with the back of a greased spoon, and press 1 tbsp poppy seeds and the remaining almonds over the top.
While still warm, score into diamonds or squares, then cool for 15 minutes until firm before separating the pieces.
tips: Roast the flour on genuinely low heat until deeply golden — this is where all the flavour comes from, and rushing it leaves a raw, floury taste.
Add the jaggery off the heat and only after the mixture cools slightly, or the residual heat can turn it hard and grainy.
Cut while warm but cool fully before lifting the pieces, or they crumble instead of holding a clean edge.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature with a glass of warm milk, or tuck a square into lunchboxes as a wholesome, keeps-for-days sweet.

variations.name: Khapli Wheat Sukhdi
variations.description: A nuttier, more nourishing sukhdi built on stone-milled khapli (emmer) wheat, an ancient low-gluten grain with a rustic, earthy flavour that stands up beautifully to jaggery and ghee. The squares are a shade darker and more wholesome, with a satisfying, slightly denser bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: ancient emmer-wheat flour adds a deep, earthy nuttiness and extra fibre to the sukhdi

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: bilona ghee roasts the robust khapli flour into a fragrant, melting base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery binds the ancient-grain flour and complements its rustic character

steps: Grease a small tray with ghee and dry-toast 1 tbsp sesame seeds in it for 30 seconds, then tilt to coat the base evenly.

Melt 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan on low heat and add 1 cup Anveshan Khapli Atta, roasting and stirring for 10 to 12 minutes until the coarser flour turns a rich brown and smells intensely nutty.
Take the pan off the heat, rest for a minute, then stir in 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder swiftly until it melts into a smooth glossy mass.
Mix in 0.25 tsp dry ginger powder, 0.5 tsp cardamom powder and 2 tbsp chopped walnuts, working quickly before it stiffens.
Tip the mixture into the sesame-lined tray, level it to about 1 cm thick with a greased spoon, and press gently so the surface is smooth.
Score into squares while warm, then leave to firm for 15 to 20 minutes before separating.
tips: Khapli flour is coarser and needs a couple of extra minutes of roasting than regular atta to lose its rawness.
The pinch of dry ginger is a traditional digestive touch that suits this heartier, winter-friendly version.
If the mixture sets before you can spread it, warm the pan for a few seconds to loosen it again.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these earthy squares with masala chai, or pack them as a high-fibre energy bite for travel.

variations.name: Gond Dry-Fruit Winter Sukhdi
variations.description: A fortified winter sukhdi in the tradition of postpartum tonics, studded with puffed edible gum, mixed nuts and warming dry ginger. Richer and crunchier than the everyday square, it doubles as a strengthening morning bite through the cold months.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: extra ghee is needed to fry the edible gum and to keep this nut-heavy sukhdi tender

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery sets the tonic sukhdi and adds iron-rich sweetness

steps: Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan on medium and fry 3 tbsp edible gum in small batches until each piece puffs white and crisp, about 30 seconds, then drain and crush coarsely.
In the same pan lightly toast 0.33 cup chopped mixed nuts for 1 minute and set aside with the gum.
Add the remaining ghee to make up 0.6 cup total, melt on low, and roast 1 cup whole wheat flour for 9 to 10 minutes, stirring, until golden-brown and nutty.
Take off the heat, rest a minute, then stir in 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder until fully melted and smooth.
Quickly fold in 0.5 tsp dry ginger powder, 0.5 tsp cardamom powder, 0.25 tsp nutmeg powder, the crushed gum and the toasted nuts.
Press the mixture firmly into a greased tray about 1.5 cm thick, score into squares while warm, and cool for 20 minutes until set.
tips: Fry the gond until it fully puffs and shatters when pressed; any hard centres stay unpleasantly chewy.
This richer version needs slightly more ghee to stay soft, as the nuts and gum absorb some of it.
Store in an airtight jar and eat one square each cold morning — it keeps well for two to three weeks.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve a square with warm turmeric milk on winter mornings as a traditional strengthening treat.

variations.name: Sesame-Multigrain Sukhdi
variations.description: A crunchier, wholesome reinvention using multigrain flour and a heavy hand of toasted sesame, giving the squares a nutty, brittle-like character and a boost of fibre and calcium. The sesame plays off the jaggery like a chikki, making these a more textured, everyday-healthy sukhdi.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Multigrain Atta
ingredients.note: a blend of grains adds fibre and a complex, hearty flavour that suits the sesame beautifully

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: ghee roasts the multigrain flour and carries the toasted-sesame aroma through the squares

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: jaggery and sesame together give a chikki-like depth to this sukhdi

steps: Dry-roast 4 tbsp sesame seeds in a pan on medium for 2 minutes until they pop and turn golden, then set aside, reserving 1 tbsp for the topping.
Grease a tray and scatter the reserved 1 tbsp sesame across the base.
Melt 0.5 cup Anveshan Ghee in a heavy pan on low, add 1 cup Anveshan Multigrain Atta, and roast for 9 to 10 minutes, stirring, until browned and fragrant.

Take off the heat, cool for a minute, then stir in 0.75 cup Anveshan Jaggery Powder until it melts into a smooth mass, and mix in 0.5 tsp cardamom powder, 2 tbsp chopped cashews and the toasted sesame.
Pour into the sesame-lined tray and spread evenly to about 1 cm thick with a greased spoon, pressing the surface smooth.
Score into squares while warm and let firm for 15 minutes before lifting out the pieces.
tips: Roast the sesame separately just until it pops, so it stays crunchy rather than burning in the flour.
Multigrain flour browns faster than plain atta, so watch it closely in the last two minutes.
For extra crunch, press a light layer of sesame onto the top as well before it sets.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these nutty squares with a cup of ginger tea, or crumble over warm milk for a quick fortified breakfast.

variations.name: Classic Surti Undhiyu
variations.description: The grand Surti winter casserole, a slow-cooked medley of surti papdi, purple yam, baby potatoes, sweet potato, small brinjals and raw banana layered with fried methi muthia in a fragrant green masala of coriander, green garlic and fresh coconut. It is sweet, savoury and herby all at once, the centrepiece of every Gujarati winter feast. Traditionally cooked upside-down, undhiyu rewards patience with meltingly soft vegetables.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Undhiyu is generously oiled the Surti way; groundnut oil carries the green masala deep into the vegetables

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The gentle caramel note balances the green masala the way Surti cooks intend

steps: Make the muthia by mixing ¾ cup besan, 1 cup chopped methi, 1 tsp ginger-chilli paste, ½ tsp turmeric, a pinch of salt and 1 tbsp oil into a firm dough; shape into 12 small ovals and deep-fry in some of the Anveshan Groundnut Oil for 3 minutes until golden, then drain.

For the green masala, grind 1.5 cups coriander, ½ cup green garlic, ½ cup grated coconut, the remaining ginger-chilli paste, 2 tbsp sesame seeds, 3 tbsp crushed peanuts, 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and 2 tsp salt into a coarse, thick paste.
Slit the 6 brinjals and 8 baby potatoes crosswise and stuff them generously with the green masala, reserving the rest of the masala for layering.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a heavy pot on medium, add the surti papdi and tuvar lilva with 2 tbsp reserved masala, and saute for 3 minutes.

Layer in the purple yam, sweet potato, raw banana, then the stuffed potatoes and brinjals, spooning the remaining masala between layers; add ¼ cup water, cover tightly, and cook on low for 30 minutes without stirring.
Tuck the fried muthia on top, cover again, and steam 10 more minutes until every vegetable is fork-tender; fold gently once and serve hot.
tips: Do not stir undhiyu while it cooks; gently shake the pot instead so the soft vegetables and muthia keep their shape.
Add the fried muthia only in the last ten minutes, or they soak up liquid and fall apart.
Undhiyu tastes even better an hour after cooking once the masala settles, so make it slightly ahead of your meal.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the classic Surti way with hot puris or thepla, a wedge of lime and jalebi on the side for the beloved undhiyu-jalebi winter pairing.

variations.name: Kathiyawadi Undhiyu
variations.description: The bolder Saurashtra version, cooked matla-style in a heavy pot with a fiery red garlic-chilli-sesame masala instead of the Surti green paste. It skips the sweeter yam and banana and leans on smoky heat, roasted peanuts and a hit of jaggery to round it off. Rustic and robust, it is undhiyu for those who like their winter food with a kick.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Fries the red garlic masala to a deep, smoky aroma before the vegetables go in

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: A Kathiyawadi touch that softens the fierce red-chilli heat

steps: Mix ¾ cup besan with 1 cup chopped methi, ½ tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, a pinch of salt and 1 tbsp oil into a firm dough, shape 12 muthia, and deep-fry in a little of the Anveshan Groundnut Oil for 3 minutes until crisp; drain.

Pound 12 garlic cloves coarse, then mix with 3 tbsp Kashmiri red chilli powder, 3 tbsp sesame seeds, 4 tbsp crushed peanuts, 2 tbsp coriander-cumin powder, 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, ½ tsp turmeric and 2 tsp salt into a thick red masala.
Slit the 6 brinjals and 8 baby potatoes and pack them with the red masala, keeping the rest aside.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a heavy pot on medium, add the leftover red masala, and fry for 90 seconds until the raw garlic smell turns nutty and the oil runs red.
Add the surti papdi, tuvar lilva and sweet potato, toss to coat, then nestle in the stuffed potatoes and brinjals; add ⅓ cup water, cover, and cook on low for 30 minutes.
Lay the fried muthia over the top, cover, and steam 10 more minutes until everything is tender and glossy with the red masala; fold gently and serve.
tips: Fry the red masala until the oil separates before adding vegetables; this cooks out the raw chilli and deepens the colour.
Balance the heat with the jaggery to taste; Kathiyawadi cooking loves the sweet-hot contrast, so adjust rather than omit it.
Keep the pot on the lowest flame with a tight lid to mimic the slow matla cooking that makes this version smoky.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with thick bajra rotla, a dollop of white butter and sliced onion, the hearty Saurashtra plate that stands up to the fiery masala.

variations.name: Pressure-Cooker Quick Undhiyu
variations.description: A streamlined one-pot undhiyu for busy days that captures the green-masala soul in a fraction of the time by pressure-cooking the vegetables and stirring in ready muthia. It keeps the core papdi, tuvar and brinjal but skips the elaborate stuffing and layering. Faster, lighter and still convincingly Surti.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Enough to bloom the masala and gloss the vegetables without the traditional flood of oil

steps: Grind 1 cup coriander, ¼ cup green garlic, ⅓ cup grated coconut, 2 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, 1 tbsp sugar and 1.5 tsp salt into a coarse green paste with a splash of water.
Heat ⅓ cup Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pressure cooker on medium, add the green paste and ½ tsp turmeric, and saute for 2 minutes until fragrant and the raw smell fades.
Add the surti papdi, tuvar lilva, halved baby potatoes and quartered brinjals, tossing to coat them evenly in the masala.
Pour in ½ cup water, close the lid, and pressure-cook for 2 whistles on medium, then let the pressure release naturally.
Open the cooker, gently fold in the ready methi muthia, and simmer uncovered for 3 minutes so they warm through and soak up the masala.
Check the vegetables are fork-tender, adjust salt, and serve hot with a scatter of extra coriander.
tips: Cut the potatoes and brinjals to a similar size so they cook evenly in the short pressure time.
Two whistles is enough; over-cooking turns the papdi mushy and the brinjal to paste.
Add the muthia only after releasing pressure so they stay intact instead of disintegrating.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with hot phulka rotis and a bowl of plain curd for a quick weeknight Gujarati dinner that still feels festive.

variations.name: Baked-Muthia Healthy Undhiyu
variations.description: A lighter reinvention where the methi muthia are made with wholegrain khapli atta and baked instead of fried, and the whole casserole is finished with far less oil. Purple yam and sweet potato keep it earthy and satisfying while the green masala stays true. It is undhiyu you can enjoy without the post-feast heaviness.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Wholegrain emmer makes the baked muthia hearty and fibre-rich instead of fried and heavy

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Just enough to bloom the masala and brush the muthia before baking

steps: Mix ¾ cup Anveshan Khapli Atta with 1 cup chopped methi, 1 tbsp ginger-chilli paste, ½ tsp turmeric, a pinch of salt and 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil into a firm dough, shape 12 muthia, brush them lightly with oil, and bake at 200C for 18 minutes, turning once, until golden.
Grind 1.5 cups coriander, ½ cup green garlic, ½ cup grated coconut, the remaining ginger-chilli paste, 2 tbsp sesame seeds and 2 tsp salt into a coarse green masala.
Slit the 6 brinjals and stuff them with a spoon of the green masala each.
Heat the remaining 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a heavy pot on medium, add the leftover masala and ½ tsp turmeric, and saute 2 minutes until fragrant.
Add the surti papdi, tuvar lilva, purple yam and sweet potato, then set the stuffed brinjals on top; add ⅓ cup water, cover, and cook on low for 25 minutes until tender.
