Fold in the baked muthia, cover, and steam 5 minutes more so they absorb the masala; serve warm.
tips: Baked khapli muthia stay firmer than fried ones, so add them near the end and fold gently to keep them whole.
Steam the vegetables on the lowest heat with a tight lid; the reduced oil means they cook mostly in their own moisture.
If the pot looks dry midway, add a couple of spoons of hot water rather than more oil to keep it light.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with khapli-atta rotis and a bowl of cucumber raita for a wholesome winter meal that goes easy on the stomach.

variations.name: Classic Gujarati Vaal Nu Shaak
variations.description: A beloved Gujarati home curry of dried field beans simmered soft in a sweet-and-sour gravy balanced with jaggery and tangy kokum. The vaal's gently bitter skin is exactly what gives the dish its distinctive earthy edge against the mellow sweetness. Thick, comforting and quietly complex, it is everyday thali food at its finest.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Blooms the tempering that flavours this earthy field-bean curry

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The sweet counterweight to the vaal's bitterness and the kokum's sourness

steps: Soak 1.5 cups dried vaal overnight in plenty of water, drain, and pressure-cook with 2 cups fresh water and ½ tsp salt for 4 whistles until the beans are soft but still hold their shape.

Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pot on medium, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then add ½ tsp hing and 1 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste and saute for 30 seconds.
Stir in ½ tsp turmeric, 2 tsp coriander-cumin powder and 1 tsp red chilli powder, cook for 20 seconds off the fiercest heat so the spices do not scorch.
Add the cooked vaal with its liquid, 4 kokum petals and ½ cup more water, and simmer uncovered on medium for 10 minutes so the flavours meld.
Stir in 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and the remaining salt, and simmer 5 more minutes until the gravy thickens and turns glossy sweet-sour.
Fold in 3 tbsp grated coconut, garnish with coriander, and serve hot.
tips: Keep the vaal skins on; they carry the mild bitterness that defines this dish, and peeling makes it taste flat.
Balance the sweet, sour and salt at the end by tasting, since jaggery and kokum strengths vary batch to batch.
Soaked and cooked vaal freezes well, so batch-cook and freeze to have this curry ready on a busy day.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with soft rotli and steamed rice, or ladle over plain khichdi with a spoon of ghee for a classic comforting Gujarati dinner.

variations.name: Kathiyawadi Vaal Nu Shaak
variations.description: The robust Saurashtra rendition, thick with a pounded garlic and red-chilli masala and finished with a smoky red tempering. It trades kokum and coconut for a punchy, garlicky heat softened only by a whisper of jaggery. This is vaal for a rustic meal, meant to be mopped up with bajra rotla.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Fries the pounded garlic-chilli masala to a deep, smoky base

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Just a touch to round the fierce garlic-chilli heat

steps: Soak 1.5 cups dried vaal overnight, drain, and pressure-cook with 2 cups water and ½ tsp salt for 4 whistles until soft.
Pound 10 garlic cloves coarse and mix with 2 tbsp Kashmiri red chilli powder and 2 tbsp water into a loose red paste.
Heat 4 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil on medium, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 12 curry leaves for 20 seconds, add the chopped onion, and fry for 4 minutes until golden.

Add the garlic-chilli paste and fry for 90 seconds until the raw smell fades and the oil turns red, then stir in the chopped tomato, ½ tsp turmeric and 2 tsp coriander-cumin powder and cook 4 minutes until pulpy.
Add the cooked vaal with its liquid and ½ cup water, simmer on medium for 10 minutes until the gravy thickens around the beans.
Stir in 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder and the remaining salt, simmer 3 minutes, garnish with coriander, and serve.
tips: Fry the garlic-chilli paste until the oil separates for the signature smoky Kathiyawadi depth; rushing it leaves a raw taste.
Keep this version thick and clingy rather than soupy so it sits well on a rotla.
For extra Saurashtra punch, finish with a spoon of hot oil bloomed with a pinch of extra red chilli powder poured over the top.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with bajra rotla, a knob of white butter and raw onion for a hearty rustic Saurashtra plate.

variations.name: Lilva Vaal Nu Shaak
variations.description: A tender winter version made with fresh green val beans instead of dried, cooked quickly in a light green masala of coriander, green chilli and coconut so they stay sweet and just-soft. Brighter and lighter than the dried curry, it celebrates the short season of fresh vaal. A squeeze of lemon keeps it fresh rather than jammy.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Coconut Oil
ingredients.note: Its light sweetness suits the fresh green beans and coconut masala

steps: Grind 1 cup coriander, 3 green chillies, ⅓ cup grated coconut and 1 inch ginger into a coarse green paste with a splash of water.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Coconut Oil in a pan on medium, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 15 seconds, and add ¼ tsp hing.
Add the green paste and ½ tsp turmeric and saute for 2 minutes until the raw smell fades and the oil edges the masala.
Add the 2 cups fresh val beans, toss to coat, then pour in 1 cup water and 1 tsp salt and bring to a gentle simmer.
Cover and cook on low for 10 to 12 minutes until the beans are just tender and the gravy has thickened lightly.
Stir in 1 tsp sugar and 1 tbsp lemon juice, simmer 2 minutes, and serve fresh and bright.
tips: Fresh lilva cooks fast, so check at ten minutes; overcooking greys the beans and dulls their sweet flavour.
If using peeled lilva, reduce the water slightly as skinned beans release moisture more readily.
Add the lemon off the heat to keep its brightness, since boiling it makes the sourness flat.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with phulka rotis and a bowl of plain rice, a fresh, light winter shaak that pairs well with a simple dal.

variations.name: Jain Vaal Nu Shaak
variations.description: A no-onion, no-garlic version built entirely on the flavours of ginger, asafoetida and a sweet-sour tamarind-jaggery base, so the vaal's earthiness shines without any allium. A tomato-free gravy keeps it true to Jain preferences while staying rich and satisfying. Gentle, warming and completely faithful to the dish's soul.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: Carries the hing-and-ginger tempering that stands in for onion and garlic

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Balances the tamarind sourness in this allium-free gravy

steps: Soak 1.5 cups dried vaal overnight, drain, and pressure-cook with 2 cups water and ½ tsp salt for 4 whistles until soft.
Heat 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pot on medium, splutter 1 tsp mustard seeds and 1 tsp cumin seeds for 20 seconds, then add a generous ¾ tsp hing so it fizzes.
Add 1 tbsp ginger paste and 3 slit green chillies, saute 30 seconds, then stir in ½ tsp turmeric and 2 tsp coriander-cumin powder off the fiercest heat.
Add the cooked vaal with its liquid and ½ cup water and simmer on medium for 10 minutes.
Stir in 2 tbsp tamarind pulp and 2 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder with the remaining salt, and simmer 5 minutes until the gravy is glossy and balanced sweet-sour.
Garnish with coriander and serve hot.
tips: Use a generous pinch of hing to build savoury depth in place of onion and garlic; it is the backbone of Jain cooking.
Add the tamarind and jaggery together and taste, adjusting each so neither the sour nor the sweet dominates.
For a fully Jain meal, ensure the vaal used has not sprouted, as sprouted beans are avoided in strict Jain diets.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with plain rotli and steamed rice, or with a simple moong dal khichdi for a soothing satvik meal.

variations.name: Classic Doodhi Handvo
variations.description: The definitive Gujarati savoury cake: a coarsely ground rice-and-mixed-lentil batter fermented overnight, folded with grated bottle gourd, and cooked slowly to a deep golden crust over a soft, tangy crumb. A lavish sesame-mustard tempering pressed into the surface makes every slice crackle.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: wood-pressed gingelly oil in the tempering and around the edges builds handvo's signature crackling crust

steps: Rinse and soak 1 cup rice with 0.5 cup chana dal, 0.25 cup toor dal and 0.25 cup urad dal for 4 to 5 hours, then grind coarsely with a little water into a thick idli-like batter.
Stir in 0.75 cup whisked yogurt, cover, and leave to ferment in a warm spot for 8 hours or overnight until it smells pleasantly sour and rises slightly.

Squeeze 1.5 cups grated bottle gourd and fold it into the batter with 1.5 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp salt; just before cooking, sprinkle in 1 tsp eno and mix until airy.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a heavy non-stick pan on medium, crackle 1.5 tsp mustard seeds, 2 tbsp sesame seeds and 0.5 tsp asafoetida with 12 curry leaves for 40 seconds, then pour half over the batter and reserve the rest.
Pour the batter into the same pan in an even layer, drizzle the reserved tempering on top, cover, and cook on low for 18 to 20 minutes until the base forms a dark golden crust.
Carefully flip the handvo, add 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil around the edges, and cook uncovered for 10 to 12 minutes until both crusts are crisp; cool slightly and cut into squares.
tips: Grind the batter coarse, not silky — a little grit gives handvo its characteristic hearty texture.
Cook strictly on low heat; rushing on high burns the crust before the inside sets.
A well-fermented batter can rest in the fridge overnight and be brought to room temperature before adding eno.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the crisp golden squares warm with green chutney and sweet tamarind chutney, or a simple bowl of masala chai.

variations.name: Instant Rava Handvo
variations.description: A same-day handvo that skips soaking, grinding and fermenting: semolina and gram flour are whisked with yogurt, rested briefly, and lifted with fruit salt. It bakes up just as golden-crusted and savoury, ready in under an hour for a weeknight craving.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: neutral wood-pressed groundnut oil crisps the instant handvo base evenly and keeps it light

steps: Whisk 1.5 cups semolina and 0.5 cup besan with 1 cup yogurt and 0.5 cup water into a thick lump-free batter, then rest for 15 to 20 minutes so the rava swells.

Stir in 0.5 cup grated carrot, 1.5 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1.25 tsp salt and 1 tbsp lemon juice, loosening with a splash of water to a thick pouring consistency.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a small pan, crackle 1.5 tsp mustard seeds, 1 tsp cumin seeds, 2 tbsp sesame seeds and 12 curry leaves for 40 seconds until the sesame is golden.
Stir half the tempering into the batter, sprinkle in 1.5 tsp eno, and fold gently until the batter turns visibly frothy.
Immediately pour into a heavy non-stick pan greased with 1 tbsp oil, drizzle the remaining tempering on top, cover, and cook on low for 15 to 16 minutes until the base is deep golden.
Flip the handvo, add 1 tbsp oil around the edges, and cook uncovered for 8 to 10 minutes until crisp on both sides, then cut into squares.
tips: Add the eno only at the last moment and cook straight away, or the batter loses its lift and bakes dense.
Rest the batter long enough for the semolina to absorb the yogurt, otherwise the handvo tastes grainy.
For a browner crust, sprinkle a few extra sesame seeds into the greased pan before pouring the batter.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm wedges with coriander-mint chutney and a hot cup of adrak chai for a quick evening snack.

variations.name: Lasaniya Green Masala Handvo
variations.description: A fiery Kathiyawadi-style handvo where a fresh green paste of garlic, green chilli and coriander is beaten through the batter, giving a punchy, herb-forward cake with real heat. Extra garlic in the tempering and a scatter of crushed peanuts make this the boldest version on the table.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: gingelly oil carries the pungent garlic tempering deep into the crust and crisps it beautifully

steps: Soak 1 cup rice with 0.5 cup chana dal and 0.25 cup urad dal for 4 to 5 hours, grind coarse, stir in 0.75 cup yogurt, and ferment for 8 hours until slightly risen and sour.
Grind 8 garlic cloves, 5 green chillies and 0.5 cup coriander into a coarse green paste, and beat it into the fermented batter with 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1.5 tsp red chilli powder and 1.5 tsp salt.
Just before cooking, sprinkle in 1 tsp eno and fold until the batter turns light and airy.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a heavy non-stick pan, crackle 1.5 tsp mustard seeds, 2 tbsp sesame seeds, 3 tbsp crushed peanuts and 12 curry leaves for 40 seconds, then stir half into the batter and keep the rest.
Pour the batter into the pan in an even layer, drizzle the reserved tempering over, cover, and cook on low for 16 to 18 minutes until the base is deep golden and crisp.
Flip carefully, add 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil around the edges, and cook uncovered for 10 to 12 minutes until both sides crackle, then cut into squares.
tips: Keep the garlic-chilli paste coarse so you get little bursts of heat and pungency through the cake.
The crushed peanuts in the tempering add a Kathiyawadi crunch — toast them just until fragrant.
Adjust the green chillies to taste, but this version is meant to be assertively spicy.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve these fiery squares hot with cooling plain yogurt and a wedge of lemon to balance the heat.

variations.name: Baked Palak-Corn Millet Handvo
variations.description: A nourishing oven-baked handvo built on ground millet and oats instead of rice, folded with spinach and sweet corn for a fibre-rich, protein-forward cake. Baking gives an even, all-over crust with far less oil, ideal for a lighter, wholesome bite.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Multigrain Atta
ingredients.note: a blend of millets and grains makes a wholesome, high-fibre base that bakes into a firm cake

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: a modest drizzle of gingelly oil is all the baked handvo needs for a crisp top and nutty aroma

steps: Whisk 1 cup Anveshan Multigrain Atta, 0.5 cup ground oats and 0.5 cup besan with 1 cup yogurt and a little water into a thick batter, and rest for 15 minutes.
Fold in 1 cup finely chopped spinach, 0.5 cup sweet corn, 1.5 tbsp ginger-green chilli paste, 0.5 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder and 1.25 tsp salt.
Preheat the oven to 200C and grease a baking tin with a little of the sesame oil.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil in a small pan, crackle 1 tsp mustard seeds and 2 tbsp sesame seeds with 10 curry leaves for 40 seconds, then stir half into the batter.
Sprinkle 1.5 tsp eno over the batter, fold until airy, pour into the tin, and drizzle the remaining tempering and the last 1 tbsp oil over the top.
Bake for 30 to 35 minutes until the top is firm and golden and a skewer comes out clean, then cool for 10 minutes before cutting into squares.
tips: Squeeze any excess water from the chopped spinach so the batter does not turn runny.
Grind the oats fresh and coarse; store-bought oat flour can make the handvo gummy.
This baked version keeps well for two days and reheats into an excellent high-fibre breakfast.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve the wholesome green-flecked squares warm with thick yogurt and coriander chutney, or pack cold into a healthy tiffin.

variations.name: Classic Gujarati Lilva Kachori
variations.description: A prized Gujarati winter kachori with a crisp, flaky shell hiding a coarsely crushed filling of fresh tuvar lilva, coconut and sesame, sweetened with a little jaggery and warmed with ginger and green chilli. The contrast of shatteringly crisp pastry against the moist, sweet-savoury pea filling is irresistible. It appears in every Surat and Ahmedabad sweet shop the moment fresh lilva hits the market.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Wholegrain emmer gives a nutty, flaky shell that fries crisper than plain maida

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: 3 tbsp goes into the pastry as moyan for flakiness; the rest deep-fries the kachoris

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: The gentle sweetness that defines the Gujarati lilva filling

steps: Rub 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil into 1.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with ½ tsp salt until the flour clumps when pressed, then knead in about 0.4 cup water into a stiff, smooth dough; cover and rest 30 minutes.
Coarsely crush the 2 cups fresh tuvar lilva in a mortar, keeping the mixture chunky rather than a paste.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan on medium, add 1 tsp crushed fennel and 2 tsp ginger-green chilli paste, saute 30 seconds, then add the crushed lilva, ½ tsp turmeric and ½ tsp salt.
Cook the filling for 5 minutes until dry, then stir in ⅓ cup coconut, 2 tbsp sesame seeds, 1.5 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder, 1 tbsp lemon juice and coriander; cool completely.
Divide the dough into 12 balls, roll each into a 3-inch disc, place a spoon of filling in the centre, gather the edges to seal, and flatten gently into a stuffed kachori.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil to a moderate 150C and fry the kachoris in batches on low-medium for 6 to 7 minutes, turning, until pale golden and crisp; drain and serve warm.
tips: Fry the kachoris on low-medium heat; high heat browns the shell before the inside crisps and leaves it doughy.
Dry the filling well before stuffing, as any moisture makes the kachoris burst open in the oil.
Seal the edges without cracks and rest the shaped kachoris a few minutes before frying so the seams hold.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with sweet tamarind-date chutney and a sharp green chutney, alongside masala chai, the way Gujarati farsan shops plate them.

variations.name: Baked Khapli Lilva Kachori
variations.description: A lighter, oven-baked kachori where the wholegrain khapli shell turns crisp with just a brush of ghee instead of a deep fry. The lilva filling stays true, savoury and fennel-scented, so you get the winter treat with far less oil. Ideal for those who want the crunch without the indulgence.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its nutty grain bakes to a satisfying crisp shell without frying

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: 3 tbsp enriches the dough; the rest brushes the kachoris for a golden bake

steps: Rub 3 tbsp Anveshan Ghee into 1.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with ½ tsp salt until crumbly, then knead in about 0.4 cup water into a stiff dough; cover and rest 30 minutes.
Coarsely crush the 2 cups tuvar lilva, keeping it chunky.

Heat 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee in a pan on medium, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds and 1 tsp crushed fennel for 20 seconds, add 2 tsp ginger-green chilli paste, then the crushed lilva, ½ tsp turmeric, 1 tsp coriander powder and ½ tsp salt.
Cook the filling for 5 to 6 minutes until dry and fragrant, stir in 1 tbsp lemon juice and coriander, and cool fully.
Roll the dough into 12 discs, stuff and seal each with the filling, flatten gently, and arrange on a lined tray; brush the tops with the remaining melted Anveshan Ghee.
Bake at 190C for 25 to 28 minutes, turning once halfway, until the shells are golden and crisp; cool a few minutes before serving.
tips: Roll the shells a little thinner than for frying so they crisp through in the dry heat of the oven.
Brush ghee on both sides during baking for even browning, since the oven will not coat them the way oil does.
These stay crisp for a day in an airtight box and re-crisp beautifully with 5 minutes back in a hot oven.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve warm with a bowl of thick sweetened curd and green chutney for a lighter tea-time plate.

variations.name: Mini Cocktail Lilva-Matar Kachori
variations.description: Bite-sized party kachoris where fresh lilva teams up with sweet green peas and crunchy cashews in the filling, all wrapped in tiny crisp shells perfect for a starter platter. The peas add extra sweetness and colour while the cashews give richness. Made small so guests can pop one whole with a dab of chutney.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Rolls thin for delicate mini shells that stay crisp on a platter

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: 3 tbsp for the dough moyan; the rest fries the mini kachoris crisp

steps: Rub 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil into 1.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with ½ tsp salt, then knead in about 0.4 cup water into a firm dough and rest 30 minutes.
Coarsely crush 1 cup tuvar lilva and 1 cup green peas together, keeping the mix chunky.

Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan, fry 3 tbsp chopped cashews for 1 minute until golden, add 2 tsp ginger-green chilli paste, then the crushed lilva-peas, ½ tsp turmeric, ½ tsp garam masala and ½ tsp salt.
Cook the filling 5 minutes until dry, stir in 1 tsp sugar, 1 tbsp lemon juice and coriander, and cool completely.
Roll the dough into 20 small 2.5-inch discs, place a teaspoon of filling in each, seal and flatten into little kachoris.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 150C and fry the minis on low-medium for 5 to 6 minutes until crisp and pale gold; drain and serve.
tips: Keep the fillings and shells small and uniform so every mini fries evenly and looks neat on a platter.
Fry a test kachori first to check the seal and oil temperature before committing the whole batch.
Shape these a few hours ahead and fry just before guests arrive so they are served hot and crackling.
variations.servingSuggestion: Arrange on a platter with small bowls of mint chutney and sweet chutney, and top each mini with a drizzle of chutney and a pinch of sev for a chaat-style starter.

variations.name: Green Garlic Lilva Kachori
variations.description: A pungent winter version where the lilva filling is loaded with fresh green garlic, coriander and mint for a herby, savoury bite with no sweetness at all. The green-garlic aroma perfumes the whole kachori and pairs beautifully with the earthy peas. It is the choice for those who find the classic too sweet.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Its rustic flavour suits the bold green-garlic filling

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: 3 tbsp as moyan for the shell; the rest fries the kachoris golden

steps: Rub 3 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil into 1.5 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta with ½ tsp salt, knead in about 0.4 cup water into a stiff dough, and rest 30 minutes.
Coarsely crush the 2 cups tuvar lilva, keeping it chunky.
Heat 2 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil in a pan on medium, crackle 1 tsp cumin seeds for 15 seconds, add ⅓ cup green garlic and 3 minced green chillies, and saute 1 minute until the garlic wilts.
Add the crushed lilva, ½ tsp turmeric and ½ tsp salt, cook 5 minutes until dry, then stir in the mint, coriander and 1 tsp amchur and cool fully.
Roll the dough into 12 discs, stuff and seal each with the herby filling, and flatten into kachoris.
Heat the remaining Anveshan Groundnut Oil to 150C and fry on low-medium for 6 to 7 minutes until crisp and golden; drain and serve hot.
tips: Add the mint and coriander after the filling comes off the heat so their fresh aroma survives into the kachori.
Green garlic can be watery, so cook the filling until fully dry before stuffing to prevent bursting.
Amchur here replaces the classic jaggery, keeping this version tangy and savoury rather than sweet.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with a sharp lemon-coriander chutney and a cup of ginger chai for a savoury winter snack.

variations.name: Classic Gujarati Methi Thepla
variations.description: The definitive Gujarati travel bread, thin rounds of khapli wheat and gram flour kneaded with fresh fenugreek, curd and a whisper of jaggery to tame the bitterness. Rolled fine and cooked supple rather than crisp, theplas stay soft for days, which is why no Gujarati suitcase leaves home without them. Faintly sweet, spiced and endlessly comforting with a spoon of pickle.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Low-gluten emmer keeps the theplas bendable even after a day in the tiffin

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: 1 tbsp softens the dough; the rest lightly cooks the theplas supple, not crisp

ingredients.name: Anveshan Jaggery Powder
ingredients.note: Dissolved into the curd, it balances the methi's edge the Gujarati way

steps: Stir 1 tbsp Anveshan Jaggery Powder into ⅓ cup sour curd and set aside for 5 minutes until it dissolves into a smooth cream.

In a wide bowl combine 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, ¼ cup besan, 2 tsp sesame seeds, ½ tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp ginger-green chilli paste and 1 tsp salt, rubbing the spices evenly through the flour.

Add 1.5 cups chopped methi, the jaggery-curd and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee, then knead in only about ¼ cup water a splash at a time until a soft, smooth dough forms; the methi and curd supply most of the moisture. Rest 15 minutes.
Divide into 12 balls and roll each very thin, about 7 inches across, dusting lightly so the sesame does not tear the surface.
Cook each thepla on a medium tava for about 45 seconds until pale bubbles form, flip, smear ¼ tsp Anveshan Ghee, and press gently until soft brown freckles cover both sides, roughly 90 seconds total.
Stack the cooked theplas in a covered container so trapped steam keeps them soft enough to fold into quarters.
tips: Add water very cautiously; curd and wilting methi can turn the dough sloppy fast, and a stiff dough will not roll thin.
Cook on steady medium heat for supple theplas; too hot a tava makes them crisp and prone to cracking when folded.
These keep soft for two to three days at room temperature, making them the ideal train and flight food.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with chhundo, a bowl of thick curd and masala chai, or roll around aloo bhaji for a portable lunch.

variations.name: Tikha Masala Methi Thepla
variations.description: A bolder, garlicky thepla for those who like heat, with extra red chilli, crushed garlic and ajwain worked into the dough and no sweetness to soften it. Cooked with a touch more oil, it develops crisper edges while staying pliable in the middle. This is the punchy version that needs nothing more than a glass of chaas.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Holds up to the bolder spicing while staying soft and foldable

ingredients.name: Anveshan Groundnut Oil
ingredients.note: 1 tbsp in the dough and the rest on the tava for crisper, spicy edges

steps: In a bowl mix 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, ¼ cup besan, 2 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp ajwain, ½ tsp turmeric, 2 tsp coriander-cumin powder and 1 tsp salt.
Add 5 crushed garlic cloves, 3 minced green chillies, 1.5 cups chopped methi, 3 tbsp curd and 1 tbsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil, and rub everything through the flour.
Knead in about ⅓ cup water gradually into a soft, pliable dough and rest it, covered, for 15 minutes.
Divide into 12 balls and roll each into thin 6 to 7 inch rounds on a lightly floured surface.

Cook each on a medium-hot tava for 1 minute until bubbles rise, flip, drizzle ½ tsp Anveshan Groundnut Oil around the edges, and press until deep golden crisp-edged spots form, about 2 minutes per side.
Stack in a cloth-lined box; they will stay soft in the centre with pleasantly crisp rims.
tips: Crush the garlic coarsely rather than pasting it so little pockets of garlic flavour stud each thepla.
Bloom the ajwain in the residual tava heat by pressing the raw side down first; it deepens the aroma.
Serve these fresh, as the crisp edges are part of their appeal and soften if stored too long.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve hot with garlic pickle, a wedge of raw onion and a tall glass of salted buttermilk to balance the heat.

variations.name: Multigrain Sattu Methi Thepla
variations.description: A high-fibre, protein-rich thepla built on multigrain atta and roasted-gram sattu instead of besan, with a spoon of flaxseed for extra nourishment. It is nuttier and heartier than the classic yet stays soft thanks to curd in the dough. The everyday-healthy thepla for lunchboxes and long journeys alike.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Multigrain Atta
ingredients.note: A blend of grains gives these theplas extra fibre and a deeper, nuttier taste

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sattu
ingredients.note: Roasted gram flour adds protein and binds the dough in place of besan

ingredients.name: Anveshan Sesame Oil
ingredients.note: 1 tbsp in the dough and the rest on the tava for a wholesome, toasty finish

steps: Combine 1.5 cups Anveshan Multigrain Atta, ½ cup Anveshan Sattu, 2 tbsp ground flaxseeds, ½ tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 2 tsp ginger-green chilli paste and 1 tsp salt in a bowl.
Add 1.5 cups chopped methi, ⅓ cup curd and 1 tbsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, and rub everything through the flour until crumbly and evenly green-flecked.
Knead in about ⅓ cup water gradually into a soft dough; sattu absorbs water fast, so add the last splashes slowly. Rest 15 minutes.
Divide into 12 balls and roll each into thin 6 to 7 inch rounds, dusting with a little multigrain atta.
Cook each on a medium tava for about 1 minute, flip, smear ½ tsp Anveshan Sesame Oil, and press until golden-brown freckles cover both sides, about 90 seconds total.
Stack the cooked theplas in a covered box to keep them soft and foldable.
tips: Rest the dough a little longer if it feels stiff; the multigrain and sattu need time to hydrate for soft theplas.
Grind the flaxseeds fresh, as pre-ground flax goes rancid quickly and can turn the theplas bitter.
These heartier theplas keep you full longer and hold up well for two days in a lunchbox.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of thick curd, a spoon of green chutney and a side of cucumber for a nourishing, balanced meal.

variations.name: Kasuri Methi Dudhi Thepla
variations.description: An all-year thepla for when fresh methi is out of season, using aromatic dried kasuri methi and grated bottle gourd for moisture and softness. The dudhi keeps these theplas remarkably tender and light while the kasuri methi delivers a concentrated fenugreek fragrance. A clever pantry-and-fridge version that travels just as well.

ingredients.name: Anveshan Khapli Atta
ingredients.note: Pairs with juicy grated dudhi to give an especially soft, tender thepla

ingredients.name: Anveshan Ghee
ingredients.note: 1 tbsp in the dough and the rest on the tava for a soft, fragrant finish

steps: Crush 3 tbsp kasuri methi between your palms and mix it with 2 cups Anveshan Khapli Atta, ¼ cup besan, ½ tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, 1 tsp coriander-cumin powder, 2 tsp sesame seeds, 2 tsp ginger-green chilli paste and 1 tsp salt.
Squeeze the 1 cup grated dudhi lightly to remove excess water, then add it and 1 tbsp Anveshan Ghee to the flour and rub through.
Knead into a soft dough using only the moisture from the dudhi, adding a spoon of water only if it feels dry; rest 15 minutes.
Divide into 12 balls and roll each into thin 6 to 7 inch rounds on a floured surface.
Cook each on a medium tava for about 1 minute, flip, smear ¼ tsp Anveshan Ghee, and press until soft golden spots appear on both faces, roughly 90 seconds total.
Stack the theplas in a covered container so they steam soft and stay foldable.
tips: Squeeze the grated dudhi only lightly; you want most of its moisture to soften the dough so you barely need extra water.
Rub the kasuri methi between your palms before adding it to release its full aroma into the flour.
This version is a lifesaver when fresh methi is unavailable and keeps soft for two days on a journey.
variations.servingSuggestion: Serve with a bowl of aam ka chhundo, plain curd and hot chai, or pack with dry aloo sabzi for a tiffin.
